# Patrologia Latina, volume 149 — English translation

# Patrologia Latina, Volume 149

## Complete Course of Patrology

Or Universal Library, complete, uniform, convenient, economical, containing all the holy Fathers, Doctors, and ecclesiastical writers who flourished from the apostolic age to the time of Innocent III; the chronological reprinting of all monuments of Catholic tradition that have survived through the first twelve centuries of the Church, according to the most accurate editions, carefully collated with one another and with several manuscript codices, and corrected with the greatest diligence; continuously illustrated with dissertations, commentaries, and variant readings; enlarged with all works discovered after the publication of the most extensive editions issued during the last three centuries; furnished with particular analytical indexes following each volume and each author of any importance; adorned with chapters properly arranged within the text itself, as well as with headings distinguishing the upper margin of each page and indicating its subject matter; expanded by works both doubtful and apocryphal, or else possessing some authority in relation to ecclesiastical tradition; enriched with two general indexes: one of subjects, by consulting which whatever each Father has written on any topic may be seen at a glance; the other of Sacred Scripture, from which the reader may readily discover which Fathers commented on the individual texts of the books of Scripture and in which passages of their works they did so. An exceedingly accurate edition, and easily preferable to all others if one takes into account the clarity of the type, the quality of the paper, the integrity of the text, the perfection of the correction, the variety and number of the works reprinted, the very convenient format of the volumes, consistently similar throughout the whole work, the low price, and especially this collection—single, methodical, and chronological—of six hundred fragments and minor works previously scattered here and there, but now for the first time gathered in our library from works belonging to every age, place, language, and form.

## Second Series

In which appear the Fathers, Doctors, and ecclesiastical writers of the Latin Church from Gregory the Great to Innocent III. Edited by J.-P. Migne, publisher of the Universal Library of the Clergy, or of complete courses in each branch of ecclesiastical learning.

The Patrology has been issued in two editions, one Latin and the other Greek-Latin. Two hundred volumes of the Latin edition are sold for one thousand francs; three hundred volumes of the Greek-Latin edition for eight hundred francs. The purely Latin edition embraces all authors, both Western and Eastern; the latter, however, are supplied in it only in Latin translation.

# Preliminary Observations

## § I. The Author and Sources of the Deeds

[Col. 0009A]

The *Deeds of the Bishops of Cambrai* [Note: The author himself did not give this title. He prefixed to his work neither a general title nor his own name, but entitled only the individual books: the first, “The First Book on the Deeds of the Bishops”; the second, “The Second on the Monasteries Situated within the Diocese”; the third, “The Third Book on the Deeds of Bishop Gerard.” Only later writers gave the entire work, together with its continuations, this title. Thus Lambert of Arras, bishop, in a charter of the year 1067: in the deeds of the bishops of the churches of Arras and Cambrai—that is, in our Book I, chapter 30. The Chronicle of Marchiennes, in our *Annals* VIII, 427, refers to it as “from the deeds of the bishops of Cambrai,” which is our first book. The *Chronicles of the Abbey of Saint Andrew of Cambrai* I, 6, says concerning Erluin, Gerard, Lietbert, and Gerard: “Whoever wishes to know them more fully will be able to find them in their deeds,” namely in our first and third books and in the *Deeds of Lietbert and Gerard II*. The Gaugerician Excerptor, in the passage to be printed below and cited in our *Annals* VII, 440, says: “What is contained in this volume concerning Lord Lietbert, Bishop of Cambrai, has been taken from the book of the deeds of the bishops of Cambrai”; and shortly afterward: “Here begin excerpts from the book of the deeds of the bishops of Cambrai.” Later, speaking of the separation of the sees of Cambrai and Arras, he says: “If anyone wishes to know more fully, let him consult the deeds of the bishops.” Finally, Rodulfus, in his *Life of Lietbert*, calls that part of the *Deeds* which concerns Lietbert, in chapter 2, the *Life of Lietbert*, but in chapter 28 calls it “the episcopal deeds.”]

Was first composed, at the command of Bishop Gerard I [Note: I, preface: “At the command of our lord Bishop Gerard,” who held the see from 1012 to 1051.], by a certain canon of Blessed Mary [Note: II, 23. He calls the estate of Lambras “the estate of the holy Mother of God,” two lines after calling it “our estate”; I, 85: “of this church,” namely of blessed Mary of Cambrai; II, 11: “in our church.”], who, if not born at Cambrai, nevertheless lived there from his youth [Note: II, 5: “I saw [him] as a young man.”], and was familiar with Gerard [Note: Compare III, 12: “My lord bishop used to relate”; 22: “My lord bishop used to tell us”; there: “The lord bishop often related”; 26: “We learned this from the lord bishop’s account.”].

He wrote at Cambrai [Note: I, preface: “Our cities, namely Cambrai and Arras”; 4: “this city of ours”; 7: “these cities also”; 21: “in this our city”; 80: “of this church”; 92: “from this city”; 96: “this city”; 103: “from this city”; 114: “to this city”; II, 11: “in our church”; there: “among us”; 12: “to this neighborhood”; 29: “our city.”], arranging the work in three books from the beginning [Note: I, 122: “of which it will be narrated in the third book.”], and, up to III, 34, immediately and continuously with his pen after recently recovering from an illness [Note: Compare II, 8.] during the years 1041–1043 [Note: II, 23. Concerning the monastery at Henim: “Recently Robert appointed canons there,” which took place in 1040; III, 21: “Herbrand, who is now [living],” who died around the year 1045; III, 23: “Otto, who is now [living],” who died on 25 May 1045; ibid.: “Waleran, who is now a commendable abbot,” who died already at the end of 1043.].

Chapters 35–60, however, neither preserve the chronological order of the earlier chapters nor are they well arranged; they were merely noted down and thrown onto paper, as though for the use of a future book. They therefore seem to have been written somewhat later, perhaps at the same time when the author revised the earlier material and enlarged it both in the margin and on attached slips, while Gerard was still alive [Note: For everywhere, both in these additions and throughout chapters 35–60, he is called “lord.”], though not long after 1044 [Note: Nothing in all this extends beyond that year.].

His style is indeed not very elegant and is interspersed with not a few barbarous words [Note: Such as *addexterare*, “to assist”; *adrumari*, “to be beaten”; *alimonia*, “nourishment”; *amicare*, “to befriend”; *ampliorare*, “to enlarge”; *annonari*, “to receive provisions”; *atrium*, “cemetery”; *bachania*, “revelry”; *camisia*, “shirt”; *campus*, “field”; *capitaneus*, “captain”; *caraxare*, “to scratch or write”; *caraxatura*, “writing”; *cervicatus*, “stubborn”; *clangorium*, “clamor”; *clepere*, “to steal”; *clericus*, “student”; *cluere*, “to be renowned”; *debriatus*, “drunk”; *dequeri*, “to complain”; *didragmare*, “to weigh two drachmas”; *dissitudo*, “distance”; *doctrinare*, “to teach”; *duricors*, “hard-hearted”; *ememor*, “forgetful”; *epacare*, “to appease”; *eulogiose*, “blessedly”; *expilator*, “plunderer”; *expletio*, “completion”; *exsumptuare*, “to spend”; *frigoritici*, “sufferers from chills”; *funebritas*, “mourning”; *gaudiosus*, “joyful”; *guerra*, “war”; *gutteria*, “throat disease”; *herbidare*, “to graze”; *inconcare*, “to shape into a basin”; *infiscare*, “to confiscate”; *inimicare*, “to make hostile”; *lactare*, “to suckle”; *matricularius*, “register-keeper”; *ocdenarius*, “an eight-denarius coin”; *peccarium*, “sinful”; *perdonare*, “to pardon”; *pinguamen*, “fatness”; *pompare*, “to boast”; *prebendae*, “prebends”; *prediatus*, “provided with estates”; *prepotestas*, “great power”; *profluvia fides*, “overflowing faith”; *rapinator*, “plunderer”; *regimonium*, “government”; *repatriare*, “to return to one’s homeland”; *revadiare*, “to pledge again”; *sacellarius*, “treasurer”; *saepissimus*, “very frequent”; *senior*, “elder”; *sermentatus*, “sworn”; *siriaticus*, “Syriac”; *turgor*, “swelling”; *solatiari*, “to console”; *subtolarium*, “a raised floor”; *tranquillare*, “to calm”; *tribua*, “truce”; *ultissimus*, “most extreme.”], yet it is simple, very far from verbal bombast, and does not pursue similar sounds at the ends of sentences.

He employed very many sources: Gregory of Tours; the *Deeds of the Frankish Kings*; Flodoard’s *History of Reims*; the letters of Hincmar; the *Annals of Saint-Vaast*; Einhard [Note: I, 42.]; Saint Gislenus [Note: These are lost. We know them only from the Hainaut chronicle of Jacques de Guise, who quotes certain passages from them for the years 937, 975, 984, 1000, 1005, and 1035. Our author copied from them the material for 975, 984, and 1000, and doubtless much more that can no longer be recognized from the lost annals themselves. — The distinguished Wilmans pointed out that the Annals of Rothnacum should also be counted among the sources of the work. See volume IX of our *Annals*.]; catalogues of the bishops of Cambrai; the lives of Saints Ursmarus and Erminus by Anso, of Autbert by Fulbert, of Vedastus by Alcuin, and of Leodegarius, Salvius [Note: *Acta Sanctorum*, June, volume V, p. 200.], Gislenus, Landelinus, Amatus [Note: Ibid., September, volume IV, p. 128.], Aichadrius, Hugh of Rouen, Gaugericus, Maxellendis [Note: *Acta Sanctorum Belgii* IV, 572.], Aldegundis, and Gudila; Wibold’s *Book on Dice*; the letters of Gerard I; charters from the archives of Cambrai, Lobbes, and Maroilles; and the accounts of Gerard I and others [Note: III, 12, 22, 23; I, preface, 10, 34; II, 3, 12.].

He used these sources in such a way that sometimes he copied them whole and sometimes excerpted them, freely changing the wording. Indeed, the actual charters still preserved at Cambrai clearly show that he did not always reproduce even the charters with the accuracy customary in his age. We have noted this [Note: I, 27, 39, 64, 77.] so that excessive authority may not be attributed to medieval writers in such matters when the charters themselves no longer survive.

But this was a fault of his age, not of carelessness or falsehood. Everywhere he wished to write the truth [Note: I, preface: “Nothing doubtful, nothing fictitious has been inserted … otherwise it is better to be silent than to bring forward falsehoods”; ibid. 2: “We judged it more prudent to remain silent than to fabricate something legendary”; ibid. 28: “It is better to be silent than to fabricate something legendary”; compare chapter 4.]; and although he often made mistakes, especially in chronology [Note: For example I, 8, 16, 42, 49, 50, 60; II, 21, 32; III, 13.], he never knowingly transmitted falsehoods. Nor does he pursue miracles excessively, nor does he try to embellish the poverty of events with inventions. Although he is intellectually limited and was not born to write history, he is nevertheless straightforward, and his credibility is corrupted neither by anger nor by partiality.

## § II. Was Balderic the Author of the Deeds?

These are the certain facts about the author that we know from the work itself. No other testimony about him survives except three letters [Note: They are as follows.

“Gerard, Bishop of the Church of Cambrai or Arras, sends greetings to Hubert, a religious bishop. I am sending to you Balderic, formerly secretary to the pious Lietbert and serving me, his nephew, in the same capacity, so that he may console you in the Lord concerning your doubts. He is a learned man, and is imbued with the matters of the people of Morins, as his recent chronicle of your people and mine indicates. He will explain to you what belongs to your see, and from him you will learn what you desire. I rejoice at your improved health and wish you to bear affliction more willingly; for whoever wishes to avenge himself will find vengeance from the Lord. It is most just that a bishop spare everyone, since he daily asks God to spare him. Learn that it is characteristic of a good shepherd to suffer and endure, to set his face like the hardest stone, and not to be confounded. In all things give thanks to God, clinging wholly to him alone; thus you will not feel the offense of the wicked. Given at Cambrai in February, in the year 1082.”

Colvenerius does not say where he obtained this letter.

The second is:

“Raynaldus, Archbishop of Reims, sends greetings to Balderic, cantor of the people of Morins. You ask me, dear friend, for my judgment concerning your *History of the Church of Cambrai and Arras*. What I have learned about it from Brother Sigebertus I now write back to you. Like a diligent bee flying devotedly around the places of the pious, you seem not to have passed over any place from which you did not pluck something with incredible diligence. Thus the wonders of God and the saints will not be in the land of forgetfulness, and you have built for generation and generation. Until now, therefore, enough has been granted to your modesty and restraint; grant the remainder to the prayers of the devout and to the will of the pious deceased prelate, and do not take away from the dead what you consecrated to him while alive with tireless industry and a mind attentive even to the smallest matters. Release it from your hands, so that it may circulate in churches and monasteries. My mind also foretells that this work will bring you glory, serve posterity, and now become a delight and ornament to both churches. Given at Reims on the Ides of January, in the year 1094.”

Colvenerius likewise gives no indication of its origin.

The third, “taken from the archives of the Church of Amiens,” is:

“Godefrid, Bishop of the Church of Amiens, sends greetings in the Lord to his beloved fellow-brother Balderic, Bishop of Noyon. God has raised me, unworthy as I am, to this pastoral care, so that I may do what is worthy of the devotion of the flock. Since, therefore, this diocese contains very ancient foundations of churches, and since most of the cloisters have already been destroyed by human injury, I earnestly beg you in the Lord—so that these things may not be handed over to perpetual oblivion, but remembrance of the holy places may encourage the minds of the faithful toward the propagation of divine worship, and so that God may become propitious toward our wickedness through many intercessors and grant mercy—that, girding yourself for this holy labor, or rather persevering in the labor, you become the transcriber and writer of our diocese and church, just as you have been a faithful pen of the swift-writing scribe in the churches of Cambrai and Morins. Do not hide your talent in the earth, and in doing good do not grow weary. The archdeacon Peter greets you, as do I, your fellow-servant in Christ’s sheepfold. Farewell there. I wrote at Saint-Quentin, my delight, near the town of Péronne, in the year 1108, in May.”

To these Colvenerius adds “an epitaph that could be seen before the destruction of the city of Morins in the choir of the cathedral church”:

“Peter Balderic, cantor of this church and Bishop of Noyon, died on the day before the Kalends of June, in the year 1112 from the incarnation of the Word and in the fifteenth year of his episcopate, full of merits and illustrious for his Cambrai chronicle.”

It is not known where he obtained this. Terouanne, however, was destroyed in 1551. Dom Rivet has already remarked: “This inscription is not original, and was made only afterward, from the letter of Saint Godefrid, Bishop of Amiens.”]

From these letters, which owe their preservation to Colvenerius, he was the first to infer that the author of the *Deeds* was Balderic, son of Aibert, lord of Sarchinville: first chaplain and secretary of Gerard I, then secretary of Lietbert and Gerard II; afterward canon and cantor of the Church of Morins; then archdeacon of Noyon; and finally Bishop of Noyon and Tournai. He was said to have died at Morins in 1112 and to have been buried there in the choir.

But Petrus Boschius [Note: *Acta Sanctorum*, August, volume II, p. 668. Colvenerius and Boschius are the only writers worth consulting; all the others merely repeated what they had said, adding absolutely nothing new. Miraeus, *Opera diplomatica* I, 80; Cousin, *History of Tournai* I, 152; Sanmarthani III, 819; Vossius, *On Latin History*, p. 387; *Gallia Christiana* IX, 999; Ceillier, *General History of Ecclesiastical Authors* XXI, 76; Fabricius, under the relevant entry; Bouquet VIII, preface, and X, 196; Baur in Ersch and Gruber’s *Encyclopaedia*; Thierry, *Letters on the History of France*, no. 17, all follow Colvenerius. Paquot III, 633, folio edition; Rivet in *Literary History of France* VIII, 400; Bouquet XI, 122; and Leglay in the *Universal Biography* LVII, 310, and in his edition, agree with Boschius in holding that our author was different from the Bishop of Noyon, but accept all the remaining conclusions that Colvenerius draws from the letters: namely, that the author was called Balderic; that he was secretary to Lietbert and Gerard II; that he continued his third book through Lietbert’s death; that in 1082 he went to Hubert, Bishop of Morins; and that, after composing the Chronicle of Morins, he died as cantor around 1097.]

Has shown that Balderic the bishop, whom the Church of Noyon itself calls its shepherd, was not imported from elsewhere, nor another man, but its own son, brought forth from its own womb; that, received into its lap, it nursed him at its own breast; that, after weaning him, it raised him itself; and that from the very beginnings of his cradle, through the stages of ages and ranks, it claimed him entirely for itself, so that it might rejoice to have a father in its son, a ruler in its pupil, and in its own canon and archdeacon Balderic a pontiff [Note: These are the words of a letter written by R., the dean, and the entire chapter of the Church of Noyon to Lambert, Bishop of Arras, published by Baluze, *Miscellanea* V, 309, from a manuscript of Arras of unquestionable reliability. Yet a charter of Rabod, Bishop of Noyon, dated 7 December 1093, presented by Simon’s *Chartulary of Saint Bertin*, p. 206, and by Guérard, lists among its witnesses: “The sign of Balderic, archdeacon.” It therefore appears that Balderic, later bishop and already archdeacon of Noyon in 1093, cannot have been cantor of Morins in 1094, as Raynaldus’s second letter asserts.]

—cannot be the same man as our author, whom his own words show to have lived at Cambrai from his youth until at least 1044, and whom these letters say did not go to the people of Morins until 1082 and was still living there in 1094.

We must therefore suppose either that Gerard was mistaken, so that, knowing that the Cambrai Chronicle had been written by a Balderic but not knowing which Balderic, he had in mind the Balderic whom he knew best, the bishop; or that the entire letter was fabricated, which Boschius suspects of the other two as well, for more than one reason.

Indeed, they have something apocryphal and, so to speak, vague about them. Their coloring is more recent, not what was customary at that time. In the first, a Chronicle of Morins is mentioned as having been written before the author had gone to the Morini. In the second, the Cambrai Chronicle—which we know was composed before 1044—is represented in 1094 as still unpublished, although the first letter, from 1082, mentions it as sufficiently well known. In the third, an old man—if he were our author—would be invited to write history at a minimum age of eighty-eight.

Furthermore, the origin of the first two letters is completely unknown. Although Colvenerius, a man of the highest learning and religious integrity, certainly was not one who knowingly presented falsehoods as true, it is nevertheless neither impossible nor inconsistent with the esteem rightly due to his memory that he could have been deceived by documents fabricated long before his time.

Therefore both the letters themselves and the conclusions based solely upon them—the name Balderic; the office of secretary to Lietbert and Gerard I; the transfer to the Morini; and the Chronicle of Morins [Note: This Chronicle is mentioned nowhere except in the first and third letters. Colvenerius adds: “It was preserved in the archives of that church until the time of Philip of Luxembourg, Bishop of Morins and Le Mans, who died at Le Mans in 1519. He ordered it to be transferred from Morins to the College of Saint Benedict in the city of Le Mans.” But Dom Rivet searched for it there in vain. Le Long lists a manuscript of the same work in the Fouchet Library, *Bibliothèque historique de France*, no. 3310. The learned Cambrai abbot Mutte, however, had already doubted whether such a Chronicle had ever existed at all.]—if they are not to be entirely rejected, nevertheless remain so doubtful that they are virtually as though they did not exist.

Much more probable—indeed, almost certain from the author’s own testimony [Note: II, 4.]—is the conjecture of Boschius [Note: *Acta Sanctorum*, August, II, 668, and *Acta Sanctorum Belgii* II, 278.], according to which our author, in addition to the *Deeds*, and indeed before them, also composed the *Life of Saint Gaugericus* from two older works.

## § III. The Deeds of Lietbert

We have seen above from the author’s own words that he wished to lay down his pen with Gerard I. But Colvenerius—and all the others followed him—also attributed the *Deeds of Lietbert* to the same author, induced by the single fact that in manuscript 2 they are placed after the third book.

Yet Colvenerius himself says that they were written there by another hand, and one somewhat more recent. It therefore seems almost certain that they were not present in the primary manuscript, the source of manuscript 2 [Note: Note also the erasure in manuscript 2 at the end of III, 60, undoubtedly made by that other, more recent hand. The erasure shows that something had originally been written there indicating that the work ended at that point.].

Sigebertus [Note: In 1054.], Rodulfus, the biographer of Lietbert, the author of the *Chronicle of the Abbey of Saint Andrew of Cambrai*, and the scribe of the Copenhagen manuscript [Note: *Archives* VII, 440.] were already reading these materials in the book of the deeds of the bishops of Cambrai. But it by no means follows that the author was the same.

For he certainly would not have passed over the final seven years of his patron Gerard in such deep and abrupt silence; nor, I believe, would he have left untouched until after 1076 a book completed in 1044—for it was only then that the *Deeds of Lietbert* were composed [Note: This is shown by the fact that Lietbert is only rarely called “lord,” a term that the author could not have omitted when writing during his lifetime.].

Although the style does not differ greatly in coloring, the effort to end each individual part of a sentence with a uniform sound is nevertheless much more evident than in the preceding work. Rodulfus, moreover, calls this part of the *Deeds* the *Life of Lietbert* [Note: *Life of Lietbert* 2.], a name he could scarcely have used unless it had been separated from the earlier material. The Cambrai abbreviator and the French translator likewise show that, because they began with Lietbert, there was, so to speak, a division at this point in the *Deeds*.

We have therefore separated the *Deeds of Lietbert* from the third book, which was composed more than thirty years earlier and intended by the author for the affairs of Gerard alone. We give them from manuscripts 2, 2*, and 7, in which alone they are read.

## § IV. The Deeds of Gerard II

We have restored the *Deeds of Gerard II* from manuscripts 7 and 7*, where they are inserted so closely into another work composed in 1180 that they might seem to be a single work by one author.

But anyone who examines the matter more carefully will immediately see that what is said there about Gerard was written shortly after his death in 1092 [Note: Compare chapter 9 at the end.], and by an author different from the author of the *Deeds of Lietbert* [Note: For he pursues the practice of ending sentences with words of equal sound to such an extent that in the coloring of its style it is quite different from the *Deeds of Lietbert*.]. The remainder was added only in 1180, excerpted from the *Deeds* of the succeeding bishops.

The French version, which will be mentioned shortly, prevents us from believing that only excerpts of the *Deeds of Gerard II* are found here. For the French version was made not from manuscript 7 but from the *Deeds* themselves, and agrees with our text almost word for word in the section on Gerard II, while in what follows it is much fuller.

Here too, therefore, as in the case of Lietbert, we have separated the material that in manuscripts 7 and 7* and in the edition of Dom Brial XIII, 476—the only edition hitherto—forms a single work.

## § V. The Deeds of Manasses and His Successors; the Excerpts of Saint Gaugericus; the Cambrai Abbreviation; the French Version

We no longer possess the *Deeds* of the succeeding bishops in their entirety. Only through two excerpts and the French version can we conjecture what they were like.

In the year 1180, a monk, apparently of Saint Gaugericus [Note: We infer this from the extensive account of Saint Gaugericus in chapters 4–6 and 9, which he added on his own, since it was not present in the *Deeds*.], after writing the *Deeds of Lietbert*, his *Life*, and the *Deeds of Gerard II* in a single volume [Note: This is our manuscript 7.], intended to indicate summarily the succession of bishops from that time to the present, over approximately one hundred years—that is, from the year 1090 of the incarnation of the Word to 1180.

He therefore attached to Gerard’s *Deeds* the account of the succeeding bishops, excerpted from their own *Deeds* [Note: “Let him consult the deeds of the bishops,” chapter 1.], so closely as though it were a single work. He added nothing of his own except chapters 4, 6, and 9, concerning Saint Gaugericus, while omitting certain matters that, as we have indicated in their proper place, must be supplied from the French version.

Of this excerpt we possess only the beginning, extending to the year 1095. The remainder has perished through the mutilation of manuscript 7*, from which Dom Brial XIII, 476, printed it, and of manuscript 7, the autograph, from which we printed it.

In 1191, a canon of Cambrai [Note: Compare chapter 26.] abridged the *Deeds of Lietbert and his successors* rather briefly and, apparently from the death of Nicholas onward [Note: I infer this because in chapter 19 he completely omits the last part of that decade and immediately passes to the successor, rather abruptly and as though suddenly deprived of his sources. He himself cites the *Deeds of Burchard* in chapter 13.], continued them on his own down to the year 1191.

Although he changed the wording of the *Deeds* very extensively and sometimes reached a different judgment about individuals from that expressed there, his work is nevertheless extremely useful when compared with the French version for restoring those *Deeds*.

It was afterward continued by someone else, but these materials have perished. The work was published from the single manuscript 9, now lost, in the book *Supplement or Continuation of the Cambrai Chronicle Attributed to Balderic, from 1054 to 1196*, Cambrai, at Saint Berthoud, 1786, octavo; afterward in Dom Brial XIII, 534, with the beginning derived from the *Deeds of Lietbert* omitted.

We give it from both editions, introducing our own division of the chapters.

Finally, at the end of the thirteenth century [Note: “In the time of Enguerran de Créqui, as is shown by the catalogue of bishops at the head of the manuscript.” BRIAL.], someone translated the genuine, unabridged *Deeds of Lietbert and his successors* into French. He translated them in the somewhat more verbose manner customary at that time, but altogether with sufficient accuracy.

In the sections concerning Lambert and Gerard II, he omitted nothing and added nothing. In what follows, where the *Deeds* themselves have perished and judgment is possible only from the excerpts, he seems to have omitted very little and to have added nothing except five passages [Note: Chapters 28, 31, 32, 38, and 39.] taken verbatim from Lambert Waterlos’s *Chronicle*.

If these additions are removed, this version adequately supplies the lost *Deeds of Manasses and his successors*. It is therefore regrettable that it ends already in the year 1135, because the end of the only manuscript, 10, has been lost.

Dom Brial was the first to publish it from this source, XIII, 476. Leglay printed certain excerpts [Note: Pages 544, 551, 553, 554, 557–564, 571, 572.].

We present all the material again from manuscript 10 itself, beginning with the year 1092, omitting entirely the *Deeds of Lietbert and Gerard II*, since they contain nothing new, and adding our own division of the chapters. We indicate everywhere in the margin the passages in which the Gaugerician Excerptor and the Cambrai abbreviator relate the same events.

## § VI. Continuation of the Abbey of Saint Andrew of Cambrai

[Col. 0016C]

These are the portions of the *Deeds of the Bishops of Cambrai* that have come down to us.

We possess one continuation that did not derive from them, a very brief account of the years 1051–1179, by a monk of the Abbey of Saint Andrew of Cambrai [Note: Compare the beginning: “in this church.”]. After Dom Brial XIII, 533, and Leglay, p. 308, we append it from the same single manuscript 3 used by them.

The *History of the Bishopric of Arras* [Note: The authors of the Cambrai and Arras accounts are unknown—“he was killed by hands.” In manuscripts 7 and 7*, used by Brial XIII, 533, and from him by Leglay, p. 351.]—the ending of which Brial and Leglay published—does not belong to the *Deeds*, since it was composed by a cleric of Arras around 1172 and does not touch German affairs in any way.

Nor should we have published the *Deeds* in which the city of Arras is restored under Urban to its ancient dignity, edited by Baluze [Note: *Miscellanea* V, 237, from a manuscript of Arras, now at Bologna (*Archives* VIII, 406), whose fifteenth-century copy I saw in the library of Arras.]. They may indeed be compared with the *Deeds* with some usefulness, but they have a wholly different author, an Arras writer living around 1102, and contribute nothing to our history.

[Column 17A] The *Gesta* were neither widely read nor frequently copied during the Middle Ages. Lambert, bishop of Arras, used them in 1097 [Note: [Column 17C] In a charter apud Baluzium, *Miscellanea* V, 380.], Sigebert in 1105, Rodulf in the *Life of Lietbert* before 1130 [Note: [Column 17C] Some have thought him to be that famous abbot of Saint-Trond; but less correctly, as the *Necrology of the Holy Sepulchre of Cambrai*, in the municipal library of Cambrai, no. 734, shows. There, in a twelfth-century hand, the following is read: [Column 17D] “On the second day before the Nones of July died our Rodulf, monk and priest, who described, in a single volume and in brilliant language, the life of our lord and patron Lietbert, bishop of the church of Cambrai, the labors that he endured for that same church, and the end of his present life.” The author was in Greece with Lietbert in 1064 and wrote before 1133; for by then the *Chronicle of Saint Andrew of Château-Cambrésis* had already copied him. His work, already published twice, by Dachery, *Spicilegium* II, 138, and in the *Acta Sanctorum*, 23 June, we have decided not to reprint, since, being for the greater part compiled from the *Gesta of Lietbert*, it can scarcely be counted among the sources of history. Chapters 1–15, 28, 44, and 53–57 are taken intact from *Gesta pontificum* I, 114; III, 1; and *Gesta Lietberti* 1–7, 14, 8, 16–24; Rodulf merely diluted them with inflated turns of phrase and poetic and biblical flowers. The very few things that he inserted from his own material we have excerpted in the notes to the *Gesta Lietberti*. He copied chapter 46 word for word from Lietbert’s charter apud Miraeum, [Column 18C] *Opera diplomatica* I, 155. Chapters 16–27, 29–43, 45, 47–52, and 58–66 are the author’s own, except for a great many verses of Virgil with which he embellished Lietbert’s journey. Of these, however, whatever is worth knowing has already for the most part been excerpted by the *Chronicle of Saint Andrew* I, 15; II, 22–29, [Column 18D] 31; the rest we have given in the notes to that same *Chronicle*, so that it is no longer necessary to search for grains in this chaff.], the *Chronicle of Saint Andrew of Château-Cambrésis* in 1133, Andrew of Marchiennes in 1194, the *Chronicle of Marchiennes* in 1200 [Note: [Column 18D] Written at the request of Abbot Simon, who presided from 1191 to 1201; cf. our *Annals* VIII, 427.], and James of Guise about 1380 [Note: [Column 18D] He used them only rarely, and not the *Gesta* themselves so much as a certain French epitome of them, which he calls the *History of Cambrai*; nevertheless, under the same name he calls Rodulf’s life of Lietbert. Cf. our *Annals*, vol. IX.].—The manuscripts, however, are these:

## § VII.—Manuscripts

**1) C. of Saint-Ghislain**, now The Hague, Royal Library, no. 303, purchased from the books collected by Leloup; parchment, small folio, 88 leaves, 28 lines on each page. It was written throughout by one hand in the eleventh century, in ink so dark that here and there entire words already escape the eye; some of these a second, twelfth-century hand attempted to restore near the beginning of the work. Numbers are prefixed to only the first eight chapters; from the ninth onward they cease. The first letter of each chapter is red; only a few at the beginning of the work are ornamented. The headings are written in red ink, but both the difference in orthography and the fact that the scribe often left insufficient space—so that the rubricator was forced to use the margin as well—show that the rubricator was someone other than the scribe.

Throughout the manuscript [Note: [Column 18D] Specifically in these places: I, 5, 7, 10, 12, 17, 21, 23, 27, 40, 48, 52, 58, 64, 71, 93, 104, 114, 116; II, 5, 11, 12.] another hand, somewhat neater but plainly contemporary, entered additions in generally darker ink: sometimes on erasures, sometimes between the lines and in the margin, and sometimes on sewn-in slips, now shorter, now longer; indeed, it supplied entire chapters in this way. It also corrected every slip of the pen made by the principal scribe and the rubricator, frequently altered the orthography, and supplied words omitted by them, whether by accident or deliberately. I believe this hand to be that of the author himself, revising his work in a second edition—for in these passages he speaks of himself [Note: [Column 18D] I, 7: “as we mentioned above”; 10: “in our days”; 23: “I considered it necessary to insert into this work”; 27: “we discovered.”]; all the other manuscripts contain only what this corrector added, not what the first scribe wrote. The whole character of these corrections and additions is the same as that which we see in the autograph manuscripts of Thietmar, Liudprand, Sigebert, and others. [Column 18A] Finally, another hand, from the end of the twelfth or beginning of the thirteenth century, made certain corrections in I, 20 and 68.

The manuscript now contains only the first and second books. It ends in the middle of the next-to-last page of a complete gathering. On the blank space—one and a half pages—left by the scribe, another contemporary hand wrote: “From the decrees of blessed Pope Gregory, concerning what monks …,” which has no connection whatever with our work. But in Colvenerius’s time, when he used it at Saint-Ghislain, a third book was also present, extending to the middle of chapter 49, ending at the word where it stood at the end of a gathering; the following leaves, with the end of the work, had been lost. Those leaves still existed near the end of the twelfth century—for the scribe of manuscript 2 then copied them—but by the fourteenth century they were already lost, since manuscript 3, written at that time, no longer contained them. [Column 18B] All the other manuscripts derive from this primary manuscript [Note: [Column 18D] This is demonstrated above all by passages I, 4, 20, 40, 64, 68, 89, 93, 104, 108; II, 7, 48.]. Colvenerius used it; Pertz recovered it again in 1835; and in 1839, at The Hague, with the most generous assistance of the distinguished Holtrop, keeper of the Royal Library, we collated it anew with the greatest possible accuracy.

**[2] C. of Saint Mary of Arras**, now lost, but still used by Colvenerius, who calls it more recent than the Saint-Ghislain manuscript. That it had already been copied before the end of the twelfth century is clear from the fact that at I, 20 and 68 it contains what was read in the primary text of manuscript 1, not what the twelfth-century hand wrote above the erased passages. Its headings are written in red, as in manuscript 1, which it reproduced generally with considerable accuracy; it inserted only one addition, at I, 3. After the end of the third book there was a *Gesta Lietberti*, but “written by another hand, and that a somewhat more recent one,” according to Colvenerius. The final leaf, together with another containing III, 48 and half of chapter 49, was already missing when manuscript 2* was copied from ours. We know this solely from Colvenerius, a thoroughly trustworthy witness, who refers to it in his notes as “a.”

**2*) C. of Saint-Vaast**, now of the city of Arras, no. 666; paper, folio; copied by several hands from manuscript 2 in 1482, but rather carelessly. Wherever the scribes could not read the text, they left a space, often indicating in the margin with the word *desunt* (“missing”) that words were lacking. One entire gathering, containing I, 46–106, has since disappeared. I collated it myself.

**3) Royal Parisian C.**, no. 5533a, formerly belonging to Baluze; parchment, quarto, fourteenth century; written most elegantly and with the greatest accuracy. The chapter headings are in red; there are none in the third book. Here and there space was left where the copyist could no longer read a word in manuscript 1, but this happened rarely. It ends in the middle of III, 49, and in the same hand adds a very brief continuation, “After this … Savine,” which we shall give after the *Gesta*. I collated it myself.

**4) C. of Affligem**, later of the Society of Jesus at Antwerp, now Brussels, Burgundian Library, no. 7675; paper, folio, sixteenth century. It contains the *Gesta*, the *Chronicle of Egmond*, [Column 19B] and Andrew of Marchiennes. It sometimes altered the division of the chapters on its own initiative, joining several together. After the end of the second book, in the same hand, it copied what another hand had inserted there in manuscript 1; immediately afterward it added the third book, without a title. In the margin another hand wrote: “Thus it is found in the manuscript exemplar of Lord Preudhomme, canon of Cambrai.” It ends in the middle of III, 49; nothing is lost. I collated it myself.

**[5] C. of Rouge-Cloître**, now lost, but still seen by Colvenerius and designated by him as *r*. He says that it was written on paper, and rather imperfectly, about sixty or seventy years earlier. Many things in it were altered arbitrarily, and new names substituted for old ones. It has chapter summaries only in the second book, and not complete ones. [Column 19C] The scribe proceeded with the greatest arbitrariness: III, 18–49 was compressed into the space of a single line. It ended in III, 49, in the middle of a page.

**6) C. of Saint Peter of Hautmont**, now Douai, Municipal Library, no. 800, written by Anthony, a monk at Hautmont, at the end of the twelfth century; parchment, octavo. I discussed it in our *Annals* VIII, 428. Among other things, it contains the second book of the *Gesta*, entirely without a title. The scribe worked fairly accurately, except that he omitted several passages at will. The chapter headings are red; there are no numbers. I collated it myself.

**7) Copenhagen C.**, Tott. no. 520; parchment, quarto, late twelfth century; formerly belonging to the Church of the Holy Martyrs Florentius, Hilary, Martin, and Peter, but apparently written at Cambrai, at Saint-Géry. It contains the *Gesta Lietberti* and his *Life*, to which the scribe, [Column 19D] without any title, added on folio 40 the *Gesta Gerardi* and a continuation excerpted from the *Gesta* of the succeeding bishops. It ends on folio 40 at the end of a gathering; the following leaves are lost. Our Waitz maintains that the manuscript of this continuation is an autograph; he collated and described it in our *Annals* VII, 440.

**[7*] C. of the Holy Sepulchre of Cambrai**, now lost, but seen by Dom Brial, who published from it the *Gesta Gerardi* and the Gaugerician continuation, XIII, 476. It seems to have been copied from manuscript 7. It already ended with the conclusion of chapter 8 of the continuation lost.

**8) C. of Gembloux**, now Brussels, no. 5468; parchment, folio, eleventh century. At the end, added without a title by another hand of the late eleventh century, it contains our chapters I, 94–98 and 104. I recorded all its readings.

**[9] A twelfth-century chartulary**, designated A, from the archives of the cathedral church of Cambrai, according to Dom Brial XIII, 534. At the beginning it contained the abridgment of the *Gesta* prepared by a canon of Cambrai, which Dom Brial published from it, together with a continuation written by another hand, but so mutilated that scarcely anything certain can properly be extracted from it. We do not know from which manuscript it derives.

**10) C. chained in the church of Cambrai**, now Cambrai Public Library, no. 884. After a catalogue of the bishops down to Enguerrand de Créquy, it contains a French version of the *Gesta*, which Dom Brial published from it, XIII, 476. The end of the manuscript is lost.

The editions are these:

**COLV.)** *Chronicon Cameracense et Atrebatense, sive historia utriusque ecclesiae*, in three books, written nearly six hundred years ago by Balderic, bishop of Noyon and Tournai. Now published for the first time and illustrated with notes by George Colvenerius. Douai, from the press of I. Bogard, 1615, octavo.* This is the first edition. Colvenerius possessed our manuscripts 1, 2, and 5. He used the more elegant and fuller manuscript 2 as his foundation, but corrected it from manuscript 1 wherever he thought necessary; he indicated in the notes at least some of the readings of manuscript 1 that seemed important, while from manuscript 5, as a recent and interpolated witness, he drew only a few readings. In the preface he discussed the author at greater length, but there he allowed himself to be misled by the three letters that he was the first to publish; this, however, should in no way be held against him, [Column 20C] since that letter from Noyon had not yet been published by Baluze. His commentary, finally, though somewhat more extensive, still contains much that remains useful today, and we have used it with benefit. We know through Colvenerius alone the manuscripts 2 and 5 and the third book of manuscript 1, now lost; and since Colvenerius excelled among the foremost in solid learning and careful accuracy, his book must be numbered among the finest editions of the authors produced by the Middle Ages.

**BOUQ.)** Dom Bouquet and his continuators inserted several excerpts from Colvenerius’s edition in volumes VIII, 278; X, 196; and XI, 122. Dom Brial, however, XIII, 476, 533, 534, published from our manuscripts 3 and 10 and from the now-lost manuscripts 7* and 9 the materials that we have explained above to be the *Gesta Gerardi*, the Gaugerician excerpt from the *Gesta*, the Cambrai abridgment, and the French version. Although he did not sufficiently understand their origin, sources, or authority, he nevertheless deserves credit for having been the first to bring them to light.

**LEGL.)** *Chronique d’Arras et de Cambrai, par Balderic, chantre de Térouane, revue sur divers manuscrits et enrichie de deux suppléments, avec commentaires, glossaire et plusieurs index, par le docteur Le Glay. Paris, 1834, octavo.* In this book the editor chiefly wished to make the knowledge and historical studies of the Middle Ages—which he loved so much that they turned him from a physician into an archivist—once again known and welcome to his countrymen, and to lead them back to the very sources from which they ought to learn history, sources already almost buried in oblivion [Note: [Column 21D] Preface, p. 10: “At a time when provincial patriotism is awakening, it is natural that each region should inquire somewhat into its own past and know what it was doing when it had an independent existence and did not form a suburb of Paris. Ibid., p. 29: Since it is now demonstrated that history can be investigated thoroughly only with the aid of original documents, why should the study of these documents not enter into classical education? Could not every royal college have a course in palaeography and diplomatics applied to our national history? Young Germans, when they leave their classes, know the *Scriptores rerum Germanicarum*; they have read Gregory of Tours [Column 22D] and Einhard, two French writers whose existence our students scarcely suspect. If at last we want the young to have sound ideas about a past that until now has been shown to them in such false colors, it is time to put them into direct contact with that past itself. The eyewitnesses are there; why not make them speak?”]. Therefore, in publishing the author’s words, he followed Colvenerius, consulting here and there manuscripts 2* and 6. He devoted much more effort to the commentary, which is indeed more extensive; yet even so, we gladly read an author who knows how to treat such matters in a way that makes us seem not to be reading a scholarly work but listening to a cultivated man, as he is, recounting them with a certain pleasing elegance. He also increased the usefulness of the book by being the first to publish there the third part of the chronicle of Saint Andrew of Château-Cambrésis, until then unknown. We owe the opportunity to present it in full below to the kindness of this amiable man.

The principle of our edition was as follows. Since we had recognized that manuscript 1 had been corrected by the author himself, we have given the first and second books of the *Gesta* entirely from it, indicating everywhere with the greatest fidelity its corrections, additions, and slips of the pen. From the other manuscripts we have noted only those readings by which either the manuscripts themselves and their character may be recognized, or corrections and lacunae in manuscript 1, caused by the ravages of time, may be supplied. We have likewise given the third book from manuscript 1 as far as the middle of chapter 49; although the manuscript itself is now lost, Colvenerius’s excellent accuracy compensates so fully for its absence that only very few uncertainties remain. [Column 22A] We supplied the end of the book from manuscript 2—that is, from Colvenerius—and from 2*. We are the first to separate the *Gesta Lietberti* from the preceding material, presenting them from 2, or Colvenerius, 2*, and 7, the only manuscript to supply their conclusion, which had until now remained unpublished. We restored the *Gesta Gerardi* from 7 and its copy, 7*, made by Dom Brial. Since the *Gesta* of the succeeding bishops no longer survive in full, we have presented three short works from which they can be supplemented: namely, the Gaugerician excerpt, fuller here than in Dom Brial, from the autograph manuscript 7; the Cambrai abridgment, whose sole manuscript, 9, no longer exists, from the two editions prepared by Berthoud and Brial, but omitting the beginning copied word for word from the *Gesta Lietberti*; and the French version from manuscript 10, also omitting its beginning, whose source still survives. Finally, we present the continuation of Saint Andrew again from the single manuscript 3. In the notes we have borrowed from Colvenerius and Le Glay whatever we found correctly stated there, especially geographical material, always scrupulously adding their names; in addition, we have chiefly attempted two things: to explain the chronology as accurately as possible, and to print everywhere in smaller type what has been taken from other writers [Note: [Column 22D] We enclose these in parentheses. EDITORS OF THE PATROLOGY.].

**L. C. Bethmann**

[Column 21]

# [GESTA OF THE BISHOPS OF CAMBRAI]

## PREFACE TO THE FOLLOWING WORK

[Column 21C] At the command of our lord Bishop Gerard [Note: [Column 22D] The first Gerard, who held the see from 1012 to 1051.], insofar as we have been able to investigate the matter truthfully, we have committed to writing both the antiquity of our cities—namely Cambrai and Arras—and also that of their pastors. We did not rely on talent, but were compelled by the dignity of the one who gave the command: he preferred to expose our smallness before the most learned ears rather than allow the order of so many ages and the sequence of so many events to remain silent any longer. Although these matters have been set down in rustic language, [Column 22C] they nevertheless appear sufficiently clear. Nor should the reader be rashly disturbed by the fact that we have rendered such ancient matters in modern form, since nothing uncertain and nothing fictitious has been inserted, nor indeed anything except what we found either in the annals and histories of the Fathers, or in the deeds of kings, or in the charters still preserved in the archive of that church, or what we received as seen and heard from reliable informants. Otherwise, it is better to be silent than to bring forth falsehoods [Note: [Column 22D] He seems to have imitated Sulpicius Severus, whose final words of the prologue to the *Life of Saint Martin* are: “Otherwise I would have preferred to be silent rather than speak falsely.” COLV.].

# BOOK ONE

[Column 21]

### 1. The reason for founding cities is first indicated

[Column 21C] It is said that the first reason given by the founders for building cities [Note: [Column 22D] Cf. Cicero, *Tusculan Disputations* V, 2. COLV.] was that human beings, wandering everywhere like wild beasts—ruled neither by custom nor by culture under the guidance of reason, knowing nothing either divine or human, and whose blind and reckless desire, the ruling power of the mind, through error and ignorance abused the strength of the body for its own satisfaction with destructive accomplices—should come together within fortified city walls; that they should learn to practice faith and preserve justice, and should become accustomed to obeying others of their own will; and that they should regard not only the undertaking of labors for the sake of the common good, but even the loss of life, as worthy of acceptance. This reason, although it may seem not unworthy—for it was neither base nor absurd that people hidden among fields and woodland shelters should be rendered gentle and tame instead of remaining wild and savage—nevertheless pointed, within the plan of ordering Providence [Note: [Column 23] “of God” is added by manuscript 5.], to a far higher purpose of things. Through it, human prudence, while thinking that it was providing for its own needs, usefully served the coming generations: namely, so that by their very walls they might seem to be building nothing other than, so to speak, royal structures in which the holy Mother Church, soon to come into being, would possess the chief stronghold of her dignity and an apostolic see.

For the Pentateuch of Moses says that, after the Hebrew people had been recalled from Egyptian domination, God promised and bestowed upon them, through mystical gifts, the cities of the nations to possess, according to the Psalmist’s words: “He gave them the regions of the nations, and they possessed the labors of the peoples” (Psalm 105:44). Thus, too, the cities of the western regions, which paganism had ennobled with walls and marvelous structures, are occupied by the Church spread throughout the world, like strongholds of royal majesty.

### 2. The founders of Cambrai and Arras are unknown; Julius Caesar, however, after crossing the Alps and reaching Arras among the Gauls, subdued the commander Commius

But enough about the reason for building cities. Concerning their founders, there is generally disagreement, to such an extent that even the origin of the city of Rome cannot be carefully ascertained. For some assert that it was founded by the Trojans and Aborigines, others by Evander, and others by Romulus. Therefore, we should not foolishly condemn historians or commentators who give differing accounts, because antiquity itself created the error. But if the true account of so great a city does not appear, it is not surprising that uncertainty should exist concerning the origin of others.

Since I am about to mention the holy fathers whom God’s provident ordering appointed to preside over the church of Arras or Cambrai, I ought to have recorded in writing the founders of these two cities. But since neither history, nor annals, nor even surviving tradition has preserved their names or memory [Note: [Column 23] Manuscript 1 reads *supestes* (“surviving”).], we have judged it more prudent to remain silent about them than to fabricate some fable. The same reasoning applies to the dates of their foundation: since their founders are unknown, the dates must also remain unspoken, except that anyone who rereads the histories of Julius Caesar will not fail to recognize that Arras was counted among the older and more distinguished cities.

After Caesar had subjected almost the whole world of the East to Roman rule and made the kings of the nations tributary, he saw that the fortunes of war had favored him and planned to add the western regions also to his empire. Therefore, after crossing the Alps and forcing the Gauls [Note: [Column 23] “seeing … and the Gauls” stands in an erasure, but was written by the same scribe.] to surrender or slaughtering them by the sword, he came, surrounded by military forces, to Arras, which lay at the farthest edge of Gaul. The citizens resisted him under the leadership of Commius, a man distinguished by long military service and passionately devoted to the safety of his people and homeland. Caesar was indignant that they dared resist Roman power, before which the farthest reaches of India lay open, the Assyrian and Egyptian peoples obeyed, Macedonia and the whole region of Palestine served, and even Scotland—which owed nothing to the lands—and Saxony, inaccessible because of its marshes and enclosed by impassable regions, already trembled. Finally, everything was subject except what was inaccessible because of excessive heat or cold, and therefore outside the Roman Empire because it was likewise outside human use. Indignant at this, he pressed the siege with even greater force.

The conflict continued most vigorously on both sides until the aforementioned Commius [Note: [Column 23] Manuscripts 1 and 3 read *comes* (“count”).], unable to withstand the strength of the Roman prince, was forced, together with the citizens, to surrender. Some loudly demanded that the attempt at rebellion and the delays of the siege be avenged upon the man’s head. A crowd gathered, as the Romans streamed together to witness his arrival. Some wished to see him cast down whom they had shortly before observed placed in the highest honor and presiding over the supreme command; others strove to mock the captive; others marveled at the many and changeable turns of human affairs. Most wisely lamented, thinking that the same things might happen to themselves in the misfortunes of others.

More than the rest, Caesar was moved by the natural gentleness of his spirit: he saw before him the proud warrior of a little while earlier, suddenly subjected to the power of enemies, awaiting the outcome of his fate at another’s nod, shipwrecked in life, exiled from hope, and uncertain of safety. So powerful are the turns of battle that a brief change can make unequals of those who were once alike, when the powerful are cast down or the afflicted are raised up. Accordingly, the better party—namely, those who possessed honor and toward whom Caesar’s counsels were more inclined—offered milder advice.

Yet the greatest factor in the man’s safety in Caesar’s eyes was his devoted love for his homeland and his proven excellence in military affairs. Observing in him steadfast loyalty and an outstanding spirit, Caesar advanced him among the foremost men of military affairs and among his royal counsellors; through him he afterward accomplished many distinguished deeds of valor. Since he was brave in war and good in counsel, and frequently routed countless forces of the enemy with a small band, it is not part of the present undertaking to recount everything. The places near Maroilles [Note: [Column 24D] Maroilles.] still appear to this day with embankments thrown up, where the Roman battle lines had pitched their camps.

### 3. King Clodio entered Cambrai with a great army after sending scouts, killed the Christians, and took possession of the city

Finally, although the founder and date of the city of Cambrai are not certainly known, the fact itself shows that it held a name and reputation among the older cities: it is often mentioned in the written deeds of the ancients [Note: [Column 25] Manuscripts 2 and 2* add: “For the book which, at Julius Caesar’s command and by decree of the Senate, was entitled *On Cosmography* by the wisest men, where it distinguishes all the famous places throughout the Roman world, also includes Cambrai and clearly shows how far it is from the fortress of Bavay, namely eighteen miles.”].

The history of the Franks likewise relates that, after Gaul had been handed over to be struck by the pagan sword in accordance with the sentence of divine sanction, under the emperor Justin [*(Deeds of the Kings of the Franks)*: King Clodio lived in the castle of Dispargum, in the territory of the Thuringians, in the region of Germany. In these parts—that is, southward, on this side of the Rhine—the Romans lived as far as the Loire River. Beyond the Loire the Goths ruled. The Burgundians, following the sect of the Arians, lived beyond the Rhône, adjoining the city of Lyon. Clodio, however, sent scouts to the city of Cambrai, where the Romans living there were already practicing the Christian religion. He himself [Column 25B] later crossed the Rhine with a great army, entered the Carbonarian Forest, and took the city of Tournai. From there he came as far as the city of Cambrai and stayed for a short time; he killed the Romans whom he found there. From there he occupied the territory as far as the Somme River.]*

### 4. King Clovis, the fourth after Clodio, killed his cousin Ragnachar in battle because he had not admitted him into the city

The text of that same history also indicates that King Clovis, the fourth after Clodio, left his cousin—or nephew—Ragnachar as guardian in the city of Cambrai while he remained in the lands and cities that he had occupied as far as Orléans. When he returned at a certain time, Ragnachar, proud in worldly arrogance and having changed his allegiance, denied him entry into the city.

Because of the obscenity of his conduct and his insolence, Ragnachar had made the Franks hostile to him, especially because [*(Gregory of Tours II, 42)*: He was unrestrained in lust and burned with such a Venus-like fire that he did not restrain his desires from the wives of either citizens or relatives. This indeed became for him the cause of his deadly ruin. For the Franks, inflamed by this notorious disgrace, devised means by which the king’s destruction might be brought about and reported their plot of treachery to King Clovis. He bribed the traitors with promises and deceived them with debased gold. Their agreement was that they would abandon their king when they met the enemy in battle.

Accordingly, taking a strong force from his own men, Clovis led an army against Ragnachar. Ragnachar himself prepared to meet the king in a pitched battle. He sent scouts to observe Clovis’s army, but failed to detect the deceit of the messengers, who fraudulently encouraged the king’s boldness by exaggerating the size of his forces. Such were the words of the messengers when he asked them [Column 26A] with which army the stronger force was accompanied [Note: [Column 25] “fraudulently … to them” was omitted by manuscript 3, which left a space; manuscript 4 could not read it either, except for “fac . . . . . . forces was encouraged, such was . . . .” Hence it appears that both manuscripts 3 and 4 were copied from this manuscript 1.]: “By yours,” they said, “and by your Faroni’s.” He himself, unaware that this had been deceitfully contrived, on account of his counsellor Faro, whom he alone had placed in charge of the affairs of the kingdom, preferring him to the leading men of the palace—for whenever some gift or food was brought to him, he was accustomed to say, “Let these be for me and my Faro”—when the kings therefore met, these men abandoned their lord in the very clash of battle, fleeing down the slopes and turning their backs to the enemy in feigned terror.

Ragnachar was seized and killed. When the traitors muttered against the king because of the debased gold, he is said to have answered that they deserved such a reward, since they had willingly led their lord to death; it ought to be enough for them that they were allowed to live, lest they pay the penalties of their detestable treachery under torture [Note: [Column 25] The whole of what follows in this chapter was supplied on a sewn-in slip, apparently by the scribe himself.].

We read in the *Deeds of the Bishops of Reims* (Flodoard I, 13) that, when the aforementioned King Clovis—as becomes clear later—had been baptized by Saint Remigius and Saint Vedast, together with his sisters and a great army of Franks, a considerable part of the Franks, still unbelieving and not yet converted, remained for some time with that prince Ragnachar in the places beyond the Somme River, that is, in the city of Cambrai, in unbelief. At length, by the ordering of heavenly grace, but with Clovis victorious, that same Ragnachar, a follower of crimes and shameful acts, was bound by the Franks and handed over by his own men, as we have just said, and killed; and the whole people of the Franks was converted and baptized into the faith of Christ through blessed Remigius,] as we read there.

But we rather believe that this was accomplished through blessed Vedast. For we have never heard that Saint Remigius preached the word of God to the people in our regions; rather, we know that blessed Vedast was sent by him and by the newly baptized king to our city for the conversion of the people. Therefore, we believe that Vedast was the author of this undertaking.

### 5. The savagery of the pagans and the slaughter of the Christians are described.

Therefore, the plan of the work undertaken requires that I pursue in writing the fathers of both sees, or those who succeeded to the pontifical throne. Now it is certain that these were two mother-church sees, which are presently governed under the direction of one shepherd; this can easily be understood from the descriptions of Pope Dionysius, who distinguished each see from the others by assigning particular boundaries to all the provinces, just as Bishop Hincmar also defines the matter in his books [Note: ED. 44, ed. Sirmondi II, 719.]. [Note: Observe that formerly Cameracum and Atrebatum were two sees, which are now united. The author himself added this in the margin.]

Blessed Vedastus united these two sees under one administration, because he found them exceedingly devastated after the many attacks that we have mentioned and shall mention. But a certain obscurity of antiquity has withdrawn their first fathers from our memory—or rather, the persecution of the pagans overturned the churches of Gaul because of the sins that demanded it. This persecution is said to have raged so fiercely against the Christian people that the Christians who lived at that time celebrated the divine mysteries in hiding places. If any were discovered by the pagans, they were either beaten or slaughtered with the sword; many were suffocated while concealed in caves or underground pits [Note: Le Glay reports that such places still exist throughout the territory of Cameracum, at Villers-Plouich, Inchy-Beaumont, and Beaumetz.].

Thus, as the priests died, the sacred offices were interrupted, and everything pertaining to the observance of sacred worship was relaxed. As the ruins fell upon them, some threw themselves down, [Col. 0027B] while others were burned in the fires of their country. Yet a few persevered in their office to the very end, encouraging one another not to place the duty of sacred religion behind their own safety, since it was the safeguard of salvation. They rightly judged that, if they devoted to piety what necessity demanded, they were being treated justly; and that it would be most beautiful if they were permitted to be buried in the bosom of their homeland. For what benefit would it be to escape and live on after religion? It was better to die together with a pious duty. If anyone abandoned it through fear of danger, that was sacrilege; if anyone fulfilled it, that was a sacrifice—the victory of pious suffering.

Thus the mitred priests were sacrificed among their own victims, and, clothed in priestly stoles, they lay upon the ground among the bodies of the slain. Nor had such slaughter raged only among the sacred ministers; it also tormented the remaining populace with a most miserable massacre. Thus human and divine things alike were stained. Had not David also spoken of these people:

> “The nations have entered into your inheritance; they have defiled your holy temple; they have made the dead bodies of your servants food for the birds of the sky; they have poured out their blood like water around Jerusalem, and there was no one to bury them” (Psalm 78:1–3).

For at that time the nations had likewise entered into God’s inheritance, to carry everything away; the temples of God were polluted by the hands of the wicked, and the unburied corpses of the slain lay exposed as food for birds and the voracity of beasts. Blood was poured out so that it might stagnate in the temple, and no one remained to bury the dead, because fury passed from the living against the dead, and from the dead against those who still lived. Gaul, you were paying the price of your ancient savagery. [Col. 0027D] If anyone were to recount the slaughter of the slain, he might think that the Babylonians had returned to Jerusalem.

[(FLOD. I, 6.)] Blessed Jerome mentions this persecution in his letter *On Monogamy*, when he lamented the barbarian persecution to Aggerundia, a noble widow, exhorting her to persevere in widowhood and recalling, among other things:

> “Innumerable and most savage nations have occupied all Gaul. Whatever lies between the Alps and the Pyrenees, enclosed by the Ocean and the Rhine, the Quadi, Vandals, Sarmatians, Alans, Gepids, Heruli [Note: Thus in 1, 2, and 3; *herulei* in 5.], Saxons, Burgundians, Alamanni—and, O mournful commonwealth!—the Pannonian enemies have devastated. Indeed, Assyria has come with them. Mainz, once a noble city, was captured and overthrown, and many thousands of people were slaughtered in the church. The Vangiones were destroyed by a long siege; the powerful city of the Remi, Amiens, Arras [Note: Jerome, together with the other cities, also laments the destruction of Atrebatum. The author added this in the margin.], and the extreme peoples of the Morini, Tournai, and the Nemetes were transferred into Germany. Aquitaine, the province of the Nine Peoples, and the provinces of Lyon and Narbonne were entirely laid waste except for a few cities, and even those are ravaged from outside by the sword and from within by famine,”

and so forth.

### 6. Saint Vedastus, directed by divine grace, comes to this province and leads King Clovis—compelled toward the worship of the Christian faith by the less favorable outcome of a battle—to Saint Remigius for baptism.

Thus, while this tyrannical fury raged against the Church of Christ, the city of Atrebatum remained without a priestly ruler until the time of Saint Vedastus. The church had been destroyed, the place reduced to solitude, and made a dwelling-place of wild beasts.

[(Life of Saint Vedastus.)] “This holy confessor of God and outstanding preacher came into these regions, by the direction of divine grace, in the time of the most powerful king of that period, Clovis of the Franks, for the salvation of many.”

Let us set down in writing the order and cause of this event, insofar as brevity permits. The aforementioned ruler was still entangled in the errors of pagan superstition, [but he had a religious wife, initiated into the sacraments of baptism, named Chrothildis (Life of Vedastus),] the daughter of King Chilperic, whom her brother, King Gundobad, had killed after disputes had arisen between them.

This most Christian queen daily entreated the king, urging him to turn from the worship of idols to the worship of the one true God, so that the unbelieving husband might be saved through the faithful woman (1 Corinthians 7:14). But the king paid little heed to the queen’s counsel, because he believed that, through the aid of his gods, everything that appeared to have happened successfully to him had come about [Note: *omibus* in 1.]. The queen, anxious about the king’s salvation rather than the power of the kingdom, saw that the king had rejected the counsel of salvation and asked the Most High to provide an opportunity by which the king, compelled in this way, might at least take hold of the occasion for his salvation.

[(Life of Vedastus.)] “The king therefore declared war against the Alemanni, but he did not find them unprepared, as he had wished. For they gathered a strong force, met the king near the banks of the Rhine, and attempted to defend their homeland by military valor.”

After the Franks had invoked their gods for the king’s assistance, they began to lose heart at the very moment of engagement. Their right hands grew weak, and, overcome by terror and fear alike, they were tormented more by despair of life than by the prospect of defeat.

Seeing his army scattering, the king, displaying strength of spirit beyond the power of terror, forbade the soldiers to tremble and inflamed them more ardently for battle, so that they might value the danger of death less than the triumph of glory. As standard-bearer, he himself recalled the ranks, drove his horse first against the enemy, and the others followed with a great shout and fought fiercely.

The Alemanni, on the other hand, superior in strength and number and fighting for their lives and the freedom of their homeland, began to press the Franks vigorously: some pierced the retreating soldiers with arrows, others with weapons, and others with crossbows. But when the king saw that, after the loss of many men, the army was falling apart and could not hold its ground, and that the gods he had invoked had not come to his aid in the present danger, he called upon the most powerful God of the Christians, whom the queen had urged him to worship. In his desperation, he bound himself by a vow that, if his fortunes were changed and he returned victorious from the enemy, he and his army would be washed in the sacred font.

Immediately their strength was restored and their ranks re-formed. With the help of the Trinity they attacked the enemy and defeated almost all of them, except those whom flight or surrender preserved for life. Understanding that the enemy had been overcome not so much by his own valor as by God’s gift, and bound to Him by the vow of faith he had made, [Life of Vedastus:] “the king soon went to the town of Toul, having heard that blessed Vedastus was serving God there in praiseworthy devotion.”

When he explained to him the reason for his arrival and announced that the outcome of the battle—which had turned against him after the invocation of the gods—had come to a favorable conclusion through the name of Christ, the man of God gave thanks to God, [Col. 0029C] who had deigned to open his kingdom to the nations. He began to announce the ministry of the Catholic faith to the king and, instructed by evangelical declarations, led him to the venerable man of God Remigius, who at that time held the chief authority of the church of Reims.

[(FLOD., I, 15.)] “He was a man formed by wisdom and virtues, whose marks of spiritual excellence the Gallic people testify to, having been converted through him to Christ.”

[(Life of Vedastus.)] “Pope Hormisdas had once entrusted him with carrying out his duties in Gaul. Vedastus therefore led the king, who was hastening toward the fountain of life. On the journey the man of God restored the light of his eyes to a certain blind man who was crying out to him, not without the amazement of the nobles of the palace, and even of the king, whom the manifestation of the present miracle kindled with fervor for the Christian faith. A church built as a testimony to this power can be seen to this day; there divine benefits are granted to those who pray and believe.”

### 7. Blessed Vedastus brought wine from a dry vessel; after being ordained bishop by Saint Remigius, he restored a cripple’s ability to walk and sight to a blind man.

The king, having been baptized together with his nobles, returned to the royal scepter; [Col. 0030A] Saint Vedastus, however, remained for some time with blessed Remigius. A great number of nobles and religious people gathered around him because of the celebrated reputation of his way of life [Note: *regiosorum multos* in 1.].

Among them, one man, moved more than the others by love of heavenly teaching, was accustomed to visit him familiarly. One evening, as the sun was sinking toward sunset, he did not wish to send the man away without the provisions of charity. He therefore asked a boy to bring wine. When the boy reported that all the wine had been exhausted because of the multitude of guests, Vedastus, undoubting in the riches of faith, caused precious wine to overflow from a dry vessel.

Blessed Remigius, observing in him the marks of an exemplary way of life and spiritual gifts, judged it unworthy that the light of a heavenly lamp should remain enclosed in darkness, when it would shine more brightly for the salvation and illumination of many. With King Clovis’ support, therefore, he sent the bishop ordained by God’s providence to evangelize the cities of Cameracum and Atrebatum.

Thus it is clear [Note: *Liquet.*] that, the more earnestly this king had loved the sees of his fathers, the more approved a shepherd he had appointed there. For, as stated a little above (ch. 4), he was more especially concerned with those sees than with the others; and therefore, moved by greater zeal [Note: That is, eagerness or love, as in II, 5.], he tried to enrich the parish with pastoral government. He considered no one better than blessed Vedastus both for taming the savage people and for stirring them to the grace of faith, since it was through him that he himself had acquired the Catholic faith.

It should also be noted, as we touched upon above (ch. 5), that these two parishes had formerly enjoyed a dual episcopal administration; but now, because this holy pontiff found them devastated, they are gathered under one administration [Note: The author himself supplied *colliguntur* on a sewn-in slip. He likewise supplied the words *Clodoveo* and *providentiam* above the line, and wrote *Favente rege*, *Cameraco et Atrebato dirigit* in an erasure.].

[(Life of Vedastus.)] “At the entrance to the city of Atrebatum he gave one lame man the power to walk and another blind man sight; they had cried out to him, the one deprived of light, the other of the ability to walk. On entering, he was astonished by the city’s lamentable ruin. For he learned that in ancient times the worship of the sacred faith had flourished there; but because of the offense of its inhabitants, by the hidden yet just judgment of God, that city, together with the other cities of Gaul and Germany, had been handed over to the pagan and faithless king of the Huns, Attila, for plunder. Because of the savagery of his spirit, he knew how to show reverence neither to the priests of God, as we lamented above, nor to the churches of God; rather, like a most savage storm, he devastated everything with sword and fire.

“While he searched to see whether any sign of the church remained, no trace of the ancient temple appeared, because the site had already grown wild with brambles and thorns; and where once there had been choirs of singers, there appeared the lairs of wild beasts. At last, after examining the fragments of the walls more carefully, he found the altar of the holy Mother of God, Mary. Although it lay amid the ruin of the walls, he did not doubt that it had still been preserved unharmed by divine providence.”

From this the holy man understood—and we too are enabled to understand—that the stronghold of the episcopal chair had once stood there, especially since Pope Dionysius, who, according to the authority of the chronicles, held the Roman see 263 years before Pope Hormisdas, who lived in the time of blessed Vedastus, left these cities also—Cameracum and Atrebatum—listed among the others and equally distinguished with their parishes when he established each diocese with defined boundaries and decreed that the more eminent sees should be metropolitan, while the inferior ones should be suffragan [Note: Pope Dionysius included Cameracum and Atrebatum among the other episcopal sees in his description. The author added this in the margin.].

[Note: He had originally written, “that he left this city also listed” in 1; the author himself corrected it to the reading now found.]

### 8. At the synod held in the city of Vienne by Saint Mamertus, Saint Remigius sent Saint Vedastus in his place; there the co-bishops decreed, among other matters, that the fast observed for three days before the Ascension of the Lord should be maintained.

[(Life of Vedastus.)] “After restoring the buildings of the temple, blessed Vedastus devoted the peoples of the surrounding province from the worship of idols to divine worship, demolishing the shrines of the gods and raising churches to the height of supreme splendor. Knowledge of the divine law shone everywhere; the name of Christ was heard on everyone’s lips.
