As for the signs and wonders that divine power displayed through him, since the brevity of this writing cannot contain them, the book of his life gives a fuller account to inquisitive readers.

“In his time a synod held in the city of Vienne is recorded. Almost all the bishops of Gaul, summoned by blessed Mamertus, gathered there; [Col. 0031C] and they themselves asked that blessed Remigius come, since he was exceedingly learned in divine utterances and most eloquent by the privilege of outstanding grace. But the holy man, weighed down by old age and detained by bodily weakness, sent blessed Vedastus there as his associate in the duties entrusted to him” [Note: Henschenius explained that what is contained here is more than doubtful, *Acta Sanctorum*, February I.].

“For at that time, as blessed Gregory, bishop of Tours, writes in the *History of the Franks*, unheard-of portents had terrified the citizens of that city. [*History of the Franks.*] A profound depression of spirit had fallen upon them because of a very great earthquake, the sudden destruction of many churches, and the shaking of collapsing palaces; the continuing portents seemed to announce that the end of the world and the final day of judgment were approaching. Moreover, many beasts—wolves, bears, and deer—wandered about there. Entering through the city gate and devouring many people, they did this throughout the entire year.

“When the solemn day of Easter arrived, Saint Mamertus, bishop of that city, was celebrating the sacred mystery during the vigil, and the royal palace, which rose above the higher part of the city, was set ablaze by divine fire. The bishops recognized that this punishment of divine indignation had occurred because of human offense, and by common counsel decreed that the fast which is observed for three days before the Ascension of the Lord should be maintained. It is observed in all the churches of Gaul to this day. Thus the tribulation and destruction themselves ceased.”

### 9. Blessed Vedastus departed from this world, and a column of light illuminated his departure.

[(Life of Vedastus.)] The outstanding priest of God, Vedastus, ruled the church of the aforementioned city for approximately forty years. Blessed Remigius kindly recalls him in his testament, writing as follows (FLOD. I, 18):

> “To the church of Atrebatum, for which, by God’s authority, I consecrated my dearest brother Vedastus as bishop, I have assigned, from the gift of the aforementioned ruler”—that is, Hludowicus (Clovis), whom I received from the sacred font—“two estates for the support of the clergy, namely Orcos and Sabucetum.”

[(Life of Vedastus.)] His death was indicated by a column of light, visible as a luminous path extending from his cell all the way to heaven; it was soon illumined by the holy day of his ensuing death. It was remarkable that, amid the lamentations of those weeping, the voices of people singing on earth were heard in heaven.

He was buried in the church of the blessed virgin Mary, not far from the altar itself, toward the southern side. He rested in that place for some time, until, when the Lord revealed it, he was happily transferred by the holy men Autbertus and Audomarus to the place where his memory now shines, as is read in the book of his life and more fully in the deeds of blessed Autbertus. In that translation blessed Audomarus is said to have avoided, by recovering his blindness, the corruptible gift of light that he had received. A diligent reader will find the miracles performed after his death elsewhere.

### 10. [Note: The author himself wrote this and the following chapter on a sewn-in slip.] Concerning a man sustained in the field through the advocacy of Saint Vedastus

We have received from eyewitnesses a few events that occurred in our own days through the merits of this blessed confessor, and we have judged that they should by no means be passed over.

In the territory of Dernium [Note: Perhaps Ergny, arrondissement of Montreuil, or Erny-Saint-Julien, arrondissement of Saint-Omer. Le Glay. Perhaps it should be read *Dervensi*. The name *Pagus Dervensis* survives in Moutier-en-Der. P.] certain wicked robbers, coveting another man’s small property, attacked a man from the household of Saint Vedastus with malicious accusations. For that reason, seeking their advocate in court, they challenged the man himself to single combat, which country people call “the field.”

He promised that his advocate would appear within the period established for settling this legal matter, took up a bag and staff, and hurried to the monastery of the man of God. Proclaiming his case, he implored the abbot’s advocacy. But the abbot declined to provide assistance because of the difficulty of the long journey; rather, he advised him to await divine aid [Note: *expectaret* in 1.].

Completely desolate, the man returned to his own home. Trusting solely in the Lord’s mercy, he did not consider abandoning the legal proceeding he had undertaken. Therefore, on the appointed day, presenting himself for judgment, he claimed that the advocacy of God and Saint Vedastus would benefit him, and confidently declared that he would oppose no other shield than his bag to settle the combat.

By divine mercy it came to pass that, when the other combatant, carefully armed, had engaged him and struck his unarmed bag with a mighty blow, such a thick and dense mist immediately rose between them from that very bag that neither could see the other.

### 11. Concerning a man also liberated through Saint Vedastus

In a certain church located in the episcopate of Liège and dedicated in honor of Saint Vedastus, a particularly wicked robber seized a man through fraudulently contrived accusations. With the man’s hands tied behind his back and a rope placed under his armpits, he dragged him away to be tortured more harshly.

When he saw that the man had immediately been freed from heaven, he leapt down from his horse and, supposing that the man had somehow freed himself, beat him badly and bound him again more tightly. After mounting his horse, he suddenly saw that the man had again been loosed; in fury he seized him by the hair, beat him, and bound him a third time by the genitals.

Before long, however, he saw that the man had been released. At last, overcome, he judged that he must be beaten by divine power. No one can doubt that this was granted by God through the merits of Saint Vedastus.

### 12. After Vedastus, Dominicus succeeded; afterward Vedulfus, and then blessed Gaugericus

After blessed Vedastus, Dominicus succeeded to the pontifical throne, and Vedulfus succeeded him. From this man and his other successors, the church of Cameracum received a special seat of authority, although it had long been without priestly government, as Atrebatum also had been, ever since the slaughter of the barbarian persecution had devastated the churches of Gaul.

Nevertheless, no one will rightly doubt whether some rulers had presided over this church earlier, since this can easily be understood from the descriptions of Pope Dionysius, as was expressly shown above (ch. 5, 7) [Note: The author supplied the words *ut supra expressius ostensum est* between the lines.]. Or it may be understood from the fact that King Clodio killed the Romans whom he found there as Christians.

Although Vedulfus the bishop may perhaps have performed some memorable deeds, it is uncertain whether, through negligence or because of the scarcity of writers—by which many things often grow old in silence—his fame has not survived to our own time. Apart from this, in the deeds of blessed Gaugericus [Note: In the older accounts, *Acta Sanctorum*, August II, 670; *Acta Sanctorum Belgii* II, 273.], who succeeded him in the pontificate, we read that he was removed from human affairs and passed to better things. From this it may be understood that he was a man of such merit that not punishments for guilt but rewards for innocence should be rendered to him; this is what it means that he “passed to better things.”

### 13. [Life of Gaugericus III, 1; Note: Composed by our author before the *Gesta*; cf. *Acta Sanctorum*, August II, 670; *Acta Sanctorum Belgii* II, 308.] Concerning Bishop Bertoaldus

After the death of blessed Gaugericus, Bertoaldus succeeded to the pontifical see. He was of noble Frankish lineage, an apostolic man and distinguished by the endowment of virtues.

Moved by love and veneration for blessed Gaugericus, for whom he had always burned with affection as for a son, he placed his bed, spread with bedding, in the chamber of the holy man from which he had sent his soul to heaven. He did this not out of the presumption of a slippery spirit, but because he was confident that no hostile, phantasmal ambush would trouble that place, which so great a man had consecrated by the event of his death.

When he rested there one night, blessed Gaugericus appeared to him in a vision, addressing him gently and kindly, so that, by promptly removing the bed, he might remember to atone for the guilt of his presumption if he wished to have Gaugericus favorable to him. He immediately removed the bed as he had been ordered, and dedicated an altar to the Lord in memory [Note: *in honore* in 5.] of blessed Gaugericus in the same chamber. Having placed relics of the saints there, he adapted it for divine worship. Sacred celebration is still carried out there to this day, and vows are also paid to God.

### 14. Bishop Bertoaldus attended a synod with Saint Arnulfus and many others, where matters necessary for the Church were discussed (A.D. 625).

We also find in the deeds of the bishops of Reims (Flod. II, 5) that Bishop Bertoaldus himself attended the synod celebrated by Sonnatius, bishop of Reims, together with Theodoricus of Lyon, Sindulfus of Vienne, Sulpitius of Bourges, Medegiselus of Tours, Senocus of Eauze, Leontius of Saintes, Modoaldus of Trier, Chunebertus of Cologne, Richerius of Sens, Donatus of Besançon, and many other bishops whose names brevity has omitted.

Saint Arnulfus is also found to have attended as bishop of Metz. Many useful matters were read as having been established at this synod, concerning how the affairs of the Church should be handled.

For example, concerning clerics: if any should dare to bind themselves by an oath of rebellion or by a written conspiracy and should contrive plots against their bishop through crafty allegation, then, if they refused to correct themselves after being admonished, they were to be entirely deprived of their own rank.

Likewise, if any judge, whatever his rank, should presume to oppress a cleric by public sanctions, or, for whatever causes, to constrain him without the knowledge and permission of the bishop, or should presume to afflict him with insults or injuries, he was to be deprived of communion.

Likewise, if anyone voluntarily committed homicide and did so not while resisting violence but by inflicting violence in a fit of passion, communion was not to be given to him at all; nevertheless, if he performed penance, communion as viaticum was not to be denied him at the hour of death [Note: *violente* in 1 and in Flod.].

Likewise, if a cleric wished to leave one city and travel to other cities or provinces, he was to be commended by letters from his bishop; if he departed without such letters, he was by no means to be received.

Likewise, if anyone established in any rank or office, or supported by authority, should dare, after the bishop’s death, to seize property of any kind placed in the houses or fields of the Church before the opening of the testament or the hearing, or should presume to break the barriers of the Church and touch or search the furnishings placed inside the church’s house, he was to be entirely excluded from the communion of Christians.

Likewise, clerics of any rank were not to approach the court for their own affairs or for ecclesiastical affairs in any other way, nor dare to plead cases, except those which they had been expressly permitted to conduct with the bishop’s permission and counsel.

Likewise, no one, whether supported by royal authority, by any other power, or by his own presumption, was to dare to seize or carry away widows who had asked to be consecrated to the Lord, or girls consecrated to the Lord. If both parties consented, they were to be deprived of communion.

Besides these, many other matters were discussed. Although they were quite useful, we who favor brevity have judged that they should be passed over.

### 15. [Life of Gaugericus III, 3.] During the time of this prelate, a thief was apprehended in the basilica of Saint Gaugericus when Saint Gaugericus revealed him.

During the time of this bishop, a certain thief entered the basilica of Saint Gaugericus in the dead of night and wished to strip the holy man’s tomb, which glittered with gold and gems in a work of astonishing craftsmanship. But the man of God appeared in a vision to his doorkeeper, informed him that his memorial was being attacked by robbers, and ordered him to permit the captured thief to depart without injury. And so it was done.

### 16. Ablebertus, or Emebertus, of holy descent, is added.

After Bertoaldus, blessed Ablebertus succeeded him. This is the name by which he is listed in the catalogue of bishops, but the inhabitants and neighbors called him Emebertus [Note: Our author is greatly mistaken, confusing Ablebertus, who died about A.D. 640, with Emebertus or Hildebertus, the brother of Saint Gudula, who became bishop around A.D. 705; see ch. 33. Everything narrated in this and the following chapter concerns this Emebertus, Saint Gudula’s brother.].

[(Life of Gudula.)] He was born in the district of Brabant, of parents distinguished both by the nobility of their life and by their lineage: namely, his father Witerus, a count and holy man, and his mother Amulberga.

He also had four holy sisters: Reinildis, Sarachildis, Ermenlindis, and the most blessed Gudula, younger in age but no less outstanding in holiness. Before she was born, she was announced by an angel to her most blessed mother. She strove to surpass her days by good works and shone with many virtues and miracles, as the published book of her life indicates.

That book also declares the bishop Ablebertus to have been renowned for extraordinary holiness and conspicuous for the nobility of his character—something that should not be doubted, especially since he was born of such holy and distinguished parents [Note: Sc. *protestetur*. Colv.].

When he heard that the tomb of the aforementioned sister, Gudula, who had already been buried for three days, had been violated by a pestilential robber, he groaned and bound the robber with the chain of anathema. Indeed, with an uttered curse, he also obtained this result, so that, with signs bearing witness, it might at least not be hidden from posterity: if the offender were a man, he would become lame or disabled in some way; if a woman, she would never be free from the condition commonly called *gutteria* [Note: Goiter.].

And this is marvelous to relate: the book itself testifies that the entire offspring of that family afterward suffered this condition. From this it may be understood that the man was of superior merit.

### 17. He was buried at Martinas but transferred to Melbodium.

He possessed, as they say, an estate called Martinas [Note: It seems to be Merchten in Brabant. Le Glay.], extremely wealthy in households and abundant possessions. He had made the church of the Mother of God [Note: The church of Cameracum.] its heir, but he had lost it, we do not know for what reason except perhaps through the attacks of the pagans.

When the day of his calling arrived, he died in the same district, in a village which the inhabitants of the place call Ham [Note: Ham near Vilvoorde.], and departed from the world. He was buried there, then carried to Martinas, and afterward transferred to Melbodium, where he now rests and awaits the day of the resurrection.

### 18. Concerning Saint Autbertus

After him, blessed Autbertus succeeded to the pontifical see [Note: A.D. 633, according to Ghesquière in *Acta Sanctorum Belgii* III, 535.], an outstanding man distinguished by the merit of his life, in the time of Dagobert, king of the Franks.

Because of the familiar friendship with which he loved him uniquely, the king gave one royal estate to the brothers who served in the church of blessed Mary, where the man of God exercised the office of the pontifical chair. It was called Oneng [Note: Onnaing, between Valenciennes and Condé. Colv.] from ancient times.

The deeds of this blessed man have not been fully disclosed because of the scarcity of writers. Apart from this, in the deeds of the saints who lived in his time, we have found a few passages in which he is commemorated with celebrated remembrance; of these we shall briefly relate some.

As he was carefully planning to promote a certain boy, whom he had received from the sacred fonts and entrusted to the sacred letters, to the sacred orders, the devil deceived him with deceptive words and drew him back toward worldly pursuits. Taking wicked and seditious men to himself, the boy began to harass, drag away, and rob travelers.

As he persisted more attentively in these practices and the blessed man lamented his downfall, one of his accomplices, suddenly carried off to punishment [Note: Clearly, the punishment of hell, as is evident from the Life of Saint Autbertus. Colv.], struck the young man, who was permitted to see these things, with great horror. After the terrifying vision, an angel appearing from heaven declared to him that he too was destined for such punishments because he had abandoned the man of God, Autbertus.

Seized by this terror, the young man was received by the holy man, nourished, and advanced all the way to the priesthood. Whoever has leisure will find many miracles of his in the book of his life, even to the present day.

### 19. [18.] [The same source.] He consecrated the church of Saint Gislenus, cultivated Saint Vincentius, and veiled Saint Waldetrudis and Saint Aldegundis. [The same source.]

At nearly the same time, blessed Gislenus, having departed from Athens, was accused before blessed Autbertus after disputes had arisen. Autbertus, recognizing the causes of the false accusation, judged him not only undeserving of condemnation but received him with great veneration. Taking blessed Amandus with him, he consecrated the church which Saint Gislenus had built in honor of the apostles.

He formed blessed Vincentius—formerly called Madelgarius—who had been occupied with the affairs of secular life and was distinguished both by military duties and by marriage into the royal family, with such fervor of divine love that, laying aside his military belt and dissolving his marriage, he took the monastic habit and bound himself under the rule of holy conduct.

His wife, namely blessed Waldetrudis, took with her her sister, who had dedicated her intention of virginity to the Lord. Both received sacred veils from blessed Autbertus: one at the mountain called Castrilocus [Note: Mons.], the other at the place called Melbodium [Note: Maubeuge.]. They devoted themselves to divine worship until the end [Note: *de seculo seculi* in 1.].

There was also at Melbodium a monastery built by blessed Aldegundis, which the holy pontiff consecrated in honor of the blessed virgin Mary and the holy apostles. He brought with him religious men, as the published book of her life indicates [Note: Thus in 2 and also originally in 1. But in this manuscript a hand of the late twelfth century—not our author’s—erased the words “whom the published book of her life indicates,” and wrote, partly in the erasure and partly in the margin, the following excerpted word for word from the Life of Saint Autbertus: “namely blessed Amandus, Abbot and co-bishop Ursmarus, as well as Audoenus, bishop of the city of Rouen, and also Humbertus, bishop and abbot of blessed memory, together with the abbots Etto and Eloquius, and Erminus, a most illustrious man, he dedicated it.” At the very top of the following page he wrote: “Saint V. at Atrebatum, in honor of the blessed God-bearing Mary.” The same wording is found in 3 and 5. It therefore appears that manuscript 2, which does not yet contain this material, had already been copied from 1 before the end of the twelfth century.]

### 20. (19.) (Same source.) Saint Vedast was transferred

At Arras, too, a church had been dedicated in honor of the blessed Mary, Mother of God; in it stood the throne of the episcopal dignity. In this church the blessed Vedast, whom we mentioned above [Note: [Col. 0037D] Chapter 6 and following], rested not far from the altar, with his tomb turned toward the southern quarter. The blessed Autbert, after an angel had indicated to him the place where an oratory was to be built and after the church had been founded, transferred him, taking with him the blessed Audomar, bishop of Thérouanne. During this translation the same blessed Audomar, although he was blind, recovered the sight he had lost suddenly, treating the restored light as a small matter; and in memory of so great a miracle a church is still known to have been built there in honor of the blessed Autbert [Note: [Col. 0037] Thus in manuscripts 2 and originally 1; but the same late-twelfth-century hand erased *presentis seculi* in manuscript 1 and wrote *tanti miraculi* instead; manuscripts 3, 4, and 5 also have the latter reading.].

At the divinely designated place the man of God built a monastery and, from his own possessions, gave to the church whatever was needed for the use of those serving it, according to the circumstances. The account of this matter is shown more fully in the little book of his life. The blessed Vindicianus, who succeeded him in the episcopate, for reasons that arose, gave the abbey to King Theodoric, retaining for himself the privilege of pastoral governance.

The blessed Autbert, after entrusting his people to the worship of the Lord’s faith, happily completed his life; he was buried in the church of the blessed Peter [Note: [Col. 0037D] Now Saint-Géry. Concerning the date of his death, see Ghesquière, *Acta Sanctorum Belgii* III, 537, who assigns it to the year 669. But the Vedastine Annals say: “In the third year of the reign of Justinian, in the year 687 of the incarnation of the Word, the body of Saint Vedast, by God’s providence and through angelic revelation, was transferred from the episcopal see by the two holy bishops Autbert and Audomar, after 118 years of his episcopate. When this translation had been completed, the bishop Autbert, a man of holy and worthy memory, departed to the Lord; Vindicianus succeeded him, himself also magnificent in merits and works.” The Minor Annals of Elnon, although not very reliable in their chronology, have under the year 676: “Saint Vindicianus governs the bishopric of Cambrai”; and under 686: “The body of Saint Vedast is transferred from the episcopal see to Nobiliacum.” Moreover, the Blandinian Annals have under 697: “The translation of Saint Vedast, 128 years after his death.”], which had been built outside the walls of the city of Cambrai; now, however, after the walls had been enlarged and the monastery improved, he rests within the walls of the city itself [Note: [Col. 0037] Manuscript 1 has *urbis*.].

### 21. (20.) (Annals of Vedast; compare the Life of Leodegarius.) Vindicianus succeeded as bishop, and concerning the martyred Saint Leodegarius

After his death (in the year 670), the blessed Vindicianus undertook the governance of the see of the same church during the reign of King Theodoric, son of Clovis by the most prudent Queen Balthild.

This Theodoric, after his brother Chlothar—who had earlier succeeded to his father’s kingdom together with his mother Balthild—assumed the supreme power of the kingdom, despite the resistance of many of the Frankish nobles, especially because of Ebroin, who was exceedingly troublesome to them as master of the royal household. Accordingly, rising against Theodoric and Ebroin, they shaved the hair from the heads of both and confined them in the monastery of Luxeuil in Burgundy; and they accepted as king over the entire realm their third brother Childeric, who ruled in the regions of Austrasia. They appointed Saint Leodegarius, bishop of Autun, over the king’s household.

But not long afterward the Franks, unable to endure the king because of his frivolity and insolence [Note: [Col. 0039] Omitted in manuscript 1], raised a rebellion and killed him. Thus Theodoric was restored to the kingdom, and Ebroin to his former rank. Having been instructed by the most wicked counselors, Ebroin supposed that he had been driven from his former power by the faction of the bishop just mentioned. He therefore subjected Leodegarius to the most cruel tortures and, after having him led through the territory of Arras, ordered him to be beheaded at a place called the Forest of Saint Leodegarius [Note: [Col. 0039D] The Bois de Lucheux. Le Glay.]. He was buried in a village called Sercin [Note: [Col. 0039D] Sercin is the name of the place situated in the middle of the village of Sus-Saint-Léger. Le Glay.], which lies on the boundary between the bishopric of Cambrai and that of Thérouanne [Note: [Col. 0039] The author himself wrote “Cambrai and Thérouanne.”].

### 22. (21.) (Life of Leodegarius.) Concerning the body of this martyr

When the bishops Ansoaldus, Hermenecharius, and Saint Vindicianus contended over the body of this martyr [Note: [Col. 0039] Manuscript 1 has *Vincentiano*], Ansoaldus obtained it by lot. Soon afterward the fame of his miracles, spread throughout the surrounding regions, became widely known even at the royal palace.

At that time, among the other nobles, Ansoaldus, bishop of Poitiers, and Hermenecharius, bishop of Autun, as well as Saint Vindicianus, happened to be present. The first of these, wishing to claim the body of the holy martyr by virtue of the privilege of his monastery and kinship; the second, asserting the rights of his bishopric; and the third—that is, the blessed Vindicianus—declaring that the place of martyrdom and burial, which the martyr had received in his diocese by God’s will, belonged to him: they had settled this entirely reasonable dispute among themselves until, by the judgment of the other bishops, three letters bearing the names of these three men were subscribed, covered together beneath the altar cloth, and placed there after a common prayer. By the indications thus given, it was declared that the holy body belonged to the bishop of Poitiers.

### 23. [Note: [Col. 0039] This entire chapter is missing from manuscripts 1, 3, 4, and 5; it survives in one copy of manuscript 2, designated 2*. Without doubt the author had supplied it in manuscript 1 on an attached slip, which was later lost.] (22.) A miracle concerning Saint Amatus, which occurred at Cambrai in the time of Bishop Vindicianus

During the time of this bishop, something remarkable also occurred in our city, which I have judged necessary to insert in this work. (Life of Amatus.)

At that time, while the aforesaid King Theodoric was raging against the saints of God, the blessed Amatus, bishop of the church of Sens, was appointed for exile and confinement by the devil’s prompting. He was sent far from those regions, to be held under guard at the municipality in Vermandois called Péronne [Col. 0039D], under the custody of the most reverend man, the abbot Ultanus. The king intended, of course, that the man whom he did not dare to kill by the sword should at least be worn down by the long tribulation of exile.

After Saint Ultanus had died, the impious king feared that the holy bishop might return to his homeland. He therefore chose a certain man named Mauruntus, son of Duke Adalbaldi and Saint Rictrudis, sent him to Péronne, and ordered him to take the blessed bishop with him and keep him under suitable guard elsewhere.

The distinguished athlete of God did not delay obeying this command. Hurrying to carry out what had been ordered, he brought the exiled saint away with him, treating him honorably. As they were making their way toward the district of Ostrevant, it happened that they turned aside to the city of Cambrai for refreshment.

While the others were busy with the necessary arrangements, the most blessed bishop, always intent upon that portion which Mary, according to the testimony of the Lord, chose as the better one, entered the church of the holy Mary, Mother and Virgin of God, not far from their lodging. There it became perfectly clear how dear he was to the Lord.

For when he entered, his eyes, as commonly happens in shadow, were dazzled and weakened by the brightness of the sunlight. Being therefore less able to see, he used a ray of sunlight, which shone through a hole in the wall, as a servant. Tired from the journey and laying down his material burden so that he might take up the spiritual one more lightly, he unknowingly placed his cloak and sleeves upon the ray of sunlight as though upon a staff extended there.

The sun itself received them and, while he lay prostrate in prayer, supported them in service. Meanwhile, after arranging what was necessary in the house, the blessed Mauruntus followed the saint’s footsteps. When he entered the church and discovered the saint’s garments hanging from the sun, he proclaimed the wonder of God with praise, threw himself at the feet of so great a man, and, confessing his ignorance, asked forgiveness if he had sinned against him.

He had not previously served him properly, since he did not yet know that the man possessed such merit before God. But the most gentle bishop mercifully forgave him [Note: [Col. 0039] Omitted in manuscript 2*]. Soon afterward, having recovered their strength, they resumed the journey they had begun. Easing their labor by the sweetness of divine speech, they reached Hamaticum [Note: [Col. 0040D] Hamage, near Marchiennes. Le Glay.].

They remained there for a very long time and made considerable progress. Finally, leaving the monastery of Hamaticum, the holy bishop was taken out and led to Broilum [Note: [Col. 0040D] Bruel.]. There he ordered a cell to be built for himself beside the basilica. Whenever it was appropriate, he remained there and ceaselessly wearied his body with vigils, prayers, and fasts, until the Lord called so distinguished a soldier from earth to heaven (in the year 690).

### 24. (23.) (Life of Maxelendis.) How, in the time of this holy man, the virgin of God Maxelendis was martyred and her killer was blinded

At approximately this time, a certain virgin in the territory of Cambrai, born of very noble parents, was accosted by a young man who was not lowborn but was base in character, so that she might be joined to him in lawful marriage.

She could not be broken—neither by gold or gems nor by any kind of ornament—so as to abandon her resolve of virginity and be joined, as noble women commonly were, to a powerful man. Nor was she willing to listen to her parents concerning such a proposal.

The young man, despairing of love and finding an opportunity when he could attack the girl alone in her father’s house, gathered a crowd of wicked companions. They surrounded the entire house, broke in, and searched every part of it. At last, after examining more closely the little room in which the virgin was hiding, they found her and dragged her violently to the place where a basilica has now been built in honor of all the saints, especially Saint Vedast, and also in veneration of the holy virgin herself.

Then the deadly executioner, gnashing his teeth, drew his sword and killed her with a blow. As soon as he saw the virgin’s blood, he was struck blind by the just judgment of God.

She was buried in the basilica of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul and of Saint Sulpicius the confessor, which was built in a village called Pomeriolas [Note: [Col. 0041D] It is not Pommereul, but Saint-Souplet; within its territory a field is still called Pommereul. Le Glay.].

### 25. (24.) (Same source.) How the blessed bishop brought the virgin’s body back to the place of her killing, and Harduinus recovered his sight

Three years after her martyrdom had been completed, a noble matron named Amaltrudis was divinely warned that she should approach the blessed Vindicianus, bishop of Cambrai, so that he, together with his clergy and the neighboring people, might bring the sacred body back with the greatest reverence to the place of her killing, because the Lord had determined to glorify that place with signs and miracles.

As soon as the blessed bishop heard the woman’s report, he took care to fulfill it. Harduinus, who had killed her, was still living in the darkness of his blindness, though in the utmost misery and disgrace. When he heard that the sacred body of the virgin was being brought back to the place mentioned, he condemned and acknowledged his sin, ordered himself to be led out to meet the body, and prostrated himself before the bier.

As soon as the bearers of the sacred body reached him, he recovered his sight. He ran to the bishop and related all that had happened to him. On the occasion of this manifest miracle, therefore, the bishop addressed the people and buried the holy body in the church mentioned above (in the year 673).

### 26. (25.) How he obtained confirmation from Pope John of the privilege concerning the possessions of the church of Saint Mary at Arras

We found this written account: the venerable bishop, the man of God, enlarged the church of Arras dedicated to the holy Mary, Mother of God, from his own possessions and also together with King Theodoric. He increased it with villages, churches, lands, mills, and other resources. Then, when the aforesaid king was seated in a general assembly, he entirely excluded secular and judicial authorities from that church by episcopal authority, in the presence of many fellow bishops, who together with the king gave their support, in a written privilege confirmed by Pope John.

The privilege reads as follows:

> “To the holy and universal church’s most blessed guardian, John, Roman pope and bishop of bishops, Vindicianus, the least servant of the servants of God: whatever may be most fortunate in Christ the Lord.
>
> Let your fatherhood, and all the children of the holy Church of God, know that if we contribute anything from our possessions to holy places or to the substance of the poor, we confidently believe that this will undoubtedly be repaid to us in eternal blessedness.
>
> Trusting in such great mercy and goodness of the Lord, in the assembly of our venerable bishops, before the most pious King Theodoric at a general court, we have ratified this letter and wish what has been ratified to remain so forever.
>
> The law of the ancients also demands that whoever wishes to sell, transfer, or give away anything from his own possessions should have the right, according to the Salic Law, to attach his written instrument.
>
> Therefore let all the faithful, present and future, know that by episcopal authority this episcopal privilege has been established by the aforesaid King Theodoric, so that it may be preserved inviolate from this day forward.
>
> By episcopal authority we exclude all secular and judicial powers, and every claim and every invasion, from the church of Saint Mary of the city of Arras. But so that the canons serving God there may be permitted to live peacefully now and for all time, we separate them from every worldly disturbance.
>
> If, however, a circumstance should arise in which our successors should prefer to make grants or benefices from possessions belonging to the use of the clergy, we forbid this.
>
> By the prohibition of anathema and by episcopal authority we further establish that the monastery itself, together with these villages—Belrenio [Note: [Col. 0041D] Beaurains. Colvenerius.], Medonivilla [Note: [Col. 0041D] Moyenville. Colvenerius.]—with sixty holdings between those two villages, eleven cultivated estates, and two churches with their entire endowment and all their appurtenances; Aquis [Note: [Col. 0041] Manuscript 1 has *Aquisgrani*, but *grani* was erased.] [Note: [Col. 0041D] Aix-les-Fampoux. Colvenerius.], in the district of Arras, with its church and endowment and all its appurtenances; Friscinicurte [Note: [Col. 0041D] Fresincourt. Colvenerius.], with all its appurtenances; Batzala [Note: [Col. 0042D] Basseux. Colvenerius.], with its church and all its appurtenances; Berleta [Note: [Col. 0042D] Berlette, in the arrondissement of Saint-Pol, but the canons of Arras possess nothing there. It seems that the reading should be what a later hand corrected in manuscript 5: *Boyletta*, Boille, whose domain—situated between Arras and Bapaume—is held by the chapter of Arras. Colvenerius.]; Squavia [Note: [Col. 0043A] [Note: [Col. 0043C] Ecoivres. L.]], with its church, endowment, and all its appurtenances; Ors [Note: [Col. 0043C] Ors, near the fortress of Cambrai; but the chapter possesses nothing there. Colvenerius.], with all its appurtenances; Sautscido [Note: [Col. 0043C] Either Sauchy-Cauchy or Sauchy-l’Estrée, or Sus-Saint-Léger. L.], with its appurtenances; Radonivilla [Note: [Col. 0043C] Ronville. Colvenerius.], with one mill on the stream of the Crientio [Note: [Col. 0043C] The Crinchon, a stream running through Arras, especially suitable for purple-dyeing workshops, in which the city was especially distinguished in Roman times.]; another mill at Dominica Curte [Note: [Col. 0044C] Demencourt, in the suburb of Arras. Colvenerius.]; Maraculo [Note: [Col. 0044C] Maroeul, in the diocese of Arras. Colvenerius.], in its entirety, with its church and endowment; a small tithe [Note: [Col. 0043] Manuscript 1 has *decima* for *decimancula*.] in Rodulf’s court [Note: [Col. 0044C] Roclincourt. L.]; likewise in Vinziacum [Note: [Col. 0043] Manuscripts 1, 3, 4, and 5 have *Viuinziaco*; manuscript 2 has *Unziaco*.] [Note: [Col. 0044C] Onzain. Colvenerius.], shall from this day and for all time remain in the power of the canons serving God in this monastery.
>
> Let no one presume to inflict any trouble upon the canons concerning any of the possessions we have mentioned, which the renowned king has assigned to that place for the use of the clergy, from his own possessions and from others by royal decree. Rather, let them be permitted to possess everything peacefully, so that they may more freely implore the mercy of God for the peace of the holy Church of God, for the life of the king and his wife and children, and for the stability of the kingdom.
>
> If anyone proves to be an observer of this privilege issued by us [Note: [Col. 0043] Manuscript 1 has *nobis*.], let him receive reward from the Lord, blessing from you and from all of us in the present life, and eternal life in the future. Amen.
>
> But if anyone should disregard our authority and wish to violate this episcopal authority confirmed by our hand, we send him to your clemency, so that you may permit what has been confirmed by us to remain stable—not only through you but through all our bishops who are with you.
>
> May almighty God, who placed the teaching of truth in the chair of unity, make you mindful of and understanding toward him; and may it please you, for his sake, to remember me also in your prayers.”

And he replied:

> “To Vindicianus and the bishops dwelling with him in the regions of Gaul: brotherly visitation and fatherly blessing.
>
> Hear the sentence that I pronounce. If anyone among your successors, whether a count, the greed of judges, or any opposing person, should wish to diminish or remove from that place this gift or confirmation which you have decided to make or ratify for the sake of God and out of divine love, we condemn him by apostolic judgment. By episcopal authority we exclude him from the thresholds of the holy Church of God, separate him from the assembly of the heavenly powers, and exclude him from the kingdom of God. By the prohibition of Saint Peter, the doorkeeper and key-bearer of Christ and of the heavenly kingdom, we forbid him, and with Judas, the betrayer of our Lord Jesus Christ, we assign him a lot, so that on the day of judgment, shaken by mourning, he may suffer in hell with the devil and his ministers, without joy. Amen.
>
> I, John the pope, have confirmed and ratified this privilege issued by my insignificance.
>
> I, Marinus, vicar of the apostolic see, have confirmed and ratified it.
>
> I, Andrew, bishop, have subscribed.
>
> I, Bonibertus, bishop, have subscribed.
>
> I, Laurentius, bishop [Note: [Col. 0043] Omitted in manuscript 1], have subscribed.
>
> I, Pedelbrandus, bishop, have subscribed.
>
> I, Nautor, bishop, have subscribed.
>
> I, Hilarius, bishop, have subscribed.
>
> I, Constantius, bishop, have subscribed.
>
> I, Martinus, bishop, have subscribed.
>
> I, Christophorus, bishop, have subscribed.
>
> I, Thomas, bishop, have subscribed.
>
> I, Felix, bishop, have subscribed.
>
> I, Audoinus, archbishop, have subscribed.
>
> I, Austregisilus, bishop, have subscribed.
>
> I, Ravengarius, bishop, have subscribed.
>
> I, Silvinus, bishop, have subscribed.
>
> I, Leodegarius, deposed from the see of Autun by the impious judge Ebroin, have written and subscribed.
>
> Given on the eighth day before the Ides of May, in the seventh year of the reign of our lord King Theodoric, in the second indiction (in the year 685).
>
> I, Vindicianus, bishop, at the command of the lord King Theodoric and at the request of John, the supreme pontiff, have written and subscribed.”

### 27. (26.) How the man of God Vindicianus, together with Saint Lantbertus, consecrated a church in the village of Hunolcorth

Moreover, the aforesaid bishop Vindicianus consecrated, in a settlement which lies approximately seven miles from the see of Cambrai and which the ancients called Hunolcurt [Note: [Col. 0044C] Honnecourt; compare II, 10], a monastery in praise of God and in veneration of Saint Peter. He summoned to himself not a few fellow bishops, together with the most precious blessed Lantbertus, the martyr of Liège, and established clerics and nuns there.

Afterward the man of God spent some time in the village of Savia [Note: [Col. 0044C] The same place mentioned above as Squavia, Ecoivres.], his own estate, in the oratory of Saint Martin. He had already become quite distinguished through the sacred evidence of his works; and by frequent conversations, exhortations, and apostolic preaching he had stirred many people there to carry out the rule of a wholesome life [Note: [Col. 0043] The author himself supplied the remainder of this chapter on an attached slip, placing the sign ::: after *excitaverat* and repeating it at the beginning of the slip. The other manuscripts begin a new line; manuscript 4 wrote in the margin: “Something seems to be missing here.” Colvenerius begins a new chapter and supplied a title of his own, found in no manuscript.].

(27.) We found an old charter in the archive of the church of Saint Huntbertus. Under the presence and favor of this holy bishop, the holy man himself, who at that time was abbot, wrote it concerning the village of Maceriae [Note: [Col. 0044C] Maizière-sur-Oise. L.]. It reads as follows [Note: [Col. 0043] Henschenius published the following diploma from the Maricolan manuscript, bearing the seal of Saint Humbert, in *Acta Sanctorum*, March III, 560. We therefore add below the passages in which it differs from our text, so that the degree of confidence to be placed in this sort of material may be apparent.]:

> “In the twelfth year of the reign of our lord Childeric, the glorious king, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of April [Note: [Col. 0043] The words “15. Kal. A.” are absent in the Maricolan manuscript] (in the year 672).
>
> I, Chonebertus, in the name of God [Note: [Col. 0043] The Maricolan manuscript has *Humbertus*], although an unworthy sinner, thinking of the fear of God and the reward of eternal good, and of the cleansing of my sins—for Scripture says: “Make friends for yourselves from the mammon of iniquity, so that they may lead you into the eternal dwellings of the saints”; and again it says: “Make for yourselves alms-bags that do not grow old” [Note: [Col. 0045] The Maricolan manuscript omits the words beginning “and again it says” through “that do not grow old”]—therefore I give, intending that this gift be given forever, to the sacred monastery called Maricolas, which the illustrious Huntbertus [Note: [Col. 0045] The Maricolan manuscript has *Radobertus*, which is correct; the founder was not Saint Humbertus himself but Radobertus, otherwise called Chronebertus or Chunebertus. Our text’s error may have arisen from this form of the name, *Chunebertus*.] once built by his own work, where I myself, an unworthy sinner, seem to preside as abbot [Note: [Col. 0045] These words are omitted in the Maricolan manuscript], consecrated in honor of holy Mary, mother of our Lord Jesus Christ, and of Saints Peter and Paul the apostles, and of the other lords who are venerated in that basilica, situated in the district of Famenne [Note: [Col. 0045D] The ancients called the district *Fanum Martis*; later writers named it after the river flowing through it, the Hainaut. Folcuin, *Gesta of the abbots of Lobbes* I.], on the stream called the Helpre [Note: [Col. 0045D] The Lesser Helpe, near Maroilles, flowing into the Sambre. L.]:
>
> “that is [Note: [Col. 0045] Omitted in the Maricolan manuscript], the greater part of our possession in the village called Maceriae, situated in the district of Laon on the river Oise, which I formerly purchased from my grandmother, the woman consecrated to God Audeliana [Note: [Col. 0045] The Maricolan manuscript has *Andiliana*], for a stipulated price by a contract of sale. This includes the lordly holdings where Audiliana herself lived, as well as those we later built, cultivated lands [Note: [Col. 0045D] That is, cultivated fields.], male and female slaves.
>
> “These holdings, therefore, with their lands, clearings, and pastures, in their entirety, by this text of our deed of gift, which we asked the notary Ulfinus to write, we now transfer from this day for possession to the same basilica of Saint Mary at Maricolas [Note: [Col. 0045D] Maroilles on the Helpe in Hainaut, in the diocese of Cambrai.].
>
> “All the things named above we have assigned to that monastery, so that the monks themselves or our successors may from this day receive them for possession as their own right and dominion, both the lands and houses, buildings, dependents, vineyards, woods, meadows, pastures, waters, and the courses of waters, without the intervention of any judge [Note: [Col. 0045] The Maricolan manuscript adds: “advocacy and harassment”]. Let them have the power in their own hands to retain, give, sell, exchange, or do whatever they wish with these things.
>
> “Therefore in this letter we determine that no further claim may afterward arise for any other reason between the servants of God and our heirs [Note: [Col. 0045] Omitted in the Maricolan manuscript].
>
> “If, however, after us—which we do not believe will happen—anyone from among our heirs or any opposing person should wish to come against or violate this gift which we have ordered to be made, let him first incur the anger of the threefold Majesty, be anathema, and let his name be erased from the heavenly book of the living [Col. 0045D] and not be written with the righteous. Let him instead be the companion of Judas Iscariot, who betrayed the Lord [Note: [Col. 0045] The Maricolan manuscript omits the words beginning “but let him be” through “who betrayed the Lord”]. And if he refuses to make amends, may God change his mind, and in that judgment let him receive what Ananias and Sapphira received in this life. Moreover, let him be compelled by the fiscal authority to pay ten pounds of gold and ten pounds of silver [Note: [Col. 0045] The Maricolan manuscript omits the entire clause beginning “Moreover” and ending “silver”].
>
> “Nor, if he makes any claim, shall he be able to vindicate anything [Note: [Col. 0045] Omitted in the Maricolan manuscript], and may our reward thereafter advance toward salvation.
>
> “If any documents, whether earlier or later, should ever be produced by any trick or device in our name among our relatives or among outsiders, or should appear at any time, let them be recognized as forged and remain void. But [Note: [Col. 0045] The Maricolan manuscript has *et*, “and”] let this present gift made by me remain firm and inviolate for all time, supported by the stipulation of suitable witnesses—namely, the lord Vindicianus, bishop, and my brother Fulbertus, and others [Note: [Col. 0045] The Maricolan manuscript has “and others”].
>
> “Done at Maricolas. I myself, Chonebertus [Note: [Col. 0045] The Maricolan manuscript has *Humbertus*], although a sinner and abbot, confirm this with my own hand.”

### 28. He was buried on the Mount of Saint Eligius

Concerning the life of this most blessed bishop and most glorious confessor of Christ, we have related a little—either because we think that, owing to the rarity and negligence of writers, it was neglected, or because we believe that the writings perished amid the stormy seditions through which, as we said above, the holy churches had continually suffered shipwreck (chapter 5). This certainly should not be doubted. For it may have happened that, when churches were overthrown by such great upheavals, the books in which the course of this holy man’s life and miracles was contained also perished, given over to laughing winds [Note: [Col. 0046D] That is, given over to the winds and made the plaything of breezes; compare II, 4, where they rejoice that the envious breezes carried off most of these things.].

Since, however, for the reasons mentioned above, it is also uncertain how long he governed the church of Cambrai, and which persons attended his funeral [Note: [Col. 0046D] That is, his burial], it is better to remain silent about these matters than to compose something legendary.

Let it suffice to know with certainty that, as a reward for his labor, he departed to Christ on the day of his death, the fifth day before the Ides of March [Note: [Col. 0046D] In the year 713, according to the Vedastine Annals], and was buried in the basilica, at the place called the Mount of Saint Eligius. When he had once fallen ill at Brosella [Note: [Col. 0046D] Apparently Brussels. L.], a territory of his diocese, he himself had ordered that he be transferred there because the blessed Eligius had made his dwelling a place of lodging there, and the blessed Vindicianus had clung to him with the familiar practice of affection.

### 29. A certain cleric, unknowingly insulting the tomb of the holy man, is deprived of sight and then illuminated again

After a long time, when the Lord had already determined to glorify his saint, an event occurred that would make the merits of the one lying there evident through clearer signs.

At Arras there were sons of noblemen who were being instructed in the literary disciplines under a teacher. The time had come when these boys, at the request of the same teacher, were to make ink for the scribal art. The place where the man of God lay buried was already full of brambles and thorns, and no inhabitant lived there, because the place had long been deserted owing to the attacks of pagans.

Witnesses to the event I am relating survived down to our own times. For when the aforementioned clerics [Note: [Col. 0047D] That is, students, little clerics] were exploring the thorny growth of the surrounding woodland, they happened by chance to turn aside to the basilica. While those who had the more mature understanding prayed, the younger ones examined the interior layout of the church more curiously.

One of them, approaching the tomb of the man of God rather carelessly, saw that the earth had opened and made a fissure from top to bottom. Taking up a mattock, he began, as though insulting the saint, to probe the hollow by digging at it.

Immediately struck with blindness, he began groping for a guide and calling out for a guide. Those present were terrified by the sudden change in the event and each feared more for himself, lest he be punished by a similar sentence.

When they questioned the boy, who had been deprived of his sight, about the cause, he replied that this had happened to him because of the rash insult he had inflicted on the one buried there. After discovering a plan for a remedy that would bring salvation, they advised the boy to appease the anger aroused by so great a punishment by surrendering his head [Note: [Col. 0047D] That is, by promising that he would become a monk].

And so it was done. As soon as he had recovered his sight, the boy returned, having been chastised in no small degree.

### 30. How Bishop Fulbertus honorably transferred the holy body of the blessed Vindicianus

The fame of this miracle therefore resounded throughout the neighboring region and stirred people far and wide to venerate so great a man. Bishop Fulbertus, astonished by it, and the fifteenth bishop after him, decided to transfer the holy body. He found it honorably enclosed in a stone coffin (around the year 940). His archdeacon Honoratus, as they say, who lay beside him, he left undisturbed.

### 31. How a blind man is illuminated by the merits of Saint Vindicianus

Moreover, in the territory of Arras there was a woman who had an only son. Although his eyes were open, light itself had been denied him for a long time. His mother took him with her to the tomb of the blessed Vindicianus. When they arrived, she had him offer a wax candle upon the altar and then prostrated herself for a short prayer.

By the manifest power of God the boy recovered his sight. He began to return by the direct road, without hesitation and without requiring anyone to guide him.

### 32. Likewise, a certain blind woman recovered her sight

There was likewise a woman of no ignoble birth in the territory of Ponthieu, but she was weakened by the loss of her sight. Having prepared provisions for the journey, she intended to travel to Rome, to the thresholds of the apostles, in order to receive healing.

On the night before the morning on which she had prepared to set out, she was divinely warned to hurry to the tomb of the blessed Vindicianus with her offering; there, she was told, she would receive the exchange of her desired light.

At daybreak she was placed in a cart and fulfilled what she had been instructed to do. When she came to the tomb of the man of God, as soon as her eyes touched the earth, they were opened, and she returned home rejoicing.

### 33. Many were punished with various tortures because they violated his church

In the time of the former Emperor Henry, when disputes arose between Baldwin [Note: [Col. 0047D] The Fleming] and Count Arnulf [Note: [Col. 0047D] Of Valenciennes; compare chapter 115], Baldwin gathered a force and expelled Arnulf from Valenciennes, since Arnulf was inferior in numbers. That fortress had been subjected to the authority of Henry.

The emperor, angered by the insolence of the affair, himself also blockaded the fortress (in the year 1006). King Robert of the Franks came to him with an immense multitude in order to renew their friendship, and Richard, duke of the Normans, came as well.

That people, fierce and unquiet [Note: [Col. 0048D] That is, unquiet], and burning with zeal for avarice, had not left even the churches of God free from their raids. As they traversed the province of Arras, they afflicted the country with miserable slaughter.

Some of them came to the Mount of Saint Eligius, which we discussed above (chapter 28), and heard that the monastery was filled with much money and accumulated wealth. They formed a band and attempted to break into the church.

When the clerics resisted, one man, inflamed with barbarian fury, brandished a weapon and struck down one of the priests at the very entrance of the church. The others, burning with grief at the killing of their brother, resisted more stubbornly.

When this created a difficulty and the attackers could not break into the church, one of them, armed with a mad spirit, climbed up over the roof of the church, forced his way inside through the ceiling, and began unexpectedly striking the men from behind.

Those who were present were thrown into confusion when they saw the enemy among them. While defending their rear, they left the front open to attack. The invaders rushed in, killed many people, and, contaminating the holy things with bloody hands, carried away the church’s treasures and even the priestly vestments.

Yet they did not enjoy themselves for long. As soon as [Note: [Col. 0048D] That is, immediately after] they had divided the spoils among themselves, many of them were seized and tormented by a demon. Some had their tongues burned; others had their tongues cut off by their own bite; many were punished with the miserable torture of having their legs burned.

The report of this event struck terror into the others, lest the savage plague also consume them because they had touched the spoils taken from that church.

The count [Note: [Col. 0048D] Richard, duke of the Normans. Colvenerius], as soon as he had returned to his homeland, conducted an inquiry concerning the treasures mentioned and, under oath, had every item repaid down to the smallest quarter.

One of those who had taken part in violating the church kept a bell for himself. After concealing it for a long time, he was eventually compelled to confess what he had denied at the urging of greed, when one part of his body had already begun to die.

An embassy was therefore sent to the keepers of the matricula [Note: [Col. 0049D] That is, the custodians of the church, who kept the register of the baptized—*les marguilliers*]. He restored twice as much, and thus was returned to his former state of health.

34. Hildebert succeeded, then Hunold, and thereafter Hadulf. Hildebert [Note: Or Emebertus; concerning him see above, ch. 16.] succeeded blessed Vinditian in the episcopate (718). Hunold succeeded him. After Hunold’s death [Note: In the year 718, according to the Annals of Saint-Vaast. Others say that he died on 9 January 717.], Hadulf was elected to the episcopal throne. Some assert that he was the son of Saint Ragnulf the martyr; concerning him, those faithful persons who survived into our own times testified that they had witnessed many miracles at his tomb.

[Col. 0049B] 35. Bishop Engranus raised him, and at his elevation a woman was freed from a demon. Hadulf was buried in the church of the holy apostle Peter, which stands within the walls of the fortress of Arras beside the monastery of Saint Vedast [Note: He died in 728, according to the Annals of Saint-Vaast, the Petavian Annals, and the Annals of Lorsch.] (728). In the course of time his holiness was manifested by many extraordinary and wondrous signs. The sacristan of the monastery of Saint Vedast, the principal witness of these events, disclosed to Engranus, bishop of Cambrai, the visions that he had frequently seen. Engranus, therefore, recognizing him as a trustworthy witness, raised the saint’s body. During this elevation, to reveal the merits of the holy man, a certain woman was miraculously freed from an unclean spirit. Accordingly, the bishop, rejoicing, addressed the people and proclaimed the solemn commemoration of blessed Hadulf among the saints.

[Col. 0049C] 36. Concerning Bishop Trawardus. After Hadulf, Trawardus was appointed to the see (728).

37. (36.) Concerning Bishop Gonfridus. After him, Guntfridus, rector of the same monastery, became bishop [Note: He carried out the translation of Saint Landelinus on 15 June 770. It therefore appears that Albericus did not become bishop before the end of 770. He died on 7 January 790. At Cambrai, in the public library, there still exists manuscript no. 619, a book of Irish canons written at his command, as the subscription at the end, added in the scribe’s own hand, testifies: “Here ends the book of canons which Lord Albericus, bishop of the city of Cambrai and Arras, ordered to be made. Thanks be to God. Amen.” See our Annals, VIII, 432.].

38. (36.) Concerning Bishop Albricus. After his death, Albricus succeeded him (770).

39. (37.) Concerning Bishop Hildoardus. After Albricus, Hildowardus succeeded him (790), in the time of Charlemagne. In the twelfth year of his episcopate, as is clear from the same tablets, he ordered two beautifully carved ivory panels to be made. He survived until the time of Louis the Pious [Note: The author himself inserted *H. a. u. a. t. L. P. s.* (“He survived until the time of Louis the Pious”) between the lines.], and, taking care to equip the church with many benefits, obtained from the emperor himself the following privilege of immunity [Note: I have seen the original charter of this privilege, still preserved in the archive of Cambrai, signed by the emperor’s hand and secured with his seal; I append its various readings.]:

[Col. 0049D] “In the name of the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ. Louis, by the providence of God’s ordering, august emperor. When, for love of divine worship, we favor the just and reasonable petitions of God’s servants, we do not doubt that we are fortified by heavenly grace. Therefore let the diligence and sagacity of all our faithful, present and future [Note: The charter reads “and future.”], know that the venerable man Hildoardus, bishop of the city of Cambrai, brought before our sight the privileges of immunity of our grandfather [Note: The charter reads *auu* (“grandfather”).], namely King Pippin [Note: The charter reads “of King Pippin.”], and of our father, the most excellent Emperor Charles of blessed memory. In these it was inserted how that same father of ours and the preceding kings had held the aforesaid see—which is in honor [Note: The charter reads “which is in honor.”] of holy Mary, Mother of God [Note: The charter’s form is *genetrix*; the customary form is *genitrix*.] and ever-virgin—for the love of God and the tranquility of the brothers dwelling there [Note: The charter reads, “the tranquility of the brothers there, always under ...”], under complete protection and defense of immunity [Note: The charter reads “defense.”].

“Nevertheless, for the security [Note: The charter reads *firmitatem*, “security,” in the accusative.] of the matter, the aforesaid bishop requested of us [Note: The charter omits “of.”] that we confirm by our authority the authority of those kings [Note: The charter reads “authorities of those kings”], in the love of God and in reverence [Note: The charter reads *reverentiam*, “reverence,” in the accusative.] for holy Mary, Mother of God. We willingly assented to his petition, and thus granted everything and confirmed it by this document of our authority.

“Therefore we command and order that no public judge, nor anyone whatsoever exercising judicial power [Note: The charter reads *quislibet*, “anyone whatsoever.”], dare enter, in our time or in that of our successors, the churches [Note: The charter reads “or” instead of “and.”], places, lands, or remaining possessions of the aforesaid church, which in the present time the said church justly and lawfully holds or possesses in any counties or territories under the authority of our empire [Note: The charter reads “within our empire”], or those possessions [Note: The charter reads *eas*, “those,” rather than *ea*, “those things.”] which thereafter shall have been bestowed upon the same church by Catholic men [Note: The charter reads, “bestowed upon the same church by Catholic men.”], in order to hear cases, exact fines, provide lodgings or provisions, take sureties, or distrain [Note: The charter reads *distringendos*, “to distrain”] the men of that church, both free and enslaved, who dwell upon its land [Note: The charter reads “who dwell there”]; nor may anyone presume to enter to demand any payments [Note: The transmitted text has *redditiones*; the charter reads *redibit.*, an uncertain variant], or seek unlawful pretexts, or to exact anything mentioned above [Note: The charter adds “entirely.”].

“But let the aforesaid bishop and his successors be permitted to possess in peaceful order, under the protection of our immunity [Note: The charter reads, “with the things and persons subject to it under the protection of immunity.”], the said church together with its cells, possessions, and persons lawfully subject to it; and let them faithfully obey our imperial authority, and, for the stability of ourselves and of the whole empire granted to us and preserved by God [Note: The charter reads “granted”], together with the clergy and people subject to them, freely implore God’s mercy.

“Whatever our treasury could have exacted from these matters, we have perpetually granted for the maintenance of the lamps of that church. It was also contained in the same privilege of our lord and father that, if any duke, count, vicar, or anyone exercising judicial power should presume to violate the authority of our lord and father [Note: The charter reads “of our lord and father.”] or of the preceding kings [Note: The charter reads, “to violate the authority conferred upon and confirmed for the aforesaid church by our lord and father or by the preceding kings.”], he should be judged liable to six hundred solidi: two parts, namely, should be assigned to the archive of that church, and the royal treasury should receive the third, so that no one might dare to commit such an act [Note: The charter reads “might dare.”].

“We likewise confirm this by our present authority, so that, just as it was conferred and confirmed by our lord and father or [Note: The charter reads, “or by the preceding kings, conferred upon the aforesaid church.”] by the preceding kings, so henceforth it may be preserved inviolate [Note: The charter reads, “so also henceforth.”].

[Col. 0051B] “Indeed, so that this authority may be believed more securely [Note: The charter reads “more certainly”] by the faithful of holy God’s church and by our own faithful, we have confirmed it below with our own hand and ordered it to be marked with the impression of our ring.

“Sign of Louis, most serene emperor.

“I, Durandus the deacon, have reviewed it in place of Helisachar.

“Amen.

“Given on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of May, in the third year, with Christ’s favor, of our lord Louis the most pious Augustus, in the ninth indiction [Note: The charter reads: “Helisachar reviewed it. Given on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of May, in the third year of the reign of our lord Louis, with Christ’s favor.”] (816). Done at Aachen, in the royal palace [Note: The charter reads “in the royal palace”], in God’s name. Amen [Note: The charter reads “done happily in God’s name.”]”

It is also found that he took part in the synod [(Flodoard, II, 18)] which Archbishop Wulfarius of Reims held in the church of Noyon with other fellow bishops in the year 814 from the incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ. There a dispute was examined between Wendilmarus [Note: Of Noyon.] and Rothardus [Note: Of Soissons.] concerning the boundaries of their parishes.

40. (38.) Concerning Halitcharius, to whom Archbishop Ebo addresses the following letter with humility (ibid., 19). Halitcharius succeeded Hildowardus [Note: He is thought to have died on 4 July 816. Certainly he still received a diploma from Emperor Louis on 14 April 816; see Miraeus II, 930.], a man apostolic in learning and catholic in faith. At the request of Ebo, archbishop of Reims, he composed six books on remedies for sins and on the order and judgments of penance [Note: Published by Canisius in *Antiquae Lectiones*; see Fabricius, s.v.]. Ebo’s letter to him is preserved as follows:

“To the most reverend brother and son in Christ, Halitcharius the bishop, Ebo, an unworthy bishop, sends greetings. I do not doubt that your charity knows how great a concern weighs upon us because of ecclesiastical discipline, because of the many necessities of our subject people, and, in addition, because of the worldly oppressions by which we are daily harassed. Therefore, as I told you, I have been quite unable to extract from the sayings of the Fathers and also from the judgments of the canons a penitential work for the use of our fellow priests, because when the mind is divided among many things, [Col. 0052A] it becomes less capable of each individual task.

“This is what greatly troubles me in this matter: the judgments concerning penitents in the little works of our priests are so confused, so diverse and mutually contradictory, and supported by the authority of no one, that they can scarcely be distinguished because of their disagreement. Consequently, when people come seeking the remedy of penance, they are utterly unable to assist them, both because of the confusion of the books and because of the slowness of their understanding.

“Therefore, dearest brother, do not refuse us yourself—you who have always flourished with a burning spirit in divine disciplines and with diligent care in meditation upon the Scriptures, in the fullest leisure. I beg you, take up without a word of excuse the weight of this burden, imposed upon you by me indeed, but to be lightened by the Lord, whose burden is light. Do not fear or dread [Col. 0052B] the magnitude of this work, but approach it manfully [Note: One manuscript reads *uidenter*; the author himself wrote *uiriliter* above it. Manuscript 2 has *uiriliter*, with *uidenter* written above; manuscript 3 has *uiriliter* in the text and *fidenter* above it; manuscript 5 and Flodoard have *fidenter*.], because he will be with you who said: ‘Open your mouth, and I will fill it.’

“For you know well that small things suffice for the small, and that a poor crowd cannot approach the table of the great. Do not deprive us of the knowledge of your devotion; do not put the lamp lit within you under a bushel, but set it upon a lofty lampstand, so that it may shine for all your brothers who are in the house of God. As a learned scribe, bring forth for us what you have received from the Lord.

“His grace will accompany you along the path of this labor—he who, when two disciples were traveling, added himself as a third companion on the road and opened their understanding so that they might understand the holy Scriptures. May the Paraclete Spirit, with every teaching of truth and perfect knowledge of charity, illumine [Note: “Or irradiate” was written above the line in manuscripts 1 and 3; manuscript 2 has *unde*; manuscript 2* has *resplendeat vel irradiet* in the text. Flodoard, according to Colvenerius, wrote *resplendeat* (“may illumine”), which a later writer changed to *repleat* (“may fill”).] your heart, dearest [Col. 0052C] brother. Farewell.”

41. (39.) Halitcharius replies by letter to Ebo (ibid.). To this the same Halitcharius replied as follows [Note: Manuscript 1 reads *atque*]:

“To the lord and venerable Ebo, archbishop in Christ, Halitcharius, the least servant of Christ, sends greetings. After I received, venerable father, the letters of your blessedness, in which you graciously urged me not to allow the sharpness of my mind to sink into idle and sluggish leisure, but to devote myself vigilantly each day to the knowledge and meditation of sacred Scripture, and, in addition, to gather into a single volume a penitential work from the judgments of the holy Fathers and the canons, this command seemed to me hard, very difficult, and terrifying: that I should undertake this burden, which I know prudent men had left unfinished.

“I resisted your will at great length—not rebelliously and stubbornly, but warned by the slowness arising from my own weakness. For, troubled by this concern, I judged it necessary to suspend myself for a time from the presumption of writing. Yet, just as I understood the difficulty of the work imposed upon me, so I neither wished nor ought entirely to resist the authority of the one imposing it. I was certain that the dignity of your command would assist my weakness far more than the difficulty of my ignorance would burden me. Farewell.”

42. (40.) He brought many precious relics of the saints from Constantinople (A. Einhard, year 828). He was sent to Constantinople by Emperor Charles [Note: Rather, by Louis.], and, as he himself reported upon his return, was honorably received by Emperor Michael. From there he carried away many precious relics of the saints—namely, of Saint Stephen the protomartyr, Cosmas, Antimus, bishop of Nicomedia, and Theodore the martyr—which are still preserved in the church of blessed [Col. 0053B] Mary. He also brought ivory panels, with which books are seen to have been covered there.

In his time (A. Einhard, year 818), King Louis the Pious, passing through Cambrai, returned to Aachen to spend the winter. The blessed bishop, receiving in peace the sleep of death with his fathers, was buried on Mount Saint Eligius (830)].

43. (41.) Blessed Theodericus succeeded him; Archbishop Ebo chose him as his judge in a synod. After him, Theodericus received the office of high priest from Louis [Note: After Halitcharius, bishop of Cambrai, had died, Theodericus was ordained by order of the lord emperor. Annals of Saint-Vaast, year 830. But the authors of *Gallia Christiana* assign Halitcharius’s death to 25 June 831; see Mabillon, *Annales*, year 650.], a man of proven holiness and divinely illuminated by the spirit of prophecy.

In his time, Lothair had deprived his father, King Louis, of imperial power, with the consent of false bishops, especially Ebo, archbishop of Reims. When the princes recognized that Louis had been unjustly deposed, and the same bishops who had previously consented began to cry out in his favor, he was restored to his former honor. [(Flodoard, II, 20.) After this, a synod was convened in the church of Saint Stephen at Metz. The emperor accused Ebo before all others of having falsely charged him and, on the basis of those same false accusations, having driven him from the kingdom, stripped of his arms, and, without confession or conviction, expelled him from the church’s communion contrary to ecclesiastical regulations. Ashamed of the charges brought against him and acknowledging that he had acted wrongly, Ebo, so that everything might be completed legally in the synod, chose bishops as his judges according to the African canons. Among them he also summoned Bishop Theodericus.] [Col. 0053D]

In the year of our Lord 832, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of December, he ordained clergy in the monastery of Lobbes [Note: See Folcuin, *Gesta of the Abbots of Lobbes*, 11.]. In the year 844, at the request of Abbot Haribertus, he also dedicated a monastery at Vasler [Note: Walers-en-Fagne, on the borders of Hainaut and Picardy.].

44. (42.) He sought and found the holy body of blessed Vedast at the monks’ entreaty. At that time the Danes, ravaging wickedly throughout the vicinity of this diocese, were attacking the churches. Therefore the man of God Theodericus, moved by the pious warnings and entreaties of the monks [Col. 0054A]—since it was doubted and uncertain in what place they believed the most precious body of Saint Vedast had been laid—sought and found it in the year 852 from the Lord’s incarnation. Once it had been found, he made such preparations that, if fear of the Danes should force them to flee, they could carry it elsewhere.

[45. (43.) He produced a written account in the synod concerning Ebo’s deposition and Hincmar’s ordination (Flodoard, III, 11).] In the days of this man, the honorable Bishop Hincmarus, after Ebo had been deposed, while he was in the seventh year of his episcopate in the same church, held a provincial synod at the city of Soissons, in the monastery of Saint Medard, together with Venilo, archbishop of Sens; Amalricus, bishop of Tours; and this Theodericus, bishop of Cambrai; and many other bishops and abbots, with the glorious King Charles also seated in their midst (853). There they dealt with certain necessary matters concerning the church of God.

At this synod, certain canons and monks of the church of Reims came forward and cried out that they had been suspended by their archbishop from the administration of ecclesiastical orders, although they had previously been advanced by Ebo. Judges were therefore chosen from both parties—that is, from the archbishop’s side and from among the complainants—and, after hearing the cases on both sides, they judged that, if Archbishop Ebo had remained in his position and had canonically ordained these brothers, they ought to minister; but if he had been unjustly deposed and canonically restored, and had ordained them after his canonical restoration, then they likewise ought to minister without question.

The ordainers of Hincmar were then questioned about Ebo’s deposition and Hincmar’s ordination. Bishop Theodericus of Cambrai rose and presented before the prince and the synod a written account containing the order of Ebo’s deposition. The question was then examined how a bishop who had been deprived of office ought to be restored. Since Ebo had not been canonically restored and, moreover, had been condemned by the apostolic see when Pope Sergius confirmed his deposition, so that he was to remain only in lay communion, it was decreed that whatever Ebo had done in ecclesiastical ordinations after his deposition should, according to the tradition of the apostolic see, be considered invalid—except for holy baptism, which had been perfected in the name of the Holy Trinity—and that those ordained by him should be deprived of their ecclesiastical ranks.

Then one of the deposed brothers brought forward a written complaint, in which it was stated that they had allowed themselves to be ordained by Ebo because they had seen the suffragan bishops of the church of Reims assemble together with letters from Emperor Lothair and restore Ebo. They also produced letters supposedly confirmed by the hands of Bishop Theodericus and the other bishops of the same diocese. When these letters had been read and proved false [Col. 0055A], the men were ordered to be deprived of communion, because they had presumed to make such accusations against bishops.

When these matters had been settled, Archbishop Hincmar recovered his place as primate. Many of his writings survive, which he composed concerning the catholic faith and the preservation of catholic law.

46. (44.) Hincmar’s writings to Theodericus and to certain others (ibid., chapter 21). Among them is a letter to Immo, bishop of Noyon, asking him to give counsel and assistance to Theodericus, bishop of Cambrai, concerning a certain disobedient man who did not fear God and did not respect ecclesiastical ministry.

He also wrote to Theodericus himself concerning a certain Hetto, a vassal of King Lothair, upon whom Theodericus had imposed penance by common consent, although Hetto claimed that he had been absolved by the aforesaid Theodericus. He wrote also concerning a certain priest whom Theodericus had excommunicated and on whose behalf the Roman pope had sent Hincmar a letter, which Hincmar forwarded to Theodericus.

Likewise, he wrote concerning the absolution of the aforesaid Hetto; concerning possessions of the church of Reims which Theodericus was asking to have assigned to him by lease; and to Maion, the illustrious count, expressing thanks for the kindness and care that he showed toward Lord Theodericus, bishop of Cambrai, a holy man, and toward his church.
