He also wrote to King Lothair [Note: Manuscript 1 reads “of the king.”], son of Emperor Lothair, asking that permission be granted for the election of a bishop for the church of Cambrai. He wrote also to Gontarius, bishop of Cologne, asking him to intercede with King Lothair and to work for the canonical election of a bishop of Cambrai after the death of the venerable bishop Theodericus [Col. 0055C]. For Theodericus had died. He wrote a second and a third time concerning the same matter, affirming that in his lifetime no bishop ought to be ordained there except according to the rule.

47. (45.) While Lord Theodericus was preaching, his thigh was broken. We learned the following account of this event from certain people who lived near his time. As he was proceeding to a certain place in his diocese to enforce ecclesiastical discipline, while he was still about three miles from the city, he perceived in spirit the danger of his impending fall and disclosed it to those accompanying him, saying:

“Know, brothers, that a dangerous fall is threatening us not far from here.”

When his companions advised him to avoid the place, he replied:

“By no means, my brothers, must we flee from God’s will. He strikes in order to heal; therefore he wounds in order to cure.”

He had not yet finished speaking when suddenly a certain beggar came to meet him. As the man bent forward to greet the bishop, the mule on which the bishop was riding was frightened by the movement of the man greeting him, suddenly leaped aside, and, striking the bishop’s leg as he fell, broke it; the animal then continued into the open field. The companions caught the falling bishop and carried him in their own arms back to the city.

48. (46.) An unheard-of miracle concerning a certain robber excommunicated by the holy bishop. Later, a certain man devoted to military affairs but intent upon the practice of plunder was accustomed, by frequent raids, to devastate the possessions of Saint Mary that lay in the territory of Arras. The bishop often summoned him on this account. When he refused to put an end to his wrongdoing, the bishop judged that his fury should be struck by the rod of apostolic authority.

He summoned him once, twice, and a third time; but when the man resisted, he excommunicated him. To increase the guilt of his condemnation, the man not only refused to acknowledge his guilt, but began to despise the bishop’s excommunication even more violently, rejecting it with swelling words and threatening still greater violence from his tyranny. Suddenly, amid the blasphemy of the raging man, the wretched one was struck by God’s judgment and died, his entrails poured out through the secret passage of nature. He was buried far from the city beside the public road, where, even in death, he was not deemed worthy to have a portion with the faithful.

As a manifest judgment of divine punishment, the earth surrounding the place of burial burned for three cubits around from the bottom upward, so that, as fire issued from hidden channels, it split open. While this was strange and terrifying to those who saw it, they were even more astonished that for three years neither dew nor rain fell upon that field, nor did any grass appear.

When the three years had been completed, the man of God was one night carried upward in ecstasy and saw the wretched man being tormented by an extraordinary and terrifying punishment. Moved by his most miserable fate, as soon as he returned to himself, the bishop took with him those whom he wished and went as far as the burial place. After explaining his plan, although he had no authority to do so, he ordered one servant who had remained attached to him for his necessary services to undertake the dead man’s cause and, granting that servant the option of freedom as the reward for carrying it out, ordered him himself to complete on the dead man’s behalf the prescribed measure of penance [Note: That is, “so that he might fulfill this.”]. Afterwards, the earth was seen to grow green again [Note: The author wrote this phrase on an erasure extending over two and a half lines.].

49. (47.) During his time the temple of Saint Gaugericus was begun, and he died in that same year. In the days of this blessed bishop, namely in the year 863 from the incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of July, construction was begun on the church of Saint Gaugericus. It was later completed honorably, but in the time of Rotradus, the third bishop of that see after Theodericus himself, it was burned by the Normans together with the city, as is related below (chapter 61) [Col. 0056D].

In the same year, on the Nones of August, Bishop Theodericus, summoned to receive the reward for his labors, ended his days and was buried in the monastery of Saint Autbertus. But in the time of the third Emperor Otto [Note: This is false: he was the first; see chapter 79.], under Fulbertus, bishop of the same see, he was translated to Germany, as will be related below.

50. (48.) After him the church was without a shepherd for three years, while Hilduinus was installed contrary to the canons. After his death (863), the church of Cambrai was without pastoral governance for approximately three years. The dispute arose between Hincmar, archbishop of Reims, and the emperor Lothair [Note: Our author is mistaken in attributing to Emperor Lothair what was done by his son, the younger King Lothair. The emperor had already died in 855 and therefore could not have appointed Theodericus’s successor, since Theodericus is known to have died only in 863. Nor could Nicholas have addressed letters to that emperor, since Nicholas was not made pope until 858. Colvenerius has already noted the error.].

The emperor had indeed bestowed the dignity of the episcopate upon a certain cleric, Guntbertus. But the archbishop, recognizing that this was contrary to the sacred canons, resisted with all authority, together with his fellow bishops. He placed all the clergy and soldiers of that church under an anathema and forbade them to presume to maintain any agreement or association with the adulterous shepherd; they were merely to lend him the usufruct of the land that belonged to the emperor.

Therefore, after remaining only a short time, Guntbertus departed unwillingly. Thereafter the emperor introduced a certain cleric named Tetboldus; but, frustrated by the same opposition, he withdrew. Finally, he decided to place Hilduinus, his kinsman and also his chaplain, over that church. But because this was contrary to canonical law, Hincmar likewise refused him his blessing with all his might.

While they continued in this dispute, the church, deprived of pastoral governance, was falling into ruin. Consequently Pope Nicholas, deeply angered, repeatedly expressed his displeasure in letters to Lothair—and even to Hincmar, as though he were negligent and careless in this matter.

We find that Hincmar sent the following letter to Pope Nicholas [(Flodoard, III, 12)]:

“To the uniquely and singularly revered lord, father of fathers, honored with supreme veneration, the most reverend Pope Nicholas: Hincmar in name, though not in merit, bishop of Reims and servant of the people of God.

“In the letter of your holiness, sent through Bishop Odo to the bishops in the kingdom of Lothair concerning the injury done to the church of Cambrai, I have reread your authoritative inquiry asking through whose neglect that church had remained without a shepherd for more than ten months. Therefore, lest I be judged negligent and incur the anger of your apostolate, I submit to your authority that, after letters had been sent to Lothair, to the bishops of his kingdom, and to Hilduinus, who had irregularly occupied that church, the injury continued up to the present, even before you sent those letters.

“I had repeatedly and as far as I could admonished King Lothair, both through envoys and by letters, until he replied to me in a royal letter that Hilduinus had sent his own envoy to your authority and that he ought to make no other arrangements concerning the aforesaid church than those he had already made, until he received a reply from you.”

51. (49.) Hilduinus is expelled, and Saint John is substituted. Thus the aforesaid dispute between the emperor and the archbishop continued until Emperor Lothair died and Hilduinus was expelled. In the year 866 from the Lord’s incarnation, John, a bishop of holy memory, was appointed in his place by the younger Lothair, son of Emperor Lothair, through the ordering of divine grace.

He had been brought up at the royal court and served in the office of cantor. On the surface of his tomb there is said to have been carved in marble the following inscription [Note: That is, “inscribed”]:

> I had been brought up in the magnificent court of kings,  
> In which I served under the name and office of cantor.  
> Not by my own merits, but solely by the mercy of the Thunderer,  
> I was made bishop in this city;  
> By God’s favor I taught it always to despise  
> The allurements of the world and to pursue true joys.  
> Now, after the separation of flesh and soul has taken place,  
> I complete the seventh day after the sixth Sabbath [Note: That is, the seventh feria; see Du Cange.],  
> Until, at Christ’s coming, the spirit resumes its limbs,  
> On the eighth day, now shining forth.  
> You who read this inscription, brother, pause for a little,  
> And say that I may deserve eternal rest.

[52. (50.) (Flodoard, III, 21.) John took part in the ordination of Bishop Bertulfus. Hincmar, whom we mentioned shortly before, had sent him to the ordination of Bertulfus, archbishop of Trier, by order of King Charles, together with Hincmar, bishop of Laon, and Odo, bishop of Beauvais, at the request of Adventius, bishop of Metz [Note: The author himself wrote this above the line.], and Arnulfus, bishop of Toul, of the same diocese of Trier. He instructed them how the matter ought to be carried out properly according to canonical and apostolic authority, so that they might depart in no respect from the sacred rules through either negligence or presumption.

[Col. 0058C] 53. (51.) Many writings of Archbishop Hincmar to Lord John. To this man—that is, to Lord John, bishop of Cambrai—who had asked that letters of recommendation be given him for his journey to Rome, to be presented in the name of Lord Hincmar to Pope Adrian, Hincmar replied that, if John wished to go to Rome to render service to the emperor in such a way that this service would not be contrary to the service owed to God, he would gladly give him canonical letters; but if he intended to go on behalf of the case of King Lothair, which had long been disputed between Lothair and his wife, Hincmar could not give him letters of recommendation in that matter and dared not give letters that would be blameworthy, since he ought not do so. This was especially so because Lord Adrian had recently sent John letters bearing his authority through Actardus, bishop of Nantes, in which he had indicated that he was following the disputes which the apostolic see, through his predecessors Benedict and Nicholas, had pursued in this case. Hincmar warned John not to allow what had been done in this matter to be weakened in any way, and informed him how Waldrada had been excommunicated.

He added that he could not, without the counsel of his fellow bishops, give John letters of release, especially concerning an uncertain matter.

He also wrote concerning the death of Lothair, urging John to come to King Charles without delay.

He wrote concerning a certain priest of the diocese of Cambrai who had castrated himself. John, repeatedly urged during visitation to take action in the matter, did not know what the sacred canons decreed about it. Hincmar advised that counsel be sought and that careful investigation be made into the manner in which the act had been committed, and that meanwhile, by indulgence, the same priest should remain in his order until a provincial synod determined what ought to be observed, provided that the decision was found to be contrary neither to the Gospel precepts nor to the decrees of the saints.

He also expressed thanks for benefits often bestowed upon him by John and asked him to seek Augustine’s sermon on the fall of a monk and a widow, send it to him for copying, or have it copied and bring it to the next synod. He likewise asked that Bede’s exposition of the Proverbs of Solomon be brought to the same synod.

He informed him also that the Roman pope had sent certain instructions to King Charles and to the bishops of his kingdom, concerning which it was necessary to deliberate in synod. For this reason the king had sent letters to the metropolitans of his kingdom, commanding them to summon their fellow bishops to the same synod.

He wrote concerning a tenth part which John had reportedly taken from an ancient royal chapel and added to another chapel that he had recently consecrated. Since this was contrary to the rules, Hincmar advised him to correct it if it had indeed been done.

He wrote concerning a certain priest who had appealed to the see of Reims, complaining that he had suffered injury at the hands of his own bishop: his priestly office, together with his possessions, had been placed under interdict, although he had neither confessed voluntarily nor been canonically convicted of the tumult and homicide that had been committed. He had been present at the event and, while unwillingly defending himself, had taken up arms and wounded a man, though not the man who had been killed [Note: Flodoard reads *eum qui* (“the man whom”).].

In these letters Hincmar showed from sacred authority what discretion ought to be observed in such a case and what chapters of the sacred canons ought to be applied. He wrote other matters also to the same man.]

### 54. (52.) Charter concerning the possessions that he acquired in the Condroz district for Saint Mary

This John acquired from a certain Macharius possessions in the Condroz district [Note: [Col. 0059D] Le Condroz, between Dinant and Liège.] belonging to the church of holy Mary, Mother of God, by an agreement made between them and set down in a charter as follows:

> “He possesses his worldly goods well who purchases everlasting rewards with earthly and perishable things. Therefore, in the name of God, I, Macharius, and my wife Gondrada, reflecting upon the love of God and the eternal reward of good things, for the remedy of our souls and for the soul of our lord and master John, bishop of Cambrai, donate and transfer to the church of holy Mary, Mother of God, certain of our possessions—which he himself graciously gave us for this purpose and which the lord emperor Lothar, through his mercy and by his charter, granted him as his own property—situated in the Condroz district, where the aforesaid venerable bishop, lord John, appears to preside.
>
> “These are: in the village of Huy [Note: [Col. 0059D] Huy, where the Hoioul flows into the Meuse.], on the river of that same name, Hoi, a church in honor of holy Mary, Mother of God; a demesne estate with buildings [Note: [Col. 0059D] Structures.] belonging to it, with four bonniers of arable land [Note: [Col. 0059] *Bonnier* is consistently written *bunu* here, except that twice *br* is written, namely of forest, *br. CC.*, and later of arable land, *br. XXXIII.*] [Note: [Col. 0059D] A *bonnier*, a measure of land, not everywhere of the same size, but generally equal to one and a half hectares. [Col. 0060D] It is still in use in Belgium.], and two hundred bonniers of woodland. There are two mills there.
>
> “In another place, in the village of Haidis, a demesne estate with buildings and an orchard on the river Sclēvus, belonging to it are thirty-three bonniers of arable land, nine bonniers of meadow, one hundred bonniers of woodland, and six servile holdings; there is one brewery [Note: [Col. 0060D] Brewery.].
>
> “In another place, in the village of Bacilla, a demesne estate with buildings on the Gorbia, belonging to it are forty-seven bonniers of arable land, three bonniers of meadow, fifty bonniers of woodland, and four servile holdings; there is one brewery.
>
> “In another place, in the village of Halogis, on the river Pauleia, three holdings, containing thirty-five bonniers of arable land.
>
> “In another place called Falmana, in the village of Grandchamp, a demesne estate with buildings, belonging to it are thirty bonniers of arable land, two hundred bonniers of woodland, and eight holdings serving there. And in the place called Glevo there is one holding.
>
> “In another place, in the village of Harsanium, on the river Wenna, a demesne estate containing twelve bonniers of arable land, two bonniers of meadow, and fifty bonniers of woodland, situated in the place called Carcinio; four uncultivated servile holdings [Note: [Col. 0060D] Uncultivated.] serving there, one of which is situated in Carcinio, while another is in Wadingo on the aforesaid river.
>
> “These amount altogether to thirty-one holdings, and, between the arable land and meadows belonging to the demesne, one hundred and forty bonniers, and six hundred bonniers of woodland and more, apart from the commons located in the place called Carcinio, and everything pertaining to the aforesaid places, in its entirety: cultivated and uncultivated lands, roads, watercourses [Note: [Col. 0060D] A waterway, aqueduct.], meadows, pastures, woods, commons, waters and their courses, and male and female slaves, of whom there are one hundred and fifty.
>
> “For this reason we transfer all the things stated above to the possession of the aforesaid holy church of God at Cambrai, so that, as long as we live, we may be permitted to cultivate and possess them by usufruct; and that the child named Achildus, whom our wife Gondrada bore to another man, and the children who may be born to us from that same wife, if they survive us, may likewise have them during their lifetimes, by usufruct for cultivation and possession. Thus, after our departure and that of our children from this life, all these things, in their entirety and with all improvements, shall return to the aforesaid holy church of God at Cambrai.
>
> “Likewise, in compensation for this benefit, our same lord John, bishop, with the consent of the faithful clerics and laymen mentioned above of Cambrai, gave us from the possessions of the church of Saint Mary of Cambrai the estate called Villare, situated in the Hagnois district on the river Unctius, where it has a demesne estate, with one hundred and twelve bonniers of arable land belonging to it, four bonniers of meadow, approximately one hundred bonniers of woodland between Villare and the place called Harilegias, and one church.
>
> “In Gentlinio, with an ecclesiastical holding containing twelve bonniers of arable land, and two mills.
>
> “In Villare itself, two holdings and two breweries. The holdings serving the aforesaid demesne estate are twelve cultivated holdings [Note: [Col. 0061D] Cultivated.], and twelve others newly brought under cultivation, which still cannot pay the full rent, sixteen being uncultivated [Note: [Col. 0061D] The number is missing in manuscript 1; no space was left.]. There are nine farmsteads in Villare itself, which ought to pay six solidi; “8” is stated, and they are uncultivated [Note: [Col. 0061] The number is missing in manuscript 1, with no space left.].
>
> “In the place called Grandovillare, between a farmstead and arable land, three bonniers.
>
> “In another place called Munliacum, between a farmstead and arable land, three bonniers. These amount altogether to forty-four holdings; and the male and female slaves belonging to Villare, together with whatever pertains to the aforesaid place, with all its appurtenances and entirety—cultivated and uncultivated lands, roads, watercourses, meadows, pastures, woods, waters and their courses—are included.
>
> “Our lord John, bishop, granted all these things to us on the following condition: as we stated above, during our lifetimes we shall have authority over both what we gave and what we received; likewise, the aforesaid Achildus and our other children who may be born from my aforesaid wife, if they survive us [Note: [Col. 0061] Manuscript 1 reads *nobint*.], shall likewise, during their lifetimes, have authority to cultivate and possess them by usufruct. For this usufruct we have agreed to pay two solidi each year, which we shall arrange to pay during our lifetimes; likewise our children, during their lifetimes, shall arrange to pay them to the church of Cambrai on the feast of the Purification of holy Mary. If we appear late or negligent in paying this rent, we shall provide security for it and make compensation to the aforesaid holy church of God.
>
> “Nor shall we in any way have authority to give, exchange, or alienate these possessions or slaves, except for preserving and improving them during our lifetimes. After our departure and that of our children from this life, all the aforesaid things, in their entirety and with all improvements, shall return to the holy church of God at Cambrai.
>
> “If, however—as we do not believe will happen—anyone among our heirs or successors should attempt to oppose this donation or lease, or disturb it, may he incur the wrath of almighty God and of the holy Trinity and be excluded from the thresholds of the holy church of God. Moreover, let him be compelled to pay ten pounds of gold and thirty pounds of silver to the fisc. And let this donation, together with the lease, remain firm and stable, supported by formal stipulation.
>
> “Enacted in the city of Cambrai, before the altar of holy Mary, on the Ides of April, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 885 [Note: [Col. 0061D] There is an error in this number. The thirty-fifth year of Charles began on 20 June 874; in the succession of Lothar, the fifth year began on 9 September 873; the seventh indiction fell in the year 874. Therefore this charter can only have been written in 874 or 875.], in the seventh indiction and the thirty-fifth year of the reign of our lord Charles, king, and in the fifth year of the succession of King Lothar. I, John, bishop, have reread this donation and confirmed it with my own hand.
>
> “Sign of Macharius and his wife Gondrada, who requested that this donation, together with the lease, be made and confirmed. I, Ernaldus, unworthy priest and manual notary, wrote this donation at the command of lord John, bishop.”

[Col. 0062C] 55. (53.) He freed the church of Laubies from the disturbance caused by the men of Charles

At length, as the discord between the partisans of Charles and those of Lothar increased, the church of Lobbes was being seriously shaken—so much so that, after the place had been utterly destroyed, it was thought that those serving there would be driven out. The bishop, however, acting according to divine counsel, wrote a *polyptych* in the year 868 [Note: [Col. 0062D] This is explained in Folcuin, *Gesta abbatum Laubiensium* 13: “In the fourteenth year of his reign, therefore, Lothar ordered a record to be made of our estates, which they call a polyptych. This record was made by Bishop John.”], which is still preserved in that church. Having separated all the invaders of the church from the fellowship of Christians by apostolic authority and with the confirmation of the neighboring bishops, he thus left the church unharmed amid so great a shipwreck.

### 56. (54.) (FLOD. III, 22.) Hincmar, bishop of Laon, chose him as his judge at a synod

We find this in the writings of the bishops of Reims: Hincmar, bishop of Laon, was rigorously prosecuted by Archbishop Hincmar, his uncle, at a synodal assembly on account of many offenses and disgraceful conduct. He therefore, in accordance with the African Council, sought chosen judges; among them he also obtained lord John.

### 57. (55.) He was buried outside the monastery of Saint Mary, in the church of the Holy Cross; but Bishop Gerard transferred him to the monastery

After lord John himself fell asleep in Christ in the year 879, he was buried in the basilica built in honor of the Holy Cross beside the monastery of Saint Mary, on its southern side. There he rested until the time of Bishop Gerard, who succeeded him as the thirteenth bishop of the see.

The aforesaid basilica had by then partly collapsed; and although some of it still appeared to stand, its old age threatened ruin. When the bishop himself decided to enlarge the aforesaid monastery as far as the tomb of Bishop John, he raised the body from the grave with fitting reverence and buried it inside the monastery.

There, afterward, a number of miracles are attested to have occurred. People afflicted by chills and by various illnesses came there and were granted the recovery they desired.

### 58. (56.) A crippled man is granted healing at the tomb of Saint John

There is still living a man named Walterus [Note: [Col. 0063] The author himself wrote “W. n.” above the name.], whose illness, although his limbs were fully developed, had from childhood deprived him of the ability to walk and of the other functions of his body. For, as his nerves withered, his ankles had become fixed to his legs, so that they could not be separated by any effort.

His mother had him carried on a pallet to the tomb of the man of God, and there she remained for several days in prayer with her son. When the Nativity of holy Mary arrived, celebrated on 6 September, during the very offices of Matins, when he happened to fall asleep for a little while, he saw—as he still reports—that a certain old man stood beside him; at his touch his legs were strengthened.

He was thereafter supported for several years from the revenues of the church. [Note: [Col. 0063] The author himself added “He ... was supported.”]

### 59. (57.) Concerning a crippled boy restored to health through the merits of the blessed bishop

It seems that the following event, too, was bestowed by divine mercy through the merits of the holy man. We know that a certain boy named Heribertus, from the household of Saint Gaugericus, is still alive. Three years after his birth, such weakness overtook his little legs—perhaps because the tendons had contracted—that for nearly another three years he had no use of his feet. [Note: [Col. 0063D] That is, of his legs.]

His mother, therefore, grieving incessantly, carried her only child, placed in a vehicle, through many places sacred to the saints. But after obtaining no benefit from any medical treatment, she finally placed him before the tomb of this blessed bishop.

Not long afterward she brought him back walking, through the operation of divine mercy and because the merits of this holy bishop obtained healing for him. We therefore believe that this was reserved for the holy man by the providence of God, so that his great merit might be clearly revealed by the miracle itself, as the event confessed. Many others, finally, have been cured of various illnesses.

### 60. (58.) Concerning Bishop Rotradus

Rotradus succeeded Saint John in the episcopate. He lived in the time of the emperor Arnulfus [Note: [Col. 0063D] He is slightly mistaken about the chronology: Rotradus died at the beginning of 887, as appears from chapter 62, whereas Arnulf assumed the kingdom only toward the end of November.]. The southern Franks, seeing that the strength of the emperor Charles, son of Louis the German, was inadequate for governing, deposed him and raised Arnulfus to the imperial throne.

### 61. (59.) At this time the city of Cambrai, together with the church of Saint Gaugericus, was burned by the Normans

During his time as well, the storm of the Northmen roared miserably throughout this whole region. In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 881, on 28 December, they entered Cambrai and devastated the entire city with fires and killings. To crown their fury, they burned the holy and venerable church of Saint Gaugericus and returned to their camps with immeasurable booty.

Returning again around the feast of Saint Peter, they reached the city of Arras. After killing everyone whom they found there and ravaging the entire surrounding land with sword and fire, they returned to their own territory.

Amid the storms of this revolt, the bishop was summoned and ended his life in the year 887. He was buried in the church of Saint Aubert.

### 62. (60.) Bishop Dodilo succeeds him

After Rotradus, Dodilo assumed responsibility for governing the church. In the year of the Lord 887 [Note: [Col. 0064D] 888 according to the Annals of Saint Vaast.] and on 17 March, he was ordained bishop. [Note: [Col. 0064D] Annals of Saint Vaast.]

He assigned one estate belonging to his jurisdiction, named Buxerias [Note: [Col. 0064D] Boussy, between Cambrai and Bapaume. Colvenerius.], for the maintenance of the brothers who served in the church of blessed Mary.

### 63. (61.) Many letters that Archbishop Fulk sent to Bishop Dodilo and to certain others

We find in the *Gesta* of the bishops of Reims (FLOD. IV, 6) that Fulk, archbishop of that see, sent Dodilo letters concerning the hearings that Dodilo had appointed for him, to which he had paid no attention. He warned and requested him to make every effort to come to the next hearing, wherever King Odo should be with the bishops, when they were to settle the matter then under consideration concerning Hildegard and Irmengard.

He should also have the accusers of Irmengard, and those who had ordered that the priest be deprived of his sight and suspended, together with all who had obeyed that infamous order or had been the perpetrators of this crime, admonished [Note: [Col. 0063] “Let them admonish,” in manuscript 1.] and summoned canonically, so that they might take care to present themselves at the assembly.

In another letter, he gives thanks for the same matter, because Dodilo had received his admonition devoutly and had come fully prepared on the appointed day. Yet Fulk appears to be angry that, although an ecclesiastical matter was being dealt with, Dodilo had wanted to send word to him not through a cleric but through a man of lay status.

Lord Fulk himself, partly detained by the service of his lord and partly hindered by bodily infirmity, had been unable to come as agreed. He also reminds Dodilo that he ought to remember how he had once acted toward him: how, without the king and without anyone advising the king’s party, he had pressed by every means to have Dodilo attain the episcopal dignity, when he was not yet fully known; how he had acted on his behalf as though on behalf of a most dear brother, because he had believed—and still believed—that Dodilo possessed simple prudence, sincere faith, and firm and unchanging steadfastness.

He had also hoped that Dodilo would be his collaborator and helper in all things. Through that sincere affection which he believed Dodilo possessed, Fulk says that he was admonishing him, ordering him to put aside every delay and occupation and to take care to be present at the agreed gathering of the bishops, without exception of any cause except bodily illness.

He should also have the persons mentioned above, whom Fulk had identified in another letter, canonically admonished, so that, prepared for the solemn assembly of the bishops on the appointed day, they might take care to present themselves.

In another letter, written together with his fellow bishops Dido of Laon, Hetilo of Noyon, Riculfus of Soissons, and Herimandus of Thérouanne, he informs Bishop Dodilo that the aforesaid bishops had assembled in the city of Reims to deliberate concerning the seizure by Baldwin. Fulk had written to Dodilo about this, urging him to admonish Baldwin to come to his senses from the wicked arrogance of his rashness.

But since Dodilo had replied that he had been unable to come to the same bishops because the sword of the Northmen had cut off his journey, Fulk expresses his sympathy with him over the common disaster.

As for what Dodilo had requested concerning Baldwin, Fulk agrees that Dodilo should diligently correct him by admonishing, exhorting, and reproving him, so that he might reform his wickedness, setting before him the divine judgments of the holy Fathers. He also states that letters from the bishops themselves were being sent to Baldwin.

Fulk urges Dodilo that, if Baldwin is present, the letters should be read to him; if he is absent, Dodilo should send them to him through his archdeacon, who should also make Baldwin understand them. If the archdeacon too should be unable to approach him, Dodilo should have the letters read publicly in his presence, in the place where Baldwin had seized the religious foundation.

Thereafter, unless Baldwin repented, no monk, canon, or any properly Christian person should associate with him, if he did not wish to become entangled in the bond of anathema.

If Hetilo should also come to the city of Arras, Dodilo should meet him, so that they might carry out canonically whatever needed to be done concerning this matter, and he should report to Fulk by letter whatever they did there.

Fulk orders Bishop Hetilo by letter to set out with the king’s faithful men for Arras, doing as far as possible what he had found indicated in another letter that he was to do.

In another letter, concerning what he was suffering at the hands of Dodilo, bishop of Cambrai, Fulk asserts that, although he had done him good, Dodilo was repaying him with insults. He calls Hetilo as a witness to how he had advanced Dodilo to better things with fatherly and simple kindness.

He also explains how the devout man Rodulfus had assigned to the church of Reims an abbey situated in Hetilo’s parish, entrusting to it at the same time the body of the blessed Pope and martyr Calixtus, which he had obtained and brought from the city of Rome. [Note: [Col. 0065] Manuscript 1 reads “of the same.”]

Fulk states that he had courteously asked the aforesaid Dodilo to come to the fortress of Arras and from there honorably raise the relics of the aforesaid martyr and escort them as far as the monastery of Saint Quentin (FLOD. IV, 16).

He had also asked Hetilo to come to that monastery and accompany the sacred body until lord Fulk himself arrived and was able properly to receive it and escort it to the city of Reims, where it was to be kept until, peace having been restored, it could be returned to its proper place, situated in Hetilo’s parish. [Note: [Col. 0065] Missing, with space left, in manuscripts 1 and 3.]

But when Dodilo ought to have done what was requested, he instead, setting aside the respect due to their filial and fraternal relationship, met the procession midway and snatched the holy relic from the hands of those carrying it. He kept it with himself, saying that he would return it to no one unless it were deposited with Hetilo, in whose parish it was recognized to have been. He had done this as a new pretext for fraud, so that he might hand the sacred body over to a certain Count Hucboldus.

For this reason Fulk asked Hetilo to send his messenger to Dodilo, rebuke and correct him with fatherly and fraternal affection, and remind him how, solely out of regard for religion and for the faith that he believed to be in Dodilo, Fulk had installed him in the episcopal see without waiting for the king or any other prince.

Hetilo should warn Dodilo to withdraw from the rash course he had begun, lest he compel the archbishop to do something against him that Dodilo himself would not want. Fulk also earnestly begs Hetilo not to support Dodilo in such a matter, but to favor the just party in everything, and not only to consent to the treasure of heaven entrusted by the aforementioned man to the church of Reims being restored to its city and basilica, but also to assist in this with all his strength.

### 64. (62.) Charter that he obtained from King Arnulfus confirming the possessions of Saint Mary

Finally, governing the church with great effort, he worked to secure it with many advantages. At his request, King Arnulfus also confirmed by the following charter the immunity of the church of holy Mary, Mother of God:

> “In the name of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, Arnulfus, king by the grace of God. When, for the love of divine worship, we favor the just and reasonable petitions of God’s servants, we do not doubt that we are fortified by heavenly grace. Therefore let the diligence and prudence of all our faithful, present and future, know that the venerable man Dodilo, bishop of the city of Cambrai, presented before us the immunities of our predecessors of blessed memory, namely King Pippin and the emperors Charlemagne and Louis. In these it was inserted how those aforesaid predecessors of ours, for the love of God and the tranquillity of the brothers residing there, had always held the aforesaid see—which is in honor of holy Mary, Mother of God and ever-virgin—under the fullest protection and defense of immunity.
>
> “For the security of the matter, however, the aforesaid Bishop Dodilo asked us to confirm by our authority the charters of those kings, out of love for God and reverence for holy Mary, Mother of God. We willingly agreed to this through the intervention of our venerable bishop Salomon, and thus granted everything in full and confirmed it by this charter of our authority.
>
> “Therefore we decree and command that no public judge or anyone exercising judicial authority dare, in our time or that of our successors, enter the churches, places, lands, or other possessions of the aforesaid church—which the church is now known to hold or possess justly and legally in any districts or territories under our authority, or which Catholic men may hereafter grant to that church—in order to exact lawsuits, fines, lodgings, or provisions; to take sureties; to distrain any of the church’s people, whether free or enslaved, residing on its land; or to demand any payments or unlawful pretexts. Nor may anyone presume to exact any of the things mentioned above.
>
> “Rather, let the aforesaid bishop and his successors possess, in quiet order and under the protection of our immunity, the possessions of the aforesaid church, together with its cells and the possessions or people legally subject to it; let them faithfully obey our command, and, for the stability of ourselves and of the whole empire granted to us by God and to be preserved, freely implore the mercy of God together with the clergy and people subject to them.
>
> “Whatever our fisc might otherwise have been able to exact from these possessions, we have perpetually granted for the furnishing of the lamps of that church. [Note: [Col. 0067] The original charter seen by Colvenerius reads *ad habendum* rather than *adhibendum*.]
>
> “Furthermore, we establish that no duke, count, viscount, or anyone exercising judicial authority presume to violate our authority or that of our predecessor kings. [Note: [Col. 0067] The author himself added the word *auctoritatem*; according to Colvenerius, it was absent from the original charter.] If anyone does so, let him be liable to royal proceedings and, in addition, be judged liable for six hundred solidi: two parts to be assigned to the archive of that church, and the third to be received by our royal fisc, so that no one may thereafter presume to dare anything of this kind. [Note: [Col. 0067] Manuscript 1 reads *videre* rather than *audere*.]
>
> “We therefore confirm this by our authority, so that, just as the aforesaid church received and had confirmed these things from our predecessors of blessed memory, so they may henceforth remain inviolably preserved.
>
> “And so that this authority of ours may be believed by the faithful of the holy church of God and by our own people with greater truth and certainty, we have confirmed it below with our own hand and ordered it to be marked with our ring.
>
> “Sign of lord Arnulfus, most invincible king. Wichingus, chancellor, have recognized it in place of Theotmarus, archchaplain.
>
> “Given on 6 June, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 894, in the twelfth indiction, in the seventh year of lord Arnulfus, most pious king. Enacted at Worms, happily, in the name of God. Amen.”

[Note: [Col. 0067] After this word the author himself placed a sign, and on a separate slip, repeating the same sign, wrote: “Here, after the walls had been built ... was buried on the northern side.” But immediately afterward, correcting himself, he drew a line in the margin with the same ink from that sign to the word *confirming*, thereby indicating that this addition belonged not to chapter 64 but to chapter 65. Ignoring this line, manuscript 3 attached the addition to chapter 64; manuscript 2—or at least Colvenerius, who represents it—places it after chapter 65 but makes a new chapter of it, adding a title of his own, which manuscripts 1 and 3 do not have.]

### 65. (63.) He took part in the consecration of Heriveus, archbishop of Reims (FLOD. IV, 11)

He took part, together with the others, in the ordination of Archbishop Heriveus: namely, Riculfus, bishop of Soissons; Otgarius of Amiens; Mantius of Châlons; Rodulfus of Laon; Otfridus of Senlis; and the other diocesan bishops, who gave their consent and confirmed the decree of this ordination.

[(64.) After building the walls, he enlarged the city’s fortifications to such an extent that he enclosed within the circuit of the walls the monastery of Saint Aubert, which had stood outside. He also solemnly consecrated the monastery built for the Mother of God on the Kalends of August. He made a silver altar panel, which we saw in our own day, as well as a silver vessel that the subdeacons carry in their hands on feast days, and a chalice, together with other church ornaments.

He also consecrated the monastery of Lobbes, taking with him Stephen, bishop of Liège. [Note: [Col. 0067D] Compare Folcuin, *Gesta abbatum Laubiensium* 18. The consecration took place after 901, the year in which Stephen assumed the bishopric of Liège. Dodilo therefore died between 902 and 911.] Overtaken by death amid these works, he ended his life and was buried in the monastery of Saint Mary itself, on its northern side.]

### 66. (65.) Stephen succeeds him and makes peace with Count Isaac at a synod before the archbishop

Stephen succeeded Dodilo in the episcopal see. He was sufficiently instructed in both ecclesiastical and secular disciplines, enlarged the possessions of that church, and confirmed them by royal charters.

[(FLOD. IV, 19.) He took part in a synod held by Sculfus, archbishop of Reims and successor of Heriveus, at the village of Trosly in the year 924. Along with the bishops of the diocese of Reims, several counts also attended.

At this synod Count Isaac came to make satisfaction for the wicked acts he had committed against the church of Cambrai: he had deceitfully seized and burned a certain fortress belonging to Stephen, bishop of that city. For this crime, having been formally accused at the synod, he made peace with the aforesaid Bishop Stephen for one hundred pounds of silver, through the efforts of Heribertus and the other Frankish counts who were present.]

### 67. (66.) At his request King Charles restored this immunity concerning the prebends of the brothers of Saint Mary

At his request also, King Charles renewed the following charter concerning the prebends of the brothers of the church of holy Mary, Mother of God—a charter that had been lost when the city was burned:

> “In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, Charles, by the favor of divine clemency king of the Franks, illustrious man. Whenever we reasonably provide for the needs of churches and the welfare of those serving God, we confidently believe that this can contribute in every way both to the salvation of body and soul and to the stability of the entire kingdom granted to us by God and to be preserved.
>
> “We wish the diligence of all our faithful, both present and future, to know that the venerable man Stephen, bishop of the holy church of Cambrai, came to our majesty and informed us that the clerics of his aforesaid see had possessions assigned for their sustenance. They had also held a royal charter concerning them, formerly granted by King Zwentibald; but when that city was burned, the charter too was consumed by the voracious flames.
>
> “Therefore, concerning this matter, he humbly petitioned our piety to restore that loss through our munificence. Out of love for God and for the brothers serving God there, we willingly agreed to do so, and ordered this authority to be renewed for their protection concerning the possessions which they have hitherto held justly and legally in whatever manner.
>
> “Therefore we decree and proclaim that the clerics of the aforesaid church may freely grant among themselves, according to their wishes, their own houses, which they have in the city, to whomever they wish within the congregation of that place, solely by hereditary right, or through sale and purchase, or exchange, or plainly through conveyance.
>
> “Moreover, the territory of the monastery which was outside the city, and likewise the estates assigned for their use—namely, in the district of Cambrai, Carnières [Note: [Col. 0069D] Carnières.], Lis [Note: [Col. 0069D] Either Vieslis or Neuveslis, by the stream of the Selles, four leagues distant from Cambrai. Colvenerius.], Venzenzias [Note: [Col. 0069D] Venzenzias, or Venzelzeias, as the original charter still preserved at Cambrai has it. It was a place where Cateau-Cambrésis was later built. Perhaps, however, Vendegies-sur-Ecaillon is meant. Le Glay.], Muntiniacum [Note: [Col. 0070D] Montigny.], Gualtercurt [Note: [Col. 0070D] Later Wahiercourt, a ruined village formerly situated between Ribécourt and Marcoing, in the area which still retains the name Wiercourt. Le Glay.], Gundreceias [Note: [Col. 0070D] Honnechies, near Cateau-Cambrésis. Le Glay.]; in the county of Hainaut, Oninium [Note: [Col. 0069] The original charter has this reading; manuscript 1 has *omnium*.]; in the Vermandois district, Toriniacum; in the Soissons district, Carisiolum—together with male and female slaves, cultivated and uncultivated lands, meadows, waters and their courses, mills, breweries, woods, and everything belonging to the aforesaid possessions of the brothers, shall be held and possessed by the clerics of that place, present and future, in perpetuity, with the authority to do with them, solely by hereditary right, whatever they may justly decide by common decree and unanimous consent.
>
> “If anyone—which we do not at all suppose—should attempt to oppose this decree of ours or inflict any injury, let him be judged liable for six hundred solidi, so that two parts of this sum may go to the brothers of that place and the third be received by the royal fisc. Moreover, let him in no way be able to recover what he has unjustly attempted, so that no one may thereafter presume to usurp anything of this kind.
>
> “And so that the authority of this edict may possess irresistible force forever, we have strengthened it with our own hand and ordered it to be adorned with the honorable impression of our ring.
>
> “Sign of Charles, most glorious king. Hugo, notary of royal rank, subscribed in place of Heriveus, archbishop.
>
> “Given on 20 December, in the fourteenth indiction, in the nineteenth year of the reign of Charles, most glorious king, in the fourteenth year of his restoration, and in the first year since he obtained the greater inheritance (the year 911). Enacted at the estate of Cruztiacum, happily, in the name of God. Amen.”

68. (67.) The charter by which the king confirmed the abbeys that he had granted to this bishop. [Note: [Col. 0069] In 1 and 4, *commisit* (‘entrusted’) is a correction by a thirteenth-century hand.] King Charles likewise granted to this man the abbeys of Marellias [Note: Maroilles.] and Crispin [Note: Crepin, near Condé.], at the request of the counts whom we shall mention shortly afterward, and confirmed the charter concerning this matter in the following form [Note: The charter itself seems to have perished. I saw a copy from the thirteenth or fourteenth century in the Lille archives; Colvenerius could have had only two copies in the Cambrai archives.]:

> “In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, Charles, by the favor of divine clemency king of the Franks. The religious life of Christians appears to subsist under a twofold government, namely, the royal and the priestly. Therefore it is fitting that the priestly order be increased and exalted by the munificence of royal honors, so that royal dignity may long remain seated upon the throne of the kingdom under the rod of equity, in accordance with what God says of himself in Wisdom: ‘Through me kings reign, and judges discern the decrees of the laws.’
>
> “For this reason, let the devotion of all the faithful of God’s holy Church know that the venerable counts Hagano and Rodulf, approaching our serenity, humbly requested that we grant to holy Mary, Mother of God, under perpetual secular subjection, a small monastery called Marellias, in the county of Hainaut, upon the banks of the river Helpra, where Saint Hunbert lies bodily, in the church dedicated in honor of Saint Peter, for the holy church of Cambrai, over which Bishop Stephen presides, a man indeed vigorous throughout the whole kingdom [Col. 0070D]. [Note: [Col. 0069] *committeremus* (‘we should entrust’) in 1, corrected by the same thirteenth-century hand; also in 3.] [Note: All the manuscripts have *Marellias*, as does one of the two copies of the charter seen by Colvenerius. The Lille copy and Colvenerius’s other copy have *Maricolas*. After this word the same thirteenth-century hand adds *tuendam* (‘to be protected’); the same is found in 3. The same thirteenth-century hand has it also in 3 and 5.]
>
> “Therefore, recognizing that their request is appropriate, we devoutly assign this small monastery, with all its appurtenances, to the aforesaid see of holy Mary, to be held there perpetually.
>
> “Then the venerable Count Sechard himself requested that we grant to holy Mary, for the aforesaid see of Cambrai, another small monastery called Crispin, in the aforesaid county of Hainaut, on the river Hon, where Saint Landelin lies in the church dedicated in honor of Saint Peter. The aforesaid Sechard held this small monastery as a benefice. Let it be held there perpetually, with all its appurtenances [Note: *respiciendam* (‘to be regarded as belonging to it’) in 1, corrected.]
>
> “And so we have done. But at the request of the aforesaid counts, for the remedy of our soul, we permit the aforesaid Bishop Stephen, in the places granted to his church—that is, Marellias and Crispin—to establish a market and collect the toll from it. [Note: This is what 1 originally read. But the thirteenth-century hand erased the words *ob ... aecclesiae* and wrote in the erasure *ob remedium animae nostrae duabus prescriptis ecclesiis, hoc est M.* (‘for the remedy of our soul, to the two aforesaid churches, that is, M.’). 3 has the same reading.] Around these places, for the distance extending one league, neither a count nor any judicial authority shall have the power to exercise jurisdictional fines; nor shall anyone, present or succeeding, attempt to carry out against those aforesaid small monasteries of the church of holy Mary of Cambrai any withdrawal, seizure, division, opposition, disturbance, contradiction, prejudice, or violence.
>
> “Rather, together with their villages and their dependencies—namely, churches, buildings, woods, meadows, pastures, lands, waters and watercourses, mills, fisheries, roads, vineyards, and the dependents dwelling upon them—and whatever in all things is justly and legally attached to them, we hand them over to holy Mary for the aforesaid see, to be held and possessed [Note: After *habendum possidendum* had been erased, that hand wrote *conservandum, amplificandum* (‘to be preserved and increased’). The same appears in 3 and 5.]; and let the administrators of that church [Note: After *rectores ejus ecclesiae* had been erased, that hand wrote *fratres ipsarum ecclesiarum* (‘the brothers of those churches’). The same appears in 3 and 5.] henceforth do whatever their own and their people’s utility requires.
>
> “Therefore, with diligence, we have drawn up this charter of confirmation; we confirm it with our own hand for the service of holy Mary [Note: After *sanctae Mariae* had been erased, that hand wrote *fratrum* (‘of the brothers’). The same appears in 3 and 5.], and we have ordered it sealed with our ring.
>
> “The sign of the illustrious King Charles. Gauzelin the notary, in the place of Rotger, archbishop and chief chancellor, has recognized this.
>
> “Given on the sixth day before the Ides of September, in the eighth indiction, in the twenty-eighth year of the reign of the glorious King Charles, the twenty-third after the restoration of his reign, and the ninth after the acquisition of the greater inheritance (8 September 921). Enacted at the palace of Heristal, happily, in the name of God. Amen.”

[Col. 0072A] 69. (68.) Lord Stephen, having completed his course, departed from this world. This bishop, born in the county of Alsace, made the church of holy Mary, Mother of God, over which by God’s authority he presided, heir to the property belonging to him by private right. He obtained many things from the kings and transferred them to that church; he bestowed a large body of dependents; moreover, he worked to restore certain properties of the church that had been taken away from the bishopric. He was overtaken by death in the land of his birth, from which he had ordered that he be brought back to his own see, and ended his days in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 934, on the third day before the Ides of February. [Note: The Necrology of Saint Mary of Cambrai, from the beginning of the twelfth century, has the same day. But Flodoard, in his Annals, records the following under the year 933: “Archbishop Artold ordains Fulbert bishop of the city of Cambrai”; compare Flodoard, *History of Rheims* IV, 24. Flodoard, like our author, begins the year from the Nativity of Christ, not from Easter.]

70. (69.) Fulbert is introduced as bishop. Fulbert, succeeding Lord Stephen, obtained the prerogative of the episcopal see through the favor and support of Duke Gislebert. [Note: *Hinc* (‘thence’) in 1.] Born in the county of Brabant, specifically in the village of Wiluva [Note: Below, III, 49, it is called *Wileve*. Perhaps this is the parish of Woluwe, where the monastery of Rouge-Cloître is situated. Colvenerius: the stream near Vilvoorde is also called Woluwe.], he was a man well instructed in good morals and continually labored to strengthen the see of God’s holy Church with many benefits.

71. (70.) The dispute between Isaac the proud count and Bishop Fulbert; nevertheless, the count is expelled when the bishop prevails. At that time Count Isaac possessed the small monastery of blessed Hunbert, over which, as we said a little above (chapter 68), King Charles had placed Bishop Stephen. He held as a royal benefice, by royal right, the royal and wealthy abbey of the most holy Gaugeric with all its dependencies [Note: *Possidebat—tenebat* (‘possessed—held’) was written by the author himself in the erasure.], namely, half the fortress of the city of Cambrai, together with half of the public revenues and also one of the two mints.

Because the city was administered under a divided lordship, when it occasionally suffered shipwreck, the rulers themselves collided with one another in the disputes that arose between them. Among their officials there was always heard a harsh sedition over the collection of revenues; violent and serious disturbances continually grew on both sides. Gradually aroused by a more serious movement, these advanced so far that the parties often took up arms.

The magnanimous count received these and similar events impatiently; inflamed with rage by excessive indignation, he raised his neck in such swollen pride against the lord bishop that one day he ordered him, together with his people, to flee as quickly as possible, intending afterward, alone, to possess without distinction the affairs of the entire city.

The bishop, terrified, yet trusting in God’s mercy, promised that he would obey such a proud command. But, so that the shameful disgrace of his flight might remain hidden from the people, he requested a delay until evening. The count granted this without difficulty, being all the safer because he did not at all regard the bishop as someone who would dare evade his commands.

Having obtained this, the bishop’s mind was drawn in different directions. He considered what he could undertake first amid such great and sudden troubles. Without delay, following divine counsel, he quietly ordered all his friends and faithful supporters to be summoned with the utmost care during this brief interval, and sought their advice concerning his affairs.

That night provided him with such a force of men that, by God’s will, the decision was reversed: at dawn they drove the unsuspecting enemy outside the city, while he himself, composed in spirit, sat with his followers in his proper seat.

After several days had passed, the count returned with a strong force, recovered his strength, and attacked the city again. Inflicting many disturbances, he harassed the bishop for some time. Finally, through repeated clashes, a serious conflict between them grew.

72. (71.) When Emperor Otto, at the request of King Louis, had answered the king’s need against his enemies, he visited Fulbert at Cambrai. Meanwhile (938), the prince of the Gauls, namely Hugh who was called the Great, and William, the most ferocious duke of the men of Rouen, were attacking their king Louis with continual hostility and fighting one another on both sides for a long time without interruption.

Seeing that he could not overcome the savagery of his enemies without outside help, the king thought he should bind Emperor Otto to him as an ally. Otto was the son of King Henry, whose sister Gerberga he had married. He therefore sent envoys to invite him to this undertaking with entreaties.

Otto, immediately and familiarly girded by fraternal appeals, ordered his dukes and princes to prepare for war. Once provisions had been prepared, he moved his camp without delay in accordance with the request (946). Reaching Paris first and then Rouen, he devastated all the neighboring regions and there brought forth a sufficiently pitiable calamity.

After exhausting his enemies through retaliation, when he was preparing to return home, he decided on the very journey back to pitch camp at the city of Cambrai, intending to visit how Lord Fulbert the bishop was conducting himself in ecclesiastical affairs.

[Col. 0073D] 73. (72.) Emperor Otto grants the abbey of Saint Gaugeric to the bishop and confirms it with the following charter. When he arrived there, the lord bishop received him with great familiarity and served him with the utmost reverence through friendly attentions. He made a humble complaint about the assaults inflicted upon him by the aforementioned count.

After hearing the case, Otto, being compassionate, felt the bishop’s troubles just as the bishop himself did. Following the appropriate counsel of his men, and judging the private count according to the law of the realm, he transferred to God’s holy Church, for perpetual possession, the abbey of Saint Gaugeric together with all the properties mentioned above from which the dispute had begun, and also the other abbey that we mentioned above [Note: Maroilles, chapter 68], belonging to the holy Church of Mary, Mother of God.

He confirmed this grant in writing as follows:

> “In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, Otto, by the favor of divine clemency king. Let all our faithful, present and future [Note: Missing in 1.], know that, for the love of God and of the holy and ever-undefiled Virgin Mary, Mother of the same God and our Lord Jesus Christ, and for the salvation of our soul, and also at the intercession of our faithful—namely, Archbishop Frideric, our beloved brother Bruno, Duke Cuonrad, Duke Herimann, and our other faithful—we grant from this day and hour to holy Mary, for the see of the church of Cambrai, over which the venerable Bishop Fulbert, by God’s favor, appears to preside, the entire abbey of Saint Gaugeric, with all the things and possessions belonging to it at home and abroad, just as it has hitherto appeared to have been held justly and legally by our right.
>
> “We likewise grant every public service or exaction belonging to the aforesaid monastery. No count or any minister of the public authority shall have power there to hold a court, impose a ban, exact fines, or exercise any other jurisdiction. Rather, everything shall remain under the authority of the bishop who, by God’s assistance, shall preside over that church by succession, henceforth and forever, just as until now they belonged to the right and authority of our power.
>
> “And so that the authority of this grant may, throughout the succession of ages, possess an unshakably firm force in God’s name, we have confirmed it below with our own hand and ordered it strengthened by the impression of our ring.
>
> “The sign of Lord Otto, the unconquered king. I, Bruno the chancellor, have recognized this in the place of Rotbert, archchaplain.
>
> “Given on the second day before the Kalends of May, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 947, in the sixth indiction, in the thirteenth year of the reign of the pious King Otto. Enacted happily at the palace of Aachen, in the Lord. Amen.”

74. (73.) The bishop separated Count Amulric and Isaac’s daughter, whom he had married, because of their consanguinity. Another count from the county of Hainaut, Amulric by name, a man most noble by birth and most fortunate according to the splendor of worldly glory, took as his wife the daughter of the aforementioned Count Isaac.

When Bishop Fulbert learned this through the reports and disclosures of many people, he discovered that the bridegroom and bride were related by close kinship and had therefore been joined contrary to law. After consultation, he canonically separated them from one another and prescribed a measure of penance by which this great crime was to be expiated.

Their parents and friends bore this painfully and sorrowfully. At times they frightened the bishop with the harshness of threats; at other times they approached him with entreaties and costly gifts. They even promised very rich estates, hoping that—whether compelled by their threats or swayed to another opinion by desire for the promised gifts—he might perhaps reunite the separated couple and permit them thereafter to remain joined without disturbance.

The bishop was deeply moved by this appeal, but because fear of the Lord outweighed everything in him, he disregarded their threats. And, lest he should be bought off and depart from the rule of canonical law, he rejected their promises. Rather, in accordance with the prophet’s rebuke, unwilling “to make alive the souls that die” (Ezek. 13:19), he did not yield at all to their entreaties, but permanently separated them by the judgment of his full authority.

From this it clearly appears that no storm of threats could move him from his purpose in accordance with the law, and no desire for worldly gifts could ensnare him. Yet today we often see men who, compelled either by the terror or favor of a more powerful person, or avid for the profits of avarice—if I may dare say so—corrupt the discipline of ecclesiastical institution by evil deeds.

75. (74.) The Hungarians, after devastating this region, came as far as the city. Unable to conquer it, they burned the entire suburb together with the church of Saint Gaugeric. During those same days (953), the Hungarians were raging violently through the regions of this province: they took Christians captive, profaned sacred worship, and burned churches.

Terrified by this, Bishop Fulbert foresaw the impending ruin with watchful care. He diligently fortified the city and concealed in the monastery of Saint Mary the most blessed Gaugeric, a most precious treasure, suspecting with prophetic insight what the outcome soon proved.

For after several days had passed—specifically, in the year 953 from the Lord’s Incarnation, on the eighth day before the Ides of April—the Hungarians, advancing with greater eagerness and displaying their military discipline, swooped down upon this city. They remained for three days and produced a plague of every kind.

Since our men were very few against so many, they had taken refuge within the safety of the walls. The Hungarians burned the suburban buildings without resistance and plundered the property of the citizens. Finally, delighted by their successful progress, they turned their warlike efforts toward the city’s fortifications. Attempting a breach, they achieved nothing because our men defended themselves fiercely.

Therefore, exhausted, they pitched their tents not far from the city, in the meadows beside the river Scald, to refresh themselves with rest and food, intending afterward to return for the city’s destruction.

Our men, however, were not entirely idle, nor did they suffer the city’s losses without retaliation. When they saw that the enemy had withdrawn a little and that the king’s nephew—whose name has escaped me—a man skilled in the arts of war, was walking last along the walls, Odo, a man sharp in counsel and prompt in mind, immediately selected some of his bolder companions. Love of their country’s ruin had infused these men with contempt for death. They suddenly pursued the enemy, intercepting him on a shorter path.

Surrounded by a multitude, he considered retreating shameful. Being a man of immoderate spirit, he rushed into battle while his companions fled. Soon surrounded from the side, he was nevertheless beheaded and killed, at the cost of some of our men.

Having thus won the victory, they fixed his head upon a spear and hung it at the top of the wall—a joyful spectacle to them, but a miserable one to their own people.

When King Bulgio—such was his name—heard this, he was inflamed with fury and lamented the pitiable death of his companion. Eager to avenge his nephew’s death, and more bitter than usual, he returned with his men against the city.

Then, while those outside raged fiercely and those within resisted bravely, the battle continued for a long time on both sides, and weapons of every kind were employed. The grief over their kinsman’s head persistently inflamed the Hungarians; love of their homeland and their final hope supplied our men with courage.

During this, the grieving bishop at one moment assailed the Mother of God with prayers, and, prostrate before the bier of the most blessed Gaugeric, repeatedly implored him to be their defender. At another moment he ran through the defenses, encouraging and instructing his men individually: they were to fight manfully and battle as unconquerable men. The battle against foreigners belonged to God, he said, and victory would be theirs.

Meanwhile, since the exhausted Hungarians achieved nothing by their attacks, they judged it wiser to lift the siege. Offering their faith as surety for pardon and safety, they put forward this agreement—whether composed in deceit or in good faith is uncertain: if their head were returned to them, they themselves would restore all the booty and all the captives, as well as everything whatsoever they had seized in this region, down to the smallest item; thereafter they would end the fighting and establish peace.

Our men, however, suspecting greater deceit, rejected their request.

The Hungarians, enraged still more and irrationally, thought it an easier undertaking to burn the church. Abandoning the attempt to storm the walls, they vied with one another in shooting flaming missiles at the roof of the church.

At this, our men were finally seized by some consternation of mind, and severe weakness caused by fear began to prevail: they feared that the enemy would overcome them and that no place of defense remained for them.

Indeed, while the Hungarians shot without interruption and the victorious fire now held the roofs almost beyond recovery, one of the clerics, named Serraldus—strengthened, I believe, by God’s power—quickly climbed onto the church carrying a small vessel of water. Relying upon ropes that he had skillfully tied above to the beams of the belfry [Note: *Campanile* (‘bell tower’).], he extinguished the fire by sprinkling water. Running swiftly across the roof, he thwarted all the enemy’s efforts.

Wonderful to relate: moving about in full view of the adversaries and exposed to their weapons, yet protected—as the event itself demonstrates—through the merits and intercession of the most blessed Mother of God and Saint Gaugeric, he rescued the church from destruction by his own labor.

Thereupon the courage of our men rose. Feeling divine assistance, they cast aside their fear and attacked with stronger spirits in order to resist.

When the enemy saw that victory was impossible by any means, they withdrew from the siege with shame and grief. But whatever they had previously left untouched in the suburb, they burned completely in their fury. If they happened to find anyone capable of fighting, they immediately slaughtered him; whatever survived death and fire they reserved for captivity.

After this, something even more grievous and lamentable occurred. They attempted to force their way into the beautiful and venerable basilica of Saint Gaugeric, externally distinguished by splendid buildings and, as they thought, internally filled with abundant wealth. But the canons, together with a multitude of common people, resisted with the utmost determination, and the Hungarians could not accomplish their purpose.

Some threatened to burn it; many others, seeing the difficulty posed by its lead roofs, thought it better to leave it alone. They yielded to this difficulty and were already departing when a certain frenzied cleric, sitting in the belfry, shot an arrow into their midst.

Fiercely provoked, they returned to the monastery in greater numbers to avenge the insult. After attacking for a long time, they finally broke in and struck down many of the people whom they found inside. They also killed the clerics Ansfrid, Anselm, Grinbert, Teoderic, and Gention.

At last, setting fire beneath the ceiling, they overthrew the venerable church only after a long and difficult undertaking. The buildings of the lofty structure were burned, and—lamentable to relate—the roofs collapsed in a vast ruin. The lead with which the upper roofs had been covered melted and flowed in streams here and there down every slope, flooding the streets and filling the surrounding ditches.

After gathering the captives, they departed with immeasurable booty.

76. (75.) He endeavored to restore Saint Hermes to his former place. While the Danes were also raging no less violently around this province and, as is clear to those who read the histories themselves, were burning the holy houses of God, blessed Hermes, martyr of Christ, whom Pope Alexander baptized at Rome, was first carried from the Brabant village of Ronasce [Note: Renaix, in Flemish Ronse, between Oudenaarde and Grammont.]—specifically, from the monastery that Saint Amand built—to the monastery of the village of Ende [Note: Inda or Kornelimünster.], situated near Aachen. He was then transferred as far as Cologne and remained there for a considerable time.

After several years had passed, a great dispute arose between the two communities of clergy, namely, the people of Ronse and those of Ende. Once the Danes had departed and the affairs of God’s holy Church had been restored to prosperity, the people of Ronse sought to bring back their patron. The people of Ende unanimously opposed them and insisted on retaining him, regarding him as a precious treasure.

This quarrel continued between them for some time. The people of Ronse, however, having been overtaken by wiser counsel, approached Lord Bishop Fulbert humbly. Repeatedly recounting the course of their lamentation, they earnestly implored him: since the holy martyr had been transferred from his parish, he should strive with every effort to bring him back from those who had taken him by force.

The bishop recognized the justice of their case and labored by every means until he compelled the body of the blessed martyr to be returned to its proper place.

In return for so great a benefaction, the aforesaid brothers willingly gave to the holy mother church of Cambrai a village called by its inhabitants Newehova [Note: Nieuwenhoven, near Grammont and Ninove. Colvenerius.].

77. (76.) King Otto, renewing the immunities of Saint Mary, granted the toll of this city, together with its mint, to the bishop. At the request of the bishop himself, Emperor Otto also confirmed, so that it might be restored, the charter of immunity that his predecessor Charles had established over the see of Cambrai. In addition, he transferred to it the entire toll together with the mint of that city, and thereafter separated all exactions belonging to the royal treasury through the following charter:

> “In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, Otto, by the favor of divine clemency king. When we favor the just and reasonable petitions of God’s servants for the love of divine worship, we do not doubt that we are strengthened by heavenly grace.
>
> “Therefore, let the diligence and sagacity of all our faithful, present and future, know that the venerable Fulbert, bishop of the city of Cambrai, presented before us the immunities of blessed memory belonging to our predecessor Charles. These contained the statement that our aforesaid predecessor, King Charles, had always kept the aforesaid see—which is dedicated in honor of holy Mary, Mother of God and ever-Virgin—under the fullest protection and defense of immunity, for the love of God and the peace of the brothers dwelling there [Note: *Habuissent* (‘they had held’) in 1 and 3.].
>
> “For the security of the matter, the aforesaid Bishop Fulbert nevertheless requested that we confirm, by our authority, the authority of that king in love and reverence for holy Mary, Mother of God. At the intervention of our beloved Bishop Rihharius [Note: Bishop of Liège. Colvenerius.], we willingly agreed, and thus granted and strengthened it through this charter of our authority.
>
> “Therefore we command that no public judge, nor anyone exercising judicial power, dare enter, now or in future, the churches, places, lands, or other possessions of the aforesaid church that the said church presently holds or possesses justly and legally in any counties or territories within the jurisdiction of our empire, or those that shall henceforth be granted to that church by Catholic men [Note: Missing in 1.], in order to hear cases, impose fines, demand lodging or provisions, take sureties, distrain the men of that church—whether free or servile—dwelling upon its land, or seek any payments or unlawful pretexts.
>
> “Rather, let the aforesaid bishop and his successors lawfully possess, in peaceful order and under the protection of our immunity, the properties of the aforesaid church, together with its cells, possessions, and men subject to it; let them faithfully obey our imperial authority and, for the stability of ourselves and of the whole empire granted and preserved for us by God, freely implore God’s mercy together with the clergy and people subject to them.
>
> “Whatever our treasury could have exacted from these things, we have perpetually granted for the making of lights in that church.
>
> “Moreover, by our largesse we grant to the aforesaid bishop and his successors the entire toll together with the mint of their city of Cambrai, on this condition: nine parts shall be assigned to the bishops’ uses, while the tenth part shall perpetually serve the needs of the brothers of that congregation as our alms.
>
> “Furthermore, we decree that no duke, count, viscount, or anyone exercising judicial authority dare violate this constitution of ours or of our predecessor kings [Note: Missing in 1 and 3.]. If anyone does so, let him be liable to royal proceedings and, in addition, be judged guilty of six hundred solidi: two parts are to be admitted into the archives of that church, and the third part is to be received by our royal treasury, so that no one may thereafter dare attempt such a thing.
>
> “Thus we also confirm this through our authority: just as it was granted and confirmed to the aforesaid church by our predecessor of blessed memory, so let it henceforth be preserved inviolate.
>
> “And so that this authority of ours may be believed more truly and certainly by the faithful of God’s holy Church and by our own faithful, we have confirmed it below with our own hand and ordered it marked with the impression of our ring.
>
> “The sign of Otto, the most serene king. I, Bruno the chancellor, have recognized this in the place of Rotbert [Note: The original charter has *Ruodpert*.], the archchaplain. [Note: After this, the original charter, according to Colvenerius, has: ‘Given on the third day before the Kalends of June, in the year 940 from the Lord’s Incarnation, in the thirteenth indiction,’ which our less accurate manuscript omitted. But there must be an error in the day. For Otto issued two charters in the city of Salze on the fourth day before the Kalends of June, and therefore could not have been at Ingelheim on the following day.]
>
> “In the fifth year of the reign of Otto, the most serene king (940). Enacted at Ingelheim [Note: *Ingele* in 1.], happily in the name of God. Amen.”

[78. (77.) When King Otto asked for Saints Gaugeric and Autbert, the bishop gave him the body of Saint Theoderic and that of another man (see *Life of Autbert*). At that time this glorious prince Otto was devoting particular attention to the construction and restoration of churches. Having already established fourteen episcopal sees of magnificent dignity, he also built a certain metropolitan church called Magdeburg.

After obtaining many relics of saints from his bishops, he asked Bishop Fulbert to give him the bodies of Saints Gaugeric and Aubert. He considered his metropolis certain to be most fortunate if it were supported by the patronage of such great confessors.

Fearing to reject this request, the bishop hesitated uncertainly. Yet, because of the many benefits that Otto had already bestowed upon him, as we have said, he promised to fulfill the request, lest he should appear ungrateful [Note: Missing in 1.].

In this matter the anxious bishop turned his undecided mind in opposite directions. Seeing the difficulty of the undertaking, he realized that either granting or refusing the request would be dangerous for him. If he refused, the emperor’s goodwill would be offended; if he granted it, the future ruin of his province would result, since it would be deprived of the patrons through whom it had merited temporal safety and hoped for heavenly blessedness.

Caught between these alternatives, the bishop at last provided for himself by prudent reasoning. Taking into confidence a few of his men whom he trusted with secrets, he secretly opened the tombs of two priests and took their bodies: namely, the body of Saint Theoderic the bishop, whom we mentioned above (chapter 49), and that of another whose name has escaped me [Note: According to Molanus, Rotradus. *Natal.
