SS. Belgii*, 5 August.]. Wrapped honorably in biers, and together with some joints of Saint Autbert, he presented them to the emperor.]

If anyone desires to know this more fully, let him read the book that Fulbert, the most beloved teacher, wrote on the life of Saint Autbert at the command of Lord Bishop Gerard.

I will not say that this occurred without God’s gracious providence. Blessed Theoderic, a man of God, deserved this reward from the Lord and this veneration from the people; and it also occurred so that our province would not be deprived of its defenders. Even if he had wished to withdraw them, I confess that he could not have done so in any way.

What feeling do you think the citizens would have had if they saw their advocate Gaugeric taken from them—the one through whom the happy city of Cambrai was gloriously illumined and spread its name throughout all nations? Indeed, I believe that they would not have yielded even to the emperor himself.

[79. (78.) At the synod at Engulenheim, through the testimony and assistance of Fulbert, Artold is restored and Hugh expelled (Flodoard IV, 35). At the synod convened at Engulenheim before both kings, namely Otto and Louis, together with Marinus, the representative of the Roman see, and many fellow bishops, Fulbert was present (948). There the course of the dispute concerning the bishopric of Rheims between Artold and Hugh was debated.

When Artold himself, while his rival Hugh was absent, had presented his complaints before the kings and all who were present, a certain Sigebald entered, a cleric of the aforementioned Hugh, and brought letters that he had carried from Rome and had already disclosed at another synod at Mouzon. He asserted that these same letters had been given to him at Rome by Marinus himself, who was present.

The lord Marinus ordered that they be read before the synod [Note: These words are absent in 1. In 3, *qui d. e. c. s. r. jussit* (‘who, being present, ordered that the letters be read’). In Flodoard: ‘Marinus, producing the letters that Sigebald himself had carried to Rome.’].

When they were read, it was found, as the letters themselves admitted, that Wido, bishop of Soissons, Hildegarius of Beauvais, Rodulf of Laon, Fulbert of Cambrai, and all the other bishops of the diocese of Rheims had sent those same letters to the apostolic see for the restoration of Hugh to the see of Rheims and the expulsion of Artold.

After the reading, Fulbert rose together with the other bishops named in those letters and rejected them. He declared that he had never before seen or heard of them and had given no consent to their dispatch.

When the cleric could not contradict him, although he protested against them with accusations, Lord Marinus proposed to the entire synod that they should provide counsel and a proper judgment concerning such an accuser and informer of accusations against bishops.

After the informer had been publicly refuted for having brought false charges, the synod read the chapters concerning such accusers, judged him, and unanimously decreed that he should be deprived of the honor he enjoyed and, according to the provisions of the chapters, sent into exile.

He was therefore deprived of the ministry of the diaconate that he held and, rejected from the presence of the synod, departed.

As for Bishop Artold, who had made himself acceptable to every synod and had not avoided synodal judgment, they decreed, praised, and confirmed that he should retain and govern the bishopric of Rheims in accordance with the ordinances of the canons and the decrees of the holy Fathers.]

### 80. (79.) Berengarius succeeds Fulbert in the episcopal see

Berengarius succeeded Fulbert in the episcopal see and assumed the full administration of the bishopric (in the year 956). He was indeed born of a noble family of Germany [Note: [Col. 0081D] Flodoard, *Annals*, under the year 956: “Fulbert, bishop of Cambrai, dies, and the bishopric itself is granted to a certain Berengarius, a trans-Rhenish cleric, nephew of Bovo, once bishop of Châlons, who is ordained at Reims by Archbishop Artoldus.” The *Necrology of Saint Mary of Cambrai*, from the beginning of the twelfth century, records: “On the sixteenth day before the Kalends of September [17 August], Fulbert, bishop, died; he gave land at Durith for the use of the cantor.”], but was also closely related to Emperor Otto. Since he was more involved in secular than ecclesiastical affairs, he raised his spirit with a certain impulse of arrogance through the distinction of his illustrious lineage; but, once he had undertaken the office, he incurred hostility through attacks upon his character and way of life. He is also said to have been of such great fierceness that he appeared barbarous to his own people not only in language and nationality but also in conduct [Col. 0081D]. For the more the authority of his royal lineage supported him, the more fiercely he often harassed the people.

Thus, sometimes because of the immoderate volatility of his character and partly because of the ferocity and disobedience of the citizens who resisted him [Col. 0082A], difficult sedition arose among them; at other times there was an irreconcilable clash. Yet although he caused such great disturbances and inflicted such unrest, we can attribute this not so much to the bishop as to the insolence of his citizens, whom we have always heard to be disobedient and rebellious toward all their bishops because of their ferocity.

### 81. (80.) The citizens, terrified by the princes whom he brought with him, humbled themselves and received the bishop

At a certain time, however, when he had gone to Germany on the emperor’s service and remained there for some while, the citizens, gathering with one and the same resolve and forming a unanimous conspiracy, bound themselves together so tightly that, when the bishop was expected to return, they excluded him from the city by denying him entry [Col. 0082B].

When, after completing his affairs, he returned toward the episcopal see, the civic conspiracy became known to him during the journey itself. At once, therefore, because he saw that his own men were inferior both in strength and in number to so great a crowd, he retraced his journey under the disgrace of profound humiliation and approached Bruno, who at that time held the monarchy of the kingdom under his brother. He laid out his case in a speech and earnestly begged that, supported by Bruno’s assistance, he might forcibly break into the closed see and exact due vengeance upon the rebellious people for the injury he had received.

Having obtained without difficulty a large army, he also approached Arnulf, count of Flanders, and, promising him the village of Lambras [Note: [Col. 0082D] Near Douai], enlisted him as his associate, indeed as his helper. When the citizens learned that he was returning with so great an aid [Col. 0082C], they decided to look to their own interests. Concealing the movements of their rebellion as far as possible, they sent messengers so that he might come without suspicion. He therefore returned to the city with only his own men, since the others had gone back, and entered it without difficulty.

### 82. (81.) He extorted Lambras from Count Arnulf and detached two villages, Coureng and Ferroras, from the Church

Not long afterward, because of the frivolity of his insolence, he forcibly took back from the aforesaid Count Arnulf the village of Lambras, for which he had enlisted him, threatening him that, if he dared to reclaim it, he would burn all Flanders for him.

Moreover, he detached the two villages, Coureng and Ferroras [Note: [Col. 0082D] Ferrières, near Cateau-Cambrésis. Colvenerius.], from the church of holy Mary, Mother of God, and granted them as a benefice to a certain knight.

[Note: [Col. 0081] In the second manuscript *Condreng* is written above the line; hence Colvenerius thinks that this was the village of Gundreceias mentioned above, chapter 67.]

### 83. (82.) He attacked the citizens, killing some and blinding others

After some interval of time had passed, remembering the dishonor inflicted upon him by the people, he summoned allied forces and attacked the unwary citizens in a sudden assault. Striking them as they scattered, he pursued them as far as the monastery of Saint Gaugericus.

What a strange spectacle! For at once armed men, bursting into the threshold of the most holy church without reverence, killed some, while others they dismembered by cutting off their hands and feet. They gouged out the eyes of some; others they branded on the forehead with red-hot iron [Col. 0083A]. Then, in his frenzy, he ordered the spears of those who had been killed and other spears that had been taken to be piled up on a cart, and hastened to send them to his own estate, namely to the village called Betendorth [Note: [Col. 0083] Thus in the first and third manuscripts *Betencorth*, according to Colvenerius; this was Béthencourt between Cambrai and Cateau-Cambrésis], to display the pomp of his vengeance and victory to his retainers.

### 84. (83.) He died after being struck by Saint Gaugericus during the night

I cannot cease to marvel at the deed of this bishop, who did not fear to violate the church of the most blessed confessor—a church which Walter the castellan, a most inhuman young warrior, knew well enough to revere in a similar affair in our own days [Col. 0083B].

One day, coming from somewhere with his men, Walter happened to encounter two brothers, Aldo and Baldwin, who were his bitterest enemies. Immediately, spurring the horse on which he was mounted, he flew after them; with his spear almost touching their backs, threatening them with imminent death, he pursued them as they fled to the very foot of the hill, though they were already nearly nine paces from the monastery.

When he saw them approaching the refuge of the most holy church and calling upon the holy confessor for help, he was afraid to pursue them farther. At last, bursting out with these words, he said: “Know that today you have been snatched from me by the intercession of blessed Gaugericus!”

If, then, a man of great savagery learned, through love of God and reverence for his confessor, to spare his enemies and show restraint, how much more ought a bishop to have done so, even in consideration of the priestly office that he held?

Yet because he sought no escape or hiding place from so great a crime, nor any form of repentance, he paid a fitting recompense of punishment not long afterward. For when he had gone to Cologne and was resting one night in his bed, blessed Gaugericus appeared to him while he was half awake, evidently rebuking him for his offenses and then striking him heavily with the staff he carried in his hand.

Immediately awakening, he groaned with deep lamentation. Calling his chamberlains, he disclosed the vision in order and indicated the danger that had befallen him. After struggling for some time because of this blow—it is certain—he died not long afterward [Col. 0083D] and was buried in the basilica of Saint Gereon.

[Note: [Col. 0083D] We learn from a diploma of Otto I, first published by Leglay from the Cambrai archive, that he was still alive in 958. The diploma was granted at Cologne on the Ides of June 958 to the church of Cambrai, where the venerable Bishop Berengarius is known to have presided. If Engrannus truly occupied the see for only three years, as our author states in chapter 87, Berengarius must have died in 962 or the following year. I searched in vain for the day of his death in the Cambrai necrologies.]

The chaplains, that is, the clerics of this church [Note: [Col. 0084D] Namely, of Saint Mary of Cambrai], rashly suspected on the basis of accusations of some kind [Col. 0084A], fled after abandoning the pontifical ornaments.

### 85. (84.) Engrannus is appointed in his place

After Berengarius’s death, Engrannus, formerly a monk of the monastery of Saint Peter at Corbie, was promoted to the episcopal throne through the influence of the aforesaid Bruno, the chief archbishop, with whom he had acquaintance and familiarity on account of the brothers’ affairs which Engrannus administered beyond the Rhine.

Engrannus was adequately instructed in both ecclesiastical and secular disciplines and possessed remarkable charity toward his flock. Full of every gentleness, he filled the dignity of the bishopric with such religious earnestness that he seemed in no way to exceed the proper standard of a monk. For he was always laboring in the pursuit of ecclesiastical cultivation and instructed the flock entrusted to him by the example of an innocent life and the formation of good character [Col. 0084B].

### 86. (85.) He went to the general assembly to claim the village of Perrona, and took a church from his cleric because he had not carried out his command

He also enriched the church from his own property, and if anything was taken away, he strove to recover and restore it through a public judgment.

At that time, Bruno, duke or archbishop, is said to have held a general assembly with many princes and bishops at a certain village whose name does not come to mind [Note: [Col. 0084D] Perhaps Compiègne, in 959; compare the *Annals of Flodoard]. At this assembly, matters concerning the peace and religion of the holy Church of God and the condition of the kingdom were dealt with beneficially and appropriately.

Bishop Engrannus also decided to go there, intending to claim the village of Saint Mary called Perrona [Note: [Col. 0084D] Near Binche, between Mons and Charleroi. Le Glay; compare chapter 112], which the inhabitants of Hasbania held as a benefice. He ordered his chancellor Wido to carry with him the charter of that village, which he had found in the church archive, so that through it he might make his claim more openly and certainly [Col. 0084C].

When he arrived there and was prepared to present his claim, he asked the chaplain for the charter. Realizing that he had indeed consigned his lord’s command to oblivion, he froze in great astonishment and finally replied that he had forgotten it. Thus the embarrassed bishop returned home; and, bearing this impatiently, he took from the chaplain the church located in the village of Salliacum [Note: [Col. 0084D] Sailly].

### 87. (86.) Bishop Engrannus died and was buried by Hadulfus, bishop of Noyon

Finally, while he was enlarging the monastery of Saint Mary with every effort and undertaking toward the western side, he was overtaken by death—his citizens’ faults demanding it—and left the work unfinished. After governing the church for three years, he departed to Christ [Col. 0085A].

[Note: [Col. 0085D] Folcuinus, abbot of Lobbes, certainly a highly trustworthy witness when speaking of himself, records the following in *Deeds of the Abbots of Lobbes*, chapter 28, as having occurred in 965: “He caused Folcuinus to be ordained at Cologne in the imperial presence.” He was therefore ordained by Engrannus, bishop of Cambrai, on the very feast of the Lord’s Nativity, a festival which Otto in fact celebrated at Cologne only in the year 965. It follows that Engrannus did not die before 26 December 965. Yet he cannot have died much later if Ansbertus truly held the see for five years and Wiboldus for one, as our author states in chapters 88 and 91.]

Hadulfus, bishop of Noyon, attended his funeral and honorably buried him in the monastery of the holy Mother of God on the southern side.

### 88. (87.) Ansbertus succeeds him in the bishopric and established eight canons in the church of Saint Autbertus

Ansbertus followed him. He was learned in literary disciplines and was then equally a monk of the monastery of Arras and archdeacon of the church of Cambrai. Later, because he supervised the affairs of Saint Vedastus in the district of Baduensis, he became known to the emperor and attained the height of the episcopal chair.

Having contributed from his own resources as circumstances required, he appointed eight canons in the church of Saint Autbertus [Col. 0085B]. As we have already said concerning his predecessors, and as we shall later say concerning his successors, he endured serious and numerous injuries from his own soldiers and struggled for a long time against their insolence.

To quiet their arrogance, he enlisted as his ally a certain illustrious count named Arnulfus, securing him through many benefices.

[Note: [Col. 0085D] Either Arnulf the Younger, count of Flanders from 27 March 965, or the man mentioned below in chapter 95.]

With his help he overcame the stubborn men [Note: [Col. 0085D] That is, the insolent or contumacious; compare Ecclesiasticus 16:12] and enjoyed peace for a while. He therefore governed the church for five years; then, having been gathered to his fathers, he was honorably buried in the aforesaid church of Saint Autbertus.

### 89. (88.) Wiboldus is appointed, and the regular game that he devised is set out below

Wiboldus followed him, archdeacon of the church of Noyon, a man adequately instructed in both secular and ecclesiastical disciplines.

For clerics who loved gambling, he skillfully devised a regular game, so that, exercising themselves in schools through it, they might become accustomed to overcome vices by charity and avoid secular and contentious gambling. He began this game in the following manner.

[Note: The following game, when it is read separately in the manuscripts, as in Brussels no. 2088, is generally called Wiboldus’s “regular game.” It seems to owe its origin to the Pythagorean game, or *Rythmomachia*, which I discussed in our *Annals*, VIII, 383, 488—provided that the latter is older than Wiboldus. Houillon treated this game of Wiboldus in a French poem, *Le jeu du seigneur Wibold*, Cambrai, 1832, octavo.]

[Note: We have already published it separately under Wiboldus, under the year 965, in *Patrologia*, volume CXXXIV, column 4007, according to the edition of the distinguished D. Leglay. But, lest the text—indeed a very brief one—and at the same time the notes of the learned German editor be missed, since they shed considerable light on a text enveloped in great obscurity, we think it worthwhile to reprint it here. —Editor of the *Patrologia*.]

> “In Aeolic Greek, *klēros* means ‘lot’; hence in Latin *cleronomia* means ‘inheritance’ and *cleronomus* ‘heir.’ From this they are called clerics, because they belong to the lot of the Lord. *Kanon* in Greek means ‘rule’ in Latin; hence regular canons are so named.
>
> “Since this same canon forbids clerics to be gamblers—because gambling was invented and perversely practiced by the faithless and those lacking hope of good things—it is entirely fitting that, having abandoned vices, each person should draw virtues for himself with precision. Therefore, from the same kind of gambling of which we have spoken, I wish to construct a clerical game, or, so to speak, a regular one—not to mock anyone, but for the sake of exercise.
>
> “No one who understands the words of the Gospel, ‘On these two hang all the law and the prophets’ (Matthew 22:40), is unaware that Charity holds primacy over all the virtues. Where such profound greatness dwells, it produces from itself a vast and richly fruitful offspring of virtues.
>
> “Let us therefore place Charity, named together with her many offspring, and assign to each individual virtue numbers corresponding to its several lots according to such a rule that a number may neither be contained in this [arrangement] which that [lot] cannot determine, nor may this lot display what that number cannot discover.”

[Note: The construction seems to be this: “so that a number cannot be contained in this [number] which that [lot] cannot determine, and so that it is not lawful for this [lot] to display what that [number] cannot discover.” The meaning is that dice cast in any manner can never produce numbers that are not also found in one of the fifty-six lots; nor does any of these lots exhibit numbers that cannot at some time arise from dice. In brief: as many combinations as there are dice-results, so many lots are present.

Boethius the Bishop, whom Colvenerius cites, explains the passage as follows: “Wiboldus says that he will assign to each virtue a number that belongs to it alone and that one would seek elsewhere in vain. Understand this as referring to the upper surfaces of the dice, whose individual numbers you are required to seek on the side of the virtues. For example, if, when the dice are thrown, you obtain three twos, you will find these beside Compunction and nowhere else. But if you take three twos as the number six, you will find the same number in Justice and Peace.”]

“Beginning with the principal of the principals, and proceeding through two and the others up to six, by a threefold rotation of itself and of those numbers, let it contain the twenty daughters of the holy Mother and end in Wisdom.”

[Note: That is: the principal number, 1, proceeds to six, first by 1 from 1 to 6, then by 2 from 2 to 6, then by 3 from 3 to 6; and so forth. This three-part sequence produces twenty-one combinations, or lots, containing the twenty virtues besides Charity, the mother of them all.]

“Then the number two, beginning with Compunction, will end with Reverence after encompassing fifteen of the same [daughters of holy Mother Charity]. From there the number three, beginning with Piety, will encompass ten and end with Exomologesis [Confession]. Thus the number four, beginning with Maturity, will encompass six and end with Weeping. Likewise, beginning with Cheerfulness, the number five will encompass three and close with Continence. But the final number six, like the first, rejoicing in Simplicity, shall possess Humility as guardian of the virtues.”

[Note: That is, it occurs in no other lot: neither 6. 6. 6. nor 18 occurs anywhere else in the whole table except in this single lot; likewise 1. 1. 1. and 3 occur only once, in the first lot.]

[Note: “The number two, beginning with Compunction, will close with Reverence after encompassing fifteen of the daughters of holy Mother Charity; then the number three, beginning with Piety, will encompass ten virtues and end with Exomologesis; likewise the number four, beginning with Maturity, will encompass six virtues and end with Weeping; and beginning with Cheerfulness, the number five will encompass three and end with Continence.”]

“Taken together, these make fifty-six. If we examine them more carefully, we shall observe that this progression of numbers, ascending from three to eighteen—”

[Note: That is, the fourth column, which contains the sum of each lot.]

“—assigns to each of the virtues its corresponding number. The first, second, last, and next-to-last each receive one virtue; the third and third-from-last each receive two;

[Note: That is, they receive virtues. The first sum (3), second sum (4), last (18), and next-to-last (17) occur only once each in the whole column and each measures a single virtue; the third (5) and third-from-last (16) occur twice each; 6 and 15 three times; 7 and 14 four times; 8 and 13 five times; and 9, 10, 11, and 12 six times. When corresponding numbers are paired—the first with the last, the second with the next-to-last, and so on—they always make 21.]

the third and third-from-last each receive two; those between them, joined similarly from beginning and end toward the four middle numbers, receive three, four, or five virtues, and always express the number twenty-one in relation to one another.

“Thus 3, 4, 17, and 18 each determine one virtue: Charity, Faith, Continence, and Humility. Numbers 5 and 16 determine two each: Hope and Fortitude; Weeping and Compassion. Numbers 6 and 15 determine three each: Justice, Peace, and Compunction; Confession, Sighing, and Cheerfulness. Numbers 7 and 14 determine four each: Prudence, Chastity, Fear, and Joy; Reverence, Contrition, Constancy, and Understanding. Numbers 8 and 13 determine five each: Temperance, Mercy, Providence, Sobriety, and Shrewdness; Wisdom, Virginity [Note: The first edition reads *virginitatis*, “of virginity”], Mortification, Innocence, and Solicitude. Numbers 9 and 10, 11 and 12 distinguish six each: Obedience, Discernment, Goodness, Delight, Simplicity, and Piety; Perseverance, Modesty, Sweetness, Hospitality, Patience, and Indulgence; Long-suffering, Gentleness, Frugality, Zeal, Prayer, and Judgment; Kindness, Poverty, Mildness, Love, Vigilance, and Maturity.”

[Note: Manuscript II reads *omnes* (“all”); Colvenerius corrected it to *senas* (“six each”).]

“And to return to each point: by the number three, what word shall we designate except Trinity, whose sanctifying name returns to the unity of its own beginning? What else by the number four than the trumpets of the four evangelists?”

[Note: The third edition reads “evangelical trumpets”; the first reads “crowds of evangelists.”]

“Taken together, these reveal that most holy grace, sevenfold and full of gifts of grace. The number seven, spoken twice, and joined with three and four—seventeen and eighteen—shows how 3, 7, and 4 return into one another. We may also assign 10 to the commandment of the Decalogue, which once operated under the Law and now under grace, and 8 to the eighth age, which has not yet begun.”

[Note: Manuscript 1 reads *ñ*; manuscript 5 *n*; manuscript 2 *non* (“not”); Colvenerius corrected the text.]

“But it was more appropriate to mention these three at this point. Therefore, whoever loves in the ear of his heart the sound of the holy Gospel’s trumpets, loves the holy Trinity with inward devotion, and desires to preserve it to the end by the sevenfold grace, should seek to possess Charity, in which the whole law is fulfilled (Romans 13:8); Faith, without which it is impossible to please God (Hebrews 11:6); Continence, so that he may abstain from vices and thus be able to retain the virtues; and Humility, by which the person who gathers virtues carries dust in the wind (Gregory, *Homily* 7 on the Gospels). Let him strive to exercise these virtues once possessed—charitably, faithfully, continently, and humbly—so that he may reach their fullness.”

[Note: Manuscript 1 reads *que* (“and”) for *qua* (“by which”) after “Humility.”]

“We may join the five senses to the number five; taken three times and with unity added, it rises to sixteen.”

[Note: Perhaps *scilicet* (‘namely’) is to be read three times.]

“For if we discipline these five senses through physics, logic, and ethics, so that we may always return to the unity of Charity, which is God (1 John 4:8), we shall possess naturally, rationally, and morally these virtues which appear to be marked by the two numbers.

“The number six, whose sixth part is 1 and whose third half is 3, because it is a perfect number, well constituted by its own parts, may be assigned to the perfection of a work.”

[Note: Manuscript 1 has *IIIa* (‘a third’).]

“Repeated in this way and with three added, these make 15.”

[Note: Manuscripts 1 and 2 read *replicatos* (“repeated ones”) for *replicatis* (“having been repeated”).]

“Let us therefore be perfect in works of good action, and strive to climb the fifteen steps of the psalmist, so that we may deserve to behold the holy Trinity in Zion (Psalm 84:8); and assuredly we shall not be without the virtues expressed by these numbers.”

[Note: That is, we shall not be without those virtues which are expressed by these numbers.]

“Again, seven is present, filled with spiritual grace, producing fourteen through two. Let us therefore pray to that same Spirit to grant us passage through the practical life to the theoretical life, so that we may deserve to be admitted to his virtues.

“But since above we referred to eternity—”

[Note: Manuscript 1 reads *se* (“itself”) for *Sed* (“but”).]

[Note: That is, the eighth age which has not yet begun, as our author expressed it above. It is therefore unnecessary, with Colvenerius, to write “the eighth age.”]

“—of which the title of the psalm says, ‘For the end, for the eighth,’ this may be compared with eight, just as we said below that ten would be present. If five are added to it, they will explain thirteen.

“It is also fitting that the five senses be subordinated to the eighth life, because not only does one fail to deserve this life—unless their appetitive pleasure is restrained by the bridle and reins of spiritual discipline—but one also fails to deserve that life which is lived from Abel through the giving of individual white robes until justice is turned into judgment and the saints possess a double portion on earth (Isaiah 61:7).”

[Note: Manuscript 1 reads *appetus* for *appetitus* (“desire”).]

[Note: Manuscript 1 reads *coexerceatur* for *coerceatur* (“is restrained”).]

[Note: Manuscript 1 reads *singulorum* (“of individuals”) for *singularum* (“of individual [robes]”).]

[Note: That is: “Unless the appetitive pleasure is restrained, one not only fails to deserve this [eighth life or age, namely eternal blessedness of body and soul], but also fails to deserve that life of the soul alone which is lived from Abel through the giving of individual white robes”—in white garments, compare Revelation 6:11; 7:13—“until the coming of that eighth age, or the last day, when justice is turned into judgment.” The word “not” must be supplied from the following “nor.”]

“Now 9, 10, 11, and 12 remain at the summit. The first shines consecrated by the nine orders of heavenly citizens; the second by the ten words of the Law; the third by the worthy fruits of repentance; the fourth by the twelve heralds of the New Testament.

[Note: Manuscripts 1 and 3 read *sedm* (“seven”) for *novem* (“nine”).]

“The fifth, because, as it is written, ‘In many things we all offend’ (James 3:2): whoever transgresses the ten commandments and stumbles in the eleventh, crowned with the splendor of twelve gems—”

“—so that the nine former losses may be repaired, let him return through the commandments of the ten and be clothed in the eleventh with the Church’s sackcloth coverings, so that he may at some time say with the psalmist: ‘You have turned my mourning into joy,’ and the rest (Psalm 29:12).”

[Note: The first and fourth editions have a corrupt reading: *p. q. duoq. dicem ps. 1. 4*.]

> “Since, then, we have arranged the virtues and numbers in whatever manner, let us now decide how they ought to be drawn. Let us therefore take three dice, each having six faces marked with different numbers—the largest, six; the others always one less, down to the unit—so that together they make twenty-one. Let us mark each of our five vowels, namely A, E, I, O, V, upon them in the same order, so that, repeated four times, they correspond to one another. Yet let the letters be written in such a way that A begins on the first die, E on the second, and I on the third, beginning with the unit, always in a straight line and ending with the same letter, as follows:

> [lacuna: the source contains a diagram that is not preserved in the supplied text]

> “Once these arrangements have been made, we wish the numbers that are to be calculated to be sought, as in the game mentioned above, always in their proper order, according to what the lot dictates.”

[Note: The first edition reads *ditaverit*, “will have enriched,” rather than *dictaverit*, “will dictate.”]

> “We omitted Y, the sixth and Greek vowel, not only because we have no present need of that language and do not fully observe the rules of our native grammarians, but also because we strive to make our work concise and to conduct our little game in a popular manner.”

[Note: Construe: “We omitted Y, the sixth Greek vowel, not only because … we do not observe [the rules of native orthographers], but because we strive to conduct the jest or game of our work concisely and in a popular manner.”]

> “As for the consonants—since sixteen remain in the alphabet, except for Q, which grammarians call superfluous and which we have not counted because it can easily be understood here from its companion V, without which it loses the force of a letter, and because the number seventeen seemed, for completing what we intended, like an intercalary addition—we must therefore insert the consonants, just as the vowels are placed upon squares, into one triangular pyramid having four surfaces, as follows:

[Note: Manuscript 1 reads *remanet excepta q. per gramatici s. n. quique*: “remain, except Q; [which] grammarians call superfluous; and which.”]

> [lacuna: the source contains a diagram that is not preserved in the supplied text]

> “This, however, shall be governed by the following rule: if even one of its lower consonants is found in the name of the virtue whose vowels have been separated, it shall count in place of all the others. And what the upper surface of its square demonstrates, this lower surface of the pyramid—that is, its base—will demonstrate.”

[Note: That is: in the dice, the numbers—or rather letters—of the upper surface have value; in the pyramid, the letters of the lower surface have value.]

> “Nor is this without reason, since the body, whose likeness these consonants retain while those vowels represent the soul—whether the body is properly adorned by its natural composition, diminished in some part, or increased by monstrous excess—appears to possess either a whole spirit or none at all. When that spirit departs, let this lower element, from which it was taken, return [to it]; let that spirit return to the Lord who gave it (Ecclesiastes 12:7).”

[Note: Manuscript 1 reads *siu* for *seu* (“whether”).]

[Note: Colvenerius explains that vowels are compared to the soul and consonants to the body. But the passage seems corrupt: *et quae* should perhaps be altered to *et qui*, that is, *quasi*, “as though,” so that the sense is “whose likeness these [consonants] retain, those [vowels] representing, as though, the soul”; or, as Pertz proposes, *in eque*, “equally,” giving: “those [vowels] equally representing the likeness of the soul.” The latter is much preferable.]

> “Thus, when the dice and the triangle have been cast together, and their individual letters have been examined, we must immediately return to the margin containing the numbers together with the virtues. When, as stated above, we find the discernment belonging to one vowel in the similarly three-part arrangement, we must mark the virtue which it has on its side. [Note: The text had *quae omnes* (“which all”); Colvenerius corrected it to *quam* (“which”).] If we can, we should join its visible vowels to the vowels of that virtue, and thereby become its sole possessors, so that our fellow players may no longer claim that same virtue for themselves in the same game.”

[Note: Manuscripts 1 and 4 read *c potest* in place of *compotes* (“possessors”).]

> “By this method of disputing, taking turns, alternating, and playing in a circle, let them divide all the virtues among the lots. If they are not divided between them on an equal scale, let those who have surpassed the others by even one virtue rejoice that precedence in the rest has fallen to them.”

[Note: Colvenerius prints *superabundaverint* (“have exceeded”); manuscripts 1 and 3 have *superabundavit … prelaturam* (“has exceeded … precedence”).]

> “This is to be observed, however: Charity, which is twofold, should, if necessary, be counted as two virtues.”

[Note: That is, if the players have obtained an equal number of virtues.]

> “Because only one of its letters is missing—namely A—it should be tested a second time after the first throw.”

[Note: Manuscript 1 reads *eclipsin. i a. bina*; it preserves the phrase concerning the loss of one letter, A, and a second trial.]

[Note: Charity has three units on its side. In the dice, three units consist of A on the first die, E on the second, and I on the third. Charity cannot arise as a lot unless the dice show these three units on their upper surfaces. But if one demands all the vowels of the word *Karitas* [“Charity”], one A will be lacking, since the word consists of two A’s and one I. Wiboldus therefore allows a second throw, to test whether the upper surfaces of the dice will yield two A’s and one I. Or, alternatively, the single die bearing E on the unit must be thrown again, so that, if it produces A, the vowel requirement for the word *Karitas* will be completed; otherwise the entire throw will be void. —Colvenerius.]

> “Until the sixth hour of that day, the higher-ranking players should call their lower-ranking pupils and advise them to strive to obtain through good morals the virtues that their lot lacks.”

[Note: Manuscript 1 reads *debe ut virtutes* (“must [that] the virtues”); after a space of several letters, the scribe of the copy he was transcribing could no longer read the text. Manuscript 3 has precisely the same gap.]

> “The lower-ranking [players] too, recognizing *niati tessere* [reading uncertain], and, as though [their] superiors [lacuna] teachers [lacuna], must not dare to address them by any other name than ‘masters.’”

[Note: In manuscript 1 the text is *inferiores qq niati tessere c. a. v. s. prelatis pedagogis*, with spaces after *quoque* and *prelatis*: the scribe could no longer read the words at those points. Manuscript 3 has precisely the same reading; *tessere* is absent from manuscript 2. Perhaps the missing word was *nominatim* (“by name”).]

> “But if it happens that neither can overcome the other, let both, equally possessing the virtues of the other, always be united in one Charity and rejoice in the name of brotherhood.

> “The same game may perhaps be made more effective and more agreeable in another way: each person, having cast only three dice, may pay attention not to the force of the individual elements but to their combined total, and may boast that he possesses as many virtues as he finds crowned with the number specified above.”

[Note: The first and third editions read *alia*, “another.”]

> “We set these things before you, reader, so that, if your pen demands anything, you may usefully add it or remove it by correction. [Note: Manuscripts 1 and 3 read *acnectas* for *adnectas* (“add”).] Do not, however, introduce anything blasphemous; and if you do not wish to praise it, at least do not destroy it.

> “But if the game seems worthless or produces weariness in your mind, at least let the useful arrangement of the numbers and the beloved investigation of the virtues, together with the exercise that is not idle, turn your mind toward it, so that you may be exercised by the comparison of numbers and rejoice in the accumulation of virtues.

> “If you conquer while acquiring these things, you will have no arrogance; if you are conquered, you will have no shame. If you have acquired less, you must be obedient; if more, you must be diligent in obedience.

> “To all who pursue these virtues in Christ and recall them in action and conduct, may there be grace and peace forever.”

> “The name of the author is sought in these dactylic verses themselves:
>
> If by numbers: the first makes [it], and the second the initial letter,
>
> And the eighth, ten twice taken; and thus by nines
>
> The third is inserted; the fourth is then two;
>
> The fifth is four and ten; next, finally, the sixth
>
> Is read in elevens, the seventh in twice two; and
>
> The final order ends in numbers three times six.”

By which, taken together, the theoretical sum is consecrated:

“Virginity of the soul shines forth, and the ten commandments;

Whoever keeps them secures for himself the joys of heaven.” [Note: That is: If the author’s name is sought through these dactylic verses (hexameters), take it as follows. The first and second letters, together with the eighth, make twice ten (that is, the twentieth letter of the alphabet, V); thus the third letter is inserted as nine (the ninth letter, I); from this the fourth is read as two (the second letter, B); the fifth as fourteen (O); then finally the sixth as eleven (L); the seventh as twice two [Col. 0094C] (D); and the final sequence limits the name at three times six (S). When these are brought together—that is, when the ten verses are written together—the theoretical sum becomes the sacred mystical total, namely the word *Virginitas* (“for this word is composed of ten letters,” COLV.). “The virginity of the soul and the ten commandments shine forth” (“the ten verses represent the number of the Decalogue,” COLV.); whoever keeps them secures for himself the joys of heaven. Thus VIBOLDUS is produced.]

“This game instructs the learned clergy to proceed with the tabulated scheme,

So that they may be able to compose the names of the virtues.”

90. (89.) Where the leading men of Cambrai asked the king to grant them Wibold as bishop. The leading men of Cambrai—for he traced his distinguished lineage from them—acclaimed him with one and the same will and, sending letters to the emperor, urgently requested with great enthusiasm that he be granted to them as bishop. Once the emperor learned of his good reputation, he readily yielded to their requests in willing good faith; granting his assent, he gladly fulfilled their embassy.

91. (90.) He travels to Italy to the king concerning the grant of the bishopric; but, exhausted by the summer journey, he died not long after his return. As soon, therefore, as Wibold learned that the emperor had consented, and as the leading men of the aforesaid city were also pressing their request, he hastened to the emperor, who was then staying in the regions of Italy, to undertake so great an office. [Note: Otto was there in 962–964 and from 967 to the middle of 972. Since Engrannus was still alive on 25 December 965, and since, according to our author, his successor Ansbertus occupied the see for five years and Wibold for one, this journey can fall only in the summer of 971 or 972. If 972 is posited, Wibold’s death would fall in the middle of 973, and thus after Otto I’s death. Yet in the following chapter we read that this same Otto still gave him Tetdo as successor; Wibold’s year must therefore apparently be assigned from the middle of 971 to the middle of 972.] It was summer, a circumstance that greatly hindered him both on his journey there and on his return. For when, after receiving so distinguished an office, he was returning, he was so exhausted by the blazing heat [Note: *torrentem* (“raging,” or “blazing”), reading 1.] that, when he reached the church, he could scarcely move the bell [Note: This bell was called Aldegundis. Whenever the bishop was present at Cambrai, it was rung every evening [Col. 0095D]. When he became bishop and entered the church for the first time, he himself rang it, confirming under oath that he would restore it if it should ever be broken. This happened in 1396 and 1416; in the latter year, after it had been recast, it received this inscription:

“I ring late when the bishop is present, and I hang for his dangers;

Then, for other reasons, I summon the congregation.

Formerly I was Aldegundis, as my name declares.

I was ordered to be restored, while Plonchet directed the work,

When M had been taken once, and C four times eight by eight reduced.”

LE GLAY.]—that is, the bell whose ringing ought to announce that he was claiming for himself the dignity of the bishopric—because of the distress of his illness. He presented to the church of the Mother of God a Gospel book beautifully adorned with gold and jewels, as well as many books that he had brought with him. Afterwards his illness became so severe that he governed the church for scarcely the span of one year. Departing from this world, he was buried in the same basilica of Saint Mary, on the south side.

92. (91.) The monk Rotbert’s request is rejected, and Tetdo is installed as bishop. On the day of Wibold’s death, determined by lot among the fathers, a certain man named Rotbert, a monk at the estate of Solemia, eight miles from this city, was administering the affairs of Saint Dionysius. Hearing of the bishop’s death, and captivated by secular honor, he judged that the leading men of the city should be won over with money. He gave them generous gifts and promised them much greater ones, if they would ask the emperor to make him bishop by common consent. They immediately sent an embassy to the emperor, having been bribed [Note: *oberrati*, “having gone astray,” reading 1.], and requested that, with his own consent, he deign to grant them as bishop the man whom they had chosen.

But the emperor saw that, because he had previously granted Wibold according to their choice and had readily yielded to their requests, they perhaps wished the power of admitting a bishop to remain reserved to their own discretion as well. Therefore, with complete opposition, he refused to give effect to their embassy [Col. 0094C]. But, forestalled by a higher counsel, he elevated Tetdo to the office of pastoral governance. Tetdo was vigorous in holy conduct, by no means uneducated, descended from the foremost and greatest families of Saxony, and provost of the church of Saint Severinus at Cologne. Although he resisted—for he had heard of the evil conduct and ferocity of the people of Cambrai—he was nevertheless suitably appointed. After his ordination had been completed, the venerable man of God, having put his necessary affairs in order, came to the seat granted to him, intending to visit the flock entrusted to him. Yet scarcely could it be expressed in words how many injuries, insults, and adversities he later endured from his own people!

93. (92.) Concerning the injuries that the bishop suffered from his soldiers. At that same time there was a certain man named Johannes, powerful by birth among both the people of Cambrai and those of Vermandois, who held precedence over the others in the city through the office of mayor under episcopal authority. But the greater and more powerful he was than the others, the worse and more ferocious he was toward the bishop.

To pass over the rest, the venerable bishop, the man of God, had prepared heaps of stones and lime, as well as every kind of material, with which he intended to enlarge the church of blessed Mary, Mother of God. But, while the work was in progress, necessity required him to depart to the emperor. While he was away, the aforesaid castellan had the heaps of building materials carried to him and used them to lay the foundations of a house with a magnificent structure in the same castle.

When this was reported to the bishop after his return, he groaned deeply and, through prolonged lamentation, stirred divine mercy to avenge the audacity of so great an outrage. Not long afterwards, having gathered the aid of a large army, he drove Johannes from the territory of the city. Fleeing into the district of Vermandois, specifically into the castle of Saint-Quentin, he was sheltered for some time under Count Albert, with the support of friends and relatives. There, after asking for assistance, he gathered so great a number of followers that, at one point, bursting forth unexpectedly from hidden ambushes, he devastated the villages of the surrounding region with miserable plundering.

The bishop was therefore often terrified and, wondering how he might restrain a robber of such savagery, was stirred by various thoughts and deliberations. While he was considering these matters, a certain Walter, a vassal of the castle of Lens [Note: Lens.], distinguished by the eminence of his secular power but full of cunning and intellectual craft [Note: *versuta*, “crafty,” reading 1.], surrounded him with the support of factions. He promised that, if the bishop would enfeoff his son—who bore the same name—with whatever Johannes held, and would receive him in Johannes’ place, Walter would defend the city steadfastly against the violence of that tyranny with all his strength and would overcome Johannes through frequent attacks.

Therefore the bishop gladly received him and, without difficulty, granted him what he requested. But afterwards Walter, undermining the reliability of the aforesaid promise by his words, not only failed to help the bishop [Note: *juvavit*, corrected from *juvit*, reading 1.], but, more troublesome than the former man, inflicted many and various injuries upon the bishop and his successors. Johannes, meanwhile, lamenting that his possessions had been seized by another heir, grew harsher and did not restrain himself until the bishop, compelled by repeated harassment, restored to him nearly as much benefice as he had lost.

94. (93.) Concerning the death of the emperor Otto and the succession of his son Otto. At that time the most holy emperor Otto, most faithful protector, standard of justice, devoted worshiper of the Church, hope of peace, and lover of religion, advanced in age and full of days, happily departed to Christ (7 May 973). After his death, his most glorious son Otto, although still a young and inexperienced man in the first flower of youth, was nevertheless good in counsel, vigorous in war, and—in brief—very like his father both in character and in name. He undertook to guide the reins of the empire.

But because he was younger, Henry, duke of the Bavarians, raised his neck against him with all his presumed and determined efforts, disdaining to be subjected to his rule. As a result, after some interval of time, their conflict proceeded as far as war [Note: *ense*, “by the sword,” readings 1 and 3.]; but not long afterwards, as I shall relate later, when Henry had bent back beneath the yoke of surrender, peace and concord were established between them.

95. (94.) Concerning the fury of Rainerus and Lantbertus against the emperor. When the emperor’s death became known far and wide, Rainerus and Lantbertus—the sons, namely, of Rainerus [Note: Of Rainerus III, or Long-Neck, count of Hainaut. At this same point, read Folcuin complaining in the *Gesta* [Col. 0096D] of the abbot of Lobbes, chapter 26. In a Gospel codex of the church of Cambrai, no. 309, from the tenth century, a hand of the late tenth or early eleventh century wrote the following at the end: “These are the names of the evildoers who burned the churches of our … together with Count Rainerus: Count Albert; Rainuwalo; Rotbert; Setwinus; Baldricus; Hildebrandus; Ratholo; Fastradus; Fulcuinus; Borgardus; Tetmarus; Sarawardus; Rotlandus; Lietselmus; Arnulfus; Johannes; another Johannes; Otmarus; Rotmundus; Tietselmus; Lochardus; Wiamarus; Stephanus; Euremarus; Amolricus; Gerardus; Gonterus; Amolricus; Fulcradus; Hubaldus; Arnulfus; Fredericus; Rotbertus; Landricus; Otselmus; … Ohuldus; Tietselmus; Goismondus; Gonzo and his son; Harduinus; Gontmarus; Gotselo.”], whom Archbishop Bruno, while the emperor was still alive, had often corrected by reproving his insolence, his plunder, his attacks upon the Church, and his many crimes, and had often pacified by appeasing his servile conduct with benefices—yet, since he could in no way suppress his ferocity, swollen with Syrian arrogance, Bruno finally condemned him to perpetual exile and handed him over to his brother (957). He first granted his land to the nobleman Richarius [Note: Before *Richario* there was originally the sign *facto*; the author himself wrote above the same word *duci Godefrido* (“to Duke Godefrid”): “first to Duke Godefrid, then to Richarius,” readings 2 and 3; “to Duke Godefrid, also called Richarius,” reading 5.] and, after Richarius’ death, to Warner and Raynald. When they too had died [Note: The Liège, Floreffe, and Marchiennes Annals, all derived from one source, contradict this at the year 973. There was a battle at Péronne between Rainerus and Warner. Sigebert combined this account with ours under the year 973 as follows: “Rainerus and Lantbertus, gradually recovering their strength, return from Francia and engage in battle at Péronne with Warner and Raynald, who had occupied their father’s county; they kill them and many others, and, after fortifying the castle of Buxude above the river Haine, harass Lotharingia.” In this passage he has added nothing but the words “they kill them and many others.” This is the only testimony known to me that contradicts our author. If it is correct, Godefrid and Arnulf cannot have received the county of Hainaut from Bruno, but only later from Otto II. This Godefrid was the Elder, count of Verdun. Delewarde, *Histoire de Hainaut* II, 208, considers Arnulf to have been the son of Isaac, count of Cambrai and Valenciennes. The count of Flanders, as Mejerus, Lipsius, and others maintain, he cannot be, in view of Otto’s diploma reported below in chapter 112, from the year 1001, where Arnulf is likewise called count, since Arnulf the Younger of Flanders had already died in 988.], he granted it to the most noble counts Godefrid and Arnulf, and expelled the aforesaid sons from their ancestral territory because of the same insolence.

These men, I say, on hearing of the emperor’s death, returned to their ancestral territory, recalled by certain criminals who hated peace—sons of Belial—and, wishing by force to reclaim their father’s land, fortified the castle of Bussud above the river Haine [Note: Boussoit on the river Haine, near Binche. That the castle had already been captured on 21 January is shown by Otto’s charter, which I copied at Ghent in the archive of Saint Bavo: issued on the twelfth day before the Kalends of February, in the year of the Lord 974, indiction 2, in the thirteenth year of the reign of Lord Otto and the fourth of his empire. “Actum Bosgut in the name of the Lord. Amen” (in Miraeus I, 49, it is incorrectly read *Bosgrat*). The emperor had still celebrated Christmas at Utrecht. LE GLAY.] There they raged as much as, and more than, they were permitted [Note: *dum dum*, repeated in reading 1.].

When the young emperor heard this, he gathered an army, surrounded the castle with a siege, demolished it, and sent the captured rebels into exile (January 974). Bishop Tietdo also took part in this siege. After these events, he approached and attacked the aforesaid duke of Bavaria, who, as we have said, was resisting him with his followers; but, by the will of God, he very quickly defeated him, brought him ready to surrender, and subjected him to imperial authority.

96. (95.) Where the same plunderers turned their backs in battle against the emperor’s faithful men. Meanwhile the aforesaid brothers Rainerus and Lantbertus, driven by poverty and imitating their ancestral ways, persisted in plundering and, disrupting the public peace, harassed those who were less powerful in whatever way they could.

Finally, going into the territory of the Carolingians, they enlisted to their aid Charles, the brother of King Lotharius, a man devoted to evil conduct, and likewise Otto, son of Albert, count of Vermandois, together with many other plunderers. They craftily bewailed their own misfortune: they had been disinherited, stripped of their patrimony, made exiles from their father’s dwelling; the land in which they had been born was being denied to them; therefore they begged for allied arms to avenge the wrong.

With these men supporting and accompanying them, and their military practices restored, they hastened toward the hill of Castrum. There, in the year 976 of the Lord’s Incarnation, they attacked the emperor’s faithful men, namely the counts Godefrid and Arnulf. Those men, however, aroused with no less courage, gathered the forces they had present and emerged from the fortification. Exposing themselves to the sudden danger, relying on no unexpected aid except God’s, they joined battle. After a long struggle on both sides, they nevertheless gained the fruit of victory.

When these men had withdrawn to their own territory, Otto [Note: Son of Albert of Vermandois. COLV.] soon seized that estate of Gogic [Note: Gony in Arouaise. COLV.] from Arnulf by an assumed claim, because it adjoined his own property. After fortifying a castle there, he harassed this city, since it was not far away, with frequent incursions.

97. (96.) King Lotharius of the Carolingians unexpectedly attacks the emperor Otto; Otto therefore gathers an army and devastates his kingdom. Afterwards, when the emperor had pacified his kingdom and subdued by his strength all who had previously resisted him, he remained quietly and prosperously occupied with matters belonging to God at the palace of Aachen, around the feast of Saint John (978).

Suddenly King Lotharius of the Carolingians, his nephew, wishing to deprive him of the empire, prepared to attack him by a secret expedition so unexpectedly that Otto could learn of it only the day before the attack [Note: *resistere*, “to resist,” readings 2, 3, and 8; *rescire*, “to learn,” reading 3.]. Since he thought that, taken unawares by this affair, he presently lacked the means of resisting, he left the place with his entire household and withdrew to Cologne. He rightly judged that he ought to yield for a time, so that afterwards he might be better able to resist deliberately.

When King Lotharius arrived there but, frustrated in his arrangements, failed to encounter him, he remained there while the Franks rioted [Note: That is, “the Franks were behaving outrageously,” reading 8.] and plundered, and he ravaged the region with much destruction. Otto, returning, hastened to send him an embassy, openly declaring that, in revenge for such treachery, he would set no traps or ambushes for him and would not steal upon him by deceit; rather, after removing every fraud, he would proceed on the Kalends of October to weaken the power of his kingdom.

Meanwhile, therefore, the emperor ordered the dukes and princes of his land to be summoned, armed for war. Calling them together, he gravely explained the whole cause of the affair [Note: *insinuans*, “explaining,” reading 8.] and resolved to lead an expedition against Lotharius. At his exhortation they all inclined their hearts to him; indignant at the insult inflicted upon them, they unanimously formed a conspiracy with one another, as though they were one man, and promised that, out of loyalty to his father, who had lovingly nourished them, they would serve him to the end of their lives.

After gathering and compelling these men, he moved such a large army that no one afterwards could remember having seen one so great, either before or since. And, lest his previous embassy deceive King Lotharius, he entered his kingdom on the appointed day. Using his successes well, he devastated first the territory of Rheims, then that of Laon, and also that of Soissons, and finally the region of Paris with various forms of destruction. Yet, instructed by his father’s character, he respected the churches and even preferred to enrich them with lavish gifts.

Then, to display the glory of his victory, he sent word through an embassy to Hugh, who was residing in Paris, that Alleluia should be sung for him with such magnificence as he had never heard. He summoned a great number of clerics and ordered *Alleluia te martyrum* to be sung at the place called the Mount of Martyrs with voices so raised that Hugh himself and all the people of Paris, astonished at what they heard, marveled [Note: *admiraretur*, “marveled,” reading 8.].

98. (97.) Where Lotharius pursues Otto, but, because the river Aisne lay between them, battle is postponed. When he thought that he had exacted an adequate return for his vengeance, and judged that he ought to withdraw to winter quarters, he recalled the cavalry and arranged his return around the feast of Saint Andrew (29 November), with winter already approaching. Having retraced his route and rejoicing in the successful outcome of his deeds, he ordered his camp to be pitched above the river Aisne.

But because this river, whenever rains occur, is accustomed to swell so greatly that it cannot be crossed without boats, Count Godefrid [Note: The Elder, count of Ardennes and Hainaut.] suggested and urged that he hasten past it, lest so large a force of soldiers encounter some obstacle in a difficult crossing. A few servants nevertheless remained behind. They were bringing up the rear, transporting the baggage and military equipment, and, because of the burden’s exhaustion and the darkness of the night already descending, decided to postpone their crossing until the following day.

On the next day Lotharius, having gathered as many men as he could, although inferior in number, drew confidence from his awareness of the shame involved and secretly pursued the enemy as far as the aforesaid river. Terrified by his unexpected attack, the men carrying the military equipment thought they could save themselves by swimming; but when the waters suddenly rose, their strength failed and they were drowned.

That very night the channel rose so high that, because of the difficult and inaccessible bank, neither side could reach the other. This, I believe, was arranged by God’s will, so that an immeasurable slaughter might not occur on either side. Although Lotharius, they say, had joined the battle despite his inferior numbers, he nevertheless captured the pack animals and shattered the vehicles, which in times of danger were regarded as more of a burden than a use.

A boat was then prepared, and through messengers Otto sent word to Lotharius that, if he had enough eagerness for battle, he should either cross to fight after taking hostages—lest, if some of his men had crossed while many more still had to cross, he should suspect that the route was being blocked by deceit—or, conversely, Otto himself would take hostages from Lotharius, recross the river, and return against him. They would then join battle with one another, and whichever of them God favored would obtain the imperial rule of the kingdom crowned with victory.

On hearing this, a certain count named Goisfridus [Note: Grisagonella.] burst out and said aloud: “Why should so many men be cut down on both sides? Let both kings come together alone, and, while we watch from a distance, let them face the whole danger themselves in single combat. Once one has been struck down, let the rest be spared and submit to the victor.”

At this, Count Godefrid likewise said indignantly: “We have always heard that your king was held cheap by you, though we did not believe it. Now, however, since you yourselves admit it, we are entitled to believe it. Our emperor will never fight while we remain at rest; he will never risk himself in battle while we are unharmed. Yet we do not doubt that he would be victorious if he were matched in single combat with your king” [Note: At this point reading 8 adds: “Meanwhile, someone who had served God for a long time in seclusion foretold that none of those who had been responsible for this scandal would live beyond seven years. And events proved it so.” Cf. Alpertus, *Monumenta Germaniae Historica*, SS IV, 697.].

99. (98.) Bishop Tetdo is shaken by many rebellions and troubles from his own vassals. While the kings were thus at odds with one another, it is already difficult to say by how many storms of factional violence Bishop Tethdo was battered by his own vassals. They knew that the emperor, the torturer of evildoers, was occupied with the affairs of the aforesaid war. Therefore, gathering confidence in their impunity, they repeatedly inflicted injuries upon the bishop by deceitful suggestions, since he was a simple man and ignorant of the language of the region.

At one point Walter, entirely depleted of truth [Note: “He has already brought forth his offspring and has nothing more,” COLV.], pretending loyalty by deceit and creating the fear of a plausible danger, mocked him. He fraudulently announced that King Lotharius was prepared to come with a gathered force to burn the city and bring destruction upon the entire surrounding region.

Terrified by this, the bishop gave Walter a great payment and promised more if, by any means, he could avert the designs of so great a calamity [Note: That is, “could completely pacify it,” COLV.]. Pretending that he was sending an embassy to friends and relatives serving in the royal household, supposedly so that they might calm the king, Walter returned to the bishop after several days. He boasted that, through his own entreaties and ingenuity, the expedition that had been prepared had ceased because the king had been pacified.

By this fraud he won the bishop’s favor and received a great abundance of gifts; indeed, together with other benefices, he extorted the estate called Lambras.

Heriwardus did the same on one occasion. He had previously abandoned the bishop because of his disloyalty and joined the plunderers whom we have already mentioned, namely Rainerus and Lantbertus. But, having made little progress among them, he later returned to the bishop under the appearance of loyalty. Through crafty factions and flatteries, under a certain appearance of familiarity, he purchased the bishop’s favor for himself. At one point he devised intrigues against him through a suspicious and plausible story, asserting that Rainerus and Lantbertus were preparing to devastate the bishop’s possessions.

The bishop truly accepted this falsely composed suggestion and was constrained by no small anxiety. He promised Heriwardus a substantial payment if, by any exercise of ingenuity, he could appease them so that they would not come. Heriwardus immediately pretended to go to them to confirm the suspicion raised by his falsehood and to appease them, but turned aside elsewhere. Returning a little later, as though he had obtained peace, he demanded what had been promised to him.

On this man and on others who wickedly deceived him, the bishop spent so much that even now the episcopal seat, and the whole diocese as well, seems to lament that it has been torn apart. Under the same pretext Heriwardus also arrogated to himself the advocacy of several estates, supposedly for their defense, but devastated them through continual exactions more than an enemy robber would have done.

100. (99.) Concerning the death of Bishop Tetdo, and what divine mercy accomplished at his command during the celebration of Mass. During this period, after Arnulf the Elder, count of the Flemings, had died, King Lotharius immediately invaded his possessions—namely, the abbeys of Saint Amand and Saint Vedast, together with the castle. He also invaded Douai and everything as far as the river Lys, with all its dependencies.

This certainly struck great fear into the bishop, who reasoned that the king might soon occupy his own city as well, since it was nearby. Thus continually afflicted by these and similar disturbances, he wasted away with grief and sometimes reproached himself with tearful complaint, saying:

“What have you done, most wretched Tetdo? What have you done, leaving your homeland and coming among barbarians? Behold the plain but deserved recompense for your merits: that you abandoned your father, Saint Severinus.”

[Note: Our author has confused certain matters here. Arnulf the Elder died on 27 March 965, and King Lotharius invaded French Flanders in the same year. But, as we saw above in chapter 87, it is certain that Engrannus still held the see of Cambrai on 25 December 965. Therefore neither Arnulf’s death nor Lotharius’ invasion can have occurred during Tetdo’s episcopate. Perhaps our author confuses this with Lotharius’ later expedition toward Aachen in 978. Moreover, he relates that Tetdo, out of fear of Lotharius, withdrew to Cologne and died there. But in January 974—nine years after that invasion—the bishop was still besieging the castle of Buxude with the emperor. He therefore could have withdrawn to Cologne only later; to suppose that he did so out of weariness from the invasion of 965 in the year 975 or 978 would be excessively absurd.]

Meanwhile the bishop, attempting to swim out of so great a shipwreck, returned to Cologne. And, lest he be battered any longer by such blows, he was, I believe, seized by illness through God’s mercy and departed from this world. He was buried in the basilica of Saint Severinus.

Nor must we pass over what, granted to him by heavenly mercy, we have learned from reliable informants. One day, while he was celebrating the sacred mystery in the monastery of Saint Mary upon the altar of the holy Savior, and when the point had come at which, according to priestly custom, he was to offer the Lord’s body to his mouth, suddenly, in a wondrous manner, the consecrated substance of the most holy body was raised from heaven at the bishop’s command and leapt into his hands, while the ministers looked on in amazement.

[Note: “Nor”—the author himself later supplied the words in the margin. But when the codex was cut apart by the bookbinder, the first letters of each line were cut off: in the first line, *Nec p*; in the second, *quod ei a*; in the third, *te con*; in the fourth, *relat*; and so forth. We supply these lacunae as Colvenerius supplied them from manuscript 2. Manuscript 3 reads: “Non p.; quod superna p.; c. a. c.; majoribus a.; Q. n. d. d. i. m. s. M. ante a. s. S, s. m. c. e. u. v. esset, q. c. dominicum more s. offerre d. mirum in m. de sacrosancti c. mysterio ad n. episcopi; the remainder is missing,” with the space of one line left blank.]

101. (100.) Duke Charles entered Cambrai for its protection and committed many evils. After his death, the cause of a much harsher pestilence arose, and the church of Cambrai was shipwrecked amid storms far more violent. The emperor was far away from the borders of his kingdom, staying to conquer the Slavs against whom he had marched, while the Lotharingian princes who had been left behind were uncertain what they should do about restoring the bishop.

They had already heard that King Lotharius had occupied the episcopal possessions of Arras, and therefore feared that he might seize the city of Cambrai as well by a sudden attack. Accordingly, the counts—Godefrid, than whom no other was more distinguished in character, and Arnulf, who was no less outstanding in counsel—being greatly troubled, approached Duke Charles, the brother of King Lotharius. Emperor Otto had placed Charles over Lower Lotharingia, having won him over by many benefices so that he might resist his brother’s movements more powerfully alongside him.

The counts, after conferring together, urged him to enter quickly the city deprived of its shepherd, defend it from his brother’s attack and from every other invader, and bind the vassals of that place to loyalty toward the emperor by oaths and hostages, until the emperor returned to his homeland and restored a bishop.

Charles readily agreed to this plan, but, handling it badly, did not carry it out with equitable execution. Accompanied by a large force, including the aforesaid counts, he came into the city; but, being as he was inept and slow-witted, he engaged in detestable usurpations, so that he appeared more a robber than a protector, more a violator than a guardian.

The aforesaid counts, therefore, indignant and moved to anger, left him there and returned to their own lands. Charles, meanwhile, having found the opportunity and favor of the place and sufficient food for all, sent for his wife. He ordered a bed to be prepared for her in the bishop’s chamber with complete presumption. He consumed all the resources intended for the bishop’s needs in extravagant feasts and lavish banquets. He squandered the church’s treasure, sold prebends, and even, having purchased the business of ecclesiastical administration, arrogated to himself the right to distribute it to those who bought it [Col. 0103B]. Thus he carried the burden of complete disgrace for so long, until the emperor returned and restored matters to a better condition.

102. (101.) Rothard assumed the episcopal see. When the frosts of winter’s harshness had settled upon the land, the emperor recalled his army from the war and returned on Christmas Day to the estate of Polida, his own seat [Note: Otto II celebrated Christmas at the palace of Polde twice, in 974 and 979. But he did not set out against the Slavs in 974, but in 975 and 977. Therefore the year intended here must be 979.] (979).

When the vacancy of the church of Cambrai was reported to him there, by the common vote and acclamation of the Lotharingians, and indeed at the urging of Nocher, bishop of Liège, he bestowed the episcopal vestment upon Rothard, a man born of noble lineage and adorned with pious character. He judged that Rothard, by the gentleness of his disposition, might restrain the savagery of the people of Cambrai [Note: “will be able to subdue,” *Werde swingen konnen*.].

Having received the dignity of this gift, Rothard visited the flock entrusted to him and went to the city around the beginning of Lent (980). Not long afterwards he was ordained by Albero, archbishop of Rheims, with the greatest reverence, since he had maintained friendship and familiarity with him from childhood; they had been fellow students, specifically in the schools of the monastery of Gorze [Note: Gorze.], from their earliest years.

### 103. (102.) The same bishop demolishes the castle of Vinciacus

When this venerable man undertook the supreme governance, he encountered many grievous and inexplicable affronts. For the entire city, as stated above (chs. 93, 99), was suffering in various ways not only from attacks by outsiders but also from assaults by its own inhabitants; no peace intervened. But, to pass over the rest, nothing was more grievous than what he suffered at the hands of the aforementioned Otto, the invader of the castle of Gogicus [Note: [Col. 0103] Something such as “had fallen upon” seems to have been omitted; cf. ch. 96.], who pressed them with attacks so great and so frequent that he had made all the farmers of the villages, and even the inhabitants of the entire city, tributary to him.

Moreover, to press them with an even heavier assault, he was hastening to fortify a castle beside a little village called Vinciacus [Note: [Col. 0104D] Vinchy.]—it lies four miles from this city—and indeed he would have done so had the bishop not discovered it in time. For while that man was fortifying it and stubbornly laboring at the undertaking with various kinds of toil, the bishop, roused by the bad news, sent without delay a delegation to the aforementioned counts Godefrid and Arnulf, together with other Lotharingians, asking them to gather their troops and hasten to come to him to destroy the hostile work.

They cautiously mustered their companies and, without delay, came by night to the bishop, bringing him exceedingly abundant and very strongly armed assistance. When morning came, the bishop, supported by such a force and accompanied also by his citizens and peasants, attacked the fortified site. With God’s help, he demolished the embankment and leveled with the sand the turreted castle, which was already almost complete [Note: [Col. 0103] “Embankment” is printed as *agere* in witness 1.]. This won him the greatest glory for his courage.

Then, at one moment terrifying the tyrant by force, at another enticing him with gifts, he finally overcame him in every way and brought him to peace with himself. Thus restoring public peace and quiet, he turned almost everyone’s goodwill toward himself, except that of his castellan Walter. This man, however, stirred up many troubles against the bishop and inflicted many disturbances, although the bishop had given him much and increased his possessions with many benefices.

Afterward the venerable pontiff completed the monastery of Saint Mary, which, as we said (ch. 87), Bishop Engrannus had begun but, hindered by the same disturbances mentioned above and soon overtaken by death, had left unfinished. He covered the altar of holy Mary, Mother of God, with a golden panel adorned with precious stones. He also had a large chalice and paten made of the purest gold. He fashioned at his own expense two large and sufficiently resonant bells, which still hang in the tower he built. He assigned the village called Villaris [Note: [Col. 0104D] Villers-Pol, near Quesnoy. COLV.] to the altar of Saint John, for the use of the brothers of that same church of Saint Mary.

### 104. (103.) The emperor begins war against the Saracens, is defeated, and dies soon afterward

After some time had passed, the emperor Otto and King Lothair made peace with one another, having entered into an alliance, and both kingdoms rested in the tranquility that had been established (980). Meanwhile, Otto had gone to Rome and heard that the Saracens were raging through the lands of Apulia. Thus, like a bold young man, strong in hand and boiling with spirit, he hurried the enterprise and allowed no delay (981).

Without postponement, and supported by only a few men whom he had with him, he set out and crossed over to that region. He would not wait for his own men, who were to follow him at intervals along the route, but soon and rashly joined battle with the enemy. For the habit of victory and ignorance of retreat had armed him.

When the engagement took place (982), although he was far inferior in number, he inflicted great slaughter upon the enemy; nevertheless, being defeated, he lost the glory of victory. For courage without counsel is transformed into recklessness [Note: [Col. 0105] The words *Qui—illesus evasit* were at first absent from witness 1, which proceeded immediately with *convertitur. Unde cum probro*, etc. But the author himself deleted the words *Unde cum—estimavit* by drawing lines through them; inserting a sign after *convertitur*, he supplied on an attached slip all the words *Qui—illesus evasit*, prefixing the same sign. In witnesses 2 and 8 the words *Unde, cum—estimavit* are absent, but witnesses 3 and 5 have them.].

Thinking that he should save himself by flight, since he could not escape by land, he quickly plunged into the sea. He saw a little boat belonging to the enemy, which by chance he had noticed not far from the shore without suspecting anything, and with an eager but exceedingly difficult swim he climbed aboard. The rowers, taking pity on him when he was already almost exhausted, brought the boat alongside and received him. Thinking him very different in appearance and unknown to them, they asked the reason for his misfortune.

At last, recognizing from their barbarous speech that he had incautiously fallen into the hands of his enemies, he immediately learned to deceive through fear. As a shipwrecked man among enemies, he sought the means of escape by whatever method he could. He pretended to be a certain man from the maritime city of Bar, a person abounding in great wealth, who had nevertheless suffered shipwreck through an error in navigation. He promised that they would be richly rewarded for their trouble if they brought him there unharmed.

Thus won over, when the rowers had brought their boat to the aforementioned city according to the emperor’s wish, the delighted emperor secretly conveyed the whole matter through intermediaries to Bishop Theoderic of Metz and the other leaders of his people, who had taken refuge in the defense of that city. They, grieving over the king’s danger, thought that he had been captured. He cunningly instructed them to bring him gifts as though they were going to reward the sailors.

They immediately and gladly embraced the unexpected command. They carried the emperor’s chests and the rest of the royal furnishings to the boat, and brought along a very swift horse as well. While the sailors were attending to the gifts that had been brought, the emperor sprang lively from the boat, mounted the horse, and—thus deceiving the enemy—escaped unharmed, contrary to expectation, as I believe, with the Lord’s help.
