Thereupon, departing in disgrace and inflamed with shame, he judged that, with better counsel, he should seek a military force with which to renew the battle. Nevertheless, overtaken by death in the meantime, he died shortly afterward (983, December 7). He was buried at Rome, in the portico of Saint Peter.

### 105. (104.) King Lothair of the Carolingians and Duke Henry of Bavaria each strive for the imperial power of the Lotharingians; the royal child is seized by Henry but later recovered by force

When this became known everywhere, a twofold stain of evil suddenly arose in the kingdom. For, as is characteristic of disturbed morals—or rather of worldly ambition—King Lothair and Duke Henry of Bavaria revived their ancient hatred [Note: [Col. 0105] *Retrudescunt* in witness 1.]. They exchanged peace for war and, seeking to wrest the prerogative of the kingdom from the surviving free namesake—what they had been unable to do while his father was alive—turned their attention to usurping imperial power. For the proximity of the place favored one, while kinship favored the other.

Duke Henry was indeed holding the royal child, treacherously abducted, in custody. Against the will and grief of the other princes, he was depriving him of imperial favor. Meanwhile, after Wifred, bishop of Verdun, had died (982 or 983), Lothair entered the city (984), despite the resistance of many of the bishop’s military retainers, though some others consented, and with a presumed claim to it. He then threatened that he would also seize the bishopric of Cambrai.

At this, Bishop Rothard was moved by no slight terror. Nevertheless, employing the wisest counsel, he approached the king humbly and, through gentle entreaty, purchased his favor to such an extent that, after first capturing the city of the Liégeois and first subjugating several of the Lotharingian princes, he himself too was afterward subjected without difficulty.

Having obtained peace, though with his hope suspended, he rested for the time being, until, with the Lord’s help, his own princes had forcibly wrested the captured child, the emperor’s son, from the hands of the man holding him and restored him to his paternal right. This child [Note: [Col. 0105D] Otto III.] afterward increased in both strength and age and became so powerful that King Lothair returned to him the captured city of Verdun and Count Godefrid [Note: [Col. 0105D] Lothair was prepared to return Godefrid, but only under certain conditions. Because Godefrid refused to accept them, he did not recover his freedom until Lothair had finally died.] [985].

### 106. (103.) The letter sent by the monks of Lobbes to Rothard, bishop of Cambrai, and Notker, bishop of Liège

We do not think it inappropriate to insert what the monks of Lobbes, long deprived of a shepherd, wrote when they approached in a letter (990) the lord bishops Rothard and Notker of Liège, asking that Heriger be appointed abbot for them. Their letter was as follows:

> “To the venerable lords and fathers, Bishops Rothard and Notker, the humble community of Lobbes, most devoted in the duties of faithful prayer.
>
> “Long deprived of a shepherd, and for a very long time lacking the diligent care of a ruler, we approach your fatherhood in submission, since God has willed that one of you should oversee our souls and the other our bodies [Note: [Col. 0106D] The monastery of Lobbes was subject in spiritual matters to the bishop of Cambrai and in temporal matters to the bishop of Liège.]. We ask you to provide us with an abbot who will be what the name signifies: one who will both provide the necessary care for our bodies with paternal affection and not neglect the salvation of souls through the vigilance of a shepherd; who will not diminish his care for interior matters through his occupation with exterior affairs, nor abandon his provision for exterior matters through his concern for interior ones; lest, devoted to outward affairs, he fall away from inward things, or, occupied solely with inward matters, fail to provide his neighbors with what he ought to provide outwardly.
>
> “Let his command or teaching be scattered through the minds of his disciples like leaven of divine justice. Let him strive to be loved more than feared, and in his commands—whether according to God or according to the world—let him be prudent and discerning. Let him strive with the concern appropriate to human capacity after the other things drawn from blessed Benedict.
>
> “For pursuing these aims, we have been unable at this time to find anyone more suitable than the lord Heriger, a man who, God as our witness, has lived among us for many years as a brother, not according to his own estimation but according to ours [Note: [Col. 0107] Corrected in this manner by the editor; witnesses 1 and the others read otherwise.], and who has been of great benefit to us, while fulfilling for many of our number the strenuous office of teacher and educator.
>
> “Although, by his own testimony, he lacks the catalogue of virtues which blessed Benedict requires of an abbot, he has nevertheless always possessed the outlook of a good intention for aspiring to these goods, according to the evangelical saying: ‘If your eye is simple, your whole body will be full of light’ (Matthew 6:22)—that is, whatever the work may be in public, let the intention nevertheless remain good in secret.
>
> “You should know that our unanimity is not lacking in his election, in accordance with the institution of our rule, which commands either that the congregation be made altogether concordant in this matter or that even the smallest part prevail through sounder counsel. For if anyone, even secretly, is not in agreement with this election, he has pronounced judgment upon himself, without your conscience contradicting it: that he wishes to be wholly useless and unproductive.
>
> “We testify before Jesus and his dreadful judgment that, to our knowledge, he has not aspired to the governance of souls through money or ambition—ambition being the first item in the fourfold subdivision of pastoral care. But how he teaches, that is, whether he knows from where to bring forth new things and old, is certain to be sufficiently present in him, both for you and for us.
>
> “As for how he lives—which we have recognized as the most important matter, and as the matter most likely to trouble his conscience—we who were of sounder counsel have impressed upon him the consolations of blessed Benedict, which are expressed in these words:
>
> “‘While he avoids accounting for the affairs of others, he is made solicitous about his own; and while he supplies others with correction through his admonitions, he himself is made corrected from his vices. For he is exceedingly like a pagan and a publican who, reproving others, is unwilling to be irreproachable, since blessed Benedict himself says: “Whatever he teaches his disciples to be contrary, let him judge in his own actions not to be done.”
>
> “‘And concerning anxiety over lesser possessions he says: “Nothing is lacking to those who fear God” (Psalm 33:10). And: “The Lord will not afflict the soul of the righteous with hunger” (Proverbs 10:3). And: “I was young, and now I am old, yet I have not seen the righteous forsaken nor his offspring seeking bread” (Psalm 36:25). Therefore, “Seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things will be added to you” (Matthew 6:33).’
>
> “Finally, under the solemnity of divine fear, we set before him the saying of blessed Pope Gregory (Pastoral Rule 1.5) concerning those who can be of benefit but refuse to preside:
>
> “‘They will be held guilty at the dreadful judgment for as many persons as they could have benefited here.’
>
> “Since he has given his assent to these things, we promise him, with you and the others as witnesses, the good of obedience according to our rule; and, subject in all things to your authority, we shall adequately fulfill toward him the submission that accords with our way of life.
>
> “Let not your excellence and prudence think that in this election we wished merely to employ flattering words and serve the buskins of eloquence. Rather, from a true and sincere heart we have drawn forth for your greatness those things which we know to be necessary for our desolation and for the man himself who has been elected.”

### 107. (106.) The irregular conduct of Abbot Fulrad, and how he set the count of Flanders and Bishop Rothard at enmity

At that time Fulrad, a monk in name only, presided over the abbey of Saint Vedast. Living irregularly, he stripped the profession of the holy name of the dignity of honor. For, having wickedly neglected the concerns of pastoral care, he was excessively entangled in worldly affairs; and, with the desire of the flesh acting as his procurer—I shudder to say it—he utterly falsified the appearance of the holy habit.

What he ought to have spent for the needs of the church or of the brothers, alas, he shamefully squandered among the gatherings of his mistresses. For this reason the bishop often summoned him secretly, judged him strictly, and rebuked him severely. But when, hardened by an incorrigible obstinacy, he did not sufficiently desist from what he had begun, he was publicly reproved and struck by right of the apostolic authority’s rod.

Afterward, however, putting on the appearance of penitence and resorting to satisfaction, he confessed his fault and asked forgiveness, and was granted absolution. But as time went on, he again clung to his former wickedness. So that he might pursue his own filth more freely, he began to introduce a new source of hatred between the bishop and Arnulf [Note: [Col. 0107D] Rather Baldwin the Bald, who became count of Flanders after Arnulf in 988. The author himself shows below, in ch. 116, that Baldwin must be understood here: he says that Fulrad sowed false accounts of discord between him and Count Baldwin, as stated above.] the count of Flanders and his faithful men, so that the bishop, troubled by hostility toward the count, might cease correcting his wickedness.

This crafty instigator added to the growth of discord a deceptive and plausible assertion: namely, that he possessed privileges of Saint Vindician, bishop of that same see, confirmed by apostolic authority. In these, he claimed, it had been decreed that the monks of Saint Vedast were not to show deference to the bishop of the church of Cambrai [Note: [Col. 0109] *Abere* in witness 1.]. He drew this false argument from the fact that blessed Vindician, in his own time, had excluded all disturbances from the monastery of Saint Vedast by a written command, so that the monks might live in peace according to the rule of Saint Benedict and serve God—not so that, living disorderly [Note: [Col. 0109] Witness 1 reads *inordinante*.] and shamefully, as this man and his companions did, they might depart from their purpose.

This man, who was attempting to evade the bishop’s discipline and correction and, contrary to the authority of evangelical and apostolic instruction, to shake his neck free from submission to the bishop’s yoke, misunderstood the saying of Saint Benedict, where, treating of the appointment of an abbot, he says among other things:

> “The bishop to whose diocese the monastery itself belongs.”

Anyone who has leisure to examine carefully what this means should investigate the writings of that same volume.

This wretched man had indeed become forgetful of how humbly and reverently his predecessors once approached the lord Theodoric, bishop of that same see, at the time when the Danes were miserably raging throughout the neighborhood of this diocese (see ch. 44). They implored him because, being unequal to so great a burden and afraid to undertake so difficult an affair without the bishop’s authority, they wished him to move the body of Saint Vedast from the place where it had been found and, after placing it upon a bier, to prepare it for removal elsewhere because of fear of the Danes.

The bishop, appropriately anticipating the wishes of his people, readily fulfilled all that they asked. Through the exercise of his authority, he had that most precious treasure transferred, amid a multitude of people, to the church of Beauvais. From those same brothers he duly received the greatest praises and thanksgivings.

After a very long interval [Note: [Col. 0109D] “Distance” or “separation.”], when the lands had become quiet after the Danes’ departure and the same monks were preparing to bring the holy body back to its former seat, blessed Bishop Theodoric had long since died. They therefore decided to invite his successor Dodilo, the fourth bishop, to undertake this matter. They sent him entreaties and requested the authority of his presence.

He, satisfying their desire, proceeded to the aforementioned church of Beauvais. After the holy treasure had been restored to its own place with the greatest reverence, he addressed the people and, by his episcopal authority, commended the annual day of the translation of the holy body, July 15, to perpetual celebration. For this reason the blessed bishop was rewarded by those same brothers with demonstrations of respect and honorably heaped with generous praises.

But these expressions of goodwill and reverent submission, which his predecessors had shown to all the bishops of this diocese, Fulrad and his followers wickedly consigned to oblivion [Note: [Col. 0109] Witness 1 reads *oblioni*.]. They refused to be subjected to the bishop, contrary to evangelical and apostolic decrees.

Later, however, he was proved to be subject by the force of much authority. Finally, coming to his senses, he was bent back—though unwillingly—under the yoke of submission. For whoever strives to avoid the bishop’s yoke is also shown to be fleeing from Christ.

No one is gathered into the unity of the church without the condition of episcopal ministry, especially since the Lord himself, the lawgiver, is shown in the Gospel in many ways to have been subject, together with his disciples, to priests. He himself bears witness when he says: “I have not come to abolish the law but to fulfill it” (Matthew 5:17). To disciples subject to wicked priests he says: “Do what they say, but do not do what they do” (Matthew 23:3).

### 108. (107.) He obtained the confirmation by royal commands of the immunities concerning the possessions of Saint Mary

He acquired for the church of holy Mary, Mother of God, the estate called Fontanas [Note: [Col. 0110D] Fontaine-Notre-Dame.], which is not far away. He also obtained the confirmation by Otto III of the immunities granted to the church by earlier emperors, through a charter of the following kind:

> “In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. Otto, king by the favor of divine clemency.
>
> “When, for love of divine worship, we favor the just and reasonable petitions of God’s servants, we confidently believe that we are fortified by heavenly grace. Therefore let the diligence of all our faithful, present as well as future, know that the venerable Rothard, bishop of the city of Cambrai, brought before our sight the immunities of blessed memory belonging to our grandfather Otto and to his namesake, our father, the august emperors [Col. 0110C]. In these documents it was inserted how the aforesaid august emperors had always held the aforementioned see—which is dedicated to the honor of holy Mary, Mother of God and ever-virgin—in the fullest protection and under the defense of immunity, for the love of God and the tranquility of the brothers residing there.
>
> “For the security of the matter, the aforesaid Bishop Rothard asked us to confirm by our authority the authority of that king, out of love and reverence for holy Mary, Mother of God. Accordingly, at the intercession of that bishop and of our other faithful, Hildebold, the venerable bishop of the church of Worms, and Nothger, the honored prelate of the church of Liège, we consented; and thus we granted everything and strengthened it by this command of our authority.
>
> “Therefore we command and order that no public judge, count, or anyone whatsoever exercising judicial power dare enter, in our time or in that of our successors, the churches, places, fields, or other possessions of that church—which the aforesaid church now justly and legally holds or possesses in any counties or territories under our authority, or which shall hereafter be bestowed upon the same church by Catholic men—for the hearing of cases, the collection of fines, the provision of lodging or transport, the taking of sureties, the coercive disciplining of the men of that church, whether free or enslaved, living upon its land, or the exaction of any payments or unlawful pretexts. Nor shall anyone presume to demand at all the things mentioned above [Note: [Col. 0111] Missing in witness 1.].
>
> “But let the aforesaid prelate and his successors possess in quiet order, under the protection of our immunity, the property of the aforesaid church, together with its cells, possessions, and persons legally subject to it; let them faithfully obey our imperial authority; and, for the stability of ourselves and of the entire empire granted and preserved for us by God, let them freely entreat God’s mercy, together with the clergy and people subject to them [Note: [Col. 0111] The words *Dei misericordiam* are missing, with a space of approximately six letters left in witnesses 1 and 3.].
>
> “Whatever our treasury might have been able to exact from these things, we have perpetually granted for the provision of the lamps of that church [Note: [Col. 0111] Witnesses 1 and 3 read *concinanda*.]. Moreover, by our generosity [Note: [Col. 0111] Witness 1 reads *largitionem*.] we grant to the aforesaid bishop and his successors every toll, together with the mint of his city of Cambrai, on the condition that nine parts be assigned to the bishops’ uses, while the tenth part shall perpetually serve the needs of the brothers of that congregation as our alms.
>
> “Furthermore, we establish that no duke, count, viscount, or anyone whatsoever exercising judicial power presume to violate our authority or that of our fathers, the kings [Note: [Col. 0111] That is, “royal authority”; cf. ch. 64.]. If anyone does so, let him be liable in royal proceedings and, in addition, be judged liable for six hundred solidi, namely, so that two parts may be assigned to the archive of that church and our royal treasury receive the third [Note: [Col. 0111] Witness 1 reads *tertia*.]. Thus no one may thereafter presume to attempt such a thing.
>
> “We also confirm this by our authority, so that just as the aforesaid church received and had confirmed these privileges from our grandfather and our father of blessed memory, so they may henceforth be preserved inviolate. And so that this authority of ours may be believed more truly and certainly by the faithful of holy God’s church and by our own faithful [Note: [Col. 0111] Witness 1 reads *est*.], we have confirmed it below with our own hand and ordered it marked with our ring.
>
> “Sign of the lord Otto, most glorious king.
>
> “I, Hildebold, bishop and chancellor, have recognized this in the place of Archbishop Willigis.
>
> “Given on the fifth day before the Kalends of July, in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 991, indiction 4, and in the eighth year of the reign of Otto III. Done at Nijmegen, successfully. Amen.”

[Note: [Col. 0111] In witness 1 the following diploma was added afterward by the author himself on a now-lost sheet, though Colvenerius had still seen it. It is missing from witness 5, but can be read in witnesses 2 and 3.]

> “In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. Otto, king by the favor of divine clemency.
>
> “If we readily make ourselves approachable by the pious prayers of the faithful, it should be believed that we shall remain steadfast in our principate and endure as those who will remain in eternal blessedness. Therefore let the diligence of all our faithful, present and future, know how, fulfilling the petition of Bishop Notker, as well as of Hildebold and our other faithful, we have given one forest (*forastum*) to Bishop Rothard of the church of Cambrai, for the church of Saint Mary, for the remedy of our soul and those of our parents. It extends in length from Mount Sauvlonir [Note: [Col. 0111C] This appears to be Montplaisir, near Câteau. LE GLAY.] to the place where the two Elprae fall into the Sambre; in breadth, from the village called Basius [Note: [Col. 0111C] Barzy, canton of Guise. COLV.] and the place called Gurgunces [Note: [Col. 0111C] Gourgonce, near Barzy. COLV.], as the Sambre and the two Elprae flow, up to the inner bank of the farther Elprae.
>
> “We have secured this by our ban, namely, on the condition that no person, great or small, presume to hunt within the bounds of the aforesaid forest (*forastum*) except with the permission of the aforesaid Bishop Rothard and his successors. Rather, he and his successors shall hold the right of hunting by our royal gift and may grant permission to hunt to whomever they please.
>
> “And so that this gift of our donation may remain firm, we have ordered this command to be written and signed by the impression of our seal, and have confirmed it with our own hand, as appears below [Col. 0112C].
>
> “Sign of the lord Otto, most glorious emperor.
>
> “I, Hildebold, bishop and chancellor, have recognized this in the place of Archbishop Willigis.
>
> “Acted on the eighth day before the Kalends of May, in the year of the Lord’s incarnation [997] [Note: [Col. 0111] A space was left for the number in witnesses 1, 2, and 3. Of the three copies of this charter preserved at Cambrai in Colvenerius’s time, two had the year 995 and the third 983. Indiction 8 fell in the year 995; but at that time Otto was not yet emperor, since he was not crowned until May 21, 996. In May 997 Otto was in fact staying at Aachen; for this reason we would assign the charter to that year, except that our author immediately states that Rothard’s successor, named in this charter, traveled to Rome with the emperor, where he too was elevated to the summit of imperial power and consecrated by Gregory, who himself was not consecrated pope until May 3, 996. There must therefore be an error in the diploma.], indiction 8, and in the first year of Otto’s imperial rule [Note: [Col. 0111] The words from *anno* through *amen* are missing.]. Done at the palace of Grannum [Note: [Col. 0112C] Aachen.]. Amen.”

### 109. The death of Bishop Rothard

Meanwhile Bishop Rothard, called to receive the reward for his labor, departed from this world [995] [Note: [Col. 0112C] *Necrologium Beatae Mariae Cameracensis*, now Bibliothèque de Cambrai no. 165, thirteenth-century copy: “On the fifteenth day before the Kalends of September, Bishop Rothard died.”]. He was buried beside the monastery of Saint Mary, on its southern side. Over his tomb one of his familiar associates, a provost named Godelinus, built an oratory of the apostles Simon and Jude and of Saint Severinus.

### 110. Erluin succeeds him and is ordained at Rome

After him Erluin was appointed (995). He was archdeacon of the church of Liège and learned in both ecclesiastical and secular affairs; by often wearing down the thresholds of princes, he had become renowned far and wide.

Bishop Notker of blessed memory advised him to hasten to Mathilda, with whom Erluin himself was familiar—namely, the daughter of the elder Otto, the emperor, and abbess of the church of Quitinaborch [Note: [Col. 0113D] Quedlinburg.]—so that through her support he might attain the dignity of the episcopate.

A certain man named Azelinus, from the village of Truncinis [Note: [Col. 0113D] Drongen, near Ghent.], son of Count Baldwin of Flanders by a concubine and later bishop of Paris, also approached Sophia, the sister of the young emperor, with money, so that through her influence he might obtain the summit of the episcopate.

The emperor was therefore petitioned by both sides, but, by God’s providence, he was inclined more toward the request of the other party. For, without Sophia’s knowledge, he had agreed to her aunt Mathilda and on the solemn feast of Saint Dionysius entrusted the pastoral governance to Erluin.

Having received so great a gift, Erluin sought the city entrusted to him. But when he discovered that the possessions of his predecessor Rothard had been devastated by Walter and by others who ought to have been the church’s soldiers, he groaned.

At about the same time (991), Arnulf, archbishop of Reims, had been deposed from the episcopal rank for many crimes, especially for disloyalty to his lord [Note: [Col. 0113D] That is, against his lord Hugh Capet.]. In his place sat Gerbert, than whom no one afterward proved more learned.

Nevertheless, while certain bishops were debating the matter, it was determined that because Arnulf had been degraded without the knowledge and authority of the pope of the Roman see, a legitimate recourse to that same see remained open [Note: [Col. 0113] This is Colvenerius’s conjecture; in witness 1, after *pa*, approximately five letters have been erased. Witness 1 reads *prevaleret*.].

Therefore, since a prolonged dispute existed between them, Erluin traveled to Rome with the lord emperor, who was also to be elevated there to the summit of imperial power, in order to be ordained by the pope (996, March). But shortly before they arrived, after Pope John had died (May 3), Bruno—later called Gregory—was elevated to the apostolic see with the consent of the Romans (May 21). The emperor was therefore consecrated by him and received the imperial diadem, while Erluin received the summit of priestly pontifical office.

### 111

Afterward, while a synod was being held there before the emperor, with the pope presiding together with bishops, abbots, and priests, and the necessary affairs of the church being thoroughly discussed [Note: [Col. 0113] Witness 1 reads *nessariis*.], Bishop Erluin rose and solemnly laid before them a complaint concerning the plunderers of his parish. He also brought forward publicly the fact that, as we stated above, he had recently found the possessions of his predecessor devastated by Walter and others.

Therefore, with the pope confirming the matter—or rather, with the bishops, abbots, and all who were present also giving their assent—he obtained the preparation of a document of the following kind [Note: [Col. 0113] After this word, witness 1 leaves the rest of the page blank; the next page begins at the top with “The New Castle,” written in exactly the same hand and ink. The bull is therefore missing, although the scribe intended to supply it. The same thing was done in witness 3. Colvenerius provided the bull from witness 2, and we insert it here in brackets because the author intended it to be supplied, as shown by the word “of the following kind.”]:

> [“Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God . . .” (See *Patrologia*, vol. CXXXVII, col. 904.) “Written by the hand of Petrisgionus, notary and scribe of the holy Roman church, in the month of May and in indiction 9. Fare well in Christ. + In the first year of the pontificate of the lord Gregory, supreme pontiff and universal pope of the church, in the first year, and in the eleventh year of the empire of the lord Otto III, emperor [Note: [Col. 0113D] False. It was the first year of the empire and the thirteenth of the kingship.”]]

### 112. He Fortified the New Castle by Royal Authority [Col. 0114B] (996)

After these events had taken place, the bishop returned to the see entrusted to him. Once the soldiers had been pacified, he found the land of his parish quiet, except for a few villages around the forest of Thiérache [Note: [Col. 0113D] The forest of Thiérache extended from the sources [Col. 0114D] of the Sambre to the borders of the county of Namur. Le Glay.], which certain extremely dangerous soldiers from Laon and Vermandois frequently disturbed by covert attacks and often ravaged by open invasions.

Therefore the bishop, concerned for the matter, obtained an imperial order to fortify a castle at the village of Perrona [Note: [Col. 0114D] Today Le Câteau; cf. ch. 86.], on the River Selle [Note: [Col. 0114D] Selle. Le Glay.]. This village had long before been taken away from this church, but, as we related earlier [Note: [Col. 0114D] Our author is mistaken; he related nothing on this subject.], had been restored by King Cendebold in the time of Bishop Dodilo; afterward, however, we do not know how, it had again been withdrawn and granted as a benefice to powerful men. Nevertheless, by means of the properties that Bishop John had acquired for this church in the county of Condroz and in Hesbaye, Erluin redeemed it. In this village, then, around which the aforementioned plunderers were raging most violently, he obtained by imperial command the construction of a fortified castle, so that it might be an obstacle to robbers and a protection of liberty for the peasant inhabitants all around.

We have decided to append the charter of immunity in the following form:

> “In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. Otto, by the favor of divine clemency, august Roman emperor.
>
> “If we strive to exalt the possessions and increase the honors of places devoted to divine worship, we know and truly believe that this should be proclaimed not only with human praise but also rewarded with divine recompense. Therefore let all our faithful, both present and future, know that we have granted to Erluin, venerable bishop, at the intervention of Bishop Leo and the others, the right, authority, and permission to establish, regulate, and construct a market, together with coinage, tolls, the ban, and all the services of the public authority, on a certain possession of the holy Church of Cambrai, at the place called the Castle of Saint Mary, formerly called Vendelgeias [Note: [Col. 0115] *que* for *quod* in 1.], which is situated in the county and pagus of Cambrai and in the county of Count Arnulf [Note: [Col. 0115D] Concerning him, cf. above, ch. 95.].
>
> “We grant the aforesaid market, coinage, tolls, ban, and the entire public function in perpetuity to the holy Church of Cambrai, on the condition that no duke, margrave, or count, nor any other person, shall have any authority over the said market except with the permission of Bishop Erluin and his successors.
>
> “Therefore, by imperial power, we order and decree that all persons visiting, going to, conducting business in, or residing at the said market shall, both on their journey there and on their return, enjoy the same peace as merchants lawfully possess in the market of the city of Cambrai.
>
> “Accordingly, whoever attempts to break or violate the aforesaid market shall pay a ban of our jurisdiction equal to that which, as the law requires, those who rashly disturb the market of Cambrai must pay.
>
> “And so that the authority of this grant of ours may remain more firmly established, we have ordered this document to be sealed after strengthening it with our own hand.
>
> “The sign of Lord Otto, unconquered Caesar.
>
> “Heribert, chancellor, recognized this in the place of Archbishop Willigis.
>
> “Given on the eleventh day before the Kalends of May [April 21], in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1001, indiction 14; in the seventeenth year of Otto III’s reign and the fifth of his empire. Done at Ravenna, successfully. Amen.”

### 113. Concerning the Injuries Inflicted by the Soldiers, and How He Enlarged the Monastery of Saint Autbert and Elevated the Episcopal Residence [Col. 0115C]

From those very soldiers whom he had appointed as guardians of his castle, he suffered many injuries. Nevertheless, after they had been defeated, peace having been negotiated and an agreement established, he found rest.

At his command, a certain archdeacon of his, Godefrid, enlarged the monastery of Saint Autbert, which lies within the city walls. The bishop himself, for the support of the brothers, returned one village, namely Avesna [Note: [Col. 0115D] Avesne-le-Sec, near Bouchain. Colv.], and granted another, Tiliodium [Note: [Col. 0116D] Tilloi, near Cambrai. Colv.], so that the service of God might increase and the number of the brothers multiply. The bishop also founded the episcopal residence, elevated by imposing buildings.

### 114. Concerning the Death of Otto III and the Succession of Henry

Meanwhile, when conflicts arose between the counts—namely Baldwin [Note: [Col. 0116D] The Bald, 988–1036.] of Flanders and Arnulf [Col. 0115D] of Valenciennes—an extremely bitter discord grew up, which, advancing even to war, repeatedly disturbed the peace of this city.

Because Bishop Erluin was on familiar terms with Count Arnulf, as with a companion in their common submission under the emperor, Baldwin inflicted many hardships upon this city. His fury increased still more when he heard of the death of Emperor Otto III. [Note: [Col. 0115] The following words, *at the same time … comets appeared*, were not originally in manuscript 1: between *siquidem* and *imperator* only one word of about seven letters could be read. The author himself deleted that word, placing a sign of deletion over it, and added in its place on an attached slip the words *at the same time … comets appeared*. Manuscripts 2 and 3 still saw and copied this addition; manuscript 5 no longer had it, and nothing now survives from it except the holes made by a needle in the parchment and a little thread.]

At that same time (1000), the emperor, having gone to Rome, was staying in the ancient palace on the Aventine. Like a young man, bold in strength and powerful by birth, he was contemplating something great—even impossible—and was attempting to raise the power of the Roman Empire to the might of the ancient kings. He also intended to reform ecclesiastical customs, which the greed of the Romans was corrupting through depraved commercial practices, according to the standard of the earlier grace.

To accomplish this more effectively, he showed the Romans the highest favor of familiarity. Preferring them to his own Germans, since they were inhabitants of the place and knowledgeable about its customs and practices, he kept them as his counselors and foremost associates. This was surely well and prudently arranged, if it had reached its intended result. But neither happened.

For the more favorably he treated the Romans, the more proudly they displayed their insolence. Very often excessive familiarity gives birth to contempt. Moreover, because he exercised both observance of the law and the standard of justice with impartial moderation, indignation soon arose; and, as their unrestrained inequality of character dictates, they were driven from love to hatred and exchanged friendship for sedition.

The discord grew so far that, making a sudden attack, they killed a certain distinguished young man, Mazelin, who was a friend of the emperor. Finally, they shut up the emperor himself [Note: [Col. 0115] Manuscript 4 omits *himself*.] in the aforementioned palace with a force gathered for the purpose, for three days, so that neither food could be brought to him [Note: [Col. 0115] Manuscript 3 reads *they gave*.], nor could anyone go out to him or enter to see him (June 1001).

He would scarcely have escaped the danger if Henry, duke of Bavaria—who, as will become clear below [Note: [Col. 0115] Manuscript 3 reads *in the subsequent events*.], afterward put on the royal insignia—and Hugh, margrave of Italy, had not come to his aid.

These men, who were outside in their camps, were stunned by the sudden reversal of events. Uncertain what they should undertake, they judged that the rash audacity of the enemy ought to be calmed more prudently by words than provoked by arms. Thus, approaching them peacefully, they soothed their fury with gentle speech. Saying that they would establish peace [Note: [Col. 0115] Manuscript 3 reads *enter into peace*.], they obtained access after the siege had been lifted.

When they had entered the elder’s presence, they informed him that the besiegers’ force was invincible and that they had no safe hope except in flight [Note: [Col. 0115] Manuscript 2 reads *defection*.]. Therefore they secretly and skillfully led him outside, away from his enemies.

Thus the emperor went out together with Pope Gerbert, who was called Sylvester [Note: [Col. 0117] Manuscript 2 reads *Rome*.], and traveled through Ravenna and the cities of other provinces, gathering aid to avenge the injury inflicted upon him.

While he was pursuing this purpose, he was seized by illness and, overtaken by death, ended his life in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1002 [Note: [Col. 0117] The year-number is missing in manuscript 3, with a space left blank.].

In that same year, before he died, many portents were seen in the sky. On a certain day, the nineteenth day before the Kalends of January—that is, January 24, 1002—around the ninth hour, something like a burning torch descended from the riven sky toward the earth in a long course resembling lightning. Its brilliance was so great that not only those who were outside in the fields but also those indoors were struck in the eyes when the light burst through every opening [Note: [Col. 0117] Manuscript 3 reads *bursting in*.].

While the fissure in the sky gradually vanished, as the elements drew closer together [Note: [Col. 0117] Manuscript 2 reads *returned*.], meanwhile—marvelous to relate!—it appeared to take shape like a serpent, with its head increasing in size and with blue feet [Note: [Col. 0117] Manuscript 3 reads *which*.]. Shortly afterward it disappeared, to the great astonishment of the many who watched it.

In that same year comets also appeared. The emperor set out to wage war against the Romans with a large expedition, but died on the way. His princes, dukes, and bishops nevertheless brought his body back with honor, and he was buried in the church at Aachen, where he rests in peace.

After his death, the princes of Lotharingia chose Henry, the son of the aforementioned Duke Henry of Bavaria, for royal rule: a man pious in character, prudent in counsel, vigorous in war, and a close kinsman of the deceased emperor.

Meanwhile Baldwin, having gathered a large force, laid siege to the castle of Valenciennes. Because Arnulf was far inferior in numbers, Baldwin drove him out and presumed to claim the castle. After these events, King Henry, aroused to action, repeatedly summoned Baldwin to justice; but Baldwin continually resisted and despised his summonses.

A few days later, therefore, the king, supported by a multitude of his princes and also accompanied by King Robert of the Franks and Duke Richard of Normandy, attacked the same castle in anger and fell upon Baldwin. But because the sins of the people demanded it—and indeed because some of his own men, through treachery, withdrew their support—his hope was frustrated. Accomplishing nothing, he returned home (1006).

### 115. The Bishop, Fearing Baldwin, Goes to the King

Afterward Baldwin considered Bishop Erluin the instigator of this siege and threatened that he would exact strict vengeance upon him and upon the very heart of the entire city.

The bishop, terrified, entrusted the administration of the city and the affairs of the public authority to his archdeacons and leading soldiers. To avoid being imprudently crushed by that threatening tyrant, he sought the king.

He remained there until the king, having gathered a large body of soldiers, invaded the castle of Ghent in order to ravage the land (1007). After capturing some of Baldwin’s leading soldiers, he terrified Baldwin so greatly that Baldwin soon became submissive, came to make satisfaction on behalf of his entire family, returned the castle of Valenciennes to the king, and, giving hostages and taking an oath, promised that thereafter he would preserve loyalty and peace toward him.

Later, however, the king was oppressed by serious and numerous rebellions. Therefore, so that Baldwin might be of assistance to him, he granted him the castle of Valenciennes as a benefice.

### 116. Concerning the Fury of Abbot Fulrad, and How, After His Deposition, the Abbey Was Given to Richard

For a while the bishop obtained peace, but he was not at all free from the insolence of the aforementioned Fulrad, who did not cease in any way from renewing the same disgraceful practices that Rothard had suppressed.

Because the bishop had often summoned and sternly and canonically rebuked him, Fulrad sowed false fabrications of discord between the bishop and Count Baldwin, as we have said above [Note: [Col. 0117] Ch. 107, where the matter concerns the bishop and Arnulf, count of Flanders.]. He was plainly currying favor with the count, claiming that he possessed the privileges mentioned above.

Unhappy man! He did not recall blessed Augustine, who says that those dispute wickedly against the keys of the Church who strive to abolish the ecclesiastical authority which they plainly acknowledge to reside in bishops. Otherwise, the Church, which possesses authority in the episcopate, could in no way have the power of binding and loosing.

But Fulrad, disregarding the bishop’s sacred admonitions, persisted more and more in his seductions and did not withdraw from his wicked undertakings. Thus he was often publicly rebuked by Erluin, no less than previously by Rothard; yet he constantly resisted and defended himself with brazen cunning. Nevertheless, he was bound by the bond of anathema.

Moreover, to crown his fury and increase his condemnation, moved by the devil as his incanting instigator against the bishop, he raised his neck in such swelling pride that, having gathered a large force and with Count Baldwin’s consent, he set fires among the bishop’s goods in the territory of Arras.

Yet, by the dispensation of divine mercy [Note: [Col. 0117] Manuscript 1 reads *despensatione*.], the enormity of his crimes could not long remain hidden from the count. Once fully discovered, he paid the price of his slanders.

For when the count finally perceived the nature of his wicked schemes, he was grieved to realize that he had long been deceived by his frauds. Understanding that Fulrad’s accusations had been accumulated more through deceit than supported by truth, he justly transferred all the charges to the accuser himself.

At Arras, therefore, after a council had been convened in the very cloister of the monks (1004), he invited the bishop, as the church’s teacher and master. He set out the matter before the brothers and, with the bishop listening, asked how Fulrad had governed the abbey up to that time.

When it was discovered that Fulrad had taught nothing of religion inwardly and had badly dissipated the goods outwardly, the bishop, after he had been rebuked legally and canonically, sent him into custody. Heribert, a monk of good repute, assumed the abbacy.

He was full of perfect and irreproachable conduct and religious simplicity, but was less suited to repair and reorganize the many things that his predecessor had destroyed. For this reason the count, with the bishop’s advice and appointment, entrusted the removed abbey to Richard, a most religious man [Note: [Col. 0119D] Abbot of Saint-Viton of Verdun, who died in 1046.].

Richard so thoroughly trained the brothers in the rule of disciplined religion and worked so diligently to increase their material resources that, with God’s favor, no abbey in our region was superior in religious observance or richer in resources.

After Fulrad’s wickedness had been extinguished, Richard also remained always subject to the lord bishop with complete reverence and obeyed him in all things, as was fitting, with an unstained seal of love [Note: [Col. 0119] From here to the end of the chapter, the author himself supplied the text in the margin.].

Fulrad, however, taking with him the money that he had stolen from the possessions of Saint Vedast, went to the Church of Reims. Having lamented the necessities of his sufferings, he intended to bend Archbishop Arnulf, who at that time presided over the church, by offering gifts and seeking his advice.

He bribed the archbishop and his ministers with a price, so that, having supposedly been deposed through prejudice, he might perhaps obtain access to the archbishop’s private favor through his authority. For the archbishop himself was degenerate in spirit. Although he could in no way prejudice the aforementioned ecclesiastical constitution, he was nevertheless greedy for gifts and accepted what was offered, caring more for his own avarice than for Fulrad’s cause.

While Fulrad suspended his hopes in the expectation of this support for some time, he led a shameful life in the city itself and conducted business with Jews. Meanwhile, wretched man, overtaken by death and struck by divine vengeance, he died unrepentant and unconfessed (1004).

### 117. Concerning the Death of Walter the Castellan

Meanwhile Walter the castellan, seized by a serious illness, sent a delegation and begged the bishop to grant his land as a benefice to his son Walter, so that his son might serve as a soldier while retaining the secure use of his paternal inheritance.

The bishop, believing that the son would be far more intolerable than his intolerable father—as later events proved—refused his request. Nevertheless, yielding somewhat, he replied that he would do so if Walter first corrected, by making satisfaction, the transgressions he had committed against the Church and the poor of Christ, and also returned the village of Salliacum, which he held against the bishop’s will.

He had granted this village to his wife on the following condition: that she serve the bishop [Note: [Col. 0119D] That is, himself, namely the bishop.] in women’s work, and that the wickedness of her lord [Note: [Col. 0120D] That is, her husband.] should cease.

But because the bishop himself had received no change from either of them—that is, neither did the wife provide the promised service, nor did he see the man’s savagery cease—he sought to recover the village.

Although Walter was already near death, worn down by an incurable illness, he in no way came to his senses and amended his conduct. Calling his soldiers to him, he bound them by oath to loyalty toward his son. He admonished and urged them that, if he should happen to die, they should observe his son with complete devotion, faith, and goodwill, and stubbornly support him against the bishop.

After some time had passed, Count Baldwin also came to visit the bishop, who was suffering from illness. Walter, almost dying, had drawn him there by appeals for aid to his son.

Not long afterward Walter ended his life in that very illness, bringing his evils to an end amid such wickedness.

### 118. Concerning the Fact That, When the Bishop Was Dying, Walter, Walter’s Son, Invaded the Episcopal Residence

The bishop too, suffering from a prolonged illness, awaited the day of his calling.

Walter, however, resembling his father both in savagery and by nature [Note: [Col. 0120D] That is, similar to his father.], and in every way reflecting his father, did not cease raging against the bishop. The bishop’s illness increased Walter’s ferocity.

Therefore the bishop, often deeply angered, intended to strike the insolence of the usurper with the rod of eternal damnation. But, persuaded by the pleas of some of his men, especially Seiher of Lens, Walter’s uncle, he postponed this for a while.

Seiher, a prudent counselor, restrained his nephew’s pride, now by entreaty, now by the severity of threats; and he humbly soothed the bishop’s rightly aroused anger with gentle pleas. In this way he pacified them, on the condition that Walter pay twenty pounds of silver for his offenses and promise that he would remain quiet thereafter.

Then the bishop gently and kindly urged him to keep faith with his words and, if overtaken by death he should leave this human life in that illness, to hold the Church faithfully and courageously until another shepherd succeeded him.

But Walter wickedly forgot this and failed to put it into practice. For a few days later, as the illness grew worse, the entire residence echoed with the bishop’s dissolution, so that he was thought to be dead outside.

As soon as Walter heard this, he rejoiced. Armed with a multitude of his men, he broke down the doors and furiously burst into the clerics’ houses. He also handed over the bishop’s stables to plunder after seizing the horses.

The bishop, whose eyes were already growing dim and whose strength had failed, listened with immense difficulty to this fury. With a deep sigh he groaned bitterly that insult was being offered to him while he still lived. Raising his hands slightly toward heaven, he called upon the supreme Judge to condemn this robber on the day of vengeance. Thereafter, still filled with this indignation, he gave up his spirit on the third day before the Nones of February [February 3] [Note: [Col. 0120D] Annals of Quedlinburg, 1012: “Erluin, bishop of Cambrai, died, and Gerard was ordained in his place.” [Col. 0121D] Necrology of Saint Mary of Cambrai, now Bibliothèque de Cambrai, no. 219, early twelfth century, copied from an older source: “On the third day before the Nones of February Bishop Erluin died; he gave a third free prebend for the use of the brothers” [Col. 0122D].] (1012).

### 119. Concerning the Burial of the Bishop

Meanwhile, while his people mourned, the funeral was prepared with due ceremonial observance, and the body was carried with appropriate veneration to the monastery of Saint Mary [Note: [Col. 0121] Manuscript 1 reads *of his memory*.].

During his burial, while the others were wailing, Walter raged noisily with joy, wholly devoted as he was to plunder and robbery.

Finally, so that he might omit no kind of wickedness, he took his brother Seiher with him and went armed in fury to the monastery where the funeral rites were being performed. Turned aside by no sense of reverence, he drove the chaplains who were rendering the final rites away with drawn swords, all the way to the altar of Saint Mary—a pitiable spectacle.

With matters thus thrown into confusion, he postponed the burial until Richard, the aforementioned abbot of the monastery of Arras, arrived and buried the bishop in the monastery of Saint Autbert, on its northern side.

### 120. Concerning Walter’s Savagery

It is difficult to express how grievous a storm settled upon the devastated city and how great a ruin overwhelmed the condition of the commonwealth.

Walter, the source of the entire storm, raged within the city with an inborn ferocity. Taking Robert of Perrona as his accomplice in such wickedness, he presumed, as an alien heir, to occupy the episcopal residence.

Growing ever more savage and violating the customs of his fathers, he inflicted intolerable injuries upon the wretched citizens. Whoever did not give money was dragged into chains.

Nor did foreign robbers fail to ravage the surrounding area. Presuming that they had free security for robbery after the bishop’s death, they laid everything low.

I leave it to the judgment of everyone to determine how unjust this was: that Walter, as lord, should seize everything according to his desire and yet not even protect it from other brigands.

No one was free from Walter’s injuries except those who appeared in some way to share his views. He impoverished his own people and enriched foreigners, so that through their praise he might spread the glory of a good reputation among the barbarians.

Very frequently the complaints of the lamenting citizens were exchanged among themselves [Col. 0122A]: they said that they had no patron but a public plunderer, and that no remedy remained for them except to withdraw somewhere farther away and escape the fury of such a beast.

For they considered any exile more tolerable than their own home, where the days were spent in plunder and the nights in fear.

### 121. How Seiher, Walter’s Brother, Lost Hope of the Bishopric

To secure an even freer authority for his fury, Walter sent his brother Seiher to the emperor, with the contrived proposal that he should be elevated to the episcopate.

But when, during the journey itself, he heard that the bishopric had been given to another [Note: [Col. 0122D] That is, after he heard it.], he returned home, frustrated in his hope.

### 122. The Embassy of Azelin, Who Also Sought This Bishopric, Is Rejected; It Is Given to Gerard [Col. 0122B]

Azelin had long been eagerly striving for this bishopric. As we stated after Rothard’s death, Sophia favoring him, he had aspired to the episcopate (ch. 110).

Even shortly before Lord Erluin departed from this world, Azelin, thinking to advance his ambition, hastened to send envoys to the emperor. Through them he hoped perhaps to purchase the emperor’s goodwill and attain the privilege of the episcopate.

Carrying out his orders, they approached the emperor’s presence. They announced that Lord Erluin was near death and, promising large gifts, begged that the episcopal office be granted to Azelin, so that he might rejoice that what he had been unable to obtain after Rothard, he could at least secure after Erluin.

They were told to await the bishop’s end and returned home with some hope. But while they were returning, they heard of Erluin’s burial, retraced their journey, and again approached the emperor. Announcing that the bishop had died, they earnestly requested that the honor be granted to Azelin, offering valuable gifts.

When they were rejected, the emperor, following the common counsel of his people, decided instead to give the office to his chaplain Gerard (1012). He will be discussed in the third book.

[Col. 0121] **HERE ENDS THE FIRST BOOK, ON THE DEEDS OF THE BISHOPS.**

**HERE BEGINS THE SECOND, ON THE MONASTERIES THAT EXIST WITHIN THE EPISCOPATE.**

## Preface

[Col. 0121D]

Having spoken of the deeds of the bishops as memory brought them to mind [Note: [Col. 0121] Manuscript 6 reads *brings them to mind*.], and having treated, as far as the dryness of my small intellect permits, their various actions up to the end [Note: [Col. 0122D] That is, up to the last bishop, Colv.] of Lord Gerard, who is bishop now, the first book demands an end.

As for the second book, the order of the work seems to require that it begin with that same Lord Bishop. But, setting that aside for the moment, we have decided, with an interruption of the order, to discuss the monasteries that lie within the jurisdiction of the episcopate. We shall show what each place is, what worship is practiced there, what bodies of saints it contains, and what kind of servants there are.

Since, then, we are going to speak of each in turn, let us begin with the monastery of the blessed and glorious Mary, Mother of God, so that what surpasses the others in its principal title [Note: [Col. 0123] Manuscript 4 reads *presides over*.] may rightly be preferred to the others in every respect.

### 1. First, Concerning the Monastery of Saint Mary, and a Certain Man Who Was in Danger There and Was Later Restored to Health

Indeed, we have often heard that this place [Note: [Col. 0123] Manuscripts 1, 2, 3, and 5, and the first hand of 6, read *this place*; the present reading was corrected to *this one*.] is made illustrious by divine miracles for the praise and honor of the Mother of the Lord. But we grieve that, through the negligence of scribes, its memory has grown stale and been withdrawn from recollection [Note: [Col. 0123] Manuscript 6 omits the following material through chapter 4.].

We cannot remain silent about a few things among the many, whether those we learned from eyewitnesses or those we ourselves recently saw.

In the time of Bishop Erluin, a certain mason or carpenter named Helfridus was compelled by necessity to climb the bell tower of this monastery. But when his foot slipped on the slippery surface, he fell half-dead onto the ground in the choir itself, in the sight of many. He fell with such force that, even if some prophet had happened to promise that he would live, the crack in the excavated pavement where he fell would undoubtedly have appeared able to refute the prediction [Note: [Col. 0123] Manuscript 1 reads *excavated*.].

For the collapse of the pavement, which had long been present, testified to the severity of the danger and, rather than offering any hope of recovery, plainly foretold imminent death.

Immediately people rushed to him in astonishment and with human compassion, and they grieved pitifully over so sudden a calamity. His relatives, overcome with sorrow, sadly reproached the Lord and especially murmured against Saint Mary in elegiac language [Note: [Col. 0123D] That is, “elegiacly,” or in a lamenting manner.], saying:

> “Why should service be offered to her who allowed one serving her to fall into danger?” [Col. 0123C]

At last he was lifted up and placed on a bed. Not from hope of recovery, but rather out of human compassion, they carefully and vigorously anointed him with medicinal treatments. Gradually restored, he was later, I believe, through the merits of Saint Mary coming to his aid, returned to health and lived for a long time afterward.

It is also established by very reliable report that many others have been freed from various calamities.

### 2. Concerning the Falling Bell Tower, Restored to an Upright Position Through the Merits of Saint Mary

Recently, Lord Bishop Gerard, intending to enlarge and improve the head of the monastery together with its crypt—as appears from the work, which is now almost completed—ordered the ancient buildings to be demolished from their foundations (1021 or 1023) [Note: [Col. 0123D] Lord Gerard began constructing the head of the monastery of Saint Mary, Mother of God, at Cambrai, on the eighth day before the Kalends of April [March 25], from 1021, in the tenth year of his episcopate, with great and marvelous display, according to the *Chronicle of Saint Andrew of the Castle of Cambrai* I.8. But our author himself says below, III.49, that, impeded by disturbances, he could not begin it until March 1, 1023.].

Thus, when the workmen had long struggled with one and the same purpose to demolish the walls according to the plan, part of the structure was torn down. Suddenly, under repeated blows, the ancient masonry, tottering because of its age, broke at the summit and dragged down a vast ruin with a tremendous crash as far as the site of the bell tower—more than anyone had expected [Note: [Col. 0124D] That is, more than could have been estimated. Colv.].

At the crash, clergy and laypeople alike, small and great, all terrified, suddenly rushed out of their houses. Seeing the danger of the impending collapse, they were especially distressed at the fall of the bell tower.

For the more elevated the structure was and the more heavily it was burdened by the weight of the bells, the more imminent—and also the more serious—its collapse appeared. Indeed, it leaned so far toward the east under its own suspended weight that no one who saw it could doubt that its destruction threatened immediate danger.

While the people cried out and called upon God’s mercy, suddenly, in a marvelous manner, through the merits and intercession, as we believe, of the glorious Mother of God, the collapse paused for a moment and the tower was restored to an upright position [Note: [Col. 0124D] That is, to a straight position.]. The remaining roof, the collapse having ceased [Note: [Col. 0124D] That is, “the ruin,” as immediately below *after it had collapsed* is used in place of “after it had fallen.” Colv.], was secured.

The beams were torn from the upper buildings and shattered everything upon the corner of Saint Mary’s altar, which the bishop had ordered to remain untouched. When the beams had fallen, the relics of the saints that had formerly been placed in the consecration of that altar were found unharmed by divine will.

### 3. Concerning the Bishop’s Brother, Cured There

In those same recent days, Elbertus, the bishop’s brother, who had become a monk from a layman [Note: [Col. 0124D] Of Saint Andrew of the Castle of Cambrai; he died in 1047 according to the *Chronicle of Saint Andrew of Cambrai*, on the fifth day before the Ides of May, and according to the Necrology of Saint Mary, on the fifth day before the Ides of May.], was restored to health from a long illness there, as we ourselves plainly saw.

He had intended to come to Cambrai out of fraternal affection. But while he was making the journey, he was seized by such a serious illness that he could not reach the city. He was received by the brothers at the monastery of the martyr Priectus [Note: [Col. 0124D] Saint-Prix, near Saint-Quentin. Colv.] and spent a long time there in intolerable pain [Col. 0124C].

When, after being somewhat restored by medical treatment, he could scarcely sit on a horse, he nevertheless had himself carried to his brother—though not without difficulty. There he suffered so severely for a long time that they declared he would soon die.

It happened that, after a lengthy illness, on the solemn night of the blessed confessors Vedast and Amandus, he decided to enter the monastery of Saint Mary, carrying staffs, in order to celebrate Matins.

Miraculously visited by God, he recovered so completely that, setting aside for a while the staffs by which he had been supported, he stood upright and felt the remedy of his illness that very day, to the amazement of many.

There can be no doubt that this gift may be attributed to the merits of Saint Mary, Mother of God, and of the aforementioned confessors.

[Col. 0124D] **4. On the site of the monastery of Saint Gaugeric, most glorious father.** After the monastery of Saint Mary, we thought it not inappropriate to place second the monastery of blessed Gaugeric, most glorious confessor of Christ and [Col. 0125A] bishop of that same city [Note: [Col. 0125] *estimamus* (“we think”) in 6.]. For it is very fitting and entirely appropriate that, since the city of Cambrai is sustained under the protection of the Mother of the Lord, and since it is exalted by the renown of his name, we should likewise place his house in this work next to the house of that same Lady Virgin.

For in the time of this bishop, as is clear to those reading his Life [Note: [Col. 0125D] The earlier Life, in *Acta Sanctorum*, August II; *Acta Sanctorum Belgii* II, 276. From “At its summit …” to “house of sacrifice” it is copied verbatim.], on the summit of the hill where the monastery now stands there was a grove of ancient madness, that is, a grove dedicated by idolaters in former times, according to demonic rites, for the destruction of souls. Therefore this man of God, worthy of joyful remembrance, inspired by divine counsel, resolved to cut down the grove; and when the idols had been utterly uprooted, he built a basilica in honor of blessed [Col. 0125B] Medard (around the year 600). Thus he made a place devoted to impurities into a house of prayer and sacrifice, while wisely providing for himself there a mausoleum for his repose and a dwelling of welcome [Note: [Col. 0125] The following material through chapter 9 is absent in 6.].

For when, after the thirty-ninth year of his episcopate, the almighty King and most generous Dispenser had called his most valiant soldier to receive the recompense due for his labors, he was honorably buried in that same basilica, as he had previously arranged, and awaits the day of resurrection. Immediately, therefore, kings and princes and all the most powerful men, stirred by the signs and wonders with which he had shone forth in many ways before his death, and astounded by still greater works which the merciful and compassionate Lord graciously continued to perform through his merits after his death, flocked from various regions to the tomb of the most holy man [Col. 0125C], imploring that they might be aided by the patronage of so great a man, and offered exceedingly rich gifts.

At once, through the abundance of these resources, the monastery was enlarged with every diligence, and a numerous company of brothers was appointed in perpetuity to serve God and his most holy confessor. This house, situated on the brow of the hill, plainly seems to indicate that its distinguished inhabitant always trampled earthly things underfoot and longed for heavenly things with his whole desire.

Afterward the place was enriched by assistance of various kinds and so greatly increased through the many benefactions of good men that, as the documents preserved in the church archive attest [Col. 0125D], they bestowed not only the richer and more fertile estates around and near the monastery, but also, in far-removed regions, various revenues—so to speak, benefits of every kind. That place, once pre-eminent both in elegance and in every advantage, offered abundant grace and the greatest honor to the whole province and greatly distinguished the city by the excellence of its dignity. For it was a venerable and royal abbey, flourishing in complete sufficiency, whose manifold grace one would have thought impossible to augment.

[Col. 0126A] But after it was miserably ravaged and destroyed, along with the other churches of Gaul, first under the persecutions of the pagans and then of the Hungarians, as we briefly touched upon in the first book, the sins of mortals having demanded this punishment, not only could it not be restored to the favor of its former state, but—what is more grievous—it fell ever farther and farther, plunging into ruin.

For because the weakness of the rulers could not by their foresight simultaneously restrain such varied possessions, situated both far apart and nearby, the most wicked plunderers from the surrounding area, in an already corrupt age, had taken away what good men had contributed for the salvation and remedies of souls, as human ambition’s love is accustomed to do. Worse still, some of the rulers themselves had not avoided the snare of fraud: they too robbed, stole (*cleperent*) [Col. 0126B], and stripped the place [Note: [Col. 0125D] That is, “stole.” Greek *κλέπω* (*klepō*), “I steal.” Plautus likewise has: “snatch, steal, seize, plunder.” *Patrologia Latina* editor.].

And what shall I say? Once there was a more numerous company of brothers; now, because of poverty, their number has fallen to fifty, and through the efforts of Bishop Gerard they take their daily food together in the refectory. In memory and veneration of this father of ours, monasteries—and also more numerous basilicas—have been built not only nearby but in distant regions, where divine benefits are granted to those who ask, and where divine clemency graciously performs many indescribable miracles of power to the praise and glory of the most holy confessor.

The miracles that we have learned occurred here from trustworthy narrators, or that we constantly see occurring ourselves, exceed all measure because of their multitude and cannot be confined within any numerical limit [Col. 0126C]. Of these, the greater part, people are pleased to say, has been carried away by the envious wind [Note: [Col. 0126D] Compare I, 28.]; only a very few, which could not be concealed, we briefly touched upon in the first little book. Yet anyone who wishes will be able to find them fully recorded in that volume entitled *The Life of the Saint Himself* [Note: [Col. 0126D] By our author, in *Acta Sanctorum*, August II; *Acta Sanctorum Belgii* II, 278.].

**5. On a demoniac who was healed.** But so that this page may rejoice and be glad that it bears a holy and joyful name, I have decided to append a few things that I myself, then a young man, saw in recent times. Besides very many people of both sexes suffering from frenzy whom I had seen restored to health there, I shall mention separately one who, I think, could not be compared with any of them because of the excess of his madness.

He was foaming at the mouth and gnashing his teeth. Although his hands were bound behind his back and he was pitifully beaten by his own people, he could scarcely be restrained from devoting himself with all his strength to every kind of bacchanalian frenzy, the devil urging him on with violence. He was always saying forbidden things; suddenly leaping upon the unwary, he often bit people.

When he had been brought to the monastery of the most blessed confessor with great difficulty, he continued to rage no less for several days, so that no one dared to confront him [Col. 0127A]. Yet it was not long before, through the pious intercession of his patron and the merciful visitation of the heavenly physician, he recovered the use of a sound and unimpaired mind. His family returned home rejoicing, while Gerard—for that was his name—resolved to remain in the monastery, serving God and his most holy confessor.

After he had served there familiarly with the greatest devotion for a long time, it happened that one day the inclination to visit [Note: [Col. 0127D] That is, “desire” or “affection,” as in I, 7.] his father’s estate invited him. As he was traveling toward it, though he was not yet far away, he encountered, as he himself used to relate, a priest adorned with gray hair, handsome in face and attire. The priest addressed him in these words:

“Where are you going?” he said.

And he replied: “It is already a long time, my lord, since I have served the most holy father Gaugeric for the benefits he has bestowed. But now I am eager to return to my homeland to visit my parents and see how they are.”

“It is better for you,” he said, “to remain, lest you appear ungrateful for the benefit bestowed.”

But, moved by affection for his parents and setting aside the warning he had received, he proceeded a little farther; immediately he was seized by the demon much more severely than before, being so deranged that he intended to stone everyone he encountered. Many people could not easily capture him; bound with straps, he was dragged back to the monastery. Because, instructed by the devil, he was hurling insults against the Catholic faith, he was now assailed with threats and now shaken by scourges. Yet no one could restrain the false chatter of his rabid mouth until, amid scourges and bonds, he was thrown down before the tomb of the holy [Col. 0127C] man [Note: [Col. 0127] The words “before the tomb of the holy man” were inserted between the lines by the author himself], and exhaustion overcame him with sleep.

When he awoke after a little while and rose, his mind was immediately restored by divine power. Everyone marveled and wept for joy as he prostrated himself before the tomb in great confusion, shame, and repentance. He confessed his fault and begged forgiveness for his error. Finally, having become entirely composed in mind, he devoted himself faithfully to monastic services, not daring to leave the place again until, after a long time, he obtained permission from the brothers to go to Rome.

It should be noted that the blessed Gaugeric was undoubtedly the priest whom we said had shortly before appeared to him.

**6. On a cripple who was healed.** There is still a man serving in the monastery named Hildebert, whom we know was restored to health after a long illness through the merits of the holy man. For almost an entire year he was so afflicted by some kind of disease that, with most of his body already as if dead, he could perform no service for ordinary human activities.

His father sadly acknowledged that, in the hope of restoring his health, he had spent part of his small estate without any benefit on the frequent hiring of physicians, and he could not discover what further course to pursue. In this distressed state of grief [Col. 0128A], a sound and salutary plan finally occurred to him: namely, to seek the medicinal assistance of blessed Gaugeric, since the sick often received health there and every kind of demoniac or lunatic was freed.

Therefore, after reaching this decision, he brought the sick man to the monastery, placing him in a vehicle. He vowed that, if he were restored to health, he would dedicate him forever to the service of the most blessed Gaugeric. Why prolong the little story? He lay there for a short time and obtained the grace of divine healing. In return for so great a benefit, he served the monastic community and afterward continued to live in the monastery.

**7. On a fire extinguished through the merits of Saint Gaugeric.** In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1027 [Note: [Col. 0127] 1 has “1o o XXo VIIo”; it is uncertain whether the VIIo belongs to the year or denotes the day of the Ides. The others have exactly the same form.], on the Ides of July [Col. 0128B], a vast and destructive fire broke out in the city itself. A large part of the city had already been burned, and the flames, raging and driven by the winds, grew stronger until they reached the houses situated near the holy man’s monastery and enveloped them in an unavoidable and devouring destruction.

Now an even greater fear arose concerning the threatened burning of the church. For it was perhaps beyond doubt that, if the neighboring dwellings were burned, the church and monastery themselves would be seized by the fire. As the flames grew stronger, a still greater fear weighed upon everyone; and when flaming masses flew through the air, the entire population and clergy roared with a cry raised to heaven.

Immediately two clerics, with the approval of the others, hastened to the holy tomb. Driven by a boldness born of fear, they drew out the silver casket containing the body of the most holy [Col. 0128C] man and, lifting it quickly, carried it toward the raging flames. At once, through the operation of divine clemency and the support of the holy man’s merits, the entire fire subsided and became so inert that one would have thought it had been sprinkled from above with a dew-laden shower.

Many other things also present themselves for narration, but the narrow brevity of this little book does not permit it. And what shall I say about the multitude of different sick people who flock there daily and recover their health? Why mention these things when they always appear more plainly to the eye than in words? Recently, indeed, God be thanked, he restored me myself to health when I was suffering intolerably from fevers.

**8. The author adds his own affliction.** The severe inconvenience of the fever that held me for a long time now compels me to abbreviate my words [Col. 0128D]. For although the affliction has now been driven away and, God be thanked, I am recovering somewhat in body, my mind is still weakened by the recent pain, and it does not possess sufficient strength to write at length. Let us therefore meanwhile continue the task of this little work with a compressed pen.

**9. On Saint Aubert.** The monastery of Saint Aubert, served by a few canons, is situated within the walls of the city. There, divine benefits are granted to those who ask, and, with God’s cooperation, many miracles are performed for the glory of his confessor. It is certain that many of these have been lost through the scarcity of writers and the sloth of memory [Col. 0129A].

**10. On Hunulchort.** Let us pass to the monastery of Saint Peter in the village of Hunulchurt [Note: [Col. 0129] *Hunulchurh* in 1 and 3; *Honulfocurte* in 6; *Honulficurte* in 2], where I found in writing that Saint Pollina rests. This illustrious man, named Amalfridus, founded it with his wife Ghildebertana (in the year 677), and placed his daughter Auriana in charge of the nuns. Once it flourished in religion and wealth; now, after it was granted as a benefice to military men, it has been reduced to a few canons.

**11.** [Note: [Col. 0129] This chapter, at first contained in seven lines, was later expanded by the author in an erasure and an attached slip.] **On the village of Barala.** In the village also called Barala by its inhabitants [Note: [Col. 0129D] Baralle, between Cambrai and Arras. COLV.], there once existed a monastery of a canonical community, said to have been founded by King Clovis [Col. 0129B] and consecrated by blessed Vedast in honor of Saint George. The arm of that same martyr was kept there.

That it was exceedingly wealthy and venerable is shown by its marble columns and the beautiful ancient buildings that still remain. In the days of Bishop Dodilo (around the year 881), the canons saw the frenzy of the Normans raging everywhere throughout this province and, as we mentioned above, those men burning the holy houses of God after profaning sacred worship. They therefore brought the sacred relics, together with all their necessary belongings, to our church, where they were humanely received by the bishop himself.

After they had remained there for some time, when they thought that the enemy had withdrawn and requested permission to return to their own place, the bishop, unwilling to agree, advised them to postpone their departure for a time [Col. 0129C]. He warned them to beware the treachery of the enemy, whose return was suspect; they should not rashly trust an empty supposition but await definite security.

When they heard the bishop’s advice, they remained for some time. A few days later, however, they again approached the bishop, asserting that the enemy had gone away, that everything was safe, and that their departure was secure.

The bishop said to them: “What rashness is moving you? I do not believe what you assert; perhaps your judgment is deceiving you. Remain still, I advise you; stay here. In the meantime, nothing necessary for your use will be lacking with me. Moreover, that people is fierce and cunning and spares no one. If you fall into their hands unprepared, you will pay a heavier penalty for your premature boldness.”

But when they stubbornly persisted in their request and insisted without a doubt that everything was safe, he added [Col. 0129D]: “Since this is your decision, so be it! I place the choice in your hands. Nevertheless, I shall retain with me that precious relic of the arm, arranging matters in this way as a kind of presage, so that, if—as the outcome later proved—the enemy should attack, a treasure of such importance would not perish.”

Having received this permission and prepared provisions for the journey, they began their return with such obstinacy—foolish men, who had not followed the bishop’s advice [Col. 0130A]. They had not yet traveled three miles from the city when they were intercepted by unexpected enemies and fell by the sword.

Their monastery too was destroyed; the entire surrounding region, except for fortified places, was cruelly plundered. The little church was later rebuilt, but only one priest presided over it. That sacred arm has remained with us in this manner down to the present day.

**12. On the village of Sancti** [Note: [Col. 0129] This chapter, originally occupying four lines, was expanded by the author himself in an erasure and in the margin.]. Not far from here, at Sancti [Note: [Col. 0130D] Sains-les-Marquion. LE GLAY.]—this being the name of the place—there is said to have been a basilica of maidens, where Saint Saturnina rests.

This virgin was born in Germany of illustrious parentage and, from childhood, vowed her virginity to the Lord. When her parents planned to marry her according to worldly custom, she preferred to preserve the integrity of her chastity for her heavenly bridegroom and shunned a human marriage-bed. Seeing that she could neither resist her parents’ will nor escape the desire of her insolent suitor, she secretly left her father’s house and fled.

When she reached this region, she completed the course of her life by martyrdom near the aforementioned village.
