The man to whom her parents had promised her pursued her as she fled, all the way to that place. When the venerable virgin saw him from a distance behind her, she trembled all over and did not know how to escape the bites of the attacking beast.

What could she do? Immediately, being a simple creature, she placed herself among the shepherds who were pasturing their flock there, intending in this way to conceal herself from her pursuer. But the young man, having tracked her down, rushed upon the innocent little sheep like a hungry wolf and beheaded her with his drawn sword [Col. 0130C].

At once, as the ancient accounts dare to assert, she took her own head in her hands and, while the people watched, carried it as far as the church in that village, which stood in honor of Saint Remigius. Therefore, a monastery was built by faithful Christians in her honor, and a community of girls was assigned to it. But because of the causes mentioned above, it was reduced to the service of a single priest.

There is also an ancient account that, long afterward, the Saxons—for what reason is uncertain—came to this region and, passing through the village itself, heard of its sacred reputation and carried away part of the holy virgin’s body.

**13. On the monastery of Saint Mary of the people of Arras.** [Col. 0130D] Let us now come to the territory of Arras. The monastery of Saint Mary, where the principal seat of the episcopal chair once stood, has forty canons.

In our own days, Rodulfus, treasurer of that church, enlarged it with the counsel of Lord Bishop Gerard. The place would be venerable and less in need of support, were it not for the proud magnificence of the Count of Flanders, whose stronghold rises beside it and has sometimes been accustomed to oppose it [Col. 0131A].

There, beside the altar of Mary, Mother of God, which blessed Vedast had consecrated in his lifetime, many exceedingly precious relics of the saints were discovered in the second year of Bishop Gerard (1013). For approximately three years divine clemency worked various miracles to make them glorious. Lepers were cleansed, the crippled were restored to the use of their limbs, and many who suffered from different illnesses were cured and given health.

**14. On Saint Vedast.** In the castle of Arras there is the monastery of Saint Vedast, which, as we said above (I, 20), was built by Saint Aubert. It rejoices in the religious observance of monks and is illuminated from heaven by many miracles of power.

**15. On two basilicas.** Within the same castle, two canonical basilicas also lie nearby: one, namely, in honor of Saint Mary, and the other of Saint Peter the Apostle [Col. 0131B].

**16. On Maraculum.** In the village of Maraculum [Note: [Col. 0131D] Maroeul d’Arras.] there is also a monastery of canons, where Saint Bertilia rests; she gave this very estate of hers to Saint Mary.

**17. On Albiniacum.** Again, in the village of Albiniacum [Note: [Col. 0131D] Aubigny, arrondissement of Saint-Pol. LE GLAY.], there is a monastery of canons, namely that of Saint Chilianus, who is said to have been a Scot.

**18. On the monastery of Saint Vindician.** Likewise, on Mount Saint Eligius—for that is what the place is called—there is also a monastery of canons dedicated to Saint Vindician, bishop of Cambrai. After it was granted as a benefice to military men, it was reduced, through the diminution [*imminutione?*; Col. 0131C] of its resources, to a small number of brothers.

**19. On Lucau and Pas.** Moreover, in the villages of Lucau [Note: [Col. 0131D] Lucheul, near Doullens.] and Pas there are two canonical basilicas. After these too were granted as benefices to military men, they fell into poverty.

**20. On the cell of Saint Savior.** There is a village belonging to the property of Saint Vedast, named Berclaus [Note: [Col. 0131D] Billi-Berclau, on the River Deûle. COLV.], situated in marshland, suitable for livestock because of its ample pastures, and entirely well suited also to the use of monks.

Therefore Abbot Leduwinus [Note: [Col. 0131D] Of Saint Vedast, c. 1022–c. 1041.], considering the suitability of the place, resolved to found a monastery there, provided that episcopal authority also approved. Two purposes would thereby be served quite appropriately: namely, that he could assign there some of the monks who had gathered in greater numbers at the monastery of Saint Vedast, and that the church’s surrounding properties could be held more securely.

Accordingly, he decided to approach Lord Bishop Gerard at a synodal assembly and, before the entire synod, requested permission to carry out his plan. Having obtained it without difficulty through the bishop’s authority, he hastened to build the monastery and secured permission for it, once completed, to be consecrated by the lord bishop himself.

The bishop changed the name of the place and decreed that it should be called the Cell of Saint Savior.

**21. On the castle of Douai.** Moreover, at the castle of Douai [Note: [Col. 0131D] Douai.] there is a monastery of canons, where the bodies of the saints Maurontus [Note: [Col. 0131D] That is, Maurontus, Saint-Morand. COLV.] and Amatus lie.

It should be known that, before the establishment of this castle, the toll custom—which is now collected in the castle itself, because of the imposing power of the Count of Flanders, according to a practice changed from the former one [Col. 0132B]—was paid at the village of Lambras, belonging to the holy Mother of God. It was a royal domain, but in the time of Bishop Stephen King Charles granted it to Saint Mary to possess.

At that time the harbor was also located there. After the settlement of this castle began, however, the use of the shipping route was transferred there, and only half of the toll is paid to our village.

In this village King Childebert was buried by chance [Note: [Col. 0131D] That is, by chance; for afterward he was transferred to Soissons and buried in the basilica of Saint Medard beside his father Chlothar, according to Gregory of Tours, IV, final chapter. Our author took everything that follows in this chapter from that account, though with considerable verbal alteration. He is mistaken about the name: it was Sigebert, not Childebert.]. When he was preparing to go and besiege his brother, who at that time was staying at Tournai, blessed Germanus, bishop of Paris, had foretold with prophetic spirit [Note: [Col. 0131] *presaga* in 1 and 2, but corrected here in 4.] that he could not complete such an undertaking if he pursued it with the intention of bringing about his brother’s death.

But he paid no heed to the blessed bishop’s words and prepared to carry out his plan. Yet, so that the holy bishop’s prophecy would not prove empty, death overtook him on the very journey, and he was buried in the aforementioned village of Lambras.

**22. On the monastery of Lens.** At the castle of Lens [Note: [Col. 0132D] Lens in Artois. COLV.] there is likewise a monastery of canons, where Saint Vulganus rests; he is said to have been a Scot.

**23. On the village of Henim.** In the village called Henim [Note: [Col. 0132D] Hennin-Liétard, between Douai and Lens.] there is also a basilica in honor of Saint Martin, formerly served by only one priest. Recently, however, Rotbert of Arras, considering the remedy of his soul, assigned twelve canons there at his own expense, with the counsel of Bishop Gerard (in the year 1040).

**24. On the village of Belgicus.** Likewise, in the territory of Arras, in the village called Belgicus by its inhabitants [Note: [Col. 0132D] Now unidentified. Colvenerius has already shown that it can be neither Belgeville, nor Belge on the River Ternoise, nor Blangiacum, since these places were never in the diocese of Arras. He also mentions Bellovacum in Artois, Belle near Aubigny, and Berlette at the source of the Scarpe, but notes that no traces of a collegiate church or monastery exist in any of them. The following etymology of the name Belgicus [Col. 0133C] rests solely on our author’s authority. Isidore, *Etymologies* XIV, 4: “Belgica is a city of Gaul, from which the province of Belgica was named.” Compare our *Annals*, vol. IX, p. 305.], there stands a canonical basilica of Saint Remigius, where, they say, divine miracles frequently take place from heaven [Col. 0133A].

It should be noted that this place once stood out to such a degree that our entire region, even down to the present, was called Belgica after it.

**25. On the village of Hasnum.** In the village also called Hasnum there was once a royal and exceedingly wealthy abbey, where the bodies of Saints Marcellinus and Peter rest for the most part. Now, because the customs of the degenerate age have been corrupted, we mourn that the place has become desolate and impoverished, with only a few clerics serving there.

**26. On Marchiennes.** At the village of Marchiennes [Note: [Col. 0134C] Marchiennes.], the glorious virgin of God, Rictrudis [Note: [Col. 0133] Erased in 1; deleted in 2. “The glorious matron Rictrudis” in 5. Compare below III, 8, and Du Cange, s.v. *virgo*.], built a monastery from her own wealth and estates, with the counsel of Saint Amandus, who at that time was held in high esteem. After assigning nuns to serve there, she herself also guided the reins of governance as abbess [Col. 0133B].

During her life, and to some extent after her death, religious observance greatly increased there, and ecclesiastical practice regularly flourished. But as the world, always corrupted for the worse, grew more degenerate, the order of the girls themselves also began to be corrupted and perverted; and this increasingly depraved custom had continued in their degenerate successors down to the present.

Recently, however, the aforementioned Abbot Leduwinus, through the efforts of Bishop Gerard and Margrave Baldwin, expelled the women who were living shamefully from the cleansed site and installed monks who would serve God and the aforementioned virgin, who rests there, better and more religiously [Note: [Col. 0133] Thus in 2 and 6; *religiosus* in 1.].

**27. On Hamage.** Not far from here, in the village of Hamage [Note: [Col. 0134C] Hamage, near Marchiennes.], the blessed handmaid of Christ Eusebia, the daughter of the aforementioned virgin, also built a church from her inherited property [Col. 0133C]. After establishing nuns there, she too endowed it generously, according to her means, as abbess. Now, because of its great decline into secular ways, it scarcely has a few canons.

**28. On Denain.** Again, in the village of Denain [Note: [Col. 0134C] Denain, between Douai and Valenciennes.], the blessed Rainfredis founded a cell from property belonging to her own right and, after establishing nuns there, herself also governed it as abbess.

This [Note: [Col. 0133] In 1 this chapter originally ended as follows: “But this … [lacuna] … canons.” The scribe himself—not the author—later erased the five or six words that had stood between *autem* and *canonici*, and later wrote *i. i. incli* above the erasure; he supplied the remainder, *natam … praefecit*, in the margin, using exactly the same ink as for everything else. He forgot to delete the word *canonici*. Later, when the codex was cut down by the bookbinder, the first letters of each line were cut away: *natam*, *nici*, *donec*, *mni Ge*, *Leduwi*, *moder*, and so forth. These are still read and printed by 2 and 6 as we gave them above. Manuscript 4, already defective, has: “p. i. inclining … p. c. inhabited … with the counsel of Lord G. b. and … of the abbot … in the time … [lacuna] … OF THE VILLAGE,” etc. Manuscript 3 has: “through poverty a few … with the counsel of Lord G., b., and L., a. m. At that time the count restored it to its former condition and there installed … of Saint Benedict, E. p.” Finally, 5 gives the whole passage in this altered form: “But afterward, on the advice of Lord Bishop Gerard and Abbot Leduwinus, Count Baldwin restored it to the former condition of the nuns, and there introduced nuns of Saint Benedict, although previously they had been regular; over them he set as abbess E. p.”]

But afterward, when poverty had brought it low, a few canons inhabited it, until, through the counsel of Lord Bishop Gerard and Abbot Leduwinus, Count Baldwin in recent times restored it to its former condition. There he installed nuns according to regular discipline and placed over them an abbess named Ermentrude [Col. 0134A].

**29. On the village of Haspro.** At the time when the Normans, especially with the tyrant Rollo as their instigator, raged through this kingdom as through other regions, and, as we said above (I, 61), the sins of Christians demanded it, burning the churches of the saints indiscriminately, the bodies of the saints—namely Aycadrius and Hugh—were brought, amid such a storm of terror, from the monastery of Jumièges [Note: [Col. 0134C] Jumièges.], situated on the River Seine not far from the city of Rouen, to the village of Haspro, which lies no more than ten miles from our city.

Whether this village had previously belonged to the aforementioned monastery, or whether at that time it had been given by a king or some prince, for the remedy of his soul, as a place of refuge for the saints, we cannot say with certainty.

Certainly, blessed Aycadrius, who had been appointed abbot by Saint Philibert, the most distinguished abbot of that monastery, was governing the sacred community there and shone forth in the conduct of his life and the radiance of his virtues. Inspired by divine grace to imitate his holy way of life, the holy man Hugh, bishop of Rouen and son of King Karloman, abandoned the reins of his episcopate and renounced worldly cares, desiring with his whole heart the discipline and habit of monks. Instructed by the sacred conduct of his master, he shone forth perfected in every kind of virtue.

What manner of men they both were is made clear to those who read their Lives. With these relics thereafter remaining at this village, a monastery was established and monks were assigned to it [Col. 0134C]. In their honor, the pious and merciful God graciously performed many—indeed, very celebrated—miracles of power, to such an extent that none of the neighboring powerful men or those passing through on military expeditions had previously dared to inflict any outrage upon the place.

But because the abbot of the monks lived far away and, owing to the difficulty of the distance, used to visit them very rarely, they followed the world in loosened freedom and, living irregularly, were in danger until the time of Bishop Gerard, since they were without a ruler.

Seeing this, the bishop often admonished the abbot to correct the situation. But because, as we have said, he lived far away, he delayed the correction. It happened, however, that the bishop, traveling through this village on some ecclesiastical business, informed the aforementioned Abbot Leduwinus—for he was his traveling companion—of the monks’ shameful conduct [Col. 0135A].

He urged him with sound, indeed entirely suitable, counsel that, if he had any property of Saint Vedast in the vicinity of the aforementioned monastery, he should exchange it for this monastery, which was adjacent to his own, and strive to improve this place for the sake of eternal reward.

During this conversation Leduwinus hesitated uncertainly, yet seemed to refuse as though the matter were difficult. Not long afterward, however, having carefully and diligently considered the opportunity, the abbot who had received the salutary advice informed the bishop that he would carry out the admonition if he could obtain the exchange from Abbot Theoderic [Col. 0135B].

The bishop, therefore, rejoiced and immediately sent an embassy to approach Abbot Theoderic, showing him the danger to his soul if he did not take care of the matter in time. Since he was situated far away, he ought to exchange the place; but if he refused, the bishop would join forces with Margrave Baldwin, expel the false monks, and use all his authority to reform the place.

The abbot, applying suitable judgment to the matter, decided to comply with the bishop’s commands. Having received the properties of Saint Vedast that lay around his own vicinity, he handed over the village of Haspro to Abbot Leduwinus (in the year 1024).

This exchange was made before King Robert of the Franks and before the counts—Baldwin of Flanders and Richard of Rouen—and was confirmed by them [Note: [Col. 0135C] Miraeus assigns this exchange to the year 1044 on the basis of a charter of Leduwinus, published in *Opera Diplomatica* I, 265, where the following is found: “To the Prince of eternity … I, Leduwinus, abbot … But in our time, namely in the year 1044 of the supreme and true pontiff Jesus Christ, the matter was investigated through Gerard, bishop of Cambrai and Arras, and, after inquiry and reconsideration, it was arranged that, with the counsel of the elders, the neighbors, and our brothers, we should receive by gift from Count Richard and Abbot Theoderic of the monastery of Jumièges the cell called Haspra, because it was nearer to us; and they should likewise possess Anglicurt, a cell nearer to themselves, by our gift. The witnesses to this matter were Richard the count, who made the gift; Robert, his brother, the archbishop; Richard, son of Richard; Robert, his brother; Warinus, bishop of Beauvais, a brother of our congregation. Done at Rouen, in the month of January, on the octave of Epiphany, in the sixth indiction, while the most serene King Robert of the Franks was reigning, in the twenty-eighth year of his reign.” But the reference to the forty-fourth year is plainly erroneous and must be changed to the twentieth; for Robert’s twenty-eighth year was 1024. Moreover, Archbishop Robert died in 1037, Warinus in 1030, and Abbot Theoderic already before 1030. Colvenerius therefore rightly determined that the year of this exchange was 1024; and James of Guise likewise gives 1024 (ed. Fortia IX, 246).].

Abbot Leduwinus, therefore, as a capable builder, improved the place with the greatest zeal, for the praise and veneration of the saints who rest there, and busied himself in adorning it with new buildings and a regular cloister.

## 30. On Valentiana

In the fortress of Valentiana there is a monastery of canons, which Count Arnulf, with the counsel and authority of Bishop Rothard [Note: [Col. 0136C] Thus, sometime between 979 and 995.], built in honor of Saint John the Baptist; and, having furnished it with possessions as appropriate, he assigned twelve canons to it.

## 31. On the Monastery of Saint Salvius

Not far from here there once stood a little church of Saint Martin; now, however, there is a canonical monastery, also held in veneration of Saint Salvius, bishop and martyr.

[(V. Salv.) At that time Saint Salvius, wholly longing for the heavenly homeland, left the helm of his bishopric for the sake of pilgrimage; setting out abroad, he resolved to devote himself to preaching. Thus, proceeding from place to place, he proclaimed the word of God to the people and devoted himself especially to the celebration of Masses. But when he had come into that very neighborhood and was one day crossing from the port of Valentiana to the village of Condatum, he was captured through an ambush laid by a certain wicked man and confined in custody. After his priestly garments and episcopal ornaments, which he had brought with him, had been seized, he was beheaded [Col. 0136B]. Religious men buried him in the aforesaid church of Saint Martin. Then, both immediately and afterward, as many people proclaimed his miracles, it became clear how great and worthy of honor he had been, as is found in full in the book of his passion. Therefore the prince of the region, Karl Martel, struck with astonishment, enlarged the place for the salvation of his soul from the Valentianian fisc and from other possessions; assigning it an adequate endowment, he established canons there.]

## 32. On Marecolae

The holy man of God Huntbertus, distinguished for holiness and greatly renowned, likewise departed from the territory of Laon and chose the village of Mareclias [Note: [Col. 0136C] Maroilles.] as the place of his holy way of life. There, from his own possessions and estates, he built a monastery by apostolic authority in honor of the holy Mother of God and of the holy apostles Peter and Paul [Note: [Col. 0136C] Cf. I, 27; *Acta Sanctorum Belgii* IV, 117.]. Having established brothers there for service, he himself also serving the Lord, shone forth sufficiently renowned for signs of virtue and for the merits of his teaching and life. There, completing the labor of this life, he lies buried and rests in peace.

This abbey, as we explained more fully in the first book, was entrusted by the first Emperor Otto, son of King Henry [Note: [Col. 0136C] He was our Otto; for above, I, 68, he himself related that King Charles had handed it over to Bishop Stephen in the year 921.], during the episcopate of Bishop Fulbert, to the church of the holy Mother of God of Cambrai.

## 33. On the Village of Waslero

In the village of Waslero [Note: [Col. 0137D] Wallers-Saint-Hilaire, or Wallers-en-Faigne. According to Fulcuin, however, ch. 4, it was not Landelinus who founded this monastery, but Ursmarus.] the blessed Landelinus also founded a monastery for a few brothers, and placed over it Saint Dodo, a man of good memory. He, renowned for sacred conduct, led a life of innocence; and there, laying down the burden of frailty, he happily rests in peace.

## 34. On the Village of Fescau

In the village of Fescau [Note: [Col. 0137D] Fussiaux, near Avesnes. Le Glay.] there is also a monastery where, in truth, the holy man of the Lord, namely Hetto the Scot, came under the guidance of divine providence and lived for some time. At last, completing the course of his pilgrimage, he departed to Christ. To make his merit manifest, divine mercy deigned to perform many signs of virtue. Accordingly, certain religious men gave the holy man resources from such great possessions [Col. 0137B] that several canons might be admitted.

## 35. On the Monastery in the Village of Alto Monte

Nor shall I pass over the village that they call Altum Montem [Note: [Col. 0137D] Hautmont, near Maubeuge.], and not without reason so named, since the blessed Vincent, together with the many religious men who had been with him, made it elevated by his way of life.

(V. Auth.) [This Vincent was, in fact, an outstanding count, namely the husband of Saint Waldetrudis. In secular eminence he was exceedingly powerful both in possessions and in lineage; nevertheless, instructed by the learning and frequent admonitions of the blessed Bishop Autbert, he withdrew far from the pomp of secular military service and resolved rather to dedicate himself to the service of God.]

Thus, while he was anxiously seeking a place in which to pursue his way of life, divine mercy was not lacking to fulfill the holy man’s desire [Col. 0137C]. For one night the Lord sent snow and sprinkled the whole surrounding region with snowy dew, except for a small area which he reserved to be sprinkled in the form of a cross in the aforesaid village. The man of God understood, by a higher plan, that this had happened from heaven in response to his desire. Assured, therefore, by the divine sign, he immediately founded a monastery in that same place at his own expense. His teacher Autbert, bringing in religious men who were with him, dedicated it in honor of the apostles Peter and Paul.

There the holy man lived happily and strove to lead a life of admirable holiness. Many religious men had gathered to his pious way of life; and, after handing over estates and personal possessions, they lived with the holy man and bound themselves to the norm of the regular life. But when the place had begun to be enlarged by kings and princes and had become populous through the number of the brothers, he withdrew to a more secluded place so that he might devote himself to God more freely. I shall speak of that place a little later.

Afterward, the religious life of the monks grew for a long time according to his pattern and example. But, as poverty stealthily entered through the incursions of pagans and even through the frequent disturbances of their own people [Col. 0138A], the monastic order was reduced to a canonical one and remained so until the time of Lord Gerard, the bishop. Seeing this, the bishop, by the command of Emperor Henry and with the counsel of Count Heriman [Note: [Col. 0138D] Of Eiham or Verdun; cf. III, 6.], and with the consent of his brother Godefrid—namely, the bishop’s brother, who held that place in the fisc on the part of Count Heriman—improved its condition. Having made Fulcoin abbot, he restored it to its former order (in the year 1016). This abbot of good memory, carrying out the office of his name with the greatest zeal and labor, both taught inwardly the practice of the Rule and adorned the whole place outwardly, as suited the circumstances of the time and its still-new condition, with beautiful buildings and necessities for the monks’ use.

## 36. On the Monastery of Maubeuge

It must also be said that in Maubeuge [Note: [Col. 0138D] Maubeuge.] there is a monastery of women, which the blessed virgin of Christ Aldegundis built from her own estates for the practice of her way of life. The blessed Autbert also dedicated it, bringing in many men with him. This praiseworthy virgin, sister of the previously mentioned Saint Waldetrudis, was instructed by the blessed Autbert and received the veil of devout religion. There, leading a life of innocence with a very large company of sisters, she laid down the burden of the body and went forth to meet her heavenly Bridegroom with a burning lamp.

## 37. On the Monastery of Lobbes

We must pass on to the monastery of Lobbes [Note: [Col. 0138D] Lobbes.], which, from the sacred beginnings of Saint Landelinus, gradually reached the title of such honor as it now possesses.

[(V. Autb.) We read in the book of his life that, in his earliest youth, this Landelinus was imbued by the blessed Bishop Autbert with letters and sacred morals; but afterward, deceived by the devil, he fled from his pious teacher, rejected the clerical state, and joined a band of robbers. After the most kindly teacher had recalled him from error through long mourning and unceasing prayer, received him like a father receiving his son, and restored him, wounded as he was, through gentle correction and benevolent consolation, he advised him to withdraw to the place mentioned above, then deserted, so that he might correct his errors with greater discipline and live more correctly.

After the building of his dwelling had been completed and it had been consecrated in honor of the apostles Peter and Paul [Note: [Col. 0138D] According to Folcuin, *Gesta abbatum Lobbiensium* 4, Ursmarus ultimately did this, in the year 697.],—having received a few men of pure life with him,—he fulfilled his teacher’s admonitions and commands equally in conduct and in deed. Progressing from day to day, he rose to the summit of the most holy life.

When the place began to flourish through the holy man’s devout way of life and, through the generosity of kings and any powerful men, became as rich outwardly in possessions as it was inwardly in its number of monks, he soon withdrew from there. Since he desired to be more strictly devoted to God, he sought a more secluded place, of which we shall speak shortly.

(V. Ursmari.) As he was about to withdraw, he placed in that location the blessed man of God Ursmarus, endowed with devout morals, a consecrated bishop only for the purpose of missionary preaching [Note: [Col. 0139D] That is, for preaching the word of God to the nations, and not assigned to any particular place. Colv.]. He too, born in the village of Fleon [Note: [Col. 0139D] Floyon.], which lies below the forest of Thiérache [Note: [Col. 0139D] The Forest of Thiérache, on the borders of Picardy.], presented the brothers with the pattern of an innocent life and spent his days in good works.]

Under this teacher, and afterward under the blessed Erminus, whose monastery we shall discuss below, the place flourished, and, as is still evident, ecclesiastical custom fully grew there to the glory of God.

## 38. On the Monastery of Saints Ursmarus and Erminus

Let us next add the dwelling-place of the repose of these blessed confessors of God. There was a parish church subordinate to the aforesaid monastery, situated nearby, namely on the summit of a hill. The monks themselves, as well as all the neighboring inhabitants living around it, were commonly brought there for burial. When they died, the most blessed men Ursmarus and Erminus were also carried there to be buried. To manifest their merits, divine mercy deigned to perform many miracles.

But since we touched only briefly above on Saint Ursmarus (ch. 37), it is not inappropriate to explain something also about Saint Erminus.

[(V. Ermini.) This man, certainly praiseworthy in life and greatly renowned, was born in the territory of Laon. Progressing from day to day in good works, he shone forth in the practice of every virtue. Because the fragrance of his good reputation spread far and wide, the blessed Ursmarus [Col. 0139C], who governed the aforesaid monastery [Note: [Col. 0140D] Lobbes.], summoned him frequently. Understanding that the day of his calling was approaching, he chose him as rector of the monastery [Note: [Col. 0139] “The monastery,” 1.] after himself, as his equal in office, minister, and bishop (in the year 711). Having thus been appointed as his deputy in the administration, he devoted himself more earnestly to divine worship. Instructed by the example of his teacher, he carefully cared for the sheep entrusted to him.]

He also expended his estate at Ercli for the use of the brothers. After both had been called to their reward—first the blessed Ursmarus (in the year 713), then the man of God Erminus (in the year 737)—and had been buried in the aforementioned parish church, that place was endowed with so many and such great benefactions that, in modern times, when it had become a monastery, canons were sent there.

## 39. On Mons-Castrilocus

In the village of Castrilocus [Note: [Col. 0140D] Mons.] there are also two monasteries: one for women,

[(V. Autb.) which Saint Waldetrudis, wife of the aforementioned Saint Vincent and sister of the blessed Aldegundis, built. For when her blessed husband Vincent, having abandoned the shipwreck of the world, sought the harbor of a monastery, she too, inspired by divine mercy [Col. 0140A], resolved to trample upon the world. Intoxicated by the holy Spirit and strengthened by the blessed Autbert, she assumed the habit of the holy veil. Then, from her dowry benefits and personal estates, she founded the monastery itself in honor of Saint Mary, according to the decision and authority of Saint Autbert, her patron. There, having taken in not a few women of her household, she led a life of praiseworthy purity and prepared for herself the lamp of an unquenchable light, intending to go forth to meet her heavenly Bridegroom.]

The other monastery is one of canons of Saint Germanus.

## 40. On the Cell of Saint Gislenus

Not far from here, in a place they call the Cell, there is a monastery of the monks of Saint Gislenus.

[(ibid.) This man, instructed by an angelic vision, departed from Athens and directed the course of his pilgrimage to that very region. With the authority of the holy Autbert and with the assistance of Saint Waldetrudis, to whom he had then been bound by familiar affection, he founded that monastery (around the year 640).]

How great and what sort of life he lived, the book composed about his life will abundantly declare.

## 41. On the Village of Crispinium

In the village of Crispinium [Note: [Col. 0140D] Crépin.] there is a monastery of canons. As we said a little above (ch. 37), Saint Landelinus, leaving the monastery of Lobbes because of the multitude of brothers, entrusted its governance to the man of God Ursmarus and properly arranged its affairs; then, having completed the perfection of a purer life, he departed to Christ. Buried in peace, he shone forth through many virtues.

This little abbey, as can be seen in the royal charters in the first book (I, 68), is said to belong under the authority of the church of the holy Mother of God of Cambrai. But, as invasions by foreign peoples stealthily brought disorder, or as it was severed during a change of kingdom, it was taken into the benefice of military men.

## 42. On the Village of Condatum

At the village of Condatum [Note: [Col. 0140D] Condé, on the Scheldt.] there was formerly a royal and wealthy women’s abbey in honor of Saint Mary; now, because of poverty, it is a monastery of a few canons. There the holy man of God Wasnulfus, a Scot by birth, completed the course of his pilgrimage and, buried with the fathers, fell asleep in peace (around the year 700). Through his merits he illumined the whole place with miracles.

## 43. On the Village of Lutosa

There is also a monastery of canons in honor of the apostles Peter and Paul, in the village called Lutosa [Note: [Col. 0140D] Leuze, between Ath and Tournai. Le Glay.]. The blessed Amandus built it. It is a wealthy abbey where the venerable man of God Baidilo rests; he is said to have brought the body of Saint Mary Magdalene from Jerusalem to Burgundy, to the place called Vercelliacum.

## 44. On the Village of Rotnasce

In the village of Rotnasce [Note: [Col. 0141C] Renaix, between Oudenaarde and Grammont.] there is a monastery of canons, also built by Saint Amandus in honor of the same apostles, where the precious martyr of God Ermes rests. We are especially astonished that Ludovicus Pius gave this place, so ancient and so wealthy, as subordinate to the monastery of Inda [Note: [Col. 0141C] Inda, or Cornelimünster, near Aachen.].

## 45. On the Village of Iham

There is also a place on the River Scheldt called Iham, where in modern times the honorable Count Godefridus [Note: [Col. 0141C] Son of Godefridus of the Ardennes. Cf. *Auctarium Affligemense* of Sigebert, years 1005–1033.] and his wife Mathildis, a memorable noblewoman,—for it was their estate, suitable for their needs,—established a fortified castle, a landing-place, a market, a toll station, and other commercial activities. Within the castle they founded a monastery in honor of Saint Mary and assigned canons to it.

Outside it, Herimanus, their son, built two monasteries: one dedicated to Saint Laurence, the other to the holy Savior. Now, since the place has recently been established, it flourishes in every sufficiency; nevertheless, it would be more prosperous if it were not repeatedly shaken by hostile incursions. This it suffers especially at the hands of the enemies of God because of the stability of the kingdom and the loyalty owed to the emperor.

## 46. On the Village of Sumgeias

Let us also return to the place which, as we said, the blessed Vincent sought after leaving the brothers at Hautmont.

[(V. Autb.) The inhabitants now call this place Sungeias [Note: [Col. 0141C] Soignies, between Mons and Brussels.]. There the man of the Lord, withdrawn from the crowds of the population and accompanied by brothers, built a monastery. Having happily completed the course of this life, he lies buried in peace together with his son Landricus, bishop of Meaux.]

## 47. The Monastery in the Place Called Maslinas

At Maslinas [Note: [Col. 0141C] Mechelen.] there is also a monastery of canons, where the precious martyr of God Rumoldus rests. A Scot by birth, he led the life of a hermit and was martyred there. This monastery, built in ancient times, has been greatly enlarged by royal benefits.

## 48. The Monastery of Saint Guntmarus

Not far from here there is a monastery [Note: [Col. 0141C] Lier, on the Nete, near Mechelen. Le Glay. Cf. *Acta Sanctorum*, October V, 678.] of canons, which the illustrious man of God Guntmarus, a layman, built from his own estates (around the year 775). Buried there, he awaits the day of resurrection.

[Note: [Col. 0141] Here Book I ends in the middle of the penultimate page of a complete quire, with none of its leaves missing, on the final recto leaf. Another contemporary hand immediately added: “From the decrees of blessed Pope Gregory: that monks everywhere should minister in the priestly office,” etc. These words fill the final page of the codex and the blank half of the penultimate page left by the scribe. The same material is read here in Book IV, but a later hand, having erased it, wrote beside it: “These things are to be omitted as extraneous.” They had in fact been added in another script in the manuscript exemplar of Saint Gislenus.

Of the third book, not even a trace now appears in Book I; yet Colvenerius still saw and published it. Since we have learned from the first and second books that his reliability in editing and annotating was excellent and truly precise, we follow him as a trustworthy witness when recording the readings of Manuscript I throughout the third book, which survives today only in Manuscripts 2*, 3, and 4, but formerly also existed in Manuscripts 1, 2, and 5.]

# BOOK THREE. ON THE DEEDS OF BISHOP GERARD

[Note: [Col. 0141] Thus Colvenerius from Manuscript 1, apparently; cf. I, 122. Manuscript 4 has no title at all. In Manuscript 3 it reads: “Lord Gerard is made bishop of Cambrai. He is the one who completed and dedicated the church of Cambrai. Book Three.” Colvenerius added the chapter headings throughout the book himself; we have removed them, since they are not found in the manuscripts.]

## 1

As we said above, Lord Emperor Henry, acting with the unanimous counsel of his princes, bestowed upon Gerard, his chaplain, still a deacon, born of noble parents among the Lotharingians and Carolingians, at the village of Erwitte [Note: [Col. 0141C] Today Erwitte in Westphalia; thus the emperor was staying there in the year 1012, certainly not in 1013. Pertz.], on the Kalends of February, the gift of the bishopric [Note: [Col. 0141C] Colvenerius, and many after him, assign Gerard’s succession only to the year 1013, because he is said to have been given the bishopric by the emperor on the Kalends of February, whereas Erluinus died only on the third day before the Nones of February. But everyone agrees that the events narrated in the following chapter took place in the year 1012. And Henry, who, as our author states in I, 122, had already learned through the mission of Bishop Azelinus, before Erluinus’s death, that the bishop was near death, could easily have granted Gerard already then what Azelinus had likewise thought it not inappropriate to request from him while the bishop was still alive. Gerard’s charters provide no help. In a charter of the year 1046, published by Miraeus, *Opera diplomatica* I, 55, it is clear that one should read “in the eighth year of King Henry, in the thirty-fifth year of Lord Gerard’s episcopate.”] [in the year 1012].

When he was a boy, Albero, archbishop of Reims, took him away with the permission of his parents, both because of their relationship and because of the estates which he held by hereditary right in that region on his mother’s side; he raised him familiarly in his household while Gerard lived under the canonical rule. Under Albero’s generous instruction, he had gained a sufficient understanding both of the standard of ecclesiastical religion and of the discipline of worldly propriety.

After Gerard had been invested with the episcopal office [Note: [Col. 0142C] That is, “given” the office; he was ordained at Reims, cf. the following chapter. Le Glay.], the emperor kept him with him on that day and the next, namely the Feast of the Purification of the glorious Mother of God, Mary [Col. 0143A]. On the third day, however, granting him permission to depart, he ordered the abbots Richard [Note: [Col. 0143D] Of Saint-Vanne at Verdun.], Berthaldus of Inda, and Count Herimanus [Note: [Col. 0143D] Of Eiham; cf. II, 3, 2, 4, 6, 8.] by an embassy to escort Gerard and lead him all the way to the city entrusted to him.

While these men were accompanying him and, on his journey, were almost passing beneath the fortress of Valentiana, Count Baldwin [Note: [Col. 0143D] Of Flanders, “the Bearded.”], having heard the outcome of the matter, hurried to meet him, intending also to accompany him. Supported by such a large company, Gerard reached the city and was received by the people and clergy with joyful and most dutiful celebration.

When the royal envoys heard of the aforementioned violence of Walter (I, 120), they rebuked him sharply and indignantly; indeed, they asked with what spirit he had dared, together with other evil men, to seize even the episcopal residence [Col. 0143B]. Immediately putting forward a false defense, he deceitfully asserted that he had planned to act in this way not for the sake of plunder but for protection against the attack of Count Baldwin, of whom he was wrongly suspected.

They replied that this was far removed from the truth and supported more by deceit than by good faith, especially since he had left his own possessions untouched but had consumed the episcopal property in reckless expenditure. At last, with severity, they advised the misguided man to withdraw from his insolence after reforming his conduct [Note: [Col. 0143D] That is, *descisceret*.], and, having corrected his past actions, to maintain fidelity toward the bishop in the future. He immediately promised this with great solemnity; but, as will later become clear in many ways, he falsified his words.

## 2

After some time had passed (in March 1012 [Col. 0143C]), Lord Gerard, having arranged his affairs and bound his vassals and clergy to himself by oath, went to the emperor at the village called Nijmegen [Note: [Col. 0143D] Nijmegen. The king stayed there in March 1012.]. He also brought Count Baldwin along with the other faithful men of the emperor. There the emperor granted him the village of Walcheren as a benefice [Note: [Col. 0143D] More likely “the island.”].

In that place he had Lord Gerard ordained priest in his presence. Then, granting him permission to return, he ordered him to come to the church of the people of Liège on Holy Easter Day to serve him, bringing Walter with him as well.

When Gerard returned, he again found many evils. He was grievously assailed by the complaining cries of the poor: Walter beat some of them and continually harassed others with unusual exactions. Rebuking the tyrant for these actions, Gerard pointed out the dangers to his soul. But Walter, listening disobediently, completely distorted these salutary admonitions.

When Easter approached and the bishop planned to go to the aforesaid church to serve the emperor according to his instruction, he ordered Walter, together with his other faithful men, to prepare to travel with him. When Walter refused, the bishop himself hurried with his other men to meet the emperor in the city of Liège at the appointed time [Note: [Col. 0143D] “The Annals of Hildesheim, 1012: The king celebrated Easter at Liège. From there he proceeded to Bamberg; there the venerable monastery was consecrated on the second day before the Nones of May. The Annals of Liège, 1012: King Henry celebrated Easter at Liège.”]. Presenting the service owed to him, he complained about Walter’s injury and disobedience.

After this the emperor urged Gerard to travel with him to the city of Bamberg, in order to dedicate the new bishopric; there, in the emperor’s presence, Gerard would be ordained bishop by apostolic envoys and by the many fellow bishops and abbots who were to gather there for the dedication—*encenia*, from Greek καινός, “new” [Note: [Col. 0144D] A dedication, from *kainos*, “new.”]—of the church.

Although Gerard knew that he would be ordained more honorably and with greater discipline amid royal magnificence and Lotharingian skill, he replied that, captivated by affection for the place in which he had been raised, he wished to be ordained by no one except the metropolitan archbishop of Reims. He was considering the matter prudently and appropriately, lest he himself perhaps appear to oppose the custom of the metropolitan see, as Bishop Erluinus had received ordination at Rome because of the aforementioned dispute (I, 111).

When the emperor heard this, he recognized that Gerard had a higher-minded plan and readily agreed. Granting him permission to return, he gave him a book containing the consecration of clergy and the ordination of a bishop, so that he might be consecrated through it and perhaps not be ordained irregularly by the undisciplined men of the Carolingian region. Thus he soon returned to his own country with honor and prosperity.

Not long afterward, having prepared provisions and setting out for the church of Reims with his leading men, except Walter, the pontiff was ordained with the greatest reverence [Note: [Col. 0144D] The *Chronicle of Saint Andrew’s Castle of Cambrai*, written in 1133, states at I, 3: “He received the episcopal blessing on the fifth day before the Kalends of May.”] [April 27].

Thus elevated, he revisited as quickly as possible the sheep entrusted to him, but was in no way free from Walter’s insolence. His ears, moreover, were not closed to the complaints of the poor—those whom Walter, as has been said, tormented outrageously and, after plundering their meager possessions, confined in chains.

Therefore the emperor, again gravely stirred by the bishop’s outcry and angered also by the memory of such disputes as Walter had previously practiced against Erluinus, sent illustrious men, namely Counts Godefridus [Note: [Col. 0144D] Son of Godefridus the Elder, count of Verdun and later duke of Lower Lotharingia.] and his brother Herimanus, to this city [Col. 0144D]. He ordered them to make a man of such savagery come to him. He was surely astonished that, although Walter called himself the city’s castellan and advocate, he never attended the royal court.

The counts, obeying their lord’s commands, met Walter and, rebuking him in no gentle expressions of indignation as ungrateful for his former reconciliation and guilty of insolence, complained bitterly. He had not merely rendered his promised reform void; he had also, by increasing his tyranny, further provoked the bishop’s anger. He was attempting to usurp for himself the entire authority over the matter, while leaving the bishop only the name and appearance of honor. They therefore advised him to proceed to the emperor’s strict judgment.

Terrified by this, he immediately assumed the appearance of incredible repentance. One would have thought that he would never again fall; offering hostages with an oath and piling up entreaties, he humbled himself with complete submission for every kind of satisfaction [Note: [Col. 0145D] That is, “of every kind,” *jeder Art*.]. So much so that Lord Bishop Gerard himself, moved by pity, softened the angry counts by his prayers.

At the bishop’s request the counts were appeased and passed over all suspicion [Note: [Col. 0145] Thus Manuscripts 4 and 5; Manuscripts 1, 2, and 3 read *precorgrediuntur*.]. Having accepted five hostages of high value, they judged it appropriate to yield to Walter’s entreaties, on the condition that, if he did not satisfy the bishop within the appointed court session, he would afterward go to appear before the emperor for judgment.

The hostages themselves also swore this before the entire people: if he violated the agreement in any way, they would immediately follow the bishop and utterly abandon Walter.

## 3

After these events, and not long afterward, Walter not only voided his promise but also greatly increased the assault of his fury. For while Bishop Gerard was staying for some time with the emperor at the siege of the city of Metz (August 1012), Walter, suspecting I know not what evil, immediately changed his allegiance, ravaged the bishop’s external possessions, and even consumed the city’s suburb with fire.

When this was reported to the bishop, he was exceedingly astonished that Walter had done this, especially since he himself had done Walter no harm and was awaiting the agreed court session under an unbroken pact of faithfulness. Walter, however, pretending repentance for the broken treaty, cleverly anticipated a refuge suited to his presumption. The more seriously he realized that he had offended the bishop, the higher a protection he sought as a hiding place [Note: [Col. 0145] Manuscript 4 reads *suffragium*.].

He secured King Robert and Count Odo [Note: [Col. 0145D] Of Champagne.] as intercessors and helpers, and obtained their promise that they would appease Lord Bishop Gerard and ask pardon for his rashness. But because they were occupied with another matter, they delegated Bishop Harduinus of Noyon, together with other envoys, to Bishop Gerard as their substitute.

Seizing the favorable time for penitents, they came at the beginning of Lent (in the year 1013), having brought Walter back, to seek pardon. Softening the bishop’s anger with the soothing power of their prayers [Note: [Col. 0145] Manuscript 3 reads *delimento*; Manuscript 2* reads *delimente*.], they all descended into supplication.

The bishop, whom one might have thought most obstinate and inexorable, judged it right not to despise their petitions [Note: [Col. 0145] Colvenerius conjectured this reading; the manuscripts have *vili pondere*.]. After the hardships of domestic necessities had been lamented on both sides, he granted assent to their prayers, though under agreements of the following kind, confirmed by the oath of his friends.

## 4

At that time it happened that precious relics of many saints were found beside the altar in the monastery of Saint Mary of Arras (cf. II, 13). Since divine mercy worked signs and wonders of various kinds to reveal their merits, a very large multitude came together for almost two full years, not only from the neighboring districts but also from distant regions [Col. 0146B].

## 5

At that same time, when, after Bishop Nocherus of blessed memory, Baldricus had obtained the dignity of the church of Liège (in the year 1008), he resolved to take Count Lantbertus [Note: [Col. 0145D] Of Leuven; concerning him, cf. I, 96.] into his friendship, since he was a relative and therefore likely to become a helper of the homeland.

Bishop Gerard, however, repeatedly made known that he had discovered Lantbertus’s treachery and urged Baldricus not to take him into his friendship. He was a deceitful man, empty of faith; his cunning was to be feared. Subsequent events proved this to be true.

For when the bishop was fortifying a castle at the village of Huvardas [Note: [Col. 0145D] Hougarde, near Tienen. Cf. *Life of Baldricus*.], in order to strengthen peace and terrify evildoers, Lantbertus, seeing this as an obstacle to his own fury, immediately changed his allegiance. Gathering a strong force and taking Count Robert of Namur [Note: [Col. 0145] Here and in the second occurrence, Manuscript 1 has *Roberto*, Manuscripts 3 and 4 *Roberto*, Manuscript 5 *Rotbodo*, and Manuscript 2 *Rotboldo*. In the third occurrence, Manuscripts 1–4 have *Rotbodi*, while Manuscript 5 has *Rotbboldi*.] as his associate, he was not ashamed to attack the bishop.

After putting everyone else to flight, he handed over only Count Herimanus [Note: [Col. 0146D] Of Verdun or Eiham, brother of Duke Godefridus; cf. ch. 1.], who considered flight dishonorable, to the custody of Count Robert. Herimanus had withdrawn into the church of Saint Gorgonius, since all had fled and hope of resistance had been removed; there he was captured (October 10, 1013).

Although this was a matter of great concern to his friends, who were deeply grieved that he might be detained for a long time, divine mercy, which surpasses everyone’s wishes, brought it to a better outcome. The mother of Count Robert [Note: [Col. 0146D] Ermengardis, daughter of Duke Charles.], acting with sound judgment, promised to return Count Herimanus to his friends if, in exchange for so great a transaction, they would restore for her the favor of Herimanus’s friends and of the emperor, whom she had offended.

When Bishops Gerard and Baldricus learned this, they approached the emperor, who was celebrating a synod at a place called Confluentia [Note: [Col. 0146D] The *Annals of Quedlinburg*, 1012: “King Henry, coming to Confluentia for the feast of Saint Martin, held a great synod and dealt with Theodoricus of Metz … for the purpose of condemning him.”], and was discussing the bishop of Metz, who had adhered to his enemies [Col. 0147A]. They obtained the emperor’s favor for him, as the countess requested. Thus Count Herimanus was released from captivity without Lantbertus’s knowledge.

### 6

There is, moreover, a monastery in the district of Hainaut, in a village called Altusmons [Note: [Col. 0147] *valle* in 2*.], which, as the reader encounters later [Note: [Col. 0147D] That is, *retro*; for as the reader proceeds in reading, he leaves what precedes behind him.], Saint Vincent, having been made a monk from a layman through the preaching of blessed Autbert, built from property belonging to him under the monastic rule; and under royal authority it flourished to no small degree for many years. When, however, the causes of the various disasters that we read about came upon it, it was granted to counts as a benefice and gradually declined into such a state that, with the monks compelled by poverty, it was entrusted to the custody of a few clerics.

As time passed, it happened that Arnulf, the father of our lord bishop, received it in exchange as a benefice from Count Herimann. When he heard of the antiquity and profound veneration of the place, he wished, as a sound-minded man, to restore it to its former condition; but, as the causes of war intervened, he could not. After his death, it passed by inheritance to Arnulf’s son, Godefrid of Florennes [Note: [Col. 0147] Colv. corrected this to *Arnulfo*; the manuscripts read otherwise.] [Note: [Col. 0147D] Godefrid of Florennes; cf. II, 35.]. Divine mercy supported the desire of this man, who wished to improve it. For at that very time (1012) his brother was raised to the episcopate; and with his advice as well as his assistance, the canons were expelled and the monastic life restored under Lord Abbot Richard [Note: [Col. 0147D] Of Saint Vanne of Verdun.] (1016).

Richard later decided to appoint Fulcuin as his successor. Accordingly, Lord Bishop Gerard and Abbot Richard presented him to the emperor to be invested with the abbacy. For no one except the emperor or a bishop has the right to bestow an abbey, although their advocacies may be entrusted to laymen. Fulcuin, having thus been installed, with much labor and with the assistance of the lord bishop, fortified the monastery—which he had found deserted—with a cloister and other buildings, as well as with the regular service of the brothers. Having thus renewed it, the lord bishop consecrated it on the Kalends of May in honor of the holy apostles Peter and Paul, as it had been before. The abbot, however, could not endure the incursions of the clerics who had been expelled unless the lord bishop restrained them by his authority.

### 7

At the same time, after the death of Duke Otto (1013 or 1014), son of Charles—the deceased duke of Lower Lotharingia [Note: [Col. 0147D] Sigebert dates Otto’s death to 1005, but incorrectly, as is clear from our account.]—Godefrid, mentioned earlier [Note: [Col. 0147D] Chapter 2. Of Verdun; son of Godefrid the Old and brother of Count Herimann of Eiham, or Verdun.], attained the dignity of duke through the intercession of Bishop Gerard and by the support of the emperor’s leading loyal men [Col. 0148A].

An old and fiercely burning discord had long existed between him and Count Lantbert. Although Bishop Gerard knew Lantbert’s fickle loyalty and unstable character, he nevertheless reconciled them through an intervening peace, lest Lantbert, by some trick, should harm Godefrid in so new an honor. Thus promoted to so lofty a position, Godefrid discharged his loyalty to the emperor with honor and the greatest courage. Indeed, no one could better extend peace throughout the fatherland or calm wars. With him directing the counsels, the emperor subdued the necks of the proud and conquered his enemies.

### 8

Near the castle of Mons there is a little spring [Note: [Col. 0148D] This spring of Saint Waldetrudis still exists in the great forest of Mons, on the right-hand side of the road leading to Brussels, nearly a mile from the city of Mons, beside ancient ruins of walls called the walls of the pagans, in the district known as Castrum. Even today it is not without veneration. Colv.], preserved for many years by the inhabitants in honor of Saint Waldetrudis. There the sick are said to recover their health, after being bathed, through the merits of the holy Virgin [Note: [Col. 0147] *matronae* in 3; cf. II, 26.].

Once, when a certain woman went there to bathe because of an illness, she found the spring as if sprinkled with fresh blood; and while she was bathing, her face appeared bloodstained. On account of this portent, the lord bishop predicted that wars were impending; and the subsequent event itself showed that this was so.

### 9

Finally, as time went on (1015), the aforementioned Lantbert, together with his nephew Rainer, the son of Rainer, broke the treaty and again stirred up hostility against Duke Godefrid and his brother Herimann. The conflict advanced through mutual blows until they met in the field of Florennes and engaged in a fierce battle (September 12). By the just judgment of God, Lantbert was killed and fell, together with a great slaughter of his men [Col. 0148C].

Afterward, Rainer and Heinricus, the son of Lantbert, entirely imitating their father’s conduct, launched attacks against many of the emperor’s loyal men and gravely offended the emperor by their human deeds and outrageous behavior [Note: [Col. 0147] The manuscripts read *ita*; Colv. conjectures *inhumanis*]. Bishop Gerard, seeing that the lord emperor was occupied with other affairs, wisely provided, as far as he could, for the safety of the fatherland. With the assistance of his fellow bishops, namely Albaldus [Note: [Col. 0148D] Or Adelboldus of Utrecht.] and Haimo [Note: [Col. 0148D] Of Verdun.], he obtained, through an intervening peace, the emperor’s favor for the wrongdoers themselves.

### 10

After these events, Rainer sought to restore friendship by having the daughter of Count Herimann joined to him in marriage [Col. 0148D]. But because of the consanguinity that was alleged, this was entirely displeasing to Bishop Gerard, who considered it unlawful [Col. 0149A]. Nevertheless, afterward, taking the advice of his fellow bishops, he kept silent against his will, since they proposed the admonitions of blessed Gregory given to his disciple Augustine.

When Augustine was instructing the English through the preaching of the word of God and cultivating them in the faith of the Christian religion, Gregory advised him that, if he found a man and woman joined in the fourth or fifth degree of descent, he should permit them to remain joined even if they were unwilling [Note: [Col. 0149D] That is, unwilling to be separated. Colv.], for the sake of propagating the new Christianity. Children would be born from them who would observe the law more faithfully. It was therefore better to consent to this, lest there should perhaps be some loss to the ancient Christianity. For if such a man became his son-in-law, there would be hope of peace; otherwise, shipwreck for the fatherland.

### 11

There was also at that time a certain Count Gerard [Note: [Col. 0149D] Gerard I, Count of Alsace, son of Count Everhard by Eva, sister of Empress Cunigund.], disgracefully puffed up with secular pomp. By many attacks he provoked the emperor, and all the emperor’s rebels and disloyal subjects, as though he were the head and lord of all evil, perpetrated every kind of wrongdoing under him.

Having prepared a strong force, he went one day toward the neighborhood of Duke Godefrid, believing the duke to be unprepared, intending to rage there with burnings and plunder. But suddenly, awakened by messengers, the duke gathered those whom he had at hand and, trusting in his loyalty to the emperor as well as in God’s mercy, went against the enemy. Entering battle, he gained the victory after Gerard had been put to flight and his only son [Note: [Col. 0149D] Sigifrid; cf. Thietmar VII, 45.] had been wounded, captured, and afterward killed (1017, August 27). This event struck great fear into the remaining disloyal men and brought peace and tranquility to the fatherland [Col. 0149C].

### 12

Afterward, a battle took place in the field of Florennes (1015, September 12), where Count Lantbert was killed and brought his tyranny to an end, while not a few men on the other side were also slain. Since the lord bishop used to recount something remarkable and memorable about this event, I have thought it appropriate to record it.

That very night, when Lantbert was heading toward Florennes to fight, he committed incest by sleeping with a certain nun at Nivelles. She fastened precious relics into the clasp of his shirt so that, through their merits, he might escape danger in the battle. When they arrived, he put on a coat of mail over his other garments and, as is customary among fighting men, fastened the mail tightly to the helmet placed on his head [Note: [Col. 0149D] It appears that “helmet” has dropped out. Colv.], while deliberately keeping the relics beneath it, attached to the clasp of his shirt.

Relying on this protection, he fought as though impenetrable to iron, until, by God’s will, the holy relics suddenly burst through the intervening garments and the coat of mail and came to rest at a distance [Col. 0150A] upon a heap of stones, wrapped in a white cloth. Immediately the count, deprived of his strength, fell dead from his wounds.

One of those pursuing the count saw how the relics had leapt out while the others were killing the enemy; he found them and hastily hid them in his own boot. After the battle, when he returned home, he began to fall gravely ill in that very thigh. As the illness worsened, he was compelled to confess how he had found the holy pledge. When this was reported to Count Herimann, whose soldier he was, Herimann eagerly sought the relics and obtained them; nevertheless, he later yielded them to the emperor when the emperor requested them.

The lord bishop could not believe the incest mentioned above until he himself, together with Bishop Baldric, carefully investigated the matter in that same monastery. There the nun, overcome with shame, finally confessed her guilt.

### 13

After the battle of Gerard that we have already mentioned, the lord bishop and Duke Godefrid, together with the emperor’s other loyal men, suppressed with great effort the rebellions that the emperor’s brothers-in-law [Note: [Col. 0149D] Gerard and his brothers, sons of the empress’s sister. [Col. 0150D] Thietmar records this in Book VIII, chapter 9, under the year 1018: “Duke Godefrid and Count Gerard were reconciled by imperial authority.”] repeatedly stirred up against the order of the kingdom. They also obtained the duchy for Herimann, Duke of Bavaria [Note: [Col. 0150D] Our author is mistaken: it was Heinricus, the empress’s brother; cf. Thietmar VII, 39, 48.], who had been deprived of it (December).

### 14

At the same time, after the death of Baldric, bishop of Liège (1018, July 29), Vulpodo was appointed in his place. By the emperor’s command, Bishop Gerard led him to the same church and installed him in the episcopal see by bestowing the bishopric upon him. Endowed with every religious virtue, he displayed the standard of justice to his people and left examples of upright conduct and innocent life [Col. 0150C].

### 15

In those same days, a monk named Engebrand presided over the abbey church of Lobbes (1007–1020). But while living in a worldly manner under the appearance of the regular habit, he attacked the very name of his office. For inwardly he taught nothing of religion, while outwardly he shamefully squandered the church’s property.

Therefore the two bishops, Gerard and Vulpodo, took counsel together about what they should do. The latter acted because the church lay in his parish, the former because the abbey lay in his territory. They attempted to expel him and finally succeeded, though not without great effort (1020). He afterward declared that he had been deposed without legal judgment and raised such persistent complaints against the bishops that, when a court had been summoned, the same bishops assembled again with many abbots and canonically deprived him of his office by law, after he had confessed and been defeated before the entire people.

In his place, by divine grace’s prior arrangement, they appointed Richard [Col. 0151A] (September 22), a man of profound religious devotion [Note: [Col. 0150D] Already abbot of Saint Vanne of Verdun and Saint Vedast of Arras.]. He had edified the monks with spiritual instruction and had also worked to increase the external resources, as can now be seen.

### 16

At that time Abbot Richard also decided to release himself from the governance of the church of Arras, both so that he might serve God more freely and so that he might make clear to everyone that he had taken up the burden for a heavenly rather than a human ambition. With the counsel of Bishop Gerard, he appointed in his place Leduin, a layman who had been made a monk of devout religious life.

### 17

After Heribert, the venerable bishop of the church of Cologne, died (1021), Peregrinus was appointed in his place. In that same church, on the feast of the apostles Peter and Paul, he was ordained in the presence of the emperor, with many bishops—and also the lord Bishop Gerard—standing by (June 30).

After this ordination the emperor went to Nijmegen. There he decided to bring aid to his men, whom the Greeks were oppressing in the regions of Apulia, namely around the cities of Salerno, Benevento, and Capua, where they were raging. Having prepared provisions for the journey, he set out (August) and brought the lord Bishop Gerard with him as far as the monastery of Sanctas [Note: [Col. 0151C] Sains-les-Marquion, chapter II, 12.]. He honorably presented him with great and excellent gifts—gold, cloaks, and also a precious silver vessel—and allowed him to return home with affection and goodwill.

After completing the journey, he attacked the Greeks and surrounded the city of Troy with a siege (1022, May) [Note: [Col. 0151] With everything that follows omitted, the text passes immediately to chapter 49, as follows: “Thus, omitting the many attacks inflicted by that Walter upon the lord Gerard, the lord Gerard himself, after he had first committed the city entrusted to him…”]. There, remembering the lord Bishop Gerard, he sent him gifts again, expressly conveying every token of goodwill [Col. 0151C].

### 18

After the bishop’s father had died, the lord bishop, at Florennes, out of reverence for the place where he had been born and also for the salvation of his father’s soul, completed the monastery of Saint Gingulf, which his father had left unfinished. From his own property and that of his brothers he also founded another monastery of Saint John, distinguished less by the beauty of its buildings than by the strength of its workmanship.

He consecrated the former for clerics and the latter for monks, with the approval of Baldric, bishop of Liège, in whose parish they lay [Note: [Col. 0151C] The former means Saint Gingulf; at Saint John, it is sufficiently established that the Rule of Saint Benedict had been in force from the beginning. In the original Gembloux manuscript of Sigebert, a hand of the middle of the twelfth century wrote the following under the year 1010: “In the monastery at Florennes, monks were appointed in place of the clerics who had served there until that time”; under 1015: “Bishop Baldric acquired the abbey of Florennes for the one whom he presided over in the episcopate of Liège”; and under 1088: “The monastery of Saint John at Florennes was burned in the sixty-second year of its consecration,” from which it would follow that it was consecrated in 1026. But this is false, since both our account and the Life of Baldric, bishop of Liège [Col. 0152C], show that the consecration took place during the episcopate of Baldric, who died on July 29, 1018.].

Finally, that abbey [Note: [Col. 0152C] Saint John’s. Richard is the famous abbot of Saint Vanne, Saint Vedast, and Saint Peter of Lobbes.] was entrusted to the governance of Lord Abbot Richard and confirmed by the authority of the great emperor Heinricus. It began to flourish and afterward, thanks be to God, flourished more and more both in abundance of resources and in the holiness of its monks.

### 19

There was also a certain place, uninhabitable because of its forests and marshes [Note: [Col. 0151] “Afterward they settle inhabitants” in 2*. 3. 4.], which the inhabitants called Mereweda [Note: [Col. 0152C] Merwede, between Gorinchem and Dordrecht. For the whole chapter cf. Albert, *On Diverse Times* II, 20; Thietmar VIII, 13.]. There the river Meuse and the river Waal, flowing out from the Rhine, converge. Previously no one except hunters and fishermen was accustomed to live there, and it was a common possession in fishing and hunting of the bishops—namely those of Trier and Cologne—as well as of several abbots.

Theodoric, son of Arnulf of Ghent, had withdrawn there. He held a share in the rule of the Frisians and, because he regarded the Frisians with suspicion on account of his father’s death—for they had killed him—he had retreated there. After establishing a sort of fortified settlement, he, a foreign invader, had presumed to occupy the land itself and also to constrain merchants sailing there with an extremely heavy tax.

Therefore, when Emperor Henry was roused by the outcry, and especially compelled by the warning of Bishop Albaldus [Note: [Col. 0152C] Of Utrecht.], to whom the greater portion of that common property belonged, he ordered Duke Godefrid and the bishops of Cologne, Utrecht, and Liège to assemble an army (1018).

As they traveled in accordance with the royal command, an event occurred along the way which, in my opinion, should not be passed over in silence. Bishop Baldric had built a crypt in the village of Utrecht, in the monastery of Saint Mary, with an altar already erected above it [Col. 0152C]. When, after prayer, he went out on that very day and was about to board a ship in order to depart with the army, a remarkable thing happened: when the altar was overturned, the entire structure collapsed.

Many therefore regarded this as an evil omen, whether for the bishop’s public affairs or his private affairs, as the outcome soon proved. He himself had set out with the others, but, quickly overcome by illness, remained in a village called Herewardus [Note: [Col. 0152C] Herwerden.] [Note: [Col. 0151] Colv. reads this way; 2* has *fertur*, 3 has *Herewarda ut fertur*, and 4 likewise.].

The others, however, advancing with an innumerable multitude, attacked Theodoric and the few Frisians he had with him [Note: [Col. 0152C] At Vlaardingen, near Schiedam, on the right bank of the Meuse, where the sea enters.], undoubtedly expecting to defeat them. For who could doubt that so great an army, of such strength, would prevail [Col. 0153A] [Note: [Col. 0153] *ambigeret* in 2* and in the corrected text of 4.], especially since they excelled in military experience and discipline and were striving to please the emperor?

When they had engaged at close quarters, suddenly, it is uncertain who, assailed by diabolical prompting, twice burst forth in this dreadful cry: “Flee, flee!” Terrified by this, the Lotharingians, through some hidden judgment of God unknown to us, all took flight (July 29). How great and how pitiable a slaughter occurred among them is not for the present work to explain.

They suffered not so much from the enemy’s sword as from fear, and while fleeing among the ships they were endangered in great numbers [Note: [Col. 0153D] That is, in large numbers.], plainly fulfilling what is written: “One shall chase a thousand, and two shall put ten thousand to flight” (Deuteronomy 32:30).

Duke Godefrid, whom the success of the battles had inflamed, found himself surrounded on every side [Col. 0153B]. Considering it shameful to flee, he alone rushed into battle while his companions were fleeing. After killing those against whom he had charged, he was surrounded from the side and, although wounded, was captured [Note: [Col. 0153] Colv. corrected the manuscripts’ *capere*—found in 1, 2, 2*, and 3—to *capitur*; 4 has *tandem capite*.].

Theodoric, fearing to keep so great a man in captivity, took precautions for his own rash act and allowed him to depart, so that he might purchase the emperor’s favor for himself.

On that same day—and, as many conjecture, at the very hour when the battle took place—Bishop Baldric died in the aforementioned village [Note: [Col. 0153D] But Thietmar VIII says that he died at Tiel on the same day.], although his body was carried to Liège for burial.

The lord Bishop Gerard, summoned by a message to bury him, did not delay in going. Moved by fraternal affection, he rode swiftly throughout the entire night. When he was traveling near the castle of Mons, still unaware of the battle that had occurred, he first learned of the battle and of the duke’s capture. Thus moved by a twofold feeling, he hastened on his way and continually questioned everyone he encountered about the battle.

Before he reached Liège, news was brought to him that the duke had returned. Immediately, therefore, through this sudden change of circumstances, not only the bishop but many others as well exchanged the grief they had conceived over the bishop’s death for the joy they felt at the duke’s safety.

The bishop hurried to meet him at the castle called Argentolum [Note: [Col. 0153D] Argenton, between Gembloux and Namur.]. He was received there with honor and heard the entire course of the battle.

It should nevertheless be known that, nearly four months before that battle, a comet had appeared, more remarkable than usual, especially in its form, resembling an enormous beam [Col. 0153D] [Note: [Col. 0153D] Albert contradicts this in *On Diverse Times* II, 20: “Before this portent appeared in the sky, a battle had broken out near the shore of the ocean” [Col. 0154D].].

### 20

In those days, a certain abbot named Simon presided over the monastery of Saint Gislenus in the village of Cella, which we mentioned above (II, 40). Living in a worldly manner, he was selling off the church’s property. After his death (1015), he reduced it to such poverty that scarcely four monks remained.

The lord bishop, foreseeing this, sought an abbot and presented the holy man Wenric to the emperor to be endowed with the dignity. For although the abbey was poor and small, it nevertheless depended upon the royal hand.

Having become abbot (1015 or 1018), when he reached the monastery entrusted to him, he was astonished at everything that had been dissipated. He not only lamented the losses of the present but afterward also suffered many attacks by robbers, of whom very many lived there.

One of them, named Aldo, a notorious plunderer, inflicted many injuries. He was so lifted up by presumption that he sometimes moved about within the cloister with his plunder and weapons [Col. 0154B].

Therefore the bishop repeatedly appealed to Count Rainer [Note: [Col. 0154D] Of Mons.], who was deaf to him, since he too was a plunderer and was accustomed to favor plunderers.

It happened that, while traveling elsewhere, the lord bishop passed through that monastery. When he arrived, he found the aforementioned robber and entrusted him, after capturing him, to Albaldus, bishop of Utrecht.

After the passage of a year, the lord bishop, softened by the entreaties of many, allowed him to return, provided that he promised and solemnly swore that he would withdraw from robbery and remain faithful to the church with complete devotion. But breaking this promise, he afterward did not cease his insolence.

Not long afterward, however, he was struck down by death through God’s mercy. Nevertheless, with many of his men pleading for it, and without the bishop’s knowledge, he was buried in the cemetery itself.

How wicked this had been was revealed by divine mercy. For two years later, when others were digging a grave for burial near his tomb, no trace was found of his entire body except a single shoe [Note: [Col. 0154D] *Subtolare*, a shoe; hence the French word *soulier*.]. Through this, everyone is given to understand how great a condemnation awaits the wicked in hell.

### 21

After the death of Lord Abbot Wenric, Count Rainer appointed two abbots, one after the other, presuming in this way to claim the abbey for himself. Because this was unlawful, the lord bishop rejected it by his authority, since, as we said above (chapter 6), no one except the emperor or a bishop ought to entrust an abbey.

Afterward the emperor, at the lord bishop’s urging, raised to office the man whom he wished, namely Herbrand, who is still living [Note: [Col. 0154D] He died around 1045.], as was fitting. He too suffered many evils at the hands of Count Rainer.

### 22

Among these events, this too deserves to be committed to memory: in those days something happened in a certain village of the diocese of Utrecht, which the lord bishop used to tell us had been reported to him by Bishop Albaldus [Note: [Col. 0155D] Bishop Adalbold, in office from 1010 to 1027.].

Among the Waterland Frisians, near that parish, it is customary either for very few or for no one to wish to receive the Eucharist on Easter Day. On that day, therefore, a priest in a certain village of the same diocese, intending to feed the people with heavenly nourishment, urged the little community to come and receive the sacrament of heavenly life.

While they delayed according to their custom, one man who was more prominent than the others, driven by diabolical inspiration, did not fear to blaspheme the mystery of Christ. He said that he would rather have a beaker [Note: [Col. 0155D] A cup.] full of beer [Col. 0155B] than that heavenly banquet of the table.

To increase the others’ hesitation, he added that everyone who received the heavenly nourishment on that day would die within the same year. Terrified by this, they all, like ignorant people, withdrew from the Lord’s table.

The blasphemer, however, went as usual to a tavern and drank an excessive quantity of beer. Then, having mounted a horse while drunk, as he was traveling elsewhere with his armed attendant, he was immediately struck by divine vengeance. Falling from the horse, he broke his neck and gave up his spirit. Nevertheless, because he was the chief man of the village [Note: [Col. 0155D] *Meier*, mayor.], he was buried in the atrium [Note: [Col. 0155D] That is, the cemetery. Colv.].

How great a crime this had been, divine mercy wonderfully revealed not long afterward. Nor should it be passed over that, at the very hour when his master fell from the horse, the armed attendant was miraculously blinded; afterward, however, he repented and, by God’s mercy, received back his sight.
