At that time Bishop Albaldus was staying with Emperor Henry in Saxony. When he heard of this affair and learned that the blasphemer had been buried in the atrium, he groaned deeply. Judging it utterly unworthy that an unbeliever should share in the burial place of the faithful dead, he immediately ordered him to be disinterred.

But because no one dared do this out of fear of the man’s relatives, the bishop himself, leaving the emperor and passing through the same village, had the blasphemer dug up. He then ordered him to be dragged far away with a rope tied to his foot.

As he was being dragged—although he had lain beneath the tomb for nearly fifteen days—he vomited beer over a distance of one mile, astonishingly as though he had just drunk it [Col. 0155D].

Because the lord bishop often recounted this, I considered it right to write it down, so that it would not remain unknown to later generations: that all unbelievers might be shaken with terror, while the faithful might rightly rejoice.

### 23

We have also learned from the lord bishop’s account of a most remarkable event that occurred in those days to Albert, Count of Vermandois, brother of Otto, who is still living [Note: [Col. 0155D] He died on May 25, 1045.]. Divine mercy repaid him fittingly, and we do not wish to pass it over.

This count, devoted to every kind of wickedness, exercised the faculty of speech in slander, perjury, buffoonery, and every form of depravity. After he had done this for a long time, he was finally struck, by the just judgment of God, with a severe and intolerable illness and paid the penalty. Terrified by reflection on his crimes, he—through the devout advice of the monk Waleran, who at that time was provost under Abbot Richard of the monastery of Saint Hunegundis [Note: [Col. 0155D] Humolaria, or Homblierès, near Saint-Quentin. [Col. 0156D] “Waleran, the abbot, died toward the end of 1043, and his successor Bernard occupied the position in the same year, 1043, in which Otto, Count of Vermandois, confirmed to the monks of Humolaria the donation of an estate at Courcelles.” *Gallia Christiana* IX, 1077.] but is now, thanks be to God, an abbot of good reputation—adopted a false penitence, intending afterward to serve the Lord under the monastic habit (around 1016).

After his head had been tonsured and he had taken the habit, he recovered somewhat from that illness. But soon, at the devil’s prompting—for he had wholly clung to him—he returned to his vomit. On the advice of his mother and other supporters, who said that he had done this in a fit of madness, he again exchanged the cowl for a military cloak.

Immediately he was struck once more by an unavoidable illness. And, so that a recompense worthy of his merits might be evident to all, his tongue was found to have been consumed by divine fire.

When the hour of his death was approaching, foolish canons brought him the body of the Lord. After he had tasted it, he gave up his spirit in these final words: “The iron,” he said, “which the clerics brought me has killed me” [Note: [Col. 0155] *Canonici* in 2.].

When the aforementioned monk came again to visit him and wished to discover the hidden fire in his mouth, he opened the dying man’s mouth only with great difficulty using a knife. He showed his mother, brother, and the other bystanders the tongue, miserably burned as far as the palate [Col. 0156C]. In this way he plainly indicated God’s manifest judgment and the fitting recompense for the man who, as long as he lived, corrupted his tongue with every kind of wickedness.

Because this was reported to the lord bishop by a reliable informant, namely the monk himself, I have committed it to memory in honor of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that all who hear of it may be terrified if they are wicked, while the good may rightly rejoice.

### 24

At that time the lord bishop was also present, together with many other fellow bishops, at the consecration of Berold, bishop of Soissons, in the church of Soissons itself.

There Azelin, bishop of Laon, accused Harduin, bishop of Noyon, with every kind of cunning and deceit. In the presence of the fellow bishops who were there, he proclaimed him an outcast [Note: [Col. 0155] Colv. reads *extorret*.] and unworthy of fraternal fellowship.

To substantiate the matter, he publicly produced documents falsely bearing the name of the lord pope, in which he claimed that Harduin had been anathematized for many crimes. Having deceitfully enticed several fellow bishops to support this, he also thought that he could entice the lord bishop.

The lord bishop, however, avoiding his fabrications, disagreed entirely, although he was not unaware of some lapses of Harduin. He judged that Harduin certainly ought not to be condemned by the judgment of one at whose advice he had committed the alleged crimes. For he had heard from their chaplains that Harduin, at Azelin’s urging, had done certain shameful things.

Their dispute was debated for a long time and progressed so far that, driven by diabolical inspiration, they grew furious enough to fly to arms. The lord bishop, partly lulling them with soothing words [Col. 0157B] and partly pricking each of them with canonical rods, managed with the greatest difficulty to calm them for a time.

### 25

After the death of A., archbishop of Reims [Note: [Col. 0157D] Arnulf, who died in 1023, or, according to the *Annals of Mouzon*, in 1021.], Azelin of Laon acclaimed a certain layman named Ebulus, formerly his secretary and confidant in his cunning, and obtained the king’s consent through his flatteries.

He was a man without any discipline, who knew no literature except a few syllogistic arguments, with which he used to mock ignorant and simple people. Under the appearance of learning, he had long been striving toward the summit of so great an honor, and he was increasing his hope with much money, which he shamefully accumulated through usury.

Azelin had sought this for a long time and now labored especially hard so that through him he might exercise his own cunning more freely. When the lord bishop was summoned to Ebulus’s ordination and consecration, he protested vehemently. He declared it unworthy—as the outcome later proved—and contrary to the divine words, in accordance with the apostle’s saying, “not a novice” (1 Timothy 3:6), and he rebuked it in an emphatic contradiction.

### 26

Nevertheless, as time went on, when he saw that the man could not be corrected, he was led by the fraternal admonition of the fellow bishops to whom he had attached himself and assembled for a synod that they were going to celebrate at Mont-Saint-Marie [Note: [Col. 0157D] Mont-Notre-Dame, near Bazoches, not far from the city of Soissons [Col. 0158D].].

There Azelin, fearing Harduin’s objections, whom he regarded with suspicion, took precautions for himself by distorting Harduin’s arguments and handed one of the bishops a letter that he had written concerning Harduin’s offenses, so that it might be read.

When it was read aloud in public, it was heard that there was an anathema among them—namely, against Harduin, who was standing there. When the reading was finished, the synod was thrown into confusion and a great dispute arose. Nevertheless, the matter was deferred to another synod for more careful examination.

### 27

At that time, seeing that, through the king’s weakness and in consequence of his sins, the condition of the kingdom was collapsing completely, that rights were being confused, and that ancestral custom and every form of justice were being profaned, the bishops Berold of Soissons and Waleran of Beauvais thought that they would greatly assist the commonwealth if they followed the judgment of the bishops of Burgundy [Col. 0158A].

These latter, deprived of every authority, made a common decree that they and all other men should bind themselves under oath to preserve peace and justice.

Moved by this device of the aforementioned bishops, the fellow bishops of upper Gaul conspiring together also urged the lord Bishop Gerard to share their opinion. He, carefully considering the causes, thought it best to refuse outright. Understanding that their counsel was both disastrous and impossible, he gave no assent.

He replied that it would be not so much impossible as unfitting if they presumed to claim for themselves what belonged to royal authority. In this way too, he said, the order of the holy Church would be thrown into confusion, although it is commanded to be administered by two orders of persons, royal and priestly. To the one is assigned prayer, to the other fighting.

It belongs, therefore, to kings to suppress rebellions by force, calm wars, and extend the bonds of peace; to bishops belongs the task of urging kings to fight courageously for the safety of the fatherland and praying that they may conquer.

This decree was therefore dangerous for everyone: all would have to swear or be subject to anathema. For everyone would be entangled in a common sin if they used a device of this kind.

Thus the other fellow bishops secretly reproached and condemned the dissenting bishop, saying that he was not a friend of peace because he disagreed with those who desired peace.

Later, however, overcome by the repeated urging of his own people, and especially compelled by the prayers of the abbots Leduin [Note: [Col. 0158D] Of Saint Vedast.] and Rotric [Col. 0158C] [Note: [Col. 0158D] Of Saint Bertin.], he reluctantly yielded.

But what he had protested against beforehand was afterward proved by the outcome. Scarcely any of them escaped the crime of perjury.

28. Thus the lord bishop, armed with divine instruction, bravely defended the laws of the Church as best he could, and stood unconquered against all his opponents. He therefore rightly reproved the archdeacons of Liège, who, led either by love of money or by favor toward friends, allowed those excommunicated from their very cradles, who had spent their entire lives in every kind of wickedness, to be buried together among faithful Christians; and he admonished them by fraternal correction to abhor this practice, in the following manner:

> “Gerard, by the grace of God, though unworthy, bishop, to the archdeacons of the holy Church of Liège: may you make good by blameless conduct what the distinction of your title demands. Since I am always concerned, with fraternal affection, about the acts of your charity,” etc.

(For the remainder, see Gerard, *Patrologia*, vol. CXLII, col. 1313.)

29. Thereafter he corrected Adalbero, bishop of Laon, who had presumed to sell the episcopal office which he held to Wido the cleric—namely, the nephew of Bishop Berold—and intended to place him alongside himself on the episcopal see, in the following letter:

> “To the lord Adalbero, bishop of the holy Church of Laon, Gerard, by the grace of God, his fellow bishop. Although up to now we have been unmoved by the various rumors of the people concerning you,” etc.

See the work cited above, col. 1317.

30. He wrote similarly to Archbishop Ebalon, who had consented to this:

> “To Ebalon, archbishop, Gerard, a fellow bishop of no merit. Since we have heard that a certain novelty of detestable usurpation is growing up within your diocese,” etc.

See the same work, col. 1318.

31. To the bishop of Soissons, concerning whom we spoke above:

> “To Berold, bishop in name and merit, Gerard, a fellow bishop of no merit: whatever is most excellent for living blessedly. Since we have heard that a novelty of detestable custom is growing up within the holy Church,” etc.

See the same work, col. 1318.

32.

> “Gerard, bishop in name, not in merit, to Leduin, abbot, and to the whole congregation living under him of our holy father Vedast, and to all who devoutly read this page: may life and peace from God, who is life and glory to all who believe in him, be multiplied. Since we have recognized that you are a son of holy mother Church, imitating your merciful Father, God,” etc.

See the work cited above, col. 1319.

33.

> “Gerard, bishop in name, not in merit, to G., abbot: may he be strengthened by increases of virtue. Recently the archdeacons of Liège held a council concerning Hezelin and our niece, said to be his wife; and we are astonished, now that we have learned the truth, at what judgment they rendered among themselves and how they rendered it.
>
> “For we have heard that the same Hezelin has now said for the first time that he had intercourse with her only once; a fact which until now he kept silent about, although he had repeatedly been summoned on this matter before many assemblies. From these he often returned, moreover, sprinkled with the blush of shame because of the impossibility of such a claim. In truth, his silence meant nothing other than giving assent to those who contradicted him.
>
> “Therefore he ought no longer to have been heard on this matter before a synodal council, where the proven truth of the speakers’ words must be examined more carefully by the masters of the council, or their falsehood refuted. But suppose that he had intercourse with her once: what, then, of the rest? Namely, that he lived with her for eight years or more, and did not know her thereafter, and that there is no hope that in the future she should be expected to live otherwise?
>
> “In discerning these matters, let the teacher of the Church, the apostle Paul, be heard. Writing to the Corinthians, he says: ‘Let the husband render the due to his wife, and likewise the wife to her husband’ (1 Cor. 7:3). Then he continues: ‘Do not defraud one another, except perhaps by mutual consent for a time, so that you may devote yourselves to prayer; and return again to the same relation, lest Satan tempt you because of your lack of self-control’ (ibid., 5).
>
> “Let those who judge such matters explain to us what the Apostle wishes to be understood when he says, ‘except perhaps by mutual consent’; or whether the wife’s due could have been discharged, by their mutual consent, through intercourse only once during eight years.
>
> “But if they strive to seek something further, let them hear what the same apostle says elsewhere: ‘Do you seek proof of Christ speaking in me?’ (2 Cor. 13:3).
>
> “We have thought it necessary to write this to you so that you may set this apostolic judgment more clearly before those who know how to judge such matters otherwise than lawfully. Let them either accept it, or, if they reject it, let them put forward something they have found more reasonable.”

34.

> “To Lord Fulco, bishop of Amiens, Gerard, by the grace of God fellow bishop of Cambrai, wishes both innocence in this life and heavenly glory with the angels. That our brother Drogo, bishop of Thérouanne, is assailed by Count Baldwin with such great injuries,” etc. See Gerard, as above, col. 1321.

35. In those days (July 1023), while the emperor Henry happened to be conducting affairs, both ecclesiastical and secular, in the palace at Aachen, a provincial synod was meanwhile held in the church itself by the bishops. There a considerable dispute arose between Pilgrim, archbishop of Cologne, and Durand, bishop of Liège, concerning the monastery of Burtscheid, which each sought to subject to his own diocese.

The lord Bishop Gerard, wishing to settle the dispute by the testimony of truth, publicly reproved them, saying that the bishops of Liège had consecrated five abbots of that monastery without any opposition from the archbishop. Indeed, at the emperor’s request and at the petition of Baldric, bishop of Liège, Gerard himself had ordained the clerics of that monastery in the church of Saint Mary at Aachen, in the presence of the lord emperor, and had consecrated the monastery together with Archbishop Poppo of Trier and Haimo of Verdun. It therefore seemed to him more correct that the monastery should be subject to the jurisdiction of Liège rather than Cologne.

When the others likewise testified to this, the archbishop, moved to anger without any regard for synodal reverence, departed.

36. Nor should it be consigned to oblivion that, for several days while the synod was being held (July 1023), such dryness of the air and oppressive heat blazed forth that many mortals were thought to be collapsing from the excessive heat, and several animals suddenly fell dead. On the other hand, the marble columns of the church itself appeared to sweat with abundant and unusual moisture, so much so that it would have been enough, by chance, to wash anyone’s hands. The marble pavements, too, seemed to float as though bursting with such a quantity of liquid that the custodians of the church were thought to have deliberately sprinkled them.

Many wise men were astonished by this and did not know what to conjecture; but, judging by human appearances, they foretold the impending ruin of certain princes whom the faithful of the Church were evidently destined to mourn. And indeed it was so: shortly afterward the duke died first [Note: Godfrey of Lorraine], and then the emperor. As we shall relate later, the holy Church laments that through their deaths she suffered desolation.

37. From there the emperor departed (August) and went to the exceedingly beautiful village of Ivois [Note: Ivoi, on the river Chiers], which had been ennobled by the birth of the blessed Gaugeric. There, with the leading members of his palace, he intended to meet King Robert [Note: a gap occurs in the source], to discuss the condition of the empire and not merely worldly but also spiritual matters. He had wisely arranged this because he knew that Gaugeric had been born in that place, and he wished to come there to celebrate his joyful feast, which falls on 11 August.

The emperor, who was the greater and therefore the humbler, judged it fitting to meet King Robert, when he came to him, at Mouzon [Note: Mouzon, in the Ardennes], on the feast of Saint Lawrence; but on the following day, the feast of Saint Gaugeric, he received him with the greatest reverence.

It is not for my insignificance to unfold the details of this exceptional meeting and gathering for so great a solemnity. There assembled leaders and nobles of various nations, as well as a great number of eminent men, both bishops and abbots. Many also came in order to marvel at the imperial dignity, which fame praised so highly.

There a supreme settlement of peace and justice was made, together with a reconciliation of mutual friendship. There, too, careful discussion was devoted especially to the peace of God’s holy Church and to how they ought better to assist Christianity, which lies exposed to so many falls.

Afterward, consulting one another about where they might again meet, with the apostolic lord and with the bishops from both sides of the Alps present with them, they decided that nowhere was more suitable than Pavia.

When these matters had been completed and they ought to have parted from one another, who could adequately estimate the number and value of the gifts with which the emperor presented the king—gifts offered by the archbishop of Cologne, by the lord Bishop Gerard, and by Duke Godfrey as well? The king, wishing to give a gift to the emperor, presented whatever gifts he could so that the emperor might accept them. The emperor, however, returned all of them with thanks, being exceedingly wealthy, and retained only a tooth of Saint Vincent the martyr, so that he would not appear to have accepted nothing.

Nor did the emperor think only the king deserving of gifts. He also heaped precious gifts upon all the bishops and abbots, as well as upon the greater men, and left scarcely anyone without a present. Therefore, all who had gathered there to learn of the emperor’s magnificence, amazed at what they had seen, said that they had witnessed more than rumor had reported. I would not dare compare any king of the Persians or Arabs with him, although I had read that those peoples surpassed all nations in wealth.

38. From there the emperor proceeded to Verdun (8 September), intending to celebrate the Nativity of Saint Mary. He brought royal envoys with him, who were to hear there the response of Count Odo, explaining how he defended himself against the charges of King Robert, by whom he was accused.

On that very day the lady empress, because the lord bishop had escorted her in the procession [Note: that is, he walked at her right hand], gave him a stole decorated with gold and gems.

There, too, the lord emperor, moved by the conflict which had for some time been burning between Odo and Theodoric of Toul [Note: Duke of Upper Lorraine], brought it to an end by an imposed peace, after the castles which Odo had unjustly built had been destroyed.

Moreover, he distributed precious gifts to the monasteries throughout the city, first to the principal monastery and then to the others. Later, when he reached Metz, he distributed great wealth among the individual monasteries, leaving no good cleric or monk without a gift, as though by some presage he foresaw the day of his death, which was exceedingly near.

Finally, granting the lord Bishop Gerard permission to return to his own affairs, he apportioned a great quantity of gold with a full hand [Note: literally, “he divided by the handful”]; and afterward, saying farewell, he sent through Gerard to Saint Mary two pallia, one plain and the other marked with a golden surface in the form of a cross.

39. Thus the lord bishop returned, but was not spared Walter’s customary evils. Among these, Walter gradually began to persecute with hatred a certain young man of his, named Robert, distinguished both by noble birth and by virtue, because he suspected that Robert would oppose his tyranny.

He did not rest until he killed him, although the lord bishop, who was seeking to reconcile them, intervened, even while Robert was under a truce [Note: literally, “placed under three truces,” hence the French *trêves*, “truces,” that is, *treugae*], and although it was Sunday.

For this and other similar offenses he expelled Walter from the city. But shortly afterward, when the emperor had died in consequence of the sins of Christians, and Walter was compelled by other circumstances, he judged it advisable to receive him into the castle, though under an agreement supported by an oath.

But because he repeatedly fell into perjury and frequently repeated his customary offenses, we have decided to append the many agreements which he craftily promised to the lord bishop when he was being reconciled, so that the pious reader may admire the bishop’s patience and, with astonishment, deplore the tyrant’s boundless savagery. They are as follows:

40.

> “I will maintain the fidelity which I promised you for as long as I am your man and hold your property; and, setting aside the customs of the Karlings [Note: the customs of France], I will show you the honor which the Lotharingian knights show to their lords and bishops.
>
> “And if I commit any offense against you and am warned by your representatives to make satisfaction, I will render you such justice, unless you pardon me, as the aforesaid Lotharingian knights render to their lords and bishops.”

41. The oath which Odo, Robert, Anselm, and Lambert swore at Walter’s request:

> “From this hour forward we shall cause you no harm, whether to your life, your limbs, the bishopric of Cambrai, your lands, your castles, or any other possessions which you hold today or may acquire in the future through our counsel, saving the fidelity owed to our lords, whom we have today.
>
> “And in order to destroy this agreement, we shall not make a lord, nor shall we acquire a knight. If Walter commits an offense against you and does not make amends within two forty-day periods [Note: that is, two periods of forty days], he shall receive no assistance from our side against you. And if you warn us, we shall help you in good faith, without evil intent.”

42.

> “The agreements which we again have with our Walter are known to everyone. Previously, too, we forgave, for the love of God and of his friends, the unheard-of offenses which he committed against us, on the condition that he thereafter remain faithful to us, just as he himself and his friends then swore.
>
> “Although he has horribly and unheard-ofly broken this promise, we again pardon him on these terms, both for the love of God and at the request of King Robert, Bishop Harduin [Note: of Noyon], Count Baldwin, Count Odo, and also Otto, Robert, and his other friends who made this agreement, so that he may keep these second promises better than the first.
>
> “He shall be obedient to us in all things, as he first promised. If clerics or laymen of our Church bring any complaint against him, he shall be subject to hearing and judgment according either to law or to agreement; and furthermore, for all those to whom we can administer justice against him, he too shall administer justice through us, if they bring complaint.”
>
> “He shall wage no war from our city which would bring harm to us or to our bishopric, without our permission. If he breaks this promise and, after being warned, is summoned to justice, as has already been said, he shall make amends within two forty-day periods, in the presence of two or three friends who made this agreement. If an impediment [Note: *sonia*, or *sunnis*, meaning an impediment; hence the French *soin*] prevents them from attending, that impediment shall be proved, and we shall await the agreement for another forty-day period.
>
> “We shall observe this agreement on both sides in good faith [Note: literally, “perfect faith”], without evil intent.”

43.

> “If this son of Walter, now our hostage, should die, he shall give us another in his place, one through whom he can make us secure concerning his fidelity; and whatever he has unjustly seized from us shall, when we warn him, be determined according to the judgment of our faithful men.
>
> “If Walter dies while his son is still in our power, we shall return the son to his knights and the property of this holy Church [Note: a lacuna occurs in the source], which his father holds lawfully [Note: ‘by right’], while nevertheless preserving the agreement which he promised us and making our lord the emperor and me secure concerning his fidelity.
>
> “If I, Gerard, called bishop, die before the son is returned, he shall be returned to his father, while the agreements stated above are preserved, and provided that he gives the Lotharingian king such security as will make him secure.”

44.

> “He did not remain long in the promises stated above. Rather, falling from bad to worse, he treated the Church entrusted to me as an object of plunder and trampling, and rose up against me so violently that for three days he besieged me in this city, armed with his satellites, so that none of my men dared leave it.
>
> “For this reason Heihamp came to me, while I had Count Herman with me, and asked that I forgive him these things. I yielded to his request and to those of his friends, forgave him all these matters, and pardoned him all the penalties for the things he had made good; I ordered him to restore to the poor what he had unjustly taken from them. He agreed, but did not fulfill it.
>
> “He then again promised fidelity by oath to my lord and to me, as before, and swore that he would obey me as the Lotharingian knights obey their lords and bishops.”

45.

> “Walter, accustomed to evil, set aside all his oaths and afterward acted worse than he had ever acted before. I endured this wickedness for a long time and continually warned him to amend his conduct.
>
> “When he saw that I would no longer tolerate such things, after an agreement had been arranged between him and me, he brought Count Otto with him. Sent to account for such great evils, Walter was again defeated, made amends for everything, promised to restore to the poor what was theirs, and promised to submit to me as the Lotharingian knights submit to their lords and bishops, as he had promised before.
>
> “At Count Otto’s request I forgave him all the penalties, on the condition that he should no longer commit any offense against me; but if he did offend and was warned to come to justice, he would justify himself to me within three weeks.
>
> “For this reason Count Otto gave me Godfrey and Ivo as hostages, so that if Walter failed to observe these terms, he would receive no assistance from their side; but if the count himself violated this agreement, the hostages would come into my power, if they were summoned.
>
> “At Count Otto’s command, each hostage confirmed this to me by oath. In that agreement I forgave what Walter himself and his men had committed against me, on the condition that, if he should again offend me and be unwilling or unable to make amends, past offenses would be joined to future ones; that the judgment which his peers had previously rendered concerning his benefice would remain firm; and that he would be excommunicated without delay.
>
> “As for what concerns penance and Christianity, I did not forgive it, but included it in the agreement, so that he and his men themselves would render an account of it.”

46. Count Otto promised God, Saint Mary, and Bishop Gerard, with his hand in Gerard’s hand, that if Walter should ever thereafter commit any offense against the bishop or against the Church entrusted to him, and should be unwilling or unable to make amends, Otto would never give him or his men any assistance, counsel, or refuge which might bring harm to the bishop or to the Church entrusted to him. Walter would neither be Otto’s man nor hold Otto’s benefice without the bishop’s counsel [Note: that is, without the bishop’s permission to obtain or receive it]. Otto swore that, to the best of his knowledge, he would observe this in good faith, without evil intent.

Ivo swore that Count Otto would not, on his advice, fail to observe the aforesaid oath; and, if Otto wished to withdraw from it, Ivo would, in good faith, make him follow it if he could. If Otto fell into an offense which he was unwilling or unable to make good, Ivo would not provide him with counsel, assistance, or refuge that could harm Bishop Gerard or the Church entrusted to him. He would observe this in good faith, without evil intent, while preserving fidelity to his lord.

47. Walter gave twelve hostages to Bishop Gerard. Their names are as follows: [lacuna: the names are missing; the names are absent in all witnesses, and witnesses 2*, 3, and 4 leave not even space for them]. They swore that Walter would not, on their advice, fail to observe this fidelity; and if he fell into an offense which he was unwilling or unable to make good, then, after they had been warned, they would bring him to justice within eight days, if they could.

If he did not do this, then within another eight days, after being warned, they would come to the bishop with their benefices, in good faith. They would never give him counsel or assistance that could harm the bishop or the Church entrusted to him, and they would help the bishop against him in good faith.

48. This is also the agreement most recently made at the town of Schelmas [Note: thus witnesses 1, 2, and 2*; witness 4 reads *Schelinas*, and witness 3 *Chelmas*. The following passage, from “town” through “he supplied ornaments,” is absent from witness 2 because of an excised leaf. It is likewise absent from 2*, which leaves a space of three letters and has the marginal note, “the remainder is missing”]. To make it known to everyone, the lord bishop proclaimed it in a form of semi-Latin speech as follows:

> “Since we excommunicated him for innumerable offenses, he rose up against us in such madness that he sought to kill certain of our men because they did not favor his side, and violently compelled his soldiers who were with him, though excommunicated, to enter the greater Church of Saint Mary and other churches.
>
> “Therefore great necessity compelled us to suspend the churches from divine worship. He also inflicted many evils upon us and our people, which would take too long to recount.
>
> “At last, unable to endure his madness any longer, we expelled him from our city without taking anything of his. After his expulsion he began to rage against us even more and to plunder and burn with fire as many of our villages and churches as he could.
>
> “Later, by the order of our lord, Count Baldwin and his son brought him to Tournai, where Duke Godfrey and the bishop of Liège were present. He rendered us no justice, but, his fraud having been revealed to everyone, persisted in wickedness.
>
> “But when, at last, compelled by necessity, he found an opportunity, he confirmed this agreement in the presence of Bishop Hugh [Note: of Tournai], Count Baldwin and his son, as well as Otto and Eustace, together with us.”

[Note: The words of the agreement are absent, together with a leaf, in the copy of Saint-Ghislain. Colvenerius says that other material concerning the end of Walter is probably missing. Since neither the second witness nor the others supply anything of the kind—not even the trace of a lacuna—we believe that nothing has fallen out of the first witness. What seemed to Colvenerius to be a removed leaf may have been erased by the scribe before he copied the text, a practice frequently observed.]

49. From the time when the lord Bishop Gerard first entered the city entrusted to him, he saw the monastery of Saint Mary’s buildings to be both cramped and old, and, suspecting cracks in the aged walls, immediately turned his mind toward improving them, if God should grant him a suitable opportunity.

But, as we related above (II, 2), hindered by both internal and external disturbances, he could not begin this undertaking until the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1023, in the [blank] year of his episcopate [Note: the manuscripts leave a space for the number].

Then, relying on divine mercy and strengthened by the prayers of many of God’s faithful, in which he had placed his trust, he ordered the ancient masses of masonry to be demolished. Once this had been done, he girded himself with every effort. Like a wise architect, he worked carefully at the task he had begun, and, prudently expending the necessary funds, hastened to rebuild a work of such difficulty, fearing that he might be overtaken by death or compelled by some other circumstance to leave the work unfinished.

He realized that nothing would delay his desire more seriously than the slow transport of the columns, which were quarried nearly thirty miles from the city [Note: a brief passage is missing in one witness].

Therefore he prayed to divine clemency that it might deign to provide him with some assistance nearer at hand. One day, having mounted his horse, he searched the earth in many places throughout the surrounding region. At last, with God’s help—for he never abandons those who hope in him—in a village which antiquity called Lesden [Note: Lesdain], four miles from the city, he had the earth opened and, according to his wish, found column-stones.

Nor was this all: digging nearer still, in the village of Nigella [Note: Noyelles, on the left bank of the Scheldt], he rejoiced to find another kind of good stone. Giving thanks to God, he devoted himself entirely to this pious labor. Not to delay further: through the working of divine mercy, he completed the immense work in seven years, namely in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1030 [Note: the *Chronicle of Saint Andrew of the Castle of Cambrai* I, 21, apparently drawing on the annals of the same monastery, says that it was consecrated in 1027, on 18 October].

Afterward, as was fitting, he solemnly—and, so to speak, more than solemnly—dedicated it on 18 October. Who could worthily recount the pomp of such glory? Who, however eloquent, could restrain such dignity within the compass of words?

There one would have seen the bodies of the saints of our diocese gathered together with the people and clergy; choirs of monks and canons mingled in ranks; and not merely the interior of the city, but also the fields outside, everywhere covered with a multitude of both sexes.

It is most pious and salutary for devout hearers to recall how the lord bishop arranged the bodies of the saints around the altar. He and Abbot Richard, both dressed in garments adorned with sewn, embroidered strips [Note: that is, wearing vestments decorated with embroidered bands], lifted the most blessed Gaugeric, the supreme bishop and principal master of the holy dedication, with the greatest devotion. After hymns had been sung, while clergy and people wept for joy as they watched, they placed him in the episcopal chair, as he had formerly been.

Beside him they placed, on either side, the holy bishops Autbert, Vindentian, and Hadulf, who had themselves been ministers at that same altar; they also inserted the staff of Saint Vedast with its relics.

Then he arranged the others—namely, martyrs, confessors, and virgins—around them, each according to his proper order, as was fitting. Whoever spiritually perceived them so arranged undoubtedly believed that they were engaged in the work of the holy consecration.

But what shall we say about the solemnly established fair? What about the other solemn ornaments? These matters can more easily be admired than recounted.

After consecrating the monastery, he supplied many ornaments [Note: witness 1 ended at this word in Colvenerius’s time, as he says, because its final gathering had been lost. That gathering still survived at the end of the twelfth century, when witnesses 2 and 7 copied it, but had disappeared by the fourteenth century. Witness 3 did not have it, but, ending at *adhibuit* (“he supplied”) and in the same hand, immediately appends the very brief continuation, “After this man—Savine,” printed below. Witnesses 4 and 5 likewise end at *adhibuit*, in the middle of a page; nothing is lost. The following text is therefore supplied only from witnesses 2, used by Colvenerius, and 2*, used by us]; he enlarged the golden panel, replacing those on both sides with silver ones; he renewed the golden crosses with equally golden banners [Note: *vexilla*]; he added a golden chalice, pallia, and chasubles, and took care to provide all the other necessary utensils.

To provide lighting, he assigned two manses at Anderlecht [Note: Anderlecht, near Brussels], where the oratory of Saint John is known to stand; when necessary, their revenues would serve to repair the work of that oratory.

Moreover, he added to these the estate of Bishop Fulbert at Wileve [Note: compare I, 70].

For the restoration of the new building, he assigned eight manses at Letfringen [Note: perhaps Ledringhem, arrondissement of Dunkirk], together with their church. He gave half of the village of Ireneias [Note: perhaps Ivergny, arrondissement of Saint-Pol], together with its church, for the use of the poor.

For the prebend of the brothers he added the church in the village of Maionis, called Fontanas [Note: perhaps Fontaine-Notre-Dame, Fontaine-au-Pire, Fontaine-en-Beauvois, or Fontaine-l’Évêque], and the allod of Gertrude.

He granted them the village of Pescant, inherited from his parents, together with its inhabitants of both sexes, for their support. He divided its revenue in such a way that at the dedication of the church they would spend half of it, while they would receive the other half on the day of his ordination for as long as he lived; after he had been taken from this world, they would convert that latter share from his ordination into an annual commemoration of his passing.

He added to the bishopric the estate of Rolaincurt [Note: Baillencourt, arrondissement of Arras, or Roellecourt, arrondissement of Saint-Pol], which he received from Ragnelin; likewise another estate in Brabant at the cross of Hado.

He also assigned to the bishop’s table at the Castle of Saint Mary, surrounding which it lies, one quarter of the estate of Perrone, which he had acquired from four free men—Robert, Hubald, Athelin, and Sueto.

There he built the oratory of Saint Andrew from its foundations [Note: the *Chronicle of Saint Andrew of the Castle of Cambrai* II, 19, says that it was dedicated on 22 September 1025; for what follows, compare the charters of Gerard and Conrad II in Miraeus, *Opera diplomatica* I, 55]. He gave one third of one quarter of the aforesaid estate to the community of monks, which he supported with pious care for as long as he lived.

He wished the allod of Theoderic’s Mount, inherited by the knight Hervard and his nephew Fulco, to remain with them [Note: that is, with the monks]. He also gave Watineias [Note: Wattignies, arrondissement of Avesnes], which the aforesaid Hervard already possessed by his own right, and whatever Fulcuin and Resino appeared to hold at Briasto [Note: Briastre, arrondissement of Cambrai]; in addition, the village called Fontanas; at Petrosa, one third together with its church; the estate at Solman received from Fagala; another at Bermerenc [Note: Bermerain, on the Escaillon, arrondissement of Cambrai], from the knight Gontho; likewise half of the village which he wished to be called the Estate of Saint Andrew; and the church of Ferrerias [Note: Ferrière, arrondissement of Avesnes, or Ferrière near Le Câteau], exchanged [Note: one witness reads “the exchanged church of Ferreria”] from the brothers of Saint Mary; another church of Saint Benignus; and the churches of Ors and Wasvilare [Note: Saint-Benin, Ors, and Basuel, canton of Le Câteau]; at Viseto; and in Brabant, an allod called Ham with its church; the church of Liniaco [Note: Ligny, arrondissement of Cambrai]; another at Furnis [Note: Furnes]; another in Cambrai, that of Saint Martin, with its oven; and half of the toll of the new castle, together with both churches and one mill.

50. After some days had passed [Note: one witness reads “after these things had passed,” as Colvenerius conjectured], the final lot brought the revered King Henry to die (13 July 1024). Let the world itself, in its calamities, speak better for us of how much desolation his departure from life brought upon humanity.

At last the Saxon princes assembled at Mainz and set Conrad over themselves as king (8 September 1024). Duke Godfrey, the prince of the Lotharingians, wished to oppose their decision. He addressed the bishops of Cologne, Noyon, Verdun, Utrecht, and Liège, and received an oath from each that they would not offer him their allegiance without Godfrey’s consent, nor go to him.

The same Duke Theodoric [Note: of Lorraine] and Count Reginar of Hainaut confirmed this by oath, together with their associates.

The bishops were the first to break it—the very men who had first submitted themselves—and became an evil song of the people [Note: compare Lam. 3:14, “I have become a mockery to all my people, their song all day long”].

The lord bishop had not joined any of these agreements. Rather, after he learned that their judgment was not sound, he tried to restore them to the grace of peace [Note: one witness reads “to return them,” as Colvenerius conjectured]. Meanwhile he suspended his own approach to the king’s presence, lest this become a cause of scandal or offense to them; nevertheless, by sending envoys courteously, he cleared himself of suspicion.

Even so, he sought to placate the king of the Franks with gifts, lest the king first impose upon him the usurpation which he had resolved to carry out throughout the whole kingdom.

He also restrained Count Baldwin with moderation, lest, corrupted by Walter’s frauds, he build fortifications for himself at Cambrai.

At last, when the dukes had been bent toward peace after a year and almost half, he went with them to the palace at Aachen and willingly offered himself to the king’s submission (December 1025).

As time went on, Baldwin, son of Baldwin, wishing to equal his father, broke with him. He went to the emperor, hoping through him to obtain from the lord bishop permission to build fortifications at Cambrai, intending to rebel against his father. But the bishop opposed him and deprived him of this hope [Note: after this, one witness leaves the space of two lines and another adds in the margin, “missing”; Colvenerius made no note concerning the other witness].

[lacuna]

### 51

At Tribur, near Mainz, Emperor Conrad summoned bishops from various regions so that they might confer with one another about matters of usefulness and religion (May 1036). After some discussion of what they had said, they adopted this provision: if, as usually happens, the fast of the first month should fall in the week in which the beginning of the fast occurs, the observance of both fasts should be completed in a single office.

[Col. 0170B] In this matter the most moderate shepherd again urged that the ancient custom of the fathers be preserved, and judged that the office of the first fast should be celebrated in the following week, according to ancient custom. His opinion was submitted, appeared appropriate, and was decreed by them to be observed.

[Note: [Col. 0170C] “The beginning of the fast” is the name given to the four days from Ash Wednesday through the first Sunday of Lent. COLV. Sigebert, on the fast of the four seasons, in Martène, *Thesaurus*, I, 298.]

### 52

This kind of decree was issued by the bishops of France to be observed by the peoples subject to them. One of them said that letters had been sent down to him from heaven, urging that peace be renewed on earth. He communicated this to the others and gave them the following instructions to transmit to the people:

No one was to bear arms; no one was to reclaim what had been seized; no one was to act as an avenger of his own blood or that of any neighbor, but was to be compelled to forgive the attackers. They were to observe a fast on bread and water every Friday, and on Saturday abstain from meat and fat; and, content with this fast as satisfaction for all sins, they were to know that no other penance was to be imposed upon them for those sins.

[Note: [Col. 0169] *licet*—“although”—in manuscript 2*.]

They were to bind themselves by oath to observe these provisions. Whoever refused was to be deprived of Christianity; and when he departed from this world, no one was to visit him or commit him to burial. They also issued many other exceedingly burdensome commands, which it seemed oppressive to repeat.

Struck by this novelty in the command, and yielding to the weakness of sinners, our bishop shaped his speech on each point according to the decrees of the holy fathers. He demonstrated that the human race had from the beginning been divided into three classes: those who pray, farmers, and warriors. He gave clear evidence that each of these is supported by the others on the right and on the left:

> “While the attention of those who pray, free from the affairs of the world, is directed toward God, they owe this to the warriors: that they enjoy a secure holy leisure; and to the farmers: that they are nourished bodily by the farmers’ labors. Yet the farmers are lifted toward God by the prayers of those who pray, and are defended by the weapons of the warriors.
>
> “In the same way, the warriors, while they are supplied with provisions by the revenues of the fields and supported by the proceeds of trade, are also fostered by the holy prayer that expiates the offenses committed with their weapons on behalf of the faithful whom they protect. Thus, as has been said, they support one another.”

[Note: [Col. 0171D] That is, *annonantur*: they are nourished by provisions.]

[Note: [Col. 0170C] That is, those who pray, or priests. This division into three classes is attributed to Noah, who said to his sons: “You pray humbly; you protect; and you work.”]

> “Since the ancient page shows that Abraham, Joshua, and David took up weapons for battle at the Lord’s command, and priests gird kings with the sword, while grace reigns in our mother the Church, the bride of God, there is no fault in the office if there is no sin in the conscience. The Apostle also calls them ministers of God, saying: ‘For he is God’s minister, an avenger for wrath’ (Romans 13:4), and adding: ‘For he does not bear the sword without cause’ (ibid.).”

[Note: [Col. 0171] Manuscript 2* reads *ira* (“wrath”) for *iram* (“for wrath”).]

[Col. 0171B] That seized property ought to be returned, as the ancient commandment—that is, of the Old Testament—makes clear, is sufficiently illustrated by the example of Zacchaeus, who said to the Lord:

> “If I have defrauded anyone, I restore fourfold” (Luke 19:8).

Nor do those who reclaim their property sin, even though they hear:

> “If anyone takes what is yours, do not demand it back” (Luke 6:30).

For we read two things: that the Lord remained silent when questioned, and that he spoke when he was not questioned. His silence is no more purposeless than his word is salutary. Just as he praised Zacchaeus for returning what he had seized, so he was silent about reclaiming it, because of unavoidable necessity. But when he said, “Do not demand it back,” he permitted the perfect to do what they had resolved upon, for the cutting away of desire; he did not command it, as I have said, as a matter of necessity. Thus in the one case he did not forbid reclaiming, and in the other he permitted not reclaiming.

[Note: [Col. 0171] Manuscript 2* reads “God” instead of “the Lord.”]

[Note: [Col. 0171] Manuscript 2* omits “not” in “when he was not questioned.”]

Therefore kings, instructed by the holy fathers, established firm laws so that the Church or anyone else might justly reclaim property unjustly taken from them, and so that the person who had stolen it would be legally compelled to restore it.

[Note: [Col. 0171] Manuscript 2* reads “restitution.”]

The same judgment applies between the one who strikes a man and the avenger of his neighbor. The attacker ought to placate the avenger by satisfaction and gifts, since he has injured and offended him by depriving him of the consolations of his dead friend. Nor should the avenger be compelled to forgive without reconciliation, since the Lord sent him from the altar a reconciler bearing an offering (Matthew 5:23–24). Would that the goodwill offered by the penitent might draw him, though he is less perfect, to this reconciliation.

[Note: [Col. 0171] Manuscript 2* reads “reconciliation” instead of “reconciler.”]

[Note: [Col. 0171] Manuscript 2* reads *tutabat*; the reading is materially uncertain.]

A fast on Friday, or even on Saturday, must not be imposed generally upon everyone, since not all possess the same bodily health and the accusation of sin does not weigh equally upon all. Nor should this satisfaction be considered sufficient for all sinners. For crimes that increase day by day must be cleansed according to the decrees of the Gospel, the Apostles, the canons, and the pontiffs; and it is not fitting for those who preside to command the people to do anything contrary to these decrees. Their commands should agree with those who, made instruments of the Holy Spirit, have uttered their words or written them through his breath, lest they appear to destroy what has been established.

[Note: [Col. 0171] Manuscript 2* reads “forgiving” instead of “imposing.”]

[Note: [Col. 0171] Manuscript 2* reads *ita* (“thus”); Colvenerius reads *quidem* (“indeed”).]

[Note: [Col. 0171] Manuscript 2* omits “should command.” Colvenerius reads it.]

Those who refuse to confirm these provisions by oath should not be struck with excommunication, since human weakness is scarcely strong enough to observe a single command, much less to be bound by perjury after neglecting all these matters.

[Note: [Col. 0171] Manuscript 2* reads “to confirm” instead of “to make firm.”]

[Note: [Col. 0171] Manuscript 2* omits “is.”]

When someone is about to depart from this world for another, his mind—naturally inclined both to forget and to remember—is scattered far outside itself by the magnitude or novelty of the journey and therefore somewhat forgetful of itself. He ought to be recalled by the consolations of the devout, so that he may repent of his sins, even if he has remained hardened until that moment; much less, God forbid, should mercy be denied to him when he asks for these things.

God’s authority also said that every sinful dead person should be committed to the earth, since the sinner of all sinners, the murderer, heard:

> “You are earth, and into earth you shall go” (Ecclesiastes 3:20).

[Note: [Col. 0171] All the following material in this chapter is found in manuscripts 2 and 2* only after the words “then they returned,” at the end of chapter 54. Since it clearly makes no sense there but is very closely connected with the present chapter, I have transferred it here. The error of the scribe of manuscript 2 probably arose because, in manuscript 1, all this material—from “Concerning what we have said” to “equality”—had undoubtedly been added by the author himself on a slip sewn in separately; the scribe of manuscript 2 inserted that slip in the wrong place.]

We wish to repeat this concerning what we have said, lest anyone rashly suppose that we have not set forth the Gospel words clearly enough against the bishops’ statutes.

[Note: [Col. 0171] Manuscript 2* reads *sapere* (“to understand/know”) for *aperte* (“clearly”).]

For the Lord gave some of his commandments alike to the imperfect and the perfect, and others to the perfect alone. This is enough as evidence: when he had said to a certain young man, “You know the commandments?” and then said, “You shall not kill,” and the rest of the same kind, and when the young man had answered, “I have kept all these from my youth,” he said:

> “If you wish to be perfect, sell what you possess and give to the poor” (Luke 18:20, 22).

Elsewhere, discussing eunuchs, he said:

> “Let the one who is able to receive it receive it; for not all can receive it” (Matthew 19:12).

Nor are we unaware that someone might say that no one enters the kingdom of heaven unless he is perfect. To such a person we point out:

> “Star differs from star in glory” (1 Corinthians 15:41),

and we repeat the Lord’s words:

> “In my Father’s house are many dwelling places” (John 14:2).

The inequality of these dwelling places, so to speak according to our understanding, has been made solely according to his omnipotent will. Yet, so that equality of measure might be preserved among them, inviolable charity has been given to each toward the others. Whatever exists in each, by sharing with all, is sufficient for everything, because whatever has been made is sufficient for all through what it possesses in its own nature.

We say similar things about ourselves: our imperfection is supplied by the one to whom the prophet says:

> “Your mercy is better than lives” (Psalm 62:4).

Through this it comes about that what each will possess in heavenly life will be sufficient glory, and that they will share in the joy of all, filled with the perfection of charity, so that equality may be achieved.”

[Note: [Col. 0171] Manuscript 2* reads “is.”]

### 53

After this there was a reason why he went to Douai. There, when the assembled people called for a false peace to be established, he replied at the appropriate time with what he had received from the one who is the same yesterday and today (Hebrews 13:8), and who is not changed by tomorrow’s time.

Walter had whispered into the ears of everyone, those outside and those inside, that the bishop was unwilling to consent to peace—not because he was a son of peace, but because he sought more freely to devote himself to the practices of his wickedness. He had combined the two points stated above (chapter 52): that no one should bear arms and that no one should reclaim what had been seized. He was striving to ensure that silence would be imposed concerning the robberies and killings by which he had been sustained in the past, so that from then on, while no one bore arms, he might enjoy his accustomed evils more freely.

The bishop, who foresaw this, calmed the people and exposed Walter’s cunning. To show that he was not opposed to peace, he remitted to him his many debts—provided only that thereafter the people should seek peace from him in truth, even at a loss, if that could bring it about, of their own property, since, as has been said, he had remitted all his debts to Walter for this purpose.

[Note: [Col. 0173] Manuscript 2* reads “for” instead of “on account of this.”]

### 54

After these events, Baldwin, then count of the Flemings, began urging the bishop, as a favor to the people, to order them to confirm the peace by oath. The bishop, not even then departing from sound judgment, declared that he would command nothing other than what the law and the Gospel announce.

At last, overcome by weariness, he came with a large crowd to the designated place between Cambrai and Arras, after many bodies of saints had been brought there. Yet even here Walter was not thwarted. He walked and muttered now around the place, now outside and inside it, saying that the bishop was resisting peace, to such an extent that he stirred up the people almost to the use of force.

[Note: [Col. 0173] Manuscript 2 asks, “What was being struck?”]

The bishop, entirely undaunted, addressed him publicly in the following manner to refute his customary wickedness:

> “A painting suggests the image of the devil standing at Simon’s ear, whispering what he should say while contending against the Apostle Peter. Your conduct is no different: you stir others up toward an evil that you yourself are not capable of achieving.”

[Note: [Col. 0173] Manuscript 2 reads “customary” instead of “to refute.”]

Then he quieted the people so that they would listen and instructed them concerning the peace they wished to seek among themselves, who wanted to consume him.

[Note: [Col. 0173] Manuscript 2* reads *deinde* (“then”) for *deinceps* (“thereupon/next”).]

After speaking about the salvation of the soul, which the law of Christianity commands them willingly to preserve, he urged them to promise that they would observe it; and whenever they deviated, they would return to penance.

[Note: [Col. 0173D] That is, “that they would observe.”]

Thus encouraged, accepting his words as true, they unanimously made the promise and returned peacefully to their homes.

[Note: [Col. 0171] The material beginning “We wish to repeat this” and ending “so that equality may be achieved” belongs here in manuscripts 2 and 2*, but has been transferred above because it belongs with chapter 52.]

### 55

Emperor Conrad went to Italy (1036) to deal with the kingdom according to his desire and to attack those bearing arms against him. While he was staying there, he irreverently threw into chains certain Lombard bishops who favored the party of Odo [of Campania] (1037). The archbishop of Milan [Heribert], captured in a similar manner on another matter, saved himself by flight.

Enraged against him, Conrad set fire to the widely extended regions, leaving no human being there (March). For he had reached this agreement with the Lombards: they had collectively sworn that, whether powerful or lowly, they would by no means tolerate any lord who acted against them in a manner contrary to their wishes.

At last Pentecost arrived (May 29), which required that the king be crowned during the solemn celebration of Mass, according to custom. When a church was sought, none could be found except one small church near the city itself. And behold, from morning onward thunder began to be heard and flashes of lightning appeared with such violence that many lost their senses in their houses, while some expired during the liturgical celebrations, as Bishop Bruno [of Minden], who sang the Mass, testified.

[Note: [Col. 0173] Manuscript 2* has the abbreviated divergent phrase *a. e. tres etiam i. m. solempnia*; its exact expansion is uncertain.]

A certain royal secretary, Bertulf, also said that he had seen Saint Ambrose, stirred to indignation by the evil deeds of the king. After this, leaving the matter unfinished, Conrad turned back across the Alps (August 1038), and not long afterward was afflicted by illness. He died at Utrecht (June 4, 1039), leaving his son Henry heir to his kingdom and his labor.

[Note: [Col. 0173] Manuscript 2* omits “was afflicted by illness.”]

The bishop mentioned above went to Henry and entrusted himself to his hands; Duke Gothilo did the same, although he had been somewhat inclined to refuse.

The following signs preceded Conrad’s death. A year earlier, in April, on the eighth day before the Ides, there appeared in the sky between the eastern and southern regions what seemed to be a fiery beam of great size. Moving over the sun, which was already declining toward sunset, it appeared to fall to the earth. Its traces could be seen for a long time, as happens when clouds close after a flash of lightning.

[Note: [Col. 0173] Manuscript 2* omits *ipso* (“very”) from “in that very year.”]

In that same year in which he ended his life, there was a solar eclipse on the day before the Ides of May. And, as I said, he himself died on June 4, the second day before the Nones.

[Note: [Col. 0173] Manuscript 2* omits *solis* (“of the sun”).]

[Note: [Col. 0174D] Our author is mistaken: it was on 22 August; the preceding “55 d.” is uncertain as printed.]

### 56

In the following month of August (1039), the lord bishop came with the king to Maastricht. At the request of Bishop Nithard [of Liège], he raised the bodies of the holy confessors Gondulf and Monulf and took relics from them. There the church was consecrated in honor of Saint Servatius.

Later, at Metz, the church of Saint Stephen, the first martyr, was consecrated. At the request of Theodoric, bishop of that city, who was also present, he received precious relics of that martyr of Christ and carried them away with him.

### 57

He expelled from the city Aldo of Vido, who held the church of Saint Gaugeric in advowson and oppressed it excessively, since he had been convicted of many wicked acts. For he was extremely deceitful and estranged from its truth and fidelity.

[Note: [Col. 0175] In manuscript 2, according to Colvenerius: “The first five words of this chapter had been erased, as had the end; I was therefore able to read them only with great difficulty.” In manuscript 2*, where the distinction of chapters disappears from chapter 49 onward, the passage reads: “he carried away with him what was said to be the relic of Saint G.,” with space left for one word.]

[Note: [Col. 0175] Manuscript 2* reads *nimis* (“excessively”) for *multis* (“many”).]

He accepted a judicial combat against him—that is, a duel—by which he withdrew, that is, surrendered and acknowledged himself defeated, and he acted according to law, losing what had been adjudged to him.

[Note: [Col. 0175C] “A field,” that is, a judicial duel.]

[Note: [Col. 0175C] “He withdrew”: he yielded and acknowledged himself defeated.]

[Note: [Col. 0175] Manuscript 2* has this reading; *cui dum* is absent, and Colvenerius supplies *fiet*.]

[Note: [Col. 0175] After this point, material was erased in manuscript 2; manuscript 2* leaves space for two words.]

[Lacuna.]

### 58

[Note: [Col. 0175] Manuscript 2* leaves space for two words after this point.]

When the lord Bishop Gerard was about to dedicate a church in honor of Saint Mary, Mother of God [of Arras], he removed the altar from its proper place. When the earth around it had been dug up, many relics of saints were found there, along with the arm of Christ’s confessor Vedast, a considerable part of his head, and parts of certain other limbs.

The church itself was therefore solemnly consecrated on January 4, after the body of Saint Vedast had been brought there, together with other saints, by the monks of that place.

[Note: [Col. 0175] In manuscript 2, fourteen lines had been erased after this point; in manuscript 2*, space equivalent to one and a half lines was left.]

[Lacuna.]

### 59

A few days earlier, Lietduin—formerly a layman, later made a monk and abbot of monks—departed from this world laudably and, as we hope, reached the next world happily (circa 1044). He left grieving those whom he had instructed in every good work.

To say something briefly about him: through the unlearned wisdom of God, he showed the inflated learning of grammarians to be foolish, while carefully avoiding everything belonging to the world and faithfully fulfilling what belongs to God.

He introduced Abbot Richard, a highly religious man, and Frederick, the uncle of Count Baldwin, who had turned from the world, prudent and just. Through Richard, that place began to flourish in holy religion and worldly resources; and when he was appointed to that place, he remained nobly, as was fitting, in every good work.

[Note: [Col. 0175C] Compare Mabillon, *Acta Sanctorum Ordinis Sancti Benedicti*, sixth century, I, p. 190.]

[Note: [Col. 0175] The words “and Frederick … just” are missing in manuscript 2.]

He restored the monastery from its foundations (1031), enlarged it with every useful provision, and lived blamelessly in all the Lord’s ordinances. After God took him away, Abbot John succeeded him, elected by the brothers, with the support of the lord Bishop Gerard and Count Baldwin.

[Note: [Col. 0176C] That is, Richard; compare chapter 16.]

[Note: [Col. 0175] After the end of this chapter, when half a page was blank in manuscript 2, a later hand added the following words: “In the year 1148, on September 6, the Church of Cambrai, the Church of Saint Aubert, and the whole castle perished in one and the same fire.” COLV.]

### 60

> “To the most serene Lord Henry, august among emperors, Gerard, last of the bishops and servant of God’s servants: the gift of perpetual peace and salvation.

[Note: [Col. 0175] Manuscript 2* has the abbreviated apparatus indication *post usque ponit* (“after ‘up to,’ it places …”); the precise scope is uncertain.]
>
> “I attribute this to my sins: that God, not you, to whom I sin incessantly, has withdrawn from me in the last period of my life whatever comfort I had hitherto promised myself from you, now that I am an old man already worn out. Nevertheless, I briefly bring this to your ears, because I am not considered guilty before you concerning the fidelity that must be preserved for the common condition of the kingdom.
>
> “For thirty years we have lived in our city amid the swords of our countrymen. It is unnecessary to remind you of how much has been given to them by our Church through daily distribution, and of what was conferred upon my predecessors in the episcopate by the kings Otto and Henry of blessed memory, and was also found by me in the patrimony.
>
> “Just as your generosity has a treasurer—*saccellarius*, from *saccus*, ‘bag’—who handles the daily expenses when circumstances arise, so I too am their treasurer, so that the delay of death, or rather the repose of life, may be obtained for those who are with me, which the rod of your discipline ought to have brought about.
>
> “And whose favor could this be except that of the kingdom? On the other hand, the hand of your blow has grown heavier upon us, since our smallness has been considered less capable in your eyes.
>
> “I say this to my lord: let him think whatever evil he wishes about me, but concerning the usefulness and purpose of what is, as it were, our protection, let him not lend pious ears to just anyone. Let him consult those who know the people and the country, and let him trust usefulness more than insinuation.
>
> “Nor is it fitting for a royal person to keep as intimates those who have hitherto attacked peace and to cast away those through whom peace flourished. Believe me truly: this advice is simulated, not genuine. For that reason I delayed obeying you, because otherwise neither you nor we would have any peace remaining.
>
> “It is certainly not so surprising if, without due cause, you are more indignant with me than is just, just as Maurice was with Gregory (Gregory, *Letters* 4.31), although I am far beneath Gregory. But consider the dreadful vengeance that Maurice underwent, while he who is yesterday and today (Hebrews 13:8), whose vicarious person we enjoy, remains.
>
> “Through him who formed and united the Church from his side, we beseech you not to divide and scatter it, lest, God forbid, you be found outside it when God’s winnowing fan purifies it.
>
> “Do not admit talkative young men with Rehoboam; rather, [follow] the silent Hushai, David, the wisest prince among the three (2 Samuel 23), as you—[lacuna].”

[Note: [Col. 0176C] *Saccellarius*, or *sacellarius*, “treasurer,” *Säckelmeister*, from *saccus*, “bag.”]

[Note: [Col. 0176C] That is, “ought to have done,” *avait à faire*.]

[Note: [Col. 0175] Manuscript 2* reads “unless the matter was contrary to the kingdom.”]

[Note: [Col. 0175] Manuscript 2* reads: “if I have offended you more than is just.”]

[Note: [Col. 0175] Manuscript 2* reads “if you strip it bare.”]

[Note: [Col. 0175] Manuscript 2 has approximately two lines missing after “as you.” Colvenerius writes: “What follows to the end of Lietbert was written by another and more recent hand; nevertheless, the style suggests the same author.” The scribe of manuscript 2* wrote in the margin, “a little is missing,” and then continued with the same pen, without any distinction: “To him indeed,” etc.]

[Lacuna.]

## THE DEEDS OF BISHOP LIETBERTI

[Note: [Col. 0177] We have supplied this title; it is absent in manuscripts 2 and 2*. The excerpts begin here from the book of the deeds of the bishops of Cambrai: “Concerning the lord Lietbert, successor of Gerard, the seventh bishop,” which begins here. We have established the division into chapters.]

[Col. 0177]

### 1. (Chapter 61)

This Bishop Gerard was succeeded in the episcopate by the lord Lietbert, who was born of a noble lineage in the region of Bracat [a land of Alost, where Brakele]. From his ancestors he was entrusted as a boy to be educated under the discipline of Gerard himself.

[Note: [Col. 0177C] Bracat is the land of Alost, where Brakele is situated.]

[Note: [Col. 0177C–D] The *Necrology of Blessed Mary of Cambrai*, in the Cambrai library, manuscript no. 219, early twelfth century, copied from an older source, records: “On the fifth day before the Kalends of February, Lietbert, father of Bishop Lietbert, died. On September 6, Osburgis, mother of Bishop Lietbert, died.”]

[Note: [Col. 0177D] Rodulfus adds in the *Life of Lietbert* that Gerard was related to him by blood. But the present author’s silence on this matter creates doubt.]

This boy, endowed with a teachable intelligence and formed by the devout master’s continual instruction, was abundantly imbued with a twofold learning. When the pious father saw him growing through good studies and advancing day by day toward better things, he began to love him exceedingly and to make him a participant in his counsels. To strengthen him further in learning, he entrusted him with the direction of the schools of Saint Mary, the mother of the Church. This honor is rarely entrusted to nobles because of the labor involved; but the rarer it is, the more honorable it is judged.

[Note: [Col. 0177] Manuscript 7 reads “more rarely.”]

Through the exercise of this ministry, the young man began to attain the summit of more perfect learning and to flourish wisely among the wise. When the bishop learned of the schoolmaster’s diligence, he removed him from the instruction of boys and made him remain always in his presence and cling to his side. In his judgments, both public and private, he first made him an auditor and soon afterward a judge.

Thus it came about that, after a short time, the young man shone most effectively in divine and human affairs. When the bishop saw that he abounded in good virtues and preserved his chastity inviolate, he began to love him above all others and to conduct both private and public affairs on his advice.

[Note: [Col. 0177] Manuscript 7 reads “works” instead of “virtues.”]

Since divine clemency, wisdom, and virtue had exalted him, the bishop judged it advantageous to magnify him, conferring upon him the archdeaconate, the provostship, and the other greater ministries of the Church. Having received these honors, he used them in such a way that he was judged worthy to enjoy still greater ones.

[Note: [Col. 0177] Manuscript 7 reads *sic* (“thus”).]

[Note: [Col. 0177] Manuscript 7 omits a word here; the apparatus does not identify it more precisely.]

### 2. (Chapter 62)

After some time, old age crept upon Bishop Gerard himself, as his years inclined toward sunset. Because of this, he was already becoming weaker than before, both in divine mysteries and in human affairs. But Lietbert, whom he had nurtured from childhood and exalted with honors, assisted him greatly in both matters.

[Note: [Col. 0177] Manuscript 7 has *nutrierat* (“had nurtured”); manuscripts 2 and 2* have *nutriebat* (“was nurturing”).]

Meanwhile it happened that Walter, castellan of Cambrai, was killed by his enemies and died (1041), leaving behind his only son and his wife.

[Note: [Col. 0177D–0180] At Cambrai, at the entrance of the monastery of Saint Mary, while he was praying, as they say—we have little reliable knowledge of this—he was killed by four men who had conspired for this very purpose. *Chronicle of Saint Andrew’s Castle of Cambrai* II.8. The *Lesser Annals of Elnon* record:

> “1041. Walter, castellan of Cambrai, was killed at the door of the Church of Saint Mary while he was praying. Before paying what he owed to death, however, he wished to make amends to God, Saint Mary, and the bishop of the Church for what he had unjustly done. When the bishop refused what he offered, he died excommunicated according to the bishop’s judgment and was buried beside the Oise, on Mount Erni.
>
> “This evil progressed so far that almost the whole Cambrai region was burned with fire and utterly devastated at the command of his wife Ermentrudis.
>
> “The Flemish count Baldwin, grieving Walter’s death, took it grievously that his body had been unjustly excluded by the bishop from the atrium of the holy mother Church—unjustly, he thought, because Walter, dying before those standing by, had acknowledged himself guilty before God. For this reason, compelled by the archbishop and Count Baldwin, the bishop rightly absolved the man whom he had unjustly bound. His body was then disinterred from the place mentioned above, transferred to the monastery of Saint-Amand beside the river Elnon, and buried in the monks’ cloister before the church doors.

> “His epitaph:

> *This ditch contains the bones of Walter the prince,*
>
> *whom the Cambrai sword struck down as he prayed.*”

His wife, whose name was Ermentrudis, did not cease from the madness of her husband; rather, wandering through every kind of worse conduct, she surpassed her husband’s wickedness. Since she could not exercise her malice on her own as she wished—for her son was still a child—she took a certain tyrant named John, the advocate of Arras, as her husband and appointed him patron of herself and her son.

The boy soon died, according to what is written:

> “The generation of the wicked shall perish” (Psalm 36:28).

John, whom the boy’s mother had married and who had invaded the boy’s benefice through his mother, tried by force or deceit to transfer to himself what no law allowed him to possess. To make the matter easier to accomplish, he began to assail Bishop Gerard with great promises and to corrupt his necessary associates and friends with money.

He did not wish Lietbert, the wisest among the bishop’s faithful servants, to participate in this plan, fearing that Lietbert’s prudence and fidelity would turn him away from his undertaking. Therefore, to keep him far from the bishop’s counsel and drive him away from the city, he falsely accused him of enmity on fabricated grounds. He had disclosed to many that, if opportunity arose, he would even inflict death upon him.

Meanwhile Bishop Gerard fell ill. Oppressed by the infirmities of extreme old age and by the illness of an acute fever, he could not leave his house unless carried out by the hands of others, nor could he arrange what would be useful either to himself or to the commonwealth.

The lord Lietbert could not remain constantly with him because of the hostility and ambushes that John directed against him. He therefore stayed at the new castle of Saint Mary, which had been assigned to his custody, except when he occasionally visited the bishop for the sake of refreshment, surrounded by a gathered troop.

John rejoiced at his absence, but still could obtain nothing from the bishop, because Lietbert’s friends dissolved and rendered useless every device of his petition.

### 3. (Chapter 63)

While these things were taking place, the time of his calling arrived, and Bishop Gerard died (March 14, 1051).

[Note: [Col. 0179C–0180C] The *Necrologies of Saint Gaugeric*—Cambrai library, manuscript no. 55, copied at the end of the eleventh century from an older source—of Blessed Mary—Cambrai library, manuscript no. 219, twelfth century—and of Anchin—Douai library, manuscript no. 825, early twelfth century—together with the *Chronicle of Saint Andrew’s Castle of Cambrai*, composed in 1133, agree that the day of his death was March 14. Most assign the year 1050; others 1048.

“Colvenerius, however, cites a charter of Bishop Lietbert granted to the monastery of Saint Aubert in the year of the Lord 1057, in his seventh year as bishop; and Miraeus, *Opera diplomatica* I, 153 and 155, cites two others from 1064, in the fourteenth year of the episcopate of the lord Lietbert. It follows that Lietbert’s first year was 1051.

“Rodulfus, in the *Life of Lietbert*, written before 1131, says in chapter 10: ‘The Church of Cambrai came together, electing the lord Lietbert by unanimous agreement … After this they approached King Henry: the new elect, namely the lord Lietbert, provost and archdeacon, and the others [an abbreviated and lacunose source fragment follows: *a. a. c. o. C. a. n. destructionis suae casum flebilem et e. s. d.*].’

“In those days, while keeping watch at Cologne, he was awaiting the Sunday of the Lord’s Resurrection after the observance of Lent, intending there to consult the distinguished counsel of his palatine nobles. While he was concerned about this matter, the people of Cambrai informed him that Lietbert had been elected by everyone. On Holy Easter Day our lord Lietbert was elected by the emperor and all the palatine princes. This was done at Cologne in the imperial palace and confirmed in the Church of Saint Peter, prince of the Apostles.

“We know from Hermann of Reichenau that the emperor celebrated Easter at Cologne in 1051; in 1048 he was in Bavaria, in 1049 at Goslar, and in 1050 at Utrecht.

“Rodulfus also says that the Church of the Holy Sepulchre was consecrated in 1064, in the second indiction and the fourteenth year of the pontificate of our lord and patron Lietbert, and that Lietbert died in the twenty-sixth year of his pontificate, in the year 1076 of the Lord’s incarnation. Both statements yield 1051 as the year of the consecration. The same year, 1051, is indicated by *Chronicle of Saint Andrew’s Castle of Cambrai* II.12, where the relevant note is given. See also *Acta Sanctorum*, June IV, 585.
