“It is therefore remarkable that Simon, abbot of Saint-Bertin, in the charter-book of Saint-Bertin, edited by Guérard, p. 184, presents a charter of Baldwin, count of Flanders, dated in the year of the Lord 1056, indiction 9, on the holy day of Epiphany, with witnesses present, among whom the third is: ‘The sign of Gerard, bishop of Cambrai.’ That the name Gerard is false is perfectly clear, but the indiction agrees. Perhaps the charter read: ‘The sign of L., bishop of Cambrai’; reading the L as G, Simon supplied ‘Gerard’ by conjecture in place of ‘Lietbert.’”]

John, however, remained in the city without receiving the castellany.

After Bishop Gerard had been honorably buried, as was fitting, the lord Lietbert, provost and archdeacon, together with the other archdeacons and the household dependants of the Church of Cambrai, approached King Henry, carrying the bishop’s staff and announcing the removal of their bishop.

[Note: [Col. 0180D] *Casati*: attached to the household, dependants. At Cambrai this designation applied especially to the twenty-four free fief-holders established to hear, on the summons of the high bailiff, feudal, civil, and criminal cases within the bishop’s jurisdiction. LE GLAY.]

[Note: [Col. 0180C] “Emperor” would be more accurate; he had already been crowned at Rome on December 25, 1046.]

[Note: [Col. 0179] Manuscript 7 reads *Lotha-Karlensium*; manuscript 2, *ariensium*; manuscript 2*, *riensium*.]

When the emperor heard of the death of so great a man, he grieved for him piously, since Gerard had been beloved by everyone. He began carefully to consider whom he could appoint in his place who would be like him.

[Note: [Col. 0180D] Rodulfus recounts the matter somewhat differently in the place cited above. According to him, Lietbert had already been elected at home by the clergy and people before they went to Cologne; this election was reported to the emperor and confirmed by him.]

As he was concerned about this matter, it occurred to him that Lietbert, provost of that same Church of Cambrai, who had long been his chaplain and whom he had often found to be most faithful to himself and in many ways indispensable to that Church, appeared suitable to govern the Church of Cambrai.

[Note: [Col. 0179] Manuscript 2 reads “by his hands”; Colvenerius corrected it from the *Life of Lietbert*.]

[Note: [Col. 0180A–D] It seemed especially useful to add here excerpts concerning Cambrai found in Jacques de Guise, Paris edition, volume VIII, p. 450:

> “When he [that is, Herluin] had died, the emperor sent Gerard, his chaplain, to that see. After suffering [*passus*, editorially supplied] many injuries inflicted by his people, no less after the benefits had been conferred upon the Church, and released from the prison of the flesh, he left as his successor his foster-son, Lord Lietbert.
>
> “During the time of that Gerard, however, relics were found in the Church of Arras beside the high altar, and they are preserved there to this day. At their discovery many benefits were continuously granted to the sick for three years.
>
> “Lord Lietbert gave the Church of Beaurain, with its tithe, to the canons of Arras, together with Berles, and founded the Church of the Holy Sepulchre in the city of Cambrai, in which he lies buried and rests with great honor. The younger Lord Gerard succeeded Lietbert.”]
[Col. 0181A] p. 454. But because above, in the immediately preceding chapter, we digressed from the true order and succession of the bishops of Cambrai—namely, from the time of the death of Gerard, who was the last bishop both of the churches of Arras and of Cambrai—and abandoned the order of the bishops of Cambrai while following the succession of the bishops of Arras, here, accordingly, with God as guide, I return to the catalogue of the bishops of Cambrai, insofar as I have been able to discover it. For in the church of Cambrai, after the aforesaid Gerard, during whose time the division of the aforesaid bishoprics took place, Gerard was succeeded by Manasses, reigning alone in the single bishopric of Cambrai. Manasses was succeeded by Walter. Walter was succeeded by Odo. Odo was succeeded by Burgard. Burgard was succeeded by Lietard. Lietard was succeeded by Nicholas. Nicholas was succeeded by Peter. Peter was succeeded by Robert. Robert was succeeded by Alard. Alard was succeeded by [Col. 0181B] Roger. Roger was succeeded by John. John was succeeded by Nicholas the elect. Nicholas was succeeded by Hugh the elect. Hugh was succeeded by Peter of Corbeil [ [Col. 0181C] Corbeil], bishop. Peter was succeeded by John of Bethune. John was succeeded by Godfrey of Condé in Hainaut. Godfrey was succeeded by Guiard. Guiard was succeeded by Nicholas of Fontaines. Nicholas was succeeded by Ingelram. Ingelram was succeeded by William of Hainaut. William was succeeded by Guy of Collo-Medio [ [Col. 0181C] Colmieu]. Guy was succeeded by Philip of Margny. Philip was succeeded by Peter of Milapi [ [Col. 0181C] Mirepoix]. Peter was succeeded by Guy of Babylonia [ [Col. 0181C] Balonia. Manuscripts of Saint-Germain; Guy of Auvergne. Fortia]. Guy was succeeded by Guy of Ventadour. Guy was succeeded by Peter Andrew. Peter was succeeded by Robert of Geneva [ [Col. 0181C] Pierre de Genève? Fortia]. Robert was succeeded by Gerard of Dainville. Gerard was succeeded by John Cherclaus, during the time of the Church’s schism. John Cherclaus was succeeded by Andrew of Saint-Paul, brother of the count of Saint-Pol.

*Volume IX, p. 464. From the history of Cambrai.* In this year (1047) there was a very great mortality at Cambrai. For this reason Bishop Gerard blessed the large cemetery outside the walls of the city of Cambrai and began a small church in honor of Saint Nicholas the bishop and of the Holy Sepulchre, but he did not complete them. The dead were buried there because all the cemeteries of the city were completely filled [ [Col. 0181C] Compare Rodulfus, chap. 46].

*Ibid., p. 466. From Sigebert.* In the same year (1049) Gerard, bishop of Cambrai, died. From the history of Cambrai [ [Col. 0181C] Rodulfus, chap. 13: “The Roman emperor Henry II gave the city of Cambrai, with all its dependencies, to Lord Lietbert”]. In the year of the Lord 1049, the emperor Henry granted the temporal lordship of the entire city of Cambrai to Lietbert, newly elected bishop of Cambrai; and [ [Col. 0182C] Compare the *Deeds of Lietbert*, below, p. 492] in the same year John expelled the canons from the church of the Blessed Virgin, closed the city gates against Bishop Lietbert, and held out against him. But at last Baldwin, count of Flanders, restored the aforesaid bishop to peaceful possession of the entire city and [Col. 0182A] exiled the aforesaid John. This Bishop Lietbert was consecrated by Guy, archbishop of Reims, together with the queen of France, wife of Henry, king of the Franks [ [Col. 0182C] Compare the Chronicle of Saint Andrew of Cambrai and Rodulfus, chaps. 19–20].

*Ibid., p. 470. From the history of Cambrai.* In this year (1052), Lietbert, bishop of Cambrai, began to found the abbey of Saint Andrew at Cateau-Cambrésis.

*Ibid., p. 472. From Sigebert.* In the same year (1054), Lietbert, bishop of Cambrai, wished to visit the Holy Land and the Holy Sepulchre, as far as he could, at great expense [ [Col. 0182C] Compare the Chronicle of Saint Andrew and Rodulfus, chap. 41]; but while he was in Cyprus, he was compelled by the Saracens to return home most unwillingly.

*Ibid., p. 476. From the history of Cambrai* [ [Col. 0182C] Compare the *Deeds of the Bishops of Cambrai*, col. 191A; Rodulfus, chaps. 47–49. The year 1064. The remaining year-numbers are lacking in the sources]. In this year (1064), Lietbert, bishop of Cambrai, founded the church of the Holy Sepulchre of Cambrai, endowed and dedicated it, and installed monks there.

*Volume XI, p. 158. From the history of Cambrai.* A short time before these events (1080), Hugh, lord of Oisy, treacherously seized Bishop Lietbert of Cambrai by night in his bed, after Lietbert, exhausted, had dedicated a certain church and confirmed a great multitude. Hugh killed the bishop’s chamberlain and many nobles who were with the bishop and wished to help him. The aforesaid Hugh seized the bishop naked [ [Col. 0181] The earlier edition reads “not yet”] in his bed and imprisoned him in his own castle of Oisy. But Richildis, countess of Mons, hearing that her spiritual father had been treated in this way, gathered a large army in Hainaut and sent word to her son Arnold, then count of Flanders, that he should come to her with a suitable escort. After a few days, she and her own son Arnold entered Cambrai through Douai, devastating Hugh’s entire territory. When Hugh fled, they captured the castle of Oisy and, after killing everyone, found Lord Bishop Lietbert in chains. With the greatest honor they brought him back to the city of Cambrai [Col. 0182C] and magnificently restored him to his own see [ [Col. 0182C] More briefly in the *Deeds of the Bishops of Cambrai*, col. 190, and in Rodulfus, chap. 56]. The leading men of Cambrai, considering the victory and the honor and advantage bestowed upon them by the countess of Mons and her son Arnulf (so the text has it), began to discuss with the countess the monetary compensation and expenses to be paid. But the countess is said to have replied that she was content with the bishop’s blessing alone; and [ [Col. 0182C] Compare the *Deeds of the Bishop of Cambrai*, col. 190, and Rodulfus, chap. 56] she further bestowed upon the church of the Blessed Virgin and upon the bishop many lands, possessions, and jewels. At last she returned to her own country, to her castle at Mons.

.

[Col. 0182C] **4. (Chapter 64, 1051.)** Having therefore summoned [Note: Manuscript 7 reads “advocates”] the representatives of the church of Cambrai, both clerical and lay, he disclosed to them the decision of his will: namely, that he wished to appoint Lietbert, the provost, bishop of the church of Cambrai, whom he believed suitable for governing that church and advantageous to his own faithful service. When they heard this, everyone agreed except one archdeacon named Guo [Note: So in manuscripts 2 and 7; *Chunomen* in the *Life of Lietbert*, manuscript 2*], who was immediately shown to have opposed the proposal more out of envy than for any other reason (Mart. 31). And when this man, together with all the others, gave his consent, the Roman emperor Henry II granted the bishopric of Cambrai to Lord Lietbert. You might therefore have seen the entire palace filled with joy and exultation, and the emperor himself beginning to sing the *Te Deum laudamus*, accompanying the bishop with clergy and people all the way to the church amid the rejoicing of this hymn. The pontiff was magnified by the king and his princes with great glory, and he was received by his own people with thanksgiving and great joy. After pledging his fidelity to the emperor and fulfilling all the required formalities, the pontiff hastened to return to his own city [Note: Rodulfus, in the *Life of Saint Lietbert*, says that all these events took place at Cologne on Easter Day].

**5.** Now that John, who had remained at Cambrai hostile to him, heard through the spreading report what had happened—that Lord Lietbert, having received the bishopric, was returning joyfully—he became very angry for this reason and pondered for a long time what ought to be done [Note: So in manuscript 7 and the *Life of Lietbert*; manuscripts 2 and 2* read “what needs to be done”]. Then he summoned his henchmen together and disclosed to them the secret of his mind, saying that he would grant the newly made bishop Lietbert no entry into the city of Cambrai unless Lietbert first wished to make him castellan of that city. He therefore ordered all of them always to be ready under arms to repel that bishop unless Lietbert satisfied him by granting him this as a gift [Note: Manuscript 7 omits “to him”]. Then he violently invaded the mother church of Saint Mary and, expelling the canons, subjected the church’s treasures and whatever he found inside to his own authority, placing his armed guards there. He entered the pontifical basilica with his soldiers and, bringing his wife into the bishop’s chamber, had his own bed prepared on the episcopal bed; he ordered that he and his henchmen be supplied from the bishop’s resources [Note: The same story is told above, I, 101, of Duke Charles].

**6. (Chapter 65.)** While these things were taking place, the new bishop approached the city. John went out to meet him with an army prepared, closed the gates, and drove him far from the entrance [Note: So in manuscript 7 and the *Life of Lietbert*; manuscripts 2 and 2* read “drives him back”]. The bishop therefore turned aside to the new castle of Saint Mary, where he was received by his own people with honor and joy.

**7.** He remained there for some time, until Baldwin, count of the Flemings, returning from the king of the Franks and having to pass through that castle, found him there [Note: Manuscripts 2 and 2* read “had found him”]. The count was delighted at his episcopate and brought him with him as far as the city of Cambrai. When the count was approaching the city, he sent word to John that he and his men should leave the city and allow free entry to the arriving bishop. John, however, since he did not dare to resist, fulfilled in every respect the command of his lord the count, just as he had been ordered. Thus the bishop entered his city, led by the count, with great glory, and his adversary John was expelled with great disgrace.

**8. (Chapter 66.)** After expelling John, the pontiff took precautions for the future. Fearing that either John or some tyrant like him might enter that castellany by force or cunning, and that afterward the rightful heir, reclaiming it, might cause disturbances, he voluntarily summoned Hugh, nephew of the deceased castellan Walter, because he was the legitimate heir, and granted him that castellany [Col. 0184B]. Since this Hugh was still a child but had a certain kinsman named Anselm [Note: Of Ribemont], distinguished in character and arms, he entrusted the boy to Anselm’s guardianship together with his property [Note: “His goods,” that is, his possessions]. That Anselm governed him excellently and faithfully until the appointed time.

**9.** John, therefore, deprived of the castellany he had unjustly usurped and daring to do no harm thereafter against the bishop—for the count had forbidden him—abandoned Count Baldwin, whose liege knight he was [Note: *Ledigman*], and went to the Roman emperor Henry, whom he knew at that time to be hostile to the count of Flanders. Having become the emperor’s knight, and knowing that the emperor was preparing a second expedition into Flanders against [Col. 0184C] Baldwin [Note: Manuscript 7 adds “the count”], he promised him that he would lead his army there if the emperor would have the castellany of the city of Cambrai granted to him by Lietbert, to whom he had recently given the bishopric.

**10. (Chapter 67.)** When the emperor heard this, he was eager to come into the count’s territory to devastate it [Note: Manuscript 7 reads “he was eager”], and he became glad, thinking that he would easily obtain from the bishop what John was requesting. Before much time had passed, therefore, the emperor, with his army prepared and John appointed as guide, set out, in accordance with John’s agreement and request, to enter the territory of Flanders (1054) [Note: Manuscript 7 reads “province”]. Passing through all the intervening places of his kingdom, he arrived at the Maen [Note: Maing, according to Le Glay], a village on the River Scheldt, no more than two miles from Valenciennes [Col. 0184D], where he wished to build bridges and thus enter Baldwin’s territory, which lay before him on the opposite side of the river [Note: Manuscript 2 reads “whom”]. But Count Baldwin had already occupied the other bank with his army, by which the emperor was preparing to cross into his territory. Thus the emperor and the count sat facing one another, neither able to harm the other because of the depth of the intervening river. A section of the imperial army secretly detached itself and attempted to attack the emperor, who was sitting unprepared, by way of the city of Cambrai, and thus to defeat him unexpectedly [Note: Manuscript 2 reads “unprepared”]. This would indeed have happened had not the count, warned at the last moment by a messenger, fled with his men and left the riverbank unguarded [Note: Manuscript 7 reads “had left”].

**11. (Chapter 68.)** When the emperor saw this, he crossed the River Scheldt over bridges that had been prepared and distributed Baldwin’s territory to his army [Note: Manuscript 7 adds “the count’s”] for devastation by the enemy [Note: That is, by the army]. He therefore ravaged it with plunder and fire and reached the stream of Debullient [Note: Le Boulenrieu, near Évin, arrondissement of Béthune, according to Le Glay] with his army. [Col. 0185B] At that place the aforesaid John came before the emperor with his henchmen and asked him to have the castellany of Cambrai granted to him, in accordance with his promise, if he wished to receive further service from him and his men.

**12. (Chapter 69.)** The emperor therefore summoned Bishop Lietbert to him—for he was present—and began to demand that he grant John the castellany of the city of Cambrai. When he heard this, the bishop was troubled to the depths of his soul, since he had already granted it to the rightful heir and the most savage tyrant was unjustly reclaiming it. At last he replied that he could not do what the emperor commanded, because he had already granted it to Hugh, the legitimate heir [Note: Manuscript 7 omits “to Hugh”], according to the law of the country.

Because of the pressing necessity, the emperor wished to satisfy John’s request; but the bishop believed that he could in no way revoke what he had done. What the emperor was asking seemed easy and insignificant to him; what was being demanded seemed grave and deadly to the bishop. For if he received into his city that unspeakable man who was demanding another’s property against the law, he would have neither peace within because of his tyranny nor the ability to withstand him and his relatives outside, disinherited as they were. Thus humbled and utterly troubled, the bishop sought renewal from divine mercy, wishing his gift, lawfully completed, to remain inviolate.

When the emperor perceived that he could not obtain what he was asking by persuasion, he began to abuse force, ordering soldiers to seize the bishop and hold him in custody outside his power [Col. 0185D] [Note: That is, outside the territory under his authority]. At last, corrected by the frank counsel of his fellow bishops and friends [Note: Manuscript 7 adds “his own”], and knowing that, according to the Apostle, one must be subject to the king (Romans 13:1), he granted the emperor’s request concerning John. Thus he returned to his own authority, released from all custody.

[Col. 0186A] **13. (Chapter 70.)** After this, John once again girded himself to lead the emperor’s army through that passage, if it could in some way be done. As the man labored and sought to accomplish this very thing, the gates of that passage were opened in the middle of the night. Thus the emperor entered the passage, after inflicting a considerable slaughter upon the enemies who wished to resist. Passing through it and killing those who came against him on the right and on the left, he reached the castle of Lille [Note: Lille; Baldwin gave rise to it in 1066, when the church of Saint Peter was founded], where Count Lambert of Lens came to meet him with many men and was killed in the encounter.

From that castle he turned aside to the city of Tournai, where he enclosed in a certain fortified place a considerable multitude of chosen soldiers who were fleeing. By siege and finally by hunger he compelled them to surrender. After accepting them and shutting them up under guard in the prisons of his soldiers, the emperor returned in glory to the cities of his kingdom.

But we have strayed from our purpose: while recounting the emperor’s deeds, we have for a time been silent about the deeds of Lord Bishop Lietbert. Let us therefore set aside the emperor’s wars and the magnificent deeds of his gatekeepers [Note: *Ostiarii*], and return to the remaining deeds of the pontiff.

**14. (Chapter 71.)** When the emperor departed into the territory of his kingdom, Bishop Lietbert likewise departed and returned to his city of Cambrai. He did not reject the boy Hugh, whom he had made castellan; rather, with no less care than Anselm himself, who had been appointed his guardian and tutor, he cherished and raised him. He treated as void the gift of the castellany which he had been forced by the emperor’s violence to grant to John. The emperor piously tolerated this action and inflicted no injury upon the bishop on that account. Indeed, he restored through his own gifts and other benefits the grant that had been made to John and reconciled peace and concord between the bishop and himself. For he knew that it had been done at his own prompting and advice that the bishop had first granted the castellany to Hugh.

**15.** Thus, rejoicing because he had obtained the emperor’s favor and because John’s unjust claim had been defeated, the bishop strove by every means to exalt his city of Cambrai. The citizens, therefore, who had been reduced to poverty under the oppression of prolonged sedition, revived through the sweetness of peace, as though rising from the sepulchre of death. Through the labor and zeal of the pontiff, mercy and truth met one another throughout the city of Cambrai and all its surrounding dependencies; justice and peace exchanged kisses (Psalm 84:11). Everything was opened and unbarred, and no thief, robber, or wrongdoer was found who inflicted harm on anyone [Note: Manuscript 7 reads “each person”; the *Life of Lietbert* reads “anyone whatever”]. The clergy, filled with prosperity in the churches, rendered praises to God; the laity carried out their duties in complete peace. They called blessed the people to whom such things belonged—and even more blessed the bishop through whom such great joys of peace had sprung forth.

**16. (Chapter 72.)** Meanwhile, Hugh, who had been granted the castellany, advanced in age, and the appointed time was approaching when Anselm had to relinquish his governance and Hugh himself receive his property [Note: “His goods”]. Anselm, however, thought that the young man was not yet fit to govern [Note: Manuscript 7 has *regendum* rather than *regendam*] the castellany, and therefore wished to prolong his own guardianship if the bishop would permit it. Although the pontiff shared Anselm’s view concerning Hugh’s immaturity, he nevertheless did not wish Hugh to be defrauded of the appointed period, thinking that the young man could be recalled to the path of truth through his discipline if, through ignorance caused by his blindness, he should deviate from what was right.

Thus Anselm was entirely unable, by prayer or payment, to obtain that Hugh should not receive his castellany on the appointed day. Once Hugh had obtained the administration of his office, he immediately made public to everyone what he had kept hidden in his heart. Previously, how could you have known him, when age, fear, and his tutor restrained him all at once? But now, master of his own power, contemptuous of all authority and discipline, confusing right and wrong, he proceeds without any regard according to the perversities of his heart and his unlawful pleasures.

Can one who collects a timber-store in the city of his lord and in his marketplace by forced exaction [Note: Manuscript 7 reads *collegit* (“collected”) for *colligit* (“collects”)] [Note: “A timber-store”] [Note: That is, by violent levy, from the wood brought into the city for burning. Colville] maintain any regard for justice, when none of his predecessors had ever done so and the opposition and prohibition of his lord forbid it? Hugh the castellan established this timber-store in the city of Cambrai and placed it in the enclosure [Note: Manuscript 7 reads “it is in the cloister”] [Note: An enclosure, that is, a surrounding wall] of Saint Autbert, in defiance of Bishop Lietbert. This was the first of his injuries.

**17.** His second injury was as follows: he seized ten cows from Ermenald, the bishop’s steward and chamberlain, brought them into his own city while he himself was present, and ate them; finally he seized Ermenald himself and bound him in chains. When this was reported to the bishop, he was deeply grieved and went to the castellan’s house, wishing to know why he was holding his chamberlain in chains. But as soon as the man noticed that his lord had entered the house, he escaped through another doorway.

The bishop then cried out and adjured him in the name of his oath not to leave but to remain and give an account concerning Ermenald, whom he had seized [Note: Manuscripts 2 and 2* read “had received”]. He refused to remain; instead, mounting a horse, he fled. When the bishop saw this, he found Ermenald held in chains, had him released, and joyfully led him away with him as though rescued from the underworld.

**18.** Afterward Hugh returned home without having restored peace and, not ceasing from the perversity he had begun, added worse things to his earlier offenses. He subjected the better and wealthier citizens to insults and injuries; he shut others, without conviction or trial, in a most vile pillory [Note: *Le cep*, an iron device enclosing the feet of captives, and hence the prison itself, according to Le Glay]; amid many disgraces he tore out the beards of some.

He dragged Evremar, one of the wealthier citizens, shamefully to the public pillory. He also dragged Gerald, well known among merchants both within and outside the city, a man advanced in body and age and even respected by tyrants. Frequently rebuked by the bishop for these and similar acts, and unwilling to reform but falling ever deeper into evil, he was excommunicated by him. But he despised this as well. Seeking no mercy and promising no improvement, he went to the count of Saint-Quentin and stayed there for some time, doing against the bishop and his church whatever evil he could.

**19. (Chapter 73.)** A few days later, in the district of Cambrai no more than ten miles from the city, at a place called Porrival, he fortified a stronghold. Entering it with his henchmen, he devastated the neighboring possessions of the bishopric, plundered passersby, and inflicted robberies upon those living all around. The bishop could not endure this for long. He gathered horsemen and foot soldiers and sent them against that stronghold.

The stronghold was overpowered by assault [Note: So in manuscript 7 and the *Life of Lietbert*; manuscript 2 reads “by a leap”], hemmed in and set ablaze, and thrown down to the ground [Col. 0188C]. Thus that place was cleansed of henchmen and brigands.

That Hugh, after the destruction of the stronghold, turned to another place, which antiquity named Inchy [Note: Inchy-en-Artois, canton of Marquion, according to Le Glay], and again undertook raids and many evil actions against the bishop. The bishop was also displeased by this and led a large force of armed men to that place. The stronghold would immediately have been overturned to the ground had not Robert of Péronne, who had come to aid the pontiff, obstructed the attempt by a ruse. After these efforts had thus proved fruitless, the men of Cambrai returned to their city without having accomplished their purpose.

**20. (Chapter 74.)** Meanwhile, that Hugh began to love a certain young woman named Adam, the niece of Richildis, countess of Mons, and eagerly wished to take her as his wife. But because he was excommunicated, he did not know how or by what means he could accomplish this. Overcome by the fire of carnal love, he went to Countess Richildis and earnestly begged her to give him her niece Adam in marriage. She, overcome at last by his entreaties, agreed to his request on the condition that he first be absolved from the anathema with which the bishop of Cambrai had bound him.

What could he do? He did not greatly care about absolution, yet, burning with desire for the girl he coveted, he sought it from the bishop through intermediaries. The bishop, worn out by his many injuries, was unwilling to absolve him unless he first made, in his own hand, a relinquishment—which is commonly called *werpire*—of every benefice he possessed within the bounds of the city of Cambrai.

At last, inflamed by his desire for the young woman, Hugh did for the bishop what he requested. Publicly, before the bishop and his soldiers, and before Countess Richildis and her nobles [Col. 0189B], he renounced every benefice he possessed within the city of Cambrai. Having thus been absolved, he rendered fidelity to the bishop concerning the remaining possessions of the castellany and gave hostages for them.

**21.** Hugh did not observe this fidelity for long. Although he had promised it by oath on the feast of Saint Andrew, he broke it on the Monday after Palm Sunday [Note: Manuscript 7 reads “the feast”]. On that day of Holy Week [Note: That is, “Char-Woche”], he entered the forest of Atrévassia [Note: The forest of Arouaise began near the castle of Encre and extended as far as the sources of the Sambre, according to Le Glay] and unjustly took away with him all the beasts of burden belonging to the men of Cambrai that he found there.

Although the bishop repeatedly admonished him, on the basis of his sworn fidelity, to return them, he refused. On the very day of his absolution, which is the day before Good Friday, he even sent his lord a defiance [Note: A challenge; *Défi*, *Herausforderung*].

**(Chapter 75.)** Afterward, abandoning Cambrai, he turned to Oisy [Note: Oisy, near Arras] and did whatever evil he could [Note: Manuscript 7 reads *malum* for *malumque*] against the bishop, just as he had initially resolved to do [Note: Manuscript 7 reads *adversus* for *adversum*]. The bishop therefore sent word to him not once but more than three times that he should come before him and, in the presence of his peers, stand trial concerning his wrongdoing [Note: “To be set right”].

At last, repeatedly summoned in the name of his own land and of the fidelity he had sworn [Note: Manuscript 7 omits “in”], he came before his lord in the presence of his peers. But when questioned about the various matters, he refused to make satisfaction and departed more unjust than when he had arrived. Therefore his peers and many other nobles who had attended this court on behalf of their common cause declared Hugh guilty and adjudicated to the bishop the land that Hugh held from him.

[Col. 0189D] **22.** Hugh returned to the stronghold he had prepared for himself at Oisy after the land had been adjudicated away from him, and he did not cease to commit evil against the bishop. The bishop, however, patiently enduring all these things and casting aside fear, went around his parish, blessing the churches that were to be consecrated [Col. 0190A] and carrying out the other works of his ministry.

It happened that, in the course of this labor, he came to a certain village named Buricellum, blessed the church of the village for consecration, and, after the consecration, grew weary from confirming the people [Note: Manuscript 7 reads “the peoples”; *Vita Lietberti* reads “anointing the crowds”] and spent the night there.

The aforesaid Hugh did not remain unaware of this. Taking his accomplices with him, he reached the house in which the bishop, already in bed, had entrusted his weary limbs to rest. After breaking down the doors of the house [Note: Manuscript 7 adds “then”] and killing some who resisted, he reached the chamber in which the pontiff was sleeping with his provost Wibold and his chaplains [Note: Manuscript 2 reads “where”].

Wibold, sensing such treachery and violence, placed himself against the chamber door as though to bar it [Col. 0190B]. But, unable to resist many men alone, he was killed when Hugh himself broke down the door. Finally, that mad murderer did not hesitate to seize the bishop as he lay in bed, wearing only his shirt, carry him naked to his stronghold at Oisy, and keep him confined there under guard.

**23. (Chapter 76.)** When Count Arnold of Flanders and his mother Richildis were stirred by this report, they immediately both came to Oisy with their soldiers. Seeking the bishop with wisdom and strength, they found him without delay and brought him back to Cambrai with great glory and honor. In addition, they bestowed gifts upon the church of Saint Mary and upon the other monasteries of the city of Cambrai.

After these things had been accomplished worthily and laudably [Col. 0190C], the count of the Flemings returned joyfully with his mother to his own country. The bishop, therefore, filled with complete hatred [Note: Manuscript 7 reads *toto animo* (“with his whole heart”); the *Vita Lietberti* reads *totis animi viribus* (“with all the strength of his heart”)], pursued Hugh relentlessly until, after destroying the stronghold of Oisy, he drove him far from the borders of Cambrai.

Expelled in this manner from the territory of Cambrai, Hugh ceased all complaint against the bishop throughout the bishop’s entire life; and the land also rested from the face of his wickedness [Note: Manuscript 7 lacks “the land also rested from the face of his wickedness”; manuscript 2* lacks the text from “the land” through “and the splendid inheritance.”].

24. (Chapter 77.) Meanwhile, as old age came upon the bishop, he began to grow weak in body [Note: “to become weary,” 7.], but, concerned for eternal life, he grew strong in spirit; and he strove to transfer to the attainment of eternal life the splendid inheritance [Note: “inheritance,” 7.] that he had possessed from his predecessors for the glory of this world. For he transferred so much from his inheritances and the revenues belonging to him to the church of Saint Mary, the holy Mother of God, the church of Cambrai, by means of chartered instruments, that the canons might obtain food and drink from it on every Sunday throughout the year; yet on every Monday a Mass was to be celebrated by the whole congregation for his soul and for all the faithful departed. And since I have spoken of the charity shown toward the church of Saint Mary and its canons, I shall not wholly pass over how he conducted himself toward the other monasteries of the city.

He built the monastery of the Holy Sepulchre from its foundations [Note: It was consecrated on 25 October 1064. Life of Lietbert, chapter 49. The foundation charter is found in Miraeus, *Opera diplomatica* I, 155.], and, having placed an abbot there [Note: “thus,” 7; “he placed an abbot,” 1, 2, 2*.] with monks, suitably enriched that place with possessions and useful goods, as the present time demonstrates. In the church of Saint Aubert he established regular canons with an abbot [Note: “Here [the text] ceased in 2, because the final folio was missing. 2* ends thus: ‘he established. The abbey very much … Meanwhile, as old age came upon the bishop, he began to grow weak in body. Concerned for life, he grew strong in spirit, [and the passage continues] inheritance.’ Here ends the book of the church of Saint Mary of Arras, 1482. The following material was preserved for us by 7 and should be compared with the *Life of Lietbert*, chapter 57.] [Note: The *Life of Lietbert* inserts “4 May 1066.” Miraeus gives the charter, *Opera diplomatica* I, 157.]; he added very good altars and splendid possessions; after expelling the canons who had served there negligently, he magnificently restored their prebends from his own property. He greatly assisted Erlebold, who built the church of the Holy Cross, both with goods and with counsel, and he applied care to the number and selection of the canons chosen and installed. He had the church of Saint Vedast, which the same Erlebold built, constructed with his counsel and assistance.

I shall not omit the monastery of our holy father Gaugericus, to which he gave the tithe at Athene in this city [Note: I have corrected the text in this way; 7 has “de Mathene.”], and, together with other very good possessions, one *camba* at the foot of the mountain of that same Saint Gaugericus. He loved his clergy and laymen as a hen that gathers her chicks and shelters them beneath her wings. Thus he harmed none of his fellow citizens, since he strove to benefit everyone. Accordingly, the city that he had found deserted, when he became bishop, because of the uprising of the wars, he left populous and prosperous at his death.

He never ceased to improve the new castle of Saint Mary, the abbey of the Apostle Saint Andrew, and the monastery of Saint Humbert at Maricolis. Moreover, he gave the church of Belreim to the congregation of the church of Saint Mary of Arras. And in the monastery of Saint Vindicianus, situated near the mountain of Saint Eligius, he established regular canons; after expelling the canons who had previously served there negligently, he added much from his own goods.

Finally, amid these exercises of good works [Col. 0192B], he fell ill. He endured the illness with great patience for nearly three years and, on the vigil of Saint John the Baptist, full of days, died [Note: According to the *Auctarium Aquicinense* to Sigebert, in the year 1076; according to the *Annals of Lobbes* and the twelfth-century necrology of the Holy Sepulchre of Cambrai, on 9 Kalends of July 1076; “he gave up his spirit in the twenty-sixth year of his ordination … and … as the sun was setting on 10 Kalends of July, he departed to Christ … .” Five years before his death, he had a tomb dug for himself. On certain days he would revisit it, at first lying upon it and drenching the grave with tears and groans; afterward he would fill it with bread, meat, or other foods, which he immediately ordered to be distributed to the poor. He was buried with glory and pontifical honor in the twenty-sixth year of his pontificate, on 9 Kalends of July, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1076. *Life of Lietbert*. The twelfth-century necrology of Saint Mary of Cambrai begins: “On 9 Kalends of July died Lietbertus, bishop of holy memory and religion. He freely and lawfully gave to us, for our use, the altar of Andreleth with its appurtenances, a third part at Lietscines, and half the village of Ogeium, as is written in his charter; and at Cambrai he restored the tithe of the mint and the *matera* that we had unjustly lost; and at the village of Pasquerthrau he bought one *camba* for us from his own property, at Bolengria one oven, and in the market one *gavalum*. He lawfully confirmed many other things for us and for our church along with these, like a good shepherd, and excommunicated anyone who might violate them.” The historical note of the twelfth century, which I published in our *Annals* VIII, 428, is plainly erroneous.]. He was buried with great glory, though amid the sorrow of his sons, in the church of the Holy Sepulchre, which he himself had built and suitably adorned with an abbot and monks.

# THE DEEDS OF GERARD II, BISHOP

[Note: We supplied the title and division into chapters; they were absent from 7 and 7*, from which we publish these *Deeds*.]

[Col. 0191]

[Col. 0191B] 1. During the time when the second Henry held the Roman Empire [Note: “the emperor, the third king.”], a second Gerard succeeded his maternal uncle Lietbert in the bishopric of Cambrai, after the unanimous election of the clergy and people of Cambrai, with the assent and grant of the royal power. He was immediately consecrated at Augustodunum by Hugh of Die, at the command of Hildebrand, then the apostolic legate. On his return he was honorably received by the people of Cambrai entrusted to him.

When, at the beginning of his office, he wished to exercise its rights, to bestow the due affection upon those committed to him, and to obtain peace with his enemies, he first prepared the castellan Hugh—whom his predecessor Lietbert had tolerated as his enemy to the end—to become his man [Col. 0192C] [Note: A vassal.] and friend, both by fealty and by oath, through the aged Count Robert and the princes of Flanders. The bishop nevertheless retained in his own hands the castellan’s revenues that were contained within the city of Cambrai. As a result of that reconciliation, the lands that had been uncultivated were cultivated [Col. 0193A] [Note: “To cultivate,” in the French version.]; the abundance of goods was quickly restored, and the poverty previously endured was wholly forgotten.

2. Thus, with peace and joy prevailing among the clergy and people, both within and outside the city, the bishop resolved to visit the emperor, from whom he had received honor for the holy church of Cambrai. But he had not yet gone very far when the citizens of Cambrai, ill-advised, swore the communal oath that had long been whispered about and long desired. They were so bound together by their oath that, unless he granted the conspiracy they had formed, they all refused entry to the bishop when he returned to Cambrai. And this is what happened.

For while the bishop was still traveling through Lobbes, his faithful reported to him what the wicked people had done. He immediately returned and, seeing that his own men were inferior in number and weaker in strength than so many citizens, took with him his friend Baldwin, Count of Mons, to curb the citizens’ arrogance and destroy their profane commune. When he wished to enter Cambrai with the count’s armed force, the conspiratorial people opposed his entrance.

Nevertheless, the bishop, preferring to pity the folly of his people rather than avenge it, offered to promise them that he would at some time discuss in his court the conspiracy made against him. After this assurance had been given, the citizens happily returned home, as though their injury had been settled and forgotten. But perhaps because their sins demanded it, and without the bishop’s knowledge, the author of the affair having been removed, soldiers desirous of plundering the money of the proud citizens suddenly invaded their houses; and whoever encountered an enemy was, as an enemy, either wounded or killed.

Thus, stunned by the sudden calamity, all the citizens fled for refuge to the church of Saint Gaugericus. But at last, defeated, they were willingly handed over into the bishop’s captivity. The city was stripped; the citizens lost their money; wickedness suffered vengeance; the entire conspiracy was suppressed; and the citizens again swore fidelity to the bishop.

3. After this commune had been destroyed, a certain wicked scheme was soon devised against the bishop, but by God’s providence it took no root and did not reach completion. A respected citizen named Wibertus, a merchant known throughout many lands, had lost his brother Fulbertus—his fellow citizen and an exceptionally prudent merchant—killed among those slain in the aforementioned commune. He therefore secretly harbored continuous anger and mortal hatred against the bishop.

For this reason he made an agreement with the bishop’s enemies that he would hand over the city of Cambrai to them. But how the planned betrayal came about, I wish to explain not only to those now living but also to posterity. The same Wibertus confessed to the bishop that the treason had been arranged—not devised by him, but secretly sought from him by the bishop’s enemies so that it might be carried out through him. Since he refused to name them to the bishop, it was judged that he should be punished until he was compelled to confess those traitors.

Therefore that Wibertus was bound to a stake by judicial sentence and cruelly scourged with two rods, yet he confessed nothing further. Consequently, the bishop’s servants bound him naked, with his hands tied behind his back, and led him through the middle of the city like a traitor, outside the walls; they cut out his tongue and tore out his eyes. Finally, after he had been killed, his ashamed and grieving relatives buried him beside the public road.

With regard to the homicide committed in defense of justice, Augustine testifies that the bishop did not sin. For he says: “To kill a man is not always criminal; but to kill through malice and not according to the laws is criminal.”

4. After the aforementioned conspiracy of the citizens had been settled, and only a short time had passed, the previously mentioned Hugh the castellan renewed his hostility concerning the castellany that the bishop had retained in his own hands within Cambrai. He scattered all the bishop’s goods at Arras, both around and within the city, at Maricolis, and wherever he could. He also ravaged, burned, and consumed everywhere the goods of the churches of Cambrai.

Thus, Hugh’s persecution of many years and the continual devastation of the lands unceasingly compelled the peasants to abandon their villages. Their goods having been taken, they wandered as exiles, begging throughout foreign regions. The wise bishop, unable to endure this intolerable evil, gave two hundred marks of silver to the second Robert, Count of Flanders, because of the misery of the needy and the groaning of the poor, so that he might wholly disinherit that Hugh from the castellany and drive him far from the territory of Cambrai—or rather, of Flanders [Col. 0194C].

What more need I say? It happened accordingly: Hugh, driven into exile, took refuge in England. There he endured exile, poverty, and many adversities. As long as the prudent lord Gerard lived as bishop, he never conceived the desire to return to his homeland.

5. Since the bishop, with great foresight for the future, saw that God had granted his lands peace from the enemy Hugh, he labored during the time of peace to ensure that, if Hugh or any other enemies should ever rise against him, both he and his people would at least be strong and secure against their enemies within the city.

Behold the good provision; behold the fatherly concern; behold the excellent work, exceedingly necessary for citizens and peasants alike: to prepare and faithfully labor so that the bodies and possessions of their households might be defended within the city against hostile attack.

Therefore, with the citizens assisting, the bishop fortified the entire city around its circuit. It had first been enclosed by a wooden palisade; he strengthened it with a stone wall, deepening the ditches and building many towers into the wall. He also strengthened with a high wall the castle within the city, where both the church of the Blessed Mother of God and the monastery of Saint Aubert were located, raising a deep, formidable ditch around it.

6. While the bishop was devoted to good works, two soldiers were converted at that time by God’s grace. One was named Walterus and the other Sicherus [Col. 0195A]; both were of noble birth, adorned with good character, and filled with the fervor of the divine Spirit. Burning with the Holy Spirit, and confessing that they possessed one will and one mind, they confidently sent word that the bishop should come to them at Douai. For they wished, on his advice, to choose a place where they could serve God.

Thus, on their own estate called Aquicinctus, in a place of horror and vast solitude, they built a church with the assent and consideration—indeed, with the assistance—of that same bishop, from their own resources. From beginning to end, the bishop was their fellow-builder in all the church’s construction.

At last, when the church had been prepared, when the things pertaining to ecclesiastical worship had been suitably arranged, and when an abbot and monks had been appointed there, the venerable bishop consecrated it on the day of Saint Denis the martyr (in the year 1079), under the name and honor of Saint Savior, God Almighty.

Then the aforementioned soldiers Walterus and Sicherus handed over for the use of the monks serving God there their estates, lands, male and female servants, and everything they possessed on earth. Anselm of Ribemont also gave there two villages, Verethum and Obercicurtis; he did this with the bishop’s consent, since he held them from the bishop in fief. Many others made many gifts there, and the same bishop perpetuated them for the brothers by privileges.

The church of Aquicinctus itself promised eternal obedience and subjection to the church of Cambrai. The bishop likewise promised that he would never place an abbot there except by election of those same monks.

7. After this blessed and memorable work, the bishop strove by various efforts during the present life to prepare what he understood to belong to the advancement and salvation of his soul. Therefore, for the salvation of himself and his parents [Col. 0196A], he assigned his estates at Lietscines and Wilrehem to the church of Blessed Mary. He also gave altars whose charters are preserved [Note: In Miraeus, *Opera diplomatica* I, 75.], and there is no need to name them here.

8. He renewed the hospital of the poor beside the atrium of the Holy Cross, after demolishing the old structure, as it now appears, and also the little chapel attached to the hospital. On the feast of All Souls he consecrated it with a worthy provision of food and drink, and established that, every year, two *modii* of wheat from the hospital’s alms should be given to the parish priest so that he might sing there on Sundays, Wednesdays, and Fridays; and so that the same priest might visit the sick and bury the dead who had been counselled and given Communion in Christ.

[Col. 0196B] 9. The same bishop, like a wise architect, carried out one further work that deserves praise from all who look upon it today. He beautifully and honorably restored the venerable church of Blessed Mary, formerly burned and ruined, from its upper end as far as the choir of Saint John. He renewed the ceilings, the plasterwork, and the short windows, making them longer; and he decently crowned the capitals of the columns, which had been fixed disgracefully and had decayed on both sides.

He had also purchased excellent colors for carrying out a painting throughout the entire church; but, alas, while the work was in progress, he was overtaken by death and left it unfinished. But since a good intention is a completed work before God, he can confidently say with the psalmist: “Lord, I have loved the beauty of your house and the place where your glory dwells.” And we believe that God will have mercy on him, since the divine reading says: “Where I find you, there I shall judge you.”

He ruled the bishopric for sixteen and a half years. He died on the day before the Kalends of August [in the year 1092] [Note: The necrology of Aquicinctus, from the twelfth century, gives the second Ides of August.], and was buried in the middle of the mother church. By divine mercy, therefore, may his soul rest in peace. Amen.

# EXCERPTS FROM THE DEEDS OF MANASSES AND WALCHERUS, BY A MONK OF SAINT GAUGERICUS

[Note: We supplied the title. In 7 and 7*, all this material is appended to the preceding *Deeds of Gerard* in a continuous hand, without any distinction, as though it were a single work.]

[Col. 0195]

[Col. 0195D] 1. After the death of Bishop Gerard, many grievous evils occurred for a long time within and outside the city of Cambrai. The cause and origin of all these evils was the ambition, pride, and also the insolence of the canons of the mother church. While they strove to place one another first, while none of them tolerated anyone else being preferred except according to his own pleasure or advantage, their discord brought it about that four persons were elected, who afterward were deprived of the same dignity. Not only that, but the mother church of Cambrai itself was deprived of the subjection and obedience of her daughter, namely, the church of Arras [Note: “Or, ‘was deprived,’ is written above the line in 7.].

If anyone wishes to know these and many other evils more fully, let him consult the *Deeds of the Bishops*. We, however, intend to indicate briefly the succession of bishops from that time to the present, over nearly one hundred years—that is, from the year of the Incarnation of the Word 1090 to the year 1180.

2. When the second Gerard died (in the year 1092)—he had been the thirty-second bishop of the church of Cambrai and Arras after Saint Vedast—the clergy of the church of Cambrai, to whom the care of electing the bishop properly belonged, held differing opinions among themselves. The citizens, aroused against them, declared that no one would be bishop unless he had been chosen by the emperor and by the better part of the clergy and people.

When they heard this, the provost of the church prepared himself to carry the pastoral staff to the emperor. The church’s custodian, meeting him in opposition, stood face-to-face against him, asserting that this was his own right. While they disputed with each other over this matter, a year and more passed, with the emperor unaware that Bishop Gerard had died.

Therefore, the citizens [Note: The *Abbreviated Deeds of Cambrai*, chapter 5, adds “with their households,” doubtless from the *Deeds*.], grieved that the city and country had so long lacked the protection of a ruler, elected a certain Frenchman named Manasses. The clergy, greatly indignant at this, assembled and elected a provost named Mascelinus. When the citizens opposed this election, the clergy, weak in judgment and strength of heart, yielded very easily [Note: The *Abbreviated Deeds of Cambrai*, chapter 5, reads: “Mascelinus, a priest and provost, who nevertheless yielded voluntarily in order to avoid the fury of the people.”].

Then the citizens took from the church two silver candlesticks weighing thirty marks and a gold chalice weighing seven marks, and gave them to their chosen Manasses. Having accepted these, he proceeded to the emperor. Finding no favor there, he returned in the same clothing in which he had set out.

For he was rightly rejected by the emperor, since he had by no means been canonically elected by the people. Consequently, a more serious dispute arose between the citizens and the clergy, who supposed that it had happened through the clergy’s factional influence that their chosen Manasses had been rejected by the emperor [Note: The *Abbreviated Deeds of Cambrai*, chapter 5, adds, doubtless from the *Deeds*: “From this point the clergy were driven far from the city in great disgrace, unless, after touching the holy objects, they swore that they had hindered Manasses before the emperor neither by letter nor by messengers.” After this, the French version continues with certain material that appears to have been in the *Deeds* but was omitted by the Gaugerician excerptor, namely the whole of chapter 2.].

3. Nevertheless, while they quarreled among themselves and argued against one another in this way, an unexpected evil and an exceedingly heavy burden came upon both sides. For the people of Arras, emboldened by this prolonged disagreement, took counsel together and elected a bishop named Lambert (in the year 1093).

When this had been done, the people of Cambrai were indignant, disturbed, and agitated. Shame and grief seized them because the daughter had presumed to raise her neck against the mother, and the disciple against the mother; indeed, for many generations, and perhaps from the days of Saint Gaugericus, who was fourth after Saint Vedast to rule both sees, they had never presumed anything of the kind.

[Col. 0198A] 4. The blessed Gaugericus, who, as we said above, was fourth after Saint Vedast to rule both sees, loved and frequented the city of Cambrai more than Arras, and preferred to live there, because the clergy were certainly more honored there and the population more numerous. Hence the see of Cambrai has five archdeacons, whereas Arras has only two.

The city itself is also beautiful and distinguished above other cities, as those who have seen various cities while traveling to Jerusalem testify. There are indeed many others greater in length and breadth and richer in wealth, but not so in location and arrangement of their buildings, although this city has been disfigured by frequent fires. They also assert that no city is more similar to Jerusalem.

For just as the city of Jerusalem has the Mount of Olives to the east, so the city of Cambrai has to the east a mountain called the mountain of Saint Gaugericus. And just as on Palm Sunday the king and patriarch proceed with the clergy and people, ascending the Mount of Olives, and there receive palm branches, with which they then come to the Valley of Jehoshaphat, where the Gospel is read and a sermon is delivered to the people, so likewise in the city of Cambrai, on that very day, the entire crowd of the city gathers together. Proceeding together with the clergy and monks, they ascend the aforementioned mountain; there the palms are blessed and distributed.

Then, descending, they go to the Holy Sepulchre, and in the atrium of that church they make a station, as though in the Valley of Jehoshaphat. There too the Gospel is read and a sermon is delivered to the people.

On the side of the aforementioned mountain, as though in Bethany, there is the church of Saint Lazarus, beside which lepers live. Within the city itself are the church of the holy Mother of God, the church of the Holy Cross, the church of the Holy Sepulchre, and seven others. Beyond the bridges, outside the gate, there is the church of the Holy Savior.

What shall I say about the liberty of this city? [Note: 7 supplies “What … is said” on a sewn-in slip.] Neither bishop nor emperor imposed a tax in it; no tribute is exacted from it; finally, no army is led out from it except solely for the city’s defense, and even then in such a way that they are able to return to their homes on the same day.

Recently, in the time of Peter, son of Count Theoderic of Flanders, who had been elected after Nicholas to the bishopric of this city—but not canonically, for he was below the required age and below the required orders—the emperor Frederick, intending to set out on an expedition against Italy, ordered money to be sent to him. But neither he nor anyone else before or after him is said to have done this.

[Col. 0199A] 5. It should meanwhile be noted that Saint Gaugericus bought the aforementioned mountain from a certain townsman and built there a church under the name and honor of Saint Medard. After gathering monks, he placed his brother Landon over them.

Saint Gaugericus himself was also buried in that basilica, and his tomb is still held in veneration. If anyone asks how this place passed from the monastic order to the clerical, I shall explain briefly.

Almighty God, who loves justice and hates iniquity, offended by the crimes and misdeeds of Christians, took up, for their correction, the rod of his anger and his staff—namely, the pagan peoples, the Huns, the Normans, and others like them. At various times they departed from their own territories and invaded the lands of Gaul and Germany, overthrowing cities and castles and killing men together with women. They also burned churches and monasteries of men and women alike, killing their inhabitants.

Finally, in the monastery near us, namely Altimont, they slaughtered three hundred monks at once; they lie buried there in a single common grave. Likewise, we have learned from our elders that the monastery of Saint Medard, which, as we said, Saint Gaugericus had built on the aforementioned mountain, was destroyed by the pagans.

But lest anyone then believe, or still believe, that by their own strength, rather than by God’s will and permission, they carried out such destruction of cities and churches and such slaughter of Christians—not only sinners [Col. 0199C] but also the just—and lest it be thought that such great affliction came upon sinners for purification and upon the just for a crown, consider this example:

On Holy Saturday the Huns surrounded the city of Metz, but, distrustful of the strength of the walls, they decided to withdraw. As they were departing, the walls suddenly collapsed before them at the divine command. They themselves then entered the city, set it on fire, and killed its inhabitants. Yet they were entirely unable to burn the church of the blessed protomartyr Stephen. They wanted to, but because Christ did not want it, they could not.

At another time, likewise on Holy Saturday, the Normans invaded the city of Nantes and killed the bishop, who was celebrating the sacred baptism, together with the clergy and people.

[Col. 0199D] 6. After the sons had been chastised, and those through whom they had been chastised had themselves been crushed by a twofold affliction, the Lord raised up men devoted to him, exalted in temporal power and rich in wealth and resources. They repaired, through their devotion and the abundance of riches graciously granted to them by God, what his enemies had destroyed by their savagery and wickedness, though under God’s justice and permission.

Two of these were especially powerful: Gerard, Count of Roussillon, and Charles, surnamed the Bald, king, who at that time ruled both the Franks and the Germans.

The first is said either to have founded or restored nine churches in honor of the holy Mother of God. One of them is the church of Vézelay, which is visited with great Christian devotion because the body of Saint Mary Magdalene was brought there from Aix and buried there.

The other, namely King Charles, likewise built or restored thirteen churches in honor of the Apostle Saint Peter. One of these is the aforementioned basilica, which, as we have already said, Saint Gaugericus had built in honor of Saint Medard but which had been devastated by the pagans.

King Charles restored it and dedicated it to the name and honor of the Apostle Saint Peter. He also placed one hundred canons there and assigned them one hundred prebends. For this reason, his anniversary is solemnly celebrated in the same church every year on 2 Nones of October [6 October].

In this way that place passed from the monastic order to the clerical order, and from the name of Saint Medard to the name of Saint Peter. It is now called by the name of Saint Gaugericus because that blessed confessor had been buried in the same basilica. Later, when his body became renowned through miracles, it was raised from the tomb, placed in a silver coffin, and honorably set behind the altar of Saint Peter in an elevated position, as it may be seen today.

An altar was also consecrated in his honor before his coffin, and another altar was dedicated in the crypt beside his tomb. Nevertheless, the principal altar’s honor and dignity, as well as that of the entire church, belonged and continues to belong to the Apostle Saint Peter to this day.

Hence, during the Rogation processions, the monks of the church of the Lord’s Sepulchre proceed to the same basilica and, at its entrance, begin the antiphon: “You are the shepherd of the sheep.” Singing this, they assemble in the choir and add the vigils and collect concerning the same apostle.

7. Having inserted these matters because of the separation of the church of Arras from her mother, the church of Cambrai, let us return to our subject.

The church of Cambrai, grieving that Arras had been separated from it, elected its archdeacon, Lord Walcherus, as bishop, undoubtedly hoping that through his prudence and persistence the aforementioned division could be restored [Note: Our author omitted a few details about Walcherus from the *Deeds*. They should be supplied from chapter 3 of the French version [Col. 0200D], beginning “and they said … happily from the church.” See also the *Abbreviated Deeds of Cambrai*, chapter 6.].

After his election, he proceeded according to custom to the emperor [Col. 0200D]. Since he had been canonically elected by the clergy and people, he was also gratefully and honorably received by the emperor. The emperor gave him both the bishopric and the county of the city of Cambrai.

But while Walcherus was traveling to the emperor, the people of Arras also went with their chosen bishop to the Roman pontiff and obtained his consecration from him (19 March 1094). After receiving these approvals, each returned with favor—Walcherus with that of the emperor Henry, Lambert with that of Pope Urban—and each was received with honor by his own people: Walcherus at Cambrai, Lambert at Arras [Col. 0201A] [Note: Our author again omitted much, which should be supplied from chapter 4 of the French version, beginning “They rejoiced … joyfully.” The *Abbreviated Deeds of Cambrai*, chapter 7, also shows that some of this material was in the *Deeds*, since it contains certain passages from it.].

After these events, Walcherus humbly requested from the archbishop of Reims the favor of his consecration. But the archbishop did not dare to perform this without the permission of the supreme pontiff, who had already consecrated Lambert.

Walcherus then sought Pope Urban and found favor with him [Note: Again certain passages have been omitted and should be supplied from chapter 5 of the French version, beginning “Then he showed him the bishops,” and also “And if … he excommunicated.”]. Finally, after receiving his letters and two witnesses—namely, the archbishop of Tours and the abbot of Saint Basolus—he presented himself to the archbishop of Reims. After receiving these documents, the archbishop prepared himself to consecrate the bishop of Cambrai.

At the very moment of the consecration, however, the aforementioned Manasses arrived and opposed the carrying out of the consecration. After being examined by the metropolitan and his fellow bishops, he was excommunicated and expelled from the church.

When the consecration had been solemnly completed, Walcherus returned to his own people in peace and joy and was received by them with honor and gladness, while the clergy sang the antiphon: “Christ, rising from the dead, dies no more” [Note: A few details have been omitted and should be supplied from chapter 5 of the French version: “and I was … willingly.”].

8. Later, Bishop Walcherus went to Pope Urban and lodged a complaint about the loss of the church of Arras. Urban, displaying a compassionate feeling toward him—not sincerely, but, as later became clear, hypocritically—assigned both bishops, Walcherus and Lambert, a day and place where the matter was to be discussed.

When they had assembled, the Roman pontiff demanded that the bishop of Cambrai give him three hundred marks. When the bishop refused, the indignant pope urged the abominable Manasses—for he was present—to reclaim the bishopric of Cambrai.

When he did so, Walcherus responded to everything wisely and reasonably. He said that Manasses had been intruded by laymen contrary to the canons and had therefore been justly rejected by the emperor; that he had also been examined and excommunicated by the metropolitan and his fellow bishops; whereas Walcherus had been canonically elected by the clergy and people, approved by the emperor and the pope, and lawfully consecrated by the metropolitan and his fellow bishops, with that same pope ordering it by letter and the archbishop of Tours and the abbot of Saint Basolus serving as witnesses.

After these statements, the supreme pontiff denied everything. Those present were astonished and said that the matter ought to be handled according to the canons. The lord pope replied: “Let the canons cease; my laws shall have authority” [Note: At this point Briali’s 7* manuscript ended; what follows belongs to a single 7 manuscript.].

9. [Note: This entire chapter is absent from the French version; perhaps, therefore, it was added by our *Gaugericiana*.] Here it becomes apparent that the pope was everything, and that “so willing and so commanding,” whenever it pleased him, his will served him as reason. If he had then kept before his eyes the fear of Him who takes away the breath of princes, he could certainly have said reasonably to the bishop of Cambrai: “Brother, you have one bishopric, and that one is surely great enough for you; and although from the beginning until now both sees have obeyed one bishop, nevertheless, since two bishops have now been consecrated, I decree that this arrangement shall remain permanently established, because changing, joining, or separating the seats of bishoprics is the prerogative of the apostolic see alone.” If the supreme pontiff had said this, no one could justly have censured him for it; rather, everyone ought to have praised him, if indeed he had assigned individual pontiffs to the individual sees. But because, on account of the money that had been refused, he so abruptly and shamelessly deposed a bishop canonically elected and consecrated at his command, and set over him a man detestable to all, it is clear to everyone that he acted irrationally.

Certainly, if Walcher had given the money demanded, he would indeed have suffered the loss of his soul, his reputation, and even his money; yet he would in no way have recovered the church he had lost. Instead, the Roman pontiff would have afflicted his spirit from day to day with various schemes and wearisome delays. We know that this has often happened, and we do not doubt that it happens every day.

Nevertheless, why are we surprised that a man of the highest see, and therefore of the highest power, exceeded the bounds of power, when we see others of far lower authority, not only in churches but also in monasteries, when taking away or bestowing honors or offices, attend not to the merit or learning of their subjects but fulfill their own private hatred or affection? Hence blessed Jerome, treating of such men, says: “They confer the rank of cleric upon those whose services have won their favor.” And blessed Pope Gregory says: “It often happens that a pastor is moved toward some neighbor by hatred or favor”; and he adds: “Those who follow either their own hatred or their favor in the cases of their subjects cannot judge their subjects rightly.”

10. Thus Walcher, bishop of Cambrai, who had humbly approached the apostolic see in order to recover the church of Arras, not only failed to receive it, but also lost the bishopric of Cambrai, which he had canonically received and held, without any other fault intervening except that he was unwilling to give money to the supreme pontiff—money, to be sure, to which everything obeys.

For this reason, grieving and mourning over the injury unjustly inflicted upon him, he withdrew from the council and returned to Cambrai. As he approached the city, a procession was being prepared for him, as is customary whenever a bishop returns from the apostolic or imperial court. Having been well advised, he refused to be received with the procession [the wording is uncertain in the supplied text]. Nevertheless, he ordered that the leading persons should assemble before him on the following day, so that from his own account they might learn what had been done at the council concerning the affair in question.

When he had related the matter to those present in detail, they were all filled with the greatest astonishment. When they heard that, on account of money, [lacuna]. [Note: Here manuscript 7 ends at the end of a quire, the next being lost; cf. Waitz in our *Annals* VII, 442.]

# Abridged Deeds of the Pontiffs by a Canon of Cambrai

[Note: We have supplied the title from our own material; we give it from Dom Brial XIII, 534, who transcribed manuscript 9, now lost, but omitted the beginning of the work, concerning Bishop Lietbert.]

## [The Deeds of Gerard, 1–9]

1. After that blessed man, commendable to God and human beings, had died, Gerard, his nephew, distinguished by character and birth, was elected by the common choice of the people of Cambrai and with the consent of Emperor Henry II. At the command of the apostolic legate then residing at Autun [Note: An error, arising because our copyist failed to insert a comma between the words “Gerardi apostolici” and “apud.”], he was consecrated bishop by Hugh, bishop of Die.

After returning to his see, through the intervention of Robert, count of Flanders, he received as a vassal and friend Hugh the castellan, previously expelled by Lord Lietbert; he nevertheless retained in his own hands the revenues of the castellan that were contained within the city walls.

Therefore the citizens, conspiring together, and the bishop being absent, swore the long-desired communal oath. But the bishop, returning with a large force under the appearance of peace, and inviting the conspirators to the judgment of his court, entered the city. And behold, his soldiers, desiring the citizens’ money, fell upon the unsuspecting people and killed them; after the property of many had been seized, the survivors were brought back into the bishop’s allegiance, having renounced the commune.

When, however, the conspiracy was again formed against the bishop, a certain Wibert, who had lost his brother in the aforementioned revolt, revealed it to the bishop. But because he refused to betray the jurors, he was scourged with rods, his hands were bound behind his back, his tongue was cut out, his eyes were torn out, and, after being struck with a sword, he was buried on the public road.

2. Meanwhile, since Hugh the castellan of the bishop was harassing the bishop and his people outrageously, Robert of Flanders, induced by gifts and by the benefit of the gabelle [Note: “Gabelle.” The *Deeds of Gerard* states only that he gave the count two hundred marks of silver], deprived him entirely of his castellanship by legal right, and safely received him in England, as a fugitive seeking refuge, in a secure hiding place.

But so that the city might rest secure within, the bishop properly fortified it with a stone wall and a rampart raised from the earth’s depths; and within the city he strengthened the castle by restoring its ditches and multiplying its intricately connected towers, through an admirable work of engineering.

3. In those days the monastery of Aulne was founded as a special dwelling of God among human beings by two knights, namely Walter and Siger. Carefully advancing their purpose, the bishop granted them a site from his fief and benefices, so that it might be enriched.

The monastery of Haffligem, too, the sanctuary of God, which had been brought to him by laymen and simple people through the authority of the aforementioned pontiff, was raised to a high degree of religious distinction; to this day it retains the prerogative of the monastic order and the privilege of daily distribution to the poor.

4. In addition to all this, the bishop, looking to his future, generously assigned his allodial estates at Lestines and Wolrehem, together with numerous altars, to the uses of his canons, as is found in his privileges. He also newly repaired the hospital of the poor beside the church of the Holy Cross.

He likewise restored and improved, at great cost and expense, the church of the blessed Mother of God, formerly burned and ruined, from its upper end as far as the choir of Saint John. And so, after governing the bishopric for sixteen and a half years, he was gathered to his fathers and buried in the middle of the church of the holy Mother of God.

5. [Cf. *Gaugericiana Excerpts* 2–3.] After Bishop Gerard had been transferred to better things, a serious disagreement arose between the clergy and the people. For while the clerics, because of internal discord, delayed for a long time in making an election, the citizens, together with the casati, elected a certain Manasses, a Frenchman, as bishop. The clergy, by common vote, appointed Lord Maselin, a priest and provost.

He nevertheless yielded freely in order to avert the fury of the people, and many of the clergy joined Manasses. Accordingly, after preparing everything necessary for his journey and carrying with him from the church treasury a golden chalice and two silver candlesticks, he went to the emperor [Note: Manasses]. But, having failed to obtain the emperor’s favor, he returned to his people ingloriously, without receiving any royal benefit. As a result, the clergy were driven far from the city and suffered severely, unless, after touching the holy relics, they swore that they would hinder Manasses before the emperor neither by letter nor by messengers.

6. Amid this turmoil, the people of Arras brought to completion what they had long before conceived. At the command of the supreme pontiff, they set over themselves a bishop of their own and, taking advantage of the disputes that were grievously afflicting the people of Cambrai, shook off their submission to the church of Cambrai, with no one opposing them.

The casati, meanwhile, plundering everything at will, erected numerous fortifications throughout the surrounding region and rendered homage to the count of Flanders, so that they might hold more securely what they had seized.

Waking, as it were, from a deep sleep amid these changes of affairs, both our citizens and our clergy changed their purpose for the better. With the counsel of the archbishop of Reims and the consent of the emperor, they elected Walcher, archdeacon of their church, as pastor and bishop, in order to defend their rights against injury.

7. [French Version 4.] Trusting in God his savior, Walcher gathered his friends and companions and, after Manasses had been killed, destroyed the castle of Gouy in Artois and that of Rumilly; he also destroyed the robbers’ den at Saucit and leveled it with the ground. He devoted the first days of his vocation to these demonstrations of his future excellence [*Gaugericiana Excerpts* 7].

Later, he was presented with apostolic letters to Rainald, his metropolitan, so that Rainald might bestow upon him the office of consecration. But Manasses, his adversary, arrived, appealed to the lord pope, and forbade his advancement.

Walcher was nevertheless consecrated bishop. What he had left unfinished for the security of his homeland, he completed with great skill, subduing his adversaries and defending his own people [ibid. 8].

Meanwhile, he went to the general council that Pope Urban was holding at Clermont, intending to denounce the presumption of the people of Arras. There, unwisely, he offended Manasses, who was bringing forward many accusations against him; and, withdrawing from the council without awaiting judgment, he incurred the sentence of excommunication. The election of Manasses was confirmed by the authority of the council because of the adversary’s contumacy, although Manasses possessed less canonical standing.

8. [French Version 7.] Thereafter, when the clergy and citizens conspired with Walcher, promising always to serve him and declaring that they would abandon him under no circumstances, Manasses, archbishop of Reims and uncle of the elected Manasses, placed under interdict the entire land known to obey Walcher’s commands [ibid. 11].

As a result, many among the clergy and laity who were sound in judgment withdrew from his allegiance or association, obtaining from the archbishop that he would not delay conferring the honor of consecration upon his nephew Manasses [ibid. 12].

After this had been done, although Lord Walcher recognized that a grave danger was threatening him, he nevertheless conquered and destroyed the castles of Oisy, Bousignies, and Boussois through innumerable assaults and the courage of his soldiers.
