His city and his people were completely restored to a most welcome peace [ibid. 14–15].

But when the clergy, especially because of the sentence of interdict, were deserting his side in great numbers, he turned to Emperor Henry for counsel and aid, and Manasses was received with honor in the pontifical seat.

He did not, however, long rejoice in the devotion of his subjects. For when Walcher returned with the emperor’s messengers and soldiers, only a few accompanying Manasses through fear of those who were arriving, Manasses, stripped of the city over which he ruled only in name, abandoned it and departed, offering only a show of resistance. Thus, as if anew, the citizens and clergy were joined to Lord Walcher by the emperor’s command.

9. [Cf. ibid. 16, 18, 19.] As time passed, Robert, count of Flanders, acting on the command of the archbishop in order to obtain remission of his sins—for he had long been excommunicated—made war against the people of Cambrai. King Henry, seeking vengeance for those injuries, invaded these regions, and the following castles fell before the attack of his army: Marquion, Palluel, Inchy, Esquelbecq, and Bouchain.

But while the emperor had withdrawn into German territory for the winter season, Robert threatened the people of Cambrai and entirely repaid upon them the losses suffered by his own men. Peace was finally established on this condition: unless the emperor came during the season of grass, they would receive Robert and his successors as lords and patrons forever.

10. [Cf. ibid. 20, 21, 22, 32.] Thus, with the war suspended under the name of peace, the people of Cambrai sent word to the archbishop that he should come to them to confer the benefit of absolution. This was done, while Walcher remained at Estrées, his stronghold, which, after being thrown down from above by the leading men of the land, still preserves the traces of its ruins to this day (1103).

Walter, strengthened by the support of his people, returned again to the city. He had made peace with Godfrey, son of Anselm, whom the people of Cambrai had set over themselves against the bishop, and, though still bearing the mark of excommunication, he entered the city.

Meanwhile, Lord Manasses had been transferred to the bishopric of Soissons, which at that time lacked a pastor. The leading men and canons of Cambrai therefore went to the house of Reims to plead for Lord Walcher. But the archbishop publicly produced letters that he had newly received from the lord pope and ordered them, under the obligation of obedience, to elect a bishop immediately, because Walcher had irretrievably forfeited the dignity of the bishopric.

11. [French Version 32.] Lord Odo, abbot of Saint Martin of Tournai, was therefore elected by all and, three days after his election, consecrated bishop by that same archbishop.

After returning to Tournai, he celebrated ordinations and a synod. He possessed nothing from the royal revenues, although he had been received at Cambrai, but lived only by the support of his faithful, which they freely offered him [ibid. 23, 27, 31].

Walcher, deprived of every hope, withdrew to Obert, bishop of Liège; and afterward, visiting the threshold of the apostles, he was completely restored by the apostolic authority to the condition he had occupied before the bishopric (1104). Finally, abandoning everything for Christ and living in the monastery of Saint Nicholas in the Wood under the habit and discipline of monks, he corrected the excesses of his former life and brought his deeds to a good end [French Version 24, 26, 29, 30].

Bishop Odo, meanwhile, was received within the city by Robert of Flanders, who held Cambrai in fief from the hand of Emperor Henry. But he was driven out farther by the power of Emperor Henry, who was persecuting his own father. When the count of Flanders had been reconciled with the emperor and had freely returned our city to him, Odo found a place of refuge at his residence at Inchy, until, through the mediation of the supreme pontiff, Emperor Henry generously invested Odo with the bishopric by staff and ring, as the pope himself had granted him permission to do.

But when the privilege of such a concession, which the lord pope had granted to emperors contrary to the canons, was revoked, Bishop Odo was deposed because of the form and manner of his investiture. Reaching Aulne, he fell asleep in Christ under the command of obedience.

12. [French Version 33.] Lord Burchard, a familiar and intimate acquaintance of the emperor, succeeded Odo by common election and the emperor’s gift (1118). But because of the dispute between the pope and the emperor over investiture by staff and ring, he could not obtain consecration for two years, while many threatened him with deposition.

At last, however, through the merit of his life, by which he shone especially among his fellow provincials, and after obtaining letters from the lord pope on the matter, he received the oil of consecration, which he had long desired.

Whatever had been alienated from the episcopal mensa—namely, the tolls, the mint, and the mills—he redeemed from the hands of creditors at great expense. In every way he labored to gather what had been scattered, rebuild what had been destroyed, and preserve with no less fidelity what he had found [French Version 34, 38].

He also recovered with remarkable diligence the new castle that, as stated above, had been attached to the church of Cambrai by a gift of the emperor, freeing it from the hands of the counts Baldwin and Charles of Flanders. Robert, the last count, and his son Baldwin had held it as a benefice and fief from the emperor.

After Count Charles was killed at Bruges by a terrible act of treachery, Hugh the castellan received from the bishop, as was proper, the castellanship of Cambrai, which he had held from the aforementioned count, after rendering homage and swearing fidelity. First, however, he demolished the castle that the same Hugh had built at Crèvecoeur as a refuge for brigands.

13. [French Version 37.] At the exhortation and counsel of this bishop, a certain citizen named Werimbold undertook the path of perfection. In this city of Cambrai he redeemed the toll for a large sum of money and, finally, in the hospital of the poor beside the church of the Holy Cross, became poor for Christ and humbly devoted himself to caring for the poor.

O truly commendable bishop! Born in regions very far removed from his see and a newcomer among the people of Cambrai, he contributed more to them through his diligence than our nobles did either through worldly splendor or through the greatness of bodily descent.

Thus, after bestowing innumerable benefits upon his people and his church, as is read in his deeds and writings, full of good works and almsgiving, he migrated on the wings of the virtues into the company of the faithful.

14. [French Version 40, 42.] At the same time, Pope Innocent, passing through Cambrai with a multitude of bishops and cardinals, descended to Liège with King Lothair and the princes of Germany (March 1131), intending to discuss many matters concerning the condition of the Church. During this conference, through the king’s favor, Lietard became bishop of Cambrai.

After his consecration, as though hoping for or fearing nothing more, wholly devoted to himself and insufficiently attentive to generosity, he became hateful to everyone.

Therefore Gerard, surnamed Maufillastres, rose up against the bishop, captured and burned Nieuwkerke, and, together with the multitude of its inhabitants and the relics of the saints, five churches perished by the violence of the fire. Gerard distributed the bishop’s surrounding possessions among his own followers without opposition and possessed the rest at his pleasure.

Only Simon of Oisy, the castellan’s son, grieving over the devastation of the bishopric, bravely made war against Gerard and finally brought him back into friendship with the bishop of Cambrai. The following satisfaction was first stipulated: the knight would give five solidi, and each foot soldier twenty denarii, for the restoration of the church of the most blessed Andrew. Thus all those who had participated in the aforementioned crime were absolved, but because of their contempt for the bishop none of these payments was put into effect.

15. [French Version 43.] The provost of the episcopal household, whom the bishop was attempting to remove—so it was commonly said—in order to indulge his pleasures more freely within his own residence, openly reported to the archbishop of Reims, together with certain clerics and citizens, that the bishop, avoiding the palace because of his excessive lust, was staying in private houses; that he was selling prebends; and that he consecrated churches only for an agreed price.

The lord of Reims therefore summoned Lietard in a fatherly manner, in the presence of only five bishops, and learned from Lietard’s own mouth that the charges brought against him were not false. He ordered and advised him that, before the coming Epiphany, he should withdraw voluntarily, so that he would not be publicly convicted, and should not appear there again. Bishop Lietard confirmed, in the presence of his fellow bishops, that he would do this.

But after departing to the emperor, he requested that through the emperor’s intervention he might find mercy with the lord pope and the archbishop. There he obtained a privilege that the aforementioned provost and the bishop’s unfeudated servants should not dare, against the bishop’s will, to interfere in his offices.

When the bishop, after the appointed term had passed, failed to carry out what he had promised, letters from the archbishop and the authority of the supreme pontiff arrived, ordering him to withdraw quickly from the bishopric. In every respect he was to be pitied: a learned man, commendable for the beauty of his body, was disgracefully driven from the episcopal see amid the shame of his face and the reproach of his name because of the infamous charges mentioned above (1137).

16. After Lietard was deposed, the people of Cambrai elected a certain Otho, a canon of the Premonstratensian order, on the condition that the election should be acceptable to the emperor.

But since the emperor in no way gave his consent, two abbots, Walter of Saint Aubert and Parvuinus of the Holy Sepulchre, were sent to obtain, through the emperor’s favor, a suitable bishop for the church of Cambrai.

By God’s providence, Lord Nicholas, provost of that same church, was therefore elected. He had been raised there from his earliest years, and everyone acclaimed him, while the emperor’s favor in the matter was fully and freely obtained.

For the multitude of princes who were then present at court recognized him as their elected friend and kinsman.

Received with immeasurable joy by clergy and people, he showed at the very beginning of his vocation what he would become. Gerard Maufillastres, who violently occupied Nieuwkerke, the bishop’s castle, and the possessions of the bishopric, was returning incautiously from a conference with Simon of Oisy. The bishop seized him at Theun, his own estate, fearing no danger that he might have to undergo for the liberty of the church, and brought him captive into the city with a great multitude of armed men.

There, after receiving hostages and many oaths that fidelity would be maintained toward him in the future, and after also recovering Nieuwkerke with its dependencies, he released Gerard. In addition, he stationed his own men in the castle of Saint Aubert for the greater security of his territory and his people.

17. After these commendable beginnings, he received the honor of consecration and devoted himself solely to the exaltation of his church, to which he gave himself with complete diligence.

While everyone was rejoicing in the tranquility of peace, certain brigands from the household of Gerard Maufillastres, ravaging this land, received from the people of Cambrai a punishment worthy of their crimes.

Gerard therefore broke the peace that he had long maintained unwillingly in appearance, declared war against the bishop and the citizens, and strengthened his territory with powerful fortifications. The bishop, for his part, did not neglect to fortify Nieuwkerke with a rampart and a most secure tower.

Gerard then gathered a large force of warriors and besieged the aforementioned castle. But by a manifest judgment of God, while he pressed the attack more fiercely than the others, he alone fell, without any of his men being wounded or brought down. Dragged within the walls by iron hooks, pierced by many wounds, and buried beneath stones, he who had previously been terrible now died pitiably.

Because of his pitiable death, the leading men of the land, threatening the bishop with increasing severity, finally compelled him, amid many and various disturbances, to drive far from the borders of his territory all those who had laid hands upon Gerard.

18. But once peace had been restored externally, seditions arose within. For the citizens of Cambrai received the count of Hainaut within their walls against the bishop and made a treaty with him, because the bishop had granted the castle of Saint Aubert in fief to his nephew Simon of Oisy, contrary to their counsel and will.

Therefore, after they had demolished Simon’s house within the city as an insult to the bishop, both the count and the citizens incurred, by canonical judgment, the sentence of excommunication and interdict.

When all these disturbances had been brought to an end in peace through God’s grace and the aid of the count of Flanders [Note: Theodoric], after that famous slaughter at Crèvecoeur, Gerard’s inheritance was restored to his son after he had rendered fidelity and homage, and suitable satisfaction was made to the bishop for the aforementioned excesses.

Not long afterward, the count of Flanders began to afflict Simon of Oisy with much warfare because he had rebelled against him, and he occupied his fortifications. But the lord bishop, a man commendable in character, defended Simon above all others with counsel and aid, as his own man, his nephew, and his friend, not fearing to provoke the anger of the leading men against himself for the sake of protecting his own people.

At last, through the bishop’s mediation, they agreed upon the following form of peace: the count of Flanders received Oisy and the castellanship of Cambrai in fief from the hand of the bishop—although Simon had previously held them directly from the bishop—and the aforementioned count enfeoffed Simon with the said properties under careful terms, so that in the arrangement of peace nothing belonging by right to the bishop was lost; rather, the homage owed to Flanders increased.

19. Meanwhile, when the famous schism arose in the Roman Church between Alexander and Octavian (1160), Emperor Frederick followed Octavian’s party with his entire empire. All France, together with the rest of the world, followed the election of Alexander, and a serious dissension arose in the Church of God, as those who follow their own interests rather than the things of Jesus Christ divided the unity of Christ.

Amid this varied division, Nicholas, the bishop whose memory deserves honor, conducted himself with such moderation that he neither withdrew from obedience to the people of Reims, to whom he was subject in spiritual matters, nor offended the emperor’s party, to which he was bound to remain faithful and devoted in matters concerning his royal revenues.

Thus, amid the uncertainty of affairs, the bishop, distinguished by his works and greatness of spirit, while burdened by illness at Saint-Quentin, made satisfaction to his Lord God through contrition of heart and confession of mouth—for the sinner is heard at the hour when he groans—and, on the hill of Saint Martin near the boundary of his diocese, was freed from earthly things (1167).

He was then carried back to his see by the hands of his people and received a glorious burial in the church of the Mother of God, on the western side, never afterward to see the setting sun.

For although this man served under the appearance of secular life and conformed himself for a time to all secular people, and although he may sometimes have contracted stains from earthly contamination, he is nevertheless believed, through God’s mercy and through the multitude of benefits that he generously bestowed upon his subjects in various places, to have cast off the burden of his sins. For no good deed remains unrewarded by the Requiter of good.

20. Lord Peter, the uterine brother of Philip, the most noble count of Flanders, provost of Saint-Omer and chancellor of Flanders, was elected bishop through the influence of his brother, whose terror had spread throughout the neighboring lands and whose name was widely famous in distant regions.

Many approved the election, while very many, although displeased by what had been done, did not dare oppose it. The emperor’s consent to the election also followed. Overcome by the count’s many embassies, he accepted the elected man, although he was still in the first years of adolescence, considering it settled that the Roman curia, by dispensing with regard to age and orders, did not reject him.

While the elected bishop delayed in approaching the emperor, the people of Cambrai, wishing to provide for their future and prevent new fortifications from arising in the surrounding region, completely demolished Thun-l’Évêque, which Bishop Nicholas had built.

But when the elected bishop attacked them vigorously, they were finally compelled, at great monetary expense, to restore what they had destroyed with stubborn presumption like an untamed people.

During the days of this elected bishop, however, our city and its neighbors throughout the surrounding region remained at peace. No one dared or was able to withstand the attack of the Flemings, whose power and strength Lord Peter, though still only elected, used to protect his people and their possessions solely by the name of his election.

In all his actions, as a young and noble man, he would have been worthy of much praise, except that, gratifying his nobility from Christ’s patrimony, he never aspired to holy orders or the honor of consecration. He bore the honor of a bishop, but not the burden; he abhorred the office, yet sought the revenues of the bishopric with complete integrity.

Therefore, after several years of his election, he finally broke through to what he had long desired. Casting aside the dignity of his election and the freedom of the clerical profession, he put on military dress, fell back into the wantonness of the age and the pomps of the world, and took as his wife the countess of Nevers, so that he might beget children of the flesh. He rejected the bride of Christ, who gives birth to spiritual children without violating her own purity (1174–1175).

He did not, however, long delight in earthly things, for the breath of man is not in his own hand but in the power of Him who is terrible among the kings of the earth. He was removed from the land of his wife, died amid deep repentance for his many sins, and was buried at Issoudun [Note: Issoudun, in Berry]. He left the living an example of our mutability, having been overtaken by an untimely death.

21. Robert, provost of Aire and holder of the privilege of election in the church of Arras, was a man raised, by the remarkable prodigy of fortune, from a lowly and humble position to splendid degrees of dignity. He was treasurer of Tours, provost of Saint-Omer, Saint-Amé of Douai, and Saint Donatian of Bruges, and singularly close to Philip, count of Flanders.

Despite the protests of many clerics, he was elected pastor of the people of Cambrai by those who, amazed at fortune’s favor toward him, hoped that he would exalt their church in a singular manner—he who had himself been raised so singularly as to astonish the world.

The emperor also condescended, at entreaties, to grant him the investiture of the royal revenues. He himself first forestalled the request by making an offer and then, after sending royal messengers ahead in much greater abundance, dispatched him to be received with great glory at his see.

Established in the seat of his new vocation, he promised many things beyond the belief and expectation of his hearers and pledged that he would make his church golden. He grew presumptuous from the abundance of the goods flowing to him, yet did not know what the coming days were preparing for him.

While these matters were proceeding favorably for him, he aroused the hatred and envy of the leading men against himself. Thus, at Condé, a village of his diocese, while he was passing through with a crowd exceeding all measure, he was struck down by a few men lying in wait for him. Miserably abandoned by his own people and cruelly killed by criminals, he underwent a sudden reversal: the hand of the Most High brought him from the heights to the depths (1174).

The experience of events itself teaches us effectively that no stability belongs to human affairs, however much they may applaud themselves.

His body was therefore carried from the place of his murder to Aire, where many memorials of his generosity remain before the eyes of those who see them. There he awaits, gloriously buried, the time when he will be raised at the end to behold the face of his Creator.

22. Lord Alard, archdeacon and treasurer of Cambrai, was a man so abundantly endowed by divine gift with an overflowing supply of everything that his storehouses poured forth from one place into another, and everyone called blessed the lord and the house to which these things belonged.

Despite the protests of some, he was elected pastor and bishop, both on account of his own merits and through the influence of his leading supporters (1174).

He went to Italy to receive the royal revenues from the emperor’s hand—a grant that he effectively obtained, although certain leading men protested—and, after returning to his own people, clearly showed himself a guileless man and exceedingly gentle toward his people.

He learned, for the instruction and example of his successors, that human peace and abundance of possessions do not consist in the power of a multitude or in the dignity of preeminence, but that the Lord takes pleasure in those who fear him and in those who hope in his mercy despite their modest condition.

Nevertheless, in the days of his old age, when he was also called to higher things, he conducted himself so as to make himself loved by everyone and often showed himself diligent in carrying out the office of the bishopric that he had undertaken, beyond the strength of his body.

When his life was completed within a short time (1177), lest wickedness change his heart, he decided to be buried at Vaucelles, so that through the prayers of religious men he might obtain what he did not dare presume would come to him from his own merits.

23. After the death of Lord Alard, Lord Roger of Waurin, who held the dignity of archdeacon and treasurer in the church of Cambrai, was elected by common consent (1178). He received the investiture without difficulty from the emperor’s hand, because he had once earned his favor when he had restored the emperor and Lord Bishop Alard to unity of peace.

He was also solemnly consecrated at Rome on the Aventine Hill, in the church of Saint Sabina, by Lord William, archbishop of Reims, who had been made a cardinal there at the Lateran Council by Pope Alexander. He had been given the mitre before obtaining the dignity of consecration.

Afterward, when he had been restored to his people amid universal joy, he governed the church in the greatest peace. The only exception was that the count of Flanders, while the bishop was delayed in Rome, purchased the provostry of Nieuwkerke for a large sum of money without the bishop’s knowledge, intending to occupy the bishop’s entire right by virtue of his portion, unless the bishop, through prudent diligence, had promptly applied a remedy to so great a presumption.

Fearing neither danger of death nor exile, and with the leading men of Flanders and the count himself rising against him, he finally prevailed, at the cost of much expense and labor, in obtaining that after the count’s death the provostry should freely devolve to the bishop’s right. During his lifetime, however, the count would possess it peacefully, content with his own legal right, while assigning seven hundred pounds at his death to whomever he pleased.

This settlement was confirmed by the privileges of the emperor, the king of France, and all the leading men whose testimony could have authority in the matter.

24. Later, when discord arose between him and his citizens because the commune of the city was stretching out its hands too freely and eagerly against the liberty of the clergy, an appeal was made to the emperor’s court. There, since the principal men of the court supported the pontiff—for the conspiracy of the commune is hateful to all who love the liberty of the Church—the commune of Cambrai was solemnly condemned by the emperor, and by imperial decree the bishop was granted authority to make ordinances concerning the city and its citizens [Col. 0213C], as the peace of the Church and the bishop’s judgment should determine. A privilege was granted concerning this matter and confirmed by the testimony of the princes, and all the insignia of the commune were utterly abolished.

But when the lord bishop imprudently threatened that he would impose upon his citizens a certain yoke of the gravest servitude, although he ought rather to have tempered his severity, the citizens hastened to the emperor, returning with much money. They eliminated the name of “commune,” which has always been detestable, under the name of peace—although there was no peace—and against the bishop and the liberty of the clergy, as may still be experienced today, they brought back a privilege filled with their own will and sedition.

O first prosperity [Col. 0214A] exchanged for great misfortune, when the privilege of liberty is changed into institutions of servitude!

25. Moreover, worn down by wars and by the many persecutions of his household, as well as by the causes and needs of his friends, and as though threshed upon a threshing floor of wheat, the bishop undertook the pilgrimage with the others on that famous journey when Jerusalem had most recently been conquered by the Saracens. He desired, through the labors and sweat of his own body, to wash away what he had contracted while living among us through negligence in episcopal government and through the contagion of human fault.

After enduring many dangers, when he reached the siege of the holy city, he began to grow seriously ill. He was carried back to Tyre, resigned his bishopric, and became poor for Christ. In the habit [Col. 0214B] of the regular canons, he departed from this world (1191). Amid the lamentation of all his household who attended him, he was received into a tomb in the church of the Holy Cross. He left his own people a memorial of penitence in the extremity of his self-abasement, assigning for the daily sustenance of the canons four mencalds of flour per week, so that, with bread that never fails, he might be refreshed eternally by their prayers.

26. How many and how great benefits the aforementioned fathers bestowed upon our church may be judged more clearly from the privileges granted to us, since by their generosity an abundance of daily bread is provided for us, on condition that a heavenly reward also be granted to those who faithfully preserve the rights of their mother.

But behold, on the day of the Lord we fear being accused of infidelity [Col. 0214C], because, as though without our knowledge, every precious possession belonging to the integrity and dignity of the episcopate has perished: namely, these castles—Paluel, Oisy, Haveraincourt, Crivecuer, Wallaincourt, Busignies, Saint-Obers, Hordain—which have become for us like a nail in the eye, although they ought to be ramparts of security. The royal *forastrum* [Note: i.e. *forestum*, “forest”] also, which was given to the bishops for hunting and assigned for the defense of the imperial frontier, has so completely perished that it retains no trace even of woodland and provides no obstacle to raiders.

In restoring all these things, as the time requires, only one course remains: that, once Peter’s sword has been drawn, the other sword, which the sheath still encloses, should be effectively brought into use [Note: Here Book 9 ends. “What follows there was written by another hand, but is so mutilated that it is scarcely permissible to extract anything certain from it.” Brial].

# French Version of the Deeds

[Editorial apparatus for this Old French recension: *ot* = “had/there was” (French *eut*); *Si* = “thus” (*ainsi*); *peule* = “people” (*peuple*); *entr’ iaux* = “among themselves” (*eux*); *jones* = “young” (*jeune*); *coustres* = “custodian”; *evesquiet* = “bishopric” (*évêché*); *curoit* = “cared” (Latin *paucum curabat*); *fremerent* = “fortified” (*fermerent*); *forche* = “force”; *tenchons* = “poetic contests” (*tençons*, Latin *certamina poetica*); *fu* = “fire” (*feu*); *ahaniers* = “laborers” (*laboureurs*); *iriet* = “angered” (Latin *irati*); *eslieut* = “elected” (*élu*); *clergie* = “learning”; and *lceche* = “joy” (Latin *laetitia*, French *liesse*, *joie*). In no. 6, *la seconde domée de l’avent* means “the second Sunday of Advent”; in no. 15, *senne* means “court,” rather than a synod.]

[Col. 0213]

## 1. (Cf. *Excerpt of Gaugain* 2.) [Col. 0213D]

After the death of Bishop Gerard (1092), there was dissension and great discord between the clergy of Cambrai. Thus they did not elect a bishop for a long time. They were greatly hated and blamed by the people; and when the people saw that the canons were not making a bishop as they ought, they assembled against God and the rights of Holy Church, held a meeting, and swore among themselves that there would be no bishop—neither this man nor that man nor any other—but only one whom the emperor would send there. Then the people took counsel that they would send the bishop’s crozier to the emperor Henry III.

A nobleman named Masselin, provost of the church, came forward to carry it and said that this was his right. But Erlebaud, the church’s custos, quickly opposed him and said that it was his right. Thus they contended for a long time over who should carry the crozier, and it was not carried. A whole year passed in this way without a bishop [Col. 0214D–0215A], and the emperor did not know that Bishop Gerard was already dead.

Afterward the people assembled and elected as bishop, against God and the rights of Holy Church, a man named Manasses, young in years and character. When the clergy saw this, they were deeply troubled. They came together in chapter and, by divine inspiration, elected a noble, wise, religious man, the provost of the church, named Masselin.

When the laymen heard this, they were filled, as it were, with madness. They fiercely opposed the election made by the chapter and swore that Manasses—the man they had elected—would be bishop. They further swore that if any of the clerics opposed them, they would kill him.

Then the elected Manasses prepared to go to the emperor, and the burghers forcibly took from the church treasury seven pure-silver candelabra weighing thirty marks and a pure-gold chalice weighing seven marks, adorned with many precious stones. Thus the burghers sent their elected candidate to court; but the emperor did not receive him, and he returned in disgrace.

Then hatred and discord grew between the clergy and the people. The burghers said that the clerics had sent letters to the emperor asking him not to receive their candidate, and there were many other causes of hatred and dissension. Thus the Church of Cambrai remained widowed, desolate, and without a shepherd for a long time, and was in great tribulation.

## 2. [Col. 0215C]

At that time there was a wicked man in Cambrai named Fulk, who was the *vidame* of the city. When he saw that the Church was without a defender, he entered the bishop’s palace with many knights, seized the revenues of the bishopric, and lived outrageously upon them. He cared little for the Church’s injury and did not wish it to have a good bishop.

When the enemies of the Church saw this, they were very pleased. They took counsel together and fortified castles in order to press the city. Among them, a knight named Amouris built one at Gouy, and Manasses built one at Rumilly. Then they went to Robert, count of Flanders, and received their lands from him, contrary to their oath and to the rights of the bishopric.

They then ravaged the country with great force, so that the city, which previously had had wars of words and disputes, afterward had wars of arms, fire, and sword. They devastated the country so thoroughly that scarcely any laborers remained to cultivate the land. [Col. 0215C–D]

## 3. [Excerpt of Gaugain 3]

At the time when the city had such discord within and such great oppression from its enemies without, a great evil befell it for which there was no remedy. For when the clergy of Arras saw that the men of Cambrai were not making a bishop as they ought, they took counsel together and elected Lambert, archdeacon of Thérouanne—this was done in the year of grace 1095 (rather 1093)—and thus made him head of the member.

When the clergy of Cambrai heard this, they were extremely angry. They went to Renaud, archbishop of Reims, and asked him what counsel they could follow. He replied that they should elect a good and wise man who could sustain the Church in such great tribulations.

At that time there was in the church an archdeacon of very great worth. He told the chapter that, if they would assist him, he was prepared to go to Rome against Lambert, the elected bishop of Arras. But everyone feared the trouble of going to Rome, and they said: “Let the one who is elected go there and defend himself as he would defend himself in his own cause.” (Ibid. 7.)

Then the clergy were placed in great anguish, sorrow, and tribulation, and did not know through whom they might be freed from their enemies. They considered and took counsel together, and knew no cleric more suitable or more worthy to restore the Church to possession of its property than the archdeacon, Sir Gaucher. They said that he was well worthy of greater honor. For he was born of noble lineage, full of great learning, and well instructed in the seven arts.

There was another reason also why he should be elected: the emperor had sent them letters commanding them to elect him. Therefore Sir Gaucher was elected by the common assent of all. Without taking anything from the Church, he went to the emperor Henry III, who received him with great honor, consented to the election, and granted him lordship over Cambrai. There was great joy at the royal court, and the king himself began the *Te Deum laudamus*. [Col. 0215D–0216B]

## 4. [Col. 0216C]

While the elected Gaucher was with the emperor, Pope Urban II consecrated Lambert, the elected bishop of Arras (1094, March 19), and by the pope’s command Lambert was received at Arras with great honor.

Then the elected Gaucher returned to his city, where he was received with immense joy. At that point the *vidame* Fulk came to the bishop and became his liege man by faith and oath. The clergy and laymen then swore fealty to him.

When the good Bishop Gaucher had newly arrived at his church, he worked very hard to love his subjects, to live in peace among them, and to acquire friends for his Church. But the pride and malice of the powerful men of the country toward him were very great and continually increased.

For Hugh, Amouris, Manasses, and Ansel—as we have said above—quickly rebelled against him because they feared losing the castles they had fortified around Cambrai in order to destroy the city while it was without a bishop. They were also afraid because they had rendered homage to the count of Flanders and received their lands from him. These four men therefore inflicted great harm upon the country through the power of Robert, count of Flanders.

When the bishop saw this, he felt great pity for the poor, who were losing their possessions. He therefore humbly admonished his enemies with gentle words and begged them to cease harming his Church. But they did nothing.

After his entreaty he promised them great gifts if they would demolish the castles they had built against him and make peace with him; but they scorned all this. When the bishop saw that he could not make them his friends either by gifts or promises, he assembled a large number of mercenaries and did so well that he had seven hundred knights. He then vigorously defended his country against his enemies. (*Abbreviatio Cameracensis* 7.)

He had a castle at Gouy in Artois attacked, and by God’s help it was taken by force. Amouris, his great enemy, who had built the castle, was captured there. The bishop held him in prison for a full year. Amouris repented of the wrongs he had done to the Church, became the bishop’s friend, and swore fealty to him; thus he was released from prison.

Then the bishop had the castle of Rumilly attacked, which Manasses had built, and they labored against it for a long time. For the town was strongly fortified with high walls and deep ditches, and those within grew very proud and greatly desired to destroy the country. But a short time afterward the bishop’s men attacked it with such strength that, by God’s will, the castle was taken, and Manasses was killed there.

The bishop then had the castle demolished and leveled, and had everything committed to fire and flame. He next attacked another castle named Sauchis, which was a den of thieves. By God’s help he took it; several of the robbers were killed and some were captured. Thus the country was freed from these criminals.

When the elected bishop saw that the country was somewhat at peace, he gave many fine gifts to his mercenaries, and they departed from him very joyfully. [Col. 0216C–0217B]

## 5. [Excerpt of Gaugain 7]

At that time the elected bishop was so occupied with establishing peace in his land that he had no opportunity to have himself ordained, and he was not a priest. When he saw that there was a little respite, he went to Reims to Archbishop Renaud and asked him to ordain him priest. The archbishop refused until he should have the pope’s command.

Then the elected bishop went to Rome and begged Pope Urban II to have him ordained priest. The pope received him graciously. The elected Gaucher then showed the pope the wrongs that Robert, count of Flanders, had done to the Church of Cambrai. He also complained about the election of Manasses: how Manasses had been elected by the people against the law, and how great a tribulation he had caused after his election.

The archbishop of Tours and several other bishops testified before the pope concerning all these complaints. When the pope heard these things, he confirmed Sir Gaucher as the elected bishop and sent him by letter to the archbishop of Reims, commanding that the archbishop ordain him. At the pope’s command, the archbishop of Tours and the abbot of Saint-Basle went with him.

The pope also commanded the archbishop not to allow Manasses to inflict further injury upon the Church of Cambrai on account of his election, since that election was null. The pope likewise commanded Manasses to return the church’s treasure, which he had wrongfully carried away; otherwise he would excommunicate him.

When the archbishop saw the great favor that the pope showed the elected Gaucher, he did what the pope had commanded. He then appointed a day at Laon for the consecration of the elected bishop, with many bishops present.

At the moment when Gaucher was to be consecrated, Manasses arrived and opposed him. The great disputes and dissensions that he caused there would take a long time to recount. The assembled bishops therefore took counsel concerning these elections and declared by definitive judgment that Sir Gaucher’s election was good and lawful. Manasses was solemnly excommunicated by the bishops, deprived, and expelled from the Church; then Sir Gaucher was consecrated with great reverence.

He afterward came to his city and was received with very great honor. He was placed in the bishop’s chair by Elynant, bishop of Laon. Then, by command of the pope, everyone, great and small, was ordered to obey him.

The pope and the archbishop sent word to Robert, count of Flanders, that from then onward he should cease harming the Church of Cambrai, make good peace with it, and love, honor, and support Bishop Gaucher. If he did not do so, the pope would excommunicate him. The count willingly complied. [Col. 0217C–0218B]

## 6. [Col. 0218B]

When the bishop saw that he had been confirmed in his see, he had a very great desire to restore the Church. He first considered Lambert, who had removed such a member—Arras—from the bishopric of Cambrai. He therefore sent a solemn embassy to Pope Urban, asking him to assign him a day against Lambert, who had taken Arras in this way and was bishop there.

The pope replied very graciously that he would help him, and appointed a day during the second week of Advent, at a specified place, Clermont. He also sent word to Lambert, the bishop’s adversary, that he should be there on that day (1095).

The bishop went to the appointed day with great effort, and the pope received him with a false embrace, as later became clear. Lambert had already secretly come to the pope and given him very great gifts so that he would not be deposed; thus he had won over the pope with his smooth words.

Then the pope tested Bishop Gaucher, asking whether he would give more than Lambert, and demanded three hundred silver marks. But the bishop refused them, and for that reason he lost his case.

For as soon as Bishop Gaucher began to speak before the bishops who were there in council, and complained about Lambert, bishop of Arras, saying that the pope had confirmed Lambert as bishop against the rights of his Church, the pope became extremely angry and shouted fiercely: “Leave your rights and your canons aside, for all the laws that I have given will be authoritative.” (*Excerpt of Gaugain* 8.)

Then he commanded Manasses, who was present there, to state his complaint about his election before everyone. The bishop and all the clergy were so astonished at what the pope commanded that it cannot be expressed.

Manasses then rose and began to say that Sir Gaucher was not bishop according to law, but that he himself ought to be bishop, since he had been elected first. Manasses advanced many other arguments.

The pope repeatedly urged Bishop Gaucher to answer Manasses at once, but Gaucher wisely asked for a short delay. [Col. 0218C–0219A]

After a little while Bishop Gaucher gave his account: Manasses had been elected unlawfully, without the assent of the clergy, and had been rejected by the emperor; he had been excommunicated at Laon in a full council of bishops. Gaucher himself, however, had been elected according to the rights of Holy Church, by the common assent of the clergy; confirmed by the emperor, who had granted him lordship over the city; confirmed also by the pope in his letters; and consecrated and blessed by the archbishop of Reims. He called the archbishop to testify to this, since he was present there.

The archbishop of Reims rose and said that it was true. But the pope did not believe him.

Then Bishop Gaucher produced the letters of his confirmation, sealed by the pope himself, but the pope denied everything. After hearing both sides, the pope ordered judgment to be rendered, and Sir Gaucher became afraid and departed before judgment had been given.

The pope then had a sentence delivered with the advice of some of the bishops, though not all. He restored Manasses as bishop and excommunicated Sir Gaucher, without giving him the admonition that ought to have preceded it. (*Ibid.* 10.) [Col. 0219B]

## 7.

Sir Gaucher returned to his church, and the procession went out to meet him and intended to receive him with great honor. But because he was sad, sorrowful, and in great tribulation, he forbade them to rejoice. The next day he summoned all his friends and told them what had been done at the council of Clermont.

When the clergy and people heard this, they were greatly troubled and hated the pope intensely. They advised their bishop no longer to obey the pope unless he restored Arras to the city of Cambrai. They also advised him not to cease performing the office of bishop; but this later turned against him. [Col. 0219C]

## 8.

After these events, Fulk the *vidame*, whom we mentioned above, and Amouris, whom the bishop had released from prison, together with many other leading men of the city, began to hate their bishop. They received letters and messengers from Manasses, who promised them gold, silver, towns, and possessions if they would join him.

They wrote to him asking that he come to meet them at Avesnes in Hainaut. He came, gave them many great gifts, and they received him as lord and bishop and held their lands and fiefs from him. [Col. 0219D]

Then they advised Manasses to go to the archbishop of Reims and place the Church of Cambrai and the whole country under interdict. This was done, to increase the confusion of Bishop Gaucher.

## 9.

At that time Renaud, archbishop of Reims, departed from this world (1096, January 21). Manasses, the uncle of the Manasses about whom we are speaking, then became archbishop. Because he found the Church and the country under interdict, he maintained the interdict. All the enemies of Sir Gaucher were therefore very pleased.

Afterward, however, they did strange things. They did not keep away from the bishop; rather, they drank and ate with him and gave him counsel in his affairs, while behind his back they betrayed him. They did not cease harming the bishop except because of the common people, who greatly loved him since he was gentle and pious and had always loved and sought peace.

The great men hated him because they wished to oppress the poor, while the bishop defended them. [Col. 0220A]

## 10.

At that time great adversities befell the bishop, for he was excommunicated by Rome and by Reims. When the clerics saw the great men of the country attacking their bishop in this way, they too rose against him.

Then the archbishop of Reims sent them letters commanding them to abandon singing and the service of God unless they received Manasses as bishop and rendered him obedience. They immediately ceased.

When Bishop Gaucher heard this, he was greatly astonished. He spoke very gently to his canons and said that he wished to act according to their counsel, as their good father and good friend, provided that they would obey him and resume the singing. They replied with great disdain that they would do nothing of the kind.

Then, so disturbed by anger that they took the holy bodies from the churches, they wished to carry the relics out of the country. As they went away with all the relics, God displayed a great miracle: such an abundance of rain and such violent blasts of wind fell upon them that they could not move.

Then the bishop’s knights and sergeants pursued them. When the clerics saw them, they were greatly frightened, ran away in haste, and abandoned the relics. The sergeants returned them to the churches with great honor. [Col. 0220B]

## 11.

Amid these events the bishop grieved greatly over the adversities that his canons caused him. They assembled in the church of Saint Géry and were there as though in a place of refuge.

The bishop then sent to them very humbly and admonished them three times, very gently, not to follow wicked counsel but to remain in the city, serve God and him as they ought in good faith, and obey him.

They did nothing. Instead, they asked the bishop to grant them permission to leave the city with their bodies and possessions safe. The bishop replied very graciously that he wished them to be secure wherever they might remain. (Cf. *Abbreviatio Cameracensis* 8.)

Then the canons went to Manasses, archbishop of Reims, and said that if he would bless Manasses and consecrate him bishop, they would obey him and abandon Bishop Gaucher. This was done. [Col. 0220C–D]

## 12.

When Manasses had been blessed as bishop, great pain came upon Bishop Gaucher. Nevertheless he was not frightened; rather, he worked harder to exercise himself in good works.

In the midst of these great tribulations he had the castle of Oisy attacked. It was very strongly fortified with walls, towers, and ditches, and within it lived a valiant knight named Gossuin, the bishop’s cousin and liege man.

Because the castle was harmful to his whole country, he did not spare his cousin. He besieged it until he starved it and took it by force. Then, because he desired peace for his people, he had everything demolished and leveled to the ground, but he spared the lives of those whom he found within for God’s sake.

He then besieged another castle named Busignies and took it by force. He besieged another named Boussies and took it also. Afterward he took by force other castles, houses, and dwellings, and everything he saw that harmed his country.

For these deeds the bishop was greatly loved and highly esteemed by great and small alike. Because he kept his subjects so well at peace, he was greatly praised even by those who hated him. [Col. 0220D–0221A]

## 13.

After these events Bishop Gaucher took vengeance on the canons who had gone to Reims to depose him. He took away their prebends and possessions and gave them to the clerics who remained in his church.

Then the bishop had those clerics sing and perform the service of God very devoutly. He himself often visited them and encouraged them to do good, and he increased their temporal goods. Thus he gave them four altars: the altar of Cantaing, that of Riewe, that of Wambais, that of Wethie, and many other fine gifts.

For a short time Bishop Gaucher and his clerics were at peace and in comfort. The canons who had gone to Reims heard of this and saw that they had foolishly abandoned their church, while those who had remained were increasing spiritually and temporally. They therefore bitterly repented that, for Manasses’ sake, they had abandoned the good Bishop Gaucher.

They took counsel that they would come to him and seek mercy—for they knew him to be gentle and pious—and ask him to allow them to return to their church. He did so very graciously and restored their prebends and dignities in full, just as they had possessed them before. He also earnestly begged them to serve God devoutly.

Then they again swore fealty to him. He forgave them all their ill will and loved them for God’s sake, who commands in Scripture that one ought to love one’s enemies. [Col. 0221B–C]

## 14.

Then the canons obeyed their bishop for a short time and served him with feigned love. But a year had not passed before they broke all the fealty they had previously sworn to him, and through the devil’s instigation great discord was sown among them.

The clergy and the entire people rebelled against him. They came before him as though of one mind and said:

“Sir Gaucher, our lord, you are rebellious against the Church of Rome and against that of Reims. We will no longer tolerate this from you. Go at once to seek reconciliation and authority to perform the office of bishop; otherwise never return.”

When the bishop heard this, he was greatly astonished and feared death. He humbly asked them for a delay, for he desired to be out of their hands. By God’s mercy they granted it. (Cf. *Abbreviatio Cameracensis* 8.)

Within three days he went to the emperor of Germany, Henry, recounted everything that had happened, and earnestly begged him to make peace for him in the face of such great injuries. The emperor kept him with him for a long time. [Col. 0221D–0222A]

## 15.

While Bishop Gaucher was there, the clergy and the entire people assembled and received Manasses as bishop, contrary to the rights of the bishopric and of the emperor.

Manasses was received inside the city, conducted himself as bishop, held a synod, performed ordinations, and remained there for three months. He took the benefices from those who belonged to Bishop Gaucher’s party and gave them to his friends.

When this had been done, news came that Bishop Gaucher was returning from court with great princes sent by the emperor. When Manasses heard this, he fled from the city. Bishop Gaucher entered it, together with the emperor’s princes, who had come to discover which people obeyed the bishop and which did not.

The princes, acting on the emperor’s behalf and in the hearing of the whole people, commanded that everyone should obey Bishop Gaucher, and that whoever did not do so would be an enemy of the emperor.

Some of the clerics then departed, while others remained. The bishop asked those who remained for their faith and oath and required them to render him homage. They all did so, clergy and laymen alike, without opposition, in the presence of the emperor’s princes.

But I place little value on such fealty, for afterward they did the exact opposite. [Col. 0222B]

## 16. [Cf. ibid. 9]

At that time Robert, count of Flanders, seeing such great dissension between the clergy and the people, seized the land of Cambresis, although this was contrary to the emperor’s rights. For Manasses, archbishop of Reims, had sent him letters commanding him to destroy Cambrai and crush those who belonged to Bishop Gaucher’s party as though they were pagans.

After reading these letters, Count Robert came into Cambresis with a great army. He plundered the country and carried out great burnings, so that the land was left without laborers and was emptied of oxen, cows, and other livestock. Men and women, great and small, fled and begged throughout various lands.

Then he had a castle fortified to press the city more closely, at a town named Marcoing, on the River Scheldt, two miles from the city. Thus he cut off their access and deprived them of peace, bread, meat, wine, salt, wood, and every other produce of the land.

When the burghers saw that they were in such great tribulation and had no assistance from the emperor, they came to their bishop and said that they could neither defend the city nor resist the count of Flanders unless they received help.

The bishop sent to the emperor, made his complaint with great anguish of heart, and begged him, for God’s sake, for aid. The emperor willingly granted it. He sent the count of Louvain with two hundred knights and the bishop of Liège with three hundred, and sent word that he himself would come and make peace for them with Count Robert.

This was done. The count left the country in peace for a short time, and the knights mentioned above returned to their own lands. [Col. 0222C–D]

## 17.

When they had returned to their own land, the burghers became very afraid. For the city was poor and had few men capable of bearing arms and defending it, and they greatly feared the count’s return.

They once assembled and said: “Why do we suffer such a long death? Let us receive the count as lord and thereby have rest.”

Then they said to Bishop Gaucher [Col. 0223A] that he should allow them to form a commune and swear a mutual conspiracy for his own benefit, since otherwise they could not defend the city or themselves.

When the bishop heard this, he was deeply grieved. Nevertheless, so that the city might have greater assistance, he tolerated it.

Then they swore as follows:

“We, the burghers of Cambrai, all together swear by God and his saints, and promise by our faith, and confirm by charter, that we will faithfully guard Sir Gaucher, our bishop, throughout his life, his honor, and his person, so long as he remains at the court of the emperor Henry, his son, and his successors, according to the judgment of the bishops of the empire.

“And we swear by our Christianity that we will never fail him, and will receive no abbot, monk, cleric, or layman who is against him; and that we will preserve his rights according to the laws and customs of the bishops who preceded him.”

They swore many other things as well. Then they faithfully helped their bishop and defended the country to the best of their ability, for they had great hope in the emperor’s coming. [Col. 0223B]

## 18. [Cf. *Abbreviatio Cameracensis* 9]

Then the emperor Henry came into those regions with a very great army and entered the count’s land by force, so that the count could neither resist him nor ought to have done so, since he was the emperor’s liege man and had, through foolish counsel, undertaken action against him and his empire.

As the emperor rode with his great army, no castle or fortress remained that was not taken by force or fear and demolished. Five were destroyed in this way: the first was Marcoing, the second Paluel, the third Ynchi, [Col. 0223C] the fourth l’Escluse, and the fifth Bouchain.

The castle of l’Escluse was taken by assault and fire, and several of the count’s men were killed there.

The emperor then greatly desired to advance farther into the count’s land, but he could not, because it was a severe winter, with rain, winds, and hail, and the ground was so wet that the great army could not travel over it.

After this victory the emperor returned through Cambrai and greatly encouraged the citizens. Then he went back to his own country and made all the men of the army swear that they would return in the summer against the land of Flanders.

The emperor therefore began making vigorous preparations to return to Flanders, and had many large ships built, for he intended to attack Flanders by sea and by land.

[Col. 0223D] **19.** (Cf. ibid.) But the people of Cambrai, who were in great distress, could not wait for this; for the emperor had left them without aid, and he had wounded the count severely. Therefore the townsmen feared that he might come suddenly and destroy the city—and it nearly happened thus. For the count came by night with a large armed force, entered the city with ease, and set fire to it. The townsmen were so terrified that they did not even take up arms in their defense. Then God performed great miracles through the merits of Saint Géry: for the men of the army themselves drove one another out of the city, and thus they departed, leaving the townsmen in peace. When the townsmen saw this, they gave great thanks to God and to the [Col. 0224A] saint.

After these events the townsmen were not at all secure, and they sent word to Count Robert that he should take pity on them and grant them a truce and respite until the emperor’s arrival; and if the emperor did not return and rescue them, as he had promised, they would hand over the city and lordship to the count, obey him, and become his faithful men. The count willingly agreed to all this, and granted them a truce until the Nativity of Our Lady in September. And so that the matter might be binding, pledges were given by their oaths on both sides.

The count then hoped that within a short time the city would be his, but it did not happen so; for soon afterward he heard that the emperor was returning toward Flanders with a very great force. He therefore feared greatly that he would be disinherited, and asked [Col. 0224B] the leading men of Flanders what he should do. They replied that, since he had undertaken action against the empire and had thereby greatly disturbed the emperor, he should henceforth seek the emperor’s grace and mercy and make amends and satisfaction to him.

The count followed their counsel and went to Liège, where the emperor was with dukes, princes, counts, and bishops. There peace was made amid great rejoicing. The count rendered homage to the emperor, swore fidelity to him and to his realm, and declared publicly that from then onward he would honor Bishop Gauchier of Cambrai, support him against everyone to the best of his ability, and command that all the revenues of the bishopric be given to him.

Then the prisoners who had been captured on the emperor’s side were returned to the emperor, and those belonging to the count were returned to him; [Col. 0224C] the bishop likewise returned those whom he had captured. Thus good peace was established everywhere, and the count promised great aid to the city of Cambrai.

**20.** While Bishop Gauchier was living in great tranquility and was greatly loved by his subjects, his enemies became jealous and rebelled against him. They told him harshly that he was not obedient to the Church of Rheims as he ought to be, and they wished to receive the canons who had gone to Rheims against him. He immediately forbade them to receive any of those men, for they were enemies of the bishopric and of the whole empire.

After issuing this prohibition, the Bishop of Cambrai departed, wishing to test what the people would do. They immediately, almost as if by conspiracy, sent word to the Archbishop of Rheims that he should have the canons return to Cambrai, even though this was against the bishop’s will; and they also asked him to send someone on his authority to absolve the city from the sentence under which it lay [in the ban] (cf. *Abbr. Cam.* 10).

This was done. For the archbishop himself came to Cambrai, together with the Bishop of Laon and the Bishop of Thérouanne, and they assembled the clergy and the people at the entrance to the city. This took place in the year of the Incarnation of Our Lord 1103, on the vigil of Saint Matthew. He then entered the city, reconciled the churches and altars, and caused the clergy and people, by faith and oath, to promise that they would be obedient to the Church of Rheims.

Then he excommunicated Bishop Gauchier and did not regard him [Col. 0225A] as bishop; rather, he hated all those who aided him, and commanded that the priests, deacons, subdeacons, and all the other clergy of the city belonging to Monsieur Gauchier cease singing.

The people and the archbishop then returned to Rheims. Nevertheless, the canons whom he had caused to return to Cambrai remained there, and because of them the laymen were perjured.

**21.** (Cf. ibid. 10.) Meanwhile Bishop Gauchier was at a castle that he had had built, called Estruen. It was his refuge for a long time, and the knights of the country, both free men and peasants, obeyed him as their rightful lord.

When his wicked enemies saw that he was honored by great and small alike, they considered by what means [Col. 0225B] they might drive him from that castle. They took the previously mentioned Godefroi, son of Ansiel, made him their lord, and raised him up as defender of the city. They then granted him the revenues of the bishopric, allowed him to maintain knights in his pay, guard the country, and restrain Bishop Gauchier so that he could not harm them.

Monsieur Hue of Inchy joined himself by oath to this Godefroi in that evil enterprise, rendered him homage, and requested the castellany. Godefroi granted it to him, although he had lost it by judgment during the time of Bishop Gerard II. This grant caused great astonishment throughout the people.

Then Godefroi assembled the entire people of the city, attacked the castle [Col. 0225C] of Estruen, captured it by force, and razed it to the ground. Thus they drove their bishop from his lodging; but the townsmen of the castle in the Cambresis received him with great honor.

For a long time the land of the Cambresis was grievously troubled by this Godefroi. Bishop Gauchier complained to the emperor and to the Count of Flanders, who were very angry and threatened strongly to punish Godefroi. Godefroi repented of what he had undertaken against the empire, accepted the counsel of honorable men, and brought the bishop back to his city, restoring him to honor in his residence.

The clergy and people were greatly displeased by this, but they did not dare oppose it. Then Bishop Gauchier made great efforts to win the love of his subjects, and all the gentleness that a father ought to show to his children he demonstrated to them in his deeds.

**22.** (Ibid. 10.) At that time someone came to Cambrai bearing good news: the Bishop of Soissons had departed from this world, and the pope had appointed Manasses bishop there. The friends of Monsieur Gauchier were therefore greatly rejoiced.

Bishop Gauchier sent to Manasses, Archbishop of Rheims, a very worthy archdeacon named Ansiaux. The bishop humbly begged him for mercy, asking him to take pity on him and forgive his wrongs.

When Archbishop Manasses heard this, he became exceedingly angry. He answered Ansiel cruelly and said: “Because you bring me such news, I excommunicate you; and because you dare speak before me of the son of Antichrist.” [Col. 0226A]

Ansiaux was greatly terrified. He humbly requested absolution and feared that he might never be able to return.

Then the hatred and dispute over the Church of Cambrai were renewed, as they had been at the Council of Clermont. The archbishop then ordered that another bishop be elected at Cambrai in place of Monsieur Gauchier.

For this reason the canons of Cambrai went to Rheims to deliberate, and said to the archbishop: “Good and gentle father, for the love of Jesus Christ, do not compel us to elect another bishop. For ours is an honorable, wise, and discreet man. He loves us as a good father, supports and nurtures us, and through us begs your mercy. If you do not forgive him, it seems to us that this is an injury. For divine law says: ‘Whoever asks for mercy ought to receive mercy.’”

The archbishop did nothing in response to the canons’ request; rather, he replied that he was very pleased to have them in his presence and urged them to elect a bishop immediately.

Then some of them, who had better counsel concerning these oppressions, appealed to Rome. Others, who wished to have the archbishop’s favor, remained there and elected the abbot of Saint Martin of Tournai, named Oedes. He was consecrated on the third day, and those canons swore fealty to him (ibid. 11).

The people were greatly astonished by this. The elected bishop went to Tournai, held ordinations there, and held a synod. Then he went to Inchy and remained there for two years. The people of the surrounding country served and honored him, for, whether rightly or wrongly, he was a bishop. And since the archbishop had blessed him, the people of the country did not dare oppose him.

**23.** Now we shall speak of Monsieur Gauchier, who endured such great adversities with immense patience and did not take revenge, but awaited the justice of Our Lord.

At last, when he saw that he was burdened by such great oppressions, he left the land of the Cambresis and went to the Bishop of Liège, named Obert. Obert received him with great honor, courteously kept him with him for a long time, and loved and honored him greatly.

**24.** (Ibid.) At that time Emperor Henry gave the city [Col. 0226D] of Cambrai to Robert, Count of Flanders, to hold from him for life. Robert did so and received the revenues for as long as the emperor lived.

The count Robert then brought Bishop Oedon into Cambrai and installed him in the palace. But he had no other benefit from the whole bishopric apart from the residence, where he celebrated as bishop.

Afterward Emperor Henry was excommunicated and suffered many adversities by God’s permission. For he was excommunicated, and his son, named Henry, rose against him and took from him, together with the imperial crown, the lance, the scepter, the power, and the glory of the realm.

He was then driven out and rejected by all the princes, and thus died at Liège without a king’s honor (in the year 1106).

After these events Henry, his son, held the empire peacefully. Monsieur Gauchier went to him and complained about Count Robert of Flanders: how he had disturbed the emperor’s realm, seized Cambrai, and installed Oedon there as the elected bishop.

The emperor was exceedingly angry because of Bishop Gauchier’s sufferings and because of the injuries caused by the count and the elected Oedon. He then prepared himself with great force to come to Flanders, and came there with a very large army (in the year 1107). He laid siege to the castle of Douai, which was very strong, with walls and ditches.

The people of Flanders were greatly terrified, and the mercenaries whom the count had stationed to guard Cambrai became very afraid. They abandoned the city and fled.

The count then entered Douai, fortified it, and strengthened all the defenses of the fortifications. He earnestly urged everyone [Col. 0227B] to defend themselves courageously.

On the third day the emperor launched a very great assault. The count defended himself extraordinarily well, so that several knights on the emperor’s side were killed, and they abandoned the assault.

Then all the great princes of the emperor’s army took counsel together. They saw that nothing was being accomplished and that they would not capture the castle, so they told the emperor to receive the Count of Flanders peacefully, and that the count would render him homage and service under oath.

The emperor then received the Count of Flanders as his man. They became good friends, and the emperor gave him the castellany of the city and the town of the castle in the Cambresis only for a term, until he had installed his own bishop at Cambrai who would be [Col. 0227C] in good peace.

**25.** After this the emperor came to Cambrai in a terrifying manner. Before his arrival, however, Oedes fled, together with a large part of the clergy and people who felt themselves guilty.

Many women therefore fled with their children to the churches and towers, and the maidens hid themselves when they saw so many German, Slav, Lotharingian, and Saxon knights.

Then the part of the clergy that was not hostile to Bishop Gauchier received the emperor with great honor. The bishop himself was with the emperor and enjoyed his love and favor, as did all his people; he was also his table companion.

The emperor then had it proclaimed that all the castellans and townsmen should come into his presence. They came deeply frightened, for they feared losing their lives or limbs, yet they did not dare oppose him.

The emperor spoke very harshly to them, severely rebuked them, and said that they had been so audacious as to do many things against the rights of the empire: conspiracies, communes, and new laws. Worse still, they had received a new bishop within the city against God and against the lordship of the empire.

When they heard the emperor speak thus, they were terrified and did not know what they could answer. Since they felt guilty, they humbled themselves deeply and begged the emperor for mercy.

Then the good Bishop Gauchier began very gently to plead for his subjects, fell at the king’s feet, and said: “Most gentle emperor, do not destroy our townsmen so cruelly and with such severity; you can correct them with greater gentleness.”

The princes of the army also pleaded with the bishop and said that the emperor should take pity on so many tears.

When the emperor heard this, he restrained his anger somewhat, accepted the counsel of the bishop and the princes, and did not punish them as severely as he had intended in the rigor of justice.

Nevertheless, he did not spare them entirely. He immediately commanded them to bring before him the charter of the commune that they had made, and they did so. The emperor then annulled it and made them swear before all the princes that they would never make another.

Thus that commune was abolished, and the emperor made them swear fealty to him by faith and oath.

Because he had found them fickle, changeable, and light-hearted, he said that they should give hostages and provide security that they would remain faithful forever.

When the townsmen heard this, they were exceedingly angry but did not dare resist. Instead, they delivered to the emperor as hostages the sons of the leading men of the city.

When the king had received them, he did not put them in prison; rather, he entrusted them to several of his princes and had them carefully guarded in different places.

**26.** After these events the emperor returned to his own country (in the year 1108), and Monsieur Gauchier went with him. He was greatly honored by the emperor and his princes.

Then the canons who had fled [Col. 0228C] because of the emperor’s arrival returned to Cambrai. But the elected bishop Oedes could not enter, for the townsmen barred his entry. He therefore went to his residence at Inchy and remained there (ibid. 11).

**27.** In that year (1110) the emperor intended to go to Rome to speak with Pope Paschal. He therefore sent ahead solemn messengers, honorable and discreet men, who were to present his affairs to the pope. Monsieur Gauchier went with them and was, as it were, their master and leader.

When they came into the pope’s presence, Monsieur Gauchier spoke and presented the emperor’s case very fittingly. The pope therefore loved him greatly, held him in high regard, and considered him a wise man.

After the emperor’s business had been completed, Monsieur Gauchier made his own complaint [Col. 0228D] to the pope. He told him of the great wrongs inflicted upon him by the clergy and the people, and how they had taken the bishopric of Cambrai from him so many times because he upheld justice, aided the poor so that they would not be oppressed by the powerful, humbled the proud, drove out the ravishers, and condemned the robbers.

For these reasons they had inflicted so many persecutions upon him that he had not been at peace for a single day in his bishopric because of the malice of his enemies.

When the pope heard of Monsieur Gauchier’s great sufferings, he took great pity on him (ibid. 11), and would gladly have restored him as bishop; but because the elected Oedon was still alive, he left him in place.

The pope nevertheless granted him great favors. He allowed him to possess in the Church of Cambrai all the benefices he had ever held, and gave him certain new benefices, so that he became canon, sacristan, and archdeacon of Brabant. The pope confirmed him in these by charters and by his seal.

And so that he would not fear losing these dignities, the pope kissed him as a sign of love and sent word to the Archbishop of Rheims by his own letters that he should restore him to his former dignities. This was done in the year 1104.

**[(WATERLOS.) 28.]** The following year, Gervais, son of Huon, Count of Rethel, seized the Church of Rheims and wished to become archbishop against the wishes of some of the clergy. For Archbishop Manasses, of whom we spoke above, had abandoned his pastoral staff and become a canon regular at the Abbey of Saint Denis in Rheims [Col. 0229B], and there he departed from this world.

The following year Pope Paschal came to Troyes and held a great council there. He condemned Gervais, declaring that he was not worthy to be archbishop, and confirmed a man named Raoul.

—Two years later Emperor Henry took as his wife the daughter of King Henry of England, named Matilda; she was only eight years old.

—A star appeared in the month of June, called a comet, and cast its rays toward the south.

—Baudouin, son of Robert, Count of Flanders, took as his wife the daughter of Alain, Count of Brittany.

—Robert, count and son of Robert, Count of Cassel, died and was buried at Arras in the church of Saint Vaast. His son Baudouin became count after him.]

**29.** In that year (1111) Emperor Henry went to [Col. 0229C] Rome and led a great army with great prudence and foresight. Although he had sworn fealty to Pope Paschal and to the Romans, he nevertheless entered Rome secretly and seized the pope by force in Saint Peter’s Church, together with the cardinals and certain bishops, for he attacked them treacherously and found them unprepared.

When the Romans heard this, they began to fight the emperor with great force, and many were killed on both sides. At last the Romans drove him out of the city by force. Nevertheless, he took the captive pope with him and kept him under fairly strict guard throughout an entire Lent.

Then, on the second Sunday after Easter, good peace and concord were established between the pope and the emperor. The emperor fell at the pope’s feet and humbly begged absolution for his sins, and the pope absolved him.

He then came to Saint Peter’s Church, where the pope crowned him with the imperial crown amid great rejoicing. This was done in the year of grace 1111.

Afterward the pope granted the emperor the power to give the pastoral staffs to all elected bishops in his country and in his empire, and, so that this might be binding, confirmed it by privileges.

Then the pope told the emperor that he wished him to receive the elected Oedon as his man—an upright and honorable man—and to love and cherish him, because he had confirmed him as bishop.

The emperor was very glad when he saw that the pope was asking this of him, and greatly desired to fulfill his request (cf. *Abbr. Cam.* 11).

The emperor then returned to his country. Soon afterward he gave Oedon the bishopric and lordships of Cambrai. Oedon swore fealty to him, and the emperor then sent him to Cambrai with solemn messengers. Thus he was received with great reverence.

**30.** (Ibid.) When the bishops of the empire, the abbots, the religious, and all the orders of the clergy heard that the pope had granted the emperor such a concession, they were deeply grieved, for it seemed to them plainly to be against God.

Some of the bishops therefore went quickly to the pope, spoke to him very harshly, and sharply reproached him for making such a peace with the emperor and such an evil agreement out of fear for his body. They said that such an agreement ought not to be kept.

Thus that pact was annulled. In the pope’s presence the good bishops tore up the privilege and called it a “perverse privilege.” They then urged the pope so strongly that the emperor was excommunicated by the whole Holy Church.

It consequently became necessary for the pope to depose all the bishops who had received their pastoral staffs from the emperor in such a temporal manner. Thus Bishop Oedes was removed from the bishopric.

**31.** Afterward the canons assembled to elect a bishop. They all remembered the sufferings, pains, labors, and damages they had endured because of the disputes over their election. It therefore seemed to them that they could have peace only if they recalled Monsieur Gauchier.

Everyone agreed to this. They then brought the pastoral staff to the emperor, and the emperor willingly consented.

At that time Monsieur Gauchier was living in the city of Tournai, where he lived very honorably. The emperor sent word to him to come to him and receive the lordship of Cambrai from him.

But Monsieur Gauchier refused, because he knew that there was great discord between the pope and the emperor. He feared angering the pope and losing his favor. He also felt himself weak and old, so that no one could induce him to become bishop again.

After these events Monsieur Gauchier lived for a short while. But God took vengeance upon his enemies, for they all died before he did.

He therefore gave thanks to God and said: “Praised be God for what he has done to me. Now I willingly wish to die, since God has avenged me upon my enemies.”

Then he received good counsel and went to Saint Nicholas of the Wood, where he became a monk. He lived there very piously, performed great penance, and thus departed from this world.
