—[(WATERL.) At that time Gaudri, Bishop of Laon, was killed by the townsmen of his city.]

**32.** Now we shall tell how Bishop Oedes was elected during the discord mentioned above.

At the time when Pope Paschal made Manasses Bishop of Soissons—he had previously been elected Bishop of Cambrai in a disputed election but could not enter the city—the Archbishop of Rheims, Manasses, who was his uncle, had removed Monsieur Gauchier in order to make his cousin bishop, but he could not bring this to completion [Col. 0231A].

When the canons of Cambrai learned that Manasses was Bishop of Soissons, they went to Rheims and wished to receive Monsieur Gauchier as bishop, as their good elected candidate. But Archbishop Manasses, because of the hatred he bore him, opposed them and commanded them, under obedience and threat of excommunication, to elect another.

They did nothing, however, but appealed to Rome (cf. *Abbr. Cam.* 10).

They then returned to Cambrai. Some of the canons who remained renounced Monsieur Gauchier and elected Oedon, abbot of Saint Martin of Tournai (ibid. 11). The archbishop consecrated him, but he was not then received at Cambrai. Instead, he went to Tournai and remained in the Church of Saint Martin for two years.

Afterward Count Robert of Flanders came to him and, on the advice of certain members of the clergy, brought him to Cambrai. Oedon lived from his own resources and not from the goods of the bishopric.

This Oedes was a very learned man, a master of great knowledge, patient, gentle, humble toward all, and full of holy habits. He greatly honored the clergy and all religious orders. He attended the Holy Church day and night, like another canon. He greatly increased its temporal possessions and fed his subjects with holy teachings.

In the end great troubles came upon him. Because he had received the lordship of Cambrai from the excommunicated emperor—even though he had done so simply and without malice—the pope regarded it as a grave offense and was greatly angered, because of the discord between himself and the emperor.

For this reason the pope sent him letters [Col. 0231C] commanding him to cease governing the bishopric and forbidding him all the rights that a bishop ought to exercise.

The good man was very ill and close to death when the pope’s sentence reached him. He obeyed God and the pope very gently, died in holy obedience, and was buried in the Church of Anchin.

This was in the year of grace 1113 (June 19).

—[WATERL. In that year, in the month of May, soil and certain trees were burned by fire that came from the sky; they bore no fruit, and certain forests dried up.]

—The following year, King Baldwin of Jerusalem, brother of Godfrey of Bouillon, took as his wife the widow of Duke Roger of Sicily.

—In that year the Bishop of Arras, Lambert, died.]

[Col. 0231D] **33.** (Cf. *Abbr. Cam.* 12.) After Bishop Oedon, Monsieur Bouchard was elected bishop by the common consent of the clergy, in the year of grace 1114.

He was a simple, discreet, honorable man and a very devout priest. At that time Paschal was pope in Rome and Henry IV was emperor, and the emperor willingly consented to this election.

At that time there was great discord between the pope and the emperor. The pope excommunicated the emperor and all his actions; and if any bishop was elected within the empire and received his regalia and pastoral staff from the emperor, the pope forbade his consecration and blessing.

For this reason, although Monsieur Bouchard had been elected at Cambrai and received by the emperor and the land of the Cambresis [Col. 0232A], and although they had sworn fealty to him, he nevertheless waited two years. He hesitated to seek confirmation from the pope and consecration from the Archbishop of Rheims.

Meanwhile he devoted himself to prayers and vigils and exercised himself greatly in good works, so that by his great humility he gained the favor of the clergy and people.

His reputation for virtuous conduct spread far and wide and reached Raoul, Archbishop of Rheims, who held him in very high regard. Raoul summoned him, received him with great reverence, wrote his letters for him, and sent him to Pope Paschal with great hope of obtaining what he sought.

When the pope heard the archbishop’s great testimony, he received Monsieur Bouchard very graciously, showed him great favor, and willingly confirmed him. [Col. 0232B] He then sent him back to the archbishop for blessing, and the archbishop consecrated him at Rheims with great reverence in the month of July.

Bouchard returned to Cambrai and was received with great joy. The archbishop himself placed him in the episcopal chair with great honor.

After he had been fully confirmed, he preached a very devout sermon to the canons and his clergy. He gently urged them to serve God with a true heart, to preserve well the state of Holy Church, to follow the deeds of the honorable men who had preceded them, and he spoke many other words of good exhortation.

Then he spoke and said:

“I return to you all the rights that you ought to possess in Holy Church. I graciously grant you all the good customs that the clergy ought anciently to have, [Col. 0232C] and I confirm them, so that they may be guarded under penalty of excommunication. I promise to treat you gently and love you as a good father, and to increase the goods of Holy Church to the best of my ability.”

Then he went to the palace as bishop and found it so stripped of everything that he had nothing with which to live: neither clergy, nor knights, nor household. It was scarcely fit for a bishop.

He therefore set himself with great force to recover the possessions of the bishopric and gather together what had been scattered, restore what had been taken away, and redeem what had been sold.

For the bishops before him, through frivolity or necessity, had given away or pledged towns, woods, waters, arable lands, and many other possessions. The inhabitants and knights of the Cambresis held them unlawfully. With God’s help, the good bishop recovered them for the bishopric, together with the mills and tolls.

**34.** (Cf. ibid.) Afterward the good bishop made great efforts to regain the castellany of Cambrai and the castle in the Cambresis.

For Emperor Henry III had formerly given Robert II, Count of Flanders, the castellany of Cambrai and the grant of the castle in the Cambresis, on the condition that the count diligently guard and loyally support the bishops whenever the emperor sent them to Cambrai, and that he faithfully guard the part of the kingdom belonging to the emperor’s empire.

Thus Count Robert held the castle in the Cambresis in his hands for a long time [Col. 0233A]. Huon of Oisy, son of the castellan Huon, received the castellany from the count, rendered him homage, and swore to him that he would remain faithful.

For the reasons stated above, the count came often to Cambrai and aided them in their needs.

After a short time the count went to a tournament at Meaux and was killed there among the knights.

After him his son Baudouin became Count of Flanders. He held the land as his father had held it, and therefore wished to retain the castle in the Cambresis. The aforementioned Huon received the castellany from him, swore fealty, and rendered him homage.

Because these arrangements had been made against God and against the Church of Our Lady of Cambrai, Bishop Bouchard excommunicated Count Baudouin. Every day he had a great complaint and proclamation made, with the bell ringing, before the Body of the Lord, because of the count’s injury.

After a short time the aforementioned count went to Normandy with a very large army. He was grievously wounded in the head in battle, so that he could never be cured.

But God, who is merciful, granted him enough life for him to feel great repentance and make his confession humbly.

When Bishop Bouchard heard that no one hoped for the count’s life, he sent messengers to him and humbly begged him to return to his Church the castle in the Cambresis and the castellany of Cambrai, and, for the absolution and remission of his sins, not to allow the man who would become count after him to hold them wrongfully.

When the count heard this, he received the bishop’s [Col. 0233C] messengers very graciously. He was deeply contrite and repentant from a true heart, and, through fear of God and of the Judgment, declared that the bishop was quit of both possessions. Thus he returned to him the castle and the castellany.

The bishop then absolved him very devoutly, and so the count departed from this world in true penitence and perfect devotion, in the year of grace 1118.

**35.** After Count Baudouin, one of his cousins became Count of Flanders. His name was Charles, son of the King of Denmark, a powerful and very wise man.

He wished to hold the whole land as those before him had held it. Therefore he revoked the grant that Count Baudouin had made at his death to Bishop Bouchard of the castellany of Cambrai. He summoned Huon of Oisy, returned the castellany to him, and Huon received it from him as a fief, rendering him homage and swearing fealty.

The bishop was deeply distressed by this. He came to Count Charles with great humility, made every effort to obtain his favor, and devoutly asked through his friends that the count might be willing to return the castellany to him.

But the count would not listen to this. Nevertheless, at the entreaty of his friends, and in return for 200 marks that the bishop gave him, he returned the castle in the Cambresis to the bishop, on the condition that the count should have a residence there just as the bishop did, and that it should serve as his refuge whenever he wished.

36. After these events, the bishop sought counsel from his friends about what he could do regarding the castellany [Col. 0234A] that had thus been taken from him. They advised him to admonish the castellan Hugh to receive and hold the castellany from him, as his predecessors had held it from the bishops of Cambrai. But Hugh refused this; and the bishop immediately excommunicated him and placed all his land under interdict. The castellan was therefore deeply angered and hated the bishop with mortal hatred. (Abbr. Cam. 12.)

Then the castellan had a castle fortified at Crèvecoeur, for he desired to destroy the bishop and his city. He entered the castle with many knights and a multitude of his men, and thus pillaged the countryside, burned towns, seized agricultural laborers, killed many people, and took food from those carrying it to the city—grain, wine, meat, fish, firewood, and other produce. Thus for a long time he inflicted upon the bishop all the evils he could. When the bishop saw this, he could endure no more. He quickly assembled knights and great numbers of armed men and marched with great force against Oisy, because the castellan trusted that place most. They captured the town outside its fortification and set everything ablaze. Then they burned the towns and ravaged the surrounding country.

The next day they went with great strength to Crèvecoeur, attacked the town very fiercely, and captured it; it was burned as far as the castle. When the castellan saw this, he acknowledged his guilt and said that he was rightly suffering so much because he had made war upon his rightful lord and had done such great harm to Holy Church and to the poor. He then repented bitterly, sent messengers to the bishop, and pleaded very humbly. He offered to do homage and swear good faith, if he could obtain this from his lord, Count Charles. When the bishop heard this, he was greatly rejoiced, for he desired peace. (Ib. 12.)

The bishop then absolved the castellan on condition that he restore the castle of Crèvecoeur in the form and manner in which the town had formerly stood, and that from then on he rebuild no castle there without the consent of the bishop and the burghers of Cambrai. Hugh then swore fealty to him, and thus they became good friends together.

37. (Abbr. Cam. 13.) At that time there was in Cambrai a burgher named Wirembauz, of honorable lineage and filled with good morals. He was greatly loved by the whole city. He married the daughter of a worthy man, and they lived together for a long time [Col. 0234D] in very loyal marriage. They had children, whom they raised in the fear of God. The children were worthy and very lovable.

This worthy man and his wife often heard the word of God. They desired to abandon the world for the love of God, and vowed chastity into the hands of Bishop Bouchard. Thus they separated from their marriage in order to serve God more devoutly. The father then placed two of his sons in the abbey of Saint Aubert and gave them beautiful gifts; he placed the third son in the abbey of Saint Sepulchre and gave it great possessions. He sent his daughter to Reims, where he gave twelve gold bezants and several other gifts. Thus Wirembauz, his wife, and his children having been placed in abbeys, he devoted himself energetically to works of mercy.

At that time there was at Cambrai, at the gate of Selles beside the castle, a cruel, wicked, and narrow passage. A knight named Sir Foucars held it from the bishop as a fief. The passage was so oppressive that no one could pass there unless he paid a great deal of money. You would often have seen the poor weeping there; for if they did not have the money ready, the servants of the passage, who were extremely vicious, took from them their cloak or mantle, their tunic, the *bresce* [probably a market basket] that they were taking to market, or other pledges. (Cf. ib.)

When the good Wirembauz saw the tears, grief, and anguish endured there by the poor, he gave so much of his wealth to the bishop and to the knight mentioned above that he redeemed the passage and made it free forever. Bishop Bouchard confirmed this by privilege, and the burgher gave a large part of his inheritance there to build the bridges.

Then Wirembauz turned his attention to the hospital of the poor of Saint Julian, beside the church of Sainte-Croix, for the goods of that house had been brought to ruin through bad administration. The worthy man gave so much of his property there that he restored the house to good condition. He had great buildings constructed and several beds made for the poor to sleep in. He himself ministered there to the sick for a long time with great devotion, lived a holy life, and thus departed from this world.

38. At that time the good Bishop Bouchard was living in great tranquility, and his land was at peace. But shortly afterward a knight named Gerard rebelled against him and cruelly ravaged the Cambresis. He burned towns and houses as far as the castle in the Cambresis, destroying and leveling everything. The knights of Ostrevant also came frequently and ravaged the Cambresis.

The bishop and his people were therefore greatly dismayed. Since they could not resist their enemies, they asked Count Charles of Flanders to accept the lordship of Cambrai and to defend them against their enemies. He did so, and Emperor Henry also consented and granted it to him. Cambrai rejoiced greatly over this matter.

The count came to Cambrai many times, took great vengeance upon his enemies, and kept them firmly at peace. This was in the year of grace 1122.

[(WATERL.) After a short time great troubles occurred at Cambrai. Count Charles, through whom such great peace had come to the country, was killed at Bruges in the church of Saint Donatian during Lent, on the sixth Nones of March, together with two of his princes.]

His own men killed him while he was praying before the altar, hearing Mass, and making an offering into the priest’s hand. This occurred in the year 1127. (Abbr. Cam. 13.)

When reliable news of the count’s death arrived, the castellan Hugh mentioned above came to Bishop Bouchard. He acknowledged that the bishop was his liege lord and received from him, as was right, the castellany of Cambrai. He did homage and swore fealty to him, swore to keep good peace, and gave hostages.

[39. (WATERL.) After this Bishop Bouchard lived for a long time, devoting himself greatly to good works, and departed from this world on the third Nones of January in the year of grace 1130. At that time the fiery illness that comes from God was very severe at Chartres, Paris, Soissons, Cambrai, Arras, and many other places. But through the power of the glorious Virgin Mary and her gentle prayer it was wonderfully extinguished. Emperor Henry died; then Lothaire, duke of the Saxons, a wise man, was elected. In the town of Aalst Count William was killed, a man brave in arms but not brave in good morals. After him Thierry, son of the duke of Alsace and cousin of Count Robert, became count. Philip, son of King Louis of France, was consecrated at Reims on Easter Day in the presence of his father and mother. The city of Cambrai was burned on the eleventh day before the Kalends of August [Col. 0236B], and the city of Arras was likewise burned on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of October. That year there was a great mortality among beasts. Pope Innocent came to Cambrai and sang Mass in the church of Saint Aubert on the Monday after the second Sunday of Lent. Count Fulk of Anjou became king of Jerusalem. The church of Saint Richarius in Ponthieu was burned, together with all the castles and many people.]

40. (Cf. Abbr. Cam. 14.) After the death of Bishop Bouchard, Pope Innocent came to Cambrai with many cardinals and many bishops of France. Then he went to the German emperor Lothaire, who was a very noble man, brave in arms, and a great respecter of God.

The pope then convened a council at Liège in the emperor’s presence (in March 1131), and the emperor received the pope with the greatest reverence. [Col. 0236C] There peace and concord were established between Holy Church and the Empire, and many other holy matters were arranged there.

The emperor then announced to the pope that Cambrai had no bishop, and asked him to give the bishopric to one of his clerks named Liethard. When the pope heard this, he was afraid to do so, for he did not know whether Liethard was worthy of such an honor. Nevertheless, he agreed to the emperor’s request, and thus Liethard was elected bishop of Cambrai. The archbishop of Reims consecrated him on the sixth day before the Kalends of May in the year of grace 1131.

Once he had become bishop, he did not conduct himself as holily or honorably as was fitting for a bishop. He did not love his subjects as he ought, nor did he attract them through gentle affection; rather, he drove them away from him with harsh words. Avarice was so deeply rooted in his heart that he could endure neither company nor a noble household around him.

Afterward he was so overcome by avarice that he left the episcopal residence and went to Saint Géry. He remained there in the house of a minor canon and demanded no service from his household. When the clergy and people saw this, they were greatly distressed that the bishop lived so dishonorably, and by force brought it about that the bishop returned to his own residence.

Shortly afterward, in his great anger, he abandoned his palace and went to live at Saint Aubert. He ordered that none of his household should go with him, and for these things he was greatly hated.

41. (Cf. Abbr. Cam. 14.) At that time there was a very powerful man in the Cambresis named Gerard Maufillastres. He inflicted many evils upon the bishop and rebelled against him. He seized the bishop’s men, imprisoned them, and took away their possessions.

When the bishop saw this, he was greatly angered and demanded that Gerard return his men. But Gerard did nothing about it; instead, he asked the bishop for a truce so that he could speak with him face to face. The bishop, on bad advice, refused him.

Gerard then became utterly enraged. He quickly assembled many knights, a great force of armed men, and foot soldiers, attacked the castle in the Cambresis, and captured it by fire and force. More than a hundred people, men and women, were burned there; the town was burned, as were five churches and the relics of certain saints. In one church a priest was burned. [Col. 0237B]

Then the men of the army seized and plundered the entire town—its silver, clothing, and whatever else they could take. Afterward Gerard held the castle in his possession for a long time, together with its dependencies and all the surrounding country.

The people of the bishopric were greatly troubled by these events. They said that all these evils had occurred because of the bishop, since he had refused to grant Gerard a truce.

42. (Cf. ib.) At that time there was a powerful man named Simon, son of Hugh, the castellan of Oisy. He took great pity on what Gerard was doing to Bishop Liethard and on the fact that no one was taking vengeance for it.

He then assembled a great army, took with him the men of Cambrai, marched against Gerard, ravaged his land, and set everything [Col. 0237C] to fire and flame. Gerard was thereby reduced to such poverty and humiliation that he asked Simon for peace and friendship.

Then the castellan Hugh and the commune of Cambrai took counsel together and granted him peace. When the bishop learned this, he strongly opposed it. He said that Gerard and all his men would never be released from excommunication until Gerard had restored the churches he had burned, had returned ten thousand marks, had made satisfaction for the hundred people and the priest who had perished in the fire, had humbly come to seek mercy, and had accepted their penance.

When the burghers heard this, they despised him and refused to do anything. The bishop replied that he would therefore allow himself to be driven forever from his bishopric rather than fail to obtain amendment to the honor of God and Holy Church. [Col. 0237D]

When they heard this, they promised him a large sum of money by fraud and deceit, as later became apparent; for he received not a penny. The count of Hainaut and all his men who had taken part in burning the castle swore to observe the agreements.

The bishop then absolved the count and all his men on condition that the knights would give five sous and the foot soldiers two sous. The bishop imposed a great penance upon them, but they did not perform it and did not pay the money; thus they all became perjurers.

The bishop was then greatly hated by his citizens and by those outside the city. Afterward he was attacked from every side, and his enemies were so determined that he should not remain bishop for long.

43. (Cf. ib. 15.) At that time he was summoned to Reims. The provost of the court and several canons went there after him. They gravely defamed him before the archbishop, saying that he sold prebends and took money for blessing churches. They also accused him of avarice and other vices and said every evil they could against him.

When the archbishop heard this, he took Bishop Liethard aside and spoke secretly to him in the presence and testimony of five bishops. He said to him very earnestly:

“Now hear, dear and gentle father, what great evils and faults your adversaries openly bring against you and condemn in your life. Therefore, for God’s sake, I ask you to acknowledge your guilt, for you cannot live long in peace with such people.”

The bishop then acknowledged his guilt before the archbishop and agreed to leave the bishopric. He humbly asked the archbishop to grant him permission to receive the revenues of the bishopric until the Epiphany. The archbishop willingly granted this, on condition that he not remain in the bishopric after the day mentioned above.

This matter was kept so secret that no one knew it except the five bishops. The bishop then returned to his country and quickly went to the emperor, hoping that through him he might be restored to his bishopric.

The provost and certain burghers of the city followed him. Before the emperor they accused him of many things, including that he intended to disinherit his men. The bishop replied very vigorously and complained to the emperor that the people of Cambrai had treated him shamefully and taken away his revenues.

When the princes of the court heard this, they feared that their subjects might treat them in the same way. They urged the emperor to confirm by privilege that no one should serve in his lord’s court against the will of that lord himself. The emperor willingly did so.

The provost of Cambrai was therefore deeply troubled, for he had wished to serve his lord against his will. The people of Cambrai then returned to their country very sadly because of this privilege and concealed themselves as much as they could.

It happened that, as they were riding between Haspré and [Col. 0238D] Cambrai, because of their sins, Gerard Maufillastres captured them by chance and held them in harsh imprisonment. Before releasing them, he took from them eleven twenty-mark sums of silver. The people of Cambrai were greatly angered by this and said that they had suffered this misfortune because of their bishop.

The bishop then returned to Cambrai very joyfully because of the privilege concerning the provostry, which had been placed at his disposal. After this the bishop excommunicated all those who had seized his burghers and those who had given counsel in it.

Then he sang Mass and cursed those who would act against the privilege of the provostry, in the year *** (1135).

## ANDREAN CONTINUATION

[Note: [Col. 0239] Manuscript 3 inserts this continuation in the middle of Book III, 49, of the *Gesta*, beginning only a new line with continuous pen and ink, without a title.]

[Col. 0239]

[Col. 0239A] After this Gerard, who restored the monks to this church [Note: [Col. 0239B] Saint Andrew of the Castle of Cambrai; compare the Chronicle of Saint Andrew immediately following, I, 20; II, 9.], as they had been before, and appointed his brother Eilbert as abbot, Lord Lietbert, a man wholly distinguished for holiness, succeeded to the episcopate; after him came another Gerard; after him Manasses, a cleric of the church of Soissons; after him Walcher, a canon of the church of Tournai; after him Odo; after him Burgard; after him Lietard; after him Lord Nicholas, brother of Goswin of Monts, who died at Val-Celles in the year of the Lord 1167. He was honorably transferred to Cambrai for burial and was buried in the vestibule of the church of Blessed Mary, before the altar of Saint John the Baptist.

Peter, son of Thierry, Count of Flanders, succeeded Lord Nicholas and ruled the church for four years. But afterward, since he was young, he laid aside the clerical state and renounced his election as bishop; having taken a wife, he became count.

[Col. 0240A] [lacuna: half a line left blank in the manuscript; Note: [Col. 0239].]

Robert, who was called provost of Aria, succeeded him in the episcopate of the church of Cambrai. He governed the church while awaiting election for five months and, as is reported, was killed at Condé between two bridges by the associates of James. He was transferred for burial to Aria.

Robert was succeeded by Alard, archdeacon of the same church. He ruled the church for a year and a half and died full of days. Roger, brother of Hellin of Wanrigavo, succeeded him, a man adorned with every good and honorable quality.

In the year of the Lord 1179 he took part in the Roman council convened by Pope Alexander, and there he was consecrated bishop by William, archbishop of Reims and legate of the Apostolic See, in the church of Saint Sabina.

## APPENDIX

[Col. 0239]

### CHRONICLE OF SAINT ANDREW OF THE CASTLE OF CAMBRAI, EDITED BY THE DISTINGUISHED SCHOLAR LUDWIG BETHMANN, PH.D.

(From Pertz, *Monumenta Germaniae historica*, Scriptores, vol. VII, p. 526.)

### NOTICE

The author of the following Chronicle was a monk of Saint Andrew in the Castle of Cambrai, and was the companion and adviser of Bishop Walcher at the Council of Clermont in 1095 [Note: [Col. 0239B] III, 19.]. At Saint Andrew’s in 1133 he wrote a history of his monastery and especially of the Cambrai region [Note: [Col. 0239B] III, 42.], in three books. Of these, he took the first and second almost word for word from the *Deeds of Lietbert*, from the *Life of Lietbert* by Rodulf, and from now-lost annals [Note: [Col. 0240B] I, 5, 6, 8, 21; II, 8, 9, 15, 16, 30.]. He adds little of his own, but among these additions are some matters of the greatest value for knowledge [Note: [Col. 0240B] Such as the account of the emperor’s expedition into Flanders in 1054; II, 18 ff.]. Beginning with 1076, the third book relates events that the author partly saw and heard in his own time [Note: [Col. 0240B] III, prologue.]; except in very few matters, he follows his own observations.

This highly useful book remained entirely unknown down to very recent times. In 1787 Dom Bevenot, then a monk of Saint Andrew and later dean of Melbode, found in the Maricolan archive the unique manuscript, undoubtedly an autograph, that had formerly belonged to Saint Andrew. He published fragments from it in the *Acta Sanctorum Belgii* V, 193. The manuscript afterward disappeared, and until now it has not been possible to discover where it went. But in 1787 Dom Bevenot had accurately transcribed it, and he entrusted this copy to the distinguished physician Le Glay for further transcription.

Le Glay was the first, after Balderic, p. 353, to publish it, in 1834, though he published only the third book. In 1841, when we ourselves visited Lille, this highly esteemed man, with the kindness for which he is distinguished, allowed us to publish the first two books; indeed, he graciously offered them himself, so that now the complete work appears for the first time. We hope it will prove useful for history, while we wish it to remain a memorial of our always grateful feelings toward Le Glay.

**L. C. Bethmann**

## BOOK ONE

[Col. 0241]

### 1. On the condition of the church and the imperial power of the city of Rome

While Gregory V was laudably presiding over the holy and apostolic Roman See—the seventy-fourth after Saint Gregory the Theologian—in the year of Christ 1001, [(V. Lietb. 1)] the younger Otto was vigorously governing the imperial throne of Roman power by military strength.

Since he could not satisfy with gifts and benefits the gluttony of the Romans, which has always been and remains insatiable [Note: [Col. 0241] “salutare,” according to the Pia copy.], their madness became so inflamed that the emperor was driven from the city of Rome, not without the death of his men. Taking his expulsion grievously, he gathered the imperial forces of soldiers to avenge his injuries, but died before accomplishing this. Amid the mourning and grief of his people, he was buried with royal honors in the church at Aachen.

After this Henry, son of Henry, duke of Bavaria, by the will and providence of God, was clothed with royal purple and adorned with the imperial arms through the counsel of the Lotharingians. How prudently, bravely, peacefully, and catholicly he governed his empire is shown by the inscription of his name, by which he is called not only Augustus and Emperor, but also Orthodox and Peaceful.]

### 2. On the archbishop of Reims and the bishop of Cambrai

(Cf. *Deeds of the Bishops of Cambrai* I, 112.)

At approximately this time, after Albero, a man of venerable life, Arnulf, the twenty-first after Saint Remigius, held the archbishopric of Reims. Erluin, the twenty-ninth after Saint Vedast—who, appointed by Saint Remigius, had been bishop of the city of Arras and of Cambrai—held the church of Cambrai.

When Erluin learned from the frequent complaints of people crying out to him from various places that all Cambrai, and especially this neighboring region, was being grievously disturbed by the attacks of certain plunderers who frequently burst forth from the nearby forest called Arida Gamantia and from the neighboring castles—for by day and night they invaded villages and houses, stripped everything, and even carried off the men themselves in chains—he conceived, through the energetic ingenuity of a manly spirit, the excellent plan of preparing some obstacle against them: namely, something that would be a secure protection and certain refuge for the inhabitants and an impregnable defense against the enemy’s ambushes.

### 3. Who built the New Castle, and why and when

Therefore, after searching for a suitable place for a long time, he finally chose this little village which at that time lay around the church of the martyr Saint Quentin and had long borne the name Perona. There the river [Note: [Col. 0241D] The Savus, that is, the Selle.] flowing beneath it forms a kind of boundary dividing the lands of Cambrai and Hainaut.

He summoned a considerable number of people living nearby and far away, built a strong though wooden fortification, and surrounded it with a firm rampart. Then, having prepared the soldiers who were necessary and placing there, as circumstances required, detachments of cavalry and infantry, he set aside the old name and called it the New Castle.

Thus, both then and afterward for as long as he lived, once the plunderers had been subdued, firm peace came to the whole Cambrai settlement.

### 4. On the ordination of Bishop Erluin

Many remarkable deeds of this bishop could be recalled, but since the discourse, directed toward another purpose, hastens to its conclusion, there is no opportunity to linger over them. This one point, however, must be briefly inserted: educated in both ecclesiastical and secular affairs, he had first been archdeacon of Liège; afterward, elevated by the gift of the bishop of Cambrai, he was ordained bishop at Rome by the aforementioned Pope Gregory together with Emperor Otto.

This occurred because at that time a grave dispute was agitating the church of Reims. Arnulf had been deposed from the episcopal see on account of certain evil accusations, and a certain scholar Gerbert had been unjustly substituted in his place. After the bishops of the Reims province had long debated this matter among themselves, it finally came to this: since the aforesaid Arnulf had been degraded without the knowledge and authority of the lord pope, he should again be restored to the episcopal see by judicial sentence. And this was done.]

### 5. On the succession of the apostolic pontiffs

After the aforementioned Pope Gregory had governed the church for one year and five months, he ended his life, and John succeeded him. After sitting for ten months, John too ended his life shamefully.

Then Gerbert, also called Sylvester, whom we mentioned above, was appointed in his place. When he departed with Emperor Otto after Otto had been expelled from Rome, he accompanied him to Ravenna. He was more than sufficiently educated in the disciplines of the liberal arts and so skilled in geometry that, by sight alone, he could easily measure the dimensions of places, whether on land or in the air.

This is clearly evident from some of his short works and letters. In one of them, concerning Macrobius’s commentary, addressed to his teacher Alcuin, he discussed with probability the method and magnitude of every sphere and its diameter, cubes, solidity, area, and arithmetical arguments.

He therefore governed the church for four years, one month, and nineteen days. Feeling that death was near, he is said to have addressed himself in this verse:

“Neither the counting-board nor mathematics will help you, Gerbert.”

Enough has been said about him.

### 6. On the death of Bishop Herluin

In the year of Christ 1002, when Otto died, as we described more fully in the first chapter, Henry obtained the summit of imperial power. After Sylvester, John Sicco took charge of the church. He too died after five months and twenty-five days.

Then John Fanassus held office for one year and ended his life. The monastery of Saint Gengulf was consecrated. After John, Sergius, who is called Osporci, held office for three years. Then Benedict held it for eleven years, ten months, and twenty-one days.

In his sixth year [(ibid. I, 118)] Lord Bishop Erluin, after many labors and after the frequent tribulations he had endured from Walter, the castellan hateful to God, son of Walter, a viperous root, was finally struck by illness. Lying in bed, he awaited with close attention the time and hour of his approaching dissolution and departure.

Meanwhile the aforesaid tyrant did not cease from the frenzy of his wickedness. Hearing that the bishop was ill unto death, he became joyful and more savage than usual. He broke into the houses of the clerics and plundered whatever pleased him. He even burst into the stables, seized the bishop’s horses, and carried them away.

He added a still more execrable crime. After the bishop’s body had been carried into the church of Saint Mary, while the clerics and chaplains were performing the funeral rites according to custom, he, driven by a new kind of impulse to robbery, attacked them with drawn swords and pursued them as they fled to the altar. Thus the body remained unburied until Richard, abbot of Arras, arrived and buried it in the church of Saint Aubert on the northern side.

What tongue, however eloquent an orator’s, could express, or what pen, however swift a scribe’s, could enumerate, how many evils this Walter, his father Walter [Note: [Col. 0243] “cujus,” according to the copy.], and his nephew Hugh inflicted upon the four bishops who succeeded one another—namely, Erluin, Gerard, Lietbert, and Gerard? But let what has been said about them suffice. Whoever wishes to know more fully will be able to find it in their deeds. We, pursuing brevity, turn to set forth other matters.

### 7. On Lord Bishop Gerard

[(V. Lietb. 2.)] Thus Emperor Henry, whom we said above had succeeded Otto, hearing that Bishop Herluin had died, readily and willingly followed the advice of his men concerning the election of Gerard to the bishopric of Cambrai. Gerard was his chaplain and was born of Lotharingian and Carolingian parents. He obtained the episcopal blessing on the fifth day before the Kalends of May.

Once he had become pontiff, how holily he lived and how canonically he ruled the church entrusted to him are testified by men of sacred religion [Note: [Col. 0243D] The *Life of Lietbert* adds “still surviving in our own times”; from this it appears that the *Life* was copied from our work, not that our work derived from it.], as well as by the rebuilding and restoration of the houses of Holy Mother Church. Behold, you may see the lamp placed upon the lampstand shining in the house of the Lord, and the whole people of the bishopric rejoicing, illuminated by its ray. (*Deeds of the Bishops of Cambrai* III, 1.)

It must also be known about him that Albero [Note: [Col. 0243] “Alberto,” according to the copy.] archbishop of Reims, with the permission of his parents, took away a boy related to him and raised him familiarly under the canonical rule.

### 8. On the church of Saint Mary

As stated above, Pope Benedict, after serving in the priesthood for eleven years, ten months, and twenty-one days, departed this life, and John succeeded him. After Arnulf’s death, Lord Ebalus took charge of the church of Reims.

In the year 1021, in the tenth year of his pontificate, Lord Gerard, at the beginning of all good works, began to build the head of the monastery of Saint Mary, Mother of God, at Cambrai, on the eighth day before the Kalends of April, with great and marvelous splendor [Note: [Col. 0244D] 1023 according to the *Deeds of the Bishops of Cambrai* III, 49.], and completed it, most beautifully adorned, as it is seen to this day and forever.

### 9. On the cruelty of Walter the castellan

[(Ibid.)] Meanwhile Walter’s wickedness, which he had exercised during the days of Bishop Erluin, did not diminish at all. Rather, persisting in greater and more serious crimes, his fury increased from day to day.

Although we are weary of mentioning him again [Col. 0244B], since his crimes are so numerous and so great [Note: [Col. 0243] “quanta,” according to the copy.] that, if written down, they would require a book of their own, nevertheless we do not wish to omit saying at least a little about him. This will show that, while the lord bishop was subjected to such great affliction by the wicked enemy, he did not lack courage; and his proven virtue of patience, by which he bore everything with composure, may be regarded by all as a cause of wonder and an example. (Ibid. 39.)

For after civil disturbances, fires, robberies, and the imprisonment of citizens and poor people, which that tyrant had perpetrated whether the bishop was absent or present, he was frequently rebuked for his unspeakable outrages by his household and peers, sometimes by powerful outsiders, and even by the emperor’s envoys [Note: [Col. 0243] “emperators,” according to the copy.], whom the emperor had sent there at the bishop’s request to restrain his madness. (Ibid. 2.)

Then he suddenly assumed a certain pretense and displayed the appearance of fictitious correction. Thus, pleading for the bishop’s favor, giving hostages and swearing oaths to preserve the peace, he obtained pardon. But as soon as an opportunity arose to exercise his customary fury, all his promises were quickly annulled and scattered, and he burst forth into still worse deeds. (Ibid. 3.)

### 10. On the churches built by Lord Gerard

Amid these adversities, however, the bishop’s clear conscience could in no way be cast down from the state of uprightness or from the intention of true religion. Rather, he constantly devoted himself to building monasteries and repairing the churches of the saints.

[(V. Lietb. 2.)] The see of Cambrai, nobly adorned through his labor and zeal and raised in pontifical dignity at its head, demonstrates this. The church of Arras testifies to it, having been restored by the same pontiff after its heavenly fire more excellently and beautifully than it had been before. This is also evident from the illustrious monastery of Florennes, which he built at his own expense in honor of God and in memory of Saint John the Baptist, since he himself was descended from that place and illustrious family, and enriched it with his paternal inheritances.

What should be said of the other monasteries—of Maroilles, of the cell of Saint Gislenus, of Hautmont—where he diligently restored the monastic order, already fallen and given over to the corrupt practices of clerics, according to the rule of its former religious life, and established there abbots who followed good works by the regular path?

But the account of these matters must retain its own place. We, however, as we proposed at the very beginning of this work, now turn our words to recounting in due order the origins of our church.

### 11. How Lord Gerard built the tower of this village

We said at the outset that Bishop Erluin, in order to repel the attacks of plunderers, first established in this place—which at that time was either no village or only a small one—a fortified site called the New Castle. Through this he acquired considerable peace and quiet for the inhabitants of the whole province.

Afterward Lord Gerard, his successor, recognizing that this had been done with sound and necessary ingenuity, likewise took care to guard it diligently and, through episcopal foresight, to enlarge it into a more substantial place.

For after several years, removing the aforementioned wooden house, he built there, at no small expense, a lofty tower of squared stone, which remains standing to this day as it can be seen. Moreover, he ordered the reason for his intention and for so great a labor to be carved in formed letters upon a large stone of the wall itself, as follows:

“To the holy mother of God, Mary, Bishop Gerard built this house for the protection and refuge of the poor. Whoever preserves it for this purpose shall receive a blessing; whoever acts otherwise shall receive an eternal curse.”

### 12. How he resolved to build this church

After this, the meditation of his heart was inspired by the sight of divine mercy to the following purpose: since a house of temporary refuge had been built against visible enemies, another spiritual house, constructed nearby of excellent stones, ought also to be built against the wickedness of invisible spirits and the rulers of darkness. In it, such custodians and watchmen should dwell as would praise God forever at both times of day and night; and just as the former offered protection for bodies and perishable possessions, so this latter should become a safeguard for souls that would never die.

While he was considering this, God—who is rich in mercy, by whose inspiration right thoughts are conceived and by whose action they are carried out [Note: [Col. 0245] The copy reads *perabuntur*]—who had given him the will, also granted him the ability, preparing for him the opportunity to accomplish this desired undertaking.

### 13. How he built this monastery

At that time there was a certain knight named Heriwardus, noble by birth, who, because of the extraordinary strength of his courage, was surnamed “Iron Arm”; from him the place is also now called Heriward’s Valley. How strong his residence at Basuellum [Note: [Col. 0245D] Basuel, near Le Câteau] was can still easily be recognized from the situation of the site itself.

Since he possessed, by paternal right, many allodial estates scattered around him, he was approached by the lord bishop. Partly in exchange for something, but chiefly for the sake of his own soul and those of his parents, as well as of his son Hervardus and his grandson Fulcho, he transferred the allod of Theoderic’s Mount, of Wateneiis [Note: [Col. 0245] Restored in this form from *Gesta episcoporum Cameracensium* III, 49. The copy reads: “Tilcho’s allod of … Mount of Watenesis.”], and also this land, the site of our dwelling, and the outlying cultivated lands.

Then the lord bishop, having obtained the fulfillment of his wish, built with energetic diligence, just as he had previously conceived in his mind, an oratory in honor of Saint Andrew the apostle and friend of God, to whom he commended himself more attentively than to the other saints. He appointed twenty-four monks to serve there under sacred religious discipline and the rule of their order, and placed over them as abbot his brother, the lord Elbertus, a man of venerable life [Note: [Col. 0245D] Compare *Gesta episcoporum Cameracensium* II, 3. He died on 11 May 1047 [Col. 0246D].]

### 14. Walter the castellan’s abominable plots

I am compelled to repeat mention of Walter through almost every sentence of this work, because the order of the narrative seems in some way to require it. For while the lord bishop was laboring at the good works mentioned above and others besides, Walter, driven by a mad spirit, did not cease even briefly from the outbursts of his wickedness.

[(Gesta episcoporum Cameracensium III, 2.) For this reason, although he was repeatedly admonished by the bishop and by the emperor’s legates to attend the emperor’s court, he, alleging one excuse or another [Col. 0246C], would, by promising words, put on the appearance of a feigned correction; but not long afterward, slipping into worse behavior, he repeated even more extensively the offenses of his accustomed depravity (ibid. 39). Thus he killed a certain knight of the bishop, Robert, distinguished both by the nobility of his birth and by the vigor of his youth, whom he suspected would resist his tyranny, although the lord bishop was seeking to reconcile them and had placed them under a truce [Note: [Col. 0246D] That is, *trevia*, *treuva*, or *treuga*], and although the killing occurred on the Lord’s Day. (Ibid. 44.) He also shut up the bishop himself inside his own house for three days, surrounding it with arms so completely that neither the bishop nor any of his men dared to go out for fear of death [Note: [Col. 0245] The copy reads *ederet*.] But I now prefer to remain silent about this rather than recount more of the misdeeds of so perverse a man; for however much we say about him, it is as though we were drawing a vessel of water from a torrent: so many and so great are his wickednesses, which he did not fear to practice against the holy man and the city.]

### 15. The lord bishop’s journey to the emperor’s court

(Ibid. 35.) Meanwhile, because of this and other matters, an occasion arose for the lord bishop, taking distinguished men with him, including the count of Hainaut, to visit the emperor Henry, who at that time happened to be staying at Aachen. There a provincial synod was being held with the archbishop of Cologne and the other venerable ministers of the holy order. At it, the emperor himself and the persons mentioned above dealt lawfully and adequately with matters both ecclesiastical and secular, and with the condition and peace of holy Church.

There also the lord bishop settled, by a reasonable and synodal judgment, a very serious dispute that had long existed between the aforementioned archbishop Pilgrim and Durandus, bishop of Liège, concerning a certain village called Burcii, which each of them was claiming to assign to his own diocese.

How many and how splendid were the gifts that the emperor distributed to all the bishops, abbots, clerics, poor people, and all men of good reputation who had gathered there in countless numbers cannot easily be enumerated either in writing or in speech. For his generosity in distributing various gifts was so great that it could be compared with the munificence of no ancient or foreign king. But, touching on these matters briefly, we hasten onward to others.

### 16. The emperor’s generosity

(Ibid. 37, 38.) When the assembly mentioned above had finally been dissolved, the emperor, with his leading men, again proceeded to the village made illustrious by the birth of Saint Gaugericus, intending to celebrate the approaching feast of that confessor, which falls on 11 August. Departing from there, he went to Verdun, where he devoutly celebrated the Nativity of holy Mary, Mother of God.

On that same day, because the lord bishop had walked at the empress’s right hand in the procession, she presented him with dishes adorned with gold and gems. From there he reached Metz and distributed great riches among the individual monasteries. He passed no good man, whether cleric or monk, without giving him a gift, as though by some presage he foresaw the approaching day—which was very near—of his death.]

### 17. The splendid gifts the emperor gave him

(An. 1023.) Indeed, since the lord Gerard, more than the other bishops, adhered to the emperor’s service, he mentioned to him in friendly conversation that, among his other undertakings, he had established a new congregation of monks in honor of Saint Andrew. The emperor, as a friend of holy religion, rejoiced with kindly favor in his pious efforts and sent through him three precious gifts to our church: namely, two small golden crosses, a certain red-colored pallium, and—more precious than these and more desirable than gold and topaz—the relics of Saint Andrew. Opening the chests of his chapel, he brought forth a bone from the body of that holy apostle, which, as he declared, the emperor of Constantinople had once given him.

He also brought forth from his treasury two pallia of no small value for the holy Virgin Mary [(ibid. 39), Col. 0247D]. Finally, after giving him a very large quantity of gold, he provided him with the means to return to his own home, taking care that the day of his death, 3 July, should be held in eternal memory at this place.

### 18. The death of the emperor Henry

Thus endowed with these royal gifts, the lord bishop returned peacefully and joyfully with his companions to his own possessions. But not long afterward grave sorrow followed. For the often-mentioned emperor Henry, orthodox and peace-loving, after administering the empire successfully for twenty years, in the twelfth year of the episcopate of the lord Gerard [(ibid. III, 50)], closed his final day [An. 1024]. It is difficult to say what desolation his death brought upon holy Church, and how much harm it inflicted upon the Roman state and people. At last, the Saxon princes assembled at Mainz and appointed Conrad as their king, and in that same year he was blessed there on the Nativity of holy Mary.]

### 19. The dedication of this church

Meanwhile, the lord bishop brought honorably into this church, with great veneration and amid a multitude of clergy and people, the gifts that he had received, as stated, from the king. He retained two crosses, which are still carried in the procession of Saint Mary, and gave in exchange for them one golden cross, made with precious stones, which is still preserved among us [Note: [Col. 0247] I have corrected the text in this way; previously the copy and the manuscript itself read as shown in the *Acta Sanctorum Belgii* V, 193]. He also brought the body of the holy virgin and martyr Maxelendis and part of the body of Saint Sarius (An. 1025).

Many bodies of saints also assembled on the day appointed for the dedication, namely 22 September in the year of Christ 1025, together with the clerics and monks: Saint Gaugericus, Saint Aubertus, the precious martyr Salvius, Saint Aycadrius, Saint Gislenus, and Saint Wasnulfus. Blessed Maxelendis was also with them [Note: [Col. 0247] The copy and the manuscript both omit the words, leaving a space]. The bishop’s prudent diligence caused them to assemble for the salvation of the inhabitants and the protection of the place itself.

### 20. The possessions bestowed upon this monastery

After establishing and consecrating as abbot his brother Elbertus, whom we named above, he sufficiently endowed this monastery with villas and allodial estates. [(Gesta episcoporum Cameracensium III, 49.)] Specifically, he gave it a third part of a fourth part of the royal estate of Péroune, which he had acquired from four noblemen, namely Robert and Hubald, Ascelin and Sueno. The remaining parts of that royal estate he assigned to the bishop’s table [Note: [Col. 0247] Missing from the copy, which leaves a space; I supplied it from *Gesta episcoporum Cameracensium* III, 49], at the castle of Saint Mary around which it lies.

Among other properties, he also gave it his hereditary allod in the village of Haynau, which is Bussud [Note: [Col. 0247D] Near Binche], together with the dependent household of Saint Philibert. Since these and his other benefactions to this church are recorded in our privileges [Note: [Col. 0247] “Placed” in the copy] [Note: [Col. 0248D] Miraeus published the diplomas of the emperor Conrad and Bishop Gerard in *Opera diplomatica* I, 55], we have judged it superfluous to say more about them, lest they become burdensome to the reader.

At that same time, a freeborn knight named Tigerus, who possessed many estates around Basuellum, where he lived, and had no heir, on the advice and at the urging of the lord bishop endowed this church with all his possessions, including what is called Tiger’s Forest, so that God and Saint Andrew might restore to him his inheritance in the land of the living.

### 21. The consecration of the church of Cambrai

Pope John, whom we reported above in chapter eight to have succeeded Benedict, ruled the Church for nine years and nine months. Benedict Theophylactus succeeded him. The monastery of Florennes was dedicated by the lord Gerard, with the consent of Rainard, bishop of Liège (An. 1026).

In the following year, which was 1027 from the Lord’s Nativity [Note: [Col. 0249] *Gesta episcoporum Cameracensium* III, 49 says that it was consecrated in 1030], the monastery of Saint Mary, honorably built by the lord Gerard, was dedicated on 18 October, with many bodies of saints present.

[(Ibid. III, 50.) After these matters had been properly completed, the lord bishop, having received sound advice, judged it fitting, according to the custom of antiquity, to visit the court of the new emperor, namely Conrad, whom we said above had assumed the royal insignia after Henry’s death. For some time he had suspended his journey to the emperor’s presence, namely because he did not wish to cause offense or scandal among the people of Lorraine.

For Duke Gothelus, the bishops of Cologne, Noyon, Verdun, Utrecht, and Liège, and Duke Theodoric together with Rainer, count of Hainaut, had resisted Conrad’s appointment and had agreed under oath that they would neither give him their hands nor go to him, because they did not want him to reign over them.

After the aforementioned dukes and bishops had been brought to peace with him after a year and a half, the lord bishop went with them to the palace at Aachen and willingly offered himself in submission to the king.]

### 22. The council held at Tribur

(Ibid. 51.) At Tribur, near Mainz, the emperor Conrad summoned bishops from various regions so that they might discuss together matters of usefulness and religion. There, among other decrees of their deliberations, they issued many commands concerning the renewal of peace, fasts, denying communion to the excommunicated, and the burial of certain persons—commands that seemed burdensome to repeat.

The most moderate Father Gerard sought to restrain their less sound opinions. After delivering an address to them, he said, among other things:

“Fasting on the sixth or seventh day of the week ought not generally to be imposed upon everyone, since neither do all possess the same bodily health nor does the accusation of sin weigh equally upon all.”

He argued many other matters as well. When the council had ended, he obtained permission and returned to his own church.

[Col. 0249] END OF THE FIRST BOOK.

## [BOOK TWO]

### THIS PROLOGUE BEGINS THE SECOND BOOK

To describe briefly the abundant material of great events and to encompass in a short discourse the famous deeds of illustrious persons requires no less labor than to extend a small narrative through lengthy words. In both cases it is difficult to emerge eloquent: either one eagerly attempts what exceeds one’s strength, striving to magnify matters that are small, or one tries to compress into a brief account matters that require extensive narration.

I recognize that one of these two things has happened to me, since I presume to pluck from the many deeds of kings, bishops, and princes certain matters and express them in a few short sentences. Yet from this presumption of mine I hope perhaps to earn pardon, because I have taken care only to disclose the beginnings of our church and the gifts by which it was enlarged and brought to its present condition.

Therefore, to accomplish this, it is necessary to run through the field of Scripture, and I have endeavored to weave together this little work gathered from various flowers. May he therefore be present and favor our labor who proclaims himself to be “the flower of the field and the lily of the valleys” (Song of Songs II, 1), so that all our work, begun by him and to be completed through him, may faithfully serve him and his friend Saint Andrew.

### 1. The burning of the monastery of Saint Mary at Arras

In the year of the Lord’s Nativity 1029 [Note: [Col. 0249] The *Annales Elnonenses minores* give 1030], in the nineteenth year of the episcopate of the lord Gerard, the monastery of Saint Mary in the city of Arras was consumed by lightning on 30 July, through a marvelous but true judgment of God.

Therefore the lord bishop, afflicted with deep grief, sent a letter to Lietduinus, abbot of Saint Vedast, a man of admirable holiness, in which he disclosed the sorrow of his heart, saying after some introductory words:

[(Gesta episcoporum Cameracensium III, 32.) “Fear and sorrow have stolen upon me more than usual. Although through long practice they are old for me, they are nevertheless always made new by their increase. For whenever I look at myself according to the quality of my life, I am plunged into bitterness, because I fail in good things and persist in evil ones.

“But whenever I raise the eye of my mind to examine the things that are in the world, I see that everything lies in evil. I clearly consider how fiercely the world is being ravaged by the sword and by what blows the people are perishing; and therefore I fear that worse things are still to come, because I confess that these things are happening through our priestly sin, as it is written, with the blessed apostle Peter testifying: ‘For it is time for judgment to begin from the house of God.’ And in Ezekiel: ‘Begin from my sanctuary’ [Note: [Col. 0249] The copy reads *incipiente*].”]

### 2. White fleeces fallen from heaven at Arras

“For example, as in the present case of Saint Mary of Arras: it is clear that on 30 July fire came from heaven and burned the whole church, with everyone looking on. Therefore I greatly fear that this was a sign of the divine Lord’s anger, coming upon the children of men.

“Just as once, before the Lord’s coming, two white fleeces are said to have fallen in that place as a sign of mercy, so, as a sign of the divine vengeance that is to come upon the children of unbelief, fire came with sulfur, which, by searing, might warn the elect to flee from the face of the bow, and might burn the impious and sinners who are always disparaging Christ and the children of the Church.

“They also commonly say to the ministers of the Church concerning us: ‘These are the shepherds of the people, who are not truly shepherds but wolves. For they eat the sins of the people who receive the fruits of the Church as their daily stipend, but they do not labor at all either in devotion to prayer or in the word of preaching.’

“And therefore, whatever adversity occurs in the world—namely mortality, pestilence, and famine—they say that it is deserved and begins from the sanctuary,” and so forth.]

These and other words belong to the lord bishop, who was making complaint and grieving deeply over the extraordinarily unusual event of the aforementioned fire. But by what zeal, labor, and expense he rebuilt that church can be recognized more from the structure itself than from anyone’s words or writings. But, leaving these matters aside, let us return to our subject.

### 3. The documents of charters bestowed here by the lord bishop

In that same year (February 1030), the emperor Conrad went with a large army into Hungary. The lord bishop, wishing to bring the work he had begun to completion and ensuring that nothing was lacking to our church that might benefit our religious purpose, also taking care that the region should be defended by fortifications against any attacks that might someday occur, approached the emperor on certain matters.

At that time the emperor was holding a council with the bishops at Tribur (May 1036); the lord Gerard, honorably received by him, attended it. There he requested and obtained that all the properties he had bestowed upon this place should be strengthened by the authority of an imperial privilege. That privilege, marked with the royal seal and brought here, is preserved among us to this day.

He also added that those benefactions should be confirmed by his own privilege. Whoever takes up the task of reading it will clearly learn with what affection he loved and enlarged this place and how much kindness he showed to the monks. Moreover, he decreed that the aforesaid abbot, the lord Elbertus, and his successor, together with those celebrating with him, should always be his intimate chaplains [Note: [Col. 0251] The copy reads *constituerit*].

### 4. The death of the emperor Conrad

After the often-mentioned emperor Conrad had held the reins of the empire for sixteen years with the greatest vigor, both in wisdom and in arms, [(Gesta episcoporum Cameracensium III, 55)] he turned his journey toward the region this side of the Alps. Not long afterward, afflicted by illness, he was deprived of life at Utrecht (An. 1039) and left his son Henry as heir to his kingdom and labors.

The aforementioned bishop went to him and placed himself in his hands; Duke Gothelus likewise did so, although he had intended to withhold himself for a while. Many signs preceded Conrad’s death; although worthy of narration, we pass over them for the sake of brevity.

### 5. The death of Abbot Lietduinus

(Ibid. 59.) Two years afterward it happened that Lietduinus, who had been converted from a layman into a monk and later became abbot of the monastery at Arras, succeeding the lord Richard, departed from this world and, as we hope, happily reached the next, leaving sorrowful those whom he had instructed in every good work.

He introduced Abbot Richard, a highly religious man, through whom that place began to flourish in holy religion and worldly resources. But since an occasion has arisen to mention the lord Richard, abbot of admirable religious devotion, we judge it right to say something more elevated in memory of so venerable a monk.]

### 6. The lord abbot Richard

This Abbot Richard was born at Verdun. Later, having become abbot in name and in fact in the court of the emperor Henry, the father—or rather predecessor [Note: [Col. 0251D] More precisely, “predecessor”]—of Conrad, whom we mentioned above, he became very well known and was also extremely familiar with that emperor.

Thus [(ibid. III, 1)], when the aforementioned emperor conferred the episcopal insignia upon the lord Gerard at the village of Arntia in Saxony on the first of February and, keeping him with him, granted him permission to leave on the third day after the Purification of Saint Mary, he ordered two abbots, namely the lord Richard and Berthaldus of Enden, as well as Count Hermann, to accompany him and conduct him as far as the city of Cambrai.

### 7. The monasteries entrusted to him

As time went on, he accepted the governance of the abbey of Hautmont, which, for various reasons that I am reluctant to enumerate, had been deprived of all monastic observance. The lord Gerard and his brother Arnulf, the advocate of that place, had requested this of him.

Later, at the request of the lord bishop Gerard and Walpo, bishop of Liège, he likewise accepted the governance of the monastery of Lobbes. The monk Engbrandus, who had been in charge of that church, was living secularly: inwardly he taught nothing of religion, while outwardly he shamefully dissipated the church’s goods.

He had also governed the church of Arras for some years. But afterward, so that he might serve God more freely and make clear to everyone that he had undertaken the burden for heavenly rather than human favor, he resolved to withdraw from the governance of the church of Arras. On the advice of Bishop Gerard, he appointed the aforementioned Lietduinus in his place, and Fulcuinus, a venerable man, at Hautmont.]

This Abbot Richard, fervent beyond measure in holy religion, suddenly shone upon the monastic order, which had almost collapsed and, so to speak, been annihilated, like a lamp and a torch. He illuminated not only the monasteries entrusted to him but also those throughout the surrounding provinces by regular practice according to the rule of Saint Benedict.

We have touched briefly on these matters concerning so great a man, about whom many more things worthy of praise could have been said. But since that is not our purpose [Note: [Col. 0253] The copy reads *prepositi*], let us proceed to other matters.

### 8. The killing of Walter the castellan

Benedict Theophylactus ruled the Roman Church for thirteen years. After him, Silvester, bishop of Sabina, held the see for fifty-six days. Gregory, also called John and Gratian, succeeded him and held it for two years and six months.

At almost the same time, Walter the castellan, notorious throughout the surrounding region for his evil deeds, was killed while praying at the entrance of the monastery of Saint Mary at Cambrai by four men prepared for this very purpose by prior agreement—or so they say; we have little certainty about the matter (An. 1041).

After his death, some rest, though not for long, came to the city, the whole region, and the episcopal court. [(Gesta Lietberti 2.)] His wife Ermentrude, left with her only young son, no less wicked than Jezebel, did not cease from her husband’s madness. Surpassing his wickedness, she married a certain tyrant, John, advocate of Arras, so that, supported by his aid, she might recover the castellanate. But when her son died soon afterward, she accomplished nothing.]

### 9. The lord abbot Waldricus

After Gratian, Suigerus, who is called Clement, held the Roman see for nine months and seven days. After him, Poppo, also called Damasus, sat for twenty-three days. Bruno, also called Leo IX, succeeded him and ruled for five years, two months, and seven days.

Coming from Rome, he held a great council at Reims and dedicated the monastery of Saint Remigius, under Wido, archbishop and successor of Ebalo. At the same time Henry, son of Conrad, was enthroned at Rome with imperial dignity.

At Cambrai, old age was overtaking the lord bishop Gerard as his days approached their end, and because of it he was already becoming weaker than in his former condition.

The lord abbot Elbertus, having happily completed the course of his life, died in the year of Christ 1047, on 11 May. After him, the lord Waldricus was ordained abbot of this church by Bishop Gerard. He was originally from the village of Bracbat, called Lutosa; he had become a distinguished cleric, then chaplain to Rainer, count of Castrilocus, and afterward a monk at Florennes.

How religiously he governed this place, with what benefits he enlarged it, and with what care he nurtured his subjects is testified to this day by the outstanding fame of his name and by the properties acquired through his administration.

### 10. The village of Lutosa

(Gesta episcoporum Cameracensium II, 43.) Since mention has been made of the village called Lutosa, or, as some prefer, Laudosa, it should be known that it contains a monastery of canons in honor of the apostles Peter and Paul, which the blessed Amandus built. It is a wealthy abbey, where the venerable man of God Baidilo rests; he is said to have brought the body of Saint Mary Magdalene from Jerusalem into Burgundy, to the place called Vézelay.]

### 11. Certain monks of this place

It should also not be passed over without notice that the aforementioned abbot, the lord Waldricus, sent here from his homeland certain members of his own family to serve God—indeed, three of his nephews.

The first was Baldwin the monk, whom we saw as the sacristan of this church, endowed with marvelous charity; his day of death is 26 December. The second was Stephen, provost of this place, learned both in letters and in secular affairs; his day of death is 18 March. The third was his brother William, a layman of blameless life, who served the monks throughout his life in every equestrian duty; many of his descendants still remain to this day.

The lord bishop Gerard likewise had brought here a monk of his own family named Socleramus [Note: [Col. 0253] It cannot be determined whether the name should be read *Socleramus*, *Soeleramus*, or *Sceleramus], a man of innocent and simple life. Among other things, content with every kind of lowliness and entirely neglecting the care of his body, he devoted himself diligently to announcing the hours of the Work of God.

We saw him bent with age, his limbs supported by a staff, yet still not ceasing from his holy purpose or from continual psalmody. Supported by such ministers and sustained by such an abbot, under the patronage of so great a bishop, this most blessed church was then praised by everyone.

We avoid reporting more about these matters, lest we perhaps weary the reader.

### 12. The death of the lord Gerard, bishop

In the fifth year of the ordination of the aforementioned abbot, when the day of his calling came upon him, the lord bishop Gerard, in the fortieth year of his episcopate, was released by what we believe to have been a happy death and, by God’s gift, attained fellowship in the life for which he had long labored through so many and such great hardships and toward which he had strained with all his strength.

He died on 14 March in the year of Christ 1050 [Note: [Col. 0253D] More probably 1051; compare what we noted concerning *Gesta Lietberti* 3. The error may belong to the copy, not the author. For the fifth year of Abbot Waldricus, ordained in 1047, as our chapter 9 states, is 1051. Moreover, the fortieth year of Gerard’s episcopate, who received the staff on 1 February 1012, is 1051–1052] and was buried in the middle of the church of Saint Mary with fitting veneration.

How greatly he was loved by his people is indicated by his tomb, adorned with various stones and golden letters.

At that time Baldwin, son of the count of Flanders, married Countess Richilde, who had previously been married to Hermann, the nephew of that count.

### 13. The election of the lord Lietbertus and the journey to the king

[(Vita Lietberti 10, 3, 11, 13.)] After the lord bishop Gerard had been buried with fitting reverence and honor, the assembly of the clergy and people of Cambrai, shaken by the loss of so great a father, gathered and unanimously elected the lord Lietbertus.

The lord Gerard had carefully and religiously raised him—he was a kinsman of his own family—having been born of noble stock in the region of Brabant. He had also advanced him through each grade of the ecclesiastical order to the dignity of archdeacon and provost of the church of Cambrai. Lietbertus had always been, and especially during Gerard’s old age had become by supporting his responsibilities, his helper and fellow worker.

After making extensive preparations, distinguished men, both knights and clerics, joyfully led the elected bishop to be presented to the emperor Henry. The emperor happened at that time to be staying at Cologne, near Agrippina, devoting himself to observing the holy season of Lent.

When they arrived there, they approached the king’s presence and informed him of the desolation of their city and the whole region caused by the death of so great a patron. Weeping, they presented the pastoral staff they had brought with them and respectfully reported to him in a few words the election of the lord Lietbertus.

When the emperor heard of the death of the aforementioned bishop, whom he had always held in great veneration and affection, he grieved piously. Yet because Good Friday was at hand, a day to be devoted to the Lord’s Passion and the remembrance of sins, he remained entirely silent about the matter for three days.

But, not to prolong the account, on the day of the holy Resurrection he bestowed the episcopate upon the lord Lietbertus, long known to him as a faithful servant, in the presence of a great multitude of archbishops and members of the other holy orders, as well as the palatine nobles and dignitaries.

To show with what devotion of mind he did this, he himself began the hymn *Te Deum laudamus*, and the entire court accompanied him from the imperial palace to the church of Saint Peter with hymns and rejoicing.

When these matters had been properly completed, and our envoys had been filled with extraordinary joy, after receiving permission to depart and having arranged everything suitably, the lord Lietbertus and his companions hurried to return to their city.

### 14. The expulsion of John from Cambrai

(Ibid. 14, 15.) After this, news of what had been done was brought in advance to John—whom we said above in chapter eight had married Ermentrude, the wife of Walter the castellan, but had nevertheless been unable to obtain any grant of the castellanate from the lord Gerard, and who had therefore often plotted the death of the lord Lietbertus because Lietbertus opposed him in this matter.

Greatly alarmed, John secretly and for a long time considered what should be done. After taking counsel with his men, he resolved not to allow the bishop to enter the city when he came unless the bishop granted him the castellanate, which he eagerly desired.

Accordingly, he violently invaded the mother church of our Lady Saint Mary. After expelling the clerics, he brought the treasures of the church and everything he found inside under his own control, and stationed his armed men there.

He arrogantly entered the episcopal residence. Bringing his wife into the bishop’s chamber, he had his own bed prepared in the episcopal bed, and ordered food and provisions to be supplied to himself and his attendants from the revenues of the bishopric.

While these things were being done, the lord Lietbertus approached the city. John, meeting him with an assembled army, closed the gates and drove him far from the entrance.

Lietbertus therefore turned aside to this village and was honorably received by his own people. He stayed here for some time, until Baldwin, count of Flanders, returning from the king of France, found him and took him with him to Cambrai.

When this was reported to John, he fled and consented to free entry for his approaching lord. Thus the lord Lietbertus possessed the city in peace.

### 15. The ordination of the lord Lietbertus

As we reported above in chapter 9, after five years and two months Pope Leo was succeeded by Giehardus, also called Victor; he held the see for two years, three months, and thirteen days.

Wido, a bishop of praiseworthy life, presided over the metropolitan church of Reims. (Ibid. 16, 17.) The lord Lietbertus, a levite who had not yet attained the rank of priest, went to him with an honorable company of his people, both laymen and clerics. He was gladly received and sent by Wido to Châlons to be ordained by Bishop Roger.

Returning from there, he was fittingly marked out by episcopal consecration on the following day. Since it is not easy to describe the joy and the great gathering of the rejoicing clergy and people, we judge that we should remain silent about it, especially since we are hastening to carry out the work we have undertaken.

### 16. The emperor’s arrival in this land

The successor of the aforementioned Pope Victor was Frederick, also called Stephen, who held the see for seven months and twenty-nine days. After him, Benedict, bishop of Velletri, held it for eleven months and twenty days. Gerard, also called Nicholas, succeeded him and held it for two years, five months, and twenty-five days.

At that time the emperor Henry was again gravely angry with Baldwin, count of Flanders, whom he had once subdued to himself by ravaging and subjecting his land, because Baldwin had rebelled.

(Gesta Lietberti 9.) The lord Lietbertus, prosperously established in his see, sought to deprive the excluded John, as we have said, of every hope of obtaining the castellanate. He invested a certain young Hugh, the nephew of the castellan Walter, with it and entrusted him for education to a certain Anselm, his relative, distinguished in character and arms.

Later, however, he found and endured Hugh as a fierce enemy. When John learned this, he immediately burned with anger. Like a wounded tigress, or like a serpent that, after receiving a blow, coils its entire body into winding circles, he conceived a savage resentment. Turning various fraudulent schemes over in his panting breast, he finally gave birth to wickedness.

Why say more? He went to the emperor and boldly urged him to move against Count Baldwin. He promised that he would serve as the emperor’s vigorous army commander, since he knew the local territory and its people, if the emperor would have the grant of the castellanate of Cambrai conferred upon him by Bishop Lietbertus.
