(Ibid. 10.) The emperor was pleased by this. Thinking it would be easy to make a second invasion of the count’s territory, he promised what John requested.

Finally, after preparing an expedition with an elaborate display of royal power, he moved the army’s camp to set out in the year of Christ 1054, the fifteenth year of his reign. Passing through the intervening places and regions, he encamped and settled at the village called Maen, situated about two miles from Valenciennes, beside the River Scheldt.

### 17. That the Count Tried to Resist the Emperor

When he had ordered bridges to be built for crossing, behold, Count Baldwin appeared from the other side of the river with a large force, ready to meet him. Thus each held one bank—the one this bank, the other that—until the count, terrified when troops secretly sent by the emperor passed through Cambrai, withdrew from the position. The emperor therefore crossed freely and, devastating everything to right and left with fire, crossed the bridge of Cheri near the place called Bulliens Rivus and settled in his tents.

### 18. The Emperor’s Passage into Melentosum  
*(Ann. 1054.)*

John approached this place by night with a few armed men. It was extremely well fortified both by the narrowness of the road’s entrance and by streams of water or the depth of ditches. Pretending to be someone who had escaped by flight, and loudly imploring that it be opened to him with deceitful pleas, he finally deceived the guards with smooth speech, entered through the opened gate, killed the gatekeepers and many others, and at dawn gave the signal by the sound of a trumpet, summoning the army.

Thus passing across in companies, they entered the land of Melentosum. They laid waste by fire everything around them and settled in a camp pitched at the village called Falempin [Phalempin, between Lille and Douai].

### 19. Concerning a Certain Cleric Sent by the Count

Many remarkable deeds of the emperor on this expedition would deserve to be recorded. But since that is neither our duty nor our purpose, we shall at least recall, touching briefly on a few among many, an example that displays his extraordinary clemency.

The count had sent a certain cleric, Radulf, to the emperor’s camp to spy out and listen to his plans, when [lacuna: the source leaves the space of one word] the man, pretending to be crippled, crawled on a little stool and sat among the poor in the emperor’s tent, seeking alms. John recognized him as a man previously known to him. He nevertheless kept silent. After walking about for a while, he approached him as he lay before the emperor and his nobles; giving him his hand, he raised him up, and in the sight of everyone ordered him to stand upright and run as a healthy man.

Astonishment seized those who watched. There was a murmur of admiration, as though a miracle had been performed; and the emperor, astonished beyond belief, asked what lay behind it. Once the matter had been revealed, the man was judged liable to hanging and death. He was ordered to twist the ropes brought for hanging him himself.

“But first,” said the emperor, “let us eat. After he has eaten, he will be hanged more cheerfully.”

Royal foods were set before him. But who would taste even a little when he saw death itself threatening him? At last the emperor summoned him before his table, asked him many questions about the count, and handed him the silver spoon he was holding. He then ordered that the man be dressed in new clothes and placed on a horse, saying: “He who came to spy upon us, crawling on a stool, shall return from us exalted on horseback.”

After returning, he used to tell us, many years later, when he was already bent with old age, how great was the joy with which he had celebrated as one rescued from death, and how greatly he had praised the emperor’s magnificence even among the emperor’s enemies.

### 20. Concerning the Emperor’s Siege of Tournai

But let us now return to our subject. While Count Baldwin remained at the fortress of Isel and watched nearby as his land was consumed before his eyes by fire and plunder, most of his army and many nobles went out to attack the emperor’s camp.

[According to *The Deeds of Lietbert*, chapter 13: “But soon Count Lambert of Lens was killed and fell dead.”]

The others, seeking safety in flight, were unable to enter the village itself while the enemy struck at their backs. Fleeing like frightened birds before the face of a hawk, they directed their flight toward Tournai. Overtaken by their pursuers, they were shut up in a certain fortified town.

The emperor came there, established his quarters at Saint-Brixius, and compelled them, constricted by a severe siege and hunger, to surrender. After taking them, he confined them under guard in the military prisons of his soldiers. Thus, entering his oratory as a victor, and most devoutly singing the hymn *Te Deum laudamus* with the ministers of the sacred order chanting it with him, he rendered thanks to the Lord.

### 21. That He Gave a Golden Vessel to a Messenger

They also relate that he did another memorable deed there. A certain envoy came from his kingdom and announced that a son had recently been born to him—namely Henry, who fifty years later came into this land and by imperial power destroyed the fortresses of Bulcen, Sclusa, Incy, and other strongholds. When the envoy announced this, the emperor gave him as a gift a golden cup, which he happened to be holding in his hand for drinking.

[According to *The Deeds of Lietbert*, chapter 14: “When all had been completed, he returned with glory to the cities of his kingdom. Lord Bishop Lietbert, having received the message, returned with his companions to his own city.”]

### 22. Concerning Lord Bishop Lietbert’s Journey to Jerusalem

[Chapters 13, 12, 29, 30, and 31.]

But behold: because of the occasion provided by John’s claim to the castellany, we have undertaken to describe the emperor’s arrival and some of his deeds, and have wandered farther from the account we began and from the deeds of Lord Lietbert. Concerning that castellany, this alone need be inserted: although unwilling and reluctant, the bishop, compelled by the emperor, returned it to John. John, however, did not retain it for long, because Hugh, whom we mentioned above, received it from his guardian Anselm when he had reached adolescence. John, compelled by the emperor through both gifts and threats, thereafter kept silent about it.

When these matters had been completed, and the city and territory of Cambrai flourished under such a ruler with abundant peace and prosperous growth, the bishop, burning with holy purpose, intended to go to Jerusalem. Since the city [i.e. Cambrai] could not resist his devotion, he prepared the necessary expenses and took companions: namely Lord Walcher, archdeacon and provost of the curia; Hugh the chaplain, later dean of Saint Mary’s, whose holiness is demonstrated by the canonical cloister and the monastery of Anchin; Erlebald the judge and procurator of the city; also Erlebald the Red, restorer of the church of the Holy Cross; as well as Fulcher, archchaplain and vicedominus of the church of Arras; and many others.

He set out [in the year 1034 of the Lord’s Incarnation]. Passing through cities and fortified towns, and through the dangers of the roads, he crossed the barbarous land inhabited by the Huns. After crossing the Danube, he reached the king of the Pannonians. Passing beyond his territory, he entered vast solitudes, which are called the deserts of Bulgaria and which are inhabited by brigands of the Scythian race.

These people, living like wild beasts, are restrained by no laws and contained within no cities. They remain under the open sky and take whatever shelters the night compels them to use. They waylay passers-by, kill those whom they encounter, and plunder the rest.

[They travel in groups, carrying all their possessions with them, together with their entire household goods, children, and wives. The *Life of Lietbert*, chapter 33, adds: “They are held by no named sect of any heresy or by the divine worship of any religion; nevertheless, as we saw from those of them whom they had killed, they are circumcised in the manner of the Saracens. They are barbarians, cruel, murderous, without affection and without pity.”]

### 23. That Lord Bishop Reached Corinth

[Chapters 34 and 35.]

While Lord Bishop and his companions were passing through so many deadly ambushes of savage enemies, under threat of death and with trembling hearts, on the seventh day, amid dense forests, they saw men with crested and banded heads, wearing cloaks and broad leggings, their bodies nearly naked. Quivers hung from their shoulders, and they carried slack bows and long spears.

At this sight the others were terrified. But because the righteous man is confident as a lion, the bishop showed himself all the more cheerful. You might have seen that, by God’s will, all their fury was so greatly softened at the sight of the bishop that—wonderful to say—they withdrew from the place and in a manner showed the travelers the way.

Thus Lord Bishop and his companions passed unharmed through the deadly region and the dwellings of the brigands. Entering Dalmatia and traversing the places where Diocletian had once inflicted various punishments of death on Christ’s martyrs while building baths, he turned his course toward Isauria. Passing through it, he reached Corinth [*Chorinerum*, according to the *Life of Lietbert*]. There, hearing that the body of the holy Demetrius, renowned among the martyrs, lay at rest, he sought out the tomb.

### 24. Concerning Fulcher, Who Fell Ill unto Death

From there he proceeded until he reached Laodicea in Syria. Learning that the church of the Lord’s Sepulchre had been violently closed by the king of Babylon after the Christians had been expelled, and that the route by land had been completely blocked because of fear of the pagans, he remained in that city for three months.

When every hope of traveling by land had been removed, Lord Bishop Lietbert decided to reach Jerusalem by sea. While masters were being sought for this undertaking, naval equipment was being arranged, and the necessary provisions prepared, Lord Fulcher was struck by a grave illness. This afflicted the bishop himself and all his companions with deep sorrow.

As the sickness grew worse day by day, even to the point of death, and the season suitable for sailing had already arrived, fear and longing tormented the bishop’s mind: should he abandon his most faithful companion, or postpone the time of sailing?

### 25. How Fulcher, Near Death, Invoked Saint Andrew

[Chapter 36.]

When all hope for the life of the man lying ill had utterly disappeared, and the bishop was compelled by the sailors, who were hurrying to the port, to depart, he nevertheless visited the sick man once more. Fulcher seemed almost to be drawing his last breath in a dead body.

Addressing him now with words, now with gestures, as best he could, the bishop asked him for permission to leave. Though the sick man was already being handed over to another world, he recognized the bishop’s voice and sobs, recovered his breath [the copy reads *quumque* for *cumque*], opened his eyes, and, understanding the speaker’s words with great difficulty, likewise asked for permission to leave, as one who was departing from this world.

The venerable bishop, commending him to God with the greatest lamentation and the whole devotion of his heart, entrusted him to the apostle Saint Andrew and to the merits and prayers of the glorious queen Mary, Mother of God. Nor is it surprising that he should have commended the man he loved to those whom he honored more attentively than all others.

After this, as though bidding one another a final farewell and exchanging the kiss of peace, Lord Bishop departed.

### 26. Concerning Fulcher’s Tears and Prayer

The sick man, abandoned by the physicians and deserted by his companions, but revived by the bishop’s blessing, breathed for a little while. Then, recalling to himself the words with which the bishop had entrusted him to Saint Andrew and in which he had implored the holy Mother of God on his behalf, he drew deep sighs from his heart, tears rising in his eyes, and said—as he later testified himself:

> “O Saint Andrew, to whose protection my lord Lietbert the bishop entrusted me, and whose memory he honors in the monastery situated at New Castle: if you truly are that Andrew, handsome, the manly apostle of Christ, friend of God, whom the Lord loved as a fragrance of sweetness, come to my aid, hasten, have mercy. Dip your finger in the oil of mercy, and by your prayers and those of the Mother of God, our Lady Saint Mary, sustain my failing soul and help me in my struggle. Come to my aid, friend of God, through the secret power of Christ, your master. I am already dying.

> “What I cannot obtain for myself, ask from the mother of compassion, so that help may be given me—not on account of my merits, which deserve the punishment of death, but on account of the tears and prayers of him who entrusted me to you.”

The bishop passed that night sleepless, commending himself and his companions to God with his customary groans, and by his earnest prayers prolonging the life of his dying friend.

### 27. Concerning the Apparition of Saint Mary and Saint Andrew

[*The Deeds of Lietbert*, chapter 37.]

The fourth watch of the night was already approaching when, while the others in the house where the sick man lay were asleep, he seemed to himself, half awake, to have fallen asleep. Behold, he saw two demonic spirits standing before him, carrying an iron trident, flaming as though it had been taken from a furnace. As he himself reported, they called it the sting of death.

They said that they had brought it for the purpose of fastening it into his heart and thus driving out his soul. What fear was there, O God! What pain, what anguish! The sick man struggled, struggled and failed; he watched the blows of those threatening to strike him, and he was utterly undone, sobbing. He was undone, and between his sobs only these words could be heard:

> “Holy Virgin of virgins, Mother of Jesus, Saint Andrew!”

In this great and terrible crisis of suffering, amid the darkness and shadows of death, the place was illuminated from heaven by her most holy presence: the star of the sea, the mother of mercy, by whose intercession God’s mercy spares the sins of sinners.

She was present, I say—the hope of the wretched, the salvation of the weak, and the mighty lamentation of the demons. In her right hand she bore the sign of the life-giving cross—the hand with which she had wrapped Christ in swaddling clothes and laid him in the manger—while leaning to the left over the apostle Saint Andrew.

“Who,” she said, “has given you, most wicked spirits, such great terror of your rage and such great confidence in your power that you wish to claim for yourselves those who have been entrusted to us? What have you to do with the sick man, whom my Son restores to health through the prayers of this holy Andrew? Go away from here at once—go away!”

At her command, the demonic spirits vanished more quickly than words can say.

### 28. How Health Was Restored to Fulcher through Saint Mary and Saint Andrew

[Chapter 38.]

Then the mother of mercy looked upon the sick man with a serene expression—the expression with which, among those dining at the wedding feast, she indicated that the wine was failing; that expression, I say, with which she looked upon the grieving Theophilus; an expression of sweetness and grace.

With that expression she looked upon the sick man, already almost dead, rescued from the hands of the demons, and signified by a command that he should rise and follow his bishop. Then she departed.

When the vision had departed, the sick man, who had seemed to himself to be sleeping, opened his eyes and found himself sound and healthy, as though he had suffered no harm. He immediately called the boy who had remained with him so that, if he died, he would not remain unburied, and ordered him to bring his clothing as quickly as possible and prepare everything necessary for the road to follow the bishop.

Although the boy thought him mad, Fulcher immediately rose, called the master of the house, asked how much he owed for the expenses incurred on his behalf, paid the calculated amount, ordered his horses to be prepared as quickly as possible, and warned the boy not to forget any of his belongings.

Not only was the head of the household, whose hospitality he had enjoyed, astonished to see him restored to health, but the entire neighborhood rejoiced at his recovery. The whole city likewise rejoiced and applauded, because the man whom they had expected, in accordance with the evangelical command, to bury only later as he lay dying, they now saw in the morning driving his horse forward at a swift pace.

He himself gladly recounted to everyone who asked how great a favor the Lord had done him through his glorious Mother and the apostle Saint Andrew. Then, accompanied by his servant, he hastened at the fastest pace to catch up with the bishop, whom God’s mercy and providence still detained on the shore.

### 29.

[Chapter 39.]

While the bishop was walking along the shore, Fulcher arrived in good health. The rising sun, with its ray-like locks, already signaled the coming storm; the prudent sailors, taking precautions against it, postponed the voyage.

Meanwhile, at the third hour of the day, while the bishop walked along the shore and mourned within himself the fate of his abandoned faithful companion, those watching from a distance announced to him that Lord Fulcher was coming.

At first he was astonished; then, gathering his thoughts, he asked how they knew this. They replied that they had truly seen the horses he used to ride and his clothing. Sighing, he said:

> “It may be so. It is not Fulcher, but perhaps his servant, who is following us after burying his master. Unless by the sole mercy of God, I no longer hope to see Fulcher. Nevertheless, I do not despair of Christ’s mercy, which restored Lazarus to his sisters and the widow’s only son to her.”

While they were saying these things among themselves and intently watching those who were approaching, Fulcher appeared. O, how great was the joy, how great the gladness—may the human mind know it! It was not permitted him to relate what had happened or how, so great was the tumult and so large the crowd pressing forward to embrace him.

[Chapter 40.] After receiving his companion, Lord Bishop boarded the ship with his men at the sailors’ command. The sailors rose to their oars with all their strength.

> The wind rises astern and drives the travelers onward.  
> They leave the ports of Laodicea and fly over the sea.  
> They repeatedly traverse the straits, stirred by the surrounding lands.  
> They spread the sails, and the hollow vessel races across the water.  
> Once the ship had reached the open sea, and no land  
> appeared any longer, sky was everywhere and sea everywhere;  
> the blue waters stood above them, and rain  
> came bearing night and winter, while the waves bristled in the darkness.  
> At once the winds enveloped the sea, and black waters rose.

Thus, battered by a violent storm and placed in danger, they landed on the island of Cyprus.

[The prince of that island, whom they call *Katapant*, that is, “subordinate lord,” fearing that he might fall into the hands of the pagans, detained him from the day before the Nones of July until the day before the Kalends of August, adds Lietbert, chapter 41.]

[Chapter 41.] When they prepared to set out again for Jerusalem, they were carried back to Laodicea. But since no hope remained of going to Jerusalem, they sorrowfully undertook the return journey on the advice of the bishop of Laodicea.

[*The Life of Lietbert*, chapter 42, adds: “When many disturbances had arisen in the kingdoms of Lothair and the Franks, the emperor Henry and Henry, king of the Franks, came together for a conference in order to settle them, but they departed with the peace unfinished. Not long afterward the emperor Henry, in the presence of Pope Victor—who, having been badly treated by the Romans in matters concerning the papacy, had come to him to lodge a complaint—ended his final day.

“After his death, Count Baldwin the father and Count Baldwin the son were both reconciled with his son Henry and the queen, with the lord pope as arbiter and with the bishops and princes of the kingdom as judges, on account of the quarrels he had had with his father. Lord Bishop Lietbert attended that settlement. He was still untonsured, since, returning from his pilgrimage, he had not yet come back to his city. He had loved the count intimately from the beginning of his episcopate.”]

### 30. Concerning the Church of the Holy Sepulchre

After Pope Nicholas, as we related above in chapter 16, Anselm, also called Alexander, ruled the Roman see for nine years and six months.

[Chapter 47.] Lord Bishop Lietbert, returning from the unsuccessful journey on which, as has been said, he had desired to reach Jerusalem but had been driven back after being tossed about by various dangers on land and sea, turned his mind to another undertaking: namely, to build outside the walls of Cambrai a church in honor of the Holy Sepulchre, as it may still be seen today.

[*The Life of Lietbert*, chapter 46, presents the matter more fully as follows:

> “We shall explain more fully for what reason that little oratory was built. In the time of Lord Gerard, of holy memory, Bishop Lietbert’s predecessor, a famine arose at Cambrai and in the surrounding regions and grew so severe that the cemeteries of the city of Cambrai could not contain the bodies of the dead.

> “Lord Gerard therefore conceived the reasonable plan of having a common burial ground dug outside the city walls, which would receive the many bodies of the poor who were to be buried. Beside that place he later consecrated a church built in honor of the Lord’s Sepulchre, so that, out of reverence for so great a name, burial there might be provided for the poor and pilgrims.

> “As the years passed, he intended to improve it, but, exhausted by the burden of age, he died. Lord Lietbert himself, inspired by so great and worthy an example of his predecessor and teacher, entered upon the work of cultivating its devout beginnings. Since the church was small, he left it untouched and built beside it a monastery of larger and better design, as it is seen at present.

> “To carry out this great work, the bishop appointed as fellow workers and ministers those whom we recorded as having accompanied him on the pilgrimage to Jerusalem: namely Lord Walcher, the archdeacon, and Erlebald, judge and minister of the city.”

Everything here is reproduced verbatim from Lietbert’s charter in Miraeus, *Opera diplomatica* I, 155.]

[Chapter 49.] What he conceived in an excellent spirit, he completed most devoutly to the end. Having summoned the bodies of many saints, and with Lord Abbot Waldric assisting him, he solemnly dedicated the church, suitably constructed, in the year of Christ 1064. He established monks there to serve God, like women keeping vigil at Christ’s Sepulchre.

[*The Life of Lietbert*, chapter 49, adds:

> “It was undertaken and consecrated in the year 1064, in the second indiction, and also in the fourteenth year of the episcopate of our lord and patron Lietbert, while Pope Alexander presided at Rome.

> “And so that the monastery might not remain outside the city’s boundaries, they took care to enlarge the walls, surrounding the entire monastery building with a rampart and ditch together with the whole city. It is clear that they did this for two reasons: so that the city might be ennobled by larger buildings and a greater number of inhabitants, and so that those living around the site might be protected by the strength of the city.

> “The church which, as we have said, had remained untouched was later, as many years passed, improved and enlarged by Walter, abbot of that place, because it was collapsing from excessive age. He added relics of the saints and established there a memorial of Saint Nicholas.”]

He also had a tomb prepared for himself in the same church, in which he was buried.

[*The Life of Lietbert*, chapter 66: “There too, five years before his death, he had a tomb dug for himself. On appointed days he would revisit it; at first, lying upon it, he would drench the grave with tears and sighs; afterward he would fill it with bread, meat, or other foods, which he immediately ordered to be distributed to the poor.”]

### 31. Concerning Fulcher’s Gifts Offered to Saint Andrew

[*The Life of Lietbert*, chapter 43.]

It must not be omitted that the bishop, returning by the road mentioned above, refused to enter Cambrai before visiting New Castle, the faithful fortified town of his principality, which he honored with particular devotion because of the memory of Saint Andrew.

When he arrived there, accompanied by Lord Fulcher together with the other companions of his household, he was received with the greatest courtesy by all. After being received, he was led to pray in the church of Saint Andrew. Prostrated on the ground, he did not have to seek tears in prayer, since tears were always most familiar to him. Then, rising, he gave his blessing.

After kissing as many as he could at the proper time, he went out publicly and told everyone how many dangers he had endured on the journey. Then Lord Fulcher, in his presence, approached the altar and recounted what great things the Lord had done for him through the merits and prayers of Saint Andrew and through his glorious Mother.

After submitting his head, in the sight of everyone he gave himself to Saint Andrew, offering two ounces of the purest gold upon his holy altar. And so that perpetual service might be maintained in that place for the honor of God and the memory of Saint Andrew, on his behalf, he handed over his son named Fulcon.

After making him a monk, he bestowed great gifts of provisions upon the brothers, which he confirmed by the authority of the bishop under the force of their privileges—namely, the altar of Lelycis. In purchasing the allod of Maretz, Lord Bishop himself gave ten ounces of gold.

Fulcher also made another son a monk at Arras; we later saw him as the venerable abbot of Hunocourt.

### 32. Concerning the War in England

In the year of Christ 1066, one of the comets appeared in the western sky, extremely terrifying to behold, sending out hair-like rays like flaming spears. It followed the sun in the evening and was visible for eighteen days.

This kind of heavenly body usually portends wars, famine, or pestilence; by its very appearance it also foreshadowed a change of kingdom.

For William, count of the Normans, crossed the sea after preparing a considerable fleet and taking with him a large force. When he landed, he ordered all the ships to be completely abandoned, so that his men would have no hope of retreat.

Thus the king of the English, Harold—formerly perjured toward the aforesaid Count William, for he had sworn that he would marry his daughter [the copy reads “son”], and who had just returned from the death of his brother Tostig, who had taken up arms against him while seeking a share of his kingdom—was then roused by unfavorable messages. Gathering a huge host of English and Norwegians, he prepared for battle and advanced against the Normans, who had already built three fortifications near the seashore.

What more need be said? Battle was joined. The Normans proved victorious; the English turned their backs, and the greater part of both sides perished. King Harold too was killed and fell dead. Thus Count William obtained the kingdom and was anointed king at London on the day of the Lord’s Nativity.

### 33. Concerning the Battle Fought at Cassel  
*(Ann. 1071.)*

We have judged it worthy to insert here the battle fought in Flanders near the village called Cassel, from which other wars arose throughout the surrounding lands, together with many evils.

Robert, also called the Frisian because he had been raised in Frisia, heard that his brother Count Baldwin had died and had left behind him as heirs two sons, Baldwin and Arnulf. He was deeply grieved that for a long time he had been completely excluded by his father and brother from every honor in Flanders, since he suspected that he had not been legitimately conceived.

He could endure this no longer. Secretly entering the coastal regions of Flanders, he began, through the deceit of certain wicked men, to seize some fortifications and castles, and claimed the land for himself as far as Cassel.

When she heard this, the widowed Countess Richildis—whom we stated above, in chapter 12, had married Count Baldwin after her first husband Herman’s death—advanced against him after gathering many armies together with her two aforementioned sons, Baldwin and Arnulf. She also prepared the king of France, Philip, to assist her [the copy reads “with no forces” for “with many armies”].

[*The Life of Lietbert*, chapter 58, says:

> “But the Flemings, through whose treachery that Robert had entered Flanders, fighting deceitfully and turning their backs, caused the boy Arnulf himself to be killed in the first flower of youth. After his death and the flight of his mother, the entire marquisate fell to Robert.

> “Inflamed beyond measure by this outcome of the war, he burst into such madness that he wished to seize the rule of the city of Cambrai from the empire and subject it to his own authority. Accordingly, gathering a large army, he ravaged the villages near the city and raged throughout the entire surrounding region.

> “When he had done this not once but twice each year, reducing the whole territory of Cambrai to utter desolation, Lord Bishop repeatedly admonished him through intermediaries. He often begged him to desist from his undertaking, now by entreaty, now by payment.

> “But Robert could not even bear to listen. Inflated by the arrogance of worldly pride, he threatened not only to continue devastating the region but also to reduce the city itself to nothing unless the bishop surrendered it to him.

> “Amid these arduous labors of mortal life, amid the hidden exercises of the holy works described above, the bishop, worthy of God, was exhausted and fell into an illness which he overcame and endured with remarkable patience for three continuous years.

> “When that tyrant heard that he was sick, as though rejoicing at the shepherd’s absence, he raged again and again against the sheepfolds of the Lord’s flock. Gathering a vast army, he rushed unexpectedly upon the city, as though he intended to conquer it.

> “Lord Bishop took this very grievously and suffered more than can be expressed. He ordered that he be lifted as quickly as possible onto a carrying bed and carried through the middle of the warriors’ lines to the tyrant’s tent. He was so tormented by the pains of gout that he could not stand on his feet at all.

> “When he had been carried, as he had ordered, to the count’s tent, he saw him, gave a grave roar, and with great severity rebuked his criminal and presumptuous audacity. By episcopal authority he admonished him to withdraw from the land of his lady, Mary.

> “For he was his parishioner, insofar as the county of Arras belonged to the bishop, since at that time the churches of Cambrai and Arras obeyed one bishop.

> “Robert paid no attention. With a proud mind he mocked the bishop’s rebukes as though they were mere amusements. The bishop, supporting himself with his hands, recovered his strength and sat up on the bed. He ordered that the pastoral staff and priestly stole be brought to him. When these had been brought, he immediately excommunicated the count and his entire army until satisfaction should be made.

> “When the count saw such constancy of mind and justice in the man of God, he respected his age and the bishop’s authority—and, more truly, was struck by divine terror. At the ninth hour of the day he broke camp and, though growling and repeating his threats, withdrew as far as daylight permitted beyond the land that was being denied to him.”]

What more need be said? When battle was joined on February 22, Robert the Frisian, strong in courage and arms—or aided by fierce companions—boldly broke through and crushed the enemy’s first line. He then put the rest to flight after his nephew Arnulf, still in the first bloom of youth and not yet fit for the practices of war, had been killed in the slaughter.

King Philip himself also turned his reins and departed. At last Robert the Frisian was captured by Count Eustace and held under guard at Saint-Omer. But not long afterward the Flemings freed him by force, and he gained possession of the entire county of Flanders by power.

### 34. Concerning Lord Lietbert’s Gifts to the Church of Saint Andrew

While we have been pursuing the deeds of emperors in more extended speech, we have wandered farther from the subject of the narrative we began. Let us therefore set these matters aside for a little and turn our attention to recalling Lord Lietbert’s generosity toward this church.

Are not the altars, estates, and other benefactions that he bestowed written in the charter which, five years before his death, he came to our chapter to have confirmed?

It is pleasing to explain briefly how the altar of Lambris came to us. Lord Abbot Waldric enjoyed considerable favor and a place of intimate familiarity with the Countess Richildis of Hainaut, mother of Arnulf, whom we said was killed by his uncle, the Frisian, in the battle of Cassel. She rejoiced to receive frequent visits from him, often followed his wholesome counsel, and, insofar as worldly concerns permitted, strove to obey his admonitions.

Meanwhile, a certain Roger, a cleric of famous nobility—the provost of Saint-Omer and of Saint-Amatus of Douai—faithfully served the countess and, as procurator of her entire court, arranged all her affairs.

Gradually and silently observing the abbot’s continence and perceiving that his life was religious in every respect, Roger began to cling to him with greater affection. Thus he bestowed upon our church many gifts and tapestries that customarily hung in the presbytery, and even the altar of Lambris, with Lord Bishop Lietbert’s joyful consent. He also came to the chapter and obtained membership among the brothers, together with the provision that the anniversary of his death—which we celebrate on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of June—should always be observed in solemn remembrance.

### 35. Concerning the Village of Lambris

[*Gerard, Bishop of Cambrai, Book II, chapter 21.]

Since mention has been made of the aforesaid village, Lambris, it should be known that it was a royal estate but that, in the time of Bishop Stephen, it was given by King Charles to Saint Mary.

King Childebert was perhaps buried in this very village. When he was preparing to go and besiege his brother, who at that time was staying at Tournai, blessed Germanus, bishop of Paris, foretold with prophetic spirit that he could not complete such an undertaking if he pursued the death of his brother with such intent.

But Childebert, deaf to the blessed bishop’s words, prepared to carry out what he had decided. Yet so that the holy bishop’s prophecy would not prove vain, death overtook him on that very journey, and he was buried in the aforementioned village of Lambris.

### 36. Concerning the Venerable Pope Hildebrand

After Pope Alexander, Hildebrand, also called Gregory VII, assumed the Roman see in the year 1073.

Burning most fervently with zeal for the house of the Lord, he issued many decrees. He promulgated judgments against the incontinence of priests, decreeing that no one should hear their Masses; that their sons should in no way receive sacred orders; and that no one should receive investiture to ecclesiastical dignities from the hand of a layman. Anyone who presumed to transgress was to be entirely deprived of sacred orders.

For this reason, not only did a great conflict arise between him and the emperor, but from that time the holy Church throughout the world also suffered grave scandal. This controversy continued until the time of Pope Calixtus, the fourth pope after him.

### 37. Concerning the Death of Lord Lietbert

In the metropolitan church of Reims, Gervasius was appointed after Wido. He was a man endowed with knowledge in both fields, who devoted himself to military affairs and defended his homeland and his possessions especially with armed force.

Among other things, he devised through his own skill a cast-bronze copper stag of immense size, which may still be seen standing in the archbishop’s court. On the breast of this stag these verses may still be read:

> When Gervasius used to roam through the forests of the Cenomanni,  
> he then had deer in sufficient abundance.

Mindful that he might be remembered by his native land forever, he cast this in bronze. [(Life of Lietbert, §§22 ff.) After enduring the most serious attacks inflicted by Hugh the castellan—of whom much is related—for he was captured by him, placed in custody after the killing of the provost Wibold, and liberated by Countess Richildis—Lord Lietbert at last, weakened by old age and wearied by the service of God, suffered from a grave illness for three years; yet he never wished to be without the ministry of Lord Waldric. Thus, in the twenty-sixth year of his episcopate, on the tenth day before the Kalends of July (22 June 1076), with the clergy standing around him and praying, he happily ended his final day.]

[Col. 0267] **END OF THE SECOND BOOK.**

**[BOOK THREE.]**

**[PROLOGUE.]**

**THIS IS THE THIRD BOOK; HERE IS THE PRECEDING PROLOGUE.**

[Col. 0267C] Thus far we have described, touching upon rather than enumerating them, some of the deeds of three bishops—namely, Lords Erluin, Gerard, and Lietbert—and, as the books of the poets relate, we have in a sense recalled the golden ages that existed in their days. In this work I seem deserving of reproach, since I have presumed to record in some sort of writing the lives and deeds of such great men. For it is evident that whoever undertakes such a task displays not only the fault of his own inexperience and presumption, but also obscures, by inept words, the praises of those about whom he attempts to speak. For when the orator Homer described the virtue and deeds of Achilles, Alexander the Great, coming to his tomb, called him fortunate for having such a herald. In the preceding two books we spoke briefly of three bishops; now, in the third, mention must be made of the fourth, namely Lord Gerard II. Under him we now feel, with sorrow, that we have descended to the silver ages and, after his death, to the iron ages. Therefore the promised work must be carried out, and our discourse must be directed toward matters that we partly saw and heard in our own time.

### 1. On Lord Gerard, the second bishop

When Bishop Lietbert died (1076), and was honorably buried in the church of the Holy Sepulchre—which he himself had built from its foundations—with the greatest lamentation of clergy and people, [Col. 0268D] the entire city assembled and sent to the emperor Lord Gerard, archdeacon of Brabant and a kinsman by blood of the aforesaid Bishop Lietbert, elected with the consent of the whole people. Having received episcopal insignia from him, Gerard returned in triumph.

Then he went to Rome to receive the blessing. Pope Hildebrand, learning the purpose of his arrival, refused even to see him, declaring him excommunicated because, contrary to the decrees of the Apostolic See, the holy canons, and his own decrees, he had received the pastoral staff and ring from the hand of a layman and an excommunicate—namely, an emperor of ill repute, who, what is judged still more detestable, [Col. 0269A] was not subject to the Roman Church.

When Lord Gerard, constrained by this objection, had returned the episcopal insignia to the pope, and his companions—especially Alard, the archdeacon and provost, whom we later saw, after becoming a monk, as abbot of Marchiennes [Note: [Col. 0269D] Marchiennes.]—were afflicted with excessive grief, the pope at last, moved by the entreaties of his own people and of the cardinals, granted him his favor and sent him to be consecrated by Hugh of Die [Note: [Col. 0269D] Die in the Dauphiné. Thus I have corrected the reading, since the copy had *Hugonem Oediis*.], the venerable archbishop of Lyon and papal legate for all Gaul. Consecrated by him in due ecclesiastical form, Gerard returned successfully to his homeland, rejoicing together with his companions.

### 2. On the devastation of Cambrai

Not long afterward a reason arose that required him to visit the emperor’s court. [Col. 0269B] On his return, when he had reached the town called Laubias, he was informed that the citizens of Cambrai had formed a conspiracy and decided that no opportunity for him to enter the city would be granted. Disturbed by this news, the bishop began to consider what ought to be done. Then, having summoned a considerable force of friends, together with Count Baldwin [Note: [Col. 0269D] Of Mons.], they set out along the roads toward Cambrai.

Why say more? As they approached the gates and the inhabitants prepared to resist, they deceitfully pretended, swearing, that they had come in peace. Thus, having been allowed to enter, they quickly broke faith: they invaded houses, plundered cellars, smashed chests, and handed everything over to pillage. Carrying away gold, silver, vessels, clothing, and whatever else was desirable, they vied with one another in loading themselves with spoils in many ways. After capturing many people, each returned [Col. 0269C] to his own place. And so Lord Gerard was restored to his see.

### 3. On a certain man named Ramihrd

After this it happened that the bishop came to the village of Lambras, which at that time belonged to him, and stayed there for a little while. There he was informed by those who reported it that a certain man named Ramihrd, living in the nearby village called Scherem, was teaching many things contrary to the faith, and had already acquired, under his instruction, many disciples and a large populace of both sexes who agreed with him.

Without delay the bishop had him brought before him and questioned him about his life and teaching. When he saw that Ramihrd was answering the charges, he ordered him to be brought to the see of Cambrai so that the matter might be examined there more fully. On the appointed day, abbots and learned clerics having been summoned, he was brought into their midst and questioned about the Catholic faith.

But he professed in every respect the rule of true belief. When the bishop urged him to participate in the Lord’s sacrament as confirmation of his faith, he refused, saying that he would receive it from none of the abbots, priests, or even from the bishop himself, because they were held bound by the guilt either of simony or of some form of avarice. At these words everyone was moved to anger and declared that he was to be regarded as a heresiarch; and so the assembly dispersed.

Some of the bishop’s servants and many others led him to a certain hut and brought him inside. He did not resist, but remained fearless and, as they say, prostrate in prayer. They set fire to the hut and burned him with it. Such was the end of a man who had done and taught many things. Nevertheless, many who had attached themselves to him seized for themselves something from his bones and ashes. Members of his sect still remain in certain towns [Col. 0270B]. They are also known by his name, and practice the profitable craft of weaving [Note: [Col. 0269D] Gregory VII speaks of this matter in Letter 25, sent on 25 March 1077 to Godefrid, bishop of Paris, which Le Glay cites from Gregory’s *Register* IV.20:

“Moreover, it has been reported to us that the people of Cambrai handed a certain man over to the flames because he had dared to say that simoniacal priests and fornicating priests ought not to celebrate Mass, and that their ministry should in no way be accepted. Since this seems to us a matter of great terror and, if true, one to be punished with every severity of canonical rigor [Col. 0270D], we admonish your fraternity diligently to investigate the truth of this affair. If you discover that they extended impious hands to such cruelty, do not delay in separating from the entrance into and all communion of the Church both the authors and the accomplices of this crime; and strive to inform us by letter, as quickly as you can, of the certainty of this matter and of whatever may have been accomplished concerning the issues mentioned above.”]

### 4. On the monastery of Anchin

At approximately the same time (1079), two men of noble birth, Siger of Lohes and Walter, son of Ursion, together with many companions, abandoned secular warfare and resolved to serve God as soldiers. They chose for habitation a secluded place suited to religious life on the river Scarpe [Note: [Col. 0270D] Scarpe. For a fuller history of this foundation, see the *Anchin Continuation* of Sigebert.], surrounded by water.

They therefore approached Lord Gerard, bishop of Cambrai, since that place belonged to his parish, and asked him for permission to live there and to build a church. He not only granted what they requested, but also began to be their helper and fellow worker in the construction of buildings suitable for monks.

Hugh, too, dean of Saint Mary’s [Col. 0270C], began to devote himself to the place with every care and all his heart, supplying generously and wholeheartedly money, altars, and other necessities. Thus, in a short time, that place, exalted by God, was filled with clergy and virtuous men, and the service of God was carried on there diligently and religiously.

This community grew so greatly by God’s will that Lord Alard, a monk of Hasnon, was appointed abbot there, and nobles from the surrounding countryside and from other provinces, renouncing the world, flocked there under the rule of holy religion. This monastery, enlarged by worldly resources down to the present day, flourishes in every form of religious observance and illumines many monasteries all around it with the fragrance of holiness.

### 5. On the death of Lord Waldric, the abbot

Lord Abbot Waldric had governed this church [Note: [Col. 0270D] Saint Andrew’s.] for thirty-six years and had set before his subjects in every respect an example of good works. By his own efforts he had acquired many possessions, altars, and estates [Col. 0271A].

When the day arrived on which divine mercy was preparing to rescue him from the hardships of this world, he was suddenly seized by illness. Falling into bed, he summoned the brothers, gave them salutary exhortations, and, bidding them his final farewell, full of days, in the year of Christ our God 1083, on the Ides of June, ended his final day. He was buried in the middle of the church amid the greatest lamentation of the brothers and others.

### 6. On the election of Abbot Guiffrid

The brothers assembled to elect an abbot and chose four from among themselves. They sent them, with the pastoral staff, to the bishop, so that whichever of them he appointed abbot, the others would approve. But, judging that such an election was not satisfactory, he delayed and, having obtained a period of respite, ordered them to return.

Meanwhile Lord Peter, abbot of Beauvais [Col. 0271B], on behalf of his brother Lord Guiffrid, and the bishop of Laon, at Guiffrid’s request, sent letters of petition to Lord Gerard the bishop. Hugh the castellan [Note: [Col. 0271D] Of Oisy.] also came as a petitioner for this same man, together with many others. Encouraged by these petitions, Bishop Gerard raised Guiffrid to the dignity of abbot.

Guiffrid governed the dignity he had received vigorously for several years. But afterward, as continuous wars loomed and especially as a great famine prevailed, this church declined into poverty.

### 7. On the battle fought near the village of Castenerias

At that time a very serious dispute arose at Cambrai between the distinguished knight Oilard and John, son of Otto, over a certain village called Vinciaco [Note: [Col. 0271D] Vinchy, near Cambrai.]. They separated from one another, so that one of them—John—remained at Cambrai with his nephew Fulco and prepared for war, while the other—Odard—came to this village [Note: [Col. 0271D] Le Câteau.] and gathered a force of hired soldiers.

One day during harvest time, when both sides had gone out and, coming to the village of Castenerias [Note: [Col. 0272D] Cattenières, arrondissement of Cambrai. Le Glay.], met one another, they engaged in battle. After a fierce struggle, a few men on Oilard’s side fell, but many from the Cambrai army were killed. Ibert, the bishop’s nephew, and Ado of Belen [Note: [Col. 0272D] Bellain, arrondissement of Valenciennes. Le Glay.], distinguished men, were also killed. Fulco, together with many famous men, was captured.

Thus Oilard gained the victory and withdrew rejoicing, distributing horses and spoils most generously among his soldiers. He kept the aforesaid Fulco, his nephew, in captivity for a year; but afterward, through the intervention of the bishop and Theoderic of Avesnes, they were reconciled and remained friends.

### 8. On a woman tormented by a demon

What we saw happen here on the occasion of the aforesaid Oilard should burden no one either to read or to hear. Since this man, famous everywhere for his military power, defended the land of Cambrai with strength and arms, it happened that he once made a great raid in the district of Vermandois [Col. 0272A]. Having taken much booty and captured many people, he quickly returned with success.

A certain woman, however, grieving excessively and beyond measure over the capture of her husband and unable to endure her sharp anguish, followed alone as rapidly as she could. But it was not easy for her to catch up with them. Thus, when the day had already declined and evening was approaching, night fell. Reaching a nearby forest, unable to proceed farther, overcome by the darkness of night, grief, and bodily weariness, she wished to rest her exhausted limbs beneath a tree she had found . . . [Note: [Col. 0271D] One or two words are missing.]

### 9. On the apparition of an evil spirit

She had lain there half-awake for a long time when suddenly an evil spirit, standing before her in some visible form—as she later reported to us—approached carrying what seemed to be a cloak in his hand, put it on her, and thus took complete possession of her.

At once she leapt up, savage and wholly unaware of herself. For the remainder of the night she wandered through the forest, and when morning came she emerged from it. For a long time she roamed aimlessly through the fields until the inhabitants captured and bound her. Shouting in voices more bestial than human, she was driven to this monastery under blows.

### 10. On the liberation of the possessed woman

When she approached the threshold of the church, she recoiled as though avoiding a dreadful precipice and resisted with all her strength lest she enter. But those present pushed her—or rather carried her in—and placed her in the middle of the church on straw that had been spread there.

Although tightly bound, she rolled miserably [Col. 0272C] this way and that. Her dreadful face and blazing eyes inspired a kind of horror in those who looked upon her. Foaming at the mouth and chewing her tongue with her teeth, she spat bloody saliva upon the onlookers, so that it was plainly made known externally by what inhabitant she was tormented internally.

Moved by her terrible cries and by the noise of the crowd rushing together, we approached after several hours. Perceiving that the malignant enemy had taken up residence in her, and at the same time sympathizing with her misery, we reverently made the sign of the cross over water that had been brought with the relics of Saint Andrew and offered it to her mouth to drink.

But she angrily pushed it away from herself as far as she could, as though abhorring something deadly. The bystanders, however, forced open her mouth as she lay on her back and clenched her teeth, and began insistently pouring it into her mouth until, drawing back her breath, she received a little of the water in her throat and swallowed it.

Then you would have seen, in an instant, just as water extinguishes fire, all her fury completely abated and cooled. She seemed changed into another person and, now transformed, looked at us with a gentle face and kindly eyes and spoke in a soft voice.

As the surrounding people raised cries of praise, we could not cease either from praising or from weeping, since we saw that divine grace had manifested itself there through the merits of the holy apostle.

Immediately, freed from her bonds, she raised herself. Supporting her shaken limbs, she began slowly to move her feet, wondering how she had come there, who had carried her from beneath the tree, and how the cloak of which we spoke above had been removed from her.

But when those present explained more accurately what had happened to her, and she had fully returned to herself, she prostrated herself with tears before the altar and vowed that she would be the saint’s servant forever. Afterward, restored by food—for she had taken no nourishment for three days—and having recovered her husband, she returned home rejoicing and in good health.

### 11. On the discord between kingdom and priesthood

Pope Hildebrand [Col. 0273B] presided over the Roman See with complete religious devotion. But the emperor Henry was unwilling to agree with the Roman Church and the apostolic decrees; indeed, although excommunicated, he persecuted the bishops subject to the pope with great severity.

He claimed that his predecessors had never consented to such decrees, since they had always bestowed episcopal insignia. Moreover, victory had made him arrogant: many years earlier he had killed in battle a certain Rudolf whom the Saxons had set up as king against him. His son, the young Henry, and the marchioness Matilda also frequently prepared numerous wars against him.

After the aforementioned Hildebrand, Odo, also called Urban, succeeded him in the Roman See. He was a most wise man, first a canon of Reims, then a monk of Cluny, and afterward became pope. In ecclesiastical regulations he followed his predecessor’s footsteps in every respect.

After Gervasius, Rainoldus, keeper of the church of Tours, governed the church of Reims. Lord Gerard presided well over Cambrai. His homeland, meanwhile, was made peaceful and prosperous everywhere by the valor and prudence of the knight Oilard, whom we mentioned above. But how, and through what misfortune, the people lost so great a defender must be briefly related.

### 12. On the death of Oilard

When this man was returning one day from the court of Flanders and wished to cross the territory of Hugh the castellan, later a monk [Note: [Col. 0273D] Of Vaucelles, whose abbey he founded in 1131. Le Glay.], Hugh’s son Simon pursued him with a military force. In the little church of the village called Chaun, he shut Oilard in with only one companion—for the others had abandoned him and fled in scattered groups.

Oilard fought with remarkable courage, wielding his sword and protecting himself with his shield, until, cut down by the blows of his attackers, he slipped from their hands. Simon killed him after he had been pierced by many wounds.

Thus, after his death, his body was brought to us and buried in our cloister, where it was enclosed beneath a single marble slab. Such was his end, mourned by the whole homeland. From him we also possess many estates that he held by inheritance: at Mediolanis [Note: [Col. 0274D] Melun. Le Glay.], Beccheniis, Buhen [Note: [Col. 0274D] Bohuin. Le Glay.], Formeiis, and Fontanis.

### 13. On the plague of those afflicted by burning

In the year of Christ our God 1089, an event became known throughout the world and was recorded in the books of annals: by the just and manifest judgment of God, as the sins of the proud populace demanded it, the fire of God’s anger blazed in these regions, especially in Brabant. A miserable plague of burning afflictions arose. In the healing of many of those suffering from it, miracles of great renown were performed in several churches of the holy Mother of God, especially at Tournai, through her pious merits and glorious intercession.

Then innumerable people of both sexes flocked fearfully to the church of Tournai from different parts of the earth—not only from neighboring places, but also from distant regions and even overseas. For what each person saw happening to another’s flesh, he feared with anxious heart might happen to himself.

When they entered the church, which was entirely full of the sick, the sight was one of immense astonishment and lamentation: some, crying out with pitiful groans, were still grievously tormented by the burning plague; while the flesh of others’ feet, and of some people’s legs, had been consumed up to the knees or even the hips, leaving dry bones hanging down. Others, whose burning had already been extinguished, lay here and there like logs, unable to move anywhere except when carried.

But enough has now been said about these matters, although we must always and everywhere fear this or any other plague, and believe that divine judgments continually threaten us.

### 14. On a certain woman healed here from the burning

At the same time a certain woman, whose feet had been burned at their extremities by the aforesaid fire, was brought by cart and set down at the door of our monastery [Col. 0274C]. She uttered tearful sighs mingled with terrible cries and, carried by her attendants amid a large crowd—for everyone feared the same punishment for himself—was placed near the altar of Saint Andrew.

O, what heart of stone or mind of iron could anyone then have possessed that the weeping and sufferings of this wretched woman, continually invoking the holy apostle, would not soften at least to tears? Since no human assistance could help her in any way, the only consolation remaining was to implore the attention of divine mercy on her behalf.

Then the senior elders among us reverently took up the relics of Saint Andrew. Marking the place of the dreadful wound with them, they carried them three times around her feet in the form of a cross.

When this had been done, she gradually ceased her cries and seemed for a time to fall asleep. She saw a man with beautiful white hair, a cheerful and venerable face, and a white garment standing beside her. Just as had earlier been done with the relics, he marked the place of pain with his hand in the same manner, and all the burning was extinguished.

At once she awoke and tried to follow him as he departed. She cried out in a loud voice that Saint Andrew was present, and she was not deceived, for she had been completely restored.

We all hurried to her and saw her rejoicing beyond belief, as though revived after having recovered her spirit. We carefully questioned her about what had happened. Recalling the vision with gratitude, she gave praise and thanks to God, to the holy apostle, and to Saint Maxellendis.

But how many tears the people who rushed to the scene shed for joy, and with what jubilation they sang the hymn *Te Deum laudamus*, is something better believed than expressed in words.

### 15. On a certain brother, Albert

A certain brother of ours, Albert, was present at and assisted in witnessing this event. He was keeper of the sacred vessels and a servant of the church. What his monastic habit proclaimed, he fulfilled by the integrity of his life and conduct, insofar as this can be established by human judgment or experience.

No one should object if we briefly insert here a few—not all—of the things we saw concerning his way of life. Under Lord Abbot Waldric he received the habit [Col. 0275B] of our order. Then, learning some psalms and progressing day by day toward better things, he was eventually ordered to handle the altar vessels and perform services of this kind.

He guarded his mouth and despised his body. Beneath his outer clothing he wore a hair shirt down to his ankles. He abstained entirely from wine and more delicate foods, content with the servants’ bread; his portion of wine and the remainder of his food he carried away to the weak and sick.

No one could know with certainty, or scarcely at all, where his bed was. Rather, before the altars, wherever sleep or bodily weariness compelled him, he lay prostrate on the ground and rested.

He also confessed privately, one detail at a time, to one of our brothers—Lord Dodo, his fellow countryman and closest companion, whom we later had as abbot and overseer of the construction of this church—that the holy apostles Peter and Andrew had appeared to him and said certain things that should not be related [Col. 0275C].

What shall I say about the fact that Albert often placed bundles of firewood at night before the doors of the poor, and that wolves frequently accompanied him on the road? We also heard that he confessed that, when he was carrying alone on his shoulders one night a crucifix from Waldonicuria, all the trees beside the road bent toward him—surely because it was fitting that creation should prostrate itself before the image of the Creator.

But, so as not to prolong the account, after obtaining permission from Lord Bishop Gerard and our chapter, he set out with only one companion for Jerusalem, moved by pious intention and longing for the Lord’s [Col. 0275D] sepulchre. What happened to him remains unknown to us.

### 16. On the death of Lord Gerard, the bishop

Lord Bishop Gerard, in the sixteenth year of his pontificate, was seized by illness in this village and died in his own house when the hour of his calling came [Note: [Col. 0275D] 12 August according to the necrologies of Blessed Mary and the Holy Sepulchre of Cambrai and of the Holy Savior of Anchin; 11 August according to the Fidemiense Necrology; in Cambrai Library, MS 730, 31 July according to the *Continuation of Gaugericus*, chapter 9.].

His body was brought to Cambrai and buried in the middle of the church in the year 1092. After his death, the worst men began to emerge from every direction, and evils multiplied throughout the land of Cambrai, which had been deprived of every defender—evils that neither this page nor any other is sufficient to enumerate.

The assembly of the clergy and people of Cambrai therefore met many times to elect a bishop. But while each person presumed to speak according to his own will, they all departed together without accomplishing anything.

Finally, after many disturbances, they elected a certain cleric, Manasses, a canon and brother of the count of Soissons [Note: [Col. 0276D] John I. Le Glay.], and sent him to the emperor with great ceremony. But, accused by secret letters sent after him, he returned empty-handed and remained deprived of hope.

### 17. On the church of Arras

Meanwhile, in 1093, the clerics of Arras, seeing that the time was favorable after the great dispute among the people of Cambrai, sought an opportunity to shake their necks free from the yoke of subjection to the bishop of Cambrai. They went to Rome and laid their case before Pope Urban, tearfully imploring him to free the church of Arras, which had for so long been treated as a handmaid.

Moved by the frequent petitions of many people, especially the king of the Franks, Urban established by a privilege that the aforesaid church should henceforth and forever have the rank of a cardinal church. To strengthen this decision, he ordered a cleric of religious life, Lambert of Lille, to be ordained bishop there. Thus he separated the church of Arras from that of Cambrai [Note: [Col. 0276D] Baluzius published the account of this separation, with all the relevant charters, from the Arras codex, now at Boulogne, of the twelfth century; concerning it, see our *Annals* VIII, 406.].

### 18. On the election of Walcher

Manasses, deeply aggrieved by his rejection, went to the archbishop of Reims and earnestly begged, through his friends, that he provide him assistance [Col. 0276C]. After hearing the account of his election, confirmed by the established truth of reliable witnesses, both from Cambrai and elsewhere, the archbishop confirmed it in an assembly of the chapter of Reims.

Moreover, the people of Cambrai elected Walcher, archdeacon of Brabant and keeper of the church of Tournai, or Noyon, as bishop. Sent to the emperor, he received from him the gift of the bishopric on the day of Saint Andrew. Consecrated by the archbishop of Reims on the authority of Pope Urban, he obtained the government of the city of Cambrai.

He accomplished many distinguished deeds. He bravely destroyed many castles and fortified towns that oppressed the Cambrai region and the city. By administering justice to those who sought it, he pacified the entire province after subduing its enemies.

### 19. On the Council of Clermont

Pope Urban, coming from Rome into Gaul, assembled a council of immense numbers in the year of Christ our God 1095 at the city of Clermont, which is called *Clarus Mons*. There he issued many decrees worthy of report, established the route to Jerusalem, and dealt sufficiently and adequately with the condition of the holy Church.

Then Manasses stood in the midst and raised a protest against Lord Walcher, who had been unjustly introduced into his election and was detestably usurping the bishopric of Cambrai by invasion. To use his own words, he said: “He has intruded himself into my election.”

When the protest had ended and Walcher had answered, the astonished judges at last reached agreement and pronounced their sentence: the first election was to be considered valid, while the second, namely Walcher’s, was to be invalid.

Walcher had already withdrawn from the council, because we who had gone there with him, listening here and there, had predicted that such a judgment would be rendered against him. After the sentence was issued, Manasses was installed as bishop in Walcher’s own see. Walcher was excommunicated if thereafter he interfered in the bishopric.

We omit many details about the council, and still more about what later happened to the men themselves, including how their land of Cambrai was utterly devastated and the city was almost deserted—matters astonishing though they are—because we now consider it more than superfluous and unhelpful to recall them [Note: [Col. 0277] It seems that a word such as “discord,” “cause,” or something similar has fallen out.].

### 20. On the ordination of Manasses as bishop

When Rainoldus, archbishop of Reims, died (1096), Manasses, the provost, succeeded him. He was indeed not very learned, but devoted to almsgiving and to care for the poor. By him the aforesaid Manasses was ordained bishop.

### 21. On the journey to Jerusalem

In the year 1096, following the exhortation of the aforementioned Pope Urban, the inhabitants of the land began to undertake the road to Jerusalem, and the sound and desire to go spread as far as the ends of the earth.

Counts, princes, nobles, and common people of both sexes vied with one another in setting out. Many claimed that they saw portents and signs in the heavens. How many dangers they endured on that journey, how many bodily hardships, how great the famines, how many battles—especially at Antioch—how, through what labor and under what pressures they reached Jerusalem, and by what skill and industry they captured it on the fortieth day of the siege, after killing many Saracen soldiers; with what zeal they cleansed the Lord’s sepulchre and the holy places—this is not ours to describe. Such matters require the inscription of a more specialized and extensive book, especially since songs have been disseminated about them everywhere and certain poems have also been written.

### 22. On Lord Odo, the bishop

After the two bishops, Manasses and Walcher, had failed through their prolonged dissension over many years, Odo, a schoolmaster of Orléans who became a monk at Tournai—for that monastery began to be built through his preaching—and afterward its abbot, was elected and consecrated bishop of Cambrai (1105).

But because he did not wish to seek the imperial grant on account of the excommunication, he was entirely forbidden to enter the city.

### 23. That the emperor came to this land

Emperor Henry, repeatedly and insistently pressed by the tearful complaints of the people of Cambrai—namely, that Robert, count of Flanders, wishing to usurp dominion over the Cambrai region, had made many hostile incursions into the province and had finally surrounded the city itself with a great army and besieged it for seven days, with, it is said, seven thousand armed men ready—came into this land in 1102.

He acted bravely and successfully, burning the castles of Bulcen, Incy, Sclusa, and other fortifications, casting them to the ground, and striking fear into his enemies everywhere. But, as winter pressed upon him, he soon returned home. Yet the count did not desist from the harassment of Cambrai . . .

### 24. On comets

In the year 1106, one of the comets that presage changes of kingdoms appeared for eight days in the month of March. In the evening, after sunset, it emitted terrifying rays and struck fear into many prudent people.

Emperor Henry, whom his son had expelled from the kingdom under pretext of an apostolic sentence and driven into foreign lands, died at Liège. But because of the aforesaid excommunication, he was not buried in the atrium. His son Henry obtained the empire, which his father, while still alive, had granted him and ordered to be blessed.

### 25. On the council held at Troyes

After Urban, Rainerus, also called Paschal, received the Roman See (1099). He was praiseworthy in every respect, firmly maintaining the decrees of his predecessors, though less attentive to avarice.

Coming into Gaul (1107), he held a great council at Troyes and afterward returned to Rome.

### 26. On the arrival of the third Emperor Henry

The third [Col. 0278C] [Note: [Col. 0277D] Le Câteau.] Emperor Henry, coming into this land (October 1107) against Count Robert, who had claimed the land of Cambrai for himself, besieged Douai. But the people inside fought bravely for themselves and their homeland, strengthened by the count’s presence, and he accomplished nothing.

At last an agreement was reached—for they feared one another—and the emperor allowed him to retain whatever his father had granted him, namely this town [Note: [Col. 0278D] Rather, the fourth emperor and the fifth king.] and certain others.

Then, returning by way of Cambrai in December, he took away with him twelve sons of the city’s powerful men as hostages, so that the citizens might never defect from their allegiance to him. Thus he returned home.

### 27. That the emperor went to Rome

Not long afterward, when he arrived at Rome (1111), he met the Roman citizens and, under oath and with feigned peace, promised that he would do no injury to any of them. He swore the same thing to the pope at the entrance of Saint Peter’s church (12 February).

But as soon as he had entered the church, he broke all his promises. He seized the pope himself, who had prepared to bless him and perform the divine rites and was already coming forward, laying hands upon him while he suspected nothing of the sort. Having captured him, he had him taken outside the city [Col. 0279A] to the camp of his army, which he had left there.

What sedition and disturbance then occurred at Rome, and what division there was between kingdom and priesthood, it is not ours to explain, since no one could do so adequately. At last the pope, compelled, confirmed on oath whatever the king commanded. Thus, after this counterfeit and deceitful agreement, they departed.

Later the Romans asked the pope to excommunicate the perjured king, but he refused and never again wished to see him.

But, leaving aside what was then happening at Rome, let us return to our own affairs. As has been said, Count Robert obtained this town and frequently began to visit it, hunt, and enjoy the opportunities of the surrounding places.

Finally, he repaired the greater part of the tower that had fallen, as well as the surrounding wall, which can still be seen, except for the hall and church that Lord Gerard II built.

He himself also constructed spacious and handsome stone houses that remain to this day: one beside the church of Saint Mary at Arras, and the other in Brabant, at the village called Melun.

Thus, as long as he lived, the count held and possessed this town, as has been said.

### 28. On the death of Lord Odo, bishop

After Manasses, metropolitan of Reims, had been taken from the flesh (in 1106), Ralph, a cleric and provost of outstanding learning, was installed in his see. But a certain cleric, Gervase, relying on royal power, usurped that see for himself and at first sufficiently obstructed Ralph’s entry; afterward, however, overtaken by death, he came to rest (in 1113).

Lord Odo, bishop of Cambrai, overcome by a serious illness, had himself carried to the monastery of Anchin; there he died (June 19) and was buried in the middle of the church. His tomb, adorned with an inscribed stone, is still shown to this day.

[Note: With this inscription:

> Here lies Bishop Odo,  
> who, tested in every way,  
> was found faithful to God, though an exile;  
> he shines in heaven like a star.]

### 29. On the arrival of Lord Burchard

When this matter had thus been concluded, since in the church of Cambrai no valid election could be held because of the discord among the slanderers, the emperor was approached. After taking counsel, he sent to the bishopric of Cambrai, together with his legates, a certain cleric who faithfully obeyed him at Aachen, named Burchard.

After being received and elected, Burchard remained unconsecrated for almost two years because of the emperor’s excommunication. At last, however, through the mercy of the apostolic lord, because he had not received the gift of the bishopric from the king’s hand, he obtained the blessing.

While Count Baldwin the Younger was suffering from the long illness which he had contracted from an incurable wound, Burchard received this village and its tower from him—though not without a considerable payment made to his advisers—and thereafter restored it as free property to the jurisdiction of Cambrai.

Something must briefly be said about this Count Baldwin: he was a young man of the finest character and a cultivator of justice and peace, so much so that, in order to preserve the tranquillity of his country, he had a young man accused of theft boiled alive at Bruges in a cauldron—a death unheard-of and pitiable. Although the crowds marvelled and wept, Baldwin himself could not restrain his tears. Consequently, fear of him made wrongdoers throughout all the provinces cease entirely from their crimes.

But when he had gone to Normandy, which he was oppressing with frequent armies, he returned after receiving a mortal wound, was ill for nearly a year, and finally became a monk at Saint-Bertin. He died shortly afterward (in 1119) and rests there.

### 30. On Lord Gerland, abbot

Meanwhile, in 1117, Lord Abbot Guiffrid, wearied both by the hostile fury that was laying waste the whole country and by the famine that was oppressing the entire land with great force, held this church as a ship wandering amid the waves after losing its helm in a great storm. At last, however, coming to himself, he entered the harbor of peace and laid down the burden of his office.

We immediately held a council and elected a monk of Anchin, a man of great religious devotion and humility, Lord Gerland. Blessed by Lord Burchard, bishop of Cambrai, we received him as abbot in the year of our Lord Christ 1117.

How vigorously and prudently he governed the church entrusted to him would have become evident from the daily evidence of our affairs, had he been granted a long life.

### 31. On the succession of the apostolic lords

Paschal Raineri, whom we mentioned above, was succeeded in the Roman see by John Gaetanus (in 1118), also called Gelasius. He sat there scarcely a year; then, coming into Gaul, he died and was buried at Cluny (in 1119).

[Editorial note: The source appears to have lost something such as “successor.”]

Wido, also called Calixtus, archbishop of Vienne, was raised to the apostolic see in his place (February 1). He was a man as praiseworthy in the integrity of his conduct as he was distinguished by the nobility of his birth: he was the brother of Clementia, countess of Flanders, and therefore the maternal uncle of the younger Count Baldwin, about whom we have said something above.

This pope held the most famous council at Reims in the year of our Lord Christ 1119 (October).

[Note: The copy has MCXVIII.]

At it, archbishops, bishops, abbots, and clerics came in crowds not only from all Gaul but also from Lorraine.

At that time a certain Frederick, brother of the count of Namur, after many disputes between himself and a certain Alexander concerning the bishopric, was consecrated there by the apostolic lord.

[Note: Of Liège. LE GLAY.]

After Frederick’s death two years later, many signs are said to have occurred at his tomb. His supporters, who were also men of integrity, maintain that these signs were genuine, while his detractors contend that they were false. But only the knower of all things knows whether they were true or false.

### 32. On the death of Abbot Gerland

After Lord Abbot Gerland had governed the flock entrusted to him in this church properly for almost five years, the day of his calling had arrived. Seized by a severe fever, he died on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of May, Tuesday in Easter week (1123), and was buried before the altar of Saint Mary.

[Note: “Severe” in the copy.]

In his time Gerard, a child,

[Note: Of Crèvecoeur. LE GLAY.]

gave the allod of Fontaines to the altar of Saint Andrew for the salvation of his own soul and that of his father. A certain Gerulf, who became our monk, redeemed its arable portion for us from the canons of Saint Mary.

After Lord Gerland had been buried, Lord Dodo, a monk of honorable life, a Fleming by nation, was installed in his place. He had already begun to build the head (the principal part) of our monastery.

### 33. On the death of Emperor Henry III

After many battles and after still more campaigns in which he had made many men rebels against him, Emperor Henry finally reached an agreement with Lord Pope Calixtus, ended his life (in 1125), and was buried at Speyer with his fathers.

When his kinsmen Conrad and Frederick wished to usurp the kingdom for themselves by hereditary right, the princes of the land assembled and, abandoning them, raised a certain duke of Saxony, named Lothair, to imperial dignity.

This man, endowed with both religious devotion and military valor, also had a wife no less religious and charitable.

### 34. On the death of the count of Flanders

In the time of the aforementioned Henry, Pope Calixtus held a general council at Rome in the Lateran in the year of our Lord Christ 1123, in the month of March.

[Note: The copy has MCXIII.]

He and the emperor, after the long-standing dispute between kingdom and priesthood mentioned above, were reconciled in a firm peace.
