At that time Lord Burchard also brought before the pope a serious complaint concerning the separation of the church of Arras from that of Cambrai. The pope received his outcry kindly and appointed him a time to deal with the matter.

But death intervened (in December 1124), and he was succeeded by a certain bishop of Ostia, Lambert, also called Honorius.

[Note: “Ostiensis.”]

The latter nevertheless willingly attended to the bishop’s complaint and promised that he would determine his case; but because letters from the king of France and many others intervened, he accomplished little.

After Lord Ralph, metropolitan of Reims, had been taken from the flesh (in 1124), Rainold, bishop of Angers, was installed in his place.

At approximately the same time, Count Charles of Flanders, while he was praying prostrate in a church at Bruges (March 2, 1127), was killed by several of his knights, who had previously conspired for this very purpose, after being pierced with many wounds.

A certain castellan of his, throwing himself between the blows in order to free his lord, was likewise struck down and killed by their swords.

As soon as the fame of so great a crime spread everywhere, grief and fear struck the whole land. Immediately all the powerful men rose up to avenge the unjust death of so great a prince, especially a certain nobleman named Daniel, who was gnashing his teeth with rage. They did not cease until they had utterly wiped those murderers and all their accomplices from the land, handing them over to various and shameful deaths.

But what mourning and grief wore down the Flemish people, what battles, seditions, and fires devastated the whole country, we do not have space to recount, since it is impossible to commemorate them in words or writing.

Many composed songs in a mournful voice about the death of this count. Among them, one monk composed a sorrowful but memorable poem in metrical verse, which we have decided to insert here, both to honor its author and to arouse the reader’s admiration:

> Come here, Calliope;  
> let her supply me with strength.  
> I am composing a mournful song  
> about a noble prince,  
> whom Dacia produced,  
> born of royal stock.  
>
> His mother was Athala,  
> the daughter of a Frisian.  
> His father, made a victim  
> in a church,  
> endured death for justice  
> in Dacia.  
>
> But our Charles,  
> secretly carried off by enemies,  
> fled to his uncle,  
> the count of the Flemings.  
>
> There, at the court of the marquis,  
> the royal offspring grew in wisdom  
> and in the grace of good conduct.  
>
> When the illustrious uncle  
> died,  
> they set Baldwin  
> upon the ancestral throne.  
>
> To neighboring kings  
> he was a terror to them all;  
> he cultivated his homeland  
> and was an enemy to injustice.  
>
> His fragile flesh  
> broken by an incurable illness,  
> he became a monk at Sithiu,  
> and Charles succeeded him.  
>
> Under his rule, Flanders  
> flourished in military strength;  
> under his government  
> religion blossomed.  
>
> He increased the glory of the fathers  
> and the power of the counts;  
> he joined many lands  
> to the borders of the Flemings.  
>
> Alas, alas, great marquis,  
> worthy of a kingdom’s throne,  
> worthy in form to be a prince,  
> worthy of so great a name!  
>
> Alas, father of the Church,  
> glory of our Flanders,  
> avenger of injustice  
> and defense of France,  
> foremost leader of the good,  
> pious defender of the clergy,  
> shield of monks,  
> terror to all evil men!  
>
> While you were count of the Flemings,  
> the roads were at peace,  
> and no one dared  
> disturb your country.  
>
> Now we have become prey;  
> we are plundered on every side.  
> When the shepherd is dead,  
> the sheep are scattered for pillage.  
>
> No one follows what is just,  
> and peace dies with you;  
> with the head cut off,  
> the limbs fight everywhere.  
>
> Mourn, weep, Flanders,  
> like a daughter for her father.  
> You have no consolations;  
> your glory is perishing.  
>
> Call the neighboring kingdoms  
> to lamentation,  
> and let mourning strike the heavens  
> at your funeral.  
>
> When he did justice,  
> he suffered envy;  
> for the cause of the poor  
> he endured martyrdom.  
>
> Therefore, for justice,  
> he is crowned with glory.  
> It would be more fitting to rejoice,  
> but we cannot.  
>
> Desolation continually compels us  
> to weep,  
> for in his absence  
> everything is thrown into confusion.  
>
> The sea and England weep,  
> and all Normandy;  
> France, you more than they,  
> but less than Flanders.  
>
> Flanders, wretched as you are,  
> beat your breast;  
> tear your cheeks with your nails,  
> and do not spare your tears.  
>
> From here Italy grieves,  
> and all Sicily,  
> harsh Germany also,  
> and Lorraine.  
>
> For our misery  
> strikes the innermost parts of the earth,  
> and distant Thule  
> grieves together with Dacia.  
>
> Glacial Rhodope  
> is stunned by so great a crime.  
> Getic Ismarus  
> and Bosphorus, shut off,  
> should weep, and Spain  
> joined with Galatia.  
>
> Nor should Greece rejoice  
> while Flanders weeps.  
>
> O wretched Flemings,  
> may the open gate of hell  
> devour you utterly  
> and never vomit you forth again.  
>
> What madness, servants,  
> drove you to such deeds?  
> Like Judas,  
> you betrayed your own lord.  
>
> You have surpassed by far  
> the crime of the Lemnian women,  
> and your crimes exceed  
> the deaths wrought by the Danaans.  
>
> Therefore you have become  
> companions of the lost Judas;  
> with him, in punishment,  
> an abode awaits you.  
>
> Indeed, you have almost  
> made the innocent man wretched.  
>
> For the one who betrayed the Lord  
> fulfilled prophecy;  
> by betraying the Lord  
> he benefited many.  
>
> But your betrayal  
> brings destruction to many.  
>
> He, unknowingly, did  
> what would benefit the greater number;  
> but your madness  
> will harm many.  
>
> I never cease to ask  
> what punishment could be made  
> equal to your crime,  
> yet I find none.  
>
> No punishment is worthy  
> of such a sacrilegious people.  
>
> Every kind of torment  
> awaits you.  
> Tantalus has been purged;  
> his place belongs to you.  
>
> All the hosts of the guilty  
> yield before you.  
> Ixion now leaps;  
> he leaves his wheel to you.  
>
> You must roll  
> the endlessly revolving stone.  
>
> The machinery of the world is stunned;  
> the hidden places of Dis tremble;  
> the stars of heaven shudder  
> at crimes so unspeakable.  
>
> And we ourselves shudder;  
> with this we bring the poem to an end,  
> lest the memory of such deeds  
> defile the ages.

### 35. On the counts of Flanders

When this had thus been concluded, after the country had suffered disturbances of many kinds, the king of the Franks came to Arras (March 20, 1127) and appointed as count of Flanders a certain young man of the noblest character, William the Norman, son of Count Robert of Normandy, who was brother of the king of the English.

Not long afterward, while he was acting bravely against those who resisted him and was oppressing by a severe siege a certain castle that opposed him,

[Note: Aalst.]

he was suddenly deprived of life after receiving a mortal wound in the hand (in 1128). He was buried at Saint-Bertin amid great grief among his own people and even the lamentation of his enemies.

After him a certain Theodoric of Alsace, of the lineage of the counts of Flanders, who had already claimed certain parts of Flanders for himself, possessed the whole land after William’s death; and thus at last Flanders came to rest.

### 36. On the death of Lord Burchard, bishop

Lord Bishop Burchard, after governing the church of Cambrai for sixteen years, departed this life in the year of our Lord Christ 1129, on the day before the Nones of January, and was buried in the monastery of Saint Mary.

After him the church itself lacked episcopal administration for fifteen months.

### 37. On Gregory’s arrival in this land

At that same time, after Pope Honorius had died by night at Rome (February 14, 1130), a certain faction of the cardinals buried him immediately at dawn, almost secretly, and installed one of their own, Gregory, whom they also called Innocent, in the Roman chair (February 15).

When the other cardinals and part of the citizenry learned of this, they hurriedly assembled, dug up the buried body, completed the proper funeral rites, and buried it again according to apostolic custom. Then they installed one of their own, namely Peter Leonis, whom they called Anacletus, as pope.

Thus each of them—that is, both the aforesaid Gregory and Peter—did not hesitate, with criminal audacity, to usurp the holy see for himself.

When the Roman people, shamefully flattering the rivalry of the two men, were thrown into an uproar by a two-sided sedition, many men were killed, and at the very entrance of the church abominable murders were committed for the sake of obtaining the pontifical see.

O lamentable misery of the ecclesiastical order! O miserable and blind folly of learned men, when experts in divine law violently and not without bloodshed strive to become rulers of the Church—and, what is more grievous, apostolic rulers!

While they were contending in this sacrilegious spirit, one of them, Peter, prevailed because he was supported by the stronger Roman faction and obtained the see. The other, Gregory, fled from Rome, came into Gaul, and was received as pope by the metropolitan of Reims and especially by the abbot of Clairvaux.

[Note: Saint Bernard.]

He came into these provinces. Passing through Cambrai and traveling to Liège for a conference with the emperor, he heavily burdened the churches, including ours, with expenses.

At that very assembly at Liège, Lord Liettard, provost of Utrecht and elected bishop (in March 1131), was sent to the city of Cambrai. He was honorably consecrated at Reims on the sixth day before the Kalends of May by the metropolitan lord and was installed in the episcopal see.

### 38. On the departure of Lord Peter, abbot

At approximately the same time (in 1131 or 1132), our Lord Abbot Peter approached Bishop Liettard and, having laid down his abbatial dignity, departed released from office.

Six months later, Lord Adam, a monk of Saint Vincent of Laon, succeeded him in the year of our Lord Christ 1132. On the thirteenth day before the Kalends of July, he was solemnly consecrated by Lord Bishop Liettard in the church of Saint Aichadri at Haspre, and on that same day was received by us with due honor as the seventh abbot of this place.

### 39. On the devastation of this village and the burning of our churches

In the following year, 1133, while our church was flourishing in peace, religious quiet, and every kind of abundance, and while the village itself, enlarged with spacious houses and rich resources, was being inhabited in peace and joy, Gerard surnamed Malusfiliaster—long the worst enemy of this village from the time of his childhood and still breathing out his wickedness against it—assembled an innumerable multitude of foot soldiers and knights on the fifth day before the Kalends of May, summoned also the count of Hainaut, invaded the village, and ordered fire to be set to the huts outside it.

As if to supplement his wickedness, though we believe by divine judgment, a violent wind suddenly rose from the southern regions as he arrived. Serving, so to speak, his will, it seemed to rage so fiercely that, by fanning the fire and adding strength to it, it spread the flames throughout the village.

As the fire burned fiercely and raged along the ground in every direction, all the houses were consumed utterly more quickly than can be believed.

Our church, together with all its buildings, and the churches of Saint Martin and Saint Andrew, along with the episcopal residence, were burned by the raging flames and presented a dreadful spectacle.

Meanwhile men with women, young people with children, surrounded by the pressure of the flames, fled here and there from the face of the raging fire. At last, vainly hoping that the castle would provide them with a safe refuge, they burst into it in groups, but did not escape the danger of death.

For when the flying fire seized the bishop’s residence and the other buildings, all those who had taken refuge within the castle enclosure were hemmed in by the raging flames and had no avenue of escape. The stronger members of both sexes escaped by leaping over the wall.

You could see others falling headlong from the wall and scarcely able to rise after their limbs had been broken. Others—that is, the children—unable to go anywhere, but embracing one another—O pitiable sight!—were burned by the fire in one place, as many as twelve together, so that when they were later sought, scarcely anything but their heads and larger bones could be found. These were carried away in a single vessel and buried in our courtyard.

### 40. On the expulsion of Provost Adam from the Tower

Adam, whom his father-in-law—the provost, who was setting out for Jerusalem—had appointed provost and keeper of the tower, saw that, amid the present fire and the danger posed by the hostile people—for the armed hand of the enemy was also pressing around him—nothing remained to him by which he could resist Gerard’s strength or devices.

Having secured an agreement that he might leave freely, he surrendered the tower.

Thus Gerard gained possession of what he had always wickedly desired, and possessed it in the worst manner.

Once he had obtained his wish, he poured out the strength of his wickedness throughout the surrounding region,

[Note: Read “virus,” poison, for “vires,” strength. PERTZ.]

and, harassing the city of Cambrai itself repeatedly, laying waste the entire neighborhood, burned villages and oppressed the people with frequent plundering and levies.

Not to say more, throughout the whole country grievous evils and murders multiplied by his hand. I am already weary of recounting more about these things.

### 41. On the astonishing darkness that arose during the day

After this, when three months had passed, on the fourth day before the Nones of the following August, Wednesday, at the sixth hour of the day, the sun suddenly became visibly dark, and darkness came over the whole earth. While we were engaged in divine worship, it lasted for nearly half an hour.

This event shook everyone’s minds with wonder and astonishment at once. Certain men who thought themselves wiser said that a solar eclipse had occurred because the moon had come between us and the sun.

Reason clearly shows that this could not have happened—namely, that the sun can be eclipsed by the moon only at new moon—since it is certain that on that day the moon was twenty-four days old.

[Note: There was a total solar eclipse throughout Europe, Africa, and Asia on August 2, 1133. LE GLAY.]

Others, more plausibly, asserted that this sign of darkness foretold some new portent.

Much later, men returning from Jerusalem reported that on that very day, at the very hour of the darkness, five fewer than four hundred soldiers of the Temple had been killed by the Saracens across the river.

Nor is it surprising if God was pleased to bring darkness upon the world at the slaughter of his members, since at the death of Christ the sun and the whole world are known to have been darkened.

### 42. Conclusion of the work

From the beginning of the world until the present year, which is the year 1133 from the Lord’s incarnation, the nineteenth year of the cycle, while Lothair holds the scepter of the Roman Empire; while Gregory, called Innocent, and Peter Leonis are disputing the apostolic see; while Louis is king of the Franks, Rainold is archbishop of Reims, and Lord Liettard is bishop of Cambrai—from the beginning of the world until now, 6227 years have elapsed.

The remaining time of the age is uncertain to human investigation. For the Lord Jesus removed all inquiry concerning this matter when he said: “It is not for you to know the times or moments which the Father has placed in his own power” (Acts 1:7).

And elsewhere: “But of that day and hour no one knows, neither the angels of heaven, except the Father alone” (Matthew 24:36).

Therefore let each person reflect upon his own departure, as Holy Scripture says: “In all your works remember your last end, and you will never sin” (Ecclesiasticus 7:40).

For whenever a person departs from the world, for that person the end of the world has arrived.

## Around the year of the Lord 1080. Godfrey, monk of Stavelot

# Historical Notice concerning Godfrey

*(Chappeaville, Those who wrote the deeds of the bishops of Tongeren, Utrecht, and Liège, the principal authors, II, 516–575.)*

The author of the *Triumph of Saint Remaclus concerning the monastery of Malmedy* was a religious of the Order of Saint Benedict from the monastery of Stavelot, as is clear from the prologue to Book II. He was learned in the sacred writings, as anyone who reads this work can see.

He wrote this *Triumph of Saint Remaclus concerning Malmedy* accurately and faithfully, since he partly witnessed the events described in it and partly heard them from trustworthy people, as he himself testifies about himself in Book I, chapters 18 and 26, and elsewhere.

He flourished around the year 1085 from the Lord’s incarnation.

We have taken this work from an ancient manuscript codex of the monastery of Stavelot.

# The Triumph of Saint Remaclus concerning the monastery of Malmedy

## Prologue to the Triumph of Saint Remaclus

[Note: Concerning this entire history, the following should be read: first, the bull of Pope Leo IX, which we attach at the end of this history; second, the document and declaration of Frederick, archbishop of Cologne, which we have arranged to have printed at the end of the second chapter of this volume; third, the *Deeds of the Abbots of the Monasteries of Stavelot and Malmedy*; fourth, Lambert of Hersfeld in his chronicle, and the material found in chapter 2 of the work of Giles of Golden Valley. On the occasion of these works we have appended the *Triumph of Saint Remaclus* here.]

To the brothers of the churches of God that are throughout the Roman world: the brothers of Stavelot send greetings and sincere good peace.

In the reign of Henry IV, later Augustus of the Romans, in the year of the Lord 1071 and the fifteenth year of his reign, we write to you about what was done concerning Remaclus, the life-giving confessor of God, and concerning us, his servants, and our place. We write with hearts rejoicing in the Lord, although previously severe grief and tribulation had weighed upon us on both sides, within and without.

But since God has magnificently delivered us from all these things, through both the prayers of you who sympathized with us and the intervention of the merits of that same patron of ours, Remaclus, we give him fullest thanks, since we remain faithful to such a lord, always exposed to evils, persevering to the end.

Since, therefore, on the seventh day before the Ides of May, this celebration of divine action is to be commemorated by every generation, and since it was clearly seen to have taken place for the honor of so great and incomparable a confessor of Christ, we have considered it fitting to inform you, so that you too, if you wish, may celebrate the day of his glorification—the day on which it pleased God to make his power known among his people (Psalm 76), so that by his grace he might exalt the meek for salvation (Psalm 149).

Therefore, now and always, magnify God with us, and let us exalt his name together (Psalm 33), for he is rightly proclaimed wonderful in his saints (Psalm 67) throughout the ages.

Indeed, I would wish to raise him up, however inadequately, with our praises for these wondrous deeds. But before his excellent magnificence, by which he made this saint commendable in every virtue, our feeble intellect collapses.

Therefore we must beseech the grace of the Holy Spirit, who cooperates with him, to raise us up, so that, with the support of truth inspiring us and in simplicity of words, the history of pure narration may run freely.

For we must not make it come forth in public, adorned with the falsehood of any art, like some little prostitute, in pompous language seeking only the applause of popular favor. Rather, it should proclaim, in humble and simple speech, what and how great the things are that God has done with us.

Therefore, as has been said, since the wondrous God glorifies his bishop, we shall explain in their proper places how he made him wondrous through equally divine benefits.

But for now, lest by lingering too long we prolong the preface with something repetitive, let us proceed through this first work from its beginning, treating one by one the events worthy of remembrance.

# Table of chapters of Book One

**Chapter I.** On the dispute between the monasteries, repeatedly pursued, and on the many-year efforts of the bishops of Cologne concerning it, frustrated.

**Chapter II.** On the agreement of the men of Malmedy with Bishop Anno, and on the transfer of the body of Saint Ailulf to Cologne.

**Chapter III.** On the simultaneous conspiracy of Cologne and Prüm, and on the abbeys of Corbie, Lorsch, and Stavelot; and on their unjust transfer to them by the king.

**Chapter IV.** On the court held at Trier, and on the confirmation there of the transfer, while the abbot was unaware.

**Chapter V.** Abbot Theodoric and Duke Frederick deliberate together; a fortification is built over Malmedy; they are summoned together to court; but the duke, rejecting the matter, complains of the injustice to the king through an intermediary.

**Chapter VI.** The duke rebukes his nephew Conrad concerning the advocacy of Malmedy; and when the abbot is compelled to go to court, he sends the agent Roricus, who, after being abandoned by the king, is detained for a long time.

**Chapter VII.** The duke’s death, followed by mourning and misery; and how, as he had ordered, he is buried at Stavelot.

**Chapter VIII.** The archbishop sends Conrad to claim Malmedy for himself and to choose an abbot; Abbot Theodoric demands from the monks the promise made to him.

**Chapter IX.** The men of Malmedy are confirmed by oaths to the bishop; a severe persecution is carried on against our men; the body of our saint is brought forth publicly.

**Chapter X.** Tegeno is placed over Malmedy as abbot; but our abbot goes to Godfrey, marquis of Lombardy, for help.

**Chapter XI.** An account of the nature, character, and differing qualities of the two dukes, Frederick and Godfrey.

**Chapter XII.** Our abbot restores the saint’s body to its place; under threat of divine judgment he adjures the abbot placed over him to depart and abandon what he has unjustly possessed.

**Chapter XIII.** Duke Godfrey, having been made duke, rightly decides that the saint’s property ought to be restored to him. The bishop, delaying, did not agree to do this; and after our church and treasury had been stripped, our case remained unsuccessful.

**Chapter XIV.** The saint’s body is carried to the court at Aachen, where, by order of the bishop, it is received without any honor.

**Chapter XV.** While we mourn and proclaim our case together with the people, the insolent bishop of Speyer orders our soil to be carried away. Finally, with great sorrow and together with the saint’s body, we depart from there.

**Chapter XVI.** The king, seized by a serious illness, promises to restore everything to the saint; the bishop, likewise weighed down by grief, makes the same promise, but shortly afterward withdraws from it.

**Chapter XVII.** After the archbishop of Trier dies, Anno, whom he had unwillingly installed, is found with him; that insolent bishop of Speyer, like an unclean dog, is struck and driven away in disgrace.

**Chapter XVIII.** Again the abbot obtains from the king permission to reclaim the place; he returns to Malmedy and, bringing the saint’s body with him, restrains everyone—monks and laymen alike—under oath to the prelate.

**Chapter XIX.** The abbot comes to Rome and pursues his cases before Pope Alexander. The pope also sends letters to Cologne on his behalf, but all this was in vain.

**Chapter XX.** Gerlasius, the bishop’s agent, again invades Malmedy in the bishop’s name; but after hearing an uncertain report, he hastens his return.

**Chapter XXI.** The abbot returns from Rome, helped little by the apostolic letters. Indeed, persecution is renewed against him and us through a certain fierce man named Fredelo, and through Gerard, who afterward, by God’s judgment, was ruined.

**Chapter XXII.** The bishop travels to Rome, and the abbot follows him. They are examined before the pope and the senate and finally dismissed without any advantage to us.

# Table of chapters of Book Two

**Chapter I.** How, while the bearers of Saint Remaclus’s body were traveling toward Liège, those behind complained that they were being dragged by those in front, while those in front complained that they were being pushed by those behind.

**Chapter II.** On the relics of Saint Simetrius, and how a path was shown through the air by night from the oratory at Stavelot to the house of Saint Lambert.

**Chapter III.** The bishop of Liège comes out to meet the holy body and receives it honorably with all the clergy and people.

**Chapter IV.** The king regrets his injustice; the bishop of Vercelli admonishes the archbishop concerning it; the archbishop firmly refuses.

**Chapter V.** The archbishop leaves the brothers prostrate at Saint John’s on the island, with an uncertain answer.

**Chapter VI.** Supplication directed toward God, and the pious compassion of the clergy and laypeople who were watching.

**Chapter VII.** The saint’s shrine is lifted from the altar with a sound, and great consolation is given to those who witness it.

**Chapter VIII.** The brothers surround the king during the meal; the bishop of Bamberg postpones justice until the following day.

**Chapter IX.** They bring the saint’s body immediately onto the table, and, complaining about the delays, ask for justice.

**Chapter X.** The brothers follow the king and bishop as they leap up from the table, but are forbidden access to the palace. When the body is brought back onto the table, the structure itself collapses to the ground.

**Chapter XI.** Gonterul’s crushed and broken shinbone is restored; he is brought as far as the royal doors.

**Chapter XII.** A blind woman there receives her sight.

**Chapter XIII.** The bishop rebukes the disturbed king and orders the body returned to the sanctuary. At last chamberlains are sent, but in vain, for the body remains immovable like a stone.

**Chapter XIV.** The bishop, interpreting all these things as illusions, orders the saint’s body to be removed from the midst; but those sent return empty-handed, offering money for this very purpose.

**Chapter XV.** The king sends the bishop of Liège and his chancellor to the brothers, but accomplishes little.

**Chapter XVI.** The abbot himself comes in the evening with the bishop of Utrecht to satisfy the king. When the bishop descends, the brothers keep vigil there through the night in vain.

**Chapter XVII.** Of two blind men sitting there, one unexpectedly receives his sight.

**Chapter XVIII.** Of a dove seen by certain people coming forth from the shrine.

**Chapter XIX.** Of a jongleur who, during the vigils, extended songs about these events, and of the king listening and spending the night in woolen garments and barefoot.

**Chapter XX.** When morning came, by common agreement the holy body was carried back to the sanctuary.

**Chapter XXI.** The king prepares torments and punishments for the brothers, and the saint’s body is sent to the bishop of Bamberg.

**Chapter XXII.** After a considerable disturbance in the church, the saint’s shrine is lifted a cubit into the air; and while the bishop of Cambrai prays in the crypt, he is visited by the presence of God and the saints.

**Chapter XXIII.** Sayings of the saints are recalled as examples.

**Chapter XXIV.** A woman severely contracted is carried to the saint and immediately healed; as the people flock to this event, the church is filled.

**Chapter XXV.** The great bell gives a sound without anyone striking it; a multitude of sick people are restored to their former health more quickly than words can tell.

**Chapter XXVI.** A certain cripple in the crypt, in the presence of the bishop of Cambrai, is raised up; another, weaker than the former, carried by two chamberlains, is restored to health before all the people.

**Chapter XXVII.** While the minds of the king and archbishop remain in doubt concerning these things, a certain man brings before them the staff of a paralytic who had been healed, under oath upon his own head.

**Chapter XXVIII.** The bishop of Cambrai announces what both men had seen; and, when the king is terrified, the archbishop restores the property by means of the staff that he held in his hand.

**Chapter XXIX.** The king, breaking into the church with the force of his men, takes the saint’s staff and restores the property after humbly making satisfaction; a certain cripple is raised at that same hour.

**Chapter XXX.** An account of why the saint’s body, once carried to Aachen, performed nothing similar there, but did so here, in its own episcopal see.

**Chapter XXXI.** Of a certain matron of that city who had lost her sight and was restored to her former vision.

**Chapter XXXII.** Of a woman born blind who was granted sight.

**Chapter XXXIII.** Of a miserable man with a swelling on his head who was healed.

**Chapter XXXIV.** Of a seven-year-old girl who was paralyzed and healed.

**Chapter XXXV.** Of a cleric whose feet had been twisted from birth and who was healed.

**Chapter XXXVI.** On the following morning, counsel is held that the glorified body should be returned to its place.

**Chapter XXXVII.** Of the halt made for them at the Meuse; of the extremely celebrated praise of the schoolboys; and of the transfer of that place, confirmed to the saint by its possessors.

**Chapter XXXVIII.** A joyful return to their own place and the reclamation of Malmedy; and, on the following morning, as they were traveling toward Stavelot, the sitting of unknown little birds upon the saint’s shrine and the restoration of the saints’ bones to their proper place.

# Book One

## Chapter One

On the dispute between the monasteries, repeatedly pursued, and on the many-year efforts of the bishops of Cologne concerning it, frustrated.

[Note: Col. 0292D. The supplied source breaks off here.]

1. Since it is evident that the saint of whom we speak, Saint Remaclus, built these two monasteries, Stavelot and Malmedy, so that they might be governed by one abbot, although they belonged to different dioceses, this is clear from Harigerus, book I, chapters 55 and 56, and still more clearly from the document and declaration of Frederick, archbishop of Cologne, found in this second volume, chapter 2, note 1, where we read:

> “We carefully reread the privileges of the Church of Stavelot, in which it was found that blessed Remaclus, founder of both places—namely, Malmedy and Stavelot—after building Malmedy, chose Stavelot as the principal place of residence and burial for himself and his successors; and because that same place is a parish in the diocese of Liège, all the abbots of both places in succession ought to be consecrated by the bishop of Liège,” etc.

2. This matter was often treated absurdly in secret disputes. That frequent disputes over precedence took place between the religious of Stavelot and Malmedy is clear from the document and declaration of Archbishop Frederick mentioned shortly before, where he says:

> “The people of Malmedy have hitherto tried so far to invalidate this that, in the time of Otto II of blessed memory,” etc., as you may read in the passage cited above.

[Col. 0291C]

Since it was therefore evident that the saint of whom we speak, Remaclus, had built these two monasteries, whom almost the whole of Gaul rejoices to possess as its singular patron before God, and that he had left them to his successors under the same arrangement by which he had governed them—namely, that, although the two were not far apart, under one ruler and one law they should be of one heart and one soul (Acts 4)—it was always characteristic of the one party to suffer from a kind of disease, preferring disagreement to sincerely maintaining the bond of brotherhood.

This disease, I say, was of the soul: because one of the monasteries looked toward the metropolitan see of Cologne, while ours was enclosed within the bounds of the parish of Liège, those who belonged to the former party sought either to claim the right of domination for themselves or to provoke a quarrel in violation of the agreement.

This absurd matter, often pursued in secret disputes, when it occasionally came into the open, [Col. 0292C] was suppressed and obscured by privileges and the authority of our superiors. The archbishops of Agrippina themselves, drawn into this matter, by their fruitless efforts made our predecessor bishops wearied but not moved, whether through opportunity or force.

But now, because this period was advancing according to the wishes of those to whom every good thing was harmful, and because corrupt morals—and ambition, which has compelled many mortals to become false—had found the agreement of rulers, they undertook to accomplish what, although it had long been pursued with sufficient effort, had not previously succeeded.

From the beginning, one man succeeding another, each taking up the cause in order to perpetrate this fine deed, they had dragged it on into these unfortunate times of ours, always striving to make it happen.

## CHAPTER II. The agreement of the people of Malmedy with Bishop Anno, and the translation of the body of Saint Ailulf to Cologne.

[Note: [Col. 0293D] At that time they possessed the body of a certain man of tested holiness and faith, whom they call Ailulf. This is, I think, the same person whom Molanus names Agilolphus in *The Birthdays of the Saints*. He speaks of him as follows:

“Cologne: the feast and translation of Saint Agilolphus, archbishop and martyr of that city. He is said to have come to Joppila, according to the *Life of Saint Switbert*, on the Kalends of March, to the sick prince Pippin, and to have labored greatly to prevent him from naming as heir Charles Martel, born of the concubine Alpais. Yet he could not obtain this.

“Afterward he suffered martyrdom in the Ardennes district of Amblava, which place is so called from the name of the river flowing past it. He was buried in the church of Saint Lawrence adjoining the monastery of Malmedy and became famous through various miracles.

“Of him it is written at Malmedy in the book of the miracles of Saint Quirinus the martyr: ‘Born of noble stock, he was entrusted by his parents to Anglinus, abbot of this place, to be regularly trained under monastic discipline. Imitating the conduct of his spiritual father, he became his successor according to the will of God. Then appointed bishop of the see of Cologne, he did not lay aside the burden of the abbacy until, governing both offices with the greatest vigor, he was crowned with martyrdom at Amblava for the sake of the kingdom’s faith; and here among us, where he had presided as abbot in name and in deed, he had a place of burial for as long as God willed.’

“The commonly circulated Cologne chronicle, however, says that he was killed by enemies while being sent by Martel to the Saxons on a mission of peace, and that he was carried by Bruno, who was the brother of the emperor Otto, to Cologne, to the Steps. But I do not hesitate to assign the bishop’s death to the time of the son or grandsons of Martel, who also fought against the Saxons, because letters of Zacharias, who became pontiff after Martel’s death, were addressed to him concerning the reception of the legate Boniface.

“Furthermore, the *History of Saint Anno*, which deserves great credence, testifies that the body of Saint Agilolphus was carried from Malmedy to Cologne by Saint Anno, who deposited it in his monastery at the Steps.

“Malmedy is the second abbey of Saint Remaclus, dependent on Stavelot; formerly it belonged to the diocese of Cologne, but now, unless I am mistaken, it belongs to the territory of Liège, with respect to both jurisdictions. For while blessed Poppo presided over these places, he established by perpetual law that the people of Malmedy should make their profession of religious life at Stavelot.

“His feast falls on the last day of March; but the people of Cologne commemorate him together with his translation on 9 July, because at the end of March the Church is always occupied with the observance of Lent or with the Passion or Resurrection of the Lord.”]

The feast of Saint Peter called *ad Vincula* was at hand, and on it a royal court happened to be held among us, with a great attendance of nobles. The king was still a very young boy and had not passed beyond the years of childhood, but his mother, the empress, was sufficiently exercising the functions of government on his behalf.

Among many fellow bishops there was also Anno, archbishop of Cologne. Later, not without injury to royal dignity, he did not hesitate to transfer the right of domination to himself by a rash act: laying hands upon his lord and, as if under the pretext of protection, forcibly taking the boy away from his mother.

Because he was a man of great ability and a keen intelligence, the monks of Malmedy approached him. They thought it would be useful and advantageous to consult such a man about the purpose of their plan. After several steps by which they cautiously brought him into their intimacy, they invited him to their place, Malmedy, for a visit, and made him the guardian of their affairs, as though all their hopes and resources lay in him, thereby securing him as the ally of their fortunes.

At that time they possessed the body of a certain man of tested holiness and faith, whom they call Ailulf, and whom the annals also report to have first been abbot of Stavelot and afterward archbishop of Agrippina. By a wicked suggestion they urged Anno to request this man for himself from Lord Abbot Theoderic, so that, once he had been transferred, they might hope that the place would, as it were through him, come under his authority. Whether this was done with his consent, we do not know; nevertheless, we regarded what happened as disgraceful.

The lord abbot, as though unaware of the matter, did not delay granting the request when asked to do so. Later, although he did not perceive it at the time, this became clearly the occasion of all the evil that followed. For, as many then indicated by a kind of foreboding of evil, from that moment almost everything went against him in dealing with them.

The archbishop therefore received the venerable relics of the saint mentioned above and reverently placed them in a fitting location, with the honor due to a martyr of Christ.

## CHAPTER III. The conspiracy jointly formed by Cologne and Bremen, and the unjust royal transfer to them of the abbeys of Corvey, Lorsch, Stavelot, and Inda.

[Note: [Col. 0295D] That royal administration and protection was transferred to another person, namely the archbishop of the Church of Bremen. It should be read *Bremenensis*—“of Bremen”—as Lambert of Hersfeld reads it in his *Chronicle*.]

After this, certain men who were called counselors among them, and who were the authors of this undertaking, as it seemed . . . went to Cologne. There, with the archbishop having confirmed the plan, they returned home having obtained the fulfillment of the intention and desire we have mentioned.

On their return, they are said to have brought this message from the archbishop to their associates, insolently taunting us but rejoicing among themselves: that they should have no distrust of him or of his promise; that he would assist them in every kind of help, like a father; and, moreover, that he was as confident as if he already held them in his hands, together with the place and all its property.

By these words they were led into a confident hope and boasted that henceforth they would be more fortunate than we, since they would be able to live under him more peacefully and for a longer time, exactly as they wished.

And lest I be accused of inventing falsehoods as facts, I call upon certain suitable witnesses from among them: namely, Lambert, one of those who had approached the bishop, is said to have spoken these words. He was later overtaken by premature death and left his plan unfinished in the midst of life.

Let no one therefore suppose that we recall these evils concerning our fellow brothers because we would rather they had acted wrongly than rightly. But we consider it a sin to pass over in silence anything that the nature of the work undertaken requires us to say.

From that time, therefore, the archbishop directed his mind toward the matter, contriving and seeking every possible opportunity to obtain possession of it. His energetic and capable intelligence did not allow him to trust that any undertaking could be so difficult that this most cautious man could not bring it, once begun, to whatever outcome he wished.

After the royal dignity had been violated in the manner mentioned above, when the boy king had unwillingly come under the protection of that pontiff, the officials and nobles of the kingdom were indignant, as though their king had been deprived of his authority. They were also angered that the administration of the realm had fallen into the hands of a new man.

For at that time some accused him of exacting payment in exchange for granting each person the dignity he sought, especially ecclesiastical honors.

Understanding that this envy was being aroused against him, and with no sluggish cunning looking after his honor and reputation, he acted vigorously so that, under the pretext of an honorable matter, that royal administration and protection might be transferred to another person, namely the archbishop of the Church of Bremen.

He immediately bound this man to himself by the favor of intimacy, so that the two of them entered into this inviolable pact: each should be the mouth of the other.

Seeing, then, that everything was proceeding according to his wishes, the man of Bremen sought to establish a patriarchate in his own see. But because he lacked the strength to accomplish this, he attempted to increase his resources from what belonged to the royal jurisdiction.

And because, as has been said, the right established between the two of them by their agreement was that each should favor the other’s interests, it was not difficult for them also to obtain from the king’s simplicity whatever they wished.

By agreement with the bishop of Agrippina, Cologne, it was arranged that the man of Bremen should claim the two imperial abbeys, Corvey and Lorsch, for his diocese. How he was able to obtain them, though he had claimed them in vain, may become sufficiently clear to anyone investigating the matter elsewhere; we must pursue our own subject, not without sorrow.

The other, wishing to repay his associate the favor he had received, caused him to obtain, from royal benefices which he knew belonged to him, the royal gift of Malmedy and Inda.

Although it is painful to recall how this transfer was made almost furtively, contrary to right and justice, and not without injury to royal dignity, we have nevertheless thought it not inappropriate to hand the matter down to posterity.

## CHAPTER IV. A court is held at Trier, and there the transfer is confirmed without the abbot’s knowledge.

At that time, when the annual solemnity commemorating the martyrdom of the prince of the apostles came around, a royal court was held at Trier, not without harm to this Church.

The lord abbot had been received as a guest by the archbishop of Cologne at Saint Maximinus. He had shown him every courtesy with great devotion and charity, since, because of their former intimacy, he suspected nothing hostile being plotted against him.

But the other, having changed from a friend into a bitter enemy, did not find any equitable means by which to injure him. In his anger, therefore, he cunningly sought what he might take away unjustly.

For, while the abbot was unaware, the other laid snares behind him; like a lion, he thought nothing of fulfilling against him the Psalmist’s mournful utterance:

> “He who ate my bread has magnified his treachery against me” (Psalm 40).

At that same time, in the very court, our charters were read aloud at the abbot’s request. The king himself had renewed by his authority the decrees of the earlier emperors and had confirmed by the subscription of his hand that, just as they had remained inviolate up to his time, so they should remain thereafter.

But since he was a boy, easily swayed in either direction, and had been badly advised by the persuasive words of these officials, he immediately weakened and violated his own statutes and those of his predecessors, and without right or judge handed them over into alien hands.

At last everyone had already departed from the court, while the lord abbot had still learned nothing of the truth concerning this matter, secretly perpetrated. He considered it wicked to believe that the man whom he regarded as a devoted friend could have committed such a great crime against him without cause.

But on the return journey, when he was also offering that man the service requested of him, he was first informed of what had been done: namely, that the property of Saint Remaclus had been invaded by his agents and that he had claimed Malmedy.

Who can keep his mind from being shaken when these things are recalled, except that the sorrow which then existed has now been turned into joy? When that report reached the ears of our people, what grief and mourning struck our minds along with it! The mind was uncertain what to do or where to turn, except that it was better to commend this injustice to God.

## CHAPTER V. Abbot Theoderic and Duke Frederick confer together; a fortification is built above Malmedy; they are summoned together to court; but the duke refuses and complains of the injustice to the king through an intermediary.

When the lord abbot had therefore returned to Malmedy, he thought it useful, given the urgent necessity of the matter, to consult Duke Frederick, the common advocate of both Churches by ancient right.

At that time he was a man of such tested faith and such great integrity that it was not without reason that, after God, the abbot hoped to trust him for the defense of this wrong.

The duke himself, outstanding in noble birth no less than in piety, justice, and truth, superior to all others, promised that he would assist in every way, by action, counsel, [Col. 0297A] and aid. He said that he deeply resented what had been done and that, as long as he lived, he would never permit the separation of this Church’s property.

He added that he would rather die than fail to preserve it inviolate, just as he had received it into his advocacy.

He immediately sent word through an intermediary to the archbishop that, if he cared at all for his life together with his earthly honor, he should abandon this intention and these undertakings by every means.

Meanwhile, he planned to come to Malmedy with a military force. He sent provisions ahead in abundance and prepared and equipped whatever would be useful for defending the place bravely.

Then, to repel an enemy force, he occupied a nearby mountain with a kind of fortification, as though enemies were present, and kept watch there with his men, strengthening it with a rampart and ditch. He completed an entire month there with his expedition.

While these things were being done by the two parties, the affair was brought to court and discussed by the courtiers. Both men—the duke and the lord abbot—were declared public enemies, as though they had acted against the commonwealth.

Accordingly, letters were sent in the king’s name by those officials whose counsel, as we have said, seemed to be corrupting the dignity of royal power. The letters ordered both men to proceed to court to give an account.

The duke considered this treatment unworthy of him and indignantly rejected the summons. He complained bitterly of the injustice that the king, corrupted by the counsel of priests, had inflicted upon Saint Remaclus and himself.

Moreover, he sent the king this threatening message: unless he restored to the saint the property he had taken away, the duke, together with all his men, would be a great enemy to him and to his kingdom.

## CHAPTER VI. The duke reproves his nephew Conrad concerning the advocacy of Malmedy; and, when the abbot is compelled to go to court, he sends the agent Roricus, who abandons the abbot, and the abbot is detained for a long time by the king.

At the time when the archbishop had usurped the property of the confessor of Christ, he had taken the duke’s nephew Conrad—a vigorous man—into his service as a knight in return for the benefice of this advocacy.

Conrad, who was already hostile to the lord abbot, is said to have willingly undertaken the advocacy of Malmedy in order to pursue still more grievous enmities in revenge.

When this unexpectedly reached the hearing of the duke, his uncle, indignation struck his mind no less forcefully than the earlier report had done.

Nevertheless, after summoning him, he reproved the insolence of his spirit with paternal correction. He complained bitterly that, in offense to his uncle, and without preserving the reverence due to his honor and advancement, Conrad had dared to attempt against him what belonged to his uncle’s jurisdiction and responsibility.

When Conrad wished to clear himself, claiming that he had undertaken nothing contrary to what was good and honorable, and that, without prejudice to his uncle’s favor, he had done nothing beyond the custom of his peers, the duke threatened him not to presume any further to attempt what he knew would not turn out well for him.

Again, therefore, the lord abbot was summoned in the king’s name. If he did not hurry to court on the appointed day and at the appointed time, he was to suffer the forfeiture of all the property he held from the king.

Although he distrusted his own prospects, he did not despair of God’s mercy. He sorrowfully undertook the journey, commending himself no less to God than to the prayers of his faithful people.

The duke provided him with his own agent, Roricus, who had served as a legate, as his companion on the journey, so that Roricus might adequately plead his case and represent him before the king and his court.

But when Roricus explained in their presence the reasons for which he had come, some agreed in one way and some in another. Others—those for whom, as has been said, the court seemed to be concerned more with a private than a public matter—threw the whole affair into confusion, declaring that both men, because they had used force against the kingdom, deserved to suffer forfeiture.

When Roricus understood that this evil was being prepared no less for himself than for his lord, he returned home rashly and left the abbot in danger.

The abbot was detained at court on the advice of the archbishops; the court was then being held at Tribur, the royal seat.

There, when he tried to establish the justice and legitimacy of the case brought against him, he was examined more out of hatred on the part of the judge than according to judicial law. He was accused and treated with insults, in a manner unworthy of a man of such distinguished nobility.

For he was often ordered to surrender the pastoral staff of his office. It is said that he held so firmly to the strength of his resolve that he declared it would be taken from his hands only by force, since, with God and his conscience as witnesses, there was no evident reason for which he ought justly to suffer forfeiture.

Fixed in this position, he was detained in exile for almost an entire month, contrary to expectation, suffering the many hardships of travel no less than hunger, while every form of human assistance was denied him.

At last, after his friends obtained from the king some sort of release, he quickly withdrew to his own place, like one who, barely rescued, escapes the fury of lions.

We, therefore, fearing for his safety and life no less than for our own, and having lost hope of his return because of what we had heard through intermediaries, suddenly found him present among us, to the joy of those who had always been anxious about him and seeking news of him.

## CHAPTER VII. The duke’s death is followed by mourning and misery, and he is buried at Stavelot as he had ordered.

As soon as he had returned, we poured out tears of mutual joy. But behold, when a fresh sorrow came upon us, we were unexpectedly struck and disturbed by a grief which we lament no less irreparably than the earlier misfortune.

We heard, alas, that the duke whom we had described as indefatigable except when overtaken by death was laboring toward his end, afflicted by increasing illness, and that the defender of our Church was dying.

The lord abbot immediately hurried there to visit him. After, together with the bishop of Liège, he had administered to him all that was appropriate according to Catholic rite as his viaticum, he returned no more joyfully than if he himself had been destined to die at the same time.

On the following day the man beneath whose faith and integrity the whole world was inferior departed from this life. He left behind for us, for his own people, and for all good men a true cause of grief and pious mourning in the world.

It was therefore a time of misery to behold. His entire household grieved inconsolably. But no lesser sadness possessed us, since we had been deprived of all human assistance in the face of the danger threatening us.

Nevertheless, we were filled with no small wonder: when this man seemed most likely to benefit us, he had suddenly been taken away. Unless, because our sins deserved it, this tribulation—which could have been restrained through him—had to pass over upon us.

Thus, just as while alive he had resolved never to depart from the patronage of Saint Remaclus, so in death he fulfilled that resolve by receiving an honorable burial in his monastery.

It is sufficient to have recalled these matters insofar as the subject required, while we do not shrink from necessarily turning to the continuation of events filled with sorrow.

## CHAPTER VIII. The archbishop sends Conrad to claim Malmedy and choose an abbot for it; Abbot Theoderic demands from the monks the promise they had made to him.

When the archbishop learned that the duke had died, as though by striking down one adversary, he immediately resumed what fear of the duke had caused him to interrupt and returned to carrying out what he had begun.

He promptly sent Count Conrad, whom we mentioned above, since he was sufficiently willing for this purpose, to claim for himself what belonged by right to another and to secure Malmedy.

Moreover, he ordered all the priors and all the more capable men among the monks themselves to be brought to him on an appointed day, so that, if a suitable man could perhaps be found among them, he might set him over them as abbot.

Conrad, not sluggishly carrying out what he had been ordered to do, quickly undertook what his respect for his uncle had caused him to omit, since he burned to injure our abbot greatly.

We think it not inappropriate to repeat here a small matter that we omitted above. After the injury inflicted upon him by the archbishop, the lord abbot—distrusting his own strength against the power and intelligence of that man, which surpassed every human effort—warned the monks of Malmedy to preserve their fidelity to him, and, according to the Rule of Saint Benedict, to preserve their obedience and profession.

Although they falsely promised that they would observe everything toward him, he forbade them, under an adjuration by Christ, to receive anyone else besides himself or to allow any outsider to be admitted while he lived.

How they kept this promise became afterward clearer than daylight. He trusted them in a certain simplicity, as though they were utterly faithful, and no one could report anything so obvious about them that he would not always regard them as though innocent of this crime.

## CHAPTER IX. The people of Malmedy are bound by oaths to the bishop; a severe persecution is carried out against our people; the body of our saint is exposed in their midst.

[Col. 0299D]

When Conrad therefore sent word to them that he was coming and ordered that ample preparations be made for him, one might have seen them hastening joyfully about, running in every direction, receiving him as though he were an angel of God coming among them, and eagerly supplying themselves, the expenses, and whatever else might be useful, lest the new advocate should appear to incur any offense.

After binding the men of the Church by oaths in the name of the archbishop, he instructed them concerning the orders he had received: whether, after renouncing Abbot Theoderic, they wished to obey the man to whom they had been given.

Although a few did not agree, the greater part without hesitation quickly professed that they would do so.

When this became known to us in sorrow, grief covered us like night overtaking the light with darkness.

Some of our men nevertheless went there carrying the staff of our patron. Having reclaimed the place in his name—which proved ineffective—they returned hated by those people.

The count mentioned above took the action very badly, as though it had been done against him personally. With his spirit inflamed, he wished to avenge it both upon the monks and upon the laypeople of the Church.

Hence the greatest persecution descended upon our people, so that they did not dare proceed openly anywhere, since military ambushes had been spread everywhere.

It therefore pleased the brothers, by common counsel, to expose the venerable body of our lord Remaclus in their midst, and thus to pray more earnestly together with him who was being wronged, seeking by this means whatever remedy their grief demanded.

There was indeed just cause for all his people to grieve: their own property, which had remained inviolate until then, was about to be taken from them by unjust mortals.

From that time onward, day and night, we did not lack this mournful chant:

> “Look, Lord, for the desolation of your Church has come to pass; she who sits in sorrow has no one to comfort her except your mercy alone.”

## CHAPTER X. Abbot Tegeno is placed over Malmedy; but our abbot goes to Godefrid, margrave of Lombardy, for assistance.

[Note: [Col. 0301A] Abbot Tegeno is summoned from the monastery of Brouwilre. Concerning this abbot, placed in charge of the monastery of Malmedy, Archbishop Frederick of Cologne speaks quite openly in the charter cited earlier, in these words:

“Moreover, in the time of the lord Emperor Henry IV, through the lord Archbishop Anno, after a new separation had once again been made, a certain abbot was appointed at Malmedy,” etc.]

The people of Malmedy, therefore, although the lord abbot’s opposition to their undertaking was expressed in his name, nevertheless proceeded to Agrippina, Cologne, since the matter was going according to their wishes.

Questioned by the archbishop about their intentions and consulted concerning the appointment of an abbot, they replied that they desired this more from another source than from themselves.

After sending them back to their own place, he summoned Abbot Tegeno from the monastery of Broulwilre. The bishop, not without skill, deprived him of what was his own and made him take possession of what belonged to another.

For he truly appointed him abbot of Malmedy outside due order, compelling him to enter as though a thief coming from elsewhere, but not through the door.

Thus, when their abbot came under the protection and escort of Count Conrad, the monks of Malmedy received him on the night when the feast of Michael the Archangel was celebrated.

When he entered in the darkness of night, as though coming to steal the place, those willing to receive him brought torches and lamps to meet him.

Indeed, it would not have been unjust if one who had entered secretly by night, like a thief, had been driven away and deprived of his plunder.

At that time the lord abbot was not among us. After the duke’s death he had been deprived of both practical and advisory support and was uncertain what to do or where to turn. Nor could he find anyone among mortals comparable to the duke.

But because he knew that Godefrid, then margrave of Lombardy, surpassed others in power and rank, and that through counsel and intimacy he possessed great influence with the king and the nobles, he devoted himself entirely to him, seeking to recover his property by payment and entreaties.

At that time Godefrid was seeking to succeed to the duchy of his predecessor. The lord abbot, having agreed to the advocacy of Stavelot, preferred also to seek it from the king at the same time.

Indeed—let us say this without prejudice to him—he is reproached for having acted less rightly in this respect, because he is said to have trusted too greatly in human assistance as a means of recovery, although a defense thought capable of standing through a human being is by no means secure.

## CHAPTER XI. An account of the character, conduct, and differences of the two dukes, Frederick and Godefrid.

[Col. 0301B]

Godefrid was a powerful, energetic man and good in counsel, but in faith and truthfulness he differed greatly from Frederick.

Since the matter has brought both distinguished men into the present narrative, we thought it unworthy to pass over in silence their virtue and their conduct.

Their birth, age, and power were almost equal; their greatness of spirit and glory were comparable. But each possessed different qualities.

Frederick had innocence and integrity of life. Severity joined with honor had given him reverence and dignity. His actions themselves made it plainly understood that he had never preferred friendship, kinship, or even the exalted status of royalty to justice and truth.

[Col. 0301C]

Godefrid, on the other hand, possessed immense bodily and spiritual vigor. Excelling in war and military exercises, he acquired distinction for himself. In him eloquence was as prominent as prudence, and both were joined to a keen intelligence.

He took pleasure in extending the reputation of his name through words no less than through deeds, in pursuing the honors and dignities of the world, raising a great army, sometimes initiating wars, keeping watch over his labors day and night, and carrying out killings, burnings, and military plunder. He knew how to employ all these things, as circumstances and time required, without disgrace.

Such qualities never found a place in the other man.

For Frederick, peace was always dearer than war. Through his prudent intelligence he turned back toward peace whatever he perceived being moved against him toward war and sedition.

Whereas in the one man there was destruction for the wicked, in this man there was refuge for the afflicted.

His lord never found him opposed or blameworthy, because for him lying or perjury was always a crime. He preferred to be good rather than to appear good, and therefore attained greater glory because he desired it less.

We admit that Godefrid too possessed excellent qualities, although desire sometimes hindered them.

There was one less praiseworthy feature in him: when he was often asked for help and was able to provide it, he was said to delay more by making promises than to give assistance, as may be observed in the continuation of this text.

When the lord abbot therefore approached him, as we have said, as a most faithful friend, Godefrid gave him sufficient confidence through magnificent promises, as though the abbot would recover through Godefrid whatever he had lost.

But we have discovered that he contributed very little in this matter.

Accordingly, for his own advantage and that of the abbot, Godefrid advised him to accompany him to court, where he promised to devote great effort on his behalf.

## CHAPTER XII. Our abbot restores the holy body to its proper place; he adjures the abbot appointed over him, under threat of divine judgment, to depart and abandon what he unjustly possesses.

Meanwhile, the lord abbot went to visit the brothers whom he had left in sorrow. When he arrived, he found the venerable body of our lord Saint Remaclus deposited on the floor, where it had already lain for many days.

As though nothing more grievous could be heard, he learned that an outsider was presiding over Malmedy in its place.

It therefore seemed better to him, after consultation, that if the saint’s body were restored to its proper place with due honor, we should not for that reason be deprived of his assistance whenever he wished to give it.

And so it was done.

Afterward, acting prudently and restraining himself through patience, although he could easily have avenged the injuries inflicted upon him by that adversary, he held himself back out of benevolence and sent him a message through certain elders of our community in these words:

> “If you are acting justly, whoever you are, against me, consider it according to the judgment of yourself and of wise men. If you know that treacherously displacing another is evil, why have you, being an outsider, invaded my seat in this blameworthy manner—a seat which I have never lost by right or judgment, nor have I ever been accused of wrongdoing concerning it?
>
> “So that I may not appear to deal too harshly with you when I could rightly do so, I beg and admonish you, under adjuration by the name of Christ [Col. 0302C] and by the Rule of Saint Benedict: if you have any fear of God concerning this injustice, do not fraudulently retain what belongs to another, but depart and leave us what is our own.”

But since the other gave no definite answer to these words, those who had been sent returned without achieving what they had hoped.

## CHAPTER XIII. Duke Godefrid, having become duke, rightly decides that the saint’s property ought to be restored; the bishop refuses to comply, delaying the matter, and after our church and treasury have been stripped, our claim remains unfulfilled.

[Note: [Col. 0303C] The prophecy appears to be fulfilled which says (Habakkuk 1). The Vulgate edition reads:

> “And judgment was made, and opposition became stronger. Therefore the law was torn apart, and judgment did not reach its end; because the impious prevails against the just, therefore perverse judgment proceeds.”]

After this, the abbot proceeded with Margrave Godefrid to the court at Goslar. There Godefrid obtained the duchy together with the advocacy of Stavelot and was again elevated as military commander of Lotharingia.

The lord abbot, complaining of the injustice inflicted upon him, did not cease to make his case known, privately and publicly, to whichever bishops and dukes of the Roman Empire he could reach. He also asked them to support him in this necessity of his.

Many of them, moved by compassion of this kind, declared that the deed was unjust and kindly urged that the truth should not be concealed from the king.

At last it was decreed that the matter ought to be judged: whether it had been permissible for this to be done without cause and without a judge.

When Duke Godefrid was asked to administer the law of judgment, he rightly judged that the property ought to be restored to the representative of Saint Remaclus, since it would have been wicked to take it away from him.

Many assented equitably to this judgment. The archbishop alone resisted and contradicted it.

But, as many said at that time, after judgment had been rendered, the archbishop who contradicted it could have been decisively overcome by what was right and just if the faithful advocate, just as Frederick had done, had wished to secure the property for the saint by retaining and defending it.

He hesitated, however, because he suspected the other on account of the benefice he held from him, and avarice hindered him from doing the same.

The prophecy also seems to have been fulfilled which says:

> “Judgment was made and the judge accepted a bribe; therefore the law is overturned, and judgment is not brought to its conclusion” (Habakkuk 1).

All who were present appealed to the bishop and asked him to accept the just judgment. But since he was a man inflexible in his position, and could not otherwise escape, he accepted a postponement and deferred the matter for consideration at the next court.

From then on, the postponement was always extended from one court session to the next. And although our lord abbot was very often wearied by vain promises [Col. 0303B], he did not rest, undeterred, repeatedly proclaiming the injustice, until the gaze of mercy came from the Most High. Whatever in the Church’s possessions seemed most valuable, he always brought forward in the hope of recovering it, thinking it would benefit him to distribute it generously among friends—namely, those whom he hoped to win for himself through these benefactions. The king, valuing the treasury more highly, was himself ensnared by greed and demanded that some portion of these goods be ceded to him.

An exchange had been stipulated: if the king’s money were paid into the treasury, the good that had been taken away would immediately be redeemed in full. But once the church had been stripped and what remained had also been removed, this further accumulation of evils was added to our misfortunes, for the imperial promise remained void for us.

## CHAPTER XIV. The body of the saint is brought to the court at Aachen, where, by order of the bishop, it is received without any honor.

[Note: [Col. 0304C] Having taken up the saint’s *lipsanum*. *Lipsana* is declined only in the plural. It is the word used among us to signify relics.]

[Col. 0303C]

In that same year the royal court was held at Aachen, at the time when the observance of Lenten abstinence was being practiced. With the king’s consent, our lord abbot had obtained permission to be present there, intending to speak publicly both about his own rights and those of the sanctuary. For the king had promised that, concerning the matters in dispute, he would act justly if the commands and privileges of his predecessors could invalidate what he had done; but this too was again in vain. For the bishop’s badly fixed resolve could not be shaken at all; indeed, by his perverse ingenuity he drew even the king’s mind, which he possessed as a kind of bondman, away from the judgment of what was right.

Moreover, he had persuaded him that such a complaint would henceforth accomplish nothing. When it became clear to us that matters had come to this, by common counsel of the brothers it seemed necessary that the body of our patron Remaclus should be carried there, so that, in its presence, the adversaries might at least be moved to fear retaining his property. Accordingly, it was carried to that place, formerly within his diocese, not [Col. 0304A] without pain and groaning, accompanied by a considerable company of members of his household.

When the people of Malmedy learned of the transportation of the sacred body, they did not delay to inform the archbishop of it immediately, urgently imploring him to maintain his steadfastness and not to invalidate the pledge that he had made with them. For this reason, after approaching the king, he placed our lord abbot under the pressure of grave necessity in the king’s name: unless he forbade us to come nearer, he would entirely lose the royal gift.

Thus he came to meet us, as though intending to do this, sad and mourning; but we did not listen to him at all concerning the matter. Immediately, despite his opposition and while proclaiming himself unfortunate, we rushed forward, took up the saint’s *lipsanum* [Col. 0304B], and entered the town of Aachen. You could have heard mourning and cries such as had never occurred in our time; and, unless our sins had hindered us, we would not have hesitated to direct such tears even toward heaven itself.

But that man of Cologne was not moved from his decision by these things. Rather, because matters had proceeded differently from what he wished, he is said to have taken steps to oppose us. He forbade the clergy of the saint’s former parish to offer the due honor that was owed to the patron of all Gaul. He presumed to insult this venerable body, whose funeral rites the angels ceaselessly celebrate and whose soul possesses the joy of paradise, and to drive him away from their sight like one of the lowest mortals, as though he were his equal.

## CHAPTER XV. While we mourned and proclaimed our grief with the people, the insolent bishop of Speyer orders our “clod” to be carried away; finally, in deep sorrow, we departed from there together with the saint’s body.

[Col. 0304C]

As our lamentation and mourning continued, and we proclaimed this injustice in the house of the Mother of God, the bishop of Speyer, sent by the king, investigated the cause of the protest. After hearing only a few statements and learning nothing certain from him, we—whose courage, trusting in the Lord, stood as a wall—went up to the palace and proceeded as far as the royal doors. There, a few of us entered and stood weeping before him with our lord’s staff. The king sat as though mute and stunned and gave no answer; but the archbishop responded in his place according to his wishes, saying that our lord had done nothing unjust by giving what was his own, and that he himself had committed no wrong by receiving anything from our saint. When they replied that this could be recognized from the commands and privileges of their forefathers, if such an act had been lawful, a careful examination of the matter was postponed until the following day.

But while the people, who thought that nothing had been adequately done, continued to cry out, that insolent bishop of Speyer shouted from above: “Take your clod away from here,” he said, “along with those importunate cries, which it is improper for my lord to endure with his faithful followers.” We bore this infamous remark with great grief; but, at Duke Godefrid’s urging, lest we should later regret that some harm had been done to us, we carried the sacred body to the church of Saint Aldegund, which belonged to us, to be kept there.

But the man of Cologne, fearing that he might be overcome by the authority already invoked, or even by royal command, made excuses, hastily departed from the palace, and entrusted Duke Godefrid with acting on his behalf, relying on the duke’s oath of loyalty.

The next morning, as though already confident that we would obtain what had been postponed, we returned to the palace. For, late in the day, as the king was going to the baths, he had promised that he would do everything that was requested of him; but he committed the wrong for which he is accused of having deceived us.

After assailing Duke Godefrid with many prayers, we sent him ahead to speak for us, since he had promised to act as our advocate. In him alone the hope of everyone rested, as though he were then devoting himself wholeheartedly to our cause. But the matter turned out otherwise than we had a right to believe of him. For at that time a kind of corruption had invaded everyone: although princes were often sought out and judges spoke words intended to please, no one placed any faith at all in promises. Thus, when the commands of the emperors and of the king’s own father were read out on the spot, there was nothing with which the adversaries who wished to resist could offer opposition.

When, therefore, justice had brought the matter to the point at which the king was compelled to act rightly by the authority of himself and his father, the duke interrupted this course of action, saying that, out of loyalty, he could in no way tolerate any force being used against his absent lord. Thus he obtained a postponement until the bishop could be present at another court. That day, frustrating everyone’s hope, increased our sorrow. Again you would have seen cries and weeping of such a kind arise around the sacred body that we would have thought mercy itself was grieving from the divine throne, unless, because our sins demanded it, the prophet’s prediction seemed to be fulfilled: “A cloud has been set up so that our prayer may not pass through” (Lam. III).

But the time for showing mercy had not yet come for those afflicted in heart. By divine providence, a greater glorification of Christ’s confessor was being reserved for a more fitting time. Those who had seen us arrive in sorrow grieved even more deeply to see us return home, while joy came to our adversaries according to their desire. We also feared that, by troubling such a great priest, we had done him an injury, and that perhaps, because of us, he might come to be despised by unjust mortals and thus treated with contempt. But acting wickedly against God’s elect does not go unpunished, as what followed also made clear.

## CHAPTER XVI. Seized by a serious illness, the king promises to restore everything to the saint; the bishop, likewise stricken by illness, makes the same promise, but soon afterward the matter proceeds differently.

Not yet had the year completed its course when God’s judgment concerning these matters began to be stirred up. The king was staying at the town of Fritzlar, where he was afflicted by the distress of a serious illness [Col. 0306A]. As the disease grew stronger in the innermost passages of nature, he cried out at every moment that he was dying, overcome by the oppressive weight of excessive pain. His faithful followers suggested that this had deservedly happened to him because of the injustice inflicted on Saint Remaclus, and that divine providence had begun to avenge the wrong done to its confessor upon him. Moreover, if he wished to escape this judgment, he should not delay restoring to the saint what he had unjustly taken away—his hereditary possession.

The king, willingly, but nevertheless constrained by the extremity of necessity, called upon the bishops of Mainz and Fritzlar as sureties, together with Duke Englibert, and entrusted this property to their pledge of loyalty, so that, once it had been recovered from the Archpriest, who was then absent, they might restore it by their sworn word to the saint from whom he had taken it.

[Col. 0306B] Our lord abbot was again summoned to the court. The sureties took care to carry out the deliberation entrusted to their faith; but the archbishop refused to acknowledge that any agreement concerning this deliberation had been made. They and other faithful men tried to persuade him in this way: that the matter had not been undertaken without God’s judgment; that such a salutary counsel ought not to be rejected, since it seemed to have brought relief and healing to his lord.

But he, like a slippery snake, made for his hiding places. Having surveyed the way by which he might thrust forth his threefold tongue, he asked for a postponement. For, because of some agreement made between them—I do not know what kind—it was the case that there was nothing so difficult that the king, even under oath, would dare refuse him.
