Thus on this occasion also, to increase the misery of us all, he hardened his resolve against us.

Indeed, not long afterward he himself was visited by a similar affliction [Col. 0306C] in the hidden passages of nature. The sick man was tormented, deservedly, by the anguish of pain, but his evil and fixed resolve endured in his mind. When, having despaired of life, he was advised by his friends concerning our cause—for a false report had already reached us that he had died—he is said to have promised that he would do everything that justice required concerning the property of Christ’s confessor. But although it was hoped that the matter could be brought about according to his will, it had not been arranged according to the decision of the Most High, who intended to accomplish it more wondrously without him.

## CHAPTER XVII. After the archbishop of Trier dies, the man whom he had installed against their will is captured together with that insolent bishop of Speyer, Anno, who is driven away in disgrace, like an unclean dog beaten with blows.

[Col. 0306D]

The archbishop of Trier had died, and he himself had substituted his provost in his place. For this reason he had incurred just causes for hatred among the people of Trier, because, disregarding their election, he had imposed his own choice upon them against their will.

That bombastic bishop of Speyer was ordered to provide an escort for the new archbishop, so that, moved by divine judgment, he too might experience the punishment of the infamous crime being avenged upon him. A considerable retinue of both bishops arrived at the estate of Biettemburghe, with an abundant and lavish supply of equipment. When they had gone to sleep, behold, Theodoric, advocate of the people of Trier, burst in with an armed force, laying waste and plundering everything [Col. 0307A]. He treated the new bishop brutally and cast him into chains. But the bishop of Speyer had escaped into the church beside the altar and hidden there. When he was sought and found, he paid a deserved penalty for the retaliation owed on account of the injury he had inflicted on the saint when, in his arrogance, he had ordered our “clod” to be carried away.

For after being beaten and driven from the sanctuary, he was dragged away like an unclean dog and, uncovered and barefoot as he was, was placed upon a wretched beast and ordered to return in that condition to his own lands. Yet even this was not sufficient for the judgment of him who speaks through the prophet: “Vengeance is mine, and I will repay” (Deut. XXXII; Rom. XII). Finally, consumed by grief and sorrow over these things that had happened to him against his will, he died within the course of that year.

What his men did to their bishop is not something we have time to pursue here; as far as we are concerned, let it suffice to have said enough about them. Nevertheless, may this evil not be counted against him by God in the future, on whose account it is believed that so great and abominable a crime—the murder—could have been committed. But now let us return to the sequence of the narrative.

## CHAPTER XVIII. The abbot again obtains from the king permission to reclaim his place, returns to Malmedy, and, bringing the saint’s body with him, restrains everyone—monks and laymen alike—under oath to the prelate.

When the period of the postponement obtained by the archbishop had elapsed, our lord abbot returned to the court during the very days of the Nativity. The king was at the city of Bamberg amid that celebration, where, before him and [Col. 0307C] his nobles, the abbot once again made mention of his complaint, as was not unusual.

Despite the archbishop’s opposition, almost the entire assembly of the court wholeheartedly supported our lord abbot, even though the king, agreeing with the truth, was favorably disposed to restore the property of Christ’s confessor. His only hesitation was that he feared doing so contrary to the bishop’s will, which he regarded with suspicion.

For earlier in that same year, when the king had been with us together with the queen, they had restored this property to the saint through his staff; and when the sacred *lipsanum* had been displayed in the midst for this purpose, he himself had carried it back and replaced it in its proper place with fitting praises. We are witnesses, for we heard and saw this happen, although afterward, because he feared the bishop, it was a crime for him to deny it [Col. 0307D]. Nevertheless, now observing both the king’s goodwill and that of his nobles, the abbot began to implore him that, with his favor preserved, he might be permitted to reclaim the place as his own right, even if the bishop did not wish it.

Since the king did not reject these just petitions, and indeed everyone agreed that the act ought to be done, our lord abbot returned to Malmedy. And, lest he should seem to reclaim it fruitlessly by his own efforts, he decided that it should be done especially through the presence of the body itself, whose hereditary estate it was.

We hastened there immediately, not unwillingly, but on our journey we encountered those who opposed us. As soon as they heard among themselves of our arrival with the saint’s body, you would have seen everyone trembling in uncertainty, turning pale and bloodless, and striving with all their strength lest they be bound as though by the chain of due servitude. For they were ashamed to be called what they could not deny they were: servants of Saint Remaclus, whose benefactions and assistance in truth sustained them, although they were ungrateful.

The monks encouraged the laymen, and the laymen the monks, each urging the other to oppose the reception of the venerable body by our lord abbot, who was present; or, if it were brought in against their will by force, to leave the monastery or the place in opposition.

When the abbot learned of this, he restrained the insolence of their servile boldness, now by persuasion and then by threats, until at last they agreed, without hostility, to receive their lord. When our lord abbot was celebrating the mystery of human Redemption, so that we might offer praises to God together, not one of them took part in the solemn Mass [Col. 0308B]. They still trusted in the bishop’s power and relied upon his support, since they knew that this was not his will.

Having reclaimed the place and recalled the people of the Church under his oath, and likewise the monks—although they were unfaithful—under their rule, the abbot returned to Stavelot, suspecting nothing further that they might be plotting against him.

## CHAPTER XIX. The abbot comes to Rome and pursues his cases before Pope Alexander, who also sends letters on his behalf to Cologne; but all this was in vain.

Within a few days he himself set out for Rome and approached Alexander, pope of the Romans, in order to renew the privileges of our Church by apostolic authority [Col. 0308C]. There he adequately pursued his case, as circumstances allowed, on behalf of himself, the place, its adverse circumstances, and also the injustices that the bishop of Cologne had inflicted upon Saint Remaclus and upon him. He found very welcome consolation from the pope and from the senators of the Roman state.

For the pope himself, after rereading the decrees of his predecessors, recognized the considerable danger. He was astonished that the prudence of so wise a man could have been deceived, and that he could have acted so foolishly in these matters. Therefore, both at our lord abbot’s request and because, as the universal shepherd, he was obliged to take concern for everyone, he warned the archbishop in writing, by the authority of the apostle Peter, not to presume to condemn anyone justly on these grounds, and to beware of using force any longer against possessions that did not belong to him.

“We have learned,” he said, “of many good works proceeding from you and reaching even to the see of my lord Peter, but they seem to me to be darkened, as if by a cloud, by these presumptions of yours. God does not need anything offered to him from injustice. Why, then, are sacrifices made to him from plunder, as though someone were slaughtering a son in the presence of his father?” (Isa. LXVI). “And lest, by giving, you seem to offend Peter, leave to that saint what is his own, for Abbot Theodoric, acting as his vicar, implores our judgment.”

When the archbishop received a copy of these letters from the pope’s legate, his mind was no more softened than an adamant stone is softened by iron. While the abbot was traveling to Rome, he had not yet left his homeland when the people of Malmedy informed him of everything that had been done against them and against the place [Col. 0309A].

Because the archbishop was not then in the province, they are said to have given gifts to his procurator Gerlasius so that, acting in his name, the place might quickly be reclaimed through a countermeasure. But when he learned of these events, he restrained his anger through the steadfastness of his spirit and came from the place called Sarevelt, where he was then staying, as though he intended to avenge the injury done by our place.

It was also reported that he had then decided to build a fortress in the same fortifications of Malmedy, which he had previously strengthened against us while Duke Frederick was alive. But dissuaded by the advice of his friends from doing this, he prepared to avenge his injury by another route, through injuries inflicted in return.

## CHAPTER XX. Gerlasius, the bishop’s procurator, again invades Malmedy in his name, but, on hearing an uncertain report, hastens his return.

[Col. 0309B]

Accordingly, Gerlasius once again invaded Malmedy and reclaimed it in the bishop’s name, not fearing to lay an inexperienced hand upon the man who possessed the place itself, which he had not yet entirely abandoned to protection. For, as is now clear, no one will ever be able to take it away from him unless—God forbid—because of the presence of its inhabitants he himself first abandons his inheritance, no longer caring for it, as Jeremiah says (Jer. XII).

Nor did he endure the alien hand over him because he was repeatedly slandered and repeatedly transferred from one ownership to another, as though his hand seemed too weak for that defense. Rather, he wished his servants to be chastised for a time amid adversity, since he saw them slipping into worse things through their sluggishness; and he foresaw that, at a more suitable time, he would draw them back to himself through benefactions and miracles, even as they retreated with an adverse shoulder.

Hardly had the rash soldier accomplished what he had come to do when the monks no less than the laymen—since matters of this sort depended upon their will—fell back by agreement under foreign rule. He found it difficult to delay his return, fleeing more quickly than a thief who is pursued. For a rumor had gone out that a very large army was approaching from our region. Struck with terror, they weakened one another so greatly by their flight [lacuna] that, when their horses failed, each could scarcely make his way back home.

## CHAPTER XXI. The abbot returns from Rome, little aided by the apostolic letters; indeed, through a certain harsh man named Fredelo, persecution against him and against us is renewed, and through Gerard, who was afterward ruined by God’s judgment.

[Col. 0309D]

Meanwhile, when our lord abbot returned from the apostolic see, he brought us nothing certain except the authorized privileges. For we perceived that even that letter, a copy of which he had with him and which they said had been sent by the apostolic see to the archbishop, had contributed nothing to the advantage of our affairs.

After this the archbishop admonished Count Conrad and his own familiars concerning their loyalty to him, so that they might take steps to avenge his injuries upon the abbot and his faithful followers. But he took very badly the agreement of friendship that had become known between the abbot and the count, accusing his own soldier of disloyalty because, without his order, he had entered into relations with his enemies and had not sufficiently acted in his interest in return.

Therefore, in his name and in place of the count’s deputy, he entrusted the advocacy of Malmedy to an equally harsh man, Fredelo, so that he might press the defense of that place more vigorously and more effectively. Having received this power, Fredelo, as though he expected to gain greater favor or reward by it, devoted himself with all his strength, together with his men, to this business day and night.

Once again the greatest persecution came upon us, so that it would have been a free confession to say that they were servants of Saint Remaclus only at the price of danger. As a result, the violence of this dreadful captivity weighed heavily upon some of the better members of the Church.

But may all who rise up against us prosper in the same way as that man and his followers will have cause to rejoice for this fine deed of rising against God’s saint. For it is clear that he fell from good reputation into infamy, and thus from great wealth into poverty. Moreover, one of his men, Gerard, a man of intolerable boldness, who was no less ready and effective at slaughter and arson than at plunder and banditry, was, like a rabid animal raging against our people, plainly ruined by divine rather than human judgment.

## CHAPTER XXII. The bishop sets out for Rome, and the abbot follows him; they are examined before the pope and the senate; finally the matter is settled without any advantage to us.

After this the bishop, trusting in his own strength as though he had overcome everyone by his severity—for he had even compelled the king to agree not to raise the matter with him any further—prepared to set out for Rome, as though he intended to receive from the apostolic see an authoritative privilege concerning this property.

Our lord abbot, having been sufficiently and necessarily advised by his faithful followers, decided to be present there as well, in order to oppose him by the authority of the forefathers. The bishop, however, traveling on a royal embassy, went through Italy with power, as though he were going to complete the king’s business; but the matter turned out very differently from what reason required and fell into uncertainty.

They therefore came to the confession of blessed Peter. But the abbot, arriving first, repeated before the same authorities whom he had previously approached the same complaint. Having been duly consulted about the matter by the apostolic lord, he presented himself to the arriving bishop in a posture of satisfaction and humbled himself before the altar of the very one for whose devotion the bishop had come.

But, alas for the crime! It is said that the bishop, moved neither by fear nor by love of the sweetest Peter, did not deign to console the grieving man or look upon him in his humiliation. Rather, with the same stubbornness, he proceeded to the celebration of the divine sacraments. Again, during the very sacraments that he was celebrating, the abbot, imploring mercy, humbled himself; but even then that stubborn mind did not depart from its decision. He returned, as he had been ordered, to the apostolic see if he did not obtain what he sought. The pope and his associates, placing little value on the bishop’s religious observance, condemned this impiety.

At the Lateran, by the pope’s command, both men were summoned to a public hearing. The apostolic lord also had a legitimate judicial charge against the archbishop: he had communicated without papal authorization with his rival, namely the bishop of Parma, who was said to lie under the judgment of anathema [Col. 0311A]. Accordingly, by decree of the senate, the archbishop was ordered to be barred from the sight of the pope and of the entire Roman council unless, through a public satisfaction, he purified the offense he had committed against the right and honor of the vicar of the apostle Peter.

For this reason, when he was summoned to account, he proceeded publicly barefoot, led by the marchioness Beatrice; after making satisfaction and receiving pardon, he was admitted again into the community.

There our lord abbot, before the judges of the Roman Church and the senators of the state, set out everything for which the archbishop was liable: the entire sequence of his acts of deception; furthermore, the injustice he had committed by usurping, contrary to right, the property of Saint Remaclus [Col. 0311B]; and finally, his violation of the authority of the present pope and of the decrees of his predecessors.

At this, as though guilty of the deed, he was confused and grew pale from his conscience, especially while everyone in that assembly proclaimed the act unjust. After speaking briefly and deliberately, he gave an adequate response for the moment to the king’s Roman legate: that no one ought to inflict any force upon him disgracefully, and that he had not come there in order to lose what had been granted to him as a royal gift [Col. 0312A].

When the pope then asked him, for the love of blessed Peter and of the pope himself, to show him just human kindness, he promised that he would do so entirely, provided that both men came before the king in their homeland. After this and many other matters, both departed from Italy.

Nevertheless, the bishop obtained none of the things for whose sake he had chiefly gone there. When he returned to his homeland, he not only made void what he had promised, but also declared that the king himself had been despised in the king’s injury, so as to turn the king’s mind against the abbot into bitter hostility.

But if we wished to discuss one by one the differing loyalties of the parties, the enormous labors of our abbot, and finally the character of the whole adversity, we would find that time, rather than material, would fail us. Therefore, let us bring to an end these matters that seem full of sorrow, as though our minds, weary from the tedium of them, might gladly do so; and let us turn more willingly to those things that bring joy and gladness.

**End of the First Book**

# BOOK TWO

[Col. 0311]

## PROLOGUE

[Col. 0311B]

In the text of the preceding work we completed a very sorrowful history of the adverse circumstances that had befallen us. May the course of the work that follows now pass through the blessings that, for the glorification of his confessor, came about by God’s favor, with a joy equal to that of the apostles after the Resurrection.

For just as, after the sorrow caused them by the death of their Master, they were granted joy at his resurrection (Matt. XXVIII; Luke XXIV; John XX), so we too, who have been afflicted by sorrows no less severe for five years and more, rejoice in a comparable way at the same time in the astonishing glorification of his confessor [Col. 0311C].

But you, our lord Theodoric, most reverend of abbots, receive this little work with a mind prepared for happier things. It has been brought forth in an unpolished style from the treasury of our very small intellect, but it should be examined and corrected by your more mature judgment. We therefore ask that it be strengthened by your authority before it is spread among the public ears with its uncorrected loquacity.

## CHAPTER I. How, while traveling toward Liège, the bearers of Saint Remaclus’s body complained that they were being dragged by those in front, while those in front complained that they were being pushed by those behind.

A royal court had been announced to take place at Liège, when the solemn season of the Lord’s Resurrection was approaching [Col. 0311D]. All who had a case for judgment from the various parts of the Roman Empire were ordered to assemble there. Among them was also Father Theodoric of the monastery, to whom the king had appointed a hearing concerning the damage done to the Church [Col. 0312B]. If he could in any way bend Archbishop Anno, who had usurped Malmedy, which belonged by right to Saint Remaclus, together with all its dependencies, the king himself would order and undertake the restoration of what had been taken away.

Our aforesaid father, because he had finally expended a great deal of the Church’s treasures in vain, became wearied and, having lost confidence in all human assistance, though late, accepted the counsel of our elders. They approved the carrying of the body of our protector Saint Remaclus to that same court, in the town where he himself had once exercised the office of pontifical leadership [Col. 0312C]. Once they had agreed to this, and had gained possession of what they desired, they hastened, supported by God’s providence, to bring what they had begun to completion.

But because our departure was delayed somewhat, our lord abbot had gone ahead the day before and ordered us to follow after the sacred body had been treated with due care. Therefore, as we were setting out, the bearers in front proceeded more quickly than those behind could sustain the labors of the journey. The latter complained that they were being dragged by those in front, while the former complained that they were being pushed by those behind.

For the sacred relics, drawn onward by divine impulse, prevented the bearers from lingering in their tracks. Hence there was no doubt that Saint Remaclus wished to visit Saint Lambert, who had once become for him, while still in the flesh, a singular refuge: so that, just as one had shown compassion to the other during persecution, so now each might assist the other in recovering his possession [Col. 0312D].

The union that followed between them clearly demonstrated how pious was the intention that had preceded it. From the most sacred fellowship of their bodies came incomparable joy to us, but salutary assistance to the sick and weak. Yet more about this elsewhere.

## CHAPTER II. Concerning the relics of Saint Symetrius, and how during the night a path was shown through the air from the Stavelot oratory to the house of Saint Lambert.

[Note: [Col. 0313C] We received the relics of Saint Symetrius the Martyr, brought from Ladernaco to meet us. Concerning this martyr Symetrius, Molanus speaks as follows in *The Feasts of the Saints of Belgium*, under 26 May: “At Rome, the holy martyrs Symetrius and twenty-two others. While he was hiding and celebrating the divine mysteries in the titular church that the pious pope had built near Praxedes, the Emperor Antonius ordered them to be punished by the sword without any interrogation, in that same titular church. Praxedes collected and buried their bodies on the seventh day before the Kalends of June.

“The History of the Church of Ladernaco adds that, in infancy, he was restored to life by blessed Maternus, and that on this occasion his mother Albana, together with her child, received the sacraments of the faith and gave him the name Symetrius. He was the sixth count of Salm among the Tungri, whom Saint Maternus had baptized shortly before.

“Moreover, Saint Babolenus, who succeeded Remaclus, brought his body from Rome to Stavelot and placed it with fitting honor in the principal hereditary possession of the monastery, the estate of Lierneu, or Ladernaco. It was decreed that the aforesaid estate should acknowledge itself as a daughter of the Church of Stavelot, paying a census of one *esterling* from each house, and that each year, on the ninth day of March, they should carry the martyr’s sarcophagus to Stavelot with hymns and a procession as a sign of filial subjection.

“The place and the martyr are also mentioned in the twentieth book of the miracles of Remaclus, which belongs to Notger, bishop of Liège: ‘The estate of Ledernans,’ he says, ‘is assigned to our monastery. In it is a church of Saint Symetrius and others, illustrious for their miracles.’”]

When we had come to an estate belonging to us called Lovincias, we honorably received the relics of the holy martyr Symetrius, which had been brought from Ladernaco to meet us. They had not been brought to Liège together with the sacred body of our patron without purpose: without doubt, the worthy presence of both would increase everyone’s hope of the divine mercy that would benefit us.

[Col. 0313B] That night, while we were resting in the same estate with the sacred relics, at the hour of Matins a wondrous sign was shown at Liège to certain people who did not know that Saint Remaclus was to be brought there. It seemed that from the Stavelot oratory to the house of Saint Lambert a kind of shining road extended through the air in a brilliant path. While those who saw it wondered what the appearance of this thing signified, its meaning was immediately resolved by the arrival of so great a guest; they acknowledged without doubt that the vision had served to announce it.

We too, rising at the first crowing of the roosters from the place where we had rested, traveled the difficult road with ease, without labor or hindrance, and with joy. Nor were praises of the Lord lacking as we went, according to the ability and knowledge of the accompanying people [Col. 0313C].

Nevertheless, not far from the city, we awaited a messenger whom we had sent ahead to our lord abbot. He returned and announced that, contrary to hope and expectation, opposition had arisen to our proceeding, and that our lord bishop Theoduin did not dare receive the venerable body of the saint as it deserved, because he feared displeasing the metropolitan, who would be angry about it. Although the matter seemed uncertain, we nevertheless proceeded there quickly, without losing confidence.

## CHAPTER III. The bishop of Liège comes out to meet the sacred body and receives it honorably with the clergy and the entire people.

[Note: [Col. 0314D] “Our lord bishop, although from the beginning of this evil…” He means Theoduin, whom the preceding chapter indicates to have had a more timid spirit; now, he signifies that, at the urging of the archdeacons and other prelates, he recovered his courage and renewed his distinguished efforts for the recovery of Malmedy over the course of two full days.]

Meanwhile, the archdeacons, who were deeply distressed by the injury done to the saint, and the sound-minded clerics from every household, approached the bishop. They protested that an act contrary to fairness and goodness was being committed, and that he ought to take counsel not only for his own welfare but also for the safety of the entire city, so that so great a former shepherd of theirs, a renowned saint among the foremost saints of Gaul, might be received honorably, as was fitting, with praises of God [Col. 0314B].

They also approached the archbishop and tried to bend his mind toward agreement. Although he thought differently on other matters, in this case, lest he appear to oppose so just a desire shared by everyone, he gave his consent. At once our lord bishop prepared to go out with all his clergy, while the metropolitan remained in the palace with those who agreed with him.

Meanwhile there was an enormous press of people on every side, as crowds rushed together with praise of God. No one among those gathered escaped injury altogether, since many were thrown down by the feet of those pushing forward.

In that gathering, who could have refrained from tears? One of the soldiers of the heavenly Emperor, who had long possessed the palm of eternal glory and immortality, seemed to be approaching the court of an earthly king in pursuit of justice that ought to have been granted. Above all, the clergy had just cause for reflection: pious compassion had moved their hearts to tears at so great an injustice, and likewise at the humiliation of so great a confessor, inspiring an astonishment worthy of reverent fear.

Moreover, although our lord bishop had from the beginning of this trouble devoted himself sufficiently, as circumstances and counsel required, he now, together with his best clerics, the dukes, and those present, spent the entire two days with still greater effort, striving to lead both the king and the archbishop, guilty of this deed, away from the position they had adopted.

## CHAPTER IV. The king repents of the injustice; the bishop of Vercelli admonishes the archbishop about it, but he firmly refuses.

The king also greatly regretted having entrusted this property to hands from which, whenever he wished, he could not withdraw it without committing an injustice. People even whispered that he shared responsibility for the crime because of the decline of imperial power. The archbishop himself had hardened his mind so inflexibly that, whenever he was consulted about the matter, he resented every proposal, together with its author.

The bishop of Vercelli, as one more familiar with him, went to him to discuss the matter and, wishing to persuade him, humbly offered this counsel:

“If you would listen to just advice, most reverend archbishop, and properly consider your own salvation, it would seem most just that you should render due honor to God and grant this holy man the justice which he evidently seeks justly. We have recognized that what you are doing is unjust, and we have also recognized the danger threatening you on this account unless you change your decision. Therefore we admonish you to acknowledge his rightful claim to that holy man, to whom it has been adjudicated by the agreement of the princes and of the entire [Col. 0315B] people. The king himself greatly desires this, for he does not fear without reason that he may be drawn into the same peril. Tell me plainly what counsel I should report, for I have been sent by him to consult you.”

The archbishop replied, moved to indignation:

“Stop, brother and fellow bishop; stop importuning me with these matters, to which I have never been able to give my mind anything more seriously. For I have resolved under oath that I would rather die than allow such a decision to be weakened through me. What do you want me to say? We shall never be changed by these arguments. Even the man whom they call a saint, if he were to resume bodily form and come in person to ask for it, would by no means obtain what he requested with my permission.”

“Good, good words, I beg you,” he replied, “lest these dishonorable things be spread abroad to the ears of the public, bringing disgrace upon the pontifical order, or lest other powerful men exploit this decision as though it gave them some authority. Therefore, even if not through the prayers or counsels of friends, we nevertheless believe that you will accomplish this through the power of God.”

“If,” he said, “you should see this taken from these hands during my lifetime, may the Lord command that my spirit be taken away with it.”

O wondrous clemency of God, and patience of his holy confessor! Retribution did not immediately follow the seizure of the possession, although the archbishop would, according to his own choice, have suffered just judgments. But God is not like a man, to be appeased without cause and made conformable to clay.

## CHAPTER V. The archbishop dismisses the brothers, prostrate at his feet, to Saint John on the island with an uncertain reply.

[Col. 0315D]

On the following day, which was the Sunday of the Lord’s Resurrection, our elders went to the church of Saint John on the island, where he was celebrating the mysteries of that church’s dedication. Prostrate at his feet, they said:

“The earth is full of the mercy of the Lord” (Psalm 32). Therefore, lest you be found alien to that mercy, show us the mercy we seek, if only for the Lord’s name.

He dismissed them, as usual, with extremely cautious speech and an uncertain reply.

## CHAPTER VI. Supplication directed to God, and the devout compassion of the clerics and laypeople who looked on.

That same day, after the princes and bishops had been summoned before the king, while our lord abbot was present with the archbishop, discussion began concerning our affair.

Meanwhile, as we waited before the doors for the outcome, it occurred to all of us that, in our present necessity, no counsel was better than to implore God alone, our helper, more earnestly. Accordingly, standing in a spirit of humility at the altar of the Holy Trinity, upon which lay the venerable body of our most devout patron, we sang “Come, Creator Spirit” (*Veni, Creator Spiritus*) to the end. When we had completed it with the sweetest supplication, we recited the seven psalms with the litany, contrite in heart. Then we made a procession, singing “With a great voice, in praise” (*Magna vox, laude*), and so forth, to Saint Lambert in the crypt. From there we went to Saint Mary with the responsory “Christ, most beloved Virgin” (*Christi, Virgo dilectissima*); from there we returned to the Holy Trinity with the antiphon “You, God, the unbegotten Father” (*Te Deum Patrem ingenitum*), followed by other prayers to obtain the help of that same Holy Trinity.

But as the clerics and laypeople looked upon the faces of our men and the altered color that revealed their inward grief, they were wounded in spirit; and, gathering in a public supplication, they became like us. Stretching their hands toward heaven, they all entreated God to be favorable to us. Our supplication was by no means slight; indeed, there was also trepidation, because, seeing the reverence due to so great a confessor being brought into contempt, they feared that desolation would come upon the place and that they would have to endure still more the blasphemy of those who insulted him.

[Col. 0316C] But God, who does not forget to show mercy (Psalm 76), used this occasion to exalt his saint still higher.

## CHAPTER VII. The saint’s shrine is lifted from the altar with a sound, and abundant consolation is given to those who witnessed it.

[Note: [Col. 0316D] For the saint’s shrine, which had been placed upon the altar of the Holy Trinity. From this chapter Aegidius of the Golden Valley took the second chapter of his *Deeds of Saint Theoduinus*, which begins: “In the year 1071, on the seventh day before the Ides of May, in the sixth year of the dissension of the monasteries of Malmedy and Stavelot,” and so forth.]

After the supplication mentioned above had been completed, we surrounded the king’s presence so that at least we might obtain permission to speak before him. There we plainly experienced the providence of the almighty King, through the conspicuous and wondrous power of his miracles. For the saint’s shrine, which had been placed upon the altar of the Holy Trinity, appeared, with a sudden sound, to be lifted into the air. This greatly astonished those who were standing there, including those who, together with the custodian of the holy relics, were keeping watch; and they explained to us, who were doubtful, what they had seen, affirming it worthy of belief. We were therefore greatly consoled and, with all our strength, commended the outcome of the affair to God.

## CHAPTER VIII. The brothers surround the king at dinner; the bishop of Baveberg postpones justice until the following day.

[Note: [Col. 0318A] Where he was reclining with his men in royal splendor. Lambert of Schafnaburg expressly testifies that the relics of Saint Remaclus were brought to the king while he was reclining at dinner. Thus he writes: “After taking counsel, they say, being moved to this by a divine revelation, they lifted the bones of blessed Remaclus and carried them to Liège; and while the king was celebrating a banquet in a certain distinguished place, they set them upon the very table.”]

When we understood that the king and the archbishop were prolonging matters—for our lord abbot had already said that some people were discussing nothing definite—we reached this common decision: we ourselves should approach the king on our behalf and speak before him as the matter required.

We therefore entered the orchard, where the king was reclining in royal splendor at dinner with his nobles. We approached him with devout supplication and entrusted the opening speech to one of our number:

“King and lord,” he said, “may you live happily through the ages,

and reign victorious, as we Stavelot men desire.

“We humbly suggest to your majesty that you should see what the deed requires and recognize what you have committed against the saint of God whom we serve. Having recognized it, may you live forever with your fathers. We also beseech you, for the sake of the state of the kingdom that you possess, and for the sake of the property of the saint, which you have weakened after being corrupted by the greed of certain men, and which your most powerful predecessors bestowed upon him and confirmed—property which remained inviolable and undisturbed until these times of your rule—that you order it restored in the manner attested by the monastery’s privileges. If you wish it done otherwise, it will become a cause of danger for you.

“For our place, once honorable and wealthy, appears in your time to be utterly desolated, though the emperors before you honored it with the highest distinctions. For, since a contrary arrangement has been introduced, its best possessions are being taken away on every side. Therefore, lest you prove inferior to them, or worse in any matter of royal policy, let justice be planted in your heart, and your throne will be established forever” (Proverbs 25).

[Col. 0317C] When the king looked toward the archbishop, as though awaiting instruction from him about what should be done, and the archbishop, held silent by his greed for the property, offered no answer, our spokesman added:

“What, lord king, have you become silent because of this one man, to whom, contrary to the dignity of the kingdom, you have submitted yourself through an unworthy discipleship? And you,” he continued, turning to those seated around him, “bishops and nobles of the kingdom, why are you silent before him, afraid to speak for justice?”

At this the archbishop changed expression and said:

“What guilt have I incurred by taking something from you? Or in what way am I liable to this holy man? You have no case by which to obtain anything, and you strive in vain, for I have never touched anything belonging to you.”

The other replied:

“We seek nothing but our right, for a just cause: namely, our prebend, which you rashly invaded without due thought, with the assent of our lord king. From the beginning, the bishop and abbot who governed these two monasteries, once they had been built, wished them to be one heart and one soul in both establishments; accordingly, he left the prebend to be held as one by all succeeding generations. Therefore, for us also to wish to hold it is not injustice; but see what sacrilege it is for you to have taken it, and how great the wrong.”

But the bishop of Baveberg, who at that time was steward of the royal household, said:

“If your petition is just, my lord has decided that it will be examined tomorrow in a general judgment. For we do not allow anything unjust to grow within his rule, so long as the authority of this order is present to advise the commonwealth.”

## CHAPTER IX. The saint’s body is immediately brought to the table; complaining of the postponement, the brothers demand justice.

[Note: [Col. 0318C] “Acknowledge, therefore, to him what the whole world adjudicates as belonging to him.” Lambert of Schafnaburg also remembers this supplication of the religious men of Stavelot in these words. [Col. 0318D] “Beseeching God,” namely, the religious men mentioned above, “that, if he would show no mercy as to sons, he might at least show mercy to so great a Father, who already reigns with Christ and daily brings a complaint concerning his injuries before the tribunal of the eternal Judge.”]

[Col. 0318A]

Distrustful—or rather, doubtful—because of the bishop’s words concerning the following day, since nothing is hurried enough for an eager mind, we decided by common agreement that it was necessary to bring our patron’s body immediately. When it had unexpectedly been set upon the royal table, we said:

“Behold the very one to whom you, king, are doing injustice. Acknowledge, therefore, to him what the whole world adjudicates as belonging to him. Behold, because of that very injustice, he demands your judgment upon the earth. Take care not to neglect this, lest in heaven he seek God as judge against you.”

“Because of you,” the king said to the archbishop, “this importunate attack is being made upon us. But how long must I endure this contrary to the custom of my ancestors? Consider that, unless we change our decision and determine otherwise, we may soon place our own safety in peril because of this.”

But when the archbishop gave us no helpful answer, and instead declared that we were guilty of excessive presumption and audacity, the king once again promised, postponing the matter until the following day, that he would do us full justice according to our desire. He said that it was not opportune to decide a matter of such importance at that time.

Meanwhile, the entire assembly of bishops urged and begged that the venerable body be carried back to the church. We said:

“It is uncertain what tomorrow will bring. Nevertheless, it is no less lawful for imperial power to do what is good. For the sake of his salvation and the stability of his empire, we ask the king not to suspend us any longer through these delays and postponements.”

The queen, his wife, a woman of good character, since she could not help us, shed tears in place of prayers.

## CHAPTER X. The brothers follow the king and bishop as they leap up from the table, but are barred from the palace; when the body is brought back to the table, the structure itself collapses to the ground.

[Note: [Col. 0319C] “Thus the king, scorning the table, sprang up.” Lambert of Schafnaburg speaks of this as follows: “By this form of supplication, which had been devised to win favor, the king, becoming excessively enraged in turn, hurried away, abandoning the meal, and rushed into the palace. Filled with anger, he considered by what example he ought to punish the abbot, the instigator of so audacious a deed.”]

[Col. 0318D]

As we persisted in these petitions and in this struggle, the archbishop rose, grasped the king’s right hand, and said:

“Why, king, do you sit here in disgrace? These insolent monks have attacked you with their rustic band, offering violence contrary to law against royal authority, as though to compel us to obey their will. It is not worthy of your honor to look upon their audacity for long—men whom it is shameful even to hear openly.”

Thus the king, scorning the table, sprang up with all his men and left us bewildered but not exhausted; and he himself, no less ill-advised. We had with us that confidence by which nothing could seem more secure, yet it was not then clear what should be done, except to follow into the palace the king for whose sake we had come, if that should perhaps prove useful. When we arrived there, the chamberlains who went ahead offered the saint an indignity by repelling him at the entrance.

Who can unfold the sudden outbreak and magnitude of the lamentation among all our people, the great cry of the populace rising to heaven, the voices proclaiming this injustice to God, the flood of eloquence, or what tongue can express it? At such a moment, no honorable path of advance was open to us. For the orchard was closed on every side by the crowds of the tumultuous people. The courtiers themselves, who, moved by devout compassion, were kindly disposed toward the saint and toward us, advised that the saint’s body be carried back to the same place and set, miserably, upon the royal table before everyone’s eyes.

This seems to have happened not against the will of the Lord’s confessor. For as soon as that senseless material somehow perceived the saint’s relics, as though unable to bear that divine weight, the stoutest framework of the trestles very easily dissolved into pieces, like wax. The most sacred pledge itself was lowered to the ground and lay there in the deepest humility. Immediately the entire orchard was filled with people from the surrounding area and from the whole city, of both sexes, and the cry of the grieving people multiplied toward heaven:

“Why, just Lord, do you allow this injustice to be done on earth?”

## CHAPTER XI. Gonterulus’s crushed and broken leg is restored, and he is brought as far as the royal doors.

During the humiliation just described, one of our servants, belonging to the saint’s household, carelessly placed his foot beneath the table. When the falling mass came down, he could not withdraw his broken leg. With the help of his companions he was pulled aside, and, overcome by pain, he wished to cut through the torn skin by which his foot was hanging.

The servant’s name was Gonterulus. In his distress he rashly spoke as though reproaching the holy confessor:

“Is this your power, my lord—that what you perhaps delayed doing to deserving enemies, you preferred to let happen to me, your faithful servant who obeys you?”

He had not yet finished speaking when, with a sudden collision of the bones, the broken tibia was restored through the cooperation of divine power. He rose and stood sound upon both feet, as though awakening from sleep, the anguish having passed.

Many people ran from every direction to this miracle, and many also came from the palace to witness it. To establish that the event had been wrought by divine power, they made the young man remove his shoe; and, at the place of the injury, they saw with astonishment a mark like a red thread wound around the tibia in place of a scar.

They immediately reported the truth of the event to their lord the king and led the young man as a witness as far as the royal doors. But because of the press of the crowd, he was not admitted into the midst.

## CHAPTER XII. A blind woman is restored to sight there.

[Note: [Col. 0320B] “Meanwhile, as the confessor to be glorified was making his merits shine forth.” Lambert of Schafnaburg also confirms the multitude of miracles that followed. Thus he writes: “Thereafter, throughout the whole of the following night and day, such a multitude of miracles flashed around the saint’s body that blessed Remaclus seemed, as it were, to demand his rights through a bodily proclamation.”]

Meanwhile, as the merits of the confessor who was to be glorified shone forth, another remarkable event occurred in the presence of all who were there, at the very place where the venerable body lay.

A blind woman, brought from the nearby territory of Liège, stood there with devout supplication to venerate it. Having long lamented that she had incurred the unbroken night of blindness, she is said—

“with the darkness driven out, to have gained the light.”

Taking the cross that was there, without anyone giving it to her, she began reverently to kiss it, and then proclaimed to everyone the power of the Lord’s confessor that had been manifested in her.

## CHAPTER XIII. The bishop rebukes the disturbed king; he orders the body returned to the shrine, but the men sent for it return unsuccessfully, since it remains immovable like a stone.

[Col. 0320C]

When both events had become widely known in the palace, and the king, recognizing that some divine work was present in the matter, not without reason feared that divine vengeance might suddenly overtake him, he said to the archbishop:

“We are not acting wisely in this affair of ours and of the commonwealth. Can this light be pleasing to us, or the spirit of heaven delightful, so long as we endure so great an outcry, so great a reproach against our name, and so importunate a pursuit? Do you not see that everyone’s faces are turned toward us—not only those of the common people, but also those of the princes of my entire kingdom—who, as I think rightly and not unjustly, accuse us as guilty of this deed? I freely confess that I have never acted more foolishly than when, badly advised by you, I wronged this holy man by placing what belonged to him in your hands.”

“Let this sin rest upon me,” he replied. “Attribute entirely to me whatever crime is being charged against you because of this deed.”

“Do not too readily believe these men, most invincible king,” he continued, “whom it would be more just to punish for the unheard-of audacity of their pride. For what comparison can be made with their rashness, by which—shameful even to say—they compelled you and your men to rise from the royal table, you, I mean, lord of the entire Roman Empire? If you are wise, do you think this should be treated lightly, rather than punished by imperial authority as though they were guilty of treason?”

“Therefore do not be disturbed by what is now being said to happen here miraculously, for this saint is pretending to perform miracles here only through their efforts, in order to stir us up.

“Nevertheless, hear the counsel I think should be followed meanwhile without compromising your honor. Order the sacred body, which they have thrown upon the ground as though to hasten vengeance upon us, to be carried back to the shrine, since it is improper for you and your men to endure these importunate outcries.”

The chamberlains immediately ran to us, conveying the king’s order that this should be done. We absolutely refused, sending back through them a sufficiently appropriate explanation to the king: namely, that he should understand that this injury and contempt must have displeased almighty God, who even now suffers in his chosen ones whatever adversity is inflicted upon them. At the very least, it was fitting that, after the contempt had been followed by repentance, the body should be carried back honorably once justice had been done to the saint. If the king wished otherwise, he could attempt it in vain. For it was entirely unfitting that so great a confessor of the Lord, rejected by him until then, should go farther to seek the favor of one who was turning away from him.

Those who had come from the king therefore returned and reported that our people’s resolve was unshaken. An immediate message was sent to our lord abbot in the king’s name: since he allowed his monks to act so insolently against their lord, and moreover did not think that he himself should yield with impunity, he should be punished as one who was knowingly responsible for whatever his disciples appeared rashly to have done. If he had anything to say on their behalf, he should have the venerable body brought back as quickly as possible.

The abbot declared under Christ’s testimony that he had been entirely unaware of the deed, much less privy to its planning. He added with tears that he had never been more sorrowful, for, wholly distrustful, he feared that our plan would turn to our destruction. He therefore came to us with those ministers and courtiers, thinking that he might compel us by force or put an end to the popular disturbances. But when many resisted him, as though thousands had assembled to defend us, neither his authority nor his humble entreaty had any more power there than the king’s command previously delivered through messengers.

After this, some of the chamberlains rushed into the crowds, their spirits inflamed, and attacked the sacred body as though they would accomplish their purpose by force. When they seized the saint’s shrine from every side in order to lift it, it was felt to be fixed in place by such a divinely supplied weight that it could not be raised from that spot, like an immovable stone. Astonished, and regarding the event as divine, they returned frustrated in their purpose and reported it to the great lords with no little amazement.

## CHAPTER XIV. The bishop treats all this as fantastic, orders the saint’s body removed, but those sent return empty-handed and offer money for the task.

Since the archbishop still placed no faith in these events, but maintained that everything was being fabricated fantastically, he ordered a large number of men from the palace to go in the king’s name, impose the heaviest penalties upon us, and remove the sacred body by force.

When they rushed upon us, a tremendous cry and uproar arose among the mingled crowd. Since everyone on our side resisted those opposed to us, the matter was sufficiently well handled, though not without divine assistance.

Seeing this, they were as though stunned by the divine sign of what had happened. Having no strength to carry out the orders of their superiors, they returned to them and said:

“The matter concerns the soul; nothing, lord king, can accomplish this through your men’s force or presence. For we have experienced that something divine is present there. Unless you act through benevolence and love, whatever else you may wish will remain ineffective.

“Believe us: those faithful monks of the saint cannot be compelled by any power. Whether the saint should be moved or not, he has assented to their will.”

They all therefore prostrated themselves at his feet with tears and said:

“Lord king, if you are wisely considering your own interests in this matter, as we advise, do no harm to those in whose hands the affair lies. Satisfy their will, because, as we understand it, they have a just cause for obtaining what they seek. Nothing of yours inspires fear in them; they have the strongest of defenders. Therefore we fear the danger threatening you. We would rather redeem this from the archbishop himself at any price than allow this saint not to obtain what he earnestly demands.”

## CHAPTER XV. The king sends the bishop of Liège and his chancellor to the brothers, but accomplishes little.

But the king, considering it better to be overcome by good than to conquer by evil, sent our lord bishop to us with his other nobles to ask that we do without delay whatever he wished, if we wished to obtain from him what was being requested. He further declared that it would disgrace royal dignity and mark it with infamy if he appeared to be compelled, as though by superior power, to obey the might of his subjects.

The bishop left the king and looked down from above upon the orchard, filled on every side with people. Distrusting his ability to reach the place because his health was failing—for he was a weak man—he sent ahead the king’s chancellor, together with the abbot of Saint Lawrence, to deliver the royal embassy to the Stavelot assembly on his behalf.

When they heard the king’s command, they answered briefly, as the matter lay in their hearts:

“If the king has reason to fear for himself, as though danger were imminent—and he can easily escape it, provided that he is free to do so by administering justice—why does he delay this salvation, unaware of what tomorrow may bring? We have sufficiently recognized the purpose of his postponements, by which he has so often deferred the justice sought and promised. Why do we need to spend more words on both sides? Unless the king himself comes in person and does this, if indeed it pleases Saint Remaclus the confessor, he will not be able to move this body from here today.”

Some of the party, angered by these threats, returned a contrary report.

But they too, returning in the same way, said:

“Nothing, lord king, nothing is accomplished by this. However much labor you wish to expend, you will find them fixed in their decision.”

“Since I am accomplishing little as I wished,” he said, “they too will accomplish less through me than they desire by this plan.”

## CHAPTER XVI. The abbot himself comes with the bishop of Utrecht at vespers to satisfy the king; after the latter departs, the brothers keep the night watch there in vain.

[Col. 0323A]

Amid such great and continuous pressure, which inevitably arose from love for God’s most devout confessor, some pressing against others and others being constantly pushed by still others, no one is said to have been injured or disturbed, or to have suffered any pain beyond a slight anxiety. Yet, when this anxiety had been intensified by the excessive heat and gathered force, it immediately dissolved when a most welcome breeze began to blow.

Our lord abbot, wishing to clear himself openly of the false suspicion raised against him by the king’s officials—as though he himself, being answerable to them, were the author of this opposition—again attempted, both personally and through powerful friends, to remove such a decision from his men.

He therefore came as evening was falling with William, bishop of Utrecht. But even then he was not admitted, out of respect for so great a dignity, by that popular multitude which, as has been said, had gathered together out of love for so great a confessor in order to defend him.

When the abbot and bishop could accomplish no more against the resistance of the crowd, we gave them this reply: they should not think that we had acted so thoughtlessly or against our own interests, since, as they themselves saw, there was no opportunity for us to do anything of this kind according to our desire. Moreover, it seemed entirely improper that, when divine power had affirmed that the body could not be moved, we should presumptuously attempt to move it against the saint’s will and thereby prove ungrateful.

“I see,” said the bishop, “that no force can be applied here to any effect. It is better to leave matters as they are than to undertake anything that would be done at our peril.”

After this, as evening closed the day, we kept the night watch, not without wondrous divine assistance.

## CHAPTER XVII. Of two blind men sitting there, one is unexpectedly restored to sight.

At that very hour two blind men had fallen prostrate before the saint’s body, seeking a remedy. We sat beside them, intending to perform what was appropriate to the occasion and the time.

It happened that, through the offering of those who were making gifts there, a coin fell from the shrine before the faces of the men who appeared deprived of sight. One of them picked it up before our eyes and began to examine it carefully, as though determining whose coin it was. He immediately handed it to one of those standing nearby.

When asked whether it had previously been possible for him to see anything, he replied that he had endured blindness for a long time, but that then, for the first time, by divine action, he saw something as light returned to him.

## CHAPTER XVIII. Of a dove seen by some people emerging from the shrine.

That same night, which was exceedingly solemn for us because of the vigil, the majesty of the confessor who was to be glorified was manifested there to certain people. A white dove appeared to emerge from the shrine. Flying around and surveying the place of the vigil, like the dove that had emerged from Noah’s ark during the Flood, it soothed the minds of the grieving by portending something divine. Just as that dove signified through the olive branch that peace had been restored to the earth, so this one signified that God’s anger had been turned into mercy.

After it had circled the entire area, it appeared to fly back to the same little shrine from which it had emerged. When day had come, those who had been privileged to witness this, invoking the majesty of God and the common faith, reported so great a portent to certain of our men.

## CHAPTER XIX. Of a jongleur who sang songs during the vigil about these events, and of the king listening and spending the night in woolen clothing and barefoot.

That night a certain jongleur-singer had gone to sleep at an inn with his companion. He was immediately awakened from sleep and said:

“Please, get up; it is better for us to go there.

“This is no vain matter; believe me, we must not remain here.

“It is good to keep that venerable vigil.”

When the other refused and accused him of a delusive vision, he replied:

“I am not deceived by a dream’s mockery. I swear by God that I saw someone of venerable appearance, as though taking me by the hand, dragging me there.”

After saying this, he hurried at a swift pace to join the watchers. Not knowing what he was singing, he happened by chance to begin singing many things about the saint. As he recounted our misfortunes one after another, his song somehow consoled the sorrowful, while dancers sang along.

The king, listening from above through a window, heard with anxious attention the singer’s references to what he himself had cause to fear. Because of what had occurred, he spent the entire night in woolen clothing and barefoot, in fear and supplication.

## CHAPTER XX. At dawn, by common agreement, the sacred body is carried back to the shrine.

When morning came, everyone agreed that the sacred body ought to be carried back to the shrine. It had been sufficiently exposed as a spectacle to the arrogance of the powerful, and nothing had been accomplished except to heap greater insult upon the body that, as was said, had been subjected to injuries.

Some people coming from the court reported one thing and others another: the king’s advisers were treating us with excessive hostility and maintaining that we should suffer human judgments according to the laws, because we had offered an unheard-of resistance at that moment to royal authority.

But one of the princes called some of our men aside and, sympathizing with them from his heart, disclosed the firm decision against us: unless the saint were carried back, all human ingenuity would profit us nothing; his lord considered nothing important and could arrange nothing while it happened that the venerable body was being detained by us in this manner. All good men, he said, plainly judged that we wished to avenge ourselves in this way—something wicked—upon our common ruler.

When we heard this, after consulting our lord abbot and the brothers together, we immediately carried our only hope honorably back into the church of the Virgin Mother.

## CHAPTER XXI. The king prepares torment and punishment for the brothers, and the saint’s body is assigned to the bishop of Baveberg.

[Note: [Col. 0325C] The angry king had ordered his armed men to surround our people. Lambert of Schafnaburg agrees: “By this example,” he says, “he, filled with anger, considered how he ought to punish the abbot, the instigator of so audacious a deed.”]

[Col. 0325A]

After this, when the solemnities of the Masses had been completed, our lord, carrying the records of his predecessors, went to the palace with his men, intending to make his customary proclamation before the lords. There he learned of our plan and of that of all the others who had resisted royal authority—namely, that torture and exile were finally being prepared. He ordered those whom he had sent away to take care lest they should be discovered and punished.

For the angry king had ordered his armed men to surround ours and to spare neither monk nor layman from being dragged away for punishment. This was the plan of the archbishop, who was disturbing our affair with all his strength; and it was said that, at his instigation and through his efforts, the king had also adopted the plan of allowing the bishop of Baveberg to take away our patron’s body, which had been granted to him by the king.

But why should we delay in describing what we believe will be equally delightful for all to hear, though not without joy mingled with tears? The devout providence of the patron could no longer endure the prolonged affliction of his faithful servants. Indeed, when all human help had failed, he immediately came to our assistance, divine power cooperating with him. He had long endured insults and disgrace, and had sufficiently observed the perseverance of his people. Though, in a sense, despised on earth by the tyranny of princes, he made nearly the entire world recognize in a moment what power he possessed in heaven before the Almighty, so that, whether they wished it or not, his adversaries, bent by divine power, obeyed his will.

## CHAPTER XXII. After a considerable shaking in the church, Saint’s shrine is raised a cubit into the air, and the bishop of Cambrai, praying in the crypt, is visited by the divine presence of the saints.

[Note: [Col. 0326B] “It was the year from the Incarnation of the Lord.” From this passage Aegidius of the Golden Valley drew the second part of the second chapter of his book, which begins: “In the year of the Lord 1071.”]

The year was 1071 from the Incarnation of the Lord, and the sixth year since the severance of the Church of Malmedy from that of Stavelot, when, on the seventh day before the Ides of May, it pleased divine grace to restore her. At the hour when the sun inclines toward midday, the heavens distilled upon us a mercy we had desired.

While we were staying at Liège in the house of Saint Lambert, there was again made a sound like that of an approaching violent wind. Filling human ears, it likewise filled the church, where many had gathered from different regions. When a considerable shaking had occurred at the place where the saint’s most sacred bones rested, the shrine was plainly seen to move and to be lifted about a cubit into the air.

At that same moment, an equally great sound was made below in the crypt, where the most sacred body of the precious martyr Lambert rests. At that hour Bishop Lietbert of Cambrai was intent there upon the psalmody with his clerics. Somewhat terrified by what had happened, and with the others fleeing, he—being a man full of God and of profound understanding, who perceived something divine—remained, desiring to know the outcome of the event that had sounded forth so wondrously.

For, as he himself testified, at first a dense fog darkened that place; when it immediately disappeared, a light brighter than the sun shone forth. In the midst of that radiance, the bishop, as though transported beyond himself, saw two figures appear, shining with extraordinary brightness: namely, Remaclus and Lambert, equally most holy bishops. He heard them conversing with one another in a kind of secret murmur about what had happened.

## CHAPTER XXIII. The sayings of the saints are recalled by way of example.

Let it not therefore be burdensome to the attentive reader that we seem here to depart briefly from the history, in order to gather certain examples of similar events for the confirmation of faith in this miracle.

“Blessed Pope Gregory,” he says, “it is necessary that the saints display greater signs where the weak mind may doubt their presence. It is evident that this saint showed precisely such a sign to those who doubted concerning him. Where the saints lie in their bodies,” he says, “and especially where it often happens that blessed spirits revisit their bones, there is no doubt that they are able, as they indeed do, to show countless miracles to those who seek them with a pure mind, just as we read concerning certain others, and as the history of the Kings testifies concerning Elisha.”

Thus the merciful Jesus, in the customary compassion of his goodness, cooperated with his saint by the grace of his divinity, so that, with almost the whole world recognizing it in an instant, it might also become known to future generations how great was the merit before God of this saint, who was held in such contempt on earth by unjust men. Now let us return to the matter, so that we may faithfully discuss what follows.

## CHAPTER XXIV. A woman grievously contracted is carried to the saint and immediately healed; the church is filled as the people flock together for this purpose.

[Col. 0326D] Meanwhile, before the glorified body of our patron, something resembling a monster was carried in: a creature indeed, but not having the form of a human being in its pitiable body. It was a woman, brought from the Parisian parish to this region of ours, not without God’s direction, to seek the merits of the saints. The disease of paralysis had contracted her into the shape of a ball, with dreadful bodily suffering.

It was such a sight that, for proclaiming the omnipotence of the Savior, we called her monster-like: both ankles were attached backward to her loins; the nails of both hands were bent back into the palms; her sinews were contracted; and, with only the skin stretched over them, they had stiffened upon her dried bones.

As soon as she had been laid down before the shrine, her withered limbs began to revive by divine power, and little by little her face and bodily form were seen to be restored to their former strength. First, with her hands extended, she carefully rubbed her trembling limbs; gradually she tried to stretch herself out, with only one leg remaining weak, while the contractions of the other limbs were dissolved.

People streamed in from every direction; present were:

> Known and unknown, citizen together with traveler.

But that spacious church could not contain those who came.

The open porticoes and the buildings of the cloisters were filled with people proclaiming with one voice to heaven the mighty works of Christ. Considering the faith of those standing there at that time, what could have been added more fittingly to the praise of the Creator? Every creature seemed, in its confessor, to praise Christ the Lord together with us, as may be observed from the addition of what follows.

## CHAPTER XXV. The great bell sounds without anyone striking it, and a multitude of sick people are restored to their former health more quickly than words can tell.

After the glorification of so great a confessor, the great bell suddenly began to sound without anyone striking it. Later, when the other bells were rung together because of this miracle and were allowed to fall silent, that one continued as it had begun. It was always heard for the solemnity of God’s miracles, because, as it is thought, God, wishing to make known to everyone that he cooperated with his saint by increasing his powers, proclaimed this through signs by which it had strength to testify.

Some, however, suspected that perhaps, as is the custom of human ingenuity, this work was secretly being performed by someone. They climbed the high tower, but found nothing that could expose any such deception.

When the report spread that one person had recovered his health, a wretched multitude of blind, lame, and withered people immediately flocked together. It was openly possible to see many of them, from different kingdoms, restored more quickly than words can tell to their former health through the intervention of the merits of the most glorious patron.

Who could distinguish individually the kinds of healing bestowed there from heaven by divine remedies upon the various sick? For just as a skilled physician, knowledgeable about every disease, offers the sick person a potion or antidote according to what he knows will benefit each one, so divine grace infused heavenly medicine into each of those who came, as it pleased God.

Those who had been brought by the hands of others returned home walking on their own feet. Who there could refrain from praising God? The church, as we have said, was everywhere filled with the voices of those crying out in thanksgiving to God and rejoicing together.

## CHAPTER XXVI. In the presence of the Bishop of Cambrai, a certain contracted man is raised up in the crypt, and another, weaker than the rest, carried by two chamberlains, is restored to health before all the people.

Just as earlier it was manifest that this confessor of God worked wonders above, so it was also manifest below that the martyr of Christ worked wonders. At the same hour when the bishop mentioned above was present there, there was also a certain man asking him for alms, with all his limbs contracted.

When he heard from outside that such a work was taking place, he asked to be helped lest he be prevented from reaching the place by the crowds pressing together. But the bishop said: “Do not lose hope that you will arrive. The Lord is able, through these same merits of the saints, to bestow the same mercy upon you here.”

The effectiveness of the power immediately followed these words. For that traveler was restored and planted his ancient footprints firmly beneath his feet.

Some of the chamberlains then hurried to the royal palace and rushed in one after another. Each one who arrived later therefore announced as something new what the one who had come earlier had repeatedly declared.

“Lord king,” they said, “hear and understand what that saint can do, what he is now magnificently accomplishing. We truly testify that today we have seen wonders which God himself has worked through the merits of his confessor.”

Since the archbishop still did not believe their words, he caused the whole matter to be tested more carefully by deeds, as follows. Two of the chamberlains immediately ran out and seized a man whom they found lying in the portico, weaker than the others and not unlike the one whom we described at the beginning of the miracles.

They carried him before the presence of the saint and threw him onto the pavement like a burden, since he was wholly unable to move himself in any respect. At once one could see his limbs, by divine power, scattered and then joined together; his sinews tightened, his bones were connected, his inner organs restored, and each limb strengthened in health.

Gradually raising himself up, he grasped the altar’s horn and stood upon his feet. Thus, with a different face and appearance, he appeared in some way another man from the one he had seemed to be.

We write only what we saw; thousands of people from different nations saw these things equally.

## CHAPTER XXVII. While the minds of the king and archbishop remain in doubt concerning these events, a certain man brings, in their presence, the staff of a paralytic who was healed, under the testimony of his own head.

These events were reported to the king and archbishop as having truly happened, and because of them their minds remained in doubt. Meanwhile a certain courtier stood in their midst, whose name has escaped us. Displaying a staff as testimony, he said:

“Look! I received this token of power from a man who had been paralyzed. I saw him healed by divine power in their presence and leap up on both feet.”

Who, then, could be so opposed to the truth, so deranged in mind, as to deny all these things which we saw, indeed which we believe were carried out by God’s direction and power? It is not my intention, O king, to deceive you. If I am lying in any part of this, take my head from me.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. The Bishop of Cambrai announces what he saw of both saints, and, through the staff he holds in his hand, the archbishop restores the property to the terrified king.

While these things were being said and reported, and while the archbishop still could not in any way be bent to return what he unjustly held, Lietbert, Bishop of Cambrai, arrived and was admitted. He declared clearly before them what he had seen.

“It is not useful for you to remain seated, my lord king,” he said, “because I believe that you will eventually do what you must do later than you wish. Know that those two soldiers of the heavenly Emperor are bringing grave charges against you between themselves. Since I fear the danger threatening you, I have come to announce sound counsel. Without delay, if you do not wish to perish, restore to the saint what you unjustly took from him.”

Both bishops and dukes, together with the chamberlains, joined him in this request, asking that it be done with no feigned tears.

Then the king, as though terrified by these things, rose from his throne and turned toward the bishop.

“As I see,” he said, “I can delay this no longer, nor do I dissent from you any further in this matter. What you received from me when I had not taken proper counsel, restore if you wish, since, whether I want it or not, I shall have to return what he so evidently demands from me as his own.”

But the other said: “Since this pleases God, and it cannot be otherwise”—and he held out the staff he had been carrying—“Look, my lord,” he said, “receive the good that you gave.”

## CHAPTER XXIX. The king, breaking into the church by force of his own men, returns the saint’s property after humbly making satisfaction; and a certain contracted man is raised up at that same hour.

[Note: [Col. 0329D] The king, proceeding from the palace, stood upon the steps that rose before the church. Lambert of Schaffhausen confirms this satisfaction and humiliation of the king in these words: “While everyone was astonished at the novelty of so great an event, the king, seized by the most violent fear lest, if he delayed, heavenly vengeance might immediately fall upon him, not only restored what had been taken away, but also magnificently increased it with fresh gifts in royal generosity.”]

The king therefore proceeded from the palace and stood upon the steps that rose before the church. The church resounded with the voices of those rejoicing and praising God.

“But, as I think,” he said in amazement, “I shall arrive there too late to make satisfaction to the saint as he desires.”

Scarcely, therefore, did he reach the presence, the attendants forcing a way through the midst of the people, where the most celebrated work of divine power was taking place.

Immediately receiving from the custodian the saint’s pastoral staff, he stood and said:

> “Look, holy one, receive what I return to you as your own;  
> By forgiving me, grant pardon to me who ask.”

Thus the king, placing the staff again upon the venerable body and confessing his sin with bowed head, returned as quickly as possible. As we learned, at that same hour in which justice had been done to the saint by the king,

> A certain contracted man stood upright, sound and healthy in his walking.

[Col. 0329D] Immediately, therefore, all gave praise and thanks to God Most High, and the clergy of the city joined together in singing with due solemnity, “We praise you, O God.”

It is impossible to touch upon in writing how many and how great the miracles were that occurred afterward. Some of them, because of the crowds, noise, and turmoil of the surging people, could not come to our knowledge. Nevertheless, we thought it wrong to pass over in silence those things that we saw or learned through the faithful report of others who had seen them.

## CHAPTER XXX. An account of why he once carried to Aachen performed no similar deed there, but did so here, in his own episcopal seat.

[Col. 0330A]

It is worthwhile to add this also to the present work: although he could have accomplished this in a similar manner elsewhere, either in his own resting place or in the palace at Aachen, to which he had likewise been carried, he preferred that it be accomplished in the episcopal seat that had once been his own.

Divine grace brought about a worthy recompense: where he had formerly abandoned honors and dignities for contempt of the world, choosing to cleave more closely to God, there, through God’s administration, honor and glory were more magnificently displayed for him.

Nor should this example of his patience and piety be left unmentioned: it drew those who seemed to oppose him much more powerfully by benefits than it restrained them, as they deserved, by any blow or vengeance.

## CHAPTER XXXI. Concerning a certain matron of that city who had been deprived of her sight and was restored to her former light.

A certain matron from that city had for a long time been deprived of the light of her eyes. When she came to the venerable body to pray for herself according to her vow, immediately, through the presence of divine illumination and after the darkness had been wiped away, a most welcome light shone again in her eyeballs. In return for this gift divinely obtained, she herself gave two members of her household to the saint.
