## CHAPTER XXXII. Concerning a woman born blind and granted sight.

A certain woman had likewise been brought to this solemn miracle. Nature, as she herself confessed, had denied her the light of her eyes from her mother’s womb. Praying faithfully with the others, she brought forth the following words from the depths of her heart:

> “Holy one of God, merciful and ready to hear,  
> Who here workest such great and wondrous deeds divinely;  
> Who grantest others whatever they ask more swiftly;  
> Since I do not know the day, grant me sight and drive away the night  
> Which has long possessed me, wretched woman, from my birth.”

As soon as she raised her head with her prayer, both little eyes were opened, with a flow of blood:

> “For the power, shining like a brilliant ray, brought splendor into the gloomy shadows,  
> And soon the friendly day illumines her empty orbs.”

Seeing the unfamiliar light, she rightly praised the physician with the greatest joy. As proof of the miracle, she brought before the eyes of the people the blood still dripping from her eyes.

## CHAPTER XXXIII. Concerning a wretched man who had a scrofulous swelling on his head and was healed.

A scrofulous swelling had grown on the head of a certain wretched man. As it enlarged, it occupied his ear and face. This affliction seemed no less troublesome to the miserable man than it was most repulsive to everyone who saw it.

When he stood with the others before the shrine, all that diseased swelling suddenly disappeared. Those who had seen him before watched with astonishment as the loosened skin seemed to settle evenly back into its proper place, and nothing remained of the disease except a scar on his head.

## CHAPTER XXXIV. Concerning a seven-year-old paralyzed girl who was healed.

A woman laid down there her seven-year-old daughter, who was paralyzed. Her faith immediately obtained the girl’s healing. Those who saw the girl standing upright, healed by God’s power, lifted her above the people in their hands and magnified the merit of Christ’s confessor, with the miracle as witness.

Since we did not yet know what the effectiveness of this power was, the mother, standing nearby, cried out through her tears with the greatest joy:

“This girl whom I see came forth from my womb. A short while ago I expected only her death, because she was almost dead in every part and merely fluttered with an exceedingly faint breath.”

Then such a great cry of wonder arose from both sexes that the continuous voice, mingled with tears, seemed unable to end. Everyone exulted in the praise of God with a voice without words, with such a sound as scarcely any human ear could bear.

Moreover, to every person arriving from outside, that entire church seemed to have been filled with the glory and majesty of the Lord. Those dwelling there delighted as though from the presence of God in an indescribable sweetness, so that it could truly be said there, as it was rightly said:

> “The Lord is in this place” (Genesis 28).

On that very day the earth also seemed in some way to rejoice in this celebration of divine works, no less than heaven. For after three full months during which it had not been moistened by water, while the grasses with their shoots were almost dried up, on that same day, through divine action, it recovered all its greenness, abundant rains being poured down.

## CHAPTER XXXV. Concerning a cleric whose feet had been twisted from birth and who was healed.

As the evening sun was already declining toward its setting, while the large crowd still cried out in praise of Christ’s confessor, another wondrous work of divine power occurred, proclaiming the merit of that same pious protector.

A certain cleric had been carried to that healing veneration by his father. From his mother’s womb he had suffered from twisted feet, with his steps turned crosswise. Without delay, the same physician visited him in the midst of those standing around and offered each person the kind of medicine he knew to be appropriate.

The man immediately indicated that he felt himself healed. But to those watching, the matter did not yet provide complete certainty, because his shoes still clung to his feet in their former condition.

The chamberlains from the court and many nobles were present. They themselves, admiring God’s power and proclaiming the merit of Christ’s confessor in this man, praised it greatly after the boy’s feet had been stripped of their shoes.

## CHAPTER XXXVI. On the following morning a decision is made to return the glorified body to its own place.

> That day closes, holding praises throughout the ages;  
> The events rest during the night, and the spectacles return in the morning.

The lord abbot therefore sought counsel from his people about carrying the glorified body of the saint back to its own place. Sound counsel was given: the return should by no means be delayed, lest what had proceeded according to our vow later become any kind of impediment for us.

Accordingly, with the most honorable clergy of Saint Lambert—co-workers, as we truly confess, in those miracles—we departed from that city rejoicing, both in procession and with equal devotion. There was one voice among all, crying out in praise of Christ’s confessor:

> “Hail, holy bishop, our illustrious patron;  
> O most faithful hope for your own people, help us by your grace.  
> You are the light and glory of Gaul; protect clergy and people together,  
> For we know that you possess great power: care for the sicknesses of sin.  
>   
> Since you were brought here, you have shone forth with many miracles;  
> The whole country rejoices that you return from here with glory.  
> From this gathering of the court thanks are rendered to you,  
> And the whole court is magnificently celebrated in your name.”

## CHAPTER XXXVII. Concerning the halt made this side of the Meuse, the most famous praise of the schoolboys, and the confirmation by the landholders of the transfer of that place to the saint.

[Note: [Col. 0333A] The foundations of the church were immediately laid by the inhabitants. A parish church still exists today near the gate [Col. 0333B] and the bridge of Amaricordis. Because of that miracle it is called the church of Saint Remaclus, not far from the mountains from which the schoolboys are said to have sung the praises of Saint Remaclus here.]

[Col. 0332C] It also seems worthy of mention that, in imitation of those boys who proclaimed the Lord’s “Hosanna” to the Redeemer (Matthew 21), this too is believed to have been done in praise of this saint, though not apart from the pleasure of divine grace.

On our return, after crossing the river, when we had reached the open country on this side of the Meuse, all the citizens and foreigners together obtained from the lord abbot permission for a halt to be made there in order to hear Mass.

Meanwhile, while a delay was made and the divine office was being prepared for celebration, school groups of boys came together from the entire city as though to attend upon their revered Father. Climbing the summits of the nearest mountain, they raised their voices, as though angelic, through the clouds.

For, divided from one another as though arranged in three choral groups, they sang praise to God for the triumph of their confessor and, still more wondrously, of Christ:

> “We hold the opening of the song in a great voice of praise;  
> Then praise the Crucified in the flesh a second time;  
> Hail, festive day: in this order the praises resound.”

It is therefore not without reason that we believe this was done without the instruction of any teacher or the prompting of human suggestion. Rather, as with the other events, the aid of the Holy Trinity, faithfully invoked, determined that it should happen.

For just as the Psalmist had previously sung what was to come, so we also believe that it was fulfilled in Christ; and likewise, in this saint, because of his enemies, the praise foretold by the Lord was manifested and perfected:

> “Out of the mouth of infants” (Psalm 8; Matthew 21).

When these melodies had been completed, the boys descended to celebrate with us the solemnity of the divine mysteries, all of which were completed together with the votive offerings of the faithful.

On that same day, those who were heirs of that plot of ground handed over to the saint the place where he had rested during the halt. Since the solemn devotion of the people continued piously in his honor, the inhabitants immediately laid the foundations of a church there, which afterward, brought to completion, grew into a work of divine service.

## CHAPTER XXXVIII AND LAST. A joyful return to our own place, the vindication of Malmedy, and finally, as we journey toward Stavelot in the morning, an unknown little bird’s settling upon the saint’s shrine and the restoration of the saints’ bones to their place.

From there we departed and hastened joyfully to our own place. That very evening we brought our protector and triumphant patron to Malmedy. That place, nobly recovered in triumph, he himself, as its rightful Father, vindicated by his own power.

That place, I say, he has now vindicated eternally: at the beginning, after thorns and every kind of filth had been removed, he was its first inhabitant, and he consecrated the dwelling he had chosen for himself to divine worship. Handed over to him by King Sigebert, he governed it most honorably and left it to his successors to govern in his place.

After both monks and laymen had been lawfully recalled under the authority of the abbot, we returned from there to Stavelot in his name, possessing the security we had desired.

Thus, after innumerable miracles of divine power, the victorious bones of our divine patron were restored to their place.

Therefore let us rejoice, having obtained the patronage of so great a confessor, who, when human help was lacking, secured divine assistance for us through his merits.

Let our monastic Father also rejoice, who had been worn out by daily sorrow and for whom the labor expended on this matter had accomplished nothing after more than five years.

[Col. 0334B] Let him rejoice, I say, that such great grace has come to him beyond hope, which he could not obtain through human favor.

The private favor of the powerful and princes did not help. Human counsels accomplished nothing. Frequent journeys to and from the court were of no use. Moreover, the exhausted treasury advanced the matter not at all; neither gold nor silver, which mortals value above all else, nor gifts lavished with excessive generosity, produced any result.

But the grace of God alone, through the merit of his confessor, put an end to these miseries when he willed.

And since we too desire to bring these matters to an end, we decide that we should pause from this work for a little while, so that, if we intend to devote ourselves to writing about other things that afterward shone forth magnificently among us through him, we may meanwhile restore our strength for writing through leisure.

[Col. 0333] THE END.

[Col. 0333]

## Diploma by which the ancient dispute between the people of Malmedy and the people of Stavelot is settled.

Leo, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the religious abbot of the venerable monastery of Saint Peter and Saint Remaclus, situated at Stavelot, and to your successors, perpetual salvation in the Lord.

“Since the supreme apostolic dignity . . . .” The remainder may be seen among the letters of Saint Leo IX, in volume CXLIII of the *Patrologia*.

## In the Year of the Lord 1085. Samuel Marochianus, a Christian from the Jews.

[Col. 0333]

## Historical Notice on Samuel Marochianus

*(Possevinus, Sacred Apparatus, II, 190.)*

[Col. 0333] Samuel, commonly called Marochianus, a Jew from Fez by birth, converted to the Christian faith at Toledo in the year 1085. He wrote a useful little book concerning the coming of the Messiah, whom the Jews vainly await.

[Note: [Col. 0333] In the title of the Strasbourg edition of 1523 he is called “master of the synagogue which is in Subjulmenta, in the kingdom of Morocco.”]

He proves by many arguments that the Jews are under God’s anger and that, because of a certain grave sin in which they remain, they are in this grievous dispersion. He then treats of the vain observance of their law and of their blindness, and of the fact that the greatest sin was that by which they handed Christ over.

He also treats of Christ’s twofold coming, of his Ascension into heaven, and of the rejection of the Jews. Then he discusses the election of the Gentiles, the apostles in the place of the prophets, and the choice of Christian sacrifice, with all Jewish sacrifices rejected. Finally, he discusses the singing of Christians, which he demonstrates to be pleasing to God.

At the end he refutes the Jews from their own Muslim opponents and from the Qur’an. This little book, or letter, was written to a certain Rabbi Isaac in the year of the Lord 1000. Alphonsus Bonihominis, of the Dominican order, translated it from Arabic into Latin in the year 1339.

[Col. 0335]

## Book of Rabbi Samuel Marochianus concerning the Past Coming of the Messiah

*(Library of the Ancient Fathers, volume XVIII, page 518.)*

## Letter of Alphonsus Bonihominis the Spaniard to Master Hugh of the Order of Preachers concerning the following book of Samuel, which he translated from Arabic into Latin

[Col. 0335A] To the most reverend Father in Christ, Brother Hugh, most worthy master of the Order of Preachers and professor of the sacred page, his subordinate brother Alphonsus Bonihominis, a Spaniard, offers the obedience he promised, ready and devoted in all things.

Since, because of my smallness and insufficiency, I am not such a person as to know or be able to do anything great for you or on your behalf, or at least to assist you adequately in the labors and cares that you endure at the court for the peace of us all and of the whole order, I send you, for your consolation and some relief from your labor, an extremely ancient little book that recently came into our hands by a chance occurrence and had previously been hidden for so many years. I have interpreted it in a new translation from Arabic into Latin and now transmit it to you.

You should know, however, that among the Jews those who possess knowledge of Arabic letters take great pride in it, both because those letters are rich in the sciences preserved in the archives of the ancient philosophers, and because, since they are known to few Jews and fewer Christians, they write in them, with confidence, the secrets they wish to conceal from others.

For this reason also, as I believe, this Jew—the catechumen who is the author of this book—recorded it not in Hebrew speech but in Arabic. Yet all hidden things must be revealed sooner or later, according to the saying of the Savior.

In translating it, I wrote the biblical authorities cited by this Jew in their places in both Arabic and Latin, not as they are found in our translation according to blessed Jerome, but as this Jew wrote them when he composed the work. I did this so that no one could accuse me of having presumed in the text to add, subtract, or alter anything. In this matter all who know Arabic will be my witnesses.

I say this because this Jew does not follow our translation, as you will hear in the course of the work. As for me, I ought, as I believe, to explain him in Latin as he speaks in Arabic, preserving his manner of speech and his order as far as possible. Otherwise I could rightly be called not his translator but the corruptor of his book.

Nor would the Jews, if they saw the book written in both languages, be so thoroughly convicted by it if they saw that the authorities reproduced in Latin differed from the Arabic. But, with your consolation, Father and my lord master, this is another purpose I have in mind.

May the Lord Jesus Christ preserve you for many years in his grace and love for our order. Written at Paris by the hand of your humble servant Alphonsus, in the name of our most merciful Lord, in whom we hope.

## Preface of Rabbi Samuel

[Col. 0337]

[Col. 0337A] Samuel the Christian

[Note: [Col. 0337D] Nevertheless, while still a Jew, he wrote his book.]

To Isaac, an Israelite, greetings.

May God preserve you, brother, and cause you to remain until this captivity of ours comes to an end, this dispersion of ours is gathered together, our hope draws near, and God seals his good pleasure upon our life. Amen.

I know and have experienced that the fullness of the knowledge of our time is in you, and that you are the hope of our receiving certainty in the doubtful matters of the Law and the Prophets, through your glorious interpretations.

Therefore, desiring to become a sharer in your teaching, I set before you the outpourings [or “burnings”] of my heart concerning the matters of the Law and the Prophets, about which I am anxious and fearful. For this reason I have recourse to your abundant knowledge and wisdom, and I send you this little book, hoping that, God willing, through you I may be confirmed in the truth and have doubtful matters clarified.

## Book of Rabbi Samuel Marochianus concerning the Messiah whom the Jews rashly await

Written after 1,000 years from the final destruction of Jerusalem under the emperor Titus—that is, after the year 1072 from the Lord’s Nativity.

[Col. 0337]

## CHAPTER I. Why the Jews are under God’s anger.

[Col. 0337B]

My lord, I desire to receive certainty from you, through the testimonies of the Law, the Prophets, and the other Scriptures, as to why we Jews have been struck by God generally with this captivity in which we remain. It may properly be called the perpetual anger of God, since it has no end.

For a thousand years have now been completed, and more, since we were taken captive by Titus. We know that our fathers worshiped idols, killed the prophets, and rejected the law of God. Yet, because of all these transgressions, God did not strike them with captivity except for seventy years in Babylonia. After the appointed time he was reconciled to them and brought them back to their land.

According to Scripture, God’s anger at that time was strongest of all the angers mentioned by Scripture before those days. Nevertheless, as has been said, the punishment for such great sins lasted only seventy years.

And now, my lord, the anger of God that presently punishes us has no term or end in the Prophets. If we wish to say that this present anger in which we remain is still that anger on account of which the captivity of seventy years occurred, then, since complete satisfaction was made at that time for the sins mentioned above through those fathers of ours, we make God a liar—far be it from us—for God himself, true and glorious, imposed the appointed limit of seventy years upon that captivity through the prophets.

Therefore such an answer is not a response but an evasion or excuse, and it ought not to be proposed before intelligent people.

And if we say that in that exile God had mercy upon one part of our race and not upon another, and that he brought back those upon whom he had mercy to rebuild the Temple, as the prophet Jeremiah says, while we belong to those upon whom he did not have mercy, then the Christians will say to us that God had mercy upon those who worshiped idols and killed the prophets—and therefore also upon us, because we did not sin.

Moreover, among the sinful fathers there was a punishment of divine vengeance with a fixed term. Why, then, should our punishment, who have not sinned, be without a term?

Thus the punishment in which we remain is long and without end. A thousand years have now passed, and we cannot find the term of this punishment either in the Law or in the Prophets.

Why, then, my lord, since God punished our fathers for idolatry and for the killing of the prophets, and since both the sin and the punishment are known from Scripture—since God does not punish the same thing twice—there was punishment for those past sins, namely the captivity of seventy years.

And since God punishes universally only on account of a universal sin, it would have been necessary that, after that captivity, we all sinned before God with a sin greater than the idolatry of our first fathers and greater than the killing of the prophets. For those sins God punished our fathers for seventy years and no longer, whereas he has punished and continues to punish us for a thousand years and more, scattering us throughout the four parts of the world.

Nevertheless, whatever may happen, we belong to God in every circumstance, for there is no excuse concerning what has been said. Answer me.

## CHAPTER II. He proves that, because of a certain grave sin in which they remain, they are in this dispersion, and he argues against their observance of the Law.

Assuming, then, my lord, that we are in some very great sin [Col. 0338D], I now ask you to make clear to me whether, after God dispersed us from Jerusalem and sent us into this very long or perpetual captivity on account of that sin, we, by our own authority and free will, without any special command from God, began to observe in this captivity circumcision, the Sabbath, and the other ceremonies that we maintain according to the law of Moses. For we know that from the time when Titus destroyed the holy city, burned the Temple and the libraries, and dispersed us into this captivity—and from that time onward—sacrifice, offerings, and burnt offerings ceased to be practiced among us. Nor did God afterward promise us, through prophecy or through any certain revelation, that we should ever return to Jerusalem in our former condition; nor did he later command us to observe the practices mentioned above.

It therefore appears to follow that we received and maintain these practices not from God, but from others who were under God’s wrath. And it seems that our adversaries may rightly say to us: “Just as you observe circumcision and the Sabbath, and read in your synagogues the books of Moses and the prophets without God’s command, why do you not likewise take up sacrifice, and appoint for yourselves a priest, a king, a ruler, holy anointings, and incense? Why do you not build altars for yourselves and observe the ceremonies and everything else contained in the Law, if, by your own will and without God’s command, you observe the Sabbath, circumcision, and many other things according to your traditions? In either case you incur God’s displeasure. And if you do these things against God’s will—or if you say that it is God’s will and good pleasure that you observe them, though you cannot demonstrate this—why do you not observe those other practices as well, many of which you are able to perform? And even if those who rule over you do not permit you to appoint kings for the people, they will nevertheless permit you to do many other things, just as they permit circumcision, the books, the synagogues, and the other practices you maintain.”

And to this, my lord, we seem not to have a sufficient answer at hand. Nevertheless, whatever happens, we belong to God.

## CHAPTER III. How all Jewish observance of the Law is unacceptable to God because of the sin in which they remain

We find, my lord, God speaking through the mouth of Zechariah and saying, where he speaks of that first, brief captivity: “Thus says the Lord God to the priests and the people of the land: When you fasted and [Col. 0339D] mourned in the sixth and seventh months throughout the entire period of seventy years, did you understand that you were fasting for me, or mourning for me? I did not desire such a fast from you” (Zechariah VII).

Our translation, however, has the passage differently; I intend to write the authorities cited by this Samuel just as they appear in Arabic, not as they are in our Bible.

In the words quoted above, my lord, the Lord implies that while we Jews were in that captivity for seventy years, we were without the Law, because we neither had nor have fasting from the Law in the same way as the other observances; likewise, we were without circumcision and without the Sabbath. And without doubt none of these things has value while God’s anger remains upon his people.

That first anger of God was brief, lasting seventy years; but this one in which we now remain is long, already a thousand years and more, and no end to it is found in the prophets. I fear, my lord, that just as God sent our fathers into that brief captivity without the Law and without observances, and did not accept their fasts or their observances of the Law until the period of their punishment had been completed—that is, the seventy years—so in this final captivity he does not accept the works we have performed according to the observances of the Law.

It is therefore clear that we are now in a greater sin than our fathers were in Babylonia. Hence we are under God’s greater wrath than they were, and consequently our works are less pleasing to him, while we are more hateful to him. It is evident that they, because of the death of the prophets and because they worshiped idols, were in captivity for only seventy years; whereas we, because of a great and very grave sin, have been captives for a thousand years and more.

This captivity, my lord, is undoubtedly the one that God, through the mouth of the prophet Daniel, calls “desolation,” when he says: “Until the consummation and the end, desolation shall endure, etc.” (Daniel IX). The first captivity is called a “migration,” because after a short time they were brought back with honor to Jerusalem. But this is called perpetual desolation, in which, certainly, he will not have mercy on us, just as he did not have mercy on our fathers in Babylonia—except that he comforted them through the prophets, who promised them deliverance, and they were all together. Nothing, however, is promised to us; moreover, he has scattered us throughout all the kingdoms of the world. Nevertheless, whatever happens, we belong to God.

## CHAPTER IV. Showing that the Jews are blind

My lord, what has happened to us is exceedingly astonishing. For every day we hope for deliverance from this captivity, and we are always speaking about it; we are always speaking of our return to Jerusalem. Thus we are either blind or deceivers of the simple. For it is certain that after our dispersion, which took place through Titus, no prophet appeared among us to promise our return. Nor, after the captivity of seventy years, was there a prophet who spoke of this captivity, which has no end except at the end of the world. It has no deliverance except through the consummation of the age, because Daniel calls it an endless desolation (Daniel IX).

Hence I fear, my lord, that since such a great captivity cannot remain upon our entire people from God except on account of the greatest sin against God—a sin greater than having killed the prophets and worshiped idols, for which sins our fathers were punished—just as God does not have mercy on us in this life while we persist in the same sin, so he will not have mercy on those of us who are dead. Nevertheless, whatever may happen, we belong to God.

## CHAPTER V. That the Jews deceive others and themselves

My lord, it seems that we deceive others and ourselves, because in the books of the Law and the prophets we have God promising our nation deliverance and gathering from dispersion in many ways. But anyone who observes carefully will see that all the promises we have received either were fulfilled before the captivity of seventy years and during those seventy years, or were completely obstructed by the sins of those to whom the promises were made.

For example, I propose before you, my lord, these few words from Ezekiel: “If you do my acts of justice and keep my commandments, I will gather you from the four parts of the world, and I will raise you up, and bring you across the sea, and restore you to your holy house” (Ezekiel VI).

Behold: what the Lord promises us through Ezekiel in the words quoted above and in other passages of that same prophet’s book was already fulfilled before the captivity of seventy years. Thus all the Lord’s promises of this kind, greater and lesser, contained in various places in the sacred books, were fulfilled before we fell into this last captivity, which has no end. We are now in the thousandth year and beyond, yet we find no term for it in any book of the prophets. Nor is any promise of God concerning deliverance and gathering understood as referring to this perpetual captivity, but rather to those tribulations and dispersions that occurred before the aforesaid seventy years. Afterward, no gathering from dispersion was promised to us.

It follows that after those seventy years we must have committed that great sin on account of which God punishes us without end; we are in that sin and all remain in it. Otherwise God would not have continued to restrain his mercy toward us amid such prolonged anger.

For we see in the Scriptures that all the sins committed by our fathers before the seventy years of the aforesaid captivity were punished. I shall bring forward a few examples. Before those seventy years, our fathers who came out of Egypt sinned; and the promise made to them did not take effect for them, but they died in their sins in the wilderness (Joshua V). Moses sinned at the waters of Strife and did not merit the promised land (Deuteronomy XXXII). Aaron himself sinned and bore the punishment (Numbers XX). Eli the priest sinned and died with his neck broken (1 Samuel IV); his descendants were deprived of the priesthood, even though God had promised the priesthood forever.

Such promises, however, are always understood with the qualification that the recipients may fail to receive them because of their sins, as is evident in the kingdom of David: his carnal descendants were deprived of the kingdom. Likewise, the true and glorious God promised Abraham and his seed that they would possess that land forever; yet they frequently lost it because of their sins, and the Lord frequently restored it to them, until the final occasion on which they lost it. A thousand years and more have now passed, and there is no longer any hope of recovering it, because we all remain in the same sin on account of which we lost our land.

And, my lord, it is exceedingly astonishing that although we all agree that after the captivity of seventy years in Babylonia we sinned against God with a very great sin, there is nevertheless no one who says that this is the sin on account of which we have incurred such great evils. And if any one of us recognizes our condition and the sin on account of which we have incurred such great evils, nevertheless no one reveals it to his neighbor, nor does the one who recognizes it turn it to his own advantage; rather, we all lie prostrate.

We clearly see that during the aforesaid captivity of seventy years God was with our fathers through the prophets—namely, Jeremiah and the other prophets—and gave them Salathiel as leader, together with princes and priests. With these they left Babylon after completing their repentance and appeasing God; they built Jerusalem, the Temple, and other cities, and God poured out his mercies upon them abundantly.

Yet in this captivity there is no prophet among us, nor, as it appears, is God with us. Therefore, my lord, I shall inquire and shall not cease to seek what that sin may be, on account of which we have been in this captivity for a thousand years and more, and have neither prophet, king, priest, altar, sacrifice, anointing, incense, nor purification. Indeed, we have become hateful and contemptible to the whole world, as we are to God; only in our own hearts does pride reign, because we consider ourselves superior to the whole world.

What I think about this I shall disclose to you, my lord. Nevertheless, whatever happens, we belong to God.

## CHAPTER VI. What that sin is on account of which the Jews are in this captivity

[Col. 0342C]

Now, therefore, my lord, I fear that the sin on account of which we are in this desolation and captivity is the sin about which God spoke through the prophet Amos when he said: “For three crimes of Judah I shall turn away, or transfer, Israel, and for the fourth I shall not transfer them [Note: [Col. 0341] There is *convertam*—‘I shall turn away’—in our Bible; here he has *transferam*—‘I shall transfer’—and that better serves his argument], because they sold the righteous man for silver” (Amos II).

And we, my lord, according to our teaching, say that this righteous man was Joseph, the son of Jacob, who was sold by his brothers in Egypt. I would hold this view were it not that the divine word places this sin of selling as the fourth in the number of Israel’s sins or crimes.

The Christians themselves, to whom the study of the holy books appears to have been entrusted by God, respond to our aforesaid teaching and say that the first of Israel’s four crimes was Joseph’s sale by his brothers. As the second sin or crime, they identify the worship of the calf at Horeb. As the third crime, they identify the killing of the prophets, on account of which we were held captive in Babylonia for seventy years. And they say that Israel’s fourth crime was the sale of the righteous man—namely Jesus—who was literally sold after the aforesaid seventy-year migration.

If we, my lord, wish to maintain our aforesaid teaching and answer the Christians, we must claim that various crimes were committed in Israel before Joseph’s sale, so that Joseph’s sale may be the fourth crime. But we cannot sustain this, because the testimony of the book of Genesis is against us: it presents Joseph’s sale as the first crime of the children of Israel. And the prophet Amos expressly identifies the sale of the righteous man as the fourth crime, on account of which we have been in the captivity of which God speaks, threatening that he will not restore us again to the promised land, when he says: “And for the fourth I shall not transfer them, because they sold the righteous man for silver” (Amos II).

It plainly appears to me that we are justly punished for that fourth sin, the sale of the righteous man. A thousand years and more have now passed, during which we have made no progress among the nations, nor is there any hope of making further progress.

## CHAPTER VII. That the righteous Jesus, the God of the Christians, was unjustly sold

I tremble, my lord, and fear that this Jesus whom the Christians worship is the righteous man sold for silver according to the prophet Amos. I fear that the testimonies of the prophets that occur to me concern him, and that the Christians apply those same testimonies very openly in their teaching.

The prophet Isaiah says: “Woe to the sinful nation, to the wicked children, because they have withdrawn from God and blasphemed his holy one, and have turned backward” (Isaiah I).

The same prophet also says: “Like a sheep he was led to the slaughter; he did not open his mouth” (Isaiah LIII). He also says: “A man bearing sorrow and knowing weakness” (ibid.). Again: “He was despised, and for this reason we did not esteem him; for he was offered because he himself willed it” (ibid.). Again: “He was taken away from the distress of judgment; who shall declare his generation?” (ibid.). Again: “For the guilt of my people I pierced him, and he will give the wrongdoers for his burial and the rich for his death” (ibid.).

And I fear, my lord, that the wrongdoers were our fathers, and the rich were Pilate, Herod, and Annas and Caiaphas, as the prophet David says: “All the kings of the earth and the great ones rose up, against God and against his Christ” (Psalm II)—the aforesaid kings being the “kings,” and our fathers being the “great ones.”

And I fear, my lord, that this Jesus is the one exchanged and sold for silver of whom the prophet Zechariah, Amos, and the other prophets speak. Isaiah the prophet also speaks of him: “He will lay down all iniquities and will pray for the unbelieving” (Isaiah XIII).

I fear, my lord, that this Jesus is the righteous man of whom David says: “They delighted in the soul of the righteous man and condemned innocent blood; therefore God will destroy them, and the Lord our God will scatter them” (Psalm XCIII).

And I fear, my lord, that this is the righteous man of whom Jeremiah speaks when he says: “He is a man, and who is the one who understands him?” Likewise Jeremiah in the Lamentations: “The appearance of our face, Christ God, has been captured for our sins. To him we said: In your shadow we shall live among the nations” (Lamentations IV).

I also fear, my lord, that this is the righteous man of whom God spoke through the mouth of the prophet Zechariah: “For it shall be said on that day: What are these wounds in your hands? And he will answer: I was wounded in the midst of my house, among those who loved me, and my shepherd raised the sword over me” (Zechariah XIII).

Likewise: “They shall look upon me on that day, and upon the one whom they pierced, and they shall mourn over him as one mourns over an only child” (Zechariah XII).

I also fear, my lord, that this was the righteous man of whom Habakkuk says: “Horns are in his hands; there his strength is hidden, etc.” (Habakkuk III). The Gospel of the Christians agrees with this, where Jesus’ death is narrated and it says: “But when they came to Jesus, they found him dead, and one of them sent his spear and pierced him” (Matthew XXVII).

I tremble, my lord, that this is the righteous man of whom Habakkuk says: “You went forth, Lord, to save your people with your Christ” (Habakkuk III).

## CHAPTER VIII. How the dispersion of the Jews took place after the killing, according to Daniel

I tremble, my lord, at these matters. Who was this righteous man without sin, of whom the prophet Isaiah speaks? And who is that righteous man sold for silver, on account of whom the Lord says through the prophet Amos, in the passage cited above, that as a testimony of their crime he will not transfer them again to the promised land?

It also seems, my lord, that what Daniel writes in chapter IX has been fulfilled, where he says: “After the sixty-two weeks have been completed, Christ shall be killed; and then the people will come with the future prince, and he will destroy the city, and demolish the house, and condemn it; the sacrifice will be taken away, and perpetual destruction will be completed” (Daniel IX).

There is no doubt, my lord, that this destruction of perpetual desolation is the captivity in which we have been for a thousand years. And God plainly says through the prophet that there will be perpetual desolation after the killing of Christ, just as our desolation began after Jesus was killed. Nor did God threaten us with perpetual desolation except through the killing of Christ.

And if we wish to say that we were already in desolation before Jesus’ death, the Christians answer us that before that death there was no desolation except for seventy years, and that after this we were with God in grace and honor.

Certainly, my lord, I see no escape from this prophecy, because the fact itself proves to us that after seventy-two weeks had been completed from the rebuilding—above the years that amount to 433 years—Jesus was killed by our fathers. Afterward the leader, namely Titus, and the Roman people came and treated us according to this prophecy. A thousand years and more have now passed; nevertheless, if we are under God’s anger, we still hope in him.

And if we say that Christ is to come and has not yet come, that we shall regain the promised land, rebuild the city, and possess God’s grace and honor in our land, and that this dissolution is not perpetual, the Christians will answer that the killing of Christ, the coming of Titus and the Roman people, and the desolation worse than this, in which we have already been for a thousand years, still remain for us.

Alas, my lord, there is neither a fitting excuse nor an escape!

## CHAPTER IX. That there are two advents of Christ

I fear, my lord, that Christ has already come and has already fulfilled his first advent, because in our Scriptures we find a twofold advent of him. The first advent of Christ is described in the prophets in poverty and humility; the second in glory and majesty. Concerning both advents I shall set forth what occurs to me.

Of the first advent God says through the mouth of Zechariah: “Rejoice, daughter of Zion; behold, your ruler comes to you, poor, riding upon an ass” (Zechariah IX).

In this advent Isaiah describes him as despised (Isaiah LIII), Daniel as killed (Daniel IX), and Zechariah and Amos as sold (Zechariah IX). Yet what was written in the little book—and what I shall write—has already been fulfilled (Amos III): “We did not esteem him,” that is, we did not recognize him, as the prophet Isaiah said (Isaiah LIII), but we despised him and prevailed against him.

His glory and majesty, however, will be manifested at his second advent, when fire and flame will go before him, burn fiercely, and set his enemies ablaze all around him (Psalm XCIII), as God says through the mouths of the prophets David and Isaiah. And I fear, my lord, that Christ will judge in no other manner than with fire unto death, because we killed all the prophets [Col. 0345C] who announced him to us. God testifies against us through the mouth of the prophet Elijah in the Fourth Book of Kings: “And thus we killed that righteous man, on account of whom we are under God’s anger without end.” Nevertheless, we belong to God.

## CHAPTER X. Concerning the first advent of Christ

I fear, my lord, that God aptly describes the two advents of Christ through the mouth of the prophet Isaiah when he says: “Rise up, rise up; clothe yourself with strength, O arm of the Lord” (Isaiah LI). By saying “Rise up” twice, he indicates Christ’s twofold advent.

In detail and with clarity Isaiah describes Christ’s first advent with respect to his passion and humiliation throughout chapters fifty and fifty-three, especially when he says: “We saw him, and he had neither appearance nor beauty, etc.” (Isaiah LIII).

Isaiah sets forth his first advent when he says: “A little child is born to us” (Isaiah IX). Immediately he adds his second advent when he says: “And he shall be called the strongest giant, powerful; he shall sit upon the throne of David, to establish it from the beginning and forever” (ibid.).

The prophet Zechariah, however, describes him as poor and sitting upon an ass (Zechariah IX). And what else does this mean except that the prophet describes the first advent in humility and the second in power and majesty?

Thus Daniel describes him around the middle of his book, where he says: “I was considering, or looking in a vision of the night, and behold, one like a son of man was coming in the clouds of heaven. He reached the Ancient of Days, and they presented him before him, and he gave him power and honor and a kingdom; all peoples, tribes, and languages shall worship him and serve him” (Daniel VII).

The Hebrew has: “Tribes and languages shall honor him, and his power shall not fail, because it shall not be taken away, and his kingdom shall remain forever.”

Our translation, however, has: “Tribes and languages shall serve him; his power is an eternal power that shall not be taken away, and his kingdom shall not be destroyed.” Elsewhere: “His power shall not fail.” Elsewhere: “His power is eternal, and his kingdom shall remain forever.” Elsewhere: “It shall not be destroyed.”

And it is clear, my lord, that at his second advent Christ will sit before the Ancient of Days, who is God, for judgment, just as at his first advent he sat before our fathers, the Jews, to be judged.

The prophet David hints at these two advents of the Messiah—that is, of Christ—in a psalm when he says: “For he comes, for he comes to judge the earth” (Psalm XCVII). With respect to his first advent, which was simple, he says “for he comes”; with respect to the second, which will be with power, he says “for he comes to judge the earth.”

Zechariah speaks of his second advent when he says: “His feet shall imprint their tracks upon the Mount of Olives, etc.” (Zechariah XIV).

And we, my lord, do not say that God in his essence and nature has feet, flesh, or any of the things belonging to a body; rather, having feet is proper to every corporeal creature.

The prophet David also says what was quoted above, speaking of his second advent: “Fire shall blaze before him, and it shall set everything around him ablaze” (Psalm XLIX).

But, my lord, we do not say that God is circumscribed, so that anything could exist around him insofar as he is God. Rather, similar authorities have a literal truth in that righteous man whom the prophets describe, speaking now of his humility and now of his majesty.

Malachi speaks of this when he says: “Behold, the Lord comes, and who will be able to stand before his advent? For he himself is like consuming fire, and he will sit and melt silver and gold” (Malachi III).

Behold how that righteous man who was judged will come at his second advent. And observe, my lord, how the prophet describes him in the same chapter when he says: “Then I shall come and enter into judgment against them, and I shall be a true witness against adulterers, the wicked, and perjurers; against those who defraud the hired laborer of his wages; those who despoil orphans and widows; and those who oppress the stranger and the poor” (ibid.).

Likewise, my lord, Ezekiel describes him when he speaks of shepherds and sheep, saying: “I shall separate from them”—that is, from the righteous—“the transgressors and unbelievers” (Ezekiel XXXIV).

Our translation does not contain this, but the Arabic says as follows: “O my lord, behold: at his second advent he will separate the unbelievers from the midst of the righteous,” just as Malachi and Ezekiel also clearly say.

At the first advent none of us recognized him, because he had gone beyond the limits of human nature. As God says through the mouth of the prophet Isaiah: “He was counted among the wicked, and for this reason we did not esteem him” (Isaiah LIII). And Jeremiah says: “He is a man, and who knows him?”

And I fear, my lord, that our fathers failed and went astray at the first advent of the Messiah, and that for this reason we are in this captivity, which has no end. Nevertheless, whatever happens, we belong to God, and in him we hope.

## CHAPTER XI. Concerning the second advent of Christ, who will judge with power

My lord, I fear that this righteous judge is the one who will judge with power at the second advent, and who was the Savior at the first advent of all who believed in him, since the prophet David says of him: “The Lord has made his salvation known and revealed his justice in the sight of the nations” (Psalm XCVII).

Isaiah further says: “You shall draw water from the pools of the Savior” (Isaiah XII). According to my understanding, I take this saying to concern baptism. For at the first advent he saved through water, and at the second he will judge through fire.

And concerning this Savior it is said, my lord: “I know that my Savior lives, and on the last day I shall rise from the earth, and in my flesh my eyes shall see my God” (Job XIX).

Observe, my lord, that he calls the righteous Savior God. Yet it is certain that the eyes of the flesh will not see God. Behold, according to the Scriptures, the Savior is that righteous God of whom we are speaking; he alone can be called truly righteous, since he committed no sin, as God will testify concerning him through the mouth of the prophet Isaiah: “He committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth” (Isaiah LIII).

Neither of Moses nor of any of the prophets is it said that he is a righteous and sinless Savior, because Moses sinned, and all the prophets sinned, as you know, my lord. Therefore none of them is called righteous in Scripture; that name is reserved for this one alone.

And without doubt only those who believe in his first advent are saved. Those who do not believe have no reason to be saved at his second advent; rather, they deserve death. For those who did not believe Moses and did not obey him, though he was a sinner, deserved death; how much more do those deserve fire who do not believe in and blaspheme the righteous Lord who never knew sin? (Isaiah LIII.)

Nevertheless, whatever happens, we belong to God.

## CHAPTER XII. Concerning Christ’s ascension

My lord, we find in the Scriptures that Christ will be exalted from earth to heaven, and I fear that this has been fulfilled in the one who was killed by our fathers. The prophet David speaks of this exaltation in a psalm: “O nobles, open the gates of your dominion, and be lifted up, eternal gates, and the king of glory shall enter” (Psalm XXXII).

And observe, my lord, that they answer him: “Who is this king of glory?” And he himself will answer them: “The Lord of hosts, mighty in battle” (ibid.).

It is certain, my lord, that this righteous Lord of hosts had no battle except in his first advent. For when he sits to judge, fire will blaze around him, set his enemies ablaze all around, and consume the righteous by fire like silver (Psalm XLIX); and this will be at his final advent. No one, however, will fight against him then, and there will be no place for battle.

Isaiah further speaks of this righteous man’s exaltation: “Who is this who comes from Edom, from the land of Bosra, with his garments red, like one beautiful in his robe?” And this righteous man answers them: “I am the one who speak justice; I am the champion for salvation.” And the angels say to him: “O Lord, why is your garment red, like that of one who treads the winepress?” He answers, saying: “I alone have trodden the winepress, and there was no man with me” (Isaiah LXIII).

See, my lord, how precisely Isaiah speaks. And I fear that the response of this righteous man concerns none but us, when he says: “I trod them in my anger, until their blood was sprinkled upon my garments and all my clothing was stained. For the day of vengeance was in my heart, and the year of my tribulation has come” (ibid.).

How, then, can we hope in this righteous man, my lord, when we know that he complained about us to the angels in heaven and made known to them that he alone had trodden the winepress? And what else did he tread in his anger except us, who, after the battle he had in his first advent, have been overthrown by him and trampled down for a thousand years, with the day of vengeance still remaining at his final advent and the year of retribution in his heart?

Would that, when we killed Isaiah, we had erased the aforesaid passage from his prophecy so that it would never be read by anyone. And behold, David calls it a battle when he says: “The Lord of hosts, mighty in battle” (Psalm XXXII). Isaiah calls this a winepress.

Alas, my lord, we drink that must, of which the patriarch and prophet Jacob also speaks, as it is found in the book of the generation of creatures, concerning Judah: “He washed his robe in blood” (Genesis XLIX)—namely, in the blood of the grape, as happened to us at the first advent of the Messiah.

But what shall we do at his final advent, when people will stand before the man who judges, and fire will be prepared all around to devour those against whom he has pronounced sentence? For then there will be no time for battle, nor will he then tread the winepress, because there will then be neither place nor time for repentance or refuge, but justice: just as he himself was judged without sin being found in him, so he will judge sinners.

For God says in Solomon’s prophecy: “When the righteous man receives judgment, where will the wicked and the sinner be?” (Proverbs XI). Hence, if the righteous man will scarcely be saved, what will become then of the wicked? (1 Peter IV.)

## CHAPTER XIII. He proves still more forcefully Christ’s bodily ascension
I am very much afraid, my lord, that these testimonies of the prophets concerning that Just One—that he was sold for silver, as the prophet Amos says; that he trod the winepress, as Isaiah said; that he waged war with our fathers, as David says; that he was seized in our sins, as Jeremiah said; that he was wounded in his palms, as Zechariah said; that lots were cast over his garment, as David says (Psalm 21); that he ascended into heaven, as the same prophet said; and other things besides—cannot apply to God in his essence or divine nature, according to which he neither rises again, nor is exalted, nor sits, nor descends.

From what has been said it necessarily follows that the Just One has already come, to whom these and similar things can apply according to his bodily nature. But if it perhaps seems difficult to you, my lord, to believe that a corporeal man ascended into heaven, hear the authorities and examples from our Scriptures that occur to me.

David the prophet says of him: “God ascended on high and will save captivity; he gave gifts to men.” He also says in Psalm 67 concerning his ascension: “Sing praises to God and glorify his name; make a way for him who ascends from the regions of the west; the Lord is his name.” Again, my lord, David said of him in the psalm that you have in your heart: “Sing praises to God, who ascends above the heaven of heaven toward the east.” Amos said of him: “The Lord is he who built his dwelling in the heights.” David also says of him in the psalm: “God ascended amid rejoicing, and the Lord amid the sound of the trumpet.”

The prophet Aser said of him, chapter 2: “I saw a man descending from the heart of the sea, and he reached as far as heaven.”

[Note: These things are found in neither chapter of Haggai, nor does anything resembling or touching upon Christ’s ascension occur there; but chapter 2 does indeed concern his coming: “He will come,” it says.]

And because we do not have this prophecy, I have omitted writing many things that he adduces on this subject.

[Note: Rather, we do have it; but at that time he did not know that Haggai was called Aser in Arabic.]

Moses also says in his song: “I will raise my hand to heaven.” Isaiah likewise says: “Awake, awake, O arm of the Lord.” And Hannah, the mother of Samuel, says of him: “The Lord will give power to his king and exalt his anointed one” (1 Samuel 2). David also said: “The Lord ascended upon the wings of the winds” (Psalm 17).

These authorities occur to me as proofs of Christ’s bodily exaltation up to heaven. There are many others as well, which you, my lord, know well.

I shall now also adduce some examples from our law, since it seems to us entirely reasonable to believe that he ascended into heaven in bodily form. This is because in the Law and the Prophets we find that the true and glorious God took several holy men, our fathers, from the earth and raised them up.

If we do not doubt these men on account of their holiness and the testimony of Scripture, why do we doubt the bodily and spiritual ascension of the Just One, to whom Scripture bears a stronger testimony than to them? For, according to the prophets, he endured a harsher war and more captivities of the world than any of those mentioned above.

Moreover, my lord, without even supplying an example, you know that Methuselah and Enoch the righteous, and Elijah the prophet, were taken by God from this world in their bodies.

[Note: Read this cautiously, for concerning Enoch and Elijah alone do the Fathers teach from Scripture that they were taken alive, in their bodies, from human society. Scripture gives no indication concerning Methuselah, nor does any of the Fathers report it.]

Nor should it be doubted concerning Moses that he is in heaven in body and soul, as is said in Deuteronomy 34. God said to Moses: “Go up the mountain at night and die there”; and he went up the mountain and died. “No one has known his grave to this day” (Deuteronomy 34).

What does it signify that his grave is unknown on earth, since he was a greater and holier prophet than the others, except that God raised him up and took him, body and soul, as he took the other righteous, and raised him to the place where they are?

[Note: Philo indeed held this opinion concerning Moses, in Book 3 of *The Life of Moses*, but it is wholly foreign to the mind of the holy Fathers, since the Catholic faith teaches that before Christ’s descent into hell and his ascent into heaven no blessed person existed or had been received into heaven. Moses could indeed have risen with Christ and ascended with him into heaven, as many consider probable; but to infer from the words of Deuteronomy 34 that Moses rose immediately after his death and was taken up into heaven is an obvious error. See Book 9 of the Dominican theologian Malvenda’s *On the Antichrist*, chapter 8.]

Nor should we be surprised at this that the light and subtle air could carry bodies so dense and heavy. We know that water, which in its rarity is like air, when it pleased the omnipotent power, carried the bodies of the children of Israel in their departure from Egypt (Exodus 14). And when the sacrifice was accepted, fire descended from heaven, lifted up, and carried away the bodies of the sheep and oxen that were offered to God.

Moses and Elijah, moreover, prophesied concerning the raising of that Just One (Genesis 5), as did other prophets. Therefore, if we ought to believe in the bodily elevation of the holy men mentioned above, why are we unbelieving concerning the elevation of this Just One, and that he was raised into heaven, of whom there are so many testimonies of the prophets in the Scriptures, as has been said?

It could also be suggested that God clearly took up the holy men mentioned above, about whom no one doubts, so that human hearts might be prepared for the end and so that they would not doubt the ascension of his own Just One.

There is also another reason why our people themselves doubt: his first coming was hidden, and its manner was extraordinary, as Isaiah says: “He is a man, and who will know him?” (2 Kings 2; Deuteronomy 39.)

The same prophet also says: “A virgin will conceive and bear a son” (Isaiah 53). It should be observed here that he says nothing about a father according to the flesh, and this is connected with what he says elsewhere: “We did not regard him” (Isaiah 7).

Jeremiah says: “God created a new sign upon the earth: a woman will encompass a man, etc.” (Isaiah 53).

Micah also says: “Therefore God will give them up until the time when she who is in labor gives birth” (Micah 5).

It should be noted that the prophet makes no mention of the husband of this woman in labor, since he is speaking of the birth of this Just One, who alone was born outside the customary order and course of flesh—that is, from man and woman—as was foretold of him through the mouth of Isaiah when he says: “Hear, house of Jacob: God will give you a sign: a virgin will conceive and bear a son, etc.” (Isaiah 7).

All the other holy men who have been mentioned were born of woman and man, conceived carnally in sin, and all were sinners. Even Moses, holier than his prophetic parents, sinned and confessed through his own mouth that he had sinned. But concerning this Just One Isaiah says: “He never sinned, and no deceit was found in his mouth” (Isaiah 53).

Concerning all the other holy men God says through the mouth of Job: “Among all his holy ones none was found without corruption” (Job 4). The prophet Jeremiah says: “The hearts of men are perverse” (Jeremiah 17).

## CHAPTER XIV. On the blindness of the Jews, who do not believe that Christ has come and do not understand

I fear, my lord, that what the Lord said through the prophet Isaiah has been fulfilled in us: “Blindness has fallen upon Israel until the fullness of the gentiles has entered” (Isaiah 59). And again he says: “They will hear with hearing and not understand; they will see with sight and not recognize, because the heart of this people has been made gross” (Isaiah 6).

And again in the same chapter: “Blind the heart of this people and close its ears, lest perhaps they learn, turn to me, and I heal them.”

Isaiah said: “How long, Lord?” And he said: “Until the cities are desolate and the house remains without an inhabitant” (ibid.).

Daniel also said: “Close the words and seal up the prophecy” (Daniel 12).

Jeremiah says: “The sin of Judah is written with an iron stylus upon a diamond stone and extended over the breadth of their heart” (Jeremiah 17).

Isaiah, in chapter 1, says: “The ox knows its owner, and the ass its master’s manger; but my people has not understood” (Isaiah 1).

And again Jeremiah says: “The kite, the swallow, and the stork know the time of their coming, but my people has not known me” (Jeremiah 8).

All these things, my lord, were said because of us, since we did not recognize the coming of that Just Lord.

And concerning us the Lord said through Isaiah: “Bring out the blind people who have no eyes, and the deaf who have no ears; behold, they are all gathered together” (Isaiah 43).

What did the Prophet intend by these words except that God rejected us because we did not recognize the time of this Just One soon enough? He gathered the gentiles to himself in faith in our place.

David, astonished at this, said in the psalm: “This is the change of the right hand of the Most High” (Psalm 76).

Nevertheless, we belong to God in this our present downfall and in this captivity of ours, which has no end and in which we have now been for a thousand years. Yet this happened so disastrously to our fathers, who worshiped idols, killed the prophets, and wholly transgressed the Law.

## CHAPTER XV. He demonstrates the rejection of the Jews on account of their faithlessness and the election of the gentiles on account of their faith

I fear, my lord, that because we do not believe in this Just One, what God said through the mouth of Isaiah has therefore happened to us and been fulfilled: “The prophecy will be like the words of a sealed book, which will be given to a reader, and it will be said: ‘This book is sealed; I do not know what is in it.’ Then he will give letters to one who does not know how to read: ‘I am not a reader’” (Isaiah 29).

What greater sealing of a book is there, my lord, than the sealing with which God has closed our hearts? It is now a thousand years and more, and we cannot understand through the prophecy handed down to us by the prophets concerning the coming of this Just One.

For this reason God said elsewhere through the prophet: “Jerusalem will be desolated, and the holy house will fall” (Isaiah 3). He also said: “Our land is desolate, our cities have been burned with fire, and Zion will remain like a hut in a ravaged vineyard” (Isaiah 1).

This, my lord, has now lasted a thousand years and more.

Isaiah also said: “Lord God, I will exalt your name, because you have made a city into a mound and a house into a ruin, so that it may not exist forever” (Isaiah 25).

And he said: “He will crush the peoples with the crushing of a potter’s vessel, in which no part remains for carrying a coal of fire or drawing a drop of water” (Isaiah 30).

What Daniel said has also been fulfilled, my lord: “After Christ was killed, perpetual desolation will remain” (Daniel 9). We have been in that desolation for a thousand years and more.

Isaiah also said: “Desolation has been left in the city, and their land will hiss with a hissing forever” (Isaiah 24).

Jeremiah said: “Call them rejected silver, because the Lord has cast them away” (Jeremiah 9).

Isaiah also said: “Walk in the light of your fire and in the flames that you have kindled for yourselves” (Isaiah 50). We have been in those flames for a thousand years.

Amos likewise said: “The house of Israel will fall, and there is no one to raise it up” (Amos 5).

It seems to me, my lord, that God brought this ruin upon us after the coming of this Just One, after no prophet arose among us and none will arise, as was prophesied to us, because we remain in unbelief, refusing to accept his faith and denying him.

Hosea also said: “When a woman lay upon the earth and gave birth, God said: ‘Call his name Without Mercy, because I will not have mercy on this people’” (Hosea 1).

And if God has cast us away and does not have mercy on us, as we have experienced for a thousand years and more, what benefit is there in our possessing the Law, circumcision, and the Sabbath?

Isaiah said: “Bring out the blind people, just as the true and glorious God brought us out from our land” (Isaiah 24). This has now lasted a thousand years and more.

The same prophet also said: “True error has gone away” (Isaiah 26).

And what is ancient except our Law, which has departed from us, my lord, together with the king, the sacrifice, the incense, and the altars? What worse thing could happen to us, and what is it that we are awaiting?

Do we not see that he scattered us into dispersion throughout the four parts of the world, as Moses, Jeremiah, Isaiah, and the other prophets told us? Nevertheless, we belong to God and turn back to him in every circumstance.

## CHAPTER XVI. He demonstrates the rejection of the Jews on account of their faithlessness and the election of the gentiles on account of their faith

I fear, my lord, when we say among ourselves, “I and you also are sons of Jacob and Israel,” because what God says through the mouth of Isaiah has now been fulfilled: “God will kill you, O Israel, and will call his servants by another name” (Isaiah 65).

I tremble that we may be those servants upon whom that name is to be bestowed, according to what Moses said in Deuteronomy 28: “The gentiles will be at the head, and the unbelieving people at the tail,” as we have been for a thousand years and more.

Jeremiah also spoke of them: “The earth will be filled with the faith of God and will overflow like the water of the sea.”

Solomon said of them: “Lord my God, when a foreigner comes to your holy house and invokes your blessed name, hear him, Lord my God, so that the whole earth may learn to fear your name, as your people Israel does” (1 Kings 8).

In what, then, shall we glory, my lord, and why do we despise the gentiles, since the prophet Solomon made them participants with us in the fear of God and in the holy house? Perhaps God cast us out of this house as unworthy and gave it to them.

Moses also said of them: “Thus says the Lord my God: The whole earth will be filled with the glory of the Lord” (Numbers 14).

David said of them: “All the ends of the earth will remember and turn to the Lord, and a thousand generations” (Psalm 21).

Isaiah also said of them: “O holy house of David, your light has come, and the glory of the Lord has risen over you, etc. The gentiles will walk in your light, and kings in the splendor of your rising. Lift your eyes around you and see: all these have gathered and come to you; the sons of strangers will build your walls, and their princes will serve you” (Isaiah 60).

Who are these sons of strangers, my lord, who came to the house of God, except the gentiles who served idols and were strangers to God, together with their princes and kings? God said that they would walk in the light of the holy house, while we would be in darkness outside it; and this has been the case for a thousand years.

The same prophet further said of them: “You will call a nation that you did not know, and nations that did not know you will come to you” (Isaiah 53).

As we plainly see in fact, this has now been the case for a thousand years and more: Christ, sent according to the Law given to us, came, and the gentiles who did not know the Law came to him, and he gave them a new, pure, holy Law.

Again, in chapter 45: “They agreed together, and their kings were gathered in the faith of God” (Isaiah 45).

And I fear, my lord, that the following was said concerning them in the same chapter: “Gather together and come, all you gentiles who have been saved by God from among the gentiles” (ibid.).

Isaiah said concerning the people: “They sought me, though they did not ask; they found me who were not seeking me” (Isaiah 65).

Jeremiah says of them: “All will gather in the name of the Lord, in the holy house, and they will not walk in the perversity of their hearts” (Jeremiah 3).

The same prophet said of them: “All the gentiles will come to you from the ends of the earth and will say: ‘Our fathers inherited nothing but falsehood and iniquity’” (Jeremiah 16).

Zephaniah said of them: “It has been granted to the gentiles to speak together in the name of the Lord, and they will serve him shoulder to shoulder; every person from his own place, and all the islands of the gentiles” (Zephaniah 3).

Zechariah said of them: “Rejoice, house of Zion, because I will come to you and dwell in your midst on that day, and the gentiles will draw near to God in their multitude” (Zechariah 2).

The same prophet says in chapter 8: “Thus says the Lord God of hosts: Many gentiles will come from many places, and one man will say to his neighbor: ‘Let us go and seek the Lord God for good’” (Zechariah 8).

And these things, my lord, have now been fulfilled and are plainly being fulfilled before our eyes. You see peoples and languages reading the books of the Law and all the Prophets and the Psalter. Having abandoned their idols, none of them believes through Moses, Aaron, or any of our prophets, nor does anything of their former idolatrous faith remain from the time when they believed in that Just One of whom Habakkuk says: “You went forth, Lord, for the salvation of your people, for salvation with your anointed one” (Habakkuk 3).

## CHAPTER XVII. On the giving of life to the gentiles and the killing of the Jews, as will also be seen in the following chapter

I fear, my lord, that the victorious and glorious God gives life to those gentiles through faith and kills us through our unbelief, just as he says through the mouth of the prophet Isaiah:

“Because I called and you did not answer, thus says the Lord God: Behold, my servants will eat, but you will hunger. Behold, my servants will drink, but you will thirst. Behold, my servants will rejoice with gladness of heart, but you will be shaken because of the bitterness of heart. And God will kill you, O Israel, and will call his servants by another name, by which he blessed those who are blessed upon the earth. Amen” (Isaiah 65).

We will see those who have received this name blessed by God upon the face of the earth, while he has scattered us—namely, in captivity throughout the four parts of the world—for a thousand years.

The traces of God’s wrath appear plainly in us, not for correction but for destruction. This is the killing with which God threatened us, saying that he would kill Israel. Those living gentiles whom he calls servants will receive the name that God promised, but not before the death of our former name, according to the order of God’s words through Isaiah.

The hunger and thirst that we suffer are not hunger for bread or thirst for water, but the barrenness of hearts and souls and a famine of the word of God, as the prophets declare through the mouth of Amos (Amos 8).

And you, Lord, know this more fully than I do. Nevertheless, we belong to God in everything that happens to us.

## CHAPTER XVIII. How the gentiles, given life through faith, possess the pure observances of the new Law

I fear, my lord, that these gentiles have been given life for a thousand years, ever since Jesus died in Jerusalem, because they had nothing good before they believed in God, in Christ, and in the apostles. Perhaps they were those fish and beasts of which the prophet Habakkuk speaks, which have no leader.

These gentiles, purified through faith, have their fasts and observances of the new Law, and they possess all those things pertaining to purity that are contained in the ancient Law of the Jews.

You see that in every language and every place, in East and West, there are gentiles confessing the name of the Lord. They do not believe in him through Moses or any of the prophets, although they are diligent in the Law and in the books of all the prophets. God called them through the disciples of the Just One, who went forth with God for their salvation, as the blessed and glorious God himself foretold through the mouth of the prophet Habakkuk.

These disciples of his were our sons, from the sons of Israel, who are called by another name, apostles.

For I greatly fear, my lord, that these are those of whom God said through the mouth of David in the psalm: “Their sound has gone out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world” (Psalm 18).

The words of the Prophet plainly show us that he is speaking of them and not of us, when he says: “There is no language or speech in which their voices are not heard.” This cannot refer to our Hebrew language: which gentiles obey the commandments of Moses and Aaron? Indeed, they killed the gentiles and drove them away from themselves.

But these gentiles know Moses and the prophets today, acknowledge God, and observe the new Law, as the apostles taught them. Nevertheless, we belong to God.

## CHAPTER XIX. On the election of the apostles in place of the prophets

I fear, my lord, that what the prophet Zechariah said—“I will strike the shepherd, and the sheep of the flock will be scattered” (Zechariah 13)—was fulfilled when we struck the shepherd of these children and holy apostles.

From that time we sheep have been scattered throughout the whole world, while these sons of ours, namely the apostles, arose in place of the prophets. This is evident from the fact that after them God sent us no prophet and made nothing known through a vision.

I fear, my lord, that these children are the apostles of whom God said through the mouth of the prophet Joel: “Your elders will dream dreams, and your children will see visions” (Joel 2).

Most certainly, my lord, the elders are our prophets, who dreamed of the faith of the gentiles, which those children—namely, the apostles—attained and saw.

David the prophet said of these children: “Come, children, hear me; I will teach you the fear of the Lord” (Psalm 33).

God does not use “children” in the plural except that in ordinary speech he calls Israel his firstborn. In another psalm he calls these children sons when he says: “Your sons are like newly planted shoots” (Psalm 127).

Concerning Israel, my lord, God said through the mouth of Isaiah: “The vineyard of the Lord of hosts was the house of Israel. I expected it to produce grapes, but it produced thorns. Therefore I will bring one who will destroy it by trampling” (Isaiah 5).

Concerning those aforementioned sons of God who are called apostles, God said through the mouth of Isaiah: “Not now will Jacob be ashamed, nor will his face melt away; but then, when he sees among his sons those whom my hands created, sanctified before his eyes” (Isaiah 115).

And if these children, my lord, had been sanctified before us according to the way of our Law, it would not be said of us that we were in shame. Our faces would not therefore be dissolved; rather, we would possess glory and our faces would shine. But the shame of Jacob’s faces and this desolation consist in the fact that these sons whom God created with his own hand—namely, the apostles—are sanctified before us, but not according to our Law.

For this reason God gives us to understand that our Law is not their Law.

God also said through the mouth of Ezekiel: “In those days they will no longer say: ‘Our fathers ate sour grapes, and the children’s teeth were set on edge’” (Ezekiel 18). The unbelief of the Jews will not harm the faith of the apostles, and therefore it is added: “As I live, says the Lord, this proverb will no longer be spoken in Israel” (ibid.). For none of the apostles, after receiving the faith, ever returned to our faith. Thus they do not feel the bitterness of our unbelief, as our teeth are set on edge by the sin of our fathers.

Again, concerning these children who are the apostles, my lord, God said through the mouth of the prophet Isaiah:

“From whom shall I remove myself, except from my own people? But the children who will be unbelieving: God will be their savior in all their distress; his face will guard them in his love; in his mercy he redeemed them, and he will be gracious to them throughout the length of their days.”

It is entirely true, my lord, that these children of whom we speak always remained firm. From the time when that righteous King, their teacher, redeemed them, God never departed from them, but he departed from us and was always with them.

Concerning these children who are the apostles, the wise Jesus son of Sirach also said in his book: “Hear, beloved children, and work for salvation, because God honors the father in his children” (Ecclesiasticus 3).

How that honor is to be understood, God explains through the mouth of Malachi: “God will send Elijah, who will turn the hearts of our fathers toward their children” (Malachi 4).

O lord, if God were supposed to turn the hearts of the children—that is, the apostles—toward the fathers, if this is to be understood concerning faith, then these children, the apostles, would have been with us in this captivity that has no end, just as our fathers and we are.

But since God ordained that the hearts of the fathers should be turned toward the children, what is it that we await, my lord, and what are we expecting?

Even if we do not wish to say that there are other children besides the apostles to whom the foregoing refers, those others would be in captivity just as we are, since they did not follow the way of that Just One, whom the apostles followed firmly and taught others to follow. For this reason they have the honor of the fathers, in that the fathers are said to be turned toward them.

Therefore, my lord, since our sons came to the faith of God before we did, if our hearts are turned toward the children, their hearts will be turned toward us.

And as the Most High God says: “They will be one people, of one mind in the glorious and victorious God” (Zephaniah 3). We must understand that turning as referring only to a conversion from unbelief to the faith and teaching of that Just One, who is the Master of salvation for those who believe in him.

As David said concerning him, he is the one whose priesthood will be according to the order of Melchizedek forever (Psalm 109), who offered a sacrifice of bread and wine (Genesis 16), and Melchizedek was a priest of God Most High before Aaron.

And observe, my lord, how great the difference is between the sacrifice of Aaron and that of this Just Lord:

“The Lord said to my Lord: ‘You are a priest forever’” (Psalm 109),

not temporarily, as Aaron was, who died at the age of one hundred and twenty years. Furthermore, Aaron’s sacrifice consisted of flesh, whereas the sacrifice of that Just Lord consisted of bread and wine according to the order of Melchizedek.

In these words the Lord clearly shows through the Prophet that Aaron’s sacrifice would end when that eternal sacrifice began—namely, when the sacrifice of bread and wine, destined to endure forever, began—since eternity in the priesthood was not given to Aaron as it was to Christ the priest.

God also says concerning these children through the mouth of the prophet Moses (Deuteronomy 31): “He will avenge the blood of his children and wash the land of his people.”

We killed the prophets, my lord, and he did not take vengeance on them except after seventy years. But we killed the apostles and their Just Teacher, and God exacted vengeance for these children. This has now lasted a thousand years and more.
