Through their death God cleansed the land of his people; he did not say “the land of the sons of Israel.”

David also spoke of these children in Psalm 116: “As arrows in the hand of a mighty man, so are faithful sons.”

The Prophet compares these faithful children to arrows shot from the hand of a mighty man, because almighty God sent these faithful sons to the twelve regions of the world, throughout the four quarters of the earth, bearing the teaching of the Law, the Psalter, and the Prophets.

But he did not send Moses and Aaron outside the holy house to teach. He did not send them to India, Rome, or other places outside the holy land to announce the teaching of the Law and the Prophets.

These faithful children, however, thus cast forth or sent throughout the whole world, arose before God in our place after God killed Israel and our name. David aptly suggests this in the psalm when he says: “Instead of your fathers, sons have been born to you; you will appoint them as princes throughout the earth” (Psalm 44).

Through these men the first Law was renewed according to the order of Melchizedek, who established God’s sacrifice in bread and wine, from which Abraham, the friend of God, partook.

God also changed our sacrifice through their ministry, just as he changed our name and changed our carnal Law into a spiritual Law.

If God had said to our Moses, as he said through the mouth of David to the Messiah or Christ, “You will come as a priest forever according to the Law of Moses and Aaron,” that Law would have remained. But he said: “You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek” (Psalm 109).

The friend of God partook of the sacrifice of bread and wine, and not of the sacrifice of flesh.

The word of Moses accords well with this when he says: “You shall eat the oldest of the old” (Leviticus 26), by which he means the sacrifice of Melchizedek.

And again: “When new things have come upon them”—that is, when the sacrifice of the new Law has been made public—“you will cast away the old things,” namely, your sacrifices.

Nevertheless, we belong to God at every coming.

## CHAPTER XX. On the rejection of the sacrifice of the Jews and the election of the sacrament of the Christians

I fear, my lord, that God has cast us and our sacrifice away from himself and has accepted the sacrifice of the gentiles, as he said through the mouth of Malachi:

“I have no pleasure in you, says the Lord, and I will not accept your sacrifice, because from the rising of the sun to its setting my name is great among the gentiles, who offer a pure sacrifice in my name” (Malachi 1).

Therefore, before God the sacrifice of the gentiles is purer than our sacrifice.

Moreover, God has deprived us of every pure sacrifice, while elsewhere teaching the Christians to avoid us so that they might not be defiled, just as we avoided the gentiles whenever our sacrifice was pure and acceptable before God.

[Col. 0358C] You too, my lord, know what God says about our sacrifice when he speaks through the mouth of the prophet David: “Have you perhaps seen that I eat the flesh of bulls, or drink the blood of goats (Ps. IX)?” By this God makes clear that he condemns the sacrifice of flesh. Why, then, my lord, do we detest among the gentiles the sacrifice of bread and wine, which God established and nowhere condemns, as he condemns the sacrifice of flesh, when Solomon describes it as Aaron’s, saying: “He—that is, Aaron—stretched out his hands over the altar, and offered the blood of the grape and incense to the living God, and offered our sacrifice from the grains of the earth, just as Melchizedek offered on behalf of Abraham (Ecclus. L)”?

God declares the sacrifice of the gentiles through Moses: “You shall offer God a sacrifice [Col. 0358D] of leavened bread, from the threshing floor, and from the pressing of the grape, and God shall bless you and all the works of your hands (Lev. XXIII).” We also know, my lord, that at the beginning God commanded that bread, and not flesh, be placed before the ark of the Lord’s covenant (Exod. XXV). Again, my lord, when God commanded Aaron concerning this matter in Leviticus through Moses, he said: “A man from the seed of Aaron the priest who has a blemish shall not offer a sacrifice of bread, nor any other sacrifice whatsoever (Num. XXI).”

In many places of Scripture God also commanded that a sacrifice of bread be made, and he will accept one made from the purest flour; such is the sacrifice of the gentiles today, namely, bread made from the purest flour. Mention is also made of the sacrifice of bread in the First Book [Col. 0359A] of Kings (chap. XXI): “When David came to Abimelech, the chief priest of Shiloh, he asked him for bread. He replied: ‘There is no bread here except the bread that has been offered, which it is not proper for your boys to eat, because it is holy.’”

That the gentiles place water in their sacrifice ought not to seem objectionable to us, because in the holy Scriptures we also find an example of this—namely, that a sacrifice of water was made to God and was accepted by him. We also find (II Kings XXIII) that two young men drew water from the cistern that was before the gate of Bethlehem, and the prophet David offered it to God as a sacrifice. Therefore it is not contrary to Scripture if the gentiles today place water in the sacrifice that they make to God.

We also read that Aaron made a sacrifice of bread and wine to God, and David one of water; these three are together in one pure sacrifice, although our understanding cannot penetrate this—and not like the flesh of fattened bulls. Our Elijah, as is related (III Kings III), poured water upon the sacrifice, and God sent fire from heaven and accepted the sacrifice drenched with water (III Kings XVIII). The angel also communicated Elijah in figure with bread baked under the ashes and water, when Elijah walked in the strength supplied by that food—something nature cannot ordinarily grant—for forty days, up to the mountain of God, Horeb (III Kings XIX).

This sacrifice of wine mixed with water is described most beautifully and appropriately by the prophet Solomon in the Book of Proverbs, chapter IX, when he says: “Wisdom Most High shared out her sacrifice, mixed her wine [Col. 0359C] and prepared her table. Then she sent her servants, saying: ‘Whoever is little, let him come to me’; and the foolish shall eat my bread and drink my wine mixed with water.”

What, my lord, is the table prepared by Wisdom Most High, if not the altar? What is the bread and wine mixed with water, if not the sacrifice of bread and wine and water that is made on the altar? Who are the foolish summoned by the servants of Wisdom, if not the gentiles who were ignorant of God, summoned through the apostles?

It is noteworthy that he says “my bread” and “my wine.” By this he intimates that this sacrifice is pleasing to God, and that to this exalted and spiritual banquet he did not summon our fathers, who were wise in the Law and occupied [Col. 0359D] with the sacrifice of the Law—which, being a carnal sacrifice, he did not leave to us, but deprived us of it. A thousand years have now been completed since this befell us on account of that Just One against whom we sinned. Nevertheless, we belong to God.

## CHAPTER XXI. That God rejected the abolished fasts and sacrifices of the Jews and chose those of the Christians

I greatly fear, my lord, that word which the strong and glorious God spoke through the mouth of Malachi in chapter 1, where he speaks in this way about the sacrifice of the gentiles: “From the rising of the sun to its setting, the gentiles offer a pure sacrifice to my name.”

Here I observe that our sacrifice was accepted in only one place, namely, precisely in [Col. 0360A] the holy house. But ever since God deprived us of that place of sacrifice—the promised land—and scattered us throughout the world, a thousand years have now passed. Therefore what God said concerning us has come upon us and been fulfilled, when he spoke figuratively through the mouth of Isaiah: “The vintage is complete, and there is no further gathering (Isa. XXXII).”

And also the saying of Malachi: “I have no pleasure in you, and I will not accept a sacrifice from you (Mal. CLXX).” And that of Isaiah, chapter 1: “Your Sabbaths, festivals, and sacrifice I will not receive, because you are all in my anger (Isa. I).”

This saying of Isaiah has also been fulfilled against us: “What is the multitude of your victims to me? Why do you multiply sacrifices of rams and the flesh of goats? I, however, have despised [Col. 0360B] the blood of calves, the flesh of rams and goats. When you present them before me, who will receive them from you? Do not disturb my holy stones. In vain you will offer sacrifice any longer, for I will not receive your incense, your Sabbaths, or your solemnities, because my soul has hated them. If you raise your hands to me, I will turn my face away from you. And if you multiply your prayers, I will not hear; your hands are full of blood (ibid.). And all your sacrifice is like a stinking corpse. And an exit from the court’s outer gate [the text is corrupt], and the one who slaughters a bull for me, is like one who beheads a man; and the one who offers a goat in sacrifice is like one who offers a dog; and the one who offers wine is like one who offers swine’s blood [Col. 0360C] (Isa. LXVI).”

But the abomination of sacrifices before God signifies nothing other than the changing of our carnal and gross sacrifice into the spiritual and refined sacrifice of that Just Lord, who instituted the offering of bread in place of flesh, pure water in place of the fat of flesh, and pure wine in place of blood. A human being is offered spiritually and acceptably to God, not like the animals slaughtered by us, which the prophet compares to a rotting corpse.

Why, my lord, do we not believe these things that God has spoken to us through this prophet? And what could he describe more clearly concerning our sacrifices?

God also said through Jeremiah, chapter 7: “Invite your neighbors to sacrifices and eat with them the flesh of your sacrifices, [Col. 0360D] although on the day when I brought your fathers out of Egypt I did not command them, nor did I speak to them concerning sacrifices. Instead I said: ‘Hear my voice, and I will be your God and you will be my people, if you walk in all that I command you; it will go well with you.’”

But they did not listen, nor did they incline their ear to my word—and you, my lord, are the one who knows this. Nevertheless, we belong to God in all that has happened to us.

## CHAPTER XXII. He proves the rejection of the Synagogue and the election of the Church through the word of the Lord to Rebecca

I fear, my lord, that the saying written in chapter 25 of the First Book of the Law is understood concerning the Synagogue and the Church, when the Lord God says to Rebecca, Isaac’s wife: “Two nations are in your womb, and two peoples will come forth from your womb; one nation will overcome the other, and the elder will serve the younger (Gen. XXV).”

My lord, Rebecca alone was the mother of the Jews and the gentiles. The greater and firstborn people was the Synagogue, endowed with great honor and knowledge of God. The second-born and lesser people before God were the gentiles, remaining in unbelief and in their ignorance.

If, however, my lord, God killed Israel, as Isaiah describes, then the Synagogue, which had been greater, was overthrown, and it served the gentiles, who had been lesser, so that the word that God spoke to Rebecca might be fulfilled: “One nation will overcome the other (ibid.).”

God also spoke concerning the Church through the mouth of David: “The queen stood at your right hand, clothed in gilded apparel and adorned with varied colors (Ps. XLIV).” It is explained, my lord, that the Church of the gentiles, which is called the queen, is adorned with the diversity of all the languages that serve her, as though with a variety of colors. For all languages in the Church agree in the true exposition of the Law, the Psalter, and the books of all the prophets. The Synagogue, however, had only one language and its adornment was as though of a single color, namely Hebrew.

## CHAPTER XXIII. He proves the same thing through the words of the prophet Malachi

I also fear, my lord, because of the words repeatedly introduced above from the prophet Malachi. God said to the Synagogue: “I have no pleasure in your sacrifices, for from the rising of the sun to its setting my name is great among the gentiles, who offer a pure sacrifice to my name (Mal. I).”

Water, wine, and pure flour, from which the sacrifice is made, are pure by their very nature and need no cleansing or washing. The Synagogue, however, must wash the flesh of the sacrifices, cleanse the bellies of the souls that will be sacrificed, and wash the place of the blood and fat of the sacrifices; otherwise it would be horrifying to handle and behold. In the sacrifice of bread, wine, and water, however, nothing indecent or shameful appears.

I think, my lord, that God spoke of this sacrifice through Solomon: “A morsel of bread with love is better than a fattened calf with hatred (Prov. XVII).”

The morsel of love, my lord, is pure gentleness upon gentleness and mutual forgiveness of offenses; the fattened calf of hatred is “an eye for an eye” and the secret killing of enemies. Therefore, my lord, the sacrifice of the Synagogue is a fattened calf with hatred, while the sacrifice of the Church is a morsel of bread with love, concerning which God says: “A morsel of bread is better,” and so forth.

God also beautifully describes the Church by comparing her to a hind through the mouth of Solomon, where he says: “A hind most dear to God in her rival, whose breasts intoxicate you at all times, and whose love delights you forever (Prov. V).”

The Church is a hind beloved by God in her one rival, concerning whom and about whom it is written: “A hind most dear to God in her rival, having no equal in nobility and grace.” Then, my lord, he adds and says: “Let her breasts intoxicate you at all times; delight continually in her love.” By this is signified the sacrifice [Col. 0362A] of the Church, which will endure for all time, forever.

God compares her to a mother nursing her children. In what he says, “I will intoxicate you,” he indicates the matter of the sacrament spiritually with respect to wine; and by “breasts” he indicates that in the remaining parts of the sacrament there is delightful and sufficient nourishment, a sufficient sacrament by which the Church already enjoys and delights.

A thousand years have now passed since he deprived the Synagogue of sacrifice. That rival in whom the Church is so pleasing to God is Christ the Lord, and his breasts give perpetual wine, from which everlasting joy proceeds; he does not say that he will give flesh, fat, or blood, which make the sacrifice burdensome.

The Synagogue was like a woman who had another husband—supply: God—and lost both him and the holy house. This Church, however, was a hind in the desert without a husband, but God takes his place. Therefore the strong and glorious one himself says through the prophet Isaiah: “The secluded young women are better than those who have a husband (Isa. LIV).”

Again that prophet says: “I will make, says the Lord God, a way and rivers for drink for my chosen people; but you, Jacob, will not obey, and you, Israel, will not listen (Isa. XLIII).”

Thus we, my lord, are outside obedience and possess neither ears nor eyes; for this reason our captivity has now reached the completion of a thousand years.

I fear, my lord, our law, which has the wrath of fury ready at hand, and says: “An eye for an eye, etc. [Col. 0362C] (Lev. XXIV).” But that hind, having one unique rival, said in his glorious Gospel: “If he strikes you on one cheek, offer him the other (Matt. V).”

David speaks in Psalm XXX: “How great and how abundant is your sweetness, Lord, which you have hidden for those who fear you and completed for those who hope in you.”

It is clear, my lord, that the people of the Synagogue feared the punishments of the Law, namely “an eye for an eye,” because execution was ready at hand. But the people of the Church hope in the sweetness of God, and those who are struck in the face do not strike back. Therefore God prepared for the gentiles a great abundance of his sweetness, which he hid from the Jews. Nevertheless, and so forth.

## CHAPTER XXIV. That the song of the Christians is acceptable to God

[Col. 0362D] I am afraid, my lord, that what Isaiah said concerning the apostles applies to them: “They will manifest the Holy One of Jacob, proclaim the God of Israel, and the ignorant will receive knowledge, and the musicians will know the laws (Isa. XXIX).”

We plainly see, my lord, that for these many years the ignorant have been musicians and are teaching our law. Who are the ignorant if not the gentiles? And who are the musicians singing our Psalter and prophets in their churches if not the Christians?

Concerning these musicians, or singers, God says through the mouth of David: “Sing to the Lord a new song, for he has done marvelous things (Ps. XCVII).” What is that new song, my lord, if not the New Testament? And what is the Old if not the ancient law?

Concerning these musicians also God says through the prophet David: “Sing to the Lord, all the earth; sing a psalm to his name [Col. 0363A] (Ps. CXXXIV).” And in the same psalm: “All the families of the gentiles will sing and play to your name.” He notably says “all the families of the gentiles,” and not Israel alone.

Concerning these musicians God also says through the mouth of David: “Blessed is the people who know the song; they will walk in the light of your face (Ps. LXXXVIII).” Of them too, my lord, it is written: “The gentiles will sing a song to you in the house of my God (Ps. LXXXVIII).” Here he uses “song” antonomastically.

It has also been a thousand years since we Jews sang in the holy house. Of these singers David says: “They will sing a song in the house of God forever.” Of us he says: “How will they sing the song of God in a foreign land? (Ps. CXXXVI).”

And how can it be, my lord, that we hope to possess land and a name, when God said through the prophet Amos: “Israel has fallen and will not rise again; the virgin Israel has been cast down and will not rise (Amos V).”

The same prophet says: “Tribulation will come, and no one who escapes from them will be saved. Even if they hide themselves on Mount Carmel, my hand will cast them down from there; even if they descend into the depths of the sea, there I will command serpents, and they will bite them. And if they go into captivity before their enemies, there I will command the sword, and it will kill them. I will set my eyes upon them for evil and not for good (Amos IX).”

This is what God has done to us. A thousand years have now been completed since we sang a song and a psalm; such is our condition. Nevertheless, and so forth.

## CHAPTER XXV. That the Jews unjustly criticize the song of the Christians

[Col. 0363C]

My lord, God spoke concerning the song of the Christians through the mouth of David: “All nations, clap your hands and sing to God with a voice of praise (Ps. XLVI).” Elsewhere he says: “Shout joyfully to God, all the earth; serve the Lord with gladness. Enter into his presence—say it all: shout joyfully (Ps. LXV).” And: “Sing to the Lord, all the earth, and announce it from day to day (Ps. XCIX).”

I am afraid, my lord, ever since God said through the mouth of Jeremiah: “Teach your sons and daughters lamentation and mourning, for death has gone out through your gates (Jer. IX).”

Since God spoke concerning these musical children through the mouth of David: “Kings of the earth and all peoples, princes and all judges of the earth; young men and virgins, old men with the young, let them praise the name of the Lord [Col. 0363D] (Ps. CXLVIII).” And: “In the sacrifice of song he will honor me (Ps. XLIX),” as though he plainly said: “Not in the sacrifice of the flesh of goats, like our sacrifice.”

Isaiah the prophet also speaks concerning them: “Learning the Scriptures and the entire Psalter of David, so marked by musical art through high and low notes.”

When all these things have been considered, it seems to me that we are wrong in judging that what they offer in singing within the Church of God is a sacrifice of his praise, especially since in the Law of God we find commands and examples in this matter from David, who also says: “Praise him with harp and organ, praise him with cymbals of great praise, and let every spirit praise the Lord Jesus [Col. 0364A] Christ (Ps. CL).”

There is also an example in the Second Book of Kings, chapter VI, where we read that “David, with his head uncovered, danced with a harp before the ark of the Lord; his presumptuous wife Michal dared to rebuke him, and he said to her: ‘O foolish woman, will the Lord not see me despised as I play?’ The children of Israel, however, sounded the trumpet while they carried the ark.”

But what are we, my lord, when we mock the solemnities of those musicians, if not the foolish Michal? And who are these singers if not Christians dancing and exulting before God in humility, like David? Especially since God says: “Let every spirit praise the Lord (Ps. CL).”

If he had said “every Israelite alone,” then we could insult others. But what Isaiah said—that “the gentiles are as nothing in his sight [Col. 0364B] (Isa. XL)”—must be understood of those gentiles who existed before they gained knowledge of God through the coming of the Just One, for at that time they were pagans and idolaters. It does not refer to the gentiles who found the Lord, who offer a pure sacrifice every day in the East and in the West, as he says through the mouth of the prophet Malachi (Mal. I), as has already been cited above. And certainly, my lord, we are wrong. Nevertheless, and so forth.

## CHAPTER XXVI. He proves the apostasy of the Jews from God

I am afraid, my lord, that we apostatized from God at the first coming of that Just One, concerning whom we have introduced the authorities mentioned above and to whom everything written among us in the books of the Law and the Prophets expressly applies. Because of this apostasy, just as God has prolonged the days, he brought this captivity upon us; and if we await a savior other than that Just One, it does not profit us.

There is clear evidence that, because of the universal sin that is in all of us, so long as that sin persists in us, anger will persist over our nation without hope. Yet we await someone else, and that expectation does not profit us.

If we wish to say that this captivity is not universal and that in some part of the world we possess a king and ruler, we can quickly be accused and convicted of falsehood according to our Law. For if we Jews had a king and ruler in some part of the world, he would belong to only one tribe, namely Judah. But God decreed against Judah that there would never again be a king over Judah from that tribe. Therefore the prophet Jeremiah said: “The sin of Judah is written with an iron stylus on an adamantine stone, engraved upon their hearts (Jer. XVII).”

And since what is written with an iron stylus on an adamantine stone cannot be erased, how do we expect it to be erased? It will not be erased forever, especially since the strong and glorious God spoke through the mouth of the prophet Isaiah: “The Lord, the Ruler, takes away from Jerusalem and Judah judge, prophet, and ruler (Isa. III).”

The prophet Hosea also says concerning us: “The children of Israel will be without a ruler, without law, without sacrifice, without an ephod, without an altar, without teraphim [therap] (Hos. III).”

We know, my lord, that from the beginning of the world there were certain great and holy men before God, and at the beginning they lived long lives, such as Methuselah and Enoch and the others (Gen. V). Yet God prolonged the life of none of them beyond a thousand years.

We also find among us that the Messiah, or Christ, promised to us was born in Babylonia during that captivity which lasted seventy years. But this age of ours has reached 1,050 years. We cannot defend this story, rather than prophecy, by any reasoning, and yet we state and affirm it in our synagogues, where no outsider mixes with us.

But hear the public teaching of the Christians concerning Psalm LXXXVI: “A man will say: Zion was founded, and a man was born in her, and he himself founded her.”

In these words he names Mary the Lady by the name of the city, and says that “a man was born in her.” He does not say “such-and-such an Israelite” or “such-and-such a man,” so that you may understand that Mary’s son was never in the loins of any man.

And in the Second Book of Kings, chapter seven, this is made clear when God says to David: “When your days are fulfilled and you sleep with your fathers, I will raise up your offspring after you, which will come forth from your womb, and I will be his father, and he will be my son.”

But it would never have been possible, my lord, for someone to come forth from his father’s womb. This is expressly stated to demonstrate that Christ was not to be conceived in a woman through seed taken from a man’s loins, as other human beings are, descending both from David and from others.

God also says through the mouth of David in Psalm CIX: “From the womb, before the morning star, I begot you.” It is as though the strong and glorious God said concerning his Christ that he begot him by his will, which is the Holy Spirit, and not from seed. He says “from the womb” because Christ was born from the womb without male seed, beyond the ordinary course of nature. This is the true teaching of the Christians, which does not enter our minds; because of this, what has happened to us has happened.

The prophet David also describes Christ’s birth in the same way when he says in Psalm CXXXI: “The Lord swore the truth: From the fruit of your womb I will place upon your throne.” Nevertheless, we belong to God.

## CHAPTER XXVII. In conclusion, he introduces certain sayings of the Saracens concerning Jesus and his mother Mary

[Col. 0365D]

Certainly, my lord, although the Christians do not confront us with the sayings of the Saracens—especially those transmitted in the Qur’an and its commentaries—knowing that we would not accept them, just as they themselves do not accept them, nevertheless it would be useful for our weariness and for the strengthening of believers if they confronted us with what the Saracens say concerning Jesus and his blessed mother Mary.

For all the Saracens say that he was the Messiah whose coming had been foretold, and they place him above their god Muhammad with regard to genealogy. They confess that Muhammad’s parents were idolaters and wicked, descended from Hagar the slavewoman. They say that the Messiah was the son of Isaac and of the prophets and righteous men, in a direct line down to the blessed Virgin Mary, his mother.

Concerning Mary, the Qur’an says this, in the account of the family of Adam: The angel Gabriel said to Mary: “O Mary, God has chosen you, taught you grace, and preferred you above all women of every age. He has placed you like a new intermediary, dividing earthly human beings from the angels of God in the paradise of delights.”

All the Saracens also say that Christ, or the Messiah, received from God the power to perform miracles, to heal every disease and infirmity, to cast out demons, and to raise the dead. He knew all the secrets of hearts, and they believe that Jesus performed all the miracles mentioned by the Gospel.

The Qur’an expressly testifies to this, where it says in the chapter mentioned above that the Messiah knew and knows all things, [Col. 0366B] including the secrets of hearts. Thus Muhammad’s words were these: “Eise—that is, Jesus—knew every book and all wisdom, as well as the whole law of Moses, what people ate and drank in their houses, and what they stored in their treasuries.”

They also say of Christ, or the Messiah, that while he was in this world he despised riches and rejected carnal pleasures. He had no concubines, which are an occasion of sin and a cause of disobedience.

He also introduces in the Qur’an this evangelical saying: “Foxes have dens, and the birds of the sky have nests (Luke IX).”

Although all these things lack authority from the standpoint of those who utter them, they nevertheless agree with what the prophets said concerning the Messiah at his first coming, as is evident from the foregoing.

They also say in the Qur’an that Eise—that is, Jesus Christ—is the Word of God. This designation, “Word of God,” is among the Saracens almost a proper name for Jesus Christ, so that no other man is called by this name except Jesus, whom they call Eise in Arabic.

The Qur’an also says: “God said to Eise: ‘I am your sufficiency; I will raise you up to myself and purify you from the unbelievers.’”

Consider, therefore, my lord, that because of the captivity which the Jewish people have suffered for a thousand years, there are very few Jews in comparison with other nations. For the Saracens have multiplied and increase daily. The faith of Christ, moreover, has filled the whole world.

We, however, have been scattered everywhere by our God, and everywhere we are very few, like Reuben, to whom his father said: “You shall not increase,” and so forth (Gen. XLIX). We do not increase, while those who are hostile to us above all nations increase, and we make no progress.

The testimony of many people continually stands against us—namely, that of the Christians and the Saracens, the Qur’an and the Gospel of Christ. We do not wish to believe them, although in my judgment the Qur’an is worthless, since it plainly contains contradictions, as you yourself know; and its authors clearly appear to have known the Testament only imperfectly.

But what shall we say about the Gospel of the Christians, assuming that Christ, or the Messiah, has already come? For it contains nothing contrary to the prophets or to our Law; rather, it is the manifestation of all the prophets and the fulfillment of the promise contained in the Law, understood spiritually, as the teaching of the Christians presents it.

Nevertheless, my lord, concerning these doubts I turn to you, especially concerning the first matters that I received from the prophets. I know that you will regard the testimony of the Qur’an as almost worthless, especially since you know Arabic. For you know perfectly that Muhammad himself, who said that he was a prophet, foretold nothing of what was to come; and that he who said he was God’s messenger taught against his own God’s Scripture, like a thoroughly corrupt and utterly ignorant man.

The end. The Letter of Rabbi Samuel sent to Rabbi Isaac in the year of the Lord 1000, translated from Arabic into Latin by Friar Alfonso Bonihominis of the Order of Preachers in the year of the Lord 1339.

# IN THE YEAR OF THE LORD 1085. OSBERNUS, MONK AND PRECENTOR OF THE CHURCH OF CANTERBURY

[Col. 0367]

## HISTORICAL NOTICE

(Oudin, *Commentary on Ecclesiastical Writers*, II, 757.)

[Col. 0367B] Osbern, a monk and precentor of the Church of Canterbury, whom Guillelmus Cavus omitted, was English by nationality, a man of great piety and eloquence. Possevinus asserts in his *Sacred Apparatus* that he flourished around the year 1020, while Charles Saussayus, in book V, chapter 8, of the *Annals of Orléans*, calls him Obsernus, unless this was a printer’s error.

This is indeed what I had thought in the *Supplement of Writers*, page 322. But, after more carefully considering all the evidence, it seems more probable that this Osbern, the Canterbury monk, a familiar of Lanfranc, archbishop of Canterbury, and his contemporary, flourished under William the Bastard, king of the English, in the year 1080 and thereafter.

Concerning him, William of Malmesbury writes in *The Kings of the English*, chapter 8, where he is discussing St. Dunstan: “When I wished to say more, and not contemptible things, about the man, Osbern, the cantor of Canterbury, recalls me; he composed his Life in Roman eloquence, second to no writer of our time, and certainly, without dispute, foremost of all in music.”

By these words William of Malmesbury testifies that Osbern was distinguished in his own time. He was born at Canterbury, or at least was brought up from childhood in the church of Canterbury. Thus in book II of *The Life of St. Dunstan*, chapter 12, he writes: “Perhaps I, together with a tall boy of my own age, had served at the altar of Christ at Canterbury, and, when the service was completed, had begun to descend the steps.”

In chapter 20 of the same book he relates that Lanfranc, the archbishop, entrusted him with the office of preaching. The offices that he held in the monastery of Canterbury are recorded by a copyist’s note added at the end of the same book in the Lambeth manuscript: “Here ends the Book of the Miracles of our most blessed Father and patron, the archbishop of the Church of Canterbury, according to Osbern, a fellow monk, precentor, and subprior of this church, who was a most learned man.”

During his lifetime the church of Canterbury was consumed by fire, at approximately the time when Lanfranc assumed the archbishopric, namely in the year 1070. At that time the chief records of the Church of Canterbury perished, as did the more elegant Lives of the ancient archbishops and English saints. Only some works that had once been translated into the English language survived.

To repair this loss and compose Latin Lives of the archbishops from the English remains, Osbern suggests in the preface to his *Life of Dunstan* that his fellow monks provided him with assistance. The Canterbury obituary records his death in these words: “On the fourth day before the Kalends of December, Osbern, precentor of Christ Church in Canterbury, died.”

Of these Lives, the present Lives of Saints Dunstan and Elphege survive, together with the *History of the Translation of Elphege*. Henry Warthon published each of them, from whom we have taken most of this material verbatim, in volume II of the *Sacred England*, pages 88, 122, and 143, from a single Lambeth Library manuscript formerly belonging to the Church of Canterbury, which contains the Lives of several archbishops and saints of Canterbury.

Osbern completed his account of the Life of St. Dunstan in two books. The first deals with events that occurred during Dunstan’s lifetime; the second with miracles performed after his death. Both appear in the Antwerp *Acts of the Saints* of the Bollandists, volume IV of May, page 359, concerning which Daniel Papebrochius speaks at length on page 344 in his preliminary commentary on the Life of St. Dunstan. It also appears in Mabillon’s *Benedictine Acts*, volume V, page 654.

Warthon omitted the second book at the place cited because it contributed very little to history, giving only its preface on page 121, as he says in the preface to volume II of the *Sacred England*, no. V, page 9. Thus he composed the Life and Miracles of St. Dunstan, archbishop of Canterbury, in two books, which Laurentius Surius presents under 19 May, as Gerardus Joannes Vossius reports in book II, chapter 46, of *On Latin Historians*, page 357 in my edition.

But Joannes Mabillon was the first to publish these from the Colbert manuscript, in volume V of *The Saints of the Order of St. Benedict*, pages 659 and following. Some have thought that this was the same work as the one read under the name of the monk Osbert in Surius under 19 May.

The same Osbern also wrote the Life of St. Odo, archbishop of Canterbury, which Mabillon likewise published at the place cited, from the same Thuane-Colbert manuscript, on page 287. It is also said to survive in manuscript at Cambridge, in the library of St. Benedict’s College.

Finally, he wrote the Life and Passion of St. Elphege, bishop and martyr of Canterbury, which the successors of Bollandus published under 19 April, volume II, pages 621 and following. This too survives in manuscript at Cambridge in the college mentioned, together with the Life of St. Martin, of Odilo, of Majolus, and of others by the same Osbern.

Eadmer praised the Life of St. Elphege written by Osbern in book I, chapter 29, of *The Life of Anselm*, in these words: “He [Lanfranc] ordered that the history of his [Elphege’s] life and passion be composed with diligent care. This history, not only in plain prose for reading but also in musical melody for singing, was nobly produced at his command by Osbern of blessed memory, a monk of the Church of Canterbury. He himself, through his wisdom and love for the martyr, elevated it, marked it with distinction, authorized what had been marked out, and established it to be read and sung in the Church of God, thereby greatly glorifying the martyr’s name.”

An abridgment of this Life appears in Capgrave’s *New Legend*, and from there in Surius under 19 April, where it is attributed to Osbern and cited by Baronius and others as Osbern’s work.

The Antwerp collectors of the *Acts of the Saints* published Osbern’s genuine work, adding his *History of the Translation of St. Elphege*, from Harpsfield’s *Ecclesiastical History*; that History breaks off not far after the beginning. Henry Warthon published both works complete from the Lambeth manuscript, in volume II of the *Sacred England*, pages 122 and 143.

Both survive in the old manuscript of the Cotton Library, Otho A. 12, and in another still older manuscript, Vitellius D. 17. In both, the name of Osbern is prefixed by a more recent hand.

That Osbern was the author is established, besides the passage of Eadmer cited above and the testimony of the Lambeth manuscript, also by the Malmesbury manuscript, folios 116–139. Malmesbury praised Osbern’s book *On the Life of Elphege* and transcribed from it many things found in ours in exactly the same words.

Thus Warthon writes in the preface to volume II of the *Sacred England*, no. 6, page 9.

When the same writer had also caused to be printed under Osbern’s name, on page 78, the book *On the Life of Saint Odo, Archbishop of Canterbury*, and likewise, on page 75, the book *On the Life of Saint Bregwin, Archbishop of Canterbury*, and later thought that these works had been falsely attributed to Osbern, it seemed appropriate to reproduce here his judgment, which he gives in the preface to volume II of *Anglia Sacra*, sections 7 and 8, page 10.

> “William of Malmesbury testifies that Osbern wrote the *Life of Odo, Archbishop of Canterbury*, since, in composing his own *History of the Bishops of the English*, he used it. From several things that he adduces at that point, it can be gathered quite clearly that Osbern’s book *On the Life of Odo* which the Malmesbury writer saw was different from ours; John Mabillon had also previously observed this. Nevertheless, Mabillon published the surviving book under Osbern’s name in volume V of the *Benedictine Centuries*, page 283; and, since it was likewise attributed to that author, we reproduced it from the same Lambeth manuscript. For, apart from the fact that Bale, or Pits, mentions no other author of Odo’s *Life*, Osbern’s name is prefixed to this work in the Cottonian manuscript Otho A. 12, although by a later hand. Moreover, Jocelin, in *On English Historians*, chapter 10, says that the *Life of Odo* written by Osbern began with these words: ‘The venerable confessor of Christ, Odo, of noble but pagan parents, etc.’—the very opening with which the book published by us begins. Finally, the differences between the *Life* cited by William of Malmesbury and ours are of minor importance. Later, however, I discovered my error: in an ancient manuscript of Corpus Christi College, Cambridge, this *Life* is placed among the other works of Eadmer and is attributed to him. It must therefore be restored to Eadmer.

> “I received the brief *Life of Blessed Bregwin* from the same Lambeth manuscript, where it is placed between the *Lives* of Odo and Elphegus. From this I allowed myself to suppose that it might be Osbern’s. Later, however, I found it in John of Tynemouth’s *Sanctilogium*, at the end of the *Golden History* in the Lambeth library. Tynemouth took it from Eadmer’s fuller account of the life of the same saint, preserving for the most part the wording of that author. Eadmer’s book will be discussed below.”

Among the manuscript codices of the cathedral churches of England, no. 5996, in Thomas Gale’s manuscript codex 162, Osbern’s letters are said to exist.

As for the *Life of Saint Edward the King*, which Gerard John Vossius, in book II, chapter 46, page 380, of *On Latin Historians*, says exists in manuscript in a volume entitled *On the Life and Miracles of Certain Saints*, beginning with the *Life of Martial*, in Saint Benedict’s College at Cambridge—where, at the very end, one finds the *Life of King Edward*, abridged from a treatise of Osbern of Westminster, as Thomas James reports—I think this is not true, nor was it ever composed by Osbern of Canterbury. Rather, it was composed much later by Osbert, that is, Osbert of Westminster, around the year 1136. In his time Edward had not yet been enrolled among the saints, as is clear from his letters, which we shall discuss later.

Many people confuse this Osbern with Osbert, of nearly the same period, profession, and nationality, to whom two books are attributed: one *On the Life*, the other *On the Miracles of Saint Dunstan, Archbishop of Canterbury*. Surius published these on 19 May, but in truncated and mutilated form; John Mabillon published them complete, and, with their wounds in some measure healed, in volume III of the *Acts of the Saints of the Order of Saint Benedict*, pages 701 and following, restoring them to Osbern of Canterbury as their legitimate author.

Gerard John Vossius discusses both Osbern and Osbert in book II, chapter 48, page 380 in my copy, and chapter 49, page 409 in my copy, of *On Latin Historians*. John Leland discusses Osbern of Canterbury, a monk, in volume I, no. 4, of the *Collectanea*, where the *Life of Saint Elphegus, Archbishop*, by Osbern of Canterbury, is excerpted on page 22; and also in volume IV, no. 104, page 137. Caesar Baronius mentions him in the *Annals* under the years 840, 855, 857, and 860, and in his notes on the *Roman Martyrology* under 19 May, where he everywhere calls him Osbert. Henry Warthon discusses him in the preface to volume II of *Anglia Sacra*, sections 4, 5, 6, 7, and 8, which we have reproduced here. John Mabillon discusses him in volume VI, part I, page 113, of the *Acts of the Saints of the Order of Saint Benedict*, where he presents the *Life of Saint Elphegus*, from the Paris edition printed by Charles Robustel in 1701, in folio.

[Col. 0371]

# The Life of Saint Dunstan, Archbishop of Canterbury

By Osbern, a monk of the same Church of Canterbury.

(See *Patrologia*, vol. CXXXVIII, col. 407, under Saint Dunstan.)

[Col. 0371]

# The Life of Saint Elphegus, Archbishop of Canterbury and Martyr

By Osbern.

(Mabillon, *Acts of the Saints of the Order of Saint Benedict*, sixth century, part I, page 114, from Surius’s April volume and the Thuane manuscript.)

# Preliminary Observations

## 1

Blessed Lanfranc, bishop of Canterbury, persuaded by Saint Anselm, then abbot of Bec, that Elphegus, Archbishop of Canterbury, who had been killed by the Danes, could be regarded as a true and unquestionable martyr—as we shall say below—assigned Osbern, a monk of his own Church, the task of committing the acts of this holy martyr to writing, so that they might be read in the divine office.

Osbern obeyed the bishop’s command and published the *Life of Blessed Elphegus*, not only “in plain prose,” as Eadmer says, but also “in musical melody for singing.” We present it from Surius, adding from the manuscript of the Thuane Library the prologue which the Bollandists also published together with a longer *Life*, which they regard as Osbern’s genuine work. But since that *Life*, published in the Bollandist April volume, merely recounts at greater length the very things expressed more briefly in Surius, it seemed sufficient to include the shorter version here.

We append the history of the translation of Elphegus’s remains, which the same Osbern composed somewhat later than the *Life*, as he himself testifies at the beginning of the narrative. We first copied it from the aforementioned Thuane manuscript; afterward, however, we found it published in *Anglia Sacra* from English manuscripts. The Bollandists gave only a fragment of it, because it was incomplete in their manuscript.

## 2

The *Life of Saint Elphegus* derives authority not only from Osbern but also from Blessed Lanfranc, who is recorded by Eadmer, in book I of *On the Life of Saint Anselm*, as having approved it and delivered it to the whole English Church to be read. Eadmer speaks of Lanfranc as follows:

> “He ordered that the history of his life and passion—that is, of Saint Elphegus—be composed with diligent care. This history, written by Osbern, of blessed memory, a monk of the Church of Canterbury, at his command and with distinction, not only in plain prose for reading but also in musical melody for singing, he himself, by his prudence and out of love for that martyr, elevated still higher, authorized once elevated, and instituted to be read and sung in the Church of God; and in this respect he greatly glorified the martyr’s name.”

From this it is clear that the memory of Saint Elphegus was already celebrated in the eleventh century, since his feast was then solemnly observed throughout England, as will likewise be evident from the history of the translation of his remains. The cult of this holy martyr continued in England thereafter until the faith was renounced under Henry VIII.

Indeed, the memory of Saint Elphegus was famous not only among the English but also among other peoples. Godefrid Henschenius observed that his feast day was celebrated in the church at Dol among our Britons. His name appears not only in the English and Benedictine Martyrologies but also in the Roman, Gelasian, and other martyrologies written after the eleventh century; this is done on 19 April, which was his day of death. Osbern himself records the feast of his translation on 8 June in the history of the translation.

That he was not unknown among the Germans is evident from the eulogy which Trithemius inserted under the year 1015 in the new edition of the *Chronicle of Hirsau*. In the following year the author of the Saxon, or Magdeburg, Chronicle records his martyrdom. There he calls this blessed man “Dustein,” for some reason unknown to me, and writes as follows:

> “At the same time the Northmen, under their leader Thurkyl, cruelly put to death, according to their custom, the distinguished bishop of the city of Canterbury, named Dustein, whom they had captured together with the others, binding him and starving him. Moved by human weakness, he promised money and asked for a truce, so that, if he could not escape death by an acceptable ransom, he might at least cleanse himself through lamentation. When the truce had ended, he said to those demanding the promised payment: ‘I am here, ready for everything for the love of Christ, so that I may deserve to become an example of his servants. But if I seem to you a liar, it was not my will but my poverty that caused it.’

> “While they were raging, the leader Thurkyl rushed up and said: ‘Do not, I beg you, do this. Everything I possess, except the ship, I willingly surrender, lest you sin against Christ the Lord.’ But those unrestrained men poured out innocent blood with ox-heads and showers of stones. Immediately one of their chief men, becoming weak in his limbs, recognized in himself that he had sinned against God’s chosen one.”

All the English writers known to me remember this holy man, insofar as they took his acts from Osbern. If anything worthy of particular remembrance concerning Saint Elphegus occurs in them, we shall present it in the form of notes to his *Life*.

For now it is enough to mention that Saint Elphegus presided over the general Council of Enham, attended by all England, which was held under King Ethelred on the holy day of Pentecost. By the king’s command not only all the bishops of the kingdom but also the other nobles assembled there. Many measures were enacted for the proper establishment of ecclesiastical discipline; these are found in Spelman, volume I of the *Councils of England*, and in Labbe’s volume IX of the *General Councils*.

## 3

No one, as it seems to me, can deny that Saint Elphegus must be counted among the true martyrs, after Saint Anselm proved that the title of martyr was owed to him no less than to Saint John the Baptist. Eadmer recounts this at greater length in book I of *On the Life of Saint Anselm*. It seemed appropriate to quote his words here, since many have passed them over, although they contribute greatly to the glory of this holy bishop.

He tells the matter as follows:

> “Lanfranc was still, as it were, an inexperienced Englishman, and certain customs which he had found in England had not yet settled in his mind. Accordingly, relying on substantial reasoning, he changed several of them by the sole deliberation of his authority. While he was occupied with changing these practices, and had Anselm with him as a like-minded friend and brother, he spoke with him one day in a more intimate manner and said:

> “‘These English among whom we live have established for themselves certain saints whom they should venerate. When I sometimes consider who these men were, according to their own account, I cannot turn my mind away from doubt concerning the merit of their holiness. And behold, one of them rests in the holy see over which, by God’s favor, we now preside: Elphegus by name, a good man indeed, who in his own time presided there in the rank of archbishop. They count him not only among the saints but also among the martyrs, although they do not deny that he was killed, not for confessing the name of Christ, but because he refused to redeem himself with money.

> “‘For when, to use the English expression, his rivals and the pagan enemies of God had captured him, and yet, out of reverence for him, had granted him the power to ransom himself, they demanded an enormous sum of money from him for this purpose. Since he could obtain it in no way except by despoiling his own people of their money and perhaps subjecting some of them to detested poverty, he chose to lose his life rather than preserve it in such a manner. I wish to hear what your brotherhood thinks about this.’”

And thus, like a newcomer to England, he briefly laid these matters before Anselm.

## 4

Yet when we examine historically the cause of Blessed Elphegus’s death, we see that it was not only this, but that another and earlier cause existed. He was captured and killed by a cruel death not merely because he refused to ransom himself with money, but also because, when his pagan persecutors were burning the city of Canterbury and the Church of Christ situated there, and were killing his fellow citizens with atrocious death, he tried, with Christian freedom, to resist them and turn them from their unbelief.

But Anselm, as a prudent man answering a prudent man according to the question put to him, replied simply as follows:

> “It is clear that one who does not admit even a light sin against God does not hesitate to die; much more would he not hesitate to die before offending God by some grave sin. Indeed, it seems a graver sin to deny Christ than, for the sake of redeeming one’s life, to burden one’s own people for a short time by taking away their money. But Elphegus refused to do this lesser thing.

> “He would therefore have been still less willing to deny Christ, if a mad hand, by threatening him with death, had forced him to do so. Hence it may be understood that his breast possessed extraordinary justice, since he preferred to give his own life rather than, by disregarding charity, scandalize his neighbors. For this reason he was far removed from the ‘Woe’ which the Lord threatens against the one through whom scandal comes.

> “Nor, I think, is he counted among the martyrs without reason, since he is truly proclaimed to have willingly endured death for such great justice. Blessed John the Baptist, too, who is revered and believed by the whole Church of God to be the preeminent martyr, was killed not because he denied Christ, but because he refused to remain silent about the truth. And what difference is there between dying for justice and dying for truth?

> “Moreover, since, as Sacred Scripture testifies—and your fatherhood knows very well—Christ is both truth and justice, whoever dies for justice and truth dies for Christ; and whoever dies for Christ is regarded as a martyr, according to the testimony of the Church. Blessed Elphegus suffered equally for justice, just as Blessed John suffered for truth. Why, then, should anyone doubt more about the true and holy martyrdom of one than of the other, when the same cause holds both in the endurance of death?”

## 5

> “Reverend Father, reason itself teaches me that these things are true, insofar as I can discern; nevertheless, it belongs to your prudence both to correct me and recall me from this view if you think otherwise, and, by teaching the Church of God, to show what ought chiefly to be thought in so great a matter.”

To this Lanfrancus replied:

> “Brother, I greatly approve and venerate the subtle discernment and discerning subtlety of your intellect. Taught by your firm reasoning, I trust, with the help of God’s grace, that henceforth I shall honor and venerate Blessed Elphegus from my heart as truly a great and glorious martyr of Christ.”

He later carried this out devoutly; indeed, he ordered that the history of his life and passion be composed with diligent care:

> “This history, not only in plain prose for reading but also in musical melody,”

and so forth, as above in section 2. These things are related by Eadmer in the *Life of Saint Anselm*.

## 6

Furthermore, the English writers clearly report that during the same persecution by the Danes, when Canterbury had been occupied by the barbarians, many people suffered martyrdom. Among them, the Benedictine Martyrology, under 30 July, mentions Leotrona, abbess of the monastery of Saint Mildrith, together with many monks and nuns. Roger of Hoveden should be read on this matter under the year 1011, where he gives a lengthy account of this disaster.

But now the *Life of Elphegus* is to be presented.

# Here Begins the Prologue of Osbern the Monk

[Col. 0375]

[Col. 0375B] Osbern, an unworthy son of the holy metropolitan Church of Canterbury, to all who remain in the faith of Christ: grace and peace from God our Father, and the Lord Jesus Christ, and the Holy Spirit of them both.

If the heavenly judgment decreed severe punishment against the man who preferred to put the money he had received away in a cloth rather than deposit it at the money-changers’ table, I do not think I ought to be blamed if, avoiding the danger of that judgment, I set before others for recognition what I myself have learned about the glorious martyr of Christ, Elphegus.

It will belong to divine providence to grant, as a benefit of its recompense, that I, speaking truthfully, and they, hearing profitably, may find neither my labor in a somewhat arduous narrative nor their participation in a usurious deed a cause for regret.

Another considerable reason also invites me to write: we often accuse those of sluggishness who, although they know of deeds performed in their own times for the honor of the Most High, have not wished to transmit them to later generations through the duty of recounting them. We ought either not to condemn their negligence, or else to bring forth the very things that we have been able to learn as worthy of remembrance, lest in the matter for which we condemn our predecessors we appear all the more deserving of condemnation by those who come after us.

I promise to relate the truth of these events in such a way that, stripping away whatever embellishment of words may be present, I shall profess that I am reporting nothing which I have not received either from those who saw it or from those who heard it from eyewitnesses—men outstanding in both trustworthiness and authority. I deliberately avoid naming them, because I do not wish to stain the first fruits of my discourse with barbarous names.

Nevertheless, I found some things written about these matters not without usefulness, and I judged that their statements, taken from those writings, should be inserted in the present work in an appropriate order.

Relying, then, upon the aid of him through whose gratuitous goodness we are whatever good we are, and through whose abundant mercy we understand whatever good we understand, let us touch the psaltery and touch the lyre as well: with the one, let us proclaim the martyr’s everlasting glory in exultation; with the other, let us venerate him by imitating his bodily sufferings. And just as, at the command of Lanfranc, the unconquered master of all Latin eloquence and archbishop, we formerly exalted this man in musical melody, so now, compelled by the reasons we have mentioned, let us exalt him in an oratorical narrative.

# Here Begins the Life

[Col. 0375]

## 1. Elphegus Embraces the Monastic Life. He Builds the Monastery at Bath

Deriving the beginning of his birth from the most illustrious ancestry, Elphegus ordered his life with great prudence and the utmost humility. His parents, admiring the nobility of his mind and the innocence of his life, entrusted him to be instructed in literary knowledge and the wisdom of the Christian religion.

He directed the whole study of philosophy toward loving God, always desiring to know him, obey him, and subject himself to his yoke. Touched, therefore, by the spirit of the Majesty, he neglected his paternal inheritance and, although he was his mother’s only beloved, forgot her maternal grief. He abandoned the world and assumed the religious habit in a monastery named Derhirst.

[Note: [Col. 0375D] Also called Diherst or Derheste. Bede calls it Doherhusta; in his time it was a notable abbey. In the time of William of Malmesbury, however, it was nothing more than an empty image of antiquity, as he himself says in book II of *On the Bishops of the English*, in the section “On the Bishops of Winchester.” It was situated in Gloucestershire, restored by Saint Edward the King, and given to the monks of Saint Denis in France. Elphegus is said to have been a professed member of this monastery in a charter of King Henry VI, *Monasticon Anglicanum*, volume I.]

There he began to drive away private desires and personal wills, to submit himself to the service of all, to present himself as a kind of instrument for everyone, to love God without weariness, and to devote himself to fasts and vigils. He made every effort to benefit whomever he could; and those whom he could not benefit, he at least tried not to harm.

After spending several years in the monastic life, when he saw that the time of youth was passing, he sought to take up the path of a stricter life and to enter into a solitary contest with the ancient enemy. Leaving the monastery, he came to a place called Bath—that is, “the Bath.”

[Note: [Col. 0377D] Many more recent writers say that he had previously been at Glastonbury, before becoming abbot. Since the Bollandists refused to admit this on the authority of the *British Antiquities*, the author of *Anglia Sacra*, volume II, proves it from the *History of Glastonbury* found in volume I of the *Monasticon Anglicanum*. The monastery at Bath which Elphegus is said to have established here seems to have been different from the celebrated monastery of nuns built in the seventh century, which afterward passed to secular canons, and where Benedictine monks lived under King Edgar. Unless one says that it was destroyed by the barbarians, restored by Saint Elphegus, destroyed again by the Danes, repaired once more, and finally converted into a cathedral church.]

There hot water rises from the earth and supplies the use of baths according to one’s wishes. Building himself a dwelling there, he enclosed himself within it and afflicted his body with extraordinary rigor through fasting and abstinence.

In a short time nobles of every kind flocked to him, revealing the wounds of their souls and seeking from him counsel for salvation. Thus it came about that within a brief period a considerable crowd of monks gathered there.

## 2. He Exhorts His Followers to Greater Perfection

The holy man strongly reproved those who changed their worldly clothing but did not change their lives.

> “Does not the man seem full of falsehood who displays himself as what he is not, while he pretends one thing in his clothing and carries another in his heart? It is holier not to change one’s clothing than to neglect one’s life beneath the clothing.”

When he had completed a very spacious dwelling and imposed upon his disciples the law of sobriety, teaching them to restrain carnal desires, he himself shut himself up in a narrow little cell. Nevertheless, the brothers brought to him their most important causes and business.

Meanwhile, many of the monks, forgetful of their faith and profession, slackening the reins of obedience, began in the middle of the night to eat food secretly, devote themselves to drunkenness, indulge in lust, and, as far as hidden boldness allowed, practice everything dishonorable.

Against this capital crime the anger of God raged and struck them alike. One night, while Elphegus was keeping the sacred vigil as usual, he heard voices and disturbances within the monastery. Going outside, he saw a certain brother miserably afflicted and lying on the ground. Men of horrible appearance and filthy clothing stood over him, whipping him with bull-hide thongs and fiery serpents.

As he wailed and, in the anguish of his pain, uttered dreadful cries, his torturers reproached him with these words:

> “You did not obey God, and neither did we obey you.”

Saying this, they drove his soul from his body. When the saint saw this, he dissolved entirely into tears and returned to his cell. When the brothers saw what had happened, they confessed their error, did penance, and changed their way of life for the better.

## 3. He Becomes Bishop of Winchester

After Ethelwold, bishop of Winchester, died, a considerable dispute arose between the monks and the clerics concerning the election of a bishop.

The clerics of that Church were living a most wicked life and in every respect contrary to the decrees of the canons. Although they had often been corrected by the aforementioned bishop, they refused to amend their evil ways; indeed, they wished stubbornly to defend the things they had done wickedly. By royal decree it was therefore decided that they should be expelled and that others, more worthy, should serve in their place.

Thus, after the clerics had been consigned to exile, monks who feared the Lord were admitted. As a result, in the election of the bishop, the clerics wanted a cleric and the monks a monk, each group wishing to support a candidate who favored its own will.

When Saint Dunstan saw this, he took refuge in prayer, humbly asking God, to whom knowledge of the future is open, to deign to show who would be suitable to govern the Church. As he multiplied his prayers devoutly, Blessed Andrew the Apostle appeared to him and spoke this oracle:

> “Why are you sad, dearest one? Why do you utter such mournful complaints with tears? Rise, lay your hand upon Abbot Elphegus, and appoint him bishop of the desolate Church. Let no one’s power prevent you, for this judgment concerning him has proceeded not from man but from God. And so that I may not leave you anxious about me, I am Andrew, the apostle of the Son of God; know that I am the most diligent guardian of your salvation.”

Thus Dunstan, restored to confidence, consecrated Elphegus bishop as he had been commanded and sent him back with honor to his see.

## 4. His Virtues as Bishop. He Distributes the Church’s Treasures to the Poor

Elphegus adapted himself so well to the character of everyone that he was dear to all, and no one—as rarely happens among human beings—envied his glory. He showed the greatest mercy toward everyone; toward himself, however, he seemed impious and cruel.

[Note: [Col. 0378D] William of Malmesbury adds, in book II of *On the Bishops of the English*, in the section “On the Bishops of Winchester,” that Elphegus never ate meat unless he was ill, and that at night he was accustomed to go alone to the river, where he kept vigil immersed up to his loins in praise of God, doing this without the knowledge of his own people.]

For in the winter cold and frost, while sleep held everyone else at night, he himself would secretly rise from his bed with bare feet and wearing only a tunic, go outside, and spend the time until dawn in prayer. When he entered the dining hall to eat, he generally rose from the table almost as empty as when he had approached it. His body became so wasted by extreme emaciation that, when he raised his hands, stretched out with the sacrament, he could see the brightness of the air through the joints at the center of his palms.

He knew how to adapt his speech and disposition to every class of people. He permitted none of his parishioners to beg publicly, nor did he allow a poor person from another place to depart empty-handed. He considered it an immense and dreadful crime if a human being wished to claim as his own what nature had established as common to all.

Accordingly, he argued earnestly that no one could be a member of the Lord’s body if he was unwilling to help the needs of the poor. For if the other members of the body suffer with one member that is suffering, it is clear that the member of that same body which does not know how to feel compassion when another suffers does not belong to it.

When the resources that could have been assigned to the poor from the Church’s lawful income were exhausted, he ordered that the Church’s treasures, which he himself had accumulated in abundance, be distributed. He taught that churches possessed the most splendid things for this reason: so that in a time of prosperity they might serve honor, but in a time of necessity, usefulness.

[Note: [Col. 0379D] It is remarkable that nothing is said here about the translation of Saint Ethelwold, whose remains, according to William of Malmesbury, Elphegus translated: “He raised the bones of his predecessor,” he says, “in the twelfth year after his burial, persuaded to undertake it by certain signs, and not slight ones.”]

### He Is Transferred to Canterbury

When Blessed Dunstan perceived that his death was approaching and feared that the Church of God might be disturbed by a succession of wicked men, he struck the ears of divine mercy with anxious prayers, asking that he might have Elphegus as his successor. His request was immediately heard and the promise was granted, although what had been promised was not fulfilled at once.

I think this was delayed for two reasons: first, so that it might become clear to everyone how greatly God loved Dunstan, to whom, after his death and long afterward, he so faithfully granted what he had so kindly promised him while he was alive; and second, so that Elphegus might encounter the circumstances capable of advancing him to the glory of martyrdom.

[Note: [Col. 0380D] After administering the see of Winchester for twenty-two years, which he had assumed in the year 984.]

In the year of the Lord 1006, and in the 578th year after the arrival of the English in Britain, Elphegus, in the fifty-second year of his age, became Archbishop of Canterbury.

As he was traveling toward Rome to obtain the pallium and entered a certain town for the sake of lodging, the townspeople, seeing an unknown man and consulting their own greed, broke into the house, plundered his possessions, and compelled him to leave, stripped of all his belongings, by words and blows.

He bore his own injuries gently, but grieved moderately over those of his companions, and retraced the road by which he had come. He had not yet gone far from the town when dreadful voices seized its walls, threatening the citizens and buildings with swift destruction.

Without delay, devouring fire began to consume the town. As the flames grew violently and no hope of escape remained, they approached the holy man, confessed their offense, and asked forgiveness. At once the saint, having compassion on them, poured out prayers to God, and the destructive fire was immediately extinguished and ceased.

[Note: [Col. 0380D] What is reported by Bollandus and other authors is omitted here: namely, that while he was in Rome he learned of the death of Kenulf, his successor in the bishopric of Winchester and formerly abbot of Burg, who had purchased the see of Winchester with money.]

After his belongings had been restored to the bishop and he had received the pallium from the pope, he returned home safely. The virtue of chastity so dominated him that no one dared, in his hearing, utter an obscene word or report a shameful deed. He was also a comforter of the poor, a lifter-up of the oppressed, and the sole refuge of the afflicted.

## 6. The Danes Lay Waste to England

At about this time Sweyn and Turkill, princes of the Danes, inflicted a stain upon the land of the English, as their sins deserved. When Sweyn was horribly killed by divine judgment, Turkill inherited the leadership of that evil succession and ravaged many provinces of England with slaughter and fire.

King Ethelred, being unwarlike because he was weak, showed himself in deed a monk rather than a soldier. The men of the country, corrupted by wealth and bound by pleasures, considered nothing honorable except the bodily and individual advantage of each person.

Thus, while everyone feared for himself and his own possessions, all abstained from war; no one attempted to engage in a struggle for the common cause. Yet the struggle ought to have been undertaken for this very reason: so that each person might fight as splendidly as possible for what he wished to be his own.

In this great crisis, therefore, Elphegus regularly approached the enemy and preached the word of life to them. He ransomed captives at his own expense and diligently fed those oppressed by hunger. Thus, as much as he was honored and venerated by the faithful people, so much was he despised and mocked by the unbelieving.

But he, preferring to be called “Beelzebub with the Lord” rather than “Rabbi with the Pharisee,” did not cease to devote himself to the work he had begun: strengthening the faithful in faith and calling the unbelieving to the faith.

## 7. Eadric, Prefect of the Kingdom, Joins Them

The king had appointed a certain Eadric prefect of the whole kingdom. He was a man of humble birth, but his tongue had won him wealth and nobility. He was clever in mind, smooth in speech, and had surpassed all mortals in envy and treachery, as well as in pride and cruelty.

His brother first insulted the nobility of Canterbury freely in the king’s presence, and afterward violently seized the things that had come to each person by inheritance. The same nobles killed him and burned his house.

His brother sought vengeance from the king. The king refused his request and declared that his brother had been justly killed. The prefect therefore entered the palace with ten thousand men gathered around him and tried to avenge his murdered brother.

When he made little progress, he sought the aid of the Danes—not merely to defeat the men of Canterbury, but to invade the borders of all Britain and, after victory, divide the kingdom by equal portions. Thus they entered into a pact, gave and received their right hands, demanded and offered oaths, and first resolved to lay waste to Canterbury.

When Bishop Elphegus heard this, he summoned the people and said:

> “Be courageous; keep God before your eyes. Fear nothing except him who can destroy both body and soul in Gehenna. Preserve humility and patience. For Christ, although he was God and the Father had placed all things in his hands, did not wish to take vengeance upon his enemies, but ordered that the sword stained with the blood of Malchus be returned to its sheath.”

[Note: [Col. 0381D] Bollandus adds that Saint Elphegus prepared his fellow citizens to endure this siege by episcopal blessing and participation in Holy Communion.]

## 8. They storm Canterbury. The wretched condition of Canterbury

When at last the city had been besieged by the Danes for twenty days, and the citizens had exhausted everything they had prepared for the necessities of life, the bishop sent someone to urge the Danes to abandon their undertaking, spare the innocent people, and beware lest they insolently abuse the scourge of divine correction, temporarily permitted for the chastisement of His children.

But the Danes disregarded the message and steadfastly began to construct towers, batter the wall with rams, and hurl flaming torches. And behold, a devouring fire was kindled throughout the houses and, driven by the south wind, spread farther and farther. Then a pitiable deliberation arose among the citizens: whether, abandoning the defenses of the walls, they should rush to their own homes, or, neglecting those homes, devote themselves to the defense of the city. Private affection prevailed over the common good—the sweet memory of their children, and the natural compassion born of the duty to protect one’s family. Thus they ran and snatched their wives and dear children from the midst of the flames, only to see them immediately struck down by the enemy’s sword.

And behold, when the city had been breached, the army entered. A terrible din arose from the shouting voices and the blaring trumpets, so great that all the foundations of the city seemed to be shaken. Some were slaughtered by the sword, others consumed by flames, many hurled headlong from the wall, and some, suspended by their private parts, died. The matrons, compelled to reveal treasures they did not possess, were dragged by their hair through all the streets of the city and finally thrown into the flames. Little children, torn from their mothers’ breasts, were pierced with spears or crushed to pieces beneath a wagon driven over them.

But Saint Elphegus, unable to endure such devastation of his people, while he was surrounded in the church by a crowd of monks, suddenly slipped from the hands of those holding him and escaped from the church. Running to a place filled with corpses, he thrust himself among the enemy’s ranks and cried out:

“Spare them, spare them! And if you recognize yourselves as men, cease persecuting the innocent young. This is not victory, when the innocence of infants is destroyed; nor can anything done in war against the simple and gentle be counted as glory. Here am I, who have always rebuked the crimes of your impiety with free speech; here am I, who have fed, clothed, and ransomed captives whom you had fined and imprisoned. Let your anger rage against me instead.”

## 9. Saint Elphegus, taken captive, is thrust into prison. His charity toward his persecutors

He was immediately seized. His throat was gripped in their hands, impeding the voice of the speaker; his palms were bound with fetters; his cheeks were cut with fingernails; and his sides were beaten with fists and kicks. They also burned down the church [Note: The author cited by Bollandus reports that only four monks and eight hundred men escaped death in this great slaughter; other English writers follow him. See Roger of Hoveden, who says that Ailmar, abbot of Saint Augustine’s, was granted permission to depart.], consumed the Lord’s flock by the edge of the sword, and kept the bishop for seven months in a cramped prison.

Meanwhile the wrath of God began to rage against the murderous people to such a degree that, within a short time, two thousand of them were struck down by dreadful intestinal torments, while the rest of the multitude, similarly afflicted, awaited a similar end. The faithful people admonished them to repent of their sins and make satisfaction to the bishop. But they delayed, believing that this evil had happened to them by chance.

In the meantime, the plague prevailed over all the people who were trying to bring about the bishop’s death. Now ten, now twenty at a time were carried off by terrible pain in the bowels and head, striking great fear into the survivors. Therefore, after a council had been hastily summoned, they soon ran to the bishop and tearfully begged pardon for the crime they had committed. They brought him out of prison and led him honorably before the public gaze of the people.

The bishop said to them:

“Although your insatiable cruelty does not deserve pardon, nevertheless the example of the Lord teaches us what we ought to do. When He had deigned to wash the feet of His disciples, He did not exclude the one whom He foresaw would betray Him; rather, He fed him with the most holy bread. By the word of His power He struck down the ministers of the Pharisees, and by immediately raising them up He healed those same men. And—an outstanding sign of great goodness—those whom He sees daily resisting the heavenly commandments with stubborn hearts, He still allows to live while He sits in heaven, indeed even to surpass others in human affairs. Therefore, since I earnestly desire to become a devoted imitator of His examples, forgetting the burning of the city and the slaughter of the innocent—forgetting, I say, the former impiety committed against me—as He Himself interceded with the Father for those who crucified Him, so I will intercede with Him for my tormentors.

“Bring at once the bread of salvation, which will be given back to you, so that, refreshed by it and having obtained the benefit of the salvation you desired, you may either give thanks to the Savior or remain more criminal and blasphemous.”

After he had given everyone bread blessed by himself, he delivered them all from the deadly plague.

## 10. How ungrateful they were toward him. He is mocked by the devil

When they had been restored to health, the four leaders sent word to the bishop. First they thanked him for the benefit he had conferred; then they demanded that he pay three thousand marks if he wished to retain his life and freedom. When he refused to do so, they bound him and, subjecting him to unheard-of tortures on the day of the Lord’s Resurrection, thrust him back into prison.

While he was giving praise to God amid all these things, behold, an evil spirit appeared to him in the form of an angel. He falsely claimed that he had been sent from the heavenly courts so that he might lead him out of the squalor of the prison for the common salvation of the nation. He said that Elphegus should not fear being called a cowardly soldier, since he was neither more humble than Peter nor stronger than Paul: one of them had been carried away in a basket, while an angel released the other when he was weighed down by the prison’s chains. Christ also, to escape the hands of those who were stoning Him, left the temple and, by the command of the Gospel, granted His followers permission to flee.

Smeared, as it were, with these words as with ointments, he left the prison and followed the spirit.
