After they had crossed several floodwaters through the darkness of night, the evil one suddenly disappeared. Then the saint, recognizing the devices of his destructive guide, drew anguish from the depths of his heart. Throwing himself into the midst of the marshes, he implored the Savior with abundant tears, saying:

“O giver of life, O only merciful one toward the race of Adam, why have You abandoned me, an old man, of Your grace, although in the flower of my age You never used to abandon me? You allow one whom You preserved so mercifully for so long to perish, cast away at the end! How often have I found You as my savior amid the shipwreck of this life? Let me now, I beg You, experience You as my consoler in this deception of the devil, my helper in times of need and in tribulation. Behind me is the prison; before me the river; darkness surrounds me, and its author is near. Elphegus is enclosed by every hardship. The poor man has been abandoned to You alone; You will be the helper of the orphan.”

## 11. He is brought back by an angel

He did not cease to call upon the divine ears with these and similar words. And behold, a young man appeared to him, clothed in golden splendor and carrying the banners of the divine sign. He said:

“Where are your feet dragging you? Where is the force of your flight taking you? Where is the malice of your guide taking you? Is this how one goes to the crown—by fleeing the struggle of the contest? Or how can the palm of victory shine for one who, in his eagerness to run, refused to reach the limits of the course?”

When the priest replied that he was not fleeing but had obeyed the command of a divine messenger, the young man said:

“This was not a command of the Divinity, but a scheme of diabolical wickedness. He wished not so much to lead you out of prison as to lead you astray outside prison. For your pious deeds of the past constrain him, as does the present consolation of the Holy Spirit, which is always with you in such tribulations. His presence gives steadfastness to all, steadfastness gives victory, and victory gives glory. Return, therefore, to the place of the lost crown, assigned to you from heaven, knowing that tomorrow the Father will honor you in heaven with that greatest honor: that you may be with His Son forever.”

[Note: Elphegus is already said above to have understood the devil’s snares; nevertheless, this account is also related in the same way by Bollandus.]

## 12. Tortured in prison, he is visited by Saint Dunstan

Thus Elphegus, recalled by the angel to the place of combat, joyfully awaited the hour when he would receive his crown from God. But when he was near the point of entering the prison, he was seized by a crowd of executioners and afflicted with tremendous blows. Moreover, after the brain of his head had been shattered, he was shut up half alive in the dungeon. There they kindled a fire and, every hour of the day, poured in whatever produced or nourished the foulest smoke; then they closed the prison doors.

After a great part of the night had passed, the house began to receive a share of heavenly grace, breathe the fragrances of eternal life, and resound with hymns sung by the honey-sweet voices of the saints. When blessed Elphegus saw these things, he beheld the former archbishop Dunstan standing beside him, glorious in face and clothing, and addressing him with outstretched hands:

“To you, invincible soldier of the eternal King, to you we have come to honor you with our service, sent by Him who granted you victory over the enemy and prepared an everlasting crown for you in heaven. Behold those in whose fellowship you will enjoy eternal life after the death of the flesh: the citizens of the heavenly Jerusalem and members of God’s household—if in love you patiently make up in your flesh what is lacking of Christ’s sufferings.

“We have seen the manifold sufferings of the city, the burning of the churches, the slaughter of your children, your shame under chains, and, after the benefits you bestowed, torments doubled against you. Therefore, strengthened by the power of the Godhead, receive willingly what remains, knowing that the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the glory that will come, which will be revealed in you. One day will be given to punishment, but the reward will be continual and eternal.”

## 13. Again tortured, he is struck with an ax

Meanwhile his bonds were loosened, and all the wounds of his body were completely healed. Elphegus walked, singing with those who sang and rejoicing with those who rejoiced.

When morning came, he was led from the prison with a considerable armed force and, placed upon a beast, was dragged to judgment. They said to him:

“Pay the gold, or today you will be a spectacle to the world.”

He replied:

“I offer you the gold of divine wisdom, so that, abandoning the vanity you love, you may turn your devotion toward the one living and true God. But if with stubborn minds you reject the counsel of God announced to you through me, you will surely perish by a death worse than that of Sodom, nor will you take root forever in this land.”

Then the devil’s minions rushed upon him, struck him down with the backs of their axes, and covered him with stones. Bending his knees, he poured forth this prayer to God:

“Jesus Christ, only-begotten Son of the Most High God the Father [Bollandus: “only-begotten Son of the Most High Father”], who came into this world through the womb of the undefiled Virgin to save sinners, receive me in peace and have mercy on these men.”

He fell to the ground, then rose again and said once more:

“Good shepherd, unique shepherd, protect the children of the Church whom, as I die, I commend to You.”

Then a certain man rushed forward—one whom Elphegus himself had received from the sacred font—and drove an ax into his head. [Note: Bollandus says that he did this, moved by an impious pity when he saw Elphegus suffering too long at the threshold of death. In no. 35 Roger and William of Westminster call him Trun or Trum; he was a Dane.]

Immediately resting in eternal peace, he sent his victorious spirit triumphantly to heaven on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of May.

The Danish leaders, wishing to obscure both their own crime and Elphegus’s glory, decreed that his body should be thrown into the river, thinking that the enormity of their crime could more easily be concealed if his memory were removed from human beings. But what the Danes prepared for Elphegus as an insult, Christ prepared for him as glory.

Immediately the entire multitude of the people whom he had taught to abandon error advanced in arms. They preferred to perish together with the dead man rather than hand over to the devouring waters the body through whose ministry they had received the mystery of sanctification. Thus the body, protected by the opposing people, was neither submerged nor buried.

In the evening, the senators of both sides met to settle the dispute arising from so great a contention according to their own reasoning. It was agreed by all that they should jointly entreat the saint, so that, if he possessed any power with his God, he might display the strength of that power in this uncertainty.

“Behold,” said the Danes, “a branch cut from an ash tree, entirely stripped of sap and bark. If, when morning comes, the light finds it green after it has been dipped in this man’s blood, it will be clear that we have killed a just and holy man; and how you bury him will be in your hands. But if the wood remains in its former dryness, we shall say that you have erred in your devotion to him, and it will be our decision what we wish to do with the corpse.”

## 14. He shines through miracles. His body is transferred to London

When this condition had pleased and been accepted by all, so that it might be clear to everyone that Elphegus lived after death, the dry wood began to put forth leaves within the space of a single night. What the Danes had planted in the earth in the evening, they saw flowering when they rose in the morning.

Having no further grounds for opposition, the Danes began to rush eagerly into the dead man’s embrace, press repeated kisses upon him, offer their necks beneath him, and utter tears and lamentations. The body was carried on the shoulders of his enemies to the tree distinguished by his triumph, accompanied by countless miraculous signs displayed from heaven through the mighty power of God. At once the sick were restored to health, the blind received sight, the deaf heard, the mute spoke, and movement was restored to the lame. A house of prayer was also built over him there, and many Danish nobles, regenerated there, were converted to the faith of Christ.

When the people of London had heard all these things in order, they transferred the body to London at great expense and buried it honorably.

In the year of the Lord 1012, as the Sabbath of Easter week was drawing toward evening, Saint Elphegus, with the crown of martyrdom, departed to the Lord on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of May, in the seventh year of his episcopate and at the age of fifty-nine.

Against the authors of his death the wrath of God raged so fiercely that one duke is said to have killed himself with his own hand [Note: He is said to be Haco in the account of the translation which we shall shortly present.]; another drove a stylus into his throat; a priest who stubbornly concealed the martyr’s cross was killed with a sword; and another man of the same order, recklessly wearing the bishop’s sandals, was tormented by a demon before the entire people.

Such fear then seized all the Danish leaders that the earth could scarcely hold them. They entrusted themselves to the storms of the sea, thinking that they could escape the martyr’s anger on the open waters, since the land could not protect them from it. But as soon as they had been carried out into the deep, one hundred and sixty ships, driven by contrary winds, sank into the depths of the sea. Sixty-five others, having reached unknown regions, were miserably killed by the inhabitants, as though they had come with hostile intent.

The most wicked Turkill remained in England, the leader of evil, soon to be a robber for a short time but destined to remain forever the prey of a condemned spirit.

## 15.

After not a little time had passed, the Danish prince Canute came to England with a great fleet. Having broken with Turkill because of certain matters badly and treacherously handled, he destroyed whatever remained of the wicked people and drove the duke himself into Denmark with only six ships.

When the duke reached land, the Danish leaders suspected that he might stir up civil war. He was therefore immediately driven through every part of the region, and at last was killed by the common people of low birth and cast out to wild beasts and birds.

After this, the Danish prince Canute, seeing his people continuously slaughtered by the English army and nearly forced by the difficulties of the situation to surrender, summoned all the wiser Englishmen who had taken refuge with him and consulted them about the reason so many adversities had befallen him.

They all replied with one voice:

“It is the prophecy of the holy martyr Elphegus. When he had been surrounded by your fathers, he foretold that they would not take root forever in the kingdom of the English, but would perish by a death worse than that of Sodom. Therefore, if you wish to make him favorable to you in your own time, promise him that, if success attends your affairs, you will take care to return his relics honorably to his see.”

After he had firmly made this promise, he obtained peace shortly afterward, then half the kingdom after the peace, and the whole kingdom after the half.

When rest had been granted everywhere from all the tumult of war, the king remembered what he had once promised blessed Elphegus. He sent an embassy and summoned Archbishop Egelnoth. They found the martyr’s body, which had been buried for ten years, incorrupt and untouched, and brought it to Canterbury with the greatest honor, placing it reverently in a sarcophagus.

# HERE BEGINS THE TRANSLATION OF THE SAME SAINT, BY THE SAME AUTHOR, OSBERN

*(Mabillon, Acta Sanctorum Ordinis Sancti Benedicti, sixth century, part I, p. 123, from a manuscript of the Thuane Library.)*

## 1. The author’s preface

Because we once committed the venerable passion of the blessed martyr Elphegus to written records, it has also seemed fitting to gratify the desire of those who ardently wish to know how his most sacred body was transferred from London to Canterbury. We briefly mentioned at the end of his passion that it had been transferred, but we did not explain the manner of the translation. We shall now explain it.

## 2.

In the year 1012 from the Incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ, in the tenth indiction, as the Sabbath of Easter week was drawing toward evening and the Sunday of the Easter Octave was beginning, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of May, the most glorious bishop of the city of Canterbury, Elphegus, dying in the most glorious cause—for the sheep entrusted to him by God and together with those sheep—received the unfading crown of eternal glory, in the seventh year of his patriarchate and in the fifty-ninth year of his birth.

His venerable body, recovered from the place of his martyrdom either through favor or by purchase from the faithful people, was carried to the city of London and buried in the church of the blessed apostle Paul, amid countless flashing miracles of grace. Immediately the sick were restored to health, a clear light poured upon the blind, the gift of hearing was granted to the deaf, the lame walked with a straight step, and divine benefits most readily came to all who faithfully asked.

But the avenging wrath of God did not permit those who had caused his death to pass without terrible punishment.

## 3. The authors of Saint Elphegus’s death are punished

To touch briefly on a few matters among many, I propose the following: the duke Hacon piercing himself with his own blade; a practitioner devoted to the disciplines of astrology driving a stylus into his throat; a priest who stubbornly concealed the martyr’s collar-cross being killed by the martyr’s own hands; and another man of the same order, recklessly wearing the martyr’s sandals, being possessed by a demon and most cruelly tormented before the entire people of the city of London until he was dragged by his feet.

Because of these events, such intense fear seized all the Danish leaders that the earth could scarcely hold them. They entrusted themselves to maritime storms, thinking that they could escape the martyr’s anger on the open sea, since the land could not protect them from it. But as soon as they had been carried into the deep with foaming oars, one hundred and sixty ships, driven by contrary winds, were submerged in the depths of the sea. Forty others, and also twenty-five, reached foreign and unknown regions and were miserably killed by the inhabitants, as though they had come with hostile intent.

The bold and evil prince Turkill nevertheless remained in England, soon to be a robber for a short time but destined to remain forever the prey of a condemned spirit.

For after a short time had passed, the Danish prince Cnut came with a great fleet to the land of the English. Having broken with Turkill because of certain matters handled badly and treacherously, he erased whatever might remain of the wicked people, just as writing is erased with a stylus, and drove the duke himself, protected by only six ships, into Denmark.

When the duke reached land, the Danish leaders suspected that he might stir up civil war. He was therefore immediately driven through every part of that region, and at last was killed by the lowborn common people and miserably cast out to wild beasts and birds.

Thus those who had killed the holy and honorably renowned archbishop Elphegus were removed from land and sea.

[Note: English manuscripts read *diffidensque* (“distrusting”) instead of *dissidensque* (“breaking with”). Canute was first chosen by the Danes, who were ravaging England, to replace his father Sweyn; then, after King Ethelred’s death, he was also recognized as king by the English. Finally, after King Edmund’s death in 1017, he ruled alone in England; he did not compel Turkill into exile until several years later.]

## 4. The occasion of the translation. It is carried out under King Cnut’s care

But the Danish prince Cnut, seeing his people continuously and most cruelly slaughtered by the English army and already nearly forced by the difficulties of the situation to surrender, summoned all the wiser Englishmen who had taken refuge with him and consulted them about the reason so many adversities had befallen him.

They all replied with one voice:

“It is the prophecy of the venerable martyr Elphegus. When he had been surrounded by your fathers through a cruel interrogation, he foretold that they would not take root forever in the kingdom of the English, but would perish by a death worse than that of Sodom. Therefore, if you wish to make him favorable to you in your own time, bind yourself to him by this promise: when success has come to your affairs, you will take up his venerable relics from the place where they were buried and endeavor to transfer them, according to the custom of the ancients, to the seat of his patriarchate.”

The prince agreed to the senators’ counsel, and the declaration of divine reconciliation followed the counsel. For not many days later Cnut obtained peace; after peace, half the kingdom; after half, the whole kingdom.

When rest had been granted everywhere from all the tumult of wars, he remembered what he had once promised blessed Elphegus. He sent an embassy and summoned Agelnot, who at that time held the highest priesthood in the holy Church of Dorobernia. He was a holy and good man and greatly favored by the king because he had anointed him with sacred chrism.

On the Saturday of the vigils of Pentecost, Agelnot arrived in London. He sent word to the king, who happened then to be going down to the baths, that he was present and would await in the church of the blessed apostle Paul whatever the king wished to determine.

When the king heard this, he immediately rose from the bath, covering his naked body only with a cloak, put simple sandals on his feet, and hastened toward the bishop. He ordered all the soldiers of his household—whom the Danes call *Huscarles*—to act as follows: some were to stir up disturbances at the farthest gates of the city; others were to occupy the bridge and the riverbanks under arms, so that the people of London could not hinder them as they departed with the saint’s body.

## 5.

When the king entered the church, he embraced the archbishop and kissed him. Then, with the doors immediately shut, he said in a joyful yet trembling voice:

“This is the day that the Lord has made; let us rejoice and be glad in it. This is the day of which the Lord spoke, on which the treasure of the relics of Lord Elphegus is to be transferred from the house of his lodging to the house of his patriarchate.”

At these words the priest was shaken beyond description. He did not know why the king had summoned him and, in great anguish of spirit, said:

“May almighty God not count it against you, my lord king, that you wished to do this without telling me your intention, so that I might have come better instructed and fully prepared, lest I perish in the middle of this great city. Or, if you were pleased to undertake so difficult a task, why did you at least not bring men who could serve as workers in it? The stone placed at the entrance of the tomb is so heavy that it could scarcely be moved by many pairs of oxen, let alone rolled by the two monks who alone are present. This is an ill-considered undertaking. A different time and different strength must be considered.”

The king, greatly strengthened in the Lord, replied:

“In this, holy Father, it will most clearly appear whether that blessed man wishes to cross over with us: if he himself, by his power, makes possible what is impossible for human beings. Difficulty has always been accustomed to give birth to a miracle. Therefore let your holiness prostrate yourself before God in prayer; let the monks confidently approach to open the entrance of the tomb; and I shall attend as doorkeeper at the doors of the gates.”

## 6. The tomb is opened by two monks. The body is found incorrupt

After seeking and receiving the bishop’s blessing, the monks prepared to act. One was called Godricus, formerly a disciple of the same martyr and, many years later, dean of the Church of Canterbury. From him we carefully learned all that we relate here. The other was called Elvardus—also, in some texts, Alfwardus—by the surname “the Tall,” and he had once been privileged to attend closely upon Dunstan.

They seized the iron candlestick that stood opposite, attempting to break through the upper structure, which was firmly joined together by masonry. According to the men who asserted this and called upon God as witness to their testimony, the monks had scarcely applied their hands when the smaller stones, the cement, and whatever work projected above began to fall like leaves of trees shaken at the beginning of winter.

When they reached the stone covering the open tomb, they fell forward upon the ground on bended knees, placed their shoulders beneath it, and pushed it. Immediately they dragged it aside with an easy movement. This was truly more astonishing than could be believed: as we have said, the stone that many pairs of oxen could not have dragged was rolled aside by only two monks with a light push.

The king and the archbishop, terrified with amazement, hurried up. With tearful eyes they looked inside and saw the former instrument of the Holy Spirit [Note: The body of Saint Elphegus remained incorrupt even in the time of William of Malmesbury, as he himself states in Book I of *On the Bishops of the English*, in these words: “That his body, still bearing traces of fresh blood, has remained ignorant of the stain of decay to this day—I have said this elsewhere, and it need not be repeated as a common report.”], lying incorrupt and showing no trace of decay anywhere in the whole body. Counting the sequence of years, they discovered that it was the tenth year since the same saint had been buried there.

The king then cried out loudly for joy and poured forth a prayer mingled with tears:

“Father, most holy, sweeter than every delight; Father, most blessed, more precious than all the treasures of the world, have mercy on this sinful king. Let neither my own unworthiness nor the cruelty that my parents exercised against you, contrary to justice and goodness, stand in my way. I acknowledge you as the most powerful friend of the eternal King, and from now on, for as long as I live, I appoint you as my advocate. Save me; save everyone. Since you are able to save with eternal salvation, deign to depart with us, so that you may bring great joy to your children.”

## 7. He is transferred. The king’s devotion toward the martyr

The chief priest of God himself approached to handle and lift the venerable body with his own hands. He was anxious, however, because he could find nowhere a board on which it could be carried to the ship. While he stood uncertain in great despair, he noticed a wooden board beneath the body, extended lengthwise and breadthwise exactly to its measure, as though the original buriers had placed it there for this sole purpose: so that at some later time the saint might be lifted from it without any difficulty and with his body unharmed.

Thus made joyful and unexpectedly cheerful, they took a linen cloth that the monk Godricus had brought with him for the bishop’s service and wrapped the sacred limbs together with the wood beneath them. But when part of the body still remained uncovered, the aforementioned monk ran to the altar of the apostle Saint Paul, seized the shroud lying above it, left half a pound of gold in place of the shroud, and quickly returned to wrap what remained.

Then, lifting the precious treasure of the precious body onto the monks’ shoulders, they descended by a narrow road leading to the river Thames. The king and the archbishop followed them, each directing the whole attention of his mind toward God.

When they had begun to approach the river, behold, the royal ship came toward the approaching martyr. Its prow was adorned with gold, and it was filled with deacons and armed soldiers. The king quickly leapt aboard, extending his arms to receive the martyr; then, stretching out his right hand, he brought in the bishop.

After the larger vessel had moved away, the king sat holding the rudder and steering the ship toward the opposite bank of the river. One might have seen the great power of God favoring the martyr’s service: on one side, the bridge and all the riverbanks were lined with soldiers in armor; on the other, one could hear sham disturbances being stirred up at the farthest gates of the city. One could observe the king guiding the ship, a noble rower pulling the oars, the archbishop praying, and the holy monks rendering service.

## 8.

As soon as they reached the land, the king was the first to leave the ship. He placed the body upon a vehicle and then sent it ahead with a strong troop of soldiers. He himself sat with the archbishop at the far end of the bridge until those who had gone before were farther away from the city, for he feared an attack by the citizens.

Then he rose and, in refined jesting, teased the archbishop:

“You are freed. By my service you have been rescued from the danger of death, from which you thought you could not be freed. Now go safely to the saint and humbly pray that he favor our times. I would go with you if I were not occupied, as you know, with the great affairs of the kingdom. The queen lives in Kent with my son Hardacnut; I shall order her to meet you with all the nobility.”

The archbishop, separated from the king, followed those who had gone ahead with a great crowd of *huscarles*. When he had come so near that dust could be seen rising into the sky from those who had gone ahead and were constantly looking back, those who had preceded them suspected that the citizens had left the city. They therefore promptly sent forward a few monks, their attendants, and the martyr.

The others, arriving at the village of Plunstede, occupied the narrow places and arranged three battles with three companies. Their hearts were prepared to die for love of the blessed martyr. But when they saw the standard of the cross close at hand, they recognized as companions those whom they had feared as enemies, and found a joy greater than they had imagined.

## 9. Elphegus is received at Canterbury. He is placed in the church of Saint Saviour

As they proceeded and spent that same night in a village called Earhetha, an infinite multitude from Kent met them: foot soldiers mingled with horsemen, women with men, the old with young men. Each group led its own choirs, striking harps, and conducting the procession with rejoicing as though it were the Ark of the Lord’s Covenant.

You might have believed that the children of Israel sang in no other way, either when the prophet of God Moses led them out from the midst of the Red Sea on dry feet, or when King David transferred the Ark of the Lord from the house of Aminadab to his own city.

But when the citizens of Canterbury heard that the father of their life and companion in death had arrived, they leapt forth joyfully to meet him, like Jacob, awakened as if from deep sleep on account of Joseph and dissolved in tears of joy. They rejoiced that they could see again the man whose manifold benefits their parents had experienced both in life and in death.

The monks of Christ’s Church rejoiced more than all the others. They adorned the church with solemn ceremony and put on Levitical and priestly vestments. Some led the procession with bells rattling in repeated movements; others carried lamps, Gospels, and jeweled crosses in their hands; and they went out to meet him with melodious voices beyond the city’s long walls.

He was then received with the ineffable rejoicing of the whole city of Canterbury and transferred to the church not of the Teacher of the Nations, as formerly, but of the Savior of all [Note: The cathedral church of Canterbury was dedicated to Christ. Saint Elphegus was transferred into it from the cathedral church of London, which rejoiced in Paul as its patron.]. While alive, he had always cherished this church with love and strengthened it by his power; for its sake, and together with it, he had endured death.

He was placed there, not as one newly mourned with loud cries, but honored as one living forever with God.

10. He shines with miracles. Feast of the Translation.—When the third day dawned, Queen Emma arrived with all the nobility who were with her, and, after presenting gifts of various kinds of precious things, gave thanks to the living God, who, for the honor and glory of his name, had brought back with such magnificence the man whom the enemy had carried away with such disgrace, to the blasphemy of God. And so that the most holy father might show his sons some small sign of his grace, after seven days he restored speech to a certain mute man, and another, after Paul, who was bound in iron, he set free by breaking the iron. These are the joys of today’s festival, this is the solemnity of the day, which was therefore established to be celebrated every year in the Church of Canterbury on the sixth day before the Ides of June, so that it might not be erased by any forgetfulness—namely, that blessed martyr Elphegus had deigned to be transferred from a foreign place to his own.

And although we celebrate the day of his passion together with all the others, nevertheless we ought to celebrate the day of his translation alone above all others. For on that day we had one and simple cause for rejoicing; on this day, however, we have received gifts of double joy. There we proclaim that he was raised into heaven; here, that he was crowned in heaven and given to us on earth by God. Blessed is the Son of God, who crowned him in heaven and mercifully gave him to us on earth, who lives and reigns as God with the Father and the Holy Spirit throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## Epitaph of Saint Elphegus

[Col. 0393]

Nobility of character joined to a noble lineage  
Strives to ennoble this holy man.

As a boy this bishop clung to divine works;  
As an old man he strives to exchange the law of youth.

Having experienced the stroke of the axe,  
He enters the joys of heaven and rejoices to possess the celestial realm with the just.

Boundless praise to God, who leads his own,  
Destined to reign with him, to the stars through so many and such great triumphs.

## In the Year of Our Lord 1084. Blessed Bartholomew, Abbot of the Major Monastery

[Col. 0393]

## Historical Notice on Blessed Bartholomew

*(Mabillon, Acts of the Saints of the Order of Saint Benedict, sixth century, part II, p. 384.)*

[Col. 0393A] 1. After regular discipline had been restored by Saint Majolus, abbot of Cluny, in the highly renowned Major Monastery at Tours, that place, once so celebrated but which had lain entirely neglected for many years, soon recovered its former splendor to such an extent that thereafter no other monastery was considered superior to it either in reputation for holiness or in the number of its monks. How renowned it was toward the end of the eleventh century we may learn from the beginning of Book Four of Orderic Vitalis’s *Ecclesiastical History*, where he concludes his distinguished eulogy of the Major Monastery in these few words:

> “For the Major Monastery,” he says, “was begun by the most holy Martin, archbishop of Tours, and there, by God’s inspiration, the devotion of good men grew and multiplied. In our own times Albert and Bartholomew, Bernard and Hilgotus, and William of Nantes presided over this monastery as abbots. By their holiness and goodness they benefited many and, famous far and wide, shone forth valiantly for those nearby and those from abroad.”

2. It is not possible here to discuss individually the almost countless holy places that were subject to the Major Monastery at that time under the name of priories, in which monks were established under the rule and jurisdiction of the abbots of that same monastery. Certainly there was scarcely a province, city, or diocese throughout all Gaul that did not at that time desire to have monks of the Major Monastery among its people. Bishop Isembert of Poitiers praises the monks of the Major Monastery, “living in a holy vocation,” in a charter issued for that monastery under Abbot Albert.

It is worthy of note, however, what Orderic Vitalis relates in Book Three about a certain nobleman, Radulf, son of Geroi and surnamed Hero because of his outstanding deeds, who at that time became a monk in the Major Monastery and offered a remarkable example of repentance.

> “Radulf,” he says, “abandoning the enticements of the world, fled to the Major Monastery. There, having become a monk under Abbot Albert, he earnestly begged God that he might be disfigured in body by the incurable disease of leprosy, so that he might be cleansed in soul from the filth of sins. He obtained what he piously requested, and after nearly six years from his conversion he died happily.”

Albert died in the year 1063; his memory is recorded in the necrologies of Saint Benignus of Dijon and Saint-Germain-des-Prés on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of June. Bartholomew was appointed in his place, and he became more celebrated than the other abbots of this monastery.

3. The Life of Bartholomew was preserved in a manuscript codex of the Major Monastery, as we have learned from several of our notes. Indeed, an anonymous author, a native of the Major Monastery, who wrote a little book on the deeds of the bishops of Tours and the works of the abbots of the Major Monastery, states that “the Life of Bartholomew, full of miracles and virtues, is preserved in the library.” Yet, by some misfortune, we do not know what, that codex disappeared a few years ago. We deeply regret this loss, since the history of this Benedictine age could have been greatly illuminated by that Life; nor do any suitable monuments survive elsewhere [Col. 0395A] for setting forth, as fully as the matter requires, the illustrious deeds of this blessed abbot.

Therefore, lest the memory of so great a man be absent from these Acts of the Saints, it seemed appropriate to collect here into one place whatever we were able to find about him in various authors and in several ancient charters. To these we shall finally append a notable fragment of the history of the Major Monastery, taken from a manuscript codex of the Cistercian monastery of Villers in Brabant, in which many matters—and matters especially worthy of attention—that occurred under Abbot Bartholomew and his successors at the Major Monastery are narrated at greater length. At our request, this little work was copied by the Reverend Father Albert de Chambley, prior of Villers, who sent it to us in the year 1672.

[Col. 0395B] 4. The anonymous monk of the Major Monastery mentioned above is mistaken when he writes that Bartholomew was appointed to govern his monastery in the year 1004 and presided over it for twenty years, that is, until the year of Christ 1024. I would readily have supposed that this error had entered through a scribal fault, by the omission of the two letters LX, had that same author not revealed his error elsewhere in a similar way, asserting that Bartholomew was the fifth abbot after Saint Majolus had restored regular discipline in the Major Monastery.

It is certain, however, from various records that nine abbots intervened between Majolus and Bartholomew. It may be gathered from many charters of donations preserved in the archives of the Major Monastery that Bartholomew assumed the government of the abbey in 1064, although it must be admitted that several of them seem to record his election in the preceding year. I believe this occurred because of the disturbances raised against Bartholomew by Geoffrey surnamed the Bearded, count of Anjou, to whom the city of Tours was then subject.

For Geoffrey not only attempted to subject the lands of the Major Monastery to his authority; he also demanded that Bartholomew receive the pastoral staff from him. When Bartholomew steadfastly refused to do so, and after suffering much at his hands, he was forced to remain for a long time outside the borders of the region. Hence we infer that, although Bartholomew had already been elected abbot in 1063, he may nevertheless have entered upon the governance of his monastery only in the following year, namely 1064.

Here, however, we must report what is found on this matter in the *Deeds of the Counts of Anjou*, written in the following century by an anonymous monk of the Major Monastery, who dedicated his work to Henry, king of the English. Thus it reads in chapter 10, volume X of Achery’s *Spicilegium*, p. 484.

5. “How great Geoffrey the Bearded’s greed and avarice were, and also his cruelty and pride, and how God resisted and humbled him, as it is written, ‘God resists the proud,’ and, ‘God breaks all pride,’ may be seen in the present account. The devil, whose food and delight from the beginning of the world has been to corrupt holy things, disturb peace, obstruct good works, and oppose the election and most holy blessing of Bartholomew, abbot of the Major Monastery, contrived to harass them by every means in his power.

He therefore incited the count of Tours, Geoffrey by name and surnamed the Bearded, to subject the Major Monastery to his dominion and to compel its abbot to receive the pastoral staff from his hand. The flock of blessed Martin at the Major Monastery, astonished and bewildered by such an unheard-of proceeding, began to consider and say how it could come about that so great and longstanding a royal authority, and the particular glory of lord Martin, always preserved inviolate by emperors and kings from ancient times and even from their own days—for while he lived he appointed his own abbot there, named Galbertus, who now rests buried there—should in the present age be subjected to the dominion of anyone except a king, as always, or its own abbot.

“For they said: ‘We have not insignificant commands of emperors and kings, as well as very many privileges of the apostolic authorities, by which this place of ours, in reverence for our pious father, lord Martin, who founded it, possesses a special dignity and glory. It has never been subject to anyone except either a king or the proper abbot of Saint Martin. In the same way it has been separated from the authority of every prelate, except insofar as necessity in the ordering of monks requires the involvement of the Church; and we are well able to defend ourselves against those who would do otherwise.’

“Accordingly, with one mind and by common decree, the same flock came to the aforementioned count and reported all these things to him: namely, that he should not permit this abbey of the Major Monastery, nor the monastery itself, to come under anyone’s dominion except that of its own abbot, lest the honor and glory of so great a father—which continually increases in heaven—should in any way appear diminished on earth, after having hitherto been preserved inviolate by so many kings, fathers, and princes.

“But the count obstinately—or rather, forcefully—persisted in his position and threatened to destroy the place if this were done. The monks repeatedly and reasonably approached the count, and through ecclesiastical and secular persons of prudent and sound counsel they endeavored to calm his agitation. But the more the count saw the monks resisting his will, the more violently he became enraged, and the more indiscreetly he threatened not only the place but the monks themselves; and he fulfilled his cruel threats by cruel deeds.

“For wherever his power reached, he attacked the Major Monastery and its dependent places, trying to destroy them utterly; he violently seized and ravaged the monks’ possessions and the property of the monastery’s people; and he began to look more closely for ways to satisfy his savagery even against the bodies of the monks, so that what is written might be fulfilled: ‘The sinner watches for the just man and gnashes his teeth at him’ (Psalm 36:12). The persecution became so savage and grew so intense that even the count’s secular men marveled at his unrestrained conduct and, while cursing the count, prayed to God for the monks.

“But when the monks had endured these things for a long time with patience and could no longer withstand the dangers threatening them, they resolved to increase more devoutly the prayers they poured out for their persecutors according to the Gospel command. They went barefoot to the body of blessed Martin, taking with them the weak and the lepers whom they supported from the monastery’s food and clothing, and whose prayers they were confident would have the greatest efficacy before the Lord. There, persisting unanimously in prayer, they implored God and the merits of the saint to temper in his mercy that most savage plague, lest their persecutor destroy their place, from which he himself would later descend to hell to suffer punishment.

“After this, they also sent their petition to the abbot of Cluny, a man worthy of commemorative remembrance, named Hugh, humbly beseeching him and the holy congregation of Cluny to pray for God’s mercy to mitigate so great a persecution, and furthermore asking that the abbot himself deign to console the Major Monastery by his presence. Since he was benevolent by nature, he kindly granted their request.

“When he reached the Major Monastery, he consoled the brothers, and they went to Tours to see the count. Falling at his feet, they humbly begged him to cease at last from that persecution, but in vain. For the count, fixed in his savagery, was moved neither by the monks’ tears nor by the abbot’s entreaties, nor did he restrain himself even slightly from persecuting the monks.

“When they returned to the monastery, the abbot also returned to Cluny, accompanied by the abbot of the Major Monastery. Before the latter departed, however, he received the sacred priestly orders; for when he had been elected abbot, he was still serving in the ministry of the diaconate.

“Meanwhile, God, who raises up the oppressed and does not abandon those who hope in him, was not sleeping as he guarded spiritual Israel. He did not delay any longer in having mercy on the affliction of his servants, who, as it is written, had already received double for their sins. Since he is almighty and just, he caused the count’s injustice justly to rebound upon his own head.

“For it to become clear how unjust that count had been toward the abbot and those monks, and so that it might appear by how just a vengeance he deserved punishment for attacking that holy church so irrationally, God—who is always wondrous in his saints—deigned to perform a remarkable miracle on behalf of his faithful.

“After the count had despised Abbot Bartholomew, the abbot of Cluny, and the monks, and had refused to heed them, a short time later his brother, named Fulk, rose up against him with a powerful force and did not cease persecuting him until he had captured him, deprived him of his rank, and held him captive for many years. Afflicted there and, through divine vengeance, given over to a reprobate mind, he lived afterward for more than thirty years in that misery, deserving pity even from his enemies.

“Certainly by a just judgment he was deprived of freedom both of body and of mind; justly was he miserably oppressed throughout his life by the power of one man, since he had raged against the Lord and sought to crush many servants of God under unjust servitude. By a just judgment he lost forever the dominion he had held, because he had raged with unjust tyranny against the Lord’s possessions.”

6. When this storm had subsided, Bartholomew returned to Tours and devoted himself entirely to settling the disputes that had arisen between the monastery itself and many of its neighbors. Numerous agreements were made concerning these matters. Bartholomew invited some to peace by entreaties, others by admonitions, and some even by payments of money.

Among the chief documentary witnesses to this matter is a letter of his to Ernaldus, whom others call Arnaldus, bishop of Le Mans. It was written because Ernaldus was attempting to rescind the donation of Vivoin to the Major Monastery made by his predecessor Wilgrinus and confirmed by the chapter of Le Mans. We shall publish it in full below.

Bartholomew added gifts to this letter in order to calm the bishop’s anger, which had been stirred against the monks of the Major Monastery. Finally overcome by these means, Ernaldus withdrew from the entire dispute.

7. As the reputation for holiness of Bartholomew and of the monks living under his rule increased, the institution of the Major Monastery spread through various provinces of Gaul. Bishops and other noblemen requested monks from that place either to inhabit new monasteries or to restore to better condition old ones in which regular discipline had grown lukewarm. Indeed, their name reached even foreign nations.

Thus William the Conqueror, after defeating Harold, the invader of the kingdom of England, founded at the very site of the battle a distinguished monastery in honor of Saint Martin. For this reason he wished it to be called Battle; and he summoned monks from the Major Monastery at Tours and settled them there, with one of their number elected abbot, as the writers of English history relate.

The origins, possessions, and various privileges of this monastery, which was situated in the county of Sussex, are discussed at length in the *Monasticon Anglicanum*, volume I, p. 310. Several charters are also reported there, both of William himself, the monastery’s founder, and of other kings of England; there is no need to reproduce them here.

At about the same time, that is, in the year 1067, Radulfus Paganellus, a noble Englishman, “gave” to the abbot and monks of the Major Monastery the church of the Holy Trinity that he possessed at York, “desiring to restore the service of God that had perished in it . . . so that,” he says, “through their continual prayers I may deserve to have a share in the blessed resurrection in the future.” He then added various possessions for the support of the monks, all of which Pope Alexander II confirmed. His charter is reported in the aforementioned volume of the *Monasticon Anglicanum*, p. 564, where more is found concerning that priory of the Holy Trinity.

8. Nor should it be thought that the many cells which were then subject to the Major Monastery were begged for by the abbot or monks of that place. On the contrary, those to whom some monks from this congregation were granted considered that a favor had been done to them. Such respect was accorded to their holiness, as could be proved from the many surviving charters of donation.

It seemed appropriate to reproduce one of these in full as a specimen. It is the charter of a certain Gervasius, a nobleman of Le Mans, concerning the church of Saint Guingaloeus at Château-du-Loir, which he transferred to the monks of the Major Monastery for their possession. It reads as follows:

> “I, Gervasius, devoted to secular military service, concerned for the salvation of my soul, and considering that by my fasts and prayers I cannot reach God, thought that in some way I should commend myself to those who serve God in such matters day and night, so that through their intercession I might deserve to find that salvation which I could not find by myself.
>
> “Since, therefore, I wished for this reason to contribute something of this kind to such men for the support of their present life, but did not possess among my goods anything that I could worthily offer them, hope concerning God’s mercy arose in me: if I could restore to their former condition those things which my ancestors had bestowed upon God for the use of his servants, but which had now been abandoned and laid waste, I might obtain forgiveness of my sins and everlasting salvation for my soul.
>
> “There is therefore in the district of Le Mans, at Château-du-Loir, a church built in honor of Saint Guingaloeus, to which my ancestors contributed many things for the use of those serving God there, and for which they appointed canons to perform that service of God. When war arose between Count Geoffrey and the lord of that castle, and the same count was destroying everything around the castle with sword and fire, he did not hesitate to seize and ravage the property of this church also, as he did the rest. Thus many of the canons, compelled by poverty, fled and abandoned the church they served.
>
> “From that time onward the divine office began to be celebrated more negligently in the church itself, and its possessions declined each day and fell into a worse condition. Considering this, and grieving especially that God was not being served in the aforesaid church with the dignity, honor, and reverence that were appropriate, I began anxiously to consider whether I might find such men as would both honorably frequent divine worship in that church and restore the property belonging to it, now almost destroyed, to its former strength.
>
> “By their prayers supported, I—namely Gervasius—as well as my father Rotbertus, my mother Elizabeth, my wife Aremburgis, my grandfather Amelinus, my grandmother Hildeburgis, and Gervasius, archbishop of Reims—who together founded that place—might obtain forgiveness of sins and salvation from the Lord.
>
> “Accordingly, after seeking the counsel of my nobles and friends and also of the bishop of Le Mans, Lord Ernaldus, I asked Lord Bartholomew, abbot of the Major Monastery, to come to me, and I earnestly begged him to receive from me, into the lordship of Saint Martin, this church of which we are speaking, with everything belonging to it; and to establish monks there who would diligently serve divine worship day and night.
>
> “When, by God’s gift, I deserved to obtain this from him, I handed over to him the aforesaid church, with all the possessions subject to it, with which it had been endowed up to that time, just as the canons of that place held them on that day, together with all the other things that it had formerly possessed and of which it had been stripped by the tyranny of evil men. I also promised that I would recover them for him and restore them, as it had held them before, to its right.
>
> “I granted all these things free and undisturbed by every customary exaction, vicariate payment, or other tax, just as my ancestors had lawfully bestowed them upon the same church. Thus it shall be lawful for the congregation of the Major Monastery and its successors, together with the abbots who govern them in their time, to possess it in perpetuity, without any contradiction from me or from any of my successors.
>
> “Whatever they decide should be done concerning it, they shall have free power to do, arrange, and dispose of it, in whatever manner they wish and consider best, both now and in the future. It shall depend upon the judgment of the aforesaid abbot and of those who succeed him as abbots of the Major Monastery how many brothers, and of what quality, are to be sent to the aforesaid place.
>
> “I made this donation with the consent and authority of my mother and of all my brothers, as well as of all the canons of that place. So that it might remain stable and unshaken forever and might not thereafter fear that anyone would bring a legal claim against it: I, Gervasius, four thousand solidi; my mother Elizabeth, one hundred solidi; Adam, ten pounds; Rotbertus, ten pounds; Gervasius the cleric, one hundred solidi; Ursus the canon, forty solidi; Haimo the canon, thirty solidi; Rannulfus the canon, forty solidi; Odricus the canon, thirty solidi; Guido the canon, forty solidi; Fulcodius the canon, sixty solidi; Gualterius the canon, twenty solidi; Herbertus the canon, forty solidi; Teduinus the canon, forty solidi; Witernus the canon, fifteen solidi; and Guarnerius the canon, twenty solidi.
>
> “Let this be known to all: from the money of Lord Gervasius which we gave him, the canons received their own money.”

> “Names of the monks who received the place: Bartholomew, abbot; Fulchardus, monk; Gualterius, monk; Ernaldus, monk; Adraldus, monk; Ansegisus, monk; Guillelmus, monk; Girulfus of Relliac, cleric; Guarinus, cleric; Doselinus, cleric.”

9. We have a letter of G., priest of Lyons, to Radulfus, bishop of Tours, edited by Cordesius after the letters of Hincmar. In it he begs the same prelate to obtain from Bartholomew, abbot of the Major Monastery, someone from his community to preside over the abbey of Savigny.

> “I beg you, with great kindness, to admonish and entreat Lord B., abbot of the Major Monastery, on our behalf and yours, and to beseech him earnestly not to delay in providing for me, his beloved, and for the desolate brothers who seek his mercy. Let him send a father; let him send a shepherd who will guard his flock with such care that no entrance may be opened anywhere to the ancient enemy through which he could ever break into that flock.”

The same reputation for holiness that led many to transfer their possessions to the Major Monastery also moved certain others, including men of noble birth, to give not only their property but themselves to the monastery. Among these were Fulk of Boeria, who had transferred to the monastery, under Abbot Albert, the church of Saints Cyricus and Julitta and many other things; Solomon of Sablé; Beringerius of Saint-Loup; and many others who are mentioned in various charters.

10. We have thought it worthwhile to present these matters from among the many things concerning Bartholomew, whose deeds it may perhaps someday be possible to pursue at greater length, if his Life, distinguished by virtues and miracles and formerly preserved in the manuscript codex mentioned above, can ever be recovered.

His name was entered into the Benedictine Martyrology by Hugh Menard on February 23; those who subsequently compiled Benedictine calendars followed him. On the following day he is praised by the Bollandists among those passed over, and rightly so. For in the little book already cited, by the anonymous author of *The Deeds of the Bishops of Tours and the Works of the Abbots of the Major Monastery*, he is said to have died on the sixth day before the Kalends of March. There it is also said that he was “buried on the left side by the altar of the Apostles” and that he enlarged his church with “many dependencies.”

Although the altar’s dedication has changed, his tomb can still be visited in the chapel of the Annunciation of blessed Mary, beneath a small stone laid in the pavement, where this brief inscription is found:

> Here lies Bartholomew, formerly abbot of this place.  
> He died in the year 1084.

He is not celebrated with any public cult; therefore it was sufficient to designate him by the title “blessed.”

We append here a miracle performed by him, which John of Dol, lord of Combourg in Brittany, committed to writing, as it was extracted from an old copy of the Major Monastery. Brandricus and Hugh, who are called archbishops in that account, were prelates of the church of Dol. For no one is unaware that the bishops of Dol claimed this title for themselves until the time of Innocent III, although the metropolitans of Tours protested. At last, under Innocent III, the cause of Dol failed, and the bishops of Dol were left only the cross and other insignia of archbishops.

11. “John, called of Dol, lord of Combourg, to all the faithful, greetings in the Lord. I have determined to declare for the knowledge of those to come what I heard and learned from the report of many people: namely, that Maino, son of Theonigete, gave to God and to blessed Martin of the Major Monastery, and to Abbot Bartholomew and the monks of that monastery residing at Combourg, the church of Saint Martin of Gugnen [or Qugnen] and the church of Saint Martin of Voel, with all their appurtenances, to be possessed in perpetuity.

“For at one time that venerable abbot had come down into Brittany to visit the houses he possessed in that region, and he came to Combourg for the sake of lodging. Then the aforementioned Maino came to him, asking him to go down to Gugnen to visit his sons Haimo and Gauterius, who were being held by a serious illness. He went down, placed the sign of the cross upon their foreheads, and immediately they fell asleep; after sleeping, they were restored to complete health.

“When he saw this, and heard that the aforementioned abbot had healed a leper’s mouth with a kiss and had changed water into wine, the aforementioned Maino and his father Theonus the elder gave him the churches named above, with the consent of their sons Haimo and Gauterius. Alanus, son of Floaudus, also granted to the same abbot and to the monks of Combourg whatever right he held in the church of Gugnen.

“The monks established the priest Gauterius there, presented him to Archbishop Brandricus, and in Gauterius’s time they received a third part of the tithe of Gugnen. I, John, heard these things from many people, and I saw what follows: namely, that Haimo, priest of Gugnen, resigned his office in the presence of Archbishop Hugh and acknowledged that the aforesaid church belonged to the jurisdiction of the monks. Haimo received the church from the hand of William the prior, and the prior William presented him to Archbishop Hugh; Hugh approved this and confirmed his approval with his seal.

“Let everyone also know that Alanus, son of Jordan, and Eudospina approved the donations of their predecessors concerning the church of Gugnen and renewed them in the presence of Archbishop Hugh, these men witnessing: William the prior; the monks Turpinus and Durandus; Master William of Soissons; Evano-Cato; Norman of Litre; his son Geoffrey; Philip of Boteniguel; Master Herveus; Gauterius Brasart; and many others.

“Moreover, in the presence of these witnesses, the aforesaid Alanus, through the hands of Archbishop Hugh, gave the church of Trunchet with all its appurtenances, with Gauterius, the master of that place, and all his brothers consenting.”

[Col. 0403]

## Letter of Blessed Bartholomew, Abbot of the Major Monastery, to Ernaldus, Bishop of Le Mans

*(Mabillon, Acts, volume IX, p. 387.)*

[Col. 0403A] To the lord and venerable E., by the grace of God bishop of the people of Le Mans, and to the entire illustrious flock of the most blessed confessor Julian, Brother B., humble abbot of the Major Monastery, with his brothers, sends faithful prayers.

We are greatly astonished, venerable lord bishop, at what your prudence intends by bringing a charge against us concerning the altar of Vivoin. From your goodness we had expected that, if a charge concerning that altar arose against us from elsewhere, we would have in you an unconquerable defender against all accusers.

For you know that your predecessor, Bishop Wilgrinus, ever to be remembered with devotion, gave us that altar to hold in perpetuity without relief, with the consent of all the leading men of your Church, indeed of the entire chapter of the most blessed Julian. Because of this donation, we—namely, the monks of Saint Martin—and you, the canons of Blessed Julian, are so bound and united in the charity of Christ that, having been admitted into the fellowship of all our good works, we should have you as eternal sharers in whatever good we might thereafter merit before God through prayers or almsgiving, with a pact established between us and you that we should do for your canons at the death of each one what you should do for our monks.

So that no one of our successors might ever attempt, through ignorance or on any pretext, to sever this unity of ours in the Lord, a document concerning this matter was carefully drawn up by you. So that it might possess inviolable firmness, it was strengthened and confirmed by the authority of Lord Bishop Wilgrinus himself and of all the leading men of your Church.

Since your prudence knows all these things well, venerable lord father, how has the reason of your mind and your ancient kindness fallen into so deep a sleep that your excellence does not fear to inflict so evident an injury upon your brothers? And if regard for a brother’s injury does not move you, do you consider it nothing or something insignificant that you should in any way violate and destroy what the Church of Le Mans, episcopal dignity, and canonical authority established by common counsel?

In this matter, how has the holy church of the most blessed Julian deserved so badly of you—the church that appointed you as its ruler and shepherd, which you ought to honor and exalt with all your strength, since it first freely honored and exalted you? What has it deserved that, when all the Churches of France and Aquitaine, indeed of all Gaul, possess this dignity—that no successor presume to violate what has once been confirmed in their chapters—you should not fear to strip the Church of Le Mans of the dignity it has possessed for so many centuries down to your time?

Why should the holy mother Church of Le Mans be inferior among all the Churches of Gaul, so that while all the others, great and small, possess the firm authority of their chapter, the mother Church of Le Mans should possess no authority?

If any secular person, however powerful, dared to do this, it would indeed have been fitting for the bishop, together with all his clergy, for the love of God and his Church, to seek death willingly rather than consent in any way to the dishonor of his Church.

But however these matters may stand, illustrious flock of the most blessed Julian, we earnestly admonish you not to permit yourselves to be stripped of your ancient dignity for any reason.

Finally, so that you may know our judgment concerning this matter, we have resolved never to bring to trial a matter so lawfully and so authoritatively confirmed.

Farewell.

## Appendix

[Col. 0403]

## Deeds Accomplished in the Major Monastery in the Eleventh Century
[Col. 0403C] **1.** Furthermore, as we return to our subject, let us set forth, with whatever literary skill we can, those things which divine munificence has deigned to accomplish among us and toward us, unworthy though we are, both for the praise of His name and for the edification of posterity. We think, not without reason, that the souls of the faithful are reported to seek the suffrages of the Major Monastery, in which such great benefits are performed, both for the living and for the dead, through prayers and almsgiving. For why should the fulfillment of vows not be obtained there, where that mighty and exalted priest Martin gives his patronage? He was the humble and steadfast imitator of the most humble Master, Jesus Christ, and, above all through the merits of humility, can obtain both the perpetual sanctification of that same place of his and absolution from sins for those who come there faithfully to pray.

Nor is it incongruous, if God revealed it, that the aforesaid solitary either saw or disclosed something concerning the zeal and effectiveness of the brothers of that monastery in the worship and frequent celebration of the sacraments, which we have related above. For, as we ourselves observed, it was the custom of that monastery that, on account of the abundance of priests, the uninterrupted celebration of Masses continued from the first light of dawn until the hour of dinner. This was performed with such dignity and reverence that it seemed more an angelic than a human service.

Therefore, we do not think that we should pass over their praiseworthy and exemplary custom, observed from ancient times, concerning deceased brothers. Whenever one of the brothers had recently died, his confessor was questioned publicly about the penance imposed upon him. When this had been heard, one might see all the brothers, moved by extraordinary compassion, taking up the burden of their brother one after another: one seized upon the psalms, another the Masses, another the fasts, and yet another the disciplines of scourging. Thus that apostolic saying was fulfilled in wondrous order: “Bear one another’s burdens” (Galatians 6:2). At last, the deceased, released from the imposed obligation of penance, passed, as we believe, free into rest, and the community obtained grace. Amen.

**2.** The abbot of this monastery also, named Bartholomew, frequently devoted himself to private prayers. Once, while he was praying, two brothers who had died during his tenure appeared visibly to him and said:

“Indeed, Father, you keep vigilant in prayer both for yourself and for the flock entrusted to you; but know also that correction must be applied to them. For among them there are some who are not sufficiently concerned for their deceased brothers—this man and that man”—and they named certain individuals. “Act, therefore, and, when you mention the dead in the presence of the whole community, exhort everyone, individually and collectively, not to neglect or defer rendering to their deceased brothers the dues established by the holy Fathers. For we tell you this in the word of the Lord: whoever, while he lives, does not pay his deceased brothers what he owes them, whatever is paid for him by others after his death will benefit not himself but those to whom, through his negligence, he remains indebted.

“As for those whom we have named explicitly, you will summon them privately and rebuke them more severely for their correction; thereafter instruct them by admonition and command alike. If they neglect this, let them know that a terrible judgment threatens them.”

After saying this, they disappeared. The abbot, however, diligently carried out what had been entrusted to him. The negligent became watchful thereafter as a warning, and the good were made better.

**3.** What one’s own faith can accomplish is demonstrated by the faith of another; this is also clearer than daylight in baptism and is shown by certain institutions of the saints. Among the other practices of the monks, we discovered something outstanding and full of faith: whenever one of them is at the point of death, all hasten to him, setting aside every other business. Neither eagerness to eat, nor the need for sleep, nor any occupation in God’s service, nor any administration of public usefulness—however great—can wholly recall or delay anyone from gathering, individually and collectively, to bring assistance.

Moreover, no one comes empty-handed or unarmed; all hurry to protect the dying man armed with the weapons of faith and with the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God. For whenever the sign of that final necessity has been heard, they all immediately begin the Creed of the Catholic faith on behalf of the dying man, bearing witness that he lived in this faith and departs from the body in this faith. In this way, the ancient enemy may not dare to assail him as he returns to his Creator, since he hears the testimony of faith resounding everywhere.

The Lord deigned to show by a clear sign how salutary this practice was in the monastery of the Major Monastery. For while a certain brother was at the point of death, some of the brothers, according to the solemn custom of that church, stood around the dying man’s bed, strengthening his departure with prayers and supplications. One of them had his eyes opened, and behold, he saw an angel of the Lord seated at the altar and awaiting the brother’s soul. He also saw the devil standing nearby, so that he might hinder the departing soul.

When the brother’s soul had left the body, it was seen in the form of a little child sitting above its own body and, as though trembling, fearing the presence of the evil one. Then suddenly the voice of the assembled community was heard, crying out for the brother and saying: “I believe in one God.” At their testimony the confounded enemy withdrew. Then the holy angel, at the voice of the cantor proclaiming the responsory, “Come to his aid, saints of God; meet him, angels of the Lord,” took up the brother’s soul and led it all the way to heaven, as the man to whom this had been divinely revealed had foreseen.

**4.** In the same monastery there was a religious man named Hildebrand, to whom, on account of the merit of his life, the abbot had entrusted the sacrament of confession.

[Note: [Col. 0405] Thus the copy reads; below, however, he is called Hildebertus once and again. In section 13 below, Hilidebrandus senior occurs again.]

One of the brothers, approaching death, disclosed the secret of his conscience to the aforesaid religious man, and then departed this life. But after not many days, at midnight, while the brothers were customarily resting in their beds, behold, that brother who had recently died stood above the bed of the wakeful Hildebert and began to call out in a loud voice, saying:

“O Father Hildebert, having confessed my sins to you as Christ’s vicar, I believed, according to the faith of the Church, that I was saved from them. But behold, the demons are exacting their penalties from me with terrible severity.”

And he replied: “You confessed to me as to Christ the Lord, and I shall answer for you to Christ the Lord on the day of judgment.”

At this profession of such great faith, the confounded demons withdrew. The deceased then gave thanks to his confessor and escaped liberated from the hands of his enemies. In this event God showed us both the malice of the enemy toward us and the unconquerable power of holy confession.

**5.** A certain secular priest abandoned the world and professed himself a monk in the monastery of the Major Monastery. After receiving the monastic sacraments, he was one day lying in a bed in the infirmary. He called to himself the brother entrusted with the care of such matters and said:

“Bring me the lord abbot, because I have recalled to mind certain matters from my former way of life which I ought to confess to him.”

The brother replied: “At midday, according to his solemn custom, the lord abbot is making up for the vigils of the night with sleep, and no one dares to wake him at this hour. When the signal for None has been sounded, I shall enter to him freely and bring him to you.”

The sick man answered: “Necessity has no law. But, lest I perhaps be burdensome to him, I will confess to you, in his place and stead, since I have been entrusted to you by him; for extreme necessity presses me.”

Without delay, the sick man, repentant of his fault, confessed it, devoutly embraced the satisfaction imposed upon him, and, according to the custom of the sacrament, was absolved from guilt.

When these things had been done and they were both sitting there, he said: “Now I have to fight with savage enemies. Therefore, do not go away anywhere; comfort me by your presence and devote yourself to prayer. For you will not see those with whom I shall fight; indeed, they have assumed a form quite suitable to their dreadful appearance, namely, that of ravens.”

He had spoken, and suddenly his entire face was changed. His eyes swelled with blood-filled veins and, rolling about, presented a terrible sight. His distorted mouth spewed forth foam stained with blood, while none of his limbs enjoyed any repose.

Meanwhile the brother who was present began to tremble—for who would not be terrified at such a sight? Overcome by fear alone, he fell to prayer. The agony of the combatant continued for as long as the attendant took to complete the seven penitential psalms and the litany.

At last the sick man returned to himself and said to the brother standing beside him: “Behold, brother, with God’s protection I have escaped the enemies. You, who have stood beside me as though laboring together with me in my struggle, now allow yourself a little rest. For during the coming night you must keep vigil with me, since I shall depart from you.”

The outcome followed his words, and that very night, as he had foretold, he was released from the body. O how great is God’s clemency! While keeping a man in the body, He allowed him both to fight against demons and to conquer them in battle, so that by the labor of the struggle he might cleanse away his past errors and make known to his soul the hour of its absolution.

**6.** At approximately the same time, a certain layman from the castle of Saint Martin, who had become a convert in the same monastery, was hastening toward death. He was lying in a room of the infirmary, so that neither others would suffer inconvenience from him nor he from others.

At midday, behold, demons resembling Ethiopians in visible form entered and surrounded his bed. One of them, more terrifying and taller than the rest, climbed onto his bed and stretched his entire body over him, so that he even pressed his mouth against the man’s mouth.

The sick man, entirely unable to move beneath the weight of the one lying upon him, did what he could: he spat from his mouth into the face of the demon pressing upon him. Unable to bear this, the devil sprang backward and, as though wishing to avenge a personal insult, turned to crafty devices.

Finally, before him he displayed immense quantities of silver and gold and costly garments, along with choruses of girls and bands of living horsemen, so that he seemed to see even those whom he recognized. Amid these things the devil, as though exulting, said to him:

“Behold, wretch, the glory that you abandoned before the time of misery, voluntarily subjecting yourself to misery. With these things you could still be flourishing, if you had not rejected our counsels.”

But he steadfastly replied in opposition:

“We too flourished, but that flower was transient. Now let me glory in nothing except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ!”

At these words the crowd of demons vanished like smoke. And behold, blessed Martin, crowned with episcopal mitres, stood before the sick man and said:

“Come, brother, be strong in the Lord, and do not let the snares of the wicked deceive you. For they have fallen from your side and from your right hand; they will approach you no more.”

He added: “Do you recognize me?”

When the man denied this, he said: “I am Martin, the protector and provider of this place, under whose protection you have taken refuge.”

At these words the man strained to leap from the bed. After the vision had departed, those serving him found him with one foot outside, as though he had wished to embrace the saint’s feet.

Then he summoned the steward of the infirmary and said: “Make haste to provide me with the mystery of holy anointing, for my lord Martin has so commanded me. After I have received it, know that I shall neither speak nor taste anything further. The one from whom I heard these things is entirely trustworthy.”

Without delay he was anointed according to the custom of the faithful, and, as he had foretold, for as long as he lived afterward he neither spoke nor tasted anything.

**7.** In the same monastery, a boy named John, still under ten years of age, was given to the religious life by his parents from the castle of Saint Martin. His maturity in childhood, together with the maturity of his understanding, was admirable.

No one saw him relaxed in laughter; no one saw him exceed the discipline of silence; no one saw him indulge in sleep with his peers during the vigils, as is customary. A certain simplicity, joined with gravity, shone in his face, and the modesty of innocence cherished his childish eyes, so that, by some divine gaze, he chastened the frivolity of those who looked upon him and inspired them with fear of God.

The Lord, hastening to lead forth his venerable old age—though not a long one—from the midst of iniquities, permitted the innocent boy to be afflicted with bodily troubles before the years of innocence had passed. As these increased day by day, the religious boy, knowing that his end was near, asked the abbot of the place, named Garterius, to come to him.

[Note: [Col. 0407] There was no abbot of the Major Monastery by this name. It should undoubtedly be read as Garnerius, who presided from 1137 until 1155.]

With a humble and contrite heart he confessed his sins, faithfully requested the monk’s blessing, and devoutly received it. He was then anointed according to apostolic tradition. After this he was strengthened by the life-giving sacraments.

Then, when the banner of the Lord’s cross was presented to him, nothing childish, beyond his years, appeared in him. With what devotion he embraced the cross! With what pious tears he watered it! With what sobs, as he gazed upon the image of the hanging Lord, did he become conformed to His passion!

When these things had been performed according to custom, he was placed in bed. He was carried, as was the custom of that church, into the church of Saint Benedict. When the attendants asked whether he required anything to be provided for his bodily needs, he uttered nothing mortal at all. Instead, in the voice of David, he invited the boys who had washed their robes in the blood of the Lamb to praise the Creator, saying:

“Praise the Lord, you boys; praise the name of the Lord. Let the name of the Lord be blessed, from this time forth and forevermore.”

Repeating these two verses of the psalm again and again, he breathed forth his final spirit, joined, as we believe, to the company of those whom he had invited to praise God at the hour of his death.

**8.** A certain priest from Saint-Spano, named Herveus, had set aside the dignity of his order and was devoted to both secular affairs and pleasures. His money increased enormously, invested at interest; and the more it increased, the more it possessed him.

Nevertheless, this alone nourished within him, however sluggishly, some hope of future salvation: he revered religious men, and especially the monks of the Major Monastery, with the greatest honor. Finally, while healthy and still flourishing in the world, he gave himself and his possessions to them. Yet even then he did not abandon the world, whose chains ensnared him.

At last, the greedy hand of death, which strikes with an equal foot the huts of the poor and the towers of kings (Horace, *Odes* 1.4.13), afflicted him severely by touching him with bodily illness. Feeling and fearing that the hour of death was near, he sent word for the aforesaid brothers of the Major Monastery to come to him in haste. First, after making a humble, lively, lamenting confession of his sins, full of bitter tears, as was fitting, he distributed part of his substance among his fellow brothers and the poor. He handed over all the rest of his movable and immovable possessions, as well as himself, to the aforesaid brothers.

Moreover, he summoned his debtors from every quarter and decreed that whatever was owed to him should henceforth be owed to the monks and repaid at the appointed times.

Among the others came a certain godfather and intimate friend of his, to whom, without anyone knowing except the two of them, he had lent sixty pounds. The man spoke deceitfully to him as he lay there:
