“My lord, I fear for myself at the disclosure of so large a sum. Although I owe it to your kindness, I would not wish anyone to know of our secret, just as no one knew of it before. Nevertheless, under the pledge of my faith and the oath I have sworn, I promise you that I shall repay it and shall do so on the day you assign me.”

The sick man replied: “There is no need for you to swear to me. Having experienced your faith, I am not incredulous regarding what you promise me. Let the matter be confirmed only by the holy kiss of peace and faith.”

The other gladly embraced this and, under the pledge of his faith and sacred order, promised that he would pay the debt to those persons and at the time the sick man should determine.

The priest therefore instructed the debtor to restore the money in his place to the brothers of the Major Monastery and granted him a period of one year for repayment.

When these things had been completed, he was clothed in the sacred garments of religion and carried to the monastery. There he received the monastic sacraments according to the rite of the religious life. His evil acts of his former life had been condemned by a good end, and he rested in peace.

A year had now passed, but the debtor neither paid the debt nor asked for an extension. Since no one had witnessed the matter, he thought that after the man’s death the entire profit had remained to him.

But the deceased, concerned that the monks might negligently fail to collect the debt owed to their community, took care lest they lose what he had ordered to be repaid to them.

One day, therefore, he appeared in monastic habit to the chaplain of the church over which he had presided, as the chaplain was traveling to Tours. The chaplain recognized him in broad daylight and, remembering that he was dead, was shaken with great terror at his first sight.

The deceased said to him: “Do not be afraid. Arm your forehead with the sign of the Lord’s cross, and confidently hear what I shall say. I have been permitted to appear not to harm you, but to benefit you and others.”

He added: “You know how disastrously I lived for a long time. I would truly have been lost, and without remedy, if the immense mercy of the Lord had not aided me through the prayers of the holy brothers of the Major Monastery.

“Nevertheless, I endured the pains due to me in purgatorial fire. If all the torments that can be endured in mortal life were compared with them, those torments would seem very light—indeed, they would scarcely deserve to be called torments.

“Now, placed in refreshment, I await an even greater blessedness before the universal judgment; but the dissimulation of that deceitful fellow priest of ours delays me. For he has passed beyond the deadline I set for him to repay my debt to my lords, the brothers of the Major Monastery.

“You shall now go to him on my behalf and announce that he must no longer delay doing what he promised me, under the pledge of faith and the kiss of peace, that he would repay. If he carelessly allows the day that I assign him through you to pass, let him know without doubt that his soul will suffer the vengeance of the Supreme Judge.”

After saying this, the deceased disappeared.

The chaplain, prompt and diligent, carried out the command. He went to the priest, recounted the vision concerning the deposit, and urged him to repay the debt. But the priest protested that the chaplain had been deceived by an insane fantasy and that he had never been indebted to any dead man in any respect.

Without delay, when the day set by the deceased through his intermediary had passed, the debtor was seized by immense pains and feared that he was about to breathe his last. Thus, although late, he confessed that no one could escape the judgment of the God who sees all things.

What more is there to say? He summoned the aforesaid monks through the intermediary, first repaid the debt, and then handed himself and all his possessions over to them, following at the end the pious footsteps of his creditor.

In this deed the Lord truly demonstrated, to those who understand rightly, both the gentleness of His mercy and the strictness of His judgment.

**9.** There were two brothers in the same monastery, men of honorable life and praiseworthy conduct. One of them was sent to England at the abbot’s command. Changing his sky but not his mind (Horace, *Epistles* 1.2.27), he also lived there religiously.

It happened that, when the days of his life had been completed, he fell asleep in the Lord. On the very night in which he had departed this life, he appeared to his brother, who was resting among the community of the brothers, and said:

“Come, brother. Behold, today the Lord has called me from this life. As I am about to reach the rest of the saints, I need provisions for the journey—namely, the benefit customarily owed to me by our brothers.”

The other, awakened from sleep and reflecting upon the vision, gave it little credence, treating it as a dream. Meanwhile the brothers rose for Matins. During the singing, as sometimes happens, he fell asleep briefly and saw the same vision again.

He therefore began to consider somewhat more anxiously what he had been warned of by the repeated vision. After Matins they went to sleep, and behold, the deceased met his brother in a vision, earnestly urging him—now warned for the third time—to announce his death to the abbot and the brothers and, out of fraternal love, to demand from them the benefit owed to him.

When morning came, the brother was concerned about his brother, especially since he had been warned by the threefold vision. He called aside one of the officials responsible for the order, explained the matter in sequence, and asked his advice.

The official replied: “As you know better, it is not our custom to pay anyone what is owed unless a written notice is brought by which the date of death may be established, especially in a matter involving sleep, whose deception is so often false and empty.”

Without delay, that same day a messenger arrived carrying a written notice in which the brother’s death and its date were recorded. The date, moreover, was that very day.

The office for the dead was celebrated according to custom, with everyone supposing that the anniversary of his death was already at hand. But his brother, more diligent on his behalf than the others, went outside, supposedly to speak more carefully with the bearer of the notice about his brother’s death.

The bearer, however, could not be found, nor could anyone be found who said that he had seen him.

When the brother of the deceased considered together the miracle of the threefold vision and the sudden arrival and disappearance of the messenger, he learned through truthful report that his brother had departed on that same day—not on an anniversary, but on the very day on which he had seen the vision and the messenger had arrived.

It became sufficiently clear how abundant the Lord’s mercy is: He permitted the deceased to demand what was owed to him, and He showed how concerned we ought to be lest we negligently fail to pay what is owed to our deceased brothers.

**10.** There was a brother in the same monastery named Urricus, who possessed skill in the management of temporal affairs. He served as steward in the cell called Tavent.

He was exceedingly harsh and inhuman. Sometimes he withheld part of the ration assigned to the brothers, and, when they complained, he was forced unwillingly to return what belonged to them. But from the dead he withdrew or altered for the worse the benefits that had been established for them all the more freely because one who defended their rights was found only rarely.

It happened, therefore, that two brothers who had departed this world appeared to him as he slept and rebuked him in harsh words for the injury inflicted upon the dead.

He remained hardened and, in the morning, treated the vision as a dream and as nothing. The deceased therefore came to him a second time in a vision, protested against the injury, and threatened him with impending punishments unless he restored the losses. But even then he remained unchanged.

On the third occasion they came and inflicted such severe blows upon him that he lay in bed for a year and a half, as though at the point of death. At last he scarcely recovered, but afterward he was never able to regain his former bodily vigor.

From this, reader, infer what awaits in the future those who defraud the dead of what is owed to them, since even in the present the Judge permits the dead themselves to exact bodily punishment.

**11.** A certain brother left the same monastery and returned to the world, denying that he was a monk. Although, as a deserter from that holy profession, he behaved shamefully before God, he nevertheless conducted himself honorably before men.

Finally, having been ordained a priest in the diocese of Cambrai, he was assigned to a church. There he served as priest for a long time and, so far as outward appearances went, legitimately governed the people entrusted to him by his office and rank.

Because he possessed considerable worldly prudence, he amassed a great deal of money. He also took a woman as his companion, as testimony to that final form of chastity permitted to secular persons, and fathered children by her.

The fourth watch had already passed, and he was still asleep, when behold, God, the fountain of mercy, wonderfully awakened him. First, by destroying his wife and children through death, He cut from his mind the comfort of his wife and the carnal sweetness of his children. Then, afflicting him with bodily illness, He cast him down upon a bed.

At last coming to himself, he began to reconsider with groaning of heart and sweat from his inmost being what he had been, from where he had come, what had happened, and what unavoidable sentence awaited him at the end.

He therefore said:

“Behold, my years resemble the feathers of a swan” (Ovid, *Tristia* 4.8.1). “And behold, deprived, as was fitting, of every comfort, I remain like a dry tree and a useless trunk, fit only to serve as fuel for eternal fire. Truly, and deservedly, I find myself left alone, since I abandoned the holy congregation’s fellowship, worthy of God and angelic.

“Woe to me, wretched man! When I could have returned to them, I was unwilling; but now, when I desire to do so too late, I am unable.”

Saying such things to himself, he wept copiously. At last, encouraged by hope through God’s mercy, he said:

“Certainly I shall do what I can even now. For I believe and trust that He who mercifully received the thief confessing himself upon the cross will not reject me either, even at the end, if I truly repent.”

He spoke, and put his words into action. Through messengers he summoned the brothers of the Major Monastery whom he could find nearby. He revealed to them his way before the Lord and, because he doubted that his weakened health would allow him to come there to make legitimate satisfaction, he humbly begged them to exercise upon him, according to the discipline of their order, the punishment of blows with rods. He also asked them mercifully to grant him again the sacred habit of religion which he had cast aside.

There was no reason to delay this plan, since both the penitent’s supplication and the outcome of the impending danger pressed for it.

After these things had been done, and after they had celebrated Matins there during the following night, the sick man gave himself over to sleep. Behold, he saw Martin, crowned with an episcopal mitre, standing at his right with a multitude of men clothed in white; he also saw Saint Benedict with a company of monks. On the other side stood the devil and his angels.

The devil began:

“You act unjustly by approaching this man, who, after deserting you, delivered himself over to me. Now he is about to receive the rewards of the long service by which he served me, yet you visit him as though he were righteous on account of one hour’s tears and a momentary repentance.”

Merciful Martin replied:

“You do not know, wretch, the inexhaustible riches of divine goodness. Through the Prophet He thunders words contrary to a hard life, saying: ‘At whatever hour the sinner groans, all his iniquities will be consigned to oblivion.’ And He who Himself subdued your tyranny by the trophy of His cross says: ‘I have not come to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance.’”

After saying this, he turned with Saint Benedict toward the man lying there and said:

“By the grace of the Savior and by the power conferred upon us by Him, we absolve you from all sins. Henceforth live more correctly, and do not sin any further.”

He added:

“Recover from this bed of illness. You will return to your mother, the Church, from which you departed. There, following the entire path of satisfaction according to what your teacher, whom you see present here, has decreed, take the greatest care not to conceal from the Father of the monastery anything that might trouble your conscience. For you will not live much longer.”

When he had said this, both sleep and the vision departed. Without delay he summoned the brothers and related in order what he had seen and heard. He indicated that he had been divinely healed, prepared a carriage in which he could travel with his possessions, and came to the Major Monastery.

He brought with him twenty-five thousand solidi and eight silver vessels, as well as the horses on which he had arrived, and assigned them to the Father of the monastery. Then he humbly begged for mercy and requested admission, allowing nothing to be relaxed for him that would prevent him from completing the entire discipline of satisfaction.

A few days passed, and behold, he was again cast down upon a bed. When, after the mystery of holy anointing had been completed, he adored the Lord’s cross, he saw the devil standing nearby.

Looking in the opposite direction, he anxiously searched with his eyes to see whether he might again behold the protectors whom he had seen before. The demons could not tear the saving banner of the cross from his hands until he declared that his blessed patrons had come to guard him.

Trusting in their presence, he turned to the devil and said:

“Behold, bloody beast, I have protectors against you. Martin the mighty bearer of the sign is present; Father Benedict is present also. I do not fear what man can do to me.”

After saying this, he breathed out his soul with a joyful face into the hands of the saints who had come. Thus it was divinely shown how great is the innocence of many before God, with whom the repentance of sinners has such power.

**12.** Count Fulk, on his way to Jerusalem, came to Tours on the feast of Pentecost, so that the archbishop might impose upon him, according to custom, the sign of the holy cross for so great a pilgrimage.

When this had been done, he stood at the windows of the hall overlooking the Major Monastery with two priests who were to accompany him. While he was discussing some secret matter with them and waiting for his fellow soldiers and table companions after the solemnities of the Mass, he looked out and saw the first [perhaps: pinnacle] of the Major Monastery so consumed by immense flames that it seemed to be burning to the ground.

Terrified by the sight, he said:

“Behold, the Major Monastery is being consumed by fire. Do you see,” he said, “what kind of flame now dominates above?”

The priests, seeing it, grieved and marveled together. Without delay, the count summoned some of his soldiers and ordered them to ride there at a swift pace and report to him what had happened.

They mounted their horses, hurried there, came to the Major Monastery, and inquired about the fire, but found no mention of it at all. The count waited for them.

When they returned and reported that they had neither seen nor found anything of the kind, the anxious count discussed the vision with his priests. One of them said:

“My lord, this vision was shown by God and is entirely worthy of the undertaking you have begun, of the present solemnity, and of the reverence due to the place in which it appeared to you. For, inspired by the Holy Spirit, you have today taken upon yourself the Lord’s sign; and on this day the Holy Spirit descended upon the apostles in fire. The place of the Major Monastery is worthy to be the place where He should show Himself descending, since so great a community, inflamed by that same Spirit, dwells there together.”

The illustrious man was pleased by this worthy interpretation of a worthy vision. Without delay, on the following day he came there, recounted the vision to the community, and asked to be made a brother and participant in its benefit. From then on he treated the place and its inhabitants with fitting reverence.

**13.** Because of the dryness of the air, sterility of the earth was threatening, and the disequilibrium of bodies was warning of pestilence for human affairs.

The community of the Major Monastery therefore made a procession for the impending calamity to the tomb of blessed Martin, going barefoot and carrying the relics of the saints. There they celebrated Mass. When they wished to return, however, they were entirely unable to lift or move the body of blessed Corentin, which they had brought with them.

Many attempted it, but their labor was fruitless and failed nevertheless. Then there was great sorrow and mourning among all, since they had come expecting to obtain benefits but were being punished by an irreparable loss.

At that moment an old man named Hildebrand struck the bier with the staff he carried in his right hand and said to the saint:

“Come, Breton, Breton. We certainly know the pride of the Britons; and behold, I suppose you are emulating the golden tombs of Martin and Bricius because yours is poor and wooden. Now, therefore, return with us without fear, and we shall clothe you in gold, as they are.”

After saying this, he turned to the bearers of the bier and said:

“Place your shoulders beneath the burden. In the name of the Lord, do not hesitate.”

When they carried out his command, they lifted the saint with the greatest ease. After an antiphon had been begun, they returned home, filled with joy after their sorrow.

14. A layman who had entered the religious life in that same monastery learned the psalms and, after living religiously in that monastery for fifty years, never wished to go out to the outer cells to stay there. He lay in the church arranging the lamps, sweeping the floors, wiping the walls, and diligently applying himself to whatever holy services he was able to perform. Every day he recited the Psalter in order; after Matins he never allowed himself the repose of a bed. But when excessive weariness compelled him, he yielded his frail body to necessity in the place of refuge, while remaining in the habit of the saints. 

The solemn feast of blessed Martin had arrived. When the solemnities of Matins had been completed, the other brothers returned to their beds for the sake of rest. But he, having fatigued himself with private prayers and bendings of the knees, withdrew to the aforementioned place of refuge. While he was briefly carried away by a light sleep, as commonly happens in the morning hours, behold, two figures in venerable attire, radiant with splendid faces, stood before the altar. One said to the other:

“Lord Martin the glorious will today display his presence to this blessed place out of reverence for this solemnity; and he commands that this brother also, who hears us and has shown no ordinary devotion to him, be led out of the body tomorrow. For this reason I speak these things deliberately, even while he is listening, so that at an hour of such great and imminent necessity he may be found prepared.”

When these words had been spoken, the vision disappeared and the sleep withdrew. Therefore he awaited the final hour, which was so near at hand, with anxious and fearful prayers. When morning came, the brother reported to the abbot what he had seen and heard. The abbot, however, treating the dream as insignificant, declared that dreams should not be trusted. Nevertheless, he ordered him, with permission granted, to be anointed. Having done this, and fortified also with the Lord’s mysteries, he remained healthy and unharmed with the others in the community. On the following night, around Lauds, his bodily strength suddenly began to fail; no longer able to stand, he was led in the arms of those carrying him to the infirmary.

When morning arrived, out of renewed good devotion he received the sacraments of the Lord’s body and blood. After drinking wine following the blood, he expired in the hands of those who bore him. Thus Martin took to himself, on his own feast, one devoted to him; thus Christ rewarded with subsequent glory the gift of preceding grace. Amen.

15. Let us also relate a certain miracle which, through the operation of divine mercy, we do not doubt occurred in our own times.

Two of the monks of the Monastery of Saint Martin the Great—Junianus, priest of Calumnensis, and Burgardus, provost of Litinensis—were traveling by boat from their obediences, carrying with them one hundred and forty shad, which they had purchased for the refreshment of the brothers, and were making their way to reach the Great Monastery. When they came to a very dangerous place, where, because of the weirs and mills—which are especially numerous there—anyone can scarcely make his journey safely without injury, the anxious monks, in order to avoid the danger, ordered their servants to remain in the boat and strive diligently to steer it.

The servants, however, took the boat-rope and went down onto the land, so that by pulling vigorously they might cross the shipwreck-threatening passage more quickly. But the cunning enemy, who never ceases to oppose all good things, disturbed their undertaking for a little while—not, however, to their loss or disgrace, but for the praise and glory of the name of our Lord Jesus Christ.

For when the servants, cleaving the waves under proper guidance, had labored to pass through that narrow gate, and the monks, proceeding along the bank, had pulled their boat forcefully with the rope stretched out, wondrous to say, the rope suddenly broke as though it had been cut. Perceiving this, the servants, and seeing death impending over them, escaped only with difficulty, clinging with their hands to the boards of the mills.

The boat immediately sank—not by filling with water, as usually happens, but, more dangerously, with its stern and prow turned downward toward the ground, it began to float upside down upon the waves. Meanwhile the monks cried out in a loud voice:

“O blessed Father, holy Martin, by your holy prayers and merits save the fish in that boat, which we were carrying for your sons and servants.”

After the little boat had floated for a long time, driven about by the waves of the river, the monks and servants, neither believing nor hoping that anything at all had remained in it, at last dragged it to land with great labor. When they had turned it over and raised the stern upward—the stern that had floated upside down for so long—they saw their fish motionless and safe, lying in order just as they had placed them. Not one of all those intended for the brothers of the Great Monastery had been endangered in the water.

Thirty fish, however, which they had placed separately in order to distribute them to fishermen and people of that sort, fell into the water and perished. The servants’ belongings were also submerged in the river, but the monks’ book—that is, the Breviary—remained as unharmed as the brothers’ fish.

When the monks and servants, and everyone who was present, saw this, they were filled with great joy and glorified God, who never abandons those who hope in him, who not only hears the voices of his faithful crying out to him, but also fulfills the desire and intention of their hearts, as the Prophet testifies in a certain passage:

“The Lord has heard the desire of the poor; your ear has heard the preparations of their hearts.”

16. Since Scripture says, “It is good to conceal the king’s secret, but it is honorable to reveal and confess the works of God,” we have recognized that it is useful to leave in writing for our posterity a certain vision which divine mercy deigned to reveal in our own times at the Great Monastery.

Once, a monk of the Great Monastery, a man of good reputation named Oddo, provost of Saint Gemma, perceived that he had been afflicted with a mortal illness at the place of his obedience. He ordered himself to be brought as quickly as possible to the Great Monastery. When he had been placed in the brothers’ infirmary and had been somewhat examined in his illness, at last he began to enter upon the way of all flesh.

When this became known to the prior, who, as the day was already growing late, had visited him in order to investigate the nature of his illness, he informed three brothers, after Compline had ended, that they should come to watch over him—as was the custom of that church once a man had become so close to death—and spend the whole night beside him in psalms and prayers.

The brothers therefore obeyed the prior’s signal without delay. They hurried to the infirmary and, sitting around the brother who lay at the point of death, persevered in psalms and prayers almost until midnight. When the hour was already approaching at which the brothers are customarily warned to rise for Matins, behold, one of the three brothers mentioned above, named Gergonius, with his eyes open and looking upward directly—not in a vision—saw a very beautiful bird, entirely white in the form of a dove, coming over the sick brother, who was close to death, through a ray of great radiance. It began to fly above his breast and, flying, to circle around him.

Before that bird flew down, the sick brother was suffering severe anxiety and was excessively tormented by the pangs of death. But when it arrived, it quickly made him peaceful and calm, and thereafter he uttered neither such great lamentations nor such grievous gasps. After it had circled him for some time and had in turn flown over his breast, the brother likewise surrendered his spirit to the Lord, and the bird ascended by the way through which it had descended.

Let no one regard this as incredible; rather, let us give right faith to the works of God and continually render due thanks to him, who always visits his own with loving consolation and grants and prepares heavenly joys for those who hope in him.

17. A venerable man, who was both provost and archdeacon of the church of Clermont, was accustomed to come every year for the feast of blessed Martin and at the same time to visit the monastery of the Great Monastery. When he saw that great religious fervor was flourishing there, he was inflamed with a devout desire for its manner of life.

On one occasion, therefore, when he was about to come, as usual, for Saint Martin’s feast, he had his treasures, silk garments, and a great quantity of other wealth brought with him. After devoutly attending the sacred offices throughout the entire night and day of the solemnity, he withdrew with his retinue to the lodging. While conversing after the meal, he said to his men:

“Tomorrow, while you rest from your labor, I alone shall go out for a little while and return for dinner. Therefore do not be anxious about me, but make preparations for us.”

When morning came, the nobleman put on the humbler clothing of one of his servants and came to the Great Monastery. Having found Abbot William [Note: He governed the monastery from 1104 until 1124, and was called William of Comborn.], he fell at his feet and earnestly requested that, for the love of Christ and blessed Martin, monastic life be granted to him. The pious abbot, regarding his humble and submissive petition with favor, kindly granted what he humbly requested.

From there he returned to his own men, who were all amazed at how or in what manner he had gone about in such clothing. Having resumed his garments and concealed his vow, he spent the whole day in gladness. Finally, on the following day, he saw his journey being prepared, as though he were about to return to his homeland. He secretly instructed the guides of his retinue that, as soon as they first came to the Great Monastery, they should turn aside there.

Thus, after prayer had first been celebrated, he asked to be led to the abbot. The abbot rose to greet him—for by the herald of fame he had already learned who he was—and joyfully received him with the kiss of peace. He also asked him, as custom and hospitality required, to ease the labor of his journey by resting there and not to disdain accepting the benefit of the house, for holy Martin both provides its expenses and grants the will to expend them.

Then the nobleman said:

“Lord, I neither disdain nor reject the benefit of blessed Martin and of you. You received me as a monk, and I have come today for that very purpose.”

The abbot marveled that he had not seen him there before. The nobleman replied:

“Do you not remember receiving yesterday a certain poor cleric, dressed in such and such a manner, as a monk?”

“I remember that,” said the abbot.

“I am he,” replied the nobleman. “Now, if it pleases you, receive me and what is mine. If any of those who are with me has been touched by the same desire for this way of life, I ask that he be received with me for God’s sake.”

The abbot rejoiced; the clerics were saddened. Nevertheless, two of them remained, while the others departed in grief.

Having become a monk, the more exalted he had been in the world, the humbler he showed himself. Not long afterward he was made sacristan, and companions of good life, suitably attentive to his charge, were assigned to him. But as he advanced more and more in God, he began to consider how he might serve all the brothers in such a way that no one would know.

At night, when the others gave themselves over to rest, he secretly drew water for everyone and filled the washbasin. After he had done this for a long time, the solemnity of All Saints arrived. When the others returned to their beds after Matins, he undertook his accustomed work. Having completed it as usual, he returned to the oratory and devoted himself to prayer.

And behold, from that part of the church where Saint Martin’s bed is located, he heard the sweetest voices of an immense multitude. Raising his head, he saw three persons adorned with episcopal mitres; the one in the middle appeared to surpass the others both in dignity and in countenance. Then he saw many abbots and countless throngs of monks, all joyful and jubilant in sweet melody.

Meanwhile that archbishop began the responsory: “R[esponsory], Grant to us”; and having spoken and repeated the R[esponsory], he completed the office. [Col. 0419A] The second was performed for the dead. The third was for the community of that place.

That archbishop began the antiphon: “Surround this city, O Lord.” And he added the R[esponsory]: “Let there be peace within your strength,” and the Collect:

“O God, who prepare a dwelling in heaven for those who renounce the world, enlarge the temporal habitation of this holy community with heavenly goods, so that they may be held together as one by the bond of brotherly charity; that, sober, they may keep the precepts of continence; that, simple and peaceful, they may acknowledge that the grace given to them was given freely; that their life may agree with their name, and their profession be perceived in their works. Through our Lord, etc.”

When these things had been completed, that blessed and glorious procession began to return by the way it had come. But he, looking more attentively and recognizing some whom he knew to have died, addressed them, asking who these persons were.

They replied that the one walking in the middle of the bishops was Martin, who surpassed the others in the eminence of his countenance just as in his merits; that Fulgentius and Corentinus walked beside him; that the abbots of that place followed, and then the monks, who enjoyed no small share of the fruits of their labor through Martin’s merits, and who proceeded in the order in which they had migrated to Christ.

They also declared that Abbot Odo [Note: He succeeded the William praised above and held office until 1137.], who was then in charge of the place, would be summoned to their fellowship in that same year. They further related that blessed Martin, with that most holy and ever exceedingly numerous company of his disciples, very often visited the monastery in procession.

After hearing these things, the venerable man hastened to awaken some of his companions—namely, Guarnerius, later abbot of that same place, and several others. Awakened from sleep, they heard the voices of the singers and were privileged to see some of the last members of the procession.

How blessed, and how pure, we judge to have been the conscience of the man who, while still living in the body, was granted to contemplate the glory of Martin and of the saints accompanying him!

## In the Year of Our Lord 1085. Bernard, Count of Besalú

### Letter of Bernard, Count of Besalú, to Bernard, Abbot of Marseille

He asks him to undertake the government of the monastery of Ripoll through his monks, in order to remove simony from it.

(D. Martène, *Amplissima Collectio*, I, 473.)

To the lord B., venerable abbot of the Marseillais, and to the entire holy congregation serving Christ under his care, Bernard, count of Besalú, [lacuna] and the attainment of the heavenly prize.

Since I do not doubt that whatever is rightly and devoutly done by me and by secular men such as myself, though wicked, in this age is obtained through the prayers of spiritual men, I therefore judge that it ought, by my decision, to be referred to those through whose intercession it is rightly believed to have been obtained, so that, through their thanksgiving and most provident care, what was begun by the unworthy may attain the state of rectitude.

Therefore let your pious concern know that I have cleansed myself from every contagion of heretical depravity, through the aid of the Mother of God and, as I believe, through your intercession and that of the other faithful, concerning the monastery of the Mother of God of Ripoll—which, from the time of Lord Bishop Oliba, had been badly possessed by Simoniacs and had fallen into disgraceful commerce.

With the assistance of Lord Guifred, archbishop, Berengarius, bishop of Girona, and William, bishop of Ausona, I expelled from that place and government the pseudo-abbot Miró, who, after the prohibition of the Apostolic See, had attempted to obtain its administration through simony, together with all his followers, without any possibility of restoration.

After he had been driven out, I sought how, and by what arrangement, I might thereafter guard that holy place against every heretical ambition. My magnates, and especially this archdeacon and his associates, suggested to me that I should not hesitate to subject it to your lordship and your institutions, if I wished it henceforth to remain free from the perverse machinations of heretics.

Because of my love for the Mother of God, and because the dignity of your venerable name, my lord abbot, has been poured into me, it did not seem difficult at all to assent immediately to their sound counsel and promptly send them to you, so that they might summon you by the messengers whom I used as counselors for this undertaking, and so that what they have testified with their tongues I might likewise affirm by my letter.

Therefore I wish you to know that, if your delay does not prevent it, I am prepared to place the monastery in question under your jurisdiction and to confirm it by my own hand to God and to Saint Victor in a document drawn up by you, so that it may never have another abbot except one whom you, Lord B., and your successors choose according to the considered judgment of the regular community of Marseille.

For the present, we ask only that Lord Girbertus, who has long been familiar with all the rights of the monastery, should, at your command, first take charge of it, lest the entire people become less religious than is fitting if they are not permitted to have the man whom they seek.

So that everything which I must do toward you and your place may be carried out quickly and more effectively than can be written here, come, my lord abbot, swiftly to me together with these messengers and some of your community, not without Lord Girbertus . . . and after whatever may be required for the stability of this undertaking has been requested and received. Finally, let the man whom we desire . . . be advanced by careful effort, so that what has been done by you may pass through the ages to your successors.

Since we have learned, through the advance report of fame, that you are opponents of vices and cultivators of virtues, we therefore desire, with God’s assent, that through you this noble monastery—which, out of reverence for all religion and learning, once deserved to be the head and model of all Spain—be restored to its former condition. Thus, when your diligence has restored to it the reverence it formerly possessed, may you receive from the Son of that Virgin an increased crown of glory.

But if, for love of God, you do not deign to undertake so worthy a matter, it will be necessary for us to seek elsewhere those with whom and through whom we may lay aside the poison of our bitterness. You know what we desire; pray that we may be able to accomplish it.

Therefore, I shall do everything, and more than what the count of Barcelona did for you concerning the monastery of Saint Mary of Crassa, while I hasten to secure the freedom of Marseille in this matter—except that I shall not permit you there to fear either the sword or the club.

[Note: The monastery of Blessed Mary of Crassa, formerly called Orbieu from the nearby river and also Novales from its pleasant valley, was founded in the diocese of Carcassonne by Abbot Nebridius, later archbishop of Narbonne. Charlemagne confirmed its foundation in the eleventh year of his reign, that is, 778.]

I have taken care to add this at the end so that, if he should refuse to accept it, whatever the Almighty should see being done there contrary to what ought to be done may from this point be attributed to your fault and not to mine; for he knows that I speak these things with a truthful heart.

May your holiness prosper in the Lord.

[Note: The monastery of Ripoll, in French Ripouille, was a distinguished Benedictine monastery in the diocese of Ausona, founded in 888 by Count Wifred of Barcelona.]

[Note: Oliba, or Oliva, was bishop of Ausona and abbot of Ripoll and also of Cuixà. He was the brother of Count Wifred of Cerdanya and died in 1047.]

### Charter of Bernard, Count of Besalú

He subjects the abbey of Ripoll to the monastery of Saint Victor of Marseille.

(At Martène, cited above, p. 475.)

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. I, Bernard, by the grace of God count of Besalú, am a donor to almighty God, to Saint Mary, to the holy martyr Victor of Marseille, and to Bernard, abbot of that monastery, and to all his successors, by this document of my donation.

I give them the monastery of Saint Mary of Ripoll, with all the property belonging and rightfully pertaining to it, on the condition that Bernard himself and his successors always choose and send abbots there who will perform the service of God in that monastery, maintain the Rule of Saint Benedict there, and cause it to be maintained; and that the abbots and the entire community of that monastery always be obedient in all things to the present abbot of Marseille and his successors.

Let this always be done for the service of God and for fidelity to me, Bernard, and my successors; and let the see of Saint Peter of Ausona and the orthodox bishops of that place have there what they ought justly to have.

If—and may it not happen—the abbot or abbots elected there, or their community, should not observe the Rule of Saint Benedict and should prove disobedient, the abbot of Marseille shall always have the right, whenever he wishes, to come there, admonish them so that they may be corrected, and convert them from evil to good.

But if they should rebel and refuse to believe his admonitions, the abbot of Marseille shall always have the power to expel the wicked and send good men in their place. For the love of God and divine charity, the count of Besalú and the bishop of Ausona shall be his helpers in doing this.

This shall remain firm and unalterable for as long as the monastery of Saint Victor continues to stand regularly and those dwelling there maintain the Rule of Saint Benedict. It shall not be lawful for me, the aforesaid Count Bernard, or for any of my successors to break, alter, or diminish this donation in any way.

All this has been done because that place, on account of its Simoniac abbots, remained almost without religion and without the Rule of Saint Benedict. Therefore, whoever has been a helper and supporter of this undertaking and has given assistance to those living there according to the Rule shall first receive a blessing from God and shall have a share and fellowship in all the prayers and good works performed in the aforesaid monastery, or in the monastery of Marseille, and in Tomer, Saint Paul’s, Saint Mary of Crassa, Saint Cucuphas of Vallès, and at the see of Ausona, or in all the cells of the monasteries mentioned above; moreover, they shall obtain eternal recompense.

Whoever is also opposed to this our institution and, at the devil’s instigation, attempts to break it on any pretext, shall incur the wrath of God and remain a companion of all sacrilegious persons and of those condemned in hell, unless he repents and comes to make satisfaction.

This was done on the fifth day before the Kalends of January, in the year 1070 from the Incarnation of Christ, the tenth year of King Philip.

Sign of Bernard, count, who ordered this document of donation to be written and confirmed it with his own hands at the customary sign in the chapter of Ripoll, before everyone.

+ William, by the grace of God bishop, confirmed this of the church of Ausona.

+ Andrew, abbot of Saint John, confirmed this.

+ Bernard, deacon and canon, confirmed this. Heribald, canon of the see of Ausona, confirmed this. William, principal notary, confirmed this.

Sign of Raymond, viscount of Cardona; sign of Udalard Bernard; sign of Peter Bernard; sign of Bernard Wifred of Porcella; sign of Pontius Blidgarius; sign of Arnold Arnold; sign of Peter Adalbert; sign of Udalard Gaufred; sign of William Bernard, archdeacon of Guardia; sign of Bernard Raymond, his brother; sign of Bernard Miró.

Bernard the monk, who wrote this document of donation.

[Note: The monastery of Saint Paul of Tomer, formerly a distinguished Benedictine house in the diocese of Narbonne, was erected into an episcopal see suffragan to the metropolitan church of Narbonne by John XXII, while the monks nevertheless continued there; only in 1615 were they given secular dress by Paul V.]

[Note: The monastery of Saint Cucuphas was built in the district of Vallès by Louis the Pious; after being destroyed by pagans, it was restored by King Lothair.]

## In the Year of Our Lord 1085. Saint Anastasius, Monk and Hermit

### The Life of Saint Anastasius, by Walter

(At Mabillon, *Acta Sanctorum Ordinis Sancti Benedicti*, sixth century, part II, p. 487, from a manuscript of the church of Saint Martin of Doydes.)

## Preliminary Observations

1. We here present a Saint Anastasius who has until now been unknown in the Benedictine calendars. Walter, previously unknown to us as an author but, as is clear from the composition of the Life itself, a serious man, wrote his Life, if I am not mistaken, not long after the blessed man’s death.

We owe this Life to the most illustrious churchman Antonius Petrus Bertier, bishop of Rieux, who most graciously shared with one of our own a manuscript containing it, obtained from the parish church of Saint Martin of Doydes. He immediately transcribed it and sent it to us, so that it might be inserted into the Acts of the saints of our order.

2. The author of the Life did not state the year in which the blessed man’s life ended, nor do ancient documents available elsewhere provide us with this information. We must therefore investigate whether anything in the circumstances of his life can shed light on this obscurity. Since these circumstances are tied to definite periods, they may help determine the sequence of his remaining actions.

We learn from the Life itself that blessed Anastasius withdrew to the monastery of Saint Michael, called “in Periculo Maris,” around the middle of the eleventh century, at the time when an abbot infected with the stain of simony—whose name the author withheld—was in charge of the monastery.

We conjecture that this occurred around the year 1058 or the following year, because during those two years no abbot of the monastery of Saint Michael is mentioned in its catalogues or ancient documents. Perhaps a man marked by simony was not deemed worthy of a place among the abbots of that house.

Indeed, nowhere do we read that the other abbots who presided over that monastery in this century were touched by the plague of simony. We know that Fulco, the author of *The Monastery of Neustria*, introduced a certain man as abbot of Saint Michael during these two years and says that he attended the coronation of King Philip in 1059. From this it is clear that the abbey was not vacant for two years.

But that author failed to notice that the Fulco, abbot of Saint Michael, who attended Philip’s inauguration, was not abbot of the monastery of Saint Michael of the Mount, but of Saint Michael in Théorascia, in the diocese of Laon. This is certain not only from the published catalogues of the abbots of Saint Michael in Théorascia, but also from the instrument of the coronation of King Philip itself, cited by Chesne in the historical works of France and by Marlot in the metropolitan history of Reims. There Fulco is expressly called abbot of Saint Michael of Laon.

Although we do not know by what accident, the word “Laudunensis” fell from the pen of Philippe Labbe in volume IX of the Councils.

3. We have discovered another chronological indication in the Life of blessed Anastasius, derived from his journey to Spain. The same author of the Life testifies that Anastasius undertook this journey at the command of Pope Gregory VII and at the direction of Hugh, abbot of Cluny.

We assign this journey to approximately the year 1074, shortly after the restoration of King Alfonso, when Gregory had already reached the second year of his pontificate.

For we do not think that Anastasius was one of those whom Saint Hugh later sent to Spain to restore monastic discipline there. Those men remained in Spain, occupied with newly constructing various monasteries or at least restoring old ones; many of them were also raised to episcopal rank.

Anastasius, however, had gone there solely to announce the Gospel of Christ to the Saracens. When he realized that he was laboring in vain, he returned to Gaul.

4. Since we learn from the author of the Life that, after returning from Spain, Anastasius spent seven years at Cluny and three more in solitude, we already have ten years after 1074. If we add one or two years that he may have spent traveling or preaching the word of God in Spain, we may conjecture that the blessed man departed to heaven around the year 1086. Until more certain evidence appears, we have thought it appropriate to retain that year.

5. As far as we know, no martyrology records the name of this holy man—not even the Benedictine one.

Nevertheless, he is venerated in the parish church of Saint Martin of Doydes (Doydes), or, as the author of the Life calls it, Devotensis, in the diocese of Rieux, where his entire sacred body was preserved until the sixteenth century. At that time it was scattered by the raging Calvinist heretics, except for several particles enclosed in a silver reliquary, which the faithful rescued from their fury and placed in a safe location.

For several years these relics have been visited by the illustrious bishop of Rieux mentioned above. Having examined and approved them by his authority, he has permitted them to be displayed for the veneration of the faithful.

Not far from that village there is a spring commonly called the Spring of Saint Anastasius, where it is remembered that the holy man once quenched his thirst. It is frequented by the neighboring peoples because they say that the burning fevers are calmed by drinking its water; they report that this has been established by the experience of many.

## [The Life of Saint Anastasius]

### The Prologue Begins

1. Walter sends every prosperity and the fulfillment of good devotion to Peter, subdeacon of the Church of Devotensis, and to his brother Bernard.

You compel me, by persistently urging your request, to commit to writing for the edification of posterity the Life of blessed Anastasius the confessor. I do not see that this can be undertaken by me without difficulty, nor does it suit my abilities, lest the life of a holy man should seem to be diminished rather than celebrated more fully through the inadequacy of the writer’s talent.

Nevertheless, lest I appear to oppose your request—which, although I am little suited to it, I ought in all things to obey—I shall undertake it safely under the protection of your command. For if I am anything or possess any ability, I ought to attribute it to the Lord.

Moreover, since I profess to be your friend, it is not fitting for me to omit any service by which I may in any way assist you, since, as a certain wise man says, “Friendship consists only in the devotion of asking and the diligent willingness to obey.”

To this is added pure devotion, which can compel me—even if all the things mentioned above were absent—to persist boldly in completing what you ask. For when you so earnestly entrust this task to me, you are providing for the edification of posterity; and when you wish the life of the holy confessor, the most glorious Anastasius, to be disclosed for the praise and honor of God, so that it may be an example to those who come after and a testimony to the holiness of that same man, you give me reason to proceed.

Therefore I ask and earnestly entreat you: if through carelessness I have investigated too little, if through the poverty of my talent I have omitted something, or if I have added something deserving removal, may the reader not hesitate to add what he sees deserves addition or to cut out what he judges, by the mark of a wayward pen, ought to be corrected.

Finally, the devotion of those making the request can excuse me; as I have often said already, it compelled me to dare what distrust of my talent had advised me not to attempt.

### The Life of the Glorious Anastasius Begins

2. Anastasius, the most glorious confessor of God, was born in Venice and, according to the dignity of this world, shone illustrious by his lineage, born of a father and mother who were not of the lowest rank.

Regenerated from the very cradle by the water of baptism, he was handed over by his parents from his earliest years to literary studies. In these he applied himself so diligently that he seemed thoroughly imbued with every aspect of both Greek and Latin letters.

He was therefore distinguished in intellect, learned in speech, adorned in character, and beloved by everyone, so that those who had borne such a son were called fortunate.

But because the man of God had read in the sacred books that the wisdom of this world is folly with God (1 Corinthians 1), and had heard Truth itself say in the Gospel, “Unless someone renounces all that he possesses, he cannot be my disciple” (Luke 14:33), he began, not without divine grace, to call these things to mind and turn them over within himself: he would suffer grave loss if, for the sake of earthly things, he lost heavenly ones.

After turning these thoughts over for a long time, he finally resolved that, in order to do penance for his offenses, he would commit himself to the monastic habit.

But since, once one’s hand has been put to the plough, it is shameful to look back and make a crooked and useless furrow, the holy man Anastasius wished first to mortify himself with fasts, vigils, and prayers, so that he might test whether, after taking up the monastic habit, he could persevere firmly in his chosen course and not draw back.

He therefore first deprived himself of wine, in which there is lust; he began to fast on Wednesdays and Fridays, though in such a way that he sometimes ate meat. He devoted himself for the most part to prayer and vigils.

### 3

But when in this way he had restrained his flesh for some time [Col. 0427C], and had already, so to speak, kept it on the path of a good purpose, he abandoned meat dishes. He then began to devote himself so intensely to vigils and prayers that he fasted from one Sunday to the next. When he had again subjected himself to this discipline for some time, he became so strengthened that he even seemed firm and sufficient for his purpose. He therefore resolved to make satisfaction and accomplish his purpose.

Having abandoned his parents, home, and relatives, and seeking a suitable place where he might assume the monastic habit, he came to the British Sea, to a place called Portus Herculis [Note: [Col. 0427D] Everyone knows the monastery of Mont-Saint-Michel, or Mount Tumba, most famous for the multitude of pilgrims.] which is also called, by another name, Mount Saint Michael in Peril of the Sea. There he found a large community of monks, religious in every respect, except that the abbot had entered by simony; and there he received the habit he desired. The man of God was entirely unaware of the abbot’s simony.

After a year had passed, it happened that, while he was sitting with a certain brother [Note: [Col. 0427D] This seems to have been Robert, a monk of Saint Michael’s, who, at Anastasius’s request—perhaps this Anastasius—composed a commentary on the Song of Songs. The prologue and beginnings of both books into which the work was divided are found in volume I of the *Analecta*, p. 125. Certainly, at this very time both men were living in the monastery of Saint Michael.], and after a conversation had taken place concerning the strengthening of the soul, a question concerning the life of the holy Fathers was raised among them, and they had discussed it for a long time and at length, the conversation eventually turned to the abbot. The man of God Anastasius learned that the abbot was a Simonist and had entered the abbacy through the immense sum of money he had paid. Greatly grieved, and declaring that he had been deceived by a diabolical fraud—for he had sought a place suitable for his purpose and had nearly fallen into the snare of the wicked enemy—he departed from there and entered a certain island at the very entrance of the aforesaid sea. There, in a certain basilica of Mary the Mother of God, he began to live alone, devoting himself to fasts, vigils, and prayers.

### 4

When his life of exceptional conduct had become distinguished there for some time and his reputation had spread far and wide, the venerable abbot Hugh, who at that time presided over the monastery of Cluny [Col. 0428B], went out with many brothers to visit the monasteries again, at the urging of brothers who were serving God in various and distant places. It therefore happened that he reached the British Sea. Having heard of the life and conduct of the man of God Anastasius, he sent two of the brothers to the island, to the aforesaid basilica, and instructed the man of God to come out to him for a conversation; for, having heard of his good conduct, he desired to see him.

When the latter heard of the arrival of the venerable abbot, he came out with great joy. The abbot received him honorably and carefully inquired about his life and conduct. When he had heard everything from him, including how he had left the place where he had received the habit because of simony, and had understood his vow, he rejoiced greatly over his good conduct and encouraged him in God’s service by every means available to him.

As the abbot repeatedly spoke for several days about the life and conduct of the Cluniac brothers, he admonished the man of God and earnestly entreated him to go with him to Cluny, where he could fulfill his vow and provide the other brothers with an example of good conduct. The man of God Anastasius consented to his request and set out on the journey with him.

When he came to Cluny, he enjoyed great affection and humble familiarity among all the brothers. He loved them all with one accord, and by the example of his life he directed them all in God’s service. For a long time he led a remarkable life, offering himself as an example of good conduct. When the other brothers went to the refectory at the appointed signal, the man of God remained at prayer; and when everyone else rested at night, he rose and prayed for almost the whole night on his knees. He lived content with bread and water, and even took this as though in an instant. Once a year he went out into deserted or precipitous places [Col. 0429A] to observe the Lenten fasts; and then he mortified himself beyond measure with prayers, fasts, vigils, and genuflections.

### 5

At this time, by the command of our holy father Pope Gregory VII and after three exhortations from his venerable abbot Hugh, he entered Spain to preach to the Saracens. There, in order to prove the certainty of the Christian faith and eradicate the hardness of the Saracens’ cruelty, he wished to pass through a blazing fire after the solemn celebration of Mass. But the Saracens would not agree to his condition—namely, that if he crossed from here to there unharmed, they would seek the grace of baptism.

When they refused in any way to turn back from the blindness and hardness of their hearts, he shook the dust from his feet against them as a testimony and returned to his monastery [Col. 0429B].

After his return, when nearly seven years had passed, it happened that the venerable abbot, at the urging of certain brothers—laymen and nobles—wished to go into Aquitaine. These men were renouncing the world and wished to enter the monastic habit. Thus it happened that he took the man of God Anastasius with him, for Anastasius was learned in all the divine Scriptures and powerful in exhorting and edifying the brothers.

When they had traveled through a large part of Aquitaine exhorting the brothers, they eventually came to the region of Toulouse, where they were to receive the count of the town of Appamia, together with his wife and sons, into the monastic way of life.

Meanwhile, the time was also approaching when the man of God Anastasius was accustomed to observe Lent in deserted or precipitous places [Col. 0429C]. Since he was therefore very anxious and reflected upon the matter day and night, he eventually chose the nearby Pyrenean Mountains as a suitable place for this purpose, where he could observe Lent and devote himself for a time to the eremitical life.

The abbot reluctantly gave his consent to his request, because he was the staff and, as it were, the pillar of the other brothers. Yet because he recognized Anastasius’s constancy in God’s service, he did not wish to delay his good vow. Compelled and sorrowful, he therefore granted what he asked.

When they were about to part from one another, the venerable abbot, weeping and falling upon his neck with tears and sobs, urged him to remember him and to intercede with God for him and for the other brothers. Finally, bidding him farewell, he returned to the monastery with the other brothers [Col. 0429D].

### 6

The man of God Anastasius, who desired nothing except to fulfill his vow, set out toward the mountains with great joy. As he approached them, and could already mark out each place without any obstacle intervening, he chose for his dwelling the highest mountain, called Abriscola, because in the region where it was situated it rose above the other mountains.

Leaving a certain brother whom he had brought with him at the foot of the mountain, in a church there, he climbed the mountain alone. He made a sufficiently narrow dwelling from branches, together with an altar on which he could offer the sacrifice.

Then, amid continual snow and cold, he served God, devoting himself intensely to fasts, vigils, and prayers. He required nothing for food except bread baked beneath the ashes and water, which he received only in measured quantities from the brother he had left below the mountain.

While he remained there, and his way of life became known throughout the surrounding region, many began to visit him, and many gathered around him to hear from him the word of life and to learn about the remarkable life he was leading. They also sustained him with temporal goods, from whom they themselves were refreshed by divine nourishment.

But the man of God accepted absolutely nothing from them for bodily use, for he did not seek to be enriched by the people [f. *divitari*, “to be enriched”]; he even refused to live from the Gospel. Whatever was offered, he distributed through the hands of certain brothers to the poor whom he knew to lead good lives and whom he considered suitable for receiving it.

### 7

Meanwhile, as he sought to please God alone [Col. 0430B] and burned with all the ardor of his mind for this purpose, that ancient enemy, skilled in doing harm and adversary of the human race, began to envy his good works and to seek day and night an opportunity to enter and harm him.

When he found absolutely nothing in his conduct that he could seize upon, and had no power over him, he contrived at least to drive him from his cell.

It happened that one day, after the man of God Anastasius had finished praying, he came out of his little cell and sat outside with two brothers who had come to him. The ancient enemy appeared and set fire to his cell and to the altar he had made for offering the sacrifice.

But the man of God looked up, saw the fire, and recognized the snares of the wicked enemy. He therefore rose and went as far as the cell, commanded the enemy to depart, and opposed the sign of the cross to the fire. At his command the enemy withdrew, and at the sign of the cross the fire was extinguished.

When this event was reported everywhere, the native inhabitants in particular began almost all to gather around him and commend themselves to his prayers. They also sought penance from him for their sins. For nearly the three years that he remained in the desert, so many people flocked to him that often all the surrounding mountains seemed to shine with candles, which those who came lit before his cell.

He often told those who came that he was unworthy of their visit, that he was a monk from whom they were seeking penance, and that he had no permission either to preach or to receive penitents [Col. 0430D]. But what did this accomplish, when they nevertheless came in very great numbers and stirred him to preach with their tears and prayers?

### 8

But since God wished to reward his labor and call him from the prison of the flesh, so that his crown might be greater, he willed that his temporal life should end in obedience.

It happened that the venerable man, the abbot of the aforesaid church of Cluny, burned with a desire to see his brother. To the extent that Anastasius’s presence benefited the other brothers and his life strengthened them, he recognized the same degree of loss in his absence. Therefore he sent him the following letter through certain brothers, by which he recalled him to the monastery of the other brothers:

“ To his most beloved son Anastasius, brother Hugh the sinner sends greetings and wishes for a blessed [Col. 0431A] resurrection and the glorious fellowship of the elect.

I am surprised, dearest son, that for so long I have heard nothing about you and have received no knowledge of your life. Therefore I instruct your affection that, if it seems good to you, you should come down to visit the brothers, so that, as I have said, your desirable presence may strengthen and encourage them [Note: [Col. 0431] Here several words are missing, which could not be read.]. Farewell, and pray for the brothers.”

When the man of God Anastasius received the letter of his blessed father, the abbot, he rejoiced greatly and gave thanks to God for deeming him worthy to recall him to his brothers.

### 9

Having therefore left the desert, he reached a place called *Ad Verum Corpus* of the blessed martyr Antoninus, which is otherwise called Fredelas. There, when the people asked him to transfer the body of the blessed martyr to a new place and he was preparing himself to fulfill their request, a sick man was brought before him who had long been afflicted by fevers.

After Anastasius sprinkled him with blessed water that he had consecrated and marked his forehead with the sign of the cross, the man became so completely healthy that it was as though he had never felt illness. Whoever he sprinkled with the same blessed water, regardless of the illness by which they were afflicted, he restored to health.

### 10

When the report of his departure was heard, people gathered from every direction. They grieved and mourned that they were being left by so great a Father, a consoler in tribulation and a protector in adversity. With tears and weeping they begged him not to abandon those whom he had been accustomed to cherish and whom he had never failed to refresh with the nourishment of the divine word [Col. 0431C].

But the man of God, whose reward for his labor was now at hand, so that his crown might increase through obedience, as we said above, wished to obey his father, the abbot, who was recalling him. Not even the feverish illness that severely afflicted him could turn him back from this.

After delivering an address of divine admonition and exhortation, he departed and reached a place called Devotas. There, as his fever grew stronger, he began to fall seriously ill, to such an extent that through this illness he was certain of the dissolution of his body.

When he was urged to rest for a while to relieve the pain and to bathe in order to cool himself, he denied himself both, adding that ever since he had learned the monastic way of life he had used no bath and had not even applied water to wash his feet or head [Col. 0431D].

Having therefore completed the course of his race, and about to receive the crown of righteousness in the company of the saints, he—the monk, hermit, and confessor—departed to the Lord on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of November.

His sacred body was honorably buried there in the basilica of Saint Martin. There, as a testimony to his holiness, God works many miracles very frequently at his tomb. But lest we seem tedious by recounting them one by one, let us try to explain a few in sequence, passing over many.

### 11

A certain virgin was held possessed by three demons, who tormented her so greatly that they had even made her mute. She was taken to many holy places so that she might recover her health. Finally, the demons gave the response that they would not leave the possessed body unless she were brought to the body of the aforesaid blessed confessor Anastasius.

Those who were taking her therefore said among themselves where they might find him, and sought the place where the saint’s body rested; for many still did not know that he had recently departed from the world.

When they heard that he had been buried at the basilica of Saint Martin at Devotas, they brought her there bound with ropes. As they approached the place, the demons cried out:

“Why are you burning us, Anastasius? Stop tormenting us, and we will leave; stop scourging us, and we will depart from the possessed body. We have been led through many bodies of saints, and we withdrew from none of them so scourged. You alone burn us; you alone torment us; you alone harm us.”

Dragging her with their hands, they thrust her into the church and stretched her out beside the tomb of the blessed confessor.

All who were present fell on their knees and prayed with tears that God might deign to show those standing there the power of his mercy and, as a testimony to the holiness of his confessor, might deign to free her [Col. 0432C].

They had scarcely completed their prayer when, behold, the demons came out of the girl. When she rose, she spoke normally and testified that she had been freed and was suffering no harm.

### 12

A woman who had remained blind for seven years was also brought there. After the nightly vigils had been completed, she stood before the tomb of the holy Confessor; while the Gospel was being read during the celebration itself, she recovered her sight.

A certain cleric who suffered from frenzy was likewise brought to the same place, bound with chains and ropes, so that he might recover his health. Whenever an attack of mental disturbance came upon him, if he could seize anyone, he would claw and bite him [Col. 0432D].

After he had spent three vigils before the tomb of the blessed confessor, he recovered his health and departed freed from all frenzy. Thereafter he suffered nothing of his former illness.

## APPENDIX TO THE LIFE OF SAINT ANASTASIUS

### On the Discovery of the Body of Saint Anastasius

### 13

It is known, manifest, and completely certain, according to the report of trustworthy nobles of the place of Saint Martin at Devotas [Col. 0432D], that the body of Saint Anastasius, whose location had been unknown and unrecognized, was revealed on the seventh day before the Kalends of July in the following manner.

There was a devout woman of that place who kept many vigils in the basilica of Saint Martin. A voice from heaven said to her: “Know that the body of Saint Anastasius is in the place where you pray, and that it lies there.” This was announced to her once, a second time, and a third time.

Therefore, confident in the revelation, she informed the priests, clerics, and elders of the place. They dug deeply into the place she indicated, with devotion and confidence, but found nothing [Col. 0434A].

Again, a voice from heaven told the same devout woman that they should dig deeper in the same place and would find the holy body. This was done, and they found the holy body.

There was a great solemnity at the aforesaid place on account of its discovery, and it is celebrated daily. People from the surrounding regions devoutly gather for the same solemnity, in honor and for the adornment of that confessor and monk, the holy master Anastasius, whose soul possesses paradise.

## Letter of Saint Anastasius the Monk to Abbot Gerald

### On the Truth of the Body and Blood of Christ the Lord

*(The work of Lanfranc, edited by Dom Luca D’Achery, p. 21, in the notes to the Life of Lanfranc.)*

[Col. 0433B]

To Lord Gerald, formerly an abbot and son, now, by God’s favor, a venerable Father, brother Anastasius, servant of the Lord, who is what he possesses.

You have ordered me, venerable Father, concerning the body and blood of the Lord, to disclose to your holiness whatever my smallness perceives—or rather, believes. May you accept this brief account according to my limited ability, while the purity of the faith remains unharmed.

I believe, rejecting every accursed doubt, that the most holy body of the Lord, which is consecrated daily on the altar through the ministry of the priest, is truly his flesh that suffered on the cross, and that his blood is truly the blood that flowed from his side, as Truth itself testifies: “My flesh,” he says, “is truly food, and my blood is truly drink. Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood remains in me, and I in him” (John 6:52; [Col. 0433C] Matthew 26:26; Mark 14:22).

When he offered bread to the disciples, he said: “This is my body, which will be handed over for you” (Luke 22:19). Therefore, trusting these and similar words of the Lord, just as I know that no other body was handed over for our salvation except his own, so I believe that no other flesh is eaten for the remission of sins than that which was born of the Virgin Mary and rose from the tomb. Nor do I doubt that I drink no blood other than that which flowed from his side.

But those who assert that after consecration it is materially bread, and only figuratively—not truly—the body of the Lord, are carnal-minded and err gravely against the faith, because they believe their bodily eyes more than the testimonies of truth [Col. 0433D].

That bread and flesh are called a sacrament or figure by such a consecration, however, I not only do not reject; rather, gathering this from the reason of faith, I embrace and approve it in a catholic manner.

For no one who thinks correctly doubts that it is orthodox to call him bread, since Truth itself says: “I am the living bread who came down from heaven. And the bread that I will give is my flesh for the life of the world” (John 6:51).

It is called a sacrament because, under the visible appearance of those things that are seen, the flesh is consecrated more secretly by divine power, so that inwardly, in truth, there is what is believed through the power of faith [Col. 0434B]. It is called a figure when something other than what is perceived by bodily sight and taste is understood.

For Christ, the Lamb of God, who is glorified at the right hand of the Father, who now dies no more and over whom death will no longer have dominion, is sacrificed in the mystery of so great an oblation in memory of his passion.

Therefore, after the consecration of so great a mystery, I believe that I receive the true Eucharist of the Lord’s body, while nevertheless in no way denying that it is present in figure or sacrament. Otherwise, if I believed that the Lamb of God were devoured by teeth without a sacrament or figure, I would incur a great crime, as Father Augustine says.

Indeed, I enjoy the truth more abundantly insofar as, with the Holy Spirit enlightening me, I perceive more fully that figure or sacrament is present [Col. 0434C].

These things, therefore, most blessed Father, which I have said, I would support most devoutly with the sayings of many holy Fathers, if, I confess, I did not fear making this letter too long. I shall insert only three testimonies of eminent teachers, so that I may satisfy you that I either believe most rightly, or have investigated these matters with diligent vigilance and keen inquiry and weighed them on the careful scales of understanding.

The most blessed Cyprian, speaking to the people in the work in which he discusses this savory joy, says: “Receive in the bread what hung upon the wood; and receive in the cup what flowed from the side.”

The distinguished teacher Augustine spoke these same words and expressed the same meaning in his sermons to the newly baptized [Col. 0434D].

Saint Ambrose, in the book he published on the Sacraments, says: “Because it is the very flesh of Christ in the sacrament, and the blood: the flesh that hung upon the cross, and the blood that flowed from the side, taken from the Virgin Mary—not another, but the very same.”

Behold, Father Gerald, you have the most truthful testimonies of the most truthful witnesses.

If you take pleasure in knowing how our other Fathers, sharing this same belief, agree with them, seek what blessed Hilary commends in the eighth book of *On the Trinity*; what the golden-mouthed Pope Gregory confirms in the fourth book of the *Dialogues*; what the most holy Cyril, with the hundred and fifty who were assembled at Ephesus, proclaims; what the great Pope Leo discusses in his sermon for the seventh month; what Jerome, the interpreter of divine law, declares in his exposition of Exodus; what the venerable Bede examines in his sermon; what Paschasius, a catholic man, clarifies concerning the same sacrament; what the aforesaid Father Augustine examines and discusses in *On the Words of the Lord*, in his exposition of John the Evangelist, sermon twenty-six, in *On the Feast of the Innocents*, in his letter to Bishop Boniface, in book four of *On Christian Doctrine*, and in the title of Psalm 33 [Col. 0436A]—and, by discussing, examines.

If you seek diligently, you will undoubtedly find, as I have said, that all agree and in no way disagree. Indeed, because they are intoxicated by the abundance of the Lord’s house, it is no wonder that they glory in belching forth the same holy and pure things from their honeyed mouths.

As for what I have said, Father, at your command and according to my very limited ability, with a heart full of confidence, I humbly ask that you not be surprised if you do not find me weighing the loquacious arguments of the Aristotelians or Chrysippeans, or drawing a little stream from the river of Ciceronian eloquence. But remember that we simply pluck fruits in the garden of the divine page, whose roots are gloriously fixed in heaven.

Farewell.

## In the Year of Our Lord 1085: Saint Anselm, Bishop of Lucca

### Historical and Literary Notice

*(Oudin, *Commentary on Ecclesiastical Writers*, II, 710.)*

[Col. 0435B]

Saint Anselm, bishop of Lucca, was a Mantuan by birth. William Cave speaks of him very briefly in his *History of Ecclesiastical Writers*, under the year 1071, p. 617.

He was made bishop of Lucca in Tuscany by Pope Alexander II in the year 1073 and was sent to King Henry to obtain confirmation. From him he received investiture by ring and pastoral staff. Soon afterward, moved by repentance for what he had done, he laid down the staff and, having renounced the episcopate, withdrew to the monastery of Cluny. He remained there until Gregory VII recalled him to govern the Church; in the year 1073 he resumed the episcopal office.

In 1077 Gregory sent him as legate to the Milanese, together with Gerald, bishop of Ostia, in order to unite them with the Roman Church. In 1084 the same Gregory, whose cause he had always defended with the utmost zeal against the Emperor Henry [Col. 0435C], appointed him to act as legate throughout Italy, so that he might receive into the bosom of the Church all who had defected from the emperor.

Thus Cave in the place cited.

He was a man distinguished for holiness and learning, clearly the greatest supporter of Pope Gregory VII. Bellarmine and Labbeus discuss him in their book *On Ecclesiastical Writers*. To these I add that in many manuscripts there is attributed to him a distinguished *Collection of Ecclesiastical Canons*, which is preserved in manuscript in the library of Saint-Germain in Paris, codices 765 and 766, as well as in the Royal Library of France and in the Barberini Library at Rome, as Stephen Baluzius reports in his little work *On the Emendation of Gratian*, published in Paris in octavo in 1672 by François Muguet.

Read this both in the preface to the reader, no. 19, and in the notes on p. 641 [Col. 0436B].

Dom S. Luca D’Acherius had promised an edition of this *Collection* in his *Spicilegium*, but did not produce one, perhaps thinking that it did not belong to Anselm of Lucca.

For the reasons given by Baluzius, this work formerly seemed to me to be by Hildebert, bishop of Le Mans, in whose period it fits very well; he is known to have attempted something similar, and may have added to the end of his work certain decrees of Innocent II, which are found at the end of this *Collection* in some manuscripts.
