But after considering the evidence more carefully, I later judged this *Collection* to be genuinely worthy of and properly attributable to Anselm, bishop of Lucca: first, because the work suited Anselm, the foremost defender of Gregory VII; second, because many men in Italy at that time were engaged in compiling collections of this sort, such as Deusdedit and Gregory the priest; and finally, because it is found in manuscripts dating close to Anselm’s time.

Baluzius testifies to this in his preface to the emendation of Gratian, or to Antonio Augustinus’s discussion *On the Emendation of Gratian*, no. 19:

“I recently obtained another codex, and a very good and very ancient one, through the kindness of the excellent and most learned Dom Luca D’Acherius, from the library of the monastery of Saint-Germain in Paris. It contains no title at all, however, nor the author’s name. This book surpasses those seen by Antonio Augustinus in that it approaches the age of Anselm, and [Col. 0437A] contains no decrees of Roman pontiffs who held the apostolic see after the year 1086.

“There is also another work of this sort in manuscript in the Royal Library. Its codex is not particularly old, having been written only in the preceding century, although it is clearly copied from an older one. At the front are placed certain matters concerning the manner of celebrating a council; afterward, in place of a title, follows this: ‘Here begins the table of contents of the books which blessed Anselm, bishop of Lucca, composed in this volume as separate books from cases of equal kind.’

“Shortly below it is written: ‘Here begins the authentic and concise Collection of the rules and judgments of the holy Fathers and authoritative councils, made in the time of Gregory, the most holy pope, by blessed Anselm, bishop of Lucca, his diligent imitator and disciple, who completed this work eagerly at his command and instruction’ [Col. 0437B].

“Finally, in an old codex of this *Collection*, a copy of which was sent from the Barberini Library, D’Acherius communicated to Baluzius the following words written in the title, which assign the book to Anselm, bishop of Lucca:

“‘In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, here begins happily the series of this book, which Saint Anselm in Italy, who was pontiff of the Church of Lucca, a prudent and catholic man, fervent in the faith of Christ, gathered from the entire body of the canons and holy Fathers.’

“Stephen Baluzius thinks that the title is misleading and that this book has certainly been heavily interpolated, as Antonio Augustinus correctly noted, because it contains many decrees of Urban II and of later pontiffs, during whose time Anselm had ceased to live.

“Indeed, there are many things that seem to disqualify this *Collection* from belonging to Anselm, bishop of Lucca. First is the authority of the ancient writer of Anselm’s Life, edited by Sebastian Tengnagel. When reviewing the works of his master and lord, this writer makes no mention of this *Collection*. It seems that he would not have omitted so distinguished a work if it had then been known to have been composed by Anselm.

“Next comes Sigebert of Gembloux, a monk and writer of this period. When he lists in his *Chronicle* and in his book *On Ecclesiastical Writers* the books composed by Anselm, he does not say a word about this *Collection*.

“Finally, Trithemius, who had seen so many books, did not see this *Collection of Canons and Decrees* attributed to Anselm, bishop of Lucca, although he maintains complete silence concerning it.

“Antonio Augustinus had not taken account of these considerations, yet he seems to have leaned in this direction, judging that the *Collection* was not Anselm’s. Accordingly, he conjectured that it belonged to Hildebert of Le Mans, who is known to have attempted something similar.”

Thus Baluzius in the preface to Antonio Augustinus’s *On the Emendation of Gratian*, no. 19.

But these arguments are entirely negative and can prove nothing, especially since, on the contrary, several manuscripts exist in Italy and France in which this *Collection of Canons* is expressly attributed to Anselm, bishop of Lucca.

For, as those who corrected the *Corpus of Canon Law* attest—the work printed in Rome in the buildings of the Roman People by order of Gregory XIII, in three folio volumes in 1582—among the manuscripts they used for this emendation and correction are two manuscript codices of the *Collection of Canons of Anselm, Bishop of Lucca*. One is in the Vatican Library; the other belonged to a private and learned man, Jerome Parisetti, and we believe it later came to the Barberini Library.

If some canons in certain manuscripts of this *Collection* are found to be much later than Anselm, these are interpolated defects, not valid arguments against Anselm—especially since no canons later than Anselm are found in the oldest codices of Saint-Germain in Paris.

Hildebert, bishop of Le Mans, is believed to have attempted something similar because among his letters there is found a certain preface to a collection of canons from councils and holy Fathers, which some have thought belonged to him. But it has no connection with Hildebert. It is the preface of Ivo, bishop of Chartres, to his *Decretum*, which rashly or accidentally entered Hildebert’s letters in the old editions.

Printed under Anselm’s name are two books against Guibert the antipope and his followers, in defense of Pope Gregory VII, as well as certain *Collections*, or *Sentences*, gathered from various authors, by which it is demonstrated that the resources and possessions of the Church are not under the power of the king or emperor. Both works are found in Henry Canisius’s *Ancient Readings*, volume VI, pp. 202 and 235, and in the Lyon edition of the *Library of the Fathers* of 1677, volume XVIII, p. 602.

But learned men competent to judge these matters consider that neither little work is anything other than an assortment of excerpts from Anselm’s *Collection of Canons*, obtained elsewhere by Canisius.

For it is certain that this *Collectaneum*, or *Collection of Canons*, was made by Anselm in support of Pope Gregory VII against the antipope Guibert, and that the pope’s judgments against those who seize the goods and possessions of the Church were gathered from earlier authors.

Those who possess copies of Anselm’s *Collection of Canons*, bishop of Lucca, can easily test whether this conjecture is true by comparing them with these printed works [Col. 0438D].

In both works Anselm cited the forged letters of Isidore Mercator. In book I, against Guibert the antipope, he calls as witnesses pseudo-Clement, letter 3; pseudo-Pius, letter 1; and pseudo-Fabian, letter 3. In book II, pseudo-Callistus, letter 1; pseudo-Stephen, letter 2; and pseudo-Marcellinus, letter 2.

He also inserted into the *Collection of Canons* almost all the letters of pseudo-Isidore, divided into sections.

These are the words of the most learned Blondel in the *Prolegomena to Pseudo-Isidore*, chapter 18, p. 98.

Baronius, under the year 1086, the year of Anselm’s death, reports other writings of his from that anonymous author of his Life [Col. 0439A], who was his penitentiary—and, indeed, in the author’s own words:

“From many and diverse volumes of the most holy Fathers he compiled one considerable body of canonical judgments.

“He also compiled one *Apology* from various volumes of the holy Fathers, by which he defended, with canonical arguments, the judgment of the Lord Pope and all his actions and commands.

“He wrote many little books with his own hands. On the Lamentations of Jeremiah he composed a most sweet exposition.

“At the request of the most blessed Matilda he also expounded the Psalter with great clarity—briefly, indeed, but usefully—up to the passage, ‘We have blessed you in the name of the Lord.’ There he brought his exposition to an end.”

In the latest edition of the great *Bibliotheca Veterum Patrum*, published at Lyon in 1677 by the Anissons, four brief works were printed under the name of Saint Anselm, bishop of Lucca. They had first been edited around 1654 by Luca Wading, historiographer and librarian of the Order of Friars Minor, and dedicated to Marcantonio Franciotti, cardinal of the Holy Roman Church and bishop of Lucca. Lucas Wading himself discusses them in *Writers of the Order of Friars Minor*, p. 240.

They are these: *Expositions on the Lord’s Prayer*, on the *Angelic Salutation*, “Hail Mary,” and on the antiphon *Salve Regina*, printed in volume XXVII, or the Supplement, of this *Bibliotheca*, pp. 436ff., together with the metrical *Meditations on the deeds of Our Lord Jesus Christ*, which begin: “Now leave, O soul, the bed of sleep,” etc.

The first little work, on the Lord’s Prayer, begins: “Our Father, who art in heaven, O boundless clemency! O ineffable goodness,” etc. The second, on the Angelic Salutation, begins: “Hail Mary, full of grace, the Lord is with you: To you, Lord God, I give thanks,” etc. The third, a meditation on the antiphon *SALVE REGINA*, begins: “In order to salute blessed Mary the Virgin, you must first consider her greatness,” etc. The fourth, *On the Deeds of Our Lord Jesus Christ*, is as described above, etc.

Regarding this fourth work, *On the Metrical Deeds of Our Lord Jesus Christ*, Arnoldus Wion speaks of it in the Benedictine *Martyrology* under 18 March, where he attributes it to Anselm, bishop of Lucca. Lucas Wading, however, who printed it in the Anissonian Lyon edition of the *Bibliotheca Sanctorum Patrum*, volume XXVII, p. 444, notes that it is so defective that it does not deserve to bear the name of Saint Anselm, bishop of Lucca.

I know this much for certain: whether all these verses are attributed to Anselm of Lucca, to Anselm, archbishop of Canterbury, or to Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux—as many other works have likewise been mixed into their writings—they are works of the thirteenth century, or at the latest of the declining twelfth century. Moreover, as the compiler of this latest edition of the *Bibliotheca Veterum Patrum* adds, this work contains much that is unworthy of a serious man such as Anselm, bishop of Lucca, was.

Although Arnoldus Wion inserted this poem into his *Martyrology*, it is not thereby made more distinguished, since pigs smell one way and dogs another; nor is everything found in a manuscript necessarily approved by an earlier age.

As for the other three little works mentioned above, Antonius Possevinus records them from a Mantuan manuscript in the *Apparatus sacer*, under “Anselm of Mantua,” volume I, p. 86. Lucas Wading was the first to attribute them to Saint Anselm, bishop of Lucca, in the cited edition. Yet they had previously been attributed to Saint Bonaventure, Doctor of the Church, at the end of the work entitled *Stimulus amoris*, part III, chapters 16ff., pp. 235ff., in the Paris edition of 1647 in folio, printed by Nicolaus Wivenais on the Rue de la Cithare. They do not appear, however, in the Venetian edition of 1611, printed by the heirs of Hieronymus Scotus, in the treatise of Saint Bonaventure called *Stimulus amoris*.

Anyone, even a one-eyed man, who has glanced through the Bonaventurian *Stimulus amoris* will find that these three little works are mere additions appended by some unlearned Franciscan to that work, with which they have no connection and no harmony. Any prudent person will therefore admit that they are merely a scrap attached to it.

These works are so far from being capable of bringing any honor or reputation to Anselm or Bonaventure that, on the contrary, they are wholly unworthy of being attributed to such great and serious—so they are held to be—Doctors of the Church. They are the productions of some anonymous childish, ridiculous, and deranged writer, so boorish—indeed so indecent—in his expressions that I am amazed that Lucas Wading, otherwise an educated and prudent man, dared to attribute them to Anselm, bishop of Lucca.

Works bearing such titles do nothing except expose grave ecclesiastical writers to contempt and ridicule, and orthodox and sound doctrine to uncertainty, through the most insolent obscenities of language and jesting about the mysteries of Scripture.

Let us now see from the words of the works themselves how absurd, imprudent, and even insane this anonymous writer was in his expressions.

In the *Exposition on the Lord’s Prayer*, near the beginning:

“What more have I to do with earthly honors, since I am a son of God? It would be a greater disgrace for me to desire any earthly honor whatever than for an emperor’s son to desire the office of cleaning latrines. What more have I to do with earthly riches, since I am heir of an eternal kingdom? It would be more disgraceful for me to care about earthly riches, however great, than for an emperor’s firstborn to care about horse manure.”

What could be more tasteless than these comparisons? There is no doubt that the writer who repeatedly dragged into the discussion the unfamiliar comparison of a latrine and horse manure smelled of the latrine himself. Then, a little later:

“O exultation, O wonder, O marrow-deep melody, because you are my Father!”

What could be sillier than this expression, “marrow-deep melody”? What is this word “marrow-deep”—how Latin it is! How excellently the words “O marrow-deep melody” are joined together! As if melody were either in the marrow or proceeded from the marrow of the bones! Did the holy Fathers, grave in judgment, pure in expression, and sound in faith, speak in this way?

Again, somewhat later:

“Wonderful condescension, most worthy dwelling of Christ in us! I, the foulest and most abominable sewer of sins, am able, through the boundless clemency of my God, to be his tabernacle.”

Here again the anonymous writer returns to manure and the latrine, which he had scarcely laid aside long enough for me truly to call this anonymous writer a dung-man, since he so often recalls manure and latrines. Countless such low, ridiculous, rustic, and indecent expressions are available; they show that this man possessed very little talent and was barbarous in intellect and language.

Read these three little works—the *Exposition on the Lord’s Prayer*, the *Angelic Salutation*, and the antiphon *SALVE REGINA*. They are entitled *Contemplations* and were printed in 1521 at Paris in quarto under the name of Master Martin de Magistris, doctor of theology, by the press of Jodocus Badius Ascensius, of whom we shall speak later under the year 1460.

Let us now consider the *Exposition on the Angelic Salutation*, or *Meditation on the Ave Maria*, which is no less inferior to these absurdities. At the beginning it says:

“You who preserve and govern all things, and who have deigned to enlighten me, the foulest filth and detestable disgrace, full of abomination and unworthy of all life—indeed, of existence itself—so that I know that you have a mother; and you have granted to me, most unworthy as I am, that I may and dare to salute her.”

This manner of speaking suggests a man carried away, but one belonging to the fourteenth century, when such expressions, at once ecstatic and rustic, were admired and used. The ancient Fathers of the Church certainly possessed profound humility, but they testified to it in their writings with much more prudent words and more solid expression.

When this anonymous writer calls himself “the foulest filth and detestable disgrace, full of abomination,” he shows that he has not yet forgotten the latrine and horse manure about which he spoke in the *Exposition of the Lord’s Prayer*. When he calls himself unworthy of all life, indeed of existence, he shows that he is a writer of the later period, when these expressions were employed affectedly in the scholastic schools as though they signified the greatest mysteries.

Toward the middle of this little work:

“Bear with me, Lady, because I am setting forth the Angelic Salutation, though I do not live angelically, but rather diabolically. I am terrible, yet I presume to salute you.”

I shudder, I confess, at Lucas Wading, who honored so insipid an anonymous writer with the name of Saint Anselm, bishop of Lucca. Who among the Fathers, up to and including the twelfth century, ever said in his writings—even if he was most humble—that he lived not angelically but rather diabolically?

Later he says:

“Therefore, Hail, O chain-like Hail, which binds the heart to the Virgin and separates it from earthly things; which binds the wretched to the most merciful, the servant to the Lady, the son to the mother, with the firmest bond. O lovable Hail! Let him who wishes to be chained by love come forward to salute; and when he has saluted from the heart, let him be bound more and more strongly. The more strongly he is bound, the more willingly will he salute.”

Who among the Fathers of the first twelve centuries ever heard such a foolish exclamation as “O chain-bearing Hail! Let him who wishes to be chained by love come forward to salute”? What sort of adjective is “chain-bearing”? What sort of expression is “to be chained by love”? Unless I am mistaken, these words belong to the age either of Ruusbroec or of Gerson, in which a person was considered more devout and even more learned in proportion as he spoke more barbarously and foolishly.

The third little work, the *Meditation on the Salve Regina*, was not merely first published by Lucas Wading but was published again. For this meditation is found in virtually all editions of the works of Saint Bernard from 1556 to 1640. At last, however, it seemed so absurd, unlearned, and foolish that in the latest editions of those same works it was expelled from the Bernardine corpus by Johann Merlane Horst, a German, and Jean Mabillon, a Frenchman, both learned and critical scholars.

By what right, then, did a meditation judged unworthy of Bernard pass into the name and legal possession of Anselm, bishop of Lucca? If it was unworthy of Bernard, it was likewise unworthy of Anselm, both of Anselm bishop of Lucca, to whom Lucas Wading attributed it, and of Anselm, archbishop of Canterbury, to whom others assign it.

“O Lady,” it says, “who snatch hearts away by sweetness, have you not, lady, snatched away my heart? And where, I ask, have you placed it, so that I may be able to find it? Have you perhaps placed it in your bosom so that I may not find it? Have you perhaps placed it between your breasts? Perhaps you put my heart there so that what had grown cold toward you might be warmed! O snatcher of hearts, when will you return my heart to me? Why do you thus snatch away the hearts of the simple? Why do you do violence to your friends? Do you perhaps always wish to keep it?”

Even this single question proves the anonymous writer to have been a buffoon and a fool, whom indiscriminate zeal drives toward silly and indecent questions, if the words are taken literally as they stand. What a startling ecstasy! “O snatcher of hearts, when will you return my heart to me?” What madness in the writer: “Have you perhaps placed it between your breasts?” These words reek of some ecstatic eccentric whom God intended this anonymous writer to be.

I have spoken somewhat sharply against Wading, who too carelessly attributed such little works to Anselm, bishop of Lucca. Certainly they detract from the honor of many holy Fathers of the Church, whom noble talent and serious judgment have made venerable to us, when absurd and foolish works are wrongly assigned to them through indiscriminate zeal.

The writings of the ancients must be weighed not by their bulk but by their excellence, reason, judgment joined with piety, and seriousness. I have treated this matter at somewhat greater length than is our custom in order to defend the honor of Anselm of Mantua, later bishop of Lucca, and of Bonaventure, cardinal of the Holy Roman Church and Doctor, whom I judged to have been attacked through the substitution of foolish little works.

Anselm, bishop of Lucca, died in 1086, on 18 March, and was buried at Mantua, his homeland. Bellarmine and Labbe discuss him in the places cited above; Antonius Possevinus in volume I of the *Apparatus sacer*, p. 86; Natalis Alexander in *Selected Chapters of Ecclesiastical History*, eleventh century, volume XV, chapter 3, where he treats ecclesiastical writers; and Gerard van Maastricht, professor of law and history at the University of Duisburg, in *History of Ecclesiastical and Pontifical Law*, no. 260, pp. 301–303, published in Amsterdam in 1686 in octavo.

[Col. 0443]

# LIFE OF SAINT ANSELM, BISHOP OF LUCCA, BY B., HIS DISCIPLE AND PENITENTIARY

*(Mabillon, Acts of the Saints of the Order of Saint Benedict, volume IX, p. 472.)*

## PRELIMINARY OBSERVATIONS

[Col. 0443A] 1. The author who wrote the following little book indicates his own age in more than one place and presents himself as a contemporary and disciple of Anselm, as in §§ 19, 20, 21, 24, and 29. He designates his name only by the initial letter B. in § 43:

“Concerning our most blessed father and patron, Saint Anselm, bishop of Lucca … I, B., his sinful priest in penitence—not, I say, his son but his servant—promoted by him with many tears to this same order,” etc.

This B. was therefore a penitentiary; and this is confirmed by § 42, where, speaking of a certain wounded German, he says: “At last we too were summoned, so that, after imposing penance upon him, we might give him Communion.”

Wading suspects that this author was called Bardus. In his commentary on this Life, § 1, he observes from the records of the church of Lucca that Bardus, a deacon and primicerius of that church, always remained attached to our Anselm together with Lambert, the archpriest, and followed him even into exile. Wading considers it no objection that this Bardus is named in those records only as a deacon. For it can be inferred from the author’s own words that B., the author of the Life, had long been a deacon: in § 45 he says that the blessed bishop promoted him, with many tears, to the order of the priesthood, undoubtedly while both were living in exile.

That he belonged to the church of Lucca is likewise indicated by these words in § 24, where Anselm ordered them to sing the Psalms carefully and meditatively, and otherwise rebuked them harshly.

The Life of blessed Anselm was published by Tegnagel, Surius, Wading, and the Bollandists. Wading consulted several manuscript codices and supplied the work with commentary.

2. Apart from various martyrologies and more recent writers, ancient authors who flourished in Saint Anselm’s own age speak of him: Domnizo the priest in his poem on Countess Matilda; Paul of Bernried in the *Acts of Gregory VII*; Berthold of Constance in his continuation of Marianus; and others.

Above all they praise him: Hugh, archbishop of Lyon, and another Hugh, abbot of Flavigny, in his *Chronicle*. Describing the election and ordination of Hugh, bishop of Die, under the year 1084, the latter says that Hugh came to Rome in December to receive the orders and found there, awaiting a similar event, Lord Anselm, the elected bishop of Lucca—“a man worthy of every proclamation of praise, now blessed,” he says, “by a happy departure, in whom all praise may safely be sung.”

He then adds:

“With this Hugh of Die, therefore, he was bound by such a strong bond of familiarity and affection, and although they had separate lodgings they clung so closely to each other in the Lateran palace, that to those who knew their unanimity it seemed strange to see one without the other. Indeed, the prefect of the city, as though by a certain presage of truth, called one of them ‘day’ and the other ‘light’: for day is not without light, and light accompanies day. For the splendor of justice and piety shone in their conduct; their steadfast friendship, ignorant of change, outweighed all else. They were old men, not through length of life but through maturity of character.”

While they were therefore staying in Rome and awaiting the day of their consecration, messengers of King Henry came to Rome, asking that the Lord Pope, Gregory VII, should not consecrate them contrary to the custom of their predecessors, since they had received only the election to their bishoprics, not the gift of investiture through royal authority.

The author finally adds that the pontiff agreed in the case of the elected bishop of Lucca to postpone his consecration until he had received the investiture of the bishopric as a royal gift, but refused to agree in the case of the bishop of Die.

3. These matters may shed light on the Life that follows, as may the letter of the aforementioned Hugh, archbishop of Lyon, to Countess Matilda. He urges her, according to her custom, to assist the Roman Church in the election of the future pontiff after the death of Victor III, whom Urban II succeeded with difficulty.

“You have in this matter,” he writes, “most faithful helpers and kindly advocates of your devotion before God: namely, our most pious father of holy memory, Pope Gregory VII, and blessed A., bishop of Lucca. Just as, while they were still alive, they instructed you in all piety and justice, so now, from that bosom of eternal rest into which we trust they have been received, they will commend the work of your charity by their merits and prayers; and they will inspire in the depths of your devotion the love of eternal life with which they are ineffably satisfied.”

This letter was published in volume II of the *Spicilegium*.

4. How much Anselm labored to restore common life among the canons of the cathedral church of Saint Martin at Lucca is clear from §§ 5ff. of the following Life. Whether the effort achieved its result during his lifetime is not so clear.

I infer that some canons finally adopted the common life under his successor Rangerius from the following formula of profession, which we find in an old codex of the church of Lucca:

“I promise stability in this place, obedience to God and to blessed Martin, and to Bishop R., who now is, and to those who shall canonically succeed him. I promise to keep the goods of the church, and whatever I acquire through ecclesiastical office, in common and without fraud, and to obey the provost canonically appointed. + + +.”

This was done in Saint Donatus by Martin the priest, Henry, and Mascarus. Those canons therefore lived separately from the others in the church of Saint Donatus.

In another codex, now in the possession of Florentinius, a physician of Lucca, the following is read concerning such canons:

“Here begins the order of the canons who come for conversion. The novice who is about to make profession shall come before the altar after the offering, and the assembly of the brothers shall stand around him; and he shall bend his knees three times. The novice shall say this verse: ‘Receive me, O Lord, according to your word,’ etc.

“Then the novice shall rise and read this profession:

‘I, Brother N., offering myself, surrender myself to the church of Saint Donatus, and promise stability in this place and obedience to the prior; I profess the canonical life and life without property.’”

After this, in the same codex, follow the Rules of Saint Augustine and blessed Benedict, together with this Life, by Gregory the Great.

[Col. 0445C] 5. As for Anselm’s works or writings, the following are enumerated in § [.....] of the Life that follows: the *Apology for Gregory VII*, the *Exposition on the Lamentations of Jeremiah*, and an exposition on certain Psalms.

To these add the *Collection of Canons*, comprising thirteen books. The *Apology* was edited first by Heinrich Canisius and later in the *Bibliotheca Patrum*. Wading published one letter and several little works attributed to Anselm at Rome in 1657. Our manuscript Saxon chronicler has a fragment of this letter, as does the abbot of Ursperg.

Berthold of Constance cites certain verses from Anselm’s commentary on the Psalms. We have a handwritten copy of the *Collection of Canons*, transcribed from a Vatican codex, from which it will suffice for the present to excerpt the following.

## BEGINNING OF THE TABLE OF CONTENTS OF THE BOOKS

[Col. 0446B] “Which blessed Anselm, bishop of Lucca, composed in this volume as individual books on corresponding causes.”

Book I: On the power and primacy of the Apostolic See.

II: On the freedom of appeal.

III: On the procedure for accusing, giving testimony, and judging.

IV: On the authority of privileges.

V: On the ordination of churches, and on all their rights and status.

VI: On the election and ordination, and on all the power or status, of bishops.

VII: On the life and ordination of clerics.

VIII: On those who have fallen.

IX: On the sacraments.

X: On marriages.

XI: On penance.

XII: On excommunication.

XIII: On vengeance and unjust persecution.

This is sufficient as a specimen.

# LIFE OF SAINT ANSELM

[Col. 0445]

*(See Patrologia, volume CXLVIII, column 905, among the Gregorian monuments.)*

[Col. 0445]

# TWO BOOKS OF SAINT ANSELM, BISHOP OF LUCCA, AGAINST GUIBERT THE ANTIPOPE, IN DEFENSE OF GREGORY VII, THE LEGITIMATE ROMAN PONTIFF

*(Canisius, *Ancient Readings*, volume VI, p. 199, from the library of the cathedral church of Regensburg.) (G)*

## BOOK ONE

[Col. 0445D] It is characteristic of good minds to fear guilt where there is none; it is characteristic of the rejected to put themselves first and to criticize some people for foolish opinions and others for unworthy merits.

They disdain being corrected, while suspecting that those who correct them are wiser than themselves. They gladly tell others what they understand, so that they may appear to know matters that are more subtle, more useful, and unknown to others.

When they possess understanding, they investigate not themselves but always other things, so that they may appear to know more. They do not examine their own deeds but investigate those of others.

Yet by the just judgment of almighty God it comes about that, because they did not possess the fear of God and did not set God before their eyes (Psalm 53), and because they refused to walk in his law (Psalm 77), they vomit up the riches they devoured, and the Lord draws them out from their belly.

And as the Apostle says: “Because they did not approve of retaining God in their knowledge” (Romans 1), “God delivered them over to a reprobate mind” (ibid.). For the Holy Spirit of discipline flees deceit and withdraws from thoughts that lack understanding.

“Upon whom,” he says, “shall I rest, if not upon the humble and gentle, and upon him who trembles at my words?” (Isaiah 66.) And elsewhere: “With the simple is my conversation” (Proverbs 3).

When he departs, the ancient serpent pours such venom into the foolish and darkened heart, and so intoxicates the one wholly enslaved to the poison of deadly deception, that he tastes the bitter as sweet and the sweet as bitter; believes darkness to be light and light darkness; and finally asserts that good is evil and evil good (Isaiah 5).

Thus it happens that, from two mutually agreeing unclean spirits, a fullness of pride established in a house abandoned and empty of God, accompanied by every vice, occupies it at the end of the world (Matthew 12); once occupied, possesses it; once possessed, prostitutes it, so that it now appears smaller in its beginning and, as the ages advance, seems to have developed into full maturity.

For the Devil said: “I will set my throne in the north, and I will be like the Most High” (Isaiah 14). Of his father or associate the Apostle says: “He who is exalted above all that is called God or that is worshiped” (2 Thessalonians 2).

[Col. 0447C] Listen, therefore, most wicked of all men—you who must now be called by that name, since you did not fear to bark against your Lord and Master—and recognize what belongs properly to you.

I wrote you a few words with great sorrow and sincere affection, so that, recognizing your error, you might return to your senses and do penance for your sins. But because your words are iniquity and deceit, and you refused to understand in order to do good (Psalm 35), listen meanwhile to what the Lord cries out against you through the prophet:

“Thus says the Lord God: This is Jerusalem; I placed her in the midst of the nations, with lands around her. But she despised my judgments, so as to be more wicked than the nations, and my commandments more than the lands around her. For they rejected my judgments and did not walk in my commandments.

“Therefore thus says the Lord God: Behold, I am against you, and I myself shall execute judgments in your midst in the sight of the nations. I shall do in you what I have never done and what I shall never again do, because of all your abominations. Therefore fathers shall eat their sons in your midst, and sons shall eat their fathers” (Ezekiel 5).

Since you see these things fulfilled in your own times, and Truth says, “I shall do what I have never done in you and what I shall never again do,” it is necessary for you to ascribe an unheard-of judgment to yourself, since the new and unprecedented abomination of your time has consigned you, your Lord N., and through you your accomplices to a new curse:

“This is the mother Jerusalem,” and the rest.

The adulteress who now belongs to your party once appeared to be Jerusalem—namely, the holy Church, daughter of King David. But, alas, she has been corrupted by her brother and defiled from head to foot. All her beauty has departed from her; she has become like the widow who was mistress of the nations, because the king of Babylon possesses her.

For when the Lord says to blessed Peter, “I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew 16), and, “Upon this rock I will build my Church” (ibid.), and, “Feed my sheep” (John 21), and elsewhere, “My dove is one” (Song of Songs 6), whatever is corrupted through the usurpation of another’s right is shown to be no longer Christ’s bride but an adulteress, no longer free but a slave.

As blessed Ambrose says:

“I am approached by counts and tribunes so that through me the delivery of the basilicas might be completed. They say that the emperor has commanded by his own right that everything under his authority must be handed over. I replied: If he were asking me for what is mine—that is, my estate, my silver, or my right of this kind—I would not resist, although everything that is mine belongs to the poor. But what belongs to God is not subject to imperial power.”

And shortly afterward:

“It is not lawful for me to hand it over, nor is it expedient for you, emperor, to receive it. A private house may not be violated under any law; do you think that the house of God may be taken away? It is alleged to the emperor that everything is permitted to him and that all things belong to him. I reply: Do not burden yourself, emperor, by thinking that you possess any imperial right over the things that belong to God. Do not exalt yourself; but if you wish to rule longer, be subject to God. For it is written: ‘Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s’ (Matthew 12). Palaces belong to the emperor; churches belong to the priest. You have been entrusted with authority over public walls, not sacred ones.

“Again, I am told that the emperor has ordered me to say: ‘I too must have one basilica.’ I reply: You may not have any. What have you to do with an adulteress? For she is an adulteress who has not been joined in a lawful marriage to Christ. By ancient law, authority was given to priests, not usurped.”

It is therefore established that this Church is not the true Church but an adulteress, since, as blessed Cyprian says:

“Whoever, separated from the Church, is joined to an adulteress is separated from the promises of the Church. Nor will he reach Christ’s rewards who has abandoned Christ’s Church. He is alien, he is profane, he is an enemy; he cannot have God as Father who does not have the Church as mother.”

Hence blessed Gelasius also says, among other things:

“God willed that what must be arranged for the Church should belong to priests, not to the powers of the world; and if those powers are faithful, he willed them to be subject to his Church and to its priests. Let the emperor not claim another’s right for himself, nor the ministry assigned to another.”

And shortly afterward:

“Christian rulers are accustomed to obey the decrees of the Church, not to place their own power above them.”

Do not therefore say that you have undertaken the care of the universal Church. For how has the Church been entrusted to you, when it is clear that you did not enter through the door, which is Christ, but climbed in from another place like a thief? (John 10.)

The Apostolic and universal Church already had its shepherd. To speak of blessed Gregory, our father, as Cyprian wrote of Cornelius:

“He was made bishop by the judgment of God and his Christ, by the testimony of nearly all the clergy—or, to speak truthfully, of all of them—by the support of the people who were then present, and by the assembly of the ancient priests and good men. No one had been made bishop before him; the see of Alexander and the see of Peter, or the rank of the priestly chair, was vacant.

“Once it had been occupied and he had been ordained by God’s will and by the consent of all of us, whoever now wished to become bishop had necessarily to remain outside, nor could he possess ecclesiastical ordination who did not preserve the unity of the Church.

“Whoever he might be, even if he vaunted himself greatly and claimed much for himself, he was profane, alien, and outside. And since a second cannot exist after the first, whoever was made after the one who alone ought to exist was not a second but no one.”

[Col. 0449B] These are the judgments of God which you rejected, and the commandments in which you refused to walk, surpassing the wickedness of all nations when you descended alive into hell.

We therefore believe that all nations are justified in comparison with your crime, because, after receiving the gift of the Holy Spirit and the powers of the age to come, you not only refused to glorify God as God but, establishing unjust laws against his commandments, closed off every path of pardon for yourselves unless you return to the unity of the mother Church, from which you have been cut off and which alone possesses the right to bind and loose.

For the Lord says: “You have received freely; give freely” (Matthew 10). “He who does not enter through the door is not the shepherd of the sheep” (John 10). “Whatever you bind on earth shall be bound also in heaven” (Matthew 16).

Your king, however, continually sells his bishoprics, issuing edicts that no one shall be recognized as bishop who has been elected by the clergy or requested by the people unless royal favor has preceded it—as though he himself were the doorkeeper of that door of which Truth says: “The doorkeeper opens for him” (John 10).

But you have climbed in from another place and approached without being called by God. Do not usurp for yourself the care of so great a government.

For, as has already been said, if Gregory was in the Church—and he was acknowledged as such even by you—and if no one could condemn him as judge, it is clear that you, cut off from the root of the Church, have withered and possess no power or right.

As blessed Cyprian says in writing to the priest Magnus:

“There is one Church, which cannot be both inside and outside. If it is with Novatian, it was not with Cornelius. But if it was with Cornelius, who succeeded Bishop Fabian by legitimate ordination, Novatian is not in the Church and cannot be counted as a bishop.”

And shortly afterward:

“We find that in such a crime not only the leaders and authors but also their accomplices are assigned to punishment unless they separate themselves from the communion of the wicked. The Lord commanded through Moses:

“‘Separate yourselves from the tents of these most wicked men, and do not touch anything that belongs to them, lest you perish together in their sin’ (Numbers 16).

“And what the Lord had threatened through Moses he fulfilled. Whoever did not separate himself from Korah, Dathan, and Abiram immediately paid the penalty for impious fellowship.

“By this example it is shown and proved that all who mingle themselves through irreligious presumption with schismatics against their superiors and priests will be liable to every guilt and punishment. The Holy Spirit also bears witness through the prophet Hosea and says:

“‘Their sacrifices are like the bread of mourning; all who eat them are defiled’ (Hosea 9).

“He teaches and demonstrates that all who have been contaminated by their sin are joined in punishment with the authors themselves.”

Warned by these and countless other saving commandments, we detest—not the sacraments of the Church, as you falsely claim—but schismatics and sacrilegious men, from whose murderous hands the divine sacraments have withdrawn themselves.

And with our Catholic mother Church I shall pursue her enemies, and I shall not turn back until they fail (Psalm 17).

The Church venerates her own holy thing which you possess outside her—that which you received to your own harm—because you perished through its good odor; but she persecutes you as Sarah persecuted the maidservant, who nevertheless conceived and bore a child from the seed of Abraham (Genesis 16).

Understand, therefore, how the mistress still persecutes the maidservant, so that you may be taught what blessed persecution is. And know that Christians should not quarrel even for the sake of justice, if you allow the matter to be properly explained to you, so that the words “against the Catholics” may be added, and you may not rebuke Christ, who says, “Compel them to enter” (Luke 14), along with many other passages that you will hear in what follows.

Augustine the blessed says against the Donatists:

“If it is the Church herself that suffers persecution, and not the one that inflicts it, let them ask the Apostle which Church Sarah signified when she was persecuting the slave woman. For he says that our heavenly mother, Jerusalem, the free woman, that is, the true Church of God, was prefigured in that woman who afflicted the slave woman (Gal. IV). But if we examine the matter more closely, she persecuted Sarah more by her arrogance than Sarah persecuted her by restraining her. The slave woman was injuring her mistress; Sarah was imposing discipline upon her arrogance.

“Furthermore, I ask: if good and holy men persecute no one but merely suffer persecution, whose voice do they think is heard in the psalm where we read, ‘I shall pursue my enemies,’ and so forth (Ps. XVII)? If, then, we wish to speak or acknowledge the truth, there is an unjust persecution inflicted by the wicked upon the Church of Christ. The blessed persecution is that which she suffers on account of injustice.”

Again:

“As for what those who refuse to have just laws enacted against their impieties say—that the apostles did not request such measures from the kings of the earth—they fail to consider that the time was then different, and that everything must be done in its proper time. For which emperor at that time had believed in Christ, so that by enacting laws against impiety for the sake of piety he might serve Him, when the prophetic word was still being fulfilled: ‘Why did the nations rage?’ (Ps. II), and what follows? What is stated later in the same psalm had not yet come to pass: ‘Serve the Lord with fear’ (Ps. II). For when do kings serve the Lord with fear, unless by forbidding and punishing with religious severity those things that are done against God’s commands?”

The same author elsewhere:

“Where is what these people are accustomed to shout: ‘Whom did Christ use force against? Whom did He compel?’ Behold, they have the Apostle Paul. Let them recognize in him Christ first compelling and afterward teaching; first striking and afterward consoling (Acts IX).”

Again:

“I do not approve of everyone having permission to kill, unless perhaps he is a soldier or holds a public office, so that he does not do this for himself but for others or for the state in which he himself also resides, having received lawful authority, if this is appropriate to his person. Those who are driven away from doing evil by some terror may perhaps thereby be helped. This is why it was said, ‘Let us not resist evil’ (Matt. V): not so that we might take pleasure in vengeance, which feeds the mind upon another’s misfortune, nor so that we should neglect the correction of human beings. Thus one is not guilty of another’s death if, after enclosing his own property with walls, someone is struck and killed by the collapse of those walls. Nor is a Christian guilty if his ox kills someone by goring him, or his horse by kicking him; nor, for that reason, should Christians refrain from having oxen with horns, horses with hooves, or dogs with teeth.

“But consider how the Apostle Paul took pains to bring it to the tribune’s attention that certain desperate men were plotting against him, and therefore received armed escorts (Acts XXIII). If those criminals had fallen upon the weapons, would Paul have acknowledged their bloodshed as his crime? Far be it from us to suppose that, if something evil happens to anyone against our will through the good and lawful things we do or possess, it should be imputed to us.”

Again:

“If Christian discipline condemned all wars, the Gospel would more appropriately give this counsel to soldiers seeking the way of salvation: that they should throw away their weapons and withdraw altogether from military service. Instead, it was said to them: ‘Extort money from no one, accuse no one falsely, and be content with your pay’ (Luke III). By commanding them to be content with their own pay, He certainly did not prohibit military service.”

Again, to Boniface:

“Do you complain bitterly about battle? I do not want you to hesitate: I shall give you and your men useful counsel. Take up arms in your hands; let prayer strike the ears of the Author, for when battle is joined, God watches with the heavens opened, defends the side that He sees to be just, and grants victory there.”

Again:

“Do not suppose that no one who serves with military weapons can please God. Saint David was among such men, and the Lord bore witness to him with such great praise. Many men of that time were likewise so employed; among them was the centurion who said to the Lord, ‘I am not worthy that you should enter under my roof’ (Matt. VIII). Therefore consider this first when you arm yourself for battle: your bodily strength too is a gift from God. In this way you will consider how not to act against the Lord with God’s gift. So be peaceful while waging war, so that by conquering you may bring those whom you overcome to the benefit of peace.”

Augustine likewise, to the presbyter Donatus:

“You are displeased that you are being dragged toward salvation, although you have dragged so many of us toward destruction. For what do we want except that you be seized, brought before us, and preserved so that you may not perish?”

Pope Pelagius:

“Do not let the empty talk of men delay you—those who say that the Church practices persecution when she either restrains crimes that are committed or seeks the salvation of souls. Such inventors of rumor are mistaken: only he persecutes who compels someone to do evil. Whoever punishes evil that has already been committed or prevents it from being committed does not persecute but loves. For if, as they think, no one should be restrained from evil or drawn back toward good, human and divine laws must necessarily be abolished—laws that, at the urging of justice, establish punishments for the wicked and rewards for the good. Both the authority of canonical Scripture and the truth of the rules handed down by the Fathers teach us that schism is evil and that such evil must also be suppressed through external powers.”

Again, elsewhere:

“Do not suppose that it is anyone’s sin if such people are restrained. Divine grace and worldly laws alike have established that those who are separated from the unity of the Church are also restrained by secular authorities. Nor is there any greater sacrifice that you can offer to God than arranging that those who rage to the destruction of themselves and others should be checked with appropriate force.”

Jerome, on Ezekiel, book three:

“He who strikes down the wicked insofar as they are wicked, and possesses the instruments of slaughter, is a minister of the Lord.”

Augustine, on Psalm 118:

“There is an unjust mercy, of which it is written in the Law, ‘You shall not pity him’ (Deut. XIX). In the Book of Kings we read that Saul incurred offense for this reason: he pitied Agag, king of the enemy, whom the divine sentence had forbidden to be spared (I Kings XV). If someone, moved by the pleas of a robber’s children and softened by his wife’s tears, thinks that the robber should be released, although he still has the inclination to rob, will he not hand over innocent people to destruction by freeing one who is planning the destruction of many?”

As for the plundering of those who have been cut off from the Church, let our Fathers answer.

Augustine:

“Whatever was possessed by the party of Donatus, the Christian emperors ordered by devout laws to be transferred, together with the churches themselves, to the Catholic Church. If, however, we consider what is written in the Book of Wisdom, ‘Therefore the righteous took the spoils of the ungodly’ (Wis. X), and likewise what is read in Proverbs, ‘The wealth of the wicked is stored up for the righteous’ (Prov. XIII), we shall see that the question is not who possesses the property of heretics, but who belongs to the fellowship of the righteous.”

Likewise, the blessed Gregory to Velox, master of the soldiers, among other things:

“Now it has seemed useful that some soldiers should be sent there. Let Your Glory take care to admonish and encourage them to be ready; and when an opportunity arises, speak with our most glorious sons Martius and Vitalius, and do whatever, with God’s help, serves the interests of the state. If you learn that Ariulfus is setting out either here or toward the Ravenna side, strive to attack him from the rear, as befits brave men.”

Likewise, to Maurinus and Vitalianus, among other things:

“Glorious sons, be vigilant, because, as I have learned, the enemy has gathered his forces and is said to be stationed on the coast. If, with God angered against him, he should wish to make his way here, plunder his position as far as the Lord enables you.”

Having carefully considered these passages, you will know that we teach the truth, not undo it through false preaching; that through arrogance you have been handed over to a reprobate mind and have charged our holy Father with a crime; and that you have not understood the sayings of the holy Fathers which you included in your letter.

We preach these things and others like them, and with great anguish of heart we strive to free ourselves from these necessities of ours. We cry out to the Lord our God in this tribulation, asking that He may subject you humbly beneath His hand and order our days in His peace. Indeed, the merciful physician cuts with great pain one who would die if he were not cut; with many tears a father binds his delirious son. Finally, the righteous rejoices, giving glory to the Lord’s name, when he sees vengeance (Ps. LVII), yet the great number of those who perish always torments his heart.

It is indeed true that it has not been granted to take up iron weapons even for the sake of justice, insofar as this concerns the perfection of justice and the adornment of the house of God. Nor does the Apostle praise the fact that there are disputes among the saints; nevertheless, he said: “Appoint as judges those who are of no account among you” (I Cor. VI). And although he wished everyone to be as he himself was, he nevertheless allows each person, on account of lack of self-control, to have his own wife, and commands that the husband render the marital debt to his wife and the wife to her husband (I Cor. VII).

Although Truth itself had first said in the Gospel, “Do not swear at all” (Matt. V), and “Let your speech be ‘Yes, yes; no, no’” (ibid.), it nevertheless added: “Anything beyond this is from evil” (ibid.). It did not say, “is evil,” but “is from evil,” as if it had said: If it should be necessary to swear, and if you are compelled by the evil of the unbelief of others, swear—not without cause and not by your own choice.

This is why Moses, as a moderation of vengeance, said, “An eye for an eye, a tooth for a tooth” (Exod. XXI), so that by this more merciful course he might take away the opportunity for killing.

Would that Catholics had no struggle against flesh and blood (Eph. VI), so that they might live in peace and attain such perfection that all would desire the palm of martyrdom, and that there were no one whom the minister of God—an avenger unto wrath against one who does evil, and who does not bear the sword without cause (Rom. XIII)—would have to punish.

But we have not mingled ourselves in anyone’s blood, nor, with God protecting us, shall we do so, nor do we rejoice in the destruction of those who die. We prohibit everyone from avenging a personal injury, so that they may look to the Judge who promises, saying, “Vengeance is mine; I will repay” (Rom. XIII).

We desire to defend the orphan and widow with arms, even carnal arms, and to protect the holy Church—not [to defend] those who are parties in the cause, except on behalf of the commonwealth under whose rule the Churches as a whole stand. We do not covet their money or land; rather, we earnestly strive and desire that the wealth of the wicked be stored up for the righteous and that the righteous take the spoils of the wicked, yet with the intention that they may win them over, and that they distribute in charity not only what belongs to those people but even all that is their own.

It is not, therefore, the blood of the Saxons that cries out against us; it cries out against you together with the whole world, which shudders at the corruption of your crime. Heaven cries out, earth cries out, the entire Church of the righteous cries out—both the Church that is still on pilgrimage and the Church that already reigns with Christ. Christ cries out; the Father cries out on behalf of the Bride of His Son; the Holy Spirit cries out, interceding for her every day with inexpressible groanings (Rom. VIII).

You are tearing apart and rending the Church, because you have cut off your own portion from her unity and have split her into pieces more cruelly with the sword of schism than through the crime of idolatry, so that now it is not chaff among the grain but branches cut off from the vine that are thrown into the fire.

For you are tearing apart the members of the Catholic Church, which you have invaded throughout the whole kingdom—a kingdom that, having fallen within, will not be able to stand long without—and, after reducing them to slavery like a worthless slave, you bring them under your domination and enslave the freedom belonging to divine right to your service. You say that everything is subject to the emperor’s law: bishoprics, abbeys, and absolutely all the churches of God, although the Lord says, “My Church” (Matt. XVI), “my dove” (Song II), “my sheep” (John XXI).

Paul says: “No one takes this honor upon himself except one who is called by God, as Aaron was” (Heb. V). In your faction, who is appointed except one whom either favour with interest exhausted (exhausto fenore; reading uncertain), or a gift from the hand, or a gift from the tongue, or a gift from service has attracted? Who is chosen for his character, his integrity, or the uprightness of his life? Therefore the wolves must be pursued, and all those must be avoided who are promoted for the purpose of becoming heretics, who possess the leprosy of Gehazi together with his wealth, and who, by a wickedly acquired payment, have gathered not so much a patrimony of possessions as a treasury of crimes.

Since, therefore, you have neither given freely nor received freely (Matt. X), and since, turning away from the Lord’s commandments, you are accursed (Ps. CXVIII), and since you do not obey the apostolic commands, we fear being joined to you. For the blessed Ambrose says:

“If there is any Church that does not possess the foundations of apostolic truth, it must be abandoned, lest it be able to inflict some stain upon you. For it has matured under these laws, been cultivated by such teachings, and propagated through such institutions. He who opposes these things, who disregards them, who hides this lamp of truth under a bushel (Matt. V), is not a shepherd of the Church but an enemy, and the Lord will demand from his hands the blood of those who perish (Ezek. III).

“If, then, you do not dare to say that Christ is the cause of the destruction of those to whom He was sent and who did not hear His voice, and if you do not dare to attribute to Paul the folly of the Gentiles and the scandal of the Jews (I Cor. I), restrain your tongue from slandering us as well. We are compelled to speak the truth, just as the Lord threatens through the prophet: ‘The priest who enters and departs without giving a sound shall die’ (Exod. XXVIII). Again: ‘Accursed is he who withholds his sword from blood’ (Jer. XLVIII).”

Pope Innocent:

“An error to which one does not resist is approved, and truth, when it is not defended at all, is suppressed.”

Again, the same author:

“To neglect to drive away the wicked when you are able to do so is nothing other than to encourage them; nor is he free from the reproach of hidden complicity who ceases to oppose an open crime.”

Pope Pius:

“What benefit is it for one who does not defile himself with another’s error if he grants consent to the one who errs? Without doubt, he fights against the commandments—and so does the one who grants consent to the one who errs.”

Clement:

“It is most certain that neither friendship, nor kinship, nor the exalted status of a kingdom ought to be more precious to a person than truth.”

Fabianus:

“He who fears almighty God in no way consents to do anything against the Gospel, against the apostles, against the prophecies, or against the institutions of the holy Fathers.”

Leo:

“He who does not recall others from error demonstrates that he himself is in error.”

Augustine:

“Whoever conceals the truth through fear of some authority provokes God’s anger against himself, because he fears a human being more than God.”

Gregory:

“He appears to consent to the one who errs who does not intervene to cut away what must be removed so that it may be corrected.”

Therefore, as was said above, if something evil happens as a result of what we do for a good and lawful purpose, it will not be imputed to us.

But as for what you say—that we have undertaken the care of the universal Church, though unwillingly—were you, while life was still with you, to be drawn into so monstrous a crime as to violate the marriage-bed of your mother and father? And if you endured violence, why do you not at least now, as an adulterer, repent?

As for your entreaty, by Jesus, that I no longer deceive, delude, or mislead the most noble of women, I call God to witness that I intentionally covet nothing earthly or carnal in her or from her. Without ceasing I pray that I may soon deserve to be snatched away from this wicked age, worn down by extreme weariness, because I see that my sojourn is being prolonged (Ps. CXIX). I serve day and night in guarding her for my God and for my holy mother, the Church, by whose command she has been entrusted to me.

I hope that, through God’s grace, abundant reward will increase for me in guarding her—she who does not scatter her possessions in vain but stores up for herself in heaven an unfailing treasure, which the moth does not destroy and where thieves neither break in nor steal (Matt. VI). She is prepared, for the defense of justice, not only to distribute all earthly things but even to struggle unto bloodshed for your shame and reverence, for the glory and exaltation of the holy Church, until the Lord places His enemy in the hand of a woman.

But you, remember from where you have fallen and repent (Rev. II), so that perhaps the Lord may forgive you (Acts VIII), and so that, once peace has been restored to the Church, we may deserve to attain the fulfillment of our desire.

Lay aside the tiara; remove the crown (Ezek. XXI); put on mourning garments. Become as much humbler and more despised by all as, above all others, you have raised the horn of your arrogance.

Tell your king to recognize his crime, unheard-of among all other generations: he has now brought two adulterers upon his mother. Let him weep with you over the calamities of the whole world, especially over that calamity of which we spoke above, which by the just judgment of God followed upon a new crime with a new one.

Come to the grieving mother, the Church, who sighs for you, so that she herself may offer an acceptable sacrifice to the Lord on your behalf. For she alone is the one through whom the Lord willingly accepts sacrifice; she alone confidently intercedes for those who err. Outside her, whoever is found will perish when the flood reigns; outside her, whoever eats the lamb is profane, and the Law forbids its flesh to be carried outside (Exod. XII).

In many respects you are with her, but do not rejoice in this. Rather fear what follows in the same psalm: “They have defiled his covenant” (Ps. LIV). Just as Christ, bound and scourged, did not benefit Pilate and Herod, so His sacraments contribute more to your impiety and destruction.

Come confidently to the richness of the Church, your mother, from whose womb you have strayed, so that you may be joined again to her. For God is powerful enough to graft you in again; nothing is impossible for Him. Certainly she will rejoice over you, rush upon your neck, clothe you in the first robe, and sacrifice the fattened calf for the prodigal son.

May almighty God, who wills that no one perish and who loves sinners beyond a mother’s love, illuminate your heart with the splendor of His grace and lead you back to the way of salvation, so that you may recognize what His good, pleasing, and perfect will is.

## HERE BEGINS BOOK TWO

[Col. 0455]

[Col. 0455C] With the merciful assistance of the Lord our God, who by His wondrous will governs and directs both us and our words, we gird ourselves to answer those who say that Christ’s Church is subject to royal power, so that the king may, according to his own pleasure, by request, by payment, or for free, appoint pastors over it and transfer its possessions either into his own jurisdiction or into that of anyone he pleases.

And, so that we may not prolong our introduction, it seems necessary first to explain how it is certain that the blessed Apostle Peter, the first pontiff of the Church, initially sent chief pontiffs to the patriarchal sees of the East and afterward to the cities of the West. This task belonged especially to him, since Christ, the Son of God, had principally entrusted him with the keys of the heavenly kingdom, commanded him to feed His sheep, prayed specifically for his faith not to fail, and ordered him to strengthen his brothers in that same faith.

We do not doubt that the other apostles also, whom we know to have preached in various regions of the world, likewise sent pastors to the individual cities of those regions in which each one preached the word of God.

And when, taught by the Holy Spirit, they understood that the rulers of the world would come to the faith, and that in later times, driven by avarice, some of them would wish to subject the Church of God to their authority and, by their own power and pleasure, appoint pastors over her, they opposed these wicked efforts among the other canons which they established for the protection of religion and ecclesiastical discipline. Their constitution reads as follows:

“If any bishop, using secular powers, obtains a church through them, let him be deposed and separated, and let all who communicate with him be likewise separated” (Apostolic Constitution).

If anyone argues that this constitution, which is attributed to them, is not authentic, he is an overturner of the holy Seventh Universal Synod of 350 Fathers, as well as of the Council of Antioch, by which it is taught to be authentic; consequently, he will be judged a heretic. For Callistus, Gregory, and certain other Roman pontiffs, as is known to the attentive reader, strengthened their own constitutions by the authority of these same apostolic canons. Stephen IV and John VII, as Anastasius says in the preface to the Seventh Synod, judged that fifty chapters of these same canons should be received with the fullest force of authority.

After the apostles had died, the Churches throughout the world inviolably preserved the custom handed down by them: when the pontiff of any Church died, its clergy and people, by common deliberation, appointed as their pastor someone from their own clergy or from the clergy of another Church.

This most holy and God-pleasing custom remained whole and unimpaired until the multitude of the faithful began to enrich God’s churches with extensive possessions. Then, when the spirit of ambition intervened, some began to seek the bishoprics of their own Churches, others even those of other Churches, and through the wicked commerce of Simon to promise their supporters money that they did not even possess.

The Roman pontiffs most worthy of God, who held the primacy of the priesthood throughout the whole world—namely Boniface, Celestine, Leo, Gelasius, Symmachus, Hormisdas, Gregory, and others—seeing this, condemned from that time and forever the Simoniac heresy, which had first been condemned by Peter. Others strengthened the ancient custom by decretal constitutions, establishing that no one from another Church should be placed over a different Church, unless perhaps someone who was worthy to preside over his own Church could be found there, something which they believed could scarcely ever happen.

The most Christian emperors, therefore—Constantine, Constans, Valentinian, Theodosius, Arcadius, Honorius, Charles, Louis, and others similar to them in empire and religion—never presumed to violate this custom handed down by the apostles. They enriched with extensive gifts the Churches built either by themselves or by others, and did not wish to claim for themselves any dominion or jurisdiction over the clergy or the affairs of the Churches. Indeed, as we shall show below, some of them prohibited by law anyone else from claiming such authority.

By contrast, the Eutychianist emperors Zeno and Anastasius are said to have been the first to subject the holy Church of God to themselves, to the extent that they banished Catholic bishops into exile and, setting aside apostolic tradition, appointed men who agreed with them in their sees.

Before their time, certain heretical emperors are indeed said to have harassed Catholic bishops in many ways; but they are nowhere said to have interfered in the election or promotion of any pontiff. Under these same Eutychianists, both at Constantinople and in the other cities, an innumerable multitude of the faithful—clergy and people alike—is reported to have existed. They absolutely refused to receive their pseudo-bishops. From this it is plainly and clearly evident that the clergy and people rejected those pseudo-bishops because it was evident that they had been promoted by the aforementioned rulers without their election, in contempt of God and for the increase of error.

To support what we are saying with an example: Anastasius, librarian of the holy Roman Church, in the Chronicle which he translated from Greek into Latin—a work compiled from the most ancient Greek chronicles by certain Greek worshipers of God, namely Theophanes and George, whom he praises highly in the preface to that same book—writes the following, among other things, about the reign of Anastasius:

“In the twentieth year of the reign of Anastasius, after John, the heretical bishop of Alexandria, had died, Dioscorus the Younger was appointed bishop of Alexandria. When he came to Constantinople to intercede with the emperor on behalf of the Alexandrians, because of the killing of Calliopius, the Augustal prefect’s son, the orthodox publicly assailed him with insults as he proceeded, believing that he had come in opposition to the true doctrines. Therefore, after he had interceded concerning the homicide, he departed hastily.

“The cause of the killing was this: after that same Dioscorus had received the laying on of hands, crowds of country people withdrew, saying: ‘Unless he becomes bishop according to what the canons of the holy apostles contain, he will not be received.’ The rulers, however, enthroned him. Dioscorus then came to Saint Mark, and when the clergy arrived, they vested him a second time and consecrated him again. Thus, coming to Saint John, he completed the service.

“When Theodosius, son of Calliopius the Augustal prefect, and Acacius, master of the soldiers, were there, the disturbed crowds began to insult the prefect’s son because he praised the emperor Anastasius. When a quarrel had arisen, some of them rushed upon the prefect’s son, removed him from his seat, and killed him. Acacius, the master of the soldiers, killed as many as he was able to seize. When the emperor heard this, he was angered against them; but Dioscorus intervened and appeased him.”

Behold those who first dared to violate the apostolic tradition concerning pontifical promotion; behold the men by whose example the rulers of the world first sought to promote their own pontiffs in the Church of God.

And, to continue what we have begun: certain Greek emperors followed the examples of these heretics, appointing their own bishops in the cities of their kingdom. But, by God’s favor and through the merits of the apostles who live and preside in Rome, they spared the city of Rome in this matter. Nevertheless, they decreed that the written election decree of the future pontiff, subscribed by the clergy and senate, should be sent to them before he was consecrated.

Although this is often recorded as having been sent to those same emperors, they are nowhere said to have altered the election of the Romans. Their successors, superior in piety and religion, entirely rejected this practice because it was contrary to God: the Church should not be left without a pontiff until the bearer of the decree had gone and returned.

Thus it is read in the Roman Pontifical:

“For Benedict, a Roman by birth, received the commands of the most merciful emperor Constantine addressed to the venerable clergy and people of the city of Rome, by which he granted that whoever had been elected pontiff should immediately be consecrated without delay.”

Therefore, whoever observes that other Greek emperors wished the decree to be sent to them before the consecration should also observe that they never rejected the Roman election; and he should further observe that their successors entirely rejected the practice because it was contrary to God.

Let us therefore review the decrees of the holy Fathers concerning the promotion of pontiffs, so that we may know what rights they preserved for emperors of their own times or of any other period in these matters.

Leo, the eminent teacher and first pontiff of the Roman Church, writes the following, among other things, to Anastasius, bishop of Thessalonica, who exercised the authority of the Roman pontiff over more than forty bishops of Illyricum and Greece:

“Concerning the person to be consecrated as bishop and concerning the consent of the clergy and people, let the metropolitan report to Your Fraternity.”

A little later:

“When a metropolitan has died and another is to be appointed in his place, the bishops of the province should gather in the metropolitan city, so that, after the will of all the clergy and all the citizens has been examined, the best man may be chosen from among the presbyters or deacons of that same Church.

“When the election of the highest priest is under consideration, let the man be preferred to all others whom the consent of clergy and people has unanimously requested. If, however, their votes should be divided among different persons, then, by the judgment of the metropolitan, the one should be preferred at the altar who is supported by greater zeal and greater merits—provided that no one is ordained against the will and without the request of the people, lest the city despise or hate an unwanted bishop, since it was not permitted to have the one it wanted.”

The same author again:

“No reason permits those to be counted among the bishops who were neither elected by the clergy, nor requested by the people, nor consecrated by the provincial bishops with the judgment of the metropolitan.”

Celestine:

“Neither let outsiders and strangers, nor those previously unknown, be placed over deserving citizens in their own Churches, to the exclusion of those who have earned the good testimony of their fellow citizens.”

Again, in the same place:

“Let no one be given as bishop against the will of the people. Let the consent and desire of the clergy, the people, and the order be sought. Then let someone from another Church be chosen only if, among the clergy of the city itself in which the bishop is to be ordained, no one—something we do not believe will happen—can be found. For those who are there must first be rejected before men from other Churches can rightly be preferred.

“Let each person enjoy the fruit of his service in the Church in which he has passed his entire life through all its offices; let no one intrude upon another’s stipend. Let the clergy have the freedom to resist if they see themselves being overburdened, and let them not fear to reject those whom they recognize as being thrust upon them from outside. Otherwise, if they are not to have a fitting reward or free judgment concerning the one who is to govern them—”

Gregory to Bishop Gaudiosus, among other things:

“Therefore let Your Fraternity hasten to go to the aforesaid Church and quickly admonish the clergy and people that, after removing disagreement, they should with one and the same consent seek as their priest a man who is in no way rejected by the venerable canons. When he has been requested, solemnly elected, confirmed by the subscriptions of all, and presented to us with a letter bearing the testimony of your affection, let him come to be consecrated.

“We also admonish you not to permit anyone to be elected from another Church unless, among the clergy of that city itself, no one worthy of the episcopate—something we do not believe will happen—can be found. Above all, take care that persons of loose conduct do not presume to aspire to the merit of any manner of life, and that you do not, God forbid, incur danger to your rank.”

From the Council of Nicaea of 318 Fathers, chapter 6:

“It is altogether clear that if anyone has been ordained contrary to the will and knowledge of the metropolitan bishop, the great and holy council has judged that he ought not to be a bishop. But if, after the common consent of all has been reasonably approved according to ecclesiastical rule, two or three persons, driven by hostility, oppose it through contention, let the judgment of the majority of the priests prevail.”

From the Seventh Universal Synod, held by the five patriarchs with 350 Fathers under the pontificate of Hadrian I, chapter 3:

“Every election of a bishop, presbyter, or deacon made by rulers shall remain invalid, according to the rule which says: ‘If any bishop, using secular powers, obtains a church through them, let him be deposed and separated, and let all who communicate with him be likewise separated.’”

From the Eighth Synod, likewise universal, held by the five patriarchs with 240 Fathers under the pontificate of Nicholas I:

“This holy and universal synod, in agreement with the earlier councils, has defined, established, and promulgated by lawful authority that the promotions and consecrations of bishops are to take place by the election and decree of the bishops. No lay ruler or powerful layman may insert himself into the election or promotion of a patriarch, metropolitan, or any bishop, lest disorderly and inappropriate confusion or contention arise from this—especially since no layperson possessing power ought to have any authority in such matters. Rather, let such a person be silent and attend to his own affairs until the election of the future pontiff has regularly been completed by the college of the Church.

“If, however, any layperson is invited by the Church to deliberate and cooperate, such a person may, with reverence, comply if he should wish to obey those who summon him. For in this way the Church regularly promotes for her salvation a pastor worthy of her.

“But whoever among secular rulers or powerful persons, or any layman of another rank, attempts to act against the common, harmonious, and canonical election of the ecclesiastical order, let him be anathema until he obeys and consents to what the Church has shown that she wishes concerning the election and ordination of her own prelate.”

Likewise from the Council of Antioch of 122 Fathers:

“If any presbyter or deacon obtains the Church of the Lord through secular authority, let him be cast out, and let both him and the one who ordained him be entirely cut off from communion, and let them be under anathema, like Simon Magus by Peter.”

From the synod of Pope Symmachus with 218 bishops:

“It has not pleased us that laypeople should have any authority to establish anything in the Church, to which the necessity of following remains, not the authority of commanding.”

In the same synod:

“When the pontiff has died, if the election of the entire ecclesiastical order inclines unanimously toward one person, let him be consecrated bishop. But if, as usually happens, different factions begin to arise, let the judgment of the majority prevail.”

From the Roman Pontifical: “Benedict, a Roman by nationality, enacted a decree in the church of blessed Peter the Apostle, in which seventy-two bishops and thirty-three Roman priests took their seats, with the clergy present, under penalty of anathema: that no one, while the Roman pontiff was alive, or while the bishop of his own city lived, should presume to speak or form a faction for himself, except on the third day after his deposition, when the clergy and the sons of the Church had assembled; and then the election was to take place.”

From the same source: “Stephen, a Sicilian by nationality, having assembled the bishops of all Tuscany and Campania, with twelve Frankish bishops and Roman priests likewise sitting in council, held a council in the Constantinian church in the presence of all the clergy and [Col. 0461D] people. There he condemned Constantine, the neophyte usurper of the apostolic see. After the sacred canons had been brought forward and carefully examined, the council pronounced its sentence under the ban of anathema: that no layman, nor anyone from another order, should ever presume to be promoted to the sacred honor of the pontificate unless, ascending through the distinct grades, he had first become a cardinal deacon or priest.”
