From the council of Leo IV, of fifty bishops, chapter 5: “If anyone should presume to oppose the election of the Roman pontiff by the priests, or by the noble primates, or by the rest of the clergy of this holy Roman Church, let him be anathema, as it is read that the council of blessed Stephen decreed. [Col. 0462A] Likewise, the election of the pontiff does not pertain to laymen at all.”

From the Council of Laodicea, chapter 12: “It must not be permitted that the crowd should conduct the elections of those who are to be advanced to the priesthood.”

Likewise, from the decree of Pope Celestine: “The people are to be instructed, not followed; and if they do not know what is permitted and what is not permitted, we ought to admonish them, not give them our consent.”

Having thus reviewed the authorities of so many holy Fathers, both Latin and Greek, it is clear that they attributed no right whatsoever to imperial power in the election or promotion of pontiffs. Indeed, some of them prohibited under anathema—that is, separation [Col. 0462B] from God—that any lay power should claim anything for itself in these matters.

Certainly, under the Roman pontiffs mentioned above, there are said to have been very powerful emperors ruling not only the East but also the West: Valentinian and the younger Theodosius, Marcian, Maurice, and Phocas. And when the aforementioned universal synods—that is, the first and the seventh—were being conducted at Nicaea by so many Fathers, the most Christian emperors Constantine, and likewise Constantine and his mother Irene, are recorded as having been present. It is also recorded that the eighth universal synod was held at Constantinople at the request and in the presence of the great emperor Basil.

Thus, when the first of these synods decreed that no bishop should be appointed without the council of his metropolitan, while the seventh prohibited the election of the three sacred orders by princes, and the eighth forbade under anathema that the election of pontiffs be controlled by lay power, did the emperors who were present complain that this was being done as an insult to them, since nothing concerning the election of pontiffs was being referred to their authority? Certainly not. Rather, they are recorded as having embraced the constitutions of the holy Fathers, and some of them strengthened them with their own subscriptions after the subscriptions of the five patriarchs.

Likewise, when the aforementioned Roman pontiffs happened to issue decrees concerning the election of pontiffs, did the emperors of their times complain that this was being done as an injury to their imperial authority? Certainly not.

There are, however, certain people among those against whom we are writing [Col. 0462D] who think they have discovered something impressive in their own defense, when they introduce Gregory and Ambrose as having been promoted to the pontificate by secular rulers. That this is frivolous and false will become clear from an evident examination, when their elections are compared with chapter 8 of the synod, which we cited above. For although many years separated them from one another, they nevertheless appear so harmonious that both the synod and their election or promotion are shown to have been carried out by one and the same Spirit of God.

Thus their acts describe or record the following:

“Although Gregory resisted with all his strength, the clergy, senate, and Roman people unanimously chose him as their pontiff. But when he could not escape the general decree, he finally pretended that he would consent, [Col. 0463A] and secretly sent a letter to the emperor Maurice, whose son he had received from the holy font, entreating him never to give his assent to the people so that they might raise him to the glory of this honor. But the prefect of the city, named Germanus, intercepted his messenger, seized him, tore up the letters, and sent the consent expressed by the people to the emperor. The emperor, giving thanks to God for the friendship of the deacon, because he had found the opportunity to confer upon him the honor he desired to give him, ordered that he be ordained.” (From the Acts of Gregory.)

Likewise, in the Acts of Ambrose:

“When the people cried out more and more loudly, ‘Let your sin be upon us,’ and he saw that his intention could accomplish nothing, he prepared to flee. He left the city in the middle of the night, thinking that he was going to Ticinum, but in the morning he was found at the city gate of Milan called the Roman Gate. When he had been found and was being guarded by the people, a report was sent to the most merciful emperor Valentinian, who received it with the greatest joy, because the judge whom he had sent was being sought for the priesthood.”

From these passages and from the chapter cited above it is therefore perfectly clear that the aforementioned pontiffs were elected according to the ancient custom. But since they absolutely refused to be promoted, and since, in the one election, the prefect, acting in place of the Romans, sought the assistance of Maurice, while in the other the people sought the assistance of Valentinian, it is plainly evident, in accordance with chapter 8 of the synod, that the Church invited secular powers to assist her and that, at that time, they acted not by command but by obedience.

This does not seem to us impermissible if it happens that some worthy person gives his consent to his own promotion, while royal power happens to be present in the same diocese, as Valentinian is recorded as having been present in Milan at that time. But to seek such assistance outside the diocese, when the ruler might be absent for a long period, is utterly absurd, since the laws of the holy Fathers have established that they must not leave a church without a pontiff for three months.

As for what is read in the Tripartite History—that the emperor Valentinian said to Ambrose, “God has entrusted souls to you; I entrust bodies”—anyone who reads it will understand how badly it agrees with what precedes. For it seems entirely contradictory both that he said this and that he refused to consent to the election of the pontiff by himself, as the same account relates. This does not conflict with our position, since blessed Gregory affirms that this same History is faulty and rejected by the Roman Church.

There are also those who object that Nicholas the Younger established by a decree of a synod that, when the apostolic pontiff died, a successor should be elected and that his election should be reported to the king. After the election had been held and, as stated, reported to the king, the pontiff was then to be consecrated.

If this is to be admitted as having been done reasonably, we reply, in order to refute it, that the aforementioned king and his nobles made themselves unworthy of that constitution. First, after the aforesaid Nicholas had reproved the archbishop of Cologne for his excesses, they bore it with great resentment and, as far as they were able, deposed him from the papacy for this reason; they also forbade his name to be mentioned in the canon of consecration. Therefore his decree ought in law to be null, because although, according to their own judgment, he was regarded as pope by the whole world, he was not pope for them—as though whether someone was or was not pope depended not on God’s will but solely on theirs. For the Roman pontiff, as wise people know, cannot merely be deposed; indeed, under no Christian law can he be judged by anyone.

Second, although that same decree had provided that the election of the pontiff at Rome should be conducted by the Roman clergy and people and afterward reported to the king, they themselves violated the decree and elected those whom they had no right to elect: first Cadalus of Parma, [Col. 0464B] and afterward Wibert of Ravenna. They clothed them in the insignia of the apostolic office, calling apostates “apostolic men,” the forerunners of Antichrist.

Moreover, the aforementioned Wibert, or his supporters, in order to attribute the support of the decree to their own party, added certain things to it and altered others. Thus they made it so inconsistent with itself that few, if any, copies agreeing with one another can be found. What kind of decree is it when it appears so different from itself that one does not know what in it ought principally to be believed?

But finally, let us strike with an invincible sword: the aforementioned Nicholas, being only one patriarch, together with any council of bishops, could not abolish—indeed, could not even alter—the aforesaid decrees of the five holy patriarchs, which do not conflict with the faith: those of the Roman, Alexandrian, Antiochene, Jerusalemite, and Constantinopolitan patriarchs. And, as may be inferred from the number attached to the aforementioned synods, more than 250 holy Fathers are recorded as having established these constitutions in their own times. In them they are not found to have granted anything to royal power in the election or promotion of pontiffs. Rather, as stated above, while the most Christian emperors were sitting with them and raising no objection, they are recorded as having prohibited such action under perpetual anathema.

If this is to be claimed on the basis of the custom of the Greek emperors, or of the election of Ambrose or Gregory, it is clear, as stated above, that those very emperors rejected such a practice as contrary to God, while the election and promotion of those same pontiffs were, however improperly, brought into agreement with the eighth synod.

Although the decree under discussion is entirely weakened by the aforementioned laws of the Church, let us nevertheless see what the laws of the Church and of the secular world say about it once more, so that it may be completely nullified.

From the synod of Pope Hilary, chapter 4:

“What each bishop has unlawfully committed, or has found to have been committed by his predecessors, he will condemn if he wishes to avoid his own danger. For whatever he does not cut away in another, he will find in himself.”

Gelasius to the bishops Cresconius, John, and Messala, among other matters:

“Just as it is fitting for a successor to preserve the statutes of his predecessors when they are legitimate and just, so he ought also to correct their evil deeds.”

Pelagius to the military commander Armentarius, among other matters: [Col. 0465A]

“After the rights of the Church have been confirmed by the authority of the intervening documents as well, the pontiff must in no way be permitted to have the freedom—or, if he wishes, the license—to depart from them.”

Adrian to Engelramnus:

“Constitutions contrary to the holy decrees of the Roman prelates are of no effect.”

Gregory, in the Register:

“It is plainly established by imperial constitution that things done contrary to the laws are to be regarded not only as useless but also as undone.”

From the Roman laws:

“From the sacred response, let substance be taken only insofar as the aids of the laws support it.”

Likewise:

“A general command is to be preferred to a special privilege.”

And again: [Col. 0465B]

“Rescripts contrary to the law shall have no validity, however they may have been obtained. For judges ought to follow more closely what the public laws prescribe.”

And below:

“Personal rescripts that agree with the law shall be valid according to ancient custom, and the conclusion of the case about which our rescript speaks shall be considered settled by the terms of the sentence already pronounced. But if anything special brings injury to the laws and to justice, let it be abolished and eradicated.”

Likewise:

“Those sacred grants made in response to the desire of each petitioner shall prevail and be put into effect which agree with the rule of law and the laws; but those which may have been obtained by deception or false petitions shall provide no remedy to the petitioners.”

Having reviewed these authorities, it is clear that the aforesaid decree is of no effect and never possessed any legal force. In saying this, I do not prejudice the memory of blessed Pope Nicholas, nor do I detract in any way from his honor; I am following the judgments of the Fathers, which were established by the Spirit of God. He was, after all, a human being, and he could have been deceived into acting contrary to what was right.

Nor is it surprising that this happened to him, since one of his predecessors is found to have decreed something and afterward, having adopted better counsel, to have changed it. Boniface II is indeed recorded to have established by decree that the deacon Vigilius should succeed him in the pontificate. Because the Roman clergy regarded this as contrary to the canons, it was committed to the fire by the same Boniface in the presence of the clergy, before the confession of blessed Peter the Apostle.

Certainly, if the aforementioned Nicholas had been shaken by fear of God and had then seen so many judgments of the Fathers collected together and had recognized how harmoniously they opposed his decree, he would have done the same.

Blessed Augustine also composed the book of Retractations to correct what he had previously written carelessly, and he urges every wise person to do the same in these words. For in the preface to that book he says:

“No one except an impudent person will dare to criticize me by pointing out my errors. But if someone says that I ought not to have said things that afterward displeased even me, he speaks truly and supports me: for he is criticizing things of which I too am a critic. But let each person receive what I am doing as he wishes. Nevertheless, in this matter also I ought to heed the apostolic statement, which says: ‘If we judged ourselves, we would not be judged by the Lord’ (1 Cor. 11).” [Col. 0466A]

The excommunication terrifyingly pronounced in the aforesaid decree is believed to have been inserted by Wibert or by his supporters, since it is expressed quite differently in the older copies of the same decree.

That excommunication will indeed come upon those who inserted it there in their own favor, and upon those who presume to say that it must be feared: upon the former, so that they may fall into the pit they dug and so that the snare they concealed may seize them; upon the latter, because they trembled with fear where there was no fear, since the Lord is in the righteous generation.

For if he is in the righteous generation, he was in the Fathers mentioned above, and he spoke through them. Therefore their curse is to be feared as God’s curse. Concerning the curse of those who do not obey the decrees of those Fathers, the same Lord says through the prophet: “I will bless your curses” (Malachi 2); and again: “They will curse, but you will bless” (Psalm 108).

Solomon says: “As a bird flying contrary to its course, and as any sparrow passing by, so an undeserved curse will come upon the one who sent it” (Proverbs 26).

This I say against the decree by whose authority Wibert defends himself, to show that he is what he is not and never can be.

As for the number of years during which this damnable custom is said to have continued—that secular power should promote pontiffs according to its own will—it cannot rightly be pleaded as a justification. For among various customs, the one that should chiefly be followed is that which, when it began, had Catholic Fathers as its founders, following the footsteps of their own earlier Fathers, just as the Fathers of the seventh and eighth synods followed the statutes of the holy Roman pontiffs, and those pontiffs followed the custom observed throughout all the Churches from the time of the apostles.

The perversity introduced by secular rulers does not prejudice that holy custom, however many years it may have prevailed. Otherwise, our Lord God would be at fault, since he freed the children of Israel after they had been held in bondage for a very long time, first under Pharaoh and then under Cyrus or Darius, and after the passage of five thousand years redeemed the human race, which had long been held in the slavery of the devil, by his own death. [Col. 0466D]

Moreover, since adultery is forbidden by the laws of the Old and New Testaments, if certain kings have committed adultery, will later kings think that they are permitted to commit adultery on the authority of their predecessors? Far from it.

It is certainly established that crimes committed by kings against the laws must in no way be followed, while the laws trampled underfoot by them must remain in force. Hence the holy martyrs of God and the Roman pontiffs inserted the following in their statutes:

“It is not permitted for an emperor, or for anyone who observes piety, to presume to do anything contrary to the commands of the divinity. For an unjust judgment or decision, arranged by judges out of fear of or at the command of a king, shall have no force. Nor shall anything stand that has been done contrary to the constitution of evangelical, prophetic, or apostolic teaching, or to that of the holy Fathers; and whatever has been sanctioned by unbelievers and heretics shall be utterly annulled.” [Col. 0467A]

Likewise, Adrian to Engelramnus the bishop, chapter 48:

“Likewise, by a general decree we establish that whoever among kings or powerful persons henceforth believes, or permits, the rigor of the canons to be violated in any respect shall be subject to accursed anathema and shall always stand guilty before God as a betrayer of the Catholic faith.”

Again, the same author to the same person:

“Constitutions contrary to the holy decrees of the Roman prelates are of no effect.”

But if every plant that the heavenly Father has not planted will be uprooted, and if, as stated above, whatever has been done by unbelievers and heretics will be utterly annulled, should this impiety of the Eutychianist emperors not be annulled and uprooted? Certainly, anyone in the clergy who is not vehemently inflamed by his office to tear up such great wickedness from the house of God by the roots is not consumed with zeal for that same house of God and is regarded before God as a mute dog unable to bark.

For who does not see that this pest is a seedbed of the Simoniac heresy and a lamentable destruction of the whole Christian religion? When it is hoped that episcopal dignity can be obtained from a ruler, God’s Church is abandoned, while its own bishops and clergy are disregarded. Some pour enormous sums of money into the purses of courtiers so that they may earn their support for such a wicked promotion; others serve for more than ten years in the secular court at the cost of endless expense, enduring heat, rain, cold, and every other hardship with the utmost patience; others constantly wish for the death either of their own pastor or of the person whose honor they covet; one person intensely envies another, thinking that what he hopes for himself may be snatched away by that other.

Indeed, alas, they sometimes rush into such great an offense against God that this dignity is granted even to slaves and fornicators. Once such men have obtained what they sought in this way, the secular powers who have sinned do not dare to rebuke them, because they remember that they were promoted by those same powers; indeed, they were promoted so that they would not dare to rebuke them.

These men receive milk and wool, but by living most wickedly they neglect the salvation of everyone. Thus what is written is fulfilled: “Wicked priests are the ruin of the people” (Isaiah 24). And again: “As is the people, so is the priest” (Hosea 4).

Priests do not seem to differ from the people when each eagerly strives to entangle himself in popular activities. For although no one serving God should involve himself in secular business, some of them pursue not the study of the canons but that of dogs and hawks, along with the other luxuries of the world. Others, as though God praised in a priest what he condemned in a rich man, clothe themselves in the skins of foreign animals and, abandoning their cathedral churches, attend upon emperors, even though the canons, created by the Spirit of God, forbid pontiffs to visit royal palaces and instead command them, if anything needs to be proposed, to communicate it through their deacons.

Although the same sacred canons forbid, under threat of punishment, any pontiff to be absent from his cathedral church for three Sundays, some of these men scarcely manage to visit their churches three or four times a year, and even then barely once in an entire year. And, so that they may not sin alone but may become what is written—“a snare of the young” (Isaiah 62)—they give the clergy an example of likewise abandoning their churches and serving in royal courts in the hope of becoming bishops.

It is objected that, in order to perform the divine offices for rulers, clerics ought to reside in their court—as though it were not more just before God and more fitting among human beings for each bishop, when a ruler happens to be present in his diocese, to send suitable and devout clerics to celebrate the divine mysteries for him, and, for as long as the ruler remains there, to order others to succeed one another in their service.

Wishing to oppose the great calamities that result from the promotions described above, Gregory VII, in a Roman synod of fifty bishops, with a multitude of priests and abbots sitting in council, established decrees entirely consonant with the holy Fathers mentioned above, saying:

“If anyone henceforth receives a bishopric or abbey from the hand of any layperson, let him in no way be counted among the bishops, nor let any hearing be granted to him as a bishop or abbot. Moreover, we forbid him the grace of blessed Peter and entrance into the Church until, by repentance, he abandons the position which he has undertaken under the crime both of ambition and of disobedience, which is the sin of idolatry. We establish the same concerning lower ecclesiastical offices and dignities.” [Col. 0468C]

Likewise:

“If any emperor, king, duke, marquis, count, or any secular power or person whatsoever should presume to grant the investiture of bishoprics or of any ecclesiastical dignity, let him know that he is bound by the penalty of the same sentence.”

Since it has been demonstrated by the authority of the saints that the election of pontiffs is not subject to secular power, it is worthwhile to bring forward the constitutions enacted for this reason by the most Christian emperors, so that it may become clear whether they wished to claim any legal right in this matter.

For the glorious emperors Charles and Louis established the following in the first book of their Capitularies:

“Not ignorant of the sacred canons, and so that the holy Church may more freely enjoy her honor in the name of God, we give our assent to the ecclesiastical order: namely, that bishops should be chosen through the election of the clergy and people, according to the statutes of the canons, from their own diocese, with respect for persons and acceptance of gifts excluded, and on account of the merit of their life and the gift of wisdom, so that they may be able to benefit those subject to them by word and example.”

Certainly, this constitution is seen to agree so completely with the constitutions of the holy Fathers that, even if it had been promulgated by the Council of Nicaea or by any of the universal synods, it would be believed to have been spoken no less by the Spirit of God through the mouths of these emperors than through that synod.

For this constitution teaches that this is the honor and this the freedom of the holy Church: that the clergy and people should elect their own pontiff. It recalls that the statutes of the canons are to be observed in the election. It attacks and prohibits the Simoniac heresy. It demonstrates that the merit of life and wisdom are to be sought in the election of a pastor. And, remarkably, it seems briefly to touch upon what blessed Gregory writes concerning a pontiff:

“That each person ought to consider how he comes to the pontificate, how he should teach once he has come to it rightly, and how he should live once he teaches rightly.”

It is therefore clear, by the authority of the holy Roman prelates and of the Fathers of the holy universal synods, the seventh and the eighth, that the election of pontiffs ought to belong to the clergy and people of each church. It is also clear that the most Christian emperors—Constantine, Constans, Valentinian, Theodosius, Arcadius, Honorius, Charles, Louis, and the others distinguished by faith and religion—did not violate the same custom observed from the time of the apostles.

It is further clear that the most Christian emperors Constantine the Great, and likewise Constantine, Irene, Basil, Charles, and Louis, removed the aforesaid election from secular power by law. Even if their enactments had not prohibited this, the authority of the patriarchal sees would have deserved no less obedience.

For God is recorded to have said not to emperors but to pontiffs: “Whatever you bind on earth shall be bound also in heaven, and so forth” (Matthew 18). Likewise, to the first pontiff: “Feed my sheep” (John 21). Likewise, to all the apostles: “Go and teach all nations” (Matthew 28).

The authority of the patriarchs is so great that anyone who attempts to oppose their synodal constitutions is plainly proved to be a heretic. Whatever they jointly establish as to be followed is to be observed by the whole Church; whatever they teach is to be rejected is to be rejected. Their common judgment is never to be retracted by anyone, unless perhaps by those very men themselves.

God placed the foundation of the Christian faith in their sees through blessed Peter, who occupies those sees, in such a way that if one of the three principal patriarchs should fall, two would remain standing; and if two should fall, since Christ was entreated that Peter’s faith should not fail, the faith of the one Roman patriarch—by which he confirms his brothers—would never fail.

Christ our God has already deigned to demonstrate this in the universal synods, which have been celebrated universally eight times since his ascension. When one or two fell away from the faith, the Roman patriarch, though assailed and shaken in the foundation of that same faith, nevertheless stood immovable.

“For heaven and earth will pass away, but his words will not pass away,” he who said: “You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church, and the gates of hell will not prevail against it, and so forth” (Matthew 16).

Let secular powers therefore beware of following what the Eutychianist emperors devised, lest—God forbid—they be punished together with those whose wicked actions they preferred to imitate. Let them permit the holy Churches of God to use their own right and honor: namely, according to the enactments of the holy Fathers, to choose and promote their own pontiffs.

Since we have said above that this pest is a seedbed of the Simoniac heresy, it is worthwhile to rise up against the priests of that heresy and to bring forward the judgments of the Fathers concerning their priesthood and sacrifice.

In the letter of the seventh universal synod addressed to Pope Adrian, the following is read among other matters:

“Those who have laid hands, or do lay hands, through money, divine Peter the Apostle, whose chair your holiness has inherited, deposes as he deposed Simon Magus. For the impious heresy of Macedonius and those around him, who attacked the Holy Spirit, is more tolerable. They, in their madness, confess that the Holy Spirit is a creature and a servant of God the Father and the Son. These men make their own holy spirit a servant.

“For every master who possesses something, if he wishes, sells either a slave or something else that he owns; likewise, the person who buys it, wishing to become master of what he has purchased, acquires it by the price of money. So those who carry out this wicked act insult the Holy Spirit, sinning equally with those who blasphemed by saying that Christ cast out demons by Beelzebub (Luke 11); or, to speak more truly, they are compared with Judas the traitor, who sold Christ to the Jews, the killers of God. Since the Holy Spirit is consubstantial with Christ, they themselves will be his betrayers. And without doubt the grace of the Holy Spirit—that is, the holiness of the priesthood—is not in them. For those who have not received it do not possess it. Peter said to Simon: ‘You have neither part nor share in this matter, because you thought that the gift of God could be possessed for money’ (Acts 8).”

The twenty-eighth canon of the apostles, as well as their Acts, and the Third and Fourth Books of Kings, likewise declare wholly alien from the priesthood anyone who at any time has given or received money in connection with the laying on of hands—whether before the laying on of hands, during the laying on of hands, or after the laying on of hands. For “to receive” means to receive at any time.

Likewise, from the final letter of the same synod:

“Therefore, every bishop, priest, or deacon convicted of having given or received the laying on of hands for money shall fall from both the priesthood and his rank. Perhaps some say: ‘We are doing penance for the sin, and the Lord will forgive it.’ This is true, because God receives all who do penance and, through penance, forgives sins that have already been committed.”

And below:

“But because, according to the Apostle, a priest ought to be irreproachable, anyone who consecrates someone for money, or has been consecrated for money, is alien from the priesthood, as all the children of the Church, instructed in the canonical disciplines, know.”

Likewise, from the letter of Pope Paschal sent to the people of Milan:

“If someone objects that not the consecrations themselves are sold, but the things that result from consecration, he seems to say something, but in fact understands nothing at all. For just as a bishop or abbot of the bodily Church can accomplish nothing without bodily and external possessions, just as the soul cannot live temporally without the body, whoever sells one of two things without which he cannot possess the other leaves neither unsold.

“The sacred canon of Chalcedon completely destroys this objection, since it forbids a procurator or defender of the Church, or anyone subject to the Church, to be ordained for money to such an extent that it also cuts down, with the sword of anathema, those who participate in so great a crime.”

What more is there to say? If, as true heretics, Simoniacs and neophytes who have been anathematized and excommunicated are separated from the Church, who does not see that the masses and prayers of such priests provoke God to anger against the people, whereas we had believed that God could be appeased by such men?

For it is written: “The place of the true sacrifice is not outside the Catholic Church.” And again: “Avoid a heretical person after the first and second correction” (Titus 3).

When, therefore, we do not avoid such bishops, abbots, or other clerics, but listen to their masses or pray with them, we incur excommunication together with them. To believe that such men are even priests is altogether erroneous, since Peter says to Simon:

“May your money be with you for destruction, because you thought that the gift of God could be possessed for money” (Acts 8).

When it says “you thought,” he is condemned not for having done the thing but because he believed that he could do it; and thinking is less than believing. In what follows—“You have neither part nor share in this matter” (ibid.)—it is plainly shown that nothing of sacred ordination is received through this promotion.

Likewise, from the Register of blessed Gregory, to Sigius, among other matters:

“Why is it not considered, why is it not understood, that the blessing is turned into a curse for the one who is promoted so that he may become a heretic?”

Likewise, in the same work:

“It is an altogether grave crime, beyond what can be expressed, to sell the Holy Spirit, who redeemed all things.”

Likewise, Ambrose, in the Pastoral:

“This is precisely what I lament too deeply: that when the archbishop specifically ordained someone as a bishop for money, he ordained a leper.”

Likewise, in the same work:

“What he received was money; what he gave was leprosy.”

Likewise, in the same work:

“By giving gold, you lost it, and you did not acquire holy grace.”

So much for the priesthood of the Simoniacs. Now let us examine the judgments of the Fathers concerning their sacrifice.

Cyprian, in his letter to Cornelius:

“Does anyone suppose that something so great and so important could happen in the Church of God without God’s knowledge or permission, and that priests—that is, God’s stewards—would not be ordained according to his judgment? To think this is to lack the faith by which we live; it is not to honor God.

“But priests are not ordained according to his judgment when they are made outside the Church, just as the Lord himself says in the Twelve Prophets: ‘They have appointed kings for themselves, but not through me’ (Hosea 8).”

And again:

“Their sacrifices are like bread of mourning; all who eat them will be defiled” (Hosea 9).

And through Isaiah the Holy Spirit cries out and says:

“Woe to you, rebellious children, says the Lord. You have made a plan, but not through me, and you have made an alliance, but not through my Spirit, adding sin upon sin” (Isaiah 30).

Jerome, on the Twelve Prophets:

“God hates the sacrifices of heretics and casts them away from himself. Whenever they assemble under the name of the Lord, he will detest their stench and close his nostrils. To say that he hates, casts away, and does not smell them is human language, so that we may recognize God’s disposition through our own words.

“Even if they offer holocausts, even if they seem to fast, give alms, and promise chastity—things that are true holocausts—the Lord does not accept them. For he does not look at the greatness of the sacrifices but at the will of those who offer them.”

Pelagius to Viator and Pangratius, among other matters:

“You ought to abstain from the sacrifices, or rather the sacrileges, of schismatics.”

Likewise, in the same letter:

“What a schismatic consecrates is not the body of Christ. For no one can assert, without the Apostle’s condemnation, that Christ can be divided. It is established, as has often been said, that there is one Church, which is the body of Christ, and that it cannot be divided into two or more parts. For in the same way, when someone departs from it, it ceases to be the Church. There is one temple in Jerusalem; whoever divides himself must necessarily sacrifice to idols.”

Gregory, in the Register:

“We can in no way call it a consecration when it has been celebrated by excommunicated men.”

These matters are so clear and manifest that they require no elucidation. For they most plainly demonstrate that the priesthood and sacrifices of the Simonians are invalid, although someone has written that, just as in the baptism of the Simonians, so also in their sacrifice the power of the Holy Spirit cooperates—namely, not so that the sacrifice itself is true and salutary for them, but for those to whom it is administered. This is most clearly refuted by the statements of the Fathers cited above, and especially [Col. 0472D] by the saying: “Their sacrifices shall be to them as bread of mourning; all who eat them shall be defiled” (Hosea IX). For the administration of baptism and of the Lord’s-body sacrifice cannot in every respect be compared as though they were conferred in the same manner. When necessity presses, anyone who has been baptized is permitted to baptize, provided that he uses the interrogation of faith, the name of the Trinity, and triple immersion. This permission was granted on account of one who is threatened by the danger of death, so that, if one were then to run to a priest and the priest were not present, it might not suddenly prove impossible to find someone to administer baptism. Only priests, however, are permitted to confect the Lord’s body; and this is not necessary for one who has not been baptized and is immediately about to die. Baptism precedes reception of the Lord’s body, [Col. 0473A] and therefore it is necessary that a person be baptized by anyone at all before the dying person seeks the Lord’s body. It is more grievous, indeed, for someone to depart from human affairs without baptism than for someone who has been baptized to die without communion in the Eucharist, although one who could receive both will not be saved without both. For the one who said, “Unless someone is born again of water and the Spirit, he will not enter the kingdom of God” (John III), also said, “Unless you eat the bread of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you will not have life in yourselves” (John VI). I have spoken of the power to receive both because a child newly born and newly baptized cannot eat the Lord’s flesh, although it can barely swallow his blood when it has been poured into its mouth. [Col. 0473B] For what is said—“Unless you eat”—must, I think, be understood of those who are able to eat. No one says this of one who cannot eat, but of one who can.

When these matters have been reviewed, it seems necessary to say that the heresy of the Arians, Sabellians, Macedonians, and Photinians, and every general heresy, has ceased from attacking the holy Church of God—and that, if any heresy is thereafter thought capable of arising, it will cease because God fights on behalf of the same Church. This heresy, however—that of the Simonians—which at the beginning of the Church’s birth immediately took up arms against it, will continue to attack it until the end of the age, as the devil finds standard-bearers and followers for himself, and will not cease to do so for the Church’s testing. “For there must be heresies,” as the blessed Apostle says, “so that those who are approved may become manifest” (I Corinthians XI). [Col. 0473C]

It must be observed, however, that Christ God, who promised to build his Church upon the rock of faith, set the apostle who was the first of all heretics against it—namely, so that just as the Church, that is, the multitude of believers, knows that it must always follow Peter’s faith, so it might remember forever to flee the poisonous and deadly fellowship of that same wicked heresy, against whose head the chief of all Christians is known to have hurled the dart of a curse. Since these things are so, whoever, according to his ability, ceases to oppose this pestilence will have a share with Simon and his followers, as the blessed Gregory says: “Whoever, according to the position of his office, does not vigorously stand against the heresy of the Simonians and the Neophytes should not doubt that he has a share with him who first committed this abominable crime.” [Col. 0473D]

It must also be known that it is one thing to be a heretic and another to be a schismatic. A heretic is one who abandons the faith of the Catholic Church and chooses to follow the path of his own error or that of another. Likewise, according to blessed Isidore: “One who interprets Holy Scripture otherwise than the meaning required by the Holy Spirit, by whom it was written, may be called a heretic, even if he has not departed from the Church.””

A schismatic, however, is one who pretends to confess the right faith but arrogantly despises the traditions of the holy Fathers and, through some hostile intent, cuts himself off from the unity of the Church.

Likewise, according to Saint Augustine: “A heretic is one who does not follow Catholic truth. A schismatic is one who does not embrace Catholic peace.” [Col. 0474A]

Likewise, Pope Pelagius, in his *Register*, introduces blessed Augustine defining schism in a letter to the patrician Valerian; among other things: “Consider whether those are not schismatics who have separated themselves from the most exalted and manifest authority of the apostolic sees.”

Likewise, the same Pelagius, in his letter to Viator and Pangratius, introduces Augustine saying: “Whoever rashly believes against the authority of those Churches that have been deemed worthy to receive the apostolic sees and letters will not be able to drive away from himself the monstrous crime of schism.”

Since these things are so, it is clear from them that those who follow the authority of the apostolic Churches are the Church; but that those who, contrary to the prescribed authorities of the apostolic sees and the holy Fathers, attempt to ordain more than two hundred bishops in the Church of God are schismatics in every respect. [Col. 0474B]

“According to the Council of Antioch, however, if a schismatic persists in creating disturbances and seditions in the Church, he is to be restrained by external authorities as a seditious person.” — “For many things,” says Augustine, “must be done even against the unwilling, with a certain benevolent severity, for the sake of those whose welfare ought to be considered rather than their will. For in correcting a son, however severely, paternal love is never lost. Yet what he would not wish is done so that he may suffer; and even though unwilling, he appears to suffer in order to be healed.”

[Col. 0474C] Likewise Pelagius to the patrician Valerian: “Only the one who compels someone to evil persecutes him. But whoever either punishes an evil already committed or prevents it from being committed does not persecute but loves. For if, as some think, no one should be restrained from evil or drawn back toward good, human and divine laws would necessarily be abolished; for, with justice urging them, they establish punishment for the wicked and rewards for the good. Schism, however, is evil and must also be suppressed by external authorities.” [Col. 0474D]

Therefore, if, as is clear from these statements, schismatics are to be suppressed by external authorities, are the Simonians not likewise to be suppressed by them? Do they offend less? On the contrary, they offend more. For if Christ the Son of God, his Spirit, and the Father are equal in all respects, will not the Jew and the Simonian, who sell the one and the other respectively, be equals? Furthermore, since it is established from the authorities cited above that the Simonian buys the Paraclete, while the Jew is plainly shown to have bought Christ, will it not be established that they are to be regarded as equal in wickedness and merit? Indeed, this seems to be the case.

It is therefore clear that the Simonians, as the first and foremost heretics, are to be rejected by all the faithful and, if they do not repent when admonished, are also to be suppressed by external authorities. “For it is to be feared,” says Gregory, “that anyone, according to his office and position, may not burn fiercely against them and oppose their detestable error with all his strength.” [Col. 0475A] “For error,” says Pope Innocent, “which is not resisted is approved, and truth, when it is not defended at all, is suppressed.” Likewise he says: “To neglect, when you are able to drive out the perverse, is nothing other than to encourage them.”

Augustine: “Whoever conceals the truth through fear of any authority provokes God’s anger upon himself, because he fears a human being more than God.”

Ambrose: “To consent is not only knowingly to permit evil to be done, but also not to pursue evil deeds.”

Gregory: “Whoever does not correct what must be cut away commits it.” Likewise, in the *Moralia*: “Often we are left undisturbed and unshaken if, for the sake of justice, we do not take care to oppose the wicked. But if the soul has been inflamed with desire for eternal life, if it already beholds the true light inwardly, if the flame of holy fervor has been kindled within it, then, insofar as the place permits and the cause requires, we must offer ourselves for the defense of justice and oppose those who rush into injustice, even when they do not seek opposition from us. For when they strike the justice that we love in others, they nevertheless pierce us by their blow, even if they appear to honor us.” [Col. 0475B]

And since some offend through ignorance, others through negligence, and still others through the obstinacy of pride, it is best first to deal more lightly and gently with these people and with the schismatics, and to pray for them, “lest perhaps,” as the Apostle says, “God should give them a reprobate mind, so that, if they come to their senses, they may escape from the snares of the devil, by whom they are held captive” [Col. 0476A] (Romans I; II Timothy II). But if the Simonians and schismatics alike do not yield to reason, they are to be cut off from the body of the Church as incurable members and, as has been said, suppressed by external authorities.

It must be known that Augustine wrote to a certain Peter concerning all heretics and schismatics: “Hold most firmly, and do not doubt in any way, that every heretic and schismatic, no matter how many alms he gives or even how much blood he sheds for Christ, is destined with the devil and his angels for eternal fire unless, before the end of this life, he is incorporated into and restored to the Catholic Church.” [Col. 0476B]

Thus far enough has been said against those who claim that the Church of God and the ordination of its pontiffs are subject to royal authority, and against the priesthood and sacrifice of the Simonians. It remains now to speak of the resources of the Church, which those same people contend must remain under royal control.

[Col. 0475]

# COLLECTIONS OF SAINT ANSELM

*(In Canisius, Ancient Readings, vol. VI, p. 235.)*

## TO THE READER

In the manuscript codex that we used, the following statements were appended. They seem to have been collected by Anselm himself from various authors, and in them he seeks to demonstrate that the resources of the Church are not in the power of a king or Caesar. It follows that what comes next is either a second part of the second book or the third book of the entire work. Whether, however, nothing is missing, you may reasonably doubt.

## [COLLECTIONS]

### Albinus, in the Second Book on Matthew

[Col. 0475C]

“Jesus found in the Temple those selling oxen, sheep, and doves, and the money-changers sitting; and when he had made something like a whip from cords, he drove them all out of the Temple, the sheep and oxen as well, and poured out the money of the money-changers and overturned their tables” (Matthew XXI; John II).

Oxen, sheep, and doves were bought for the purpose of being offered in the Temple. The money-changers sat at tables so that the price of the sacrifices might readily be assessed between those buying and selling them. They therefore appeared to be selling lawfully in the Temple, because they were bought in order to be offered to the Lord in that same Temple. But the Lord himself, unwilling that anything belonging to earthly commerce—even commerce thought honest—should be displayed in his house, drove out the unjust dealers and expelled them all together with the things in which they traded. What, then, my brothers, do we think the Lord would do if he found people quarrelling in disputes, wasting their time in chatter, dissolving into laughter, or entangled in any other crime, when he saw in the Temple people buying sacrifices to be offered to him and hastened to drive them out? [Col. 0475D]

[Col. 0476C] We have said this on account of those who, having entered the church, not only neglect the intention of praying but also increase the very things for which they ought to have prayed; and who, moreover, pursue those who rebuke them for such folly with insults, hatred, or even slander, thereby adding sins to sins and, as it were, weaving for themselves an exceedingly long rope through their heedless accumulation of them, without fearing that they will be condemned by the examination of the strict Judge. For we read twice in the holy Gospel that, when the Lord came into the Temple, he expelled such dealers: first, namely three years before his Passion, as we learn from the subsequent writings of the Evangelist John; and again in the very year in which he suffered, when, five days before Passover, he came to Jerusalem seated on a donkey. Everyone who thinks rightly understands that he carries out this same action in the Temple of the holy Church through the examination of his daily visitation. [Col. 0476D]

Therefore these things are greatly to be feared, beloved, and dreaded with fitting apprehension; we must diligently take care that, when he comes unexpectedly, he does not find in us something perverse for which we rightly ought to be scourged and expelled from the church. Above all, this must be observed in that place which is specially called a house of prayer: we must do nothing foolish, lest with the Corinthians we hear from the Apostle, “Do you not have houses” for conducting or discussing temporal affairs, “or do you despise the Church of God?” (I Corinthians II.) The prophet likewise says to the Jews: “My beloved has committed many crimes in my house” (Jeremiah VI). [Col. 0477A]

Indeed, we should rejoice because in baptism we ourselves have become the Temple of God, as the Apostle testifies when he says: “The Temple of God is holy, and that is what you are” (I Corinthians III). We ourselves are the city of the great King, of which it is said: “Its foundations are in the holy mountains” (Psalm LXXXVI)—that is, the foundations of the Church rest upon the solidity of the faith of the apostles and prophets. [Col. 0477B] But it is greatly to be feared because the Apostle first added: “If anyone violates the Temple of God, God will destroy him” (I Corinthians III). And the just Judge himself says: “I will destroy from the city of the Lord all who work iniquity” (Psalm C).

Rejoice because the solemnity of Passover is enacted in us when we strive to pass from vices to virtues; for Passover means “passage.” Rejoice because the Lord deigns to visit our breasts—namely, his own city—and to illuminate this Passover of our good action by the presence of his compassion. But we must greatly fear lest he find us in his city doing something other than what he loves, and lest he, as a strict retributer, show himself to us as one whom we do not love; lest, finding us in the Temple as money-changers, or sellers of oxen, sheep, [Col. 0477C] or doves, he condemn us.

Oxen signify the teaching of heavenly life; sheep, works of purity and devotion; doves, the Holy Spirit. For a field is ordinarily cultivated with the help of oxen; and the Lord’s field is the human heart cultivated by heavenly teaching and rightly prepared to receive the words of God. Sheep innocently provide their fleeces for clothing human beings, and the Spirit descended upon the Lord in the form of a dove.

Those sell oxen who offer the word of the Gospel to their hearers not out of divine love but with an eye to earthly profit. The Apostle censures such people because they proclaim Christ “not sincerely” (Philippians I). Those sell sheep who perform works of devotion for the sake of human praise; of them the Lord says: “They have received their reward” (Matthew VI). Those sell doves who give the grace of the Spirit that they have received not “freely” (Matthew X), as commanded, but for a reward; who confer the laying-on by which the Spirit is received, even if not for monetary gain, nevertheless for the favor of the crowd; and who bestow sacred orders not for the merit of life but for favor. Those lend money at interest in the Temple who serve heavenly things deceitfully but earthly matters openly within the Church, seeking their own interests rather than those of Jesus Christ (Philippians II). [Col. 0477D]

The Lord shows what reward awaits such fraudulent workers when, having made a whip from cords, he drove them all out of the Temple. Those are expelled from the portion and lot of the saints who, placed among the saints, either falsely perform good works or openly perform evil ones. He also drove out the sheep and oxen because he showed that both the lives and the teaching of such people are rejected. [Col. 0478A]

The cords with which he scourged the impious and drove them from the Temple are the increase of evil actions, by which material is supplied for condemning the reprobate by the strict Judge. Hence Isaiah says: “Woe to those who draw iniquity with cords of vanity” (Isaiah V). And Solomon says in Proverbs: “His own iniquities capture the wicked, and he is bound with the cords of his sins” (Proverbs V). For one who accumulates sins upon sins, by which he may be condemned more severely, gradually lengthens, as it were, the cords by which he is bound and scourged.

He also poured out the money of the money-changers whom he had expelled and overturned their tables, because at the end he will take away from the condemned reprobate even the form of the very things they loved, in accordance with what is written: “The world will pass away, and its desire as well” (I John II). [Col. 0478B]

And to those who were selling doves he said: “Take these things away from here; do not make my Father’s house a house of commerce” (John II). He commands that the sale of doves be removed from the Temple because the grace of the Spirit must be received freely and given freely. Hence Simon Magus, who wished to buy this grace with money in order to sell it for a higher price, heard: “May your money be with you unto perdition; you have neither part nor lot in this matter” (Acts III).

It should be noted that not only are those sellers of doves who, by conferring sacred orders, seek payment in money, praise, or even honor making God’s house a house of commerce, [Col. 0478C] but so also are those who exercise a spiritual rank or grace in the Church, which they have received by God’s gift, not with a simple intention but for the sake of some human recompense. This is contrary to the words of the Apostle Peter: “Whoever speaks, as the words of God; whoever ministers, as from the strength that God supplies, so that in all things God may be glorified through Jesus Christ” (I Peter IV). Therefore, whoever is of this kind, if he does not wish to be removed from the Church when the Lord comes, should remove these things from his actions, lest he make God’s house a house of commerce.

### In the Same Work

“Out of zeal for his Father’s house, the Savior expelled the impious from the Temple.”

[Col. 0478D] Let us also be zealous, dearest brothers, for the house of God, and insofar as we can, let us strive to prevent anything perverse from being done in it. If we see a brother who belongs to the house of God swollen with pride, accustomed to slander, enslaved to drunkenness, enervated by luxury, disturbed by anger, or subject to any other vice, let us strive, insofar as our ability permits, to chastise and correct what is polluted and perverse. If we cannot amend anything of this kind, let us endure it only with the sharpest grief of mind. Above all, in the very house of prayer, where the Lord’s body is consecrated and where the presence of angels is always believed to be present, let us use all our strength to prevent anything foolish from being done, anything that might impede our own prayer or that of our brother.

### On John

“Jesus, bending down, was writing with his finger on the ground” (John VIII).

[Col. 0479A]

Through Jesus’ bending, humility is expressed; through the finger, which is flexible through the articulation of its joints, the subtlety of discernment is signified. Through the ground, moreover, the human heart is represented, which is accustomed to yield the fruits of either evil or good actions.

When the Lord was asked to judge the adulterous woman, he did not immediately pronounce judgment. First he bent down and wrote with his finger on the ground, and only then, after being earnestly entreated, did he judge. In this he teaches us figuratively that, when we observe any faults in our neighbors, we should not judge them by rebuking them before we have humbly returned to our own conscience, carefully examined it with the finger of discernment, and diligently distinguished what pleases or displeases the Creator within it, in accordance with the Apostle’s saying: “Brothers, if someone is overtaken in any transgression, you who are spiritual should restore such a person in a spirit of gentleness, keeping watch over yourself, lest you also be tempted” (Galatians VI). [Col. 0479B]

When they persisted in questioning him, he straightened up and said to them: “Let the one among you who is without sin be the first to throw a stone at her” (John VIII). The scribes and Pharisees had set traps for the Lord for this reason: they thought that he would either prove merciless in judging or unjust. Foreseeing their deceits, he passed through them as a thread passes through a spider’s web, displaying in every respect the judgment of justice and the gentleness of compassion.

Behold the moderation of mercy: “The one among you who is without sin.” Behold again the justice of judgment: [Col. 0479C] “Let him be the first to throw a stone at her.” It is as though he had said: “If Moses commanded you to stone such a woman, see to it that he commanded this not sinners but the just to do. First fulfill the justice of the Law yourselves, and then, with innocent hands and a pure heart, come together to stone the guilty woman. First perfect the spiritual ordinances of the Law—faith, mercy, and charity—and then turn to judging carnal matters.”

After judgment had been pronounced, the Lord again bent down and wrote on the ground. In accordance with ordinary human custom, it may be understood that the Lord wished to bend down and write on the ground before his wicked tempters so that, directing his face elsewhere, he might give free opportunity for departure to those whom he foresaw would leave more quickly after being struck by his answer than continue questioning him. Finally, when they heard this, they went out one by one, beginning with the elders. [Col. 0479D]

Figuratively, however, he admonishes us by the fact that, both before and after delivering judgment, he bent down and wrote on the ground. Thus, both before we correct a sinful neighbor and after we have rendered him the service of due correction, we should examine ourselves through a worthy investigation of humility, lest perhaps we be entangled either in the same offenses that we rebuke in them or in any other crimes. For it could happen that the very person who judged a murderer deserving of death might himself, through hatred of his brother, be found guilty of death before the eyes of the Creator. Similarly, one who accuses a brother of the crime of fornication might fail to see in himself the crime of pride. Therefore the judge of another’s crime is commanded to write it on his own heart with the finger of discernment, lest he be found guilty in himself.

What remedy, then, what means of salvation remains for us amid such dangers, except that, when we see another sinning, we immediately bend down—that is, humbly consider how fallen we are by the condition of our weakness if divine compassion does not sustain us—and write with our finger on the ground, that is, carefully weigh through discernment whether we can say with blessed Job: “For my heart does not reproach me throughout all my life” (Job XVII). [Col. 0480A]

### From the Decrees of Pope and Martyr Stephen

[Col. 0480B]

The ecclesiastical vestments with which the Lord is served must be both consecrated and respectable. No one should use them for purposes other than ecclesiastical and worthy divine offices, nor should they be touched or carried by anyone except consecrated persons. Otherwise the vengeance that struck Belshazzar may come upon those who transgress and presume such things and cause them to fall into the depths. Make this known in the regions where you reside and to all whom you can, and ensure that it is observed by apostolic command and authority. For those who are ours and those entrusted to us in the apostolic see and in the universal Church have all professed that these things must be observed now and in future times.

### Pope Innocent to the Bishops of Apulia

The canons established at Nicaea exclude penitents even from the lowest clerical offices.

### From the Decrees of Pope Siricius

[Col. 0480C]

It was also fitting for us to provide that, just as no cleric is permitted to undertake penance, so after penance and reconciliation no layman may ever attain clerical rank. For although they may have been cleansed from the contagion of all sins, they should not receive the instruments for administering the sacraments if they were formerly vessels of vices.

### From the Decrees of Pope Leo I

No layman, supported by any influence, should ascend to the first, second, or third rank in the Church before reaching that distinction through legitimate stages of advancement. For what we now tolerate as somehow venial will later be unable to remain unpunished if anyone presumes to usurp what we absolutely forbid. Remission of sin does not grant permission to sin, nor may what could in some way be permitted thereafter lawfully be committed with impunity. [Col. 0480D]

### From the Twelfth Council of Toledo

If a deacon or priest commits a capital crime, he is to be deprived of the honor of his office and confined in a monastery, where, for as long as he lives, he is to receive only lay communion.

### From the Canons of Pope Sylvester

No lector or acolyte should dare to touch the sacred vessels, and no subdeacon should hand to another anything already consecrated by a priest. For one thing is a minister and another an assistant; unless he merely supports what the priest places in his hands, blessed by the priest’s own mouth. [Col. 0481A]

### From the Same Source

If anyone wishes to earn clerical rank, it is right that he should serve one year as doorkeeper, twenty years as lector, ten years as exorcist, five years as acolyte, five years as subdeacon, and five years as deacon. Thus let him approach the honor of the presbyterate. After serving six years in that order, if he has the favorable vote of all—not through payment or an invasion arising from greed, and without breaking through anyone’s rank—let him be chosen by the entire Church for consecration as bishop, with no member of the Church objecting and with the entire Church in agreement. And the bishops said: “It is approved.”

### Pope Innocent on the Time to Be Spent in the Clergy

[Col. 0481B] The periods established by the elders must certainly be observed among them, so that no one quickly becomes a lector, quickly an acolyte, quickly a deacon, or quickly a priest. For if they remain for a long time in the lesser offices, both their life and their service are tested, so that afterward they may come to the priesthood after having completed the meritorious stages of service, and may not seize in advance what a proven life deserves.

### From the Decrees of Pope Zosimus

The periods to be observed in each rank are as follows. If someone has given his name to ecclesiastical ministries from childhood, he should remain continuously among the lectors until the twentieth year of his age. If he comes when already older and advanced in years, he should nevertheless, if after baptism he desires immediately to devote himself to the divine service, be retained for five years either among the lectors or among the exorcists. Thereafter he should serve four years as an acolyte or subdeacon, and then, if he deserves it, approach the blessing of the diaconate. In that order he must remain for five years if he has conducted himself blamelessly. Thereafter, with the stages of service given in support and with evidence of his own faith, he may earn the priesthood of the presbyterate.

From that position, if a life more strictly devoted to good morals has advanced him, he should hope for the highest pontificate. This law must nevertheless be observed: neither a bigamist nor a penitent may be admitted to these ranks. The defenders of the Church who come from the laity are likewise bound by the aforesaid observance if they have proved worthy of belonging to the clerical order. [Col. 0481C]

### Sylvester at the Synod Confirming the Council of Nicaea, with 275 Bishops Subscribing

[Col. 0481D] I admonish all of you, united associates, concerning the revenues of the Church: four parts are to be made, and each portion is to be assigned. The Church is to have one part for its own support; the pontiff, one; another is for the poor or pilgrims; and the fourth is for the priests and deacons together with the remaining clergy, with the pontiff himself administering everything.

I also establish this rule: if someone from the clergy or the presbyters of any place, in what is held in common, passes from this world, and has no one from his family, whatever his poverty possesses is to be contributed to the Church by his associates, and the portions are to be made as stated above.

The Nicene Synod in turn subscribed to and approved this synod, as Pope Leo IX bears witness in his letter to Michael and Leo, bishops. There, introducing the first chapter of this council, he speaks thus concerning the apostolic see: “You are indeed doing prejudice to one concerning whom neither you nor any mortal is permitted to render judgment: the most blessed and apostolic pontiff Sylvester, who, by divine decree, and with his spiritual son, the most religious Augustus Constantine, with the entire Nicene Synod approving and subscribing, decreed that the highest see be judged by no one.” [Col. 0482A]

### From a Decree of Pope Alexander

Since the authority of the sacred canons commands that the Church’s resources be divided into four portions, one of which is to be spent on the poor, another on the buildings of the churches, a third to be given to the bishop, and a fourth to the clergy, just as individual portions are to be granted to the poor and to the churches, [Col. 0482B] so likewise the remaining portions are neither to be bought nor sold by the bishop or clergy, but are to be assigned to them in the same manner for the proclamation of the Gospel and for the labor of their office.

### From the Decrees of Pope Gelasius

Four portions are to be made from both revenue and the offerings of the faithful, insofar as the resources of each church permit, as was reasonably decreed long ago: one for the pontiff, another for the clergy, a third for the poor, and a fourth to be applied to the buildings.

Just as it is the priest’s responsibility to pay the full amount mentioned to the ministers of the Church, so the clergy should understand that they must not insolently demand anything beyond the sum assigned to them. The amounts assigned to ecclesiastical buildings should truly be devoted to this work; the restoration of the places of the saints should make this evident. For it is wicked if, while sacred buildings are neglected, a bishop converts to his own profit the expenses designated for them. [Col. 0482C]

Likewise, even if he appears able to demonstrate that he has distributed the portion assigned to the poor according to divine accounting, nevertheless, in accordance with what is written—“so that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven” (Matthew V)—it ought also to be proclaimed by present testimony and not be silenced in the praises of a good reputation.

### From the Council of Mainz, Presided Over by Boniface, Archbishop and Martyr, by the Authority of Pope Zachary, Chapter 10

The churches established in ancient times are not to be deprived either of tithes or of any possession, so that these may be assigned to new oratories. [Col. 0482D]

### From the Same, Chapter 41

Whoever holds an ecclesiastical benefice must assist fully in restoring the roofs of the church or repairing the churches themselves, and must render the ninth and the tenth.

### From the Council of Aquileia, Chapter 3

No priest is permitted to celebrate baptism in another place except in the same place where baptisteries have always existed from ancient times.

### From the Same Council, Chapter 3

The tithes given by the faithful people are to be brought into the baptismal churches. The priests who have been appointed over those same congregations are to care with all diligence for the Christian people entrusted to them, and the people are to offer their tithes to their own priests. The priests are to divide them into four portions, as the ancient rule of the Fathers contains: one for themselves, one for the clergy, one for the poor, and one for the restoration, lights, or incense of the churches. We further establish that the aforesaid priests are to have, near their church or within their own dwelling, an appointed place where the fourth portion—which we have instructed is to be given to the poor—is to be deposited. [Col. 0483A]

### From the Register of Pope Leo IV

Concerning tithes, it has seemed right not only to us but also to our predecessors that they should be given to congregations only where the sacred baptisms are administered.

### Pope Gelasius to the Bishops Maximus and Eusebius

[Col. 0483B] Although ancient rules state that the parishes assigned to each church by the original arrangement cannot be taken away for any reason, lest, through a very bad custom and the rashness of an evil example continually increasing, universal confusion arise everywhere, we recently ordered in our decrees that everything which had been invaded in this way should be restored.

But since those who seize things think that persistence in retaining their crime can create a law for themselves, we wish you to carry out what we decreed between our brother and fellow bishop Constantine, priest of the Church of Comiscana, and the representatives sent by the bishop of Ancona. At that time we wrote out the form to be followed in other matters as well.

Therefore, by no presumption do we permit the established condition of parishes, which has endured with the permanence of an eternal age, to be changed. For neither the negligence of a pontiff, nor a temporary abandonment that may arise through carelessness, nor an acquiescence produced by laziness, nor an instruction obtained through furtive petition can tear apart a diocese once constituted, from which the devout people has always assembled for regeneration and confirmation. [Col. 0483C]

### The Same to the Archdeacon Justinus and Faustus: On Dividing the Church’s Property into Four Parts

We have judged it appropriate to make provision for you and your reputation, so that, in place of your bishop, someone may be appointed among you who will likewise administer everything in his name. Thus you should bring all estates back under your care, and you should not think that any single plot of church land is to be assigned to any cleric as his portion, lest it be diminished through carelessness and negligence. Instead, you are to bring to the bishop the entire amount of the rent collected from all rural and urban estates.

From this collection, however, an account must be made of what is seen to be required for causes or expenses arising from necessary needs, so that it may be set aside from the common fund. From the whole rent, the four portions or the offerings of the faithful are in every respect to be made, so that the bishop takes one for himself, another the cleric distributes according to his judgment and choice, and a third he causes to be distributed to the poor in the knowledge of all. [Col. 0483D]

As for what belongs to the buildings, we decree that it is to be paid out at the bishop’s direction through your expenditure. If anything remains from the annual expenses, it is to be placed in chests under the custody of a suitable person chosen by both parties, so that, if a greater building project arises, it may serve as assistance; these funds can be preserved through the diligence of successive periods. Alternatively, a possession may be purchased that will serve the common interests. [Col. 0484A]

### From the Council of Orléans, Chapter 7
Everything that is offered to God is to be regarded as consecrated—vineyards, lands, forests, utensils, clothing, livestock, and other possessions—so that whatever is offered to churches is without doubt offered to Christ, who is their bridegroom.

On the same matter. From the Council of Rouen, chapter 3.

All tithes of the land—whether from the fruit of trees or from crops—belong to the Lord, and are consecrated to him. Oxen, sheep, and goats that pass beneath the shepherd’s staff: whatever comes as the tenth shall be consecrated to the Lord. It shall not be selected, whether good or bad, nor shall it be exchanged for another. If anyone exchanges it, both what he exchanges and what is received in exchange shall be consecrated to the Lord and shall not be redeemed. But because many are now found unwilling to pay tithes, we decree that, in accordance with the commandment of our Lord, they be admonished once and a third time; if they do not correct their conduct, they shall be bound by the sentence of anathema until they make suitable satisfaction and amendment.

From the Council of Chalon-sur-Saône, chapter 3.

Certain brothers also complained that there were some bishops and abbots who would not allow tithes to be given to the churches where those tenants heard Mass. Therefore this holy assembly decreed that bishops and abbots shall arrange for tithes to be brought to the churches from the fields and vineyards that they possess for their own support or that of their brothers; but the members of the household shall give their tithes where their children are baptized and where they hear Mass throughout the entire annual cycle.

From the Council of Toledo, chapter 36.

Of those offerings, moreover, which are made at the altars, one quarter shall faithfully be delivered to the bishops, two parts to the clergy, and, according to some authorities, one tenth each year shall be a third part, or the whole in the third year. Nevertheless, following the Romans, we decree that the bishops shall receive each year one quarter, or the whole in the fourth year.

From the Council of Mainz, chapter 8.

According to the canons, the offerings of the faithful must be divided into four parts: one for the bishop, another for the clergy, a third for the poor, and the fourth to be reserved for the restoration of the churches.

From the Council of Agrippina.

Likewise, the tithe given by the faithful is to be called God’s census, and therefore must be rendered in full. According to the canon of Toledo, one third of it ought to belong to the bishops. We, however, do not wish to exercise this authority, but wish to receive from it only one quarter each year, following the usage of the Roman pontiffs and the observance of the holy Roman Church. If anyone is found to oppose this contentiously—whether cleric or layman—he shall be deprived of communion and judged by synodal censure.

[CANONICAL COLLECTION.]

[Col. 0485]

MAY’S NOTICE ON THE FOLLOWING COLLECTION OF CANONS.

(*Spicilegium Romanum*, vol. VI, pp. 312–394.)

I shall place Saint Anselm of Lucca, who lived with Gregory, his close friend, first among the scholars of canon law. At Gregory’s urging, as is believed, he wrote his canonical treatise, divided into thirteen books. At least until his own time, no work was considered more copious, more learned, more celebrated, or more useful. The summaries of his work, now published by me, will demonstrate this.

But concerning this distinguished work of Anselm I shall offer only a few words, almost none at all, because many others have spoken about it, most recently the illustrious P. Augustine Theiner (*Critical Investigations*, chapter 6 [Note: [Col. 0485] See the first appendix below. EDITORS OF THE *PATROLOGIA*.]), whose immeasurable knowledge of canon law, drawn from ancient sources, who could equal? He concludes his excellent discussion of Anselm’s *Collection* as follows:

“Finally, the single and unanimous judgment of learned men is that Saint Anselm of Lucca’s collection should be printed.”

In fact, Lucas Wadding, Lucas D’Achery, Andreas Rota, and M. A. Monsacratus either promised or intended to publish Anselm. Yet all of them were diverted from their undertaking, partly by the mass of the work—which also frightens me—and partly by other circumstances. Thus, after so many discussions and promises concerning him, Anselm still lies within the drawers of manuscript libraries.

The Vatican library of the supreme pontiff preserves at least seven manuscripts of Anselm. Two of them are extremely old and nearly contemporary with the author, although both lack the eleventh book, On Penance; this book, however, is attractively supplied from a more recent copy.

Surrounded by these riches of Anselm, what was I to do? If I entrusted the whole work to the press, I lacked the leisure necessary to prepare so great a work as it deserves. For who does not see that the innumerable canons cited by Anselm, the ancient Fathers, authors of civil law as well, and witnesses of various kinds must each be sought in their proper places and tested by the touchstone, lest—what once happened to Gratian—an annoying confusion of authorities and works arise, and spurious writings be accorded equal standing with genuine ones? This confusion in Gratian was at last purged, though only with great labor and vigilance, by Antonius Augustinus, the Roman correctors appointed by the supreme pontiff, and finally by Sebastian Berardus, after four volumes had been published.

As I considered these matters, nothing seemed more suitable, for the time being, to reveal Anselm’s work than to transcribe here, literally, the rubrics or titles of a great many chapters. For, as I have said, I do not encompass all parts of Anselm’s work, since that would be foreign to the purpose and nature of a specimen. Moreover, in every old or weighty writing there are usually passages that ought not to be brought forward without appropriate explanations.

Would that Anselm had prefixed a prologue to his work, in which there would undoubtedly have been much worthy of knowing! Nevertheless, no manuscript containing the author’s prolegomena has so far been found.

[Col. 0485]

THE CANONICAL COLLECTION OF SAINT ANSELM, BISHOP OF LUCCA, DIVIDED INTO THIRTEEN BOOKS.

THE CHAPTERS OF THE FIRST BOOK BEGIN. It concerns the primacy and excellence of the Roman Church.

[Col. 0485A] 1. That after Christ the priestly order began with Peter. 2. That the most holy Roman Church was established by the Lord as the head of all churches. 3. That blessed Peter handed on to his successors the power granted to him. 4. That superiors are not harmed when they are hated by their brothers on account of justice. 5. That whoever grieves the pope does not receive Christ. 6. That we ought not even speak to someone to whom the pope does not speak.

[Col. 0486A] 7. That the Lord granted blessed Peter precedence over the other apostles, with their consent. 8. That, following the pattern of the apostles, a certain distinction was made among bishops, although the see of blessed Peter takes precedence over them. 9. That the Roman Church presides over all churches, just as it was given to blessed Peter to take precedence over the other apostles. 10. That the Lord built his Church upon one person, namely Peter.
