[Col. 0487A] 11. That no one should dissent from the Roman Church, which is the head of all churches. 12. That it is wholly unfitting to depart from the rules of the Roman Church. 13. That the Roman Church has never erred from the faith. 14. That the pope ought to assist the universal Church and correct whatever is harmful within it. 15. That the Church of Antioch is subject to the Roman Church and must not dissent from its disposition. 16. That the Lord endowed the Roman Church with the priesthood of blessed Peter; that the first salvation lies in not departing from the ordinances of the Fathers; and that Catholic religion has always been preserved in the apostolic see. 17. That the Roman Church was placed above all others by the very voice of the Lord and Savior. 18. That the apostolic see is the support of all bishops and the summit of all churches. 19. That no one may judge the first see. 20. That all churches must preserve the statutes of the Roman Church. 21. That no one should presume to judge or revise the judgment of the apostolic see. 22. That the apostolic see is the head of all churches. 23. That the Roman Church possesses, by a singular privilege, the power of binding and loosing. 24. That the prelate of the apostolic see is to be judged by no one except God. 25. That the pope entrusts his duties, and even those of his see, to another—also to a subdeacon of his see—when he cannot be present. 26. That the pope may not remain silent about what can give rise to complaint. 27. That bishops should refer questions of faith to the apostolic see whenever doubt arises. 28. That, by divine institution, the pope ought principally to care for all the churches. 29. That matters which appear difficult to judge are to be judged by the authority of the Roman Church. 30. That the Roman Church received its primacy from the Lord, and that Mark did not dissent from his teacher, Pope Peter. 31. That all Catholics should follow what the apostolic see teaches.

[Col. 0487D] 32. That the pope should care for the condition of all the churches. 33. On the same matter. 34. On the same matter. 35. That the Roman Church is the mother of all churches and has never erred from the faith. 36. That the apostolic see never fosters heresies but destroys them. 37. That the ship of blessed Peter is not disturbed. 38. That it is not permissible for the apostolic prelate to conceal or remain silent.

[Col. 0488A] 39. That the apostolic prelate receives from blessed Peter the confidence and authority to defend the faith. 40. That the pope bears a greater obligation than all others to correct. 41. That the tradition of the Roman Church is observed by the other churches, which received their beginning from it. 42. That the Scriptures must not be understood otherwise than the holy Fathers taught. 43. That, out of reverence for his see, the pope is compelled to be diligent on behalf of all. 44. That one must not depart from apostolic institutions. 45. That no one should presume to violate the decrees of the apostolic see.

[Col. 0488B] 46. That the apostolic see presides over the universal Church. 47. That the see of blessed Peter has the right to judge the whole Church, but no one has the right to judge it. 48. That the apostolic see can, without a synod, absolve those who have been unjustly condemned. 49. That the apostolic see ought, by its authority, to preserve the decree of every synod that it has confirmed. 50. That whatever is decreed at the apostolic see without apostolic authority shall be null. 51. That Peter received the keys of the kingdom of heaven in order to open it to others. 52. That the authority to convene general synods has been entrusted solely to the apostolic see.

[Col. 0488C] 53. That the pope is to be judged by God alone. 54. That no one may usurp, without its consultation, what has been granted to the apostolic see. 55. That Saint Peter did not hand over the right of binding and loosing to Linus and Cletus [Note: [Col. 0487] This is speaking according to the opinion of those who hold that Linus and Cletus were not pontiffs and successors of Peter, but merely his assistants.]. 56. That in the one Catholic Church the true sacrifice is offered to Christ. 57. That the truth of the faith must be sought from the apostolic see. 58. On the request that the Council of Nicaea be confirmed by apostolic authority. 59. On the request of the Egyptian bishops concerning the seventy chapters of the Council of Nicaea. 60. That the Roman Church has always remained and will always remain spotless.

[Col. 0488D] 61. That the see of blessed Peter is the mother of priestly dignity and the teacher of ecclesiastical order. 62. That no one has the right to violate divine institutions or those of the apostolic see. 63. That the Roman Church established all ecclesiastical dignities, and that whoever attempts to deprive it of its privilege falls into heresy. 64. That whoever eats the Lamb outside the Church entrusted to blessed Peter is profane. 65. That Christ prayed especially for Peter’s faith.

[Col. 0489A] 66. That the Roman Church obtained its primacy from the Lord himself; that Peter and Paul consecrated it by their death on the same day; and that it is the first see, Alexandria the second, Antioch the third. 67. That, by evangelical authority, the Roman Church is first of all, and that Peter and Paul died on the same day. 68. That the Roman Church obtained its primacy not from synodal but from evangelical institutions. 69. That Peter and Paul are teachers of the nations, founders of the martyrs, and princes of the priests. 70. That no one can approach the body of blessed Paul, or his sudarium, from whose chain filings can sometimes be taken, and sometimes not.

[Col. 0489B] 71. That the world is governed by the authority of pontiffs and the power of kings, yet royal power must be subject to the pontiffs. 72. That emperors must obey priests, not command them. 73. On the steadfastness of Pope Agapetus against the emperor Justinian, whom he finally humbled at his feet. 74. On the obedience and honor that the emperor Tiberius showed to the pope. 75. That emperors have no right to concern themselves inquisitively with spiritual affairs. 76. That Pope Stephen advanced Pippin to kingship. 77. On the obedience and humility that King Pippin showed to Pope Stephen.

[Col. 0489C] 78. That Pope John VIII, together with the bishops, senate, and Roman people, elected and confirmed Charles as king.

[Col. 0490A] 79. On Charles, king elected as Roman emperor. 80. That, at the request of Pope Adrian, King Charles captured Desiderius, king of the Lombards, and that he himself was honorably received at Rome. 81. That King and Patrician Charles gave and restored to the Church of Saint Peter provinces, cities, fortresses, and many other possessions. 82. That legates of the apostolic see must be sent to the king with great honor. 83. That Pope Adrian refused to send legates to Constantinople unless the emperor and the Augusta guaranteed their safety, and unless they first anathematized what had been done without him; and that the bishop of Constantinople should not be called universal. 84. That obedience must be offered by the Augusti to apostolic admonitions. 85. On the oath made by King Otto to Pope John. 86. Pope John’s letter to the emperor Justinian, and the emperor’s letter to the pope, concerning the confirmation of the Catholic faith against Jewish and apostate perfidy. 87. On Justinian’s profession that the first and greatest good is the right confession of the Christian faith. 88. That priesthood and empire greatly adorn human life; concerning the election and adornment of bishops; and concerning the condemnation of simoniacal perversity.

THE CHAPTERS OF THE SECOND BOOK, which concerns the primacy of the Roman Church and the freedom of appeal.

[Col. 0489]

[Col. 0489C] 1. That more difficult judgments should be referred to priests. 2. That everyone should follow the religion taught by the divine apostle Peter. 3. That appeals should not be made merely to cause pointless delay. 4. That more difficult cases and greater matters should be referred to the apostolic see if an appeal has been made. 5. On the same matter. 6. That all who are oppressed must appeal to the Roman Church, from which all major ecclesiastical cases must receive their conclusion. 7. That all who need to flee to and appeal to the Roman Church must do so without impediment, and that no bishop may be judged or heard except in a synod convened by apostolic authority. 8. That a bishop who has been accused may freely appeal to the apostolic see, must come when summoned, and must not return unless equipped with formal letters. 9. That no one may settle the cases of bishops without apostolic authority, although neighboring bishops may investigate them.

[Col. 0490C] 10. That, through the remedy of appeal, a defective case may be restored, and that even when punishment has been assigned, the voice of appeal must not be denied. 11. That in more serious cases accused bishops should flee to the apostolic see, which should arrange to reconsider their matter either itself or through its vicars. 12. That primates should examine an accused bishop, but should not pronounce a sentence of condemnation without apostolic authority.

[Col. 0490D] 13. That doubtful and more important cases must be concluded by the apostolic see. 14. On the same matter. 15. That one stained by another’s error, or departing from his own purpose, or disobedient to the apostolic see, must not be received. 16. That the Roman Church has the right to judge everyone, but no one has the right to judge it; and that it has the power to absolve those unjustly condemned and to condemn those who ought to be condemned without a synod. 17. That nothing concerning one fleeing to the Roman Church may be judged without its command; but if anyone presumes to act otherwise, he shall be removed from office.

[Col. 0491A] 18. That the cases of bishops who are appealing, and all major matters, must be reserved to the apostolic see. 19. That whoever refuses to obey the commands of the apostolic see is excluded from divine and pontifical offices. 20. That no metropolitan should presume to conduct the cases of bishops or others except those belonging to his own diocese. 21. That the pope ought to care for all churches, and that the see of blessed Peter is the mother of priestly dignity and the teacher of ecclesiastical order. 22. That the pope restores bishops unjustly condemned through fear of rulers and orders all their possessions to be returned. 23. That the apostolic see can absolve those bound by others, but no one can absolve those bound by it. 24. That the pope can reopen the judgments of condemned persons. 25. That the apostolic see has the power to convene synods and judge all major ecclesiastical cases. 26. That the privileges granted to the Roman see concerning the convening of councils, judgments, and the restoration of bishops were granted so that it might come to the aid of all the oppressed. 27. That truth, the more often it is harassed, shines forth more clearly. 28. That matters which cannot be concluded elsewhere should be transferred to the apostolic see.

[Col. 0491C] 29. That any disagreement arising between brothers should be referred to the apostolic see. 30. That cases of the churches examined by bishops should be confirmed by the apostolic see if they are to remain valid. 31. That the purification of bishops must not take place without the consent of the Roman pontiff or other pontiffs. 32. That the pope ought to weigh the decrees of the canons so that, insofar as possible, he may moderate whatever the necessity of the times requires to be relaxed. 33. That no assembly convened without the pope’s consent should be called a council, and that more difficult questions should be referred to him. 34. That the final disposition of cases was entrusted to the apostolic see by the Lord himself, and that priests must not be accused before public judges.

[Col. 0491D] 35. That the final judgments of bishops must be referred to the Roman see, and that no others should be placed over their churches until their cases have been justly concluded there. 36. That an accused bishop must not be constrained by a foreign judge, but that his case should be decided among his own bishops; the final decision, however, must be referred to the apostolic see. 37. That the apostolic see has the authority to assist the universal Church and to correct and amend what is harmful. 38. That the more difficult questions of individual provinces should be referred to the apostolic see.

[Col. 0492A] 39. That no synod can be regularly convened without the authority of the apostolic see; nor can a bishop who has appealed to it be condemned without it. 40. That no one should be judged on the basis of suspicion, and that the apostolic see alone has, from the time of the apostles, the privilege of judging bishops. 41. That the apostles established for their successors that neither councils should be celebrated nor bishops condemned without the sentence of the Roman pontiff; and that, just as blessed Peter was first among the apostles, so the Roman Church has primacy over all churches. 42. That it was granted to the Roman see from the time of the apostles, and confirmed in the Council of Nicaea, that no bishop should be condemned or expelled without its sentence.

[Col. 0492B] 43. That all must observe what the apostolic see observes. 44. That neither a council may be celebrated nor a bishop condemned without the apostolic see. 45. That Pope Julius rebuked those who had held a council and condemned bishops contrary to his sentence, and that he received those bishops and restored them to their churches. 46. That a council is invalid unless it has been confirmed by apostolic authority. 47. That special privileges have been granted to the apostolic see concerning the convening of councils, the judgments and restoration of bishops, and the supreme affairs of the churches.

[Col. 0492C] 48. That in episcopal cases the pope’s sentence must be awaited. 49. That bishops must receive ordinations, doctrines, and restorations from the apostolic see, and must decide nothing concerning major cases apart from it. 50. That whoever regards his metropolitan or the other bishops as suspect should appeal to the apostolic see; and that it has the power to restore those unjustly condemned and excommunicated and to return their possessions to them, because it is the head of all churches. 51. That accusers and accused bishops should meet before the pope, and that their cases should there be reconsidered and either confirmed or overturned, as was customary according to the ancient rules. 52. That disputes between clerics and laypeople should be settled by the neighboring bishops, but greater disputes should be transferred to the Roman see.

[Col. 0492D] 53. Whenever doubt arises concerning the faith, bishops must refer the matter to the see of blessed Peter. 54. That the pope customarily attends provincial councils not in person but through legates. 55. That no one should judge the judgment of the apostolic see, whereas it judges all. 56. That if anyone has been deposed by the judgment of the provincial bishops, he should approach the pope, who, if it seems right to him, may reconsider the case. 57. That more difficult questions should be referred to the apostolic see. 58. That those oppressed by neighboring bishops or by their metropolitan should appeal to the apostolic see and suffer no harassment in the meantime until the matter is concluded there.

[Col. 0493A] 59. That a metropolitan, together with all the neighboring bishops, may examine major ecclesiastical cases, but may not decide them, condemn a bishop, or convene a synod without the authority of the apostolic see. 60. That the statutes of one’s superiors must in no way be neglected, nor may what has not been granted be usurped. 61. That bishops cannot regularly convene a synod apart from the apostolic see. 62. That the judgment must be renewed if the Roman Church judges that it should be renewed. 63. Just as there was a distinction of power among the apostles, so that one was preeminent over the others, so it has been arranged among bishops that individual bishops preside over individual provinces, although the Roman Church presides over all of them. 64. On the attack against the archbishop of Reims on behalf of Bishop Rothard, whom the archbishop condemned after he had appealed to the apostolic see. 65. That no one can be judged by those of lower dignity or rank. 66. That the Church of Constantinople, like all the others, must be subject to the Roman see. 67. That no one should assume honor for himself, just as Christ did not glorify himself but was glorified by the Father. 68. That even the cases of clerics of lower rank must be concluded before the apostolic see when time or circumstances require it.

[Col. 0493C] 69. That the sentence of the apostolic see must be issued only after such extensive deliberation that it requires neither reconsideration nor alteration, unless it was issued in a form permitting reconsideration.

[Col. 0494A] 70. Let anyone who composes defamatory words against the pope, or attempts to dishonor any of the patriarchs, be anathema. 71. That the apostolic see has from ancient times been accustomed to perform consecrations, ordinations, and depositions within Italy, the various provinces of Spain, and throughout the boundaries of Illyricum. 72. That the pope ordained the bishop of Ravenna; concerning the obedience of the archbishop of Milan; and concerning the consecration of the bishop of Pavia. 73. That if a bishop is condemned by neighboring bishops, no other may be ordained in his place while he is appealing to the apostolic see, unless the apostolic see itself determines otherwise.

[Col. 0494B] 74. That some matters cannot be overturned by any means, while others must be moderated according to necessity and consideration of ages, so long as this is not contrary to the evangelical commandments and the decrees of the Fathers. 75. That no prejudice could be inflicted upon the Council of Nicaea by the multitude assembled at Rimini, because the Roman Church gave it no assent. 76. That bishops must observe what has been judged by the Roman Church. 77. That accused bishops must either be condemned by apostolic authority or supported by its assistance. 78. That no one should condemn a bishop apart from apostolic authority. 79. That an accused or judged bishop may freely appeal to the pope against the neighboring bishops, and that the pope should reconsider his case; meanwhile no other bishop should be ordained in his place. 80. That if an accused person considers his judge suspect, he may appeal.

THE CHAPTERS OF THE THIRD BOOK, which concerns the procedure for accusing, giving testimony, and judging.

[Col. 0493]

[Col. 0493C] 1. That murderers, adulterers, those bound by every kind of crime, infamous persons, laymen, and all who are not their equals should not accuse or harass bishops. 2. That those who take up arms against the Fathers and trample upon priests or churches are infamous. Such persons cannot accuse bishops. [Col. 0493D] 3. Anyone who has fallen away from his undertaking and has not obeyed apostolic commands is infamous. 4. An enumeration of the faults by which persons are branded infamous. 5. Likewise, who are infamous and unable to accuse bishops; and that, if the statutes of the Fathers begin to be undermined, they are to be strengthened again by apostolic authority. 6. That an infamous person ought not to accuse, and how one ought to accuse or judge, and so forth. 7. That those who persecute the holy Fathers are to be regarded as infamous and excluded from the Church until they make satisfaction. [Col. 0494C] 8. Concerning those who are not to be received and are considered infamous. 9. That one who has abandoned the rule of his law or religion, or has neglected what has rightly been prohibited, is not to be admitted to an accusation. [Col. 0494D] 10. That corrupters of morals are worse than robbers of property. 11. That accusers of priests ought not to be heard unless their life and intention have first been examined. 12. That bishops are not to be arraigned by the people, and the matters on which they are likewise not to be accused. 13. That those who today or the day before yesterday were enemies cannot accuse or give testimony. 14. Likewise, on the same matter: that those who cannot be priests ought not to accuse priests. 15. That suspects, enemies, habitual litigants, persons of depraved conduct, and those who neither hold nor teach the right faith cannot be accusers. 16. On the same matter. [Col. 0495A] 17. That no foreigner is to be an accuser or judge, nor a slave, freedman, suspect, or infamous person. 18. Likewise, concerning those who are not to be admitted to accusation and testimony. 19. Likewise, on the same matter. 20. Likewise, concerning those whom it is not permitted to accuse; and that the accused should not have judges other than those whom he himself has chosen or whom the apostolic see has appointed with his consent. 21. That permission to accuse or give testimony is to be denied to those who have neglected the dignity of the Christian religion and name, the rule of their own law or undertaking, or matters prohibited by rule. 22. That no one may drag a cleric before a secular court without the consent of the bishop. [Col. 0495B] 23. On the same matter. 24. That an infamous and sacrilegious person may not give testimony against a Christian, and that ecclesiastical judges should not hear a case that is not covered by the laws. 25. That neither laymen nor those whom the laws of the world do not admit should presume to accuse bishops or clerics. 26. That those who live with enemies, and all laymen, are likewise to be removed from accusations against clerics. 27. That an accused cleric is to be heard in his own province; that a judge’s sentence issued in the absence of the accused is invalid; and that the slander of a betrayer is not to be heard. 28. That neither clerics should admit laymen, nor laymen clerics, in their respective accusations. [Col. 0495C] 29. That if a layman has a case against a cleric, he should approach the bishop. 30. That if a bishop has erred in the faith, he is first to be corrected; if he does not amend, he is to be accused before the apostolic see. 31. That the accusation of bishops should be brought only by suitable and thoroughly proven men. 32. That an accused bishop is not to be deprived of communion unless he refuses to come on the appointed day. 33. That an absence arranged by those evading judgment is of no benefit to them. 34. That detractors and supporters of enemies are to be excluded from an episcopal accusation, and that in a doubtful matter no definitive sentence is to be given. [Col. 0495D] 35. That whoever has a case against pastors or their churches should first await correction charitably; but if he has presumed to harass them beforehand, he is to be excommunicated. 36. That those who expose the fault of their superiors are to be condemned by the sentence of Ham, who did not cover his father’s nakedness. 37. That no one can be condemned by human examination whom God has reserved for his own judgment. 38. That accusations against priests or pastors should not be brought indiscriminately or too readily. 39. That an accused bishop should choose twelve judges for himself, who shall decide his case justly; but the conclusion of the case is to be referred to the pope. [Col. 0496A] 40. If a bishop is detained on a criminal charge outside the time of a synod, he is to be heard by twelve bishops. 41. That lower orders should not accuse higher orders; and the number of witnesses by which a bishop, priest, deacon, subdeacon, and others are to be condemned. 42. That sheep cannot rebuke their pastors unless the pastors have erred in the faith; and that those who have been stripped of their property should not be summoned to a synod until their goods have first been restored to them. 43. That no one may accuse a bishop or any cleric before secular judges. 44. On the same matter; and that a person summoned to a synod must be given adequate time. Otherwise he need not answer unless he wishes; and accusers and accused are to be heard equally. [Col. 0496B] 45. That no one is to be judged unless he has lawful accusers present. 46. That no metropolitan may hear the cases of anyone without the insistence of the bishops of his province. 47. Concerning bishops expelled without Roman authority: their property is to be restored to them. 48. That no one may presume to excommunicate a bishop who has been stripped of his property. 49. Likewise, that everything is to be restored to those who have been stripped, and that they are to be given as much time as they were deprived of, before they are summoned to a synod. 50. That a bishop lawfully summoned to a synod should come; if he cannot, he should send a legate in his place. He himself, however, is not to be excluded from communion unless he delays coming for six months or more. [Col. 0496C] 51. That a judge should not issue his sentence before the truth of the matter has been reached after the points at issue have been dealt with, and that considerable adjournments are to be granted for investigation. 52. That no accusation or testimony is to be accepted in writing, but only by the person’s own voice, in the presence of the one against whom the charge is brought. 53. That the person, faith, and conduct of those accusing the Lord’s priests are to be carefully investigated. 54. That accusers must be free from every suspicion and infamy and must be of right faith and good life. [Col. 0496D] 55. That proceedings conducted against absent persons are to be annulled. 56. That persons lower in rank should not accuse those higher in rank; that in a doubtful matter no definitive sentence is to be given; and that no absent person is to be judged. 57. Concerning those who cannot accuse bishops, and that bishops should not answer charges before all their property has been restored. 58. That neither false, hostile, nor suspect persons are to be accepted in an accusation. 59. That those who lay crimes to the charge of bishops should do so in person, provided that they themselves are irreproachable. 60. Likewise, concerning those who are not to be admitted to an accusation. 61. That no one should be rash in pronouncing sentence, [Col. 0497A] or believe statements indiscriminately, or judge or condemn anyone before true and just proof. 62. That nothing is to be done against any accused person without a lawful accuser. 63. That an accused bishop is not to be condemned except by apostolic authority, or after confessing, or after being canonically convicted. 64. On the same matter, and concerning the number of lawful witnesses. 65. That a priest should not judge anyone unless that person has confessed or been convicted. 66. Concerning excommunicated persons being heard by neighboring bishops. 67. That the condemnation or acquittal of one whose case has not been carefully examined is invalid, and that no one should be condemned because of a confession extorted from him. [Col. 0497B] 68. That in ecclesiastical affairs, even after the case has been pleaded, it is permissible to withdraw and postpone the matter if necessary, but not at all in secular affairs. 69. That accused persons cannot accuse others until they themselves have first been cleared. 70. That no one should at the same time be accuser, judge, and witness, but that each role should be separately held by a suitable person. 71. Likewise, concerning those who cannot accuse priests; and that each bishop is to be heard in his own province, together with the freedom of appeal. 72. That every accusation is to be concluded within the province unless the apostolic see has been appealed to. 73. On the same matter. [Col. 0497C] 74. That when a synod has been lawfully assembled, a bishop is to be heard by all the bishops of his province if the accusers are lawful; otherwise, the accused is not to be wearied. 75. That a judge should not issue his sentence until the accused himself either confesses or is justly convicted. 76. That in every case careful inquiry is to be made into what the matters are, how they occurred, and what kind they are. 77. Concerning the bringing of a criminal charge, and that the accuser incurs the penalty of the accused if he cannot prove what he alleged. 78. That provinces are to have their own judges unless the pope decides otherwise. 79. That no one should complain against a bishop before first approaching him amicably. 80. That bishops expelled from their sees without apostolic authority are to be restored, and only then answer the charges. Those who have intruded into their places are to be excluded from the Church. [Col. 0497D] 81. That judges and accusers must be free from suspicion. 82. That the guilty person evades judgment just as the innocent person seeks it. 83. Just as no one should be condemned without a just judgment, so matters justly judged should not be delayed. 84. That an unjust judgment or decision arranged through fear of, or at the command of, some powerful person has no validity. 85. That an emperor may not do anything contrary to the apostolic rules. [Col. 0498A] 86. Concerning permission to accuse and give testimony: when, where, and how it is to be exercised. 87. Pope Gregory’s memorandum to John the defensor, concerning how he should proceed regarding certain bishops unjustly condemned, certain priests, and others. 88. Concerning Dioscorus the bishop. 89. Concerning the condemnation of Dioscorus the bishop, who, when summoned to the synod, refused to come. 90. That Dioscorus was not condemned on account of the faith, but because he pronounced excommunication against the lord Pope Leo. 91. That the memory of Eutyches is to be condemned, and the venerable remembrance of Flavian magnified. 92. Concerning the condemnation of Macarius, with the apocrisiarii of the Roman Church presiding. [Col. 0498B] 93. Concerning the bishops restored by Pope Julius, Liberius being sent into exile and Felix consecrated in his place. 94. That Pope Agapitus held a synod at Constantinople against the Theopaschites, in which he deposed Anthimus and consecrated Mennas. 95. That Pope Vigilius came to Constantinople and excommunicated Mennas. 96. Concerning councils assembled by apostolic authority against various heresies. 97. That the pope added the honor of regional office to the defensores and allowed them to sit among the clergy. 98. Likewise, that Pope Gregory increased the honor of the Roman defensor. 99. That the bishops who had come together at Rome on account of the things said by the adversaries against Pope Symmachus refused to pronounce a sentence against him, but commended the matter to God’s judgment. [Col. 0498C] 100. Concerning the assembling of a synod in the city of Chalcedon. 101. That the emperors came together for the Council of Chalcedon not to display power, but to confirm the faith. 102. That if anyone who has a lawsuit seeks the judgment of bishops, it is immediately to be granted to him; and no judge may dare to revise what they have confirmed. 103. That bishops and the other ecclesiastical orders are not to be dragged before public courts. 104. That administrators of secular dignities, when summoned by bishops and ecclesiastical persons, should carefully examine and redress their complaints. [Col. 0498D] 105. That governors should receive letters of communion when they are promoted, and should be under the care of the bishop in whose place they exercise the governorship. 106. That those who act insolently against the sacred canons blaspheme the Holy Spirit. 107. On the same matter. 108. Concerning Pope Liberius and his admonition. [Note: [Col. 0497D] Namely, his address to the Roman clergy.] 109. Concerning the exile of Pope Liberius and Felix, ordained on the advice of Liberius. 110. Concerning the canonical condemnation of Nestorius. [Col. 0499A] 111. Concerning John of Antioch and the bishops whom he unjustly condemned. 112. By which canons or rules judgment should be rendered. [Col. 0500A] 113. Concerning clerics not being harassed by secular authorities. 114. On the same matter. 115. That an excommunicated person should not be admitted to an accusation.

## Chapters of Book Four

Which concerns the authority of privileges.

[Col. 0499]

[Col. 0499A] 1. That the privileges of churches and monasteries are to remain inviolate. 2. That the privileges of churches and monasteries, established by the authority of the holy Fathers, should not be overturned by wickedness or altered by innovation. [Col. 0499B] 3. That anyone who abuses the power entrusted to him deserves to lose his privilege. 4. That it is contrary to the priestly undertaking to confuse the privileges of a monastery and disturb its peace. 5. That privileges and ordinances arranged in the presence of the pope are not to be overturned or altered by anyone. 6. That just as the pope must defend and preserve the privileges of his own church, so he must defend and preserve the rights of each individual church. 7. That things arranged for the sake of religious peace are not to be violated. 8. That no one may claim monasteries for himself against the founder’s will. [Col. 0499C] 9. That once established, such arrangements are not to be disturbed by any opposition. 10. That the city of Constantinople should possess its own glory and not seek another’s. 11. That emperors should obey bishops. 12. That emperors should possess the privileges of public law, while priests should possess authority over the arrangements of all the churches. 13. That clerics should freely enjoy their own property. 14. That faithful Christians should enjoy perpetual security. 15. That guardians of sacred places should suffer no harassment. [Col. 0499D] 16. That privileges granted to churches are to remain inviolate. 17. On the same matter. 18. That whoever violates the privileges of a church must pay twelve pounds of gold. 19. The emperor’s privilege concerning venerable places. 20. Likewise, a privilege concerning the freedom of clerics and monks. 21. Likewise, concerning the needs for which the churches of individual cities are to possess immunities. 22. That no one may dare to remove from churches in any manner sacred vessels, vestments, or other gifts. 23. That the governor of a province should punish with capital sentence the injuries inflicted upon churches or ecclesiastical persons. [Col. 0500A] 24. That a bishop should ordain throughout the churches as many clerics as seem suitable to each. 25. That no one may dare to raise further a question concerning the Christian faith, which has been confirmed by the most reverend synods. [Col. 0500B] 26. That whoever despises what has been promulgated by the apostolic authority for the Catholic faith and ecclesiastical discipline is to be anathema. 27. On the same matter, and that the privilege has been established by Christ. 28. That it is not permitted for the pope to alienate or exchange church estates in perpetuity, except perhaps houses in the city for clerics, captives, and pilgrims. 29. That the other bishops and priests are to be bound by the same law as the supreme pontiff. 30. That privileges possessed for thirty years are not to be removed or violated by any secular person. 31. That no one should claim the patrimonies of the Roman Church; and if anyone removes anything from them in any manner, let him be anathema. [Col. 0500C] 32. Likewise, on the same matter. 33. That the Emperor Constantine granted the pope a crown and every royal dignity in the city of Rome, in Italy, and in the western regions. 34. Concerning the provinces and cities that the emperors granted to the Roman Church and confirmed by written decree. [Note: [Col. 0499D] This is a diploma of the Emperor Louis.] 35. On the same matter. [Note: [Col. 0499] Namely, these are diplomas of the emperors Otto and Henry.] 36. Likewise, on the same matter. 37. That no one should usurp the property of blessed Peter, conceal it [aciens, reading uncertain], or fail to render the service owed. 38. Concerning the distinction between divine law, public law, and private interests. 39. That the first see is to be judged by no one. [Col. 0500D] 40. That no king should permit the authority of the canons to be violated. 41. That bishops are to be elected from the clergy and people of their own diocese. 42. That property granted to churches should suffer neither division nor loss. 43. That the pope asks the emperor to restore to him the rights and possessions of the Roman Church. 44. That each church’s honor is to be preserved for it. 45. That the Pannonian diocese has been assigned to the privileges of the apostolic see. 46. That the enactments of the apostolic see and of the holy Fathers are to be observed irrevocably. 47. Likewise, on the same matter. 48. Likewise, on the same matter. [Col. 0501A] 49. That the limits of each priest’s jurisdiction should suffice for him. 50. That whatever has once been decreed against any heresy must always remain unshaken. 51. Confirmation of the privileges granted to the most holy churches. [Col. 0502A] 52. That privileges granted to Catholics do not benefit heretics. 53. Likewise, confirmation of the privileges granted to venerable places. 54. Concerning the private property of clerics, treated as military property. 55. That not only bishops but also priests are permitted to preach the word.

## Chapters of Book Five

Which concerns the law, organization, and condition of the churches.

[Col. 0501]

[Col. 0501A] 1. That the Church is one, although it has different members. 2. That one who does not preserve the unity of the Church is profane. [Col. 0501B] 3. That the Church is called the house of God, the dove, and the bride, and that it has received the power of binding and loosing. 4. That new basilicas are not to be consecrated without the authority of the apostolic see. 5. Likewise, on the same matter. 6. That a public Mass is not to be celebrated in a church that was dedicated without the pope’s consent. 7. Concerning the consecration of a church with a solemn endowment, in which the founder retains no proprietary right. 8. That no layman, apart from the pope, may establish anything in a church—that is, may make any ordinance. 9. That a layman has no authority to establish anything in a church or to dispose of its resources. [Col. 0501C] 10. On the same matter. 11. That the pope grants permission to consecrate a church. 12. That the pope, who ought to have care of all the churches, entrusts the duty of visitation in the Capuan Church to another bishop. 13. Concerning the consecration of a church if the altar is moved. 14. That altars in which there are no relics are to be destroyed. 15. That the status of parishes is not to be changed for any reason. 16. For three reasons, holy places may be transferred. 17. That church timber is not to be made available for lay use. [Col. 0501D] 18. Concerning the penance of one who burns a church. 19. That church resources possessed for thirty years are thereafter to remain stable. 20. That a church which does not possess the foundations of apostolic preaching is to be abandoned. 21. That the churches of the Arians are to be consecrated as Catholic churches. 22. That the dedications of churches and priests are to be solemnly celebrated each year; and if there is doubt concerning a church’s dedication, it is to be consecrated again. 23. On the same matter. 24. That the pope entrusts two dioceses to one bishop. 25. On the same matter. [Col. 0502A] 26. That the parishes or possessions of churches peacefully possessed for thirty years are to remain undisturbed. [Col. 0502B] 27. That thirty years’ possession of territory does not remove a legal claim. 28. Concerning thirty years’ possession within a single province. 29. That an oratory is not to be consecrated without the authority of the apostolic see. 30. That one who persecutes God’s priests and plunders churches is sacrilegious. 31. That monasteries or hostels for pilgrims built from money given for sacred orders do not contribute to a reward, but are harmful. 32. How church money is to be safeguarded. 33. That provision must be made for religious persons so that they have suitable places, lest, suffering need, they become idle. [Col. 0502C] 34. That tithes are the tribute of needy souls. 35. That tithes should be given only to the congregations. 36. That one who removes estates handed over for divine uses is to be regarded as sacrilegious. 37. On the same matter. And that church property should not be private but common. 38. That what is given for the common benefit is not to be applied to private uses. 39. That it is sacrilege to retain what is left to holy places. 40. Concerning those who violate holy places and remove something from them. 41. Concerning those who seize another’s property or ecclesiastical offerings. [Col. 0502D] 42. That ecclesiastical persons may reclaim, together with its fruits, property alienated from churches. 43. That baptism is not to be performed in a monastery. 44. That no one may presume to give or receive church property except the bishop or one to whom this has been entrusted. 45. That even if excessive necessity presses upon a bishop, he should nevertheless not distribute the church’s revenues unless he has first reported the matter to the primate of the province. 46. That whoever violates the house of God and removes anything from it is to be deprived of communion. 47. That church possessions are not to be alienated except to religious clerics, monasteries, or pilgrims, and even then only temporarily. [Col. 0503A] 48. That church vessels and furnishings are to be sold for the redemption of captives. 49. That tithes are not to be possessed by laymen. 50. That sacred things belong to no one and should not be alienated except for captives. 51. That whoever wishes to convert should leave half of his possessions to the church to which he is subject, and then go to a monastery. 52. That no abbot may hold tithes or firstfruits without the authority of the apostolic see or of his own bishop. 53. Concerning a certain abbot appointed by Pope Gregory. 54. That no monastery is to be established without the knowledge of its bishop, and that all monks are to be subject to the bishop. [Col. 0503B] 55. That consecrated monasteries may not be turned into secular lodging places. 56. That if someone seeks church property from kings, the request is to be considered invalid, and the petitioner himself is to be deprived of communion. 57. If anyone removes the resources of churches or hostels for pilgrims, he is to be excommunicated as a killer of the poor. 58. Concerning the freedom of monks and monasteries. 59. That monasteries are to be relieved from the burden imposed by clerics. 60. That clerics should not be placed over monasteries. 61. That a monastery is to suffer no legal challenge concerning those things which it has possessed for forty years. 62. That bishops, stewards, orphanage-superintendents, or hospice-superintendents are to possess nothing by inheritance except what they possessed before the hour of their ordination. [Col. 0503C] 63. Those who are against the peace of the Church are either to be stripped of their possessions or, after being beaten, assigned to exile. 64. That church property is to be divided into four portions: one for the bishop, another for the clerics, a third for the poor, and a fourth for churches to be restored. [Col. 0504A] 65. On the same matter. 66. Likewise, on the same matter. 67. That bishops should not oppress their subjects, and that church revenues are to be divided according to the merits of the work performed. 68. On the same matter. 69. That church property is not to be given away, exchanged, or sold except with a view to improvement. 70. That one monastery may not even be exchanged for another monastery. 71. What a bishop should do if several heirs contend over one church. [Col. 0504B] 72. On the same matter. 73. That a monastery is not to be taken away unwillingly from its founders. 74. That Mass may be sung and the dead buried in a monastery. 75. That a church is not to be consecrated if it is established that a body has been buried in it. 76. Concerning those who suppress or deny the documents of churches. 77. Concerning ecclesiastical traditions that are to be observed and do not harm the faith. 78. That from both the old and newly acquired revenues of a church, a quarter is to be given. 79. Concerning observance of the Lord’s Day. 80. On the same matter. [Col. 0504C] 81. Concerning loaves and other things offered upon sacred altars. 82. On the same matter. 83. Concerning ecclesiastical ordinances being moderated according to the circumstances of the time.

## Chapters of Book Six

Which concerns the election and ordination, and every power or condition, of bishops.

[Col. 0503]

[Col. 0503C] 1. That while the pope is alive no one may aspire to the papacy; and concerning the election of another if he, while still living, has made no provision for it. 2. That no one should doubt that the one whom the summit of apostolic dignity justly elevates is holy. [Col. 0503D] 3. Likewise, concerning the election of bishops, that it be conducted with pure minds and that no payment intervene. 4. That no one cause any impediment in the election of the Roman pontiff. 5. That every election of a bishop, presbyter, or deacon made by princes be invalid. 6. Concerning those who assert that they were elected by the people. 7. That outsiders not be placed over those who have served well in their own churches. 8. That the people are not permitted to conduct the election of bishops. 9. That the election of bishops ought not to arise from favor, but from the judgment of the most careful examination. [Col. 0504C] 10. Concerning a certain man elected bishop whom the blessed Pope Gregory rejected and caused another to be elected and consecrated. 11. That while a Roman or other pontiff is alive, no one presume to conduct an election. [Col. 0504D] 12. Concerning the election of the pontiff. 13. That the cardinals may excommunicate and expel an invader of the apostolic see. 14. That all cease from ambition, and that the pope whom the clergy elected with the consent of the people remain in office. 15. He who is to be elected bishop must not be a layman, a neophyte, or the husband of a second wife or of a widow. 16. That all the provincial bishops assemble for the election of the metropolitan bishop; but if they divide between two candidates, the one supported by the better merits is to be preferred. [Col. 0505A] 17. That a principate which sedition has extorted or ambition has seized, even if not evil in its conduct, is nevertheless pernicious as an example of its origin. 18. That he prepares a grave injury for himself who elevates an unworthy man to the episcopate. 19. That those to whom the governance of the Church is to be entrusted demonstrate the good path through lengthy probation. 20. That no lay prince or powerful person intrude upon the election or promotion of bishops. 21. That a bishop not be elected from another church unless no worthy candidate is found in his own. 22. That a bishop not be elected from another church if a worthy man is found in that church. 23. That the bishop of Milan was ordained at the pope’s command. [Col. 0505B] 24. That monks or laymen ought not to reach the highest priesthood except through the degrees of the Church. 25. That no Roman be elected pontiff unless he is one of the cardinals. 26. Who is a neophyte; and that he not leap prematurely to the highest orders. 27. Concerning laymen who are tonsured for the sake of ambition and suddenly become priests. 28. That, according to the proper meaning of the name, he is not a bishop who loves to preside rather than to benefit. 29. That it is wretched for one who was never a disciple to become a teacher. 30. That he who imprudently consecrated a neophyte ought to lose the right of ordination. [Col. 0505C] 31. A directive concerning the election of the bishop of Imola and the consecration of the bishop of Como. 32. That in the election of the Roman pontiff no one dare intervene except those whom ancient custom admits. 33. Concerning the ordination of a bishop. 34. That all the suffragan bishops of any archbishop elect and ordain him. 35. That the ordinations of bishops ought not to be long delayed. 36. That the metropolitan ordain his subjects, and that they likewise ought to ordain him. 37. That he ought not to be bishop who was made one without the knowledge of the metropolitan. [Col. 0505D] 38. That a crowd is not permitted to conduct the election of priests. 39. What sort of person he ought to be who is to be elected bishop. 40. That the bishop to be elected give or promise nothing to anyone. 41. Concerning a bishop who has been ordained but not received into his diocese. 42. That the lord pope delayed the consecration of a certain bishop because he still had a wife and children, through whom ecclesiastical property commonly comes into danger. 43. Instruction concerning what an ordained bishop ought to do. [Col. 0506A] 44. That a bishop worthy of election ought to be chosen by all the clergy and the entire people, with the assent of the provincial bishops. 45. Concerning the order of consecration of the supreme pontiff. 46. Concerning the order of the consecration of bishops. 47. Likewise, concerning the ordination of bishops: how, on what day, and at what hour it ought to be carried out. 48. That a bishop ought not to be ordained by fewer than three bishops. 49. How bishops are to be consecrated. 50. That no one ordain a bishop without the knowledge of the metropolitan, and that not even one bishop alone may do so. 51. Whenever prelates are ordained in the principal four sees, they ought in turn to send synodical letters in which they profess that they observe the general synods. [Col. 0506B] 52. Concerning the authority of the four councils, in a synodical letter of the holy Pope Gregory. 53. Concerning ordination on Holy Saturday after baptism. 54. Concerning ordination to be celebrated on Holy Saturday of Easter. 55. That an elected bishop, if any opposition arises, be cleared of the charge by five bishops. 56. That a dying bishop ought not to appoint another bishop in his place as though he were his heir. 57. On the same matter. 58. That once a pope has been ordained by common consent, whoever intrudes while he is alive shall be profane. 59. He who has withdrawn from the unity of the Church can possess neither the authority nor the honor of a bishop. [Col. 0506C] 60. That he lose his privilege who abuses the power granted to him. 61. That no one be ordained against his will. 62. That he who performs unlawful ordinations lose the power of ordaining. 63. That unlawful ordinations be avoided. 64. That those who have received this dignity from the laity not be counted or heard among the bishops or abbots; and the same is to apply to the lower orders. 65. That lay authorities not presume to confer ecclesiastical dignities. 66. Concerning the sacrifices of bishops that are performed against the will of God. 67. That the people ought to separate themselves from an evil prelate and elect another who is worthy. [Col. 0506D] 68. That those who have been neither elected by the clergy, nor sought by the people, nor canonically consecrated not be counted among the bishops. 69. That no one attain the episcopate through ambition. 70. That laymen not suddenly become priests, nor do so through the Simoniac heresy. 71. On the same matter. 72. On the same matter. 73. That those ordained by heretics receive condemnation rather than consecration. 74. On the same matter. And that other women not live with priests except those whom the canons permit. [Col. 0507A] 75. That one must abstain not only from the gift of money, but also from the gifts of service and speech. 76. He is a Simoniac who distributes rewards for an election. 77. Whoever does not burn vehemently against the Simoniac heresy and the heresy of neophytes shall have a share with those from whom it began. 78. Concerning the condemnation of those who buy or sell the gift of God. 79. Concerning the condemnation of the Simoniac heresy. 80. That anyone who has given or received a sacred order for money be deposed from his rank. 81. That bishops or anyone from the clergy ought not to be ordained for money. 82. Just as with sacred orders, so also with the pallium: it ought not to be given through favor or petitions. [Col. 0507B] 83. That nothing of value be given for ordination or for the use of the pallium, letters, or the pastoral staff. 84. That if any metropolitan, within three months of his consecration, has not sent to the apostolic see to present his profession of faith and receive the pallium, he lose the dignity entrusted to him. 85. That the honor of the pallium ought not to be given unless the merits of the case demand it and the petitioner makes a forceful request. 86. That whenever the pallium is granted, certain privileges must always also be granted by the apostolic authority. 87. That an archbishop ought to use the pallium only at Masses. 88. That no bishop or deacon use the dalmatic without the permission of the apostolic see. [Col. 0507C] 89. Concerning the authority of the bishop of Arles. 90. That the pallium be used only during the solemn celebration of Masses. 91. That Saint Gregory confirms the election of a bishop and grants the pallium. 92. On the same matter. 93. That the pallium ought not to be given to anyone except after the customary profession of faith. 94. That transfers of bishops may be made by apostolic authority, with common counsel and for the common good. 95. That priests ought not to transfer to churches for the sake of greed. 96. That if a bishop, scorning his own city, transfers to a greater one, he lose both his own and the other. [Col. 0507D] 97. That transfers of bishops may be made for a cause of necessity or usefulness. 98. That an episcopal see may, for a reason of necessity, be transferred to another place within the same diocese. 99. Concerning an expelled bishop incardinated in another church, and concerning the avoidance of unlawful ordinations. 100. That the pope may unite two bishoprics into one. 101. That a bishop who has voluntarily transferred to another city ought to be removed, and another ordained there. 102. That a bishop may not abandon his church, just as a husband may not abandon his wife. [Col. 0508A] 103. That a church be judged only by its own bishop; but if it is persecuted in its own place, let it flee to another. Or if he is to be transferred for the sake of usefulness, he must not do this on his own initiative. 104. That a bishop or the other orders ought not to transfer from place to place. 105. That Saint Peter commanded that in cities where the chief flamines once existed there should be primates and patriarchs, and that where the archflamines had been, there should be archbishops. 106. On the same matter. 107. That a province is one which has ten or eleven cities with bishops and one king. 108. That metropolitans govern their provinces, while the authority of the apostolic see remains intact. 109. That primates should be in the larger cities, where the pagans once called their leaders “primates” because of their more important affairs. [Col. 0508B] 110. That bishops not go to the imperial court unless they receive a formal letter from the Roman Church. 111. That no bishop go to the imperial court unless summoned by religious emperors. 112. That bishops who are in the *canalis* [reading uncertain], when going to the imperial court, make careful inquiry. 113. Concerning Bishop Serenus, who was unwillingly taken to the imperial court because of the inhumanity of his conduct. 114. Likewise, that bishops not proceed to the imperial court unless they have consulted the apostolic authority. 115. That no one subject to ecclesiastical discipline approach the emperor except with the advice of the metropolitan or of the other bishops. [Col. 0508C] 116. Here begins the formal letter issued by 318 bishops and by Atticus, bishop of the city of Constantinople. Concerning formal letters. 117. That no bishop ordain, retain, or judge another’s cleric without that bishop’s consent. 118. That no bishop interfere in any matter belonging to another’s parish unless asked. 119. On the same matter. 120. On the same matter. 121. That a bishop not lightly issue letters of release to anyone. 122. That no one be called universal. 123. On the same matter. 124. That the pope may restore a condemned bishop. [Col. 0508D] 125. That bishops take their seats and subscribe in the council according to the time of their ordination. 126. That no one presume to undertake what has not been granted to him. 127. That a teacher or pastor who has strayed from the faith must be corrected by the faithful. 128. That the pastors of the Church are often corrupted, so that those who follow may fall more deeply. 129. That we make greater progress through common and reciprocal prayers than through private and individual ones. 130. That the Church not be entrusted to the governance of the inexperienced and uneducated. 131. That bishops, when celebrating the sacrifice, have with them as witnesses seven or eight deacons on solemn days. [Col. 0509A] 132. That bishops always have priests and deacons with them as witnesses. 133. That clerics or elected monks serve as the bishop’s chamberlains. 134. That every church having a bishop also have an administrator of its property. 135. That a bishop ought not to have wicked men in his company. 136. That every bishop have his own steward; or, if he neglects this, let the clergy elect one. 137. That a bishop not entrust the Church’s property to secular men. 138. That Church property not be entrusted to secular men. [Col. 0509B] 139. That episcopal dignity be withdrawn from the city that kills its own bishop. 140. Concerning the three persons: the shepherd, the hired hand, and the thief. 141. That children born of adultery may be promoted to the priesthood. 142. That a bigamist or one who has a concubine cannot be a bishop, presbyter, deacon, or hold any other such office. 143. That the lofty seats of bishops signify their contemplation and authority. 144. That a bishop’s judgment is greatly to be feared, even when unjust; and that one must not associate with those with whom he does not associate. [Col. 0509C] 145. That pastors cannot please both wolves and flocks alike. 146. That the faults of those below are especially attributed to negligent rulers. 147. That priests and ministers of the altar abstain from secular concerns. 148. That what has been unlawfully done be destroyed. 149. That Christian princes ought to bow their heads before bishops, not judge over their heads. 150. That help should be sought from the emperor when necessary. 151. Concerning the synodal oath. 152. Concerning the oath of bishops returning from schism to Catholic unity. 153. That Bishop Leo cleared himself by an oath before the most holy body of blessed Peter concerning a certain sinister rumor. [Col. 0509D] 154. Concerning the faith of the holy Fathers, which is to be preserved in the Church. 155. That bishops subject to the ordinance of the apostolic see be presented annually, on the Ides of May, at the thresholds of the holy apostles Peter and Paul. 156. That the blessed Gregory says he does not recognize those who refuse to observe the canons, censuring their negligence. 157. That bishops are not ordained for secular affairs, but that laymen ought to attend to these. 158. That a bishop, presbyter, or deacon must not beat faithful Christians who sin. [Col. 0510A] 159. That the bishop have ecclesiastical property under his authority and distribute it through presbyters and deacons. 160. That if a bishop has personal property, he may leave it to whomever he wishes, but not Church property. 161. That if presbyters, while there is no bishop, sell anything belonging to the Church, it be restored to the Church. 162. That a bishop have the power to administer ecclesiastical property, and not entrust it to his household members, relatives, or brothers. 163. That the bishop of Syracuse and the other bishops of Sicily must never receive more than two solidi from any presbyter of their diocese under the name of the cathedraticum. 164. That no priest presume to usurp anything belonging to his own titular church. [Col. 0510B] 165. That a bishop not be permitted to exact anything beyond the statutes of the Fathers from a priest, another cleric, or holy places. 166. That bishops ought not to exact any money from their clerics or monks for the sake of shameful profit. 167. That a bishop may not alienate property acquired during his episcopate, but may dispose as he wishes of property he possessed beforehand. 168. That a bishop may not alienate treasures, sacred vessels, or other such things except for the redemption of captives. 169. That a bishop ascend to his order through each successive grade. 170. Concerning Pope Marcellinus, who, under compulsion, offered incense and later became a martyr. [Col. 0510C] 171. That every Sunday and on the birthdays of the martyrs, “Glory in the highest” be sung. 172. That presbyters, together with the pope, recite the canon on feast days. 173. Concerning the blessing of chrism and sacred oil. 174. That a bishop may not be absent from his own church for three weeks. 175. That no one may leave the principal see and proceed to another church in the diocese. 176. That a bishop not be occupied with secular cases. 177. On the same matter. 178. That a bishop must not be negligent, but diligent toward his children and the poor. [Col. 0510D] 179. That a metropolitan do nothing outside his own parish. 180. That a bishop alone cannot depose a deacon or presbyter. 181. Concerning those who invade parishes which they think belong to them. 182. That the popes first used colobia, which were later changed into dalmatics. 183. That a bishop or abbot may not give Church property to princes or to relatives, except as charitable gifts to the poor. 184. That bishops or clerics may not adorn themselves with splendid clothing. 185. That nothing is easier, yet nothing more condemnable before God, than the sacred orders when they are pursued according to human standards; but when pursued according to God, nothing is more difficult or more blessed. [Col. 0511A] 186. That good princes ought to build churches and protect and honor priests. 187. On the same matter. 188. That bishops ought not to flee to secular judges. 189. That a layman send a bishop under suitable custody. [Note: [Col. 0511] The text concerns a pseudo-bishop being sent to the apostolic see.] 190. That schismatics be restrained by the public authorities. 191. Concerning false and apocryphal books, that they not be used for reading. 192. Which books are to be read. [Col. 0511B] 193. That no apocryphal books whatsoever are therefore to be accepted. 194. Concerning the brief appended list of books received into the canon of the Holy Scriptures. [Col. 0512A] 195. That nothing besides the canonical Scriptures be read in the Church. 196. Concerning parishes that have never had bishops. 197. Concerning those who dare to perform ordinations in another’s church or province. 198. That twice a year the bishops assemble in the province wherever the metropolitan wishes. 199. Concerning a bishop unwilling to go to the church entrusted to him. 200. If a bishop is ill, how another may succeed him. 201. That whenever bishops go out to confirm infants, they not be burdensome to their subjects. 202. A letter of Pope Urban II affirming that buyers and sellers of churches are Simoniacs, and that the Masses of wicked priests are to be rejected.

## CONTENTS OF BOOK SEVEN

This book concerns the ordination of presbyters, deacons, and the remaining orders.

[Col. 0511]

[Col. 0511B] 1. That all should live in common, especially those who desire to serve God irreproachably. 2. On the meaning of the term “cleric”; that the Lord is the portion of clerics, and that they themselves belong to the Lord’s lot. 3. On the common life of clerics, and of those who cannot live continently. 4. Likewise, on the common life of clerics, and that the property of the Church must not be converted to uses other than ecclesiastical ones. [Col. 0511C] 5. On the cloisters and workshops of clerics. 6. That clerics living in common may not possess private property. 7. On deacons and religious persons, that they should live canonically. 8. That adolescents placed among the clergy should be assigned to a most approved elder. 9. Which laymen cannot attain the clerical state. 10. That one who has married a widow, whether before or after baptism, must not become a cleric. 11. That a cleric must not be a bigamist. 12. That a penitent must not become a cleric. 13. That a cleric must not marry either a widow or a woman who has been dismissed. [Col. 0511D] 14. That one who has not married a virgin must not aspire to sacred orders. 15. That the unlearned, the physically mutilated, and penitents must not aspire to sacred orders. 16. That those baptized or rebaptized outside the Catholic Church must not enter sacred orders. [Col. 0512B] 17. On those who must not be promoted to sacred orders. 18. That penitents, although cleansed from sin, nevertheless cannot attain the honor of the clerical state. 19. That pardon was formerly granted to penitents, bigamists, and husbands of widows in such a way that such men were not thereafter promoted. 20. That one who is unwillingly sent to a monastery to perform penance must not be permitted to attain the priesthood. [Col. 0512C] 21. That no one should admit a man from overseas to the clerical state except on the testimony of five bishops. 22. That no one from among the penitents should be ordained a cleric. 23. That unknown persons and strangers must not be admitted to sacred orders. 24. On those who cannot attain sacred orders. 25. That no bishop should promote another bishop’s servant against his master’s will. 26. On slaves not to be ordained; or, if they are ordained, that they be restored to their masters. 27. On the same matter. [Col. 0512D] 28. Who penitents are, and to which orders they may attain. 29. That no layman should ascend to the priesthood except through the successive degrees. 30. That no layman should be admitted to a sacred order, with the clerics who have already served in the Lord’s army being passed over. 31. Which laymen may be promoted to the clerical state. 32. That one who deliberately cuts off a limb from himself must not be admitted to the clerical state; if it happened accidentally, he is not prohibited. [Col. 0513A] 33. On eunuchs and those who have castrated themselves. 34. That priests, after receiving their order, should not lose it if their bodies are accidentally debilitated. 35. That one who comes to the priesthood contrary to the canonical forms, and his ordainer, should both be deprived of their honor. 36. That it is not permissible to ordain a neophyte or a layman inconsiderately as priest or deacon. 37. That unlawful ordinations must not be performed. 38. That the ordination of priests or Levites should be solemnly conducted at the proper time. 39. That sacred orders should be conferred at the beginning of the Lord’s night, or in the morning, with the fast continued throughout that same day. 40. On the celebration of the ordinations of priests and deacons at fixed times. [Col. 0513B] 41. That boys must not be admitted to sacred orders, and that there must be no venality in ordination. 42. That those who wish to serve in the Church’s army must ascend step by step from the lowest degree. 43. Through which periods and by which degrees one must ascend from childhood to the highest priesthood. 44. On the same matter. 45. On the order of consecration of the ecclesiastical orders. 46. On the same. 47. That a priest and a deacon are ordained by one bishop alone. 48. How the psalmist, that is, the cantor, is ordained. [Col. 0513C] 49. On the ordination of the doorkeeper. 50. On the ordination of the lector. 51. On the ordination of the exorcist. 52. On the ordination of the acolyte. 53. On the ordination of the subdeacon. 54. On the ordination of the deacon. 55. On the ordination of the priest. 56. That deacons should preserve their order and not involve themselves in the duties of priests. 57. On the order and duty of deacons. 58. That deacons owe honor to priests, and the clerics following deacons owe them honor. 59. On the obedience of deacons toward priests. 60. That the deacon should administer the Eucharist to priests. [Col. 0513D] 61. That the deacon should sit when ordered to do so by the priest. 62. That the deacon should sit in the presence of the priest. 63. That the deacon should wear the white garment only during the time of his office. 64. That the minor orders should be subject to the greater. 65. That deacons are, as it were, the eyes of the bishop, and must inspect the church and teach the laity. 66. That in each city there should be seven deacons to attend upon the bishop. 67. That the ministers of the sacred altar should not sing, but devote themselves to preaching and almsgiving. [Col. 0514A] 68. That in church one must sing to God not only with the voice but also with the heart. 69. On the ministry of deacons, without whom priests have the name but not the function. 70. That a certain man became a deacon through necessity, although, after his wife’s death, he had had children by a maidservant. 71. That deacons should not go about wearing shoes fastened with straps. 72. On an archdeacon whom his bishop cunningly wished to promote and then depose. 73. That archdeacons ought to guard the property of the Church more strictly. 74. That the bishop’s residence should be entrusted to the steward. 75. That one ordained in the Roman Church should not depart from it thereafter. [Col. 0514B] 76. On a certain man whom Saint Gregory made an acolyte and sent back to serve his bishop. 77. That the pope may permit clerics of one Church to be ordained in another. 78. What should be received from a bishop, what from a priest, and what from a deacon. 79. That seven deacons, and an equal number of subdeacons, were ordained throughout the city of Rome. 80. On the seven subdeacons who were placed over the seven notaries. 81. That the regions, as in the city of Rome, should be divided among deacons in each city. 82. That the deacon must wear the stole on his left shoulder. [Col. 0514C] 83. That the deacon must not sit in the presbytery when the divine rites are being celebrated, nor distribute the Lord’s body while a priest is present. 84. That the subdeacon must not use the orarium, nor leave the host behind. 85. That lectors and cantors must not use oraria. 86. That priests are greater than deacons, and that formerly the priest was what the bishop is.

[Note: [Col. 0513D] Anselm adduces nothing in the text except Jerome’s celebrated letter to Evangelus (Vallarsi edition, no. 146). Since highly learned men have often explained it and asserted the necessity and superiority of the episcopate over the presbyterate, there is no need to discuss it further here.]

87. That, according to canonical institutions, the life of the man to be ordained priest must be investigated; and that in every church a priest and minister are necessary. 88. That persons to be promoted should be carefully examined, and that priests should always recite the names of the apostolic pope and of their own ordainer. [Col. 0514D] 89. At what age it is appropriate to ordain a priest. 90. On the promise of those who are promoted to the ecclesiastical degrees. 91. That priests are called “presbyters” not because of age but because of wisdom. 92. That if deacons do not wish to be promoted to the rank of presbyter, suitable acolytes and subdeacons should be ordained, and should be preferred to them in honor and advantage. [Col. 0515A] 93. On clerics who do not obey their bishops when the bishops wish to promote them. 94. That no one can be reconsecrated. 95. That no one should be ordained absolutely.

[Note: [Col. 0515D] That is, without a specific title or assignment to a definite ministry, as in the text.]

96. That a priest must remain in the Church in which he was ordained. 97. On those who do not remain at all in the churches to which they have been advanced. 98. That no cleric should be enrolled in the churches of two cities. 99. That clerics ought not to move from place to place. 100. That a cleric must not be counted among the clergy of two churches. 101. That each ecclesiastical office should be entrusted to a separate person. [Col. 0515B] 102. That clerics should do nothing beyond what the authority of their own office permits. 103. That priests may be ordained from among monks. 104. That priests ordained by men of whom it is doubtful whether they were bishops should be ordained by a Catholic bishop if they are useful. 105. That priests should not appear outside their houses without priestly dress. 106. That parish priests, when they are ordained, ought to receive an official letter from their own priest. 107. That ignorance, the mother of error, must be avoided above all by priests. 108. That when a priest or deacon is appointed over parishes, he must make a profession of chastity. [Col. 0515C] 109. That ignorance is intolerable in priests. 110. That no priest is permitted to be ignorant of the canons. 111. Which books priests must necessarily study. 112. On prayers and supplications. 113. On the prefaces observed by the Roman Church. 114. That no one should invade the boundaries or rights of another parish. 115. That one who buys an order is a Simoniac and must be removed from the office of that order. [Col. 0515D] 116. On the ways in which chorepiscopi and priests differ from bishops. 117. That chorepiscopi should presume nothing concerning the office belonging to high priests. 118. That priests must not aspire to episcopal office. 119. On the same matter. 120. That priests should touch those baptized with chrism on the forehead where bishops are absent. 121. That formerly the bishop was the same as the priest.

[Note: [Col. 0515D] Anselm recites nothing else in the text except the well-known passage of Jerome from his Commentary on Paul’s Letter to Titus 1:5.]

[Col. 0516A] 122. That priests who consecrate Christ’s body can also bless and preach to the people. 123. That bishops should honor clerics, and clerics should honor bishops. 124. How bishops and priests ought to bind and loose. 125. That clerics take precedence over monks. 126. That Masses may be sung only in consecrated places. 127. On the same matter. 128. That a priest should not celebrate Mass with fewer than two others. 129. That only consecrated priests should celebrate Masses, and only in a consecrated place. 130. That priests alone should not celebrate Masses, nor in just any place. [Col. 0516B] 131. That if a priest cannot complete the office he has begun, another priest should complete it in his place. 132. That no one except the Lord’s priests should dare to preach. 133. That priests who govern well should be regarded as worthy of double honor. 134. That priests and Levites should not have intercourse with their wives. 135. On women living in close association with clerics. 136. That priests should not live with women except those whom the canonical regulation permits. 137. That the law of continence is the same for ministers of the altar as for bishops and priests. 138. That deacons must not live with women either. [Col. 0516C] 139. That subdeacons must not have carnal marriage. 140. On the same matter. 141. That clerics should not go alone to women’s dwellings, nor converse with them alone. 142. That the concubines of clerics should be sold, while penance should be imposed on the clerics. 143. That women should not live in clerics’ houses except those whom the Council of Nicaea permits. 144. That when clerics reach puberty, they should profess either marriage or chastity. 145. That clerics or continent men should not go alone to virgins or widows. 146. That a greater must not be blessed by a lesser. [Col. 0516D] 147. That one must not ask who preaches, but whom each person preaches. 148. That superiors who seek their own interests are hirelings. 149. That everything which bishops, priests, or any clerics, wherever they are ordained, acquire in any church must belong to that same church. [Col. 0517A] 150. That clerics must not sell Church property without the bishops’ knowledge, nor bishops without consulting the priests. 151. That priests must not be greedy. 152. That a cleric must not attempt usury through another person either. 153. That clerics must not be leaseholders or merchants. 154. That clerics must not receive interest. 155. That clerics should inform the pope if they see their bishop acting against the pope’s command or causing loss to the Church. 156. That if clerics see a bishop, priest, or deacon violating the statutes of the Roman pontiff, they themselves must report it. 157. That priests and deacons ought to know everything belonging to the Church. 158. That priests and the other faithful should not sit in church while the Gospels are being read. [Col. 0517B] 159. On clerics behaving arrogantly toward their bishop; and that a monastery should restore to the bishop the conditions which its founder established at the time of its consecration. 160. That no one from the clerical order should enter public office. 161. That a cleric who plots against his bishop should be handed over to the secular court. 162. That clerics, except Romans, must not use small cloths (mappulae). 163. That no one should receive a cleric belonging to another bishop against that bishop’s will. 164. That foreign clerics must not minister without letters of recommendation. 165. That buffoonish clerics should be rejected. 166. If any powerful person strips someone of his property and, when admonished by the bishop, does not restore it, let him be excommunicated. [Col. 0517C] 167. On the fast of clerics before Easter and on Mass during the night of the Nativity of the Lord. 168. On the season of Lent. 169. At which times of the year the Ember days are to be celebrated. 170. That each person should offer offerings for his truly Christian dead, and that their priest should commemorate them. 171. Why the third, seventh, and thirtieth days are celebrated for the dead. 172. For which dead the sacrifices or offerings of the living are beneficial. 173. That one should not grieve excessively over dead friends. [Col. 0517D] 174. That no one should turn episcopal residences or monasteries into common lodging places. 175. That priests and deacons should not preside over monasteries unless they have changed their way of life. 176. That no abbot should be chosen in a monastery except one worthy in deeds and morals. 177. That if anyone wishes to enter religious life in a monastery, he should first be carefully tested. 178. That monks must not, on their own authority, expel or appoint abbots for themselves. 179.
