That when someone becomes a monk, all his property becomes the property of the monastery. 185. That monks must not make one another godparents. 186. That no one should disturb monasteries, but that the bishop of the place should take care to arrange their affairs and interests. 187. That clerics should not be entangled in secular business, [Col. 0518B] nor be appointed in any way to guardianship or administration. 188. That deacons and priests are ordained only at a fixed time, but the other clerics at any time. 189. On clerics taking up arms. 190. On the sale of objects that derive from consecration. 193. That Masses cannot be celebrated by such persons. 194. On an (un)ordained man, if he has usurped orders for himself. 195. On clerics who pass over to secular courts. [Col. 0518C] 196. That clerics appointed or ordained in parishes, monasteries, and martyria should remain under the authority of their own bishop. 197. On those who move from their own parish to another and then depart altogether. 198. On those who have abandoned the monastic vocation. 199. That an ecclesiastical person must not be compelled to give testimony. 200. On those who have married a widow or a divorced woman, or have consented to homicide. 201. On consecrated virgins. 202. On widows not to be veiled by bishops. 203. On the violation of the vows of monks and virgins. 204. On clerics or monks who do not remain in [Col. 0518D] their vocation. 205. That young women must not be made abbesses, and that a virgin should not be veiled except at the age of sixty. 206. That women consecrated to God and nuns must not touch sacred vessels or consecrated altar cloths, nor carry incense around the altar. 207. That an offering should be made by everyone on Sundays. 208. On the offering and the kiss of peace. 209. On the loaves to be blessed.

Here begin the chapters of the Council of Piacenza, which was celebrated by Pope Urban II.

[Note: [Col. 0517D] We know that Urban II’s pontificate occurred after the death of Saint Anselm. But it has long been established that certain additions were made to Anselm’s manuscripts, as the difference in handwriting also often demonstrates. [Col. 0518D]]

There are twenty chapters.

## CHAPTERS OF BOOK EIGHT, Which is on Those Who Have Fallen

[Col. 0519]

[Col. 0519A] 1. That those from the clergy who have fallen should themselves, together with their property, be handed over to the poorest monasteries, where they may do penance; or, if they have parents, that the parents should receive the property and provide them with necessities. 2. From which offices ministers of the altar should abstain if, after ordination, they have intercourse with their wives, and which offices they may perform. 3. That no one may remain a cleric after penance: this has been established through the strictness of discipline, not from a despairing refusal of mercy. 4. That husbands of widows and men who have contracted numerous marriages be excluded from all ecclesiastical offices. 5. On the same matter. 6. That Pope Siricius granted penitents, bigamists, and husbands of widows the ranks which they then held, ordering that such men not be promoted further. [Col. 0519B] 7. That bishops or those in the succeeding orders who handle the sacred mysteries, if they do not abstain from their wives, should be removed from ecclesiastical office. 8. That priests and Levites should not have intercourse with their wives, because they are occupied with daily ministry. 9. That clerics who do not abstain after a third admonition should be excommunicated. 10. On the condemnation of an incontinent priest. 11. On those who are promoted to the priesthood and are conscious of sins committed before their ordination. 12. That fornicating bishops must be deposed. 13. On those who have been advanced to the honor of the priesthood without examination. 14. That a bishop, priest, or anyone who is [Col. 0519C] in the clergy may clear himself if witnesses are lacking. 15. That priests who cannot clear themselves of fornication should be removed from ministry. 16. That conspirators against their bishops should be removed from every rank. 17. That anyone who has brought a false accusation, plotted against, or reviled his bishop should be deposed and handed over to the secular court. 18. That if a cleric or monk has conspired, or has contrived a false accusation against bishops or clerics, he should fall from his own rank. 19. On clerics who have fallen into heresy and later been converted. [Col. 0520A] 20. That those who have fallen from sacred orders must not be restored to sacred ministry even after penance. 21. That a priest who, after being deposed, has celebrated Mass should be deprived of communion in the body and blood of the Lord until the day of his death. 22. On fallen deacons and priests, that they must not return to sacred orders, and that fallen subdeacons should receive communion among the laity. 23. On the bodily purity of bishops. 24. On those who return from heresy to the Church. 25. That another should be restored in the place of a fallen bishop. 26. That after a fall a priest can neither remain in sacred order nor be restored to it. 27. How those who have been unjustly deposed should be restored by bishops before the altar. [Col. 0520B] 28. That no one should rashly communicate with those who have fallen. 29. On those who have fallen, to whom communion was granted because of penance and the laying on of hands when they were in danger of death. 30. That the rigor of antiquity concerning the fallen should be preserved until the pope’s authority and counsel. 31. On those who were captured after fleeing and, under compulsion, uttered something belonging to pagan ritual: they should not be removed from communion. 32. Those who fail to carry out the better courses that they have resolved upon have fallen in the eyes of God. 33. How greatly the merits of the saints can help those who have fallen, especially when the day of judgment arrives. 34. That clerics of the Donatists should be received in the honors they hold. [Col. 0520C] 35. That those who have fallen should not be restored to their order. 36. That those who received sacred orders in exchange for abandoning an accusation should be deprived of those same orders. 37. Who may be restored after a fall, and who may not. 38. On clerics who have married wives without consulting their bishop. 39. How those who have transgressed should be received when they return to the Church.

## CHAPTERS OF BOOK NINE, Which is on the Sacraments

[Col. 0519]

[Col. 0519D] 1. That in offerings for the sacraments nothing should be offered except bread and wine mixed with water. 2. That the sacrifice of the altar should be celebrated on a pure linen cloth consecrated by a bishop. 3. That the sacrifice should be celebrated to God by those who are fasting. 4. That neither wine alone nor water alone should be offered in the chalice. 5. From what the Lord’s chalice should be made. 6. That one must follow not human custom but the will of God. [Col. 0520D] 7. That we ought to receive the heavenly food for this purpose: that we may pass into the flesh of the one who became our flesh. 8. That the Lord’s flesh is truly food, and his blood truly drink. 9. That we eat Christ’s body so that we may be participants in eternal life. 10. On those to whom it is permitted to receive communion on every Sunday. 11. On the same matter. [Col. 0521A] 12. That when an evil person receives the Lord’s sacrament, he nevertheless does not make it evil. 13. That baptism should not be administered except at Easter and Pentecost, unless necessity compels it. 14. That the proper times for baptism have been fixed, namely Easter and Pentecost. 15. That, according to the Apostolic See, baptism should not be administered on Epiphany. 16. On the recitation by those to be baptized. 17. That when the person being baptized is immersed three times, the sacrament of a three-day burial is signified. 18. That only one person should come forward to lift an infant from baptism. 19. That one father may serve for a catechumen both in baptism and in confirmation. [Col. 0521B] 20. That if someone from a marriage has held another’s child for some sacrament, they are certainly regarded as godparents. 21. If someone is baptized while remaining in unbelief, he received either no remission or remission only for a moment. 22. Unless one who has been reborn is confirmed by a bishop, he cannot be a perfect Christian. 23. That all the faithful receive the Holy Spirit after baptism through the laying on of the bishops’ hands. 24. That baptism saves those who are about to die, but confirmation with chrism is necessary for those who will live. 25. That confirmation with chrism belongs to bishops alone. [Col. 0521C] 26. That the laying on of bishops’ hands is more venerable than baptism. 27. That no one can be saved without baptism, and that without it no one should partake of the Lord’s body and blood. 28. That an infant partakes of the Lord’s body and blood when he becomes a member of Christ in baptism. 29. That the laying on of hands may be repeated.

[Note: [Col. 0521] For example, for reconciling a heretic, or something similar, but not for repeating the sacrament.]

30. On renewing the chrism each year. 31. That those baptized by heretics should be confirmed by the laying on of hands alone. 32. On the same matter. 33. That the gift of God, which is charity, can neither be possessed nor given outside the Church. [Col. 0521D] 34. That heretics and schismatics, whatever they may possess, do not possess charity. 35. That the sacraments are administered by the wicked as well as by the good. 36. That the sacrament of baptism can both be possessed and administered among heretics. 37. That the same sacraments are complete everywhere. 38. That remission is given through the dove’s groaning, whoever performs the baptism. [Col. 0522A] 39. That heretics possess the sacraments and Scriptures for appearance, not for salvation. 40. That if remission of sins comes through the power of the sacrament, then the heretic is like the greedy man; but if it comes through merit, neither the greedy man nor the heretic receives it. 41. That the wicked cannot defile Christ’s sacrament. 42. That God’s sacraments are correct everywhere. 43. ## FIRST APPENDIX: A DISSERTATION ON THE CANON COLLECTION OF SAINT ANSELM OF LUCCA

*(Augustinus Theinerus, Critical Investigations, p. 563.)*

## A DISSERTATION ON THE CANON COLLECTION OF SAINT ANSELM OF LUCCA

[Col. 0535C] Of all the collectors of canons who preceded Gratian, the most holy and learned was St. Anselm of Lucca. He was designated bishop of Lucca in 1075 by Anselm, formerly bishop of Lucca, who under the name Alexander II had been raised to the supreme leadership of the Church in 1051; he was duly consecrated by St. Gregory VII, Alexander’s successor.

[Note: [Col. 0535C] It is worthwhile to hear Domnizo, a priest of the Order of St. Benedict, a Canossan, and a contemporary of St. Anselm, speaking about our saint (*Life of Countess Matilda*, by Domnizo, book II, chapter 3, in Muratori, *Scriptores rerum Italicarum*, vol. V, p. 369 [Patrologia, vol. CXLVIII]):

> I believe that no one like him existed at that time.
>
> Fulfilling the double office of monks and pontiffs  
> night and day, he chastised his body as an enemy;  
> a Catholic, unmarried, and equally pious and sober.  
> The faithful truly grieve over his death;  
> the schismatics rejoice, for he was opposed to them.  
> The countess, to whom he had been entrusted by Gregory,  
> buried him mournfully and kindly, as was fitting;  
> Mantua committed Anselm’s limbs to the earth.  
> Of him, O Christ, you showed Matilda what was flourishing,  
> for by your virtue he performed many miracles.  
> This servant of yours became one of the saints,  
> a sign, as it were, of weakness to the Catholic party;  
> and the countess rejoices in triumph, praying. ]

Because of the exceptional holiness with which he was endowed, the celebrated countess Matilda of Tuscany chose him to hear her confessions. He vigorously defended St. Gregory VII, both by his deeds and by his writings, as Paul of Bernried, a monk of the Order of St. Benedict in Bavaria and a contemporary of St. Anselm, relates; he endured hardships and persecutions on his behalf with completely fearless courage. St. Anselm, an immortal ornament of the Church and of the Order of St. Benedict, of which he had been a member, died in exile at Mantua on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of April in the year 1086.

St. Anselm wrote various works in defense of the Church and of its supreme hierarch, Gregory VII. Some of these have been printed; others, as the saintly bishop’s penitentiary and biographer has already noted,

[Note: [Col. 0536D] “We know that many things were divinely expounded to him from the sacred Scriptures, some of which we have in writing from him, while we retain others in memory. He wrote many little books with his own hands: he compiled one *Apology* from various volumes of the holy Fathers, by which he defended and approved by canonical arguments and orthodox authorities the judgment of our lord the pope and all his deeds and commands. He made a most lucid exposition of the Lamentations of Jeremiah. At the request of the most blessed handmaid of God, Matilda, he also expounded the Psalter most lucidly—briefly indeed, but usefully—up to the passage where it says: ‘We have blessed you in the name of the Lord.’” (*Life of St. Anselm*, § 20, p. 654, in the Bollandists, *Acta Sanctorum*, under 18 March, vol. II, p. 654, and in Mabillon, *Acta Sanctorum of the Order of St. Benedict*, sixth century, part II, p. 480, Venetian edition. The same *Life of St. Anselm*, together with various works of the same saint, was published by the celebrated Luca Wadding in Rome in 1657, quarto.)]

are preserved in memory and, as may be conjectured, lie hidden in libraries. The foremost place among his works is unquestionably occupied by the celebrated *Collection of Canons*, which he very probably prepared at the urging and persuasion of Gregory VII. This is indicated by the title of the work, which is found in a codex written before the middle of the thirteenth century in the distinguished Barberini Library and reads as follows:

> Here begins the authentic and compendious Collection of the rules and judgments of the holy Fathers and authoritative councils, made in the time of Gregory, the most holy pope, by the blessed Anselm of Lucca, his diligent imitator and disciple, who eagerly completed this work at his command and instruction.

The same inscription is found in the paper Vatican codex no. 3531, as well as in two Parisian codices: one of the Royal Library and the other of the library of the celebrated Maurist monastery of Saint-Germain-des-Prés. All of these, however, are copies of the aforementioned codex.

Although this inscription does not seem to have been attached to the work by St. Anselm himself, nothing can be inferred from that fact which overturns our opinion, since it was written by the very hand by which the codex itself was written and can therefore be regarded as the testimony of some contemporary of St. Anselm. Moreover, this Barberini codex seems to have been written at Lucca. At its beginning there are both a deed of manumission and the script we usually call *formata*, written for the use of the church of Lucca. The celebrated Dom. Mansi, formerly archbishop of Lucca and a most learned editor of the sacred councils, copied this deed of manumission from our codex and published it in print.

[Note: [Col. 0537D] *Amplissima Collectio conciliorum*, vol. XVIII, p. 221.]

Furthermore, the same codex contains certain verses about St. Anselm’s work which seem to have the same author as the inscription, and which we are pleased to set down here:

> In the name of the Trinity,
>
> of the holy and undivided one,
>
> here happily begins
>
> the sequence of this book;
>
> which, namely, from Italy,
>
> Anselm, who was also pontiff
>
> of the Church of Lucca,
>
> a prudent and Catholic man,
>
> fervent in the faith of Christ,
>
> selected from the whole body
>
> of the canons and holy Fathers.

As for the manuscripts of Anselm’s work, they differ greatly among themselves. On this subject, consult what the learned brothers Ballerini discuss.

[Note: [Col. 0537D] *On the Ancient Collections of Canons*, etc., part IV, chapter 13, pp. 640–643, cited edition [*Patrologia*, vol. LVI, *Works of St. Leo the Great*, III, at the beginning].]

The manuscripts have, to be sure, been interpolated in many places, and numerous documents are found inserted in them which are earlier or later than Anselm.

Among the later materials are the chapters of the synod held at Piacenza in 1109, as well as certain decretal letters of the supreme pontiffs Urban II, Calixtus II, Paschal II, and even Innocent [Col. 0538B] II. Hence, we think, it happened that some denied that this collection should be attributed to St. Anselm of Lucca. Their futile arguments have been learnedly and skillfully demolished by the Ballerini brothers, to whom we therefore refer benevolent readers, since in this dissertation, which we have entitled *On the Collection of the Canons of St. Anselm*, we shall provide only those things which escaped the sagacity of those men or which can better clarify the nature and character of Anselm’s work.

The documents that, as we have said, were added to Anselm’s Collection are scattered about at the end of the individual books. Thus, at the end of the seventh book in the Barberini Library codex, there are the decretals of Innocent II, which the celebrated Sarti published in print.

[Note: [Col. 0538C] *On the Distinguished Professors of the Archigymnasium of Bologna*, vol. I, appendix no. 5, pp. 191–194. Bologna, 1769, folio. [Col. 0538D]]

Here we shall give another letter of the same Innocent II, entered at the end of the tenth book in Vatican codex no. 1364, folio 255. The same codex contains at the end of the sixth book another letter of Urban II, addressed to his beloved son Lucius, provost of the church of St. Juventius at Pavia, which Mansi made public.

[Note: [Col. 0538D]

*Amplissima Collectio conciliorum*, vol. XX, pp. 660–663. The letter of Innocent is: “That people should not be prohibited from receiving the monastic habit at the end of life, nor from being buried in monasteries, unless they are excommunicated.”

> “Innocent, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brothers R., archbishop of Milan, Ar. of Como, and J. of Lodi, bishops: greetings and apostolic blessing.
>
> “It has come to our ears that, contrary to the privileges of the Roman Church, you are attempting to establish certain new and unheard-of rules in your parishes, namely, that henceforth no secular person is to be buried in the cemeteries of monasteries, and that if anyone, overtaken by illness, asks to become a monk, he is under no circumstances to be received. We therefore command you and all your clergy to desist entirely from such presumption, and by apostolic letters we order you to permit freely, according to the custom hitherto observed, those who decide during life or at death to convert or be buried in monasteries, unless they have been excommunicated. Given at the Lateran, 9 May.”]

Gratian inserted almost the entire same letter of Urban the Pope into his *Decree*, C. 1, q. 3, c. 8.

Many of these documents—whether earlier or later than Anselm—which are found in manuscripts of Anselm’s Collection also occur in those collections that were excerpted from Anselm’s Collection.

[Note: [Col. 0539D] Ballerini, cited work, part IV, chapter 15, pp. 657–661.]

This is especially evident from the Collection composed shortly after the year 1089 by Bonizo, bishop of Sutri and a contemporary of St. Anselm, which he entitled *Decretal*, or *Syntagma of Ecclesiastical Decrees*; from those prepared by the priest Gregory and Deusdedit;

[Note: [Col. 0540D] Ballerini, cited work, part IV, chapter 14, pp. 646–656.]

and also from the Anselmian excerpts, namely the Viennese and Cassinese, and finally from that most extensive Collection of Canons, often cited by us, which formerly existed in the celebrated library of the Society of Jesus in Paris but is now preserved in Berlin in the library of the distinguished Savigny. It could therefore very easily have happened that documents of this kind were taken from those collections, all of which bear the greatest similarity to Anselm’s work, and added to the codices in which Anselm’s Collection was being copied.

But something must now be said about Anselm’s manuscript codices. In preparing our investigations into the works of Anselm and Gratian, we examined both Vatican and Parisian codices. The Parisian codices can contribute little or nothing to the matter, since they are all more recent and, as we noted above, were copied from Roman codices—namely, the Barberini codex and Vatican codex no. 4993—with only a few additions that other Anselmian codices, perhaps Vatican ones, supplied. [Col. 0539C] The Vatican codex just mentioned, written on paper and of no value, was produced at the order of the Sacred Congregation for the emendation of Gratian’s *Decree*. The copyist seems to have used all the Vatican codices of Anselm’s work in preparing his own codex and to have incorporated into it the chapters that one manuscript contained in greater number than the others. The Roman correctors used this codex more than the others; hence, we believe, it happened that many chapters which Gratian presents as borrowed from Anselm’s Collection are not found at all in the genuine codices of that work.

The Barberini codex, which closely resembles the Vatican codex just mentioned, contains only the first seven books of the Collection and can contribute little or almost nothing to textual criticism because it has been too heavily interpolated. The most learned Sarti, an ornament of the Camaldolese Order, who is acknowledged to have deserved greatly of the history of the predecessors of civil and canon law, included a careful and diligent description of this codex in his work, *On the Distinguished Professors of the Archigymnasium of Bologna*, which he published.

[Note: [Col. 0540D] Cited work. Compare note 25 above.]

It remains to say a few words about the other two Vatican codices, marked nos. 1363 and 1364. The latter is incomplete and lacks the eleventh book. Both are parchment manuscripts [Col. 0540A] of great elegance, written, it seems, in the middle of the twelfth century. Codex no. 1364, however, is far superior and written with remarkable care. Although we used these two codices more than the others, we by no means neglected to consult the rest, especially where they seemed capable of contributing something to the restoration of the sequence of the chapters, which we found disturbed in almost all the codices of Anselm’s work.

Anselm divided his work into thirteen books, each of which contains a greater or smaller number of chapters, according as the subject to be treated required. It is useful to set out here the rubrics of the books together with the number of their chapters from the work of the Ballerini brothers:

[Col. 0540B] **Book I.** On the primacy and excellence of the Roman Church. Alternatively, *On the power and primacy of the apostolic see*. Chapters 90, alternatively 91 or 94.

**II.** On the freedom of appeal. Alternatively, *On the primacy of the Roman Church and the freedom of appeal*. Chapters 78, alternatively 81 or 82.

**III.** On the order of accusing, testifying, and judging. Chapters 117, alternatively 124, 127, or 131.

**IV.** On the authority of privileges. Chapters 55, 56, or 57.

**V.** On the ordinations of churches, and on all their law and status. Alternatively, *On the ordination, law, and status of churches*. Chapters 71, alternatively 83 or 93.

[Col. 0540C] **VI.** On the election and ordination, and on all the power or status, of bishops. Chapters 201, alternatively 203 or 207.

**VII.** On the life and ordination of clerics. Alternatively, *On the life and ordination of priests, deacons, and the remaining orders*. Chapters 207, 209, or 213.

**VIII.** On those who have fallen. Chapter 39.

**IX.** On the sacraments. Chapters 74, alternatively 69.

**X.** On marriages. Chapters 63, alternatively 68, 70, or 76.

**XI.** On penance. Chapters 174, alternatively 179.

**XII.** On excommunication. Chapter 75.

**XIII.** On just vengeance and persecution. Chapters 28, alternatively 29 or 34.

[Col. 0540D] As regards the method Anselm employed in compiling his work, we find that he departed in no respect from the footsteps of his predecessors. He inserted into his compilation the decretal letters of the supreme pontiffs, sometimes whole and sometimes torn into parts; in receiving these, he must be said to have used Burchard of Worms’s *Decree* rather than that other Collection dedicated to Anselm.

We consider it entirely unnecessary to explain at greater length the manner in which Anselm used Burchard’s *Decree*, since this has been demonstrated sufficiently and more than sufficiently by the most learned men Antonio Agustín and Stefano Baluzi. We cannot, however, omit this one point: Burchardian chapters occur very rarely in the first seven books of Anselm, whereas in his remaining books Burchard’s *Decree* was used extremely frequently. In compiling those earlier books, Anselm consulted the Collection dedicated to Anselm [Col. 0541A]

[Note: [Col. 0541C] Let these few examples prove the point. The following chapters of the Collection dedicated to Anselm passed into the work of St. Anselm.

*Ans. dic.*, book I, chapters 1, 10, 11, 17, 20, 21, 24, 27, 31, 38, 41, 42, 52, 64, 65, 67.

*Ans. Lucens.*, book III, chapter 1; book II, chapter 4; book I, chapters 67, 34; book II, chapter 47; book I, chapters 14, 17; book II, chapters 8, 49, 75; book I, chapter 35; book IV, chapter 29; book II, chapters 62, 37, 25.

*Ans. dic.*, book II, chapters 81, 86, 192, 194, 195.

*Ans. Lucens.*, book VI, chapters 164, 167; book VII, chapters 108, 109, 110.

*Ans. dic.*, book III, chapters 28, 32, 36, 44, 46, 52, 68, 73.

*Ans. Lucens.*, book III, chapters 34, 30, 13, 35, 55, 14, 44, [Col. 0541D] 46.

*Ans. dic.*, book IV, chapters 138, 141, 151, 152, 156, 157, 158.

*Ans. Lucens.*, book VII, chapters 60, 59, 58, 57, 55, 54, 52, etc.

These Anselmian chapters just mentioned occur in no other Collection of canons than the one dedicated to Anselm.]

and used it in the same way in which, as we have often observed, it was used by other collectors of canons.

Yet, besides those documents of papal decretals which Anselm excerpted both from Burchard’s *Decree* and from the Collection dedicated to Anselm, certain other decrees of supreme prelates are found in Anselm of Lucca’s work, and these appear to have been taken from the very repositories of the Roman archive. To these we believe that some excerpts entitled “From the Book of the Roman Pontiffs” should be referred. They present purely historical matters and differ in many respects from the events narrated by Anastasius the Librarian in the work commonly known under the same title, *Book of the Pontiffs* [Note: [Col. 0541D] See what the learned editors of Anastasius the Librarian’s *Book of the Pontiffs*, L. A. Muratori, Blanchini, and Vignoli, note concerning it. The inquiry of the most learned Pertz, the recent editor of the monuments of Germany, concerning our Anastasius, in his *Italian Journey*, published at Hanover in 1823, is also not without value.].

There also frequently occur passages taken from the *Daily Book of the Roman Pontiffs* [Note: [Col. 0541D] The *Daily Book of the Roman Pontiffs* was first printed by the learned J. Garner, S.J., at Paris in 1680. Mabillon, in *Museum Italicum*, vol. I, p. 33ff., added certain unpublished documents as an appendix to the *Daily Book*; these, together with the *Daily Book* itself published by Garner, were reprinted by J. Chr. Gottfried Hoffmann, *Nova scriptorum et monumentorum collectio*, Leipzig, 1735, second volume, quarto; and by P. J. de Riegger, Vienna, Austria, 1792, octavo.], as well as from the *Roman Order* [Note: [Col. 0542C] On what should be thought concerning this book, consult the learned editors of the documents of the *Roman Order*: Georg Cassander, Melchior Hittorp, Georg Ferrarius, J. Mabillon, Edmond Martène, and Durand.]. Some of these preserve the genuine title of the documents, while others contain numerous monuments of that kind which are of the greatest importance for elucidating the ancient discipline of the Church. Thus, to give only one example, book VI, chapter 49 contains the celebrated constitution of John P. VIII concerning the rights of cardinals, which Mansi printed in his Collection of councils [Note: [Col. 0542C] Volume XVII, p. 247.].

[Col. 0542A] As we have already noted, no decretal letters of the Roman pontiffs are found in the genuine Collection of St. Anselm that are later than the decretals issued by St. Gregory VII; nevertheless, the canons of that same pontiff, issued in Roman councils, have been inserted into the Collection. Moreover, the decretal letters cited by Anselm often have fuller and more accurate titles in his work than they have in other collectors of canons; subscriptions, too, have very frequently been added to them [Note: [Col. 0542C]

Compare book V, chapter 6, distinction 1, *On consecration*, chapter 7: “Given on the Ides of April.” Book V, chapter 7: “Given on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of August.” C. 16, q. 7, c. 26; book V, chapter 19: “Given on the Ides of May, in the consulship of Asterius and Praesidius, illustrious men.” C. 13, q. 1, [Col. 0542D] c. 1.

Book V, chapter 47: the decree of John P. VIII concerning violators of churches, first published by Baluzi in *Miscellanea*, vol. VII, p. 352, Paris, 1705, octavo; and vol. I, p. 402, of Dom. Mansi’s edition, Lucca, 1751, folio; and in his *Amplissima Collectio conciliorum*, vol. XVII, p. 244. Book V, chapter 51: the decree of St. Leo P. IX against the exemption of monks, with a fuller title than that read in the acts of the councils: “Leo, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to all the faithful in Christ throughout Italy. Given at Rome, on April 20, in the fifth indiction.”

Compare the Collections of councils of Labbe and Cossart, vol. IX, col. 484; Hardouin, vol. VI, part I, p. 961; Coleti of Venice, vol. XI, p. 1353; Mansi, vol. XIX, p. 670. These few examples will suffice.]

Indeed, Anselm sometimes cites them even in decretal letters in which they are absent from the actual registers of decretals. Thus, for example, book X, chapter 6 presents the letter of Gregory the Great to Velox, master of the soldiers [Note: [Col. 0542D] *Register of St. Gregory*, book II, letter 3, p. 101 of the Venetian edition, vol. VII.] together with the subscription: “Given on the fifth day before the Kalends of October, in the tenth indiction.” According to the learned Maurist editors of St. Gregory’s works, this subscription is found only in one, and that a very ancient, Colbertine manuscript in Paris, as well as in the collection of St. Gregory’s letters prepared by Paul the Deacon. Gratian borrowed this letter almost in its entirety from Anselm in C. 23, q. 8, c. 17, omitting only the title. Pseudo-Ivo inserted only a small fragment of the same letter into his work (part X, chapter 70).

As for the sacred canons of the councils, especially the Greek councils, Anselm borrowed almost all of them from the Collection of Dionysius Exiguus. Nevertheless, he also used other versions of the Greek canons: both the version presented by the genuine Collection of the canons of the Spanish Church, recently—namely, in 1821—published under the care and at the expense of the Royal Academy of Madrid, and the version closely related to it, which was received by Pseudo-Isidore into his collection. He also frequently gives two versions of one and the same canon, namely the Isidorian and the Dionysian. Finally, another version of the Greek canons occurs somewhat more frequently in Anselm’s work. It differs greatly both from the versions just mentioned and from the version which we find in the ancient Italian Collections, and which we therefore call the ancient Italian version.

To make the character of this version clearer, we have thought it appropriate to present here the Greek text of several canons together with their version which we call the ancient Italian version. The Ballerini brothers were the first to gather this version diligently from ancient Italian manuscripts [Note: [Col. 0543D] In *The Works of St. Leo*, part I, vol. III, pp. 473–622. Venice, 1757, folio.], and the celebrated Mansi later inserted it into his very extensive Collection of councils [Col. 0543B] [Note: [Col. 0543D] Vol. VI, pp. 1109–1230.]. It should meanwhile be observed that Gratian, who received almost the whole of Anselm’s work into his *Decree*, completely neglected this version peculiar to Anselm. For this reason we trust that students of textual criticism will receive these specimens with gratitude.

## BOOK XI, CHAPTER 36, from the Council of Ancyra, chapter 20

“Women who commit fornication and kill their offspring, and those who cause what has been conceived in their womb to be expelled, the ancient decree removes from the Church until the end of their life. But now it has been determined more humanely: let them do penance for ten years.”

The Collection of the Savinian manuscript, book X, chapter 32, has the opening words of this canon somewhat differently: “The ancient Fathers decreed: until the end of their life.”

[Col. 0543C] **Ancient Italian version**

“Those who have committed fornication and kill their children and hasten to cause an abortion: the first decree forbade them until the end; but, something more humane having been determined, they may obtain it; we decree for them a period of ten years, according to the degrees that have been established.”

In the Ballerini brothers, at the place cited, p. 488, and in Mansi, vol. VI, p. 119.

The Greek text of this canon reads:

“Concerning women who fornicate and destroy what is born, and who hasten to produce abortions: the earlier rule prohibited them until their departure [from life], and they concur in this. But, finding something more humane, we have prescribed a period of ten years, according to the degrees that have been established.”

[Col. 0543D] In Mansi, vol. II, p. 520.

## BOOK VI, CHAPTER 141, from the Council of Chalcedon, chapter 26  
### Every church having a bishop must have a steward

“Since, as we have found in certain churches, bishops administer ecclesiastical property without stewards, it was decided absolutely that every church having a bishop must also have a steward from its own clergy [who must administer ecclesiastical property with the consent of his bishop, so that, when the administration has been without witnesses, ecclesiastical property may not be administered so as to bring dishonor upon the pontiff. If they do not do this, we judge them subject to the holy canons].”

[Col. 0544A] **Ancient version**

“Since in certain churches, as we have found, ecclesiastical property is administered without stewards, it was decided that every church having a bishop should have a steward from its clergy, administering ecclesiastical property with the will of his bishop, so that the administration of the church might not be without witness, and so that through this the property of that church might not be dispersed and reproach brought upon the priests [or priesthood]. But if he does not do this, he is to be subject to the sacred canons.”

In the Ballerini brothers, p. 622; in Mansi, p. 1230.

The Greek text of this canon:

“Since in certain churches, as we have heard, the bishops administer ecclesiastical affairs without stewards, it was decided that every church having a bishop should also have a steward from its own clergy, administering the ecclesiastical affairs according to the judgment of his own bishop, so that the administration of the church might not be without witness, and so that thereby the affairs of the church might not be scattered and reproach brought upon the priesthood. But if he does not do this, he is to be subject to the divine canons.”

Mansi, vol. VII, p. 368.

Gratian received this canon of the Council of Chalcedon twice: from the Pseudo-Isidorian version, D. 89, c. 4, and from the version of Dionysius Exiguus, C. 16, q. 7, c. 21.

Chapter 156 of book VII of St. Anselm’s Collection presents a very short fragment of canon 24 of the Council of Antioch in our ancient Italian version.

Besides those Greek conciliar canons which Anselm borrowed from the versions just mentioned, he also took many chapters from the chapters of St. Martin of Braga and of Pope Hadrian. The former frequently occur with the title “From the council of Martin, pope of Braga,” or “From the decree of Martin P.” Gratian presents many of them in his *Decree* under the same title, “of Martin P. of Braga,” or “of the council of Martin P.” [Note: [Col. 0543D] D. 50, c. 44; C. 26, q. 5, c. 3; and C. 32, q. 5, c. 9. The remaining passages from these chapters of Martin of Braga that passed into Gratian are: D. 18, c. 15; D. 23, c. 32; D. 24, c. 7; D. 27, c. 1; D. 28, c. 12; D. 30, c. 17; D. 34, cc. 12, 17, and 18; D. 44, c. 12; D. 50, cc. 8 and 22; D. 54, c. 7; D. 55, c. 9; D. 63, c. 6; D. 64, c. 7; D. 65, c. 2; D. 92, cc. 3, 4, and 9; D. 95, c. 11; C. 1, q. 1, c. 67; C. 1, q. 7, c. 22; C. 6, q. 4, c. 2; C. 8, q. 1, c. 4; C. 9, q. 3, c. 1; C. 10, q. 2, cc. 7 and 8; C. 11, q. 3, c. 7; C. 12, q. 1, c. 20; C. 14, q. 4, c. 4; C. 15, q. 8, c. 4; C. 17, q. 4, c. 38; C. 21, q. 5, c. 5; C. 26, q. 5, c. 3; C. 26, q. 6, c. 6; C. 26, q. 7, c. 13; C. 27, q. 1, cc. 8 and 26; C. 32, q. 7, c. 9; C. 33, q. 4, c. 9; D. 1, *On consecration*, c. 29; D. 2, *On consecration*, cc. 4 and 18; D. 3, *On consecration*, c. 7; D. 4, *On consecration*, cc. 59, 116, and 124.]

We believe that this gave rise to the fact that some wished to attribute such chapters to Martin P. I and dared to accuse that most holy pontiff of corrupting the ancient ecclesiastical discipline, because he had permitted bigamists to remain in the lower grades of orders. Some more recent writers went so far in their insolence as to cite these chapters of Pseudo-Martin P. in support of their opinion and to maintain that bishops, even in our own times, could grant a dispensation from irregularity for the reception of minor orders. But how far this is from the truth, no one is unaware; and Pope Sixtus V thoroughly and completely refuted such quibbles [Note: [Col. 0545D] Fagnanus, in his commentary on chapter 2, *On bigamists*, vol. I, p. 450. Venice, 1709, folio.].

In the alphabetical index which we prepared of the principal Collections of canons used by Gratian, we have retained the false title of Martin of Braga wherever we found it in the ancient Collections.

Moreover, as is well known, the chapters of St. Martin of Braga are inserted in all the manuscripts both of the spurious and of the genuine Isidorian Collection [Col. 0545B]. Jacobus Merlinus first published them together with the Pseudo-Isidorian Collection, and thereafter they passed into almost all the Collections of councils. Mansi reprinted them from the recension of García Loaysa and P. Labbe, S.J. [Note: [Col. 0545D] *Councils*, vol. IX, pp. 845–860.], as did Justellus [Note: [Col. 0545D] *Bibliotheca juris canonici veteris*, vol. I, appendix, pp. 7–32. Paris, 1661, folio.] and Hardouin [Note: [Col. 0545D] *Collection of councils*, vol. III, p. 390.]. Since the latter notes that he found these chapters in the extensive manuscript Collection of canons of the Paris College of the Society of Jesus, he seems to have been speaking of no other Collection of canons than the one contained in the Savinian manuscript, which we have mentioned several times. For that manuscript was once kept in the library of that college of the Society of Jesus in Paris, and the Collection itself was taken in its entirety from the work of Anselm of Lucca.

Later collectors of canons who cite chapters from the decrees or council of Martin the pope did not in any way have before their eyes the Collection of the Savinian manuscript, as the Ballerini brothers believe [Note: [Col. 0545D] At the place cited, part IV, chapter 2, pp. 578–582. Antonio Agustín discussed these chapters of Martin of Braga most learnedly in *On the Emendation of Gratian*, first dialogue, dialogues X, XI, and XII, in Galland, vol. II, pp. 290–314, cited edition; and after him Carlo Sebastiano Berardi, professor at Turin, in *Gratian’s Genuine Canons Distinguished from the Apocryphal, Corrected on the Authority of More Accurate Manuscripts, and the More Difficult Ones Explained with a Convenient Interpretation*. Venice, 1777, vol. I, chapter 33, pp. 292–309.], but the work itself of Anselm of Lucca.

As for the chapters of Pope Hadrian, Anselm inserted them either singly or several together in succession. Those which are found singly, scattered here and there in different books, are frequently entitled “From the decree of Pope Hadrian”; but when he received a series of them, he prefixed to them the customary title [Col. 0546A]. Thus, for example, after chapter 85 of book III, the following chapters of Pope Hadrian are presented: 22, 50, 52, 53, 54, 55, 72, and 80; and they bear this title:

“Here begin the chapters collected in scattered form from the Greek and Latin canons, the Roman synods, and the decrees of Roman prelates and princes, and delivered at Rome by the blessed Pope Hadrian to Angelram, bishop of the city of Metz, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of October, in the ninth indiction, when he was attending to his own affair.”

The complete series of the chapters of Pope Hadrian, preceded by this same title, exists in very many ancient manuscripts of the Pseudo-Isidorian Collection, and from there Anselm undoubtedly drew his chapters. Gratian very frequently cites these chapters [Note: [Col. 0545D] C. 2, q. 3, cc. 3 and 4; C. 2, q. 6, c. 40; C. 2, q. 7, cc. 50 and 33; C. 3, q. 5, c. 7; C. 3, q. 6, cc. 16 and 18; C. 3, q. 7, c. 1; C. 3, q. 11, c. 3; C. 4, q. 6, c. 4; C. 5, q. 1, c. 1; C. 5, q. 3, cc. 1 and 2; C. 5, q. 6, cc. 1 and 5; C. 6, q. 1, cc. 2 and 6; C. 11, q. 1, cc. 48 and 49; C. 25, q. 4, c. 3; and C. 25, q. 1, c. 11.], and Antonio Agustín published them in full, furnished with a learned commentary [Col. 0546B] [Note: [Col. 0546D] *Works*, vol. III, pp. 349–369. Lucca, 1767, folio. Mansi reprinted the chapters of Pope Hadrian together with Antonio Agustín’s commentary in *Collection of councils*, vol. XII, pp. 903–936. See also what C. Seb. Berardi notes concerning these chapters in *Gratian’s Canons*, etc., vol. I, pp. 350–355, cited edition.].

Besides these ecclesiastical monuments, St. Anselm also received several fragments from Roman law and from the capitularies of the Frankish kings, insofar as they concern ecclesiastical affairs. For the use of Roman law, see what Reisach stated in the dissertation on this subject which he appended to our investigations [Note: [Col. 0546D] In our collection, dissertation IV.], where one will also find an index prepared by the celebrated Savigny, in which all the chapters Anselm borrowed from Roman law are recorded.

Gratian, as we have already observed several times, made the greatest possible use of St. Anselm’s Collection in preparing his *Decree*, to such an extent that, if one excepts the celebrated Collection of canons which we call the *Tripartita* and Ivo’s *Panormia*, he must be said to have used no canonical work so frequently [Col. 0546C]. When the celebrated Roman correctors noticed this, they added in the margin to each of Gratian’s chapters taken from Anselm’s work the number of the corresponding book and chapter.

Moreover, in excerpting St. Anselm’s work, Gratian retained precisely the same method which, as we have demonstrated, he observed with respect to the *Tripartita* Collection and Ivo’s *Panormia* [Note: [Col. 0546D]

Gratian followed the order of Anselm’s work insofar as possible; a few examples will prove this.

*Ans.* book I, chapters 11, 16, 31, 37, 39, 57, and 65.—C. 24, q. 1, cc. 18, 15, 16, 10, 13, 22, 25; book I, cc. 20, 25, 54.—C. 9, q. 3, cc. 13, 14, 15.—book I, cc. 33, 44, 46, 50.—C. 25, q. 1, cc. 1, 2, and 4.

*Ans.* book II, chapters 6, 7, 8, 10.—C. 2, q. 6, cc. 8, 6, 4, 2.

*Ans.* book III, chapters 6, 13, 15, 17.—C. 3, q. 5, cc. 13, 2, 4, 7. Book III, chapters 65, 66, 67.—C. 1, q. 1, cc. 20, 4, and 5.

*Ans.* book V, chapters 1, 2, and 3.—C. 24, q. 1, cc. 18, 19, 20; book V, cc. 4, 5, 6, 12, 16, 1 [lacuna] 21, 22, 23.—D. [Col. 0547C] 1, *On consecration*, cc. 6, 5, 7, 19, 36, 38, 21, 22, 16. Book V, cc. 59, 60, 61.—C. 18, q. 2, cc. 25, 26, 27; [Col. 0547D] book V, cc. 72, 73, 74, 75.—C. 16, q. 7, cc. 40, 36, 35, 33.

*Ans.* book VI, chapters 27, 28, 29, 30, 31.—D. 79, cc. 9, 4, 3, 5, 6. Book VI, cc. 42, 43, 54, 56.—D. 64, cc. 6, 8, 1, 5; book VI, cc. 64, 65.—C. 7, q. 1, cc. 5 and 6. Book VI, c. 91.—95, 97, 99, 100.—D. 100, cc. 1, 2, 9, 7, 8, 5, 11, 4. Book VI, cc. 100–106, 107–111.—C. 7, q. 1, cc. 34, 43, 31, 34, 35, 42, 44. Book VI, cc. 121, 123, 129, 130. C. 23, q. 8, cc. 26 and 27.—D. 99, cc. 4 and 5.

*Ans.* book VII, chapters 2–8.—C. 12, q. 1, cc. 5, 8, 9, 3, 10, 11, 14, 1. Book VII, cc. 18–20, 21–23, 32–34.—D. 50, cc. 60, 56, 58.—D. 98, cc. 1–3.—D. 55, cc. 6, 7, 12. Book VII, cc. 38–40.—D. 75, cc. 3, 4, 7. Book VII, cc. 48–55.—D. 33, cc. 20, 19, 18, 17, 16, 15, 11, 7. Book VII, cc. 56–58, 66 and 67, 108–110, 114 and 115.—D. 93, cc. 13–15.—D. 92, cc. 1 and 2.—D. 38, cc. 3, 5.—D. 68, cc. 4 and 5.

*Ans.* book VII, cc. 140–142.—D. 81, cc. 20, 21, 30, [Col. 0548C] 31.—Book VII, cc. 185, 186.—C. 18, q. 2, cc. 19 and 20.

[Col. 0548D] *Ans.* book IX, chapters 22, 23, 25.—D. 5, *On consecration*, cc. 1, 2, 3.

*Ans.* book X, chapters 7–9, 18–20.—C. 27, q. 2, cc. 30, 46, 49, 19, 21, 22.—Book X, cc. 27, 28.—C. 30, q. 3, cc. 1 and 2.

Book XII, cc. 45–47, 49–50, 53, 54–56, 64 and 65.—C. 23, q. 5, cc. 42–45.—C. 24, q. 3, cc. 26–28, 31.—C. 23, q. 4, cc. 37–39, 18, 4.

*Ans.* book XIII, chapters 3 and 4, 10–12, 15, 16, 28 and 29.—C. 23, q. 1, cc. 1–3.—C. 23, q. 5, cc. 1–3.—C. 23, q. 4, cc. 42 and 43, 48 and 49.]

. He received Anselm’s chapters either whole or divided into parts [Col. 0547A] [Note: [Col. 0548D] Thus, from Gr., chapter 152 of book XI, he divided it into six parts: D. 1, *On penance*, chapters 50–56.], and sometimes joined two or three successive chapters into one while retaining their titles. He often added a few words to the chapters, while in other cases he omitted certain words. The titles which were longer in Anselm, Gratian shortened; he did the same with the summaries customarily prefixed to individual chapters. He omitted almost all the subscriptions to the decretal letters, which Anselm very frequently gives.

In view of this, there is no doubt that, with the help of Anselm’s Collection, many chapters of Gratian whose titles have either been lost or corrupted can be restored, and that the text itself—which is sometimes found more complete and more correct in St. Anselm’s Collection than in Gratian’s *Decree*—can be emended. [Col. 0547B] It would be excessively long and entirely foreign to our purpose if we wished to annotate individually all the chapters of Gratian’s Collection which can be corrected with the help of Anselm’s Collection. Nevertheless, we shall give a few examples here, so that it may be clear how important Anselm’s work is for those who strive, by means of criticism, to produce a more accurate text of Gratian’s *Decree*.

## BOOK IV, CHAPTER 3. “A privilege absolutely,” C. 11, q. 3, c. 63

Gratian borrowed this chapter solely from Anselm, but gave it the title: “From the register of Gregory the Great.” Anselm gives its genuine title: “Simplicius P. to John, bishop of Ravenna.” Hardouin, vol. II, p. 803; Mansi, vol. VI. Burchard, book I, chapter 29, and Pseudo-Ivo, part V, chapter 140, likewise present the same fragment under the genuine name of Pope Simplicius, but much more fully and richly. In the Savinian manuscript, book I, chapter 13, he followed Anselm exactly, as it were “from the fingernail,” but falsely entitled the chapter: “Pope Leo, surnamed the Great.”

## BOOK IV, CHAPTERS 14, 15, AND 19. “In every city.” — “All whom.” — “We decree.” C. 23, q. 8, c. 23

Here Anselm presents three mutually different fragments of secular laws: laws 16 and 26 of the *Theodosian Code*, *On bishops, churches, and clerics* (XVI, 27), and law 22, title *On holy churches* (I, 2). Gratian received these three fragments in full, but joined them together. The Savinian manuscript and the manuscripts of St. Anselm’s work preserved in the royal library at Paris present the complete constitution of the emperor Justinian, law 22, title *On holy churches*, whereas Gratian and the Vatican Anselmian manuscripts present only a fragment of it. From this it is clear that Gratian used a Roman, or at least Italian, copy of Anselm.

For the rest, concerning these fragments of laws and their use in ecclesiastical monuments, compare the learned J. Daniel Ritter in his edition of the *Theodosian Code*, vol. VI, part I, pp. 49 and 65. Leipzig, 1713, folio.

## BOOK IV, CHAPTER 39. “No one.” C. 9, q. 3, c. 13

Gratian received this chapter from Anselm in full, but falsely entitled it: “Pope Innocent.” Anselm and the author of the Collection of Zaragoza, book I, chapter 1, and book V, chapter 1, give the title: “Pope Sylvester in a council of 277 bishops.” The chapter was taken from chapter 20, act II, of the constitution of Pope Sylvester fabricated by Pseudo-Isidore; Hardouin, vol. I, p. 290, and in Peter Coustant, *Letters of the Roman Pontiffs*, appendix, p. 50, Paris edition, 1721, folio. The Savinian manuscript and the Vatican Anselmian manuscripts add at the end of the chapter: “All the bishops, and forty-five priests and seven deacons, and Constantine Augustus and his mother Helena, subscribed.” Gratian, as well as Ivo in the *Panormia*, deleted this subscription. Ivo furthermore presents our chapter under a double title: “In the decrees of Innocent: Pope Sylvester, presiding in a general synod, said: No one.” What more is there to say? We see that the source of Gratian’s title has thereby been discovered.

## BOOK V, CHAPTER 1. “There is one Church.” C. 24, q. 1, c. 18. “The Lord speaks to Peter.”

[Col. 0548C]

The passage which Anselm presents here is taken from St. Cyprian’s book *On the Unity of the Church*. Another fragment of this Cyprianic passage, “The Lord speaks to Peter,” occurs in the same work of Anselm, book I, chapter 11. Polycarp, book VII, title 3, received both fragments from Anselm, but joined them into one, placing the latter before the former. Gratian appears to have followed Polycarp in receiving these two fragments, since he presents them in precisely the same order, merely cutting away a few words.

Moreover, Gratian presents again, with slight alteration, the following golden Cyprianic words inserted into our fragment: “He who does not hold the unity of the Church, does he believe that he holds the faith? He who resists and opposes the Church, does he trust that he is in the Church?”—D. 93, c. 3: “He who abandons the chair of Peter, upon which the Church was founded, should not trust that he is in the Church.” Gratian excerpted this passage from the *Tripartita* Collection, part III, title 9, chapter 18, and from Pseudo-Ivo, part V, chapter 361. Both the author of the *Tripartita* Collection and the author of Pseudo-Ivo’s *Decree* prefix certain words to our fragment: “He who does not hold Peter’s unity, does he believe that he holds the faith?” Gratian deleted these, having transferred them into the argument or summary of the chapter: “He is not in the Church who does not follow the chair of Peter.”

Our passage in this wording is entirely absent from the ancient Vatican and Gallican manuscript codices, but is found in certain others, likewise ancient, as the Roman correctors and the most learned editor of St. Cyprian’s works, Stefano Baluzi, have noted. From this one may observe how unjustly adherents of modern criticism accuse our Gratian as a corrupter of the texts of the holy Fathers.

## BOOK VI, CHAPTER 49. “Granted.” C. 12, q. 2, c. 26

Gratian took our passage from Anselm, omitting only certain words; the author of the Collection of Zaragoza, book IV, chapter 74, likewise followed Anselm. Gratian divided it into two parts, inserting the later fragment, “Of venerable baptism,” below D. 4, *On consecration*, c. 17, in his *Decree*. Gratian [Col. 0549C] gave the later fragment another title, namely “Pope Gelasius to the clergy and people of Tarentum,” apparently following Ivo, who presents this chapter (*Panormia*, book I, chapter 21) under the title “Pope Gelasius to the clergy and people of Tharentum.”

The author of Ivo’s Pseudo-*Decree* presents the same chapter twice: first under the title “Pope Gregory to the clergy and people of Tarentum” (part I, chapter 63), and then under the title “From the Council of Worms,” chapter 10 (part I, chapter 202). In the first place, Pseudo-Ivo had Ivo’s *Panormia* before his eyes; in the second, Burchard’s *Decree*, where in book IV, chapter 7, this chapter appears with the title “From the Council of Worms,” with only its opening changed from “Sacrosanct baptism” to “Venerable baptism.”

[Col. 0549D] In fact, this chapter, together with the opening “Sacrosanct,” is found among the canons issued at Worms in the year 868: in Hartzheim, *Councils of Germany*, vol. II, p. 868; Hardouin, vol. V, p. 737; and Mansi, vol. XV, p. 871.

As for the title of our chapter which Pseudo-Ivo presents in part I, chapter 63, it undoubtedly arose through the carelessness of scribes, since the chapter preceding this one in Pseudo-Ivo’s work bears the title of Gregory responding to Augustine.

It should further be observed that nearly the same words of this chapter are found in a capitulary decree of Pope Gregory concerning Martianus the bishop, Georgius the priest, and Dorotheus the subdeacon, who had been sent as envoys to Bavaria: in Hardouin, vol. III, p. 1681; Hartzheim, vol. I, p. 36; and Mansi, vol. XII, p. 258. Mansi [Col. 0550A] received both chapters—both the one from Anselm’s Collection and the one from Gratian’s *Decree*—among the decrees of Pope Gelasius I, *Amplissima Collection of councils*, vol. VIII, pp. 87, 120, 135, and 139. See also Hardouin, *Collection of councils*, vol. II, pp. 930 and 936.

## BOOK VI, CHAPTER 89, D. 100, c. 3

Anselm, like Polycarp, reads more correctly: “Your fraternity knows.” This is how the letter of St. Gregory the Great to John, bishop of Corinth, reads, of which our chapter is a fragment. Book V, letter 59.

## BOOK VI, CHAPTER 100. D. 100, c. 4

Anselm and Deusdedit give the genuine title: “Pope John VIII to Wuilibert, bishop.” The same title is found in another letter of that pontiff sent to our bishop. [Col. 0550B] Mansi, vol. XV, p. 209. Mansi likewise lists our chapter under this title among the fragments of the letters of Pope John, at the place cited, p. 242.

## BOOK XIII, CHAPTER 33. “If anyone.” C. 1, q. 3, c. 7

This chapter is entirely absent from the genuine manuscripts of the Anselmian Collection, and appears to have migrated into Anselm’s Collection from the Collections of Deusdedit, Gregory the priest, Bonizo, and others, which share a common origin with Anselm’s work. The Collection of the Savinian manuscript, likewise, book IX, chapter 247, presents the same chapter with the title: “Pope Paschal in a letter to the Church of Milan, in book VII.” Ivo presents the same chapter under the title “From the decrees of Pope Paschal,” chapter 18, evidently taken from an old, as yet unidentified Collection of canons.

[Col. 0550C] Pseudo-Ivo (part II, chapter 84) has inserted the complete letter of Pope Paschal I under the same title. The celebrated Mansi reprinted it from a very ancient Lucchese manuscript of Burchard of Worms, belonging to St. Martin, *Amplissima Collection*, vol. XIV, p. 378ff., unaware that it was already found in Pseudo-Ivo’s *Decree*.

## C. 12, q. 5, c. 17. “He decreed”

This chapter too is found falsely in certain manuscripts of Anselm’s Collection, book III, chapter 98. Burchard, book XII, chapter 20, and the Collection of the Savinian manuscript, book XII, chapter 109, present the same chapter under its genuine title: “From the council held at St. Medard, chapter 4.” Gratian retained precisely the same title.

This fragment, otherwise much more complete, [Col. 0550D] occurs in the capitulary of Charles the Bald (title XI, chapter 8, among the works of Jacques Sirmond, vol. III, p. 70, Paris, 1696, folio; and in his *Councils of Gaul*, vol. III, p. 89; in St. Baluzi, *Capitularies of the Frankish Kings*, vol. II, p. 53; Hardouin, *Collection of councils*, vol. V, p. 53; and Mansi, *Amplissima Collection*, vol. XVII, p. 39, in the appendix), as well as in Regino, *On Ecclesiastical Disciplines*, book II, chapter 319, p. 333, edition of Stefano Baluzi, Paris, 1671, octavo.

This fragment is entitled in Charles the Bald’s capitulary “from the Synod of Soissons of the year 853,” although it is not found among the canons of that council, which was held at Soissons in the monastery of St. Medard in 853. See what the learned Hartzheim, *Councils of Germany*, vol. II, p. 563, and P. J. de Riegger, in his edition of Regino, note at the cited place, [Col. 0551A] p. 333, Vienna, Austria, 1765, quarto, observe.

Mansi correctly inserted our canon, received by Gratian together with three others presented elsewhere by Burchard from the same council at St. Medard, into his acts of the Council of Soissons of 853. *Collection of councils*, vol. XIV, p. 995.

Moreover, the author of the Collection of the Savinian manuscript added certain words at the end of this chapter which are found nowhere else: “But if not, let each one do penance for the perjury he has voluntarily committed.”

These few remarks on St. Anselm’s Collection will suffice, since it is entirely foreign to our purpose here to illustrate the whole work with critical notes; moreover, this would be exceedingly tedious and wholly useless unless we were at the same time to provide the text of the entire Collection. Nevertheless [Col. 0551B], since frequent mention is made both of our Collection and of the works of Antonio Agustín, Stefano Baluzi, and others, as well as in the annotations that the Roman correctors appended to Gratian’s Decree, some people, having been led into error, have said that St. Anselm’s Collection had already been published in print. Perhaps not a few were deceived by the fact that the most celebrated and learned Andreas Schottus, S.J., in the eulogy he delivered at the funeral of Antonio Agustín, while recalling the deceased man’s works, says:

> “For the elucidation of sacred law, after the two Antonios, Gaddo [Demochare] and Contius, who labored on Gratian’s collections, [Col. 0552A] at Lérida he published, as I have said, the complete Collections of Anselm of Lucca: a rare and useful work” [Note: [Col. 0551D] In Galland, p. 589, vol. II, cited edition.].

Who does not see that the orator was here speaking of the edition that Antonio Agustín prepared of the ancient collections of decretal letters—namely, those of Bernard of Pavia and others? Gregorio Majansius, the most celebrated Spanish jurist of his time, had already noticed this [Note: [Col. 0551D] “The History of the Life of Anselm Agustín, archbishop of Tarragona, which Gregorio Mayansias Siscarus, a nobleman of Valencia, keeper of the library of the kings of Spain and interpreter of the Justinian Code at the University of Valencia, was writing in Spanish; Fabio Prospero Cenamius and Giovanni Battista Montecatinius, patricians of Lucca, translated it into Latin.” Among the works of Antonio Agustín, vol. I, p. XLI. Lucca, 1776, folio.].

Many learned men began planning to have St. Anselm’s Collection printed. Lucas Wadding, the most celebrated compiler of the annals of the Order of Friars Minor, considered the matter several times, as the preface he prefixed to the little works of St. Anselm, published under his care, demonstrates. But, carried off by a premature death, he left this undertaking to posterity. If we trust Stefano Baluzi [Col. 0552B] [Note: [Col. 0552D] Preface to Antonio Agustín’s dialogues *On the Correction of Gratian*, § XIX, p. 215. In Galland, vol. II.], Lucas D’Achery too had St. Anselm’s work already prepared for the press; and it is exceedingly regrettable that he did not carry his plan through, since the complete and ancient codex preserved in the celebrated Benedictine library of Saint-Germain-des-Prés was lost during the French Revolution. The learned men Andrea Rota [Note: [Col. 0552D] *Historical Notices of St. Anselm*. Verona, 1737, quarto.] and Michelangelo Monsacratus [Note: [Col. 0552D] *A Letter of St. Anselm, Now Published for the First Time, Together with Annotations on St. Anselm’s Manuscript Decree*. Lucca, 1821, octavo.] also seem to have entertained the same plan. But we have not been able to inspect their works. At last, the unanimous opinion of learned men is that St. Anselm of Lucca’s Collection should be printed.

## ON THE ANSELMian CODEX PRESERVED IN THE LIBRARY OF THE MOST SACRED VATICAN BASILICA

[Col. 0551]

[Col. 0551C] The Collection presented by this codex, marked number 118 C, has been regarded by many as identical with the work of decretal material comprising St. Anselm of Lucca’s Collection. Although the Ballerini brothers had already demonstrated that this opinion was false [Note: [Col. 0552D] Cited work, p. IV, c. 13, § 8, p. 648.], they nevertheless contributed nothing by which the character of this work might be clarified. For that reason, let us offer here a few observations about it.

The collection of canons of which we are speaking has been excerpted entirely from Anselm’s work, and it comes still closer to that work than do the Collections of Bonizo, Deusdedit, and Gregory. In arranging it, the author followed almost the same procedure and method that, as we have often observed, were followed in the Savinian Collection at Berlin, as well as in the Anselmian excerpts—one preserved at Vienna and the other at Cassino [Col. 0551D]. He did indeed consult Anselm’s work, but reduced the number of books to nine, prefacing each with a general title, which we set out here:

**Book I.** On the power and primacy of the apostolic see.  
**Book II.** On the election of prelates.  
**Book III.** On the consecration of churches and their rites. [Col. 0552C]  
**Book IV.** On the sees of bishops and the authority of preaching.  
**Book V.** On excommunication.  
**Book VI.** On accusation.  
**Book VII.** On the unity of the Church.  
**Book VIII.** On marriage and adultery.  
**Book IX.** On kidnappers and thieves.

The individual books contain more or fewer chapters, to which, in the same way as Gregory—commonly called *Polycarpus*—did, certain general titles or brief summaries have been prefixed. When canons are cited from different councils bearing the same name, the councils are not distinguished by numbers; the number of the canon is also often absent, as we likewise observed in the decretal letters of the Roman pontiffs and in fragments of the holy Fathers, writers, and ecclesiastical works [Col. 0552D]. Apart from the bare names of councils, pontiffs, and other writers, nothing else appears, and in many chapters the titles have been completely omitted.

Then, in each book, there are numerous titles written in red, which appear very similar to rubrics [Col. 0553A]. These often encompass three, four, or even more chapters, but most frequently no more than one. Sometimes—and indeed quite often—twenty, thirty, forty, or even fifty chapters follow one another, with no other title prefixed to them apart from such a heading; and, as their contents show, they do not belong at all to the preceding title. From this it could reasonably be concluded that such headings are nothing other than general lists of contents, distinct from rubrics and added by the author at his discretion. Moreover, neither the individual chapters nor the titles are distinguished by numbers.

There is no preface at all, and several passages in different books of the Collection have been written into the codex by another and later, though ancient, hand. In addition, here and there the codex contains some leaves that are either entirely or partly blank [Col. 0553B]. Nevertheless, I would not dare assert with the Ballerini brothers that the work itself is incomplete, since nowhere is it apparent that the author intended to publish the work completed in every respect. If we wish to investigate how it came about that our collection was attributed to St. Anselm of Lucca, it is certainly impossible to explain this by the fact that the codex bears the title *Anselm’s Decree*. For that title was added by a later hand, and much later. Rather, the structure of this work of ours, together with its very great similarity to Anselm’s Collection, led learned men into error. When they saw that the individual books of our work began with precisely the same chapters with which the corresponding books [Col. 0553C] in the Anselmian Collection began, and when they found among the titles many that had been taken word for word from the titles of Anselm’s chapters, they concluded that the whole work itself was entirely identical with Anselm’s work of decretals [Note: [Col. 0553C].

It would take too long if we wished to demonstrate here in detail how our Collection corresponds with Anselm’s in all its parts. A few examples will suffice:

- Book I, chapters 1–8, 9–20, 23–30; Anselm, Book I, chapters 1–8, 10, 11, 13, 14, 15, 16, 17, 18–21, 22–31.
- Book II, chapters 1 and 2, 4–10. Anselm, Book VI, chapter [Col. 0553D] 35. Book VII, chapter 109, 30. Book VI, chapter 74, 17, 18, 19, 137. 21.
- Book VIII, chapters 1–3, 3–7, 9–11. Anselm, Book X, chapters 1, 2, 5, 20, 18, 19, 29, and 39, etc.]

.

Moreover, there are very many chapters in our Collection that are found neither in Anselm’s Collection nor in those of the others who followed him more closely, such as Bonizo, Deusdedit, and Gregory [Col. 0554A] [Note: [Col. 0553D] We transcribed Book IV, folio 47, from the Irish Collection. We have been unable to find it anywhere else, and it concerns the ancient penitential discipline of the Irish and English Churches:

> “The holy Irish synod, presided over by Leo, bishop of the Holy Roman Church, in the time of Charles, king of the Franks, together with Theodore, archbishop of the English and Irish, and many bishops from those regions, speaks as follows concerning the fall of priests:
>
> “If a priest, at the prompting of the devil, falls into fornication, and, through God’s mercy, takes refuge in the remedies of penance, he shall make expiation for four years in the following manner. First, for forty days and nights he shall purify himself, withdrawn in a secure place, on bread alone. When these have elapsed, during the first year he shall continue in the same way on bread and water, except on Sundays and the principal Easter festivals, when he may use wine and all foods [Col. 0554C], except meat alone. On the other days he shall be content with water and bread alone; and then, taking account of the person’s condition, he may be allowed a little wine, legumes, milk, fruit, small fish, and vegetables, as his confessor shall judge appropriate. When the first year has passed, he shall immediately become a participant in the sacred body and blood. In the choir he shall sing the Psalms with the brothers last, and shall come [Col. 0554D] to the peace; he shall perform lesser offices. In the second year he shall complete three customary fasts each week on bread and water. When two years have been completed, if he has repented according to the prescriptions, the bishop may restore him to his rank.” Cf. Distinction 82, chapter 5.].

Fragments drawn from Roman law are likewise very frequent. Some of them, especially those excerpted from the *Digest* and the *Code*, appear to have been written into the codex by a later hand around the beginning of the thirteenth century. The same hand wrote the *Book of Accusation* that the Ballerini brothers published from our Collection. It is entirely uncertain whether the author took such chapters, omitted by Anselm, from another Collection, and which Collection he himself consulted. Nevertheless, he seems to have used Burchard of Worms’s *Decree* very frequently, since he incorporated many chapters from it into his own work [Note: [Col. 0554D].

Here are some examples:

- Book III, chapters 3, 6, and 12, from Burchard, Book III, chapters 63, 225, 90, 41, 39.
- Book V, chapters 2, 4, 7, 12, 22, 23. Burchard, Book XI, chapters 38, 31, 43, 36, 48.
- Book IX, chapters 1, 2, and 4. Burchard, Book V, chapters 39, 55, 53.]

.

It remains to see how our Collection stands [Col. 0554B] in relation to Gratian’s *Decree*. There can be no doubt that Gratian both knew and used it, since many passages that are entirely absent both from Anselm’s Collection and from those other Collections that the Roman correctors used to emend Gratian’s *Decree* are found in our Collection and were received from it by Gratian into the *Decree*. Thus, for example, from Book II, folio 23, of our Collection come Causa 19, Question 2, canon 10, and Causa 19, Question 3, canon 2; from Book III, folio 33, Causa 16, Question 7, canons 13 and 17, and Causa 16, Question 2, canon 1 [Col. 0554D] [Note: Causa 16, Question 2, canon 1. Our Collection has: “John, pope VIII, to Isaac, bishop of Syracuse,” and additionally gives the date of the decretal: “Given on the day before the Kalends of April.” Gratian more correctly has: “to Isaac of Langres.” Mansius published another decretal letter of John VIII to the same bishop of Langres among the letters of that pontiff, no. 96. *Most Extensive Collection of Councils*, vol. XVII, p. 83.], and canon 6; Causa 1, Question 1, canon 124; from Book IV, folio 37, Distinction 1, *On Consecration*, canon 68; Distinction 33, canon 3, from Book V, folio 58; Causa 24, Question 3, canon 17; Causa 11, Question 3, canon 73; Causa 7, Question 1, canon 22; Causa 24, Question 3, canon 17; Causa 25, Question 6, canon 4; Book VII, folio 83, Causa 7, Question 1, canon 8; Causa 1, Question 1, canon 56. In an uninterrupted series [Col. 0554C] Gratian received from Book IV, chapters 16, 17, 18, and 19, the following in the *Decree*: Causa 11, Question 3, canons 21, 22, 23, and 24; from Book IX, chapters 5 and 6, Causa 14, Question 5, canons 2 and 3. We think it superfluous to set out more examples of this kind here, since these few already make abundantly clear how important our Collection is for emending many passages in Gratian’s text.

As for the time when this Collection of ours was compiled [Col. 0555A], it appears to have been prepared shortly after St. Anselm’s death, since, apart from certain decretal letters of Urban II and Paschal II, no more recent document occurs in it. These decretal letters, moreover, are almost the same as those found in other interpolated codices of St. Anselm’s Collection. This wonderfully confirms the opinion expressed above—namely, that documents of this kind were incorporated into Anselm’s Collection from Collections more closely related to it.

The codex was written toward the end of the twelfth century; but the Collection itself appears to have been compiled in Italy, for the names of both Gallican and German councils are given with many errors. Thus, for example, the councils called “Magotiense,” “Warmiense,” “Avirense,” “Gabilense,” and [Col. 0555B] “Ludinense” occur in place of *Magontinum*, *Wormatiense*, *Cabillonense*, *Lugdunense*, and so on. Similarly, the name of Pope Anicetus is always written *Anitius*; by this spelling the Italian compilers are distinguished from others.

As is customary with the Collection, we set out the rubrics here.

## BOOK I. On the power and primacy of the apostolic see

1. That in the Old Testament, after Christ the Lord, the priestly order began.  
2. That Peter was granted the right of binding and loosing, and should transfer it to his successors.  
3. That superiors are not harmed when they are hated by their brothers because of the strictness of justice; rather, God’s love is thereby more greatly won for them.  
4. That after Christ no one is received who has grieved the pope. [Col. 0555C]  
5. That Christ granted St. Peter, with the apostles’ consent, that he should be first among them.  
6. That we ought not even to speak with one to whom the pope does not speak.  
7. That, following the pattern of the apostles, a certain distinction was made among bishops, yet the see of blessed Peter presides over them all.  
8. That the Roman Church presides over all Churches, just as blessed Peter was given precedence over the other Churches.  
9. That the Lord built the Church upon one person, namely Peter.  
10. That no one should dissent from the Roman Church, which is the head of all Churches.  
11. That one must in no way depart from the rules of the Roman Church.  
12. That the Roman Church has never departed from the faith.  
13. That whatever is harmful in the universal Church the pope ought to correct or amend. [Col. 0555D]  
14. That the Church of Antioch, subject to the Roman Church, should not dissent from it.  
15. That the first condition of salvation is to preserve the rules of right faith and not to depart from the statutes of the Fathers, just as Rome has remained a Church enriched by the priesthood of blessed Peter.  
16. That the Roman Church has been preferred to all others not only by the decrees of the canons but by the voice of the Savior himself.  
17. That the pillars of the Churches, namely the bishops, have been strengthened upon Peter’s foundation.  
18. That the first see is judged by no one.  
19. That priests, or all the Churches, must preserve the statutes of the holy Roman Church if they do not wish to be deprived of its communion.  
20. That no one should presume to reopen or judge the judgment of the first see.  
21. That the apostolic see is the head of all Churches. [Col. 0556A]  
22. That the Roman Church has, by a unique privilege, the power of binding and loosing.  
23. That the pope is to be judged by no one except God.  
24. That the pope should entrust his functions to another whenever he cannot be present; a subdeacon can do this as well.  
25. That bishops should refer matters to the apostolic see whenever there is doubt concerning the faith.  
26. That the pope ought chiefly to care for all the Churches.  
27. On the authority of the apostolic see: care must be applied according to the needs of the time.  
28. On the primacy of the Roman Church, and that Mark the disciple did not dissent from blessed Peter.  
29. That the pope ought to care for every condition of the Church.  
30. That all who wish to be true sons should know and follow what is done in the Roman Church according to sacred rite.  
31. That the apostolic see never fosters heresies [Col. 0556B] but destroys them.  
32. That it is not permissible for the apostolic see to remain silent, because it presides over all.  
33. That the apostolic see received from blessed Peter the confidence to defend the right faith throughout the whole Church.  
34. That the pope bears, more than all others, the responsibility of correcting.  
35. That the other Churches ought to observe the tradition of the Roman Church, because they received their beginning from it.  
36. One must not think differently about the writings from what the holy Fathers taught.  
37. That one must not depart from apostolic statutes.  
38. That no one should presume to violate the decrees of the apostolic see, because this pertains to the most powerful priest, the pope.  
39. That the apostolic see can absolve those unjustly condemned without a synod. [Col. 0556C]  
40. That no one ought to observe the canons more carefully than the apostolic see.  
41. That whatever is decreed at the apostolic see without the apostolic authority shall be void.  
42. That the authority to convene general synods has been entrusted solely to the apostolic see, and that no such synod can exist without its authority.  
43. That St. Peter did not hand over the power of binding and loosing to Linus and Cletus, although he associated them with himself.  
44. The petition of the Council of Nicaea that it be confirmed by apostolic authority.  
45. The petition of the Egyptian bishops, concerning the seventy canons of the Council of Nicaea, addressed to the authority of the apostolic see.  
46. That no one may violate the divine institutions or those of the apostolic see.  
47. That the Roman Church instituted all ecclesiastical dignities. [Col. 0556D]  
48. That Christ was especially entreated for Peter’s faith.  
49. That the Roman Church obtained primacy from the Lord himself; that the two apostles Peter and Paul consecrated their cause by death on the same day; and that this see is first, the Alexandrian second, and the Antiochene third.  
50. That the Roman Church obtained primacy not through synodal but through apostolic institutions; and that St. Peter and Paul were crowned on the same day in the city of Rome.

52. That emperors ought to obey priests, not command them.

54. That emperors are not permitted to concern themselves inquisitively with spiritual affairs.

76. On observance of the decrees of the Roman pontiffs.  
77. On disobedience to the canons.  
78. On the authority of the four councils.  
79. That a council should be held twice a year.  
80. At what time a council is to be held.  
81. That one must not depart from apostolic teaching.  
82. On the councils that we ought to use.  
83. On ecclesiastical institutions to be adapted according to the circumstances of the time.  
84. On the remedy to be applied in a temporal emergency.

SECOND APPENDIX: SPURIOUS OPUSCULA.

(*Bibliotheca Veterum Patrum*, Supplement, vol. XXVII, col. 436.)

[Col. 0567]

F. P. LUCA WADDING, OF THE ORDER OF FRIARS MINOR, PREFACE TO THE FOLLOWING OPUSCULA.

Two little works of the most holy man are lacking to us: namely, the *Commentary on the Lamentations of Jeremiah* and the *Commentary on the Psalms of David*, the latter of which he was unable to complete because death overtook him. Although we have diligently sought them, we have not yet been able to find them; if they should ever appear, we shall publish them in a more complete edition. In the meantime, we are working on the collection of canons which Anselm completed in thirteen books, and which some call the *Decree of Anselm*. When, by God’s favor, we have completed it according to its divisions, cleansed it of corruptions and errors, and furnished it with notes where necessary, we shall eventually bring it to light.

Arnold Uvion attributes the following little works to Saint Anselm (*Uvion* in his notes for 18 March), and Possevinus testifies (*in Apparatu*) that they exist and are attributed to Anselm in very large parchment codices in the library of the monastery of Saint Benedict at Mantua.
