The most eminent lord, Cardinal Francesco Barberini, protector of the Benedictine order, out of his longstanding and singular kindness toward me and his natural benevolence toward all cultivators of good letters, arranged for this exemplar to be sent from there in complete fidelity. Yet some may think these works humbler in style than befits the gravity of so great a man. Nevertheless, the conjectures commonly formed from differences of style often prove slight and deceptive. For it is clear that holy teachers do not preserve the same speech and method in all their works, especially those who, in addition to excellence of doctrine, add holiness of life and, inflamed by sparks of piety, are often carried toward God. At times they rebuke others more gravely with God’s words; at times they address God more humbly in their own prayers. According to the variety of subject and matter, they now elevate and now lower their language, nor do they judge that the same tone of voice should be used with a persecutor of the Church and with the creator of the world.

The Spirit within nourishes humble thoughts of the heart and outwardly produces gentle whispers of the voice, in the sight of the One for whose honors they often cry out with a vehement spirit and, as though with a trumpet, raise their voice, announcing to the people their crimes and to the houses of princes their sins. One must consider with whom someone is speaking and what matter is being discussed, and accordingly moderate one’s language so that it is fitting in every respect. At one time Anselm fights against the tyrant Henry in the field; at another he thunders in writing against schismatics. Yet in the inner chambers of his room he was always occupied inwardly with something divine and contemplated heavenly things (*Life*, no. 30), which he afterward brought forth in reverent language. There is therefore nothing surprising if he teaches gravely and prays humbly; if he sharply turns the sacred Scriptures against tyrants and meditates on the divine mysteries with the affection of a humbled mind.

The author of his *Life* reports that he wrote many little books with his own hands (no. 25). What if these were among them? Certainly, in that very house in which he professed the monastic and contemplative life, all the following little books of contemplation, each bearing his name at its head, are carefully preserved. Let it therefore be permitted to append these to the preceding works, at least so that they do not perish.

[Col. 0569]

I. MEDITATION ON THE LORD’S PRAYER. (G)

[Col. 0569A] 1. “Our Father, who are in heaven, hallowed be your name,” etc.

O supreme clemency! O ineffable kindness! O marvelous condescension! O the length, breadth, height, and depth of divine love! I am most worthless clay, detestable corruption, a most wicked creature; and yet the God of gods, King of kings, and Lord of lords calls himself my Father. “When you pray,” he says, “say: Our Father,” etc. Since the Truth itself says this, it is utterly true. And I know that he loves me incomparably more than an earthly father or mother—indeed, more than I love myself.

From such a Father, then, my heart will be lifted like an eagle’s, and I shall now despise the lower regions of this heaven. What have I to do with earthly honors, since I am a son of God? It would be a greater disgrace for me to desire even the greatest earthly honor than for an emperor’s son to desire the office of cleaning latrines. What have I to do with earthly riches, since I am heir of an eternal kingdom? It would be more shameful for me to care about even the greatest earthly riches than for an emperor’s firstborn to care about his horses’ dung. What have I to do with carnal delights, with earthly things, however great? It would be more detestable for me, a son of the supreme King, to be attracted by any seductive creature than for an emperor’s son to be attracted by the foulest filth.

What good, beautiful, useful, or desirable thing can attract me, since I am heir of the fountain of all piety and goodness? In relation to him, all things are only a kind of likeness and shadow. I shall therefore approach my Father, who wants nothing else except that I should possess him. Shall I then be negligent? Shall I rest? Shall I be intent on other things? Certainly, with impetuosity, setting everything else aside, I shall run to him. It is enough for me if I possess my Father, and therefore I shall strive toward him with my whole heart.

I shall look at nothing, see nothing else but my God, because the eye of my mind is wholly directed toward him, since he has attracted my soul so greatly. “Our Father”—O honey and honeycomb in my mouth, when I call you my God and my Father! O unspeakable sweetness! O immeasurable joy! O ineffable jubilation, when I dare to call you Father! O exultation! O wonder! O innermost melody! For you are my Father. What more should I claim? What more should I say? What more should I ask? You are my Father.

2. But where are you, my Father? Where are you, if you are everywhere? Indeed, because you are everywhere, how is heaven your dwelling place? But for this reason, most kind Lord, you wish us to say, “Our Father, who are in heaven”: so that you may raise us from earthly things to heavenly things, where your power, wisdom, and goodness shine forth most clearly; so that there, my Father, our conversion and our dwelling may always be with you, so that we may ask you for heavenly things, not earthly things; or at least so that, having become spiritual heavens, we may be your dwelling place within ourselves.

What, then, will delay us? What will draw us back? What obstacles will prevent us from living a heavenly rather than an earthly life, so that you may dwell within us? O worthy wonder, marvelous condescension, and most worthy dwelling of Christ in us! I, most foul filth and an abominable sewer of sins, can, through the immense clemency of my God, be his tabernacle. And I, who am full of corruption and stench, shall become God’s holy temple, the seat of wisdom, and the dwelling place of the Holy Spirit!

O happy day! O blessed hour, when I shall possess such a guest! I shall hold him and not release him until I bring him in—or rather, until he himself brings me into his house above, Jerusalem, my mother, and into the chamber of my mother, that is, into the innermost repose of contemplation, where delicate souls lie and rest (*Song of Songs* III).

3. “Our Father, who are in heaven, hallowed be your name,” etc.

O how well this follows, how perfectly it continues, how elegantly this petition is ordered in relation to what was said above—namely, “Hallowed be your name” in relation to “Our Father, who are in heaven”! For filial devotion and heavenly contemplation turn the entire soul of the reverent son toward the heavenly Father, so that he cries out and says, “Hallowed be your name,” as though he were saying: “I do not ask for earthly riches, delights, or honors, but that I may be wholly converted into you, wholly divine.”

“Hallowed be your name”—that is, may the rational part of me, illumined by your wisdom and cleansed of every error, ambiguity, and darkness, possess the most holy—that is, the purest—knowledge of you.

4. “Your kingdom come,” so that my irascible power [f. will], strengthened by your power, may ascend to the sublimity of your kingdom.

“Your will be done,” so that my concupiscible power, sweetened by your goodness, indeed perfected by your love, may rest fully in what pleases you, so that, from the true friendship of love, willing and refusing may be one and the same.

Or: “Hallowed be your name,” with respect to the pure knowledge of the intellect. “Your kingdom come,” with respect to the fervent desire of the affections.

5. “Your will be done on earth as it is in heaven,” with respect to the perfect obedience of action.

Therefore may your name, which is eternally most holy, be hallowed in us, so that whatever we see, whatever we hear, whatever we understand and feel, we may order entirely toward your most holy name; so that your holy name may be in us, free from earth and pure; so that, shaken free and cleansed from every curiosity and vanity and every useless fantasy, we may always recognize you alone in all things, most pious and most holy Father.

May the eye of our mind be directed unceasingly toward you, eternal light. May I always behold you, who are in all things and from whom all things are, in all things; may I recognize you in all things. O how sweet and delightful it is never to remove the mind’s gaze from you, the sun of justice! O how sweet, lovable, and wondrous to our eyes is the brightness of your rays!

“Hallowed be your name. Your kingdom come.”

Now, Lord God, the kingdom of this world has occupied my soul—indeed, it has wholly scattered it, wholly torn it, wholly defiled it, wholly blackened it. Your beloved bride, my soul, my whole heart, my whole mind, my whole affection, has been claimed by the vanity—indeed, the foulness—of this world. Therefore I feel only what belongs to the world, desire what belongs to the flesh, and think and love only earthly things.

I have become the ashes of this world, and under the prince of this world I diligently strive to serve as a soldier. But, Lord, am I not your creature? Therefore “your kingdom come,” so that the prince of this world may be cast out, so that you alone may reign in me, you alone dwell in my mind, your kingdom wholly occupy me, wholly claim my desire, and you alone refresh my affection.

What do I seek? What do I want? What do I desire? Where do I wander? Where do I rush about? Why am I distracted? Your kingdom is enough for me, Lord; therefore “your kingdom come.” From now on, may I think of nothing, desire nothing, love nothing except your kingdom. May my refreshment be there; may my dwelling be there; may my whole manner of life be there.

You alone are good, you alone beautiful, you alone lovable, you alone desirable, lover of souls. You alone rule me; you alone guide me; you alone attract me; you alone possess my whole heart, zealous lover of souls. In you alone may my breast be sweetened; in you alone may my heart rest. Fill my whole mind. With impetuous desire may I ascend to you, the center and kingdom of all souls. Therefore “your kingdom come”; “your will be done on earth as it is in heaven.”

This I want, this I desire, this I long for with all the inner depths of my soul: that in me, through me, and for me, not my will but yours may be done; that I may be wholly yours and wholly strive toward your honor alone.

For this I was made, for this I was born: to seek your honor alone. I shall no longer bend toward my own appetite; I shall no longer seek my own advantage; I shall no longer consider the affection of friends; I shall not think about what is bitter or sweet, honorable or base. I shall strive only to fulfill your good pleasure in all things, whether difficult or easy, harsh or gentle. With impetuosity, fervent desire, and anxious concern, I shall seek to accomplish whatever pleases your will.

May this alone be sweet to me, this alone joyful, this alone easy and delightful and lovable, however harsh, difficult, and bitter it may be, if in it I seek to fulfill your will.

O joy, delight, and innermost exultation—to expose myself wholly and entirely, always and everywhere, to all your honor that I may in any way put into effect! O that I alone could fulfill all your services, my Lord! I rejoice more, I approve more, and with all my limbs and inner being I desire more fully to spend myself for your honor and to satisfy your divine will than to enjoy any or all heavenly and divine delights.

For if, for your sake, my Lord, I were wholly torn apart and accepted every suffering and death for your honor, I would rejoice in them more than in any delight I could have even in the heavenly homeland—unless, perhaps, that delight contributed as much or more to your honor. And even then I would desire it not because of the delight but because of your honor. For I was not made to console my own vanity but to honor your magnificence.

What is greater for me? What is sweeter? What is more lovable to me than to be wholly dissolved into your honor? O joy! O jubilation! O every rejoicing consolation for me, that I may do something, however difficult, for your honor.

This is the joy of the angels, the heavenly desire, the reward of the homeland: to be able to serve you wholly, to be carried wholly toward you, to be perfectly conformed to your will, and to marvel at your honor and magnificence. I do not doubt—indeed, I am certain—that the angels and holy souls rejoice more in the magnificence of your honor than in the magnificence of their own glory.

And therefore “your will be done on earth as it is in heaven”: in heaven, that is, in the heavenly spirits; and on earth, that is, in us human beings. May we serve your will with such readiness, fervor, and willingness, and be wholly conformed to your will, insofar as our strength permits.

6. **Give us this day our daily bread.** [Col. 0573B] O how well he orders these words, how elegantly he joins them to what has preceded! Although this may be explained of material and spiritual bread, for the present let us explain it chiefly of sacramental bread. And, as I have said, there is here an excellent order in God. Who is so worthy, who so humble, for receiving this sacrament, for offering the Son to God the Father, as the one who—as was said above—has ordered himself wholly toward God with respect to understanding, affection, and action; who has offered his entire self to God, consumed his whole self in sacrifice, been annihilated in himself and wholly carried into God; who now seeks not what is his own but what is Jesus Christ’s (Phil. II)? Such a one can receive Jesus Christ in this sacrifice, ask Jesus Christ, and offer Jesus Christ to God for himself and others. [Col. 0573C] Therefore the true Master placed before this petition: “Hallowed be thy name,” and so forth; and he follows it most fittingly, joining it to those words: “Our bread,” and so forth.

The one who went out from the Egypt of sins—there, “Hallowed be thy name”; and who crossed the Red Sea of raging storms, with the Egyptians submerged, on dry feet—there, “Thy kingdom come”; and who in the desert of contemplation attended to God alone and dedicated himself wholly to God—there, “Thy will be done on earth as it is in heaven.” Now, hungry in this desert, he asks the heavenly Father for manna, that is, heavenly bread: “Give us this day our daily bread.” He who once sat in Egypt beside the pots of meat, now despising them, seeks, asks for, and obtains only the living bread [Col. 0573D] that came down from heaven.

O unheard-of condescension of Christ! O wondrous jubilation of the mind! My God, my bridegroom, my love, has become my food. The reward of the saints, the joy of the angels, the Word of God the Father is my nourishment. The light of the world, the Sun of heaven, the Wisdom of God is the refreshment of my soul. The Virgin’s offspring, human redemption, the glory of heaven has become my food. What more do I desire? What more can attract me? Far be it from me, Lord, that since my heart possesses so noble a food, it should be moved by anything else in the whole world! How, I ask, after such a noble, sufficient, sweet, and delightful food, could my heart take pleasure in things empty, disgraceful, and unclean? How, I ask, could [Col. 0574A] my heart for even a moment be separated from this most noble food? And if I cannot receive it sacramentally above, at least let my heart never cease to ruminate upon it spiritually.

Truly, it seems wondrous—more than wondrous—how, in the face of the sweetness and excessive fervor of this ardor, the heart does not fail over this food. You alone, good Jesus, be my food and my refreshment; you alone will I hunger for. I will eat you with eager and insatiable appetite, and always remain hungry for you. What is sweeter than you? What is more pleasant? What is more lovable, good Jesus? You alone I wish to eat; you alone I desire to chew. May you always grow sweet to me in my heart. Your scent alone ought to refresh the whole world—how much more your nourishment! If we are refreshed and live by the word that proceeds from your mouth (Matt. IV), what will it be to receive the eternal Word itself with the mouth and chew it with the teeth of the heart? [Col. 0574B] How could my heart not delight in you so greatly that it forgets everything except you? If something earthly—or rather, the likeness of something earthly—sometimes occupies my heart so much that I forget other things, how could your truest presence not refresh and intoxicate me so greatly that I forget the whole world, and even myself?

Therefore, heavenly Father, grant us this daily bread today. But today, Lord God, give us this bread, so that we may have it present here and always in the present. May this food always be spiritually present here, so that it may never know past or future. But the good Jesus says “today,” so that we may say: Why, I ask, do you hasten so greatly to be with us? Why do you not defer until tomorrow—for what do you see in us? What do you perceive in us, what do you recognize in us, that you are so intoxicated with love for us? What do you gain by us? What do you find in us? What fruit will you have from us, that you do not know how to delay?

If love for us so urges you that you cannot defer, but immediately wish to be with us—though you gain nothing from us—while we are the most fetid corruption, unworthy even to be called your most worthless creature, how can we delay, since you so greatly desire to be with us, when we seek you, the supreme good, the spotless mirror, and the consolation of the angels? You, good Jesus, do not wish to delay, as you show; nor do we any longer wish to delay. Today, therefore, we ask you, so that today we may have you. [Col. 0574C] For your instruction is not empty; it would be so if we asked and did not obtain. Since, then, we immediately ask for and desire you, and you yourself desire this, come to our heart, for our heart rises to you.

You are intoxicated with us, and we with love for you. You draw us impetuously to yourself and yourself to us—O weight of love! Now, with every delay removed, let the mutual embrace take place, and in your arms let my soul fail, absorbed by the heat of love. When I felt your embrace, you tore up my spirit; first you fed it, then intoxicated it, and finally lulled my soul to sleep with your embraces and kisses, and it rests in your arms. You do not cast it away, unworthy though it is. You do not reject it; rather, clasping it to yourself, you cry out and say: “I adjure you, daughters of Jerusalem, that you do not stir up or awaken my beloved until she herself wishes” (Song III). [Col. 0575A]

7. Yet I still marvel at your clemency, good Jesus. Why did you say “daily”? Do you wish to be our food every day? Is it not enough for you to dwell in us and remain with us for one day? Why do you always wish to be with us? What have we done for you? I do not know what to say about such great benevolence, for in those treasures of clemency my spirit fails, unable to contemplate even a small spark—their abyss is so immense. Therefore I know how to say nothing except this: Since you wish always to be with us, may we at all times be with you and never depart from you, our most gracious bridegroom and most delightful food.

Thus, Lord, join us to yourself by your love and devotion, so that we can neither depart from you nor wish to do so. Therefore: “Give us this day our daily bread,” and so forth.

8. **And forgive us our debts, as we also forgive**, and so forth.

O good Jesus, you have most graciously and urgently offered the noblest food to us, your unworthy little servants. But what then? I fear being invited to Queen Esther’s banquet like Haman (Esth. VII), even if that is not your intention, good Jesus; nevertheless, I fear. What, then? A most sumptuous banquet has been prepared. The messengers—that is, the holy angels—press me; hunger awakens and compels me; yet I do not dare approach, because I have sinned.

What shall I do? I am in distress on every side. But certainly I know what I shall choose. I shall go to my heavenly Father, [Col. 0575C] of whom it was said above: “Our Father, who art in heaven,” and I shall say: “Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you. I am no longer worthy to be called your son; make me as one of your hired servants” (Luke XV)—that is, “Forgive us our debts.”

O blessed recognition of guilt, which earns the father’s embrace! Perhaps, in the fervor of love, I shall dissolve and be changed into another man amid his embraces, and in some measure be able to eat of the fatted calf.

Forgive us our debts, then. O wondrous condescension of our God toward us! We despised him and exchanged him for the vilest corruption; yet he urges us to ask forgiveness, because he wishes to forgive us our debts along with our offenses. He did not wish to grant this to the angels. How, I ask, good Lord, can you look upon us any longer, since we have so shamefully cast you away from us? [Col. 0575D]

Since you yourself, then, urge us to say, “Forgive us our debts,” forgive— forgive us, because you have already paid the debt for us. You have already offered yourself as a sacrifice for us. You are the one who teaches us to say, “Forgive us,” and so forth; you can do this. Has peace not already been made? Has the banquet of peace not already been celebrated, and is it not celebrated every day?

Forgive us our debts, then, as we also forgive our debtors. O blessed debt of our neighbor! O happy offense, which we may plead before God for the remission of our own debt! Therefore let us not sadden such brothers when people offend us, insult us, afflict us, rob us, and take what is ours; rather, insofar as it is possible, let us rejoice and exult over them for our own sake, because by forgiving these things to our neighbors we shall be able to plead [Col. 0576A] for the remission of our debt. There is no doubt that this plea has great virtue and great efficacy, since our supreme Advocate and Judge teaches it to us.

Therefore, if we forgive others, we are forgiven. Forgive us our debts, then, as we also forgive our debtors.

9. **And do not lead us into temptation.**

For what good does it do me, Lord, to be baptized, or washed after contact with a dead body, if I touch the dead again (Lev. XI)? It is not enough for me, Lord, that you forgive sins already committed, unless you also guard me from sins that threaten. I am exceedingly ready to sin, and unless you guard me, I shall rush headlong into sin without restraint.

Therefore, if, for our testing, humility, and exercise, [Col. 0576B] you wish and permit us to be tempted, nevertheless do not allow us to be brought into temptation. What benefit did Haman gain, who was elevated by King Ahasuerus above all the princes, when afterward, puffed up with pride, he was hanged upon the wood? (Esth. VIII.) What benefit would anything I have asked in the preceding words bring me unless you preserve me in goodness amid temptations?

Therefore: “And do not lead us into temptation.” Do you wish, good Jesus, that we should ask this because you permit us to be repeatedly goaded by temptations, so that we may have recourse to you? You employ every means and every path by which you can draw us to yourself, because you wish to have us with you.

When tempted, therefore, let me flee to my Father’s embrace, so that he may receive me as I flee and encourage me in my fear. I shall say to him: “And do not lead us into temptation,” and so forth. This is what my Father wills, desires, and awaits [Col. 0576C]: that I run to his refuge, embrace, and bosom; that, utterly distrustful of myself, I trust in him alone. Therefore: “And do not lead us,” and so forth.

**But deliver us from evil.**

It is true, Lord, that we are worthy of every evil, because we despised you, who are every good. But behold, most merciful Father, your infinite mercy, not our detestable wickedness; and lift from us, your little and infirm children, the unbearable burden, and deliver us from the evil that oppresses, distracts, draws us back, and delays us from the good. Deliver us, your children, so that we may be free; [lacuna] and above all deliver us from that horrible and terrible eternal evil, lest we be deprived of your desirable vision—which all our bones dread. [Col. 0576D]

For what would it have profited me to have been your creature, unless I possess you and, wholly and entirely, am carried into you in eternal life, which may you grant us, who are blessed forever? Amen.

### Another Exposition

All the foregoing can also be explained in this way:

“Our Father” is placed first so that we may approach him with confidence.

“Who art in heaven,” so that we may seek and savor the things above, not the things upon earth.

“Hallowed be thy name,” with respect to the illumination of faith.

“Thy kingdom come,” with respect to the raising up of hope.

“Thy will be done,” with respect to the conformity and perfection of charity.

“Our bread,” and so forth, with respect to the nourishment and support of temperance, [Col. 0577A] which is exhibited above all in the bread of the Eucharist.

“And forgive us,” and so forth, with respect to the correspondence and balance of justice, through what follows: “As we also forgive,” and so forth.

“And do not lead us into temptation,” with respect to the act of prudence, which consists in guarding against ambushes.

“But deliver us from evil,” with respect to the act of fortitude, which consists in enduring adversities.

Amen.

### Another Exposition of the Same

We may also explain the foregoing petitions with reference to what we shall possess in our heavenly homeland.

“Hallowed be thy name,” with respect to the open vision: that is, what we now see through a mirror in an enigma, may we then see purely and without earthly obstruction, without any intermediary, face to face.

“Thy kingdom come,” with respect to firm intention, so that we may reign forever. [Col. 0577B]

“Thy will be done,” with respect to consummated love, which wholly transforms the lover into the beloved. Then “as in heaven and on earth” is to be explained as meaning: as it is done in the angels, so let it be done in human beings.

“Our daily bread,” and so forth, with respect to the sweetest enjoyment. “Daily” is then to be explained as “continuous,” because there is always day there; and “today” is to be explained with reference to eternity, which has neither past nor future but is all at once, and is better indicated by the present.

“And forgive us,” and so forth [Col. 0578A], in which the coming of the jubilee year is requested, when all debts are forgiven to true Jews—that is, to the penitent and the just—and people forgive one another’s debts, while God forgives all debts to such people.

“And do not lead us into temptation,” and so forth, in which that beauty of peace is requested of which it is said: “My people shall sit in the beauty of peace” (Isa. XXXII), and so forth; where there will no longer be Satan or any evil encounter.

“But deliver us from evil,” as if he were saying: Lead us to that state which is perfected by the gathering of all good things and made joyful by the absence of every evil, where we shall truly be delivered from evil.

This final exposition requires great wonder, wondrous devotion, inward exultation, and the full payment of praise. It contains wondrous and ineffable treasures of contemplation. But I am not sufficient, nor worthy, to distribute them or to place my unclean mouth there, especially since I dare not enter the court of King Ahasuerus uninvited (Esth. IV). Therefore, let what we have said above suffice for our simplicity while we remain outside in the courtyard.

May Christ himself extend toward us, as a sign of clemency, the golden scepter [Col. 0578B] (Esth. V), so that we may enter confidently to him and reign with him forever. May he himself deign to grant this, who is blessed forever. Amen.

[Col. 0577]

## II. MEDITATION ON THE SALUTATION OF THE BLESSED VIRGIN MARY

That is, the “Hail Mary.”

[Col. 0577C]

1. **Hail, Mary, full of grace, the Lord is with you**, and so forth.

To you, Lord my God, I offer whatever thanks I can from the depths of my heart: you deigned, for us unworthy ones, to assume our nature, to be carried in a virginal womb, and, being born from that Virgin, to be nourished by her milk, cherished in her lap, and subjected to her authority—you who preserve and govern all things. You deigned to illumine me, fetid corruption and detestable disgrace, full of abomination and unworthy of every forgiveness and clemency, so greatly that I know I have a Mother. You granted this to me, most unworthy of all, that I may and dare to salute her.

For you did not deal thus with every nation, nor did you manifest this supreme benefit to them (Ps. CXLVII). Where, Lord, is that special people of yours whom, by your powerful hand and outstretched arm, you led from the land of Egypt through the desert into the promised land by so many signs and wonders of your magnificence? (Ps. CXXXV.) Is this not the people, Lord, to whom you promised this benefit? Why, then, did you reserve this supreme benefit not for those worshipers of yours but for us idolaters and unbelievers? Why for the few of us, when many—indeed, almost innumerable—peoples are ignorant of it?

Are you not, Lord, the creator of all, and did you not make everyone in your image? [Col. 0578C] Are secrets not customarily revealed to friends? Why now, Lord, to enemies—and especially to me, who am infected from the crown of my head to the sole of my foot and wholly strive toward what is contrary to your will? Why, Lord, have you given such a noble gift, such an excellent treasure, to your most faithless and wicked servant?

Does it not seem to you, Lord, that I mock rather than honor your Mother? How will the proud dare to salute the humble—indeed, the most humble; the most impure, the most chaste; the most vain and earthly, the heavenly—indeed, the most divine; the most impious, the most holy; the son of the devil, the Mother of God? Where, good Lord Jesus, is reverence for your Mother? Why do you permit such a one to salute her?

But, most merciful Jesus, because of your excessive love toward us, is it not enough that for our sake you submit to every mockery and display, without also permitting polluted lips to address your Mother, who now sits at your right hand, so that you may inflame our hearts with love for you and for her? For there is no doubt that we are utterly unworthy, and I firmly believe that there is no heavenly angel capable of saluting her as she deserves—how much less I, the most unworthy of creatures!

[Col. 0579A]

2. It seems wondrous that wretched human beings do not tremble and quake to salute so great a Lady. But this is exceedingly detestable: to utter her name with the mouth while treating vain, useless, indeed wicked, things in the heart, and to address her with one’s back turned.

The most blessed Virgin must be saluted with complete devotion and reverence, and she seeks those who approach her devoutly and reverently. She loves them, nourishes them, and receives them as her children.

O blessed is the one who rejoices in such a noble Mother, embraces her in the heart, and imitates her in action! O happy is the one who strives, according to his ability, to conform himself to the Mother of God! Such a person is certainly one who, having despised every creature, clings to God alone with singular love and, crucified with Christ, thirsts for the salvation of souls.

O wondrous indeed: how is the heart of one who salutes such a Virgin not carried away in exultation? [Col. 0579B] He addresses the Mother of God and contemplates God made man from her. He sees the lowest joined to the highest, and the highest to the lowest, through her love.

How, I ask, does our mind not melt in this salutation, when we see that God loved us so greatly that he deigned to become our brother from a virginal womb? He is now our mouth and our flesh. O excessive and ineffable outpouring of divine goodness! With what devotion, I ask, ought our heart to pour itself out toward such a Virgin, through whom we have deserved to become God’s brothers and coheirs?

Our mouth ought to overflow with wondrous sweetness when we salute so sweet and gracious a Lady and bless her fruit. Her fruit is most pleasant and sweet, and it grows sweet in the mouth and heart of the wise.

Wondrous is the fruitfulness of this Virgin: when she is devoutly saluted, she sends her most sweet fruit into the heart of the one who salutes her; and the more someone rejoices in her fruit, the more he obtains from her. Unless you say, “Enough,” she will never cease.

O wondrous Lady, it seems astonishing that we do not take such delight in saluting you that, apart from you and your fruit, we become ignorant of everything else. How, I ask, can a person not be so intent upon you, because of your exceeding sweetness, that, drawn out of himself, he even becomes unaware of himself? O snatcher of hearts! O absorber of minds! O melter of sins!

3. **Hail.**

Why, Lady, do you make us pregnant with your fruit? Why do you impregnate us with our God? Why do you fill clay with heaven and make the most vain into lords? Why, I ask, do you intoxicate us with love for your Son, when we are able to offer nothing either to you or to him?

What benefit is it to you, lover of souls, that we love you and your Son with our love? Are the heavenly things not enough for you? Why do you seek our hearts, when they are so fetid and earthly? Take them, huntress of souls, and cherish them in the lap of your grace.

For who can escape the radiance of your brightness and the rays of your mercy? No one can hide from your heat (Ps. XVIII), because heaven and earth are full of your benefits. Wherever we go, the outpouring of the virginal womb meets us.

Behold, then, you have ensnared us on every side with your benefits and have always and everywhere spread the snares of your goodness, so that we cannot reasonably flee from you, sweetest Mother, but must always rest in the lap of your sweetness. [Col. 0580A]

Run, then, from every side, human beings, and let us salute so noble and gracious a Virgin.

4. **Hail.**

Have patience, Lady, that I proclaim an angelic salutation while I do not live angelically; rather, I am dreadful and devilish, yet I presume to salute you. I certainly trust in your excessive goodness, and, inflamed by love for you, I do not fear to salute you, although I am exceedingly unworthy.

Hail. What is sweeter to me, Lady, than your “hail”? O wondrous “hail,” which intoxicates the devout heart with a certain heavenly sweetness! Certainly the one who devoutly salutes her can now say: “My soul melted” (Song X), when I saluted my Lady. “My heart and my flesh failed” (Ps. LXXII), while I addressed my Lady.

Who would not fail in you, sacred Virgin, when he sees, preceded by this salutation, that you are pregnant with the Son of God? Who would not fail when he sees the Son of God carried in your womb and nourished by your milk?

What, then, do you hear more willingly, O Lady, than the salutation by which you are acknowledged as Mother of God, when people rejoice in you in such a way that they always pour themselves back into him whose Mother you are? For I do not think that, as Mother of God, you wish to be saluted or known in any other way.

You are a crystal gate, and through you you wish us to be joined to your Son. But “hail”—and truly, hail! For your “hail” opens our heart.

O admirable and super-admirable “hail,” by which demons are driven away, sinners weep, children rejoice, the angel gives thanks, the Word becomes incarnate, and the Virgin becomes pregnant! Certainly, it is the “hail” by whose fruit creatures are renewed, human beings redeemed, and angels restored. [Col. 0580C]

Therefore let every creature proclaim your “hail” without end.

O sweetest and most delightful “hail,” by which earthly things rejoice, heavenly things exult, and the highest are joined to the lowest. O “hail,” which illumines the intellect, satisfies the affections, lifts the mind to heavenly things, enlightens the spirit, sweetens the breast, and disciplines the flesh—therefore, hail!

O chain-like “hail,” which binds the heart with the Virgin and separates it from earthly things; which binds most firmly the wretched with the most merciful, the servant with the Lady, and the son with the Mother. O admirable “hail”! Let the one who wishes to be chained by love approach to salute you; and when he has saluted you from the heart, he will be bound more fully and strongly. The more strongly he is bound, the more willingly he will salute you.

Thus, hail, my Lady, and may love increase itself mutually until the heart of the one who salutes fails from sweetness. O love of the Virgin, you make the lover divine; you make one who has been polluted by much filth virginal.

Therefore, hail, my Lady, my Mother—indeed, my heart and my soul, Virgin Mary.

5. **Virgin Mary, hail.**

O sweetest name, sweetest name, most delightful name—the name of Mary! What have I done? What have I presumed? How have I exceeded myself, that I dare name you? Who has ever heard such a thing: that a son of perdition, a sack of sins, a servant of demons, should presume to name you?

O love of me! The name of the Mother of God! Love does not know how to show reverence. Pardon me, Lady, for saying that I love you; and if I am not worthy to love you, you are worthy to be loved.

Who, O Lady, will cease to love you, through whose benefits we obtain grace [Col. 0581A] and glory? Through you, Lady, bonds are broken, sins loosed, vices conquered, broken things strengthened, lost things recovered, old things renewed, weak things fortified, little things magnified, lowly things exalted, beginnings advanced, imperfect things perfected, and perfect things brought to completion. The heart is cleansed, the mind shines again, the spirit is inflamed, the breast melts, the appearance is adorned, the pilgrim is betrothed, the bride is led across, and the soul is released.

O soul! Through you, Virgin Mary, it possesses these things.

6. **Hail, Mary.**

Truly, Mary: the star of the sea, transforming the world completely; Lady, rising above all the choirs of angels to the right hand of her Son; star of the sea, directing us and sharing our bitter sea; Lady, protecting us. You are the star of the sea in chastity, bitter in compassion, but Lady in power.

O Lord my God, what shall we repay you for all that you have given us? Or what can we do for you—or what do we do—since, while we are situated in a sea of every bitterness, surrounded on every side by darkness, excessively far from the harbor of salvation, driven by whirlwinds and storms toward shipwreck, indeed almost submerged by an overwhelming tempest, you have given us, through the radiance of the Virgin Mary, so noble a consolation, so sweet a companionship, so effective an aid, so pious a support, and such a star?

O truly blessed night, happy darkness, and glorious obscurity, which deserved to be illuminated by such a star! Truly, “this night is my illumination in my delights” (Ps. CXXXVIII).

O glorious Virgin, if you are the star of the sea, I always wish to be in the sea during this life, so that you may always be my star. Always in the sea, so that I may always be in perfect bitterness: mourning over my sins, intimately sharing in the sufferings of crucified Christ, grieving and suffering with compassion over the wretchedness and vices of souls.

I always wish to sail upon this threefold sea, so that I may always have the guidance of this star. Woe to those who are living in delights and do not know—or rather, do not wish—to enter this sea, because they will lack this sweetest star.

Let tribulations run from every side and hem me in with unheard-of bitterness; I shall not fear, for you are with me (Ps. XXII). Indeed, you truly shine upon me when I am surrounded by anxieties and deprived of every human aid, when the waters have entered even to my soul (Ps. LXVIII).

Let the whole structure of this world attack and goad me, a sinner rejected and repudiated by every creature and most worthy of every evil, I ask, so long as the marine star is with me. [Col. 0581D]

O happy will I be when I have been reviled, trampled upon, and troubled by everyone, and have been received by this star! She is the star of the sea, and shines upon those placed in bitterness.

O how sweet and delightful it is to the eyes to see this light! O how good and lovable an exchange: to abhor every consolation of the world and cast it far from oneself, irretrievably, in exchange for the radiance of the star of the sea! A single illumination from this star is worth more than possession of all worldly things.

Who would not joyfully enter the sea of every bitterness, compassion, and suffering where this star shines? Let the perfect heart not be afraid, for it is impossible for shipwreck to occur while this star shines, nor can any cloud intervene unless one wishes it.

O my Lady, in this sea you are for us the ship that supports and carries us; the anchor that steadies and strengthens; the rudder that directs and sets straight; the sail that draws us onward and shades us; the shining star that reveals the harbor of salvation—indeed, that obtains and preserves it.

Who, then, would not willingly enter this sea of compunction, suffering, and compassion, where you help us and minister to us in everything?

7. Indeed, to dare say more, you are Mary, made a bitter sea because of the suffering of your Son and your compassion for our iniquities—not because you suffer anything distressing, but I consider your mind as you lived in this life beside the cross.

Let us, then, enter this twofold sea: by sharing in compassion with your crucified Son and with your heart pierced together with his, and by grieving inwardly over our iniquities, which were the occasion of so great a death, if we wish to enter your heart, which has become “a great and exceedingly spacious sea” (Ps. CIII). [Col. 0582B]

Who, then, would not willingly enter this sea in order to enter the Virgin’s heart? Those certainly enter your heart well, and are continually in your heart, who continually ruminate upon the passion of your Son.

For it is impossible, most pious Mother, to enter the wounds of your Son without entering your heart, because those wounds are perpetually situated in your heart. Just as those stigmata will always be in your Son’s body, so they will always be in his Mother’s mind.

Who, then, will delay? Who will any longer be sluggish about entering this vessel? It is sweet to hear about you, sweeter to think about you, and sweetest—indeed, exceedingly delightful—to enter your heart through the wounds of Christ.

Let no one depart from Christ’s dishonor and wound if he does not wish to depart from your heart. There a person becomes wholly virginal, wholly holy, wholly divine; he forgets himself, thinking only upon the things of the Mother and the Son.

8. **Hail, Mary.**

Without woe for soul or body: without the soul’s woe of weakness, which would make it difficult for you to do good; without the woe of ignorance, which would prevent you from recognizing or choosing the good over the evil; without the woe of malice, which would make you inclined toward evil.

As regards the body: without the woe of pain in giving birth; without the woe of subjection, since you did not obey a husband, but rather he obeyed you; without the woe of weariness in nourishing children.

“Mary”: this name is interpreted as “star of the sea” and “bitter sea.” It is called, I say, “star of the sea” at the birth of the Son, and “bitter sea” in the passion of the Son.

For just as iron touched by a magnet turns toward it, so the iron hearts of sinners turn toward you, as though toward the heaven of the saints who praise you.

You were a bitter sea because of the goodness of your Son, because of the kind of his death, and because of the vision of that death. You were Lady because of your dignity, as Mother of the King; because of your virtue, as the first among virgins; and because of your place, since your throne is above the thrones of the angels.

9. **Full of grace**—of humility, reverence, silence, gentleness, prudence in solitude, and virginity.

The blessed Virgin is full of grace with respect to the Lord, who looked upon her humility (Luke I); with respect to the angels, whose virginity was also akin to hers; and with respect to human beings, for whom she brought forth the Savior.

Or, “full of grace,” because she was a virgin against the flesh, poor against the world, and humble against the devil.

**The Lord is with you:** as a father is with his daughter, governing; as a son is with his mother, obeying; as a guardian is with one whose treasures he guards; as a child is with his nurse; as a bridegroom is with his bride; as a king is with his queen.

Finally, “the Lord is with you” by nature, by grace, and by glory.

By nature: existing excellently, knowing presently, and persisting in power.

By grace: through infusion, operation, and revelation.

By glory: because in reason there is fullness of light, in the will fullness of peace, and in the memory continuation of eternity.

**Blessed are you among women:** because you were sanctified in the womb; because your soul was preserved from sin; because in you the tinder of sin was extinguished; because you were filled with every good and every virtue; because your womb was privileged; because you conceived without seed, carried without burden, and gave birth without pain; because you were specially praised by all Christians; because at death you were met by Christ himself, by all the saints, and by the angels; and so forth.

[Col. 0583]

## III. MEDITATION ON THE “SALVE REGINA,” AND SO FORTH

[NOTE.]

This title is prefixed in that very large Mantuan manuscript, concerning which perhaps the reader will hesitate when he sees this little work attributed elsewhere to Saint Bernard and circulated among his works. The meditation is indeed the same in both places, but the one is more abbreviated and this one twice as long. Neither, however, will be regarded as Anselm’s if Bernard, who lived later, added those final words: “O clement, O loving, O sweet Virgin Mary,” in the city of Speyer; so most writers report. Others maintain that he recited it with the customary threefold genuflection but did not add it. [Note: [Col. 0583D] See Eylengren, in the Chronicle of Speyer.] Possevinus accordingly warns the reader to examine whether it is rightly attributed to Bernard.

The author of this and of the preceding meditations must certainly be considered the same—one especially devout and accustomed to contemplating divine mysteries.

[Col. 0583B]

1. To salute the blessed Virgin, you must first consider her greatness; for she could not be elevated closer to her Son than by being called the Mother of the Lord.

Therefore, exulting and admiring the magnificence of our Mother, approach her devoutly, reverently, and confidently, and say: “Hail.” Having said this, recoil from the magnificence of the Mother of God into your own smallness. Say:

“Have patience with me, Lady, because I, the vilest of human beings, dare stand before so great a Lady, and presume to salute you as Queen of heaven, Lady of the angels, and Mother of my God. But I trust in your goodness, Lady—humble and kindly in humility—that you will sustain me, utterly unworthy though I am.

“Although you are the ark of God, incomparably nobler than the ark of the Old Testament, and I far more ignoble, nevertheless, when I touch you with my heart and salute you with my mouth, I do not believe that I shall be struck down; rather, I believe that I shall be inflamed by your love and heard in all things by your most generous mercy.

“Therefore, ‘Hail, Queen’: under your rule, Lady, I wish henceforth to serve as a soldier. I commit myself wholly to your dominion, so that you may govern and direct me completely. Do not leave me to myself, for I am far too conscious of myself. Whatever you leave to me, know that it will be most wretchedly destroyed.

“But since I am full of misery, and from the sole of my foot to the crown of my head I produce putrefaction and horror, how will so noble a creature deign to govern me?”

Certainly, because you are the Queen of mercy.

## 2.

And who are subject to mercy, if not the miserable? Thus you are the Queen of Mercy, and I am the most miserable of all your subjects, the greatest sinner. How then, Lady, will you not exercise toward me the effect of your compassion? Truly, Lady, you are Queen of Mercy, because in this life there is no one so desperate, so miserable, for whom you cannot obtain saving mercy, if he turns toward your rule.

Certainly, Lady, when I look upon you, I see nothing but mercy. For you became the Mother of God for the sake of the miserable. You gave birth to mercy for the miserable. On every side, Lady, you are surrounded by mercy; you seem to desire only to show mercy. You are deeply concerned for the miserable; you adopted them as your children and wished to govern them, Lady, and therefore you are rightly called Queen of Mercy.

Why then, Lady, should we henceforth be afraid? What should we fear? Why do we not come to you with swift steps? And who will not receive from you whatever he asks? Certainly, I do not know—unless it be one who does not recognize himself as miserable. For no one submits to your rule except the miserable, or one who recognizes himself as miserable and trusts in your mercy.

Let only those tremble who consider themselves just—those proud and presumptuous people who do not submit to your rule—and also those miserable ones who do not seek your mercy. Let us, then, the miserable, console ourselves with you henceforth; let us now dwell with you, Lady; let us embrace you from the depths of our minds, because you are life.

## 3.

Life indeed, who conquered the death of pride through humility; who obtained for us the life of grace; who gave birth to the life of glory—and there is no doubt that you have rescued natural life from many dangers. For in all things you set yourself against death as life, whenever it seems expedient.

O wondrous life, who strive to make the dead alive! Through you, Lady, there is a return from deprivation to possession. O life that fears no death, drives death away, and makes mortals immortal! O truly lovable life, desirable life, delightful life! O life that does not grow old, but rather restores the aged to youth! O life, reducing carnal lives to nothing! O life truly opposed to the life of the world! Whoever wishes to possess you must afflict himself, reject pleasures, and despise every delicacy; and the more thoroughly he has been put to death to the world, the more fully will he possess you.

O divine life, strengthening by your power, obtaining and breathing forth divine wisdom, and quickening through divine goodness! If you are my life, why do you not continually quicken my life? Who will grant me always to rejoice in the benefit of this life?

Truly, you are sweetness: by obtaining mercy you drive away the bitterness of sins; you acquire for us the sweetness of grace; you lead those who contemplate you into the pleasantness of the heavenly homeland, and at last bring them to possess it.

O sweet Lady, whose mere memory sweetens the affections; whose greatness, when meditated upon, elevates the mind; whose beauty gladdens the inward eye; whose immeasurable loveliness intoxicates the heart of the one who meditates upon you!

O Lady, who ravish hearts with your sweetness—you have now ravished my heart, Lady; and where, I ask, have you placed it, so that I may be able to find it? Have you placed it in your bosom, so that I may find myself? Have you perhaps placed it between your breasts? Perhaps you put it there so that what had grown cold might be warmed, set aflame by your love, and become unable to separate itself from you.

O ravisher of hearts! When will you restore my heart to me? Why do you thus ravish the hearts of the simple? Why do you do violence—or rather, show benevolence—to your friends? Do you perhaps wish to keep it? When I ask you for it, you smile at me; and immediately, lulled to sleep by your sweetness, I rest. When I return to myself and ask for it again, you embrace me, sweetest Lady, and immediately I am intoxicated by your love.

Now I cannot distinguish my heart from yours. Nor do I know how to ask anything else of you except your heart. But since my heart has thus been intoxicated and lulled to sleep by your love, govern it together with your own; preserve it in the blood of the Lamb, and place it in the side of your Son, so that it may feel only what you feel, love only what you love, and be with you not on earth but in heaven.

O blessed is the heart to which it is given always—or almost always—to meditate upon the Lady; to glory continually amid the delights of the Lord; and also to suffer with the Passion of the Son.

O wondrous and lovable sweetness of the heart, to which all other things—even father, mother, and children, or whatever pertains to them—seem most foul and bitter!

O sweetest Lady, possessing the sweetest fruit; drawing hearts most sweetly; bestowing the sweetest gifts; promising every sweetness; making hearts most sweet! O how sweet you are, my Lady! O truly, how sweet—and how exceedingly sweet in delights! You possess the sweetest breasts of compassion and are supremely blessed.

Then shall I attain what I seek; then shall I possess what I hope for, because you are our hope.

Are you not the Lady of the kingdom? Are you not the Mother of the reward, namely Christ, who is the reward of the good and the blessed? Are you not the one who desires so greatly that we be exalted? Do you not love us incomparably more and procure our good more than an earthly mother does?

If, then, you wish to make us glorious—and indeed you do wish it—who will be able to prevent it? For what else do you have to do except present the Son? He himself is our merit, our reward, and our glory.

Let those who know your name hope in you, for you do not abandon those who seek you, Lady (Psalm 9). Certainly, those who hope in you will renew their strength; they will take wings like eagles, run and not grow weary, call and not fail (Isaiah 40).

Who will not hope in you, who help even the despairing? And who will not hope in you, through whom the prayers of the fathers were heard, the prophecies of the prophets fulfilled, and their promises brought to completion? What could the patriarchs and prophets desire, Lady, that they did not obtain through you?

If the ancients received all these things through you, how will we—who are your children, already redeemed by the blood of the Only-Begotten—not receive whatever we wish to ask? I do not doubt that, if we come to you, we shall receive what we desire.

Let the one who despairs hope in you; let the one who is failing run confidently to you; let the one who wishes to obtain something come to you, saying: “Hail.”

Who, henceforth, can prevent us from greeting you, since you are thus Mother and Lady, our life, sweetness, and hope? Since you are Queen, who can hinder us from revering you?

Let not only human beings, but every creature, greet you as Mother of God. Through you, Lady, all things have been restored, and through you all things recover their Creator, so that they may be subject to him in due order.

Certainly, it seems astonishing that the whole world ceases from greeting you, rather than praising and saluting you continually at every moment. But what is it to greet you twice, except to revere you as Lady of angels and of human beings? And what is it to repeat the greeting, except to offer you reverence without end?

What is it to greet you and greet you again, except to ask salvation and the growth of salvation from you, Lady? Why do we greet and greet again, except that through you, Lady, we may be kept safely both inwardly and outwardly?

What is “I greet,” and again, “I greet,” except that I expose both aspects of the human person to your reverence? Why, moreover, did I greet you and greet you again, except that through you I might possess God and humanity—indeed, through you, your Son?

Why did I greet you, except that I might render you prepared to fulfill my desires; and why did I greet you again, except that you might be ready to accomplish them? Or certainly, at first we wished to greet you in order to commend you; secondly, in order to rejoice in the glory of your Son after this misery.

First, Lady, you are to be greeted so that through you we may obtain grace; secondly, so that through you we may come to glory.

## 5.

To you—to you truly—for you, Lady, gave birth to God and man. You alone, Lady, destroyed heretical depravity; you alone are Lady of the kingdom; you alone are the governess of the reward.

To you, our mother; to you, our nurse; to you, our helper; to you, certainly, who wash us from the dregs of sins; who console us even when we cry in our cradles; who give milk to hungry infants. The weak and failing are supported by your arms; you truly strengthen the wounded and lead the sick to salvation.

You have become not only mother and nurse, but also physician of the miserable: you do not abandon those who abandon; you receive those who flee; you are Queen, Empress, and Lady of the angels. With caresses you entice us, with delights you cherish and nourish us.

To you we cry out. How could we not cry out, Lady, when we suffer wounds and feel blows, when we are surrounded and terrified on every side by enemies? We cry out, distressed and oppressed by countless miseries. We cry out because of anxiety of heart, emptiness of stomach, bitterness of pain—or perhaps because of the immensity of our love for you.

We cry out. May no sleepiness toward us overtake you, who guard us day and night. Why do you sleep, Lady? Arise; help us.

We cry out also to disclose our need, because necessity compels us to cry out. We also cry out to invoke your compassion, Lady. For because of this crying my throat has become hoarse.

Why, then, do you permit me to be afflicted any longer? If you delay too long, I shall lose my voice from crying out, and I shall no longer be able to call to you. Alas for me! What shall I do then, when you can neither heed nor hear me? What shall I do then, Lady, when I have been entirely abandoned by you? What shall I do when you can no longer offer me your breasts?

Come quickly, Lady; help the one who cries out, lest I fall into the hands of the enemy. Run, hasten, Lady; in your mercy help your most wicked and faithless servant who cries out to you, and rescue him from the enemy’s hands and from the dangers of your foe.

If nothing else ought to move you, Lady, surely it should be that your enemy dares treacherously to attack us, your little servants; you ought to hasten as quickly as possible. Run and free us, Lady, in order to restrain their pride. Run, lest the enemy boast of ruling over your dependents. Run, lest they say: “Where is their Lady, in whose clemency they trusted?”

Do not wonder, Lady, that we cry out, because we have been driven very far from you. In a distant land we have squandered our portion. If we were near, we could speak more clearly; and therefore, mindful of your breasts, we cry out to you.

Exiles from our homeland, exiles from the divine vision; exiles also from grace, exiles from maternal consolation! O my soul, why are you not separated from the body rather than exiled from your Lady? If you are exiled from your mother, you are exiled from Christ the Head. And how can you, miserable one, walk without a head? Would it not be monstrous to walk without a head?

Alas for me! Why have I been banished into so long an exile? When shall I see God my Savior? Or when shall I at least be able to look upon my Lady?

I do not doubt, Lady, that if we, as exiles, cried out to you from the heart, we would fully possess you and your Son. Why, then, do we wish to rest here as citizens? Why do we not long for our homeland? Why do we not desire to embrace our sweetest Mother? What do we not desire—to dwell with her and with her Son?

O Lady, while we are exiles here, establish us in such a way that we do not cease seeking you and your Son here as though we were already secure in our homeland. Yet establish us in the body so that in mind we may always be citizens with you.

## 6. Sons of Eve

Truly, sons of Eve: proud, presumptuous, ambitious, greedy—at least for books and knowledge, and would that it were not so in any other matter!—gluttonous, carnal, and disobedient; in short, following Eve herself in everything. We are inclined toward evil and difficult to move toward good.

And if it happens that someone produces some offspring of good works, we often bring it forth with a certain pain and sorrow of heart, while we commit evil with joy. Our own evils are not enough for us; rather, just as Eve inclined Adam to evil, so we also incline others toward evil.

And just as she excused herself, so we excuse ourselves in our failings—or at least, if we can, shift the blame onto others. We grow weary of feeding upon the tree of life, namely Christ the Lord, contemplated upon the cross, and we apply our hands to the forbidden tree.

We do not care to be consoled through contemplation of the delights of paradise; rather, we wish to dwell in the filth of sins and handle every kind of vanity—or, to speak truthfully, chew the most stinking dung.

Alas, what unheard-of madness, vanity, and blindness! For we prefer, through immense toil and sweat, to acquire worthless things and our own death, rather than, with all sweetness and delight, not only to acquire life but somehow also to possess eternal life and taste the Lord of glory.

And unless you had helped us, Lady, perhaps we would have reached the deepest depths of hell. There is nothing, Lady, that can excuse us, because in everything we imitate not you but Eve—or rather, we surpass her in evil.

Therefore, recognizing this through your merciful assistance and hoping through you, Lady, to be lifted from such misery, we sigh toward you, Lady. We sigh because of the absence of a good mother, desiring to come to you, Lady. We sigh, longing to see your Son.

We sigh like little children panting for the breasts; like children—and unworthy ones—stretching toward your maternal embraces. We sigh toward you out of desire. We sigh toward you with inward love, being deeply intoxicated by your love.

For nothing but your love, by which we are inwardly intoxicated toward you, Lady, compels us to sigh toward you—[perhaps: in longing].

Who could fail to love you and sigh toward you with longing? You are the restoration of all things, the furnace of love, more beautiful than the sun, sweeter than honey, the treasure of goodness, the mirror of uprightness, the example of every holiness. You are lovable to all, approachable to all, delightful to all.

You are the seat of wisdom, the river of clemency, the ray of divinity; and no one can hide from your heat. Thus we sigh toward you from the depths of our being, out of desire and love.

We sigh—and with vehement pain—for anxieties press upon us on every side. How, then, should we not sigh toward you, consolation of the miserable, refuge of the expelled, liberation of captives, bride of the mature, Queen of the starry ones, Lady of all, even of enemies? There is no one who can oppose your will.

And therefore, so afflicted and so miserable, we sigh toward you, such a Lady: so sweet, so gentle, helper in all things, tree of life, root of consolation.

## 7. Groaning and Weeping in This Valley of Tears

Do you not see, Lady, that we are completely filled with bitterness? Within, we groan; outwardly, we weep; we lie in this tearful place.

Burdened by sins, we groan; weighed down by troubles, we weep; overwhelmed by miseries, we weep; deprived of help in the valley of tears, we groan, unable to see the Sun of Justice.

We weep while serving our enemies; we are in the valley of tears, asking for your help. This is truly the valley of tears, into which all tearful things flow, all groaning things run, and toward which all mournful things rush.

To this valley the demons of the underworld had flowed; here is the punishment of our first parents, the misery of the ancients. What more can I say? I neither suffice nor know how to recount the detestable things of this valley.

Come, then, our Advocate! O praiseworthy and exceedingly lovable clemency of the Savior, who has deigned to grant such noble assistance to those so afflicted!

O truly wondrous kindness of our God, who gives you, Lady, as Advocate to his guilty ones, so that, with your Son appointed Judge between us and God the Father, you may obtain for us whatever you wish.

For there can be no doubt that he will not condemn so openly those whom the advocacy of your compassion preserves. O wondrous mercy of our God toward us! Lest we flee from his clemency, he not only wished to share with us a Judge who would be God and man—that is, Christ, from whom the sentence must be pronounced—but wished to appoint the entrails of mercy, his Mother, the Lady of glory, as our Advocate, so that we, the guilty, might find not judgment but assistance, not punishment but an eternal reward.

Therefore there is no reason to fear that you will not have mercy on the miserable, incline toward the side of the sentence that you defend, and obtain for us the grace for which you pray on our behalf.

I know well that after the sentence there is no appeal to a higher authority, because although the Judge is human—and you are his Mother—he is nevertheless also God, the Son of God the Father. For I do not see, Lady, how anything could be denied you, or how through you we could fail to possess the heavenly homeland.

And this too is that wondrous compassion: this is certainly what our God wishes; this is what he desires; this is why he appointed you as our Advocate.

Nothing remains, then, Lady, except for you to turn your merciful eyes toward us. I do not doubt, Lady, that if you look upon our miseries, your compassion will not be able to delay its effect.

Wondrous and lovable are the rays of your eyes, by which you draw us to love and lead us to complete salvation, so that we may not fear the poisoned eyes of the basilisk.

O poisoned eyes of Eve, why do you not present yourselves to the eyes of the Virgin, if you wish to receive perfect healing? For the rays and brightness of her eyes drive away darkness, scatter the armies of demons, cleanse the vices of minds, kindle frozen hearts, and finally draw them toward heavenly things.

O blessed are those, Lady, whom your eyes behold! Turn these eyes, then, gracious Lady, toward us.

## 8. And Show Us Jesus, the Blessed Fruit of Your Womb, After This Exile

O wondrous womb, which was able to receive the Creator! O praiseworthy womb, which deserved to conceive redemption! O desirable womb, from which flowed the desire of minds, the river of graces, the reward of glory!

O womb—not a womb, but the empyrean heaven! In this womb was the price of the lost, the happiness of the blessed, the Lord of the angels.

O blessed breasts! O my Lady! O fountain of compassion, lake of holiness, river of goodness—your womb, Lady!

O happy womb, which gave birth to the Sun, restored the whole world, recovered the heavenly homeland, and moreover bestowed it! O how precious the womb that brought forth medicine for the sick, life for the dead, and paradise for the just!

O ivory womb and seat of wisdom! O rounded, lathe-turned womb, and height of glory! O lovable womb and sweetness of the soul! O elevation of minds, intoxication of hearts, and sweetness of sinners!

Your fruit, Lady, is certainly a blessed fruit from the beginning of its origin. This is Jesus, the Son of the living God. This is our Savior, Christ the Lord.

In the sweetness of this fruit, the understanding is lifted up, the affection is enlarged, and the desire of each is brought to rest. Reason becomes clear, affection sweetens, and intention is purified.

In the sweetness of your fruit the whole heart melts as it tastes your fruit. Show us this Jesus, the blessed fruit of your womb, after this exile.

May we, seeing him, possess him; seeing him, be filled with blessedness; seeing him, be carried away into him; seeing him, be poured out into him; seeing him, be transformed into him—so that, thus made divine, we may no longer belong to ourselves but be wholly transformed into him.

O merciful one! O loving one! O sweet Mary! Merciful toward the needy, loving toward those who beseech you, sweet toward those who love you! Merciful toward penitents, loving toward those making progress, sweet toward contemplatives!

Merciful in liberating, loving in giving, sweet in giving yourself! Merciful in consoling, loving in advising, sweet in caressing! Merciful in appearance, loving in action, sweet in affection!

Merciful in conception, loving in sight, sweet in embrace; merciful to the afflicted, loving to the abandoned, sweet in love toward the just.

Merciful toward those subject to you, loving toward those already corrected, sweet toward the specially beloved. Merciful toward those who ask, loving toward those who seek you, sweet toward those who knock at you; merciful toward those who marvel, loving toward those who rejoice, sweet toward those who taste you.

Merciful toward the poor, loving toward the despised, sweet toward the devout. Merciful toward those who have been elevated, loving toward those who have been transformed, sweet toward those who have melted away.

O merciful one! O loving one! O sweet Virgin Mary. Hail, Mary, full of grace; the Lord is with you.

# IV. Meditations on the Deeds of Our Lord Jesus Christ (G)

## [NOTE]

Arnoldus Wion attributes the following rhythms to Anselm; and the Mantuan manuscript codex places his name and these titles before them. Similar pieces, with the same rhythm, are found in Bernard.

These poems are certainly pious and filled with devout meditations. In the first, the author is weightier, more serious, and more concise in singing the mysteries of Christ; in the second, he is more expansive, pouring himself out completely into soliloquies and devout affections toward the Blessed Virgin. He frequently intensifies the vehemence of her sorrow, the languor of her spirit, and her lamentations during the Passion of Christ.

But the view that the Most Holy Virgin possessed perfect dominion over all her actions, affections, and powers, and permitted nothing indecorous or discordant within herself, is the judgment of the ancient and more authoritative Fathers [Note: See Suárez, *In partem tertiam*, volume II, disputation 4, section 3, and disputation 41, section 2.].

The author himself makes the same point in the first rhythm: “But,” he says, “sorrow does not strip the virginly bearing from the Virgin.” He seems different in the second, where throughout, both in the sequence of the meditations and in the words, he agrees with the little work on the Lamentation of the Virgin Mary interspersed among the works of Saint Bernard. What if the author of that little work is also the author here? In any case, we have added marginal notes to the rhythm.

## Prologue

**[Col. 0591A]**

Leave now, soul, the bed of slumber;  
Let languor, torpor, and vanity be driven outside.  
Within, let the heart seethe with the torches of love,  
Recalling the wondrous deeds of the Savior.

Mind, affection, and reason, come together;  
Do not continue to occupy yourselves with trifles.  
Away with distraction, wandering, and cares,  
While the mind handles the mysteries of life.

Above all, let the reader be warned  
Not to run hastily through the following little work.  
Rather, by reading slowly, let the meaning unfold,  
So that devotion may be drawn from the very words.

## The Mysteries of Christ’s Life

My sweetest Jesus, Lord and Creator of the heavens,  
Omnipotent King of all things,  
Who could sufficiently marvel at the deeds  
That the salvation of the miserable compelled you to endure?

The love of souls drew you from heaven,  
For whose sake, abandoning your splendid palace,  
You entered the miserable valley of tears,  
Undertaking hard labor and a bitter journey.

## The Annunciation

An angel is sent by you to the Virgin,  
Through whom your Incarnation is announced.  
But while the Virgin is diligently greeted by the angel’s voice,  
She asks in wonder about the sequence of events.

“When the Holy Spirit makes you fruitful,” he says,  
“And the Power of the Most High overshadows you,  
You will bear the one whom the people will call the Son of God;  
And the Father will give him an everlasting kingdom.”

## The Incarnation

You immediately descended at the Virgin’s consent  
And chose the temple of her chaste breast.  
You entered the chamber of the poor Virgin,  
Where you assumed the substance of our flesh.

## The Nativity

Preserving inviolate the seal of modesty,  
The Virgin gives birth to him whom she conceived as a virgin.  
It is not fitting that the vessel of the flower should be defiled,  
Nor that God should take away his Mother’s virginity.

You who rule heaven, earth, and the underworld  
Do not disdain now to assume the form of a servant.  
For nine months you remain in the womb;  
Thus you are made a little lower than the angels.

How powerful is your kindness! How loving your power!  
He who surpasses heaven and earth is born upon the way;  
Joseph and Mary render him their service,  
And an angelic harmony praises him in song.

## In the Manger

**[Col. 0592A]**

Divine majesty, how greatly you humble yourself  
When you deign, as God, to arise from a woman!  
Do you rejoice, King of heaven, in a palace?  
No; you recline in a small manger.

Jesus, whom the angelic host venerates,  
Is not born adorned in purple garments;  
Rather, he is laid in very humble swaddling clothes,  
And thus, in poverty, detests the glory of the world.

The princes of kings’ offspring ordinarily rejoice,  
And noble wet nurses offer their breasts;  
But the Son of God refuses to have these things,  
Preferring to show himself born among shepherds.

## Infancy

The Virgin alone, mother of the Son of the Most High Father,  
Pours out milk from her consecrated virgin breast;  
With a welcome kiss she consoles him as he cries,  
Stills him, cherishes him in her lap, and holds him in her blessed bosom.

O happy mother, rejoicing that you alone give birth!  
How sweetly you delight in the one born!  
With what devout embraces you embrace Jesus!  
With what generous services you minister to him!

O condescension of God, how wondrously it is shown!  
Power is governed; God is humbled.  
Height is subjected; what is long is made short.  
Depth becomes level; breadth is narrowed.

Joy is saddened; salvation grows weak.  
The living Bread hungers; power is sustained.  
The everlasting Fountain from which heaven drinks thirsts.  
Who, seeing these wonders, would not marvel?

## Circumcision

You who were born under the Law observed the Law.  
Circumcised, you began the payment of our price,  
When you offered your blood to the Father for us.  
Then, too, you received your proper name.

## The Adoration of the Magi

With the star as guide, you led the Magi to yourself,  
Whose mystical gifts you wished to receive as homage.  
Crossing into Egypt, you escaped the enemy,  
Leaving in this an example for the weak.

## Presentation in the Temple

You are presented in the temple by virginal hands;  
As a little child, you are carried in the arms of the just old man,  
Through whom you are prophetically proclaimed as God.  
You are called the Light of the Nations and the Glory of Israel.

## Disputation in the Temple

Afterward, when already twice six years old,  
You are sought by your Virgin Mother among the crowd of acquaintances;  
You are found in the midst of the teachers in the temple,  
Listening and asking wondrous questions about hidden matters.

“Son,” says your Mother, “what have you done to us?  
Have you come, Jesus, to attend to the things of your Father in this way?  
You have been sought for three days—why have you hidden thus?  
Yet you have not refused to be subject to human beings.”

From this point until the Savior’s thirtieth year,  
I marvel where the writer’s pen has gone.  
Perhaps this is suggested to the reader’s mind:  
The deeds of his youth should not be made too public.

## Baptism

Afterward, when baptized, he washed away our sins;  
By the touch of his sacred body he consecrated the waters.  
The Holy Spirit descended and illumined him,  
And the Father’s voice openly declared him to be the Son.

## Fasting in the Desert

**[Col. 0593B]**

Here, sweetest Jesus, you entered the wilderness,  
And there afflicted your body with fasts.  
Dwelling among wild beasts, you confounded Satan,  
And thus left an effective example for all.

## The Calling of the Apostles

When you chose to make your deeds known  
And preach repentance to the world,  
You began to gather disciples to yourself,  
Such as the world ordinarily considers worthless.

You reject philosophers and call fishermen;  
Those whom the world despises you make teachers.  
To confound the strong and disperse their swelling pride,  
Through these men you subject the rulers of the earth to yourself.

## Miracles

From this point you illumined the world with wondrous signs.  
Approving marriage, you entered a wedding feast  
And changed water into excellent wine.  
With a few loaves you fed many thousands.

At your word alone the dead are raised;  
Every kind of illness is immediately healed.  
You command the sea and winds, and they are no longer troubled;  
You command the demons, and at once they flee.

## The Announcement of the Passion

Most kind Jesus, after such illustrious deeds  
You announce bitter things to the disciples.  
The hearts of those ignorant of such matters are immediately troubled;  
You judge that you must be sacrificed upon the altar of the cross.

You travel through cities and fortresses teaching the people;  
You grow weary, hungry, and thirsty as you go about;  
You are often troubled by enduring harsh things  
And bearing the evils of a faithless crowd.

## The Triumph of the Palms

You proceed to Jerusalem seated on a donkey;  
The rejoicing crowd comes out to meet and receive you.  
They spread garments along the road, cutting branches of palm,  
And a procession of children praises you as you advance.

## Deeds in the City

Foreseeing the fate of the doomed city, you weep for it.  
In the temple you sternly threaten those engaged in commerce.  
The rulers immediately grow jealous, a people of impure mind,  
Asking by what right you presume to do such things.

## Judas’s Betrayal

Preaching daily, you await the time  
When you will suffer death for the life of the world.  
The impious plot how they may seize you;  
They promise Judas a price so that you may be betrayed by him.

## The Supper

After this you celebrate the supper with the disciples,  
Whom you feed with the mystery of your body.  
Washing the feet of each, you humble yourself;  
Afterward you strengthen them with the nourishment of the word.

## Prayer in the Garden

Then you openly foretold your death to the disciples
