Therefore be ready for us, the guilty, Lady,  
and, entreated, hear the least of them—me.  
Remember for whom you were so greatly exalted,  
and for whom your Son was tormented.

Deign to hear my prayers, Lady,  
and now and always come to my aid;  
make me be struck by your wounds and those of the Lord,  
and continually feel them devoutly in my heart.

[Col. 0622C] O broken by sorrows, standing beneath the cross,  
full of bitterness from the wounds of your Son!  
Give me a share of your sorrow; do not be sparing,  
you who have been called generous, free, and *guara* [reading uncertain].

O my confidence, Mother of the Savior,  
pierce me at once with the sword of your sorrow;  
enrich me with the gift of perfect love,  
and speak to my soul the power of your grief.

Now, now, present in spirit, singular Mother,  
speak something of your sorrows,  
something that may please your dear servants  
and sprinkle them with bitter tears.

[Col. 0622D] The Mother Grieves with the Son

“Importunate soul, why do you cry out to me in this way,  
when you remember and love me so little?  
But you say that you have heard pious reports about me,  
and for this reason you cry out to me so boldly.

Now, if you wish to hear the sufferings of my mind  
as I grieved with my crucified Son,  
cast away the vanities of your wandering heart,  
and offer the lamentations of a compassionate spirit.

Do not listen to these things without weeping,  
where you see me grieving in this way with my Child,  
where the Maker of heaven shed many tears,  
where the Ruler of the sun endured death.

And first I address you, assuring you concerning that  
which you sometimes ponder about me:  
that I observed all the wounds  
[Col. 0623A]  
that my Son received while enduring them.

Know that sorrow pressed upon me so greatly  
that it almost destroyed the strength of my body together with my senses;  
but my Son’s immeasurable love compelled me  
to behold all the torments that he himself endured.

Whenever I saw some pain inflicted,  
I immediately weakened as though dying;  
but, through the force of love, I revived at once  
and eagerly watched my Son’s torments.

For my whole heart dwelt with him,  
whom I loved unspeakably more than myself.  
Therefore, whatever my Son endured  
weighed upon my heart inconsolably.

[Col. 0623B] For my heart was harshly bound to him,  
tormented with him by blows and slaps, spitting,  
mockery and blasphemies, and greatly tortured  
by his harsh scourging.

With Jesus my heart was crowned with thorns,  
burdened with him by the weight of the cross,  
dragged with him to the place of Calvary,  
and embittered by his drink of gall.

I saw him stripped and subjected to great pains,  
wholly bloodied with his delicate blood.  
With Jesus my heart was stretched and nailed.  
Behold, you see my heart entirely lacerated.

Contemplate, O soul, my heart nailed  
and often pierced together with my Son;  
but my heart was especially burdened by this:  
[Col. 0623C] that it was not deprived of life by these punishments.

But indescribable torments tortured me  
when the wicked raised the cross upward;  
for they made it stand with a violent thrust  
and afflicted Jesus beyond expression.

O, if you knew how greatly this pain burdened me,  
how much it widened Christ’s wounds in his hands,  
how deeply he himself sighed,  
and how bitterly he then wept!

I stood beneath the gallows, Mother of the true God,  
seeing the Lord of all things suffer;  
I grieved inwardly over his appearance,  
whom the Jews had made deformed by torture.

In the greatest weakness and grievous pain,  
[Col. 0623D] I raised my eyes to Jesus again and again.  
‘Woe! Woe!’ I cried as best I could. ‘Woe, my Son!  
I bore you, Jesus, for these sufferings.’

I looked many times at my Son hanging,  
cruelly nailed and stretched upon the cross,  
the only just God hung among the guilty;  
and in grief I almost lost my senses.

In the greatest anguish I saw my Son,  
and was utterly unable to help him.  
I uttered groans, sighs, and sobs;  
I poured forth many bitter tears.

I saw his holy and delightful face,  
sweeter and more gracious than the tongue can express,  
wholly tearful from so many anguishes,  
bloodied, bruised, and also stained.

[Col. 0624A] For his eyes shed such abundant tears  
that they grew dim from the quantity of weeping,  
since no one was present to wipe them;  
but many mocked the grieving Lord.

The worthy head of my Son hung down, exhausted,  
for there was no place where it could rest;  
apart from the thorns, it had no pillow at all.  
Its manifold pain tormented me greatly.

When I often looked upon his most beautiful hands,  
I considered them, alas, grievously lacerated,  
tormented wickedly by the nails piercing them, and—”

Which those most wicked men had driven through these [hands].

I looked upon the most worthy feet, mangled—

alas! struck with a hammer, pierced with iron—

all the limbs of the body tortured together,

[Col. 0624B] and the framework of the bones cruelly disjointed.

They tormented the taste of my Son with gall;

the Jews harassed his hearing with blasphemies;

the stench of the place tormented his sense of smell;

and all these things together greatly oppressed me.

Love compelled me to speak to my Son,

and my affectionate heart uttered words,

but, alas, excessive grief tore them apart,

so that it was wholly unable to utter the words.

My senses failing, I was already collapsing,

and, with my strength broken, I fell down in sorrow;

but, recovering my breath, with the voice I still possessed,

I immediately burst into words such as these:

“Alas! alas! My Son, alas! alas! dear offspring,

behold, these perverse men have separated me from you.

[Col. 0624C] Help me, I beg you, in my anguish;

hear my prayers; have mercy on your desolate Mother.

Through you, Son, I possessed all that was prosperous;

in you, Jesus, I was continually joyful.

Alas, now through you I am sunk in sadness,

because this unclean crowd torments you in this way.

Let me die with you through this agony,

I who nourished you yourself for this suffering.

Alas, I nursed you for slaughter;

I beg you, make me die together with you through compassion.

In yourself, my Son, you were impassible;

all this that you suffer you assumed from me.

Therefore make me die with you in this grievous slaughter,

because I exposed you to this dreadful death.

[Col. 0624D] O, who would grant that I might undergo death for you, Jesus,

you who took from me the wretched lot that was mine?

Son, why do you permit me now to be so strong?

I beg you: by dying, make me your companion.

O my joy, salvation, hope, and life,

Jesus, why do you leave me so desolate?

Why am I placed in sufferings without assistance?

Alas, all my consolations are finished.

Who will henceforth provide comfort for me?

Deign now to hear a mother’s burden,

and at least grant me some relief.

See, see, my Son, a mother’s anguish.”

Then Jesus, hearing me sigh, groan, and weep

so unceasingly and sorrowfully,

and openly seeing my anxious heart,

[Col. 0625A] seemed, in his clemency, to console me in my mourning.

O, if only you knew how he grieved with me!

Indeed, he languished far more for me than for himself,

and his suffering pressed heavily upon me;

thus suffering afflicted us both in turn.

O immeasurable weight and anguish!

Ineffable punishment and bitterness!

How greatly this condition oppressed us both,

whom immeasurable gratitude bound together!

### Christ Commends His Mother to John

As he approached death, he called to me as I wept,

appointed John as my son,

and likewise commended me to him as his mother;

then the sword of grief pierced me.

We heard the Lord, alas, half alive;

[Col. 0625B] through sorrow we could say nothing;

we saw Jesus, almost dead, speaking,

but, alas, we could not answer anything.

I was losing the jubilation of my heart,

and was dissolving wholly into many tears;

I saw the life of my soul passing away,

and was already melting under immense sufferings.

“Why have you forsaken me?”

For in this way his humanity too was being forsaken,

nor did his divinity then come to his aid;

hence he was rendered exceedingly passible,

and he was saying, “Why have you forsaken me, God?”

Soul, if you ponder this first grief,

perhaps you will possess the dew of tears;

and if you are devout and desire honor,

[Col. 0625C] meditate often on this sorrow of mine.

O immense mercy, filled with compassion,

praise and honor without end be given to you, Mother.

May all things that have been made, known and hidden,

give you thanks, Virgin, pregnant with the Word.

Now, with tears rising through compassion,

I am compelled to interrupt this discourse of yours,

to render you thanks,

and to exalt your mercy.

O my confidence, Mother of the true God,

through you I continually pray to be urged toward good,

and through you to be restrained from every evil,

and always to be filled with your sorrows.

[Col. 0625D] Would that I could now howl with tears

and die in sorrow for you, O Lady!

I beg you always to make me feel your sufferings;

deign to soften my exceedingly hard heart.

Alas, why did you go after your Son, Lady?

Alas, why did you go out to the place of Calvary?

Alas, why were you not alone at home,

lest perhaps you perish in Christ’s death?

Was not the suffering of your Son enough for us,

unless the savage people also crucified you?

Why did you make yourself, Lady of wondrous holiness,

a vessel of bitterness and suffering?

Alas, I see you not only weeping beside the cross,

but also remaining with your Son upon the cross:

Christ bodily hanging upon the wood,

but your soul hanging there and suffering.

[Col. 0626A] Alas, I contemplate your heart, repeatedly pierced,

and fastened with each of your Son’s limbs;

behold, within you you bear your crucified child,

torn by whips, thorns, blows, and nails.

O lovable, sweet, delicate heart,

alas, now utterly changed by anguish,

greatly troubled by insults and blasphemies,

made bitter by spittle, gall, and tears.

O most lovable heart, full of sweetness!

How have you been so changed into the gall of sorrow?

Give me, I beg, a share of your pain—

of your tears, wounds, and Christ’s suffering.

Then, after the Mother had been commended to the beloved disciple,

so that the sacred Scripture might be fulfilled,

the Son of God, exhausted, said, “I thirst.”

[Col. 0626B] But, alas, what a bitter drink was given him!

O Messiah, I beg your goodness:

drive gluttony and drunkenness away from me;

grant moderation in food and drink;

do not let me fall through excess.

Alas, why do I desire to be more richly fed,

or never to be satisfied with sumptuous foods?

O Jesus, do not let us take such delight,

you who deigned to drink gall for us.

Then, just as the apostle John recorded,

Jesus immediately cried out, “It is finished,”

and so commended his spirit to the Father

with a loud cry, and thus expired.

When the Lord was dying, the earth trembled;

the rocks were split, the sun closed its light;

[Col. 0626C] the dead rose again, the people mourned;

the veil of the Temple was torn, and the heavens gave no light.

If then insensible things shared in the suffering,

and the stones were split at the Lord’s death,

let human beings be ashamed who are not sorrowful

when they contemplate that the Lord Jesus died.

You truly said, Lord, through the prophet

that you wished to remove our heart of stone

and give your people a heart of flesh (Ezek. XI and XXXVI);

but, alas, it scarcely wishes to grieve as flesh.

O more than stony—ungrateful, unworthy!

O harshness of our heart, devoid of kindness!

Are we not deserving of much reproach,

[Col. 0626D] because we have so little compassion for so great a king?

O worst of hearts, hard and empty,

harder than stones, almost inhuman!

At least now have compassion, unless you are mad,

while you see what is not human suffer such things.

O Jesus, who gives gifts of grace,

I beg all your mercies:

wash away the hardened places of my heart,

and grant me tears and compassion.

Contemplate, soul, with great fervor

Jesus Christ, the physician, with his blood,

a man without beauty or attractiveness,

struck and dead for your love.

O how great are your sorrows, O God-bearing woman,

while creatures so insensible grieve!

[Col. 0627A] With what tongue can the anxieties of your mind be expressed?

What tortures are yours for your dead Son!

O who knows your sufferings, my hope,

when Jesus was pierced with a lance before you,

when that holy side was struck in this way,

whose blood is called our price?

Although the lifeless body no longer felt the blow,

it cruelly pierced your blessed heart;

the lance reddened Christ’s side with blood,

but the pain of the entire wound tormented you.

The Mother stood beside her Son’s cross;

she continually mourned with most bitter weeping,

for, with her senses extinguished, she scarcely lived,

and, alas, she lacked both voice and strength.

Falling anxiously to the ground, she lay pale,

[Col. 0627B] alive, she was dead; dying, she lived.

Alas, her soul, full of anguish, hung suspended;

though living yet dead, she did not grieve to die.

Again she raised herself and stood in sorrow,

and, weeping, contemplated the Lord hanging there.

She certainly chose to die rather than live,

while she awaited the taking down of her Son.

Then she said, lamenting, to those depraved men:

“Behold, now that your desires have been fulfilled,

take down the body for me, the wretched Mother;

or, if you wish, join me to him by killing me.

The Mother desired to touch her Son,

and raised herself upward as far as she could;

but, since she could in no way touch him,

alas, weak and exhausted, she fell heavily to the ground.

[Col. 0627C] Again she was carried upward by the force of love,

and soon embraced the cross’s instrument of execution;

she strove intensely to touch her Son,

but, alas, she was thrown down more violently upon the ground.

Lying there, she was cruelly tormented by anguish;

alas, she was overwhelmed by immense pains.

Thus she kissed the blood as it fell,

and her face was reddened by that blood.

Meanwhile two devoted disciples of Jesus,

Nicodemus and Joseph—so they were called—

having obtained permission from Pilate the governor,

came prepared to take Jesus down.

Then the Mother took up the body and arms,

and quickly drew them toward herself in deepest grief;

she rushed upon him, already taken down, with kisses,

[Col. 0627D] and could not be satisfied with her Son.

Then the Mother stood at her Son’s head,

and bathed his blessed face with tears.

Often sighing with the deepest grief,

she struck herself and uttered words such as these:

“O dearest Son, what have you done to me?

Why have these Jews handed you over to death?

Why did you wish to leave me behind you?

Come to the aid of my spirit, which is excessively sad.

O my one and only love, and my salvation,

my singular joy and consolation,

life of my soul, O Son, tell me why

you permit me to grieve for you with such bitterness?

Where is the great joy that I possessed

when, a virgin, I conceived you and gave birth to you?

Alas, now it has been changed into great sadness,

when I see you, my joy, slain.”

[Col. 0628A] But, while grieving, the Lady preserved her reason;

retaining firm faith, she despaired of nothing.

Rather, she grieved justly and wept rightly,

while she watched the Lord perish unjustly.

Then, when they wished to place the Lord in the tomb,

she began to entreat them not to do it so quickly.

They wished to consign the dead man to burial,

but she seemed to draw the body back toward herself.

Among them there arose a pious dispute of this kind,

and each of them grieved more intensely,

and wept especially for the Virgin Mother,

because she continually mourned in such anguish.

[Col. 0628B] Then angels came to the Lord’s tomb

and rendered praises to the buried Lord,

but Mary’s eyes poured forth tears,

and sobs and groans afflicted her.

When Christ had thus been placed in the tomb,

the most sorrowful Mother blessed her Son,

and, I think, commended him to the gracious Father,

groaning, weeping, and lamenting for the one who had been put to death.

Behold, he who never dies, the Lord of lords,

is buried dead by the hands of his own;

he whom neither earth nor the heavens of heavens contain

is shut beneath a stone in the manner of the dead.

Then John, to whom the Lord had commended his Mother,

namely, lifted up the grieving woman,

and entered the city of Jerusalem with her;

[Col. 0628C] and he served her well as a son.

Then the devout women who had witnessed these things,

who had followed the living Lord,

gratefully rendered service to the dead man;

buying spices, they prepared them for his burial.

Among them Magdalene seemed such a one

that she forgot the weakness of the female sex.

Going through the darkness, she feared nothing,

and found the one she had sought, from whom she was anointed.

But the Virgin, who had given birth, was occupied with weeping;

languishing, she continually mourned after her Son.

She recalled to mind how much he himself had suffered,

and pondered it through weeping in her languishing heart.

On the third day, when Christ rose again

and led captives with him from the underworld,

[Col. 0628D] an angel suddenly descended from heaven,

while a violent earthquake likewise took place.

At dawn Magdalene went to the tomb,

carrying prepared spices with her.

She feared neither weapons nor savage men,

but, fervently loving the Lord, sought him.

He appeared first to her alone.

She, now more troubled, believed that he had been taken away;

she was unwilling to hear the angels who consoled her,

and nothing could please her without the Lord.

And because she sought him more fervently than the others,

the Lord appeared first to her alone.

He immediately forbade her to touch him,

but instructed her to tell the brothers that he was alive.

[Col. 0629A] When the Lord’s agony of suffering was finished,

and the Lion from the tribe of Judah had roared,

when the Son had been raised and the dragon defeated,

you, Virgin bearing Christ, lay aside your sorrow.

Rejoicing, look, Lady, upon the immortal body,

subtle, agile, and spiritual,

which bodily torment will no longer harm,

and which will be unable to receive a deadly wound.

[Col. 0630A] If Magdalene rejoices when she sees her beloved,

who had absolved her from her sin,

rejoice much more, Mother, when you see your Son,

in such a living body, now glorified.

I beseech you, Lady, and this Magdalene:

help me to contemplate Christ’s dreadful suffering,

so that I may have a serene conscience

and be full of love for God and neighbor.

[Col. 0629]

## THIRD APPENDIX. PRIVILEGES OF THE CHURCH OF LUCCA GRANTED IN THE TIME OF SAINT ANSELM BY COUNTESS MATILDA

(Ughelli, *Italia sacra*, I, 814.)

### I.

[Col. 0629B]

In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, the eternal God. In the year 1078 from his Incarnation, on the sixth day before the Kalends of October, in the second indiction.

It is established that I, Matilda, illustrious countess of Tuscany by the grace of God, of Lombard stock, widow of Gottifredus of good memory, duke, and daughter of Boniface of good memory, the great duke and margrave of Tuscany, because, on the part of the aforesaid husband of mine, who lived according to Salic law, I seem to live according to Salic law, have lifted from the ground with my own hands an inkpot, pen, and parchment, and have handed them over for writing to Rusticus, notary of the Lord Emperor, by means of a clod of earth [lacuna] and a knotted stick or branch of a tree, and by means of a knife and glove, together with a strip of bark, according to the custom of the Salian people.

Thus, by this charter, for the remedy of my soul [Col. 0629C] and for the remedy of the souls of the aforesaid Boniface, who was my father, and of the glorious Countess Beatrice, my mother, I offer to you, God, and to the episcopate of Saint Martin, which appears to have been built within the city of Lucca, namely, my whole portion of the mountain, hill, or castle called Decimo—the said mountain, hill, or castle with its court, tower, and houses situated within and above it, together with its circuit, foundations, and every building belonging to it. Of these I hold the fourth part; and I appear to offer to you, God, and to the aforesaid church of Saint Martin, my portion itself, whole and entire, and whatever pertains to me therefrom in any manner, with its lower and upper appurtenances, and with its additions and approaches.

[Col. 0629D] I offer it on this condition: from today, in the said church and episcopate of Saint Martin, and under the authority of the bishop who shall at the time be appointed and elected there, my aforesaid portion and the aforesaid properties that we offer to the said church and episcopate of Saint Martin shall be in his power—to have, hold, possess, administer, cause to be worked, and enjoy the usufruct of them. If necessary, the aforesaid bishop shall also have permission and authority to bring actions concerning them, make claims, give responses, settle matters in every way on behalf of the said church and episcopate of Saint Martin, and defend them with this charter of offering, as he may best be able according to law, for the remedy of my soul and for the remedy of the aforesaid Boniface, who was my father, and of the glorious Countess Beatrice, my mother.

It shall always remain stable, and if at any time I, the aforementioned Matilda, illustrious countess by the grace of God, or my heirs, should attempt to make any claim against you, God, and against the said church and episcopate of Saint Martin, or against the bishop who shall at that time be appointed and elected there, concerning the aforesaid portion of the aforesaid properties which we offer to the said church and episcopate, or should seek to reclaim or withdraw anything from it [Col. 0630B]—whether we ourselves, or anyone to whom we have given or may give it by any device—and should be unable to defend it, or fail to defend it, on behalf of the aforesaid episcopate against every person, then we shall pay to the aforesaid episcopate a penalty of twenty ounces of the finest gold and forty pounds of silver. Moreover, what I have offered to the aforesaid church shall be restored twofold, at that place, according to whatever valuation it then has.

And even then we shall neither be able nor permitted to dissolve or violate this charter; rather, this present charter of my offering shall remain firm and stable for all time, perpetually unshaken, supported by a stipulation.

Nevertheless, if you do not wish to seek or grant us the role of guarantors or defenders in this matter, you shall have permission, without our personal involvement, if it is your will, to bring actions concerning it, give responses, settle matters in every way, and defend the interests of the aforesaid church and episcopate of Saint Martin with this charter of my offering, in whatever manner you may best be able according to law.

[Col. 0630D] In this way, in this form, I, Matilda, handed this charter to you, Rusticus the notary, for writing, and asked you to write it.

Drawn up at the place called Saint Cyprian, near Perugia.

[Col. 0631A] I, Matilda, duke by the grace of God, in this charter made by me. Signed by Flacopertus, judge and envoy of the Lord Emperor; Ubertus, judge of the Lord Emperor; Gerardus, judge of the sacred palace. And the sign of the hand of Robert, son of Roland of good memory: I was present when asked. The sign of the hand of Roland, son of Alilardus of good memory: I was present when asked. Rusticus, notary of the Lord Emperor, completed and delivered this charter after it had been handed over.

### II.

In the name of the Lord our God Jesus Christ, the eternal God. In the year 1079 from his Incarnation, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of October, in the third indiction.

[Col. 0631B] I, Matilda, marchioness and duchess, widow of Gottifredus of good memory, who was duke, and daughter of Boniface of good memory, who was likewise duke and margrave, make this declaration.

I, the aforesaid Matilda, marchioness, profess that by my nationality I appear to live according to the law of the Lombards; but now, on the part of the aforesaid Gottifredus, who was my husband, I appear to live according to Salic law.

I, the aforesaid Matilda, marchioness and duchess, according to my Salic law, have lifted from the ground with my own hands an inkpot, pen, and parchment, and have handed them over for writing to Cunradus, notary of the Lord Emperor, by means of a clod of earth, a knotted stick or branch of a tree, and by means of a knife and glove, or strip of bark.

Thus, by this charter, according to my Salic law, I give, hand over, cede, and offer to you, God, and to the church and episcopate of Saint Martin, which has been built and raised within the city of Lucca near the wall of that city, namely, the house and court, or mountain, hill, and castle called Castallione Besardescos, situated within the county and territory of Volterra, together with the church there whose name is that of blessed Saint [lacuna], which is situated there, together with all the ditches, charcoal-burning sites, walls, and tower that appear to be within the aforesaid mountain, hill, or castle.

[Col. 0631C] Together with all the houses and farmsteads, or small homesteads, and likewise the lands and properties belonging to the aforesaid house and court, or mountain, hill, and church, both those within the wall of the said castle and those outside it; together with the houses and farmsteads, or small homesteads, and also the lands and properties themselves, both demesne and peasant holdings, with their foundations and all their buildings or every structure belonging to them, whether courts, gardens, lands, vineyards, olive groves, chestnut woods, oak woods, holm-oak brushwood, meadows, pastures, cultivated or uncultivated properties—everything and in every respect, both demesne and peasant holdings, wherever and under whatever names they may be, belonging to the aforesaid house and court, or mountain, hill, castle, or church.

[Col. 0631D] I offer all of it in full, with its lower and upper appurtenances, and with their additions and approaches, to you, God, and to the said church and episcopate of Saint Martin, and I undertake to give, hand over, and offer it on this condition:

From today, in the said church and episcopate of Saint Martin, and under the authority of the bishop who has been or shall be appointed there for the time being, these properties shall be in his power—to have, hold, govern, cause to be worked, and enjoy their usufruct. If it should be necessary, you shall have permission and authority to bring actions concerning them, make claims, give responses, settle matters in every way, and defend them on behalf of the said church and episcopate of Saint Martin with this charter of offering, as you may best be able according to law, for the remedy of my soul.

This shall remain stable forever. And if at any time I, the aforesaid Matilda, marchioness, or my heirs, should make any claim concerning the aforesaid house and court, or mountain, hill, castle, or church situated in the aforesaid castle of Castiglione, with its appurtenances and dependencies, against you, God, and the said church and episcopate of Saint Martin, and against the bishop who shall at that time be appointed there; or if we should seek to reclaim or withdraw anything from it [Col. 0632B]—whether we ourselves, or anyone to whom we have given or may give it by any device—and if by chance we should be unable to defend the property on behalf of the said church and episcopate of Saint Martin against every person, or should fail to defend it, we promise to purchase for you the aforesaid house and court, or mountain, hill, castle, church, lands, and properties that we have offered to the said church and episcopate of Saint Martin, restoring them twofold, at that place and according to whatever valuation they then have; and, in addition, to pay a penalty of fifty ounces of the finest gold and one hundred pounds of the finest silver.

[Col. 0632C] Even then we shall neither be able nor permitted to dissolve or violate this charter; rather, this present charter of my offering shall remain firm and stable for all time, perpetually unshaken, with a stipulation appended.

Nevertheless, if you do not wish to seek or grant us the role of guarantors or defenders in this matter, you shall have permission, without our personal involvement, if it is your will, to bring actions concerning it, give responses, settle matters in every way, and defend the property with this charter of offering, as you may best be able according to law.

And I, the aforesaid Matilda, marchioness, have relinquished and departed from it; I have placed the said church and episcopate of Saint Martin in possession of it as its property and delivered it for holding. I asked Cunradus, notary of the Lord Emperor, to write this charter of offering.

[Col. 0632D] Drawn up at the settlement called Bricole.

I, Matilda, by the grace of God, whatever I am, in this charter made by me. Signed by Ubertus, judge of the Lord Emperor. I, Ardericus, judge, was present as a witness when asked. The sign of the hand of Federighus, count living according to Salic law, son of the late Lodoicus, who was duke; and of Enrichus, son of the late Eurardus, who likewise lived according to Salic law: I was present when asked. The sign of the hand of Anselmus, living according to Salic law, son of Gerbotta of good memory, who likewise lived according to Salic law: I was present when asked. The sign of the hand of Paganus, son of Rotandus of good memory, and of Idelbrandus, son of the aforesaid Paganus: I was present when asked. The sign of the hand of Enrighus, son of Sigifridus of good memory: I was present when asked. [Col. 0633A] Cunradus, notary of the Lord Emperor, completed and delivered this charter after it had been handed over.

[Col. 0634A] In the year of the Lord 1086. Udalricus, Cluniacensian monk.

[Col. 0633]

## NOTICE FOR THE FOLLOWING COLLECTION: THE AGE, HOMELAND, BIRTH, AND DEEDS OF UDALRICUS

(From Acherius, *Spicilegium*, vol. I, p. 639.)

In bringing to light the ancient Customs of the abbey of Cluny, I used two copies. One, bearing five hundred years of age, had been sent to me in 1650 by Nicolaus Camuzatius, formerly a canon of the Church of Troyes; the other was supplied by the Cluniac monastery, written in a more recent hand.

From the first I had managed to transcribe only as far as half of chapter 9 of the third book, since I was not permitted to keep it longer. I hoped, naturally, that if these Customs were ever to be published, another copy of the manuscript would once again be made available to me. But my hope was vain: although I used every diligence, both through my own letters and through those of friends and their requests, the copy could nowhere be found—especially in the library at Troyes of the Congregation of the Oratory, where I had certainly heard that it was preserved.

The author of these Customs is identified as Udalricus, distinguished alike by nobility and holiness. Of his life, here are a few details relevant to our subject:

“Udalricus, a venerable man of illustrious Bavarian descent, from the city of Regensburg, shone among all the members of his family as Lucifer among the other stars of the heavens, displaying a noble form, and so forth.”

And after much intervening material:

“He first, at the request of the most reverend abbot William of the monastery of Hirsau, introduced the Customs of the Church of Cluny into the monasteries of Alamannia. Many lovers of monastic religion observe and embrace them with such zeal and reverence as though they were rejoicing to possess royal riches. On these matters he composed two booklets in eloquent language—Udalricus says three—whose text spread far and wide through the monasteries of Alamannia and of other regions.

“If you should happen to read them, you will find written there certain rules of divine service and of other duties, as well as rules of obedience, humility, and fraternal charity. You will also be able clearly to recognize there the diligence, intelligence, and wisdom of the man. For he was a learned householder in the kingdom of heaven, bringing forth new and old from his treasure; hence he instructed many in knowledge, and so forth.”

Nevertheless, anyone who reads them will readily see that Udalricus did not compose these Customs at the time when he collected them, but that they had already been received in practice for many generations, so that there is no need to confirm the point. For this reason I have not hesitated to call them “ancient.” I know of other Customs issued later by the venerable Abbot Peter, to remedy the behavior of certain monks who had fallen into disorder; they can be seen in the Cluniac Library.

Although these regulations chiefly concern monks, many things will nevertheless be found in them that contribute substantially to clarifying ecclesiastical duties and to the proper performance of the divine mysteries—for example, the prescriptions concerning the august sacrifice of the Mass, the sacrament of Extreme Unction, the preparation of hosts to be consecrated at the altar with the greatest care and singular reverence, and other observances for rendering canonical praises to God by day and by night.

Nor should I omit the brief note that I attached to chapter 35, “On the Blessing of Grapes and Other Fruits,” to explain these words: “He presents the grapes to the sacristan, and the sacristan presents them to the priest during the Canon at the suitable and prescribed time,” and so forth.

The note reads as follows:

“Namely, at these words of the Canon: ‘Through whom, Lord, you always create all these good things,’ and so forth. At that time the faithful offered new fruits, grapes, beans, and other things of this kind, which the priest blessed upon the altar.

“Durandus, bishop of Mende, gives the same interpretation in book IV, chapter 46, number 8, of his *Rationale*, where he explains the passage of the Canon cited immediately above in these words: ‘At this place grapes are blessed,’ and so forth. For it was an ancient custom, still practiced in certain churches, to consecrate the first fruits to God, so that the faithful people might thereby profess and venerate him as the supreme creator of all things, give him thanks for the benefits bestowed upon them, and, enjoying those fruits with heavenly blessing, be enriched by them.

“This was done, moreover, by institution of Pope Eutychianus, as reported in the *Pontifical* of Damasus (Hugo Menard, in the *Book of the Sacramentary of Saint Gregory*, p. 173): ‘He instituted that fruits, beans, and grapes should be blessed at the altar,’ as is also recorded in the *Martyrologies* of Rabanus and Notker. The Council of Carthage III, canon 3, mentions grain and grapes; so too does the Council in Trullo, canon 28, and Burchard’s *Decretum*, book V, chapters 3 and 4.

“To state my own view here, it is very plausible that the words of the Canon may be explained as follows: ‘Through whom, Lord, you always create, sanctify, enliven, and bestow upon us all these good things,’ and so forth. That is: through your Son, without whom nothing that has been made was made, you continually create and produce for our good and benefit these fruits that we now offer to you and ask to have blessed by you. But concerning this interpretation, let the judgment belong to the reader.”

Another manuscript of the same Customs, compiled by Bernard, a Cluniac monk, and dedicated to Blessed Hugh, the abbot, supplied several chapters missing from both the Cluniac manuscript and the copy of Camuzatius—namely, chapters 13, 14, and 15.

So that Bernard’s preface might not wholly be lost, I think it will not be unwelcome to the reader, nor out of place here, to append a passage from it. Bernard begins as follows:

“To the most reverend lord and foremost father of the whole religious life, Lord Hugh, abbot: Brother Bernard, the last of his sons, offers whatever can be more excellent in being, speech, or thought.

“Since, Father most devoted to religion, those of Cluny were gradually entering the way of all flesh and novices were succeeding them, controversies very often arose concerning certain Customs, with different people holding different opinions, so that the novices, hearing these things, frequently left the chapter more uncertain than when they had entered, I judged it worthwhile—if your authority should command me—to investigate the truth itself with whatever diligence I could, and, whether from what I found written or from what I had learned or could learn, to gather into one volume the truer and more discerning opinions, namely, those for which more trustworthy persons, better acquainted with the order, could give testimony. In this way I would leave to posterity an examined equity, carefully recorded in writing.

“Thus, in this little work, I fulfill the command received from you according to the measure of my smallness; like a little stream returning to its source, I present to Your Excellence what I have drawn from its fullness, and so forth. Only this remains: may your prayer come to my aid, so that I may follow what I praise in you and may be strong enough to keep the way that you show and have ordered me to describe, for my salvation and your glory.

“I beg our brothers not to disdain drinking the water of truth from a wooden vessel, nor, because it flows through a leaden pipe, to despise the clear, cold water, should they happen to be thirsty. Let them learn upon which judgments they ought to rely, so that they may not depart from the path of the holy Customs.

“May almighty God, in whose hand rests all the progress of the place of Cluny, preserve your holy head safe and sound for us, so that you may see your children’s children and for a long time provide consolation to the world.”

Thus far Bernard’s preface. He was a contemporary of Udalricus and, as may be conjectured, wrote the Customs at the same time as Udalricus himself.

The reason why we have published Udalricus’s collection rather than Bernard’s is obvious: the greater renown of Udalricus’s name, and the fact that we judged his collection to have been arranged in a more polished style and better order—namely, in dialogues. This manner of writing, especially when ascetic matters or rites are concerned, instructs and persuades the mind by an easier path.

[Col. 0635]

## ANCIENT CUSTOMS OF THE MONASTERY OF CLUNY, COLLECTED BY UDALRICUS, BENEDICTINE MONK

(Acherius, *Spicilegium*, vol. I, p. 641.)

## DEDICATORY LETTER

[Col. 0635A]

To the most reverend and most devout Father, Lord William, abbot of Hirsau, and to the holy community of brothers subject to him, Brother Udalricus, an insignificant monk of the Church of Cluny, sends greetings in the Lord and his swiftest blessing, both in this life and in the future.

To remember every day both you personally and your Church, dearest Father, has truly become so habitual to my humility that now neither habit nor affection permits a single day to pass without it.

At times there also comes to me a most welcome and pleasant memory of your promise concerning the precautions to be taken against the ingenuity of certain secular men. These men, caring little about anything except this temporal life, after they have, so to speak, filled their house with sons and daughters—or if one of them should be lame or maimed, somewhat deaf or blind, hunchbacked or leprous, or afflicted with anything else of this kind that makes him in some way less acceptable to the world—offer such a child to God with the greatest eagerness, so that he may become a monk, although plainly not for God’s sake, but only so that they themselves may be rid of the burden of raising and feeding him, or so that greater provision may be made for their other children.

Therefore, to say nothing of those who are not lacking in bodily health and integrity of limb, consider what is often perpetrated by those who are half-human or half-alive in this way. If it were useful, it would be easy to name one whom no sanctity except the disgrace of a scrofulous swelling drew to the habit of holiness, and another whom nothing but a foot [lacuna]—from neither of whom, as you too can testify, came much good example.

How much less can anything be expected from those who enjoy good health, wherever so many of them have been gathered, and possess such power that the condition of the monastery lies in their hands? Everyone knows what sort of life is lived there and what vigor the regular discipline possesses, if indeed they know that such a class of monks reigns there.

It has become so familiar and customary that, if any strictness of this spiritual warfare can exist amid the dregs of our times, it exists only where there is a greater number and greater authority of those who, neither at a frivolous age nor through parental command, but of their own will and at a more mature age, [Col. 0637A] under Christ alone as their commander, have withdrawn from worldly affairs and devoted themselves to his service.

Since you have weighed this with prudence, although you yourself were brought up in a monastery, and although it sometimes happens that a lily blossoms from among thorns, nevertheless, caring for nothing so much as what contributes to caution and the genuine stability of religion, you have promulgated this law of your monastery through the mercy of God: the secular persons mentioned above must provide themselves with another nest in which to place their abortive offspring, as though disinherited.

With God watching, that familiar practice of theirs will here achieve nothing further: namely, as the prophet says, they will no longer thrust and entrust “the eggs of vipers, and what, when brooded over, breaks out into a basilisk” (Isaiah 59) upon pious souls dedicated to God, abusing them indeed as their servants and [Col. 0637B] nurses. Let each person think what he wishes about this matter; I, however, am certain that you have uprooted from the foundations that root from which alone, above all, all the monasteries that have been destroyed—whether in the Teutonic or in the Roman language—were destroyed.

Therefore, to confess what is true: because I saw you guarded by that prerogative of pious solicitude and devoted to regular discipline, although, if I wished you well, I could do nothing further that would be of any value, except, as is fitting, for the one whose name I have truly professed, there is no one else of your name and office whom my smallness could more readily favor and honor in every way. For there are also other matters that not undeservedly commend both you and this house of God very greatly.

First, because you have excluded the weaker sex from your dwelling—something that was not formerly the case—or have been fortunate enough to have such servants in daily attendance who, born free and of free parents, voluntarily humble themselves and serve you, expecting no other life than that which is heavenly and eternal. Concerning these, however, there is one thing which, if it seemed good to your benevolence, I would wish to change soon. I would certainly wish that they no longer be permitted to remain outside the cloister; you should give them our habit. And because they are not capable of serving as readers or singers together with the educated, they should carry living vines upon living elms, so to speak, as has been said to some extent, so that, just as by serving the educated they have done until now, they might attain the reward of the educated.

For if Blessed Benedict thought it appropriate that the brothers should take turns performing the kitchen duty, this duty too is found among the holy Fathers: once they had entered the kitchen, they continued thereafter in that same obedience. But if some brother, perhaps not possessing such faith as to move mountains (1 Corinthians 12), complains that you do not have sufficient resources to gather so many monks, see what God is doing through a certain Gerard of ours, born indeed of parents who were not of the highest nobility and not so well instructed in letters that many are not more learned than he; yet I know no man of such faith.

Nor would I readily judge that a greater miracle could occur than that which God continually works through him. It is not yet thirty years since, founding and building a cell in the very village of his birth, he named it Saint Mary at Charity. Since it lies on a public road, no mortal passes by who deliberately feigns not to notice, but rather experiences that saying of Gregory: guests are not only to be invited but also drawn in (Gregory, Homily 3 on the Gospels).

At present, however, it never happens in the cloister that somewhat more than a hundred brothers are not found there each day. For nearly four years it had not been convenient for the lord abbot to visit that same cell. This year he came and, in one day, gave our habit or blessing to fifty-five novices, although every year the prior had sent as many as he could to the memory of the holy apostles for the blessing.

When, on that occasion, he invited the lord abbot, if I were to recount to your charity how little grain he had, and yet with what generosity he supplied it for [lacuna] weeks, not only to us but also to all who arrived in the meantime and who flocked from every direction to hear the lord abbot, as though to some spectacle, however much confidence you may have in me, I do not know whether you would be able fully to believe the whole story.

This, however, I certainly do not lie about: as much as I have received from both places, [lacuna] the possessions of the abbey—apart from the vineyards alone—are twice as extensive. But D. G. is such a man that, if necessity should require it, he is not at all afraid to borrow as much as three or four thousand solidi.

And how could divine clemency ever abandon one who presumes upon Him, when it once again plainly sends ravens to Elijah to provide the support of temporal life? (1 Kings 17.) For what else should I call the Franks, since they are so restless, predatory, and possess nothing of the brightness of virtue? Yet among them there are sometimes men who give so generously to a faithful servant of God that within a very short time he pays off whatever he owes.

It is also familiar to him, and almost a game, to wish that he might never happen to abound greatly in the riches of this world. If the count and protector of your place knew that you were such debtors, I do not think he would in any way dare to be importunate with you; and, if his pious and religious wife added her advice, if he gave you nothing, he would also take nothing from you.

Far be it from anyone to believe that God is confined to a locality, so that what He does in Francia He cannot also do in the territory of Speyer! May His mercy be with you to such an extent that He who tests the reins and hearts may also see here that He is obeyed in His will and commandments with such simplicity and no less devotion.

What you entrusted to my smallness concerning this matter—you can see that I have not neglected it. For you have the customs of our monastery, which I have noted, however inadequately, as much as I was able to know and remember. Once you have seen them, if afterward you put aside the sheets and take no further care of them, why then did you impose so much labor upon me? I was compelled to mention this by the negligence of others, whom I knew at first to be extremely curious but in the end to have acted in precisely this way.

There are many things which I mentioned because of their connection with other matters, although it is not necessary that they be mentioned in the brothers’ assembly. But concerning those matters by which souls can be edified and merits increased, you, Father, will confer with the brothers. Let them consider their ancient customs; let them consider yours, with which it happened that you were formed; let them consider these as well; and from everything that appears better, let one body be formed which may henceforth be observed.

And if you wish this to be ratified, it is expedient that it be secured beforehand by the common consent of the brothers, lest from it [lacuna] or something prompted by ill will arise. And since God has commanded the lord P., who now resides with us, it is not inappropriate that a man of such knowledge and religion should take part in this business. If I were present, I too would not allow my name to be entirely [f., altogether] [Col. 0639B] concealed, although I may still appear to be a novice.

Remember that in the very words I wrote down, I made the two of us converse in this way because, if you recall, we spoke much with one another about the matter. And if I seem to have added anything, this too was uttered only by your mouth and your tongue, because not merely our tongue but my entire self belongs to you—not to mention that Christ has so joined us in the unity of the Spirit, in the one body that is the Church, under the one head, who is Himself.

But since my person is insignificant and obscure, my name barbarous, and my style rustic, it seemed unworthy of me ever to have mentioned a name of this kind or to have prefixed any preface, as is customary. Although this collection, whatever its quality, has three parts, and I prefixed to each of them certain clauses that imitate a prologue, I did so chiefly for your sake and for that of our other brothers, among whom I could not willingly remain silent about the good examples I had seen.

The first part concerns the divine office and what is chiefly done in the Church throughout the whole year; the second, the instruction of novices; the third, the obediences, to which the final obedience has also been added, by which each of the brothers who is about to depart from this world is called to Christ.

I took care to preface the individual sentences with chapter headings solely for the benefit of readers, so that each person may more easily find whatever he wishes. I greet most warmly the holy household of Christ over which you appear to preside—not, as the saying goes, merely along the road, but truly with the wish and desire of salvation, which I most faithfully wish for them.

In particular, I greet the particular friends of my smallness: the lord and master A., the lord S., the lord O., the lord G., and the still novice of Christ, the lord E. May the grace of almighty God be with you all. Amen.

## Prologue

[Col. 0643]

[Col. 0643A] The author relates the occasion for writing down the customs.

A few days ago our senior, the lord abbot, sent my humility to Germany. It is not important now to report why; what concerns the matter is that, on this occasion, I turned aside to the venerable man, the lord William, abbot, whose monastery is situated in the county of Speyer and in the forest called the Black Forest.

Since this Father had known me from boyhood and was very fond of me, he received me joyfully when he saw me; and, although I was making for another destination, he compelled me, like another Cleopas (Luke 24), to remain with him for several days. Meanwhile he spoke with me constantly—indeed, as far as possible, almost without interruption—about the customs of our Church. He began to speak of them as follows:

“Your Church, dearest brother, through the mercy of God, has acquired no small reputation for religious observance in our regions. We judge that there is no other like it, in life and regular discipline, among those places that have come within our knowledge. [Col. 0644A] Therefore you do much to fulfill our desire if, through your report, we are deemed worthy to hear something about the practices and institutions of your elders.

“Even if these things are not practiced by us, the mere fact that we are not unaware that you live and conduct yourselves in such a way as our weakness either would not wish or could not achieve is itself an edification in humility.”

To this I replied: “Since I am going to eat your bread, it is only right that in the meantime I should not be unprepared to obey your wishes. But one who is in such a place, almost a barbarian because of the difference of language, and who was not raised from childhood there, cannot easily know everything in the way that a native does, one who has grown up among such things from infancy. Therefore it is not surprising if I too know little about matters of this sort, since until nearly [Col. 0644B] the thirtieth year of my age I cared greatly only for worldly affairs.

“Nevertheless, I will willingly report whatever I know. So see what you wish to ask about first.”

## Book One

[Col. 0643]

## Chapter One. How Both Testaments Are Read

[Col. 0643B] **Question.** “I hear that your readings in winter and on weekdays are very long. If you please, explain all at once how both Testaments are read, not only in winter but also in summer.”

[Col. 0643C] **Answer.** “To begin with the most ancient of all the books, namely the Octateuch: this book, as is the general custom, is appointed for reading in Septuagesima both in our Church and in other Churches. On that Sunday the lessons are quite short, except that the entire prologue of *Desiderii mei* is used for the first lesson.

“During the following nights the readings are extended so that Genesis is read through in that one week, and in the church only. In Sexagesima, Exodus is begun, and together with the other volumes that are read, both are read in the church and in the refectory, so that wherever the reading ends, there the beginning is always made on the following day. If not earlier, then certainly upon the beginning of Lent, the Octateuch is read through completely; from it, however, lessons for Sundays are excepted. [Col. 0643D]

“On the other nights of Lent, the exposition of Saint Augustine on the Psalter is read, especially on the Songs of Ascents; and just as the nights then grow shorter and shorter, so too do the readings. Care must nevertheless be taken that they never become so short that the brother who makes the circuit with the covered lamp cannot walk through the entire choir and outside it, investigating whether anyone may perhaps have fallen asleep during the reading.

[Col. 0644B] “During the Passion of the Lord, the prophet Jeremiah is read; his prologue again serves for the first lesson. It is read in the church only, and in such a way that before Maundy Thursday it is finished up to the Lamentations.

“During the octave of Easter, the Acts of the Apostles are read, and only for one week; because of the shortness of the nights, it is not possible to read much. Afterward, for two weeks, the Apocalypse and the canonical Epistles are read up to the Ascension of the Lord. The Acts of the Apostles are then appointed again and read again, as though they had not previously been begun, from the beginning through Pentecost.

“Nevertheless, these same volumes are also read continuously and in their entirety in the refectory, as are, at their proper times, the Book of Kings, the Book of Solomon, the Book of Job, Tobit, Judith, Esther, Ezra, and the Book of Maccabees. All these are read in the refectory only, and not in the church, except insofar as brief excerpts from them are taken for any given Sunday.

“From the Kalends of November, the readings for weekdays are begun again. The prophet Ezekiel is appointed to be read in the church only, and is finished according to custom before the feast of Saint Martin. Although we celebrate his octave with singing and other solemn observances, the prophetic readings are not changed, nor are they changed during other octaves unless there are twelve lessons.

“The prophet Daniel and the twelve prophets are appointed, but they are not sufficient unless, as the final reading, something from the homilies of blessed Pope Gregory on Ezekiel is added.

“In Advent, the prophet Isaiah is appointed. When I was asking about him and wished to know with certainty on how many nights he too was customarily read through, I could hear no answer from anyone, except what I myself remember having seen and heard. Once, in my hearing, he was read through during six weekdays. [Col. 0645A]

“He is followed by the letters of Pope Leo on the Incarnation of the Lord and by other sermons of the holy Fathers, especially those of Saint Augustine.

“The Apostle is appointed on the Sunday that first occurs after the Feast of the Holy Innocents, provided that the Circumcision of the Lord or the Deposition of the lord Odilo does not fall on that Sunday. Concerning this I can say the same thing as above concerning the prophet, for different people have different opinions. But to testify again to what I myself saw, an Epistle such as the one to the Romans was read in its entirety during two weekdays.

“And when a certain brother who had finished the readings had brought them to an earlier conclusion, he was prohibited from doing so in chapter by our elders.

“If it happens that the Apostle is finished before Septuagesima, the exposition of John Chrysostom on the Epistle to the Hebrews is read. [Col. 0645B]

“There: I have in a manner made the circuit of the year. If you please, let us proceed further.”

## Chapter Two. Concerning Nocturns and All the Regular Hours, and Whether Anything Has Been Added to Them Beyond What Saint Benedict Established

[Col. 0645B] **Question.** “Do you usually weave anything additional into nocturns or the other hours beyond what Saint Benedict established?”

[Col. 0645C] **Answer.** “As far as I can, if I remember correctly, I will say. First, there is no antiphon so short that we do not finish it with the complete conclusion of its tone.

“What prayers Saint Benedict said after the Lord’s Prayer is unknown, since it is not found in writing. But the prayers said by us at nocturns, at matins, at terce, sext, none, and vespers are contained in fourteen versicles. If it is a weekday, with no octaves or Easter days, Psalm 50 is inserted.

“Four other psalms are added at matins and vespers, and two at compline. I have not discovered why this difference was instituted by our elders. For when four psalms beginning at nocturns are said for our departed relatives after each hour except compline, at matins and vespers they are said amid the prayers, before the final versicle, before the brothers rise from their forms and the collect is said.

“Since I remember these psalms once and for all, let me also specify them by name, so as not to delay. The first of the nocturns is, so to speak, accompanied by the first of the seven penitential psalms, and the others are likewise divided in their proper order, one being assigned to each hour. At terce, however, Psalm 50, otherwise so frequently used, is replaced by Psalm 56.

“In second place are assigned Psalms 19, 85, 22, 12, 66, 78, and 83, in this way, with pairs prefixed. In third place Psalm 69 always follows all the hours; and for the faithful departed, Psalm 141, which is still preceded after prime by Psalm 50 for our deceased abbots.

“At compline, amid the prayers, as has been said, Psalm 50 is followed again by Psalms 69, 12, and 120.

“But to return to what I briefly interrupted, and also to recall the first prayers of compline: after the Lord’s Prayer and the Apostles’ Creed have been said, there are thirty-one versicles at prime, and the confession is inserted in its proper place. At compline there are seventeen.

“On weekdays in Advent and Lent, at matins and vespers, they reach as many as twenty versicles.

“However, this diversity of prayers, and any other matters of this kind, can, if you wish, be noted separately for you on a single sheet, so that there is no need to linger over them at greater length now.

“I do not remember whether anything additional is inserted at any regular hour on any weekday that does not in some way belong to a solemnity.”

## Chapter Three. Concerning the Psalmody Customarily Said Apart from the Regular Hours

[Col. 0646B] **Question.** “I ask you to set out everything that you recite in the community apart from the regular hours.”

[Col. 0646B] **Answer.** “This is certainly longer and more varied in Lent than at any other time; and what I am now going to say I shall give chiefly according to the order observed during Lent itself.

“On all its weekdays, we precede nocturns with the psalmody from Psalm 119 through the end of the Psalter. After the four psalms that properly follow nocturns, as stated above, a procession is made to the church of Saint Mary. During the procession two psalms are sung, namely Psalms 84 and 86, followed by one antiphon and a collect.

“Matins of All Saints are celebrated. Likewise, matins for the faithful departed. [Col. 0646C] Everyone is to see that the psalmody ‘O God, with our ears’ is sung; Psalm 78 and Psalm 93 belong with it.

“The fifteen Songs of Ascents are sung, and after the Lord’s Prayer, before the collects that follow, Psalm 89; and for the faithful departed, Psalm 22.

“If the thirtieth day of a recently deceased brother is being observed, Psalms 5, 6, 114, 115, 129, 141, and 142 are said for him.

[Col. 0646D] “It is found in the Rule that Saint Benedict commands something to be added in Lent to the measure of the customary service. We do not conceal this either. At matins and vespers, after the suffrages of the saints, and at the other hours after the four psalms that, so to speak, are appended to the hours, we prostrate ourselves bodily and say two psalms: the first from the seven penitential psalms, the second from the fifteen Songs of Ascents.

“At vespers, however, four are said consecutively, because it is not customary for any psalm ever to be said aloud after compline, except when someone who knows the psalms recites Psalms 12, 42, 66, 126, and 129 while the boys pray in silence.

“The Creed of the faith, namely the Quicumque, written by Saint Athanasius—although some Churches do not remember it except on Sunday—is not omitted on any day without being said by us. On weekdays it is said together with the other psalms; on Sunday, after the prayers.

“After prime, in addition to the psalms I have already mentioned above, the seven penitential psalms also follow. After the litany, which is to be said at that same time, and before the collects that follow, [Col. 0647A] four psalms are inserted: Psalms 69, 120, 122, and, for the faithful departed, Psalm 42.

“After the chapter for the departed whose anniversary has been announced in that chapter, the same psalms are said as are to be said for the thirtieth day of any deceased person, except that Psalm 141 is omitted on that occasion.

[Note: [Col. 0647D] “For thirty”: he meant to say “for the thirtieth day after death.”]

“After regular vespers and after the psalms said by those who are prostrate, another procession is made to the church of Saint Mary, with its own canticle as well. Just as matins are celebrated for All Saints and for the faithful departed, so also are vespers.

“After supper, we return to the church with Psalm 50, just as we always do after dinner. After waiting for the servants until they too have risen from the table, [Col. 0647B] the office is celebrated—the office commonly called by our people the vigil. At one time, when there were not so many dead, it used to be performed with only three lessons and responsories, unless the anniversary of some brother occurred.

“Now, however, since no day is without many dead, this office is never performed except with nine lessons, together with the responsories and collects that follow the office. Two psalms precede it, namely Psalms 119 and 3, just as Psalms 145 and 123 precede vespers. At matins: ‘Out of the depths’ and ‘How long?’

“Thus, as far as I remember, there is no more psalmody in use among us than this.”

## Chapter Four. For What Reasons and in What Manner the Psalmody Is Reduced at Different Times

[Col. 0647C] “Moreover, its total is reduced now because Lent has ended, now in summer because of the shortness of the nights, now on Easter days and during octaves, now because there are twelve lessons.

“First, those two psalms said by the prostrate are never said except in Lent. From Maundy Thursday until the Kalends of November, or whenever any octaves are celebrated during that winter period, only the fifteen Songs of Ascents are said before nocturns.

“Likewise, not only on days with twelve lessons but also on all octave days and Easter days, the individual hours are followed only by these two psalms, Psalms 69 and 141.

[Col. 0647D] “If, during Lent itself, a feast requiring twelve lessons should occur, the psalmody used on the aforementioned days remains, as does the office for the dead; for them, however, both vespers and the nocturnal matins lessons are said. That psalmody, ‘O God, with our ears,’ is not omitted, nor are the seven penitential psalms after prime together with the litany.

“Nevertheless, because it is Lent, the psalms that remain are supplied after the chapter, and in their place thirty psalms are sung from the beginning of the Psalter, with ‘Glory be to the Father’ inserted after terce.

“After terce, since Mass for the feast itself immediately follows, at sext and thereafter at the remaining hours we ask pardon and repeat the entire psalmody as [Col. 0648A] on any other ordinary weekday in Lent, although at the hours we say no antiphons, versicles, or collects other than those of the feast itself.

“The office also remains. Concerning it, I have almost forgotten to say that after each hour Psalms 119, 69, and 141 are said; the middle one is uncertain.

“For our elders, at the time when the office was not celebrated at night in the manner in which it is celebrated in winter, did not omit to perform that office after supper on Sundays and on other days when twelve lessons were given, lest two offices remain for one solemn day. When Saint Majolus saw that this was especially burdensome for the brothers on such a day, he prescribed, in place of that office, that Psalms 119 and 141 be said after each hour.

“But to bring to a conclusion what I proposed here concerning the psalmody: on Sundays and on other feasts outside Lent that require twelve lessons, there is nothing further to say about such a diversity of psalms, apart from [Col. 0648B] the fifteen Songs of Ascents; matins and vespers for All Saints; those psalms for the thirtieth day and anniversary of the brothers; two psalms after each hour; and, if a third is added for the reason given above, this occurs only in summer.

“For from the Kalends of November until Septuagesima the office for the dead is properly performed only at night, and only that night which belongs to Sunday is without the office.”

## Chapter Five. Concerning the Collects and Versicles That Follow the Psalmody, and the Length of the Litany

[Col. 0648C]

**Question.** “I am glad, therefore, to hear that, just as you informed me above about the psalmody, so now you will also set out in order the collects and the versicles preceding the collects, without which such extensive psalmody, divided into so many parts, does not end. You should also add something about the litany that follows prime: how long and how extensive it is.”

[Col. 0648C] **Answer.** “To oblige you, and according to the same order I have followed up to now: first, before nocturns, only the fifteen Songs of Ascents are said. The first five are said for our brothers and all the faithful departed; another five for ourselves; the final five for kings and all our relatives who are still living.

“After the Lord’s Prayer has been said, a versicle and collect follow each [Col. 0648D] division. At the first: ‘From the gate of hell,’ etc. ‘Absolve, O Lord, the souls of your servants, our brothers,’ etc.

“At the second: the versicle, ‘Remember us, O Lord, in the favor you show your people’; and ‘Remember,’ etc. The collect: ‘O God, to whom it belongs.’

“At the third: the versicle, ‘O Lord, save the kings; save the male and female servants.’ The collect: ‘Stretch forth, O Lord,’ etc.

“But if it extends to the end of the Psalter, only the places of the divisions change, not the collects; then the first reaches Psalm 129 and the second Psalm 139.

“For the four psalms that follow each hour, these versicles are always said: [Col. 0649A] ‘O Lord, save the kings; save your male and female servants. Let there be peace in your strength. From the gate of hell.’ And one of these collects:

‘Almighty and everlasting God, have mercy on your male and female servants’;  
‘Direct, we ask, O Lord, your male and female servants’;  
‘Grant, we ask, O Lord, to your male and female servants’;  
‘Stretch forth, O Lord.’

“To each of these is further added: ‘And grant your peace in our times’; and ‘May the souls of your servants rest in peace.’

“For prime alone, however, since Psalm 50 is then sung for our deceased abbots, it is customary to alter the wording for them as follows: ‘Be favorable to us, we ask, O Lord,’ etc.

“Whenever the first two of the four psalms that follow each hour are omitted—as on every Sunday, on a feast with twelve lessons, [Col. 0649B] on all octave days, from the Nativity of the Lord until Epiphany, and during Eastertide—one of the versicles given above is also omitted, namely, ‘O Lord, save the kings.’

“Concerning Saint Mary: the versicle and collect are ‘After childbirth’; ‘Your grace’; ‘O God, who from the blessed Mary,’ etc. If another wording is preferred, provided it is in use, no one objects.

“In Advent there is another versicle, namely, ‘Blessed are you among,’ etc.

“At matins of All Saints, neither the chapter nor the collect is ever changed, and the same is true at vespers. The chapter is: ‘We know that for those who love God,’ etc. The collect: ‘Make us, we ask, O Lord, of blessed Mary,’ etc.

“At matins of All Saints, after the Lord’s Prayer, the versicles are: ‘After childbirth’; ‘In the sight of the angels’; ‘Most greatly honored’; [Col. 0649C] ‘The saints shall exult’; ‘Your priests shall be clothed’; ‘They shall be brought to the King, virgins’; ‘Rise up, O Lord, help.’”

At the Office of Matins for the Dead, these collects are said: “O God, to whom it belongs”; “Grant, O Lord, we beseech you, that the soul”; “Almighty and everlasting God, to whom nothing ever”; “O God, giver of forgiveness”; “O God, by whose mercy”; “We beseech you, O Lord, by your perpetual goodness”; “O God of all the faithful.” The first is for brothers recently deceased, for whom seven offices are generally to be performed in the community; the second for an anniversary recited in chapter; the third for all our deceased relatives and dependants; the fourth for deceased brothers; the fifth for all buried in our place; the sixth for our sisters and other women among our relatives and dependants; the seventh for all the faithful departed. In summer, and at the time when the office is not performed during the night, whenever twelve lessons are read from these materials, in the Office of Matins for the Dead that follows immediately, the first and second collects are omitted, because these Matins are not preceded by the office, nor are they assigned to an individual anniversary or to the recently deceased, but chiefly to our relatives and dependants, for whom the first collect is also to be said. An anniversary, however, postponed until the following day or until it is properly convenient, is then duly celebrated.

At the psalmody: “O God, with our ears”; the verses: “Show us your mercy”; “Be for us a tower of strength”; “Remember your congregation”; “O Lord, save the kings”; “Save your servants”; “Let there be peace in your power”; “From the gate of hell.” The collects are: “O God, from whom holy desires”; “Almighty and everlasting God”; “Stretch forth, O Lord”; “Absolve, O Lord, the souls”; “Almighty God, who are the God of the living.” At the psalms for a thirtieth-day commemoration, the collect “Absolve” is said.

After the regular Matins we commemorate certain saints with antiphons, verses, and collects, since it is customary for us to call these the suffrages of the angels and saints: first, of the holy cross; of the holy angels; of Saint John the Baptist; of Saints Peter and Paul; of the other apostles; of the holy martyrs; of Saint Martin; of Saint Benedict; of the holy Fathers together, Odo, Majolus, and Odilo; and finally of the confessors. The following verses come after the two psalms said by those prostrate: “O Lord, do not remember”; “Help us, O God”; “O Lord, not according to”; “Show us”; “And let there come upon.” Then follows the brief collect, “Our voice, O Lord, is,” and so forth. Several similar collects are found in the collectary; and at the end “And to recall the benefits” and so forth is always added.

At each Hour, except at Matins and Vespers, just as there is nothing intervening between the four psalms mentioned above, appended to the Hours, and these two psalms, so also the verses and collects of both groups are joined together. At Vespers, these psalms precede those of the canticles, as they do in the book of psalms itself.

The Litany begins as follows: “Kyrie, eleison; Christ, eleison; Christ, hear us,” and so forth. Thereafter approximately seventy-three saints are named. The following forty-three verses are intended for the actual divine invocation. Those which precede the collects after the Lord’s Prayer and after the other psalms are as follows: “And let there come upon.” Thereafter they are the same as those said at the psalmody, “O God, with our ears,” except for this one alone: “Let us pray for the faithful departed.”

The collects are: “O God, to whom it belongs”; “Almighty and everlasting”; “O God, who do”; “Stretch forth, O Lord, your servants”; “O God, from whom holy desires”; “From Easter until the feast of Saint Michael,” against storms, the psalms “You have blessed” and “From your house”; “Absolve, O Lord”; “O God, who are the wondrous splendor of the saints.” Sometimes other collects are added, if it seems appropriate and if the need arises for a particular cause.

At the anniversary psalms, after the chapter, the collect for deceased brothers is “Grant, O Lord, we beseech you, that the souls,” and so forth. For relatives and dependants: “Absolve, O Lord.” Hence, if at some time during Lent thirty psalms are said on account of a feast, these verses and collects follow them: “Show us, O Lord”; “Let your mercy be upon us”; “Save your servants”; “Send them help, O Lord.” For the faithful departed: “Eternal rest”; “O God, to whom it belongs”; “Stretch forth, O Lord”; “Absolve, O Lord”; “Almighty and everlasting God, who are the God of the living.”

At Vespers for All Saints, the chapter is “The saints through faith.” The collect is “Almighty God, us your servants.” At Vespers for the Dead, the same collects are to be said as at Matins, and likewise at the office. Yet if the office that follows happens to have more collects than the preceding Matins, because of the circumstances mentioned above, they are also to be used at Vespers.

Concerning the office, this must be understood: if a brief commemoration for a deceased person occurs in such a way that it is held before None, only three collects are to be said. The first is the one customarily said for relatives and dependants; the second is for the brothers of our congregation; the third is for all the faithful departed. For this reason the customary office is not to be omitted if the time and day are such that it can properly be performed after Vespers.

But the first collect for any recently deceased person, at whatever Hour the aforesaid collect is used, always retains the first place and is not changed; in that case the collect for relatives and dependants is not to be said. Likewise, if an anniversary occurs for which all the bells are to be rung, the anniversary collect takes first place. If the anniversary is for a woman, the collect for women is to be said first and in the plural.

But if one office combines both a commemoration for someone recently deceased and one for such an anniversary, the collect for the recently deceased is always placed first, since it is no longer possible for anyone to remember that person in this way. The same rule is to be observed in the appendices, at Vespers, and at Matins.

On the Lenten feasts, the Vespers for the Dead then said are especially for relatives and dependants, just as the Matins are; therefore no other collects are joined to them, nor are they arranged in any other order than at Matins.

For the psalms said after Compline, also in silence, these verses and collects are used: “For you enlighten,” and so forth; “For in you I will escape”; “The Lord is my light”; “The Lord is the protector of life”; “Arise, O Lord”; “O God, who enlighten the night,” and so forth.

## CHAPTER VI. On the solemn celebrations of Mass; and first, on the High Mass on weekdays

**Question.** How many Masses do you generally celebrate each day in the community?

**Answer.** Two: the first, of the day; the second, if it is a weekday, for the dead. To add something that you would nevertheless not willingly neglect to ask: on weekdays the Litany again usually precedes the High Mass, though it is not very long, since only three saints from each order are named. After the first collect has been said, these follow in due order:

“From whose right hand blessed Peter”;  
“Grant, we beseech you, almighty God, that among the holy”;  
“We beseech you, almighty God, that your servants”;  
“Almighty and everlasting”;  
“O God, who make”;  
“O God, from whom”;  
“Almighty and everlasting God, have mercy on your servants.”  

From the Octave of Easter until the feast of Saint Michael: “From your house, we beseech you.”

Some of these are sufficiently familiar, so that the reason for saying them is clear; but concerning some there may be doubt. The fourth is for kings and other princes; the fifth for our bishops and abbots; the sixth for our relatives and dependants; the seventh, in rotation, for the kings of Spain, together with the other collects. If there is a cause requiring it, additional collects are used—for example, for travelers, for the sick, or for any other trouble that may arise.

The entire chant is simple and follows the same form as in other churches. Only the Introit, as is customary elsewhere, is repeated three times after the second “Gloria Patri.” Concerning the verses to be offered, I know of nothing else worth reporting except that the precentor imposes whatever seems appropriate to him: sometimes one, sometimes all, especially because of the offerers. For three days of the week, all those belonging to the left choir make the offering; peace is given and received, and those who wish receive the Lord’s Body from them. For this reason three hosts are consecrated. On the other three days, those of the right choir receive peace and communicate in the same reciprocal manner, if any wish to do so.

## CHAPTER VII. For whom the collects are said in the Mass for the Dead

At the Mass for the Dead, both those of the first choir and those of the other customarily make offerings. Sometimes more collects, sometimes the more important ones, are used; but their number does not exceed ten.
