Very often the first of the collects is the same as the first at the office; its second is also the second here, for anniversaries; the third is for pontiffs, namely, “O God, who among the apostles”; the fourth for our relatives and dependants; the fifth for brothers; the sixth for the kings of Spain: “Almighty and everlasting God, in whom human nature”; the seventh for the queen of Spain, and for sisters and other women among our relatives and dependants; the eighth, “Incline, O Lord, your ear,” for our parents and blood-relatives; the ninth for all who are buried in our place; the tenth for all the faithful departed; the last for the living and the dead, namely, “Your saints.”

The other collects and the persons for whom they are said have already been listed elsewhere. But just as the order of the collects is sometimes changed at the office, so it is changed here in turn, either because of someone recently deceased or because of an anniversary. After twelve lessons, moreover, just as the Matins for the Dead are always assigned to our relatives and dependants, so the Mass for the Dead is assigned to the Roman pontiffs. Therefore the first collect is then to be said for them, and two from the middle are omitted—the same two that are assigned at Matins to our relatives and dependants.

The remaining collects retain the order mentioned above. But, to recall those which I said are to be omitted after twelve lessons, so numerous are those who have professed in our congregation that we are very rarely without such deceased persons, for whom seven offices together with seven Masses are to be performed. Consequently, no other collect is said first so frequently as the one appointed for such persons, namely, “O God, to whom it belongs.”

But if an anniversary occurs for which all the bells are to be rung, the anniversary collect is to be placed first. If the first Mass is to be celebrated for someone recently deceased, whether the body of the deceased is present or not, the first collect ordinarily said for relatives and dependants is to be said for him, namely, “Almighty and everlasting God, to whom nothing ever.” Once it has been said, it is not to be said a second time for relatives and dependants on that occasion.

But if both such an anniversary and a first Mass for a brother recently deceased occur together, the rule I already stated elsewhere concerning the office applies here also: the collect for the recently deceased is placed first, and the anniversary collect follows. This too must be noted: the first Mass for a recently deceased person is never to be said unless the office has first been performed.

There is not much that needs to be said about the chant of the Mass for the Dead, though I think this should not be omitted. Whenever the service is performed with greater solemnity than usual, whether for someone recently deceased or for an anniversary, the first of the boys, clothed in a cope, directs the choir. The Gradual—or what others call the Responsory—is sung by two boys dressed in white, and, when the verse is finished, the Gradual is repeated from the beginning. Sometimes an anniversary is celebrated with such distinction that the two boys who are again to sing the Gradual are clothed in silk tunics, and two brothers wear copes to sing the Tract, which nevertheless is sung quite rarely.

## CHAPTER VIII. On the High Mass on Sundays

On Sundays, at the High Mass, the Introit is customarily repeated halfway after the verse, and in full after the “Gloria Patri.” The “Gloria in excelsis Deo” is never omitted except in Advent and from Septuagesima until Easter. Only one collect is to be said. The Gradual is sung by two boys dressed in white, and, when the verse is finished, it is repeated from the beginning. The Alleluia is likewise sung by two.

Everyone sings the Offertory verse. Yet, since only one person offers, five hosts are offered together, so that those who wish may communicate. Everyone receives the kiss of peace. Once consecrated, four of the hosts are exchanged with those in the pyx and are kept continually in the golden dove hanging above the altar, especially for the sick, so that, whatever may happen to them, the viaticum is ready. They are exchanged by the hand of the deacon every Sunday, for this reason: lest through being kept for a long time they should in any way deteriorate.

## CHAPTER IX. Likewise, on the Morning Mass on Sundays

Let us now come also to the Morning Mass on those same days. It is ordinarily no different from the High Mass, namely, the Mass of the day. After the first collect, the second is of the Trinity. Then follow all the collects that are said at the High Mass on weekdays, and finally “Your saints.”

It is sung without the Apostles’ Creed, unless it happens that the rural people are summoned to hear the same Mass because of some trouble; then the Creed is not omitted. If it is Lent, it is without the Tract; if it is Eastertide, with only one Alleluia. The prior alone offers one host. He receives the kiss of peace from the deacon, to be given outside the choir to one of the people. The deacon also communicates according to custom.

## CHAPTER X. On the Sunday procession

When the Morning Mass is finished, salt and water are immediately consecrated by the priest who will sing the High Mass, except perhaps on certain other principal feasts. On those occasions someone other than the priest who will sing the Mass, girded with a stole, performs the consecration. After it has been completed, he first sprinkles with holy water the pavement around the High Altar and the other nearby altars, and then the brothers.

One of them, with the cross continually beside his left side, and another carrying the consecrated water before him, makes a circuit of the offices of the cloister, saying one collect of blessing at each. First, the infirmary; second, the dormitory; third, the refectory; fourth, the regular kitchen; fifth, the cellar.

While awaiting him, the community makes its first station in the church of Saint Mary, where one collect concerning her is also to be pronounced in a singing tone; the second station is before the dormitory; the third before the refectory; the fourth together with him in the vestibule of the church; the fifth, from Easter until Pentecost, at the Holy Cross, where it is again customary for that one collect to be said.

There is no time to name each collect here, since they are sufficiently familiar, except for two, which I do not know whether they are likewise customary among the Germans: one to be said while singing before the church door, namely, “Lord Jesus Christ”; the other in the choir, “The way of all the saints.”

## CHAPTER XI. On the diversity of solemn celebrations

**Question.** On other feasts, if you do not hold a procession, do you nevertheless retain and observe everything else that is to be observed on Sundays, or is there anything that you customarily add?

**Answer.** There are several feasts on which nothing more is done than on any Sunday. There are others on which this is added: those who are to sing the Invitatory are dressed in white; and, after the priest has read the Gospel following the Nocturns, he returns to the choir in a white garment, so that, clothed in white, he may incense the altar at the Gospel canticle. This is done at the Deposition of Saint Hilary; in the Octave of the Epiphany; on the Feasts of Saint Agnes, Saint Agatha, and Saint Matthias; at the Deposition of Saint Gregory and Saint Benedict; at the Annunciation of Saint Mary; in the Octave of the Ascension of the Lord; at the Deposition of Saint Confortia the virgin; in the Octave of Saint John the Baptist; at the Translation of Saint Martin; in the Octave of the Translation of Saint Benedict; at the Deposition of Saint Brictius; in the Octave of Saint Martin; at the Deposition of Saint Clement; in the Octave of Saint Andrew; at the Nativity of Saint Lucy; and at the Deposition of Saint Sylvester. The same is customarily done on five Sundays: the First Sunday of Advent; Septuagesima; Quadragesima; and Palm Sunday.

There are others that surpass these in that the choir stalls are covered with carpets; five candles are lit before the altar at Vespers and Matins, whereas at other times there are only three; the priest incenses the altars while wearing a cope; at those same Hours two boys sing the Responsories and pronounce the “Benedicamus”; at the Nocturns only two readers, and no more, sing the fourth, eighth, and twelfth Responsories; that same twelfth Responsory is sung again; at the High Mass all who know how to sing are dressed in white; after the Alleluia a certain melody of neumes is sung, which some call the Sequence.

This occurs at the Deposition of Saint Maurus; the Nativity of Saint Vincent; the Conversion of Saint Paul; the Nativity of the apostles Philip and James; the Finding and Exaltation of the Holy Cross; the Deposition of Saint Martial; the Reception of the relics of Saint Gregory; the Nativity of Saint James; the Deposition of Saint Germanus; the Finding of Saint Stephen; the Octave of the Assumption of Saint Mary; the Nativity of Saint Bartholomew; the Nativity of Saints Julian and Hermes; the Beheading of Saint John the Baptist; the Nativity of Saint Marcellus the martyr; the Reception of Saint Marcellus the pope; the Nativity of Saint Giles; the Nativity of Saint Maurice; the Nativity of Saint Dionysius; the Deposition of Saint Luke; the Nativity of Saint Aquilinus; the Nativity of the apostles Simon and Jude; the Nativity of Saint Quintinus the martyr; the Deposition of Odo the abbot; and the Nativity of the apostle Thomas.

Among these feasts, however, the Finding and Exaltation of the Holy Cross have this prerogative: at the High Mass everyone wears a cope.

There are also certain feasts superior in this respect: two hanging cloths are suspended in the choir and six in the presbytery [Note: Col. 0655D. Dorsalia: a dorsale, Acherius says, is a cloth or curtain and tapestry placed at the back or hung on walls.]; the two who sing the Invitatory wear copes, as do all those at the High Mass; at Vespers and Matins the Gospel canticle is sung three times, divided into three sections: first before the final verse [Note: Col. 0656D. Something appears to be missing here.], and the third after the “Gloria Patri,” by everyone together; the hymn of Terce and of the two following Hours is sung with a more solemn melody than on other days, and Prime with a melody even more solemn than on Sunday; when the High Mass is finished, all the bells are rung.

This is done at the Nativity of Saint John the Evangelist and of the Innocents; at the Circumcision of the Lord; at the Deposition of Saint Odilo; at the Nativity of Saint Marcellus the pope; at the Nativity of Saint Fortunatus; at the Chair of Saint Peter, if it occurs outside Lent; on the three days of Easter and Pentecost; at the Deposition of Saint Majolus; in the commemoration of Saint Paul; in the Octave of Saints Peter and Paul; at the Translation of Saint Benedict; at the Nativity of Saint Lawrence; at the Nativity of Saint Mary; at the Nativity of Saint Matthew; on the feast of Saint Michael; and at the Nativity of Saint Andrew.

It must be noted, however, that Matins are excepted on the three days of Easter and Pentecost, and that the antiphons are not sung again, nor are they at the Nativity of Saint Marcellus the pope or of Saint Matthew.

There are still others that surpass these: four sing the Invitatory; each Responsory is sung by two or more; at Vespers and Matins adults, not boys, sing the Responsories; two incense with thuribles; at the Morning Mass and the High Mass only one collect is to be said; seven candles are lit before the altar; four hanging cloths are suspended in the choir and eight in the presbytery. This is done at the Nativity of Saint Stephen; at the Epiphany; at the Presentation of the Lord; at his Ascension; and at the Nativity of Saint John the Baptist.

The three days after the first—not only of Easter and Pentecost but also of Christmas—also have this feature concerning the first collect at the Morning Mass.

There are others to which this is added: the entire church is adorned with hanging cloths from end to end, and crowns are lit; during the Nocturns the principal altar is incensed three times, at the third, seventh, and eleventh lessons; and the thurible is then carried by the priest who performed the incensing, wearing a cope, generally to the brothers, both in the choir and outside the choir. This occurs at the Chains of Saint Peter; on the feast of All Saints; at the Deposition of Saint Martin; and at the Dedication of the Church, if it occurs outside Lent.

Only five principal feasts in a certain sense reach the highest degree: the Nativity of Saints Peter and Paul; the Assumption of Saint Mary; and three Sunday feasts. These have the special feature that at the Nocturns all the bells are rung in place of the small bell (scilla), and afterward not singly but two together, as also at Vespers; the triangular object hanging before the rood is lit; those three great candles behind the principal altar, and the seven at the Holy Cross, remain lit from Vespers until Vespers—or rather until Compline; at the Nocturns three hanging cloths of different colors are placed one by one upon the principal altar and removed in turn: the first at the end of the Responsory, the second at the end of the eighth, and the third after the Canticles; and a procession is performed through the cloister with such solemnity that not only crosses but also the Gospel book, candlesticks, and every other movable ornament are carried.

The Octave of Pentecost, the commemoration of the Holy Trinity, and the Annunciation of Saint Mary, if they are celebrated outside Lent, lack only this in comparison: the three cloths are not placed upon the altar at the Nocturns in the same manner, and the procession is not performed with that equipment.

The Prose, or what others call the Sequence, is sung only on the five principal feasts, on the Epiphany, on the Ascension of the Lord, at the Translation of Saint Benedict, and at the Nativity of Saint Maurice.

This too must be understood concerning these feasts: if two are celebrated consecutively and the preceding one is of greater reverence, the entire second Vespers is said from the preceding feast, while from the following feast only the antiphon and collect are used.

Whatever feast is celebrated during Lent receives no greater honor in any way than an ordinary Sunday, except for the five mentioned above.

## CHAPTER XII. On the Lord’s Supper

**Question.** You have spoken a little about both weekdays and solemn days—how they differ, and how some of the solemn days are more solemn than others—but you have not yet spoken specifically about any season or day of the year that possesses its own particular and distinctive character. Therefore, if you are willing, as you promised, to do what I ask according to our wishes, begin with some day, so that you may prescribe a kind of definition of the particular features of each day or season. Just as earlier you explained how the two Testaments were to be read, so now make again a kind of circuit of the year.

**Answer.** Believe me, Father, this circuit that you now ask for is not a light undertaking, and I have very little confidence in my strength that, if I begin in a way that will be useful, I shall be able to complete it. Nevertheless, in the name of Christ, and for love of so dear a petitioner, I shall try not to omit as much as I can. But before the strength I possess fails altogether, it is fitting to choose a more difficult place from which to begin, since even someone weary can sometimes proceed over level ground.

In the whole course of the year, no day has a service so elaborate and so lengthy as Maundy Thursday. Therefore let this be the goal, as you request: both the point from which to begin and the point to which we return.

On those three nights alike that precede the Sunday of the Resurrection, it is unnecessary to explain how fifteen candles are arranged before the Nocturns, so that one is extinguished before each psalm, since that custom is sufficiently well known and is general throughout all the churches in these regions. The fifteen Songs of Ascents are said in silence, though the custom of prostrating oneself over the stalls at each division is not omitted.

On the first night all the bells are rung for the Nocturns. On that night and the two following nights, we perform the Nocturns in the same manner as the canons, with the psalms, lessons, and Responsories reaching the number nine. The first three lessons are from the Lamentations of Jeremiah. In these, however, we do not imitate the canons to such an extent that we appear to sing them rather than read them, as they commonly do in many places, and we suppress the alphabetic letters entirely.

The next three are from Saint Augustine’s treatise on Psalm 62; the final three are from the Apostle. On the first night they begin at this passage of the Epistle to the Corinthians: “First of all, when you come together in church, I hear that there are divisions among you.” On the second night, at this passage of the Epistle to the Hebrews: “Let us hasten to enter into that.” On the third night, at this passage of the same Epistle: “Christ, appearing as High Priest.”

There is likewise no need to say that the Nocturns and all the Hours are begun without the verse “O God, come to my assistance,” though with the customary invocation of pardon, and that none of the antiphons ends with a determination of tone. The lessons likewise are neither begun nor ended in the customary manner.

When Matins reaches “Praise the Lord from the heavens,” however, each boy stands beside his custodian. In the middle of the two boys stands one of their teachers, who holds both of them by their sleeves until Matins is finished. After the Gospel canticle, with whatever antiphon has been sung, they prostrate themselves over the stalls. Each one silently says the prayers, “I said,” with the psalm “Have mercy on me, O God,” and the collect “O God, from whom Judas,” and so forth. At a signal given by a sound from the lord abbot, they rise and, with lanterns bearing light brought by the boys’ teachers, go to the dormitory.

When dawn has appeared sufficiently for no other light to be needed, the bell is rung. They rise from their beds and hurry to the church. After the prayer has been made, Prime begins with the hymn, as do the three following Hours; its final verse, which concerns the Holy Trinity, is omitted. The customary psalms are sung with their antiphons and tone.

During the prayers, when the point of confession is reached, the lord abbot gives a signal with a sound, so that the familiar psalms may be omitted. When they have risen after the prayers, they sing the seven psalms without the “Gloria,” followed by the Litany with all its appendices. When it is finished, they do not alter what they customarily observed on weekdays throughout Lent: they do not put on their shoes before hearing the signal, and they precede Terce with three prayers. This is changed on that day only in that the Morning Mass does not immediately follow Terce.

Before they leave the church, new shoes, suspended from three poles, are brought into the chapterhouse by the chamberlain’s servants, and the poles themselves are placed upon four stakes fixed in the ground. There, besides the proclamation of the day and of the moon and the sentence from the Rule that is customarily read there, whatever else is said by the priest and the community is spoken in silence. On those three days nothing else is read in chapter except from the Rule.

To continue what I began concerning the shoes: after the sentence from the Rule has been expounded, the chamberlain and his assistant rise at the command of the lord abbot, and through them the shoes are distributed; each pair has the name of one of the brothers written on it. Those who receive new shoes return the old ones, thoroughly washed—if, indeed, they have had more than one pair for daily use—so that they may be given to the poor.

The number of brothers in the cloister is announced, so that an equal number of poor may be admitted to the Maundy; in addition, as much as seems appropriate is provided for the friends of our lord abbot. Immediately the priest who is to sing the Morning Mass sings Mass for these poor at the altar of the Holy Cross, and one oblate is given to each of them. Since it would be rash to allow people whose consciences are unknown to communicate indiscriminately, these poor must first have been selected by the dean of the town, and they must in no way be persons who ought not to enter the cloister.

In the hospital, two portions of food—beans and millet—are given to those who are to be fed; the almsgiving servants wash their feet beforehand with warm water. There was an ancient and quite reasonable custom that on this day, on the preceding day, and on the following day—and throughout the year whenever something of this kind was to be done—the matter would be announced in chapter as something new and appropriate to the season by one of the boys. If he said anything incorrectly, he was not a person whose word could not be challenged.

Now, however, I do not know why this has been changed. If the lord abbot and the prior are absent, the precentor, or some other brother well versed in the matter, rather than a boy, is ordered to perform this duty.

After chapter, the psalms for the anniversary of the brothers are sung aloud on that day, although on the two following days they are sung in silence. When the board has been struck, the brothers speak in the cloister, and again after Sext.

After None, the priest dressed in white, together with the others who are to serve at the High Mass, makes a procession to consecrate the new fire, singing Psalm 50. Before the procession the cross, holy water, and thurible are carried, though without fire, so that after the new fire has been consecrated it may be sprinkled and incensed for the blessing. The prayer is: “Lord God, almighty Father.”

They return through the middle of the church to the choir, singing Psalms 53, 56, 59, and 79. On that day the light on a pole is carried by the church custodian; on Good Friday by the prior; on Holy Saturday by the lord abbot or the priest. A precious stone, beryl, from which the fire is produced, is kept under the custody of the apocrisiarius. He brings it only to the precentor, so that the fire may be drawn from it; on that same day, in the procession, the same chief custodian of the church carries it.

But to return to the day under discussion: when they have come into the choir, the stalls are folded up, as is customary on days when pardon is not to be requested. After all the bells have been rung, Mass is sung festively, but without the “Gloria in excelsis”; and after the verse “Gloria Patri,” the Introit is not said again. The deacon wears a dalmatic, the subdeacon a tunic, and those who sing the Gradual wear copes.

Everyone receives the kiss of peace, and everyone communicates. During those four days no brother is to omit communicating, even if some such event should happen to him while asleep.

When Mass is finished, the board is struck as a signal for the prayer of Vespers, which they perform prostrate, after the stalls have again been unfolded. Meanwhile the Lord’s Body is placed by the priest behind the altar. It is put in a golden paten, the paten between golden dishes, and the dishes in turn between silver boards made for the Gospel book.

When it is carried from the altar with candles and abundant incense, after those who served at Mass have removed their vestments, everyone follows the lord abbot, who goes before them—he sits in the choir in the meantime—and they go to the refectory. There each person receives only a portion (mixtum) from his allotted pound, and spiced drink is served to them. When they sit down, and when they rise, they say nothing from the verse, but merely perform the customary actions before and behind.

Meanwhile the poor who have been brought into the cloister are ordered to sit down. The brothers come to them and stand in order on the other side of the cloister, with the seniors nearer to the poor. The lord abbot himself, or the precentor, imposes the antiphon “The Lord Jesus,” and pardon is requested by everyone.

The Maundy begins: two together wash and dry the feet on one side, while on the other two boys separately do so with their teachers and with the infirm. Psalm 66 follows the aforesaid antiphon, “A new commandment,” which is repeated after each verse of that psalm. Then Psalm 118 follows, in which it is repeated again after every eight verses.

When the point is reached at which water is provided for the hands of the poor, the other antiphons pertaining to the Maundy are also sung. After the board has been struck once, the singing ceases. A blessing is given over the wine that is to be served, in silence; together with it, two pennies are given to each poor person by each brother.

When everyone has bowed, the verse is to be said, and the collect by the lord abbot, as on the other days when the Maundy for the poor is performed—so quietly that it cannot be heard. In the same manner, after the psalm “Have mercy on me, O God” has been imposed and the customary actions before and behind have been made, they return to the church.

Meanwhile, while the Maundy was being performed, the board was struck as many times as the bells are customarily rung for Vespers. But as the community entered, many boards had been prepared, which, in place of all the bells, were struck by the church custodians standing at the entrance of the church.

Vespers is sung in the manner of the canons, a boy beginning with five psalms, and it is ended in the same way as the Office of Matins. Do not therefore suppose that at the other Hours any psalms were said other than those customarily used.

All the altars are completely stripped. The board is struck in place of the cymbal, and in the refectory in place of the bell. There, again, as in chapter, everything that is to be said except the lessons is spoken in silence, and they return to the church in this manner.

For the Mandatum, which is to be performed among the brothers, the weekly servers first wash the brothers’ feet and do not wipe them; the lord abbot, following them, both washes and wipes them again. Three brothers also assist him: one supports the brothers’ feet while they are being washed, another brings the water, and another changes the towels. Whereas on other occasions two brothers’ feet are washed with one basin of water, here the water is used for only one brother. Since so great a multitude of brothers is assembled—sometimes, indeed, more than two hundred—the day would not suffice if the lord abbot alone performed the Mandatum in this way. Therefore another brother from among the seniors is also appointed, to perform it similarly on the other side; and, if it seems necessary, two more are appointed.

Before all these men, together with the lord abbot, bring water to wash the brothers’ hands, their feet are washed outside the chapter house by brothers who have been designated for this task. Only those who have washed the brothers’ feet on the first or second occasion perform the movements forward and backward in the middle of the chapter house before sitting down. Since one of them is the lord abbot, the brothers then rise first when he comes to seek his seat, and the prior, who had been sitting in his place, withdraws slightly and gives him the place.

All this was arranged in the chapter house immediately after the shoes had been distributed. In addition to the customary antiphons belonging to the Mandatum, there is a hymn by Flavius, the first bishop of Chalon, *Tellus ac aethera jubilent in magni coena Principis* (“Let earth and heaven rejoice at the great Supper of the Prince”). On this day, and for this Mandatum, it is sung after the first antiphon, with its first verse repeated after every verse.

When everything has been completed, the singing ceases and the church custodian strikes the board as a signal. The deacon enters dressed in an alb and stole and carrying the Gospel book. He is preceded by a church doorkeeper carrying a lectern on which it is to be read, and by three conversi, likewise dressed in albs, carrying candlesticks and incense. As they enter, the entire community rises and does not sit again until one verse from the Gospel has been read. The reading begins at the passage, “Before the feast of Passover,” and continues to the passage, “Rise, let us go from here.” Then, when the board has been struck, the brothers also rise and go to the refectory, with the deacon leading the procession.

There, those who washed and wiped the brothers’ feet also pour wine for everyone and kiss their hands. Those who served in the chapter house assist them by bringing the wine. The deacon, who is still standing at the step and reading, and those standing with him, are also served. The wine is poured into cups brought by them, and others place it on the principal table, so that when the reading is finished they may sit down there, perform the customary gesture forward and backward, and drink.

Compline is to be said in silence. From that point onward, except for the night offices and the morning offices, no regular Hour is performed in any other manner until the Saturday of Holy Week. If any brother who is staying outside wishes to attend the Easter solemnity, he must have arrived on Wednesday. But if through negligence it should happen that someone—whether one of our professed brothers or an outside monk—does not come until those three days themselves, after every Hour has ended, once the brothers have risen from their stalls at the sound, he is to receive the customary blessing. No one, however, kisses him from the moment of the Lord’s Supper, when peace was generally given in the Church, until peace is given again on the aforementioned Holy Saturday at Communion.

## CHAPTER XIII. Good Friday

On Good Friday everyone must come to Prime barefoot. When it has ended in silence, the seven psalms follow openly together with the litany, which will lack none of its proper verses and collects. The brothers go out to sit in the cloister and, beginning together, chant the entire Psalter.

Terce and the two following Hours are sung in the church of Saint Mary, because the greater church is meanwhile swept, and the dust raised there does not settle so quickly. For the procession that is again to be made to the new fire, all who are to serve at the Mass must be dressed in albs.

The tract *Domine audivi* (“Lord, I have heard”), begun by the cantors, is sung so that after each verse its first verse is repeated, now with the tract *Eripe me, Domine* (“Deliver me, Lord”) entire, now with it in half; the other tracts are sung by the cantors alone. The Passion is read without a greeting, although on the other days the greeting is not omitted.

When the collects contained in the missal have been completed, two priests dressed in albs and chasubles, who are to bring the cross, withdraw to the place where the cross is located outside the choir, on the right. While carrying it, they sing these three verses: *Popule meus* (“My people”), sung by two other men, followed by *Quia eduxi te* (“For I led you out”) and *Quid ultra* (“What more”). Each of these verses is followed by the two others singing *Agios o Theos* (“Holy God”), and by the choir singing “Holy God.”

The bearers of the cross present and uncover it—for until then it is covered—and impose the antiphon *Ecce lignum crucis* (“Behold the wood of the cross”); everyone asks forgiveness. Then follow the verse *Beati immaculati in via* (“Blessed are the undefiled in the way”); the antiphon *Crucem tuam* (“Your cross”); the verse *Deus, misereatur nostri* (“May God have mercy on us”); the antiphon *Dum fabricator* (“While the Maker”); the verse *O admirabile* (“O wondrous [cross]”); and the hymn *Crux fidelis* (“Faithful cross”), sung responsorially.

The floor is spread with carpets, especially for those dressed in albs who are to adore the cross. The priest goes first, after removing his chasuble and stole. The boys adore it next, followed by the sick. When the cross is taken away, the antiphon *Super omnia ligna* (“Above all trees”) is imposed, and forgiveness is sought a second time. If any layperson wishes to adore the cross, a place is given to him behind the altar.

On the preceding day, under the direction of the precentor, only so much of the Eucharist was reserved as would again enable everyone to communicate. The community proceeds again with incense and two candlesticks to the place where it was stored, so that it may be broken and divided as it is to be received, by the two senior priests dressed in albs and chasubles. One of them holds the chalice containing unconsecrated wine. It is carried in this manner to the altar, where the priest says only the Lord’s Prayer and the collect *Libera nos* (“Deliver us”). Although *Per omnia saecula saeculorum* (“For ever and ever”) is said openly, *Pax Domini* (“The peace of the Lord”) does not follow, because the sign of peace is not given on that day.

Formerly there was such careful observance that, after everyone had communicated, whatever remained was consumed with great reverence and caution by the same priests who had brought it, so that absolutely nothing remained for the following day. I know no other practice than this, unless it is the general custom of other churches; but this is not now given much attention here. On this day, as on the other, whatever remains after Communion is reserved.

After everyone has communicated, the board is struck so that the evening prayer may be held. The brothers go out to wash their feet and put on their shoes. When they return, all the boards are struck together, and Vespers are sung in silence, with the same psalms as on the preceding day, except that the first is removed and Psalm 143 is put in its place at the end.

In the refectory there is nothing except bread and raw herbs. Wine infused with spices is given more for almsgiving than for anyone to drink. The same is done a second time when they go again to the refectory, as though they were going to drink in the customary manner. But they rise from the collation for the *Charity*, and no one at all presumes to abstain from the wine then served, so that each person tastes at least a little.

Immediately after Vespers the church custodians begin carefully washing each altar above: first with water, and afterward with wine. For this task they do not even lack a sponge, which absorbs each of the liquids, so that the altars may be washed more cleanly with it.

**Question.** Was the principal altar bare when the Lord’s Body was given?

**Answer.** Not at all; meanwhile it was covered with a single linen cloth.

**Question.** In that passage of the Passion, “They divided my garments among themselves,” is anything of the sort represented by you?

**Answer.** Certainly. Two small cloths are placed on the altar and, at the same moment, are pulled away from either side by two brothers. But, to admit what is true, I concealed this deliberately, because, although it is not an evil, it is nevertheless not done in accordance with the Apostle’s testimony that he walks by faith and not by sight (2 Corinthians 5). But, omitting this, allow me to continue, so that the order already begun may be maintained.

## CHAPTER XIV. Holy Saturday

On Holy Saturday, immediately after Matins, not only are the altars covered, but the whole church is also adorned with hangings. No linen is placed on any altar unless it has been thoroughly washed. After chapter and after Sext, the brothers speak in the cloister.

After the procession has been made following None, the deacon first reads the praise of the candle. At one point in it, where “O happy fault” and the statement that Adam’s sin was necessary were at one time not well received, the lord abbot did very well, some years ago, to have them scraped away and to forbid their being read any longer.

On the candle itself the precentor writes the year of the Lord’s Incarnation, the concurrent number of the indiction, and the epacts. When the passage *Suscipe, sancte Pater, incensi hujus sacrificium vespertinum* (“Receive, holy Father, the evening sacrifice of this incense”) is reached, the deacon makes a cross in it with five grains of incense, placing them in holes prepared beforehand. When *Rutilans ignis ascendit* (“The shining fire rises”) is read, the candle is lit for the first time.

The following then takes place: the reading *In principio* (“In the beginning”); the prayer *Deus qui* (“O God, who…”); the second reading *Factum est* (“It came to pass”); the tract *Cantemus Domino* (“Let us sing to the Lord”), sung in full by two men; the prayer *Deus cujus* (“O God, whose…”); the third reading *Apprehendent septem mulieres* (“Seven women shall take hold”); the prayer *Deus qui nos* (“O God, who…”); the tract *Vinea* (“The vineyard”); the fourth reading *Haec est haereditas* (“This is the inheritance”); the tract *Attende* (“Give heed”); the prayer *Deus qui Ecclesiam* (“O God, who [formed] the Church”); the tract *Sicut cervus* (“As the deer”); and the prayer *Concede* (“Grant, we beseech you”).

The triple litany is sung by two cantors, who also lead the choir while dressed in copes. They chant the petitions, and each choir responds separately. At each name of a saint, except the angels, those by whom the name is pronounced bow; the precentors do not bow. We do not concern ourselves with Baptism, nor is it celebrated by anyone in our church.

As soon as the litany begins, the stalls are covered with carpets. When it ends, the cantor announces, *Accendite* (“Light [them]”). The candles before the altar are lit, and all the bells are rung. The stalls are covered with carpets. Mass begins with *Kyrie, eleison* (“Lord, have mercy”); *Gloria in excelsis* (“Glory in the highest”) follows, and everything else is performed solemnly.

No candle is carried before the priest as he proceeds to the altar, nor before the Gospel—only incense. Then, for the first time, if any priest wishes to sing a private Mass, he may receive permission to do so, and he likewise begins with *Kyrie, eleison*. On the Lord’s Supper it was possible to sing even without permission before the greater Mass, but without a candle, because the new fire had not yet been consecrated.

On this day, although *Agnus Dei* (“Lamb of God”) is not said, peace is nevertheless given and received by everyone, and, as I mentioned above, everyone communicates. When Mass is finished, the two bells are struck together.

At Vespers, as with the bells that follow, they are struck in pairs, and the customary psalms are sung: first *Confiteamur* (“Let us confess”) with *Alleluia* according to the melody; the antiphon *Crucifixus* (“Crucified”); the responsory *Angelus Domini* (“The angel of the Lord”); and the hymn *Ad Coenam* (“To the Supper”).

At the Gospel canticle, after the antiphon—which is sung three times—the melody of the antiphon itself is nevertheless sung again with *Alleluia*. The collect is *Deus qui hanc* (“O God, who [have made] this…”).

The procession customarily made to the church of Saint Mary is changed to the holy cross, as on every Saturday, but now with the responsory *Dum transisset* (“When he had passed over”), followed by its verse, and with the collect pronounced in the musical tone: *Dicite in nationibus* (“Tell it among the nations”); *Deus qui pro salute* (“O God, who for the salvation…”).

The General Mandatum would have been performed, except that it was performed on the Lord’s Supper. This too was established by the blessed Father Odilo: if the principal feasts that occur on the Saturday evening—“which, as it is written, dawned on the first day of the week,” that is, on Sunday—should fall then, the Mandatum is to be anticipated to the preceding Thursday, so that the brothers, who are to undergo longer vigils, may not also be burdened with the labor of the Mandatum.

This rule is observed for five principal feasts; the lord abbot added the commemoration of the Holy Trinity, the Chains of Saint Peter, the Feast of All Saints, Saint Martin, the Hypapante of the Lord, and the Dedication of the Church.

## CHAPTER XV. The Night and Day of the Lord’s Resurrection

On the night of the Lord’s Resurrection I know well enough that our performance of the night offices does not agree with yours. For the psalms, readings, and responsories alike reach the number twelve, although there are only three antiphons: the first is sung over the first six psalms, the second over the other six, and the third over the canticles.

As for first ringing all the bells in place of the *scilla*; placing three hangings over the altar; carrying incense around three times during the night offices; and repeating the eighth and twelfth responsories after they have once been sung—all this may be passed over, since, to say what you may remember, I have already spoken of it above when I mentioned the differences among solemnities.

At the morning praises, the melody of each antiphon is repeated with *Alleluia*. On the day itself, since each Hour has its own antiphon, as can readily be seen in the antiphonary, at Vespers *Alleluia* alone is sung over the psalms instead of an antiphon, in the melody of *Jesum quem quaeritis* (“Jesus whom you seek”).

After the blessed water, the procession proceeds to the church of Saint Mary with the antiphon *Vidi aquam* (“I saw water”), and so forth, with *Gloria Patri* (“Glory be to the Father”), together with the responsory *Veniens a Libano* (“Coming from Lebanon”), or another responsory that nevertheless does not end without *Alleluia*. The antiphon *In die resurrectionis meae* (“On the day of my resurrection”), with *Alleluia*, follows, as does *Sedit angelus* (“The angel sat”), with the verse *Crucifixum* (“The crucified one”). At the entrance to the church: the antiphon *Christus resurgens* (“Christ rising again”); on returning to the choir: the antiphon *Et valde mane* (“And very early”).

**Question.** On such a day, is the collect to be said that you mentioned above at a certain point, namely *Via sanctorum* (“Way of the saints”)?

**Answer.** Certainly; nor does it ordinarily remain on any Sunday. This kind of chant for the procession is not changed on any Sunday until Pentecost, except that, in place of the final responsory, another responsory or an antiphon of Saints Peter and Paul is sung, while the verse *Crucifixus* remains.

You do not need to hear again how Mass is celebrated on this most holy day, if you properly remember what was said above about the differences among solemnities. What I did not say there, however, is that the Introit is sung three times, because it has two verses. Two pairs of cantors, one on each side—or more, if it seems appropriate—are appointed to sing the sequence, and the choir responds with neumes.

Certain tropes are added to *Agnus Dei*, and the Communion is repeated after its verse. One verse is added to the hymns of all the Hours, namely *Quaesumus, auctor omnium* (“We beseech you, Author of all things”); and the final verse is changed to *Gloria tibi, Domine, qui surrexisti* (“Glory to you, Lord, who have risen”), and so forth. This is observed until the Ascension of the Lord.

The preface *Te quidem omni tempore* (“You indeed at all times”) is to be said at both Masses throughout this entire week. There is also another custom: whenever there are twelve readings and one and the same collect is said, it is said both at Vespers and at the Gospel after the night offices, at Terce, at Mass, and again at Vespers. On this day and during this week, however, this is observed except at Vespers alone, as was stated above concerning the vigil of Easter.

## CHAPTER XVI. Monday and the Days of the Greater Week

After Sunday has passed, on Monday and on the other days and nights of the same week, only two bells are rung for the night offices, as on ordinary days. The offices are performed with twelve psalms, arranged according to the weekdays, but only three readings are taken from the Gospels. One boy sings the invitatory.

At Matins all the bells are rung, and thereafter everything is performed festively. The antiphons that were sung at Matins on Sunday are then sung one by one at each Matins until Saturday; at the other Hours, antiphons from the Gospel are used.

At the night offices and at Vespers, only *Alleluia* is sung over the psalms, formed according to the melody of the antiphons. On Monday, for example: *Postulavi* (“I asked”), *Angelus autem* (“But the angel”), and *Jesum quem quaeris* (“Jesus whom you seek”). On Tuesday: *Et ecce terrae motus* (“And behold, there was an earthquake”), *Prae timore* (“From fear”), and *Nonne cor nostrum* (“Was not our heart…”). On Wednesday: *Erat autem* (“Now it was”), *Et respicientes* (“And looking back”), and *Scio quod Jesum* (“I know that Jesus…”). On Thursday: *Stetit Jesus* (“Jesus stood”), *Oportebat* (“It was necessary”), and again *Jesum quem quaeritis* (“Jesus whom you seek”). On Friday: *Nonne sic* (“Was it not so”), *Et ingressae* (“And they entered”), and *Crucifixus* (“Crucified”).

Of each of these three, the first is always used for the first six psalms of the night offices, the second for the other six, and the third at Vespers.

On Saturday: *Noli flere* (“Do not weep”), *Venit Maria* (“Mary came”), and *Vespere autem* (“But in the evening”). On that day also, at the other Hours, only *Alleluia* is sung: at Matins, *Angelus autem*; at Prime, *Et ecce terrae motus*; at Terce, *Prae timore*; at Sext, *Erat autem*; and at None, *Et respicientes*.

At the morning Mass throughout the entire week the office *Resurrexi* (“I have risen”) is sung. If for three days it is celebrated with only one collect, on the other three all the collects that are to be said at the morning Mass on any Sunday are said.

Likewise, for three days the greater Mass is generally performed in copes, and after the *Alleluia* certain Gallican neumes are sung. For the other three days it is performed in the manner of Sunday. At Vespers also these psalms are not changed—*Dixit Dominus Domino meo* (“The Lord said to my Lord”) and the others—until Vespers on Saturday.

## CHAPTER XVII. The Eighth Day, and How *Alleluia* Is Sung at All the Hours Thereafter

You have already heard incidentally, in connection with other feasts, how the eighth day of Easter is to be celebrated; what follows is now added.

At Vespers no psalms other than the ferial psalms are said. At the night offices there are no responsories other than those sung on the first night of the Lord’s Resurrection, and these continue to be sung in the same way throughout the following week.

The morning Mass is *Quasi modo geniti* (“Like newborn infants”). The greater Mass is the same, except that the Introit alone is changed: instead of *Resurrexi*, the first *Alleluia* is *Post dies octo* (“After eight days”).

From that day onward, although *Alleluia* is always sung at all the Hours until the Ascension of the Lord, I have found no antiphonary that specifies in what definite order so many *Alleluia* chants ought to be sung. I asked with particular care a certain young man of keen intelligence, who had already lived in the cloister for twenty-five continuous years, what he thought and knew about the matter. What he reported to me I report here.

On every Sunday: at the first night office, *Postulavi*; at the second, *Angelus autem*; at the canticles, *Et ecce terrae motus*; at Lauds, *Prae timore*; at Prime, *Surgens autem* (“But rising”); at Terce, from the Gospel, *Ut multa quidem* (“That many indeed”); at Sext, *Erat autem*; at None, *Et respicientes*; and at Vespers, *Jesum quem quaeris*.

On Monday, when, as I may say, no fewer *Alleluia* chants are required—only one fewer, because the canticles are not then said—the *Alleluia* chants are sung in the same order as above: *Postulavi*, *Angelus autem*, *Et ecce terrae motus*, *Prae timore*, and from the Gospel *Erat autem* and *Et respicientes*. At Matins: *Jesum quem quaeris*.

On Tuesday: *Stetit Jesus*, *Oportebat*, *Nonne sic*, *Qui sunt hi sermones* (“What are these words?”), from the Gospel *Et coegerunt* (“And they compelled”), *Mane nobiscum* (“Remain with us”), and *Nonne cor nostrum*.

On Wednesday: *Noli flere*, *Venit Maria*, *Et ingressi* (“And having entered”), *Et valde mane*, from the Gospel *Ite nuntiate* (“Go, tell”), *Iterum venit Maria* (“Mary came again”), and *Scio quod Jesum*.

On Thursday, the order is the same as on Monday. On Friday, the same as on Tuesday, except that at Vespers *Vespere autem* is sung. From the Gospel: *Multa quidem* (“Many things indeed”), or *Mitte manum tuam* (“Put out your hand”), *Ego sum Pastor* (“I am the shepherd”), and *Modicum et non videbitis me* (“A little while, and you will not see me”).

On Saturday, the order is the same as on Wednesday, except that at Vespers *Alleluia* is sung. Whatever Gospel is read during the week, an *Alleluia* from it is sung at Terce each day.

## CHAPTER XVIII. The Monday after the Octave of Easter, and the Customs Then Initiated

After the octave of Easter, Monday is almost a new beginning of ordinary days. Certain customs therefore begin that had not previously been practiced on ordinary days.

First, as I have already not concealed elsewhere, before the night offices only the fifteen Gradual Psalms are said. Morning Lauds follow them, with no psalm inserted at all. After Lauds and the other Hours, two of the customary psalms remain: the first and second, and between the prayers Psalm *Miserere* (“Have mercy on me”). Nevertheless, after Prime it is not omitted for our deceased abbots, nor are the Matins for the dead, nor *Deus auribus* (“O God, with your ears”), nor the seven psalms with their appendices after Prime.

After the psalms for the thirtieth-day commemoration of a recently deceased person, they return to their beds, unless the day is already so bright that writing can be distinguished in a book. If dawn is only beginning to appear, they put on their shoes and, without removing anything else, lie there with their feet extended beyond the bed until they hear the sound that signals rising. This sound should always be made at such an hour that, after a brother has washed his hands and face, combed his head, and said three prayers in the church, he can begin to see well enough while sitting in the cloister to read.

**Question.** I should like to know what sort of prayers these three prayers you mention should be, and how long they should be.

**Answer.** Certainly, as far as I know, no fixed measure is prescribed for them, because they are not performed communally. Each person makes them individually and separately as soon as he first comes into the church. One of the seniors, however, taught me as a novice to say seven psalms between the three prayers. But let each person pray whatever he wishes. Nevertheless, once the boys have left the church and begun to read, if someone then delays so that he does not also go out to sit for the reading, he easily incurs a reprimand in chapter.

Since three prayers are likewise made communally before the night offices, after Compline, and in winter on ordinary days before Terce, I may perhaps say something about what you have asked. Concerning those made after Compline, I never heard any question raised about saying anything more for each than the Lord’s Prayer alone. When the others were under discussion, the lord abbot eventually approved and decreed that the Lord’s Prayer should also be said for these, but slowly, carefully, and attentively.

Nevertheless, the prayers before Terce are not customarily brought to an end as briefly as those after Compline, nor are those before the night offices—especially on the longer nights—as brief as those before Terce. The other prayers that precede each Hour are nothing more than this same Lord’s Prayer. Only at Vespers are they extended somewhat further according to the ancient custom, so that, if it seems appropriate, the Apostles’ Creed may be added.

Having inserted these remarks out of order in answer to your question, let us attend to the cycle you set before me, and about which I cannot help being concerned until it is somehow completed: as the litany follows Prime, so the morning Mass follows the litany; chapter follows, with permission to speak.

**Question.** How long does this permission and time for speaking usually last?

**Answer.** When I first came to the monastery, a priest who wished to sing a private Mass could finish it during that interval. This now rarely happens, because the number of brothers has increased. While offerings are made at both Masses, while peace is given and received, while this and that is disputed in chapter about one matter or another, and while so many are served in the refectory, a considerable part of the day is consumed. Yet none of these things can remain in its proper order with our observance preserved and intact. For that reason the time for speaking must necessarily be shorter. If we speak somewhat less, no one in the order considers that any harm has been done.

When the signal for Terce has been sounded and the prayer has been made, they sit in the choir reading until the priest and the others who are to serve at Mass have put on their vestments. After Mass they sit again in the cloister, reading with great discipline and silence, until the boys, having received the *mistum*, come out of the refectory and begin to read aloud. As soon as the church custodian hears them, he does not delay striking the signal for Sext.

And so that you do not think we are burdened beyond measure by vigils, because the night is already beginning to grow so short while the customary psalmody after Matins is not reduced, the chief church custodian has been charged—as though by a perpetual legal obligation—with ensuring that throughout the whole summer midday occurs only after dinner has been completed. At that same moment the brothers generally settle down to rest, although they are more intent on reading than on resting.

None, at which they are to rise, will be so late that, after they have drunk in the refectory and again received permission to speak, I would not rightly call that same time for speaking, and the interval before Vespers, nonexistent rather than short. More often, before everyone has sat down in the cloister and before any brother has spoken even one word, the signal for Vespers is sounded—and there is the end of speaking.

Afterward, whatever has to be done is very rarely not performed in such a way that nothing at all is allowed to intervene between one task and the next. The bells are rung quickly, and meanwhile they have nothing else to do except sit in the choir and read. After Vespers comes dinner; after dinner, the servers’ dinner; after the servers’ dinner, the office for the dead; after the office, the collation; and so to Compline.

## CHAPTER XIX. The Third Week after Easter and the Rest until the Ascension of the Lord

In the third week after Easter, responsories from the Apocalypse are begun and sung for two weeks. Afterward the responsories *Si oblitus fuero* (“If I should forget”) are sung until the Ascension of the Lord.

When either set of responsories has been sung on one Sunday, on the next Sunday the final responsories of the night offices are changed to these shorter ones: *Surrexit Dominus de sepulcro, Alleluia* (“The Lord has risen from the tomb, Alleluia”). The same is done during the octave of the Ascension of the Lord and on the preceding Sunday.

## CHAPTER XX. The Feasts of the Saints Occurring from Easter to Pentecost

From Easter to Pentecost, whenever a feast of the saints occurs, however worthy of reverence and observance it may be, no more antiphons are sung at the night offices than one *Alleluia* alone over each group of six psalms, except at the Annunciation of Saint Mary and the Passing (*Transitus*) of Saint Benedict.

At the morning praises, if the feast has proper antiphons, as do the feasts of the holy apostles Philip and James or of the holy cross, these are not omitted but are sung at Lauds and the other Hours. If, however, it has only antiphons common to any of the saints, such as *In coelestibus regnis* (“In the heavenly kingdoms”), and so forth, these are sung neither at Lauds nor at any regular Hour. Instead, only *Alleluia* is sung, in the same manner as the melody of those antiphons.

It is sung in the following order: over the first six psalms of the night offices, *Alleluia* in the manner of *In velamento* (“In the veil”); over the other six, in the manner of *Lux perpetua* (“Everlasting light”); over the canticles, in the manner of *Ego sum vitis* (“I am the vine”); at Lauds, in the manner of *In coelestibus* (“In the heavenly [kingdoms]”); at Prime, in the manner of *In velamento*; at Terce, in the manner of *Sancti et justi* (“Holy and righteous”); at Sext, in the manner of *Lux perpetua*; at None, in the manner of *In coelestibus*; and at Vespers, in the manner of *Ego sum* (“I am”).

If proper antiphons are available, as for Saints Philip and James, then over the canticle not *Alleluia* but the antiphon *Ego sum vitis vera* (“I am the true vine”) is sung.

**Question.** Do the antiphons of the saints themselves nevertheless remain sung in this manner?

**Answer.** Not at all. For during this period they are also sung every day, namely at the suffrages of the saints, at morning Lauds and at Vespers, from *All Saints*. To explain this one by one would delay someone who is hurrying on to other matters, and is unnecessary for anyone who is attentive and remains in the monastery.

## CHAPTER XXI. The Rogation Days

On the Rogation Days, after the night offices and the Lauds for the dead have ended, they go to sleep and sleep longer than usual, namely until sunrise. For that reason they omit the midday rest and are not awakened by the customary sound. Nevertheless, once the boys have begun to read, they do not remain lying down any longer.

After Prime and the three psalms that follow, before the seven psalms are said, the psalmody left over from after Matins is inserted, namely *Deus auribus* (“O God, with your ears”); and, if the thirtieth-day commemoration of a deceased person is being observed, *Verba mea* (“My words”). Immediately after the seven psalms and the litany, Mass follows—not the customary Mass for the dead, but the Mass of the day with the usual collects, and finally the collect *Sanctorum tuorum* (“Of your saints”) added as well. Everyone makes an offering for it, but only one host is consecrated, and peace is received from one person.

In chapter, after the verse *Pretiosa in conspectu Domini* (“Precious in the sight of the Lord”), *Deus in adjutorium* (“O God, come to my assistance”), and so forth, is by no means said, nor do they speak in the cloister. After Terce the boys receive the *mistum*.

After Sext the *scilla* is rung. Everyone goes up to the dormitory as though to rest for a short while. When the signal is heard, they leave their shoes by their beds, descend barefoot, wash their hands and faces, comb their heads, and come into the church. After the prayer has been made, one of the boys imposes the antiphon *Exsurge, Domine* (“Arise, Lord”); after *Deus auribus* follows the verse *Ostende nobis* (“Show us”); *Kyrie, eleison*; the Lord’s Prayer; Psalm 66, and on the following day Psalm 69; the verse *Et veniat* (“And may it come”); and the collect *Mentem familiae tuae* (“The mind of your family”).

The relics of the saints, enclosed in small crosses, capsules, and *nuxae*, are distributed among the brothers by the secretary, so that they may wear them suspended from their necks. [Note: [Col. 0669D] *Nuxis* or *nuscis*, that is, clasps.] Before they go out, all the bells are rung.

The cross, blessed water, and Gospel book are carried before the procession. The conversi go first, followed by the boys and the cantors, with the priors last. When they come to the door of the church vestibule, two servants stand there with a double bundle of staffs, and each brother takes one staff. They return the staffs at the door of the church to which they are proceeding. There, after an antiphon or responsory concerning the saints whose patronage is established in that place has been sung, with the collect added, they make a prayer with the customary inclination.

None is sung. It is also to be sung in the monastery when the church custodian strikes the signal at the appropriate Hour, and by the sick who were unable to go out for the procession. Mass is again celebrated for the day. After the first collect, only one other is added, a commemoration of the saint whose confession is located there.

When the Gospel has been read, the obedientiaries whose duty it is to serve the brothers at table receive permission to return. At the same time, two brothers dressed in copes but barefoot, who are to receive the procession at the church door and sing the litany again briefly in the choir, also return. They sing it with the melody and verses composed for this purpose.

Vespers for the faithful departed are to be said; the office will remain.

## CHAPTER XXII. The Ascension of the Lord

How the Ascension of the Lord is to be celebrated is also found among the other solemnities. What remains to be said is the following.

At Vespers on the vigil, the collect is *Adesto supplicationibus nostris* (“Be present to our supplications”).

On the day of the Ascension itself, the antiphons sung at Lauds are also sung at the other Hours, except for the one that, as is always customary, is omitted, namely the one over the hymn of the three boys. At Vespers alone: *Alleluia* in the manner of the antiphon *Pater sancte* (“Holy Father”). This is also sung each day thereafter and, at the canticles, at morning Lauds until Pentecost, in the manner of *Sic veniet* (“Thus he will come”); at Terce, in the manner of *Illi autem profecti* (“But they went forth”); and at the night offices and the other Hours in the same manner as previously after Easter.

In the procession on the aforementioned day they do not come to the church of Saint Mary, but proceed only through the cloister as far as the church vestibule. There the station is made with the antiphon *O Rex gloriae* (“O King of glory”). The chant before or after it is nothing other than the responsories belonging to that day: first *Eduxit Dominus* (“The Lord led forth”); another, *Ponis nubem* (“You place the cloud”); and finally in the choir, *Viri Galilaei* (“Men of Galilee”).

Likewise, with a responsory, a procession is customarily made to the holy cross at Vespers and at morning Lauds.

To the hymns of all the Hours, as at Easter, the verse *Da nobis illuc sedula devotione tendere* (“Grant us to strive toward that place with diligent devotion”) is added, as well as *Gloria tibi, Domine, qui scandis* (“Glory to you, Lord, who ascend”). This continues until Pentecost.

At the octave, however, at morning Lauds and Vespers, the same collect is always to be said first, *Concede, quaesumus* (“Grant, we beseech you”). It is not observed on the following Sunday alone.

Since there are not many collects for the Ascension, suitable collects from Easter are also selected for the other Hours, such as *Omnipotens sempiterne Deus, deduc* (“Almighty and everlasting God, lead…”), and *Deus, qui ad aeternam vitam* (“O God, who [have called us] to eternal life”), and so forth.

The preface *Qui post Resurrectionem* (“Who, after the Resurrection”), and so forth, is said no more than on the first day at both Masses, and on the octave at both Masses.

It should be noted that the psalm *Ad Dominum* (“To the Lord”), which together with the psalm *Voce mea* (“With my voice”) is customarily said in the twelve readings as the office for the dead, is not to be said in this solemnity or in similar ones, because in ancient times the office was not performed on such days.

## CHAPTER XXIII. The Vigil of Pentecost
In the vigil of Pentecost, after the chapter-reading they speak; after Terce they keep silence; after Sext they go to their beds in the same manner as they do during the Rogations, until the beginning of the office that is to begin before None. Its first reading is “God tested”; this is followed by the collect without a greeting, “O God, who in Abraham.” The second reading is “Moses wrote.” Tract: “Give ear, O heaven.” Collect: “O God, who through the prophets.” The third reading is “Seven women shall take hold.” Tract: “A vineyard was planted.” Collect: “O God, who bring us to the heavenly [realm].” The fourth reading is “Hear, O Israel.” Collect: “Unchangeable God.” Tract: “As the deer.” Collect: “Grant, we beseech you.”

The litany is sung in the same manner as at the vigils of Easter; the Mass itself likewise follows that pattern in every respect, except that it has the chant for the offertory, and that the Agnus Dei is to be said together with the Communion. They dine before Vespers. At Vespers, as on Holy Saturday, no psalms other than the ferial ones are to be said, namely “Let them confess”; collect: “Grant, we beseech you,” etc.

## CHAPTER XXIV. On Pentecost itself and the following week

As is fitting, no less honor is given to the coming of the Holy Spirit than to the Lord’s Resurrection. Whatever was performed out of reverence for the solemnity on that night and on that day is also to be performed on this occasion; only at Matins, after each antiphon, its melody is not repeated with the Alleluia in the same way.

For the evening procession: a responsory. For the morning procession: a responsory. On the day itself, for that procession, no chant other than those antiphons from Easter is sung as far as the church vestibule; there, omitting the verse “Crucified,” the station is held with the antiphon “Today they have been fulfilled.” At the entrance to the church and at the holy Cross: the responsory “They appeared to the apostles”; in the choir: the responsory “The Holy Spirit.”

Although all the Gauls do not greatly value the sequences of the Germans, nevertheless, through the efforts of blessed Father Odilo, who also supported it among our own people, this one alone—“May the grace of the Holy Spirit be with us”—has obtained that it should be sung at our place on this day.

At its Vespers, “Alleluia” is sung over the psalms as the antiphon “They were speaking.” At Matins on Monday: “When they were all together.” At Terce: “Filled.” Since these three antiphon melodies, once they have received their place, are not changed, at the other hours other antiphons are sung, both from Easter, and from the Gospel, and from the Ascension of the Lord. In these, no other arrangement is observed unless the precentor makes provision for it and points it out to the one who is assigning the chants, so that none may be left which is not sung again by us during this week, as though each were bidding a final farewell.

The hymns of the hours once again do not lack an added verse, namely “Christ, now most merciful,” and “Let praise be to the Father.”

## CHAPTER XXV. On the eighth day of Pentecost

The eighth day of Pentecost is celebrated not so much as an eighth day as in commemoration of the Holy Trinity. At its first Vespers also—something rarely done on other occasions—one antiphon from the Holy Trinity is sung over each psalm.

The chapter-reading both at Vespers and at Lauds, and also at Terce, is “Blessing, and splendor, and wisdom.” Hymn: “O blessed light of the Trinity.” After the Gospel “There was a man of the Pharisees” has been proclaimed, no homily on it is read; instead, there is a sermon of Saint Gregory Nazianzen, namely “On today’s solemnity.”

There is a procession with a responsory to the holy Cross, as also after Lauds. At Nocturns: “You, unity of the Trinity.” At Lauds: “Splendor of the Father’s glory,” though with a more solemn melody than usual.

Although the melodies of those hymns sung at Easter are so plain and straightforward, and on the very sacred day of the Lord’s Resurrection are no more solemn than if the same hymns belonged to some, so to speak, ordinary day, this practice, handed down to us through the simplicity of our elders, is still maintained. If there were a suitable person who might suggest and urge this upon the lord abbot, perhaps he would order it corrected, as he has already done with many other matters.

On the aforementioned day, the morning Mass is of the Holy Spirit; at it the preface “Who, ascending above all the heavens” is not omitted, just as it is said at both Masses throughout the preceding week. For the procession through the cloister and the station in the church vestibule, the same chant is sung as on the preceding Sunday at the holy Cross; then they return to the choir with responsories concerning the Holy Trinity.

The principal Mass is of the Holy Trinity, but without a Gradual and with two Alleluias. At Sext: chapter-reading “The grace of our Lord”; collect “Lord God, almighty Father.” At None: “Everything that is born,” or alternatively “There are three who bear witness”; collect “Our minds, we beseech you, Lord.”

At Second Vespers, the final antiphon over the psalms contains no other words than those of the chapter-reading, “Blessing and splendor.” Therefore the chapter-reading is changed so that “Blessed be God and Father” is said. An antiphon of the Holy Spirit is sung, “Today they have been fulfilled”; of the holy Cross—or rather, of the Lord’s Resurrection—“Christ, having risen,” with the appropriate collects that follow.

## CHAPTER XXVI. On the week following the octave of Pentecost

**Question.** Do you observe an octave of the Holy Trinity?

**Answer.** Not at all. Nevertheless, the principal Mass is sung throughout the entire week as a Mass of the Holy Trinity, and at Vespers an antiphon is sung over the Gospel canticle.

Once Sunday alone has passed, we immediately return to the four psalms to be said at each hour and to asking forgiveness at the beginnings of the hours. At Nocturns on ordinary nights, nothing more is read than what Saint Benedict prescribes: one very short reading with a corresponding responsory.

There is another practice established for the Monday of this week. Since however many of the dead are buried at our place, the lord abbot has specifically ordained that their memory should on this occasion be observed with the greatest devotion. The same is customarily done throughout all our houses by his command.

For this purpose, after regular Vespers and the suffrages of the saints, before proceeding to the church of Saint Mary, all the bells having been rung at length, Vespers for the faithful departed are celebrated in the choir, and afterward the office is performed in the same manner. On the following day, the morning Mass is to be celebrated with greater devotion, and private Masses are to be sung by all the priests for the same persons.

At Masses, at Vespers, at the office, and first at Lauds, the collect “O God, by whose mercy” is to be said. Twelve poor people are to be abundantly refreshed with bread and wine, together with an addition of meat; and mercy is to be shown by providing bread and wine to all other poor people who arrive.

## CHAPTER XXVII. On the Ember fast in June

Before proceeding farther, we must also remember the Ember fast. Since it occurs four times in the year, on each occasion the principal Mass on its Saturday is not preceded by a litany, nor are more collects than those belonging to the office to be said at it; neither is an offering made nor the peace received except by one person; nor are unconsecrated hosts provided in the refectory, as is customary on other ordinary days.

This fast, which takes place in June, is never observed before Pentecost, even if its regular appointed time occurs earlier; but if it falls within Pentecost week, it is not postponed.

**Question.** And how do you then do both things, the fast and the solemnity?

**Answer.** In this we make no mistake. To begin with, on the first day of the fast—that is, Wednesday—after the chapter-reading everyone sits in the cloister for reading. When it seems appropriate, the signal is rung for Terce. After the prayer has been said, they put on white garments, and after Terce, copes.

The office “The Spirit of the Lord” is sung. For it, however, a ferial reading from the Acts of the Apostles and the ferial Gospel are read. After Sext they go up to the dormitory as though to rest. When the signal has been heard, they come down, wash their hands and face, and enter the church. After the prayer, and after the priest has been vested with his assistants, the office “O God, when you went forth” is appointed.

Since two readings are given at it, two collects are also said, and no more. The first reading is from the Book of Wisdom; the Gospel concerns the five thousand men who were fed with five loaves and two fish. The chant “Alleluia” is not sung at all, but only the responsory, or what others call the Gradual.

They eat once, after None, and abstain from fat. On the days of fasting that follow, nothing is to be done differently, except that they do not generally put on copes or white garments, and the collects said on ordinary days are not omitted at the principal Mass.

If this same fast happens outside Pentecost, nevertheless no offices other than those customarily belonging to Pentecost are sung. On the Saturday, after the offertory, the person who has sung the responsory and read the reading, apart from the Epistle, while wearing white, customarily removes his garment.

The cantor who leads the choir, wearing a cope, does not prostrate himself while the others kneel for prayer; and for the prayer that takes place before None he leaves the choir.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. On the feasts of the saints occurring after Pentecost

**Question.** On ordinary nights at Nocturns, if a reading such as you described above is assigned continually, how do you observe the commemoration of saints for whom twelve readings are nevertheless not performed?

**Answer.** You advise well. For saints of this kind, three readings are indeed given, with three responsories as well. These readings are excerpted from some sermon or homily that seems especially suitable for the occasion. It was not done in this way, however, during the Easter season: if three responsories were sung for saints, the readings were nevertheless taken from the book that was to be read during that week.

And, to add something further concerning these same saints, at Nocturns neither the hymn nor the ferial psalms are changed on their account. The invitatory, chapter-reading, verse, and collects concerning them are to be said. At Lauds, the antiphons are certainly changed for them, and the individual psalms are assigned according to the saints concerned; at the remaining hours the antiphons continue until the Mass office. With the office, their commemoration is entirely closed and completed. Afterward, at the hours that follow the office, there are neither antiphons nor anything else concerning them.

But if it happens that their memory is to be observed on a Sunday, after regular Vespers on Saturday, antiphons concerning them are sung, followed by a collect. At Nocturns, together with the invitatory and the Gospel, the four final readings are about them; afterward they are treated fully at Lauds and in the morning Mass. In all other respects, what belongs to Sunday is observed.

It should also be known that on ordinary days, whatever collect concerning the saints has been said at Vespers is not changed at Lauds, Terce, or the principal Mass.

## CHAPTER XXIX. On the fasts customarily observed on Wednesday and Friday

If our weakness permitted it, it would be fitting, according to the ordinance of our teacher Saint Benedict, for us to fast immediately after the octave of Pentecost on every Wednesday and Friday. Nevertheless, we do not entirely omit this practice: we observe it in some manner on one of the aforementioned weekdays and on its eve.

On that day we keep silence after Terce. After Sext we go up to the dormitory, pretending rather than actually taking a midday rest, because the signal is soon rung for us to return to the church, where we are to make a barefoot procession. We remove our shoes in the cloister near the channels, so that our feet will be ready to be washed.

The procession begins in the same way as during the Rogations, with prayers, an antiphon, a psalm, and a collect. All the bells are not rung, but only two. It begins before the entrance of the boys. Thus, singing something for sins, such as the antiphon “Be merciful,” and another, “Have mercy, Lord,” we proceed through the cemetery to the church of Saint Mary. At its entrance, both the chant and the collect concern our Lady.

We kneel on the forms for prayer. The lord abbot appoints Psalm 145 for those buried in the cemetery, and the priest follows with the collect “O Lord, by whose mercy.” The litany begins, proclaimed by two persons, and with it we come through the cloister and the church vestibule into the choir.

As has already been stated, we fast on the first day; afterward, in place of fasting, we frequently undertake some manual work. Whenever we fast in summer for any reason, the practice of silence after Terce and of ascending to the dormitory during Sext is not changed.

If it is Wednesday or Friday, we make the barefoot procession as I have just described, with the sole exceptions of the vigils of the holy apostles Peter and Paul and of the Assumption of Saint Mary—provided, of course, that these should happen to fall on such a day.

The practice is also suspended if we bury one of the dead, or if a person of such rank and dignity arrives that we make a procession for him, or if we send our large reliquary chests containing the relics of the saints to one of our villages, as often happens because of fear of plunder and robbery. In such cases we all go out wearing white garments, after all the bells have been rung, as far as the outer gate, and we show the same reverence when bringing them back.

## CHAPTER XXX. On manual work

**Question.** You touched briefly on manual work. Say a little more about it; tell me, I mean, what this manual work is and how it is done.

**Answer.** Certainly. So that I do not lie about what I have often seen, it was nothing other than removing new beans, not yet fully ripe, from their pods; or pulling weeds and useless plants from the garden, including those that choked the good plants; and sometimes shaping loaves in the bakery.

To explain how this is done: on the day appointed for it, as soon as the brothers have risen and the prayers have been said, the signal is rung for Prime. Omitting the other psalms, the litany alone follows, and then the morning Mass. The chapter-reading is also shortened more than on other days.

They do not go to Saint Mary with psalmody, as is customary, but after the board has been struck and “Bless” has been said beforehand, the lord abbot announces: “Let us go to manual work.” The psalmody that was interrupted after Prime is appointed. They proceed in procession, with the boys first and the priors last.

When they have reached the place of work, everyone turns toward the east and takes his place in order.
