At the end of one psalm they bow forward and backward; then, with the lord abbot proclaiming it, they say this verse: “O God, come to my assistance,” etc. This is followed by “Lord, have mercy,” the Lord’s Prayer, and the verse “Our help.” After bowing again, they begin to work.

This is the psalmody sung while they work: first, what remained after Prime and after the chapter-reading; afterward, all the regular hours in the canonical manner, beginning with Prime. During these prayers, Psalm 5 is also inserted, together with the seven psalms divided among the other hours. The three that remain are said in their entirety during the prayers of Compline.

Before Compline itself, Vespers for the faithful departed are held. The psalms that are customarily said for relatives after Terce and after the two hours that follow are appended.

If the lord abbot decides that they should work longer, the psalmody is extended with the psalm “To the Lord, when I was in distress,” through to the end of the Psalter; then “Glory be to the Father,” etc., is also said from the beginning, inserted after three psalms.

When the psalms for relatives have been completed, the lord abbot, whenever he wishes, signals the brothers to stop working and orders them to come closer to him. He commands that something be read, but something to be finished quickly, because he himself is going to give a sermon on it. He speaks about some subject of this kind, especially concerning the life of the Fathers, that will edify the hearers.

When this is finished, the psalmody is appointed again and they return to work. As soon as the boys reach the threshold of the cloister, they raise the volume of their voices. They do not stop in the chapter-house until the community is before the chapter-house. When the lord abbot proclaims the verse “Our help,” everyone bows forward and backward; then, after “Bless” has again been said beforehand, they are given permission to speak.

Thus None is also accelerated more than on other days. Once the time for speaking has arrived, they are compelled to return again to manual work.

This is the psalmody they then undertake: first, the psalms for relatives, which are customarily said after Vespers; Vespers of All Saints; Vespers for the faithful departed, with the antiphons of the Office for the Dead, without Lauds, which are always reserved for the night: “O God, give ear”; “My words.”

Afterward they begin the psalmody at the point where they had interrupted it previously. When they have returned, a sermon is customarily given in the cloister on that occasion. Rising from it and bowing forward and backward, with the lord abbot proclaiming the words in full, they again say this verse: “Blessed are you, Lord God.” This is followed by “Lord, have mercy” with the customary addition, and finally the verse “Our help.” After they have bowed forward and backward, permission to speak is given.

If the lord abbot thinks that they should drink after the work is finished, after the signal has been rung for Vespers and they have prayed, they go to the refectory when the cymbal is struck, and a drink made with honey, wine, and wormwood is served. It should be known that whenever this happens, afterward they do not drink during Collation, as they sometimes do.

But if they work only once, the sermon is held in the cloister, and the verse is not delayed, so that “Blessed are you, Lord” is said immediately. And if twelve readings are to be given on the following night, they do not work twice.

If they go to the bakery to make bread, on account of this work they do not postpone the psalms for relatives or the seven psalms that follow Prime. After the chapter-reading everyone washes his hands, but does not dry them; then, with the psalmody appointed, they proceed to the bakery.

The boys—or anyone who has healthy hands—do not handle anything made from the kneaded flour. Those who shape the loaves afterward do not touch their faces at all, whatever sweat may be on them, nor do they open their mouths for the psalmody, lest some saliva should leap into the dough.

No mention is customarily made of a sermon then, nor is that manual work closed with any other verse than “Our help is in the name of the Lord.”

## CHAPTER XXXI. On the third Sunday after Pentecost and its week

After the commemoration of the Holy Trinity, on the first Sunday that occurs, responsories from the Book of Kings are sung until the Kalends of August. Then they are taken from the Book of Solomon until the Kalends of September.

Once these have been sung on one occasion, on the other Sundays at Nocturns the third, seventh, and eleventh responsories are sung concerning the Holy Trinity; the fourth, eighth, and twelfth are the shorter ones, such as “The earth is the Lord’s.” Similar ones are also sung if a feast of a saint with twelve readings is observed, provided that it is not one of the greater feasts but one of the kind represented by any Sunday.

This applies not only during this season but always afterward whenever Easter has occurred. Concerning this Sunday and its week, it is not irrelevant if I say somewhat more than about the others, because some practices used on these days in divine service are also maintained on every Sunday and throughout every week until the Advent of the Lord, unless they are changed for some feast.

First, at Vespers on Saturday, the chapter-reading is “Blessed be God.” This is always the same both on ordinary days and at Sunday Vespers.

On the following nights there are three invitatories in rotation, namely “In your hand” and “Let us adore the Lord.” For the canticles: “Alleluia” as the antiphon “From Zion.” At Lauds over the three psalms: “Alleluia,” such as the antiphon “I say to you.” Proper antiphons are used for the canticle of the three young men. For the following psalm: “Alleluia,” as the antiphon “In the Lord he will be praised.” Chapter-reading: “Blessing and splendor.”

At Prime: “Alleluia,” as the antiphon “It is a garden enclosed.” Chapter-reading: “To the King of ages.” Collect of the Holy Trinity, which is always to be said at this hour and on this day throughout the whole year and is not to be changed for any feast, however important.

After the consecration of salt and water: antiphon “Sprinkle me.” At the procession’s departure for the church of Saint Mary: an antiphon or responsory concerning her. Through the cloister, one of these three antiphons: “When we have come”; “Let us pray, our most beloved”; “Almighty God, we beseech you.” If something further must be added, the antiphon “Forgive us, Lord.”

At the station in the church vestibule: the antiphon “May God bless us,” or some responsory concerning the Holy Trinity. Returning to the choir: an antiphon or responsory concerning the holy apostles Peter and Paul.

At Terce: “Alleluia,” as the antiphon “Virgin of Christ.” Chapter-reading: “God is love.” At Sext: “Alleluia,” as the antiphon “Among those born.” Chapter-reading: “Each must bear the other’s burden.” At None: “Alleluia,” as the antiphon “They nodded”; chapter-reading “For you were bought.” Collect at Sext and None: “O God, who behold”; “We beseech you, your grace.”

On ordinary nights, the chapter-reading at Nocturns is “Watch.” At Lauds: “The night has passed.” At Prime: chapter-reading “Peace and truth”; collect “Lord God, Father, who in the beginning.” Both of these are so fixed on ordinary days that they are never separated from them.

At Terce: chapter-reading “Heal me, Lord.” At Sext and None, the same as on Sunday; the collects are those marked in the collectary. At Compline: chapter-reading “But you are among us”; collect “Visit us, we beseech you.” These are immovable, so that whether the day is ordinary or solemn, they are never changed.

If the day is not Sunday but nevertheless has twelve readings, the collect at Prime is “At this hour of this day, we beseech you.” I have passed over what is more familiar, such as the antiphon over the Gospel canticle at Vespers on Saturday, “She is like a sister”; the responsory from the same book; and at Lauds and Second Vespers, material from the Gospel—or the fact that on ordinary nights at Lauds there is material from that canticle, and at Vespers again from the Gospel.

On that Saturday whose following night begins some responsories, the ferial responsory is not sung at Vespers; instead, one of the responsories about to be begun is sung.

If you remember what I mentioned above in other places, then, even without my saying it now, you can know that the collect belonging to each Sunday is to be said on Saturday at Vespers, after Nocturns at the Gospel, at Lauds, at the morning Mass, at Terce, at the principal Mass, and at both Vespers.

On ordinary nights, the collectary contains the collects to be said at Nocturns, Lauds, and Vespers. And if the priest wishes not to be criticized, he should take care not to say one that is unknown, but one that suitably imitates the Gregorian style, both in its modesty and in the humility of its words.

## CHAPTER XXXII. On the Nativity of Saint John the Baptist

Among those born of women, according to the Lord’s own testimony, no one has arisen greater than John the Baptist. It is therefore not unfitting that his solemnity should also be celebrated more solemnly than those of other saints.

His Nativity is celebrated with an octave. There are no more saints for whom this is done; only four other feasts are observed in the same way: the Nativity of the holy apostles Peter and Paul, the Translation of Saint Benedict, the Assumption of Saint Mary, and the Burial of Saint Martin.

To state first what they all have in common: on the first night, after Lauds and the preceding Vespers, a procession is made to each of their altars, except on the Nativity of the apostles Peter and Paul, whose honor is represented by the principal altar itself. It is performed with some responsory, followed by some collect, pronounced in the tonal manner.

Throughout the week of each feast, forgiveness is not requested at the beginnings of the hours, nor do they kneel on the forms for the prayers. Likewise, at each hour no less psalmody is omitted than during the Easter season whenever twelve readings were not performed.

The eighth day is entirely solemn and is to be conducted with twelve readings. If a Sunday occurs during it, nothing other than material concerning the saints themselves is read or sung.

On ordinary nights, even if it is the summer season, three readings are nevertheless given with three responsories. The principal collect that was said on the first day at the principal Mass is afterward always to be said until the eighth day at Lauds, Terce, the principal Mass, and Vespers.

The preface, however, is said only on the first day at both Masses, and on the eighth day only at the principal Mass.

This is the one point in which the Nativity of Saint John and the Translation of Saint Benedict differ from the others: on the eighth night, the final responsories of Nocturns are among the shorter ones, such as “The righteous shall flourish like the palm.” This is nevertheless common to all the same feasts that occur in summer: if a Sunday intervenes, similar responsories are sung.

Having briefly stated what, as I said, they commonly share, we must now consider what properly belongs to the commemoration of Saint John.

At Vespers of the vigil: collect “Grant, we beseech you, almighty God, that your household.” At the Gospel during the night: “Grant, we beseech you, almighty God.” This is also repeated throughout the octave.

At Lauds: “O God, who have brought this day”; this is repeated at Terce, at Mass, and at Vespers, where it is entirely concluded.

I do not know whether I can say anything that you do not already know from what I related above concerning the solemnities.

**Question.** I have not forgotten those matters. Nevertheless, there is something I would still gladly hear: in what order are the antiphons said at Nocturns and at the other hours during the octave?

**Answer.** I did not fail to ask this also of the brother whom I mentioned above. I know nothing else about these octaves or the others except what he told me again. As evidence of his testimony: if the solemnity of the day occurs, for example, on Friday, then on the following Saturday, in the first Nocturn over the psalms, the antiphon is “Before I formed you.” The second antiphon is “For all things.”

At Lauds again over the psalms: “Elizabeth, of Zechariah.” Over the Gospel canticle: “They nodded to his father.” At Prime: “Do not be afraid.” At Terce: “The Lord sent.” At Sext: “Behold, I have appointed.” At None: “The Lord from the womb.” At Vespers: “John is his name.” At the Magnificat: “Because you did not believe.”

On Sunday, in the first Nocturn: “He made my mouth.” In the second: “He who formed me.” At the canticle and at Lauds: material concerning Saints John and Paul. After the Gospel canticle: “His mouth was opened.” At Prime: “Elizabeth.” At Terce: “They nodded.” At Sext: “Among those born.” At None: “And you, child.” At Vespers: “From the womb of old age.” At the Magnificat: “And they all placed.”

On Monday, in the first Nocturn: “He made my mouth.” In the second: “He who formed me.” At Lauds: material concerning Saint Irenaeus and his companions. Concerning Saint John: the antiphon “He shall be called John.” At Sext: “Kings shall see.” At None: “He shall be called a Nazarene.” At Vespers: “He himself shall go before him”; also “The child who has been born.”

On Tuesday, in the first Nocturn: “For he shall be great.” In the second: “Among those born.” At Lauds: material concerning Saint Leo; concerning Saint John: “You, child.” The morning Mass is of Saint Leo. Therefore at Prime alone there is an antiphon concerning him; at Terce, “John is his name”; at Sext, “He himself shall go before him”; at None, “From the womb.”

At Vespers the material is not concerning Saint John, but Saint Peter; the first antiphon is “Blessed will you be.” For this reason the octave offices are also changed, so that nothing more is said concerning Saint John except after regular Lauds and Vespers: one antiphon and one collect.

Nevertheless, his eighth day is celebrated in full, both with twelve antiphons at Nocturns and with twelve readings and responsories.

## CHAPTER XXXIII. On the Nativity of the apostles Peter and Paul

The vigil of the Nativity of the holy apostles and the vigil of the Assumption of Saint Mary have something distinctive, something not customarily done at any other vigil of the saints. At the principal Mass all the bells are rung, and, apart from the fact that the angelic Hymn and the Alleluia are not sung, everything else is performed solemnly.

The choir, as they say, is led by one person in a cope. The responsory is sung by two persons in copes. The subdeacon is vested in a tunic, the deacon in a dalmatic; one person makes the offering, and all receive the peace. “Lord, have mercy,” the Sanctus, and the Agnus Dei are each sung with the ordinary melody.

At the first vigil, as I mentioned above, there is the Burial of Saint Leo the pope; at the following one, the Burial of Saint Eusebius the priest. A morning Mass is sung for them. Nevertheless, the general offering is not omitted, and the peace is received by one person.

After the first collect, all the remaining collects are for the dead. The same is customarily done whenever the same Mass is celebrated for the welfare of the living. It is not, however, customary ever to do this when there are twelve readings.

But let us return to the Nativity of the holy apostles. Some years ago the lord abbot decreed that these antiphons should be sung over the psalms of Nocturns, the first of which is “In the streets.”

The Gospel is followed by the collect that was said at Vespers, namely “O God, who taught your Church through your apostle Peter,” although at Lauds and at the principal Mass the collect “O God, who on this day” is said. If this should occasionally occur, it does not prejudice the general custom concerning collects: whenever collects of this kind are said at Vespers, they are also said at Lauds and at the other corresponding times.

On the day itself, when the procession is to be performed solemnly, if it is Sunday, it takes place before Terce. I think this is because the consecration of salt and water is to be carried out according to custom. If it is any other weekday, it takes place after Terce. The same practice is observed for the Assumption of Saint Mary and the Nativity of the Lord.

For the procession itself, the responsory “What do people say?” is customarily sung, and another, “The great Saint Paul.” At the station: the antiphon “Today has dawned for us?” Returning to the choir: the responsory “Whatever you bind”; another, “Saint Paul.”

The hymns of the hours are enlarged by the verse “You, just ones of the age,” etc.

Second Vespers is celebrated jointly for both apostles, but a collect is to be said separately for each: first for Saint Peter, then for Saint Paul, with the corresponding antiphon and collect.

The collect said at the principal Mass on the first day is changed to: “O God, who taught your Church through the preaching of your apostles Peter and Paul.” It is to be said throughout the week of the octave.

Since their individual commemoration is also observed on the following day, the collect at the morning Mass is for Saint Peter alone. At Lauds and Vespers there are an antiphon and collect for Saint Peter, just as there are at these hours for Saint John, though for John they are said without a greeting.

The third day is also the eighth day of the Nativity of Saint John the Baptist. On it we commonly commemorate both apostles at the aforementioned times, not on the fourth day according to the reckoning that we proposed above, for example, since it is Saturday.

In the first Nocturn: antiphon “Take my yoke upon you.” In the second: “For my yoke.” Responsories 1 and 3 are of Saint Peter; 2 is of Saint Paul.

At Lauds: “The apostle Peter and Paul.” At the Benedictus: “Unseparated faith.” At Prime: antiphon “Into all the earth.” At Terce: “I no longer call you servants.”

The Mass office, with all its appendages, is no different from a general office of the apostles, as on the other days within the octave, except for the collect, which alone properly concerns Saint Peter and Saint Paul.

At Sext: antiphon “For they will hand you over.” At None: “Rejoice and exult.” At Vespers: “Glorious princes of the earth.” At the Magnificat: “These are holy men.”

On Sunday, in the first Nocturn: antiphon “The apostle Peter.” In the second: “Unseparated faith.” At the canticle: “You who have left everything.” At Lauds: “Blessed are the peacemakers.” At the Benedictus: “The holy and true light.” At Prime: “This is my commandment.” At Terce: “Greater love.” At Sext: “You are my friends.” At None: “In your patience.” At Vespers: “At the regeneration.” At the Magnificat: “O doorkeeper of heaven.”

On Monday: the Translation of Saint Martin. Although at Nocturns the other responsories, together with all the antiphons, concern his life, the third, seventh, and eleventh concern matters belonging to any confessor; the same applies to those antiphons at Lauds.

On Tuesday, in the first Nocturn: antiphon “Princes of the peoples.” In the second: “For they will hand you over.” At Lauds: “This is my commandment.” At Prime: “Greater love.” At Terce: “You are my friends.” At Sext: “Blessed are the peacemakers.” At None: “In your patience.” At Vespers: “Blessed will you be.” At the Magnificat: “These are the two olive trees.”

On Wednesday, since it is the eighth day and is to be conducted with twelve readings, both the antiphons and the responsories at Nocturns alternate between these two apostles.

Since I found this in no antiphonary, I took care to note it from the brief itself, and so I also communicate it to your affection.

At Nocturns:

1. “In the streets.”
2. “He who worked.”
3. “Peter said.”
4. “I know whom I have believed.”
5. “The apostle Peter.”
6. “For me to live.”
7. “It came to pass.”
8. “You are a chosen vessel.”
9. “When Peter arrived.”
10. “The great Saint Paul.”
11. “Peter placing.”
12. “The good fight.”

Responsory 5: “You are the shepherd of the sheep.”  
6: “There is laid up for me.”  
7: “I have prayed for you.”  
8: “Saint Paul.”

Antiphon: “Glorious princes of the earth.”

Responsory 9: “Blessed are you, Simon Bar-Jonah.”  
10: “The great Saint Paul.”  
11: “Whatever you bind.”  
12: “These are the two olive trees.”

At Lauds: antiphons “The apostle Peter and Paul,” etc.; “O doorkeeper of heaven,” etc.; “At the regeneration”; “Unseparated faith”; “The holy and true light.”

## CHAPTER XXXIV. On the Translation of Saint Benedict our Father
The deposition of our master, Saint Benedict, falls during Lent. It is therefore not appropriate, on his account, to celebrate it with an octave, since on that occasion we cannot properly do what we do at his translation and celebrate it with an octave. Concerning how that translation took place, and what sort of person brought his holy bones into Gaul, we are not without clear testimony in written sources. On the first night, and on the other nights of the octave, the very beautiful sermon of Lord Odo on this same Father is read at the nocturns.

But, to return to matters that are clearer, let us proceed [Col. 0682D] to the order of the antiphons to be sung at each hour throughout the octave. In this matter someone like me could easily make a mistake if he did not have something written down somewhere beforehand. Therefore, so that we may keep to the calendar once begun, the feast in question, if it falls on Monday or Tuesday, is arranged as follows.

At the first nocturn: antiphon, *Fuit vir vitae* (“There was a man of life”); at the second, *Ab ipso pueritiae* (“From his very boyhood”); at matins and lauds, antiphon, *Beatus vir Benedictus* (“Blessed is the man Benedict”); another, *Erat vir Domini* (“There was a man of the Lord”); at prime, *Dum in hac terra* (“While he was in this land”); at terce, *Liberiori genere* (“Of a freer family”); at sext, *Relicta domo* (“Having left his home”); at none, *Recessit igitur* (“He therefore withdrew”); at vespers, *Hic itaque* (“This man, then”); another, *Sanctissime confessor* (“Most holy confessor”).

On Wednesday, at the first nocturn: antiphon, *Compassus* (“Moved with compassion”); at the second, *Expetitus a fratribus* (“Sought by the brothers”); at matins and lauds, *Erat vir Domini* (“There was a man of the Lord”); another, *Gloriosus confessor* (“Glorious confessor”); at prime, [Col. 0683A] *Cumque sibi conspicerent* (“And when they perceived for themselves”); at terce, *Inito consilio* (“Having taken counsel”); at sext, *Tunc ad locum* (“Then to the place”); at none, *Tantam gratiam* (“So great a grace”); at vespers, *Qui dum eremum pergeret* (“While he was proceeding to the desert”); another, *O beati viri Benedicti* (“O [feast] of blessed Benedict”).

On Thursday, at the first nocturn: *Fuit vir vitae* (“There was a man of life”); at the second, *Ab ipso* (“From him”); at matins and lauds, *Gloriosus confessor* (“Glorious confessor”); another, *Vir Domini* (“Man of the Lord”); at prime, *Dum in hac terra esset* (“While he was in this land”); and the rest as on Tuesday, except at the *Magnificat*: *Orabat S. Benedictus* (“Saint Benedict was praying”).

On Sunday, at the first nocturn: *Fuit vir vitae* (“There was a man of life”); at the second, *Compassus* (“Moved with compassion”); at the canticles, *Hic itaque* (“This man, then”); at matins and lauds, *Puer quidam parvulus* (“A certain little boy”); at prime, *Beatus vir Benedictus* (“Blessed is the man Benedict”); at terce, *Vir Domini* (“Man of the Lord”); at sext, *Gloriosus* (“Glorious”); at none, *Vir Domini* (“Man of the Lord”); at vespers, *Oramus te* (“We beseech you”); another, *Exsultet omnium* (“Let all rejoice”), and so forth.

Concerning the eighth day, I have nothing else to report beyond what I have already stated above. There is, however, one point I have not yet mentioned: at second vespers, over the psalms, the four antiphons that were used at the first nocturn are sung. This is customary not only on this feast but also on others, when the antiphons of the nocturns are more like these—drawn from the lives of the saints—than from the text and subject matter of the psalms.

[Col. 0683B]

## CHAPTER XXXV. The blessing of grapes and other fruits

In many missal books there is a blessing of grapes, especially for the feast of Saint Sixtus, martyr and pope. But if they are not yet ripe, the church custodian watches for the time when they first ripen, so that he may have them brought to the church. Once brought, he presents them to the sacristan, [Col. 0683C] and the sacristan, during the canon at the appropriate and previously appointed moment, [Note: [Col. 0683] “Previously appointed,” namely, Acherius says, with reference to the words “Through whom, Lord, you create all these good things,” and so forth.] presents them to the priest so that he may bless them.

Afterward they are distributed by the priest in the refectory in place of the wafers. This is not omitted even if the day is Sunday. There are also three other kinds of things that are customarily blessed in the refectory: new beans, fresh bread, and must. The procedure is as follows. The reading is begun first; after its first verse, the priest stands in the middle of the refectory before the principal table, and, after the greeting, blesses each item. For the beans: “Bless, Lord, these fruits.” For the bread: “Bless, Lord, this creature of bread.” For the must: “Almighty Lord Jesus Christ, who with five loaves and two fish fed five thousand people,” and so forth.

## CHAPTER XXXVI. The Assumption of Saint Mary

[Col. 0683D]

At vespers on the vigil of the Assumption of Saint Mary: over the psalms, the antiphon *Tota pulchra es* (“You are wholly beautiful”); collect, *Deus qui Virginalem* (“O God, who [made] the virginal…”); at the evening procession, responsory *Super salutem* (“Beyond salvation”); the same collect as above. At the nocturns the sermon of Saint Jerome, *Cogitis me, o Paula* (“You compel me, O Paula”), is read. Although it is of such great excellence, the Gospel is not announced at the ninth lesson; rather, all the lessons are taken from that same sermon. Gospel: *Repleta est Spiritu* (“She was filled with the Spirit”); collect: *Veneranda nobis* (“Make [her] venerable for us”). The same is used for both subsequent processions. At [Col. 0684A] morning lauds, terce, and the principal Mass: collect, *Famulorum tuorum* (“[Hear] the prayer of your servants”), which is to be said throughout the entire octave. At the morning procession: responsory *Gaude, Maria* (“Rejoice, Mary”).

On the feast day: antiphon *Tota pulchra* (“You are wholly beautiful”). Through the cloister: responsory *Quae est ista* (“Who is this?”); another, *Ista est speciosa* (“This one is beautiful”); at the station, *Gaude, Maria* (“Rejoice, Mary”); at the entrance to the church, antiphon *Hodie beata virgo* (“Today the blessed Virgin”); responsory *Beata es virgo* (“Blessed are you, Virgin”). At the principal Mass the Creed is sung, as also at all feasts of blessed Mary. At vespers the psalms are *Dixit Dominus* (“The Lord said”), *Laetatus* (“I rejoiced”), *Nisi Dominus* (“Unless the Lord”), and *Memento* (“Remember”), except at the Purification of the Lord.

Concerning the order of the antiphons to be sung at all the hours throughout the octave, I do not think it necessary to say anything else except that at the nocturns of each night antiphons from the nocturns of the first night are also used, and likewise at morning lauds antiphons from the morning lauds. At the other hours these antiphons are customarily sung, the first of which is *Ecce tu pulchra es* (“Behold, you are beautiful”). The office throughout the octave is *Salve, sancta Parens* (“Hail, holy Mother”); on the eighth day, *Gaudeamus* (“Let us rejoice”). To all the hymns of the hours is added *Gloria tibi, Domine, qui natus* (“Glory to you, Lord, who were born”), and likewise to all feasts of Saint Mary.

## CHAPTER XXXVII. What is sung in September

In September, responsories from the Book of Job are sung for two Sundays. Likewise, for two Sundays, responsories are taken from the Books of Tobit, Judith, Esther, and Ezra. If some feast occurs on those Sundays and would prevent the responsories from the aforementioned books from being sung at their proper time, the feast itself is deferred to the following day for this reason, so that neither one nor the other need be omitted.

Here the responsories for the Holy Trinity are also omitted, as are the shorter ones from the Psalter, so that they are not sung at the nocturns among the other responsories. Here begins the practice that whenever responsories are sung at the nocturns or at morning lauds with *Gloria Patri* (“Glory to the Father”), *Sicut erat* (“As it was”) is added to them. Until now this was done from Easter until vespers; from this point onward, however, it is done not at vespers but, as stated, at the nocturns and morning lauds, until Easter comes again. It should nevertheless be understood that if a feast is celebrated in such a way that two people sing the first responsory together, this addition is not observed.

## CHAPTER XXXVIII. The Exaltation of the Holy Cross

[Col. 0684D]

At the Exaltation of the Holy Cross, as also at the Finding of the Cross, something is done contrary to the custom of other feasts. For although first vespers belong to the Holy Cross, at the nocturns all the psalms and eight lessons are taken from the saints; but then, over the canticles, there is again material concerning the Holy Cross: *Domine, audivi* (“Lord, I heard”). The first division occurs at the verse *Pro iniquitate* (“For iniquity”); the second at *Egressus est* (“He went out”). Afterward, not only the four final lessons and morning lauds, but all the remaining hours are devoted to the Holy Cross.

On the Exaltation itself, after terce has ended and before the Mass office begins, a cross covered with a pall is carried by two monks in albs before the principal altar. They uncover it and begin the antiphon *Ecce lignum crucis* (“Behold the wood of the cross”); everyone asks forgiveness, and, with carpets spread on the ground, they prostrate themselves and adore the cross in their albs. Meanwhile another antiphon follows the one just named, namely *Crucem tuam* (“Your cross”), which is repeated at each verse of the psalm *Deus misereatur* (“May God have mercy”), followed afterward by any other antiphons concerning the Holy Cross. Once the cross has been adored by the community, it is lifted while the antiphon *Super omnia* (“Above all things”) is sung, and forgiveness is again requested by everyone.

The psalms at vespers are *Dixit Dominus*, *Confitebor* (“I will confess”), and so forth. Over them the same antiphons are sung as at morning lauds, except that the first is omitted.

The most blessed Father, Lord Odilo, considered it highly appropriate that on the day when the cross was adored there should be a fast. For this reason he established—and almost as a lawful ordinance imposed upon our church—that if the Exaltation of the Holy Cross fell on a Wednesday, Friday, or Saturday, the date of the Ember fast should not be observed on that occasion but should immediately be kept during that same week.

It should further be known concerning the Holy Cross that a principal Mass is customarily sung for it every Friday, from the octave of Easter until the Advent of the Lord, and from the octave of Epiphany until Septuagesima, unless it is omitted because of the office of a saint, the office for a fast, or an octave. Nevertheless, the ferial Epistle or ferial Gospel is read.

## CHAPTER XXXIX. Eating only once from the Ides of September

[Col. 0685C]

From the Ides of September onward, we eat only once a day. On ordinary days we make no change to the arrangement that we followed throughout the summer whenever a fast occurred. Likewise, on days with twelve lessons, since we are to eat twice, we do everything as before.

## CHAPTER XL. Customs beginning on the Kalends of October and lasting until the Kalends of November

From the Kalends of October until the Kalends of November, responsories from the Book of Maccabees are sung. At the nocturns the hymn is *Primo dierum* (“At the beginning of the days”); at lauds, [Col. 0685D] *Aeterne rerum Conditor* (“Eternal Creator of things”). From this point onward the midday rest is entirely discontinued.

If there are twelve lessons, after dinner we sit in the cloister for reading until the servers have risen from the table. The greater bell is rung, and after prayer the lesser bell is rung so that None may be sung. We go to the refectory as usual to drink, but water is no longer served.

On ordinary days, when dawn appears, the bell is rung, and we immediately hurry to the church dressed in our nocturnal garments. After a brief prayer, we sing prime, followed by seven psalms and the litany. If it should sometimes happen, through the negligence of the church custodian, that the day is not yet bright, we sit in the choir with our heads covered, while the boys sit with their teachers in the chapterhouse, until we can read by the light of day. [Col. 0686A] We devote ourselves to reading until terce. The bell is rung, and only then do we put on our daytime shoes. After washing our hands and face and combing our hair, we go to the church and, prostrating ourselves in prayer, wait for the boys. When they enter, the bell is rung; we say three prayers, the bell is rung again, and terce is sung, together with the morning Mass.

We are permitted to speak not only after chapter but also after sext, although that interval is usually very brief. It lasts no longer than the time needed for the priest and the others who are to serve at the principal Mass to wash their hands and prepare to vest. The bell is rung so that we may all come together for prayer. When it is finished, the litany is begun, and those whom I mentioned above vest for the ministry of the Mass. [Col. 0686B] If it is Wednesday or Friday, we remove our shoes upon hearing the signal, before coming to prayer, so that we may make the procession barefoot.

When Mass has ended, the bell is rung for none, and we pray before going out to wash our feet. If it is not a day on which a procession takes place, we nevertheless wait in the choir, reading, until the servers have been able to eat dinner; then the bell is rung again for none. Although I have not yet said this, the same practice is observed throughout the summer whenever the day is a fast day.

## CHAPTER XLI. Customs in November

From the Kalends of November, responsories are sung from the [Col. 0686C] books of Ezekiel, Daniel, and the other minor prophets. On ordinary days, and when there are no octaves, once we have risen we do not return to bed. Here we again begin what was omitted from the Lord’s Supper: we sing thirty psalms before the nocturns.

Likewise, the Office of the Dead, which we perform until after vespers, we now customarily perform after the nocturns, with the Office of the Dead joined also to morning lauds. The remaining psalmody is sung, as usual, in the church of Saint Mary. It is joined continuously to regular morning lauds, beginning with the first psalm and its appendices.

Here too, if you wish to follow our order in every respect, you must remember that after the office has been performed at night, there is no [Col. 0686D] need, on days with twelve lessons, to sing after each hour the psalm *Ad Dominum cum* (“To the Lord when…”) in place of that office. Saint Majolus originally decreed that the psalm *De profundis* (“Out of the depths”) should be said together with the aforementioned psalm; but afterward Lord Abbot changed it to the psalm *Voce mea* (“With my voice”). He added that, if the office were performed at night, that psalm should nevertheless never be omitted on that account.

At times it is assigned not only for the office but also for the thirty-day commemoration of a brother recently deceased. If neither of these occasions occurs, it is nevertheless often sung after all the hours for the faithful departed.

The frequently mentioned Father, namely Lord Odilo, a man truly characterized by mercy, considered how difficult some of the brothers might find it to proceed barefoot in the severe cold of winter. Therefore, out of piety, he permitted such a procession on Wednesdays and Fridays from the Kalends of November until the beginning of Lent.

[Col. 0687A]

**Question.** I should like to know what sort of interval there is after the psalmody in the church of Saint Mary has been completed; what in particular is your work during that time; and where the community remains.

**Answer.** I shall answer each question briefly. The interval is regulated so that the cloister prior, together with the assistant, can walk around the entire cloister. He looks to see whether all the cloister doors are closed; he inspects the dormitory from end to end, and also the latrines. He goes to the infirmary to see in every respect how the sick are doing. He returns through the church of Saint Mary to the Greater Church. [Col. 0687B] He does not leave unvisited any altar to which one of the brothers might go, so that he may see who is there or what that person is doing.

The brothers, leaving the church of Saint Mary together—except for those who need to go to the latrines—return to the choir. Each sits in his own seat with his head covered. The young men who are under supervision sit beside their supervisors. Great care is taken that they do not sit together in such a way that they lack between them a trustworthy mediator of good reputation.

After covering his head, each person does whatever he thinks appropriate or is able to do. To recall myself as an example, sometimes I prayed with particular attention; sometimes I meditated on the psalms; sometimes I was so weighed down by sleep that, whether I wished it or not, I fell asleep while sitting there. [Col. 0687C] If anyone wishes to pray more privately, he rises and withdraws to an altar. He does not remain there long, however, so that another may likewise have a place to pray, since there are very few altars in comparison with the multitude of brothers.

In this diversity of occupations, perhaps many are not unlike me. The boys sit in the chapterhouse and learn the chant from one of the precentors. If the winter is extremely severe, there is a workshop in which a large fire is prepared by the brothers who served as cooks during the previous week. Everyone, both older and younger, may freely go there, though with the utmost seriousness, as is proper at such an hour.

From this point until the Lord’s Supper, on ordinary days the hymn of compline is always *Christe, qui lux es* (“Christ, who are the light”), provided that there are no octaves.

[Col. 0687D]

**Question.** But after vespers, when you neither eat dinner nor perform the Office of the Dead, what else do you do?

**Answer.** We go to the dormitory, put away our knives, remove our daytime shoes, and put on our nocturnal shoes. We sit in the cloister for reading. The bell is touched so that we may wash our hands and come to the refectory to drink. We sit again for reading, and the bell is rung for the collation.

You should also know for certain that, although it sometimes happens against our will—and never deliberately—that when we go to bed the light of day is not yet clearly gone, we are able to endure among other things such lengthy readings. These would surely be as burdensome to hear for certain of our [Col. 0688A] fellow soldiers, who wish to change both their ancestral customs and their very homeland, as a mass of lead would be to carry. It is no wonder that those who do not wish to sleep with us are likewise unwilling to keep vigil with us.

Since I have begun speaking of this, let me add what else I know of the same kind. On the feast of the holy apostles Peter and Paul, the nocturns and morning lauds are so lengthy that they always begin while it is still fully daylight and never end until it is still fully daylight. Since you can understand that on that day it would not be a late hour when we went to bed, it once occurred to me to mark the hour with a ray of sunlight. On the following day, when we sang none, I saw the ray in the same place, so that not even a moment separated the preceding compline from the following [Col. 0688B] none. Thus we were able to attend the vigils cheerfully and with some devotion, and it was not necessary, after being satisfied with sleep, to become oppressed by sleep again in the church.

Brothers who come to the monastery from outside have more than once been bound by this command and condition: they must never dare to arrive after compline. If a brother who was present at vespers in the cloister has neglected to eat before compline, he is not permitted to eat after compline for any reason, except if he is burdened by such an illness as, for example: on one occasion I saw the cellarer occupied all day receiving wine, [Col. 0688C] and he paid no attention at all to dinner. After compline he asked Lord Abbot for permission to eat, but obtained absolutely nothing; and so, whether he wished it or not, he went to bed without having eaten.

If you were to see at what hour we make every effort to sleep during Lent, you would certainly admit that we can rise early enough for the nocturns. I have said these things as though they were exceptional, so that you may know that we do not wish to spend the night in feasting.

## CHAPTER XLII. The feast of All Saints and the commemoration of all the faithful departed

[Col. 0688D]

At the feast of All Saints, at both vespers neither the psalms nor the antiphons are changed. As throughout the year we sing daily for them the psalms *Confitebor* (“I will confess”), *Credidi* (“I believed”), *In convertendo* (“When the Lord restored”), and *Eripe me* (“Deliver me”), so we do here. The hymn is also *Christe Redemptor* (“Christ the Redeemer”), but with music as solemn as the day itself is solemn.

The *Kyrie, eleison* (“Lord, have mercy”) before the Lord’s Prayer is also treated differently. On other days, at all the regular hours, we say it from both choirs; on this day, however, at vespers and morning lauds, we say it only twice. The same practice is followed throughout the year. At vespers and morning lauds no prayers are said other than these verses: *Post partum* (“After childbirth”); *In conspectu angelorum* (“In the presence of the angels”).

Although on the following day twelve lessons are held for Saint Caesarius and the other saints, after vespers all the bells are rung for a longer time, and the vespers of the dead are also sung. At night, after morning lauds of All Saints, the Office of the Dead is performed together with morning lauds, and a morning Mass is celebrated with the greatest solemnity for all the faithful departed; each priest also celebrates a private Mass for them.

[Col. 0689A]

At vespers and at the other offices, however, nothing more is said concerning the collects than one single collect, namely *Fidelium, Deus* (“O God of the faithful”). This was decreed by Father Odilo: just as a commemoration of All Saints is customarily made on the preceding day, so on the following day a commemoration of all the faithful departed is to be made. Anyone who has read his Life can learn there quite well why this pious Father established it.

To complete what remains, twelve poor people are to be abundantly fed with bread, wine, and meat. Any other poor people who arrive are all to receive mercy in the form of bread and wine. [Col. 0689B] Since our meal is, not without reason, more lavish because of all the saints than because of all the faithful departed, on the feast of All Saints whatever bread and wine remains at table is given as alms.

From this example Lord Abbot also derived the practice—which, if you remember, I mentioned elsewhere—that after the octave of Pentecost a special commemoration is made in each of our houses for those who are buried in that particular place.

## CHAPTER XLIII. The feast of Saint Martin and the customs that begin then

Our celebration of the feast of Saint Martin with an octave derives from the first abbot of our house, [Col. 0689C] our own Lord Odo. He was born at Tours, was a foster-son of Saint Martin, and was also a canon there. Accordingly, he himself composed the antiphons—not the ancient ones but new ones—that we now sing at the Deposition of the holy confessor and bishop; he himself composed the hymn; and he himself, as stated above, instituted the octave.

His Life is composed in a brilliant style and is especially admirable for its account of his virtues. Our holy Fathers did not wish, here as at the Assumption of Saint Mary, that any Gospel other than the Life itself should be announced at his Deposition, or that any homily other than the Life itself should be read.

To all the hymns of the hours this verse is added: *Martine, par apostolis* (“Martin, equal to the apostles”). If you wish to know again in what order the antiphons for the hours are sung throughout the octave, [Col. 0689D] we have no smaller supply of antiphons than at the aforementioned Assumption of Saint Mary. Therefore we customarily do now what we did then: we sing the ancient antiphons of the nocturns at the nocturns on the weekdays, and those from morning lauds at morning lauds. The new ones, which I have already said were dictated by Saintly Father Odo, we distribute among the daytime hours.

For the nocturns attached to the eighth day, since they have a complete office both in antiphons and in responsories, we sing the ancient ones on that occasion.

Because the days are already so short, from the feast of Saint Martin until the Purification of Saint Mary, whenever we eat twice a day we do not wait for the servers with none after dinner. Rather, as soon as we rise from the table, we enter the choir, stand in the order in which we ordinarily stand at the hours, [Col. 0690A] and sing none; afterward the servers sing it separately. We no longer return to the refectory to drink before vespers.

During the octave of Saint Martin, and during the octaves of the Nativity and Epiphany of the Lord, we eat twice. After morning lauds we sleep, and afterward sing prime. We do not, however, omit the Office of the Dead from its proper place between the nocturns and morning lauds.

## CHAPTER XLIV. Advent of the Lord

During Advent, whenever there are twelve lessons, we abstain from fat. Nevertheless, *Gloria in excelsis* (“Glory in the highest”) is not sung, although on the feast of Saint Andrew the Apostle it is retained so that his octave may be celebrated with a complete office in every respect.

At prime [Col. 0690B] the chapter is changed, as also in Septuagesima, so that instead of *Regi autem saeculorum* (“To the King of the ages”) *Domine, miserere nostri* (“Lord, have mercy on us”) is said.

On every Sunday until the Nativity of the Lord, after the Alleluia a sequence is sung. The commemoration of the Holy Cross after vespers and morning lauds is omitted until after the octave of Epiphany. Thus, after first vespers of Advent, the procession is made not to the Holy Cross but to Saint Mary, with the responsory *Missus est* (“He has been sent”). After morning lauds: responsory *Ecce Virgo* (“Behold, the Virgin”); collect *Deus, qui salutis* (“O God, who are [the source] of salvation”), or *Deus qui de beatae* (“O God, who [are] of the blessed…”); *Gratiam tuam* (“Your grace”); *Benedicta* (“Blessed”).

On the feast day: responsory *Ave Maria* (“Hail, Mary”); through the cloister, antiphon *Venite omnes* (“Come, all”); another, *O quam casta Mater* (“O how chaste a Mother”); finally, as usual, something concerning the apostles is sung.

The aforementioned antiphons are not changed on the other Sundays. [Col. 0690C] Nor is the chapter at terce, *Ecce dies veniunt* (“Behold, days are coming”), changed until the last Sunday, when *Gaudete in Domino* (“Rejoice in the Lord”) is to be said.

On ordinary days at morning lauds and vespers, as I have already mentioned elsewhere, these prayers are said: *Oremus pro omni gradu Ecclesiae* (“Let us pray for every order of the Church”).

**Question.** Will you again make processions with a responsory at morning lauds and vespers on the other Sundays?

**Answer.** Certainly not.

**Question.** And which antiphons do you sing at the regular hours?

**Answer.** On each Sunday, the antiphons that were sung at morning lauds are also sung at prime and the following hours. On ordinary days, no others are sung [Col. 0690D] than the daily ones, until the week of the Ember fast.

## CHAPTER XLV. The week of the Ember fast

If the vigil of the Nativity of the Lord falls on Saturday, the Ember fast is held during the preceding week. On the Monday of the week before that, it is never deferred on this occasion, so that at morning lauds these antiphons may be begun: *Ecce veniet Dominus* (“Behold, the Lord will come”).

On this occasion, because of these antiphons and others beginning with the letter O, there are in the antiphonary antiphons that are almost entirely unused. These are sung at the daytime hours. For example, on Monday: at prime, antiphon *Dicit Dominus* (“The Lord says”); at terce, *Consurge* (“Arise”); at sext, *Elevare* (“Lift yourself up”); [Col. 0691A] at none, *Ponam in Sion* (“I will place [it] in Zion”).

Of these ferial antiphons, one—*Nolite timere* (“Do not be afraid”)—is always reserved, so that on the feast of Saint Thomas the Apostle it may be sung after morning lauds as a commemoration of the Lord’s Advent, unless it happens that the feast itself is transferred from its proper place and day.

It is transferred if it falls on Ember Friday and is celebrated on the preceding Thursday; or if it falls on Saturday or the following Sunday, in which case it is celebrated on Monday.

On Ember Wednesday the responsories *Clama in fortitudine* (“Cry out with strength”) are begun. On the three nights when these same responsories are sung, the Gospel is announced, and no more than the customary homily on the Gospel is read. The first homily, however, is much shorter than the following two. I myself, if I remember correctly, [Col. 0691B] have sometimes heard that more was read and that material from the sermons of the holy Fathers was added; but our elders later censured this. You must therefore choose whichever of the two alternatives you prefer.

**Question.** On Saturday, since you have no proper antiphons except those of the vigil of the Nativity of the Lord, what do you sing?

**Answer.** As you know, we have two sufficiently suitable antiphons ready to be sung, since they are taken from the psalms themselves: *Ad te, Domine, levavi* (“To you, Lord, I have lifted [my soul]”) and *Exspectetur sicut pluvia* (“Let it be awaited like rain”). To these we add those that have remained unused for the feast of Saint Thomas, or, if we see any others from another place that are more suitable.

If the precentor and sacristan are sensible and diligent, they will not make many mistakes in a matter of this kind. It is their responsibility to provide everything belonging to this category.

[Col. 0691C]

**Question.** Then, after you have sung all the morning antiphons in question once, what do you do if the Nativity of the Lord has not yet arrived?

**Answer.** What difference does it make? We repeat them a second time; obviously, we do nothing else.

## CHAPTER XLVI. The vigil and feast of the Nativity of the Lord

[Col. 0691D]

Once, a certain little book happened to come into our hands which pretended to have been written many years ago. Among other things, it stated that it was our custom on the Nativity of the Lord for Lord Abbot and the cellarer to perform the kitchen service together with the deans.

I did not wish to pass over this in silence, so that you may observe how holy our house was at its beginning, although this example of humility and religious devotion is no longer possible now, except with the greatest inconvenience. For after our vine extended its branches as far as the sea, and its shoots not merely to one river but to many rivers, so many brothers and so many guests flock to the most holy solemnity that Lord Abbot must answer each of them concerning so many different matters. It would therefore be entirely impractical for him at that time to occupy himself with washing beans. At another time he is no more excused from this service than are the others; but on this occasion the stewards of the estates, who are called deans, are quickly listed—however many of them arrive for this purpose—although not all of them serve, but only as many as they themselves decide and deem necessary.

[Col. 0692A]

On the vigil of the Nativity of the Lord, the nocturns are held as on any ordinary day, preceded by thirty psalms. None of the remaining psalmody that is customarily sung either in the choir or in the church of Saint Mary before morning lauds is retained.

At the nocturns the homily of Origen, *Quae fuit necessitas* (“What necessity was there?”), is read. At morning lauds, with the forms folded and carpets spread, after one bell has first been rung according to custom and prayer has been made, all the bells are rung. No psalms other than those appropriate to solemn feasts are sung: the ninety-second psalm and those following it.

The responsory *Judaea et Jerusalem* (“Judea and Jerusalem”) is sung by two people; the altar is incensed. Prime is not separated from these morning [Col. 0692B] lauds, nor are the seven psalms with the litany separated from prime in the usual manner. The psalm *Miserere* (“Have mercy”) is also said for deceased abbots, although two other psalms, the preceding and the following one, remain, as also afterward at all the hours.

Three prayers are said standing before terce, because once morning lauds have begun, throughout that entire day we do not kneel, except at the litany and when the Nativity of the Lord is announced in the chapterhouse. For this reason, when the morning Mass for the faithful departed has ended, the bell is rung at length for the chapterhouse, so that everyone can assemble. When the Nativity of the Lord is announced, as stated above, we all customarily fall on our faces and lie for some time in prayer.

After chapter we are permitted to speak, and again after sext, because throughout the coming week we are to maintain complete silence, except when speaking in chapter and at confession.

[Col. 0692C]

The principal Mass is celebrated solemnly: the subdeacons wear tunicles, and the deacon a dalmatic; the one who holds the choir wears a cope, as does the one who sings the gradual.

At the evening procession: responsory *O magnum mysterium* (“O great mystery”); collect *Deus, qui salutis* (“O God, who are [the source] of salvation”).

On the night of the Nativity of the Lord, before rising for the nocturns, four candles are lit at the four corners of the cloister; they burn continuously until day. A fifth is placed in a translucent marble vessel in the middle of the washroom.

Although the solemnities of the Mass are celebrated three times, we do not omit the fifteen Gradual psalms before the nocturns. The first three lessons are from the prophet; [Col. 0692D] the fourth is from the Book of Wisdom, *Ego sapientia* (“I, Wisdom”); the ninth and the two following lessons are from the homily of the priest Bede on the Gospel *In principio* (“In the beginning”); the twelfth lesson is the homily of blessed Pope Gregory on *Exiit edictum* (“A decree went out”).

The Gospel to be read is the account of Christ’s genealogy according to Matthew. Collect: *Deus, qui hanc sacratissimam noctem* (“O God, who have made this most holy night…”).

We proceed with the responsory *Confirmatum est* (“It has been confirmed”) to the church of Saint Mary, where morning lauds are also sung in the customary manner for All Saints, together with *Verba mea* (“My words”).

At the ninth lesson of the nocturns, servants are sent into the regular kitchen so that, when we leave the church of Saint Mary, a fire may be ready for us. Hot water, basins, and towels are also prepared there, so that we may wash our hands and face.

When the greater bell has been heard and rung for a short while, [Col. 0693A] we assemble at the church. After the priest and the other ministers have vested—for no prayer is made in the choir at that time—the bells are rung so that Mass may be sung: *Dominus dixit ad me* (“The Lord said to me”).

For this Mass, three singers wearing copes hold the choir, as also at the second Mass. Candlesticks are placed on both sides of them, with shining candles upon them. Those who are to sing the responsory or Alleluia, after singing what has been assigned to them, join the three singers mentioned above, and together conduct the choir. The same arrangement is customarily followed at the subsequent Mass.

After the Alleluia, the sequence is sung jubilantly. The Creed is sung, one host is offered, and peace is received from one person.

Morning lauds are sung; collect: *Concede, quaesumus, omnipotens Deus* (“Grant, we beseech you, almighty God”). Nothing from the suffrages of the saints is omitted, nor are those [Col. 0693B] two familiar psalms that accompany the hours in all celebrations with twelve lessons.

We go to the dormitory to rest for a while. When it seems appropriate to the church custodian, the greater bell is rung again so that we may come to the church. The Mass to be celebrated on that occasion is preceded by a prayer as the boys enter.

Whatever was sung for the solemn office at the first Mass is also sung at this one. Three hosts are offered and consecrated, so that any brother who wishes may communicate. Peace is to be received by all.

No other morning Mass is sung on that day.

When the first signal is sounded for terce and prayer has been made, we all put on albs. As I mentioned much earlier, if it is Sunday we immediately make the procession; if it is another day, then after terce we first go to the church of Saint Mary [Col. 0693C] with the antiphon *O beata infantia* (“O blessed infancy”); through the cloister, antiphon *O Maria Jesse* (“O Mary of Jesse”); another, *O quam casta Mater* (“O how chaste a Mother”); at the entrance to the church, responsory *Descendit de coelis* (“He descended from heaven”).

At terce the antiphon *Hodie intacta Virgo* (“Today, untouched Virgin”) is sung. When we reach the place where *Omnes Christum adoremus* (“Let us all adore Christ”) is sung, everyone customarily asks forgiveness. The verse *Memento salutis* (“Remember salvation”) is added to the hymns of the hours, together with *Gloria tibi, Domine* (“Glory to you, Lord”).

## CHAPTER XLVII. The octaves of the Nativity of the Lord and of Epiphany
The Octave of the Nativity of the Lord cannot be celebrated continuously in the same way as the octave of the Lord’s Resurrection, because of the solemnities that follow it—namely, those of Saint Stephen, Saint John, and the Holy Innocents. Concerning these, as is fitting, when the nocturnal office is performed together with the other hours and the Mass offices, only the morning Mass of the Nativity of the Lord, namely *Puer natus est*, is to be sung at the church of Saint Mary. For three days only two collects are to be said: one for the Nativity of the Lord and one for the solemnity at hand; yet they are not to be joined under a single *Per Dominum nostrum*, and so forth. The same is done at the feast of Saints Sebastian and Fabian, although on the other occasions, apart from both Masses, only one collect is said, but in the plural concerning both saints, namely *Infirmitatem nostram*, and so forth.

The Epistles and Gospels alternate in the same order in which they were read at the three Masses celebrated during the first night or day. On the Nativity of the Innocents, other churches do not sing *Gloria in excelsis* or *Alleluia*, but we pay no attention to this. [Col. 0694A] Over the evening psalms are sung the antiphons *Sinite parvulos*, *Angeli eorum*, *Sub throno Dei*, and *Cantabant sancti*. The two following days, provided that neither is a Sunday, are made like the Thursday or Friday that occurs in the greater week of Easter.

On the first night the Gospel *Exiit edictum* is proclaimed, but a different homily follows, namely that of Saint Gregory. The office of the principal Mass is *Dominus dixit*. On the second night the Gospel is *Pastores loquebantur*, and the offertory is *Lux fulgebit*. Except that the introit itself is changed to *Puer natus est*. On the third day the Deposition of Saint Sylvester, pope, is to be observed with twelve lessons.

**Question.** What is the reason, dearest one, that, as far as I see, you intend to say nothing at all about the antiphons? Indeed, if you do not consider them important, as you admit, we ask you to arrange them not only for these two days, but also for whatever other days you see require them, up to the last day of the Theophany.

**Answer.** Your affection will certainly find this no difficulty, since it is not a very laborious task. First, even if I never mention it, you can nevertheless know that, if an antiphon is found from the text of the nocturnal office, it is more appropriately sung over the nocturns than another. But if none of this kind is available, the antiphon *Verbum caro factum* may be sung; another is *Beatus venter*. At morning Lauds, *Genuit puerpera*; another, *Angelus ad pastores*. At Prime, *Illuxit nobis*; another, *In principio*. At Terce, *Verbum caro*; another, *Propter nimiam*. At Sext, *Christus Deus noster*; another, *Ecce de quo*. [Col. 0694C] At None, *Ecce advenit*; another, *Exsultemus*. At Vespers, the same psalms are used with their antiphons as on the day itself; the last of them is sometimes *De profundis*, sometimes *Memento, Domine*.

To state it once for all: these antiphons are still sung on the feasts of the Circumcision of the Lord, the Epiphany, its octave, and the Hypapante of the Lord—at the latter only at Second Vespers—and again at Second Vespers on those Sundays that occur from the octave day of the Nativity of Saint John the Evangelist up to the octave day of the Epiphany. At those Vespers, no other psalm is last except *De profundis*.

On the Circumcision of the Lord the same antiphons are used at Morning Lauds and the daytime hours; the first is *O admirabile*, with the collect *Deus, qui salutis*. At Vespers, at the Gospel, at Morning Lauds, and at the principal Mass, the collect is *Concede, quaesumus, omnipotens Deus*. The morning Mass is *Vultum tuum*; the principal Mass, *Puer natus est*. At both Masses the Epistle is *Apparuit gratia*, and the Gospel is *Pastores loquebantur*, to which is added, as it stands in the Gospel text itself, *Et postquam consummati sunt dies octo*.

The Deposition of Saint Odilo, such a dear and familiar saint, means that on the octave day of the Lord’s Nativity there can be no other commemoration of Saint Stephen than one with a single antiphon and collect. On the octave day of Saint John and of the Innocents, the office is conducted in the same way as on any ordinary day that nevertheless falls within some octave. After the nocturnal office, with Morning Lauds, we say at its proper place *Deus, auribus nostris*; and after Prime, the seven psalms with the litany. If there is a commemoration of someone, it is to be observed with only three lessons. Thus, at the nocturns, the hymn and the antiphon over the psalms are from the Nativity of the Lord; everything else is from the saints mentioned above, until the principal Mass has been completed. Over the evening psalms there is only one antiphon, and that is from the Nativity of the Lord.

On the vigil of the Epiphany, the collect at Vespers is *Deus illuminator*; at Morning Lauds, the antiphon over the psalms is *O admirabile*, with the following antiphons assigned also to the following hours. At Mass: *Dominus dixit ad me*; collect, *Corda nostra*; Epistle, *Apparuit benignitas*; Benedictus responsory, *Alleluia, Dominus dicit*; Gospel, *Defuncto Herode*; offertory, *Laetentur caeli*; [Col. 0695B] Communion, *Exsulta, filia*. We do not fast on that day.

As regards the solemnity and its octave, the Epiphany and its octave resemble the Ascension of the Lord, except for the procession held after Terce on the day of the Ascension. For the rest, recall what I said there, so that you may observe the same here. On the actual day of the Epiphany, the same antiphons are sung at Morning Lauds and at the daytime hours. On weekdays at the nocturns, if antiphons from the text of the nocturns are lacking, the antiphon *Vidimus stellam* may be sung; another is *Tria sunt munera*; another, *Admoniti magi*. At Morning Lauds, any one of those five Morning-Lauds antiphons may be sung over the psalms. At Prime, *Lux de luce*; if it is a Saturday, *In sole posuit*, as also on the vigil of the Epiphany; at Terce, *Interrogabat magos*; at Sext, *Videntes stellam*; at None, *Descendit Spiritus*; at Vespers, *Vox de caelo*. There are other antiphons not only from the Epiphany but also from the Nativity of the Lord, and I see no difference whenever you wish to substitute them for these.

## CHAPTER XLVIII. On the Purification of Saint Mary

Concerning the days or weeks that follow the octave of the Epiphany, I think I have nothing new to report that you do not know, except that, for the procession on Sunday, the antiphons from the Nativity of the Lord are not changed until the Purification of Saint Mary, unless Septuagesima should come first.

Therefore, to say something about the solemnity just mentioned: on the vigil, the collect at Vespers is *Perfice in nobis*, which is repeated at the principal Mass after another collect has first been said, in order to complete it. For the evening procession, the responsory is *Cum inducerent puerum*; at Morning Lauds, *Gaude, Maria*.

On the day itself, after Terce—or, if it is a Sunday, before Terce—the procession proceeds to the church of Saint Mary with the antiphon *Cum inducerent* and another, *O beata infantia*. The collect that follows is *Exaudi, quaesumus, Domine*. Afterwards a prayer is said at each regular hour, and all make the customary inclination both before and behind. The candles that are to be consecrated are consecrated there with this blessing: *Adesto supplicationibus nostris*; another is *Domine Deus, creator*. After their consecration they are sprinkled with holy water, incensed, and distributed.

While the candles are being lit, the antiphon *Lumen ad revelationem* is sung, with the canticle *Nunc dimittis*. After the candles have been distributed, the prayer is *Domine Deus, Pater omnipotens, lumen*, and so forth. Through the cloister the antiphon is *Ave, Maria*; another is *Adorna thalamum*. At the vestibule of the church, at the station, the responsory is *Responsum accepit Simeon*; at the entrance of the church, *Hodie beata Virgo*; likewise the responsory *Cum inducerent*.

At the offertory, after the host and wine have first been offered, candles are also offered as the deacon begins. From that day, at the twelve lessons, None is postponed until the servers have risen from the table; afterwards they go to the refectory to drink.

## CHAPTER XLIX. On Septuagesima and Lent

At Septuagesima, fat is buried together with the Alleluia, so that afterwards no one may taste it until Easter. [Col. 0696B] For the Sunday procession through the cloister, the antiphon is *Cum sederit Filius*. At its Vespers, and on all ordinary days up to Lent, the responsory is *Spes mea, Domine*; at Morning Lauds, *Adjutor meus esto*.

The office for the dead is also changed: it is no longer said after the nocturns, but after Vespers; after each hour in the twelve lessons, *Ad Dominum cum tribularer*. At Morning Lauds, the office for the dead is held after the Morning Lauds of All Saints.

On Quinquagesima, since from then on we eat neither cheese nor eggs, after Vespers we have at supper a general serving of eggs cooked in pepper. Throughout the rest of the year it never happens that anything else is provided on that occasion besides bread alone, and, if they happen to be available, raw apples, or those very thin things made on a marked iron from a sprinkling of flour, which people of the Roman tongue call *nebulae* and our own people call *oblatae*.

## CHAPTER L. On the Beginning of the Fast and on Lent

At the beginning of the fast it is established that neither at the nocturns nor at the other hours is any chapter read except one concerning the fast. At Terce and the following hours there are collects for sins, the first of which is *Exaudi, quaesumus, Domine*; at Morning Lauds and Vespers of that day, the same collect is used. At the nocturns, the collects are the same as those said throughout the year on ordinary nights. For the procession, the psalm *Deus misereatur* is followed by the collect *Concede nobis, quaesumus, Domine, praesidia*.

The priest alone, clad in a stole, blesses the ashes in this way: *Deus, qui non mortem*. When he begins to place them on each person, the cantor also begins the antiphon *Immutemur habitu*.

## CHAPTER LI. On the Sundays of Lent

On every Sunday up to the Passion of the Lord, the same chapter is used at Vespers, Morning Lauds, Terce, and again at Vespers: *Hortamur vos*. No hymn concerning the fast is sung, but the same hymns as on Sundays outside Lent. At Sext and None the collects are likewise the same, but the chapters concern the fast.

For the procession, these two antiphons are sung alternately until Easter: *Christe, Pater misericordiarum* and *Cum sederit*. On the first Sunday, at the eight nocturnal lessons, the sermon is by Maximus, namely *Licet nobis, dilectissimi*. On the second Sunday, since it has no other collect than *Deus, qui conspicis*, this is said at Terce; the following collects from the ordinary days are said at Sext and None.

## CHAPTER LII. On the Monday of Lent

On the Monday of Lent, hymns concerning the fast begin at Morning Lauds, Terce, and the following hours. Only the nocturns seem to have committed some offense here: although during Advent and so often on solemnities they have a special hymn, in Lent they have lost it. Even at so short an hour as Terce there is no hymn other than the customary one, namely *Ternis ter horis numerus*. And although this is so among us, it is not so among the monks of Italy, nor among those of the apostolic see and the Roman Church; among them, whatever the other hours have on this occasion, the nocturns have as well.

There are still other things that customarily begin on the aforesaid Monday: two psalms said by those prostrate at each hour; and the greater prayers at Morning Lauds and Vespers, namely *Oremus pro omni gradu Ecclesiae*. In the chapter no sentence from the Rule is read other than one concerning Lent.

A brief catalogue is also read of the books distributed to the brothers for reading during the preceding year. When each brother is named, he rises and returns the book given to him; and if he has not perhaps read it through, he asks pardon for his negligence.

**[Note: [Col. 0697D] “For indulgence.” Rather, “for negligence.”]**

A carpet is spread there, on which those books are placed; the books that are distributed again are handed out together with the catalogue. For this purpose a somewhat larger table has also been made.

If a feast requiring twelve lessons occurs on that same day, two lessons are then read in the chapter and two sermons are given: the first concerning the feast, the second concerning Lent. After the distribution of the books, permission is given to fast, but in such a way that they fast with discretion and moderation, lest they lose bodily health, especially health needed for the exercise of this kind of life, namely the active life.

Observe also with what humanity our fathers wished Lent itself to begin. On that day, as they saw fit, we have at the meal bread better than usual and warm, a general serving of fish if it can in any way be found, and spiced drink; yet no bell is rung for the serving of that drink.

On Wednesday and Friday, after None, the brothers leave the church, remove their shoes, and return in that condition for the procession. On those occasions no prayer is said beforehand; instead, as the boys enter, they immediately begin the antiphon *Exsurge, Domine*.

## CHAPTER LIII. On the Ember Fast in the Month of March

In the month of March, whatever may be the date of the Ember fast, it is nevertheless never observed before the first week of Lent. If the date has not yet arrived in that week but will come later, nevertheless on the Wednesday of that first week two lessons are read at the office of the principal Mass and two responsories are sung; on the Wednesday when the fast itself is observed, only one lesson and one responsory are used.

I do not know whether this custom first arose through deliberate care and zeal or through negligence, except that I know this practice is contrary to the usage of many churches, both in the Roman tongue and in the Teutonic. Those offices that belong to the same fast, although written for the first week of Lent, do not therefore cause any office to be postponed if the fast is not observed in that week, except the office belonging to Saturday. Only this office is reserved for the Saturday of the fast. On this one occasion also, instead of the hymn of the three boys, *Benedicite* is sung, not *Benedictus*.

## CHAPTER LIV. On the Passion of the Lord and Palm Sunday

[Col. 0698B]

On the Passion of the Lord, *Gloria Patri* is sung at the entrances even when no responsory is sung, although in this too we act contrary to the usage of other churches.

On Palm Sunday, at the morning Mass only one collect is to be said, and the Passion is not read, but only that Gospel lesson, *Cum appropinquaret Jesus*. All priests who have celebrated private Masses are also instructed to be ready for the two processions that must be held on that day.

The first takes place after the morning Mass, with salt and water consecrated, as is customary on every Sunday, through the cloister. The later one takes place after Terce, with branches and palm branches consecrated before the principal altar, proceeding to the church of Saint Majolus, with everyone clothed in white.

The branches themselves are blessed with these collects. When they are distributed, the antiphon *Pueri Hebraeorum ramos* is sung; another is *Pueri Hebraeorum vestimenta*. As they leave, all the bells are rung; the antiphon *Cum appropinquaret Dominus* is sung, and *Cum audisset populus*; the responsory *Contumelias et terrores*; and another responsory.

At the entrance of the church, from the saints whose memory is observed there, an antiphon or responsory is sung. At the station, the antiphon is *Ave, Rex noster*; the collect is from those saints. The Lord’s Prayer is said with the customary inclination, and a sermon is given to the people.

[Col. 0698D] On the return, *Collegerunt* is sung. Some singers go ahead; clothed in copes, they receive the community in the vestibule of the church with these verses: *Gloria, laus*. At the entrance of the church, the responsory is *Ingrediente Domino*. The tract is sung only by the four singers, while the community sits on both sides in complete silence, just as it is also silent during the other tracts.

For the Passion and the offertory, when the branches or palm branches are offered, everyone must be present, and no one may be absent on the pretext of any obedience. In former times on that Sunday the office for the dead was not said, nor is the psalm *Ad Dominum cum tribularer*, which serves as its substitute, said now.

## CHAPTER LV. On Feasts Occurring in Lent

As much as I thought needed to be said about feasts occurring in Lent, I have not left unmentioned elsewhere. Nevertheless, to touch on it briefly again: at every feast, something is added to the psalmody that would neither be added nor said if the feast occurred outside Lent. This is what happens.

First, after Vespers of All Saints, Vespers for the dead are also held; and for them, at night after Morning Lauds, the psalmody *Deus, auribus*. After Prime, the psalm *Miserere*; for our deceased abbots, the seven psalms and the litany. After the chapter, thirty psalms. After Terce, the Mass of the feast itself is sung festively as well.

At Sext and the remaining hours we ask pardon and repeat the entire psalmody, as we repeat it on every other ordinary Lenten day, although at the hours we say no antiphons, chapters, verses, or collects other than those belonging to the feast itself. Otherwise only the office remains again, in whose place the aforesaid psalm is sung after each hour.

If a feast occurs on a Sunday, it is postponed and celebrated on Monday. After the Monday following Palm Sunday, if any feast occurs, it too must be postponed until the Thursday of the following week.

The reason concerning the other days is obvious, so that you yourself may understand it. Each of them contains certain matters resembling principal solemnities, to which nothing else ought to be preferred—except on Tuesday, when, because we are to be shaved, we must speak in the cloister, something never permitted during the twelve lessons.

On Wednesday Lent is, as it were, brought to a close. On that day the Mass office is somewhat longer because of the two lessons, the tract, and the Passion of the Lord. Therefore our predecessors decreed that on that day not only should no other feast be celebrated, but neither a procession nor the office for the dead should be held.

[Col. 0700B]

Blessed be God, by whose grace what I wished has now somehow been completed, dearest Father. For, having begun with the Lord’s Supper, I have returned again to the Lord’s Supper. To this my host, so kind and generous toward my humility, said: “You too, dearest one, ought to be invited to the supper of our poverty; and if anything remains to be asked, let it be reserved for tomorrow.”

# BOOK TWO. ON REGULAR DISCIPLINE

## PREFACE

[Col. 0699C]

It was already the second day since I had come to the monastery. I first recall having begun the matters set out above. Having perhaps inquired into the condition of the place, I learned that, after the vintage of the current year had been completed, only eight cartloads of wine had been gathered for the brothers’ provisions. Nevertheless, the Father of the monastery reduced the customary measure of wine on no day, not only for the monks but also for those living outside the cloister who had voluntarily devoted themselves, from free and well-born men, to become servants of the servants of God.

Between both groups, as I believe, nearly thirty men were present almost every day. You would have seen a pious and holy contest between the abbot and those men: the abbot’s contest was for charity, theirs for frugality. Thus, when the Hypapante of the Lord was approaching on that occasion, I still saw six cartloads remaining in the brothers’ cellar.
