Amazed at such an example of sobriety, when I first saw the Father of the monastery I addressed him as follows: “If God grants that these sons and pupils of your holiness, Father, be as temperate in delicious food as they are in wine, then it is very likely that, with God’s help, through that chief cook Nabuzardan they will not lose their dwelling of peace.”

To this he replied: “In the name of Christ, they do not fail daily to test how much they can resist that same most savage enemy, who attacks and provokes them every day. But since Scripture says, ‘Every idle man is ruled by desires,’ the assistance of your affection will not be useless if you occupy us still further with those religious instructions of which you disclosed some part yesterday. Occupied with these, perhaps we shall think less about returning to the pots of Egypt or desiring anything of that kind. Thus, if the ancient people of the Fathers built the tabernacle of the covenant, may you, our Bezalel, construct the sanctuary of the mind with its varied furnishings of regular discipline.

“For this reason we ask to hear today, especially concerning novices, and the precepts by which they must be instructed and formed, so that they may be able to conduct themselves regularly among you.”

“Now,” I replied, “you are asking me to teach what I have never deserved to be a master of. I have never been considered worthy to sit upon the chair of this school, as a teacher of novices. Nevertheless, I shall not refrain from beginning to report whatever I have happened to know about this subject.”

## CHAPTER I. On the Varieties of Novices

There is, then, some variety among these novices. They come not only without the habit, as laymen and clerics, but also with the habit, already made monks; and such men differ in three ways.

Some come from distant and foreign monasteries, intending to profess again and thereafter remain with us. Some come from our cells and have already received the abbot’s blessing, either because of illness or because of the distance of the place, while their profession has meanwhile been postponed and reserved until they reach our house.

Some come from one of our monasteries that has its own abbot without the lord abbot of this monastery. Although they receive a blessing and make profession there, they are nevertheless regarded by us in every respect, in life and after death, as though they had been with us. As soon as these men arrive, they enter confidently and without delay; and according to the time at which they were received in the aforesaid monastery, they will not be deprived of their proper rank here either.

All the others are not allowed to enter until, in accordance with the word of Saint Benedict, they have first spent one night in the guesthouse. Before they enter, they must also be instructed how to make their petition: first, so that they know how to ask pardon according to our custom. When prostrate and asked by the lord abbot what they want, each is to say: “I wish to have the mercy and grace of God and your fellowship.” After he has replied, “May God grant you the fellowship of his faithful,” they rise and come to his feet.

If someone is, as I said above, from one of our cells, he is invited in while the brothers are seated in chapter. After asking pardon, he is ordered to sit last among the brothers, because he has not yet made profession.

Someone from a foreign monastery likewise asks pardon and sits wherever he is ordered, according to the will of the lord abbot and the judgment he forms of the person. From the day on which he makes profession, however, he too will sit last, unless it seems good to the lord abbot to advance him. If the abbot is absent, the prior may receive such a person, but he may not hold a chapter without the lord abbot’s command.

A cleric or layman who is not yet experienced in our life must be instructed more carefully, as the Rule prescribes, about how hard and harsh the things are that he must endure if he comes under our obedience. This obedience compels him to possess no authority over his own will, but to depend entirely on another’s command.

They are led into the church, where they remain seated until they are clothed. At the principal Mass, after the litany has ended, the layman is led into the choir, ordered to sit on a chair placed opposite the principal altar, and crowned after his hair has been cut. His beard is shaved, and he is marked with the insignia of Christ’s training.

Then he rises and follows his master, to whom the novices have been entrusted, to the adjoining vestry. There all are to be clothed, and their clothing must be entirely like ours, except that, as long as they are without the blessing, they will lack only the cuculla.

## CHAPTER II. How They Are to Conduct Themselves in the Novices’ Cell

Afterwards the hood is sewn to their froccus, so that, while living among us, they may not appear conspicuous through any noticeable difference. When they are few, they do not sleep separately, because they never enter our dormitory unless they have been blessed. In the refectory and other places, however, they are not separated from us at all.

If there are enough of them to make it seem appropriate, then, after the hood has been removed, they have their own cell, where they not only sleep and eat but also remain continually separated from the community. They attend the divine office with us and come into chapter only until the sentence of the Rule has been read and explained; then they immediately leave for the collation.

At each hour, except the nocturns, they follow the boys who go ahead of them to the church and stand in the lesser choir; no one dares to mingle with them. When the community is in the church of Saint Mary after Morning Lauds and Vespers, they do not enter, but wait outside after the others have gone out. Then they approach more closely and stand in order, bent forward, until everyone has passed.

They do the same after each meal, at a suitable place prepared for this purpose. There again they stand inclined while the community leaves the refectory, and the community passes by them with a similar inclination.

When they are going to eat, they leave the church before the community and, after washing their hands, proceed to the regular kitchen to bring each his own portion of beans. To bring the general serving or the pottage, as many of them rise from the table as are needed and as the one serving them in the cellarer’s place directs.

They too have readings and a bell, and in other ways imitate the same discipline that we observe in the refectory. If one of them has to come from the church to his cell, he does not presume to do so without taking at least one companion.

I would not claim that I can even remember how many and how varied are the things they must then be taught. Nevertheless, I do not omit what I can briefly touch upon, because what is begun by me may perhaps at some time be completed or at least enlarged by another.

Certainly, even if it may be considered a small matter unworthy of mention, every novice must nevertheless be instructed with considerable care to know how to bow according to the Rule: not with his back curved, as is familiar to certain negligent persons, but in such a way that his back is lower than his loins and his head lower than his back.

By custom we call this inclination “forward and backward,” because it begins facing east and ends facing west. We make it first before the nocturns and after Compline, namely after the three prayers have been completed. For the rest, whenever we assemble in the church, chapter, or refectory, we make it on entering or leaving; but in the church on Sunday, a prayer is first said.

If we go to the church after lunch, supper, or collation, we do not make the inclination unless a regular hour follows at that very moment and has been completed. Likewise, during an office sung in the daytime, we do not bow until its end.

Whenever we come to the church of Saint Mary, after the annual psalms, when we return to chapter, we bow only once before the striking of the board.

In the choir, whenever we change station for either Mass, we bow. At Mass, the older brothers stand first, nearest the principal altar; at the regular hours, they stand last, at the end of the choir. The exception is Terce during the twelve lessons, because the morning Mass usually precedes that hour and the principal Mass follows immediately; for this reason, I think the station is not changed.

The aforesaid student of Christ is instructed in this not so much by hearing as by seeing.

## CHAPTER III. On Silence and the Workshops in Which It Is Kept

He must also carefully learn the signs by which, while silent, he may in a certain way speak. For after he has been joined to the community, he is permitted to speak only very rarely. There are workshops in the cloister in which our fathers have handed down and established that perpetual silence is to be kept: the church, the dormitory, the refectory, and the regular kitchen.

In each of these, by day and by night, if he speaks even one word within the hearing of anyone, he does not readily merit pardon without judgment. If he names an antiphon, responsory, or anything of that sort without a book, and has not seen it in the book at the same time as he uttered the word, this is judged nothing other than a clear violation of silence.

## CHAPTER IV. On the Signs Used for Speaking

To give some examples of these signs, let us begin with those concerning food.

For the sign of bread, make a circle with both thumbs and the two fingers next to them, because bread is usually round.

For bread cooked in water, which is usually better than the daily bread, first make the general sign for bread, then add this: place the inside of one hand upon the back of the other and move the upper hand around as though anointing or moistening it.

For rye bread, commonly called *turta*, first make the general sign, then add this: make a cross across the middle of the palm, because this kind of bread is usually divided into four parts.

For a small cake, which is given in addition to the customary pound on the five principal feasts, place the two fingers next to the thumb, slightly separated, diagonally over the corresponding two fingers of the other hand, likewise separated.

For beans, place the first joint of the thumb beneath the tip of the index finger and make the thumb project over it.

For eggs, with one finger imitate the prolonged picking of a shell upon another finger.

For pottage made with vegetables, draw one finger over another as though cutting herbs to be cooked.

For the general sign of fish, use the hand to imitate the movement of a fish’s tail in water.

For cuttlefish, separate all the fingers from one another and move them in that manner, because cuttlefish also appear to have many such appendages.

For eel, close both hands as though holding and squeezing an eel.

For lamprey, with a finger imitate on the jaw the spots that the lamprey has beneath its eyes.

For salmon or sturgeon, after making the sign for fish, add this: place the fist, with the thumb raised, beneath the chin, which signifies pride, because the very proud and wealthy commonly have such fish.

For pike, after making the general sign for fish, add a sign of speed with the hand, because the pike swims faster than other fish.

For trout, add this: draw a finger from one eyebrow to the other, because women have bindings in that place and because *truita* is always spoken in the feminine gender.

For millet, make a circle with a finger, because millet itself turns around in the pot with a spoon.

For fritters, or, as others say, *frigdolae*, grasp the hair with the fist as though you wanted to make it curly.

For cheese, join both hands obliquely as though pressing cheese.

For *fladones*, after making the general signs for bread and cheese, bend all the fingers of one hand, hollow the hand, and place it on the surface of the other hand.

For *rufeolae*, or, as the Teutons say, *cratoni*, after making the general sign for bread, use two fingers to imitate the small folds made in them, on the side where they are folded and somewhat rounded.

For milk, touch the little finger to the lips, because an infant sucks in that way.

For honey, let the tongue appear slightly and apply the fingers as though you wished to lick them.

For fruit, especially pears or apples, close the thumb together with the other fingers.

For cherries, add this: place a finger beneath the eye.

For raw leek, extend the thumb and the finger next to it together.

For garlic or radish, extend a finger toward the slightly open mouth, because of the kind of odor perceived from them.

For water, join all the fingers and move the hand obliquely.

For wine, bend a finger and bring it to the lips.

For spiced drink, close the hand and imitate grinding.

For a drink seasoned with honey and wormwood, separate the index and middle fingers from the others, and also separate those two from each other as you move them, because wormwood is divided in its leaves.

For mustard, place the thumb beneath the front joint of the little finger.

For vinegar, rub the throat with a finger, because its sharpness is felt in the throat.

For a bowl, extend the hand broadly.

For the cup that holds the daily measure of wine, incline the hand downward and hold it hollow, with the fingers slightly bent.

For a glass flask, after making the preceding sign, add this: place two fingers around the eye, so that the brightness of the glass may be signified by the brightness of the eye.

For a *staminea* (a woollen garment), hold its sleeve with three fingers—the little finger and the two next to it.

For breeches, add this: draw the hand downward along the thigh, as one who dresses himself in breeches.

For a froccus, hold its sleeve in the same manner as the sleeve of the linen garment is to be held.

For a cuculla, add this: touch the hood behind with two fingers.

For sleeves, hold the sleeve of the froccus and add the sign used for breeches.

There are many more things that I could mention, but now that I remember to whom I have been speaking, I see that it was not necessary to say so much about this matter or, as that poet says, “to carry wood into the forest” (*Horace, Satires* I.10.34). Therefore, to be silent at last about these matters, which, as I think, you know better than I do, we must consider what follows, so that I may speak of things which, since you have neither seen nor heard them before, may gain somewhat more favor through their novelty.

And since the subject is the instruction of novices, let us proceed as far as possible in order through that discipline by which the man who wishes to live among us is continually bound.

## CHAPTER V. How a brother should rise for Nocturns

At the first sound of the signal for Nocturns, he hastens immediately to rise. Before throwing off his covering, he puts on his cuculla and covers his legs with it before rising from his bed. He does not leave the bed carelessly, but arranges it properly, spreading the covering over it. He does not enter the necessarium unless his head is covered with a cap. He is accustomed to come into the church before the boys, and is careful to attend the three prayers that are made when the signal has ended.

## CHAPTER VI. Of the offenses for which he asks pardon

[Col. 0705B]

If he has not attended, he will ask pardon in chapter, as he will also if he has omitted any of the regular hours—unless he is a priest, so that meanwhile he may sing Mass—or if he has omitted the conference, or chapter without permission, or the general meal. Prostrating himself for prayer, he draws his froccus backward over his elbows and knees, so that it does not hang down over his feet to the ground.

If it should happen in any way that he does not arrive before the *Gloria* of Psalm 94, or before the *Gloria* of the first psalm at any other hour, he enters the choir and comes to the altar step. There he honorably and deliberately asks pardon on his hands and knees, extending the edge of his froccus slightly so that he can place his hands upon it. Rising, he bows more deeply toward the altar. From then on he will not move until the hour has ended; while the others bow, he bows only toward the altar.

But if it seems good to the lord abbot, he sends a brother to him to tell him to withdraw. He bows slightly to this brother’s beckoning hand, and, having made the bow before and behind, withdraws to his station. There he again asks pardon as before, bows toward the community, and the community bows toward him.

## CHAPTER VII. How he should conduct himself at the regular hours

At the *Gloria* of each psalm that is sung at the regular hours, he does not keep his hands in his bosom, but puts them into his sleeves and gathers the sleeves together, so that, when he bows to the ground, they do not reach it. For that bow must be very low, and not merely the same as the bow made at other psalmody.

If he wishes to sit during the psalmody, he takes care not to sit beside someone else who is sitting, but in such a way that one stands while the other sits; and they should offer one another the opportunity to sit. Wherever he sits, he never lets his sleeves hang carelessly to the ground. If his hands are inside his bosom, the sleeves are gathered crosswise outside it.

If he has left the choir for some reason, or if he comes afterward, when the hour has already begun, he bows toward the front of the church, and bows to everyone who is likewise going to bow. He never bows toward the high altar unless his hands have been taken out of his sleeves and his head has been lowered almost to the ground; toward the other altars, and toward the crucifix in chapter, he bows more moderately.

If he knows the psalms and has made a mistake in any verse, he asks pardon before him in the same manner described above for asking pardon at the altar step after arriving late. He bows reverently to the lector at the step, both when the lector makes the bow before and behind and when he goes to the reading and returns.

## CHAPTER VIII. How he should carry the wooden lantern at Nocturns

If, during the readings, the brother who carries the wooden lantern comes to him and, thinking that he is asleep, directs the light toward his face, then, if he is awake, he bows reverently once more.

But if he has fallen asleep and the lantern has been placed before him, once awakened he first surveys the right-hand choir with it; returning through the middle, he surveys the outer choir, and finally the left-hand choir. If he finds someone asleep, he directs the light toward his eyes three times. If the person does not awaken at the third time, he places the lantern before him, so that, once awakened by it, he too may carry it in the same way.

## CHAPTER IX. With what discipline he should return to bed

Returning to bed, he again settles himself with due discipline. He does not remove his cuculla before drawing the covering up over his elbows. Then he carefully folds the cuculla that he has removed and places it at his head.

However much heat he may feel, he never uncovers more of his body than his feet, arms, and head.

## CHAPTER X. How he should rise in the morning and what he should do immediately

[Col. 0706C]

At the sound customarily made in the dormitory at dawn to awaken the brothers, he does the same thing as at the signal for Nocturns. He rises as quickly as possible, and on that occasion puts on no shoes other than those made for daytime, unless perhaps he has undergone bloodletting. He takes care not to forget his knife, which he must carry with him.

After washing his hands and face, when three towels are hanging together in the cloister, he dries himself only with the one assigned to those like him, since one is for the boys, another for the cantors, and the third for the unlearned.

He combs his head and makes three prayers in the choir, in front of and nearer to the altar than the seniors, just as at Nocturns. At Nocturns also, after the boys begin to read, he does not remain there long.

## CHAPTER XI. How he should sit and walk

When sitting for the reading, he sits so that an ulna’s width is between himself and the person sitting beside him. He always draws the front parts of his froccus into his lap so that his feet can be clearly seen. He also gathers the *girones*, which some call “arrows,” on both sides, so that they do not lie scattered on the ground.

Wherever he walks, he always walks with his head lowered. If he is ever seen with his neck held erect, the matter is not overlooked or left unmarked.

## CHAPTER XII. How he should come to confession

If he needs to come to confession for some offense, he approaches whichever priest he especially wishes. Standing before him, he draws his right hand out of his sleeve and places it on his breast: this is the sign of confession.

The priest rises, and he follows him as he goes before him into chapter. First, he asks pardon before him, prostrated with his whole body. When the priest orders him to rise, he sits down and tells him what he has to say.

If something happened to him during the night that we modestly call “frailty,” he must say the seven penitential psalms before confession—or, if he does not know the psalms, the Lord’s Prayer seven times—and after he has confessed, he must do what the priest orders him.

On that day he does not kiss the Gospel book, go to the kiss of peace, or approach the offering.

## CHAPTER XIII. How and when he should put on his garments

[Col. 0707B]

We have a private washing place with a water supply. There he washes his undergarment to the extent that it has been soiled by the discharge; or, if he has his change of clothing at hand, he changes what he is wearing. He does not presume to approach any of the places mentioned above before doing so.

He never changes while wearing only the cuculla, unless he is also wearing a pelliceum or froccus, lest anyone see any part of his nakedness.

The garments he removes he immediately folds. He wraps the undergarment in the stamineum and fastens both garments together with its sleeves. He also observes the time for changing clothes, which is only before Prime, or, if Prime is sung together with Matins, before Terce.

He should know that this is also the time for confession: after chapter, for as long as the psalms for the anniversary of the brothers are being said. On solemn days, changing is permitted until the Matutinal Mass; during Lent, for three days in which silence is kept in the cloister until Sext.

## CHAPTER XIV. If he is a cook, at what hour he should attend to his cooking

If he has undergone *coctio* (“cooking,” as they commonly say), he neither inspects nor binds the treatment according to custom except before Prime; or, if Prime has been joined to Matins as mentioned above, before Terce; and after Vespers, provided that he does not break silence on this account.

Freshly washed cloths must be kept ready at hand, so that he has no need to say anything. He never sits during the Athanasian Creed. He approaches the offering neither earlier nor later than his turn.

## CHAPTER XV. How he should wash his garments

After this, if he wishes to wash any of his garments, he finds in the regular kitchen a bronze vessel intended solely for this purpose, in which water may be heated and lye prepared.

In the cloister there is a very large hollowed-out trough with several separate compartments, so that the stamineum may be washed in one part and the undergarment in another. Before chapter he puts them into hot water to soften them. After the striking of the board, he washes them, but no longer than the period during which permission to speak lasts.

If it is a fast day, he is not forbidden to wash after Terce. If it is Lent or an ordinary day, he may wash not only after Terce but also after Sext, even though we do not speak in the cloister.

Whatever he washes, however it has been washed, he removes after the washing hour and dries it, so that it does not lie there dirty and rough—especially where the whole community will see it when leaving the refectory.

## CHAPTER XVI. How he should not leave the regular hour except for unavoidable necessity

When he hears the signal that is rung for Prime, he enters the church with the others. Since the ringing of the signal is properly prolonged until seven psalms can have been sung, he may sometimes, if he wishes, leave for a bodily necessity after the boys have passed through.

On returning, he washes his hands, so that, when the time comes for the offering, he will not have to go out again. If he goes out so frequently, he will find this matter also reserved for chapter.

Nor does he see anyone leave while any of the regular hours is being sung during the day, except for an unavoidable necessity—for example, if blood is flowing from the nose.

## CHAPTER XVII. How he prepares for chapter, and what he should do if he is conscious of any offense

When the bell is rung for chapter, he pulls his stamineum down all around him and arranges it properly, so that he may be ready if, in any way, he is accused and ordered to seek judgment.

When the lord abbot says, “Bless,” he bows. When the proceedings of chapter begin, if some offense has happened to him in any way, which another person has seen and is properly able to report, he anticipates the accusation, asks pardon, prostrates himself with his whole body, and confesses his fault.

However much he confesses, he does not ask pardon more than once for the offense he has confessed. But if another person has reported him, then each time he hears himself reported he asks pardon each time.

If, while sitting and hearing an accusation against himself, he answers anything before asking pardon, he is ordered to prostrate himself and receives one blow on his own froccus.

Afterward, for the offense of which he has been accused, he accepts whatever the superior decides: either to be beaten or to be assigned a lesser penalty. I am not speaking here of matters that belong to a graver offense.

## CHAPTER XVIII. Of a lesser offense

When sent into a lesser penalty, he conducts himself as the Rule itself prescribes.

During the prayers of Nocturns and of all the regular hours, he lies prostrate at the step. He does not make the offering, kiss the Gospel book, approach the kiss of peace, or come to table with the others.

But if a feast day requiring twelve readings occurs, he is released from lying prostrate and from not eating with the others. In church he does not abstain from the reading, from undertaking the chant, or from the other matters I have mentioned.

When an ordinary day arrives, he again enters into the state in which he was previously, until he is absolved.

He is absolved especially when he is lying prostrate at the step and a brother is sent to him to indicate that he has been absolved. Absolution is also customarily given in this way if, after having been assigned to the same offense, he should later happen to be accused again for some wrongdoing and beaten.

If this does not happen, he is not absolved unless the community has first seen his satisfaction, whether as he lies at the step or for one hour.

## CHAPTER XIX. How he should stand wherever he is standing

When standing before the lord abbot, or wherever he may stand, he is also careful to keep his feet placed evenly together. While standing, he never spreads them apart from one another.

## CHAPTER XX. Of things that may be done only at the hour for speaking

[Col. 0709B]

When he leaves chapter, if it is a day on which speaking is not forbidden, he takes a book and sits before saying a single word. He says absolutely nothing while standing; whatever he says, he says in a low voice.

His speech and hearing concern only spiritual matters or those things of which this present life cannot be deprived.

If he needs to ask the chamberlain for something, he asks then. If he needs to cut his nails, he cuts them then. If he needs to wash his dish and platter, he washes them then. If he needs to sharpen his knife, he sharpens it then on the whetstone that hangs in the cloister for this purpose.

If he needs to spread something from his clothing in the sun, he spreads it then, and remembers carefully to remove it before the conference—or, if there are twelve readings during the following night, before Vespers.

If he wishes to visit one of the sick brothers, he visits him especially then.

If he is without an obedience concerning guests, he speaks to none of the servants except with permission.

He calls nothing his own individually, but says “our” for everything, except in speaking of his father and mother. In their case he may permissibly say “my” and “mine.”

If he addresses a brother, he never addresses him by his bare name unless he adds “lord.” He calls the boys “brothers.” Likewise, when he is going to say someone’s proper name, he always puts “brother” first.

## CHAPTER XXI. Of bloodletting

[Col. 0709D]

If he wishes to have blood let, he asks permission at the very hour when he leaves chapter.

To describe the procedure in order: after receiving permission, he goes to the cellarer and tells him his wish, so that the cellarer may arrange for the servant appointed to this task to be ready after the Gospel of the greater Mass.

At that moment he leaves the church, puts on nocturnal clothing—which he will wear for the next three days—and does not enter the choir. Taking from his bed the bandage needed for this purpose, he goes to the regular kitchen, where he uncovers and warms his arm. He summons the aforesaid servant by a sign alone from the cellarer and takes him with him to the place for bloodletting.

Before doing anything else, he makes the bow before and behind and says this verse three times:

> “O God, come to my assistance” (*Deus, in adjutorium meum intende*),

as he also does for manual work; and he adds the rest as it is prescribed there.

Bloodletting then begins. He keeps silence, except to say a few words about what is being done.

Afterward he rises and immediately goes to the refectory, where he eats a little of his pound and drinks wine, as he also does on the following two days. At dinner, if the others have a special portion, he receives the general portion; at supper, three eggs.

If it is winter—from the Kalends of October until Lent—and the brothers generally eat only once, he then has supper after Vespers.

On the second and third days, when he comes to the refectory after chapter, he says the verse for the meal together with the boys and receives three cooked dishes. On the fourth day, he receives a quarter of a cheese, or its equivalent in value.

On that day he returns to the choir at Prime wearing daytime clothing.

At Nocturns during these three nights, if he falls asleep, no one disturbs him with the hidden signal; rather, he may rest for a while in his bed. Nor is he permitted to ask pardon in chapter if something is reported against him and he is ordered to stand and bow for pardon.

He takes care not to have blood let on a day before whose following night there will be twelve readings, except during Lent. Then he always has blood let after Vespers on Saturday, because he will not fast on Sunday.

On Sunday, because he is going to make a procession outside the cloister, he also puts on daytime clothing. After Compline, of the three prayers he makes only one, and then he goes out.

## CHAPTER XXII. With what discipline he should remain in church for the solemn Masses

[Col. 0710C]

To return to the point from which I briefly digressed: if, while speaking, he hears the signal for a regular hour, and if he is in the cloister, he does not finish the word he has in his mouth, but immediately falls silent and hastens to attend the prayer.

He sits in the choir and applies himself to the reading until the priest who is going to sing Mass has been vested. When he hears the first stroke of the second signal, however, he immediately stops and rises. The same applies to the two signals rung for Vespers and whenever all the signals are rung.

He carefully observes the pardon he asks, so that he never asks it later or earlier than the others. When the others lower themselves, he lowers himself; when they rise, he rises, for the bows, prayers, and orations.

When the others are not reading and are attending only to the divine office, he too never opens a book to read, especially in the choir, except sometimes the antiphoner for the greater Mass, because of a more difficult chant that is being sung at that time; or the hymn book at Vespers, because of a hymn that is to be sung then.

If he is the hebdomadary, he may look in the collectary for whatever he needs. If he is the lector in the refectory and is still a young man under supervision, he may, if he wishes, preview the reading in the choir for both Masses.

He does not like frequently to make the hand-signs used for speech, especially when the community is watching. Whenever he makes them, he makes them reverently and out of necessity, never without a useful reason. Just as he restrains the other members of his body, he also restrains his sight from wandering.

When Mass has ended, he sits in profound silence at the reading until the boys return from the *misto*.

## CHAPTER XXIII. With what discipline he should remain in the refectory

At the hour of dinner or supper, if he has not gone up to the dormitory, he washes his hands and immediately enters the refectory.

At his seat, after making the bow before and behind while standing, he reverently awaits the lord abbot, unless he is so ill that he cannot stand; then he sits.

He eats absolutely nothing before the reading has begun and before he has received the offering from the priest’s hand—provided, however, that it is an ordinary day and that he has not received Communion that day.

He tastes nothing from the general portion before it has been blessed. He never brings anything to himself except salt and water, unless he happens to be serving the community generally and comes to his own seat.

If something is brought to him by another, he reverently extends his hand toward it and bows slightly. If something is directed to him either by the lord abbot himself or by the prior sitting beside him, he rises completely and bows more deeply. However much he may wish to abstain, he nevertheless does not fail to taste it.

He brings his dish especially to the brother sitting above him beside him, so that the brother may eat. If that brother refuses, he brings it to the one below. If the second also refuses, however much of the food remains that he did not or could not eat, he does not send it farther to any other brother for any private favor. He merely moves the dish away from himself, so that the server may remove it.

With regard to crumbs, he takes the greatest care that not even the smallest piece fall to the ground and be wasted. With his knife he scrapes them from the table, so that finally they may be gathered into the dish with a little grass fan and taken to the alms.

As long as he has not been separated from the community to be with the sick, he does not taste even one grain of pepper, nor does he take any drink in any way on account of an illness, except in the refectory and apart from the Eucharist.

Nor does he ever drink except while holding the cup with both hands, and never except while sitting.

If it should happen from time to time that he is not present at the beginning while the others are seated, then, coming afterward to the step, he asks the lord abbot by a sign for permission to eat. When the abbot assents, he does and says by himself what he would have done and said with the others: the bow before and behind, and the verse.

If it is dinner, he says, “The eyes of all,” and so forth; if supper, “The poor shall eat,” and so forth. Bowing, he says, “Glory be to the Father”; standing upright, he blesses with hand and mouth, saying, “Let us pray. Bless, O Lord,” and so forth. He bows to the lord abbot and withdraws to sit down.

If he ever needs to rise from the table before the others, he again comes to the step and asks permission to leave by extending his open hand slowly from his breast.

After receiving permission, he bows as though turning around and says the verse. If it is dinner, he says, “Let them confess,” and so forth; bowing, “Glory be to the Father”; standing upright, “We give you thanks,” and so forth. If it is supper, he says, “He made a memorial,” and so forth, and “Blessed is God,” and so forth.

After making the bow before and behind, he proceeds slowly, singing the psalm *Miserere*, to the door of the refectory. There he bows toward the principal table and says everything that is said in the church by the priest or by the community, namely, “He has scattered abroad, he has given to the poor,” and so forth. Finally, after making the bow before and behind, he leaves.

If the brothers eat only once that day, he says no other verses than those belonging to supper, together with “We give you thanks.” He never does both on one occasion, arriving later than the others and rising earlier.

## CHAPTER XXIV. Of his conduct after dinner and after supper

[Col. 0712B]

After the meal, silence is imposed on him for this period with greater strictness than at any other time. According as the time or the order of the day requires, he either sits in the cloister reading or singing, or, if he goes to sleep and wishes to read, he reads while lying down, arranged as though he wished to fall asleep immediately.

He avoids not only the signs made with the hand, but also directing even a glance of his eyes toward any brother’s bed, so as to look at it even for a moment.

After None, whether he is thirsty or not, he does not fail to go with the others to drink.

Whenever supper is eaten after Vespers, after supper he goes up to the dormitory, puts down his knife, removes his daytime shoes, puts on nocturnal clothing, and comes to sit in the cloister.

During the hour in which he sits there, he is so devoted to silence that, even if he happens to write something, being only somewhat skilled in writing, he must not let either the parchment or the pen itself make any sound at all.

If he comes down from the dormitory later than the others, he places his feet so quietly that, even if his walking is seen by others, it cannot be heard by anyone.

## CHAPTER XXV. With what discipline he should settle himself after Compline

After Compline, when the three prayers are again made, he takes the last place for these prayers, and the seniors the front places.

After being sprinkled by the priest with holy water, he comes to the church door with his head covered by a cap and does not uncover it again until he has settled himself in bed.

Let these few things, as they have come to mind, be said from among the many matters in which all novices should, if possible, be instructed before they are joined to our community.

## CHAPTER XXVI. Of the confession and petition of the novices

In their secular life, whatever they have committed against the salvation of their souls, they confess everything to the lord abbot.

Afterward, when it seems good to him, he orders them to come before him again in chapter. When they have come and asked pardon, after they have risen he again explains to them, as before, something of the austerity of regular discipline. Among other things, he does not fail to say that it is better for them to return to the world without a blessing than, after receiving a blessing, not to persevere thereafter.

But if they, on the contrary, promise complete obedience and stability, he finally consents to confirm them with a blessing.

He commends them to the brothers’ prayers and, if it seems appropriate, sometimes orders one psalm to be sung for them after each hour on that day.

## CHAPTER XXVII. Of the blessing of the novices

They come forward in pairs or groups of three.

The blessing is properly to be performed after the Gospel of the greater Mass, and it is begun in this way. Each has written out how he is to make his profession, as follows:

> I, Brother N., promise stability as a monk, conversion of my conduct, and obedience according to the Rule of Saint Benedict, before God and his saints, in this monastery constructed in honor of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, in the presence of Lord N., abbot.

Each reads this from his own written declaration and places the declaration upon the altar, where it is to be kept permanently. If he does not know his letters, another reads it for him, but he makes some mark with his hand on the declaration.

They ask pardon three times on their hands and knees, also saying three times this verse:

> Receive me, O Lord, according to your word (*Suscipe me, Domine, secundum eloquium*), and so forth.

Each time the community answers them in the same way. At the third time, adding the *Gloria Patri*, they make a circuit, still on bent knees, and afterward prostrate themselves for prayer.

The lord abbot, standing, begins the *Kyrie, eleison*, the Lord’s Prayer, and the psalm *Miserere*, preceded by these versicles:

> Save them, and so forth.  
> Send to them, and so forth.  
> Let nothing prosper, and so forth.  
> Be to them, and so forth.

The following collects of blessing follow:

> God of mercies, and so forth.  
> O God, who through the coeternal one, and so forth.  
> Lord Jesus Christ, who are the way, and so forth.  
> Holy Spirit, who are God, and so forth.

He blesses the cucullas with:

> Lord Jesus Christ, who, and so forth,

and sprinkles them with holy water.

When their blessing is finished, the novices rise from prayer, remove their frocci, and put on their cucullas.

While each is removing his froccus, the lord abbot says to him again:

> May the Lord strip you, and so forth.

While he is putting on the cuculla:

> May he clothe you, and so forth.

They go around the entire choir so that all the brothers, beginning with the lord abbot himself, may kiss them.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. Of their conduct during the three days after the blessing

[Col. 0713D]

During these three days they do not uncover their heads, which remain covered by the cap. They sleep in their cucullas, speak absolutely nothing, make the offering at the kiss of peace, and come to Communion. They do not omit Communion even if something has happened to them while sleeping.

On the third day, after the priest has kissed them, he removes the cap from their heads. From then on they may speak and remove their cucullas, like the other brothers.

If one of them is ill and, as they say, has received the blessing “for assistance,” and has been unable to keep silence because of his illness, he also covers his head while the others who are being blessed cover theirs. He similarly performs everything that they perform during those three days, so that what had previously been omitted may be supplied.

Therefore, from that day onward they are no longer separated from chapter. According to the grace given to each of them, the lord abbot orders them thereafter to serve in the church: those who know how are to read and sing, while those who are capable of nothing else are to carry the candlesticks and thuribles.

In the case of those who are priests or levites, however, he carefully examines how they were ordained, what their knowledge is, and what their conscience is like. He tests their conduct for some time before permitting them to undertake this ministry.

In particular, anyone who was a priest before he came is entirely forbidden to exercise the office until, after frequent observation, he has learned with what manifold care such a sacrament is handled among us.

To mention this here: both the person being examined and those who, after examination, are ordered in any way to serve must carefully attend to their written declaration in chapter, so that each may observe whether some service has been assigned to him, whether it is to be performed in the church or outside it.

## CHAPTER XXIX. Of the hebdomadary cantor and of the person appointed to begin the invitatory, a reading, or a responsory

If he has been appointed for the invitatory, when he begins it while standing at the step with his colleague, or when he finishes it, he makes the bow before and behind on both occasions.

If, among the two who are to sing the invitatory, he is the one appointed first, he will also be the hebdomadary. Throughout the entire week he imposes the office of the greater Mass. On Sunday and on any similar day, when all the signals are to be rung, it belongs to him to begin ringing the first bells. He then puts on the cope, so that the choir may be held together by him. He also places in the thurible the incense brought to him, with which the Lord’s body is to be incensed before the consecration.

When the brothers are at the kiss of peace and Communion, he may sit.

Whenever there are twelve readings during the week, he imposes the antiphon at all the hours except Vespers. At Vespers he imposes it only on a feast such as that of the Holy Trinity, or on one more solemn than that.

When we are all vested in white for the greater Mass, the duty of the greater Mass belongs not to him but to the armarius.

If he is not the hebdomadary but has nevertheless been appointed for one of the antiphons of Nocturns, after imposing it, when the first verse of the psalm has ended, he makes the bow before and behind.

When going to read, he bows deeply as he approaches and withdraws. Except on an occasion when the community has not yet sat down, he does not bow so deeply. After reading, he again comes to the step and not only makes the bow before and behind, but also precedes it with the pardon on his hands and knees.

It should also be noted as one of our customs that, if he reads a prophecy—especially where nothing historical is present—on Sunday nights, he does not say at the end of the reading, “Thus says the Lord,” but “But you, O Lord.” The same words are also said at the end of every book of the prophets that has been read aloud.

If he has been appointed for a responsory, he bows moderately, both before imposing it and afterward, when the verse or the *Gloria Patri*, if it is to be added, has ended. After the verse, he lowers himself in a bow for a short time. If he is to sing with another, he sings at the step.

## CHAPTER XXX. Of the hebdomadary priest

If he has been assigned to exercise the priesthood and has sung the greater Mass during the present week, he will sing the Matutinal Mass in the following week.

He should know by heart a considerable amount of what he is to say: first, the three collects for the canticles of the fifteen degrees before Nocturns; or, if the psalmody continues to the end of the Psalter, the collects for the suffrages of the saints; the collects for the offices of the dead; those for psalms for associates (*familiares*); and those for the psalmody *Deus, auribus*.

He should also know our customs in many respects, especially in the saying and arranging of collects, so that he never says anything in the community that in any way differs from them. However learned he may think himself about everything, he should nevertheless not disdain frequently to ask the cantor and the armarius about each matter.

Whenever there are twelve readings, after Nocturns he is to read the Gospel. He does not leave the choir before the singers, taking turns, have reached the verse:

> “The heavens and the earth are full,”

and then, having quickly washed his hands, he enters the sacristy. Vested in an alb, stole, and chasuble, and after that verse has again been begun:

> “Throughout all days,”

he comes forward, reverently holding the Gospel book with both hands, leaning it against his breast. As he approaches, he places it in the middle of the altar and, with incense, makes the sign of the cross over it only once.

He bows for prayer, especially at the Lord’s Prayer. At the final verse of the hymn mentioned above he rises, takes the book from the altar after kissing it, and proceeds to the lectern. The entire community turns toward it and bows.

When Matins begins, he does not move from his place until he has said the *Gloria Patri* with the others. Bowing slightly, he withdraws when they rise. He always hastens, however, so that he is back in the choir before the first psalm ends.

He handles the incense as follows: first he incenses the front of the altar; then, holding the incense-bearing hand out, he makes three motions over the surface in different places across the breadth of the altar, and one motion crosswise. He then incenses the rear right corner of the altar, followed by the left corner.

He also incenses each of the smaller altars near the choir and the altar of the Holy Cross, making over each one only the sign of the cross with incense.

On ordinary days, whenever there are two meals, before the signal is rung for Terce he washes his hands according to custom, so that, after making the prayer, he may immediately vest in priestly garments and impose Terce.

When Terce has ended, after the litany preceding Mass has been sung as far as the verse “All saints,” he leaves the choir to put on the chasuble also and come before the altar with the procession.

If it is a day on which there is only one meal, he vests while the litany is being sung. If a procession is to be made, as on Wednesday and Friday in Lent, he does not vest until the procession itself has also been completed.

As he approaches, he too carries the missal on his left arm. After placing it at the right corner of the altar, he bows for prayer, especially the Lord’s Prayer, or, if he prefers, “Holy Lord,” and so forth.

He kisses the altar and the Gospel book. He gives the deacon room to stand near the right corner of the altar; he himself stands near the left. Bowing toward the deacon, who likewise bows, he says the confession. Its form is prescribed so that neither at Mass nor at the hours when it is to be said is it expressed in more words than these:

> I confess to God and to all his saints, and to you, Father, that I have sinned in thought, word, and deed; through my fault. I ask you to pray for me.

**Response:**

> May almighty God have mercy on you and forgive you all your sins; may he free you from every evil; may he preserve and strengthen you in every good work; and may he lead you to eternal life. Amen.

At the Epistle he sits until the Gospel is reached.

To the deacon who is about to read he gives this blessing:

> May God have mercy on you and bless you.

On that occasion he stands near the right corner of the altar, and the deacon near the left.

Here it is not inappropriate to recall with what diligence and care the consecration and communion of the Lord’s body and blood are observed. First, for this very purpose, a small cupboard was made before the face of the high altar, very well joined and lined inside with cloth. Nothing else is stored in it except those utensils necessary solely for the solemn celebration of Masses generally performed in the convent, especially two golden chalices with patens of different sizes; and two corporals, [Col. 0716C] one double, as all corporals ordinarily are for private Masses, the other single. The smaller chalice with the double corporal is for the morning Mass; the larger with the single one for the principal Mass. For one single corporal always lies at the left-hand corner of the altar, as I learned from our predecessors, so that it may be at hand in case of danger from fire; against this danger, if it should happen, many believe that a corporal spread out is of great value. There is also a medium-sized silver paten, and a golden bowl with a cover of the same metal, joined by the work of a craftsman; there are ampullae for supplying wine and water, for wine is also customarily offered in an ampulla before consecration. There is a silver ewer with its appendage for washing the hands; there are several little linen cloths, without which the individual sacred vessels are neither lifted nor carried anywhere.

The cupboard itself has a shelf in the middle, so that the more sacred things may be above and the others below. At the beginning of Mass it is unlocked by the chief custodian of the church, or by his assistant who is hebdomadary at that time. It is entirely covered above with a cloth, and he places the paten there together with the corporal. Holding the chalice with a linen cloth stretched lengthwise over it and covering it above, he carries it to the water vessel, which is always made of tin and kept in the church in a suitable place, so that all the chalices used for private Masses may be washed there. At that point the hebdomadary carefully washes the chalice, pouring in water twice; and if he is not a priest or levite, he asks [Col. 0717A] someone of one of those two orders to act as his substitute, as on Wednesday and Saturday. Having put his hand inside, he also rubs the chalice well at the bottom, lest it should perhaps acquire a slight odor because of the frequent pouring in of wine. Thus washed, it is carried back and placed on the cupboard.

The subdeacon anticipates the washing of his hands, so that he may be ready for the ministry of the chalice. Meanwhile, while the Gospel is being read, he takes the chalice together with the corporal and paten, checks whether any water has remained in it during the washing, and pours it into a basin made of brick tiles near the altar, just as another has been made somewhat farther away, where the same subdeacon and the other assistants wash their hands over it. He stands beside the priest until the Gospel is finished. He places the corporal on the altar, retaining the chalice and paten; [Col. 0717B] he accompanies the priest, who goes a little way toward the brothers, so that each may make an offering. The deacon brings water and a towel and presents them reverently. After washing his hands, the priest approaches the altar and—speaking properly here of the principal Mass—takes and spreads either corporal: the one that always lies on the altar or the one brought by the subdeacon. He carefully presses together the thumb and forefinger of each hand, lest he should touch the corporals with the fingers with which he will shortly touch and handle the hosts.

When the offering has been completed, the priest also washes his hands, likewise taking care afterward not to touch anything with the fingers with which the Lord’s body is to be touched. The subdeacon carries the hosts to the deacon, who stands beside the altar and covers himself, so that from among them he may choose three as he wishes for consecration. Therefore, leaving the paten with the hosts on the altar, the wine that has been offered is poured by the subdeacon himself into the other chalice, and he leaves only as much as suffices for consecration. He himself does not mix water with it, since he is permitted to pour in neither wine nor water; but he gives the ampulla of water, brought together with the chalice, to the deacon, so that the deacon may mix it. He also gives him a little cloth, so that the outside of the chalice may be carefully wiped, lest any wine or water remain on the exterior and be lost.

On this occasion the deacon does not refrain from separating the fingers of which I spoke above, since he has already placed the hosts that he was going to place. Then, when the chalice has finally been placed on the altar, the subdeacon returns with the paten and ampulla, sets the paten filled with hosts on the cupboard, and puts the ampulla in the place where it is customarily kept. He takes another silver paten stored inside the golden bowl, carefully wipes it with the whitest cloth, which hangs continuously near the cupboard for this very purpose, and afterward wraps it honorably and reverently in a linen cloth.

Meanwhile the priest censes the chalice and the host, making three crosses and one sort of circle with incense over both. He also censes toward both corners of the altar, the right and the left, as far as he can extend his hand, while keeping his feet motionless. Then he returns the thurible to the deacon. The deacon first censes the priest, drawing the chasuble between his arms toward the feet; afterward he censes the face and surface of the right-hand corner of the altar, and finally the face and surface of the left-hand corner. [Col. 0718A] If it is a feast day, he censes the five principal altars nearest to the choir, as well as the altar to which the convent went for Vespers and morning praises, where a candle burns both by night and by day.

It should be noted that on all feast days and Sundays the aforementioned altars are censed twice at the principal Mass: first, after the priest and deacon have made their confession, and again after the offertory. The same is done at the lesser Mass, for which all the bells are rung. On ordinary days incense is offered once at the principal Mass, namely after the offertory, and only the sacred offering on the principal altar is censed. At the principal Mass, unless the bells are rung, incense is never offered.

It should also be known that, whether three or five hosts are consecrated, the priest always takes the middle one. With it he makes the crosses in the chalice, divides it, and places one particle in the blood; he does not neglect to communicate himself with the middle portion and the deacon with the remaining one.

After the deacon has censed the altar—or, if it is such a day, the altars—and, if a bishop or abbot happens to be present, has returned the thurible to him while he stands beside the ciborium column, from whom he is also censed, he remains there inclined, as at the first and last collects, until the priest says, “For ever and ever” (*Per omnia saecula saeculorum*). Having turned around, if someone wearing a cope is in the choir, he first censes that person; then, beginning on the right, he carries the thurible in the same manner and order described above to those in the greater or lesser choir. He does this additionally in the lesser choir: he goes out first to the right and afterward to the left.

After this, going out, he censes those who are outside the choir, beginning at the entrance to the choir on the upper side; then the others, as they stand in their stations around it; and finally the smaller altars near the choir, which are not censed by the deacon—at the front and on the right and left sides. He does not presume to extend his hand over the altar. If he encounters a priest celebrating Mass there, either he himself or the deacon, if it can suitably be done, offers him the thurible. The priest censes the altar or sacred offering and returns the thurible to him; the deacon or the other man, having turned back, reverently censes him and does not neglect to arrange the chasuble between his arms.

When he hears “For ever and ever,” etc., before the preface, if he has already returned from censing the altars, or if he is present there, as on ordinary days, he goes behind the priest. If he has not yet returned, as soon as he returns he does the same. The subdeacon follows the deacon, holding the paten, covered as described above, with his hand raised upward. During the twelve lessons one of the assistants customarily does this, remaining behind the subdeacon. When they arrive there, they bow more deeply, and afterward stand upright until the *Sanctus* begins.

From this point the priest performs everything in the same way as it ought to be performed at any private Mass, as has been said elsewhere. One of the assistants—there should always be two—stands with a fan near the priest and, once the infestation of flies begins, does not neglect to drive them away from the sacrifice, from the altar, and from the priest himself until the end. The deacon, subdeacon, and one of the assistants, if it is a feast day, afterward remain inclined and intent upon prayer.

The deacon observes when the priest, having bowed at “We humbly beseech you” (*Supplices te rogamus*), straightens himself. Then he too rises and withdraws to a place before the aforementioned cupboard in order to wash the four fingers with which the Lord’s body is to be touched and divided. It should be known that, not only for the soul of the person who donated the little ewer from which the water is poured and the basin into which it is received, but also after the offertory, both he and the priest, while washing their hands there, say this collect: “Let us pray. Absolve, O Lord, the soul of your servant,” etc., loudly enough for the conversi serving them to hear and answer, “Amen.”

After washing and drying his fingers, he returns to the place where he had first remained inclined. Bowing more deeply, he immediately rises, then stands and carefully watches for the moment when the priest begins to make crosses over the sacrifice at “Through him, and with him, and in him” (*Per ipsum et cum ipso et in ipso*). As soon as he sees this, he approaches the altar moderately and step by step. First he kisses the right-hand corner of the altar, then the priest’s right shoulder; afterward, with the two middle fingers of his right hand, he removes the corporal from one side, [Col. 0719C] while the priest removes it from the other. With the same fingers he holds the chalice through its middle and manages to raise it slightly while the priest says “For ever and ever,” etc.; afterward he replaces the corporal on it from the same side. Finally, returning behind the priest to the place where he had previously been, he again remains inclined until the subdeacon offers him the silver paten.

The subdeacon does not rise before this, nor does he leave the place where he has remained inclined behind the deacon since the *Sanctus* began, until the priest says “Our bread” in the Lord’s Prayer. Then he withdraws, proceeds reverently, and lets the linen cloth fall from the paten. Holding the paten with part of the linen wrapped around his hand, he deliberately allows a portion of the same cloth to hang down, so that the deacon too, with his middle fingers wrapped in the cloth, may receive the paten from him after kissing his hand and offer it to the priest when the Lord’s Prayer is finished. He does not, however, separate his thumb and forefinger, just as he did not separate them when he raised the chalice with the priest.

It should be known that whatever the subdeacon does with the aforementioned paten on ordinary days is customarily done during the twelve lessons by the assistant who ordinarily remains behind him. After the deacon has offered the paten to the priest, he remains inclined near the right-hand corner of the altar, attentive to prayer if he is wise, until “For ever and ever” is said.

The priest takes the paten with his middle fingers and places it on the corporal at the foot of the chalice. After he has broken the host, he places one particle, as is customary, [Col. 0720A] in the chalice and two on the paten, and covers both with the corporal. First, however, he carefully rubs and shakes over the chalice the fingers with which he touched it, lest anything from the Lord’s body should have adhered to them during the breaking. Meanwhile, closing his hands with the greatest care and placing them against his breast in the form of a cross, he turns first to the deacon, who bows reverently and, after the kiss of peace, arranges the chasuble between the priest’s arms with his two middle fingers; the priest gives him peace, then gives it to the subdeacon, and as he proceeds opposite the convent, to the two assistants. Finally, coming to the step before the lectern, he gives peace to the rest, as we have decided should be noted, throughout the entire convent on the five principal feasts.

On other days, except for Saturdays on which Ember-day fasts occur, and except for the fasting Masses during the feasts of Lent and the other fasts in which a feast of the twelve lessons occurs—when one host is offered and peace is given to one person by the deacon—the distribution of peace proceeds as follows. On Tuesday, Thursday, and Saturday, the right choir always goes to receive peace, except for anyone to whom such an event occurred during the night; on Monday, Wednesday, and Friday, the left choir does so. On Sundays they go alternately: one choir on one Sunday, the other on the next, just as hymns, antiphons, and psalms are begun alternately by one choir in one week and by the other in the next.

If they are vested in copes or albs, they go to peace according to the dignity of their order: first the priests, in the order in which they are priors; second the deacons; third the subdeacons; then the others, as their order requires; and finally the conversi. If some are in copes, some in albs, and some in frocks or cowls, those in copes go first according to the dignity of their order, then those in albs, and finally those in frocks or cowls, always according to the order in which they entered the conversion or were raised by the lord abbot, whether they are cantors or conversi.

It should nevertheless be noted that if the lord abbot, for any reasonable cause, has raised a conversus in chapter and in the refectory, he will still preserve that order. But for peace and communion, as also for holy water, he will go according to the order of conversion. On ordinary days the conversus who serves with the candlestick, because he is dressed in an alb, goes first to receive peace after the priest has come to the step.

While the priest proceeds to give peace, the deacon approaches the altar and breaks and divides the two hosts—or, if there are more, as on Sundays—which the priest did not divide. He sets them apart, so that he himself may communicate from one and the priest from the other; and if he finishes before the priest returns, he nevertheless withdraws nowhere. As soon as the subdeacon and assistants have received peace, they do not neglect to wash their hands in the basin near the altar. The subdeacon carries back the golden paten belonging to the chalice, which he had placed on the cupboard, puts it on the altar, and also lays out the linen cloth crosswise on the altar. Then he stands inclined between the reclinatory and the right-hand corner of the altar until he returns. Upon returning, he takes from the paten the small portion of the Lord’s body that he is to consume, using the two middle fingers of his left hand, and extends the paten slightly toward the deacon. Taking the portion over the chalice, he afterward gives the same chalice containing the blood to the deacon.

One of the assistants takes the bowl from the cupboard and holds it, together with the linen cloth, over the reclinatory. This reclinatory, I think, was made especially for this purpose between the two columns of the ciborium. The deacon places on it the paten on which the Lord’s body has been divided. He also gives the chalice containing the blood to the subdeacon, who stands inside between the reclinatory and the altar. The subdeacon holds it inclined, as close as possible to the bowl. The deacon communicates first, and afterward the others approach from outside in the order in which they went to receive peace, apart from those in albs. Before communicating, all of them—both those in albs and the others—ask pardon and kiss the priest’s hand.

If anyone who is not of the choir that goes to receive peace wishes to communicate, he signals the person responsible for maintaining the order. If the lord abbot or prior is absent, he approaches both for peace and for communion in his proper order. Each person must draw so close to the bowl that, if during the reception of the Lord’s body it should happen to fall, whether from the mouth of the recipient or from the hand of the one administering it, it cannot fall anywhere except into the bowl.

To however many people he gives the sacred body, he first dips it for each one into the blood.

[Note: [Col. 0721D] *Intinguit* (“he dips”). Another manuscript adds: “Although this is contrary to the custom of other churches, some—especially our novices—are so inexperienced that, if they received the blood separately in this way, there would be no occasion on which they did not at some time incur serious negligence.”]

After all who wish have communicated, and finally the subdeacon—who by custom must always communicate at the principal Mass, except on days when only one host is consecrated—and after the person holding the bowl has communicated, if any part of the Lord’s body remains, or if it seems appropriate, the bowl is covered. The person holding it does not move away until the priest, having received the chalice from the subdeacon, drinks the blood and the wine with which he afterward washes the chalice. This wine is poured for him by the same subdeacon, who holds the ampulla in one hand and, with the other wrapped in the linen cloth that he had placed on the altar with the paten, raises the foot of the chalice.

The deacon, after receiving communion, comes near the cupboard to wash in another chalice with wine the fingers with which he handled the Lord’s body, with the assistant who remains there.

[Note: [Col. 0721D] *Supererat* (“remains”). The same manuscript mentioned above reads: “The assistant who remains also approaches with another chalice outside the reclinatory, so that the priest may wash over it with wine the fingers with which he handled the Lord’s body, just as the deacon does as soon as he has communicated and before he folds the corporals. The priest then drinks this wine, which the second assistant pours again so that the chalice may be washed on both sides.”]

The assistant pours the wine from the ampulla and raises the foot of the chalice. After washing them, the deacon first wipes them on the chalice and then on his face. He applies the part with which he wiped them and drinks the wine, turning toward the east. Then he hastens to fold the corporals, to move the missal from the left-hand corner of the altar to the right, and to turn toward the place where the next collect is to be said.

As soon as the priest has consumed the blood and the wine with which he afterward washed the chalice, the subdeacon receives the chalice from him, kissing his hand, and receives from the deacon the chalice paten, taking it from the altar after a corporal has been placed over it. He replaces the other corporal in its proper place on the altar. Then the person holding the bowl raises it higher and goes before the left-hand corner of the altar. The subdeacon remains with the chalice before the right-hand corner, behind the priest, holding the chalice with one hand and, with the other, the paten, slightly raised with the corporal.

Meanwhile the entire convent asks pardon before them, out of reverence for the Lord’s body and blood.

It should be known that if anyone arrives after the common request for pardon, he must ask pardon either in the choir or outside it, as the case may be. Likewise, after anyone has communicated apart from this communion, he customarily asks pardon, sometimes before the altar of Saint John, sometimes elsewhere.

As soon as the assistant who remains has poured wine over the deacon’s fingers, he comes outside the reclinatory carrying another, smaller chalice with the ampulla that he supplied to the deacon; afterward he receives it back from him, so that the priest too may wash the fingers with which he handled the Lord’s body. These fingers may never be washed in the chalice of the principal Mass. After the wine has been consumed, more wine is poured into the chalice so that it may itself be washed a little, and the priest drinks it. Whenever he consumes either the blood or the remaining wine, he turns his face toward the altar or toward the east.

The person who carries the candlestick, after the priest has returned from giving peace, immediately takes it and holds it raised before the step. He does not put it down before “Through our Lord” (*Per Dominum nostrum*) has been said in the first collect after communion. At the same time the subdeacon with the chalice and the assistant with the bowl depart. During the twelve lessons, two conversi with two candlesticks and a third holding the thurible approach and depart before the step in exactly the same manner as has been described for ordinary days.

It should be known that whenever no more than one host is consecrated at the principal Mass, that Mass is sung with the chalice of the lesser Mass and the double corporal. Then neither is the silver paten brought out, nor is the aforementioned bowl brought, nor does the subdeacon, after receiving the chalice following communion, remain behind the priest. Nor does the conversus serving with the candlestick, after the priest has drunk the wine poured into the chalice following the washing of his fingers, continue to be covered.

It should also be known that every Sunday the Lord’s body is changed. While the priest proceeds to give peace, the newly consecrated body is placed by the deacon in a box of bark; what had been consecrated on the previous Sunday is taken from it, divided by the same deacon, and the brothers receive communion from it. Only the two particles of the host that the priest divided are not changed.

While the familiar psalms are being said after Terce, the deacon removes the aforementioned box from the dove, which hangs continuously above the altar. He wipes its exterior carefully with a linen cloth to remove dust and places it beneath the covering at the right-hand corner; when Mass is finished, he replaces it in the same place.

After the subdeacon and assistant have departed from before the altar, each carries his own items back to the cupboard. There, however bright the day may be, the subdeacon and assistant carefully inspect by candlelight both the paten on which the Lord’s body has been broken and the chalice, to see whether anything, however tiny, of the Lord’s body may remain. If either sees that something remains, he does not presume to touch it with his hand, but raises and consumes it only with his tongue, if the particle is such that it can suitably be consumed. If it is extremely tiny—so to speak, indivisible and like an atom—he receives it, if possible, with wine in the chalice in which the priest and deacon wash their fingers; he raises it and separates it.

If it has adhered in such a way that this cannot be done with wine, he nevertheless applies his tongue briefly to the place where he sees it and thus consumes it. Afterward he again pours wine over the paten. If he knows that nothing, however small, remains there, he nevertheless does not omit to pour wine over it once with the greatest care; he first consumes that wine poured over it. Then he washes with other wine the same chalice from which he drank the wine poured over the paten, or he immerses it in the wine with which either he or the assistant washed the inside of the chalice of the principal Mass. He consumes it, pours the remaining wine into the chalice of the principal Mass, and rinses its interior all around. If the assistant has communicated, he drinks it; otherwise, the subdeacon, after consuming the wine poured over the paten, immerses it in the chalice over which the same paten was poured, as has been said, and consumes it. In that case he does not wash it with other wine, unless he later discovers that something has remained there.

The other assistant must hold a candle for this careful inspection and diligently unfold the three linen cloths. If the subdeacon is serving as custodian, it is the custodian’s duty to hold the candle. Two linen cloths must be placed over the chalice of the principal Mass, and again over the chalice of the lesser Mass; thus the sacred vessels are arranged in their proper place. Even if they have completed this before the end of Mass, none of them should therefore go away undressed.

As the priest withdraws from the altar, he gives the missal to the deacon to carry back. He himself folds the stole and maniple, unless—as at the principal feasts—they are gilded; in that case they are to be folded by the sacristan.

On ordinary days unconsecrated hosts are carried to the refectory, so that they may be distributed by the hands of the priest to those who have not communicated that day. This is customarily done in the following order: first he gives some of those hosts to the lord abbot; afterward, since there are three tables, he goes to the right of the lord abbot, to one table, then to everyone on the other side, and so returns again to the right. Each person kisses the hand of the distributor. Whenever he blesses, he makes three crosses toward the principal table, toward the right, and toward the left; for the drink he makes only one.

After Compline, before the third prayer is finished, he leaves the choir for the holy water, so that he may sprinkle each person with it.

Since I have mentioned the priest once, I will add here what further concerns him specifically. If he wishes to sing a private Mass, he signals a conversus with the sign of the cross, which is the sign of a sung Mass. The conversus immediately follows him to the place where the utensils for solemn Masses are stored. He lights a candle, places the priest’s vestment on his left arm, and the missal on top of it.

The priest first washes and dries his hands, places the host with a spoon on the paten, and also washes and dries the chalice. He pours wine and water into two ampullae; he carries them in his left hand and the chalice, with the paten and corporal placed upon it, in his right. Thus, preceding the conversus who follows him, he proceeds to the altar where he is to sing. He unfolds its folded cloth and places the chalice and missal there.

Provision has also been made, neither unexpectedly nor inadequately, for the vestment: at each altar there is a board on which it may be placed, and a projecting piece of wood fixed into the wall on which the ampullae may be set. A small towel also hangs ready at hand, with which the priest, after vesting, dries the fingertips with which he necessarily touches the sacred objects.

From there, beginning Mass, he reads straight through the entire chant pertaining to it, as our fathers prescribed, rather than ever daring to sing it. When he reaches the offertory, he observes everything with the same care and diligence customary at the principal Mass. When Mass is finished and he has returned, he does not then omit to wash the tips of his fingers again, especially because of the chalice and because he must carry back the corporal.

To say still more about the priest’s rule: when he is vesting for a private Mass, if the signal is rung for a regular Hour and he has not yet placed the stole around his neck, he removes his vestments, stops the Mass, and goes to the Hour. Likewise, while the Hour is being sung, if he has finished Mass and can come into the choir before the *Gloria* of the first psalm, he leaves the conversus with the vestment, folded or unfolded, and he himself goes to the Hour. But if he cannot come, neither he nor the conversus moves from the place until the Hour is finished.

These are the occasions on which priests may sing such Masses without permission: every day before Prime, provided Prime is not joined to morning praises, as happens more often in winter; after the chapter until Terce; or, if there is a chapter, after Terce until Sext; and also after None, provided the brothers have not gone to sleep.
