Sometimes a priest may receive permission after the Gospel of the principal Mass; this is nevertheless censured if he wishes to make a regular practice of it.

## CHAPTER XXXI  
### On the subdeacon and on the singers of the Gradual, Alleluia, and Tract

The subdeacon who is to read the Epistle, when he goes with the priest to the altar, carries the Gospel book and places it in the middle of the altar. He does not carry the cushion unless it is a solemn day. When he begins the reading, and again when it is finished, he makes the gesture before and behind at the very place where he is to read.

Those who sing the responsory, or the Alleluia, or the Tract or canticle, are to do the same. Since on ordinary days these are sung communally by the convent, if another feast occurs during the week, they are to be sung again by those who previously sing them on Sunday. If everyone is in copes or albs, the armarius indicates whomever he wishes to sing them. He does the same for the prose, whenever it is to be sung; for this, no gesture before or behind is to be made either at the beginning or at the end.

## CHAPTER XXXII  
### On the deacon

The deacon customarily precedes the priest to the altar. When the priest bows for prayer, he too stands similarly inclined; when the priest rises, he performs the gesture before and behind. He approaches to kiss the left-hand corner of the altar, then stands opposite the priest so that he may make his confession in response to the priest’s confession.

He presents the incense, and after it has been placed in the thurible he also presents the thurible itself. When he later receives it back, if it is a solemn day, he censes each of the altars nearest the choir, especially the rear corners of the principal altar itself. When the priest sits, he too sits, but only after the priest has indicated it; he does not sit without the priest’s permission. When the Gospel is finished, he makes the gesture before and behind. Likewise, when Mass is finished, he never says “Go, the Mass is ended” (*Ite, missa est*) unless the *Gloria in excelsis* has also been sung.

## CHAPTER XXXIII  
### On the church servants and those whom we call ministers of the altar

Besides the duty of carrying the thurible and candlesticks, the servants carefully observe that they are never absent from the priest’s service. Whenever the levites vest themselves for any divine work, after the work has been completed they remove those vestments, or, if they need water and a towel, they do so in order to wash their hands.

Likewise, whenever either of them censes the altars, one of those same servants continually accompanies them. What seemed necessary to say about those whom we call ministers of the altar has been set out above.

## CHAPTER XXXIV  
### On the reader at table

When the solemnities of the principal Mass have ended, the reader at table comes to the step, makes the gesture before and behind, and, with the entire convent responding, pronounces three times this verse: “O Lord, open my lips” (*Domine, labia mea*), etc.

The priest continues with this blessing: “Save your servant,” etc.; “Send him help,” etc.; “The Lord guards you,” etc.; “May the Lord guard your entrance,” etc.; “May he take away from you the spirit of pride,” etc. Again the person who is to read bows as before.

Before the general meal he tastes bread and wine, according to the prescription of Saint Benedict. At the morning or principal Mass, after the Gospel, he takes the book in which the reading is written, withdraws to the lesser choir, and attends to what is to be read. If he is a young man placed in custody, he does not withdraw in this way but reads within the choir itself.

The book from which the reading is to be given is carried to and from the refectory by the reader who reads for the servants. Since none of the brothers has tasted anything before the reading has been introduced, as soon as the lord abbot or prior has sat down, the reader asks for a blessing and hastens to begin the reading. When it is finished, he comes to the step and makes the gesture before and behind.

If during the week he omits the reading on one day and asks another brother to read in his place, he is not reproved. If he does so more often, except on account of illness—and if he has not demonstrated this by asking pardon in chapter—he is noted.

## CHAPTER XXXV  
### On the cooks

There are customarily four weekly cooks. Their first duty, after the signal for Vespers has been rung and the prayer has been said, is to go to the kitchen to receive the beans. After Vespers they wash them carefully, pouring in water three times, and leave them overnight in that water in a well-covered cauldron.

When those who served during the preceding week wash the brothers’ feet at the command given to them, these cooks, girded with a cloth, dry them and provide towels for the hands. When the foot-washing has also been completed, they come before the lord abbot and make the gesture before and behind.

Likewise, after the morning praises of Sunday have been completed, they come to the step and give thanks to God for the completion of the service performed, saying three times, with the response of the entire convent, this verse: “Blessed are you, O Lord,” etc. When they are about to perform the same service, these men ask God’s help, saying: “O God, come to my assistance,” etc. The priest is to say these verses and collect for them: “Save your servants,” etc.; “Turn, O Lord,” etc. Prayer: “O God, to whom belongs the humble,” etc. For these men: “Save them,” etc.; “Send them,” etc. Prayer: “Merciful and most loving,” etc.

Even before the convent, they leave the church of Saint Mary so that they may put on their shoes and meanwhile go down. While the convent is at the necessary place, they wash their hands and face. As is customary, they make three prayers in the church, if they are able to enter; if not, near the church doors.

When they enter the kitchen, they wash the beans again with three waters and then put them on the fire. When the cauldron begins to boil and the foam rises, they continually remove it with a crosswise spoon, lest the beans floating together with the foam be thrown out. They also stir them frequently at the bottom with the same spoon, lest, when they are to be eaten, they taste of smoke.

When the skins of the beans begin to open, they do not allow them to remain longer on the fire. They cool them again with cold water three times, stir them again this way and that with a spoon, and put them into a single bowl with a very well-fitted lid. The inside of the cauldron in which they were cooked is also washed until it is clean. Once it has been removed from the fire, another is immediately hung up, so that the water may be heated in which the bowls are to be washed.

The board, too, is leaned against the wall; after the bowls have been washed, they are set upon it to rest, and water is poured over the entire upper surface of the board and it is scrubbed with brooms. First, however, after making the customary inclination, they again say three times the same verse that they said in choir; but here, on the third occasion, they add “Glory be to the Father,” etc., together with the Lord’s Prayer and the verse “Our help,” etc. Having again made the customary movement forward and back, they finally lean the board against the wall.

They sing all the regular Hours according to the custom of the canons. They insert Vespers for the faithful departed at its proper place, and at the end “My words.” The water with which the bowls are washed is poured in to be heated for cooking the vegetables.

But if the morning praises are completed late, as sometimes happens, especially on the principal feast days and in summer, and the signal for Prime must be rung earlier, then, before doing anything else, they attack the Hours with the board already leaned against the wall. For if anything remains that they have not sung before Prime, it is not customary for it to be sung publicly after Prime. When this is finished—or, on ordinary days, after the Gospel of the morning Mass—they put the vegetables into the cauldron, [Col. 0727C] and after Chapter they put the beans into the other one again.

They take bacon which, after it has been cooked somewhat with the vegetables, they squeeze so that the fat may be poured over the beans. Nevertheless, not all withdraw from the principal Mass for this purpose, but only two, especially if any of them are illiterate. These must previously have obtained permission from their fellow workers to hear some private Mass. As stated above, these men pour out the fat; through them the beans are heated again.

If they think that, because of slow cooking, more water should be poured over the vegetables, they first heat as much as they wish to add in a frying pan, because vegetables have the property that cold water gives them an inferior taste. They must therefore also take care, when the vegetables are to be put into the cauldron, that they are washed with no water other than hot water. They are not seasoned with salt or sprinkled with fat until they have been thoroughly cooked, lest the salt perhaps disappear during a longer delay. If one of the cooks wishes, he may lawfully taste a little of the bean water itself, to test whether it has been properly seasoned.

For the mixtum they accept only what Saint Benedict prescribes: a fourth part of bread, apart from its pound, and likewise of wine.

When the Hour has ended and the brothers are about to eat, they quickly leave in order to serve the beans. The senior cook, if he knows the task well and is physically able to perform it, puts the beans into the bowls with a spoon made for this purpose. The others carry them to the tables, beginning with the principal table.

The vegetables, by contrast, are usually served in the opposite order, beginning with the last table. When the bowl containing the vegetables has been placed before the lord abbot—or before the prior, who has placed it there—the server asks the presiding officer, with a moderate sign of permission, that the small bell may be sounded. When he gives assent, the server inclines slightly; then, coming to the bell, he rings it long enough for each person to swallow whatever he may have had in his mouth, so that all may be ready to answer the priest’s blessing. While that blessing is being completed, the aforesaid server stands bowed before the steward, and then makes the customary movement forward and back.

What is given between the beans and the vegetables is usually a *pitancia* on three days of the week—that is, Monday, Wednesday, and Friday—and a *generale* on the other three. We call *generale* what is given to each person in an individual bowl; *pitancia* what is given to two persons in one bowl. For example, sometimes, instead of a *pitancia* served in a bowl, there is one piece of uncooked cheese or four eggs; for the *generale*, there are five eggs, and the cheese is never served except cooked.

If the dish is *generale*, it is served beginning with the last table, and the bell is rung for this just as it is for the vegetables. The *pitancia*, however, is served beginning with the prior. The weekly kitchen servers have no duty whatever concerning this; rather, the cellarer serves it with those whom he indicates for the task. Whatever is *generale*, they bring out—unless it is fish, which the cellarer himself places before each person who signals to him.

If there is another *generale*, one of them again rings the bell and collects only those bowls in which the beans and vegetables have been served. Because of these bowls, one man always remains in the kitchen to wash them while they are still freshly soiled, using the same [Col. 0728C] water with which they were washed at dawn, lest, if the remnants of the food should harden, the difficulty of washing them become greater.

The same care is taken with the cauldrons, so that they too are washed, if not earlier, at least before the meal of the servers is finished. The hearth, moreover, is carefully covered, so that on the following day it may be found still alive and not extinguished.

After Vespers, when the beans have again been washed, they say, in thanksgiving, the aforesaid verse, “Blessed are you, O Lord,” etc., in the same manner in which they said the other verse in the morning. But if they wish, they may take two days off from washing the bowls, namely Monday and Friday. On these days the cellarer cannot, according to custom, object if the bowls, carried to the cellar at dawn, are entrusted to his servants to wash with greater care.

When Saturday comes, after None [Col. 0728D] or after Vespers, they sweep the kitchen. All the dirt produced by the ashes or wood is piled outside the door, so that it may be carried away by the cellarer’s servants. They heat water for the *mandatum*, and on that day the verse “Blessed are you, O Lord” is postponed until the *mandatum* has been completed and the reading at the meal in the refectory has also ended.

On the following Saturday, because our aqueduct has muddy water, they sweep both washrooms: the one for the use of the church and the one for washing the hands. They also sweep the latrines and gather against the wall the remnants of hay spread throughout the week. If it is summer, throughout that week they serve water in the refectory after None.

## CHAPTER XXXVI. On the kitchen utensils

[Col. 0729A]

These are the utensils that must never be lacking in the kitchen.

First, three cauldrons: one for beans, another for vegetables, and a third together with an iron tripod, so that if anyone wishes to wash his clothes, he can make lye.

Four bowls: one reserved for holding the beans when they have been half-cooked; another into which the aqueduct flows and in which the vegetables are washed before being put into the cauldron; a third for the bowls; and a fourth solely for receiving hot water for the *mandatum* and for the shaving water used by the brothers while shaving. Those who served during the preceding week must also heat the water for this last purpose.

Likewise, four spoons: one for the beans, another for the [Col. 0729B] vegetables, a third, not so large, for squeezing out the fat, and a fourth made of iron for covering the hearth with ashes. There must also be a pair of tongs of the same kind for arranging or dispersing the fire.

Four pairs of sleeves, so that the sleeves of the brothers’ woollen garments may not be soiled by the familiar blackness of the kitchen.

Two pairs of *palmariae*, as they are called in the vernacular; they protect the hands from the heat of the cauldron when it has just been removed from the fire and must be moved or tilted.

Three hand towels, which are also changed every Thursday; the brothers should by no means wipe their hands on the usual towels that hang in the cloister.

One knife for cutting bacon, together with a whetstone for sharpening it.

One pan for heating water, if necessary, and for melting fat; [Col. 0729C] another, very small, pierced with tiny holes in the bottom, so that the fat itself may be strained.

One box in which salt is kept; one chest in which all the smaller objects are stored.

One pitcher for drawing water; and two brooms with which the cauldrons are swept after cooking.

Two pieces of netting suitable for washing both bowls and cauldrons.

Two boards for the bowls: one on which they are placed after the meal, however imperfectly washed; the other on which they are placed at dawn, when they must have been washed completely.

Two seats, commonly called benches; one low, four-footed stand on which the bowl containing the vegetables is placed when they are to be put into the cauldron.

One large millstone likewise, on which the cauldron is again placed, [Col. 0729D] whether it contains beans or vegetables being served; another stone on which another bowl is placed, from which the bowls are washed during the meal.

One bellows for blowing the fire; one wicker fan for fanning it.

One pole for supporting the cauldrons; another for moving the fire.

One channel in which lye is continually kept for the frequent washing of hands.

Also two triangular frames, each made of three pieces of wood, although formed with unequal angles; they can be turned this way and that like doors. Chains hang from these frames. By means of them the cauldrons are suspended, filled with water near the aqueduct, and then drawn without effort all the way [Col. 0730A] to the fire.

It should also be known that, for no necessity, anything else is cooked in the regular kitchen besides beans and vegetables, nor any other kind of pulse. Indeed, when the beans themselves are young enough to be seasoned with pepper as a delicacy, they are not cooked by the brothers but by the servants in another kitchen.

Only the scribe, if he wishes to mix ink, is not forbidden to do so.

If anyone wishes to grease his shoes, he must choose a suitable hour: in summer, before Prime; in winter, before Terce; and, if None is not celebrated, after None—provided that the servers do not have further duties to perform.

The boys, too, make in the same kitchen, with their masters, whatever candles they need.

## CHAPTER XXXVII. On those who perform the *mandatum*

[Col. 0730B]

The list closes with the three men appointed for the daily *mandatum* [Note: [Col. 0729] *Mandatum*: an ecclesiastical term used for the washing of feet, because the antiphon “A new commandment I give,” etc., is then sung from the Gospel], which begins at the start of the fast and continues every day until the Kalends of November, whether the meal is eaten once or twice; it is performed after supper.

When the community leaves the church, after the verse, those who are to perform it gather at the door. After the psalm “Have mercy” has been begun, they proceed to the alms house, where they find three poor men sitting with their feet uncovered. They also ask pardon before them.

When the psalm has ended and the antiphon “A new commandment,” etc., has been begun, they wash, dry, and kiss the feet of the poor. After first washing their own hands, they provide water and a towel for the hands of the poor.

When the small bell has been struck, the singing stops; the bell is then rung, and the blessing is given over the bread and wine to be distributed to the poor. The bread is placed in their right hands and the wine in their left, and both their hands are kissed.

They incline themselves for the prayer, which is as follows:

“Show us.”  
“Lord, have mercy.”  
“Our Father.”  
“We have received mercy, O God.”  
“You commanded.”  
“Prayer: Be present, O Lord, at the duty of our service,” etc.

After making the customary movement forward and back, and beginning the aforesaid psalm again, they withdraw.

When they come to the brothers sitting in the cloister, they proceed bowed, and the brothers, as they pass, likewise rise somewhat while bowed. Reaching the choir with the same psalm, they again say the Lord’s Prayer [Col. 0730D] and the verse “And let it come upon.” Prayer: “Direct our actions, we beseech you, O Lord.” The whole rite concludes with the customary inclination.

Our speech, too, must be concluded here.

“Will you also grant me permission to depart? When I have completed what has been enjoined upon me, I shall be able, if you wish, to return; and if anything has now remained unfinished, I hope then to complete it in prayer.”

“This,” he said, “is what we desire and what we ask: since we do not now dare to detain you against your will, when you have returned, may you by no means return by any route other than through us, so that what you began for the benefit of our souls and with such devotion, you may bring to completion.”

# BOOK THREE. ON THE INDIVIDUAL OFFICES

[Col. 0731]

## PREFACE

[Col. 0731A]

Blessed Jerome advises in one of his letters that we who are reckoned by the name of monks should rarely accept when asked, and never ask when asking others. When I had read this—to confess what is true—it pleased me so greatly that thereafter I could not be forgetful of that saying.

As I have already mentioned elsewhere, when our elder, the lord abbot, had sent me to Alemannia, specifically to the king and to a certain bishop who possessed royal wealth, I happened to suffer some need of supplies for the long journey home. Nevertheless, unable to remove from my memory what the aforesaid philosopher of Christ had advised, and what I myself had approved so thoroughly, I set a guard upon my mouth against the goad of the pressing necessity, so that I asked nothing at all from the persons mentioned, while they too gave nothing at all of their own accord.

Thus, still in need, I returned to the lord abbot William, who, when I had earlier departed from him, had adjured me to return to him after completing the embassy that had been entrusted to me. I could not properly omit this. And what did he do? Certainly he did not wait to be asked for anything by me. For whatever I had needed, before I even knew it, he provided in full and compelled me, whether I wished it or not, to accept it.

Moreover, he continued to offer me every service and attention that he could in any way judge to belong to charity. Thus, when I was burdened by my long hair and sought a barber, he would not allow me to have anyone other than himself. [Col. 0731C] Likewise, when I was about to offer the sacred Host and sought a minister for this, he would not allow me to have anyone other than himself.

Without pretence he imitated the one who came not to be served but to serve. A special lover of the whole religious life, and especially devoted to our monastery as to another paradise, he earnestly asked me to complete whatever still remained to be said about our usages. To accommodate him, I have therefore begun this third book.

## CHAPTER I. On the election of the abbot

I have not yet said anything about the offices—or, to speak in the language of the Rule, the obediences. Since the principal of all these is the obedience owed to the lord abbot, let it also be the beginning of our account.

His original election has, as it were, this lawful and perpetual rule: no mortal usually takes part in it except those alone who are professed members of our Church.

The lord abbot whom, by God’s gift, we presently have, when he was prior of our house, prostrated himself in that place and in the general Chapter, and chanted the first seven of the fifteen Gradual psalms. Then the lord prior himself, rising while the others still remained prostrate, said this prayer, without the Lord’s Prayer:

“We are present, O holy Lord Spirit; we are present, held back indeed by the enormity of our sin, but specially gathered together in your name. Come to us, be with us, and graciously enter into our hearts. Teach us what we should do and by what way we should proceed; show us what we ought to accomplish, so that, with your help, we may be able to please you in all things.

“Be the salvation, the counsellor, and the accomplisher of our judgments—you who alone, with God the Father and his Son, possess the glorious name. Do not allow us to disturb his justice, you who love perfect equity, so that ignorance may not drag us to the left, favour may not bend us, and the acceptance of a gift or of a person may not corrupt us.

“But join us effectively to yourself by the gift of your grace alone, so that we may be one in you and deviate from the truth in nothing. Just as we have been gathered in your name, so may we uphold justice in all things with a moderating compassion, so that here our judgment may dissent from you in nothing, and in the future we may receive eternal rewards from you for our good conduct.” [Col. 0732B]

At the end all answered, “Amen.” The prior then addressed them as they sat again, urging them in no way to doubt the presence of divine grace. He also promised, to the best of his ability, that they could not possibly elect anyone—not even the least of the boys—to whom he would not willingly and without any arrogance be obedient.

When blessed Father Odilo was asked on his deathbed what he thought about his successor, he refused to name anyone. He merely mentioned several persons of rank and proven worth, excluding the prior, and approved that whoever might be elected from among them, all the rest should consent.

When this had been reported in Chapter on that same occasion by a certain brother who had been present at the end of the holy Father’s life, the cloister prior was compelled by the other senior men, the former having been passed over, to be the first to declare what he thought should be done concerning the election.

He hesitated, but at last, overcome by reason and unable to avoid answering, named and elected the prior. Thereafter no one uttered even the slightest murmur against this judgment; all praised it together.

Only the elected man protested, asserting that they had not given him good counsel. If they knew what he would become, he said, they would already have found him to possess this severity and this presumption in a lesser office, since he had already presumed to do many things that other priors had by no means presumed to do.

Tears, too, flowed abundantly amid his words, so that it was plainly understood—according to the saying of a certain writer—that one thing was ready upon the tongue while another was shut up in the breast.

But whatever he might allege achieved nothing. The antiphon “Confirm this, O God” was begun, and Psalm 57, “If indeed,” was sung in a loud voice; and thus he was led into the church.

The prayer “Direct our actions, we beseech you, O Lord” followed. The elected man was set in the abbot’s place, and the hymn “We praise you, O God” was begun. At its second verse, each of the brothers, asking pardon, began to kiss him.

Such was the ambition of the first elector toward the privilege of electing, and such was that of the elected man toward obtaining the prelacy. Since this is not unworthy of the memory of posterity, may those who come after us also wish to imitate it.

On the following day the archbishop of Besançon was invited to Chapter, and the election was announced to him. He was asked to bless the elected man according to the solemn rite. He agreed, promising with the greatest eagerness to do so—not merely because he had been asked, but because he would do whatever even the least of them should command.

Three times, moreover, he adjured them by episcopal authority that if anyone had a different opinion concerning the person elected, such that his ordination could not be legitimate and according to God, he should neither remain silent nor conceal it, but should bring it forward publicly at that moment.

When he found that there was no such person, whatever he had said in this matter was concluded; the election was again confirmed in the presence of the archbishop, and the antiphon “Confirm this, O God,” together with the psalm mentioned above, was again begun as they proceeded into the church.

On the third day, namely the Feast of the Chair of Saint Peter, when the elected man was to be blessed, he was clothed in an alb, stole, and cope; the archbishop was clothed likewise, as were two other abbots who led the elected man in their hands to receive the blessing.

Carpets having been spread before the altar, all four prostrated themselves together in adoration. The litany was sung briefly. After the final “Lord, have mercy,” and after the Lord’s Prayer, the bishop rose and said:

“And lead us not into temptation.”  
“Save your servant.”  
“Send him help.”  
“Here he will receive a blessing.”  
“O Lord, hear.”  
“The Lord be with you.”

Then the blessing followed. When it had been solemnly completed, the hymn “We praise you, O God” was sung again, and, as before, they kissed the man newly confirmed by the blessing.

Having briefly set forth these things about the lord abbot by way of example, let us return to what generally belongs, without respect of persons, to our order and to anyone who has held the office of abbot.

## CHAPTER II. On the lord abbot

The lord abbot is accorded singular reverence everywhere, as is fitting.

First, in church, whenever he has begun an antiphon and has inclined after beginning it, everyone also inclines toward him. As long as he is present in the community, it is never omitted that he is noted at the eighth responsory and at the twelfth lesson; for the latter, everyone rises when he comes and goes. Yet he makes the customary movement forward and back not at the step, as the others do, but near his own seat, still in the middle of the choir, so that they need not stand longer on his account.

For this reason, when the lesson has ended, he himself remains above and does not descend until they have risen for the “Glory be to the Father” of the sung responsory.

If a responsory is sung at the step and he is the one who sings it, he sings it from his seat with his fellow singers approaching him and standing behind him.

The cantor always comes to him beforehand to announce whichever antiphon he is to begin, or whichever responsory is to be sung.

It also belongs to him to read the Gospel whenever it is to be read after Matins. No one other than he begins the antiphons for the Gospel canticles that are to be sung either at Matins or at Vespers.

The priest who is about to offer incense first carries it to him, so that it may be placed in the thurible by his hand. Likewise, the deacon comes to him before the Gospel, and the one who leads the choir before the Offertory.

Whoever gives anything of this sort into his hand, or receives it from him, whether in church or outside, kisses his hand.

Whoever has kissed him, except at the solemn celebration of Mass, asks pardon both before and afterward.

His bed is in the middle of the dormitory near the wall. He himself makes the sound by which the brothers are awakened at dawn to rise. If he should happen to sleep so deeply that the boys rise before him, they do not begin reading as vigorously as usual, but in a subdued voice, lest he be awakened harshly by them.

If he comes into the kitchen to warm himself and finds the brothers occupied with psalmody, they remain completely silent out of reverence for him until he has gone out.

The signal that is rung and at whose dismissal the Hour begins is not discontinued until he or his substitute arrives, so that he is not left waiting.

If he comes afterward to Chapter or Collation, when the brothers are already seated, they not only rise but also lower their feet from the stool to the ground.

Whenever they hear his name recited in the short book, if he is present, everyone inclines, as he himself does.

If there is doubt about some custom, whatever he defines concerning it is thereafter held as law. It is reserved to him alone to send any brother, as they say, into more serious guilt.

## CHAPTER III. On graver guilt and other kinds of faults

[Col. 0734C]

A brother who has incurred such a fall comes to Chapter with his feet bare. The opening of his woollen garment is loosened on the right and left so that he can pull his arms through it and tie the garment, sleeves included, around his thighs. He takes a bundle of rods in his right hand, while his cuculla hangs in a suitable fold from his left. A brother appointed for this purpose walks before him.

Coming thus into the sight of the lord abbot, he places the rods and cuculla before him and asks pardon. Ordered to rise, he sits on the ground and places the cuculla over his knees. He is beaten as much as seems appropriate to the lord abbot.

After this, the abbot orders him to go out and dress. On returning, he prostrates himself again. When he hears the lord abbot say, “Go away,” he immediately bows his head, puts on his cap, and goes to the place designated for such men. There he remains, sleeps, and eats at the time and in the manner prescribed by the lord abbot.

At all the Hours he stands near the church door wearing his cap until the community begins the “Lord, have mercy.” Then, removing his cap, he prostrates himself full length upon the ground. He does not rise until the Hour has ended, and, if the brothers are to go out, until they have all been able to leave.

When they enter Chapter, he likewise prostrates himself, and afterward withdraws to his small private room.

At both Masses he remains in the corner of Chapter adjoining the church. No one speaks to him, not even the man who serves him. The food brought to him is not blessed.

Nevertheless, the lord abbot deliberately sends certain senior brothers to him to exhort him to accept with gratitude whatever temporal correction has been inflicted upon him, so that he may be reconciled to divine grace.

When it seems appropriate, the abbot also agrees with these same seniors that they should ask pardon in Chapter for the guilty man and for his absolution—especially if they have truly found and can testify that, because of his guilt, he possesses a troubled spirit and a contrite and humbled heart.

With the common consent of the brothers, the abbot agrees to show him mercy and sends for him. The brother strips in the same manner as before; after he has been beaten upon his arrival, he puts on his cuculla at the lord abbot’s command.

He falls at the feet of the abbot and of every one of the brothers, from the greatest to the least, one by one. He asks pardon again and is ordered to go out to dress. After dressing and returning, he asks pardon once more.

He is ordered to sit last and to be last of all in every place.

Meanwhile he does not communicate, does not come to the kiss of peace, and does not kiss the Gospel book in church. He is not noted for the lesson or for the singing as the others are. He alone is not barred from the kitchen, in order to serve there, or from performing the *mandatum*.

After each Hour has ended, he asks pardon on his knees, though he does not turn toward the altar for this.

Whenever all the brothers wear white garments because of some feast or procession, he too is clothed in white.

Finally, if the lord abbot sees that it would be expedient and that the brother’s humility merits it, and if the brothers have petitioned him in Chapter, he calls the brother to rise and come into the midst. When the brother asks the customary pardon, the abbot speaks in words appropriate both to the cause and to the person and restores him to his former status, so that he may no longer suffer separation from the others.

If at any time a higher-ranking person is advanced, he falls at that person’s feet, as does anyone else, both in church and in Chapter.

There are still other kinds of correction among us, which are administered not only by the lord abbot but, if necessary, also by the prior.

I have heard the lord abbot say, most truthfully, that no monastic Church is dishonoured because some brother commits such an act; rather, what plainly brings disgrace upon us is that something wicked is committed and then left without worthy correction.

Therefore, if someone is publicly reported to have committed some disgraceful act, he is usually corrected in the presence of the people as well, so that those who have learned of his offence may also learn of his correction.

With everyone who wishes to see watching—and especially in the middle of the public square—he is stripped, bound, and beaten.

But if the fault is not among the more serious offences, and he has perhaps argued dishonourably and irreligiously with someone in the hearing of the people, then, for such conduct, when Sunday comes, at the beginning of the morning Mass, while the people are gathering at the church, he stands barefoot near the church doors and holds a fairly large book in his hand.

He does not put on his cap, so that he may be recognized by everyone. He speaks to no one entering or leaving. A servant always stands beside him and tells those who ask why such a penance has been imposed upon him. He does not leave that place until the Mass has ended.

If anyone is disobedient and rebellious in any way, the brothers, according to custom, do not wait for an order to seize him. They themselves immediately rush upon him and capture him. Once he has been captured, they do whatever seems appropriate, sending him either to prison or to the *bogae*.

The prison is a place into which one descends by a ladder; it has neither a visible door nor a window. The *bogae* also include some lighter and some heavier forms of confinement, so that the prisoner may be unable to ascend to the dormitory; in that case, he sleeps elsewhere under guard.

If the disobedient man has in some way displayed his disobedience outside Chapter, the board is immediately struck so that the brothers may assemble in Chapter.

Someone might also speak something so presumptuous in the presence of the lord abbot or prior that, on this account as well, the board would be struck; this is the signal for assembling.

Whenever it happens that the lord abbot and one of the brothers are speaking together, and the brother senses anger and indignation against him on the part of the lord abbot, he does not delay but immediately asks pardon, prostrating himself with his whole body.

No one passes before him, wherever he may be, without making a deeper inclination.

In church, the priest himself stands behind him wearing an alb, stole, or even a cope.

In a procession for which those serving at the principal Mass are dressed in white, he walks before everyone. In the procession for which all are dressed in white, as at the greater feasts, he wears a cope.

In the community, if he wears a woollen cope or puts on his cap, no one reproves him for doing so whenever he wishes.

When entering the refectory to serve him, one brother holds bowls and another a towel. He provides water for the hands of clerics and of monastic pilgrims who dine with us and travel on foot without a mount. Such men sit at the principal table.

If he wishes to send anything to anyone from the refectory, this is permitted neither to the prior nor to anyone else, but only to him.

If he is in the infirmary, he also customarily sends his charitable portion from there to any brother in the refectory; the brother who receives it inclines no less carefully than if the abbot were present.

After night has fallen, lanterns are carried before him everywhere, both within the community and outside, as far as the bed. The man carrying the lantern serves him both in putting him to bed and in getting him up.

If he has received the *mistum* when he is going to the refectory, he must have a reading at table. If he returns fasting at the hour when the brothers, having eaten after Sext, have already supped a second time after Vespers, he does not eat with them on that occasion but waits until they have risen, because the person who sits by the bell must never remain behind; when the community leaves, he too must leave.

If he has gone to Rome or stayed for some time in other lands, when he returns he is received in procession, with everyone generally dressed in white. If it can suitably be done that same day, after some regular Hour has ended, he goes ahead of everyone who is about to leave the church and stands or sits near its door. The brothers who were with him on the journey remain with him, and he kisses each person as he leaves.

If that day is not suitable, he does the same thing on the following day after Chapter.

For his arrival they have in the refectory a *generale* of fish, or something of equal value, and spiced wine.

The brothers who travel on the road in his service continually take care to remain close beside him, lest at any time they happen to be absent when he sings any regular Hour. If one of them should be absent, he does not sing that Hour afterward without the abbot’s permission.

Whenever they pass through any large town, they never fail, according to custom, to put on their caps.

But, to return to the cloister: every Sunday the lord abbot is assigned with the boys to the *mandatum*. He also does what the others do not: he gives two denarii to the poor man whose feet he washes, and he gives money to the boys so that they may distribute it to the poor.

Whenever he is about to hear the confession of these boys, their master leads them as far as the entrance to Chapter and waits there for their return.

When he is assigned to the kitchen, although there are otherwise only four men, he is usually the fifth.

For two weeks in the year, if he is present and well, no one other than he is ever assigned to the principal Mass: namely, on the Sunday of the Resurrection and on Pentecost. On those days, however, another priest, at the cantor’s direction, says the regular Hours—except Vespers and Matins—and gives the blessing in the refectory.

On those principal days, he is clothed for the Gospel canticle no less splendidly than the lord abbot, so that he may incense the altars together with him and hold the collectary in his service.

On the Nativity of the Lord, the Nativity of the holy apostles Peter and Paul, and the Assumption of Blessed Mary, because these feasts do not occur on Sunday any more than on other days, the lord abbot is not assigned for the whole week but only for the days of each feast.

For as many of the greater feasts throughout the year as he is able and willing, he sings the principal Mass, Vespers, and Matins.

## CHAPTER IV. On the greater prior
When the prior is to be appointed, the lord abbot first consults the seniors of the community; [Col. 0737D] afterward he reports his decision in chapter, and all approve what seems right to him. The man whom he has chosen, if he has good sense, asks pardon and excuses himself, saying that he is unfit for such an office. Finally, when obedience has been commanded and imposed upon him, he does nothing but bow; he sits on the left of the lord abbot. When they have risen from chapter, they go with the customary psalmody to the greater church; there the new prior goes forward and backward, saying three times this verse: “O God, come to my aid,” and the whole convent responds in the same way. The lord abbot himself gives him this blessing:

> “We humbly beseech your omnipotence, most merciful Father, that you may deign to pour upon this servant of yours, whom we dedicate to your service and that of your servants, the spirit of wisdom, understanding, and discernment. Grant that in this house of yours he may act in such a way and administer the office entrusted to him in such a way that he may both please you and, with your help, fulfill perfectly the benefit of your servants, and that for this reason, both in this age and in the age to come, he may receive from you, the most gracious bestower, the reward of his labors in the company of your saints. Through the Lord,” etc.

When he is to be released from office, he sends with him the verse, “Blessed are you, O Lord, who have helped me,” and he is released with this blessing:

> “Lord Jesus Christ, who are a generous rewarder and merciful giver to those who piously serve you, answer with your customary kindness the labors of this servant of yours, who until now has labored faithfully in this house of yours and, by obeying you and your servants, has administered with your help the office entrusted to him; show yourself a gracious remunerator. Grant that he may remain continually in this house and receive from you the reward of his labors, both here and in the recompense of the righteous, and that he may not doubt, with the fullest faith, that you are the giver of all good things.”

From the hour of his appointment onward, after the lord abbot, he takes charge of all matters and affairs pertaining to the monastery, both spiritual and temporal. All who hold any obedience look to him; and if they are going to undertake anything of particular importance, none of them acts without his counsel and assent. In the left choir he stands highest, and in the refectory at the upper table, which is on the right of the lord abbot; and if the latter is absent, he sits in his seat. Outside the refectory, however, no mortal is permitted to send him anything. In the refectory he sends to whomever he wishes whatever he wishes.

If he goes to obediences that are nearby and in the surrounding area, he takes with him two brothers and one provision-servant; if farther away, for example into the province, two provision-servants and three brothers, one of whom is in charge of his servants and baggage and carries the priestly vestment with which there is a silver chalice. As long as he is in the cloister, he has neither a chaplain nor any other vestment for Mass than any other brother has, nor any private money. When he has returned from outside, he hands over to the chamberlain whatever of this kind he has brought, and receives from him whatever he needs. This [Col. 0738D] was prescribed by our fathers [lacuna], lest that evil plague of proprietorship, especially dangerous to monks, should in any way creep in.

Yet although in every respect, as stated above, he acts in the place of the lord abbot, especially in his absence, I do not know how it has happened that he has lost this privilege in the church alone, so that I have seen the precentor and the armarius, although not yet very old, have the twelfth lesson, while the prior had the eighth. Whoever wishes may praise this; my still-small understanding does not know how it can deserve praise.

## CHAPTER V. On the deans who are overseers of the estates

His assistants in temporal matters are those brothers who are overseers of the estates and whom, according to our custom, we call deans. Concerning their particular rule, so to speak, I shall report something. All whose obedience lies within half a day’s journey must come to the monastery every Saturday before vespers; for they neither put on washed clothes nor ever shave anywhere except there.

On the day they come, after each of the hours they go forward and backward, and one collect is to be said for them, together with the verse: “Almighty and eternal God, disposer of our times and life,” etc.; “We beseech you, almighty God, [to grant] these servants,” etc.; “Almighty and eternal God, have mercy on these servants,” etc. The verses that precede are two: the first, “Save [us]”; the second, “Turn again, O Lord,” or “Behold, how good,” or “Blessed are those who dwell [in your house].”

When the collect has been said three times for them, it is not to be said a fourth time, except that, without the greeting and with only the preceding verses, one says: “May almighty God have mercy on you.” This, however, is never done for the lord abbot or the prior.

When they are about to depart, after each hour has ended, they raise their hand and, making the sign of the cross with it toward the lord abbot or prior, ask permission to leave. When he has assented and they have again bowed toward the step as is customary, the priest continues with these verses and this collect: “Save your servants,” etc.; “Send them,” etc.; “Attend, O Lord, to our supplications, and [bless] the way of your servant,” etc.

Those who spend only one night outside the cloister do not, on account of this alone, have a collect either when they leave or when they return. If it happens that someone who has come departs again that same day and returns the next, he is not deprived of what he would have had on the preceding day had he remained.

If two or more are going away and are to eat with the servants either before the brothers’ general meal or afterward, they do not sit at one table, but each sits in his own place as a safeguard of discipline; nor does anyone ever eat without the convent unless he has first received a blessing. If someone has already left the cloister and prepared himself to mount his horse immediately, and it happens that he hears the signal for any regular hour while he is still within the monastery enclosure, he returns to the hour after setting down his traveling equipment. He must not again fail to speak to the lord abbot or prior, nor leave without his permission.

Before mounting his horse, he first puts on his cape, before girding his frock with a strap. He never loosens the bridle of his horse in order to make it run, nor does he himself ever run on foot, except for two things: for a dead person and for a fire.

Once on the road, if it is a weekday—a day on which permission must be requested at each hour—whenever he has sung any hour, he too dismounts, removes his cap from his head and his gloves from his hands, asks pardon, and says the Lord’s Prayer. Rising from this, he makes the sign of the cross, asks pardon again, and, when the hour is finished, continues on his way. No summer heat causes him to ride without his frock, wearing only his cowl. Such a servant, whether beardless or with a shaved beard, is not ordinarily included in his retinue.

At the deanery itself, the servant who supplies him with food and drink never does so wearing only a shirt or only breeches, unless he is also clothed in a frock or fur garment and hose. If, while eating, the dean says something briefly to him concerning what he presently needs, he avoids any longer conversation on other matters.

Before he eats, after the appointed verse has been said, something from Holy Scripture is also read, either by another person or by himself; and likewise at the end, before he rises after the meal. He never beats any of his household for any offense. He is never without the testimony of another brother who remains continually with him.

If a woman of such a kind comes from another place that he cannot refuse her hospitality, he never sits with her at one table, nor does he ever accept anything from the woman’s hand. At all times after night has fallen, unless some such necessity arises and prevents it, he does not delay Compline any further; and if he has removed his cowl, he says no word, either by night or by day. He also takes care never to place it anywhere more than one cubit away from himself.

If he removes his frock because of the heat, he may sit in his cowl, but only if he has neither a tunic nor a fur garment beneath it, and nothing other than his woolen garment. He gains nothing by cleverness unless he diligently cultivates fields and vineyards and raises livestock and pack animals. He keeps nothing hidden or entrusted to a stranger’s house; this has been utterly anathematized by our elders.

When the grain and wine have been entirely gathered, the prior comes, as is customary, and sees whatever there is in the cellar and whatever there is in the granary. He leaves as much as seems appropriate for the dean’s provisions, for arriving guests, and for agricultural work; whatever remains he orders to be brought to the monastery.

If the dean should at some time begin to fall ill and be in the cloister with the other sick, he no longer takes charge of the obedience until he is well; thereafter his entire administration is again in the prior’s hands. If one of his associates, out of their longstanding familiarity, sends him anything, it is presented not to him but only to the cellarer, so that it may benefit him no more than all the other sick. After whatever it is has been consumed, the infirmarian informs them from whom and through whom he received such kindness.

## CHAPTER VI. On the cloister prior

[Col. 0740D]

The cloister prior is in every respect the deputy of the major prior. He is present wherever the lord abbot goes and wherever the prior goes; he remains continually in the cloister and chiefly bears the burden of the entire order. For this reason, however, he has no particular precedence in the choir, except that, in the prior’s absence, he offers first, comes forward first for the kiss of peace, and goes first to the holy water.

Whenever twelve lessons are read, he gives permission to one of the white-robed brothers to offer the hosts. This, however, is something he never omits on any day: after Compline, having received the blessing, he withdraws to stand near the church door so that he can observe each one and see how they bow toward the altars and toward the priest by whom they are sprinkled.

After all have gone out, he takes a covered lamp from the hebdomadary, with a candle burning inside it, puts on his cap, and makes a circuit of the entire cloister. First he sees whether the almonry, the regular kitchen, the refectory, and the novices’ cell are closed and bolted; whether anyone still remains there, and why, before the cellar; and he examines what is being done in the infirmary and whether the sick have already retired, and how they are; if any of them has remained in the church of Saint Mary, he goes up to the dormitory, carrying with him anything he may have found neglected in the cloister, and inspects all the seats of the necessary-house from one end to the other.

If he finds any negligence in these matters, he complains about it in chapter the following day. In winter he makes another circuit during the interval that ordinarily falls between nocturns and matins; on that circuit he also goes around all the brothers’ beds and all the church altars.

To conclude briefly concerning his office: if the lord abbot and the prior are absent, not only do all the obedientiaries who are in the cloister obey his command, but the deans themselves do so for whatever work may be required. If he receives a monk from another monastery, he may grant him fraternal fellowship in every respect, except chapter, which he reserves solely to the lord abbot.

He also has his own assistants: one who fills his place in his absence in all matters that, as they say, are to be done immediately; the circuiters; the masters of the boys; and the guardians of the young men.

## CHAPTER VII. On the circuiters

[Col. 0741C]

The duty of the circuiters is to note every negligence, both minor and major, that can in any way occur against the order, and to complain of it in chapter. For this reason they go around the entire cloister not once but many times a day, so that there may be neither place nor hour in which any brother who has committed such a thing can feel secure that it will not be detected and made public.

Accordingly, the obedientiaries, who cannot avoid sometimes speaking about their obediences while others are silent, immediately rise if they see one of the circuiters approaching, and briefly indicate what necessity they have for speaking. The circuiters show such deference to the lord abbot and the prior that they never go where they know them to be; for, as it is written: “A disciple is not above his master.”

## CHAPTER VIII. On the boys and their masters

When a boy comes wearing secular or clerical clothing, the chamberlain leads him to the wardrobe, where he is clothed in the same manner as any novice, except that he is given a linen shirt instead of a woolen garment. When it seems right to the lord abbot, he orders the cap to be removed from the boy’s frock and blesses a cowl to be given to him.

He also orders one of the brothers to offer the boy in place of his parents. The brother, having the petition he is about to make written down, confirms it with the mark of his own hand, then reads it aloud and places it in the hand of the lord abbot. It is as follows:

> “I, Brother N., offer to God and to his holy apostles Peter and Paul this boy, named N., in place of his parents, with the offering in his hand and the petition, the altar cloth wrapped around his hand, to the name of the saints whose relics are contained here and of the lord abbot N. who is present. In the presence of witnesses I hand him over to remain according to the Rule, so that from this day it may not be permitted him to shake his neck free from the yoke of the Rule; rather, let him acknowledge that he must faithfully observe the institutions of that same Rule and serve the Lord with the others with a thankful heart. And so that this petition may remain firm, I have confirmed it below with my hand and delivered it to witnesses for their ratification.”

The boy himself receives with the offertory a paten and chalice, with the host placed upon it and wine poured in. The vicar then wraps the boy’s hand with the altar cloth, so that he may offer both the boy himself and his sacrifice to be received by the priest.

Afterward he is clothed in the cowl. His blessing is thereafter deferred until the lawful age—that is, at the latest, until he is fifteen years old. When the lord abbot wishes to bless him, he reports the matter to the brothers in chapter; the young man immediately asks pardon and, released from school, comes to the feet of the abbot. Nevertheless, he does not leave the other boys until the hour of the blessing.

Like the other novices, he makes profession. The blessing of the cowl is not repeated; nor is it removed or put on except as it was before.

The boys who are in our community are never more than six, and their masters are two, if not more, but never fewer. Their discipline is as follows.

First, they sleep together in the dormitory, with each of their beds separated from the beds of their masters. No one else dares approach them. If one of them needs to go to the necessary-house at night, he first wakes by a sound the master lying near him. The master rises, lights a lamp, places it in a lantern, and makes the other boy rise. With one of them holding the lantern above them, the master walks between them; in this way he leads them there and back, and does not extinguish the candle until both have been put back to bed.

When everyone has risen for nocturns, the boys and their masters go together to the necessary-house, as I have already said regarding the two. Their seats are marked out in the middle by two wooden circles, on which no one dares sit when they come. They do not put on their caps like the others except while sitting; when they rise, they stand bareheaded, waiting for one another.

Their principal master sees to it that they do not approach the church until all have been able to assemble and to sing the seven psalms quietly and carefully. Only then does he come solemnly with his pupils and lights, and he himself concludes the three prayers of the brothers, which they perform on that occasion or after Compline.

At nocturns—or, indeed, at all the hours—if the boys commit any offense in psalmody or in another chant, by dozing or by committing anything of that kind in any way, the matter is not postponed. Without delay they are judged, stripped of frock and cowl, and beaten in only their shirts either by the prior or by the aforementioned [Col. 0743A] master, with light, smooth, rounded willow rods provided for this purpose.

Every day at dawn, as soon as they have sat down in the cloister, before doing anything else, they read aloud three psalms beginning, “Have mercy,” etc. No one comes to confession before he has heard these psalms begun.

At all the hours their faces are turned toward the west, I think so that they may be seen by the priors who usually stand on that side. When the prayers are reached, the two younger boys on either side turn toward the choir; the third, who is older and stands nearer the altar, turns toward the altar, except at Compline and at Prime.

Then, for confession, two of them arrange themselves facing the altar on one bench, with one master between them, as also happens at the litany and at each prayer performed in the presbytery; when the confession is to be said, the third runs up. At both Masses, during which the priors also change places, they all turn together toward the choir. They do likewise on Saturday at the procession to the Holy Cross held at vespers and matins, at the twelve lessons at Terce, and at any procession that we may sometimes make for a person of such standing who has arrived.

If we are sometimes clothed in copes for such a procession, they wear only white robes; yet at the solemn celebrations of Mass, if the convent is clothed in copes, they too are clothed in silk tunics. At the Secret and the Canon, if the convent bows or even prostrates itself, they stand upright, except for the Lord’s Prayer alone; and one of their masters likewise remains standing and continually watches them.

In the cloister and in chapter, where each sits separately, they have individual tree-trunks for seats, and are so separated from one another that one cannot touch the other’s clothing in any way. In the church their arrangement is different because of the benches, which are sometimes present and sometimes removed. On weekdays they are removed to make transverse forms, on which some of the brothers prostrate themselves for prayer and ask pardon at the beginning of the hours. Only one bench remains, on which the eldest of the boys sits transversely; meanwhile, during the singing of the regular hour or any other psalmody, he sits with his face turned toward the west.

During the intervals—for example, from the matutinal Mass until chapter; after the prayer of Terce, immediately followed by the major Mass; after the prayer of None, while the brothers are still fasting; after the evening prayer; and at the Canon of Mass, if he is sitting—he turns his face toward the east.

The other boys, if they have benches, sit upon them with their faces turned toward the choir; if they do not, they sit on the ground, always in the same manner as the eldest sits on the bench. At the lessons of nocturns on feast days and during octaves, they sit beside the straight form.

When the forms are transverse, they sit so that one of the benches on which they sit is also transverse, while the masters sit opposite them on the form that is always placed in the middle of the choir. If the brothers are keeping vigil with psalmody beside a dead person, the boys from the right choir sit at the head, and those from the left at the feet.

When a procession is to be held to receive someone who has been brought in from outside dead, the boys go out first, immediately behind the cross. When they have reached the vestibule gate, they keep their faces opposite one another until the prior says the collect, “Absolve, O Lord.” They withdraw slightly to one side so that those carrying the cross and the other processional insignia can pass.

Following them into the church, they leave them near the door so that the dead person may be surrounded by them; they themselves extend as far as the altar of the Holy Cross and stand there, with the masters between them, on the left side, so as not to impede the priest, who is to approach the altar three times to incense it.

When this has been completed and the dead person has been carried to the tomb, they move from the left into the middle of the church and, keeping their faces continually turned toward the altar, begin the antiphons and psalms. In every procession held through the cloister they always walk behind the cross. On Palm Sunday and during the Rogation processions, they walk between the lay brothers and the singers.

Chapter is not held with them on the five principal feasts: the Purification of Saint Mary, Palm Sunday, and the Ascension of the Lord; whenever they shave, whenever they bathe, whenever they wash their clothes, and whenever we perform manual labor; or whenever we have a dead person who, at the hour of chapter, is still unburied. Their own chapter is received without a bow, with only the preceding blessing.

One boy complains of another if he knows of such a thing concerning him; and if someone is discovered deliberately to have concealed it, both the one who concealed it and the one who committed the offense are beaten. On that occasion, however, a single bell is customarily rung, so that the household servants to whom bread is to be given may come to receive it. Once it has been heard, none of the boys is stripped, and the chapter itself is brought to an earlier end.

During the time of conversation, sometimes the cellarer and sometimes the chamberlain comes to them to hear whether they need anything that can be remedied through them. After the major Mass they receive the mixed refreshment (*mistum*); but if it is a fast day, or winter, or another day on which food is eaten only once, then they receive it after Terce. From the Kalends of October until Lent, if, as I said, food is eaten only once, their meal consists not merely of bread, but something else, whatever it may be, is also set before them.

Throughout the summer, on Sundays at supper, mercy is shown to them in the form of milk. If one of them is so small that he needs it, bread and wine are brought to him in the cloister itself, where he sits. At the washing place, as at the necessary-house, they have a special place of their own.

When they are in the refectory, they do not approach any table before the verse; they stand in the middle of the refectory, or sit with their masters, until the person who is to sit at the bell comes. They are distributed among the tables, each placed before such brothers as will not overlook any negligence they observe in them while eating.

They do not run about to bring salt, a bowl, or anything else to any brother, nor do they accept anything from anyone except what is given generally to all. If the lord abbot sends them something or the cellarer gives them something, only the boy who stands at the principal table, if the lord abbot or prior indicates to him that he needs bowls, goes to the master. The master rises, asks for them from the kitchen, and places them before the boy so that he may carry them; through him he also sends whatever each person sitting at the bell wants.

That boy, because of the guests who more frequently sit at that table, always carries two small knives. If one of them becomes so ill that he cannot stand properly, then, with the prior’s consent, the master provides him with a small table and a napkin, so that he may sit in the place where he ordinarily stood.

After lunch or supper they leave together and proceed between the two choirs, after None, when the brothers drink, and at the collation, last of all, and before the lord abbot or prior.

Whenever they enter the church as a group, they enter on the eastern side and the convent on the western side. No hour and no general meal begins without them, unless at least two of them are present. Wherever they pass through the cloister, the brothers rise slightly and bow toward them, both on account of the two and on account of all of them.

They do not turn aside either to the necessary-house or anywhere else unless two of them are always together, with one of their masters between them. If the convent is absent, the master does not sit but stands before them at the necessary-house.

The servants also, when leaving the refectory, if they are sitting in their usual place, bow toward them, and the boys rise toward them. If some of the boys arrive late for a regular hour, later than the “Glory” of the first psalm, the others do not therefore come and stand at the step.

Likewise, if they remain away from the refectory until the verse has been said, they do not ask permission to eat, but merely bow forward and backward in their place; their accompanying master, however, maintains the custom on both sides.

If a boy coming from outside is about to enter the cloister, two other boys are led to the cloister door to meet him, and he is presented to the convent together with them. After the hours, they receive the blessing in the presbytery with the others who have come, while he stands before them.

If one of them is to be taken to the infirmary, two other boys come there with him. As long as he remains there, he is entrusted to a most careful custodian, who watches over him day and night. At night, wherever he goes, he carries a lantern before him and also carries a staff.

If he eats meat, he puts on his cap and comes with the other sick to the greater church; yet he does not enter the section containing the altar of Saint John the Baptist. When the others enter, he remains outside near the vessel of holy water, so that he can be seen by everyone.

The principal master of the boys frequently visits him while he remains in the infirmary. When he first sees that the boy has recovered sufficiently, he brings him back in the same way in which he had taken him there and joins him to the other boys, who are about to enter the church for Prime or Terce if it is winter and a weekday. Before this, however, on that same day he is abundantly provided with meat. In chapter, because of his offenses, he does not ask pardon as the other sick do.

This is the service that they are properly to perform. At all the regular hours they recite the individual verses of the psalms; on weekdays they intone the antiphons and whatever is sung at the matutinal Mass. At matins and vespers they sing the responsories and recite the verses, and in summer at nocturns they recite that very short, single lesson.

In chapter no one reads except them—although never in the refectory—and they read by turns at the collation. The board that the major prior or the cloister prior strikes five times to grant permission to speak is to be carried by their prior.

Likewise, in winter, whenever the brothers speak for a second time after Sext, after they have left the church everyone falls silent until the youngest of the boys has pronounced “Benedicite” in a loud voice. He must likewise say it when they leave their chapter or when, after receiving their breakfast in the refectory, the brothers are speaking.

They are marked for kitchen duty together with their masters, and in groups of two. Nevertheless, they do not rise from the dormitory for it before the signal, nor do they leave the choir before the familiar psalms have been completed, except for the matutinal Mass after the offertory. They do not serve in the refectory, nor wash the brothers’ feet in chapter; instead, for everything they themselves cannot suitably do, they have their masters as substitutes.

On the days when a procession is to be made barefoot, they first clean with brooms and water the channels in which the brothers are to wash their feet. If the lord abbot or prior orders a psalm to be sung for several days, they bow when they hear it, because it is especially their concern that it not be omitted.

Since they read the Martyrology and the Memorial of the Brothers every day, they are responsible for knowing and noting when the thirtieth day after each person’s death has been completed. They are also responsible for informing the almoner for how many brothers the anniversary is being observed, so that he may receive the same number of portions; and they inform the church custodian when all the bells are to be rung for each anniversary, which has been carefully noted individually in the Memorial.

Every Wednesday, if it is a weekday, and every Saturday, they wash their shoes after vespers. They also customarily wash their clothes before the Nativity of the holy apostles Peter and Paul, before the Translation of Saint Benedict, and before the Assumption of Saint Mary. They do not, however, hang them out to dry on the line [or “rope”; text reads *horda*], as the other brothers do, but merely lay them down in the cloister garden.

At a regular hour for which only one signal is rung, such as Prime, they pray in the choir at the place where those for whom two signals are rung pray in the presbytery near the altar.

In the morning they rise at the signal, or when Prime is sung with the dawn appearing, as on weekdays. From the Kalends of October to the Kalends of November they do not go to the necessary-house before going to church, but afterward, when the hour has ended, if they wish, or after the prayers have been said.

After Compline they say their prayers without the convent, and before the convent does so; they must leave the necessary-house before the convent comes there. Their principal master stands before them with a rod until all have been put in place, and their faces are well covered.

Likewise, when they rise, if they rise late, the rod is immediately upon them. After matins, at the time when everyone is again going to sleep, if dawn has not yet appeared, then, while the master holds the rod in his right hand and the candle in his left, they are undressed and quickly put to bed.

If dawn has become somewhat bright, they fasten the candles atop the lanterns, put on their shoes, and recline on their beds, so that they may rise without any delay at the signal; the whole convent must do the same. Their bread and general allowance are no less than those of the other brothers.

If one of the brothers, returning from outside, kisses all the brothers, he does not kiss the boys, nor do they kiss him, just as they do not kiss in the church at the kiss of peace. Their feet are not washed for the Mandatum, nor do they themselves wash anyone’s feet.

When they serve in the kitchen, their masters usually see to it that the dormitory and necessary-house are suitably illuminated, and that two candles are placed in the necessary-house at nocturns; these last only until the convent departs. If it happens to be night when they leave the refectory after supper, they come into the choir, take the candles out of the lanterns, and hold them high for as long as they are in the choir.

If they need to take a book or the breviary board to a place other than where they usually sit in the cloister, they never take it without the master’s permission. Twice a week they come to confession, which is heard only by the lord abbot, the major prior, or the one who holds the office. They confess standing; and if the prior is to hear them, he comes to them and leads them there and back, while one confesses and the other sits meanwhile.

No one else ever sits on the tree-trunks on which they usually sit, not even any of the pedagogues themselves. They have a separate chest containing the razors with which they are shaved. The boys are shaved separately with their masters; and however many masters there may be, they never leave the boys for any reason without the principal master’s permission. They must never be left with only one master.

Their seating in the cloister is arranged so that the boys sit near the wall and the masters at the cloister grating, in such a way that they can continually watch them. No one dares pass directly between them.

Wherever they may be, however narrow the place and however large the crowd of brothers, everyone takes care not to come so close that any of the boys’ clothing is touched.

And, finally, to conclude concerning these boys: I have often seen with what care they are guarded day and night, and I have said in my heart that it would scarcely be possible for any king’s son to be brought up with greater diligence in a palace than the smallest boy at Cluny.

## CHAPTER IX. On the guardianship of the young men
A brother who is of such an age as still to be beardless, even if he has voluntarily renounced the world, and even if he is of the best reputation, is nevertheless by no means free from custody. Sometimes, moreover, even those who have been brought up in the monastery, if they refuse to be men in their conduct, gain nothing from reaching manhood by way of release from custody.

When someone has been placed under it, his bed in the dormitory is first situated near the bed of his custodian; without him he neither ever approaches nor leaves it. At night, wherever he goes, he carries a lantern before him, while his custodian takes care that he has a lighted candle. If the custodian has led him to the latrine, after he himself has risen he keeps looking at him continually, although the lantern is also before him. If he needs to rise during the night, he wakes his custodian, lights the lantern, and goes to the latrine; the custodian does not extinguish the lantern before he has been put back to bed. For the custodians always light and extinguish them.

If he has led him to church, he does not leave him until he reaches the choir; and in the refectory he remains with him until he is inside the doorway and in the presence of the community. If he has been assigned to the kitchen, he does not come to him before the sound of the signal.

At the three prayers which they properly perform before nocturns, or after compline, and likewise during the day at the three prayers which in winter are performed before prime, or in summer after the signal, they are never separated from one another. When the community proceeds to holy water and to other processions, if they are under different custodians in the order of custody, they go up or down to the custodian; the custodian, however, does not alter his own order, except perhaps on account of one who was in the more serious fault and who, after being received into brotherly fellowship, [Col. 0748C] is nevertheless the last of all, or one wishing to flee who has been unwillingly dragged back and restrained.

If a deacon or subdeacon under custody is scheduled to read the Gospel or Epistle, and something happens to him so that he cannot read, he does not on that account call upon anyone, either by word or by sign, who is his equal and placed under similar custody, to read in his place. Rather, the matter is made known to his custodian, with the testimony of his own custodian, so that the custodian of a brother of the same order may speak to the brother in turn about the reading. Or, if the one who is to read prefers, he reports his inability earlier to the librarian, so that the latter may promptly arrange whom to assign the duty of reading.

Each of these brothers, if—as they say—they wish to take precautions for their own backs, takes the utmost care in every place that they do not stand together or sit together in church, in the chapterhouse, or in the refectory without an intermediary; nor do they bump against one another when the community proceeds in such a dense crowd that this sometimes happens as they enter or leave the church, or when they put books away in the little bookcase situated in the cloister. This is not neglected even if their status is still in the middle of the choir, with one on one side and the other on the other, so that they stand in such a way that their backs are not turned directly toward one another.

## CHAPTER X. On the precentor and librarian.

The precentor and librarian obtained the name *armarius* because the library, also called an *armarium* by another name, is customarily in his hands. This is an office which, according to custom, no one deserves unless he has been brought up in the monastery.

The official under discussion properly has one assistant, who both sings with the boys and prepares the brief list of readings and responsories, as well as other services. As for the names of the brothers who are to read, sing, or do anything else, no one but he assigns them—unless he himself wishes his second to do so, and that second possesses the requisite diligence and judgment.

To touch briefly on his continual occupation: the entire ordering of divine service in the church depends on no one more than on him, and in this matter he has no superior except the lord abbot alone. Whatever he wants sung is sung; whatever he wants read is read—in church, in the refectory, and at collation—and in all such matters everyone must always obey him.

If, however, he presumes against custom or neglects something, this is entirely passed over for the time being, until complaint is made in chapter.
