At the Gospel canticles, at morning praises, and at vespers he imposes the antiphon, except for what the lord abbot is to impose at the twelfth lesson. This librarian, as long as he is in the community, does not assign himself to any reading or responsory, so that, if the lord abbot should not read, he may himself be ready to read in his place.

If an error is made in a tone, no one’s expertise overrides his, and everyone must heed and follow him above all others. He alone is not reproved if he names an antiphon or responsory without a book and directs a brother to sing it. He also imposes all the verses of the offertory. However softly any chant may be sung, no one else dares raise it to a louder voice.

Every day at dawn, after the three boys have read through the psalms, as is customary, he immediately comes to them so that the boy who is to read in chapter may hear the reading. If the boys have in any way offended, especially by singing, by reading carelessly, or by learning the chant insufficiently diligently, they receive from him a discipline proportionate to their fault.

Nevertheless, he himself, and the others as well, takes the greatest care when beating them—not only that they do not touch their flesh with the hand, but also that his garment does not adhere to their garments. Their cheeks are never struck with the palm; if correction is needed, only the master who leads them may pull their hair. No one else may do so.

For this reason, as long as he or his assistant remains among them, the principal master of the boys, whom I mentioned above, neither reads nor does anything else, except continually to watch the librarian and the boys. The book from which the reading is made is always placed between them in such a way that one of the cloister columns lies between the reader and the listeners.

The readings which are to be read at nocturns, and the responsories, are properly heard after none, and during Lent after sext; but never after vespers.

Whenever a solemn or morning Mass is to be sung, once the priest has vested with the other ministers, the librarian is never absent by custom: first, so that he may see whether all the persons who are to serve are present, and indicate anything he knows needs to be indicated. He does the same whenever the Gospel is to be read after nocturns, or whenever those who are to sing the invitatory put on albs or copes. He is the principal organizer of the entire matter.

If a sick brother is to be anointed with the oil of the sick, or, if he has died, is to be carried out for burial, or if someone brought from outside is to be received, the care belongs to him: how the priest is to vest, how the Lord’s body is to be brought, how he is to be communicated; and which collects the prior is to say over the dead brother, while he is washed, while he is clothed, before he is brought into the church, and what is to be sung; how the grave is to be blessed; which collects are to be said at its blessing, which at the burial, and which after the burial. In all [Col. 0750B] these matters he is to be the principal director.

He receives the brief notices concerning deceased brothers who arrive, records them on the reading desk, and distributes other written notices among the brothers traveling through the various provinces of the earth. Nor does he forget, when a brother has died, the thirty Masses which are properly entrusted to six brothers on his behalf. Indeed, I do not know whether anyone does more than he for all the processions, at which absolutely nothing is sung except what he has imposed.

Finally, whatever such new matter may arise to be done, he must be especially mindful and diligent about it. I mean, for example, when new beans, or new bread, or must is to be blessed in the refectory; or when a guest of such dignity arrives that, after the procession has been completed, a reading must first be recited before him, as the Rule prescribes; or when, after manual work, something has to be read; or when the hair and beard of any novice are to be shorn at his public profession. For each of these and similar matters he takes and brings the appropriate book, and ensures that there is no negligence either regarding the person or regarding what the person is to say.

If a bishop is present—whether of our order or of such a reputation that the lord abbot or prior thinks he should give the blessing in church—he supplies the stole, book, and staff, and imposes this verse: “Humble yourselves for the blessing.”

At Christmas, Easter, and Pentecost, the better singers, as the librarian judges, are assigned to the office of the principal Mass and to holding the choir. They nevertheless do not presume to approach on their own unless he gives them the copes with his own hand; these are always prepared at the head of the choir stalls by the principal sacristan from among the best. He also adds to those assigned in order as many as the entire width of the choir can accommodate. None of them presumes to withdraw, approach for the kiss of peace, sing Mass, or leave his assigned place, even if he is one of the more important persons, except at his direction.

If it happens that neither the prior nor his vicar is in the choir, then, if he sees that it is necessary, he may move brothers from one choir to the other and grant permission to anyone who asks to leave. The thurible is first brought to him by a lay brother, unless it is our abbot, or some bishop or abbot, to whom it is presented out of respect for the order.

In all other matters, whatever the order of the aforesaid librarian may be, he does not lose his precedence. He does not approach for the kiss of peace, nor does his assistant; meanwhile, while the peace is being given, he sings “Lamb of God” with the verses appropriate to it. Nor does anyone among those assigned to the gradual or alleluia take part unless he himself has indicated them by handing them booklets.

He also tells the priest in what tone to begin “Glory to God in the highest,” and, if necessary, tells the deacon “The Mass is ended.” Four sing the sequences, two on one side and two on the other, that is, on the left and the left [as printed; the wording is uncertain]. He himself is added as a fifth, especially beside the two on the right, who always begin the first verse, so that, if they should perhaps disagree, he is at hand to support them.

He also precedes the others somewhat in removing the cope and in moving forward and backward, so that he may hurry to remove each person’s garment, and so that he himself may be the first to put his hand to ringing the little bells, just as he did at the beginning of Mass.

If a notation or brief record of this kind is to be made, it is not made on the daily tablet but on another, somewhat larger one, specifically assigned to feast days. Among us another useful record is also customarily made, but because the librarian is otherwise so occupied, it is sometimes entrusted to another brother who is mindful and diligent: namely, that all those who have served in the kitchen be recorded in order, lest through forgetfulness anyone happen to perform that duty more frequently than another.

## CHAPTER XI. On the chamberlain.

Our chamberlain personally goes out and receives, at the proper time, as many coins as we can obtain from our villages. Of these, however, he returns a third part to the deans, because they have need of so many things—not only for farming but also for themselves, since they stay there more often, and especially for guests, who plainly could not be received at all without inhumanity.

From those villages which are so far away that neither the wine nor the grain produced there can reach us, the produce is sold on the spot and the price is brought to the chamberlain. Finally, whatever gold, silver, or animals are donated to us from any source, he receives in full, except for what I am about to say.

If someone gives us ten shillings or less, these are always assigned to the cellarer, solely so that he may show some charity to the weaker and somewhat delicate brothers, beyond what is generally given to everyone. If a cow happens to be donated to us, he receives that also as support for the cow-barn under his administration. Sheep and oxen go to the dean of the village: sheep for the manure with which the fields are enriched, and oxen for plowing.

Cloaks and gold or silver vessels which can be used for the service and adornment of the church are received by the sacristan. Apart from these, as has been said, everything comes into the hands of the chamberlain, and not undeservedly, because it frequently happens that, from all the things produced annually, we have absolutely nothing to support our temporal life except what has been purchased with money. Since this occurs only from time to time with food, everything pertaining to clothing must be purchased not from time to time but continually and entirely.

Each brother is given every year a new frock and a new cowl, so that both are ready and sewn before Christmas. A new fur garment is given every second year, at the feast of Saint Michael; meanwhile, when the community is in the refectory for the meal, it is placed on his bed. Again, at the feast of Saint Martin, footcloths are given. As for shoes, I have explained elsewhere how they are given on Maundy Thursday.

With regard to woolen shirts and undergarments, or any other such items, nothing else is prescribed except that, when they have grown old and are no longer useful, they are to be washed and returned by the brothers to the chamber, and other ones are to be assigned.

To state this once for all: whatever can regularly and customarily be possessed for the clothing of each brother consists first of two frocks and two cowls; two woolen shirts and two undergarments; two pairs of shoes with straps; one pair of felted shoes for winter nights and another pair without felt for summer nights; two pairs of leggings; three fur garments, or one of them a tunic in place of the third; a fur cap; and five pairs of footcloths.

For the bed there are a pillow, a coverlet, a quilt, bedding, a small girdle with which the undergarments are fastened, a neck-strap, a woolen garment, a belt from which the knife with its sheath hangs, a wooden comb with its sheath, and a needle with thread and sheath.

A priest and deacon generally have three undergarments, so that if something of that kind should happen to them during the night, they may readily change them. If the chamberlain, out of mercy, adds a tunic to someone who already has three fur garments, or gives someone a pair of sheepskin leggings or bindings for weakened legs, neither the giver nor the recipient deserves much reproach for it.

But beyond these provisions, whoever wishes to have anything more of this kind is certainly judged to possess it neither as a matter of justice nor of mercy, but out of great excess. All the fur garments are of sheep’s wool; the coverlets are of sheep, cat, or hare fur, and never of any kind of greater value. The frock and cowl are made of cloth such that together they are worth no more than eight shillings, in currency containing more copper than silver.

Whenever the chamberlain has bought or sold something, after the transaction has been completed in full, he voluntarily adds or returns some coins to the merchant with whom he has dealt, according to the nature of the business and the person involved, because of Saint Benedict’s command that our goods should always be sold more cheaply than those of other people.

Whenever the chamberlain or his junior, who carries the key to the chamber, speaks in the cloister, he must never be absent. At that time he is to hear from each person what this or that brother needs, and he does not neglect to come even to the boys, to ask them whether there is anything they lack. Thus he supplies on that occasion whatever must be supplied, lest, if the brothers ask him at another hour when silence is in force, they be unable to observe silence.

A brother whose fur garment, woolen shirt, or undergarments are so torn that they can still be mended places them at dawn in one of the arches of the chapterhouse assigned for this purpose. The chamberlain’s junior comes and carries them outside to the tailors. After vespers he brings them back and places them in the same place, so that the person to whom they belong may collect them.

Likewise, anyone who needs his shoes greased first washes them with water let down through the channel from the water supply. The chamberlain’s junior then takes them and treats the shoes as he does the other items. But if a brother wishes to grease them himself, he takes the grease and does so in the regular kitchen before prime; or, if prime is sung together with morning praises, before terce; or after the brothers’ meal, when they eat only once.

Our elders have handed down that, when Lent begins, however many poor people arrive, all are to receive alms and a blessing consisting of meat. Besides the concern he has for the brothers’ clothing, nothing should occupy the chamberlain more than this very almsgiving. Our pigsty and larder contribute little to it, for they are never so full that the money alone, issuing from the hand of the chamberlain, is not required. To say nothing else, this happened in the present year: those who counted the poor testified that there were seventeen thousand, to whom two hundred and fifty bacon sides were distributed in the name of Christ.

## CHAPTER XII. On the apocrisiary.

The apocrisiary is the one who guards the church’s treasury, and in whose hands is whatever is offered by the people at the altars. So that he may be able to fulfill his office worthily, the assistance of several brothers is assigned to him. Among them, however, one is usually more distinguished, and it principally belongs to him to act in the apocrisiary’s place when he is absent or engaged in some other task outside the community.

The church door is also specially entrusted to one man, who always closes and opens it at the proper time. A man is carefully chosen for this who is grave in conduct and not easily given to laughter, lest those entering or leaving detect any frivolity in him. He is absolutely forbidden, when closing or opening the door, to extend even a foot beyond it for any reason.

Since he always remains on watch in the church, he sleeps and reads there. Beyond the others, he alone is assigned the duty every Saturday of thoroughly scraping the basins and the bowls of the candlesticks in which the candles burn, so that no residue of dripping wax remains. With equal care he cleans the entire pavement around the high altar, and he does not neglect to sweep the pavement of that altar and of the other altars with a broom.

He also closes and opens the church doors in different ways at different times. Since he always opens them for nocturns, both in winter and in summer, in winter he nevertheless always closes them after the office sung during the night, and they remain closed until the little bell is sounded for terce. When the morning Mass has ended, he closes them, and they remain closed until the bell is rung for sext. Then they are opened, and after Mass has ended they are closed until vespers. After vespers the regular doors are closed and remain so until nocturns.

In summer, however, since they are closed immediately after the regular morning praises, they are opened at prime and remain open until the morning Mass has ended. They are then closed and opened again for the Mass; after it they are shut until vespers, and when vespers has ended they are entirely closed until nocturns.

During Lent, on weekdays, they are closed after the morning Mass and reopened immediately after the bell has sounded following sext; they are not closed until vespers has ended. At the twelve readings, both in winter and summer, they are opened at the bell which is sounded after chapter. He nevertheless diligently ensures that, if anyone knocks on them by day or night, he is completely ready to open them.

Thus, when the community proceeds to Saint Mary’s, he always remains in the church, lest some negligence occur in his absence. The others perform their weekly turns, each beginning on Sunday at nocturns, in the manner prescribed for them; each must carefully attend to what he is to do.

First, as I said, at nocturns, after the clock has struck, he rings the little bell, and continues until he sees the boys coming. After the three prayers have been said, he rings one of the larger bells until the psalm “I rejoiced” (*Laetatus sum*). Second, he rings the smaller bell for a while at “Lord, have mercy” (*Kyrie, eleison*), until the Lord’s Prayer with its collect has ended. Third, he does likewise. Fourth, all the bells are rung; or, if it is a weekday, two are rung at the final division of the Songs of Ascents.

At the penultimate psalm, the weekly server lights two candles fixed to candlesticks before the altar and extinguishes the third, which had been burning in the basin behind them. He also takes care at the readings to light the candle by which the reading is to be made at the final nocturn.

Thus, at the ninth reading, which is from the Gospel, a third candle is still burning before the altar; he lights another behind the altar and uncovers the golden altar panel, which until then had been covered with a cloth. He takes the Gospel book from the altar and carries it to the vestry. After the Gospel has been read, when the priest returns, he takes it from his hand and replaces it where he had first taken it.

When the time comes for the morning priest to say the collect, he provides and brings a candle for this as well. Then, after extinguishing all the candles around the altar, he relights the one that had previously been burning in the basin, so that it may burn by day and by night unless it is extinguished because other candles have been lit.

He also lights another candle and fixes it to a candlestick, to be carried in the procession customarily made to Holy Cross and Saint Mary. At Holy Cross he precedes the community, fixing small burning candles to each column until the community has departed. At Saint Mary’s he lights one candle in the basin and another before the church doors.

When dawn appears, the priests begin to sing private Masses. For these the weekly server provides everything necessary, so that, when the priests first arrive, they find everything ready. He unlocks the cupboard, which has been constructed with no less care than the one before the face of the high altar, of which I mentioned something elsewhere. In this cupboard, for private Masses, chalices with corporals, approximately seven hosts, and candles are stored, without which no Mass is to be sung; also larger and smaller cruets, the larger for wine and the smaller for water; and a pewter pitcher with which wine is brought from outside; and two others with water, so that one may be used for washing the hands and the other for washing the chalices.

No water intended for mixing into the sacrifice is poured from any other vessel than this water; the smaller cruets are filled from it. The wine from which the sacrificial wine is to be taken is not kept elsewhere in the cellar, but in a sealed cask from which nothing can be drawn unless it is opened with a key.

Whenever the weekly server approaches it, before taking any wine he carefully washes not only his hands but also the stave and the bottom of the cask around the stave. As I have said, it is his responsibility to ensure that the church never lacks either water or wine, and therefore that at night, if a sick person needs it, it is ready so that he may receive Communion.

If it is the time and day on which prime is sung with the beginning of daylight or before dawn, he properly puts on his shoes for the seven daytime psalms, and washes his hands and face like the cook. Returning with the large pitcher full of water for the litany, before the litany is entirely finished he rises and hastens to bring wine and water.

On such a day he does not uncover the altar panel until he has rung the little bell that gives the brothers the signal to put on their shoes; in summer, or in winter when there are two meals, he postpones it until prime.

He is careful to ring the signals that are to be rung at each hour at the proper time, but he presumes nothing unless commanded by a superior and according to what has been established by custom. When the time comes for the brothers to wash their hands before terce or none, he stands beside the entrance to the church; as soon as he sees that the boys have washed, he does not delay ringing the signal.

He acts in the same way whenever, after Mass and before sext, he hears them reading after they have already received the *mixtum* [the mixed wine and water]. He does not interfere in signaling the other hours except insofar as he is commanded, as stated above.

For both Masses he provides and brings whatever is needed. First, he washes the golden chalice with which the priest is to make the offering, as I have already mentioned elsewhere. On Sunday or any other feast, since the offering for both Masses is made by only one person, he likewise brings only one paten and one cruet with wine. After the Gospel has been read, he lifts the cruet and gives it into the prior’s hands for him to offer to the one who approaches.

At the principal Mass the prior indicates to those who are wearing albs that they are to offer on his behalf. For those who wish to communicate, five hosts are sent on Sunday; on other days, whether private or solemn, only three, except on the greater feasts, such as the feast of Saint John the Baptist, when the prior ensures that enough are sent for everyone to be able to communicate.

On weekdays, at the morning Mass, since everyone offers, the weekly server takes care that among the medium-sized chalices made for this purpose, and among the cruets with wine, there are five, together with an equal number of patens containing hosts. He places them in order outside, near the choir, on a table covered above and lined inside with a cloth, so that the brothers may take them from there to make the offerings with their offertories.

At the principal Mass, since only one choir offers, only three chalices or cruets are prepared. The weekly server stands in the left choir, holding in his hand a golden paten and a larger paten filled with hosts, which he distributes individually to those offering with a golden spoon.

When the priest, deacon, and other ministers assemble in the vestry for either the principal or the lesser Mass to be sung, he always prepares the Gospel book, which the subdeacon carries as they process.

When the time of the meal arrives, so that no further Mass may be sung that day, he counts the chalices to see whether he has them all. He also counts the missal books and the priestly vestments which lie opposite in the cupboard. He carries the pyx containing unconsecrated hosts to the refectory; from these, as I said above, those who did not wish or were unable to communicate take a preliminary portion.

When the meal is over, he leaves the refectory first with the same pyx, in order to ring the little bell in the choir. At vespers he lights the candles as at nocturns. When vespers has ended and the brothers have first gone out, he takes one of his companions and covers the golden altar panel with a cloth.

If collation is so late that a fire is needed, he carries three lighted candles to it and places them in the basins suspended there for this purpose. At the washing of the feet he never fails to bring one burning candle.

After compline, as he makes his rounds, he arranges in order on the lowest peg the loops of all the bells which are to be rung only for nocturns, so that at nocturns he cannot err by grasping one thing instead of another.

On Wednesday and Saturday he carries all the larger and smaller cruets to the water supply and washes them most carefully, using a particular iron instrument provided for this purpose, with which he can scrub them at the very bottom.

To say something about the apocrisiary himself: from what is offered by the people at the altars, he gives the tenth coin and all the bread to the almoner, and the cheeses and eggs to the cellarer. He is also charged with arranging certain anniversaries, for example that of Emperor Henry.

On such a day he sees to it that the brothers have a good general meal in the refectory, especially, if he can obtain them, well-peppered fish and spiced drink. Everything else that comes into his hands he spends principally on repairing the church’s roofs and walls, so that they do not in any way fall into disrepair, and on lighting, and on anything else that may be necessary and useful for the church.

He gives candles to the refectory, and to the infirmary as many as are needed; likewise to the chamberlain, the guest master, the lord abbot, and the prior, as many as are needed, since they never sleep without light. So that he may never lack the means for all these things, this same apocrisiary also has a sufficiently good village, with tithes, vineyards, and fields.

## CHAPTER XIII. How the hosts are made.

Since what pertains to the Eucharist and to the Lord’s body ought to be carried out with the utmost reverence and care, it is appropriate that the manner of carrying it out should not be passed over in silence.

First [Note: [Col. 0757] First. What follows, and the next two chapters, have been copied from another manuscript codex.]

Whenever it is necessary to make hosts, they are made especially before Christmas or the day of the holy Resurrection. Since the nights are longer during the winter season, the brothers may work longer before the meal; after the meal, however, it is not permitted to perform this work.

The grain from which the hosts are to be made, however good and naturally pure it may be, is nevertheless selected grain by grain and carefully washed, and this is done by no persons other than the brothers themselves. It is then gathered into a sack—not an ordinary one, but one sewn and reserved exclusively for this purpose from good cloth. The tied sack is entrusted to a servant who is not frivolous.

He carries it to the mill, washes both millstones, covers them above and below with curtains, clothes himself in an alb, places it over his head, and ties on a shoulder-cloth, that is, an amict, so that nothing of his face except his eyes can be seen. Thus he grinds, and thus he sifts the flour, after first carefully washing the sieve as well.

If the principal custodian of the church is not a priest or deacon, he seeks a deputy to complete this work. With the prior’s permission, he also seeks out two others from those orders who are knowledgeable about the matter, and one lay brother.

When nocturns has ended, these four prepare themselves, wash their faces and hands, and comb their heads. They then withdraw to the altar of Saint Benedict, where they sing morning praises; they also sing prime together and the seven psalms with the litany, postponing the rest of the psalmody for the time being.

Then the three who belong to one of the orders clothe themselves in albs and shoulder-cloths, as was said above concerning the servant—for there are albs and amicts assigned exclusively to this task. One of them sprinkles the flour and kneads it very vigorously (sic) on an exceedingly clean board with a rim around it and a slightly raised surface around the edge, so that the water cannot run off.

They sprinkle it with cold water, because hosts made from it are whiter. The other two form the hosts. The water is carried in no other vessel than the one customarily used for carrying it to Masses.

The lay brother holds the iron implement in which they are to be baked and puts on gloves. Six hosts can be placed in the implement at once. Therefore a board is placed between the bearer of the implement and the makers of the hosts, and two poles are fixed into this board, with a crosspiece laid across them; the implement is placed on this crosspiece for loading the hosts.

Those which have not been baked are scraped with a knife, and the scrapings fall downward into a dish set on the board and continually covered with a cloth, except when the hosts are being scraped.

They sing the psalmody that remains, and, if they wish, the hours of Saint Mary. At all other hours they observe complete silence. They take the greatest care that not only their saliva but even their breath in any way reaches the hosts.

Only the lay brother, if something is needed, makes it known briefly to the servants, who make the fire only from dry wood specially prepared for this purpose. The workers who make the hosts themselves do not eat that day with the brothers but rather with the servants. As relief from such great labor, they receive at lunch from the apocrisiary’s stores a special portion and spiced drink.

## CHAPTER XIV. On washing the corporals.

[Col. 0758B]

Whenever the corporals of the most holy ministry are to be washed, they are washed by the ministry of priests or Levites with the greatest honor, with the same care and diligence which was defined above as necessary for making the offerings.

For this task, the spring or autumn season is properly chosen. Spring is chosen because, once the harshness of winter has passed, the air is already purer. Autumn—that is, after the Ides of September—is chosen because there is no longer such an abundance of flies as in summer, whose stains are more difficult to wash away.

For this service they have very tall bronze vessels devoted to no other use. After vespers, the corporals are dipped twice in cold water in the church and rubbed in the hands. Water is poured in again a third time, and they remain in it through the night. In the morning water is poured in as before, into the basin over which the chalices are washed.

They are then carried outside to the workshop of the secretary, where they are to be washed. There the servants prepare a very clear lye and strain it most carefully. Nevertheless, it is never poured out unless the corporals have first been wrapped on the surface in cloth, lest, if anything of the kind remains in the lye, it reach the sacred coverings.

After they have been thoroughly washed and dried somewhat, they are dipped again into a dressing made clear and liquid from the finest flour, and are then dried completely. Meanwhile they are by no means left without a custodian, especially one who will drive away flies and little worms settling on them.

The cord on which they are stretched for drying is not neglected but washed; it is also continually kept in a pouch reserved exclusively for this purpose. When the same corporals are smoothed with a glass hemisphere, a cloth is placed beneath them, and they are never put directly on bare wood.

## CHAPTER XV. On the Relics of the Saints: How They Are Escorted or Received

Whenever, because of some urgent necessity, the relics of the saints must be carried somewhere outside the monastery, they are to be escorted with the following ceremonies. First, the sacristan arranges them in an ornamented bier. Then he supplies the brother under whose obedience they are to be carried, and also another senior brother to whom the prior specially entrusts custody of those relics, with everything necessary: namely, two candlesticks, a cross, a censer, a vessel of blessed water, three banners, a curtain as well, and a little bell carried by two men, together with vestments and other things suitable for ecclesiastical use. [Col. 0759A]

When they are to be brought out from the church, everyone puts on white garments. Then the prior censes the holy body and entrusts it to two white-clad cantors, who carry it as far as the castle gates. All the bells are rung, and the appropriate responsory is begun by the cantor. The procession goes first; after it follow the bearers of the sacred relic, then the children, finally the cantors, and lastly the lay brothers.

[Col. 0759B] When they have reached the gates, the laymen receive what has been entrusted to them. When the responsory has ended, and the prior has begun the psalm *Ad Dominum, cum tribularer* (“To the Lord, when I was troubled”), the procession returns in the same order.

Likewise, when it is brought back, all the brothers first put on white garments, and the two larger bells are rung. Then, with the procession going ahead—that is, with the blessed water, censer, cross, and candlesticks—they proceed in every respect similarly and in complete silence as far as the castle gates. There the prior takes the censer and censes the holy relics. When the cantor has begun the responsory and all the bells are sounding, the relic is received in the same manner in which it had gone out.

When the image of blessed Peter is received, the cantor first begins the antiphon *Tu es Pastor ovium* (“You are the Shepherd of the sheep”). At its beginning the entire community bows deeply, with their hands lowered to the ground. Then the abbot or prior pronounces the versicle *Exaltent eum in Ecclesia plebis* (“Let the people exalt him in the Church”), followed by the collect *Deus, qui apostolo tuo Petro* (“O God, who to your apostle Peter…”). When this has been completed, the cantor begins the responsory, and the image is carried to the church in the order described above.

## CHAPTER XVI. On the Shaving of the Brothers

Among the other matters which the chamberlain must attend to, it is worthwhile that he not forget to provide the razors with which the brothers shave. Accordingly, one brother is specially appointed to care for them. [Col. 0759D] He keeps them in a small, locked chest placed above, beside the entrance to the dormitory. Whenever he wishes, and sees that there is need, he carries it into the cloister; there, sitting in one part outside the community, he sharpens and prepares the razors. In addition to the other hours when the community sits in the cloister for Mass and the office, he is permitted to devote himself to this work.

When the time comes for the general shaving, the brothers form, as it were, two lines for sitting: one along the cloister screen and the other near the wall. In one line are the razors; in the other, through the almoner, bowls are distributed to each man. No one dares move from his place, but they wait with discipline until the person carrying the bowls and razors reaches each of them.

Whoever shaves another removes his frock and shaves in his cowl. The one being shaved remains in his frock, removes his cowl, and places it beside him. If he happens to leave to fetch hot water, he carries the neatly folded cowl on his arm.

While they are shaving, the psalmody *Verba mea* (“My words”) is sung, preceded in the same way as in the kitchen; in addition, at the end, the familiar psalms are sung until Vespers. The psalms belonging to Vespers are not sung. Otherwise, until the psalmody has been completed, there is the strictest silence, except that the one who shaves first says, “Bless [us]” (*Benedicite*).

No one presumes to cut his hair with scissors beforehand, nor to do so without first putting his cowl back on. Before he has been completely shaved, if the signal is sounded for any hour, he puts on his cowl over his frock, puts on his cap, and goes to the church; he does not, however, enter [Col. 0760B] the choir but stands apart.

If someone arrives after the hour appointed for shaving, he is not shaved except with the prior’s permission, or after None, when they speak in the cloister; and even then only in the warming house. There, as in the cloister, the sick are shaved one day before the community.

The appointed shaving times during the year are these:

1. Before the vigil of the Nativity of the Lord. Between that feast and Septuagesima there is no fixed interval, since the number of weeks varies; the prior determines how it can most conveniently be done.
2. Beginning at Septuagesima, three weeks are always allowed to pass from one shaving to the next.
3. Before Easter, shaving is done on the Tuesday of that week, especially because on that day they have permission to speak in the cloister.
4. After Easter, on the Sunday *Misericordias Domini* (“The mercies of the Lord”).
5. Before the Rogations, on the Thursday of that week, provided that no intervening feast prevents it.
6. Before Pentecost. Since the number of weeks from that day until the solemnity of Saints Peter and Paul again varies, shaving at that point is likewise left to the prior’s decision.

After this, there is no uncertainty about any of the appointed times, since customarily they always shave for the Translation of Saint Benedict, the Chains of Saint Peter, the Assumption of Saint Mary, her Nativity, the feasts of Saint Michael, Saint Luke the Evangelist, Saint Martin, and the Advent of the Lord.

## CHAPTER XVII. On the Baths

It is customary for everyone, after shaving, to bathe immediately as well. But there is not much to say about our baths. We bathe only twice a year: first, before the Nativity of the Lord, and then before Easter. For this purpose the dean of the village supplies servants and firewood throughout the preceding week, so that each man may bathe in a tub, or without a tub, using hot water. Each is allowed whichever option he prefers.

If, when the bell sounds, someone has already entered the bath and has thereby omitted one regular hour, this is not counted against him.

## CHAPTER XVIII. On the Cellarer

The cellarer is appointed and absolved with the same blessing as the prior. Once appointed, he must know how varied the service to the brothers in the refectory must be.

So far as I have been able to learn, and so that I may not remain silent about it, I shall say nothing of the beans supplied every day—and not without fat, unless it is a fast day—or of the chopped and cooked vegetables which are served according to what can be obtained. Apart from these, three days a week—Monday, Wednesday, and Friday—we have only a *pitantia* (additional dish); on the other four days we have the general portion, together with the fish served on Sunday and Thursday, provided that fish can be found at a reasonable price. If there are no vegetables, the general portion continues.

Likewise, whenever there are twelve readings, there is a general portion. On such feasts as, for example, the Translation of Saint Benedict, both the general portion and the *pitantia* are served. Moreover, on the five principal feasts, beans are replaced by cuttlefish or *fladones* [a kind of pastry or prepared dish]. [Col. 0761B] On those occasions, in addition to the customary bread, they usually receive one small cake made with eggs and flour.

There are also many anniversaries. If one falls on a day when, according to custom, a *pitantia* is served, the meal is changed for their sake together with the general portion. The cellarer keeps a written list of such days and every Saturday holds a conference with the prior and the chamberlain, or with their deputies, concerning each day of the coming week, so that whatever ought to be served on each day may be provided in good time.

He also records in his memorandum the total number of pigs and rams owed by our obediences, so that he may immediately raise the matter if any part of the total is lost through the negligence of an obedientiary. Several nearby little villages are likewise attached to the cellarer’s obedience. [Col. 0761C] From them he feeds his horses; he stays there to purchase fish or to construct devices by which fish are caught.

If any brother is so ill that he cannot rise from bed, the cellarer comes to him every day at first light together with the infirmarian. He asks him about everything he can have and what he thinks would be suitable, so that he may prepare something for his refreshment.

Whenever the general portion of fish is served, everything must be arranged immediately after Sext—or, if the fast lasts that long, after None—in bowls on the table in the cellarer’s vestibule. Thus the prior, on arriving before sitting down at the signal bell, can see what is in each bowl: whether it is equal, and whether it has been divided so that the priors do not receive larger or better portions. Particular care is taken here to prevent favoritism.

On the day when the cellarer’s sentence is read in chapter, the brothers receive a good general portion, or a *pitantia* and spiced drink, which must always be ready while the sentence is being read. At the following chapter he again asks pardon and confesses himself guilty of many negligences arising from his obedience. The prior absolves him and commands that Psalm 50, with its collect, be sung for him by everyone together at Saint Mary’s.

If it should happen that, at the hour of the meal, the bread or something else has not been cooked, it is also the cellarer’s responsibility to remove the hammer so that the bell cannot be struck; meanwhile the brothers sit in the choir for the reading.

These are the cellarer’s assistants.

The first acts in every respect as his substitute when he is absent and answers for everything for which the cellarer himself usually answers.

The second receives the grain; we also call him the granary keeper. When the harvest has been entirely gathered, the prior informs him how many *modii* are to come from each obedience, and whatever he hears once he keeps in his account until it has been delivered.

The bakers are under his authority. When they receive the grain, they are to return two kinds of bread, so that, whatever may be the quality of other provisions, the bread served to the brothers may nevertheless be of the best quality. Thus one *modius* produces 120 pounds of this kind of bread, and 50 pounds of the next kind.

If the bakers commit any negligence—either by failing to return the customary number of pounds or by making the bread less good than it ought to be—their aforementioned master brings them before the prior and the cellarer. At the latter’s command, they are stripped and corrected with blows; at that very moment they are restored with bread and wine.

What I said elsewhere concerning the dean is always observed by everyone: discipline is never inflicted on any servant except before the midday meal.

In the same way, the granary keeper is in charge of the fullers who wash the brothers’ clothes. Every Tuesday, after the Gospel of the morning Mass has been read, he leads them into the cloister to the chest into which the clothes are put from above through an opening.

Another brother, entrusted with observing and remembering what the fullers receive, and what they return when they come again on Saturday after None—or in Lent after supper—meets him there. He sits there again to ensure [Col. 0762C] that none of the brothers, especially any uneducated one, is so negligent as to take clothing other than that on which his own name is written. For this too is an ordinance of our fathers: no one is to omit having his name written in ink on his linen garment, and on his undergarments with thread.

The woodcutters are also under the granary keeper’s authority. With donkeys they bring wood from the forests, not only for the oven but also for the kitchen.

Every day after chapter, or, if there is only one meal, after Sext, the signal bell is sounded. Then all members of the household who are to receive bread come to the granary keeper. He also makes sure that the beans do not run out.

He does not sleep in the dormitory but in the infirmary, because he frequently has to retire later than the others. The brother who travels through the obediences with the donkeys to collect and bring back the grain usually sleeps there as well.

## CHAPTER XIX. On the Keeper of the Wine

The third assistant of the cellarer is the man who receives and guards the wine. Once the vintage has been completed, the prior informs him, just as he informs the granary keeper about the grain, how many cartloads of wine he is to expect from each obedience.

When the brothers are to receive spiced drink, he asks the chamberlain for what is necessary and receives it from him; he himself has the individual spices ground and mixed.

He sleeps in the cellar with the cellarer, and never without a lamp, for which the chamberlain supplies the fat, as he does also for the dormitory and the infirmary.

## CHAPTER XX. On the Gardener

The gardener must be subject to the cellarer, so that if there is anything in the garden which the cellarer wishes and knows to be useful for the service of the brothers, the gardener may obediently provide it to him without delay.

He is in no way permitted ever to dare omit the midday regular hour, unless on some day a necessity requires him to remain there. In that case he asks permission from the prior.

## CHAPTER XXI. On the Refectory Servant

There are two keys to the refectory. The cellarer always keeps one, so that if a brother should happen to arrive at midday or after Compline, he can show him hospitality.

Likewise, after the prior and everyone else have sat down, if someone has not yet sung Compline for some reason and suffers thirst, he may drink with the cellarer’s permission. If he was within the monastery enclosure, he is to drink at Vespers, as has been said, if he needs to do so. But no brother in good health is ever permitted, for any reason, to eat anything after Compline.

The refectory servant has three other brothers under him. First, every day immediately after chapter, they lay out the tablecloths. They set out spoons and loaves. If the loaves are somewhat scorched, they have knives with which to scrape them; they also have small cloths, which they first hang around their necks, so that while scraping the loaves they can properly lean them against their chests.

After the Gospel of the principal Mass has been read, they bring wine to be distributed in *justitiae*. [Col. 0763D]

> **Note:** In this passage, *justitia* means a little vessel or cup containing the measure prescribed for each person; from this it acquired the name *justitia*, “measure.”

Whatever they bring or do, they always take care that no servant appears in the refectory at their invitation.

If there are two meals, after Vespers, when the man who has eaten his entire pound and drunk his wine has finished, half a pound is then placed before him. Nothing is subtracted from the *justitia*, however, which must always be given on that occasion as well. If they do not eat again at some point, they nevertheless never fail to drink again.

This is what especially belongs to the senior refectory servant. Whenever spiced drink is served, he pours it into small measures and rings the signal bell, which hangs at the end of the refectory solely for this purpose. Although it is also rung for the blessing of spiced drink on any feast or anniversary, it is not rung when the spiced drink is given for the lord abbot returning from a journey, for someone returning from the infirmary to the community, for the arrival of the prior, for the cellarer’s sentence, or when any other familiar person shows them charity.

It is also his responsibility every Sunday and every Thursday to change the three hand towels which constantly hang in the cloister for wiping the hands.

He must also know on which days all the refectory tables are to be entirely covered with tablecloths. This is whenever all the brothers wear white garments for the principal Mass; on five Sundays, except those I have already mentioned elsewhere; and on the vigils of the five principal feasts, on which a general portion is always served.

On other days, only half the tables, apart from the principal table, are covered, and in such a way that neither bowls nor *justitiae* are placed on the tablecloths.

## CHAPTER XXII. On the Keeper of the Guesthouse

The keeper of the guesthouse receives guests who are pilgrims, or who come for no other reason than the salvation of their souls, with every kindness. Whatever they need, he asks from the cellarer; and if the cellarer happens not to have it, he asks the chamberlain to procure it without any excuse.

First, however, I shall speak about people who share our way of life and manner of living. If an abbot, or even a private monk, arrives from a distant place and does not know our order well, the keeper leads him into the cloister. But first he humbly explains our custom to him: namely, that, if he wishes, when entering the church he should ask pardon at the threshold and prostrate himself in prayer, even if it is a feast day.

The keeper remains constantly with him and shows him at which places he should pray: first at the Holy Cross, then in the choir at the principal altar, and at Saint Mary’s; or, if the church is not closed and some laypeople are inside, only at the altar of Saint John, which is in the right section of the church, [Col. 0764C] and at Saint Mary’s.

When the hour of the meal arrives, the abbot sits at the principal table, but not at the signal bell, because, as I mentioned above, he is not instructed in our order. In the church he is allowed to give the blessing to the readers and to place incense in the censer.

But if the hour arrives when the servants have already sat down to eat, he does not sit at the principal table; nor does he ask permission to eat at the step from the one sitting at the signal bell, as the others do. He merely says the versicle before the table at which he is going to sit. Since he has arrived late, he remains there after the servants depart and completes the second versicle in the same place.

If he seeks admission to our society, after the matter has been discussed in chapter to the extent that our prior thinks appropriate, someone is sent for him. When he arrives, the community rises to greet him; he asks pardon for the society itself, and receives it with the book. He is invited to sit, and is not permitted to ask pardon again.

His companions, however, ask pardon three times, on their hands and knees, facing the prior, while the brothers incline toward them on the right and left.

If he is a person who is to be received with a procession, whether he belongs to our profession or to another, after he has been received something from the divine page is read before him.

If he belongs to the clerical order, and it seems appropriate for him to eat in the refectory, he also puts on clerical dress. Having been brought to the cloister door, he waits until he is invited. Then the lord abbot—or, if he is absent, the prior—offers him water for his hands and proceeds to ring the signal bell. When it has been heard, the keeper of the guesthouse brings in the guest, who sits at the principal table.

If he is a bishop, he gives the blessing to the reader. Whatever the brothers’ food may be, the guest is nevertheless to be served generously together with the prior.

When the brothers rise from the table, the keeper of the guesthouse leaves the refectory last with him. Walking slowly with him and singing Psalm 50 outside the cloister door, he finishes in the same way as the community, with the versicle and inclination.

If laymen or clerics are admitted to the society in chapter, they do not ask pardon.

If they are eager to see the workshops of the cloister, after obtaining permission from the prior at one or the other Mass, when the community is in the church the keeper of the guesthouse leads them first into the almonry, then into the cellar, kitchen, refectory, novices’ room, dormitory, and infirmary, where the brothers do not speak and he himself says not a word.

He must take every precaution that no one ever enters wearing spurs or clad in leather hose.

To ensure that there are always people able to serve the guests properly, it has been decreed that the servants of the lord abbot, the prior, and the chamberlain who customarily ride with them are all to receive their pound and their *justitia* from the hand of the keeper of the guesthouse. They are to come daily into his presence and observe whatever he commands.

If any of them leaves without his permission, he will lack his *justitia* that day.

In addition, two donkeys are assigned to the guesthouse to bring wood every day, so that, when guests arrive, a supply of wood is ready. When such guests are present, a candle that burns throughout the night in the guesthouse is ordinarily never lacking.

If the guests are of sufficiently high rank, the keeper of the guesthouse gives his servants who have served them some charity from the remains of the food; whatever is left over, the almoner must receive in its entirety.

The cloister door is to be closed by him every night after Compline, and the door of the church vestibule, just as the outer door of the walls is closed by his servant. The cloister is not opened before daybreak, and when the brothers rest at midday it is likewise secured.

## CHAPTER XXIII. On the Stable Keeper

There is a brother entrusted with the obedience of caring exclusively for the horses and mules; he is called the stable keeper.

When he sees that guests have been received in the guesthouse, he immediately considers what should be allotted to their horses. If anything is lacking, he goes to the chamberlain so that it may be purchased.

Before the guests themselves depart, he gives new shoes to all their animals that are unshod. He also ensures that a hammer is always at hand; it is attached by an iron chain to the gate.

## CHAPTER XXIV. On the Almoner

Just as all pilgrims who travel on horseback are received by the keeper of the guesthouse, so all who travel on foot are to be received by the almoner. The exception is a legate who brings letters: the keeper of the guesthouse receives him.

After receiving each person, the almoner asks the granary keeper for one pound of bread, and for those departing the following day, half a pound for the meal. He gives wine to those arriving and departing in the same measure, namely half a *justitia*.

Thus, during Advent—except on the days when there are two meals—and in Lent—except on Sundays—and throughout the year whenever fat is omitted in accordance with the canonical observances, as during the Rogations, the vigils of the apostles and other saints, and the Ember Days, whatever wine remains for the brothers in the refectory is all received by the almoner. [Col. 0766B] The same applies to bread, and throughout the year to spiced drink.

He gathers and stores this wine so that visiting pilgrims may always have some of it. On the day when he receives bread from the refectory, he not only asks the granary keeper for it but distributes from that bread to as many pilgrims as he can; whatever he sees that he lacks, he asks from the granary keeper.

He also receives as many full portions as there are anniversaries of deceased brothers: full provisions of bread, wine, beans, and general portions.

For every recently deceased brother who made profession in our congregation, wherever he died, a portion is provided for thirty days. If he cannot obtain beans from the regular kitchen, he asks the granary keeper for them again. For the general portion the cellarer sometimes provides meat.

The almoner himself also purchases meat with the money given to him by the church as his tithe. In this way he arranges to be able to give meat more frequently to pilgrims, and to give one penny to each person who departs, provided that he can determine that they will not remain longer in our place or return within a year.

There are also eighteen poor people who receive portions. Every day the almoner’s servant receives from the cellarer an equal number of *justitiae* of wine and from the granary keeper an equal number of pounds of bread, as well as beans for four days of the week. On the remaining three days they receive only vegetables from the garden assigned to almsgiving.

On the greater feasts they also receive meat instead of beans, and in the course of the year there are twenty-five days on which they receive meat.

For clothing, they receive annually at Easter nine cubits of woollen cloth, and at the Nativity of the Lord a pair of shoes. They are also under this discipline: they sleep together in a single workshop, and must never dare omit attending all the night offices, unless one of them is so ill that he cannot rise from bed. Otherwise, whoever fails to come will not receive his *justitia* that day.

The brother who makes the rounds at the altars during the second nocturn, when he comes out with the lantern to them in the nave of the church, observes this. He carefully notes whether any of them is absent and informs the almoner.

The almoner, knowing that there are times when their provision is of this kind, also customarily gives them a *pitantia* in rotation. Every day he receives from the refectory whatever remains for the brothers, both of the general portion and of the *pitantia*: one half is assigned to the cooks who are laymen. From the half that falls to him, he customarily gives a similar share to his servants. He also gives them half a pound of bread, except to their senior, to whom he gives a full pound; each of them also receives a full pound from the granary keeper.

There are six servants:

- one senior, as I have said, who serves the recipients of portions, as well as other poor people and pilgrims;
- one doorkeeper of the almonry;
- two who go every day with two donkeys to the forest for wood;
- two providers for the two ovens, from which some assistance comes to the alms according to the custom of the region and country.

In addition, three brothers’ portions are assigned to almsgiving: for the most blessed father, lord Odilo; for Henry I, emperor; for Fredeland and his wife; and for the kings of Spain.

Although the Maundy, or foot-washing rite (*mandatum*), is not carried out by the brothers throughout the entire year, almsgiving never ceases. In winter, the almoner’s servant washes the feet of three poor people with hot water and gives each of them a pound and a *justitia* of bread of the same kind as the brothers have in the refectory.

In addition to all this, twelve cakes are given every day, each weighing three pounds. They are to be distributed to orphans and widows, the lame and blind, old men and old women, and all needy people who arrive.

It is also part of the almoner’s office to go through the entire village once a week, looking for any poor sick person lying there. If the person is a man, he enters to visit him himself; if a woman, he stands at the door and sends his servant to her with bread and wine, and with whatever other provisions he can obtain that are better.

The rushes scattered in the church and cloister are to be provided by the almoner. Six times a year he has both places swept and the entire pavement covered with newly acquired rushes: at the Nativity of the Lord, Easter, Pentecost, the Nativity of Saint John, the Assumption of Saint Mary, and the feast of All Saints.

For this reason, before those feasts arrive, he is also given six cakes: in winter, over three weeks; in summer, over two, since rushes can then be obtained more easily.

On all the feasts at which we sing two responsories each, as on the six feasts mentioned above, he scatters fresh rushes throughout the entire church and cloister. On the other solemnities, such as the Translation of Saint Benedict, which we celebrate in copes, and on those which we celebrate in white garments, as well as on all the Sundays of Lent, he does not neglect to scatter rushes throughout the church, wherever the schola sits, in the cloister, and in the middle of the chapter house.

## CHAPTER XXV. On the Infirmarian

The infirmarian has a cook and kitchen set apart for the service of the sick. He too asks the cellarer, and no one else, for whatever he needs. He never lacks the duty of preparing in good time whatever must be prepared for the sick for their meals.

When the community eats twice, those who are not lying in bed do not omit attending the principal Mass until the Gospel has been read. They leave for Saint Mary’s to sing Sext and do not, as a rule, delay any longer before eating.

But if the community fasts until None, the sick sing Sext immediately after chapter—or, if chapter is before Terce, as from the Ides of September until the Kalends of October, immediately after Terce—and eat.

Therefore, whoever eats meat has three courses at dinner and one at supper. At supper they always hurry so that it is never necessary to omit Compline. Those who abstain from meat but remain in the infirmary, because they are not healthy enough to eat with the others in the refectory, also eat at the same times.

In Lent, however, all the sick sing Vespers immediately after None and perform the other offices that follow, then proceed to the table without delay.

Outside Lent, if a general fast occurs, as on the Ember Days, they again sing None after the Gospel of the principal Mass and then eat.

There are sometimes sick brothers who do not leave the infirmary for an entire year or longer. If they are strong enough, they are permitted to sit with the community in the morning, to offer the Mass at Matins, to come to chapter and to Compline, and nevertheless to eat with the other sick.

If a brother’s illness is plainly of such a kind that it does not greatly impair his ability to fast—for example, loss of sight and blindness—then, when the community eats once, he too is not forbidden to eat once.

[Col. 0768C] Returning again to the infirmarian himself: after the prayers have been said at Matins, he receives the lantern and goes around the beds of all the sick to discover whether any of them has not yet risen and for what reason he has remained behind.

It is also his responsibility, if anyone cannot rise from bed, to come at first light with the cellarer—as I have already stated elsewhere—so that together they may determine what should be prepared for the sick man’s refreshment.

At the proper hour he hurries to the kitchen of his office and makes the cook prepare what must be prepared. At the proper hour he invites the sick to eat, and he himself sets before them the courses that are to be served.

Whatever they do not eat, if it is of such a quantity, he does not put away again. He has a little cupboard in which he stores such things, as well as candles and apples. Pepper, cinnamon, ginger, and other health-giving roots are rarely, if ever, lacking there, so that something beneficial to a sick person may always be readily available—perhaps for someone suddenly struck by an attack, or, if useful, so that spiced drink may be prepared for him.

The chamberlain readily supplies the infirmarian with such resources.

To the servants who serve the sick he gives a *pitantia* from the remains of the food; what remains he returns to the granary keeper as bread and to the cellarer as meat. If there is anything of such a kind that it can honorably be served again to the sick, he keeps it for them.

He never omits a regular hour without permission, unless the lord abbot or prior happens to be in the infirmary. If he omits it on their account, this is not recorded against him.

After Compline he brings blessed water and sprinkles all the beds of the sick. When the time has come for everyone to have retired, he carefully inspects the necessaries (latrines) with the lantern.

## CHAPTER XXVI. On the Servants Belonging to the Infirmary

Since I mentioned above the servants belonging to the infirmary, I shall say a little more about them. There are customarily three: two who sleep in their presence and serve them at table.

They are subject to this discipline: while the sick are eating, they must never sit or stand in their presence, lest they happen to hear one of them say something—as people do while eating—which it would not be appropriate for servants to know or to spread through them.

Each of them stands or sits outside at a distance, and, when necessary, is summoned by any sick brother with a sound. When he has done what he was called for, he quickly goes out again.

The third servant is assigned especially to wash the cloths needed for the *cocturae* of all the *fratres cocti* (“cooked brothers”), as they call them [the technical wording is uncertain]; to make the fire; and to heat the water with which the bowls are washed.

All of them sometimes go together and sometimes in turn to the forest, where they cut wood. It is brought back with one donkey, so that the sick may have a fire whenever they wish. For this purpose alone, the granary keeper must always feed a very good donkey, and no servant drives it except one of those mentioned above.

## CHAPTER XXVII. On the Sick

[Col. 0769C]

A brother who begins to grow so ill that he cannot keep up with the community asks leave in chapter and declares that he is ill. He is ordered to stand outside the choir, so that he may sit as he wishes, and the cellarer takes care that he is not left in the refectory without a dish of food. When two or three days have passed, if his health has not improved, the prior invites him to the infirmary. On the second or third day, if he has still not recovered even slightly, the prior visits him again at the hour of dinner, has meat brought, and orders him to eat. From that occasion onward he goes nowhere without a staff, and not without his head covered by a cap.

He comes to church for both the morning Mass and the principal Mass, although he attends the principal Mass only until after the Gospel. If he does not enter chapter, nevertheless he listens to what is read in chapter—namely, a sentence from the Rule or from the Gospel—and he attends collation. If the community is to discuss the brothers’ negligences, he must not be inquisitive about hearing this. He immediately withdraws from the doorway where he has been listening while reclining; nevertheless, as is customary, he remains silent until chapter has ended. [Col. 0769D]

Before sitting at table, he washes his hands at the infirmary lavabo. During the meal, if total silence has not been imposed on him as in the refectory, nevertheless he has no license for excessive talking. After dinner too he is not permitted to devote himself to chatter; instead he immediately lies down in bed, or, if it is a time when the brothers are not taking their midday rest, he goes, if he prefers, to the chapel of Saint Mary. There, again, after supper he sits or lies down while the brothers are seated in the cloister for reading. [Col. 0770A]

The circuiters frequently visit the infirmary and carefully inquire how the sick men are faring. If the infirmarian again notices any negligence, especially in talking, he reports it in chapter. The prior then sends someone to them from chapter, and afterward comes to them himself once, and a second time to administer correction. A sick brother may be such that, if he does not amend, he may at times even experience the rod.

But when someone has recovered sufficiently to return to the community, he asks the prior for permission to return. His day shoes are greased, and on the following day he puts them on in order to return. When the first signal is rung for Prime—or, if it is the time and day on which Terce is sung before chapter—he stands near the door of Saint Mary and waits for the boys. When he sees them passing, he follows them into the church and so rejoins the community. [Col. 0770B]

When he has come into chapter and, after the reading, the prior has ordered the brothers to speak about their order, he immediately rises and, asking pardon, says as follows:

> “I was in the infirmary; I did not observe our order as I ought.”

And the prior replies:

> “May God forgive you.”

He bows very deeply toward the prior, toward the right and toward the left, and in the same way each group bows to him. Then, in the place of penance, he is assigned to sing seven psalms, or, if he does not know them, the Lord’s Prayer seven times.

If anyone is so ill during Advent or Septuagesima, he is not permitted to abstain from meat. Whenever he recovers—even if it is in the middle of Lent or on Palm Sunday—he asks pardon in chapter, as is customary for the eating of meat. [Col. 0770C]

## CHAPTER XXVIII. On the anointing of each brother

A brother who feels that, as his illness worsens, he is soon going to depart from this world confesses his entire conscience to the lord abbot or the prior and asks to be anointed with the oil of the sick. If he is so weak that this is necessary, two brothers lead him into chapter between them. He asks pardon and confesses himself guilty of many negligences against God and against them. The prior pronounces absolution over him, with everyone answering, “Amen,” and he likewise answers them.

He is brought back and placed on a low bed, so arranged that the brothers can stand around him on every side. After chapter, the weekly priest, vested in an alb and stole, proceeds with the oil of the sick, holy water, a cross, and two candles in candlesticks, followed by the community. Psalm 50 having been appointed, the priest first says this collect:

> “Almighty and everlasting God, who through your blessed Apostle said: ‘Is anyone among you sick?’ etc.”

Seven psalms are appointed with these antiphons:

> “Heal me, Lord, for …” etc.

Psalm: “Lord, do not rebuke me in your anger.”

Antiphon: “There was a certain royal official.”

Psalm: “Blessed are those whose …”

Antiphon: “Lord, my servant …”

Psalm: “Lord, do not rebuke me in your anger.”

Antiphon: “A contrite heart.”

Psalm: “Have mercy.”

Antiphon: “Lord, come down.”

Psalm: “Lord, hear.”

Antiphon: “Lord, I am not worthy.”

Psalm: “Out of the depths.”

Antiphon: “When the sun had set.”

Psalm: “Lord, hear.” [Col. 0770D–0771A]

Meanwhile the priest performs the anointing in this manner. He coats his thumb with oil and, with his thumb, makes the sign of the cross over both eyes, saying:

> “Through this anointing, and through his most tender mercy, may the Lord forgive you whatever you have sinned through sight.”

Likewise, over both ears: “Through hearing.”

Over both lips: “Through taste.”

Over the nose: “Through smell.”

Over the hands: “Through touch.” (The priests do this on the outside.)

Over the feet: “Through walking.”

Below, over the groin: “Through the heat of lust.”

He washes his hands; and the wash-water is customarily poured out only in a clean and secluded place.

Then, if the sick man does not receive Communion, the priest himself adds all the following collects, preceded by these verses:

“Save him,” etc.

“Send to him,” etc.

“Let nothing prosper,” etc.

“Be to him,” etc.

Prayer: “O God, who restored your servant Hezekiah,” etc.

“Look upon, Lord, your servant in …” etc.

Another: “O God, who are the creator of your creature,” etc.

“O God, who for the human race,” etc.

“O God of the heavenly powers,” etc.

“Holy Lord, almighty Father, eternal God, who know the frailty,” etc.

“Hear, Lord, our prayers,” etc.

“May this servant be preceded,” etc.

“Lord our God, who [our offense …],” etc.

“Be present, Lord, to our supplications,” etc.

“Grant, we ask, Lord, to this servant of yours,” etc.

“O God of the human race,” etc. [Col. 0771B]

But if he is about to receive Holy Communion, the collects mentioned above are said by another person. Meanwhile the priest himself, leaving the cross and holy water behind, returns to the church with the twin candlesticks in order to bring the Lord’s Body. The man who is to receive it first asks pardon. The priest first incenses it, breaks it, and holds the portion he is to bring over the chalice; both the chalice itself and the priest’s hands are covered with the whitest linen cloth. Everyone who meets him asks pardon.

In the meantime care is taken that the sick man’s mouth is washed, since he is to receive the Lord’s Body. He receives it dipped in wine; after drinking it, he also drinks the ablution of the chalice, then a second ablution of the priest’s fingers, and finally a third ablution of the chalice. The cross is brought to him to kiss. He also kisses—as though taking his final farewell—first the priest, then all the brothers, and even the boys. The community returns, with Psalm 50 appointed again. [Col. 0771C]

## CHAPTER XXIX. What is to be done at the end of life

When a brother has reached such an illness, one servant is assigned to him who has nothing else to do except attend to the sick man. At night, moreover, all the servants who are in the infirmary keep careful watch, lest his death occur unobserved. A cross is fixed opposite his face, and the light of a candle does not fail until broad daylight. [Col. 0771D]

If there is a brother sufficiently devout who, out of a special affection, wishes to remain awake with the sick man, the prior willingly grants his request, especially if he is the sort of man who can sing the canonical hours for the sick man and read the Passion to him when he approaches his final moments.

When the servants who are greatly practiced and experienced in such matters see that the hour of his death is now approaching, they spread out a haircloth, sprinkle ashes over it, and lift the sick man from his bed and place him upon the haircloth. One of them strikes a board against the cloister door with repeated and almost continuous blows.

Since this is the signal of someone about to die, all the brothers immediately rush together when it is heard. For although a man of our order is altogether forbidden, for any reason, ever to exceed a grave and measured pace, it is nevertheless commanded that he run to a dying man and also to a fire.

But if this striking of the board occurs during either Mass, or while a canonical hour is being sung, all who are standing outside the choir rush together. Those in the choir do not do so, except those to whom the prior gives a sign, and the officials who are to perform some duty at the funeral. [Col. 0772A–B]

If they are still sitting in the refectory and the reading has not yet ended, those same men also rush out, although, after the dead man’s body has been washed and carried into the church, they must return there again so that the reading may be completed and the customary psalm sung.

Those who come running sing and repeat the greater Creed, so that the faith of the brothers may bring assistance to the one who is departing. But if his death is delayed somewhat, a litany is to be recited, with the lord abbot or the prior leading it. After each saint’s name, “Pray for him” is to be added. It is to be prolonged as the time permits and according to what can be foreseen or judged concerning the condition of the departing man. [Col. 0772C]

When the names of the saints have been completed, the following is immediately added:

“Be gracious; spare him, Lord.”

“Be gracious,” etc.

“Deliver him,” etc.

“From the evil sword, deliver him, Lord.”

“From everlasting death, deliver him,” etc.

“From the burden of sins, deliver him,” etc.

“From dreadful darkness, deliver him,” etc.

“Through your cross, deliver him,” etc.

“Through the intercession of all the saints, deliver him,” etc.

“Sinners, we ask you, hear us.”

“That you may remove from him the scourges of your anger, we ask you.”

“That you may free his spirit from the place of distress, we ask you.”

“That he may await the day of judgment with confidence, we ask you.”

“That you may cause him to be counted among those who please you, we ask you.”

“That you may cause him to be separated from the number of the wicked, we ask you.”

“That you may command him to be cherished with eternal joys in the land of the living, we ask you.”

“That you may cause him to obtain the rewards of eternal life, we ask you.”

“That you may deign to defend him from the deadly destroyer, we ask you.”

“Lamb of God,” etc.

“Spare him.”

“Lamb of God.”

“Grant him rest.”

“Lamb of God.”

“Have mercy on him.” [Col. 0772D]

But if he has not yet died, the community withdraws, and a few who remain begin the Psalter. When they are no longer in doubt that he has died, the priest says these collects:

“Brothers, with pious remembrance and affection.”

Another: “O God, to whom all things live.”

“Receive, Lord, the soul of your servant.”

As the community goes out to sit before the chapel of Saint Mary, it sings Vespers for the dead, the office, and Matins, with no collect other than this one, which always follows:

“Almighty and everlasting God.”

If a brother dies while the community is at a canonical hour or at Mass, the community afterward does not come running in this way, but comes at a measured pace while singing Vespers for the dead. [Col. 0773A]

As soon as he has died, the lay brothers voluntarily hurry out to ring all the bells, and at length, in order to bring another cross, holy water again, candlesticks, and a thurible. When these have been brought, incense is made over the dead man, and holy water is sprinkled over him.

Shortly afterward, together with the things that have been brought, he is carried out into the small courtyard, where he is to be washed. But no brothers carry, wash, or place him in the grave except those who resemble him either in the order or outside the order.

It is the infirmarian’s duty to provide hot water; it is the chamberlain’s duty to provide the things in which he is to be dressed. He is placed on a board reserved for this purpose alone, stripped, and washed from the crown of his head to the sole of his foot. Only his private parts are covered with an old woolen cloth. [Col. 0773B]

He is dressed in a woolen garment, a cuculla, night stockings, and a sudarium (cloth) made of the same fabric as the woolen garment, as are the stockings. These stockings are longer than the others and are not sewn open at the end. The hood of the cuculla is sewn down over his face on both sides toward the chest; his hands are folded over the cuculla above it, and the cuculla itself is tightened by sewing it at various places, so that it is loose nowhere. The night garments are likewise sewn together.

During the washing, all the washers who know the psalms do not cease from psalmody, and the priest says this collect:

“Receive, Lord, the soul of your servant.”

After he has been dressed, incense—which throughout this time had continually been maintained—is placed over him. He is sprinkled with holy water, placed in the bier, and covered from above. He is carried as far as the door opposite the community. When the community has reached the end of a psalm, the prior observes this and strikes the board only once. [Col. 0773C]

The psalmody being dismissed, with everyone bowing, the Lord’s Prayer is said, and the prior continues:

“And lead us not into temptation,” etc.

“From the gate of hell.”

Prayer: “O God, giver of life,” etc.

Another: “O God, eternal lover of human souls.”

The responsory “Come to his aid” is appointed. Likewise, “Alas for me,” etc.

In the procession the boys follow the cross, then the priors, then the lay brothers, and finally those carrying the dead man. The dead man himself is placed before the altar of Saint Mary until this collect has been said for him:

“O God, giver of forgiveness.”

Again the responsory “Do not remember,” and afterward “I sin every day,” are appointed. Once the ringing of all the bells has begun, he is carried into the greater church and placed upon the choir stalls. A cross with candlesticks is fixed at his head. [Col. 0773D]
