From that hour until he is carried to the grave, psalmody is not omitted unless a general Mass or a canonical hour is being sung. When the signal is first rung for it, the psalmody ceases, except at Matins alone; then it continues until the boys enter.

When the community is in chapter or in the refectory, the prior orders some brothers to remain. If it is the time when the brothers ordinarily sleep around midday, they do not sleep that day.

If the dead man died somewhat before the sound was made in the dormitory, he is buried that same day; otherwise, not. [Col. 0774A] The following night is divided into three watches: the first is performed by the right choir, the second by the left, and the last, after Matins, by the boys with their teachers.

If it is a winter night—from the Kalends of October until the Lord’s Supper—the entire Psalter is to be said at each watch. In the evening, the office and Matins with Lauds are said for the dead, always with “My words” added.

But if it is summer, only one hundred psalms are to be said from the Psalter. If the brother’s death occurs after Compline, the Psalter is not begun unless all the offices that follow the brother’s death have first been completed: Vespers for the dead, the office, Matins with Lauds, and “My words.”

The morning Mass is sung for him, and everyone must attend it in order to make an offering. After the deacon has incensed the altars, he also incenses the dead man. [Col. 0774B]

When the grave has been made, this collect is to be said over it:

“O God, who founded …”

When the principal Mass has ended—or, if it is Lent, after the signal for Vespers has been rung and the Vespers prayer has been said—the prior strikes one of the larger bells somewhat three times. The brothers assemble, and candles are distributed by the church custodians.

The priest who is to bury the dead man is vested in an alb and stole. The armarius, having taken another brother, begins:

“Lord, have mercy; Christ, have mercy; Lord, have mercy,” etc.

When everyone has answered together, they bow down, and the priest, without a greeting, says these collects:

“Do not enter into judgment.”

“Grant, we ask, Lord.”

“Incline, Lord.”

Between these are inserted the responsories:

1. “She is clothed.”

2. “I know, Lord.”

3. “Deliver me, Lord.”

“Verses,” etc.

The priest also incenses the principal altar and the body of the dead man three times. The antiphon “Into Paradise” is appointed with Psalm 117. [Col. 0774C]

The procession differs in this respect: the novices and lay brothers follow the boys, and the senior brothers come afterward. The sick also stand in the church of Saint Mary with candles.

The community, arriving first at the cemetery, spreads out in the form of a crown. During the burial it sings the following psalmody with antiphons:

Antiphon: “Open.”

Psalm: “Give thanks.”

Antiphon: “I shall enter.”

Psalm: “As the deer longs.”

Antiphon: “This is the resting place.”

Antiphon: “Remember.”

Antiphon: “From the earth.”

Psalm: “Lord, you have searched me.”

Antiphon: “Do not enter into judgment.”

Psalm: “Lord, hear.”

Antiphon: “Let every spirit.”

Psalm: “Praise.”

Antiphon: “Absolve, Lord.”

Canticle: “Blessed.”

As soon as the priest comes to the grave, he says these collects:

“We beseech your mercy.”

Another: “O God, with whom …”

The grave is incensed both before and after it has received the dead man, and holy water is sprinkled over it. [Col. 0774D]

A wooden cover is placed over the dead man. The priest first throws a little earth over him with a spade and then adds these collects:

“Let us pray.”

“Dearest brothers.”

“O God, who impose punishments on the just.”

“The debt of the human body.”

“Indeed, the presumption …”

When these things have been done, he withdraws from the grave together with the cross and proceeds to the middle of the cemetery. There the boys stand, their faces turned toward the east, and they sing psalms, as does the whole community.

There, after the Lord’s Prayer has been said in silence, he adds:

“And lead us not into temptation.”

Verse: “Do not enter into judgment.”

Collect: “To you, Lord, we commend …”

After the candles have been extinguished, Psalm 50 follows. Again, with the Lord’s Prayer:

Verse: “From the gate of hell.”

Collect: “O God, by whose mercy …”

After the customary bow has been made and seven psalms appointed, the community returns in such a way that on this occasion the senior brothers are ahead of the boys. In this order, when they have reached the choir, they prostrate themselves with the same psalms. The priest, having now removed his alb and stole, concludes with this collect:

“Absolve, Lord, the soul of your servant.” [Col. 0775A]

The bells whose ringing began immediately when the dead man was carried out do not cease until the priest has withdrawn from the grave.

On the day on which the dead man is buried, all the priests sing Mass for him. On the following day, whatever bread or wine remains from supper is given as alms for him. His seven-day and thirty-day observances are also begun.

The seven-day observance is conducted as follows: for seven days the community generally sings the office and Mass for him.

The thirty-day observance is conducted as follows: for thirty days a full provision with beans and the general offering is given as alms for him; the psalmody customarily said after Matins is said for him, as well as the psalm “With my voice,” which is customarily said at all the hours. Then “My words” is also said for him, and thirty Masses are sung for him by six priests, beginning with the prior. When each has finished his Masses, he announces in chapter that another may begin on the following day. This is never interrupted on account of any feast, except on five days of the year: the Nativity of the Lord, his Resurrection, and the three days preceding that same Sunday of the Resurrection. [Col. 0775B]

As soon as his clothing can be washed, all of it except the coverlet is carried into chapter so that it may be divided among the brothers if they need it. Whoever receives anything from it is ordered by the prior to remember the dead man with such psalmody—or, if he is a priest, with as many Masses—as the prior then sees fit to prescribe.

The coverlet is not brought or distributed there because the brothers have it more as an act of mercy than according to that regular constitution, of which Saint Benedict makes no mention. [Col. 0775C]

When all has been completed, the prior again pronounces absolution over him. Thereafter, whenever his anniversary comes, his provision is again given as alms.

The Mass that is then to be sung for him is sometimes prevented by a feast. Nevertheless, whatever Masses are next sung for the dead are sung no less for him than for the others; but the psalmody “My words” is not postponed. [Col. 0775D]

## CHAPTER XXX. If someone dies in one of the cells

If a brother who has been sent to a particular cell dies there, he also receives there the thirty Masses mentioned above. When the notice of his death reaches us, the office and Mass are performed for him, with all the bells rung. Thereafter, both there, where he has been buried, and among us, his seven-day observance, thirty-day observance, and anniversary are to be conducted in the same manner.

## CHAPTER XXXI. What is done for each brother in the individual obediences

To admit what is true, I cannot easily say what is done in our cells for every brother who has died among us or elsewhere. When the notice arrives, the office is performed, and every priest sings Mass for him; those who are not priests say fifty psalms or the Lord’s Prayer that many times. [Col. 0776A]

Nevertheless, there are few places in which a provision is not given for him. In some it is given for seven days, in others even for thirty days, and always on his anniversary. All this has been arranged and ordered by the lord abbot according to what he has recognized as the capability and resources of each place.

## CHAPTER XXXII. On the death of the lord abbot

In addition to all these things, the following are to be added when the lord abbot departs this life. He is to be laid in the tomb wearing all the priestly vestments. The four brothers who sing the verses of the three responsories are dressed in copes, and the four who carry him to the tomb in albs. [Col. 0776B]

For a full year, a provision is to be added to his alms, not only among us but also in all our monasteries and cells. Thirty Masses are to be sung for him, if there are enough priests to perform this.

His anniversary is also observed in the following manner. First, all the bells are rung at length for Vespers for the dead; on that occasion Vespers is sung in the choir before the procession to Saint Mary. Likewise, the office and Mass are celebrated festively and with a tract, sung by two men. On that day the brothers receive in the refectory a general meal of fish, if it can be obtained, and spiced drink. Twelve poor people in the hospital are refreshed, not only with bread and wine but also with meat, if it is a day on which meat may be eaten; otherwise, provision is made of something equivalent. [Col. 0776C]

## CHAPTER XXXIII. On one who dies during Lent and is to be buried on a day with twelve lessons

If one of the brothers dies during Lent and is to be buried on a day that is solemn with twelve lessons, a Mass for the dead is sung for him after Prime, with only these three collects:

“Almighty and everlasting God.”

“O God, giver of forgiveness.”

“O God of the faithful.”

Nevertheless, neither the festive Mass after Terce nor the fast-day Mass after None is omitted for this reason. But if the burial occurs on Sunday, a fourth collect is added, namely:

“Your saints.” [Col. 0776D]

Likewise, if someone is to be buried on any of the three days immediately preceding Easter, he is buried without a Mass for the dead being celebrated at that time.

If someone is to be buried during the Rogation days, a Mass for the dead is sung for him after Prime, and the Rogation Mass after Terce. No offering is made at the latter, nor is the peace received, except by one person.

If someone is to be buried on a day when we cannot conveniently alter the tonsure, he is buried immediately after chapter once the board has been struck. For as long as he remains unburied, it is not permitted to speak or do anything else in the cloister, except devote oneself to the psalms for the funeral.

The armarius alone does as much writing as is necessary: he writes the dead man’s name in the Memorial of the Brothers and prepares the notices that are to be sent to the cells on his behalf. [Col. 0777A]

There are some congregations, not only of monks but also of clerics, which have an association and fraternity with us. When their notice of a dead man reaches us, or ours reaches them, the office and Mass are performed, followed afterward by the seven-day observance with offices and Masses.

There are also many faithful Christians, both poor and rich, who, when they have been brought into our chapter, ask that they too may deserve to share our fraternity. Their request is granted, and they are given a book, so that they may have a portion and share in all the good works performed in any way, whether in prayers or in almsgiving, not only among us but also in all places that appear to belong to our jurisdiction. [Col. 0777B]

For all these people, as long as they remain in this temporal life, Psalm 68 is sung specially at each hour, and whenever the collect “Stretch out your protection, Lord, over your servants,” etc., is said at the principal or morning Mass, it is added for them. [Col. 0778A]

After they have died, at the Mass and office for the dead, the collect “Almighty and everlasting God” is assigned to them specifically, whenever it is not the first in the order of the collects. Likewise, the Lauds for the dead that are sung on the following night after every solemn day with twelve lessons are said for them without an office.

Moreover, four times a year—that is, after the First Sunday of Lent, after the feast of the holy apostles Peter and Paul, and after the feast of All Saints—special commemoration is made of them with office, Mass, the seven-day observance, the thirty-day observance, and the provision, in the same way as is customary for any absent brother who has died in one of our cells. [Col. 0778B]

Since this has been reported quite clearly above, there is no need to report it a second time. The additional provision is that twelve poor people are refreshed; what is done less is that Mass is not sung for them by each individual priest.

## In the Year of Our Lord 1087. William Calculus, Monk of Jumièges

[Col. 0777]

## HISTORICAL NOTICE

*(Fabricius, Bibliotheca mediae et infimae Latinitatis, vol. III, p. 147.)*

William Calculus, a Norman, a coenobite or monk of Jumièges of the Order of Saint Benedict, wrote eight books of a *History of the Normans*. In the first four books he abridged Dudo’s *History on the Customs and Deeds of the First Dukes of Normandy*; in the fifth, sixth, and seventh he continued it from the death of Richard I, or from the year 996, up to the conquest of England by William I the Conqueror in 1066, and dedicated these seven books to the same William, whom he calls the orthodox king of the English by the will of the supreme King.

After some years had passed, in addition to the conclusion of Book VII concerning the death of William I, which occurred in the year 1087, he added an eighth book on the deeds of William II, king of the English; Robert, duke of the Normans; and Henry I, king of the English and duke of the Normans, as well as on the beginning of the reign of Stephen, who succeeded Henry in 1135.

[Note: This is how it appears in the edition of André Du Chesne, which is divided into eight books. In the Cambden edition there are seven books, because Books III and IV are each counted twice as Book III. Vossius, p. 405; Oudinus, vol. II, p. 1112; and others therefore also count seven.]

[Note: But whether the account of the deeds of Henry I, king of the English, and of William was added by William himself after the death of William I, or was instead written by another monk who was the author of Book VII, is called into question by the letter William prefixed to his work, addressed to William I, and still more strongly by Orderic Vitalis. For Orderic writes that William ended his narrative after the battle of Senlac, using these exact words: “William, also called Calculus, a monk of Jumièges, carefully reworked Dudo’s material, abbreviated it gracefully, and added the deeds of his successors up to the subjugation of England. After the battle of Senlac, he completed his narrative and presented it to King William, the most subtle of his race.” Oudin.]

The work appeared in William Camden’s *Scriptores rerum Anglicarum, Northmannicarum et Cambricarum*, Frankfurt, 1602, folio, pp. 604 and 691, and, corrected from two manuscript codices, in André Du Chesne’s *Northmannici*, Paris, 1619, folio, pp. 215 and 317.

The manuscript codex that was in the Hohendorf Library, III, p. 246, has now been transferred, together with the other treasures of that library, to the Imperial Library. [Col. 0779]

## THE EIGHT BOOKS OF THE HISTORY OF THE NORMANS BY WILLIAM CALCULUS, MONK OF JUMIÈGES

*(André Du Chesne, Ancient Writers of the History of the Normans, explaining their deeds in Gaul, England, Apulia, the Principality of Capua, Sicily, and the East. Paris, 1619, folio.)*

## LETTER TO WILLIAM THE ORTHODOX KING OF THE ENGLISH

### On the deeds of the Norman dukes

[Col. 0779A]

To the pious, victorious, and orthodox William, king of the English by the will of the supreme King, William, a monk of Jumièges and the most unworthy of all monks, [wishes] Samson’s strength for crushing enemies and Solomon’s depth for discerning judgment.

Most prudent and most serene king, I have woven together this work on the deeds of the Norman dukes from various excerpted manuscripts, in accordance with the smallness of my ability. I have dedicated it to your exalted person and have decided that it should be entrusted to the library of chronicles, among the chief responsibilities of lay dignity, for the recollection of the ancient fathers and as an example of most pious deeds.

I have worked it out clearly for every reader, not adorned with the graceful grandeur of rhetoricians, nor with the marketable charm or polish of refined speech, but conveyed in an untrimmed style and a simple manner through straightforward language. [Col. 0779B]

Your Majesty is surrounded by distinguished men, highly learned in literary expertise. They circle the city with drawn swords, drive out the plots of the wicked, and strive to protect Solomon’s roof with the vigilant defense of divine law. Many people, in many ways, have proved how the vigor of your exceptionally subtle intellect, bestowed upon you through the privilege of the heavenly dispenser, is effective not only in the conduct of arms but in everything to which you devote attention and which you propose to consider.

Therefore receive with a kindly hand the little gift of our very small labor, and recall through these pages your own and your ancestors’ famous deeds, most worthy of celebrated remembrance.

I gathered the beginning of the narrative up to Richard II from the history of Dudo, a learned man, who carefully sought from Count Rudolph, brother of the first Richard, what he committed to writing for transmission to posterity. The remainder I offer as my own gift: partly what I learned from the reports of many men equally trustworthy for confirming the truth, through their years and experience of events; partly what I learned with my own eyes, as the most certain judge. [Col. 0779C–0780A]

But if someone who has perhaps been devoted to the sacred schools should mark me down, on account of such an undertaking, as presumptuous or guilty of any other fault, let him know the purpose of this little work, which I do not consider useless: namely, that the virtues of the best men, the most excellent both in secular and divine affairs, virtues that happily live in the eyes of God, may also live profitably in human knowledge.

For it is not fitting that one whom the narrowness of cloister walls confines, walls embraced with the utmost devotion for the sake of the expanse of the heavenly Jerusalem, and whom both the reverence of his habit and the profession of his life separate from the world, should delight in being flattered by the gentle but dangerous smile of popular favor or become entangled with the world through its allurements. [Col. 0780B]

Here you have, most wise ruler of kingdoms, both the peace and the wars of your most pious and glorious father, the great duke Robert, and of your earlier ancestors. They were princes renowned in earthly warfare, yet, with the most sincere faith, the liveliest hope, and the most ardent charity, they pressed toward heavenly things and proved themselves especially valiant soldiers and most devoted servants of Christ.

May the Emperor who presides over the eternal empire—trusting in whom you have joyfully triumphed over and crushed, through marvelous successes, countless obstacles of the most savage dangers—himself, the most powerful protector, protect you in all that you undertake. May he, by governing, support the prudence he has bestowed upon you, until, after completing your course most happily beneath the worldly diadem, you are taken up into the palace of true and supreme blessedness, adorned with the ring of everlasting glory and the robe, pious, victorious, and orthodox king. [Col. 0780C]

## BOOK ONE OF THE HISTORY OF THE NORMANS

### How Hasting oppressed Neustria before the arrival of Rollo

[Col. 0781]

## CHAPTER I. How the strength of the Franks, which had long flourished, was changed, and why they were consequently less able to resist the savagery of the pagans

[Col. 0781A]

From the time when the Frankish people, having recovered their strength, threw off from their own neck the yoke of Roman ferocity and bent their beastlike necks beneath the rule of kings, the Church of Christ, having grown vigorously and bearing fragrant fruits, flourished as far as the western boundaries.

In that age, the kings themselves were vigorous in warfare and supported by the strength of the Christian faith; everywhere they constantly carried away the strongest triumphs over their enemies. Under their rule, Christ’s vineyard grew and produced countless branches of the faithful. From it, indeed, very many sheepfolds of monks sprang forth, which, like bees from their hives, brought honeycombs from the many flowers of the world into the heavenly dwellings. [Col. 0781B]

From these, the structure of the everlasting Jerusalem was raised; before the gaze of the eternal King they shine like bright stars throughout unending ages.

This Church, endowed with vigorous strength, flourished for many generations of the Franks under different kings, until, when the four sons of the emperor Louis disagreed among themselves, the kingdom of the Franks began to be shaken from its great glory by the loss of peace. The conflict reached such a point that, having gathered forces from every side, two parties fought against two others at Fontenay, a village in the territory of Auxerre, instigated by the devil, and, in the most wretched manner, satisfied their hatred with the bloodiest slaughter of Christians among themselves.

By nearly depriving their country of every military defense through the repeated battles and the crowds of soldiers, they left it weak and exposed to invasion by barbarians or any other enemy. [Col. 0781C]

At that time the pagans, with a son of King Lothroc named Bier—“Iron Ribs”—pouring forth from the regions of the Norsemen or Danes, and with Hasting, the most wicked of all the pagans, directing his expedition, harassed the inhabitants of the sea-coasts with continual disasters. They destroyed cities and burned abbeys.

But who this Lothroc was, or from whose stock he descended, we shall say below. For now, however, let us first say a little about the situation of Dacia.

## CHAPTER II. On the three parts of the earth, and in which of them Dacia lies, and on its situation
Having described the whole mass of the world, and carefully measured the circuit and surface of the earth, cosmographers, understanding that the entire land is everywhere enclosed on all sides by the perpetual boundary of Ocean and measured by the fourfold heavenly axis, divided it into three parts, reckoning Asia, Europe, and Africa.

But since [Col. 0782A] we have mentioned the divisions of the earth, it does not seem useless briefly to recall what blessed Augustine says about them in Book XVI of *The City of God*:

> “Asia,” he says, “extends from the south through the east to the north; Europe, however, from the north to the west, and from there Africa from the west to the south. Hence Europe and Africa appear to occupy two halves of the world, while Asia alone occupies the other half. But those two parts were made because between them there enters from Ocean whatever waters flow between the lands and make this great sea for us. Therefore, if you divide the world into two parts, East and West, Asia will be in one, while Europe and Africa will be in the other.”

Having briefly stated these matters, let us return to our subject. Europe, intersected by the channels of very many rivers [Col. 0782B] and named according to its various provinces, is bounded by the limits of territorial divisions. One of these regions, the most extensive and richest of the others in the innumerable multitude of its inhabitants, is called Germany. In it the river Hister, arising from the summit of Mount Athos, enlarged by sixty tributaries, flowing in great abundance and turbulently from south to east, and dividing Germany from Scythia as far as the point where it is received by the Scythian Sea, is called the Danube.

Accordingly, across the broad expanse extending from the Danube to the boundary of the Scythian Sea dwell savage and barbarous peoples. They are said, according to barbarian custom, to have burst forth in many different ways from the island of Scanza, surrounded on every side by Ocean, like a swarm of bees from a hive or a sword from its sheath, and to have spread in various directions. [Col. 0782C] There is there a very extensive tract of Alania, a remarkably spacious region of Dacia, and a greatly extended expanse of Getia. Of these, Dacia stands near the middle, fortified in the form of a crown and like a city by immense Alps. The fierce peoples who inhabit the winding stretches of its extended expanse are warlike at Mars’s prompting: namely, the Getae, who are also called Goths; the Sarmatians and Amaxobii; the Tragoditae and Alans; and very many peoples who inhabit the Maeotian marshes.

## CHAPTER III. On the origin of the Goths, and where they first lived

The sacred writings plainly testify that Noah had three sons. The youngest of these, named Japheth, begot a son whom he called Magog by his proper name. His Gothic offspring, deriving its name from the resemblance of the final syllable of its father’s name, multiplied so greatly that it spread itself in many ways through different regions of the earth and claimed for itself the aforesaid island of Scanza [Col. 0783A] within the strait of the sea.

There, increasing greatly through the successive courses of time, it produced from itself two peoples of the Goths, exceptionally strong in arms. One of these, with its king Thanause, emerging from its sheath, invaded and seized the farther Scythia, later waging war for a very long time against Vesosis, king of the Egyptians, who was attempting to make war against it.

Their wives, afterward called Amazons, distressed by their husbands’ prolonged absence, rejected intercourse with men and took up arms, appointing as their leaders two queens, Lampeto and Marpessa, bolder than the others. With their right breasts burned away for the throwing of weapons, they attacked all Asia and, for nearly a hundred years, subdued it beneath the yoke of a most oppressive rule. But enough about them here. [Col. 0783B] Whoever desires to know everything should read through the deeds of the Goths; let our pen now turn to the matters proposed.

## CHAPTER IV. That the Danes descend from the stock of the Goths; why they are called Danes or Northmen; and why this same people multiplied so greatly

Thus another band of Goths, leaving the island of Scanza—which was like a workshop of peoples or a sheath of nations—with its king named Berig, gave a name to the place as soon as they came out of their ships and set foot upon the land. In memory of the place from which they had burst forth, they called it Scanza.

From there, extending farther onward, they occupied the Maeotian marshes within the Germanic inlets, measuring out very many regions over a wide area. In the second settlement of these regions stood Dacia, also called Danamarcha. It had many kings, deeply imbued with remarkable philosophical learning, namely Zeutan, Dicineus, and Zalmoxes, as well as many others. Hence the Goths were always wiser than almost all barbarians and nearly comparable to the Greeks.

For they assert that the god Mars arose among them, and that they appeased him by the shedding of human blood. They boast that the Trojans came forth from their stock, and that Antenor, expelled from the city together with two thousand soldiers and five hundred men because of the betrayal he had committed there, escaped and, passing through the sea’s many winding routes, reached Germany; afterward he reigned in Dacia and named it Danamarcha after a certain Danao, a king of his own stock. [Col. 0783D]

For this reason the Dacians are called by their own people Danai or Danes. They are called Northmen because in their language the north wind is called *North*, while a man is called *Man*; hence they are named Northmen, that is, northern men. But whether this or something else was the case, the Danes are nevertheless known to derive their origin from the Goths.

After this they grew through such great increases that, when the islands had become filled with people, very many of them were compelled by a law established by the kings to migrate from their native homes. They multiplied in this way because they were excessively devoted to luxury and joined themselves to many women. For a father expelled all his grown sons from him except one, whom he left as heir to his own authority. [Col. 0784A]

## CHAPTER V. How Bier, son of Lothroc, king of Dacia, was expelled from his homeland according to the customary practice, together with his tutor Hastingus

This law remained unshaken through the reigns of many kings, until King Lothroc, whom we mentioned above, succeeded his father in the kingdom. This king too, summoned by the laws of his ancestors, was compelled by the lot to renounce his son, named Bier Iron-Side, from his kingdom with a great company of young men, together with his tutor Hastingus, utterly fraudulent, so that, seeking foreign kingdoms, he might acquire for himself foreign settlements by force of arms.

He was called Iron-Side because no shield was set before him; rather, standing unarmed in the battle line, he would withstand unharmed any force of weapons. He had been infected by the most powerful poisons of his mother. Hastingus, proscribed and exiled from his homeland together with his young charge, sent an embassy inviting from the neighboring provinces men light-minded and eager for war to this expedition, and gathered an innumerable army of inexperienced fighters.

What more is there to say? Ships are built, shields renewed, breastplates repaired, coats of mail and helmets polished, swords and spears sharpened, and the army carefully equipped with every kind of weapon. Then, on the appointed day, the ships are pushed out onto the sea; the soldiers hasten to them, standards are raised, and sails are spread to the winds. Swift wolves are carried forth to tear the Lord’s sheep, offering human blood to their god Thor [Col. 0784C].

## CHAPTER VI. How they came into the kingdom of the Franks and first devastated the Vermandois district

Having been jointly intoxicated by the blood of this libation, with a favorable wind blowing, they attacked the port of Vermandois in the year 851 from the Lord’s incarnation. Leaping from their ships, they immediately handed the whole county over to Vulcan. They also burned the monastery of Saint Quentin in savage frenzy, perpetrating a wicked mockery against the Christian people.

Emmo, bishop of Noyon, was likewise cut down by their sword together with his deacons, and there was slaughter among the people, deprived of their own shepherd. Then they attacked the bank of the Seine and established a siege at Jumièges, with their fleet stationed there. [Col. 0784D]

That place is rightly called Jumièges because those who will not groan there in the avenging flames groan there for their offenses. Some, however, think that it was named from *gemma*, “gem,” because, like a jewel in a ring, it shines through its position and the abundance of its fruits.

This place, constructed in the time of Clovis, king of the Franks, by blessed Philibert with the assistance of Queen Balthild, grew to such an extent that its community reached nine hundred monks. There a very great multitude of bishops, clerics, and noble laymen gathered, rejecting worldly pomp in order to serve Christ the King, and subjected their own necks to a most salutary yoke.

When the monks or inhabitants of the place learned of the pagans’ arrival, they fled. Some hid their possessions underground, while others carried them away with them; with God’s help they escaped. The pagans, finding the place empty, set fire to the monastery of Saint Mary and Saint Peter and to all the buildings, reducing everything to desolation.

After this destruction had been carried out, the place, which had long flourished with such splendid honor, all its inhabitants expelled and its buildings overturned, began to be a lair of wild beasts and birds. Its walls remained solidly raised upward, while dense shrubs and thickets of trees grew everywhere from the earth for nearly thirty years. [Col. 0785A]

## CHAPTER VII. On the destruction of Neustria, which extends transversely from the city of Aurelianis as far as Paris

[Col. 0785B]

From there, plowing their way along the channel of the Seine, they reached Rouen and burned it, perpetrating a dreadful mockery against the Christian people. Seeking the interior of France, they invaded with Northmannic savagery almost the whole of Neustria, which extends transversely from the city of Genabum to Paris.

They ranged everywhere, devastating everything through very frequent incursions: at first on foot, because they lacked skill in riding; afterward mounted on horses, they wandered everywhere according to our custom. Meanwhile, they established their fleet’s station on an island situated beneath the monastery of Saint Florent, as though it were a refuge from every danger, and built huts there like a fortified settlement, where they could keep their captive herds bound in chains and, for a time, restore their own bodies after labor, ready immediately to serve the expedition.

From there they made sudden raids, carried now by ships and now by horses, and destroyed the entire surrounding province. On their first arrival they burned the city of Nantes in a conflagration. Then, traversing the region of Angers, they burned the city itself. They plundered and devastated the strongholds and villages of Poitiers and the whole country from the sea to that same city of Poitiers, filling everything with slaughter.

Later they reached the city of Tours by ship, filling it with slaughter according to their custom and finally handing it over to the flames, after ravaging the whole surrounding region. Not long afterward, seeking the upper reaches of the Loire by ship, they reached Orléans and sold the captured city for gold; then, withdrawing for a time, on a second arrival they destroyed it by fire. [Col. 0785D]

Why should I extend my account by recalling the disasters of Neustria alone? Or did only the five cities mentioned above suffer the losses of destruction?

## CHAPTER VIII. How the city of Paris and Beauvais were destroyed, as well as Poitiers and the other neighboring cities, from the very shore of Ocean eastward as far as Auvergne

What of Lutetia Parisiorum, the noble capital, once resplendent with glory, abounding in wealth, fertility of soil, and the most peaceful tranquility of its inhabitants—a city that I might rightly call a marketplace of peoples? And what of Beauvais, what of Noyon, and those once most distinguished cities of Gaul? Did they too fall beneath the incursions and hostile sword of those same barbarians? [Col. 0786A]

It is painful to recount the destruction of the most noble monasteries, both of men and of women devotedly serving God; the slaughter of populations of no small standing; the captivity of matrons; the violation of virgins; and all the unspeakable forms of torture that victors are able to inflict upon the defeated.

What shall I say of the immense affliction of the Aquitanian people, once the nurse of wars, but then presenting a cold right hand to war? For when it had destroyed within itself the best men of its native soil, the region then lay open as prey to foreign peoples.

From the very shore of Ocean, so to speak, eastward as far as Auvergne, the most renowned city of ancient Aquitaine, no region was able to retain its freedom, no town or village, and finally no city that did not fall beneath the savage slaughter of these pagans. Poitiers, the most fertile city of Aquitaine, bears witness to this; so do Saintes, Angoulême, Périgueux, Limoges, and certainly Auvergne, as well as Bourges itself, the capital of the Aquitanian kingdom. [Col. 0786B]

## CHAPTER IX. That, after France had been afflicted by the oppression of the pagans for nearly thirty years, Hastingus, sailing to Rome in order to subject it to his lord Bier, was driven by a storm to the Italian city of Luna

After Gaul had been lamentably worn down, as we have already indicated, by these and similar calamities for nearly thirty years, not without the guilt of certain persons, Hastingus, desiring to raise his lord to greater heights, began more attentively to deliberate with his companions about an imperial crown. Finally, having taken counsel, they crossed the sea under sail and resolved to seize Rome by a clandestine attack.

But when a violent storm arose, they were driven by the wind to the city of Luna, which was called by this name because of its beauty. The citizens, terrified by so great a fleet, closed the city’s barriers with gates, fortified the defenses with spears, and urged one another to resist.

When Hastingus learned of their boldness, supposing that this must be Rome, he began with every effort to devise how he might invade it by deception. Finally, he sent agents of his treachery to the bishop and the count, instructing them to say that he had not landed there of his own will but had wished to return to his homeland; that they were peaceful and henceforth sought peace; and that he, oppressed by a fatal illness, humbly begged them to make him a Christian.

When the bishop and the count heard this, they rejoiced and established peace with the most wicked enemy of peace. Entry into the city was granted to both peoples. [Col. 0786D]

## CHAPTER X. How Hastingus, supposing that Luna was Rome, captured it by deception when he could not take it by force, and destroyed it

At last the criminal Hastingus was carried to the church, immersed in holy baptism; the cunning man emerged as a most rapacious wolf. The bishop and the count received him from the font to their own destruction, and from there he was carried in the arms of bearers to the ship, smeared with chrism.

After this, in the dead of night, he was placed in a coffin wearing his coat of mail, signaling to the others to put on their armor beneath their tunics. Thereupon an intolerable lament arose throughout the army: Hastingus, the new convert, had died. The shore of the sea resounded with grief at the death of so great a leader.

Then he was carried from the ship to the church on the shoulders of bearers. The bishop put on sacred vestments, intending to sacrifice the holy offering for the deceased. The commendation of the soul was performed, so that the body, already buried in the abyss as an instrument of crimes and perdition, might be committed to burial.

But behold, he leaped from the coffin and cut down the bishop and the count with his sword. Then, with lupine fury, he and his men raged among the people. After these deeds of death had been perpetrated, the house of God became a theater: young men were slaughtered, old men butchered, the city plundered, and the walls demolished from their foundations.

## CHAPTER XI. That, when the pagans discovered that the city was not Rome, they divided; and that Bier, wishing to return to Danamarcha, died near Frisia; while Hastingus, having made peace with King Charles, received the city of Chartres from him as a stipend and lived there

[Col. 0787B]

After the destruction of this city had been completed, the pagans discovered [Col. 0788A] that they had in no way captured Rome. Fearing that they would accomplish nothing further—especially since news of their profane deeds had already reached Roman ears—they took counsel and arranged their return.

Bier, the author of the entire destruction and king of the armies, while returning to his native land, suffered shipwreck and scarcely reached a port among the English, with many of his ships sunk. From there he returned toward Frisia and died there.

Hastingus, however, approached Charles, king of the Franks, and sought peace. Having obtained it, he received from him the city of Chartres as a stipend. Thus France breathed for a while from the crash of tumults, while the sentence of vengeance due for the enormity of their crimes was suspended, through the propitiating mercy of the most merciful Christ, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit ineffably rules the world through the ages. [Col. 0788B]

# SECOND BOOK OF THE HISTORY OF THE NORTHMEN

Containing the deeds of Rollo, first duke of Normandy

[Col. 0787]

## CHAPTER I. On the nobility and valor of Rollo’s father, and how the young men of Dacia who had been registered by order of the king for expulsion came to Rollo and his brother Gurim to seek aid against the king

[Col. 0787C]

After the intervals of many years had passed, and France had been somewhat lulled to sleep after the crash of these disturbances, Danamarcha once again, scattering fire-bearing brands of destruction by the law of extermination, decreed that very many recruits, young men blossoming in youthful vigor, should be expelled from their native soil according to the law of their ancient fathers.

In those days there was an old man in the regions of Dacia, extremely wealthy in the abundance of all things and surrounded on every side by a countless multitude of soldiers. He had never subjected his neck to any king, nor entrusted his hands to anyone’s hands by commending them in gratitude for service. Possessing nearly the whole kingdom of Dacia, he claimed for himself the lands bordering Dacia and Alania, and subdued their peoples to himself by force and power through very many battles.

He was preeminent in valor beyond all the other peoples of the East, and excelled all others through the amassed abundance of every virtue. When he died, two sons survived him, vigorous in arms, trained in war, very handsome in body, and exceedingly strong in courage. The elder was called Rollo, while the younger was called Gurim.

The young men who had been registered by royal command for extermination approached them, bending the knee, lowering their faces, and earnestly begging in humble voices. With one accord they said:

> “Bring us help; come to our aid. We shall remain under the protection of your guardianship and shall constantly perform your service. Our king, however, wishes to expel us from Dacia and deprive us entirely of our farms and benefices.”

Then the two brothers replied to those who were pleading humbly:

> “We shall gladly help you, and we shall make you dwell secure in Dacia from royal threats, and shall enable you peacefully to retain your property.”

When they heard this, the young men kissed the feet of Rollo and Gurim and immediately returned rejoicing over the princes’ words.

Meanwhile, a report of established truth was spread, reaching the ears of the king of Dacia: namely, that the mighty duke, the father of Rollo and Gurim, had attained his final destiny. Then the king, recalling the earlier evils that that duke had inflicted upon him, summoned all the leading men of his realm and said:

> “You are not unaware that the father of Rollo and Gurim has died. I shall therefore attack their territories, seize their cities, strongholds, and most fortified places, avenge the father’s deeds upon his sons, and satisfy myself by crushing them beneath their misfortunes. I ask you to prepare yourselves and your people to complete such tasks.”

When the date of departure had been fixed, they returned with their men from wherever they had come. At once the fierce youth of Dacia, eagerly awaiting the intense heat of these concerns, prepared what was useful for the expedition. Some, assisted by the craftsman’s art, made light shields and shining spears. Others sharpened darts, swords, and axes on whetstones.

The unexpected report of this matter reached the ears of Rollo and Gurim, and they were disturbed by the words of the message. They summoned a numerous force, an appropriate body of men in the flower of youth, and a multitude of those of middle age, the old, and those registered for expulsion; then, raising their right hands, they ordered silence. [Col. 0789A]

## CHAPTER II. How, after Rollo rebelled against the king for five years, the king deceitfully sought peace from him

When the people’s tumult had been completely quieted, and Rollo had been solemnly seated upon an elevated and fitting platform, he began in honeyed speech:

> “I address you whose youthful ardor burns and who surpass the others in the flower of valor. With prudent purpose, imitate your revered fathers, grandfathers, and great-grandfathers. Grow strong like men and take courage; do not disdain to meet them suitably in equal turns of battle.  
>   
> “The king of this realm is planning to overcome us, invade the monarchy of our dominion, destroy us and all of you, and seize the hereditary land of our rule. Before he makes it subject to his government, let us anticipate him and occupy his land, resisting his arrival with hostility.”

Immediately, all were delighted by these words. With their armies gathered together, they invaded the royal territory and devastated it completely, with Vulcan raging.

When the king heard this, he marched against Rollo and his brother Gurim for battle. After fighting for a long time, he turned his back and fled to the protection of the cities. Rollo then buried the dead of his own army but left the king’s dead unburied.

When the duel between the king and Rollo had continued for the space of five years, the king sent him the following message in peaceful words but with deceit:

> “There is nothing between you and me except the bond of kinship. So that the commonwealth may rest, I beg you to permit me wisely to possess what is mine by right and what my father held; while you shall have what is yours by right. Let peace and concord between you and me be joined [or: settled] by an unbreakable bond.”

Then Rollo and Gurim, their soldiers, and those registered for expulsion praised the peace. When a time had been fixed for swearing friendship, each came to the appointed meeting, and, enriched by mutual gifts, they were bound together in alliance.

## CHAPTER III. How the king attacked Rollo’s cities by night, concerning the death of his brother Gurim, and concerning Rollo’s arrival at the island of Scanza with six ships

At last the treacherous king, brooding in a hostile heart over the deceit of the fraud he had conceived, summoned his former army, marched against them by night, invaded their territories, concealed an ambush near the walls of the city, and began the attack.

Then Rollo and his brother Gurim, together with those who were with them, leaped out of the city and pursued the king, who had turned his back and was pretending to flee. When Rollo had passed beyond the place of the ambush, part of the king’s men emerged from their hiding places and attacked the city. Finding it empty of armed defenders, they burned it and carried away as spoils all its furnishings.

Some others followed Rollo as he drove the king away with hostile ferocity. When the king saw that the city had been burned and that the ambush had succeeded, he turned back and fought against him. After many on Rollo’s side had been killed, his brother Gurim fell in battle. [Col. 0790A]

Seeing himself between the two armies—one pretending to flee, the other having emerged from hiding—and seeing his brother dead, Rollo, scarcely escaping after being torn by many wounds, withdrew from them with a few companions.

Then the king besieged and captured the cities and subdued the people who opposed him. Rollo, unable to remain in Dacia because of the king and distrustful of his own position, attacked the island of Scanza with six ships. Then Dacia, deprived of its pious leader, its patrician, and its most powerful champion, shaken by great lamentation, began to weep exceedingly.

## CHAPTER IV. On the warning given to Rollo in a dream to seek England, and on his victory over the English

[Col. 0790B]

After he had remained sorrowfully for a long time on the island of Scanza, burning with anxious thoughts that tormented his mind and planning to avenge himself upon his enemies, many of those whom the royal ferocity had driven from Dacia returned to him.

When his limbs were weary with labor and he was overcome by sleep, a divine voice sounded to him, saying:

> “Rollo, rise quickly. Cross the sea swiftly by ship and go to the English. There you shall hear that you will return safely to your homeland and enjoy perpetual peace there without loss.”

When he had related this dream to a certain wise and Christian man, the man interpreted it in these words:

> “As the course of future time declines, you will be purified by holy baptism, become fully worthy to be a Christian, and pass from the error of the wavering world to the English—that is, to the Angels—where you will at last arrive and possess with them the peace of everlasting glory.”

Immediately he fitted sails to the ships, adorned them with oars, and loaded them with grain, wine, and hides. Crossing the sea swiftly under sail, he attacked the English and expected to remain there peacefully for a long time.

When the country people of that territory heard that Rollo the Dacian was approaching, they drew up a large battle line against him and attempted to drive him from their borders. He advanced to battle without hesitation, according to his custom, met them, felled many of them, and harassed the backs of the rest as they turned in flight with his spear.

Finally, gathering a larger number of country people than before, they again directed their battle line against Rollo and tried either to kill him or to escape by flight [the text may require “to make him flee”]. [Col. 0790D]

But he, trained by the practices of war and made exceedingly fierce by the necessity of battle, wearing a helmet magnificently adorned with gold and dressed in triple [possibly “three-layered”; the printed reading is *trilici*] armor, advanced swiftly and without hesitation against the armed bands that railed against him and rushed upon him. With his victorious hand he fiercely [the printed text is uncertain: *imma niter*] struck down thousands of them, pursuing the fugitives at a swift pace and capturing many of their leaders.

Then he returned to the place of battle, buried the bodies of the slain in the earth, carried away the others who were wounded, and bound the captives to the ships.

Now tormented by a threefold uncertainty—whether he should return to Dacia, proceed to France, or afflict the English land with war and claim it for himself—he began to be anxious and exceedingly sad.

## CHAPTER V. On his dream and on the interpretation of that dream given by a certain Christian

[Col. 0791A]

While he remained anxiously troubled by such disturbances, and while the people of the region were submitting themselves to his authority through the bond of fidelity, one night, as sleep’s Lethean stillness gently spread through his limbs, he seemed to see himself standing upon a certain lofty mountain in a very high region of France.

At the summit of that mountain there was a clear and fragrant spring. He saw himself washed in it and cleansed by it from the contamination of leprosy and the itching disease with which he was infected.

While he still remained upon the summit of that mountain, he saw many thousands of birds of different kinds and varied colors around its base, on every side and in all directions. They had left wings that were even crimson. He could not comprehend with his sharp and narrowed gaze the inexhaustible extent of their multitude, which spread far and wide.

Moreover, with orderly movement and flight, he saw them alternately yielding place to one another as they approached the spring of the mountain and washed themselves in it by suitable swimming, just as they are accustomed to wash themselves at the time of future rain. When all had been wonderfully anointed, he saw them take their proper places without distinction of kinds or species and, without any contentious quarrel, share a common meal almost amicably. He also saw them build nests through hurried labor, carrying off small branches, and willingly submit to the command of his authority.

When he awoke and remembered the vision he had seen, he summoned the leading men, together with the leaders whom he had captured in battle, and without hesitation recounted the entire sequence of the vision. He asked them what mystical meaning they thought the vision had.

Then, while all were silent, one of the captives, imbued with the faith of Christian religion and touched by the omen of divine inspiration, explained the mystical meaning of the vision, saying:

> “The mountain of France upon which you seemed to stand signifies its Church. The spring that was at the summit of the mountain signifies the baptism of regeneration. Through the leprosy and itching disease by which you were infected, you will understand the crimes and sins of your commission. That you were washed in it and cleansed by it from the disease of leprosy and itching signifies that you will be regenerated by the washing of holy baptism and cleansed from all sins.  
>   
> “Through the birds of different kinds having crimson left wings, whose immeasurable extremity you could not exhaust with your sight, understand men of different provinces bearing shield-like arms, who will become your faithful followers; you will perceive an innumerable multitude of them gathered together.  
>   
> “Through the birds immersed in the spring, washed in it by turns, and eating through a common meal, understand a people polluted by the contagion of ancient deceit, to be washed in a typical baptism and nourished by the food of the most holy body and blood of Christ.  
>   
> “Through the nests that they made around the spring, understand that the walls of the devastated cities will be rebuilt. Birds of different species will obey you; men of different kingdoms, reclining in your service, will obey you.”

At these words of marvelous interpretation Rollo rejoiced. He released from their bonds the interpreter of his vision and the others whom he had captured in war and, after enriching them with various and diverse gifts, sent them joyfully back to their homes. [Col. 0792A]

## CHAPTER VI. On Alstemus, the most Christian king of the English, with whom Rollo entered into an unbreakable treaty of friendship

At that time the most Christian king of the English, named Alstemus, adorned with every title of goodness and fully worthy to be the protector of the most holy Church, governed the reins of the English kingdom with the greatest piety.

Rollo immediately sent his envoys to him and told them what they should communicate to his ears. When they came to him, they spoke with devout affection, their faces lowered:

> “The most powerful patrician and most distinguished duke of the Dacians, Rollo, our lord and protector, offers you faithful service and your friendship an unshaken gift.  
>   
> “Great misfortune, lord king, has been suffered by us in the kingdom of Dacia, and, alas, we have been fraudulently expelled from it. The east wind, hostile to us, drove us, afflicted by the swelling force of violent storms, to your borders, deprived of every protection of hope and safety.  
>   
> “When we attempted to return to Dacia and avenge ourselves upon our enemies, icy winter opposed and blocked us. Frost crusted the earth and afflicted the pliant branches of the grasses and trees; the rivers, restrained by a dense mass of icy crusts, built a wall for us, and the water did not provide us with a favorable route.  
>   
> “Certain soldiers living near the frontier of our arrival, hearing of it, drew up a very large battle line against us, attacked us, and challenged us. Unable to sail either beneath the ice or upon it, we resisted their boldness, disarmed and captured many of them in battle.  
>   
> “We shall not devastate your kingdom, nor shall we bring any booty seized anywhere back to our ships. We ask for a truce in which to buy and sell, because at the time of the approaching spring we shall depart for France.””

When the king heard this, he lowered his head and replied with a cheerful face:

> “No land produces men more distinguished than Dacia, or more excellently trained in arms. Many have reported to us the widely spread noble lineage of your lord, as well as your misfortunes and labors, and also the treacherous faithlessness of the king of Dacia. No one is more just in deeds than your lord; no one is greater in arms.  
>   
> “Set aside the cares of this matter. Be secure from weapons, free from the burdens of battle, and exempt from every evil. Let it be permitted you to buy and sell anywhere in the lands under our authority. We beg you to urge your lord to honor us by coming to us, for I desire to see him and to console him in his misfortunes.”

The envoys departed and reported to Rollo everything they had heard. Immediately Rollo proceeded boldly and without hesitation toward the king, who was coming to meet him. They embraced one another, exchanged kisses, and, while the troops of both armies withdrew, sat apart.

Then King Alstemus addressed him first:

> Strong in lineage, shining with the brilliance of deeds,  
>   
> Loftier than all in character and merit,  
>   
> Let us be joined together in a single pleasing covenant of faith.  
>   
> Be, I ask, a part of my soul and forever my companion,  
>   
> And I ask you to settle in our lands,  
>   
> So that you may be cleansed of your defilement by saving baptism.  
>   
> Behold, take within the world of our dominion what your deeds deserve.  
>   
> Be mindful of me; and I shall likewise always be mindful in every matter.  
>   
> And if you now wish to depart for other shores,  
>   
> If a fierce and savage people should presently make war upon me,  
>   
> Unprincipled, not preserving faith or maintaining its obligation,  
>   
> Then, as you are able, bring aid, saving me through steadfast effort,  
>   
> And I shall come to your assistance in like manner.  
>   
> My shield shall shelter you in mutual battle.

## CHAPTER VII. On the storm suffered by Rollo as he sailed from England to the kingdom of the Franks, and how he landed on the shores of the Welsh

[Col. 0793B]

Then Rollo, rejoicing at the king’s words, is said to have replied:

> “I return thanks to you, most excellent of all kings, for your freely offered benefits; and whatever you have proposed should be done between you and me, make it as I desire. I shall not remain long in your kingdom, but will go to Francia as quickly as I can. Wherever I may be, I shall remain your friend, joined to you by an unbreakable bond of affection.”

When he had said this, they became most inseparably allied and were wonderfully enriched by the exchange of gifts; then each returned with his own men to his own land. Throughout the whole winter, Duke Rollo had ships and the supplies necessary for the journey prepared with diligent care. He also enlisted the English soldiers of flourishing youth who had become his men and were to travel with him. [Col. 0793C]

When, at the beginning of summer, an abundance of softly gleaming flowers smiled forth, and white, fragrant lilies flourished among purple blossoms, Rollo, always mindful of the vision that had warned him to proceed to Francia, boarded ship after the fleets had been given their sails. When the ship had advanced with gentle winds to the middle of the sea, and they saw nothing but the sky spread above the surface of the water, the envious spirits, knowing that these men were to be cleansed in the name of Christ through baptism and were to attain the glory they had lost, came groaning upon them and stirred up dangers.

The winds also rushed from their seats, and, as the sea gaped open, raised enormous waves from the lowest depths into a precipice and up to the stars. The sky thundered with repeatedly flashing lightning, and a black night of dense darkness settled upon them. [Col. 0793D] Their oars broken, the sails could not withstand the fury of the winds. Thus, exhausted of strength, they entrusted everything to the winds. The ships tossed here and there as though over mountains and valleys, threatening sudden death to all.

Then Rollo stretched out his hands, prostrated himself upon the ship, and uttered the following words in a humble voice:

> O almighty God, filling the heavens with light,
>
> who hold the heaven and earth, whose power  
> endures through the ages and, embracing all things  
> within an eternal circuit;
>
> you who desire me, by the gift of a vision,  
> to become a worshiper of Christ, though infected  
> with the vices and filth of sin,
>
> as the brief course of future time passes by,
>
> willingly receive my vows and graciously favor my prayers;
>
> calm the raging waves and restrain their destructive force,
>
> [Col. 0794A] rescuing us from these disasters and hardships;
>
> compress, soothe, and soften the sea  
> surging too violently in a furious whirlwind,
>
> and make it peaceful.

When these prayers had been completed, the sea immediately grew calm as the storms abated. The winds soon opened out the immense stretches of sea with the desired breeze, and they brought the ships, shattered by the storm, to the shores of the Walgrenses.

## CHAPTER VIII. How Rollo defeated the rebellious Walgrenses, Rainerius, duke of Hainaut, and Radebold, prince of Frisia; and concerning twelve ships laden with provisions and an equal number filled with armed soldiers, which Alstemus, king of the English, sent to him while he was staying there

When the Walgrenses heard that a barbarian people, violently battered by the sea-storm, had been carried to their shores, [Col. 0794B] they gathered a multitude of countrymen and attacked Duke Rollo, who had scarcely escaped from the stormy sea. He, roused according to his custom, advanced against them to fight, sent many of them slain by the sword to the underworld, and either drove the rest into flight or captured them.

While he remained for a long time ravaging Walgras [perhaps Walcheren, among the islands of Zeeland, where Flushing is situated], Alstemus, the most Christian king of the English and pre-eminent among all kings in virtue, remembered the friendship by which he and Rollo had bound themselves in everlasting alliance. He therefore sent the distinguished duke in Walgras twelve ships loaded with grain, wine, and bacon, and likewise twelve ships filled with armed soldiers.

Rollo, delighted by these gifts, sent back to the king envoys richly laden with very great presents and with thanks, instructing them to declare that he would serve the king. [Col. 0794C] The Walgrenses, however, judging that Rollo would remain in Walgras permanently because of the abundance of grain transported to him, summoned Rainerius of the Long Neck, of Hasbain and duke of Hainaut, and Radebold, prince of the region of Frisia. Gathering an army from other districts, they attacked Rollo.

He advanced against them repeatedly and without hesitation, killed many thousands of them, and drove Rainerius of the Long Neck and Radebold the Frisian back to their camps. Then he devastated the whole land of the Walgrenses and consumed it with fire.

Afterward, angered on account of this deed, he quickly attacked the Frisians and began to ravage their land. The Frisians then swiftly gathered a great host of peoples and added to themselves a multitude of commoners dwelling along the border of Frisia. [Col. 0794D] Having prepared many battle lines, they attempted a sudden assault upon Rollo, who was staying by the river Almera.

Rollo and those who were with him, however, waited for the beginning of the battle on bended knee, covered by the protection of their shields and enclosed within the terror of their weapons, while the flashing points of their swords were locked together in close formation. The Frisians, thinking their number extremely small, entered a battle that would not benefit them. But the Danes leapt forth, fell upon them, and struck them down to extermination. They captured several princes and led an innumerable host to the ships.

The remaining Frisians, losing confidence in themselves, thereafter became tributaries and obeyed Rollo’s commands in everything. [Col. 0795A] After the tribute of Frisia had been gathered, increased, and delivered, he immediately spread the sails into the open sea, turned the prows toward the lands of Rainerius of the Long Neck, and desired to take vengeance upon him, since he had come to Walgras with the Frisians who had already been defeated in battle.

Having traversed the sea, he entered the channel of the Scheldt. Ravaging the land on both sides, he came against Rainerius of the Long Neck to a certain abbey called Condatum. Rainerius fought many battles against him, but Rollo emerged victorious and powerful from them all. The land was devastated, and both armies suffered misfortunes. A severe famine arose, because the land was no longer broken by the plow. The common people were afflicted by want and worn down by famine and war. All despaired of living, deprived of the means of sustenance.

One day, while Rainerius was staying in an ambush [Col. 0795B] and secretly wishing to fall upon the Danes, the Danes gathered from every side surrounded him. Since he fought very fiercely, they captured him and brought him bound to Rollo.

On that same day, Rainerius’s men, seeking to capture some of the Danes who were lying in concealment, attacked twelve of Rollo’s foremost soldiers and captured them by their steadfast courage. Then Rainerius’s wife, weeping and wailing over him, summoned her princes and sent them to Rollo, asking him to return her husband in exchange for the twelve captured companions.

Rollo immediately received the embassy and sent back the following reply:

> “Rainerius will not be returned to you, but will be beheaded, unless you first return my companions, and, in addition, give me all the gold and silver of his dukedom, under oath according to the Christian religion, as well as the tribute of this region.”

[Col. 0795C] Soon Rainerius’s wife, distressed by the mournful embassy, sent the captured companions back to Rollo, together with all the gold and silver she could find anywhere. She also sent him what had been assigned to the sacred altars, as well as the tax of that dukedom, with an oath that she had no more metal and could obtain no more. In humble and supplicating words she begged Rollo to return her husband.

Moved by pity and by the voices of those who supplicated him, Rollo had Rainerius of the Long Neck brought before him and addressed him in peaceful words:

> “Rainerius, duke and most fierce soldier, sprung from the proud blood of kings, dukes, and counts: what injury had I formerly done you, on account of which you fought against me with the Walgrenses and Frisians? If you now wish to rage, you lack both weapons and attendants. [Col. 0795D] If you wish to slip away from us by flight, you cannot escape, since you are now captured and entangled in fetters.
>
> “I have repaid you, as I did the Frisians, in kind for the evils you inflicted upon me without cause. Your wife and your princes have sent me, on your behalf, whatever gold and silver they were able to recover. I shall return half of the accumulated gift to you and send you back to your wife. From now on, grow gentle and rest; let there be no discord, but everlasting peace and friendship between you and me.”

When he had said this, Rainerius’s legs were released from their fetters. Rollo immediately made him his ally, enriched him with very great gifts and presents, and returned him to his wife, along with half of the embassy’s gifts.

## CHAPTER IX. How, in the year 876 of the Incarnation of the Word, Rollo came to Gemmeticum and then to Rouen; and concerning the peace which Archbishop Franco sought from him and obtained

[Col. 0796A]

When these matters had been settled, the Danes, with their duke Rollo, set their sails to the winds. Leaving the channel of the Scheldt and crossing the sea, in the year 876 from the Lord’s Incarnation they entered the banks of the Seine and, with the wind blowing according to their wishes, came to Gemmeticum. There they placed upon the altar in the chapel of Saint Vedast, across the river, the body of the holy virgin Ameltruda, which they had carried from Britain. That chapel still bears the name of this virgin.

Franco, archbishop of Rouen, learned of their arrival and saw that the city walls had been utterly destroyed to the ground by the savagery of the enemy. Completely despairing of assistance for resistance, [Col. 0796B] he judged it safer to seek peace from them than to provoke them in any way to his own destruction. He hastened to them, requested peace, and obtained the desired peace through a firm pact between them.

After this, the Danes hurried to the city walls, driving their ships forward as quickly as possible, and brought them, filled with a great number of soldiers, alongside the gate to which the church of Saint Martin is attached. Considering carefully by land and sea the defenses of the city, which they judged to be fortified by the advantages of its position, they unanimously determined that it would become the head of the entire county.

## CHAPTER X. How Rollo, coming with his men along the channel of the Seine, established at Archas, called Hasdans, a certain fortress, where he fought against the Franks, killed many, and put their duke Rainaldus to flight; and concerning the destruction of the fortress of Mellentum

[Col. 0796C]

Having gained possession of Rouen, Rollo, with a crafty heart, deliberated with his men about the uprising at Paris and thirsted, by pagan instinct, for the blood of Christians like a wolf. They loosed their fleet, plowed the river Seine, and established a naval station at Hasdans, which is called Archas.

Then Rainaldus, duke of all Francia, having learned of the sudden arrival of the pagans, advanced against them with the strong might of his armies on the river Authura. He sent ahead Hastingus, who was still staying in the city of Chartres, together with other envoys because of his knowledge of the language.

Hastingus came near the course of the water and addressed them in these words:

> “Alas,” he said, “most powerful soldiers, from what shores have you been carried here, what do you seek in this region, or by what name is your lord known? [Col. 0796D] Tell us. We are indeed envoys of the king of the Franks, sent to you.”

Rollo replied to him as he asked:

> “We are Danes, and exercise equal lordship. We have come to expel the inhabitants of this land, wishing to bring the country under our authority. But who are you, who speak to us so courteously?”

Hastingus answered:

> “Have you ever heard of a certain Hastingus who, coming here from your regions as an exile with a multitude of ships, greatly devastated this kingdom of the Franks and reduced much of it to a wasteland?”

Rollo replied:

> “We have heard of him. For Hastingus began as a good man and completed everything with a bad end.”

Hastingus then said:

> [Col. 0797A] “Do you wish to submit to King Charles?”

Rollo answered:

> “By no means. We shall submit to no one; whatever we acquire by arms, we shall claim as our own right. If you wish, report this to the king whose envoy you boast of being.”

Hastingus promptly reported all this to his duke.

Meanwhile Rollo and those who were with him made themselves a defense and barrier in the form of a fortress. They fortified themselves all around with an embankment of excavated earth, leaving at the site of the gate a space of considerable breadth, which remains visible to this day.

The Franks came at dawn to the church of Saint Germanus. There they heard Mass and partook of the body and blood of Christ. Then, riding onward, they saw on the bank of the river the ships and the Danes within the fortification of excavated earth, and attacked the broad, open entrance of the gate.

The Danes lay down inside, [Col. 0797B] here and there across the level ground of the fortress, and covered themselves with their shields, so that their number might appear extremely small. Rotlandus, standard-bearer of Rainaldus, with the line that led the army, violently rushed through the remarkably broad entrance upon them and began to fight.

But the Danes rose up and in a moment killed Rotlandus and his followers. When Rainaldus, Hastingus, and the other counts saw all those men dead, they turned their backs and eagerly sought flight.

After this, Rollo swiftly occupied the town of Mellentum with his ships. Having overturned it, he killed all its inhabitants by the sword.

## CHAPTER XI. By what deception Count Tetboldus bought the city of Chartres from Hastingus, and how Hastingus himself, after selling everything, departed abroad and disappeared

[Col. 0797C] Count Tetboldus, considering that he had found an opportune moment to deceive Hastingus, falsely approached him with these words:

> “Why,” he said, “most illustrious man, do you languish in sloth? Do you not know that King Charles wishes to seek your death because of the Christian blood you unjustly shed in former times? He remembers the evils that you then wickedly inflicted upon him, and therefore has decided to expel you from the land. Your hand also, as he himself says, is allied with the pagan Rollo for the destruction of the Franks. Therefore, before long, you will be utterly destroyed by them. Take thought for yourself, lest you be punished without having taken precautions.”

Terrified by these words, Hastingus immediately sold the city of Chartres to Tetboldus. After selling [Col. 0797D] everything, he departed abroad and disappeared.

## CHAPTER XII. The renewed war of Ragenoldus, prince of Francia, against Rollo and his death; the annual siege of the city of Paris; and the destruction of the city of Bayeux, where he captured a certain maiden named Popa, by whom he fathered William and his sister Gerloc; and how his army slaughtered the citizens of Évreux while he himself was besieging Paris with some of his men

Rainaldus, unable to bear the disgrace of his flight, gathered a larger army and suddenly attacked Rollo again. Rollo anticipated his attempt, cut down some of his men with swords, and drove away others who were fleeing shamefully. A certain fisherman of the Seine, attached to Rollo, pierced Rainaldus with a spear and laid him dead upon the ground.

Then Rollo weighed anchor and, rowing swiftly, [Col. 0798A] made for Paris, surrounding it with a siege after immediately bringing booty from every direction. While he remained there, scouts arrived and reported that the city of Bayeux was empty of defenders and could very easily be captured without loss to any victor.

Rollo immediately withdrew his ships from the siege and came to Bayeux under full sail. After capturing it, he partially overthrew it and killed its inhabitants. There he captured a most noble maiden named Popa, daughter of the illustrious Berengarius. Not long afterward, according to Danish custom, he joined her to himself, and by her fathered William and a very beautiful daughter named Gerloc.

After the city had thus been demolished, Rollo quickly returned to Paris. While he was pressing its conquest with battering rams and siege engines, he sent an army of soldiers to the city of Évreux [Col. 0798B] to destroy it and slaughter the bishop, named Sibor, together with his people.

When they arrived there and found that the bishop had escaped by flight, they killed all the citizens and returned to their duke with very great booty. Terrified by these events, many peoples of Francia paid tribute to Rollo, while many others resisted him.

## CHAPTER XIII. Concerning Elstannus [Alstemus], king of the English, who requested his aid against rebels through envoys and received it; and how Rollo, returning from there, subdued the English at the king’s request and, enriched with very great gifts and assistance, divided the counts of his army, sending some by the channel of the Seine, others by the Loire, and others by the Gironde, to plunder the intervening provinces by swift navigation

[Col. 0798C] While these things were occurring, envoys of Elstannus, king of the English, arrived, bringing supplicating words to Rollo and asking him to bring aid to the king as quickly as possible. Certain rebels had indeed conspired against him and taken up arms.

Sympathizing with the king’s anxiety, and despairing of the conquest of Paris because of the difficulty of access and the great abundance of provisions within it, Rollo abandoned the siege and attacked the English. When he arrived there, he subdued the rebels by force, and, after receiving hostages, made them obedient to their king.

Then, having again selected a multitude of young men and received great gifts from the king, he returned to Francia. Immediately dividing the counts of his army, he sent some by the channel of the Seine, others by the current of the Loire, and others by the river Gironde, to plunder the intervening provinces by swift navigation. [Col. 0798D]

Rollo himself returned again to Paris and began to attack the city and ravage the land of his enemies.

## CHAPTER XIV. How Charles, hearing of Rollo’s return, requested and obtained peace from him for three months; and how, when that period had ended, Rollo sent his men in every direction to plunder as far as Burgundy

When King Charles heard that Rollo had returned from the English territories after successful operations, he sent Franco, archbishop of Rouen, to him, instructing him to cease harassing the Franks and to grant him a truce of three months. After this was obtained, the land rested for a short time from the pagans’ plundering.

When the three months had ended, Rollo, thinking that because of the security he had granted [Col. 0799A] he was considered worthless by the Franks, began fiercely and cruelly to ravage the provinces, tearing apart, afflicting, and destroying the people.

His men went toward Burgundy, sailing along the Yonne into the Saône. Ravaging on every side the lands adjoining the rivers as far as Clermont, they invaded the region of Sens, plundered everything, and returned to Saint Benedict against Rollo.

When Rollo saw the monastery of Saint Benedict, he did not wish to defile it, nor did he permit that province to be plundered on account of Saint Benedict. He did, however, attack Étampes and destroyed the whole surrounding land, taking many captives. From there he came to Vilemelt, plundered the neighboring lands, and then hastened to return to Paris.

## CHAPTER XV. How, while he was besieging the city of Chartres, Richard, duke of the Burgundians, attacked him with his own army and that of the Franks; and how, while Rollo resisted bravely, Bishop Antelmus unexpectedly sprang from the city with armed men carrying the tunic of the holy Mother of God and attacked him from behind. Thus Rollo yielded not to the Burgundians but to divine power

[Col. 0799B]

At last Rollo surrounded the city of Chartres with a siege. While he was attacking it with siege engines and artillery, Richard, duke of the Burgundians, arrived with his own army and that of the Franks and fell upon him.

Rollo engaged him and resisted fiercely with his men, until Bishop Antelmus unexpectedly sprang from the city with armed men, carrying before him the veil (*supparum*) of holy Mary, Mother of God, and attacked Rollo from behind, striking at him.
