At last Rollo, seeing himself and his men in the extremity of death, decided to yield to the enemy for the moment rather than fight at the cost of his men. By prudent counsel, not through cowardice, he withdrew from the battle.

## CHAPTER XVI. Concerning the part of the army that withdrew to a certain mountain; and concerning Count Ebulus of Poitiers, and how he hid in a fuller’s house because of the Northmen

A certain part of Rollo’s army, retreating while the Franks pursued, came to Leugas and climbed to the summit of a certain mountain.

Count Ebulus of Poitiers, arriving late for the battle, discovered that the pagans had occupied the heights of the mountain. Immediately pursuing them, he surrounded its steep slopes with soldiers so that they could not escape.

But in the middle of the night [Col. 0799D] the Northmen burst violently through the Frankish camp and escaped without loss of life. Ebulus, suspecting that Rollo had fallen upon them, entered the house of a certain fuller and hid there trembling throughout the night.

At daybreak the Franks learned that the pagans had escaped. Spurring their horses, they began to pursue them. When they found them, they did not dare to attack, because the Northmen had fortified themselves in the manner of a fortress with the bloodstained corpses of animals. Since nothing had gone favorably, the Franks quickly withdrew; thus the Northmen freed themselves and joyfully returned to their duke.

## CHAPTER XVII. How, when Rollo, inflamed with fury, was devastating Francia with increasingly severe oppression, King Charles gave him his daughter and the coastal land from the river Epte to the Breton borders, together with Brittany itself as a means of livelihood, since the land had been plundered and was deserted [the aforesaid land was deserted]; on condition, however, that he become a Christian; and how the king, Robert duke of Francia, and the other nobles and bishops swore that the same land should be possessed forever by Rollo and his heirs; and how Rollo, unwilling to kiss the king’s foot, ordered one of his soldiers to kiss it for him

[Col. 0800A]

Enraged by these misfortunes and by the death of his soldiers, Rollo intensified the attacks of the rest of his men against the Franks and urged them with all their strength [Col. 0800B] to demolish or destroy the country because of the destruction of their companions.

What more is there to say? Like evening wolves, the pagans rushed upon Christ’s sheepfolds; churches were set on fire, women were led away captive, the people were slaughtered, and universal mourning arose. Finally, the Franks, oppressed by these calamities, appealed to King Charles with lamenting cries, all proclaiming together that the Christian people were perishing through pagan incursions because of his negligence.

Deeply moved by their complaints, the king summoned Archbishop Franco and sent him quickly to Rollo, instructing him to say that, if Rollo became a Christian, he would give him the coastal land from the river Epte to the Breton borders, together with his daughter named Gisla.

Franco accepted the embassy, completed the journey, and explained everything in order to the pagan duke. Rollo gratefully received his words after consulting with his men [Col. 0800C] and granted the king a truce of three months from pagan devastation, so that peace might be established between them during that period by a firm treaty.

When the appointed time arrived, the king came with Robert, duke of the Franks, to the place designated as Saint-Clair, across the river Epte. Rollo remained on this side, surrounded by ranks of soldiers. Messengers passed back and forth, and, with Christ’s favor, peace was established between them. Rollo swore fidelity to the king by oaths, and the king gave him his daughter together with the land mentioned above. He also added the whole of Brittany to supplement his resources, while the princes of that province, Berengarius and Alanus, swore oaths to Rollo.

The coastal land now called Normandy, because of the daily incursions [Col. 0800D] of the pagans, lay uncultivated, overgrown with forests everywhere, untouched by plow or hoe. The king first wished to give Rollo the province of Flanders as a means of livelihood, but Rollo refused to accept it because of the obstruction caused by its marshes.

When Rollo, on receiving the duchy of Normandy from the king, refused to kiss the king’s foot, the bishops said to him:

> “Whoever receives such a gift ought to seek the king’s foot with a kiss.”

He replied:

> “I shall never bend my knees to anyone’s knees, nor kiss anyone’s foot.”

Compelled by the pleas of the Franks, he ordered one of his soldiers to kiss the king’s foot. The soldier immediately seized the king’s foot, carried it to his mouth, and, standing upright, planted a kiss upon it, causing the king to fall backward. Great laughter arose, and great tumult among the people. [Col. 0801A]

Moreover, King Charles, Robert duke of the Franks, the counts and nobles, the bishops and abbots, swore by an oath of the Catholic faith to the patrician Rollo that they would preserve his life, his limbs, and the honor of the entire kingdom concerning the designated land, so that he might hold and possess it and hand it on to his heirs, and so that the succession of descendants might possess and cultivate it through all the passing years, from generation to generation.

When these matters had been nobly completed, the joyful king returned to his own territories, while Rollo proceeded with Duke Robert to the walls of the city of Rouen.

## CHAPTER XVIII. How, in the year 912 of the Incarnation of the Word, Rollo and his army were baptized; how he gave a portion of the land of his province to the more venerable churches before dividing it among his officials; and concerning Brenneval, which he gave to Saint Dionysius the Areopagite

[Col. 0801B]

In the year 912 of the Lord’s Incarnation, at the blessed font called that of the Holy Trinity, Rollo was baptized by Franco, archbishop. Duke Robert received him from the font and gave him his own name.

After Rollo had been baptized, during the seven days in which he remained in white garments, he honored God and the holy Church with devout gifts. On the first day he gave a very large tract of land to the church of Saint Mary of Rouen; on the second, to the church of Saint Mary of Bayeux; on the third, to the church of Saint Mary of Évreux; on the fourth, to the church of Saint Michael the Archangel situated upon the mount in the danger of the sea; on the fifth, to the church of Saint Peter and Saint Audoenus in the suburb of Rouen; on the sixth, [Col. 0801C] to the church of Saint Peter and Saint Aichadri at Gemmeticum; on the seventh, he gave Brenneval with all its appurtenances to Saint Dionysius.

## CHAPTER XIX. How he divided the land among his men, rebuilt the destroyed churches and the walls of the cities, and subdued the Britons who rebelled against him

On the eighth day of his purification, after he had removed his chrismal garments, he began by word to measure out the acquired land and distribute it among his counts and his other faithful men.

When the pagans saw that their duke was a Christian, they abandoned their idols, accepted the name of Christ, and unanimously hastened to baptism. After this, Robert, duke of the Franks, having successfully accomplished the matters for which he had come, returned joyfully to Francia.

Robert, duke of the Northmen, [Col. 0801D] having prepared a great array of wedding gifts, took the daughter of the aforementioned great king into the companionship of his bed according to Christian custom.

He provided security for all peoples who wished to remain in his land. He divided that land among his faithful men by measuring it with a cord, and rebuilt the whole region, which had long been deserted. He reconstructed it, filling it with his own soldiers and with peoples who had arrived from elsewhere.

He imposed upon the people perpetual rights and laws sanctioned and decreed by the will of the princes, and compelled them all to live together in peaceful conduct. He rebuilt the churches that had been utterly overthrown and restored the numerous temples of the pagans that had been destroyed. He repaired and enlarged the walls and fortifications of the cities. He subdued the rebellious Britons and sufficiently nourished the entire kingdom granted to him from the provisions of the Britons.

## CHAPTER XX. Concerning the law he established that no one should support a thief; and concerning the peasant and his wife whom he ordered to be hanged for stealing a knife and a plowshare

[Col. 0802A]

After this, within the borders of Normandy he established a law that no one should support a thief. If anyone were discovered doing so, both were to be hanged on gallows.

Not long afterward, in the village of Longapetentis, a certain farmer, having suspended his work in order to repair something, returned home, leaving his straps in the field together with a knife and a plowshare. His wife, as unfortunate as she was deranged, secretly carried everything away, wishing to test the duke’s edict.

The farmer returned to the field and, finding that the objects were gone, asked his wife whether she had them. When she denied it, he approached the duke and asked that his tools be returned to him.

The duke, immediately moved by pity, ordered that the man’s loss be compensated with five solidi [Col. 0802B] and that all the people throughout the surrounding area be compelled to undergo an examination by the ordeal of the red-hot iron. When, by God’s judgment, the man had been acquitted, the farmer’s wife was seized by the officials. Forced by blows, she confessed her guilt.

The duke said to the farmer:

> “Did you know beforehand that this woman was a thief?”

The farmer replied:

> “I knew.”

Then the duke said:

> “Your own mouth condemns you, wicked servant.”

And immediately he ordered both of them to be hanged on the gallows.

Many other deeds worthy of recounting are also commonly told about him. I shall briefly relate one of them here.

While he was eating after a hunt in the forest overlooking the channel of the Seine near Rouen, surrounded by crowds of attendants, he sat beside a lake which, in everyday speech, we call Mara. Sitting upon the pool, he hung golden bracelets on an oak tree. [Col. 0802C] They remained untouched there for three years because of fear of him.

Because he performed that memorable deed beside Mara, the forest itself has therefore been called Rollo’s Mara down to the present day.

By such terrors and others like them, Duke Rollo restrained the people—both because of his love of justice, which he owed to the divine laws, and for the harmonious and peaceful life of his subjects, and for the tranquil condition of his own honor. Thus he governed the duchy entrusted to him by God peacefully for a long time.

## CHAPTER XXI. Concerning the two soldiers of King Charles whom he ordered to be punished

Charles the Simple, son of Louis surnamed “Did-Nothing,” was Rollo’s father-in-law. At one time [Col. 0802D] he sent two soldiers to his daughter Gisla. She kept them secretly with her for a long time, unwilling to reveal them to Rollo.

When he learned of this, he became angry and, considering them spies, ordered them to be brought out and, once brought out, slaughtered in the market where goods were sold.

When Robert, duke of the Franks and Rollo’s godfather, heard that, because of the killing of the two soldiers, the bonds of the peace joined between the king and Robert, duke of the Northmen, had been broken and destroyed, he rebelled against Charles. Invading the kingdom of Francia, he was anointed king on the third day before the Kalends of July.

Before the year was completed, however, Charles fought against the invader of the kingdom at Soissons and, with God’s help, defeated and killed him. But while Charles was returning victorious from the war, the wicked Count Herbert met him and, under the false appearance of peace, compelled him to turn aside to the fortress of Péronne for lodging. There he deceitfully captured him and held him until death. [Col. 0803A]

Duke Robert had married Herbert’s sister, by whom he fathered Hugh the Great. When Charles had been captured, he raised to the kingship, on the counsel of the nobles of Francia, Rodulf, the noble son of Richard, duke of the Burgundians, whom Charles had received from the sacred font.

Ogiva, Charles’s wife and daughter of Elstannus, king of the English, terrified by her husband’s misfortunes, fled to her father in England with her son Louis, fearing greatly the hostility of Herbert and Hugh the Great.

## CHAPTER XXII. How, after his wife died without children, he again joined himself to Popa, whom he had had before his baptism; concerning the oath of loyalty which he made the Northmen and Britons swear to his son William; and concerning his death

[Col. 0803B]

Duke Rollo, who was also called Robert, after his wife had died childless, taken by death, took back the repudiated Popa, by whom he had already fathered a son named William, and again joined himself to her. [Col. 0804A]

But now weakened by age, labors, and battles, in which he had consumed all the strength of his youth, he deliberated with all his might about the disposition of his duchy— to whom and in what manner he should leave it.

Having summoned the nobles of all Normandy, together with the Britons Alanus and Berengarius, he presented to them his son William, blooming in the most beautiful flower of youth. He ordered them to choose William as their lord and to place him at the head of their military force.

Then, soothing them all with persuasive words, he subjected them to his son under an oath of fidelity. After this he lived for one five-year period, and, worn out by old age, put off his human condition in Christ, to whom are honor and glory forever and ever. Amen.

[Col. 0803]

# HISTORY OF THE NORTHMEN, BOOK THREE

## Concerning William, the second duke, son of Rollo

## CHAPTER I. Concerning the uprightness of Duke William’s conduct; how the Franks envied him because he extended the boundaries of his duchy in every direction; and how he defeated the Breton counts Berengarius and Alanus when they rebelled against him

[Col. 0803C]

After Duke Robert had been freed from the burden of the flesh, his son William, governing the entire dominion of the Norman duchy with prudent authority, eagerly strove in his heart to preserve unshaken faith in Christ the King.

He was tall in stature and handsome in appearance, with shining eyes, gentle toward the kindly, but terrifying to his enemies like a lion, and strong in battle like a giant. He did not cease extending the boundaries of his duchy in every direction.

This circumstance furnished the leading men of Francia with fuel for hostile invasion, audacity, hatred, and envy. At the same time, [Col. 0803D] the Britons Berengarius and Alanus, departing from the fidelity they had pledged to him, attempted with presumptuous boldness to withdraw from his authority and thereafter to serve the king of the Franks.

The duke quickly suppressed their recklessness. He ravaged Brittany in a hostile expedition for as long as necessary and overthrew many of their towns, until he expelled Alanus, the instigator of all the wickedness, from the kingdom and compelled him to go to the English. Berengarius, however, he mercifully reconciled to himself.

## CHAPTER II. How certain Northmen, under a certain treacherous Riulf, wishing to expel him entirely from the kingdom, were defeated by him with a small band of soldiers while they were besieging the suburbs of the city of Rouen, at the place still called the Field of Battle; and how, while returning victorious from the battle, he learned that a son had been born to him by the most noble maiden Sprota at Fécamp, whom he ordered to be called Richard at baptism

[Col. 0804C]

Having defeated these men, while the devil stirred up a great many wicked persons, internal conspiracies again arose against him. For a certain Riulf, inflamed with the madness of treachery and joined by many men infected with the poison of discord, took up arms and set about driving him completely from the realm. He gathered a multitude of men from every side and, after crossing the bed of the Seine, established a siege around the suburbs of Rouen, intending either to expel the duke from it or to seize and wickedly kill him, with Normandy claimed for himself.

Seeing, therefore, that he was thus besieged by his own men, the duke began in many ways to consider how he might safeguard his welfare and honor and restrain his soldiers from fear of so audacious a conspiracy. At last, after being indecently provoked by insults from a certain Bothon, his steward, he took up arms and, bursting into the rashly established camp with three hundred mailed soldiers, struck down the greatest part of them with swords and sent them to the underworld; he put the others, who hid themselves in various forest thickets, to flight. Riulf, deprived of the support of his comrades and lying concealed among the fugitives, escaped by the aid of flight.

The duke, having thus routed his enemies, reviewed the number of his own men and found that not one of them had perished. The place where this conflict occurred has since been called Pratum-belli, “Meadow of Battle.” As he was returning from the battle, a messenger was sent to him by the prefect of the castle of Fécamp, bearing the news that a son had been born to him by a certain most noble girl, Sprota, who had been joined to him according to Danish custom. Overjoyed, he immediately sent orders to have the child taken to Bishop Henry at Bayeux, so that, washed in the sacred font by the bishop’s hands, he might be called Richard, after his father. The bishop gladly carried out his command, anointed the boy with chrism, and sent him back to Fécamp to be brought up.

## CHAPTER III. How many counts and dukes from foreign regions, attracted by the fame of his goodness and virtue, frequented his court—especially Hugh the Great, duke of the Franks; William, count of Poitiers; and Herbert of Vermandois—and how William sought and obtained his sister Gelroc as his wife, while Herbert, at Hugh the Great’s urging, joined his daughter to him in marriage.

[Col. 0805B]

Having achieved a conspicuous triumph over the rebels and grown stronger in power, the duke began in many ways to spread the distinguished fame of his virtues among foreign nations, so that counts and nobles of kingdoms from various parts of the world, frequenting his court, would return joyfully to their seats, enriched with many gifts.

Attracted by these reports of his extraordinary nobility, Hugh, duke of the Franks, William, count of Poitiers, and Herbert, while the duke was laboring in the sports of the hunt in the Forest of Lyons among the rutting stags, came to him to congratulate him on his prosperity. Receiving them with great expenditure and ceremony, he often discussed with them the arrangement of various secular affairs.

During these private conversations, William, count of Poitiers, asked for his sister, named Gelroc, so that she might be joined to him in lawful marriage. The duke gladly favored his petitioner’s wishes. With Hugh’s counsel, he drew up the betrothal agreement and celebrated the wedding, then sent William joyfully back to his own country with many gifts.

Herbert, delighted by the promptness and magnificence of this wedding celebration, and wishing by an alliance with so great and generous a man to extend both his own name and his posterity, gave his daughter to the duke at Hugh the Great’s urging. The duke brought her from her father’s house to the fortresses of Rouen with an innumerable company of soldiers.

## CHAPTER IV. How, at the request of Æthelstan, king of the English, he restored Louis to his paternal kingdom and, with the support of Hugh the Great, the bishops, and the other leading men of the Franks, raised him to the royal throne after anointing him with holy oil; and how, after five years, the Franks again conspired against him and plotted to drive him from the kingdom.

[Col. 0805D]

When Æthelstan, king of the English, heard of the illustrious duke’s magnificent reputation, he sent him ambassadors with many gifts, asking him to undertake to restore Louis—his own nephew, the son of King Charles—to his paternal kingdom, and, for love of him, to forgive Alan the Breton, who was hostile to him, for the offenses he had committed.

The duke willingly agreed to his request. He forgave Alan what was owed to him and, by command, allowed him to return to his own country. He recalled Louis from overseas and, with Hugh the Great’s support, together with the bishops and the other leading men of the Franks, anointed him with holy oil and elevated him to the kingdom.

When Louis had governed peacefully for one five-year period, the Franks again conspired against him, plotting to drive him from his kingdoms.

## CHAPTER V. How Louis, compelled by necessity and wishing to enter into a treaty of friendship with Henry, king of Germany, could not persuade the king to agree except through William, the margrave of the Northmen; and how Louis, earnestly seeking the duke, obtained through him the treaty and assistance he sought from King Henry.

Compelled by their wickedness, Louis sent messengers to Henry, the king beyond the Rhine, saying that he wished to discuss certain matters with him in conference and to establish a firm treaty of friendship. The king replied that he would in no way agree to enter such a treaty unless it was supported by Duke William.

When Louis heard this through messengers, he immediately approached the duke, intending to seek his aid against the designs of the Franks. The duke received him honorably, as befitted a king, and promised that he would assist him in every way. Moreover, they spent some time together pleasantly at royal banquets.

The duke first sent the soldier Tedgerius to King Henry; then the two of them, with a great army, promptly followed him to the conference. Hugh the Great and Herbert, leading men of the Franks, were also added for this business. Thus, after hastening their journey, the two kings met on the river Meuse, at a place called Veusedus. Henry’s army pitched its tents on one side of the river, and Louis’s directly opposite on the other.

Between them, William, both most faithful and most prudent, proposed useful and honorable counsels. As he arranged, the two kings confirmed the terms of their friendship with oaths. After this Louis turned back with his men and returned to France, expressing the greatest thanks to the duke for what he had accomplished with valor.

## CHAPTER VI. How, when Duke William was returning from the conference of the kings, he received Louis’s son from the sacred font at Laon at Louis’s request, and gave him the name Lothair.

As the king was returning from the conference, a messenger arrived and announced that a son had been born to him by his wife Gerberga. Exceedingly joyful, he immediately begged Duke William to receive the child from the sacred font and call him Lothair, after his own name.

The duke gladly obeyed these words of affection and set out for Laon to fulfill the request. After carrying out the royal ceremony, he hastened back with his men toward the Northmen’s borders.

When all the clergy of Rouen learned of his arrival beforehand, they went out to meet him at the city gates with songs of praise, while citizens of both sexes called out from the battlements: “Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord.” Amid the harmonious voices of clergy and people, he was brought into the church of Mary, Mother of God. After prayers had been poured out to God, he proceeded, surrounded by a large retinue, to his own house to dine.

## CHAPTER VII. On the occasion when Duke William restored the monastery of Jumièges, previously destroyed by the pagans.

[Col. 0807A]

At the same time, two monks from the territory of Cambrai, from a village called Hespera—namely Baldwin and Gundwin—happened to return to Jumièges. Entering the vast wilderness of the place, they began, with the greatest labor, to clear and level the land as best they could by cutting down the trees, and to toil there with the work of their hands.

Duke William, arriving there during a hunt and finding them, began to ask them from what regions they had come and what those remarkable buildings had been. At once the servants of God explained the whole matter to him in order and offered him the charity of barley bread and water.

Since he had disdained to accept it because of the lowliness of the bread and water, he entered the forest and found an enormous boar, which he immediately began to pursue. But when the boar, turning back as the mastiffs were set upon it, broke the hunting spear and charged at the duke with headlong force, it knocked him down and savagely mauled him.

After a little while, having recovered his senses and sound mind, he returned to the monks, received from them the charity he had rashly despised, and promised to restore the place. He therefore sent workmen and cleared it of branches and brambles. Repairing the monastery of Saint Peter, which had partly fallen into ruin, he properly roofed it. He fortified the cloister and all the buildings and, reducing them to a smaller scale, made them habitable.

## CHAPTER VIII. On the twelve monks and their abbot Martin, taken from the monastery of Saint Cyprian and sent to him by his sister, the countess of Poitiers, at his request, so that he might install them in the place mentioned above; and how the duke, wishing to become a monk, was prevented by that abbot; and on the oath of loyalty which he compelled the Northmen and Bretons to swear to his son Richard.

[Col. 0807C]

Meanwhile he sent messengers to his sister in Poitiers, whom Count William had married, instructing her to send him monks whom he could install in the aforesaid place. His sister gladly supported his request, arranged the expenses of the journey, and sent her brother twelve monks, taken from the monastery of Saint Cyprian, together with their abbot, named Martin.

The duke was greatly delighted by their arrival. He received them at Rouen with the greatest joy and, surrounded by companies of soldiers and every mark of honor, led them to Jumièges. He handed the place and the entire estate over to the abbot; he had bought it from the landholders with gold, and he bound himself by a vow to become a monk there.

He would have fulfilled his vows, had not the same abbot opposed his intention, because his son Richard was still a very young boy. The abbot feared that, because of the boy’s weakness, the country might be disturbed by the machinations of wicked men.

Nevertheless, the duke took from him a monk’s cowl and tunic, carried them away with him, placed them in a chest, and hung its silver key from his belt. Afterward he departed and returned to Rouen, distressed that the abbot had forbidden him.

He summoned all the Northmen’s and Breton leaders and fully disclosed the decision of his mind. They were profoundly astonished by his words and, overcome with amazement, remained unable to say what they should answer. At last, scarcely recovering their breath, they broke out in lamentation:

“Why, most serene lord, are you abandoning us so suddenly? Or to whom are you entrusting the rule of your duchy?”

The duke replied:

“I have a son named Richard. I ask you, therefore, if you have ever felt affection for me, now to show it to me with a willing heart, so that you may place him over you in my stead; for what I have vowed to God will inevitably be fulfilled by me in deed.”

Unable to oppose his will, they gave their assent, though sorrowfully, and agreed on this among themselves. He sent messengers to bring the boy Richard from Fécamp and presented him to them. Since all willingly confirmed their loyalty to him by oaths, the duke placed the whole duchy of Normandy and Brittany under his authority.

Immediately sending him to Bayeux, he entrusted him to Bothon, the chief of his military force, to be brought up there. Thus instructed in the Danish language, he would be able to give clear answers to his own people and to foreigners.

We have prefaced this account concerning Jumièges in order to show how great the duke William’s devotion and pious purpose were toward him.

## CHAPTER IX. How Herold [Aigrold], king of the Danes, expelled from the kingdom by his son Sueno, came to Normandy with sixty ships and was received with due honor by Duke William, who granted him the county of Coutances for his support.

[Col. 0808C]

Meanwhile, as fame proclaimed the strength and piety of so great a prince, Herold, king of the Danes, expelled from the kingdom by his son Sueno, came humbly to Normandy with sixty ships full of armed soldiers.

The powerful and generous duke received him with fitting honor and granted him the county of Coutances for his support, until he could build ships, enlarge his army, and recover his kingdom with a stronger force of soldiers.

## CHAPTER X. How Duke William, moved by the misfortune of Count Herluin, besieged and captured the castle of Monastériol, which Arnulf of Flanders had taken from him, and restored it to Herluin.

At that time Arnulf, count of Flanders, a crafty man, unable to restrain himself within the boundaries of his own jurisdiction when enticed by greed, sought in his pride of domination to trouble many who lived nearby.

Among his other schemes of wickedness, he inflicted the gravest injury on a certain count named Herluin and fraudulently took from him the castle called Monastériol. Since Herluin had been entirely deprived of assistance by Hugh the Great, his lord, he sorrowfully approached the lord of Normandy to seek help.

The prince, endowed with both goodness and greatness, sympathized benevolently with his misfortune. Gathering an army, he hastened to attack the town. He quickly occupied it by siege and, after rousing his soldiers, captured it by force. He then restored it to Herluin, again fortified with provisions.

Returning from there, he went joyfully to Rouen because of his successful deeds. At that time Franco, archbishop of Rouen, died, and Lord Gunardus [Gimardus] succeeded him.

## CHAPTER XI. How Arnulf, grieving over the town that had been taken from him, sent Duke William a deceitfully peaceful message that he should come to Pinchiniacum to discuss a treaty of friendship with him.

Meanwhile Arnulf of Flanders, breathing forth dire poison from his treacherous heart and grieving with savage spirit over the town that had been taken from him, began in his heart to plot the duke’s death with many leaders of the Franks.

Those men, infected by the deceitful trickery of an inhuman man and abominable murderer, unanimously conspired for the death of the excellent prince, binding themselves to this crime by oath.

Arnulf, wishing to accomplish by deed what he had conceived in his fraudulent mind, sent messengers to Duke William, saying that he wished to have friendship with him, establish an unbreakable peace, and, for love of him, forgive Count Herluin the offense he had committed. He added that, if he were not detained by gout and arthritis, he would gladly come to the duke’s court for this purpose. Finally, he earnestly asked William to designate a place where Arnulf could meet him for a mutual conference.

The duke, wishing to restore peace to his duchy, and because he ardently desired to assume the monastic habit, set out for the appointed place at Pinchiniacum, on the river Somme, with an innumerable force of the finest soldiers, in hope of settling so important a matter. There the army of Arnulf was stationed on one side of the river and William’s on the opposite side.

## CHAPTER XII. How the four traitors—namely Henry, Balzo, Robert, and Riulf—killed the duke on an island in the river Somme at Arnulf’s command; how a silver key was found in his sash, beneath which he kept a monk’s cowl and tunic in a chest; and how his body was taken back to Rouen.

There was an island in the middle of the riverbed. After exchanging kisses, the two dukes sat down there to discuss the matters for which they had come.

Arnulf, imitating the custom of the traitor Judas, spun out a spider’s web for a long time with songs and evasions. At last, after they had sworn the oaths of friendship and exchanged many kisses of peace, they parted from one another as the sun was sinking toward the west.

But as William was crossing the river, Henry, together with Balzo, Robert, and Ridulph [Riulfus]—four sons of the devil—called him back with shouts and reported that their lord had neglected to disclose a better plan.

When William turned his boat back toward the bank, as soon as he touched land they drew their swords and—alas!—killed the innocent man, who could receive no help from his own men because of the depth of the flowing water. They immediately sought the aid of flight and left the most pious man’s body lifeless.

Berengerius and Alan the Bretons, as well as the leaders of the Northmen, seeing their lord being killed, filled the shores with cries and wailing but could give him no assistance.

After a little while, when they had brought his body back to themselves and stripped it, they found a silver key hanging from his sash. Beneath it lay a very rich treasure: namely, a monk’s tunic and cowl. Had life remained with him, he would undoubtedly, on returning from this assembly, have taken these garments when he became a monk at Jumièges.

They placed him on a bier and brought him as quickly as possible to Rouen amid multiplied mourning. The clergy and people of both sexes came out to meet him at the city gate, and with sorrowful sobs carried him into the church of Saint Mary, the perpetual virgin.

They then sent to the city of Bayeux and summoned the boy Richard to his father’s burial. There they unanimously renewed their oath of loyalty to him and placed him under the guardianship of Bernard the Dane, so that he might be kept more securely within the city walls under his watchful and faithful care.

The most holy duke William completed the course of his life on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of January, while King Louis held the kingdom of the Franks, in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 943, during the reign of our same Lord Jesus Christ, who lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.

# HISTORY OF THE NORTHMEN. BOOK FOUR

## On the First Richard, Son of Duke William

[Col. 0809]

## CHAPTER ONE. How Richard, still a boy, succeeded his father William.

[Col. 0809D]

When the most pious and most blessed Duke William had been transferred, as we believe, among God’s elect, his son Richard, marked by the distinction of the highest nobility, like a shoot cut from a sweet-flowing tree and taking root in its first flowering, began to send forth the fragrant blossoms of a most pleasing childhood and to shape his generous spirit under the discipline of a tutor.

Restraining the impulses of his youthful heart from unlawful desires by noble self-control, and rejecting the frivolous pursuits of his tender age, he devoted himself wholeheartedly to the teachings of the wise. Whatever soundness or prudence he caught with his ear, he immediately entrusted to his discerning memory, as the occasion required.

When the leading men of the Franks heard of Arnulf of Flanders’s most heinous treachery and the mournful death of Duke William, many grieved.

## CHAPTER II. How King Louis of the Franks came to Rouen, fraudulently took the boy Richard with him to France, and, as the boy’s guardian, subjected the duchy of Normandy to his own authority.

Some accomplices of the murderer, however, who had previously pretended to be his closest friends, revealed the poison long concealed within them once the inner secrets of their hearts had been exposed.

King Louis, believing that a door to great honor had opened for him, forgot the benefits and loyalty the duke had always shown him. Pretending that he wished to consult the Northmen about the duke’s death, he hastened quickly to Rouen.

Rodulphus, Bernard, and Anslech, guardians of the entire duchy of Normandy, received him with royal honor, as befitted so great a king, and submitted themselves to his service, ostensibly out of loyalty to their very young lord.

When the king saw the fertility of the land, the healthfulness of the waters, and the abundance of the forests, he was caught by desire and deceitfully began promising them that he intended otherwise—namely, to turn everything to his own advantage.

He sent orders for the boy Richard to be brought into his presence. Seeing that the boy was endowed with exceptional beauty, he decided that he should be raised in his palace with boys of his own age.

Meanwhile a harsh rumor shook the entire city: Richard, the pledge of their hopes, was being disgracefully detained in the king’s custody. At this, the citizens, mingled with bands of soldiers, ran through the city with drawn swords and burst into the king’s court, hastening with savage purpose to kill him.

When the king learned of their tumult, he was greatly terrified. On Bernard the Dane’s advice, he seized the boy in his arms, displayed him to the furious crowd, and thus restrained their wild agitation.

Wishing entirely to calm the agitated spirits of the Northmen, the king, on the advice of his men, granted the boy Richard his paternal inheritance, after securing their oath of loyalty to himself. Receiving the boy into his own protection, he promised them—though deceitfully—that he would return him to them properly instructed in courtly disciplines.

## CHAPTER III. How Louis, blinded by Arnulf’s gifts, threatened to burn the hamstrings of the boy Richard, duke of the Northmen.

[Col. 0811D]

When these matters had been settled, the king bitterly endured in the hidden anger of his heart the disgrace he had suffered from the Northmen. He returned to France with the boy Richard, supposedly to avenge his father’s death violently upon Arnulf of Flanders.

Arnulf, fearing that King Louis might attack him with a hostile force, and wishing to cleanse himself of the crime of treachery, sent messengers with ten pounds of gold. He declared before the king that he was free of guilt in William’s death and promised that, if the king ordered it, he would certainly expel the killers from their homeland.

Yet he insisted that Louis ought to remember the insults and reproaches which he and his father had endured from the Northmen for so long. To prevent him from languishing in prolonged distress, he said that the best course would be to confine the boy Richard under strict guard after burning his hamstrings and to burden the Northmen with the heaviest taxes until they were forced to return to Denmark, from which they had emerged.

The king, therefore, blinded by gifts and the crafty snares of the traitor, absolved the man who deserved hanging from his crime and turned his anger against the innocent boy, imitating Pilate, who released a murderous man and condemned Christ to the punishment of the cross.

Thus, while he was staying at Laon-La-Fère, he met the boy returning from fowling and assailed him with the bitterest insults. He called him the son of a prostitute who had of her own accord taken another woman’s husband, and threatened that, unless he came to his senses concerning such conduct, his knees would be cauterized and he would be deprived of every honor.

Other guards were appointed, and orders were given that he should be kept under close watch lest he escape.

## CHAPTER IV. How Osmund, the boy’s steward, freed him from strict custody by a stratagem, and, taking him from Laon-La-Fère, brought him as far as Senlis to Bernard, his maternal uncle.

When Osmund, his steward, heard of the king’s exceptionally harsh sentence and understood what would follow, he was dismayed and sent a messenger to the Northmen, reporting that their lord Richard was being held by the king under the mournful yoke of captivity.

When this became known, a three-day fast was immediately proclaimed throughout the whole country of the Northmen, and continual prayer was offered to the Lord by the Church for the boy.

Osmund, having taken counsel with Yvo, William of Bellême’s father, urged the boy to pretend to be ill, lie in bed, and appear so gravely sick that everyone would despair of his life. The boy promptly obeyed his advice and immediately lay down as though he were at the point of death.

When the guards saw this, they neglected their custody and went here and there to attend to their own affairs. By chance, a bundle of hay lay in the courtyard of the house. While the king was dining and the streets had been cleared of citizens, Osmund tied the boy to his shoulders with the bundle, as though he were carrying fodder for a horse, and crossed the city walls.

When he reached the house of his host, he quickly mounted a horse and, taking the boy, fled as rapidly as possible to Codiciacum. There he entrusted the boy to the men of the castle, while he himself rode through the night and arrived at Senlis at dawn.

Count Bernard was astonished to see him arrive so early and carefully asked how matters stood concerning his nephew Richard. When Osmund had revealed the whole sequence of events and had made him happier than usual, they immediately rode swiftly in search of Hugh the Great.

After explaining the plan, they took an oath of the holy faith to help the boy. Then they came with a very large army to Codiciacum, joyfully removed him from there, and brought him to the city of Senlis.

## CHAPTER V. How Bernard the Dane wisely nullified the counsel Hugh the Great had given Louis against the Northmen.

[Col. 0813A]

King Louis, realizing that his plan would fail, began through his messengers to demand Hugh the Great’s loyalty from him. When they reported that Richard was not held under the authority by which Louis had supposed Hugh controlled him, but under the protection of Bernard, count of Senlis, Louis, losing hope of recovering him, sent to Arnulf of Flanders and instructed him to meet him quickly so that they might consult about these matters at a village called Restibulus.

While the two men were arguing there from opposing sides about what should be done, Arnulf finally added:

“We know that Hugh the Great has long been of one mind with the Northmen. It is therefore expedient for you to blind him with gifts. Grant him the duchy from the Seine to the Northmen’s sea, reserving the city of Rouen for yourself, so that, deprived of his assistance, this treacherous people may be compelled to leave the country altogether.”

Persuaded by these words, the king immediately summoned Hugh the Great through his messenger to a conference at a village called Crux, near Compiègne.

When Hugh arrived and heard the king discussing the distribution of cities and counties, he preferred, blinded by greed, to be enlarged in honor as a perjurer rather than to preserve unshaken faith with his friend Richard.

Accordingly, they departed from the place after swearing an expedition against the Northmen. Once armies had been gathered on both sides, the king began attacking the territory of Caen, and Hugh that of Bayeux, with plundering and fires.

When Bernard the Dane learned this, he followed the counsel of Bernard of Senlis and immediately sent messengers to King Louis, instructing them to speak as follows:

“Why, most powerful king, are you laying waste to your own homeland, especially when it is peaceful and quiet for you, with no one resisting? Cease, therefore, from plundering your own people and make use of the service of the Northmen’s soldiers. Why do you harass them with fires, when the city of Rouen lies open to you? Accept their service with a benevolent spirit, so that with their aid you may avoid the schemes of your enemies.”

## CHAPTER VI. How Louis came to Rouen and was received by Bernard the Dane and the other citizens, and how, at his command, Hugh the Great ceased ravaging Normandy.

[Col. 0813D]

Greatly delighted by this embassy, Louis forbade his soldiers to plunder and hastened as quickly as possible to the city.

When he approached, all the city’s clergy came out to meet him at the gate with many praises, calling out with the crowds of the people: “Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord.”

Then the king went to the royal banquet and began to dine splendidly, with Bernard the Dane serving him. While he was already warmed by wine during the meal, Bernard said to him:

“Today, most serene king, a most joyful day has dawned for us, since we have begun to be royal. Until now we have served the duke; henceforth we shall serve an unconquered king. Let Bernard of Senlis keep his nephew Richard; may we have you as lord and king for a long time!

“Indeed, he gave you a ruinous piece of advice who persuaded you to lose the strength of the entire Northmen’s army. Whom could you have failed to terrify with the immense power of that army? They are subject to your rule just as we are, and they desire to serve you with willing hearts.

“Why, then, did you arm your enemy Hugh against us with twenty thousand warriors? Has he not always been hostile to you and constantly quarreled with you?”

Pleased by these and similar words, the king immediately sent messengers to Hugh the Great, ordering him to withdraw from the borders of the Northmen. He also sent him this message: that it would be foolish to give such great possessions to another, when he could acquire them lawfully and peacefully for his own support without anyone opposing him.

When this was reported to him, Hugh the Great was greatly angered and withdrew as quickly as possible, abandoning the expedition and restraining his soldiers from ravaging Normandy.

The king remained at Rouen for some time and appointed Rodulphus, surnamed Torta, as prefect over the county, so that he might collect taxes annually from the subjects and decide all rights and every matter in that province.

Worse than the pagans, Rodulphus demolished from their foundations all the monasteries that had been burned by the pagans and that stood along the banks of the Seine, carrying away their stone to repair the city of Rouen.

When he came to Jumièges, he attacked the monastery of Saint Mary and overturned it. He would have destroyed it completely from its foundations had not a certain cleric named Clement bought two towers from the workmen for a price. They remained standing until the time of Archbishop Robert, who restored that church.

After arranging matters according to his will, the king returned joyfully to Laon.

## CHAPTER VII. How, through Bernard the Dane’s resourcefulness and King Herold of the Danes’ action, King Louis of the Franks was captured and held under strict guard in the city of Rouen.

Meanwhile Bernard the Dane feared that, on his return, King Louis and Duke Hugh might oppress the Northmen with even heavier hardships. He therefore secretly sent messengers to Herold, king of the Danes, who was still staying at Cherbourg, instructing him to join the soldiers of Coutances and Bayeux in a land expedition, while Herold himself, with a hostile fleet, harassed Normandy by raids from the sea. In this way, when King Louis came to meet him in conference, Herold might avenge the blood of his friend William upon his enemies.

The king readily followed this advice. Sending his ships to sea and spreading their sails wide, with the northwest wind blowing he reached the shores of Corbon’s saltworks, where the river Dives pours itself in a swift current into the stormy sea.

As usual, rumor flew and immediately struck the ears of the Franks: pagans had seized the maritime shores with a large multitude of ships.

Bernard the Dane and Rodulphus Torta also sent a messenger to King Louis and informed him of this misfortune. Gathering a powerful army, Louis came as quickly as possible to Rouen.

From there he sent word to King Herold of the Danes to meet him at the ford called Herluin’s Ford. He intended to make clear to anyone who wished to know why Herold was attacking the borders of his kingdom.

This greatly pleased King Herold, who had resolved with all his strength to avenge the duke’s death.

When the two kings met on the appointed day and discussed at length among themselves the unjust killing of Duke William, a certain Dane noticed among the others Herluin, count of Monastériol, for whose sake the duke had died. Inflamed with zeal for his friend, he immediately pierced him with a lance and struck him dead on the spot.

Lambert, Herluin’s brother, and the other Franks bitterly lamented his death and, stirred to fury, suddenly rushed upon the Danes to fight. The pagans bravely received them and, while Mars raged, sent eighteen leaders, together with countless others, headless by the sword into the fire-breathing underworld.

Others, hastening to hide themselves, wandered here and there through various hiding places, seeking refuge for their lives.

King Louis, escaping capture by King Herold through the speed of his horse, fell into the hands of a certain soldier. He promised the man many things so that he would not betray him and hand him over to the enemy. At last, overcome by the king’s tears, the soldier secretly took him to an island in the Seine.

When Bernard the Dane learned this from those who reported it, he immediately sent men to seize the soldier and put him in chains. Compelled by his own necessity, the soldier unwillingly revealed before them the man he intended to rescue in return for a reward.

The king was then removed from the island and, by Bernard’s order, confined under strict guard at Rouen.

## CHAPTER VIII. How Queen Gerberga, seeking help from her father, Henry, king beyond the Rhine, against the Northmen, did not obtain it; and therefore gave her son and two bishops as hostages for her husband, King Louis.

When Queen Gerberga heard that her husband had been captured by the Northmen, she grieved and, in deep distress, quickly approached Henry, king beyond the Rhine, her own father. She asked him to organize a very large army, besiege Rouen, and violently rescue her husband from there.

When King Henry heard of her misfortune, he replied that this had rightly happened to her husband, because Louis had wickedly violated the faith he had once sworn to Duke William by capturing his son.

“Try,” he said, “to help him through your own efforts, my daughter, for at present I must attend to matters of my own.”

When the queen heard these words from her father, she quickly returned to France, having accomplished nothing favorable. Then, approaching Hugh the Great as a suppliant, she asked him to wrest her lord from the Northmen.

Duke Hugh sent Bernard of Senlis and summoned the Northmen to a conference at Saint-Clair. When they had gathered there and had disputed at length about the king’s surrender, Hugh the Great finally said:

“Give us back our king, and in exchange receive his son, on the condition that, when we return here at the proper time, we establish peace between us by a firm treaty.”

This pleased the Northmen. In exchange for the king, they received hostages: his son and two bishops, Hildier of Beauvais and Wido of Soissons.

When these matters had been successfully completed, the king, rejoicing at his escape, returned to Laon, and the Northmen went back to Rouen.

## CHAPTER IX. How the Northmen brought back their lord Richard from France, how the hostages were returned, and how Herold returned to Denmark.

After this, the Northmen sent to Bernard of Senlis and recalled from there their elder Richard with a great army. At the appointed time, the king, having summoned a military force, came with the bishops of Francia to the River Epte, together with Hugh the Great; the Northmen met them on the opposite bank of the river with the boy Richard [Col. 0816B]. As messengers passed between the two sides, peace, with Christ’s favor, was established between them by firm treaties, and after oaths had been sworn the hostages were returned—the king’s son having died at Rouen. When these matters had been properly completed, King Louis returned to Laon, and the boy Richard to Rouen.

Rodulf Torta, the prefect of the city, immediately began to treat him harshly and to afflict his household with want and hunger, refusing to provide them with more than twelve coins for their daily sustenance. Therefore the duke, inflamed with fierce anger, quickly drove him from the city and compelled him to go to Paris, to his own son, the bishop of the city. When these matters had been settled, the land of the Northmen grew quiet before the duke. King Herold, however, returned not long afterward to Denmark [Col. 0816C] and was reconciled with his son Swein.

## CHAPTER X. How Hugh the Great betrothed his daughter Emma to Duke Richard; how King Louis and Count Arnulf of Flanders, terrified by this, sought the aid of King Otto against Hugh the Great and Duke Richard; and how Otto, having devastated Hugh the Great’s land, attacked Rouen in an attempt to conquer it

After these events, Duke Hugh, observing the boy Richard growing stronger, betrothed his daughter, named Emma, to him, with the consent of Bernard of Senlis and after oaths had been sworn on both sides, so that when he reached maturity and the flower of youth, he might unite her to himself by the law of marriage. This affair greatly terrified King Louis and many of the nobles of Francia, but above all Arnulf of Flanders, the instigator of the entire plot. [Col. 0816D]

When Louis learned that these dukes of great power had been joined by the bond of love, he feared that their efforts might remove him from the summit of the kingdom. Accordingly, at Arnulf’s advice, he sent Arnulf of Flanders across the Rhine to King Otto, instructing him that, if Otto utterly crushed Hugh the Great and subjected the land of the Northmen to his dominion, he would unquestionably hand over to him the kingdom of Lotharingia, which had been promised to his father, King Henry, the king across the Rhine, on account of the battle successfully fought in the field of Soissons, with his aid, by Charles, Louis’s father, against Robert.

Otto rejoiced when he heard what he had long desired. Having prepared everything suitable and necessary for so great an undertaking, he left his kingdom like a mighty storm [Col. 0817A] and, joined by the armies of King Louis and Arnulf of Flanders, fell upon Hugh the Great with many legions of soldiers. After destroying everything that belonged to Hugh outside the fortified towns, he directed the full strength of the war against the Northmen, intending to drive them from their homeland. He sent ahead a certain nephew of his with a large force to terrify the city of Rouen.

When this nephew attacked the city and found the Northmen hiding within the walls, he supposed that they were all incapable of fighting. He therefore ordered his soldiers forward and began vigorously to assault the gates. But the Northmen suddenly threw open the gates and burst out with savage courage. They ravaged their adversaries in so great a storm of violence that the king’s nephew was struck down upon the bridge, and scarcely a few escaped [Col. 0817B] from the battle.

## CHAPTER XI. How Emperor Otto, King Louis, and Arnulf of Flanders shamefully fled from the siege of Rouen; and concerning the death of Louis, whom his son Lothair succeeded

King Otto, following slowly with King Louis and Arnulf of Flanders, arranged his legions of soldiers and approached to besiege the city. When he saw that it was unconquerable, and heard of the death of his nephew, he began secretly to consult with Arnulf, inside the church of Saint Peter and the blessed Audoenus, situated in the suburb of the city, about handing Arnulf over to the Northmen together with his own men. There too, in fearful counsel, he made arrangements to withdraw on the following day.

But Arnulf, having recognized this snare of treachery, folded up his pavilions and tents, loaded the pack animals, and at the dead of night fled hastily with his army. The others remained in great terror, frightened by the sound of the departing horses. At dawn Otto and Louis arose, and when they learned that Arnulf had fled, they immediately turned back along the road by which they had come, abandoning the siege.

As they departed, the Northmen pursued them so vigorously, killing them with swords, that the fallen were found along various roads like slaughtered two-year-old sheep. Many of them, while wandering through the remote clearings of the forests, were captured and dragged throughout the land of the Northmen. This was the end of King Louis, who not long afterward departed from human life after many sorrows. At that time, when Gunhard, archbishop of Rouen, died, Hugh succeeded him.

## CHAPTER XII. How Hugh the Great, approaching his end, entrusted his son Hugh to the protection of Duke Richard; and how the same duke took Emma, Hugh’s daughter, as his wife after her father’s death

Finally, Duke Hugh, worn out by old age and seeing the last day of his life drawing near, summoned the princes of his duchy and, with their counsel, endeavored to commend his son, named Hugh, to Duke Richard, who was flourishing in the bloom of youth, so that, protected by Richard’s guardianship, the boy might not be caught by the treacheries of his enemies.

After Hugh’s death, the same duke took his daughter, named Emma, from her father’s house [Col. 0818A] and, as he had formerly betrothed her, brought her into the walls of Rouen with the greatest celebration and honor, joining her to himself by the law of marriage.

## CHAPTER XIII. How Count Theobald of Chartres gave Queen Gerberga counsel against Duke Richard, and how this same plot was disclosed to the duke by two of Theobald’s soldiers

Meanwhile Count Theobald of Chartres, after certain disputes had arisen, began to oppose Duke Richard, laying waste his lands by plundering raids. When Richard learned of his rash attempts, he vigorously suppressed them with a strength worthy of so great a man.

Theobald, perceiving that his undertaking was achieving less than he had hoped, began to whisper malicious words about Duke Richard to Queen Gerberga, persuading her that, while Richard lived, Lothair, her own son, could never hold the kingdom of Francia in peace. For this reason, he said, it was supremely necessary that she strive with all her strength to drive so great an enemy from the land.

The queen, believing these words, immediately sent a messenger to Bruno, archbishop of Cologne and duke—her brother, that is—asking him to assist his nephew and to strive, if any way presented itself, to capture Richard, the most dangerous adversary of his kingdom. Bruno at once sent a certain bishop to the duke, to persuade him to meet him in the district of Amiens, saying that the king wished to reconcile himself with Richard and to subject the kingdom of Francia to Richard’s authority.

Deceived by these words, the duke, hastening toward the place to which his joyful hope called him, set out quickly [Col. 0818C]. As he went, two soldiers of Theobald met him. One of them said:

“Where are you going, most illustrious of men? Do you wish to be duke of the Northmen, or a keeper of sheep outside your homeland?”

After saying this, he fell silent. The duke asked him:

“Whose soldiers are you?”

The other replied:

“What concern is it of yours whose? Are we not your men?”

The duke immediately understood that the words of these informers were directed toward warning him and urging him to take the necessary precautions. He therefore courteously bade them farewell, giving one of them a sword with a hilt shining with four pounds of gold, and rewarding the other with a bracelet of the same weight in pure gold.

Then he swiftly turned back and came safely to Rouen. In this way Bruno was deceived and returned, his treacherous plots having been exposed [Col. 0818D].

## CHAPTER XIV. How King Lothair, having gathered Duke Richard’s enemies—namely Count Baldwin of Flanders, Geoffrey of Anjou, and Theobald of Chartres—wished to deceive him but could not

When so great a deception had been emptied of its force, King Lothair, urged by Theobald, once again turned to another pretext for concealed treachery. He sent an envoy to the duke, furnished with words such as these:

“How long, duke,” he said, “do you refuse to render me the service you owe? Do you not know that I am king of the Franks, to whom you ought to render military service, and whose commands and counsels you ought by no means to oppose? Are not the enemies of both you and me rejoicing at our disagreement? Therefore turn back, now and immediately, from these disputes born of an obstinate spirit, and hasten your journey to meet me, so that, joined thereafter by indissoluble bonds of peace, we may enjoy the benefits appropriate to us through mutual harmony. Let the king rejoice in so great a duke, and the duke in his dearest king.”

Lured by these evasive words of the false embassy, the duke immediately informed the king that he would come of his own free will. The king rejoiced greatly at this. He summoned the duke’s enemies—namely Baldwin of Flanders, Geoffrey of Anjou, and Theobald of Chartres—and hastened to the River Helne for the detestable meeting.

The duke, for his part, sat with his military force on the opposite bank of the water. Wishing to learn what was being done among the king’s party, he sent some of his men to report back and to speak with the king about his companions and friends. When the messengers found the aforementioned counts preparing to attack the duke, they immediately returned at a rapid pace and urged him to leave the place, lest, while the royal treachery took him by surprise, his enemies should rejoice in his death as they met him in battle.

At once, urged on by his men, the duke crossed the River Deppe, halted for a while, and prevented the pursuing enemies from crossing at the ford, until, avoiding the royal force, he quickly returned with his men to Rouen. Thus the king’s treachery was exposed openly, and the duke recognized the hostility he bore toward him.

## CHAPTER XV. How King Lothair captured the city of Évreux and handed it over to Theobald; how Duke Richard ravaged the county of Chartres and the county of Dunois; and how Theobald, coming with an army to the estate of Ermentrude, fled from there in disgrace and with great loss because of the duke

[Col. 0819C]

Seeing, therefore, that the purpose of his desire was being held in contempt, the king returned furiously to Laon, intending not long afterward, at Theobald’s urging, to attack Normandy with hostility. Scarcely pausing to gather counsel, he assembled forces of Burgundian and Frankish soldiers, attacked the city of Évreux while its citizens were off their guard, surrounded it with a siege, and captured it by the trickery of Gislebert, surnamed Machel. He immediately handed the city over to Count Theobald, so that Theobald might conquer the homeland.

When the king withdrew from the city, Duke Richard followed close behind him and ravaged the entire county of Dunois or [Col. 0819D] Chartres with battles and fires. After destroying everything that belonged to Theobald, he returned home with immeasurable booty.

Soon afterward Theobald, in reciprocal retaliation, secretly gathered a column of troops and, to the duke’s disgrace, pitched his tents and huts at the estate of Ermentrude, establishing a camp of most hostile enemies. But the prudent and mighty duke crossed the bed of the Seine in the silence of the deep night. At dawn he fell upon them and routed them with such slaughter that six hundred and forty of them perished, while the rest, wounded, fled through various forest paths.

Theobald himself, shamefully fleeing with a few companions and hiding along the remote tracks of the woodland, reached Chartres in confusion. In support of his flight, with Christ returning his deed upon him, his son died that very day, and the whole city of Chartres was consumed by fire [Col. 0820A].

The duke of Normandy returned to the battlefield, found the dead, and, moved by compassion, ordered them to be buried. He commanded that the wounded be carried gently to Rouen and treated there by physicians, and that, once healed, they be returned to Theobald.

## CHAPTER XVI. How Duke Richard sought and effectively obtained the aid of Herold, king of the Danes, against the Franks

Seeing that the king’s many plots were threatening him and that the Frankish counts were united in raging against him, the duke sent envoys to Herold, king of the Danes, asking him to come quickly to his aid and, with a multitude of pagans, to crush the fury of the Franks to the ground [Col. 0820B].

The king not only received the duke’s envoys gladly but also sent them back to him enriched with the greatest gifts, promising that he would send aid to him with all speed.

What more is needed? At the king’s command, ships were pushed out to sea. Pagan youth was prepared for so great an expedition, and an innumerable army was equipped with shields, coats of mail, helmets, and every kind of weapon. Then, on the appointed day, the standards were raised. With favorable winds balancing the sails, and with the ships swiftly crossing the sea, they came to the shores of the Seine.

When the duke learned of their arrival, he rejoiced greatly and went out to meet them. With him leading, they rowed along the bed of the Seine and were carried swiftly to Givold’s Ditch. There they cast anchor and took counsel about the overthrow of Francia.

Then suddenly [Col. 0820C] they burst from the ships and burned the entire surrounding country with deadly fire. Men and women were chained together and carried away; villages were plundered; cities were desolated; castles were overthrown; and the land was reduced to a wilderness. Mourning arose everywhere, and not a dog barked throughout the county of Theobald.

Wherever these resources failed, they immediately invaded the royal estates. Whatever they took from the Franks, they leased to the Northmen for a small price, so that the Northmen might possess it. The land of the Northmen remained free from pagan plunder, while Francia, with no one resisting, was carried away captive.

## CHAPTER XVII. How King Lothair and Theobald, compelled by necessity, fully restored everything they had taken from Duke Richard, and concerning the conversion of the pagans at the duke’s urging

[Col. 0820D]

While these events were taking place, a synodal assembly of bishops gathered at Laon to investigate why the Christian people were being afflicted by such disasters. At last they sent the bishop of Chartres to the duke to ask him for what reason such execrable severity had proceeded from a most Christian and devout man.

When the bishop learned from him of the king’s treacheries and of Theobald’s seizure of the city of Évreux, he immediately asked for and obtained a truce from the pagan incursions. During this truce, the bishops were to bring King Lothair to a suitable place, where he would make satisfaction to the duke with a willing heart.

When Theobald heard that the king was seeking peace without his counsel, he feared that the whole burden of the rebellion would fall upon him. He therefore quickly sent a monk to the duke, declaring that he repented with all his strength of the offenses he had committed against him, and that he wished to go to the duke’s court and return the city of Évreux to him.

When the duke heard this, he was pleased and, after granting him a guarantee of safety, allowed him permission to come to him. Theobald came with his companions and not only returned the city to the duke; after friendship had been restored, he also departed joyfully from him with many coins.

As the appointed day of the meeting approached, the duke ordered a pavilion of remarkable size to be constructed at Givold’s Ditch, in the camp of the pagans. There Lothair, withdrawing with his leading men, made satisfaction to him through agreed treaties and sworn oaths.

After the duke had completed these matters beneficially, he converted many of the pagans to the faith of Christ through sacred admonitions. Others, who intended to remain in paganism, he sent to Spain. There, waging many wars, they destroyed eighteen cities.

## CHAPTER XVIII. How, after his wife Emma died without children, the same duke married Gunnor, and concerning the duke’s descendants

At this time his wife Emma, the daughter of Hugh the Great, died without children. Not long afterward, he betrothed in Christian fashion a certain maiden named Gunnor, descended from a most noble Danish family, to himself in marriage.

By her he fathered sons—namely Richard, Robert, and Malger—and two others, as well as three daughters. One of these, named Emma, married King Ethelred of the English. By her the same king fathered Edward and Alfred, the latter killed much later through Godwin’s treachery.

The second, called Hadvis, was joined to Geoffrey, count of the Bretons, and bore the dukes Alan and Eudon. The third was Matilda, who married Count Odo; of her there will be discussion later.

He also fathered two sons and an equal number of daughters by concubines. One of the sons was called Geoffrey, the other William. The former was count of Eu. After he died, his brother received the same county, which his heirs still possess by right of succession, although Count Gislebert, the son of Count Geoffrey, held that county for a short time before he was killed.

This Gislebert fathered Richard, a most valiant knight. Both Richard himself and his sons—Gislebert, Roger, Walter, and Robert—loved the church of Bec with great devotion and enriched it with extensive possessions. They imitated their grandfather, Count Gislebert, who assisted the venerable Herluin, the first abbot and builder of that church, both with counsel and with material resources in founding it.

In a later account, at the appropriate place, we shall speak of that church and of its aforesaid abbot as the narrative requires. For now, it is enough to have mentioned these matters briefly in advance.

## CHAPTER XIX. How Duke Richard, building a church at Fécamp in honor of the Holy Trinity, adorned it with various ornaments; concerning the abbeys of Saint Michael of the Mount and Saint Audoenus, which he restored; and how, after Lothair’s death, Hugh Capet was elevated as king, and after his death some time later, his son Robert succeeded him

[Col. 0822A]

Since Duke Richard was distinguished by the growth of many good works, among his numerous undertakings of highest renown he built at Fécamp a church of remarkable size and beauty in honor of the divine Trinity, and adorned it in many ways with marvelous decorations.

He also restored certain abbeys: one in the suburb of Rouen, in honor of Saint Peter and Saint Audoenus; another on the Mount called the Mound, in veneration of the archangel Michael. He endowed them with communities of monks.

At the same time, Hugh, archbishop of Rouen, died, and Robert, the son of the same duke, succeeded him [Col. 0822B]. After Lothair, king of the Franks, died, Hugh Capet, son of Hugh the Great, was placed in his position by everyone, with the support of Duke Richard.

Hugh took up arms against Arnulf of Flanders, who refused to serve under him, and with a strong force took Arras from him, together with all the townships he held on this side of the river called the Lys. Grieved by this misfortune, Arnulf approached Duke Richard as a suppliant and devoted man, asking him to reconcile him with the king and the princes of Francia.

For this purpose the duke went to a meeting with King Hugh. He not only reconciled Arnulf with him but, through his entreaties, restored to him everything that had been taken away. At that time the same King Hugh died, and his son Robert, a most devout king, succeeded him.

This duke therefore flourished even more abundantly through the privileges of this blessedness, because whenever he heard that men were at odds, he made them harmonious either personally or through his envoys, as Scripture says: “Blessed are the feet of those who bring peace.”

He was tall in stature, handsome in face, sound in body, adorned with a long beard, and crowned with a head of white hair. He was a most devout benefactor of monks, a prudent supporter of clerics, a despiser of the proud, a lover of the humble, a supporter of the poor, a guardian of orphans, a pious defender of widows, and a generous redeemer of captives.

## CHAPTER XX. How Duke Richard, approaching his end, appointed his son Richard over the Northmen, and concerning his death at Fécamp

While this jewel of Christ, fragrant in secular dress with these and similar flowers of good repute, was flourishing, he began to be severely weakened by bodily illness [Col. 0822D]. He summoned Count Rodulf, his maternal brother, and sought his counsel concerning the disposition of the homeland.

Rodulf, overcome by profound grief and for a while rendered speechless, at last recovered his breath and gave the duke this answer:

“Although, dearest brother and most serene lord, you seem to be deprived of bodily strength, nevertheless, while we rejoice to embrace you in this life, it is your responsibility to make provision for the condition of the whole homeland.”

When the duke heard this, he summoned his leading men from every side and presented his son Richard before them, commending and appointing him with these words:

“Until now, my excellent comrades, I have presided over your military service. Now, since God calls me and illness grows worse, you can no longer have me among you as I enter the way of all flesh, having laid down the burden of corruptible life.”

When he had spoken these mournful words, the entire household was immediately shaken by groans and tears. At last, when the weeping had subsided, they assented to the duke’s will and, pledging their fidelity to the young Richard, unanimously acclaimed him as prince.

Afterward, as his illness grew worse, the duke was laid upon his bed. Raising his eyes upward, he breathed out his spirit, full of days, amid words of prayer.

[Col. 0824A]

Up to this point I have collected these events as they were related by Count Rodulf, the brother of this duke, a great and honorable man. I leave them written for posterity in the style of a scholar.

Duke Richard the First died at Fécamp, with the peoples weeping and the angels rejoicing, in the nine hundred and ninety-sixth year from the incarnation of the Lord. Our Lord Jesus Christ lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit, forever and ever. Amen.

# HISTORY OF THE NORTHMEN, BOOK FIVE  
## Concerning the second Duke Richard, son of the preceding Richard

[Col. 0823]

## CHAPTER ONE. Concerning the honorable conduct of the second Richard, both in secular and divine affairs

[Col. 0823B]

Since in the preceding books we have raised up Richard, duke of the Northmen, that most precious jewel of Christ, with fitting titles of praise, and have properly set him into the ring of the eternal King, it seems worthwhile that the carbuncle arising from him should occupy a second setting—corresponding both to his name and to the eulogy of his most distinguished nobility—in the person of Richard, his son.

This son was highly conspicuous for his military triumphs and worthy of being honored with no lesser celebration of praise. Spreading the rays of his brilliance under a glorious name through the several quarters of the world, within the boundaries of his duchy he marked out almost the whole land of the Northmen as one church of Christ through the abundant growth of good works [Col. 0823C].

He was exceedingly vigorous in arms, and everywhere nobly commanded armed legions of soldiers, accustomed always to gain victory over his enemies. Although he was devoted to secular activity, he was wholly Catholic in faith and benevolent and devoted toward the worshipers of God.

Under his rule many sheepfolds of monks grew strong. Like bees emerging from many baskets of holy works, they carried forth the clearest honey into the heavenly treasuries.

## CHAPTER II. How wisely he suppressed the unanimous conspiracy of the peasants, which they were contriving against the peace of the homeland

While he was thus overflowing with such abundant virtue, at the beginning of his youth a certain poisonous seed of dissension arose within the duchy of the Northmen [Col. 0823D].

For the peasants, acting in unanimous agreement and holding many assemblies throughout the various counties of the entire land of the Northmen, resolved to live according to their own wishes. Thus, both in the clearings of the forests and in the exploitation of the waters, they might use their own laws, with no one standing in their way before the barrier of established law.

To make these decisions effective, two envoys were chosen from each gathering of the raging populace, to carry their decrees to an inland assembly for confirmation. When the duke learned of this, he immediately sent Count Rodulf [Col. 0824B] with a multitude of soldiers to them, so that he might break up the rustic ferocity and the peasants’ assembly.

Without delaying over the command, Rodulf promptly seized all the envoys, together with certain others. He then cut off their hands and feet and sent them back useless to their people, so that their fellows might restrain them from such actions and be made cautious lest they suffer worse consequences.

When the peasants had experienced this, they quickly abandoned their assemblies and returned to their plows.

## CHAPTER III. Concerning the rebellion of William, the duke’s natural brother, to whom he had given the county of Oximus; how this same William was captured and later reconciled with his brother; how he received from the duke the county of Eu as a gift, together with Lezcenina; and concerning the sons of this William

[Col. 0824C]

At this same time, the insolence of certain wicked men made the duke’s firstborn half-brother on his father’s side, named William, arrogant and rebellious. He had received from the duke, as a gift within their fraternal association, the county of Oximus, so that he might render him the military service required of him. But, enticed by the cunning of evil men, he despised the duke’s authority and withheld himself from the service of his fidelity.

Although the duke repeatedly rebuked him through envoys, William refused to abandon his undertaking. With the counsel and aid of Count Rodulf, he was captured and thrust into the tower of the city of Rouen, where for five years he paid the penalty of his rashness.

He also overcame, in frequent disturbances of battle, certain of his retainers who persisted in their rebellious purpose: some he deprived of life, and others he drove into exile from his territories.

After five years, William, through the plotting of one of his soldiers, slipped from the tower by a very long rope through a higher window and began his flight [Col. 0824D]. Hiding by day so that those searching for him would not find him, and traveling by night, he finally decided within himself that it would be more equitable for him to attempt his brother’s mercy at the risk of his life than to seek the aid of some king or count, which might ultimately profit him nothing.
