With this purpose in mind, he was making his way when one day he found the duke exercising himself in the sports of the hunt in the forest of Verneuil. Immediately he threw himself flat upon the ground at the duke’s feet and mournfully begged forgiveness for his offense [Col. 0825A].

Moved by mercy and with the favor of Count Rodulf, the duke immediately raised him from the ground. When he learned from William himself how he had escaped, he not only forgave his errors but also thereafter loved him with a kindly heart as his dearest brother.

Not long afterward he gave him the county of Eu and gave him a very beautiful girl named Lezcenina in marriage, the daughter of a certain most noble man named Turquetil.

By her he fathered three sons: Robert, who after William’s death became heir of that county; William, count of Soissons; and Hugh, bishop of Lisieux. When these matters had been settled, the land of the Northmen grew quiet before the duke.

## CHAPTER IV. How King Ethelred of England, who had married Emma, the duke’s sister, sent an army to subject Normandy to himself; and how Nigel of Coutances defeated them utterly

[Col. 0825B]

About this time King Ethelred of the English, who had Emma, the duke’s sister, as his wife, desired to harm the duke and bring disgrace upon him, after certain causes of dissension had arisen. He therefore ordered a very great number of ships to be pushed into the sea and commanded soldiers from his entire kingdom to assemble at them on a day he appointed, properly armed with coats of mail and helmets.

The English gladly obeyed his commands and gathered unanimously at the ships. When the king saw the large and well-equipped force of the army, he summoned the commanders of his military force and disclosed the purpose of his mind. With stern royal authority, he ordered them to ravage and destroy all Normandy with plunder and fire as they went, sparing only the Mount of the archangel Michael, lest they burn with fire a place of such holiness and religion.

He also ordered them to capture Duke Richard, bind his hands behind his back, and, after subjecting the homeland, bring him alive into the king’s presence. After issuing these commands, he ordered them to depart with all speed.

They drew their ships out to sea and, cleaving the waters under wind-filled sails, reached the shores of Sara after crossing the expanse of sea. Bursting from the ships, they immediately consigned the coastal regions to deadly fire.

When Nigel learned this from scouts, he gathered the soldiers of Coutances together with a multitude of common people, suddenly attacked them [Col. 0825D], and destroyed them with such slaughter that absolutely no one remained to report their deeds to posterity.

One of them, exhausted by excessive running, had remained behind at a distance. When he saw the misfortune of his companions, he was terrified by fear and, forgetting the weakness of his body, ran as quickly as he could to the ships, announcing the destruction of the others to the guards.

All together, they withdrew to safer places and, distrusting their lives, rowed into the inlet of the sea. They spread their sails upward and, with the swiftest course and a favorable wind, hastened to their king.

When he saw them, the king immediately began to demand the duke from them. But they replied:

“We did not see the duke at all, most serene lord, but fought against a ferocious people from a single county, at the cost of our own destruction. There are not only very brave warrior men there, but also fighting women, who with the shafts of their water jars smash the brains of the strongest of the enemy. You may know that all your soldiers were killed by them.”

When the king heard this, he recognized his folly and shamefully grieved.

## CHAPTER V. How Geoffrey, count of the Bretons, sought and received Duke Richard’s sister Hadvis as his wife, and how she bore Alan and Eudon

Geoffrey, count of the Bretons, observed that Duke Richard was prospering in everything and increasing daily in strength and wealth. He judged that his own position would be more securely fortified and his power further strengthened if he enjoyed Richard’s friendship and aid.

Therefore, supported by the counsel of his men, he entered the Breton territories and sought the duke’s court with a very large display of soldiers. The duke received him honorably, as befitted so great a man, detained him for some time amid an abundant display of wealth, and showed him the greatness of his power as he wished.

When Geoffrey saw that the duke treated him with such distinction, he began to consider within himself that, if he were joined in marriage to the duke’s sister, named Hadvis, a stronger bond of affection would be woven between them. The girl was very beautiful in body and most pleasing in the uprightness of her conduct.

Accordingly, after their friendship had been established, he asked with all his strength that she be given to him. The duke gladly favored his wish and, with the Northmen’s princes consenting, gave him the woman he sought in Christian fashion [Col. 0826C].

After the wedding had been celebrated with immeasurable honor, he soon afterward allowed them to depart joyfully, laden with immense gifts. Geoffrey later fathered by her two sons, namely Alan and Eudon, who after his death ruled the land of Brittany for a long time with the greatest strength.

## CHAPTER VI. Concerning the cruelty of Ethelred, king of the English, toward the Danes who were living peacefully with him in England; and concerning certain young men of the same people who escaped and announced to Swein, king of Denmark, the death of their relatives

While the prosperity of Normandy flourished under so excellent a ruler in the condition described above, Ethelred, king of the English, polluted during his reign a kingdom that had long flourished under the glory of mighty kings with so great a crime of wicked treachery that even pagans judged the deed abominable and horrifying.

For he ordered the Danes, who lived throughout his kingdom in unanimous harmony with his people and suspected no danger of death, to be killed suddenly in a single day. He also ordered the women to be buried in the earth up to the belly, and their breasts cruelly torn from their chests by savage dogs set upon them; and he ordered nursing infants to have their brains dashed out against the doorposts of their houses. No crimes or offenses had been committed by them.

While at London, on the day appointed for this decree, this heap of slaughtered victims was being piled up without end by the savagery of the executioners, certain young men, swift in agility, made their way to a ship [Col. 0827A]. By rapid rowing along the bed of the Thames, they sought the open sea as a refuge for their flight.

After crossing the long breadth of the water, they finally reached the desired harbor of Denmark and announced to King Swein the bloody destruction of his people. The king was then struck inwardly by immense grief. He summoned the leading men of his entire kingdom, laid out the whole sequence of events before them, and carefully asked what should be done.

Moved by the distress and mourning of their friends and relatives, they all resolved, as if with one voice, that their blood must be avenged with all their strength.

## CHAPTER VII. How King Swein, having gathered an army, reached the county of York, then dismissed his army and came with several ships to Duke Richard of Normandy at Rouen to seek peace; concerning the pact established between the Northmen and the Danes; how the people of York, Canterbury, and London surrendered to the same king; and how King Ethelred fled with his wife and sons to Richard, duke of the Northmen

[Col. 0827B]

Having heard this, the king ordered all who lived under his rule to prepare without delay. He sent mounted couriers in every direction and appointed a day on which he commanded soldiers eager for gain to come from foreign kingdoms for this expedition. When the appointed time arrived, an immense army immediately hurried to the ships. Then the royal standards were raised aloft; the sails were spread to the winds, and, driven forward across the intervening expanse of sea, they were carried to the territory of York. There the king, leaving his army behind with some ships, proceeded to Duke Richard at Rouen to seek peace. When the duke had treated him royally for some time, while both he and his soldiers recovered from the labor of so long a voyage, they established an enduring peace between them—namely, on the condition that throughout the successive ages of the kings of the Danes and the dukes of the Normans, and of their heirs, it should remain permanently firm between them, and that whatever the Danes had taken from their enemies they should restore to the Normans as compensation. If any Dane were weak or wounded and needed the assistance of friends, he was to recover among the Normans, as though in his own house, under secure protection. To ensure that this agreement remained valid, the leaders on both sides confirmed it by the terms of oaths.

When the king had accomplished these matters as he wished, the duke rewarded him with worthy gifts, and he returned joyfully to his own men as quickly as possible. Once he had rejoined his army, he immediately committed the kingdom of the English to avenging flames. Seeing, therefore, that no one came to York’s aid, the people gave hostages and submitted to his rule. From there he departed and advanced to the bank of the Thames. When the people of Canterbury came there, they likewise submitted themselves to his authority. Then, having pulled up the ships’ anchors and cleaving the river’s channel, he established a siege at London. The Londoners, unable to withstand his assault, unwillingly bowed their proud necks beneath the yoke of his servitude.

King Eldred, however, residing at Winchester, saw that the English had utterly abandoned him. Taking the treasures from the earth, he went with his wife and sons, Edward and Alfred, to Duke Richard in Normandy. Received by him with due courtesy, he spent the whole period of his residence at Rouen with the duke amid great displays of wealth.

## CHAPTER VIII. On the death of King Sweyn at London; how his son Cnut, succeeding his father, again led an army against the English; and on Eldred’s return to England and the Danes’ victory at Ashingdon.

While Sweyn was at London arranging the affairs of the kingdom, he was overtaken by illness and died. The Danes embalmed his body with spices, placed it on a ship, and hastened to convey it to Denmark for burial. After it had been buried, his son, named Cnut, took up his arms, vigorously strengthened his army, and exerted all his efforts to prevent them from shrinking from a renewed expedition. Finally, by sending envoys, he summoned two kings to his assistance: namely, Lachman of the Swedes and Olaf of the Norwegians. Coming to his aid with their forces of soldiers, they reinforced the strength of his entire army by their valor.

Meanwhile, when these things were taking place, King Eldred heard of Sweyn’s death. Having made every preparation for sailing, he returned joyfully to his kingdom with his wife, but left his sons Edward and Alfred with their uncle. King Cnut, however, having gathered legions of soldiers from every direction, emerged from his kingdom like a mighty whirlwind and fearlessly challenged the stormy sea. When the ships had been launched into the deep, he was carried toward the English under full sail. From there, making for the River Thames, he quickly landed in the territory of London.

The English, gathered from the whole kingdom at Ashingdon, came out to meet him and his men as they disembarked from their ships, and brought upon him a most bloody battle, to their own destruction. The king fought them savagely, with the spirits of his legions roused to fury, and slaughtered them with such carnage that no human being could calculate how many thousands of the English people fell on that day.

## CHAPTER IX. How, after the death of Eldred, king of the English, King Cnut of the Danes took his wife Emma and fathered Hardacnut by her, who later succeeded him.

The victorious king returned with his men to his ships. Then, moving swiftly and confidently, he surrounded London with a siege. Within the city King Eldred fell seriously ill, and as the disease in his body grew worse, he departed this life not long afterward.

When King Cnut heard of the king’s death, he took precautions for the future on the advice of his faithful advisers. After a few days he removed Queen Emma from the city and joined her to himself in Christian marriage, giving the entire army her bodily weight in gold and silver as her price. In due course she bore him a son named Hardacnut, later king of the Danes, and a daughter named Gunhilda, who married Henry, emperor of the Romans.

The people of London, moreover, despairing of their safety as they were suffering from prolonged hunger, opened the city and voluntarily surrendered themselves and all their possessions to the king. When these matters had been completed, the whole strength of the English kingdom came under King Cnut’s rule. We have woven these events into the sequence of this work in order to show the origin of King Edward to those who did not know it. Now let the narrative return to its subject, from which we have digressed for a little while.

## CHAPTER X. On the dispute between Duke Richard and Odo, count of Chartres, concerning the castle of Dreux; how the same duke fortified the castle of Tillières on the River Avre; and how the Normans defeated Odo and the two counts who assisted him.

In those same times, Odo, count of Chartres, took from her brother’s house one of the duke’s sisters, named Matilda, with many gifts, and lawfully joined her to himself in marriage. The duke gave her half of the castle of Dreux as her dowry, together with the land adjoining the River Avre. After some years had passed, this same Matilda, by God’s ordering judgment, died without children. After her death, when the duke sought to reclaim the aforementioned land, Count Odo began to oppose him with excessive cunning, unwilling to leave him peaceful possession of the custody of the castle of Dreux.

Therefore the duke, having summoned the Bretons together with the legions of the Normans, came hostilely to the River Avre and built a castle, which he called Tillières. Taking provisions from Odo’s territory, he filled the fortification most abundantly. He left in it Nigel of Coutances, Ralph of Tosny, and Roger, his son, as commanders with their soldiers.

After successfully accomplishing these things, he withdrew from there, ordering each man to return to his own home. Count Odo, however, secretly summoned counts to his aid—namely, Hugh of Maine and Waleran of Meulan. Riding all night with their forces of soldiers, they came at dawn to the castle of Tillières, with standard-bearers leading the way.

When the aforementioned nobles saw them, they left guards inside the town, burst out with their men in a sudden assault, and joined battle with them. Immediately, with God’s help, the duke’s forces struck them down so thoroughly that, after many had been killed and very many wounded, the survivors fled through trackless places and, staggering, sought the dark hiding places of the forests.

Odo and Waleran, seeking some means of preserving their lives, concealed themselves in the fortification of the castle of Dreux. Hugh, however, when the horse on which he was mounted had been killed, fled on foot to a sheepfold and hid beneath the earth the coat of mail he had been wearing. Then, wrapping himself in a shepherd’s cloak and tirelessly carrying the sheepfolds’ hurdles on his shoulders from place to place, he urged the Normans to pursue as quickly as possible the enemies who were shamefully fleeing not far ahead of them.

When those men had withdrawn, he followed the forest paths with the shepherd leading the way and finally reached Le Mans after three days, his feet and legs miserably bloodied by brambles and thorns.

## CHAPTER XI. How two pagan kings came from overseas to Duke Richard’s aid against the Franks.

When the duke saw that Count Odo had fallen into such great folly, he sent envoys to summon two kings, together with a pagan multitude, from overseas to his aid—namely, Olaf of the Norwegians and Lachman of the Swedes. The kings received the duke’s envoys suitably, sent them back with many gifts, and announced that they themselves would come shortly afterward.

Then, gathering together with their armies, they cut through the foaming sea with the few sails of their ships and quickly reached the shores bordering Brittany. The Bretons, recognizing their sudden approach, gathered from every part of the kingdom and supposed that they could catch them unawares while they were intent on plunder.

The pagans, however, discovered their stratagem and employed a certain ruse. Across the level ground through which they knew the Bretons would come, they dug very deep trenches, narrow at the surface, so that the approaching horsemen, with the horses’ legs broken, would fall disgracefully onto the ground and thus be more easily killed by the sword.

The Bretons came and immediately rushed savagely upon the enemy. But, brought down by the pagans’ traps, they suffered such slaughter at once that scarcely a very few escaped from the battle. The barbarians then advanced farther, besieged the castle of Dol, captured it, and burned it with fire, killing its inhabitants together with Solomon, the advocate of the place.

Then, raising their anchors, they returned to the sea, and with their fleet under sail were carried to the mouth of the Seine. Entering the river’s channel, they reached Rouen by swift rowing, and Duke Richard, greatly rejoicing, received them with appropriate royal honor.

## CHAPTER XII. How Robert, king of the Franks, made peace between Duke Richard and Odo.

Robert, duke of the Franks, heard that the pagans had inflicted such disgrace upon the Bretons and that Duke Richard had summoned them to curb the insolence of Count Odo. Fearing that France might be devastated by them, he summoned the leaders of his government and ordered both of the disputing men to come to him at Coldres.

After hearing there the causes of the disagreement on both sides, he calmed their spirits and immediately restored them to concord, on the following terms: Odo was to retain the castle of Dreux, while the duke was to recover the land that had been taken from him; and, conversely, the castle of Tillières was to remain permanently in its existing condition, in the possession of the duke and his heirs.

When these matters had been settled according to his wishes, the duke returned joyfully to his own kings. He rewarded the kings with suitable gifts of royal magnificence and allowed them to return gladly to their own lands, prepared to come back whenever he needed their aid.

The Swedish king, moreover, delighted by the Christian religion, rejected the worship of idols and, together with some of his people, converted to the faith of Christ at the urging of Archbishop Robert. After being washed by him in baptism and anointed with holy chrism, he returned joyfully to his kingdom, rejoicing in the grace he had received. Later, betrayed by his own people and unjustly killed by the faithless, he entered the heavenly kingdom as a glorious king and martyr. Even now he shines among that people through miracles and virtues.

## CHAPTER XIII. How Duke Richard married Judith, sister of Geoffrey, count of the Bretons, and on the offspring he had by her.

Duke Richard, concerned about the succession of offspring, heard that Geoffrey, count of the Bretons, had a sister named Judith, remarkably beautiful in body and distinguished by every kind of moral goodness. He asked for her in marriage through envoys.

Geoffrey, eager to advance the proposal with willing spirit, made haste to prepare everything appropriate for so great an undertaking and brought her as far as the shrine of the archangel Michael. There the duke received her with suitable honor and joined her to himself in lawful marriage.

Over the passing years she bore him three sons: Richard, Robert, and William, who in his youth took the monastic habit at Fécamp. She also bore three daughters. One, named Adeliz, married Rainald, count of the Burgundians, by whom she had William and Guy. The second married Baldwin of Flanders. The third died a grown woman but still a virgin.

Later, Count Geoffrey, setting out for Rome to pray for the fulfillment of his desire, left all Brittany under the guardianship of the duke, together with his two sons, Alan and Eudo. After visiting the holy places, he was overtaken by death on his return journey.

## CHAPTER XIV. How Robert, king of the Franks, with Duke Richard’s help, restored the castle of Melun to Burchard.

At that time, while Burchard, count of the castle of Melun, was staying at the court of the king of the Franks, one of his soldiers, named Walter, blinded by gifts, secretly stole the castle from him by treachery and handed it over to Count Odo.

When the king learned of this, he promptly ordered Odo to leave the castle voluntarily, since he had unjustly usurped it. But, trusting in the strength of the place because the Seine flowed around it, Odo replied to the king through envoys that, as long as he lived, he would never return it to anyone.

The king, greatly angered by these words, summoned Richard, duke of the Normans, to a conference and laid before him the disgrace of this insult to his royal dignity, asking that the duke’s most welcome loyalty come to his aid, lest he be crushed by so great a mockery of presumption on the part of his own men.

The duke, unable to endure the insult offered to the pious king, gathered an army of astonishing size, came to Melun as quickly as possible, and besieged it from one side of the river, while the king took up position on the other. Thus, from both sides, they battered the castle day and night with a great storm of engines and siege machinery.

When the people of Melun saw that they could not withstand such a force of enemies, they suddenly opened the gates, drove out the arrogant rebel against the duke, and admitted the duke with his men. The duke, sparing the multitude, immediately sent the traitor to the king and instructed him to dispatch soldiers. The king restored the castle to Burchard and ordered the traitor and his own wife to be hanged on the gallows, repaying them with the fitting punishment for their conspiracy.

After this, Duke Richard, having completed matters properly, returned to his own lands with the king’s blessing. In his time the Normans were always accustomed to put their enemies to flight, but never to turn their backs.

## CHAPTER XV. How, with Duke Richard’s help, Robert, king of the Franks, obtained the duchy of Burgundy, which Duke Henry of that land had left to him at his death, despite the opposition of the Burgundians.

After three years had elapsed, Henry, duke of the Burgundians, died without children, leaving Robert, king of the Franks, heir to his duchy. The Burgundians refused to receive him in their proud arrogance; instead, they sent Count Landry of Nevers into Auxerre to rebel.

Hastening to suppress their swollen efforts of presumptuous insolence, King Robert summoned Duke Richard with a large Norman army and besieged Auxerre for so long that he subdued Landry and the city to his rule after taking hostages.

From there he departed and pitched his camp for a siege before the castle of Avalon. After assaulting it with great force for three months, Burgundy was devastated, and the townspeople, compelled by scarcity of provisions, surrendered it to the king through the counsel and assistance of the duke.

Having properly completed these matters according to his wishes, the king appointed guards in all the castles and placed his son Robert over the duchy. Thus, with the arrogance of the rebels broken, peace was restored. Then the king returned to France, and the duke with his men returned to Normandy.

## CHAPTER XVI. How Rainald, count of the Burgundians beyond the River Saône, married Adheliz, Duke Richard’s daughter.

Having learned of the duke’s reputation for marvelous deeds, Rainald, count of the Burgundians beyond the River Saône, sent envoys and sought his daughter, named Adheliz, in marriage. Having obtained her, he took her from her father’s house, brought her into Burgundy with great honor, and joined her to his bed according to Christian law.

Much later, however, when the seeds of disputes had arisen, he was deceitfully captured by a certain count of Chalon named Hugh, thrust into a prison under harsh custody, and bound in extremely heavy fetters.

When the duke learned of his son-in-law’s intolerable distress, he immediately sent envoys to Hugh with a direct command that, without difficulty or delay, he should allow the duke’s son-in-law to go free for love of him. Hugh thought little of the duke’s embassy. He not only refused to release Rainald but arrogantly ordered that he be guarded even more strictly by additional guards.

When this was reported to the duke, he immediately ordered his son Richard to gather the Norman army in one place, enter Burgundy, and avenge the duke’s injury with all his strength. The young man willingly carried out his father’s orders and prepared everything necessary for so great an expedition.

Finally, he departed his homeland like a violent storm, driving everything before him. After completing the journey with an innumerable multitude of Normans, he invaded Burgundy and surrounded the castle of Milinand [Milbiand] with a siege.

The inhabitants of the place, trusting in the security of their fortification, immediately began to provoke the enemy to their own destruction with weapons and arrows. The Normans, roused to the fiercest fury, attacked the castle all around with great force, suddenly captured it, and burned it to the ground with its men, women, and little children.

From there they directed their march toward the city of Chalon and consumed its territory with fire. Hugh, realizing that he could in no way resist the strength of so great an army, carried an equestrian saddle on his shoulders, fell on his knees before the young Richard, and begged forgiveness with humble supplication for the rashness he had committed.

After forgiveness had been granted, he restored Rainald and, having given hostages, promised Duke Richard by oath that he would make satisfaction at Rouen for what he had done. When these matters had been completed according to his wishes, the young Richard returned with his men to his father.

## CHAPTER XVII. How, when Duke Richard was approaching death, he placed his elder son Richard over the duchy.

Although Duke Richard had become widely renowned through the distinction of his outstanding deeds, he nevertheless remained a constant worshiper of Christ, so that he was rightly called the most devoted father of monks and clerics and the tireless supporter of the poor.

While he was flourishing under these and similar titles of virtue, he began to be severely weakened by bodily illness. He therefore summoned Archbishop Robert and all the leaders of the Normans to Fécamp and informed them that he was already entirely wasting away.

Immediately, intolerable mourning arose throughout every dining hall of the house. The monks and clerics lamented mournfully over the loss of so dear a father. The faces of the nobles streamed with tears at the loss of their unconquered duke. The crowds of the needy also mourned along the roads of the town over the deprivation of their comforter and patron.

Finally, after summoning his son Richard, and on the advice of the wise, he placed him over his duchy, and his brother Robert over the county of Hiesmes, so that from there he might render him the service he owed.

At last, after energetically arranging everything that seemed to pertain to the worship of God, he departed this life in the year 1026 from the incarnation of the Lord, entering upon the way of all flesh, while the same Jesus Christ reigned in the divinity of the Father’s majesty and in the unity of the Holy Spirit, throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

# BOOK SIX OF THE HISTORY OF THE NORMANS

On the third Richard and his brother Robert, namely, the sons of the second Richard.

## CHAPTER ONE. How Richard III, although he remained only a short time in control of the duchy, nevertheless imitated his father’s goodness.

Thus far the deeds of the preceding dukes of the Normans have been displayed openly in the unpolished brilliance of our style. It now seems fitting that those who flourished in the age of our own time should receive an appropriate place in the arena of this scholarly exercise. We have learned of their deeds partly by observation and partly through the reports of truthful witnesses, and we have resolved to disclose them to the knowledge of many, insofar as the poverty of our composition permits.

Richard, therefore, a young man who survived his father in the duchy, although he lived only a short time afterward, was, just as in the meaning of his name, also his heir in the highest standard of nobility. Highly capable in military arms, he was nevertheless wholly Catholic in faith and kind and gentle toward the worshipers of God. He governed the military bands with balanced judgment and rejoiced in the enjoyment of continual peace.

## CHAPTER II. On the dispute between him and his brother Robert, and on Richard’s death after peace had been made.

Yet the treacherous enemy did not allow him to enjoy the increase of the peace he desired for long. Through the cunning of certain malicious men, he stirred up his brother Robert against him to rebel.

After two years, Robert despised Richard’s authority and withdrew with his followers into the castle of Falaise to resist him. Duke Richard, eager to restrain his raging brother’s rash attempts and recall him to the obedience owed by a subject, surrounded him with a siege inside the castle’s circuit, together with a multitude of enemies.

After assaulting it for some time with repeated blows from battering rams and crossbows, Robert finally abandoned his treachery. They gave one another their right hands, returned to their former concord, firmly established peace, and departed from one another.

Duke Richard then dismissed his army and returned to Rouen. There, while accompanied by some of his own men, he died of poison, as many reported. This occurred in the year 1028 from the incarnation of the Lord.

Richard had a young son, Nicholas, who by the allotment of earthly inheritance lacked a share in it, so that God himself might be his portion here and forever. From infancy he was devoted to learning and was raised in the monastery of Saint-Ouen in the suburb of Rouen. He bore the monastic yoke for a very long time.

After Abbot Herfast died, Nicholas succeeded him in the governance of that monastery, which he held for almost fifty years, during the time of William, duke of Normandy and great king of England. Finally, in the year 1092 from the incarnation of the Lord, in the month of February, he died during the time of Robert II, duke, and William, archbishop of Rouen.

Now let us return to our subject.

## CHAPTER III. How Robert succeeded his brother Richard; on his character; and on the dispute between him and Archbishop Robert.

When Duke Richard descended from the summit of worldly rule and, as we believe, ascended to the heavenly kingdoms, his brother Robert was appointed by all to the rule of the entire dominion. Although he was harsher in character toward rebels, he proved gentle and kind toward the well-disposed, and pious and devoted toward the worship of God.

For this reason he always deserved to enjoy the delight of lasting peace, except for what he willingly chose for himself at the advice of wicked men. Thus, at the beginning of his rule, regarding Archbishop Robert with suspicion, he surrounded Évreux with a hostile siege.

The archbishop, wishing to avoid his savage assaults, shut himself within the city walls with an armed force. Finally, after giving his word that he would be allowed to depart, he left and went into exile to Robert, king of the Franks, and struck Normandy with a pontifical anathema.

Duke Robert, therefore, having countered the cunning of the wicked and recognizing that he had acted without due consideration in everything, recalled the archbishop from France and restored him to his former honor. Later, repenting of his wrongdoing, he took him into his counsels, as befitted so great a man, and thereafter remained faithful to him.

## CHAPTER IV. How the same Duke Robert besieged William of Bellême inside the castle of Alençon and compelled him to surrender.

After removing from himself all the instigators of discord and bringing their minds under the discipline of peace through generosity, he began to follow the counsels of the wise and, through diligent industry, to advance with great strength toward the highest honors.

Many of the good began to exalt his upright character and peaceful deeds with praise, while some of the wicked attributed them to cowardice. From the company of the latter, William of Bellême, son of Yves, dared to test his courage. From the castle of Alençon, which he held by right of benefice, he rashly attempted, through rebellion, to wrench his stubborn neck from the yoke of service.

The duke came swiftly with military forces to crush his atrocious insolence. He confined him within the fortification that supported such presumption until William sought the duke’s mercy and, barefoot, carried an equestrian saddle on his shoulders to make satisfaction.

Although William’s submission was feigned, the duke not only forgave him everything but also returned the town to him and quickly withdrew from the place. William, however, breathing out a deadly poison hidden in his narrow breast, restrained himself for a short time from open treachery; not long afterward he openly returned to the same crime of perjury.

He was exceedingly cruel and greedy, and he had four sons like himself: Warin, Fulk, Robert, and William. After Warin had cruelly deprived Gunher of Bellême, a good and lovable soldier who suspected no evil and was instead smilingly congratulating him as a friend, of his head without cause, he was immediately seized by a demon and strangled in the sight of his companions who were present.

Again William, having sworn falsely, grew so fiercely hostile against the duke that he boldly sent his sons Fulk and Robert with a force of soldiers to harass Normandy by plundering. Many of the duke’s household retainers, however, quickly went out to meet them boldly, joined bloody battle with them within the pass of Blavou, and, with God’s help, crushed them severely.

There Fulk, the son of the perjurer, was slaughtered, and almost all the soldiers were cut down. His brother Robert, wounded, barely escaped from the battle with a few men. Their father William, already seriously ill, learned that they had perished in this way. Struck inwardly by grief of heart, he immediately breathed out his soul.

Thus, after the duke’s enemies had been defeated, the rebellion in those regions disappeared thereafter.

## CHAPTER V. How Hugh, bishop of Bayeux and son of Count Ralph, wished to hold the castle of Ivry but could not.

Meanwhile, while these things were taking place, Hugh, son of Count Ralph and bishop of the city of Bayeux, observed that Duke Robert wished to follow the counsels of the prudent and abandon his own. Employing a certain cunning deception, he secretly supplied the castle of Ivry with sufficient arms and provisions.

Then he appointed guards and hurried to France in order to recruit soldiers there who would help him resist courageously. The duke, hastening to anticipate his fraudulent schemes, gathered the Norman forces and seized the same castle in advance by laying siege to it, closing every opportunity for anyone to leave or enter.

When Hugh saw himself excluded from entering it, concerned for those confined within, he requested permission from the duke through envoys to depart and immediately led them away from there. He himself also remained in exile for some time with the men he had summoned. The duke, having removed the guards from the castle, received possession of the fortified place upon its surrender.

## CHAPTER VI. How Baldwin, count of Flanders, sought and obtained for his son Baldwin the daughter of Robert, king of the Franks, to his own disadvantage unless Duke Robert of Normandy brought him aid; and on the death of Robert, king of the Franks, whom his son Henry succeeded.

At the same time, Baldwin, the Flemish leader, wishing to ennoble his offspring with royal ancestry, sought out Robert, king of the Franks, and asked that his daughter be given to his son Baldwin.

He obtained her from the royal palace, carried her to his own home in a cradle, and carefully raised her until she reached marriageable age. As soon as his son began to enjoy the embraces of the noble girl, relying on the royal relationship, he drove his father from his own soil, after the Flemings had withdrawn their allegiance from him.

Abandoned shamefully by his own people, Baldwin hurried to the duke of the Normans to request assistance against his son. The noble duke, pitying the man’s misfortune, gathered the strength of his soldiers and, like a dreadful whirlwind, departed his homeland and attacked Flanders, devastating it with destructive flames.

Advancing to a castle called Chioca, he immediately overthrew it and burned everything that stood within it. The remaining nobles, seeing this and fearing that they would suffer the same fate, abandoned the son, returned to the father, and sent hostages to the duke.

The young Baldwin, realizing that he could in no way withstand the duke’s intolerable incursions, sent envoys to him with the humblest pleas, asking that, through the duke’s mediation, he might be reconciled with his father.

The man of supreme benevolence favored his desire and petition with a sympathetic affection. After exchanging the kiss of peace, he immediately persuaded both men to return to their former concord. Thus, after the disputes had been suppressed, they continued thereafter in peace and love, as was fitting.

The duke himself, after destroying the rebels’ possessions, returned to Normandy with his army unharmed. At this time Robert, king of the Franks, died, and his son Henry succeeded him.

## CHAPTER VII. How the same duke helped Henry, king of the Franks, against his mother Constance.

King Henry had obtained the kingdom of the Franks while his father Robert was still alive. Later, however, his mother Constance treated him with such stepmotherly hatred that, with the counts conspiring against him, she sought to remove him from the royal throne and planned to place his brother Robert, duke of the Burgundians, in his stead.

On the advice of his men, Henry fled to Robert, duke of the Normans, with twelve retainers and at Fécamp asked him, in virtue of the loyalty owed to him, to support his cause. The duke received him honorably and honored him with many gifts. Not long afterward, properly equipped with horses and arms, he sent him to his paternal uncle, Count Malger of Corbeil, ordering him to afflict with fires and engines all whom he saw defecting from Henry’s allegiance in those regions.

The duke himself stationed a very strong force of soldiers in all his castles bordering France and violently attacked the rebels in repeated conflicts until, their necks bent and all their possessions consumed, they were compelled to be reconciled to their king and the attempts of their wretched mother were utterly frustrated.

At that time Robert, heir to the power and cruelty of William of Bellême, had for several years been harassing the neighboring people of Maine and the Normans. While undertaking an expedition beyond the Sarthe, he was captured by the people of Maine and held in prison for two years at the castle of Ballon.

After two years, William, son of Geroy, and other nobles of Robert gathered an army, summoned the count of Maine to battle, and, fighting bravely, drove him from the field. There they captured Walter of Sordes, an outstanding soldier, together with his two excellent soldier-sons. Despite William’s opposition, they wickedly hanged him on the gallows.

Walter’s other three sons were at Ballon. When they learned of the atrocious death of their father and brothers, they became fiercely enraged, violently broke into the prison, and miserably killed Robert of Bellême, crushing his head there with axes.

After his death, his brother William Talvas succeeded him in his honor. He was worse than all his brothers in every kind of wickedness, and immoderate depravity continued to flourish among the heirs of his descendants down to the present day.

## CHAPTER VIII. How Duke Robert, proceeding against Alan, count of the Bretons, built the castle of Carrouges [Carrucas] not far from the River Couesnon.

Alan, count of the Bretons, lifted up by the pride of arrogance, stubbornly began to withdraw himself from the service of Duke Robert. The duke therefore moved an innumerable army against him and established, not far from the River Couesnon, a castle which he called Carrouges, both to protect the Norman frontier and to subdue the arrogance of the presumptuous man.

From there he invaded Brittany and committed the entire county of Dol to devouring flames. After accomplishing these things splendidly, he returned to Normandy with immense booty.

After his departure, Alan, wishing to avenge the insult inflicted upon him, pursued him immediately with a large army in order to destroy the county of Avranches. Nigel and Alfred, surnamed the Giant, the aforementioned castle’s commanders, came out to meet him with their men. Fighting him, they immediately ravaged the Bretons with such slaughter that the fallen appeared scattered across the open fields and along the banks of the aforementioned river like sheep.

Alan, therefore, returned sadly to his own country and reached Rennes in disgrace.

## CHAPTER IX. On the abbey of Bec, its first abbot and venerable founder Herluin, and his successor Anselm.

Around this time, namely in the year 1034 from the Lord’s incarnation, Lord Abbot Herluin, abandoning secular life in the fortieth year of his age, received the habit of sacred religion from Herbert, bishop of Luxeuil. Later, ordained priest by the same prelate and appointed abbot, he became the beginning of the monastery of Bec. But since we have mentioned so great a father, we gladly insert somewhat more fully in these pages of the annals, for the memory of posterity, certain details about him and the church [Col. 0838D] he built.

His father traced his origin to the Danes, who first possessed Normandy; his mother was related by close kinship to the dukes of the Morini, whom modern people call Flemings. His father was Ansgot, and his mother was named Helois. Count Gislebert of Brionne, grandson through his son, Count Godefrid, of Richard I, the first duke of Normandy, kept Herluin with himself, most favorably received among all the leading men of his court, and had him brought up there.

He was extremely capable in arms and bore them with no less courage. All the members of the great families throughout Normandy counted him among their chosen warriors, and raised him up for every military undertaking and in the cultivation of his body. He turned his mind away from dishonorable things, while he devoted all his zeal to honorable matters, which are highly esteemed at court. At home and in war he could not endure not being foremost among his comrades. For these reasons he won not only the exceptional favor of his lord, but also made for himself a very great reputation with Robert, duke of the whole country, and with the lords of foreign regions, together with familiar access to them.

He had already passed thirty-seven years in this most agreeable condition of life when at last his mind began to be inflamed by love born of divine fear, and to grow lukewarm toward love of the world, gradually becoming colder day by day. Turning the eye of his heart away from outward things toward himself, he went more frequently to church, prayed devoutly, and often burst into tears. Having entirely abandoned amusements, he was now less often at court. The only thing that detained him there was his effort to win his estates for God along with himself. He achieved this by obtaining them from his lord through persistent service: his master transferred to him both the authority over and the service of whatever paternal rights his brothers possessed, men born to him of equal rank. Since he was becoming worthier and more nobly born in true nobility than his brothers, it was not considered unjust or dishonorable that they should rightly be subject to him.

At once, in the village called Burnenvilla, he undertook a substantial work for the service of God, and completed it in a short time. He not only supervised the work but carried it out himself, digging the earth, removing the soil from the ditch, carrying stones, sand, and lime on his shoulders, and personally setting them into the wall. While others were absent, he gathered together whatever the work required, [Col. 0839C] excluding idleness from every part of the day. As much as he had formerly been delicate through swollen vanity, so much more patient was he now, through true humility, in enduring every kind of labor for God’s sake. Except on the days when it was forbidden, he ate once a day, and then only a simple and quite sparing meal, after completing the day’s work.

He learned the first elements of letters when he was already nearly forty years old. With divine grace assisting him, he progressed so far that even among those thoroughly learned in grammar he was rightly regarded as admirable in explaining and understanding the meanings of the divine Scriptures. To make it clear that this was accomplished solely through the efficacy of divine grace, he devoted only the night hours to this study, since he never interrupted the execution of his daytime work on account of reading. He immediately tore down his paternal houses and built dwellings for the servants of God.

When the church he had built had been consecrated by Herbert, bishop of Lisieux, he cut his hair and, laying aside secular dress, received from the same pontiff the habit of sacred religion, having already proved himself a strong soldier of Christ through so many dangers. Two of his own men took up the yoke of the same order with him. Later, after being consecrated priest by the aforesaid prelate, he was placed in charge as abbot, with several more brothers already added to his leadership. Those whom he had received to govern he ruled very strictly, but according to the custom of the fathers who had gone before him.

You might see the abbot, once the office had been completed in the church, carrying seed on his neck and a rake or hoe in his hand, leading the way in agricultural work, while all the monks continued at rural labor until the end of the day. Some cleared the field of briars and thorns; others carried manure on their shoulders and spread it. Some hoed, others sowed; no one consumed bread in idleness. At the hour appointed for the office, all gathered in the church without exception. Their daily food was rye bread and herbs with water and salt. The water was nothing but muddy, since there was no spring within two miles.

His noble mother likewise devoted herself there to such service for God. After giving to God the estates she possessed, she performed the duty of a servant, washing the clothing of the servants of God and carrying out with the greatest care whatever menial work was assigned to her.

Then, after some time, he was warned in a vision that, having abandoned the solitary rural place, which entirely lacked suitable advantages, he should transfer his dwelling to a place belonging to him, which was called Bec from the stream flowing there, a mile from the castle called Brionne. This place lies within the Brionne forest, in a low valley enclosed on either side by wooded hills, convenient in every respect for human use. Because of the density of the woods and the refreshing stream, many wild animals gathered there. There were only three houses belonging to three mills, and very little habitable land.

After a fairly substantial church had been built and consecrated within a few years, he constructed a cloister with wooden columns and established the brothers there, according to the custom of the country, to remain there and go nowhere else. Various disputes, therefore, which often arose within, began to cause him much sorrow [Col. 0840C] and anxiety. For there was no one at all in the cloister to preside over their settlement, while the necessity of accumulating expenses compelled him to remain outside. Since he had often entreated God about this matter, divine mercy supplied him with a suitable helper, sufficient to support everything that had to be done [variant: was being done].

There was then a certain man born in Italy, whom the Latin world acknowledges with the highest love and honor, under the full weight of its debt, because he restored learning to its ancient condition: his name was Lanfranc. Greece herself, the teacher of the nations in liberal studies, willingly listened to and admired his pupils. Leaving his homeland, he came to Normandy with many scholars of great renown. He therefore visited Bec, which was nowhere considered a poorer or more wretched monastery. At that time the abbot happened to be occupied with building a furnace and was working with his own hands. Deeply revering and loving his humility of spirit and the dignity of his speech, Lanfranc became a monk there.

Thus he lived for three years in solitude, amid the scarcity of people, rejoicing that he was unknown there, a stranger to everyone except the very few with whom he sometimes spoke. When news of this event emerged, rumor spread it far and wide, and the most distinguished reputation of the man soon raised Bec and Abbot Herluin throughout the world. Clerics arrived, sons of dukes, the most famous teachers of Latin schools, powerful laymen, and men of high nobility [Col. 0841A]. Many, out of love for him, bestowed many lands on the same church. The place of Bec was immediately enriched with ornaments, possessions, and noble and honorable persons. Within, religion and learning greatly increased; without, the supply of everything necessary began to abound fully. Thus the domain of the monastery, which at its beginning had possessed only enough land for the buildings required, extended within a few years for miles.

Not long afterward, because of the multitude of inhabitants, what the Lord said through the prophet Isaiah happened there: “The place is too narrow for me; make room for me that I may dwell.” For since the multitude of brothers gathered there could no longer be contained by the spaciousness of the buildings, and since the site was proving harmful to the health of those living there [Col. 0841B], the venerable Lanfranc began urging Abbot Herluin to construct a larger monastery and its workshops. Herluin was terrified by the mere suggestion of so great an undertaking, greatly distrusting the strength of his failing age. When he refused in any way to agree, by divine will the presbytery of the monastery collapsed. At last he yielded, placing the most certain hope in God and trusting greatly in the help of his counselor, through whose work all good things came to him. He began a new monastery and workshops in a much healthier location—a very great and worthy work, to whose dignity many richer abbeys do not rise.

To begin this work, it was not his own resources, which were very small, but his greatest faith in God that strengthened his spirit. By gathering everything together he accumulated such resources that from the day [Col. 0841C] on which the foundations were first laid until the setting of the final stone, neither materials nor funds were lacking.

When three years had been completed, and only the basilica itself still remained unfinished, the venerable Lanfranc, the initiator of the work, was compelled by the petitions of both the Lord and the leading men of Normandy to become abbot of the church of Caen. Meanwhile William, duke of the Normans, seized the hereditary kingdom of England for himself and brought its rebellious power under whatever laws he wished by force of arms. Then he turned his mind toward improving the condition of the churches.

Therefore, at the counsel and request of Alexander, supreme pontiff of all Christendom, a man outstanding in life and learning, and with the most willing assent of all the nobles of the English kingdom and the Norman realm, King William chose the aforementioned teacher for this task, the advice he chiefly and exclusively accepted. He was brought to England by various inducements and assumed the episcopate of the church of Canterbury, which holds primacy over the transmarine islands.

Enriched by extensive lands and made wealthy with gold and silver, he fulfilled the command given in Exodus: “Honor your father and your mother, so that you may live long upon the earth.” In every way he showed kindness toward his spiritual father and mother, the Church. How great his fruitfulness afterward was in England is most fully attested by the ecclesiastical order, renewed everywhere.

The monastic order, which had utterly fallen into lay dissolution [Col. 0842A], was reformed according to the most approved discipline of monasteries. Clerics were restrained under the canonical rule; the people, freed from the vainness of barbarous rites, were instructed in a proper form of believing and living. The number of the noblest and best men, both clerics and laymen, gathered there from many parts of the world, reached a total of one hundred [variant: extended to a hundred].

The new church had not yet been consecrated, because it awaited consecration from the very man whose counsel had begun it and whose assistance had completed it; he was earnestly asking this of God. God, who had shown himself gracious to him in all other matters, granted his petition its desired fulfillment, satisfying his whole desire in this matter. For it was consecrated by the man he had desired with an honor far greater than he could have presumed.

Thus, on the tenth day before the Kalends of November, in the year 1077 from the Lord’s Incarnation, Lanfranc, revered by the whole holy Church and supreme pontiff of the transmarine peoples, arrived to complete by consecration the church which, inspired by God, he had begun, and in whose foundations he himself had laid the second stone with his own hand.

All the bishops of Normandy, the abbots, and other religious men assembled. The nobles of the kingdom were present. The king, occupied with other business, could not attend. Queen Matilda would gladly have been present had she not been detained by royal affairs. Nevertheless, she was present through a benefaction appropriate to her generosity. The heavenly King did not wish an earthly king to place the final hand upon the work of his grace, reserving entirely for himself the joy of its completion. Within sixteen years, at the sole expense of the poor, he completed the monastery with all its workshops—a beautiful and very great work.

The most distinguished counts of the kingdom of France were also present, along with many other nobles of that same kingdom, clerics, and monks from all the neighboring provinces.

After some time had passed following the dedication, the venerable Father Herluin began to be entirely deprived of the use of his limbs, and, long before the annual return of that very day, obtained what he had desired. For in the following August, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of September, a Sunday, he became completely bedridden. After the brothers had celebrated Vespers, when the day and the daytime office had ended [Col. 0842D], he completed the course of human life in a happy passage. It was during the approaching night, which dawned into Sunday, on the seventh day before the Kalends of September.

A monument was made for him in the chapter house, an eternal memorial of his good deeds for his sons. When those who intend to speak of spiritual pursuits gather together in the proper manner, the memory is presented of the man who, from a tyrant became religious, from one thoroughly secular became wholly spiritual, and was the first founder and abbot of that place and order.

## Epitaph

This stone covers him who produced  
all the buildings you see around,  
a monk formerly a layman.

After three times eleven years,  
and three and four, he did not know letters;  
afterward he died learned.

He passed four times eleven years  
in the monastic life,  
properly dividing his days in half.

When Phoebus brought forth his ninth rising  
under Virgo,  
he closed his day and week  
by departing this life.

He was Herluin, if anyone asks his name;  
may God grant him with the saints  
whatever belongs to them.

## Another

Looking upon this tomb, learn from the inscription  
who lies buried here.  
To know who he was is the road of virtue.

When here he had reached four times ten years of life,  
he despised the things that had belonged to the world  
through love of God.

Thus changing his condition,  
from a soldier of the world he suddenly became  
a soldier of Christ, a monk formerly a layman.

From then on, joining to himself communities of brothers  
according to the custom of the fathers,  
he ruled and nourished them  
with the care by which he taught them.

All the many buildings you see here  
he alone founded,  
not so much through wealth  
as through the merits of faith.

The Scriptures he had not learned as a boy  
he afterward knew,  
so learned that scarcely could the unlearned  
follow him.

Death’s cruelty carried him away from us  
as we wept,  
on the fifteenth day of August.

Father Herluin, thus you joyfully ascend  
to the heavenly realms,  
for on the basis of your merits  
we may believe this of you.

The same venerable Father died on the seventh day before the Kalends of September, in the eighty-fourth year of his age and the forty-fourth of his monastic life. A few days later, Anselm, who was then prior of the same place, was elected abbot in his stead. How great his religion and how great his wisdom were, anyone who reads the book written about his life will easily discover.

That revered man also wrote several works worthy of remembrance, which we have taken care to append below. While he was still prior at the monastery of Bec, he wrote three treatises: the first, *On Truth*; the second, *On the Freedom of Choice*; the third, *On the Fall of the Devil*. He also wrote a fourth, which he entitled *On the Grammarian*. In it he responds to a pupil whom he introduces as debating with him, and proposes and resolves many dialectical questions.

He also composed a fifth little book, which he called the *Monologion*. In it he alone speaks, speaking with himself; silently, by every rational method, he seeks and discovers, and proves and establishes by invincible reasoning what true faith thinks about God, namely that it is so and cannot be otherwise.

He also composed a sixth book, small indeed, but great in the weight of its propositions and most subtle contemplation, which he called the *Proflogion* [printed form; commonly known as the *Proslogion*]. [Col. 0843D] In that work he addresses either himself or God.

He also wrote a seventh book of letters to various people, responding to their various affairs or instructing them to attend to matters that concerned him. He produced an eighth, *On the Incarnation of the Word*. This work, written in epistolary style, he dedicated and sent to Urban, supreme pontiff of the holy Roman Church.

He published a ninth book, which he called *Why God Became Man*; a tenth, *On the Virgin’s Conception*; and an eleventh, *Prayers to Various Saints*, which many call *Meditations*. In these, it readily appears to readers how great a sweetness of heavenly things had filled his mind.

The twelfth, and final, treatise of his was *On the Procession of the Holy Spirit*. For at the council of Bari he had refuted the Greeks, who denied that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Son. Taking up this subject, he composed the book at the request of Hildebert, bishop of Le Mans.

And since we have said something about this venerable man, we gladly summarize the course of his life.

Born of noble parents in the city of Aosta, which borders Burgundy and Italy, he pursued literary studies in various places and came to Normandy. At the monastery of Bec, where at that time the great Lanfranc mentioned above held the office of prior, Anselm became a monk of Bec in the twenty-seventh year of his age, at Lanfranc’s urging and counsel, together with other fellow students whom Lanfranc instructed in both divine and secular letters.

There he lived as a cloistered monk without ecclesiastical office for three years; then he was prior for fifteen years after the aforementioned Lanfranc, archbishop of Canterbury, of blessed memory. Thereafter he was abbot for fifteen years, following the venerable Herluin, of pious memory, the first abbot of that place. From there he was raised to the archbishopric of Canterbury after the revered Lanfranc, and governed it for sixteen years.

In the seventeenth year of his archbishopric, the forty-ninth of his monastic life, and the seventy-sixth of his age, he departed from the world on the eleventh day before the Kalends of May, on the Wednesday before the Lord’s Supper. That year his final Easter occurred, namely on the seventh day before the Kalends of May.

Having said these things in anticipation about the founder of the monastery of Bec, naming with reverence the venerable Herluin and his successor, the renowned man Anselm, in divine matters, let us return to the sequence of the deeds of the dukes [Col. 0844C] of Normandy, from which we had digressed briefly.

## CHAPTER X. Of the fleet which Duke Robert arranged to send to England in aid of his kinsmen Edward and Alfred, the sons of King Æthelred

At the time when Æthelred, king of the English, as we related above, was driven from his kingdom by Sweyn, king of the Danes, and fled to Normandy, he left two sons, Edward and Alfred, with their maternal uncle Richard to be raised. They had been brought up within the court of the Norman dukes, and the duke treated them with such honor that, as though they were his brothers, he adopted them to himself in the closest bond of love.

Having long pitied their exile, he sent ambassadors and instructed King Cnut that, now fully satisfied with their expulsion, he should spare them and, even at that late hour, return their own possessions to them for the sake of his love for them. But Cnut did not yield to his salutary advice. He sent the ambassadors back with their business unfinished and carrying no joyful message.

Then the duke, inflamed with the blush of intense fury, summoned the leading men of his duchy and ordered a great fleet of ships to be built with haste. He gathered it from every part of the Norman coast and, within a short time, carefully equipped it with anchors, weapons, and the strongest men. He caused it to lie at Fécamp on the shore of the sea.

Then, when the signal had been given and the sails spread high, they were driven by a violent storm toward the island called Jersey and, amid great danger at sea, were cast back home [Col. 0845A]. I think this happened by God’s agency on behalf of King Edward, whom he intended to reign in the future without bloodshed.

While they were detained there for a long time because an adverse wind continued to blow, the duke was tormented by incredible sorrow and a fierce temper. At last, seeing that he could in no way cross the sea, they turned the prows of the ships and, rounding the shoreline, reached the mount of Saint Michael as quickly as possible.

## CHAPTER XI. That he sent part of the same fleet to afflict Brittany, and concerning the restoration of peace between him and Alan, count of Brittany

Duke Robert entrusted part of the fleet to Rabello, a most valiant soldier, and sent it to afflict Brittany with fires and plunder. He himself, having gathered a cavalry army, prepared to attack it from the other side.

Alan, therefore, realizing that grave danger threatened him from both directions, sent an embassy and urgently summoned to himself Robert, their maternal uncle, namely the archbishop of the Normans. When he had recounted to the archbishop Brittany’s fatal destruction and the duke’s fierce expedition being prepared against him, the prelate pledged his faith, took him under his protection, and brought him to the mount of Saint Michael at Tombelaine, where he obtained mercy for him from the duke, who was preparing to attack him.

Soon, with Christ’s favor, their excessively rigid hearts were brought to peace, so that, every movement of dissension being calmed, serene harmony united them and made Alan, bound by sworn fidelity in the duke’s service, wholly submissive as a suppliant [Col. 0845C]. After this, the duke sent ambassadors and ordered the sailors to withdraw from their attack on Brittany.

## CHAPTER XII. That Cnut, king of the English, offered through his ambassadors half the kingdom of England to Edward and Alfred out of fear of Robert, duke of the Normans; and that the same duke, setting out for Jerusalem, placed his five-year-old son William in charge of the duchy of Normandy

When these matters had been fully settled, behold, ambassadors sent to Duke Robert by King Cnut arrived, announcing that he wished to return half the kingdom of England to the sons of King Æthelred, with peace secured during his lifetime, because he was being heavily afflicted by bodily illness.

For this reason the duke interrupted his naval expedition and postponed what he had begun, first wishing to return from Jerusalem, which he had long desired with the greatest devotion. Considering that this life is wasteful and fleeting, and turning over in a pious and blessed heart the Lord’s words addressed to the rich—“Woe to you who have your consolation”—he chose to become a poor man of Christ rather than be burned in the fires of Gehenna.

He therefore summoned Robert the archbishop together with the leading men of his duchy and disclosed to them that he wished to undertake a pilgrimage to Jerusalem. All were greatly astonished by these words, and many feared that in his absence the country would be thrown into confusion.

Presenting to them his son William, whom he had fathered as his only child at Falaise, he earnestly demanded that they choose him as their lord in his place and appoint him leader of his military forces. Although the boy was held in the most tender stage of childhood, they were all greatly heartened by the prospect of his succession. In accordance with the duke’s decision, they immediately acclaimed him their prince and lord with willing enthusiasm and pledged him fidelity by oaths not to be violated.

After Duke Robert had completed these matters according to his wish, he entrusted his son, until he reached lawful age, to faithful and prudent guardians and advisers. Having appropriately arranged the affairs necessary for governing the country, he bade everyone a pious farewell and undertook that most holy pilgrimage with his noble retinue.

What tongue or speech could describe the alms he distributed daily to the needy? Or what widow, orphan, or impoverished person existed who was not assisted at his expense? At last, having completed the journey, he reached the venerable tomb in which the most holy body of the heavenly King had lain. Who among men could recount how many times over eight days he washed it with streams of tears, or with how many gifts of gold he adorned it?

## CHAPTER XIII. That the same Duke Robert, returning from Jerusalem, died in Christ at the city of Nicaea

[Col. 0846C]

Thereafter the duke, pious and beloved of God, unwillingly turned back toward the city of Nicaea after worshiping Christ with sighs born of inward sobbing and visiting the holy places. At Nicaea, seized by bodily illness, he sought the way of all humankind and, in the year 1035 from the Lord’s Incarnation, died at the command of the divine summons, on the sixth day before the Nones of July, with the angels rejoicing.

I do not consider it unworthy to believe and record with the pen that it pleased the Ruler of the eternal heavenly Jerusalem—whose burial place he had also venerated on earth—to take him, amid the labor of this life, into fellowship with everlasting glory, lest his blessed soul, already made radiant by the splendor of so many good works, should gather stains after becoming entangled in worldly affairs.

His followers also buried him in the basilica of Saint Mary, within the walls of the city of Nicaea; our Lord Jesus Christ reigning in the glory of the Father’s majesty, with the Holy Spirit coequal in all ages. Amen.

# Seventh Book of the History of the Normans. Of Duke William, who subdued England by arms

[Col. 0847]

## Chapter I. What hardships William endured as a boy at the beginning of his rule, through the perversity of certain men

[Col. 0847A]

Having related in order the deeds of the great Duke Robert and made them known to attentive ears through diligent investigation, it seems fitting that the narrative should turn to his son William, setting down for posterity by what sweat of labor he escaped the snares of his enemies and manfully thrust their beastly necks beneath his feet. For in many pages of Scripture it is found that the house of a son is overthrown by the wickedness of an iniquitous father, whereas, conversely, it is more firmly strengthened by the merit of a good one. Thus Christ established the house of Duke Robert, after he had rejected secular pomp, while rewarding him with an everlasting palm and afterwards raising up his son William to a royal throne when his enemies had been defeated.

Nevertheless, it is pleasing to make known to future generations by what triumphs of victory he became illustrious in the duchy, as the order of matters most truthfully ascertained shall dictate, lest deeds that shone gloriously in the time of our age be concealed through idle negligence. This duke, deprived of his father in his boyhood years, was trained toward the growth of liberal conduct by the prudent care of guardians. During his early youth, many Normans who had strayed from fidelity to him raised strongholds in various places and built for themselves very secure fortifications. Trusting boldly in their protection, diverse commotions immediately arose among them, seditions were stirred up, and cruel burnings of the land were perpetrated everywhere. In so great a storm of dissensions Mars raged fiercely, and no small band of warriors was vainly consumed.

## Chapter II. Of the war between Tustin of Bastenborc and Walchelin of Ferrières, and of the death of Osbern, son of Herfast

Hugh of Montfort, son of Tustin, fought with Walchelin of Ferrières, and in that conflict both were killed. Moreover, the monstrous fury of certain men burst forth and prevailed excessively to the injury of the country. Indeed Count Gilbert of Eu, son of Count Geoffrey, shrewd and strong, guardian of the boy William, yet his lord, was killed one morning while riding and speaking with his godfather Wascelin of Pont-Erchenfray, suspecting no evil, together with Fulco, son of Geroie. This evil was done at the treacherous instigation of Ralph of Wacy, son of Archbishop Robert, by the cruel hands of Odo the Fat and the bold Robert, son of Geroie. Then Turold, tutor of the young duke, was killed by the faithless deserters of the country.

[Col. 0848A] Osbern also, chief steward of the household, son of Herfast, brother of Countess Gunnor, was one night, while sleeping securely with the duke himself in the duke’s chamber in the valley of Rouen, suddenly slaughtered in his place by William, son of Roger of Montgomery. For Roger was then in exile among the Parisians because of his treachery, and his five sons—Hugh and Robert, Roger and William, and Gilbert—were zealously engaged in dreadful crimes in Normandy. But William, for the crime described above which he committed, received his deserved recompense from God not long afterwards. Barno of Glos, Osbern’s steward, wishing to avenge the unjust death of his lord, gathered armed fighters one night, came to the house where William and his accomplices were sleeping, and immediately slaughtered them all together, as they deserved.

## Chapter III. How Roger of Beaumont, son of Humphrey of the Vieilles, overcame Roger of Tosny at his father’s command

Roger of Tosny, of the line of Malahulc, who had been the paternal uncle of Duke Rollo and had vigorously acquired Normandy with him by crushing the Franks, was a powerful and proud man and standard-bearer of all Normandy. This man had set out while Duke Robert was abroad in Spain, where many valiant deeds had been performed against the pagans through him. But after some time he returned to his own country. Learning that the boy William had succeeded his father in the duchy, he was greatly indignant and proudly scorned to serve him, saying that a bastard ought not to rule over him and the other Normans. For William had been born of Duke Robert’s concubine, named Herleva [Herlotta], daughter of Fulbert, the duke’s chamberlain; and, as a bastard, he was despised by native nobles, especially those born of the lineage of the Richards.

Yet after the duke who had gone to Jerusalem died, a certain worthy knight, Herluin, married Herleva, and by her begot two sons, Odo and Robert, who later attained conspicuous eminence. Roger, therefore, relying on a multitude of helpers, dared to rebel against the young duke. He openly despised all his neighbors and devastated their lands, especially those of Humphrey of the Vieilles, with plundering and fire. Unwilling to endure this any longer, Humphrey sent his son Roger of Beaumont against him with his household. Roger of Tosny rashly despised him and, fearing nothing, boldly engaged him in battle; but there he was killed with his two sons, Helbert and Elinant, and left victory to his enemies.

[Col. 0849A] There Robert of Grantmesnil received a mortal wound, from which he died three weeks later, on the fourth day before the Kalends of July. Before his death, moreover, he divided his land equally between his two sons Hugh and Robert, and entrusted to them his youngest son Ernald, that they should treat him well as a brother until he reached maturity.

## Chapter IV. That the same Roger built the abbey at Préaux and married Adeline, daughter of Count Waleran of Meulan

Roger of Beaumont, having overcome his adversaries, gave thanks to God who grants victory, and throughout his life strove to labor at good works. Among these he built a monastic community on his estate at Préaux, and always remained faithful to Duke William against all men. Therefore he became more eminent than all his forefathers and ancestors. For he married Adeline, daughter of Count Waleran of Meulan, by whom he begot two sons, Robert and Henry, later counts of great power. Robert, indeed, flourished as count of Meulan for more than twenty-seven years after his maternal uncle Hugh; and Henry received from King William in England the earldom of Warwick.

After the aforesaid slaughter, in which Roger and Robert of Grantmesnil and very many others fell, Count Richard of Évreux, son of Archbishop Robert, took Roger of Tosny’s wife in marriage and begot by her William, who now rules the people of Évreux. His brother William joined to himself Hadvise, daughter of Geroie, the widow of Robert of Grantmesnil. Meanwhile Duke William, with God’s favor, grew in age and strength and advanced in judgment and strength of character. Observing how greatly the fury of his own people had trampled Normandy, he gathered manly strength in his boyish breast and strove to draw his father’s magnates to love for himself, instructing them by entreaties and commands not to act without discipline. On the advice of his elders he chose Ralph of Wacy as his guardian and made him commander of the Norman forces.

[Col. 0849D] Certain of the magnates, who love God and justice, willingly obey the duke as their lord, keep faith with him, and faithfully strive to subdue rebels to him. But the sons of discord, who delight in dissensions and endeavor to afflict those wishing to live innocently, seeing that by themselves they could not harm the simple folk as much as they wished, devised how they might with shameless face procure the overthrow of the country. They therefore approached King Henry of France and scattered his firebrands throughout the Norman borders in every direction. I would name them in writing if I did not wish to avoid their implacable hatred. Yet, to speak in the ear of those standing around you, they were none other than those who profess themselves most faithful and whom the duke has now heaped with greater honors.

## Chapter V. That King Henry of France burned the castle of Tillières, which the Normans had surrendered to him for peace, and also Argentan

[Col. 0850A]

Driven to fury by the senseless instigation of the traitors, King Henry, having forgotten the benefit once bestowed on him by Duke Robert, decided that he would in no way be reconciled with him so long as he saw the fortress of Tegularias remaining in its former condition. The Northmen, standing firm in loyalty and wishing to avert the king’s intrigues for the safety of the boy, resolved to do what they afterward regretted. Gilbert, surnamed Crispin, to whom Duke Robert had formerly entrusted the fortress, as soon as he recognized the extremely unwelcome decision, rejected their attempt and immediately shut himself inside it with a strong force of armed men to resist them. The king, observing that access to the stronghold was being denied him, gathered together armies of both Franks and Northmen and hastily surrounded it with a siege. What more need be said? At last Gilbert, overcome by the duke’s entreaties, sorrowfully surrendered the fortress, which he saw immediately burned with the greatest anguish of heart before everyone’s eyes. When the king had carried out these acts according to his desire, he withdrew from the place. But not long afterward he approached the count of Exmes and burned Argentom, the duke’s town, with devouring flames; and thus laden with booty, he abandoned those districts. Then, returning by the route on which he had come, he reached the castle of Tegularias and invalidated the oaths that he had sworn to the duke—that none of his men should restore it for four years. For he rebuilt it [Col. 0850C] with haste, fortified it most abundantly with soldiers and provisions, and then, since he had already satisfied his wishes, departed joyfully.

## CHAPTER VI. How Tursten Guz wished to hold the castle of Falaise against Duke William but could not; and concerning Richard, his son
