Tursten, surnamed Guz, son of Ausfrid the Dane, who was then governor of Exmes, perceived that the young duke had yielded somewhat to the king and was already, as though defeated, enduring in some measure the oppression of the royal hand. Inflamed by the zeal of disloyalty, he hired royal soldiers for pay and took them as accomplices to fortify the castle of Falaise, so that it would not serve the duke from there. As soon as the duke learned of this evil-minded attempt, [Col. 0850D] he gathered forces of Northmen from every direction and hastily besieged the castle. At that time Ralph of Wace was commander of the army and assisted his duke with all his strength. When the soldiers had been roused, they immediately fought with such great courage that they brought down part of the wall in an instant. And if night had not separated the combatants, they would undoubtedly have completed entirely the deed they most ardently desired. Tursten, realizing that he could not endure such great enemy forces any longer, asked the duke for permission to withdraw; and so, fleeing from his homeland as an exile, he departed. After this, Richard, Tursten’s son, served the duke most faithfully and thereby reconciled his father to the duke; he himself also acquired much greater possessions than his father had lost.

## CHAPTER VII. How Malger, son of the second Richard by his second wife Popia [Papia], succeeded Archbishop Robert; and concerning William of Arques

[Col. 0851A]

When Robert, archbishop of Rouen, died, Malger, brother of Duke Robert, succeeded him. For Richard Gunnor’s son, after Judith’s death, took another wife named Popia, by whom he fathered two sons, namely Malger, the archbishop, and William of Arques. This William, while the duke was already flourishing in adolescence, received from him the county of Talou, on the understanding that he should remain faithful to him in return for the benefaction. Raised up by the nobility of his lineage, he founded the castle of Arques on the summit of the mountain itself. Then, having assumed tyrannical power and supported by royal aid, he dared to lift his heel against the duke. The duke, seeking to draw him away from his madness, ordered him through envoys to come and render him service. But he treated this embassy with contempt, and with great confidence fortified and armed himself to resist. The duke, having summoned the strength of the Northmen, came against him as quickly as possible to subdue his pride; he raised siegeworks at the foot of the mountain, established a castle there, made it impregnable through the strength of brave men, and, departing, left it supplied with provisions. This action did not remain hidden from King Henry. The king therefore gathered forces and came with the greatest haste to fortify the upper town, ordering his army to pitch camp at Saint-Albino. When the duke’s soldiers learned of his arrival, [Col. 0851C] they sent some of their own men to see whether they might perhaps draw certain enemies away from the royal assembly and catch them unawares while they remained in hiding. When they had reached the place, they drew away a considerable part of the army and led them into an ambush while pretending to flee. Immediately, however, those who had seemed to flee turned their faces and began to strike them fiercely, so that in this encounter Count Ingelrann of Abbeville was killed after being pierced with many wounds, while Hugh, surnamed Bardulf, was captured together with many others. When the king learned this, he sent provisions into the castle for which he had come, and, grieving over the loss of his soldiers and the disgrace, withdrew. Not long afterward William, afflicted by hunger, unwillingly surrendered the castle with his men and himself departed into exile from his native land. Finally, with his wife—namely, the sister [Col. 0851D] of Guy, count of Ponthieu—he sought Eustace, count of Boulogne, and, receiving food and clothing in his household, remained an exile until his death.

## CHAPTER VIII. How, when King Cnut of the English died, his son Harold succeeded him; and concerning Edward, still an exile

At that same time Cnut, king of the English, died, and his son Harold succeeded him, born of a concubine named Ælfgifu. When Edward heard of the death he had long desired, he was still living with the duke; he immediately crossed the sea with forty ships full of soldiers and landed at Southampton. There he encountered an innumerable multitude of Englishmen awaiting him for his destruction. Engaging them at once, he quickly sent a considerable number of them to Orcus. Remaining victorious, he returned with his men to the ships. Seeing that he could not obtain the kingdom of the English without a very large number of soldiers, he turned the prows of his ships and returned to Normandy with very great booty.

## CHAPTER IX. Concerning the betrayal of Alfred, Edward’s brother, by Count Godwin; and how Hardecnut, son of Emma, Edward’s mother, succeeded his brother Harold, and how Edward succeeded Hardecnut and married Edith, Godwin’s daughter

Meanwhile his brother Alfred gathered a considerable number of soldiers, sought the port of Wissant, crossed from there, and came to Canterbury. Advancing inland into the kingdom, he met Count Godwin. The count received him under his protection, but that same night played the part of the traitor Judas toward him. For, after exchanging the kiss of peace and sharing food with him, in the middle of the dead of night he had him sent, with his hands bound behind his back, to King Harold at London, together with some of his men. He scattered Alfred’s soldiers partly throughout the English region and partly killed them disgracefully. When Harold saw Alfred, he immediately ordered his companions to be beheaded and Alfred himself to be led to Ely and deprived of his eyes. Thus the noble and excellent man Alfred died, unjustly killed. Harold himself died not long afterward, and was succeeded by his brother Hardecnut, who had come from Denmark and was born of Emma, Edward’s [Col. 0852C] mother. After he had been established for a short time at the height of the kingdom, he recalled his brother Edward from Normandy and made him live with him. But after existing for not quite two years, he departed from human life and left Edward heir to the entire kingdom.

At that time the fierce contriver of deceit, Godwin, was the most powerful count in England and held a large part of the kingdom of the English by force. He had claimed it either through the nobility of his ancestors or by violence or fraud. Edward, therefore, fearing that he might be harmed by so powerful a man or by his customary deceit, and acting on the advice of the Northmen, whose faithful support strengthened him, graciously forgave him for the unworthy destruction of his brother Alfred. And so that firm affection might continually remain between them, he took his daughter Edith as his wife in name only. For in truth, as they say, both preserved perpetual virginity. Edward was, indeed, a good man: gentle and humble, pleasant and patient, merciful, the protector of the poor, and the legitimate restorer of English laws. Many times he saw divine mysteries and uttered prophecies that were afterward confirmed by the outcome of events; and he ruled the kingdom of the English successfully for nearly twenty-three years.

## CHAPTER X. Concerning the cruelty of William Talvas and William, son of Geroy, who became a monk of Bec

William, surnamed Talvas, after the head of his brother Robert had been crushed in prison with axes, obtained all his father’s estate through the assistance of his own men, and especially of William, son of Geroy. Yet he by no means turned his steps away from the treachery of his ancestors. He took in marriage Hildeburg, daughter of a certain most noble man named Arnulf, and by her afterward fathered Arnulf and Mabilia, the mother of a most cruel offspring. But because the woman was well-mannered and ardently loved God, she did not consent to her husband’s wicked factions. For this reason he hated her intensely. Finally, one morning, while she was going to church to pray to God, he had her suddenly strangled on the road by two of his parasites. Then he betrothed to himself the daughter of Ralph, viscount of Bellême, and invited many neighboring nobles to the wedding. Among them he summoned William, Geroy’s son, a man of exceptional courage. [Col. 0853B] His brother Ralph, surnamed the Clerk because he was abundantly learned, and Mala-corona because, while devoted to military exercises, he poorly maintained the dignity of the clerical state, foreseeing from the omen that grave misfortune threatened him, warned his brother not to attend in any way the foul, deadly marriage of a bigamist. William, however, disregarding Ralph’s dissuasion, came unarmed to Alençon with twelve soldiers. Talvas, finding him there suspecting no evil but rather, as is customary, rejoicing at the wedding of his friend, immediately seized him without cause as though he were a wicked traitor and ordered his retainers to guard him carefully. Later he went hunting with his wedding guests. His attendants, whom he had secretly ordered to do this, led William outside; and while all who witnessed it mourned—alas, what grief!—they deprived him of his eyes and disfigured him by cutting off the tips of his nose and ears. When this crime became known, many grieved and were inflamed with anger against Talvas and attempted to avenge such wickedness. After three years, William Geroy’s son approached the venerable Abbot Herluin and became a monk in the monastery of Bec, which the aforesaid father was then building in honor of holy Mary, Mother of God.

## CHAPTER XI. How Duke Richard gave the two districts Monasteriolum and Escalfou to Geroy, who married Gisla, daughter of Tursten of Montfort

This Geroy, whose descendants we are discussing, is said to have sprung from a noble lineage of Franks and Britons. He came with William of Belesme to the court of Duke Richard, by whose gift he obtained two districts in Normandy, Monasteriolum and Escalfou. While he was seeking the duke, he lodged in the house of Tursten of Montfort. There, happening to see his daughter Gisla at table, he fell in love with her; he requested her from her distinguished parents and obtained her. In time she bore him seven sons and four daughters, whose names are these: Ernald and Fulk, who perished with Count Gilbert; William and Ralph (Mala-corona); Robert, Hugh, and Geroy; Heremburg, Emma, Adelaide, and Hadwisa. From these a military company of sons and grandsons was propagated, one that appeared an object of overwhelming terror to the barbarians in England, Apulia, Thrace, and Syria. After William Talvas, as we said above, had so savagely dishonored William—who was superior in age and judgment among the descendants of Geroy—through envy, Robert and Ralph, excellent soldiers, rose up manfully with their brothers and kinsmen and sought to avenge their brother’s grievous injury. They devastated all Talvas’s land with plundering and fires; they came armed without resistance as far as the gates of his fortifications and boldly challenged him to come out and fight at close quarters. But because he was timid and possessed no strength in warfare, he did not dare to engage the provoking enemies in the field. Thus he was often mocked by the descendants of Geroy.

## CHAPTER XII. Concerning Arnulf, son of William Talvas, and his brother Oliver, a monk of Bec

[Col. 0854B]

At last, when his son Arnulf observed these things, he rebelled with the consent of his nobles against his father, who was hateful to everyone. He disgracefully expelled him from his fortifications and compelled him to wander miserably in exile until his death. He seized his paternal possession but did not avoid wickedness; therefore he deserved to perish by a sorrowful end. For one day he went out to plunder with his retainers and, among other things, seized a pig belonging to a nun. She followed him lamenting and earnestly begged that the little pig she had raised might be returned to her for God’s sake. Arnulf disregarded her pleas, ordered the pig slaughtered and prepared for eating by the cook, and, serving pieces to his own belly, ate from it much too late. But he did not go unpunished. For that same night he was strangled in his bed. Some people’s account, moreover, asserts that he was killed by his own brother Oliver. We, however, not only do not affirm such a great crime of such a man, but utterly refuse to believe it. The aforesaid Oliver afterward lived honorably for a long time in military service and, having grown old, left the world by God’s will. Then, under Lord Anselm, at that time abbot and now archbishop of Canterbury, he piously received the monastic habit in the monastery of Bec, and under Lord William, the abbot, wore it there laudably for many years.

## CHAPTER XIII. How, after Arnulf’s death, his uncle Ivo, bishop of Sées, possessed his land by hereditary right

[Col. 0854D]

Finally, after Arnulf had been wickedly killed, as we related above, his uncle Ivo, bishop of Sées, received the castle of Belesme and whatever belonged to it by right; and he held it lawfully for as long as he lived, having made peace with the descendants of Geroy and his other neighbors. He was indeed shrewd, handsome, and affable, very fond of joking, and desirous of peaceful tranquility. But the treachery of the wicked does not cease to disturb the rest of the good. Accordingly, in the time of Bishop Ivo, Richard, Robert, and Avesgot, sons of William surnamed Sorengus, took a band of criminals as their accomplices and ravaged without reverence the entire country around Sées. Finally, they invaded the church of Saint Gervase [Col. 0855A] and stationed a band of plunderers there. Thus they made a den of thieves and a stable for horses out of a house of prayer. The aged and religious bishop Azo of that city had destroyed the walls and, from the stones of the demolished wall, built a church to Saint Gervase the martyr, where the episcopal seat had long afterward been established. When the venerable Ivo saw the Sorengs raging so wildly in his days that they did not hesitate to make a thieves’ pit and a brothel for prostitutes in God’s temple, he grieved intensely, touched by noble anger, and devoted all his strength to the liberation of God’s church. Once, therefore, while returning from Duke William’s court and passing through the district of Exmes, he brought Hugh of Grandmesnil and other barons with their troops and had the Sorengs vigorously attacked in the monastery tower. [Col. 0855B] But they resisted boldly and, fighting for themselves, wounded many with hurled weapons. When the bishop saw this, he ordered the neighboring houses to be set on fire. The parishioners immediately obeyed the bishop’s orders. The fire, fanned by the wind, ran to the church, invaded it, and consumed it, while severely tormenting the impious men raging within. At last, when the Sorengs saw that they could not endure the violence of the flames, they seized their weapons and fled from there in disgrace.

## CHAPTER XIV. Concerning the sons of William Sorengus—Richard, Robert, and Avesgot—and how they died a fitting death

The just and merciful God took the desecration of his church hard and did not delay imposing the deserved punishment upon its violators. For the three brothers who had led the aforesaid invasion were not long afterward killed by God’s just judgment, while they were devoting themselves above all to brigandage and plunder, without confession and without the saving viaticum.

Richard, the firstborn, was sleeping securely at night in a poor hut beside a certain pond. Immediately a powerful knight named Richard of Saint-Scholastica, whose land he had devastated, surrounded the little house with his household. Sorengus, awakened, came out of the hut and, fleeing, tried to leap into a stream. But a peasant whom he had previously tortured in chains got ahead of him; crushing his head with an axe, he immediately killed him there. Then [Col. 0855D] his brother Robert plundered booty with his men one day around Séez, and while returning was wounded by peasants pursuing him and died immediately. Finally, Avesgot entered Cambremer against Albert, son of Girard Fleitel, and began to rage there with military fury; but when a spear was thrown down from above, he was struck in the head and soon perished.

Behold, in these men we have truly seen fulfilled what we have heard: “If anyone violates the temple of God, God will destroy him.” Let plunderers and church-breakers, having learned of the destruction of their like, beware lest, while committing similar deeds, they at last perish by a similar punishment. And if untroubled prosperity accompanies them for a little while, let them not boast securely on that account. They ought certainly to know that the joy of the world passes away like smoke after a short time and acquires lasting sorrow, or, as a certain excellent versifier says in his poem while rebuking the wicked:

> You rejoice evilly, because at last you will receive  
> The fruit of wickedness: darkness, fires, and grief.  
> For God, a pious giver yet also a just avenger,  
> Protects what is his and punishes what is hostile.

When the sons of discord had been overthrown, as stated above, the simple people around Sées were allowed to breathe somewhat in peace. The noble Bishop Ivo strove to roof the church and rededicated it on 2 January. But because the walls had been damaged by the force of the flames, they collapsed that same year before Lent.

## CHAPTER XV. Concerning the council held by Pope Leo at Reims and his rebuke of Ivo, bishop of Sées, on account of the burned church of Saint Gervase

[Col. 0856B]

At that time holy Pope Leo came to Gaul, consecrated the church of Saint Remigius, archbishop of Reims, and transferred his body to the church newly dedicated. Then the same pope held a great council at Reims and severely rebuked negligent bishops and abbots. Among them, as they say, he said to Ivo, because of the burning of the church: “What have you done, traitor? By what law ought you to be condemned, since you dared to burn your own mother?” Ivo, eloquent in speech, openly confessed that he had indeed done wrong, but said that he had been gravely compelled to commit that crime lest worse things be done by criminals against the sons of the Church. Then he accepted penance according to the command of the prudent pope [Col. 0856C] and applied himself to restoring the church of Saint Gervase. Accordingly, he traveled to Apulia and from there to Constantinople, and collected a great deal of money from his wealthy relatives and friends together. By the emperor’s gift, he brought back a precious gift from the wood of the Lord’s Cross. Returning to Sées, he began to build a church so large that his successors Robert, Girard, and Serlo were unable to complete it for forty years.

## CHAPTER XVI. How William Talvas, brother of Bishop Ivo, gave his daughter Mabilia, together with her land, to Roger of Montgomery

Meanwhile, after William Talvas had been expelled from his land by his son, as we related above, [Col. 0856D] he wandered for a long time, miserable and despised by everyone, through other men’s houses. At last he sought Roger of Montgomery and freely offered him his daughter, named Mabilia; he also granted him all the honor that he himself had lost through his wickedness and indolence. Roger, who was strong, upright, and mature in counsel, saw that this arrangement would benefit him and agreed to everything. He received the wandering man into his house and lawfully joined his daughter to himself in marriage.

The woman mentioned above was small in body, very talkative, quite ready for evil, clever and witty, and excessively cruel and bold. In time she bore five sons and four daughters, whose names are these: Robert and Hugh, Roger the Poitevin, Philip and Arnulf; [Col. 0857A] Emma, Matilda, Mabilia, and Sibyl. These daughters surpassed their brothers in character. For they were generous and honorable, affable toward the poor and monks and other servants of God. Their brothers, however, were savage and greedy, fierce oppressors of the needy. How crafty, military, or treacherous they were, or how far they rose above their neighbors and equals, and how they again fell beneath them because of their crimes, it is not ours to relate here, since we have resolved to disclose the deeds of the great Duke William. Therefore, leaving them aside, let the pen now return to the foregoing sequence of the narrative.

## CHAPTER XVII. How, after Hugh, bishop of Bayeux, died, Duke William appointed his uterine brother Odo in his place; and concerning the battle at Val-es-Dunes

[Col. 0857B]

The duke, now flourishing like spring in the most delightful vigor of youth, began wholeheartedly to embrace the worship of God, to remove the company of the ignorant from himself, and to make use of the counsels of the wise. He became powerful in military affairs and strong in worldly prudence. Around this time Hugh, son of Count Ralph, bishop of Bayeux, died, and the duke entrusted the aforesaid bishopric to his brother Odo. After the aforesaid Odo had been consecrated as bishop, he enlarged the episcopal church in honor of holy Mary, Mother of God, making it new, and, having increased the number of skilled clerics, wonderfully enriched it with many ornaments. He himself lived in the episcopate for nearly fifty years.

As the duke daily increased in the advantages of many virtues, he encountered a cruel companion, namely Guy, son of Rainald, count of Burgundy, who had been raised with him from childhood and to whom he had once granted the castle of Briouze as a gift intended to bind his loyalty more firmly. For, ensnared by the arrogance of pride, Guy began, like Absalom, to turn many nobles away from the duke’s loyalty and entangle them in the abyss of his treachery. He even attached Nigel, governor of Coutances, to this conspiracy and drove him, together with many others, entirely away from the service that he owed the excellent prince under the obligation of oaths.

The most prudent duke, therefore, considering that he was being so greatly deserted by his own men and that they were continually being strengthened by the protection of their dependents, feared that he might be driven from the height of the comital dignity and that a rival might be appointed in his place. Compelled by necessity, he sought King Henry of France for assistance. Then at last, remembering the benefit once bestowed on him by the duke’s father, the king gathered the forces of the Franks together, attacked the county of Exmes, and came to Val-es-Dunes, where he encountered an army of innumerable armed men, filled with the most savage spirit and threatening battle against him with drawn swords.

The king and duke, not at all fearing their ferocious attacks, engaged them in battle after the soldiers had joined in successive charges; and they immediately destroyed them in such a slaughter that those whom the sword did not kill were swallowed by the river Orne as God struck fear into them and they fled. Blessed was that battle, in which on a single day the castles of the arrogant and the homes of criminals collapsed. Guy, having escaped from the battle, sought Briouze [Col. 0858A] and, closing the bars of the gates, shut himself in there for a while, hoping to be freed. The duke, pursuing him successfully after the king returned to France, enclosed him within a siege, establishing fortifications on both sides of the river called the Rille. Guy, seeing that he could escape from the place by no means, was overcome by the calamity of hunger and, compelled by his friends, was forced to submit and seek the duke’s mercy, repenting of what he had done. The duke, moved by compassion for his misery and on the advice of his men, mercifully spared him; after recovering the castle of Briouze, he ordered Guy to remain with his household in his own house.

All the nobles who had strayed from the duke’s loyalty, observing that he had partly destroyed and partly blocked every means of escape, surrendered their stiff necks to him as their lord by giving hostages. Thus, with the castles everywhere overthrown, no one afterward dared reveal a rebellious spirit against him. The aforesaid battle therefore took place in the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1047.

## CHAPTER XVIII. How Duke William recovered the castles of Alençon and Domfront, which Count Geoffrey of Anjou had invaded

Geoffrey, count of Anjou, surnamed Martel, a man crafty in every respect, frequently afflicted certain people living nearby with various disasters and intolerable hardships. Among them, he fraudulently captured Count Theobald and consigned him to custody for so long that he violently extorted from him the city of Tours, together with several castles. Then, when certain sparks of dispute had arisen, he began to move savagely against Duke William and to devastate Normandy violently through plunder, placing seditious guards inside the castle of Domfront.

The duke, surrounded by an armed force, attacked it under the pretext of inspecting it. When he saw that it was surrounded on every side by extremely rugged and lofty cliffs and inaccessible for assault, he summoned the strength of the Northmen, enclosed it with very strong castles, and blocked the routes of departure. While he remained for some time in this military position, scouts arrived and announced that he could capture the castle of Alençon without loss to his own men. He immediately stationed guards within the fortifications and, riding all night with his army, came to Alençon at dawn. [Col. 0858D] There he found certain men in a town situated across the river mocking him with insults. Rousing the spirits of his soldiers most fiercely, he began to storm the place at once and, setting it on fire, burned it with deadly flames. He ordered the mockers, in the presence of everyone staying below at Alençon, to be deprived of their hands and feet. Without delay, as he had commanded, thirty-two were mutilated.

For they had beaten hides and fur garments as an insult to the duke and had contemptuously called him a furrier, because his mother’s parents had been furriers [pollinctores, embalmers].

The guards of the castle, recognizing the duke’s severe harshness, became afraid; and, lest they suffer the same things, they immediately opened the gates and surrendered the castle to the duke, preferring to give it up rather than endure such grave tortures at the cost of their men’s limbs. Having carried this out manfully and admitted his soldiers, the duke returned with the greatest speed to Domfront. When the people of Domfront heard what the duke had inflicted on his fellow soldiers and considered that no one could help them, they surrendered themselves and their castle to his dominion.

Leaving from there after placing guards, and proceeding farther to confound Count Geoffrey, he came to Ambrières. There, on the bank of the river, he founded a castle and sufficiently fortified it with provisions and soldiers. Having suitably completed these affairs, he returned to Rouen, the metropolis of Normandy.

## CHAPTER XIX. How, after removing William Werlenc from the county of Mortain, he appointed his uterine brother Robert in his place

[Col. 0859B]

At the same time William, surnamed Werlenc, of the lineage of the great Richard, was count of Mortain. Once a certain young man from his household, named Robert Bigot, approached him and said: “I am oppressed by poverty, my lord, and in this country I cannot earn the profit I need. Therefore I shall now go to Apulia, so that I may live there more honorably.” William said to him: “Who persuaded you of this?” He replied: “The want that I suffer.” The count said: “If you are willing to believe me, you will remain here with us. For within eighty days you will have such a time in Normandy that whatever you see necessary for yourself, you will be able to seize with your hands without penalty.”

The man, accepting his lord’s advice, remained, and not long afterward, through his kinsman Richard of Avranches, obtained access to the duke. One day, while speaking privately with the duke, he reported to him, among other things, the count William’s statement quoted above. The duke summoned William to him and asked why he had made such a speech. William could neither deny it nor venture to explain the intention of his words. Angry at this, the duke said: “You have resolved to disturb Normandy with seditious tumults, and, rebelling against me, you have wickedly decided to disinherit me; therefore you promised a time of plunder to a needy soldier. But, by the Creator’s gift, peace remains with us forever, as we need it. You, however, depart from Normandy as quickly as possible, and do not return here again while I live.”

After William had been expelled and had miserably gone to Apulia with only one armed attendant, the duke immediately raised up his brother Robert and granted him the county of Mortain. Thus he harshly overthrew the proud kinsmen of his father and honorably exalted the humble relatives of his mother. But, as the common proverb says, a fool is scarcely corrected by words or examples, but only by blows, nor does he become afraid until he receives dreadful blows. This will become clearer from an example in what follows.

## CHAPTER XX. Concerning the rebellion of William Bucacius, count of Eu; and how, as an exile, he received the county of Soissons as a gift from King Henry of France

As we have made clear above, Duke Richard of Normandy, son of the first Richard, gave the county of Eu to a certain uterine brother named William. By Countess Lescelina he had three sons: Robert, William, and Hugh, afterward bishop of Lisieux. The middle one, William, surnamed Busac, wishing to claim the duchy for himself, began to raise his neck against the duke with threats and harassment. But the strong prince, unwilling to yield to him, gathered an army and besieged the castle of Eu until he captured it; he compelled his rebellious kinsman William to go into exile.

William then sought King Henry of France and tearfully explained to him what had happened. The king, receiving him kindly as a soldier noble in lineage and appearance, sympathized with his misfortune and granted him the county of Soissons together with a noble wife. From her the now-prosperous exile afterward received distinguished offspring, who to this day nobly maintains his father’s honor. At last, after the servants of discord had been expelled or overthrown, all Normandy rested beneath the wings of a favorable peace.

## CHAPTER XXI. How Duke William married Matilda, daughter of Baldwin of Flanders and niece of King Henry

Now that the duke was flourishing in youthful strength and had passed beyond the years of adolescence, his nobles began to discuss with him more attentively the succession of offspring. Hearing that Baldwin, count of Flanders, had a daughter named Matilda, descended from royal stock, very elegant in body and generous in spirit, he requested her from her father as his wife, sending envoys on the advice of his men. Baldwin, the magnate, greatly rejoiced at this proposal; he resolved not merely to give the requested girl but also to escort her with innumerable gifts all the way to the castle of Eu. There the duke arrived surrounded by bands of soldiers, betrothed her to himself in lawful marriage, and brought her into the walls of Rouen with the greatest rejoicing and honor.

In time she bore him four sons: Robert, who afterward held the duchy of Normandy for a while; William, who ruled the kingdom of England for thirteen years; Richard, who died young; and Henry, who succeeded his brothers, both the king and the duke; and four daughters. Concerning all of them, both men and women, the following book, which will be entitled Concerning the Deeds of the Most Noble King [Col. 0860D] Henry, will treat, with God’s help, according to our modest ability.

## CHAPTER XXII. Concerning the monasteries that were built in Normandy in the time of Duke William

In those days the inhabitants of Normandy enjoyed the greatest tranquility of peace, and the servants of God were held in the highest reverence by everyone. Each of the nobles vied with the others in building churches on his estate and enriching monks who would pray to God on his behalf with his possessions. Since we have said that the nobles of Normandy at that time were especially eager to build monasteries on their estates, it is pleasing to name those who built monasteries in that province during that period.

First, therefore, I shall mention Duke William himself, father of his country. He began and enlarged the monastery of Saint Victor at Cerisy, which his father, Duke Robert, had begun before departing for Jerusalem; afterward he himself built the monastery of Saint Stephen and his wife Matilda the monastery of the Holy Trinity at Caen.

William, son of Osbern, a relative of Duke William, a powerful man and praiseworthy in both spirit and bodily strength, built two monasteries in honor of blessed Mary, Mother of God: one at Lire, where he afterward buried his wife Adelina, daughter of Roger of Tosny; and another at Cormeilles, where he himself was buried after his death.

Roger of Beaumont, son of Humphrey de Vieilles, also built two monasteries on his estate at Préaux, one for monks and the other [Col. 0861B] for nuns.

Roger of Montgomerie, father of Robert of Bellême, unwilling to appear inferior in anything to his peers, nobly built two churches in honor of Saint Martin—one in the suburb of the city of Sées, the other in his village of Troarn—and placed there companies of monks who would serve God. He also built a third at Almenêches for the use of nuns. Lescelina, countess of Eu, aided by her sons Robert, count of Eu, and Hugh, bishop of Lisieux, courageously built the monastery of monks of Saint Peter upon the Dive and the monastery of nuns before the city of Lisieux. Her son, the aforementioned count of Eu, built the monastery [Col. 0861C] of Saint Michael at Le Tréport. Roger of Mortemer, son of the first William of Warenne, founded the monastery of Saint Victor on his own land.

[Note: Son of Walter of Saint-Martin, brother of the first William of Warenne.]

Richard, count of Évreux, built in that same city the monastery of the Savior for the use of nuns. The same viscount, completing at his own expense a monastery of the Holy Trinity at Rouen on the hill overlooking the city, established monks there to serve God. Count Robert of Mortain built the monastery of Grestain; Hugh, later count of Chester, built the abbey of Saint-Sever. Eudes “with the cap” (cum capello) built the church of the Holy Trinity at Écaquelon; Baldwin of Reviers also built another at Montsbourg; and Nigel, viscount of the Cotentin, built the monastery of the Savior. William Talvas I, who, after clearing a forest, had built a castle called Domfront on a certain hill, constructed from its foundations the monastery [Col. 0861D] of Saint Mary at Lonlay. Ralph Taisson and his brother Erneis built the church of Saint Stephen at Fontenay; and Ralph of Tosny built the monastery of Saint Peter at Castillon.

Certain monasteries of that province, older than these, which had been destroyed while the Northmen were still pagans, were rebuilt through the zeal of good princes. Rollo, the first duke of the Northmen, at the beginning of his conversion gave many possessions to the church of Saint Mary of Rouen, and to those of Saint Mary of Bayeux and Saint Mary of Évreux, and to the monasteries of Saint Peter, Saint Ouen, Jumièges, and Saint Michael of the Peril of the Sea. William, his son, completely restored the monastery of Jumièges. Richard, his son and successor, restored the monastery of Fécamp, Saint Michael of the Mount, and Saint Ouen at Rouen. Richard II greatly enlarged the monastery of Saint-Wandrille and the other monasteries rebuilt by his predecessors. His wife Judith founded the church of Saint Mary at Bernay. Richard III, however, cut off by an untimely death, neither established nor renewed any monastery. But his brother Robert, before departing for Jerusalem, began to build the monastery of Saint Vigor at Cerisy. [Col. 0862B]

At that same time the venerable Abbot Herluin began to build the monastery of Bec in honor of Saint Mary; we briefly touched upon this in the preceding book. If anyone wishes to know more fully about his conversion and manner of life, let him seek out and reread the book concerning the life of that venerable father, written in elegant style by the religious man Gilbert Crispin, later abbot of Westminster, a man distinguished both by the nobility of his family and by secular and divine learning. In it he will find sufficient material to satisfy his desire. The monastery of Saint Taurinus, Saint Leufredus, the monastery of Willar, and the monastery of Saint Amand within the city of Rouen must also be counted among the older foundations. From this it is clear that they had first been destroyed and were rebuilt again. [Col. 0862C]

## CHAPTER XXIII  
### The restoration of the monastery of Saint Ebrulf at Ouche by William Giroie and his nephews Robert and Hugh of Grandmesnil

At that time Robert of Grandmesnil, seeing the prosperity of the world perish in an instant, decided with his brother Hugh to build an abbey of monks. In his childhood he had acquired knowledge of letters, but afterward, having somewhat interrupted his studies, he had been the duke’s squire for five years. Later, girded with a military sword by the duke, he received great gifts. But not long afterward, as has been said, at God’s prompting he rejected everything and firmly resolved to build a monastery and become a monk. When William, son of Giroie, heard this, he was very glad. Approaching Robert and Hugh, he spoke as follows:

“I hear, my dearest nephews, that you are fervent in the worship of God and indeed wish to build a monastery for monks. I therefore rejoice greatly, and gladly promise that I will help you in this work. But what place have you chosen for this construction, and what will you contribute there to those who serve Christ?”

They replied: “At Noyers, with God’s help. We wish to establish a stronghold there for Him, and we will give our churches, tithes, and whatever else we can, according to the ability of our poverty.”

William said: “Saint Benedict, the master of monks, commands that a monastery be established in such a way that all necessities—namely, water, a mill, a bakehouse, a garden, and various crafts—can be carried on within the monastery, so that the monks have no need to wander outside, since this is wholly disadvantageous to their souls. The countryside around Noyers is indeed sufficiently fertile, but an abundance of woodland and convenient water, which monks especially need, lie far away.” [Col. 0863A]

When they asked him to express what seemed best to him concerning this matter, he said:

“In the time of Clotaire, king of the Franks and son of Clovis—the first of the kings of the Gauls to be baptized, by Saint Remigius, archbishop of Reims—Saint Ebrulf was born at Bayeux. Among the royal nobles he shone through the nobility of his lineage and wealth. Rejecting the pomp of the world for the love of God, he became a monk, and after some time went into the wilderness with three monks. There, indeed, he thought he could remain hidden from men and fight more strongly against the devil with God’s help.

“As he prayed devoutly to God on bent knees, asking Him to show him a suitable place of habitation, an angel sent by God appeared to him and led him to Ouche. This servant of God then, while Chilperic and Sigibert, sons of Clotaire, were reigning, founded a monastery there. He terrified the robbers who inhabited the forest with useful threats and exhortations, and made them abandon their brigandage and become either monks or farmers. There, for the love of God, he patiently endured great poverty and gathered an outstanding multitude of faithful monks. There he raised two dead men in the name of the Lord, and performed many other miracles which it would take too long to enumerate. [Col. 0863C]

“Finally, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 596, in the eightieth year of his age, while Gregory, the supreme teacher and apostle of the English, occupied the apostolic see, blessed Ebrulf departed this world on the fourth day before the Kalends of January and received from the Lord in heaven the reward for his labors.

“Then, nearly three hundred years later, in the time of Charles the Simple, son of Louis, surnamed ‘He-Has-Done-Nothing,’ our Creator wished to punish the multiplied crimes of His people dwelling in these regions. With His permission, therefore, Hasting, the son of perdition, came into Neustria and burned Rouen [or Beauvais] and other cities. He also destroyed many monasteries of the holy fathers, namely those of Philibert at Jumièges, Wandregisel at Fontenelle, Ebrulf at Ouche, and Saint Martin at Tours, which is called the Great Monastery, as well as many others belonging to monks, clerics, and nuns. Some of these were afterward restored by good princes, while others still lie in desolation.

“Perhaps, dear nephews, this very lengthy speech of ours is wearisome to you; yet if you receive it with a kindly spirit, I think it will prove useful to you. Now I will briefly reveal what I am turning over in my mind, so that you may know my proposal. Let us, with God’s help, restore the monastery of Saint Ebrulf at Ouche, gather there faithful monks who will fight against the devil, and hand over to them all our churches and tithes. Let us also, together with our brothers, sons, and nephews, serve them until death. For we ought not to rule over them but to serve them, so that through their prayers we may deserve assistance and one day be blessed in the delight of paradise.” [Col. 0864A]

When Robert and Hugh had gladly accepted these words and carefully investigated the character of the place, the magnanimous hero William added:

“The place at Ouche, to which God directed the venerable Ebrulf through His angel, is entirely suitable for the poor in spirit, to whom the kingdom of heaven is promised. For the ancient basilica of Saint Peter still stands there, and a broad field surrounds it, where gardens and orchards can be made. The land is uncultivated and barren, but the Lord is able to prepare a table in the wilderness for His servants. There are no fish-filled rivers or abundant vineyards, but a dense woodland and convenient springs for drinking are available. The bodies of many saints also rest there, and they will rise again in great glory on the last day. You have now heard what I most earnestly desire; consider what you wish to do.”

When they approved his counsel and promised to follow him in all things, the prudent William continued:

“If it pleases you, let monks be sought at once and established at Ouche with such freedom that neither we nor our heirs may demand any revenue from them, except one thing alone: that the servants of God support us with their prayers. And lest we should ever, at the devil’s instigation, harass them in any way, let us voluntarily entrust the aforesaid monastery to the duke of all Normandy, so that he may protect it against us, our descendants, and all mortal men. Thus, if we should violently demand from them anything beyond spiritual benefit—whether service or gift—we may be salutarily restrained by princely severity and cease to trouble God’s recruits against their will.” [Col. 0864C]

After this they went together to the duke and clearly explained their desire to him. He kindly favored their wishes, then confirmed a charter of his authority at the Lion’s Wood and delivered it to the bishops and barons of Normandy for confirmation. Archbishop Malgerius of Rouen signed first. Then the prelates signed: Hugh of Lisieux and Odo of Bayeux; William of Évreux; and Gilbert, abbot of Castillon. At that point Lord Theodoric, a monk of Jumièges, was elected, and the care of the abbey of Ouche was entrusted to him.

[Col. 0864D] In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1050, in the fourth indiction, while Pope Leo occupied the apostolic see and Henry II, the most Christian Augustus, son of Conon, duke of the Saxons, ruled, the monastery of Saint Ebrulf at Ouche was restored by the aforesaid nobles, William Giroie and his nephews Robert and Hugh of Grandmesnil. There the venerable Theodoric, a monk of great religious devotion, was solemnly consecrated before the altar of Saint Peter by Hugh, bishop of Lisieux, on the ninth day before the Ides of October, a Sunday.

In the following year the noble Robert, founder of the monastery, became a monk there, and afterward endured many labors in the administration of God’s servants. Not long afterward William Giroie was sent to Apulia for certain reasonable causes. While he was beginning his return, he died at Gaeta on the Nones of February. His son William de Monasteriolo, a knight of great eminence in Apulia, oppressed the Greeks and Lombards by force of arms and subjected them to the vicar of the holy apostle Peter.

## CHAPTER XXIV  
### How Archbishop Malgerius returned the archbishopric to the duke and he appointed the monk Maurilius in his place

At that time Malgerius, archbishop of Rouen, began to lose his judgment, and, led by folly, returned the archbishopric to the duke. The duke confined Malgerius on the island called Guernsey [Ghernervia] and, by decree of a synod, entrusted the metropolitan see to Maurilius, a monk of Fécamp distinguished by many virtues. [Col. 0865B]

At that time discord also disturbed the Normans and compelled them to shed the blood of neighbors who preferred war to peace. Indeed, ever since the Normans had begun to inhabit the fields of Neustria, it had always been the custom of the Franks to envy them. They therefore incited their kings to rise against the Normans, asserting that the lands they possessed had been violently stolen from their ancestors.

King Henry, greatly angered by these claims—or rather by the most malicious suggestions of his rivals—invaded Normandy with two hostile armies because of the duke’s power. He sent one army, composed of men of chosen nobility and courage, to lay waste the territory of Caux, placing his brother Odo in command. He himself led the other army with Geoffrey Martel to destroy the county of Évreux. [Col. 0865C]

When the duke saw himself and his men being oppressed in this way, he was deeply and nobly grieved. He immediately selected soldiers and sent them with the utmost speed to crush the destroyers of Calceium. He himself went with some of his men toward the king, so that he might suffer punishment if he could in any way draw one of the king’s attendants away from his side.

When the Normans came upon the Franks, they found them at Mortemer occupied with fires and the violation of women. Battle was joined with them at once in the morning and, amid the continual slaughter of those falling on both sides, lasted until the ninth hour. At last the French were defeated and fled, and the Normans quickly informed the duke of the outcome by messengers.

He was exceedingly joyful at this news and, wishing to drive away King Henry, terrified him by the message. The duke’s messenger approached the royal camp and, standing by night on a nearby hill, began to shout loudly. When the royal guards asked who he was and why he was shouting in this manner at such an hour, he is said to have replied:

“My name is Ralph of Tosny, and I bring you a mournful message. Go to Mortemer, lead your wagons and carts there, and bring back the corpses of your dear ones. The Franks came against us to test the military strength of the Normans, and they found it far greater than they had wished. Their standard-bearer Odo was shamefully put to flight, and Guy, count of Ponthieu, was captured. All the rest were either captured or killed, or barely escaped by fleeing with all their strength. Report this at once to the king of the Franks on behalf of the duke of Normandy.” [Col. 0866A]

When the king learned of the misfortune of his men, he withdrew sorrowfully from the Norman invasion as rapidly as he could and did not attempt to come against them again. This battle took place in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1054.

## CHAPTER XXV  
### How Duke William built the castle of Breteuil and entrusted it to William, son of Osbern; and concerning his wife

Afterward the duke built, opposite the castle of Tillières, which the king had formerly taken from him, another stronghold no less formidable, called Breteuil to this day. He entrusted it to William, son of Osbern, to guard against all who opposed him. [Col. 0866B]

This legitimate and generous man took Adela, daughter of Roger of Tosny, as his wife. By her he fathered two sons, William and Roger the Proud, and one daughter, who afterward married Count Ralph, a Breton by birth, and went with him to Jerusalem in the days of Pope Urban.

The aforesaid hero founded two monasteries of monks in honor of Saint Mary, Queen of Heaven. One was at Lyre, where he buried his wife Adela; the other was at Cormeilles, where he himself rests and where his son Ralph, a monk from childhood, long served God. He himself, together with Duke William, thoroughly subdued the English and obtained the county of Hereford, with a large part of the kingdom, through judgment and strength.

Finally, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1070, he went with Philip, king of the Franks, into Flanders, wishing to assist Baldwin, the nephew of Queen Matilda. Robert the Frisian, however, with the army of Emperor Henry joined to his forces, unexpectedly attacked them in battle on the tenth day before the Kalends of March, the Sunday of Septuagesima. When Philip and the Franks fled, he killed Baldwin, his nephew, and Count William with the weapons of his men. He afterward held the duchy of Flanders for a long time and, when he died, left it to his sons Robert the Jerusalemite and Philip. But let us now return to the order of the history.

## CHAPTER XXVI  
### The reason why two monasteries were built at Caen

Duke William, being repeatedly reproved by certain religious men because he had married a woman related to him, sent messengers to consult the Roman pope about the matter. The pope, wisely considering that if he ordered a divorce a grave war might perhaps arise between the Flemings and the Normans, absolved husband and wife from guilt and imposed penance upon them.

For he commanded that they should establish two monasteries, in which prayers should diligently be offered to God on their behalf by both sexes. They gladly fulfilled this command in deed. At Caen one abbey was built in honor of the Holy Trinity, and the other in honor of Saint Stephen the protomartyr.

In the monastery of the Holy Trinity, a choir of nuns daily sings praises to God. The servant of God Matilda, its abbess, presided over them for nearly forty-eight years. There Queen Matilda was buried in the year 1081 of the Lord’s Incarnation, on the third day before the Nones of November. There also Cecilia, her daughter, was consecrated to God and remained for a long time in His service. [Col. 0867A]

In the monastery of Saint Stephen, an army of monks resists the demonic phalanx. Its first abbot was Lord Lanfranc, a monk of Bec. He was Lombard by birth, gentle and religious in conduct, and exceedingly skilled in both secular and spiritual learning. After several years, with the support of Pope Alexander, he assumed the archbishopric of Canterbury; after a long time, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1100, he died on the sixth day before the Kalends of June.

After him, William the monk, son of Radbod, bishop of Sées, governed the church of Caen. He too later assumed the archbishopric of Rouen after John, the metropolitan. Then Gilbert of Coutances, a shrewd man, became rector of Caen. During his tenure Duke William of Normandy and king of the English died at Rouen in 1087, on the fifth day before the Ides of September, and was honorably buried in the church of Saint Stephen at Caen. [Col. 0867B]

Let these anticipatory remarks suffice. The venerable Theodoric, after governing the monastery of Saint Ebrulf for nearly eight years, returned the care of souls to Archbishop Maurice and Bishop Hugh because of certain disturbances stirred up against him by Lord Robert of Grandmesnil, who was then prior. Thus released by them, as a son of peace he resolved to go to Jerusalem.

When he came to the island of Cyprus with a bishop of venerable life who was making a pilgrimage, and reached a certain church of Saint Nicholas, he prostrated himself on the ground before the altar and prayed for a long time. There, while praying, he gave his blessed spirit back to God on the Kalends of August. When the islanders learned of the holiness of such a pilgrim, they buried his body in the church. Through his merits, many miracles of healing were divinely displayed among the sick.

## CHAPTER XXVII  
### How Duke William stormed and captured the city of Le Mans and the castle of Mayenne

The magnificent Duke William, after suitably defeating the forces of the Franks, remembered the insult inflicted upon him by Count Geoffrey and for several years directed his arms against the city of Le Mans. Who could possibly explain with how many attacks by soldiers and how many campaigns of armies he afflicted it?

At last, after the people of Le Mans had been defeated and the castles throughout the county subdued, they gave their right hands to the duke and pledged their faith to him with the strongest oaths. Among them, in order to tame their insolence, he established two fortified towns at Pont-de-Braye, or Barbello, and entrusted them to his soldiers for defense.

The castle of Mayenne, belonging to a wealthy soldier named Geoffrey, still resisted. The duke attacked it for some time after bringing up his armies, then captured it and burned it by means of two boys who had secretly entered to play with the children of the townspeople. [Col. 0868A] He rebuilt it afterward and handed it over to his guards.

## CHAPTER XXVIII  
### How King Henry of the Franks lost his army at the ford of the Dive and was afterward reconciled with the duke, to whom he returned the castle of Tillières

King Henry, desiring with all his strength to avenge the injury inflicted upon him by the duke, took Geoffrey, count of Anjou, and invaded Normandy on a second campaign with a very large army. Passing through the county of Exmes and penetrating into the region of Bayeux, he finally turned toward the ford of the Dive by the road of return.

When the king had crossed, half of the army remained behind, unable to cross because the river had overflowed, its waters pouring forth like the sea. The duke attacked them fiercely and engaged them immediately before the king’s eyes. He struck them down in such slaughter that those whom the sword did not destroy were scattered along the Norman roads by the violent force of dreadful captivity. [Col. 0868B]

When the king saw the destruction of his men, he withdrew from the Normans as quickly as he could and did not attempt to come against them again. Considering the duke’s excellence, he sought his friendship and returned to him the castle of Tillières, which he had formerly taken away.

The aforementioned king was highly warlike and possessed great courage and piety. He took Matilda, daughter of Julius-Clodius, king of the Rugians, as his wife and fathered by her two sons, Philip and Hugh, and one daughter.

[Note: Some call her Anna; she was his second wife, whereas Matilda was his first.]

After he had ruled the kingdom of France for nearly twenty-five years, he received a potion from John, the most skilled of physicians, as a remedy for bodily health. But when the poison produced excessive thirst, he disregarded the physician’s order and, accepting a drink from a chamberlain while the doctor was absent, drank before the purgative had taken effect. As a result he became extremely weak and died that same day after receiving the holy Eucharist. He established his son Philip as his heir in the government of France and entrusted him to the guardianship of Baldwin, the Flemish nobleman.

## CHAPTER XXIX  
### How Duke William, because of the accusations of certain men, expelled some of his barons from Normandy

At that time, when certain slanderers accused their neighbors and peers out of envy, Duke William was provoked to immense fury and expelled his barons from Normandy—namely Ralph of Tosny, Hugh of Grandmesnil, and Ernald, son of William Giroie. [Col. 0868D]

He also expelled Abbot Robert from Normandy without guilt or synodal judgment, because he came from the bold lineage of the Giroies. Robert had already governed the monastery of Saint Ebrulf for three years. In his place he appointed a monk named Osbern.

Robert went to Rome and laid his case before Pope Nicholas. But since that pontiff died shortly afterward, Robert obtained no redress through him. Finally, the venerable Robert went with eleven monks to Pope Alexander and, on his command, sought out Robert, duke of Calabria, his countryman. [Col. 0869A]

He was honorably received by him, and a site for building an abbey was granted to him in the city named Brixa. The Bretons, it is said, had formerly left their borders at the command of the Romans, who then ruled throughout the entire world. Later, at the Romans’ order, they founded the city of Brixa on the shore of the Calabrian Sea. But after many years various disturbances of war destroyed it.

For every year the Agareni came by ship into Italy and, while the Greeks and Lombards who inhabited the land lay sluggish in cowardice, exercised their cruelty against them through threats. They burned cities and strongholds, destroyed churches, and took men and women captive. They did this frequently for many centuries.

## CHAPTER XXX  
### When the Normans first went to Apulia and concerning the Norman princes under whose leadership the Apulians were subdued

[Col. 0869B]

Then, in the time of Emperor Henry, son of Conon, and of Robert, duke of the Normans, Osmund Drengot, a bold soldier, went to Apulia with certain other Normans. He had killed William surnamed Repostellus, a very distinguished knight, while hunting in the presence of Duke Robert. Fearing the duke’s anger and the wrath of the noble relatives of that eminent knight, he withdrew to Apulia, where, because of his great excellence, the people of Benevento honorably retained him.

Afterward, following the example of the aforesaid Drengot, agile young Normans or Bretons were stirred to seek Italy at various times. At first they began courageously to assist the Lombards against the Saracens or Greeks, and repeatedly crushed the barbarians in war. Thus they became objects of fear to all who had experienced their strength.

Once the Lombards had attained security, however, they began to despise the Normans and withhold from them the pay they owed. When the Normans noticed this, they set one of their own number over them as prince and turned their arms against the Lombards. They then captured fortifications and forcibly subjected the inhabitants of the land to themselves.

The first to command the Norman forces in Apulia, while they were still newcomers and serving as mercenaries of Waimalchus, duke of Salerno, was Turstin surnamed Scitellus, a man highly experienced in many forms of excellence. Among the other signs of his courage, he snatched a goat from a lion’s mouth; then, when the lion raged because its goat had been taken, he seized the lion with his bare hands and threw it over the wall of the aforesaid duke’s palace like any puppy. [Col. 0869D]

The Lombards, moved by envy against him and wishing for his death, led him to a certain place where a monstrous dragon lived with a great multitude of serpents. When they sensed the dragon approaching, they immediately fled. Turstin, unaware of the trick, saw his companions fleeing and, astonished, asked his shield-bearer the reason for such a sudden flight. Suddenly the fire-breathing dragon came upon him and attacked the head of his packhorse with its gaping mouth. Turstin drew his sword, struck the beast courageously, and immediately killed it. But he himself, infected by its poisonous breath, died on the third day.

His shield—which is wondrous to relate—the flame bursting from the dragon’s mouth burned completely in an instant. [Col. 0870A]

After Turstin’s death, the Normans chose Ranulf and Richard as their princes. Under their leadership, avenging Turstin’s death, they rebelled fiercely against the Lombards. After some time, Drogo, son of Tancred of Hauteville and a man of Coutances, became prince of the Normans in Apulia. He was praiseworthy in Christian religion and military excellence. Wazo, count of Naples and his godfather, murdered him before the altar while they were keeping vigil in the church of Saint Lawrence on the fourth day before the Ides of August, as Drogo invoked God and Saint Lawrence.

His brother Humphrey succeeded him in the principate and subjected all Apulia to the Normans. When he perceived that the end of his life was approaching, he entrusted his son Abelard to his brother Robert—whom, because of his craftiness, he had nicknamed Wiscard—together with the duchy of Apulia.

Robert surpassed his brothers, who were all dukes or counts, in courage, judgment, and eminence. He subjected all Apulia, Calabria, and Sicily to himself. After crossing the sea, he invaded a large part of Greece and, in battle, shamefully defeated and put to flight with his immense army Alexius the emperor, who had wickedly rebelled against his lord, Michael Augustus.

He also did many good works and restored several bishoprics and abbeys. As we said above, he kindly received Lord Robert, abbot of Saint Ebrulf, and granted him a small church situated on the shore of the Calabrian Sea and dedicated in honor of Saint Euphemia, virgin and martyr. [Col. 0870C]

But Robert, being magnanimous, founded a great monastery there and gathered a large multitude of monks to serve God in that place. The bishops and noblemen loved and venerated the aforesaid Father Robert and assisted him with all their strength. He cared little for his own body, but adequately nourished those subject to him with food and clothing, and disciplined and ordered their minds by regular observance.

He therefore governed the aforesaid monastery for nearly seventeen years and happily departed to the Lord on the Ides of December.

## CHAPTER XXXI  
### How Harold swore fealty to Duke William but, after King Edward’s death, broke it by perjury

[Col. 0870D]

By God’s arrangement, King Edward of the English, lacking succession by offspring, had previously sent Robert, archbishop of Canterbury, to Duke William, designating him as heir to the kingdom allotted to him by God. He then sent Harold, the greatest in wealth, honor, and power among all the nobles of his dominion, to the duke, so that Harold might swear fealty to him concerning the crown and confirm it with oaths according to Christian custom.

As Harold was hastening to come for this business, he sailed across the strait and landed at Ponthieu, where he fell into the hands of Guy, count of Abbeville. The count immediately seized him and his companions and thrust them into custody. When the duke learned of this, he sent messengers and forcibly secured his release. He kept him with him for some time and brought him on the expedition against the Bretons.

After Harold had confirmed his fealty to the duke concerning the kingdom with several oaths, the duke promised that he would give him his daughter Adela together with half the kingdom of England. Finally, he sent Harold back to the king with many gifts but retained his handsome young brother Wulfnoth as a hostage.

At last King Edward, having completed the course of his blessed life, departed this world in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1065. Harold immediately invaded his kingdom, breaking by perjury the fealty he had sworn to the duke.

The duke at once sent messengers to him, urging him to recover from this madness and to preserve, with fitting submission, the faith he had promised by oath. But Harold not only scorned to listen to this; he also treacherously turned the entire English people away from the duke. [Col. 0871B]

After the hostile sword had killed King Griffith of Wales, Harold took as his wife his beautiful widow Aldith, daughter of the distinguished Earl Algar. In those days a comet appeared in the northwest. Extending three rays far outward, it illuminated most of the south for fifteen nights and, as many asserted, signified a change in some kingdom.

## CHAPTER XXXII  
### How Duke William sent Earl Tostig to England, and how, out of fear of Harold, he fled to the king of Norway

The duke sent Earl Tostig to England, but Harold’s military forces, guarding the sea, drove him back by force of arms. [Col. 0871C] Unable to enter England safely and unable to return to Normandy because the wind opposed him, Tostig approached Harold Hardrada, king of Norway, and humbly begged him to help him. The king readily granted Tostig’s request.

In that same year Lord Osbern, abbot of Saint Ebrulf, died on the sixth day before the Kalends of June, after governing the monastery for five years and two months. He was a good man and attentive to those subject to him. The prudent Mainnerius, a monk of the same monastery, succeeded him. With God’s help and the favor of favorable times, he built a new church and all the buildings suitable for the monks.

After governing the monastery for twenty-two years, during the time of the negligent Duke Robert and Gilbert Maminot, bishop of Lisieux, he died on the eleventh day before the Nones of March. [Col. 0871D] He left the administration of the abbey of Ouche to the most accomplished Serlo, distinguished by knowledge of the Scriptures and eloquence. After two years and three months, Serlo assumed, by the grace of God, the bishopric of Sées.

## CHAPTER XXXIII  
### The death of Count Conan of Brittany

At the time when Duke William was preparing to go to England and claim it for himself by arms, the bold Conan, count of Brittany, attempted to frighten him by sending the following message:

“I hear,” he said, “that you now wish to cross the sea and obtain the kingdom of England for yourself. I rejoice greatly at this, but I beg you to return Normandy to me. Robert, duke of the Normans, whom you pretend to be your father, when he was going to Jerusalem, entrusted all his inheritance to my father Alan, his cousin. But you, with your accomplices, killed my father Alan by poison at Winchester in Normandy. You invaded his land, which I could not possess because I was a child, and you have held it to this day against justice, although you are illegitimate. Therefore either return to me the Normandy that is owed to me, or I shall bring war against you with all my strength.” [Col. 0872A]

When he heard this, Duke William was somewhat frightened. But soon God deigned to rescue him by frustrating the enemy’s threats. One of the Breton nobles, who had sworn fealty to both counts and carried this message between them, smeared poison on the inside of Conan’s trumpet, reins, and gloves. He was Conan’s chamberlain.

At that time the count of Brittany had besieged the castle of Gunther in the county of Anjou. When the soldiers in the town surrendered to him, he was bringing his men inside. Meanwhile Conan incautiously put on his gloves, touched the reins, and raised his hand to his mouth. By this contact he was infected with poison and shortly afterward died, while all his men mourned him.

He was very prudent and honorable and a lover of justice. Had he lived longer, it is said, he would have accomplished many good works and would have been useful in governing the realm. The traitor, conscious of his guilt, immediately fled from the expedition and reported Conan’s death to Duke William.

## CHAPTER XXXIV  
### The number of ships that Duke William brought to England

[Col. 0872C]

Willelmus, therefore, having become secure, turned the full force of his fury against the English. Considering that Harold was daily growing stronger, he ordered a fleet of three thousand ships to be rapidly and carefully built, and had it lie suitably at anchor in Ponthieu, at Saint-Valéry. He also assembled a vast army from Normans, Flemings, French, and Bretons; and he filled the prepared fleet with both powerful horses and very strong men, equipped with coats of mail and helmets. When everything was ready, with a favorable wind blowing and the sails spread high, he crossed the sea and landed at Pevensey, where he immediately built a fortress with a very strong rampart and entrusted it to reputable knights. [Col. 0872D] Then he hastened to Hastings and quickly fortified another position there.

But while the Normans were entering the kingdom that he had usurped, Harold was engaged in battle against his brother Tostig. In this conflict he killed that brother of his, as well as Harold, king of Norway, who had come to aid Tostig. This battle took place on the Nones of October, a Saturday, and in it almost the entire Norwegian army was slain by the English. Victorious from there, Harold returned to London, but he could not long rejoice in the murder of his brother or remain secure, because a messenger soon announced to him that the Normans were present.

## CHAPTER XXXV  
### That the tyrant Harold rejected the counsel of his mother and brother, who urged him not to wage war against the Normans

[Col. 0873A]

When he heard that fiercer adversaries had risen against him on the other side, he once again prepared himself manfully for battle. For he was very bold and honorable, exceedingly handsome in his whole body, charming in speech, and agreeable to everyone. Moreover, while his mother and other loyal friends were advising him against the war, his brother, Count Gurth, said to him:

“Dearest brother and lord, your excellence ought to be tempered by the moderation of prudence. You have now returned exhausted from the battle against the Norwegians, and yet you are hurrying again to fight against the Normans. Rest, I beg you; be willing to consider carefully with yourself [Col. 0873B] what you promised under oath to the count of Normandy. Beware lest you incur perjury and, for so great a crime, fall together with the strength of our nation, becoming thereafter a lasting disgrace to our race. I am free from every oath and owe nothing to Count William. I am therefore ready to fight boldly against him for my native land. But you, my brother, remain peacefully wherever you wish and await the outcome of the war, lest the glorious freedom of the English perish through your destruction.”

When Harold heard these words, he became exceedingly angry. He rejected the counsel that seemed beneficial to his friends, and provoked with insults his own brother, who was advising him faithfully. He also struck his mother insolently with his foot, since she was trying too earnestly to keep him with her. Then [Col. 0873C] for six days he gathered an innumerable multitude of English, hastening to forestall the unwary duke; riding throughout the night, he appeared in the field of battle in the morning.

## CHAPTER XXXVI  
### How William, duke of the Normans, defeated the rebellious English

The duke, taking precautions against the enemy’s nighttime raids, ordered his army to remain under arms from the beginning of darkness until the welcome light of dawn. At daybreak on Saturday, he arranged his troops in three divisions and, undaunted, advanced against the terrifying enemy. He joined battle with them at about the third hour of the day, and the fighting continued until night, with men dying on both sides in the slaughter. Harold himself, advancing in the first line of the troops, was pierced by deadly wounds and fell. [Col. 0873D]

But after the English had stood bravely in the conflict throughout the entire day and discovered that their king had been overwhelmed by death, they began to despair of their own safety. As night approached, they turned their faces and sought the aid of flight. Thus, when the Normans saw the English fleeing, they pursued them vigorously throughout the whole of Sunday night, to their own destruction. For tall grass covered an ancient embankment, where the Normans, rushing forward at full speed with horses and weapons, plunged headlong; and as one suddenly fell upon another, they destroyed one another in turn. There, as they say, nearly fifteen thousand perished.

Thus almighty God, on the day before the Ides of October, punished innumerable sinners from both battle lines in different ways. For, with the madness of the Normans raging, many thousands of English were slain on Saturday [Col. 0874A]—men who long before had unjustly killed the innocent Alfred, and who on the preceding Saturday had mercilessly slaughtered King Harold, Count Tostig, and many others. The same judge also took vengeance on the English during the following night and cast the raging Normans into a blind abyss. For they had immoderately coveted another’s property contrary to the commandment of the Law, and, as the Psalmist says, their feet had been swift to shed blood. Therefore, they encountered destruction and misery in their ways.

## CHAPTER XXXVII  
### That the Londoners surrendered to him, that he became king of the English at London on the following Christmas, and concerning the abbey of Battle

[Col. 0874B]

After these events, the vigorous Duke William, returning from the slaughter of his enemies, went back at midnight to the field of battle. When the morning light of Sunday had dawned, after the spoils of the enemy had been distributed and the bodies of his dear companions had been buried, he set out on the road leading to London. Then he turned aside toward the city of Wallingford, and, after crossing the ford of the river, ordered his troops to pitch their camp there.

From there he departed and attacked London. His advance troops, arriving in the streets of the city, found many rebels there, striving with all their might to resist. Engaging them at once, they brought no small grief upon the city because of the numerous deaths of its sons and citizens. At length, when the Londoners saw that they could no longer hold out against him, they gave hostages and submitted themselves and all their possessions to the most noble victor. [Col. 0874C]

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1066, therefore, William, duke of the Normans—whom our pen is not sufficient to praise—fashioned a noble trophy from the English, as has been said above. Then, on the day of the Lord’s Nativity, he was elected king by all the nobles of both the Normans and the English, anointed with sacred oil by the bishops of the kingdom, and crowned with the royal diadem.

The place where, as we said above, the battle was fought has from that time to this been called Battle. Moreover, King William built there a monastery in honor of the Holy Trinity, established monks and the order of the Major Monastery of Saint Martin of Tours, and richly endowed it with the resources necessary for the slain of both sides.

## CHAPTER XXXVIII  
### Concerning his return to Normandy and the death of Archbishop Maurilius, whose successor was John

[Col. 0874D]

Soon afterward he returned to Normandy and ordered the church of Saint Mary at Jumièges to be dedicated with great honor. While this sacred mystery was being celebrated there with the utmost reverence, in the greatest devotion and festivity, he himself, always an earnest and devoted worshiper of the Bridegroom of these nuptials, was present with the most devout spirit.

This dedication was completed in the year 1067 of the Lord’s Incarnation, on the Kalends of July, by these bishops: namely, Maurilius, archbishop of Rouen, and Baldwin of Évreux. Maurilius, the chief pastor, still living in that month, laid down the burden of the flesh on the fifth day before the Ides of August and departed free and joyful, now destined to live with his king Christ. [Col. 0875A]

John, bishop of the city of Avranches, succeeded him: a man exceptionally distinguished by nobility, happily imbued with spiritual wisdom, and supremely endowed with worldly prudence. He was, in keeping with the nobility of his birth, the son of Count Rudolph.

Since we have mentioned this Rudolph, it is pleasant briefly to recall some earlier events. Richard I was the son of William Longsword. When he was still a boy, after his father’s death, the king of the Franks detained him in France as though he were an exile. His mother, Sprota, driven by necessity, entered into the companionship of a certain very wealthy man named Asperlengus. Although wealthy in other respects, this man was accustomed to hold the mills of the valley of Rueil on lease. From Sprota he fathered a son, Rudolph, of whom we are speaking, and several daughters, who were later married into noble families throughout Normandy.

When the aforementioned Richard had obtained the duchy of Normandy, which the king of the Franks had fraudulently taken from him, it happened one day that his men went hunting in the forest called Weura. Among them was Rudolph, the duke’s uterine brother. As they explored the forest’s byways and hidden places during the hunt, they found an enormous bear in a certain valley. The hunters turned to flight, leaving the young man alone and giving him the opportunity to display his valor.

For he feared the disgrace of cowardly flight more than the ferocity of the beast. He stood his ground and, although young in years, was strong through his innate greatness of spirit; he threw down the raging animal that was attacking him. His companions, returning after their flight and learning what had happened, reported the young man’s courage shamefacedly to Duke Richard. The duke rejoiced and gave him the forest of Weura with its appurtenances. The valley in which he killed the bear is still called Bear Valley.

He also gave him the castle of Ivry [in one manuscript, Virey], from which he was called a count. Rudolph took as his wife a woman named Eremberga, very beautiful, born in a village in the territory of Calvados [Calcivi], called Cavilla [Cachevilla]. By her he fathered two sons: Hugh, later bishop of Bayeux, and John of Avranches, who eventually became archbishop of Rouen.

He also had two daughters. One married Osbern of Crépon, by whom William, son of Osbern, was born. Richard of Bellafago married the other, and by her fathered Robert, who succeeded him, and several daughters, one of whom was married to Hugh of Montfort. Since we have incidentally mentioned this Hugh, we have thought it useful to say briefly something about his predecessors.

Turstin of Bastenburg had two sons, William Bertrand and Hugh with the Beard of Montfort. This Hugh, as well as Henry of Ferrières, was killed in a certain conflict that they had begun against one another. The son of this Hugh was a second Hugh, who later became a monk of Bec. This Hugh had by the daughter of Richard of Bellafago one daughter, [Col. 0875D] whom Gilbert of Gant married. By her he fathered a fourth Hugh, who married Adeline, daughter of Robert, count of Meulan; by her he fathered his firstborn son Robert and others.
