We called him the fourth Hugh because the second Hugh, after the death of his first wife, married another, by whom he fathered a third Hugh and his brother Robert; but they died abroad and without children. Robert of Bellafago became a monk of Bec toward the end of his life, where his sons Richard and William are piously preserved. His successor was Robert Baviel, his grandson through his daughter. Having said these things in anticipation, let us return to the order of the history.

## CHAPTER XXXIX  
### How Count Eustace of Boulogne was driven back from Dover Castle, which he had besieged while King William was in Normandy

[Col. 0876B]

While the victorious king, remaining in Normandy and devoting himself in his customary honorable manner to the pursuit of good works, increased his titles of piety and enlightened his beloved homeland by his presence, Eustace, count of Boulogne, corrupted by the cunning of certain English living within the county of Canterbury, attempted to attack the fortress of Canterbury.

Crossing the sea in the dead of night, he besieged it at dawn with a large army and began to assault it with all his strength. But the soldiers of Odo, bishop of Bayeux, and of Hugh of Montfort, to whom the defense of Canterbury had been entrusted, realizing that, with their lords absent, they had been unexpectedly besieged, were inflamed with generous courage. They immediately opened the gates, rushed out together, joined battle, and drove all the attackers away from the siege in disgrace. Eustace, turning toward the sea, fled indecorously from there by ship with only a few men.

The others, fleeing toward the slope of the mountain that rises above the sea and is exceedingly rough with rocks and crags, all threw themselves headlong down from it, God inspiring terror in them, and paid the just penalties for their crime. Thus it happened that those whom the sword did not overthrow were torn apart by the terrible harshness of the precipitous mountain, as the judgment of the heavenly judge took vengeance by crushing the reckless.

## CHAPTER XL  
### That the brigands of England, preparing a rebellion, built the castle of Durham, and concerning their destruction

[Col. 0876D]

King William, having now arranged everything according to his desire for which he had come, entrusted the rule of the Norman duchy to his son Robert, who was flourishing with youthful vigor. He himself, returning to the English kingdom, again found many of the same people whose fickle hearts a treacherous conspiracy had turned away from loyalty to him.

For the brigands had conspired throughout the country that, on the first day of the fast, the soldiers whom he had left to defend the kingdom should be killed everywhere while hastening barefoot to church, as Christian religious practice customarily requires penitents to do, and that in this way they might more easily disturb him as he returned from Normandy.

But when God exposed the machinery of their treachery, directed against him, they feared the sudden arrival of the great conqueror. Following secretly the counsel of great terror that urged haste, they fled to a part of the county of Cumberland inaccessible alike by its waters and forests. There they built, with a very strong rampart, a fortress which in their own language they called Durham. From there they frequently made various raids and hid there for some time, awaiting the arrival of Svend, king of the Danes, whom they had summoned to their aid through messengers.

Then, sending envoys to bring forth the disastrous schemes of their wickedness, they brought the men of York over to their side. Joining with them, they fortified the city with an abundance of weapons and pay, and strengthened themselves for resistance. They set over themselves as king a certain boy named Edgar, descended by lineage from the nobility of King Edward. [Col. 0877B]

When King William learned of their reckless acts and designs, he brought out the Norman forces and marched as quickly as possible to crush their obstinacy. The rebels, trusting in their courage and strength, rushed out of the city and immediately drew up their line against the royal army. They were at once so thoroughly routed that very many were killed and the rest were forced to take refuge within the walls of the town.

The Normans followed them immediately and burst with them into the circuit of the wall behind which they had taken refuge. By sword and fire alike, they destroyed almost the entire city, from boy to old man. The instigators of the whole plot, however, escaped the destruction of death by ship along the river Humber.

## CHAPTER XLI  
### How Brian, son of Eudon, count of Lesser Brittany, defeated the two sons of Harold together with the army of the king of Ireland

[Col. 0877C]

Meanwhile, the sons of King Harold withdrew from their association with those men and, together with many native allies, approached Dermot, king of Ireland, seeking assistance. With his support, they soon gathered for themselves a considerable force of soldiers from his kingdom.

Then, with sixty-six ships, they returned as quickly as possible to the English coast at the place they judged most suitable. In the manner of the most savage pirates, they attempted to destroy the people of the land through plunder and fire.

Brian, son of Eudon, duke of Lesser Brittany, met them there armed with his men and immediately joined battle with them in two engagements on the same day. After killing seventeen hundred warriors, together with some nobles of the kingdom, the survivors fled from the conflict and, with the protection of their ships, escaped the destruction of death as best they could. They carried back to the Irish the greatest grief over the loss of their loved ones. Indeed, if night had not separated the combatants, all of them would have been shaved away by the razor of death.

## CHAPTER XLII  
### That King William, traveling through England, built many castles for the defense of the kingdom

Finally, the assassins hiding within Durham, having learned of the misfortunes of so many people united in the same madness through pernicious conspiracies, still dared to persist in their distress with weapons and flight. Fearing the royal expedition against them, they deliberately adopted the course appropriate to such ill-considered recklessness and withdrew to the more remote coastal strongholds, accumulating dishonorable wealth for themselves by piratical robbery.

But the king, instructed by the prudence with which he knew how to advise a ruler in every matter, carefully surveyed the undefended parts of the kingdom. To repel the enemy’s raids, he established extremely secure castles in suitable locations and fortified them with the choicest strength of soldiers and an abundant supply of pay.

At last, when the storm of wars and rebellions had subsided for a while, he both controlled the reins of the entire English monarchy more powerfully and enjoyed its glory with greater prosperity.

## CHAPTER XLIII  
### Concerning the death of Robert Wiscard, duke of Apulia, his excellence and that of his descendants, and the circumstances in which his nephew Roger became king

[Col. 0878B]

At this time Robert Wiscard, a Norman by birth, duke of Apulia, died. Having dismissed his first wife on account of consanguinity—for by her he had fathered a son named Bohemond—he married Sichelgaita, the eldest daughter of Gaimar, prince of Salerno, with the support of Gisulf, the girl’s brother, who had succeeded their father Gaimar. Her younger sister Gatteclima [Gatteclinia] married Jordan, prince of Capua, son of Richard the Elder and father of Richard the Younger. His father founded the city called Aversa.

Robert Wiscard had by Sichelgaita three sons and five daughters. His daughters were married with such distinction that one of them was joined in marriage to the emperor of Constantinople. This Robert defeated two emperors in battle: Alexius of the Greeks in Greece and Henry of the Romans in Italy. Henry was thoroughly defeated; when he heard of Duke Robert’s reputation, he trusted neither the strength of the Saxons and Alemannians nor even the walls of the city that is the head of the world. Finding no safety there, he fled in haste.

Bohemond, although he possessed extensive lands, eventually went with the other Normans and French to fight against the Saracens, who at that time held nearly all the cities of Romania. After finally defeating the pagans and subjugating the cities of Antioch, Jerusalem, and many others, Bohemond obtained the principality of Antioch. His heirs succeeded him: namely, his son Bohemond, born of Constance, daughter of King Philip of France; and after him Raymond, son of William, count of Poitiers, who had married the daughter of the second Bohemond.

When Duke Robert departed this life, his son succeeded him. He was the firstborn of his second wife and was named Roger, with the surname Bursa. When this Roger also died, and his sons after him, Roger, his cousin—the son of Count Roger of Sicily, brother of Robert Wiscard—obtained sole possession of both Apulia and Sicily.

In the course of time this man became king from being a duke, because of a dispute between two Apostolic pontiffs who had been ordained at Rome at the same time: namely, Innocent II and Peter Leonis. The latter granted Duke Roger permission to wear the royal diadem because the duke favored his party. This occurred around the year 1130 from the Lord’s Incarnation. The two men lived together for nearly eight years.

## CHAPTER XLIV  
### Concerning the death of William, king of the English and duke of the Normans, and his burial at Caen

Having briefly related these matters in anticipation, let us now come to the end of the deeds of William, king of the English and duke of the Normans. In order to spare our readers’ weariness, we have touched upon some matters concisely. If anyone wishes to know them more fully, let him read the book of William of Poitiers, archdeacon of Lisieux, which contains these same deeds abundantly and in eloquent language. Moreover, Bishop Guido of Amiens published on the same subject a work not unworthy of attention, written in heroic meter.

But, so that we may now bring our discourse to an end, let us disclose, according to the opinion of certain people, the cause of his death.

After this victorious king had successfully completed many wars and numerous expeditions in Normandy, England, Lesser Brittany, and also Maine, he attacked and committed to avenging flames a certain town named Mantes, the property of Philip, king of the Franks. At that time Philip was aiding Robert, the duke’s son, who was waging war against his father. The cause of this disagreement was that King William did not allow this son to do as he wished with the duchy of Normandy, although he himself had made him his heir after him.

When King William had attacked and given the town of Mantes over to the avenging flames, the weight of his armor and the strain of shouting as he encouraged his men allegedly caused the fat of his intestines to melt, and he began to fall seriously ill. Although he lived for some time afterward, he did not enjoy his usual health.

At length, having arranged his affairs and granted the kingdom of England to his son William, he ended his present life in Normandy at Rouen, on the fourth day before the Ides of September. As he had ordered, his body was transferred to Caen and buried with royal honors before the high altar in the church of Saint Stephen, which he himself had built from the foundations.

Only one of his sons, Henry, attended his father’s funeral—the one worthy eventually to possess the paternal inheritance alone, which his brothers held piecemeal after their father’s death. The same king died at nearly sixty years of age, in the fifty-second year of his duchy in Normandy, in the twentieth year of his reign in England, and in the year 1087 of the Lord’s Incarnation.

With our same Lord Jesus Christ reigning with the eternal Father in the unity of the Holy Spirit, throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

# EIGHTH BOOK OF THE HISTORY OF THE NORMANS
## Concerning Henry I, king of the English and duke of the Normans

## CHAPTER I. Prologue to the deeds of King Henry, in which he is briefly shown to be better than his brothers

[Col. 0879C]

Since the preceding book treated of the acts of William, king of the English and duke of the Normans, it will not seem unfitting that this book—which is being composed as the seventh in the history of the deeds of the Norman dukes [Note: [Col. 0879] But it is the eighth book of the History of the Normans, as the heading of the manuscript which we have followed has it.]—should set before the age to come, and especially before posterity, for imitation, the life, conduct, and, to no small extent, the deeds of Henry, the most noble king, son of the aforesaid William. Nor without reason does this number suit that man, who excelled greatly not only in nobility of mind but also in bodily excellence, namely in the true combination of three and four. Moreover, it happened that the same king whom we have undertaken to describe is found in the [Col. 0879D] seventh degree of the genealogy of the Norman dukes, if one begins the reckoning with Duke Rollo, who was the founder of this lineage.

But, in order that the continuity of the history may be maintained, something must first be said, even if briefly, about his brothers, William king of the English and Robert duke of the Normans, whom he alone succeeded [Col. 0880C]; especially since this contributes to the commendation of the subject undertaken. For just as painters customarily lay down a rust-colored ground so that the red laid over it may shine out more brightly, so perhaps, if the aforesaid brothers are compared with this man, he will shine more brilliantly by comparison with them. This may be observed in a few words. In one of them—I mean William—liberality toward secular men was praised, but religion, which he held in great contempt, loudly complained. Robert was deservedly extolled by fame in military affairs, but that same quality truly showed him to be less useful in maturity of counsel and in the government of the duchy. But Henry alone, embracing those qualities which seemed honorable in each of them, and likewise possessing those qualities which, as we have said, they lacked [Col. 0880D], was judged nobler not only than they but than all the princes of his time. But because these matters will be set forth more fully in their proper places, lest we seem to make a digression at the very beginning, let us henceforth pursue the order of the matters proposed.

## CHAPTER II. That William, Henry's brother, after the death of William their father, crossed into England and became king; that Robert obtained the duchy of Normandy; and that this same Robert gave the county of the Cotentin to Henry and afterward took it away

[Col. 0881A]

Accordingly, when William, king of the English, had been removed from human affairs, his son William crossed the sea at Toques as quickly as he could, was received by the English and the French, and was anointed king at London, in Westminster, by Lanfranc, archbishop of Canterbury, and his suffragans. For his brother Robert had left Normandy before their father's death, taking it ill that his father did not allow him to dispose at his own will of either the duchy of Normandy or that of Maine [Col. 0881B]. He had long before been designated heir of the former, while during his father's life he sought the government of the latter because Margaret, daughter of Herbert, formerly count of Maine, had been betrothed to him; although, before he attained her marriage-bed, that maiden, devoted to Christ, died at Fécamp.

While he was staying in Ponthieu at Abbeville with young men like himself—the sons, that is, of the Norman magnates, who outwardly rendered him obedience as though to their future lord, but were in truth drawn by a desire for revolution—and was especially ravaging the borders of the duchy of Normandy by raids and plundering, he heard the news of his father's death. He therefore came at once to Rouen and received that city and the whole duchy without any opposition. When his adherents urged him quickly to recover by arms from his brother the kingdom of England, which had been snatched from him, he is said to have replied with his customary simplicity, indeed with something close to imprudence: “By the angels of God, if I were in Alexandria, the English would wait for me and would not dare to make a king for themselves before my arrival. Nor would my brother William himself, without my permission, venture upon what you say he has presumed, on pain of his life.” At first he spoke thus, but after he learned the course of events, no small discord arose between him and his brother William.

Meanwhile their brother Henry remained in Normandy with Duke Robert. His father, when dying, had given Henry five thousand pounds in English money [Col. 0881C]. His brother Robert also gave him, or, as others maintain, mortgaged to him, the county of the Cotentin. But he did not enjoy it for long. For, having found certain paltry pretexts, though at the prompting of evil men, Robert seized Henry at Rouen when he was contemplating nothing of the sort, and disgracefully extorted from him what he had given.

## CHAPTER III. Concerning the agreement made between William, king of the English, and his brother Robert, duke of Normandy, and how they besieged their brother Henry at Mont-Saint-Michel

After this, when some time had passed, William king of the English and Robert duke of Normandy made an agreement with each other [Col. 0882A], although Robert himself could easily have had the kingdom of England a little before, had he not been too heedless. For Count Eustace of Boulogne, the bishop of Bayeux, the count of Mortain, his uncles, and other Norman magnates crossed the sea with a great military force, occupied and held Rochester and several other castles in the county of Kent for his use; but while they awaited Duke Robert himself, who at that time was indulging himself in Normandy more than befitted a man, they were long besieged by King William. Since he for whose sake they had undergone so great a danger did not come to their aid, they left the fortifications which they held in disgrace and returned home.

At length there was made between them at Caen, as we have said, with the assistance of Philip, king of the Franks—who had come to aid the duke against King William, then staying with a huge army of English and Normans at the town of Eu—an agreement of some sort, shameful and ruinous so far as Duke Robert was concerned [Col. 0882B]. For King William was allowed with impunity to keep whatever he had occupied in Normandy through the treachery of the duke's men, who had handed over to that king the strongholds which Robert had entrusted to his own soldiers so that they might harass his brother from them. The strongholds which he held in this manner were Fécamp and the town of Eu, which Count William of Eu had handed over to him with his other fortresses. Stephen, count of Aumale, son of Odo, count of Champagne, and nephew through his sister of the elder William, king of the English, had done likewise [Col. 0882C], as had many others dwelling beyond the Seine.

Although they ought to have helped and provided for their brother Henry, so that, as brother of their king and son of a king, he might live honorably, they attempted to expel him from all his father's land. Hence it happened that on one occasion they besieged him at Mont-Saint-Michel. But while they labored there fruitlessly for a long time and finally fell out among themselves, Count Henry came out freely and, through the ingenuity of a certain native, received the very strongly fortified town called Domfront. For that native, being a noble and wealthy man, was indignant to endure any longer the oppressions which Robert of Bellême, a fierce man of inhuman mind, then lord of that castle, inflicted upon him and his neighbors [Col. 0882D]. Henry thereafter guarded it with such diligence that he held it in his own lordship until the end of his life. About this time, when John, archbishop of Rouen, died, William, abbot of Saint Stephen at Caen, succeeded him.

## CHAPTER IV. That, when King William returned to England, Henry restored the county of the Cotentin to his own control

When King William returned to England, Henry, with the consent of King William and the aid of Richard de Reviers and Roger de Mandeville, not sluggishly restored to his own control the greater part of the county of the Cotentin, which had previously been fraudulently taken from him [Col. 0883A]. Since Count Hugh of Chester had proved faithful to him in this matter and in most of his other necessities, Henry granted him outright the castle called Saint-James, in which that count at the time possessed nothing except the custody of the fortification of the town itself. The elder William, king of the English, had founded it on the boundary of Normandy and Lesser Brittany, when, before the English war, he was leading an army against Conan, count of Brittany, son of his cousin Alan, who did not obey him. In order that the hungry Breton raiders might no longer harm undefended churches or the common people at the farthest edge of his land by predatory raids [Col. 0883B], he established it to repel them and entrusted it to Richard, governor of Avranches, father of the aforesaid Count Hugh.

## CHAPTER V. That the men of Maine, observing that Duke Robert was occupied by many disturbances in Normandy, made Helias, son of John of La Flèche, their count

Meanwhile, seeing Duke Robert occupied by so many disturbances in Normandy, the men of Maine entered into a plan with Helias, son of John of La Flèche, a valiant and energetic man and the most powerful in that province, that he should marry the daughter of a certain count of Lombardy, namely the niece of Herbert, formerly count of Maine, through his eldest daughter [Col. 0883C]. They believed that by this means they could shake from their necks the yoke of the Norman dukes' dominion. They did not need to spend long in persuading him, since the man already named, having long anticipated their proposal with his own desire, brought their purpose in this matter to effect without any delay.

Neither he nor his advisers was deterred from this presumptuous rebellion by the fact that the region of Maine had anciently been under the dominion of the Norman dukes, or that within our memory William, the most noble duke of the Normans and afterward the most fortunate conqueror of the English, had liberated these same men of Maine from the oppression of the elder Geoffrey Martel, secured them under his protection, ruled them as his own while he lived, and at his death left them to be ruled by his successors [Col. 0883D]. Thus it came about that, soon after that king's death, Duke Robert, of whom we are now speaking, at the beginning of his duchy, led an army of Normans against them and restrained them when they were already attempting the obstinacy of rebellion within his own borders.

## CHAPTER VI. That, when Anselm, abbot of Bec, was raised to the archbishopric of Canterbury, William, a professed monk of the same house, succeeded him

At the same time, when Anselm, abbot of Bec, was raised to the archbishopric of Canterbury, William of Beaumont, a man of no slight religious devotion and a professed monk of the same monastery, succeeded him in the government of that house [Col. 0884A]. In the following year Pope Urban came into Gaul and assembled a council in the city of Auvergne, also called Clermont, to deal with ecclesiastical matters. Among the other salutary measures which he took there, he urged the faithful, both present and absent, to go to Jerusalem for the remission of their sins, in order to free the holy places from the power of the pagans, by whom they were then possessed and defiled.

## CHAPTER VII. That Robert, duke of Normandy, having mortgaged his duchy to his brother William, king of the English, went to Jerusalem.

[Col. 0884B] Therefore, in the following year, moved by this divine exhortation, almost all the soldiers of renowned valor from the western region—both the illustrious and the rest of humbler station—undertook the journey of holy pilgrimage. Inflamed by this desire, Robert, duke of the Northmen, sent word through a messenger to his brother William, king of the English, that he should hasten to Normandy and hold his duchy until Robert’s return, while supplying on the way his own needs and those of his followers from the abundant treasures of the English.

The king William, delighted by the message of this embassy, crossed over into Normandy and lent Duke Robert ten thousand marks of silver, on the condition that, for as long as the duke remained on the aforesaid pilgrimage, he himself should hold the duchy of Normandy as security for the money, restoring it to the duke when Robert, on his return, had repaid the sum specified to him. After these events, Count Henry went to King William and remained with him altogether. The king granted him the counties of Coutances and Bayeux in their entirety, except for the city of Bayeux and the town of Caen. At this time the aforesaid King William built a certain castle called Gisors on the border of Normandy and France. His brother Henry, often mentioned above, who by divine providence succeeded him, made it impregnable by surrounding it with walls and lofty towers.

## CHAPTER VIII. On the valor of this William in the affairs of the kingdom, and how he persecuted the Church of God and its servants

Concerning this William, we could insert in the pages of these Annals [Col. 0884D] that, once and again, he led an army against the Welsh and subdued them when they rebelled against him in their own territory; and that, meeting with his army King Malcolm of Scotland, who had brought an army into England, he compelled him to accept whatever agreements he wished.

We might likewise report that, when he heard that Helias, count of Maine, had besieged his own men in the city of Le Mans, with Count Fulk of Anjou aiding him—for Helias had first taken that city from the king’s men, but the citizens had restored it to the king, whereupon Helias had besieged them again—William, I say, having heard this while he was in England, summoned the soldiers who happened then to be with him and ordered the absent to follow. Coming to the sea, and finding the wind contrary for crossing to Normandy, he entered the open sea against the wind, saying that he had never heard of any king who had perished in a shipwreck. Having crossed the sea, as though contending against the force of the elements, he drove the aforesaid counts from the siege merely by the report of his arrival.

These things, I say, and others like them, we could truthfully relate about him, were it not that, because he persecuted many of God’s servants and the holy Church to no small degree—and consequently performed repentance late and, as many wise men believe, fruitlessly—we judge it appropriate, for the order of the history, merely to touch briefly upon his deeds and to proceed to explain at greater length the acts of his brother and successor, Henry of blessed memory, who greatly honored religious men and the Church of God by protecting and assisting them.

While this William was governing the kingdom of England, Morell, nephew of Robert de Mowbray, count of Northumberland, slaughtered the aforesaid Malcolm, king of Scotland, who was making raids in England, together with his eldest son and most of his army, within the borders of England. This Robert, however, when he attempted against the will of his lord to seize certain royal fortifications adjoining his county, was captured by King William’s soldiers. By the king’s command he remained in those bonds for a long time and, when King Henry was already reigning, eventually died in that prison, worn out.

Many said that this was retribution inflicted upon him because he had treacherously killed the king of Scotland, the father of the most noble Matilda, later queen of the English. Henry, by then king, gave the land he possessed in Normandy and most of the aforesaid county to Nigel d’Aubigny, an illustrious and honorable man.

Nigel later married Gundred, daughter of Gerard de Gournay, by whom he fathered a son named Roger de Mowbray. While still a child, Roger succeeded his father, who had become a monk of Bec and had bestowed a large possession in England upon that place. Gerard himself, at the request of his father Hugh de Gournay, who was a monk of Bec, gave many things to the same church. At last, while traveling to Jerusalem with his wife Edith, sister of William, count of Warenne, he died on the journey. His wife, returning from there, married Drogo de Moncey, by whom Drogo had one son named Drogo.

Gerard was succeeded by his son Hugh, who, by a sister of Ralph, count of Vermandois, fathered a son named Hugh. We have briefly mentioned these matters in advance here, concerning the friends and benefactors of the monastery of Bec; now let us return to the order of the history.

## CHAPTER IX. On the death of the same king in the New Forest, and how his brother Richard had previously died there, and on the cause of their deaths according to popular belief

Therefore, as we said above, when Robert, duke of the Northmen, went to Jerusalem in the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1096 [Col. 0886A] and pawned the duchy of Normandy to his brother William, king of the English, it happened after some time that the same king went hunting one day in the New Forest. There, on 2 August, he was struck in the heart by an arrow carelessly shot by one of his attendants and died in the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1100, in the thirteenth year of his reign.

In the same forest, Richard, William’s brother, had also died earlier, while their father was still alive. While hunting in a similar manner, he was injured by the blow of a tree that he had failed to avoid properly; shortly afterward, he departed from human life. Many said that these two sons of King William perished in that forest by God’s judgment because, in order to enlarge the forest, he had destroyed many villages and churches around it.

## CHAPTER X. How his brother Henry succeeded him and took Matilda, daughter of the king of Scotland, as his wife

[Col. 0886B]

After King William had been killed, as we have related, his brother Henry immediately had his body carried to Winchester and there buried it in the church of Saint Peter before the high altar. After the burial, he came to London and, with all the French and English consenting, received the royal diadem at Westminster on the fourth day after his brother’s death.

Many rejoiced that they had now been granted a king born of a king and queen, and born and raised in England. So that this king might live lawfully, in the same year he married the venerable Matilda, daughter of Malcolm, king of Scotland, and Margaret. How great in holiness [Col. 0886C] and in secular as well as spiritual knowledge both queens were—Margaret, namely, and Matilda—the book written about their lives describes in plain language.

Nor should it be omitted that, by Anselm, archbishop of Canterbury of holy memory, this same Matilda was betrothed to the most noble King Henry at Westminster on the feast of Saint Martin, and on the same day adorned with the royal diadem. King Henry was a man endowed with many virtues: a follower of justice and peace, a lover of religion, a most zealous punisher of the wicked and of thieves, and a most fortunate victor over his enemies—not only eminent princes and counts, but also kings of the greatest renown.

## CHAPTER XI. How he fathered by her a son named William and a daughter who later married Henry, emperor of the Romans

[Col. 0886D]

By his second wife, Matilda, queen of the English, he fathered one son named William and one daughter, who resembled her mother in honor as well as in name. When this girl was scarcely five years old, Henry V, king and fourth emperor of the Romans and Germans, sought her in marriage. Having obtained her through distinguished bishops and counts acting as envoys, he received her into his kingdom with the ineffable generosity [joy] of both parents and solemnly betrothed her at the next Easter at Utrecht.

[Col. 0887A] The archbishop of Cologne consecrated her as queen at Mainz on the feast of Saint James, with the other bishops assisting, especially the archbishop of Trier, who reverently held her in his arms during the consecration. He then ordered that, once consecrated queen, she should be carefully brought up until the proper time for the wedding, so that in this upbringing she might learn the language and shape herself according to Teutonic customs. We shall speak more fully below about this most noble empress.

The aforesaid William, son of King Henry, who was born after his sister Matilda the empress, though we have placed him before her because of his male sex, died an untimely death when he had already reached young manhood. As he was crossing from Normandy to England, between Barfleur and Southampton, the ship struck a rock in a dangerous place at sea which the inhabitants call the Cataracts; he and many of his father’s nobles perished in the shipwreck.

This single event somewhat clouded the fortune of the most excellent king, although in all other matters the most agreeable good fortune smiled upon him. Having mentioned these matters in advance, let us return to the order of events.

## CHAPTER XII. How Robert, duke of the Northmen, returning from Jerusalem, crossed into England, intending to take the kingdom from his brother, and how they were reconciled

Not much time had passed after King Henry undertook the government of the kingdom of England when his brother Robert returned from Jerusalem [Col. 0887C] and recovered the duchy of Normandy, which he had pawned to his brother William, without producing any money, although he had the sum he had received from that brother with him, so that he might return it if necessary and have it ready if anyone demanded it.

When he heard that his brother Henry had been established as king of the English, he began to grow angry with him and threatened him greatly, because he had dared to assume the kingdom of England. For this reason he began to prepare as large a fleet as he could. When it was ready, he crossed into England.

King Henry, whose whole confidence was in God, quickly assembled a large force of English soldiers and advanced against him, prepared to expel him and all who had come with him from English soil. He would certainly have accomplished this quickly by God’s favor [Col. 0887D], had not his brother made peace with him on these terms: that the king himself should pay him thousands of marks of silver every year in perpetuity. The same count, however, forgave this sum to Queen Matilda, his brother’s wife.

After peace had been made between them, Count Robert remained in England for some time. When he had stayed there as long as he wished, he returned to Normandy.

## CHAPTER XIII. How, after this agreement had been broken, Henry captured him in battle at Tinchebray and thereafter wisely governed the duchy of Normandy together with the kingdom of England until his death

The aforesaid peace between them did not last long. Count Robert, believing too readily those who preferred discord between them to peace, began to seek opportunities and to stir up his brother against him.

King Henry could no longer endure this, and he was especially indignant that his brother had so squandered his paternal inheritance, namely the duchy of Normandy, that he possessed almost nothing except the city of Rouen—indeed, he might perhaps have given that away like the rest, had this not been unlawful for him on account of its citizens. Indignant at this, I say, he crossed the sea as quickly as he could and soon afterward assembled a considerable army. He besieged the city of Bayeux and, capturing it quickly, almost completely destroyed it. Then he captured Caen.

After some time, while he was besieging a castle of the count of Mortain called Tinchebray [Col. 0888B] and laboring to capture it, his brother Count Robert and the count of Mortain, believing that they would avenge themselves upon King Henry and utterly destroy him from the land, attacked him with a great force and a violent charge. But when God’s judgment came upon them, both were captured, along with many others, by King Henry’s men and brought before him.

In this way God granted the God-fearing king a bloodless victory, just as he had once done for the emperor Theodosius, his servant. In this encounter none of Henry’s men fell, while scarcely sixty from the opposing side were killed.

After the battle had ended and peace had been restored to the wretched province, which had nearly been destroyed through the count’s imprudence, King Henry took all Normandy and all the castles of the count of Mortain under his own authority. Having thus pacified the whole land, he returned to England, bringing with him his brother Count Robert, the count of Mortain, and certain others whom he chose; he kept them in free custody until the end of their lives.

This battle took place at Tinchebray between Henry, king of the English, and his brother Robert, duke of the Northmen, in the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1106, on 27 September. In the same year, in February, a comet had appeared, terrifying kings and dukes with the prospect of changes in kingdoms.

Count Robert ruled the duchy of Normandy for nineteen years, except for the period during which he remained on the journey to Jerusalem. This Robert was a very brave soldier and accomplished many noble deeds, especially when Antioch and Jerusalem were captured from the Saracens by the Christians. For governing the duchy, however, he was less useful because of his simplicity and because he lent too ready an ear to frivolous counsels.

## CHAPTER XIV. On Sibylla, wife of Duke Robert, and his son William, and how this William became count of Flanders

When he returned from the journey to Jerusalem, he took as his wife Sibylla, sister of William, count of Conversano, by whom he fathered one son named William. This countess was beautiful in appearance, honorable in conduct, and endowed with wisdom. When the duke was absent, she herself managed the affairs of the province, both private [Col. 0889A] and public, better than he would have done had he been present.

She lived only a short time in Normandy, deceived by the envy and faction of certain noblewomen. The aforesaid William, son of Duke Robert, later became count of Flanders. How this happened, let us explain briefly.

When he was already a young man and was living in exile in France, his father—as we have said—being held in the bonds of King Henry, it happened that certain traitors killed Charles, count of Flanders, in a church while he was attending the sacred mysteries. When the queen of the French, wife of King Louis, heard this, she gave her sister in marriage to the aforesaid William and brought it about through her husband that he was made count of Flanders. For Charles had died without a son.

[Col. 0889B] Yet William was not far removed from kinship with the counts of Flanders. Queen Matilda of the English, his grandmother, was the daughter of Baldwin with the Beard, count of Flanders. This Baldwin had two sons, Baldwin and Robert. Each of them took a wife while their father was still alive.

Baldwin, the elder son, married the countess of Hainaut, by whom he fathered two sons, Arnulf and Baldwin. Robert, however, married the widow of Florentius, count of Frisia. By Florentius she had one daughter. Wishing to remove her far from her paternal inheritance, Robert gave her to Philip, king of the French. Thus the county of Frisia remained to the girl together with her mother, and Robert was surnamed the Frisian.

Baldwin, count of Hainaut, died before his father Baldwin, and his elder son Arnulf succeeded him. At last, when Baldwin, count of Flanders, died, and Arnulf, count of Hainaut, ought to succeed him as his grandson through his elder son—and was also striving to do so—King Philip of the French came to his aid. His aunt, Queen Matilda of the English, sent him William, son of Osbern, with an armed force of soldiers.

But Robert the Frisian, his uncle, joining with his own forces the contingents of Henry, emperor of the Northmen and Germans, unexpectedly attacked them on Septuagesima Sunday. He put King Philip of the French to flight and killed his nephew Arnulf and William, son of Osbern, count of Hereford. For this reason he possessed Flanders until his death.

## CHAPTER XV. On William, count of Hereford, and his succession

The aforesaid William, count of Hereford, was an honorable and upright man and was related to the dukes of Normandy not only through his father but also through his mother. His father Osbern was the son of Herfast, brother of Gunnor, countess and wife of Richard I, the first duke of Normandy. His mother was the daughter of Ralph, count of Ivry. This Ralph was the uterine brother of the aforementioned Duke Richard.

William married Adeliza, daughter of Roger de Tosny, by whom he fathered two sons: William de Braose, who after his death possessed the land [Col. 0890A] that he had in Normandy; and Roger, to whom the county of Hereford fell by the allotment of inheritance. He also had two daughters. One, named Emma, was married to Ralph de Waiet, a Breton by birth, who was count of Norwich. But when he attempted, against his fidelity to William the elder king, to hold the fortification of Norwich, he was expelled and exiled from the kingdom of England. He went with his wife to Jerusalem, leaving one daughter named Itta, who later married Robert, count of Leicester, son of Robert, count of Meulan.

Thus it happened that Lire, Glo, Breteuil, and much of the land that William, son of Osbern, the grandfather of his wife, had possessed in Normandy came into the possession of that same count after the death of William de Breteuil, his wife’s maternal uncle. By her he fathered one son and several sons.

After William, son of Osbern, had been killed, as we have said, his son William de Breteuil, who had succeeded him, began to claim the town of Ivry because it had belonged to Ralph, count of Ivry, his grandmother’s father. At that time the same castle was held in his dominion by Robert, duke of Normandy, just as his father, King William, had held it throughout his life.

Countess Albereda, wife of Count Robert, had begun to build a very strong tower on the summit of the mountain overlooking the castle; it still stands today. Count Robert of Meulan, who guarded that tower, exercised the office of viscount in the aforesaid town.

By his customary cunning, he brought it about that the castle was restored to William de Breteuil, but on this condition: in return for what he then held in that town, he should possess Brionne, adjoining his land, forever by a grant from Duke Robert.

From ancient times that town had been one of the proper residences of the dukes of Normandy. Hence they had always held it in their dominion, except that Richard II had given it to his natural brother, Count Geoffrey, and his son Count Gilbert had held it after him. After Gilbert was killed, however, it returned to the dominion of the dukes of Normandy.

Since Roger, son of Richard, was reclaiming the same castle because his grandfather, Count Gilbert, had previously possessed it, as has been said, Count Robert of Meulan, desiring to avoid all disturbance, prevailed upon Duke Robert to give Roger, son of Richard, a certain town called Humet, situated in the county of Coutances, not only to settle that claim but also in exchange for the small sum of money which Roger had given the duke for this purpose.

Many of the ancients say that Richard, Roger’s father, had earlier received the town of Tonbridge in England in return for reclaiming the same castle. They assert that the league of Brionne had been measured all around with a cord, and that when the same cord was carried to England, the league of Tonbridge measured out the same distance, exactly as the Brionne mile is demonstrably still preserved.

After some time, it happened that Goel of Breherii-Valley treacherously captured his lord William de Breteuil and held him in captivity for so long that William was compelled to grant him a certain illegitimate daughter of his own together with the castle of Ivry.

[Note: [Col. 0891D] One manuscript has “Virey” instead of “Ivry,” and so everywhere.]

By her that man of Belial fathered William Lovell, Roger the Stammerer, and others, in whom the wickedness and deceit of their father, like evil seed, still persists to the destruction of the innocent.

After William de Breteuil had been freed from his bonds, mindful of the injury inflicted upon him by the traitor, he dared to undertake an enterprise worthy of remembrance. He summoned Philip, king of the French, with a very large army, and Robert, duke of Normandy, by immense gifts. He also supplied from his own resources everything necessary for them and for all their men who were willing to accept his support.

[Col. 0891B] He almost completely destroyed the castle of Breherii-Valley and all Goel’s land, and, besieging Ivry for so long that the traitor despaired of his possessions, he compelled him to restore it. Thus William ultimately possessed that castle securely as his own for the remainder of his life.

When William was approaching the end of his life, he made a certain young man, Ralph de Waiet, his nephew through his sister Emma, heir to his estate. But Eustace, his natural son, during his father’s funeral occupied and fortified all his fortifications and held all his father’s land peacefully for a long time through this seizure. This continued until his wife Juliana, an illegitimate daughter of King Henry, acting with excessive arrogance and relying on support against the king’s will and fidelity, expelled her guards from the fortification of Breteuil.

For this reason the king, angered, rightly deprived him of the whole inheritance which he had possessed until then not by hereditary right but by his own seizure—or rather by the king’s clemency. The castle of Ivry [Ibrey] was indeed restored to Goel and his sons. Robert, count of Leicester, later received the remaining land, as we have already said, together with his wife. Eustace was therefore left only the town of Passais.

Since we have treated at greater length this matter concerning William, son of Osbern, whom we mentioned above, let us now return to what we had begun to say about the counts of Flanders.

## CHAPTER XVI. On the death of William, count of Flanders

Therefore, to the aforementioned Robert, count of Flanders, Henry [Col. 0891D], king of the Saxons and emperor of the Romans, gave the county of Cambrai, and Robert rendered him homage for it. The same Robert fathered two sons, Robert and Philip.

Robert, surnamed the Jerusalemite because he was present when Jerusalem was captured by the Christians, fathered Baldwin, who succeeded him. When this Baldwin died from a wound that he had received in a battle at a certain castle called Aucum in Normandy, his kinsman Charles succeeded him. After Charles was killed by treachery, as has already been said, William, son of Robert, duke of Normandy [Col. 0892A], held the same county of Flanders, as we stated above.

But he survived only a short time, having been struck by a mortal wound during the assault on a certain town. He died on 27 July in the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1128. He was buried in the church of Saint Bertin the Confessor, and was succeeded by Thierry of Alsace, a kinsman of the earlier counts. King Henry of the English married him to the sister of Geoffrey Martel, count of Anjou.

Robert, duke of Normandy, father of the aforesaid William, died in England at the castle of Bristol, belonging to his nephew Robert, count of Gloucester, to whose custody King Henry had entrusted him. He died on 10 February and was buried in the church of Saint Peter at Gloucester, in the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1134. Having conveyed these matters in advance, let us now return to the order of the history.

## CHAPTER XVII. How, after the death of Philip, king of the French, his son Louis succeeded him, and on the origin of the counts of Évreux and their descendants

About this time Philip, king of the French, departed from human affairs, and his son Louis succeeded him. After William, archbishop of Rouen, died, Geoffrey, dean of Le Mans, obtained the same episcopal seat.

A short time afterward William, count of Évreux, died. Since we have mentioned this city, we wish to trace briefly the earlier origin of its counts.

Robert, son of Richard I, the first duke of Normandy, archbishop of Rouen and count of the city of Évreux, contrary to ecclesiastical custom took a wife, like any layman, and fathered two sons: Richard, who succeeded him in the county, and Ralph of Wace.

Count Richard, by the widow of Roger de Tosny, who had been killed in a certain battle, fathered the aforesaid William, who succeeded him, and one daughter, who married Simon de Montfort. By her were born Amaury and his sister Bertha.

Before her, however, Simon had had two wives. By the first of these he fathered his elder son, namely another Amaury, and his sister Elizabeth. After that Amaury was killed, Ralph de Tosny—

[Note: [Col. 0891D] The remainder of this chapter and the following chapters XVIII, XIX, and XX, together with the beginning of XXI, are also missing from the Gemmeticensis manuscript.]

[lacuna]

## CHAPTER XVIII. On the discord between King Henry and Amaury, count of the city of Évreux

[Col. 0892D]

## CHAPTER XIX. On the war between Louis, king of the French, and Henry, king of the English

## CHAPTER XX. How, after making peace with King Louis, King Henry returned to England, and on the death of his son William

## CHAPTER XXI. On the disagreement between the same king and Walerannus, count of Meulan, and how it ended

[lacuna]

Finally, with the troops arranged in the manner of combatants, and with mounted archers—of whom the royal army had a very large number there—sent ahead on the enemy’s right, a shout arose on both sides, as is customary at the beginning of battles. But before the soldiers’ divisions joined, the count’s side had almost given way under the persistence of the archers, who shot at it continuously on the right, where it lacked the protection of shields.

It would be tedious to proceed through every detail, but, hastening to what follows, we shall briefly explain the outcome of the affair.

When the battle had begun, Count Walerannus was subsequently captured. All those famous and wealthy soldiers who followed his banners were also captured, although some, after falling into the hands of the enemy, escaped by flight with the agreement of certain of their close associates whom they had in the royal army [Col. 0893B]. Among these were Amaury, count of Évreux, and William Lovell of Ivry.

This battle was fought by the commanders of Henry, king of the English, against Walerannus, count of Meulan, in the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1124, on 26 March, not far from a village called Bourg-Théroulde.

## CHAPTER XXII. With what prudence the same king ruled his land in peace

After Count Walerannus had been placed in bonds together with his companions, King Henry had the tower of Watteville utterly demolished. Moreover, after subduing the town of Brionne by force rather than voluntary surrender, he punished by blinding the man who had held it for a long time after the count’s capture.

Terrified by this, the men guarding the castle of Beaumont, lest they suffer similar treatment, surrendered it to the king. Thus, after all that disturbance had been quieted, the king held in his dominion both the count’s land and that of the others who had been captured with him.

After several years, however, Count Walerannus was pardoned and released from his bonds, and was permitted to possess his land again, while the king retained only his fortifications in his own hand. Some of his fellow captives remained in their bonds for as long as that king lived.

From the time Count of Meulan was captured in the aforesaid battle, complete peace prevailed both in the duchy of Normandy and throughout the kingdom of England for the entire decade that King Henry survived, although his nephew William, during the short time in which he held the county of Flanders, tried as far as he could to disturb it.

But since the wise king surpassed almost all the princes of his time in mercy and wealth, through the one—namely, mercy—he showed consideration to the churches, monasteries, and poor men of his land; through the other, that is, the limitless abundance of his treasures, he stationed many hundreds of soldiers in different places near his enemies, so that they might repel them by force of arms from plundering churches or the poor.

Thus it happened that even that land of the renowned Emperor Henry, which lay on the borders of the other provinces, was rarely harmed by any hostile injury, let alone the land farther away from them. For, as has been said, the multitude of soldiers whom the most excellent prince adequately supported at his own expense and honored with gifts stood against them.

## CHAPTER XXIII. What he did, for love of justice, concerning the moneyers who had debased the coinage throughout almost all England

I shall relate something that occurred while the aforesaid discord between the king and the count of Meulan was still continuing. In it both the severity of his justice toward the impious and his contempt for money in comparison with uprightness will become evident.

While he was engaged in military affairs in Normandy, it happened that, through some perverse corruption, almost all the moneyers of the English kingdom manufactured tin coinage in which scarcely a third was silver, whereas the same coin had customarily been made entirely of silver.

When the royal soldiers happened to receive some of this counterfeit money in Normandy as their pay, and were unable to buy anything with it because it was not legitimate, they complained to the king about its falsity. The king therefore became angry, both because of the injury to his soldiers and, even more, because justice had been violated. He issued his judgment, ordering and commanding those whom he had left in his place in England to punish all moneyers who could justly be accused of this wickedness by cutting off their right hands and their genital members.

O man who defended justice and most fiercely punished iniquity! O, if he had been willing to accept a ransom for the limbs of so many wicked men, how many thousands of talents could he have gained from it! But, as we have said, he despised money for the love of justice.

## CHAPTER XXIV. On the death of William, abbot of Bec, and on the goodness of his successor, the venerable Boso

[Col. 0894C]

At this time William, abbot of Bec, died, and lord Boso succeeded him. Concerning Boso it became a matter of debate whether he deserved more reverence and glory from men because of his exceptional knowledge of secular and spiritual matters, or because of his exceptional observance of the monastic order.

Many powerful men, distinguished by both secular and ecclesiastical rank, honored him with intimate friendship: they revered him as a father, feared him as a teacher, and loved him as a brother and a child. To him they entrusted the counsels of their souls; to him they entrusted a kind of watchtower from which the ecclesiastical orders might be surveyed.

The watchful care of such a man—whom the distinction of wisdom and holiness alike had endowed with the greatest authority—could promise considerable security to their most excellent concerns. As we have said, King Henry—or rather the unanimous consent of the entire convent—appointed him abbot of the monastery of Bec. He resisted no less from love of submission than from fear of higher rank.

Abbeys, monasteries, synods, and courts revered him: as prudent, so eloquent; as just, so discerning. He tastes the rule of nature but does not feast upon it; he never favored money or influence, whether giving judgment in court or delivering a decision in council. He showed himself both gentle and severe, with a most fitting alternation between the two: merciful toward no person, but a relentless persecutor of every vice [Col. 0895A], a pious enemy.

But lest we seem to stray too far from the deeds of the renowned king, let us return to relate what we promised concerning his daughter Matilda, the Augusta empress.

## CHAPTER XXV. How, after the death of the Emperor Henry, King Henry brought his daughter Matilda, the empress, back to England and married her to Geoffrey, duke of Anjou, by whom she had three sons, Henry, Geoffrey, and William
When, therefore, Henry IV, august Roman emperor, died before old age—namely, in the year 1125 from the Incarnation of the Lord—the most powerful king of the English, Henry, sent nobles and had his daughter, the empress, brought back to England with great honor. Although the most eminent princes of the Roman court, having experienced her prudence and the grace of her character, desired during the lifetime of her imperial husband to have her rule over them in every respect, they followed her for this reason as far as the court of her father, to ask precisely this of him. When the king absolutely refused their petition—for he wished her, after his death, to succeed by hereditary right to the kingdom of England—he made the more powerful bishops, archbishops, and abbots, as well as the counts and magnates of the whole English kingdom, promise her, under the strictest oath of loyalty, that they would strive with all their strength so that the same Augusta, after her father’s death, might obtain sovereignty over Greater Britain, which is now called England. Whether they did this is of no concern to me to say.

As time passed, however, her father, wishing to be rid of the hostility and importunity of Fulk, count of Anjou, Tours, and Maine—for there had long been hostility between them on various grounds—although she was unwilling, gave the same empress in marriage to Geoffrey Martel, son of the aforesaid Fulk. Geoffrey succeeded his father in the countship when Fulk became king of Jerusalem. By her the same marquis fathered three sons: Henry, Geoffrey Martel, and William, legitimate heirs to the English principality, not only through Henry, their grandfather, but also through Matilda, their grandmother. Each spouse, in a different way, touched closely upon the kinship of the ancient kings of England, as is contained in the book written about the life of that queen. Because of its account of the events and in honor and memory both of the mother from whom it was produced and of the daughter for whom it was produced, we might perhaps append that book to this work.

## CHAPTER XXVI. How the kings of the Franks descend from the lineage of the counts of Anjou

Let no one—and certainly not the august empress herself—consider it wholly unworthy that, after the bed of the emperor, she entered into marriage with the count of Anjou. For although the count of Anjou is of much lower dignity than the Roman emperor, anyone who consults the deeds of the kings of France will find from what noble stock the counts of Anjou descend. There he will also find that the kings of the Franks who rule that kingdom in our time derive from the offspring of the aforesaid counts.

For after the account of the death of Charles the Bald, the same deeds contain the following—not in the same words, perhaps, but with the same meaning:

“When Louis, son of Charles the Bald, died, and his son Charles the Simple, still a boy, was entirely unable to govern the reins of the kingdom, while two sons of Robert, count of Anjou, a man of Saxon descent, survived—namely, Odo the prince, under whose guardianship Louis had left his son Charles, and his brother Robert—the Burgundians and Aquitanians chose the aforesaid Odo as their king. He ruled the kingdom of the Franks most ably for thirteen years and nobly defended it against the Danes, who at that time were devastating Gaul.

“When Odo died, Charles the Simple recovered his kingdom, and Robert, Odo’s brother, became prince of the Franks under Charles. But because he was not given the portion of the principality that his brother Odo had held before he was chosen king, Robert rebelled against King Charles. Having himself been anointed king, he reigned for one year, but afterward was killed in the battle of Soissons by the army of Charles the Simple.

“Nevertheless, his son Hugh the Great became prince of the Franks after him. Hugh was born to the daughter of Herbert, count of Vermandois. This Herbert captured Charles the Simple by treachery as he was returning victorious from the aforesaid battle, and Charles himself died in his captivity.

“The aforementioned Hugh the Great fathered, by the daughter of Otto, king of the Saxons and afterward Roman emperor, Hugh Capet and his brothers. This Hugh, after the line of Charlemagne had been set aside, was anointed king over the Franks. While he was still alive, in the first year of his reign, his son Robert was associated with him in the kingship. Robert was a most devout king and a man highly instructed in literary learning by Gerbert the monk and philosopher, later Roman pope.”

I have inserted this account of the deeds of the Franks into this little work, wishing to make known to those who do not know it the nobility of the counts of Anjou, and that the third family of the kings of France—for kings have been created successively from so many families from the beginning of that kingdom until now—has come from their lineage in the manner we have described. It is therefore not altogether unworthy that the daughter of the king of the English was joined in marriage to a man closely related by blood to the kings of France. [Col. 0896D] Now let us return to the order of the events proposed.

## CHAPTER XXVII. How devoutly the aforesaid empress distributed her treasures among various churches and the needy while she was ill

The often-mentioned Empress Matilda, while she was once ill at Rouen, displayed to those living then and to those who would come after sufficient proof of her prudence and religion. She distributed with such a devoted hand not only the imperial treasures, incomparable treasures that she had brought with her from Italy, but also those which royal—or rather paternal—munificence had bestowed upon her from the inexhaustible treasures of the English, among churches of various provinces, religious men and women, the poor, widows, and orphans, that she did not even spare the silk mattress on which she lay during that illness, but ordered it to be sold and its price distributed to lepers.

Nevertheless, in this distribution she showed herself more ready toward the church of Bec than toward the many monasteries of Neustria, not to say all of them. She gave it gifts of such variety, and of such precious material and workmanship, that Byzantium itself would have considered them very dear, and which could remain honorable until the end of the world—always representing the devotion and love of the august empress toward that church, and in turn impressing more firmly upon the hearts of those who lived there the memory of their distinguished lady. To designate each item by description or name would be tedious. It is delightful to behold them even for the greatest visitors, those who have often seen the treasures of noble churches. If a Greek or Arab visitor passed through that place, he too would be drawn by the spectacle’s delight.

We believe—and it is right to believe—that the most just Judge of all will repay her a hundredfold, not only in the future but also in the present age, for what she gratefully expended upon His servants with a hand both generous and devout. That it also belonged to the reward of the present time is beyond doubt: when, by God’s mercy, her adverse illness had subsided, she recovered her health and completely renewed her monks—the monks of Bec—who, striving with continual labor in prayer for her recovery before and above all others, had almost collapsed from the effort, but were wholly restored by the breath of her returning health.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. How, when she was despairing of recovery, she asked the king to be buried at Bec; concerning her affection for that church; and how she was restored to health

Nor should this be suppressed in silence; rather, as one might say, it should be transmitted to the age to come, written in capital letters: before she recovered, she asked her father to permit her to be buried in the monastery of Bec. At first the king refused, saying that it was not fitting for his daughter, the august empress, who once and again in the city of Romulus, the head of the world, had proceeded adorned with the imperial diadem by the hands of the supreme pontiff, to be buried in any monastery, however renowned for religion and reputation. Instead, she should at least be carried to the city of Rouen, the metropolis of the Normans, and placed in the principal church, where her ancestors—by which I mean Rollo and his son William Longsword, who subdued Neustria by arms—lay, and where she too should be placed.

When the king’s decision had been conveyed to her, she sent him word that her soul would never be happy unless, in this one matter at least, her will were fulfilled. O woman, distinguished for virtue and sounder judgment, who thought so little of worldly pomp in the disposition of her body! For she knew that it is more beneficial for the souls of the dead that their bodies be buried where prayers for them are offered to God more frequently and more devoutly.

Her father, therefore, overcome by the piety and prudence of the Augusta, although he was accustomed to surpass others in both virtue and piety, yielded and granted that her will and request concerning her burial should be carried out at Bec. But, God willing it, as has been stated, she recovered and was restored to perfect health.

Having thus commemorated the august empress in its proper place, as is fitting, let us say something, even briefly, about the other children of King Henry, although they were begotten in a less suitable manner, for the sake of providing an account of the facts.

## CHAPTER XXIX. How King Henry married Adeliza after the death of his wife Matilda, and concerning the children he fathered elsewhere, whose firstborn was Robert, count of Gloucester, who received the inheritance of Robert son of Haimon together with his daughter

After the death of the second Matilda, queen of the English and mother of this august empress, as was said above, King Henry married Adeliza, daughter of Godfrey, duke of Leuven, and cousin of Eustace, count of Boulogne. He had no offspring by her. Nevertheless, that king had six sons and seven daughters, although, as we said, they were begotten in a less honorable manner.

To his firstborn, Robert, his father gave in marriage a most noble maiden named Sibyl, daughter of Robert son of Haimon, specifically a granddaughter through Mabilia, daughter of Roger of Montgomery, father of Robert of Bellême. He granted him the greatest inheritance, both in Normandy and in England, which by hereditary right belonged to the aforesaid maiden.

By her he fathered five sons—namely, William, his firstborn, and his brothers—and one daughter. The chief place of the inheritance that Robert acquired together with the aforesaid maiden is the town called Torigni, situated on the boundary of the counties of Bayeux and Coutances, about two miles from the river called the Vire, which divides those counties on the nearer side. After it had come under the authority of Robert, the king’s son, that town was fortified against every hostile attack with lofty towers, strong walls, and steep ditches cut into the rocky mountain itself; it was also surrounded and rendered inaccessible for the most part by water collected in ponds.

Although the surrounding land is less suited to producing abundant crops, the town itself is populous, filled with merchants of various wares, adorned with both public and private buildings, and not lacking gold and silver. The king also gave him the land of Haimon the steward, the uncle of his wife.

Moreover, because it was not enough for the king’s son to possess vast estates without the name and honor of some public dignity, his pious father gave him the county of Gloucester. Richard, this count’s brother on his father’s side, perished with his brother William in the oft-mentioned shipwreck. The other three—Rainald, Robert, and Gilbert—were still young and without a settlement. The fourth, namely William of Tracy, was removed from human affairs shortly after his father’s death.

Of the daughters, one, named Matilda, married Rotrou, count of Perche, and had one daughter by him. This Countess Matilda was afterward drowned with her brothers in the aforesaid shipwreck. Another, also named Matilda, was given to Conan, count of Brittany Minor, and bore him a son named Hoel and two daughters. The third, Juliana, was given to Eustace of Pacy, by whom she had two sons, William and Roger. The fourth was given to William Goiz. The fifth was given to the viscount of Beaumont, whose castle is situated in the county of Maine. The sixth was given to Matthew, son of Bouchard of Montmorency. The seventh, born to Elizabeth, sister of Waleran, count of Meulan, remained unmarried.

## CHAPTER XXX. How, when Geoffrey, archbishop of Rouen, who had once succeeded William, died, Hugh, abbot of Reading, obtained the same see

[Col. 0899B] About this time, when Geoffrey, archbishop of Rouen, died, Hugh, the first abbot of Reading, succeeded him. A short time afterward, Pope Innocent II came to Rouen on King Henry’s business and was received and escorted by the same king with immense attentions, as befitted an Apostolic man. In the same way, long before, when Pope Calixtus had come to him for ecclesiastical matters at his castle called Gisors, situated on the edge of his duchy, the king had received him in royal fashion and sent him back laden with royal gifts.

## CHAPTER XXXI. Concerning the castles that King Henry built in the duchy of Normandy, and how by his wisdom he established peace not only in his own land but also in distant regions

King Henry built very many castles both in his kingdom and in his duchy. He also improved almost all the others built by his predecessors, not only towns but even the most ancient cities. The names of those he constructed in Normandy, on the edge of his duchy and at the borders of the provinces, are these: Driemcurtis; New Castle, situated on the bank of the river Epte; Verneuil; Nonancourt; Bonmoulin; Mont-Colmiae; Pontorson; and others that I deliberately pass over so as not to delay.

By the wisdom and goodness granted to him by God, he maintained peace not only in his own land but also in kingdoms far away. He held the Welsh, who were always rebellious against the English, so subject that throughout their entire land either he himself or his magnates built fortifications against their will. While he lived, they themselves possessed no fortification within their own jurisdiction except the mountain called in the language of the English Sneundune [Snowdon], that is, “snowy mountain,” because snow continually remains there.

Some people, and not without justification, as many thought, considered one thing in him worthy of reproach. Since he had in his hands the fortifications of some of his barons and also of certain neighboring men whose lands bordered his duchy, he sometimes fortified them as though they were his own, surrounding them with walls and towers, so that those men, trusting in them, might not do anything against the peace of his rule. But many did not know with what intention he did this, and for that reason they criticized it.

## CHAPTER XXXII. Concerning the churches and monasteries that he built, his generosity toward Christ’s servants, and his other pious acts

The illustrious King Henry, whose deeds we are recounting, was exceedingly generous not only toward the powerful of this world but also—and this is greater and more useful—toward religious people. The bishops, abbots, poor monks, and communities of nuns of France and Aquitaine, as well as of Burgundy and Italy, testify to this, for they received considerable annual benefit from him.

In England he built from the foundations the abbey of Saint Mary of Reading on the river Thames, enriching it with ornaments and possessions, and established monks of the Cluniac order there. He also built another church at Cirencester in honor of Saint John, established regular canons there, and provided them with sufficient necessities.

Likewise, in Normandy at Rouen, he almost completed the church of Saint Mary of the Meadow, which his mother had begun long before. He adorned the place with a cloister, monastic offices appropriate to the monks, and a surrounding wall; he granted it several estates, both in Normandy and in England, for the use of those serving God there, together with precious ornaments. He would have granted greater things as well, had life lasted a little longer, according to his promise.

Because that place belonged to the church of Bec, being the patrimony of Lord Herluin, the first abbot and founder of the monastery of Bec, he established monks of Bec there to serve God. He always honored the abbots and monks of that church wonderfully and held them in the greatest reverence, especially Lord Abbot Boso. We experienced this within our own memory, when the same king annually gave that venerable man a considerable sum of money to support the provisions of his community and to receive guests, whom Boso honored and entertained splendidly—indeed, beyond his means—not so much from the abundance of his possessions as from the breadth of his charity.

Although the king’s generosity made these gifts not only for the sake of the abbot but also because of the good reputation of the monks, whose prayers he frequently sought to commend himself to, either personally or through a messenger, the following shows that he honored that abbot more than his predecessors in this particular respect: during the rule of the aforesaid abbot he devoutly gave the church of Bec at times one hundred pounds of silver, and very often one hundred marks of the same metal, whereas previously he had scarcely reached a quarter of the aforementioned sum in giving anything to that church.

He proclaimed by deed as well as by word that Boso surpassed the other persons of his kingdom in holiness and in both spiritual and worldly counsel. This was especially evident during the two years in which that holy man was continually afflicted by severe illness before his death: whenever the king traveled through the neighboring regions, he never passed by without turning aside to visit him, and whatever Boso requested from him for the needs of his own monastery or of another, he gladly obtained.

Several dwellings for God’s servants were built, both in the kingdom of this illustrious king and in distant provinces, through his counsel and generous munificence. As for the church of Cluny, to say nothing of smaller establishments, he built most of it at his own expense and assigned great possessions in England for the redemption of his soul. He did the same for the church of Saint Martin of the Fields.

He also provided various kinds of assistance for constructing the buildings of the monks of Tiron, except for the dormitory, which he wished to have built entirely from his own resources in memory of himself. His munificence likewise completed the hospice for those suffering from elephantiasis who lived at Chartres, a very great and marvelous work.

Moreover, his inexhaustible generosity made the Alps, hitherto almost impassable, passable for those seeking the thresholds of the apostles or other holy places. Why should I mention that he annually sent, with a devout hand, abundant assistance both in arms and in other necessities to the soldiers of the Temple at Jerusalem, who constantly fight against the Agarenes in defense of the Christian religion?

He also gave the Hospital of Jerusalem a certain piece of land in the county of Avranches, on which those servants of Christ built a village called the Village of God, fortified by royal munificence with great privileges.

Furthermore, the church of Blessed Mary in the city of Évreux, destroyed through his pious—so to speak—severity and rebuilt again, surpasses nearly all the churches of Neustria in beauty. For when, as has often been said, the same city had been burned by the king because of the discord caused by Almaric, and the church of the episcopal see could not be spared from the fire, the king afterward granted that church such revenues that, once renewed for the better, the total revenues of that bishopric were thereby permanently and greatly increased.

## CHAPTER XXXIII. Concerning his death, and how his body was carried to England and buried at Reading

It would be a lengthy task to enumerate and examine each of his pious deeds, or those relating to the administration of public affairs, his knowledge, and his probity. The church with its poor bears unfailing witness to one aspect of these matters; the court, not only of the English but also of distant provinces, together with its nobles, bears witness to another.

We, therefore, mindful of the benefits generously bestowed upon us both by him and by his daughter, the august Empress Matilda, and not wishing to be judged ungrateful, have not neglected, as far as our ability permits, continually to repay him in spiritual matters. We have endeavored, from the few deeds of his that we have mentioned, to suggest to those living now and to those yet to come a beneficial remembrance of the many deeds that we knowingly passed over—if only they would not disdain to imitate them.

After a long reign, the often-mentioned Henry, king of the English and duke of the Normans, died on the fourth day before the Nones of December, in the year 1135 from the Incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ, in Normandy, at Royal Village, situated in the Forest of Lyons, which by metonymy they call Saint-Denis. He had reigned in England for thirty-four years and four months. He had governed the duchy of Normandy for twenty-nine years and four months.

His body was carried to England and honorably buried in the church of Saint Mary at Reading, which he had built from its foundations at his own expense. May Christ, King of the ages, grant him forgiveness of his transgressions through the prayers of his mother and mercifully bestow upon him the joys of the blessed. He lives and reigns as God with the Father and the Holy Spirit, throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## EPITAPH FOR HIM

How little things avail, how wealth amounts to nothing great,

King Henry proves, the living king, friend of peace.

For he had been richer than all others,

Whom the office of ruling had set above the western people.

Yet against the assaults of death, what use were gems, cloaks, garments,

The varied wealth of the earth, or castles, to him?
