Hence pale and wicked Death, giving equal lot to the lowly,

Stretches out her foot and strikes at his hall.

When grim fever, on the first night of December,

Stripped the world of him, it multiplied the world’s evils.

For when the father of the people, peace and protector of the humble,

The pious man himself, falls, the impious man rages, oppresses, and burns.

Let the English people therefore mourn, and the Norman people weep in turn.

You die, Henry: then peace, now grief, for both.

## ANOTHER BY THE SAME AUTHOR

In judgment, riches, accessibility, and fitting severity,

Admirable—beyond telling—to those suffering violence, terrible to criminals,

Outstanding, wealthy, not difficult of access, revered:

Here lies Henry, once king, peace, and glory of the world.

## ANOTHER BY THE SAME AUTHOR

Victor, pursuer, avenger, protector, lover

Of wars, peace, crimes, the realm, and goodness,

This tomb contains the king known in every place,

Henry, once terror, now the same man’s ashes.

## CHAPTER XXXIV. Concerning the four sisters of the aforesaid king, of whom Adela married Stephen, count of Blois, and concerning Adela’s children

Of the daughters of the first King William of the English, sisters of the illustrious King Henry, whose deeds we have now recounted to some extent, I wish, for the sake and love of their brother, to insert something concerning them at the end of this little work.

Their firstborn, named Cecilia, a virgin consecrated to God, presided for many years over the monastery of the Holy Trinity in the town of Caen, after Matilda, the first abbess of that place.

The second, Constance, was married to Alan Fergant, count of Brittany Minor, the son of Hoel, who had succeeded Conan, and died without children. Consequently, after her death the same count married a daughter of Fulk Rechin, count of Anjou, by whom he fathered the younger Conan, who succeeded him, as was mentioned above.

After Geoffrey Martel, a man of great probity and the firstborn son of the aforesaid Fulk, count of Anjou, was killed by treachery, his other son, named Fulk, succeeded him. This Fulk was born to another wife named Bertha, sister of Almaric, count of Évreux. After he received the daughter of Helias, count of Maine, together with her county, he fathered by her two sons—Geoffrey Martel, of whom we have already said a little above, and Helias—and an equal number of daughters.

One of these daughters married William, son of Henry, king of the English; after his death at Fontevrault, she assumed the religious habit. The other married the count of Flanders; after his wife’s death, he went to Jerusalem and, having married the daughter of Baldwin II, the recently deceased king, became the third king of the Jerusalemites.

For after the city of Jerusalem had been captured by the Christians, Duke Godfrey, brother of Eustace, count of Boulogne, was the first to rule it. Out of reverence for our Redeemer, who in some city had borne the crown of thorns for us sinners, he never wished to be adorned with a royal diadem. After his death, his brother Baldwin became the first king there, and he was succeeded by another Baldwin, the first Baldwin’s nephew. As we said, Fulk, count of Anjou, married that Baldwin’s daughter.

The third of King William’s daughters, named Adeliza, had been betrothed to Harold the traitor before the English war; but after Harold had been punished with a fitting death, she married no one and died a marriageable virgin.

The fourth, named Adela, married Stephen, count of Blois, by whom she had four sons—William, Theobald, Henry, and Stephen—and one daughter.

William, the firstborn, received from his father the lordship of Sorey [Soleil] to govern. Henry, count of Eu, son of Count William, married his daughter, although they were bound by close kinship; by her he had three sons and one daughter.

Theobald, a man praiseworthy in every respect, although a layman, revered and supported religious men with extraordinary devotion. He succeeded his father in the county of Blois; he also purchased the county of Troyes from his uncle Hugh and possessed it together with the county of Chartres. He took as his wife the daughter of a certain count of Bohemia [Behania], by whom he had several sons and daughters.

His brother Henry, a Cluniac monk from childhood, afterward received first the abbey of Glastonbury as a gift from his maternal uncle, Henry, king of the English, and later the bishopric of Winchester.

Stephen, also made count of Mortain by the same king with his support, married Matilda, daughter of Eustace, count of Boulogne, and granddaughter of the second Matilda, queen of the English, through her sister Mary. Since that Eustace had no son, Stephen himself, on account of his wife, became heir both to the county of Boulogne and to the great possessions that his father-in-law had held in England. By her he fathered several sons and daughters.

This Stephen became king of the English after the death of his maternal uncle, King Henry. For when that king died in Normandy, his daughter Matilda, once empress, whom he had long before established as heir to his kingdom, was staying in the county of Anjou with her husband, Geoffrey, duke of that county, and their sons. Shortly before her father’s death she had left Normandy, somewhat angered against him, because the king refused to reconcile himself freely with William Talvas, although she repeatedly pleaded with him on William’s behalf. He did not do this out of contempt for his beloved daughter, but so that he would not be feared less by William himself or by his other princes if he remitted William’s offence readily and without punishment.

## CHAPTER XXXV. How Roger of Montgomery was born from one of Countess Gunnor’s granddaughters, and concerning Roger’s ancestors

This William, son of Robert of Bellême, was born to the daughter of Wido, count of Ponthieu. Robert was considered hateful to that king and to many other wise men because of his excessive cruelty. When Robert had finally been placed in chains, in which he also died, King Henry captured his noble town, Bellême, and gave it to his son-in-law Rotrou, count of Perche.

Although the district of Bellême did not belong to the duchy of Normandy but to the kingdom of France, Philip, king of the Franks, had formerly given—or, as some say, sold—the lordship of that district to his kinsman William the Elder, king of the English and duke of Normandy.

Ivo of Bellême, Roger’s predecessor, was a powerful and wise man. Through his counsel, Richard I, while still a boy held in the custody of the king of the Franks, was rescued, through the agency of Osmund, the boy’s squire. Ivo’s son was William of Bellême, who fathered another William, surnamed Talvas, the father of Mabel.

Roger, count and son of Hugh of Montgomery, took this Mabel as his wife, together with all her father’s inheritance, whether in the district of Bellême or in the Sées region beyond the river Sarthe. Roger himself was born from one of the granddaughters of Countess Gunnor [Note: From Joceline, daughter of Wevia, as the manuscript book has it]; and therefore he also possessed immense estates in various regions of Normandy.

By Mabel he fathered five sons and four daughters. His son Robert of Bellême succeeded him, a man wicked in every respect. As we have already said, by the daughter of Wido, count of Ponthieu, he fathered William Talvas, his successor.

This Talvas had by his wife Ala, who had formerly been the wife [Note: Rather, daughter, as Orderic Vitalis notes] of the duke of Burgundy, two sons and an equal number of daughters. Of the sons, the firstborn, Wido, became count of Ponthieu while his father was still alive. One of the daughters married Ivhello, son of Walter of Meduana, by whom she had several sons. The other married the third William of Warenne, count of Surrey.

The aforesaid Roger of Montgomery took part in the English war and received from William, king of the English, the counties of Arundel and Shrewsbury as a gift.

## CHAPTER XXXVI. An account of how Gunnor herself was first joined in marriage to Richard, duke of Normandy

Since we have mentioned Countess Gunnor because she was the mother of Roger of Montgomery’s mother, who was that countess’s granddaughter, I wish to commit to the memory of writing, as I learned it from the ancients, how that same Gunnor entered into marriage with Count Richard.

Count Richard, having heard of the beauty of the wife of a certain forester who lived not far from the town of Arques, in a village called Schecheville, deliberately went hunting there, wishing to test whether what he had learned from the report of certain people was true. He lodged in the forester’s house and, captivated by the beauty of his wife’s face, ordered his host to bring his wife, Sainfria by name, to his chamber that very night.

When the forester reported this to her with sadness, she, as a wise woman, consoled him, saying that she would substitute in her place her sister Gunnor, a maiden much more beautiful than herself. And so it was done.

When the duke learned of this deception, he was delighted that he had not sinned by taking another man’s wife. By Gunnor he fathered three sons and an equal number of daughters, as is found above in the book written about the deeds of that duke.

When the same count wished to have one of his sons, named Robert, made archbishop of Rouen, certain people answered him that this could by no means be done according to the decrees of the canons, because his mother had not been formally married. For this reason Count Richard joined himself to Countess Gunnor in Christian marriage. The sons who had already been born to her, while the marriage ceremony was being performed, were covered together with their father and mother under a cloak; and afterward Robert was made archbishop of Rouen.

## CHAPTER XXXVII. How the same countess gave her sisters and granddaughters in marriage to the nobler men of Normandy, and concerning their descendants
Gunnor herself, apart from Sainfria, had two sisters, [Col. 0905D] Wewa and Awelina. One of them, with the assistance of the countess herself, who was a woman of great prudence, married Turulf of Pont-Audemer, who had been the son of a certain man named Torf; from him, moreover, certain villages are still called Torfvilles. This Turulf’s brother was Turchetil, the father of Anschetil of Harcourt. Turulf had by the same woman Humphrey of Vieilles, the father of Roger of Beaumont.

The third of Countess Gunnor’s sisters married Osbern of Bolebec, by whom she had Walter Giffard the First and Geoffrey, the father of William of Arques. This William was the brother [Col. 0906A] of Matilda, whom William the Chamberlain of Tancarville took as his wife; by her he had a son named Rabel, who succeeded him. The aforesaid Walter married one of the daughters of Gerard Flatel; the other, namely Basilia, the widow of Ralph of Wacey, was married by Hugh of Gournay, whose succession and descendants have been discussed above.

This Walter had Walter Giffard the Second and several daughters, one of whom, named Rohais, married Richard, son of Count Gilbert. This Gilbert had been the son of Geoffrey, Count of Eu, namely the natural son of the first Richard, Duke of the Northmen. This Gilbert had two sons: the aforesaid Richard and Baldwin. Baldwin likewise had three sons, Richard, Robert, and William, and the same number of daughters.

Richard, Baldwin’s brother, [Col. 0906B] had by Rohais four sons—Gilbert, Roger, Walter, and Robert—and two daughters. One of the daughters was married to Ralph of Telgers; by her were born Fransval, Henry, and Robert Giffard.

Gilbert acquired, after his father, the land in England that his father had possessed. His brother Roger obtained the land in Normandy. This Gilbert, I say, had by the daughter of the count of Clermont three sons—Richard, who succeeded him, Gilbert, and Walter—and one daughter named Rohais.

Richard married the sister of Ranulf, the younger count of Chester, and had by her three sons: Gilbert, who succeeded him, and his brothers. Richard himself died prematurely, killed by the Welsh, [Col. 0906C] who, after hearing of King Henry’s death, rebelled savagely against the English.

When his uncles Roger and Walter had died without children, Gilbert, the son of Gilbert, acquired their lands by hereditary right, with their own consent. He married Elizabeth, the sister of Waleran, Count of Meulan, and by her had a firstborn son named Richard.

[Note: [Col. 0905] This is that Richard who, as Count of Pembroke and surnamed Strongbow, first opened Ireland to the English.]

Robert, Richard’s son, was succeeded by his own firstborn son, born of one of the daughters of Waltheof, Count of Huntingdon. This Waltheof had three daughters by his wife, the daughter of the countess of Albemarle; that countess was the uterine sister of William, the elder king of the English.

Of these daughters of Count Waltheof, the firstborn was taken by Simon of Senlis, together with the county of Huntingdon; by her he had a son named Simon. After Count Simon’s death, David, the brother of Matilda II, Queen of the English, married his widow, and by her had one son, namely Henry. When his brothers Dudecan and Alexander, kings of the Scots, had been removed from this life, he himself assumed the kingdom.

The second daughter, namely Judith, was married by Ralph of Tosny, as has already been stated. The third was married by Robert, Richard’s son, as we have just mentioned.

[Col. 0907A] Since we have mentioned Countess Gunnor’s sisters, it is also fitting to say something about those who were related to her in the second degree of kinship, as we have learned from the ancients.

The countess therefore had by her brother Herfast a nephew, Osbern of Crépon, namely the father of William, Count of Hereford, a man in every respect deserving of praise.

The aforesaid Gunnor had many nieces, but I have heard only which husbands five of them married. One of them was married to the father of the first William of Warenne; by her was born that same William, later Count of Surrey, and Roger of Mortemer, his brother. Another was married to Nicholas of Bascheritville—commonly called Bacqueville—from whose descendants were born William Martel and Walter of Saint-Martin. [Col. 0907B] The third was married to Richard, Viscount of Rouen, the father of Lambert of Saint-Sauveur. The fourth was married to Osmund, Viscount of Vernon, by whom was born the first Fulk of Anet, together with several daughters, one of whom was the mother of the first Baldwin of Reviers. Hugh of Montgommery married the fifth; by her was born Roger, the father of Robert of Bellême.

## CHAPTER XXXVIII. On the occasion by which Stephen, Count of Mortain and nephew of King Henry, succeeded him in the kingdom

But, to return to the matters from which we digressed because of these genealogies: when Henry, King of the English, died, his nephew Stephen succeeded him in the very month of his death. For while that count was residing in the county of Boulogne, having heard of his uncle’s death [Col. 0907C], he quickly crossed the sea and, with the help of his brother Henry, Bishop of Winchester, obtained the crown of the kingdom.

As was stated above, at that time Matilda was the king’s heir in the region of Anjou. Nevertheless, she obtained Domfront, Argentan, and Exmes, her father’s castles, as well as three others, namely Mont-Cerisy, Gorre, and Ambrères [Amberras]. In the meantime she granted these to Juhel of Mayenne, on condition that he faithfully assist her in acquiring her inheritance. For the same Juhel claimed that those three fortresses, namely the ones last mentioned, were in his land.

The daughter of Adela, daughter of William, King of the English, whom we mentioned above, married Richard, Count of Chester, the son of Count Hugh. This Hugh [Col. 0907D] was the son of Richard, Viscount of the Avranchin. When Richard and his wife had died in the shipwreck mentioned so often, together with William, King Henry’s son, Ranulf, Viscount of the Bessin and Richard’s cousin, acquired his county.

When this Ranulf died, he was succeeded by his son Ranulf, a man vigorous in military affairs. Richard, the son of Gilbert, married this Ranulf’s sister, and had by her three sons. Finally, this Richard was killed by the Welsh, as was stated earlier.

The aforesaid Count Ranulf took as his wife Matilda [MS: *Sibyllam*, “Sibyl”], the daughter of Robert, Count of Gloucester; by her he had two sons, Hugh and Richard.

## CHAPTER XXXIX. How Adela, Countess of Blois, assumed the habit and way of life of a religious woman at Marcigny in the time of Lord Peter, Abbot of Cluny; and how she died in the second year after the death of her brother, Henry, King of the English

[Col. 0908A]

When Stephen, Count of Blois, the husband of Adela, daughter of William, King of the English, died, she governed the county nobly for some time, because her sons were still too young to administer its government. When they had grown up, she assumed the habit and way of life of a religious woman at Marcigny in the time of Lord Peter, Abbot of Cluny, and remained there commendably in God’s service until the end.

She died in the second year after the death of her brother Henry, King [Col. 0908B] of the English.

## CHAPTER XL. On the violent wind that occurred before the death of King Henry; and how many of the nobles of the English kingdom died in the same year or the year after King Henry’s death

In the year in which that King Henry was taken from human affairs, a violent wind arose in Normandy and in many other regions shortly before his death, namely on the vigil of the Apostles Simon and Jude.

Not long after his death had passed—during the same year or the following one—many of the princes of the English kingdom died by God’s judgment: namely William, Archbishop of Canterbury; the Bishop of Rochester; the Bishop of Exeter; Richard, [Col. 0908C] son of Gilbert, as has already been stated; Robert, Richard’s son, his uncle; Richard, Baldwin’s son, the cousin of the last two mentioned; and also the second William of Warenne, Count of Surrey.

He was succeeded by his third son William, born of Elizabeth, daughter of Hugh the Great, Count of Vermandois. The aforesaid countess had first been married to Robert, Count of Meulan, by whom she had three sons and the same number of daughters.

## CHAPTER XLI. On the sons of Robert, Count of Meulan, and the sons of his brother Henry, Count of Warwick

Of his sons, two—namely Waleran and Robert, who were twins—succeeded him. Waleran [Col. 0908D], the firstborn, received the county of Meulan and the land their father had possessed in Normandy. Robert received the county of Leicester [*Legreeestriae*; alternatively, *Legiecestriae*] in England.

After her first husband had died, their mother married William of Warenne, the second Count of Surrey, by whom she had one son, namely William the Third, and two daughters. The elder of the daughters was taken as wife by Count Roger of Warwick.

This Roger was the son of Henry, Count of Warwick, the brother of Robert, Count of Meulan; he was born of Margaret, sister of Rotrou, Count of Perche. By her he had Henry, several other children, and two daughters.

The aforesaid Roger succeeded his father in the county of Warwick. One of his brothers born after him, namely Robert of Neubourg, possessed [Col. 0909A] the land that their father had held in Normandy. This Robert was a devoted lover and benefactor of the church of Bec.

He married Godechild, the sister of Roger of Tosny and daughter of the second Ralph; by her he had several sons, namely Henry and his brothers.

## CHAPTER XLII. On the death of Lord Boso, Abbot of Bec, and his successor

About this time Lord Boso, the fourth abbot of Bec, a man whose life was praiseworthy in every respect, died, and was succeeded [Col. 0910A] by Tetbald, prior of the same place.

William, Duke of Aquitaine, also died not long afterward. Louis, son of the King of the Franks, took his only daughter and the duchy itself as his wife. When Louis’s father died on the Kalends of August of that same year, the younger Louis succeeded him, becoming King of the Franks and Duke of Aquitaine, in the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1137; in that year there was a very severe drought.

In the same year Lothair, Emperor of the Romans and Germans, died. He was succeeded by Conrad, the nephew of Henry IV, who had ruled as emperor before Lothair.

# ADDITIONS TO THE HISTORY OF THE NORTHMEN

[Col. 0909]

[Col. 0909B] Having touched briefly, rather than pursued at length, upon a few matters among the many concerning the illustrious King Henry mentioned above, we have judged that a certain miracle should be appended—a matter no less worthy of beneficial narration than of wonder—which also compelled us, as it were, to return to the beginning of the history.

How great Rollo’s humility was after he had received the faith of Christ became plainly known to everyone from one thing he did.

At a certain time, after he had made peace with the King of the Franks, men came to him from Rouen and began to ask him to have the body of Saint Audoenus brought back from Francia. It had once been transferred there through fear of him, when he had first taken Normandy.

“We are sad,” they said, “and deeply grieved that we have lost our archbishop in this way.” When the count heard this, he ordered the King of the Franks to return his priest to him; if he did not do so, he should know beyond doubt that he could in no way remain at peace with him.

The King of the Franks, however, not wishing to cause him trouble over this matter, returned his priest to him as he had requested. The duke then ordered that the body of Saint Audoenus be brought back from there and restored to his church, from which it had been carried away.

The monks who had guarded it while it was in Francia carried it back as far as a certain village one league from the city of Rouen. When they arrived there, being quite tired from the journey, they stayed there that night so that, rising in the morning, they might, if possible, carry Saint [Col. 0909D] Audoenus back to his own place.

When they rose in the morning and wished to carry him into the city, they could not move him in any way. Then the monks, very sad and deeply grieved at what had happened to them, sent word to the citizens that they could not move Saint Audoenus’s body from the place where it had lain that night.

When this was reported to the count, who was then at Rouen, he replied that this tribulation had rightly befallen them because of Saint Audoenus’s body. If they had thought correctly and possessed right understanding, they ought to have gone to meet him in procession and with great devotion.

After this the count ordered [Col. 0910B] the archbishop and all the people of Rouen to go with him to Saint Audoenus in woolen garments and barefoot, and to implore his mercy as devoutly as they could, asking that he not regard their foolishness or negligence but be gracious to them and permit himself to be transferred from that place to the city where he had been archbishop.

Then the duke himself, first of all, as he had instructed the others, reached the village where Saint Audoenus was, dressed in wool and barefoot. When he arrived there, he immediately prostrated himself with all the people who were with him before the bier and prayed as follows:

“Saint Audoenus, good archbishop and our advocate, permit [alternative *permitte*, singular “permit,” for printed plural *permittite*, also “permit”] your body to be transferred to the city where you performed the office of bishop and frequently bestowed sacred [Col. 0910C] blessings. And I give to your church and to you the whole territory that lies from this place to the walls of the city.”

At once the count and the people, lifting the bier on their shoulders, began to carry the holy body away with the greatest ease. Thus they carried it joyfully and exultantly all the way to its church.

As a result of this event, some called that little village *Longum Peanum*, because the count had made so long a journey there barefoot. If anyone asserts that this was not a sign of great humility, it can truthfully be said of him that he does not know what great humility is.

Another event is said to have happened to the same count at the time when he first made peace with the King of the Franks.

One day, while the duke was at Rouen, toward evening many men were standing before their houses, which were beside the bank of the Seine. While they were there and looking at the same water, they saw a mounted man crossing over the water and coming all the way to them.

Greatly astonished by this, when he reached them they began to ask him who he was and where he came from. He replied:

“You see that I am one man. Today I left Retiers in Brittany very early; at the sixth hour I ate at Avranches, and by evening I arrived here, as you see. If you do not believe me, go to the house where I dined, and you will find my knife, which I inadvertently left there.”

Then they sent word to the count, who, as I have said, was then in the city, about the man who had crossed over the waters without any injury. When the count heard this extraordinary report, he ordered the man to speak with him before departing.

The man sent word back to the count that he should wait for him until the first hour on the following day. But when morning came, he rose and went on his way without speaking to the count.

When the count heard that he had departed in this manner, he said that the man had lied, and therefore thought that he must have been some phantom who had wished to deceive them in this way.

Some who had been present then said that, as it seemed to them, he had not lied to him, because he had sent word that he would come not by the count’s first hour but by his own. For his first hour had been much earlier than the count’s, and therefore what he said had been true.

Nevertheless, while he sat that night by the fire of his host and the host questioned him about many things, especially about that count and whether that lineage would long endure, he replied that it would endure for a long time and that their duchy would continue manfully through the seventh generation.

When the host asked what would happen after the seventh generation, he would answer nothing. Instead, from a little stick that he held in his hand, he began to draw furrows through the ashes of the fire. When his host pressed him intensely to say what would come after the seventh generation, he used the stick in his hand to mix up the furrows he had made in the ashes.

From this they inferred [Col. 0911C] that after the seventh generation the duchy would either fail or suffer great dissensions and tribulations. We now see that this has been fulfilled to a great extent, since we have outlived King Henry, who is shown to have been the seventh in the place of this lineage.

Rollo was the first of this genealogy. William Longsword, his son, was the second. Richard, William’s son, was the third. Richard, Richard’s son, was the fourth. Robert, Richard’s son, was the fifth. William, Robert’s son, who possessed not only Normandy but also England, succeeded in the sixth place. After him, in the seventh degree, were his sons, of whom only Henry ultimately possessed Normandy and England until his death.

[Col. 0911D] In the agreement made between the Franks and the Northmen in the time of the first Richard, when Louis, King of the Franks, who had been captured by the Northmen, was restored, the Danes enlarged Normandy from the river called the Andelle to another river called the Epte. Others, however, say from the Epte to the Yser.

It was also established in that agreement that the Count of Normandy would perform no service to the King of the Franks for the land of Normandy, nor serve him in any other way, unless the King of the Franks gave him a fief in Francia from which he would owe him service.

Therefore the Count of Normandy performs homage and fealty to the King of the Franks from Normandy alone, for his life and for the honor of his landed possession. Likewise, the King of the Franks performs fealty to the Count of Normandy for his own life and for the honor of his possessions [Col. 0912A].

There is no other difference between them except that the King of the Franks does not render homage to the Count of Normandy, whereas the Count of Normandy does so to the King of the Franks. At that time the Danes acquired this liberty for their kinsmen, the counts of Normandy.

Of Richard, son of the first Richard, it is said that he was the father of his country and especially of monks. Throughout his entire time Normandy abounded in every good thing, and such peace existed in Normandy during his rule that even plowmen did not dare carry the iron tools of their plows from their fields back to their homes.

If any of these tools were stolen, the count ordered the plowman to come to him, and he himself restored in full whatever had been lost through theft.

Thus in his lifetime something happened similar to a deed of his ancestor Rollo. When the wife of a certain plowman heard the duke’s prohibition, one day she stole a knife and a plowshare, wishing to test what the count would do about it.

The peasant came to his plow the following day, and, not finding his tools, went to the count and reported what had happened to him. The duke ordered money to be given him with which he could repair the loss.

When he returned home, he told his wife what the count had done for him. She replied: “That is good now, because he himself would have the money and she herself what he had lost.”

When he heard this, and not wishing to act disloyally, he returned to the count the money that had been given him and reported what his wife had done. While keeping him there for some time, the count sent orders that his wife’s eyes be torn out [Col. 0912C] because of the theft she had committed.

When the peasant returned home and found his wife punished with the deserved penalty, he said to her angrily: “Do not steal again, and from now on learn to observe the count’s commands.”

This count greatly enlarged the lands and ornaments of the church of Fécamp, which his father, the first Richard, had built. He was also accustomed to hold his court there almost every year during the solemnity of Easter.

Sometimes, during that solemnity, he and his wife would carry before the altar of the Holy Trinity a large vessel filled with textiles, censers, candlesticks, and certain other ornaments, covered with a very fine pall, and offer it there to God for their sins.

On that same day, after the masses and before going to his court and eating with his barons, he would come with his two sons, Richard and Robert, into the monks’ refectory. The boys, bringing dishes through the kitchen window as the monks were accustomed to do, would hand them to their father, and he himself would place the first courses before the abbot and afterward before the monks.

When he had done this with great humility, he would come before the abbot, receive his permission, and then go joyfully and happily to his court.

Sometimes he would send the abbot from his table a silver dish full of fish and tell him to keep it and do with it as he wished.

This Richard gave much not only to the church of Fécamp [Col. 0913A] but also to other churches. One day he came to Jumièges and rested there that night. Rising in the morning, as was always his custom, he went to the monastery to pray; after praying, he placed a little stick upon the altar.

After he had departed, the sacristans came to the altar, thinking they would find there either a mark of gold, an ounce, or something of that kind. They found the little stick instead and began to wonder greatly what it signified.

At last they asked him what it meant and why he had placed it upon the altar. He replied that it was Vinmonasterium, namely a certain manor, which he was giving them for the sake of his soul.

# IN THE YEAR OF THE LORD 1087. POPE VICTOR III

[Col. 0913]

## HISTORICAL NOTICE

(Ciacconius, *On the Lives of the Roman Pontiffs*, II, 342.)

[Col. 0913B] Pope Victor III, who before his pontificate was called Desiderius and in the world Dauferius, was born at Benevento in Samnium, his father being the prince of that city. Brought up with complete care while still a boy, he grew into a young man of remarkable and renowned uprightness.

Moved by a desire for the solitary life and the preservation of chastity, he abandoned a virgin bride born of the highest rank, secretly and without his parents’ knowledge sought the desert, and received the monastic life from a certain holy monk named Hyacinth, not far from Benevento.

For a long time he lived most chastely in the monasteries of the Holy Trinity at Cava, of Saint Sophia near Benevento, and of Tremiti on an island in the Adriatic Sea; finally he lived in the vast desert of Majella, filled with holy men.

By a letter of Pope Leo IX to Hyacinth, the prior of the desert, Desiderius [Col. 0913C] was forced to leave Majella and returned to the monastery at Benevento. Pope Leo, who was then staying at Benevento, recognized his uprightness, virtue, and religious devotion and, through the efforts of Humbert, Cardinal of Silva Candida, and Frederick the chancellor, made him a cardinal deacon of the Roman Church.

When Leo died, Desiderius obtained permission from Victor II and withdrew to the monastery of Cassino under Abbot Peter, where he had resolved to devote himself, with the other monks, to divine philosophy.

Made provost of the monastery at Capua, he displayed the greatest evidence of skill, prudence, and integrity, so that Stephen IX, formerly abbot of Cassino, considered him worthy of that abbey. At Stephen’s direction, he was designated by the monks and sent by him as a legate of the Apostolic See to Constantinople, together with Cardinal Stephen and Maynard, later Cardinal Bishop of Silva Candida, both monks of Cassino.

When they reached Bari in Apulia and heard of the pope’s death, they returned to Cassino. There Desiderius, with Humbert of Silva Candida and Peter of Tusculum presiding—bishops who had fled Rome because of the ordination of Benedict X—was placed in the abbatial seat by the unanimous vote of all the monks, as the twenty-seventh abbot after Saint [Col. 0914B] Benedict, in the year of salvation 1058.

He accompanied Nicholas II, elected at Siena, on his journey into Picenum. At Auximum, on the day before the Nones of March, a Saturday in the Ember season, Nicholas ordained him cardinal priest of Saint Cecilia; on the following day, Sunday, he consecrated him Abbot of Cassino.

Returning to Cassino, Desiderius had the monastery and its church, disfigured by age, rebuilt from the foundations. He had it dedicated by Alexander II with solemn rites, while an immense crowd of people flocked to the celebration.

He added many ornaments, arranged for the writing of very many books, and founded several towns and castles for the protection of the monastery. He recovered many possessions taken away by various princes and increased the revenues, majesty, and splendor of the monastery to a remarkable degree.

At his request, many members of the congregation were appointed by the Roman pontiffs of his time as cardinals, archbishops, and bishops. He was an especially devoted supporter of the Catholic party throughout his life: with Nicholas II against John Mincius; with Alexander II against Cadalus; and finally with Gregory VII against Guibert, whom he steadfastly opposed.

For this reason, shortly before his death, Gregory VII himself, in the presence of the cardinals, proposed Desiderius—who was to be designated the chief pontiff—as the man whose virtue might restore the Roman See, which had almost collapsed under the most dreadful schism, and bring it back to its former dignity.

After Gregory VII had been duly buried, the bishops and cardinals and the others who supported the Catholic party, all of one mind and striving with all their strength to sustain it, summoned as many people as they could from every region to the papal election [Col. 0914D]. Most of them came.

On Pentecost itself, Desiderius instructed them all concerning what Gregory had ordered about the ordering of the Church. He also approached the princes with them and urged them to provide assistance to the Church at a most necessary time.

When the cardinals and bishops learned this, they all agreed upon Desiderius. [Col. 0915A] Rejecting their judgment, however, he withdrew to the monastery and stirred up Romans and Lombards, by letters and messengers, to embrace the Church.

When the heat of summer had subsided, Prince Jordan attempted to bring Desiderius to Rome, intending to declare him pope even against his will. He could not persuade him, and thus the papal business came entirely to nothing that year.

On the day before Pentecost, when the election assembly had been summoned, all the clergy and lay supporters of the Catholic party begged him to consent to assume the Roman pontificate and not allow God’s Church to be held by an adulterine pontiff.

He rejected their pleas with the same firmness as before and replied that he would endure anything rather than accept so great a burden. [Col. 0915B] When they heard this, since it was late in the day, they all went to their homes.

The following day, when he was entreated to name the person he judged most suitable, he consulted the Roman consul Cinthius and named the Bishop of Ostia; most of the others inclined toward the bishop of Ostia.

Then a certain cardinal said: “God forbid that we should have anyone but Desiderius as pontiff!”

At these words the others, encouraged, seized Desiderius by common consent and led him to the church of Saint Lucia. After he had been duly elected and given the name Victor III, they clothed him in a scarlet cloak; they could not put the white one on him because he resisted.

After four days Victor left Rome and went to Ardea and Terracina. There he declared that he did not wish to be pope, laid aside the cross, cloak, and other papal ornaments [Col. 0915C], and returned to Cassino. Neither Jordan nor the bishops or cardinals could in any way bring him back to Rome.

The assembly at Capua was held during Lent in the year 1087. When it was over, all the clergy and laity suddenly persisted in troubling him with renewed prayers that he resume the papal dignity.

After he had rejected these prayers for two days, at last the duke, the prince, bishops, and cardinals fell at his feet to entreat him, and he yielded. On the twelfth day before the Kalends of April, the feast of Palm Sunday, he confirmed the earlier election, taking up again the cross and cloak.

After celebrating Easter at Cassino, he advanced toward the city with the princes of Capua and Salerno, took his seat outside the portico of Saint Peter, and, with the outstanding efforts of his supporters, recovered the church held by the antipope Clement [Col. 0915D].

On the seventh day before the Ides of May—that is, on the Sunday after the Ascension—the Romans came out to the Vatican. Victor was duly consecrated by the bishops of Ostia, Tusculum, Porto, and Albano, and was installed in the deaconry of Saint Lucia at the Septizodium and in the sacred see.

After eight days he returned to Cassino and from there, at Matilda’s request, went back to the city. He was received with the greatest courtesy and stayed for eight days in the Vatican. On the feast of Saint Barnabas he celebrated the divine service in Saint Peter’s church, and on the same day, with Matilda’s help, entered the city and took up residence on the island that belonged to him.

On the day before the Nativity of the Apostles, the antipope Clement, wishing to celebrate the sacred rites in Saint Peter’s church according to custom, induced certain Romans to cross the Tiber under arms and occupy the church.

Although they captured the other places, they could not enter the church held by Victor’s supporters. Clement therefore celebrated at midday in the church of Saint Mary in the Towers.

After these events, Victor, in order to break the insolence of the Saracens who were in Africa, held a council with the bishops and cardinals, summoned a huge army from every part of Italy, handed it the banner of Saint Peter, granted a plenary indulgence, and sent it to Africa. Through that army one hundred thousand enemies were slain and their greatest city captured.

There was no more distinguished victory in those times, since it was announced in Italy on the very day on which it had been won in Africa.

In Germany, Henry, fighting unsuccessfully against the Saxons, lost four thousand [Col. 0916B] soldiers by God’s will, so that at last he might cease persecuting his Church and harassing it with calamities.

Some writers say that many portents appeared at this time: domestic birds, such as hens, geese, pigeons, and peacocks, fled to mountainous places and became wild, while fish, both river and sea fish, perished in part.

Certain cities were also so shaken by an earthquake that at Syracuse a great basilica collapsed while vespers were being celebrated and crushed everyone who was in the church, with only two miraculously surviving, namely a deacon and a subdeacon.

Some say that at this time the body of Saint Nicholas was transferred from Myra, a city of Lycia, to Bari in Italy, after resting there for 745 years, and was held in the greatest reverence and honor, as Marianus Scotus, a man of great learning and singular way of life, records in his *History*.

From there Victor turned against Clement the false pope and his faction and, in August of the year 1087, summoned a council at Benevento, calling together all the bishops of Apulia and Calabria.

While the Beneventan synod was still being conducted, the pontiff began to suffer from a severe attack of dysentery. Three days later he hurried back to Cassino with the bishops and cardinals.

Feeling that death was approaching, he asked them, in accordance with the will of Pope Gregory, to make Otho, Cardinal Bishop of Ostia, pope after his death. Presenting him with his own hand in the presence of the cardinals and bishops, he said:

“Receive him and place him in the Roman see, and have him act in my place in everything in which you are able to do so.”

After these arrangements, three days later he happily migrated to Christ in the same monastery, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of October, in the year 1087.

Some writers say that he died from poison given to him in the chalice while he was celebrating the sacred rites, through the plots of the emperor and the antipope. This, however, is not incompatible with the disease of dysentery, since poisons sometimes produce dysentery by corrupting and weakening the intestines.

The see was then vacant, because of the difficulty of the times, for five months and twenty-two days.

His body was buried in the Cassinese chapter house, of which monastery he had been abbot before his pontificate, in a marble tomb bearing this epitaph:

> If anyone should wish to learn who I was, or what,  
> what kind of man and how great, golden writings teach it.  
>   
> My stock was that of the great; Benevento was my homeland;  
> Desiderius is my name, and you, Cassino, are my glory.  
>   
> Spurning [MANSI: *sternens*, “laying low”] my untouched bride, my mother, my homeland, and my kin,  
> I hastened here and became a monk.  
>   
> Then, made abbot, I strove in due course  
> to renew this place, as it is now seen.  
>   
> Meanwhile I had been renowned in the Roman city  
> as a priest of your Church, blessed Peter.  
>   
> Having held that office for twenty-nine years (six lustra less one year),  
> I then, as Victor, climbed the apostolic throne.  
>   
> After scarcely four and a half months had passed,  
> being sixty years old (twice six lustra), I am buried here in death.  
>   
> The final light of the sun stood in the Virgin’s sign  
> when the true Sun, God himself, took me from here.

[Col. 0917]

## ANOTHER HISTORICAL NOTICE

(Mansi, *Councils*, vol. XX, p. 630.)

[Col. 0917B] Victor, a native of Benevento and descended from a noble lineage, whose name had previously been Desiderius, was elected pope—Victor III, the third of that name—from the Cassinese monastery and the bishopric of Ostia, on the advice of Gregory VII, who was already dying, after an interregnum of almost one year, in the year 1086 of Christ our Redeemer. Consecrated on the seventh day before the Ides of May of the following year, he turned his military expedition against the wicked Saracens who continually harassed the shores of Italy and carried off Christian captives. With what fortune and success Leo of Ostia relates in these words:

“After consultation had therefore been held with the bishops and cardinals, he assembled an army from almost all the peoples of Italy, entrusted them with the banner of blessed Peter the Apostle, and sent them under remission of all sins against the unbelieving and impious into [Col. 0918B] Africa. With Christ as their leader, they entered Africa and killed one hundred thousand combatants, capturing and destroying their chief city. Moreover, lest anyone doubt that this happened by God’s will, on the very day when the Christians emerged victorious, the victory was also announced in Italy.”

After Guibert and the other schismatics had been condemned and excommunicated by synodal judgment, “he happily migrated to the Lord,” says the same Leo of Ostia, on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of October, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1087. He was buried in the apse of the chapter house itself, where three days before his death he had ordered a grave to be prepared for him. The epitaph inscribed on his tomb is found in Leo of Ostia, composed in these verses. (See above in the earlier notice.)

[Col. 0917]

## DIPLOMATIC NOTICE

(Jaffé, *Regesta Romanorum pontificum*, no. 447.)

The one surviving bull of Victor III was issued through the hands of … the bishop of Segni and librarian of the Roman Church.

[Col. 0917]

## ON THE DEEDS OF DESIDERIUS, ABBOT OF MONTE CASSINO, LATER POPE VICTOR III

(Mabillon, *Acta Benedictina* IX, 585.)

[Col. 0917B] Desiderius obtained full governance of the abbey upon the death of Stephen, abbot of Cassino. Leo of Ostia calls him the fourth founder of the monastery; together with his continuator, he recounts his life and distinguished deeds at length in the *Chronicle of Cassino*, which is entirely devoted to Abbot Desiderius. We shall borrow the account of his life from that work, omitting what has no relevance to our subject. Leo begins his prologue as follows:

[Col. 0918B] “The deeds of Desiderius from the *Chronicle of Cassino*—The author’s reliability. Desiderius, the thirty-seventh abbot of this monastery and the fourth restorer and renewer of this place, held office for twenty-nine years and five months. The first founder and builder of this monastery was the most holy Father Benedict; the second was Petronax; the third, Aligernus; and this Desiderius of ours was the fourth. In him, indeed, almighty God appears in our own time to have fulfilled even bodily that evangelical promise in which it is said: ‘Amen I say to you, that everyone who has left house or brothers, or sisters, or father, or mother, or wife, or children, or lands for my name’s sake shall receive a hundredfold and shall possess eternal life’ (Matthew 19).

“The material of the deeds of this truly admirable and singular man of his order is so rich, so varied, and finally so abundant that it could not have seemed unworthy of writing even to Jerome himself, had he been present, or to Sulpicius. Yet I, although the most inexperienced of all and wholly unequal to so great a work, both out of obedience to the most holy Oderisius—for he is the very man who succeeded Desiderius in governing the monastery—and because of the great affection that Father Desiderius himself deigned to show me from almost my infancy—for when I had scarcely passed my fourteenth year, he received, instructed, nurtured, and advanced me with the greatest kindness in this holy place—observing also with grief that, along with the usefulness of so great a work, the memory too of so great a man would through the negligence of writers gradually pass into oblivion and consequently into contempt, shall nevertheless undertake, although I cannot do so fittingly, elegantly, or adequately, to touch upon his works in some fashion, trusting in God’s help, and to commit them imperfectly to writing for the glory of God and of so great a man, for his holy memory, and for the consolation of his sons, our brothers.

“I judge it more equitable to accept, through obedience [Col. 0919C] and devotion, the stigma of ignorance than to remain entirely silent about such precious material. I consider it wholly unworthy that, although I cannot report everything, I should not strive to relate at least something about so many and such great works of his—following the exceedingly prudent practice of hunters pursuing wild beasts: although they cannot capture them all, they by no means neglect to catch as many as they can.

“And because the works of so great a man are very numerous and almost countless, I confess that I shall omit even much that I know. Had I wished to write everything, I would certainly have composed a lengthy and disproportionate History, although I do not doubt that many of our people who remember these things together with me will on that account reproach me. But, usefully taking account of my readers’ weariness, I judged it sufficient to write only those matters most worthy of narration. For if some things are found less fully in our writings, they are displayed more clearly than daylight in his works.

“Since, with Christ’s help, I desire to begin here, I learned the beginnings of this man’s life from those who had been his companions from his infancy. I also learned many things from his own truthful mouth, since in his great kindness he often allowed me to remain close to him; I heard some things from certain elders; and finally I both saw many things with my own eyes and was present at almost all of them until his death. Therefore I wish to make my reader completely certain that in this little work I shall add nothing from outside and write nothing about him unless I have learned it to be true. I remember that I read, with simple understanding: ‘You will destroy, O Lord, all who speak lies’ (Psalm 5:7), except, of course, for the other interpretation by which this statement is affirmed concerning heretics.

“But if anyone, led by envy or malice, should refuse to place faith in these things and should suppose instead that I undertook this work out of a desire to win favor, let him hasten here, if he wishes, open his eyes, and see; and, considering without jealousy through the things that are visible those also that cannot be seen, let him wonder and believe. Once he believes, let him offer praises and thanks for this to the Giver of all good things, and thus finally recognize that I have written little about his many deeds, and very little about his greatest ones.”

### Desiderius’s lineage; his piety as a boy

[Col. 0920B] Desiderius, therefore, tracing his bloodline from the most noble origin of the princes of Benevento, began from the earliest beginnings of childhood to be noble in spirit rather than in flesh, and chose from, so to speak, his mother’s breast to devote himself more to God’s service than to the vanities of the world. Although still a little boy, he made a practice of attending church, gladly hearing and reading the sacred lessons, frequently engaging in conversations about them with certain religious men, and striving to express in himself whatever he could learn from them about good conduct.

But his father, wishing to involve him in worldly affairs and, since he was his only son, loving him with a unique affection, intended to extend the name of his own nobility through his posterity. When the boy began to reach adolescence, he therefore sought to betroth him to an equally noble girl and to hasten by every means the strengthening of the relationship between the two families. But because the Spirit of God had kindled Desiderius’s heart with its fire toward contempt for the world, the excellent boy intended to act quite otherwise than his father had planned. By whatever secret gestures he could, he indicated that he desired the desert rather than marriage, and he would have satisfied his desires had not his parents’ vigilant guardianship, their exceptional love, and their immense concern prevented him.

### He flees to the desert and assumes the monastic habit

[Col. 0920D] Not many days later, when his father had been killed by the Normans—as God had ordained—Desiderius, having somehow found the opportunity he had long desired, began by every means, although secretly, to strive to bring forth in action the desire he had conceived in thought.

He therefore disclosed his entire plan to a monk well known to him, a sufficiently prudent man in worldly affairs named Jaquintus, from whose account I learned this. He revealed his vow, made his intention clear, and earnestly begged him to assist him confidently in this matter. “You know, my father,” he said, “how my relatives have bound me to this wretched world. But, to tell you the truth, I resolved long ago to devote myself to God. By God himself I implore and beseech you: according to what you know and are able to do, release me from these bonds and secretly transfer me, free to serve God more fully, to some most remote solitude.”

What more is there to say? Jaquintus promised him assistance in everything but ordered him to beware lest this proposal be from demons. When, however, he recognized that the young man’s heart was firm in Christ, and after testing him again and again by visiting him, found in him always the same resolve as before, one day, toward evening, they mounted horses together and left the city as if for a ride, accompanied by several servants. They reached the church of Blessed Peter, surnamed Major, situated near the same city. Entering it as if for the sake of prayer, they left the horses and the sword with which Desiderius was then girded with the aforementioned servants outside the doors, as though for safekeeping.

Then, already late, they proceeded by a small rear door of the church and began their journey. Since the place to which they had decided to go was no more than eight miles away, they were confused by the darkness and by fear alike, and reached it only with difficulty on the morning of the following day. When Santari, a man of God who lived a solitary life there, saw them, he was greatly astonished and rejoiced. He immediately led them into his cell, repeatedly kissed Desiderius, and began carefully to ask why they had come.

When he learned Desiderius’s intention, he was profoundly amazed that a boy so noble, so delicate, so rich, and especially so dear to his parents had approached in such fervor to serve the Lord under so strict a purpose, spurning all the pageantry and vanities of the world. But because he knew that nothing was difficult or impossible for God, he offered him the greatest praise and thanks. At Desiderius’s own insistence above all, he immediately stripped him of the old man with his deeds, and then clothed him with the new man, who is renewed in the knowledge of God. When Jaquintus returned at once to his own home, Desiderius remained alone with Santari.

### His monastic habit is forcibly removed

[Col. 0921C] His servants, as has been said, waited for him in vain outside the church with his horses and weapons. When at last they learned of his departure, they returned quickly to the city, which was already near nightfall, and with anxious hearts reported to his mother and relatives what had happened. His mother spent that night in tears; at daybreak his relatives and kinsmen mounted horses and dispersed through the various neighboring districts to search for him. Finally, suspecting what had happened and having confirmed it through the evidence of his servants, they reached Santari’s cell.

They immediately entered it by force and found him wearing the monastic habit. In great anger they attacked the aforementioned servant of God with severe insults and many reproaches. They dishonorably stripped Desiderius of the sacred garment, tearing it apart with their own hands, and clothed him again in his former clothing, although he was unwilling and resisted. Finally, placing him on a horse and holding the reins themselves, as though leading some great prize before them, they returned to the city in triumphal fashion.

Who could attempt to recount here his mother’s tears and complaints, together with the counsels she vainly pressed upon Desiderius, and the rejoicing of his relatives—or rather of the whole city? For almost an entire year [Col. 0922A] he lived under strict guard in his mother’s house, secular in dress alone but celibate in mind; and no one could persuade him in any way either to marry or to undertake any worldly action. Thus the Lord, who intended to appoint him a faithful and energetic steward of his household, preserved him pure and free from every stain of carnal contamination. Hence all the citizens rightly regarded him as remarkable and desirable.

### He flees a second time

But when his mother no longer suspected that he would flee again, and since she could not keep him with her as a married man, she tried to make him a cleric. She first allowed him to go to the episcopal residence, which was quite close to her house, under guard, and later, as her confidence increased, more often by himself.

At that time the superior of the monastery of Saint Sophia was a man named Siconolfus. Knowing Desiderius’s desire perfectly, he did not dare speak with him during the day, lest suspicion revive, but very often conversed with him at night in the episcopal residence. After not many days, he came to him at night with horses, as he was accustomed to do, secretly led him, dressed in a hooded monastic garment, to Salerno, and swiftly returned to Benevento.

Desiderius then approached Prince Guaimarius, who was related to him by blood. He explained the reason for his arrival and begged that, since his parents’ obstinacy prevented him from living as a monk in his homeland, he might be permitted to serve God peacefully in Guaimarius’s presence. If he could obtain this favor, he would never leave; but if Guaimarius would at some point have to return him to his relatives, he asked that he be granted permission instead to go elsewhere.

Guaimarius was exceedingly delighted by his arrival and greatly astonished at such fervor in so young a man. He granted his request, kept him with him for several days, and solemnly promised that he would not return him to anyone against his vow. Finally, at Desiderius’s request, he sent him to the monastery of the Holy Trinity, called La Cava, situated not far from Salerno.

His relatives pursued him [or, according to an alternative reading, anticipated this], and by great and repeated prayers importuned Guaimarius to return Desiderius to them. But since the prince remained faithful to his promise to Desiderius, Landulfus, prince of Benevento, worn down by the entreaties of Desiderius’s mother and relatives, came in person to Salerno and requested that Desiderius be restored to his kinsmen.

The monastery of Saint Sophia was situated not far from the walls of the city of Benevento. It had been founded by Arichis, duke of Benevento, for religious women, as Leo himself explains more fully in book 1, chapter 9, of the *Chronicle*. Later it passed to men and remained for a long time subject to the Cassinese monastery, as the same author relates. Ughellus published its *Chronicle* at the end of volume VIII of *Italia sacra*. Finally, after various vicissitudes, it was united by Clement VIII, in 1590, with the congregation of the regular canons of Saint Savior of Bologna, as Lubinus notes in his *Notice of the Abbeys of Italy*. The monastery of La Cava, mentioned below, is discussed in various places in this and the preceding volume.

### He is forced to return and is received at the monastery of Saint Sophia

[Col. 0923A] At last permission was obtained for Desiderius to return to Benevento on the condition that he be allowed to remain at the monastery of Saint Sophia under monastic profession, without anyone’s hindrance or opposition. When they reached Benevento, all his relatives and the whole city rushed out together to meet him, and the prince escorted him to the monastery with the entire company.

Gregory, then a very prudent and energetic man, was abbot of that monastery. He received Desiderius with great joy, since Desiderius was desirable to everyone, and then, for the first time, ordered that his name be changed and that he be called Desiderius; until then he had been called Danferius.

### He transfers to the monastery of Tremiti, then to the desert; he is forced to return

[Col. 0923B] After he had lived there for several years under a highly religious rule and had often reflected that it was impossible to become a perfect monk in his own homeland, news of the monastery of Tremiti eventually came to his attention. It was situated in the Adriatic Sea, near an island formerly called Diomedes, about thirty miles from the mainland.

Since he had long before become acquainted at Benevento with the abbot of that place, he went there with difficulty, though he obtained permission, and devoted himself to a sufficiently austere way of life, in which he spent a considerable time. But because the abbot loved him so greatly that he wished to hand over the abbacy to him while still alive, whereas Desiderius directed his mind toward subjection rather than leadership and therefore decided that he ought to leave the place, the same abbot, on one occasion when he was going out to inspect the monastery’s affairs, asked Desiderius to accompany him.

Desiderius gladly embraced this opportunity to depart and considered that he should not delay. When they had gone together, as circumstances required, to the court of Count Transmundus, the count’s wife—greatly delighted at Desiderius’s arrival because he was her kinsman—obtained from her husband that he retain Desiderius with him for a time, even against the abbot’s wishes. Desiderius himself, he says, was the cause of this retention.

Hearing at that time of the celebrated name of the hermits living on Mount Majella, and desiring to hasten there and serve God in greater seclusion, he asked the aforementioned count to send him there; [Col. 0923D] this was done. After he had remained there for about three months—from the beginning of February, namely, until the third Sunday after Easter—the aforementioned Jaquintus was sent there with a letter from the pope to the prior of that hermitage. In the letter the prior was commanded under threat not to presume to retain Desiderius any longer; Desiderius himself was likewise ordered not to dare to prolong his stay there any further. Thus he returned to the monastery of Saint Sophia.

### He becomes known to Pope Leo and joins Alfano

Not many days later, the most holy lord Pope Leo returned from the transalpine regions and entered Benevento. Since Desiderius had long been known and greatly loved by Humbert, bishop of Silva Candida, he became known and very familiar to the pope through Humbert and through Frederick, then chancellor. He frequently assisted the pope in the service at the altar and often read the Gospel at his Masses.

At that time the aforementioned pontiff went down into Apulia to fight the Normans. Defeated by them through God’s judgment, he returned to Benevento, appointed Vodelric, whom he had brought with him, as archbishop, and after about nine months returned to Rome and died.

Meanwhile Desiderius, having fallen into considerable illness because of excessive abstinence and many vigils, went to Salerno for treatment. While he remained there for some time, Alfano, later archbishop of that same city, a most prudent and noble cleric, became closely associated with him. Desiderius frequently urged Alfano’s soul toward contempt for the world and eventually prevailed upon him to become a monk, provided that he were first permitted to go to Jerusalem, as he had long intended.

After they had confirmed this agreement between them, Desiderius returned to Benevento. Not many days later he sent word to Alfano to come to him. Alfano refused, or rather was afraid to leave Salerno. Desiderius therefore went to him again and, because Alfano feared certain enemies, led him out of the city at night dressed in Desiderius’s own hooded garment and brought him with him to Benevento.

When noblemen and clerics of every kind began frequently to visit Alfano and to honor him appropriately because of his great prudence, his intention of traveling to Jerusalem gradually began to grow cold. He declared that he would never, under any circumstances or at any time, separate himself from Desiderius’s side. Thus they spent some time at the monastery of Saint Sophia.

### He visits Pope Victor and withdraws to Cassino

Then news suddenly spread that Pope Victor had come to Rome from the transalpine regions and would shortly be traveling to these parts. Terrified by this report, Alfano—who undoubtedly knew that his brothers would be accused of the murder of Prince Guaimarius—decided to forestall the pope and earnestly asked Desiderius to go with him.

Since Desiderius possessed remarkable skill in singing and considerable knowledge of medicine, and had brought several books on that art from home, he confidently believed that he would be regarded as someone of importance in the supreme pontiff’s court. Having prepared and arranged as many medicines as he could, they set out for the Roman pontiff in Tuscany together with the archbishop of that city, and found him staying at Florence.

In a short time they gained the greatest familiarity with him and were treated with considerable honor. But after they had remained there for some time, Desiderius learned for certain that the pope would not come to these regions at all and would soon travel beyond the mountains. At the same time he realized that remaining in the pope’s court was wholly useless to his purpose. He therefore began by every means to urge Alfano to seek permission from the pope immediately to return.

A man named Peter had recently been elected abbot of this monastery by the brothers. To report his election, he had sent two brothers from this place to the pope. Desiderius therefore, finding the opportunity he had long desired, approached the Roman pontiff with Alfano. They prostrated themselves together at his feet and asked permission to withdraw. They also requested that, for the sake of living more religiously, the pope send them there with the monks who had come to him from the Cassinese monastery, and commend them by letter to the abbot and brothers.

The pope consented. Accordingly, they were sent with those brothers to this monastery. Received honorably by the abbot, associated with the brothers, and living among them for some time with great decency and humility, they were greatly loved by everyone and received monastic consecration from the same abbot. Frederick was more than sufficiently delighted at their arrival.

### A vision; he is placed over the monastery at Capua; Alfano

During these days Desiderius had a vision not to be disregarded, whose meaning was soon commended by the event itself. He saw himself standing together with Alfano in a lofty and very beautiful tower situated beside the brothers’ chapter house. In it Father Benedict appeared to be seated on a most dignified throne.

When they were astonished and afraid at the vision and did not dare approach any nearer, blessed Benedict cheerfully beckoned to Desiderius and, extending his hand, ordered him to sit beside him. But Alfano, since he had not been called by Benedict, as though bearing this indignantly, left the house.

This vision seemed most clearly to foretell both that Alfano would not remain long in this place and that Desiderius would assume in this monastery the role of Father Benedict. Not long afterward, therefore, Alfano was requested by Prince Gisulf. He was first made abbot at the monastery of Saint Benedict in Salerno and subsequently obtained the archbishopric of that city.

Desiderius, meanwhile, was sent to the monastery at Capua as superior. Count Richard of Aversa was then besieging Capua. But when Pandulf, prince of that city, wished to impose upon Desiderius certain unworthy and superfluous obligations, in accordance with the custom of earlier times, Desiderius, firm-hearted as he was, considered it wholly unfitting to agree to them. He left Capua, approached Richard, obtained from him security for all the monastery’s possessions outside the city, and from that time formed with him a close bond of friendship. He remained for some time among the dependencies of that monastery, leaving only a very few brothers in the monastery and summoning the others to himself.

The Alfano mentioned here is famous among ecclesiastical authors for various short works, which Peter the Deacon lists in chapter 19 of his *On the Illustrious Men of Cassino*. Marus made further observations about him and his writings in his notes on this passage of Peter the Deacon. Trithemius, Baronius, Vossius, and others frequently praise him. Some of his shorter works were published by Martinengius, Ughellus, Surius, and others. Arnold Wion says that he was numbered among the saints, but I have been unable to find his name in any sacred calendars.

As for Desiderius, he renovated the church of Saint Benedict within Capua, as is related in book 4, chapter 33, of the *Chronicle*. Pope Paschal II consecrated it under Abbot Oderisius. Under Leo X this abbey was transformed into a college of canons, which for some time was governed by a secular abbot. Later Clement VIII entrusted it to Cardinal Bellarmine, archbishop of Capua. Finally, through Bellarmine’s agency and with the approval of Paul V, it passed to the Jesuits, as Michael the Monk relates in the *Capuan Sanctuary*. He says that before the church came into the possession of the Fathers of the Society, it had been adorned with ancient paintings and mosaics; in its apse these three verses were read:

> Desiderius, who is also Victor, bishop and abbot,  
> Began this work, which Oderisius, the excellent abbot,  
> Completed, Benedict, to adorn it in your honor.

### Pope Stephen X; Desiderius is elected abbot of Cassino and sent to Constantinople; the pope dies

After the aforementioned Frederick had first been elected abbot of this place and had finally been ordained Roman pontiff, Desiderius went to Rome in August, summoned by Frederick himself, together with twelve other brothers from this place. There he was struck by Roman fever and returned here after a few days.

When the same pope came to this monastery about four months later, he soon afterward was seized by a grave illness and brought almost to the point of death. He summoned the priors of this monastery and gave them the option of electing as abbot whomever they wished.

After they had consulted among themselves and, as is customary in such matters, proposed now one man and now another for election, the common agreement of all at last settled upon Desiderius. With one voice they begged the pope to grant him to them as Father.

The pope declared that this election pleased him greatly. Desiderius had long been well known to him at Benevento, dating from the time of Pope Leo; and since Abbot Peter had received Desiderius less than two full years earlier, the pope had become bound to him by great familiarity. While still in his chamber, therefore, he confirmed the brothers’ election, saying that although at that time the monastery possessed many religious and spiritual men endowed with great integrity and prudence, they could not have chosen anyone from their community more suitable for this office.

Since he had resolved, while he lived, to entrust the abbacy to no mortal, but had long intended to make Desiderius apocrisiarius to the emperor at Constantinople, he decreed that if Desiderius returned while the pope was still alive, he would himself hand the abbacy over to him; but if he died before Desiderius’s return, the entire community was to receive Desiderius as abbot without any opposition when he came back.

He gave Cardinal Stephen and Mainardus, later bishop of Silva Candida, as companions for Desiderius’s journey. In the letters he sent to the emperor, he mentioned that Desiderius had been elected abbot of Cassino, and he sent him away, ordering him to hasten back as quickly as possible after completing the embassy.

Desiderius therefore, striving to fulfill the duty entrusted to him, took with him whatever was necessary for so great a journey and began the journey with the companions assigned to him. He proceeded to the monastery of Saint John, called at Veneris, in order to embark there. After he had remained there for several days in vain and did not dare to put out to sea because of the harsh weather, he went from there to Siponto.

There he boarded a ship bound for Bari. Through a certain bishop who had gone to Mount Gargano for prayer, he asked that he be commended to the brothers and that they be told he had put out to sea. But when he was delayed for some time at Bari as well because of the storm, he tried to send another messenger here, who reported that, because of the bad weather, he was still staying at Bari.

By divine providence, what had until then delayed Desiderius from receiving the honor of this place happened in such a way that on the very day this messenger arrived here, our brothers who had set out with the pope returned, the pope having died and been buried at Florence. Our brothers immediately met in council and hastily sent two brothers who were to recall Desiderius and announce the pope’s death to him.

### After the pope’s death, he abandons the journey and returns to Cassino; he is made abbot

Desiderius had by then sufficiently prepared everything necessary for the journey he had begun and was just about to sail with Argyrus, master of Bari, when, on Palm Sunday toward evening, he received the messengers sent by our brothers. They declared that the pope had died and that all the brothers had sent them in haste to recall him. He was therefore to return as quickly as possible and assume the governance of the monastery, while everyone eagerly awaited him, as the Lord had ordained.

Desiderius was stunned by the sudden death of the pope. He immediately summoned his companions and disclosed what the messengers had reported. Together with Argyrus they began to consider how they might return before the pope’s death became widely known. They had no doubt that once his death was learned, the Normans would either capture them or obstruct their journey.

They immediately purchased, or otherwise obtained, several pack animals for themselves and their companions. Setting out on the Monday after Palm Sunday, they came to Robert Guiscard, then merely count of the Normans in Apulia, but later duke of all Apulia, Calabria, and Sicily. They asked that they be allowed to pass safely through his territory.

Although Robert had already learned that the pope had died, he was a man of the greatest kindness and granted them safe passage. He also gave Desiderius three horses, which he still needed. Thus, with God prospering everything, they returned without hindrance and arrived at the city of San Germano rather late on Holy Saturday.

Very early on Easter Sunday they came up here and, according to the monastery’s custom, entered the brothers’ chapter house. Humbert, bishop of Santa Rufina, and Peter, bishop of Tusculum, presided, together with Cardinal Stephen and Mainardus, the companions of Desiderius.

As we related much earlier (book 2, chapter 101), the aforementioned bishops, Humbert and Peter, had then been fleeing from Rome to avoid the ordination of Mincius and were traveling to Benevento to celebrate Easter. But by God’s arrangement, our priors invited them to remain and retained them, honoring them on the occasion of so great a feast.

After the solemn sermon for that great day, Humbert, who was fully informed about the entire arrangement, summoned Desiderius. On behalf of all the brothers, he commanded him to accept the obedience of the abbacy, just as the pope had formerly arranged.

Without any delay or waiting for a reply, all immediately rose, received Desiderius, carried him to the church with the greatest praise, and honorably seated him in the abbatial chair. Everyone was filled with immense joy and gladness, both because of the solemnity of Easter and because of his appointment.

This occurred in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1058.

### He Repairs the Monastery Buildings

After Desiderius had assumed the abbacy, he began by every means to apply himself and strive [Col. 0928C] so that what was said of him might truly be said. Seeing, therefore, that all the workshops and service buildings of the monastery were cramped in space and misshapen in form, and that through both age and neglect they were falling into ruin—so much so that they all seemed to be covered with adjoining roofs, while the exit of one was joined to the entrance of another—he was indeed stirred in spirit to undertake their renewal. Yet he was also troubled, since he had almost no resources set aside with which to begin so arduous a work.

First, therefore, as though wishing to test whether he was capable of accomplishing anything, he completed with sufficiently creditable workmanship the palace which Abbot Richerius had formerly begun on the eastern side of the monastery and brought up as far as the upper story; next to it, toward the church, he built a small but entirely adequate building in which books could be stored. When he saw that this had turned out successfully for him [Col. 0928D], he also undertook to build from the foundations the house in which the abbots were accustomed to live. This house, attached to the church on the northern side, was visibly supported below by the poorest wooden forks and constructed for the most part of wickerwork. To it he joined the palace with an apse that the ancients were accustomed to call “Todericus.”

Then, with God inspiring and prospering him, he no less energetically undertook to renew the dwelling that contained the resting brothers in several small rooms, each divided according to its limited size—specifically, on the southern side of the earlier building—which he intended to demolish completely in order to make room for the cloister. For, because of the summit of the mountain, where there was scarcely any level ground, the earlier monks had barely managed to construct here, beside the apse of the church, something resembling a very small cloister [Col. 0929A].

This house was therefore completed at a length of 160 cubits, a width of 24 cubits, and a height of varying extent, owing to the unevenness of the mountain, though everywhere considerable. After fitting it out quite beautifully with fir beams, he covered it with tiles and adorned it with various colors.
