Without delay, proceeding in the same manner, he completely demolished the old chapterhouse and renewed it; he decorated it with a plastered enclosure all around, glass windows, and a beautiful pavement of various marbles, then covered it with tiles and painted it with an exceptionally pleasing variety of colors.

### He Founds a New Castle

At this time Desiderius is said [Col. 0929B] to have built, with the assistance of Duke Adenulf of Gaeta, a new castle against the people of Fratte, who were hostile to the people of Minturno and to the neighboring towns within the territory of Cassino, after he had unsuccessfully attempted to pacify them by arguments and benefactions.

### He Becomes a Cardinal Priest; Vicar of the Apostolic See; Council of Melfi

He now deals with the ordination of Pope Nicholas, who had succeeded Stephen. That pontiff sent word to this monastery, as Leo continues, that the lord abbot should meet him as soon as possible while he was traveling to the Marches, namely so that at the approaching fast of the month of March he might receive both the rank of priest and the office of the cardinalate.

On the first Sunday of Lent, therefore, after all the necessary preparations had been made, he set out and joined the apostolic pontiff at the monastery of Farfa [Col. 0929C]. There he was received by him with extraordinary friendliness and honor, and he departed with him for Osimo. There, on the second Saturday of Lent—which at that time fell on the day before the Nones of March—the same apostolic pontiff ordained him cardinal priest; on the following Sunday he received the consecration of the abbacy and obtained from him a highly honorable privilege, in accordance with the custom of his predecessors.

Moreover, in virtue of the dignity of his cardinalate and for the honor of the most holy Father Benedict, the same apostolic pontiff granted him his own authority throughout Campania and the Principate, as well as Apulia and Calabria, as far as the river Pescara where it flows into the sea. After this, having received permission to return, he came to Rome and on the following Sunday, the middle Sunday of Lent, solemnly celebrated Mass at the church of Saint Peter. Accompanied by an innumerable crowd of Romans, he was led with the greatest acclaim to the titular church of Saint Cecilia across the Tiber; thus he returned to this monastery on the feast of Saint Benedict.

Since the same pontiff had invited him to Rome for the sake of the paschal festival, he returned there, and after the feast left the city and proceeded to the Apulian city of Melfi, where the pontiff had then decided to hold a council. At that synod, when Richard, prince of Capua, was present with many others, he was admonished by the aforementioned Pope Nicholas and made a grant to Saint Benedict of the monastery of Saint Mary at Calena, together with its dependencies [Col. 0930A].

Angelus de Nuce reproduces the grant praised here in his notes, dated 23 August, in the second year of Prince Richard’s rule. That monastery, situated near the city of Vesta, was later united by Eugenius IV, in 1446, to the congregation of the Canons Regular of the Lateran, as Lubinus observes in his *Catalogue of the Abbeys of Italy*.

### The Monasteries at Salerno

At that time Gisulf, prince of Salerno, in response to Desiderius’ complaint on this matter, restored to this holy place the cell of Saint Benedict at Salerno, which the violence of the Salernitans had hitherto withdrawn from the right of our monastery. But when he had removed the abbot and appointed there a provost according to the custom of our cells, the people of Salerno, [Col. 0930B] bearing this very indignantly, began to press the prince to allow that monastery to remain organized as it had formerly been.

Compelled by their request, the prince offered in its entirety to this monastery the monastery of Saint Lawrence, built within the city of Salerno and belonging to him by hereditary right. Nevertheless, he did not invalidate the restitution that he had previously made concerning the aforesaid cell, and so forth. The author goes on at length concerning the charters of the monastery of Salerno belonging to the Cassinese monks, which had first been hidden and later torn apart. After various fortunes, the monastery of Saint Benedict was finally given by Clement VIII, in 1591, to the Olivetan monks.

### Monks Raised to High Dignities; Princes Robert and Richard as Friends

At a later time, when the aforementioned pontiff again came into these regions, while staying at Acerra he ordained Lord Oderisius, son of Oderisius, count of the Marsi, and a monk of this place from childhood, as a deacon in the Lateran church [Col. 0930C].

Afterward, in the city of Aquino, having deposed the bishop Angelo because he was a novice and recklessly wasteful of ecclesiastical resources, and because he had long since been excommunicated by Pope Leo of holy memory for certain wicked acts, he consecrated as bishop Lord Martin, a Florentine by birth, a thoroughly religious and prudent man and formerly one of the prior monks of this place.

Peter, bishop of the sees of Venafro and Isernia, a native of Ravenna and our monk, was also consecrated at that time. During those same days he confirmed Richard in the principality [Col. 0930D] of Capua and Robert in the duchy of Apulia, Calabria, and Sicily, after first receiving from them an oath of fidelity to the Roman Church, together with the investiture of an annual census of … .

Since the course of the history has already brought mention of these two magnates—Robert and Richard—who, more than all other men of their time, loved, enriched, and protected this place, and who throughout their lives were exceedingly devoted, faithful, and intimate friends of our Desiderius, it seems worthwhile to insert briefly in this little work how each of them was advanced to the honor of his dignity.

Richard came to this monastery and was received with extraordinary honor and solemn procession. Everything pleased him greatly. When the elders asked him to protect the place, he most devoutly promised that henceforth he would be its most faithful defender against all who might oppose it, and so forth. In all these successes he always gave thanks to God and to Father Benedict, declaring with complete certainty that he was assisted by the saint’s merits and raised up by his prayers.

As for the lord abbot, although he had already made him his closest friend while presiding at Capua, as we said above, he nevertheless revered him in every way as though he were his father, entrusted himself to his counsels, and willingly obeyed him in everything as though he were his lord [Col. 0931A].

### The Grant, Acts, and Donations to the Monastery of Cassino Are Here Merely Indicated

In the first year in which the prince was made ruler together with his son Jordan, following the custom of earlier princes, he issued a general grant to this monastery, and so forth. The author relates, as he does in the following chapter, many things that Richard did in favor of the monastery of Cassino.

In chapter 19 he lists various donations made by Gregory, the Roman consul; Baldwin, count of Valle Sorana; Pandulf, count of Venafro; Landulf, count of Miniano, who came to conversion; and other devout and distinguished men. There is no point in listing them individually here.

### He Provides Ecclesiastical Ornaments

Meanwhile Desiderius burned with an immense desire to acquire ecclesiastical ornaments, of which we had hitherto been exceedingly poor, from every possible source. Yet, by God’s gift, this good desire could not prove ineffective in so great a man, as will become clear in what follows [Col. 0931C].

Bringing some items from his own resources and borrowing others from his closest Roman friends, he assembled 180 pounds in value and redeemed nearly all the ornaments of Pope Victor that had been pawned here and there throughout the City. They were as follows:

A large *diarodanum* cope, woven entirely with gold on every side and furnished with gold fringes; a large *diacitrinum* chasuble, decently adorned all around with gold bands; another *exametum*, likewise bordered all around with a fringe; a similar *exametum* dalmatic, marked with gold and white at the head, feet, and sleeves; a *diapystis* tunic with a very ample border, golden at the feet, sleeves, and shoulders; nine gold-woven stoles with maniples and half-belts [Col. 0931D]; and a *diarodanum* cloth with gold bands for the faldstool.

It is also pleasing to record here the individual items that, from the time of his ordination until the renewal of the major basilica, he either made or acquired for the church’s equipment; the remaining items we shall describe more fully later.

He covered and gilded the pastoral staff with silver. Before the altar he made a golden panel set with gems, weighing about ten pounds, as well as a gold thurible with gems and enamels, weighing two pounds. He had a book of Epistles for Mass copied and decorated it with one golden cover and another of silver.

He also had a copy of the Rule of Saint Benedict richly ornamented inside and covered outside with silver. Likewise, he did the same for two altar sacramentaries, two Gospels, and one Epistolary [Col. 0932A]. Until that time both the Gospels and the Epistles had been read from a complete Missal; how inappropriate that was at the time is now sufficiently apparent.

He did the same for another little book containing processional prayers. He also made a little book for singing before the altar, or on the step, and attached to it ivory covers magnificently carved and decorated with silver.

He had the book *The Life of Saint Benedict, Saint Maurus, and Saint Scholastica* copied with the greatest care. He also made silver doors for the entrance to the choir, weighing about thirty pounds.

He made wooden seats around the choir, with their backboards, outstanding in both carving and painting. He also erected, outside the choir, a wooden step of the same workmanship, quite beautiful and in the manner of an ambo, from which the lessons at night, as well as the Epistles and Gospels at Masses on the principal feasts, were to be read [Col. 0932B].

During those same days, when rumor had spread that the king was coming to Italy, he went without delay to Amalfi. There he bought twenty silk cloths called *triblata*, so that, if it should prove necessary, he would certainly have something to give the king for the protection and honor of this monastery.

At that time he also acquired there a silver pitcher weighing seven pounds, which he assigned for the ministry of holy water during Sunday processions, together with another pitcher of the same metal and weight that was later given to him.

Since the king had returned from his journey, he immediately ordered all the *triblata* to be made into copes [Col. 0932C]. Seeing the bronze doors of the bishop’s church at Amalfi, and finding them very pleasing to his eyes, he at once sent the measurements of the doors of the old church to Constantinople, where he had very beautiful ones made. For he had not yet decided to renew the church, and for this reason the doors themselves were made as short as they have remained to the present day.

### The Election and Schism of Cadalo Are Merely Indicated

Meanwhile, after the apostolic pontiff had died at Florence, and so forth, the author deals with the election of Alexander II and the schism of Cadalo.

### The Holy Mountain Is Struck by Lightning

Desiderius had nearly completed the fifth year of his administration when, by divine permission, this monastery was struck by lightning, more terribly than usual. One day, while the brothers were customarily celebrating the Office of Prime in the church, lightning suddenly slipped down from heaven and struck the priest serving that week, a man of good reputation named Manno, who was standing in the choir, killing him instantly. It threw the others who were standing nearby to the ground as though lifeless.

It also struck and killed a certain novice who was standing outside the choir before the great cross. In the chapterhouse it split the official tables and left the record-keeper himself as though dead. It tore apart and threw down the painted image of Abbot Richerius on a panel in the same chapterhouse, and it struck in many other parts of the monastery. This happened on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of February.

Therefore, after taking counsel with the brothers, the venerable Father decided, in order to appease God’s anger, that throughout all the months the first Friday should be observed communally by everyone as a day of abstinence, and that Mass should accordingly be celebrated especially while proceeding barefoot. He also ordered that throughout the year, on every day, a prayer against lightning should be recited at public Mass and at the special offices of the psalms [Col. 0933A].

Moreover, when Lord Peter Damian came to this monastery and by word and example kindled in everyone whom he could reach a fervent zeal for God’s service, he eventually obtained, with the lord abbot’s permission, through a voluntary offering by the entire congregation for the remission of all sins, that throughout the year they should be content with bread and water on Fridays and that each person should receive a discipline after making confession [Col. 0933B]. In addition, they were to undertake a three-day fast every year at the beginning of Lent.

Many times Desiderius pondered and prayed that it might be revealed to him what caused the previously mentioned scourge to wear down this place so frequently. One night Father Benedict appeared to him in a vision and, among other things, explained in response to his anxious question that it was nothing other than the devil’s snares and the ancient envy directed against this place.

I myself remember that, when I was still living in the monastery school, one night lightning struck the church and the bell tower six times during the second nocturn alone, and so forth.

### The Mission to Sardinia Is Prevented

At about the same time, envoys from Barisone, king of Sardinia, came to this monastery [Col. 0933C]. Through them the king sent two large and excellent cloaks to Saint Benedict and asked that some brothers from our congregation be sent to establish a monastery for him. He promised that the greatest honor and advantage would accrue to our interests in his kingdom if, through our efforts, the practice of monastic religion—until then unknown in those regions—should thereafter become established among them as he had observed it flourishing among us.

The venerable Father immediately made a considered decision and chose twelve of the best brothers of this monastery. He abundantly supplied them with books of Holy Scripture, various implements of ecclesiastical service, numerous patronages of saints, and equipment of many kinds. He also appointed an abbot to preside over them and sent them there with great honor aboard a ship from Gaeta.

Nevertheless, by God’s permission and Satan’s obstruction, the undertaking could not be brought to completion at that time. For the Pisans, driven by the greatest hatred of the Sardinians, when our men had already crossed over successfully to the island called Lily and, having disembarked in small boats, were waiting for a favorable time to sail, suddenly came upon them with armed ships. Treating both our men and all the others indiscriminately and with extreme violence, they plundered everything.

Moreover, they were already preparing to cruelly hang the leader of the aforementioned embassy, unless, when one of our men offered him a monastic habit, he immediately put it on [Col. 0934A]. After this they burned the ship, restored only the clothing to our men, and returned home laden with everything else and greatly pleased.

Our brothers from the monastery of Lucca, diligently searching for the monks who had been scattered by them in various places, found them all and brought them back in vehicles to their own monastery, except for four who had already departed to Christ. Later, although at different times, nearly all of them returned to us in the same year, and so forth.

Those pirates then divided all the other goods among themselves and handed the reliquary to one of their number … . When he had at some time entered the room in which it was kept, he suddenly collapsed and died. When this became known, great terror immediately seized everyone. On the following day they came barefoot and, with immense reverence and honor, removed the aforementioned relics from there [Col. 0934B]. They transferred them to the bishop’s residence with great praise of God and placed them there to be treated with the honor that was due to them.

### Monasteries Established in Sardinia

Meanwhile the king of the Sardinians, having received from the Pisans satisfaction worthy of such great injuries, sent word again to this monastery that he remained even more ardently committed to his former devotion, and that we ought not on account of what had happened to neglect the matter.

After nearly two years, he finally received with great enthusiasm two brothers who had been sent there. He granted them by charter the church of Saint Mary at a place called Bubalis, as well as Saint Elias of Monte Santo together with the entire mountain, for the establishment of a monastery [Col. 0934C], along with many colonists and slaves and extensive property and possessions.

Another king of the same Sardinia, named Torchytorius, emulating him in this good work, likewise drew up a charter of his offering and sent it to this monastery, namely concerning Saint Vincent of Taberna, and so forth, to establish a monastery from them … .

An envoy was also sent to the Pisans by Pope Alexander together with our monk, so that, unless they wished immediately to experience an apostolic anathema, they might restore in full the property of Saint Benedict which they had wickedly seized … . When they had made satisfaction … they returned to Desiderius’ favor.

### Distinguished Cassinese Men

Since the aforementioned apostolic pontiff was extraordinarily devoted to this monastery, and since the archdeacon Hildebrand both suggested and urged him, whenever he could obtain brothers from this house from the lord abbot, he either associated them with himself in ecclesiastical service or honorably promoted them as bishops or abbots [Col. 0934D].

He summoned Todinus, son of Berard, count of the Marsi, to Rome and appointed him a deacon in the Lateran patriarchate. He also consecrated Aldemarius—of blessed memory—a prudent and noble cleric of the city of Capua and once the notary of Prince Richard. Aldemarius had been my teacher at my conversion and had earlier been appointed abbot over the brothers sent to Sardinia. After returning to the monastery, he was consecrated both cardinal and abbot in the church of Saint Lawrence called *Forismuros* [Col. 0935A].

He also ordained Ambrose of Milan, likewise a prudent and quite learned man, bishop of the Church of Terracina. He appointed Gerald, a most learned cleric in every respect and a German by birth, archbishop of the Church of Siponto.

At the same time Milo, provost of the monastery of Capua, became bishop of the Church of Sessa. Peter, called son of Athenulf, a member of the Capuan nobility who later became a cardinal at Rome, was sent at the request of the prince of Salerno to the abbacy of Saint Benedict at Salerno, which we mentioned above.

At that same time the apostolic pontiff granted Desiderius a solemn privilege which, among other things, concerned the complete liberty of this monastery. He prohibited by apostolic authority any bishop of any church, other than the Roman pontiff, from presuming in any way to exercise jurisdiction not only in our principal church but also in all our cells, wherever they might be located [Col. 0935B].

At that time, when Hildebrand, archbishop of Capua, swollen with a certain arrogance, attempted to murmur against this authority, we publicly lodged a complaint about the matter in the Roman synod. Convicted by the privileges of the apostolic see, he confessed that he had sinned, and so forth.

### The Monastery of Tremiti

Moreover, since many disgraceful and unspeakable things were being reported at that time concerning the rulers of the monastery of Tremiti—which, as many privileges of the Roman pontiffs testify, had belonged to us from ancient times—the apostolic pontiff granted Desiderius authority to investigate and regulate it as he thought best [Col. 0935C].

After he had removed Adam, the abbot of that place, having convicted him of many crimes, Desiderius entered the aforementioned island accompanied by Counts Robert of Laurotello and Peter of Lesina, the bishops of Troia, Dragonara, and Civitate, and the abbot of Terra Maggiore. There he honorably appointed Transmund, son of Oderisius, count of the Marsi, as abbot: at that time he was a young man of truly outstanding character, possessing considerable ability in wisdom and letters and trained here from childhood in honorable conduct [Col. 0935D].

But in the end he yielded to the counsels of the place’s worst brothers—indeed, of those whom our abbot himself had instructed him to obey. For after our men had returned, a few days later he put out the eyes of three of the senior monks of that place and cut out the tongue of another. They had been accused before him by their companions of plotting a rebellion on the island.

When this was reported to our Desiderius, he received it with the greatest indignation and severity and was overcome by profound grief: first because of the misery of those who had suffered, then because of the cruelty of the man who had ordered it, and finally—and this was most important and most grievous to his heart—because of the disgrace brought upon this place.

Since the solemnity of the dedication of our church was expected to take place in that same year, Transmund was kept back so that he could attend it and receive a sentence corresponding to his guilt [Col. 0936A]. When he came, Desiderius rebuked him in the assembly of the entire monastery with exceptionally harsh and deserved correction, subjected him to a more severe penance, and did not permit him to return there again.

The archdeacon Hildebrand, however, entirely approving of what Transmund had done and insisting that he had acted not cruelly but vigorously and deservedly against wicked men, eventually, before the year had ended, with some difficulty secured him from the lord abbot. He first entrusted to him the abbacy of Saint Clement on the island of Balvensis [variant: Pennensis] and shortly afterward added the dignity of the bishopric of Balvensis, and so forth.

### He Builds a New Basilica: Its Description

Thus the venerable abbot, divinely established in every prosperity and tranquility through the merits of our most blessed Father Benedict, and held in such great honor by everyone around him that not only ordinary people but even their princes and dukes gladly obeyed him and strove in every matter to submit to his will as though to that of their father and lord, resolved—clearly not without divine inspiration—to demolish the old church and build a new one more beautiful and more magnificent [Col. 0936B].

Although many of the earlier monks then regarded this as an excessively difficult and impossible undertaking, and tried by prayers, arguments, and every means to turn his mind away from the intention, since they believed that so great a work could not be completed during his lifetime, he trusted in God and promised himself and awaited God’s help alone for everything undertaken on God’s behalf [Col. 0936C].

In the ninth year of his administration, therefore, and in the year 1066 of the Incarnation, in the month of March, in the fourth indiction, after first constructing beside the house of the sick a basilica of Saint Peter—not very large, but one in which the brothers could meanwhile assemble for the divine offices—he undertook to demolish from its foundations the aforesaid church of Saint Benedict. It was inadequate to so great a treasure and so great a congregation of brothers, both because of its smallness and because of its ugliness.

Since it had been built on the very summit of the mountain, exposed on every side to the violent blasts of the winds, and had frequently been struck by fiery lightning, he decided, trusting in God’s help alone, to cut away the rocky crest of the same mountain with fire and iron and to level, by digging down into the lower ground, as much space as would suffice for the foundations of the basilica [Col. 0936D].

After appointing men who would carry this out with all their strength and greatest diligence, he himself meanwhile went to Rome. There he visited his closest friends and distributed money generously and appropriately. He bought in abundance columns, bases, decorative marble lilies, and marbles of various colors. He transported all these from the City to Porto, from Porto by sea through Roman waters to the tower of Garigliano, and from there to Sinuessa by hired ships with great confidence. From there he had them carried by wagon to this place, not without immense labor.

And, to make you marvel still more at the fervor of the faithful who served him, the first column was brought up here from the very beginning of the mountain by the strength of the necks and arms of a multitude of citizens alone. For at that time, in order to increase the height, the ascent of this mountain was extremely steep, narrow, and rough. Desiderius had not yet conceived the idea of leveling and widening the same road, as he did later [Col. 0937A].

At last, after the whole area of the basilica, except for the sanctuary, had been leveled with no small difficulty and everything necessary had been prepared in the greatest abundance, he immediately hired highly skilled craftsmen, both Amalfitans and Lombards. After laying the foundations in the name of Christ, he began the construction of the basilica: its length was 105 cubits, its width 43 cubits, and its height 28 cubits.

After setting the bases in place, he raised ten columns on one side and the same number on the other, at intervals of nine cubits. In the upper parts he established fairly large windows: twenty-one long ones in the nave, six in the sanctuary, four round ones, and two in the central apse. He also raised the walls of both porticoes to a height of fifteen cubits and divided them with ten windows on one side and the same number on the other.

Meanwhile, as he arranged to bring the sanctuary level with the floor-level of the basilica—which was reckoned at about six cubits—he dug down less than three ordinary cubits and suddenly discovered the venerable tomb of Father Benedict [Col. 0937B]. After consulting religious men and deciding that he must not presume to alter it in any way, he immediately covered the tomb again with precious stones in the very place where it had lain, lest anyone be able to steal anything from so great a treasure [Col. 0937C]. Above it he constructed, transversely across the basilica—that is, from north to south—a marble chest of Parian marble, five cubits long, in exceptionally beautiful workmanship.

In this way the sanctuary remained at its former elevation, so that from its floor down to the floor of the basilica one descended by eight steps, beneath the very large vault that hangs over the sanctuary, apart from the step by which the altar is approached from every side.

In the greater apse, on the eastern side, he established the altar of Saint John the Baptist, precisely where Father Benedict had formerly built his oratory. On the southern side he placed the altar of the Blessed Mother of God, and on the northern side the altar of Blessed Pope Gregory [Col. 0937D]. Beside the apse with its two chambers he built a house for storing the treasury of ecclesiastical service; this house is customarily called the sacristy. He joined to it another building of the same workmanship, in which the ministers of the altar were to prepare themselves.

Since, for the sake of widening the church, he had taken away a considerable part of his own chamber, he consequently made that same chamber, adjoining the aforementioned sacristy, larger and more beautiful than the former one. Beside it, near the portico of the principal church of Saint Nicholas, he founded a small but very beautiful building with a curved wall. From it as far as the outermost front of the basilica [Col. 0938A], he extended, in similar workmanship, a highly venerable oratory of the apostle Saint Bartholomew.

On its front, near the doors of the greater church, he erected from square and enormous stones a marvelous tower, commonly called the bell tower. He also made an atrium before the church, which in the Roman manner we call Paradise. Its length was seventy-seven and a half cubits, its width fifty-seven and a half cubits, and its height fifteen and a half cubits. It had four columns on each of the two façades and eight on each side, standing upon four-part bases.

On its southern side he also constructed beneath the pavement of the atrium, with arched workmanship, a very large cistern of the same length. Before the entrance to the basilica, and likewise before the entrance to the atrium, he ordered five vaults to be built above, which we call *spiculi*.

On the western side of the atrium, at each corner, he erected a very beautiful basilica in the manner of a tower: on the right, one dedicated to Saint Michael the archangel; on the left, one dedicated to Blessed Peter, prince of the apostles. From within the atrium, one ascended to them by five steps.

Outside the vestibule of the atrium and these same basilicas, since the ascent to the church was very steep, he excavated the mountain itself to a length of sixty-six cubits and the same width, and to a depth of seven cubits. Thus one ascended from the bottom to the vestibule of the atrium by the twenty-four marble steps that he established there; the passage had a width of thirty-six cubits.

### The Ornaments

Meanwhile he sent envoys to Constantinople to bring craftsmen skilled in mosaic and marble-work. Some of them were to adorn the apse, the arch, and the vestibule of the greater basilica with mosaic; others were to pave the entire floor of the church with a variety of different stones [Col. 0938C].

The degree of perfection possessed by the masters of these arts who were then sent to him may be judged from their works. In the mosaics, each person seems almost to see living figures and every kind of verdant plant; in the marbles, one might think that flowers of every color were blooming in beautiful variety.

Since Latinity had neglected the skill of these arts for five hundred years and more, and by God’s inspiration and cooperation had now deserved to recover it in our own time, this man of complete prudence took care that many of the monastery’s boys should be diligently trained in the same arts, lest the knowledge of them be lost from Italy again [Col. 0938D].

Nor did he acquire only such craftsmen. He also secured for himself exceptionally devoted artisans from among his own men in every craft that can be practiced in gold, silver, bronze, iron, glass, ivory, wood, plaster, or stone. But these matters belong elsewhere.

Now let us describe, as best we can, how he partly adorned the basilica after its construction and finally consecrated it. He covered the whole building—that is, the sanctuary, both porticoes, and the vestibule—with leaden roofing, and clothed the apse and the greater arch in mosaic. Around the broad curve of the apse he ordered these verses to be written in golden letters:

[Col. 0939A]

> That, with you as guide, the fatherland may enjoy the blessings won for the righteous,  
>   
> Desiderius has built this hall for you, Father.

In the apse, here and there beneath the feet of Saint John the Baptist and Saint John the Evangelist, he ordered these verses to be written:

> This house is like Sinai, which bears sacred laws,  
>   
> as the Law once promulgated here shows.  
>   
> From here went forth the Law that leads minds up from the depths.

And, having been made widely known, it gave light throughout the regions of the world. He enclosed all the windows, both those of the nave and those of the façade, with panels fitted together with lead and glass and joined by iron. Those situated in the sides of the two porticoes he constructed of gypsum, though with almost the same ornamentation. Then, after placing a coffered ceiling upon beams, wonderfully adorned with various colors and figures, he also painted all the walls with a sufficiently beautiful variety of every color. He paved the entire floor of the whole church, together with the adjoining oratories of Blessed Bartholomew and Blessed Nicholas and also his own chamber, with a truly remarkable and hitherto unknown profusion of cut stones. But especially noteworthy is the pavement beside the altar and in the choir, where the steps by which one ascends to that altar are distinguished by slabs of precious marble in an appropriate variety. He also enclosed the front of the choir, which he placed almost in the middle of the basilica, with four large marble panels: one of porphyry, another green, while the remaining two, and all the others around the choir, were plain.

He likewise ordered the vestibule of the church to be adorned above with exceedingly beautiful mosaic, together with the arches over the lintels; from there down to the bottom of the pavement, he had the entire façade of the basilica covered with gypsum. He also covered the arches of that vestibule on the outside with mosaic and had these verses of the poet Marcus written there in letters of gold. Ordering the other three sides of the atrium to be painted, inside and out, with various scenes from both the Old and the New Testament, he paved the whole of it with marble; above, he covered it with a coffered ceiling and tiles. He likewise had the vestibule of that atrium, with its twin towers, painted, roofed, and paved with marble in the same manner.

### It Is Dedicated by a Pope

When all these works had been completed within five years, with God prospering and assisting them, Desiderius resolved to dedicate the basilica with the greatest solemnity and immense rejoicing, for everlasting remembrance. He therefore approached Alexander, the pontiff of the highest see, and most devoutly invited him to come for that same dedication. Since Alexander willingly consented, Desiderius also summoned his archdeacon Hildebrand, the other cardinals, and the Roman bishops, as well as very many of the city’s clergy and nobles, with the warmest familiarity.

The day of so great a solemnity was fixed, after consultation with the apostolic lord and the cardinals, on the Kalends of October; letters of invitation from that same apostolic lord were sent to all the bishops of Campania, the Principate, Apulia, and Calabria. When the fame of this event had therefore spread far and wide, such a multitude of bishops, abbots, monks, clerics, magnates, nobles, commoners, and men and women of every condition from almost the whole of Italy converged on the appointed day that it would have been easier for anyone to estimate the number of the stars in heaven than the number of all those people.

Thus all the workshops of the monastery, and even the roofs of all the workshops; all the roads of the mountain from bottom to top—and what shall I say?—all the houses of the city, all the streets, and all the broad spaces of the neighboring fields, far and wide, were packed and crowded with the assembled throngs for these great solemnities. Meanwhile, during the three continuous days immediately preceding and following the solemnity, the provisions—bread and wine, and a great variety of meats and fish—were supplied in such abundance that scarcely anyone could be found in that immeasurable multitude who did not say that he had received enough.

Ten archbishops were then present at so great a celebration: Hildebrand of Capua, Alphanus of Salerno, John of Naples, John of Sorrento, the archbishop of Amalfi, Gerard of Siponto, Bisantius of Trani (Trandisis), Arnaldus of Acerenza (Acheruntinus), Hugh of Otranto, and Oiretanus [perhaps Oristano in Sardinia].

There were also forty-three bishops: John of Porto, John of Tusculum, Ubaldus of Sabina, Erasmus of Segni, Peter of Anagni, Honestus of Veroli, Ambrose of Terracina, Leo of Gaeta, Martin of Aquino, Palumbus of Sora, Pandulfus of Marsica, [the bishop] of Balva, [the bishop] of Penne, William of Teano, John of Caiazzo, [the bishop] of Rosella, Goffridus of Aversa, [the bishop] of Nola, [the bishop] of Avellino, Maraldus of Paestum, Stephen of Troia, Robert of Florence, [the bishop] of Melfi, [the bishop] of Lucera, [the bishop] of Campodraconaria, Roger of Civita, Nicholas of Termoli, Peter of Guardiagrele, William of Larino, Maynardus of Ariano, [the bishop] of Serni, Albert of Boiano, [the bishop] of Salpi, John of Canosa, William or Guibertus of Ruvo, Constans of Venosa, Ignatius of Morubio, John of Vigili, Baldwin of Melfi, John of Giovinazzo, Peter of Monopoli, Datto of Ostuni [or Stunensis], Drogo of Taranto, Goffridus of Perugia, and Theobaldus, the elected bishop of Castellaneta, who was consecrated bishop on the day after the dedication.

We have inserted in another typeface the proper names of these bishops that are not found in Leo, from a manuscript booklet on this Dedication which Antonio Caracciolus made public at Naples in 1626 from the Cassinese library, together with Erempertus’s epitome and other ancient monuments. But Leo lists many more than the author of this booklet: namely, the archbishops of Amalfi and Oireto, and the bishops of Balva, Penne, Rosella, Nola, Avellino, Lucera, Serni, Salpi, and Melfi. The booklet, however, includes Peter of Venafro and John of Picenum, who are absent from Leo. In the bull of Alexander II, which the same Caracciolus cites from the original document, John, bishop of Cales, is replaced by John, bishop of Claudiopolis.

The following also subscribe: Hildebrand, archdeacon of the Holy Roman Church; Peter Damian, bishop of Ostia; Firminus, cardinal of the Holy Roman Church; Leo, cardinal . . .; Stephen, cardinal-priest; Landulfus, cardinal-priest; Leo, cardinal-priest, on behalf of all the cardinal-priests, deacons, and clergy of the Holy Roman Church.

As for the magnates, Leo continues: Richard, prince of Capua, with his son Jordan and his brother Rainulfus; Gisulfus, prince of Salerno, with his brothers; Landulfus, prince of Benevento; Sergius, duke of Naples; and Sergius, duke of Sorrento. Duke Robert was at that time besieging Palermo and therefore could not attend so great a solemnity. There was also a great attendance of the counts of the Marsi and of Balva, and of Borellus’s sons. As for the other powerful men or nobles, both our own countrymen and Normans, there was absolutely no possibility or means of listing either the names or the innumerable number of all those from the surrounding lands.

With the profound devotion and immense joy of all these people, and with the greatest honor and distinguished glory, the basilica of Blessed Benedict, together with its five altars, was dedicated on that same day, the Kalends of October, in the year 1071 from the divine Incarnation, in the ninth indiction, on a Saturday. The apostolic lord himself blessed the two central altars, dedicated respectively to Blessed Benedict and Saint John. The altar situated on the southern side in honor of the holy Mother of God was blessed by John, bishop of Tusculum; the altar on the northern side, dedicated to Blessed Gregory, by Ubaldus, bishop of Sabina; and the altar of Saint Nicholas was solemnly dedicated by Erasmus, bishop of Segni.

The relics of those saints were then deposited in the individual altars, and we have thought it appropriate to insert them here. In the altar of Blessed Benedict are relics of the holy apostles Philip and James, etc. In the altar of Saint John . . . . . . . oil from the lamp of the Holy Sepulchre, which each year, in a very wondrous manner, is kindled from heaven on Holy Saturday in the sight of all, etc. Above all these things, we must not omit that, at the time of the construction, relics of Saint Philip were reverently placed in little bronze boxes in the capitals of the individual columns of that basilica, together with . . . hairs of Saint Remigius the bishop, etc. In the four corners of the bell tower are these relics: wood of the Lord, etc. In the cross of the bell tower: wood of the Lord, part of the head of Saint John the Baptist, etc. In the façade of the church, in the bronze cross: wood of the Lord, a stone, etc.

### Indulgences Granted

When the solemn celebration of the masses had been completed, absolution from sins was granted, by apostolic authority, both to those who happened to be present then and to all who, out of devotion to so great a solemnity, might come there during the eight continuous days. Everyone returned to his own home with the greatest and most immense joy.

Yet, because of the grace of the aforesaid absolution, such a continual stream of people of every sex and age came here from all directions throughout those same eight days that one might almost have thought that none of those who had crowded in on the first day had returned home.

> Nor is there an end to the peoples gathering in dense columns;  
> nor rest: they hasten from night into daylight,  
> and are unwilling to wait for the day.
>
> The peoples of Lucania gather, the Apulian youth gathers,  
> and the Calabrians, and all whom either sea washes,  
> while all Latium resounds around them on left and right;  
> and Rome herself, powerful through the sacred monuments  
> of the great ones of heaven, through Peter and Paul,  
> rejoices to grow less crowded, pouring thousands  
> toward the lofty walls of Cassino.
>
> Devotion, the love of Benedict, conquers the hard journey;  
> and nourishing faith also conquers it. God is believed  
> to be present there in all matters [variant: “of all”],  
> and Benedict is the glory of Christ Most High.

Surely anyone would consider himself completely wretched and unbelieving if he did not strive to take part, at least at the end, in so great a solemnity. From that time onward the glory of so great a celebration began to be proclaimed throughout the Christian world. Henceforth this place, although it had long been famous and renowned through the merits of Father Benedict, began to be regarded as much more renowned and glorious; and the name of Father Desiderius, already for a long time great and celebrated among many, was thereafter spread throughout the whole West with still greater fame and honor. Everyone praised him as possessing the greatest prudence and religious devotion, and he was rightly judged superior to all the abbots of his time everywhere, not only in the western and eastern regions but throughout the world.

Some therefore came here out of a desire to see Desiderius; some to behold the temple, so widely known and celebrated; and finally some to live in this most holy monastery and serve God for as long as they lived. Many people from many distant parts of the earth began to gather here. Desiderius received them cheerfully, and it came about that within approximately two years the number of the community had reached nearly two hundred.

The devotion that began to be shown toward that venerable Father by various kings and powerful people of both sexes was attested by supplicatory letters and fitting gifts, in which they earnestly commended themselves and all their people to his prayers and to those of the brothers living under him. This solemnity of the dedication is recorded in the Benedictine annals and by Ferrarius in his *General Catalogue*, under 1 October.

### Gifts of the Empress Agnes

Nor does it seem right to remain silent about the worthy religious devotion of the Empress Agnes. Like another queen of Sheba, led by a great desire to see another Solomon and another temple, she came here from the farthest borders of Germany. Staying there for almost half a year, she rejoiced to see that the things she had heard about this place were, both in divine and in worldly terms, much greater than she had understood, and she declared—rightly judging that the place, the Father, and the brothers ought to be celebrated throughout the world among the members of their order—that they deserved this renown.

She offered Blessed Benedict magnificent gifts, as befitted her imperial dignity: a *diasper* chasuble, woven entirely with gold on every side; also a white vestment, most beautifully adorned with embroidery at the shoulders, head, and hands, and likewise encircled at the feet by an embroidered band about a cubit wide, together with an amice and a breast-piece; two purple copes adorned with precious golden bands; a fringed rose-colored cloth with gold, to be placed before the face of the high altar; and also a large pallium decorated with elephants, which they call a *dorsal*; a Gospel book (*Euglium*), with a cast-silver cover, worked in relief and beautifully gilded; and two silver candlesticks, likewise cast, weighing twelve pounds.

### Ornamentation of the Basilica

Now, after the dedication of the church, it is pleasing to describe the remaining ornamentation, so that we may thereafter proceed more freely to Desiderius’s achievements both in buildings and in every other kind of magnificence.

He therefore sent one of the brothers to the aforementioned imperial city with letters to the emperor and thirty-six pounds’ weight of gold, ordering him to have made there a golden panel for the front of the altar, with very beautiful gems and enamels. With these enamels he had some scenes from the Gospel, but almost all the notable stories of the miracles of Blessed Benedict, represented.

The Roman emperor received this brother of ours with the greatest honor; for as long as he remained there, he treated him and all his companions courteously and respectfully, and granted him imperial permission to produce whatever ornaments he wished there.

The brother therefore also had four bronze screens cast, to be placed before the altar on either side, between the choir and the sanctuary. He likewise had a bronze beam cast, with fifty candlesticks, in which an equal number of candles were to be placed on the principal festivals; beneath it, thirty-six lamps hung from bronze hooks attached to the same beam. This bronze beam, supported by bronze arms and hands, was attached to a wooden beam which Desiderius had caused to be beautifully carved and adorned with gold and colored pigments. He placed it above six silver columns, each four and a half cubits high and weighing eight pounds, on the front of the choir.

Beneath that beam he hung five round icons, while above he placed thirteen square ones of equal size and weight. Of these, the aforesaid brother sculpted and gilded ten of the square panels at Constantinople in thick silver; some weighed fourteen pounds each and others twelve. He had all the round ones surrounded only by a four-pound silver rim; the rest he had painted with colors and figures in the Greek manner. Desiderius ordered three other square icons, of the same metal and dimensions, to be made by his own craftsmen in a wholly similar style.

A certain nobleman also sent from the imperial city another round icon to Blessed Benedict. It was covered on both sides with wonderfully sculpted and gilded silver and surrounded externally by silver bosses in a circle. Later, another like it was ordered to be made, and both were hung on either side in the canopy over the altar.

The aforesaid brother also brought with him from Constantinople two large and seven small cast-bronze *ceraptata* [possibly candelabra or lamp-bearing fixtures], very beautiful.

Desiderius further had another beam made of silver, weighing approximately sixty pounds, likewise sculpted and gilded. He placed it in the great arch before the altar, upon four partly gilded silver columns, each weighing ten pounds and five cubits high. He also made two large silver crosses, each weighing thirty pounds, whose figures projected in quite marvelous repoussé work, and set them beneath the aforesaid beam between the same columns, on either side, upon marble supports.

He covered the other three faces of the high altar with eighty-six pounds of well-sculpted and gilded silver. The faces of the other three altars were adorned on three sides with old panels. He also covered the four beams beside the canopy of the altar externally with silver similarly sculpted and gilded; internally he adorned them with petals [perhaps sheets] and colors. Two of them were six cubits long and weighed twenty pounds each; the other two were four and a half cubits long and likewise weighed twenty pounds each.

He also had six large candlesticks made from extended and sculpted silver sheets, three cubits high, each weighing six or five pounds [perhaps “equally”]. They were to be set in a straight line before the altar and lit with great torches on the principal festivals.

He made a wooden pulpit for reading or singing, much finer and loftier than the earlier one, reached by six steps. He made it exceptionally beautiful with various colored pigments and sheets of gold. Before it he set, upon a porphyry base, a silver column weighing twenty-five pounds, partly gilded in the manner of a great candlestick and six cubits high. Upon it the great candle to be blessed on Holy Saturday was solemnly to be raised.

He also made a *pharus*, that is, a very large crown, of approximately one hundred pounds of silver. It measured twenty cubits in circumference and had twelve towers projecting outward; thirty-six lamps hung from it. He suspended it outside the choir, before the great cross, by a very strong iron chain distinguished by seven gilded knobs.

Having now written, as best we could, about the construction, consecration, and partial decoration of the new basilica, let us return, together with our Desiderius, to the completion of the monastery’s other buildings.

### The Other Buildings of the Monastery

After the solemn dedication of the basilica had been completed, Desiderius saw that, with divine power assisting and through the merits of Father Benedict, everything he had begun had reached the perfection he had desired. He therefore became bolder—or rather, more capable—and resolved with great determination to enlarge the entire circuit of the monastery. As he had already done with some buildings, he also resolved to renew the remaining workshops, including those which he himself had constructed before the building of the church.

First, desiring to enlarge the cloister, which was plainly still far too small for so large a community, he immediately demolished the old refectory. It had been attached rather awkwardly to the side of the church and, at the front, to the chapter house; he himself had enlarged it twice at different times. He then built it farther away, in the area of the future cloister, beside the southern side of the church atrium, making it handsome and sufficiently large. He adorned it throughout with various colors by the art of painters, added a coffered ceiling upon beams, and covered it above with tiles. He also installed in it a very beautiful and elevated reading desk, which he covered very neatly with gypsum and thereby made an object of admiration for all.

That building was ninety-five cubits long, twenty-three cubits wide, and fifteen cubits high. It had an entrance on the eastern side and an apse on the western side, before which the abbot’s very broad table could be seen set crosswise. On the southern side it had fourteen windows, three around the reading desk, and only two on the northern side; it also had two round windows in each façade. All were skillfully made of glass, gypsum, and lead.

Beside this building, on the southern side, he erected the brothers’ kitchen, sufficiently large and beautiful, in two adjoining vaults supported by a single column. Between it and the refectory he set steps and a door through which whatever was needed could be brought into or carried back from the refectory. On the other side of the kitchen he established a storeroom, from which whatever was needed could be supplied both to the refectory and to the kitchen.

After this, since the space of the cloister still seemed insufficient for so great a multitude of brothers, this truly magnanimous and exceedingly confident man undertook to demolish completely the dormitory and chapter house which he himself had once built at great expense and with great care, as well as the old infirmary, and, in the process of enlarging the cloister, to make those buildings larger too.

Since he intended to erect the outer wall of the dormitory much farther away from the other, on a great mountain precipice, he laid a foundation wall five cubits thick for the sake of maximum strength and extended it lengthwise for a distance of two hundred cubits. He raised it to a height of thirty cubits, leaving a distance of twenty-four cubits from the inner wall. On the southern side it had twenty large windows, three of which were supported by three small marble columns. This building, much larger, stronger, and more beautiful than the former one, was carefully roofed with brick through the skill of the builders and decorated with colors by the art of painters. Beside it, at its farther end, he also constructed the brothers’ wardrobe: small, indeed, but sufficiently adequate and attractive.

### Reverence for the Bodies of the Dead

When these works had been completed after about three years, he began to excavate the mountain that lay in the way: one hundred and five cubits lengthwise, forty-nine cubits wide, and approximately seven cubits deep. He then established the chapter house transversely on the eastern side, so that the inner angle of its façade was joined to the outer angle of the church’s façade, while its apse seemed to approach the dormitory.

That building was fifty-three cubits long, twenty cubits wide, and eighteen cubits high. On one side it had nine very beautiful glass windows, and on the other an equal number; in the northern façade it had three round windows, and in the southern façade two likewise round windows. It was sufficiently adorned with a coffered ceiling, pavement, and very costly paintings.

While these excavations were being made, we experienced such a frequency of earthquakes that on one day we felt seventeen tremors, and on several other days sometimes four, sometimes two, and at times six or five tremors each day. Many of us thought that this had not happened without reason, since countless graves at that place had necessarily been violated, and they may have belonged to holy men. Earthquakes, in fact, usually occur very rarely in this place.

But because a great precipice remained on the inner side of the dormitory, he built vaulted chambers beside the same building and leveled the area by filling the rest with earth and stones. Likewise, in front of the refectory, at the front of the cloister, he constructed a very large cistern beneath a curved vault. Only then did he make the entire surface of the cloister level. Immediately afterward he established covered walks with arches all around, upon one hundred and ten small marble columns, and extended the whole cloister to a length of one hundred and five cubits and a width of seventy-five.

Since the part adjoining the greater basilica would not have had a suitable entrance into that basilica if it had been brought to the same level as the rest, he made vaulted walks both below and above it, and installed marble steps at each of its two corners by which one could descend to the other areas. He made the whole circuit—fifteen steps toward the chapter house and thirteen from the refectory—and paved it with stone floors in the Byzantine style and adorned it with beautiful paintings.

Without delaying over this, once it had been completed, he lowered the upper floor of that palace, which Richerius had begun and he himself had completed, from its former elevation to the level of the cloister, and established it there as a place of rest for the sick brothers.

On the western side of the cloister, beside the cistern mentioned above, he suitably arranged the novices’ room. There the novices themselves were to meditate, rest, and eat according to the rule. Thus at last he taught the brothers, who until then had been more than sufficiently disturbed and troubled by so many works, to devote themselves thereafter to the regular order in an orderly and therefore stricter manner, once they had been settled in a station of rest both convenient and pleasant.

When all these works had been completed according to his wishes, and the inner workshops of the brothers had been finished most suitably as he had desired, he applied himself tirelessly and vigorously to completing the monastery’s exterior buildings as well.

First, on the western side, he raised a very strong wall and set up a gate nearly thirty cubits outside the old one, made of squared and cut stones. Above it he secured a very strong tower, raised upon four large columns, with a massive vaulted chamber. Since outside there was an immense precipice while inside there was a great mound, he dug away the mound and made the precipice passable with its stones and earth, though along a sloping path. Beside it, just outside the gate, he built a very large hospice.

Finally, he enclosed the entire monastery with a continuous wall, fortified in the manner of cities. Then, on the northern side, he built a palace of no small size to receive all kinds of guests. He also constructed the old one with such elegance that many pilgrims who came here, unaware of what it was, repeatedly gathered there as though to pray in a church.

While these works were in progress, Desiderius did not cease laboring to acquire ornaments for the church and, by whatever means and through whatever ingenuity he could, to obtain from every direction objects suited to its beauty.

### The Church of Saint Martin Is Built and Dedicated

Recognizing, therefore, with Christ as his guide, that everything had happened for him as he had desired, Desiderius now turned his whole heart to renovating the church of Blessed Martin, which alone, or almost alone, remained among the old buildings within the monastery’s circuit.

After demolishing the former basilica of that same Blessed Martin and laying foundations in the name of Christ, he began the construction of the church: forty-three cubits long, twenty-eight cubits wide, and twenty-four cubits high. It had nine windows on one side and the same number on the other. He also raised the walls of both porticoes to a height of sixteen cubits and distinguished them with four windows on one side and an equal number on the other. Those in the nave he enclosed with panels fitted together with lead and glass and bound with iron.

In the façade of the same church he arranged three windows, and one in the apse, and ordered them to be made with similar ornamentation. Those in the porticoes he constructed of gypsum, but with equal elegance. He raised nine columns on one side and the same number on the other.

Beside the church, with a curved wall, he built a small but very beautiful house for the service of that church. He had marvelous stone screens made before the altar of Blessed Martin. He decently covered the apse with mosaic and had these verses written there in letters of gold:

> Once this place had been dedicated  
> to demonic rites, and in this temple  
> Apollo had been worshiped.
>
> But when Father Benedict hastened here,  
> he turned it to the honor of almighty God  
> and to the name of Saint Martin.
>
> Desiderius, after a hundred lustrums had passed,  
> overturned this ancient and small building,  
> renewed it, adorned it, and enlarged it.

How conspicuous and beautiful the pavement of that church is, and how richly it is laid with a great variety of marbles, is visible to everyone’s eyes. He also ordered a very beautiful reading desk to be constructed there, decorated with gold and colors through the skill of painters.

Before the altar of Blessed Martin he ordered Desiderius to have made a silver panel, gilded and beautifully sculpted, weighing forty-four pounds. Upon it he had almost all the stories of Blessed Matthew the Evangelist and Saint Martin, Christ’s confessor, carved.

He also had bronze doors made at the entrance to the same church. Beside that basilica he built a small dwelling in which he himself might stay, adding beams and covering it above with tiles.

When, with the Lord’s assistance, he had completed these works according to his wishes, he had the basilica of Blessed Bartholomew solemnly dedicated on the third day before the Nones of January by John, formerly a monk of this monastery and later bishop of Sora, together with the entire community of the brothers. In its altar he deposited a substantial portion of the apostolic body in a silver reliquary. In it he also placed these relics: a stone from the Holy Sepulchre, and relics of Saints John and Paul, Vitus, Januarius, Hermes, and the Forty Martyrs.

Desiderius was held in such authority and favor by the Roman pontiff that, in any churches or monasteries deprived of their own pastor, he had the right to appoint bishops or abbots from among his own brothers, whenever he wished.

Not long afterward, he also had those small buildings which we said had been placed like towers at the corners of the atrium—one by the same John, the other by Leo, bishop of Aquino—dedicated with great joy on the fourth day before the Ides of September.

In the altar of the blessed archangel Michael he deposited relics of Saints Nicander and Marcian, John and Paul, Vitus, Mercury, and Catherine, as well as the names of Saints Apollinaris the bishop, Protus, and Hyacinth. Leo, bishop of Aquino, consecrated the altar of the prince of the apostles to the divine name, in the presence of the lord abbot and the entire community of the brothers, with great joy and devotion.

The following relics were deposited in that altar: some of the five barley loaves; and relics of the holy apostles Peter, Matthew, and James; of Nazarius and Celsus; Januarius; Felicissimus and Agapitus; Sergius and Bacchus; Nicander and Marcian; Aurelius; Protasius; Fortunatus and his companions; and some of the garments of the three boys.

### Matters Irrelevant to the Author’s Purpose Are Omitted

Up to this point Leo of Marsi brought the Cassinese Chronicle. What follows was added by Peter the Deacon, as he himself bears witness in the Prologue to Book IV, which he dedicated to Abbot Raynald. But since he inserted many things that do not pertain to illustrating the life of Desiderius, we shall henceforth present only those that serve our purpose, omitting the rest.

In chapter 35 he discusses Alberic, Alphanus, Amatus, and Constantine the African, Cassinese monks whose little works he lists. These may likewise be seen in that author’s booklet *On Illustrious Cassinese Men*.

### Pope Alexander Restores a Demoniac and Grants Privileges to the Monastery

At a later time the aforesaid Pope Alexander, leaving the City, came to this monastery. Desiderius received him with honor. When Alexander had entered the abbot’s chamber, which was built beside the church of Saint Nicholas, a certain demoniac was delivered by him, etc.

The same most holy pontiff also issued a privilege to Father Desiderius concerning the monastery of Saint Mary in Palladium, etc.

### The Monastery of Saint Angelus at Formis

At about the same time Prince Richard, by a formal grant, offered to Blessed Benedict the church of Saint Angelus, which is called *ad Formas*. Earlier, in the time of Abbot Baldwin, we wrote at greater length about how it was granted to us by Pope Marinus.

But because the archbishop of Capua was retaining it at that time, the aforesaid prince, wishing to establish a monastery there, exchanged it with him approximately seven years earlier, giving in return another church . . . . . and offered the aforesaid church to the Cassinese monastery. Since the place was very pleasant and highly suitable for a monastery, he humbly asked Desiderius to take particular care of it out of affection for him.

Desiderius did so, taking from the monastery of Albaneta half of all its movable property and sending there with it half of the monks of that place. He began to build it entirely anew, as magnificently and spaciously as it is seen today, and within a short time gathered there more than forty monks to live according to the rule.

### Gifts from the Emperor of Constantinople

About this time Michael, emperor of Constantinople, sent Father Desiderius many gifts through messengers whom he dispatched to him, asking that they continually implore the mercy of almighty God on his behalf, for his children, and for the well-being of his empire.

Moreover, out of reverence for Father Benedict and for the salvation of his own soul, he established by a decree sealed with a golden bull that each year this monastery should receive from the palace of the Constantinopolitan Empire twenty-four pounds of gold and four pallia, for the support of our community.

### Monasteries Given to Cassino

Count Borellus, son of the elder Borellus, having deservedly gained Desiderius’s familiarity through certain services he had rendered at this place, devotedly offered to blessed Benedict the monastery of Saint Peter called Avellana. His father had handed it over to blessed Dominic forty-four years earlier for construction, and Borellus himself had enriched it with a very extensive grant of land, together with its churches, tenants, and absolutely all its appurtenances and possessions—an estate of approximately five thousand *modii* of land—and so forth.

Theodinus, Oderisius, and Bernard, counts of the Balva family, likewise, not long afterward, offered to this monastery the monastery of Saint Peter situated in the valley of Lacu, and another monastery of hermits at a place called Pratum Cardosum. These too had been founded by blessed Dominic only a few years earlier. They made the donation in the same manner, and so forth. These monasteries were discussed in the earlier part of this age, in the Life of Saint Dominic, abbot of Sora, under the year 1031.

In that same year Leo and Girard, consuls of Fondi, together with Richard, surnamed “of the Eagle,” offered to this place the church of Saint Onuphrius with its appurtenances. Since the site was suitable for constructing a monastery, Desiderius, wishing to establish one there, had it raised to the condition in which it is now seen through Girard, provost of Saint Nicholas at Pica, who became the fifth abbot of this monastery after him.

### The Pontiff Decrees against Invaders of Church Property

At the same time, the pontiff of the Church of Rosello, coming to this monastery, deposited a considerable sum of money there. When this was reported to Prince Jordan, he sent soldiers and ordered that the same money be taken from the church treasury and brought to him.

The brothers replied: “We absolutely do not give to any living person the money entrusted to Father Benedict. Let us place it in the treasury; then let whoever dares remove it take it from there.”

But when the soldiers heard this, and, intoxicated by a diabolical impulse [*sic*], they removed the money from the church treasury and carried it to the prince.

When so great, so monstrous, and unheard-of a crime came to the ears of Pope Gregory, he could not tolerate leaving the offense of such presumption unpunished. Fearing that, following the example of this outrage, our church might again be violated, he interdicted the divine office in Father Benedict’s church and ordered all the altars to be stripped. He declared that, in the face of so great a crime, he could justly reproach Desiderius and the brothers for excessive negligence and for a timidity requiring severe punishment, and that he ought to be moved more gravely against our congregation, were he not restrained by the love with which he had always cherished this place.

Indeed, he said that he would consider it more tolerable for the villages and castles belonging to us to be given over to plunder and devastation than for this holy place, famous and venerable throughout all Christendom, to be exposed to the danger of such disgrace.

Yet the right hand of God did not long delay its vengeance after the office had been interdicted in our church. For the prince, author of so great a crime, lost his sight after receiving the money.

The same Pope Gregory, while sitting in council, decreed that if any Norman or any other person invaded the estates, monasteries, villages, or possessions of this Cassinese monastery, and, after being admonished twice or three times, did not amend his conduct, he should be subject to excommunication until he came to his senses and made satisfaction to the Church.

### Various Matters Omitted

Chapter 48. Peter deals with the pious monks Guinizone and Gebizone; we shall speak of them below. In the two chapters that follow, he discusses at greater length the disputes between Pope Gregory and Emperor Henry, and then the conversation between that same emperor and Desiderius. There is no opportunity here to pursue these matters in detail.

### Union with the Cluniac Brethren

Around this time Hugh, the venerable abbot of Cluny, a man of the most illustrious life and reputation, came with great devotion to the threshold of Father Benedict. The venerable Desiderius received him honorably, as was fitting for so great a man. The two men decreed that the fellowship of the Cluniac brethren should be joined to our congregation, and that the memory of the Cluniac congregation among us, and of our congregation among them, should be perpetually maintained both in life and in death.

He adds some remarks about Gregory and Randisius, pious monks whom we discussed in the first part of this age, p. 103 and following, where we praised this very chapter of the Cassinese Chronicle, together with several other passages from Peter’s continuation, under the name of Leo, as is commonly done.

Furthermore, Angelo de Nuce, in his notes on this passage, produces a letter of Desiderius to Peter Damian, in which Desiderius promises him, both while alive and after his death, his own prayers and those of the entire Cassinese congregation and of his successors.

### Pope Gregory and Others Are Kindly Received

Robert Guiscard freed Pope Gregory, whom Emperor Henry was holding under siege in the fortress of Sant’Angelo, and, says Peter, brought him as far as this monastery. Our abbot supported the apostolic pontiff until his departure, together with the bishops and cardinals who had followed him.

### Gift of the Holy Cross

At this time a certain nobleman of the city of Amalfi, renouncing the world and all worldly things, came to this place. Desiderius gladly received him and made him a monk. The man, most devoted to blessed Benedict, offered a considerable portion of the wood of the saving and life-giving Cross, ornamented with gold and precious stones and placed in a golden icon. He himself had taken it from the imperial palace at Constantinople during the conspiracy formed against Emperor Michael.

After this Desiderius went to Capua. Seeing that the workshops of the monastery of Capua already lay in ruins, he resolved to restore it. After the former church had been demolished, he ordered other craftsmen to be brought in to make the column capitals with marvelous workmanship. Calling Benedict, the provost of that place, to him, he instructed him to devote particular attention to the restoration of the church, setting aside all other matters.

Obeying his command, Benedict constructed the basilica of Father Benedict, as it is now seen, extremely beautiful, and so forth.

### Death of Robert, an Outstanding Benefactor

In this year—namely, as Angelo de Nuce notes, 1085—in the month of July, on the feast of Saint Alexius, Robert Guiscard, duke of Apulia, died, and so forth.

It does not seem inappropriate to append here, in part, a summary of the donations of this duke and of his wife Sichelgaita, for the knowledge of posterity. More than almost all mortals of his time, they strove to love, exalt, and honor this place, Father Desiderius, and our congregation.

In Chapter 58 Peter lists those donations individually; in the following chapters he records others made by different noblemen. In Chapter 62 he deals with Guaifer, whom he also praised in *On Illustrious Men*, chapter 29, where he is called Benedict, who is also named Guaifer.

### Desiderius Has Several Books Copied; Their Titles Are Given

Desiderius devoted himself with the greatest diligence not only to buildings but also to the copying of books. He ordered several codices to be copied at this place. Their titles are as follows:

Augustine: *Against Faustus*; *On the Work of Monks*; *On the Lord’s Sermon on the Mount*; fifty homilies on the Epistle to the Romans; sermons on the Epistles of Paul; *On Genesis Literally*; his Epistles; his *Pastoral Rule*; *On the Baptism of Infants*.

Ambrose: *On Events in the Church of Milan*; *On the Patriarchs*; *On the Faith, to the Emperor Gratian*; his sermons.

The Register of Pope Leo; the Register of Pope Felix; the Rule of Basil; Jerome on Ezekiel, on the Epistles of Paul, and on the twelve prophets; Eugesippus; the sermons of Severianus; the History of Anastasius; the History of the Lombards, Goths, and Vandals; the history of Bishop Jordan concerning the Romans and Goths; the History of Gregory of Tours; Josephus, *On the Jewish War*; the history of Cornelius, together with Homer; the History of Erchempert; Bede on Tobit; *On the Holy Places*.

A large Gospel book decorated with gold and precious stones, in which he placed these relics: a piece of the Lord’s wood and pieces of the garments of Saint John the Evangelist.

The sermons of Pope Leo; the sermons of Gregory Nazianzen; *The Teaching of the Fathers*; a sacramentary with a martyrology; another sacramentary; *The Episcopal Order*; Gualfridus, *On Offices*; *On the Rule*; four books of the *Passionary* for the entire year; two daytime antiphonaries, to be kept constantly in the choir; a nighttime antiphonary; the *Lives of the Fathers*; the *Institutes of the Fathers*; the Acts of the Apostles with the Catholic Epistles and the Apocalypse; the Epistles of Paul; *Paralipomenon*.

Commentaries on the *Song of Songs* by Origen, Gregory, and Berengarius; John Chrysostom, *On the Restoration of the Fallen*; the dialogue that he himself composed with the deacon Alberic concerning the miracles of the monks of this place; another dialogue; a dialogue on the life of Saint Benedict; Hilary, *On the Mysteries* and *Hymns*; Sedulius, *On the Gospels*; Juvencus, *On the Gospels*; a medical book; a Psalter; Cresconius, *On the Libyan Wars*; verses of Arichis, Paul, and Charles; the verses of Paulinus; Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods*; the Institutes of Justinian; his Novels; Terence; Horace with geometry; Ovid, *Fasti*; Seneca; Virgil with Theodorus’s eclogue; Donatus.

### Famine

At this time thieves entered the cellar of our monastery at night and, stealing meat, cheese, and bacon, filled their sacks with these provisions. When they went outside and tried to lift the sacks they had filled, they were completely unable to do so.

Then, leaving their burden behind and attempting to flee, they went around the monastery’s enclosures throughout the course of the night, but were entirely unable to find any way out, and so forth.

At this time, moreover, a very severe famine occurred throughout almost the whole of Italy. Desiderius therefore consulted with the brothers and distributed food generously to those in need.

### After the Pontiff’s Death, He Refuses the Papacy

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1085, in the eighth indiction, when the venerable lord Pope Gregory VII, whose memory is forever to be revered, was being held at Salerno by a serious illness, three days before his death he was asked by the bishops and cardinals who were then present together with Desiderius what arrangements he wished to be made for the Roman see after his death.

He replied that, if they could ever do so in any way, they should promote Desiderius to this office. Besides being at that time the first cardinal priest of the Roman Church, Desiderius possessed the greatest prudence, singular religious devotion, and extensive friendships among the surrounding princes.

If they could not bend him to this, they were to hasten, after his death, to elect as pope whichever they could first obtain among Hugh, archbishop of Lyon; Otto, bishop of Ostia; and the bishop of Lucca.

Having made this arrangement, Gregory died on the eighth day before the Kalends of June—that is, on Sunday—and was honorably buried inside the church of Saint Matthew the Apostle and Evangelist. He had occupied the pontificate for twelve years, one month, and three days.

Since the Roman Church had been left without a shepherd, and heretics and schismatics were striving to invade it like wolves, Desiderius, together with the bishops and cardinals and also the devout laymen who had until then remained faithfully in Catholic unity and in obedience to Pope Gregory, began unanimously to consider how he might arrange the Church in the most proper manner.

They therefore sent for and assembled from every direction persons suitable for this office, so that by unanimous agreement they might elect from among them someone who, with the grace and help of God, would be suitable and capable of so great an order.

Afterward the bishops and cardinals came to the abbot mentioned above. They began to appeal to him concerning the judgment of the deceased pontiff and to implore him most urgently to aid the Church, which was endangered in such a crisis, by accepting the papacy.

He obstinately refused to accept the papacy, but promised that, by whatever other means he knew and could employ, he was ready to serve the Roman Church.

On Pentecost, when the bishop of Savina and Gratianus came from Rome, Desiderius went to meet them and recounted to them the words he had exchanged with Pope Gregory concerning the ordering of the Church. Together with them he also approached Prince Jordan and Count Raynulf, urged them to serve and assist the Roman Church, and found them most willing to undertake everything.

He then began pressing the cardinals strongly to deliberate as quickly as possible about the person to be elected pontiff, and to send letters to Countess Matilda, asking her to ensure that the bishops mentioned above, as well as all those judged suitable for so great an office, should come to Rome without delay.

While they neglected to do this, they secretly plotted with Prince Jordan to impose pastoral responsibility upon the same abbot. By many arguments they tried to bring him to Rome by whatever means, thinking that they could force the office upon him.
