Sensing this, he began in every way to refuse and oppose them. He therefore returned to this monastery and again began urging the Normans, Lombards, and everyone else whom he could reach to serve the Roman Church. He found many of them willing and ready to undertake the task.

Because the heat of summer was excessive, however, they postponed going to Rome until the heat had diminished and the unhealthy season had passed.

When the prince, having hired an army for this purpose, came into Campania in order to go to Rome, accompanied by several bishops of these regions together with Desiderius, the latter—suspicious of the plans described above—refused to proceed any farther. He said that unless Prince Jordan, Count Raynulf, and the Roman bishops gave him their pledge in his presence that they would use no force against him in this matter and would permit no one else to do so, he would not go with them under any circumstances.

When they refused to do this, the matter at that time remained unfinished.

### He Is Elected

Almost a year had passed in such uncertainty. There was no shepherd in the apostolic see, no one was caring for the Lord’s flock, and Guibert, the heresiarch, was tearing apart the sheep redeemed by Christ’s blood together with his followers.

Around the celebration of Easter, the bishops and cardinals of the Roman Church came to Rome from various regions. They sent word to the abbot mentioned above that he should come to them as quickly as possible, together with the Roman bishops and cardinals who were then staying with him and with Gisulf, prince of Salerno, who had arrived from the Cisalpine regions, so that they might deliberate together about the ordering of the Roman Church.

Suspecting nothing—that they were already considering something concerning him, since no one was now mentioning him—he took all those men with him and reached the city of Rome.

On the day of his arrival, the eve of Pentecost, Desiderius urged that the summit of the pontificate be entrusted to someone whom either they or he considered suitable. But both the Roman clergy and people utterly refused to consent.

Throughout that day, a great multitude of all who supported the Catholic party, clergy and laity alike, came to him. Toward evening they all gathered together—bishops and cardinals as well as the other Romans who persevered in fidelity to blessed Peter, prince of the apostles—at the deaconry of Saint Lucia, which is beside the Septizonium.

There they all began unanimously to entreat Desiderius with many prayers not to refuse the Roman pontificate. They implored him by everything divine and human to help the Church, which was in peril and shipwreck. Many times they all fell at his knees, with some of them weeping.

But Desiderius, who had long since resolved to spend his life in quiet and who preferred to end his days in divine pilgrimage, began to refuse in every possible way and firmly promised that he would never consent.

They pressed him forcefully and insistently; he resisted more forcefully and persisted more stubbornly, saying:

“Know for certain that if you inflict any violence upon me in this matter, I shall return to Cassino as soon as I can, and I shall never involve myself in it in any way. As for you, by doing this you are making a great mockery both of yourselves and of the Roman Church.”

Since the hour had grown late and night was already approaching, each returned to his own place.

Early the next morning, on Pentecost Sunday, they all again came to him unanimously and began repeating the same request. He nevertheless persisted in the decision he had once made.

When they saw that they were accomplishing absolutely nothing, the priests, cardinals, and bishops told Desiderius that whoever he advised them to choose, they would be ready to elect.

After consulting with Cencius, consul of the Romans, he finally decided that the bishop of Ostia should be elected pope.

After this they asked him to receive the pontiff whom they were going to elect at the Cassinese monastery and to support him and all his companions until the Church was restored to peace, just as he had done for the aforementioned Pope Gregory.

Desiderius most willingly promised to do this, and, with the staff he was carrying in his hand, formally pledged them his faith concerning the matter.

But when they were already about to decide upon the bishop of Ostia, one of the cardinals suddenly declared that this election was contrary to the canons and loudly announced that he would not consent under any circumstances.

Although the others argued that, given the circumstances and the necessity, it had to be accepted for the time being, they could not bend him to their view.

But, as wise Solomon testifies: “There is no wisdom, there is no counsel against the Lord” (Proverbs 21:30).

At once the bishops and cardinals, together with the clergy and people, grew angry at Desiderius’s stubbornness. Seeing that they could accomplish nothing with him through prayers, they resolved to complete the matter by force.

Finally, therefore, they all seized him together, with one accord and one mind, and dragged him, unwilling and resisting, to the church of the aforementioned martyr of Christ, Lucia. There, electing him according to the custom of the Church, they gave him the name Victor.

Since they had done all this, as we have said, against his mind and will, he did wear a red cope, but they were never able to make him put on a white one.

### He Leaves Rome and Remains at Cassino

At that time the emperor’s prefect, dispatched by the duke and his mother because of the hostility arising when the bishops and cardinals, despite the efforts of the prince of Salerno, had refused to consecrate the archbishop of Salerno, gathered day and night in the Capitol against the newly elected pontiff, together with several men hired with illicit money, and inflicted severe persecutions upon him.

After four days the newly elected pontiff left Rome and came to Ardea. He remained there for three days, then departed for Terracina. From there he laid aside the cross, the chlamys, and the other insignia of the pontificate, and no one could ever persuade him to use them again in any way.

He resolved that throughout the whole of his life he would rather end his life in divine pilgrimage than submit his neck to the heaviest burdens of so great an office.

Every day he was confronted with prayers and very frequent tears. The great dangers of the Churches were placed before him, as was the destruction of countless souls, for which divine indignation was being directed against him in the clearest terms.

Thus he returned to Cassino.

For the course of an entire year, however, his purpose of mind remained so immovable that no arguments whatsoever could turn him from the exhortations and prayers of those who appealed to him.

Nevertheless, the cardinals and bishops who were with him did not remain quiet. They began pressing Prince Jordan to hasten and go with them to Rome for the consecration of the newly elected pontiff.

The prince came to this monastery with a large army, but, unwilling to go farther partly because of the elected pontiff’s dissuasion and partly because of fear of the summer, he turned back.

### Council at Capua; He Is Consecrated at Rome and Returns to Cassino

In the following year, during Lent, a council of bishops was assembled at Capua. The aforementioned elected pontiff presided over the council together with the Roman bishops and cardinals. Cencius, consul of the Romans, was also present with other Roman nobles, as were Prince Jordan and Duke Roger with nearly all their leading men.

After the council had ended, the clergy and laity once again unexpectedly pressed him with many prayers and tears, while he suspected nothing of what they were planning. He remained unmoved for two days.

Finally, when the duke and the prince, together with the bishops and the other Catholic men, lay at his feet with their tears flowing, he was compelled by many arguments and prayers and at last, though with difficulty, yielded. He confirmed the earlier election by resuming the cross and purple, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of April—that is, Palm Sunday.

He then returned to Cassino and celebrated Easter there.

After the festival had ended, he went to Rome with the prince of Capua and the prince of Salerno. Crossing the Tiber with everyone near the city of Ostia, he was detained by a serious illness and pitched his tents outside the portico of Saint Peter.

Since the Ravennate heresiarch Guibert, who had seized the papacy while Pope Gregory was still alive, was holding Saint Peter’s church with an armed force, the church was attacked and recovered by the prince’s soldiers, with God’s help, before a full day had passed.

On the Sunday after Ascension Sunday, many Romans and almost all the inhabitants of Trastevere came solemnly to meet him in an immense crowd. The elected pontiff was consecrated according to ecclesiastical custom by the Roman bishops—namely, those of Ostia, Tusculum, Porto, and Albano—with many cardinals, bishops, and abbots assisting. He was placed in the apostolic see on the seventh day before the Ides of May.

On that same day the body of Saint Nicholas, confessor of Christ, was brought to Bari from the city of Myra, where it had rested for 775 years.

The aforementioned pontiff remained in Rome for approximately eight days and then returned to this monastery together with the princes named above.

### He Goes to Rome; Disturbances There

After a short time Countess Matilda came to the city and, through envoys, appealed to the same pontiff with great entreaties so that she might be granted the enjoyment of seeing him and of speaking with him. She suggested that this had been her principal reason for coming to Rome.

Bodily illness compelled him not to leave the place, but because he had resolved to expose himself even to the greatest dangers for the benefit of the holy Church, he undertook the journey by sea.

When he reached the city, the countess, her army, and the other faithful of blessed Peter received him with the greatest devotion and courtesy. He remained for eight days at the church of Saint Peter.

Then, on the feast of Saint Barnabas, he solemnly celebrated Mass upon the altar of Saint Peter. On that same day, with the assistance and support of the aforementioned countess, he entered Rome through Trastevere.

At that time he held under his jurisdiction all Trastevere, a very large part of the Romans and nobles, nearly the entire populace, the fortress of Sant’Angelo, the basilica of Saint Peter, and the cities of Ostia and Porto. He was staying at the Island in Rome, which was likewise under his authority.

On the day preceding the feast of the apostles, a certain messenger arrived, supposedly from the emperor’s side, and drove all the consuls, senators, and Roman people away from the imperial crown. Suddenly the Romans arrived and seized everything except the church of blessed Peter. They could not enter that church itself, which the men of the aforementioned pontiff held from above.

But because the force of the heresiarch Guibert was very large, the men on Pope Victor’s side, unable to withstand so great a host of enemies, withdrew into Trastevere or into the fortress of Sant’Angelo.

By midday the Ravennate heresiarch celebrated Mass in the church of Saint Mary in the Towers. He had captured both bell towers by placing fire and smoke beneath them. But when the sun was already declining toward sunset, those who had occupied the church openly descended with their weapons and withdrew.

Thus, alas, what grief! On the day when the apostolic and universal church of blessed Peter was especially celebrating his feast, it lacked every office, both by night and by day.

In this way the hope of the heresiarch Guibert was frustrated, for he had desired to celebrate Mass there on the solemnity of the apostles.

The next day the heretics washed the apostolic altar, and Mass was celebrated there. On the following day everyone returned to his own place, and the same church returned to the power of Pope Victor.

At that same time, when certain pilgrims came to blessed Benedict for the sake of prayer, a certain man, a canon, met them. When they asked him who he was, he replied that he was the apostle Peter.

They asked him: “Where are you going?”

The holy Apostle replied: “I am going to my brother Benedict, so that I may celebrate with him the day of my Passion; for I cannot remain in Rome. My Church is being oppressed by various storms.”

When the men later disclosed this to the brothers, the brothers established it as a memorial for posterity that they should celebrate the feast of so great an apostle solemnly and with the greatest devotion, just as they celebrated the feast of Father Benedict.

In the following chapter he deals with the various disturbances stirred up by Guibert and his followers, and with the coronation of Henry.

### Expedition to Africa

Meanwhile the same apostolic pontiff Victor burned with an immense desire to confound, trample down, and crush the infidelity of the Saracens living in Africa.

After consulting with the bishops and cardinals, he gathered a Christian army from almost all the peoples of Italy and handed them the banner of blessed Peter the Apostle. Under the remission of all sins, he sent them against the Saracens living in Africa.

With Christ as their leader, they came down against the African city. Attacking it with all their strength, they captured it with God’s assistance, killing 100,000 fighting men from the Saracen army.

So that no one might doubt that this happened without divine will, on the day when the Christians achieved victory over the Saracens, this event was also divinely revealed in Italy.

### Synod at Benevento

The aforementioned Pope Victor III left the city and came to this monastery. After associating the bishops and cardinals with him, he solemnly dedicated the church of Saint Nicholas at Pica.

In August, he decided to celebrate a synod with the bishops of Apulia and Calabria and with those of the Principate, and he went to Benevento. There the same apostolic pontiff presided and said: “Your charity knows,” and so forth.

He included much in his address against Guibert, whom he anathematized. He then complained against Hugh of Lyon and Richard, abbot of Marseille, as deserters.

He declared that the company of excommunicated persons must be avoided so completely that the faithful ought rather to live and die without the sacraments than be polluted by communion with them.

In volume II of Acher’s *Spicilegium*, p. 405, there is a letter of Hugh of Lyon to Countess Matilda in which he attempts to refute the charges brought against him in this matter.

In another letter to the same Matilda, Hugh attacks Desiderius at great length. Abbot Hugh of Flavigny inserted the letter in full in his *Chronicle of Verdun*, printed in Labbe, volume I of the *New Library*, p. 233.

But these calumnies are dispelled by the unanimous agreement of the more serious writers of this age, who celebrated Victor with many praises.

Thus our anonymous Saxon manuscript chronicler says of him under the year 1085:

“Pope Hildebrand, who is also Gregory VII, dies in exile at Salerno and is buried there in the church. With the agreement of the Normans from Apulia, of the most powerful woman Matilda throughout Italy, and of all who shared their party, Desiderius, Roman cardinal and abbot of Cassino, a true servant of Christ, is substituted for him, although he resisted greatly in both heart and body, and is named Victor.

“For, while suffering from a serious illness, he was brought unwillingly—indeed, as a captive—to this supreme dignity. He obtained by his prayers that within a few days he should be taken from this life.”

Trithemius says nearly the same under the year 1085 in the Saint-Gall edition of the *Chronicle of Hirsau*, and he also frequently praises the same pontiff elsewhere.

What happened after the Council of Capua we may learn from Peter, who continues the Chronicle.

### Abbot Oderisius

At the same council the same pontiff fell seriously ill. After the council had continued for three days, he hastily returned to Cassino. Ascending to this monastery with the bishops and cardinals, he ordered himself to be carried into the brothers’ chapter house.

Under the strictest anathema, he forbade any of his successors to dare sell or alienate the land-dues (*terraticum*), churches, villages, or any possessions belonging to this Cassinese monastery.

Likewise, he forbade any monk to dare draw up a charter or document without the knowledge of his abbot. If anyone did so, it was to be invalid.

He also then established that all the monasteries under the authority of our Cassinese monastery should provide a meal for our congregation each year.

After this decree had been made with the unanimous consent of all the monks, while the bishops mentioned above were seated in the chapter house and confirmed it, he appointed as abbot the lord Oderisius, a highly religious man and a Roman deacon who was then serving as provost in our monastery.

Afterward, having summoned the same bishops and cardinals, he admonished and instructed them to strive, as quickly as they could, to elect Otto, bishop of Ostia, as pope, in accordance with what his predecessor Pope Gregory had long before decreed.

Since Otto was present, Victor took him by the hand and handed him over to the other bishops, saying:

“Receive him, and set him in order for the Roman Church; and until you are able to do this, regard him in everything as my representative.”

After arranging and decreeing these matters, he ordered a tomb to be constructed for him in the apse of that same chapter house. On the third day afterward he happily departed to the Lord, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of October, in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1087, 579 years after the passing of Father Benedict.

He had governed this monastery for twenty-nine years, four months, and sixteen days; in the apostolic see, he had served one year from the beginning of his election, and four months and seven days from his consecration.

Sigibert writes in his *Chronicle* under the year 1086 that Victor died after being consumed by dysentery. Others say that he perished by poison. For this reason some bestowed upon him the title of martyr, since in this way he could be said to have been killed by his enemies with poison in defense of the Church.

## He Leaves Behind Many Ornaments

Furthermore, the same Pope Victor left these ornaments in this monastery at his death. Almost all of them, after the dedication of the church, he acquired partly himself together with the brothers of this monastery and partly recovered from others who had deposited them as pledges [Col. 0959D]:

Five gilded *diaspra* chasubles, and three without gold; three gilded *diarodana* chasubles; two *diapisti*, and another saffron-colored one; seven gilded purple chasubles, five other purple ones, and two *exametae*; the chasuble of John the physician; six everyday chasubles and four Lenten ones; eight prepared dalmatics and eleven others; five prepared tunics and nineteen others, for incense five. Thirty-eight gold-ornamented copes and eighty-seven others; 193 linen albs and ten silk ones; nineteen gilded stoles with their maniples; three silver stoles with their maniples; eighteen other stoles; seven half-girdles; three gold *fanones* for subdeacons and fourteen others; two large gilded shirts with their amices, and seven other silk ones [Col. 0960A].

One altar cloth for Saint Benedict, with one face decorated with pearls and another gilded face; three coverings with gold and two without gold; eleven large and excellent *circitoria*. For the altar of Saint John, five *circitoria* and five coverings. For the altar of Saint Mary, one purple face with gold, one covering with enamels, four *circitoria*, and four coverings. For the altar of Saint Gregory, one golden *circitorium* and four others without gold, four coverings, nineteen large backcloths, and thirty small backcloths; seven door hangings [*ostiaria*, or *hostiaria*].

Twelve golden chalices with their patens—seven larger and five smaller; one golden straw or tube with an angle; two Saxon silver chalices and seven other silver ones; two silver tubes; two golden censers [Col. 0960B], two silver-gilt ones; two very large other silver vessels; and eight other silver ones. One pair of crystal candlesticks; another silver pair with an onyx vessel; another silver pair with crystal apples; and five other candlesticks. Two large silver lanterns and one everyday lantern.

The Gospel Book belonging to him; the emperor’s Gospel Book; Pope Stephen’s Gospel Book; the empress’s Gospel Book; two Gospel Books of Brother Firmus; the Gospel Book of Abbot Aligernus; two Sacramentaries with silver; two Epistolaries, one with a gold cover and the other with silver covers; the Rule of Saint Benedict with silver covers; a large silver reliquary with gems and enamels; two silver chests; two large golden crosses with gems, two other smaller golden ones [Col. 0960C], and three silver processional crosses; a candlestick; a ewer with its basin; a Greek censer; another with niello; and a ewer with enamels.

All these were of silver. A golden pyx with enamels for the Body of the Lord, and another larger silver one with niello; three small cups made of mother-of-pearl; two onyx chalices; two pairs of silver basins; one hundred pounds of unworked gold; two golden stoles; an imperial *fanon*, entirely of gold; twelve imperial *scaramangae*; a silver crown over the altar of Saint John, with five crosses, and another Greek cross; a gilded silver crown decorated with precious stones and bearing six crosses; another crown over the altar of Saint Benedict, bearing three crosses decorated with precious stones; at Saint Nicholas, a silver crown and a cast silver cross; eleven silver crowns that he found in the old church.

Let this brief account of the life and character of the most reverend Pope Victor III, and of the renewal or adornment of this place, suffice. Moreover, as long as the orbit of this world revolves, his praiseworthy merit continually receives increase through Jesus Christ our Lord, who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit forever and ever. Amen.

Here we append the epitaph that to this day is seen inscribed on his tomb in the chapel of Saint Bertharius.

## Epitaph of Pope Victor III

*(We have already given it above.)*

## The Memory and Relics of Victor; His Minor Works

Of what we have said about Desiderius, or Victor, from Leo and his continuator Peter, there is almost nothing to add, since it is not our intention to bring here what is found about him in the commonly circulated authors. The Benedictine calendars and Ferrarius, in his *General Catalogue of the Saints*, celebrate his memory on September 16, the day that was his last.

His sacred bones were transferred from the ancient tomb to the chapel of Blessed Bertharius in 1515. When that same chapel, begun many years earlier, had finally been completely finished in 1666, the relics of the blessed pontiff were solemnly placed there on the right side of the altar by the most illustrious prelate Angelo de Nuce, at that time abbot of Sacro Monte and later archbishop of Rossano, as he himself relates in the notes to chapter 73 of Book III of the *Cassinese Chronicle*.

Victor also earned a place among ecclesiastical writers. Peter the Deacon lists his minor works in chapter 18 of *On the Illustrious Men of the Monastery of Cassino*:

> “He published, together with the deacon Theophilus, four books concerning the miracles performed by Blessed Benedict and by the monks of Cassino. He also composed the chant of Blessed Maurus, and so forth. After becoming pontiff, he wrote several letters to Philip, king of the Franks, and to Hugh, abbot of Cluny. Of these, three books of dialogues have been published; the fourth has not yet been found.”

[Col. 0961]

# Letters of Pope Victor III

### I. To the Empress, for the remission of the tribute of the Holy Sepulchre  
*(1086)*

[Note: [Col. 0961D] I would be mistaken if an error had not entered the title of this letter; nor do I doubt that this letter was written to Alexius, then emperor of Constantinople, and not to some empress of the East or West. Certainly no one is unaware that Alexius laid ambushes not only for armies hastening toward holy expeditions but also for pilgrims arriving from the West. His greed is demonstrated by this very golden bull, written in letters of gold, in which he confesses that, driven by need, he had removed sacred offerings from the churches. There he indeed forbids this to be done in the future; but even if he later refrained from stripping the churches, the reports commonly given by the historians of that period show that he was no more restrained in harassing pilgrims.]  

For the remission of the tribute of the Holy Sepulchre.

[Mabillon, *Benedictine Annals*, Appendix to vol. V, p. 647.]

[Col. 0961B]

Victor, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his glorious and beloved daughter in Christ, A., empress Augusta.

We are compelled by the duty of the Apostolic See, dearest daughter in Christ, not to withhold appropriate admonitions from persons great or small. In this matter, indeed, we ought to insist all the more upon those of higher rank, the more we know that they are able, in temporal affairs, to benefit or harm Christ’s poor.

Therefore, wishing that your dignity may not in the future be condemned for the temporal oppression of pilgrims and the poor, but glorified [Col. 0961C] for relieving them, we announce and beseech you in the Lord Jesus to cause the extremely severe and intolerable tribute imposed by your officials upon the ambassadors and visitors of His holy and glorious Sepulchre to cease.

To say nothing of the other burdens that they suffer throughout your empire, in two places alone they are so grievously oppressed that three gold pieces are exacted for each horse, and a *toditem* from every two foot-travelers [the term is uncertain in the supplied text]. Moreover, they forcibly seize the horses of these ambassadors and harass them for as long as they wish.

Unless you swiftly drive this evil danger from your realm by an imperial edict, know that it will redound—God forbid!—upon your soul, because whatever is committed by inferiors concerns their superiors, and those who do such things and those who consent to them will be punished with equal penalty [Col. 0962B].

For our part, as is fitting, always mindful in goodness of you and of your venerable ancestry, we desire and pray that you govern yourself and your people in such a way that you may acquire a good name—which is better than great riches—and may happily enter in the future into the joy of your Lord.

We both desire and pray that your excellence may remain forever in good health. We admonish you also to remember, as befits you, the Roman Church, your first and proper mother, and always to venerate her. Indeed, she continually remembers you for good and venerates your ancestral lineage.

### II. Victor III confirms, at the request of Bishop Ursus, the possessions of the newly established bishopric of Ravello  
*(1087)*

[Ughelli, *Sacred Italy*, I, 1182.]

[Col. 0962C]

Victor, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son in Christ, Ursus, bishop of Ravello, forever.

Since, by the disposition of heavenly clemency, God has granted Blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, and his successors throughout the nations the power to establish, arrange, rule, and govern the Churches, we too, according to our ability, being concerned for all the Churches, diligently strive by right to arrange, rule, and govern what the mercy of God has inspired in the secret place of our mind.

Therefore, assenting to your pious wishes and just petitions, we grant you and by our authority command that you and your successors forever have, retain, and possess by episcopal right whatever has newly been acquired, or may thereafter justly be acquired, as belonging to the city of Ravello, newly distinguished by the honor of episcopal dignity.

But if any king, margrave, duke, prince, patrician, count, viscount, or any person, great or small, should presume to act against this sanction of our decree, let him first be separated from participation in the Body and Blood of Christ [Col. 0966A]. If, after being canonically summoned once, twice, or three times, he should not make satisfaction but persist in his wickedness . . . . we decree that he is excommunicated and condemned.

We grant to you and to your successors free authority in your diocese, without anyone’s . . . . to prepare chrism, dedicate churches, ordain clergy, and celebrate whatever belongs to the order of the episcopate.

Given at Capua through the hands of . . . . bishop of Segni and librarian of the Roman Church, in the year from the Incarnation of Our Lord Jesus Christ 1088; in the first year of the pontificate of Pope Victor III, indiction 10.

[Col. 0965]

# Sermon of Pope Victor III

Delivered at the synod of Benevento: On the condemnation of Guibert; on avoiding recent schismatics. — Canons of the council.

[Baronius, *Annals*, year 1087, vol. XI.]

[Col. 0965B]

Your affection knows, dearest brother bishops—and this is not hidden from the whole world—how many adversities the holy Roman and apostolic See, which by God’s authority I serve, has endured; how many blows, finally, it has received from the brokers of the Simoniacal heresy, so that the pillar of the living God seemed already almost shaken and tottering, and the net of the supreme Fisherman seemed to be torn apart by swelling waves and to perish by shipwreck.

For Guibert, the arch-heresiarch who, while my predecessor of holy memory, Pope Gregory, was still alive, invaded the Roman Church—the forerunner of Antichrist and standard-bearer of Satan—does not cease to scatter, slaughter, and tear apart Christ’s sheep.

As the instigator and inciter of evils, who could recount the insults, persecutions, and disasters that he inflicted upon Pope Gregory [Col. 0965C]? He himself, the author of the conspiracy, stirred up conspirators against him; drove him from the City; as far as lay in him, installed a Simoniac and perjurer in the priesthood; aroused the Roman Empire against him; incited peoples and kingdoms; and—in something unheard-of since the beginning of the world—though himself excommunicated and condemned, dared to excommunicate the holy pontiff.

He does not cease to profane the Roman city with sacrileges, killings, perjuries, conspiracies, crimes, and the mockery of every vice. Inflamed by the treachery of Simon Magus, he summoned the accomplices of his wickedness to so impious and execrable a deed. Having compelled an imperial army, he became the invader of the Apostolic See, contrary to the evangelical commands [Col. 0965D], contrary to the decrees of the prophets and apostles, contrary to the canons and the rights of the Roman pontiffs. With no prior judgment of the cardinal bishops, with no approving vote of the Roman clergy, and with no consent sought from the devout people, he became in the holy Roman Church the head of all wickedness and destruction [Col. 0966B].

But when the power of almighty God had called the aforementioned pontiff Gregory, after many labors and struggles, to eternal rest, and when the bishops, cardinals, and provincial prelates, together with the Roman clergy and people, had unanimously placed our insignificance—resisting and opposing in every way—over the Apostolic See, Guibert, fearing neither the judgment of the eternal Emperor, still does not cease to persecute Christ and His sheep, for whom He shed His blood.

Therefore, by the authority of God and of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, and of all the saints, we deprive him of every priestly office and honor and, separating him from the thresholds of the Church, bind him with the bond of anathema.

Moreover, you know—and know well—what schemes were devised and what pressures were brought upon me by Hugh, archbishop of Lyon, and Richard, abbot of Marseille. Out of pride and ambition for the Apostolic See, which they had long secretly desired, when they did not obtain what they wished, they created schisms in the holy Church.

Richard had indeed worked at Rome with the cardinals and bishops against our election. Hugh, however, shortly afterward came to us, prostrating himself at our feet; while offering us, the supreme pontiff, the service owed to us, though unwillingly and reluctantly, he requested and received from us a legation in the regions of Gaul.

Thus, as long as they saw our insignificance resisting the election that had been made and approved by them, they persisted by every means in preventing us from casting off the burden imposed upon us for the benefit of the Church [Col. 0966D]. But when at last they perceived that we were yielding, the furnace, sated, vomited forth the flame it had long conceived.

Therefore, seeing that the unanimity of all the brothers firmly opposed them, they were immediately separated from communion with them and with us.

Accordingly, by apostolic authority we command that you take care to abstain from them and do not communicate with them at all, because they have voluntarily deprived themselves of communion with the Roman Church. For, as blessed Ambrose writes: “Whoever separates himself from the Roman Church is truly to be regarded as a heretic.”

We also decree that if anyone hereafter receives a bishopric or abbacy from the hand of any lay person, he is in no way to be regarded as bishop or abbot, nor is any reverence to be shown him as bishop or abbot. Moreover, we forbid him the bosom of blessed Peter and entrance into the church until, repenting, he abandons the position that he has taken under so great a crime of ambition and disobedience—which is the sin of idolatry. We decree the same concerning lower ecclesiastical ranks and dignities.

Likewise, if any emperor, king, duke, prince, count, or holder of any secular power presumes to confer a bishopric or any other ecclesiastical dignity, let him know that he is bound by the same sentence; since the three hundred and eighteen Fathers at the Council of Nicaea excommunicated all such sellers and buyers, decreeing that he who gives and he who receives is anathema. Whoever communicates or prays with such bishops, abbots, or other clerics, or hears their masses, is punished by one and the same sentence of excommunication; indeed, they cannot even rightly be considered priests.

Penance and communion, moreover, are to be received from no one but a Catholic. If no Catholic priest is present, it is better to remain without visible communion and to communicate invisibly with the Lord than, by receiving it from a heretic, to be separated from God. For, as the Apostle says, “What concord has Christ with Belial? Or what share has a believer with an unbeliever?” (2 Corinthians 6). Every heretic, moreover, is an unbeliever; and a simoniac, because he is a heretic, is therefore an unbeliever. Although Catholics may be unable visibly and bodily to receive Christ’s sacred communion because of threatening heretics, nevertheless, so long as they are joined to Christ in mind, they receive His communion invisibly.

Accordingly, whatever I have happened to hear or see in the apostolic regions, I shall endeavor, life permitting, to conclude in two other little books [Col. 0967A]. And, to remove every scruple of doubt from readers, I shall append, for each matter, the names of the persons from whom these reports came to me, judging it better to remain entirely silent than to relate anything false or corrupted.

### Theophilus

Since Scripture says, “The mouth that lies kills the soul” (Wisdom 1:11), why did blessed Paul, when he was committed to prison custody together with Silas, assert that he was a Roman, when it is perfectly clear that he was not a Roman but a Jew?

### Desiderius

Far be it from the hearts of the faithful to believe that the preacher of truth and teacher of the nations ever fell into falsehood! Blessed Paul both was and was not a Roman.

He was not a Roman because he had not originated from the city of Rome [Note: [Col. 0967C] Saint Paul was a Roman citizen by hereditary right; and he was born to this status not because he was born in the City itself, but because his father was a Roman citizen. For he was born at Tarsus, which was the metropolis of Cilicia and had obtained municipal rights from the Romans, so that the people of Tarsus were counted Roman citizens and enjoyed the privileges of Roman citizens. See Lorin, commentary on the Acts of the Apostles, chapter 22, verse 28.].

But he was a Roman because the entire Jewish people, like almost the whole world, at that time lived under the dominion of the Roman Empire. Or he could be called Roman for another reason: *Romanus* means “exalted,” and he could most suitably and justly call himself exalted because he had no hesitation in declaring himself so, as he himself says: “Our citizenship is in heaven” (Philippians 3).

### Theophilus

I confess that what you say is very pleasing to me, but please begin now to relate what you promised.

### Desiderius

The matter I am about to narrate is very unusual, and is confirmed by the testimony of our elders, concerning the most reverend man [Note: [Col. 0967D] Apollinaris was made abbot of Cassino in the year of the Lord 817, and is honored with the title of sanctity in the Benedictine Martyrology under December 5. Peter the Deacon described his deeds at length in the manuscript Book on the Origin and Life of the Just of Cassino, chapter 26. See also Leo of Ostia, *Chronicle*, Book I, chapter 18.]: namely, Abbot Apollinaris of our monastery, whom, with God’s favor, though unworthy, I serve. His holiness, kindness, and generosity were made most plainly evident to almost everyone living in this province.

One day, compelled by necessity, he was inspecting the monastery’s estates and came to the river Liris [Note: [Col. 0967D] The Liris, also called the Caritianus, is the principal river of Campania and separates it from Latium. Its sources are seen on Mount Apennine above the city of Sora.]. Since there was no boat by which he could cross the river, full of faith and fortifying himself with the sign of the holy cross, he approached the riverbank. Clothed as he was and wearing his shoes, he entered the river and proceeded [Note: [Col. 0967D] In the same way, Saints Frontosius and his fellow martyrs, carrying their severed heads, walked over the waters of the river called the Yla. Saint Hyacinth, of the order of Preachers, walked over the waves with dry feet, spreading his cloak over them, and led his companions across with him. Marulus reports that Nazarius and Celsus also walked over the waves when they had been thrown into the sea, Book III, chapter 3. The glorious Charitina, in the year 308, with a stone tied around her neck, was submerged into the depths of the sea, yet crossed the waters as though over solid ground and reached the shore; see Surius, October 5. The martyr Quirinus, according to Prudentius and Eusebius in their chronicles, in the year 314 was tied to a rock and thrown into a river, yet swam out and calmly walked over the water, while the waves supported and carried the rock. It is read in the *Lives of the Fathers*, Book VI, little book 2, no. 2, that the water solidified beneath the feet of Abbot Bessarion. Blessed Oringa, also called Christina, a virgin in Etruria, likewise fled across a river with dry feet so that she would not be forced to marry.] and reached the opposite bank with dry feet, so that not even his shoes appeared to have become wet.

Consider, I beg you, how great was this man’s holiness, religious devotion, and merit before almighty God: although still burdened by the weight of the body, he was permitted to walk upon the fluid element as though upon dry land. In this deed he was evidently made like the prince of the apostles, who, at the Lord’s command, walked upon the waves with dry feet.

### Theophilus

I certainly observe it and am profoundly amazed, since in our times—when, according to the prophet’s prediction, “The holy man has failed, truths have diminished among the children of men; there is none who does good, not even one” (Psalm 13)—almighty God has deigned to perform such things.

### Desiderius

If you consider, dearest brother, what the Lord deigned to promise His disciples—“Behold, I am with you all the days, until the consummation of the age” (Matthew 28)—you will be able to rejoice rather than wonder.

### Theophilus

[Note: [Col. 0968D] In the year of the Lord 846, the Agarens, or Saracens, a populous people, inflicted great damage upon Italy and devastated almost all the Roman provinces with fires and plunder. Leo of Ostia, *Chronicle*, Book I, chapter 26; Baronius under this same year.]

I do rejoice, and I rejoice exceedingly; but I beg you, continue what you have begun.

### Desiderius

At the time when the people of the Agarens, having transported their fleet, were devastating Italy far and wide, I do not consider it worthy of silence how almighty God delivered this monastery from their hands.

After they had consumed everything around them with fire and sword, they also came to the churches of the most holy Peter and Paul and plundered them. Then, taking the Appian road, they attacked the city of Fundi and burned it with fire [Col. 0968C]. All who lived there were either killed or captured by them.

Departing from there, they arrived in the vicinity of our monastery, across the river Liris. Since night was already approaching the land, they pitched their camp, intending at dawn to destroy the entire monastery from its foundations or carry off as booty whatever they could find there. And, being exceedingly thirsty for blood, they intended to slaughter with the sword all the brothers whom they found there.

When this terrible, monstrous, and fearful danger had been announced at the monastery, all the brothers, struck by immense fear, fell prostrate upon the ground, earnestly beseeching the divine majesty [Col. 0969A] graciously to receive their souls, whose bodies, because their sins demanded it, He had determined to hand over to so sudden and terrifying a death. For they did not believe that they would live any longer in this world, seeing the sword of death so close upon them.

Thus, throughout the whole night, with their heads sprinkled with ashes, they devoted themselves to vigils and prayers. The most reverend Abbot Apollinaris, whom I mentioned above [Note: [Col. 0969D] Bassatius was made abbot of Cassino in the year of the Lord 837, according to Leo of Ostia, *Chronicle*, Book I, chapter 23; he died in 856, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of April.], appeared in a vision to Abbot Bassatius, a religious man, and addressed him, saying:

“Do not be afraid or let your heart be troubled. You will not be captured by the Agarens at this time, nor, with the right hand of God protecting you, will they be able to inflict any harm upon you. Rather, they will soon turn back and attempt to reach their own borders. From now on you will remain safe and unharmed, because the most holy Father Benedict has obtained your salvation from almighty God. He himself has come to help you, and we have all come together with him.”

Then the venerable Abbot Bassatius awoke from sleep, summoned the brothers together, and related what he had seen and what had been revealed to him. He urged them to beseech almighty God without delay.

They, now confident in divine mercy, became joyful, praising and blessing the Lord, and spent the rest of the night in prayers and supplications. The air had been so calm that not even a thin cloud could be seen in it, when suddenly the sky thickened with clouds, thunderclaps resounded, repeated flashes and lightning gleamed [Col. 0969C], and such a rain poured down upon the earth that the river Liris, overflowing widely, seemed like a sea.

At daybreak the barbarians rose from their camp and approached the riverbank, carefully searching to see whether they might find a boat or ford by which they could cross the river. But when every hope of crossing had been taken from them, stirred by savage rage, they gnawed at their hands and fingers because they had been frustrated of their hoped-for booty and had remained empty-handed. They burned the cells of our monastery situated across the Liris, then turned their army around and began to depart as quickly as possible.

When they had reached the place where the aforesaid river Liris flows into the sea through a broad mouth, they abandoned all the horses they possessed, disabling their legs and cutting their tendons, because they could not take them with them. They themselves, however, boarded ships, gave their sails to the winds, and, cutting through the sea on a direct course, reached Sicily. They hoped to touch dry land quickly.

Suddenly they saw a small boat darting swiftly here and there over the waves among their ships. A cleric of venerable gray hair and another monk appeared to be sitting in it. When they eagerly asked them where they were coming from, and why they were returning so happy, energetic, and heavily laden, they declared that they were coming from Italy and had there delivered everything to fire and sword. They boasted that they had also stripped the houses of Peter and Paul, as well as that of Benedict.

“And who are you,” they asked, “who strive to question us so anxiously, carefully, and inquisitively?”

“We are called Peter and Benedict, one of us by one name and the other by the other—the very men whose houses you boast that you invaded. But how great our virtue and power are, you will learn very soon.”

After they had said this, they vanished from their sight.

Immediately, winds raged from every direction and the waves swelled. So violent a storm suddenly arose that all the ships were either dashed against one another or driven upon the rocks and wrecked. Thus, out of that entire host of pagans, scarcely a few survived who could report these things to the citizens who had sent them.

Almighty God indeed permitted their churches to be devastated by them for a time, but He did not allow them to rejoice long over so great a crime. In this deed I seem to see fulfilled what Blessed Father Benedict had once promised his disciples, saying:

> “After laying aside the burden of the flesh, I shall be more present to you, beloved sons, and by God’s grace I shall remain your constant fellow-worker.”

Also fulfilled was what the Lord said to Blessed Peter:

> “You are Peter, and upon this rock I shall build my Church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it” (Matthew 16).

He did not say, “They will not be able,” but “They will not prevail.” For the gates of hell are the pagans, heretics, and Jews, who then appear to have power against the Church of God when through them the Lord permits His faithful to be scourged. But they will not prevail, because almighty and merciful God does not allow them to enjoy perpetual triumphs over His Church.

Thus the Apostle also exhorts us, saying:

> “We suffer tribulation, but are not crushed; we are in difficulty, but are not abandoned; we suffer persecution, but are not forsaken; we are humbled, but are not put to shame; we are afflicted, but do not perish” (2 Corinthians 4).

### Theophilus

What you say pleases me greatly.

### Desiderius

The priest John, of holy memory [Note: [Col. 0969D] Peter the Deacon described the deeds of John, a man Apulian by origin and name, distinguished for holiness as abbot of Lucera [or Lucensis], in the manuscript Book on the Origin and Life of the Just, chapter 33. See also Leo of Ostia, *Chronicle*, Book II, chapter 92. He is listed among the blessed in the Benedictine Martyrology under February 22. He was alive in the year of the Lord 1055.], who for some time held the office of dean in our monastery and afterward became provost of your monastery, which was built within the city of Lucca—many monks who knew him and still survive bear witness to how great his obedience and humility were.

As for the wonders that the divine majesty deigned to perform through him, since many have slipped from my memory, I shall relate the few that I remember. This man of God devoted himself to fasts, vigils, prayers, and especially the giving of alms. By the Lord’s generosity he merited such a grace of tears that there could be no doubt that those tears, issuing from so simple and humble a heart, were able to obtain much from God.

When the fame of his holiness had spread brightly throughout that entire city, a woman possessed by a demon and gravely afflicted was brought to the monastery [Col. 0971A] over which he presided. Those who had brought her bound him with earnest entreaties to pray to the Lord for her. He summoned the brothers, entered the oratory, and poured out prayers to the Lord for her amid many tears. Immediately, he drove the demon out of her.

But I will not keep silent about what I learned from truthful men who related it concerning this same venerable man—a matter so well known that it is scarcely hidden or unknown to anyone dwelling within the walls of the aforesaid city of Lucca.

The wife of a certain distinguished man lay confined to her bed by illness. As her condition grew steadily worse, she was brought to the point of death, so that for three days she lay without consciousness or speech and was regarded as though dead. When all who were present had utterly despaired of her life, someone was sent to the man of God, asking him to offer prayers and sacrifices to the almighty Lord on her behalf. But he, being benevolent in spirit and ready to respond to the petitions of those who implored him, immediately put on his priestly vestments and approached the altar to offer sacrifice to almighty God.

When her name was mentioned during the sacred celebration of Mass, she, in her own house, situated far from the monastery, answered from the bed on which she lay as though lifeless, as if someone were calling her. When those present asked what she was saying, or to whom she had replied, she said: “Is not Lord John, the superior, here? For he himself called me, and I answered him.”

Struck with amazement at so unusual, so celebrated, and so astonishing a miracle—both because they saw her, who had been lying almost lifeless, now nearly healthy and unharmed, and because she reported that she had heard the voice of one situated so far away—they immediately arranged to send messengers to the monastery, so that they might learn what the servant of God was doing and report it. They were without doubt convinced that the woman had not risen so quickly from her bed and given her answer without reason.

When those who had been sent entered the monastery’s oratory, they found the man of God standing beside the altar and offering sacrifice for her to the Lord, the author of that distance. Carefully noting the hour, they discovered that she had risen from her bed and given her answer at the very moment when she was named during the sacred celebration of Mass.

Pope Saint Alexander, of blessed memory [Note: This was Pope Alexander II, elected in the year of the Lord 1061; he died at Rome, renowned for miracles, in 1073.], was a man of the greatest eloquence and learning. He first governed the Church of Lucca and afterward the Roman Church. From his lips I happened to hear the account I am now relating concerning this venerable man.

When the aforesaid pontiff had once been seized by fever, had fallen seriously ill, and was being exhausted more severely each day as his illness increased, he suddenly recalled what he had often heard rumor relate about the aforementioned servant of God: namely, that anyone suffering from fever who drank from the water that flowed from his hands when he washed them after the celebration of Mass was immediately restored to health and freed from the illness [Note: This miracle is also related by Leo of Ostia, Book II, chapter 92, and by Baronius under the year of the Lord 1070, no. 22. In the Greek nation as well, there is evidence of this pious practice of drinking water with which a priest washes his hands after the celebration of Mass, in order to drive away various illnesses; the exceedingly learned Leo Allatius bears witness to it in *On Certain Greek Opinions*, no. 6.].

He therefore secretly sent people who were to bring him a little of that water. When those who had been sent brought the water he had requested, he immediately drank it and was so suddenly restored to his former health that no sign of that illness remained in him.

There was also another venerable man of virtuous life, named Guinizzo [Note: Guinizzo lived around the year 1080, at the time when Henry governed the Roman Empire and Basil the empire of Constantinople. He was plainly a remarkable man, distinguished for holiness and radiant with the spirit of prophecy; he is listed among the saints in the Benedictine Martyrology under 26 May. His acts appear to have been written by Leo of Ostia, Book III, chapter 47, and by Peter the Deacon, *On the Origin of the Just of Cassino*, chapter 30; the dialogues of Desiderius are also mentioned in that passage.], a monk in mind and habit. Coming to our monastery from farther Spain, he led a solitary life for a considerable time in this neighboring forest, and there ended his life in the service of the omnipotent Lord Jesus Christ.

Concerning this venerable man, John, abbot of the monastery of Saint Vincent, situated near the source of the river Volturnus, who had been very close to him, was accustomed to relate many marvelous things to me while he was still exercising the office of superior in our monastery. His disciple, named Januarius [Note: Januarius is mentioned in the Life of Guinizzo written by Peter the Deacon, *On the Origin of the Just of Cassino*, chapter 30.], was a monk of great obedience and great abstinence.

On one occasion, his master, the venerable Guinizzo, sent him to Aquinum to have repaired the tools with which they were accustomed to work. He went to the house of a blacksmith and, offering payment, asked him to repair those tools. But the blacksmith began to mock him, saying: “How can this solitary, so ruddy and so fat, exist on bread and water?” [Note: Saint Cassius, bishop of Narni, was likewise accused of drunkenness by Totila, king of the Goths, on the basis of the redness of his face; Saint Gregory rises to refute that accusation in *Dialogues* III, chapter 6.] “That redness, it seems to me, comes more from wine than from water.”

But Januarius replied: “Today I shall show you whether my redness comes from nature or from habitual drinking of wine.”

When the iron placed in the fire had become intensely hot, and the blacksmith, taking it with tongs, had placed it upon the anvil, sparks flew in every direction and illuminated almost the whole house. By chance, the iron slipped from the anvil and fell to the ground.

The venerable Januarius, seeing that the iron had fallen from the anvil, bent down, took the burning iron in his bare hand, placed it upon the anvil, and urged the smith to strike it as quickly as possible. When those who were present saw so great a miracle, they were overcome with extraordinary fear, fell at his feet, and humbly begged his forgiveness for the mockery they had practiced against him. Thus all that mockery was turned into veneration—the mockery which foolish men had rashly presumed to inflict upon God’s servant.

When the venerable man had therefore returned to his master and to his cell, he was severely rebuked by him for yielding to those who insulted him and presuming to perform such things before human eyes. When Januarius asked how he knew this, or who had told him, Guinizzo replied: “He who granted you the power to do it also granted me the power to know it.”

**Theophilus.** Since the Lord says, “Let your light shine before men, so that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven” (Luke 12), why is it that holy men conceal their good works and strive with every effort to prevent them from being seen by anyone?

**Desiderius.** [Note: These words appear to have been taken from Saint Pope Gregory’s *Homilies on the Gospels*, homily 11.] Although holy men sometimes display their works publicly, their intention nevertheless remains hidden. Through what they do inwardly, they do not seek praise outwardly, because they wish both to provide their neighbors with an example of good work and, through the intention by which they desire to please God alone, always to remain concealed.

I mean that they desire their good works to be hidden when they see that their disclosure will bring no gain to souls and no benefit to the salvation of their brethren. But when they perceive that through such disclosure they can gain something for the glory of almighty God, then they allow their good works to be declared and made known, because they seek not their own praise but that of their Creator.

**Theophilus.** The explanation is sufficiently clear, and I do not think that anything further need be sought from it.

**Desiderius.** I have also judged it worthy to append to this little book the things that the religious monk John, who lives as a solitary under the discipline of an anchorite in this neighboring forest, is accustomed to relate about this distinguished man, Guinizzo. He said that while he was still living in his monastery in the city of Benevento, one day a servant of God told him and the other brothers who were present:

“Know for certain that today some great man from among the monks has departed this world for the Lord at Monte Cassino.”

When they heard this, they were astonished that he could have seen the soul of a man departing from the body nearly eighty miles away. Not believing it, they carefully investigated the matter. It was discovered that the venerable man had indeed breathed out his soul on the very day when the aforementioned servant of God, situated at Benevento, had learned of it.

Nor will I remain silent about what I learned from the brothers concerning the monk Mancuso, whom I myself saw while he was living in the monastery and who died in our own time. He had come here from the regions of Apulia for the sake of conversion, and was received by Richerius [Note: Richerius became abbot of Cassino in the year of the Lord 1038 and died in 1055; this miracle is therefore found to have occurred within that period. See Leo of Ostia, Book III.]—our predecessor as abbot—and joined to the community of the brothers.

Thus, although he lived bodily in the monastery, he lived in the world in his mind and was always pondering earthly things. Every discipline of the Rule seemed burdensome and intolerable to him. He then began asking the abbot for permission and devising many excuses by which he might revisit his homeland and parents.

His abbot repeatedly admonished him to advance for the better, day by day, along the way of truth that he had once undertaken and to bring it to its completion, laying aside all sluggish negligence and striving with the utmost effort. Otherwise, according to the Lord’s saying, “The one who puts his hand to the plow and looks back is not fit for the kingdom of heaven” (Luke 9), he might prove unfit for the kingdom of heaven; and, imitating Lot’s wife, who was changed into a pillar of salt (Genesis 19:16), he might present a dreadful spectacle to everyone.

Nevertheless, his mind, once possessed by the evil one, did not rest at all. Each day he wearied the abbot and the brothers with his petitions, repeatedly demanding that they allow him to revisit his homeland. When he saw that his hope of returning had been frustrated, he secretly left the monastery, seeking the darkness of night like a fugitive slave. At the devil’s instigation, he returned to his homeland like a dog to its vomit [Note: How destructive a homeland is for a monk is related by Cassian in *Conferences of the Fathers*, Book V, chapter 32, in the story of Abba Machetes. He did not even dare to open a packet of letters brought by his parents but handed it over to be burned, saying: “Away, thoughts of my homeland; burn together, and do not try to call me back again to those things from which I fled.” Simon Miletius writes that a place is shown today on the descent of Monte Cassino toward San Germano where a dragon appeared to a monk who was unwilling to remain in the monastery and later left it; he says that the demon had been transformed into the form of a dragon. But what is related by Theoderic in the Life of Saint Dominic, Book III, chapter 2, is altogether remarkable. See also Saint Jerome, letter to Heliodorus, *On the Praise of the Solitary Life*, and Saint Ambrose, *On Flight from the World*. Let those monks therefore take heed and beware who not only do not abandon their homeland or leave their parents and friends, but daily, for the sake of their own desires, pursue the courts and favor of the powerful. Would that this vice did not belong to our own age!].

He remained in his parents’ house and began to live there in a worldly manner, just as he had long conceived in his mind. But when his abbot repeatedly admonished him through messengers to return to the monastery’s enclosure, and he, disregarding the salutary admonitions, neglected to obey, the abbot deprived him of communion.

Not many days later, when he had been slightly weakened by illness and was sitting upon his bed, he saw a huge lion enter through the doorway and approach him with its mouth open. Terrified at the entrance of the savage beast, he began to shout loudly, saying: “Run, run! This lion is trying to devour me.”

The lion, roaring, rushed upon him, bit him, seized his thigh, and tore away a very large piece of flesh. It then disappeared, leaving him mangled and half dead.

When several people, astonished by the sound of his cries, came running, they saw no lion, but found the mangled and half-dead monk lying on the ground. When they lifted him from the ground and he had recovered his breath somewhat, he disclosed in order everything that had happened to him and earnestly begged his relatives and neighbors to take him back to the monastery as quickly as possible.

His relatives complied with his wish and carried him to the cell of our monastery situated opposite the town of Ascoli. After he had recovered his health there, he returned here to the monastery and, having received penance for the sin he had committed, lived for many subsequent years in the habit of holy conduct.

**Theophilus.** This monk, as I see it, was handed over visibly for a time to the lion—that is, to the devil—so that afterward he might deserve to be freed invisibly and forever from his power.

**Desiderius.** Do you also wish me to tell you how almighty God has always rescued this monastery from the hands of tyrants and, through the merits of blessed Father Benedict, protected it from the attacks of its enemies by the right hand of his divinity?

**Theophilus.** Tell me whatever you wish, for I profess that I listen to all these things with eager spirit, devoted mind, and attentive ears.

**Desiderius.** Pandulph, prince of Capua [Note: That this Pandulph was the fourth prince of Capua, who died in the year 1050, is shown by the exceedingly learned Camillus Peregrinus in *History of the Lombard Princes*. Leo of Ostia recounts his deeds in Book II, chapters 60, 64, and 84; Baronius does so under the year 1038, no. 3.], was a very powerful and wealthy man. By robbery, by shedding human blood, and by cruelly taking cities, towns [Col. 0975C] and the estates of the surrounding inhabitants, he subjected them to his dominion. For a long time, without any compassion and insatiably, he practiced the violation of women, murders, robberies, and the seizure and sale of the goods of churches.

After plundering and carrying away enormous wealth from the churches of Christ, he sacrilegiously seized all the castles, villages, and estates of this monastery, driven by greed, so that he left the monks not even one peasant to cultivate the fields, nor any fields for a peasant to cultivate. Moreover, he carried away the entire treasury of this monastery and stored it in a fortress that he had built not far from the city of Capua, on the mountain called Saint Agatha the Martyr [Note: The mountain of Saint Agatha is now called San Nicola. See Saint Capuanus Michael the monk in the notes to Saint Offa.]. There he had gathered and deposited many spoils belonging to orphans, widows, churches [Col. 0975D], and the poor.

When almighty God wished to put an end to such great crimes, and when the tears and cries of orphans, widows, and the poor, as well as the prayers and supplications of God’s servants, had been admitted into the sight of his Divinity, he inspired the mind of Emperor Conrad—just as it is written, “The heart of the king is in the hand of God” (Proverbs 21:1)—to return to Italy and come to Rome in order to avenge the wrongs done to His churches and rescue them from the hands of tyrants (in the year 1038).

When he had entered Italy with a large army and reached Rome, he decided to send some of his best men from his own retinue to Capua, to command Prince Pandulph through them to restore, without any further delay, the goods of Saint Benedict that he had unjustly taken, to release the noblemen and men of every condition whom he held captive in prison, bound with heavy iron chains, and to return their possessions to them without delay.

He had no intention of coming to these regions himself if Pandulph could carry out what he ordered through the men he had sent. But almighty God, who hardened Pharaoh’s heart because of the many evils he had inflicted without cause upon God’s people, so that he would not believe Moses, his servant, who was displaying signs and wonders with marvelous power (Exodus 10:1), also hardened this man’s heart, so that he would not obey the imperial command.

When those whom the emperor had sent arrived at Capua, they held many fruitless discussions with Pandulph and returned to the emperor without accomplishing anything. But when the emperor saw that he had been despised by the prince, he was moved to anger, left Rome with his army, came to Cassino, and ascended to the threshold of blessed Father Benedict.

When the hour for the brothers’ chapter had arrived, he entered the chapter house and, after the brothers had assembled together, asked them to pray to the Lord for him. There, before them, he testified that he had come to these regions for no other reason than to rescue the monastery of blessed Benedict from the hand of the most savage tyrant.

Afterward, having asked for their blessing, he left that place and came to Capua. The retainers of the aforementioned prince, who were holding the monastery’s goods for their own use in accordance with his commands, learned with certainty of the Augustus’s arrival and fled in all directions. Thus it happened that the monastery recovered in a single day all the castles, villages, and estates that had been taken from it, and that the goods which the ministers of wickedness had gathered there for another’s use came into the power of the monks.

It therefore seems to me that what blessed Father Benedict once foretold to his disciples when they were grieving over a shortage of bread came to pass for them: “Today they would have less, but tomorrow they would have abundantly.”

The aforementioned Augustus then entered Capua and removed Pandulph from the honor of the principate, appointing another in his place. Pandulph himself fled from that city and withdrew into the fortress that he had fortified with the greatest care on the summit of Mount Saint Agatha the Martyr.

By divine providence it came about that everything he had acquired over many years through robbery, perjury, and the shedding of the innocent blood of many people, he lost within the space of a single week. Of all the many and great towns he had acquired, nothing remained to him except the fortress we have mentioned. And the children of those whom he had forced to beg by taking away their possessions have continued to this day to go here and there begging.

Who could doubt that all this happened to him through the merits of blessed Benedict, whose goods he had squandered, driven by wicked greed?

**Theophilus.** There can be no doubt about this matter, since the aforementioned emperor testified before the brothers that he had crossed over to Rome for no other reason than the defense of the monastery of Saint Benedict.

**Desiderius.** At another time (in the year 1049), a certain Capuan named Pandulph, having gathered horsemen from among his friends and neighbors everywhere and assembled a considerable number of soldiers, attempted, at the devil’s instigation, to attack and capture a castle belonging to this monastery called Conca.

He departed from the city of Capua with his followers as the day was already declining toward evening. He set out so that, traveling throughout the night, he might attack and capture the aforementioned castle before daybreak, while everyone there was still sleeping securely. After they had left the city and advanced some distance, they reached the place from which they had decided to travel—not by day but by night, so that no one would see them. While they lingered there briefly, the desired night arrived.

Like children of darkness, loving darkness more than light, and paying no attention to what the Lord says in the Gospel, “The one who walks at night stumbles” (John 11), they began to travel across the fields of a certain estate and hasten as quickly as possible toward the attack on the aforementioned castle. They bloodied their horses’ flanks with the spurs and, thinking they were traveling along a straight route, rode throughout the entire night around the aforesaid fields [Note: Leo of Ostia affirms in *Chronicle*, Book II, chapter 81, that the things related by Desiderius were also reported to him by one of those who took part in that great mounted expedition. Peter the Deacon also relates them in his manuscript sermon *On the Octave of Saint Benedict*. All this occurred in the year of the Lord 1049.].

But by the marvelous arrangement of God’s work, when morning came they found themselves in the very place where night had overtaken them. Thus, frustrated in their desires, confused, and marvelously exhausted, they returned empty-handed to their own homes.

At another time [Note: Around the year of the Lord 1038. Read Leo of Ostia, *Chronicle*, Book II, chapter 65, and Peter the Deacon’s manuscript sermon *On the Octave of Saint Benedict*.], when the fishermen of this monastery had cast their nets into the sea to catch fish for the brothers’ meal, a certain Norman, puffed up in mind and swollen with pride, came upon them in a furious mood. As such men are greedy for plunder and insatiably eager to seize the property of others, he seized one of the fishermen, stripped off the garment he was wearing, and immediately put it on himself.

Then he entered the little boat and began forcing the fisherman to draw up the nets from the depths so that he might take away and carry off with him whatever fish were found in them. When the fisherman refused and said that he wished to catch fish for the monks’ meal, not for the Normans’, the Norman beat him severely and threw him into the sea [Col. 0977D].

When that same Norman, eager for the spoil of the fish, began to pull the nets up from the depths by himself and gather the fish, he suddenly fell from the boat and, trapped beneath the water, breathed out his life. But—marvelous to say—the wave cast his dead body onto the shore before the fisherman whom he had thrown into the water could reach it by swimming alive.

At another time [Note: Leo of Ostia mentions this in *Chronicle*, Book III, chapter 62, and Peter the Deacon in his manuscript sermon *On the Octave of Saint Benedict*.], thieves entered the storeroom of this monastery by night and, stealing meat, cheese, and bacon, filled their sacks with them. But when they went outside and tried to lift the sacks they had filled, they were utterly unable to do so.

Then, abandoning their burden and attempting to flee, they wandered throughout the whole night here and there within the monastery’s enclosure, wholly unable to get out. When morning came and they saw themselves still inside the monastery’s enclosure, terrified and conscious of their guilt, they did not know what to do.

At last, after reaching a decision among themselves, they went out through the monastery gate and, as though they had committed no wrong, mingled with the others who were leaving the monastery for various tasks, hoping in this way to escape. They proceeded slowly, so that no suspicion might arise, and stopped not far from the monastery.

Meanwhile, the cellarer entered the storeroom to provide the brothers with their customary provisions and found the filled sacks lying before the entrance. Astonished and unaware of what had happened, he asked what had been stored there. When he saw that the stolen goods had been put back, he was disturbed by the loss, went outside, and found everything that had been stolen in the very sacks.

Greatly astonished, and now understanding what had happened, he immediately summoned two or three boys and sent them along the road descending the mountain, in case they might find the thieves who had done this. Carrying out his orders, they left the monastery and, after advancing a short distance, found the thieves standing beside the road on the mountainside.

They had almost passed them and, since the thieves were known to them, had no suspicion of them. They quickly continued along the road they had begun. But the thieves, terrified by divine power and made almost insane, began to shout after them:

“We know, sirs, that you have come to apprehend us. But have mercy on us! We carried nothing away; we left everything that had been stolen at the very entrance of the storeroom.”

Hearing this, the boys seized them, bound their hands behind their backs, led them to the monastery, and presented them to the brothers still tied with their bonds.

There were some who, insufficiently cautious with regard to the Lord’s commandment, judged that the thieves should be beaten and then released. But the others, whose minds were devout in the Lord and who were more earnestly concerned to fulfill the divine commands, released them from their bonds, refreshed them with food and drink, and permitted them to depart as free men.

O marvelous kindness of the Lord Jesus Christ, marvelous compassion, marvelous patience that he taught! Although it is written in the Law (Leviticus 19; Matthew 5), “You shall love your friend and hate your enemy,” and although the command was given that hand should be repaid for hand, tooth for tooth, eye for eye, and retaliation for retaliation, he himself wished to command that we love our enemies, do good to those who hate us, greet those who do not greet us, give our cloak to the one who takes our tunic, and return good for evil to those who persecute us!

**Theophilus.** I confess that what you relate is exceedingly pleasing to me.

**Desiderius.** What I am about to relate is marvelous and exceedingly astonishing [Note: It is related by Leo of Ostia in *Chronicle*, Book II, chapter 60, and by Baronius under the year 1038, no. 11], but it is so well known to many that no one ought in any way to doubt it.

At a certain time Sergius, master of the soldiers who governed the city of Naples, went hunting in the forest on Holy Saturday, accompanied by his retainers, in order to catch a boar. They stretched out nets to pursue it and, with the dogs, spread themselves together throughout the forest, here and there. Before the boar, fleeing from the snare of the net, could become entangled, however, it was overtaken by the hunters, pierced, and captured.

Since the hour was already late and the sun, declining toward sunset, was casting an almost black shadow over the earth, the aforementioned master of the soldiers, fearing that darkness would overtake him, took the game he had captured and began returning home as quickly as possible with all his retinue. He ordered only one boy, named Pythagoras, to gather up the nets and follow him swiftly.

When the boy who had been left behind had gathered the nets and was following his master along the direct road, two monks of exceedingly venerable appearance suddenly came to him on the way. Terrified by fear, he asked who they were. They said to him: “Do not be afraid; only follow us.”

As they walked together for some distance through the same forest, they came to a place that was extremely muddy and dreadful to behold. There they showed him, miserably, Pandulph, prince of Capua, whom I mentioned above and who had died not long before, bound with iron chains and submerged up to his throat in the mud of that pool [Note: Pythagoras’s vision of Pandulph’s damnation should apparently be understood of the fourth prince of Capua of that name, who died in 1050. Camillus Peregrinus proves this in his *History of the Lombard Princes*, in the succession of the abbots of Cassino under Richerius. He also points out that another vision, given to a certain solitary concerning the damnation of another Pandulph, is related by Peter Damian in his letter to Dominic, chapter 13; by Leo of Ostia, Book II, chapter 84; and by Baronius under the year 1038, nos. 12–13. That other vision concerns Pandulph surnamed Caputferreus, prince of Capua, who lived until 981, not the fourth prince of Capua, who died in 1050. He also clearly demonstrates that this account does not conflict with the other histories.].

Meanwhile, two very black spirits, making whips from twisted wild vines, bound him by the throat, plunged him into the depths of the pool, and then drew him upward again. When they had done this repeatedly, the boy Pythagoras addressed him, although with trembling voice, asking him to tell him why he was suffering such things.

Weeping and wailing, he immediately gave the boy this answer:

“Although, O boy, countless and infinite punishments have been prepared for me because of my innumerable crimes, I nevertheless suffer the punishment you see for no other reason than the golden chalice that, driven by sacrilegious greed, I stole from the monastery of Saint Benedict and failed to return even when I was dying.

“But I earnestly beg you, and adjure you by Jesus Christ, the Lord and Savior of all—whose commands I, wretched man, despised and for that reason was plunged into this chasm of death—to go yourself to Capua, or send a messenger to my wife, who will tell her both of the torments I am suffering and that she must return the chalice to the monastery of Saint Benedict.”

But Pythagoras said: “What good will it do if I tell her? She will not believe either that I saw you or that you are suffering such things.”

Pandulph replied: “Give her this sign from me: that Pandulph, son of Guala, is holding the chalice itself as a pledge, and that, once the solidi that we owed him have been paid to him, she should recover it and return it without delay to the monastery of Saint Benedict. I beg you not to delay in making this known to her.”
