After he had said these things, the vision vanished from the boy’s eyes.

As soon as the boy returned home, he was seized by illness and died within a few days. He disclosed to everyone who came to him what he had seen and what had been said to him.

Pandulph himself, who held the chalice as a pledge, happened at that very time to be traveling to Naples for some reason unknown to me. He reported that he had heard all these things from Pythagoras’s own mouth. Through him, Pythagoras also sent word to Pandulph’s wife at Capua of everything he had seen concerning her husband and of everything her husband had commanded him.

But she, looking to her own interests rather than those of her husband, was unwilling to repay the sum that her husband had lent. She therefore took no steps either to recover the chalice or to return it to the monastery.

**Theophilus.** It is exceedingly astonishing and must be considered with great care why almighty God wished to show such things to this boy, since the man shown to him was not freed from his punishment—or why, when so many and such great crimes had been concealed, he appeared to be tormented for the single golden chalice.

**Desiderius.** That this man was seen in punishment and was not freed from it when his wife disregarded the return of the chalice happened through the just, though hidden, judgment of almighty God. Through his pious and benevolent providence, it was made known to human beings so that anyone who hears these things may be afraid and restrain both mind and hands from robbing churches.

Otherwise, a person may fail to repent before death, and after death his parents and relatives may be unwilling to perform the deeds by which he himself might be freed from punishment. Thus it may happen that he possesses eternal punishments because of those relatives, while he, having set aside the fear of God during his life, did not at all fear committing such deeds, and in that other life no longer deserves forgiveness because he neglected to earn it through good and holy works in this one.

That he appeared to be judged for the golden chalice alone, while his other crimes remained unmentioned, plainly shows how powerfully, how terribly, and how miserably he was tortured for his many other and immeasurable crimes, since the theft of a small chalice tormented him so harshly and cruelly. For we related above that he had said to the boy Pythagoras that many immense torments had been prepared for him because of his other offenses.

Nor should we be greatly surprised that the one who saw him amid punishments was immediately seized by illness and died not long afterward, if we consider what happened to Daniel, the man of desires and truthful interpreter of visions. After the vision of spiritual mysteries, he immediately fell ill and, as he himself testifies, languished for many days (Daniel 8).

If so great a man could not bear the things he saw spiritually, but was immediately seized by illness and remained sick for many days, what is surprising if this boy, devoted to worldly concerns and burdened by carnal desires, could not bear a vision of spiritual things, but, seized by illness, was brought to the point of death?

In all these matters, however, divine judgments are to be feared rather than investigated. They are great and inscrutable, as the Psalmist testifies when he says: “Your judgments are a great abyss” (Psalm 35). Paul also testifies, saying: “O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God! How incomprehensible are his judgments and unsearchable his ways! For who has known the mind of the Lord, or who has been his counselor? Or who has first given to him, so that he should be repaid? For from him and through him and in him are all things. To him be glory and dominion forever and ever. Amen” (Romans 11).

# BOOK TWO

In this book are discussed the miracles performed by Saint Benedict and by other monks in the monastery of Cassino through divine power.

[Col. 0981]

Having brought the first book, as best I could and as I had promised, to its conclusion, I shall now, with God’s help, undertake to write the second. In it I shall endeavor to bring together the remaining miracles that have occurred in this monastery, or that have been performed by the monks of this holy community wherever divine clemency has granted such things in our own times, insofar as they come to our memory.

When I was still a layman and was passing through the years of adolescence, I will not silently pass over what I heard from many people in the city of Benevento about John [Note: [Col. 0981D] John, the third abbot of this name and the thirtieth after Blessed Benedict, descended from an illustrious lineage of Beneventan citizens. He received the abbacy in the year of the Lord 997 and held it until the year 1010.], then archdeacon of that same Beneventan Church and later abbot of this holy monastery. Since this John sprang from an illustrious family and, what is more important, while living religiously [Col. 0981C] strove in every way to please the almighty Lord, he was so loved by clergy and people that, after the death of the archbishop of that city, they all unanimously desired the highest priesthood for him.

Another man in the same Church, a deacon named Alix [Note: [Col. 0981D] Alix, the fourth Beneventan archbishop, was raised to the archbishopric by Pope Sylvester II in the year of the Lord 1000, at the request of the emperor Otto III, but was not received by the people, as is recorded in the *Chronicle of the Archbishops of Benevento*. An unworthy thing for a religious man—but the customs of our age have reached such a point that what pagans shun and abominate is regarded by our political men almost as law: they teach that it is permissible for a good and wise man, especially a ruler, to lie; that it is lawful to set traps for others; and that, from desire to rule, one thing may be kept locked in the heart while another is ready upon the tongue [Col. 0982D]—mocking Sextus Pompeius, who, although it would have been easy for him to kill his adversaries after breaking faith and thereby gain power over the whole world, valued faith more highly than empire. They are so shameless that they dare teach that religion and virtue ought to serve empire, and that a ruler may, as circumstances require, cast off faith confirmed even by an oath just as he casts off a buskin. Such are the things in which they glory. Would that those who strive to contrive deceits and ensnare others might be frustrated in their hopes, and that the birds they hunt might elude them and fly away—as happened to Archbishop Alix, who did not obtain his quarry! O how far removed this is from the earliest centuries, when Christians preferred to die rather than lie even once, as Justin Martyr writes, *Apology* 2!], was striving with all his might to attain the episcopal office, and had no regard whatsoever for the means by which he might achieve it. But while the same John remained archdeacon, he despaired of being able to reach the summit of so great an honor.

As he revolved these thoughts daily in his mind, a vain idea would not allow him to rest. One day, when the two had sat down in a secluded place and no one else was with them, they began speaking together about the fragility of this wretched life, the joy of heavenly and everlasting life, [Col. 0982B] the punishment of sinners, and the eternal glory of the just. Accordingly, they agreed to abandon the glory of this world and assume the habit of a holy way of life; and, so that they might be more faithful to their agreement, they confirmed their decision by an oath. Then they fixed a day on which they would seek the threshold of Blessed Benedict at the fortress of Cassino and serve the Lord Jesus Christ under the rule of his teaching.

When the appointed day arrived, on which they were to undertake the journey, Alix—who carried one intention in his heart and another upon his lips—said to the archdeacon John: “Dearest brother, since something of my property still remains, which I wish to arrange according to God’s will, I beg you to go ahead. As soon as you have assumed the habit of holy life, send me word; once I have completed these matters, I will hasten to follow you as quickly as possible.”

The archdeacon came to the monastery of Blessed Father Benedict and, as soon as he had assumed the sacred habit, sent word to his companion as they had agreed. He reported that he had already submitted his neck to the rule of holy discipline and urged him to come quickly, as he had promised. But as soon as Alix heard this, he became elated because he saw that the man who had surpassed him in the Church had withdrawn; and he wholly denied that he could go to him or enter so narrow a path. Thereafter he strove with all his strength to acquire the dignity and summit of the episcopal office.

But the almighty and just God arranged matters otherwise than he had hoped. For when the emperor Otto had left Germany and entered Italy, after arranging Roman affairs as he thought fit, he went to Benevento. Alix became so close to him that the emperor ordered him to be elected bishop, although the Church refused. Later, when the emperor returned to Rome, Alix asked him to have the Roman pontiff consecrate him; after his consecration, the emperor sent him back to Benevento. Then the emperor, struck by fever, died several days later by divine providence.

Alix, returning to Benevento, did not even dare approach the city walls. He was driven away in disgrace, and the citizens chose another bishop for themselves. The almighty God did this as vengeance upon evildoers and praise for the good: the man who, led by desire for honor, had deceitfully sought to expel his brother from the Church was himself expelled from his homeland and ended his life in exile [Col. 0983B] on foreign soil.

Besides these matters, I heard the following from Leo, a man of venerable life who died a few years ago, and from other veteran monks. After the same John had spent several years in the monastery under the rule of holy discipline, he asked his abbot for permission, went to Jerusalem, and lived for six continuous years in God’s service on Mount Sinai. Later, in Greece, he stayed for some time on the mountain called Hagionoros [Note: [Col. 0983C] Peter the Deacon also mentions John’s pilgrimage to Mount Hagionoros, or the Holy Mountain, formerly called Athos, in the Macedonian province of Greece, in his manuscript work *On the Origin of the Just of Cassino*, chapter 35, and Ostiensis in *Chronicle*, book II, chapter 22.]. What happened to him there, however, seems to me by no means to be passed over in silence.

An anchorite living on that same mountain was visited or known by very few people. [Col. 0983C] One day, the brother who served him and brought him food on appointed days brought the venerable man John, mentioned above, to that servant of God. As he himself later used to recount with tears to his disciples, the anchorite received him kindly, as was fitting. After they had spoken at length about the joys of heavenly life, the servant of God said to those who had come:

“Come, brothers, for now it is time to take bodily nourishment, lest you grow weak on your return journey. You ought not to leave us fasting, since you have undertaken so arduous a journey for this purpose.”

Saying this, he prepared the table and set out the meal. [Col. 0984A] When, after prayer, they had finally sat down at table, marvelous to relate, an enormous bear came from the neighboring forest and appeared before the faces of the diners, carrying a honeycomb filled with honey.

[Note: [Col. 0983D] Quite a few saints are reported to have had certain wild animals as companions, either giving them food or receiving it from them. Recall the remarkable life of Elijah and the service of the ravens, which continually brought him bread in the morning and meat in the evening; likewise the animals mentioned in the *Life of Paul the First Hermit*, although innovative heretics commonly hiss at such miracles of the saints. This, as Saint Augustine says in book XXI, chapter 3, of *The City of God*, is their entire argument: they think that what they have not experienced cannot exist. They also seem unaware that God often restored to holy men the dominion over beasts which he had granted to the first parent before sin. See the Venerable Bede in the *Hexameron*, and Philo the Jew, *On Rewards and Punishments*. The great Antony also commanded the beasts not to harm his small harvest, as Athanasius records in [Col. 0984C] chapter 25 of the *Life*. Pachomius, as we read in chapter 10 of his *Life*, crossed a river with the aid of crocodiles, which carried him with complete submission, setting him down wherever he commanded. The ancient Simeon, likewise, as Theodoret reports in the *Philotheus*, chapter 6, ordered two lions to escort guests and bring them back from the road on which they had gone astray. Many other examples occur throughout the histories of the saints.]

When they, greatly terrified, tried to flee, that venerable anchorite restrained them and warned them not to be afraid, saying that it had already been many years since almighty God, in his mercy, had very often sent him through that beast the gift of this honey-sweet nectar. After the meal, they rose from the table, more satisfied in spirit than in body, and, having received his blessing, returned to the monastery.

Not many days later, the most blessed Father Benedict appeared to the same John in a vision. Holding in his hand a pastoral staff, he urged him to return as quickly as possible to Cassino, to his monastery. [Col. 0984B]

The next morning, John disclosed the vision in detail to the abbot of that monastery, a religious man. The abbot, being prudent and discerning, recognized God’s will in the vision and said:

“Brother John, hasten quickly to return to your monastery, lest you appear disobedient to that great Father who appeared to you in a vision. For, as I understand it, almighty God has determined to place you over his flock and has chosen you in his mercy to feed his sheep faithfully.”

John obeyed the vision and the admonition. Leaving the lands beyond the sea, he returned under Christ’s guidance. He was made superior by the most religious man John, who was then in charge of the brothers, and not long afterward—because that abbot was already physically weak and unable to bear the burden of so great an office—he was appointed abbot by that venerable Father, with the counsel and election of all the brothers.

The former abbot, relinquishing the abbacy, withdrew into a neighboring forest, where he lived as a solitary until the end of his life and completed his days in the service of almighty God.

Nor should what I heard about Felix [Note: [Col. 0984D] Peter the Deacon also discusses Blessed Felix in his work *On the Origin of the Just*, chapter 37. For what Desiderius relates belongs to the year 1052, as may be seen in Camilus Peregrinus, *Catalogue of the Abbots of Cassino under Desiderius*.]—a monk of this monastery—be passed over in silence.

On one occasion, for some reason I do not know, I happened to be in the city of Teate. The bishop and clergy of that Church received me kindly and amicably,[Note: [Col. 0984D] The bishop of Teate mentioned here is believed to have been Arnulf, whom the most learned Abbot Dom Ferdinand Ughellus, in volume VI of his manuscript *Italia sacra*, shortly to be published, judges to have held office about the year 1049 and to have had Acto, of the counts of the Marsi, as his successor. [Uncertain bibliographical fragment:] *On the Ancient Affairs of the City of Teate*—a patrician conspicuously accomplished in humane and sacred learning, in a style sufficiently elegant and learned.] and, for the sake of prayer, led me to pray. After praying, I went to the right side of the church, where I saw a small chapel and an altar. When I asked the bishop and clergy in whose honor the altar had been erected, they answered that it had been dedicated in honor of Blessed Felix, confessor of Christ.

When I asked who this Felix had been, they told me that he had been a monk of the Cassinese congregation. Sent by his abbot to those regions to preside excellently over shepherds, he had ended his life there. Since almighty God worked many miracles at his body, his superiors had removed it from the place where it had previously lain and buried it in this church beneath the altar, as you see.

Accordingly, a memorable event recently performed there was being recounted through the generosity of almighty God.

[Col. 0985B] A certain blind man, stumbling with his feet against every obstacle, came before Felix’s altar to beg the merciful Lord. Prostrating his whole body upon the ground, he prayed with groans and sighs that, through the merits of Blessed Felix, the Lord might have mercy upon him. Immediately the darkness of blindness was driven away. He rose so sound and whole that, to everyone’s astonishment, he began to see with his own eyes the light which he had always desired to hear others describe.

**Theophilus.** I should like to know whether this venerable man, who shone so brightly, gave any sign after his death, while he was placed in this life, of the merit of his life.

**Desiderius.** I have not learned that this venerable man gave any indication of his virtues while he lived in this world. Nevertheless, almighty God often acts so that those who strive to serve him with devoted minds, although while living in the flesh they display no sign of their sanctity, may not remain concealed after death as to the merit they possessed. Thus, when their extinguished bodies are seen to shine with miracles, human minds may be kindled more ardently in his service.

**Theophilus.** I admit that I am pleased by what you say. But, I beg you, continue what you have begun, so that, while I hear the things I greatly desire to hear, my weary spirit may be refreshed toward love of the heavenly homeland.

**Desiderius.** A certain Gregory, a monk of the highest religious devotion, was said to have lived in this monastery. As I remember hearing from many of the brothers of this place, while he remained in the present life he strove most diligently to serve almighty God under the rule of monastic discipline.

When he had completed the course of his life and departed from this world, such a fragrance spread from the place where he lay lifeless that the sweetness of that scent suddenly filled the entire monastery, as though one corner of a house had been wonderfully sprinkled with it. While everyone marveled, refreshed by the ineffable sweetness of the fragrance, and no one knew what it was, a messenger suddenly arrived in haste from the infirmary and reported that the monk Gregory had died.

Thus almighty God wished to show how great this man’s merit had been, since, as his soul departed, such a wondrous fragrance filled the entire monastery [Note: [Col. 0985D] This is also reported by Leo of Ostia, book III, chapter 50, and by Peter the Deacon, *On the Origin of the Just*, chapter 44.].

Another man, named Angelus [Note: [Col. 0985D] Angelus the monk is mentioned by Peter the Deacon in his manuscript work *On the Origin of the Just*, chapter 39, and in a manuscript sermon on the octave of Saint Benedict, as well as by Leo of Ostia [Col. 0986D], book III, chapter 42.], was said to have been a monk in this monastery. Indeed, his life was not unlike his name. When, struck by bodily illness, he had closed his final day, a demoniac happened to enter the kitchen. Suddenly the man began to make a din; leaping furiously from the ground, he rose into the air and cried out loudly, complaining that he was suffering at Benedict’s hands:

“See what Benedict has just done to me! He has taken the soul of the monk Angelus away from me and carried it off with him because of the little hood he wore on his head.”

While all who were present listened in astonishment to his words and did not understand what he meant, suddenly the signal by which the death of a brother is customarily announced sounded. At once all the brothers hurried to the infirmary and found the monk Angelus already dead. From this it was plainly shown that the ancient enemy had been unable to harm his soul in any way, since before the brothers he had displayed himself as so sad and mournful at Angelus’s death.

**Theophilus.** Please tell me why the devil is so hostile to the human race that, from the beginning of a person’s birth until the end of life, he works by every means to turn human beings away from the commands of their Creator and to lay whatever snares he can for those journeying toward the eternal homeland.

**Desiderius.** The reason is evident. The ancient enemy, who strives to make himself equal to his Creator, suffered a great fall and was plunged into the abyss of the deep pit. Therefore he is hostile to the human race in every way, because he sees humanity ascending to the place from which he himself, cast down through pride, fell irrecoverably. Hence, at the passage of God’s elect, he is seen to make a terrifying din, rage, and gnash his teeth.

A certain Azzo [Note: [Col. 0986D] Azzo flourished in the year of the Lord 1022. See Leo of Ostia, book II, chapter 34, and Peter the Deacon, manuscript work *On the Origin of the Just of Cassino*, chapter 40.] was also a monk of sufficiently religious life. He restored with every effort the church of Blessed Michael the Archangel in the valley called Regis, which the most Christian emperor Louis had built with magnificent workmanship but which was later destroyed by the Saracens. There he gathered brothers for the service of almighty God, as far as he could.

After he had completed several years there in God’s service, already well advanced in age, he returned to our monastery, from which his abbot had sent him. Worn out by old age and illness, he lay in a bed in the infirmary, drawing his final breath as one about to die. Many of the brothers kept watch around his bed, occupied with hymns and psalms, [Col. 0987A] awaiting his departure.

A certain brother [Note: [Col. 0987D] His name was Peter, as Ostiensis reports, book II, chapter 34.], who still survives and lives with us in the monastery, was then a young man but is now advanced in age and character. He was resting in the dormitory with the other brothers when, suddenly, in the middle of the night, he looked up and saw in a vision Blessed Michael the Archangel coming through the dormitory. He had recognized the archangel’s face from an image. Another angel followed in his footsteps, walking somewhat farther behind.

Seeing him, the brother said: “Lord, are you not Blessed Michael the Archangel?”

He replied: “I certainly am.”

The brother asked: “Where are you going, lord?”

“To the infirmary,” he answered, “to take Brother Azzo with me, for the time has come.”

After these words, the vision disappeared. The brother immediately awoke, rose, and hurried to the infirmary. He found that Brother Azzo had already breathed out his soul from his body. From this it is plainly understood that Blessed Michael had carried him away with him, since he testified that he had come to take him.

A certain brother in our monastery, Stephen the Venetian [Note: [Col. 0987D] This miracle is also recounted by Peter the Deacon, manuscript work *On the Origin of the Just of Cassino*, chapter 42, and by Leo of Ostia in *Chronicle*, book III, chapter 42. Stephen the Venetian lived around the year 1080.], was so called. Coming from the regions of Venice, he lived most diligently in the habit of holy religious life. The excellence of his humility, patience, and obedience was perfectly evident to all who were then gathered there in the service of almighty God.

When the time had come for his worthy way of life to be rewarded by the most just Lord, he was afflicted by illness and, with the brothers standing before him, closed his final day.

At that time a very religious old woman named Agundia, a virgin in mind and body, lived in the habit of a nun near the church of Blessed Mary Ever-Virgin, situated in the city built around the foot of Mount Cassino. As was her custom, before the clergy of that city had risen to offer the nightly praises to God, she stood before the church of the Mother of God and prayed to almighty God with groans, tears, and sighs.

Suddenly, in the middle of the night, she looked up and saw a pillar of fire coming out of the cell in which the infirm brothers were accustomed to rest and rising toward heaven. She immediately ordered a messenger to enter the monastery and carefully inquire whether any of the infirm brothers living in that cell had departed from this world.

The messenger who had been sent quickly climbed the mountain, entered the monastery, and went to the infirmary. There he found Stephen, the religious monk, dead. Inquiring more carefully, he discovered that Stephen had given up his soul at the very hour when the pillar of fire had been seen by the servant of God rising into the heights of heaven.

Another man in our aforesaid monastery, named John the Venetian [Note: [Col. 0987D] John the Venetian is mentioned by Peter the Deacon, *On the Origin of the Just*, chapter 41 [Col. 0988D], and by Leo of Ostia, book III, chapter 42.], was a monk of remarkable patience, obedience, and humility. How great was his merit before the Lord Jesus Christ became exceedingly clear after his death.

A certain brother, whose name has slipped from my memory [Note: [Col. 0988D] He is called Ramicus by Peter and by Leo of Ostia.], happened to suffer a rupture in the groin, so that, when the membrane was torn, his internal organs slipped between the flesh and the skin. He went to John’s tomb and, prostrating himself upon it, asked from the depths of his heart, with tears and groans, that John pray to the Lord for him. He undoubtedly believed that he could recover health through the merits of a man who, while in this life, had striven with all his strength to serve almighty God.

After he had lain for some time praying upon the tomb, he was restored to health so completely that not even the slightest sign of his former illness seemed to remain in him. [Col. 0988B]

The monk Smaragdus, who still survives and lives in our monastery, related to me the account I am now giving. He said that he had heard it from Leo, a venerable priest—his own uncle—concerning the monk and priest Antony.

Antony was by no means poorly educated in secular and divine literature. From adolescence until the end of his life he lived in the monastery mentioned above and was known to nearly everyone in this province. One day, when an accident occurred, he suffered a rupture in a more private part of the body, as the aforesaid priest had heard from his own lips. As the illness increased, he was worn down by severe pain every day and began considering whether he should bring in a physician to cut or cauterize him, if by some means he might recover his health.

Yet he feared that, if the physician operated, he might die, as often happens; and, if he did not undergo the operation, he thought that he would have to endure continual pain, which is worse and more dangerous than death itself. As he turned these matters over within himself for a long time, he believed that one remedy remained: he should go to the tomb of Blessed Benedict and implore his mercy, hoping to be saved through the patronage of the man under whose guidance he had devotedly placed himself after withdrawing from the world.

He immediately entered the church, humbly prostrated himself before the altar, and prayed for a long time, asking that almighty God might grant him health through the merits of so great a Father. When his prayer was completed, he rose from the floor on which he had lain prostrate, gathered dust from the ledge of the altar, tied it in a cloth, and placed it upon the spot where he suffered. The next day he was found so completely healed that no sign whatsoever of his former illness remained in him. [Col. 0988D]

Concerning Paul [Note: [Col. 0988D] The same things are related about the monk Paul by Ostiensis, book II, chapter 55, and by Peter the Deacon, manuscript work *On the Origin of the Just*, chapter 43. He flourished in the year 1035. See Sanctus Capuanus, Michael the monk, *On Saint John the Primicerius and Paul the Provost*.], a monk of holy religious life, I remember hearing the following from brothers who are still alive in the present world and knew him very well; I will take care to relate it.

When Paul came to our monastery for the sake of his salvation (in the year 1022), he was devoutly received by Abbot Theobald, a religious man who was then presiding over the brothers with great honor. The venerable Father ordered Paul to live in the monastery of Blessed Father Benedict, which had been built within the city of Capua. When Paul arrived there, he bound himself so strictly under the rule of holy discipline that, for this reason, he was considered admirable by everyone.

But the omnipotent, merciful, and gracious God deigned to show after his death how pleasing his worthy way of life had been to him in this world. After Paul had spent several years in that monastery practicing a religious, honorable, and God-pleasing life, he was struck by bodily illness and, at the Lord’s command, sprang out from the prison of flesh. [Col. 0989B]

A certain bishop of venerable life, coming from the regions of Gaul, was traveling for the sake of prayer to the church of Blessed Michael the Archangel built on Mount Gargano. When he reached the city of Capua, he lodged beside the church of the protomartyr Stephen [Note: [Col. 0989D] In the *Chronicle of Cassino*, book II, chapter 55, and in Peter the Deacon, chapter 43, it is called the church of Saint Lawrence, not of Stephen.].

Finally, when he rose from his bed in the middle of the night, he stood before the aforesaid martyr’s church and offered his prayers and tears to the nearby ears of almighty God. Suddenly, when he turned his eyes toward the eastern quarter, he saw a splendid light, like the rays of the sun, flying wondrously through the air from the monastery. As he gazed for a long time in astonishment at the light he saw, the signal sounded in the monastery by which the departure of a brother was announced.

He immediately understood that someone among the brothers, a man of great merit, had departed from this world and, together with the light itself, penetrated the heights of heaven. He summoned the clergy, related what he had seen, and immediately sent a messenger to the monastery to discover who had died there. When the messenger entered the monastery, he found that the venerable monk Paul had breathed out his soul from his body. [Col. 0989C]

The very religious monk and priest John [Note: [Col. 0989D–0990D] Peter the Deacon also treats this miracle in his manuscript book *On the Origin of the Just*, chapter 36.], whom I mentioned earlier, had abandoned the governance of the monastery and withdrawn into the solitude of the desert. He remained a solitary in the neighboring forest until the end of his life, devoting himself there to fasts, vigils, and prayers and striving with attentive mind to serve almighty God.

When he departed from this light during the time of Abbot Theobald (in the year 1022), a monk named John was living most diligently in God’s service in the monastery of Blessed Lawrence the Martyr near Capua. One night, before the brothers rose for the vigils, he rose from his bed as usual to pray to almighty God. While he stood praying to the merciful Lord with attentive mind, he suddenly looked up and saw a brilliant light in the air; within it he saw the soul of the venerable John penetrating heaven. [Col. 0990A]

At dawn, wishing to learn more certainly what he had seen, he went to Andrew, who was then superior of the monastery’s cell situated within the same city of Capua. He related in detail what he had seen and earnestly begged Andrew to send a messenger to this monastery to investigate the matter carefully.

Andrew, eager to comply with his request, immediately sent a messenger who was to learn diligently what had been reported and return quickly to announce it. As the messenger hurried along, another man coming from the monastery met him on the road. He announced to the brothers living in the aforesaid cell at Capua the death of the servant of God.

Upon careful questioning, the first messenger learned that the servant of God had been taken from this light at the very hour when John, the religious monk living at Capua, had seen him miraculously penetrate heaven. The two men then returned to those who had sent them: one reported the servant of God’s death, and the other reported the vision that had been seen concerning him. [Col. 0990B]

From the testimony of many brothers [Note: [Col. 0990D] This miracle is also mentioned by Peter Damian in a sermon preached on the vigil of Saint Benedict, and by Leo of Ostia in *Chronicle*, book II, chapter 65.], I learned the following, which I took care to record in this little work of ours. Although Peter, the venerable bishop of Ostia, inserted it elegantly and appropriately into the sermon he composed with great brilliance to be read at the vigils of Blessed Father Benedict, I nevertheless decided to include it among the other miracles which almighty God has deigned to display in our time—or in the memory of our elders whom we ourselves saw and learned about from their reports—in our monastery. Perhaps that sermon has not come into everyone’s hands, and someone may learn of this event in our little book and praise God for his wonders, since at all times he nourishes the tender minds of his people with fresh food.

For a certain period, from the beginning of May until the end of July, the air was so dry that the parched earth, cracked by frequent fissures, did not seem capable of being moistened even by the smallest drops. One day a peasant, wishing to burn the straw of the wheat harvest in his field so that he could cultivate the ground more freely, carelessly placed a fire he had brought beneath it. As the fire gradually licked the straw and raised its flame high, a gust of wind drove it into the neighboring forest beneath the monastery, despite the peasant’s resistance.

The forest supplied the fire with an infinite amount of fuel. The flames ran here and there along the sides of the mountain and threatened, while people watched from every direction, to burn down the entire monastery. The brothers, terrified and disturbed by the crackling flames, sprang from their beds with awakened minds—for the event occurred while they were resting at midday. Seeing such an immense and sudden danger and utterly unable to devise any way of resisting it, [Col. 0991A] they immediately turned to divine protection.

With all their strength and from the depths of their hearts, they began to implore almighty God that, through the merits of Blessed Father Benedict, he might rescue the monastery from the fire by whatever means he wished, since they had completely despaired of defending it by human effort. Some prayed with their hands raised toward heaven, others with their bodies prostrate upon the ground, others on bended knees, and others with their heads bowed to the earth.

Suddenly, a small cloud gathered along this side of the mountain and, by divine command, spread itself above its summit. It immediately poured out such a heavy rain that it extinguished the entire fire and completely saved the monastery.

Let us therefore, brothers, strive to live religiously and piously and, by serving God, acquire such a patron’s favor. For just as, through his merits, a cloud covered the summit of this mountain and, pouring out abundant rain, extinguished the fire, so likewise, if we earnestly and devoutly entreat him, with good works going before us, we shall, by the mercy of God, be freed from the flame of burning vices. [Col. 0991B]

On another occasion [Note: [Col. 0991] This miracle is also recounted by Peter the Deacon in his manuscript sermon on the octave of Saint Benedict.], as I learned from those who knew the matter very well, the brothers of this monastery were building a church of Blessed Scholastica the virgin within the city of Gaeta, so that when they went there to purchase various necessities they might have a place of shelter. One of the laborers was breaking stones at the top of a cliff overlooking the sea at the head of the city, stones intended for building the church walls.

As he struck the stones more intently with his hammer, the hammer slipped from its handle, fell down the enormous precipice that opened there, and dropped into the sea. Greatly saddened by the loss, the laborer immediately went to the brothers who were building the church walls and sorrowfully reported what had happened.

When all hope of recovering it had disappeared and they had decided that another hammer should be made with which to break stones for the church’s construction, one of the brothers said:

“Let us go down there, brothers. Perhaps Blessed Benedict will restore the hammer to us through his merits. Once he miraculously drew a tool out of the depths of a lake for a Goth, restored it to him, and sent him back rejoicing to the work he had begun.” [Col. 0991D]

The proposal pleased the others. They went down to the sea and boarded a small boat. Rounding the bay of the city, they came to the place beneath the aforesaid precipice where the hammer had fallen from the laborer’s hands. The water there was so deep that no hope of recovering it by any human device remained.

Trusting in the help of almighty God and the merits of Blessed Father Benedict, they cast the handle into the sea. In a marvelous manner, the iron immediately adhered to the handle. They drew it out, gave thanks to God and Blessed Benedict, and returned joyfully to their work.

**Theophilus.** I remember that this miracle was performed in the Old Testament by Elisha and, in the New, by the most holy Father Benedict. But when I consider how far the merits of these men and those men differ, I confess that I conceive an even greater admiration in my mind for this miracle recently performed.

**Desiderius.** We ought not, dearest brother, to attribute this deed so much to these men as to the one whose merits they trusted in when they attempted it. But would you like me to tell you something about those possessed by demons who, through the generosity of divine mercy and with the merits of Blessed Benedict assisting them, were healed in this monastery of his? In this way the minds of those listening may grow stronger and stronger in the praises of God and be kindled in many ways toward love of the supreme Divinity.

[Col. 0992B]

**Theophilus.** Continue with whatever you wish to say for the edification of your listeners. I declare that I gladly listen to these things.

Desiderius. A certain boy, sleeping in the guesthouse on a little bed together with his father, rose in the deep silence of night to relieve himself. Suddenly an enormous lion appeared before him, roaring through its teeth and ready to tear him apart with its claws. Terrified beyond measure, he cried out and collapsed to the ground. At the sound of his voice, his father immediately rose in alarm from the bed and hurried anxiously to him, asking with the utmost concern why he had cried out and what had happened. Trembling and trembling with fear, the boy reported that he had seen a huge lion coming toward him. His father soothed him with kind words, took him in his arms, and carried him back to the bed.

But the devil, who had appeared to him in the form of a lion, entered him and, after several days, began to torment him most violently. When he was brought to the church before the altar of the Most Blessed Benedict, he lay prostrate on the pavement with his eyes closed. In a marvelous manner, whoever entered through the monastery gate he immediately identified by name, saying: “Such-and-such a man is now entering the monastery through the gate.”

A certain brother, having gone down from the monastery to the city on a matter of obedience, received twelve denarii from someone and, secretly taking them for his own benefit, put them into his bosom. When he had returned to the monastery and approached the boy at the place where he was being tormented, the devil immediately began, through the boy’s mouth, to denounce him before the brethren, saying: “This monk, contrary to the rule of his order, received twelve denarii from such-and-such a man for his own advantage and keeps them hidden in his bosom.” When the brethren therefore asked whether the accusations that the ancient enemy was making through the mouth of the afflicted boy were true, the brother immediately cried out, confessing his guilt, and admitted that it was entirely so.

Another brother, whose name I omit so that he might not suffer shame, had been brought to our monastery from another monastery for the sake of his salvation. One night, at the hour of nocturnal vigils, he was reciting in the church a reading from the Old Testament, as was customary while the brethren sat in their places; the afflicted boy happened to be present. Suddenly the devil cried out through the boy’s mouth, declaring that he knew perfectly everything that was being read and that he had been present there. Then, adding the following words to the reader’s words, he reproached him:

“But if I wished to relate before those present what I know about you, I could certainly bring great shame upon you.”

And it was indeed discovered that this brother had lived a thoroughly worldly life in his monastery. After the brethren had prayed for a long time for the afflicted boy before the tomb of the Blessed Father Benedict, he was restored to health, so that he was no longer seen to be tormented by the evil spirit.

At the same time, another little boy saw an enormous Ethiopian standing upon the roof. Greatly terrified, he immediately took flight. But the same demon pursued him to the door of the house, struck him to the ground, and immediately entered him, tormenting the wretched boy severely. After he had often been brought for several days to the oratory at the tomb of the aforesaid Father, the demon who had invaded him departed by the merits of that same Father, and did not thereafter dare to approach him.

Another man, named John, who is now advanced in age and still lives, serving in the house for the sick, was from the province of the Marsi, where he had been born. When he was held by a most evil demon, his relatives brought him to the monastery in the hope of recovering his health. They firmly believed that, through the merits of the Blessed Benedict, he could receive healing, for they had heard that many people afflicted by various illnesses had been restored to their former health at his threshold. After a short time, the enemy was expelled from John, and when he had recovered his health, he brought great joy to those who saw him.

The monk and priest Theodoricus, who still lives and resides with us in this monastery, leading a religious life, had a nephew whom he loved very much while still in the world. The ancient enemy entered this nephew—not, however, so as to torment him openly, but by secretly inflicting an illness and making him appear to observers as though he were paralyzed. The aforesaid uncle therefore had him brought to him for the recovery of his health, trusting in the merits of the Blessed Father Benedict.

But when the boy remained ill for some time in this monastery, suffering as he had suffered before, and no one suspected that he was possessed by a demon, one day his uncle brought him to a venerable man named Lambertus, who lived as a solitary in the nearby forest beside the church of the holy martyrs Cosmas and Damian, so that he might receive his blessing. The man of God gave him blessed bread and ordered him to eat it. When the boy had put what he had received into his mouth and tasted it as he ate, the demon that had until then lain hidden within him, unable to endure the blessing of so great a gift, revealed the cause of the illness by making a great noise, shouting, and leaping here and there.

After the boy had returned to the monastery with his uncle, and it became known openly that he was possessed by a demon, he was led into the oratory, where all the brethren gathered together to pray to the omnipotent Lord for him. When the prayer and psalmody had been completed, at the sixth hour the brethren went to the refectory to refresh their bodies, leaving two or three monks with him. While those who had remained tearfully implored divine mercy for him, asking that, through the intercession of His most blessed confessor Benedict, the Lord might deign to free the captive man, a monk of venerable white hair appeared standing before the altar to the afflicted man. He commanded the ancient enemy, with powerful authority, to depart from him.

Immediately the demon made a great assault and came out of the possessed man with vomiting; thereafter he did not dare to approach him. It was unquestionably established that the old man was the Blessed Maurus, whose relics the brethren who had remained in the church with the possessed man had placed upon his breast with great devotion and hope. After he had been freed from the demon, the man became a monk and continued in this monastery with the other brethren in the service of Jesus Christ our Lord.

A certain peasant lived nearby in a fortress called Saint Angelo. Every year, together with his household, he celebrated as devoutly as he could the feast of the Blessed Nicholas, confessor of Christ. On the day when the faithful celebrated his sacred solemnity, he went with his wife and their son, who was still a boy, to the basilica consecrated in the saint’s name, in order to offer an oblation to the Lord.

After the solemn rites of the Mass had been completed and they had participated in the communion of the sacred body and blood of the Lord, they returned to their home. The boy then asked his father for permission to inspect the fields. His father restrained him, saying:

“It is not fitting, my son, to go into the fields today to work them, because, although unworthy, we have received the divine sacrament, and the feast of our patron, namely the most blessed Nicholas, is being commemorated everywhere by all with great devotion.”

But the boy, yielding to childish frivolity, could not obtain from his father what he had requested. Disregarding his father’s orders, he secretly slipped away from the house and went alone to inspect the countryside.

After he had spent some time in the field and saw the sun inclining toward setting, with shadowy night already almost hanging over the earth, he went to a nearby forest to cut wood and carry it home, so that he would not appear to return empty-handed and might thereby regain the favor of his father, whose words he had despised.

When he had begun to arrange the wood into a bundle, he suddenly sensed what seemed like the sound of a violent wind coming toward him. Raising his head, he saw an exceedingly black bird, shaped like a vulture, flying through the air above him with great force. It placed itself not far away, directly in the path along which the boy would have to return.

As he watched it, terrified and trembling with fear, it transformed itself into the appearance of an exceedingly black boy, whose hair was bristling and standing erect and whose garments seemed to end in a reddish color. Thus it presented itself to him.

While the boy, frightened as he was, contemplated what he saw, the ancient enemy addressed him in this manner:

“Become wholly mine, boy, and come with me to the bank of this nearby river. There I will give you a great abundance of gold and silver, so that you may return home laden not with wood but with gold and silver. As long as you live, you will surpass all your relatives and neighbors in wealth and enjoy upon earth a noble and more luxurious life.”

The ancient enemy made this promise not because he intended to give the boy what he offered, but so that he could drown and kill him in the river. But the boy, repeatedly invoking the name of Christ, tried to arm himself with the sign of the cross, and in a tearful voice gave this reply:

“Far be it from me—far be it from me ever to become the servant of anyone except the omnipotent God, who created me, and my father, who begot me.”

As he repeatedly made the sign of salvation upon himself, the demon who had appeared withdrew from him toward the nearby river’s waters, plunged into them with a great uproar, and there began to hiss like serpents, bray like asses, bellow like bulls, and roar like lions. He filled the poor boy with such terror that the entire forest seemed to whirl around him in a dizzying vortex.

When he was almost lying lifeless on the ground and had no idea at all what to do, suddenly an old man appeared standing beside him. He had a mitred head, was radiant and clothed in a white vestment, and said to him:

“What are you doing here, when the later hour is already advancing and, with everyone departing, the fields have been left almost deserted? Rise as quickly as possible and hurry home, lest, if you remain here any longer, you fall into grave danger.”

The boy rose from the ground and bent down to lift his little bundle. At that moment the old man who had appeared to him disappeared.

Then the evil spirit once again thrust itself before his eyes and began to address the boy in the same words as before. Nevertheless, the boy emphatically refused to do what it urged. Weeping and wailing, he fell to the ground and, as best he could and knew how, implored the mercy of Jesus Christ, the Savior of all, to come to his aid.

Immediately the venerable old man who had appeared to him earlier appeared again and urged him to rise more quickly, take up the wood, and carry it away. At his arrival, the enemy who had appeared to the boy vanished like smoke.

We believe that this old man was the blessed Nicholas, whose feast the aforesaid peasant had devoted himself to celebrating on that day. At the old man’s command, the boy rose from the ground, lifted his bundle, and returned home with the greatest speed. As he later reported, the bundle of wood became so light for him that it seemed to have no weight at all.

After he had returned home and remained there for a short while, the demon who had appeared to him entered him and began to torment him horribly. Both parents were thrown into confusion, grieving and crying out, while the entire household gathered around.

When they saw that they could offer him no help, they found a saving course of action: they brought him to the monastery and to the threshold of the Blessed Benedict. They laid him down at the venerable tomb on the right side of the altar, tearfully begging the Lord for mercy. There, exhausted and violently tormented, the possessed boy fell asleep.

While he lay sleeping in this weariness, he suddenly seemed to see his side opened, and from it a man of exceedingly radiant appearance, clothed in a white garment, emerged. He felt the boy’s abdomen and chest for a long time, then ordered him to rise and depart.

Immediately awakened, the boy rose so completely healed that he no longer felt any demonic disturbance within him. I heard all these events in their sequence from the mouth of the boy himself, who had suffered them and related them tearfully.

Theophilus. I greatly marvel at what you say happened to the boy, and trembling before the judgments of the omnipotent God, I am astonished that He permitted him—who had devoutly celebrated the feast of the Blessed Nicholas together with his father and had received communion of the Lord’s body and blood—to be handed over to an unclean spirit.

Desiderius. If you consider how great a sin it is not to obey one’s parents, since Scripture says: “Honor your father and your mother, so that you may be long-lived upon the earth” (Exodus 20:12). And again: “It is better to obey than to sacrifice, and to listen than to offer the fat of rams, because rebellion is like the sin of divination, and refusal to submit is like the crime of idolatry” (1 Samuel 15:23–24). And Solomon says: “Listen, my son, to your father’s discipline, and do not abandon your mother’s teaching, so that grace may be added to your head and a necklace to your neck” (Proverbs 1:8–9). And elsewhere: “How evil in reputation is the one who abandons his father, and cursed by God is the one who provokes his mother” (Ecclesiasticus 3:18). You will recognize that this happened by the just judgment of God.

God therefore permitted this boy to be scourged for his disobedience. Yet in His customary compassion He did not allow him to remain longer under the same blow, so that everyone might understand from this how much danger disobedience brings and how humbly one ought to submit oneself to obey one’s parents.

Theophilus. The words of your reply appear to have satisfied my question.

Desiderius. In the diocese of the bishopric of Teano there is a noble monastery near the foot of Mount Majella, built in honor of Saint Liberator and subject to this monastery of Cassino.

[Note: Concerning the monastery of Saint Liberator in the diocese of Teano, see Leo of Ostia, *Chronicle*, book I, chapter 44, and the most learned Lucius Camarra, *On the Ancient Affairs of the City of Teano*. What occurred there is also read in a manuscript sermon of Peter the Deacon, *On the Octave of Saint Benedict*.]

A great multitude of brothers dwells there, serving Christ the Lord, the true King, and, according to the command of the nourishing Blessed Benedict, serving as soldiers under him.

At a certain time, while the brethren of that monastery were resting in the silence of night according to custom, a certain venerable man dressed in monastic clothing appeared to one of them and exhorted him to rise quickly from the bed on which he lay. When, awakened by his command, the brother rose swiftly, the man said to him:

“Hurry and awaken all the brethren. Insist with loud cries that they rise quickly and go to the church, because this cell in which they are resting is about to collapse with the utmost suddenness.”

Obeying the command, the brother began to cry out in a loud voice:

“Rise, brothers, rise, and leave this cell as quickly as possible, because it is about to collapse at once. Do not remain in it any longer and thereby, God forbid, be crushed by its ruins.”

When the brethren awoke, disturbed by his cries, they asked how he knew this. He related in order what he had seen and what had been said to him. The brethren immediately left the place quickly, entered the church, and, after the bells had been rung, began to sing the nocturnal office to the Lord according to custom.

While they were performing the customary offices with attentive minds, the aforesaid house suddenly collapsed completely with a great crash. The frightened brethren hurried there, anxiously investigating whether any of their number had been crushed by the ruin. As they moved the fallen material this way and that, they found that one of the brothers, weighed down by old age, had remained unharmed beneath the ruins surrounding him on every side. They brought him out and carefully asked how he had escaped.

He replied:

“When the house, completely collapsing, was falling upon me, suddenly a radiant man dressed in monastic clothing stood beside me. He supported with his arm the ruin that was already falling upon me and threatening to crush me, and he preserved me unharmed, as you yourselves see.”

This man is believed to have been the blessed Benedict. Earlier, with fatherly compassion, he had rescued the flock of the Lord that served under his direction through his warning and protection; and now he defended with the hand of his solicitude an old man who was unable to flee.

A certain brother in the same monastery was also named John.

[Note: This is also related in a manuscript sermon of Peter the Deacon, *On the Octave of Saint Benedict*.]

Pressed down by age and illness, he was drawing his last breath. One day, when some of the brethren had come to him according to custom to sing the morning praises, he restrained them with whatever voice he could muster, saying:

“I do not want you to sing the canonical hours for me any longer, because the lord abbot has just come to me with many brethren dressed in white garments to visit me. While singing the morning office to me, they said that after a short while they would come here and take me with them.”

While the brethren who had come to him attentively watched this vision and anxiously awaited whether what he had reported was true, after the space of one hour that brother gave up his spirit with great exultation.

From this we can understand that it was the Blessed Father Benedict who appeared to him with that company dressed in white and took him with him, as he had promised. I found these events, which I have related, written in a certain old little page in a sufficiently unskilled style, and I have now endeavored to add them to our little book.

Since the omnipotent God sometimes reveals His wonders not only in great things but also in the smallest, so that the faith of believers may increase more and more and every creature may burst forth in praise of its Creator—for He is seen to care with fatherly compassion for all things granted for human use—I will not neglect to relate in part what happened concerning the lamps in our church in our own times, as I learned from Gregory, a venerable monk who still serves as custodian of that church.

[Note: What is related about the lamps is also confirmed by Leo of Ostia, *Chronicle*, book III, chapter 38, and Peter the Deacon in a manuscript sermon, *On the Octave of Saint Benedict*. Related to these miracles is what Venantius Fortunatus expressed in verse, drawn from Sulpicius Severus, *Dialogues* 3.3, concerning Saint Martin:

“Though the flask has fallen upon the marble pavement, it stands upright:

nor do the stones break the glass, nor the vessels lose their liquid.”]

One day, one of the custodians had lit a lamp in the oratory before the altar and, having applied the flame, raised it almost to the ceiling. Suddenly it fell and landed on the pavement before the altar. God is marvelous in His works! It was not only unbroken: neither was the oil spilled, nor was the flame that had been lit in it extinguished.

At another time, when the aforementioned Gregory wished to refill a lamp before the image of the Savior painted above the church doors, he found it hanging in the air by its little hooks, extended in such a way that it was supported by absolutely no material. He immediately summoned the brothers who were standing nearby and showed them what he had witnessed, so that they might be witnesses to so great a miracle.

Moreover, at another time in this same church of the blessed Benedict, on the night preceding the day on which his feast was celebrated, as I learned from those who were present at this miracle, one of the custodians was refilling a lamp before the image of that same blessed Benedict during the vigils. Suddenly it fell and crashed onto the pavement, yet remained unharmed. It was then raised upward three times and fell three times; and, even more marvelously, by the power of God preserving it, it could neither be broken, nor have its oil spilled, nor have the light burning in it extinguished.

Many other miracles of this kind involving lamps have taken place in the oratory of this monastery. Since they are very simple, however, we have judged it unnecessary to write them down. We have written these things so that, because they are small, they might not appear entirely unworthy of consideration.

There is one event that slipped from my memory in the preceding book, which I had promised to relate to you: how the omnipotent God often rescued this monastery from the hands of tyrants. We have thought it appropriate to record it in this second book, lest it slip from memory.

[Col. 0998D] In the time of our predecessor Athenulphus,

[Note: Athenulphus was abbot from the year 1011 and lived until 1022, during which period the events related by Desiderius took place. See Leo of Ostia, *Chronicle*, book II, chapter 71, and Peter the Deacon in his sermon *On the Octave of Saint Benedict*.]

when the estates of this monastery were being fiercely harassed by the count of Aquino, and neither the prayers of the monks nor reverence for the nourishing Father Benedict, who had been the founder and builder of this monastery, could soften his spirit or induce him in any way to desist from injuring this place, the aforesaid abbot was compelled by necessity, after seeing that the man’s ferocious spirit could in no way be appeased, to bring into the possessions of this monastery some Normans who at that time were coming to Italy under contract with our princes, so that through them he might protect those possessions from the aforesaid count.

After they had received in abundance both houses in which to live and provisions by which they might be sustained, they began, like vigorous soldiers, to defend all the property belonging to the monastery nobly and faithfully on every side, driving the enemies far away.

While the aforesaid abbot and the man who had succeeded him in the second rank of governance were still alive, the hired soldiers remained quite honorably in their allegiance. But after those men had been taken from this life and the fortune of our princes had changed and begun to waver somewhat, the Norman cohort that had been admitted for our defense gradually became faithless and hostile to us. Day after day, like a dog and a serpent, it moved toward our destruction, taking away from us now this thing and now that, and, driven by sacrilegious greed, reducing everything to domination under its own authority.

Thus it came about that from so great and extensive a possession nothing remained for our use and benefit except the city situated at the foot of Mount Cassino, together with the estates of four or five villages. Even these were oppressed by them every day—for barbarian greed knows no limit—as they took away our wealth and gave us misery and poverty in return.

After they had continued to do this without any compassion for a considerable period of time, the merciful and gracious Lord resolved in His goodness to assist His servants, who were suffering from hunger and want. The most blessed Father Benedict appeared in a vision to a certain peasant who was staying in the field of one of our little villages and ordered him to go out and follow him.

As that peasant fixed his mind upon the vision, it seemed to him that the most blessed Benedict, with the staff he carried in his hand, was expelling by powerful strength from the boundaries of this land all the Normans who had invaded the monastery’s possessions, driving them empty-handed of their goods and burdened with disgrace from the inheritance of his monastery.

That same year, the aforesaid Norman cohort, growing more insolent in its audacity than usual and seeking our ruin, occupied the fortress called Saint Andrew, so that it might retain more securely what it had taken from us. This event brought their spirit to domination and ours to despair.

After they had gained possession of the fortress, they gathered together one day and entered the aforesaid city of Cassino with great arrogance. There, by God’s will, they were overcome by the city’s inhabitants. Some of them were killed or captured, while the rest fled and withdrew into the fortification of the aforesaid fortress.

The inhabitants of the land then formed a united force, with assistance arriving from all the neighboring areas, and turned their attention to besieging the fortress. I am about to relate a marvel. After the siege had been established, while spears and missiles were hurled fiercely from both sides, the Normans’ own weapons, as though blown back by a gust of wind, wounded those who had thrown them.

What more need be said? When they saw that they were thus being attacked by themselves and could no longer resist, they recognized that it was hard for them to kick against the goad and understood that the divine right hand was fighting against them. They surrendered and handed themselves over to the abbot and the monks. The monks scarcely succeeded in protecting them and sending them back to their comrades who were staying in the town of Aversa.

Thus it came about that from that time onward, through the merits of the blessed Benedict, the land in which we live has remained unharmed by their attacks and continues secure under the protection of that holy man.

The form of this little book compels us to hasten toward its end. But the goodness of obedience, which is first among the other virtues, does not permit us entirely to pass over in silence the virtue of a certain brother who pursued it with complete humility of heart even unto death, imitating Him who became obedient to the Father unto death (Philippians 2) and left us alike an example of obedience and patience.

This brother of our congregation, named Raynerius,

[Note: Peter the Deacon also discusses Raynerius, a monk of Cassino killed by robbers, in *On the Origin of the Just Men of Cassino*, chapter 45.]

was young in age but old in character. Many of the brethren who still survive and knew him very well testify that he possessed such humility and obedience that, on this account, he was considered remarkable by everyone.

One day his abbot ordered him to go into the territory of Teano to perform some work for the benefit of the monastery. As always, he was cheerful and ready for obedience; he hastened to fulfill the command and set out on his journey.

As he traveled and had already covered a considerable distance, he was killed by the robbers of a certain powerful man named Oderisius. Acting on that man’s orders, they were watching the road to seize anything they could take from the possessions of this monastery. They stripped him of everything he was carrying and killed him.

His body could not be brought to this monastery, either because of the enemies’ ambushes or because of the distance, but was committed to the ground in a nearby church. Yet God deigned to show how acceptable his obedience had been to Him through what occurred at his lifeless body.

Many people suffering from illness began to hurry to his tomb and, after recovering their health, return home unharmed. Among them was Count Atto, the son of the great Count Atto and also the son-in-law of the aforementioned Oderisius.

[Note: They were alive in the year of the Lord 1053 and were leaders of the Italians against the Normans. See William of Apulia, book II of *The Norman Deeds in Italy and the Kingdom of Naples*.]

When he was severely weakened and tormented by fevers, Atto came to the tomb of Raynerius, led there by his reputation. He prostrated himself in prayer, and when the fever departed, he rose so healthy that he felt none of the ill health from which he had previously suffered. Giving thanks for his recovered health, he offered an excellent pallium upon the tomb in repayment for so great a gift and departed joyfully.

Since we have begun to mention the wonders of God, I do not think I should pass over in silence what happened to me personally, since Scripture says: “It is good to conceal the secret of a king, but it is honorable to manifest and reveal the works of God” (Tobit 12).

When I was still a child and suffering violently from fevers, John of blessed memory, a priest of venerable dignity who at that time was renowned for the service of God in our city of Benevento, came quickly to visit me. After sitting for a short time with the others who had arrived and seeing that I was being severely afflicted by a tertian fever, he was moved by the charity he felt toward me. He rose, covered his face with tears, and, invoking the Lord in a gentle voice, placed his hand upon my head. Immediately the fever that had been tormenting me so fiercely fled and departed.

What I learned from Leo, abbot of the monastery of the holy apostle Paul,

[Note: In response to the arguments of John Bosco, reported in the Floriac manuscript concerning the jurisdiction of the monastery of Saint Paul outside Rome during the time of Abbot Leo and whether it belonged to the Cassinian or Cluniac congregation, Lauretus replied in *On the Existence of the Body of Saint Benedict on Mount Cassino*, chapter 25. The miracle of the aforementioned holy martyrs Protus and Hyacinthus is also related by Leo of Ostia in *Chronicle*, book II, chapter 48, and by Peter the Deacon in the manuscript book *On the Origin of the Just Men*, chapter 46.]

situated two miles from the city of Rome, where his most sacred body is revered and worshiped, shining with signs and miracles, I will take care to write at the end of this little book.

He said that the most reverend Adam, a very holy monk and custodian of this church of our monastery, had told him the following. One day, when that venerable Adam had gone out through the monastery gate to perform some task, two young men dressed in monastic clothing met him at the very entrance of the monastery. After he had carefully greeted them and asked who they were, he heard from them that one was called Protus and the other Hyacinthus.

Astounded, he asked why they had come. They replied:

“We have come to visit the brothers who today commemorate our memory with devout minds.”

It was indeed the day on which, having shed their blood for Christ and with Christ granting it, they had earned the palm of martyrdom.

Adam stood there for a short time in astonishment. When they had entered the monastery and continued on their way, he came to himself and, wishing to learn more certainly what he had heard, pursued them at a rapid pace.

He searched for them carefully throughout the monastery, here and there, but could not find them. He began asking everyone he met where the monks were who had just entered the monastery after speaking with him. They all declared that they had heard of no one entering the monastery except Adam himself.

From this it is plainly understood that those who had appeared to him were truly the holy martyrs Protus and Hyacinthus, whose feast was being celebrated on that day. I learned from Firmus, a veteran monk of this monastery and Adam's own nephew, that all these events had taken place in that order, as Adam himself had told me while I was in Rome.

Let the prayer of this day end here, so that, with this book concluded in honor of such great martyrs, and our spirit refreshed during the course of this night, we may come faithfully to relate the remaining Acts of the saints, assisted by the prayers of those martyrs and of all the saints.

# BOOK THREE

## Which concerns miracles performed elsewhere

[Col. 1001]

[Col. 1001C] Having completed, with the grace of Christ accompanying us, the two little books in which we described the miracles of God performed, by His generosity, either in this monastery or in the cells subject to it, let us now proceed, with the Lord’s permission, to the narrative of the third.

Since the remaining miracles that took place outside the precincts of this monastery—things that we have learned by sight or hearing—still remain to be written in the other two little books, it seems worthwhile to me to begin from the very head of the Church and then, proceeding in sequence with my pen, to come to each of its members.

While, therefore, through the negligence of priests, Italy was gradually straying from the straight path of religion and being undermined, the evil custom grew to such an extent that, with the authority of sacred law disregarded, divine and human things alike were confused. Thus the people sold the right of election; the priests sold the right of consecration; and they sold the gift of the Holy Spirit—which divine authority had ordained should be received and given freely—for money paid and accepted into their hands, driven by avarice. Consequently, scarcely anyone could be found who, undefiled by the contagion of this Simoniac plague, observed the Lord’s commandments with pure hearts before God.

[Note: See Lauretius on the *Ostian Chronicle*, book II, chapter 78; Peter Damian, vol. I, book II, epistle 10; Baronius, year 1057, no. 15 and following, and year 1074, nos. 28, 29, 57; and Genebrard’s *Chronicle* at the year 1074.]

[Note: The plague of the Nicolaitans had gained such strength in those centuries, especially in Germany, that clerics not only openly entered incestuous marriages but also defended them most shamelessly. Almost all were being carried headlong over the precipices of vice, like maddened horses racing uncontrolled across the fields of their pleasures—especially if what Lambert of Hersfeld relates about those times is true. It must nevertheless be observed that not all clerics had sunk so deeply into incontinence as to take wives. Rather, some among them, being especially incontinent, stirred up tumult against the decree of Gregory VII, who followed the footsteps of his predecessors in preserving clerical continence. They said that it was better to marry than to burn, and that while Gregory denied the customary course of nature, he was loosening the reins on fornication and impurity. Under this pretext they took wives. Thus what the prophet Malachi had said in the first chapter truly befell the priests of that age: “You have turned aside from the way, and have scandalized many in the law; you have made void the covenant of Levi. Therefore I have also made you contemptible and low among all the peoples” (Mal. 2). See Opusculum 5 of Blessed Peter Damian, entitled *On the Privilege of the Roman Church*; Baronius, year 1074, nos. 28, 29, 57; and Bellarmine, *On the Clergy*, chapter 19.]

[Col. 1003A] The common body of clergy therefore proceeded along the road of unrestrained license, with no one restraining it. The priests and deacons themselves—who ought to handle the Lord’s sacraments entrusted to them with pure hearts and chaste bodies—began, like laymen, to take wives and to leave the children they had fathered as heirs by testament. Some bishops too, abandoning all shame, lived together in the same house with their wives.

[Note: The bishop of Toul was specifically summoned by Gregory VII to the synod of 1075 to give an account of simony and of cohabitation with a woman whom he kept as his wife. O the disgrace of that age! See Baronius, year 1074, no. 57.]

This most vile and detestable custom flourished especially within [Note: Pope Stephen X, emulating the zeal of Phinehas, ordered all the incontinent clerics in Rome who had persisted after Pope Leo IX’s prohibition—including perhaps some who were married, or, more properly, public concubinarians—to leave the assembly of the clergy and the church choir. Shame and decency had perished; and as ecclesiastical discipline gradually collapsed, the plague of every vice and depravity increased day by day. See Baronius, year 1057, no. 15 and following.] the City, from which the standard of religion had once spread everywhere through the Apostle Peter himself and his successors.

Accordingly, while for several years certain men held the papal chair in name alone, [Note: Benedict IX, also called Theophylact, son of Alberic, count of Tusculum, was a boy of twelve when, through his father’s bribery and tyranny, he was thrust into the Roman see in the year of the Lord 1034. O deed deserving to be mourned with an entire fountain of tears! Whoever wishes to know what sort of man Benedict was thereafter, and how shamefully he lived, together with his unhappy condemnation to hell, should read Baronius at the year 1033 and following; the Deacon in the *Life of Benedict*; and the other writers of the lives of the Roman pontiffs. It was certainly horrifying and detestable to see a boy sitting upon the lofty chair of Peter. For what does the Church not suffer when princes meddle in rights that are not theirs? What does the burning desire for office not attempt?]

a certain Benedict—Benedict in name, but not in conduct—the son of a consul named Alberic, following the footsteps not of Simon Peter but rather of Simon Magus, claimed for himself the highest priesthood, having scattered a considerable amount of money among the people. How shameful, filthy, and detestable his life became after he had obtained the priesthood, I shudder to relate. I shall begin instead by narrating how almighty God deigned to look upon the face of the Church.

After he had for some time committed robberies, murders, and other abominations against the Roman people without interruption, the people assembled because they could no longer endure his wickedness. They drove him from the papal chair and expelled him from the City. In his place they installed another—namely John, bishop of Sabina—[Note: John, bishop of Sabina, who was called the antipope Sylvester III. Baronius, year 1044, no. 2.] disregarding the canonical decrees, though not without payment.

John occupied the Roman chair for no more than three months. Benedict, however, attacked the City on every side with his relatives. Since he was descended from the consuls of the land, and since they possessed great power, John was driven from the City in disgrace and returned to his bishopric.

Benedict therefore recovered the priesthood he had lost, but did not in the least change his former ways, according to what is written: “A young man according to his way, even when he grows old he will not depart from it” (Prov. 22). And because it is difficult for an old heart to conceive new things, he persisted, as before, in the same wicked and perverse deeds.

When he saw that, because of his crimes, he was despised by both clergy and people, and perceived that the reputation of all his misdeeds filled everyone’s ears, he finally found a solution. [Note: Benedict yielded the see at the urging of Saint Bartholomew, abbot of Grottaferrata, a disciple of Saint Nilus.]

For, being devoted to pleasure and preferring to live like Epicurus rather than like a pontiff, he relinquished the highest priesthood to an archpriest named John, who at that time appeared more religious than the other clerics in the City, receiving from him a considerable sum of money. [Note: Others call this John Gratian; he later became Gregory VI. Although Desiderius is found to have reproached him for simony, it must nevertheless be understood that Desiderius reported these things about Gregory because he was regarded in this way by almost all the uneducated, and especially by his rivals. The cause, arising from Gregory’s zeal and charity, was not yet well known to Desiderius; and for that reason Gregory suffered calumny, bearing the name not of a legitimate pontiff but of a usurper, although in truth he should rather be called the liberator of God’s Church than infected with the stain of simony, as Otto of Freising faithfully relates.
