Although he was deposed as a simoniac by the council of Sutri, in the presence of the emperor Henry II, nevertheless the most serious and learned men of that age—and inveterate enemies of the simoniacs—including Peter Damian, who even addressed letters to Gregory VI, and Hildebrand, who later deliberately wished to be called Pope Gregory VII in order to show that Gregory VI had been the true pontiff and had been wrongly expelled by Henry for no other real reason—whatever pretext the emperor might finally allege—than that he had been elected without consulting the emperor, held, I say, that this council had done what it could not justly do and that Gregory had been an excellent and most holy man.

They believed that the money he had paid should be called not the purchase of the see but rather the redemption of an oppressive situation. It had been necessary to drive out the three invaders of the Apostolic See, so that the transaction deserved to be called a settlement rather than simony, and therefore lawful, as Laymann teaches, book IV, treatise 10, chapter 8, no. 23, citing Cajetan, Soto, Suárez, and Lessius. Gregory Polydore writes in the *Gregorian* that God himself testified by a miracle to the innocence of Gregory VI. See also Baronius, year 1044, no. 6.]

Benedict withdrew to his own castles and left the City. [Col. 1005A]

Meanwhile John, to whom the name Gregory had been given, administered the priesthood for two years and eight months. King Henry—who at that time ruled Germany, Pannonia, Saxony, and Italy—entered Italy and approached the City of Rome in order to receive the imperial crown from the Roman pontiff and thereafter to be called Augustus (in the year 1047).

Before entering the City, however, he summoned a council in the city of Sutri, bringing together many bishops, as well as abbots, clerics, and religious monks. He sent bishops to John, who was called Gregory, asking him to come so that ecclesiastical affairs—and especially the affairs of the Roman Church, which seemed at that time to have three pontiffs simultaneously—might be discussed under his presidency.

But these actions had been undertaken deliberately. For a long time the king had already resolved that, with the counsel and authority of the entire council, he would justly expel those three men who had unjustly invaded the Apostolic See, and that one man, elected by clergy and people, would be ordained to govern the Lord’s flock diligently according to the statutes of the holy Fathers.

The aforesaid pontiff, therefore, entreated by the king and the other pontiffs, was summoned to Sutri, where the synod had assembled. He went gladly, hoping that, once the other two had been deposed, the pontificate would be confirmed to him alone.

But after he had arrived and the synod had begun to deliberate and investigate the matter, he recognized that he could not justly administer the honor of so great a priesthood. He leapt up from the papal chair, stripped himself of the pontifical vestments, asked pardon, and resigned the dignity of the highest priesthood. [Col. 1005C]

[Note: Pope Gregory, a most holy man, seeing that a dreadful schism would arise unless he renounced the pontificate, imitated Gregory of Nazianzus, who voluntarily abdicated in order to restore peace to the Church. Gregory likewise, with the same spirit and courage, voluntarily withdrew from the papal see; such was the necessity imposed by the wickedness of those times.]

After this, the king entered the City. The Roman clergy and people were assembled in the church of Blessed Peter the Apostle, together with the bishops who had gathered for the aforesaid synod. By common agreement they elected Clement, bishop of Bamberg, [Note: Suidgerus of Bamberg was made pope under the name Clement II in the year of the Lord 1047. Some writers say that he died after being poisoned, departing unexpectedly from this life beyond the Alps on 9 October, a Friday.] since no person suitable to so great a priesthood could then be found in the Roman Church. They enthroned and installed him in the Apostolic See to govern the Lord’s flock.

After he had exercised the priesthood for no more than nine months, he departed this life. Damasus, a native of Germany, supported by royal authority, succeeded him and obtained the priesthood. [Note: The emperor Henry III sent Poppo, bishop of Brixen, a man of great renown, to Rome to be consecrated pontiff in the year 1048; he was called Damasus II. According to some, this occurred on 17 July, a Sunday. He died at Praeneste on 9 August, a Tuesday; his body was brought back to the City and buried at the church of Saint Lawrence outside the walls. Some report that he was removed by poison through the agency of Benedict IX, the invader of the see.]

Damasus administered the priesthood for no more than twenty-three days and then died. He was succeeded by Leo, about whom our present narrative is concerned. [Note: Leo IX was elected supreme pontiff in the year of the Lord 1049. He had previously been called Bruno, bishop of Toul, son of Hugh, count of Dagsburg, and was a monk of the Toul congregation of Cluny, descended from a noble family of the Franks. He was consecrated at Rome on the Ides of February, after first hearing the voice of angels singing: “I am considering thoughts of peace and not of affliction.”]

Leo was in every respect an apostolic man, born of royal stock, endowed with wisdom, distinguished by religion, and thoroughly educated in all ecclesiastical learning. He was one who, as it is written, began to invoke the name of the Lord. I also saw him and was privileged to enjoy his familiarity. Often, when he celebrated Mass in the church, I stood with him at the divine altar wearing the sacred vestments, and I read the Gospel to him.

Through him all ecclesiastical pursuits were renewed and restored, and a new light seemed to arise for the world.

He frequently summoned a priestly council, removed priests, deacons, and other clerics who had not been regularly ordained, and appointed in their places men capable of ministering worthily to the worship of the true and supreme God. Every day, through himself and through his disciples whom he sent everywhere, he showed the peoples the way of the Lord, preaching it in writing and speech.

Always walking by the apostolic path, he also imitated apostolic men in miracles. I have heard many things about him; but since I am occupied with many affairs and cannot recount each one, I shall strive to relate a few of the many, so that whoever reads this in the future may recognize how great was this man’s merit.

[Note: This was Gregory VII, previously Hildebrand, a Tuscan by birth, created pope in the year of the Lord 1073; he died in 1085. His sanctity is venerated in the Roman Martyrology on 15 May, although schismatics and heretics—especially Melchior Haiminsfeld Goldast in his 1607 edition of the *Imperial Constitutions*—attacked Gregory by accusing him of simony.

To refute that calumny, Gregory proved his innocence by receiving the divine Eucharist. He urged King Henry, for whose benefit that calumny had been fabricated, likewise to receive Communion as a testimony to his innocence concerning the crimes of which he was accused, invoking Christ, who is received in the Eucharist, as witness. The king, conscious of his own guilt, refused to do so.

Gregory’s final words as he was dying were: “I have loved justice and hated iniquity; therefore I die in exile.” Baronius, year 1085, and Nicholas Sanders in *On the Visible Monarchy of the Church*, Genebrard in his *Chronicle*, and Sigonius in *On the Kingdom of Italy* defend Gregory. Moreover, Gretser, in his *Apology for the Most Holy Gregory VII*, produces nearly fifty witnesses to Gregory’s innocence. Consult also Marianus Scotus and Lambert of Hersfeld, who flourished in those very times and arranged the genuine and uncorrupted acts of Gregory year by year.]

I learned what I relate from the account of Gregory the pontiff, who had been raised and ordained subdeacon by Leo and who now occupies the apostolic summit in the City of Rome, illuminating Christ’s Church by both words and example. I ought to believe his words as though I were present at that very moment and had seen everything with my own eyes.

At a certain time, when the venerable pontiff Leo was staying in Gaul, occupied with ecclesiastical affairs, he received from an abbot of the monastery of Saint Remigius the Confessor of Christ a wooden cup, offered to him as a blessing-gift. He greatly cherished it out of love for so great a pontiff, and, when seated at table at mealtime, was accustomed to drink from it, preferring it to golden and silver vessels.

One day, therefore, as he sat at table and the cupbearer was about to hand him the cup as usual, it fell from the bearer’s hand through some negligence of which I know nothing and was immediately broken into pieces. When the most blessed pope asked twice and three times for wine, and the cupbearer delayed coming for this reason, he was informed that the cup from which he was accustomed to drink had fallen from the bearer’s hand and been broken.

When he heard this, he was deeply saddened—not so much because of the loss of the cup as because he saw that he had been deprived of a vessel received from the monastery of Saint Remigius as a gift of blessing. He said to those standing beside him: “Bring me the broken cup.”

When it had been brought to him and he saw both fractures, he prayed to almighty God that, through the merits of Blessed Remigius, he might restore the broken cup, which he cherished so greatly for love of him. Immediately he joined one part to the other, and at that very moment it became solid, so that no sign remained that it had ever been broken. All who were present marveled and cried out in his honor. [Col. 1007C]

[Note: The miracle of Saint Pope Leo’s broken cup is also recounted by Saint Bruno, bishop of Segni, in the *Life of Leo*, and by Baronius, year of the Lord 1049, no. 28.]

He began to attribute this not to his own merits but to those of Blessed Remigius, from whose monastery he had received the gift through charity.

**Theophilus.** In this miracle, or in one of the two, I hear that the first miracle of Blessed Father Benedict—though the matter was different—was similarly renewed, when he rejoined the *capisterium*—the kneading sieve or trough—after it had been divided into pieces. (*Gregory, Book II of the Dialogues.*)

**Desiderius.** Meanwhile, dearest brother, you must be silent, so that, keeping your mind attentive, you may learn greater things about him. At another time, as Pope Gregory mentioned above related to me, a certain bishop of Gaul had been suspended from the episcopal office by that same pontiff Leo.

One of the bishop’s priests, named Gibertus, eloquent in speech and by no means uneducated in letters, had promised the bishop that he would go to Rome and, by his clever arguments, deceive the blessed pontiff himself and obtain the restoration of the office that had been taken away. Having accepted money from him, he came to Rome.

When he had presented himself to the most blessed pontiff, he began to turn this way and that like a crafty serpent, excusing his bishop with rhetorical words and demanding, with flattering and most humble petitions, that the office which, as he asserted, had been unjustly removed should be restored.

But when what he requested was denied, and he could not deceive the pope as he had hoped, he devised another stratagem, lest he appear to return without result to the bishop from whom he had received a considerable sum of money. He approached the chancellor of the Apostolic See and, after offering him payment, persuaded him to give him secret letters, sealed with the apostolic seal, to carry to his bishop. These letters indicated that the episcopal office and the favor of the Apostolic See had been restored to him.

The blessed Leo was not unaware of this matter. He immediately summoned the aforesaid priest, took the money that he had offered, placed it in his hand, and said: “May your money be with you for your destruction, because you attempted to possess the gift of God secretly by means of money” (Acts 8).

Divine vengeance immediately followed his words, so that from that day until now he has wandered everywhere out of his mind, and no house or enclosure has been able to keep him for more than two or three days. [Note: This miracle is also reported by Baronius, year of the Lord 1049, no. 29.

The severity of the crime of simony was likewise demonstrated by the punishment of the emperor Justin, who fell into a disease of brain-fever and madness, so that he understood absolutely nothing of the things that were happening. Nicephorus, *History*, book XVII, chapters 33 and 39. Antiochus too is reported to have been punished by such a penalty, in 2 Maccabees 9.

Why, then, do the loins of those who now do not fear but, with brazen faces, profess impiety, not dissolve with terror? Those who trust in the persuasive words of human wisdom are later seen as though fevered and bereft of mind, and experience the truth of the saying: “A person is tormented by the very things through which he sins.” O how terrible God is in his counsels concerning the sons of men!]

From this it is plainly understood that whoever, with reckless daring, attempts either to deceive or to provoke to anger the one who dwells in righteousness unquestionably offends the Lord. Such a person will feel the Lord’s avenging anger against himself—an anger which, although he had not experienced it, he rashly neglected to avoid.

**Theophilus.** It is as you say. But, I ask you, if anything further about the virtue of so great a Father comes to mind, continue without hesitation.

**Desiderius.** While the most blessed pontiff Leo had administered for five years, piously and with the greatest religious devotion, the priesthood divinely entrusted to him, he departed from this unstable light to Christ, who is the true and eternal light. The citizens of heaven rejoiced, and he was carried by angelic hands. [Note: Saint Leo IX, supreme pontiff, died in the year of the Lord 1054, on 19 April, a Tuesday. He was entered among the saints in the Roman Martyrology after having held the pontificate for five years, two months, and eight days.]

Paradise was opened to him, and he was received into the fellowship of the saints. But unhappy was the world, which did not deserve to possess such a pontiff for long. After his death, many great miracles became manifest through the Lord’s granting, both at his tomb and in other places. [Note: For the miracles of Saint Leo performed both during his life and after his death, see Saint Bruno, bishop of Segni, in the *Life of Leo*; Wibert, archdeacon and contemporary of Leo; the bishop of Ostia in *Chronicle*, book II, chapters 86 and 88; and Baronius, year of the Lord 1049 and following.

That holy pontiff, among the countless marks of his goodness, whenever he remained in Rome, used to go three days each week from the Lateran church to Saint Peter’s, in private clothing and barefoot, singing psalms and praying at night with two or three clerics. This is affirmed by the bishop of Ostia in the cited *Chronicle*, book II, chapter 88.]

I shall omit the other miracles and append only two to this little book for the sake of edification, since I am hastening to narrate the deeds of others.

Pope Victor, who had succeeded him in the administration of the priesthood, did not believe the reports related to us by truthful men. He had heard of Leo’s miracles and that the Lord performed such things through him, but he did not grant them credence.

Yet, as the Apostle says, “Tongues are a sign not for believers but for unbelievers” (1 Cor. 14), and almighty God wished to teach him by experience what, although heard from many, he had been entirely unwilling to believe.

A certain bishop of Chur [Note: His name was Dietmar. On the Kalends of February in the year 1040 from the birth of Christ, he was placed over the bishopric of Chur in Rhaetia, near the Rhine River; he died in 1070 after having presided over it honorably and most usefully for thirty years. See Guilmann, book IV, *On the Affairs of the Helvetians*, chapter 2, and the *Chronicle of John Walther.]—whose name has slipped from my memory—had come from Germany with the aforementioned Pope Victor and was staying in Rome in his service.

This bishop had a boy who had been mute from his mother’s womb. He fed and clothed the boy for the sake of his own soul and was accustomed to take him with him wherever he went. In the boy’s empty mouth there seemed to be not even the slightest indication of a tongue.

The bishop too, because of the miracles performed at Blessed Leo’s tomb, possessed a mind as unbelieving as the pope’s.

One day, therefore, having already obtained permission, he decided to return to the seat of his bishopric. He entered the church of Blessed Peter the Apostle for the sake of prayer. After commending himself attentively to Blessed Peter, together with his attendants he mounted his horses and hurried out of the City along the road leading to his homeland, leaving the boy behind in the same church.

When he had gone some distance from the City, it suddenly came back to him that he had left the mute boy in the church of Blessed Peter. He immediately stopped and sent back some of his servants to retrieve the boy.

When they entered the basilica of the prince of the apostles, they saw the boy standing before the tomb of Blessed Leo and speaking with those who were standing around. While they marveled and asked how this had happened, the boy said:

“After my master left me in this church and departed, I came here to the tomb of Blessed Leo, in case almighty God might deign, through his merits, to restore to me the function of which I was deprived. I was not cheated of the desire I sought with all my heart. As soon as I had lain weeping for a little while before his revered memorial, I immediately recovered my voice and rose speaking, as you yourselves see.” [Note: Baronius also reports this great miracle of the healing of the mute, year of the Lord 1054, no. 45.]

From that day onward—and this was even more marvelous—a tongue began gradually to grow in his mouth, where it had been absent, so that within a few days he fully recovered his tongue and spoke words without impediment.

Those who had been sent took care to lead the boy to the bishop. They brought him back speaking through the merits of Blessed Leo, whereas they had left him silent.

The bishop then returned and approached the Roman pontiff, showing what almighty God had deigned to accomplish through Blessed Leo. From that time they began to proclaim everywhere his venerable merits, which previously they had refused to hear when others reported them.

**Theophilus.** They are pleasing because they are marvelous, but even more because they are new.

**Desiderius.** The illustrious Maximus, a citizen of the city of Rome, recently related to me what I am about to tell concerning the same venerable bishop.

There was a certain soldier named Bernard, a man of utterly wicked mind, who displayed himself as opposed to the Apostolic See in every way he could. But in a battle fought against the neighboring inhabitants around the City, who had conspired with Cadalus, bishop of Parma, [Note: Concerning Cadalus, see Baronius, year 1064, nos. 29, 30 and following.] who at that time was attempting to invade the Apostolic See, Bernard engaged the soldiers defending the Roman Church and was pierced and killed by the just judgment of God.

After hearing reports of the miracles that almighty God displayed to the faithful through the merits of Blessed Leo, he not only refused to believe them but also ridiculed and blasphemed them with sacrilegious speech.

One day, when he appeared in a gathering of the people and conversation arose among them about the signs and virtues of Blessed Leo, he began to mock them, saying: “If he is a saint, as you say, let him contract my finger.”

Those standing nearby restrained him from speaking in such a manner about a holy man, and he left when the gathering broke up.

But then, as it happened, a dog that was following him attacked a pig it found in the street. Bernard hurried forward so that the pig would not be torn apart, and he attempted to seize the dog by laying hold of it. Immediately, however, the pig bit his finger with its open mouth. [Note: See Baronius, year 1054, no. 46.]

From that day until the end of his life he had a contracted finger and could not extend it at all. Thus the man who had dared to ridicule God’s servant himself became an object of ridicule to everyone because of his contracted finger.

Let this suffice concerning so great a Father, Blessed Leo. Since we are hastening to narrate the deeds of others, let us leave to someone with leisure the task of writing the many and even more marvelous things that are told about him.

What the Lord says in the Gospel—“My Father is working until now, and I am working” (John 5:17)—we see fulfilled daily, and ancient miracles renewed in new times.

The things I am about to relate are so famous that they are known not only throughout the diocese of Florence, where they occurred, but also throughout all Tuscany and in the city that is the head of the world, Rome.

[Note: Peter of Pavia, surnamed Simonacius, son of Theuzo of the Mediaebarba family, entered the episcopate in the year of the Lord 1062.]

A certain cleric named Peter secretly obtained the episcopal see in the aforesaid city of Florence by money given and through royal support. After he had been kindly received by the clergy and people, as was fitting for a bishop, it soon became widely rumored throughout the diocese that, stained by the plague of the Simoniacal heresy, he had purchased with money what, by the Lord’s command, is ordained to be received and given freely. When this dreadful and utterly detestable report first reached the religious and then the ears of the common people, many began to withdraw from communion with him.

[Note: Andrew of Genoa relates in the *Acts of Saint John Gualbert*, chapter 62, that Peter’s father exposed his Simony.]

[Note: A very serious letter written by the Florentine people to Pope Alexander II concerning this matter is extant; it contains the entire sequence and truth of the affair.]

Burning with divine zeal, they took care to inform the Roman pontiff of everything they had learned about the matter. He summoned a gathering of bishops and called that same bishop to appear, so that he might investigate the matter carefully. But when the bishop had presented himself before the synod and accusers were shouting against him from every side, he attempted to clear himself by oath. After the matter had been debated for some time in the presence of those assembled, a delay was granted, so that perhaps, brought to his senses by it and fearing divine judgment, he might humbly confess what he stubbornly denied, and thus not be removed forever from the altar if he withdrew from this present altar, at which he could not justly minister.

Meanwhile the people divided into two parties. One, which preferred the love of God to gifts, followed the clerics and religious monks who had undertaken to establish the case against the bishop; the other, which loved gifts and favor, followed the bishop. As the people repeatedly quarreled among themselves, with one side obstructing the other, the conflict grew so intense that they often came to blows, even to the shedding of blood.

[Note: This was Saint John Gualbert, abbot of Vallombrosa, whose sanctity is honored in the Roman Martyrology on 12 July.]

When these things had continued for a long time and neither party yielded to the other, the most reverend John, abbot of the monastery called Vallombrosa, was frequently summoned to this conflict. Moved by zeal for God, he came with his monks and did not cease exhorting and preaching to the bishop, and threatening him with the divine examination and judgment, urging him to repent of the crime he had committed, to resign humbly from the priesthood he had not lawfully acquired, and not to become a source of harm to himself and to his subjects, to whom he ought to have been a source of increase.

He frequently set before him the Gospel passage describing how the Lord Jesus drove the sellers and buyers of doves from the Temple, overturned their seats, and poured out the money of the money-changers (John 2:15). In this he showed that anyone who, driven by greed or lifted up by vainglory, attempted to acquire or sell for a price the gift of the Holy Spirit, signified by the dove, should know that he would undoubtedly be expelled from that heavenly temple and eternal altar.

But the bishop, nevertheless desirous of the honor of this present life, regarded the holy man’s admonitions as worthless. Rather, he stubbornly attempted to defend himself with arms, words, and every means at his disposal.

When the venerable abbot saw that his words were accomplishing nothing, he summoned both parties of the people and said:

“Since words are of no avail, let us proceed to a sign. Let a pyre be built and kindled with fire beneath it; let one of our number pass through it, so that, with the Lord deciding, it may be proved whether what we say about the bishop is true or false.”

Both parties approved the judgment. A pyre was immediately constructed, twelve feet in measure. Within it a narrow path was left, wide enough for only one person to pass through. This path too was covered with burning wood, so that no place there would be free from flame.

[Note: For the width, length, and height of the pyre, see Thomas Boz, *On the Signs of the Church*, Book IX, sign 35, chapter 5, §18; Antonio Yepes, *Chronicle*, cent. 6, chapter 4, volume V; S. Atth., *Saint Antoninus*, part 3, title 15, chapter 17, §5; Gonon and Surius in the *Life of Saint John Gualbert*; and other authors cited by Diego de Franchis, *History of the Monastery of Vallombrosa*, Book XI.]

[Note: Because of human unbelief, and because other human means of discovering the truth were lacking, examination by fire was admitted in ancient times, though only after lawful accusation in the courts. This may be observed in Ivo of Chartres, letters 74, 205, 251, 252, 254, and 280, and in Rosweid, *On the Faith of Heretical Servants*, chapter 12. Hence it was called “divine testimony,” as in letter 232. Arnulf, accused in the Council of Reims, chapter 30, says: “I shall hand over my servant to the bishops; as he walks through fiery plowshares, he will make God’s judgment concerning you clear by manifest signs.” Thus Copres proved by fire that the Catholic faith was true, in Book II, chapter 9, of the *Lives of the Fathers*, edited by Rosweid. Andrew of Spoleto, a Franciscan, likewise refused to decline being surrounded by flames before the king of Mauritania and his princes, wishing to show that the teaching of Christ which he preached was true, and he remained unharmed among them for a long time. A certain Franciscan, and likewise Jerome Savonarola, were also prepared to enter the fire at Florence to undergo the ordeal. See Peter Delfino, Book IV, Letter 68, addressed to Peter Baronius on 15 April 1498.]

[Note: He was of the most noble Aldobrandini family, and of such humility that he willingly undertook the care of cows in the monastery. Later, because of the remarkable prodigy of fire, he was called Peter Igneus; he was then made cardinal bishop of Albano and enrolled among the blessed on 8 January in the Benedictine Martyrology. See Baronius, under the year 1063, no. 57.]

While these preparations were being made, the aforementioned abbot John ordered his disciple Peter—the most reverend man who was later ordained bishop in the city of Albano and who still survives, governing that same Church—to put on the sacred vestments and offer sacrifice to Almighty God. Then, trusting in God’s mercy, he was to enter the flames of the burning pyre without hesitation.

Obeying his father’s commands, after offering sacrifice to God, Peter removed his chasuble, approached the fire, and said in a loud voice:

“I beseech you, Almighty God: if Peter, who is called a bishop, is stained by the plague of Simony, show by the judgment of your Holy Spirit that your Church may no longer be polluted; grant that I may pass unharmed through this fire. But if we, full of deceit and driven by envy, have brought this charge against him, let the heat of this fire consume me, abandoned by your grace.”

Having said this, and fortifying himself with the sign of the holy cross, he boldly entered through the middle of the flames. When he was surrounded by fire on every side, so that no one could see him at all, and everyone already thought that he had been consumed, he suddenly burst out on the other side, accompanied by Christ’s grace. Not only his clothing, but not even a hair on him, appeared to have suffered any injury from the fire.

Yet, as that venerable man later recounted, while he was walking through the middle of the flames, a small cloth fell from his hand.

[Note: The Roman Order calls it a *mappula*; it was used to wipe the discharge of the eyes, nose, and mouth. Others call it a *sudarium* or an arm-cloth.]

When he was almost out of the fire, he realized that he was not carrying the cloth in his hands. Considering that it had fallen into the fire, he returned through the middle of the flames, retrieved the cloth, and carried it out with him. Then all who were present, seeing so great and astonishing a miracle,

[Note: This prodigy—or, rather, this Babylonian miracle—occurred in the presence of almost eight thousand clerics and laypeople of both sexes and of every age at the monastery of Septimianum, five miles from the city of Florence, in the year of the Lord 1063, on 16 February, a Wednesday in the first week of Lent. Baronius mentions the event in his *Annals* under that year, but it is narrated at length in the *Life of Saint John Gualbert* and in Thomas Bozius, *On the Signs of the Church*, Book IX, sign 35, chapter 5. On the left of the monastery’s principal church the place can be seen where Peter passed unharmed through the fire; several verses are carved there in memory of the event. More wonderfully still, the monks who live in that monastery testify that even to the present day such a fragrance of sweet odor issues from the aforesaid place that almost everyone marvels at the abundance of its perfume, as a sign and evident proof of the miracle.]

gave immense thanks to God. The opposing party immediately became one, and they expelled the aforesaid bishop from the church.

[Note: Peter bore the most just sentence with such equanimity that, after being tonsured, he even wished to embrace the monastic life within the monastery of Septimianum. See the distinguished Abbot Ughelli, of outstanding knowledge and expertise in sacred history, in his *Sacred Italy*, volume III, under the bishops of Florence.]

Afterward, moved to repentance, he changed his clothing and appeared to lead a religious life under the rule of holy discipline.

**Theophilus.** I rejoice in wonder and wonder in joy that, in the time of our mediocrity, I behold that ancient and glorious miracle of the three youths, when they came forth from the furnace of blazing fire whole and unharmed in every part of their bodies.

**Desiderius.** The venerable Pope Gregory, whom I mentioned above, often used to tell me what the Lord wished to reveal, in his presence, against that same Simoniacal heresy.

“When I was a subdeacon,” he said, “and had been sent to Gaul by Victor, pontiff of this apostolic see, of blessed memory, to investigate ecclesiastical affairs, I took care to convene a council of bishops, so that, with them present, we might discuss ecclesiastical matters. In the same city where the synod was being held there was a bishop whom many accused of having purchased his episcopal dignity for money.

“The bishop was therefore summoned and came before the assembly. When we began to exhort him with salutary admonitions to confess humbly the charges brought against him, his conscience already acknowledging them, he utterly despised our words, both because he was bishop of that city and because he relied on the support of the local count and was full of pride. But when he saw that we and the other bishops present were constraining him under the rule of justice, contrary to his expectation, and that he had no opportunity to escape, he stubbornly began to deny what previously he had scarcely been willing even to hear.

“As the discussion dragged on, and a large part of the day had been consumed, while he nevertheless persisted in his obstinate denial, it seemed appropriate for us and the other religious bishops present to adjure him and commit the entire judgment to a manifestation of the Holy Spirit.

“‘In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, whose gift of grace we have heard that you purchased, we adjure you to tell us the truth of this matter. But if you attempt to continue denying it as you have begun, may you be unable to name the Holy Spirit until you confess what is true.’

“The bishop was highly eloquent, and we entreated him to name the Holy Spirit. He named the Father and the Son quite clearly, but, in a marvelous manner, he was completely unable to name the Holy Spirit. Then it became clearer than daylight to everyone present that he had purchased with money the episcopal dignity, which is bestowed only by the generosity of the Holy Spirit’s grace. Then, shaken by the power of the Holy Spirit, the bishop was compelled humbly to confess before everyone what, previously inflated with pride and having set aside the fear of God, he had rashly dared to deny.”

**Theophilus.** Since the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are one, and it is not lawful to think anything different concerning the Father and the Son from what one thinks concerning the Holy Spirit, why, in pronouncing the names of the Father and the Son, did he have a free and eloquent tongue, but, at the sole name of the Holy Spirit, as though it were preeminent, a tongue that was mute and entirely bound?

[Note: See Baronius, volume XI, under the year of the Lord 1055, no. 17; Hugh, abbot of Cluny, was also present at this prodigy.]

**Desiderius.** It occurred by the just judgment of God that the man who, with a flattering tongue, had purchased the gift of the grace of the Holy Spirit—which is both given and received freely—should, when pronouncing the name of the Holy Spirit in particular,

[Note: The Simoniac was unable to express “Holy Spirit” because the gifts of grace are attributed to the Holy Spirit, and the Simoniac had committed an offense against them by selling them. From this let those who, promoted to ecclesiastical dignities by money, sit in the temple of God learn how foul, how monstrous, and how dreadful the crime of Simony is. Let them remember that, by comparison with the Simoniacal heresy, all other crimes are regarded as almost nothing, and that Saint Ambrose called it an unpardonable offense. Would that the customs of our age did not produce such monsters, and that the aconite of Tartarean bitterness might be removed as quickly as possible—for I use the words of Peter Damian—lest, God forbid, deadly poison spread.]

have no use of his tongue.

[Col. 1015A] Alferius was abbot of the monastery of the Holy Trinity, built by him on the side of the mountain that rises above the sea between the cities of Salerno and Amalfi.

[Note: Saint Alferius, a Salernitan monk of Cluny, first abbot of the monastery of Cava and disciple of Saint Odilo, rested in peace in the year of the Lord 1050, on the day before the Ides of April. See Baronius under that year, no. 16.]

I myself partly witnessed his religious and God-loving life, since I stayed with him for some time on familiar terms, and I learned the rest from the reports of others. It would be wrong to pass over in silence the miracle that divine power deigned to work through him, and which I learned from very many people.

As he was once going to the city of Salerno on business for the monastery, walking along a road cut into the mountain, he fell downward with the horse he was riding over an immense precipice. The cliff rises so high above the sea that it appears to extend more than fifty paces downward. While those traveling with him, supposing him certainly dead, were exceedingly sad and weeping, they descended by a detour toward the sea, hoping that they might at least find him somehow and commit him to burial.

When they were walking quickly along the soft sands beside the shore at the foot of the mountain toward the place where he had fallen, they found him safe and unharmed on the road, sitting upon the horse with which he had fallen and hastening toward Salerno along the road he had begun. Astonished, and entirely unable to understand how the event had occurred, they began to give thanks to God and to raise their voices loudly, almost in tumult. But he suddenly silenced them and said:

“If you wish to enjoy my blessings, tell no one, as long as I live, what you have seen happen to me.”

[Col. 1015C] It is also said of him that he raised a dead man to life. To those who knew him and his life thoroughly, this certainly seems not at all incredible.

[Note: Saint Alferius was succeeded by Leo, his disciple and nearly his equal in holiness, as Baronius reports under the year 1050.]

The abbot Leo, who succeeded him in governing the monastery, had been educated under his direction and, serving him as provost, adhered to him familiarly more closely than the other brothers. He recently told me that, at one time, secular men came to him to visit him and enjoy his prayers.

Wishing to provide them not only with spiritual nourishment but also with bodily refreshment, Alferius ordered the aforesaid Leo, his provost, for the sake of charity, to set the table for them and prepare a meal. Leo replied that he had nothing with which he could provide them to eat except bread and wine and five hen’s eggs; but he did not know how those eggs could be divided among them, since there were seven men.

“Make haste,” said Alferius, “and prepare those same eggs over the fire as quickly as possible, then bring them to me so that I may set them before the guests.”

Leo ran and, as he had been ordered, boiled the eggs and brought them to him. Alferius took them, blessed them, and from the five eggs gave each of the seven men one—an astonishing thing.

**Theophilus.** When I consider that five eggs were so increased in distribution among seven men that each received one in equal share, I see in a certain sense the miracle by which the Author of all things satisfied five thousand men with five loaves (Matthew 16:9).

**Desiderius.** My father’s aunt, a woman named Bella,

[Note: Theodata, or Theodorada, wife of Duke Romuald, in the year of the Lord 682 attached to the church of Saint Peter a monastery of nuns of great devotion. Its remains can still be seen at the foot of Mount Saint Felix. Paul the Deacon, *History of the Lombards*, Book VI, chapter 1.]

lived in the monastery of the blessed Apostle Peter within the city of Benevento, wearing the habit of a nun from the first bloom of youth until the end of old age. Although she had been betrothed to a man, she secretly fled from her parents’ house and hurried to the monastery. There she dedicated her virginity to Almighty God; and, because she had disdained to have an earthly bridegroom on earth, she undoubtedly deserved to have a heavenly one in heaven.

She herself used to tell me about her abbess, whose name was Offa.

[Note: Offa lived around the year of the Lord 1070.]

Before assuming the governance of the monastery, Offa had lived for a long time on the mountain called that of Saint Agatha the Martyr, near the city of Capua, and there had led an eremitical life.

[Note: See Michael the monk of Capua, in his notes on Saint Offa.]

Afterward, having assumed the governance of the monastery, one night, while the sisters were still resting, she entered the oratory and took a censer in order to burn incense on the altars as usual. When she wished to place incense in the censer, it fell from her hand, and, the lamp having been extinguished by the wind, she could not find the incense.

[Note: Because of her devotion alone, she would go around the altar secretly and by herself with incense. Peter Damian also relates this event, though somewhat differently from Desiderius, in Book VIII, Letter 5.]

Suddenly someone stood beside her, held her hand, and gave her the incense that he had placed in the censer. So great a fragrance emanated from that incense that, throughout the remainder of the night until the third hour of the day, it filled not only the church but the entire monastery with marvelous sweetness. From this it is undoubtedly understood that it was an angel of the Lord who gave that incense such a fragrant odor.

This same most devout abbess, after having presided diligently over the virgins for many years and never ceasing to instruct the servants of God entrusted to her through words and example, was struck by bodily illness and came to the point of death. When she lay at the end of her life, already near the moment when she was to return her soul to Christ, whom she had served, she rose from her bed in the sight of everyone present, as though to the height of three cubits in the air, and stood with her hands extended toward heaven. After praying, she placed herself again upon the bed and breathed out her final spirit.

From this it can be recognized how great her abstinence had been. While she lay sick in bed, many honorable men and women came to visit her and urged her to take some food to sustain her weakened body. But she, unaccustomed to delicacies, said:

“If you bring me some strained legumes, perhaps I shall be able to taste a little of them.”

O abstinence worthy of praise in a woman! While ill, she used strained legumes as the greatest of delicacies.

After she had died and been buried in the church, a certain peasant carrying grain happened to pass through that same church one day. Disregarding the merit of the woman buried there, he set down his sack of grain upon her tomb and, tired, sat beside it to rest for a while. Suddenly, by divine power, the sack was lifted from the tomb and thrown far away, scattering throughout the church all the grain with which it had been filled.

The peasant was utterly terrified. From that day he learned how greatly the people of God should be honored while they are in the body, since divine power wished to show that even when their bodies have died and been placed in a tomb, they must not be despised by anyone.

Another nobleman from the same city of Benevento had come to the monastery for some reason and, unaware of what he was doing, happened to sit upon her tomb. Suddenly such a severe pain seized his entrails that, shouting and wailing, he thought he would die at that very hour.

At his cries, the virgins in the monastery immediately ran to him and told him whose tomb was beneath him. After asking forgiveness for his ignorance, he deserved to receive healing from heaven through the merits of the servant of God.

In the same city there is a monastery called Saint Sophia,

[Note: On the monastery of Saint Sophia, see Leo of Ostia, Book I, chapter 9, and the *Chronology of the Archbishops of Benevento* by Marius de Vipera.]

subject to this monastery of Cassino. In it there was a monk who, from childhood, had lived a holy and most humble life. Before reaching the years of adolescence, he was overcome by an excessive illness and brought to the point of death.

When the brothers gathered at his passing, they began to commend his soul to God with hymns and psalms and to invoke more earnestly the assemblies of the saints for his assistance. As his illness increased, he died. But while water was being prepared to wash his body, he lay lifeless for almost an hour.

While those present continued in prayer and psalmody, suddenly his entire body trembled, and, gradually returning to life, he sat up on his bed, to the amazement of everyone. Then, when questioned, he began to tell them what he had seen after leaving the body:

“When my soul was departing from my body while you were singing litanies and invoking the saints of the Lord, the saints whom you invoked immediately came to my aid in answer to your prayers.”

They asked him whether he could recognize those whom he had never seen. He replied:

“I recognized Saint Benedict and Saint Gregory. I saw the blessed Donatus and Felix, together with the other saints who rest in this church, coming to my aid. Among them, our patron Saint Mercury appeared shining like a brilliant star.”

When they asked him whether he would remain in this life, he answered:

“Not at all. For the blessed Mercury promised that he would come today to take me to himself.”

The outcome proved that what he had said was true. On that same day he was taken from this light and was undoubtedly received by those whom, while dying, he had previously seen coming to his aid.

Finally, while I was staying in that monastery, I saw one of the witnesses who had been present, a survivor named Sicenolf. He declared that he had seen and heard all these things exactly as they have been related.

*(Here ends the third book. The entire fourth book is missing from the autograph manuscript of the Vatican Library bearing the number 1203. This manuscript, written in Lombard script, is known to have once been used by the fathers of the monastery of Cassino.)*

[Col. 1017]

## Epitaph of Abbot Apollinaris, by Desiderius the Abbot, later Victor III

*(Dom Tosti, History of the Abbey of Cassino I, 12.)*

[Col. 1017D]

Here lies buried Abbot Apollinaris, a father.

Let something else known of him be said: M [lacuna]

You, good young man, fled the world,

Entirely apostolic, a true friend of all;

You became an abbot, fragrant through every effort, unwilling

To be anything but least: humble, devout, generous, and just.

With dry feet you crossed the Liris by the gift of the Father,

Thus imitating Peter and Placidus as well.

You draw down the swollen one; you convert him, and he becomes blessed.

[Col. 1018D]

While the Agarene plague ravages every pleasant place,

already dead to the flesh, an exalted envoy of God,

you are sent from on high as a messenger to the sons of your people,

Saying: “God has shown mercy to Mount Cassino

Through the prayers of the true servant, Father Benedict.””

Here is the fourteenth abbot, serene in mind;

For eleven years you lived here, not without sufferings.

The revered Desiderius transfers and places you here:

Be favorable to us, O revered and honored father.

## Before the year of the Lord 1099. William of Apulia

### The Historical Poem of William of Apulia on the Deeds of the Normans in Sicily, Apulia, and Calabria, down to the Death of Duke Robert Guiscard, Addressed to Roger His Son, with Notes by the Distinguished Men John Tiremaeus and Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz

*(In Muratori, *Writers of the History of Italy* V, 245.)*

[Col. 1019]

## Preface by Ludovico Antonio Muratori to William of Apulia’s Norman Poem

In the eleventh century of Christ, something marvelous happened in Italy. A number of brave men departed from Normandy, a province of Gaul, and came to Apulia as travelers in the year 1016, thinking of anything but war. There they were incited by a certain Melo against the Greeks who still ruled the region. Fortune immediately smiled upon these vigorous men. When they realized that there was an abundance of opportunities there and an easy way to grow rich among an unwarlike people, they enlisted new comrades from their own nation, gradually undertook greater enterprises, conquered many cities and towns, and finally, under Robert Guiscard and his brother Roger, brought all Apulia—which we now call the Kingdom of Naples—and all Sicily beyond the Strait under their rule.

These immense deeds and great events were plainly worthy of being committed to writing by historians and transmitted to distant ages. Nor were writers lacking, as this very collection of historians will make abundantly clear. We shall therefore give first place to William of Apulia, an excellent poet who described in hexameter verse the deeds of the Normans in Apulia, Calabria, and Sicily, and who is for this reason mentioned by Vossius among the Latin historians.

We have found no record, either in his own work or in anyone else’s, of who he was. It is certain that this writer flourished while Robert Guiscard lived and reigned, for he chiefly records Robert’s deeds; indeed, he also records his death and ends his poem at his funeral. Robert was taken from the living in the year of Christ 1085. But since the poet also mentions Pope Urban II as still living at the beginning of the poem—Urban had occupied the See of Peter from the year 1088—he must have written after that year and before 1099, when that pontiff died. He dedicated his poem to Roger, the son of Duke Robert.

The first person who arranged for this history to be printed in type was John Tiremaeus, an advocate of the treasury in the province of Rouen. He published it at Rouen in 1582. But because the book was extremely rare—so rare that Duchesne himself, whom others call Quercetanus, did not know it while collecting the Norman historians—the most celebrated Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz brought it forth again, inserting it on page 578 of volume I of his writers dealing with Brunswick, printed at Hanover in 1707. More recently John Baptist Carusius reprinted it from Leibniz for the third time in volume I of his *Historical Library of the Kingdom of Sicily*.

This writer clearly indicates that a marriage was celebrated between Robert’s daughter and Hugh, son of Azzo, Marquis of Este, the renowned ancestor of the dukes of Brunswick and Modena. This was the reason Leibniz added the ancient poet and historian to his collection. I too indicated this in Part I, page 12, of my *Este Antiquities*.

William therefore had an even stronger claim to be included among the Italian writers, since he was an Italian and dealt with events that occurred in Italy. I have chosen to retain the prefaces and certain notes with which Tiremaeus and Leibniz illuminated various passages of this poem, since they are not useless to the reader. Moreover, not only Neapolitan and Sicilian history, but Italy as a whole owes much to this poet, because, in those ages of ignorance, he brought commendable eloquence and facility to the shaping of verse, and describes most things as though he had been an eyewitness.

[Col. 1021]

## To the Most Noble and Learned Lodovicus Balliol, Most Worthy Abbot of Lonley and Sillé  
### John Tiremaeus, Hautenois, Advocate of the Treasury in the Province of Rouen

When, most noble Balliol, I was returning several years ago from Argentona, where I had gone to visit my excellent father during our annual recess, the religious house of the abbey of Bec-Hellouin invited me hospitably to stay there on my journey and received me generously.

There, while I admired both the character of the people and the beauty and magnificence of the place, I eventually began a conversation about the library. When I was brought into it, I inferred—for this is easily conjectured from the remains—that in better times it had once been a repository of books of every kind.

As I examined the remnants of so great a treasure as carefully as circumstances allowed, my eyes finally fell upon several miserable sheets, badly assembled and scarcely holding together, which dust and moths had long been ravaging. Moved by pity for this loss, I willingly extended my hand and roused them from their idle and utterly destructive decay. When at last I had wiped away their grime and looked more eagerly to see what they contained, I found, among other things that could scarcely be read because of their antiquity, the historical poem of a certain William of Apulia concerning the deeds performed in Sicily, Apulia, and Calabria by Robert Guiscard, the most valiant leader of the Normans.

Although I had never seen it anywhere and supposed that it had hitherto been read or seen by very few, two things especially compelled me to investigate it. First was my love of our common homeland: wherever the glory, splendor, and ancient virtue of that homeland shine forth, I am delighted by them above all else and without satiety, as I ought to be. The second was that I understood our ancestors—brave and magnanimous men—to have always preferred to be authors of deeds rather than writers of them in spreading the glory of their name throughout the world. Hence it happened that their

“Hidden virtue differs but little from buried inactivity.”

(*Horace, Odes* IV.9).

For this reason I judged it wrong that a man who considered himself wholly born for the commonwealth or for his homeland should allow whatever writings by foreigners existed in praise of that most illustrious and warlike nation to remain any longer in darkness.

Therefore, after I had borrowed the old sheets for a time from my religious hosts, I read through the poem they contained from beginning to end, as they say, applying my eyes and mind as closely as I could. Nor was I content with that: I also took care to have it transcribed diligently, so that I could more easily share it with certain learned friends of mine, men of sincere and refined judgment.

Their judgment was entirely the same as mine: given the scarcity of writers who have embraced in writing any memory of the deeds of the Norman people, no one among our own authors had been found who had illuminated in letters the history of that outstanding leader, Guiscard; among foreign writers there were indeed very few, but no one who had written about him specifically in verse, or more plainly and truthfully than this William of Apulia.

He was a contemporary of the times whose history he composed and, a circumstance that gives him authority and credibility, was to a large extent an eyewitness of the events.

Nor will I deny that my friends and I, moved by the love we bear our homeland, wished this work possessed those two brightest lights of any writing, in which ears especially delight: elegance of language and sweetness of composition. For many passages seemed harsh and, so to speak, low—passages whose humility lowers the dignity of the events rather than expressing them according to their merit and worth. Thus, perhaps not without justification, one might apply to them what the poet once wrote:

“Those who smear splendid deeds

with foul verse.”

*(Horace, Epistles II.1.136.)*
But we did not think that this ought to be an obstacle preventing this Apulian, abandoned for so many centuries, from deserving both illumination and protection—especially since any fair-minded judge of these matters would easily conclude that, if he lacked the highest elegance and ornament of poetry or of the Latin language, this was the fault not of the man but of the uncultivated age in which he lived. When I therefore resolved, with the approval of learned men, to bring both light and deserved freedom to this foreign yet distinguished herald of Norman virtue, it seemed worthwhile to choose you, most noble Balliol, under whose most fortunate auspices this book, at last rescued from long darkness, might appear in public and be defended by your perpetual patronage.

Nor do I fear that any person of sound mind will rashly accuse me of having done this carelessly or without sufficient consideration. Indeed, I rather think that the author himself, if he were alive, would have acted in the same way; and I have no doubt that, if I had acted otherwise, I should have incurred the hostility of his offended spirit. For when an outsider describes in Latin verse so many victories, trophies, and deeds successfully accomplished in various places by that most noble and illustrious Norman, to whom among mortals, I ask, could this entire work—whatever its worth—more rightly be inscribed, given, or dedicated than to you? You yourself are a Norman, and you excel in such antiquity of lineage and nobility of ancestry that your family not only gave Guiscard companions in glory and renown who were by no means inferior, but also produced for the Scots John Balliol, their most valiant king, and Edward, his son, a brother-in-law to Philip of Valois, king of the French.

Moreover, you stand out so greatly in the excellence of your character that in this age of ours you appear second to no one, whether in every field of liberal learning or in the glory of virtue and wisdom. But as for the judgment of others, let it be put aside; I need only know that this counsel of mine is approved by you alone. There is no doubt that you will approve it most willingly. Accept, then, out of your supreme love of letters and of men of letters, this ancient client of Norman nobility, reborn through my efforts; and protect him, as he asks of you, against all enemies of virtue and all who envy the renown of our ancestors.

For the rest, I ask you to convince yourself that whatever labor and effort we have devoted to correcting this book and explaining the notes we have added, all of it, until we can provide something better, is likewise offered to you as a kind of pledge of your former goodwill toward me and as a perpetual testimony before everyone of my gratitude and exceptional respect for you.

Farewell.

[Col. 1023]

## TO THE READER

[Col. 1023A]

If these verses do not possess as much of the flavor of the Aonian Muses  
as the songs of Maeonides and Virgil,  
nevertheless you will not read here the trifles of the underworld, the cups of Circe,  
the Cyclops, Harpies, monsters, or any such things.  
Truth-telling Phoebus does not concern himself with Greekish dreams,  
nor does the modest Muse stain her face with cosmetics.  
You have, reader, a poet such as Platonic polity—or rather the pious law of Christ-worshippers—would not banish.  
With sure faith, and in verses not wholly unacquainted with the Muse,  
he has related the deeds of his own age: matters seen with his own eyes,  
comparable in arms, counsel, and piety with those of his native land.  
You will learn of the brave hearts of the Norman people,  
who came to Italy from the Gallic Ocean,  
not as exiles or as a people defeated at home, but as lovers of military glory,  
and as a people in need of a settlement because of their countless numbers.  
Therefore read him—not as though he were the best of poets,  
but because, as a historian, he certainly ought to be regarded as excellent.

[Col. 1023]

## PREFACE OF GODEFROID WILHELM LEIBNIZ

In his *Introduction to the Collection of Writings Serving the History of Brunswick*, no. XXXIX.

[Col. 1023B]

The powerful margrave Azo, of Estense origin, descended through Cuniza from the heiress of the ancient Guelfs and was the father of Guelf, duke of Bavaria, who propagated the family in Germany and whose line still survives in the princes of Brunswick. By another wife he had sons, Hugh and Fulk. Hugh married a daughter of Robert Guiscard, prince of the Normans, who held Apulia, Calabria, and Sicily, famous for his great achievements and founder of the kingdom of the Two Sicilies, whose title his son Roger bore. For at that time the name “Sicily this side of the Strait,” or “mainland Sicily,” referred to what we now call the kingdom of Naples; while the island of Sicily was called the kingdom of Trinacria.

The historian of the House of Este knew nothing of this marriage, any more than he knew the succession of Azo’s children and wives. Since, however, the contemporary poet William describes Hugh’s marriage, we have wished to add him to the writers of our history, although he has been seen by very few. Gaspar Barthius, a man of immense reading and a distinguished searcher-out of obscure writings, speaks of this author as follows in his notes on William the Breton, p. 774:

“There exists a poem by William of Apulia, once published and praised by many learned men, but it has not come into my hands, much to my annoyance at the perversity of fortune. In the copy communicated to me by the most distinguished Feller, son of the most learned professor of Leipzig and now secretary to the most serene duke of Weimar, the eminent Nicolaus Heinsius had written the following inscription: ‘This is a very rare book, otherwise unpublished, which the distinguished Emeric Bigot gave me.’”

[Col. 1023D]

“Certainly it must have escaped the diligence of Quercetanus, who, publishing the writers on Norman affairs in a proper volume and in the format called folio, omitted this work, although it had already appeared under the following title: *The Five Books of William of Apulia on the Norman Deeds in Italy and the Kingdom of Naples*, Rouen, at the shop of Richard Petit and Richard Lollemant, 1582, quarto, p. 52.”

The editor calls himself Jean Tiremaeus Hautenoeus, advocate of the treasury in the province of Rouen. He says that he found the book in the religious house of the monastery of Beccobelvin, and he inscribes it to Louis Balliol, abbot of the monasteries of Lonley and Sully.

It is worthwhile to summarize the subject of the work briefly, so that what is scattered throughout the author’s account and obscured by his diction may be understood more easily.

### Book One

At the beginning he says:

> My mind impels me to tell under whose leadership  
> the Norman people came to Italy.

He declares that he undertook this work at the urging of Roger and of Pope Urban II himself. Urban began to sit as pope in 1088 and died in 1099; from this one may estimate the age of our poet. He relates that certain Normans, when they had entered a church on Mount Garganus dedicated by vow to Saint Michael, found there the distinguished Melo, driven out by the Greeks and called Baro. Melo persuaded them to attack the Greeks and supplied them with weapons.

Turnicius, the Greek catapan, was defeated; but in the following year his successor Basil in turn defeated Melo by the river Aufidus. Melo went to Henry Augustus and obtained assistance, but died while it was being prepared. Abandoned, the Normans returned to Campania and hired out their hands and arms now to one, now to another, of the Lombard princes.

At last they settled in the city of Aversa and appointed as their leader among them the distinguished Ranulf, who fathered Jordan, and Jordan fathered Richard. A certain Lombard named Ardoinus, who had been wronged by Dochianus, a Greek commander, again incited them against the Greeks. They then chose twelve of the noblest from their entire number and, equipped with five hundred horsemen and seven hundred foot soldiers, captured Amalfi.

Loaded with booty, they then disregarded the orders of their leaders and served Adenulf, prince of Benevento. They captured in battle the son of Basil, who had once driven out Melo, and joined to themselves by treaty Bari, Monopoli, and Juvenacum, cities that had revolted from the Greeks.

The Normans who were in Aversa then passed from Adenulf to Guaimar, prince of Salerno. The rest elected Argyros, Melo’s son, as their leader; he was fighting Maniaces, the Greek commander. Meanwhile Constantine Monomachus came to the Greek imperial throne. He incited Argyros and his men against Maniaces, who was hostile to him.

The Aversans also came to Argyros’ aid. Among them were Rudolph, Ranulf’s successor in governing Aversa, and William Iron-Arm, son of Tancred, whose brother was Guiscard, later duke. Maniaces fell in that war.

### Book Two

While Argyros held Bari, he also occupied Hydruntum. From there he dismissed the Normans and was besieged at Bari by Guaimar. Finally he returned to Constantinople. The Normans again entered the service of Guaimar of Salerno; from there some attached themselves to Count Peter and others to Drogo, the son of that same Tancred.

Peter, their kinsman,

> He founded Andria, and from there built Coretum,  
> Buxilias, and Barolum upon the sea’s shores.

I think that “to build” is what our author calls “to fortify.” At last Peter was captured in battle by Humphrey and Drogo. Argyros returned from Constantinople with money and urged the Normans to fight for the Greeks against the Turks, whom the author, following Greek writers, calls Persians.

But when they refused to leave Apulia, he tried to crush them, summoning Pope Leo IX as well. Drogo and Guaimar had by then died, and the Normans were without a leader. Drogo’s brother Humphrey, however, survived him, and Richard the Norman governed Aversa in the manner of a count. Yet Robert Guiscard, the brother of William, Drogo, and Humphrey, surpassed all the others in valor.

In the battle fought with Pope Leo, the Lombards abandoned the Germans. The Swabians resisted with great courage, but were eventually slaughtered; the pope, excluded from Benevento by its citizens, was captured. The Normans gained possession of all Apulia. Humphrey granted Calabria to his brother Robert, but soon afterward his death provided Robert with the opportunity to obtain both it and Apulia.

Pope Nicholas II, after holding a synod at Amalfi, created Robert duke and restored to him, under the law of feudal tenure, the lands he had occupied and offered to the Roman Church. Thus the poet says of Robert:

> Hence all of Calabria and all Apulia  
> were granted to him, and the domination of the people’s homeland extended into Latium.

But from the time of the Ottos the emperors of the West had claimed Apulia and Calabria for themselves. What Otto II had begun was continued by Henry II; after capturing Benevento, Troia, Naples, Capua, Salerno, and other places, he had even granted lands to the Normans because they had fought bravely. Therefore Henry IV and the other emperors denied that anything could be taken from imperial authority either by the pope or by the Normans. Our author concealed all these matters.

Meanwhile Robert repudiated his first wife on the ground of consanguinity—by whom he had fathered Bohemond—and married Sichelgaita, daughter of Guaimar, prince of Salerno, and sister of Gisulf, his successor. By her he had three sons and five daughters. He then defeated his brother Humphrey’s son Abelard and the other rebels.

### Book Three

The third book relates how Robert, after defeating the Greeks in a naval battle, finally wrested Bari from them in the third year. He then prepared, through his brother Roger, for war against the Saracens of Sicily and soon took Palermo himself.

Next he stripped Peter Trano, son of Count Peter, of his possessions and captured Gisulf, his wife’s brother; thus he gained possession of Salerno and Amalfi. At that time this city flourished through the gathering of merchants and was frequented by foreigners through constant voyages.

> Here Arabs, Indians, Sicilians, and Africans are known.  
> Here, they say, the mariner’s compass was discovered,

although our author says nothing about this. After arranging matters there, Robert returned to Troia.

> While he lingered by the walls of the Trojan city,  
> a noble margrave named Lambardus arrived,  
> accompanied by many nobles of his homeland.  
> He was called Azo, and he brought with him Hugh,  
> his illustrious son, so that the duke might give him his daughter.

After this matter has been explained at greater length, the poet then relates how the duke brought his other kinsmen and rivals into proper order, taking away part of their territories and restoring part.

### Book Four

The fourth book relates how Michael, called Parapinaces, son of Constantine Ducas, was deprived of the empire:

> … his brother, his companion, having been driven away,  
> he becomes a monk; Robert’s daughter grieves  
> that her betrothed has been deposed,  
> and the unhappy man is forced into exile.

Michael the emperor had indeed betrothed his son Constantine to Robert’s daughter Helena, so that he might resist the Turks with Robert’s assistance, as the Curopalates records.

Our poet then speaks of the other sons-in-law Robert had. Among them:

> From the regions of the West—of Iberia—whom Barcelona trembled before,  
> the distinguished count Raymond came to this city,  
> asking that the duke’s daughter, who was to marry, be given to him.  
> The elder daughter was given to him in marriage; the other married  
> an excellent count, illustrious in the lineage of the Franks.  
> He was called Ebalus, one who knew not how to yield to an enemy.

I have discovered that this Count Ebalus was of Rochefort. His fame was then so great that the pope created him commander of an expedition against the Saracens of Spain.

Thus Hugh of Este, son of Azo and brother of Guelf, was connected by marriage to so many illustrious families. Shortly afterward Robert, reconciled with Gregory VII, came to Rome and confirmed his loyalty to him by oath. It was believed that he had secretly agreed with the pope that he would receive the crown of the Roman Empire, which had been taken from Henry.

Meanwhile Robert crossed over to Greece to avenge the wrong done to his son-in-law and daughter. But when he learned of Gregory’s danger—Henry and the rival pope Guibert were pressing him—he returned to Italy. Leading to Rome an army of six thousand cavalry and thirty thousand infantry in full strength, he freed Gregory, who was besieged in the Mausoleum of Hadrian, and thus in the same year defeated both the emperor of the East and the emperor of the West.

### Book Five

The fifth book, which is the last, describes Robert’s final expedition to Greece, from which he was not to return. Accompanied by his son Roger, he crossed the Adriatic Sea with one hundred ships and died during the expedition.

Meanwhile Gregory died in exile at Salerno. The returning forces suffered shipwreck, and Robert was buried in the city of Venosa among his brothers.

[Col. 1027]

# THE HISTORICAL POEM OF WILLIAM OF APULIA ON THE DEEDS OF THE NORMANS IN SICILY, APULIA, AND CALABRIA

Written up to the death of Duke Robert Guiscard and addressed to his son Roger.

## BOOK ONE

[Col. 1027B]

Ancient poets sang the deeds of ancient leaders;  
I, a new poet, shall undertake to publish the deeds of new ones.  
My mind impels me to tell under whose leadership  
the Norman people came to Italy, what reason they had for remaining,  
and under what leaders they followed and gained triumph in Latium.

Spare your poet, O illustrious Roger, worthy offspring  
of Duke Robert, who sings lofty things according to his strength.  
Your willing obedience to whose authority  
makes me bold, because the pure devotion  
which I offer supplies the powers that labor and skill  
and natural ability deny me.

And the reverent request of Father Urban  
forbids me to be slow, because I fear more to sin by refusing  
the commands of so great a pontiff  
than by following his gracious instructions.

[Note: Pope Urban II lived, according to John Tiremaeus, and was elected, according to Leibniz, in the year of salvation 1088. At the same time Roger, son of Robert Guiscard, duke of Apulia, was reigning.]

After it pleased the powerful King to change  
the times along with kingdoms, so that Apulia,  
long possessed by the Greeks, would no longer be inhabited by them,  
the Norman people, distinguished for equestrian ferocity, entered  
and, after expelling the Achaeans, ruled Latium.

When the north wind, which their native language calls *North*,  
bore them to the shores of the northern region,  
from which they had departed to seek the lands of Latium,  
and when the word *man* among them is what is called *homo* among us,  
they are called Normans—that is, “northern men.”

Some of them climbed the heights of Mount Garganus,

[Note: Mount Garganus in Apulia, by the Adriatic Sea. — Leibniz.]

[Note: Volaterranus, book III of the *Geography*, writes that Robert Guiscard expelled from Sicily the Saracens who, in the year of salvation 914, had occupied Apulia, Calabria, Naples, and Mount Garganus. — Leibniz.]

[Col. 1027D]

to pay you, Michael the Archangel, the vows owed. There they saw a certain man dressed in Greek fashion, named Melo.

[Note: The reading is *Meles* in Theodorus Fazellus, later Decade, book VI, chapter 1. — Leibniz.]

They marvel at the foreign garment of an exile  
and at the unusual coils of the turban fastened about his head.  
While they looked at him, they asked who he was and where he came from.

He answered that he had been born a Lombard and was a free citizen of Bari,  
but that he had been driven from the borders of his homeland  
by Greek cruelty.

[Note: In the year of salvation 1018; so Tiremaeus. — Around 1011, a revolt had arisen in Calabria and Apulia. — Leibniz.]

While the Gauls sympathized with his exile:

[Col. 1028C]

> “How easy a return I should have, if you were willing,” he said,  
> “with several men of your people helping us!  
> For he declared that the Greeks could quickly be driven out  
> with the aid of these men, if easy effort accompanied them.”

They promise to give him the protection of their people  
and to restore him swiftly to his homeland whenever he might be able to return.

After they had therefore returned to their ancestral borders,  
they soon began urging their people to seek Italy with them.  
They told them of Apulia’s fertility and of the sloth inherent in its people,

[Note: The marginal reading was *Graecis* (“to the Greeks”); this reading may perhaps be more correct. — Tiremaeus.]

and urged them to undertake the course that they alone could accomplish. They said that a prudent leader  
would be found there, under whose leadership an easy victory over the Greeks could be won.

With the minds of many therefore aroused, some prepared to go,  
since they had scarcely any resources at all; others,  
because they wished to undertake even greater things than great ones.  
There was in everyone the same desire to acquire wealth.

They set out, taking whatever each thought necessary  
to carry in order to complete the journey according to his strength.

After the unarmed Norman people had crossed Rome,  
they halted, exhausted by the labor of the journey, on the shores of Campania.  
Rumor flew through Latium that the Normans had landed.

When Melo learned that the Gauls had reached Italy,  
he approached more quickly and gave weapons to those who lacked them;  
he compelled his companions to hasten, armed, along with him.

Until then the Latins had marveled at the unaccustomed  
and countless snows that had fallen in that season,  
and most of the wild animals had perished in their downfall;  
nor was it permitted for the trees that had fallen  
to rise again from it.

After this portent had been observed, in the following spring  
Melo bought weapons in the Campanian regions

[Note: In the year 1017, or shortly before; so Leibniz.]

[Col. 1029B]

and, raging to attack the Apulian territories, led the Normans there.  
The Norman people first had him as their leader.

All Apulia trembles at the Gauls in the regions of Italy,  
and many of them perished under their overwhelming severity.

At last the report reached the ears of Turnicius,

[Note: Perhaps *Tumitius* or *Tomitius*, a name customary among the Greeks. Leo Tomitius was hailed emperor by the soldiers in 1046. — Leibniz.]

who had been the Greek catapan, sent from the city  
to which Constantine, the city’s founder, gave his name,  
and over which Constantine and likewise Basil  
then ruled: that fierce Gauls had come, hired by Melo,  
who had rebelled against both rulers  
and was urging the Normans to ravage the Apulian territories.

When Turnicius had received this report,  
he quickly directed the Greek forces against the enemy.  
He did not prepare the first engagements himself,  
but through a lieutenant whose surname was Pacianus  
and whose name was Leo.

[Note: Leo Pacianus. — Leibniz.]

He led many Pelasgians to war beside the bank of the Fertorius,  
a place also called Arenula,

[Note: The river Arena is on the southern side of Sicily and is so called because it contains white sands around the surrounding mouths. Theodorus Fazellus, book VI, chapter 4 of the first Decade. — Leibniz. However, this place called Arenula must be sought in Apulia, since the Normans had not yet crossed over to Sicily. — Editor.]

The month of May was an especially suitable time for Mars;  
kings customarily go forth to war at that season,  
and at first fortune was equal in battle on both sides.

Turnicius then followed with his companions,  
after his soldiers had been reinforced; but he turned his back  
and withdrew, having been defeated. In this battle Pacianus fell.

Victory increases the Normans’ powerful strength.  
They learned from experience that the Greeks possessed no strength,  
and discovered that they were not bold but cowardly.

The fame of the empire informs its rulers  
that the Normans, under Melo’s leadership, were ravaging Apulia.

When the court heard this, it judged him an enemy;  
if he were captured, it ordered that he be beheaded.

Basil was ordered to march against him the following year  
with a large Greek force.

[Note: Basil of Constantinople regained the empire in the year of salvation 977. — Leibniz. This has nothing to do with the matter. Leibniz was mistaken both in name and in chronology, attaching here a note concerning Basil, who reigned in the tenth century; it should have referred to the Basil placed in command of the Greek army in the eleventh century. — Editor of the *Patrologia*.]

Basil, who had become catapan, had the surname Bajianus.

[Note: Sigonius calls him Bubaganus; he was the catapan of the emperor Basil. — Leibniz.]

The Greeks call this office *catapan*; we use the word for the whole:

[Note: Among the Greeks, *catapan* means the prefect or commander of the entire army. — Leibniz.]

whoever among the Danaans holds this office  
organizes for the people everything that is useful to them  
and supplies each person with everything he ought to receive.

Near Cannae, where the river Aufidus flows,

[Note: The river Aufidus in Apulia, called the Ofanto by the Italians. — Tiremaeus.]

the two sides fought around the Kalends of October.

[Note: 1019, as is believed. — Leibniz.]

Melo, not strong enough to resist with his small force,  
turned his back, deprived of a large part of his men.  
Ashamed to remain defeated in his native land,  
he went to the Samnites and stayed there.

Afterward he sought the assistance of Henry, king of the Germans,

[Note: Henry I, king and emperor, 39. — Tiremaeus. Henry, surnamed “the Holy.” — Leibniz.]

who, calm in his customary manner,  
received the suppliant and promised him the gift of nearby assistance.

But Melo, forestalled by death, could not return.

The king Henry buried him, as is the royal custom:  
he accompanied the funeral rites all the way to the tomb  
and adorned the grave of the buried man with a royal poem.

[Note: In the *Life of Saint Henry*, book XXII, it is recorded that Ismael—corrupt, I think, and a familiar name substituted for the unknown Melo—appointed prefect of Apulia by the emperor, died at Bamberg and was buried in the chapter house of the Great Monastery. — Leibniz.]

After Melo’s death, whose assistance the Gauls  
had hoped would come, their entire hope failed.  
Mournful, they returned to the shores of Campania  
and pitched their tents nowhere in any fixed place.

The diminished number of their people terrified them,
