as did the large force of the enemy standing around them.

Therefore no place seemed safe for them:  
sometimes among mountains, now in valleys far removed.

But when they no longer hoped that assistance could be prepared,  
since to the defeated all circumstances seem troublesome  
and fortune itself is thought to aid the victors,  
and when, wandering and unstable, they had already roamed through many places  
and could settle nowhere in a fixed abode,  
a nearby dispute at last gave them the advice to remain.

For they knew that a Lombard possessed greater strength;  
they attached themselves to him and faithfully remained with his assistance,  
so that through his service they might be protected from the others,  
and so that, if they obtained favorable turns in the war,  
their fame might become illustrious.

For this reason they measured out a suitable place for a camp,  
one overflowing with water, herbs, and trees alike,  
which supplied the people with everything necessary.

Soon they chose one of their own, an outstanding man named Ranulf,

[Note: Ranulf, first duke of the Romans. — Leibniz.]

[Col. 1031A]

to be commander of the army, whose orders it would not be lawful to resist.

When they were preparing to fortify the site of their first settlement,  
a dense marsh on every side, together with a great abundance of croaking frogs,  
prevented them from fortifying the settlement.

Not far from there they found another place suitable for their stations.  
With no inhabitant of the homeland giving them assistance,  
they tried to fortify it for their own defense;  
and, once the fortification had been made,  
they were pleased to join themselves to a certain man

[Note: Pandulf IV. — Leibniz.]

who was prince of Capua.

He was then the first and most powerful of the princes of Latium.  
The allies, hastening to be protected by this prince,  
ravaged the territories and increased the number of their enemies by force of arms.

But because the meditations of the worldly mind  
are inclined toward avarice, and money prevails everywhere,  
they continually attached themselves to whichever man paid more,  
despising now one, now another.  
Everyone was pleased to serve the man  
from whom he received the greater payment.

They loved wars among peoples more than treaties of peace  
and, according to their strength and the circumstances of the time,  
weighed the changes of service; the more they gave,  
the more supporters they had.

A great desire to rule supplied wars to those princes;  
each wanted to be more powerful.  
One and another sought to subject the rights of the other.

From this fuel arose disputes, battles, and deaths;  
for this reason countless evils increase among mortals.

Alas! Miserable are those who strive for anything in the world:  
after enduring countless vain labors for empty praise,  
they will suffer even more once they leave worldly things behind.

The Normans never approved the complete victory  
of the Lombards, lest punishment return upon themselves.

They prevented every faction from being utterly overthrown,  
now adding their favor to these, now to those.  
Gallic cunning deceives the Italians  
and permits no full triumph to be seized from the enemy.

Thus the discord of Latium restores the despairing Gauls  
to the hope that had previously been destroyed.

In this way they increased both their strength and their resources.  
If any dangerous neighbor fled to them,  
they welcomed him gladly.  
All whom they saw coming, they instructed in their customs and language,  
so that one people might be formed.

After several years, the army of the Gauls founded the city of Aversa,

[Note: Aversa, a city situated between Naples and Capua. — Leibniz.]

safe under the count Ranulf.

[Note: *Consul* is used for “count.” — Leibniz.]

This place, rich in resources, is also useful and pleasant;  
it lacks neither sown fields, fruits, meadows, nor orchards.  
There is no more agreeable place in the world.  
The prudent judgment of the aforementioned noble count chose it.

From his distinguished stock came Richard,

[Note: William of Jumièges agrees, book VII, chapter 43. But Leo of Ostia, book II, chapter 67, relates that Asclettin the Norman married Ranulf’s sister, succeeded him in the county of Aversa, and fathered Richard, the father of Jordan and grandfather of Richard II. Pandulf, prince of Capua, had made Ranulf count of Aversa. Richard I later seized the principality of Capua in 1053. See Leo of Ostia, book III, chapter 16. — Leibniz.]

[Col. 1032A]

who later succeeded him and than whom no one was more courageous,  
no one more generous. He fathered Jordan,  
who was no less than he in virtue; and Jordan then fathered Richard,  
who, though still a young man, possessed strength worthy of a man.

After Ranulf had completed the walls of Aversa,  
he sent messengers to his homeland to make the Normans hurry  
and to report how pleasant Apulia was:  
that the poor would soon become wealthy  
and that the rich would have much more to possess.

After hearing these things, many poor and wealthy men alike arrived.  
The needy hastened so that the burden of poverty might be lifted,  
and the rich so that they might seek the best opportunities.

Meanwhile, after much time had passed,  
the Gauls were no longer feared in the Italian regions,  
because the catapan Basil had driven the Normans away  
by defeating Melo, the enemy of the empire.

Suddenly Ardoinus came to Aversa,

[Note: The Lombard Hardoinus led the Normans. After he had struck down a certain Saracen during an expedition, he was deprived of the horse he had won for himself in battle; desiring to avenge this injury, he conceived the plan of taking Apulia from the Greeks. — Tiremaeus.]

and with many men brought along with him  
made all Apulia tremble.

He was a Lombard and wished to drive out the Greeks.  
I shall explain why he was hostile to them  
and why he led the Gauls.

While Michael the Epileptic

[Note: Commonly called “the Paphlagonian”; he became emperor in 1034 and died in 1041. — Leibniz.]

was presiding over the imperial throne,  
he ordered arms to be taken against the Sicilian enemies  
who did not cease ravaging the Calabrian borders.

Michael Dochianus was sent to accomplish this task.  
Having powerfully assembled many horsemen and foot soldiers  
from every direction, he restrained the Sicilian enemies.

Among those assembled was Ardoinus, together with certain followers of his,  
some of the Greeks left behind after the slaughter,  
and a populace of Lombards mixed with certain Gauls  
who had been fugitives when Basil waged war.

When Dochianus returned from his victory over the enemy  
and paid rewards to the soldiers in the city of Regina,

[Note: Regina was once a city of immense power; for this reason many maintain that its name became the word for a city, as though it were a royal city. — Tiremaeus.]

Ardoinus could receive none of the gifts given to the Greeks  
and remained wretched and unrewarded.

He therefore angrily summoned his men  
and accused the Greeks of shameful avarice,  
because gifts that ought to be given to men  
were bestowed upon an idle people,  
although a Greek is almost like a woman.

Angered by these insults, Michael ordered that Ardoinus,  
according to Greek custom, be stripped and beaten,  
so that after being severely scourged with leather thongs  
he would regret his offense.

Driven by the tortures of so great a disgrace,  
and unwilling to leave the punishment unavenged,  
he secretly abandoned the Greek camp with his people.

A troop of Pelasgians sent to pursue him  
found him in the field. When it tried to engage him,  
it gave way; and after fifty Pelasgians had been killed there,  
Ardoinus hastened to Aversa.

He told the Normans everything that had happened to him  
and vehemently reproached them:

Since Apulia is a land of such manifold usefulness,  
why should it be left in the possession of effeminate Greeks,  
when theirs is a cowardly race,  
whom drunkenness, the companion of gluttony, often makes weak,  
who have frequently been put to flight by the smallest enemy,  
and who, heavy in their clothing, are suited to display  
garments rather than arms?

Although compelled by the valor of the Danaans  
the Normans had previously left the Apulian fields;  
now, stimulated by him, they prepared to return.

When their numbers and strength had increased, they all gathered  
and chose twelve of the noblest as leaders—  
men distinguished by lineage, dignity of character, and age.  
Others obeyed these leaders when they were advanced to the countship;  
the countship was their honorary title

[Note: The title of countship was also, for us, the name of an office until the time of Hugh Capet. — Tiremaeus.

It also signified a territory, since a countship was assigned to each man at the same time. — Leibniz.]

[Col. 1033B]

and the territory with which they were endowed.

They divided all the lands among themselves, unless hostile fortune opposed them.  
They set out the individual territories that by lot  
were to fall to each leader, together with the revenues of each place.  
Under this arrangement they hurried together to war.

At that time no imperial army  
was heard of in those regions. The entire Greek matter was quiet,  
and rumor reported that war against the Sicilians  
was being conducted only in a period of calm.

As the Normans entered the Apulian fields,  
Melfia was suddenly captured.

[Note: Melfi, or Melfia, a city in Apulia. — Leibniz.]

Whatever they plundered they carried to that city.  
There Basil, whom I mentioned above, had previously built  
a modest dwelling, seeing that the place offered unexpected advantages.

Now, through the influx of population, it is regarded as a distinguished city,  
the most famous in the Italian regions, rich in the pleasant fertility  
of its situation, lacking neither grain nor streams,  
and distinguished by ducal honor in the part where it lies.

When the Normans heard that Michael had returned  
from the shores of Sicily, they prepared for war,  
although the force of the Greeks was large  
and their own people very few.

Their infantry numbered only five hundred,  
while the cavalry contingent numbered seven hundred.  
A few men protected by shields were defended by coats of mail.

The armed foot soldiers were ordered to surround  
the right and left flanks; some cavalrymen were joined to them,  
so that the infantry might be more secure with their accompaniment.

They ordered them under no circumstances to leave the field,  
so that they could be received back if they were put to flight by the enemy.

After they had been arranged and stationed in this way on both sides,  
the cavalry wedge withdrew a little way into the distance.  
A single Greek wedge was sent against it.

For the Danaans do not usually loosen all their cohorts  
in the first engagement, but first send one legion  
and then another, so that the increased strength of their own men  
may weaken the enemy and increase their terror.

Thus, when the leader of the cavalry sees the enemy resisting,  
he suddenly rushes forward with the more select soldiers  
who remain with him. In this way he customarily  
blunts the enemy’s strength completely  
while restoring the courage of his own men.

When the lines of both sides had joined,  
a great battle took place beside the swift waters  
of the river Lebentus.

[Note: Perhaps *Sebethus* or *Labentus* should be read. — Tiremaeus. But if the battle was fought at the city of Melfi, as William seems to imply, and on the Apulian plain, I do not know whether Tiremaeus’ conjecture is successful.]

The Danaans were defeated, and the army of the Gauls  
bravely pursued them. The Apulian plain received many bodies,  
but the river received still more.

The Argive people, indeed, struck with excessive terror,  
fled trembling. Neither the roughness of the terrain  
nor the rushing waters prevented them,  
as it prevents a fugitive from throwing himself headlong.  
The riverbed engulfed more men drowned in the stream  
than the sword had delivered to death.

The Gallic people struck some with arrows, others with swords,  
and the Greeks suffered a great slaughter in various ways.

Michael escaped with a few men and climbed a mountain.  
He seemed to have reached the summit of the neighboring mountains.

Victory increased the Gauls’ strength and courage,  
and they no longer feared waging war against the Danaans.

Just as a hawk, accustomed to seize smaller birds  
without hesitation, hesitates to attack a larger bird,  
but, if it can overcome even one crane,  
will not afterward fear the swan  
and will no longer dread confronting great birds,

so the Gauls, having gathered their forces,  
again led to the river said to be the Aufidus,  
near Cannae, all whom Michael was able to bring with him.

The Gauls returned to battle, as they had done before.  
Michael yielded to them; the defeated Pelasgians fled;  
many were killed, and the life of the fleeing Dochianus  
was saved by the aid of his armed attendant.

His horse happened to stumble as it entered the river. Michael, almost already  
within the grasp of the hostile crowd, escaped  
when his attendant led his own horse.

The Normans were encouraged all the more  
as their fortunate success in arms increased.

Michael, defeated, sought the heights of Mount Pelusium.

From there he sent messengers to the Greek army  
then stationed in the Sicilian regions,  
ordering it to come and restore the forces  
of which he stood in need after being driven away by the enemy.

The victorious Normans decided to return to Melfia.  
There, after collecting the spoils of the Achaean people,  
they remained for a while in peaceful quiet.

They laid out twelve streets according to the number of their counts  
and built an equal number of houses for the counts in the city.

But because earthly honors always belong to earthly inhabitants...

They incur hatred by refusing the commands of the counts, whom the fierce Gauls had preferred to themselves and wished to preserve. They preferred to place a native of Latium before their own people; they loved Adenolfus, the name of this prince of Benevento—men whom perhaps he himself had compelled to change their former pledge [Col. 1034D] by giving gold or silver. What does the ambition for wealth not compel one to undertake? It can overthrow sound judgment and loosen the rigid bonds of loyalty.

After hearing the report that Dochianus’s army had arrived in the Sicilian regions, and being informed that Dochianus needed reinforcements, he hastened to the Calabrians and to whatever men could be gathered from every quarter, in order to avenge the bodies of his men, which lay unburied in the fields and waters.

[Col. 1035A] Some were present with the Greeks whom the worst error had made insane, and who took their name from its author. The common people call them those who say that the Father suffered together with Christ. With one finger they impress the sign of the cross upon their forehead, and they taught that the Son had no person different from the Father, and that the Holy Spirit likewise had this same person.

These men hastened together to the war, all of them united in purpose, so that the forces Michael had lost might be restored. Nevertheless, he forbade Michael to remain commander of this army, under whom the administration of the Roman empire had continued, because he had achieved no success against the Normans. He ordered Exaugustus to assume this office and lead the Danai into battle.

[Col. 1035B] This man is said to have been begotten by that Basil who, under the command of Melo, had forced the Gauls to turn their backs. From there Michael Dochianus returned to the Sicilian shores.

Exaugustus addressed those entrusted to his command as follows:

“May your manly prudence, vigorous in its condition, not permit you to possess womanly hearts, men. What cowardice continually compels you to flee? Remember your ancestors, whose valor subjected the whole world to them.

“Hector, the bravest of men, fell by Achilles’ arms. Troy collapsed, consumed by the fires of Mycenaean rage. [Note: [Col. 1035D] Leibniz corrects printed *Michaenei* to *Mycenaei*, “Mycenaean.”] India knows how great Philip’s strength was. Did not Alexander, his most valiant son, subject the mighty kingdoms of many peoples to the Pelasgians?

“Among the western peoples and throughout all the regions of the world, the fame of the Greeks used to be an object of fear. What nation, after hearing the name of the Greeks, dared to stand in the field? Scarcely did towns, camps, or cities render their enemies safe from their power.

“Stand firm, I beg you, remembering the valor of your ancestors, and do not let confidence in your feet make you degenerate. He deprives the enemy of strength who dares to stand manfully. Take care to follow the first footsteps of your forefathers. Let flight now be displeasing; let the whole world recognize that you are brave men.

“The people of the Franks are not to be feared in war, unequal as they are to us in number and strength.”

By these words he inflamed the courage of the Greeks, and ordered all the Argolics to leave the mountains and seek the level plain. He established the camp on the plain.

[Col. 1035D] The Gauls sent scouts, prepared to observe the Danai. They reported that they were ready for battle and that, although their commander’s mind had changed, many feared nothing. Leaving their comrades on the mountain, so that they might return safely if necessity arose, the native inhabitants descended to aid the Danai.

Both peoples assembled on the level plain. A fierce battle then took place, as each side strove for victory.

[Col. 1036A] Now these men fled and drove others to flight; now the others did the same. While the Argives pressed the Gauls fiercely for a long time and were already almost victorious, Galterus suddenly burst into the midst of the enemy, urging the fleeing Normans to return to the battle. He was one of the chosen counts, the distinguished son of a friend. The Achivi had never experienced a more serious conflict; many soldiers fell there, and many heroes perished together.

The wretched Exaugustus, led by Adenolfus, was bound before the victor’s horse, for the enemy desired to display the splendor of his triumph. In that year victory fell to the Gauls three times.

With the Danai thrown into confusion, there was now no hope of a trophy. Everything was surrendered above the splendid Apulian walls of Bari.

[Note: [Col. 1035D] Bari is otherwise called Barium, a maritime city of Apulia. It was completely destroyed by William I, king of Sicily. TIREM.]

[Col. 1036B] At that time Monopolis, Juvenacus, and many other cities, rejecting their treaty with the Greeks, entered into an agreement with the foreign Franks.

Then, since God no longer wished his empire to endure, Michael died.

[Note: [Col. 1035D] Michael Calaphates, the nephew of Michael the Paphlagonian through his sister, succeeded him in the year of salvation 1043. Constantine Monomachus succeeded him in the same year. [Col. 1036D] LEIB.]

His nephew Michael succeeded him, and was likewise called Constantine. To obtain some assistance from him, the Apulian people sent Synodianus. When he arrived and first landed at Hydruntum, he sent envoys to the allied Frankish cities, asking that he be received; they refused to obey his request. He wished to restore the army, but, since many soldiers had been killed and scattered, he was able to retain only a few men. For this reason Synodianus did not leave the city walls.

[Col. 1036C] Nevertheless, he issued an imperial order that he should return. During this period, while the prince of Salerno, Guaimarius, was making many promises to himself,

[Note: [Col. 1036D] The Guaimarius mentioned here is called Guamarinus by others; he was prince of Salerno. TIREM.]

the Norman people rejected Adenolfus’s service. Only the citizens who had turned away had given themselves to Guaimarius’s rule; the other Gauls whom Apulia contained wished to serve Argyros, the son of Melo. His father had previously worked to introduce the Gauls and was the first to strive to bestow gifts upon them in Italy.

Argyros, poor though bold and noble, denied that he could rule so great a people, since he had no silver or gold to offer. They declared that they loved not gold but Argyros himself, whose father had been gracious to them. He granted the people’s request. At night he led with him from Bari the men who were foremost in age and judgment, and, when they had been brought to the church of Saint Apollinaris, he addressed them as follows:

“Since I have no means of payment by which I could enrich a powerful people, I wonder why your people wishes to place me before itself. For I know that you need many different things, and, when I do not provide them, I shall regret that I am unable to do so.”

They replied:

“With you as our prince, no one among us will be poor or needy. Under your leadership fortune will favor us; and, once you have become our prince, the paths of counsel which it used to reveal to us under your father’s leadership will be opened to us through you.”

When they had said this, they immediately raised him up unanimously; by common prayer he was made prince.

[Note: [Col. 1037D] Among the Franks, as among the Caninefates, according to Tacitus, it was customary to place the chosen king upon a shield and carry him aloft on their shoulders. TIREM.]

Meanwhile Maniacus, full of wickedness, came to Hydruntum with a great array of Danai.

[Note: [Col. 1037D] Maniacus is Georgius Maniacus the Byzantine, who was prefect of Constantine Monomachus, emperor at Constantinople and king of Sicily. LEIB.]

He had been ordered by Michael to enter Latium. In him there was nothing worthy of praise except his appearance. He was proud in mind and overflowing with savage ferocity.

After dismissing his fleets at Hydruntum, he stirred up his hostile army to attack the cities held by the Franks. He first spread through the fields of Monopolis.

[Col. 1037B] Maniacus killed many; some he hanged from trees, while he slaughtered others after cutting off their heads. The tyrant dared to inflict an unheard-of kind of execution upon infants: because they had been captured, he buried the living body of a boy in the earth, leaving the head protruding above it. In this way he killed many and took care to spare no one.

Afterward he approached Matera,

[Note: [Col. 1037D] Matera is a city in Apulia, called Acherontus by Livy. LEIB.]

where the camp of the Carthaginian commander is said to have been fixed when Hannibal subjected Italy to the Africans. In the fields, with a furious mind, he slaughtered two hundred captured farmers.

Neither child nor old man, monk nor priest, was safe from punishment. The unjust man pitied no one.

Meanwhile Michael, who had sent this Maniacus, was captured and blinded; after being blinded, he was driven from the citadel. This was done by the sisters Zoe and Theodora.

[Note: [Col. 1037D] Zoe, the widow of Michael the Paphlagonian, adopted Michael Calaphates as her son. After he had assumed the insignia of power and, ungrateful, exiled his mother, the source of his imperial dignity, he was captured by the conspiring people and deprived of the use of his eyes; Zoe was restored to the imperial power. [Col. 1038D] LEIB.]

[Col. 1037C] The first was the wife of Michael’s uncle until this man’s succession. Because he himself refused to share the kingdom with her, thinking that she ought to be disinherited with the senate’s opposition, he was deprived of sight and captured. Zoe was joined in marriage to Constantine Monomachus.

[Note: [Col. 1038D] Constantine Monomachus was Zoe’s third husband. LEIB.]

Maniacus was hostile to him, and he to Maniacus,

[Note: [Col. 1038D] Fazellus says that the disagreements between Maniacus and Monomachus arose from the hatred which the Roman clergy exercised against Maniacus. LEIB.]

because each had abused the other’s mistress.

The throne, entrusted to Monomachus by the jealousy of power, shook the tyrant’s mind with excessive terror, and, driven by hatred and anger, he reported his shameful grievances. He commanded all those whom he had led with him to Argos; once he had made himself prince, no one was to obey Monomachus.

The treacherous man assumed imperial dress for himself and did not fear to take upon himself the name of the holy empire.

[Col. 1037D] After Monomachus had assumed the dignity of the throne, he ordered Argyros to strive to win over the Gauls, to arrange that they join his own faithful supporters, and to promise them great rewards.

[Col. 1038A] Argyros, unwilling that imperial glory should be lost to him, restrained the Normans from besieging Trani, which alone at that time supported the Greek forces, and ceased devastating the neighboring places.

Meanwhile the imperial messenger who had arrived bearing very great gifts was captured by Maniacus. They inflicted various punishments upon him. Maniacus had him cruelly tortured by applying horse dung mixed with cleansing material to his nostrils, ears, and mouth, and then killed him in the stable.

When he himself saw that he possessed so great a weight of gold, he began to be excessively elated and returned from there to Tarentum. He distributed a great deal of gold among the Argolics, so that they might be more favorably disposed toward him. He assumed the imperial purple, and his right foot was adorned with red leather, which the one who undertakes the care of the empire customarily wears.

[Col. 1038B] From there he came to Bari surrounded by many soldiers, hoping to deceive Argyros with promises. He attempted to reconcile the Gauls to himself so that Argyros might become his colleague against the empire of Monomachus. If he could obtain their assistance, he hoped that his forces would be able to kill the enemy and retain for himself, with little effort, the diadem taken from Constantine.

His hope was empty. He could persuade neither the Normans nor their prince to change their minds; despised, he withdrew from them. Therefore, since he departed full of intense fury at having been rejected, he divided the army into four parts and ordered them to go raiding in every direction.

[Col. 1038C] Most of the people and livestock were led away to Tarentum.

[Note: [Col. 1038D] Tarentum was a city of Calabria at the far end of Italy, near the borders of the Salentines; it was founded by Tara, son of Neptune. LEIB.]

At the same time Argyros, sent by Constantine with many talents of gold and silver, offered gifts to the Normans and asked them to assist him, so that with their aid Maniacus might kill the enemy of the holy empire. He asserted that, once the enemy had been defeated, they would earn very great rewards according to their wishes.

Accordingly, many Normans were made enemies of Maniacus, not by love of money but by their affection for the commander Argyros. The counts of Aversa also came voluntarily with many of their men. Tancred’s son, their greatest hope, was present: William, ready for war, accompanied by the count Rodulfus of Drengot,

[Col. 1038D] who had governed the city after Ranulfus’s death.

[Note: [Col. 1038D] The city of Aversa. LEIB.]

William’s noble name terrified the Danai. Because he was strong, he was said to have iron arms.

[Col. 1039A]

[Note: [Col. 1039D] William Iron-Arm, son of Tancred. LEIB.]

For he possessed great strength and courage.

His brother Robert was the man who later obtained the duchy, Guiscardus.

[Note: [Col. 1039D] Many called Guiscardus “Erroneus,” because he wandered through the lands, but the following derivation is more pleasing and more appropriate to our usage. Even in our own time we commonly call a cautious and clever man “Guiscard.” TIREM.

The surname Guiscardus denotes a prudent man. *Wys* means “wise,” and *Wyssen* means “to know.” The editor of Rouen observes that in his own time *Guishard* commonly signified “clever.” [Col. 1040D] From Robert Guiscard and Roger, the sons of Tancred of Hauteville in Gaul, the lineage of the Norman princes in Italy was propagated. LEIB.]

—prudent in every undertaking.

Trusting in the company of so many counts, Argyros hastened against the enemy. Maniacus had come to the river Taram,

[Note: [Col. 1040D] It may perhaps be read *Tarum*, which is a river. TIREM.

Leibniz read *Tarani*, but the first reading should be retained.]

and had measured out his camp there for some days.

But, shut up in the city of Tarentum, he could not withstand the arrival of so great a people. The Gauls came to the river and, having taken possession of the empty Greek camp, advanced as far as the bridge.

The waters of the sea flowed around it on both sides; between the lofty opposing cliffs the water was cut off in such a way that the city could be crossed to with the bridge’s assistance. The route which now seemed short to a traveler would appear long to one circling along the shore.

[Col. 1039B] For Tarentum, enclosed for the greater part by the sea, would soon have become an island if a modest hill had not intervened.

William challenged the Achivi enclosed within the walls to battle, but they never came out from the walls to join combat. No force of the river was more terrifying to the enemy than the spear of so great a commander.

Thus a zealous snake-charmer, wishing to capture an asp, tries by various arts to draw it out from the earth’s entrails, where it remains hidden and safe. Here he blocks one ear so that it may not hear anything harmful; with its tail fastened, the other part is fixed in the earth.

The Danai pretended not to hear the Gauls calling them to battle and, having put up the bars, remained in the city.

When the Gauls saw that the Pelasgians did not wish to come out to battle, and when the strength of the city’s position deprived them of hope of capturing its walls—for the site was extremely well fortified—they withdrew. After remaining in the city for a short time, Maniacus returned to Hydruntum.

Again Argyros came, as did Theodorus; the former arrived with many soldiers, the latter with many fleets, prepared by imperial command to hasten against Maniacus. They shook the enemy’s mind with various terrors, and, wavering in spirit, he fluctuated now this way, now that.

At last, compelled by excessive fear to leave the city, he established his camp beside the sea, where the rocks had been cut away, in a difficult place.

[Col. 1040B] No access to it could be made by anyone. He caused the ships placed upon steps among the cliffs to cling there, so that, once the sea had been pacified, he might cross over. Some men whom he believed had especially disturbed the waters he tortured and burned with fire.

Before the sea waves had been completely calmed by tranquil weather, he sought the ships and crossed the sea. That crossing, however, profited the wretched man nothing. When the army deployed by Monomachus met him, he fell and paid the penalty for his crimes with his body.

[Note: [Col. 1040D] In this engagement Maniacus was wounded in the chest, fell from his horse, and died in his own blood. TIREM.]

[Col. 1039] Here ends the first book.

## The Second Book Begins

[Col. 1039C] Argyros, having driven the enemy from the borders of Latium, went to Hydruntum with a large company and many men. The city was handed over to him, and the citizens rejoiced in this prince.

From there, returning to Bari, he permitted the Gauls to depart. They went to serve Guaimarius at Salerno. The prince Guaimarius, trusting in their strength, led them with him back to Bari and besieged it.

He ordered Argyros to obey him, leave the city, and cross over to the Greeks. Argyros refused to obey the instructions of the man giving the order. Nevertheless, since he did not dare to engage in battle, he guarded himself in the city, being unfit for combat, while devastating the fields and the pleasant cultivated lands of Bari.

Guaimarius returned to the walls of his own city.

At that time Constantine governed the laws of the empire. He ordered Argyros to come to him as quickly as possible.

[Col. 1039D] Argyros favored the imperial commands. Carried across the waves of the Adriatic, he approached the city of the empire in a calm spirit. The man who governed the city received him as he came out with great honors.

Meanwhile, the people whom he had ruled attached one party to Count Peter and another to Drogo, the son of Tancred. His brother William, who had lived for only a short time during Drogo’s rule, had been said to possess iron arms. If he had been permitted to live, no poet could have set forth his praises. So great was his integrity of character, so living his valor.

All Italy trembled before Unfredus and his brother Drogo, although at that time Peter, their close kinsman, was richer than they. He founded Andria, then built Corato and Busilias, and built Barolo on the sea coast.

His fame had risen above that of the other counts. But Count Unfredus and his brother Drogo laid aside their pride, because, while he prepared to enter the struggle, the unhappy man, losing prosperous times, was defeated and captured. With fortune’s wheel turned, it began to exalt Tancred’s sons.

The previously mentioned ruler of the empire consulted Argyros as to how he might drive the Gauls from the shores of Italy; for he had discovered that they could no longer be driven out.

[Col. 1041A] Therefore, prepared to approach others with a plan, he hoped to deceive with promises those whom he knew to be strong in arms and unconquerable by arms.

For he heard that the Norman people was always inclined toward greed, and that whoever gives more is loved more. A large amount of money, much silver, precious clothing, and gold was entrusted to Argyros to carry, so that the Normans might be deceived and, departing from the borders of Hesperia, quickly cross the sea, expecting to earn great rewards in the service of the empire.

He also ordered that, if they refused to cross, what was to have been given to them should be given to others, whose fierce attacks would crush the Gauls.

Argyros obeyed. He crossed into Apulia as ordered, summoned the Frankish counts, and promised to give them great gifts if they crossed over to Argos, leaving Latium, where they were engaged in a serious struggle with the Persians. He swore that they would be gratefully received by the one who ruled the empire, and promised that they would be enriched with great resources.

The Greeks’ crafty promise did not escape the cunning of the people that wished to rule Latium. They declared that they would not leave Apulia while they were assembling, unless perhaps a stronger crowd came against them, drove them out, and crushed them.

The admirable Leo was ruling the Roman see at this time.

[Note: [Col. 1041D] Pope Leo IX, the ninth of that name, began his pontificate in the year of salvation 1049. He had previously been called Bruno and was bishop of Toul. TIREM.

He had previously been called Bruno and was bishop of Toul. LEIB.]

When the Apulian people heard of the pope’s arrival, it began to bring various complaints and to accuse the Gauls of different crimes. Mixing truth with falsehood, Argyros sent messages to the pope and repeatedly begged him to free Italy, which lacked liberty, and force the unjust people to depart, since Apulia, oppressed beneath their yoke, was being ruined.

[Col. 1041C] The earlier Norman leaders, Drogo and Guaimarius, had died at this time: one had been killed by the citizens and kinsmen through treachery at Salerno; the other by the natives, because he trusted them too much, and was killed at Pontelario.

[Note: [Col. 1041D] While Drogo was striving to enlarge his dominion and fortifying the cities of Apulia, he was surrounded at the town of Montolium by the ambushes of the Lombards and Apulians and killed through the treachery of Visone, an Apulian by birth. LEIBNIT.]

The Gallic people complained to the pope that it was without a ruler. Nevertheless, it came to meet him with as many troops of cavalry and infantry as it could muster. They had heard that some men from Latium had arrived with a large army, and that the pope was accompanied by countless Alemanni and Teutons, prepared for war.

[Col. 1041D] Although the Normans shone in splendid armor, they feared to resist such great armies when they saw them. They sent envoys to request a treaty of peace and to ask that the pope calmly accept their service. They all declared that they were ready to obey the pope, that they did not wish to offend him, and that they wished to learn from him the duty he required.

[Col. 1042A] If it pleased him, they asked him to be their lord and declared themselves faithful.

The Teutons, whom their hair and appearance had made exceptionally handsome and tall in body, mocked the shorter-looking Norman bodies and paid no attention to their envoys, since they were not equal either in number of people or in strength. They approached the pope, proud in words and spirit:

“Order the Normans to leave the Italian lands, cast down their arms, and return to their ancestral borders.

“If they refuse, we wish you neither to accept a treaty of peace from them nor to heed their envoys. They have not yet tested the swords of the Teutons. Let them perish by the sword, or be compelled to depart; unwillingly, let them leave the land which they do not wish to leave voluntarily.”

Although the pope resisted the arrogance of the proud people in various ways, he could not calm their spirits. The most worthless dregs of the Italian people—the Marcher people, deservedly rejected by honorable Latins—gave them hope.

Although many Italians abound in great valor, fear, flight, and luxury were innate in these men; the German contingent did not seem large.

The Normans returned in confusion, peace having been denied, and reported the Teutons’ swelling reply.

The time was already near the cutting of the wheat harvest, but the farmers had not yet gathered the green sheaves. Because the Frankish people lacked bread, they toasted the sheaves over a fire and ate them after they had been scorched. Such was the life they led beside the rebellious camps, which served the Teutons on every side and gave them nothing required for bodily existence.

[Col. 1042C] After his brother Drogo’s death, his surviving brother Unfredus was regarded as one of the foremost nobles among the Frankish people.

[Note: [Col. 1042D] Unfredus, the third son of Tancred by his wife Trezenda. TIREM.]

Then there was Richard, recently chosen count in the city of Aversa, and, shortly before, Robert had followed his brothers. By his magnanimous valor he surpassed his elder brothers; he took part in that war.

His surname was Guiscardus, because neither Cicero possessed such cleverness nor Ulysses such craft.

Among them were Peter and Galterus, the sons of a distinguished friend; also Aureolanus, Ubertus, Musca, Rainaldus, Count Hugo, and Count Girardus. The latter had been placed over the Beneventans, while the others governed the Thelesines.

[Col. 1042D] The virtue of Rodulfus, count of Boiano, accompanied these men—he was powerful both in counsel and in arms.

Scarcely three thousand knights followed these nobles, along with a few infantrymen. Because they had lacked bread for three days, all preferred to seek arms and die honorably in battle rather than have such great men overcome by the disgraceful death of hunger.

[Col. 1043A] The Alemannic people, surrounded by a large body of attendants, trusted vainly in the fleeing Lombard crowd’s assistance. It believed that the Normans would turn their backs at the first encounters or be destroyed.

But victory in war depends neither on number, horses, people, nor arms, but on the one to whom it is granted from heaven.

Between the Teutonic and Norman forces there was a hill. An innumerable Apulian, Balbense, Campanian, Marsan, and Thelesine people had come to assist the former. The Teutonic commanders Guarnerus and Albertus brought no more than seven hundred Swabians.

This people was courageous and bore fierce spirits, but was not skilled at using horses. Against their blows the sword was more effective than the lance. Their horses were not skillfully turned by their hands, nor did their lances deliver powerful blows; their swords, however, were especially long and exceedingly sharp. They often cut through a body struck from the crown of the head, and, once dismounted, they stood firm-footed. They preferred to die fighting rather than turn their backs, and were more formidable in this way than while they were cavalrymen. Such was the boldness of the people that had joined itself to the people of Italy.

The German counts Transmundus and Atto commanded them, as did a descendant sprung from the line of Burrellinus.

They hastened to war together, along with Maldrefus [printed *Maldrefiis*], an inhabitant of the maritime plain, and Rofredus, the father-in-law of Rodulfus of Molinara, whose castle was called Guardia.

[Col. 1043B] And there were many others whose names I do not know.

The Romans, Samnites, and Capuans also sent assistance here, nor did Ancona withhold its resources. The Spoletans came here, together with the Sabines; the Firmani also came. It cannot be enumerated in my verses how great a host arrived, striving to erase the name of the Frankish people.

With the Teutons, all these men had pitched their tents beside a river called Fertorius; a nearby city bore the name given it by its own citizens.

When the Normans learned that hope of peace and flight had been denied them, and that they had no place to which they could flee, they climbed the hill to observe the enemy camp. After viewing the camp, they armed themselves and appointed Richard, count of Aversa, to the right wing.

[Col. 1043D] He was to approach the Lombards; a renowned troop of cavalry accompanied him in front. Unfredus was chosen commander of the central division, to oppose the brave Swabians in battle. Robert, his brother, was ordered to guard the left wing with the Calabrian people, so that, whenever he saw that assistance was needed, he might hasten to aid his companions and restore their strength.

The Teutons had armed two wings opposite the two wings of the Normans. All the Italians stood massed together on the other side; for in the contest of war they did not know how to arrange their lines in proper order.

Richard first began to move his arms against them and attacked boldly. The Italians, overcome by his force, did not withstand him; trembling seized them all.

[Col. 1044A] Turning to flight, they scattered at a run across level ground and steep places. The force of the flight itself compelled many to fall; they were cut down by javelins and sword.

As when, where doves have gathered, a hawk attacks them in its swift flight from above, making them seek the rocky ridges of a lofty mountain, yet capturing those whom it itself catches, so that they can no longer seek any refuge, so the Italians, turning their backs, scattered before Richard.

But neither the men whom he captured nor those who clung to their companions gained anything from flight. A very great number of the Latian people died there in battle; the greater part fled.

The Swabians, not slow to arms, prepared their battle line against Unfredus. At first Unfredus attacked them from a distance with missiles; he himself was attacked in turn by hostile weapons. At last both peoples came together with swords. Marvelous blows were struck on both sides by the swords. There you would have seen human bodies cut from the crown of the head, and horses felled together with their riders’ bodies.

[Col. 1044B] When Robert saw that such enemies were pressing his brother fiercely, and that Unfredus was unwilling to yield to them in any way, he rushed courageously into the midst of the enemy, accompanied by the assistance of Count Girardus and followed by the Calabrians, whose leadership had been entrusted to him.

He boldly pierced some with his spear, cut down others with his sword, and inflicted terrible blows with his powerful hands. He fought with both hands; neither his lance nor his sword was ineffective wherever he wished to direct his hand.

Three times he was thrown from his horse; three times, recovering his strength, he returned to the fight greater in arms. Fury itself supplied him with goads.

[Col. 1044C] As when a roaring lion fiercely attacks smaller animals, and, if it begins to find anything that resists it, becomes enraged, and its anger is inflamed still more by larger creatures, so that it leaves nothing unavenged—this it drags away, that it devours, even what cannot be eaten, scattering and crushing the whole flock to destruction—

so Robert did not cease to strike down the opposing Swabians with varied slaughter. He cut some down with his foot and others with his hands; he severed one man’s head together with his body; he split another’s belly and chest; he pierced the ribs of another after cutting off his head. He made great bodies equal to smaller bodies severed from them, and showed that the palm of valor does not belong only to large bodies, since smaller men often abound in courage.

[Col. 1044D] No one in this war, as was demonstrated after the wars, whether victor or vanquished, ever delivered such mighty blows.

Returning after the great slaughter of the Ausonian people, one part of whom had fled while the other had remained dead beneath swords and spears, Richard saw that the Teutons still resisted his allies and cried out:

“Alas! Although we believed that the war was at an end, victory has not yet reached its conclusion.”

He rushed without hesitation into the midst of the enemy.

Since these men now had no hope of flight and no hope of safety, they resisted more fiercely, but resistance did them no good. The splendid ranks of Richard surrounded them on every side, and the great cause of victory became the ruin of the enemy. The wretched men were killed in various slaughters.

[Col. 1045A] Of so great a people not one survived.

This outcome of the war filled the pope with grief. Afflicted by profound mourning, he fled to the city. But the citizens did not receive the pope with proper respect, fearing that he might be burdensome to the victorious Normans.

The Norman people venerated him on bended knees, begging forgiveness. The pope graciously received them as they bowed, and all together kissed his feet.

He admonished them in pious words and blessed them. He complained bitterly because the messages of peace had been rejected, and, weeping for the dead, prayed for his brothers.

When Argyros heard of the success of the great prosperity enjoyed by the Normans, he was afflicted by no small anxiety. For he saw that he could accomplish the imperial commands neither by fraud nor by arms: he could not move the Franks from Latium or force them to depart.

Argyros did not possess a force large enough to resist them in battle, nor could promises move them to seek other borders, nor could gifts persuade them.

While meditating on this, he left Bari and crossed the sea. He returned to his lord, reported in full the answers of the fierce people and the recent events of the war against the Teutons.

Constantine then ceased to love Argyros, and he was no longer, as he had previously been regarded, the intimate counselor of the emperor.

After suffering exile, he lived for a long time in misery and, afflicted by bodily distress, is said to have ended his life wretchedly.

The courage of the victorious Normans grew greatly.

[Col. 1045C] No Apulian city rebellious against them now remained. All surrendered or paid tribute.

Then Count Unfredus, avenger of his brother’s death, punished all those who had shared in the fatal plot. He beheaded some, pierced others, and hanged many. Remembering Drogo’s death, he wished to spare no one. The memory of his brother’s death lay fixed deep in his heart and, as a greater source of fury, inflamed him.

Terrifying to all, he subjected many cities to himself. The Trojans began to pay tribute to the count.

The citizens of Bari, Trani, and Venusia served him, as did the citizens of Hydruntum and the city of Acerontum.

[Note: [Col. 1045D] Trani is a city of Apulia, which Colenutius thinks was formerly called Trajonopolis. TIREM.]

[Note: [Col. 1045D] Venusia is a city of the Apulians, and the Sabelli are often read in place of the Venusians, because, after the Sabelli had been driven out, the Romans settled the Venusians in their vacant places. [Col. 1046D] TIREM.]

He granted his brother Robert the acquisition of Calabrian lands. The young man was patient of labor, prudent, and had hands ready for every task.

[Col. 1045D] Robert was also ingenious, always seeking lofty things and loving praise and honor. If victory came to him through art or arms, he valued it equally, because what violence often cannot accomplish is achieved by the cleverness of the mind.

Distinguished in eloquence, he gave excellent answers immediately whenever someone consulted him and asked his advice; he knew how to give it wisely.

He rejoiced in the Calabrian charge granted to him. He had previously gathered some knights around him, carrying out as much plundering as he could, especially in those regions which his brother held.

Whatever could be captured, he divided equally among everyone. All were dear to him, and he himself was dear to all.

While he was dining with Unfredus, he was captured. He wished to rise against his brother with a sword, but Gocelinus held him fast with his hands. He was then handed over to the guards; after he had been held for a considerable time, his brother released him and granted him the cities and castles of the Calabrian region, providing him with the support of knights.

Eager to take possession of the land, he displayed love toward everyone. No ruler strove to be regarded as more approachable or humble than he.

Everywhere the Norman people possessed a distinguished name, but the Calabrians, who had not yet experienced its valor, were terrified by its great ferocity.

When Robert entered as commander, supported by no small number of soldiers, he ordered plundering and fires to be carried out everywhere throughout the land. He also ordered the inhabitants to be stripped of their possessions, and commanded that everything which might inspire fear be done, while delaying the soldiers whom he had sent away from his brother.

He harassed the Calabrians not with a large but with a savage army.

As he moved from place to place in search of plunder, unable to capture any castle or city, he contrived by his skill to approach a certain place. Its ascent was difficult, because a very large crowd of inhabitants lived there, and the monastic community there did not allow any foreigner to enter.

The cunning man devised a useful deception. He ordered his people to claim that a certain man was one of their dead. He was placed upon a bier as though he were dead, and ordered to conceal himself beneath a cloth smeared with wax and spread over his face, as is the Norman custom for covering corpses. Swords were hidden beneath the body, inside the bier.

The body was carried to the monastery gates for burial. The ignorant inhabitants, whom living men could not deceive, were deceived by the fiction of the dead man. While the funeral appeared to be proceeding in a simple manner, the man who was believed to be awaiting burial suddenly rose.

His companions drew their swords and attacked the inhabitants of the place, who had been deceived by the trick.

What could the foolish men do? They could neither defend themselves nor find anywhere to flee. All were captured. There, Robert, you first established a fortress.

The monastery, however, was not destroyed, nor was the monastic community rooted out from the place.

[Col. 1046D] Gathering a large army in that fortress, Robert began to be dearer to his men, because he was called a vigorous count, skilled in arms and shrewd in counsel in this region. Among those who accompanied him were several knights, one of whom was called Torstenus, another Arenga, and another Rogerus, strong in the conduct of wars.

He was given certain towns of the land. At this time the Apulian prince, weakened, ordered…

Unfredus should come swiftly to his brother.

[Col. 1047A] Robert hastens; when he sees his brother ill, he weeps in compassion and the brother’s arrival gives great comfort to the sick man. He asks the one who has come to be ruler of his lands when he dies, and guardian of his young son, whom his age prevents from becoming ruler. The anxious brother agrees and says that he will do everything he commands.

Unable now to restore his weakened limbs to health, Unfredus dies [Note: [Col. 1047D] The death of Unfredus occurred around the year of salvation 1052. LEIB.]. All Apulia weeps in tears for the death of its father. He, a kindly father of his country, ruled it peacefully, and adorned his life with uprightness. He did not strive to oppress the people with cruel tyranny; cultivating justice, he preferred to pardon many offenses rather than injure justice. He was buried near the brothers mentioned above, in the seat of the monastery of Venosa.

[Col. 1047B] When Robert had duly completed the funeral rites, he returned to the Calabrians and immediately besieged the city of Cariati, intending, once it was captured, to terrify the remaining cities.

Meanwhile he learned of the arrival of Pope Nicholas [Note: [Col. 1047D] Nicholas, the second pope of that name, was of Allobrogian origin and had previously been called Gerardus; he was created supreme pontiff in the year of Christ 1059. TIREM.]. A large part of the cavalry was dismissed from the siege, while a smaller part accompanied him.

Melfi received him, and there the pope was received with great honor; he had come to those parts to deal with ecclesiastical affairs. For priests, deacons, and the entire clergy in that region were openly joining themselves in marriage. There the pope held a council [Note: [Col. 1047D] More correctly this is attributed to Calixtus and Gregory; see *presbyteri* 27, distinction; *Nullum*, distinction 28. TREM.], with a hundred bishops summoned to the synod and supporting him. He urged priests and ministers of the altar to bear the weapons of chastity [Col. 1047C], and called upon them, commanding them to be spouses of the Church, since by law a priest cannot be a devotee of lust. Thus he completely uprooted the wives of priests from those regions, threatening that those who despised the decree would be struck by anathema.

When the synod was finished, at the request of many, Nicholas bestowed ducal honors upon Robert [Note: [Col. 1048D] Robert was created duke of Calabria and Apulia by Pope Nicholas II. TIREM.].

Of all the counts, he alone was made duke by papal grant, binding himself by oath in faithful allegiance to the pope. Thus all Calabria and Apulia were granted to him, together with dominion over the people of the Latin homeland.

The pope returned to Rome, while the duke, with a great cavalry force, returned to besieged Cariati, where the greater part of the cavalry that had earlier been dismissed had remained faithful to him. The people of Cariati, disturbed by the duke’s return [Col. 1047D], unable to resist, surrendered themselves and their city to him. This people first called him duke and saluted him as duke in the Calabrian regions; from there he proceeded to the other places.

Then powerful Rossano and armed Cosenza [Note: [Col. 1048D] These are neighboring cities in Calabria. TIREM.], and also wealthy Gerace, submitted to him; almost all Calabria became subject to him.

When the renown of his power had begun to increase [Col. 1048A], he began to send ambassadors to Gisulf, son of Guaimarius, who would convey his words to that nobleman. He requested the marriage of Gisulf’s sister, since he himself was then without a wife, his first wife having been rejected on account of consanguinity [Note: [Col. 1048D] Her name was Abderada. LEIB.]. By her Buamundus had been born, a vigorous offspring [Note: [Col. 1048D] And by his earlier wife, whose name was Abderada. TIREM.], distinguished for extraordinary valor and destined to become powerful.

At first Gisulf rejected Robert’s messages—not because he could unite his sister with a greater or nobler man, but because the Gauls seemed to be a fierce, barbarous, and savage people. The first rejection of a wife produced a period in which another had to be given; at last the prince consented, and gave you, Duke Robert, his elder sister in marriage.

[Col. 1048B] The younger Gatelerina, called Sichelgata [Note: [Col. 1048D] Some call her Sengregaita. LEIB.], afterward married Jordan, a nephew [the antecedent is unclear in the transmitted wording]. He, prince of Capua, matched in virtues of character the virtues of both the duke and his father.

After a marriage into so great a nobility, Robert’s noble name began to grow. The people who once had been forced to serve, now bound only by the obligation of ancestral right—for the Lombard people knew that Italy had been subject to this woman’s great-grandfathers and grandfathers—began to honor him.

She bore him three sons and five daughters, an outstanding offspring of both sexes for the future.

The glory of Robert, which had begun to undergo such great increase, thereby acquired no small amount of envy, since, while men envied his virtues, twelve counts, as they were called by the people, conspired together to hand him over treacherously to death. When they happened to see that the time was favorable for this, Goffridus, Gocelinus, and Abagelard, son of Unfredus, who was demanding back his paternal rights, were the principal instigators of the plot.

When the duke therefore learned of the conspiracy of the counts, he prepared for war. He burned fiercely against them all, captured some and drove out others, and afflicted the bodies of certain men with various punishments.

Fearing the duke’s anger, Gocelinus fled to Argos. Terrified, Goffridus hastened to the castle of Mount Pelusium. Since he could not take it by arms [Col. 1048D], he captured it by cunning: with promises he deceived the castle’s guardian, Godefridus, giving him certain things and promising him more, as well as a castle stronger than the one he possessed.

Goffridus had not possessed the whole lordship of Mount Pelusium; he had granted Godefridus half of it. But because he had promised him dominion over the whole of the more distinguished castle, namely Ojanum, Godefridus, desiring to rule alone [Col. 1049A], ordered Robert to withdraw from the siege, feigning his own return. But as soon as he learned that Goffridus was absent, Robert was to return safely to the castle and enter it, and, after receiving the keys, hand Ojanum over to him. By this stratagem Godefridus surrendered the castle to him.

He received Ojanum, but who afterward would trust him? He was called a traitor by the entire people of Latium.

Thus the prudent cunning of the astute duke repeatedly overcame by craft what he could not overcome by arms.

After subduing his enemies and capturing castles everywhere, he prepared to besiege the people of Bari. There was no city in Apulia whose wealth could surpass Bari; rich in resources and full of strength, he besieged it, so that, once the leading men of so great a city were defeated, he might fill the smaller cities [Col. 1049B] that remained unsubdued with terror. It was considered greater than all the cities contained in the Apulian land. The duke fortified his camps with soldiers and filled the sea with ships brought from Calabria.

The citizens appealed for the aid of the Holy Empire. Those who had conspired with the citizens there sent ambassadors and all together requested imperial assistance. The duke ordered the citizens to give him the houses of Argyrus, which he knew stood higher than the neighboring buildings. Having acquired them, Robert climbed up through them and hoped from there to bring the whole city under his authority.

The people of Bari gave the duke harsh replies. He vigorously attacked the native inhabitants of the city, strong men not slow to engage in battle. Carefully undertaking the approaches to the gates with wooden screens, under which he arranged armed men lying in ambush, he built a tower that projected above the walls. Beside it he placed a stone-thrower on each side [Note: [Col. 1049D] *Petraria*, a kind of siege engine. LEIB.], and attached a machine of another kind with which he could overthrow the walls.

Nor did the citizens defend the city less vigorously. They did not remain shut within the walls, but stood fighting with the duke before the city’s fortifications. They drove some away by fighting and struck others down with blows, as is the custom of war; the enemy drove them away, and they in turn drove the enemy away. Each attacked and was attacked; one struck again and was struck in return.

Just as when two boars fight with their teeth extended, one’s mouth dripping with saliva against the other, sharpening its teeth so that it may inflict sharp wounds, and with powerful blows they strike each other’s backs in turn—now wounded in the foot, now in the ribs—each fiercely resists and neither wishes to yield until their wounded limbs, exhausted by the blows and by the loud cries, teach one boar to seek flight and the defeated one withdraws [Col. 1049D].

The Normans pressed on fiercely, and the citizens resisted no less fiercely. A machine of another kind was added to the walls, so that once the city’s walls had been overthrown, an open approach would be available to the Normans, which the closed defenses denied them on every side. The sea did not make the place an island, but only a narrow tongue of land; the duke’s tents had been pitched on this side.

By placing masses of material in the sea and filling one part of it, he prevented the Bari ships from putting out, and built a harbor and bridge for his own men. After a fortification had been placed upon the bridge with earthworks, the inhabitants nowhere had an opportunity to emerge from the city, and the Norman fleet safely guarded the harbor.

But the citizens seized the tower, and the greater part of the sea-bridge fell when they overthrew it. The people of Bari defended their city by land and sea.

Later, when Robert despaired of taking Bari’s walls by combat, he began to make many promises to the city’s nobles, whose nobility held greater power in the city and whose influence was stronger. After gathering the leading men, he believed that the lesser citizens could be attracted by promises and gifts. He often made threats in order to instill terror among the citizens, and worked by every means for the city’s surrender, which he ardently desired to obtain.

Rumor reported that Gocelinus would come to their aid with many imperial ships. The crafty duke stationed scouts to capture him.

The praetor of Bari was Stephanus, assigned to the people of Bari by imperial decree, surnamed Pateranus [Note: [Col. 1049D] Stephanus Pateranus, whom others call Sebastophorus [Col. 1050D]. TIREM.], an honorable and generous man, praiseworthy in every pursuit except that he had undertaken the death of so great a duke.

There was a soldier of Bari who had once received a grave insult from the duke. Ready for every evil, fickle, irritable, and bold, he was urged by Stephanus to approach the duke’s camp and, taking the unsuspecting duke by surprise at night, hand him over to death by striking him with the deadly point of a spear. Stephanus promised him much gold if the duke should perish.

Remembering the insult inflicted upon him and eager for profit, the soldier departed by night and surveyed the camp on every side. Seeing that nothing obstructed him, he reached Robert’s lodging, which Robert himself had covered with straw and enclosed with branches, so that he might be protected from the cold of winter.

After supper had ended, the soldier came and examined the duke’s seat as he sat at dinner. He thrust the spear through the branches into the place where the duke had been sitting. But an abundance of phlegm had accumulated in his mouth and caused him to bend his head beneath the table [Note: [Col. 1050D] The Apulian had fallen asleep. TIREM.]; thus the place was found empty of the spear, and he delivered blows in vain.

[Col. 1050D] He returned in flight, and rumor spread through the whole city that the duke had died. The citizens rejoiced, and the entire people raised a cry of joy to the heavens. While they were shouting, the duke arrived and, himself a witness to his own safety, shouted that the citizens were pouring forth their cries in vain. When they heard the voice of the man shouting, the shouting ceased, and the words of their joy came to an end together with the end of their cries.

[Col. 1049] The second book ends.

THE THIRD BOOK BEGINS.

[Col. 1051]

[Col. 1051A] Meanwhile Michael [Note: [Col. 1051D] Michael the Elder was emperor of Constantinople in 1058; when he abdicated the empire, Isaac Comnenus obtained it. LEIB.] governed the rights of the Roman Empire with his brother, who was called by the name Constantine [Note: [Col. 1051D] Constantine Ducas, emperor of Constantinople, reigned in the year of salvation 1063, for seven years. Eudocia bore him three children, Michael, Andronicus, and Constantine—those two before he obtained the empire, and the latter afterward. Thus this passage must be understood of Michael, son of Constantine Ducas. TIREM.

[Col. 1052D] The author here means Michael and Constantine. LEIB.].

Their rule was destructive to the Greeks, because, always setting wars aside, they devoted themselves to leisure, while shameful idleness corrupted those captured by the allurements of deceitful luxury.

During their time the terrified Christian people who inhabited the delightful regions of Romania fled when the Turks entered from the eastern shores. Most of them fell, killed by the wicked swords of the Turks; and when the cities were captured, the entire subject population, paying tribute to them, fled.

Against these enemies the rulers sent no cavalry because of their cowardice. Therefore, by decree of the senate, their mother Eudocia, who loved her husband more than her lineage, was married to the distinguished knight Romanus [Note: [Col. 1052D] Eudocia ruled together with her sons in the year of salvation 1070, month 7. LEIB.] [Col. 1051B], whose surname was Diogenes [Note: [Col. 1052D] Romanus Diogenes ruled for three years from 1071, from Biblianadros. Others, however, date the beginning of his reign to the year of salvation 1068, placing Diogenes in the empire before Constantine Ducas. TIREM.], because his beard was forked.

Assuming the government, he chose to undertake the various affairs of war for himself, while leaving peace to his stepsons. Ready to act, he entered into war with the Persians, who were ravaging the unfortunate Argos. He experienced various outcomes of war against them.

Often indeed he drove the Persians away in battle as victor; often both peoples fought with equal fortune.

At last, while he himself assigned countless companions to guard the cities, whose service had come under his authority and whose universally recognized good faith had become known everywhere, he remained with only a few of the better soldiers in the camp.

A great number of Persians, with their king, suddenly surrounded him and strove to break into the camp. They engaged in terrible battles, eager to seize the imperial camp; driven back in the first and second engagements, they withdrew.

At last Romanus’s anxious prudence, despairing of defending the camp, placed the lives of his men above everything. Seeing that they were gravely exhausted by war and hunger, he ordered that everything substantial in the camp—every precious garment and all vessels of gold or silver—be carried out and scattered through the camp, so that, if the Turks happened to break into it, the sight of these things might make them desist from harming the Greeks [Col. 1051C].

The money was gathered by unwilling servants preparing for flight, and the Danaans were forced to pass a sleepless night.

When day arrived, that innumerable Persian people came and surrounded the camp on every side. Arrows flew everywhere; a hailstorm of arrows covered the entire air. Since the Argives could no longer endure it, the Turks broke in and every fortification was shattered. But the Persians, intent more on plunder than on striking the soldiers [Col. 1052A], allowed many to escape.

The lord of the Greeks was recognized by the eagle insignia—conspicuous in its golden brilliance, fastened to his breastplate—as he cut down the enemy spears with his sword and did not cease defending himself.

By chance a flying arrow wounded his unwary limbs. Thus at last he was captured with some of his men.

After plundering the camp, the Persian phalanx led Romanus to its own camp and seated him in an eminent place, beside the Persian king.

The king asked what Romanus would have done if he had been captured by him. Romanus replied:

“If you had been subjected to me or to my men, I would order either that your head be cut off or that you be hanged on a forked stake.”

The king replied that he would never commit such an act [Col. 1052B], but that henceforth Romanus would enjoy perpetual peace with him, which he himself had often requested through ambassadors. He also promised to give his baptized daughter to him as a wife, so that the peace might thereby be made firmer.

After treaties had been established under these conditions, the Persian ruler sent Romanus back to his own people, giving him very great gifts. He released the captives and honorably escorted them as they traveled across the long extent of the lands, then permitted them to depart.

But the stepsons did not approve the benefits of the peace that had been secured. They were less capable of guarding the Greek forces, and it was not further decided that Romanus should return to the rights of the imperial citadel.

When Diogenes learned that these men had become his enemies, relying on Persian aid he attempted to stir up various forms of civil war against them.

When the stepsons saw that they could not resist him, they tried to lure him away by a deceitful peace. Unaware of the fraud and carrying messages of peace, they sent twelve bishops with Gocelinus, whose affection Romanus had so often experienced that he did not hesitate to trust him as a friend.

Romanus trusted the bishops and Gocelinus. Made secure by the oath and the pledge of faith, which he himself requested and which was given, the wretched man was pleased by the imperial promise of a return—uselessly, since as soon as he reached Heraclea he was captured and, after being captured, deprived of his sight. He whose imperial name had been so noble became a monk.

Now the two brothers guided the kingdom with peaceful reins [Col. 1052D].

Yet their tyranny did not remain wholly unavenged. For the son of Romanus, adding the Armenians to his allies, deprived the Persians of their eastern lands [Col. 1053A], ravaging them with sword and fire.

At that time the treacherous Persian people began to rise against Romania through slaughter and plunder. That people could not yet have been brought back under the laws of the Empire, unless the nation of the Gauls, more powerful than every other people in the strength of its arms and stirred by a heavenly command, had overcome the enemy and restored it to freedom. God was breathing upon them and had inspired them to open the paths to the holy Sepulchre, which had long been closed.

The men by whose counsels the blinding of so great a man had been carried out were captured in misery and, expelled from the palace, were forced to pay the deserved penalties. Those who had advised that the innocent man be punished were themselves, being guilty, subjected to various tortures.

A messenger, an imperial legate, arrived at the city of Bari [Col. 1053B] and begged that aid be given to the wretched citizens.

Ships suited to piracy were prepared according to custom, and grain and arms were ordered to be carried in them. With these, the fleet could cross safely to the city, while the sailors’ fear and the city’s scarcity would be dispelled.

By imperial command Gocelinus was placed in command of these ships. Fear of the duke of Italy had driven him out, and he was hated because he had conspired against him. He arrived swiftly with the armed ships to encourage the trembling citizens. He was already near the city and hoped to enter safely at night when suddenly Robert’s fleet came against the Danaan fleet.

Gocelinus had come to restore Robert’s enemies. During the night the duke’s ships willingly entered battle [Col. 1053C], since they knew the places and therefore found it easier. The combat was more difficult because the other people aboard the ships knew the region least of all.

After great exertion, Gocelinus’s ship was finally captured, and he himself was brought captive before the duke. Another Danaan ship was sunk; the remaining ships barely escaped.

The Norman people, inexperienced in naval warfare, returned victorious, increasing the prince’s hope. He realized that the Danaans had brought by ship not merely assistance for the citizens of the city, but forces that would greatly hinder the siege; at the same time he rejoiced in the novelty of the naval victory. Henceforth he hoped to engage in naval battles with the Normans more confidently.

Gocelinus spent his life confined in a long prison and, after enduring various dangers, met the end of his labors with the end of his life [Col. 1053D].

The city had now been under siege for a third year. At last, exhausted by many forms of suffering, it was overcome—more by hunger, however. At that time Argiritius was considered the leading man of the city. When the duke induced him to begin the city’s surrender, it was not difficult to overcome the remaining citizens; for the leading men can bend the hearts of the lesser people toward whichever side they wish.

[Col. 1054A] Robert showed the citizens a calm affection. Because he always held dear all those whom he had won over, he himself was loved by all.

The duke returned to the inhabitants the fields, estates, and farms that had been taken either by force or by cunning. He restored what had been lost; he himself inflicted no harm upon the citizens and permitted no one else to inflict any injury upon them. To the surrounding peoples, who had been accustomed to pay tribute, he granted quiet freedom from the Norman levy.

Moved by pity, he did not wish to handle Stephanus’s white hair as an enemy. Rather, forgetting the killing that Stephanus had attempted, he strove to treat him kindly. When Bari had been captured, this man, to the amazement of many, was kept in unguarded custody and left unpunished [Note: [Col. 1053D] Concerning Stephanus Pateranus, see above, Book I.].

After remaining for several days in the conquered city [Col. 1054B], he ordered arms to be prepared at the expense of the people of Bari, so that they might hasten with him wherever they would see him hastening.

With his people he led them to the city of Regina [Note: [Col. 1053D] Regina is a city in Calabria. TIREM.].

Rumor reported that not far from the shore there was a fish, enormous in body amid the Adriatic waves, of an incredible form such as the people of Italy had never seen before. The breeze of spring had driven it there, toward the fresh waters.

By various devices the duke’s ingenuity began to pursue it. As it descended into nets made of rope, with the entire weight of iron attached to the net, it was submerged in the sea. At last the sailors cut it repeatedly with various blades, deep down beneath the surface. With difficulty the monster was dragged to shore and made a spectacle for the people [Col. 1054C]. There, by order of the duke, it was cut into pieces.

Thus a long supply of food was provided for him and his men, and for all who remained among the Calabrian shores. The Apulian people also shared in it everywhere.

The cut backbone measured four palms in circumference. After remaining there a little while, Duke Robert proceeded toward the city of Regina.

While he was staying there, because a bridge had been built, the entire place is now called the Bridge of Guiscard.

The people of Bari, following his command, prepared everything that was required for the walls of Regina.

There the duke took soldiers and prepared ships, and crossed the Sicilian sea with many companions.

Although narrow, the passage is difficult to cross: Scylla [Note: [Col. 1053D] Scylla is near the promontory of Pelorus, where there is a town called Sciglum, named Scilaeum by Pliny. TIREM.] and Charybdis [Note: [Col. 1053D] Charybdis is a whirlpooling sea, called Galofarus, almost Calofanos, by our people. There fires are lit at night as a signal for sailors seeking the harbor; both places are fatal to ships. TIREM.] present various dangers. One turns ships around, while the other dashes them against the rocks.

The aid of his brother Roger, already gathered to a large extent in the Sicilian regions, increased the duke’s hope. At that age Roger was inferior to none in valor; none of his brothers, however distinguished, undertook so noble a war [Note: [Col. 1054D] Roger Bosso, the younger of Tancred’s sons, was summoned to Sicily by the people of Messina. He twice routed and defeated the Saracens at Messina and eventually captured it. LEIB.].

For he always fought against the Sicilians, enemies of the divine name, desiring to exalt the holy faith by which we all live [Col. 1055A]. In his youth he especially cultivated this work, until the subjugation of the Sicilian people became a worthy cause for his rest.

Trusting in this companion and leading a large force with him, the duke did not despair of taking Palermo by siege [Note: [Col. 1055D] Palermo, the oldest city in Sicily, where kings customarily received golden crowns. In its greatest temple the kings and bishops of Sicily are buried; no private person is. TIREM.], which he had heard was nobler than the other cities of Sicily.

Surrounded by Robert’s numerous soldiers, the city was afraid. Its inhabitants repaired the walls and towers, prepared arms and men, closed the openings that had been exposed, and stationed frequent guards throughout the city.

The duke ordered armed cavalry to approach the gates, so that they might provoke the enclosed enemy to battle. By his cunning power he ordered that everything capable of inflicting punishment and hardship should likewise be brought upon the citizens.

The Sicilians came out through the gates, unable to endure remaining inside [Col. 1055B], and, once outside, resisted with bold spirit. But they could not withstand the fierce Normans, worshipers of Christ, while the Agarene people resisted; they were unable to endure it. They fled, and our men followed, striking many down with swords and many with spears. From the tops of the walls missiles flew everywhere. They tried to wound our men with stones and javelins lying ready. Our men, driving them back by force from the city walls, happily returned to their camp.

Then the people of Palermo tried to summon Africans for aid. With their forces joined to their own, they undertook at sea the war which they had not dared to undertake on land; they believed the sea more favorable for fighting.
