Accordingly, after equipping their ships, they made ready the proper equipment for naval war [Col. 1055C]. To repel the blows of stones and javelins, they came to battle with manly resolve, covered everywhere with red felt coverings, so that they might live or die according to the lot of men.

The duke ordered the Normans, Calabrians, and people of Bari and Argos, whom he had captured, to fortify themselves with the body of Christ. After receiving it, he ordered them to enter battle with the blood.

Thus the faithful crowd, protected by such food, advanced in prepared ships, in which they were superior.

The treacherous people filled the sea with the sound of trumpets and horns and with the cries of mighty voices.

The worshipers of Christ, seeking only the aid of the eternal Prince, whose flesh had nourished them, were terrified by no blaring. They opposed them fiercely and struck and shook the enemy manfully.

[Col. 1055D] At first the African and Sicilian ships resisted. At last, compelled by the divine will, they yielded. When they sought flight, some of their ships were captured; others sank and perished, while most barely escaped through the repeated stroke of their oars. As they entered the harbor, they soon stretched chains across it, with which they were accustomed to block the approaches from the sea.

Even after these were broken, the worshipers of Christ captured some of their ships and burned many others. This victory gave the duke’s spirit strong courage.

From then on, attentive to the city’s capture, he worked by various efforts to penetrate it.

[Col. 1056A] He had the foot soldiers equipped with slings and arrows and ordered the armed cavalry to advance with him.

The foot soldiers approached the wall and shook the fortifications with stones and arrows. The hostile people came out from the city and opposed them. Unable to withstand them, the foot soldiers scattered in flight. When the duke saw them dispersed across the fields, he immediately ordered all the legions, at the signal for battle, to engage without delay. Like a vigorous commander, he encouraged his men with voice and hand.

For a short time the Sicilians remained in the mixed combat, but at the sight of the duke they were terrified and turned their backs.

The duke struck and urged his men to strike the backs of the perverse people. He did not cease cutting down the enemy until they reached the opposing gates of the city.

The people accompanying the duke wounded the enemy with various injuries—some with swords, some with spears, many with sling-cast stones, and most with arrows. Then, stepping over the bodies of the slain, he tried to reach the city gates with the fleeing Sicilians, so that he might bring an end to such great labor by capturing it.

But while the citizens closed and barred the gates, they shut out a considerable number of their own people. The hostile attack filled the city with such terror that they allowed all those excluded to be slaughtered.

Although Robert saw the cavalry scattered after the long engagement, he urged them to persist in their undertaking:

“Men, your courage has endured various labors. Either now it will be worthy of praise, or now worthy of rejection. The city hostile to God, ignorant of divine worship, subject to demons, and stripped of its ancient strength, already trembles as though broken. If it sees you pressing on powerfully, it will devise no means of resistance. But if you falter, tomorrow it will restore its strength and resist more fiercely. While you see that the time has come, run; with Christ’s mercy, what is difficult to capture will be opened. He himself makes difficult labor easy. Trusting in this leader in war, bring the battle to an end, and let us all hasten to attack the city.”

With these words Robert inspired the hearts of his men.

They hurried up the walls by means of ladders and promised that they would be ready to fulfill the duke’s will.

Thus a good charioteer, when he sees that swift horses are yielding in their running, spares them and allows them to pause; then, when their breath has been restored, he makes them resume their course and drives them on with repeated goads until they complete their run and, though beaten, pass those whom they are accustomed to surpass, under the cautious guidance of their master [Col. 1056C].

When the duke perceived that all his men were laboring to take the walls, he too busied himself with carrying the ladders, anxious that they should advance upward. Then he ordered his men to proceed to the heights.

They hurried together to climb the walls. Opposite them, the entire people of Palermo stood upon the walls, scattered across the battlements.

The labor was the same for both peoples, but their reasons were different: one desired to capture the city, the other to defend it. One side stood for itself, for its children, and for its wife; the other strove to please the duke by subduing the city.

[Col. 1057A] While both peoples struggled with such great effort, the action of fortune was favorable to Robert and disastrous for the city. Suddenly a body of cavalry emerged, and, while it sought the heights of the walls by means of ladders, the Sicilian defenders, roaring, turned their backs.

The New City was captured, while they were shut up within the Old City.

The Agarene people, seeing that they had been stripped of all their strength and that every hope of safety had failed, humbly begged that he, in pity for their misery, would regard their plight and not repay them with punishment equal to their deeds. They surrendered everything to the duke and asked only to remain alive.

After surrendering themselves, they deserved to obtain the favor of the merciful duke [Note: [Col. 1057D] Palermo was captured in the year of salvation 1071.]. Life was promised to them freely; he did not wish to proscribe anyone. Keeping faith with his promise, he sought to harm no one of them [Col. 1057B], although they were gentiles.

He examined all his subjects with an impartial balance. Glorifying God, he destroyed all the structures of the wicked temple. Where the mosque had previously stood, he built a church of the Mother Virgin. The place that had belonged to Muhammad and the demon became a dwelling of God and a gate of heaven for the worthy.

He ordered strong military works to be prepared, so that his people might remain safely in the camps against the Sicilians. He added wells and useful supplies to the camps.

After taking several hostages and preparing the camps, Robert, victorious, returned to the city of Regina. He left at Palermo a soldier of that same name, who was given authority to be regarded as its emir.

He immediately permitted all those who had been captured at Bari, together with Stephanus Pateranus, to depart for Argos [Col. 1057C]. Since the most merciful duke was releasing his enemies unpunished, they were pleased with him as if they loved him.

With the people of Bari, the Calabrians, the hostages from Palermo, and his own soldiers, the duke went to the walls of the city of Melfi. This was the chief of all the cities, and it still is of all those contained in the Apulian land.

The counts of that region and distinguished men from everywhere gathered together. Each wished to see again the face of so great a prince. Only Peter, son of the previously mentioned Peter, refused to approach him.

After his brother Goffridus, the elder, had died, paternal right had passed into his hands, together with the rights of his nephews, until the offspring of his brother, Richard, had reached an age legally suitable for ruling.

[Col. 1057D] The duke suspected Peter because he had utterly refused to apply his strength when the duke was going to the Sicilian borders.

Nevertheless, the duke put aside his apprehension and summoned him. Saying that Taranto had been granted to him by his brother, he demanded back the right to his brother’s gift. Peter himself refused to return what had been overcome by his father’s arms.

For this reason a serious dispute arose between them.

Peter came to Andria, prepared for various wars, and began to undertake them. He ordered new weapons to be prepared, increased his military force, sought support, and everywhere labored to keep everything belonging to his jurisdiction secure.

Meanwhile the duke prepared to subjugate by siege the city of Trani, a place of distinguished name, filled with wealth, arms, and a numerous population [Col. 1058A].

Peter led twelve chosen horsemen to the city, so that he might attract the citizens to his side by his counsels and strengthen them when they saw him. One man prolonged his speech, when suddenly Robert and his army, spread across the fields, appeared everywhere.

The besieged citizens, already fifteen days within the walls, gathered around Peter. They begged him to favor the city’s surrender. They could no longer endure the city’s losses.

At first he was burdened with excessive grief by this; he refused. At last, weeping and compelled by them, he asked with his companions to be permitted to depart freely. Thus he allowed the city to surrender to the duke.

[Col. 1058B] As he departed, he did not permit himself to be seen by the duke, and he absolutely refused to see the duke himself, since he considered it horrifying to behold the duke’s face.

The people of Juvenacum surrendered, as did those of Buxilia. Buxilia had belonged to Peter; Juvenacus was the friend of Peter, whose father had been Peter’s paternal uncle. Because he had given assistance to Peter’s brother, the duke hated him, and also because he had attempted to approach the Dalmatian borders without the duke’s permission.

Having learned these things, the duke, desiring to bring Peter under his authority, prepared to surround Coretum with a siege.

When Peter heard that the duke was surrounding this castle with camps, he did not dare to contend with him by arms. He was received safely within the walls of Andria. While he had gone out from Andria to carry booty from Trani, and fifteen horsemen had followed him, Guido had led forty horsemen into the city.

At the duke’s command, his wife’s brother suddenly emerged with troops spread across the fields. They captured Peter and forced him to present himself—or rather, to be presented—to the duke, after he had first denied the accusation.

This capture brought the duke’s labors to an end.

But at last Peter, bound by an oath of allegiance, was released, and he recovered everything that he had lost. He departed free, deprived only of Trani, which was left to the enemy [Note: [Col. 1057] Read “with honor.” Certainly below Gisulfus is said to have been deprived of the honor of Salerno. LEIB.].

Meanwhile the populous people of Amalfi frequently sought the aid of the distinguished duke. For a long time they had paid annual tribute to him, because Gisulfus was attacking them with threats and continually disturbing them by land and sea.

Robert, stirred by the people’s complaint against Gisulfus, ordered Gisulfus to cease harassing the Amalfitans, who had been accustomed to bring annual tribute to Robert, and not to violate the ancient treaty of friendship. He said that the affection due to a brother-in-law ought to compel Gisulfus to desist, and promised to render the due return.

When Gisulfus received these instructions from the ambassadors who conveyed them, he returned proud words. He denied that the duke would enjoy peace with him unless he rendered him the services fitting for a servant.

Unable to endure the reply of such arrogance, the duke, accompanied by an innumerable people, hastened to Salerno and prepared a siege by land and sea.

The fourth month of the siege had been completed. Such hunger had invaded the wretched citizens that they could scarcely live by eating the corpses of dogs, horses, mice, or asses [Col. 1059A].

A certain citizen, leaving his father behind in the city, was present in the camp. A dog, which had been raised in his father’s household, detected him with its keen nose and came to him. He gave it food, and after it had eaten enough, he would skillfully place some loaves in a sack around its breast, supplies sufficient for a day’s life.

The dog, returning at swift speed—wonderful to relate!—and delaying nowhere, carried them back to its own dwelling.

Thus the shrewd one prepared provisions both for his master and for himself.

Some, unable to endure such hunger, went out, and in the eighth month the citizens opened the breached walls to Duke Robert,

wherever a more suitable entrance could be found.

[Col. 1059B] The city captured from Gisulf terrified Robert. He climbed the tower that, built on the summit of the mountain, rises above the city; its approach is difficult by nature and by artifice, and no stronger fortress anywhere in all Italy seemed to exist.

Robert stormed the fortress with all his strength. But when a powerful stone-throwing engine had struck the fortress from above with the force of a hurled rock, a splintered piece of wood wounded Robert’s noble chest, who had been careless; yet before long, with God’s help, the wounded flesh recovered.

Restored to health, he strove more vigorously to conquer Gisulf. [Note: [Col. 1059D] Robert was Gisulf’s brother-in-law. TIREM.] When Gisulf saw that his fortune had been placed in extreme danger, since little hope remained for his safety, he surrendered himself and his possessions to the duke’s discretion.

[Col. 1059C] He asked only that he be granted freedom to depart; relinquishing to the duke the right he possessed, he went away free.

Having been stripped of his honor at Salerno, he first sought Pope Gregory. The pope received him kindly, and the Campanian territory was handed over to him.

Robert rejoiced over the city and the conquered fortress. To ensure that the treacherous people would not later resist him, he fortified the summit of the fortress with loyal guards. In a lower position he made an impregnable stronghold, where his subjects could remain safely.

No city of Latium is more delightful than this city. It abounds in crops, trees, and wine, and you lack neither apples nor nuts, nor beautiful palaces:

[Col. 1059D] nor is feminine beauty absent, nor the uprightness of its men. One part occupies the plain, another the mountain, and the land or sea supplies whatever you might wish.

With this acquisition he acquired Amalfi as well.

[Col. 1060A] This city appears rich in resources and crowded with people. None is wealthier in silver, clothing, gold, and countless other goods; and many sailors dwell in the city, skilled in opening the routes of sea and sky. [Note: [Col. 1059D] We owe the Amalfitans the invention of the mariner’s compass and the Digest of Justinian. LEIB.]

Various goods are also brought here from Alexandria and from Antioch of the king; it crosses many seas. Here Arabs, Indians, Sicilians, and Africans are known. This people has become famous throughout almost the whole world, bringing merchandise to sell and delighting in bringing back what it has purchased.

After bringing all these matters under his authority into proper order, the duke himself revisited Troy. [Note: [Col. 1059D] Troy was a city in Apulia, built around the year 1016 of salvation by Catapan Basil and Constantine, the brothers of Emperor Constantine; later it became the capital of Apulia. TIREM.] While he was staying within the walls of Troy, a certain distinguished Lombard marquis arrived, accompanied by many nobles of his homeland. He was called Azo. [Note: [Col. 1059D] He means Azo, who held a large part of Lombardy and Liguria, from whom the princes of Brunswick and Este descend. LEIB.] He brought with him Hugh, his illustrious son,

[Col. 1060B] and requested that the duke’s daughter be given to him as a bride. He summoned the counts and nobles, and all whom the duke thought he should consult about the matter.

On the advice of these men, Robert’s daughter was given to Azo’s son. They celebrated the wedding torches according to custom, both by feasting and by distributing many gifts.

When everything required by the order of marriage had been completed, the duke pressed the counts and all the powerful men, asking for gifts so that the joyful husband and wife might depart with sufficient presents. For previously, when another imperial child had entered the marriage chamber of Michael, [Note: [Col. 1060D] Namely, of Michael Doukas, who began to reign in 1071 and lost the empire in 1078; this event must therefore have occurred in the intervening period. LEIB.] they had given him no assistance whatsoever. They all grieved together, as though astonished that the duke was demanding tribute, but they were unable to resist him, and they supplied mules, horses, and various gifts.

[Col. 1060C] Adding his own gifts to those he gave his son-in-law, he prepared a fleet and sent him back to his own country with great honor.

The Norman counts frequently complained among themselves that the duke treated them so badly and oppressively. They concealed for a long time the anger in their treacherous hearts. [Note: [Col. 1060D] “Through hatred of the present condition, states are changed,” writes Tacitus. TIREM.]

At last, after taking counsel, they shared their plans with Jordan, the son of Richard, and disclosed everything to his uncle, Count Rannulf. Once these men had joined them, Peter and Goffred, with open treachery of mind, began to attack the duke by war.

Abagelardus, heir mindful of the lost land, son of Unfred, [Note: [Col. 1060D] Several writers say that, after Unfred’s death, Bagelardus succeeded him, and that he was deprived of his principality by his uncle Robert Guiscard. LEIB.] did everything he could to harass the duke, together with Guidilo, to whom he had given his sister in marriage. Nor was Baldwin absent from their efforts, learned in speech and skilled in arms.

[Col. 1060D] Count Henry and Count Amicus were with them; Robert, count of Monte Scabioso, more learned than these men, was also present. [Note: [Col. 1060D] Robert, count of Monte Scabioso, and Goffred were Robert’s nephews through his sister. TIREM.] He was Goffred’s brother, and, returning, brought both of them ready for fighting on foot.

[Col. 1061A] They were born of the duke’s sister. Anger inflamed the nephews against him, who wished to excel all others. All these men attempted to deprive the duke of his honor.

This dissension shook not only the places of Apulia, but also prevailed along the shores of Calabria and Lucania, and likewise in Campania. Fear of the enemy was everywhere. The fury of brigands raged in every direction, and the number of plunderers increased throughout the regions of Italy. The Norman host turned toward various sides.

But although there were more enemies than troops in the duke’s army, the better part always remained loyal to Robert in war.

The city of Trani was restored to Peter and Abagelardus. Having given his wife and child, Argyricius gave them the distinguished city of Bari, which the duke had entrusted to him.

Yet, although these cities had been removed from their authority at that time,

[Col. 1061B] the people of Juvenacium, loyal out of love for the duke, did not withdraw from him. With one accord they desired to obey him faithfully.

Argyricius urged them to return to Amicus the city that had been his. If they were unwilling to return it, he threatened to hand them over to the duke, together with the children whom the duke had formerly entrusted to him as hostages. Yet they did not put this loyalty second to their love for their children; disregarding their affection for their offspring, they declared that they would preserve it for the duke forever.

To acquire this city, Amicus went there with a large retinue and with Count Peter’s company.

Argyricius arrived at the besieged city with the people of Bari, Trani, and Choreti. [Note: [Col. 1061D] Choritus is a town in Tuscany, founded by King Corithus. TIREM.] The people of Andria also arrived with those of Buxentum.

The people of Juvenacium, neither terrified by the siege nor by arms,

[Col. 1061C] stood firm and bravely. They took care to defend the walls, stationed guards, and fiercely resisted those who pressed them from outside. The besiegers fought; the city resisted. Although it had been attacked by land and sea, it could not be captured by any stratagem.

By chance, a messenger was ordered to bring fabricated reports from the city of Bitonto. But William, son of Yvo, to whom the duke had granted the city, discovered them cautiously.

“Look,” said the messenger, “Roger, Robert’s son, is here, and the duke has given him many troops of cavalry and infantry to lead. Believing that he had hurried here, all those whom the duke had led to besiege the city, so that Amicus might bring it under his control as a captured city, fled.”

Although the duke heard that so many rebels had gathered, he was shaken by no fear. By stratagem or by arms he overcame them all, drawing them with gentle admonitions. He subdued some by war; crafty and bold, he knew both methods. He took away their camps from some, while he urged others with flattering words to surrender what could not be obtained by violent warfare.

Thus, after dismissing his cavalry near the Bradano River, he departed with part of his Calabrian forces toward the Calabrian coast and made peace with the people of Cosenza. [Note: [Col. 1061D] Cosa, with a simple or doubled s, is a city in Calabria, now called Cosano. Cicero mentions the municipality of Consa in book 5 of Against Verres. TIREM.] [Col. 1062A] Accompanied by them he departed, but first distributed whatever he could to the obedient people.

He hastened to fight all the disloyal. He received Juvenacium’s loyal people.

From there, taking several horsemen, he first attacked Bari with violent force, where he knew Abagelardus was. The people of Bari, relying on their numbers and on the leadership of the man whom they followed, since he was powerful in the duke’s warfare, engaged the duke.

But Abagelardus’s cuirass was pierced by a spear. He could not protect his pierced body with his armor; wounded in battle, he could no longer withstand the attack. His people fled as far as the city walls.

Robert, victorious, soon prepared to approach Juvenacium. A loyal crowd hastened to come out to meet him. Who could express such great thanks,

[Col. 1062B] as he returned to each one? They all praised the people because they had placed the preservation of their promised faith above their dear hostages.

Then, kissing everyone, he said: “Do not be afraid. Amicus will not harm any of the children, since he is seeking by every means to have my favor restored to him.”

The people replied to him in this way: “Believe that we are ready to follow all your commands. We entrust the entire care of our children to God, since no love will be able to remove us from love for you. We ask only that you remain the guardian of our affection, and be our ruler with kindness.”

When he heard the people’s prayers, he favored those who prayed.

Their tribute was remitted for three entire years; a pact granting them half was given to them forever.

[Col. 1062C] Having dismissed them in this manner, he hastened to return to Salerno. On his return he gave hostile villages and conquered camps to his soldiers, and frequently fought battles in different places.

Fortune lent its aid to him. While treacherous Ascoli was attacking him, Baldwin was captured in a cavalry engagement, and a castle called Vico was taken by force. [Note: [Col. 1062D] Asculum is said by Ptolemy to be today Ascolo, and this is the place called Asculum Satrianum. TIREM.] Here Gradilo was captured and deprived of his sight and testicles; but Baldwin was allowed to retain his limbs unharmed. Nevertheless, guards confined him in prison because he had favored Abagelardus.

After these deeds, he reached Salerno, where he had set out to go.

Envoys came to the duke from Jordan, seeking a treaty of peace. The duke, foreseeing many advantages that would soon disappear if the discord did not cease,

[Col. 1062D] answered the envoys with calm goodwill. He established a truce and arranged a day for negotiations.

The envoys returned with great joy, because they had been received by him so graciously, and they brought back the happy news.

Everything they reported greatly pleased Jordan.

Meanwhile, the duke arranged to send some chosen horsemen to Juvenacium. He ordered them

[Col. 1063A] not only to benefit his own men but to harm his enemies, and to harass them in whatever way they could.

After these men had arrived by a long route—for they were not permitted to proceed directly—following winding paths because many enemies were present, they began to attack the duke’s enemies bravely.

Those who had previously been accustomed to carry out raids now grieved that they had to suffer them themselves; they could no longer travel safely.

Prince Jordan and the duke resolved to go to Sarno on the appointed day. A firm peace was made between them, and a similar agreement was concluded with Rannulf. One was Jordan’s paternal uncle, the other his maternal uncle.

When these matters had been settled, the Apulian duke sought his camps. At Spinazzola, [Note: [Col. 1063D] Spina is a city in Italy, whence the name Spinales. TIREM.] a fortress that Amicus had fortified with walls and arms,

[Col. 1063B] where his son was present with not a few soldiers, he captured the horsemen and all the others. Only Amicus’s son escaped by flight.

Fearing the loss of more, Amicus asked for peace. The duke graciously favored him, and, after receiving hostages, gladdened the sorrowful fathers by returning their children; the mothers of Juvenacium ceased their lamentation.

These treaties terrified the proud nephews of Count Robert and of Duke Goffred. Their uncle did not consider the wrongs that had been endured, but, forgetful of his anger, granted them pardon when they asked for it.

Relying on these allies and accompanied by a large force, the duke besieged Bari; Argyricius, Abagelardus’s father-in-law, alone had avoided peace.

He received the duke into the city. When his son-in-law had been expelled from the peace and from the city, the duke was restored to Argyricius’s favor.

[Col. 1064A] Since Abagelardus did not enjoy the duke’s peace, he abandoned the lands of his ancestral right and went as an exile to the lands of the Danaans. When Alexius was ruler, [Note: [Col. 1063D] Alexius. LEIBN.] he received him kindly and generously, treated him honorably, and gave him many things. But death, envious and concerned to spare no one, overtook his youthful limbs.

Although he had believed that he would return as a powerful man, with insignia and triumphs of various kinds, he died and was buried in exile among the Greeks.

With the people of Bari joined to him and his forces increased, the duke besieged Trani, which had rebelled at Peter’s instigation.

There the duke left his wife during the siege. He himself went to Tarentum with many soldiers and immediately took it, after besieging it by land and sea.

[Col. 1064B] After setting up camp, he victoriously besieged the fortress of Aneti. From there a pitiable anxiety afflicted Count Peter, because fortune, which seemed to favor the duke, appeared hostile to him. He sought peace and pardon.

Through the envoys whom he had sent, the duke replied that Peter should give him, together with Trani, the fortress of Aneti; unless he did so, he would not deserve to enjoy the duke’s peace.

Peter went to the camp in neglected clothing. He entered, asking for pardon and a peace treaty. He summoned the guards of the fortress and ordered them to come down from the towers. They obeyed and handed the walls over to Robert.

He also handed over Trani, so that he might receive the duke’s favor, and by oath became his faithful subject.

Thus the shrewd and bold duke knew how to bend stiff necks and how to put an end to wars.

[Col. 1063] The third book ends.

# THE FOURTH BOOK BEGINS

[Col. 1063C] After Michael had been cast down from the throne, [Note: [Col. 1063D] This Michael was called Parapinaces, son of Constantine Doukas. He was removed from the empire, and Nicephorus Botaneiates was substituted in his place in the year 1081 of salvation. LEIB.] whose savage will had burned indignantly against the innocent Roman, after his associate brother had been rejected, he became a monk.

Robert’s daughter grieved at the deposition of her husband; the wretched man was forced into exile. After subduing the surrounding cities and fortresses, the duke left Apulian territory and prepared to go to Salerno.

A distinguished count, Raymond, had come to this city from the western regions, before whom Barcelona trembled. He asked that the duke’s daughter be given to him in marriage. The elder daughter was given to him as a bride; the other married an outstanding count, distinguished by the lineage of the Franks.

This man was called Ebalus. He did not know how to yield to an enemy; he was skilled in leading warlike lines into battle, eloquent, and strong in speech and in action.

[Col. 1063D] In those days Pope Gregory came to Benevento, [Note: [Col. 1063D] Gregory VII became supreme pontiff in the year 1073 of salvation. TIREM.] arrived. This city was subject to the Roman pope and belonged to him, and the pope took it badly because the duke had besieged the city.

Robert hurried to the pope’s city to obtain pardon for this offense. He prayed, and, kissing the Father’s feet, [Note: [Col. 1064D] “Of the saint” is lacking. LEIB.] he was received. His person seemed worthy of the honor due to so great a power, and the pope made him sit down.

They held a private consultation for a long time, with everyone else excluded. Then the pope summoned his faithful men. By the pope’s secret orders, these matters were disclosed to them. A book of the Gospels was brought forward.

The duke swore to the pope that, as long as he lived, he would observe the laws of perpetual loyalty to the holy Church, to which the whole world is subject.

The pope was said to have promised him the crown of the Roman kingdom, because King Henry had been condemned by him for the crimes he had committed.

[Col. 1064D] For he had not feared to sell holy churches, he revered the perverse doctrine of Simon, [Note: [Col. 1064D] Simony gave rise to the greatest disputes between Pope Gregory and Emperor Henry. TIREM.] and he granted no one a pontifical dignity except those who had offered the greatest gifts.

He had also committed shameful incest and dared to enter upon shameful adultery. [Note: [Col. 1065D] Henry expelled Agnes, who admonished him about what should be done regarding religion, from every administration; after she had gone to Rome, she did not survive long. TIREM.] He led an unjust life, sacrilegious and adulterous, having no associations with honorable people, but always loving gatherings and societies of the reprobate.

Because these vices were opposed to the virtue of the holy Pope Gregory, he judged Henry should be deposed from the kingdom. He commanded the Saxons to declare that he was no longer their king and to resist him with all their strength.

He summoned the dukes Guelf and Rudolf and urged them, on behalf of Peter and Paul, to resist Henry, against whom Simon had risen.

The crown was thought to have been granted to Rudolf. [Note: [Col. 1065D] Rudolf, duke of Swabia, was substituted for Henry, stripped of the title of king, with the consent of the dukes and envoys who had assembled at Forchheim. TIREM.]

He, joined by a large force of Saxons, declared war against the venerable pope’s enemy.

Many of the people remained attached to the condemned king, recalling the right of their fathers and unwilling to introduce another heir into the kingdom. A grievous struggle arose on both sides.

They were a hard people, unwilling to yield under great blows. On one side the Lotharingians, on the other the Saxons, struck at one another competitively and returned wound for wound. Each side stood firm, striving in turn to resist.

It is said that thirty thousand men were killed there. Yet neither people yielded. Rudolf died, and both exhausted peoples were depleted.

Henry, rejoicing at Rudolf’s death, as though he had thereby become the victor, labored to attack the pope, whom he knew had deposed him from his kingdom. He attempted to come with a large force to besiege Rome.

[Col. 1065C] When the prudent pope learned this, he sought to secure the duke’s support, so that he himself might hasten, ready for arms, to assist him in his difficulty [Note: [Col. 1065D] Robert Guiscard entered Rome, rescued Pope Gregory from the Lateran fortress, and restored him there in the year 1084 of salvation. TIREM.], and suppress the enemy’s strength.

After a perpetual peace treaty had been concluded at Benevento, Gregory returned to Rome, while the duke went to Salerno. Here, Matthew, he built for you a church of wondrous beauty in the city, and a noble hall was prepared for himself.

The insult inflicted on his son-in-law [Note: [Col. 1066D] Michael Doukas. LEIBN.] and on the rejected child, in the august seats, inflamed the duke’s heart with no small concern. This grave injury seemed to many to have been done to the duke, and he desired to go and avenge it.

An old man named Nicephorus had taken up the reins of the kingdom. [Note: [Col. 1066D] Nicephorus Botaneiates, who had expelled Michael from the empire by what stratagem, was himself driven out by Alexius Comnenus. TIREM.] He was sluggish in war, yet shrewd in mind and cautious against hidden dangers. Unwarlike, he feared more than he was feared.

Alexius, commander of the army, supported him. Vigorous in arms and strong through crafty calculation, he was distinguished in character and born of distinguished parents.

From the earliest flowering of his youth, this man spent many years of his life in arms. If anything serious had to be done, he did not hesitate to undertake it when the holy imperial authority commanded him.

[Col. 1066A] The enemies of the empire, Basilacius and Brienus, [Note: [Col. 1066D] Brienus was defeated by Alexius’s valor. TIREM.] distinguished Greeks, powerful in wars and resources, were defeated by this commander; each yielded to the victor.

Brienus was defeated in battle and captured while engaging him not far from the city. Basilacius was defeated and withdrew to the Alexian fortress.

While each was hastening to engage the other, their camps were placed opposite one another as day declined. During the night, prudent Alexius pretended to flee. He abandoned the camp, but did not remove all his equipment; some tents remained standing.

The abandoned flight and the pack animals made the story credible the following day, and the equipment left behind suggested that no enemy was prepared against them. When Basilacius saw no one there ready for hostile war, he ordered his own men to leave the abandoned camp and move around it,

[Col. 1066B] instructing them to report if they encountered any disturbance from horses or troops.

No voice of the watchmen, no sound or neighing of horses could be heard. Basilacius hoped that everything was safe and believed that the enemy, terrified by his forces, had fled.

He was weighed down by sleep after dining to excess, and the entire force lay quiet in the camp. Alexius, brought by hidden paths, suddenly burst upon the enemy and terrified them.

Because darkness obstructed them, no safe place was visible anywhere. There was no hope of escape; they were captured and killed.

Sleep and the violent effect of wine had given them much sluggishness. They could neither flee nor return to their weapons.

Basilacius was deprived of his sight and captured. [Col. 1066C] He was sent to you, Nicephorus, himself unable to see, but destined to be seen by you, against whose empire he had presumed to rebel.

Thus the energetic and cautious victor Alexius overcame many enemies of the empire by arms and by strategy.

The duke, wishing to cross the sea, ordered arms to be prepared and commanded his soldiers to await him at Otranto. He had ships fitted out and himself delayed at Salerno, seeking gifts and reinforcements from every direction.

He continually sent letters here and there, urging his loyal companies to sail with him in armed ships. The undertaking seemed strange to many, especially to those whose wives and dear children were at home. They did not wish to undertake such military service, but the duke added threatening words to his gentle requests and compelled many to hasten.

[Col. 1066D] Everyone assembled at Otranto, as ordered. The duke selected Dalmatian ships suitable for carrying burdens, which that people had sent at his request as assistance.

He filled them with arms, horses, money, and men and sent them to Corfu. [Note: [Col. 1066D] Corfu, formerly Corcyra. LEIB.] This island is not far from the city of Otranto, [Note: [Col. 1066D] Hydruntum, or Hydrus according to some, is a city in Calabria on the Ionian Sea, now called Otranto. TIREM.] and with gentle winds blowing they crossed quickly to it.

After the ships had been dismissed, the duke’s horsemen fiercely invaded the island and struck fear into all who lived around it.

The old man previously mentioned had by this time been driven from the seat of the kingdom. The warrior Alexius [Note: [Col. 1067D] Alexius deprived Nicephorus both of liberty and of citizenship, and under the agreement granted the soldiers three days in which to plunder the city. TIREM.] expelled him in anger, since it was not without injustice toward his brother that the brother had been removed because of him—that brother who had strengthened the empire with all his power and won so many triumphs over the enemy.

With all the legions of the empire accompanying him, Alexius found the city empty of defenses and easily overcame the old man. He was forced to become a monk.

The invaded city was given to the soldiers for three days to plunder. [Note: [Col. 1067D] Alexius Comnenus acquired the empire of Constantinople in the year 1085 of salvation. LEIBN.] Nor did they fear to violate with profane hands even the holy places, atrocious as they were in themselves.

[Col. 1067B] Alexius led them, in order to be more feared by the city, having obtained control of the empire through war.

He courteously showed no small honor to Robert’s daughter. He had heard that Robert wished to come and was striving to make peace with the duke, so that in this way he might turn the duke’s mind away from his undertaking.

But the duke’s resolute mind did not know how to yield from its purpose. After delaying for a short time at Otranto, he awaited the arrival of his wife and of the many counts whom he knew would become companions of his journey.

A certain deceiver came to him from the Greeks, falsely claiming to be Michael, wrongfully demanding the imperial right that had been taken from him. He presented himself as an exile, weeping.

The duke received the weeping man honorably and generously and offered him kindly service with calm goodwill. The entire credulous people also rose and greeted him with bowed necks.

The duke took this man as his companion, so that the cause of his journey might appear more just, and brought him with him as he crossed the sea.

But shortly before he crossed, the king’s messages urged him to hasten, asking him—of the king whom the pope had marked for deprivation of his kingdom—to give assistance against the pope and the arrogant Romans, who had become rebels without justification.

At that time the king had come to Rome and besieged it. [Note: [Col. 1067D] King Henry IV of the Romans, mentioned above, after defeating Matilda at Parma, proceeded toward Rome with hostile intent and established his camp in Nero’s meadows. TIREM.]

Although the duke gave a favorable answer, the envoys returned without any benefit.

He reported everything to Pope Gregory, whom he supported with a pure mind, including the news about the condemned king. He acknowledged that he would never have undertaken that journey if he had been able to foresee the king’s hostile arrival.

But since he had already made such extensive preparations, he declared that he could not withdraw from so great an undertaking.

Meanwhile his wife arrived, and, at the request of the counts, he summoned his distinguished offspring, Roger, while a great crowd watched. In the sight of everyone he designated him as heir and placed him above all others,

[Col. 1068A] himself being the most worthy heir to those over whom he had been placed.

This son, adorned with the character of so great a father and with paternal virtues, showed by the cultivation of his earliest excellence what sort of character he would possess.

The duke gave Roger the whole of Latium as his rightful possession, together with all the lands of Apulia, Calabria, and Sicily.

Robert, count, and Gerard were placed in charge of him. One was born of the duke’s brother, the other was his most faithful companion; both loved virtue and uprightness.

He asked them not to refuse the pope whatever assistance they could provide.

He hastened the journey he had begun. With fifteen Liburnian ships he plowed the Adriatic. The island of Corfu trembled at the approach of so great a prince, supported by chosen soldiers.

The force that had gone ahead captured the city of Botrontum. From there it received Corfu in surrender, a city endowed with natural and constructed defenses; after hostages had been given, the entire island paid tribute.

Sailors plundered Butrint, which they had captured by force.

Bohemond, a cavalryman of great courage, his other son, born of his first wife, was placed over all the companies of cavalry and infantry that the duke had led. He himself commanded that the entire people obey him.

The father besieged Dyrrachium from one side, and the son from the other. They strove to overcome the city, which was besieged by land and sea.

George had often urged the duke to hasten there, because he had heard that Nicephorus had been driven from the throne.

But the ships, having endured the summer season, suffered shipwreck and obstructed the journey. The ship on which the duke was present was broken apart on every side by violent storms, and he was scarcely granted the opportunity to escape.

The loaves brought to restore the bodies were soaked by the rains and ground into pieces; heaps of them, cast upon the shore by the waves, lay in foul-smelling piles.

The duke grieved that the journey he had prepared could not be completed.

Because the storm of air and sea did not abate, and because it caused long delays, Palaiologus led many Argives to Dyrrachium. George was driven from the city by trickery, and Alexius rejoiced that the enemy sent against him had been expelled.

Nevertheless, once he learned that the time had come, the duke did not wish to be diverted from his undertaking. The island of Corfu first submitted.

From there he captured Aulon as well, together with certain coastal cities. Hearing that Dyrrachium was now more strongly fortified,

[Col. 1068D] he besieged it. Once a wealthy city, it had been especially covered with large tiled walls.

Pyrrhus, king of the Epirotes, ordered it to be called “Epiduarum.” [Note: [Col. 1068D] It should be called Epiduarum. LEIB.] He had not hesitated, allied with the people of Tarentum, to endure the Romans’ strenuous wars.

Afterward, having suffered frequent warfare and various hardships, it was emptied of men and reduced to nothing.

[Col. 1069A] Later Zethus and Amphion rebuilt the destroyed city on a smaller scale and ordered it to be called Dyrrachium. The duke surrounded it with a siege.

No small fear seized the citizens of the besieged city. They stationed watchmen, placed reliable guards throughout the city, reported that the duke’s siege had been undertaken by command, and arranged to ask the envoys for assistance.

The duke attempted to attack the city by every means and constructed a wooden siege tower of remarkable workmanship.

A huge stone-throwing engine was erected above it, casting great missiles to destroy the city walls.

The citizens continually saw the camp growing, everything being ravaged, large spoils being amassed, and winter houses being built to withstand the cold.

Compelled to abandon the vain hope that had deceived them—that the enemy would withdraw—

[Col. 1069B] they began to believe that the duke intended to remain and would not depart until he had subjected this city as he had subjected the others.

They sent envoys and asked why he himself had come.

The duke replied that Michael, unjustly expelled from the seat of the kingdom, had come so that he might be restored to his honor.

They promised that the entrances to the city which he requested would never be denied once Michael had been seen.

Surrounded by the sound of horns and trumpets and by the music of stringed instruments, the man who had pretended to be Michael was led forth in imperial fashion, crowned according to custom and encircled on every side by singing crowds.

When the citizens saw him with one accord, they mocked the sight with laughter, saying: “This man used to carry bowls full of wine to the tables of Lyaeus, and he was one of the lesser cupbearers.”

After Alexius learned that Robert had invaded his cities,

[Col. 1069C] fearing that he might subject Dyrrachium as well, he prepared to meet the duke there with a large force. He warned the people allied with him to resist the duke by fighting at sea.

This was no inexperienced or timid naval people. Populous Venice had sent it, at the empire’s request—a people rich in resources and rich in men. Its territory lies where the innermost gulf of the Adriatic waters extends beneath Arcturus.

The walls of this people are surrounded by sea, and no one can pass from one house to another unless carried by a small boat. They always live upon the waters. No people is stronger in naval warfare or in steering ships across the sea.

[Col. 1069D] Alexius urged them, for the sake of the besieged citizens, to bring assistance, bring their ships, and fight against the duke’s ships, so that, once these enemies were defeated in war, it would be easy to begin the land battle.

The imperial command obeyed, despite the duke’s weakened people, and they hastened to go and fight with the duke’s ships.

It was already becoming evening when the duke’s ships came to meet them. But because night was approaching, both sides postponed the battle.

At dawn of the following day, the rising light drove away the shadows, and each people prepared for naval war.

[Col. 1070A] Because the Venetian people was more experienced in this warfare, it rushed forward boldly. [Note: [Col. 1069] The Venetian commander was Domenico Selvo. TIREM.] The duke’s fleet was terrified and fled back to the harbor, so the battle ended.

When daylight returned for the third time, a large Venetian force approached the harbor and attacked Robert’s ships.

The Ragusan people, accompanying the duke with Dalmatian ships, filled the sea with dense showers of missiles.

Nevertheless, they did not dare to take the ships far from the harbor, since the proximity of the camp had made the harbor safe.

The Venetians cut the ropes and violently pushed some ships away from the shore; the crowd drove them off by force.

This event did not terrify the duke’s undaunted mind. It was considering another course and was still prepared to fight. He decided to bring in other ships, capable of carrying and inflicting greater exertion.

[Col. 1070B] Alexius gladly heard of the deeds of the victorious force. The islands that had customarily paid tribute to Robert, when they learned that the duke’s ships were stronger at sea, proposed to become rebels with equal fierceness.

An imperial edict resounded. [Note: [Col. 1069] An edict. LEIB.] By command of the empire, lest the enemy, foreseeing the war and taking precautions, avoid the dangers to come, every passage through the mountains and rivers was fortified.

Thus Alexius hoped to rush upon an unsuspecting enemy and overcome the unconquered duke by a hidden assault.

He led innumerable companies drawn from various peoples. A vast multitude of barbarian forces accompanied the Greeks.

Nevertheless, Basil was sent ahead with two thousand chosen horsemen and ordered to reconnoiter the camp of Duke Robert.

[Col. 1070C] He was a Mesopotamian, experienced in the varied hardships of war, and he followed the commands of the one giving orders.

When he had already come near the city of Butrint, word arrived that the duke’s horsemen were not far away, carrying considerable booty, although many of them had already been wounded by the arrows of the Turks whom he had brought.

They unanimously resolved that it was better to die in battle than to yield shamefully to the Greeks. They turned against the enemy, closing their ranks, where they prevailed by their preparation.

The Turks were terrified when they saw the enemy turn and resist them fiercely, striking hard.

Basil could not maintain his line while it was fleeing and was captured in flight. The Norman battle line hastened to present the captive to the duke.

Robert questioned him closely about everything: what Alexius was attempting against him, what he intended to undertake, and how many troops he had mobilized for war.

After the duke learned that the hostile arrival was near and with how many forces Alexius was attacking him, he summoned all the nobles he had brought with him. When they had been called, he disclosed everything he knew and consulted them about what had to be done.

Some of them, whose minds were fierce, proposed that several men leave the camp by stratagem and meet the approaching enemy without hesitation, in order to terrify their assault.

The duke replied that it was better not to withdraw from the camp until the imperial force had been seen more closely, and he declared that the art of victory was sought in vain, since victory was granted to no one except from heaven.

Although he knew that excellent horsemen were present with him, he did not wish to be rash in beginning the engagement.

He was told that the opposing force was innumerable, and he did not yet know the character of the men.

Therefore, shrewdly and intelligently, he arranged them all before his own forces and prepared everything that was needed. He did not wish to await the enemy’s wedges close to Dyrrachium, where, if they came suddenly, the mountains and plains would be covered with them like locusts.

The sun was already near the Ocean. Therefore neither side wished to undertake battle; they gave their limbs to rest.

Alexius had ordered all the people of Dyrrachium, after the enemy had engaged, to strive to come behind them,

[Col. 1071B] so that the duke would be unable to make himself safe either to the rear or to the front.

When day came, the prudent duke burned their camp, so that, once the duke had departed, no one would be permitted to rush in.

He himself first stirred up his companies for battle and moved many forces against Alexius.

The Calabrians, together with the Lombards, were terrified, and all...

He who had been a sailor under the duke nearly sought flight, and at the first encounter the duke’s cavalry itself was terrified, while the enemy’s attack pressed heavily upon it. Having crossed the river, he came upon certain narrow and unsuspecting places. The duke, so that no one could come from the city against him or proceed toward the city, had had the bridge destroyed. While these constricted places hindered the passage of his men, they were covered on every side by a violent cloud of missiles; no greater hailstorm of arrows, it is said, had ever been seen, and the place, which had begun to be secure, was no longer so.

Meanwhile, since they were able neither to fight nor to retreat and spread out backward, they struggled by rushing into the sea, because the tightly packed crowd itself hindered them no less than the enemy did. Such a harsh confinement seemed unbearable to the Normans. The imperial army, thinking that they had been overcome and exhausted, attacked them, eagerly hoping to capture the defeated Venetian fleet, which was floating nearby on the waves, and thirsting for plunder. The horses and various baggage were seized, which the duke’s hastening army had left behind in its eagerness for battle.

Meanwhile, after the crowd had withdrawn, it was scarcely able to join the duke at sea. He had passed beyond the ruinous danger of that unfavorable place with great exertion; he was at the forefront, although the battle line that had previously been ordered here had been altered. The confinement of the place had forced everything to be changed in that lamentable terrain.

He rejoiced to find his men present and, as their commander, first encouraged them with a few words, loudly declaring that their only protection would lie in arms. If they turned their backs on the Greeks, he threatened to slaughter each one like cattle and foretold to the captives a life equal to death.

With these exhortations he kindled the hearts of his men. Although he saw the countless troops of Alexius’ party hastening toward him, he rushed against the enemy without distrust, trusting in the honor which the pope, supreme shepherd of Peter, had granted him, and in the merits of Saint Matthew, whose church he had built.

Relying on Saint Matthew, he rushed boldly against the enemy and, fierce in battle, engaged them not far from the besieged city. Alexius was defeated, and his men turned their backs, for more than five thousand of the Argolic people were slain in this battle. A large part of the Turks also perished with the Greeks, and a varied glitter of weapons and horses was captured. The diverse and splendid standards of the Danaans were taken as well. Scarcely could thirty horsemen of the duke’s people be seen among the slain.

Alexius lamented that the enemy had prevailed over him, although he had neither an equal number of troops nor equal resources. He himself withdrew wounded. In tears and without glory he was compelled to return, although he had vainly hoped for the glory of triumph.

Robert’s wife happened to be wounded in this battle by a certain arrow. Terrified by the wound, and expecting no assistance, she had nearly surrendered herself to the enemy, whose ship she wished to board because she feared the imminent dangers of death. God rescued her, unwilling that so great, noble, and venerable a matron should become a laughingstock.

Constantine, stripped of the honor of the kingdom, died in this battle and was buried with fitting honor. Greece lost many nobles at Dyrrachium, whose unburied corpses decay across the fields. The duke did not wish to remain long in the Alexian camp because of the rotting corpses.

The faithful Venetian people, obeying the commands of the empire, held the city of Dyrrachium. Having departed from that city, the duke reached a river called Divalus. There he built himself a fortress and settled in various places those who had accompanied him, so that, when the frost of winter bore down, they could live in safety.

The Venetian people inflicted various punishments upon most of those who had crossed over with the duke but had not followed him into battle. They assigned the refugees to servile occupations; they confined others in the prisons of the workhouse; those sent back to their homeland were handed over by others to the Greeks.

Among the people of Dyrrachium whom the Venetian land had sent was a distinguished man named Dominicus. He hated a certain man because that man did not share the counsel which Dominicus was proposing to many of his associates. That group sought to have this man as its leader; it was said that the Venetian duke had fathered him.

Dominicus tried to deprive him of his leadership. He summoned to himself a certain Barinus from among the refugees, a man dear to him and proven by the steadfastness of his loyalty. He advised him to seek Robert’s camp by night and to say that he wished to disclose his own advantage to the duke. He also told him to urge the duke to hasten to a place called Petra.

That place is near the church of Saint Nicholas. Robert went there with a small number of soldiers. Summoned by the refugee, the Venetian met him and readily promised the surrender of Dyrrachium, unless the duke refused to grant him what he requested. He willingly pledged under oath that what Dominicus sought would be fulfilled: his niece would be given to him as a wife.

After their conversation each secretly returned. They first determined at what time Dominicus would carry out the surrender and at what time the duke would return. The day agreed upon by both was now approaching.

The duke selected certain men from Cosenza, whom he knew to be swift in movement; he joined to them certain chosen horsemen. Hastening toward the city during the quiet of night, he carefully sent the refugee ahead, so that he might report to him what needed to be done in the city.

The Venetian had already been waiting for him for a considerable part of the night when sleep overcame him. The refugee Barinus soon forced him to awaken and announced the duke’s arrival. The duke ordered him quickly to admit his trusted men into the city without favoring anyone. Barinus returned and sent the duke’s infantry in first; he entrusted to them the buildings and districts that lacked guards.

During the night they caused no disturbance. At daybreak the entire city perceived, amid various trumpet blasts, that the enemy had entered. Every Venetian seized his arms, except those whom that domestic enemy had lured by his promises to Robert. Each inhabitant, once the enemy had got above them, dug a defensive ditch within the fortifications so that the enemy would not have an easy descent upon the city.

The duke had ordered his troops to hasten from the camp that same night. When he heard the voices of his men, he hurried up and sent them through every gate. Thus, when the inhabitants saw themselves attacked from within and without, the confused Venetian army cried out that the Venetian forces had proved faithless, and every Venetian fled from the city.

Some were killed, some captured, and some fled to the Adriatic Sea; thus the fugitives escaped by driving their ships onward. All the Venetians who had resisted with arms, as well as the son of their duke, were captured when the city was taken, and the fleet was driven from the shore.

Thus the duke brought Dyrrachium under his authority. What he could not conquer by arms, he subdued by a victory of stratagem; and he rejoiced that everything he had promised the Venetian had been fulfilled for him after the surrender.

Meanwhile the people of Troy and Ascoli, one unwilling any longer to fulfill the customary obligation of tribute, the other grieving over the destruction of its walls, united in purpose and attacked Roger, the distinguished heir of the duke. Famous for his judgment and his arms, Roger resisted with whatever forces he could muster, shut up in the citadel of Troy. At last, when his allies and certain of his father’s men hastened to his aid, he rushed out of the citadel in fury and punished the rebellious people with various tortures. He cut off one man’s hand, another’s foot; he deprived one of his nose and another of his testicles; he disfigured some by removing their teeth and others by cutting off their ears.

Such is often the hidden rage of a captured tigress when, shut in, she can vent her fury upon no one. If by chance she can escape after breaking through her restraints, she devours and seizes everything she sees and displays an unaccustomed fury. Even a lion flees the encounter with the raging creature, although it is smaller in body, while he is the stronger.

After a year had passed, Robert again crossed the Adriatic waters to the Apulian territories by ship. He had entrusted the entire people to his firstborn son, whose name was Bohemond, and likewise to Brienus.

When the duke discovered that the people of Canosa were in rebellion against him, he besieged them and razed the besieged city to the ground.

“Rex” is used here in the sense of a ruler or governor. [LEIB.]

Hermanus, a ruler, had been born to the same mother as Onfredi’s son Abagelardus, though the two did not have the same father: she had been joined to two men. Each brother was a distinguished soldier in arms, but both yielded to the powerful Robert, whose power scarcely had an equal anywhere in the world.

After the destruction of Canosa, Robert planned to go to Rome against Henry, the enemy of Gregory, the Roman prelate. For a long time a great barbarian host had delayed there for two years; it had broken the high walls with siege engines and demolished many towers of the unconquered city. The Transtiberine district had already submitted to him, while Gregory had been shut up in a certain fortress.

This was the mausoleum of Hadrian. [LEIB.]

It was sufficiently fortified and seemed, because of its astonishingly laborious construction, impregnable to anyone. A guard of faithful men had also fortified it.

When Henry learned that Robert had undertaken such preparations and was bringing arms against him with such great equipment, King Henry fled. The duke’s courage terrified him, as did his valor, already known throughout the world. Fearing to await him, he withdrew to a safe place.

Robert, hastening to Rome, pierced by force the walls of the distinguished city. [TIREM: The part of the city destroyed by Robert lay between the Lateran and the Capitol.] Nevertheless, with the help of a few supporters of Gregory and after certain buildings had been burned, he violently freed the pope, who had already been under siege for so long.

He led Gregory with great honor to Salerno. [TIREM: Gregory died there.]

After the duke’s departure, the Roman citizens, eager for Henry, again yielded to him. He himself had granted them the Ravennate Guibert, whom Henry publicly invested with the pontifical crown in the Lateran basilica. [TIREM.] Guibert, rising with equal criminal intent, presumed to seize the rule of the Apostolic See; the populace called him Clement.

After bringing the Roman troops back from the city to Salerno, the duke dismissed them; no army equal to his ever remained in that place. He had led six thousand horsemen and thirty thousand infantry to Rome. Thus, at one and the same time, the two rulers of the lands were defeated: this Alemannic king and that supreme ruler of the Roman Empire. [TIREM: These victories bear witness to Guiscard’s outstanding valor.]

One of them, rushing to arms, was overcome by arms; the other withdrew solely through fear of the name he had heard.

[Col. 1073] The fourth book ends.

THE FIFTH BOOK BEGINS.

[Col. 1075]

When Alexius learned that Robert had crossed the sea, he tried to restore his diminished forces and to break through the absent duke’s camp. Two powerful men held these positions by strength and counsel: the duke’s son Bohemond and Brienus.

Not far from Jamna, a city of no little renown, the people of Alexius’ party had established their camp. Alexius fortified that position in many ways with a barrier of wagons. Its proximity to the open plain made it easy to penetrate, but iron caltrops obstructed every approach, so that, when the enemy loosened the reins and let the horses go, the horses’ feet would be pierced.

But while a fog obstructed the Danai’s view, the Normans secretly reached that place through rough ground thick with vines and full of reeds. Alexius resisted them for a short time when they met, but he was unable to withstand their continued pressure. Defeated, he sought flight and withdrew.

After his second defeat in battle, he made for the splendid city of Thessaly which the common people call Salanichin. [TIREM: After his defeat, Alexius fled to Salanichin, that is, Salonica, formerly Thessalonica.]

Since he knew that the outcomes of wars are various, he still tried to return to battle. Bohemond, rejoicing more in a bold army than in a numerous one and exulting in the honor of having captured Civisci, besieged Larissa, renowned for its distinguished name. He had heard that the imperial treasures had been carried there and that the city was filled with great wealth.

From this place Achilles, the author of the Trojan disaster, had gone forth.

Alarmed by the siege of his city, Alexius came with an innumerable host and engaged the Normans in manly battle. The force accompanying Brienus gave way before them as they fought.

Seeing a considerable army on the hills, Bohemond believed that the imperial ruler himself was present. He rushed upon the trembling enemy and pursued the Greek army as Nisus pursues larks. The Greeks turned their backs, but so great a cloud of dust enveloped both sides that neither could see where the other was going. The defeated Greeks sought the shelter of the forests.

The victor returned to the mountains after killing some of them, watching to see whether further battles might be prepared against him. When Alexius learned that the enemy had withdrawn, he approached the Larissan camp with a large force.

The infantry left in the camp, unable to withstand the enemy pressing them with greater strength, were defeated. Most were killed, while the smaller part fled. Whatever spoils the victorious crowd had gathered from every place, Alexius carried away.

A messenger hastened to the mountain to announce the adverse outcome to Bohemond, who had expected to be the victor. He grieved that his men had been defeated; yet he himself feared nothing and sought to reunite his companions who had been scattered. Misfortune could not terrify the man’s mind. Rather, he lamented that the city, already freed from the siege, had now been defeated and subdued.

Night had now arrived and, exhausted from battle, urged them to give their bodies to rest. Bohemond sought a shady valley nearby, which provided everything suitable for himself and his men; there they gave their bodies over to sleep.

Three days later, two powerful Greek armies gathered to prepare for war against Bohemond. One was led by the German Augustus Melisianus; the other by a relative named Adrianus.

Remembering their accustomed valor, the Normans rushed swiftly to arms. Accustomed to escaping the fleeing Greeks on foot, they hastened back to the walls of Larissa, where Alexius himself, shut in, did not dare to leave, though he had been defeated so many times. The fleeing Turks were likewise shut up in the city.

The Norman people could not remain long while those men were besieged, because the land, having suffered the labor of plundering, refused them food for sustenance, and their provisions had been lost in the camps recently captured. With his soldiers divided, Bohemond sought the districts of Ebellona for the necessities of life, while Brienus sought Castorea.

Alexius, leaving behind a large part of his men at Salonica, returned to the seat of his own city, which had been founded by Constantine and had taken its name from him.

Meanwhile the Venetian people returned with their ships repaired and, meeting no opposition, entered the city of Dyrrachium, because few citizens remained in the city; an extraordinary calamity had scattered the inhabitants everywhere.

After remaining for fifteen days, the Venetians tried to empty Dyrrachium of its useful goods. But the secure fortification, protected by garrisons left behind by the duke, denied them control of the castle. When they saw that it could not be captured, they withdrew.

On hearing that the duke’s son had returned and that many ships had entered together by sea, they erected beams and constructed a small city. After assembling a wooden fort, the prudent people placed there all the equipment of their fleet and settled themselves within it.

Thus, beneath their little shelters, they remained safely at sea during the cold season, in the face of rainy winters.

Winter was now yielding, and the gentle breezes of spring were blowing, when everyone proceeded with all the ships to Corisus; the island pleased them all. The commander of Alexius’ fleet, Mabrica, had come there.

From there many sailors decided that Venice should be revisited, so that their departure might take place by mutual agreement and each might return to the homeland of his companions.

They decided that this should be done because Robert’s return was being delayed too long; prolonged business concerning the disposal of their possessions was the reason for the delay.

During that period Robert was occupied with great concern in waging especially important wars against Jordan. He wished to leave nothing unfinished and therefore did not himself wish to return to Latium.

Prince Jordan, terrified by the report of Henry’s arrival, did not meet him in arms in order to defend himself and his territories. Instead, he established firm peace treaties with him and submitted to him. He gave his son as a hostage, and together with his offspring he presented many gifts of gold solidi.

He did this so that he would not be deprived of his hereditary right to rule, if the king should be granted passage into the Apulian fields.

Since it had yielded to his jurisdiction—the jurisdiction of Jordan [the reference is uncertain]—the duke ravaged that man’s lands with iron and fire. Then Jordan’s nephew sought peace and received what he requested from Pope Gregory, after everything had been settled before he returned to the borders of the Greeks. He begged the pope to dedicate the church he had built in honor of Saint Matthew, and the pope graciously granted the petitioner’s request.

When these matters had been completed, Robert turned his attention to the undertaking which he had long been considering. He therefore selected sailors and those whom he knew to be most suitable for military service and had them accompany him to Tarentum.

When the entire fleet had assembled there with its people, he equipped it with magnificent military preparations; the ships were filled with provisions and arms. He went with these companions to the harbor of Brindisi, which seemed safer. He feared crossing at Otranto, although that crossing was shorter, because autumn was beginning and the calm summer had withdrawn.

Fearing that a sudden storm might cause delay at Otranto and damage the ships, he took refuge with his fleet in the safe harbor and prudently awaited favorable winds.

Then, bidding farewell to his wife who stood on the shore, and at the same time to the people who remained there with his wife, he began to depart from the Ausonian territories, never to return.

He crossed the Adriatic Sea with 120 armed ships, accompanied by his son Roger, who sought to imitate his father in military vigor and in a gracious friendliness toward all.

He also led cargo ships, whose capacity was their proper function; he filled them with horses, provisions, arms, and various supplies required for use at sea.

That army crossed the sea, assembled by the other son of the distinguished duke, whom he had left in command.

They spent nearly two months on the shore, compelled by severe weather to postpone the war. When calm weather returned, they left the harbor and prepared a naval battle against the Venetian ships and the Greek chelandia.

The duke led five triremes; he entrusted five to Roger, five to his brother Robert, and five to Bohemond.

These were supported by an accompanying force of smaller vessels.

The Greeks brought countless chelandia to the war. Another group, relying on nine tall triremes, which Venice knew to be especially suitable for battle, saw that Robert’s ships were inferior to its own and boldly engaged them.

Supported by the Greek chelandia placed between them, they wounded the enemy with countless missiles hurled from above and threatened to hurl great weights of iron, lest the hostile fleet draw near.

Scarcely anyone on the ship carrying Roger into battle was found uninjured. Roger himself was wounded in the arm, yet stood there, unwilling to yield to the resisting enemy. Forgetful of the wound inflicted upon him, the ardor of honor—which is accustomed to accompany victors—spurred him on.

His father, often adorned with distinguished triumphs, summoned him and ordered him, once summoned, to separate the chelandia from the larger fleet. Eager to obey his father’s command, he hastened to follow the order. With the five triremes entrusted to him, he prepared to carry the war against the chelandia.

While he fought, the Greeks offered no resistance but fled in every direction, as birds do not dare oppose a flying eagle, and hares are forced to flee in fearful haste lest they be seized and become food for its hooked claws and ravenous beak.

Once these had been driven away, the Venetian fleet stood alone.

When Robert and his sons saw that the Greek ships had been routed and only the triremes remained, they fiercely attacked them with their own ships. Their assault and impact were so violent that, after seven ships had been sunk, the Venetian fleet hoped it could not escape. But it was of no use for only two ships to remain in the battle; all were compelled to yield to the enemy. The duke triumphed according to his customary manner.

After his triumph over the fleet, the victor brought two thousand of those fighters to the harbor with him, namely those who had resisted most strongly and whose courage had been greatest.

Besides these he counted another five hundred who had been captured. Seven Argolic ships were captured in this battle while the Greeks were fleeing.

Those who had faithfully guarded the fortress of Corif were released from the siege they had endured while the duke, so greatly feared, was absent.

Next he arranged to bring along both the victorious and the defeated ships and to place them in safe stations while winter frost bore down.

With sagacious planning he led them to the river Glycaeus. There he stationed the ships and sailors and ordered them to remain until the season of summer should return peacefully.

He himself led his cavalry to Bunditia to spend the winter with them and remained there.

The harsher-than-usual frost forced the people who lived near the river Clicaeus to languish. Most of them suffered the hardships of cold and hunger and perished. The pestilence grew so severe that, before the third month had fully passed, nearly ten thousand men had been carried off by death.

Nor was the remaining army free from such slaughter. Within a short time the disease destroyed five hundred horsemen in a common disaster, and a large part of the common people also fell. No horseman, sailor, or any man was able to escape the ruin of imminent death.

Yet these misfortunes did not break the duke’s spirit. He remained strong and undaunted in every adversity.

His son Bohemond, falling ill, asked his father to permit him to return to the shores of Italy, which abounded in many physicians and medicines. Although unwilling, Robert consented to the one who wished to depart, desiring to restore the health of so distinguished a son.

He gave him what was necessary for his departure. When Bohemond had left, he ordered Roger to go with his soldiers to Cephallenia, which had rebelled during such a storm, so that it might be subdued and restrained when the island was captured.

He knew that the Greek cities everywhere were to be terrorized. Roger obeyed his father’s orders, hastened with the duke’s troops to the appointed city, and besieged it.

The duke returned to the ships stationed on the river Glycaeus and tried to lead them away, eager to subdue the arrogant Greeks by sea no less than by land. Fierce in spirit, he worked to prepare war both with horses and with the fleet, so that every island might be thrown into confusion when the ships were brought up and might pay the imperial tribute into the duke’s treasury.

When summer returned, the supply of water diminished, and the riverbed no longer flowed with enough water for the sailors to lead the ships down the river.

The duke, who by skill makes difficult labor easy, learned that the river lacked its usual flow. The waterway ran through a narrow channel, and so he ordered many stakes to be brought and driven into both banks of the river, joined together with wickerwork.

With many branches cut from many trees, he constructed lattices and filled them above with sand, so that the water, scattered disorderly, might be gathered into one channel.

The riverbed thereby became higher and more capacious, and the flowing water was compelled to provide a navigable course for the ships, which were brought unharmed back to the waters of the sea.

At this time the venerable Pope Gregory died at Salerno. [TIREM: Pope Gregory’s death occurred in 1085.]

Neither personal affection nor love of gold ever bent him; he always resolved to maintain strict justice. Joy could not make his heart excessively glad, nor sorrow make him sad. He was the comforter of the sorrowful, the way of light, and a teacher of honesty. He restrained the arrogant by laws and supported the humble.

He was the terror of the wicked and the shield of the upright. By scattering the seeds of the saving word, he never ceased to call the faithful people back from vices to the character by which one goes to heaven. His life did not depart from his teaching. He was neither unstable nor light as a reed.

When he heard of the death of so great a man, the duke could not restrain his tears. Neither the death of his father, nor that of his son, nor that of his wife would have compelled him to weep more, even if he had seen either of them in their final hour.

His grief at the death was great because the bond of love between them had been great during their lives. Neither had ever withdrawn from the other’s affection after they had once strengthened their mutual treaties of peace.

The church of Saint Matthew, where the pope was buried, ennobles the city with the treasure of so great a body. Since the translation of the apostle Matthew makes it a city of lofty renown, and since the merit of this vicar increases when he is laid there, the duke would have chosen it above all cities as his place of residence, if he had been permitted to live.

But after the death of Gregory the prelate, it was not permitted to him to return to the places in Latium which he had left.

The noble Roger, the duke’s son, continued without interruption to terrify Cephallenia with threats. The island was proposed to Robert as one to be conquered, and his son had been sent to capture it.

As Roger was boarding a ship so that he might return to inspect the camp, he was first seized by fever. The blazing dog-star had begun, whose fiercest summer heat is usually harmful to mortals at that season.

His wife had arrived from Italy not long before and was present in the camp while the duke returned to the camp of his son, leaving the people behind with the fleet.

When she learned that Robert was feverish—on whom all her hope rested, since he was such a husband—she tore her garments, wept, and hurried to him at a swift pace, as though her husband had already failed. Seeing that his final hour was near, she tore her cheeks with her nails and, having ripped apart her hair, left it disheveled.

“Alas!” she cried. “What shall I do, most wretched woman, or where shall I, unhappy, be able to go? Will not the Greeks, when they hear of your death, attack your son, your wife, and your people, for whom you alone were glory, hope, and strength?
