Your presence protected them, because, while you were present, no enemy among your people feared threats or an encounter.

“Although the opposing battle line was crowded with many troops, those whom your encouragement had made secure dared to engage in war, and worldly valor could never resist once it had seen you.

“Look, your son is being left to be devoured by wolves, and your wife, and your people, who can never be safe without you. Since you were the courage of our people, once you are lost, the people will no longer be courageous.

“Any cowardly mob will be able to surpass them. Impious death, spare the man whose destruction will destroy so many with him. I beg you, yield to these prayers, though you know not how to yield; at least wait until you lead us back to our own people, so that a safe place may receive us after your death.

“Ah, wretched woman that I am! I plead in vain with death, which has always been ungrateful to the one who pleads and has never spared anyone.”

Roger likewise, weeping with his mother, raised great cries with groans to heaven. He lamented that he had been deprived of his father before he was either fully aware of what he possessed or knew how to prepare to possess it completely and follow his father’s deeds of virtue.

Who could look with dry eyes upon the tears of the assembled people? Who would be so patient, so hard-hearted, as not to share the sorrow of so many sufferers?

Amid all these tears, after receiving the body and blood of Christ, Robert was stripped of his life. Thus, in exile, the limbs of the powerful prince released his spirit, deprived of his body, and he died. [TIREM: Robert Guiscard died, according to Onuphrius and Sigonius, in the year of salvation 1085; Colenutius gives 1082.]

He had been accustomed, when present, to inspire strong courage in others, so that his men suffered no fear. His wife could not bear to leave the man’s body in the lands of the Greeks and tried to return it to his own country. She boarded the galley which she knew to be the swiftest and crossed with Robert’s body aboard, so that, dead, he might bring consolation to Latium when he returned, although while alive he had not been permitted to return to his own realms.

Roger went to his father’s camp and anxiously announced his father’s death to all the people. He sought their counsel, for he confessed that, unless he returned quickly, he would be deprived of the honor of his father’s authority, since his father had declared him to be his heir.

They all promised him with faithful hearts that, just as they had served his father, they were ready to serve him. They unanimously asked that he be their coadjutor in crossing the sea, and he granted the people’s request.

Nevertheless, he begged them to await him until Cephallenia, the island where he had left his companions, should be captured. He said that the people left behind in the siege ought not, by right, to call him faithful if he refused to return to inspect their camp and failed to announce to them his father’s death, which he had reported to the others, and his own departure.

After saying this, he returned to the camp of his siege and announced that his father had died and that he wished to depart.

Each man replied that he would do whatever Roger had done and that he did not wish to abandon the beginnings of his service, provided that suitable and appropriate compensation were given to him.

When Roger had thus withdrawn and gone to his own camp, the people remaining in the other camp were shaken by such terror that they had no hope of escaping alive, as though life and safety were being denied them.

If all the Greeks, the Persian people, and the Agarene people had attacked them, and if people from every region of the world had poured in and sought, armed, to attack the unarmed, their fear would not have been greater than this fear. The death of one man was the cause of terror to many. They feared that, once the duke was dead, they would be unable to resist even a few of the countless peoples whom they had usually defeated while he was alive.

Thus, although one man had often been stronger than ten thousand, two men were proved capable of routing a thousand.

Terrified that the enemy might attack with a larger fleet, the people tried to preserve the smaller ships, so that, having crossed the Adriatic Sea, they might escape their fear.

Such was their terror that they cared neither for their possessions nor their cloaks. They set everything aside and, with suppliant prayers, begged the sailors to take only their bodies aboard the ships.

Although the ships were farther from the land, some mounted horses to reach them, and, leaving the horses behind, placed only their bodies aboard. Others swam, so that by swimming they might climb onto a ship.

Nevertheless, most of them, because they could not return by ship, remained behind and surrendered themselves to the Greeks. Those who had been feared now began, in their timidity, to serve the Greeks, their fierce courage having been driven away.

The ships had now been brought alongside the Apulian shores when an intolerable storm shook the swollen sea. Many sailors suffered shipwreck there. Part of the people perished with the fleet, and the ship which had carried the noble body was broken apart by the storms. The corpse, which had fallen into the sea, was drawn out with difficulty, lest harmful stench should emerge from it.

The duke’s wife, always endowed with prudent counsel, ordered his entrails and heart to be buried at Otranto, and the remainder of the body was preserved with much spice. From there she had it carried to the city of Venosa, where the tombs of his earlier brothers had been built. The duke was buried near them with great honor.

The city of Venosa shines, adorned with such tombs. From the time of Charlemagne or even of Caesar, the earth has never produced brothers equal to those buried here. A church was built at their command, whose splendor stands out above that of this city. May the Three-in-One King grant it the gift of pardon.

[Col. 1081] The fifth book ends.

Roger, you recognize that our verses are written for you. The poet, with joyful mind, has striven to serve you. Cheerful donors have always deserved cheerful authors. You, a duke more worthy than the Roman duke Octavian, be, I beg you, for me a hope of good fortune, as he was for Maro.

The end.

[Col. 1083]

A BRIEF NORTHMANNIC CHRONICLE (1041–1085), BY AN ANONYMOUS AUTHOR, NOW FIRST PUBLISHED FROM THE MANUSCRIPT CODEX OF THE CHURCH OF NARDÒ.

NOTICE BY LUDOVICO ANTONIO MURATORI

We possess many chronicles, both distinguished and published, in which the glorious deeds of the Northmannic people in Apulia, Calabria, and Sicily are described. As has been established, our collection will include them one by one. I now add to the published works this brief account, previously unpublished, which begins with the year 1041 and continues to the death of the most celebrated prince Robert Guiscard, duke of Apulia—that is, to the year 1085.

The date of its composition seems to be indicated by its final lines. At the end, we read: “Roger, his son, succeeds Robert, the father of William III, duke of Apulia, who is now happily ruling.” Robert Guiscard left behind Roger, surnamed Borsa, who also succeeded him in the duchy of Apulia. Roger, by his wife Adela, fathered William, who succeeded his father in the duchy in the year 1111 and held it until the year 1127, when, toward the end of July, he exchanged life for death.

This prince is mentioned by Falco of Benevento, Alexander of Telese, Orderic Vitalis, and other writers. Therefore this little history appears to have been written before 1127 and is consequently not without value. I owe it to the noble and exceptionally learned lover of letters Ignazio Maria Como of Naples, who obtained a copy from the distinguished and learned Pietro Polidoro.

Polidoro himself reports that this little book was copied from the manuscript codex of the episcopal archive of the Church of Nardò and collated with another belonging to the distinguished Jacopo de Franchis and with one belonging to a member of the Taviani marquises. The Nardò codex appeared to have been written around the year 1530; the other, from the form of its script and other indications, was believed to have been written toward the end of the twelfth century or the beginning of the thirteenth.

I do not know by what process three years were omitted after the year 1074. This little work too will be useful when chronological disputes arise concerning the earlier deeds of the Northmannic people in Apulia and Sicily.

THE NORTHMANNIC CHRONICLE BEGINS: CONCERNING EVENTS CARRIED OUT IN JAPYGIA AND APULIA AGAINST THE GREEKS

[Col. 1083A] In the year 1041, the Northmen, under the Lombard leader Arduino, first invaded Apulia with a large and powerful army.

In the year 1042, in the month of March, the Northmen engaged in battle in Apulia with Michael the imperial Protospatharius, who was called Dulchianus, and defeated him. In the month of May they fought again, and again the Greeks and the Protospatharius were defeated. Many cities and places in Apulia that belonged to the Greeks and to the emperor Michael were captured; Constantine succeeded Michael in this year.

In the year 1043, the magister Maniaces, with a Greek army, fought against the Northmen near Matera, and there was great slaughter in both armies.

In the year 1045, Argyrus of Bari, the imperial catapan and duke of the Greeks, went to Tarentum against the Northmen and defeated them. He then went to Trani and was defeated by them under William Iron-Arm, who was designated the first count of Apulia.

## Year 1046

A battle was again fought in Apulia between the Greeks and the Northmen. The latter routed and scattered the Greek army; their leader was Duke Drogo, who became the second count of Apulia.

## Year 1048

The Northmen went against the Greeks in Calabria, invaded it, and defeated the Greeks near Tricaricum. Humphrey captured Troia and built a fortress at Bachareza.

[Col. 1084A] **Year 1051.** Drogo was killed in Apulia, and Humphrey succeeded him.

**Year 1052.** A battle was fought with Argyrus, the Greek catapan, and his army was again routed by the Northmen near Tarentum. A battle was likewise fought near Croton in Calabria, and Sico the protosphatharius was defeated. Northman rule became powerful in Calabria and Apulia, and their power and the fear of them increased throughout the whole land.

**Year 1053.** The Northmen waged war against Pope Leo, the Beneventan prince, and the imperial catapan in the principality of Benevento. Prince Rudolph was routed, and Pope Leo was captured by Humphrey and the Northmen; a great slaughter took place in the month of June.

[Col. 1084B] **Year 1054.** The emperor Constantine, surnamed Monomachus, died. After him Theodora ruled, Constantine’s [daughter?] and sister of the empress Augusta Zoe.

**Year 1055.** Humphrey fought a battle with the Greeks near Oria and defeated them. Count Geoffrey captured Neritonum and Ditium. Count Robert marched against Callipolis, and the Greek army was again routed in the territory of Tarentum. Hydruntum and the fortress of Minerva were captured.

**Year 1056.** Humphrey died, and Count Robert entered into possession of Apulia; he was called Guiscard. [Col. 1085A] A battle was fought near Tarentum in the month of September, and the Greeks were defeated. A great slaughter of men took place from Tarentum to Hydruntum, and all the cities and lands came under Northman rule [or homage; *dominio vel hominio*]. The Augusta Theodora died, and Michael, called Stratonicus, succeeded her.

**Year 1057.** Michael was deposed from the empire, and Isaac became emperor.

**Year 1058.** There was a great famine in the territory of Tarentum and in Calabria. Afterwards plague came, and in the month of May very large numbers of people and animals died.

**Year 1059.** Count Robert of Apulia was made duke of Apulia, Calabria, and Sicily by Pope Nicholas in the city of Melfi, and he rendered him homage for the whole [Col. 1085B] land. The emperor Isaac renounced the empire, and Constantine Ducas became emperor.

**Year 1060.** In the month of May the city of Tarentum was captured by Duke Robert. Afterwards he marched against Brindisi and captured it. Count Malger marched against Oria and drove the Greeks from it. In October Miriarchus arrived with an imperial army and fought a great battle against Robert and Malger. He routed the Northmen and recovered those cities, together with other lands and Hydruntum.

**Year 1061.** In January Count Roger entered Manduria, while Duke Robert captured Acerenza. He marched against the Greeks who were besieging Melfi and routed them.

**Year 1062.** Duke Robert captured Brindisi again, [Col. 1085C] routed the Greeks, and captured Miriarchus in battle. Afterwards he marched against Oria, captured it again, and built a fortress at Mejana.

**Year 1063.** In April Count Geoffrey died, and his son Godfrey captured Tarentum. He then marched against the fortress of Motula, captured it, and took its castle.

**Year 1064.** Count Robert captured Matera in April. In June Count Godfrey captured Castanetum. In September Count Malger died, and afterwards his count William died at Tarentum.

**Year 1067.** Mabrica, with a large Greek army, routed the Northmen and again entered Brindisi [Col. 1085D] and Tarentum. Afterwards he marched against Castanetum and recovered it. Constantine Ducas died and left the empire to his wife Eudocia and their sons. She then married Romanus, called Diogenes, who became emperor.

**Year 1068.** Count Godfrey besieged Mount Pillosus and captured it in June. In October Hydruntum was captured again, and the Greeks were driven from it.

**Year 1069.** A battle was fought on the plain of Litium, and the Greeks were routed. Duke Robert captured Gavinum, Obbianum, and Bari.

**Year 1070.** Duke Robert marched against Brindisi. Count Godfrey came with a large and strong army in ships, and a cruel battle and slaughter of men took place between them and Mabrica during the siege.

[Col. 1086A] **Year 1071.** The same Duke Robert captured Brindisi. His brother Humbert died. The emperor Romanus was deposed and blinded, and Michael Ducas, the son of Constantine, succeeded him.

**Year 1072.** The same Duke Robert went with a naval army to capture the island of Sicily. Count Godfrey besieged Palermo and captured it. In June the glorious Robert entered Palermo, drove the Saracens from it, and celebrated a great triumph.

**Year 1073.** In January the Northmen and Count Petronius captured the city of Trani. The glorious Duke Robert, returning from Sicily, routed [Col. 1086B] Count Petronius near Bari and captured it again; Count Petronius became hostile to Roger.

**Year 1074.** The same Duke Robert went into Campania and captured many cities, including the city of Salerno, and became hostile to Pope Gregory.

**Year 1078.** Count Petronius captured Trani. Michael Ducas was deprived of the empire by Nicephorus, called Botaniates, who became emperor.

**Year 1079.** Count Petronius entered Bari again. Count Abailard marched against Troia, routed Bohemond, the son of Duke Robert, and besieged and captured Ascoli. Duke Robert recovered it again. Afterwards a battle took place there, and Abailard [Col. 1086C] was routed with his soldiers. He fled to Constantinople and died there, an enemy of Duke Robert.

**Year 1080.** Duke Robert again entered Tarentum and Castanetum. Afterwards he marched with an army against Bari, routed Petronius, and captured it again together with the city of Trani. In June he was reconciled with Pope Gregory, and the whole territory that Duke Robert held in Apulia, Calabria, and Sicily was confirmed to him by the pope. The emperor Nicephorus was deposed, and Alexius became emperor.

**Year 1081.** Michael Ducas, who had been expelled by Nicephorus, came to Brindisi and asked Duke Robert for assistance against Alexius. Duke Robert [Col. 1086D] went with him to Hydruntum and equipped a naval force of many ships on his behalf. Then he went with the same Michael to the island of Corcyra and captured it. Afterwards he marched against Dyrrhachium with fifteen thousand men. A battle was fought at Dyrrhachium, and Alexius was routed by Robert. Duke Robert captured Dyrrhachium and won a great victory over him against the Greeks.

**Year 1084.** Pope Gregory was besieged in Rome by King Henry, who had appointed Guibert, archbishop of Ravenna, as pope, thereby creating a schism in the Church; Henry was crowned there by Guibert. Gregory summoned Duke Robert to his aid with a very large number of Northmen in the month of May. Robert freed him and brought him to Salerno, [Col. 1087A] while King Henry was driven from the city of Rome and returned to Germany.

**Year 1085.** Duke Robert came to Brindisi with a large and powerful Northman army. In April he put to sea in ships and went against the Venetians to attack Cassiopi. A battle was fought at sea, and the Venetians were defeated by Duke Robert. Pope Gregory died at Salerno in May, [Col. 1088A] and the duke himself died at Cassiopi in July. His body was brought back to Brindisi in September and buried in the church of Saint Sabinus in the city of Venosa, as he had ordered before his death. His heart and entrails, however, were buried at Hydruntum. Roger, his son, succeeded Robert; Roger was the father of William III, duke of Apulia, who now rules happily.

[Col. 1087] **The Northman Chronicle ends.**

# BEFORE THE END OF THE CENTURY  
## Geoffrey Malaterra, Benedictine monk

# Geoffrey Malaterra’s Sicilian History

Edited according to the evidence of the ancient manuscripts by Giovanni Battista Caruso; now collated again with the earlier editions and purged of many errors.

(*In Muratori, Rerum Italicarum Scriptores*, volume V, p. 537.)

[Col. 1087]

# Muratori’s Preface

A second writer on Norman affairs now follows in our Collection: Geoffrey, a monk of the Order of Saint Benedict, surnamed Malaterra, who relates the deeds accomplished by the Normans in Apulia and Sicily during the eleventh century. This writer was a contemporary of William of Apulia and treated the same subject as he did, though he perhaps wrote some years later. He too begins with the first arrival of the Normans in Apulia and brings his History down to the eleventh year of the pontificate of Pope Urban II, the seventh indiction, and the third day before the Nones of July—that is, to the year 1099, when that same pontiff was taken from the living on the fourth day before the Kalends of August.

He too is a weighty author and for that reason especially worthy of recommendation, since he attempts to assign the events he records to their proper years, thereby providing much illumination for chronological arrangement. He also wrote this History at the command of Roger, count of Sicily, who was the brother of Robert Guiscard; from this one may understand the esteem in which he was held by that prince. He dedicated it to the bishop of Catania in these words:

> “To George, bishop of Catania, of blessed memory: Brother Geoffrey Malaterra, deriving his surname from his predecessors.”

The published text must doubtless be corrected here, and *agnomen* (“surname”) should be written instead. From this we learn—as I had formerly noted in the *Estensian Antiquities*, p. 344—that the title “of blessed,” “good,” “pious,” or “holy memory” was also bestowed upon the living. Geoffrey then mentions the religious habit with which we are girded. These words, together with those that follow, sufficiently indicate that he served under the rule of Saint Benedict.

Rocchus Pirrus noted in his *Notice of the Church of Catania* that, after the Saracens had been expelled from Sicily, Roger the Norman, conqueror and count of Sicily, appointed Ansger, a Benedictine monk drawn from the Calabrian monastery of Saint Euphemia, to the church of Catania. Thus the Church of Catania was established from the beginning under the regular discipline of the Order of Saint Benedict, so that the same man was abbot of Catania and bishop. This custom continued into later centuries. Ansger, from the year 1091, when he was appointed bishop of Catania, occupied that see until 1124, as the documents cited by Rocchus Pirrus demonstrate. I therefore think that we should accept the conjecture of the distinguished Mabillon in the *Benedictine Annals* under the year 1098: in place of George, whom the published History of our Geoffrey names, Ansger should be restored. Indeed, copyists could easily have corrupted the relatively unfamiliar name Ansger.

Since Geoffrey seeks refuge with the bishop of Catania, so that, relying on such aid, he may fear less those who attempt to bite him with an enemy’s tooth and may enjoy the support of his prince, Mabillon likewise believes that Geoffrey was seeking protection both against rivals and from his prince, namely Robert, at whose command he undertook to write this History in plain language. But it seems certain to me that the prince was not Robert, since at that time no Robert ruled Sicily and Guiscard had already died, but rather Roger, count and prince of Sicily itself. This is especially clear because Geoffrey himself openly reveals in his Preface that he wished to hand down to posterity the triumphs of the most famous prince Roger—for that was what Roger had commanded—and to relate how he first subjugated Calabria and then Sicily by armed force. These things apply to Roger alone, namely the brother of Robert Guiscard.

Our Geoffrey was by no means born in Italy. He excuses himself for perhaps having omitted certain matters or described them in a less orderly manner according to their dates, since he came from the lands beyond the mountains and had only recently become an Apulian, or at least a Sicilian. If we are willing to accept Gerard John Vossius’s account in book II, chapter 47 of *On Latin Historians*, Geoffrey was a Spaniard. But Vossius fell into a double error. First, in book III, chapter 6, he presents this same Geoffrey to us as though he were different from the one he had mentioned above, saying that the book of one was edited by Hieronymus Zurita and that of the other by Domenico Portonari. Yet the writer and the work were the same: Zurita first published the same work at Zaragoza in the printing house of Domenico Portonari in 1578.

Second, I think Vossius supposed Geoffrey to be Spanish because he heard, from the report of others—that is, from Possevino—that Geoffrey’s History had been published in Spain, and Possevino assigned this writer to Spain. Vossius could not weigh the matter correctly, since he did not then have Geoffrey’s book in his hands, as he did later when he composed the third book of *On Latin Historians*. In Spain, however, and even among the writers of *Hispania Illustrata*, historians born under other skies were published more than once, although they had never been able to see Spanish soil.

The opinion of the distinguished Pagi in his *Critique of Baronius* under the year 1099 therefore comes closer to the truth: he judged that Geoffrey was born in Normandy, a province of Gaul. Geoffrey certainly calls the Normans “our” Normans everywhere. It is easy to understand that he came to Sicily, whether voluntarily or by invitation, from nowhere other than Normandy, since a Norman prince, after conquering so many provinces, had established a kingdom for himself in Sicily, and for many years other Normans had already been accustomed to gather there to share in the fortunes of their people.

For this reason, I believe that Orderic Vitalis, the celebrated writer and monk of the monastery of Saint-Evroul in Normandy, made an honorable mention of our Geoffrey. Speaking in book III, p. 483, of the dukes and counts of Apulia, he writes:

> “Concerning their worthy deeds and vigorous achievements, Geoffrey the monk, surnamed Malaterra, recently produced an elegant little book at the urging of Roger, count of Sicily.”

Finally, as we have said, Geoffrey’s History was first published by Hieronymus Zurita and dedicated to the learned Antonio Agustín, archbishop of Tarragona. It was then reprinted at Frankfurt in 1606, in volume III of *Hispania Illustrata*, under the care of the distinguished Giovanni Pistorius. Finally, in 1723, it appeared again, enlarged with variant readings, through the work of the distinguished Giovanni Battista Caruso in his Collection of Sicilian Writers, using the ancient manuscripts that he lists in his Preface.

I have all the more right to insert it into this Collection of ours because its author deals chiefly with Italian affairs. And, so that the learned reader may lack nothing from the earlier editions, I shall arrange for the prefaces and letters of those who preceded me to be printed as well.

[Col. 1089]

# Giovanni Battista Caruso’s Brief Notice of Malaterra and His History

Orderic Vitalis, an Englishman and Geoffrey’s contemporary, praised the History of Geoffrey Malaterra in his *Ecclesiastical History* [Note: [Col. 1089] Book III, p. 483, in the *History of the Normans*], where he discusses the Normans ruling in Italy, especially Robert Wiscard and his brothers, saying:

> “Concerning their worthy deeds and vigorous achievements, Geoffrey the monk, surnamed Mala-Terra, recently produced an elegant little book at the urging of Roger, count of Sicily.”

Cardinal Baronius also frequently commended the authority of the History of Geoffrey Malaterra, confirming his own narratives from it, when he said:

> “Geoffrey the monk, who at that time both saw and wrote these things that he was observing.”

He later added [Note: [Col. 1089] Volume XI, under the year 1097, p. 667 of the Roman edition, and p. 682]:

> “This Geoffrey, a Benedictine monk by profession, has been named; his work, venerable plainly on account of its very antiquity, lay almost buried among the ancient monuments of the kings of Aragon until our own age.”

Vossius, supported by no evidence, thought that Geoffrey was a Spaniard [Note: [Col. 1090] *On Latin History*, p. 390], but he seems rather to have been a Norman.

This History, indeed, lay hidden for several centuries, since the art of printing had not yet been invented. Nevertheless, several manuscript copies of it existed among learned men and those interested in the affairs of Sicily, as may be seen in Pirrus [Note: [Col. 1090] *Notice of the First Church of Palermo*, after the expulsion of the Saracens, no. 4, p. 90]; some of these copies still survive. Among the oldest, written in an ancient script with contracted letter-forms, I saw the copy preserved in the library of the Marquis of Jarratana.

I also saw an ancient copy kept by Don Octavius Montaperto, prince [Note: [Col. 1091A] [This note appears in column 1091, but the callout number (6) has not been printed in the text.] At the end of book I, Caruso had likewise warned readers that, after beginning the edition, he had found another manuscript in the College of Palermo, from which he recorded further variant readings. We have fitted all of them into their appropriate places and, according to custom, designated that manuscript by the initials C. P. MURATORI.] of Raffadali. It had come to him from Don Fabio Montaperto, his kinsman and abbot of Saint Michael of the city of Troina. It is either that very copy, or at least one copied from it, which Pirrus wrote [Note: [Col. 1091A] Book II, *On the Church of Troina*, p. 454] had been found by the aforesaid abbot in the same monastery and later, in 1555, transferred by order of the viceroy to the royal chancery.

Hieronymus Zurita had another copy in his hands, which he made public in print at Zaragoza in 1578 through the press of Domenico Portonari. For the poems found in that copy [Col. 1092A] are absent from the two manuscripts mentioned above. Zurita’s edition was printed again by Giovanni Pistorius, provost of the Church of Wrocław, in volume III of *Hispania Illustrata*, at Frankfurt in 1606. We have undertaken to reprint Zurita’s edition for a third time, adding only in the margin certain variant readings from the Jarratana manuscript, by which the errors marked with an asterisk by Portonari may be corrected.

[Col. 1091]

# To Antonio Agustín, Archbishop of Tarragona, Excellent Prelate

[Col. 1091B] Your lifelong studies, excellent prelate, without any interruption, bear witness—with the greatest benefit to this age—to the honor that, for the most just reasons, you have always accorded to the ancient past in every study of the arts and sciences, especially in the accomplishment of great undertakings. We know that you venerate and cherish this one pursuit above all others and esteem it beyond every pleasure and every rest from human cares. You have always desired, with good reason, to admire it and bring it before the eyes of all when you undertook the greatest embassies on behalf of the state.

Enriched by its abundant resources and ornaments, you have advanced greatly toward those things that are most useful to the whole Christian commonwealth amid the grievous disasters of our times, when so many terrors and dangers already seem to be present and imminent. Against the impious insolence of heretics, who attempt by their treachery to violate the holy Catholic Church—which divine Providence, though always afflicted, continually receives and never allows to collapse—and to stain the other peoples of the faithful with sacrilegious crime, you have energetically provided and labored for the glory of God in that office which was especially yours.

That service of exceptional labor, which has brought you the highest esteem among men distinguished for learning, is demanded and earnestly requested of you by the most serious and learned men: namely, that you have gathered into so many volumes the innumerable decisions and decrees of the holy Fathers and supreme pontiffs, and the sacred synods that had fallen into oblivion. Through your singular diligence and vigilance, as you devoted yourself wholly to the sequence and illumination of the sacred constitutions, you have added the greatest possible abundance to canonical sanctions and decrees.

Moreover, everyone greatly admires you for this: while engaged in the grave and continuous interpretation of sacred sanctions, you promote the study of every branch of learning and, through constant and intense occupation, devote every effort to contemplation and to knowledge of the liberal disciplines. You never cease to assign to the studies of gentler literature, as a kind of relief and relaxation, not merely the times of games and holidays—as the most studious men are accustomed to do—or what they call spare hours, but all the time in which we live, and by which life is chiefly sought and sustained, and in which we share a common breath.

From this come those riches and ornaments of intellect whose fruits you have obtained so abundantly and fruitfully that, when you descend to these studies of ours as though to a lighter amusement and a popular delight for the relaxation of the mind, you unfold and openly display greater treasures of every kind of learning than those who have worn away all their leisure and time in meditation on common letters or more polished humane studies.

But since it was neither the purpose nor the judgment of my work to touch upon your praises—praises that the fame of all mortals celebrates through the intellects of the most serious men—I shall nevertheless confess that I have seized this opportunity: you are the most serious defender, guardian, and prelate of antiquity, and through the protection of your name these very ancient writers of history may first come into the light. They handed down to posterity, more than four hundred years ago, the arrival of the Norman princes in Italy and the deeds accomplished by them in Campania, Apulia, Calabria, Bruttium, and the island of Sicily.

Neither their uncultivated and neglected language, their meager sequence of events, nor the crude verses of the monk Geoffrey—however dull and rough, or disordered and metrically faulty—dissuaded me from bringing into public view events that, so far as I know, no author had transmitted to this day. Indeed, I thought myself so far from being open to the charge of foolishness in this edition that nothing could have been more natural than to append to these writers on Norman affairs the poetic work of Bartholomew of Neocastro, an ancient Sicilian writer. He gave it the title *Messana* and composed it in fifteen books of hexameter verse.

Although the work was not constructed through any impulse of keen or sound judgment, nor through artistic composition, but with an enormous and ponderous structure, it was devoted to the deeds of Peter, king of Aragon, in Sicily against Charles I, king of Sicily of that name, [Col. 1092C] I became entirely convinced that a loss of words is tolerable, whereas knowledge of events, causes, and outcomes is immeasurable.

This is clear and belongs to ordinary practical wisdom: the chief and primary wisdom is that by which we take greater pleasure in knowledge of the events themselves, even when transmitted in the poorest composition, than in superfluous and diffuse speech. The ideas that ought to remain fixed and, as it were, stamped upon our minds come from the events themselves; and especially because language ought to flower and overflow most abundantly from the transmission of the events themselves.

Therefore, since you have never lacked extraordinary care in discharging the whole office of sacred affairs, pontifical authority, and the rest of your jurisdiction, and since in so great an office and charge you have never ceased to benefit students of learning everywhere, I am led by great hope—for your supreme seriousness is joined with singular courtesy, and you are fortified by such gentleness—that you will not disdain or reject this very small gift, as though it bore some distinguished mark of quality.

Perhaps it may provide the fruit of some slight usefulness and benefit, and may reveal the memory of ancient events which the most diligent investigators of antiquity strive, through every inquiry, to discover in the pursuit of truth.

The reason and plan that moved me to add these writers to the indexes of the deeds of the kings of Aragon was this: not to mention that, for three hundred years, the kings of Aragon had inserted themselves into the Norman line through a double relationship, all the territories that had been acquired and won through so many victories by the Norman and later Swabian princes came afterwards to the kings of Aragon—by hereditary right, by the right of war, and by the grant bestowed by the Church through public deliberation as a benefice—by a heavenly and divine allotment.

At Saint Engratia, outside Zaragoza, in the year of the Lord 1578, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of May.

[Col. 1094A] Your Most Illustrious Lordship’s most devoted servant,

**Hieronymus Zurita**

[Col. 1093]

# Domenico Portonari of the Orsini to the Reader

[Col. 1093A] In publishing these books of Geoffrey the monk and Alexander the abbot—ancient authors who wrote the deeds of the Norman princes, so that they might be added to the indexes of the deeds of the kings of Aragon—we were especially hesitant and, from the beginning, began to feel some distrust because we had obtained only a single copy and lacked the support of another manuscript. That support is normally of the greatest assistance, since it removes scribal errors through careful investigation and, as it were, by tracing them to their source.

Those who undertake the proper task of correcting books are moved by careful consideration to avoid above all the danger that, driven partly by ingenuity and partly by a certain overconfidence, they may slide not merely into different interpretations but frequently into contradictory ones, and that they may cruelly mutilate the authors whom they are attempting to correct.

Therefore, so that no more serious wounds might be inflicted upon these authors through such corruption—for although they did not seem likely to possess great antiquity, they nevertheless deserved, in return for the events they transmitted to posterity, that due honor be paid to them—we thought it better to place a mark beside the corrupt passages. Thus each person, according to his own greater ingenuity and skill, may, as far as possible, heal defective pieces and corrupt sections, cutting them out where necessary and punctuating the remaining structure appropriately.

For it seemed wholly fair that wounds which we cannot restore to uncorrupted health should not only be left unulcerated but not even touched, so that their proper work and task may remain intact for those who, with easier and more suitable judgment, are able to bring aid and health even to desperate sores. It is enough for us, and more than enough, to have brought these authors into the light, since through our work they have obtained the possibility that their health and former condition may at some time be restored by others.

Moreover, we consider it scarcely doubtful that these writers of history flourished in their own homeland through private patronage and through the distinction of friendship with those princes who, at their urging, transmitted their deeds to posterity. It should seem surprising that neither any of the ancient writers nor, in more recent memory, Abbot Trithemius—who searched all libraries with incredible diligence—made mention of them, and that although they lay hidden for more than four hundred years, they were preserved almost entirely safe from every danger.

Geoffrey was frequent in that merit, with great care and diligence, of noting definite intervals of time. This is not only highly pleasing but a complete source of delight, without weariness or satiety. Abbot Alexander, however, was so negligent in this respect that, although he was present as an eyewitness to the events and saw them himself, he nearly destroyed the sequence of the deeds.

I would not wish this matter to be omitted: Queen Alberia, the wife of King Roger, whom the same writer extolled as a woman of exceptional religious devotion and worthy of praise, was the daughter of Alfonso, the great king and prince of Spain. He freed Toledo, the royal city, and the cities of the Carpetani and Oretani from the impious rule of the Saracens. Roderic Jiménez, archbishop of Toledo, calls her Geloira, while our writer calls her Elvira. Thus her son, whom Alexander calls Anfus and to whom the honor of the principality of Campania was assigned, bore the name of his maternal grandfather, King Alfonso.

[Col. 1093]

# Book I Begins: On the Acquisition of the Kingdom of Sicily, Calabria, Apulia, and the Island of Sicily by the Glorious Prince Robert Guiscard and the Brothers Who Came from Normandy

Compiled by Geoffrey, a religious and honorable man, a monk of Saint Benedict, at the request of the illustrious prince Roger, count of Trinacria, who brought Sicily back from the faithless tyranny of the Saracens to the devotion of Christ.

# Here Are the Chapters of the First Book

[Col. 1093D]

The chapters of this book are distinct and various,

which our page ought to place beneath headings here and there,

so that whatever you wish may be found more quickly by searching.

1. First it tells what part of France Normandy is.

[Col. 1094C] 2. Under Duke Rollo, Norway sends pirates across the sea. They overrun it; the king comes to meet them in order to keep them away from it. He postpones battle, makes a treaty, and becomes their lord. The boundaries enclosing their homeland are noted. Let the rhythm cease; let prose speak if anything further remains.

[Col. 1094D] 3. The custom of the Norman people concerning Hauteville.

[Col. 1095A] 4. Concerning Tancred, his first and second wives, and his children.

5. How Tancred’s first sons, William, Drogo, and Humphrey, leaving Normandy, came to Apulia.

6. How, after first serving the prince of Capua, they passed from him to the prince of Salerno.

7. How they first crossed over with the Greek Maniaces to wage war against Sicily.

8. How Arduino was struck down by Maniaces.

9. How Melfi was built by the Normans, and concerning the embassy sent by the Greeks and the first encounter that they had with the Greeks.

10. Concerning the second battle beneath Mount Pillosus.

11. Concerning Tancred’s younger sons, who followed their elder brothers [Col. 1095B] to Apulia after them.

12. Concerning the death of Count William.

13. Concerning the death of Count Drogo.

14. Concerning Leo the pope, and how he was captured by the Normans.

15. How Pope Leo was honorably released by the Normans.

16. Concerning Robert Guiscard: how he fortified the castle of Saint Mark and how he went on foot with the Slavs to plunder.

17. Concerning Robert Guiscard and Peter of Turra.

18. How Robert Guiscard became count of Apulia.

19. Concerning Roger, Tancred’s younger son.

20. Concerning Roger, who, invited by Robert Guiscard, went from Calabria to Apulia.

21. Robert Guiscard and Roger go with an army to Reggio.

22. Roger comes to Reggio with very great booty.

23. Roger leaves Robert Guiscard in anger.

24. Roger is kindly received by his brother William, and Scalea is granted to him.

25. Count Roger steals horses.

26. The men of Amalfi are captured by Roger.

27. Famine occurs in Calabria.

28. The rebellious Calabrians treacherously capture the castle of Leucastrum, killing many men there.

[Col. 1095D] 29. Concerning the peace made between Robert Guiscard and his brother Roger.

30. Robert Guiscard repudiates his wife Alberada and marries Sikelgaita; Roger and Guiscard are reconciled.

31. Robert Guiscard marches against his brother William before he celebrates his wedding.

32. Roger fights a battle with the Greeks at Saint Martin.

33. Robert Guiscard and Roger go to the aid of their brother Geoffrey.

34. After Guillamato has been defeated, both brothers go to Calabria.

35. Guiscard becomes duke.

36. While Guiscard remains at Reggio, Roger [Col. 1096A] attacks the fortresses of Calabria.

37. How Squillace was captured.

38. How Serlo, the son of Tancred, was driven from Normandy into Brittany.

39. Concerning the military service of that same Serlo.

40. Concerning Tancred and Apro.

# The Chapters of Book II Begin
I. Count Roger first enters Sicily. II. Duke Robert entrusts Rhegium and the whole of Calabria to be administered; he himself goes into Apulia. III. Becumen, the amir of Sicily, expelled by his own men, meets the count at Rhegium. IV. At Becumen’s advice, Count Roger goes into Sicily again. V. Count Roger fights with the men of Messina. [Col. 1096B] VI. Count Roger obtains by a vow the calming of the troubled sea. VII. That booty taken from pagans is not displeasing to God when offered in sacrifice. VIII. The men of Palermo come by boat to the Strait, intending to prevent our men from crossing. IX. Seeing that their crossing is being obstructed, our men implore assistance. X. Crossing by night without the enemy’s knowledge, the count captures Messina. XI. A certain Saracen killed his fleeing sister when she faltered. XII. Realizing that they had been outwitted, the men of Palermo withdraw; the duke crosses unhindered. XIII. The duke and the count arranging Messina as they pleased, they go to besiege Rametta. [Col. 1096C] XIV. The Christians of the Val Demone offer gifts to the count and the duke. XV. The duke and the count attack Centuripe. XVI. Our men make camp on the plain of Paternò, beside the river Gèdeta. XVII. A battle is fought between our men and the Saracens. XVIII. Because winter is near, the expedition is dissolved, and the Christians surrender Troina. XIX. The count takes a wife. XX. After the wedding has been celebrated, the count therefore goes into Sicily. XXI. The count withdraws from the duke in anger. XXII. Becumen is killed in Sicily. [Col. 1096D] XXIII. The duke goes to besiege his brother the count at Mileto. XXIV. The count captures Gerace by treachery, and the duke is captured at Girace. XXV. The duke’s soldiers invite the count to come to his brother’s aid. XXVI. While besieging Girace, the count frees the duke from captivity. XXVII. The castle that the duke had fortified at Melito is broken by the count’s soldiers. The duchess flees to Tropea. XXVIII. The duke divides Calabria with the count. XXIX. The Greeks plot treachery against the count at Troina. XXX. Captured by the Saracens, the count frees himself with his sword. [Col. 1097A] XXXI. The count goes into Calabria. XXXII. The count fights with the Arabs of Castrogiovanni. XXXIII. The battle of Cerami, where Saint George appeared. XXXIV. The Pisans invite the count to come to besiege Palermo. XXXV. When the enemy are terrified, the count’s soldiers climb the Tower, which was later called Gato. XXXVI. Our men are harassed by the men of Taranto. XXXVII. The duke attacks Agello. XXXVIII. A castle is built at Petralia. XXXIX. The duke besieges Montemaggiore. XL. The duke besieges Bari. XLI. Count Roger fights with the Saracens. XLII. Doves announce to their people in Palermo that they have been defeated. [Col. 1097B] XLIII. With the aid of Count Roger, the duke captures Bari. XLIV. Scylla is reconciled to the duke. XLV. Palermo is captured. XLVI. Serlo is killed.

## THE CHAPTERS OF THE THIRD BOOK BEGIN.

I. Castles are built at Paternò and Mazara. II. Guiscard besieges Salerno. III. The men of Amalfi make peace with the duke. IV. Salerno is surrendered. V. Count Roger besieges Abagelard at Santa Severina. VI. The duke recovers Santa Severina. At the castle of Sant’Agazio the duke besieges Abagelard. VII. Count Roger builds a castle on Mount Calataxibet. [Col. 1097C] VIII. The Africans destroy Nicotera. IX. The Africans are defeated at Mazara. X. Hugh of Gircea is killed at Catania. XI. Trabia is compelled by siege to surrender. XII. Castro Nuovo enters into alliance with the count. XIII. The emperor Michael comes to the duke. XIV. The duke prepares a fleet for Greece. XV. The count besieges Taormina. XVI. Evisandus is killed on the count’s behalf. XVII. The Golafri from Africa are seen beneath Taormina. XVIII. Taormina is captured. XIX. The church of Troina is founded. XX. The count besieges the Jaceans and the Cinese. XXI. He captures them. [Col. 1097D] XXII. The count gives his daughter to the count of Provence. XXIII. A chaste marriage is praised. XXIV. The duke goes to Romania. XXV. The duke besieges Durazzo. XXVI. The duke fights with the Venetians. XXVII. The duke fights with the emperor. XXVIII. The duke captures Durazzo. XXIX. The duke captures Castoria. XXX. Bennavet enters Catania by treachery, and shortly afterward Catania is recovered by our men. XXXI. Angelmartus rises against the count at Gerace. [Col. 1098A] XXXII. Messina is fortified with towers. XXXIII. Pope Gregory recalls the duke from Romania. XXXIV. When the duke returns, the treachery of the peoples is suppressed. XXXV. Having summoned his brother, the duke goes against the prince of Capua. XXXVI. Jordan rises against his father. XXXVII. The duke goes to Rome and captures it. XXXVIII. The Romans are rebuked. XXXIX. Bohemond defeats the emperor in battle. XL. The duke goes to Romania again. XLI. An eclipse of the sun occurs. The pope dies, as do the duke and the king of the English. XLII. Roger is made duke.

## THE CHAPTERS OF THE FOURTH BOOK BEGIN.

[Col. 1098B]

I. Benarvet lays waste Nicotera. II. The count engages Benarvet. III. The Pisans attack Africa and offer it to the count to retain. IV. Duke Roger and his brother Bohemond are reconciled. V. The count besieges and captures Agrigento. VI. Chamut becomes a Christian; Castrogiovanni is surrendered. VII. The count ordains bishops throughout Sicily. VIII. King Philip of the Franks seeks the count’s daughter as a wife. IX. Mihera enters Maia. X. Bohemond overruns Cosenza. [Col. 1098C] XI. Mihera becomes a monk. XII. The count besieges Butera. XIII. Pope Urban comes into Sicily to speak with the count. XIV. The count takes Adelaide as his wife. XV. The men of Noto are reconciled to the count. XVI. The count goes to Malta. XVII. The duke and the count capture Cosenza. XVIII. Jordan dies. XIX. Simon is born. XX. Duke Roger falls ill. XXI. William of Grandmesnil enters Rossano. XXII. The duke and the count besiege the castle-town. XXIII. The count gives his daughter to the son of the emperor of the Germans. [Col. 1098D] XXIV. The duke and the count go to besiege Melfi. XXV. The king of Hungary takes the count’s daughter as his wife. XXVI. The count besieges Capua with Duke Roger and Prince Richard. XXVII. Pope Urban, journeying toward them, attempts to establish peace. XXVIII. Capua is captured and restored to Prince Richard. XXIX. Pope Urban grants the count the legation of Sicily and Calabria.

## THE LETTER OF THE RELIGIOUS MAN GAUFREDUS, MONK OF BLESSED BENEDICT, BEGINS

Sent by the same man to the venerable Father, the lord bishop of Catania.

[Col. 1099]

[Col. 1099A] To George of blessed memory [Ansgrio], bishop of Catania, Brother Gaufredus, bearing from his predecessors the surname Malaterra, who, having lived an unhappy worldly course with Martha, seeks to be raised up, with Lazarus as a brother, into the happiness of Mary’s repose.

Since, most holy Father, I recognize that, by a certain special intimacy, I am joined to you—though unworthy—by the religious habit with which we are girded, whereas the other bishops appear, so far as their clothing is concerned, to belong to another institution, I also enjoy a special hope in you, presuming upon you more than upon the others, and I ask you to be my protector in all affairs. Through you, therefore—or at least in your presence—I ask that this book be judged, so that through the favor of your authority it may become more pleasing to the prince, or, if perhaps some rivals rise up, may be presumed to be bitten less severely out of reverence for you. Yet you should know, whether you or anyone else approaches as a reader or indeed an interpreter of this book, that if you find things reported in a somewhat disordered sequence, not according to the times in which the events recorded occurred, or discover that some matters have been passed over through forgetfulness, these things should be attributed as faults not so much to me as to the reporters—especially since I was not personally present at the times when these events took place. Rather, you should recognize that I came from the regions beyond the mountains and had only recently become an Apulian, or indeed a Sicilian in the full sense.

If, however, there is a question concerning the uncultivated quality of my poetry, you should know that, even if I had the ability to pour forth something clearer or more ornate, the command of the prince himself urged me to write in plain and easily understood language, so that whatever was said might be more readily clear to everyone. [Col. 1099C] Whether, then, this or that objection is brought against me, I seek refuge beneath the shelter of your protection, so that, relying upon such great assistance, I may fear less those attempting to bite me with hostile teeth and may enjoy the support of our prince.

To all throughout Sicily to whom the episcopal or clerical name is assigned: Gaufredus Malaterra, together with the designation of the name and its meaning.

By the tradition of the ancient philosophers, it has become customary among the human race, destined to have descendants, to transmit to posterity the deeds of strong men, recorded in writing, lest memorable actions perish in silence together with those by whom they were performed; rather, when entrusted to letters and read or learned by future generations, they somehow make those by whom they were done live, as it were, through the memory of their life. Sallust commends this practice (*Catiline* 1), that praiseworthy rhetorician among historians, who at the beginning of his book wrote as follows:

> All human beings who strive to excel other animals ought to exert themselves with the utmost effort, lest they pass through life in silence like cattle, which nature fashioned bent forward and obedient to their belly.

Instructed by such authors, who recited the histories of earlier times, the most renowned prince Roger, deciding to entrust to posterity his laborious triumphs, achieved not without great danger—namely, how he first subdued Calabria and then Sicily by armed force—ordered me to apply myself to dictating the labor of this work. But because, in view of his preceding kindness toward me, I cannot refuse whatever he has commanded, I enter upon it timidly, with a less learned style and a feeble poetry, like one ignorant of swimming entering a very deep pool. I am especially afraid of you and of your indignation toward me, since it was you, rather than I, famished of the bread of such knowledge, who ought to have undertaken such a work, being intoxicated with the clearest spring of the grammatical art. [Col. 1100B]

But the aforementioned prince, recognizing that you are occupied with greater duties—sometimes laboring with Martha in the care of the churches, sometimes with Mary in blessed contemplation—spares you, lest he recall you from a better purpose. Me, however, as though I were unoccupied and devoted to no exercise, he strives by a certain stroke of his hand to make more watchful.

I therefore ask you, remembering what Scripture says, “Bear one another’s burdens, and so you will fulfill the law of Christ,” and what is said elsewhere, “When one brother helps another, both are consoled,” to extend the foot of your favor in support of my feeble song, so that, fortified by the shield of your authority, I may fear less the attacks of detractors and the hostile teeth of those who attempt to gnaw at the words or deeds of others. [Col. 1100C]

There are indeed some who, when they have attained whatever degree of knowledge and have consequently won the favor of human praise, overflow with such envy beneath their swelling brows that they do not wish to have anyone near them equal to themselves in letters. If it happens that they possess another person’s work, they do not cease to attack it with a biting tooth through disparagement, fearing that their own praise will be diminished by another’s. To such men the saying of Scripture may appropriately be applied: “Knowledge puffs up”; but what follows—“love builds up”—does not follow in them.

There are others, by contrast, whom knowledge and character ennoble to such a degree that the more deeply they are intoxicated from the philosophical spring, the less they are carried away by pride. Fixing the step of their mind always in humility, they do not gnaw at the words or deeds of others; rather, whatever they hear expressed less elegantly, they correct gently within themselves, not in public, lest those others perhaps be scandalized. [Col. 1100D] And, in order to make such men pleasing to the powerful of this age, they strive to exalt them in words, considering their praise or gain as their own. I ask that their affectionate goodwill be invited toward me.

Whatever I dictate that you judge should be corrected and adorned with the roses of your knowledge, I shall regard as such, so that the vineyard plowed by you and watered by the cultivation of your knowledge, yielding richer fruits, may attain greater praise and favor for the prince.

## GAUFREDUS MALATERRA, BENEDICTINE MONK: SICILIAN HISTORY

[Col. 1101]

## BOOK ONE BEGINS

### CHAPTER ONE. The first section concerns Normandy, which is a part of France.

[Col. 1101B]

Normandy is a certain homeland in the regions of Gaul. It was not always called Normandy; rather, it was once the royal fisc of the Frankish kings and, together with all that belonged to it, was called France by the general name. This continued until the very brave duke Rollo, a pirate from Denmark or Norway, having gathered a large force of brave soldiers who entrusted themselves to the sea in a naval army, ravaged Frisia and all the maritime places toward the west. At last he landed in the harbor where the river Seine, flowing down into the sea, enters it. Penetrating by its channel with a very large fleet into the deeper regions of France, and having observed the pleasantness of the places, he was moved to embrace this land above the other regions through which he had passed and to adopt it as his own. [Col. 1101C]

For it is exceedingly rich in fish-bearing rivers and wild forests, especially suited to the practice of falconry, fertile in grain and other crops, abundant in fishponds, and a nourisher of livestock. For this reason they began, springing forth from both banks, to subjugate the inhabitants of that region to their rule.

### CHAPTER TWO

Under Duke Rollo pirates cross the sea from Norway;

They invade this land. The king comes to repel them;

He postpones battle, makes a treaty, and becomes their lord.

The king who at that time ruled France, Louis, as we believe the second, learning that enemies had invaded the gates of his realm, was at first indignant. He mobilized an army and set out to meet the enemy, intending to keep both the duke and his men away from his borders. But when he realized that he could not do this without great loss among his own men, fearing the uncertain turns of war and sparing the blood of his people, he followed the counsel of his elders and accepted the terms of peace and the service which they offered him. He granted them as a benefice the greater part of the land they had invaded. [Note: [Col. 1101D] C. P. “It is therefore extended.”]

Thus, that land [Note: [Col. 1101D] C. P. “to them.”], granted to them, extended from the district of Pontin, which it has on its eastern side, along the English Sea adjoining it on the northern side, as far as Brittany, which closes its western boundaries; on the western and southern side it is bounded by the district of Maine as far as Chartres, and from Chartres it is enclosed by the Vexin and Beauvais as far as Pontin. [Col. 1102B]

Duke Rollo received this territory, assigned to him by the king of the Franks, as an hereditary fief. He distributed it among his people as he judged appropriate, reserving the more valuable portions for his own uses. Since we have touched briefly upon the extent of the land, it also seems useful to say something about the customs of the people.

### CHAPTER THREE. On the custom of the Norman people of Hauteville.

This is an exceedingly shrewd people, avenging injuries in the hope of gaining more elsewhere, despising their ancestral fields, greedy for profit and domination, feigning every kind of character, and occupying a certain middle ground between generosity and avarice. Their princes, delighted by a good reputation, are exceedingly generous; the people know how to flatter and devote themselves to eloquent studies, to such an extent that you might even regard their children as rhetoricians. [Note: [Col. 1101D] C. P. “studies of eloquence.”]

Unless restrained by the yoke of justice, this people is utterly unbridled. It is enduring of labor, hunger, and cold whenever fortune requires it [Note: [Col. 1102D] C. P. “demands it”], and devoted to hunting and the practice of falconry. It delights in the luxury of horses and of the other equipment and clothing of military service.

From their own name, therefore, they gave the land its name. For *north* in the English language means the northern region. And because they had come from the north, they also called the land itself Normandy. [Note: [Col. 1102D] “Called Normans, [they called] the land also Normandy.”]

In this province there is a city called Coutances, in whose territory there is a village called Hauteville—not, indeed, merely because it is situated upon some lofty mountain, but, as we believe, through some omen foretelling the future events and prosperous successes of that village’s heirs, who, with God’s help and their own vigor, would gradually climb to the summit of higher honor. For we do not know whether divine providence, observing what pleased it among the heirs of the earlier generations, or certainly among those who would come later, or among both, advanced these heirs to such a degree [Note: [Col. 1103D] C. P. “to what extent”] that, as was promised to Abraham, growing into a great nation and extending their rule by arms, they subjected the necks of many peoples to themselves. We shall pursue this by touching upon it gradually in our writing.

### CHAPTER FOUR. On Tancred, his first and second wives, and his children.

There was a certain soldier of extremely noble birth who possessed, by hereditary right, this village left to him by his ancestors. His name was Tancred. He took as his wife a woman distinguished in character and lineage, named . . . . . [Note: [Col. 1103D] C. P. “Moriella.”] By her, through legitimate succession, he later had five sons who would become counts: namely William, surnamed Iron-Arm, Drogo, Humphrey, Gaufredus, and Serlo.

When their mother died, and while their father’s still youthful age did not yet deny him continence, he celebrated a second marriage, abhorring illicit unions and preferring to be content with one legitimate wife rather than stain himself with the shameful embrace of concubines, mindful of that apostolic saying: “Let each man take a wife to avoid fornication.” And what follows: “God will judge fornicators and adulterers.”

The woman whom he married was called Fressenda. In nobility and character she was no inferior to the first. Within legitimate bounds she bore her husband seven sons, who would be of no less worth or dignity than the brothers mentioned above. Their names we list here: first, Robert Guiscard, afterward prince of all Apulia and duke of Calabria, a man of great counsel, intelligence, generosity, and courage; second, Malgerius; third, William; fourth, Alveredus; fifth, Humbert; sixth, Tancred; seventh, Roger the younger, afterward conqueror of Sicily and count.

The mother nurtured her sons with the greatest care and maternal affection. She embraced those who were not her own sons but her husband’s by his previous wife with such love that you could scarcely distinguish, unless you learned it from some circumstance, which child was a son and which was not. Consequently, she was loved all the more by her husband and highly esteemed by those living around them.

As the children’s age allowed, they passed beyond their boyhood years. When one after another had reached adolescence, they began to devote themselves to military disciplines, practicing with horses and weapons and learning to defend themselves and attack the enemy.

### CHAPTER FIVE. How Tancred’s first sons, William, Drogo, and Humphrey, departing from Normandy, came to Apulia.

When they saw that, as the old men living nearby were dying, their heirs were quarreling among themselves over the inheritance, and that the portion which had fallen to one person, divided among several, was insufficient for each, they began to deliberate among themselves so that something similar might not happen to them in the future. Thus, by common agreement, the elder brothers, being more mature than the younger ones still remaining, first departed from their homeland and sought profit by military service in various places. At last, with God guiding them, they arrived in Apulia, a province of Italy. [Col. 1104A]

### CHAPTER SIX. How, after first serving the prince of Capua, they passed from him to the prince of Salerno.

Having heard that hostilities had intensified between two very famous princes—namely, the prince of Capua and the prince of Salerno—because certain disputes had arisen between them, they offered themselves to the prince of Capua, seeking to gain something through military service, since they had found the road by which they came to be the nearer route. They remained there for some time and accomplished many things bravely, receiving their reward. [Col. 1104B]

But when they recognized the Capuan’s stinginess, they rejected him and passed over to Gaimar [Note: [Col. 1104D] C. P. “Gaimarius”], the prince of Salerno. He received them honorably because of the military reputation that had already made them renowned throughout Apulia, and especially because they had crossed over to him from a prince who was hostile to him. Inflamed with loyalty to him by many gifts, they harassed the Capuans with various and frequent raids and ravaged the entire province all around, as though a pestilential calamity were thundering everywhere. [Note: [Col. 1104D] C. P. “they added.”]

The men of Salerno, avenging their prince’s injuries everywhere, undertook the same work without weariness, and they restrained those who had previously rebelled against the prince to such an extent that all the surrounding regions lay quiet and pacified.

But the Lombards, an exceedingly envious people, always suspicious of anyone who was virtuous, secretly disparaged them before that same prince, biting them with a hostile tooth. They urged him to drive them away, saying that, if he did not, it would easily come about that a people of such cunning and such vigor—and, they added through the malice of their hearts, of such treachery—would, once the prince had been disinherited, take possession of his inheritance through their own craft.

By these same arts they easily twisted the prince’s heart, already inclined toward their counsel, for the worse. Yet although the prince, yielding to the wicked advice of his men, was preparing to do what they urged, he feared the vigor of the brothers and therefore did not dare to disclose openly what he was secretly planning.

### CHAPTER SEVEN. How they first crossed over with the Greek Maniac to conquer Sicily.

There was a certain Maniac, a Greek by nationality, appointed by the emperor of Constantinople as governor of the territories in Calabria or Apulia that belonged to his authority. He planned to land in Sicily in order to conquer it for the empire’s advantage, and he gathered auxiliaries from every quarter.

Accordingly, in the emperor’s name he sent word to the prince of Salerno, as a friend of the empire, that he should send to assist the imperial cause those men who were reputed to have defeated his enemies. He also promised that they would be rewarded with many prizes.

The prince, having found an opportunity by which he could honorably dismiss them, summoned them. When they came, he urged them to undertake the mission for which he had been asked to send them. To encourage them more readily, he enumerated in words the rewards that had been promised and also promised gifts of his own. [Col. 1105A]

They, however, attracted not so much by the prince’s command as by hope of the things promised, prepared what was necessary and reached Maniac. Maniac rejoiced greatly at their arrival and placed great confidence in their assistance. Having prepared a fleet, they invaded Sicily with a large army. [Note: [Col. 1105D] C. P. “he invaded.”]

Because they landed beside the shore, they first attacked Messina, which lay nearby, and compelled it to enter into a treaty with them by surrender. Although there were at Messina very brave soldiers of its own people who, advancing from the city, struck the Greeks very hard in the engagement, when the Greeks retreated an opportunity was nevertheless opened for our men to join battle.

The men of Messina, not yet having tested our men’s valor, began at first to press forward fiercely. But when they saw themselves harassed more than usual, as though recoiling from the warfare of a new people, they turned their backs and fled before our men almost to the city, while our men cut down the hindmost of them.

Maniac, having gained the city through our men’s efforts, began to value them and to encourage them in military service with gifts and promises. [Note: [Col. 1105D] C. P. “to rouse them.”]

From there they advanced, testing the deeper regions of Sicily and subjugating everything, until they reached Syracuse. A certain Arcadius ruled that city and, hostile to our men, inflicted many defeats upon them. William, the son of Tancred, who was called Iron-Arm, was exceedingly angered by this. He attacked Arcadius, rushed upon him, and, engaging him bravely, struck him down with the strength of his spear and killed him. From then onward, therefore, he enjoyed the greatest admiration for his renown among both Greeks and Sicilians. [Col. 1105C]

The Sicilians, gathering as many as sixty thousand men, attempted to offer battle to Maniac and his forces in the region of the city of Troina. William, Tancred’s son, made fierce by the renown of his military service, brave in arms [Note: [Col. 1105D] C. P. “in arms”], anticipated the Greeks in battle. Once the battle had begun, he engaged the enemy with only the soldiers of his own people, before the Greeks reached the place of combat.

Acting bravely, he felled many [Note: [Col. 1106D] C. P. “he fells”] and put the rest to flight, becoming the victor. When the Greeks reached the place where the battle had taken place, while our men were pursuing the enemy, they seized the spoils and divided them among themselves, reserving no share for our men, who had driven the enemy from the field.

### CHAPTER EIGHT. How Arduin was struck down by Maniac.

When our men, returning from the pursuit of the enemy, learned this, they regarded it as an injury. Through a certain Italian named Arduin, who belonged to our men and knew the Greek language, they summoned Maniac to account, asking whether he had divided the spoils inadvertently or by deliberate contrivance.

Maniac, angered as though they had dared to oppose his authority, although he was permitted to deal with those same spoils as he pleased, ordered that they be beaten with clubs throughout the camp and insulted with abuse, to the dishonor of our people.

When Arduin returned and reported such things, our men took the matter grievously and decided to rise against the Greeks. But Arduin, scarcely restraining them, gave the more useful counsel: namely, that, concealing his anger, he should approach Maniac himself in more elegant clothing, until, with the others less suspicious, he could obtain by whatever trick from Maniac’s notary—whose friendship he enjoyed—a written document allowing them to cross the Strait more freely.

While he was contriving this, Maniac, unaware of what was being done, praised the soldier’s goodwill and promised gifts, while nevertheless laughing derisively with his men. As soon as Arduin had obtained the document from the notary, pretending that he had some business to conduct in Calabria, our men secretly advanced by night as far as Messina and crossed the Strait without hindrance.

Then, heading toward Apulia, they ravaged Calabria and every place they knew to belong to the Greeks, ranging through the land. In this way they reached Apulia. [Col. 1106B] But, recognizing the treachery of the prince Gaimar, they did not go over to him. Instead, while laying waste to the province, they adopted the plan of subjugating it for themselves.

### CHAPTER NINE. How Melfi was built by the Normans, concerning the legate sent by the Greeks, and concerning the first engagement they had with the Greeks.

Since the inhabitants of that land were without a castle in which they could defend themselves [Note: [Col. 1106D] C. P. “the inhabitants”], they built a castle called Melfi. While only five hundred soldiers were there, the Greeks who ruled that land gathered a very large multitude from Calabria and Apulia, as many as sixty thousand armed men, and began to advance against them in order to drive them from their borders.

They sent a legate ahead and ordered them to choose whichever they preferred: either to fight with them on the following day or, if peace were granted them, to withdraw unharmed from the territory they had invaded. [Col. 1106C]

The legate sent for this purpose was mounted upon a most beautiful horse. A certain Norman named Hugh, surnamed Tudextifem [Note: [Col. 1106D] C. P. “Tudebufem”], began to touch the horse with his hand. To send the Greeks a wondrous message about himself and his companions, by which they might be terrified, he struck the horse on the neck with his bare fist and felled it with a single blow as though it were dead.

The other Normans sprang forward and raised up the Greek who had fallen together with the horse. He lay on the ground as though lifeless, although he had been injured only by fear. They dragged the horse as far as a certain precipice and threw it down.

When the Greek had scarcely recovered his senses through the consolation of the Normans, they gave him a better horse, and he reported to his companions that battle had been arranged. But when he had reported only to the leaders of his people what had happened, they, struck by wonder and fear, suppressed the matter among themselves, lest, if it were openly told, the terrified army should flee.

When morning came, at first light the Normans met them, and the two sides fought fiercely in a very sharp engagement. Among those taking part in this battle were two of Tancred’s sons, William Iron-Arm and Count Drogo; none of their brothers had yet followed them.

They, acting as the bravest soldiers, encouraged their companions and themselves fought courageously. After laying many of the enemy low, they finally put the rest to flight. Pursuing them and cutting down those at the rear, they won the victory. Many of the enemy were drowned in the river called Oliveto while trying to swim across it.

### CHAPTER TEN. On the second battle beneath Montepeloso.

Defeated but not yet exhausted, encouraging one another and having gathered a much larger army, the Greeks prepared for battle again under their leader Anno, who had been sent for this purpose by the emperor of Constantinople.

The Normans, not sluggish in war, met them beneath Montepeloso. Fighting bravely, they demonstrated that they did not wish to flee battle but rather, as though from delight, sought it.

As the Greeks fought vigorously against them in the engagement, the Normans had already begun to grow weary from the excessive slaughter. William was suffering from a quartan fever and, because of the extreme illness that oppressed him, could not take part in the battle. He lay at a distance, awaiting the outcome.

When he saw that his men were now fighting less bravely and were almost failing, in indignation and anger he forgot the illness that oppressed him, seized his arms, and threw himself into the midst of the enemy like a raging lion. Reviving his men with exhorting words, he acted bravely and put the enemy to flight, their commander Anno, leader of the army, who wore a tail, having been killed like an ox. [Note: [Col. 1107D] “With leader Anno, who …”]

Losing confidence in their own strength and trusting less in fortune, they fortified their camps and no longer dared to fight with the Normans except with walls between them. But even the walls could not protect them against the Normans. [Col. 1107C]

For the Normans harassed them with frequent raids, uprooted their vineyards and olive groves, and plundered their herds, flocks, and everything else necessary for use, leaving nothing outside the camps. They also surrounded the camps themselves while the Greeks were shut inside and attacked them.

They prepared the engines necessary for this work, employing highly skilled craftsmen, and by striking the walls and towers repeatedly with blows they demolished them to their foundations. When the walls had been breached and the entrances lay open, they rushed in and seized everything for themselves. Consequently, the remaining camps all around, seeing this happen to one another, voluntarily submitted themselves to the Normans’ authority.

### CHAPTER ELEVEN. On Tancred’s younger sons, who followed their elder brothers to Apulia.

The younger brothers, whom their age still compelled to remain at home, learned through report that their elder brothers, acting bravely in Apulia, had climbed to the summit of greater honor and domination. As soon as their age permitted, they too followed them, leaving only two behind in their homeland, lest the inheritance or the lineage belonging to them should be alienated. [Col. 1107D]

As they departed, they scarcely persuaded those who remained to stay behind. They prevailed chiefly by promising that, if the heirs followed them, they would benefit them from what they were going to acquire. [Note: [Col. 1107D] “They too followed them, leaving two in the homeland so that the inheritance belonging to them might not be alienated.”]

But it would be too long for this work to insert, by touching upon each matter individually, how they acted in Apulia. [Note: [Col. 1108D] “How he acted in Apulia.”] This much is attested not only by us but also by the facts themselves: they subdued the whole homeland by arms and brought it under their authority.

As a great multitude of their own relatives, countrymen, and parents, as well as of the neighboring regions, followed them in the hope of profit, they, tireless givers, received these men as brothers and enriched them with horses, arms, clothing, and various gifts. They also bestowed lands upon some of them with the utmost generosity, preferring the assistance of brave soldiers to all the riches of this world.

For this reason, nothing they undertook passed them by in vain. Hence that Gospel saying also came true for them: “Give, and it will be given to you.” For the greater the gifts they distributed, the greater the gains they acquired.

### CHAPTER TWELVE. On the death of Count William.

When the elder brother, namely Count William, died after illness had overtaken him, great grief seized all the Normans. They had no hope of possessing any longer a man of such counsel, so brave in arms, so generous toward them, so approachable, and so well-mannered.

But after his funeral rites had been celebrated with the greatest care and with great mourning, as was customary and entirely fitting, the second brother, Drogo, assumed dominion over all Apulia. He was, to speak briefly, a man praiseworthy in every respect.

He appointed his brother Humphrey as count, with Abagelard [Note: [Col. 1108D] C. P. “Adagelard”] mentioned in the transmitted wording; the precise syntactical relation is uncertain, at the castle called Lavel, by the counsel of the Apulians and Normans. He placed Robert Guiscard in Calabria, fortifying for him a castle in the Crati valley at a place called Scribla, so that he might fight against the people of Cosenza and those who were still rebellious in Calabria.

### CHAPTER THIRTEEN. On the death of Count Drogo
Therefore the Lombards, the Apulians—for they were always a most treacherous people—having secretly arranged a conspiracy throughout all Apulia so that all the Normans might be killed on an appointed day, when Count Drogo was staying at the castle of Monte Olio, which the inhabitants corruptly call Montolium, at first light he hurried to the church, as was his custom. Just as he was entering the church [Col. 1108D], a certain man named Risus, the count’s godfather and bound to him by oaths, was hiding behind the door. Breaking his sworn bond, he received him with a sword; and Drogo, together with many of his men, was killed, though a few escaped. Yet in various parts of Apulia many more perished in this treachery.
