Hunifred Abagelardus [Note: [Col. 1108D] C. P.: Adagelardus], disturbed by his brother’s murder and claiming the honor due to himself, attacked the castles that his brother had possessed. Binding to himself the Normans who had escaped the danger of the conspiracy, he rose to avenge his brother’s death. After besieging for a long time the castle in which his brother had been killed, he finally conquered it. He subjected the murderer of his brother, together with those who had supported him [Col. 1109A], to various tortures, and by their blood somewhat extinguished the anger and grief of his heart.

## CHAPTER XIV. How Pope Leo the Apostolic was Captured by the Normans

The Apulians, still not exhausted by their treacheries, sent secret envoys to Pope Leo IX, inviting him to come into Apulia with an army. They said that Apulia rightfully belonged to them and that, in the time of their predecessors, it had belonged to the jurisdiction of the Roman Church; they promised to bring him assistance, while describing the Normans as unwarlike, feeble in strength, and few in number. Although he was, as usual, extremely prudent, ambition nevertheless seized him. Having received an army of Germans from the emperor as an auxiliary force, and trusting in the aid of the Lombards, he entered Apulia [Col. 1109B].

The count, however, judging it more honorable to end his life with honor than, after undertaking that honor, to be deprived of it while still alive and thereby live in disgrace, mobilized his army and boldly met the enemy. Having drawn up his forces and entered the battle, he began the first encounter with great vigor, as was his custom. But the terrified Lombards attempted to protect themselves by flight, abandoning the Germans in the battle. The Germans fought bravely, having no refuge except in their weapons; but as the Normans prevailed, almost all of them fell.

The Apostolic, seeking the refuge of life through flight, withdrew as a fugitive within the city of the province of Capitanata called Cimitata. The enemy pursued him and besieged the city with armed troops. They carried earthworks, prepared engines for capturing the city, and terrified the inhabitants with threats, demanding that they surrender the Apostolic. Those men [Col. 1109C], ever most treacherous, having secured no agreement beneficial to the Apostolic except one by which they themselves might be protected, drove him out through the gates. The enemy received him and, out of reverence for the holy Roman Church, prostrated themselves at his feet with great devotion, asking his pardon and blessing. They also escorted him with every humility as far as the place where the army had fixed its camp and tents.

The Apostolic gratefully accepted their legitimate goodwill, granted them pardon for their offenses and his blessing, and conceded to them, from Saint Peter, all the land that they had overrun and all that they might thereafter acquire toward Calabria and Sicily, to be held by them and their heirs as an hereditary fief, around the year 1052.

## CHAPTER XV. How Pope Leo was Dismissed by the Normans with Honor

[Col. 1109D]

As the Apostolic returned to Rome, Count Hunifredus escorted him honorably for as long as he wished. When he granted him permission to return, Hunifredus went back to Apulia and found the entire land peaceful and obedient to him. For a long time he governed it in peace, so that scarcely anywhere within his dominion could a robber or anyone daring to oppose his commands be found.

He therefore made two of his brothers counts: Malgerius in Capitanata, and Guilielmus in the principality. [Col. 1110A] But when Malgerius died and left his entire county to his brother Guilielmus, Guilielmus affectionately granted it to his brother Gaufredus.

## CHAPTER XVI. Robert Guiscard: How He Fortified the Castle of Saint Mark and Went on Foot to Plunder with the Slavs

While Robert Guiscard was staying at Scribla and vigorously attacking the Calabrians, he saw that his men were growing weak because of the unhealthiness of the place and the difference in climate. Seeking a healthier place—not, however, to avoid the enemy like a coward retreating backward and retiring farther [Note: [Col. 1109D] C. P.: “inside.”], but rather, as though gaping toward the enemy, moving into a nearer stronghold—he fortified the castle called Saint Mark.

But after he had fortified the castle [Col. 1110B], he could find no course of action to undertake. The people living around it had removed everything they possessed to the nearest castles, lest it be seized by the Normans. One evening the steward who presided over his entire household asked him what he or his soldiers would eat on the following day, saying that he had neither food nor money with which to buy it; and even if he had money, nothing could be found anywhere that could be approached peacefully.

Guiscard, who had with him as many as sixty men called Slavs [Note: [Col. 1109D] C. P.: Scalanos], men familiar with the whole of Calabria, whom he had made his most faithful companions by sending them gifts and rewards, asked them whether they knew of an accessible place where plunder could be obtained. They replied that beyond the mountains they knew a very extensive place, reached by a most precipitous route through exceedingly deep valleys [Col. 1110C], but that it could not be brought out without great danger.

Robert is said to have answered them as follows:

“Come now, safest guardians of my life, will you allow Guiscard—and yourselves as well—to be afflicted by hunger? For the sake of acquiring food, uncertain fortune must be tested even at the risk of life. For we have heard that those who make the attempt often escape triumphantly, but no one who has died of hunger is praised.

“Go,” he said, “nighttime raiders. Their drunkenness prevents the Calabrians from being sufficiently watchful. Since they are celebrating this day, they will, according to custom, have devoted themselves to feasts and drinking.” [Note: [Col. 1110D] C. P.: “They devoted themselves to feasts and drinking.”] “Go ahead of me” [Note: [Col. 1110D] C. P.: “Go before me,” etc.]; “I will follow with armed soldiers” [Note: [Col. 1110D] C. P.: “with two hundred armed soldiers,” etc.].

Thus, after his bed had been prepared and he had already been laid down, he rose at night without anyone knowing [Col. 1110D]. Wearing a poor garment and the sandals that they use instead of shoes, and disguising himself like one of those departing, he joined them in their midst. Having become their unknown companion for the whole night, he spoke a word to none of them. He did not even dare to clear his throat, lest by doing so it be discovered who he was. Since they belonged to the same people, he did not entirely trust them.

When they reached the place of the plunder, they gathered in front of themselves whatever they found there. Robert himself, making frequent leaps and brandishing his spear, urged his companions to hasten their return. Before daylight, however, those who had suffered the loss, realizing that their goods had been taken, pursued the soldiers in order to recover the plunder.

Guiscard saw the pursuers approaching rapidly and heard his companions boldly encouraging one another so that they would not be deprived of their booty. To make them still bolder, he now revealed who he was.

“Guiscard,” he said, “is here, sharing your labor. With me you will suffer no danger. Be stout-hearted, and let us rise against the enemy. For, if God favors our fortune, we shall easily prevail.”

Having said this, he met the enemy with the greatest fury. While fighting, he killed many, captured more, and put the rest to flight; thus he became the victor. After receiving the spoils of his triumph, he made mounted soldiers out of his foot soldiers. Now secure, he led the captives with him, going ahead and leaving a few men behind to drive the plunder.

When his soldiers, as daylight rose, realized that armed men were approaching the castle, they suspected them of being enemies. Not knowing where their lord was, they searched the entire castle, calling for him loudly. When they failed to find him, they were thrown into confusion; nevertheless, they boldly rushed out of the castle and hastened to meet those whom they suspected to be enemies.

Robert, meanwhile, spurring the horse on which he sat, approached them at a gallop, repeatedly shouting “Guiscard!” Thus recognized by them, he made them all joyful at his presence and at the success of his fortune. Yet they strongly reproached him for having ventured on such a deed and warned him not to attempt anything similar again, lest the fortune that had now smiled on him should, if tested again, turn for the worse.

Thus enriching the castle with plunder and the ransoms of captives, he harassed the Calabrians greatly through repeated raids.

## CHAPTER XVII. Robert Guiscard and Peter of Turra

[Col. 1111C]

It must not be passed over in silence how he captured Peter of Turra, who was staying at Bisignano. This Peter was an extremely wealthy citizen of Bisignano, and, excelling all the others both in counsel and in courage, ruled over them all. Peter and Robert Guiscard were accustomed to meet frequently, as though for a friendly conference, to discuss the many disputes that arose among their people.

Guiscard knew that Peter possessed immense wealth and dominated the castle above all others. He therefore began to consider how, through Peter, he might gain possession of the castle and seize the money that he owned. After turning this over in his mind for a long time, he finally consulted with his men.

One day, without any treaty having been made between them, Guiscard and Peter came outside the castle of Bisignano [Col. 1111D] to the field where they were accustomed to converse. Guiscard saw that a very large crowd had come with Peter. He therefore sent a messenger ahead to say that he did not wish to mingle with the crowd, lest some disturbance arise among them for one reason or another. Instead, he proposed that the companions of both sides move farther away and that the two of them meet alone in the middle to converse.

He had nevertheless told his own men what he intended to do and instructed them to come quickly to his aid when necessary. Peter agreed to what Guiscard had sent word of, taking insufficient care for himself. Leaving his companions at a distance, he hastened alone to meet Guiscard in the middle of the field.

They sat down and spoke to each other for a long time. When they rose to depart, Guiscard, observing the man’s enormous size and bulk, placed little doubt in his own strength. He was, after all, extremely presumptuous in everything [Col. 1112A] and daring in attempting great deeds. Seizing Peter around the middle, he placed him across his neck and began carrying him toward his own men.

The companions of both sides came running: the people of Bisignano to rescue Peter, and the Normans to assist their lord. Guiscard, while Peter struggled violently, brought him to his own men, sometimes carrying him, sometimes rolling him, and sometimes dragging him.

The Calabrians, now despairing of Peter and unwilling to fight the Normans on his behalf, fled into the castle of Bisignano. The Normans, rejoicing as though in a triumph, brought Peter with them as far as the castle of Saint Mark. There he was held captive for some time. After paying an astonishing sum of money, he freed himself from captivity; but because the citizens would not agree to it [Col. 1112B], he was entirely unable to recover the castle.

When the Calabrians learned of this and similar acts of Guiscard’s cunning, they—an exceedingly fearful people—trembled before him. They said that no one could be compared with him in arms, intelligence, or strength.

## CHAPTER XVIII. How Robert Guiscard Became Count of Apulia

Having received so much money, Guiscard generously rewarded his men and strengthened them in loyalty to himself. By continually harassing the people of Bisignano and Consentia, the Marturanenses, and the neighboring province, he compelled them to enter into a treaty with him, on the following terms: they were to retain their castles but pay only service and tribute [Col. 1112C]; and they pledged this by oaths and hostages.

Count Hunifredus, meanwhile, was governing Apulia in the greatest glory and with praiseworthy peace. Overcome by illness, he died—a grief to relate. When Guiscard, who at that time was staying at Saint Mark, heard this, he hastened toward Apulia in great anguish of heart. Received by the leading men of his homeland, he was made lord and count of all the land in place of his brother.

Having put his affairs in order and reconciled all Apulia to himself in peace, he could not forget what he had first conceived in his mind. Now extended over a greater dominion and strengthened by greater forces—namely, by an increased number of soldiers—he again turned his attention to completing what he had begun.

Having mobilized his army and assembled what was necessary for the expedition, he directed his forces toward Calabria [Col. 1112D]. Passing through the territory of Consentia and the Marturanenses, he remained for two days beside the hot springs, on the river called the Noce, so that he might refresh the army, fatigued by the difficulty of the journey, and examine the land more carefully.

From there he continued as far as the castle called Scyllacium. Proceeding along the seacoast, he reached Rhegium. After inspecting the situation of the place for three days, he saw that he could bend the citizens of the city neither by threats nor by blandishments. Certain affairs recalled him toward Apulia, and he prepared to return. As he departed, Leucastrum, Maja, and Canalda made peace and surrendered themselves.

## CHAPTER XIX. Roger, the Younger Son of Tancred

Roger, the younger brother, whom youthful age and affection for his parents had until then kept at home [Col. 1113A], followed and came to Apulia. Guiscard was exceedingly pleased at his arrival and received him with the honor that was fitting. He was a very handsome young man, tall in stature and elegant in body; extremely eloquent, shrewd in counsel, prudent in arranging affairs, pleasant and affable to everyone, strong in body, and fierce in warfare. By these qualities he soon earned universal favor.

Since he was factional and, as is usual at that age, eager for praise, he attached to himself all who were inclined toward faction and gladly and most generously shared with them whatever he could obtain.

Guiscard, wishing to test his brother’s steadfastness and military boldness more certainly, sent him into Calabria with only sixty soldiers to fight many thousands of enemies [Col. 1113B]. Roger advanced boldly and pitched his camp on the highest summit of the Vibonian mountains, fixing his tents there so that, visible from far and wide, he might more easily frighten the inhabitants all around.

When this became known throughout all the cities and castles of that province and throughout the entire valley of Salinarum, everyone was terrified. They sent envoys seeking peace, gave many gifts, and feebly surrendered their strongest castles into servitude. They bound themselves by oaths and hostages.

## CHAPTER XX. How Roger, Invited by Robert Guiscard, Went from Calabria to Apulia

Having organized the land according to his and his brother’s allegiance as he wished, Roger sent his brother a great deal of the money he had received through envoys, reporting how he had conducted his affairs. He himself fortified with the greatest care the castle called Incifola [Col. 1113C], strengthening it with towers and defensive works and supplying it with armed soldiers. He had adequately brought in everything necessary for food.

Guiscard received the money sent to him by his brother and was greatly pleased when he learned of his vigor. Desiring to speak with him, he sent word that Roger should hasten to come to him. Roger brought only six soldiers with him, leaving the others to guard the castle he had built and to keep the province under pressure so that no treacherous acts might be attempted. He came to Apulia to his brother, who received him properly. They exchanged reports of their affairs and spoke together in mutual conversation. [Note: [Col. 1113D] C. P.: “They rejoiced.”]

## CHAPTER XXI. Robert Guiscard and Roger Go with an Army to Rhegium

[Col. 1113D]

Roger remained there until, by common counsel, they had prepared what was necessary for the expedition. Then, crossing the mountain ridges of Calabria with a very large force of cavalry and infantry, they advanced toward Rhegium.

When they reached the valley of Salinarum, Guiscard [Col. 1114A] heard that the people of Rhegium had shut inside the city all the provisions available in the surrounding area, leaving nothing accessible to the army. He foresaw that hunger might force the army to abandon the siege of the city. He therefore sent his brother Roger with three hundred soldiers toward the castle called Geracium to plunder, earnestly warning him to seize whatever he could that was necessary for food and bring it to the army at Rhegium. He himself proceeded by the direct route and hastened to besiege the city.

## CHAPTER XXII. Roger Comes to Rhegium with Great Plunder

Roger, eager to carry out what had been entrusted to him for the favor of his brother and the entire army, searched the highest hills and the deepest valleys [Col. 1114B]. Like a faithful and industrious bee, he returned to the army heavily laden with an enormous amount of plunder, and revived the troops, who were already almost exhausted, with the abundance of supplies.

Guiscard, however, seeing that he was making little progress against the city and that the army was being troubled by the severity of winter, lifted the siege and gave permission to depart. He himself withdrew with a few men to spend the winter at Maja.

## CHAPTER XXIII. Roger Leaves Robert Guiscard in Anger

Roger had too little with which to reward his soldiers [Note: [Col. 1113D] “Roger, with certain of his soldiers, had too little with which to reward them.”], and they themselves were becoming increasingly importunate in demanding it from him. He therefore asked his brother for assistance.

But Robert, influenced by the counsel of wicked men, although generous toward the others, began to be more restrictive toward Roger than was proper. He saw that, because of Roger’s valor, the young soldiers of all Apulia were more inclined to follow him than himself. He consequently feared that Roger might grow insolent against him and wished to compel him, through want, to remain content with a few men in his company.

Roger, however, being a man of great spirit, knowing this, left his brother and went to Apulia [Col. 1114C]. [Note: [Col. 1113D]

“He, feeling himself to be so treated by his brother, withdrew and went to Apulia.”

C. P.: “Lest he should regard himself as degenerate from his brother or unworthy, but might gradually climb to higher things, as his brother had done and as he himself was now, with fortune favoring him, doing, he left his brother in anger,” etc.]

.

## CHAPTER XXIV. Roger is Kindly Received by His Brother Guilielmus and is Granted Scalea

When his brother Guilielmus, count of the entire principality, heard this, he sent envoys and invited Roger to come to him. He promised that Roger should receive jointly whatever Guilielmus possessed and affirmed that, apart from his wife and children, he wished to hold nothing as his own separately from him [Col. 1114D].

Roger came and was received with the honor that was fitting. He stayed with Guilielmus for some time. Finally, he received from him the castle called Scalea [Note: [Col. 1114D] C. P.: Ascla, and likewise thereafter]. From there he made many raids against Guiscard and harassed the surrounding region.

When this was reported to Guiscard, he went with an army to besiege the castle just mentioned. Guiscard was devastating the olive groves and vineyards adjoining the city. Guilielmus, however, repeatedly engaged his soldiers and, by the strength of his spear [Col. 1115A], struck them down in military fashion, reducing their numbers.

When Guiscard saw that he was making little progress against the city and that the number of his men was steadily decreasing, he withdrew from the place after taking counsel, lest he be burdened by an even greater loss.

## CHAPTER XXV. Count Roger Steals Horses

Not long afterward, peace was temporarily made between them through intermediaries. Invited by his brother, Roger went to serve him with forty soldiers loyal to himself. There he suffered considerable hardship, but he was supported in many ways by the thefts of his armed retainers.

We do not mention this to his disgrace. Rather, since he himself ordered it, we shall continue to write even more humble and blameworthy things about him, so that it may become clear to many how laboriously and amid how much hardship he rose from profound poverty to the highest summit of wealth or honor.

He had a certain armed retainer named Blettiva [Col. 1115B; Note: [Col. 1115D] “A certain Blettina”], before whom he concealed nothing that he intended to steal. He himself, still a poor young man but later destined to become an extremely wealthy count [Note: [Col. 1115D] “While still living, he was destined to become an extremely wealthy count, [and] was the cause”], desired certain horses that he had seen at Melfa in a certain man’s house. He persuaded this retainer to go with him and carry them away by night theft.

## CHAPTER XXVI. The Men of Melfi are Captured by Roger

After diligently performing his brother’s service for a period of two months, Roger had received from him nothing as a reward for himself and all his men except one horse [Col. 1115C]. Although he had not read it, he nevertheless seemed to know by instinct that Sallust’s proverb:

> “To strive in vain and, in the end, by exhausting oneself to seek nothing but hatred is the height of madness” (Cat. 61);

and that fortune is necessary for one who serves well.

Seeing that fortune favored him less in relation to his brother, he argued at length with him. He returned the agreement that they had made between themselves for a time, went back to Scalea, and that very evening sent his soldiers from the castle called Narencium to plunder the territory of Guiscard. Thus he ravaged the province.

While he was waiting at Scalea for those whom he had sent to plunder, a certain man named Berver [Note: [Col. 1115D] C. P.: Benerus], coming from Melfa, announced that Melfitan merchants were passing from Melfa toward [Col. 1115D] Melfa, not far from the castle.

On hearing this, Roger was exceedingly pleased. Mounting his horse, he rode out with only eight soldiers to meet the merchants at Gisenualdum and Carbonaria. He captured them and led them to Scalea. He seized everything they had with them and even made them ransom themselves.

Strengthened by this money, he became a generous distributor and gathered one hundred soldiers to himself. With these he tore apart all Apulia through frequent and varied raids, making Guiscard so anxious that he forgot the conquest of Calabria and nearly lost what he had already acquired.

## CHAPTER XXVII. Famine Occurs in Calabria

In the year 1058, a very great disaster and, as we believe, a scourge of God’s wrath, sent by divine judgment in response to sins, afflicted the entire province of Calabria over the course of three months—namely, March, April, and May—to such an extent that the inhabitants, seeing death threatening them through a triple disease, though one of these dangers alone would have been sufficient to endanger life, scarcely believed that they could escape any one of them, much less all three raging together with such fury.

For on one side the sword of the Normans raged, sparing scarcely anyone. On another side, with strength exhausted, famine seethed through their languishing bodies [Col. 1116B]. As a third plague, the frost of mortality flowed down horribly, striking scarcely anyone who remained untouched [Note: [Col. 1115D] “But the battle of mortality flowed down horribly, scarcely allowing anyone to escape, passing through everything to such an extent”], and ran like a fire raging with loose reins through a dry bed of reeds [Note: [Col. 1116D] “Boiling with reins”].

Those who possessed money had nothing to buy. They sold even their own freeborn children [Note: [Col. 1116D] “Their children”] into slavery for a paltry price. But since they could not find anywhere to spend the money for the benefit of their food, they were tortured, adding to their grief, as though by a fourth calamity: the loss of their children through a useless sale [Note: [Col. 1116D] “Their loss was inflicted because of the loss”].

They ate meat without bread. Some had no wine; when their drink was seasoned with water [Note: [Col. 1116D] “For those who had it, they were sustained by watery drink”], it caused dysentery and brought many low, while it made others suffer from an enlarged spleen. When the natural heat was excessively flooded with stronger wine [Col. 1116C], the heart, whose strength bread did not sustain, paid the penalty for the same destruction; yielding to an internal fever, it was forced into weakness.

The holy observance of Lent, handed down in accordance with catholic teaching by holy and religious Fathers, was dissolved by hardship to such an extent [Note: [Col. 1116D] “It was dissolved; they used raw meats, fruits of trees, or bark as food”] that not only the eating of milk or cheese, but even the consumption of meat, which had been permitted at other times, was violated even by those who had previously appeared to possess some degree of decency.

Thus the green plants and vegetables from which stews are usually made had been taken away by the sterility of the earth. When they were found, they seemed, after being cooked, to have been spoiled by a certain frost of corrupted air and to do more harm than good when tasted.

They attempted to make bread from river reeds and the bark of certain trees, together with chestnuts and the nuts of oaks or holm oaks, which we call acorns [Col. 1116D], after taking them from the pigs, drying and grinding them in a mill, and adding a small amount of millet.

Raw roots, eaten with salt alone, produced swelling of the belly and pallor of the face, obstructing the vital organs. Mothers, through a cunning motivated by affection, shamefully strove with violent boldness to snatch food from the very mouths of their children rather than give it to them.

Thus they were worn down by the triple scourge until the new crops [Col. 1117A]. When the new crops arrived, famine was indeed driven away; but the sword of mortality became sharper. For the bodies, emptied by hunger and unaccustomed to food, were restored all the more intemperately by abundant nourishment contrary to their condition, and therefore perished all the more quickly.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. The Rebellious Calabrians Treacherously Capture the Castle of Leucastrum, Killing Many There

At last the Calabrians, a most treacherous people, seeing that, because the brothers were quarreling among themselves, no one was rising against them [Note: [Col. 1117D] C. P.: “visiting them”], began to shake off the yoke of the Normans and to pay neither the service nor the tribute that they had sworn to pay.

Accordingly, having arranged a treachery under the pretense of loyalty, they seized the castle of Leucastrum [Col. 1117B] and killed in a single day the sixty Normans who had been left there to guard the castle.

## CHAPTER XXIX. The Peace Made Between Robert Guiscard and His Brother Roger

When this was reported to Guiscard, he saw that he was losing ground in Calabria and that all Apulia was being thrown into disorder. He therefore summoned his brother through envoys and made peace with him, granting him half of Calabria, from the ridge of Mount Intefoli [Note: [Col. 1117D] C. P.: Niclefoli], Mount Scyllacium, which had already been acquired, as far as Rhegium, including whatever they would acquire.

## CHAPTER XXX. Robert Guiscard Repudiates Alberada and Marries Sigelgaita; Roger and Guiscard are Reconciled

[Col. 1117C]

After these events, Robert Guiscard had a respectable wife of his own people and distinguished lineage, named Alberada. By her he had a son named Marcus, whom they also called by another name, Bohemond. Counting the relationship between them, and unwilling to act contrary to the canonical sanctions, he dissolved the marriage. He joined in marriage with himself the daughter of Gaimarius, the prince of Salerno, named Sigelgaita.

## CHAPTER XXXI. Robert Guiscard Goes Against His Brother Guilielmus Before Celebrating the Wedding

In the year 1058 from the Incarnation of the Lord, after becoming betrothed to her at Salerno, and before they came together, Robert entrusted the girl to the care of his brother Roger [Col. 1117D]. He himself went to destroy [the passage is corrupt]—Gisulf, his own brother, whom he had established as count of the principality in her inheritance, being exceedingly hostile to him. [Note: [Col. 1117D] “So that he might act according to the wish of Gisulf, the girl’s brother, the two castles which Guilielmus...”] [Note: [Col. 1118D] “He himself nevertheless.”]

He then returned to Melfa and celebrated the solemn wedding.

## CHAPTER XXXII. Roger Fights the Greeks at Saint Martin’s

After these matters had been completed, Roger returned Scalea to his brother Guilielmus with thanks. At Guiscard’s request he came to Calabria, possessing the castle of Melito, which his brother had assigned to him hereditarily [Col. 1118A], and began attacking the rebellious Calabrians in every direction.

One day, while he was besieging the castle of Oppidum [Note: [Col. 1118D] C. P.: Oppium], the bishop of Cassino and the provost of Gerace—whom we call a provost—raised a very large army and went to attack the castle called Saint Martin in the valley of Salinarum, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1059.

When this was reported to Roger, he withdrew from the castle he was besieging and, hastening at a rapid pace, flew to the place where he heard that they were. He attacked them and then, as though surrounding them, scarcely allowed a single one to escape. From their spoils, horses, and weapons he made all his men wealthy.

For this reason, although Calabria was not entirely obedient, it nevertheless trembled at his proximity and was less willing than before to provoke him.

## CHAPTER XXXIII. Robert Guiscard and Roger Go to Aid Their Brother Gaufredus

[Col. 1118B]

Robert Guiscard was asked by his brother Gaufredus, count of Capitanata, to come with assistance against those resisting him in the land called Gitium, which he had begun to subdue in order to extend his borders. Trusting greatly in the valor of his brother Roger, Robert invited him to come to him as quickly as possible, intending to go there with him.

Roger accepted the invitation and, recognizing his brother’s need, hastened with the utmost care to his brother’s assistance. Although he was occupied with arranging his own affairs, it had always been his custom to treat the interests of his friends as his own and to come to their aid.

Thus, having mobilized an army, the two of them directed their forces to assist his brother [Col. 1118C]. They attacked and captured the castle of Guillamatus [Note: [Col. 1118D] Guilliniacum]. They brought Gualterius, who ruled the castle, captive to Apulia and put out his eyes, lest, if he ever escaped from captivity while retaining his sight, he should again become a nuisance to his brother.

This man had a sister, who was carried away into captivity with him. She is also said to have been of such extraordinary beauty that, if she ever went to bathe in the sea, or placed her legs for the sake of experiment in some fish-filled river, the fish, delighted by their whiteness, would swim toward her so that they could even be caught by hand.

## CHAPTER XXXIV. After Guillamatus was Conquered, Both Brothers Go to Calabria

[Col. 1118D]

Then Count Gaufredus, having obtained the castle of Guillamatus [Note: [Col. 1118D] Guilliniacum] with his brother’s assistance, began vigorously to subdue the entire province of Teacina.

Robert Guiscard, however, withdrew with his brother Roger into Calabria. There he arranged many matters for his and his brother’s advantage. He went raiding as far as Rhegium, while Roger remained in Calabria; then he himself returned to Apulia to spend the winter there.

## CHAPTER XXXV. Robert Guiscard is Made Duke

After winter had passed, Robert burned with great desire to acquire Rhegium [Col. 1119A]. He carefully prepared provisions and the other necessities and assembled a very large army in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1060. He came to Calabria, took his brother with him, and, at the time when the harvests were beginning to be gathered, arrived before Rhegium and besieged it.

The inhabitants defended themselves vigorously, as though fighting for their lives. The two brothers, each vying with the other in encouraging his men, stirred them to attack the castle. When the enemy occasionally sallied forth, the brothers performed many deeds of valor.

Roger, lest he be said to rouse others to warfare while fleeing himself, placed himself before his companions in every engagement. He attacked and killed a certain very strong man of enormous size who had been insulting the Norman army with many taunts and whom everyone praised as a giant [Col. 1119B]. Roger struck him down with the force of his spear.

After this man had been killed in such a manner, the others inside the castle were terrified. They saw that engines had been prepared for capturing the city and were being brought right up to it. Distrusting their own strength, they made an agreement that two men who appeared to rule the others might depart with all their people. All the rest, however, surrendered the city and submitted themselves to Norman rule.

Those who departed withdrew into the castle called Scillacium.

## CHAPTER XXXVI. While Guiscard Remains at Rhegium, Roger Conquers the Castles of Calabria

Robert Guiscard received the city and thus attained the fulfillment of his long desire [Col. 1119C]. He was made duke with triumphant glory. He gave great thanks, with fitting recompense, to his brother and to the rest of the army, through whose aid he had reached such a summit of honor.

He sent his brother with the army through the cities and castles of the entire province, so that they might submit to his rule. Meanwhile, he himself rested from his labors at Rhegium.

Roger, not ignorant of this kind of work, led the army wisely. Within a short time he gained eleven very famous castles, now terrifying them with threats, now soothing them with blandishments. He did so thoroughly that throughout Calabria no castle dared to resist, except Xillanum [Note: [Col. 1119D] C. P.: Scyllacium], which was held by those who had departed from Rhegium.

## CHAPTER XXXVII. How Scyllacium was Captured

[Col. 1119D]

Roger besieged Scyllacium. When he saw that it could not be captured quickly, and that his army was being wearied by the labor, he built a certain castle before its gate. He supplied it with soldiers to harass Scyllacium and with everything necessary for the soldiers, then dismissed the army from the campaign.

Those who had entered Scyllacium from Rhegium saw that they were being harassed excessively by the men whom Roger had placed in the new castle and that they could not endure this for long. They therefore boarded a ship by night and fled to Constantinople.

The people of Scyllacium summoned Roger, made peace in the year of the Lord 1060, and surrendered the castle. Thus all Calabria, in the presence of Duke Guiscard and his brother Roger, became quiet and lay pacified.

## CHAPTER XXXVIII. How Serlo, Son of Tancred, was Driven from Normandy into Brittany

[Col. 1120A]

But lest anyone suppose that those who did not come to Apulia with their other brothers were of less worth than the rest, and that for this reason they remained in Normandy, a few things must be said about Serlo. While he was being esteemed among the more distinguished soldiers in Normandy, he suffered an injury from a certain powerful man and, while striving to avenge himself, killed him. Unable to bear the anger of Count Robert, son of Richard II and father of the most renowned King William of the English, he withdrew to Brittany. After remaining there for some time, he won everyone’s favor by his valor; and, seeking peace from Count Robert through envoys, but failing to obtain it, he harassed Normandy with many raids.  
[Col. 1120B]

## CHAPTER XXXIX. On the military service of that same Serlo

When Count Robert had once besieged a castle on the border of France and Normandy called Taulerias, a certain French knight repeatedly came out from the castle and sought single combat with the Norman army, overthrowing many men. The count, fearing loss among his own men, had forbidden everyone to confront him; thus he gave his men an excuse, so that when they avoided what was dangerous, they could attribute it not to fear but to the prince’s prohibition.

When this was reported to Serlo, who at that time was staying in Brittany, he could not endure the disgrace of his people. Accompanied by only two squires, he came to Taulerias and, at first light, offered single combat before the gate, waiting while leaning upon his spear from horseback. The man accustomed to overthrowing others, indignant, came rushing toward him in splendid armor upon a spirited horse, with the greatest fury. He asked who Serlo was and urged him to withdraw from the place and preserve his life. When Serlo revealed his name but refused to withdraw, the two engaged fiercely, and the overthrower of others was himself brought down by a powerful thrust of the lance.

With many on both sides watching, though not knowing who he was, Serlo became the victor, to the glory of the Normans. Placing the severed head beneath his lance, he hurried back to Brittany through the midst of the camps of his own people, speaking to no one.  
[Col. 1120D]

The count therefore sent an envoy and ordered him to investigate who the victor was and to command him to come to him. When it was reported that this Serlo was the son of Tancred, that he had come from Brittany because his people had driven him out in consequence of a dispute, and that, since the prince was angry with him, he was avoiding the prince’s wrath and willingly enduring exile from his homeland, though in poverty, until the prince’s anger subsided and he himself ordered his return, the count was moved by compassion. Unwilling to remain deprived of so great a man, he ordered Serlo to be summoned to him.

He went out to meet him, granted him his favor, safely restored him with a kiss, returned what he had lost, increased the possessions belonging to his wife, and retained him among his closest associates. [The wording *inter sib* is uncertain in the supplied text.]

## CHAPTER XL. On Tancred and the boar

[Col. 1121A]

It is neither improper nor unworthy of remembrance to say something about Tancred, the father of so many sons. In the time of his youth, devoted to military exercises and traveling through the courts of various regions and princes, he gained much by performing many deeds in his eagerness for distinguished renown. When he was in the household of Richard II, count of the Normans—the fourth after Duke Rollo—in one of those days the same prince went hunting. For, as is customary among the wealthy, he took considerable delight in that pursuit, and he stirred up a boar of astonishing size, which they call a singular beast.

It was the prince’s custom, as it is that of many other powerful men, that no one except himself should presume to kill an animal that he himself had started. But while the dogs pursued the boar more swiftly and the count followed more slowly because of the dense thickets and thorny terrain, the boar, fearing that the more aggressive dogs would tear it apart, found a certain rock and used it as a wall behind its tail, presenting its tooth-filled head to the dogs in self-defense.

Thus, while the hunter’s dogs were deprived of assistance and the boar was already making great slaughter among them with its foaming teeth, Tancred happened upon the scene. Although he knew the prince’s custom, he nevertheless hastened to aid the dogs. At the sight of him, the boar abandoned the dogs and rushed upon him with a firm charge. But Tancred, being a man of great strength, received it with a daring sword—not by striking it with a blow, but by driving the sharp point through its exceptionally hard forehead as far as its vitals—and brought the hilt against its forehead. Nothing of the very long sword remained outside the boar’s body except the hilt.

After bringing it down and leaving the sword embedded in its forehead, Tancred withdrew farther away so that the count would not discover that he had done it. When the count arrived, astonished to see the dead boar, he ordered his companions to examine it and determine whether it bore any wound. When they discovered the sword still fixed in its forehead, he marveled at the force with which it had been driven in and asked whose sword it was, so that the perpetrator of the deed might not conceal himself. [The supplied Latin at this point is textually uncertain.]

When it was discovered that Tancred had done it, the count and everyone else extolled him with the highest praise. Although he had already been held in esteem, from then on he was regarded even more highly; and afterward he served at the count’s court with ten soldiers under his command.  
[Col. 1122B]  
[Note: [Col. 1121D] *Demum*—“finally” or “afterward.”]

Now, since we have written not everything that might be worth remembering, but only the few things we learned by report from the brothers themselves about what was done in Apulia, or certainly in Calabria, although in a rustic style, let us turn our attention to what happened in unbelieving Sicily and to the manner in which that land, rebellious for so long, was subdued. Yet we shall do so in such a way that, whenever the opportunity requires, those things later done in Apulia, or Rome, or Greece will not be passed over in forgetfulness but will be treated in their proper place.  
[Note: [Col. 1121D] *Qualiter ne*—“and how not” (variant reading).]  
[Note: [Col. 1121D] “What was previously done in Apulia, etc.”]  
[Note: [Col. 1121D] “So that they might not pass into oblivion in their proper place.”]

[Col. 1121] Here ends Book One.

# BOOK TWO BEGINS

[Col. 1121]

[Col. 1121C] If it is asked why, after Calabria, or part of Apulia, has been described—not completely, however, with regard to everything that happened there—we pass to describing Sicily, making what seems again to be a digression, it should be understood that each matter to be described demands its proper place according to the time at which it occurred. The sequence of the narrative must be woven along a straight course, so that what happened earlier comes first, while what happened later is written afterward.  
[Note: [Col. 1121D] “Let it be asked why.”]  
[Note: [Col. 1122D] “It is to be reduced to the same style; it should be understood that each matter to be described…”]  
[Note: [Col. 1122D] “It is.”]  
[Note: [Col. 1122D] “It testifies.”]  
[Note: [Col. 1122D] “What follows is added.”]

For when Count Roger first set out to conquer Sicily, he did not abandon what he possessed in Calabria. Rather, whenever necessity required, he would dismiss the army temporarily into Sicily and return himself to arrange his own affairs. Often, too, he crossed as far as Apulia to bring assistance to his brother the duke, or at least to give counsel in greater and doubtful matters, as a vigorous soldier and a man of great wisdom.  
[Col. 1121D]

## CHAPTER I. Count Roger first enters Sicily

The most elegant young Count of Calabria, while staying at Reggio with his brother the duke after the whole of Calabria had been conquered, heard of unbelieving Sicily and saw it nearby across the very short stretch of sea. Since he had always been eager for dominion, he was seized by the ambition of acquiring it. He regarded this as profitable to himself in two respects, namely for soul and body: if he recalled that land, devoted to idols, to divine worship, and if he temporarily possessed and distributed in God’s service the produce or revenues of the land that the people ungrateful to God had appropriated for themselves.

Turning these thoughts over in his mind, and not a tardy executor of the things upon which he had fixed his attention, he explored Sicily with only sixty soldiers, committing himself by sea to the most dangerous, though short, passage between Scylla and Charybdis. He crossed over to test the military strength of his people.

Near the harbor where they landed stood a populous city. Since it derived its name from the harvest—because the harvests of the entire region, as much as was formerly paid in tribute to the Romans, used to be gathered there—it was called Messina. Its citizens, a very large multitude, learned that their enemies had invaded their territory and were greatly angered, especially because they saw that the enemy force was small. Bursting out through the city gates with tremendous force, they advanced to seize them.

But the count, as always exceedingly shrewd and skilled in warfare, first feigned fear. When he had drawn them some distance away from the city, he attacked, rushed upon them with the greatest ferocity, and put them to flight. Cutting down the hindmost of them and appearing to the fleeing men as an abhorrent and threatening pursuer, he drove them all the way back to the city gate. After taking the spoils and horses of those whom he had overthrown, he boarded his ships and returned to Reggio, to his brother the duke.

## CHAPTER II. Duke Robert entrusts Reggio and all Calabria to be administered; he himself goes to Apulia

Duke Robert then returned with his brother Count Roger to spend the winter in Apulia. Since some time had passed since he had withdrawn from there, he found his affairs, as though blunted at the point and less orderly. Throughout the winter he restored them by his prudent counsel and repaired them completely.  
[Note: [Col. 1123D] “Mending” or “repairing.”]

He gave many gifts to the Apulian princes, who rejoiced with him over the duchy newly acquired for him, and warned them that an expedition toward Sicily would be undertaken in the coming summer.

## CHAPTER III. Becumen, admiral of Sicily, expelled by his own people, comes to Count Roger at Reggio

Count Roger, leaving the duke in Apulia, returned to Reggio in the first week before Lent. There came to him at Reggio Becumen, admiral of Sicily, who had been routed in battle by a certain prince named Belcamed, because he had killed the husband of his sister, an honorable young man of his people named Beneclerus. As a fugitive, he approached the count and urged him with many appeals to attack Sicily.  
[Notes: [Col. 1123D] “Betumen.” “By Elcarmedo.” “Beneclerus.”]

## CHAPTER IV. On Becumen’s counsel, Count Roger again goes to Sicily

The count was very pleased by his arrival, received him honorably, and, following his advice, went into Sicily before the winter had ended—namely, in the week immediately preceding Lent. Taking Becumen with him, he invaded Sicily with one hundred and sixty soldiers, crossed the Strait, and proceeded toward Clibana.  
[Note: [Col. 1123D] “Taking Bittumen with him, since he knew the country, and crossing the Strait to Clibanum.”]

While, under the guidance of Becumen, who had defected to him, he was traveling by night toward Melacium, not far from the city of Messina, he encountered a certain Saracen, very famous among his people for military skill—namely, the brother of Beneclerus, on account of whose killing Becumen had been expelled from Sicily. The man had learned on the previous evening that the count had entered Sicily with an armed force. Relying too confidently on his military strength, he had advanced from Messina as a nocturnal enemy, seeking to acquire a military reputation for himself by harming the enemy.

Count Roger, unarmed except for a shield and the sword with which he was girded, went ahead of his companions, while a squire followed behind him with the weapons, and he kept his eyes intently on every side. When he detected the approaching man beneath the pale light of the moon, judging that it would take too long to receive his weapons from the squire, lest the man, if he caught sight of him in the shadows, should flee, Then he attacked him with the sword alone and, striking him through the middle with a single blow, cut him in two. He gave the horse and spoils to one of his men.

From there he passed through Melacium and Rametta, taking a great quantity of booty, and returned to the three *batus* [perhaps “lakes”] near the Strait, which are called Praroli, to spend the night. The next day he advanced as far as the Outer Waters, or “Sweet Waters,” and sent the booty he had taken by ship to Reggio.  
[Notes: [Col. 1124D] “Lakes.” “They are called Caroli.” “To the Sweet Waters.” “They place it on ships to be transported.”]

## CHAPTER V. Count Roger battles with the people of Messina

The people of Messina thought that, since some men had boarded the ships, they could more easily seize the others as though they had been divided into two groups. They therefore all came out of the city with cavalry and infantry and advanced to attack. But because the wind was unfavorable, none of the armed men had entered the ships. When the count learned that they were approaching him, he sent ahead his nephew Serlo—namely, the son of his brother Serlo, whom we mentioned above at the end of the first book—so that, if they wished to flee, as they did, they would have less freedom to do so. He himself followed more swiftly and intercepted them as they attempted to escape, barely escaping with his life from so great a multitude.

## CHAPTER VI. Count Roger obtains the calming of the disturbed sea by a vow

While the people of Messina mourned the wounds—or, according to another reading, the deaths—of their men, the count passed near the city and went to lodge on the island of Saint Hyacinth, not far from the city. At first light he advanced to attack Messina, as though it had been exhausted of strength.

But the remaining people of Messina, though few, defended themselves with the women as well, who were armed along with them. They defended the towers, fortifications, and themselves with eager determination, as though fighting for their lives. The count, fearing that Sicily might be aroused by such an action and rush upon him, returned to his tents and began to consider the crossing back toward Reggio.

When the troubled sea threatened a dangerous crossing, the count, employing wise counsel, had resolved to give all the booty he had captured to Saint Andronius, for the rebuilding of his church near Reggio. It had recently been destroyed. And so, as we believe, through the merits of that saint, a favorable breeze arose, the sea grew calm, and, making itself passable, allowed them to cross safely.  
[Note: [Col. 1124D] “Saint Anthony.”]

## CHAPTER VII. That booty taken from pagans is not unacceptable to God as a sacrifice

Lest this deed—their offering of booty to God—appear contrary to the canonical sanctions because of the saying, “Whoever sacrifices a victim from plunder, or from the substance of the poor, is like one who sacrifices a son before his father” (Ecclesiasticus 34), it should be understood that this saying applies especially to the substance of Christ’s poor. Of these it is also said elsewhere: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew 5).  
[Notes: [Col. 1125D] “Of the poor.” “To these, whose kingdom is heaven.”]

We know that those people were not Christ’s poor, since they confess God neither with their mouth nor with their body. But it does not seem absurd to offer to God what is taken from those who use, without gratitude, gifts whose giver they do not acknowledge.  
[Notes: [Col. 1125D] “If anything.” “It is not absurd to offer.” “They use them ungratefully.” “And so forth.”]

## CHAPTER VIII. The people of Palermo come by ship to the Strait to prevent our men from crossing

Throughout March and April, Count Roger prudently arranged matters in Calabria and energetically prepared another expedition toward Sicily, with ships and the other necessary supplies. When May began, the duke came from Apulia to Reggio with a very large cavalry force and also sent a naval army to come by sea.

Belcamuer, admiral of Sicily, hearing that an expedition toward Sicily was being prepared, sent from Palermo to the Strait ships called Catti, to prevent the enemy from crossing. For several days they blocked the passage of the enemy. Although our naval army was very large, theirs was larger and had stronger ships. Our men had only a greater abundance of Germandi and galleys; the Sicilians had Catti, Golafri, and Dormundi, as well as ships of various construction.  
[Notes: [Col. 1126D] “Roc Kilias.” “Cochleas and Galafros.”]

## CHAPTER IX. Seeing their passage obstructed, our men implore a helper

Seeing their passage obstructed in this way, the duke, after taking counsel with his brother the count and with wise men, invited divine aid. He ordered the army to confess to the priests, receive penance, and all receive Communion.

Together with his brother, he vowed that, if God granted them the land by divine assistance, they would henceforth devote themselves more fully to God. They firmly held in mind what is written: “In all your affairs take God as your helper, and you will have prosperous results”; also, “There is no counsel against the Lord”; and, “There is no difficulty in advancing where the Holy Spirit is present as co-worker.” With tearful contrition of heart they implored God, in all that they planned to do, to be their director and their stronger governor.

## CHAPTER X. Without the enemy’s knowledge, Count Roger crosses by night and captures Messina

[Col. 1126A]

Count Roger saw that the enemy were stationed on the opposite bank facing his army and that no progress was being made. He therefore turned, as was his custom, to cunning devices—as though he had read the question, “What difference does it make whether victory is achieved by arms or by deceit?” He gave the duke this advice: the duke should remain there with the army and continue to display himself to the enemy, while Roger proceeded with one hundred and fifty soldiers as far as Reggio, brought ships from there to himself under cover of night, crossed the sea without the enemy’s knowledge, and invaded Sicily.

The duke refused, fearing the loss of his brother, and said that he did not wish to gain anything through his brother’s death, but preferred his brother’s life to every advantage. Nevertheless, after sending the ships ahead to Reggio, Count Roger followed with three hundred soldiers. As always presumptuous in warfare and an undertaker of great ventures, he crossed the sea heedless of the enemy—[Note: [Col. 1126D] “heedless enemies”—] and landed at a place commonly called the Monastery.  
[Note: [Col. 1126D] Another reading: “of the Three.”]

He sent the ships away so that none of his men might flee to them, and advanced to attack Messina. Finding it undefended—for he had killed its defenders long before—he captured the city and demolished its towers and fortifications. Those whom they found were killed; some others fled to the ships of the people of Palermo. This occurred in the year 1060 from the Lord’s Incarnation.

## CHAPTER XI. A certain Saracen killed his sister when she faltered in flight

[Col. 1126C]

Among those fleeing was a certain young man from one of the more noble citizens of Messina. He had an exceptionally beautiful sister and was trying to take her with him as he fled. But the girl, being a delicate young maiden of weak constitution, unaccustomed to exertion, began to falter from fear and the unfamiliar speed of the flight.

Her brother encouraged her most tenderly with words, but when this produced no result and he saw that her strength was exhausted, he attacked and killed her with his sword, lest she remain among the Normans and be violated by one of them. Although he was drenched in tears because of the sweetness of his affection for his sister—for she was his only sister—he preferred to become his sister’s killer and mourn her dead rather than allow his sister to become a transgressor of her law and be ravished by someone who did not observe that law.

## CHAPTER XII. The people of Palermo, recognizing that they had been outwitted, withdraw; the duke crosses freely

[Col. 1126D]

After the city had been captured, the people of Palermo realized that they had been outwitted by the enemy. Fearing that the sea might again become rough if they remained there longer, forcing them to land and exposing them to oppression by the enemy, they withdrew in confusion, turning their sails back toward the place from which they had come.

Count Roger sent the keys of the captured city to the duke, instructing him to hasten to him by sailing safely. Thus, when the sea had been cleared of the enemy and the passage lay open without danger, the duke crossed with the entire army at a favorable speed and came to Messina. Finding his brother safe, they rejoiced greatly.

## CHAPTER XIII. The duke and count arrange Messina according to their will and go to besiege Rametta

After wisely arranging their affairs for eight days and securing the city according to their will with various guards, they left the cavalry army at Messina and both brothers turned toward Rametta.

The people of Rametta had already learned that a very large multitude of Messinan warriors had fallen before their small force. Fearing that something similar might happen to them, they were terrified when the enemy approached. They sent envoys to seek peace, surrendered the city and themselves to the brothers’ authority, and, with books of their superstitious law placed before them, confirmed their fidelity by oath.

## CHAPTER XIV. The Christians of the Demenna Valley offer gifts to the count and duke

They then withdrew with the greatest joy over their success. Having learned the weakness of the enemy people, they became bolder and lodged beneath Scabatripoli. The next day they reached Fraxini, and from Fraxini they proceeded to the meadow of Maniaci.

Here the Christians living in the Demenna Valley were tributaries under the Saracens. Rejoicing at the arrival of the Christians, they went out to meet them and offered many gifts and presents. They adopted this as their excuse before the Saracens: they did not do this out of love, but in order to protect themselves and what belonged to them. They promised that they would preserve their loyalty to the brothers inviolate.

The brothers, for their part, received them with the greatest warmth and promised to bestow many benefits upon them if God granted them the land. They then dismissed them in peace and proceeded as far as Centuripe.

## CHAPTER XV. The duke and count attack Centuripe

Although the people of Centuripe were not unaware of the brothers’ valor, they did not shrink from death. Since they were unwilling in any way to submit, they armed the defenses of the city and themselves.

Our men attacked the city courageously. But when they saw that their own forces were being harassed by slingers and archers and that they could make no progress toward the city without suffering losses, they abandoned the assault—especially since they heard that a battle with the Saracens was about to take place. They reserved their men for that battle, lest they be harassed or reduced in number.

## CHAPTER XVI. Our men make camp on the plain of Paternò beside the river Gùedeta

After leaving Centuripe, they made camp on the plain of Paternò and set up their tents. Seeing the spacious plain and judging it a suitable place for battle, they remained there for eight days, wishing the Saracens to offer them a battle arranged in that place.

But when they learned from Becumen’s scouts—for Becumen had defected to the count at Reggio and accompanied them as a faithful companion and guide—that a battle was not yet ready, they advanced farther inland and lodged at Saint Felix beside underground caves. They captured most of these caves by assault, killing many of their inhabitants.

From there they advanced to the mills before the castle of John, on the bank of the river called Guedeta in the language of the people there, which in Latin is interpreted as “river of the marsh.” There they made camp.

## CHAPTER XVII. Our men engage in battle with the Saracens

Bechamet gathered together a large multitude of Africans and Sicilians and offered the enemy the battle he had long been preparing, in the year 1061 from the Lord’s Incarnation.

The duke divided his army into two parts, for there were only seven hundred men in all. He organized two battle lines and assigned one to his brother, as was his custom, so that Roger might strike the enemy first. He himself followed with the other, exhorting his men vigorously with words.

Similarly, Bechamet, who had fifteen thousand armed men, organized three battle lines. With these he first approached the enemy with the utmost boldness and entered into battle. Our men, fighting bravely in the first encounter as was their custom, overthrew many and put the rest to flight. Pursuing them while cutting them down, they killed as many as ten thousand as far as the Castle of John.  
[Col. 1128C]

Thus they gained the victory, and some were enriched with such abundant spoils that a man who had lost one horse in the battle, receiving ten in return, would not hesitate to enter a similar army for comparable profit.

The next day they advanced nearer to the castle and lodged for one night beside the lake between the Castle of John and Irancuum.  
[Note: [Col. 1127D] Another reading: “Naurcium.”]

On the following day they set up their tents on the mountain called Calataxibet. But because the mountain was too confined and insufficient for the army’s lodging, they moved to the plain of the Springs.

Count Roger, unable to tolerate rest and constant in labor, took three hundred young men with him and went as far as Agrigentum to plunder and inspect the land, devastating the entire province by setting it ablaze. When he returned, he filled the entire army abundantly with spoils and booty.

They remained there for a month, afflicting and ravaging the whole province with various raids, but they were unable to prevail against the Castle of John. In that same year the duke built the Castle of Mark.

## CHAPTER XVIII. Because winter is approaching, the expedition is dissolved, and the Christians surrender Traina

Foreseeing the approach of winter, they dissolved the expedition. They left Becumen at Catana in his allegiance—and in possession of his own jurisdiction—to harass Sicily in the meantime. They fortified Messina with soldiers to guard it and with whatever the soldiers would need. After crossing the Strait, the duke withdrew to Apulia to spend the winter, while the count remained in Calabria.

In midwinter, within the season of Christ’s Nativity, Count Roger again crossed the sea with two hundred and fifty soldiers and went to plunder as far as the city of Agrigentum, harassing the whole country. The Christians of the provinces came to meet him with the greatest joy and assisted him in many ways.

From there he reached Traina. He was welcomed with joy by the Christian citizens who lived there, entered the city, arranged matters according to his will, and celebrated Christmas there.  
[Note: [Col. 1129D] Another reading: “he celebrated.”]

## CHAPTER XIX. Count Roger takes a wife

[Col. 1129B]

A certain envoy came from Calabria and announced that Abbot Robert of Saint Euphemia had sent word to Count Roger concerning Delicia, his sister, a niece of the Norman counts brought from Normandy [the supplied text is corrupt], that he should hasten to celebrate the marriage.  
[Notes: [Col. 1129D] “In the aforesaid.” “Brought to the count.”]

The count was greatly delighted when he heard this. He had desired her for a long time, for she was beautiful and of distinguished birth. As quickly as he could, he returned toward Calabria and hastened to see the young woman whom he had long desired. Coming to the Valley of the Salines, or “of the Saltworks,” at Saint Martin, he lawfully betrothed the girl, led her to Melito amid the greatest musical celebration, and held the solemn wedding there.  
[Note: [Col. 1129D] Another reading: “Valley of the Salmarines.”]

## CHAPTER XX. After celebrating the wedding, Count Roger goes to Sicily

[Col. 1129C]

After the marriage had been completed, he stayed with his wife for some time, but he could not forget what he had set his mind upon. He prepared an army and took the squire Roger with him. Leaving the young woman in Calabria, he again invaded Sicily, detained by no entreaties from his weeping wife.

He summoned the Saracen Becumen from Catana through an envoy and took him with him. Then he advanced to besiege Petralia. The citizens, partly Christian and partly Saracen, took counsel among themselves, made peace with the count, and surrendered the castle and themselves to his authority.

The count fortified the castle according to his will, supplied it with soldiers and paid troops, and came to Traina. There he likewise strengthened the city and urged Becumen to go and harass Sicily, applying himself to the count’s advantage. He then presented himself in Calabria to his wife, who longed for him and was anxious for his safety, and made her exceedingly happy by his arrival.

## CHAPTER XXI. The count withdraws from the duke in anger

Count Roger possessed no castle in his own territory outside his brother’s power except Melito. He therefore asked his brother to grant him what had been promised when the two had been reconciled at Scalea after the brother had invited him there—namely, half of all Calabria. He especially wished to provide a suitable dowry for his young wife, who was still a girl and had been born of such distinguished lineage.

Although the duke was generous with money, he was somewhat sparing in distributing lands, and he kept putting off his brother by evasions. When the count realized his brother’s craftiness, he could no longer tolerate being delayed by deceptions. He sent to the leading men throughout Apulia, presenting the matter for judgment and seeking what had been promised him.  
[Notes: [Col. 1129D] “Sending to them, and so forth.” “And when.”]

When this too produced no result, he broke the pact between them and withdrew from his brother in anger. He came to Melito and vigorously fortified the castle, bringing in the best soldiers he could find from every quarter to the detriment of his brother.  
[Notes: [Col. 1130D] “The best as well.” “Recruiting.”]

Although it was plainly unjust for his brother to act against him, he nevertheless preserved his legality and refrained from harming his brother for forty days. He did this lest, if his brother reconsidered his conduct toward him within that period, he—the one who had complained of injury—should instead be judged to have been the injuring party.  
[Note: [Col. 1130D] Another reading: “should be declared.”]

He preferred that the wrongful blame for this disagreement be turned upon his brother rather than upon himself.  
[Note: [Col. 1130D] “Unjust.”]

## CHAPTER XXII. Becumen is killed in Sicily

Becumen traveled through Sicily, and, as the count had asked, brought as many people as he could into allegiance to our people. Those whom he could persuade less readily, he did not cease to harass with attacks.

When he was hastening to attack the castle of Antulium, formerly his own, a certain Nichel, once a soldier of that same Becumen and more powerful than the others, deceitfully sent peaceful words. He instructed Becumen to come with only a few men, separated from his own forces, to a designated place, as though the people of Antulium wished to be reconciled with him.

Because Becumen had previously bestowed many benefits upon them when they were on good terms with him, he suspected little fraud and did not delay in coming as he had been instructed. The people of Antulium, having discovered the plan conceived by Nichel with his poisonous heart, first pierced Becumen’s horse with a spear, lest its rider, if he were wounded first, should detect the treachery and escape more freely on the unharmed horse while wounded.

After throwing down the horse, they also stabbed Becumen on the ground and made him breathe out his final breath of life in his blood.

When the Normans heard this—the men whom the count had stationed at the castles of Traina and Petralia—they were greatly troubled, for they had guarded those strongholds especially under Becumen’s authority. Abandoning the castles, they went to Messina to defend it.

## CHAPTER XXIII. The duke goes to besiege his brother the count at Melito

The duke, angered that his brother had withdrawn from him, gathered an army and went to besiege him at Melito, in the year 1062 from the Lord’s Incarnation.

Although at that time the count was suffering from a fever—for he had been at Gerace, called there by certain affairs, and had himself fallen ill there because of the unfamiliar and corrupted air, losing some of his men—he nevertheless met his approaching brother as an enemy with the greatest ferocity on the mountain called Saint Angelo.

After overthrowing many men from his brother’s line with the strength of his spear in military combat, he drove them back by an attack, lest they establish a castle on that mountain, or at least on the neighboring mountain called Green Mountain, as they had planned.

Once the city had been besieged, ambition for glory and youthful age impelled many on both sides to practice warfare. Thus, while many advanced in military fashion, a certain young man named Arnold, from the count’s side—his son-in-law, for he was the brother of the young countess—who was well suited to military exercises, was himself overthrown and killed while attempting to bring down another. It is painful to say.

As a result, immense grief and lamentation arose, not only among those whom he had assisted, but even among those who were attacking from outside. While his sister celebrated the funeral rites with much mourning and carried out the burial as was fitting, the count, who grieved no less than the sister, burned for vengeance. He attacked the enemy, overthrew many in military combat, and killed them.

The duke, seeing that his men were harassed daily by such engagements and were making little progress, fortified two castles before the city, thinking that in this way he could more easily wear down the besieged with weariness and hunger.

But the count harassed those castles every day. When he knew that the duke was in one of them, he attacked the other; when he saw that the duke was coming to its aid, he abandoned it and crossed through the middle of the city to the other. Thus he continually alternated the fighting from one position to another.

## CHAPTER XXIV. The count captures Gerace by treachery, and the duke is captured at Gerace
One night, then, Melitus set out with one hundred soldiers and came to Geracium. Entering the city, which the inhabitants had handed over to him, he fitted it out for his own use. When the duke heard this, filled with the greatest anger, he strengthened the castles that he had established before Melitus with soldiers and, with his entire army, pitched his tents outside the city toward Geracium. [Col. 1131D]

The people of Geracium had indeed sworn allegiance to him long before; nevertheless, they had not surrendered the city for him to use at his pleasure, lest, if he should establish a castle within it, he might completely subjugate them all according to his will. The duke, however, knew a certain prominent man of the city named Basilius. Invited by him to dinner, the duke entered the city with his hood covering his head so that no one might recognize who he was, and went alone to his host’s palace to eat. Once inside, while suspecting no evil and, before the food had been prepared, conversing with the wife of the man who had invited him, the townspeople learned through one of the household servants that the duke was within the city. Suspecting treachery, they were thrown into no small disturbance.

The whole city was thrown into an uproar as people rushed together from every side. All ran to arms and went with furious force to the house where he was, intending to drag him out. The man who had invited the duke, recognizing the impiety of his fellow citizens but lacking the strength to restore him, tried to save his own life by fleeing toward the church; but he was pierced by the sword of his native land and fell dead. His wife too was treated with such great brutality by her fellow citizens that, pierced through to the entrails with a stake, she was compelled to end her life in a dishonorable death.

When he saw this, it is not surprising if the duke despaired of his life, especially since he saw a citizen being killed by citizens, a friend by friends, and rulers by their subjects with a savage sword and such fury, without any remembrance of an earlier kindness. An unarmed soldier stood amid the threatening weapons of raging enemies—formerly the conqueror of many thousands of foes—transferring the leonine ferocity that was in some way innate in him into the gentleness of a lamb. But when he saw that the wiser men, who foresaw the outcome of the affair, were urging that the disordered fury of the ignorant crowd, which had little foresight regarding what harm or gain would result if he were killed, should be restrained, he recovered some courage and began to address them in these words:

“Do not, do not let yourselves be deceitfully lifted up by excessive joy, lest fortune, now smiling upon you but hostile to me, by that very smile give you a sign of the adversity that you will have to endure in the future, since no power is assigned to anyone without divine disposition. Consider by what judgment you have been granted power over me, and refer it among yourselves. For I have not been brought here by your strength; nor did I enter in order to contrive any evil against you. You made your oath of allegiance to me, and I know that I have in no way violated the agreement that I promised you. Perhaps this has happened for your benefit or instruction, so that your allegiance—whose stability we have come to know—may present you to us as more deserving of favor and reward.

“To seize one man by chance, not by military means, after breaking a treaty and lying, and to take his life without resistance, is no cause for praise. Nor, as I think, will you gain anything useful from me. My death will not remove the yoke of my people; rather, they will blaze up more fiercely against you in revenge for me. I have very loyal soldiers, brothers, and kinsmen, whom no consideration will be able to reconcile if, by perjury, you stain your hands with my blood. Wherever on earth what you have done is proclaimed, you will incur everlasting disgrace, because of your perjury, together with all the succession of your race—especially if, without investigation, I should suffer any wrong at your hands.”

At these words, the wiser men of the city showing him favor, the ignoble crowd, its tumult quieted, placed the duke in captivity until they could take counsel about what should be done with him.

## CHAPTER XXV. The duke’s soldiers invite the count to come to his brother’s aid.

[Col. 1133A]

The duke’s army, which had pitched its tents outside the gate, heard that the duke [Note: “duke”] had been thrust into captivity [Note: “captivity”] in such misfortune. Greatly disturbed on every side, they debated among themselves, uncertain what should be done. At last, after accepting the better counsel, they hurried by messengers to inform the count of what had happened. [Note: “To inform the brother of what had happened to the duke.”]

They knew the uprightness of his character. Although, in seeking some dispute with his brother, he displayed his contention against him, nevertheless, when he considered their blood relationship, he would love his brother as a brother and, forgetting every injury inflicted upon him, would prefer rescuing his brother’s life, placed in such danger, to any profit. [Note: “With.”] They therefore invite the brother to come to the aid of his brother in distress. Once the duke had been rescued, they promise that they themselves will provide assistance and that the dispute between the two brothers would be settled according to law. [Notes: “He invites”; “distress”; “they will provide.”]

## CHAPTER XXVI. The count besieges Geracium and frees the duke from captivity.

The count, disturbed by the evil report of his brother’s misfortune and wholly overcome with tears by affection for his brother’s blood, humbly entreated his men to hasten with him to rescue his brother. Seizing his weapons, he flew as swiftly as possible to Geracium. He invited the townspeople to come outside the walls and speak with him under the protection of a treaty, and addressed them as follows:

“Come,” he said—[Note: “Also: ‘Come, then.’”]—“my friends and faithful men. You have learned that my enemy and kinsman, who came to besiege me, has been captured, and you hold him in allegiance to me.” [Note: C. P.: “Behold, I begin to test your allegiance, and because you hold my brother besieged for me,” etc.; “my”; “in my allegiance,” etc.] [Note: “Behold, I am beginning to test your allegiance, and because you have besieged my brother for me,” etc.; “my”; “in my allegiance,” etc.]

“Since your allegiance has advanced so far against me, I wish to take revenge upon him by your counsel, but not by your hands or weapons. He has provoked me to such anger that it is not enough for me that he should die by any weapons other than my own. Therefore, lest your allegiance, thinking that it is rendering me a welcome service, should do this, know that it is utterly forbidden to you.

“Hasten, then, by handing my enemy over to me. For the present it will be enough that you learn about his punishments. Satisfied with your counsel, I shall make him end his life amid tortures. Let there be no delay in handing him over; for no consideration will draw me away from the siege of this city until I avenge the injuries that he has inflicted upon me.

“Behold, his entire army, no longer enduring his injuries, has rejected him, transferred its allegiance to me, and chosen me as its duke. Behold, I was judged unworthy to possess even a little land under him; once he is dead, with fortune favoring me, I shall receive all that has hitherto belonged to his jurisdiction.

“I am not someone whom you can prolong matters against by evasions. If you attempt to delay any longer, behold, your vineyards and olive groves will presently be uprooted. Once your city has been besieged by us and our engines have been prepared, no defenses will protect you against us. If you are captured unwillingly, the punishments promised to an enemy will likewise be promised to you.”
