After this speech, the people of Geracium, terrified, obtained permission to return to the city, report these things to their fellow citizens, and take counsel together. After taking counsel, they were uncertain whether the words they had heard from the count had been spoken deliberately, so that he might rescue his brother, or from genuine hatred. They therefore demanded an oath from the duke that, if he were released by them and escaped his brother’s threats, he would not, as long as he lived, cause any castle to be established within their city.

Because they failed to perceive the duke’s cunning, they were deceived by that oath. For what the duke swore he would not build, the count—without swearing—completed not long afterward, to their grief. After receiving the oath, they led the duke outside the city and returned him to the count, while many of the Normans wept for joy. They promised, with many assurances, that from then on they would be faithful to both brothers.

## CHAPTER XXVII. The count’s soldiers destroy the castle that the duke had established at Melitus. The duchess flees to Tropea.

The duke and the count looked upon one another. As once Joseph and Benjamin did, when what had seemed harsh unexpectedly turned toward prosperity, they burst into tears and enjoyed mutual embraces. The duke promised the count that from then on he would not withhold what he had promised him. The count escorted the duke as far as Saint Martin, then went from there to Melitus.

The count’s soldiers who were at Melitus, having heard that the duke was being held captive, attacked and captured his castles that he had established before Melitus. They kept captive the soldiers whom they found there and strengthened, with their own soldiers, the castle that he had established at Saint Angelo; but they demolished the other, which appeared more vulnerable. The duke’s wife, suspecting that she would be widowed, fled to Tropea.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. The duke divides Calabria with the count.

When the duke heard this, remembering the wrong rather than the favor, he was moved by the greatest indignation and refused to carry out the agreement that he had promised his brother, until both the castle of Saint Angelo and the soldiers who were being held captive were restored to him and the injury inflicted upon him was addressed according to law. The count, wishing to remove every opportunity for his brother to carry out his will, returned the soldiers and restored the castle and everything that had been held within it.

But when he saw that even this did not soften his brother’s disposition so that he would grant him justice, he entered the castle of Messianum after its inhabitants had handed it over and declared his hostility to the duke. The duke, seeing that the castles that he had possessed before Melitus [Col. 1135A] in that province had been taken from him—[Note: “The better castle that he possessed in that province had been taken from him,” etc.]—and knowing that all Calabria could easily be thrown into turmoil through them, divided Calabria with his brother in the valley of Gratensis, after summoning his brother to himself and fulfilling the agreement with him. [Note: “Summoning his brother to the bridge, where Guiscard, having at last fulfilled the agreement with him, [divided] Calabria,” etc.] He then went into Apulia.

The count returned to receive his share of Calabria. But when he saw that his men throughout Calabria were poorly supplied with horses, clothing, and weapons because of the sedition that had hitherto existed between himself and his brother, he went to demand tribute from them. On reaching Geracium, he regarded them as almost more disloyal and therefore more hateful than the others. To extort more from them, he pitched his camp far outside the city.

When the people of Geracium cited the oath that the duke had sworn to them, the count replied: “Since half of Geracium is mine, the duke can preserve the terms of his oath in his own portion, so that it is not violated. But I, who may do whatever I wish in my portion, am bound by neither oath nor promise.” The people of Geracium, realizing that the duke had cunningly deceived them through the oath, attributed the matter to their own folly. After making an agreement with the count, they turned him away from the castle that they had acquired through the treaty by means of money rather than arms.

## CHAPTER XXIX. The Greeks at Traina plot a deception against the count.

The count, generously rewarding his men with weapons, horses, and everything else that was necessary, and prudently arranging the land that had fallen to him among his faithful followers, again attacked Sicily with three hundred men to wage war. He took with him his young wife, although he heard that she was unwilling. [Note: “Fearful, and to some extent …”]

When he came to Traina, the Christian Greeks who had received him there once before welcomed him again, though not with as much eagerness as previously. He strengthened the city, adapting it to his purpose, although the nature of the mountain on which it lies made it sufficiently defensible. Leaving his wife there with a few men, he went around attacking the neighboring castles.

The Greeks, always that most treacherous race, were offended by nothing except that the count’s soldiers were lodging in their houses. Fearing for their wives and daughters, one day, while the count was staying at Nicosinum for the purpose of attacking it, they saw that only a few men had remained with the countess. Suspecting that they could easily prevail against them and thus shake off their yoke by driving them from the city or killing them, they began to attack.

But our men, although few, were nevertheless most ready in spirit and arms. Once they recognized the deception, they swiftly rushed to arms and, defending their lady and themselves vigorously, resisted with the utmost force until night separated the combatants. The count learned through a messenger what had happened and flew back with all speed. The Greeks had already cut the city in half between themselves and the Normans and had made a kind of fortification for their defense. He attacked them, but for the moment with little success. [Col. 1136A]

At last, five thousand more energetic Saracens from the neighboring castles, hearing that the Greeks were at odds with our men, rejoiced greatly and had already gone to them to offer assistance. With their support the Greeks were strongly defended. For as they were detained by continual attacks—first attacking and then defending themselves—and were prevented from seeking food by plundering in different places, as they had been accustomed to do, they were greatly weakened by hunger, by the heat of unceasing battle, and by vigils, all of which were quite incompatible with one another.

Everyone was so occupied with his own concerns that even the count himself scarcely had anyone to prepare food for him except his wife and armor-bearers. While they were detained within the city by continual defense so that they could not go out to plunder, outside, everyone’s eyes were fixed on the danger that, if he attempted to rob with only a few men, he would be discovered. The threat of either course deterred him.

Consequently, such poverty prevailed among them that they could neither seize anything nor obtain it from one another by favor or receive it through mutual exchange, since almost everyone, from the count himself to the humblest retainer, was equally in need. They also suffered such a shortage of clothing that the count and countess possessed only one cloak between them, which they used in turn according as the greater necessity fell upon either.

The Greeks and Saracens, however, for whom the whole countryside lay open at will and favored them, were filled with abundant supplies. They did not need to wander anywhere in search of food, since all Sicily voluntarily supplied them with whatever was necessary, eagerly bringing it to them.

Our men, although afflicted by such poverty, and groaning among themselves under the heat of hunger, labor, and vigils, concealed their weakness from one another so that they would not discourage each other. They tried to feign a certain cheerfulness in face and speech. But the young countess could quench her thirst with water; her hunger, however, having nothing else with which to restrain it, she knew how to curb only with tears and sleep.

Although food did not sustain the unceasing combat [Note: “As regards food, which was not food”], the enemy’s attacks prevented it from ceasing. Sometimes, lest they be scorned by the enemy if they rushed to arms only when attacked—[Note: “They would be seized if they did not rush to arms when attacked”]—the ferocity innate in their spirits represented their strength even to those who wished, with keen intelligence, to conceal it. [Note: “To those unwilling.”]

## CHAPTER XXX. The count is captured by the Saracens and frees himself with his sword.

[Col. 1136D]

One day, then, when battle had begun, the count, mounted on his horse, placed himself among the enemy in order to aid his men. When the enemy recognized him, they attacked him with greater force, pierced his horse with spears, and, throwing both horse and rider to the ground, seized him with their hands. They tried to drag him, like a resisting bull to the sacrifice, to a safer place where he could be punished. [Col. 1137A]

The count, placed in such danger and not forgetful of his former deeds—[Note: “Not forgetful of his claims”]—sought to draw the sword with which he was girded [Note: “Wielding it”]. Waving it vigorously in every direction, like a sickle cutting down a green meadow, he killed many and, with his right hand alone and God’s help, freed himself. He inflicted such slaughter upon the enemy that, just as fallen trees lie scattered by the wind in dense forests, so the corpses of the enemies whom he had killed lay all around him.

The surviving enemies withdrew into their fortification. Having lost his horse, the count carried away its saddle, so that he would not appear to be hurrying like a frightened man, and returned on foot toward his own men.

Our men had now been placed in such a difficult situation for four months. The harshest winter that had occurred in those regions that year became an opportunity for their liberation but a source of ruin for the enemy. Near the city of Aetna, which lies not far away in the same province, the city is accustomed at certain times to suffer the fiercest heat from the burning eruption of the sulphurous mountain; at other times it suffers the harshest inundation of storms, tempests, snow, and hail.

Therefore the enemy, accustomed to the heat of baths, began, when colder air blew, to grow slower in the watches and guard-duty of the city. They tried to kindle their natural warmth within themselves by drinking wine, and, as usually happens, sleep followed the wine. When our men discovered this, they too deliberately began to appear slower. Although they kept the most attentive watch, they suppressed their shouting and pretended that they were not keeping watch, so as deceitfully to make the enemy feel more secure.

One night, therefore, when the count, as always tireless in every labor, was renewing the night watches with his armed men beneath the freezing winter sky, while they were most carefully intent upon their own interests [Note: “He was attentively conducting the watch”], and had discovered that the enemy, weighed down by sleep within their fortifications [Note: “Among”], had no one among so great a multitude keeping watch, he silently broke into their camp [Note: “Their castle”]. Seizing the unsuspecting enemy with his armed force [Note: “And thus, with armed force”], he killed many and captured the fortification. More were taken prisoner; the rest sought refuge in flight.

Porinus [Note: C. P.: “Polorinus”], who had been the chief author of the treachery, was hanged with those who had principally supported him, as an example to the others, and deprived of life. Many others were subjected to various punishments.

After taking the spoils in triumphal fashion, our men, who had hitherto been in want, were filled with such an abundance of grain, wine, oil, and other necessities that they could rightly recall, by analogy, what Elisha said when God suddenly and unexpectedly granted abundance at Samaria: “Tomorrow at this hour a measure of fine flour will be one shekel at the gate of Samaria” (2 Kings 7:1), although on the preceding day none could be found at any price, however great.

## CHAPTER XXXI. The count goes to Calabria.

[Col. 1138A]

Having arranged his affairs and strengthened the city more securely according to his will, the count went toward Calabria and Apulia to acquire horses for his men to replace those they had lost. Leaving his wife and soldiers at Traina, he departed. Although she was young, his wife began to show such energetic concern for defending the castle that she went around it daily and, wherever she saw improvements needed, took care that watches should be kept. Speaking kindly to all the others whom her husband had left behind when he departed, she urged them to provide carefully for whatever had to be guarded, promising them many rewards upon her husband’s return. She also recalled the danger they had already endured, so that by acting negligently they would not fall into something similar.

## CHAPTER XXXII. The count battles the Arabs at the Castle of John.

[Col. 1138B]

The count returned from Calabria and Apulia laden, like a most industrious bee, with the things necessary for his soldiers, and gladdened all his men by his arrival, distributing among them horses and everything else they needed.

After allowing the horses that he had brought to recover for several days from the labor of the journey, he learned that Arabs and Africans who had come from Arabia and Africa—as though to bring assistance to the Sicilians, but in fact to seek profit—were staying at the Castle of John, numbering as many as five hundred. Wishing to test the valor of their army, he directed his forces there.

He sent ahead his nephew Serlo with thirty soldiers, so that by showing themselves before the castle they might provoke the enemy to come out and fight. He himself hid with the rest in ambush at a certain place, intending that when the enemy vigorously pursued his men, who would deliberately pretend to flee out of fear, he might suddenly burst from the ambush and more easily seize the enemy, who would have been drawn far from the castle.

When the Arabs who were in the castle saw the approaching force from a distance, they rushed out to meet them with the greatest violence. They pursued the fugitives and, overtaking them, slaughtered them so completely that only two of our men reached the place of ambush unharmed.

When the count saw that some of the men he had sent ahead had been captured and others thrown down, he burst from the ambush with leonine force, met the enemy, and began the battle. The two sides fought vigorously against one another. After a long and fierce struggle, however, with God favorable to him, the count became victorious when the pagans fled. He pursued the last of the enemy for more than a mile, killing them. Laden with spoils, he returned joyfully to Traina, and the city was filled with rejoicing.

Wishing to harass the Sicilians everywhere, he went to Calatabutor to plunder [Note: C. P.: “Calatabaturum”]. Returning from there toward the Rocks of the Castle of John, he attempted, in case he might draw the Arabs out of the castle, and brought back very great booty.

Then, wishing to become acquainted with the deeper regions of Sicily, he advanced farther and came as far as Buterum [Note: “Buterium”]. There he took a considerable amount of livestock and brought back many captives with him, lodging at Avator [Note: “Anattor”]. The next day, because he had lost several horses through the length of the journey, the excessive heat, and the lack of water, he spent the night at Saint Felix and from there came to Traina.

## CHAPTER XXXIII. The battle of Cerami, where Saint George appeared.

The Africans and Arabs, having gathered with a very large army together with the Sicilians in order to make war upon the count, were reported to be approaching in the year of the Incarnation of the Word 1063. The count went eagerly to meet them with his men and climbed to the summit of the mountain above the river Cerami so that he might observe them more fully.

He saw them across the river on the ridge of another mountain. After looking at one another for a long time, alternately, and neither side crossing toward the other, the Saracens moved first and returned to their camp, where they had been staying. The count, for his part, returned to Traina. For three days they looked at one another across the intervening river, and neither side dared cross toward the other.

On the fourth day the Saracens moved their camp and encamped on the mountain where they had displayed themselves for three days, lest they should appear to be retreating backward. Our men, unwilling to endure any longer the proximity of the enemy, confessed themselves to God with great devotion in the presence of priests, accepted penance, commended themselves to God’s mercy, and, trusting in his aid, went to bring battle to the enemy.

But when, halfway there, they received news that Cerami was being attacked by the enemy, the count directed his forces there. He left his nephew Serlo with thirty soldiers to enter the castle and, by defending it until the count arrived, hold it. The count himself followed with one hundred soldiers, for he had no more.

Serlo entered the castle but did not wait for the arrival of his uncle, who was following. Instead, like a raging lion, he burst through the gates against the enemy and inflicted great slaughter. Although the enemy numbered thirty thousand, apart from the infantry, whose multitude was without number, Serlo—who had only thirty-six soldiers—turned them all to flight. This accomplished, we can clearly recognize that God was a supporter of our men. Human strength could neither have dared nor, much less, accomplished so great and unprecedented a deed in our times.

If, then, with the prophet we wonder how “one pursued a thousand”—for we recognize that this happened to these men as once to the children of Israel—we can certainly answer ourselves, without falsehood, in the prophet’s words: “Because their God avenges them, and the Lord had shut them up in the depth of their iniquities, with the nail of his anger.” I say “their God,” not because they knew him by worshiping him, but because, although unworthy and ungrateful to their Maker, they were nevertheless his creatures.

I say “their God,” moreover, in accordance with what we are taught by the Apostle, where he says: “For the same God is Lord of all, rich toward all who call upon him.” If anyone should try, by dialectical reasoning, to make this statement contradictory, saying, “If God is rich toward those who call upon him, it follows that he is poor toward those who do not call upon him,” the answer must be that the Godhead itself suffers neither increase nor diminution and does not admit of more or less in its nature, but, always remaining in the same state, is equally able to do all things.

If we are forced to call him poor, this is not in relation to himself, but in relation to those who show themselves unworthy to receive from God the riches of his mercy.

The count followed his nephew with one hundred soldiers and came to Cerami. Learning that the enemy had been defeated by his nephew, he was considering whether to pursue them and defeat them more completely. Some men, however, urged him not to do so, saying that the victory granted by God through his nephew was sufficient, lest by pursuing farther, Fortune’s wheel should turn and the outcome become worse.

Then Ursellus of Baliol [Note: C. P.: “rebuking”] threatened the count that he would never bring him aid either there or elsewhere unless he engaged the enemy in battle. When the count heard this, he angrily heaped many insults upon those who were trying to dissuade him, and immediately went to offer battle to the enemy, toward their camp, for they had fled there.

The enemy, having recovered their strength, hastened to meet our men boldly, forming two battle lines. The count likewise formed two wedges from his own forces. He assigned one to his nephew, Ursellus, and Arisgotus of Pozzuoli, so that they might strike first as the advance force. He followed with the other, going into battle while invoking God as his helper.

The enemy’s first line avoided Serlo and our first line, wishing to seize the mountain above our men, and encountered our final line, which the count was leading. When the count and Ursellus of Baliol [Note: “Ballionis”] saw their men, as was usual, more fearful because of the great multitude of enemies whom they were confronting [Note: “Were dreading”], they tried to drive fear from them with such exhortations:

“Rouse your courage, O most valiant recruits of the Christian army. We have all been marked with the name of Christ, who will not abandon his seal unless offended. Our God, the God of gods, is almighty. Everyone who distrusts God, trusts in man and makes flesh his arm. All the kingdoms of the world belong to our God, and he will grant them to whomever he wishes.

“This people is rebellious against God, and strength that is not ruled by God is quickly exhausted [Note: “Will be exhausted sooner”]. They glory in their own power, but we are secure in God’s protection. For it is not honorable to doubt that those whom God precedes cannot stand before us. Because Gideon did not doubt God’s aid, he struck down many thousands of enemies with a few men.”

As these words were being spoken while they hastened toward the battle, a certain splendid knight appeared in armor, mounted on a white horse. A white banner was tied to the top of his lance, and above it was a shining cross. As though advancing from our line to make our men more ready for battle, he burst with the greatest force into the enemy where they were most densely packed.

When our men saw him, they became more cheerful. Repeatedly invoking God and Saint George, and moved to tears by joy at so great a vision, they followed him most eagerly as he went before them. Many also saw a banner containing a cross hanging from the top of the count’s lance, placed there by no one except through divine agency.

The count exhorted the foremost men of his line. Arcadius of Palermo, who was advancing most eagerly before our line while reproaching it, was armed with a shining *clamucium*, which we use in place of a cuirass. When battle began, the count engaged him with great force, struck him down by the strength of his lance, and killed him, putting fear into the others.

Arcadius had been the most distinguished warrior among his people, and they believed that no one could resist him by arms. The *clamucium* with which he was clothed could not be pierced by any weapon except by striking from below upward between the two iron pieces joined by chains; it could be damaged more by craft than by force. [Notes: “Claviculus”; “by one”; “and chained”; “overcome by force.”]

As the two sides fought fiercely, our men, because of their small number, were so hemmed in amid the multitude that surrounded them that scarcely any of them could break through except by making a disturbance with their weapons. Seeing our men cut down the dense ranks of the enemies surrounding them, as a furious wind disperses a dense mass of clouds, and as the swiftest hawks strike down a weakened, scattered flock of birds, [Note: “Seeing such a density of pagan and Sicilian enemies existing together and surrounding them,” etc.]

After the battle had raged for a long time, the enemy could no longer endure the assault of our men and tried to save themselves by flight rather than by arms. Our men pursued boldly and killed all whom they caught at the rear. Thus they became victorious, and as many as fifteen thousand of the enemy fell.

Our men, laden with the spoils of triumph, returned as far as the enemy camp and lodged in their tents, claiming the camels and everything else they found as their own. The next day they attacked the infantry, numbering about twenty thousand, who had fled and occupied the cliffs and steep places of the mountain. They killed most of them, while they sold the rest after defeating them and received an immense sum of money.

After remaining there for some time, they were burdened by the stench of the rotting corpses of the slain enemy. Abhorring the stench, they returned to Traina.

The count, recognizing that he had obtained so great a victory through God and Saint Peter’s patronage, was not ungrateful for the benefit bestowed upon him. As a testimony to his victory, he sent through one of his men, named Meledius, four camels—which he had received among the other spoils after triumphing over the enemy—to Pope Alexander, who at that time was wisely and catholically exercising at Rome the office of blessed Peter.

The Apostolicus rejoiced more over the victory granted by God over the pagans than over the gifts sent to him. By apostolic blessing and the authority he exercised, he granted the count and all who would assist in gaining Sicily from the pagans and permanently retaining the land gained for the faith of Christ an absolution from their offenses, provided that they repented and guarded against them in the future. He also sent a banner marked with the authority of the Apostolic See at Rome, so that, trusting in the protection of blessed Peter as their reward, they might rise up more securely to wage war against the Saracens.

## CHAPTER XXXIV. The Pisans invite the count to go and besiege Palermo.

[Col. 1142B]

Therefore the Pisan merchants, who were accustomed to come to Palermo frequently for the sake of maritime trade and profit, wishing to avenge certain injuries suffered at the hands of the Palermitans themselves, assembled a naval force from every quarter and, committing their sails to the winds across the sea, made landfall in Sicily at the port of the Val Demone. They sent an envoy to the count at Troina, where he was then staying, instructing him to meet them at Palermo with a mounted army; they themselves would bring him assistance in capturing the city, since the prospect of such a reward drove them to seek vengeance for the injury inflicted upon them.

But because certain affairs detained the count, he postponed going for the moment, instructing them to wait a little while, until the matters to which he was then attending had been settled. They, however, accustomed by long practice to commercial profits more than to military exercises, unwilling to wait lest they be deprived of their accustomed gains for too long, and intending to attack Palermo by themselves, directed their sails toward that city’s harbor. But terrified by the very great multitude of the enemy, and for that reason daring not to advance from their ships at all, they merely cut the chain that closed the harbor from one side to the other [Note: [Col. 1142D] C. P.: “from one bank to the other”] and, reckoning this according to the custom of their people as a great achievement [Note: [Col. 1142D] “the greatest”], returned to Pisa.

The count, therefore, seeing that summer was approaching—a season which, because of the excessive heat produced by the proximity of the blazing Dog Star, would prevent the undertaking of numerous cavalry expeditions—decided in the meantime to go to Apulia to his brother the duke, while the oppressive summer passed. But, so as not to leave his wife and the soldiers remaining with her without pay, he sent his army out in battle formation to plunder Golisano on the first day, Brocato on the second, and Cefalù on the third.

Thus, after filling Troina with abundant provisions, he gave many exhortations to his soldiers: they were to keep the city under the most vigilant watch, prudently guard against enemy incursions, and not advance too far from the city in any direction should some intervening circumstance arise. He himself went toward Apulia with his brother to discuss what should be done next. After they had discussed many matters together, at last, when the heat had abated, he accepted one hundred soldiers from his brother as auxiliaries and went with two hundred soldiers to plunder the territory of Agrigento.

### CHAPTER XXXV. The Count’s soldiers, after terrifying the enemy, climb Turron, later called Galzonis.

When he was returning from there with very great booty, he ordered his soldiers’ booty to proceed ahead of them. He himself, with the remainder, advanced between two wedges, taking care that he not be thrown into confusion by any hostile attack from the front or, especially, from the rear.

The Africans and Arabs, eager to avenge the victory taken from them in the battle at Cerami and at some time, with fortune favoring them, to recover the renown they had lost there, learned by a messenger that the count had gone raiding with seven hundred picked soldiers. They concealed themselves in ambush along the road by which he had to return.

But when our men who were marching ahead reached the place, the enemy suddenly rose against them. Forgetting the boldness to which they had hitherto been accustomed, they acted feebly and began to avoid the danger of death by flight rather than by arms. Seeking help, they climbed a certain mountain surrounded on every side by precipices, with only a single narrow entrance remaining open.

The enemy, however, killed part of the armed men who were escorting the booty and seized the booty itself. The count, who was following behind, heard the uproar and hurried forward. When he learned what had happened, he was filled with the greatest indignation and anger. He tried with immense shouts to call his men back in vain from the mountain they had climbed, so that they might seek vengeance upon the enemy with him. At last he himself climbed Turron and called each of his men by name, addressing them lest they later excuse themselves for having been absent:

“Have you, who until now were most valiant, been so drained of strength,” he said, “that, without remembering any military glory, you have been plunged into the depths of rotten cowardice and can no longer draw breath? Remember your ancestors, and also our people and the valor for which we have hitherto been renowned; avoid the marks of future disgrace. Remember how many thousands of enemies you destroyed at Cerami with fewer fighters than you have now. Fortune, then smiling upon you, is ruled by the same power as now. Take up your former strength again. After flight, victory is the restoration of honor to those who act bravely.”

After saying much more of this kind in reproach, he scarcely managed to revive them with his exhortations before hurrying into battle and engaging the enemy. Acting bravely, they defeated the race that had rebelled against God; the booty was recovered. Our men, made victorious, were enriched with the spoils of triumph.

They returned joyfully to Troina, except that they were deeply saddened by the death of Walter of Simula [Note: [Col. 1143D] C. P.: “by the death of Walter alone”], who, worthy of military distinction above all the others, had fought bravely in the engagement but—painful though it is to say—had lost the flower of his youth, pierced by the enemy [Col. 1144A].

### CHAPTER XXXVI. Our men are troubled by tarantulas.

The duke Robert, while he was in Apulia, knew that his brother was being harassed by the enemy through repeated incursions. Unwilling to remain without a share in the profit, and wishing also to become a participant in the labor, he assembled a very large army from Apulia and Calabria and set out toward Sicily.

When the count heard that his brother was approaching, he hurried joyfully to meet him at Cosenza, a city of Calabria. Proceeding from there, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1064, they crossed the sea at the Strait of Messina with only five hundred soldiers. They traversed all Sicily without hindrance, since no one dared attempt anything against them, and reached Palermo. At the duke’s command, they pitched their tents on a mountain later called Tarantinus, because of the abundance of tarantulas by which their army was greatly troubled there—an order of which he later repented.

For the whole mountain was infested with tarantulas, and it offered men and women an indecent, though they escaped it, ridiculous lodging. A tarantula is a worm resembling a spider, but it has a sting whose venom produces a savage puncture. It fills all whom it stings with a great poisonous inflation, and they are so tormented that they cannot in any way suppress the very inflation which emerges indecently through the anus with a crackling sound. Unless a furnace-heated or some other especially hot application is quickly applied, they are said to incur danger to their lives.

Some of our men were troubled by this indecency and were finally compelled to change their location. They sought a safer place nearer the city where they could pitch their tents. After remaining there for three months, they made no progress toward the city, since the Palermitans resisted them bravely; but they afflicted many of the surrounding places with extensive devastation.

When they saw that at that time they could not prevail against the city, they moved their camp and went to attack Bughāmum. Since the inhabitants of that fortress resisted feebly, they completely destroyed it and brought away all its inhabitants as captives, together with the women and children and all their possessions. Then, wishing to return toward Calabria, they pitched their tents not far from the city of Agrigento, since the road lay more directly that way [Col. 1144D].

The citizens of that city, trusting their own strength more than was necessary, burst through the gates and fell upon them with a great uproar. Pretending to yield while fleeing, they pursued the unsuspecting enemy as far as the gates of their own city [Note: [Col. 1143D] “And the unsuspecting enemy, yielding as they fled…”].

The duke then withdrew, came to Calabria, and dismissed the expedition. He restored the Bugamans whom he had brought away as captives to Scribla, which he had abandoned [Note: [Col. 1144D] “They led them to Scribla, which they had abandoned”], and had them settle there [Note: [Col. 1144D] “The Bugamans”].

### CHAPTER XXXVII. Agello is attacked by the duke.

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1065, after destroying the fortress of Policastro, he brought all its inhabitants to Nicotera, which he founded that same year, and had them settle there.

Before Duke Robert went toward Palermo and pitched his tents on the mountain of the tarantulas, the duke and Count Roger had already captured the fortress called Regale in the territory of Cosenza [Note: [Col. 1145D] C. P.: “Ragel”] and arranged it according to their will.

In the same year, the duke went to attack a certain fortress called Agello in the territory of Cosenza and besieged it for four months. The people of Agello, coming out of the fortress while the enemy pitched their tents closer, tried to drive them farther away with slings and arrows. Thus, the two sides engaged one another bravely in mutual slaughter.

But when our men, provoked to the greatest indignation, attempted to break through against the enemy at the points where they were most densely gathered, Roger, son of Scolcand [Note: [Col. 1145D] “Scotland”], was pierced by a spear and thrown from his horse. When his nephew Gissibert [Note: [Col. 1145D] “Gilbert”] tried to lift him up [Note: [Col. 1145D] “while”], he too was thrown down, and both were killed.

The duke and the whole army were greatly disturbed by their deaths, for they were exceedingly dear to them among their companions. He ordered their bodies to be buried at Saint Euphemia, where an abbey was then newly being established in honor of holy Mary, the Mother of God. He bestowed upon the same church their horses and the other possessions they had, for the salvation of their souls.

The people of Agello, recognizing that by this and similar acts they had gravely offended the duke, sought peace from him, lest, if they persisted in rebellion and were captured by force, he should, in his anger and without remembering any mercy, kill them all together as they deserved.

Although the duke was eager to seek revenge upon them with punishments, nevertheless, so as not to delay longer by postponing the matter, since he had other intentions, he made peace with them. He decided to receive the fortress, once they had surrendered it, under his authority and arrange it according to his will.

### CHAPTER XXXVIII. A fortress is established at Petrelegium.

Count Roger, intent upon acquiring Sicily, could not endure rest. He traversed everything, terrifying the inhabitants with frequent incursions, and was so habitually devoted to continual labor that he was always more threatening in one place or another. Not even the darkness of night could deter him from leaping from place to place and attempting everything himself. His presence terrified the enemy more than anything else; they were so frightened by his frequent rapid movements that they thought he was nowhere absent.

But because, when he was present with his own men, the enemy discovered that he was absent elsewhere, his men were sometimes harassed by hostile incursions. Therefore, in 1066, at Petrelegium, he most carefully fortified a stronghold with towers and defenses outside the gate. He could take refuge there more easily if necessity arose, and from its vicinity the nearest places, once more attentively subdued, could quickly be bound to him by alliance. By this means he conquered a very large part of Sicily and subjected it to the yoke of his dominion [Col. 1146A].

Finally, the sons of Tancred naturally acquired this custom: always eager for dominion, they would not tolerate anyone who possessed lands or estates near them without rivalry, insofar as their strength permitted. Either those people had immediately to become their subjects and serve them, or they themselves would take possession of everything by their own power.

### CHAPTER XXXIX. The duke besieges Montepiloso.

Duke Robert, who had claimed this custom for himself more than the others, accordingly undertook to compel his nephew Gauridus of Conversano—for he was the son of his sister—to render him service from Montepiloso, just as he did from the many other fortresses he held under his authority.

Gauridus, however, had not received Montepiloso from the duke, as he had the others; he had won it from the enemy by his own valor, while the duke had provided him no assistance. When he refused to do this, the duke brought up his army and went to besiege the same fortress. After many military actions had been carried out on both sides, he finally compelled him to promise and render service from that fortress, just as from the others.

### CHAPTER XL. The duke besieges Bari.

The duke, therefore, seeing that everything he undertook merely by beginning it was prospering for him with fortune favorably smiling, had nearby, not far from Montepiloso, the very famous city called Bari. It still adhered faithfully to the emperor of Constantinople [Note: [Col. 1145D] “adhering”], but was rebellious toward the duke. By whatever agreements he could make with the emperor [Note: [Col. 1146D] “Which he had, by whatever agreements he could, with the emperor also”], and urgently pressing for an attack upon that city in order to make its people more favorably disposed toward himself [Note: [Col. 1146D] “Inflamed”], he proceeded against it.

In the year of the Incarnate Word 1067, he went to besiege it with a cavalry force and a naval army [Note: [Col. 1146D] “He went to attack it”]. Since the city, situated as if at a certain angle, projected into the sea, he enclosed the side open toward the land with his cavalry, while extending ships across the sea from one shore to the other. He fastened each ship firmly to the next with iron chains, as though constructing a fence, and thus surrounded the entire city so completely that no means of departure from the city was open on any side.

He also constructed two bridges, one from each shore, and extended them farther into the sea until they reached the ships’ ropes from both sides, so that, if the people of Bari attempted any attack against the ships, the soldiers could come to their aid more readily by a direct route.

At first the people of Bari held all that was being done in contempt and treated it as worthless. Displaying their ornaments and costly treasures hanging in view, they heaped many insults upon Guiscard and, trusting in their towers, began to assess the outcome of events too lightly.

This did not deter Guiscard from his undertaking. Rather, the mind of a man burning with ambition was fixed with greater determination on persevering in what he had begun, because they said that more precious things were contained within the walls; he hoped all the more ardently to gain them. He answered them with a smile:

“What you display is mine,” he said, “and because you present it to me voluntarily, I receive it gratefully. Remain faithful for the time being in preserving it. When you grieve over its loss, I shall one day be generous in distributing it to you.”

Thus, inflaming his men with exhortations and promises to conquer the city, he declared that the reward for their labor and service lay within the walls.

He himself went around the walls, transported embankment material, surrounded the city with fortifications, constructed battering rams and the other machines necessary for capturing the city, instructed his men, harassed the enemy, and strove by continual pressure to instill fear.

The people of Bari, seeing that the duke’s steadfastness persisted without interruption beyond what they had expected, and that the food within the city was being uselessly consumed by the unarmed populace—women and children—with no opening by which to bring supplies to the enemies surrounding them, prepared by deceit to endanger the duke’s life, since they could not do so by force.

They agreed upon a price with a certain frivolous man and paid him to attempt, as he left the city, to strike the duke with a dart [Note: [Col. 1147D] “the city”] [Note: [Col. 1147D] “They paid him to attempt it. His mind was diseased”].

Amerinus, therefore, seized by avarice and captivated by the desire for the reward, hurried to carry out what appeared to him such a noble deed [Note: [Col. 1147D] “to perpetrate it”]. Having received from those instructing him a dart smeared with poison, he left the city and, pretending to be one of our men, threw stones with a sling toward the enemy above the walls. In this way he deceitfully made his way around the camp in order to observe it.

As evening came on and night hastened to block out the sun’s rays, the hour of supper approached. The duke was sitting in his tent, made from the leafy branches of trees. Amerinus came from behind and, with a wall of branches between them, first believing that he had clearly seen the duke with his eyes and then recognized him by his voice, forcefully hurled the dart he had received for this purpose. He caught hold of part of the duke’s clothing, but, with God protecting him, the duke remained unharmed, and the dagger was fixed in the ground.

Believing that he had wounded the duke, and having lost the dart after striking ineffectively, Amerinus thought nothing would serve him better than to flee. As quickly as he could, he made his way back inside the city.

The duke’s servants, terrified by this deed, rushed outside. Once they discovered the deception, they stationed guards and watchmen around the duke with greater vigilance than usual. At his command they hired masons, who by first light quickly completed a house.

### CHAPTER XLI. Count Roger fights with the Saracens.

At that time Count Roger was staying in Sicily, traversing everything in a hostile manner through frequent incursions. Sometimes he pressed people to submit to him by rewards; at other times he terrified them with threats. By continual activity he usually inflicted losses upon some of them, and by harassing the enemy without respite he frightened them so greatly that they were scarcely safe even within their fortifications, and nowhere else at all.

Night and day, evening and dawn, gentle and harsh winds alike were equally sources of fear and danger. Therefore the Sicilians, having held counsel among themselves, decided that they would rather die than prolong their unhappy life amid such continual unrest. They prepared to test the fortune of war against the count.

Accordingly, in the year of the Incarnate Word 1068, while the count was setting out to plunder the region around Palermo, they suddenly confronted him at Michelmir with an army gathered from every quarter and of immeasurable size.

When he saw them from a distance, he roared all over, gathered all his men together, and said to them with a smile:

“Come, nobility of our noble predecessors! Fortune, favoring you, brings of its own accord to meet you the booty which you had planned to seek farther away, sparing you labor so that you will not grow more weary on the journey. Behold the booty granted to you by God. Take it from those who are unworthy of it. Let us use it by dividing it, in the apostolic manner, according to each person’s need.

“Do not now recoil from those whom you have already defeated so many times. If they have changed their commander in their minds, the commander under whom they presume to do this is of the same nation and character [Note: [Col. 1148D] “of the same nation and character, changed, etc.”], and indeed of the same region [Note: [Col. 1148D] C. P.: “religion”], as the rest. But our God is unchangeable. If the integrity of faithful hope is not changed in you, neither will his decision concerning triumphant assistance be changed.”

After saying this and prudently arranging his men in battle formation, he engaged the enemy. Our men fought bravely, and the hostile force was so completely defeated that scarcely anyone survived from such a multitude to carry news of the outcome to Palermo. Our men, meanwhile, were greatly enriched by the spoils of triumph.

### CHAPTER XLII. The doves announce to Palermo that its people have been defeated.

It is the custom of the Saracens to raise doves at home, feeding them grain soaked in honey. When they travel farther away, they take the males with them in little baskets. Thus, whenever fortune brings them some new event about which they want those at home to know, they write their news on small pieces of paper, suspend them from the birds’ necks or beneath their wings, and release the birds into the air. In this way they hasten to inform their anxious households whether everything is proceeding favorably for their absent friends.

The little bird, attracted by the sweetness of the honeyed grain which it had often been accustomed to taste at home, hastens back and delivers the notes to those who know its custom.

The count seized such baskets with the birds among the rest of the spoils. He released the birds with notes stained with blood, thereby announcing to the people of Palermo the outcome of their unhappy fortune.

The entire city was shaken. The tearful voices of children and women rose through the air toward heaven [Col. 1149A]. Joy was born for our men, and sorrow for them.

### CHAPTER XLIII. With the count Roger’s assistance, the duke captures Bari.

At that time a certain Greek named Argerius [Note: [Col. 1149D] C. P.: “Argeritius”] governed the city of Bari under the emperor. After counsel had been held among the other citizens concerning the circumstances and the place [Note: [Col. 1149D] “After counsel had been held, and concerning the place”], he secretly sent to the emperor of Constantinople, through a certain man leaving the city named Diogenes [Note: [Col. 1149D] C. P.: “Diogerius”], a written account of the city’s and its citizens’ hardships and of the enemy’s attacks.

He reported that the city, which alone persisted in loyalty to the emperor, was being shaken on every side by hostile incursions and that, unless help came quickly, they would lose it through lack of provisions. He stated that, with the third year now approaching [Note: [Col. 1149D] “With the enemies surrounding them, and the citizens weakened by the long struggle, etc.”], they were surrounded by the enemy and, exhausted by the prolonged conflict, were preparing to surrender [Note: [Col. 1149D] “were prepared for surrender”]. Unless the emperor retained the city, no hope would remain for the recovery of their homeland, which had been overrun by the enemy [Note: [Col. 1150D] “No hope”] [Note: [Col. 1150D] “is preserved concerning its recovery”].

The envoy, diligently seeking to carry out faithfully what he had been charged to do, covered the great distance in a short time and came to Byzantium. He went to present the letters to the emperor and added an exhortatory speech urging him to provide assistance.

The emperor, having received and read the letters, sent him to Durazzo and had a fleet prepared. He appointed as its commander Gocelin of Orencho [Note: [Col. 1150D] C. P.: “a certain Gozelin of Corinth, a Norman by nation”], a Norman by nation and second in the palace after the emperor, because he was distinguished in arms and skilled in counsel. With large forces, he planned to send assistance to the people of Bari.

The man who had been sent, ordered by the emperor to return to Bari, secretly entered the city through the enemy lines by the same route by which he had departed. He reported what had been done and explained a signal by which they could recognize from a distance that assistance was coming. He instructed them to make a similar signal from each fortress toward those approaching: namely, to light bundles of wood, and warned them not to turn away from a particular harbor.

The people of Bari, cheered by this news and hurrying more than necessary—for nothing seems to be done quickly enough to a desirous mind—lit the bundles on the following night. With shouts and praises, they displayed their joy more openly than usual.

Among our men the question arose as to what they intended by this action. Conjectures were made concerning many matters, and arguments were advanced from every side; the wiser men discovered the truth: assistance was evidently coming to them by sea.

Count Roger of Sicily had arrived to assist his brother the duke, having recently been invited by him. He possessed leonine ferocity in every battle, yet prudence governed him and favorable fortune accompanied him.

Acting shrewdly in this matter, he ordered men to go out each night to observe whether ships approaching across the sea could perhaps be seen from a distance. Then, in the middle of one night, lanterns burning like stars were suddenly seen far away at the top of the mast of each ship.

When the count discovered this, he hurried out with an armed force, trusting in his many oarsmen, and hastened to meet the enemy. The enemy, seeing them from a distance and supposing that they were the people of Bari coming out in joy to meet them, made less adequate preparations for defense.

The count recognized from afar the ship of Gocelin, who was the enemy commander, distinguished from the others by two lanterns, and ordered his men to direct their attack toward it.

While they fought bravely, some of our men boarded one of their ships with such force that, when they ran carelessly toward one side under the weight of their armor, one hundred and fifty of our armored soldiers were submerged.

The count defeated Gocelin in battle. Taking him, disarmed, into his own ship, he returned gloriously and in triumph to his brother.

The duke, however, was tormented by fear that his brother might be lost in the battle. He could neither come to his aid nor, if Roger died, find another equal to him. Nevertheless, when he was told that Roger had returned victorious and unharmed, he declared that he believed no one until his own eyes had satisfied him. With tears, he repeatedly asked whether Roger was safe, examining him closely.

The count presented Gocelin to the duke as a captive, magnificently equipped in the Greek manner.

The people of Bari, therefore, no longer able to endure the enemy, having been disappointed in their hope, surrendered and entered into an alliance with the duke.

In the year of the Lord 1070, the duke, having attained the fulfillment of his desire, gave thanks to his brother and to the entire army. After arranging the city according to his will, he sent his brother ahead to Sicily and soon afterward, with his customary army, resumed the expedition toward Palermo.

He spent the entire months of June and July at Otranto, having a mountain cut down so that a descent to the sea might be made more easily and horses brought aboard the ships. The people of Durazzo were therefore greatly terrified, fearing that he would cross the sea with his army and come to attack them. On this pretext they sent him a mule and a horse, ostensibly as a mark of honor, but in order to spy out the situation.

### CHAPTER XLIV. Scyllum is reconciled to the duke.

At that time Costa Condomicita, who had long before fraudulently taken Scyllum from the duke [Note: [Col. 1150D] C. P.: “Stilium”], fearing that, if the duke pretended to cross by ship toward Sicily, he might turn aside and besiege Scyllum [Note: [Col. 1150D] “Stilium”], was reconciled with the duke and returned the fortress. He explained that he had been compelled to commit such an injury by the following circumstances:

The duke had appointed a certain Stratigotus named Costa Peloga, who, carried away by excessive insolence, treated every free man and woman with insults, sparing not even his own relatives. Among other things, wishing to extort from a certain freeborn matron named Regina a golden hen with its chicks, which she was said to possess, he had confined her in captivity after tearing her with blows.

Costa Condomicita was being held in the duke’s service on the island of Crotone. When what had happened was reported to him, he considered the injury done to his grandmother as done to himself. Pretending illness, he asked the duke for permission to go home for treatment and entered Scyllum [Note: [Col. 1151D] “Stilium”] on Christmas Eve.

When the Stratigotus heard that he had arrived, he sent him a gift of fish through a servant and asked how matters stood with the duke. Costa, as though plotting no evil and concealing his anger, sent back his thanks. But he had not forgotten what he had resolved in his mind.

After they had eaten, he secretly surrounded the more powerful men of the city and displayed his complaint concerning the injury inflicted upon him and his grandmother. When they replied that such things had rightly happened to him, he made no excuses, but declared that he regretted the deed and promised that he would attempt to undo what had been inflicted, provided only that he obtained their assistance [Col. 1151B].

Having thus secured the faith of many, he spent the entire night sleepless, attaching to himself everyone he could. At first light, while all those unaware of the plan were, as that day required, serving God’s praises in the church, he approached the gate of the castle with thirteen men girded with swords and cloaks. The rest, having received the signal, waited at the doors. The gatekeeper, suspecting nothing, opened it for him as for someone known.

He entered with his companions, went into the Stratigotus’s lodging, and seized the weapons he found. Then, wishing to forestall the Stratigotus, he ran as quickly as possible toward the church.

A shout therefore rose from every side. When the Stratigotus discovered the ambush, he leapt through a window and fell down a precipice. While seeking refuge by flight among the citizens, all of whom hated him, he was captured and brought back.

Because Costa Condomicita was his kinsman and wished to spare him, the people condemned the Stratigotus. Thus he paid the penalty with tortures and was killed by those against whom he had committed his crimes. Those whom he had imprisoned were freed, and they openly turned away from allegiance to the duke.

For nearly six years afterward, the duke’s rebels caused him great disturbance in various places throughout Calabria. We record this here so that those in authority may beware of allowing their subjects to be drawn away from their allegiance by wicked ministers.

### CHAPTER XLV. Palermo is captured.

The duke, having prepared provisions and everything else suitable for an expedition, followed his brother, whom he had sent ahead, and came to Catania, where the count was. Pretending that he was going to attack Malta, as though he had despaired of Palermo, he was nevertheless encouraged by his brother. Then, advancing from there with a large cavalry force and naval and infantry troops, he came to Palermo.

He blockaded the city with ships from the Ocean, stationed his brother the count on one side, and himself, with the Calabrians and Apulians, surrounded the walls from the other wing.

For a period of five months, while the enemy kept the city under the most vigilant defense, he nevertheless persisted in harassing them by attacking it together with his brother. Both men, inflamed with equal ardor, went around everything, instructed their men, arranged every detail, threatened the enemy, gave generously to their own men, promised them still greater rewards, were the first and most frequent to appear, and left nothing unattempted.

The duke had machines and ladders most skillfully joined together for scaling the walls. He secretly entered the gardens with three hundred soldiers on the side where the naval army was stationed and instructed his men to harass the city from that direction. He had likewise taught his brother to act from the side where he was positioned.

When the signal was given, those who had been instructed did not delay in carrying out their orders, but rushed forward with a great din. The entire city rushed to arms, and the people who ran to its defense amid the tumult advanced rapidly.

The side that had been less carefully guarded began to give way. The Guiscardians placed their ladders and climbed over the wall. The outer city was captured, and the gates were opened with iron tools so that their allies could enter.

The duke and the count, with the entire army, took shelter within the walls. The deceived Palermitans, realizing that the enemy was behind them inside the walls, withdrew into the inner city, seeking refuge there.

Night brought the tumult to an end. On the following morning, the leading citizens approached and spoke with both brothers after a treaty had been arranged. They said that they did not at all wish either to have their law violated or to abandon it, provided they were certain that they would not be compelled or crushed by unjust and novel laws.

Since present fortune thus urged them to surrender the city, they promised to remain faithful in service, pay tribute, and confirm this by an oath according to their law.

The duke and the count gladly accepted what was offered, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1071.

First of all, as faithful imitators of Scripture, which says, “Seek first the kingdom of God, and all these things will be added to you” (Matthew 6:33), they restored with great devotion and in Catholic fashion the church of the most holy Mother of God, Mary. In ancient times it had been an archbishopric, but at that time it had been violated by the impious Saracens and made into a temple of their superstition. They enriched it with an endowment and ecclesiastical ornaments.

They recalled and restored the archbishop, who, having been expelled by the impious, was carrying out the worship of the Christian religion as best he could in the poor church of Saint Cyriacus, although he was a timid Greek by nation.

Afterward, once the castle had been fortified and the city arranged according to his will, the duke retained it as his own property. He granted his brother possession of the Val Demone and of all the rest of Sicily that had been acquired—and that, with his assistance, as he promised, would yet be acquired, not falsely.

### CHAPTER XLVI. Serlo is killed.

While these events were taking place, Serlo, son of Serlon and therefore the nephew of both of these princes, whom we mentioned earlier, was staying at Cerami to protect the province from the incursions of the Arabs, who were said at that time to be residing at the Castle of John, having been so ordered by the duke and the count. For half of all Sicily had fallen, by agreement of the duke and the count, to be divided between Serlo and Arisgotus of Puteoli [Col. 1153A], because Serlo was their kinsman, while both men were exceptionally distinguished in counsel and arms.

The Arabs who were staying at the Castle of John were exceedingly hostile to Serlo because he had often harassed them, and by continual plotting they sought to contrive his downfall either by deceit or by arms. A Saracen of some importance at the Castle of John, named Brahen [Note: [Col. 1153D] C. P.: Braclem], had entered into an alliance with Serlo in order more easily to deceive him. According to their custom, each had adopted the other as a brother through the ear, and they had mutually accepted this relationship.

After arranging his treachery with his companions, Brahen sent Serlo a salutary little gift with friendly words. Among other things he added this:

“Let my adopted brother know that on such-and-such a day only seven Arabs, by deliberate boastfulness, intend to come and raid your land.”

When Serlo heard this, he began to treat it as a joke. Taking insufficient precautions for himself, he summoned no one from the neighboring fortresses to his aid. When the appointed day had come, he withdrew thoughtlessly to go hunting.

The Arabs who had devised the plot then departed from the Castle of John with seven hundred cavalry and two thousand infantry. Not far from Cerami, in hidden places, they set an ambush. They sent only seven soldiers, as Brahen [Note: [Col. 1153D] Braclem] had told Serlo, to withdraw Serlo from Cerami after they had taken their prey.

A cry arose, and the inhabitants of the province were thrown into tumult. From the place where he had gone hunting, Serlo heard the citizens shouting. But because he had gone out unarmed, he sent a messenger to Cerami to bring him weapons and summon his men. He himself went forward to inquire what had happened, since the uproar was becoming more threatening [Col. 1153C]. When he was told that seven soldiers were carrying off the booty, he seized the weapons brought to him and, imprudently following his adopted brother’s deception with more credulity than was necessary, advanced beyond the ambush [Col. 1154A].

When the men burst out from the ambush and the enemy were discovered behind him in a dreadful storm of weapons, Serlo, distrustful both of his ability to fight and of the possibility of escape, ran with the few men who were with him toward a rock that from that day was called Serlo’s Rock. After climbing it, he used its rearward slope as a wall. He fought bravely for a long time, but since no help came from elsewhere, his struggle was in vain. At last he was pierced through and fell, and of all who had been with him no one escaped except two who had hidden among the corpses of the dead.

After disemboweling Serlo, the Saracens cut out his heart. They are said to have eaten it in order to take into themselves his courage, which had been so great. They sent the heads of the slain to the king in Africa as a mark of honor. Serlo’s head, however, was placed on a stake and carried through [Col. 1154B] the streets of the city. A herald proclaimed that it belonged to the man by whom Sicily had been attacked more than all the others, that the enemies had been defeated with no comparable survivor, and that Sicily would henceforth easily fall to their share [Note: [Col. 1154D] C. P.: easily].

When news of these events was brought to our princes at Palermo, the whole army was thrown into confusion. The count was overwhelmed by unbearable grief at the loss of his nephew; the duke, wishing to restrain his brother from lamentation, tried to conceal his own sorrow in a manly fashion.

“Let women be permitted to lament,” he said; “but let us gird ourselves with arms for vengeance.”

Therefore, since the two brothers were each striving separately to secure their own advantage, except that whenever necessity pressed upon them one summoned the other and they came in turn to aid one another, let us bring this book to an end as we begin another, so that in what follows we may alternate our style, now treating each of them separately and again together, as the events themselves require [Col. 1154C].

[Col. 1153] Here ends the second book.

# BOOK THREE

[Col. 1153D]

Since the arduous deeds and splendid triumphs of the two great men—namely, Duke Guiscard and Roger, count of Sicily—must now be set forth, sometimes separately and sometimes together, as we promised our writings would do, it would be fitting, if adequate resources were available, for a more limpid poetic style and the pen of a nobler philosopher to commit to writing the deeds that shine in this noble record. Otherwise, when the clearest liquid is offered for drinking, even the thirsty may recoil from it because of the stench of an unclean vessel.

But since poverty prevents us from drinking through golden tubes, we sometimes use a leaden tube, intending at least to taste the sweet liquids [Col. 1154D]. Therefore, whoever attempts to examine the sequence of this history should attend not to deceptive inventions of words but to the grand triumphs of the men worthy of remembrance. For the things inserted here are subtitled not to my praise or yours, but to the praise of those who earned it by their deeds.

Since, by the prince’s command, the time for writing is pressing upon us—and what has hitherto been neglected has therefore been drunk only sparingly—the urgent haste of that same prince prevents us from returning to the fountain from which we might draw what could be poured forth more clearly.

# CHAPTER ONE. Fortresses are built at Paternion and Mazara

[Col. 1155A]

The most famous prince of Sicily, Roger, remaining in Sicily after he had taken Palermo, while his brother the duke departed from Sicily toward Calabria and Apulia on his customary expedition to pursue his interests, retained for himself, with the duke’s agreement, a small part of his brother’s departing army, attracting them by rewards and promises.

He then began to subdue Sicily from every side and harassed it greatly by continual incursions. Although until then he had acted vigorously, intending to share fully with his brother whatever he acquired, he was now determined that everything he acquired should fall to his own portion. Like a hungry lion greedy for prey and unable to endure rest, he allowed himself to range everywhere, to be the first to undertake the most dangerous enterprises, and to leave nothing unattempted [Col. 1155B].

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1073, he fortified two castles: one at Paternion to harass Catania, and another at Mazara to subdue the neighboring province.

The duke, however, coming from Sicily into Calabria, fortified a castle at Rossano, a city of that province, to the grief of its inhabitants.

# CHAPTER TWO. Guiscard besieges Salerno

Gisulf, prince of Salerno and brother of Sigelguta [Note: [Col. 1155D] C. P.: Sigelgaita], the wife of Duke Guiscard, wishing all the coastal districts from Salerno to the harbor called Ficus, as well as Arecum and Saint Euphemia, to belong to his jurisdiction [Note: [Col. 1155D] “Maritimanos”], and hearing that part of them was being invaded daily by Guiscard [Note: [Col. 1156D] “Diatim pervadere,” to invade daily], turned his hostility against the duke. He disgraced with insults everyone attached to the duke whom he could capture, and did not conceal that he was hostile to our people.

Duke Guiscard, who had promised him friendship, bore this patiently at first and told the envoys that it would be fitting for him to desist from what he had begun. But when he saw that the prince’s evil purpose was growing worse the more he tried to soften it, he renounced the treaty that existed between them and prepared implacable hostility against the man who was hostile to him.

Because, however, hostilities had grown hot between him and Prince Richard of Aversa, he feared that Gisulf might receive help from Richard against him. He therefore made peace with Richard, hiring him with certain agreements to assist him, and went with a large force to besiege Salerno [Note: [Col. 1156D] “Quem fecit, et statum pennam” (“whom he made, and the established penalty”; reading uncertain)].

# CHAPTER THREE. The people of Amalfi make peace with the duke

The people of Amalfi, who hated Gisulf, were afraid of being punished by him, because they had been the killers of his father when he was attacking them in order to subject them to himself [Col. 1156A].

Invited by the duke to come by ship and serve him in besieging the city, their leading men went hurriedly to speak with the duke, with the agreement of some others. The duke then tested them with shrewd agreements, compelling them by threats if they refused, and at last forced them into an alliance: if they stood against Gisulf, all Amalfi, once subjected to him, would be bound to him by hereditary treaty.

When the duke promised everything they desired, he left part of his army behind to besiege the city and led the remainder with him. Together with those who had come from there, he went to Amalfi, received the city, which the citizens had surrendered to him, built four castles in it, and fortified them with his soldiers. From there he returned to Salerno with a large force of the people of Amalfi.

Thus he kept the Amalfitans in fear of Gisulf, should they in any way escape the hand of Guiscard.

# CHAPTER FOUR. Salerno is surrendered

[Col. 1156B]

The duke surrounded Salerno with naval forces, infantry, and cavalry. By frequent attacks and engagements he terrified the inhabitants on every side, and wore them down so severely that no route remained open for bringing in food, despite their resistance. He forced them into such hunger that, as we learned from the reports of those who were present, some of those shut up inside even ate mice.

Abagelard, son of Count Hunifred and therefore the duke’s nephew, had entered Salerno to aid Gisulf because of the hostility between himself and the duke, on account of the inheritance that the duke was withholding from him [Col. 1156C]. When famine grew severe, Abagelard secretly departed from Salerno by night and withdrew to the Calabrian city of Santa Severina, where he became hostile to the duke.

The duke sent word to his brother in Sicily that he should go and besiege his nephew Abagelard at Santa Severina, and he did not send the message in vain. He himself continued unremittingly to harass Salerno and finally compelled it to surrender.

Since Gisulf was his sister’s brother—the maternal uncle of his brother’s children—the duke granted him freedom to depart wherever he wished. He retained the city by his own power and fitted it with castles and fortifications according to his pleasure.

# CHAPTER FIVE. Count Roger besieges Abagelard at Santa Severina

[Col. 1156D]

Thereafter, unable to endure rest and failing to neglect any labor wherever some prospect of gain appeared, the duke went to Santa Severina, where he had invited his brother to join him, to besiege his nephew Abagelard. Finding that his brother, whom he had invited for this purpose, had besieged the city from one side, he himself took up position on the other.

Abagelard came out of the city daily to challenge our men to battle. Since he often and vigorously engaged them in turn, many deeds appropriate to warfare were accomplished [Col. 1157A].

When the duke saw that he was making little progress against the city, he held a council with his men and fortified three castles. He assigned one to Hugh Falco and another to Rainald of Simula, to harass the city; the third he entrusted to Herbert, Hugh’s brother, and Custinobarbus, Rainald’s brother [Note: [Col. 1157D] C. P.: Tristomo Barba].

Having thus ended the expedition, he withdrew into Apulia. Not long afterward, at Cava, he captured Count Heremann, Abagelard’s brother, in an engagement and sent him to his brother Roger to be confined in the tower at Melito.

While Heremann was being tortured in a dark prison in chains, Abagelard, moved by brotherly compassion, made an agreement with the duke: if the duke would return the city to him, he would receive his brother in exchange. The duke gave his word, deceiving him by this trick, that when they came to Gargano—for so a certain castle was called—he would return his brother to him, free from captivity.

Abagelard, unsuspecting and failing to notice the crafty meaning of the words, left the city and handed it over to the duke. He then remained with him for some time, vainly expecting the return of his brother.

When they reached Rossano, Abagelard spoke more sharply with the duke because the matter was being delayed too long, and urged him to hasten toward Gargano. The duke then revealed the deception and declared that he would not go to the place he had mentioned within the next seven years.

When Abagelard realized that he had been trapped by the craftiness of the words, he argued vehemently with the duke, departed in anger, and withdrew with his men into Apulia, taking up a rebellious position in the castle of Saint Agadius.

# CHAPTER SIX. The duke recovers Santa Severina; at the Castle of Saint Agadius the duke besieges Abagelard

[Col. 1157C]

The duke knew that Abagelard was striving to stir all Apulia against him as far as he could. He therefore raised an army, pursued him, and went to besiege him. But because the castle was extremely strong by nature, fortification, and defensive works, and because the men inside fought bravely, the longer he persisted in attacking it, the more he was troubled by the losses of his own men than he advanced against the castle.

Abagelard’s grief over the loss of his brother increased day by day. The chains in which his brother was held tormented him no less than they tormented his brother, whenever he thought of them. Therefore, repeatedly trying to improve his brother’s situation by every kind of agreement [Col. 1157D], he finally managed, though only with difficulty, to obtain permission to surrender the castle, receive his brother, and depart with his own freedom.

After receiving his brother, they departed together, crossed the sea, and went over to the emperor of Constantinople.

# CHAPTER SEVEN. Count Roger builds a castle on Mount Calataxibet

The most famous prince of Sicily and its conqueror, Roger, remained in Sicily, acting vigorously in all things. No pleasure drew him away or allowed him to be absent from the enemy. Poverty, labor, the threats of the enemy, the continual combat that threatened, wakefulness, and even a harsher life did not deter him from what he had begun. Rather, the more he was shaken by hardships, the more ardently, with the steadfastness naturally implanted in his human spirit, he strove to conquer rather than be conquered, driven by his desire for dominion.

Although he desired everything, he was especially troubled by his eagerness to possess the Castle of John. If he gained it, he knew that he would have it, as though it were a secure instrument [Note: [Col. 1158D] C. P.: “to use as a scourge”], for ranging at will throughout all Sicily.

Driven by this great and urgent desire, in the year of the Incarnate Word 1074 he fortified a castle on Mount Calataxibet. By supplying it with soldiers and everything else necessary [Col. 1158B], he made it a most dangerous threat to the Castle of John.

# CHAPTER EIGHT. The Africans destroy Nicotrum

The African Saracens, members of the household of the king of Tunis, set out at his command. Committing their ships to the winds across the sea in the manner of pirates, they went to lie in wait along the coasts toward Sicily and Calabria.

Thus, in the month of June, on the eve of Saint Peter, they landed at Nicotrum by night. They overwhelmed the unsuspecting citizens, who were weighed down by wine and sleep according to the custom of the approaching festival and were overcome with joy. They killed some while they were half asleep, captured others, and carried onto their ships even the children with the women and all the movable goods [Col. 1158C].

They burned the entire castle with fire and, urging on their rowing, withdrew into the open sea. On the following day they came closer to the shore and, when friends wished to ransom the children and the weaker members of the household, they accepted the price and put them out of the ships, thus lightening their load. The rest, who seemed likely to be useful, they carried away. Then, committing their sails to the winds, they set out joyfully to revisit the native fields from which they had come.

# CHAPTER NINE. The Africans are defeated at Mazara

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1075, because the previous year had turned out favorably for them at Nicotrum, fortune appearing to favor their will [Col. 1158D], they became more insolent than their success warranted through their greed. Thinking that a similar outcome would occur, they boarded their ships and sailed toward Sicily to test their fortune.

They tried the island by sailing around it and finally landed at Mazara. Leaving their ships, they attacked the city with great force and broke in. They then besieged the castle below for eight days, while its defenders resisted bravely.

When the count learned through a messenger that the castle and his men were being harassed by the enemy, he secretly entered the castle by night with an armed force. At first light he burst out through the gates and engaged the enemy in the city street before the castle. Fighting bravely according to his custom, he won the victory. After killing many, he pursued the rest as they fled, driving the last of them into the sea.

Mazara was rescued from the enemy by the count’s valor. A groaning report was carried to Africa by the few who escaped. Thus fickle Fortune laughed at men whom she had first enticed by favorable successes, deceiving them with the hope of earlier outcomes.

# CHAPTER TEN. Hugh of Gircea is killed near Catania

When certain necessities called the count away from Sicily, he departed toward Calabria and placed Hugh of Gircea in charge of defending Sicily. Hugh possessed great valor and was also of distinguished birth, coming from the province of Le Mans [Note: [Col. 1159D] C. P.: “He had given him Catania with his daughter by his former wife, all …”].

The count ordered him not to leave the city in pursuit of the enemy if Bernarvet, who lived nearby at Syracuse, should make any incursion against him. He was to beware Bernarvet’s cunning tricks.
