But Hugh’s youthful spirit was ardent for warfare and eager for praise. Paying too little attention to what had been forbidden him, he began striving to accomplish, before the count’s return, some noble deed by which he might earn military renown.

He therefore advanced as far as Traina and brought Jordan, the count’s son, with the count’s household troops to Catania. Bernarvet, meanwhile, gathered a large army of chosen soldiers, approached by night, and hid in ambush in concealed places not far from Catania. He sent thirty [Col. 1159C] picked soldiers ahead to Catania, intending that they should provoke the enemy to battle and draw them farther from the city.

Hugh and Jordan, burning with eagerness for battle, urged their men on and departed from the city with great force. They sent thirty picked soldiers to reconnoiter the ambush, while they themselves hastened to follow more carelessly.

The scouts passed beyond the place of the ambush. When those following had come all the way to it, the enemy burst out from their hiding places and rose against them in a dreadful onslaught. The men who had gone ahead saw the ambush behind them, but, with the enemy between them and their comrades, they could not return to their own side. They fled and escaped to Paternion.

Our men, however, tried to engage the enemy bravely. Hugh, the count’s son-in-law, was killed with many others [Col. 1159D]. Jordan, unable to withstand the enemy, escaped to Catania with a few companions.

Bernarvet returned happily to Syracuse with the spoils.

When the count learned of this report through a messenger, he hastened back. Raising his army against Bernarvet, he attacked and completely destroyed the castle called Zotica. He killed the men and sent the women and children to Calabria to be sold, in the year of the Incarnate Word 1076.

But because the prince’s spirit, almost destroyed by grief at the killing of his son-in-law, could not be restored except by greater vengeance, he sought a more extensive revenge. He advanced as far as the province of Noto and devastated everything so thoroughly that he even burned the standing crops completely. The time of threshing was approaching, and they could not be carried away. He added that he would do the same in various places throughout Sicily, and in that year he inflicted the greatest poverty upon the island:

> Hunger therefore arises, because vengeance has taken away the loaves.

# CHAPTER ELEVEN. Trablas is forced to surrender by siege

After the year of the Incarnate Word had passed,

[Col. 1160B]

and, added to a thousand, seven times eleven,

the count sets an expedition in motion in the month of May.

The ships spread their sails across the sea, with the west wind assisting.

The bronze instruments sound; the sea applauds with rejoicing as the trumpets blow.

The fleet of great Alexander was not more beautiful [Note: [Col. 1159D] C. P.: “was”].

The breeze smiles together with Fortune; the warlike youth rejoices.

The trained musicians play the cithara, and the drums resound.

They set out to attack Trablas; the waters do not swell [Note: [Col. 1159D] “They go”].

But the count crosses over on horseback with a warlike front,

through the depths and heights of the rocky mountains,

supported by a great multitude of warlike young men.

When the sun touches the shields gleaming with gold

and the shining helmets,

it throws back its radiance into the eyes of those who look.

All the mountains glitter above the bright stars.

[Col. 1160C]

The horses snort and neigh; the mountains likewise resound [Note: [Col. 1160D] “Echo”].

A thousand standards flutter in the light breeze.

With terrifying appearance they hasten toward Trablas.

The enemy see them and shudder at this cloud of weapons.

Trumpets resound over land and sea, to strike fear into them.

The shout beats all the way to heaven; below, the enemy tremble.

They surround the city on every side, by sea and dry land [Note: [Col. 1160D] “The city is surrounded”].

The sailors are shaded by sails; on land they plant their anchors.

Some of the cavalry strike at the front lines; others pitch their tents.

They repeatedly rush into battle and engage bravely.

The enemy strives to resist, but is greatly hemmed in [Note: [Col. 1160D] C. P.: colliditur, “is struck down”].

[Col. 1160D]

After the battle there is mourning in the castle; our men add the lyre.

The enemy, distrustful of their strength, finally seek peace.

The count yields; they return the castle [Note: [Col. 1160D] “They submit to his authority”] and submit to his rule.

They enter into a treaty according to their custom, but do so with grief.

From this same city a narrow tongue of land, pressed by the sea on both sides, extends farther into the sea and abounds in very rich pastures. In time of war the herds and the city’s other animals were accustomed to graze there. Since, according to custom, they would go out daily because of the enemy who were threatening, our men, observing them across the narrow intervening gulf, began, as is customary among such people, to be stirred by the desire to acquire them, if they could do so by some stratagem.

Jordan, the count’s son, applied himself especially to carrying out this undertaking, striving to win for himself, above all others, a military reputation. At last, being an exceedingly presumptuous man and eager for praise, he held counsel with his companions. One evening he chose a hundred soldiers for himself, boarded the ships without his father’s knowledge, crossed over to the island by night, and, after landing, withdrew. Before daylight, he hid in ambush in a hollow of the island.

When night had passed and the shining sun had illuminated the earth, the entire population of the city mentioned above came out from the city, as usual, to pasture their animals and spread out across the island [Note: [Col. 1161D] C. P.: “the whole population of the aforesaid city”].

Jordan, who was hidden in ambush, saw that the herd had advanced some distance from the city. He burst out from his hiding place with leonine force, rushed forward as far as the city gate, gathered the animals, and hastened to drive them toward the ships so that they could be taken aboard [Col. 1161B].

When the citizens saw that the island had unexpectedly been overrun by the enemy, they rushed to arms. With the greatest force they burst out from the city, as many as ten thousand of them, and unwisely pursued the enemy in order to recover the herd.

When Jordan saw that they had advanced farther from the city, he abandoned the herd and met the enemy with leonine ferocity. Battle was joined, and the fighting was fierce on both sides. Jordan, however, who was highly effective in engagements, made his men more eager by exhorting them in words. Fighting bravely, he struck down many and put the rest to flight. He won the victory and, cutting them down, pursued them all the way to the city gate [Col. 1161C].

Then he returned to the ships. After the great booty had been joyfully brought aboard [Note: [Col. 1161D] “freely”], he returned unharmed to his father with triumphal praise.

Terrified by this event, the city was compelled to surrender, as we have said. Once he had obtained the city, the count arranged the castle and the other fortifications according to his pleasure. He supplied them with soldiers and everything those soldiers needed, surrounding them on every side with towers and strong defenses.

But the neighboring province, firmly enclosed on every side, was very strongly fortified and therefore continued to resist and rebel. The indefatigable count began to harass it with frequent incursions, intending to bring everything beneath his authority. Within a short time he compelled as many as twelve very famous castles to submit to his dominion in obedience. He distributed them among his soldiers and granted them to be held from him together with all their appurtenances [Col. 1161D].

After thanking the whole army for the service rendered to him, he dismissed it. He himself withdrew to Bricca to rest from his labor.

# CHAPTER TWELVE. The Castle of Novum enters into alliance with the count

At that time a certain Saracen named Bechus possessed the Castle of Novum and lived there. He was a man of great extravagance and arrogance. By his frivolity he sometimes subjected even his own retainers to various insults, making them less loyal to him [Col. 1162A].

One day he became angry with his miller, summoned him before him, and disgraced him with blows. The miller pretended to bear this very heavily. He set his mind on avenging so great an insult and silently considered by what means he might repay it, whether by damaging his master’s property or by injuring his body.

It happened that one evening he gathered accomplices from among his subordinates, broke into and occupied a certain rock that rose above and dominated the entire castle, and sent a messenger to the count at Bricca. He reported that he had acted in loyalty to the count and asked him to hasten to his assistance.

When the count received this news, he was greatly delighted. He hastened there as quickly as possible with as many men as he could gather.

Bechus, meanwhile, tried in vain to attack the miller, while attempting by flattery and promises to reconcile him to himself and make him abandon what he had begun [Col. 1162B]. But when the count arrived, he came nearer and bound the miller to his allegiance by the most generous promises.

Since there was no access by which our men could approach the miller, he lowered a rope, and by means of it drew some of our men up to him.

When Bechus saw our men received inside the rock by the miller, he was terrified and abandoned hope of retaining the castle. He abandoned the castle, carried away whatever he could, and fled. The citizens made peace with the count and received him inside the castle.

The count, having thus gained possession of the castle, arranged and fortified it according to his will. To provide an example for others to carry out similar deeds, he rewarded the miller with many benefits and even granted him freedom.

# CHAPTER THIRTEEN. The Emperor Michael comes to the duke

[Col. 1162C]

A certain Greek, calling himself Michael, emperor of Constantinople, came to the duke in Apulia, seeking assistance in recovering the palace [Note: [Col. 1162D] “recovering”]. He said that he had been expelled from it by the treachery of his own people on Good Friday, and had been forcibly compelled to become a monk. The sole charge brought against him was that he had taken the duke’s daughter in marriage for his son.

His own son, moreover, so that no hope of recovering the palace or of securing the succession through the wife he had taken might remain, had been shamefully castrated and was banished into exile until the end of his life. Another man had been substituted in the palace in place of the expelled heir, although neither any line of descent nor even the remotest hereditary connection with the ancient emperors had invited him to that inheritance by the law of nations [Col. 1162D].

The Greeks feared that, if heirs were born from a wife of our people and succeeded in the palace [Note: [Col. 1162D] “were to grow up as successors”], our people would be given a freer opportunity to enter it, and that their nation, customarily devoted to luxury and pleasure rather than to the pursuits of war, would be trampled under the strength of our men.

They kept the duke’s daughter shut up under careful guard, lest, if she married some powerful man, the fact that she had once been crowned in the palace as the hereditary empress should lead the man she married to assert some hereditary claim to the palace through her.

Michael, therefore, having escaped from the monastery in which he had been forcibly made a monk, and having removed the monastic habit, as he claimed, came to Apulia as a fugitive. The duke received him with imperial honor. Throughout all the cities of Apulia and Calabria, he was treated with the greatest care, by processions and imperial ceremonies, at the command of that same duke.

The duke did all this deliberately, not because he intended to restore him to the palace [Note: [Col. 1163D] “Not that he intended …”]. He had heard that his son-in-law had been castrated. Having therefore lost hope of offspring from his daughter who might have a hereditary claim to the palace, he secretly worked toward this end: under Michael’s name, with the support of certain allies, he would more easily defeat the Greeks, and, once they reached the palace, seize the crown with the scepter and imperial ornaments by force and become emperor himself.

Promising only that he would provide Michael with assistance, he kept him with him for nearly two years and more in the rank with which he had begun, until the things necessary for so great an undertaking had been prepared [Col. 1163B].

At that time there were also certain men with the duke who had served in the palace during the reign of the Emperor Michael. They said that they knew Michael’s face and that this man did not resemble him at all, or even bear the slightest likeness to him. They claimed that he had come fraudulently, hoping to receive some gift from the duke.

The duke, uncertain whether this was true or not, heard much whispering among his men about the matter. Yet he was not deterred from what he had begun. Rather, while carrying out his plan, although he himself had no doubt that this was not Michael, he insisted that no one should doubt it. He deliberately praised this attitude and encouraged his men to maintain it, so that they would not dissuade him from what he had begun [Col. 1163C].

# CHAPTER FOURTEEN. The duke prepares a fleet against Greece

While arranging such matters and silently keeping them in mind,

he labors at expense so that Byzantium may become his plaything.

From every land he seeks a supply of materials.

Nothing is rejected, nor are rustic materials despised.

Even what has already been scorned may prove useful.

The foremost woodcutters are commissioned in their craft.

From every land the art of making planks is brought together.

Cut timbers fall; they are trimmed, and the cut surfaces are scraped

by craftsmen of wood. The smith applies iron to the fire.

An anchor is forged, and the form of nails is prepared.

The framework of the ship is woven together [Note: [Col. 1163D] C. P.: “covered”] and fastened above with nails.

Some cover the lowest cracks with wool,

[Col. 1163D]

while others hasten to spread liquid pitch over them.

These sew the sails; those devote themselves to the ropes.

The fleet is fitted out; not a single ship alone is prepared.

As the hero eagerly presses on so that the number may grow,

once everything has been equipped and the ships skillfully prepared,

the fleet is assembled at Hydruntum across the open sea.

# CHAPTER FIFTEEN. The count besieges Taormina

Meanwhile, while these things were taking place, in the approaching year 1078 [Col. 1164A], the count besieged Taormina and surrounded it with twenty-two castles. He closed the approaches from one to another with hedges and barriers [Note: [Col. 1163D] “Scropibus”], and also surrounded the city from the seaward side with naval forces, so that no route was open on any side by which the enemy might introduce anything into the castle or remove anything from it.

One day, while the count was crossing from one castle to another along the precipitous slopes of a rocky mountain, accompanied by a few men, a group of Slavs [Note: [Col. 1164D] “Sclavorum”] hiding among myrtle bushes burst out at a narrow point of the passage and attacked him.

If a certain Evisandus, a Briton by nationality, had not heard the clatter of weapons and placed himself between the count and the enemy, victory over the count, as they say, would have fallen to the enemy.

But God, who alone examines hearts, had foreseen the prince’s good intention in what preceded and in what would follow through him, and turned the matter otherwise than they intended [Col. 1164B]. For it is written: “There is no wisdom, there is no understanding, there is no counsel against the Lord” (Proverbs 21:30).

# CHAPTER SIXTEEN. Evisandus is killed in place of the count

When Evisandus had been killed in this way while remaining faithful to his lord, our men rushed to arms, but the enemy escaped down the precipitous slopes of the rocky mountain.

Thus, under God’s protection, the death of Evisandus took the place of the count’s life [Note: [Col. 1164D] “life”]. The count honorably rewarded his loyalty. After his body had been decently buried, he bestowed many benefits upon the needy and sacred places for the redemption of Evisandus’s soul, and not without good reason.

He traversed the mountain peaks and the valleys with them, making his way with infantry forces. From the mountain called Gibel by the inhabitants, which we call Etna, as far as Traina, he left no one of that superstition unpunished [Col. 1164C].

> There was much mourning among the soldiers for this buried man.
>
> For the Briton was dear to all because of his merit.
>
> For the merit of his faith, may he receive the lot of rest.
>
> Although death was given to him, life was thereby given to the count.
>
> Let him learn from Judas what such great fidelity may signify for him [Note: [Col. 1164D] C. P.: distat, “he differs”].
>
> He sold God, and afterward hanged himself by a noose;
>
> he purchased death, marked by his betrayal.
>
> This man gave himself willingly to the enemy’s sword,
>
> so that he might save his lord and heap up merit for himself.
>
> These two must not be placed under an equal heading, since their virtue was not equal.
>
> One was a traitor, while the other hastened to save another.
>
> This man will receive an angelic wing, that one Gehenna.

# CHAPTER SEVENTEEN. African ships called Golafri are seen beneath Taormina

[Col. 1164D]

Fourteen ships, which they call Golafri, wandering across the sea like pirates from Africa, from the kingdom of the king of Tunis, landed beneath Taormina. At dawn, our men saw them anchored not far away in the sea.

Our ships, however, after disembarking their armed men, were not fully prepared for action. The count sent a messenger to inquire who they were, for what reason and from where they had come, and whether they had arrived as enemies or bearing peace [Col. 1165A].

He added a threat: if, in the exercise of their own jurisdiction, they had done or presumed to attempt even the slightest wrong against anything belonging to him, they would nowhere escape him unpunished.

They replied under oath and by the law of their king that they were plotting no harm against anything belonging to him. Rather, by the command of the king of Tunis, they had been sent to drive from the sea any hostile pirates they might find. They were ready, if necessary, to serve the count.

The first man from each ship was therefore invited to a friendly conference, so that, if they lacked food or any other necessities, his generosity might supply them. While they agreed to the invitation and, after accepting the treaty, were preparing to come, a contrary wind rose. The ships, with the men aboard them, were driven across the waters and immediately torn away from the sight of our people [Col. 1165B]:

> Thus those whom he invites, the north wind prevents from approaching.
>
> And what he promised to give, the wind withdrew so that he would not give it.

# CHAPTER EIGHTEEN. Taormina is captured

But the count remained intent upon the things by which he had previously been held:

> He besieges and fights; the castle resists as best it can.

The struggle begins [Note: [Col. 1165D] C. P.: “continues.”]; the count strives to persist here [Note: [Col. 1165D] “Let him take care to persist.”].

Although anxiety binds him, nothing at all tires him.

He presses on and urges them, threatening the enemy with his courage.

He gives; he promises to give; he leaves nothing unattempted.

In the undertaking to which he urges his comrades, he proves himself the foremost,

Since there is a struggle, and since he is a relief to his brothers.

[Col. 1165C] He is seen ahead of his own men, while he is brought back with those behind.

Otho is first at the watch [Note: [Col. 1165D] “The Crotonian.”], Elias second;

Arisgotus third; Jordan, from there, refused to remain apart.

The comrades were heartened by this method.

An order was issued: “Is it permitted to seek provisions?”

Thus they are subdued, and our men enjoy their station.

They are prevented from the great mountain and from the lake on every side.

They are subjected to no one [Note: [Col. 1165D] “Nothing is added beneath.”]; what has been added afterward [Note: [Col. 1165D] “Earlier.”] is diminished.

Hence hunger increased, while the enemy ceased from engaging.

His strength declines; the enemy is now nearly conquered.

Secure only in the fact that a wall surrounds him on every side,

He takes care not to plant his step outside, lest he offer battle [Note: [Col. 1165D] “He fears it.”].

When bread fails, the starving people are overcome.

[Col. 1165D] Thus the count is summoned and takes possession of the fortress as he wishes.

Beneath the laurel tree the walls of Taurus bend.

When the pact has been concluded, the enemy grieves that the enemy has been received;

Yet, however much he grieves, he does not reveal it by concealing it.

He grieves for our men because his enemy was rejoicing.

If fortune thus becomes different, it is nevertheless one and the same.

For them he is recognized as sad, for these as rejoicing.

It was the sixth month, in which the burning sword rises.

[Col. 1166A] He besieged Piscibus [“the Fishes”], and withdrew when Leo was burning.

With such assistance divinely placed at his disposal,

Lest Roger appear ungrateful by despising it,

He began to consider with himself what he might offer instead.

Employing masons, he gathers them from every quarter;

He lays the foundations of a temple in the city of Traina.

By persevering at this work [Note: [Col. 1165D] C. P.: “diligent.”], he completes it in a short time.

The ceilings of the roofs of the church are joined together;

The walls are painted with varied coloring;

It is consecrated in honor of the Virgin who bore a child;

Its endowment is greatly increased with lands and tithes;

It is clothed with ornaments and various possessions.

The episcopal chair is raised with its insignia;

The sacred clergy is increased as the funds permit;

The vessels of the altar, and vestments, are more than sufficient for the clergy.

[Col. 1166B] Candlesticks, crosses, books, and wax-lights [Note: [Col. 1166D] “Acerra and thuribles.”].

Metal bells are made to summon the people;

They produce sweet melody, sounding beautifully together [Note: [Col. 1166D] “Of beautiful harmony.”].

The sacred clergy makes music with hymns of holy praise;

The prelate sows the words of the sacred law among the nations.

Divine worship is summoned by the greater number of believers.

To whom should these things be ascribed, if not to so great a prince?

He restored the sacred law, from which it had previously fallen.

By whose aid all this is accomplished, and who promulgated this law [Note: [Col. 1166D] “Added it.”].

Let us pursue the text of the book, for these things are sufficient.

A discourse repeated too insistently sometimes becomes tedious.

The following style will tell whether anything remains.

Happy Traina, rejoice; give praises worthy of your title [Note: [Col. 1166D] “Worthy of a title of praise.”].

[Col. 1166C] In you the divine legion is first restored [Note: [Col. 1166D] “Religion.”].

Messana, joined to it, serves beneath an equal shield.

## CHAPTER XIX. The Count Besieges the Jacenses and the Civenses

In the year 1079 of the Incarnation of the Word, the Jacenses, trusting in the natural strength of the mountain on which they lived and in their numerous population—for they comprised as many as thirteen thousand households—abhorring the yoke of our people, refused to perform the prescribed service and pay the tribute.

The count, however, approaching them through envoys, now sought to soften them with flatteries, now attempted to intimidate them with threats, urging them not to rise against him, not to incur guilt through wrongdoing [Note: [Col. 1166D] “Perjury.”], and not to provoke him into attacking them. He endeavored to make them withdraw from their undertaking.

But when this produced little result [Col. 1166D], he brought up his army and began to bend by force those whom he could not bend by flattery or threats.

The mountain on which they lived was fortified on every side by rocky precipices so steep that no ascent was possible from any direction, except for one narrow entrance, cut out by art, through which a path was extended for the citizens to leave and enter. At the highest point of that ascent, a gate and a wall extending lengthwise on either side protected it. [Col. 1167A]

Since this mountain, being of broad extent, could not be completely enclosed by a siege, the count established his positions especially in those places where he judged that it could become more hostile to the enemy.

The Jacenses, as though fighting for their lives, pressed on, went around everything, relaxed nothing, fortified those places where they were most afraid, and strove tirelessly to remain present with watchful care.

Since they had driven their herds and sheep with them into hidden and cavernous places of the same mountain, keeping them safe from hostile invasion, and feared less that the enemy would carry them off, they were more hardened.

But the more attentively the count saw them persist in defending themselves, the more deeply he was inflamed with anger, because he recognized that he could do them less harm.

He was not deterred from his undertaking; rather, he strove more insistently to prevail by attempting everything. [Col. 1167B]

Accordingly, he left his Sicilian soldiers—those to whom he had already distributed the island’s possessions to the extent that he had subdued it—at Parthenicum and Cortitum [Note: [Col. 1167D] C. P.: “Cornilium”], ordering them to become hostile to the Jacenses. He himself, with the Calabrians, went to besiege Cinisum, which was likewise resisting him.

Thus, at one and the same time, establishing two sieges in a single border region, though separated from one another, he held both with the greatest determination. Frequently moving from one to the other, he did not cease to exhort, press on, attempt everything himself, remain hostile to the enemy, terrify them now with threats, now with raids, flatter his own men [Note: [Col. 1167D] “His men.”], lavish many gifts, permit greater ones [Note: [Col. 1167D] “Allow.”], draw his men into loyalty to himself, and make the enemy hostile to them.

## CHAPTER XX. He Captures the Same Places

[Col. 1167C]

It was the sixth month [Note: [Col. 1167D] C. P.: “The hostile heat thunders”]; it marks the heat of summer.

One strives to inflict harm; the other strives to make him withdraw.

They inflict and suffer harm; thus, alternating, they are pressed.

Thus, with equal desires, neither enemy is lacking to the other.

It was harvest time; it exhausts those wearied by arms.

The crops are burned; this disturbance troubles the Jacenses.

And what now harms [Note: [Col. 1167D] “Jaca.”] does not go well for the Cinisenses.

They take counsel and prepare to come to the aid of the crops.

But when they cannot do so by force, they seek to add stratagems to it.

They approach the count and attempt to make him favorable to them.

They arrange a pact and lay aside the devices of deceit.

The crops are saved, and they are reconciled with the count.

## CHAPTER XXI. The Count Gives His Daughter to the Count of Provence

[Col. 1167D]

Accordingly, in the year 1080 of the Lord’s Incarnation, Raymond, the most famous count of Provence, having heard the reputation of Roger, count of the Sicilians, because of the valor that was reported of him, sent worthy envoys who could be sent from so great a man to so great a man, and requested in marriage Matilda, the count’s daughter by his first wife—a girl of exceptionally handsome appearance.

When the count had granted this, they reported it [Note: [Col. 1167D] “After it had been confirmed by oaths on both sides that it was to be carried out, and the wedding day had been fixed, those who had come, enriched by the count with many gifts, reported to their lord, with hurried steps, that they had met him, etc.”]. He rejoiced at this news not a little, for, because of the beauty he had heard she possessed, he desired her with the most ardent love.

When he heard the date of the wedding, he hastened to anticipate the day by going in person to Sicily. The count received him with fitting honor; the agreements were renewed [Note: [Col. 1167D] “By the nobles of both parties.”]; the girl’s dowry was recorded in a written instrument [Note: [Col. 1168D] “Recorded in a signed document.”]. The betrothal was celebrated in the presence of both parties [Note: [Col. 1168D] “By the prelates of both parties, by those very men.”], with prayers offered by the bishops and sacred orders according to Catholic rite.

The affection that had gradually grown between the young man [Col. 1168B] and the girl had already matured for a long time; on the first night, as is customary, it increased immensely.

Accordingly, after the wedding had been celebrated, and not without the expense of great expenditures, the father-in-law kept his son-in-law with him for some time. At length, after making him favorably disposed by gifts, as the circumstances required, and giving each of those who had come with him an individual gift according to what he knew each man to be, he prepared ships and sent him away across a calm sea with his daughter.

They, entrusting themselves to the winds with the greatest care [Note: [Col. 1168D] “Most attentively.”], with the west wind assisting [Note: [Col. 1168D] “Blowing favorably.”], brought the bride back within a short time to the place from which they had come [Note: [Col. 1168D] “They returned.”].

## CHAPTER XXII. Chaste Marriage Is Praised

The daughter rejects her father, nor was she ashamed to leave her mother [Note: [Col. 1168D] C. P.: “to leave.”].

She is joined to a foreign count and takes delight in the union [Note: [Col. 1168D] “She delights in being joined.”].

She lacks the one by whom she was raised and possesses this other [Note: [Col. 1168D] “And the other as well.”].

There is indeed much punishment when the nurse [Note: [Col. 1168D] “The mother.”] is already an adult.

Nor does she possess the one who raised her, the lustful brother.

She esteems the outsider more than the one who is her father by right.

I do not condemn this excessively, although here I engrave such things.

Nor do I forbid or avoid it, since she is joined [Note: [Col. 1168D] “Joined.”] to her husband unwillingly.

Let her love him, and by rightly preserving the bond let her honor it beautifully.

For those whom the law joins, no judgment can repel.

So that offspring may increase and not waste away through failure.

The first woman is given and joined to the first man.

Let the two be joined by such fortune that they are one flesh.

[Col. 1168D] Thus the divine law has commanded, not a foreign one.

Scripture has depicted what must be done in the future:

Let anyone who is joined to his wife in prior love

Put his father behind him, and finally put his mother behind him.

By marital right, such a lineage is preserved.

## CHAPTER XXIII. The Duke Goes to Romania

[Col. 1169A]

Accordingly, Robert, the most famous duke of Apulia and Calabria, continually urged on by Michael, who had defected to him, directing his mind toward Romania as he had begun to do, came to Hydruntum in May of the year 1081 of the Lord’s Incarnation.

Having prepared resources worthy of so great an undertaking, he sent fifteen ships across the sea to seize some city in advance, so that, when he himself followed with the rest of the army, the weak common people—most of whom were on the expedition—would have a place in which to defend themselves from an enemy attack, if necessary.

They, committing their sails to the winds, reached Corofon by night. Having viewed the island from afar out at sea and recoiled from the multitude of enemies they found there, they did not dare to disembark from the ships at all. Instead, hastening their return, they reported to the duke that all was peaceful, even if the army were larger.

The duke, therefore, greatly encouraged, brought in the supplies and ships and hastened to cross the sea with the whole fleet. Many of those left behind, to whom he had delegated the administration of Apulia and Calabria, grieved at the fear of losing him and those who departed with him, even to the point of tears, which the affection of their devotion expressed.

Some of those who were setting out with him, however, were oppressed by such dreadful fear of the undertaking to which he was directing himself, as though they were suffering from a recurrent fever; the soldiers trembled humbly.

For although the duke’s great daring and military valor are sufficiently and abundantly clear from his many exploits, even if all else were left unmentioned, this may be noted above all without doubt: he dared to attempt to go to war against so populous an empire, so powerful an emperor, and so many thousands of enemies, hoping to subjugate them with a small force. Those who took part in the enterprise testify that he had no more than 1,300 armed soldiers with him. [Col. 1169C]

Moreover, as to the forces and strength that circumstances and time supplied him, in terms of numbers—though the sight of them provided less than sufficient support—his innate military fierceness represented them to his mind as more than sufficient, as though he possessed an abundance of the troops necessary against the enemy.

By displaying a cheerful face, he revived the spirits of his men, who were less joyful through fear, and encouraged them with generous promises of the possessions and treasures of that region, as though he had already conquered it. By offering them hope of receiving these things in the future, if they wished to act bravely with him, he made them readier to attempt the dangers of military service, from which fearful calculation had sought to dissuade them. [Col. 1169D]

After forces worthy of so great an undertaking had thus been prepared in accordance with hope, the ships were guided across the sea by a skilled helmsman. With a gentle wind favoring the swelling sails, they reached the harbor of a safe landing without mishap, and part of the fleet put in at the harbor called Herico. [Col. 1170A]

Afterward, where the river Bajosa flows into the sea, he transferred to a peaceful shore.

The duke, therefore, having obtained the calm shore according to his wish, disembarked from the ships. As soon as he touched the land with his feet and had observed the beauty and situation of the places, he is said to have spoken to his men:

“O bravest soldiers, and worthy heirs who do not degenerate from the honor of your predecessors, this is the inheritance that suits you. For its acquisition you must fight with arms.

“Do not let the clamor of the ignoble common people and of the weak, though numerous, multitude of enemies terrify you. Rather, let the appearance and fertility of the hostile land urge you to acquire it as an inheritance, as well as the beauty and abundance of the things that will belong to you after the struggle, if you act bravely.”

After saying this, he attacked and captured the fortress called Casopolis on the island of Caroli. He also subjected to his own rule the other fortress, which took the name Carofium from the island’s name, together with the whole island.

Proceeding from there, he immediately went to attack the city called Avolucia [Note: [Col. 1169D] C. P.: “Avalona.”], near the fields of Pemachios [Note: [Col. 1169D] “Amathios.”], since it lay adjacent to the border where he had landed.

When the citizens heard of the duke’s arrival, they were exceedingly terrified. Distrusting their own strength in a cowardly manner, they surrendered themselves and the city to his power.

A certain fortress not far from the city [Note: [Col. 1169D] “Near the city.”], called Canna, weakened by fear at the duke’s presence—and especially because it had surrendered Avalon [Note: [Col. 1170D] “Avalona.”], which was richer in military forces [Note: [Col. 1170D] “They made surrender.”]—was likewise subjected to him [Note: [Col. 1169D] “With them, which was called Canna.”].

## CHAPTER XXIV. The Duke Besieges Duracium

[Col. 1170C]

Recognizing that fortune was going well for him,

The duke adds many things to see.

He besieges the walls of Duracium,

With the people’s armed force on every side.

Thus the city trembled, surrounded by enemies;

Its strong walls now distrust themselves;

Threatening weapons press upon the citizens;

They exchange deaths.

But the Greek people are more thoroughly worn down by hardships,

Terrified by the enemy;

The frightened people do not return harsh wounds;

Fear had taken away their strength.

A letter is sent to Constantinople.

[Col. 1170D] It reports that the enemies are present in battle.

They ask that they come with a price [Note: [Col. 1170D] “With a plea.”] to rescue those who have been seized,

So that they may not be subjected to the enemy.

## CHAPTER XXV. The Duke Fights with the Venetians

Accordingly, when the emperor received by letter the evil news of the enemy’s presence, he sent notices urging an expedition and alarmed the whole empire. With many thousands, he prepared to meet the few enemies, who nevertheless possessed greater valor.

Believing that they could easily be overwhelmed by the multitude of his own men, he ordered the Venetians to meet him at Duracium with a very large fleet, so that, if our men happened to be defeated by him there and attempted to escape across the sea in flight, the Venetians might intercept and destroy them more easily by engaging them in a naval battle.

Faithfully fulfilling his orders, they hastened with their fleet. Three days before the date fixed for them by the emperor, they were seen by our men from afar at sea, approaching Duracium.

At their sight, our men rushed to arms and hastened to meet the enemy most eagerly, intending to fight a naval engagement.

Thus, throughout the entire day, the two sides engaged one another with the greatest ferocity.

But when the day had cooled and the sun, inclining toward its setting, seemed already to be entering beneath the liquid waves of Ocean, the Venetians, exhausted by the valor of our men, promised surrender and asked for peace and a truce [Col. 1171B] until the next day, requesting that the duke make whatever pact with them he pleased.

Our men unwisely granted what they desired, and the battle was broken off for that occasion. Our men returned to their harbor.

Our men, therefore, deceived by the false promise of surrender, spent the whole night boasting as though the enemy had already triumphed, while they awaited the next day in greater security.

The Venetians, however, lightened their ships, which had been gathered with many supplies, by unloading them in the silence of night. At the top of the mast of each ship they skillfully constructed a platform for two or three men and fortified themselves with stones and javelins for throwing. Thus they prepared themselves for defense rather than surrender.

The duke, ignorant of the deception, sent at first light the stronger men of his army to receive those who, as they had promised, were surrendering themselves. He ordered them to lead the Venetians to him, with all their possessions preserved.

But when the Venetians arrived, they displayed weapons rather than surrender. They advanced toward our men with a great onslaught, while our men, having set out less prepared, avoided the battle. The Venetians safely entered the harbor of Duracium, to the shame and harm of our men.

Having thus gained free access to the city, the sailors joined themselves to the townspeople and the townspeople to the sailors. Throughout the night and day they took counsel together. After more than half the night had passed, under the pale moon they armed themselves, quickly moving the ships away from the shore. Sounding their trumpets, they advanced to offer battle to our men. [Col. 1171D]

Our men hastened to meet them and engaged in the fiercest combat on both sides.

But the Venetians, using cunning, directed beneath the waves through hidden passages in pipes a fire that they call Greek fire, which cannot be extinguished even by water. Deceitfully, they burned one of our ships, which they call the Cattus, amid the very waves of the liquid sea.

Our men, however, recognizing the deception, made an assault and completely sank another of their ships of no lesser value into the sea.

Thus, with loss balanced against loss, vengeance was more easily regarded as equal. Our men recoiled from their deception, while the Venetians recoiled from the valor of our men, and the battle was brought to an end on both sides.

The Venetians returned to the city’s harbor, from which they had departed; our men remained where they had first landed. [Col. 1172A]

## CHAPTER XXVI. The Duke Fights with the Emperor

The following day, at first light, with October approaching, some of our army were preparing to go in search of fodder when they discerned by the standards waving at the tops of the spears from afar that the emperor was approaching with innumerable forces.

There was a rush and uproar in the camp. Some were frightened; others, more ready in spirit, encouraged the less courageous and became stronger by restoring their confidence.

The duke, seeing that the battle was imminent, wished to inflame his men more ardently for their defense by taking away all hope of flight. He therefore burned all his ships that had been protected at sea [Note: [Col. 1171D] “Small ships.”], lest, when a fiercer battle threatened our men, the timid should avoid the struggle and flee in the hope of crossing back over there. [Col. 1172B]

The emperor approached and pitched his camp not far from our camp, with about four stadia between them. He drew up his army on every side [Note: [Col. 1171D] C. P.: “They themselves were silent.”], though on that day none of them dared undertake anything against our men, nor did any of our men dare undertake anything against them.

The following night the duke kept the first watch. The second watch, from midnight until daybreak, was kept by Bohemond, the duke’s son.

When morning came, the duke himself at the first twilight of day, and all our men rising, heard with the greatest devotion hymns to God together with the celebration of Mass. They confessed their sins contritely to the priests and fortified themselves with the ministrations of the sacred viaticum. [Col. 1172C]

Thus, with the battle lines arranged, they advanced step by step and in very close formation toward the contest.

The emperor, meeting them, saw such a multitude assembled on every side [Note: [Col. 1171D] “Pressed together.”] that no ascent of any mountain seemed sufficient to survey its furthest extent.

The English, whom they call Varangians, requested the honor of beginning the engagement from the emperor. Once battle had begun, they pressed upon our men most fiercely with tailed battle-axes, the weapons most commonly used by that people, and at first became exceedingly troublesome to our men.

But suddenly one of our battle lines burst out against them from the opposite side, beneath their unprotected flank. In a strong engagement it wounded them and, driving them from their undertaking, forced them to flee.

They sought the protection of life in the church of Saint Nicholas, which stood adjacent there. While some entered beneath it as far as its capacity allowed, others climbed over the roof in such numbers that the roofs themselves, loosened and collapsing under the weight, fell in [Note: [Col. 1172D] “When the structure itself was dissolved, they were crushed as they were placed beneath it.”], suffocating together those who had entered [Note: [Col. 1172D] “Their necks are suffocated, etc.”].

The emperor, seeing that the Varangians in whom he had placed his greatest hope of victory had been overcome feebly, and that our men were advancing against him in pursuit, was terrified and chose flight rather than battle.

The entire Greek army, leaving behind its tents and all its equipment, hastened, each man before the others, to become the first in flight.

Our men, therefore, having won the victory, pursued them as they fled, while the duke restrained them, though they did not flee far. Then they returned to the enemy camp. The duke lodged in the emperor’s tents; the others who arrived first took possession of the more valuable lodgings together with the spoils.

The duke, seeing that winter was approaching—for it was the month of October—left that place and built a fortress beside the river Daemoniorum for wintering [Note: [Col. 1173D] C. P.: “For spending the winter.”]. Calling it by his own surname, he named it Mount Guiscard.

From there, advancing daily with an armed force as far as Duracium, he frequently harassed the region with various raids.

The different fortresses of that province, unable to endure his attacks, made a pact with him, surrendered, and were reconciled to him.

## CHAPTER XXVII. The Duke Captures Duracium

[Col. 1173B]

At that time there was at Duracium a certain Venetian named Dominic, of noble birth, to whose charge the larger tower had been entrusted for its defense.

The duke, having gained some knowledge of his disposition through a casual conversation between them, began to tempt him in various negotiations—sometimes personally, though more rarely, and sometimes through others, lest it be discovered that a deceitful arrangement had been made between them by someone else—and to solicit him concerning the surrender of the city.

His mind, sick with desire, was easily corrupted, as avarice is mingled with luxury by those who make promises. Inclining from a good and honorable purpose, he slipped into what was worse.

The duke had a niece of beautiful appearance, the daughter of his brother William, the count of the principate. He promised Dominic that he would give him his niece in marriage, together with the inheritance appropriate to the girl. Using his influence as he pleased, and after oaths had been exchanged by both parties—Dominic swearing to hand over the city, and the duke swearing to give him his niece—the night was fixed for entering the city by treachery.

Certain that he would obtain the city, the duke constructed wooden ladders for scaling the walls [Note: [Col. 1173D] “For scaling them.”].

The Venetian, to assist the duke, lowered ropes from the wall for the approaching enemies [Note: [Col. 1173D] “Entangled.”].

And since it is written, “No enemy is more dangerous in doing harm than a familiar enemy,” the city was thrown into complete confusion by the man who ought to have protected it by force, because he freely granted the enemy the opportunity to burst into the city, under the name of Guiscard, with the sinister cry repeated again and again and the trumpets sounding. [Col. 1173D]

The citizens rushed to arms, unaware that the enemies were already with them inside the walls and in the higher tower. They attempted to resist in vain [Note: [Col. 1173D] “They were in the higher ground, and they fought in vain.”].

For three days they resisted as best they could [Note: [Col. 1174D] “Holding out.”], but in vain. At length, compelled by force, they made a pact and surrendered themselves [Note: [Col. 1174D] “They surrendered and, by surrendering themselves, made him…”], submitting their necks to the duke’s authority [Note: [Col. 1174D] “They are subjected.”].

## CHAPTER XXVIII. The Duke Captures Castoria

[Col. 1174A]

Accordingly, after taking possession of the city, the duke arranged matters according to his will and delegated Fortino of Rosana to administer it.

He himself advanced farther with the army, going to subjugate the whole province by conquering it.

Coming therefore to the city called Castoria, which refused to submit to his authority, he established a siege and surrounded it on every side. Remaining hostile for some time, he harassed it greatly, terrifying it with threats and occasionally softening it with flatteries.

Three hundred Varangians lived in that city, stationed there by the emperor as guards. The city was defended to a considerable degree by their protection and labor.

But when they saw our men persisting in the assault, they feared the appearance of the engines by which the city could more easily be conquered. Taking precautions for the future, lest they enter into a worse pact after the city’s capture, they concluded an agreement and surrendered.

Thus, after the city had been subjugated, all the surrounding provinces, together with the neighboring fortresses, were subjected to his authority.

He treated all who came over to him with the greatest honor, increased their possessions with gifts, and made extensive use of their advice in matters that had to be done.

He did this deliberately, so that others, when they heard of these things, might more easily attach themselves to him.

His fear, moreover, made the whole empire tremble, even as far as the royal city itself.

## CHAPTER XXIX. Benarvet Enters Catania by Treachery and Shortly Thereafter It Is Recovered by Our Men

[Col. 1174C]

While these things were being done by the duke in Romania, Roger, count of Sicily, was occupied in Calabria and Apulia with the affairs of his brother as though they were his own. Meanwhile, in Sicily, Benarvet, hostile to the Christian name, was inflicting many hardships.

He was exceedingly cunning and devoted to military practice, bold and treacherous, saying one thing with his tongue while concealing and carrying another in the silence of his heart. He was prince of Syracuse and Noto, and all the Saracens who were still rebellious in Sicily relied upon his counsel.

He approached a certain pagan named Bencimine [Note: [Col. 1174D] C. P.: “Betchumne.”], whom the count had placed in charge of Catania, the greater city. By cunning circumventions he sought to persuade him to surrender the city, offering many agreements involving gifts and possessions.

The pagan, a fitting imitator of his own name, blinded by avarice and forgetful of the oaths of loyalty he had given to the count, received Benarvet deceitfully within the city at the appointed time, together with a very large number of his men, and thereby secured for himself the name of traitor forever. [Col. 1175A]

When this deed had resounded throughout the whole island, the Christians were exceedingly ashamed that so unspeakable a fraud had been found among them. The Saracens, however, rejoiced everywhere, mocking the great disgrace of the Christian name.

Jordan, the count’s son; Robert of Surda Valley; and Elias of Cartoma [Note: [Col. 1175D] C. P.: “Crotoma”]—a man converted from the Saracens to the faith of Christ, later seized hostilely by his own people at the Castle of John, and, because he refused to become an apostate by denying it, having laudably finished his life in martyrdom—advanced toward Catania with an army.

When Benarvet learned through his scouts, whom he sent everywhere to observe everything, that they were approaching, he arranged his forces outside the city for battle and came out to meet them.

He placed as many as twenty thousand infantry slightly in front of his right wing to meet the enemy, while he himself remained stationed with the cavalry legion on the left wing, awaiting the enemy.

Our men, however, numbered only 160 soldiers. They did not delay but entered the battle, invoking God as their ally.

After making a third assault upon the infantry, they were unable to bend them, since they stood immovable. They therefore turned aside from them and fell upon the cavalry. Engaging them fiercely, they caused great slaughter and put them to flight.

Pursuing them and cutting down the last of them, they drove them as far as the city gate.

Benarvet barely escaped in flight. A very great slaughter was made among the infantry.

Our men then pitched their tents before the city and pressed the siege heavily.

But Benarvet secretly left the city by night and, fleeing with the pagan traitor, withdrew to Syracuse.

Thus the city was recovered by our men.

The pagan traitor, while demanding the rewards that had been promised, was beheaded by Benarvet, lest he surrender Syracuse as he had surrendered Catania.

## CHAPTER XXX. Angelmarus Rises Against the Count at Gerace

[Col. 1175C]

A certain common soldier named Angelmarus [Note: [Col. 1175D] “Englemarus”] had served the count for a long time.

Although Angelmarus was of low birth, the count wished, as was always his custom, to reward his service honorably because of the military valor he observed in him. He therefore gave him in marriage, despite her strong resistance, the wife of his nephew Serlo [Note: [Col. 1175D] “Who”], who had been killed by the Saracens in Sicily, together with the entire dowry appropriate to her [Note: [Col. 1175D] “With the dowry.”].

She was the daughter of Radulf, count of Bajanus, and through a woman of such distinguished lineage he wished the soldier’s nobility to become more illustrious among his companions.

At Gerace, where a quarter of the city belonged to him by the woman’s dowry, after the wedding had been solemnly celebrated, Angelmarus no longer preserved the honor of humility or recalled in his mind the lowliness of his own birth. Rather, claiming in his mind the nobility of his wife, he arrogantly sought to present himself as equal in birth and dignity to the man whose wife she had previously been.

At Gerace, where the count had secured a tower, Angelmarus first began gradually to advance its defenses, sometimes openly and sometimes by concealment, until he made it an extremely strong tower. He attracted all the people of Gerace to himself by flatteries and favors [Col. 1176A], and, by exchanging oaths with them, united them in friendship.

When this was reported to the count, he noticed Angelmarus’s insolence and feared that, trusting in the tower, he might turn to some worse undertaking in the future. He therefore humbly ordered him to take down the tower to the form of a habitable house, rebuking him for having dared to undertake such a thing without consulting him.

Angelmarus, however, after taking counsel with the people of Gerace, perversely decided to resist the count rather than obey him, having forgotten—as is customary among degenerates—the favor bestowed upon him. The people promised that they would bring him assistance [Note: [Col. 1176D] “They decided that they themselves would bring him assistance.”], and he chose this disgraceful course [Note: [Col. 1176D] “He chooses.”].

When this became known to the count, he ordered the people of Gerace to destroy the tower and deliver Angelmarus into his custody [Note: [Col. 1176D] “Angelmarus.”].

They refused to do so—not so much out of loyalty to Angelmarus [Col. 1176B] as because they hated every people of our nation and desired discord among our men more than peace.

The count, preserving his lawful authority, therefore commanded that his man be distrusted from that time forward, and then, bringing up his army, proceeded to besiege Gerace.

Angelmarus, however, by cunningly soothing the people of Gerace, kept his accomplices in folly with him for some time.

But when they saw themselves hard pressed by the count both from outside and within, they too began to abandon and grow weary of their foolish undertaking.

When Angelmarus realized this, he was terrified that they would hand him over to the count and be reconciled with him. He therefore fled and departed as an exile.

His wife, however, came to the count’s mercy and, in pious remembrance of the nephew whose wife she had been, earned permission to be escorted to her husband [Col. 1176C], with all that she possessed preserved.

The count, meanwhile, after the Greeks had effected a reconciliation, recovered Gerace.

## CHAPTER XXXI. Messana Is Fortified with Towers

In the same year, the same count, having prepared considerable funds and hired skilled masons from every part of the world, began to build at the city of Messana, laying foundations, fortresses, and towers.

He appointed diligent officials to ensure that the workers were not neglected. From time to time he came in person to inspect the work, encouraging them himself and making them more eager.

Within a short time he completed the towers and fortifications with marvelous workmanship and immense height.

Because he regarded this city as almost the key of Sicily, he considered it superior to the other cities he possessed and guarded it with stricter watchfulness, assigning faithful guardians to it.

He also constructed in the same city a church in honor of Saint Nicholas with the greatest magnificence, endowed it by increasing its possessions, and appointed clergy to serve there. He furnished it with an episcopal see but united it with the see of Traina.

## CHAPTER XXXII. The Duke Is Recalled from Romania by Pope Gregory
Therefore the most famous duke of Calabria and prince of the Apulians, Robert Guiscard, while vigorously subjugating everything among the Bulgarians, received letters in the year of the Incarnate Word 1082 from Gregory, the apostolic man of the Roman See, describing his distress. Gregory urged him with many entreaties to hasten his return to the aid of the Holy Roman Church. For the emperor of the Germans, Henry, after certain disputes had arisen between them, came to Rome with an army and, after besieging the city for some time, had stormed it with fortune assisting him. Having bound the more powerful Romans to himself in alliance and subjection [Note: [Col. 1177D] “Subjugating.”], he had shut up and besieged the apostolic man in a certain tower called that of Crescentius. In his place he had installed another archbishop—namely, the Ravennate Umbertus—without the matter having been investigated, and, contrary to the holy canons, which is unspeakable, had substituted him in the chair of blessed Peter. The apostolic man was so weighed down by the siege that no free passage for going anywhere was open to him.

Although the duke gave precedence in his mind to every advantage connected with the undertaking he had begun, when he heard of the calamity of the Holy Roman Church, and that his lord—under whom he recognized that he possessed everything he had—was so grievously distressed, he preserved the faith he had pledged and his lawful obligation. He preferred to set aside his own affairs, dear though they were, for a time, and to serve the needs of the holy Church of God and of his lord. Thus, entrusting to his son Boamund, a most vigorous soldier, the completion of what he had begun, and assigning all his forces to him, he himself, with a few men and a gentle passage by oar, made land in Apulia at Otranto.

## CHAPTER XXXIII. On the duke’s return, the treachery of the peoples is suppressed.

[Col. 1177C]

At that time many men in Apulia, insolent because of the duke’s absence, had conspired against him, wishing to usurp what belonged to his jurisdiction and supposing that, being occupied with more important affairs, he would no longer trouble to return there. Hence Gaufridus of Conversano, laying siege to the city called Oria, not far from the province of Taranto, was especially troublesome, harassing it severely.

When the duke landed at Otranto and heard that the city was under siege, he hastened to approach it with a few men. The leaders of the besieging force learned through a messenger that the duke was approaching. Terrified by his presence and deterred from their undertaking, although they were numerous, they each hastened to flee from the accustomed siege and dispersed to their own places.

The citizens, thus freed from the siege that had weighed upon them, hastened to meet the arriving duke and received him with joy and every mark of obedience. Throughout Apulia, however, the rebellions stirred up by faithlessness were calmed by his presence before his eyes and fell silent as though they had never existed.

## CHAPTER XXXIV. The duke, having summoned his brother, marches against the prince of Capua.

[Col. 1178A]

The duke summoned his brother, the count, from Sicily, assembled a very large army, and marched against his nephew Jordan, prince of Aversa, ravaging the harvests. For previously, when hostilities had blazed up between them over various disputes, his anger against the prince had grown especially hot because he had heard that Jordan had recently become the emperor’s man to the detriment of the apostolic lord and had undertaken to hold his land in his service.

He therefore came with his army before the city of Capua and the castle called Aversa. Jordan was unwilling and unable to repel him; the duke remained there for eight days and more, inflicting heavy devastation throughout the province. But Jordan was a distinguished soldier and had distinguished men with him, and many military actions were carried out on both sides in various engagements.

Returning from there through all Apulia and Calabria, the duke reviewed his army and urged it to prepare provisions and supplies so that, in the coming summer, they might go with him to Rome against the emperor.

## CHAPTER XXXV. Jordan rises up against his father.

The count, having been invited by his brother, who had recently returned from Bulgaria, intended to go to meet him in Apulia. He entrusted Sicily to his son Jordan to administer, forbidding everyone to presume to oppose him in anything he commanded.

Jordan was born of a concubine, yet was a man of great strength of mind and body [Note: [Col. 1177D] C. P. “strength.”], ambitious for glory in great affairs and desirous of his own domination. For some time, secretly following the counsel of wicked young men attached to him, he had harbored a conspiracy to rise up. When his father departed, he found, as he was told, an opportunity for his evil design. By cunningly deceiving many people, before the enterprise had been disclosed, he craftily drew away their loyalty [Note: [Col. 1177D] “Having accomplished it, he draws [them] by craft, so that whoever …”], so that whatever he himself began first, they would remain as accomplices in carrying through.

Having deceived such men [Note: [Col. 1177D] “Thus.”], he finally disclosed the plot he had long been preparing. Some were displeased [Note: [Col. 1178D] “And so on.”], but more approved. Whoever [Note: [Col. 1178D] C. P. “upright.”] resisted consenting to such proposals, each of them shamefully [Note: [Col. 1178D] “Shamefully.”] urged not to wish to break the faith he had pledged. The oaths they had given to the father, they said, would remain intact, because, when he departed, he had commanded everyone to obey whatever Jordan wished or ordered [Note: [Col. 1178D] “And so on.”].

With Jordan promising many things, assent to the wicked counsel spread among them. They presumed against the interests of his father beyond what was proper or what the father himself had permitted. Jordan seized the castle of San Marco and Mistretta for himself; once his treachery was discovered, he introduced plunderers there throughout the province. He also advanced in a hostile manner toward Traina and tried to carry away the treasures of his father that were kept there, but, frustrated in his design, returned empty-handed. For the count’s loyal men, having discovered the treachery and assembling together, drove him away from those borders when he approached hostilely.

When this was reported to his father, the count hastened back. Acting prudently as a wise man, he pretended not to march against his son, lest the frightened youth should cross over to the Saracens, who were still rebellious. Instead, he attributed everything the son had done to the indulgence due to youthful age. When Jordan was told that his father had taken his actions lightly, he approached his father under a sorrowful pact, taking little precaution against those who accompanied him.

For a time the father concealed his anger and showed his arriving son a cheerful face. But after a few days, looking to the future lest, if those who had joined their son in giving such counsel were allowed to escape unpunished, others should be carried away into presuming something similar, he summoned the twelve leading men responsible for this error, one after another, without his son’s knowledge, and had them deprived of their eyes.

Having done this, and wishing to restrain his son from such an undertaking by frightening him, he summoned him and threatened to do the same to him, pretending that he did so for the sake of justice. But his loyal men—whom he had deliberately told beforehand that he would do this—held him back. Having terrified his son, he thereafter dealt with him at his own discretion, as was proper. For discipline and the rigor of justice have fellowship with peace, as the Psalmist testifies when he says: “Mercy and truth have met one another; justice and peace have kissed” (Psalm 84:11).

Mercy must indeed be pursued in such a way that justice is not made more lenient than is proper, lest vices grow too strong. Thus the prudent father, like a wise physician, subdued this very son of his by terrifying him with such severity, so as to restrain him from wickedness.

## CHAPTER XXXVI. The duke goes to Rome and captures it.

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1083 [Note: [Col. 1179D] “Of the Incarnation, all …”], after everything had been prepared with the greatest care, the duke set out toward Rome with a very large cavalry force and also with infantry troops [Note: [Col. 1179D] “Very many.”], to free Pope Gregory from the siege [Note: [Col. 1179D] “Siege.”] of the emperor and the faithless Romans [Note: [Col. 1179D] “To liberate.”]. Gregory was also called Hildebrand before he assumed the papacy [Note: [Col. 1180D] “Because Aldebrandus had assumed his own [name?].”]. He set out to fight the Caesar, if necessary [Note: [Col. 1180D] “Were [necessary].”], and, unless he yielded, with leonine ferocity [Note: [Col. 1180D] “And against.”] [Note: [Col. 1180D] “Ferocity.”].

When they had nearly arrived, however, wishing to proceed incautiously, he arranged his battle lines and sent ahead one thousand chosen soldiers with an equal number of banners. He ordered another line of three thousand men to follow slowly. He himself prudently followed with the remainder of the army, placing the infantry and all the weaker troops in front of him.

He had heard that the emperor’s soldiers had come out to meet him and that the Romans had emerged on the side of the aqueduct, but this report was false. The emperor had already dismissed a large part of his army and was staying in Rome with a smaller force than the one with which he had arrived, suspecting nothing of the kind. When he perceived that the enemy was approaching, fearing that he was inadequate to his own strength and fearing the treachery of the Romans, although they continually promised to stand by him, he withdrew in great anguish of mind. He had already departed from the city three days earlier.

The duke therefore encountered no one who, as he had suspected, was coming to meet him in battle. He approached the city freely and pitched camp before the gate where the Tusculan road extends, beside the aqueducts. He remained there for three days, surveying the city on every side.

One dawn, approaching the gate called that of Saint Lawrence, beneath the aqueduct beside the Tiber, where he perceived that the guard was smaller and that no one on that side suspected anything, he came with one thousand three hundred soldiers. Silently placing ladders against the walls, he climbed over them. He opened the gates with iron tools and brought in his men. Shouting repeatedly for Guiscard, whose army was waiting at the bridge, and terrifying the citizens, he broke open the gate by force rather than unlocking it and brought his men inside. Thus, advancing in a direct assault, he ran as far as the tower of Crescentius, rescued the pope, and, leading him away with the honor befitting him, restored him to the Lateran palace.

There the duke first, and afterward the entire army, prostrated themselves at his feet according to due custom with offerings and presented a very large treasure.

The Romans, however, regaining their strength and forming a conspiracy among themselves, assembled on the third day and attempted to rush through the middle of the city and attack our men. A cry and din arose in Rome. Our men burst out from the tables at which they had been sitting and swiftly rushed to arms. Enemies fell upon enemies; a hard front met a hard front.

Roger, the duke’s son, who was being harassed by the Romans outside the city with one thousand horsemen without his father’s knowledge, came rushing up with the greatest speed. But while the Romans pressed on bravely, no attack prevailed until the duke, shouting for fire, set the city alight and pressed forward with sword and flame. Only then, unable to endure the conflagration, did the Romans turn to flight.

The duke pursued the fugitives, cutting down the last of them all the way to the bridge. Most of the enormous city was consumed by fire, which increased as the wind joined it. Our victorious men returned to the Lateran.

The Romans, seeing that enemies threatened them within their walls and unable to endure the burden of their attacks any longer, held a council among the wiser men of the city. They chose the sounder course: to be reconciled by making an alliance with their apostolic lord rather than persist in their foolish undertaking and be scattered by the hostile sword with no profit.

Having arranged a peace, they approached him for an interview. After using many evasions in excuse for their treachery, they finally obtained pardon and were reconciled. Bound by oaths according to the pope’s and the duke’s pleasure, they entered into an alliance.

When our men departed, the city was freed from the hostile calamity. But the apostolic man, recognizing the Romans’ treachery and taking care lest he be surrounded by another siege, followed the counsel of his loyal men. For a time he left the city, avoiding the Romans’ deceit [Note: [Col. 1181D] C. P.: “And the pontiff lived for a long time in the monastery of Cassino.”], rather than remain there and, by granting them free power over him, put himself to the test of whether they would faithfully observe what they promised. He withdrew with the duke into Apulia and came to Benevento. Thus, in the regions of Apulia, Rome remained hateful to him until the end of his life.

## CHAPTER XXXVII. The Romans are reproved.

Rome, once mighty in war and flourishing throughout the whole world,

You traversed the regions, subduing the necks of the proud;

You gave laws and governed everything with reins.

Before you, commanders, princes, and empires trembled;

The necks of kings, mastered by your bonds, were bent.

Nothing proud resisted, terrified by your sword.

You arranged whatever you wished; commanders or princes

You deposed whenever you wished, making the proud into humble servants.

By these arts [Note: [Col. 1181D] “By these.”] you exercised authority, having just judges,

And while you pursued what was just, you enjoyed prosperity.

All the kings of the world sought laws from you.

The judgment given through you remained undivided.

In no long time, through such pursuits [Note: [Col. 1181D] “This: ‘far from such pursuits.’”],

You became entangled through your own deceit in shameful affairs;

As your deceit became apparent, you grieved [Note: [Col. 1181D] C. P. “You wither.”], despicable.

Now no one fears you; you offer your back to everyone.

Your weapons, blunted, lack their points.

Your laws are corrupted, full of falsehoods;

In you every evil flourishes: luxury and greed,

No faith, no order; the Simoniac plague

Oppresses all its borders; everything is for sale.

Through you the sacred order collapses; water first came forth. [Note: [Col. 1181D] C. P. supplies these lines in the margins, as Carusius noted in his Preface, distinguishing them by the same form of lettering. MURAT.]

One pope is not enough for you; you rejoice in two mitres.

Your faith is strengthened by payments that have been offered.

While this one gives, you displace that one; when this one ceases, you recall him.

You threaten that one with this one, and thus fill your purses,

Giving the whole world error by mingling these schisms.

If the first studies of noble art had not ceased in you,

No king’s victory would have yielded to you [Note: [Col. 1182D] “Could have.”].

This soldier is indeed a Norman [Note: [Col. 1182D] “A certain one is.”], who has conquered you after defeating you;

The sacred presence of the apostles does not terrify you.

Nor do the relics of the saints recall you from your undertakings [Note: [Col. 1182D] “So many.”].

Once the source of all praise, now you are a pit of deceit;

Your character is corrupted, exhausted of noble qualities;

You serve wicked pursuits, and there is no shame upon your faces.

Rise, supreme shepherd Peter; put an end to such things.

## CHAPTER XXXVIII. Boamund defeats the emperor in battle.

While the duke was serving the needs of the apostolic lord at Rome, his son Boamund, left behind by his father among the Bulgarians, was acting vigorously and was carrying out his father’s responsibilities without difficulty. He was besieging the city called Arta [Note: [Col. 1182D] “Arse.”] and, persisting in his vigorous attacks, was striving by every means to capture it.

When the emperor heard that a city belonging to him was being hard-pressed by enemies and that the duke, whom he greatly feared, had departed, he regained his strength through the duke’s absence, assembled an army, and prepared a great force to relieve the city.

Boamund, however, came out to meet him. When the battle began, he engaged the enemy [Note: [Col. 1182D] “Joins battle.”]. In the first encounter, the men who had advanced first collided and were thrown down; those following were terrified at the sight [Note: [Col. 1182D] “His followers were then terrified at the sight.”], and flight began. The emperor thought it useful to be among the first fugitives. When the emperor had been put to flight [Note: [Col. 1182D] “He says: ‘to take flight’; when he had been put to flight.”], Boamund emerged victorious.

## CHAPTER XXXIX. The duke again goes to Romania.

When this was reported to the duke as he returned from Rome in triumphal glory, he recognized that his son was not degenerate from him. He was especially pleased that, at one and the same time, the flight of two emperors had brought triumphal glory and praise to himself and his men.

Coming into Apulia, he summoned his servants from every direction and, after arranging all his affairs with the greatest order, prepared to hasten with a very large army toward Greece and to complete what he had begun.

Finally, in September, ships from all Apulia, Calabria, and Sicily were assembled at Otranto. After the necessary forces had been brought aboard, and with a favorable wind assisting him, he reached the desired harbor. He presented himself to his son and to those whom he had left with him in the farthest regions, who had been anxiously awaiting his return, and restored them to great joy.

Thus carrying out the purpose for which he had come, he disturbed the entire country by his return. Hostile to the cities, tireless in sieges [Note: [Col. 1182D] C. P. “Persisting assiduously.”], first in engagements, never absent from the watch, now terrifying the empire with threats, now soothing it with flatteries, he made it tremble before him.

## CHAPTER XL. An eclipse of the sun occurs. The pope, the duke, and the king of the English die.

We have judged it worthy to insert in this work a remarkable omen that was seen throughout Apulia, Calabria, and Sicily, especially because we believe that we are not wholly ignorant of what such a sign portended.

In the year of the Savior’s Incarnation 1084, on the sixth day of February, between the sixth and the ninth hour, the sun was darkened for the space of three hours. The darkness was so great that those laboring at some task inside their houses could not continue what they had begun except by lighting lamps; those who wished to pass from one house to another used lanterns and torches.

Before the year had passed, the meaning of such an eclipse became clear, as far as we believe, through great loss to many. For in that same year the venerable Pope Gregory, mentioned above, sought medicine from physicians for his illness, but, his remedies having failed, died.

The duke died in July, and the most famous king of the English and duke of the Normans, William, died on the ninth day of September. The duke’s wife Gayta [Note: [Col. 1183D] C. P. “Sichelgaita.”], together with his son Roger, who at that time was staying with him among the Bulgarians, and his other barons, carried out the funeral rites with due honor, though not without justice [Note: [Col. 1183D] “Justly.”], and brought the body across and buried it at Venosa.

With the enemies gone, Greece rested joyfully in freedom; all Apulia and Calabria were thrown into turmoil.

## CHAPTER XLII. Roger becomes duke.

[Col. 1184A]

Now, while the brothers Roger and Boamund were at odds, each seeking the duchy, and while many people sought advancement now from one, now from the other, pursuing their own profit, the value of the loyalty of many Apulians became clear by experience.

Roger finally became duke with the assistance of his maternal uncle, Roger, count of the Sicilians, who, while his brother was alive, had promised the duchy to him. All the castles of Calabria, of which Count Roger had previously possessed no more than some half-share, were handed over to him in full by his nephew.

Now, since the final day of so great a prince makes it appropriate to speak of him only to the end of this book, the end of this book must also be placed here, as it seems to me, so that, speaking henceforth of the new duke together with the count, we may proceed to a new book.

[Col. 1183] Here ends the third book.

# THE FOURTH BOOK BEGINS.

[Col. 1183C]

If there were material for a new and more elegant poem [Note: [Col. 1183D] “Poem.”] to be applied to the new duke, so that a more eloquent discourse, by a young man eager for new things—as is customary at such an age—might, in a new style, exact new favor from his own merit [Note: [Col. 1183D] “Of new things, as is customary through baseness, and from the heart.”], we would proceed with the sequence of the discourse while preserving the order of the earlier poem [Note: [Col. 1183D] “Poem.”], lest, by changing our style, we should seem to do this as an act of flattery.

## CHAPTER I. Benarvet ravages Nicotrum.

Accordingly, while Count Roger was intent on the interests of his nephew, so as to establish him more fully in the duchy of Calabria, or certainly in the principality and lordship of Apulia, against the will of his rivals, Benarvet prepared a fleet at Syracuse. Coming with a naval army to Nicotrum, he devastated it from its foundations.
