After plundering everything he could, he carried away men and women as captives. Then, coming to Rhegium, he plundered a church not far from the city dedicated to blessed Nicholas, and another situated in honor of blessed George. He defiled and trampled upon the sacred images, and carried away the sacred vestments and vessels, adapting them to the uses of his men.

Proceeding from there, he attacked and devastated an abbey of nuns consecrated in honor of the holy Mother and Virgin Mary, at the border of the Scyllacian territory, in a place called Roca Asini [Note: [Col. 1184D] C. P. “Rocca.”]. He carried away the nuns after dishonoring them by shameful violation.

## CHAPTER II. The count engages Benarvet.

Because of this, the count, divinely inspired with anger more than usual, rose up most ardently to avenge such an injury inflicted upon God. Beginning on the first day of October to prepare a fleet with which he might more easily surround and crush Benarvet, he completed it on the twentieth day of May.

Thus afflicting himself, he carried out processions with the greatest devotion through various churches, barefoot, during the litanies; he bestowed many gifts upon the needy and committed himself to the dangers of the sea. He set his sails toward Syracuse.

He ordered his son Jordan to come there to meet him with a cavalry army. Seeing that the ships were being driven by God’s will, cutting through the swift waves of the sea in a straight course, with neither wind nor rower pushing them forward, he could readily understand that God’s favor accompanied this expedition and that it ought to prevail over the enemies [Note: [Col. 1184D] “By favor.”].

The count, therefore, having been made more confident by an indication of victory [Note: [Col. 1184D] C. P. “By the manifestation.”], landed on the first night at Turoneum [Note: [Col. 1184D] “Tauromentum.”], on the second at Longaevum, and on the third at Resesalix [Note: [Col. 1184D] “Longina, and on the third Beselap.”].

There his son Jordan, having met him with a cavalry force, held much discussion with him about what ought to be done. After taking counsel together, they sent Philip, son of George, their uncle [Note: [Col. 1184D] C. P. “Gregory the patrician.”], in an extremely swift sailing vessel to Syracuse to investigate the whole situation.

He faithfully fulfilled his orders. By night he sailed around among the Saracen fleet as though he were one of them, for he and all the sailors who had set out with him were thoroughly skilled in their language. After prudently observing everything, he returned and reported that battle was ready and, God being favorable, that no danger threatened. He urged them to meet the enemy boldly.

It was Saturday. The count reminded his men and, as dawn broke, heard the morning hymns together with the celebration of Mass. They confessed to the priests and were initiated into the sacred mysteries. They remained there throughout the day.

In the middle of the following night, after the anchors had been drawn up, they proceeded silently. As the moon shone, they came to Syracuse, where Benarvet was waiting most fiercely with his fleet. They entered battle; both sides engaged.

Benarvet, prompted by the devil, who wished to bring his life to an end by a wretched death, recognized the count’s ship from a distance. Rushing forward with great force, he attacked it and fought fiercely, but was received even more fiercely.

For after being pierced first by a spear cast by a certain Lupinus, he pursued the count with a threatening sword when the count had leapt aboard his ship. Benarvet then tried to reach a nearby ship belonging to his men in a leap in order to flee, but he sank into the sea under the weight of the iron. Thus, by divine judgment, he was punished with a fitting vengeance and suffered the penalty for the injury he had arrogantly inflicted upon God.

The others, while attempting to flee, were pursued by our men with rapid rowing and cut down.

If Jordan had meanwhile attacked the city, it would certainly have been easily defeated and surrendered; but his father, acting less prudently, had forbidden him to do so. From May until October, therefore, while a siege was laid against the city and it resisted strongly, there was much harassment on both sides.

The citizens, however, having many Christians held captive inside the city, released them and drove them out, thinking that our men would thereby easily withdraw from the city. But when they saw that our men nevertheless persisted, Benarvet’s wife, with his son and the city’s leading men, escaped by night in two ships through the middle of our fleet, rowing with the greatest speed, and made their way to Noto.

The rest, after arranging a treaty, surrendered themselves and the city in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1085.

## CHAPTER III. The Pisans attack Africa and offer it to the count to retain.

While these events were taking place, the Pisans, who were conducting commerce in Africa, suffered certain injuries. Gathering an army, they attacked the city of the king of Tunis and captured it as far as the great tower in which the king defended himself.

But because, after conquering the city by their own strength, they were not strong enough to retain the country, they invited the Sicilian count by messengers, knowing him to be very powerful in such matters, and offered it to him if he wished to accept it.

He, however, because he had said that he would preserve friendship with the king of Tunis [Note: [Col. 1185D] “Thuminus.”], preserved his lawful obligation and delayed assenting to the latter’s injury.

When King Tunis [Note: [Col. 1185D] “Thuminus.”] could not resist by fighting, he purchased peace at a price. Being less able to resist them by arms, he used money to keep the fleet from the lands of the Christian name [Note: [Col. 1185D] C. P. “He keeps it from his borders, also promising, under the pretext of his law, that no fleet, and so on.”], while they promised not to attempt any further invasion [Note: [Col. 1186D] “To attempt further invasion.”]. He was also compelled to release the captives of the same religion whom he held.

## CHAPTER IV. Duke Roger and his brother Boamund are reconciled.

Duke Roger prudently arranged his affairs in Apulia and Calabria, acting vigorously and carefully in everything. Although he was still young, judging him by his conduct one could consider him no longer young, but an old man in character.

He was constant in military affairs, fond of the company of soldiers, approachable in conversation, generous with gifts, indefatigable in labor and vigils, a defender of churches, a consoler of the poor and sorrowful, a shield to his own men and a goad to his enemies. He judged everything justly, except that, when the feeling of compassion intervened, he was somewhat more lenient in the rigor of justice.

By these qualities, increasing in him, he quickly gained the favor of all good men.

Boamund, who had broken away from his brother out of ambition for the duchy and had already obtained the city called Oria through the treachery of its citizens, was harassing the province of Taranto and Otranto. He had bound accomplices to himself everywhere in the hope of plunder.

Roger saw that Boamund was making little progress against him—not because he was not a most distinguished soldier, but because he lacked the necessary resources for the undertaking. Moved by brotherly affection, he summoned him to himself and reconciled him, granting him a portion of their paternal inheritance.

He agreed to let him retain the city of Oria that he had seized, and added Taranto, Otranto, and Gallipoli, with all their dependencies, as well as whatever Gaufridus of Conversano held under him, together with his household.

As for the rest, if any were adversaries, Roger overthrew them by his own vigor. Wherever he was less able to manage matters himself, he used the Sicilian count as a whip against the others, and many, terrified by the count’s power, did not dare to resist him strongly.

## CHAPTER V. The count besieges and captures Agrigentum.

[Col. 1186C]

Count Roger rejoiced that all the more powerful men of Sicily had been defeated by him and that no one except Chamuto remained. He therefore devoted himself through constant deliberation to this purpose: once Chamuto had been surrounded and defeated, to bring all Sicily thereafter under his rule.

Accordingly, he brought up his army and remained at the Castle of John, while he marched against the city of Agrigentum to besiege Chamuto’s wife and children. This occurred in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1086, on the first day of April.

He surrounded the city on every side with his army and harassed it through a long siege. By applying himself to the engines prepared for capturing the city, he finally exhausted its strength. On the twenty-fifth day of July, with the enemy pressing upon it, the city opened its gates; Chamuto’s wife was found with the count’s children, caught in the captivity [Note: [Col. 1186D] C. P. “Entangled in the captivity.”].

The count therefore, having established himself in the city according to his pleasure, decided that Chamuto’s wife should be guarded by his men, with every dishonor forbidden. He knew that Chamuto would be more easily reconciled to him if he learned that she had been taken without dishonor.

He arranged the city according to his will, fortified it with a very strong castle, surrounded it with a ditch, and equipped it with towers and defenses. He harassed the neighboring castles with raids and compelled them to surrender. Thus, within a short time, he brought eleven of them under his control and bound them to himself. Their names are:

Platonio, Missor, Gastajel, Satuti, Racel, Bifar, Muclofe [Note: [Col. 1187D] “Missar, Gnastilel, Satiri, Gemellos, Raselbisar, Miclufe.”], Garo, Calatenissa—which, translated into our language, is rendered “Castle of Women” [Note: [Col. 1187D] “Castle.”]—Lerata, and Remise [Note: [Col. 1187D] “Lecata, Remunisse.”].

## CHAPTER VI. Chamuto becomes a Christian; the Castle of John is surrendered.

The count, recognizing through God’s mercy that everything was proceeding favorably for him, added the Castle of John to his plans, seeking to bring it under his control either by force or, at any rate, by craft and some arranged treaty.

One dawn, therefore, he hurried toward the Castle of John with one hundred soldiers and invited Chamuto to speak with him under an established treaty. By testing him with various circumlocutions of speech, he pressed him to surrender the castle and to convert to the regeneration of Christ’s baptism.

Chamuto, however, having learned from the example of others that, whatever the count undertook, he strove at nothing in vain when fortune favored him, and having also been secretly inspired in his heart with some inclination toward conversion to the faith, secretly arranged with his men that, at an appointed time, the count should come with an army before the castle and receive him as he fled to him with all his possessions.

For he feared that, if it became openly known that he was attempting to surrender the castle or convert to the Catholic faith, he would be killed by his own people.

The count, delighted by such a promise, returned to Agrigentum. At the appointed time, he silently gathered his army and concealed himself in ambush not far from the Castle of John, at a place previously agreed upon between them.

Chamuto loaded all his mules and horses, as though he intended to travel somewhere, and departed from the city. Deliberately, he fell into the ambush of our men and was received by them. Once the matter became known, our men attacked the Castle of John.

The citizens, exhausted by this event, were terrified and arranged a plan suited to the circumstances. After a treaty had been established, they were reconciled to the count. The castle was added to the surrender.

The count was pleased to have obtained the Castle, and stronger towers were assigned to our people for its defense. Chamuto, together with his wife and children, became a Christian, subject only to this condition in the agreement: that his wife, who was connected to him by a certain degree of consanguinity, should not thereafter be forbidden to remain with him.

Chamuto, either delaying or distrusting further residence among his own people, and fearing that the count might suspect him of some deceit or believe him less than fully, requested from the count land in Calabria, in the province of Melitina, sufficient for his own needs. The count willingly granted his request, and Chamuto withdrew there.

He lived for a long time afterward and henceforth showed himself irreproachable, wholly free of treachery toward our people.

## CHAPTER VII. The count appoints bishops throughout Sicily.

The Count, seeing that by God’s favor all Sicily, except Butera and Noto, had submitted to his rule, began, lest he prove ungrateful for so great a benefit bestowed upon him by God, to live devoted to God: he began to love just judgments [Col. 1188A], to execute justice, to embrace truth, to attend church with devotion, to stand present at the sacred hymns, to assign a tenth of all his revenues to the holy churches, and to be a considerate consoler of widows and orphans, as well as of those who mourned. Throughout all Sicily he repaired churches, himself contributing funds from his own resources in many places so that the work might be completed more easily. In the city of Agrigento he exalted the episcopal see with pontifical insignia; he endowed it hereditarily, by his charters, with lands, tithes, and various resources sufficient and properly assigned to the bishop and clergy, while fully providing ornaments and vessels for the sacred altar. To this church he appointed as bishop a certain Gerland, a native of the Allobroges, a man, as they say, of great charity and learned in ecclesiastical disciplines [Col. 1188B].

He did likewise at Mazara, fully assigning everything that would properly suffice for the prelate and clergy, and ordained as bishop a certain Stephen of Rouen, a man of honorable life. At Syracuse, adding the same provision, he raised to the pontifical dignity Roger, dean of the Church of Troina, a cleric of honorable learning, a man of good character and affability, born in the province. The people of Troina grieved greatly at his loss, since by his teaching and example he was always exhorting them to better things; and in secular affairs as well they used his counsel and eloquence as though they were a staff of support. Indeed, when the bishop was absent, he carried out the responsibilities delegated to him with complete prudence [Col. 1188C] and moderation.

At Saint Euphemia, however, he intended to ordain as bishop a certain monk, a Briton by nationality, a religious man who, after the abbot, governed the whole church with prudent moderation, so that he might obtain him for the Church of Catania [Note: C. P. “if he can.”]. He therefore went there in person and, only with difficulty, obtained this from the monks, who were reluctant to be deprived of him, although the man himself resisted more strongly than all the others. Thus, solemnly granting him the bishopric—something he is known to have done for none of the other bishops—he assigned the entire city, with all its dependencies, to its see, to be possessed hereditarily under charter and witnesses. The bishop, receiving a church that was little cultivated, as one snatched from the jaws of an unbelieving people, first devoted himself with particular zeal to the study of law; [Col. 1188D] then, within a short time, supplying the church with everything necessary, he passed from Mary’s role to the work of Martha [Note: “of Martha.”]. Gathering to himself a considerable company of monks, he compelled them, as a faithful shepherd, to submit in word and example to the yoke of a strict rule.

## CHAPTER VIII. King Philip of the Franks Seeks the Count’s Daughter as His Wife

At that time Philip, king of the Franks, had a legitimate wife of illustrious lineage, named Bertha, by whom he had fathered a son named Louis [Col. 1189A] [Note: C. P. “Ludovicum,” “Louis.”]. He had also designated before all his courtiers that the kingdom would belong to this son after him. Yet, contrary to the law of legitimate union, he caused himself to regard Bertha with hatred and attempted to cast her away from him by a writ of repudiation, contrary to the statutes of the canons. He alleged no crime against her, except that he attempted, falsely and unsuccessfully, to count consanguinity among the grounds.

He sent envoys to the Count in Sicily and requested that his daughter, named Emina, a beautiful girl whom he had by his first wife, be joined to him in marriage. The Count, unaware of the fraud he was practicing against his legitimate wife, agreed to give her to him with a rich dowry. When the appointed time had been fixed and the ships prepared, he sent her by sea as far as Saint Ægidius, with many treasures as a wedding gift, to the place where the king had said he would meet her. [Col. 1189B] He trusted Raimund, the Count of that province, to deliver her honorably to the king, for Raimund himself had long before married another daughter of the Count.

The king, however, following the advice of wicked men, was intent on taking possession of the treasures and deceiving the Count by refusing to marry his daughter. Once Raimund discovered the king’s fraud, he too began to devise another fraud: namely, that he would receive the girl honorably while concealing the deception, give her in marriage to another honorable man, and himself appropriate all the money.

But the prudent men whom the Count had sent with his household discovered, through the girl’s pleas, the fraud that was being perpetrated. They carried away the money, weighed anchor, committed the sails to the winds, left the girl with her enraged husband, and, as a gentle breeze blew, returned to the Count in Sicily with the more valuable treasures. [Col. 1189C] Count Raimund, thus partly thwarted in the fraud he had contrived, married the girl to the Count of Clermont in a lawful marriage. Thus, by God’s sole dispensation, she was solemnly married, and both the father was freed from the disgrace that the king had contrived and the daughter from any irregular and unlawful union.

## CHAPTER IX. Mihera Enters Maia

Mihera, son of Hugh Foloch, a man of great levity but a most accomplished knight, using his left hand as his right, broke out into insolence after Duke Robert’s death. He began to attack his neighbors all around him, harassing them with plunder and various raids. At that time he possessed the castles inherited from his father, Catanzaro and the Rock; but, seeking still more by force of arms and presuming even against the duke himself, he invaded and usurped the castle called Maia, through the betrayal of its citizens.

Wishing to add allies to his own forces, he became a man of Bohemond, the duke’s brother, who had already broken the treaty and conspired against his brother. Bohemond received Mihera, after he had renounced the duke, into his alliance by oaths; he received Maia, which Mihera had invaded, and all the land that Mihera held under the duke as his hereditary inheritance from his father.

## CHAPTER X. Bohemond Invades Cosenza

[Col. 1190A]

Bohemond, driven by an ambition to obtain cities through invasion and eager to surpass his brother, secretly negotiated with the people of Cosenza concerning the betrayal of the city. He promised that, if he could capture it with their help, the castle that the duke had built in the same city, detested by them, would be utterly demolished. Enticed by this promise and inclined to fraud, they agreed with Bohemond and received him within the city with his armed force. They entered into an alliance with him by oaths and, surrounding the castle, went to attack it.

When this was reported to the duke in Apulia, where he was then staying, he brought up his army and hastened there. He sent word inviting his uncle to come to his aid and not delay in meeting him at Cosenza [Col. 1190B]. For, as we have said, he used that man against all who opposed him, as though he were a scourge for terrifying others.

The Count, having prepared his cavalry and infantry, hastened to meet his nephew, who had invited him. But before either army—that of the duke or that of the Count—had arrived, the castle under attack, while resisting as best it could, was exhausted by the engines brought against it and surrendered to the enemy. It was then utterly demolished, as Bohemond had promised.

The duke, meeting the Count on the way, attacked and captured Rossano, which had agreed to Cosenza’s treachery, ravaging everything with fire. Bohemond, therefore, to avoid being enclosed within the city by a siege, withdrew to the Rock, leaving Hugh of Clermont at Cosenza to hold the people in his allegiance [Col. 1190C].

The duke and the Count, thinking that Bohemond had departed for Maia, went there intending to forestall him. But when they discovered that he was not there, they hurried toward the Rock and pitched their tents at a place called the Grove of Calupnius. There, through intermediaries, with peace established between both sides, they fixed a date for meeting at Saint Euphemia and effecting a fuller reconciliation.

Mihera agreed to this arrangement, but Bohemond did not. He delayed reconciliation and had already withdrawn to Taranto. When the appointed day drew near, Mihera requested a safe-conduct, by which he might come and depart under the treaty. It was granted, and he came; without consulting Bohemond, he was reconciled to the duke. Maia was returned and restored to the duke, to whom it rightfully belonged.

Thus, after two years of dissension, the brothers were reconciled through the counsel of the faithful men of both sides [Col. 1190D]. The duke granted Cosenza and Maia to Bohemond, as he was always most generous toward him. But this arrangement lasted only a very short time, because Bohemond had sworn to the people of Cosenza that he would not build a castle there, while the duke had made the same oath to the people of Bari. An exchange was therefore made between them: the duke received Cosenza and granted Bari to his brother in return, so that each might freely exercise whatever authority he wished in his own right, without interference. Thus, confirming their friendship by witnesses and charter, they thereafter maintained it unbroken.

## CHAPTER XI. Mihera Becomes a Monk

Mihera, therefore, having long remained rebellious while Count Roger and Radulf of Loracello [Col. 1191A] [Note: “With Lodocellus as leader, he added an additional force for a longer period of raiding.”] harassed him, saw that his offenses had exceeded the bounds of reconciliation and could no longer endure them. He assigned all his land to his son Adam, thinking that, with help from his maternal relatives, Adam might more easily resist his enemies or at least be reconciled with them. Mihera himself withdrew to Benevento and, joining the monastic life, put on the habit.

Neither the duke nor Bohemond was his friend, because he had deceived each of them in turn by breaking his treaty with them. For this reason the Count and Robert of Loracello, already asking that the duke grant them Mihera’s land, obtained it more easily.

The Count sent his knights against Adam under the leadership of Radulf of Loracello. Adam resisted their prolonged raids for some time, but was eventually brought low by scarcity. When he saw that he could endure no longer, he burned his palace and all the better houses at night, while he was being attacked, and, abandoning the castle to the enemy, withdrew in the year 1086 of the Incarnate Word [Note: A.D. 1087.].

The Count and Radulf of Loracello divided his land between themselves, as it had been granted by the duke [Note: “As granted by the duke.”], and thereafter held it as their own [Note: “By lot.”].

## CHAPTER XII. The Count Besieges Butera

Accordingly, after Count Roger had pacified all Sicily by a treaty concluded against his opponents, except that the people of Noto—in whose city Benarvet’s wife had taken refuge with her son—and the people of Butera still resisted as best they could, he brought up his army and went to besiege Butera in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1088, at the beginning of April [Col. 1191C].

## CHAPTER XIII. Pope Urban Comes to Sicily to Speak with the Count

Arming himself prudently and surrounding the place on every side in a hostile manner, he afflicted those enclosed there for some time with various hardships. But while he was laboring intently over the engines prepared to assault the castle, a legate of Pope Urban arrived with letters sealed by the pope. He announced that the pope himself had entered Sicily and ordered the Count to come to him at Troina. The pope was fatigued by a long journey: he had departed from Terracina and, because of bodily exhaustion and the mountain passes still lying ahead, did not wish to proceed farther.

The Count was anxious about what he should do. He considered it damaging to abandon the seat of war, yet, as a Catholic man, he judged it unworthy not to meet the pope, who had come to him from so great a distance [Col. 1191D]. At last, having accepted prudent counsel, he arranged matters so that he would neither abandon the seat of war nor prove disobedient by failing to meet the apostolic visitor.

He entrusted the army to his faithful men, prudent and experienced in such affairs, and instructed them to harass the enemy. He himself, with a few companions, went to meet the pope at Troina. They were joyful at their meeting, and each received the other with the greatest reverence: the pope received the Count with apostolic blessing in the role of Mary, while the Count served the pope in the necessities of the body, in the role of Martha. On the following day, they met at first light and discussed the matter that had compelled the pope to come.

A few days earlier, the pope had rebuked Alexius, emperor of Constantinople, through Nicholas, abbot of Grottaferrata, and Roger the deacon. He reproached him as a father because he had forbidden the Latin Christians living in his province to offer sacrifice with unleavened bread, ordering them instead to use leavened bread according to Greek custom—a practice entirely absent from our religion.

The emperor humbly accepted this rebuke and, through the same envoys, invited the pope in letters written on golden tablets to come with learned Catholic Latin men, so that, once a council had been convened at Constantinople, a disputation might take place between Greeks and Latins. By a common definition, they would remove from the Church of God the practice whereby the Greeks offered with leavened bread and the Latins with unleavened bread, so that the one Church of God might observe one custom.

He said that he would willingly consent to a Catholic examination and that whatever was determined by authoritative judgments, in the presence of Greeks and Latins—whether the sacrifice should be offered with unleavened or leavened bread—he would thereafter observe. He also fixed a time by which the pope should come, namely, a year and a half.

The Count advised that the journey should be undertaken, so that so great a schism might be cut away from the Church of God. But the journey was prevented by enemies of the holy Church of God who remained hostile to the pope in Rome.

The Count therefore dismissed the pope, honoring him with many gifts. He himself returned to Butera and, continuing to harass the enemy, eventually compelled them to surrender. Having thus obtained the castle, he arranged matters according to his will and sent the more powerful men to remain in Calabria, lest those who stayed there should contrive some fraud and cause an uprising.

## CHAPTER XIV. The Count Marries Adelaide

In the year 1089 of the Incarnation of the Savior, Count Roger’s wife, Elemburga [Note: C. P. “Eremburga.”], daughter of William, count of Mortain [Note: “Morintonensis.”], having died, he married another woman named Adelaide [Note: “Adelaida.”], the niece of Boniface, the most famous of the Italian margraves, namely, the young daughter of his brother, a girl of exceedingly honorable appearance.

He also married two sisters of this same girl to two of his sons, namely, Geoffrey and Jordan. But Geoffrey, before he reached marriageable age—painful as it is to say—never knew her because illness prevented it; Jordan, however, married her in a solemn wedding.

## CHAPTER XV. The People of Noto Are Reconciled to the Count

The people of Noto, seeing all Sicily bent beneath the Count and realizing that further resistance was useless, deliberated among themselves and judged it advantageous to be reconciled with him. They chose envoys from among themselves and sent them to the Count [Col. 1193A]. Coming to him at Melito, where he was then staying, they made peace in February of the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1090.

The Count therefore remitted their tribute for two years and sent with them Jordan, his son, to whom he had also given land and a wife, so that he might receive the city when they surrendered it. Instructed by his father, Jordan took possession of the city, fortified the castle, and arranged matters according to his own will while remaining faithful to his father. Benarvet’s wife, however, fled to Africa with her son.

When all Sicily had been pacified, Count Roger, not wishing to be ungrateful for the benefit God had bestowed upon him, began in every way permitted by the worldly cares that occupied him to show himself devoted to God. The more he recognized that God had raised him to a higher position in earthly honor, the more zealously he acted so that, remaining in a state of perfect humility, he might fix the step of his mind firmly there.

He summoned his soldiers, by whose help he had attained the summit of such honor, and thanked them with complete gentleness. To some he repaid the sweat of their labor with lands and extensive possessions; to others, with various additional rewards.

## CHAPTER XVI. The Count Goes to Malta

After wisely arranging all Sicily according to his will, the Count, accustomed to military exercises, unable to endure idleness, eager for labor, and desirous of gain, did not allow his body to grow unaccustomed to its habitual exertions. Instead, he considered with attentive mind and continual reflection which overseas kingdoms he should first bring under his authority [Col. 1193C].

When he learned from reports that the island of Malta was nearer to him than the others, he ordered a fleet to be prepared quickly to attack it and announced by command that his soldiers should prepare themselves for this undertaking.

While these things were being done, Mainerius, whom the Count had invited to come and speak with him at Gerentia, delayed coming. In the presence of the Count’s legate, he answered arrogantly that he never wished to see the Count except to inflict harm upon him, if he could.

When the envoy who had been sent reported this, the Count heard it and was greatly angered. He crossed the sea in haste and came from Sicily to Calabria. He sent Peter of Mortain, to whom he had entrusted his authority to a considerable extent, ordering him to raise an army throughout Sicily and hasten after him.

Peter prudently carried out what had been commanded. Within eight days he gathered a large army from all Sicily and brought it to the Count at Malo [Note: “In the meadow of May.”]. The Count then hurried toward Gerentia and surrounded the castle with a terrifying siege.

Mainerius was frightened by this. Recognizing that he had acted and spoken foolishly, he came humbly to seek the Count’s mercy. He placed in the Count’s hands his horses, mules, treasures, and everything he possessed, asking pardon.

Seeing that he repented of what he had done, the Count, as always a man of merciful heart, forgave everything except that, more as a matter of discipline than from ambition, he took a thousand gold solidi from him [Col. 1194A], to restrain him from such presumption in the future.

He then departed through the difficult terrain of the neighboring mountains and came to Cosenza. Because the inhabitants of that province were resisting the duke, he uprooted their vineyards and olive groves for three days, then withdrew to Arata. There he took counsel with his men and soon disbanded the army, ordering each man to return home and prepare for the expedition against Malta. He fixed a period of fifteen days, by which time they were to meet him at Resacramba, for he had ordered his fleet to assemble there.

This harbor differs from others because of the nature of its dryness. If someone, for the sake of testing it, takes a reed or some other hollow object and, two cubits from the shore out into the sea [Note: C. P. “one cubit”], drives it only a palm’s breadth deep into the seabed, of such a length that its hollow upper end may reach as far above the waves as one wishes, one sees the sweetest, drinkable waters bubbling upward through the hollow, although the sea is extremely salty [Note: “You may see this.”].

When the appointed day arrived, and a very large army had gathered from all Sicily and Calabria in the month of July, the Count hastened one evening to board the ships [Note: “To enter.”].

While the fleet was being prepared, Count Roger’s son Jordan had always suspected that his father would not go to Malta but would entrust him with leading the army there. At the very moment he was boarding the ships, however, the Count summoned Jordan and ordered him to remain behind with the men he selected to govern Sicily. He forbade him to enter any city or castle until the Count returned from Malta. Instead, he was to live in the tents and remain ready wherever assistance was needed throughout Sicily, awaiting his father’s return [Col. 1194C].

Jordan, hearing his father command something different from what he had expected, was struck with utter astonishment. He tried to dissuade his father from what he was saying and cried with tears that, if it pleased his father, he should rather be enrolled as a young man for so great a labor; his father, already a man of almost retired service, should refresh his body, so greatly wearied by labor, with the pleasures of rest. It would be less damaging if he, a young man of lesser worth, perished in so great a danger than if a man of such authority and such wisdom did so.

The Count was angered by his son’s words. He rebuked him severely before everyone and declared that he would never send either his son or anyone else to a place where he himself did not dare to be first. Just as he was first in possessing or distributing things, so it was fitting that he should be first in acquiring them [Col. 1194D].

Many of those who were departing returned out of affection for him and then wept. The Count boarded the ships. At his command, trumpets sounded and instruments of various kinds played melodies, each according to the skill of its musician. The anchors were raised, the sails were committed to the winds with great display, and, with a favorable breeze assisting, they reached Miletus on the second day [Note: “Malta.”].

The Count’s ship, faster than the others, reached land first. The Count disembarked, mounted a horse with only thirteen soldiers, and attacked the great multitude of inhabitants who had come to the shore to prevent his landing. He struck down many, put the rest to flight, and pursued the fugitives for a long distance, killing all whom he overtook. In the evening, returning from the pursuit, he and his entire army took lodging that night on the seashore.

At dawn the next day he approached the city more closely and surrounded it with a siege. He sent his men throughout the island to plunder. Gaytus, who ruled the city and the island, and the other citizens, little accustomed to military exercises, were terrified by the presence of the enemy. They requested permission to come freely to a conference with the Count for the sake of peace. The Count granted this, and they came to his tent to speak with him and make peace.

After employing various circumlocutions, they finally realized that they could not deceive the prince with their cunning. According to the Count’s will, they first returned the Christian captives whom they held in great numbers within the city. They also offered the Count horses, mules, all the weapons they possessed, and an immeasurable sum of money [Col. 1195B]. They fixed the amount to be paid each year, promised that the city would serve the Count, and, after giving oaths according to their law, entered into an alliance with him.

One could see the Christian captives coming out of the city, each shedding tears from the depths of his heart for joy at his unexpected liberation. They carried in their right hands crosses made from wood or reeds, according to whatever each had first found, and fell at the Count’s feet while crying out, “Kyrie eleison”—“Lord, have mercy.” Our men, seeing this spectacle, were likewise drenched with tears of compassion [Col. 1195C].

After the city had thus entered into an alliance with him, the Count arranged for the captives to be transported by ship. He hastened his return in great fear, dreading that the excessive number of captives might cause the ships to sink. But, as we believe, God’s right hand was revealed by the outcome: lifting the ships above the waves, it carried them across the sea a cubit higher than at their outward journey, when they had been burdened by a lighter load.

As he hastened across the sea on his return, he saw from a distance an island called Golfani [Note: C. P. “Golsa.”] and ordered the sails to be directed toward it so that he might conquer it. Landing there, he attacked and ravaged it with plunder; then, recognizing that it had entered into a treaty with him, he assigned it to his dominion.

Directing his sails safely across the waters in every direction, he returned to Sicily and presented himself to his faithful men, laden with an enormous amount of plunder. He summoned all the captives whom he had rescued and brought back with him and set them free. He offered them the opportunity, if they wished to remain with him in Sicily, to have a village built at his expense wherever they chose, and to receive from his resources what was necessary for earning a livelihood. He further promised to designate that same village as a *franca*, that is, a free village, because it would forever be free from every tax and servile exaction.

To those who wished instead to see their own lands and friends, he granted free permission to depart wherever they wished, providing them with the necessities of travel throughout his entire land and passage across the Strait without charge [Col. 1196A]. They themselves, rejoicing and giving thanks to the Count for their liberation, each returned to his own region. Scattered across the various realms according to their nations, they spread abroad and magnified the Count’s name.

## CHAPTER XVII. The Duke and the Count Capture Cosenza

In the year 1091, Duke Roger, angered at the people of Cosenza, who had long remained rebellious, gathered an army from all Apulia. He decided to go and besiege them in May, taking his brother Bohemond with him, and invited his uncle, the Count, from Sicily, asking him not to delay in coming to meet him there with aid [Col. 1196B].

Because of his affection for his nephew, the Count raised many thousands of Saracens from all Sicily and also recruited companies of soldiers. He hastened eagerly to the place to which he had been invited.

When the people of Cosenza heard that the enemy was approaching them, they fortified themselves with a ditch and walls, prepared weapons and everything necessary for defense, brought supplies required by nature into the city, and encouraged one another to defend themselves rather than surrender.

The duke and the Count met one another at Cosenza and surrounded the city on every side. The duke occupied the plain with his siege. The Count climbed into the mountains, where greater difficulty and a more hostile enemy threatened, and ordered his men to encircle the city with their camp.

The people of Cosenza, shut in on every side by the ditch and palisades at the prince’s command, were greatly terrified when every possibility of entering, leaving, or bringing anything inside had been removed [Col. 1196C]. Thus the struggle continued without interruption, a constant battle.

The people of Cosenza placed their greatest hope of defense in slings and arrows. They considered it dangerous to approach more closely and engage our men at sword’s length. The Count, sometimes coaxing them toward surrender with gentle words, but more often frightening them with threats, urged his men on and encouraged them. He inspected everything, left nothing unattempted, undertook first whatever needed to be done, led his men into battle, and followed behind them when they withdrew. He strove to provide for everything through prudent organization, making all more vigilant in carrying out their duties by his own example.

The people of Cosenza, having long recognized the Count’s steadfastness and abandoning hope of keeping the enemy from their borders, deliberated among themselves and prepared to surrender the city, if they might perhaps obtain forgiveness from the duke and Count for their rebellion [Col. 1196D].

First, because they knew the Count to be a man of wiser counsel, under whose direction everything was governed, they humbly entrusted the negotiations, themselves, and their deliberations to him. They would do nothing without him, since they knew that, once he had made a promise, he would give them counsel without fraud or harm to themselves wherever this could be avoided.

He received their words as a merciful man and lover of peace, as always, and arranged the matter so prudently that the duke would possess the city according to his will, while the people of Cosenza would not be deprived of reconciliation through the duke’s favor.

The duke, having obtained the city through the valor of his uncle, built a castle of masonry on a higher ridge of the city before the expedition was disbanded, to prevent such presumption in the future [Col. 1197A]. As compensation for the service rendered to him, he assigned the Count half of the city of Pausemitana [Note: C. P. “Panormitana.”]. Thus, when the expedition was disbanded in July, the duke departed for Apulia and the Count for Sicily.

The Count fortified a castle in his portion and organized the city, now held jointly, in such a way that the duke later received more than half of it, although at first, when he possessed the entire city without a partner, he had held all its revenues.

## CHAPTER XVIII. Jordan Dies

After these events had been completed, since we promised to write in the order of time whatever was done or happened, the sequence of events forbids us to pass over and omit from this book the grievous sorrow of Sicily and Calabria, although recalling the same event in the presence of many may seem burdensome, as though it renewed the pain.

There are some who, because of the excessive affection they had for the man of whom we speak, cannot restrain themselves from tears if what happened is recounted in their presence, as though the event being narrated had just occurred.

Jordan, the Count’s son, was beloved by all because of his valor. Many suspected that he would become the Count’s heir, since Gaufred—whose illness did not lessen the sorrow—had already been afflicted by elephantiasis, and the Count had no other male child. Jordan was struck by a fever at Syracuse, a city under his own authority.

When this was reported to his father, the Count hastened to arrive before death. But as the illness worsened, Jordan’s final destiny came more quickly than his father [Col. 1197C].

When the Count entered the city and saw his son’s funeral, he was seized by unbearable grief. All who had come with him became participants in his sorrow and were swept away in tearful lamentation. For many, the father’s grief drew more tears than Jordan’s death.

The entire city resounded with tearful wailing, to such an extent that even the Saracens, hateful to our people—not from love, but because of the sorrow in which they saw our people immersed—were overcome by compassion and brought to tears.

The Count arranged the funeral with due solemnity and led the body to Troina, to be buried solemnly at Saint Nicholas [Note: C. P. “to Troina through the portico.”]. He bestowed many benefactions upon that church and upon others as well for the redemption of Jordan’s soul, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1092.

The citizens of Peutarga, a city that had hitherto belonged to Jordan [Note: “Pentarga.”], heard of the death of Jordan, whom they had greatly feared, and were swept away by empty joy. Breaking out into insolence, they foolishly attempted through rebellion to throw off the yoke of our people.

The Count, however, did not delay after burying his son. With only his household, he went to besiege them and ordered an expedition from all Sicily to follow him there [Col. 1198A]. Overcoming them by force, he hanged and killed those who had been responsible for such foolish counsel, inflicted various tortures upon the rest, and subdued the city’s folly [Note: “He subdued.”].

## CHAPTER XIX. Simon Is Born

The father bereft, his son thus carried off by grave illness,

Lest he should grieve because he lacked hereditary support,

He is enriched with offspring, as by a heavenly flower.

She conceives and grows heavy; the mother’s joyful womb

Swells. The infant grows according to nature’s progress.

Father and mother pray to God that the child may be male.

He fulfills their prayers completely, as the seed is formed [Note: “Himself.”].

Nature is now made secure within the mother’s womb.

The ninth month arrives, with hope in suspense. Thus the birth hastens.

The infant emerges. No one hates him. Joy comes to everyone.

The midwives rejoice at the mother’s happiness [Note: “At the signs of the male.”].

The news that a boy has been born brings new joys.

The mother hears and therefore applauds; she becomes unaware of sorrow.

They hasten; this joy is announced to the father.

He rejoices and applauds; like incense from heaven,

He humbly offers the incense of prayers and enriches the messenger with gifts.

He orders more gifts to be distributed to the poor, as he wishes.

The grave pain of the son’s death, the burden of his fate, now removed,

Becomes light [Note: “Lenitas,” “softness/easing.”] and is forgotten in the joy of hope in the newborn [Note: “Of joy.”].

Simon, at the font, marked on the forehead by anointing with chrism,

Is endowed as heir and strengthened as the future Sicilian duke [Col. 1198C].

The Calabrians wish their swords to be joined to his.

The father fulfills the entire desire; the duke granted that it be done [Note: “While he grants it.”].

## CHAPTER XX. Duke Roger Falls Ill

Duke Roger, who had a wife of illustrious nobility—namely, Adala, niece of Philip, king of the Franks, and daughter of Robert, margrave of Flanders, whom they called the Frisian—was the father of two children by her. At Melfi, a city of Apulia, he was seized and severely tormented by a fever in the year 1093 of the Incarnate Word.

As the illness grew worse and his vital faculties were almost obstructed, nature, as the most skilled physicians themselves testified, wandered in astonishment contrary to its customary course, so that the physicians could determine the illness neither by his pulse nor by his urine, nor by any other signs used for prognosis [Note: “In such matters”; “with them in these matters”; [Col. 1198D] “Thus”; “determination of the illness.”].

Because even the physicians seemed to despair of him, a rumor, as though he had already died, disturbed all Apulia and Calabria.

At that time Bohemond was staying in Calabria. When he heard from the rumor that his brother had already died, he believed it and invaded the castles that belonged to his brother, persuading them to enter into an alliance with him by oath. He made this distinction, however: if his brother had died—as Bohemond protested he did not wish—then, while preserving loyalty to the brother’s lawful heirs, they should remain faithful to Bohemond as the loyal uncle of those heirs until they reached an age at which they would be able legitimately to govern their land.

When Count Roger heard that Bohemond was doing these things, he was angered that Bohemond had presumed to act without consulting him. He also feared that, although he might honorably accept this profession of loyalty, Bohemond might later conceal fraud beneath decorated words [Note: “Peace”] and, seized by ambition against his nephews, contrive some deception. He therefore ordered his men to pursue Bohemond and drove him from all Calabria.

## CHAPTER XXI. William of Grantavul Enters Rossano
Many others, too, on hearing the report of the duke’s death, burst into lawless behavior and tried to appropriate for themselves, by distributing them, the things that belonged to the duke. Hence William of Grantemaniol [Note: Grantemanil.], seized by the utmost greed and inclined toward insolence, entered and occupied Rossano, a city of Calabria, saying that it rightly belonged to him because he had as his wife Mabilia, the duke’s sister and Guiscard’s daughter, and therefore ought to become a participant in the inheritance. Thus, because of the weakness of the heirs, each person displayed how great his loyalty toward them would be, while appropriating for himself the duke’s possessions by distributing them.

But Nature, which had long wandered abroad, returned to possession of her own jurisdiction and began, contrary to the physicians’ expectation, to restore him to health. As his health increased day by day, he was completely restored to his former condition. When Boamund heard this, he hastened to Melfi, where he knew his brother was, to rejoice with him over his recovery. He returned the camps that had sworn allegiance to him and showed that he had not acted deceitfully in what he had done.

William of Grantemaniol, however, enticed by shameful greed, neither hastened to rejoice over his lord’s recovery nor took care to return the city he had occupied. Instead, displaying his fraud with an impudent face, he strengthened that same city as best he could and armed it against the duke, in case he should attempt to attack it. Count Roger, greatly indignant at this, nevertheless, as a prudent man, because William was his niece’s husband, sent a messenger to him and urged him to return the city and be reconciled with his lord. But when he achieved little by gentle words, he burst wholly into anger and declared that he would rightly take from him both the city he had wickedly occupied and everything which, by the duke’s permission, he had previously held, once he had been disinherited.

## CHAPTER XXII. The Duke and the Count Besiege Castriville

Thus, rather urging the duke to undertake an expedition against William than allowing himself to be removed by the duke for avenging the injury, he brought up the army; and both proceeded to besiege Castriville in the year of the incarnation of the Savior 1094.

William had devised the following covering for his fraud. When he had first been received within the city by its inhabitants, he had confirmed by oath, under an unexpected stipulation, that he would never surrender the city to anyone except Ludovise, the duke’s son—and, because Ludovise was still a little child, that after the next ten years he would renounce the fidelity he had sworn to the duke, considering this a lesser offense and disgrace than the oath he had sworn to perjurers and fraudsters. Thus greedy ambition, together with his wife’s wicked persuasion, had readily blinded the young man’s mind against distinguishing what was good and honorable. [The manuscript’s wording is somewhat uncertain.]

The duke, having summoned forces of horse and foot from all Apulia and taken his brother Boamund as an auxiliary, together with the men of Otranto and Taranto and the others who belonged to his jurisdiction, occupied the Gratian Valley on the way toward Castriville. The count, meanwhile, gathering many thousands of Saracens from Sicily and Apulia, and also forces of Christian horsemen and foot soldiers, did not delay in hastening to meet his nephew there.

William of Gratemaniol, recognizing that men of authority had conspired against him and that a siege threatened him, prepared himself as best he could for defense. While he tried to bring auxiliaries to himself from every direction—although it is customary for young men to take part willingly in such enterprises for military glory and gain—they feared both the count’s anger and the duke’s, and, despite his many promises, did not dare to join him. They were especially afraid because they foresaw that fortune was opposed to him and therefore turned him away with some dishonor.

The duke waited in the Gratian Valley for the count to arrive, advancing as far as the castle called Saint Maurus. He received the citizens’ surrender on the condition that, for as long as he lived, they would never return it to William. From there, passing as far as Rossano, he offended those who were less willing to agree with him, because William had brought the sons of the city’s more powerful citizens to himself as hostages.

But the duke had already, a year earlier, against the will of the Greeks—who for the most part ruled that city—appointed a Latin successor to the deceased Greek archbishop of the see. Since the appointee had not yet been confirmed by oath or sacred anointing, the duke abandoned the Latin election and allowed the Greeks to choose an archbishop for themselves from among their own people, according to their wishes. Having thereby won their favor, he also obtained their city’s surrender. But when he attacked the castle, he could not prevail because William’s loyal supporters resisted.

The count, arriving with his army and rejoicing that the duke had already made such progress, made camp near the castle of Tarsia, beside the river flowing down from Saint Mark, where the duke had already pitched his tents. William, invited by the count to come safely for a conference, approached him. After employing many stratagems, while concealing his fraud, he restored to the duke what he had occupied.

The duke, seeking an order for the matter, summoned William and demanded that he be reconciled to him, so that he might uphold justice according to the judgment of the count and the other prudent men present. He adjured William by oath and pledged faith to him, despite the fact that William had so long acted unjustly toward him. Conscious of his guilt and afraid of being overwhelmed by the judgment, William refused. Having received permission to depart, he returned safely to Castriville.

The duke and the count followed him on the next day with their entire army and surrounded the castle with a siege. They enclosed it by fencing it in with timber and armed forces so completely that the inhabitants of Castriville had no entrance by which they could go out or bring anything in. They possessed only a small amount of food within the walls, and, pressed by the enemy for three weeks, exhausted the provisions they had.

William then did what had initially been demanded of him: if he were received, he promised to uphold the duke’s justice. Since he did not have sureties acceptable to the duke, he offered as a pledge the property he possessed. He was made secure through the count’s intervention, with the duke’s authority, until the appointed day on which judgment would be rendered; and it was agreed that, if he could carry out the judgment, his castles would be restored to him.

When the appointed term for rendering judgment arrived, they assembled at the designated place. The duke set out his complaints against William; but William, having little legal standing and arguing weakly, was deprived by judgment of the things he held under the duke. When he tried to oppose the judgment, he lacked both power and legal right; deprived of his lands, he crossed over with his wife to the emperor of Constantinople. After remaining there for some time, he eventually returned with a large sum of money and was reconciled to the duke, a pious and merciful man. He recovered the land he had lost, except for the castle called Saint Maurus.

## CHAPTER XXIII. The Count Gave His Daughter to the Son of the Emperor of the Germans

When disagreements were said to have grown heated between Pope Urban and Henry, emperor of the Germans, and certain disputes arose between Conrad, the son of that same Henry, and his father—matters too lengthy to recount in detail—Conrad, leaving his father in anger, went to the pope and to the marchioness Matilda, who remained loyal to him. With their assistance he continued in rebellion throughout much of Italy.

Since he was a young man without a wife and lacked sufficient resources for what he had begun, at the advice of the pope and the aforementioned marchioness Matilda he asked, through Count Conrad, whom he sent to carry out this embassy, that the daughter of the count of the Sicilians or Calabrians be granted to him in marriage.

The pope also entrusted him with a letter and, addressing the count as his familiar and friend, urged him to grant the request. He said that it would bring great honor and advantage if the daughter were joined to the son of the future king as his bride, and if the young man, who remained faithful to the Holy Roman Church but lacked sufficient resources against his father, who was unjustly attacking him, were strengthened by whatever forces the father might provide to his son for defeating the enemies of the holy Church of God.

When Count Roger received this embassy and had read the pope’s persuasive letter, he took counsel with his faithful advisers, especially Robert, bishop of Trani, through whom he obtained the entire agreement with Conrad. Robert was an Italian and well acquainted with those regions. The count granted what was requested and had both parties confirm the arrangement by oaths.

When the wedding day had been fixed, Count Conrad, honored by Count Roger with many gifts, hastened back to the place from which he had come. Eagerly reporting the outcome of his embassy and announcing that the marriage had been granted, he greatly delighted his lord.

Count Roger then prepared everything appropriate for carrying out the agreement. He had the bishop of Trani and his other barons escort his daughter, richly furnished with many treasures, as far as Pisa. There the king’s son met her, received her with every honor, and celebrated the solemn wedding according to the proper rites, in the year of the incarnation of the Word 1095.

## CHAPTER XXIV. The Duke and the Count Go to Besiege Melfi

The duke Roger was still young and harbored no evil suspicion against anyone. In the purity of his heart he judged the minds of others, and, believing the Lombards as faithful to him as the Normans—because on his mother’s side he belonged to their people—he did not sufficiently recognize that their kind was hostile to our people. He entrusted his castles to them for protection no less than to the Normans.

It therefore happened that, while at Melfi he failed to take adequate precautions in doing the same, the people of Melfi began using the city and the castles that Guiscard had built there to restrain their treachery as they pleased. They gained the freedom to carry out their fraud, to cast off the yoke of our people and of the duke—because he was the executor of our customs—and to refuse to pay the established tribute and service. They even denied the duke access to the city, excluding all his loyal men.

When the duke saw the great harm inflicted upon him, he regretted too late the trust he had placed in them and sought counsel from the count and his faithful men about subduing them. He granted half the city to his uncle the count if they could subjugate it, asking him to come to his aid with the greatest care. Then, in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1096, he brought up a naval and cavalry army from all Apulia and Calabria, while infantry forces hastened forward in rivalry.

They surrounded the city with ships on the seaward side. Through the steep slopes of the surrounding mountains, they carefully arranged, by the count’s advice and labor, forces of horsemen and foot soldiers, and thus enclosed the city on every side with a siege. They would surely, as we believe, have overpowered and captured it, had not the following misfortune intervened, which we shall record under its appropriate heading.

Boamund, pretending to come to the duke’s aid and arriving after being summoned by him, proved more harmful than helpful to his brother—not, as we believe, by deliberate intention. In that same year, by order of Pope Urban, an expedition toward Jerusalem was being eagerly undertaken from every part of the world.

Boamund, who had long before invaded Romania with his father Guiscard and had always desired to subjugate it for himself, saw a very large multitude hastening through Apulia without a leader. Wishing to become their leader by binding them to himself, he placed the sign of that expedition—the cross—upon his garments.

The military youth of the entire army, both the duke’s and the count’s, eager for novel undertakings, as is customary at that age, saw Boamund’s cross. Urged by him to do the same, they rushed forward in rivalry. Taking up crosses, they bound themselves without hesitation by a vow not to advance farther against the boundaries of Christian territory until they had invaded the lands of the pagans.

When the duke and the count saw that their army had thus, for the most part, abandoned them, they sadly dissolved the expedition. Thus, although the city had been afflicted almost to the point of surrender, they were deprived of it by this misfortune.

Boamund crossed the sea. The duke withdrew into Apulia. The count returned to Sicily. The city, rejoicing in the removal of the oppression, was freed.

## CHAPTER XXV. The King of the Hungarians Took the Count’s Daughter as His Wife

The German king of the Hungarians, hearing the fame of the glorious Sicilian count Roger, sent envoys and urgently requested that his daughter be granted to him in marriage.

Although the men who had come for this purpose were honorable, the count dismissed them honorably and sent some of his own men with them, so that he would not be deceived. He replied that, if the king wished to carry out what he had begun, he should send persons of some rank or authority, whom it would be easier to believe, to confirm the matter.

Eager to fulfill the agreement, the king sent Bishop Arduino of Jovianum and Count Thomas to repeat the request. The count received them honorably and kept them with him. He sent honorable and astute men from his own household to Pannonia and had the king, in their presence, confirm by oath the performance of what had been requested.

The king readily consented and, through his duke named Alivus and other men of no lesser dignity, confirmed by oath everything that had been entrusted to him. Thus he dismissed the count’s envoys, enriched with gifts, so that they might report that the agreement had been confirmed. [Note: They should report that it had been confirmed.]

When the count received the report from his men [Note: “received”], he likewise dismissed the king’s envoys from his presence [Note: “them”], having enriched them with many honors [Note: “increased”]. He set a date by which the king was to send him his daughter.

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1097 [Note: 1097], after preparing what was necessary, in the month of May he had Henry, bishop of Lescastrum, and certain of his faithful men escort the girl with three hundred soldiers as far as the Baths. From there he had her proceed by sea toward Pannonia. [Note: “Having her proceed by sea with the girl as far as Palermo, where the girl …”] They boarded prepared ships, bringing the girl aboard with many wedding gifts [Note: “the embarkation”], and, committing their sails to the wind, were carried across the sea by a favorable breeze [Note: “will be carried”] until they safely reached the port of Alba, which belonged to the king of Hungary [Note: “the kingdom belonging to the Hungarians”].

There Count Vincurius of Bellegrata [Note: “Count Viricurius of Bellagrata”], sent with five thousand armed men, met them. Receiving her and those who had come with her in suitable fashion [Note: “receiving”], he led her to the king [Note: “him”].

Throughout Pannonia the king’s wedding was proclaimed. People came from every direction with gifts [Note: “exenia,” that is, gifts]. As is customary, a continually dense and numerous crowd gathered with the king—more countless than usual [Note: “the king has an innumerable crowd, and so forth”]—both because of the wedding and from the desire to see the new queen [Note: “the desire to see her”]. On the appointed day, in the presence of archbishops and bishops and of various orders, the girl’s dowry was publicly declared according to legal custom [Note: “according to royal custom”].

The king and queen were formally betrothed according to Catholic rites, and the solemn wedding was celebrated in tents and tabernacles made from green branches, since no houses could accommodate so great a multitude.

When the royal wedding had been completed, the king kept Bishop Lescastrum and those who had come to return with him for some time. When he saw that they were eager to depart, he dismissed them with lawful gifts. They came to the port and hastened to return by sea.

As they were already approaching the boundaries of our people and could see the land in the distance, the small vessel in which the bishop was traveling—its companions lacking weapons—was violently attacked by two pirate ships, which are called galleys. The helmsman who directed the vessel was pierced by a javelin and struck down. The ship, deprived of its rower, threatened to sink.

The bishop had no refuge in weapons, but he was unwilling to surrender to the enemy. Calling upon God’s help, he encouraged his companions. While doing the same himself, he added among other things:

“God, if, because my sins demand it, I deserve less to be heard, may I at least be heard through the grace which you have often shown that you bear toward the descendants of Tancred. For I have been intercepted here in the service of his son.”

He had not yet finished speaking when, behold, a breeze arose between them. The ship in which he was was torn away from the enemy and gave its occupants greater safety. They saw the ship, without a rower, carried in a straight course toward a nearby island, with such speed over the swift waves of the sea that the hostile vessels, pursuing with oars and sails, could scarcely prevail against its velocity.

Thus, as we believe, it was guided by divine power in a straight course, so that they safely reached a suitable harbor on the island. The harbor, filled with dense sandbanks and having a narrow and dangerous entrance that could be attempted only by experienced sailors, nevertheless opened its way to them.

When the enemies, frustrated, withdrew, the travelers reached the count across the favorable sea, landing where they intended, and explained the sequence of what had happened. Who could doubt that this lineage had been marked out by a certain divine good fortune, since in its advantages, where [lacuna] you might think it to have been, it is reported to have enjoyed so many fortunate successes, and Fortune did not allow herself to be absent even from its faithful servants whenever they carried out its affairs? Indeed, in testimony to their gracious fortune, this ship was rescued from the enemy’s attack.

## CHAPTER XXVI. The Count Besieges Capua with Duke Roger and Prince Richard

[Col. 1205B]

The count, therefore, the support of his entire lineage, excelled in abundance of resources and in the skill of wise and experienced counsel, from Rome toward Sicily, as the seas surround the land on every side. Hence everyone brought their affairs to him, so that, with his prudence, they might become more skillful in arranging their affairs—as iron is sharpened again by a whetstone—and might obtain his assistance whenever necessary.

He, for his part, cherished everyone beneath the shield of his protection and counsel, as a hen shelters her chicks beneath her wings, favoring all as a pious patron both in deed and in counsel, insofar as he could.

It therefore happened that Richard, the young son of Prince Jordan, himself prince of Aversa, had survived as a small child after his father’s death. He had long before been unjustly deprived of Capua through the treachery of the Lombards. When he had reached an age at which he could understand his situation, he saw and grieved over the injury inflicted upon him and planned to seek vengeance from its authors.

He sent prudent men humbly to his kinsman the count, asking him not to delay in hastening there to bring aid. In return for his service, he confidently granted him Naples, which was likewise resisting him, if the count could prevail.

The duke, who favored the prince’s side as his kinsman, sent a no less distinguished envoy than his own wife Adala, daughter of the marquis of Flanders, and earnestly invited the count not to delay coming with his army and bringing him aid.

The prince had become the duke’s vassal because of the assistance he hoped to receive from him. Guiscard, although a man of many arts and great strength, had never been able to extort this from Prince Jordan, whether by force or persuasion, even though Jordan was his uncle and Guiscard his nephew—that is, the son of Jordan’s sister—although he had attempted it very often.

The count was persuaded and enticed by affection for his kinsman the prince and by the many words of the duchess, whom the duke had delegated to him as an envoy and petitioner. He assembled by strong command an army such as he is known never to have possessed before, gathered from all Sicily and Calabria [Note: “steadfast”]. In the first week of April, during the second week of Easter [Note: “Pascha”], he crossed the Strait and hastened there.

He remained for a while in the meadow of Marco, waiting for the army delayed by the crossing of the sea and by the narrow passage through the rocky mountains [Note: “and the passage through the steep mountains of Consus, delaying it”]. He saw the ridges of the Calabrian mountains occupied by flocks [Note: “herds”] of cattle and sheep [Note: “sheep for use”], and also by goats, for the use of the Saracens, most of whom were part of the army [Note: “of the army”]. Thus, by comparing like with like, you might have recalled the flocks of Laban and Jacob, if you had read the account, or had learned it from some reliable informant [Note: “you might have been able to”].

When the army had been assembled, who could count the thousands of armed men, when the tents themselves, covered with bitumen, could scarcely be contained within any number? With this unusually splendid army, the count advanced in view of the Apulian territory. The Apulians had been unaccustomed to expeditions for several years. Rather than exhausting their bodies with wounds and prolonged labors, they sought to indulge and restore themselves instead of laboring to become accustomed once more to campaigns. Hence they feared the duke less, as though he were effectively deprived of the prince’s assistance, and, rising against him in various places and bursting into insolence, obeyed his commands less readily.

The duke, for a similar reason, being less convinced that the count was coming on campaign toward Apulia—for nothing is hurried sufficiently for one who desires something—hastened toward Calabria in order to withdraw and extricate himself.

As he was proceeding toward Apulia, the duke met him at Liscum, beside the castle of Orioli. They rejoiced greatly in one another. The duke hastened to withdraw his army toward Melfi, while the count, so that his flocks would not fail, continued his journey to Benevento. There he camped on the plain beside the bank of the Calore River, at the bridge of Saint Valentine.

The Beneventans, fearing his arrival, came to meet him for three days, requesting peace. The count, knowing that the city belonged by right to Pope Urban and to the Holy Roman Church, accepted fifteen hundred gold pieces and six riding horses, and ordered that the city and its crops be spared. From there he crossed the river called the Sabbato, pitched his tents, and celebrated Pentecost.

He had previously sent honorable men as envoys to the people of Capua, urging them to desist from their foolish undertaking. He told them that he wished to inflict no harm upon them, but rather, if they wished to uphold justice together with their prince, he would stand by their side with justice and protection.

When he heard from the returning envoys that they were attempting nothing and were instead persisting arrogantly in their wickedness, he moved from there and invaded the territory of Capua. At dawn he approached the city with a thousand armed men preceding the army. He militarily cast down and ruinously mocked many who had come out, and would have injured many more had not dust, raised by the horses’ feet and driven into a dense cloud by the wind, intervened.

Returning to his camp, he moved closer to the city on the following day with the entire army. He enclosed it in a siege from the southern side, surrounding it from the eastern bank to the western. The duke and the prince, besieging from the northern side with their army, strove to press the city hard.

The count, whose counsel guided everything, was more vigilant because he was more concerned and more prudent in every undertaking. He constructed a wooden bridge and arranged it across the river so that the armies of himself and of the duke could cross freely.

Thus the city was so heavily oppressed by both armies that there was no safe way out or in, by land or water. Every dawn before daylight, the count rose and crossed the bridge to inspect both armies, going to see whether they were attentive to their watches. Finding the duke and the prince still overcome by sleep, he mocked them.

They were covered with shame because they, young men to whom the matter more particularly belonged, were more sluggish, while the count, a man of more advanced age and accustomed to the hardship of wounds and labors, was more vigilant. His vigilance was an object of wonder to the entire army, and all became more watchful by his example.

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1097, Countess Adelasia conceived by Count Roger there.

## CHAPTER XXVII. Pope Urban Comes to Them and Attempts to Establish Peace

While these things were taking place, Pope Urban, desiring a meeting with the duke and the count, set out from Rome and came to Capua, where they were maintaining the siege. The count provided him with six tents for lodging and supplied an abundance of whatever expenses were necessary.

He knew what is written: “Blessed are the feet of those who proclaim peace” (Romans 10); and: “Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called sons of God” (Matthew 5); and elsewhere: “Keep peace, and the God of peace and love will be with you” (2 Corinthians 13). Above all, he knew that the care of all Christianity had been entrusted to his oversight. He therefore first approached the duke, the count, and the prince together and began to attempt to restore peace among them.

They used the count’s prudent counsel in their reply and said, in the presence of the pope, that they would enter into judgment according to the authority of blessed Peter if the people of Capua would carry out the same process under equal conditions.

The pope went inside the city to learn the same thing from the Capuans. When both sides gave their consent, he rejoiced in vain, hoping to complete the peace, and returned with the agreement. A day for the dispute was appointed.

The parties stated their cases and responded to one another according to the circumstances. The judges legally reached a conclusion against the Capuans by a weighty syllogism. When the Capuans heard that they were being overwhelmed by the judgment, they used either opposition or reasonable contradiction against the judges. Publicly displaying themselves as wrongdoers, they declared that they either would not or could not carry out the judgment.

When the pope heard this—and since he had been their intermediary for carrying it out—he was somewhat ashamed. He threatened them by invoking the sword of blessed Peter and, showing complete favor toward our party, joined it. He greatly praised the count’s steadfastness in undertaking difficult actions and declared that his life was absolutely necessary to Rome and Italy. For fear of him restrained more people from insolence than zeal for honor did.

The pope, being more intent on ecclesiastical affairs than on military enterprises, turned his mind away from the general tumult. He granted his apostolic blessing to the three princes and to the entire army, then withdrew to Benevento.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. Capua Is Captured and Restored to Prince Richard

The count, persisting with the duke and the prince in the most vigorous assault upon the city, skillfully devised siege engines for capturing it.

At first the Capuans mocked and despised them, encouraging one another to defend themselves. Nevertheless, they attempted to surrender the city to the duke or the count if they were willing to accept it while retaining possession. But the most noble princes were unwilling to accept this fraud in any way and would not consent unless the city were restored to the prince.

When the Capuans saw the prepared siege engines approaching the city, they shuddered at what they had previously treated as a joke and, on the count’s advice, submitted themselves to surrender. Using him as mediator, they scarcely obtained immunity for their fraud.

The city of Capua was restored to the prince according to his pleasure. The prince gave thanks to the duke and the count. The duke and the count then departed together at Salerno. The prince, taking possession of the city according to his will, lodged triumphantly in the highest tower.

## CHAPTER XXIX. Pope Urban Grants the Count the Legation of Sicily and Calabria

When the pope heard that the city had been restored and peace established among them, he rejoiced both that fraud had been suppressed and that peace had been accomplished. But when he heard that the duke and the count had withdrawn to Salerno, he did not wish the count to return toward Sicily before speaking with him, and therefore hastened there.

When he arrived with the archbishops at Saint Matthew, he waited in procession to receive the count with due honor. Nevertheless, because of the affectionate reverence he bore toward the count, he first went amiably to the count’s lodging to see him. After spending a long time in conversation with him, he proceeded to the procession that was waiting to receive him. On the following day they met, and each enjoyed the other’s conversation with the greatest affection.
