But the pope had earlier appointed Robert, bishop of Trani, as legate in Sicily to carry out the rights of the Holy Roman Church, without consulting the count. Perceiving that the count took this badly and would in no way consent that the arrangement remain permanent, and also recognizing that the count burned with zeal for divine fervor in carrying out all ecclesiastical affairs, the pope revoked what he had done concerning the bishop of Trani.

He then placed the legation of blessed Peter over the count throughout Sicily and, hereditarily, over Calabria belonging to his jurisdiction [Note: “and over Calabria, held as part of his jurisdiction”]. He established the following provision: as long as the count lived, or as long as any of his heirs who was an executor of his father’s ecclesiastical zeal survived, no other legate from the Roman See would be placed over them against their will. If anything belonging to the jurisdiction of the Roman Church had to be carried out, it was to be authoritatively determined by them, with the advice of the bishops of those provinces, through documents sent by the Roman See to Sicily or Calabria.

If the bishops were invited to a council, they were to send there as many and such bishops as the count or his future heirs thought appropriate, unless some matter concerning one of them had to be dealt with at the council and could not be authoritatively resolved in his presence in Sicily or Calabria. The pope confirmed this arrangement permanently by the privilege of his authority. Its text follows:

**URBAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his most beloved son R., count of Calabria and Sicily, greeting and apostolic blessing.**

Because the favor of the supreme Majesty has exalted your prudence through many triumphs and honors, and because your probity has greatly expanded the Church of God in the lands of the Saracens and has always shown itself devoted in many ways to the holy apostolic see, we have taken you as a special and most beloved son of that universal Church.

Therefore, placing the greatest confidence in the sincerity of your probity, just as we promised in words, so also we confirm by the authority of this letter that, throughout your entire lifetime, and throughout the lifetime of your son Simon or of any other person who may prove to be your legitimate heir, we shall appoint no legate of the Roman Church in any land under your authority without your will or counsel. Indeed, whatever we intend to carry out through a legate, we wish to have carried out through your agency in the legate’s place whenever we send someone to you from our side—that is, for the welfare of the churches existing under your authority, for the honor of blessed Peter and of his holy apostolic see, which you have hitherto obeyed devoutly and which you have vigorously and faithfully assisted in its necessities.

If a council is held, I shall instruct you to send me bishops and abbots from your land. Send as many and such men as you wish, while retaining others for the service and protection of the churches.

May almighty God direct your deeds according to his good pleasure and lead you, absolved from sins, to eternal life.

Given at Salerno, through the hand of John, deacon of the Holy Roman Church, on the third day before the Nones of July, in the seventh indiction, in the eleventh year of the pontificate of our lord Urban II.

[Col. 1209] Here ends the work of Geoffrey the monk.

[Col. 1209]

# APPENDIX FROM THE CODEX OF THE MARQUIS JARRATANA TO THE FINAL CHAPTER OF BOOK IV OF THE HISTORY OF GEOFFREY OF MALATERRA

[Col. 1209C]

After these events, the most pious count, entirely deprived of male offspring by the hidden judgment of God, joined himself to his wife in prayer poured out before God, hoping to beget children, and fathered sons and daughters by her.

He lived honorably into a most venerable old age, devoting himself greatly to the building of churches. He endowed them abundantly throughout his entire land, as his unbroken line of descendants still rules and preserves them, and he religiously and decently appointed men to sing the psalms. He proved to be a pious protector of orphans and widows and a generous helper of Christ’s poor.

As he, together with his sons and daughters, continually advanced toward what was better, he remained for all an example of honorable holiness. At last, when the necessary law of human existence brought about the natural dissolution of his body, he sent forth that illustrious soul, marked by such radiance and by the recognition of its merits, to the desired company of the blessed before the presence of the divine Majesty. His body was honorably buried at Mileto, in the church that he himself had founded, as befitted so great a man.

[Col. 1210C]

After him, Simon, the firstborn of his sons, received the kingdom. Living only a few years, he endured serious upheavals from the Apulians.

He was succeeded by that greatest of men, beloved and blessed by God, the one and only lion and foundation of peace: Roger, the wonder of the world, the splendor of every virtue, a wise and immeasurable hero among kings. First a count, then—through the incomparable wisdom by which God worked—worthy duke of fertile Apulia and prince of Capua, and finally king of Sicily, he greatly extended the borders of his empire far and wide through the acquisition of many lands, becoming the most powerful ruler of Tripoli, Africa, and Sicily.

Since I judge Cicero’s eloquence insufficient for recounting his praises and deeds with the singular excellence they deserve, I, who am almost nothing, fear even now to undertake a burden of such gravity, still unknown to me.

[Note: [Col. 1209] Appendix II, or a brief chronology from the above-cited Jarratian manuscript. CARUSIUS.]

In the year of the Lord 1027, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of August, Gaytus Maymonus, a Spanish Saracen, devastated, plundered, and burned Pactas and the Syracusan territory within seven days; he killed some of the inhabitants of both sexes [Col. 1211A] and took others captive.

In the year of the Lord 1032, Stratigotus Georgius, the first patrician, and Maniacus, together with the duke, captured the city of Messana, and in that same year engaged in battle. It is unknown with whom Maniacus achieved the victory.

In the year of the Lord 1060, on the Kalends of August, Pope Innocent was captured by the aforesaid King Roger, king of Sicily, in the city of Captinata.

In the year of the Lord 1101, in the ninth indiction, in the month of July, the great Count Roger, father of King Roger, died.

In the year of the Lord 1118, in the ninth indiction, Queen Adelaide of Jerusalem, mother of King Roger, died.

In the year of the Lord 1149, in the month of July, Africa was captured [Col. 1211B] by that same King Roger.

In the year of the Lord 1154, Roger, king of Sicily, duke of Apulia, and prince of Capua, died.

In the year of the Lord 1164, on the day before the Nones of February, the city of the Catanians was overturned by an earthquake; in that destruction all the monks and their bishop were crushed.

In the year of the Lord 1166, King William I, son of King Roger, died.

In the year of the Lord 1178, on the Ides of September, in the thirteenth indiction, the sun suffered an eclipse: at the ninth hour the stars appeared.

In the year of the Lord 1182 [?], Queen Margaret, mother of King William II, began to construct, build, and endow the monastery of Maniace.

[Col. 1211C] In the year of the Lord 1187, in the month of July, on the vigil of the Lord’s Forerunner, Jerusalem was captured by Saladin, sultan of Babylon.

In the year of the Lord 1189, in the seventh indiction, King William II died. In that same year and indiction, in the month of March, King Tancred was crowned king of Sicily and received in the palace of Palermo.

In the year of the Lord 1194, on the twentieth day of February, the aforesaid King Tancred died.

In the year of the Lord 1195, Lord Henry the emperor was received in the palace of Palermo on the last day of November. On the fourth day after the feast of the Nativity of the Lord, he captured King William, son of King Tancred, together with the counts and barons of this kingdom, and devastated them.

[Col. 1211D] In the year of the Lord 1198, Lord Henry the emperor died.

In the year of the Lord 1198, Frederick, son of Lord Henry the emperor, was crowned king of Sicily in the city of Palermo. In that same year, his mother Constance died.

In the year of the Lord 1200, . . . on the fifteenth day of August, in the twelfth indiction, Lady Constance of Aragon arrived at Palermo, and in that same month Lord King Frederick married her.

In the year of the Lord 1212, in the year of the birth of Lord King Frederick, in the fourteenth indiction and the eleventh year of his reign. He himself had been summoned by Pope Innocent III to the imperial crown from the sixteenth year of his life.

[Col. 1212A] In the year of the Lord 1216, a most celebrated council was held under Pope Innocent III.

In the year of the Lord 1219, in the seventh indiction, on the fifth day after the beginning of November, Damietta, the principal city of Amaleth, was captured by the faithful Christians and has been held under Christian rule.

In the year of the Lord 1220, in the month of November, in the ninth indiction, Lord King Frederick, together with Lady Queen Constance his wife, received the imperial crown from Lord Pope Honorius III. In that same year Damietta was lost by the Christians.

In the year of the Lord 1221, in the tenth indiction, Lord Frederick the emperor went with a great army against the Saracens of Jaci, captured Benaveth with his sons, and hanged them at Palermo.

[Col. 1212B] In the year of the Lord 1222, in the eleventh indiction, Lady Empress Constance died at Catania. In that same year the emperor captured Celano and expelled Count Thomas of Celano from the kingdom.

In the year of the Lord 1223, in the twelfth indiction, Lord Emperor Frederick sent his army to Gerba; he captured, destroyed, and enslaved its inhabitants.

In the year of the Lord 1224, in the thirteenth indiction, Lord Emperor Frederick sent a great army against the Saracens of Sicily. They remained in the mountains; he continually inflicted great devastation upon them each year, until they descended in great disgrace, and he made them live on the Sicilian plain, in the villages.

In the year of the Lord 1227, in the first indiction, in the month of June, [Col. 1212C] Lord Emperor Frederick II crossed to the overseas territories, and there received the crown of that kingdom. In that same year, before he crossed, Lady Empress, his wife, died. King Conrad was born. In that same year Pope Gregory assumed the papacy at Rome.

In the year of the Lord 1225, in the fourteenth indiction, Lord Emperor Frederick took as his wife Isabella, daughter of Lord King John.

In the year of the Lord 1228, in the second indiction, the emperor returned to the kingdom.

In the year of the Lord 1229, in the third indiction, in the aforesaid month of August, the emperor made peace and reconciliation with Lord Pope Gregory. At the beginning of September, in the fourth indiction, he remained at Anagni with Lord Pope Gregory for three days.

In the year of the Lord 1230, in the fourth indiction, the emperor discussed, or caused to be discussed, his Constitutions.

In the year of the Lord 1231, in the fifth indiction, the emperor sent his Constitutions throughout the entire kingdom and into Sicily through Lord Richard of Montenigro, who was master justiciar of Sicily. In that same year, in August of the aforesaid indiction, Martin Ballonus rebelled against Lord Emperor Frederick with a number of men from Messana. The master justiciar himself took flight. The aforesaid Martin, likewise out of fear of the emperor, took flight and was captured with his companions at Malta.

[Col. 1213A] In the year of the Lord 1232, in the sixth indiction, in April of that indiction, the emperor came to Messana and put the aforesaid Martin Bellion to death. In that same year he acted similarly at Syracuse and Nicosia.

In the year of the Lord 1233, in the seventh indiction, Matthew Marchafaba was appointed secretus of Sicily and Calabria.

In the year of the Lord 1234, in the eighth indiction, Emperor Frederick went to Germany.

In the year of the Lord 1235, in the ninth indiction, Emperor Frederick II took as his wife the sister of the king of England. In that same year he captured King Henry, his son, and kept him in prison until he died at Maturanum; he was buried in [Col. 1213B] the church of Cosenza.

In the year of the Lord 1236, in the tenth indiction, at the end of November, the emperor went to Lombardy with a great army; he marched against Milan and captured Corrocium of the Milanese.

In the year of the Lord 1236, in the eleventh indiction, in the month of February, King Henry, son of the emperor by his third wife, who was the sister of the king of England, was born. In that same year the emperor besieged the place called Brescia, but accomplished nothing there.

In the year of the Lord 1237, in the twelfth indiction, on the first day of August, Marchafaba the secretus died. Also in that same year Pope Gregory excommunicated Lord Emperor Frederick.

[Col. 1213C] In the year of the Lord 1238, in the thirteenth indiction, Major of Brancadoria was secretus of Sicily; William of Anglone was justiciar of Sicily, and they remained in their offices for seven months. In June of the aforesaid indiction, Hubert Fallamonica was secretus of Sicily, Peter of Calabria was justiciar, and Roger de Amicis was captain.

In the year of the Lord 1239, in the fourteenth indiction, the prelates of France were captured by Lord Emperor Frederick during the pontificate of Pope Gregory. In that same year the same pope died.

In the year of the Lord 1240, in the fifteenth indiction, Peter of Calabria was justiciar in Sicily. In that same year Roger de Amicis went to the Sultan [Col. 1213D] of Babylon.

In the year of the Lord 1241, in the first indiction, Hubert Fallamonica, by order of the emperor, went to Morocco. In that same year the Sultan of [lacuna] and [lacuna] attacked the Christians who lived in Jerusalem; they captured them, killed them, and led them away captive. In that same battle Perfectus, bishop of Saint George of Rama, was killed, together with Walter of Breteuil, lord of Joppa. In those days Lord Roger de Amicis was staying in Babylon and in Cairo with the sultan.

In the year of the Lord 1242, in the second indiction, Roger of Paris was captain of Sicily. William of Taraum was justiciar.

[Col. 1214A] In the year of the Lord 1243, in the third indiction, Lord Serrebald, a cardinal, assumed the Roman papacy; he immediately went by sea to Genoa, and afterward went as far as Lyon [Lugdunum], where he remained for six years. Also in that same year, in July of that indiction, all the Saracens of Sicily, as rebels, went up into the mountains and captured Jato and Alcamo.

In the year of the Lord 1244, in the fourth indiction, in March of that indiction, Tibald, Francis, and William of Saint Severinus, together with other counts and barons of the kingdom, captured the territory of Capaccio and its castle as rebels. Lord Emperor Frederick II besieged them, and in the middle of July of that indiction captured them all, after capturing all the men who were staying with them; he transported them away and burned them all in the land of Naples. He then seized the nobler women of the kingdom and sent them to prison at Palermo, and they never appeared again. Also in that same year, in July of that indiction, Lord Hugh of Cassino was appointed justiciar in Sicily.

In the year of the Lord 1245, in the fifth indiction, by order of the emperor, Count Richard of Caserta expelled all the Saracens from Sicily and sent them to Nocera in Apulia. Also in that same year Pope Innocent held a great council at Lyon with the transalpine prelates, but not with those of the kingdom, except Lord Richard, archbishop of Palermo, who had been sent there by the emperor.

[Col. 1214C] In the year of the Lord 1247, in the seventh indiction, Lord Emperor Louis, king of the Franks, crossed to the overseas territories and remained on the island of Cyprus in June of that indiction. In that same month he bravely crossed as far as the sea of Damietta and immediately captured that territory with great rejoicing.

In the year of the Lord 1248, in the eighth indiction, in April of that indiction, the lord king of the Franks lost the aforesaid territory of Damietta, and the Sultan of Babylon recovered it.

In the year of the Lord 1250, in the ninth indiction, in December of that indiction, Lord Emperor Frederick II died in Apulia, in the territory called Florentinum. His body arrived at Messana on the thirteenth of January of that indiction and remained day after day for several days in the church of Pactas, during the tenure of Lord Philip, bishop of that territory. It was afterward conveyed to Palermo and buried there. Lord Henry, the king, son of the emperor by his English wife, arrived at Messana on the nineteenth day of January of that ninth indiction and was received there with great joy.

In the year of the Lord 1250, in the tenth indiction, in January of that indiction, King Conrad, son of the emperor, came by sea from Germany with a great force sent by the lord prince, who was bailiff of the entire kingdom by order of [Col. 1215A] the emperor; he arrived in Apulia on the eighth of January of that indiction.

In the year of the Lord 1252, in the twelfth indiction, in October of that indiction, the city of Naples was captured by the same Lord King Conrad. In May of that same year he died and was buried at Messana. Also in that same year, in January of that indiction, the aforementioned King Henry died.

In the year of the Lord 1253, in the thirteenth indiction, in November of that indiction, Pope Innocent IV entered Naples with great rejoicing, because the lord prince wished it, and by his permission he entered the kingdom. In those days Borrellus of Anglone was killed. At the beginning of December of that indiction, Lord Pope Innocent died in the same territory of Naples and was buried there. Immediately [Col. 1215B] Lord Pope Alexander assumed the Roman papacy and remained in the territory of Naples until May of that indiction. Also in that same year, in December of the thirteenth indiction, the lord prince recovered Lucera and Achienza; John the Moor was killed there. He afterward recovered the city of Melfi and destroyed the city of Rapolla because it refused to submit to him. In February of the thirteenth indiction, the commune of the city of Messana expelled Count Peter Russo of Calabria from that city with his entire household and sent word to the lord prince to come and take Messana together with all Sicily. Later, after taking counsel to their misfortune, they sent a great army against the army of the aforesaid lord prince in Calabria, in the district [Col. 1215C] called Corona. The army of the lord prince attacked the aforesaid army of Messana and prevailed over it most disastrously: some they killed, others they wounded, others they led away, and others they captured, while few of them escaped. Also, in August of the aforesaid thirteenth indiction, the commune of Messana destroyed the territory of Taormina because it refused to obey their command. Also in that same year, in October of the fourteenth indiction, the commune of Messana sent to Rome and elected Lord James of Pente as podestà. He remained in office until the middle of May of the aforesaid indiction; Lord John of Colonna, archbishop of Messana, sent by the pope, came with him.

[Col. 1215D] Also, in the year of the Lord 1254, in the fourteenth indiction, in April, Henry of Abbot, with the army of the Val di Mazara, captured Palermo, Brother Businus the legate, and the whole of Sicily turned to the lord prince’s rule, except for Platia, Castrogiovanni, and Aidone.

Also, in the year of the Lord 1255, in the fifteenth indiction, [Col. 1216A] Count Frederick Lancia came as vicar to Sicily. After gathering the barons of Calabria, the Val di Crati, the land of Jordan, and all Sicily, he went with a great army against Platia, besieged and captured it, and killed a certain number of the inhabitants of that territory. He afterward went against Castrogiovanni and Aidone, and the inhabitants of those territories submitted to the lord prince’s rule. In that same year Philip of Aterno was justiciar.

Also, in the year of the Lord 1256, in the first indiction, Bernard of Acquaviva was justiciar of Sicily. In April of the first indiction, the lord prince Manfred came to Messana and afterward went to Palermo. There he had all the prelates and barons of the entire kingdom summoned; and at their election the lord prince was crowned king of Sicily on the tenth [Col. 1216B] day of August, in the first indiction, amid the greatest joy and rejoicing.

Also, in the year of the Lord 1257, in the second indiction, Count Frederick Maletta came as captain to Sicily, and Frederick of Avenis Arenes was justiciar.

Also, in the year of the Lord 1258, in the third indiction, in the month of May, Gobbanus the German killed that same Count Frederick Maletta before Mount Trapani. Gobbanus himself then went up the same mountain, and he, together with the inhabitants of that mountain, raised the standard of rebellion against Lord King Manfred, rejecting his name. Lord Count Frederick Lancia, with a great army, besieged the aforesaid mountain, and in October of that same indiction [Col. 1216C] captured it together with its inhabitants. He made them leave it and devastated some of them.

In the year of the Lord 1263, in the ninth indiction, Count Charles entered Rome in the summer. In April of that indiction, Lord King Manfred sent his force to Marseilles to besiege it.

In the year of that same Incarnation, 1265, in the ninth indiction, Count Charles captured the bridge of Ceprano, and the city of Naples was thrown into confusion. Afterward the same count, with his army, came to the bridge of Valentino in the territory of Benevento, and on Friday, the twenty-second day of February, he prevailed over King Manfred and his army and gained victory over him.

[Col. 1216D] Also in the year of that Incarnation, in the same ninth indiction, on Saturday, the thirteenth day of March, the city of Messana raised the banner of the aforesaid Count Charles. On Thursday, the first day of April of that same indiction, Count Philip of Montfort came as vicar to Sicily on behalf of that same Count Charles.

# In the Year of the Lord 1087. William I, Duke of the Normans and King of the English, Surnamed the Conqueror

## Deeds

[Col. 1217]

## The Deeds of William the Conqueror

Written by William of Poitiers, archdeacon of Lisieux, his contemporary.

(Duchesne, *Historiae Northmannorum. Scriptores antiqui*, p. 178.)

*(The beginning is missing.)* . . . when he lost the kingdom of England, which he owed to the violence of his father and himself, not to others. Harold, his son, obtained the same crown with the throne, having inherited in part from him a degenerate love of tyranny. Edward and Alfred, relatives of William the prince, still remained exiles at his court; long ago, when they were boys, they had fled to their uncles in Normandy [Col. 1217A] so that they would not be slaughtered. Their mother was Emma, daughter of Richard I; their father was Æthelred, king of the English. But concerning the genealogy of these brothers, and the fact that the Danes seized their inheritance by invasion, others have written sufficiently.

When, therefore, they had heard of Cnut’s death, Edward first, having crossed the sea, brought forty ships, fully equipped with soldiers, into Southampton, where he encountered a very large multitude waiting to destroy him. For the English did not wish to abandon Harold—or, what is more credible, did not dare to do so, fearing that the Danes might be present to protect him or to avenge him swiftly; they had by no means forgotten that the Danish savagery had extinguished the noblest men of their own nation. Edward immediately defeated them in an encounter with great slaughter. Considering [Col. 1217B] that the strength of the hostile land was immense and that the forces he had transported were small, he turned his prows back and returned to Normandy with rich booty. He knew that land to be a safe, generous, and benevolent home.

Not long afterward, after an interval of time, Alfred arrived at Canterbury, having been transported from the port of Itius, better prepared than his brother had previously been against violence; he too sought his father’s scepter. As he approached, Earl Godwin received him with an impious fraud and handed him over through a most wicked conspiracy. Indeed, he went out to meet him voluntarily, as though to honor him, kindly promised him his service, and gave him kisses as a pledge, together with his right hand. He also shared table and counsels with him familiarly. But in the middle of the following night, while Alfred was weakened by sleep, he bound his unarmed hands behind his back. Having conquered him by such a show of tenderness, he sent him to King Harold in London; from his retinue he likewise sent some of the others bound, assigned some separately to prison with cruel separation from one another, and horribly killed others by disemboweling them.

When Harold rejoiced at seeing Alfred in chains, he ordered the best of his attendants to be beheaded in Alfred’s presence, deprived Alfred of his sight, [Col. 1218A] and then, disgraced by being stripped and placed on horseback, had him led to the sea with his feet bound beneath the horse, so that he might be tortured by exile and poverty on the island of Ely. The life of his enemy pleased him more when it was worse than death. At the same time he intended to terrify Edward completely through his brother’s calamities. Thus the most handsome young man, most highly praised for his goodness, the king’s son and the grandson of kings, perished; nor could he survive long. As his eyes were being gouged out, the blade of a knife pierced his brain.

Therefore, Godwin, whose dead name remains infamous and hateful, we shall address you in this brief outcry. We wish, if it were possible, to deter you from the crime you committed with such malice. What detestable madness drives you? With what sort of heart do you plot an abominable deed against right and justice? Why, most cruel murderer, do you admit such utterly treacherous betrayal to the destruction of yourself and your own people? You devise—and congratulate yourself on having completed—what the rites and laws of nations far removed from Christianity detest. Alfred’s most undeserved misery brings joy to you, most wicked man, but tears to the honorable. Indeed, such things are grievous to relate.

But the most glorious Duke William, whose deeds, trusting in divine assistance, we shall teach the age to come, will strike with an avenging sword the throat of Harold, your offspring, most like you in cruelty and treachery. Through your betrayal you shed the innocent blood of the Normans; in equal measure, the blood of your own people will be shed by the sword of the Normans. We were inclined to bury this inhuman crime in perpetual silence, but we judge that even less worthy events, [Col. 1219A] when they necessarily arise in the sequence of history, must not be removed from the page, just as they must be removed from imitation.

Not long afterward Harold died, and his brother Harthacnut, born of Emma, Edward’s mother, succeeded him after returning from Denmark. He resembled his maternal family more closely; he did not rule with the cruelty of either his father or his brother, and he desired not Edward’s destruction but his advancement. Because he frequently suffered from illnesses, he also held God more before his eyes and recognized the brevity of human life. As for writing about his kingdom or his life, let us leave that to others, lest we depart too far from the subject we have undertaken.

At last there dawned a most festive joy, eagerly awaited above all by those who desired peace and justice. Our duke, more mature in understanding of honorable matters and in bodily strength than in age, takes up [Col. 1219B] military arms; the report of this brought fear to all France. Gaul had no other man who could be proclaimed such a knight and warrior. It was a delightful and terrifying spectacle to see him controlling the reins, splendid with sword, shining with shield and helmet, and threatening with his weapon. For just as he excelled in beauty when he wore the garments of a prince or of peace, so the equipment he assumed against an enemy suited him in a singular way. In him a manly spirit and outstanding courage shone forth with brilliant clarity.

Accordingly, he began with the greatest zeal to defend the churches of God, protect the causes of the powerless, impose laws that would not oppress, and render judgments that in no way departed from equity or moderation. Above all, he prohibited killings, burnings, and plunderings. For, as we have shown above, excessive license in unlawful acts prevailed everywhere. Finally, he began entirely to remove from his companionship those whom he recognized to be ignorant or wicked, while using the counsels of the wisest and best, bravely resisting external enemies, and vigorously demanding due service from his own people.

When these beginnings were already restoring to Normandy its splendor and the tranquility of its ancient condition, and were promising better things, with good men obediently helping their ruler to enjoy his customary liberty, certain men preferred to retain what belonged to them at their pleasure and seize what belonged to others. The standard-bearer of this madness sprang forward: Wido, son of Count Reginald of Burgundy, who held the very strong castles of Brionne and Vernon as a gift of the duke and had been raised familiarly with him from childhood.

But he aspired either to the principate [Col. 1219D] or to the greatest part of Normandy. He therefore joined with himself in the worst conspiracies Nigel, governor of the Cotentin, Ralph of Bayeux, the viscount, and Haimo, surnamed “the Toothed,” together with other powerful men. The kinship of the family did not restrain that wicked man’s obstinacy; nor did the liberal expenditure of such great benefits; nor, finally, did the duke’s sincere affection and supreme goodwill toward him. They killed many innocent men whom they had vainly attempted to turn to their side, or whom they had perceived to be a major obstacle to themselves. They neglected every right and took care to avoid no wrong, provided only that they might acquire greater power. Such is sometimes the blindness of ambition.

Gradually, therefore, the enterprise of that perjured alliance grew so strong [Col. 1220A] that, gathered in the most direct battle line at Val-ès-Dunes against their lord, they shook everything far and wide with tumult. The greater part of Normandy followed the standard of impiety. Yet William, leader of the avenging party, was not at all terrified by so many swords. Rushing upon them with slaughter, he inflicted such fear that the hearts of his opponents were almost torn from them and their arms weakened. Only the impulse that drove them to flight remained. He pursued them harshly for several miles, punishing them. For many, pathless places or difficult roads threw them into death. For others, on the level, well-trodden ground, speed brought ruin and crowding brought deadly collision. The river Orne swallowed not a few horsemen together with their horses.

King Henry of France took part in this battle, aiding the victorious cause. It was truly a most fruitful battle of a single day, one that should be made known to the ages: while establishing a terrifying example, it both crushed with steel necks raised too high and, by the hand of victory, overthrew many strongholds of crime, driving them down, and put our domestic wars to sleep for a long time.

Guido, having escaped in the most disgraceful manner, hastened to Brionne with a large cavalry force. This town seemed impregnable both by the nature of its location and by its construction. Besides the other defenses that the necessity of war customarily builds, it possessed a stone hall serving the needs of the fighters, around which the river Risle flowed, allowing no ford at any point. The victor promptly pursued him and established a close siege, setting castles opposite one another on both banks of the divided river. Then, by terrifying him with attacks by day, he completely blocked the possibility of escape. Finally, the Burgundian, hard-pressed also by a shortage of provisions, began sending intermediaries to seek mercy.

Moved by kinship, supplication, and the misery of the defeated man, the duke did not exact a harsher vengeance. After recovering the castle, he allowed him to remain at his court. He also preferred, for reasonable causes, to pardon his associates the capital punishments that would otherwise have been inflicted equally. I find that Nigel was punished by exile at another time because he had offended intolerably. Guido voluntarily returned to Burgundy because of the burden of disgrace. He was ashamed to endure among the Normans the contempt of all and the hatred of many. Burgundy, for its part, tolerated him unwillingly. Indeed, if he had possessed as much power as he strove for, he would have deprived his own brother William, count of that province, both of power and of life. [Col. 1220D] He spent ten years and more in arms, hunting through battles for the blood of his kinsman.

Why add further evidence, to make the proof of his wickedness clearer? Once defeated, all the Normans submitted their necks to their lord and many gave hostages. Then, at his command, they quickly and completely destroyed the fortifications built in the cause of innovation. The people of the metropolitan city of Rouen brought down to the ground the insolence they had exercised against the young count. Thereafter the churches rejoiced, because it was possible to celebrate the divine mystery in tranquillity. The merchant exulted, since he could safely go wherever he wished. The farmer rejoiced, because it was safe to break new ground and sow the hope of crops, without hiding at the sight of a soldier. [Col. 1221A] Every person of every condition and rank raised the duke to the stars with praise and wished him long life and health with all their prayers.

After this, he himself repaid the king with the most devoted loyalty, when the king requested his help against certain men who were extremely hostile to him and very powerful in obstructing him. For King Henry, angered by the insulting words of Geoffrey Martel, led an army against him and besieged and stormed his castle, called Molendinum Herlae, in the county of Anjou, with a strong force.

The French saw what envy would have preferred not to be seen: an army led from Normandy alone, a single region, larger than the entire force brought or sent by the many counts. While I was an exile at Poitiers in Aquitaine, [Col. 1221B] the same fame of the Norman count, which our countrymen attest, was widely proclaimed—fame won on that expedition. They said that among all others he excelled in intelligence, industry, and skill with his hands. The king willingly referred matters for deliberation to him and conducted the most important affairs according to his judgment, preferring him to all others in his perception of better counsel.

The king reproached him for one thing only: that he exposed himself too much to danger and often sought battle, openly rushing out with ten men or fewer. He also begged the leading Normans not to permit even the slightest battle to be joined before any town, fearing, evidently, that his courage might fall while he displayed it—the courage in which he placed the firmest defense and most splendid ornament of his kingdom. Yet what the king strongly discouraged and chastised as an immoderate display of courage, we attribute to his ardent and spirited age or to his office. By such occasional withdrawal, matters that are by no means unhelpful are sometimes discovered through investigation. Sometimes wrongdoers are intercepted, because they avoid large columns; at other times something else of the greatest usefulness is achieved.

Here is an act of the man whom we excuse, and whose remarkable apprenticeship it is all the more pleasant to remember attentively. Wishing, as it were, to elude his companions, he withdrew from the army, leading about three hundred horsemen for a little while. Then he withdrew from these with only four men and wandered about. Behold, fifteen men from the enemy’s side, exulting in horses and arms, came upon him. Immediately he charged and cast his lance, taking care to pierce the boldest of them. His thigh, however, was shattered when he was thrown against the ground. He pursued the others for four miles.

Meanwhile, the three hundred whom he had left, following and searching for him—for they feared his confidence—suddenly caught sight of Count Theobald with five hundred horsemen. A most grievous suspicion arose. They thought these men were enemies and that their lord had been captured and held in their power. Therefore, encouraging one another, they threw themselves forward, almost into a doubtful situation, to rescue him. But when the troop was recognized as friendly, they searched farther and found one of the fifteen lying there, held fast by a broken thigh. After they had gone a little farther, their cheerful lord met them, bringing seven soldiers whom he had captured.

[Col. 1222A] From that time Geoffrey Martel repeatedly declared, as he believed, that under heaven there lived no knight or soldier equal to the count of Normandy. Powerful men from Gascony and Auvergne sent or brought him horses that were commonly ennobled by proper names. The kings of Spain likewise sought his friendship through these and other gifts. This friendship was to be desired and cultivated by the best and most powerful men. For he possessed in himself the fullest reason why he should be loved by those at home, by his neighbors, and by those set far away.

Moreover, he himself worked as hard as he was able to be an ornament or assistance to his friends, and always took care that his friends should owe him as much as possible. At that time, in his youth, he ruled a single province and did not dominate kingdoms; he was about forty-five years old. If from that age, or, if you investigate his deeds more fully, from his boyhood, you consider his actions, you can rightly affirm that through him the law of fellowship or friendship was never violated.

For he remained firmly constant in his words and agreements, as though demonstrating by his actions what the philosophers declare: that faith is the foundation of justice. If he was compelled by the gravest reasons to separate from someone’s friendship, he preferred gradually to dissolve it rather than cut it off suddenly. We see this to be in accord with the judgment of the wise (Cicero, *On Friendship* 21).

King Henry unjustly alienated himself and undertook a savage enmity, led astray by the persuasion of the worst men. When he assailed Normandy with injuries that were altogether intolerable, William, to whom the defense of Normandy belonged, resisted him; [Col. 1222C] nevertheless, he gave much weight to their old friendship and to royal dignity. While the king was present, he took the greatest possible care, insofar as necessity allowed, to avoid engaging his army. He frequently restrained the Normans as well—not merely by command but almost by entreaty—since they were extremely eager to dishonor royal dignity by battle.

Elsewhere these matters will be understood more clearly, together with the magnanimity with which he himself disdained the swords of the French and of all those who had been summoned against him by the king’s command.

By William’s strength and counsel as well, after Harthacnut’s life had finally ended, Edward was crowned and sat upon his father’s throne. He was worthy of that glory both through wisdom and outstanding moral integrity and through his ancient lineage. For the English, deliberating and recognizing what was most useful to their own interests, agreed that they should yield to embassies requesting what was just rather than test the force of the Normans. They eagerly secured his return with a not very large force of Norman soldiers, lest, if the Norman count should arrive, they be subdued by a stronger hand. They knew well enough from report what he could accomplish in war.

Edward, meanwhile, gratefully considered how costly a generosity, how singular an honor, and how intimate an affection Prince William had bestowed upon him in Normandy; how beneficent he was and how closely he was joined to Edward by a line of kinship; and, moreover, how through his zealous aid he had been restored from exile to the kingdom. Wishing above all to repay him with something most worthy and most pleasing, in the manner of honorable men, he resolved to establish William, by a confirmed gift, as heir to the crown he had obtained through him. Therefore, with the assent of his leading men, he sent him, through Robert, archbishop of Canterbury, the mediator of this delegation, hostages from the most powerful family: the son and grandson of Earl Godwin.

Domestic turbulence among us has now been wholly changed into calm. But a neighboring rival had not yet entirely quieted down. Geoffrey Martel was raising against us an arm with which he was not lightly wounding himself. For, since he was exceptionally skilled in the art of war, what triumph could the Angevins, Tourangeaux, Poitevins, Bordelais, and the many regions and numerous cities that obeyed his standards not promise him? He had in fact captured by force of arms his own lord, the count of Poitiers and Bordeaux, and did not permit his captive to return by restoration to his former status until he had extorted an enormous weight of silver and gold, as well as very rich estates, together with an oath concerning the agreements. Moreover, on the fourth day after the captive’s death, following his ransom, Geoffrey took the man’s stepmother—of the highest nobility—to his own bed, accepted his brothers into his protection, and claimed the treasures, together with the whole extent of their honors and power, almost as his own possession.

He considered it a poor and disgracefully narrow confinement for his power to be shut within the boundaries of the county of Anjou. Savage greed dragged him far and wide through the possessions of others. Thus, enlarged by his acquisitions, he accomplished many notable things, acting no less through varied cunning than through resources. Among them he conquered the great wealth and strength of the Tourangeaux as well, after first crushing the valor of Count Theobald. For when Theobald was preparing to come to the aid of his beloved city—whose groaning under the hard blows of the besieging Martel, and whose near collapse, he had learned from the city itself—Martel met him with the utmost readiness and defeated him. Finally, having captured him, he confined him at Baugé together with his chief men; nor did he expel them under a milder agreement than the one by which he had previously expelled William of Poitiers. From that time he possessed the city of Tours. He likewise harassed all France by rebelling against the king.

Elated, therefore, by the success of his battles, he seized by assault a fortress of Normandy and carefully held Alençon. He had found its inhabitants favorably disposed toward him. He regarded it as a splendid addition to his name that he had accomplished something which diminished the dominion of Normandy. William, capable of defending his paternal and ancestral right, and indeed of extending it more widely, entered the Angevin territory with an army, intending first to exact retaliation by removing Danfront from Geoffrey, and then to recover Alençon.

Yet he nearly perished through the treachery of one of his own soldiers, who did not fear to pass through the enemy’s broad province. When he was approaching Danfront, he turned aside with fifty horsemen to collect what would increase their pay. A certain leading Norman, however, betrayed him to the men of the castle, revealing where and why he had gone, how few accompanied him, and that he was a man who preferred death to flight. Three hundred horsemen and seven hundred foot soldiers were sent out immediately and attacked him from behind while he was unaware. But he boldly presented his chest to them and struck down the first man whom their extraordinary daring had thrown against him. The others, their momentum immediately lost, fled back to the fortification.

He advanced by a known shortcut along the road. But he did not desist from the pursuit until the gates of the fortification snatched the fugitives away. He seized one man and held him with his own hands. This increased his eagerness to besiege the place, and he set up four castles around it. The position of the town denied a swift assault with all the force or skill available: the roughness of the cliffs drove back even the infantry, except those who could approach by two narrow and steep paths.

Geoffrey had placed in the town’s defense a select body of men to assist its inhabitants. Nevertheless, the Normans pressed their attack upon them with repeated and furious assaults. The duke himself loomed first and most terrifying. Sometimes he rode all day and all night; sometimes he hid in concealed places to discover whether anyone had been intercepted while bringing provisions, sent on an embassy, or lying in wait for his foragers. Indeed, to show how securely he moved about in hostile territory, he sometimes went hunting. That region abounded in forests rich in wild animals. He often amused himself with the flight of falcons, and still more often with that of hawks. Neither the difficulty of the terrain, nor the severity of winter, nor any other adversity could drive his unyielding courage away from the siege.

The besieged sent for Martel and summoned him by messenger, expecting him to come to their aid. They were by no means willing to abandon the lord under whom they could freely acquire profit through brigandage; this was the reason they had been enticed to settle in Alençon. They knew well how hated a robber or marauder was in Normandy, how each was sentenced to punishment according to due process, and that neither would be acquitted cheaply. They feared that the same application of the law would overtake them for their own crimes.

Geoffrey led out an enormous force of cavalry and infantry to relieve them. When William learned of this, he hurried to meet him, entrusting the continuation of the siege to tried soldiers. Roger of Montgomery and William son of Osbern, both young and vigorous, were sent ahead to reconnoiter. Through conversation with the enemy himself, they also thoroughly learned the mind of their extremely arrogant opponent.

Through them Geoffrey announced by his trumpet that William’s watch at Danfront would be aroused before tomorrow’s dawn. He described beforehand what sort of horse William would have in battle, what sort of shield, and what sort of clothing. They replied that there was no need to tire him by the longer route he had chosen, since the man for whom he was going would soon be there. In turn, they described their own lord’s horse, clothing, and weapons.

When these reports were delivered, they added considerably to the Normans’ eagerness. But the duke himself, more ardent than all the rest, urged on those who were hastening forward. Perhaps the most pious young man desired that the tyrant be destroyed. The Latin and Athenian senate judged this the finest of all his glorious deeds.

But Geoffrey, overwhelmed by sudden terror before he had even seen the opposing line, entrusted his own safety to flight with his entire army. Behold: the Norman duke now had an open road for ravaging the enemy’s wealth and erasing the rival’s name beneath everlasting disgrace. Yet he knew that it belongs to the prudent to moderate victory, and that a man is not sufficiently powerful if he cannot restrain himself when he has the power to take revenge.

He therefore decided to turn his fortunate advance elsewhere. Hastening from there, he suddenly arrived at Alençon and accomplished this difficult task with almost no battle. The town, so strongly fortified by nature, construction, and armament, came into his hands with such rapidly advancing success that he might have gloried in the words: “I came, I saw, I conquered” (*veni, vidi, vici*).

This report quickly struck the men of Danfront. They no longer trusted that they could save themselves by their shields after the flight of the famous warrior Geoffrey Martel. Accordingly, when they saw the prince of the Normans returning to attack them, they likewise hastened to save themselves by the speediest surrender.

Men of older memory report that both these camps had been founded with the permission of Count Richard, one inside the other, close to the borders of Normandy, and that they had habitually obeyed both the commands of his successors in the countship and his own. The victor later returned home and illuminated the whole homeland with renewed honor and rejoicing, while at the same time spreading his love and fear more widely among foreign peoples.

At about the same time this same prince accomplished other deeds suited to the volumes of the Annals. We pass over many things that he did at other times, either lest an expansive book burden anyone, or because we have judged that the matter was not sufficiently worthy of the writer. Besides, since we possess only limited ability in speaking, we reserve that ability for relating the most excellent deeds of all. Poets may give birth in their breasts to wars that their pens will produce, and may enlarge what they know by wandering through the fields of invention. We shall praise this duke—or king—for whom nothing beautiful was ever impure, purely, never straying a single step from the boundary of truth.

After this, almost all the leading Normans began to embrace him with extraordinary veneration. As they had earlier resisted him, so now each strove to prove his own loyal devotion to him, to such an extent that they competed to make both him and the offspring whom they then cherished only in hope their lord, by the unanimous choice of their wishes.

He himself attributed everything that had been loyally done either toward him or by him to the divine gift, as it ought to be attributed, with humble wisdom, conducting himself as a most self-controlled man at the beginning of his youth.

Counsel therefore began to be taken concerning marriage, as minds and opinions of people of different kinds commonly advise different courses, especially when an important matter is deliberated in a large court. Kings from far away would willingly give their uniquely beloved daughters to this husband, and especially wished to have as in-laws those who were their neighbors; the weight of many considerations persuaded them of this.

At that time Baldwin, the margrave of Flanders, was powerful among the peoples bordering on the Germans and the Franks, and foremost among them in authority. He was likewise most illustrious through the nobility handed down from an ancient stock. For he traced his ancestry both to the satraps of the Morini—whom modern people call Flemings—and to the kings of Gaul and Germany, even reaching a line of Constantinopolitan nobility.

Counts, margraves, and dukes were astonished as they admired him, as was the high dignity of archbishops, whenever the exceptional guest’s presence had earned the attention of imperial concern. They sought his wisdom in deliberating the greatest affairs, as though he were their friend and ally, and sought to secure his goodwill through gifts and lavish expenditure on honors.

In name he was a soldier of the Roman Empire; in reality he was its supreme distinction and glory in counsels during its greatest need. Kings, too, both revered and feared his greatness. Even distant nations know how, through frequent and grievous wars, he exhausted the savagery of emperors, until peace was finally arranged on terms dictated according to his judgment; and how he violently deprived certain kings—the lords of their own lands—of part of their territories, extorting them from them. He protected each of his own possessions with a hand that was either unconquered or, rather, indefatigable.

After France, the monarchy, together with its boy monarch, passed under the guardianship, direction, and administration of this exceptionally wise man. This margrave—far greater in offices and titles than can be briefly explained—personally presented to us at Ponthieu his daughter, a lady most welcome to us, nobly bringing her to her father-in-law and husband.

Her prudent and holy mother had nourished in her daughter something that far outweighed her father’s gifts. If one seeks her maternal lineage, one should know that her mother’s father was Robert, king of France, who, the son and grandson of kings, fathered kings. The world’s tongue will not be silent about his praiseworthy devotion to divine religion and his governance of the kingdom. The city of Rouen was free for the arrival of this bride, rejoicing in it.

At this point we are compelled to speak of a well-known event, and we cannot pass over Count William of Arques himself through the rapidity of our style as he hastened toward greater things—though the tears of his homeland show how powerful he was in his efforts beyond the bounds of what was fair and good.

Neither human nor divine law held back this ignoble and treacherous offspring of a distinguished stock, Guy—William. Nor did these restraints, nor Guy’s downfall, nor the admirable valor and good fortune of the great victor, who had never been defeated by anyone, nor the illustrious name thereby acquired, hold him back.

What ought to have raised both men toward outstanding courage and every praiseworthy deed instead plunged them into immoderate confidence and excessive ambition: namely, their exaggerated awareness of their origin. Both wrongly understood themselves to be counted among the descendants of the dukes of Normandy. Burgundio claimed to be a grandson of the Richards through the daughter of Richard II; the man of Arques claimed to be the brother of Richard III, the son of Richard II, and grandson of Richard I.

From the beginning of the prince’s rule, this man was faithless and hostile toward him. Although he had sworn loyalty and obedience, he carried on hostile actions, sometimes resisting with undisguised recklessness, sometimes through secret intrigues. Improper elevation of spirit very easily drives a man into unjust actions.

Moved by the dissensions and other evils mentioned above and arranged in some detail, he himself stirred up some as the principal leader, and incited, strengthened, and confirmed many more by his example, counsel, favor, and assistance. His schemes were numerous, restless, and prolonged. They were directed toward increasing his own greatness and opposing that of his lord, whose access he repeatedly rose up to block not only from the castle of Arques but also from the neighboring part of Normandy situated this side of the Seine.

Finally, during the siege of the aforementioned Danfront, he withdrew in the furtive manner of a deserter, without having requested permission to depart. He now wholly refused the military service that he had previously used, in some fashion, to cloak his hostility.

Because of these and his many other great and daring actions, the duke, perceiving—as circumstances warned him—that he would attempt still more and greater things, occupied the higher stronghold of the refuge in which William placed the greatest confidence. He sent a garrison into it, yet did not otherwise diminish any of William’s rights.

Indeed, William himself had first laid the foundations of that fortress as a hiding place for his incipient arrogance and madness, and had constructed it with the greatest labor on the summit of the very high mountain of Arques. Not long afterward, however, the faithless guards returned control of the castle to its founder, exhausted and subdued by promises of gifts and by various entreaties that pressed upon them ever more heavily.

Soon, inflamed by the fury that had been admitted within them, they became more savage than usual, as though they intended to exact vengeance for themselves as people diminished by injuries. Great misery arose throughout the surrounding district. Tumults, plunder, and robbery raged, threatening devastation. The castle was equipped with arms, men, provisions, and everything suitable for such an undertaking; its already strong defenses were made stronger. No place was left for peace or leisure. Finally, a most savage rebellion was organized.

When this became known to Duke William—he had received a reliable report in the district of Cotentin—he hastened from there with such speed that all the horses of his companions except six collapsed from exhaustion before they reached Arques.

The disasters reported in his province urged him on even more eagerly to confront the injury against him. He was grieved that the property of churches, the labor of peasants, the profits of merchants, and the plunder of soldiers were being unjustly taken. He intended to summon to his aid the helpless common people, whose great lamentation commonly arises in times of war or sedition.

On the road, not far from the castle itself, he encountered certain commanders of his army, men loyal to him and valued by him. They had heard through a sudden report at Rouen what the count of Arques was doing, and with three hundred horsemen they had hurried to Arques, hoping that they might be able to prevent the transport of grain and other supplies necessary for the siege.

But when they learned that enormous forces of soldiers had gathered there, and because they feared that even those who had accompanied them might cross over to William’s side—so their friends’ secret opinion had predicted before the rising of the following day—they lost confidence and returned as quickly as possible.

They reported these matters and advised him to wait for the army. They claimed that more of its forces were deserting than rumor had spread, that almost the whole neighborhood was yielding to the enemy’s favor, and that it was extremely dangerous to proceed with so few men.

But his resolve was not at all shaken by these words into fear or distrust. Strengthening them with this reply—that the rebels would certainly dare nothing against him when they saw him present—he hurried on, advancing as quickly as he could force his horse with the spurs.

His own courage drove him forward, and a just cause promised him success. And behold: when he saw the leader of the rebellion on the high mountain with a battle line of many legions, he struggled up the steep slope and forced all of them with the greatest energy to turn their backs and retreat inside the fortification.

Had the doors not been barred more quickly, he would have pursued them and, as his angry and courageous spirit demanded, cut down a large part of those ill-omened men.

We relate a deed truly accomplished, and something that nearly happened, though posterity will find it difficult to believe. Then, wishing to gain possession of the fortification, he quickly assembled an army at his command and surrounded it. It was extremely difficult to attack men whom the nature of the place defended so effectively.

Indeed, following his excellent custom of wishing to accomplish the matter without bloodshed, he shut up the savage and stubborn rebels behind a barrier built at the foot of the mountain, placed a garrison there, and later withdrew when other business summoned him, intending to spare them the sword but conquer them through hunger.

Reason worthy of remembrance also advises us to record how his pious self-restraint always avoided slaughter unless military force or some other grave necessity demanded it. He preferred to punish by exile, imprisonment, or another penalty that did not take life those whom other rulers, according to custom or the provisions of law, destroy by the sword when captured in war or when clearly convicted at home of capital crimes.

He wisely considered how terrifying an Arbiter from above observes the actions of earthly power, assigning to each according to its due both measured clemency and immoderate cruelty, and every quality of merit.

When King Henry heard that the man whose madness he had supported and advised was shut up, he hurried to bring aid, leading a considerable force of armed men and a large quantity of whatever the besieged needed.

Some of those who had been brought to the hope of achieving a memorable deed—men from the number of those left in the duke’s garrison—watched the roads by which the advancing Franks were traveling and ambushed them. And behold: a large part of the less cautious force was intercepted.

Ingelrannus, count of Ponthieu, known for his nobility and courage, was killed, along with many other distinguished men. Hugh Bardulf, himself also a great man, was captured.

Nevertheless, when the king arrived where he had intended to go, he attacked the garrison with the greatest force and with the most exasperated spirit, intending to rescue William from his troubles and at the same time avenge the slaughter of his own men. But when he perceived that the undertaking was difficult—for the enemies had easily endured the assault behind the castle’s fortifications, and the strength of the soldiers was equally firm—he hastened to withdraw lest he be driven away by a bloody death and a shameful flight.

He gained no honor, unless perhaps it was honorable to have relieved, by pay, the want of those for whose sake he had come and increased the number of their soldiers.

Then the duke returned to the siege and, after remaining for some time in battle array, nearly conquered the place. The sharpness of hunger pressed upon the besieged more fiercely and more tightly than arms.

The king was summoned again by a very humble and pitiful messenger, but he refused to come, reflecting on the previous outcome and fearing something harsher and more disgraceful.

At last, seeing amid distress that the desire to seize a principality from his own lord was misguided, he recognized that violating an oath or trust was both unjust and usually destructive; while the name of peace was pleasing and sweet, peace itself was certainly pleasant and beneficial.

He himself condemned above all the excessively rash undertaking, the utterly mad counsel, and the ruinous deed. He grieved that, while armed, he was being confined in narrow circumstances.

The supplicants obtained permission to surrender. They agreed upon nothing except their lives—nothing else either honorable or useful.

Behold a sad spectacle, a lamentable end. The Franks, famous shortly before as horsemen, hurried beyond what their weakened strength could sustain to escape with the Normans. Their necks were bruised by disgrace no less than by hunger.

Some hung upon starving pack animals whose hooves could scarcely sound or raise a little dust; others, equipped with boots and spurs, moved in an unfamiliar procession. Most of them sat upon cavalry saddles with their backs bent and weakened; some could scarcely carry themselves, staggering and swaying.

It was also possible to see the wretched and varied calamity of the lightly armed troops as they emerged.

The duke’s clemency, worthy of celebration, pitied this misfortune as it had earlier pitied Guy’s. He did not wish the exile, made destitute by an even more shameful accident, to be tortured further. Instead, he granted him his homeland with his favor, certain extensive possessions, and many revenues, judging that it was better in his case to remember his uncle than to persecute an adversary.

During this very Norman siege, several of the more powerful men defected from the duke to the king. It was plausible that they had earlier been secret supporters and accomplices of the rebels’ conspiracy. They had not yet entirely disgorged the malevolence with which they had once been inflamed against the child.

One of their number, Guimundus, who was in command of the fortress called Molendina, handed it over to the king. A royal cohort was placed in it, including Guy, brother of William, count of Poitiers, and of the Roman empress, together with military men of distinction.

But both these men and all the others who had been left elsewhere by the Franks, when they learned that the strongholds of Arques had been surrendered, stole away from our men by flight.

The Normans, however, in accordance with the law governing deserters, were reconciled to their lord with a light punishment or none at all, judging that no resources or stratagems of theirs would now be effective against him.

After this France began to burn more fiercely with rivalry and to be stirred by a new tumult. All the princes, together with the king, became bitter enemies of the Norman prince, who was already their enemy.

A painful and especially envious wound swelled anxiously in their malevolent minds: the recent death of Count Ingelrannus and of those who had been killed in the same conflict.

The memory of the Angevin count Geoffrey, driven back some time earlier by William’s shield, as we have related, inflamed them bitterly, as did the losses of many others and the disgraces inflicted upon them by Norman valor.

We explain the causes of this enmity truthfully. The king endured it with the greatest distress and defined it as an insult to himself, to be avenged as fully as possible. He had the Roman emperor as his friend and ally—no greater name of power or dignity exists in the world—and he presided over many powerful provinces whose lords or military governors served as officers in his army. Yet Count William was neither his friend nor his soldier, but his enemy. Normandy, which had long been governed under the kings of the Franks, had nearly been elevated into a kingdom; and although William’s predecessors had possessed considerable strength, none of them had undertaken such actions.

Theobald, count of Poitiers, Geoffrey, and the other leading men, grieving over this and adding a certain private indignation, considered it intolerable that they should obey the king’s standards wherever he summoned them. They wished to wage war against William—not at all as though he were a king of the Normans, but confidently and without interruption, so as to wear down still further his greatness, which he had somewhat diminished, or, if any means were available, to crush it entirely.

Moreover, certain close relatives of the king desired Normandy or part of it. Like blazing torches, they set the king and the princes on fire.

For these reasons, after a consultation shared under an ill omen, a royal edict ordered war, and an enormous army was sent into Normandy. You might have seen Burgundy, Auvergne, and Gascony hastening forth, terrible with iron—or rather all the forces of so great a kingdom, extending across all four quarters of the world. France and Brittany, however, were the more fiercely hostile because they were nearer to us.

You might affirm that Julius Caesar—or any more experienced commander, if such a one existed—leading a Roman army once assembled from a thousand nations, when Rome at the height of its prosperity ruled a thousand provinces, could have been terrified by the monstrous size of this host.

Our land naturally conceived some fear. The churches feared that the leisure of holy religion would be disturbed and their revenues seized at the whim of armed men, although they trusted that they were contending under the protection of their prayers.

The urban and rural common people, and everyone who was unarmed or less strong, were anxious and trembling. They feared for themselves, their wives, their children, and their possessions, measuring such a serious enemy as greater through fear than he actually was.

But when they remembered what sort of defender they had, and how, while still a youth—or rather a boy—he had endured the mournful disasters of his homeland through great wisdom and the greatest courage, they softened fear with hope and consoled affliction with confidence.

The duke William, however, of admirable steadfastness and struck by no fear, hurried with great courage to oppose the king, who was himself leading an enormous force and was gradually advancing from the district of Évreux toward Rouen. When he learned how the enemy had been distributed, he directed part of his own forces across the opposite bank of the Seine to meet them.

This was the arrangement devised by his skill, and it was expected to be highly advantageous: whatever soldiers could be gathered between the rivers Seine and Garonne—those many peoples whom, under one name, they call Celto-Gauls—were to invade us from one side under the king himself; while from the other side, leaders were to advance between the Rhine and the Seine, the region now called Belgic Gaul, under the king’s brother Odo and his closest companion Rainaldus.

Aquitaine also accompanied the king. Many judged it the third part of Gaul both in the breadth of its territory and in the number of its inhabitants.

Nor was it surprising if the Franks’ reckless and arrogant confidence, so strongly fortified, had some hope that our duke would either be crushed by such a mass of forces or escape through a shameful flight; that his soldiers would either be killed or captured; that his towns would be destroyed, his villages burned; that some things would be struck down by the sword and others seized as plunder; and finally that the whole land would be reduced to a foul wilderness.

But the event had a very different outcome. Odo and Rainaldus engaged under an unlucky omen, and when they saw their line being ravaged with terrifying violence, they abandoned both leadership and the aid of the sword and sought safety through the speed of their horses.

The sword of Robert, count of Aucy—great both in birth and in courage—was pressing upon their undeserving necks, together with that of Hugh of Gournay, Hugh of Montfort, Walter Giffard, William Crispin, and the other very brave men of our side.

Count Guy of Ponthieu, too eager to avenge his brother Ingelrannus, was captured, along with many men distinguished by birth and wealth. Very many fell; flight rescued the rest together with their standard-bearers.

When our defender, Duke William, quickly learned of this success, he cautiously sent out a certain well-equipped man in the middle of the night. From the top of a tree, nearer to the king’s camp, he shouted out the sad news of the king’s victory one word at a time.

The king, stunned by the unexpected message, without any hesitation roused his men to flight at the pre-dawn signal, judging it absolutely necessary to withdraw from Normandy’s borders with the greatest possible speed.

Afterward, many hostile acts were carried out on both sides, such as commonly occur between such great enemies apart from a direct battle.

At last, since the Franks most eagerly desired an end to their grievous internal dissensions, peace was agreed upon. The pact between the duke and the king was as follows: those captured at Mortemer would be returned to the king; but with the king’s consent and as a kind of gift, the duke would retain by perpetual right what he had taken from Geoffrey, count of Anjou, and whatever else he might be able to take.

Immediately, at the very meeting, the duke ordered the commanders of his army to be notified and to be ready to arrive promptly within Martel’s Angevin territory, in order to build fortifications at Ambrières. He fixed for them the same day for beginning the work as he set through messengers for Martel.

O the strong, confident, and noble spirit of this man! O the admirable valor, not easily exalted by a fitting proclamation! He did not seek to conquer the land of some weakling, but that of the fiercest tyrant, who, as the preceding events have shown, was exceptionally vigorous in warfare—one whom the most powerful counts and dukes trembled before like a dreadful thunderbolt, and whose strength and stratagems scarcely anyone bordering upon him could escape.

Moreover, to make the deed still more admirable, he did not attack the enemy while he was unsuspecting and unprepared. Instead, forty days beforehand he announced to him where, when, and for what purpose he would come.

Struck by the terror of this report, Geoffrey of Mayenne hurried to Geoffrey, his lord, and, grieving and lamenting, complained that, once Ambrières had been built with Norman resources, his land would be invaded, destroyed, and laid waste at the enemy’s pleasure.

The tyrant Martel, however, as was his custom when elated in spirit, was accustomed to presume and speak grandly. “You may deny,” he said, “that I am your lord, as though I were a base and disgraceful master, if you see me permit what you fear to be carried out.”

On the appointed day, the ruler of the Normans entered the land of Le Mans. While he was raising the castle he had threatened to build, he heard, according to a report—for rumor flies as the messenger of both falsehood and truth—that Geoffrey Martel would soon arrive.

Therefore, after completing the work, he awaited the enemy’s arrival with great steadfastness and eagerness. But when he saw that Martel was delaying beyond expectation and that both commoners and nobles were already complaining of a shortage of provisions, he decided to dismiss the army, lest he have soldiers who would be less ready for future action.

He fortified the castle with men and provisions, ordering them all to return there as quickly as possible when they received his message.

As soon as the departure of our army became known, Martel, joined by William, count of Poitiers and his own lord, and by Odo, count of Brittany, together with forces gathered from every direction, hastened toward Ambrières.

Then, after examining the position and defenses of the garrison, he prepared to attack. They prepared to cut through the rampart, but the defenders resisted. They grew heated, dared more, and advanced closer and more fiercely; both sides fought with great force.

Missiles, stones, heavy stakes, and spears struck from above. Many were killed by these weapons; others were driven back. When this bold attempt had failed, they began another. They attacked the wall with a battering ram, but when it was struck by the defenders’ pole, the ram broke.

Meanwhile, William, the founder of the fortification, learned of the exertion of his men. Unable to tolerate any delay, he summoned his army and hurried as much as possible to bring help.

When the enemy perceived that three such famous counts were riding against them, they dispersed with their enormous armies with astonishing speed—or rather, with a frightened flight.

The victor immediately attacked Geoffrey of Mayenne in war. The latter’s complaint mentioned above had especially inflamed his lord’s anger. Within a short time William compelled him to surrender in such a way that, in the most remote parts of Normandy, he submitted his hands, now subdued, and swore the loyalty that a retainer owes to his lord.

Again, when peace had been broken, the king, seeking revenge more for his disgrace than for his losses, renewed his expedition and attacked Normandy with an army indeed large, but less monstrous than before.

A greater part of his kingdom was mourning the deaths of its men or fearing their disgraceful flight, and was therefore less inclined to return against us, although it was far more eager for vengeance upon us.

Geoffrey of Anjou, not yet broken by so many adverse events, was not absent. He brought whatever forces he could collect by any means, for nothing short of Normandy’s being utterly crushed or destroyed could satisfy this enemy’s hatred and rage.

Concealing the report of their movement as much as they could, lest they be repelled immediately upon entering by the defender they had already experienced, they reached the river Dive by rapid marches through the county of Exmes, ravaging the land with enemy savagery as they passed.

They did not dare either to turn aside there or to halt. For if they were permitted to proceed farther at the speed with which they had arrived, and then to escape safely into France, they promised themselves an opportunity for great fame: they would have ravaged William the Norman’s land with sword and fire all the way to the sea, with no one resisting and no one pursuing.

But that hope, like the earlier one, deceived them. While they were lingering at the ford of the Dive, William himself arrived, eager, with a small force of men, at a fortunate hour.

Part of the army had already crossed the river with the king. And behold, the very brave avenger fell upon those who remained. He struck down the ravagers, believing it a crime to spare them when the cause of the wounded homeland demanded such action and the most hostile enemy had been caught in its very midst.

Almost all those intercepted on this side of the water fell by the sword before the king’s eyes, except those who, driven by fear, preferred to plunge themselves into the river.

But lest the rightly raging sword pursue them to the opposite bank, the river’s backwash prevented it, occupying the bed of the Dive with an irresistible mass.

Pitying and fearing for the destruction of his men, the king withdrew from Normandy’s borders as quickly as possible together with the Angevin tyrant. This energetic and famous man, accomplished in military affairs, decided with a shaken mind that it must be considered madness to attack Normandy again.

Not long afterward he departed along the way of all flesh, never boasting of a triumph that he had won over Count William the Norman—indeed, he had not secured much revenge against him.

His son Philip succeeded him while still a child. Between Philip and our prince a firm peace was established, together with a serene friendship, with all France wishing and consenting to it.

At about the same time Geoffrey Martel also died, to the satisfaction of many whom he had oppressed or who had feared him. Thus nature places an inevitable end upon earthly power and human arrogance.

The pitiable man was too late in regretting his excessive strength, his ruinous tyranny, and his destructive greed. His final days taught him what he had previously neglected to consider: that even those things which are justly possessed in this world must necessarily be lost.

He left as heir his sister’s son. Unlike him in character, though bearing the same name, this man began to fear the heavenly King and to perform good deeds in pursuit of external honor.

We know that human tongues are more ready to praise malevolence than benevolence, usually because of envy, and sometimes because of another depravity. For they commonly distort even the most beautiful deeds into their opposite through unjust corruption.
