It is therefore clear that the honorable deeds of kings, dukes, or any excellent person are sometimes condemned by the judgment of good people when they are not truthfully transmitted to later generations, so that evils not at all worthy of imitation may not, through such an example, become pleasing as a pretext for invasion or some other unjust deed.

For this reason, we consider it worthwhile to transmit as truthfully as possible how this William, whom we celebrate in writing and whom we wish to displease no one but rather to please all—both those now living and those yet to come—came into possession of the principality of Le Mans, just as of the kingdom of England, not only by a strong hand but also as one who ought to possess it under the laws of justice.

[Col. 1234A] The dominion of the counts of Anjou had long been burdensome and almost intolerable to the counts of Maine. To omit many other matters, most recently, in our own memory, Fulk of Anjou lured Herbert of Maine, the elder, to Saintes by promising him that city. There, in the midst of a conference, he had him bound and compelled by imprisonment and torture to accept the terms he had greedily desired.

In Hugh’s time, however, Geoffrey Martel repeatedly burned the city of Maine by setting it on fire; repeatedly he distributed it as plunder among his soldiers; often he uprooted the vineyards around it; and once, after expelling the man who had lawfully ruled it, he claimed it entirely for his own dominion. Hugh left his inheritance, and the same enmities, to his son Herbert. Fearing that he would be utterly destroyed by Geoffrey’s [Col. 1234B] tyranny, Herbert humbly approached William, duke of Normandy, under whose protection he would be safe. He surrendered himself to him, received all his possessions from him as a soldier receives them from his lord, and appointed him sole heir of everything if he himself should beget no other heir. Moreover, so that he and his descendants might draw closer to so great a man, he sought and arranged a marriage with the duke’s daughter.

Before she had reached marriageable age, however, he himself died of illness, and at the very end he earnestly entreated and implored his people not to seek anyone other than the man whom he was leaving them as their lord and himself as heir. If they willingly obeyed him, they would bear an easy service; if they were subdued by force, it might prove burdensome. They knew that man’s power, prudence, strength, glory, and ancient lineage very well. Living under his rule, they would be a source of fear to all their neighbors.

But disloyal men received Walter of Mantes, the count to whom Hugh’s sister had been married, as an invader, having deserted their rightful lord. William, therefore, indignant at this rejection, prepared arms to reclaim what had thus been taken from Herbert, to whom he was heir by many rights. For Maine had formerly been governed under the dominion of the dukes of Normandy. He could immediately have set the city ablaze, or utterly destroyed it, and killed those who dared such injustice, to the full extent of his intelligence and strength. Yet, with his customary restraint, he preferred to spare even the blood of the most guilty men, and to leave unharmed that very strong city, the chief place and stronghold of the land that he held.

He therefore chose this method of conquering it: by frequent expeditions and [Col. 1234D] prolonged stays in the territory itself, to inspire fear; to lay waste vineyards, fields, and villages; to seize fortified places on every side; to install garrisons wherever circumstances required; and, finally, to afflict them incessantly with every sort of hardship. When the people of Maine saw these things being done, how anxious and terrified they were, and how earnestly they desired to cast off so grievous a burden from their necks, it is easier to imagine than to describe. More than once, after summoning Geoffrey, whom their ruler Walter had appointed as his own lord and protector, they threatened to engage in battle, but never dared to do so.

At last, after the castles had been subdued and the whole county brought under control, they surrendered the city to the stronger power. The man whom they had kept at bay through a long rebellion, they received with humble and immense [Col. 1235A] honor. High, middle, and low alike made it their concern to appease the offended ruler. They ran to meet him, cried out that he was their lord, fell down and bowed before his dignity, and assumed cheerful faces, joyful voices, and the applause of congratulation. The religious orders of all the churches present there came to meet him, joining in the enthusiasm of the laity. The temples shone, adorned with the utmost care, as were the processions; incense filled the air with fragrance; sacred songs resounded.

For the victor, it was sufficient punishment that the conquered had come under his power and that the city’s stronghold was henceforth occupied by his own garrison. Walter willingly agreed to surrender, lest, by protecting what had been invaded, he should lose his hereditary possessions. The disaster inflicted by the Normans upon the territories of Mantes and Chaumont made him fear still greater losses.

[Col. 1235B] The prudent victor and devoted parent reflected that he had acted wisely for all time and for his descendants. He therefore resolved to marry his son to Herbert’s sister, whom he had brought from the lands of the Germans at enormous expense and with the greatest generosity, so that through her he himself and his descendants might possess Herbert’s inheritance—his sister’s husband and her nephews holding it by a right that no dispute could remove or weaken.

Since the boy’s age was not yet mature for marriage, he had the girl guarded with great honor in safe places until she approached marriageable age, committing her to the care of noble and wise men and women. This noble maiden, named Margaret, was more beautiful in her distinguished appearance than any pearl. But not long before the day on which she was to be joined to a mortal bridegroom, the Son of the Virgin, the bridegroom of virgins, the heavenly Emperor, took her from the human race. The pious girl burned with his life-giving fire; for love of him she devoted herself to prayer, abstinence, mercy, humility, and, finally, every form of goodness. She ardently desired to know no other union forever than union with him.

The monastery of Fécamp buried her. Together with the other churches, insofar as religion permitted, it deeply mourned that she had been snatched away by a premature death, though it had most earnestly desired her long life. For her soul, prudently watchful, awaited Christ’s coming with a burning lamp and began to honor the churches with reverence. The hair shirt by which she had proposed more secretly to subdue her flesh, discovered after she had departed this life, revealed a mind intent upon eternal things.

How far the cunning Geoffrey of Mayenne was from being favorably disposed toward Duke William was most clearly revealed when the city of Maine was surrendered. For, unwilling to witness this glorious success of his, he deserted him, driven on by grief no less envious than his treachery was fickle. In his shameless audacity he refused to remember how, when subdued, he had formerly begged for mercy. Shameless iniquity did not hesitate to violate its sworn promise.

Yet men far greater than he, though powerful, have never gloried in an everlasting name. He seemed to be doing as he pleased if he dared to challenge unconquered virtue, magnified by so many triumphs. Warned repeatedly through envoys to submit, he did not abandon his obstinate purpose. [Col. 1236A] Flight, cunning, and strong fortifications supplied him with no small confidence.

The rejected lord therefore decided to take from him the castle of Mayenne, his most cherished refuge. He judged it far better and more honorable to strike him with this punishment than to pursue him in flight and add an easy victory over a captured man to his own distinguished titles. One side of this castle is washed by a rocky and swift river—for it stands above the bank of the Mayenne on a precipitous mountain crag—and no force, ingenuity, or human art can attack it there. On the other side, stone fortifications and an exceptionally difficult approach offer equal protection.

Nevertheless, a siege was arranged, our army being brought as near as the resisting nature of the place allowed. Everyone marveled that the duke would undertake so extremely difficult a task with such confidence. Almost all thought that so many cavalrymen and infantrymen would be wearied in vain; many complained that there was no hope of raising their spirits unless, perhaps, hunger should conquer the place after a year or more. No action was being taken, nor was any action expected, with swords, lances, or missiles; nor with a battering ram, artillery, or other instruments of war, since the site was wholly unsuitable for siege-machines.

But the high-spirited commander William pressed on with what he had begun. He ordered, encouraged, strengthened the doubtful, and promised a happy outcome. Nor did the uncertain remain so for long. Behold, by his skilful plan, fires were set and seized the castle. They spread with the greatest speed in their usual manner, destroying with greater ferocity than any weapon everything in their path. The guards and defenders, stunned by the sudden disaster, abandoned the gates and the wall, and ran about [Col. 1236C] in panic, first trying to rescue their households and possessions from the flames. Then they hastened to secure their own safety by whatever refuge they could find, fearing the victors’ swords more than the fire.

The Normans rushed together with the greatest eagerness, raising joyful spirits and a simultaneous cry of congratulation. They burst in competitively and took possession of the stronghold by force. Rich booty was found: noble horses, military arms, and furnishings of every kind. As elsewhere, when substantial booty was captured, the most self-controlled and generous prince wished it to belong to his soldiers rather than to himself.

The castellan and those who had fled into the citadel surrendered themselves on the following day, trusting in no fortification against William’s skill and courage. After restoring what the flames had damaged and prudently arranging a garrison, he carried home an unprecedented triumph, as though he had overcome nature itself, amid the immense joy of the army. Geoffrey of Mayenne’s neighbors did not receive the news sadly that he had been punished by this loss; they declared that the glory of Count William alone constituted the vengeance of many against a perjurer and a robber.

At nearly the same time, King Edward of the English, in favor of William, whom he loved in place of a brother or child and had already designated as his heir, took precautions by a pledge more solemn than the one previously given. He wished to forestall the necessity imposed by death, whose hour a man of holy life, advancing toward heavenly things, judged to be near. He sent to William Harold, who would confirm his fidelity by oath, a man outstanding among all who were subject to Edward’s rule in rank and power. Previously Harold’s brother [Col. 1237A] and nephew had been accepted as hostages concerning this same succession.

Edward acted with the greatest prudence, so that Harold’s wealth and authority might restrain the dissent of the whole English people, should they desire to alter the arrangement through treacherous fickleness. While Harold was attempting to come on this business, after escaping the dangers of a sea voyage he reached the coast of Ponthieu, where he fell into the hands of Count Guy. He himself and his retinue were taken into custody—a misfortune brought about for so great a man by shipwreck.

For the cunning of avarice had taught certain peoples of Gaul a detestable custom, barbarous and far removed from all Christian equity. They ensnare powerful or wealthy men, shut them up in prisons, and subject them to insults and tortures. Thus, after crushing them in various miseries almost to the point of death, they very often cast them out after selling them for a high price.

When Duke William learned what had happened, he sent envoys at once. By entreaties and threats alike he secured Harold’s release and honorably went to meet him. Guy, who deserved well—for, compelled neither by money nor by violence, he had himself brought to the castle of Eu and presented to William the man whom he could have tortured, killed, or sold at will—received fitting thanks. William granted him extensive and very fertile lands and added enormous gifts of money.

He brought Harold, with every sufficient honor, into Rouen, the capital of his principality, where manifold acts of hospitality most delightfully refreshed those who had endured the hardships of the journey. He was naturally delighted to receive as a guest so important an envoy of his dearest kinsman and friend, whom he hoped would prove a most trustworthy mediator between himself and the English, among whom Harold was second only to the king.

When a council had been assembled at Bonneville, Harold there swore fidelity to William according to the holy rite of the Christians. As the most truthful and highly honorable men who had been present as witnesses related, Harold himself willingly specified the following points in the full form of the oath: that, as long as he survived, he would be Duke William’s representative at the court of his lord, King Edward; that he would exert all the counsel and resources at his disposal so that, after Edward’s death, the English monarchy might be secured in William’s hands; that in the meantime he would deliver Dover Castle into the custody of William’s soldiers, having fortified it at his own effort and expense; and that, in various places in that land, he would also provide other castles, wherever the duke wished them to be strengthened, together with abundant provisions for their guards.

The duke, having accepted Harold as his retainer, gave him, before the oath was sworn, the lands and entire power that he requested. For Edward’s life, already weakened by illness, was not expected to last long.

Then, knowing that Harold and those who had come with him were fierce and eager for a new reputation, and equipped with military arms and excellent horses, William took them with him into the Breton war. He treated his guest and envoy almost as a companion in arms, so that by this honor also he might make him more faithful and more obligated to himself.

All Brittany, for its part, was confidently armed against Normandy. Its leader was Conan, son of Alan. Having grown into a most fierce man and been freed from the guardianship that had long restrained him, he captured his uncle Eudo and consigned him to prison fetters; then he began to rule the province, which he had received as a paternal gift, with great savagery.

Thereafter, as a renewer of his father’s rebellion, he wished to be not a soldier but an enemy of Normandy. His lord, William of Normandy, by ancient right meanwhile set against him on the frontier the castle called Saint James, so that hungry raiders would not harm defenseless churches or the common people at the furthest edge of his land by marauding expeditions.

For King Charles of the Franks had purchased peace and friendship from Rollo, the first duke of the Normans, giving him his daughter Gisela in marriage and handing Brittany over to him in perpetual service. The Franks had sought this treaty because they could no longer resist the Gallic [Col. 1238B] sword against the Danish axe. The pages of the annals bear witness to it.

From that time onward, the Breton counts were never able entirely to free their necks from the yoke of Norman rule, although they often attempted it, struggling with all their might. Alan and Conan, the closer they were related by blood to the rulers of Normandy, the more proudly and exultantly they rose up against them. Conan’s recklessness had by then grown so great that he did not fear to announce the very day on which he would attack the borders of Normandy.

For a man of sharper nature and ardent age, confidence was greatly strengthened by a region spread far and wide and crowded with more soldiers than could be believed. In those regions, one man begets fifty, having, in barbarian fashion, ten or more wives—a practice reported of the ancient Moors, who were ignorant of divine law and modest custom.

Moreover, the population itself is devoted above all to arms and horses and scarcely at all to the cultivation of fields or to civilized ways. They sustain themselves on extremely abundant milk and very little bread. Their vast lands produce rich pastures for cattle and are almost ignorant of grain crops.

When they are not engaged in war, they live by, or practice themselves in, plunder, brigandage, and domestic slaughter. They enter battles with burning eagerness; while fighting, they rage like madmen. Accustomed to drive others back, they yield with difficulty. They rejoice and exalt themselves excessively in victory and the praise won by fighting, and they love to strip the spoils from the slain as though it were an honorable and pleasurable task.

Taking none of this terror into account, Duke William remembered the day on which Conan’s arrival had been announced and met him within his own borders. Conan, fearing that a blow like lightning was about to fall upon him, immediately fled with the utmost speed toward defensible places, abandoning the assault on the castle of Dol in his own land. That castle stood firm against the rebel and faithful to the just cause.

Ruallus, the castle’s commander, tried to stop Conan. He called after him in mockery and begged him to delay for two days, promising to obtain from him sufficient payment for this delay. But the wretchedly terrified man, listening more to fear, continued his flight and fled farther.

The terrifying commander would have pressed after the fugitive whom he had driven away, had he not recognized the manifest danger of leading a numerous army through broad, famished, and unknown regions. Whatever remained in the impoverished land of what had grown the previous year, the inhabitants had hidden with their livestock in safe places. [Col. 1239A] The crops stood unripe in the ears.

Therefore, lest the army seize as sacrilegious plunder whatever ecclesiastical goods it might find, he led back the army, exhausted by monthly scarcity, with great courage, presuming that Conan would soon beg pardon for his offense and seek his favor. But when William was already crossing beyond the boundary of Brittany, he was suddenly informed that Geoffrey of Anjou had joined Conan with immense forces and that both would be present for battle on the following day.

The conflict was therefore opened with all the greater eagerness because William understood how glorious it would be to win, in a single engagement, a triumph over a twofold enemy, both of them savage. Moreover, the fruits of that triumph would be manifold.

Ruallus, however, in whose territory the tents had been pitched, addressed a complaint to him. He said that he was indeed grateful to have been rescued by William from hostile force, if the benefit were not destroyed by the accompanying harm. For if William remained waiting, a region of only moderate fertility, already excessively depleted, would be utterly devastated. It made no difference to the farmers whether a Norman or a Breton army consumed the labor of the year and caused them to lose it. As far as he was concerned, Conan’s expulsion had served his reputation, but not the preservation of his possessions.

The duke replied that he had to consider whether a hasty withdrawal might produce an unfavorable opinion. He promised full compensation for the damage in gold. Immediately he forbade the soldiers to touch Ruallus’s crops and livestock. The order was obeyed with such restraint that a single sheaf of grain would have been more than enough to compensate for all the damage.

The battle was awaited in vain, since the enemy fled farther into the distance. After being received in his own land by his dear guest Harold, William stayed with him for some time and then sent him away laden with gifts, as befitted both the man at whose command he had come and the man for whose honour he had come to promote. Indeed, Harold’s other nephew, who had been a hostage, was returned with him for Harold’s sake.

We shall therefore address you briefly, Harold. With what mind, after these events, did you dare to take William’s inheritance from him and wage war against the man to whom you had subjected yourself and your people by a sacred and holy oath, with both tongue and hand? You ought to have restrained them, yet you stirred them up most disastrously.

Unhappily favorable were the winds that breathed upon your blackest sails as you returned; impiously merciful was the sea that allowed it to carry you, a most detestable man, toward the shore; sinister was the calm anchorage that received you as you brought the most wretched shipwreck upon your homeland.

Yet amid his occupations in military affairs, or in domestic matters, which are called worldly, the excellent prince’s devotion to divine things was outstanding—so much so that we cannot recount each instance in proportion to its greatness. For he knew not only that the flourishing principalities of this world end in a brief decline, but also that the form of the world itself passes away.

There is, however, one kingdom that stands immovably. Over it presides an ineffable Emperor with everlasting dominion, governing by providence coeternal with himself the whole universe that he created; he is able in an instant to crush tyrants too devoted to the sweetness of earthly things; and in that most glorious city, the homeland of true and supreme goodness, he disposes diadems and palaces, forever shining with immeasurable splendor, for the perseverance of his servants.

William knew that his illustrious father, Duke Robert, after the memorable achievements by which he had been distinguished at home, had laid aside the insignia of office and undertaken a foreign journey full of dangers, from desire to behold that Emperor in the heavenly Zion. He knew that Robert had humbly borne the cross upon his forehead, love in his mind, reverence in his conduct, and that Richard and his earlier ancestors, exalted by power and renowned by fame, had done likewise.

As a man of prudent soul, William had considered how wretched and disgraceful it is for those stripped of transient honor to be condemned to a dark exile, where they will burn in an unquenchable flame without being consumed, lament in misery without mercy, and mourn their errors [Col. 1240B] without forgiveness. Conversely, he knew how blessed and beautiful it is, after earthly consulships, to be enrolled as a citizen among the angels, clothed in the robe of immortality, where one will delight in every pleasure, contemplate God as he is, and rejoice forever in his praise.

A man worthy, therefore, of his devout father and devout ancestors, even while constantly engaged in arms, he never lowered his inner eye from fear of everlasting majesty. By crushing external wars with arms and restraining seditions, robberies, and plunder, he cared for his homeland as it worshiped Christ, so that the more it enjoyed peace, the less it would violate sacred institutions. It will never rightly be said that he undertook a war devoid of justice.

Thus the Christ-worshiping kings of the Roman and Greek peoples protect what is theirs and repel injuries, striving justly for victory. Who could say that it belongs to a good ruler to tolerate seditious men or robbers? Through his punishment and laws, thieves, murderers, and evildoers were expelled from Normandy.

The pact of peace, which they call the truce (Trevia), was observed with the greatest sanctity in Normandy, although the unrestrained wickedness of other regions frequently violated it. William himself humbly heard the cause of the widow, the poor man, and the orphan; he acted mercifully and pronounced judgment with complete justice. While his fairness restrained unjust greed, no powerful man or courtier dared move the boundary of a weaker neighbour’s field or seize any possession.

Villages, castles, and cities had their rights made firm and secure through him. The common people celebrated him with joyful applause and sweet songs.

He was accustomed to receive the sermons of sacred Scripture with eager hearing and a receptive taste, desiring to delight in them as in food for the soul, to be corrected and instructed by them. He also received and honored the saving host with fitting reverence, holding with sincere faith what true doctrine had commanded: that the bread and wine placed upon the altar, consecrated by the priest’s tongue and hand according to the holy canon, are the true flesh and true blood of the Redeemer.

It is certainly not unknown with what zeal he pursued and sought to exterminate from his land anyone who held a contrary perversity. From his earliest youth he devoutly observed sacred solemnities, very often celebrating them together with an assembly of religious people, clergy, or monks.

[Col. 1241A] As a young man he became a great example to the old by his daily diligence in attending the sacred mysteries. Likewise, through his careful provision, his children learned Christian piety from infancy.

Certain men shine forth as objects of lament on the heights of earthly power, throwing themselves headlong into the destruction of their souls. Their greedy malignity resists the generous will of the best rulers: it makes the construction of basilicas within their dominion difficult or wholly impossible, forbids gifts to those already built, and does not shrink from stripping them, piling sacrilege upon personal wealth.

In many churches, however, our homeland praises the Lord for those built through the benevolent favor of its prince William and enlarged by his ready generosity. He willingly granted anyone who wished to contribute free authority to do so, never harming the saints by any injury or alienating anything dedicated to them.

In his time Normandy rivaled blessed Egypt in its communities of regular monasteries. He himself was their foremost patron and, by his faithful protection, their constant guide. He showed love, honor, and care to all, but more generously to those whom a greater reputation for devoted religion commended.

O diligence worthy to be remembered, imitated, and propagated for all ages! As a ruling layman, he carefully admonished abbots and bishops concerning ecclesiastical discipline; he steadfastly exhorted them and severely corrected them.

Whenever, at his command and encouragement, bishops assembled—the metropolitan with his suffragans—to discuss the condition of religion, clergy, monks, and laity, he did not wish to be absent from their synods. He attended both to add zeal to the zealous by his presence and to provide caution to the cautious, and also so that he would not need to learn from another’s testimony how matters had been conducted—since he desired that everything be conducted rationally, orderly, and in holiness.

If word reached him of some enormous crime that a bishop or archdeacon had punished more leniently than justice allowed, he ordered the offender against eternal majesty to be kept imprisoned until the Lord’s case had been decided by strict equity. He accused the bishop or archdeacon, as adversaries of the divine party, and summoned them to judgment, where they were to receive a severe sentence.

If he discovered, on credible testimony, that a cleric or monk’s life did not differ from his profession, he gladly conversed with him and inclined his whole will toward his requests. Conversely, he did not allow even the eyes of friendship to move him to respect an infamous man because of the enormity of his life.

He cultivated intimate friendship with a certain Lanfranc, about whom it is disputed whether he deserved greater reverence and worldly as well as divine glory for his singular knowledge of literature, or for his singular observance of the monastic order. William revered him as a father, feared him as a teacher, and loved him as a brother or child.

To him he entrusted the counsel of his soul and a kind of watchtower from which the ecclesiastical orders throughout Normandy might be surveyed. For the vigilant care of such a man, who had acquired the greatest authority through the distinction both of wisdom and of holiness, could promise no small security to the best of concerns.

By a kind of devout compulsion, William appointed him abbot of the monastery of Caen, although Lanfranc resisted as much through love of subjection as through fear of higher rank. Thereafter he enriched the same monastery with many possessions, as well as silver, gold, and various ornaments. At his own generous expense he built it from the foundations, with immense size and beauty, fittingly for the blessed protomartyr Stephen, whose relics were to make it glorious and whose honor was to consecrate it.

No one can esteem too highly the services of prayers sent up to heaven. Whenever war or some other difficult matter threatened, William frequently asked for and purchased the prayers of Christ’s servants at great and ever-greater expense.

As I recall these things, the sweet memory comes to me of the Emperor Theodosius, who, before setting out to fight the tyrants, was encouraged by the oracles and responses of the monk John, who lived in the farthest Thebaid. Theodosius esteemed John above all monks, since through obedience he had attained the grace of prophecy; William likewise esteemed Lanfranc, whose speech and conduct breathed the Spirit of God.

Most good men, warped by carnal affection for those joined to them by blood, spare their relatives’ crimes and refuse to descend from the heights of dignity on which they preside unworthily. Blinded by love, they judge these relatives most mercifully, while judging others with clear sight and severity.

William, however, whose unimpaired goodness we are recording, deserves to be considered and admired more attentively because, knowing that his father’s deposition was in no way to be preferred to divine justice, he carried out God’s business both prudently [Col. 1242C] and justly against his uncle Malger, the archbishop.

Malger, son of Richard II, abused his sacred dignity as though it were his by right of birth. He was never adorned with the pallium, however—the principal and mystical insignia of the archbishopric, which the hand of the Roman pontiff customarily sends—because he was judged unfit for it.

He was not unlearned in gathering the secrets of Scripture with the eye of literal understanding, but he did not strive to govern either the lives of his subjects or his own according to the discipline they prescribe. What the piety of many had enriched by adornment, he diminished by stripping it: he should not be called its bridegroom or father, but its most oppressive lord or most rapacious robber.

He loved to provide tables excessively ample and excessively splendid, buying praise by his generosity and lavish in the guise of liberality. Repeatedly warned and corrected, privately and publicly, by the wise diligence of his young secular lord, he preferred to continue along the same path of depravity. Nor did he place any limit on his gifts until the metropolitan see was almost entirely deprived of ornament and treasure.

Very often, acts of plunder follow acts of generosity. Moreover, the offensive odor of his infamy spread because of other crimes. But we consider it foreign to reason to linger over publishing vices whose commemoration seems neither seemly nor useful to know.

He also injured the universal Church with no slight offense. Its one supreme primate, the highest bishop in the world, he did not honor with the obedience that was due. For, summoned repeatedly by apostolic command to a Roman council, he refused to go.

Indeed, Rouen was ashamed of him, and all Normandy was ashamed of an archbishop who, though he ought to have surpassed all who excelled in the form of honorable conduct, was refuted by the testimony of the lowest persons and judged worthy of degradation amid universal contempt.

The prince therefore perceived that, in a matter of such great importance, action could no longer be taken by admonitions, lest by enduring further he provoke the anger of heavenly judgment against himself. He deposed his uncle publicly in a holy synod, with the apostolic legate and all the bishops of Normandy delivering sentence by unanimous agreement, according to the authority of the canons.

He then provided Maurilius for the vacant see, bringing him back from Italy, where he had shone above the other abbots mentioned earlier. Maurilius was most worthy of the supreme archbishopric by the merit of his lineage, person, virtues, and learning.

A certain equal of his, and a diligent companion in the fellowship of anchoritic rigor, named Gerbert, whom his consciousness and reputation placed near blessedness in every holiness, he later appointed over the monastery of Saint Wandrille, intending through a spiritual abbot to restore its fallen discipline.

Both men, in the full flower of their age, contemplated the divinity and the blessedness that divinity grants. With a far keener insight of mind than Plato, they escaped the obstacles of temporal affairs by their bare profession, despising the schools which they had loved through intense application to worldly philosophy, the sweet smile of their native soil, their kin renowned for wealth and nobility, and the hope of lofty advancement.

Thus, freed by a victorious spirit, they struggled now beneath the yoke of monasteries, now in the contest of the desert, vying with the Maccabees in sweat and exertion. For unending freedom and peace, they embraced every hardship and sought no preeminence in the exile of this passing world.

The same prince raised many churches to prominence through carefully weighed appointments of bishops and abbots, but especially the churches of Lisieux, Bayeux, and Avranches. For he appointed exceptionally suitable bishops: Hugh at Lisieux, his own brother Odo at Bayeux, and John at Avranches.

In their election, their virtue prevailed in his judgment, not the high birth of those related to him. John, the son of Count Ralph, though previously a layman in rank, had long been known among the clergy—indeed, admired by the leaders of the clergy—for his learning and religious life. It was not John’s desire that sought the honour of priestly rank; rather, the bishops’ wishes sought him out as a colleague to be consecrated.

From childhood, Odo had been inscribed among the number of the best by concordant praises of the best. His fame, it is said, traveled to distant regions; but his many qualities, generosity, and humility deserve still greater recognition.

Hugo, whom we have observed with especially close familiarity, we do not hesitate to describe at somewhat greater length than the others, since we do not doubt that knowledge of him will benefit them. He was Richard’s nephew and the son of William, count of Eu, a man no less good than noble. Raised by the prince from youth to the summit of the episcopate, he soon shone with a spiritual maturity more advanced than that of old men. He was by no means marked as arrogant because of his ancient lineage, nor, because of his higher rank or flourishing age, was he either elated in spirit or wandering through slippery pleasures. With vigorous diligence he balanced the weighty office, a burden to be carried with caution. He watched attentively over the ordering of his own conduct and, with unceasing care, kept watch over the flock entrusted to his nourishment, thus revealing how keenly he saw with his inward light that he had received sacred ministry and ecclesiastical government, not domination or honor.

He enriched the holy bride with lands, treasure, and the beauty of precious ornaments. He adorned her buildings also with such lavish care that an observer might hesitate whether new ones were rising or old ones being restored. But in himself he consecrated to her a dowry more precious than gold and electrum, and more splendid than any stone or jewel. Monasteries, synods, and courts revere and love this most reverend prelate: prudent and eloquent, just and discerning. He never favors money or influence, whether when pronouncing judgment or giving counsel. Indeed, when Archbishop Malgerius was deposed, he was the ringing voice of justice, steadfastly remaining on God’s side and, for God’s sake, condemning his paternal uncle’s son.

He shows himself gentle and severe in a most fitting alternation between the two: merciful toward every human being, but an unrelenting persecutor of every vice, a devout enemy of it. He gives his subjects the most faithful counsel, comparable in prudence to loving fathers who consider not so much the wishes of their young sons as their welfare. He favors them with congratulations and assists the soldiers of the heavenly King in whatever order they serve, honoring the King himself in the reverence and love of his soldiers.

Thus he always lives humanely, and so abstinently that he continually brings his meals to each person—more often, however, to one who will not return—and offers his fasts to God. He does not refuse to be cheerful and agreeable in fellowship, nor wholly silent, nor does he reject a plentiful and sumptuous table; he tastes at nature’s command, but does not feast. He is nourished by those delights with which he desires hungry souls to be nourished eternally, which the heavenly Paraclete pours into them with most sweet sweetness: vigils devoted to prayer, the diligent celebration of the divine offices, a most intimate cultivation of the sacred library, and, finally, an indefatigable love of every holy work. [Col. 1244D] These, I say, are what he chiefly delights in; on these the excellent shepherd of the Lord’s fold, Hugo, eagerly feeds.

In adversity he wins equal praise for steadfastness, and in prosperity for moderation; he is desirous of nothing. He found tongues that delight in injuring another’s reputation so hateful that he never wished to make his ear a witness to their wickedness. He exalts his dignity by the privilege of remarkable humility, and protects his continence, his other virtues, and every pious activity with that most secure and salutary guardian. For that mystical rational breastplate of Aaron spiritually adorns his inner being, continually reminding him of the holiness of the Fathers whose names it was commanded to bear inscribed upon it.

[Col. 1245A] But lest, while we are carried away by the pleasant contemplation of the temples of a most honorable life, we go beyond due measure, let us return to the deeds of Prince William.

Two brother kings of Spain, having heard of his greatness, eagerly sought his daughter in marriage, intending by this alliance to magnify both their kingdom and their posterity. A very hostile dispute arose between them on her account. She was by no means unworthy of such a father, but entirely worthy of him, so adorned in character and so devoted to the love of Christ that, though an un veiled girl, she could have served as an example to queens and consecrated women.

The majesty of the Roman Empire admired, praised, and venerated him beyond the names of kings. In former times its most glorious ruler, Henry, son of Conrad, the august emperor, had formed friendship and alliance with William while he was still a boy, as with a most renowned king. For even then the boy’s illustrious name was carried throughout the nations.

But let me speak of the man’s greatness. Noble and powerful Constantinople, ruling over many kings, desired him as a neighbor and friend, so that with him as defender she might despise the formidable power of Babylon. In Normandy no one now dared anything against a neighbor. Every storm of domestic sedition, as well as of foreign war, had fallen silent. Bishops and counts of France, Burgundy, and still more distant provinces frequented the court of the lord of Normandy: some to receive counsel, others benefits, and most merely to boast of his favor.

His kindness was rightly called a harbor and refuge, admitting and relieving many. Strangers, seeing among us knights traveling here and there unarmed, and every road open in safety to every traveler, often wished that such blessedness might exist in their own regions! William’s valor brought this peace and dignity to his country.

Therefore, when his country once saw him lying ill in uncertain condition, it rightly poured forth tears and prayers such as might obtain life for the dead. It prayed that he who was dying would die only very slowly, fearing that, at his premature death, the storm by which it had previously been troubled might rise again; for he would then leave behind no offspring of suitable age to govern. It is believed—and most deservedly—that the supreme Arbiter of pious devotion granted health and peaceful leisure to this vigorous servant of his majesty, with every enemy defeated, so that, having deserved to be raised to higher things, he might more easily possess the kingdom once it had been seized, secure in the condition of his principality.

For a true report unexpectedly arrived that the land of England had been deprived of King Edward and that Harold had been adorned with his crown. The mad Englishman did not wait to consider what the public election might decide. On the mournful day when that excellent king was buried, while the whole nation was grieving, the perjurer occupied the royal throne amid applause, with certain unjust men supporting him. Stigand, deprived of priestly ministry by the just zeal and anathema of the apostolic authority, performed his coronation—not a holy consecration.

Duke William, after consulting with his men, resolved to avenge the wrong by arms and reclaim his inheritance by arms, although several of the leading men cleverly tried to dissuade him, calling the enterprise excessively arduous and far beyond the strength of Normandy. At that time, besides bishops and abbots, Normandy had in its councils the most distinguished men of the lay order. Among them shone certain of its brighter lights and ornaments: Robert, count of Mortain; Robert, count of Eu; Hugo’s brother, the bishop of Lisieux, whose life we have described above; Richard, count of Évreux, son of Archbishop Robert; Roger of Beaumont; Roger of Montgomery; William, son of Osbern; and Hugh the viscount.

Under the direction and industry of such men, the state could have been preserved unharmed. The Roman commonwealth, relying on such men, would scarcely have needed two hundred senators, if it now possessed as much power as it had among the ancients. Yet we have learned that in every deliberation all conceded the wisdom of the prince, as though by a divine mind he foresaw what ought to be done or avoided. “God gives wisdom to those who act piously,” says a certain expert in divine matters. But William had acted piously from childhood.

Whatever he was pleased to command, all obeyed, unless necessity stood in the way. How ships were built under his prudent direction, equipped with arms, men, provisions, and other things useful for war; how the zeal of all Normandy burned; and how he prudently arranged for those who would govern and defend Normandy in his absence—it would take too long to recount in detail.

A large number of foreign soldiers also gathered to his aid. His well-known generosity attracted some of them, but all were drawn by confidence in the justice of his cause. Every act of plunder was forbidden. Fifty thousand soldiers were maintained at his expense while unfavorable winds detained them for a month at the port of Dives. Such was his restraint and prudence: expenses were supplied abundantly to soldiers and guests, and no one was permitted to seize anything. The provincials’ herds and flocks grazed safely, whether across the open fields or through the wilderness. The crops awaited the cultivator’s sickle untouched; neither the proud overflow of the cavalry trampled them nor did the forage-gatherer cut them down. A poor or unarmed man could ride wherever he wished, singing on horseback, seeing troops of soldiers without being terrified.

At that same time Alexander, the most worthy pope of Rome, sat in the chair of Saint Peter, one whom the universal Church obeyed and consulted. For he issued just and salutary responses. Although this bishop of Lucca sought no higher rank, he was placed, by the forceful consent of many whose authority then prevailed among the Romans, with a great council assenting, in that primacy in which he was to be the head and teacher of the bishops of the world. He had earned this election by holiness and learning. Through both, he shone from the rising to the setting of the sun. Nor does the sun more unchangingly follow the limit of its course than he directed his life along the straight path of truth, correcting whatever he could find unjust throughout the world and yielding to no one.

The duke sought the favor of this apostolic prelate and explained the undertaking he was planning. Through his kindness he received a banner, as a token of Saint Peter’s support, with which he might attack his adversary more confidently and securely.

He had also recently entered into friendship with the Roman emperor Henry, son of the Emperor Henry and grandson of Emperor Conrad; by his command, Germany would come to William’s aid against any enemy, if he requested it. King Sven of the Danes likewise promised him loyalty through embassies, but he showed himself a faithful friend to William’s enemies, as you will see when you read of his losses in what follows.

Meanwhile Harold, ready to fight either on land or at sea, usually waiting along the seacoast with a huge army, sent out cleverly disguised scouts. When one of them was caught and tried to conceal the purpose of his arrival under the pretext he had been instructed to use, the duke revealed the greatness of his spirit in these words:

“Harold has no need,” he said, “to squander his gold or silver in buying the loyalty and skill of you and the others who have come to spy on us by stealth. What is being planned and prepared among us will be reported to him by an informant more accurately than he wishes and more quickly than he expects, since my presence itself will teach him. Take this message from me to him: he will suffer no adversity from us that prevents him from passing the rest of his life in security, unless he sees me within the space of a year in the place where he hopes his feet are safest.”

The leading men of Normandy were astonished at this great promise, and many did not conceal their lack of confidence. In speeches dictated by despair, they magnified Harold and diminished William’s resources. Harold, they said, had abundant treasures with which he could hire the leaders and powerful kings of his party; he possessed a very large fleet and men highly skilled in naval service, who had often experienced maritime dangers and battles. His land was as rich as it was plentiful in soldiers, and in this respect surpassed Normandy many times over. Who could hope that ships could be completed, or oarsmen found for those already completed, within a year, as had been stipulated? Who would not fear that this new expedition might reduce the beautiful condition of the homeland to utter misery? Who would not affirm that the resources of the Roman emperor could not be overcome with such difficulty?

The duke then raised the spirits of the doubters with this speech:

“We have learned of Harold’s wisdom,” he said. “It terrifies us, but it increases our hope. He will spend his own resources uselessly, dissipating gold rather than consolidating honor. He possesses no strength of spirit with which he would dare promise even the least of my possessions. But at my discretion, both what is mine and what is said to belong to him will alike be promised and given. He will certainly overcome an enemy who can give away no less of what the enemy possesses than of what is his own.

“We shall sooner have sufficient shipping; we shall not be delayed. Let him have experienced the things which we shall experience with greater success. Wars are fought by valor rather than by the number of soldiers. Moreover, lest he lose what he has seized, he will fight; we, however, have acquired by benefactions the things we receive as gifts, and we demand them. This first confidence of our party, driving away every danger, will give us the most joyful triumph, the highest honor, and the most illustrious name.”

For it was clear to this Catholic and wise man that the omnipotence of God, who wills nothing unjust, would not permit a just cause to fall—especially since he considered that he intended not so much to increase his own dominion and glory as to correct Christian practices in those regions.

At last the entire fleet, most carefully equipped, was carried from the mouth of the Dives and the neighboring ports to the harbor of Saint-Valery, where it had long awaited the south wind, by a west wind’s blowing. There the excellent prince entrusted himself to heavenly aid through prayers, gifts, and vows, with complete confidence. Neither delay nor contrary winds, nor terrible shipwrecks, nor the fearful flight of many who had pledged their loyalty could break him.

Indeed, meeting adversity with counsel, he concealed as far as he could the deaths of those who had been drowned, burying them secretly; by increasing the provisions day by day, he eased the shortage. By different exhortations he also drew back the terrified and encouraged the fearful. He contended so earnestly in sacred supplications that he even had the body of Gualeric, a confessor most pleasing to God, carried outside the basilica against the obstruction and for a favorable wind, while the assembly of those who were to depart with him joined in the same weapons of humility.

When the awaited breeze began to blow, grateful voices and hands rose toward heaven, and at the same time a tumult arose as men encouraged one another. They abandoned the land as quickly as possible and eagerly entered upon the uncertain voyage. They were driven forward with such speed that one called out for his armor-bearer, another for his companion, and many, forgetful of retainers, comrades, or necessary equipment, thought only of hastening on lest they be left behind.

Yet the duke’s fiery energy rebuked and drove into the sterns those whom he noticed trying in any way to delay. But lest, before daylight, they should reach the shore toward which they were heading and be endangered at an unfavorable and unfamiliar anchorage, he issued an order through the herald’s voice: once they had been brought out into the open sea, all the ships should rest for a little while during the night, floating at anchor not far from his own vessel, until they saw a lamp at the top of the mast. At once, when the blast of the trumpet was heard, they were to take it as the signal to continue.

Ancient Greece tells how Atrides, Agamemnon, went with a thousand ships to avenge the violation of his brother’s marriage-bed. We declare that our William sought a royal crown with more ships. It tells how Xerxes joined the cities of Sestos and Abydos, separated by the sea, with a bridge of ships. We proclaim that William truly joined the expanse of Norman soil and English territory with a single nail of his authority. We judge that William—never defeated by anyone, who adorned his homeland with famous trophies and enriched it with brilliant triumphs—was superior to Xerxes, whose host was defeated by the enemy’s hand, and was his equal even without a fleet, indeed superior in valor.

After the ships had been released at night following their rest, the vessel carrying the duke left the others far behind, proceeding more eagerly toward victory and, as it were, obeying the command of his speed with equal speed. In the morning he ordered a rower to look out from the open sea and see whether any ships were approaching. The man reported that nothing other than sea and air appeared within his view.

The anchor was immediately cast. So that fear and grief might not unsettle his accompanying band, the most courageous duke received them with an abundant breakfast, not lacking spiced wine, as though in a memorable domestic dining room, promising that all the others would soon be there, brought by God, to whose protection he had entrusted them.

The Mantuan, chief among poets, would not think it unworthy to insert into the praises of Trojan Aeneas, who was the glory and father of ancient Rome, the security and purpose of this meal. The scout was questioned again. He cried out that four ships were approaching, then that three times as many were arriving, so that the thick abundance of their sail-bearing masts resembled a forest.

How greatly the duke’s hope was changed into joy, and how he glorified the divine mercy from the depths of his heart, we leave everyone to infer. Carried forward by a favorable wind, he reached Pevensey and disembarked freely from the ships, with no battle obstructing him. For Harold had withdrawn into the region of York, intending to fight his brother Tostig and Harold, king of the Norwegians.

Nor should you wonder that his brother, moved by injuries and jealous of the honor that had been invaded, brought foreign arms against Harold, whom his own sister—utterly unlike him in character—could not attack with arms but assailed with prayers and counsel: a man disfigured by luxury, a savage murderer, arrogant through wealth acquired by plunder, and an enemy of justice and goodness. That woman of manly prudence, who understood all honorable things and cultivated a virtuous life, wished William to rule the English, for she had decided that William, whom King Edward her husband had adopted as a son, should succeed him: a wise, just, and brave man.

# WAR BETWEEN DUKE WILLIAM AND HAROLD, KING OF THE ENGLISH

[Col. 1249]

[Col. 1249B] Rejoicing at having seized the shore, the Normans occupied Pevensey as their first fortification and Hastings as their second, so that these might serve them as a refuge and their ships as a defense.

Marius or the great Pompey—each an outstanding man who earned a triumph through cunning and industry, the former after bringing Jugurtha captive to Rome, the latter after compelling Mithridates to take poison—would have been afraid, if transported in this way into enemy territory, to lead his entire army while exposing himself separately from the army with only a legion. It has been the custom of generals to send scouts rather than go themselves, preserving their own lives through foresight more than preserving their army.

William, however, with an escort of no more than twenty-five soldiers, personally explored the places and inhabitants. Returning from there on foot because of the roughness of the route, he performed an action that, though perhaps it may make the reader laugh, supplied material for serious praise: he carried on his shoulder the coat of mail of a companion-at-arms, while he supported with bodily strength and courage William, the son of Osbern, a man of the highest renown, encased in iron.

A certain wealthy inhabitant of those borders, a Norman by nationality, Robert, son of Guimara, a noblewoman, sent a message to his lord and kinsman, the duke, at Hastings, in these words:

“King Harold fought with his own brother and with the king of the Norwegians, whom people thought to be the strongest man alive beneath the sky. In one battle he killed both of them and destroyed their immense armies. Encouraged by this success, he is hastening back against you, leading a very numerous and powerful people. Against him I do not think your men are worth any more than just as many contemptible dogs.

“You are considered a prudent man; until now you have acted wisely in all matters at home and in war. Now look to yourself, take precautions, and strive not to plunge yourself through rashness into a danger from which you cannot escape. I advise you to remain within the fortifications and not engage in battle for the present.”

The duke replied to the messenger:

“For the message by which your lord wishes me to be cautious—though he ought to have offered his advice without insult—I give him thanks, and report this to him. I would not protect myself in the shelter of ramparts or walls, but would fight Harold as soon as possible. Nor would I distrust the courage of my men, believing that, by God’s will, he would be crushed by them. Even if I had only ten thousand men, they would be such as those whom I have brought to the number of sixty thousand.”

One day, while the duke was inspecting the guard of the ships, it happened that he was told, as he walked near the naval camp, that a monk had arrived as Harold’s envoy. He immediately went to meet him and addressed him cleverly:

“I am,” he said, “the closest associate of Count William of Normandy and his steward. Since you will not be able to obtain an opportunity to speak except through me, tell me what you bring. Through me he will gladly learn the same, since he has no one among his own people dearer to him than I am. When you wish to use my services at the proper time, you will come and speak in his presence.”

After the monk had disclosed the embassy, the duke, without delay, ordered that the envoy be received as a guest and treated with courteous hospitality. Meanwhile he deliberated with himself and his men how he should answer the message.

The next day, seated among his leading men, he said to the hooded envoy:

“I am William, prince of the Normans by the grace of God. Repeat now in the presence of these men what you reported to me yesterday.”

The envoy spoke as follows:

“King Harold sends you this message: You have entered his land; with what confidence or rashness, he does not know. He does remember that King Edward formerly decided that you should be heir to the English kingdom, and that Edward himself gave you a firm assurance in Normandy concerning this succession. But Harold knows that the kingdom is lawfully his, since the same King Edward, his lord, granted it to him as a gift in the last moments of his life.

“For from the time when blessed Augustine came to this region, it has been the common custom of this people that a gift made by anyone at the end of his life should be considered valid. Therefore he asks you and your men to withdraw from a land that is justly his. Otherwise he will dissolve the friendship and all the agreements he himself confirmed for you in Normandy, leaving those matters entirely with you.”

After hearing Harold’s message, the duke asked the monk whether he wished to convey his greeting to Harold as his envoy. The monk promised to take care of his safety as though it were his own. The duke immediately instructed a certain monk of Fécamp to carry the following message more quickly to Harold:

“I have crossed into this land neither rashly nor unjustly, but deliberately and under the guidance of equity. As Harold himself admits, my lord and kinsman King Edward appointed me his heir, on account of the greatest honors and many benefits that I and my ancestors bestowed upon him, his brother, and their men. He believed me to be the most excellent of all those connected with his family, the one best able either to support him while he lived or to govern the kingdom after his death.

“Indeed, he did this not without the consent of his leading men, but on the counsel of Archbishop Stigand, Earl Godwin, Earl Leofric, and Earl Siward. They also confirmed with their own hands by oath that, after Edward’s death, they would accept me as their lord and would in no way seek, during Edward’s lifetime, to occupy this country against me by any obstruction. He gave me Godwin’s son and grandson as hostages.

“Finally, he sent Harold himself into Normandy so that what his father and the others named above had sworn to me in my absence, he might swear there in person to me in person. While he was on his way to me, he fell into danger of capture, from which my wisdom and courage rescued him. He surrendered himself to me with his own hands and with his own hand confirmed to me security concerning the English kingdom.

“I am ready to prosecute my case against him in judgment, whether he prefers the law of the Normans or rather that of the English. If the Normans or English decide, according to the truth of equity, that he ought by right to possess this kingdom, let him possess it in peace. But if they agree that it must be restored to me as the due of justice, let him yield it to me.

“If he rejects this condition, however, I do not consider it just that my men or his should fall in battle, since they bear no blame for our dispute. Behold, I am ready with my own head against his to assert that the English kingdom belongs by right to me rather than to him.”

We wish this carefully established meaning of the duke’s words, rather than our own version of them, to come before the eyes of many, because we desire that he be praised forever with the favor of many. From it one may clearly gather that he was truly prudent, just, devout, and brave. For the abundance of his arguments, as is clear to anyone who pays attention, destroyed Harold’s reasoning—arguments which even Tully, the greatest authority of Roman eloquence, could not have refuted. Finally, he was ready to accept whatever judgment the laws of the nations might define. He did not wish Englishmen to die as enemies over his dispute, but wished to settle the case by a single combat between his own head and Harold’s.

When these same messages were reported to Harold through the monk as he approached, he turned pale with astonishment and remained silent for a long time as though struck dumb. When the envoy asked him twice for a reply, he answered the first time, “We proceed without delay”; the second time, “We proceed for the price.” The envoy pressed him to give another answer, repeating that the Norman duke preferred single combat, not the destruction of armies. For the brave and good man wished to announce something just and joyful and did not want many to fall, trusting that Harold’s head would fall—a head for which there was little courage and no equity.

Then Harold lifted his face toward heaven and said: “Let the Lord today decide what is just between me and William.” Blinded by desire to reign and, in his fear, simultaneously forgetful of the wrong he had done, he wished the righteous judge to bring about his own ruin.

Meanwhile, at the duke’s command, the finest horsemen were sent to reconnoiter. They quickly reported that the enemy was near. The furious king was hastening all the more because he had heard that the countryside near the Norman camp was being ravaged. He was also planning to overwhelm them less cautiously by a nighttime or sudden attack. To prevent them from escaping by sea, he had stationed an armed fleet of nearly seven hundred ships as an ambush.

The duke quickly ordered all those found in the camp to arm themselves, for most of the allied forces had gone out that day to gather fodder. He himself attended the mystery of the Mass with the greatest devotion and fortified his body and soul through communion in the Lord’s body and blood. He also hung around his humble neck relics whose favor Harold had alienated from himself by violating the oath of loyalty he had confirmed over them.

Two bishops from Normandy were present with him, Odo of Bayeux and Geoffrey of Coutances, together with a large body of clergy and some monks. That company was appointed to fight through prayers. As the duke was putting on his armor, its left side turned inward, an occurrence that might have terrified another man. He laughed at this reversal as an accident and was not frightened by it as an evil portent.

We have no doubt that the exhortation by which, briefly and as the occasion required, he added great alacrity to the soldiers’ courage was excellent, even if it has not been reported to us in all its dignity. He reminded the Normans that, under his leadership, they had always emerged victorious from many and great dangers. He reminded everyone that they must now prove by their deeds what courage they possessed and what spirit they carried, worthy of the noble achievements and great reputation of their homeland.

He said that the issue was no longer which man should live as king, but which man would escape the impending danger with his life; that if they fought as men, they would possess victory, honor, and wealth; otherwise they would either be slaughtered more quickly or, if captured, become objects of mockery to the most savage enemies. Besides this, they would be branded with everlasting disgrace. No road to escape lay open, since on one side arms and an enemy land unknown to them stood in the way, and on the other the sea and arms.

It was not fitting for men to be terrified by numbers. The English, he said, had often been thrown down and killed by the enemy’s sword; they had usually been defeated and forced to surrender to the enemy; they had never been praised for military glory. Those inexperienced in warfare could easily be crushed by the vigorous courage of a few, especially since heavenly support would not be lacking for a just cause. They need only dare and not give way; they would rejoice in triumph all the sooner.

He advanced in the following most suitable formation: the apostolic banner that had been sent ahead; infantry in the front, armed with arrows and crossbows; stronger, armored infantry in the second line; and finally troops of cavalry. He himself was in their midst, with the strongest force, so that from there he could direct every part by hand and voice.

If some ancient writer were describing Harold’s army, he might record that, as it passed, rivers were drunk dry and forests leveled into plains. For the greatest forces from every region had gathered from all sides. Some favored Harold, but all supported their homeland, which they wished to defend against foreigners, although it was not in the right. The related land of Denmark had also sent them abundant auxiliaries.

Yet they did not dare to engage William on equal terms, considering him more formidable than the king of the Norwegians. They occupied a higher position, a hill near the forest through which they had arrived. Immediately they abandoned the use of their horses and all stood as infantry, densely packed together.

The duke and his men were not terrified by the roughness of the ground, but slowly ascended the steep slope. A terrifying blast of trumpets sounded the signals for battle, and the eager courage of the Normans on both sides gave the battle its beginning—just as, when advocates plead a case in court over a theft, the first to strike with words is the one who brings the charge.

The Norman infantry therefore advanced closer, challenged the English, and directed missiles against them, bringing wounds and death. The English, for their part, resisted bravely, each according to his skill. They hurled spears, weapons of various kinds, the fiercest axes, and stones mounted in wooden frames. You might have thought that our men were immediately overwhelmed by these as by a deadly mass.

The cavalry came to their aid, and those who had been behind became first. Ashamed to fight from a distance, they dared to settle the matter with swords. A tremendous cry from the Normans on one side and from the barbarians on the other was surpassed by the clamor of weapons and the groans of the dying.

Thus for some time both sides fought with all their strength. The English were greatly aided by the advantage of the higher ground, which they held without advancing and in the densest formation, as well as by their immense numbers and very powerful bodies. They were also aided by weapons that easily found a path through shields and other defenses. They therefore endured with great courage, or drove back, those who dared to attack them with drawn swords. They wounded those who hurled spears at them from a distance.

Then behold: terrified by this savagery, the British infantry and cavalry alike, together with all the auxiliaries on the left wing, turned away, and nearly the whole line of the duke gave ground—though this is said without dishonor to the invincible nation of the Normans. The army of Roman majesty, containing the forces of kings and accustomed to victory on land and sea, once fled when it knew or believed its commander had been killed. The Normans believed that their duke and lord had fallen.

Their withdrawal, therefore, was not excessively shameful, and certainly not to be lamented, since it proved greatly useful.

For the prince, seeing that a large part of the opposing position had surged forward and was pursuing the rear of his men, ran to meet the fugitives and blocked their way, striking or threatening them with his spear. He also uncovered his head and removed his helmet, crying:

“Look around for me! I am alive, and with God’s help I shall conquer. What madness persuades you to flee? What road will be open for your escape? Those whom you could slaughter like cattle are driving you away and killing you. You are abandoning victory and everlasting honor; you are rushing toward destruction and everlasting disgrace. By departing, none of you will escape death.”

At these words they recovered their courage. He himself ran first, flashing his sword, and laid low the opposing people who, by rebelling against their king, had earned death. The Normans, inflamed and surrounding several thousand who had pursued them, destroyed them in an instant so that not even one survived.

Thus encouraged, they attacked the savage army with greater force. Although it had suffered a great loss, it did not appear diminished. The English attacked confidently with all their strength, laboring above all not to open any entrance to those who wished to break in. Because of their excessive density, they could scarcely move without being killed. Nevertheless, paths were cut into them in various places by the swords of the bravest soldiers.

The men of Maine, the French, the Bretons, and the Aquitanians pressed upon them, but the Normans did so with the greatest valor.

A certain young Norman, Robert, son of Roger of Beaumont, nephew and heir of Count Hugh of Meulan through Hugh’s sister Adeline, experienced battle for the first time on that day and performed a deed worthy of being immortalized by praise. He led a legion on the right wing, charged, and struck down the enemy with great boldness.

It is beyond our ability, and contrary to our present purpose, to relate in proportion to their merit the brave deeds of every individual. Even a writer of the greatest eloquence, who had learned that battle with his own eyes, would find it very difficult to follow every detail. We are hurrying toward this point: having finished our praise of Count William, we shall write the glory of King William.

The Normans and their allied host realized that the enemy, resisting all together, could not be overcome without excessive harm to themselves. They therefore turned their backs, deliberately pretending to flee. They remembered how their flight shortly before had provided an opportunity for the desired outcome.

Great joy arose among the barbarians, together with hope of victory. Encouraging one another with exultant cries, they abused and threatened our men, declaring that they would immediately bring them all down. As before, several thousand dared to pursue at a gallop those whom they believed to be fleeing.

The Normans suddenly turned their horses back, intercepted those men, and slaughtered them after surrounding them on every side, leaving no one alive. They used the same stratagem twice, with the same result, and attacked the rest with greater eagerness—their line still dreadful and extremely difficult to surround.

Then a battle of an unusual kind took place. One side conducted it through charges and varied movements; the other endured it as though fixed to the ground. The English grew weak and, as though confessing their guilt by their very collapse, suffered punishment. The Normans shot, struck, and pierced them. As they fell, the dead seemed to move more than the living.

The dense mass of their allies did not permit the lightly wounded to escape but killed them by crushing them. Thus fortune ran on William’s behalf to hasten his triumph.

Those who took part in this battle were Eustace, count of Boulogne; William, son of Richard, count of Évreux; Geoffrey, son of Rotrou, count of Mortain; William, son of Osbern; Haimerius, governor of Thouars; Walter Giffard; Hugh de Montfort; Ralph de Tosny; Hugh de Grandmesnil; William de Warenne; and many others, celebrated far and wide for their outstanding military distinction, whose names deserve to be commended among the most warlike men in the volumes of history. William, their duke, surpassed them in courage as greatly as he did in prudence, and therefore deservedly ought to be preferred to some of the ancient Greek or Roman commanders most highly praised in writings, and compared with others.

He led them actively, restraining flight and giving courage as a companion in danger, more often shouting that they should come than ordering them to go. From this it is plainly understood that his valor made a path and boldness for his soldiers as well as for himself. A considerable part of the enemy lost heart without receiving a wound when they saw that admirable and terrifying horseman. Three horses fell beneath him, pierced by blows. Three times he leapt down fearlessly, and the death of his mount did not long remain unavenged. Here could be seen his speed, here the strength of his body and mind. With an angry sword that disdained delay, he pierced shields, helmets, and coats of mail; with his own shield he struck down several men.

When his soldiers saw him fighting on foot, many of them exhausted by wounds recovered their courage. Some whose blood and strength were already failing, leaning on their shields, fought manfully; others, when they could do nothing else, urged their comrades on by voice and gestures, so that they should not follow their duke timidly or let victory escape from their hands. He himself was a help and a means of safety to many.

With such a Harold as the poems describe Hector or Turnus, William would have dared to engage in single combat no less readily than Achilles with Hector or Aeneas with Turnus. Tydeus, against fifty ambushers, sought the aid of a rock; William, his equal and in no respect inferior, alone did not fear a thousand. The author of the *Thebaid* or the *Aeneid*, who in those very books, according to poetic law, sings of great things as greater still, ought to consider—or perhaps complete—a work equally great and more worthy by singing truthfully of this man’s deeds [f., *conficerent*: “should complete”]. Indeed, if they were to relate in fitting verse as much as the dignity of the subject supplied, they would transfer him among their gods through the beauty of their style.

But let our humble prose, in its lowly title, conclude briefly and truthfully the battle in which he conquered as bravely as justly, commending him to the piety of rulers in the worship of the true God, who alone is God from eternity to the end of the ages and beyond.

[Col. 1255D] Now, as the day was declining, the English army undoubtedly understood that it could no longer stand against the Northmen. They knew that they had been diminished by the death of many thousands; that the king himself, his brothers, and some of the kingdom’s leading men had fallen; that all those who remained were almost exhausted; and that no support was left for them to await. They saw that the Northmen had been little reduced by the fall of the slain and, as though gaining an increase of strength through fighting, were pressing them more fiercely than at the beginning. They saw the duke’s savagery, which spared no one who stood against him, and his courage, which would not rest unless victorious.

They therefore turned to flight and departed as quickly as possible: some seized horses, some went on foot, some by the roads, and most across trackless ground. Those who were unable to flee lay in their blood, whether they were trying to crawl onward or to rise. A desire for life, burning intensely, enabled some to do what they had been unable to do before. Many corpses remained in hidden woodland places; more, having collapsed along the roads, impeded those who followed. Although unfamiliar with the region, the Northmen pursued eagerly, striking the exposed backs of the fugitives and applying the final blow to their successful enterprise. Even the horses’ hooves inflicted punishment on the dead as they ran over those lying on the ground.

Nevertheless, confidence returned to the fugitives when they found an excellent opportunity for renewing the battle among steep valleys and numerous ditches. That people, descending from the ancient stock of the Saxons, the fiercest of men, had always by nature been ready for the sword. They would not have been driven back unless compelled by overwhelming force. They had so recently defeated the king of Norway, supported by a great and warlike army—how easily they had defeated him!

[Col. 1256B] But the leader of the fortunate standards, seeing the companies unexpectedly gathered, although he thought that reinforcements had newly arrived, neither changed his course nor halted. More terrifying with part of a spear than those brandishing huge javelins, he called out in a manly voice to Count Eustace, who had turned away with fifty soldiers and was preparing to sound the signal for retreat, ordering him not to depart.

Eustace, in turn, familiarly advised the duke in his ear to withdraw, predicting that death was close at hand if he proceeded. While these words were being spoken, Eustace was struck between the shoulders by a resounding blow, whose force was immediately shown by the blood from his nose and mouth. He escaped as though dying, with the aid of his companions. The duke, utterly rejecting either cowardice or disgrace, attacked and crushed the adversaries.

In that encounter [Col. 1256C] some of the more distinguished Northmen fell, their valor hindered by the unfavorable nature of the ground. Thus, when the victory had been completed, he returned to the field of battle and found the slaughter, which he viewed not without compassion, although it had been inflicted upon the impious, although killing a tyrant in a just war is beautiful, glorious in reputation, and pleasing as a benefaction.

The flower of English nobility and youth, soiled with blood, lay spread widely across the ground. His two brothers were found nearer the king. He himself, stripped of every mark of distinction except certain signs, was recognized—not by his face—and carried to the duke’s camp. The duke granted permission for him to be buried to William surnamed Malet, and did not yield his body to his mother even when she offered an equal weight of gold for the body of her beloved son.

For he knew that it was not fitting to accept gold in such a transaction.
