He judged it unworthy that the man should be buried according to the mother’s desire, since countless others would remain unburied because of his excessive greed. It was said in mockery that he ought to lie there as guardian of the shore and sea, where, in his madness, he had once taken his seat in arms.

We do not insult you, Harold; rather, with the pious victor, we mourn and lament your ruin with compassionate tears. You conquered with an outcome worthy of you and according to your merit; you lay in blood, and you lie in a coastal tomb; and to generations yet unborn, both English and Northmen, you will be hateful. Those who regard supreme power in the world as supreme happiness commonly fall; and, to become supremely happy, they seize it and strive to retain what they have seized by military force.

Yet you were drenched in your brother’s blood, lest your brother’s greatness make you less powerful. Then you rushed madly into a second conflict so that, aided by the murder of your country, you would not lose royal dignity. Thus the disaster you had brought upon yourself dragged you down. Behold: you do not shine in the crown that you wickedly invaded; you do not sit upon the throne that you proudly ascended. Your end shows how rightly you had been raised by Edward’s gift at the close of his life. The comet, terror of kings, which flashed after the beginning of your elevation, foretold your destruction.

[Col. 1257A] But, setting aside the dirge, let us discuss the prosperity that the same star announced. Agamemnon, king of the Argives, with many commanders and kings to aid him, scarcely overthrew Priam’s single city by deception in the tenth year of the siege. What the character and valor of his soldiers were, the poems testify. Likewise, Rome, so grown in power that it wished to rule the whole world, conquered several cities, taking years over each one.

But Duke William subdued all the cities of the English with the forces of Normandy in a single day, from the third hour until evening, with little assistance from outside. If Trojan walls had protected them, the hand and strategy of such a man would quickly have cut down Pergamum. The victor could immediately have gone to the royal seat, placed the diadem upon his own head, distributed the riches of the land as plunder among his soldiers, slaughtered some of the powerful, and driven others into exile.

But he chose to proceed more moderately and to rule more mercifully. From his youth he had been accustomed to adorn triumphs with self-restraint. It would have been fitting for the English—who had brought such ruin upon themselves through their wrongdoing—to die, their flesh devoured by the throats of vultures and wolves, and for the fields to be buried with their unburied bones. But he regarded such punishment as cruel. He granted those who wished to gather them for burial full permission to do so.

After burying his own dead and arranging a garrison, he approached Hastings with the energetic prefect Romanaer, and exacted whatever punishment he wished for the slaughter of his men, whom a savage people, having been driven there by error, had attacked in battle and routed with great losses on both sides.

From there he hastened to Dover, where he had learned that an innumerable population had gathered, because the place seemed impregnable. But the English, shaken by his approach, trusted neither in the defenses provided by nature or workmanship nor in their multitude.

[Col. 1257D] The castle stands on a cliff adjoining the sea. Naturally sharp, it had been laboriously cut on every side with iron tools for this purpose, rising in the form of a wall with an extremely straight height, as far as an arrow’s flight can be measured; on one side it is washed by the sea.

When the garrison were preparing humbly to surrender, the armed men of our army, eager for plunder, set fire to the place. The flame, leaping about in its lightness, seized most of the buildings. The duke, unwilling to harm those who had begun to treat with him concerning surrender, paid the cost of restoring the buildings and compensated them for their other losses. He would have ordered stricter action against the authors of the fire, had their usefulness and large number not concealed them.

After recovering the castle, he added fortifications over eight days wherever they were lacking. The soldiers there, living on fresh meat and water, were many of them killed by a flux of the bowels, while very many were weakened to the extremity of life. Yet these adversities did not break the duke’s courage. Leaving a garrison there, together with those weakened by dysentery, he set out to subdue those whom he had defeated.

The men of Canterbury came voluntarily to meet him not far from Dover; they swore fidelity and gave hostages. The powerful metropolis also trembled with fear and, lest it fall utterly, hastened to obtain its position by obedience, without offering resistance in any way. Arriving the next day at the Broken Tower, he pitched his camp. There, suffering from a severe illness of the body, he disturbed the spirits of his attendants with a corresponding anxiety.

But, desiring the public good and unwilling that the army should suffer from a lack of necessities, he did not permit himself to delay there. Although it would have been beneficial to all, and greatly desirable, for the excellent duke to recover his health.

[Col. 1258B] Meanwhile Stigand, archbishop of Canterbury, who, just as he excelled in wealth and dignity, so wielded great influence among the English through his counsels, threatened battle together with the sons of Ælfgar and other powerful men. They had appointed Edgar the Ætheling king, a boy descended from the nobility of King Edward. The sum of their wish was evidently to have no lord whom they had not had as a fellow countryman. But he who ought to rule them, advancing fearlessly, took up position not far from London when he heard that their assembly was more numerous.

The river Thames flowed past that city, bringing foreign riches from the seaport. Although it had only its own citizens, it abounded in a populous settlement renowned for wealth and military excellence. At that time, however, a crowd of foreign defenders had streamed into it, and although the city was excessively spacious in circumference, it could scarcely contain them.

Five hundred Northmen horsemen were sent ahead. When the opposing line came out against them, they briskly compelled it to flee within the walls, giving ground as they retreated. They added fire to the great slaughter, burning whatever buildings they found on this side of the river, so that proud ferocity might be subdued by a double calamity. The duke then advanced wherever he pleased, crossed the Thames by both ford and bridge, and reached the town of Guarengefort [Walengford].

[Col. 1258D] Stigand, the metropolitan bishop, came there as well, surrendered himself to him, confirmed his loyalty by oath, and revoked Edgar the Ætheling, whom he had lightly chosen. As soon as London came into view for the duke who was advancing from there, the city’s leaders came out to meet him. They delivered themselves and the whole city into his service, as they had previously done at Canterbury, and brought the hostages—those and as many as he ordered.

After this the bishops and other great men asked him to accept the crown. They said that they were accustomed to serve a king and wished to have a king as their lord. He consulted his companions from Normandy, whose prudence no less than their loyalty he had tested, and disclosed to them what chiefly dissuaded him from doing what the English requested: affairs were still unsettled; some were in rebellion; he desired the peace of the kingdom rather than the crown. Moreover, if God granted him this honor, he wished his wife to be crowned with him. Finally, he said that one ought not to hurry excessively while ascending to a lofty summit.

Indeed, the desire to rule did not dominate him. He understood that the pledge of marriage was sacred and loved it as sacred. His attendants, on the contrary, urged him to do what they knew was desired unanimously by the entire army, although they recognized that his reasons were most praiseworthy and flowed from the secret depths of abundant wisdom.

[Col. 1259A] Haimerius of Aquitaine, governor of Thouars, was present at this council, a man whose speech was no less distinguished than his right hand. Admiring and courteously praising his modesty in asking the soldiers whether they wished their lord to become king, he said:

“Soldiers have never, or only rarely, been summoned to deliberate on a matter of this kind. We must not prolong by our deliberation what we desire to have done as quickly as possible.”

Yet those wisest and best men would not have wished to place him so high in this monarchy unless they had seen him to be especially suitable, even though they wished their own advantages and honors to be increased through his elevation. He himself, weighing everything once more within himself, yielded to so many who asked and advised him, especially hoping that once he began to reign every rebel would dare less against him and would be more easily crushed by him.

He therefore sent men ahead to London to construct a fortification in the city and prepare most of what was appropriate to royal magnificence, while he remained for the time being in the neighboring districts. Every adversity was far away, so that, if he wished, he could safely devote himself to hunting and the sport of birds.

On the day appointed for the coronation, the archbishop of York, a mature man of age, wise, good, eloquent, and a great lover of justice, addressed the English in fitting speech and asked whether they consented to have him crowned their lord. All declared their joyful consent without the slightest hesitation, as though given from heaven with one mind and one voice.

The Northmen readily agreed with the will of the English after Bishop Constantine had spoken to them and asked their judgment. But those who had been stationed in arms and on horseback as a guard around the monastery, mistaking an unfamiliar sound amid the excessive tumult for a hostile signal, unwisely set fire to a place near the city.

Thus the same archbishop consecrated the chosen king, a man equally esteemed for his holy life and unblemished reputation. He placed the royal diadem upon him and installed him on the royal throne, with many bishops and abbots present in support, in the basilica of the apostle Saint Peter, which rejoiced in possessing the tomb of King Edward, during the most sacred solemnity of the Lord’s Nativity, in the year 1066 of the Lord’s Incarnation.

For he had refused to be consecrated by Stigand of Canterbury, whom he had learned had been justly condemned by apostolic zeal with an anathema. The insignia of kings suited his person no less than his virtues proved him fit to govern. His children and grandchildren, by rightful succession, would rule the English land, which he himself possessed both by hereditary grant confirmed by the oaths of the English and by the right of war, having been crowned with the consent—or rather the desire—of the leading men of that same people.

Even if the claim of blood relationship is required, it is very well known how close a kinship connected King Edward with the son of Duke Robert: Emma, the aunt of Richard II and daughter of the first Richard, was Edward’s mother.

After the coronation had been celebrated, he did not, as is customary after an increase of honors, begin to conduct himself more laxly in praiseworthy matters. Rather, this most worthy king was kindled by a new and admirable ardor for honorable and great deeds—a title that our style gladly accepts in place of the name “duke.”

He devoted himself energetically to both secular and divine affairs, yet his heart was more inclined to the service of the King of all kings. He attributed his advancement to Him, knew that no mortal could long possess power or life against Him, and expected from Him unending glory when his temporal life ended.

Therefore, as though paying tribute to this Emperor, he generously distributed what King Harold had greedily locked away in his treasury. Merchants had been accustomed to bring abundant wealth to those lands, rich in their fertility, through imported treasure. Treasures of the greatest number, quality, and craftsmanship had been amassed, either to be guarded for the empty pleasure of avarice or shamefully consumed in English luxury.

He magnificently distributed part of them to the ministers of the completed war, and gave a great deal, including the most precious objects, to the poor and to monasteries in various provinces. This zeal for generosity was aided by a considerable revenue which cities everywhere and all the wealthy had offered to their new lord.

He sent to Pope Alexander a quantity of gold and silver for the Roman church of Saint Peter greater than can be believed when described, together with ornaments that Byzantium would regard as extremely precious. He also sent the memorable banner of Harold, bearing in woven gold the image of an armed man, so that he might return an equivalent gift for the favor of that apostolic man and at the same time beautifully proclaim the triumph, desired at Rome and beyond, over the tyrant.

How many assemblies of Christ’s servants, formerly his supporters and armed by the armour of his prayers, then joyfully sang hymns of thanksgiving for the victor—we recount only briefly. The memory of King William will be perpetually celebrated by a thousand churches of France, Aquitaine, Burgundy, Auvergne, and other regions. The greatness of his benefaction, always living, will not allow the memory of the benefactor to die.

Some received very large golden crosses, magnificently adorned with gems; most received pounds of gold or vessels made from the same metal; others received cloaks or some other precious object. He splendidly adorned the metropolitan basilica, while even the smallest of these gifts brought joy to some monastery.

I would have these things, and many others recorded in this little book, become known to dukes and kings as examples or encouragement. Indeed, gifts of the greatest delight arrived in Normandy from her beloved son, sent with the eager affection of a devoted father, while the violence of the season and sea was at its fiercest with January approaching.

But the news of the event, which she had awaited with intense anxiety, she received a thousand times more dearly. For nothing beautiful or sweet that Arabia could offer would have been so welcome to her. No day ever dawned brighter for her than when she learned with certainty that her prince, the author of her peaceful condition, was king.

Cities, castles, villages, and monasteries rejoiced greatly for the victor, but even more congratulated him as ruler. A light of unusual serenity seemed suddenly to have arisen over the entire province. Although it thought itself abandoned by its common father because it lacked his presence, it nevertheless wished him to be absent more so that he might exercise supreme power than that he might provide it with protection or further distinction while powerful.

For Normandy desired his majesty as greatly as he desired Normandy’s advantage or honor. Indeed, it was uncertain whether he loved his homeland more, or his homeland him, just as it was once questioned concerning Caesar Augustus and the Roman people.

[Col. 1261B] And you too, English land, would love and esteem him greatly and gladly cast yourself wholly at his feet, if your ignorance and injustice did not prevent you from judging wisely into whose power you have fallen. Do not prejudge him; learn his dignity more carefully, and regard as insignificant, compared with him, all the lords you have endured.

The beauty of his integrity will adorn you with the finest color. King Pyrrhus, a most powerful man, learned through his envoy that the Romans were nearly all such men as he himself was. That city, mother of the kings of the world, head and mistress of the earth, would rejoice to have produced the man who is to rule you, to be defended by his hand, governed by his wisdom, and obeyed by his authority.

His soldiers, the Northmen, possess Apulia, have conquered Sicily, defend Constantinople, and inspire Babylon with fear. Chnut the Dane slaughtered the noblest of your sons, both young and old, with excessive cruelty, so that he might subject you to himself and his children.

Would this man have wished Harold to perish? On the contrary, he wished to increase for him the power of his father Godwin and to give him his daughter, most worthy of an emperor’s bed, in marriage, as he had promised.

But if you do not agree with me about these matters, he certainly removed from your neck the proud and cruel domination of Harold. He killed the detestable tyrant who oppressed you with a calamity both servile and shameful. Such a service is considered welcome and glorious among every people.

The benefactions of the most salutary rule by which you will be exalted will, in what follows, bear witness against your envy. King William will live—he will live for a long time—and in the pages that I am pleased to write in a modest style, so that many may understand clearly the most beautiful events. Especially since the principal orators, although they possessed great power to speak gravely, are found to have used humble language when writing histories.

After he had been crowned, he arranged many matters in London wisely, justly, and mercifully: some for the advantage or dignity of the city itself, others for the benefit of the whole people, and others for the welfare of the churches of the land. Whatever laws he enacted, he enacted for the best reasons.

No one ever sought a just judgment from him in vain. Ruling injustice often conceals avarice beneath the appearance of punishing wrongdoing; it condemns the innocent so that it may seize the condemned person’s property. He condemned no one unless it would have been unjust not to condemn him. For just as he bore an unconquerable spirit against other passions, so he did against avarice.

He understood that it was the mark of royal majesty to excel in illustrious generosity and to accept nothing where equity objected. He both commanded and earnestly urged his leading men to practice justice with the dignity and diligence appropriate to them. He required them always to keep before their eyes the eternal Emperor by whose protection they had conquered.

He declared that the conquered, who were equal to the conquerors in their Christian profession, ought by no means to be oppressed excessively, lest those whom they had justly subdued be driven by injuries into rebellion. He added that they must take care not to disgrace the land where he had been born or raised by behaving shamefully toward foreigners.

He restrained soldiers of middling rank and common soldiers by suitable edicts. Women were safe from violence, which lovers often inflict. Even offenses committed with the consent of immoral women were prohibited, in order to prevent disgrace.

He did not permit soldiers to drink much in taverns, since drunkenness usually generates quarrels and quarrels homicide. He forbade seditions, slaughter, and every kind of robbery, restraining the peoples by arms just as he restrained arms by laws.

Judges, whom the common soldiers feared, were appointed, and severe penalties were simultaneously decreed for those who transgressed. The Northmen were not permitted to act more freely than the Britons or Aquitanians.

They propose Scipio and other ancient commanders as models for imitation, men who teach in their writings about military discipline. Yet the army of King William offers examples no less, or even more, worthy of praise. But let us hasten to speak of other matters, lest we remain long suspended from recounting the return that Normandy awaited with such attention.

He established a measure for tributes and all things payable to the royal treasury that would not be burdensome. He denied every place within his territories to robbery, invasion, and wrongdoing. He ordered ports and every route to be open to merchants and prohibited any injury from being done.

He did not approve Stigand’s episcopal office, which he knew to be uncanonical; but he judged it better to await the apostolic decision than to depose him too hastily. Other considerations also advised him to tolerate him for a time and treat him honorably, since his authority among the English was supreme.

For the metropolitan see he was considering a man holy in life, esteemed in reputation, powerful in the eloquence of the divine word, capable of providing a suitable model for the suffragan bishops, of presiding over the Lord’s flock, and of benefiting everyone through vigilant devotion. He was also already considering appointments to the other churches. His beginnings in ruling were entirely worthy.

Having left London, he remained for several days at the nearby place of Bercing, while certain fortifications in the city were being completed against the restlessness of a vast and fierce population. He had seen first of all that it was urgently necessary to restrain the people of London.

There Edwin and Morcar came to submit to him, men among the greatest of all the English in birth and power, the sons of the famous Ælfgar. They asked pardon if they had harbored any feelings against him, and surrendered themselves and all they possessed to his mercy. Many other nobles, rich and distinguished, did the same.

Among them was Count Coxo, whom, we have heard, the king and afterward every excellent Northman valued for his exceptional courage and integrity. As they requested, the king gladly accepted their oaths, generously granted them his favor, restored everything they had possessed, and held them in great honor.

Proceeding from there, he visited various parts of the kingdom, everywhere arranging what was useful to himself and to the inhabitants of the land. Wherever he went, no one remained under arms. No road was blocked; everywhere people came to submit or to explain their position.

He looked upon all with merciful eyes, and upon the common people with the utmost mercy. His face often revealed a compassionate spirit; many times he ordered mercy when he saw suppliants or the needy, and observed mothers pleading by voice and gestures with their children.

[Col. 1263B] He enriched Edgar the Ætheling, whom the English had attempted to establish as king after Harold’s downfall, with extensive lands, and held him especially dear because he was descended from King Edward. He did this so that the boy’s youth would not suffer excessively from lacking the honor to which he had been chosen.

Through the gift of the same generosity, many Englishmen received what they had not received from their parents or former lords. He placed energetic men brought from Gaul in charge of the castles, men whose loyalty and courage he trusted equally, together with a multitude of infantry and cavalry. He distributed rich benefits to them so that they might endure labors and dangers with willing hearts.

Yet no Gaul was given anything that had been unjustly taken from any Englishman.

[Col. 1263C] Canterbury is a noble and powerful city. It has wealthy, faithless, and bold citizens and neighbors. It could quickly receive the Danes as allies. It lies fourteen miles from the sea that separates the English from the Danes.

Within the walls of this city also he built a fortification. There he left William, son of Osbern, the foremost man in his army, to govern in his place the whole kingdom toward the north for the time being.

Of all the Northmen, he had found this man, in the manner of a father, most faithful to him at home and in war; he was also outstanding in courage and counsel, whether in domestic or military affairs, and deeply devoted to the heavenly Lord. The king knew that he was most dear to the Northmen and a source of the greatest terror to the English. More than his other companions, he had loved and exalted him from childhood in Normandy.

[Col. 1263D] He entrusted Dover Castle to his brother Odo, together with the adjoining southern coast, which, under its ancient name, is called Kent and faces Gaul more closely; it is therefore inhabited by less savage people. They had been accustomed to exchange goods with the Belgians.

It is reported—and the page of antiquity also bears witness—that this coastal region was once possessed by Gauls, who, having crossed there for plunder and to wage war, found its fields fertile and pleasing. Odo, bishop of Bayeux, had proved himself a man fully capable of managing ecclesiastical and secular affairs.

The church of Bayeux first bears witness to his goodness and prudence: while still young in age, but surpassing the old in maturity of spirit, he arranged and adorned it splendidly with great devotion. Thereafter he was useful and an ornament to all Normandy.

In synods, where the worship of Christ was discussed, and in deliberations, where worldly matters were debated, he shone equally in understanding and eloquence. Gaul, public opinion agreed, had no equal to him in generosity. He also deserved praise for his love of justice.

He never wielded arms, nor wished them to be wielded; nevertheless, he was greatly feared by armed men. For, whenever necessity required, he aided war with extremely useful counsel, insofar as he could without compromising religion.

To the king, whose uterine brother he was and whom he embraced with such love that he did not wish to be separated from him even amid arms—he had received great honors from him and hoped for more—he was uniquely and steadfastly faithful.

Northmen and Britons alike gladly obeyed him as a most welcome lord. The English were not so barbarous that they could fail to understand that such a bishop and such a governor deserved to be feared, but also revered and loved.

[Col. 1264B] Having thus entrusted the government of the kingdom, the king withdrew to Penevesellum, a place that we think ought to be mentioned among the names of sites because it was through that harbor that he first reached that shore.

The ships stood ready for the crossing, and it would truly have been fitting for them to be decorated with white sails in the ancient manner. They were to carry back a most glorious triumph and announce the joy that was most desired.

A large body of English cavalry gathered there. He had decided to take with him those whose loyalty and power he especially suspected: Stigand the archbishop; Edgar the Ætheling, a kinsman of King Edward; the three counts Edwin, Morcar, and Gallew; and several other men of high nobility.

He did this so that nothing might be changed in his absence on the advice of those men, and so that the whole people would be less capable of rebellion once deprived of its leaders. Finally, he thought that these men above all should be held in his power as hostages, since their authority or safety would be of the greatest importance to their relatives and fellow countrymen.

They were subdued in such a way that they carried out his orders with the utmost obedience. Indeed, even when he preferred to ask something of them, they heard it as though it were a command. This was especially so because they were not being dragged along as captives, but were accompanying their lord and king as close companions, and would thereby receive greater favor and honor.

For they recognized in this his humanity, from which they could expect everything good and fear nothing cruel or unjust. As for the soldiers returning to their homeland, whose loyal service he had employed in such great affairs, he gave generously to all of them at the same harbor, so that all might rejoice that they had received the finest fruit of victory with him.

Thus, when the ships had been released, with every spirit filled with joy, he was carried to his native land with favorable wind and tide. This crossing brought long peace to the sea, driving every pirate far away.

The faithfulness of the deeds, which anyone who knows them rightly admires, was made still more admirable by their speed. For around the Kalends of October, on the day when the Church celebrates the memory of the archangel Michael, he departed for that hostile land, uncertain what outcome would follow; in the month of March he was restored to the bosom of his homeland, in a manner better explained by the deeds themselves than by our writings.

Julius Caesar, having crossed over into Britain itself twice with a thousand ships (for the older name of England is Britain), accomplished no equally great deeds on his first attempt: he neither dared advance far from the shore nor remain long on the shore, although he had fortified a camp according to the custom of his homeland. He crossed over at the end of summer and returned before the approaching equinox. His legions were thrown into great fear when some of his ships were shattered by the sea’s tide or by the waves, while others were unfit for navigation because their equipment had been lost. Some communities, preferring to live in peace rather than endure as an enemy the Roman people, whose terrifying reputation extended throughout the world, gave him hostages. [Col. 1265B] But of those whom he ordered to bring hostages to the mainland, all except two ignored the order, although they knew that he was wintering in Belgium with an enormous army.

On his second expedition he transported nearly one hundred thousand Roman infantrymen and cavalry, together with a considerable number of leading men from one of the communities of Gaul and their cavalry. What, then, did this man whom we are writing about accomplish on this occasion that should be compared with Caesar’s achievements? The cavalry and charioteers of the Britons inflicted no small defeat upon Caesar, engaging him most boldly on level ground. The English, however, awaited William fearfully on a hill. The Britons attacked Caesar repeatedly in battle. William crushed the English so completely in a single day that afterward they never regained the confidence to fight him.

[Col. 1265C] When the same commander reached the river Thames, leading his army into the territory of Cassivellaunus, who was conducting the war against him, the enemy stood arrayed on the opposite bank. The Roman soldiers crossed the fords only with the greatest difficulty, rising from the water with nothing but their heads above the surface. But when the Northman duke approached the same region, the cities and municipalities came out to meet him, begging for mercy. They would have prepared a crossing for his soldiers over the river by means of a bridge without delay, if he had chosen to order it.

Caesar sent his cavalry out with fire and plunder to ravage the fields; Cassivellaunus restrained them from ranging more widely by sending against them men skilled in fighting from chariots. William, however, ordering the inhabitants to live in peace, preserved both the people and the land for himself, although he could have devastated the country as quickly as he wished.

[Col. 1265D] Caesar defended Mandubracius and his city from the violence of Cassivellaunus, and restored its rule to Mandubracius. William permanently freed the whole nation from the tyranny of Harold and himself obtained the throne, so that one ruler might govern the regions that had once been subject to many kings. The Romans captured only one man of distinction from Britain. The Northmen, had they wished, could have thrown a thousand eminent men of that nation into chains.

How much the Romans accomplished in those territories during the summer, and how much the Northmen during the winter! It is well known that winter is less suitable than summer for conducting military operations. For Caesar it had been enough for glory or advantage to make battles with the Britons, as with the Gauls, by giving orders. Indeed, he rarely fought with his own hand. This was the customary practice of many ancient commanders. [Col. 1266A] The eloquence of the *Commentaries* dictated by Caesar himself bears witness to it.

But William considered it disgraceful and of little value, in the conflict in which he crushed the English, to perform the duties of a commander unless he also performed the duties of a soldier, as he was accustomed to do in other wars. For in every engagement in which he was present, he habitually fought with his own sword, first or among the first.

If you examine more attentively the deeds of that Roman and of our own prince, you will rightly call the former rash and excessively confident in fortune, but the latter an altogether prudent man, who achieved success more through excellent judgment than through chance.

Finally, Caesar, after receiving the submission of several communities and hostages from Cassivellaunus, and after imposing a certain tribute for Britain to pay annually to the Roman people, brought his army [Col. 1266B] back to Belgium with difficulty in two transports. His ships had been repaired, but they were fewer in number than those with which he had arrived, because of the damage caused by the storm.

William was troubled by no such difficulty. The same people would obey him as their ruler and provide new ships in whatever number and form he wished, moreover adorned with precious metal and decorated with purple sails, equipped with experienced oarsmen and selected pilots. See how gloriously he returned—not dragging along, as the Romans did, a captive populace, but having in his company and service the primate of all the bishops of Britain, great abbots from monasteries across the sea, and sons of the English who, both by the distinction of their lineage and by their wealth, might be called kings.

He brought back not a modest tribute and not plunder, but [Col. 1266C] silver and gold—an amount scarcely collected from the dominion of the three Gauls—which he had received by the strictest right and which he intended to spend when the most honorable considerations required it. That land surpasses the Gauls in many ways through its abundance of precious metal. Just as its abundance of grain seems to warrant calling it “the Granary of Ceres,” so its abundance of gold warrants calling it “the Treasury of Arabia.”

Let us omit any remark about Julius Caesar that might perhaps be noted as disparaging. He was therefore an exceptional commander, learned through reading the military precepts of the Greeks, who had practiced Roman warfare with distinction from youth and had attained the consulship of Rome through valor. He successfully and swiftly completed many wars against warlike peoples and finally made Rome, which ruled Africa, Europe, and Asia, his kingdom through warfare.

[Col. 1266D] Northmannia never greeted King William, its prince, more joyfully than Italy had greeted Titus, son of Vespasian, who, because he loved what was right with such fervor, deserved to be called “the Love of the World.” The days were wintry, and were devoted to the austerity of Lenten penance. Nevertheless, everywhere they were conducted as though they were the great festivals of the finest season; the sun appeared bright with summer serenity, and the customary cheerfulness of the days was greatly increased.

The inhabitants of smaller or more remote places gathered in the cities, or wherever they had the opportunity to see the king. When he entered his metropolitan city of Rouen, the old men, children, matrons, and all the citizens came out to look upon him. [Col. 1267A] They shouted greetings to him on his return, so that the whole city seemed to applaud, just as Rome once celebrated its Pompey with applause and dancing.

The monasteries competed with one another, each asking which could show the greater devotion upon the arrival of its most beloved protector. Nothing was omitted that is customarily done in the pursuit of such honor. Moreover, if anything new could be devised, it was added. He immediately repaid this devotion with manifold generosity, giving cloaks, pounds of gold, and other great gifts to altars and servants of Christ. We have never found the offerings of any king or emperor more generous.

Likewise, churches that he could not visit in person he visited again with gifts. To the basilica at Caen, built at his own expense from the foundations in the manner and appearance of remarkable splendor, as mentioned earlier, in honor of blessed Stephen the Protomartyr, [Col. 1267B] he brought various gifts of the most precious materials and workmanship, capable of preserving their honor to the end of the age. To describe each one individually, whether by explanation or name, would take too long. It is delightful to behold them for distinguished guests and for those who have often seen the treasures of noble churches. If a Greek or Arab guest were to pass through, he too would be drawn by the same delight.

The women of the English nation are highly skilled with the needle and in embroidery with gold; the men are outstanding in every kind of craftsmanship. In addition, Germans, most knowledgeable in such arts, commonly lived among them. Merchants who travel by ship to distant regions also bring in the work of skilled hands.

[Col. 1267C] Some powerful men make gifts improperly to the saints, usually increasing their own praise in this world and their sins before God through those very donations. They rob churches and enrich others with the stolen goods. King William, however, never acquired a sincere reputation except through goodness, giving what was truly his own, with his mind directed toward the hope of an everlasting reward rather than toward glory that perishes.

The churches across the sea, which were wealthy, willingly gave him certain things to carry to Gaul, because he repaid them many times over with other goods. He knew that his homeland, no less dear to him than the kingdom, was especially remarkable for its good people, faithful to earthly rulers and greatly devoted to the worship of Christ; he found it in the condition he desired.

Our lady Mathilda had governed very well, already widely known by the title of queen, although [Col. 1267D] not yet crowned. Men of highly useful counsel assisted her prudence. Among them the first in dignity was Roger of Beaumont, son of Humphrey, a man of the highest nobility, who, because of his mature age, was more freely able to attend to affairs conducted at home. Her adolescent son had been entrusted with military duties; we have spoken briefly of his courage in the battle against Harold.

Yet since the neighboring peoples had dared no incursion, knowing that the land was almost exhausted of soldiers, we think this should first be attributed to the king himself, whose return they feared.

At the monastery of the Holy Trinity at Fécamp he celebrated the Lord’s Easter, honoring the Redeemer with the greatest reverence at the feast of his resurrection, amid a gathering of [Col. 1268A] venerable bishops and abbots. Standing humbly among the choirs of the religious orders, he compelled soldiers and crowds of common people to cease their amusements and hasten together to the divine services.

Ralph, the exceedingly powerful count and stepfather of the king of the Franks, was present at this court, together with much of the nobility of France. They gazed with curiosity, alongside the Northmen, upon the long-haired pupils of the northern region, whose beauty the most handsome young men of “long-haired Gaul” might envy. They did not yield even to maidenly grace.

As they looked upon the garments of the king and his attendants, woven and encrusted with gold, they judged worthless the things they had previously seen. They also admired the silver and golden vessels, regarding whose number and beauty things truly incredible could be told. From these vessels [Col. 1268B] so great a population drank in the dining hall, or from buffalo horns similarly adorned with metal around both ends.

Finally, they noticed many things of this kind befitting royal generosity, which they would praise at home because of their novelty. Yet they recognized that the king’s own honor was far more distinguished and more worthy of remembrance than all such things.

He spent that summer and autumn, and part of the winter, around the sea, devoting all this time to the love of his homeland. The homeland did not complain that its resources had been diminished either by this delay or by the expedition of the preceding year. Such was his moderation and prudence.

Provisions were supplied abundantly to soldiers and guests, and no one was permitted to seize anything. The animals and flocks of the inhabitants grazed safely, whether across open fields or through wastelands. The crops [Col. 1268C] awaited the farmer’s sickle untouched; they were neither trampled by the proud dispersal of the cavalry nor mown down for fodder. A weak or unarmed man could ride on horseback wherever he wished, singing as he went, seeing companies of soldiers without being terrified.

Meanwhile Odo, bishop of Bayeux, and William, son of Osbern, were each administering their respective offices in the kingdom commendably, sometimes acting together and sometimes separately. Whenever necessity required it, one quickly brought assistance to the other. Their prudent vigilance was strengthened by the sincere goodwill with which they agreed.

They loved one another and the king equally, burning with the same devotion to preserve the Christian people in peace, and they willingly accepted one another’s counsel with equanimity. They practiced the greatest [Col. 1268D] fairness, as the king had instructed, so that fierce and hostile men might be corrected and made friendly.

The lesser governors likewise worked energetically wherever each had been stationed in the fortifications. But the English could not be restrained sufficiently either by kindness or by fear to prefer tranquil peace to new and turbulent affairs. They did not dare openly rise in arms, but throughout the regions they discussed wicked conspiracies, in case they might prevail through some trick to cause harm. They sent envoys to the Danes or elsewhere, wherever some assistance was hoped for.

Some voluntarily fled into exile, so that, as outcasts, they might either be free from the power of the Northmen or return against them strengthened by the wealth of others.

[Col. 1269A] At that time Count Eustace of Boulogne was hostile to the king. Before the war he had given his son as a hostage for his loyalty in Northmannia. Those who inhabit Kent persuaded him above all to attack Dover Castle, using them as his helpers. They argued that, if he gained possession of this strongest site together with its seaport, his power would spread more widely, and the power of the Northmen would thereby be diminished.

Because they hated the Northmen, they had made peace with Eustace, who had long been their bitter enemy. They had learned by experience that he was skilled in warfare and fortunate in battle. If they had to serve someone who was not their countryman, they thought it better to serve a known and neighboring man.

It happened that the timing of the opportunity seemed to promise the outcome they desired. The first [Col. 1269B] guardians of the fortress had gone across the river Thames: the bishop of Bayeux and Hugh of Montfort, taking with them the greater part of the soldiers. Eustace therefore, after receiving news from the English, crossed over to them with his men at the dead of night, intending to catch the castle’s defenders unprepared.

He brought a fleet laden with selected soldiers, leaving behind all but very few horses. The whole neighborhood was present under arms, and a larger number would have come from farther away if the siege had lasted two days. But they found the guard less negligent than they had expected, yet stronger in defense because of fear.

The speed of the horses, knowledge of the route, and a more prepared ship enabled the defenders to escape. His most noble young kinsman, however, was captured. The English escaped all the more easily through several byways because the small number of the castle’s defenders made it difficult to pursue them in different directions.

[Col. 1269C] Eustace deservedly suffered this disgrace and loss. Indeed, if I were to bring forward the arguments advanced against him in the dispute, I would plainly prove that he had fairly and justly lost the king’s favor and the benefits he had received as gifts from the king [Col. 1270A]. Nor was the judgment mistaken that was pronounced with the agreement of the English and the French, by which he was convicted of great guilt.

But we think mercy should be shown to a person illustrious in many respects, the count in question, who, now reconciled, is honored among the king’s closest associates.

At nearly the same time Count Coxo, whom we have said was pleasing to the Northmen, died an undeserved death, one that deserves to be widely proclaimed. Therefore, so that his praise may live and the innocence of the dead may arise as an example for posterity, it is worthwhile to make it known in writing.

In ancestry and power this Englishman was nearly supreme; he excelled still more in the singular quality of his mind, which was prudent and altogether honorable. He strongly approved the king and the king’s cause. His own attendants, however, disagreed with him; they were the worst supporters and accomplices of faction.

Accordingly, they tried to turn him away from his [Col. 1270B] duty, often warning him, as though out of friendship and concern for his private honor, to defend the liberty handed down by his ancestors. At other times they begged and implored him, supposedly out of concern for the commonwealth, to abandon foreigners and follow the will of the best men of his own nation and kindred.

They offered these suggestions and others like them through prolonged and varied cunning. But when they could not move him in this way from a mind firmly fixed upon the course of goodness, they stirred up his fellow provincials to envy, which he could only appease by defecting from the king.

At last, as their hostility increased day by day, when he preferred to endure the hatred of the people and every wrong rather than violate the integrity of his loyalty, they overpowered and killed him by treachery. Thus, by his own death, that exceptional man asserted [Col. 1270C] that the majesty of his lord ought to stand.

Indeed, certain bishops were devoted to royal service, especially Adelred, primate of York. . . . The remainder is missing in the manuscript.

# APPENDICES TO THE DEEDS OF WILLIAM THE CONQUEROR

[Col. 1269]

## FIRST APPENDIX. GENEALOGY OF THE DUKES OF NORTHMANNIA

From an old manuscript codex.

[Col. 1269D] In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 896, while Charles, called the Simple, was reigning as king of the Franks, Danish pirates came out from the island of Scandza, which is called Northvega. After they had fought many battles in France and devastated the kingdom, the aforesaid Charles, having received hostages, gave them Neustria, which from that time they called Northmannia, because it was possessed by those who had come from Northvega.

Robert, therefore, called Rollo, was their first duke and count of Northmannia. This Robert fathered William, surnamed Longsword, whom the Franks killed by treachery. William [Col. 1270D] Longsword fathered Richard the Elder. He fathered a daughter named Emma, from whom Edward, king of the English, was born.

Richard the Elder fathered Richard. Richard the Second fathered Richard the Third and Robert. Richard fathered Nicholas, abbot of Saint-Ouen. Robert fathered William the Bastard, who, after Edward’s death, crossed over into England in the year of the Lord 1066 and obtained the kingdom by hereditary right, because his great-grandfather Richard the Elder was the man whose daughter Emma had borne King Edward.

This William the Bastard had three sons, namely Robert, William Rufus [Col. 1271A], and Henry, by Matilda, daughter of Baldwin, count of Flanders, who was buried at the town of Lille. After William the Bastard died, his son William Rufus was made king and Robert count of Northmannia.

While William Rufus was in a forest hunting, one of his knights, aiming an arrow at a stag, killed the king instead of the stag. After he was killed, Robert, the king’s brother, who ought to have succeeded him, was then in Jerusalem; and Henry, his brother and an unjust man, invaded his kingdom.

When Robert returned after capturing the city of Jerusalem, Henry crossed the sea, attacked his brother in Northmannia, captured him by treachery, and sent him as a captive [Col. 1272A] to England. He obtained both Northmannia and England.

He took as wife the daughter of Malcolm, king of the Scots, named Matilda, whom Saint Margaret had borne. Saint Margaret was a niece of Edward, king of the English, who had been king before William the Bastard.

By this Matilda, the aforesaid King Henry fathered William and Matilda, whom he gave to the emperor Henry the Younger in the year of the Lord 1110. But in the year 1120, when William wished to cross from Northmannia to England, he followed his father and perished by drowning, together with counts and the sons of noble Englishmen, on the eighth day before the Kalends of December.

[Col. 1271]

## EPITAPH OF WILLIAM, DUKE OF NORTHMANNIA AND KING OF THE ENGLISH

(*Literary History of France*, vol. VIII, p. 180.)

[Col. 1271B]

He ruled the fierce Northmen and Britons,  
Boldly he conquered, bravely he held them;  
And he restrained the swords of the Manceaux  
By valor, and imposed the laws of his rule.

[Col. 1272B]

Here great King William lies in a small urn;  
A small house suffices for a great lord.  
Phoebus had turned three times seven stages and two  
Within the Virgin’s embrace, and then he departed.

[Col. 1271]

## ANOTHER EPITAPH

From an old, half-damaged parchment. (Duchesne, *Scriptores rerum Normannicarum*, p. 317.)

Weep, men; mourn, nobles: the king has been dissolved into ashes.

A king born from great kings, King William, strongest in war,

King of the English and duke of Northmannia, lord of the land of Maine.

In all that he subjected to himself, and in which he placed himself above all,

More is owed to his own valor than to the thousands of his army.

Great was the valor and wisdom with which he ruled so many thousands.

King William, powerful and noble: his deeds prove that you are praiseworthy.

It ought to be written as a sign for posterity, with what valor you surpassed the others.

But what style or eloquence could encompass so many distinctions?

In fierce England, apart from a thousand astonishing battles,

[It shows] what sort of count he was in Maine, how great a duke in Northmannia.

Afterward he made himself a king from a duke, most worthy of the Roman laurel.

People of England, you disturbed the prince who loved the path of valor.

You learned what he could do, who was accustomed to conquer by arms.

Great was your destruction, but it was because of your king’s perjury.

After he had joined you to his empire, he treated you according to the judgment of a kingdom.

Thus he defeated the powerful men of England, and shut up the proud men of Denmark.

Great honor comes from such a lord; great sorrow from the end of his life.

King William, the tomb confines you, but throughout the world the people mourn you.

All mourn your wondrous deeds, your generosity, your peaceful wars.

The more the ages pass away, the more hearts sigh for you.

Whoever traveled through your homeland did not fear the violence of an enemy.

You were fear amid the multitude, security in solitude.

Now, by the law of things, there is no security; now its very numbers defend it.

Alas! After the death of so great a prince, supreme honor tends toward its end.

That fall is exceedingly mournful, which gives exile to honor.

Deprived of its powers, you lie pressed beneath long sorrows.

And deservedly so. For no powerful man, no wondrous man, was like him.

[Col. 1273]

From a tablet of the monastery of Battle in England, commonly called Battle Abbey, with this superscription:

This place is called Battle from the battle, because here  
The English were defeated and left here in death:  
They fell on the feast of the martyr Saint Calixtus.  
It was the year one thousand and sixty-six,  
When the English perished, with a comet showing the sign.

# THE WORDS OF WILLIAM THE CONQUEROR AS HE LAY DYING

*(Orderic Vitalis, book VII, p. 656, in Duchesne, Scriptores rerum Normannicarum.)*

[Col. 1283] “Burdened,” he said, “with many and grave sins, my friends, I tremble, and, soon to be dragged before the dread judgment of God, I do not know what I shall do. For I was reared in arms from childhood and am deeply stained by the shedding of much blood. I cannot in any way enumerate the evils I committed during the sixty-four years in which I lived in this wretched life, for which I am now compelled without delay to render an account to the most just Judge.

“When my father, voluntarily advancing into exile, entrusted the duchy of Normandy to me, I was a tender boy, only eight years old; from that time until now I have always borne the burden of arms. I held that duchy itself for nearly fifty-six years amid the hazards of war. Those whom I ruled often plotted against me and wickedly inflicted losses and grievous injuries upon me. They treacherously killed Turchetil, my foster-father, and Osbern son of Herfast, the dapifer of Normandy, and Count Gilbert, the father of the fatherland, together with many others necessary to the state. Thus I learned by experience the loyalty of my people.

“Many times at night, out of fear of my kinsmen, I was secretly carried from the principal chamber by my uncle Walter and transferred to the homes and hiding places of poor people, lest I should be found by the traitors who were seeking my death.

“The Normans, if they are governed by a firm and rigorous rule, are exceptionally vigorous; in difficult circumstances they all excel in unconquered strength and strive to overcome every enemy. Otherwise they tear one another apart and consume one another. They desire rebellion; they seek sedition and are ready for every crime. Therefore they must be restrained by the strong judgment of rectitude and compelled, by the bridle of discipline, to walk along the path of justice. But if they are permitted to go according to their own will, without a yoke, like an untamed wild ass, they and their princes will be covered with poverty and shameful confusion. I learned this long ago through many experiences.

“My nearest relatives and kinsmen, who ought in every way to have protected me against all men, rose against me through repeated conspiracies and nearly deprived me of all my father’s inheritance.

“Guido, son of Rainald, Duke of Burgundy, by my paternal aunt Adelisa, repaid me evil for good. For I had kindly received him when he came from another land, honored him as my only brother, and given him Vernon, Brionne, and a considerable part of Normandy. Yet by words and deeds he insulted me, openly declaring and maliciously spreading abroad that I was illegitimate, degenerate, and unworthy of rule.

“What more shall I relate? Having broken faith with me, he rebelled against me and drew away my nobles Ranulf of Bayeux, Haimo Dentatus, and Nigel of Coutances, together with many others, compelling them by his wicked counsel to become perjurers with him. Thus, forgetful of the homage and loyalty he had sworn to me, he attempted to seize the whole of Normandy.

“Therefore, while still beardless, I was compelled to take up arms against him and fight my cousin and vassal on the plain at Val-ès-Dunes. Then, with the help of God, who is the just Judge, I defeated the enemy between Falaise and Argentan [Argenton; and in another manuscript, Bayeux]. When, by God’s command, they had been overthrown, I freely possessed my hereditary right. Afterwards I besieged the stronghold of Brionne. I shut Guido inside after he had been wounded and had escaped from the battle by flight, and I did not depart until I had driven the public enemy from Neustria and obtained all his fortifications.

“Not long afterwards another most serious adversity arose against me. My uncles, Archbishop Mauger of Rouen and his brother William, to whom I had freely given Arques and the county of Calogium, despised me as illegitimate and summoned King Henry and Enguerrand, Count of Ponthieu, against me.

“As soon as I heard such rumors in Coutances, I set out, despite the advice of many who tried to dissuade me. I sent ahead a number of soldiers who were particularly eager to strike blows at Arques, and I followed with a not-large army and besieged the difficult stronghold. But before I reached the fields lying between the two rivers, the Seda and the Garumna, my advance troops intercepted Count Enguerrand as he was hastening to enter the castle. They killed him while he fought bravely—for he was a most fierce warrior—and put his forces to flight.

“By a severe siege I subdued the men in the castle and forced the perjured count into exile; throughout his life I did not permit him to return to what he had lost. I also removed by papal decree the insolent prelate who was neither devoted to God nor faithful to me from his episcopal see, and in his place I installed the venerable monk Maurilius, whom God had sent to me from Florence, a city of Italy.

“Henry, relying on royal power, inflamed by military daring, and greatly urged on by the insults of my enemies, often appeared to trample me down as though I were unarmed, to crush me in many ways, and to impose unjust rights upon me. He often entered my land with a huge force of armed men; yet he never rejoiced in the plunder of my possessions or the capture of my people.

“With great pomp and terrible threats he usually entered my borders; yet he never returned home in happiness or without disgrace. He brought with him many men distinguished for their valor, but because—alas!—they perished by the swords of my men and me, he did not lead them back.

“Once, inflamed with excessive hostility against me, King Henry sent a huge army from Gaul in two divisions to crush our estates by a double invasion. He himself led one phalanx into the diocese of Évreux, so that it might devastate everything as far as the Seine; [Col. 1286D] the other he entrusted to his brother Odo, to Rainald of Clermont, and to two counts, Radulf of Montdésir and Wido of Ponthieu, so that they might quickly enter Neustria through the fords of the Epte, invade Bray, Aumale, and the whole district of Rouen, and completely devastate it with sword, fire, and plunder as far as the sea.

“When I learned this, I promptly advanced in the opposite direction. Along the bank of the Seine I continually opposed my forces to the king’s encampments, and wherever he attempted to ravage my territory, I answered his aggression with arms and the sword.

“I sent Robert, Count of Eu, and Roger of Mortemer, together with other highly distinguished knights, against Odo and his legions. When they encountered the French near the castle called Mortemer, the forces of both sides being drawn up, a terrible battle was joined, and much blood was shed on either side. For there were brave warriors on both sides, unwilling to yield even unto death.

“On one side the Gauls raged in their desire to acquire; on the other the fierce Normans struck, burning with the hope of escape and of defending themselves and their homes. At last, with God’s help, the Normans prevailed and the French fled.

“The Normans fought this battle beyond the Seine in winter, before Lent, in the eighth year after the battle of Val-ès-Dunes. Wido, Count of Ponthieu, was then captured, while Odo, together with Rainald and the others who were swift of foot, was put to flight.

“Count Radulf too would have been captured, had not Roger, the commander of my army, aided him; for Radulf had long before done homage to him. In such a necessity Roger rendered him a beautiful and fitting service: he protected him for three days in his castle and afterwards conducted him safely home.

“For this offense I expelled Roger from Normandy, but shortly afterwards I was reconciled with him and restored his other honors. Nevertheless, I justly, as I think, took away from him the castle of Mortemer, in which he had saved my enemy; but I gave it to his kinsman William of Warenne, a legitimate young knight.

“As for Count Wido of Bayeux, I kept him in prison as long as I pleased, and after two years I received his homage on the condition that from then on he would always remain faithful to me and would provide military service wherever I commanded, with one hundred soldiers every year. Afterwards I presented him with great gifts and dismissed him honorably and in peace.

“When the conflict was over, as soon as I learned reliable reports of what had happened beyond the Seine, I sent word through Radulf of Tosny to the king of the French. On hearing this, he immediately rose by night and fled swiftly with his army; thereafter he never again, while secure, spent the night in my land.

“Thus from my childhood I have been hemmed in on every side by countless troubles, but by God’s grace I have been honorably delivered from them all. I therefore became an object of envy to all my neighbors; yet, with the help of God, in whom I have always placed my hope, I was overcome by none. The Bretons and Angevins often experienced this. The French and Flemings bear witness to it. The English and the men of Maine have learned it bitterly by experience.

“Geoffrey Martel, Count of Anjou, Conan, Prince of Brittany, and Robert the Frisian, lord of the Morini, plotted against me by many devices. But while God guarded me, although they greatly desired it and laid many traps, they never achieved their wish.

“I obtained the royal diadem, which none of my predecessors had worn; divine grace alone, not hereditary right, bestowed it. How many labors and dangerous conflicts I endured overseas against the men of Exeter, Chester, and Northumbria, against the Scots and Welsh, the Norwegians and Danes, and against the other adversaries who attempted to strip me of the kingdom of England, is difficult to recount. In all these matters the lot of victory fell to me.

“Yet although human eagerness rejoices in such triumphs, inwardly the anxiety of fear pricks and bites me when I consider that savage recklessness raged through all these events. Therefore I earnestly beseech you, priests and ministers of Christ, to commend me in your prayers to almighty God, so that he may forgive the sins by which I am heavily burdened and, through his tireless mercy, save me among his own.

“I also order that my treasures be given to churches and to the poor, so that what has been amassed through crimes may be dispersed for the holy uses of the holy places. You ought to remember how tenderly I loved you and how vigorously I defended you against all rivals.

“I never violated the Church of God, our mother; rather, everywhere, as reason required, I honored her eagerly. I never sold ecclesiastical dignities. I always detested and rejected simony. In choosing persons I investigated the merit of their lives and their instruction in wisdom, and, as far as lay within me, I entrusted the governance of the Church to the most worthy of all.

“This can surely be proved in Lanfranc, archbishop of Canterbury; in Anselm, abbot of Bec; in Gerbert of Fontenelle and Durand of Troarn; and in many other teachers of my kingdom, whose celebrated praise, I believe, resounds to the furthest ends of the earth. I chose such men as companions for conversation and found truth and wisdom in their fellowship; therefore I always gladly desired to enjoy their counsel.

“Nine monasteries of monks and one of nuns, founded in Normandy by my fathers, grew with my assistance and, by God’s help, were gloriously enlarged through the increase of many possessions that I gave them. During the time of my duchy, moreover, seventeen monasteries of monks and six of nuns were built, where great service and many acts of charity are performed daily for love of the supreme King.

“Normandy is fortified with such camps, and in them the earthborn learn to fight against demons and the vices of the flesh. I was either their founder, by God’s inspiration, or their originator, their ardent helper, and their willing encourager.

“I also freely granted all the possessions in lands or other revenues that my nobles gave to God and his saints for their spiritual salvation in Neustria and England, and with sovereign authority I freely confirmed the charters of their gifts against all rivals and attackers.

“I pursued these practices from my earliest years, and I leave them to my heirs to preserve for all time. In these matters, my sons, follow me constantly, so that here and forever you may be honored before God and men.

“Above all I urge you, my innermost being, to remain continually attached to the fellowship of the good and wise, and to obey them in everything if you wish to remain glorious for a long time. The teaching of pious teachers is to distinguish good from evil, to uphold justice in every way, to avoid wickedness with every effort, to spare and assist the weak, the poor, and the just, to restrain and overcome the proud and unjust, and to curb the persecution of the simple; to frequent the holy Church devoutly; to love the worship of the divine nature above all riches; and night and day, in adversity and prosperity alike, to obey the divine law without weariness.

“I granted the duchy of Normandy to my son Robert before I fought against Harold at Epitumo Senlac, because he is the firstborn. He has already received the homage of nearly all the barons of this country. An honor once granted cannot be withdrawn. But I know with certainty that the land subjected to his rule will truly be wretched. For he is proud, a foolish dolt, and one who must long be chastened by harsh misfortune.

“I appoint no heir to the kingdom of England, but commend it to the eternal Creator, whose I am and in whose hand all things are. For I did not possess so great an honor by hereditary right; rather, by a dreadful conflict and the abundant shedding of human blood, I took it from the perjured king Harold, and, after killing or driving away his supporters, subjected it to my rule.

“I hated the native sons of the kingdom more than was right. I cruelly harassed nobles and commoners. I unjustly disinherited many, and killed countless numbers, especially in the district of York, by hunger or by the sword.

“For the men of Deira and the peoples beyond the Humber received the army of Sweyn, king of the Danes, against me; they killed Robert de Comines with a thousand soldiers inside Durham, and in various places they slew other nobles and my most distinguished young knights.

“Therefore, moved by unrestrained fury, I hastened against the northern English like a mad lion. I ordered their houses, their crops, all their equipment and possessions to be immediately burned, and abundant herds of cattle and flocks of sheep to be slaughtered everywhere.

“Thus I punished a multitude of both sexes with the sword of such terrible famine. And so, alas, I disastrously slaughtered many thousands of that most beautiful people, old and young alike.

“Therefore I dare entrust the power of this kingdom, which I obtained with so many sins, to no one except God alone, lest after my death still worse things come to pass because of me.

“I desire that my son William, who from his earliest years has always clung to me and willingly obeyed me in everything according to his ability, may in the Spirit of God long prosper and, if it is God’s will, shine happily upon the throne of the kingdom.”

[Col. 1289]

# LETTERS OF WILLIAM THE CONQUEROR

## LETTER I. TO GREGORY VII, ROMAN PONTIFF

[Col. 1289C]

(See Gregory VII, *Patrologia*, vol. CXLVIII, col. 748.)

## LETTER II. TO JOHN, ABBOT OF FÉCAMP

(See *Patrologia*, vol. CXLVII, col. 463.)

## LETTER III. TO THE CLERGY AND LAITY ESTABLISHED THROUGHOUT ENGLAND

(Published by Selden in the notes to Eadmer’s *Historia novorum*, Appendix to the edition of Lanfranc’s works, 1675, p. 113.)

William, by the grace of God king of the English, sends greetings to both the clergy and the laity established throughout England.

Let it be known to you that, with the assent of Lanfranc, archbishop of Canterbury, and of Stigand, bishop of Chichester, and also with the counsel of my bishops and barons, I have granted and confirmed that the church of Saint Martin of the Battle—which I founded by vow because of the victory that God granted me in that place—shall be forever free and quiet from every service and from everything that the human mind can devise, together with all the royal dignities and customs that I have granted it by royal authority, as my charter testifies.

Therefore I will and firmly command that this church, together with the surrounding league, shall be free from every domination and oppression of bishops, like the church that gave me my crown and through which the splendor of our rule flourishes.

The bishop of Chichester, although the church lies in his diocese, shall not be permitted, against the abbot’s will, to lodge there by custom, either in the church or in the manors belonging to it; nor shall he make any ordinations there or burden the abbey in any way. Nor shall he exercise any domination, force, or authority over it; rather, like my own chapel, it shall be entirely free from all exaction on his part.

The abbot shall not be summoned or compelled to attend a synod, unless he wishes to go of his own accord for some matter. Nor shall he be prevented from having his monks promoted to sacred orders wherever he judges most appropriate. Nor shall anyone forbid the consecration of altars, confirmations, or any episcopal blessings to be freely performed there by any bishop at the request of the abbot or the monks.

[Col. 1290D] I also establish by royal authority and by the testimony of my bishops and barons that the abbot shall in every respect be judge and lord of his church and of the surrounding league.

When the abbot dies, an abbot shall be elected from that same church, unless perhaps—which God forbid—no suitable person can be found there. Let none of my successors presume to violate or diminish this constitution of mine, confirmed both by vow and by royal authority.

Whoever therefore acts against the liberties or dignities of this church shall be subject to forfeiture to the royal crown.

The witnesses to this matter are Lanfranc, archbishop of Canterbury; Stigand, bishop of Chichester; Walkelin, bishop of Winchester; and Wulfstan, bishop of Worcester. [Col. 1291A] All of them, in my presence and hearing, condemned with perpetual anathema those who violated these commands and constitutions of mine.

At Winchester.

Place of the seal.

## LETTER IV. TO REMIGIUS, BISHOP OF LINCOLN

(As above.)

William, by the grace of God king of the English, sends greetings to the counts, sheriffs, and all Frenchmen and Englishmen who hold lands in the bishopric of Bishop Remigius.

Let all of you, and my other faithful subjects who remain in England, know that I judged the episcopal laws which, up to my time, had existed in the kingdom of the English neither properly nor according to the precepts of the holy canons, to be in need of correction by common counsel and by the advice of my archbishops, my other bishops and abbots, and all the princes of my kingdom.

Therefore I command, and by royal authority order, that no bishop or archdeacon shall henceforth hold pleas concerning episcopal laws in a hundred court, nor bring a case that pertains to the governance of souls before the judgment of secular men. Rather, whoever is summoned concerning any matter or fault according to episcopal laws shall come to the place that the bishop chooses and names for this purpose; there he shall answer concerning his case, and not according to the hundred but according to the canons and episcopal laws he shall render what is right before God and his bishop.

[Col. 1291]

# THE LAWS OF WILLIAM THE CONQUEROR

## I

(Published by Selden in the notes to Eadmer’s *Historia novorum*, in the appendix to the works of Saint Anselm, 1675 edition, appendix, p. 114.)

### PREFATORY NOTICE

The author of the old manuscript chronicle of the Church of Lichfield says:

“In the fourth year of his reign, William, at London, by the counsel of his barons, caused all the nobles, wise men, and those learned in their own law throughout all the counties of England to be summoned, so that he might hear their laws and customs.

“And although King William had previously approved the laws of Norfolk and Suffolk, of Cambridge and Deira—where once the greater part of the Danes and Norwegians dwelt—more highly, and had ordered them to be observed throughout the whole kingdom, because all his predecessors and almost all the barons of Normandy had been Norwegians and had formerly come from Norway, nevertheless afterwards, at the pleas of the community of the English, the king yielded. They begged that he permit them to retain their own laws and ancient customs, in which their fathers had lived and in which they themselves had been born and raised—namely, the laws of Saint King Edward.

“From that day the laws of King Edward were venerated with great authority and strengthened and preserved throughout the whole kingdom above the other laws of the kingdom. These laws had in fact previously been discovered and established in the time of King Edgar, his grandfather. Nevertheless, after the death of King Edgar until the coronation of Saint King Edward—a period comprising sixty-seven years—the aforesaid laws lay dormant and were entirely neglected.

“But after King Edward had been elevated to the kingdom, by the counsel of the barons of England he revived the law that had lain dormant for sixty-seven years; having revived it, he restored it; having restored it, he adorned it; having adorned it, he confirmed it. After it had been confirmed, it was called the law of Saint King Edward—not because he had first devised it, but because, after it had been neglected and wholly consigned to oblivion from the death of his grandfather, King Edgar, who is said to have first discovered it, until his own time—that is, for sixty-seven years—it was revived by him.

“Therefore, by command of King William, twelve of the wisest men were chosen from each of all the counties of England. By oath they were charged, in the presence of King William, to make known, as far as they could, the established provisions of their laws and customs by a straight course, turning neither to the right nor to the left, omitting nothing, adding nothing, and omitting nothing through prevarication [another reading: *mutantes*, ‘altering’].

“Archbishop Aldred of York, who had crowned King William, and Hugh, bishop of London, by the king’s command, wrote with their own hands everything that the aforesaid sworn men said.

“Beginning with the laws of Holy Mother Church—they who (another reading: because) through her hold a firm foundation upon which king and kingdom stand—they proclaimed her laws, liberties, and peace, saying: ‘Every cleric,’ and so forth, as we read in Roger of Hoveden’s *Annals of Henry II*, where there is a digression concerning the kings of Norway. Almost the same things, in nearly the same words as those transcribed here, are also found in that same Roger.”

Yet the difference between the Lichfield author and Hoveden in these matters was not so insignificant that what the former, still unpublished, contains should for that reason be neglected, since the latter, who has been published, has related the same matter here in almost the same words.

Anyone who carefully considers both must acknowledge this. In the Lichfield author, however, only a portion of the same laws that Hoveden inserts follows. A portion of this kind is also found in Henry Knighton, canon of Leicester, a careful writer whose work has not yet appeared in print. Hoveden, however, has almost three times as many laws as either the Leicester or the Lichfield author. Yet among the latter two there is nothing that is not found in Hoveden.

I admit that the Lichfield, Leicester, and Hoveden authors are all ancient. The same must be said of several others who have transmitted the same account of this matter. But it is clear that none of them wrote until several centuries had passed since William, nor did those laws escape interpolation in Hoveden. For in the chapter on the Danish tribute there is mention of the younger King William.

Although I would by no means presume to determine what degree of confidence should be placed in such recent writers concerning a matter so ancient—one that generally eluded men not sufficiently occupied either with civil affairs or with legal studies—I would nevertheless wish it to be investigated more carefully.

I call them recent when I compare them with Ingulf, abbot of Crowland [Col. 1293], who in this matter ought perhaps not so readily to be called the foremost of witnesses as the only one whom it may perhaps be fitting for us to believe.

For he was not only an eyewitness of the beginnings of Norman rule in England; he also labored assiduously at King William’s court to establish the rights of his monastery. There, through his association with men experienced both in civil affairs and in legal studies, he obtained a copy of William’s laws—that is, of the laws of King Edward confirmed by William—written in the Norman language and differing greatly from those possessed by the more recent writers. He brought it with him to Crowland and added it to the end of his history.

He does not himself state explicitly in what year of William he did this. But it is plainly established that the time was after approximately the fifteenth year of William’s reign. This is worth noting because the revision and confirmation of those laws are attributed by the more recent writers mentioned above to William’s fourth year, whereas it is nevertheless quite certain, if one trusts Ingulf, that other laws—very different from them, though distinguished by the same heading and the same name—were circulated ten years or more later and regarded as genuine and as the only laws to which the authority of the king and the estates had previously been applied.

Hence perhaps the credibility of those who rashly thrust other versions upon us, beyond these, may be increased. For although the enactments of several years might have enabled many to recognize William as their author, it is nevertheless hardly probable—and no one reports—that either Edward’s laws were reviewed again under William, or that there was more than one recognition or confirmation of them. If there were in fact several, it would meanwhile have to be clearly established that the last deserved the greatest, not to say the sole, consideration.

We know sufficiently that the king’s fifteenth year had passed when Ingulph obtained his copy at the royal court in London, because William, bishop of Durham, appears as witness to a charter obtained at that time for the monastery of Crowland and found together with his published history.
