He had certainly not been appointed before the year of salvation 1081, or the fifteenth year of King William; and that charter was perhaps the genuine copy of the laws which, in William’s fourth year, had been both reviewed and confirmed by public authority.

For it is possible, and not unlike the truth, that although those more recent writers were deceived by a spurious—or at least interpolated—copy of the laws, they nevertheless faithfully learned and reported the year of the review and confirmation, since it had perhaps become a celebrated one. But let us hear Ingulph himself:

> “At the same time,” he says, “I brought with me from London to my monastery the laws of the most equitable King Edward, which my lord, the illustrious King William, had proclaimed to be authentic and to be inviolably observed throughout the whole kingdom of England under the gravest penalties, and had commended to his justices—in the same language in which they had been issued—lest through ignorance it should at some time happen that we or our people, to our grave danger, should rashly contravene and offend the royal majesty and imprudently set foot upon his most severe censures, which are frequently contained in those same laws, in the following manner.”

These words conclude his published History, with only the following addition by the editor, the distinguished Henry Savile:

> “It seems that he inserted here the laws of Edward which are missing.”

Yet we know with certainty that he did insert them there. This is evident not only from the autograph of the History itself, still preserved at Crowland in the county of Lincoln, but also from a more recent copy, written about two hundred years ago, which we have used.

Accordingly, insofar as the negligence and ignorance of the copyist, and the mouldering roughness of an obsolete and thoroughly corrupt style, have permitted, we present them here at once. They have been hastily committed to the press in the kind of Latin once used by our ancient lawyers. We have generally rendered word for word, and, because the barbarous phrase is especially suited to the subject, have preferred to interpret whatever we understood rather than transfer it into a purer style, which in such obscurity would more often—as frequently happens—cast darkness over the matter instead of bringing it light. Indeed, scarcely anyone who is not too alien to the law courts and the history of the Middle Ages will fail to understand this barbarous Latin.

To impose upon these texts the more polished vocabulary of imperial law would show that the translator had read Justinian rather than revealed the proper force of the Norman idiom. Yet I have not been wholly convinced that I understood everything I have ventured to translate here, and I have willingly left several passages to more perceptive readers. I lacked the autograph, which in the meantime I earnestly wished and strove to obtain, but in vain; and I did not wish to torment myself further with the trifles of conjecture. Wherever—as often happened—the meaning of the Norman diction entirely escaped me, I have retained it in the translation itself, set in a different type.

For I would rather openly confess myself guilty of ignorance than uselessly strain my eyesight in the thickest darkness. And among more skilled conjecturers, who, having abundant leisure, take pleasure in matters of this kind, I shall perhaps, while hurrying, serve as a whetstone, although I myself am unfit to do the cutting.

# [THE LAWS OF WILLIAM THE CONQUEROR]

[Note: [Col. 1293] The following three versions of the text are printed in parallel in Migne.]

These are the laws and customs which King William granted to all the people of England after the conquest of the land. They are the same as those which King Edward, his cousin, maintained before him.

## I

[Col. 1293]

This is to be known: the peace of Holy Church. Whatever offence a man had committed at that time, if he could come to Holy Church, he had peace of life and limb. And if anyone laid hands upon one who sought the protection of Holy Mother Church, whether it was an abbey or a religious church, he was to restore what he had taken and pay one hundred shillings as a penalty; for a parish mother church, twenty shillings; and for a chapel, ten shillings. Whoever thus violated the King’s peace in Mercian law was to pay one hundred shillings as compensation, and likewise in the case of *Heinfare* and of premeditated ambush.

## II

These pleas belong to the King’s Crown. And if anyone—a count or a provost—did wrong to the men of his bailiwick, and was convicted of it by the King’s justice, his penalty was to be double that imposed for another person’s offence.

## III

Whoever violated the King’s peace in the Danish law was to pay 144 pounds. The King’s forfeitures belonging to the sheriff were forty shillings in Mercian law and fifty shillings in West-Saxon law.

For a free man who possessed *sac* and *soc*, *tol* and *theam*, and *infangenetheof*, if he were impleaded and placed in forfeiture in the county, the forfeiture due to the sheriff was forty ores in Danish law. For another man who did not possess this franchise, it was thirty-two ores. Of these thirty-two ores the sheriff was to have ten for the King; the man who brought the plea was to have twelve as compensation against him; and the lord within whose jurisdiction he remained was to have ten. This is in Danish law.

## IV

This is the custom in Mercian law. If anyone was accused of larceny or robbery, and was pledged to come to justice, but fled, his pledge had four months and one day in which to search for him. If he could find him, he was to swear with eleven others that, at the time when he pledged him, the thief was not a thief, that it was not through him that he fled, and that he had not been able to seize him. Then he was to restore the property, pay twenty shillings for the head, four pence for the capture, a halfpenny for the *besche*, and forty shillings to the King.

In West-Saxon law, one hundred shillings was due for the hue and cry concerning the head, and four pounds to the King. In Danish law, the penalty was eight pounds: twenty shillings for the head and seven pounds to the King. If within a year and four days he could find the thief and bring him to justice, the twenty shillings which they had received were to be restored, and justice was to be done upon the thief.

## V

Whoever captured a thief without pursuit and without a hue and cry, and released him to the person to whom he had caused the damage, but the latter came afterward, was reasonably to pay ten shillings of *Hengwite* and to submit the matter to justice at the first proceeding without the permission of the justice; the penalty was forty shillings.

## VI

Whoever replevied property—namely a horse, ox, cow, pig, or sheep—which is called *forfengend* in English, was to pay to the provost the full amount: for a horse, eight pence; nevertheless, if there were no more than one hundred at the *maille*, he was to pay no more than eight pence; for a pig, four pence; and for a sheep, one penny. In the same proportion, for each of the three [variant: eight], four pence, and if there were no more than the stated number, no more than eight pence was to be paid. He was also to give pledges and find sureties that, if someone came within a year and a day to claim the property, he would produce in court the property he had replevied.

[Note: [Col. 1297] See Somner, *Glossarium ad Historiam Anglicam*.]

## VII

The same applies to property found in the ditch and to other property discovered. It was to be shown to three parts of the neighbourhood, so that he would have testimony concerning the finding. If someone later came to claim the thing, he was to give pledges and find sureties that, if another claimant demanded the property within a year and a day, he would produce in court the property he had found.

## VIII

[Col. 1299]

If one man killed another, confessed his guilt, and refused to make compensation, he was to pay from his *manbote* to the lord ten shillings for a free man. The *wera* of a thegn was twenty pounds in Mercian law and likewise in West-Saxon law. The *wera* of a villein was one hundred shillings in Mercian law and likewise in West-Saxon law.

## IX

Regarding the payment of the *wera*, the man of high blood was first to pay ten shillings to the widow and the orphans; the remainder the orphans and the relatives were to divide among themselves.

## X

As part of the *wera*, one could render a horse that had its testicles for twenty shillings, a bull for ten shillings, and a yearling for five shillings.

## XI

If one man wounded another and denied or refused to make further compensation, he was first to restore the payment for the head and the wounds. The injured man was to swear upon the saints that he could not have done otherwise, neither because of the hair, however dear it was to him, nor because of the weapon; that is, because of the pain.

## XII

If the wound came upon the uncovered face, at the brow [variant: palm], four pence throughout; and for every bone which a man drew from the wound, four pence for each bone. Afterwards, by agreement, if he placed before him honours [variant: lords], so that, if they had what he had done to him, his heart would permit him to accept from him what he offered.

## XIII

If it happened that someone cut off another’s fist or foot, he was to render half the *wera*, according to what it was worth. For the thumb, half the value of the hand. For the finger next to the thumb, fifteen shillings of the English shilling, that is, forty pence. For the long finger, sixteen shillings; for the other finger, the one that bears the ring, seventeen shillings; for the little finger, five shillings. For the nail, if he cut it off, five English shillings for each nail; for the nail of the little finger, four pence.

## XIV

Whoever violated a woman betrothed to another forfeited his *wera* to his lord.

## XV

Likewise, whoever gave a false judgment lost his *wera*, unless he could prove upon the holy relics that he had been unable to judge better.

## XVI

If someone accused another of theft, and the accused was a free man, and had no other testimony of his good faith, he was to clear himself by a full oath. Another who had previously been accused was to be named under oath. That is to say, if he could obtain lawful men by name, he was to clear himself with eleven others; and if he could not obtain them, he was to defend himself by judgment. The accuser was to swear over him with seven named men that he had not done it out of hatred or for any other reason, except to pursue his rightful claim.

## XVII

If someone was accused of breaking into a monastery or chamber, and had not previously been accused, he was to clear himself by forty-two named lawful men, with eleven others. If he had previously been accused, he was to clear himself threefold, namely by forty-eight named lawful men, with thirty-five others. If he could not obtain them, he was to go to the judgment threefold, as he ought to do threefold by full oath. If he had previously made compensation for theft, he was to go to the ordeal.

The Archbishop was to have forty shillings of the forfeiture in Mercian law; the Bishop twenty shillings; the Count twenty shillings; the Baron ten shillings; and the villein forty pence.

## XVIII

A free man who possessed agricultural property worth thirty pence was to pay Peter’s penny. For the four pence which the lord gave, his bordars, his *boner*, and his servants were to be quit.

A burgess who possessed from his own chattels property worth half a mark was to pay Peter’s penny. In Danish law, a free man who possessed agricultural property worth half a mark in silver was to pay Peter’s penny. By the penny which the lord gave, those who lived on his demesne were to be quit.

## XIX

Whoever violated a woman by force forfeited his limbs. Whoever threw a woman to the ground in order to force her paid a fine of ten shillings to her lord. If he violated her, he forfeited his limbs.

## XX

Whoever refused Peter’s penny was to have the penny taken from him by the justice of Holy Church and was to pay a penalty of thirty pence. If he were impleaded concerning it by the King’s justice, he was to pay thirty pence to the Bishop and forty shillings to the King.

## XXI

If anyone accidentally put out another’s eye, whatever the circumstances, he was to pay seventy shillings in English shillings. If the pupil remained [variant: was restored], he was to pay only half.

## XXII

[Note: [Col. 1303] See the Laws of Henry I, chapter 14.]

The Count’s relief, which belonged to the King, consisted of eight saddled and bridled horses, four coats of mail, four helmets, four shields, four lances, and four swords; the other four were hunting horses, together with palfreys fitted with bridles and halters.

[Col. 1305]

## XXIII

The Baron’s relief consisted of four saddled and bridled horses, two coats of mail, two helmets, two shields, two lances, and two swords; the other two were a hunting horse and a palfrey with bridle and halter.

## XXIV

The relief owed by a vavasor to his liege lord was to be discharged by the horse of his father [variant: ancestor], such as he had possessed on the day of his death, and by his coat of mail, helmet, shield, lance, and sword. If he had been so destitute of arms that he had possessed neither horse nor weapons, he was to pay one hundred shillings.

## XXV

Concerning any property which a man wishes to claim as stolen: if he wishes to give security and find a pledge to pursue his claim, he must name to the person who has meanwhile held it his guarantor, if he has one. If he has none, he must name his *Heuvelborh* (a surety association) and his witnesses, and produce them on the appointed day and at the term, if he has them or can obtain them. The intermediary shall deliver the property in pledge into the claimant’s own hand, and the other shall put it into the hand of his guarantor or his *Heuvelborh*. He must have witnesses that he bought it at the King’s market, and that he does not know his guarantor or pledge, living or dead. He shall swear this with his witnesses by full oath. He shall lose his chattel if they testify that he took it from a *Heuvelborh*. If he cannot obtain a guarantor or witnesses, he shall lose it; and in payment he shall forfeit his *werra* to his lord, in Mercian, Danish, and West-Saxon law.

He must not claim his lord as guarantor for what has been put in pledge, nor, in Danish law, put it into the market until it has been adjudged clear. If he can prove, through three parts of his neighbourhood, that it is of his own household, he may have it adjudged clear. For once the oath has been adjudged to him, it cannot afterwards be taken from him by the judgment of England.

## XXVI

Concerning secret murder: if a man is slain and the men of the hundred do not seize and bring the killer to justice within eight days, by showing on whose account he did it, they shall pay forty-seven marks for the murder.

## XXVII

If a man wishes to establish a covenant concerning land against his lord, he must establish it through his peers of the same tenure, whom he shall call as witnesses. He cannot establish it through strangers.

## XXVIII

A man who pleads in a court, whatever court it may be, except where the body is at stake, and is charged with having said something which he refuses to acknowledge, shall retain his word if he can establish by two credible men, in the presence of the pleader, that he did not say it.

[Note: [Col. 1307] See the Laws of Henry I, I. 31, 48.]

## XXIX

For the relief of a villein, he shall give his lord the best chattel that he has—horse, ox, or cow; and thereafter the villeins shall be in frankpledge.

## XXX

Concerning the three roads, namely Watling Street, Ermine Street, and the Fosse: whoever kills or assaults a man travelling through the country on any of these roads violates the King’s peace.

## XXXI

[Col. 1309]

If stolen goods are found, wherever that may be, together with the thief, the lord of the land and the woman shall have half of the thief’s goods; the claimants shall have their chattel if they find it; and the *borh* [variant: the faith, half] shall be lost if the thief is found within *sake* and *soke*, and the lord shall have it.

## XXXII

Concerning the *Strevvarde*: from every hundred hides there shall be one man between the feasts of St Michael and St Martin, and the *ward-reeve* shall have thirty hides free for his labour. If beasts trespass or perish, or are driven into the water, and the reeve cannot show that a cry or violence was raised, he shall make good the property.

## XXXIII

Those who cultivate the land are not to be compelled to work beyond the rent which is due; nor may a lordship remove cultivators from their land so long as they can perform the proper service. Serfs who leave their land are to be sought, lest they fail to perform the service due from their land. If a serf leaves the land on which he was born and goes to another’s land, no one may keep either him or his chattels; rather, he shall be made to return and perform the service that belongs to him. If lordships do not make other labourers come onto their land, justice shall compel them.

## XXXIV

No one shall withhold from his lord the service due to him because of any remission which the lord has granted him in arrears.

## XXXV

If a woman is condemned to death or mutilation of limbs and is pregnant, justice shall not be done upon her until she has been delivered.

## XXXVI

[Col. 1311]

If a man dies without disposition, his children shall divide the inheritance among themselves equally.

## XXXVII

If a father finds his daughter in adultery in his house or in the house of his son-in-law, he may lawfully kill the adulterer.

## XXXVIII

If a man poisons another, let him be put to death or permanently exiled. I cast your goods out because of danger of death, and you may not implead me for it; for it is lawful to harm another through fear of death when one cannot otherwise escape. And if I meddle with your goods because, through fear of death, I would not have done it, I shall have transgressed in that respect. Goods thrown from a ship shall be shared in common according to their chattels; and if anyone casts goods out of the ship without necessity, he shall restore them.

## XXXIX

If two men are partners in one undertaking and one is impleaded without the other, and through his own folly he loses, the other, who was not present, is not thereby to lose. For judgment is to be made between those parties and does not bind others who are absent.

## XL

Those who hold their land at rent shall have their proper relief equal to one year’s rent.

## XLI

Let those who have judgments to make consider carefully that they judge as they desire to be judged when they say, “Forgive us our sins.” We forbid that a Christian man be sold out of the land, especially into a country where no one knows whether he will be led away or lost, though He redeemed him with His life. Whoever raises a wrongful accusation or gives a false judgment through anger, hatred, or gain shall be in the King’s forfeiture of forty shillings, unless he can prove that he did not know how to do better; he shall lose his franchise, unless he can redeem it from the King at the King’s pleasure. And if he is in Danish law, he shall forfeit *Laxlite*, unless he can establish that he could not do better. Whoever refuses right law and right judgment shall forfeit to him who ought to have the right: if it is due to the King, six pounds; if to a count, forty shillings; if in a hundred, thirty shillings; and so to all those who hold courts in England, in English shillings. In Danish law, whoever refuses right judgment is at the mercy of *Laxlite*; nor may anyone complain to the King until he has been denied justice in the hundred or county.

[Note: [Col. 1311] See the Latin Laws of William, chapter 65, or variant 5.]

## XLII

No man shall take a kinsman or any other person into the county or outside it until he has three times demanded right in the hundred or county. If at the third time he cannot obtain right, he shall go to the county; the county shall aid him on the fourth occasion by oath. If the person against whom he complains is in default, he must obtain leave to take a *nam* (distress) for his own compensation and proof.

## XLIII

No one shall buy goods worth four pence, dead or alive, without the testimony of four men, of borough or village. If the man is challenged and he sells, he must have testimony. If he has no guarantor, he shall restore the chattel to its owner, and he who ought to have it shall have the forfeiture. If he has testimony, as we have said above, he shall vouch it three times, and on the fourth occasion establish it or restore the chattel.

## XLIV

It does not seem reasonable that a man should be required to make proof through witnesses who know that the goods were stolen, when no one sought them before the end of six months after the goods were stolen.

[Col. 1315]

## XLV

When a man is summoned and vouched as lawful, and has evaded the plea three times, and at the fourth time the summoners show his three defaults, he shall nevertheless be summoned to find a pledge and come to right. If he will not, and he is not seen alive or dead, all that he has shall be taken; the claimant shall have his chattel restored, the lord half of the remainder, and the hundred the other half. If any kinsman or friend obstructs this justice, they shall forfeit six pounds to the King. Let them seek the thief; wherever he is found in their power, he shall have no warranty of life and shall recover nothing by a prohibited plea.

## XLVI

[Note: [Col. 1315] See the Laws of Edward the Confessor, chapter 27.]

No one shall receive a man for more than three nights unless he tells him whence he came.

## XLVII

No one shall allow his man to depart from him beyond the time for which he is retained.

## XLVIII

[Note: [Col. 1315] See the Laws of Cnut, part II, chapter 126, and the Laws of Henry I, chapter 12.]

Whoever encounters a thief and knowingly lets him go shall make compensation to the value of the thief, unless he clears himself by full law that he did not know him to be a thief. Whoever hears the cry and holds back shall make amends for the delay to the King, unless he clears himself.

## XLIX

Every lord shall have his sergeant or pledge who shall keep himself so that he may obtain right in the hundred.

## L

If anyone is accused, within the hundred four men shall accuse him; he shall clear himself with a twelve-hand oath. If he afterwards fled from the accusation, his lord shall render his *wera*; and if anyone challenges the lord, saying that he went away with his lord’s knowledge, the lord shall clear himself with a six-hand oath. If he cannot or will not do so, he shall make amends to the King, and the accused shall be a villein.

### The Latin recension

The following are the laws and customs which King William granted to the whole people of England after the conquest of the land. They are the same as those which King Edward, his kinsman, observed before him.

## I. On the Right of Asylum and Ecclesiastical Immunity

The peace of Holy Church: whatever offence a person had committed at that time, if he could come to Holy Church, he was to have peace of life and limb. And if anyone laid hands upon one whom Holy Mother Church had claimed, whether it was an abbey or a religious church, he was to restore what he had taken and pay one hundred shillings as a forfeiture; for a parish mother church, twenty shillings; and for a chapel, ten shillings. Whoever thus violated the King’s peace in Mercian law was to pay one hundred shillings as compensation, and likewise in the case of *Heinfare* and of premeditated ambush.

## II. On the Privilege of the King’s Men

These pleas belong to the King’s Crown. If anyone did wrong to the men of his bailiwick—whether count or provost—and was convicted of it by the King’s justice, his forfeiture was to be double that imposed upon anyone else for a similar offence.

## III. On Violators of the Public Peace

Whoever violated the King’s peace in Danish law was to pay 144 pounds. The King’s forfeitures belonging to the sheriff were forty shillings in Mercian law and fifty shillings in West-Saxon law.

A free man who possessed *sac* and *soc*, *tol* and *theam*, and *infangenetheof*, if he was impleaded and placed in forfeiture in the county, owed the forfeiture for the sheriff’s benefit: forty ores in Danish law. For another man who did not possess this franchise, it was thirty-two ores. Of these thirty-two ores the sheriff was to have ten for the King; the man who brought the plea was to have twelve as compensation against him; and the lord within whose jurisdiction he remained was to have ten. This is Danish law.

## IV. On the Accused Thief and the Pledge Who Had Accepted Responsibility for His Appearance

This is the custom in Mercian law. If anyone was accused of larceny or theft, and was pledged to come to justice but fled, his pledge had four months and one day in which to search for him. If he could find him, he was to swear with eleven others that, at the time when he pledged him, the thief had not been a thief, that it was not through him that he fled, and that he had been unable to seize him. Then he was to restore the property, pay twenty shillings for the head, four pence for the capture, a halfpenny for the *besche*, and forty shillings to the King.

In West-Saxon law, one hundred shillings was due for the hue and cry concerning the head, and four pounds to the King. In Danish law, the forfeiture was eight pounds: twenty shillings for the head and seven pounds to the King. If within a year and four days he could find the thief and bring him to justice, the twenty shillings which they had received were to be restored, and justice was to be done upon the thief.

## V. On the Capture of Thieves

Whoever captured a thief without pursuit and without a hue and cry, and released him to the person to whom he had caused the damage, but that person came afterward, was reasonably to pay ten shillings of *Hengwite* and to submit the matter to justice at the first proceeding without the permission of the justice; the forfeiture was forty shillings.

## VI. On the Redemption of Animals

Whoever replevied property—namely a horse, ox, cow, pig, or sheep, which is called *forfengend* in English—was to pay the provost the full amount: for a horse, eight pence; nevertheless, if there were no more than one hundred at the *maille*, he was to pay no more than eight pence; for a pig, four pence; and for a sheep, one penny. In the same proportion, for each of the three [variant: eight], four pence; nevertheless, if there were no more than the stated number, he was to have and pay no more than eight pence. He was also to give pledges and find sureties that, if someone came within a year and a day to claim the property, he would produce in court the property he had replevied.

## VII. On Things Found by Chance

Likewise concerning property found in the ditch and other property discovered: it was to be shown to three parts of the neighbourhood, so that the finder would have testimony concerning the finding. If anyone came afterward to claim the thing, he was to give pledges and find sureties that, if another claimant demanded the property within a year and a day, he would produce in court the property he had found.

## VIII. On Homicide and the Valuation of the Head, or *Wera*

[Col. 1299]

If anyone killed another, confessed his guilt, and refused to make compensation, he was to pay from his *manbote* to the lord ten shillings for a free man. The *wera* of a thegn was twenty pounds in Mercian law and likewise in West-Saxon law. The *wera* of a villein was one hundred shillings in Mercian law and likewise in West-Saxon law.

## IX. To Whom the Valuation of the Head, or *Wera*, Is to Be Paid

As regards the *wera*, the man of high blood was first to pay ten shillings to the widow and the orphans; the remainder the orphans and the relatives were to divide among themselves.

## X. The Value of Certain Animals in the Assessment of the Head

As part of the *wera*, one could render a horse that had its testicles for twenty shillings, a bull for ten shillings, and a yearling for five shillings.

## XI. On the Assailant

If anyone wounded another and refused to make further compensation, he was first to restore the payment for the head and the wounds. The injured man was to swear upon the saints that he could not have done otherwise, neither because of the hair, however dear it was to him, nor because of the weapon—that is, because of the pain.

## XII. On an Inflicted Wound

If the wound came upon the uncovered face, at the brow [variant: palm], four pence throughout; and for every bone which a man drew from the wound, four pence for each bone. Afterwards, by agreement, if he placed before him honours [variant: lords], so that, if they had what he had done to him, his heart would permit him to accept from him what he offered.

## XIII. The Assessment of Severed Limbs

If it happened that someone cut off another’s fist or foot, he was to render half the *wera*, according to its value. For the thumb, half the value of the hand. For the finger next to the thumb, fifteen shillings of the English shilling, that is, forty pence. For the long finger, sixteen shillings; for the other finger, the one that bears the ring, seventeen shillings; for the little finger, five shillings. If someone cut off another’s nail, he was to make compensation with five English shillings for each nail, and for the nail of the little finger, four pence.

## XIV. On Adultery

Whoever violated a woman betrothed to another forfeited his *wera* to his lord.

## XV. On the Corrupt Judge

Likewise, whoever gave a false judgment lost his *wera*, unless, touching the holy things—the Gospels—he could prove that he had been unable to judge better.

## XVI. On the Purification of One Accused of Theft

If anyone accused another of larceny, and the accused was a free man, and had no other testimony of his legality, he was to clear himself by a full oath. If he had previously been infamous, he was to clear himself by named witnesses under oath: namely, if he could obtain lawful men by name, he was to clear himself with eleven others. If he could not obtain them, he was to defend himself by judgment. The accuser was to swear over him with seven named men that he had not done it out of hatred or for any other reason than pursuing his rightful claim.

## XVII. On One Who Has Broken into a Temple or House

If anyone was accused of breaking into a monastery or chamber, and had not previously been infamous, he was to clear himself by forty-two named lawful men, with eleven others. If he had previously been marked by infamy, he was to clear himself threefold, namely by forty-eight named lawful men, with thirty-five others. If he could not obtain them, he was to undergo the judgment threefold, as he ought to do threefold by full oath. If he had previously made compensation for theft, he was to go to the ordeal.

The Archbishop was to have forty shillings of the forfeiture in Mercian law; the Bishop twenty shillings; the Count twenty shillings; the Baron ten shillings; and the villein forty pence.

## XVIII. On Peter’s Pence, or the Roman Tribute

A free man who possessed agricultural property worth thirty pence was to pay Peter’s penny. For the four pence which the lord gave, his bordars, his *boner*, and his servants were to be quit.

A burgess who possessed from his own chattels property worth half a mark was to pay Peter’s penny. A free man under Danish law who possessed agricultural property valued at half a mark in silver was to pay Peter’s penny. By the penny which the lord gave, those who lived on his demesne were to be quit.

## XIX. On a Woman Violated by Force and an Attempt upon Her Chastity

Whoever violated a woman by force forfeited his limbs. Whoever threw a woman to the ground in order to force her paid a fine of ten shillings to her lord. If he violated her, he forfeited his limbs.

## XX. On Those Who Do Not Pay the Roman Tribute, or Peter’s Pence

Whoever refused Peter’s penny was to have the penny taken from him by the justice of Holy Church and was to pay a penalty of thirty pence. If he were impleaded concerning it by the King’s justice, he was to pay thirty pence to the Bishop and forty shillings to the King.

## XXI. On an Eye Put Out

If anyone accidentally put out another’s eye, whatever the circumstances, he was to pay seventy shillings in English shillings. If the pupil remained [variant: was restored], he was to pay only half.

## XXII. On the Count’s Relief, or *εἰσθεικτικόν* (an entrance-payment)

[Note: [Col. 1303] See the Laws of Henry I, chapter 14.]

The Count’s relief, which belonged to the King, consisted of eight saddled and bridled horses, four coats of mail, four helmets, four shields, four lances, and four swords; the other four were hunting horses, together with palfreys fitted with bridles and halters.

[Col. 1305]

## XXIII. On the Baron’s Relief

The Baron’s relief consisted of four saddled and bridled horses, two coats of mail, two helmets, two shields, two lances, and two swords; the other two were a hunting horse and a palfrey with bridle and halter.

## XXIV. On the Vavasor’s Relief

The relief owed by a vavasor to his liege lord was to be discharged by his father’s horse [variant: his father’s or paternal horse], such as he had possessed at the time of his death, and by his coat of mail, helmet, shield, lance, and sword. If he had been so destitute of arms that he had possessed neither horse nor weapons, he was to pay one hundred shillings.

[Editorial note: “I confess that I am so blind here that I cannot even supply a heading.”]

## XXV

*The supplied source ends at this heading.*
# Earlier mixed Latin/French recension (XXV–L)

## XXV. Concerning the person who wishes to accuse or reclaim livestock

If anyone wishes to accuse or reclaim livestock taken from him by theft, and wishes to give security and find pledges to prosecute his appeal, then the person who has the livestock must name his warrantor, if he has one; and if he does not have one, he shall name his *Heuvelborh*, his witnesses, and shall have them present on the appointed day and at the hearing, if he has them or can obtain them.

The intermediary shall give security for himself with five others, and the other shall place his security in the hands of his warrantor, or in the hands of his *Heuvelborh*. The latter shall have witnesses that he bought the livestock at the King’s market, and that he does not know his warrantor, whether living or dead, nor any pledge. He shall swear this with his witnesses by a full oath.

He shall lose his chattel if the witnesses testify that the *Heuvelborh* took it. And if he cannot obtain a warrantor or a witness, he shall lose it and, for [an uncertain charge], shall lose his *wergeld* toward his lord. This applies under the laws of the Mercians, Danes, and West Saxons.

He shall not summon his lord as warrantor concerning what is placed in pledge [Col. 1307]. Under Danish law, he shall not place it [in pledge] until he has been cleared; and if he can prove through three parts of his neighborhood that it comes from his own rearing, if he has cleared himself concerning the livestock. For once judgment has been given to him after the oath, he cannot thereafter recover it by the judgment of England.

## XXVI. Concerning the hundred-mult, where the accused murderer is not brought to judgment

If someone commits a *murdre*—a secret killing—and the men of the hundred do not seize him and bring him to justice within eight days, so that he may show for what reason he did it, they shall pay forty-seven marks for the murder.

## XXVII. Concerning a tenant’s action against his lord

If anyone wishes to clear an agreement concerning his land against his lord through his peers of the same tenure, whom he calls as witnesses, they shall clear him. For he cannot be cleared through outsiders.

## XXVIII. Concerning [an omitted matter]

Whoever pleads in a court, whatever court it may be, except where the King’s body is present, and someone imputes to him that he said something which he does not wish to acknowledge, if he cannot clear himself through two intelligent men who were present at the plea and saw that he did not say it, he shall recover through his own oath.

## XXIX. Concerning the relief of villeins

As the relief of a villein, he shall give his lord the best animal he possesses, whether it be a horse, an ox, or a cow; and afterward, if the villein is placed in free pledge, [the provision is complete].

## XXX. Concerning the public roads

There are three roads, namely Watling Street, Ermine Street, and the Fosse. Whoever on any of these roads kills or assaults a man travelling through the country violates the King’s peace.

## XXXI. Concerning a thief apprehended with the stolen goods, or *ἐπαυτοφόρῳ* (“caught in the act”)

[Col. 1309]

If theft is discovered in anyone’s land, together with the thief, the lord of the land and his wife shall have half the thief’s goods; and the claimants shall have their chattels if they find them, and [the lord and his wife shall have] half [the residue]. If it is found within soke and sake, the wife shall lose [her share], and the lord shall have it.

## XXXII. Concerning [an omitted matter]

For each hide of a hundred, one man shall serve as steward between the feast of Saint Michael and that of Saint Martin. The ward-reve shall have thirty hides free of service for his labor. If livestock die, perish, or are carried away by water, and he cannot show either a claim or the violence that occurred, he shall restore the livestock.

## XXXIII. Concerning cultivators and villeins attached to the soil

Those who cultivate the land must not be molested except concerning their rightful rent. Nor may cultivators be allowed to leave their lordship and their land unless they can perform their proper service. Native tenants who leave their land must not be allowed to [depart] or to sail away, since they do not perform the proper service belonging to their land.

A native tenant who leaves the land where he was born and comes to another’s land shall not be retained by anyone, nor shall his chattels; rather, he shall be compelled to return, so that he may perform the service appropriate to him. And if the lords do not cause other cultivators to come to their land, justice shall do so.

## XXXIV. That no one withhold services owed to his lord

No one shall withhold from his lord his proper service on account of any remission that the lord previously granted him.

## XXXV. Concerning a pregnant woman condemned to capital punishment

If a woman has been condemned to death or to mutilation of her limbs, and is carrying a child in her womb, judgment shall not be carried out against her before she has given birth.

## XXXVI. Concerning the goods of intestates

[Col. 1311]

If anyone dies intestate, his children shall divide his inheritance equally.

## XXXVII. Concerning an adulterer caught by the father

If a father catches his daughter in adultery in his own house or in the house of her son-in-law, he may lawfully kill the adulterer.

## XXXVIII. Concerning jettison, as under the Rhodian Law

If anyone, by force of another, is killed or violently cast out, I have thrown your goods from the ship through fear of death; you cannot bring an action against me for this. For it is lawful to cause another a loss through fear of death when danger cannot otherwise be escaped.

And if you accuse me concerning this, alleging that I did it not through fear of death, I shall be answerable for it; and the goods remaining in the ship shall be divided jointly according to the chattels. If anyone throws chattels out of the ship when necessity has not required it, he shall restore them.

## XXXIX. Concerning judgment against an absent partner

Two persons are partners in one *crichet* [uncertain term], and one of them is sued without the other; if he loses through his own negligence, the absent partner ought not therefore to suffer loss. For what has been judged between them ought not to prejudice those who were absent.

## XL. Concerning the relief of those who pay rent

For those who hold their land at rent, the proper relief shall be equal to the annual rent.

## XLI. Concerning judgments

Let those charged with rendering judgments take careful heed that they judge as they pray when they say, “Forgive us our debts.” We prohibit any Christian man from selling a person outside the land, lest that person lose his soul, which God redeemed with his own life.

Whoever raises an injury or renders a false judgment through anger, hatred, or money, shall incur the King’s forfeiture of forty shillings [Col. 1313]. If he cannot allege that he did not know how to do more justice, he shall lose his liberty unless he can redeem it from the King at his pleasure.

And if this is under Danish law, he shall incur the forfeiture of *Lahslite* if he cannot allege that he did not know how to do better, and if he has refused right law and right judgment, he shall incur forfeiture toward the person to whom this right belongs: if toward the King, six pounds; if toward a count, forty shillings; if in the hundred, thirty shillings; and toward all those who hold courts in England, the amount shall be reckoned in English shillings.

Under Danish law, whoever refuses right judgment shall be at the mercy of his *Lahslite*, and he shall not properly complain to the King because someone has failed him in the hundred or in the county.

## XLII. Concerning the seizure of a distress, called *namium*

No one shall seize any distress in the county, or by force, until he has demanded justice three times in the hundred or in the county. If he cannot obtain justice on the third occasion, he shall go to the county, and the county shall assign him a fourth day. If the person against whom he complains fails to appear, he shall receive permission to seize a distress for his own benefit and profit.

## XLIII. That no one buy anything without witnesses

No one shall buy anything valued at four pence, whether a dead or a living thing, without the testimony of four men, either from a borough or from a village. If someone claims the thing, the purchaser shall come and have witnesses. If he has no warrantor, he shall answer to the other with his chattel and incur the forfeiture owed by the person who should bear it. If he has witnesses, as stated above, after three appearances, then at the fourth he shall clear himself and return it.

## XLIV. Concerning [an omitted matter]

Moreover, it does not seem reasonable that anyone should establish proof through testimony that recognizes the thing at issue, and that no one should prove it before the six-month term after the goods were stolen [Col. 1315].

## XLV. Concerning an abandoned pledge

The person who has been accused and has testimony of his legality, and whose plea has been missed three times, shall at the fourth appearance have the summoner show the three defaults. Nevertheless, he shall be ordered to find pledge and come to justice. If he refuses, and no one has seen him alive or dead, whatever he possesses shall be seized and given to the claimant; the lord shall have half the remainder, and the hundred half.

If no relative obstructs this justice, they shall incur a forfeiture to the King of six pounds and shall seek the thief. Whoever has him in his power shall have no warrant for his life, nor shall he thereafter be able to recover a plea by way of defense.

## XLVI. Concerning guests

No one shall receive another for more than three nights, unless the person with whom he came orders otherwise.

## XLVII. Concerning servants

No one shall permit his man to depart from him once he has been accused.

## XLVIII. Concerning [an omitted matter]

Whoever encounters a thief and, without an accusation, lets him go, shall pay an amercement equal to the value of the thief, or shall clear himself by full law that he did not know him to be a thief. Whoever hears the hue and cry and neglects it shall pay the King’s amercement for the neglect, or shall clear himself.

## XLIX. Concerning [an omitted matter]

Every lord shall also have his servant or pledge, who, if he is accused, shall have justice in the hundred.

## L. Concerning [an omitted matter]

If someone is accused within the hundred and four men retain the accusation against him, he shall clear himself with twelve men. If he flees after the accusation, the lord shall pay his *wergeld*. If the lord is accused, the lord who is to be proceeded against on account of the accusation shall clear himself with twelve men; and if he cannot do so, he shall make amends toward the King and be outlawed.

---

## These are the laws of King William, rendered into Latin by the distinguished scholar Charles du Frêne, Lord of Cange, royal procurator.

[Col. 1294]

## I.

[Note: [Col. 1293] See the Laws of Edward the Confessor, chapters 6 and 7 below.]

Namely, the peace of Holy Church: whatever forfeiture anyone has committed until now, if he can come to Holy Church, let him have peace of life and limb. If anyone lays hands upon a person who has sought the Mother Church, whether it be an abbey or a religious church, he shall restore the person whom he has seized and pay one hundred shillings for the forfeiture; for a parish Mother Church [Col. 1296], twenty shillings; and for a chapel, ten shillings.

Whoever violates the King’s peace under Mercian law shall pay one hundred shillings, likewise for *heinfare* and for premeditated ambushes.

## II.

These pleas belong to the King’s Crown. If anyone, whether a count or a reeve, does evil to the men of his bailiwick and is attainted or convicted of it by the King’s justice, his forfeiture shall be double that which any other person would have incurred.

## III.

Whoever breaks the King’s peace under Danish law shall pay 144 pounds. The King’s forfeitures that belong to the sheriff are forty shillings under Mercian law and fifty shillings under West Saxon law.

Concerning a free man who has sake and soke, toll and team, and *infangentheof*: if he is sued and placed in forfeiture in the county, the forfeiture belongs to the sheriff for the King’s use—forty *orae* under Danish law. For another man who does not possess such liberty, it is twenty-two *orae*.

Of these thirty-two *orae*, the sheriff shall have ten for the King’s use; the person against whom the plea has been brought shall have twelve; and the lord within whose territory he has lived shall have ten. This applies under Danish law.

## IV.

This is the custom under Mercian law. If anyone is accused of theft or robbery and has been pledged to stand trial, and then flees, his pledge-holder shall have four months and one day to search for him.

If he can find him, he shall swear with eleven others that, at the time when he pledged him, he did not know him to be a thief; that it was not through him that the man fled; and that he could not seize him. He shall then restore the chattel and pay twenty shillings for the principal charge, four pence to the keeper of the prison, and a *mallia* or *mea alia* [uncertain reading] for the *ta besche* [uncertain term] [Col. 1298], together with forty shillings to the King.

Under West Saxon law, he shall pay one hundred shillings as the capital charge and four pounds to the King. Under Danish law, the forfeiture is eight pounds, twenty shillings for the capital charge, and seven pounds to the King.

If, within a year and four days, he can find the thief and bring him to justice, the twenty shillings he paid shall be returned to him, and justice shall be done to the thief.

## V.

Whoever apprehends a thief without pursuit or hue and cry and delivers him into the power of the person who suffered the loss, and then comes afterward, ought reasonably to give that person ten shillings as *hengwita* and make an end of the matter at the first hearing or plea. Without the permission of justice, he shall incur a forfeiture of forty shillings.

## VI.

Whoever recovers stolen livestock—whether a horse, ox, pig, or sheep, which is called *forfeng* in English—the person who possessed it shall pay, for a large animal, one shilling to the reeve, who is to receive eight pence as the *lestussun*. If there are not enough goods to make one hundred in the *mallia*, he shall pay only eight pence; for a pig, four pence; and for a sheep, one penny.

This continues up to eight animals, at four pence for each; and if there are not so many, he shall pay only eight pence. He shall give security and find a pledge. If someone else later comes within a year and a day and claims the livestock, he shall have justice in court against the person from whom the livestock was recovered.

## VII.

What has been said about livestock shall likewise be understood of every other thing found. It shall be shown to three parts of the neighborhood, so that he may have testimony concerning its discovery.

If someone later comes to claim or demand the thing, he shall give security and find pledges who shall promise that, if anyone else claims the livestock within a year and a day, he will have justice in court against the person who found the thing.

## VIII.

[Col. 1300]

If anyone kills another and admits it but refuses to make amends, he shall pay his *manbot* to the lord: for a free man, ten shillings; for a slave, twenty shillings.

The *wergeld* of a thegn is twenty pounds under Mercian law and under West Saxon law. The *wergeld* of a villein is one hundred shillings under Mercian law and under West Saxon law.

## IX.

From the *wergeld*, ten shillings shall first be paid for high blood to the widow and orphans; the remainder shall be divided between the orphans and the relatives.

## X.

In payment of the *wergeld*, a horse that has testicles may be given for twenty shillings, a bull for ten shillings, and a boar for five shillings.

## XI.

If anyone wounds another and afterward refuses to make amends, he shall first pay him the principal amount. The wounded man shall swear upon holy objects that he cannot act for a lesser compensation, nor, out of hatred, make the compensation for his *sarbota*, that is, for his pain, more costly or greater.

*(In Saxon, “sag” means pain; “bota,” compensation.)*

## XII.

If the wound inflicted upon him is such that it is visible, he shall pay four pence for the skin of the whole wound, and four pence for each of the bones extracted from the wound.

But if an agreement has been made before superior lords concerning a wound inflicted upon him by another, and if his heart has advised him and given him counsel, he shall accept from the other whatever has been offered to him.

## XIII.

If it happens that someone cuts off another person’s fist or foot, he shall pay him half the *wergeld*, according to what has been lost. For the thumb he shall pay half the value of the hand.

For the finger next to the thumb [Col. 1302], fifteen English shillings, that is, forty pence; for the middle finger, sixteen shillings; for the other finger, which bears the ring, seventeen shillings; for the little finger, five shillings.

If a fingernail is cut off, five English shillings shall be paid for each; for the nail of the little finger, four pence.

## XIV.

Whoever violates another man’s bride forfeits his *wergeld* toward his lord.

## XV.

Likewise, whoever renders a false judgment loses his *wergeld*, unless he can prove by an oath sworn upon holy objects that he did not know how to judge better.

## XVI.

If anyone accuses another of theft, and the accused is a free man who has at some time had true testimony of his lawfulness, he shall clear himself by a plain oath. A man previously defamed shall clear himself by the specified oath, namely, from the court of lawful men who are his peers, if he can obtain them; or he shall clear himself with twelve men.

If he cannot obtain them, he shall defend himself by judgment—that is, by what this law calls common purgation. The accuser shall swear with seven named men that he has made the accusation through no hatred and for no other reason than to pursue his right.

## XVII.

If anyone is accused of violating a monastery or church, or of breaking into a chamber, and has not previously been defamed, he shall clear himself with twelve named lawful men, himself making the twelfth.

If he has previously been defamed, he shall clear himself with three times the stated number of witnesses: namely, with forty-eight named lawful men, himself making the thirty-sixth. If he cannot obtain them, he shall undergo judgment three times, just as he should have undergone the oath three times.

If he has previously made amends for theft [Col. 1304], he shall undergo the water ordeal.

The archbishop shall have forty shillings from the forfeiture under Mercian law; the bishop, twenty shillings; the count, twenty shillings; the baron, ten shillings; and the villein, forty pence.

## XVIII

A free man who has thirty pence’ worth of livestock in the fields shall pay Peter’s penny. For the four pence paid by the lord, his bordars, his *bonnarii*, and his servants shall be quit.

A burgess who has half a mark in his own chattels shall pay Peter’s penny. A free man under Danish law who has livestock in the fields worth half a mark in silver shall pay Peter’s penny. For the penny given by the lord, those who dwell in his demesne shall be quit.

## XIX

Whoever uses force against a woman forfeits his limbs. Whoever throws a woman to the ground in order to use force against her shall pay ten shillings as a fine to her lord. If he has intercourse with her by force, he is forfeited in his limbs.

## XX

Whoever refuses Peter’s penny shall pay the penny by the justice of Holy Church and, in addition, thirty pence for the forfeiture. If he is sued for this by the King’s justice, the bishop shall have thirty pence from the forfeiture and the King forty shillings.

## XXI

If anyone in any circumstance puts out another’s eye, he shall make amends with seventy English shillings. If the pupil remains, only half shall be given to him.

## XXII

Concerning the relief of a count, which belongs to the King [Col. 1306]: eight saddled and bridled horses; four coats of mail; four helmets; four shields; four spears; four swords; and four other hunting animals and palfreys with bridles and halters.

## XXIII

Concerning the relief of a baron: four horses with saddles and bridles; two coats of mail; two helmets; two shields; two lances; two swords; and two other things—one hunting horse and one palfrey with bridle and halter.

## XXIV

Concerning the relief of a vavassor toward his liege lord: he shall be quit by the horse of his father, such as his father had at the time of his death; by his coat of mail, helmet, shield, lance, and sword—unless he was so destitute of all goods that he had neither a horse nor arms worth one hundred shillings.

## XXV

If anyone wishes to accuse or reclaim livestock taken from him by theft, and wishes to give security and find pledges to prosecute his appeal, then the person who has the livestock must name his warrantor, if he has one; and if he does not have one, he shall name his *Heuvelborh*, that is, his sureties, and his witnesses, and shall have them present on the appointed day and at the hearing, if he has them or can obtain them.

The intermediary shall give security for himself with five others, and the other shall place his security in the hands of his warrantor or of his *Heuvelborh*. He shall have witnesses that he bought the livestock at the King’s market and that he does not know his warrantor, nor any living or dead pledge. He shall swear this with his witnesses by a full oath.

He shall lose his chattel if those giving testimony say that the *Heuvelborh* took it. If he cannot obtain a warrantor or a witness, he shall lose it and, for [an omitted charge], shall lose his *wergeld* toward his lord.

This applies under the laws of the Mercians, Danes, and West Saxons. He shall not summon his lord as warrantor concerning what has been placed in pledge [Col. 1308]. Under Danish law, he shall not place it in pledge until he has been cleared; and if he can prove through three parts of his neighborhood that the livestock came from his own rearing, if he has cleared himself concerning the livestock.

For once the oath has been adjudged and imposed upon him, he cannot thereafter recover it by the judgment of England.

## XXVI

If anyone commits a *murdre*, a secret killing, and the men of the hundred do not seize him and bring him to justice within eight days, so that they may show by whom the murder was committed, they shall pay forty-seven marks for the murder.

## XXVII

If anyone wishes to clear an agreement concerning his land against his lord through the peers of the same tenure, whom he calls as witnesses, he shall be cleared through them; for he cannot be cleared through outsiders.

## XXVIII

Whoever pleads in a court, whatever court it may be, except where the King’s body is present, and someone imputes to him that he said something which he does not wish to acknowledge, if he cannot clear himself through two intelligent men who were present at the plea and saw that he did not say it, the matter shall return to his oath.

## XXIX

As the relief of a villein, he shall give his lord the best animal he possesses, whether a horse, an ox, or a cow; and afterward the villein shall be held in free pledge.

## XXX

There are three roads, namely Watling Street, Ermine Street, and the Fosse. Whoever on any of these roads kills or assaults a man travelling through the country violates the King’s peace.

## XXXI

[Col. 1310]

If theft is found in anyone’s land, together with the thief, the lord of the land and his wife shall have half the thief’s goods; and the claimants, that is, those who reclaim their property, shall have their chattels if they find them, together with their half. If he is found within soke and sake, the wife shall lose her share, and the lord shall have it.

## XXXII

Concerning the steward: from each hide of a hundred, one man shall serve between the feast of Saint Michael and that of Saint Martin. The ward-reve shall have thirty hides free of service for his labor. If livestock or animals die, perish, or are infected by some disease, and it cannot be shown that a claim or violence was involved, the livestock shall be restored.

## XXXIII

Those who cultivate the land must not be molested except concerning their rightful rent. Nor may a lord dismiss cultivators from his land so long as they are able to perform their proper service.

Native tenants who leave their land and deny their native status must be sought out, so that they may perform the proper service belonging to their land. A native tenant who leaves the land where he was born and comes to another’s land shall not be retained by anyone, nor shall he or his chattels be retained; rather, he shall be compelled to return and perform the service appropriate to him.

If the lords do not cause other cultivators to come onto their land, justice shall do so.

## XXXIV

No one shall withhold from his lord his proper service on account of any remission that the lord previously granted him.

## XXXV

If a woman has been condemned to death or to the breaking or mutilation of her limbs, and is pregnant, judgment shall not be carried out against her before she has given birth.

## XXXVI

[Col. 1312]

If anyone dies intestate, his children shall divide his inheritance equally.

## XXXVII

If a father catches his daughter in adultery in his own house or in the house of her son-in-law, he may lawfully kill the adulterer.

## XXXVIII

If anyone poisons another, he shall be killed or condemned to perpetual exile. If I throw your goods from a ship through fear of death, you cannot bring an action against me for this. For it is lawful to cause another a loss through fear of death when danger cannot otherwise be avoided.

If you prove that I did this not through fear of death, I shall be answerable for it; and the goods remaining in the ship shall be divided jointly according to the chattels. If anyone throws chattels out of the ship when no necessity requires it, he shall restore them.

## XXXIX

Two persons are partners in one *crichet*, and one of them is sued without the other and loses through his own negligence. The absent partner ought not therefore to suffer loss, for a matter adjudged between them does not prejudice those who were absent.

## XL

For those who hold their land at rent, the proper relief shall be equal to the annual rent.

## XLI

Let those charged with rendering judgments take careful heed that they judge as they pray when they say, “Forgive us our debts.” We therefore decree that no one sell a Christian man outside the land, especially into a country where no provision is made lest the soul perish, which God redeemed with his own life.

Whoever raises an injury or renders a false judgment through anger, hatred, or money given [Col. 1314], shall incur the King’s forfeiture of forty shillings, unless he can clear himself by alleging that he did not know how to act more justly. He shall lose his liberty unless he can redeem it from the King at the King’s pleasure.

If this is under Danish law, he shall incur the forfeiture of *Lahslite* if he cannot clear himself by alleging that he did not know how to do better. Whoever refuses right law and right judgment shall incur forfeiture toward the person to whom this right belongs: if toward the King, six pounds; if toward a count, forty pounds; if in the hundred, thirty shillings; and toward all those who hold courts in England, the amount shall be reckoned in English shillings.

Under Danish law, whoever refuses right judgment shall be at the mercy of his *Lahslite*. Nor shall a complaint be made to the King because someone has failed him in the hundred or in the county.

## XLII

No one shall seize a distress, either in the county or outside it, until he has demanded justice three times in the hundred or in the county. If he cannot obtain justice on the third occasion, he shall go to the county, and the county shall assign him a fourth day. If the person against whom he complains fails to appear, he shall then receive permission to seize a distress for his own benefit and profit.

## XLIII

No one shall buy anything valued at four pence, whether a dead or a living thing, without the testimony of four men, either from a borough or from a village. If the thing is claimed, the purchaser shall come and have witnesses. If he has no warrantor, he shall return the other man’s chattel, and the person who ought to bear the forfeiture shall bear it.

If he has witnesses, as stated above—namely, for three appearances—then at the fourth appearance he shall clear himself or return the thing.

## XLIV

It does not seem reasonable that proof should be made through witnesses who know the stolen thing, and that anyone should be required to prove or establish his proof [Col. 1316] before the expiry of six months after the thing was taken and stolen.

## XLV

The person who has been accused, and has testimony of his legality, and has abandoned the plea three times, shall at the fourth appearance have the summoners show his three defaults. Nevertheless, he shall be ordered to find pledge and come to justice.

If he refuses, and has not been seen alive or dead, whatever he possesses shall be seized and given to the claimant or petitioner; the lord shall have half the remainder, and the hundred the other half.

If any relative or friend obstructs this justice, they shall incur a forfeiture to the King of six pounds. They shall seek the thief, and wherever he is found in anyone’s power, he shall have no warrant for his life and shall not thereafter be able to recover a plea in his defense.

## XLVI

No one shall receive another for more than three nights, unless the person with whom he came orders otherwise.

## XLVII

No one shall permit his man to depart from him once he has been accused.

## XLVIII

Whoever encounters a thief and willingly lets him go safely shall pay an amercement equal to the value of the thief, or clear himself by full law that he did not know him to be a thief. Whoever hears the hue and cry and neglects it shall pay the King’s amercement for neglect, or clear himself.

## XLIX

Every lord shall also have his own servant or pledge, who, if he is accused, shall go to justice in the hundred.

## L.

If the person who is accused is concealed [Col. 1318] and is accused before the hundred by four men, he shall clear himself with twelve men. If he flees after the accusation, the lord shall pay his *wergeld*. If the lord is accused of having exceeded through his own knowledge, he shall clear himself with six men. If he cannot do so, he shall make amends to the King and be outlawed.

---

# SELDEN TO THE READER

[Col. 1317]

No one except Ingulf has transmitted these laws; nor, apart from them, do I think that any other law written in the French or Norman language of that age survives at all. Meanwhile, tradition records that William earnestly desired that this language, being his native tongue and, as it were, more faithful to the newly established government, should be spread and made common in England, and that he ordered this by decree.

I pass over what the historians say on this subject and call as witness Robert Holkot, a man, as his age regarded him, exceedingly learned. The histories relate, he writes on the Book of Wisdom, chapter 11, that when William, Duke of the Normans, had conquered the kingdom of England, he considered how he might destroy the Saxon language and make England and Normandy agree in language. Therefore he ordered that no one should plead in the King’s court except in French, and also that every boy who was sent to school should learn French, and through French, Latin. These two practices, he says, continue to this day.

This Robert flourished under Edward III and was carried off by the plague in the twenty-fourth year of that king’s reign. See Statute 36 Edward III, chapter 15.

Yet several other laws, attributed in old manuscripts to King William—apart from those attributed to King Edward and promulgated under his authority—are found. It seemed worthwhile to append these laws both because Roger of Howden has inserted them from an excessively mutilated copy, or because they have been shortened through the fault of scribes, and because I know for certain that William Lambard’s book on the ancient laws of the English, where they are indeed published but do not everywhere agree with the copy I use, is very rarely encountered by scholars.

[Col. 1317A]

# WILLIAM, by the grace of God king of the English, duke of the Normans, to all his men of France and England, greeting.

## LI. Concerning religion and the public peace

First of all, we decree that one God shall be venerated throughout our whole kingdom, that the one faith of Christ shall always be kept inviolate, and that peace, security, concord, judgment, and justice shall be firmly and inviolably observed between the English and the Normans, the French and the Britons of Wales and Cornwall, and the Picts and Scots of Alba.

Likewise, they shall be observed between the French and the islanders, and among the provinces and lands that belong to the crown and dignity, defense and observance, and honor of our kingdom [Col. 1317B], and among all who are subject to us throughout the entire monarchy of the kingdom of Britain. Thus no one shall commit any offence against another in any matter, on pain of our full forfeiture.

## LII. Concerning faith and obedience toward the king

We also decree that all free men shall affirm by covenant and oath that, within and outside the whole kingdom of England—which was formerly called the kingdom of Britain—they desire to remain faithful to William their lord, to preserve his lands and honors everywhere in that fidelity together with him, and to defend them against enemies and foreigners.

## LIII. Concerning the killing of a Norman or Frenchman

[Col. 1318A]

We will and firmly command that all the men whom we have brought with us, or who have come after us, shall be under our protection and in our peace throughout the aforesaid kingdom. If one of them is killed, his lords shall produce his killer within five days, if they can. If not, they shall begin paying us forty-six marks of silver for as long as the substance of that lord lasts. When the lord’s resources fail, the entire hundred in which the killing occurred shall jointly pay what remains.

## LIV. Concerning the right of Normans who, before William’s arrival, had been English citizens

Every Frenchman who, in the time of our kinsman Edward, was in England a participant in the customs of the English shall pay what they call *Anhlote* and *Anscote*, according to English law.

## LV. Concerning cliental or feudal law, and the immunity of free men

We will, firmly command, and grant that all free men throughout the monarchy of our aforesaid kingdom shall have and hold their lands and possessions well and peacefully, free from every unjust exaction and every tax, so that nothing shall be demanded or taken from them except the free service which by right they owe us and are bound to perform, and according to what has been established for them and given and granted to them by us, by hereditary right in perpetuity, through the common counsel of our whole aforesaid kingdom [Col. 1319A].

## LVI. Concerning night watches

We also decree and firmly command that all the cities, boroughs, castles, hundreds, and wapentakes of our aforesaid kingdom shall be watched and guarded every night in turn against crimes and enemies, as the sheriffs, aldermen, reeves, and our other bailiffs and ministers shall, by common counsel, more suitably provide for the benefit of the kingdom.

## LVII. Concerning measures and weights

[Col. 1319B]

Throughout the kingdom they shall have the most reliable and officially marked measures, and the most reliable and officially marked weights, as our good predecessors established.

## LVIII. Concerning the services of tenants or vassals

We also decree and firmly command that all counts, barons, knights, servants, and all free men throughout our aforesaid kingdom shall always have and maintain themselves properly in arms and horses, as is fitting and necessary; and that they shall always be ready and prepared to complete and perform their full service for us whenever there is need, according to what they owe us by right from their fees and tenements, and as we have established for them by the common counsel of our whole aforesaid kingdom [Col. 1319C], and have given and granted to them in fee by hereditary right.

This command shall in no way be violated, under our full forfeiture.

## LIX. That subjects strive with all their strength to preserve the royal laws unharmed
We further decree and firmly command that all free men throughout the aforesaid kingdom shall be sworn brothers, bound by oath to defend and manfully preserve our monarchy and our kingdom, to the full extent of their strength and means, against enemies; to maintain unimpaired the peace and dignity of our crown; and to administer steadfastly, in every possible way and to the best of their ability, right judgment and justice to all, without deceit and without delay. This decree was enacted in the city of London.

### LX. That sale and purchase shall take place only before witnesses and in the cities

We also prohibit the sale or purchase of any living property except within the cities, and then before three trustworthy witnesses; nor shall anyone sell or purchase any prohibited thing without surety and warranty. Whoever acts otherwise shall pay and make full payment, and shall thereafter incur forfeiture.

### LXI. Concerning marketplaces, and the recognized law of cities and boroughs

Likewise, no market or fair shall exist or be permitted to take place except in the cities of our kingdom, in boroughs, within walled enclosures, in castles, and in the safest places, where the customs of our kingdom, our common law, and the rights of our crown, established by our good predecessors, cannot perish, be diminished, or be violated. Everything must instead be done rightly and openly, by judgment and justice. For this reason castles, boroughs, and cities have been situated, founded, and built: namely, for the protection of the people and inhabitants of the kingdom and for the kingdom’s defence. They must therefore be maintained with every liberty, integrity, and due order.

### LXII. Concerning legal purgation in public proceedings

It has also been decreed that, if a Frenchman accuses an Englishman of perjury, murder, theft, homicide, or *Ran*—which they call open robbery, and which cannot be denied—the Englishman shall defend himself in whatever way he knows best, either by the judgment of iron or by combat. If the Englishman is infirm, let him find another who will do this for him. If either of them is defeated, let him find another who will act for him. If either of them is defeated, he shall pay the king forty shillings.

But if an Englishman accuses a Frenchman and wishes to prove the charge by judgment or by combat, I then wish the Frenchman to purge himself by an unbroken oath [“not by iron,” according to Hoveden].

### LXIII. The laws of King Edward confirmed

We also command that all men shall have and hold the law of King Edward in every matter, with the additions that we have established for the benefit of the English.

### LXIV. Concerning pledges for the administration of public justice

Every man who wishes to be held as free shall be placed in a pledge-group, so that his pledge-holder may bring him to justice if he commits an offence. If anyone escapes, let his pledge-holders see to it that they pay what has been charged, and let them clear themselves by declaring that they knew of no fraud in the escape.

Let the hundred and the county be summoned, as our predecessors established, together with those who ought justly to come but have refused. Let the defaulter be summoned once; if he does not come a second time, let one ox be taken; if a third time, another ox; and if a fourth time, let what has been charged—called *Ceapgyld*—be paid from that man’s property, together with the king’s forfeiture.

### LXV. Concerning slaves and their manumission

We also prohibit anyone from selling a person outside the country. If anyone wishes to make his slave free, he shall deliver him to the sheriff by the right hand in full county court. He shall proclaim him quit of the yoke of his servitude by manumission, show him the free roads and gates, and give him free arms, namely a spear and a sword. Thereafter he becomes a free man.

### LXVI. Concerning slaves

Likewise, if slaves remain without accusation for a year and a day in our cities, or in boroughs enclosed by walls, or in our castles, from that day they become free and shall remain free from the yoke of their servitude forever.

### LXVII. Concerning the manner of punishments

We also prohibit anyone from being killed or hanged for any offence. Instead, his eyes shall be torn out and his feet, testicles, or hands cut off, so that the trunk remains alive as a sign of his treason and wickedness. For punishment ought to be inflicted upon evildoers according to the magnitude of their offence. These commands shall not be violated, on pain of our full forfeiture. Witnesses, etc.

### [NOTE]

The sheets used in bringing these matters to light also supplied the laws *Concerning Forensic Procedure*. A more correct copy is found in the manuscript of John Brampton, abbot of Jervaulx, who, although otherwise a most diligent investigator of our affairs and especially of ancient laws, does not record that William established any laws beyond these. In this abbot’s work the heading is as follows, and the style is as follows.

## INSTITUTES OR LAWS OF KING WILLIAM

William, by the grace of God king of the English, sends greeting and friendship to all to whom this writing comes. I command and order that it be observed throughout the English nation.

### LXVIII. Concerning forensic procedure

If an Englishman challenges a Frenchman to combat over theft, homicide, or any matter for which combat ought to be undertaken, or in a judgment between two men, he shall have full permission to do so. If the Englishman does not wish to fight, the Frenchman who has been challenged shall defend himself against him by oath, according to the law of Normandy, through his witnesses.

### LXIX. Concerning the same matter

Likewise, if a Frenchman challenges an Englishman to combat over the same matters, the Englishman shall have full permission to defend himself by combat, or by judgment if he prefers. If either of them is infirm and does not wish to fight, or cannot do so, let him seek a lawful defence for himself.

### LXX. Concerning the same matter

If the Frenchman is defeated, he shall pay the king sixty shillings. If the Englishman does not wish to defend himself by combat or by testimony, let him defend himself by the judgment of God.

### LXXI. Concerning forensic procedure

Concerning all matters of outlawry, the king established that an Englishman shall clear himself by judgment. If an Englishman accuses a Frenchman of outlawry and wishes to establish the truth of this charge against him, the Frenchman shall defend himself by combat. If the Englishman does not dare to prove it by combat, the Frenchman shall defend himself by a full oath, without observance of verbal formulas [Note: [Col. 1321C]].

It should be noted that the divisions of the chapters are found nowhere in the manuscript copies, but were deliberately made by us, both to provide, wherever possible, easier access to the chapter headings and to assist the observations of those curious readers who pursue such matters. The numbers, which we carry continuously through the rest of the work, follow no other plan than that they begin with the first chapter of those laws transmitted by Ingulph.

The following passage may also be added to William’s institutions: a passage from John of Salisbury, *Polycraticus*, Book VIII, chapter 7:

“Having assumed the diadem of the kingdom and established peace,” he says, “he sent envoys to foreign nations, so that they might bring back from the distinguished households of every land whatever appeared to them magnificent or extraordinary [alternative reading: ‘carry away’]. Thus everything that could be found of magnificence, or rather of luxury, flowed into the wealthy island, which is almost alone in the world content with its own resources.”

There is also the following passage concerning the royal provision, found in the *Dialogue of the Exchequer*, or *Black Book*, so called by Gervase of Tilbury, as the received opinion holds, written under Henry II and preserved in the fiscal archive, which in legal terminology is called the Receipt of the Exchequer:

“In the earliest condition of the kingdom after the Conquest, the kings were paid from their estates not in weights of gold or silver but only in provisions.
