From these, the necessities of the royal household were supplied for daily use, and those appointed for this purpose knew how much came from each estate. For the pay or gifts of soldiers, however, and for other necessities arising from the pleas and agreements of the kingdom, and from cities or castles where agriculture was not practised, coined money accumulated.

Thus this arrangement continued throughout the whole time of the first King William, down to the time of King Henry his son, so much so that I myself have seen certain men who had seen provisions brought from royal estates to the court at the appointed times. The officials of the royal household also knew from which counties wheat was owed, from which various kinds of meat, and from which fodder for horses or other necessities were due.

After these had been paid according to the established measure for each item, the royal officials reckoned them with the sheriffs in sums of money: for a measure of wheat for the bread of one hundred men, one shilling; for the carcass of a pasture-fed ox, five shillings; for a ram or sheep, four pence; and for the provision of twenty horses, likewise four pence.

Later, when the same king was occupied in suppressing military disturbances in overseas and distant regions, it happened that coined money became extremely necessary to accomplish these tasks. Meanwhile a complaining multitude of peasants flocked to the king’s court, or, what seemed more grievous to them, repeatedly met him as he passed, holding out ploughshares as a sign of agriculture’s decline. They were oppressed by countless burdens because of the provisions that they had to transport from their own homes through many parts of the kingdom.

Moved by their complaints, the king, after taking the advice of the magnates, sent throughout the kingdom those whom he knew to be the more prudent and discerning for this task. Travelling around and examining each estate with their own eyes, they assessed the provisions paid from them and converted them into a sum of money.

From the total sum arising from all the estates in one county, they established that the sheriff of that county should be answerable at the Exchequer, adding that he should pay according to the scale.”

Nor should we omit what Henry Bracton, our ancient jurist, says concerning foreign service: namely, the service rendered by those who, as their subjects’ retainers, hold land on that account and assume the persons of their lords in services rendered to the king, especially military ones. This, he writes, is called royal service because it belongs to the lord king and to no other, and because it was devised in the time of the Conquest.

It is obvious that he was referring to the time of this William. For formerly, as today, his victory was designated by the barbarous word *conquest*. There are several other laws of this kind in Matthew Paris, Henry of Huntingdon, and others; since they are accessible to everyone, we pass them over. In the meantime, however, let readers beware lest they be misled in these matters by Polydore and his followers. Deceived by his own carelessness, he attributes to William as author certain laws that certainly belong to the earlier times of Saxon rule, and others that arose several centuries after William.

Since I have so far overlooked the oath sworn by King William, by which he bound himself generally to observe the ancient enactments of the English, it is not inappropriate to append here Matthew Paris’s words on that subject. He wrote the lives of the abbots of St Albans. In the *Life of Abbot Fretheric*—a vigorous and steadfast man who retained as especially dear to himself the name of King Harold, no less conquered than reigning, and who later, when the southern English resisted, as Archbishop Aldred did among the northern English, offered himself as their leader bravely but unsuccessfully—he describes the differing loyalties of the parties:

“Seeing,” he says, “that the matter concerned their very lives, the English, summoning many men, assembled a numerous and most powerful army. They appointed as their leader the handsome and mighty Edgar, in whose bosom lay all the hope of the English. Hence there arose in England this eulogy:

‘Edgar the Ætheling, England’s darling.’

Among all the English, the most effective leader and promoter was Fretheric, abbot of St Albans, a noble man, formidable in no small degree in works and strength.

The king therefore began greatly to fear for himself lest he should shamefully lose the whole kingdom that he had acquired by the shedding of so much blood, and even be killed. Instructed by the prudent counsel of the archbishop—namely Lanfranc—he began to act more mildly toward the kingdom’s leading men, humbly asking for the things that make for peace. With a serene face he summoned them to peace, though it proved a deceitful peace, as the subsequent course of events made clearer.

The English mentioned above, thinking no evil, came under the governance and leadership of Abbot Fretheric at Berkhamsted. There, after many entreaties, in the presence of Archbishop Lanfranc, the king, for the sake of peace, swore upon all the relics of the church of St Albans, and, touching the holy Gospels, while Abbot Fretheric required the oath, that he would inviolably observe the good and approved ancient laws which the holy and pious kings of England, his predecessors, and especially King Edward, had established. Thus reconciled, they joyfully returned to their homes.”

---

## II. The Council of Lillebonne, held by William, king of the English, with the bishops and nobles of Normandy at Lillebonne, at Pentecost in the year of Christ 1080, in the eighth year of Pope Gregory VII and the twentieth year of Philip, king of the French

*(Labbe, Councils, vol. X, p. 391. An authentic copy of it on parchment exists in the royal archive, which we have seen; it is also found in several manuscripts and in Orderic Vitalis, Book V of his Ecclesiastical History, etc.)*

### HEADINGS OF THE CANONS

I. That the Peace of God be firmly maintained and its violators restrained by the bishops.  
II. That bishops judge incestuous marriages according to the canons.  
III. Concerning the judgment of clerics accused of forbidden intercourse with women.  
IV. That a layman must not possess a share in ecclesiastical revenues, and what service a priest may lawfully render in that connection.  
V. That bishops demand nothing from priests beyond their lawful revenues.  
VI. That archdeacons inspect the clothing, chalices, and books of their priests every year.  
VII. That a bishop shall investigate an offence committed by a priest in the forests of the king or of his barons.  
VIII. That every year the priests offer to the mother church a denarius’ worth of wax from each household.  
IX. That a layman may neither appoint nor remove a priest from a church except with the bishop’s consent.  
X. Concerning cemeteries situated in cities, chapels, boroughs, or enclosed places.  
XI. Concerning village cemeteries.  
XII. Concerning priests whose churches are given to monks or canons.  
XIII. Concerning episcopal rights and customs.

### PREFACE

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1080, in the eighth year of the papacy of Lord Pope Gregory VII, while Philip was reigning as king of the French and William was governing Normandy as king of the English, a council was held at Lillebonne [Julia Bona or Juliobona (Lillebonne)] at Pentecost, in the presence of that same king, with William, archbishop of Rouen, also present, together with bishops and abbots, counts and the other nobles of Normandy. At this council, through the foresight of the most serene King William and on the advice of his aforesaid faithful men, the following matters were defined.

## CANONS

### I

The Peace of God, commonly called the *trevia*, shall be firmly maintained as he himself originally established it, and shall be renewed in every parish with the prescribed excommunications. Those who disdain to observe it or violate it in any way shall be judged by the bishops, who shall administer justice according to the earlier statute.

If anyone is disobedient in this matter to his bishop, the bishop shall demonstrate it to the lord in whose land he resides, and that lord shall subject him to episcopal justice. If the lord also refuses to do this, the king’s sheriff, summoned by the bishop for that purpose, shall carry it out without any excuse being admitted.

### II

Concerning those who take wives from among their own kindred, or the wives of their relatives, the bishops shall enforce canonical justice. For the king tolerates and protects no one in this matter; rather, by assisting the bishops, he admonishes them that the law of God must be firmly observed.

### III

Priests, deacons, subdeacons, and all canons and deans shall have no woman at all. If thereafter anyone is seen to incur this same fault, and has first been accused of it by the bishop’s ministers, he shall clear himself in the bishop’s court.

If, however, one of the parishioners or lords accuses him, the accused shall be granted time to speak with the bishop. If he wishes to clear himself in the same parish in which he serves, he shall clear himself before several parishioners, before the bishop’s ministers, and before the court.

If he cannot clear himself, he shall lose the church irrecoverably. The aforesaid king established this not in order permanently to deprive his bishops of the justice due to them, but because at that time the bishops had done less in this matter than was proper; once he saw their correction, he would restore to them for their good conduct what he had then temporarily taken from them as a penalty for the offence.

### IV

No layman shall have any share in the revenues of an altar, in burial fees, or in a third part of the tithe, nor shall he receive money in any way for the sale or grant of these things.

Nor shall the priest render service in this matter unless he carries his lord’s message, so that he returns to the church on the same day. He may travel through Normandy alone, carrying his lord’s provisions; if the lord wishes, he may go with him. In the meantime the priest shall care for the service of the church.

### V

Priests shall not be compelled by bishops or their ministers, by force or threats, to give anything beyond the bishop’s lawful revenues. No monetary penalty shall be demanded from them on account of their women.

### VI

Archdeacons shall inspect once a year throughout their archdeaconries the clothing, chalices, and books of their subordinate priests, but only at three places designated by the bishop in each archdeaconry, where neighbouring priests shall be summoned to display these things.

When the archdeacon comes to inspect these things, he shall have sustenance from the priests assembled for three days, if necessary, for himself on the fifth [day; the wording is uncertain].

### VII

If a priest has made satisfaction for an offence concerning the king’s forests or those of his barons, the bishop shall receive no compensation from it.

### VIII

Once a year, around Pentecost, priests shall come with their processions to the mother church and shall offer from every household a denarius’ worth of wax, or its equivalent, for lighting the church altar.

Anyone unwilling to do this shall be compelled by the priest, through his ministry, to pay it, without any monetary penalty.

### IX

A layman shall neither appoint nor remove a priest from a church except with the consent of the bishop. Yet, if he is to be rejected, the bishop shall not reject him; and if he is to be rejected, he shall not retain him. [The transmitted wording is internally repetitive.]

### X

In the cemeteries of churches situated in cities, castles, or boroughs, the bishops shall possess whatever they held in the time of Count Robert and King William, with the latter’s consent.

In cemeteries situated on the frontiers, if there is war and some people establish a dwelling there for habitation during the war, and because of the war remain in the churchyard, the bishop shall exact no forfeiture from them except what he would have received before they fled to the churchyard.

When peace has been made, those who fled there because of the war shall be compelled either to leave the churchyard or to submit to episcopal laws. Those who have remained longer in the cemeteries mentioned above shall continue in their ancient peace.

### XI

The churches of the villages shall have as much cemetery land as they possessed in the time of Count Robert, or as much as they had up to this council. In them the bishops shall have those customs which they had in the time of Count Robert or with the consent of King William, unless the bishops have granted some exemption with King William’s permission.

If, after the council, a new church is established within a village, the bishop shall establish a cemetery for it with the consideration of the lords and parishioners of that church. If a new church is built outside a village, it shall have five *perticae* of cemetery land.

### XII

If a church is given to monks, the priest who holds that church shall retain honourably whatever he possessed from it before the monks received it, and all the better because he is associated with holier men.

When he dies or becomes unable to serve in any way, the abbot shall seek a suitable priest and present him to the bishop, either personally or through his messenger. If the bishop is to receive him, let him receive him.

If the priest wishes to live religiously with the monks, he shall ensure that the church, which he entered with episcopal permission, is honourably maintained, both in vestments and books and in all other necessities for serving the church, according to the resources of that church.

If the priest does not wish to live with the monks, the abbot shall give him enough from the goods of the church to enable him both to live properly and to perform the church’s service suitably. If the abbot refuses to do this, the bishop shall compel him appropriately to do so.

The priest shall be rightly subject to his bishop and shall pay the episcopal revenues. Whatever remains beyond this, the abbot shall have for the uses of his monastery. The same rule shall be observed in the churches of canons.

### XIII

Violation of a church or churchyard, as determined above, and offences for which divine service is suspended, shall be compensated to the bishops by payment of money. The same applies to an assault on the road to a church. If anyone, in anger, pursues another into a churchyard or church, the same rule applies.

If a cleric ploughs or builds in a churchyard without episcopal permission, the same rule applies. If a cleric commits rape, theft, assault, wounding, or homicide; undertakes combat without the bishop’s permission; commits *nannum* [an uncertain term in the source]; commits an assault; unjustly seizes anything; or commits arson, the same rule applies, whether the act is committed by his fostered servant or by an inhabitant of the churchyard.

If a cleric commits adultery or incest, the same rule applies. If a priest has made satisfaction for an offence arising from his ministry, the same rule applies. The same applies to priests who have neglected to attend the synod, and to those who have failed to pay the synod-fee and *circada* at the appointed times.

If a cleric abandons his tonsure, the same rule applies. If a monk or nun who lives without a rule abandons the religious habit, the same rule applies. If a priest excommunicates violators of the Peace of God or robbers without the bishop’s permission, the same rule applies.

If someone having an estray, commonly called *weidif*, comes to the court of a priest or cleric living in the churchyard, or to the alms of that church, it shall be treated as though it were in the bishop’s churchyard. If anything is left through contempt in the house of a priest or cleric, in the churchyard of a priest, or in the hands of their fostered servant, it shall belong to the bishop. If anything is found or left in a church or churchyard, it shall belong to the bishop.

If anyone assaults, strikes, captures, or kills a priest, monk, or nun, or burns their houses in the churchyard, he shall make the same compensation. If anyone commits adultery or incest, or has intercourse with his godmother, co-mother (*commater*), or goddaughter, he shall make the same compensation.

If anyone abandons his wife, or a woman abandons her husband, without the bishop’s judgment, the same rule applies. Those who consult the dead or practise sorcery shall make the same compensation. Whoever, while denying the crime charged against him, is convicted by the judgment of iron—except in a matter concerning the Peace of God—shall make the same compensation. Whoever resists justice and allows himself to be excommunicated shall make the same compensation.

The crimes of parishioners that pertain to the bishop shall, wherever this has been customary, be examined by episcopal judgment. If an objection is made to the judgment, it shall be settled before the bishop. If the judgment of theft has been given, it shall be concluded before the mother church. If a plain legal proceeding is required, it shall take place where the plea was first held.

In the bishop’s parish no one shall dare to preach without his permission.

Whoever falls into the aforesaid offences, if he voluntarily comes to penance, shall be assigned penance according to the nature of his crime, and no money shall be demanded from him in any way.

If a layman commits rape in the churchyard, he shall make compensation to the bishop. If he commits it elsewhere, whatever the circumstances, the bishop shall receive nothing.

The bishops shall have these customs in those places where they have possessed them until now, in the time of Count Robert or by the grant of King William. Places that were exempt shall retain the exemption which they have firmly held up to this time.

In all these rights and customs the king reserves to himself whatever he has hitherto possessed.

If a priest contradicts his lord’s judgment in an ecclesiastical matter and unjustly causes him trouble by making him go to the bishop’s court, he shall pay ten shillings in compensation to his lord.

If the bishops can demonstrate in the king’s court that they possessed anything not written here in the time of Count Robert or by the grant of King William, the king shall not take it from them, provided only that they do not seize it in any way until they demonstrate in his court that they ought to possess it.

Likewise, on account of this document the king takes nothing from laymen that they can demonstrate in the king’s court the bishops ought not to possess. They shall not, however, dispossess the bishops of it until it has been demonstrated in the king’s court that the bishops ought not to possess it.

In the manuscript copy of the Council of Lillebonne, a synodal decree concerning the peace commonly called the Peace of God is placed before it. This peace begins on Wednesday and was established by William the Elder, king of the English and duke of the Normans, and by the bishops of Normandy.

“Dearest brothers in the Lord, concerning the peace commonly called the Peace of God, which begins at sunset on Wednesday and ends at sunrise on Monday, you must henceforth observe the following with the readiest spirit.

No man or woman shall assault, wound, or kill any man or woman anywhere; nor shall anyone assault, plunder, seize, or burn any castle, borough, or village during this period of four days and five nights, by any device, force, or fraud.

If anyone—God forbid—violates it by failing to observe what we command, unless he performs penance in exile for thirty years and, before leaving the bishopric, makes satisfaction for whatever he has done against the peace, we excommunicate him from the Lord God, and let him be separated from all Christendom.

Whoever knowingly communicates with him in any matter, gives him counsel or assistance, or has any conversation with him except so that he may come to penance and, as stated, leave the bishop, shall likewise be excommunicated until he makes satisfaction.

If that most wretched violator of the holy peace, after receiving thirty years of penance, dies in the place of his exile, no Christian shall presume to visit him, remove his body from the place where it lies, or take anything from his goods or possessions.

Moreover, brothers, you shall observe this peace and Peace of God concerning lands and animals, and also concerning all things that can be possessed.

If anyone takes another person’s animal, or even an obol or garment, during this peace, he shall be excommunicated until he makes satisfaction. If he wishes to make satisfaction, he must first return what he stole, or the full value of what he stole. Thereafter he shall do penance for seven years within the bishop’s jurisdiction.

If he dies before making satisfaction and undertaking penance, he shall not be buried, nor shall he be moved from the place where he died, unless his relatives make satisfaction on his behalf to the person whom he injured.

For the rest, during this peace no one except the king or the count of this land shall conduct a cavalry expedition or make war. Whoever is engaged in the king’s cavalry expedition or war shall take from this bishopric no more than what is necessary for himself and his horses to live.

Merchants and all men who pass through your lands from other regions shall have peace from you.

You shall also observe this Peace of God from the beginning of the Lord’s Advent until the octave of Epiphany, from the beginning of Lent until the octave of Easter, and from the beginning of Rogation days until the octave of Pentecost, throughout all the days.

Those who observe this peace shall be blessed with prayers offered for them; those who violate it or grant permission to its violators shall be cursed.

If anyone says that he unknowingly violated the peace, he must first swear an oath and carry the hot iron of judgment, and then do penance for seven years.”

---

## III. The ancient customs and laws of the Normans, confirmed at the council held at Lillebonne in 1080

*(Marten, Anecdota, vol. IV, col. 117, from a manuscript of St Michael in Periculo Maris.)*

### I

This is the law which King William, who acquired the kingdom of England, held in Normandy. It is written here as Count Robert of Normandy and his son and heir, William, king of England, caused it to be recalled and written down through their bishops and barons on the same day, the fifteenth day before the Kalends of August.

This is the law of the lord of Normandy: in his court, while going to court, or while returning from court, no man had *garda* against his enemy. If anyone committed an offence against his enemy on the road to court or in the court itself, knowing that the person against whom he acted was going to or returning from court, and this was proved against him, the lord of Normandy received his money and his body for the administration of justice, and he lost his land, so that neither he nor any of his relatives could claim it.

If he could prove that he had not done this knowingly, he was placed at the mercy of the lord of Normandy in respect of a monetary payment, without loss of land.

### II

On the army’s route, in the army itself, during the eight days before the departure of the appointed army, and during the eight days after the army, if anyone committed an offence, the lord of Normandy had the same jurisdiction over that offence as over an offence committed in his court.

During the aforesaid periods of the army no one was permitted to take a *vammum* [a term of uncertain meaning in the source]. If anyone took one, he was to make monetary compensation at the mercy of the lord of Normandy.

If, in the army, in the court, or on the road to the court or army, a disturbance occurred that had not arisen from a previous quarrel, and someone was wounded or killed in it, the person through whose fault this happened was to make compensation according to the measure of the offence.

### III

No one in Normandy was permitted to make a ditch in level ground unless it was such that he could throw the earth upward from its bottom without a stool. Nor was anyone permitted there to construct a palisade except in a single line, and that without battlements or projecting galleries.

On a rock or an island no one was permitted to build a fortification, and no one was permitted to build a castle in Normandy.

### IV

No one in Normandy was permitted, on account of a land dispute, to burn a house or mill, commit any devastation, or seize plunder.

### V

No one in Normandy was permitted to deny the lord of Normandy the fortification of his castle. If the lord wished to hold it in his own hand, no one could oppose him.

If the lord of Normandy wished to take as a hostage for the keeping of faith the son, brother, or nephew of one of his barons who was not a knight, no one could oppose him.

### VI

No one was permitted in Normandy to assault a man or lay an ambush in the forests of the lord himself.

### VII

No one was permitted, while pursuing an enemy or taking a *vammum*, to carry a banner or coat of mail, blow a horn, or send a little bell after the ambush had ended. Nor was anyone permitted to condemn a man by mutilating his limbs without judgment, unless he had been found in an act and offence for which he ought to lose a limb and had lost it there on the spot, and unless this was done by judgment of the lord of Normandy’s court in matters belonging to him, or by judgment of the barons’ court in matters belonging to the barons.

### VIII

No one in Normandy was permitted to commit *haufare*, arson, the abduction of a woman, or the taking of a *vammum* without a complaint being brought before the person to whom the complaint ought to be brought.

If these acts were committed, the lord of Normandy received whatever belonged to him in those places where he ought to have received it, and the barons received whatever belonged to them in those places where they ought to have received it.

### IX

No one in Normandy was permitted to disturb a merchant on account of any earlier offence. If anyone did so, he was placed at the mercy of the lord of Normandy in respect of his person.

### X

No one in Normandy was permitted to mint money outside the mints of Rouen and Bayeux, and there it was to be half silver and of the proper weight, namely eight shillings to the *helmarc*.

If anyone minted money elsewhere, or minted false money there, he was placed at the mercy of the lord of Normandy in respect of his person. If anyone minted money outside the aforesaid mints, or caused false money to be minted in those mints, he forfeited his land and money.

### XI

The matters written above have been included because they are the more necessary. Much remains outside this writing concerning the law of coinage and the other laws of Normandy; but because it is not written, [the following clause is syntactically defective in the transmitted text]: that the aforesaid Count Robert and William, concerning the law which their father had held, nor the barons concerning what they had possessed in the time of King William. No one was permitted, because of war, to capture or ransom a man, or to carry away money from a battle or conflict, or to lead away weapons or a horse.

---

## IV. Here begin the laws of Saint Edward the king, which he held in England and which William, his heir and kinsman, confirmed

### HEADINGS OF THE ECCLESIASTICAL LAWS
## I. Of clerics and their possessions. II. Of the times and days of the king’s peace. III. Of the justice of holy Church. IV. Of all tenants of the Church. V. Of accused persons fleeing to a church. VI. Of violation of the peace of the Church. VII. Of tithes owed to the Church from sheep and piglets. VIII. Of bees and many other small tithes. IX. Of those who have been judged by the king’s justice through trial by iron or water. X. Of Saint Peter’s penny, which in English is called Romescot. [Col. 1331D] XI. What danegeld is, and on what occasion it was established. XII. Of the many forms of the king’s peace, etc. Also of the manbota of the archbishop, bishop, etc. XIII. Of treasures hidden and found in the earth. XIV. What the king’s office is, and an example concerning Charles and Pippin, his brother [read: son]. XV. Of barons who have their own courts and customs. XVI. Of sacha. XVII. Of soca. XVIII. Of thol. XIX. Of theam. XX. Of infangthefe. XXI. Of the Jews. XXII. The king’s decree concerning usurers.

## PREFACE

[Col. 1332C]

After the acquisition of England, in the fourth year of his reign, King William, with the advice of his barons, caused the noble English, the wise, and those learned in their law to be summoned throughout all the counties of England, so that he might hear from them their laws, rights, and customs. Accordingly, twelve men were chosen from each county of the whole country. First, they confirmed before the king by oath that, as far as they could, proceeding along the straight path, turning neither to the right nor to the left, they would disclose the enactments of their laws and customs, omitting nothing, adding nothing, and changing nothing through deception. Beginning, therefore, with the laws of holy Mother Church, since through her the king and the kingdom possess a firm foundation on which to stand, they proclaimed her laws, liberties, and peace, saying:

### I

Every cleric, and also every scholar, and all their goods and possessions, wherever they may be, shall have the peace of God and of holy Church.

### II

From Advent of the Lord until the octave of Epiphany, the peace of God and of holy Church shall prevail throughout the entire kingdom. Likewise from Septuagesima until the octave of Easter. Also from the Ascension of the Lord until the octave of Pentecost. Also on all the days of the Ember seasons. Also on every Saturday from the ninth hour, and throughout the following day, until Monday. Also on the vigils of Saint Mary, Saint Michael, Saint John the Baptist, [Col. 1333A] all the apostles, and the saints whose solemnities are announced by priests on Sundays, and of All Saints on the Kalends of November: always from the ninth hour of the vigils and throughout the following solemnity. Also in parishes where the day of dedication is observed. Also in parishes of churches where the proper feast of a saint is celebrated.

And if anyone comes devoutly for the celebration of a saint, let him have peace while going, staying, and returning. Likewise, all Christians going to church for the sake of prayer shall have peace while going and returning. Similarly, those coming to dedications, synods, or chapters, whether they have been summoned or have business of their own to conduct, shall have complete peace.

Even if an excommunicated person has fled to a bishop for the purpose of being absolved, [Col. 1333B] once absolved, he shall have the peace of God and of holy Church while going and returning. If anyone commits an offense against him, the bishop shall administer justice in the matter. Nevertheless, if some arrogant person refuses to make amends according to the bishop’s justice, the bishop shall inform the king. The king, however, shall constrain the wrongdoer to make amends to the person against whom he has offended—first to the bishop, then to himself—and thus there will be two swords, and one sword will aid the other.

### III

Wherever the king’s justice, or anyone else’s justice, holds pleas, if a messenger of the bishop appears there, presenting a case of holy Church, that case shall first be determined. For it is just that God be honored everywhere before all else.

### IV

Whoever holds anything from a church, or has a dwelling on church land, shall not be compelled to plead outside the ecclesiastical court, even if he has committed an offense—unless, God forbid, justice has failed in the ecclesiastical court.

### V

Wherever an accused or guilty person has fled to a church for refuge, from the moment he has reached the churchyard he shall in no way be apprehended by any pursuer, except by the bishop or his ministers. If, while fleeing, he has entered the priest’s house or court, he shall have the same security and peace there as at the church, provided that the priest’s house and court stand on church land.

If he is a thief or robber, he shall return what he wrongfully took, if it is at hand. If he has utterly destroyed it but possesses his own property from which he can make restitution, he shall restore it in full to the person whom he injured. If a thief has acted in this manner according to his custom and has repeatedly escaped by chance to a church and to priests’ houses, then, after making restitution of what he took, he shall forswear the province and shall not return. If he should return, no one may presume to give him lodging unless permission has been granted by the king.

### VI

If anyone violently violates the peace of holy Church, the matter belongs to the justice of the bishops. If the guilty person evades or arrogantly despises their sentence, a complaint concerning him shall be brought to the king after forty days. The king’s justice shall bind him by surety and pledges, if he can provide them, until he first satisfies God and afterward the king and the Church.

If he cannot be found within thirty-one days, either through friends or acquaintances or through the king’s justice, the king shall outlaw him by the word of his mouth. If he is afterward found and can be detained, he shall be returned alive—or his head, if he resists. For from the day of his outlawry he bears a wolf’s head, which in English is called *Wulfesheofod*. This is the common and general law concerning all outlaws.

### VII

Of every crop, a tenth sheaf is owed to God and must therefore be rendered. If anyone has a herd of mares, he shall render every tenth foal; whoever has only one or two mares shall render one penny for each foal. Likewise, whoever has several cows shall render the tenth calf; whoever has one or two shall render one obol for each calf.

Whoever makes cheese shall give a tenth to God; if he does not make cheese, he shall give milk on the tenth day. Likewise: every tenth lamb, tenth fleece, tenth cheese, tenth quantity of butter, and tenth piglet.

### VIII

Likewise, a tenth of the profit from bees is owed. Moreover, from woodland, meadow, waters, mills, parks, fishponds, fisheries, thickets, gardens, trading enterprises, and all things which the lord gives, a tenth part must be rendered to him who gives the nine parts together with the tenth.

Whoever withholds it shall, through the justice of the bishop and, if necessary, of the king, be compelled to render it. For blessed Augustine preached and taught these things, and they were granted by the king, the barons, and the people. But afterward, through the devil’s instigation, many withheld it, and wealthy, negligent priests did not trouble themselves to undertake the labor of pursuing such payments, since they already possessed enough for the necessities of life. For in many places there are now three or four churches where at that time there was only one, and thus the tithes began to diminish.

### IX

On the day when the judgment is to be held, the bishop’s minister shall come there with his clerics, and likewise the king’s justice with the lawful men of that province, [Col. 1334D] so that they may see and hear and ensure that everything is done equally.

Those whom the Lord, in his mercy and not through their merits, wishes to save shall remain undisturbed and depart freely. Those whom the wickedness of their offense, and not the Lord, has condemned, the king’s justice shall administer justice concerning them.

The barons who have their own court over their own men shall see to it that they act toward them in such a way that they incur no guilt before God and do not offend the king. If a plea concerning the men of other barons arises in their courts, the king’s justice shall be present at the plea, since without it the plea may not be concluded.

If certain barons do not possess judicial authority, the matter shall be determined in the Hundred where the plea was held, at the nearest church where the king’s judgment will be given, without prejudice to the rights of those barons.

### X

[Col. 1335A]

Everyone who has thirty pennies’ worth of living property in his house, of his own, shall by English law give Saint Peter’s penny; and by Danish law, half a mark.

This penny must be announced on the solemnity of the apostles Peter and Paul and collected for the feast called *Ad Vincula*, so that it is not withheld beyond that day. If anyone withholds it, a complaint shall be brought to the king’s justice, because this penny is the king’s alms. The justice shall compel the penny to be rendered, together with the forfeiture owed to the bishop and the king.

If anyone has several houses, he shall render the penny from the one in which he resides on the feast of the apostles Peter and Paul.

### XI

[Col. 1335B] [Note: [Col. 1335D] This chapter appears to have been added in the time of Henry II.]

The payment of danegeld was first established on account of pirates, for they were troubling the country and devoted themselves as much as they could to its devastation. To restrain their insolence, it was established that danegeld should be paid annually—namely, twelve pennies from each hide throughout the country—to hire those who would oppose and resist the pirates’ incursions.

The whole Church, and also every piece of land that belonged to the Church in its own lordship, wherever it lay, was free and exempt from this danegeld, paying nothing at all in such a levy, because people trusted more in the prayers of the Church than in the defenses of arms.

The Church of England maintained this liberty until the time of the younger King William, who was called Rufus. When he sought assistance from the barons of England to retain Normandy against his brother Robert, surnamed Curthose, who had departed for Jerusalem, it was granted to him—not established or confirmed as law, but for this necessity—that four shillings be given to him from each hide, with the Church not excepted.

When the tax was being collected, holy Church proclaimed her claim to liberty, but achieved nothing.

### XII

The king’s peace has many forms. There is the peace granted by his own hand, which the English call *cynninger honde sealde grith*. Another is that on the day on which he was first crowned, which lasts eight days. At Christmas, eight days; at Easter, eight days; at Pentecost, eight days; and so forth below.

*Manbota*—that is, compensation to be paid to the lord for his man who has been killed—is, by English law, three marks to the king and the archbishop for their own men; but twenty shillings to the bishop of the same county, the sheriff, and the king’s steward; and ten shillings to the other barons, and so forth.

### XIII

Treasures found in the earth belong to the king, unless they are found in a church or cemetery. Even if found there, the gold belongs to the king and half the silver; the other half belongs to the church where it was found, whatever that church may be, rich or poor.

### XIV

The king, who is the vicar of the highest King, has been appointed for this purpose: to revere, govern, and defend the earthly kingdom, the people of the Lord, and above all his holy Church; to remove and destroy evildoers from it and utterly abolish them.

If he does not do this, the name of king will not remain in him; indeed, as Pope John testifies, he loses the name of king. For this reason Pippin and his son Charles, not yet kings but princes under a foolish king of the Franks, wrote to him, asking whether the kings of the Franks ought to continue in that condition, content with the royal name alone.

The answer given to them was that those deserve to be called kings who vigilantly [Col. 1336B] defend and govern the Church of God and his people, imitating the Psalmist-king who says: “He who acts proudly shall not dwell in the midst of my house,” etc. (Psalm C).

### XV

[Note: [Col. 1335D] The material that follows in Lambard under this chapter, “Of the king’s office and of the law and appurtenances of the crown of the kingdom of Britain,” together with Pope Eleutherus’s letter to King Lucius, is found neither in our manuscript nor in Hoveden.]

Archbishops, bishops, earls, barons, and all who possess sacha, soca, thol, theam, and infangthefe shall also have under their *friborg* their own knights and personal servants—namely, stewards, butlers, chamberlains, cooks, and bakers. They shall likewise have their own squires and other servants under their *friborg*.

If any of these persons commits an offense and the complaint of the neighbors against them arises, they shall hold them to justice in their own court—I mean those who possess sacha, soca, thol, theam, and infangthefe.

### XVI

*Sacha* is this: if anyone accuses another by name of something, and the accused denies it, the forfeiture arising from the proof or denial shall belong to him.

### XVII

*Soca* is this: if anyone seeks anything on his land, even a theft, the justice concerning it belongs to him if it is found—or not.

### XVIII

*Thol*, which we call toll, means that he has the liberty to sell and buy on his own land.

### XIX

*Theam* means that if someone claims an object against another, and the person against whom it is claimed cannot produce his warrantor, the forfeiture shall belong to him, and likewise justice shall be done against the claimant if he fails.

### XX

Everyone who has sacha and soca, thol and theam, and infangthefe—namely, the aforesaid customs—possesses the justice concerning a thief, of his own man, if he is captured on his land.

Those who do not possess these customs shall do justice before the king’s justice in Hundreds, wapentakes, or shires.

### XXI

It must also be known that all Jews, wherever they are in the kingdom, must be under the protection and defense of the king. None of them may submit himself to any rich man without the king’s permission. For the Jews, and all that belongs to them, are the king’s. If anyone detains them or their money, the king may recover it, if he wishes, as his own property.

### XXII

[Col. 1338A]

King Edward also prohibited usurers, so that none would remain anywhere in his entire kingdom. If anyone were convicted of exacting interest, he would lose all his own property and afterward be treated as an outlaw.

That king asserted that he had heard in the court of the king of the Franks, while he was staying there, that usury is the principal root of all vices.

# OTHER LAWS OF KING EDWARD WRITTEN IN THE NORMAN IDIOM

[Col. 1337]

## TITLES OF THE ECCLESIASTICAL LAWS

[Col. 1337A]

I. Of the peace of holy Church and the right of asylum granted to it. II. Of one who breaks into a monastery, church, or house. [Col. 1338A] III. Of paying Saint Peter’s penny, or Romescot. IV. Of those refusing to pay Saint Peter’s penny. V. Of the goods of intestate persons.

## PREFACE

[Note: [Col. 1337] The Latin and French versions of the following text are printed in parallel in Migne.]

[Col. 1337]

[Col. 1337B] These are the laws and customs that King William grants to all the people of England after the conquest of the land: the very same ones that King Edward, his kinsman, maintained before him.

[Col. 1338B] These are the laws and customs that King William granted to the whole people of England after the acquisition of the land—namely, the very same laws that King Edward, his kinsman, kept before him.

## ECCLESIASTICAL LAWS

[Col. 1337]

### I

[Col. 1337B]

That is to say: Peace to holy Church, whatever offense a person may have committed at this time; and if he can come to holy Church, let him have peace of life and limb.

If anyone lays hands upon him who has sought Mother Church—whether it is a bishop’s church, an abbey, or a religious church—let him restore what he has taken, and pay a forfeiture of one hundred shillings; to the mother church of the parish, twenty shillings; and to a chapel, ten shillings. Whoever breaks the king’s peace in Mercian law shall make amends with one hundred shillings, and likewise for *heinfare* and for a premeditated ambush.

### II

If anyone is accused of breaking into a monastery, church, or chamber, and has not previously been defamed, let him deny it with twelve lawful men, whom they call his “twelfth hand.” If he is accused a second time, let him deny it with three times that number—namely, forty-eight [read: thirty-six] lawful men, whom they call his “thirty-sixth hand.”

If he cannot have these men, let him go to the *ivise* threefold, as he ought to have gone to the threefold oath. [Note: [Col. 1337D] A type of ordeal; this is conjectural.] If afterward he makes composition for theft, let him go to the judgment of water.

The archbishop shall have forty shillings from the forfeiture, according to Mercian law; the bishop twenty shillings; the earl twenty shillings; the baron ten shillings; and the villein forty pennies.

### III

A free man who has thirty pennies’ worth of livestock in the fields must give Saint Peter’s penny. For the four pennies which the lord gives, his bordars, his *bonerii*, and his servants shall be quit.

A burgess who possesses in his own property goods worth half a mark must give Saint Peter’s penny. Whoever is free under Danish law and possesses field livestock worth half a mark of silver must give Saint Peter’s penny; and by the penny that the lord gives, those who live in his demesne shall be quit.

### IV

Whoever refuses Saint Peter’s penny shall render it through the justice of holy Church, and pay a forfeiture of thirty pennies; the parallel Latin text reads twenty pennies. If he is brought before the king’s justice, he shall pay thirty pennies to the bishop and forty shillings to the king.

### V

If a man dies without making a disposition, his children shall divide the inheritance equally among themselves.

### V. Ancient statutes in which the assembly of the whole kingdom of England is organized

*(In Acherius, Spicilegium, vol. XII, p. 557.)*

# THE METHOD OF HOLDING PARLIAMENT

[Col. 1339B]

Here is described the manner in which the parliament of the king of England and of his Englishmen was held in the time of King Edward [III], son of King Ethelred. This procedure was recited by the wisest men of the kingdom before William, duke of Normandy and the Conqueror, and king of England; the Conqueror himself ordered it and approved it, and it was used in his time and also in the times of his successors, the kings of England.

## CHAPTER I. The summons to parliament

The summons to parliament must precede the first day of parliament by forty days.

All archbishops, abbots, priors, and other major clerics who hold by county or barony by reason of such tenure must be summoned and must come to parliament; no lesser clerics need come unless their presence and attendance are required for some reason other than their tenures—for example, if they are needed for the king’s council, or if their presence is judged necessary or useful to parliament.

The king must provide such persons with their costs and expenses for coming to and remaining at parliament. Lesser clerics of this kind ought not to be summoned to parliament; instead, the king should send such experts his writs, asking them to attend his parliament.

The king also used to send his summonses to archbishops, bishops, and other exempt persons, such as abbots, priors, deans, and other ecclesiastical persons who possessed jurisdictions by virtue of such exemptions and privileges separately, ordering them to cause two skilled and suitable procurators to be elected for each deanery and archdeaconry of England, from those deaneries and archdeaconries, to come and attend parliament, undertake its business, plead, and do the same things that all and each of the persons of those deaneries and archdeaconries would do if they were personally present there.

Such procurators were to come with their warrants, sealed with the duplicated seals of their superiors, stating that the clerics had been sent for this procuratorship. One of these letters was to be delivered to the clerks of parliament for enrollment, and the other was to remain with the procurators. Thus the whole clergy was to be summoned to parliament under these two categories.

## CHAPTER II. Of laymen

All earls and barons, and their peers, must likewise be summoned and must come—namely, those who possess lands and revenues worth a whole county or barony: twenty knights’ fees, each fee being reckoned at twenty pounds, making four hundred pounds in all; or worth a whole barony, namely thirteen fees and one-third of a knight’s fee, each fee being reckoned at twenty pounds, making four hundred marks.

No lesser laymen need be summoned or come to parliament by reason of their tenures, unless their presence is useful or necessary to parliament for other reasons. In that event, they shall be treated as was stated concerning lesser clerics, who are not required to come to parliament by reason of their tenures.

## CHAPTER III. Of the barons of the ports

The king must send his writs to the Warden of the Cinque Ports, ordering him to cause two suitable and skilled barons to be elected from each port, by that port, to come and attend his parliament, to answer, undertake business, plead [perhaps: make an allowance], and do the same things that their barony would do if each and every one of those barons were personally present there.

Such port barons must come with their warrants, sealed with the duplicated common seals of their ports, stating that they had been duly elected, appointed, and sent for those baronies. One of these warrants was to be delivered to the clerks of parliament, and the other was to remain with the barons.

When such port barons had obtained permission to withdraw from parliament, they used to receive a writ under the great seal of the Warden of the Cinque Ports, ordering him to cause their reasonable costs and expenses to be paid from the community of that port, from the first day on which they set out toward parliament until the day on which they returned home.

The writ expressly stated the length of their stay at parliament, the day on which they had arrived, and the day on which they had been licensed to return. Sometimes the writ also specified how much such barons were to receive per day from those communities—some more, some less, according to the persons’ abilities, standing, and circumstances. It was not customary to assign more than twenty shillings per day for two barons, taking into account their stay, labor, and expenses.

Nor were such expenses ordinarily fixed by the court for persons elected and sent on behalf of communities, unless the persons themselves were honorable and conducted themselves well in parliament.

## CHAPTER IV. Of knights

The king likewise used to send his writs to all the sheriffs of England, ordering each of them to cause two suitable, honorable, and skilled knights to be elected by his county, to come to his parliament in the same manner as was stated concerning the barons of the ports, and with warrants in the same manner.

For the expenses of two knights from one county, it was not customary to assign more than one mark per day.

## CHAPTER V. Of citizens

In the same way, orders used to be sent to the mayor and sheriffs of London, and to the mayor and bailiffs—or the mayor and citizens—of York, and of the other cities, that they should elect, for the county of their city, two suitable, honorable, and skilled citizens to come and attend parliament, in the same manner as was stated concerning the barons of the Cinque Ports and the knights of the counties.

The citizens used to be peers and equals of the knights of the counties in expenses for coming, remaining, and returning.

## CHAPTER VI. Of burgesses

In the same way, orders used to be, and ought to be, sent to the bailiffs and good men of the boroughs, that they should elect from among themselves and on their own behalf two suitable, honorable, and skilled burgesses to come and attend parliament, in the same manner as was stated concerning the citizens.

Two burgesses were not accustomed to receive more than ten shillings per day for their expenses, and sometimes no more than half a mark. The amount was assessed by the court according to the size and power of the borough and according to the respectability of the persons sent.

## CHAPTER VII. Of the principal clerks of parliament

[Col. 1342A]

The two principal clerks of parliament sat in the midst of the justices, enrolling all the pleas and business of parliament.

It must be understood that these two clerks were subject to no justices; there was no justice of England in parliament, and they did not possess records in parliament in their own right, except insofar as a new authority had been assigned or granted to them in parliament by the king and the peers of parliament—for example, when they were assigned with other members of parliament to hear and determine various petitions and complaints corrected [perhaps: presented] in parliament.

These two clerks were immediately subject to the king and his parliament in common, unless one or two justices were assigned to them to examine and correct their enrollments. When peers of parliament were assigned to hear and examine particular petitions by themselves, then, once they were unanimous and in agreement in the judgments they were to render on those petitions, they would recite them, and, after proceedings had been held concerning them, deliver judgment in full parliament.

Thus these two clerks were principally to enroll all pleas and all judgments in the principal parliament roll, and to deliver those rolls to the king’s treasurer before parliament was dismissed. In every way, therefore, the rolls were to be in the treasury before parliament departed, while the clerks were to retain a transcript or counter-roll if they wished to have one.

Unless these two clerks held another office with the king and received fees from him sufficient to live honorably, they were to receive from the king one mark per day, together with their expenses, in equal portions. If they were at the lord king’s table, they were to receive, in addition to their table, half a mark per day, in equal portions, throughout parliament.

## CHAPTER VIII. Of the five clerks

The king shall appoint five skilled and approved clerks: the first shall minister to and serve the bishops; the second, the procurators of the clergy; the third, the earls and barons; the fourth, the knights of the counties; and the fifth, the citizens and burgesses.

Unless one of them is with the king and receives from him fees and wages sufficient to live honorably, he shall receive from the king two shillings per day. If he is at the lord king’s table, he shall receive twelve pennies per day.

These clerks shall write down their questions and the answers they make to the king and parliament. They shall attend their councils wherever they wish to have them, and whenever they are free they shall assist the principal clerks in enrolling.

## CHAPTER IX. Of cases and judgments of parliament

When a dispute, doubt, or difficult case concerning peace or war arises in the kingdom or outside it, that case shall be set out and recited in writing in full parliament. It shall be discussed and debated there among the peers of parliament.

If necessary, the king—or, on the king’s behalf, if the king is not present—shall order each rank of peers to consider the case separately. Each rank shall deliver the case in writing to its own clerk and have it recited before them at a specified place, so that they may order and consider among themselves how the matter can best and most justly be dealt with, both on behalf of the king and in their own persons, and also on behalf of those whose persons they represent.

They shall wish to answer before God and shall submit their answers and opinions in writing. After all their answers, opinions, counsels, and advice on both sides have been heard, proceedings shall follow according to the better and sounder counsel.

Where at least the greater part of parliament agrees—whether discord among them, the king, and certain magnates, or perhaps among the magnates themselves, has weakened the peace of the kingdom, the people, or the country; whether it appears to the king and his council expedient that the matter be considered and corrected through the deliberation of all the peers of his kingdom; whether the king and kingdom are troubled by war; or whether a difficult case arises before the chancellor of England or a difficult judgment must be rendered before a justice, and in similar matters—

if, in such deliberations, all or at least the greater part cannot reach agreement, then the earl steward, the earl constable, and the earl marshal, or two of them, shall choose twenty-five persons from all the peers of the kingdom: two bishops, three procurators for the whole clergy, two earls, three barons, five knights of the counties, and five citizens and burgesses. These make twenty-five.

Those twenty-five may choose twelve from among themselves and agree upon them; those twelve may choose six and agree upon them; those six may then choose three and agree upon them. Those three may not reduce the number further unless they obtain permission from the lord king.

If the king consents, the three may reduce the number to two, and of those two one may defer to the other [perhaps: agree with the other]. Thus their ordinance will finally stand over the whole parliament. In this way, by descending from twenty-five persons to one alone, unless a larger number can agree and make an ordinance, the single person, as stated, shall order matters on behalf of all, since he cannot disagree with himself.

This remains subject to the lord king and his council, who may, after such ordinances have been written, examine and amend them if they know how and wish to do so. Everything must be done there, then, in full parliament and with the consent of parliament, not behind parliament’s back.

## CHAPTER X. Of the business of parliament

The business for which parliament exists must be deliberated according to the parliament calendar and according to the order of the petitions delivered and *enfilées*—that is, filed or strung together—without regard to anyone’s person. Whoever proposed a matter first shall act first.

All the business of parliament must be recalled in the parliament calendar in the following order:

1. War, if there is war, and other business touching the persons of the king and queen and their children.

2. The common business of the kingdom, and laws to be established against defects in the original, judicial, and executive laws.

After judgments have been rendered, these are the most general matters of business.

3. Particular matters, according to the order of the petitions filed, as stated above.

## CHAPTER XI. Of the days and hours for parliament

Parliament must not be held on Sundays. It may be held on all other days except three: All Saints’ Day, All Souls’ Day, and the Nativity of Saint John the Baptist.

Each day it must begin in the middle of the first hour, at which hour the king is required to attend parliament, [Col. 1344B] and all the peers of parliament must be kept in a private place.

On feast days parliament must begin at the first hour because of divine service.

## CHAPTER XII. Of the ranks of the peers
The king is the head, beginning, and end of Parliament, and therefore has no peer in his degree; thus the first degree consists solely of the king. The second degree consists of archbishops, bishops, abbots, and priors holding by barony. The third degree consists of the representatives of the clergy. The fourth consists of earls, barons, and other magnates and nobles holding lands worth an earldom or barony, as stated above in the title concerning laymen. The fifth consists of the knights of the counties. The sixth consists of citizens and burgesses. Thus Parliament consists of six degrees. But it should be understood that, even if someone belonging to one of these degrees is absent after the king, provided that all have been forewarned by a reasonable summons to Parliament, it is nevertheless considered full.

### CHAPTER XIII. Concerning the manner of Parliament

Having first shown in what form, and how far in advance, a summons to Parliament ought to be issued to each person, and who ought to come by summons and who ought not, it must secondly be stated who, by reason of their offices, ought to come and are bound to attend throughout the whole Parliament without a summons.

It should therefore be noted that the two principal clerks of Parliament—the clerks appointed by the king and his council—and the other secondary clerks, concerning whom and whose offices more will be said later; and the chief crier of England with his under-criers; and the chief usher of England—for these two offices, namely the office of crier and that of usher, formerly belonged to one and the same person—are bound to attend on the first day.

The chancellor of England, the treasurer, the chamberlain, and the barons of the Exchequer; the justices; all the king’s clerks and knights; together with the serjeants at the king’s pleas who are of the king’s council, are bound to attend on the second day, unless they have reasonable excuses preventing their attendance. In that case they must send proper excuses.

### CHAPTER XIV. Concerning the opening of Parliament

The lord king shall sit in the middle of the greater bench and is bound to attend personally during the first six days of Parliament. The chancellor, the treasurer, the barons of the Exchequer, and the justices used to record the defaults committed in Parliament in the following order.

On the first day the burgesses and citizens of all England shall be summoned. If they do not come on that day, the burgess shall be amerced at one hundred marks, and the city at one hundred pounds.

On the second day the knights of the counties of all England shall be summoned. If they do not come on that day, the county from which they come shall be amerced at one hundred pounds.

On the third day of Parliament the barons of the Cinque Ports shall be summoned; afterward the barons, and afterward the earls. If the barons of the Cinque Ports do not come, that barony shall be amerced at one hundred marks, and an earl at one hundred pounds. The same shall be done with those who are peers of earls and barons, namely those who possess lands and revenues worth one earldom or one barony, as stated above in the title concerning summonses.

On the fourth day the representatives of the clergy shall be summoned. If they do not come on that day, their bishops shall be amerced, for each archdeaconry that has defaulted, at one hundred marks.

On the fifth day the deans, priors, abbots, bishops, and finally the archbishops shall be summoned. If they do not come, each archbishop shall be amerced at one hundred pounds; a bishop holding an entire barony at one hundred marks; and the same shall apply to abbots, priors, and others.

On the first day a proclamation shall be made, first in the hall, monastery, or other public place where Parliament is being held, and afterward publicly in that city or town: all those who wish to bring petitions and complaints before Parliament are to deliver them during the first five days of Parliament immediately following.

### CHAPTER XV. Concerning preaching at Parliament

An archbishop, or a great cleric, a learned and eloquent cleric appointed by the archbishop in whose province Parliament is held, shall preach on one of the first five days of Parliament, in full Parliament and in the presence of the king. This shall be done when Parliament has been assembled and gathered for the most part. He shall then accordingly enjoin upon the whole Parliament, in his sermon, that they should humbly beseech God with him and adore Him for the peace and tranquillity of the king and kingdom, as will be stated more fully in the following title concerning the address at Parliament.

### CHAPTER XVI. Concerning the address in Parliament

After the sermon, the chancellor of England, or the chief justice of England—that is, the person who holds pleas before the king—or another suitable, honorable, and eloquent justice, or a cleric chosen by the chancellor and chief justice, shall state the causes of Parliament, first in general and afterward in detail, standing.

It should therefore be understood that everyone in Parliament, whoever he may be while he is speaking, shall stand, except the king, so that everyone in Parliament may be able to hear the speaker. If he speaks indistinctly or too softly, he shall repeat himself and speak more loudly, or another shall speak for him.

### CHAPTER XVII. The king’s speech after the address

After the address, the king shall, in Parliament, ask the clerks and laymen—naming all their degrees, namely archbishops, bishops, abbots, priors, archdeacons, representatives, and others of the clergy; earls, barons, citizens, burgesses, and other laymen—to labor diligently, earnestly, and harmoniously to examine and deliberate upon the business of Parliament, as they understand and perceive that this is chiefly and principally in accordance with God’s will, and afterward to the honor and advantage of the king and themselves.

### CHAPTER XVIII. Concerning the king’s absence from Parliament

The king is bound in every way to attend Parliament personally, unless he is detained by bodily illness. In that case he may remain in his chamber, provided that he does not lie outside the manor, or at least outside the town, where Parliament is being held.

He must then send for twelve persons of the greater and better men who have been summoned to Parliament, namely two bishops, two earls, two barons, two knights of the counties, two citizens, and two burgesses, to see his person and testify to his condition. In their presence he must commission the archbishop of the place, his steward, and his chief justice to begin and continue Parliament jointly and separately in his name. The commission must expressly mention the cause of his absence, which ought to be sufficient, and must inform the other nobles and magnates of Parliament, together with the business and testimony of the said twelve peers of his.

The reason is that formerly there used to be outcry and murmuring in Parliament over the king’s absence, because it is a harmful and dangerous matter for the whole community of Parliament, and also of the kingdom, when the king is absent from Parliament. He ought not, and cannot, absent himself except in the case stated above.

### CHAPTER XIX. Concerning the place and seating in Parliament

First, as stated above, the king shall sit in the middle place of the greater bench. On his right shall sit the archbishop of Canterbury, and on his left the archbishop of York. Immediately after them shall sit the bishops and priors, always in a straight line, in such a manner among the aforesaid degrees and their places that no one sits except among his peers. The steward of England is bound to ensure this, unless the king appoints someone else.

At the king’s right foot shall sit the chancellor of England, the chief justice of England and his colleagues, and their clerks who are of Parliament. At his left foot shall sit the treasurer, the chamberlain, and the barons of the Exchequer; the justices of the bench; and their clerks, if any of them are of Parliament.

### CHAPTER XX. Concerning the usher of Parliament

The chief usher of Parliament shall stand inside the great door of the monastery, hall, or other place where Parliament is held, and shall guard the door, so that no one enters Parliament except one who [lacuna] ought to come to Parliament, or who has been called because of business that he is pursuing in Parliament. The usher must know the persons who ought to enter, if it is necessary to have several ushers.

### CHAPTER XXI. Concerning the crier

The crier of Parliament shall stand outside the door of Parliament, and the usher shall notify him of the calls to be made.

The king formerly used to send his armed servants to stand for a considerable distance outside the door of Parliament and guard the entrance, so that no assaults or disturbances might be made around the door through which one entered Parliament, under penalty of arrest of their persons. For by law the door of Parliament ought not to be closed, but should be guarded by the usher and the king’s armed servants.

### CHAPTER XXII. Concerning the stations of speakers

All the peers of Parliament shall sit, and no one shall stand [something is missing here] [lacuna], but when he speaks and addresses Parliament, he shall stand, so that everyone in Parliament may be able to hear him.

No one shall enter Parliament or leave Parliament except through one door. Whenever someone speaks about a matter that ought to be deliberated by Parliament, all the speakers shall stand. The reason is that he may be heard by the peers, because all the peers are judges and justices.

### CHAPTER XXIII. Concerning the king’s aid

The king formerly used to ask aid from his kingdom only for an impending war, or to make his sons knights, or to marry his daughters. Such aids must then be requested in full Parliament, delivered in writing to each degree of the peers of Parliament, and answered in writing.

It should be understood that, if such aids are to be granted, all the peers of Parliament must consent.

It must also be understood that the two knights who come to Parliament for a county have a greater voice in Parliament, in granting or opposing an aid, than the greatest earl of England. In the same way, the representatives of the clergy of one bishopric have a greater voice in Parliament, if they are all in agreement, than the bishop himself. This applies to everything that must be granted, denied, or done by Parliament.

This is clear from the fact that the king can hold Parliament with the community of his kingdom without bishops, earls, and barons, provided that they have nevertheless been summoned to Parliament, even if no bishop, earl, or baron comes in response to his summonses. For formerly there was neither bishop, nor earl, nor baron, and even then the kings held their Parliaments.

The converse is otherwise. Even if the communities of the clergy and laity had been summoned to Parliament, as they ought by law to be, and were unwilling to come for some reason—for example, if they alleged that the said king did not govern them as he ought, and specifically identified the ways in which he had not governed them—then there would be no Parliament at all, even if the archbishops, bishops, earls, barons, and all their peers were present with the king.

Therefore everything that is to be affirmed or rejected, granted or denied, or done by Parliament must be granted by the community of Parliament. This community consists of three degrees or orders of Parliament, namely the representatives of the clergy, the knights of the counties, and the citizens and burgesses, who represent the whole community of England, and not the magnates; for each of the latter is present at Parliament for his own person and for no other.

### CHAPTER XXIV. Concerning the dissolution of Parliament

Parliament must not be dissolved so long as any petition remains undiscussed, or at least before its answer has been determined. If the king permits the contrary, he is perjured.

No single member of the peers of Parliament may, or ought to, withdraw from Parliament unless he has obtained permission from the king and all his peers, and this in full Parliament; and a record of such permission must be entered on the Parliament roll.

If one of the peers falls ill during Parliament, so that he is unable to come to Parliament, he shall send excuses to Parliament for three days. If he does not come on the appointed day, two of his peers shall be sent to him to see and testify to the illness. If there is suspicion, those two peers shall swear that they will tell the truth about it. If it is discovered that he had pretended to be ill, he shall be amerced as for a default. If he had not pretended, he shall appoint a sufficient attorney before them to attend Parliament on his behalf. No healthy man can be excused if he is of sound mind.

The dissolution of Parliament ought to be conducted in this manner: a question must be put and publicly proclaimed in Parliament and within the palace of Parliament, asking whether there is anyone who has brought a petition to Parliament to which no answer has yet been given. If no one objects, it is to be assumed that everyone has been given a remedy, or at least answered so far as can be done by law. Then, namely when no one who has presented a petition on that occasion objects, we shall dismiss your Parliament.

### CHAPTER XXV. Concerning transcripts of records in Parliament

The clerks of Parliament shall not refuse anyone a transcript of his proceedings, but shall provide it to anyone who requests it. They shall always take one penny for ten lines, unless proof has first been given of inability to pay; in that case they shall take nothing.

The Parliament rolls shall be ten inches wide.

Parliament shall be held in whatever place in the kingdom pleases the king.

[Col. 1349]

## The Speech of William, Duke of Normandy, afterward King of England, to His Army before the Battle

*(Henry of Huntingdon, Book VI, p. 210, in* Rerum Anglicarum Scriptores*.)*

[Col. 1349A]

“I address you, Normans, bravest of peoples—not as one uncertain of your valor, nor as one who is not confident of victory, which has never been able to escape you through any accident or impediment. If you had once been unable to conquer, perhaps you would need to be exhorted, so that your valor might shine forth. But what need of exhortation has that which is innate in you and almost necessary?

“O strongest of mortals, what could the king of the Franks accomplish in war with all the peoples who are from Lorraine to Spain against our ancestor Hasting? As much of France as he wished, he acquired for himself; as much as he wished, he left to the king; while it pleased him, he held it; when he was satisfied, and desired greater things, he abandoned it.

“Did not Rou, my father, the first duke and founder of our people, defeat the king of the Franks in war at Paris, in the middle of his kingdom, together with our fathers? And could the king of the Franks hope for safety unless he had humbly offered both his daughter and the land which, because of you, is called Normandy?

“Did not your fathers capture the king of the Franks at Rouen and hold him until he restored Normandy to your young duke Richard, on the condition that, in every meeting between the king of France and the duke of Normandy, the duke would wear a sword, whereas the king was not permitted to carry either a sword or even a knife? Your fathers imposed this perpetual ordinance upon the great king by force.

“Did not that same duke lead your fathers as far as Mirmande near the Alps, and, fighting against the duke of that city—his own son-in-law—compel him to obey his bride?

“And lest it be too little for you to have conquered men, did he not himself also conquer the devil, wrestling with him bodily, throwing him down, and binding his hands behind his back, leaving him confused and defeated by the victor of the English?

“But why do I recount ancient deeds? When you were engaging the Franks at Mortemer, did they not place headlong flight before warfare, and spurs before weapons? But you, after Radulf, the chief commander of the Franks, had been killed, having gained fame and spoils, held fast to your natural excellence with your customary determination.

“Come, let some Englishman step forward—those whom our ancestors, both Danes and Norwegians, have defeated a hundred times in war—and let him show that the people of Rou, from his time until now, have suffered the shipwreck of war only once; then I shall depart defeated.

“Is it not therefore a disgrace to you that a people accustomed to be defeated, a people lacking in war, a people not even possessing arrows, should advance against you, O bravest men, as though drawn up for battle?

“Are you not ashamed that King Harold dared to show you his perjured face by confronting me in your presence?

“Yet I am astonished that you saw with your own eyes those who beheaded your kinsmen together with my relative Alfred through wicked treachery, and that their heads still remain upon their shoulders.

“Raise your standards, men! Let there be no limit or restraint to your deserved anger. From East to West let the lightning of your glory be seen, let the thunder of your attack be heard, and avenge the noblest blood!”

Duke William had not yet finished speaking when all, inflamed with anger beyond what can be imagined, rushed forward against the enemy in an indescribable charge according to their battle lines, leaving the duke already speaking only to himself.

[Col. 1349]

# Charters of William the Conqueror

## I. For the Church of Saint Andrew at Rochester

*(Monasticon Anglicanum I, 29.)*

[Col. 1349B]

William, king of the English, sends greetings to Walter the sheriff and all his barons, French and English, of the county of Gloucester.

Know that I have given to the church of Saint Andrew of Rochester and to Bishop Gundulf the manor of Eston, which belonged to Countess Gode, and everything pertaining to it, as fully, freely, and peacefully as the countess ever held it at her best, and as I myself also held it in my demesne, with all the customs called in English Soke and Sake, Toll and Team, and Infangenetheof.

I do this for the soul of my father, the soul of my mother, and my own soul.

Witnesses: Walkelin, bishop of Winchester; Robert, bishop of Lincoln; William the chancellor; Ranulf the chaplain; Eudo the steward; Roger Bigot; and Hugh de Evermu.

## II. For the same church

*(Ibid.)*

William, by the grace of God king of the English, sends greetings to his faithful French and English subjects.

Know that I have granted the donation which Haimo, my steward, made to the church of Saint Andrew in the city of Rochester, concerning the church which is in Tarenteford, my manor. Robert and Haimo, the sons of that Haimo, in my presence, granted the same donation of their father.

Witnesses: Robert, count of Meulan; Robert, count of Meritol; and many others.

## III. For the same church

*(Ibid.)*

[Col. 1351B]

William, king of the English, sends greetings to the bishop of Suffolk, the sheriff, and his other barons, French and English.

Know that I have granted and confirmed the gift of Roger Bigot, which he gave to the church of Saint Andrew of Rochester, namely the church of Saint Felix of Walton, with its tithes and everything else pertaining to it.

Witness of Eudo the steward. At Winchester.

## IV. For the same church

*(Monasticon Anglicanum I, 29.)*

[Col. 1351C]

William, king of the English, sends greetings to the bishop of Sussex, the sheriff, and his other barons, French and English.
