Know that I have granted and confirmed the gift of Gilbert of Tonbridge, which he gave to the church of Saint Andrew of Rochester, namely the church of Rotherfield and everything pertaining to it, whether in tithes, hunting rights, or any other matters.

Witnesses: Roger Bigot and Haimo the sheriff. At Winchester.

## V. For the liberty of the monastery of Meldun

*(Ibid., p. 52.)*

Reigning forever is our Lord Jesus Christ, who governs and rules all the elements, who also, through incomparable compassion and great majesty, sustains all things, and beautifully orders and dispenses all things, visible and invisible, according to his will.

Therefore I, William, by God’s ordering king of the English and of the other peoples dwelling round about, ruler and duke of the Normans, at the request of my most faithful wife, Queen Matilda, and of many bishops and barons, have granted to Warin, abbot of the monastery of Meldun, and to his successors, the same donation of lands and possessions which all my predecessors provided and granted to this church.

And because this church is recognized as having been founded in honor of Mary, Mother of God and perpetual virgin, and because the body of the most holy Aldhelm rests there, together with the relics of many saints, especially those of our patron and prelate of Rouen, I give and grant to this church perpetual liberty, namely the same liberty granted by King Edward.

This means that it shall be free and quit of shires, hundreds, pleas, complaints, all gelds, and customs. I also grant it Sake and Soke, Toll and Team, Infangenetheof, Donbriche, Damlokene, and Forestal.

If anyone—God forbid!—inflated by a devilish spirit should attempt to violate this royal gift of mine, let him know beyond doubt that, unless he is willing to make amends beforehand by suitable satisfaction, he will stand trembling and quaking, anathematized, before the strict tribunal of the Judge, amid the uproar of the assembled archangels.

Whoever preserves it, may he deserve to reign with the Lord Jesus Christ in the glory of paradise.

This charter of donation was made in the year from the Incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ 1081, indiction IV, in the fifteenth year of the reign of William, the most powerful king.

The following witnesses subscribed:

I, William, king of the English, confirmed this gift.  
I, Matilda, queen, signed it.  
I, Lanfranc, archbishop.  
I, Odo, bishop of Bayeux, subscribed.  
I, Osmund, bishop of Salisbury.  
I, Remigius, bishop of Lincoln.  
I, Geoffrey, bishop of Coutances.  
I, Walthelm, bishop of Winchester.  
I, Walter, abbot of Evesham.  
I, Robert, earl, subscribed.  
I, Henry, the king’s son.  
I, Halamius, earl, subscribed.  
I, Baldwin, sheriff.  
I, Robert of Dantesey.

Done at London, with Warin the abbot in attendance.

## VI. For the same monastery

*(Ibid., p. 53.)*

I acknowledge, beyond all ambiguity, that orthodox persons who do good with a pure heart will receive eternal rewards. Therefore I, Matilda, by the grace of God queen and lawful wife of William, the most vigorous king of the English, the mighty ruler of the other peoples dwelling round about, and the most noble duke of the Normans, with the same illustrious man’s will and sincere consent, and at the request of the reverend Abbot Warin, have given to holy Mary, Mother of God and most spotless virgin, and to Saint Aldhelm, in the monastery of Meldun, a certain piece of land called Gersduna, which I held as my own, to be held forever by hereditary right with everything belonging to it, for the use of the monks serving there in God’s work and pouring out prayers before the sight of divine mercy for the remission of the sins of myself and my children.

That land contains three hides and is surrounded on every side by the lands of the aforesaid monastery.

I made this gift gladly, under the rule of our supreme and immeasurable Lord Jesus Christ, in the year 1081 from the year of his ineffable Incarnation, indiction IV, in the fifteenth year of the reign of the most serene King William, in the month of February.

## VII. Confirmation of King Edward’s privilege for the church of Peterborough

*(Monasticon Anglicanum I, p. 68.)*

[Col. 1353A]

I, William, by God’s favor king of the English, at the request of Abbot Brand, approve and confirm this privilege in every respect, just as the kings written above me did. Likewise, concerning the lands of the brothers or their kinsmen which they held hereditarily and freely under King Edward—namely Scotera, Scotuna, Malmetun, Raganaldethorp, Melsingham, Cletham, Bibaldestopa, Thalcote, and Mulcham, with all their appurtenances—I grant them forever to his monastery and to the patron of that place, blessed Peter the apostle, free and quit, with all the customs called in English Sake and Soke, so that they may continually be their own property and demesne, for the infirm (*infirmas*; the printed Latin is unclear) and for every necessity of those serving God there.

Therefore let none of my heirs or successors dare to violate this, lest he perish by the sword of excommunication and possess hell in place of the inheritance of the Church.

The following were present as witnesses: Aldrad, archbishop of York; Wilwimus, bishop of Lincoln; Merleisuein, sheriff; Ulf, son of Topi; William, earl; William Maleit; Ingelvus, priest.

## VIII. For the monastery of Bath in the county of Somerset

*(Ibid., p. 185.)*

William, king of the English, sends greetings to O., bishop of Salisbury; L., abbot of Glastonbury; A., sheriff; and all the barons, French and English, of Somerset and Wiltshire.

Know that I have given to God and Saint Peter at Bath, and to John the bishop, the whole city of Bath as an alms and for the enlargement of his episcopal see and that of all his successors, for the salvation of the souls of my father, my mother, myself, and my predecessors and successors.

I have given it, I say, so freely and honorably, with all its appurtenances, whatever I or my father held there when we held it best, with all customs within and without, as I hold any city in all England most freely: with the mint, with the toll, in the fields as well as in the woods, in the market as well as in the meadows and lands, so that he may have his episcopal see there with the greatest honor.

The witnesses to this are openly declared: Walkelin, bishop of Winchester; Robert, bishop of Lincoln; Robert, count of Meulan; Henry, count of Warwick; Robert, son of Haimo; Eudo the steward; Ivo the steward; Robert, son of Gerald; Robert the dispenser; and William of Carocel.

## IX. For the church of Saint Mary at Stow

*(Ibid. I, 263.)*

William, king of the English, sends greetings to the bishops and all his faithful throughout England.

Know that I have confirmed the donation which Earl Leofric and his wife Godiva gave to the church of Saint Mary at Stow, namely Newark, Flawborough, and Wellingore, with their appurtenances.

Furthermore, at the petition of Bishop Remigius, I grant to the aforesaid church the church of Egnesham with the lands which it now possesses, on the condition that an abbot be appointed there by my counsel, who shall always administer the affairs of the churches; but the abbey shall remain in my dominion like the others throughout England.

And so that no one may have any occasion for complaint against that abbey, in exchange for the altar of Stow and four carucates of land belonging to the bishop, I grant to the bishops of Lincoln a good estate at Stafford.

I do this by the counsel and testament of Archbishop Lanfranc.

Witnesses: E., sheriff, and R. de Osli.

## X. To the men of the abbey of Stow

*(Ibid., p. 263.)*

[Col. 1354B]

William, king of England, sends greetings to the men of the abbey of Stow.

I command all of you to be as obedient to your lord, Abbot Columbanus, in all matters as you were to Bishop Remigius.

Witness: Richard de Curcy.

## XI. Concerning the exchange of Saint Mary of Stow

*(Ibid., p. 265.)*

William, king of the English, sends greetings to R., bishop of Lincoln.

I command you to maintain Abbot Columbanus peacefully and honorably, and to ensure fully that he receives his exchange for all the lands which he held at Stow, so that nothing is lacking from it, but that he has the whole of it at the same value as he held there.

Take care that I hear no further complaint about this, because otherwise I would not have consented to your making the change of place.

T. W., the chancellor, at Ou.

## XII. Charter granted to Ivo Taleboys

*(Ibid., p. 307.)*

William, king of the English, sends greetings to R., bishop of Lincoln, and to all his barons and faithful.

Know all that I grant that Ivo Taleboys may give the manor called Spalding to Saint Nicholas of the city of Angers, namely on this condition: that the church which is in the same manor, and its ministers, shall have the manor with all its appurtenances, with Sake and Soke, Toll and Team, Infangenetheof, and all other customs, as any of his ancestors held it at their best; but they shall have it only after his death, or before his death if Ivo himself wishes.

Witnesses: W., bishop of Durham; Robert, son of Haimo; William the chancellor; Eudo the steward; and Roger Bigot, at Hom.

## XIII. For the monastery of Saint Edmund in the county of Suffolk

*(Ibid. I, 288.)*

William, king of the English, prince of the Normans and of the men of Maine, to the archbishops, bishops, abbots, earls, and his other faithful subjects.

Because we believe that by God’s mercy we have been raised to the heights of the kingdom, we ought to take care to watch over the prosperous stability of the people subject to us, and especially of those who labor day and night in the service of the Lord.

Therefore we make known to the faithful of our kingdom, present and future, that Bishop Arfast reported to us and to many others that the church of blessed Edmund, in which that venerable king and martyr awaits the day of blessed resurrection with his body incorrupt, ought to be his episcopal see.

Accordingly, after the greatest dispute had continued for a long time between Baldwin, abbot of the aforesaid church, and that bishop, we judged it appropriate, with the counsel of the archbishops, bishops, and many other faithful men of ours, that the case of both parties concerning these matters should be examined in our court.

When they appeared before us on the appointed day, the bishop presented his complaint with sufficient eloquence, but was entirely lacking in documents and testimony. The abbot, on the other hand, showed how King Cnut, with the common counsel of his archbishops, bishops, and nobles, expelled from the aforesaid church the priests who lived there disorderly and installed monks.

He also showed that afterward Archbishop Ailnoth of Canterbury dedicated that church at the command of the aforementioned king; that the first abbot of that place was consecrated by the bishop of London, the second by the bishop of Winchester; and that Baldwin himself, who is the third abbot, was consecrated by the archbishop of Canterbury.

He further related in due order that for fifty-three years, without contradiction from any predecessor of the aforesaid Arfast, the monks of that place had received orders from whichever bishops they wished.

Finally, he produced the charters—namely those of King Cnut and the most glorious King Edward—in which those kings granted the aforesaid church perpetual and complete freedom from the domination of all the bishops of that county.

When Archbishop Lanfranc of Canterbury, Archbishop Thomas of York, Odo, bishop of Bayeux, my brother and count of Kent, and many other bishops, as well as my son Robert and the other princes of our kingdom who were present, heard this, they judged that the great authority of so great a place ought to remain inviolate until the end of the age.

I assented to their irrefutable judgment, as was proper, and give my consent to it.

It also pleased us, with the counsel of the archbishops, bishops, earls, and many other faithful men of ours, and at the worthy petition of Abbot Baldwin, who humbly requested our serenity, to strengthen by our charter the charters which our predecessors, the English kings—namely Edmund, Cnut, Harold Harefoot, and the illustrious Edward, by whose mercy, lineage, and gift of the Lord we possess the kingdom and are its heirs—granted to the often-mentioned church.

We do this so that the church itself, and the town in which it is situated, may be free from the domination of Bishop Arfast and of all bishops who succeed him in the course of time.

And so that this authority may remain perpetually firm and inviolate concerning that holy place in our time and in times to come, we have decreed that this charter be strengthened by the subscription of our hand and confirmed by the impression of our seal.

## XIV. For the monastery of Battle in Sussex

[Note: Concerning the foundation of this monastery, the following is read in Leland, *Collectanea*, vol. III, fol. 73: “In the year 1067 King William, rejoicing in the victory obtained over the Saxons, built the abbey of Battle and established monks there, so that, for those slain in the battle, sacrifices of salvation might perpetually be offered to God by them.”

**Verses on the monastery of Battle**

The Bastard overcame the kingdom of the English in war,

And the king hastened to establish a monastery.

Fasting, praying, and longing to know about his offspring,

He soon deserved to hear a divine answer:

“The church of Battle shall be long in feet;

For so many years shall your posterity endure in England.”

When they wished to make the church longer,

They could not exceed three hundred feet.”]

(*Monasticon Anglicanum* I, 317.)

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, I, WILLIAM, by the grace of God king of the English, make known to all, present and future, archbishops, bishops, abbots, counts, barons, and all faithful Frenchmen and Englishmen: that, when I had come to England and landed with an army in the region of Hastings against my enemies, who were unjustly attempting to take the kingdom of England from me, already armed and prepared for battle before my barons and soldiers, with the approval of all and to strengthen their courage, I made a vow to build a church in honour of God, for the common salvation, if by God’s grace we could obtain victory. When we had gained it, fulfilling my vow to God, I built a church in honour of the holy Trinity and blessed Martin, confessor of Christ, for the salvation of my soul, of my predecessor King Edward, of my wife Queen Mathilda, and of my successors in the kingdom, and for the salvation of all through whose labour and assistance I obtained the kingdom, especially those who fell in that very battle. And because at this place, where the church was thus built, God granted me victory in battle, I wished the place itself to be called Battle, in memory of the victory.

Therefore, to this church of Saint Martin of Battle I first grant, by royal authority, this privilege: that it shall have its own court in every respect, with royal liberty and the customary right to deal with its own matters and business, and to administer justice by itself. Let it be free and undisturbed forever from every subjection to bishops and from the domination of any persons, like Christ Church at Canterbury. And if any robber, murderer, or person guilty of any crime, fleeing from fear of death, should reach this church, let him suffer no harm but be entirely released; and let the abbot of that church have the right everywhere to rescue a robber or thief from hanging, should such a person come before him.

I also grant to the same church the surrounding league of land, free and undisturbed from every geld and scot, hidage and danegeld, bridge-work and castle-work, park-work and enclosures, armies and all aids, pleas and complaints, shires and hundreds, with sake and soke, toll and team, infangthief, *marpeni*, *lestagium*, *mamfocne*, *forestall*, *blodwite*, *childwite*, and theft; free from every customary burden of earthly service and from every exaction of bishops.

Again, to this church of Saint Martin of Battle I give the royal manor called Wi, with all its appurtenances, from my own royal crown, with all liberties and royal customs, as freely and quietly as I held it most freely and quietly, or as a king could give it—namely, free from every geld and scot, hidage and danegeld, bridge-work and castle-work, park enclosures, armies and all aids, pleas and complaints, shires and hundreds, with sake and soke, toll and team, infangthief, *warpeni*, *lestagium*, *hamlocne*, *forestall*, *blodwite*, *childwite*, and theft, if it should occur.

Likewise, I give two pennies from all forfeitures and pleas of all the hundreds that belong to the summons of Wi. At Dengemarsh, which is one member of Wi, I grant the same church all the maritime customs that I possessed there, together with every right of wreck. And if the fish called *craspeile* should come there, the whole of it shall belong to the abbot and monks. But if it should come ashore within the bounds of Blachemale and Horlemede and Bradelle as far as Withiburne, the church shall have two parts of that fish and its tongue, as I have always had.

I also give to the same church these manors: Alsistona, Lymenesfeld, Hom, Grammarcis, and Briswaltintona, with all their appurtenances, free and undisturbed, with the liberties and royal customs stated above. If a killing should occur within the league or in the church’s manors, or if treasure should be found, both shall belong to the abbot and monks. The church shall have its own warren in that league and in all its manors.

I also give to the same church of Saint Martin the church of Radingis, the church of Culintuna, and the church of Saint Olaf at Exeter, with their lands, tithes, and everything belonging to them. And if any of my barons or men should give anything of his own to the same church as alms, I grant them the same liberties that I have granted to the possessions which I gave to that church, and by this present writing I confirm them, with royal authority, as stated above.

Willel+mus, king. Lanfr+anc, archbishop of Canterbury. Tho+mas, archbishop of York. Maurice + bishop of London. Walkelin + bishop of Winchester. Osbern + bishop of Exeter. Gundulf + bishop of Rochester. Hugh + count of Chester. Roger + count of Montgomery. William + count of Warenne. William + son of Osbern. William + de Braose. Bernard + de Neufmarché.

## XV. For the same monastery

(*Monasticon Anglicanum* I, p. 317.)

WILLIAM, by the grace of God king of the English, to Lanfranc, archbishop of Canterbury, Stigand, bishop of Chichester, and all their successors who hold the kingdom of England, and to all the faithful, greetings.

I make known to you that the place of my victory, just as with God’s help I conquered it and, as king, possessed it freely, so I offered it freely to God and free from every exaction of all men. There I established a church in honour of Saint Martin, which I wished to be called Battle, because God granted me such a great victory in that same place that I triumphed over my adversaries, who were unjustly resisting me, and acquired for myself and my successors a kingdom due to me, to be possessed perpetually by hereditary right.

Therefore, hastening to fulfil the vow that I made to God and Saint Martin, I dedicated the same monastery to monastic religion and founded it according to the rule and observance of the greater monastery. From there I appointed Gausbert as its first abbot, for the sole purpose of establishing the rule of religious life there. It was nevertheless to remain forever free and undisturbed from every subjection and domination and from every claim of the greater monastery and every exaction of other persons, like Christ Church at Canterbury and like my own chapel, the emblem of the English crown through which I reign and through which my successors, the kings, ought to possess the kingdom of England.

We therefore decree, with the oversight both of ecclesiastical and royal authority, that when the abbot of Battle dies, all the property of the monastery, wherever it may be, shall remain free and intact, with all its rights and customs, in the hands and under the disposition of the prior and the monastic chapter of Battle. We establish and confirm this statute for perpetual observance because the abbot of Battle has no private revenues but shares them with the brothers.

Whoever, therefore, by God’s favour, is appointed abbot through the canonical election of the brothers shall be blessed there without any simony, just as Stigand, bishop of Chichester, blessed Gausbert as the first abbot in that monastery of Battle. The abbot of Battle must not squander the monastery’s alms by misusing them with his secular relatives or any others, but must exercise fraternal care by receiving the poor, pilgrims, and guests. He shall not grant rent-paying lands as fiefs, nor make knights except in the sacred clothing of Christ; and no one shall hold anything from the church’s possessions as an absolute fief, but only in return for an annual rent and the service owed to the abbot and monks.

In the house and possession of the abbot of Battle and the monks, no one, inside or outside, shall hold an office by inheritance; rather, the appointment and removal of provosts and any other officers shall rest at the discretion of the abbot and monks.

Therefore, to the monastery of Battle, and to everything belonging to it, I give and confirm forever this free immunity and unimpaired liberty of my own freedom at Battle. As a sign of the crown of our kingdom, I also commend God’s cause to the kings who shall reign in England after me, so that God may preserve it for them eternally.

Witnessed by Peter, bishop of Chester; Herman, bishop of Salisbury; William, count of Warenne; Bernard of Neufmarché; and Gausbert, now abbot of that place, with his monks, who were present when this charter was made at Winchester.

## XVI. Charter of the foundation of the monastery of Armethwaite in the county of Cumberland

(*Monasticon Anglicanum* I, p. 324.)

WILLIAM, by the grace of God king of the English and duke of the Normans, to all his faithful in Christ who shall see these present letters, greetings.

Know that, of our own free will and from charitable consideration, we have founded, built, and established forever, as a pure and perpetual alms, a house and monastery of black nuns of the order of Saint Benedict, in honour of Jesus Christ and the blessed Virgin Mary, for the souls of our ancestors and of all Christians, situated beside the water called Croglyn in the county of Cumberland.

We have also given and granted to the nuns dwelling there two acres of land on which the aforesaid house and monastery stand. We have further given and granted to the same nuns three carucates of land and ten acres of meadow, with all common rights, woods, and wastes in any way belonging to those three carucates of land, lying beside the aforesaid monastery.

We have also given and granted to the same nuns and their successors forever 216 acres of land within our forest of Ingelwood, lying on the northern side of a certain water called Tarnendelyn, with all useful woods and benefits existing upon those lands or subsequently growing there.

We have also granted to the same nuns common pasture with all their animals, for themselves and their tenants dwelling there, throughout our forest of Ingelwood, with permission to take sufficient timber there for all their buildings whenever and as often as necessary, by agreement with our foresters or with whichever one of them is present there.

We have also granted and confirmed to the same nuns and their successors a certain annual rent of forty shillings, to be received forever each year from our tenements in our town of Carlisle, to be paid to the same nuns and their successors by the hands of the keeper of our aforesaid town of Carlisle, at Pentecost and at Saint Martin in winter, in equal portions.

We also grant, for ourselves and our heirs, that the aforesaid nuns, their tenants, and their servants shall be free from paying toll throughout our kingdom of England for any animals or goods whatsoever bought in future by them or by any tenant or servant of theirs.

We also grant and confirm that the aforesaid monastery and house, with the aforesaid three carucates, two acres of land, and ten acres of meadow, shall be free in every respect and shall have all its liberties in the same manner as is granted to our monastery of Westminster, without vexation, molestation, disturbance, or injury from any sheriff, exactor, bailiff, officer, or liegeman of ours whatsoever.

We also grant to the same nuns common pasture with their animals within the vill and common of Aynltaplyth, with free entry and exit.

We further grant that the aforesaid nuns shall be free throughout all their land from the obligations of every tenant, and shall have free warren, both in the leets of our courts and in the waters, woods, lands, open grounds, and boundaries belonging or in any way pertaining to the same monastery.

All and each of the aforesaid things are to be had, held, and occupied by the aforesaid nuns and their successors forever from us and our heirs, as a pure and perpetual alms, by spontaneous will and grant.

“As the heart may think or the eye may see.”

In testimony of this matter we have caused these letters patent to be made. Witnessed by me myself at Westminster, on the sixth day of January, in the second year of our reign.

## XVII. Charter of the first foundation of the abbey of Selby

(*Monasticon Anglicanum* I, 371.)

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. Amen.

WILLIAM, the strongest, indeed the most powerful, king of all those kings under whose rule royal sceptres are governed beneath the open sky, ruling the greatest dominion of the English land, which by God’s permission and will he first acquired through signs, wondrous miracles, and then by great strength and wars in which he defeated the English, sends greetings to ecclesiastical men, as well as to his counts, barons, and all his officers.

By the providence of God’s mercy and by my goodness, inspired by divine clemency, I granted to the most devout Benedict, who earnestly requested it, permission to found a monastery in honour of our Lord Jesus Christ, his most blessed mother and virgin Mary, and Saint Germanus, bishop of Auxerre, at Selby.

In that foundation I placed, established with royal liberty, and gave from my own table Selby itself: namely, one carucate of land at Swaith, six bovates at Flarlep and Rodeliffe, half a carucate of land at Bratton, one fishery at Whitegift, and the lands given to that church by Archbishop Thomas, namely Fryston and Little Selby, both according to his oral grant and according to the tenor of his charter.

In the same way I confirmed and granted Crull—namely, one hundred lying in the county of Lincoln—and Stamford, which lies in the county of Hampshire, given by Geoffrey de la Wirche and Guy de Rainecourt. I also granted and confirmed everything connected with these, wherever situated, whether lands and possessions or other offerings which, at the prompting of the Holy Spirit, may be offered by devout benefactors and acquired in every direction by right, prayer, or payment, free, peacefully, and openly from every exaction, molestation, and vexation, as befits a royal alms and a proper abbey to hold in endless and perpetual peace.

It shall have its own court with sake and soke, toll and team, infangthief, and all the customs which the church of Saint Peter of York possesses in the highest degree, and shall hold and possess them forever.

As testimony and confirmation of this gift of alms, for the salvation of my soul and of my predecessors and successors, this charter was issued and confirmed at London, in the presence of these persons: Odo, bishop of Bayeux; Edward of Salisbury; Hugh de Port; Hugh de Montfort; Robert de Olley; Richard, son of Count Gilbert; Baldwin, his brother; Remigius, bishop; Ralph Tallebosc; Robert de Tany; Geoffrey de la Wirche; and the entire royal court.

## XVIII. For the church of the holy apostles Peter and Paul

(*Ibid.*, p. 380.)

We are warned by the example of the holy Fathers carefully to commit to the memory of writing the possessions which we know to have been granted to the holy Church by the faithful in our time, both for the benefit of those who grant them—for by their example later generations are stirred to do good—and because of the perversity of evil men, who are known to covet ecclesiastical possessions with all their strength in order to seize them.

Therefore, imitating the diligence of our predecessors, we have taken care to transmit in writing, for the knowledge of those who come after, a work of piety which the venerable Count Roger and his devout wife, named Adelaisia, offered to God in our time.

In the suburb of the city of Shrewsbury there was a fairly small church built in honour of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul. Its site seemed suitable for establishing dwellings for servants of God. The count, therefore, relying on the permission and authority of King William and of Lanfranc, archbishop of Canterbury, as well as of Peter, bishop of Chester, to whose diocese that place belonged, gathered monks there to pray to the Lord for his salvation and that of his people, in the year 1087 from the incarnation of the Lord.

For their support, he and his revered wife gave them the possessions listed below forever. First, one street adjoining the same church, with three mills and all revenues belonging to it. In English this street is called Bifosieta, which in Latin means “before the gate.”

Next, they granted them certain churches with all the possessions belonging to them, which we have specified here by name: namely, the church of Saint Gregory of Damerfeld, whose possessions are these: Estleigh, Northleigh, also Estleigh Croft, Halghton, Chinsley, Harpford, Billingsley, Newton, Tugalost, Fertecot, and Weston.

Also the church of Stottesdon, whose possessions are these: Dodelmouth, Hinton, and Prestcot.

Also the church of Diddlebury, whose possession is Spertford and half a hide of land at Corston.

Also the church of Edmundon, the church of Toenges, the church of Donnington, the church of Wellington, the church of Werecordine, the church of Ercolum, the church of Hodeneth, the church of Conedover, the church of Ness, and the church of Ballechurch, whose possessions are Prestcot, Newleigh, and Bageley.

With all these, the count and countess gave the same monastery three vills with all their appurtenances, namely Eaton, Eyminster, and Burton.

They also granted the monks the toll on timber brought into the city through the eastern gate. They further ordered that on the feast of Saint Peter, on the Kalends of August, the people of the entire province should gather at that place for a market lasting three days each year, and that the monks should have the whole toll and all profit arising from it.

Afterward the count granted that any of his barons or knights who wished might give lands and possessions of their own to that place without requiring his permission or that of his men, so that, once the alms had been completed, neither the donors nor the recipients should thereafter perform any service for him. For he established that all the monks’ land should forever be free from the geld of the knights and also from the common geld, unless he himself granted it from his own demesne.

This pious generosity of the count greatly pleased all who heard of it and strongly stirred them to love that place. Then Warin the sheriff gave those monks two hides of land in the vill called Tugaford, the tithe of Opeton, and the church of Birton with the tithe of that vill.

Rainald, Warin’s brother, gave them the vill called Leigh. Girard of Tornac gave Betton. Geoffrey gave half a hide at Herleigh. Odo the knight gave Hordleigh.

The venerable Count Roger, together with his sons Hugh, Robert, Roger, and Arnulf, granted and confirmed all these things. The witnesses were Herbert the archdeacon, Godebald and Oilerius the priests, Warin the sheriff, Robert son of Theobald, Roger Corbet, Robert the butler, and many others.

The place where the monastery itself had been built belonged by inheritance to a certain knight named Siward. Since the most pious count did not want any future dispute to arise for the monks from this, he gave Siward in exchange a vill called Longfield. Later, when Siward received the fraternity of the monks, he granted that the same vill, which he had received from the count, should come into their possession after his death.

Witnesses: Godebald, Richard of Belmes, and Richard of Mount Harold.

I, William, king of the English, granted all these things and confirmed them with my seal.

## XIX. For the church of Saint Mary of York

(*Monasticon Anglicanum* I, 397.)

WILLIAM, king of England, to Archbishop T. of York, and to his justices, sheriffs, all his barons, and his faithful Frenchmen and Englishmen of Yorkshire and Carlisle, greetings.

Know that I have granted and confirmed to God and to the church of Saint Mary of York, and to Abbot Richard and the monks serving God there, the cell of Saint Constantine with the manor of Wedderhale, the chapel of Warwick, the weir, pond, fishery, and mill of Wedderhale, which is fixed and established in the land of Coskeby. They received these lands as a pure and perpetual alms from Ranulf Meschin, count of Cumberland.

I also confirm to them, as my gift, all the pasture between the Eden and the king’s road which leads from Carlisle to Appleby, and from Wedderhale as far as Dsibeke.

Therefore I prohibit anyone else from disturbing or violating this confirmation or gift of ours made to the aforesaid monks.

Witnesses: Lucia, my wife; Henry, my brother; the knights Oder and Huddred; Enesaunt Muserdde; and others.

## XX. For the monastery of Saint Denis in France

(*Ibid.*, p. 547.)

WILLIAM, king of the English, count of the Normans and the men of Maine, to Christ’s faithful throughout the world.

The merciful and compassionate God, patient and rich in mercy, among the other commandments of his mercy, since everything a man possesses is, beyond what can be said, of little account in comparison with eternal blessedness, commanded us to store up from the things we rightly possess treasures that do not fail, saying: “Store up for yourselves treasures in heaven, where neither rust nor moth destroys.”

Moved by love of this commandment, I and my consort Mathilda, with the prudent counsel of our nobles, for the salvation of our souls and of all our children, grant to Saint Denis—whose apostolic distinction is honoured by the Gallic people—the church of Derhurst, situated in the territory and county of the city of Gloucester, with all its appurtenances.

Our illustrious predecessor King Edward gave it to our faithful Baldwin, a monk of that same saint, for his own use, before Baldwin received from him the abbacy of Saint Edmund, which he now governs; and afterward, when we had obtained the kingdom, we granted it to him ourselves.

Let this church, with everything known to belong to it, be free from every obligation. We also strengthen by this privilege the gift which the aforesaid king granted to the same saint in order to obtain eternal reward, namely Teynton with everything belonging to it, decreeing that it be free just like the church which we have granted to him, so that we and our offspring may, through the prayers of that saint and of his companions Rusticus and Eleutherius, deserve to attain prosperity in the present life and the harbour of eternal dwelling.

But if anyone should take away anything from this gift of ours, whatever his rank or power, by the authority of almighty God let him share the portion of Dathan and Abiron, unless, coming to repentance, he offers satisfaction and restitution to the saint and to the brothers of the place.

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1069, in the second year of the reign of King William, this privilege was confirmed on the second day of Easter in the monastery of Saint Swithun at the city of Winchester, while Mass was being celebrated, with these witnesses consenting:

I, William the king, have marked this gift and confirmation of ours with the sign of the + holy cross.

I, Mathilda, queen of that same king, have declared that this pleased me.

I, Richard, the king’s son, have most willingly assented to the gift of my father and mother.

I, Stigand, archbishop of the church of Canterbury, have confirmed it.

I, Aldred, archbishop of York, have confirmed it.

## XXI. Charter of King William the Conqueror concerning the foundation of the abbey of Saint Stephen of Caen in the duchy of Normandy

(*Monasticon Anglicanum* II, p. 956.)

Whoever gives anything to God or for God does not alienate it from himself but rather preserves it to be multiplied in the future, with the hope of eternal life. This is effected by the pious generosity of the Creator and by his abundant goodness toward us. Although he has no need of our goods—for the earth is his and all its fullness—he nevertheless desires to be honoured from our substance and to receive a sacrifice of praise for our salvation.

He urges us to serve him and grants us what we may return to him for his benefits. Yet the merciful Father receives what is, as it were, another’s, and repays it as though it were ours: in this world forgiving sins, and in the next receiving a hundredfold, promising himself and the heavenly kingdom.

Led by this hope, I, William, king of the English, prince of the Normans and the men of Maine, resolved to build a monastery in honour of God and of the most blessed protomartyr Stephen, within the borough commonly called Caen, for the salvation of my soul, my wife, my children, and my parents.

In case the cultivation of divine religion should at any time fail at that place through poverty, I have provided for it in the future in this way. Therefore I hand over to the aforesaid monastery the following vills of my right: Lens, Rots, Almenêches, Pont-de-Dives, and Cagny, with their cultivators and bond tenants, and so forth.

Also the land which Hugh of Rosel held at Grainville, the forest of Walpertuso, and those of Tortavalle, Folonia, and Casneto, with their waters and lands and everything belonging to them.

I also grant the entire allod which Osmund Aculeius, Richard, and Roger hold in the territory of Calvados above the Dives, and likewise everything which any allodial holders possess within the league of Pont-de-Dives.

In the land of the English, in the county of Devon, I give a manor called Rostham. In the county of Dorset, two manors: one called Frantonia and the other called Besencumbe.

In the county of Somerset, in the territory of Cross, ten hides of land and a church, with the whole tithe of that territory.

In the county of Wiltshire, the church of Cottam with all the land and tithe belonging to it.

I also grant in the county of Norfolk a manor called Welles, which William de Scocers gave to the aforesaid monastery, with the church of Northon and its land, together with the tithe belonging to that church in Essex.

Likewise, in the county of Essex I grant a small manor called Panfield—Paunfeld, a cell of Caen—and in London a certain piece of land which belonged to Leuzech, situated near the church of Saint Peter, free from geld, scot, and every other custom. Waleran son of Ranulf gave it, together with the tithe of all his land which he possesses in England, both for his own soul and for mine.

## XXII. Charter of the same glorious King William, confirmed after the dedication of the same monastery

(*Ibid.*, p. 956.)

I, WILLIAM, king of the English, prince of the Normans and the men of Maine, give to the monastery of Saint Stephen, which I built in the borough of Caen, the church of Saint Ouen of Vieux, with all the land which Milo the marshal gave in marriage with his daughter Arfast, in the territory of Venoix, Caen, and Vaucelles.

## XXIII. Charter concerning the gifts of the barons and nobles of Normandy for the same monastery, received and confirmed by the glorious King William

(*Monasticon Anglicanum* II, p. 956.)

I, Roger of Montgomery, faithful to my lord William, king of the English, prince of the Normans and the men of Maine, for the love of God, of that same lord of mine, and for the salvation of my soul, give to the monastery which he built in the borough of Caen in honour of Saint Stephen the borough of Trun, with the forest of Alge, and so forth.

I, Rainard, chamberlain of King William, give to the monastery of Saint Stephen of Caen, upon the altar, together with my son Corbel, the mill of Waimara, which I hold from the king, and so forth.

I, Serlo of Lingeuro, a man who am a sinner and in need of God’s mercy, have given from my right to the monastery of Saint Stephen of Caen the church of Bruxedelle, with three and a half acres of land and the entire rightful tithe from my demesne and my villeins, together also with one-third of the tithe from my knights, from the aforesaid vill, and from the other parishioners who come to the same church, for my salvation and that of my wife, my children, and all my relatives.

My wife and my sons have consented to this, as have my lord William, king of the English, prince of the Normans and the men of Maine, William the chamberlain, and Robert of Mowbray, from whose fief I hold the land and church of the aforesaid vill.

So that this gift of mine may remain firm and stable forever, I received from Gilbert, then abbot of the aforesaid monastery, out of charity, forty-five pounds in pennies and two marks of silver; and my son Ranulf received one good palfrey.

For this I gave the same abbot sureties, namely my son Ranulf, Arnald of Tilly, and Robert of Maisnil, so that, if anyone should ever bring a claim against Saint Stephen and this gift of mine, I or my heir would fully acquit it.

Witnesses on my side, who were also sureties: William of Poitiers and William of Hotot. On the side of Saint Stephen: William of Taisel, Auschitil of Maletot, and his son Roger.

I, Hugh of Rosel, give to the monastery of Saint Stephen of Caen the land which I hold at Grainville from the king’s benefice, with the king’s consent, and with the consent of my wife and my son Hugh, on the condition that the abbot and monks receive me into the order while I am still alive.

Witnesses: Hugh my son, Ralph of Grainville, Robert of Ros, and many others.

I receive with thanksgiving these donations which my barons and faithful men have made to my abbey for love of me and for my salvation; I grant them and, together with those confirming these same donations, strengthen and confirm them by my hand and authority. The names of those who have authenticated this charter are as follows: William, king of the English, prince of the Normans and of the men of Maine; Matilda, queen; Robert, the king’s son; William, the king’s son; Henry, the king’s son; Lanfranc, archbishop of Canterbury; Odo, bishop of Bayeux; Gislebert, bishop of Lisieux; Geoffrey, bishop of Coutances; Michael, bishop of Avranches; Gislebert, bishop of Évreux; Robert, bishop of Sées; Roger de Montgomerie, count; Robert, count of Mortain; William, count of Évreux; Roger de Beaumont; Robert, count of Meulan; Robert de Bellesme; Henry de Beaumont; Hugh de Montfort; [Col. 1368B] Montfort; Robert; Bertrand; William Bertrand; Richard, son of Turstin; Ranulf, viscount; Hugh, count; Eudo, viscount; Robert, count of Mowbray; Ingelram, son of Ilbert; Ralph, son of Ansered; William Goir; Rainard; Hugh, son of Hugh de Rosel; Cerlo de Lingaurio; Corballus the chamberlain, son of Rainard; William the canon, son of Sueri; Bernard, son of Ospac; Ralph, son of Harfred.

## XXIV. Letter of King William the Conqueror to his faithful men of Carlisle and beyond the Lyder, ordering them to receive Christianity from the bishop of Durham

*(Monasticum Anglicanum, II, 845.)*

William, king of England, to William, son of Theodoric, and to all his faithful men of Carlisle and to all who [Col. 1368C] dwell beyond the Lyder, greeting.

I command you to receive Christianity from the bishop of Durham and from his archdeacon, and to obey the aforesaid bishop in the laws of Christianity, just as you ought rightly to obey your own bishop. And see, as you love me, that henceforth you unjustly cause no further trouble there to the bishop’s ministers. Witnesses: Robert, son of Girold, and others.

## XXV. Another charter of the same king to G., viscount, and the barons of Carlisle

*(The same, p. 845.)*

William, king of England, to G., viscount, and to his barons of Carlisle, greeting.

I wish and command that you attend to matters of Christianity through the archdeacon of Durham just as you attended to them in the time of William, bishop of Durham, and so forth; witnessed by Eudo the steward.

## XXVI. Another charter of the same king concerning the lands of Lunt and Hough

*(The same.)*

William, king of England, to Thomas, archbishop, and to Bertram de Verdun and to his French and English barons of Cherivicleire, greeting.

Know that I have restored to Ranulf, bishop of Durham, all those lands concerning which there had been a dispute between him and Alan de Percy, namely Lunt and Hough, and whatever belongs to Wellenton; and you, Bertram, are to put him in seisin of them. Witnesses: William, the chancellor and count [Col. 1369A] of Meulan, and Robert, son of Haimo, at Salisbury, on the fourth day of Epiphany.

## XXVII. Charter of King William confirming the lands situated in the county of Warwick belonging to the abbey of Evesham

*(Monasticon Anglicanum, II, 852.)*

William, king of the English, to Bishop W. and Viscount R., greeting.

I command and order you to ensure that Abbot Adelwin may hold, with full honour and in peace, the lands of the church of Cheltenham—namely Saltford and Curdworth, and Milecot, and Ragley, and Arley, and Eccleshal, and Bildeburglunth, and Cralton, and Withlakesford, and Dorlitone, and the other lands which he possesses in the viscounty of Warwick—so that he may have and hold them for the use of the servants of God, with my good peace and protection. And I command you, Viscount R., not to consent that anyone do him injustice in any matter, because I do not wish to consent to this; rather, let him hold his possessions fully, with sake and soke and all customs. And if anyone should presume to do him injustice, let the abbot appeal to me, and I shall do him full justice concerning whatever he has claimed.

## XXVIII. Charter of William, duke of Normandy and king of England, by which he grants to the abbey of Fécamp in the duchy of Normandy the lands of Staning and Bermondsey in England

*(The same, II, 971.)*

I, William, by the mercy of God protector of the Normans [Col. 1369C] and also king of the English, moved by the fear and love of God and taking thought for my future, grant and confirm to the holy and undivided Trinity and to the church of Fécamp all its lands in England, namely the land of Staning and the land of Bermondsey, with absolutely all the appurtenances of those lands, with all laws and all liberties, free customs and immunities, and with all pleas, complaints, and all cases which exist or may arise, without any disturbance or diminution by any secular or judicial authority, just as possessions belonging to the royal fisc.

Therefore I command inviolably that the aforesaid lands, with absolutely all their appurtenances and their possessors, be free and quit of every customary burden of earthly servitude [Col. 1369D] and of every domination and subjection to barons, princes, and all others. Let the abbot and monks of the church of Fécamp, or their ministers, likewise possess every royal liberty and custom and all their jurisdiction over all matters and all affairs which occur or may occur in their land; and let no one except them intervene in these matters, because this is wholly a royal benefaction and free from every servitude.

Likewise, for my soul and for the souls of all my predecessors, I grant and confirm to the aforesaid church of Fécamp all its lands in Normandy, with all their appurtenances, with all the dignities, free customs, and immunities which my lord and predecessor, Richard, count of the Normans, gave as alms to the aforesaid church, free from all disturbance or diminution by any secular or judicial authority, just as possessions belonging to the royal fisc. I have learned this not only from the report of many, but also from his sealed letters.

If anyone should presume to act against this confirmation of mine, let him incur the anger of Almighty God and, under compulsion, pay one hundred pounds of gold into the royal fisc. And so that this may remain ratified and stable for all time, I confirm it by royal authority and with the sign of the cross, with the assent of my wife, my children, and my nobles, and I entrust it to be strengthened by the hands of my faithful men.

## XXIX. Charter of King William the Conqueror by which he confirms to the monastery of Fontenelle, in the duchy of Normandy, the donations of the churches of Minster, Brighton, Scorston, and Lancaster in England

*(The same, p. 974.)*

[Col. 1370C] Let it be known to all, present and future, that I, William, by the grace of God duke of Normandy and king of the English, for the redemption of my soul and the salvation of my wife and children, have granted to the monastery of Fontenelle, founded in honour of Saint Wandrille, for love of my chaplain Guncard, who became a monk there, four churches situated in English territory, with their tithes and all their customary dues, just as Guncard’s predecessor held them in the time of my predecessor, King Edward of blessed memory.

Two of these, Minster and Brighton, are in the county of Wiltshire. The fourth, Lancaster, is in the county of Dorset. And so that the donation may be ratified and confirmed, I have authorized it with my own sign, invoking anathema and a curse upon those who violate it [Col. 1370D] or wish to disturb it, and so forth.

## XXX. Charter of King William for the hospital of Saint Peter at York

*(The same, p. 369.)*

William, king of England, to all our men and liegemen, both French and English, greeting.

Know that I have given and confirmed to the hospital of Saint Peter at York that ancient alms on which the said hospital was founded: namely, from every plough-land under cultivation in the bishopric of York, one measure of grain. Witnesses: T., archbishop; Geoffrey Baynard; Ralph Paganell; and others.

## XXXI. Charter of William, king of the English, for the monastery of Fleury (1067)

*(Dom Martène, Thesaurus Anecdotorum, I, 196, from the archives of Saint-Ouen.)*

[Col. 1371A]

All who are held by this fragile and transitory life ought always to keep before their eyes the judgment of Almighty God, and to act while it is permitted, lest at his judgment they be found on the left hand with the reprobate. This applies especially to those whom God’s providence has raised above others, because the richer and more exalted they are than the rest, the more ready they ought to be to perform good works and to uphold just judgments.

Considering and diligently reflecting upon all these matters, Richard [Col. 1371B], duke of the Normans, and his brother Robert, for the redemption and salvation of their souls and those of their predecessors, gave to God and Saint Benedict the church of Saint James, situated on the border of Normandy and Brittany, together with the land and water belonging to that church.

Near this same church I, William, their successor, duke of the Normans and, by God’s mercy, made king of the English, when wars were pressing upon us and the place seemed more suitable for the purpose, built a castle for the defence of my land. Having done this, I assigned to it many things that had not previously belonged there, namely a tract of uncultivated land with its pond and toll, and the market of the cross. In exchange for this I gave Ralph, abbot, and the monks of Saint Michael a compensation and exchange, together with two fairs and a road toll.

[Col. 1371C] I constructed three ponds and made the men who were living there of their own will remain permanently. When the monks of Saint Benedict saw that the place had been improved through me, with God’s help, Hugh the abbot and many others, by common counsel of the chapter of Saint Benedict, came into my presence, asking and humbly entreating that I give them half of what I had added to the aforesaid place, on the condition that they too admit me to half of their possessions, except for the church and the things belonging to it, which were and are theirs.

I willingly agreed to their request. The division between us was as follows: of the entire castle—namely, of the mills, ovens, tolls, road tolls, fairs, markets, all jurisdictions, and all revenues and customs received from the castle itself or from its surroundings, and of everything belonging to these matters that might be improved there—I retained half for myself and gave half to them, so that from this day forward it should perpetually belong by right and dominion to Saint Benedict and the brothers of the monastery of Fleury.

Of the three ponds which I made there, I retained for myself the fishing of the upper pond; I granted the entire fishing of the middle pond to them; and of the third pond I retained half the fishing for myself and gave them half.

[Col. 1372A] Concerning the ministers, we decreed that the ministers of Saint Benedict should swear fidelity to me, and that my ministers should swear fidelity to Saint Benedict and the monks.

And because in this matter I sought and desired a recompense for my soul more than for my body, they promised me this, and I required this gift from them: that every week, for the salvation and safety of myself, my wife, and my children, and for the remedy of the souls of my predecessors and successors, they should celebrate one Mass; that they should maintain one monk in the monastery of Saint Benedict in place of myself during my lifetime; and that they should always feed one poor person.

They also promised and agreed to provide prayers, alms, and benefactions for me during my life and after my death, not only in the monastery of Saint Benedict but also in the monasteries [Col. 1372B] of Fleury. The abbot and all the monks granted this to me by common counsel. And so that this might remain firm and unbroken, I confirmed it below with the sign of my subscription and strengthened it with the assent of my wife and children, and so forth.

## XXXII. Charter of William I, king of the English, separating ecclesiastical pleas from civil cases

[Note: Concerning the date of this charter’s composition, it seems to have been around the year of the Lord 1085. For Matthew Paris, speaking under this year in *The Deeds of King William*, says: “King William had shortly before given the bishopric of Dorchester to Remigius, a monk of Fécamp; [Col. 1372D] but Remigius transferred the episcopate to Lincoln in the year 1085, and there founded a church on the summit of the hill.” This charter is among the privileges of the bishop of Lincoln, after the episcopate had been transferred.]

*(Mansi, Concilia, vol. XX, col. 605, from a manuscript codex belonging to the dean and chapter of the cathedral church of Saint Paul, London.)*

[Col. 1372C]

William, by the grace of God king of the English, to R. Bainard, G. de Mandeville, P. de Valognes, and to my other faithful men of Essex, Hertfordshire, and Middlesex, greeting.

Know, all of you and my other faithful men who remain in England, that I judged that the episcopal laws which, up to my time, had existed in the kingdom of the English neither properly nor according to the precepts of the holy canons should be amended by common counsel and by the counsel of the archbishops, bishops, abbots, and all the princes of my kingdom.

Therefore I command, and by royal authority order, that no bishop or archdeacon henceforth hold pleas concerning episcopal laws in a hundred court, nor bring a case belonging to the governance of souls before the judgment of secular men. Rather, whoever is summoned under episcopal law concerning any case or offence must come to the place which the bishop shall have chosen and designated for this purpose; there he must answer concerning his case or offence, and must do right to God and to his bishop, not according to the hundred court [Col. 1373A] but according to the canons and episcopal laws.

If anyone, raised up by pride, should disdain or refuse to come to episcopal justice, let him be summoned once, a second time, and a third time. If even then he does not come to be corrected, let him be excommunicated; and, if necessary for enforcing this, let the strength and justice of the king or the viscount be applied. He who, having been summoned, refuses to come to the bishop’s justice shall make amends according to episcopal law for each summons.

This also I forbid and prohibit by my authority: no viscount, reeve, or royal minister, nor any layman, is to intervene in laws belonging to the bishop; and no layman is to bring another man to judgment without the bishop’s justice. Judgment is to be held nowhere except at the episcopal see or in the place which the bishop shall have built for this purpose.

## XXXIII. Charter of William, king of the English, for the monastery of Saint-Riquier

*(From d’Achery’s *Spicilegium*, IV, 574.)*

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, William, by the grace of God duke of the Normans, to all the sons of the Catholic Church who have care of soul and body.

We wish it to be known to all future generations how I confirmed that the church of Scamelli-Villa should be held perpetually by Saint Riquier for the salvation of my soul, by the force of our authority [Col. 1373C]. When the abbess of the monastery of Villaris brought a claim against it, and I had been summoned by Gervinus, abbot of the monastery of Saint Riquier, the cause of this matter having been explained by him in person before the leading men of my court, I restored it to him, since judgment had determined that it belonged to him by right through the donation of my predecessors. I further gave him, as a pledge of credibility, my word that henceforth he should hold it freely under my protection, just as he had received it from my grandfather and father.

For I had observed, as the account of those who knew the case suggested, that the prebendary ought, on account of this benefice, to be duly present among them in remembrance of us. Therefore, lest our confirmation be annulled by the rashness of anyone in the future and lest we lose our merit, we caused the letters of this testament to be written.

Done in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1047, at Argentan, on the third day before the Kalends of November. The suitable witnesses to this matter are Storinstingus, Richard his son; Yvo de Bellême; Arnulf his nephew; Ralph Taxo.

## XXXIV. Charter of William, king of the English, for the Greater Monastery of Saint Martin

*(Baluze, *Miscellanea*, VII, 227.)*

We wish this to be known to all who in future times shall hear it [Col. 1374B]: I, William, by the grace of God count of the Normans, for the remedy of my soul and those of my parents, especially my father and mother, and also of my wife and heirs, grant in perpetuity to God and Saint Martin—that is, to the monks who serve God at the Greater Monastery under Abbot Albert—and likewise to their successors, the abbots and monks who shall labour in God’s service in that monastery, an entire whale’s tongue every year in the county of Coutances, at the town of Valognes, in the presence of the witnesses whose names are written below.

Whoever wishes to withdraw this alms from Saint Martin, whether in my time or in that of my heirs, let him himself also be excommunicated, and let his attempt have no effect, so that, while my alms remains stable, my memory may likewise become perpetual in that monastery.

# In the Year of the Lord 1088: Durand, Abbot of Troarn

## Historical Notice

*(Galland, *Bibliotheca Veterum Patrum*, vol. XIV, Prolegomena, p. IX.)*

Durand was a monk of Fécamp from childhood, of the order of Saint Benedict, and soon became the first abbot of Troarn, in the recently founded monastery of the diocese of Bayeux established by Count Roger de Montgomerie. He was a contemporary of Fulbert of Chartres, whom he calls the bishop of his own time and who is known to have died in the year 1028 of Christ. He wrote a book *On the Body and Blood of the Lord* against Berengar, which he divided into nine parts and which, it is believed, was written in the year 1060. He died, having reached a good old age, in 1088.

Testimonies of Orderic Vitalis, book VII of the *Ecclesiastical History*, under the year 1087, p. 658:

> “In choosing men, I investigated the merit of their lives and the teaching of their wisdom”—these are the words of William the Conqueror as he lay at the point of death—“and, insofar as it lay within my power, I entrusted the governance of the Church to the most worthy of all. This can truly be demonstrated in Lanfranc, archbishop of Canterbury; in Anselm, abbot of Bec; in Gerebert of Fontenelle; and in Durand of Troarn; and in many other teachers of my kingdom, whose celebrated praise, as I believe, resounds to the farthest ends of the earth. I chose such companions for conversation; in their fellowship I found truth and wisdom; therefore I always gladly desired to enjoy their counsels.”

And book VIII, p. 676:

> “Durand, abbot of Troarn, advanced in years, a monk from childhood, distinguished in religion and wisdom, a most skilled teacher of ecclesiastical song and divine doctrine, a harsh executioner toward himself but a gentle worker for others, after many labours in the worship of God, lay down upon his bed and, well prepared, like a prudent and faithful servant, to go to the court of his Lord, departed from this world on the third day before the Ides of February.”

Then, shortly afterward:

> “The venerable disciples reverently buried the body of the religious teacher in their chapter house, and on the white stone that was placed there they added this epitaph:”

> Here lies beneath this tomb a good and venerable abbot,  
> Durand, the standard of our monastery.  
> For the praise of the Lord he founded this present building,  
> In which we believe that God is favourable to him.  
> Under February’s eleventh light, released from the bond  
> Of the flesh, he is directed toward the angelic homeland.

# Book of Lord Durand, Abbot of Troarn, on the Body and Blood of Christ against Berengar and His Followers

*(Galland, *Bibliotheca Veterum Patrum*, vol. XIV, p. 245, from the manuscript codex of the library of Lord Bigot, senator of the Rouen mint.)*

## Preface

The labour of all the doctors is to inquire into books,  
So that the substance of divine things  
May rightly be understood, hidden beneath the form  
Of bread and wine—which, after the sacred words  
And also the sign of the cross, are nothing other  
Than true flesh and true blood  
Of the true body of Christ reigning in the heavens,  
As befits the King of kings and Lord of lords.

Let these things therefore be sufficient for those less learned,  
Drawn from many books of the earlier Fathers.  
In them the strength of faith shines forth,  
And there is provided no small advantage of harmonious brevity  
For recitation, but only for the simple.  
Let the wise go further,  
And, trusting in study, read more substantial things with understanding.

[Col. 1376] But lest anyone rashly suppose that we deserve reproach  
Because we seem to have presumed to undertake such things,  
Let him learn that we have been compelled by great wickedness:  
The heresy of schismatics wandering through the regions  
And camps of the Franks, through whom in our times  
A new error has begun, denying the venerable mysteries of Christ,  
By which the holy faith of the Church flourishes  
And is nobly established.

Therefore, lest anyone mock the humble labour of the learned,  
I confess that this little work of ours will please many.  
For I have selected the finest sayings of the Fathers of old,  
Of sincere faith, concerning the flesh and blood of Christ,  
And gathered many things together in this small book.

# Here Begins the Book of Lord Durand, Abbot, on the Body and Blood of the Lord

[Col. 1375]

## Part One

[Col. 1375] I. Since the ancient enemy, the enemy of the human race and cruel murderer, according to the apostle’s saying, goes about like a roaring lion seeking whom he may devour, we must resist him, strong in faith, without which it is utterly impossible to please God. For faith is what breaks his strength, dulls his insolence, triumphs over him victoriously, and carries away the prize of everlasting life [Col. 1377A].

For that poisonous serpent, the ancient plague of mortals, who from the beginning of the faith has spread throughout the whole world the many-formed poison of heretical perversity through vessels fitted for the destruction of his deception, now also tries through the hidden accomplices and servants of his wickedness subtly to undermine the Catholic faith and, by carefully devised arguments, to weaken the Church of Christ, founded from ancient times upon its truth.

For he has persuaded certain people, who are wise in their own eyes and perversely deceive not so much others as themselves, to hold—and through crafty whispers gradually and secretly to suggest to others that they should hold—that nothing is effected in the Lord’s sacraments according to truth, but that everything is done rather through figure and likeness.

In order cunningly to strip themselves of suspicion of heresy and to make themselves appear to agree with the Lord’s teaching, they cloak themselves in this artifice of cunning and so temper and colour the doctrine of their profane novelty that they say that the gifts brought to the altar, bread and wine, remain after consecration what they had been, and that in some manner they are the true body and blood of Christ—not naturally, but figuratively.

They even rave that the very substances of the divine offering are so corruptible and subject to corruption that they perish in the digestion of ordinary food and, when consumed in excessive quantity, can be turned into gluttony and the madness of drunkenness.

But they also feel and do not cease whispering to their confidants and to those less suspicious other things far more serious and much more shameful than these—things which, not to say openly, it is even impious merely to think faintly.

Yet I believe that such men should be questioned, and that such teachers should be consulted, as to what usefulness is produced by a profession of this kind, in which no holiness and absolutely no trace of holiness to be imitated is found, but everything is unsound and shameful and serves the dissolution of perverse morals and actions.

If such great perversity is admitted—that no truth is believed to exist in the Lord’s mysteries, but only a shadowy falsehood is asserted, together with the shameful corruption of those same sacraments that follows from it—what, I ask, remains except that the whole discipline of the Christian profession has perished?

For just as in these things the solid strength of Catholic faith and the sum of human salvation [Col. 1377D] consists, so, once these have been taken away, nothing holy and nothing meritorious will remain. For if falsehood is discovered here, where, I ask, will truth be found?

Therefore there will no longer be any fear or reverence in holy things. No one will cultivate purity of heart; no one will honour sanctity of body. Everything will be dissolved, everything altogether disordered, once the discipline of the highest integrity has ceased.

And not without reason. For who thereafter would devote himself to moderation and sobriety? Who would render worship to the fear of God where there is no majesty of truth?

Moreover, if in the Lord’s food there is a figure and not substantial truth, then Christ, who said, “Take and eat; this is my body,” is not truthful. If he is not truthful, he is not God; if he is not God, the preaching of the saints throughout the world is empty, and empty also is the faith and profession of the Catholic Church, in which the precious blood of the martyrs was poured out to no purpose and the labour of the strong athletes in the theatre of the world, with Christ himself looking on, won a triumph over the enemy in vain. And consequently there is nothing that we do and nothing at all that we hope for.

Is this the abundant fruit? Is this the rich reward for which the shameless insolence of the schismatics busies itself? O ruined foundation, followed not by a structure but by such a collapse!

But far be it from us that Christ should not be God, since he is certainly truthful, because he truly is God. If he is truthful, then what is received as he extends it, what is eaten as he offers it, although in different ways according to the difference of merits, is nevertheless truly the Lord’s body. This can be clearly discerned by the purified inner vision alone, deeply examining it in the mirror of faith, while the weakness of the outward eyes is struck blind.

Nevertheless, with an evident proclamation of Truth, the modern dogmatists and agents of Satan resist, and with rash murmuring, in an impious and shameful freedom, maintain opinions that pollute even the air itself and corrupt the minds and hearts of those who favour them.

Yet, in order to avoid the stigma of such great infidelity and more freely to evade refutation, they diminish the authority of all interpreters of divine books—of blessed Pope Gregory, Leo, Maximus, and all the others who, apart from a few, laboured by discussing matters in the authentic writings of the Church.

## Part Two
[Col. 1378C] II. But it seems wholly inappropriate and absurd that debased and filthy men, who have contributed no benefit to the Catholic Church either through integrity of life or through the usefulness of their learning, should grow so bold that they seize the fruit of the labor of so many Fathers and teachers—men through whose life and instruction the orthodox faith is known to have flourished until now, and through whose preaching and perseverance to have increased and, with God’s assistance, advanced day by day toward better things—and that they should shamelessly bend us to themselves and perversely attach us to their error. Nevertheless, it is plainly ill-advised for us to abandon those whose teachings instruct us, whose examples of holy life shape us, and whose daily miracles enlighten us, and instead cling to those [Col. 1378D] whose life is contemptible. Even if there were in them a profession of teaching correctly, it would deservedly be worthless and liable to contempt. Indeed, this would be like renouncing life and embracing death; rejecting light and becoming entangled in darkness; disavowing truth and offering our hands to falsehood.

But far be it from us to be joined in equal treachery to men so perverse and so utterly turned away from truth itself, or to confess anything less concerning the holy communion of the Lord’s body and blood than what the Catholic Church throughout the world proclaims. In it there truly exists Christ’s flesh and true blood, just as Christ himself is proved to be truthful—he who first sanctified these things and then, by his power, granted them authority and the form of sanctifying. Faithfully received, they enlighten the righteous, justify sinners, and condemn the ungodly; and, though they are not recognized as operating differently in themselves, they are recognized as producing different effects in every profession and person according to the quality of their merits. Nor should it thereafter be believed that they undergo the indignity or corruption of any injury; rather, by divine power they are poured back into spiritual operation.

Thus it is written: “The bread that I will give is my flesh for the life of the world.” The bread, therefore, is flesh, because Truth itself says: “The bread that I will give is my flesh”; but the flesh is life, and the life of the world—not corruption. For just as God and man, Jesus Christ, having completed the dispensation of human redemption, passed from death to life and from corruption to incorruption, so this divine and heavenly sacrament is rightly believed to be suddenly transformed from its visible appearance into that which he alone knows, in whom all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden—human things being joined to heavenly things through an operation sufficiently effective for that purpose. Hence the Lord says: “Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood remains in me, and I in him.”

Here, as is plainly clear to all sound-minded people, what is promised to the faithful is not the obscenity of digestion, but the reality of dwelling through the sacrament. Consequently, the divine mystery, faithfully and fittingly received, is transformed wholly by God into what it already was in part, from what had still remained subject to external sight. It sanctifies and elevates the souls and minds of those who receive it, fitting and preparing them for divine indwelling; and thereafter it rightly transforms them from death to life by its powerful efficacy, just as the Author of this gift attests when he says: “Whoever eats me will live because of me.”

[Col. 1379C] Let us now consider what the blessed teacher Augustine thought about this transformation, and what he left written on the subject in the third book of *On the Holy Trinity*. He says:

“If, then, the Apostle Paul, awaiting adoption and the redemption of his body, could proclaim the Lord Jesus Christ by signifying him differently through his tongue, differently through a letter, and differently through the sacrament of his body and blood, we do not call the membranes, ink, significant sounds uttered by the tongue, or letters written on skins the body and blood of Christ. Rather, we call that alone the body and blood of Christ which, taken from the fruits of the earth and consecrated by mystical prayer, we rightly receive for spiritual salvation, in memory of the Lord’s passion undertaken for us. When, through human hands, it is brought to that invisible form, it is not sanctified so as to become so great a sacrament unless the Spirit of God acts invisibly.

“Since, therefore, God performs all these things that occur in that work through bodily movements, first moving invisible realities—whether the souls of ministers who are human beings, or the hidden services of spirits subject to him—what wonder is it if God also does in the creature of heaven and earth, sea and air, whatever he wishes, using sensible and insensible things to signify and demonstrate him in them, as he himself knows ought to be done, without his own substance, which he is, appearing in them?”

In this statement we propose that special and careful attention be given to the point where it is said that Christ’s body is taken from the fruits of the earth and consecrated by mystical prayer through a certain divine hand. By the Holy Spirit working invisibly from the visible form, this great sacrament is unmistakably declared to be brought to an invisible form. In truth, from visible and earthly substances—that is, from bread and wine mixed with water—through the incomprehensible work of the Holy Spirit and through mystical words, the holy body of the Lord and his true blood are made, their appearance not being changed, but their nature. Nevertheless, the visible form of the same sacrament is truly brought, through heavenly commerce, among the hands of the ministers to an invisible form, so that it may become so great a sacrament—that is, wholly holiness and life for souls.

[Col. 1380B] Nor, as certain wicked men dare to fabricate in their ravings, is it dissolved into the corruption of digestion; rather, it effectively works life and salvation in the minds of those who partake. For this reason our Redeemer, the author and sanctifier of his mystery, says in the holy Gospel: “If anyone eats of this bread, he will live forever.”

When you hear “bread,” therefore, do not at all be disturbed or misled by the external appearance. Instead, attend more carefully to what follows, where the same Lord graciously and plainly explains his words and, under the appearance of a visible thing, wishes to display something else much more clearly and magnificently. For he says: “And the bread that I will give is my flesh.”

Behold how clearly it is expressed that what had previously been called something else—that is, bread—is now called flesh. It is called flesh and is called bread: bread because it is food, or because of the likeness appearing externally; flesh because it is life, and because of the truth hidden inwardly through its dispensation. It is called bread so that you may not immediately recoil at the sound of the word, as many of the disciples once did, of whom it is written: “They went back and no longer walked with Jesus, saying: ‘This is a hard saying; who can hear it?’” But it is called flesh so that you may be invited by the contemplation of so great a novelty and drawn inward by the promise of so immense a benefit.

Then follows: “For the life of the world”—life, certainly, not corruption, as the impious recklessness of modern heretics asserts: “for the life of the world,” he says. The world was formerly unclean because of the filth and stains of corrupted life [Col. 1380D] and works of iniquity, by which human nature had been contaminated both through the transgression of the first parent and through the necessity of a corrupted origin, and had become increasingly polluted as it continually declined toward worse things. But now it has been fully cleansed by the glorious blood of Christ, poured out like that of an immaculate lamb sacrificed upon the altar of the cross by the soldier’s spear, because from the place where guilt arose, grace also flowed.

For Eve was formed and came forth from the side of the sleeping Adam, and through the transgression of the commandment she brought the condemnation of death upon the world. From the side, nevertheless, of the second Adam—that is, Christ—fastened to the cross and brought into the sleep of a three-day death, blood and water flowed forth; after excluding the punishment of eternal death, they poured back the grace of everlasting life.

From there plainly comes the salvation; from there comes the life of the world. To cleanse it from every stain of sin, both original and actual, divine Providence, taking pity on human errors, provided this singular remedy. Thus, in his holy Church, already spread far and wide throughout the whole world, he established one unique and special sacrifice, by which God himself is mercifully reconciled to the world and mortal weakness, offending him by daily crimes, is reconciled to him.

Whoever contradicts this by refusing to believe rightly, or by shamelessly and impiously blaspheming, being in every respect ungrateful for divine benefits, closes against his own salvation the entrance to heavenly reconciliation. Therefore he cannot in any way attain the grace of life that has been established in so great a sacrament.
