Concerning this it was stated above: “The bread that I will give is my flesh for the life of the world.”

## PART THREE

[Col. 1381B]

### III

It is worthwhile to examine more carefully how the Lord’s flesh was offered twice for the life of the world. First, once in the sacrament, when our Redeemer himself took bread in his hands, lifted his eyes to heaven, blessed it, broke it, and then gave it to his disciples, saying: “Take and eat; this is my body.”

Hence this is also the form of the holy sacrifice, which was offered not merely once in price, when the same Son of God ascended the gallows of the cross in order that the human race might be redeemed, and offered himself to his Father as both priest and victim. This manner of sacrifice was already prefigured when, as we have said, the same Savior, now near in place and time to the death he had chosen, sanctified the visible substance of bread, saying: “Take and eat; this is my body.”

[Col. 1381C] And lest any perverse person be left an opportunity to err or to understand something else, he added: “Which will be delivered for you.” By these words all impious arguments of opinion and the false inventions of the recent heresy are excluded, since the Lord Jesus so absolutely testified that what he held in his hands and offered to his disciples was his own body—and nothing other than what was to be delivered for them.

It should certainly be considered with particular care that divine piety, which knows all things both new and ancient, just as it handed down its sacraments to its holy Church for salvation, so fortified them through both its deeds and its words, so that they could not be weakened or contradicted in any respect.

Therefore, to the words already mentioned he adds: “Do this,” as though he were saying: “What I have done by my own power, do by my authority. I act as the example; you act through imitation. Do this.”

Who? You who are mine, who are now disciples; and after you, those who have not seen and yet have believed, and therefore are truly blessed.

“Do this.” What does “do this” mean? It means: with my words and my invocation, consecrate this body and this blood. And not once, as I do, but whenever you receive it. For what purpose? “In remembrance of me,” he says—that is, so that through this you may hold my memory more firmly and recall to mind that I suffered for you; finally, so that you may be able spiritually to see me, feel me as present, and possess me without doubt.

And because I am going to die once, and death will in no way rule over me thereafter, recall my death through frequent use, so that it may be for you a salutary reminder of piety and may become a unique and powerful means of obtaining more specially the favor of my Father.

No one, even the least of the faithful, should be persuaded that a thing so divine, so salutary, and so full of power and majesty perishes through indigestion. Rather, once received, it ought to be believed to console us in the present under the hope of the future glorification that is awaited, and to prepare us by its powerful effect to earn afterward what it promises.

It seems exceedingly absurd, and is judged foreign to the matter itself, that where Christ is received, one should think of excrement. The Apostle does not grant this even to those who approve of it and are therefore rightly called “Stercorites.” Rather, it is asserted that they eat and drink judgment because they do not discern properly, while the faithful faithfully receive the Lord’s body and blood under the visible form of the divine sacrament that we celebrate.

For this reason we now remain naturally in Christ through the communion of his holy flesh, and he in turn graciously deigns to remain in us through the assumed mortality of our weakness. He incorporated us powerfully into himself by adapting himself graciously to us; and thus, through assuming our humanity, he became one with us, while through our communion with his flesh and blood he made us naturally one with him.

As the blessed Hilary also defined in the book he titled *On the Holy Trinity*, foreseeing this new heresy, as I believe, in the spirit:

“Now I ask those who introduce a unity of will between the Father and the Son whether Christ is in us today through the truth of nature or through harmony of will. For if the Word truly became flesh, and we truly receive the Word as flesh in the Lord’s food, how is he not to be considered to remain naturally in us, since he also implanted in himself the nature of our flesh?”

[Col. 1382D] Attend carefully, I ask, and note how often he repeats the words “truly” and “nature.” First he stated that the Word truly became flesh; then he asserted that we truly receive the Word as flesh in the Lord’s food, clearly indicating through these teachings that the flesh of the Word is received in sacramental food in the same manner as the Word became flesh.

Since the Word truly became flesh, it must likewise be believed that the same flesh of the Word—or rather, the Word as flesh—is truly received as food, and not through an empty figure of truth. Nor should there be any hesitation that, if what was stated first is true, what follows is consistent with the truth: namely, just as the reality of the Incarnation took place in the Word, so the true reception through the sacrament of the Lord’s flesh must be believed—flesh taken from us and now seated in heaven as a sharer in majesty.

### IV

From this point the Lord himself, in order to instruct us in the truth of this matter, says to his disciples: “My flesh is truly food, and my blood is truly drink.” What could be clearer? What could be more explicit? Behold, Truth itself testifies about himself, while the recent heresy shamelessly resists him and wickedly pursues the dense cloud of likeness and figure.

The divine sophist and heavenly rhetorician Hilary forcefully strikes back at it and tramples it down in refutation:

“How is he not to be considered to remain naturally in us,” he says, “who, born as man, took to himself the nature of our flesh, now inseparably united to him, and mingled the nature of his flesh with the nature of eternity under the sacrament of the flesh that was to be communicated to us?”

Here he emphasized “nature” a third time and in as many ways: the Word, which existed and remained from the beginning, assumed the nature of our flesh, which had not existed in him and was inseparably united to him; then he mingled the nature of his flesh with the nature of eternity. Consequently, he provided it to us as communicable under the sacrament.

Therefore there can be no doubt that human nature can reach the food of the divine flesh, which, through the ineffable commerce of the Word, has been brought even to participation in the worshipful divinity. Otherwise everything Scripture reports would be pagan and utterly senseless: “Worship his footstool, for it is holy.”

The footstool of divinity is the holy humanity of the Redeemer. Because of the truth of its inseparable union, it must be accorded the reverence of humble adoration, especially when it supplies the gift of reciprocal communion. For this purpose it was divinely instituted; for this purpose the Lord commanded it to his disciples; and for this purpose this venerable sacrament has come down to us: so that through the mystery of unity, obtained by participation in it, we may become a pleasing dwelling and kingdom of divinity, transformed from human things into divine and ineffably elevated from carnal things to spiritual ones.

### V

If, then, we do not reject what is greater, having been bestowed upon us, nor deny that what is less can be granted—namely, that under the mystery we rightly receive the flesh of Christ’s body, which is already near to us because he graciously assumed the flesh of our body, while what is above us is so because Christ was truly born as a human being from a virgin—then no room remains for doubt concerning the truth of his flesh and blood.

For, both by the profession of the Lord himself and by our faith, the sacred consecrated gift of the life-giving sacrament truly is flesh and truly is blood. Faithfully received, it brings about this result: that we are in Christ and Christ in us.

This is the cause of our life; this is our salvation: that we, who are carnal, have Christ dwelling in us through his flesh. Although he is now of a different dignity and glory from us, he is nevertheless naturally flesh, as we are. For assumption does not remove nature but glorifies it, when the Word and flesh become one.

Therefore, even now the Word made flesh remains in us who are carnal. While we run in the arena of corruptible life, Christ God arranged, through that dispensation, that he should remain in us, and by the remedy granted through his passion and the punishment of his death he provided that we might one day be raised to behold his dignity and merit it according to our measure, so that we might become like him, seeing him as he is.

And truly this is the cause of our life: Life itself died for us so that it might become our ordinary food. This also is the firm hope of the glory we are to merit, because here we hold, as a pledge, the flesh of the glorious divinity. Through it we possess Christ, who is Lord of hosts and King of glory, dwelling meanwhile in us who are carnal, while through the ministry of the ministers, with every scruple of error removed, we receive the true flesh, natural to the Word himself.

Is this not the truth? Behold once again the most discerning contemplator of the divine mystery rebukes the authors of falsehood and, urged by the Spirit of Christ who spoke in him, adds an imprecation of the punishment by which those who are guilty of so great a matter deserve to be chastised:

“Let it plainly happen to those who deny that Christ Jesus is true God that this is not true.”

We too, like him, may wish this upon them, unless they repent of their error, so that at least through the torment of punishment they may experience what they have denied.

But may the kindness of the Savior, through his truth and our faith, grant us what he promised: that we, having received the nature and property of his flesh and professing perfect unity on both sides, may remain in him and he in us, and that the desirable companionship of pious belief may become the worthy reward of the majesty graciously entering into us and of the divinity presently dwelling with us, through the suitable pledge of so great a grace and power.

## PART FOUR

### VI

Although the authority of so great a man is sufficient, I nevertheless wish to draw out certain passages from Saint Ambrose, whose authority in the Catholic Church after the apostles is regarded as preeminent, and whose abundant eloquence is both the glory and the model of the Latin language. I shall also draw out passages from the blessed Augustine, whose proven faith and manifold, useful, and renowned labor in the Scriptures are attested.

We shall further append some statements of other holy Fathers, gathered from scattered sources through careful study and no small labor, so that they may be pleasing to those who piously seek the truth concerning this matter and more than sufficient to strengthen the account of the faith.

### VII

The aforesaid Ambrose says in his book *On the Mysteries*:

“Let us now consider this matter, lest someone, seeing visible things—for invisible things are not seen and cannot be grasped by human eyes—should say: ‘Manna rained down upon the Jews; hence it is said: “Man ate the bread of angels.”’ Yet all those who ate that bread died in the desert. But this food that you receive, this living bread that came down from heaven, supplies the substance of eternal life, and it is the body of Christ.

“Consider now whether the bread of angels is greater, or the flesh of Christ, which is certainly the body of life. That manna was from heaven; this is above heaven. That was of heaven; this is of the Lord of heavens. That was subject to corruption if it was kept for another day; this is free from every corruption, so that whoever has tasted it devoutly cannot experience corruption.

“For them water flowed from the rock; for you blood flows from Christ. Water satisfied them for an hour; blood washes you forever. The Jew drank and thirsted; when you have drunk, you cannot thirst. The former was in shadow; this is in truth.”

And after a little:

“How many examples, then, do we use to prove that this is not what nature formed, but what blessing consecrated, and that the power of blessing is greater than that of nature, because by blessing nature itself is also changed?”

And after some intervening material:

“If, then, human blessing had such power that it could change nature, what shall we say about the divine consecration itself, where the very words of the Lord the Savior operate? For this sacrament that you receive is made through Christ’s word. If Elijah’s word had such power that it could bring down fire from heaven, will Christ’s word not have power to change the appearance of the elements?

“Concerning the works of the whole world you have read: ‘For he spoke, and they came to be; he commanded, and they were created.’ Therefore, the word of Christ, which could make from nothing what did not exist, cannot change what exists into what did not exist? For it is no less to give new things to things than to change their natures. Is it not greater to give new things than to change natures?

“But why do we use arguments? Let us use his own examples and establish the truth through the mystery of the Incarnation—or, according to another reading, ‘of the mystery.’ Did the ordinary course of nature precede when the Lord Jesus was born from Mary? If we seek the natural order, a woman joined to a man is accustomed to give birth. It is therefore clear that the Virgin gave birth beyond the order of nature, and that this body which we consecrate is from the Virgin.

“Why, then, should we seek the order of nature in Christ’s body, when the Lord Jesus himself was born from a Virgin beyond nature? It is truly the flesh of Christ that was crucified and buried. Therefore it is truly the sacrament of that flesh. The Lord Jesus himself cries out: ‘This is my body.’

“Before the words of the heavenly blessing, one kind of thing is named; after consecration, the body of Christ is signified. He himself calls it his blood. Before consecration it is called one thing; after consecration it is named blood. And you say: ‘Amen’—that is, ‘It is true.’ Let what the word sounds forth be felt by the heart. With these sacraments, then, Christ Jesus feeds his Church, and by them the substance of the soul is strengthened.”

And shortly afterward:

“Christ is in that sacrament because it is the body of Christ. It is not, therefore, bodily food but spiritual food. Hence the Apostle says of its type: ‘Our fathers ate spiritual food and drank spiritual drink.’ For the body of the Lord is a spiritual body. The body of Christ is the body of the divine Spirit.”

Faithfully weighed, the judgment of so great a man destroys all the tricks and every argument of the heretics, and from the opposite direction instructs and strengthens the Catholic faith. It sufficiently establishes the devotion of the faithful concerning the natural truth of the body and blood of Jesus Christ the Savior, so that thereafter it may not waver in any respect.

Since we do not have time to examine it point by point wherever this would be necessary, we pass through it briefly, urging those who will read these things to make a more careful inquiry for themselves and to strive to understand what we have passed over without discussion.

### VIII

He says:

“This food that you receive, this living bread that came down from heaven, supplies the substance of eternal life, and is the body of Christ.”

Here it is necessary to observe that he unquestionably calls the food and bread that we receive from the sacred altar the Lord’s body, and that for this reason it supplies the substance of eternal life to those who receive it with worthy devotion of heart.

And truly so. For Christ is truly life, as he himself said: “I am the way, the truth, and the life.” It is necessary that whoever faithfully receives Christ within himself should be deemed worthy to become a participant in eternal life. Far from that life is anyone who does not fear to distance himself from the holy mystery, whether by living badly or by believing incorrectly. Each person is nearer to it insofar as he lives more correctly through devotion to the true faith.

Lest anyone be able to interpret or understand “body” in another way, since the Apostle says: “There are heavenly bodies and earthly bodies,” the same teacher of Christ immediately afterward calls it Christ’s flesh, saying:

“Consider now whether the bread of angels is greater, or the flesh of Christ, which is certainly the body of life.”

The flesh of Christ is truly the body of life, because Christ himself, for whom that flesh is a substantial body, is immortal life; or because it is established that, for those who faithfully partake of him, it spiritually produces life.

And shortly afterward:

“That manna,” he says, “was a shadow; this is the body in truth.”

Manna is not improperly called a shadow, because although it truly was a heavenly creature, it nevertheless signified something other than what it appeared to be. It existed as a figure or shadow of the future mystery, not as the truth itself—a truth that was awaited and was to be revealed in the last times, when, as the fullness ordained by the providence of the divine plan before the ages was already approaching, God himself deigned to become human for human beings.

He prepared this heavenly—or rather divine—gift not as he had previously given that manna through Moses, but through his own person. He gave it to his disciples to celebrate in memory of him until the consummation of the age, when he will come openly, saying:

“Do this whenever you receive it in remembrance of me.”

From this it is plainly established that the same truth of flesh and blood exists in the sacrament that the holy Church throughout the world celebrates uniformly. It was also present in that which Christ God himself sanctified with his holy hands and distributed to those holy men who had followed him from the beginning of his preaching:

“Take and eat,” he said; “this is my body.”

And thereafter:

“Do this,” he says, “in remembrance of me.”

This word, as we believe and confess, is the word to which the consecration of the Lord’s mystery is plainly performed daily. Although it is seen by human eyes to be something else, and although it is not denied that, for useful typological reasons, it signifies something else, nevertheless it is proved to be substantially nothing other than the true flesh and true blood of Christ.

And as the blessed Ambrose said above:

“After the heavenly words, it is no longer what nature formed, but what heavenly blessing consecrated, because the power of the blessing poured down from heaven is greater than nature, since by blessing nature itself is changed from what it was into what it was not.”

Elsewhere, in his book *On the Sacraments*, he likewise says:

“This bread is bread before the words of the sacraments; when consecration has been added, from bread it becomes the flesh of Christ.”

And shortly afterward:

“If, then,” he says, “there is such power in the word of the Lord that things which did not exist began to exist, how much more operative is it that things which existed should come to be and be changed into something else?”

By this brief statement the perfidy of the heretics is more clearly destroyed. They argue against the divine sacraments otherwise than Truth itself teaches, asserting that in them there is only a figure and not the truth, and that the creature remains altogether what it was. They claim that it possesses some spiritual power through the blessing, by which it is called the Lord’s body, but that the truth of the things is not changed into anything other than what it was.

Yet Ambrose says: “This body is in truth.” He himself explains how it is in truth, saying:

“It is not what nature formed, but what blessing consecrated, because by blessing nature is changed.”

## IX

But because there are some who seem to themselves somewhat more prudent and religious than these men, who indeed say that it is Christ’s flesh, but not that flesh which Christ himself received from the holy Virgin, in which he suffered and rose from the dead, and which, alive and true, he carried up to heaven in the triumph of victory; rather, they say it is some new flesh, freshly consecrated by the blessing—this aforementioned teacher most clearly defines their error, utterly destroying it and more firmly building up the Catholic faith, by showing how one ought, according to the Truth, to understand this matter.

For he says: “It is therefore clear that the Virgin gave birth contrary to the order of nature, and that this body which we consecrate is from the Virgin.” And a little later [Col. 1387C]: “It is truly the flesh of Christ which was crucified, which was buried. Therefore it is truly the sacrament of that flesh; for the Lord Jesus himself cries out: ‘This is my body.’”

From all these statements it is clearer than daylight that the Lord’s sacraments are truly the body and blood of Christ, not only through the efficacy of power and spiritual potency, but also in the unimpaired propriety of natural truth; and that they are absolutely nothing other than the very same flesh which the Virgin conceived from the Holy Spirit and brought forth while the integrity of her inviolate virginity remained intact—contrary to human custom, but not contrary to the truth of a human body. That flesh was condemned to the suspension of the cross and subjected to the punishment of death, but afterward glorified by the triumph of blessed resurrection; it overcame the heights of heaven [Col. 1387D] and now sits at the eternal right hand of the Father. There, according to the truthful words of the apostle Paul, having been made high priest forever on behalf of human flesh, it diligently intercedes for us; yet, through the natural truth of divinity, it receives the prayers of its faithful and grants their petitions, by divine power and majesty.

Here it seems appropriate to add further testimonies of the same teacher on this subject, so that the abundance of his statements may satisfy the faithful and utterly deprive the impious of the vain and profane freedom to teach.

Thus, in the third book *On Virginity*, he says:

“See how great a people comes to the birthday of your Bridegroom, and no one returns unfed. In the end, he invited many to his wedding; but now it is not bread from barley that is served, but a body from heaven.”

And after much else:

“He was wounded in his passion, and from the wound came water and blood for the spirit’s drink unto resurrection [Col. 1388A]. For there is one Christ for us in faith, hope, and charity: faith in the washing, hope in the resurrection, charity in the sacrament.”

In the second book *On Widowhood*:

“The Lord,” he says, “Jesus supplied some with barley bread, lest they should fail on the way; to others he supplied his body, so that they might strive toward the kingdom.”

And in the book *On the Sacraments*:

“Therefore you have learned,” he says, “how bread becomes Christ’s body. And what then? Wine is poured into the chalice; but through heavenly consecration it becomes blood.”

And a little later:

“Before it is consecrated, it is bread; but when the words of Christ have been added, it is Christ’s body. And before Christ’s words, the chalice is full of wine and water; when Christ’s words have worked, there blood is produced. Then the Lord Jesus Christ himself has testified to us that we receive his body and blood. Surely we ought not to doubt his testimony and faith?” [Col. 1388B]

And in the earlier book *On the Sacraments*:

“As,” he says, “the Lord Jesus Christ is truly the Son of God—not as human beings are sons through grace, but as a son from the substance of the Father—so too is the flesh truly what he himself said it is, the flesh which we receive. But perhaps you say: ‘How is it true? I see a likeness, but I do not see the truth of the blood.’ First of all, I told you about the word of Christ, which works so that it can change and transform established kinds. Then, when the disciples could not endure Christ’s saying that he would give them his flesh to eat and his blood to drink, they were withdrawing. Therefore, so that more would not do this [al.: say this], and so that there might be something like a horror of bloodshed, while the grace of redemption nevertheless remained [Col. 1388C], you receive the sacraments in a likeness, but you attain the grace and power of the true nature.

“‘I am,’ he says, ‘the living bread which came down from heaven.’ But the flesh did not descend from heaven; that is, he assumed flesh on earth from the Virgin. How, then, did bread descend from heaven, and living bread? Because our same Lord Jesus Christ is a sharer both in divinity and in body; and you who receive the flesh become a partaker of his divine substance through this nourishment.”

In this statement, therefore, blessed Ambrose clearly explains why he previously said that the likeness of flesh or blood is seen, not its appearance: namely, because, by a providential arrangement, the appearance—that is, the truth of flesh and blood—is hidden in the sacrament, lest, if it appeared as it is, the sight of it should inspire horror in those who saw it [Col. 1388D]. “In a likeness,” he says, “you receive the truth, lest the truth itself should inspire horror in you.” The likeness is therefore displayed so that the horror of the truth may be driven away; yet the grace of the true nature, of flesh and blood, is not diminished, since true flesh and true blood of Christ are received under another likeness.

The likeness of flesh and blood is called bread and wine either because of the very truth which, although concealed, they possess, or because, in a certain respect, they are flesh and blood: rightly so called because, through their customary use, they preserve the life of those who consume them and, through natural growth, are changed into flesh and blood. Hence it was also entirely fitting that the Savior should establish that his flesh and blood be consecrated from the substance of bread and wine—things by which mortal life itself is sustained [Col. 1389A] and through which human substance continually increases, since, once taken as food and drink, they are transformed by a certain hidden force of nature into flesh and blood.

Nevertheless, in truth, after consecration the bread and wine are flesh and blood, although their appearance is concealed beneath the divinely preordained visible likeness of material things.

As the same bishop testifies in the second book of *On the Holy Trinity*:

“As a human being he says what is human, because he was speaking in my substance: ‘This is the living bread which came down from heaven.’ This bread is flesh, as he himself said: ‘The bread which I shall give is my flesh.’”

And in the eighth book:

“Let us see,” he says, “whether the prophet may be speaking of that earth which the Lord Jesus Christ assumed in the taking on of flesh and which ought to be worshiped. Thus, by the footstool, earth is understood; and by earth, the flesh of Christ, which even today we worship in the mysteries.” [Col. 1389B]

Blessed Augustine, in the book *On the Words of the Lord*:

“I remember,” he says, “my sermon: when I was discussing the sacraments, I told you that, before the words of Christ, what is offered is called bread; but when Christ’s words have been pronounced, it is no longer called bread, but the body. Why, then, does he say ‘our bread’ in the Lord’s Prayer, which follows afterward? Bread indeed, but supersubstantial bread: this is not the bread which passes into the body, but that bread of eternal life which supports the substance of our soul.”

From this so very clear teaching concerning the Lord’s sacrament, then, it is understood that that heavenly consecration is not a shadow, but truly the body and blood. But when it is called “supersubstantial bread,” not the bread which passes into the body but that which supports the substance of our soul, it is plainly evident that the Lord’s Prayer speaks not of this temporal bread [Col. 1389C] which passes into the body and is discharged into the privy, but of that which is consecrated by divine words and, once received, supports our soul.

When it is offered, it is merely bread and a temporal support for the flesh that is destined to die; but after the mystery of consecration, it is the true flesh of Christ and the immortal support of the faithful soul. Thus, under the form which it invisibly displays, it faithfully works salvation in the person who receives what is divine; it does not perish by being shamefully expelled through the stomach, but, reverently consumed, supports the substance of the soul.

## X

Paschasius too, the most diligent investigator and Catholic examiner of the divine sacrament, says in his book—as blessed Augustine is shown to have thought—the following among other things [Col. 1389D]:

“It is therefore frivolous, as it is read in an apocryphal work, to think in this mystery about excrement, lest it be mixed in the digestion with other food. Indeed, when spiritual food and drink are received, and the Holy Spirit works through it in a human being so that, if anything carnal still remains in him, it may be transferred into spirit and the person may become spiritual, what possibility of admixture can there be? Therefore, as far as eternal life surpasses this mortal life, so far does this food wholly surpass that common food by which animals too live together with us.”

See what this aforementioned man said, following the authority of the earlier Fathers.

Likewise, blessed Clement [Col. 1390A], the apostolic man, in the letter addressed to James, in which he reports that he transmitted the precepts of the apostle Peter, commands that ministers, when receiving the remnants of the Lord’s table—as was especially customary at that time—abstain from other foods for fixed intervals of hours: namely, that one who had communicated at the third hour of the day should fast until the sixth; one who had communicated at the sixth should wait fasting until the ninth; and one who had communicated at the ninth should refresh himself in the evening.

Since, therefore, after receiving the mysteries he ordered that ordinary foods be avoided at appointed times, was he troubled by any concern about the excrement of the sacraments, as though it were more precious and might be mixed with the baser food of others, and ought perhaps to be expelled through a more honorable discharge? Far from it! [Col. 1390B]

For he had not received from the apostle a discipline concerning the separation of excrements, to be handed down by him in turn as something to be observed by others. Rather, he had received a precept concerning the holy fragments of the Lord’s table, which he was to pass on to the rest.

How greatly and with what holiness and reverence these are to be treated he plainly indicates when he forbids those who share in them to approach ordinary foods immediately—not so that the indecency of admixture might be avoided (for if it occurred, it would not at all need to be avoided), but so that the ministers of holiness might be trained in greater restraint and care for a frugal life, and so that no opportunity for false speculation might be given to the inexperienced, with the punishment of a damnable offense following upon the negligent. This is what the Apostle threatens the Corinthians who, while celebrating the Lord’s Supper, indulged too freely in the allurements of appetite. He says to them [Col. 1390C]:

“Therefore whoever eats this bread and drinks the cup unworthily eats and drinks judgment upon himself, not discerning the body of the Lord.”

A great guilt is therefore incurred, and severe punishment follows, because the Lord’s mystery is not discerned—that is, it is not sufficiently distinguished from other foods—when by the inexperienced, indeed by the impious, it is asserted to be discharged during digestion.

Hence blessed Augustine says in his commentary on the Gospel of John:

“Whoever eats the bread and drinks the cup unworthily will be guilty of the body and blood of the Lord.” He was speaking of those to whom the Apostle referred when he said this: they were taking the Lord’s body indiscriminately and carelessly, as though it were any other food.

If, then, the one who does not discern is rebuked—that is, the one who does not distinguish the Lord’s body [Col. 1390D] from other foods—how is the one condemned who, pretending to be a friend, approaches his table as an enemy? Therefore, as we said above, one must take great care that the Lord’s body is not left undiscerned—that is, received indiscriminately or carelessly. It is believed not only to remove the punishment of eternal death, but also, when faithfully received, to bestow the grace of perpetual life, as the author of the same gift testifies, saying:

“If anyone eats from this bread, he will live forever.”

This heavenly sacramental bread, which restores life to mortals and drives away the penalty of death, differs by an immeasurable and incomparable distance from that bread which merely cares for bodies. Therefore, it must in no way be believed to perish, lest, where the grace of life is to be drawn in through faith, the dangerous plague of death be incurred through unbelief [Col. 1391A], as Augustine says:

“But for that man it will be death, not life, who has judged Life to be a liar.”

For he judges Life to be a liar—or, so far as he can, makes it one—who dares to alter or falsely interpret the most sacred words of the Redeemer. Consequently, for him it will be death, not life, since he thinks otherwise about Life than Life itself thinks, when it says:

“The bread that I shall give is my flesh for the life of the world.”

This bread, then, is bread in appearance, but in truth it is the flesh of the Truth and the life of the faithful world, while it is judgment for the unbeliever, just as the Truth itself, to which faith must be given, plainly prescribed. In the human being it produces life, not excrement, and purity of mind, not corruption of the belly.

It is therefore called “supersubstantial,” because it nurtures the higher substance of the human being, and invigorates and advances it [Col. 1391B]. Earthly bread, which passes into the body, cannot do this before consecration; but this bread, which supports the substance of the soul and which, after the Lord’s words, is rightly called Christ’s body rather than bread, as Augustine says, does so because it has been transformed into something else by the heavenly working of consecration.

Because this bread is spiritual and belongs to eternal life, we are under a great necessity to ask for it, as it is written:

“Give us this day our daily bread.”

If it is daily, then certainly it must also be sought daily; nor should there be a long delay in asking for it, since its life-giving and saving reception by the soul is established.

But concern about temporal and ordinary bread is forbidden in these words:

“Do not be anxious, saying: ‘What shall we eat?’ or ‘What shall we drink?’ But seek the kingdom of God, and all these things will be added to you.” [Col. 1391C]

The kingdom of God is Christ, as it is written:

“The kingdom of God is within you.”

But Christ is bread, as it is written:

“I am the living bread which came down from heaven.”

Whoever has been faithfully satisfied with this bread will not fear that the support of earthly bread will fail him.

# PART FIVE

## XI

But because [Col. 1391D] in the books of the authorities the word “figure” appears in one place and “likeness” of Christ’s body and blood in another, although this gives no prejudice whatsoever to right faith, wicked men nevertheless imagine that they have found in it a powerful defense of their error.

While they wish to seem spiritual, they are found to be far more carnal than those who are carnal—or, to put it more truly, worse than they are. For where they ought faithfully to knock, humbly to seek, and diligently to investigate the grace of a higher understanding, there they are known, through obstinacy, to rush into the snare of unbelief and the sheer precipice of perdition.

They do not strive to examine what should be followed more earnestly in the Scriptures, but what may more effectively support their foolish error. They disdain to direct their crookedness according to the norm of Scripture; instead, by violently bending and deforming its straightness, they try to twist it toward the use of their perversity. Although they cannot wholly obtain what they seek, they nevertheless grow stronger through this in the vice of their presumption, blocking for themselves the path to deeper knowledge and obstinately barring the entrance to salvation with the bolts and locks of blasphemies. [Col. 1392A]

But we, who prefer not self-will but the sincerity of truth, yield to the authority of Holy Scripture. We do not conform Scripture to ourselves; rather, we conform our understanding to it. We embrace not discord in its variety but the lines of its manifold meaning. Thus we do not deny that the Lord’s sacrament is, in a certain respect, a figure and a likeness, while nevertheless professing that in truth it naturally exists as Christ’s body and blood.

For the Apostle says to the Corinthians:

“Whenever you eat this bread and drink the cup, you will proclaim the death of the Lord.”

The clear reasoning derived from the Lord’s words reveals the meaning of this statement. When Christ was indicating to his disciples the remembrance of his passion, he said:

“This is my body, which will be handed over for you. This is the cup of my blood, which will be poured out for you. Do this in remembrance of me.” [Col. 1392B]

Since Christ, having risen from the dead, no longer dies, we proclaim his death daily so that, by invoking through it the Father’s propitiation more readily, we may obtain it; and thus the saving mystery both signifies the Lord’s death and effects human reconciliation.

Who, then, would deny that what represents the passion of the Only-Begotten, which took place once in the past, may rightly be called a likeness or figure?

Yet this likeness or figure is entirely full of truth and grace. It is full of truth because the sweetness of Christ’s flesh and blood is shown to overflow not merely potentially but naturally. I say that it is full of truth because there is nothing in it less than that flesh which hung nailed to the cross, and it is nothing other than the blood which flowed from the pierced side, as Augustine is shown to have said to the newly baptized:

“Receive in the bread what hung upon the wood; receive in the cup what flowed from the side.” [Col. 1392C]

As is plainly evident, nothing other than flesh hung upon the wood, and nothing other than the blood which was in the body flowed from the side.

It overflows with grace because it consoles us with a temporal gift, so that at last we may attain what it displays when we behold it with unveiled face. It is also full of grace because it joins us to our Head and, while we journey toward our homeland, so invigorates us that we do not fail along the way.

Finally, this figure or likeness is filled equally with truth and grace because in it we undoubtedly receive the one through whom grace and truth came to be [Col. 1392D], and that same whole reality of which the Gospel proclamation resounds:

“The Word became flesh and dwelt among us; and we saw his glory, glory as of the Only-Begotten from the Father, full of grace and truth.”

This is indeed the grace which, while the world did not know it, suddenly received it. This is the grace which found no merit and extended a benefit. Finally, this is the truth which, surpassing all understanding, was entrusted nevertheless to fishermen and either destroyed or confounded the foolish wisdom of mortals.

Let us cling to this truth with the greatest eagerness, lest we fall away from grace; and, so that we may reach him who is himself the truth, let us not neglect the pledge of so great a grace. It has been established for us in the present as the way by which true life may one day be grasped.

## XII

Moreover [Col. 1393A], so that the majesty of the divine nature may be preserved and its sincere brightness not be obscured, greater diligence must be applied, and the words must be distinguished with precision, lest a profane confusion of meanings creep in, from which perverse disagreement customarily arises.

From this came the widely spreading growth of the Manichaeans; from this the most filthy offshoot of the Arians sprang up; from this also the plague of countless schisms either took its beginning or seized for itself a pretext. From this, too, the instigators of modern heresy and the fabricators of impious doctrine prepare an accusation against the purity of faith and, so far as they can, detract from the truth of the divine mystery, because it is sometimes called a likeness or figure—as though it were a fiction and not the truth. [Col. 1393B]

But one must proceed with careful and cautious consideration, because, like many other terms, these two words are homonyms. Since they can be understood in many ways according to the variety of meanings to which they are applied, they are nevertheless sometimes placed in the divine Scriptures in such a way that they prejudice neither the truth of nature nor the property of substance.

So it is in Genesis:

“It is not good for the human being to be alone; let us make for him a helper like himself.”

When it is said that a helper is to be made for the human being, the new creation of woman is clearly indicated. She is rightly said to be like the man because, although there is a distinction of sex, woman is nevertheless nothing other than a human being: the nature is the same, the condition is the same, and where these are one, no disagreement is found.

Therefore, just as woman from man is not something other than the same flesh, and is a human being like him, so from the true body of Christ, in which the whole fullness of divinity dwells [Col. 1393C], there is established his substantial and true body, which we handle in the sacred rites of the holy Church; and the name “likeness” applied to it is shown in no way to contradict this.

Moreover, if this comparison seems to someone less effective and not sufficiently suitable to the matter undertaken, let him hear without displeasure the apostolic statement, where there is no ambiguity:

“Made in the likeness of human beings.”

Here, as is evident, the term “likeness” does not exclude the truth of humanity. Christ was truly human, although he is said to have been made in the likeness of human beings.

## XIII

Concerning “figure,” the same Apostle says elsewhere:

“Who, being the radiance of glory and the figure of his substance.”

Here let the superstitious hunters of words and fraudulent deceivers of truth [Col. 1393D] either strip Christ completely of the dignity of the Father’s substance, or cease to bring an accusation against the divine sacrament on account of the term “figure.”

For if “figure” here denies the substance, then the Son is not what the Father is. Thus, when Christ’s sacrament is likewise called a figure, it is a shadow and not the truth, as in the passage reported by Scripture:

“All these things were happening to them in figure.”

What things? The manifold benefit of the sea, the coolness of the cloud during the day, the comfort of its brightness during the night, as well as the nectar-like rains of manna, the watered moisture of the rock, and the other things recounted there.

But that manna, like the other things, is called a figure because it was one thing while foreshadowing another. What was seen was, in its entirety, substantial; but it beforehand indicated the future mysteries of Christ [Col. 1394A] through certain intellectual signs—something which it itself was not. Hence the Apostle says elsewhere:

“I do not want you to be ignorant, brothers, that our fathers ate the same food and drank the same drink.”

He means “the same” through the power of a signifying figure, not through the truth of the nature exhibited. Otherwise Christ would still be stiff and motionless in the vast stony wilderness, where that stone pouring forth water lies inert in its mass.

For it is written:

“The rock was Christ.”

But it was not Christ, the rock born from the Virgin.

This figure is therefore rightly called a shadow, since it foretold something other than what it was.

But if the Only-Begotten of the Father, God from God, is called his figure, although he differs in no way from him in substance and is no less than the one whose figure he is proclaimed to be, then it is plainly clear that the divine sacrament [Col. 1394B] too may be called a figure and nevertheless possesses nothing less than the truth of the Lord’s flesh.

This, then, is the figure of the Lord’s substance; the earlier figure was a figure of this one. There was a shadow there; here is the truth itself.

We have considered it appropriate to insert here that statement of Saint Ambrose which certain people abuse to the detriment of the holy sacrament—indeed, as experience has shown, to their own destruction. In one place the likeness of the precious blood is written; elsewhere the figure of the body and blood is set forth. By these statements, as has been said, perverse people become more deeply entangled in their error, because they do not seek the author’s meaning through the sequence of his statements, but instead attempt to establish their own folly, in which they have been worn down, from bare words; they seek to acquire authority for themselves from the name of so great a teacher and thereby defend against Catholics the heresy in which they languish. [Col. 1394C]

This will in no way succeed, nor will it happen as they wish. Rather, the matter under discussion will become clearer if what follows is properly compared with what came before, and if the sequence of the subsequent words is rightly understood from the preceding ones. It is as follows:

“But perhaps you say: ‘I do not see the appearance of blood; but it has a likeness. For just as through baptism you received the likeness of death, so also you drink the likeness of the precious blood, so that there may be no horror of bloodshed, while the price of redemption nevertheless works.’”

This is the source from which the entire disagreement among foolish people [Col. 1394D] arose—people of whom reason cries out through the Holy Spirit in the Prophet:

“The fool said in his heart: ‘There is no God.’”

He is plainly a fool who, so far as he can, strips Christ of his divinity, since he does not fear to assert that Christ lied—something which cannot in any way be attributed to God—and impiously presumes to teach that what he openly proves and declares to be truly flesh and truly blood is merely a likeness or figure. It is as though such people were saying, in such a manner and with such words—not as wise people but as senseless ones:

“There is no God.”

## XIV

To say, therefore, “There is no God” is to contradict the Truth, which is Christ, and to think perversely otherwise than he himself taught about himself; this is plainly the mark of a fool.

Or is he not clearly a fool who resists God himself over the words of a simple servant [Col. 1395A], however they may have been uttered, and brings an accusation against his clear and simple statements? The Lord says:

“This is my body, which will be handed over for you; this is my blood, which will be poured out for you. Eat and drink. And do this also in remembrance of me.”

These people say, “Ambrose says: ‘I do not see the blood, but it has a likeness’”—as though, through the words of the disciple, they were stubbornly inflicting an insult upon the heavenly Master. Although it is written, “The disciple is not above the teacher,” they diminish, so far as they can, the authority of the Master by placing the disciple above him. Thus they offend the one whom they place below no less than the one whom they place above: in both cases they are guilty, and in both they are likewise condemned.

But let us honor the servant in such a way that we always and in every respect place the Lord [Col. 1395B] first, as we ought. Let us not measure the Lord’s statement by the disciple’s words; rather, let us measure the disciple’s words by the teaching of the Master. The disciple could not have thought anything contrary to him, since he was a disciple of the truth.

But we must now consider more attentively how so great a man, whom unbelievers summon into their dispute, does not disagree with his own author, the Lord our teacher of truth, but is instead entirely in harmony with him.

A little earlier he says:

“You have learned how bread becomes Christ’s body, and wine is placed in the chalice, but becomes blood through heavenly consecration.”

Here there is plainly no disagreement, nothing whatsoever that departs from the rule of Catholic truth, nothing at all that conflicts with the Lord’s statement. Rather, these words explain how the Lord’s words are to be understood.

The Lord says, “This is my body.” Ambrose explains more clearly how this can occur, testifying that through the change of bread and wine [Col. 1395C] Christ’s body and blood are made by heavenly blessing. If, having expressed this unmistakable opinion about the truth of the Lord’s body and blood in almost the very same passage, he then forgot it, thought something else, and taught differently, he would now be contradicting not the Lord but himself. It is ridiculous even to think this, let alone to affirm it.

### XV

Let us therefore see what follows: “But perhaps you say: ‘I do not see the appearance of blood, but it has a likeness.’” First of all, observe that he represents the person of some uneducated man saying, “I do not see the appearance of blood.” To this man, who doubts and is not capable of properly considering the matter as it is, he replies: “But,” he says, “it has a likeness.” As if he were saying:

“O poor in understanding, O keen in perception—or, as the Lord says to the disciples, still weak and not yet capable of grasping divine mysteries—O foolish and slow of heart to believe, you are astonished that you hear ‘body’ and hear ‘blood,’ but because you do not believe, you do not see the appearance, that is, the reality of the flesh and blood that is within. If you truly believed it, you would undoubtedly see it. Believe, therefore, so that you may see; for to believe already means to see with the heart. While this is deferred, while the mind’s vision is awaited—purified and enlightened by the benefit of faith so that it may contemplate the depth of so great a mystery—do not meanwhile despise what appears outwardly, since it has a likeness, lest you deservedly fall under the judgment of condemnation through unbelief. Receive what is apparent, so that afterward, by means of faith, you may deserve to reach what lies hidden within.

“But it has a likeness: inwardly there is the reality of flesh and blood, produced from bread and wine by a heavenly operation; outwardly there is a likeness, lest the horror of displayed blood be able to confuse the one who approaches. ‘But it has a likeness,’ he says. Here he does not deny the very reality that he had previously affirmed; rather, he clearly declares that something exists in reality while appearing differently to the eyes. The outward likeness, therefore, does not prejudice the inward reality. This likeness does not differ from the truth but prepares faith and instructs belief; it does not diminish the benefit but increases merit; it veils the mystery but does not remove grace; it fosters and nourishes devotion, does not obstruct pious reason, restrains rashness, and exercises the work of salvation. This likeness attracts and holds you, so that the truth may refresh and advance you.

“Therefore, venerate and honor this likeness which the divine dispensation sets before you, so that you may at length become worthy not to be deprived of the benefit of the truth that is stored within. For it serves, in a certain manner, in place of a mediator: it removes horror and bestows grace.”

Accordingly, what follows is: “For just as you received the likeness of death through baptism, so also you drink the likeness of the precious blood, so that there may be no horror of blood, while nevertheless the price of redemption is effective.”

Here too he declares that the likeness of the precious blood is drunk, so that only the horror of blood may be kept far away, just as the likeness of death is received in baptism. Yet baptism is a true and effective sacrament, so that it may bury vices and confer holiness of life. Otherwise, if it were not true, how could it convey so great a benefit? And nevertheless it is called a likeness of death, although, as was stated above, it truly brings death to sins, gives birth to virtues, and supplies their growth.

Thus, too, the likeness of the precious blood is rightly imbibed, so that the horror of blood may be entirely removed; yet, just as the blood is real, so truly does it accomplish the price of redemption. Therefore, having begun to discuss the likeness introduced for the sake of a definite matter, the aforesaid teacher now ceases that discussion and proceeds, in his customary manner, to speak of the natural reality present in the Lord’s sacrament, about which, as is evident above, he had also said so much:

“‘You have learned,’ he says, ‘that what you receive is the body of Christ.’ What you receive, he says, is truly the body; the likeness serves it by the dispensation. It is the body so that it may accomplish redemption by its price; it is the likeness so that the weariness of horror may be driven away and the sincerity of devotion exercised, so that, while he believes what he does not see, the recipient may more worthily attain what the majesty hidden in the mystery promises.”

It continues:

“‘Do you wish to know by what heavenly words it is consecrated? Listen to the words. The priest says: “Make this offering for us approved, ratified, reasonable, acceptable,” which is the figure of the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ.’”

Understand his use of the word “figure” in this way: when the priest says and performs these things, he represents the Lord himself handling and consecrating his sacraments, and at the same time displaying those very things that he consecrated as the mysteries of his body and blood: “‘Which is,’ he says, ‘the figure of the body and blood.’”

It is called a figure because at that moment the simple substance of bread and wine is being presented, from which, through powerful words, the heavenly sacraments are to be effected, as the priest’s prayer teaches and indicates: “‘Make this offering,’ he says, ‘ratified’”—that is, so that it may surpass its own nature; “‘reasonable’”—so that it may please you; “‘acceptable’”—so that it may benefit us.

Or “‘ratified’”—so that it may be transformed from a figure into reality; “‘reasonable’”—so that it may commend to you the service of our devotion; “‘acceptable’”—so that it may suffice to obtain heavenly propitiation.

“‘On the day before he suffered,’ he says, ‘he took bread in his holy hands, looked up to heaven, to you, holy Father, almighty and eternal God, giving thanks; he blessed it, broke it, and gave what had been broken to his apostles and disciples, saying: “Take and eat from this, all of you; for this is my body, which will be broken for you.” Likewise, after supper, he took the cup, saying: “Take and drink; this is [al., for this is] my blood.” See: all those words up to “Take,” whether concerning the body or the blood, are the evangelist’s. From that point onward they are Christ’s words.

“‘Observe each word: “The day before he suffered,” he says, “he took bread.” Before it is consecrated, it is bread; but when the words of Christ have been added, it is Christ’s body. Finally, hear him saying: “Take and eat from this, all of you; for this is my body.” And before Christ’s words, the cup is full of wine and water; when Christ’s words have operated, there blood is produced, the blood that redeemed the people.

“‘Consider, therefore, in how many ways the word of Christ is powerful to change things into their contraries. Finally, the Lord Jesus himself testified to us that we receive his body and blood. Surely we ought to doubt his faithfulness and testimony?’”

Here blessed Ambrose plainly rebukes those who hesitate concerning Christ’s faithfulness and testimony, and with an open confession asserts that Christ’s body is truly present and his blood truly present after Christ’s words, while the natures have been changed by the power of the Lord’s utterance.

It is therefore now perfectly clear and evident why above he said that the blood has a likeness but is not seen in its appearance. “‘This,’ he says, ‘is only a likeness of blood, not blood; but,’ he says, ‘it has a likeness,’” concerning which he had said that its appearance was not seen. If he had said that, he would have entirely taken away from himself the hope of salvation and the price of redemption; and therefore he would plainly be proved contrary to Christ Jesus and to the words of his own that he had previously set forth and afterward added.

When, therefore, he said that the appearance is not seen but that there is a likeness, he in no way denied that it is truly blood, to which the appearance or likeness seems to refer; nor did he attribute something else to it or deny it by diminishing its reality. For although it is not seen in its own appearance, and although it appears to possess some likeness that it displays, it nevertheless cannot be nothing. It is truly blood, and truly from the body of God and man, Jesus Christ. It is none other than the blood that took its origin from the Virgin’s flesh and was poured out as the price of the world, as the aforesaid teacher declares shortly afterward when he says: “When the words of Christ have been added, there blood is produced, the blood that redeemed the people.”

Note each word carefully and weigh the force of the terms. “The words,” he says, “of Christ operate: ‘there blood is produced, the blood that redeemed the people,’” because surely the blood that is produced is none other than the blood that redeemed. The blood that was poured out and this consecrated blood are therefore one and the same: the true blood of the one Christ, although in a certain respect it is called a figure. Yet it is not like the manna, which was not Christ’s body but signified it; for that reason it is also called a shadow, since manna is shown to have been merely a material substance.

Thus Augustine says:

“‘But manna was a shadow; this is the truth: “The bread that I will give is my flesh”; “This is the bread that comes down from heaven.” A truly wondrous thing! Bread came down from heaven, and bread is also flesh; therefore flesh came down from heaven. Is it really so? Certainly it is, for it is written: “The Son of man who descended from heaven, who is in heaven.” Do you see how great is the unity of the Lord’s person and how great is the truth of both natures in the Lord’s humanity? Flesh is in heaven, the Word on earth—indeed, the Word and flesh are in heaven and on earth, because Christ Jesus is one person, God and man.

“‘This, however, is living bread made from the flour of our humanity and prepared by the dew of divinity. Just as a grain of wheat, ground on a revolving millstone, is sprinkled with water so that it may become bread, so that grain of wheat, having fallen into the earth through the dispensation of death in order to bear much fruit, is watered by the drops of divinity, so that it may now be not two breads but one bread. Thus the figure of God and the figure of flesh are one figure of the sacramental bread—not an empty figure, but one full of truth.

“‘That bread the evangelical woman concealed in three measures of flour until it became sufficiently fermented and suitable for human use. Having worthily tasted this spiritual bread in advance, we shall deserve to be incorporated into Christ, so that he may be in us and we may be in him. From many we shall become not many, but one bread, through the sacrament of consummated unity in him and in us.

“‘Therefore the Apostle says: “Because there is one bread, we who are many are one body.” Great labor must consequently be expended, prayer must be practiced more frequently, purity of heart cultivated, and above all the unity of charity pursued; and thus the truth of so great a grace must be frequented. For this bread is called daily when in the Lord’s Prayer it is said: “Give us this day our daily bread.”’”

Here Father Augustine continues:

“‘If it is daily bread,’ he says, ‘why do you take it after a year, as the Greeks in the East are accustomed to do? Receive daily what benefits you daily; live so that you may deserve to receive it daily. Whoever does not deserve to receive it daily does not deserve to receive it after a year.

“‘How did holy Job offer sacrifice for his children? In case they had sinned in thought. You therefore hear that whenever this sacrifice is offered, the Lord’s death, the Lord’s resurrection, the Lord’s ascension, and the remission of sins are signified—and yet you do not receive this bread of eternal life daily? Whoever has a wound needs medicine. There is a wound, because we are under sin; the heavenly and venerable sacrament is medicine.’”

These are the precious words of Saint Augustine, directed especially against those who communicate only once after nine years. When they are accused of unbelief, they pretend humility; yet if, out of humility, they suspended themselves from the holy sacrament, they would certainly not dispute brazenly against that same sacrament by thinking perversely and shamelessly clinging to the mire of a recent heresy.

But as for us, whose judgment is different, if purity of heart agrees with innocence of conduct, let us frequently participate in the divine mysteries. If, however, grave crimes weigh upon us, let us abstain from the holy things—not so that we may persist in sins, but lest we be condemned for impious presumption if, shamelessly stained with mortal vices, we dare to plunge ourselves into the very things we ought not to presume to receive.

For a time, therefore, one must abstain from the holy things, but repentance must be applied promptly, so that by ceasing from evil and cleansing life from sins through worthy satisfaction, we may strive, by restoring the grace we have lost, to be found at some time worthy of communion in the sacraments.

But whoever is free from these crimes either through innocence of life or, after falling, has been restored through subsequent worthy repentance, should communicate frequently and with humility, carefully considering his weakness and hastening, with God’s help, to abstain thereafter from even the smallest sins, never despairing of God’s mercy. For, in order to provide a daily remedy for our daily falls, he instituted this heavenly and new sacrifice to be celebrated not annually but daily, the former things having been removed, so that, nourished more frequently and thereafter refreshed, we may be renewed and enlightened by the grace of faith.

As Father Augustine says:

“‘The Jews approached Christ in order to crucify him; let us approach in order to receive his body and blood. They were darkened by the Crucified One; we are illuminated by eating and drinking the Crucified One.’”

Here no figure is written, but the Crucified One is plainly said to be eaten and drunk.

Elsewhere he also says:

“‘In the sacrament, believers drank the blood which, in their fury, they shed.’”

Here too no cloud of likeness intervenes; believers are said to have drunk in the sacrament the very blood that those acting furiously shed.

And in the book of the *Confessions*:

“‘That your Only-Begotten redeemed me by his blood; let not the proud bring accusations against me, for I contemplate my price and eat and drink and distribute it, and, being poor, I desire to be filled from it.’”

Behold, Augustine contemplates Christ as his price, and says that he eats him because he is food, drinks him because he is drink—namely, flesh and blood—and distributes him because he was a bishop; and he desires that the poor be filled from him because, being humble, he did not know disdain for the divine sacrament.

### XVI

Let us therefore believe these things faithfully and together with the faithful, so that by eating the Crucified One and drinking with them we may truly be illuminated, lest through unbelief we be darkened together with the impious.

Those unbelievers were unable to endure Christ’s declaration that his flesh was to be eaten and his blood drunk, because they did not wish to believe reverently. Nevertheless Christ God, because he willed it, was undoubtedly able to fulfill what he said and give us his flesh as food and drink. Although this may appear less evident to reason, by faith it is entirely clear.

For just as we believe that the Word became flesh and hold this without doubt, although we know by no reasoning how it happened, so also in the Lord’s sacrament we understand that the bread which is seen is nothing other than Christ’s flesh, which is received, even though we cannot comprehend or explain this.

We believe this because the very same efficacy of divine power that was the creator of the Lord’s incarnation is also always effective and powerfully operative in this heavenly sacrament.

For these reasons, and on account of the insolence of the faithless, I have judged it fitting to restrain and temper with the reins of moderation the rashness of certain people. What I have set forth is brief in view of the greatness of the subject, insufficiently elaborate in view of its majesty, yet weighed according to the balanced equity of truth—more an introductory tasting than a full discourse—so that they may not presume to scrutinize the height of the divine sacrament beyond measure, lest under the pretext of piety they incur offense.

For them the pure simplicity of faith should be sufficient: a faith handed down from ancient times and transmitted through their successors down to us. Nor should human loquacity be pursued in divine matters. Hence comes the saying of blessed Hilary:

“‘One must not speak about the things of God according to human or worldly understanding; nor, through force and imprudent preaching, should perversity be extracted from heavenly sayings that are sound, in order to produce an alien and impious interpretation.’”

This statement applies particularly to those who, by human understanding, do violence to heavenly sayings and extract impiety from them, while they corrupt the divine sacrament with the mark of shameful conduct.

## PART SIX

### XVII

There are many things in Scripture which, if exaggerated too vehemently, bring not the help of salvation but the error of destruction; they do not sharpen understanding but confuse the mind’s perception. Whoever have maintained moderation in these matters have remained in the Catholic Church; but those who have overflowed beyond measure, and with their foolish hearts closed have become empty in their thoughts, have fallen into multiple fantasies of falsehood, becoming leaders of heresy and producing schisms and divisions.

Since, as has been said, there are countless mysteries of sacred Scripture which mortals ought rather to reverence than scrutinize, I shall here add a few examples to make the matter clear. Among them is the severe divine judgment concerning the calling of the Gentiles and the rejection of the Jews. When the Apostle Paul had encountered this subject at an appropriate point in his argument, and had perceived that he was not sufficient to explain it, nor we sufficient to understand it, he suddenly burst into wonder at the divine secret:

“O the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God! How unsearchable are his judgments and inscrutable his ways!”

There is also the question of the origin of souls, about which there was extensive debate among the philosophers of the world, and concerning which two opposing lines of reasoning have been debated among the most distinguished teachers of our religion. One side was more prepared to provide solutions to the questions, while the other was more inclined toward the integrity of faith. That view prevailed which carried greater weight in relation to the truth.

So too this heavenly sacrament must be believed rather than dissected. It is better to remain, in a discreet manner, ignorant of something than to define dishonestly what concerns so great a matter, because in the one case there is the danger of presumption, while in the other there is the practice of Catholic sobriety.

Hence blessed Gregory says:

“‘We burn with fire what remains of the lamb when we humbly reserve for the power of the Holy Spirit what we cannot penetrate concerning its mystery, so that no one may presumptuously dare either to despise or to denounce what he does not understand; rather, he commits it to the fire when he reserves it for the Holy Spirit.’”

Let us therefore believe what Truth itself has defined concerning its holy body and blood, and let us profess what it deigned to reveal through the divinely inspired Scriptures so that it might be believed. Let us not be torn away from these things by any newly arising opinion. To defend them, let us spend whatever resources and strength we possess—even our blood itself, if the matter requires it.

For the sacred offering of bread and wine is truly Christ’s flesh and truly his blood. Through the mystery it represents the passion of the Only-Begotten, and according to the merits of those who receive it, it becomes for each person either the provision of life or the cause of judgment.

If, in refuting the heretics who boil over with perversity, it should be necessary to draw out something more profound from these matters, that too should not exceed the limits of probable reason and should not be deprived of the grace of complete decency. For every trace of impiety produces some deception wherever one suspects a trace of shamefulness, whereas the form of heavenly discipline and the glory of complete holiness remain established.

I believe that what has been said is sufficient for the extent of the question that arose, and sufficient for those who prefer truth to prolixity of speech. I proposed to append abundant examples drawn from the testimonies of the Fathers, so that all the faithful might be more fully instructed and defend their belief, while they might more securely mock the impiety of the faithless and more forcefully repel the questions brought against them.

### XVIII

Augustine therefore says in his book on the Psalms:

“‘He was carried in his own hands. But, brothers, how could this happen in a human being? Who can be carried in his own hands? A person can be carried in the hands of others; no one is carried in his own hands. We do not find how this is to be understood in David himself according to the letter; but in Christ we do find it. For Christ was carried in his own hands when, commending his own body, he said: “This is my body.” That body was carried in his own hands. This is the humility of our Lord Jesus Christ, which is greatly commended to human beings.’”

And shortly afterward he says:

“‘The Jews approached him in order to crucify him; let us approach him in order to receive his body and blood. They were darkened by the Crucified One; we are illuminated by eating and drinking the Crucified One.’”

Elsewhere he says:

“‘Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood remains in me and I in him. How are we to understand this? Can we also include here those of whom the Apostle says that they eat and drink judgment upon themselves, even though they eat that very flesh and drink that very blood? Did Judas, the seller and impious betrayer of the Master, remain in Christ, or Christ in him, although he ate and drank with the other disciples the sacrament of his flesh and blood, which had first been prepared by his hands, as the evangelist Luke more clearly declares?’”

Again Augustine:

“‘Let all that the Lord said about his flesh and blood, and all that he wished to be understood concerning those who eat and drink his flesh and blood, serve this purpose for us: that we should not merely eat the flesh and blood of Christ in the sacrament—as many wicked people also do—but eat and drink unto participation in the Spirit, so that we may remain as members in the Lord’s body and not be scandalized even if many now eat and drink the sacraments with us temporally, while at the end they will have torments.’”

Again, above:

“‘I am the living bread that came down from heaven. Manna also came down from heaven, but manna was a shadow; this is the truth. “If anyone eats from this bread, he will live forever, and the bread that I will give is my flesh for the life of the world.” When could flesh grasp that he called bread flesh? That which flesh cannot comprehend is called flesh; and for that reason flesh comprehends it even less, because it is called flesh. This is what they shrank from; this is what they thought could not happen.’”

And somewhat earlier:

“‘Do we not die, brothers, who eat the bread that descended from heaven? They died in the same way that we shall die. For certainly those who eat Christ will also die temporally, but they will live forever, because Christ is eternal life.’”

In the same work:

“‘“The flesh profits nothing,” as they understood it—not as I give my flesh to be eaten.’”

Again:

“‘You have eternal life in the ministry of your body and blood; and we believe and know that you are Christ, the Son of the living God—that is, that you yourself are eternal life—and that in your flesh and blood you give nothing except what you are.’”

Let the followers of Stercoranism hear what so great a teacher says: “You give nothing in your flesh and blood except what you are.” You yourself are eternal life, and you give eternal life, which is what you are; you do not give excrement, which you are not, in the flesh and blood that comes from you.

Again Augustine:

“‘The Lord spoke to us about his body and blood, calling his body food and his blood drink. The faithful recognize the sacrament of the faithful. When, therefore, while commending such food and such drink, he said: “Unless you eat my flesh and drink my blood, you will not have life in yourselves”—and he said this concerning Life—who else could he be except Life itself? But for that man who considers Life a liar, it will be death, not life.

“‘His disciples were scandalized—not all of them, but many. The Lord replied to them: “Does this scandalize you? Do you think that I am going to make portions from this body that you see, tear apart my limbs, and give them to you? What, then, if you see the Son of man ascending to where he was before?” What does this mean? Certainly he who could ascend whole could not be consumed. Therefore, from his body and blood he gave us a healing refreshment, and in a brief statement he resolved so great a question concerning his integrity.’”

Again Augustine:

“‘That your Only-Begotten redeemed me by his blood; I contemplate my price and eat and drink.’”

Elsewhere:

“‘Rightly, therefore, the martyrs are placed beneath the altar, because Christ is placed upon the altar; rightly the members of the righteous rest beneath the altar, because the Lord’s body is offered upon the altar. Nor is it without reason that the vengeance of blood is sought there where Christ’s blood is also poured out for sinners.’”

### XIX

Saint Cyril, together with the one hundred and fifty bishops assembled at Ephesus, likewise says:

“‘Proclaiming according to the flesh the death of the Only-Begotten Son of God, that is, Jesus Christ, and confessing together his resurrection and ascension into heaven, we celebrate in the churches the bloodless service of the sacrifice. Thus we also approach the mystical blessings and are sanctified, becoming participants in the holy body and precious blood of Christ, who has become the Redeemer of us all—not as though we were participating in ordinary flesh, God forbid; nor as though we were participating in that of a sanctified man joined to the Word according to the dignity of the union, or as though he possessed a divine indwelling; but truly in flesh made life-giving and made proper to the Word himself.’”

And blessed Ambrose:

“‘My flesh is truly food, and my blood is truly drink. You hear “flesh,” you hear “blood,” you recognize the sacraments of the Lord’s death—and you bring accusation against divinity? Hear him saying this himself: “A spirit does not have flesh and bones.” But whenever we receive the sacraments which, through the mystery of holy prayer, are transformed into flesh and blood, we proclaim the Lord’s death.’”

Thus far blessed Ambrose. In his words we must observe that he says that the sacraments—that is, the bread and wine, as is evident from their being called so because they are consecrated—are transformed through the mystery of holy prayer into flesh and blood. For, as Augustine says above:

“‘After the words of the sacred prayer, they are no longer believed to be bread and wine, having been transferred into something else by heavenly power, but the flesh and blood of Christ; through them we proclaim his death.’”

Hence also Eusebius of Emesa:

“‘Let all uncertainty of unbelief depart, since the one who is the author of the gift is himself also the witness of its truth. For the invisible priest transforms visible creatures into the substance of his body and blood by his word and by a hidden power, saying: “Take and eat; this is my body,” and, repeating the sanctification: “Take and drink; this is my blood.”

“‘Therefore, at the command of the one who ordered it, the heights of the heavens, the depths of the waters, and the vast expanses of the earth suddenly came into existence from nothing. With equal power, in the spiritual sacraments, the power commands through words, and the effect serves the reality.’”

And shortly afterward:

“‘Let no one doubt that primary created things can, at the command of power and in the presence of majesty, pass into the nature of the Lord’s body and blood, since he sees the human being himself made Christ’s body by the workmanship of heavenly mercy.’”

And blessed Gregory:

“‘We ought to despise the present age with our whole mind, especially since we see that it has passed away, and we ought to offer God daily sacrifices of tears and daily sacrifices of his flesh and blood. For this unique victim saves the soul from eternal destruction; through the mystery it represents to us the death of the Only-Begotten. Although, rising from the dead, he no longer dies and death will no longer rule over him, yet, living in himself immortally and incorruptibly, he is again sacrificed for us in this mystery of the sacred offering. For there his body is received; his flesh is distributed for the salvation of the people; his blood, no longer into the hands of the unbelieving, but into the mouths of the faithful, is poured out.’”
