In the dialogue of Basil and John it is likewise written:

“‘He who sits above at the right hand of the Father is nevertheless held in human hands at the time of the sacrifice and is handed over to those who desire to lick him and embrace him in veneration.’”

Doctor Leo also says:

“‘Then the offering of the sacrifice is pure and the holy gift of mercy is present, when those who make these offerings understand what they are doing. For when the Lord says: “Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of man and drink his blood, you will not have life in yourselves,” you ought to share in the sacred table in such a way that you have absolutely no doubt concerning the truth of Christ’s body and blood. For what is believed by faith is received by the mouth, and those who dispute against what they receive answer “Amen” in vain.’”

Bede likewise:

“‘Every day Christ takes away the sins of the world and washes us from our sins in his blood, when the memory of that blessed passion is renewed, when the creature of bread and wine is transferred into the sacrament of his flesh and blood by the ineffable sanctification of the Spirit. Thus his body and blood are not killed and poured out among the hands of unbelievers to their destruction, but are received by the mouths of the faithful for their salvation.’”

Paschasius, however, says:

“‘Therefore, when the Lord says: “This is my body, and this is my blood,” I do not think that he indicated any flesh other than his own—the flesh that was born from the Virgin Mary and hung upon the cross—nor any blood other than that which was poured out from his side and was then in his own body.’”

Amalarius also says in his book *On Offices*:

“‘In the bread Christ commended his body, and in the cup his blood, saying: “Eat and drink; whenever you do these things, you shall do them in remembrance of me.” Here we believe that the simple nature of bread and wine is changed into the rational nature, namely, that of the Lord’s body and blood.

“‘Great and wondrous, therefore, is the faith of holy Church, which sees with spiritual eyes what is lacking to mortal eyes. It believes that the present sacrifice is carried by the hands of angels, and it perceives that it must be eaten by the human mouth. It also believes that it is the body and blood of the Lord, and that by this bite the souls of those who receive it are filled with heavenly blessing.’”

Here it must be noted that, following the authority of the earlier Fathers, he says that the simple nature of bread and wine is changed into the rational nature of the Lord’s body and blood. For when one thing is changed into another, it is undoubtedly suddenly held to be something other than what it had been.

Therefore, the bread and wine that are brought to the altar and consecrated by the words spoken by the mouth of the divine priest, although they appear in the former appearance in which they are brought, are nevertheless believed substantially to be Christ’s body and blood—not through some empty image of a phantom, but, as blessed Ambrose, Saint Gregory, Eusebius, and holy Bede have handed down in their writings, through a heavenly change of temporal things into the life-giving and true nature of flesh and blood.

Its reception, which takes place through the human mouth together with the inner perception mediated by faith, adorns the souls and bodies of those who sincerely receive it with heavenly blessing.

But these things can be fully grasped only by the wisely faithful, to whom God has graciously revealed them through his Holy Spirit, without whom no one can say, “The Lord Jesus.” They faithfully give glory to God and firmly believe that he, who is faithful in all his words, can accomplish whatever he wills—he who, as it is written, “does great and inscrutable things.” Even if these things cannot be fully comprehended, they must nevertheless be believed in their entirety, without any scruple of mind.

XX. Although I believed that what I have gathered here from the sayings of the ancient Fathers would suffice, we nevertheless thought it would not be unwelcome to note what Fulbert, bishop of Chartres, an acute and vigorous philosopher of our own time, yet in faith, life, and conduct a disciple of Christ’s disciples, thought and wrote concerning this matter. For among other things he says:

“Because Christ was soon to raise up to heaven, away from our sight, his body, which he had once offered for us as the price of our redemption, lest we should be deprived of the present protection of that body when it was taken away, he left us the saving pledge of his body and blood—not an empty symbol of a mystery, but a body joined together by the Holy Spirit [another reading: ‘the body of Christ’]. Yet, under the visible form of a created thing, a hidden power invisibly effects this daily act of worship.”

A little later:

“What can be judged unworthy of God, who entered the Virgin’s womb, if he is poured into created virginal things? [another reading: ‘which’] And although shortly before they displayed the appearance of a simple nature, afterward, through the sanctification of the heavenly Word, true majesty is infused into them, and what outwardly appeared to be the substance of bread and wine is now inwardly the body and blood of Christ. Taste, then, and receive bread, the nourishment of the inner life—not fermented by the baker’s craft, but the life-giving food of the incarnate Godhead. Receive likewise wine, not trodden out by a sordid cultivator, but pressed from the winepress of the cross. Taste, I say, the sweetness of the heavenly dish, but do not be nauseated by the earthly flavor of the ministering element.”

And a little later:

“It is impious to doubt that earthly matter, transcending the worth of its own nature and kind, is changed into the substance of Christ; and if God was able to create creatures from nothing, he is surely able to transform those same creatures into the dignity of a more excellent nature and to pour them into the substance of his body.”

[Column 1406A] Behold what the aforementioned man, following the ancient Fathers in all things, has said.

These too are the thoughts of John Chrysostom on the same subject:

“Judas was present when Christ said: ‘This is my blood, which will be poured out for many.’ Tell me, Judas, whom did you sell for thirty pieces of silver? This is the blood concerning which you made an agreement with the Pharisees. O mercy of Christ! O madness of Judas! He was bargaining for thirty pieces of silver in order to sell him, while Christ was offering him the blood which he had sold.”

And after some intervening material:

“Now Christ himself is present, he who furnished that table; he himself also consecrates this one. For it is not a human being who makes what is set before us the body and blood of Christ, but he who was crucified for us, Christ. The priest’s mouth speaks the words, and they are consecrated by the power of God. He says, ‘This is my body’; by this word what is set before us is consecrated. And just as that voice which says, ‘Increase and multiply,’ was spoken once, yet continually produces its effect for generation, so that voice too was spoken once, yet through all the churches’ tables down to the present day, and until his coming, gives the sacrifice its stability.”

And after some intervening material:

“You hasten to the holy and terrible sacrifice. Be ashamed before the secret of the offering, where Christ, slain, has been set before us. And why was he slain? So that he might reconcile heavenly things.”

Again, shortly afterward:

“The Jews crucified Christ, and yet he generously gives the blood poured out for the salvation of those who poured it out.”

He also says to the newly baptized:

“After Jesus had died and was still hanging on the cross, a soldier approached, struck his side with a lance, and immediately water and blood flowed out: the one, a symbol of baptism; the other, of the sacrament. From his side, therefore, Christ built the Church, just as Eve, his wife, was brought forth from Adam’s side. And just as, while Adam slept, God opened his side and disclosed his members, so now, after his death, he has given us water and blood. See, then, with what food he nourishes us to satiety. He himself is the substance and nourishment of our food. For just as a woman, compelled by the nature of her affection, hastens to nourish the child she has borne with the abundance of her milk, so Christ continually nourishes with his blood those whom he himself regenerates.”

And elsewhere:

“Christ died,” he says, “to give you immortality. He hungered so that he might satisfy you with his flesh. He thirsted so that he might give you drink from his own blood.”

Again:

“You wished to eat: he became a table for you. You wished to drink: he became a cup for you, just as he himself says: ‘He who eats my flesh and drinks my blood remains in me, and I in him.’”

And blessed Gregory says:

“You have learned what the blood of the Lamb is, not now by hearing but by drinking. That blood is placed upon both doorposts when it is drawn not only by the mouth of the body but also by the mouth of the heart. The Lamb’s blood is placed upon both doorposts when the sacrament of his passion is received with the mouth for redemption and contemplated with an attentive mind for imitation.”

These sayings of so many Fathers, carefully weighed, together with what was noted above, dispel every ambiguity concerning so great a mystery and refute the impiety of heresy.

It is exceedingly astonishing that, although the Lord’s own words are sufficient in themselves, we seek examples from elsewhere to strengthen this faith. For he who says, “My flesh is truly food, and my blood is truly drink”; and, “He who eats my flesh and drinks my blood”; and, “The bread that I shall give is my flesh”; and, “He who eats me will live because of me”; and, “Take and eat; this is my body”; “Take and drink. This is my blood, which will be poured out for you”; and other such statements—he unquestionably establishes the certainty of this matter and completely removes every error of doubt.

PART SEVEN

XXI. But because there are some who are unwilling to consider these things faithfully, we decide that we must return to an abundance of examples, so that anyone who perhaps does not believe reason may at least be overwhelmed by the authority of many witnesses.

The learned Eusebius says:

“Truly, the one perfect sacrifice is to be judged by faith, not by appearance, and not assessed by outward sight but by inward effect. Hence the heavenly authority rightly confirms that ‘my flesh is truly food, and my blood is truly drink.’ Therefore, when creatures to be blessed with heavenly words are placed upon the sacred altars, before they are consecrated by the invocation of the supreme Name, the substance there is bread and wine. But after Christ’s words, it is the body and blood of Christ. What is astonishing, then, if he who was able to create by a word can also change by a word what he has created? Indeed, it seems a lesser miracle if he can change for the better what he is acknowledged to have established from nothing.”

[Column 1407C] Moreover, Bishop Hincmar, in that remarkable description which he truthfully issued for King Charles and which he ordained should be called “Solomon’s Table,” speaks as follows concerning the truth of the holy sacrament, following the other Fathers:

The Lamb, light of the world, feeding us with his own body,

May he remain in us; he will become our dwelling.

The Lamb, fountain of life, giving us drink from his own blood,

May he always, as is his custom, make us drunk and guide us.

Here is God almighty, through whom the Father made all things;

He changes the natures of things, as he himself wills.

Here, by the cross, he creates our offerings with his own words.

His flesh and blood come to be from bread and liquid.

For the body fixed upon the cross, and the blood also poured out,

Are those which Christ had already given to his own at the supper.

When we unworthy ones commemorate these things, the Redeemer,

The price of the redeemed, makes our gifts the price of the redeemed.

XXII. And in his *Epicolumnia* he says:

“The sacrifice of the body and blood of the Lord Christ, made from bread and wine mixed with water, is consecrated by ineffable sanctification through the cross and his words; and they become the true and proper body of our Lord Jesus Christ and his true and proper blood, just as he himself declared: ‘This is my body; this is my blood.’”

The aforesaid man appropriately sought to strengthen his opinion by divine authority. Thus, as though from a certain fountain, there proceeds the whole form of truth and of ecclesiastical tradition, which is preserved uniformly throughout the world.

Hence the Apostle also says:

“I delivered to you first of all what I also received: that the Lord Jesus, on the night when he was betrayed, took bread, and giving thanks, blessed it and broke it, saying: ‘Take and eat; this is my body, which will be delivered for you.’”

Consider, I ask, the prudence of the one who received, and examine the authority of the one who delivered. He changed nothing of what he had received; he added nothing new, as recent schismatics do. Rather, preserving the integrity of the meaning and the dignity of the words, he composed the very things he had received as a disciple of the truth. He inserted no mention of figure or likeness, because he intended to make known to the Corinthians, who were mishandling them, not what the Lord’s sacraments signified but what they were.

Therefore he resolved to set down not his own words but the Lord’s, so that he might obtain from the name of the Master both the weight of authority and the reverence owed to so great a sacrament, saying: “This is my body.”

Truly this divine sacrament is the Lord’s body, in which the perennial life of all remains. Hence Augustine says:

“O sacrament of devotion! O sign of unity! O bond of charity! Whoever wishes to live has where to live and from what to live. Let him approach and believe; let him be incorporated, so that he may be given life.”

It deserves careful consideration that he says, “he has where to live,” because Christ is truly without location and is the place of life in which the Christian lives; “he has from what to live,” because life comes from no other source than him; “let him approach,” therefore, by faith, not with his feet; and “let him believe” with his heart, “who wishes to live”; but let him “be incorporated” by the power of the sacraments, so that he may “be given life” through the truth of charity. Thus, through the sign of unity, he may reach the reward of incorruption, which no one otherwise attains except through that sacrament of devotion in which the fullness of truth resides.

Cassiodorus discusses its purity in Psalm 109:

“You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek.” To whom can this truthfully be applied except to the Lord and Savior, who sacramentally consecrated his body and blood in the distribution of bread and wine, just as he himself says: “Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you will not have life in yourselves”? But concerning this flesh and blood, let the human mind conceive nothing bloody, nothing corruptible, lest, as the Apostle says, he who eats the Lord’s body unworthily should eat judgment for himself. Rather, let it understand a life-giving and saving substance, made proper to the Word himself, through which the forgiveness of sins and the gifts of eternal life are bestowed.”

It was rightly said, “Let the human mind conceive nothing bloody, nothing corruptible,” because whoever still suspects anything bloody or corruptible in the Lord’s sacrament belongs to those who, for that reason, withdrew, saying: “How can this man give us his flesh to eat?” When they heard, “Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man, you will not have life in yourselves,” they imagined that they would divide it limb by limb and gnaw it with their teeth. Horrified by this, they withdrew from following Christ, because they understood in no way what they heard and could not penetrate the power of the sacrament or the force of the words. Therefore, scandalized, they said: “This is a hard saying.”

To them Augustine says at that place:

“Do you think that I am going to divide into pieces this body which you see, and cut up my members and give them to you? Certainly, he who was able to ascend whole could not be consumed. Therefore the Lord gave us a saving nourishment from his body and blood, and briefly resolved so great a question concerning his integrity.”

It is plainly well said that he “resolved so great a question”—but for those who do not reject the truth and who venerate and receive the power of the Lord’s sacrament. Those who still doubt in error, however, and who, thinking something other than what the truth holds, argue against it, remain wandering, not yet released from the knot of so great a question. To them the Lord says: “It is the Spirit who gives life; the flesh profits nothing.”

Indeed, it profits nothing to the one who does not wish to understand this divine mystery as he ought. But to one who believes rightly and receives worthily, it profits in every way. Hence Augustine says:

“Lord, good Master, how does the flesh profit nothing when you have said, ‘Unless someone eats my flesh and drinks my blood, he will not have life in himself’? Does life profit nothing? And why do we exist as we do, except that we may have the eternal life which you promise through your flesh? What, then, does ‘the flesh profits nothing’ mean? The flesh profits nothing—but how did they understand it? They understood the flesh as it is torn apart in a corpse or sold in a butcher’s shop, not as it is animated by the Spirit.”

The heretics of our own time are unquestionably like them. Possessed by a similar error, they deny the truth of the Lord’s sacrament, resisting the Truth itself, which said: “This is my body.” While they invent for themselves something other than what the truth holds, they become entirely exiled from the truth itself and lose the saving power of the Lord’s communion, whose faith they reject.

Nor is this undeserved. Wrapped on every side in the darkness of their blindness, and therefore seized by the hateful vice of obstinacy, which is characteristic of heretics, they applaud themselves for their singular knowledge and do not attend to the divine light of the Lord’s words. Nor do they yield to the opinions of so many teachers; instead, while they themselves wretchedly err, they dare to assign the mark of error to others, like the insane, who, though deranged in every respect by the violence of their passion, think that everyone else is insane.

If they had wished to consider prudently and humbly, among the opinions of the other teachers, what the aforementioned Cassiodorus says, they would have found it more than sufficient to correct their error. For he says:

“Let the mind conceive nothing bloody, nothing corruptible, but understand a life-giving substance, proper to the Word himself.”

He says “substance,” not shadow, and “proper to the Word himself,” not figure. For truly, under the appearance of bread, the real substance of the Lord’s flesh is proved to be present; and although it is true flesh and true blood, nothing corruptible and nothing bloody ought nevertheless to be believed to exist in so great a mystery, lest one who thinks in this way should receive judgment rather than salvation, failing to discern rightly the Lord’s body—a most grievous offense.

Hence Augustine, a most vigorous disputant, is found to have said in his book *On Christian Doctrine*:

“‘Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you will not have life in yourselves.’ This seems to command a crime or an outrage—but only to unbelievers, who did not wish to believe what was being said. When they heard, ‘Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you will not have life in yourselves,’ they withdrew, because, being carnal, they could not understand the sacrament which divine Wisdom was preparing but for the time being postponing. Yet they could have believed, if they had wished, together with Peter and the other apostles who remained faithful, until, after Jesus had been glorified and the Spirit had been given, they deserved to be strengthened with them in all truth.

“But because they were thoughtless in hearing and became undisciplined by refusing to give faith to the Lord’s words, it happened that they departed wrongly from the good Master, in whose discipleship they were unwilling to maintain firm constancy. They were offended by a hard saying, as it seemed to them, but one that was soon to be tempered by the simple sacrament which was already being preached, though not openly.”

Nevertheless, I would more readily pardon those who then withdrew from following the Lord. They were still carnal; they saw Christ Jesus the Lord as a carnal human being and were not yet able to raise the eyes of their hearts to contemplate heavenly mysteries. I would pardon them more readily than the people of our own time, in whom the grace of the Holy Spirit has been poured out through baptism; people who neither fear nor believe the sacred mysteries of the heavenly table, formed by divine oracles, explained and made clearer by the teaching of the holy doctors, and confirmed by manifest demonstrations of miracles. Instead, by speaking perversely, they contradict them and, with much shameful impiety of words, attempt to defame what they are utterly unable to overthrow.

Consequently, wherever they can, they never cease fabricating unjust accusations by finding some pretext either in the words or in the opinions of the elders. This is what they are known to do with the statement of blessed Augustine that we have cited. They embrace it more eagerly than his other testimonies concerning the divine sacrament because it says: “It seems to command an outrage or a crime.”

But once the perfidy of these people has been rejected with due care, let us faithfully examine what the aforementioned teacher said and what he meant in these statements.

XXIII. “It seems,” he says, “to command a crime or an outrage.”

First, it is worth considering that he says “it seems to command,” not “it commands.” For it seemed an intolerable crime or outrage to eat human flesh or drink the blood of a living person. Yet this was not commanded; rather, the saying referred to the sacrament that was already being preached.

“It seems,” he says, “to command,” not “it commands.” Here he touches upon the Jews and those who followed their error, who thought that there was a great outrage in these words of the Lord. Therefore they were horrified and went away, because they received the saying as though they were going to devour Christ with their teeth, just as dogs devour a hare or stag when they seize it alive and bloody.

But this is unacceptable and reason does not allow it. It is a crime and a great outrage to understand the matter in this way, since it must be understood otherwise. The Lord’s flesh must not be thought to be received as ordinary flesh or the flesh of some animal. Rather, it must be believed to be received spiritually through the sacrament, yet to be no flesh other than that which underwent the Passion, although the appearance of what is offered seems to be bread.

This was certainly arranged by divine dispensation, and must faithfully be believed to have been so arranged, so that human frailty—which is not accustomed to feed on human flesh—might take in through sight nothing that would cause horror, while nevertheless receiving in the sacrament the flesh of our Lord Jesus Christ no less truly than the truth possesses it. Concerning this the Apostle says: “Even if we had known Christ according to the flesh, yet now we know him no longer.”

Here he does not deny the truth of the nature assumed from us, but signifies the incorruptibility of our substance, glorified into God [another reading: “in God”] through the resurrection. Just as it is incorruptible in God, so, under a visible and familiar appearance, we receive it incorruptibly in the sacrament.

Yet the minds of those who receive so great a sacrament must be conformed and adapted to it, so that what is received in the mystery may produce an inward effect—namely, that whoever shares in such holiness should, dead to the world and to vices, afterward strive to live in the newness of life.

For this reason Augustine calls it a sign or figure in the book mentioned above, where he says:

“Therefore it is a figure instructing us to share in the Lord’s passion and to remember with sweetness and benefit, in mercy [another reading: ‘in memory’], that Christ’s flesh was crucified and wounded for us. For he shares in Christ’s passion who crucifies himself to the world and to his desires, so that he does not do whatever he pleases. And he beneficially remembers the Lord’s flesh, crucified and wounded for us, who kindly shows mercy to the needs of his neighbor, himself laying down his life for his brothers.”

When that teacher spoke in this way, he was surely directing attention to the Lord’s communion, although, according to the property of its nature, what is received is nothing other than the true and natural substance of Christ’s flesh and blood.

Therefore, whenever the Lord’s mystery is found in the writings of blessed Augustine to be called a figure, sign, or type, it must not be accepted with careless rashness. Rather, one must diligently investigate why it is so called, because so great a teacher cannot contradict himself. If he were to destroy elsewhere what he had said in one place by thinking differently elsewhere, he would unquestionably make himself a transgressor, and no one ought to place faith in his words.

But every suspicion of error in his statements must be removed in view of the correction he himself provided. Careful and laborious attention must be given to the places in which he appears to have said different things, so that one statement is not taken for another, but each saying preserves its own proper meaning in its own place.

To pass over his other statements showing that he understood the truth of the Lord’s body and blood, I shall insert what is judged to be the principal and sufficient answer to all the sophistries and crafty arguments of heretics, and what he is known to have published in an exposition of a certain psalm. From it it is clearer than daylight that he understood nothing empty or devoid of truth, nothing shadowy or counterfeit, in the Lord’s sacrament. Rather, he expressly indicated throughout that the offerings consecrated on the altar are truly Christ’s natural body and substantial blood, poured out on the cross, although at times he appears to approve that the truth itself intimates something to us, by which we may be more closely instructed and adhere to it more actively in practice.

Thus he says in Psalm 98:

“I am uncertain: I fear worshiping the earth, lest he who made heaven and earth condemn me; again, I fear not worshiping the footstool of my Lord’s feet, because the psalm says to me: ‘Worship his footstool.’ I ask what his footstool is, and Scripture says to me: ‘The earth is the footstool of my feet.’ Wavering, I turn to Christ, because I seek him here, and I find how the earth may be worshiped without impiety, how his footstool may be worshiped without impiety. For he took earth from the earth, because flesh is from the earth, and he gave us that very flesh to eat for salvation. No one, however, eats that flesh unless he has first worshiped.”

And a little later:

“When he had said, ‘Unless someone eats my flesh, he will not have eternal life in himself,’ some of his disciples—about seventy—were scandalized and said: ‘This is a hard saying; who can understand it?’ And they withdrew from him and no longer walked with him. What he said seemed hard to them: ‘Unless someone eats my flesh, he will not have eternal life.’ They received it foolishly; they thought about it carnally and supposed that the Lord would cut off certain pieces from his body and give them to them. They said: ‘This is a hard saying.’ They themselves were hard, not the saying.

“For if they had not been hard, but gentle, they would have said to themselves: ‘He does not say this without reason; there must be some hidden sacrament here.’ They would have remained with him, gentle rather than hard, so that they might learn from him what those who remained learned after the others had departed.

“For when the twelve disciples remained after the others had gone away, they reported to him, as though grieving over the death of those who had been scandalized by his saying and had departed. But he instructed them and said: ‘It is the Spirit who gives life, but the flesh profits nothing. The words that I have spoken to you are spirit and life. Understand spiritually what I have spoken. You are going to eat this body which you see, and you are going to drink the blood which those who crucify me will pour out. I have entrusted a sacrament to you; understood spiritually, it will give you life. And although it is necessary for it to be celebrated visibly, nevertheless it must be understood invisibly.’”

What could have been said more openly or plainly than this?

“You are going to eat this body which you see, and you are going to drink the blood which those who crucify me will pour out.”

Here there is nothing ambiguous, nothing that can be understood as anything other than that Lord’s body which appeared to be eaten and that blood which was to be poured out and drunk. This is plainly what the Lord himself said:

“Take and eat; this is my body, which will be delivered for you. This is the blood which will be poured out for you.”

But let us return to the earlier passage:

“Christ,” he says, “took earth from the earth, because flesh is earth; and he gave us for eating and for salvation that very flesh—not another, plainly, but the very flesh which he took from the earth.”

Behold how, elsewhere, for a definite reason, he calls it a figure and a sign, while here he openly declares that Christ’s flesh, taken from the earth, was given to us for eating. And it is certainly no flesh other than that which was born from the Virgin, endured the hanging of the cross, passed through the heavens, and was placed in the Father’s seat for the glory of human nature, governing the dominion of the world according to his will, and sharing in every respect the majesty of God. It is no longer subject to any corruption, and elevates those who receive it so that, once the distress of mortal nature has finally been conquered, they may deserve to become sharers and participants in blessed immortality.

Persisting, therefore, in the incorruptibility of its own integrity, it is believed to suffer nothing corruptible because of our fault, although in the visible mystery it appears, through the service of our ministry, not to be absent from the temporal service of the ministers. The truth, therefore, must be believed in the proper nature of the substance, and sincerity in the inestimable dignity of the sacrament. Thus true flesh and true blood must be understood without any corruption, although the appearance of bread and wine, providentially preserved, serves the temporary devotion of the ministers. When it has been received, we too may deserve to be transformed into the members of Christ, and it into us, through the truth of the nature shared by both sides—namely, ours and his, which he graciously deigned to take from us in order to make us participants in him, both now in some manner and, when this is removed, more perfectly at some future time, in him who forever remains from the Father and in the Father.

How, then, could that holy man, who so clearly defined that Christ took flesh from the earth and indicated that he had given it to us for eating and for salvation, have taught elsewhere anything contrary to his own opinion—God forbid!—and rashly and impiously declared that the Lord’s sacrament was merely a figure or sign and nothing else?

Nevertheless, the Truth itself points out that something must be done by us through the mystery. Hence the Apostle says: “Whenever you eat this bread, you proclaim the Lord’s death.” And Peter says: “Christ suffered for you, leaving you an example, so that you might follow in his footsteps.”

XXIV. Behold the sign; behold the figure to which Augustine refers: “so that you might follow in his footsteps.” That is, those who believe in him by faith and receive him in his body and blood must imitate him in the practice of good works and the sincerity of their conduct:

“He committed no sin, and no deceit was found in his mouth. When he was reviled, he did not revile in return; when he suffered, he did not threaten.”

For whoever shares in the body and blood of Christ, which was poured out through his Passion, ought to share in him through sincere kindness toward his neighbors and the gentleness of a compassionate spirit.

This is what Augustine says:

“Therefore it is a figure instructing us to share in the Lord’s passion and to remember with sweetness and benefit, in memory, that Christ’s flesh was crucified and wounded for us.”

As though he were saying: What is received in the sacrament is indeed the truth, and what is taken is true flesh and true blood. Nevertheless, through the indication of that very truth and through the example of the Lord’s Passion, which is recalled there, the devotion of all who receive is admonished to strive for the innocence of that Lamb through the merit of a simple life and to imitate the footsteps of his suffering through the mercy of fraternal compassion. For our sake he did not shrink from the insults of reproach or the injuries of suffering, and he graciously provided for all, believers and unbelievers alike, the singular remedy of his death and the benefit of life.

That this is what the same teacher truly meant, and nothing else, he makes still clearer in the preceding work—that is, in the second book of *On Christian Doctrine*—when he says among other things:

“For by the fragrance of the ointment with which his feet were anointed, the Lord gave some sign; and, after the sacrament of his body and blood had been tasted beforehand, he indicated what he wished.”

In this passage you may observe that the fragrance of the ointment was both real, according to the account of what happened, and nevertheless signified something else according to the method of allegorical interpretation; and that the foretaste of the Lord’s sacrament—that is, the reception of Christ’s body and blood—is likewise established as true according to the integrity of the events, while it is not thereby deprived of its significance.

Elsewhere, discussing the sacraments on the second day of Easter, he says:

“We are one bread and one body, though we are many, and we all share in one bread and one cup, because he who suffered for us commended his body and blood to us in this sacrament. He also made us ourselves his body, for we have become his body through his mercy.

“You did not exist, and you were created; you were brought to the Lord’s threshing floor by those who were laboring for the good—that is, by those proclaiming the Gospel. You were threshed; you began to be ground by fasts and exorcisms. Afterward you came to the water, and you were sprinkled; you became one. With the heat of the Holy Spirit approaching, you were baked, and you became the Lord’s bread.

“Behold what you have received. Therefore, just as you see that what has been made is one, so be one yourselves, loving one another, holding fast to one faith, one hope, and undivided charity.

“When heretics receive this testimony, they act against themselves, because they seek division, whereas this bread signifies unity. So too wine flows from many clusters, and now, after the pressures of the winepress, it is one in the cup’s sweetness.

“And you, after those fasts, labors, humility, and contrition, have now come in Christ’s name to the Lord’s cup as though to a cup. Where you are at the table, where you are in the cup, you are with us. For we are this together, because we drink together and because we live together.”

Thus, in many places, and thus in this statement, as well as in the preceding chapter, the aforesaid bishop indicates that the Lord’s sacrament signifies something without abolishing the faith of its truth.

But while he laboriously devotes himself to writing books, he explains himself less fully in certain passages. Consequently, to some who are less educated and not at all thoroughly trained in the sacred Scriptures, he appears difficult or incorrectly understood, and is proved to become a seedbed of error.

Nevertheless, if he were shown to have understood this matter otherwise and to have said something alien to the integrity of so great a mystery—God forbid!—one would have to bring forward in opposition the Apostle’s definitive statement:

“Even if an angel from heaven should announce to you something beyond what you received, let him be accursed.”

## XXV

Furthermore, let us hear what the Apostle himself taught and thought on this matter—an apostle whom not even an angel from heaven is to be accepted if he should think contrary to the faith:

> “The cup which we bless, is it not a participation in the blood of Christ? The bread which we break, is it not a participation in the body of Christ?”

But far be it from us to suppose that a man of such great authority in the Church of Christ thought otherwise concerning the sacrament of Christ’s body and blood than the Lord himself delivered or his own Apostle taught—he who is found to have left, in various books, so many and such important testimonies of sound faith, which no one can contradict. Indeed, one would hardly come across anyone who would write them, or even read them!

Among these is the following passage in Book Four, *On the Holy Trinity*:

> “Who, then, is so just and holy a priest as the only Son of God—not one who needed, through sacrifice, to purge his sins, whether original sins or those added from human life? And what could be taken up by all so suitably to be offered for them as human flesh? And what could be so fitting for this immolation as mortal flesh? And what could be so pure, for cleansing the faults of mortals, as flesh born in the womb and from the virgin womb without any contagion of carnal desire? And what could be offered and received with such gratitude as the flesh of our sacrifice, made the body of our priest, so that, since four things are considered in every sacrifice—whom it is offered to, by whom it is offered, for whom it is offered, and what is offered—the same one, the true Mediator, reconciling us to God through the sacrifice of peace, might remain one with him to whom he offered, make himself one in himself with those for whom he offered, and himself be the one who offered?”

And in the book *Against Faustus*:

> “The blood of Christ has a mighty voice on earth, when, having received it, all the nations respond, ‘Amen.’ This is the clear voice of the blood, which the blood itself expresses from the mouths of the faithful, redeemed by that same blood.”

Again:

> “The fact that, after seven days, the dove, once released, did not return signifies the end of the age, when there will be rest for the saints—not still in the sacrament of hope by which the Church is joined together in this present time, so long as what flowed from Christ’s side is being drunk, but already in the perfection itself of eternal salvation, when the kingdom is handed over to God the Father.”

Also, in the first book *On the Creed*:

> “How great a crime it is to kill Christ! Yet the Jews killed him, and many afterward believed in him, drank his blood, and their sin, which they had committed, was forgiven.”

In the second book likewise:

> “For his side was struck, and immediately blood and water flowed forth: water, in which the bride was purified; blood, from which she is found to have received her dowry. In this blood the holy martyrs washed their robes and made them white. Invited to the wedding of the Lamb, they came, received the cup, drank, and gave it to him to drink in return: for they drank his blood and poured out their own blood for him.”

In the book *On the Fourth Day*:

> “The first man was from the earth, earthly. What does every human being say—the earth? When he receives the blood of Christ, he says, ‘Amen.’ What is ‘Amen’? ‘It is true.’ What is ‘It is true’? That the blood of Christ was poured out. By whom was it brought about? By the disciple who handed him over. By saying ‘Amen,’ by crying out ‘It is true,’ he says this: ‘Every human being is earth.’ Behold, in the case of Judah: ‘The voice of your brother’s blood cries out to me from the earth.’ We have proved that you are watered with his blood. See, earth, how you receive this blood, because whoever receives it receives a blessing.”

Again, in the same work:

> “Respond as Cyprian responded, and Laurence and the other saints, who, having received the blood of Christ, did not hesitate to pour out their own blood for the blood which they had drunk.”

And shortly afterward:

> “See that you do not abandon the table of your Bridegroom, so that you may remain beautiful. You will eat his flesh daily and drink his blood, and you will have eternal life. The table of your Bridegroom has whole bread and a holy cup. Of this bread and of this cup he himself said: ‘The bread which I shall give is my flesh; the cup which I shall sanctify is my blood.’”

In the third book *On the Creed*:

> “Having fallen prostrate on the ground and become a disciple of the heavenly Chief Physician, he himself first drank the antidote prepared from the physician’s blood and offered it to his lovers to drink. Kings themselves drank this antidote prepared from the blood of the crucified one, and those who had been persecutors of the Church became its defenders.”

In the book *On the Cataclysm*:

> “For the Lamb is eaten during the night of this age, so that, when that morning comes which will have no evening, the sacrifice of the Lamb’s image may no longer be offered, but we may find there the Lamb himself, whom we eat daily and whose blood we drink—the perfect priest whom here we know to have been slain for our salvation.”

In the *Gospel of John*:

> “The words which I have spoken to you are spirit and life.”

> “Understand spiritually what I have said, for you will eat this body which you see, and you will drink that blood which those who crucify me are going to pour out.”

Can such great, such numerous, and such clear writings of Saint Augustine not suffice for our complete instruction concerning the truth that is in Christ’s sacraments, and serve as testimony to the same man’s sincere faith? Although, for a particular reason, he called the Lord’s sacrament a figure, did he ever think or teach that it should be understood according to the truth as anything other than true flesh and true blood?

For consider what he said:

> “You will eat this body which you see, and you will drink the blood which those who crucify me are going to pour out.”

What could have been said more openly or more clearly? Therefore, when he called it a figure, he was considering not what the Lord’s sacrament was, but what it signified.

## XXVI

But because certain perverse people have plunged from the opinion of so great a teacher into a labyrinth of error and have stubbornly attempted to lead others after them, it must be understood that many people do not understand his subtle statements at all. This is especially demonstrated by the fact that they read things they do not understand, not in order to learn, but rather to procure, through the authority of so great a man, support for the error in which they have long been languishing after being deceived, and more easily to ensnare others in the traps of deception by adapting his authority to their perversity.

Therefore, it seems necessary to persuade and admonish more earnestly that whoever encounters and reads the books of interpreters of divine things should proceed through each passage with caution. Whenever a difficulty concerning an obscure matter arises for him, he should attribute it to his own slowness rather than to an error in the teacher. Accordingly, he should strive, by his own study if he is able, to understand what is being said; if he cannot, he should hasten to learn under the instruction of a Catholic teacher; or, if he cannot grasp the matter under discussion, he should at least learn reverently to honor it. By such humility he may either come to understand what had seemed arduous and difficult, or receive from God another grace which he did not yet possess.

For just as humility acquires the benefits of virtues that were not present, so it ensures that those already acquired are not lost. Thus, since Christian humility is necessary in all the gifts of religion, it is shown to be especially useful and appropriate in this sacrament of the Lord’s tradition. In it the grace of divine power shines so brightly that it is grasped by humility rather than by human ingenuity.

A discussion of its greatness—terrible and more worthy of reverence than of investigation—is found to have been presented very appropriately in the *Dialogue of John and Basil*. For among other things it is written:

> “There were indeed things that were terrible and fearful even in those matters performed under the Law in the Old Testament before grace—for example, the bells, the pomegranates, the stones arranged upon the breast, the ephod, the mitre, the head-dress, the ankle-length garment, the golden plate, the Holy of Holies, and within it the reverent silence and solitude. But if someone considers the things established in the ordering of grace, he will judge those terrible things that came before to have been small, and he will recognize as true even through these what was pronounced concerning the Law: that what had been glorified was not glorified because of the surpassing glory.

> “For when you see our Lord sacrificed, and the priest standing by the incense and invoking God, and all alike being drenched with that precious blood, do you still think that you are among human beings, and are you not immediately transported in spirit into heaven, excluding every carnal sense from your mind, so that, with your soul bare and your perception utterly pure, you behold the things that are in heaven?”

And again:

> “Who, then, will have the madness to despise this ministry, which is so worthy of reverence?”

And a little farther below:

> “But when the priest has invoked the Holy Spirit, has sacrificed that venerable victim, and afterward touches the common Lord of all, where, tell me, shall we place him according to our estimation? For then angels also surround the priest, and the tribunal and the place of the altar are filled with heavenly powers in honor of the one who is sacrificed. This is shown even by what takes place.

> “I myself heard from someone who reported that a certain presbyter, remarkable for the holiness of his life and accustomed to see revelations, had once related that he had seen such a spectacle—that is, at the time of the sacrifice he had seen a multitude of angels, as far as it was possible for him to behold them, surrounding it in shining garments and crowning the altar, with the order in which soldiers customarily stand around their king.”

These things are written in that man’s book exactly as stated. Since they contain a revelation divinely displayed, we have thought it worthwhile to narrate elsewhere revelations found in different places as well, for they promise the greatest benefit to readers.

## PART EIGHT

### XXVII

There was a noblewoman, distinguished by birth and upright in honorable conduct, in the time of Saint Pope Gregory. On one occasion, as was her custom, she brought an offering to the altar. When that same pontiff had consecrated it with his own hands, the time for communicating arrived.

After each person had received the Lord’s communion according to the dignity of his order, a portion of the Lord’s sacrament was extended by the hand of that same bishop to the woman mentioned above, while he said:

> “May the body of our Lord Jesus Christ profit you unto eternal life.”

At this, recognizing the piece of bread that she had offered, she smiled. The pontiff, therefore, was moved, held back his hand, and placed the offering upon the altar. He addressed the people concerning the matter, then devoted himself to prayer with the faithful clergy. Rising from the ground, he found that the bread had become flesh, just as it was, and he showed it to the doubtful woman and to the others. I believe that this greatly strengthened them in the faith.

### XXVIII

After these matters have been briefly recounted, another marvel, no less useful and worthy of being briefly committed to memory in writing, seems appropriate. A certain presbyter-elect, distinguished in life and conduct, frequently celebrated the divine sacraments out of devotion. At last, confidently hoping to obtain this from divine mercy and from the merit of his diligent service, he humbly asked, while performing the divine mysteries, that the matter with which he was so familiar might be divinely revealed to him.

As he lay prostrate on the ground and was drenched with tears, an angel suddenly appeared, ordered him to rise immediately, and announced that he had obtained what he had requested. At the angel’s command he rose at once and saw with complete certainty a boy where he had left the consecrated bread.

O marvelous event! He took the boy in trembling hands, pressed him closely to his own breast, and sorrowfully and devoutly brought the boy’s mouth to his own mouth to kiss it. In this way he satisfied his burning desire for a long time by seeing, kissing, and embracing Christ. Finally, he restored the Son of God to the altar and obtained through prayers that he deign to return to his former form; and so he participated in the sacred mysteries according to custom.

### XXIX

It does not seem that we should pass over what blessed Jerome, whose authority among ecclesiastical teachers is considered preeminent, is found to have narrated in the book which he chose to call *The Lives of the Fathers*.

One of the elders, indeed great in the merit of his life but uneducated and insufficiently instructed in the Scriptures, was in error concerning the Lord’s mystery—yet, as has been said, more through ignorance than through malice. When this became known to two other Fathers, men endowed with great grace of virtue and teaching of wisdom, they hastened by agreement to visit him.

When they wished to persuade him of the truth concerning the Lord’s body and blood, he did not agree at all, but said:

> “Unless I see the matter, I do not believe you.”

When those who had assembled heard this, and were explaining the truth to that rustic old man, they imposed upon him a three-day fast with them and dismissed the gathering so that they might entreat the Lord concerning the matter. At the appointed time they met again and then proceeded to the church where the divine mysteries were being celebrated. There they awaited the outcome of the matter they had conceived in their minds.

The grace of seeing what was taking place was granted to those three alone, plainly revealed to the sight of their intellectual vision. When the loaves had been placed upon the altar, only those three saw what appeared to be a little boy lying upon the altar.

When the presbyter extended his hands to break the bread, an angel descended from heaven, holding a knife in his hand, and sacrificed that boy. He caught the boy’s blood in a cup. As the presbyter broke the bread into small portions, the angel likewise cut the boy’s limbs into small portions.

When the old man approached to receive holy communion, flesh covered with blood was given to him alone. When he saw this, he was terrified and cried out:

> “I believe, Lord, that the bread placed upon the altar is your body and that your cup is your blood.”

Immediately that portion in his hand became bread according to the mystery, and he took it into his mouth, giving thanks to God.

Then the elders said:

> “God knows that human nature cannot eat human flesh. Therefore, in his loving dispensation, he wished the proper reality of his body and blood to lie hidden beneath the figure of bread and wine.”

### XXX

We have also judged that the account read in the book *The Life of Saint Basil* ought to be inserted into our little narrative, since we believe that it can greatly assist in resolving doubt. It is reported as follows.

A certain Jew, not yet reborn in Christ but extremely curious about the divine mysteries, secretly mingled with the faithful and once entered a church in order to investigate carefully what was being done there. When blessed Basil was celebrating the Holy of Holies, and the time had come to distribute the Lord’s body to the people, he approached the altar with the others and received from the minister’s hand a portion of the sacred mystery, made flesh.

When he came to the cup to receive from it, he saw that it too was filled with blood. Astonished by the magnitude of the miracle, he returned home and explained everything he had done and seen to his wife, who knew nothing of it. When she believed, he went to Basil the next day, carefully reported what had happened and what he had seen, and, prudently recognizing the power of holy baptism and the Christian name, asked that it be given to him. He obtained it without delay.

If anyone is troubled by the apparent difficulty of this event—that a portion of the Lord’s body and blood is said to have been revealed to a pagan, indeed a Jew, who did not yet believe, and that such a thing is denied to have been possible—let him consider other signs of the Savior’s mercy, much greater than this. Let him consider how he appeared to the ignorant world clothed in flesh and how he endured death for the impious and sinners.

Let him also attend to the fact that, in the Acts of the Apostles, the grace of the Holy Spirit was unexpectedly granted to pagans and gentiles. He will observe that nothing new or incredible occurred in this matter, nothing that exceeds the faith of truth or is unworthy of the Savior’s mercy.

Concerning him Scripture says:

> “God so loved the world that he gave his only-begotten Son,”

namely, so that he might endure the hanging of the cross and the punishment of death for the redemption of the world.

He was born of the Jews, to whom he was sent by the Father as he had promised, just as he himself says:

> “I was sent only to the sheep that had perished from the house of Israel.”

It is therefore not surprising if he unveiled the mysteries of his sacraments and revealed the proper reality of his body and blood, since he had willed to give himself, according to the hereditary promise, for the redemption of those people.

[Col. 1420C] **XXXI**

The son of a certain Jew, while being educated among Christian boys in the liberal studies of letters, went one day with his companions of the same age to the basilica of the glorious, undefiled, and ever-Virgin Mary, where the solemn rites of the Mass were being celebrated. There, as a child among children, he received a share of the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ, and returned home to his father. Amid embraces and kisses, he simply recounted what he had done.

When the impious father heard this—an enemy of Christ and of his laws—he raged violently and threatened the boy, saying:

> “Because you have acted against my will, I shall now be a harsh and cruel parricide toward you, in vengeance for the insult done to our violated law.”

Having said this, he seized the boy, threw him into a nearby blazing furnace, and added wood so that he would be burned more fiercely.

Meanwhile, when the mother learned of this, she hurried there in lamentation, as though she might rescue her son. But, accomplishing nothing because of the force of the flames, overcome by grief, she threw off the covering from her head. With her hair scattered, she ran here and there, filling the entire city with her wretched cries.

At her cries the people suddenly gathered and learned the whole crime in order. Indignant, they approached the furnace, quickly removed the flames, and drew out the boy, who was found unharmed amid the fire. But they threw his father, the perpetrator of so great a crime, into the same flames by deliberate common decision; there, by divine judgment, he was burned to the bones and instantly perished.

When the boy was questioned whether he had felt the burning of the flames, he replied:

> “A woman who was carrying a little child in her arms in that basilica, where I received the bread from the table, covered me with her cloak so that the fire would not consume me.”

Here it is plainly shown that the boy saw not only the Son of God but also his holy Mother amid the sacred mysteries. Later, relying upon her protection, he escaped the burning of the flames and the danger of death.

In his innocence and childlike simplicity, he could neither invent nor lie about such a vision. The divine gift of deliverance granted to him provides sufficiently clear testimony to the truth of the matter.

But amid all this, we must carefully consider that, just as it was divinely revealed to this boy whether the sacred mystery received from the altar table is the body of the Son of God, so too the presence of his holy Mother is sometimes present, bringing her protection to those who receive it, provided that they possess the merit of simplicity and innocence during the celebration. Such people hold a singularly beloved place in God’s intimate favor, as the Savior himself says:

> “Let the little children come to me, for the kingdom belongs to such as these.”

Therefore he also calls his disciples, whom he had chosen as pure and simple, children, saying through the prophet:

> “Behold, I and the children whom God has given me.”

And in the Gospel:

> “Children, do you have anything to eat?”

## PART NINE

### XXXII

But because many things have been said concerning the truth of the Lord’s sacrament—although in an unskilled manner of expression, yet with the truth of meaning and integrity of faith preserved—I wish briefly to excuse my conscience and faithfully make known that I have dictated these things simply for the simple, and for those who lack either the depth of understanding or the abundance of books. I do not seem to be the only one who has ventured to do this.

For others, having found the same opportunity, are found to have acted in a manner deserving pardon, compelled by divine zeal to write many things against the perfidious enemies of the Church. In our time, a very great multitude of these had occupied the provinces of the Franks and were attempting to infect the surrounding regions and places with the poison of their perfidy.

The author and head of this error appeared to be a certain Berengarius, whom many of the Franks, and also some of the Northmen—either because he had taught them himself or because he had assisted them for a while in their desire to learn—favored greatly.

### XXXIII

In the year 1053 of the Lord’s Incarnation, he entered the territory of the Northmen and came to the monastery called Préaux. To its Catholic ruler, who governed the monastery vigorously and by whom he had been received honorably enough, he impiously uttered many blasphemies.

I learned this not long afterward from that same abbot, named Ansfredus, who was lamenting bitterly to me over such great impiety. The abbot tested him carefully on many points and found him similarly reprehensible and perfidious in many matters.

Leaving there, Berengarius hastened to the prince of the Northmen, whom he also subtly attempted to entangle in his perfidy. But although the prince had not yet passed beyond the years of adolescence, he nevertheless—being endowed with the merit and grace of Catholic faith—kept him under careful restraint. He detained him with him until he reached the inland seat of his kingdom, a place called Briotna [variant: Briona], where he arranged for a dispute to be held after summoning Catholic and learned men from every direction.

They came, and the matter was proposed for examination on the following day. When many wise men from all Northmannia, men regarded as numerous and distinguished, had assembled, they refuted the aforementioned heresiarch Berengarius and another cleric whom he had brought with him, in whose eloquence he had placed his hope of victory. They overcame them before everyone by such evident reasoning that they forced them into silence and compelled their assent to the words by which they defended the Catholic faith.

Berengarius, finally escaping not without shame, went to Chartres. There, when clerics of that city consulted him about the same question—for the matter had already become widely known—he gave no answer, but promised that he would respond when an opportunity was given him.

Not long afterward, therefore, he dictated letters, which I myself also read. In them, breathing out many absurdities foreign to the Catholic faith, he denounced the Roman Church—the head, namely, of all Christendom—with great rashness by the term “heretical.” Along with it he likewise defamed its ruler, the lord Pope Leo, a man whose Catholic faith, distinguished wisdom, and praiseworthy diligence were widely recognized.

While postponing his answer to those questioning him, he reported that he had been intent on refuting them both. For the appointed day of the council later held at Vercelli was then approaching.

He sent these letters, which seemed to him full of purity but were in reality filled with much vanity, to the men of Chartres who had challenged him on the question.

When the report of so great an evil grew and struck the hearts of all the faithful more forcefully, and when this poison was already spreading secretly and openly through many people, it happened that the matter reached the ears of King Henry of the Franks.

On the advice of the bishops and nobles of the kingdom, he ordered a council to be convened at Paris on the tenth day before the Kalends of November. He commanded the aforesaid Berengarius to attend the assembly of so many Fathers, either to support his statements by the authority of the Fathers despite the opposition of many, or, if he could not defend them, prudently to pass over into the Catholic faith, which he could not oppose.

Meanwhile the appointed day arrived, and a large gathering of bishops and other clerics of the holy order, as well as noble laymen, assembled at Paris. But the aforementioned Berengarius, struck by fear because of his evil conscience, delayed coming there as he had been ordered. He kept himself with Bruno, his bishop—the bishop of Angers, under whom he held the office of archdeacon—chiefly because Bruno too was known to be involved in the same error, being credulous toward so great a man.

Meanwhile the bishop of Orléans produced, in the presence of everyone and of the king—for the king was present—some writing arranged on a fairly large sheet:

> “Let your holiness order these letters, written by Berengarius, to be read if you wish. I did not receive them from him myself, but when he was sending them by courier to one of his intimates, named Paul, I forcibly seized them.”

After they had been received and handed over to be read, everyone’s ears were raised, their mouths composed into silence, and their hearts prepared to understand what the letters contained.

But during the reading a great murmur suddenly arose, and at each word expressing an absurd meaning a grave roar resounded. Thus the reading displeased everyone intensely, since it reeked of the most wicked heresy. The author of such things was therefore condemned by common judgment, as were his accomplices, and also the book of John Scotus, from which the condemned statements appeared to have been taken.

The council was dissolved and the people departed on the condition that, unless the author of such perversity repented, he and his followers were to be urgently sought out wherever they gathered, with the clerics leading the whole army of the Franks, perhaps in ecclesiastical array; they were to be besieged there until they either consented to the Catholic faith or were captured to suffer the punishment of death.

Accordingly, terrified, they were summoned not long afterward to a council concerning the state of their faith. There they publicly professed that they faithfully believed and understood matters as the Catholic Church holds them. Relics of the saints were brought forward, and, to satisfy everyone and make those present certain of the truth of the faith they had professed, they gave an oath.

But setting aside the account of such men, whom we have heard afterward returned to apostasy and to their former vomit, let us finally close the text of this little book, in which we have faithfully shown, as far as we could, the sincerity of our faith according to the authority of the ancient Fathers, applying many examples from them.

Let us glorify the almighty Lord with all our hearts, whose gift and grace it is that we believe faithfully and act well; he lives and reigns in the Trinity that is one and in perfect unity, throughout all ages of ages.

## EPITAPH OF AINARDUS, ABBOT OF DIVES, BY DURANDUS

*(Ordericus Vitalis, Ecclesiastical History, Book IV, in Duchesne,* Historiae Northmannorum Scriptores, *p. 545.)*

Here lies Ainardus, fragrant as choice nard,  
Rich in the many flowers and merits of his virtues.

By him this place was founded and built,  
With immense effort and no small expense.

This man was great, gentle in uprightness and meek as a lamb,  
Distinguished in life, eminent in teaching,

Sober and chaste, prudent, simple, and honorable,  
Strong in counsel, renowned in office.

He possessed gravity of mind and a more mature age,  
With gray hair and a slender face.

The nineteenth day before the Kalends of February,  
As February advanced, the final lot took him away, and swift death carried him off.

You who pass by, remember to pray for him as a suppliant,  
That the gracious face of God may be his sufficient satisfaction.

## EPITAPH OF MABILIA, COUNTESS AND WIFE OF ROGER OF MONTGOMERY, BY DURANDUS

*(Ordericus Vitalis, Ecclesiastical History, Book V, cited above, p. 578.)*

Born from a lofty line of illustrious parents,  
Great Mabilia is covered by this tomb.

Among famous women she shone more famously still,  
Distinguished throughout the wide world by her merit.

Sharp in intellect, vigilant in understanding, energetic in action,  
Useful in speech, provident in counsel.

Slender in form, but altogether great in honor,  
Generous in expenditure, sufficiently refined in dress.

She was the shield of her homeland, the defense of the frontier,  
To her neighbors gracious or terrible.

But since not all mortals can do everything,  
She perished by the sword, slain by treachery in the night.

And since it is now necessary to bring aid to the dead,  
Let whoever is present as a friend prove it by helping.

**In the year of the Lord 1089. Guitmundus, Archbishop of Aversa.**

## HISTORICAL AND LITERARY NOTICE

*(Fabricius,* Bibliotheca medii et infimi Latini, *Book VII, p. 171.)*

Guitmundus, Guimundus, Guismundus, Wimundus, Witmundus [Note: He is not to be confused with Guimundus the Englishman, an Augustinian, concerning whom see Leland, chapter 163, nor with Guido of Arezzo, concerning whom see above], was first a monk of the monastery of the Holy Cross of Heltonis, Saint Ouen, or Saint Leufredus, of the Benedictine order in Normandy, in the diocese of Évreux.

In the year 1070 he was summoned to England and asked by King William I of England [Note: Ordericus Vitalis IV, p. 524; Mabillon, preface to the sixth century of the Benedictines, § 58], among the Norman leaders under William II, to remain with him in England and undertake ecclesiastical governance. He refused this, however.

Returning to Neustria, or Normandy, after John, archbishop of Rouen, had died in 1079, he was designated by the king and others as John’s successor [Note: Sammarthanus, vol. I of *Gallia Christiana*, p. 576; Ordericus, p. 526]. Because rivals obstructed him, he did not obtain the archbishopric. But after securing permission from his abbot Odilo to go on pilgrimage, he was kindly received by Gregory VII and chosen among the cardinals of the Roman Church [Note: same reference]. Later, under Urban II, who began to occupy the papacy in 1088, he was created metropolitan of Aversa in Apulia, in the kingdom of Naples.

He governed the Church entrusted to him for a long time, as Ordericus testifies [Note: ibid.; add Ughelli, vol. I of *Italia sacra*, p. 488, where his successor in the archbishopric of Aversa, John, is mentioned no earlier than the year 1095]. He was still alive in 1090 and beyond. Hence it is clear that those are mistaken who say that he died in 1080 [Note: Thus Labbe, vol. I of *De sancta Ecclesia*, p. 402; Cave and others] or in 1084 [Note: Joseph Eggs, in *Purpura docta*, p. 81].

A fragment of a letter from Urban II to him survives in the second part of Gratian’s *Decree*, cause 24, question 2, canon 3; from it Latinus Latinius already observed the age of Guitmundus in volume I of his *Bibliotheca sacro-profana*, p. 81.

Thus one must either posit two Guitmunduses, or, if we follow Ordericus, it is necessary to conclude that the Anonymous of Melk is mistaken when, in chapter 102, he says that Guitmundus was made bishop of Aversa by Gregory VII.

It also agrees little with Ordericus’s account that the same author from Melk makes Guitmundus abbot of Stavelot, saying that he fled, assumed the name Christian so that he would not be recognized, became bishop of the Apulians, and argued most invincibly against Berengarius.

See, if you please, what is said above concerning Christian Druthmarus, volume I, pp. 375 and following (at the end of volume CVI of Migne’s *Patrologia*). There is also discussion there of his three books against Berengarius, written in the manner of a dialogue, with Roger, a monk skilled in the medical art, as interlocutor. At Roger’s request he undertook this work and dedicated it to him.

According to Mabillon, he wrote these books while he was still in Neustria, during the pontificate of Gregory VII, and therefore after the Roman council held under Nicholas II in 1059, which he mentions, and after Lanfranc, whom he calls his teacher, but before the Roman council of 1078.

No one, in Mabillon’s judgment, investigated Berengarius and his followers’ various opinions more accurately [Note: Compare Benedict Pictet, *History of the Eleventh Century*, p. 524 and following, where he reviews the arguments of Guitmundus’s books].

These books were published with Algerus by Erasmus at Antwerp in 1530, and afterward under the care of John Vlimmerius at Louvain in 1561, who added the writings of Paschasius and Lanfranc on this subject.

Finally, they appeared in the Paris, Cologne, and Lyons editions of the *Bibliotheca Patrum*, volume XII in Cologne and volume XVIII in Lyons, p. 440, in which edition, as in the earlier ones, the work is also appended on p. 465: Guitmundus’s *Confession concerning the Holy Trinity, the Humanity of Christ, and the Truth of the Body and Blood of Our Lord*; and finally, on p. 468, his *Oration to William I, King of the English, when he refused the bishopric*, preserved by Ordericus Vitalis, *Ecclesiastical History* IV, pp. 524–526.

## THREE BOOKS OF GUITMUNDUS, ARCHBISHOP OF AVERSA, ON THE TRUTH OF CHRIST’S BODY AND BLOOD IN THE EUCHARIST

With Guitmundus himself and Roger, fellow members of the Benedictine order, as interlocutors.

*(Bibliotheca Patrum XVIII, 441.)*

### THE FIRST BOOK BEGINS

**GUITMUNDUS**

You call me, beloved brother Roger, to a matter certainly necessary in these times, but one that ought to be entrusted to someone better than I am: namely, to discuss the truth of the Lord’s body against the questions of our age and, insofar as I am able, to refute in writing the foolishness of Berengarius of Tours.

Although my inclination—or rather my necessity—leads me toward other benefits of the soul, I nevertheless cannot fail your wishes and prayers, since I also know that your religious request serves the common good. But I ask you to grant me this one thing, which you certainly owe me in obedience: do not cease to assist me by praying more earnestly to the Lord concerning this matter. For both we and our words are in his hand (*Wisdom* 7).

**ROGERIUS**

What you ask is entirely reasonable, and one ought not to discuss such great mysteries without prayers always accompanying the discussion. Therefore, with the Lord’s help, it shall be done.

But I ask you to observe this custom for me: after hearing my objections, do not conceal anything further that you judge may rightly be brought against you—whether from Berengarius’s own book, or from the questions of many people who have repeatedly questioned you on this matter, or from your own reflections.

**GUITMUNDUS**

Concerning these sacraments, and in whatever way my conscience speaks before God, I shall disclose as much as seems sufficient, with the Lord’s help. But so that you may know more fully the cause and origin of the whole error, let us first say a very little about the man’s character and teaching.

**ROGERIUS**
You certainly speak of something fitting: for some, observing in him a certain weight, as it were, of I know not what gravity, and the pomp of his ancient learning, preferred to imitate him.

**GUITMUNDUS**

When he was still spending his youthful years in the schools—as those who knew him then report—he was so inflated by the frivolity of his intellect that he paid little attention to the judgment of his own teacher, considered his fellow students worthless, and despised the books of the liberal arts. But since he could not, by himself, reach the deeper secrets of philosophy—for he was not in fact so acute, and moreover at that time the liberal arts had grown obsolete throughout Gaul—he at least aspired, by means of novel interpretations of words, in which he still takes extraordinary delight, to claim for himself the reputation of unique learning and to pursue the glory of a certain superiority, in whatever manner he could. Thus, with a pompous bearing, a lofty position above the others, and an appearance of the dignity of a teacher that he simulated rather than demonstrated by his deeds, as well as by keeping himself deeply wrapped within his hood and by pretending to meditate at length, deceiving the unwary with the very slow, almost mournful utterance of a voice scarcely produced at last after long expectation, he professed himself a teacher of the liberal arts while scarcely knowing them.

But after he had been disgracefully confounded by the lord Lanfranc in dialectic over a fairly insignificant matter, and after God had caused the liberal arts, through that same most learned man, lord Lanfranc, to grow warm again and revive most excellently, this man, grieving that he had been deserted by his students, turned to spewing forth shamelessly the mysteries of the divine Scriptures, precisely where Lanfranc—then still a young man—had not yet applied himself very deeply, since he had hitherto been occupied with other studies.

But there too he was foolish; for “wisdom will not enter into a malicious soul” (Wisdom 1). Seeking diligently for novelties by which he might stir the hearts of everyone and draw everyone’s eyes toward himself, he preferred to be a heretic under the admiration of men than to live privately as a Catholic beneath the eyes of God. Then he brought forth those teachings that would please worldly people, though they desired always to sin with impunity: namely, he destroyed lawful marriages, as far as he could, and overturned the baptism of infants. In the one matter, the devil, through his mouth, persuaded the worst men that all women might lawfully be used; in the other, after abolishing infant baptism, he urged them to plunge with impunity into the depth of every evil, since they were to be baptized only afterward.

Read the letter of the bishop of Liège against Berengarius to Henry, king of the Franks, and you will find the very same things written there in almost the same words. In those days he also dared, in his utter madness, to pour out this blasphemy, against which, with God’s favor, we shall act. Here too he was serving the devil, so that, once the truth of the Lord’s body had been removed, those who wished to sin might be restrained from no crime by any reverence or fear of receiving holy communion. I do not now wish to delay you with the other impieties—of which he spewed out quite a number during that period. This, then, is how we have learned that this plague began. But now I shall explain how and through whom it was for a time retained, and how and through whom it was later defeated and condemned; once you know its origin, development, and downfall, you will better understand what judgment to form of it—unless you think the account too long.

**ROGERIUS**

On the contrary, I shall listen to this thirstily. I think it will contribute greatly to the matter before us.

**GUITMUNDUS**

Since his earlier blasphemies could not be endured even by the ears of the worst men—the first because of its injuries to mothers and the other consequences, the second because of its condemnation of their infants—and since he could find absolutely no place in sacred Scripture from which to defend them, especially because blessed Augustine had argued against them at great length (*On the Good of Marriage* and *On the Baptism of Infants*), he devoted himself entirely to defending this latter position. Here he also seemed to rely, as it were, upon the testimony of the senses. Nor did he find that anyone among the most holy Fathers had argued against it at comparable length—for the Church of their time had not been so greatly in need of such an argument, although many of their wisest writers clearly and lucidly recorded what they themselves held on the matter.

Thus, having gathered a few little arguments—as no heresy has ever been able to grow strong without some appearance of rational plausibility—and having also brought forward a few passages of sacred Scripture that he had badly understood, passages that are a deadly snare to many who go astray, he secretly spread the most foul poison of so great an evil in every direction he could through impoverished schoolmen, whom he had already corrupted both by the support with which he sustained them and by his seductive but distorted speeches.

Those who, in addition, accepted him in any way were people who, terrified by the apostolic judgment that says, “Whoever eats and drinks unworthily eats and drinks judgment upon himself” (1 Corinthians 11), preferred that the holy communion which they were compelled to receive according to ecclesiastical custom should either not exist at all or be something less than it was, rather than restrain themselves from their crimes to some extent out of fear of it. Thus, through such people also, the execrable plague grew a little stronger.

As soon as these teachings began to be heard openly, Catholic men were deeply stirred and found them intolerable.
