With the most blessed lord Pope Leo presiding in person, they convened a council at Vercelli. You said that you wished some matters to be discussed by us there as well; now explain what you think should be set before me.

**ROGERIUS**

Berengarius and those who follow him maintain that the Lord’s Eucharist is not truly and substantially the Lord’s body and blood, but is called so merely by an expression, because it is like a shadow and a signifying figure of the Lord’s body and blood. I would not be so greatly disturbed by this if they were merely deceived, in their carnal understanding, according to the senses—except that, as you mentioned above, they appear to advance certain little arguments and to support them with several statements of blessed Augustine. They also parade certain words of the Lord the Savior, by which the weak may perhaps be scandalized.

First I shall set forth the arguments themselves, and afterward the authorities. “Nature,” they say, “does not permit this change.” When they are shown the statement that “the Lord has done whatever he willed” (Psalm 143), they reply, “He did not will this change.” For surely it is not permissible that Christ should be crushed by teeth or broken into pieces, just as these things are crushed by teeth and broken apart.

Answer these points for the moment, if you please; afterward I shall set forth the rest. By arranging the discussion carefully and comparing your answers with each of the points I have proposed, I shall understand that you have satisfied me fully on every matter.

**GUITMUNDUS**

Since you earlier asked that I add whatever seemed to me necessary to your inquiries, understand first that not all who err concerning these sacraments proceed along one and the same path of error. All the Berengarians agree on this point: bread and wine are not changed essentially. But, as I have been able to draw out from some of them, they differ greatly in this respect: some say that nothing whatever of the Lord’s body and blood is present in these sacraments, but that they are merely shadows and figures. Others, yielding to the sound reasoning of the Church but not abandoning their folly, say that the Lord’s body and blood are indeed truly there, but are contained secretly and, so that they may somehow be received—as I may put it—are made into bread. They say that this is Berengarius’s more subtle position.

Others, though no longer Berengarians but fiercely opposed to Berengarius, were nevertheless for a time troubled by his arguments and by certain words of the Lord—as we shall discuss more fully in its proper place—and used to think that bread and wine are partly changed and partly remain. Still others, who recoil far more strongly from the irrational view of these people, but do not understand very aptly the same words of the Lord by which the others are moved, thought that bread and wine are indeed changed completely, but that when the unworthy approach to receive the flesh and blood of the Lord, they change back again into bread and wine. Against all these errors we shall attempt, as the Lord grants us strength, to take our stand.

Let us now answer the two kinds of Berengarians first. Although they differ among themselves, they have almost the same position against us and rely upon the same arguments. Both assert that nothing essential is changed in the bread and wine. Let us examine their arguments, and first investigate what they assert concerning nature. When they say, “Nature cannot endure this change,” they must either be saying this absolutely and without exception, so that it could never happen—not even if God willed it—or they must be speaking with some qualification.

If they speak absolutely and without exception, they first openly declare themselves enemies of God’s will, by affirming that something is impossible for him. Indeed, they destroy themselves whenever they recite the verse from the Psalm that you mentioned: “The Lord has done whatever he willed” (Psalm 134). For if they do not accept this verse, they recite it in vain; nor do they now believe in the Lord’s omnipotence, since they argue that nature can resist him when he wills something. If they do not believe him omnipotent, they do not believe him to be God. For he is not truly God who cannot do what he wills.

But I think they do not deny that they believe in God. Let them therefore accept that “the Lord has done whatever he willed.” At the same time, then, they must necessarily accept that the Lord made it possible for nature to endure this change, if he willed it. For if the nature of all things, when absolutely nothing existed, was brought into being by God’s will and formed into the diverse kinds of so many things, how will the already existing nature of bread and wine resist God’s will, so that it may not be transferred into something else?

What ridiculous people they are! While imagining that they are defending nature, they demonstrate instead that they do not understand nature’s power. For, as you yourself testify—you who know, through the art of medicine, the natures of foods and of human beings—every day the nature of the bread we eat and of the wine we drink is naturally transformed into our flesh and our blood.

If the human stomach, or even that of any animal, can do so much that it changes bread and wine, or whatever foods are enclosed within it, into living flesh and living blood each day, will God’s majesty and the power of his word not be able, if he wills, to transform bread and wine into his flesh and blood?

And if Christians are willing to grant God no more than the great pagan philosopher Plato granted him—namely, that the nature of things is what God wills—what could be more absurd than for what God wills to oppose God when he wills it? Therefore, unless these people are utterly without understanding, they will never make the unqualified claim that nature can undergo this change unless God wills it. Their assertion of this as something significant against us is therefore futile. It accomplishes absolutely nothing against us. No Christian believes that this change occurs except by God’s will.

Let them therefore cease their empty statement, “Nature does not permit it,” and let us ask only whether God wills this change.

“Far be it from us,” they say, “to believe that God would ever will this! For it is not permissible that Christ should be crushed by teeth.”

I ask first what they mean by “crushed.” If by “crushed” they mean touched more closely or pressed more firmly, I ask why it should not be permissible for Christ to be crushed by teeth. If they say that it is impermissible because it cannot happen, that is the very same argument they used concerning nature: nature cannot endure it. This is a thoroughly empty argument. No impossibility in created things can obstruct the will of God.

Furthermore, why could he not be pressed by teeth, when he could be touched by Thomas’s hands after the resurrection? And of the holy women who met him after the resurrection, Scripture says that “they held his feet.” There is no reason why a tooth should not be able to touch what a hand touches; for touch belongs to the whole body just as it belongs to the hands. Whatever a hand touches can therefore be touched by the whole body, and thus it can also be touched by teeth.

Moreover, what can be touched even lightly, since it is a solid body, why could it not also be touched somewhat more firmly—that is, crushed? If the Lord’s body could be touched after the resurrection by the hands of the apostle Thomas and of the holy women, why should it not today be touched—whether more lightly or more firmly, that is, crushed—by the teeth of believers? No reason appears to stand in the way.

But if they say that it is impermissible for Christ to be crushed by teeth not because it is impossible, but because it seems unworthy, I ask again why it ought to seem unworthy. Is it because Christ appears to be humbled too greatly?

Yet he did not disdain, for the salvation of the faithful, to be crushed—so far as it depended upon them—by the rods of unbelievers, by a crown of thorns, by the cross, by nails, and by a spear, in the most irreligious manner; as it is written, “He was crushed because of our iniquities” (Isaiah 53). Will he, for the salvation of those same faithful, disdain to be crushed by their teeth in the most religious manner, insofar as their teeth can crush him?

If he endured for us what was more unworthy, how will he disdain to suffer what is less unworthy? Especially since, just as it was necessary for the Lord Jesus Christ to be suspended upon the wood so that death, which had come through wood, might be conquered through the wood of the cross, so it is necessary that Christ truly be eaten: because the ancient people, by truly eating the fruit of the forbidden tree, received death—not the shadow of its fruit, but the fruit itself—while the new people, by truly eating not a shadow but the one who hung upon the tree of obedience, that is, the cross, may escape death and receive life.

Isaiah seems to have prophesied this mystery when he says:

“The Lord of hosts will prepare for all peoples on this mountain a feast of rich foods, a feast of wine, of rich and marrow-filled things, of wine purified; and on this mountain he will destroy the face of the bond that is bound over all peoples, and he will cast down death forever” (Isaiah 25).

The prophet was in Jerusalem. What, then, does “on this mountain” mean except the place where Christ was crucified? And what does “he will prepare a feast for all peoples” mean except that all peoples eat the one who hung there?

What is signified by these rich and marrow-filled foods except flesh made exceedingly rich by the grace of the Holy Spirit, in which “the fullness of divinity dwells bodily” (Colossians 3)? What is signified by purified wine except the holy blood, which is drunk under the appearance of wine? And what will happen to us through this feast? “He will cast down death forever,” he says.

But perhaps their teeth are unclean. The Apostle, however, says: “To the pure all things are pure” (Titus 1). Therefore neither a tooth nor anything else is unclean to Christ.

Certainly hands seem dirtier than teeth. With our hands we touch many kinds of filth that we recoil from bringing to our teeth. He who offered himself to be touched by hands after the resurrection will not avoid teeth because of their uncleanness.

But perhaps they fear injuring the Savior by touching him with their teeth, although they do not fear injuring him by their insolent lies. May God destroy, for their salvation, these enemies who defend him, if they do not know that the flesh of the risen Lord retained what belonged to nature and lost what belonged to weakness. To be touched is natural to flesh; to be injured belongs to weakness. Christ can therefore be touched even by teeth, in such a way that, under whatever pressure of teeth, he can no longer be injured.

Since, then, no impossibility stands in the way, and Christ’s humility is not incompatible with it—if indeed this is also advantageous for us unto life—and since no uncleanness or injury to the Savior need be feared on this account, no other reason arises why it should be forbidden for Christ to be crushed by teeth.

If “crushed” is understood as “touched more firmly,” then their utterly empty claim, “It is not permissible for Christ to be crushed by teeth,” has no force against us.

But if they understand “crushed” as “broken into pieces” or “fragmented,” then there is no longer a second argument but only one: that they say he is crushed by teeth and broken into pieces—unless breaking him into pieces means more than crushing him by teeth. Their statement must therefore be understood as though they were saying: “It is not permissible for Christ to be broken into pieces, either by being crushed with teeth—that is, fragmented—or in any other way.”

We too confess this: it is not permissible for Christ to be broken into pieces by any violence, whether by teeth or in any other manner. But if it pleases the One for whom all things are possible (Matthew 19), by the highest and inscrutable purpose of his counsel, that he should himself divide his body into parts, provided only that it no longer die, suffer injury, or undergo any corruption—for it will endure no further misery—who would dare to judge this impossible?

When they therefore argue that these sacraments are crushed by teeth and broken into pieces, and if by “crushed” they mean “reduced,” we answer: If it pleases him for whom nothing is impossible (Luke 1), who can do whatever he wills with all things, that—not through our violence but through his will operating in our ministry—his body should be divided and distributed in these sacraments without death, injury, or any disadvantage to itself, then, if we believe this, no one can point out anything improper in it.

For here, as Saint Gregory says, “his flesh is divided for the salvation of the people.”

But if it does not please him that his flesh can be divided and distributed without some disadvantage to itself, then we do not believe that these things are reduced by teeth or broken apart in any way. In that case we must understand the statement, “His flesh is divided for the salvation of the people,” not as meaning that it is diminished by being divided, but as referring to the likeness of a breaking, just as Christ is said to be sacrificed daily because of the likeness of his passion.

Although, because of the great mystery, the priest appears to divide these things, we must nevertheless believe that, when his venerable body is distributed to the faithful, our Lord and Savior does not divide himself among individuals but comes to different people through participation in himself.

We may also say that as much is present in one small portion as was present in the entire host. It is written concerning the manna that “the one who gathered more had no excess, and the one who gathered less had no deficiency” (Exodus 16).

Thus the entire host is Christ’s body, while each separate portion is nevertheless the whole body of Christ. Yet three separate portions are not three bodies, but one body. Nor do the portions themselves differ from one another as though there were several bodies, because what one portion of the whole body is, the others also are.

Therefore they should no longer be called several portions, but rather one complete and undivided host, even though, because of the great mystery I have mentioned, it appears to be divided by the priest’s action, since this is how the rite had to be celebrated.

Similarly, if these things appear to be broken by teeth or in some other way, we understand that they are not actually broken, because we believe that the same thing is contained in the whole as in any apparently separate portion.

So that no one may think that I have invented this opinion from my own understanding, I have inserted here the preface that is used throughout almost the entire Latin world on a Sunday between Epiphany and Septuagesima. It contains these words:

“[Fragment:] Eternal God: and to offer you this sacrificial victim, which is saving and the ineffable sacrament of divine grace. It is offered by many, and through the infusion of the Holy Spirit it is made one body of Christ. Each receives Christ the Lord, and in each portion he is wholly present; nor is he diminished in each, but he presents himself entire in each. Therefore we who receive communion of this holy bread and cup become one body of Christ.”

Eusebius of Emesa says the following:

“Ancient history relates: ‘The one who had gathered more had no excess, and the one who had prepared less found no deficiency’ (Exodus 16), because the sacred reception of the Eucharist consists not in quantity but in power. The body, when distributed by the priest, is present in the small portion as much as it is known to be present in the whole. When the Church of the faithful receives it, it is proved to be whole in each individual just as it is complete in all together. From this understanding the apostolic statement is derived: ‘The one who had much did not have too much, and the one who had little did not have too little’ (2 Corinthians 8).

“If we were to offer ordinary bread to the hungry, it would not reach each person in its entirety, because each would take his share in proportion, piece by piece and crumb by crumb. But when this bread is received, individuals have no less than all together. One person receives the whole, two receive the whole, many receive the whole, without diminution; for the blessing of this sacrament knows how to be distributed but does not know how to be consumed by distribution.”

We say the same even if a thousand Masses are celebrated at the same time. We believe that Christ is wholly present in each one, so that neither the diversity of priests nor the diversity of places produces many Christs or a divided Christ.

Indeed, those who believe that the Lord’s body is invisibly present at every Mass cannot oppose us on this point. For when a thousand Masses are celebrated simultaneously, and—as they themselves agree—the whole body of Christ is present in every Mass, since they too deny that the Lord’s body can be divided, then either there will be a thousand bodies of Christ, or they will confess with us that, at one and the same time, one and the same whole and undivided body of Christ can be present in a thousand places.

But they themselves do not say that there are a thousand bodies of Christ. It remains, therefore, that they must believe that in a thousand Masses celebrated at the same time there is one and the same undivided body of Christ.

Similarly, in one host, even if it appears to be divided into several parts, we do not consider that any flesh is divided among them, because each separate portion is the whole body of Christ, just as all the portions joined together are the whole body.

No one should find this incredible. Through daily experience we know that our understanding—that is, the word of our heart—when we clothe it, as it were, with a voice so that what lay hidden in our heart and was known only to us may be made manifest to others through speech, remains at the same time whole in our heart and can likewise appear wholly to a thousand people through the voice it has assumed. So far as the word itself is concerned, it can at once illumine the hearts of all, while the voice with which it has been clothed can strike the ears of everyone at the same time, whole and undivided.

If God has granted so much to a human word that not only the word itself but also the voice with which it is, as it were, clothed can reach a thousand people simultaneously, whole and entire, then no one should consider it incredible that the same can be true of the one omnipotent and co-eternal Word of omnipotent God, and of his flesh, with which he clothed the Word so that it might appear to us in a similar manner.

If someone cannot comprehend this, he should nevertheless not consider it incredible that what he can scarcely comprehend concerning the most frail and transitory human word and momentary voices, which barely exist and never endure, yet almost always experiences in practice, should be possible with God’s Word and flesh.

Blessed Augustine proves with great force that our soul itself, burdened by a body subject to decay, is not divided piece by piece among the individual limbs of the body, but is contained whole and entire in each small part of it.

He who granted our soul this power—so that one and the same undivided soul exists wholly at the same time in each of the several parts of its body—why should he be unable, if he wills, to grant the same dignity to his own flesh, so that it can be present wholly and undivided in the different parts of its body, which is the Church?

For just as our soul is the life of the body, so the Savior’s flesh is the life of the Church—indeed, by God’s grace, much more so. Through the soul the body lives, at least for a time in this world; through the Savior’s flesh the Church is enabled to live not merely in some fashion, but blessedly and eternally.

Since the wisest Solomon said that all things are difficult (Ecclesiastes), so that a human being cannot explain them, is not one who violently attempts to examine these divine mysteries by sight very much like a madman?

All God’s creatures are inexplicable miracles to us; Christ, however, is a singular miracle among all things, or above all things. If Christ can bring it about, as we have said, that each separate portion is the whole body of Christ, while all the separate portions are not many bodies but one body; if one voice strikes the ears of a thousand people and is wholly present with each one, yet is not called many voices but only one; and if the whole soul fills the thousand parts of a human body, presenting itself wholly to each part and yet remaining not many souls but one—then no reason now appears to prevent or forbid Christ from transferring bread and wine into his body and blood, as he himself taught and the Church has believed.

**ROGERIUS**

Concerning the thousand Masses that can be celebrated at the same time, you seem to me, I admit, to have explained the matter very fully and adequately. Nevertheless, I remain somewhat troubled by the division of a single host. For what I initially see as one alone appears, when I divide it, to be divided into several parts, each portion appearing smaller than what was whole [so that].

If the host were divided not by my action but spontaneously, or if after the division its size appeared not to have been altered in its entirety, I would now consider myself satisfied: each portion and all the portions together could then be one complete body without any division.

**GUITMUNDUS**

If you think that enough has been explained concerning the thousand Masses celebrated at one time, it is strange that you can be so troubled concerning one host. Before you divide the host, you see only one host; similarly, before a thousand Masses are celebrated, you see one body of Christ in heaven—if not with your eyes, then with your mind or faith.

And just as you suppose that the host is divided by your action, so one might suppose that the work of the priests causes the one body of Christ, which is in heaven, to be held simultaneously in a thousand places. But far be it from us to say that by their action or yours the one Christ is divided among several places or parts! For it is he who acts in your work—not what your sight judges, but what he himself wills.

Thus the violence of the Jews appeared to cause him to die, and yet he himself says: “No one takes my life from me; I lay it down of my own accord” (John 10). In the same way, Christ may perhaps be thought to be broken by someone’s violence; nevertheless, we must believe that he works not what the carnal senses judge, but what Christ himself wills.

Just as, after the host has been divided, each portion appears smaller to you than the whole host, so in all the Masses the Lord’s body appears less than we believe it to be in heaven. But this is so only according to the senses; and the senses, as they are often deceived in many other matters, are always deceived in this one.

But if the eye of the flesh cannot grasp this, should the eye of the mind therefore be extinguished? When Mary Magdalene, weeping at the Lord’s tomb, saw the Lord himself, was he not truly Jesus because, deceived according to her eyes, she thought she was seeing a gardener? (John 20.) Or when, on the day of his resurrection, he explained the Scriptures as a stranger to two disciples walking along the road, was he anything other than himself because it is written: “Their eyes were held, so that they would not recognize him”? (Luke 24.)

Or when the disciples, laboring on the sea, saw him walking upon the waves, who would dare say that it was not truly he because, with their eyes deceived, they thought him a phantom? (Matthew 24.) Moreover, when they saw him already in the boat with them and marveled at his miracle in the calmed sea, they did not recognize him, as may be inferred from the Gospel, until they came to land. For it is written: “When they had come out of the boat, they immediately recognized him” (Mark 6). From these words, as we have said, it may be inferred that some of them did not recognize him in the boat, perhaps because they were still astonished by the recent miracle.

What then? Should we think that he playfully deceived them? Far be it from us! He was the same everywhere; everywhere he was the truth; everywhere he was wisdom.

But through these events it had to be shown to us that, so long as we stand with weeping Mary beside the Lord’s tomb (John 20), mortifying ourselves (Colossians 3) and proclaiming the Lord’s death until he comes (1 Corinthians 11); so long as we journey as strangers on the road, absent from the Lord (2 Corinthians 5); so long as we labor on the sea of this world and the wind of temptations blows against us; so long as we walk by faith and not by sight (ibid.), although the Lord always comforts us when we weep beside his tomb, always explains the Scriptures to us when we are on the road, always stills us when we are troubled at sea, and is always present with us in the boat of the holy Church until the consummation of the age, nevertheless we do not see him except under the appearance of a stranger—especially with the eyes of the flesh—even though in these sacraments we possess nothing other than him.

And rightly so. Since the fruit of the death-bearing tree had closed the spiritual and truthful eyes of the ancient people and opened their carnal and deceptive eyes, it is just that the fruit of the life-giving cross should close the eyes of the flesh for the new people and open the truthful eyes of the mind, through which the truth is seen.

Therefore, just as no healthy person believes a sick palate when it judges bitter what is sweet to the healthy, so no one except a madman agrees with sickly carnal eyes when they judge against the healed eyes of the mind concerning that inner medicine of light.

For this matter is so great that it cannot be grasped by defective sight. It is also more beneficial for our faith to be exercised in the meantime in this way: through what takes place in this necessary sacrament contrary to the sight of the flesh, we learn to transcend visible things, hasten toward invisible things, and hold more securely to the hidden things taught by Truth, which never lies, than to what the deceptive eye displays before us.

Since, therefore, it has been shown to you that what is present in the portions of one host is the same as what is present in the many Masses celebrated simultaneously, concerning which you said enough had been explained; and since it has been demonstrated by Gospel examples and by reason that you must not judge according to the vision of the carnal eyes, explain whether you think that enough has now been said.

**ROGERIUS**

I admit that you seem to me to pursue the truth of sound faith with an appropriate argument. Nevertheless, I shall not be silent about what still gnaws at me somewhat.

Earlier you said that the priest appears to divide the host because of the mystery, which must be celebrated in this manner. If, then, I saw that after the host had been consecrated it could no longer be divided except for the sake of the mystery—which, as you said, requires that it be celebrated in this way—I would confess that the entire course of your argument was established by unshaken truth.

But since anyone seems able to divide it as he wishes, without any consideration of the mystery, my thought still suffers from certain darkness on this point. It longs to drive that darkness away, yet it cannot do so entirely and freely.

**GUITMUNDUS**
If you thoroughly review in your mind what has been said above, you will recognize, I think, that no darkness remains for you here. For both the many arguments of the ancient philosophers and daily experience teach with complete clarity that the senses are very often deceived. Indeed, as Boethius says, the senses are confused both in matters of the greatest and of the smallest kind. Hence they cannot form a pure and sound judgment about those things in which they are confused. Even concerning moderate matters, they judge not according to the truth of things but according to the disposition of the person perceiving them. Thus, to any healthy eater, if he is very hungry, even bitter things seem sweet; but to a sick person, or to one who is very full, even sweet things are bitter.

Likewise, if someone is wasting away with love for a deformed prostitute, is not her appearance exceedingly pleasing to his eyes, although it greatly offends the sight of almost all observers whose minds have not been taken captive by the same misery? If you ask the eyes about an oar in the water, they assert that it is broken; but once it has been withdrawn, reason proves, with the eyes themselves bearing witness, that it has remained intact. What shall we say about the judgment of the ears? For what sounds most absurd to the ears of a sober person delights any wanton performer through a soft song.

But why should I linger over these matters any longer? Who should be surprised if the external sense is frequently deceived, when the mind itself—the inner judge of all the senses—unless God’s grace governs it, is so often and so greatly endangered? Therefore you must not in any way be hindered, contrary to the reasonable faith of holy Church, by the fact that a weak and bleary eye thinks it sees something. For you already understand, I believe, that the eyes which the food of disobedience opened (Gen. III) must be closed by this food of obedience, so that, once the spiritual faculties which that carnal and deadly eye had closed have been restored through spiritual and life-giving food, we may no longer set our minds according to the flesh for death (II Cor. V), but, with unveiled face, contemplate spiritual things for eternal life.

And so, as long as we struggle in the contest of faith, as long as we are exiles from the Lord, our faith must diligently be exercised, so that through exercise it may be instructed, through instruction nourished, through nourishment increased, through increase perfected, and, once perfected, crowned. But what exercise of faith would there be, or what merit would the faithful possess through their exercise, if it were plainly evident to everyone’s eyes that the sacred host could be divided only by a priest and only during Mass? Who—even among unbelievers—would not assent to so obvious a miracle rather than to the reasoning of faith? Finally, the Apostle says that manifest miracles occur not for the faithful but for unbelievers; yet these sacraments are not for unbelievers but for the faithful (I Cor. XIV). Therefore it is not lawful for them to be distributed to unbelievers, nor even to be disclosed to them.

Let them not, then, be revealed to unbelievers through open miracles; let the faithful alone perceive them—not by the gaze of the flesh but by the mind. For our Lord Jesus Christ himself called these sacraments “the mystery of faith.” Why “mystery,” unless because it is hidden? Why “of faith,” unless because this ought to be contemplated not with the eye of the flesh but with the perception of faith? For, as the most holy Gregory says, faith has no merit when human reason supplies proof.

If, therefore, you have clearly understood the deceitfulness of the bodily senses—which are not to be trusted concerning even small matters, and matters ordinarily open to those same senses, much less concerning the greatest and most hidden realities contrary to the rule of belief; if you have learned that spiritual senses must be opened to spiritual sacraments, while bodily senses must be closed; and if, finally, you are satisfied that this mystery of faith must be hidden from unbelievers but will greatly benefit the faithful as an exercise through which their faith grows in merit—then, I think, you ought no longer to entangle yourself here in any darkness of perverse evasion.

In short, who could declare or even comprehend how great the glory and power of our flesh will be after the resurrection? For we shall be changed, and this corruptible body shall put on incorruption, and the body that is now animal shall rise spiritual (I Cor. XV); and what eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor entered into the human heart shall be given to us (Isa. LXIV; I Cor. II).

Since no present reason can comprehend how great a power even the flesh of the least little human being will then possess, do you impudently and carnally argue according to the senses about the body of the Savior, which all the angels venerate beyond expression? Indeed, whatever occurs to the human intellect as something that could be given to us is less than—or nothing in comparison with—that which is promised to us.

Since we believe that we shall receive what we are now unable to understand how it can happen, except that all things are possible for God, will you continue, like a child, to chatter about the body of almighty God merely because you do not possess before your bestial eyes whatever takes place? Therefore reconsider more carefully what has been said above, and hold confidently either that the Lord our God can distribute his flesh ineffably in portions without any injury to it, or—if he does not wish this—that the sacraments of his table remain undivided, either according to the explanations we have given or according to others, should God perhaps grant you better ones, even though they appear otherwise to the weakness of bodily eyes.

But if the Lord wishes what I said earlier, then Christ may indeed, not through any violence of ours but through his own condescension, be crushed by teeth according to the flesh, and his body be administered to the faithful in portions. If he does not wish it, however, no objection concerning the division and dispersion of the sacraments ought to be brought against us, since, as we have said, they can reasonably be proved indivisible and inseparable.

## ROGER

I confess that this is so. Your reasoning has adequately answered everything I raised, so that I rejoice in every respect and see nothing remaining in these matters for which I should think you ought to be troubled by me any further.

## GUITMUNDUS

Some people are understandably troubled and therefore do not believe that this change can occur because, throughout the solid course of nature, scarcely any wholly similar change can be found. For when something is substantially changed into something else, it ordinarily passes into that which did not previously exist. For example, Moses’ staff was changed into a serpent (Exod. VII): before that it was not a serpent, but then it began to be one. Yet when we say that bread is changed, we confess that it is changed not into flesh that had not previously been flesh, but into flesh that was already Christ’s flesh, without any increase of the Lord’s flesh itself.

We do not deny that this change is difficult for us to understand in this age, but we do deny that it is difficult to believe. Why, then, should this matter be a problem? We ought not to refuse to believe this great and salutary truth merely because we cannot grasp how it occurs in this life, since we necessarily hold many things by faith against which our blindness seems to struggle either much more strongly or, at least, no less strongly.

Concerning divine providence and free will, for example, although we faithfully hold both—and both must be held—human arguments appear so mutually opposed that they seem rather to destroy each other in turn than to allow either one to exist. No human mind can comprehend how that which is wholly present in one place can at the same time be wholly present in another; yet everyone holds this concerning the human voice, while blessed Augustine confirms by irrefutable reasoning that the soul is wholly present simultaneously in each of the body’s members.

And behold, the creation of all things is believed, although it cannot be grasped by human beings. For, to speak briefly, who can comprehend when that which was first made came to be? What is not yet at all does not come into being, for coming into being already belongs to existence. Once it exists, it does not come into being, since it already exists. Yet between existence and non-existence there cannot be anything belonging to that which was first made. For if there were some intermediate thing, that would have been made first, and the other later.

When, then, did that which was first made have to be made? Yet it did have to be made. For what is not without a beginning could in no way exist unless it came to be. He himself spoke, and they were made (Ps. XXXII). O wondrous coming-into-being, which must necessarily be believed but cannot be grasped by any thought!

But if anyone thinks that I am reasoning absurdly and dislikes all this, let him state what pleases him, and he will certainly find himself deficient in all his words and even in all his thoughts, if he observes carefully, concerning the first beginnings of things.

Since these matters necessarily demand faith and wholly exclude investigation, do they not reasonably require, in relation to the body of the very author himself, a simple believer and condemn an insolent investigator? Here, indeed, we ought to recall the beginning of this discussion. We proposed the matter in this way: when they say that nature cannot endure this change, let them allow the qualification “unless God wills it,” or not.

If they do not allow this qualification, but assert without exception that nature cannot endure it even if God wills it, then they do not believe that the Lord has done everything whatsoever he willed. If they do not believe that the Lord has done everything whatsoever he willed, then first they despise the canonical Scriptures, which they themselves very frequently quote—indeed, they despise the God whose Scriptures they are—and then they do not believe God himself to be either omnipotent or God.

For he is not truly omnipotent, nor truly God, who cannot do what he wills. But since such positions are utterly impious even in their own view, they must confess that the Lord has done everything whatsoever he willed. Therefore, if God wished to make this change, however difficult it may be for us, he undoubtedly made it.

It remains only to inquire whether God willed it. When, with his help, we show at the appropriate place that God did will it, whether or not it can be understood how it occurs, we shall nevertheless establish by necessary reasoning that he made it. The blindness of our weakness is not sufficient evidence against belief merely because it can never grasp this in the present life, if the necessity of evident reasoning proves that the matter is as we have said.

Christ did not command you, “Understand,” but “Believe.” It is his concern to bring about how that which he wishes to happen happens; your concern is not to investigate but humbly to believe that whatever he altogether wishes to happen does happen. For one must not first understand and then believe; rather, one must first believe so that afterward one may understand.

Nor did the prophet Isaiah say, “Unless you understand, you will not believe,” but, “Unless you believe, you will not understand” (Isa. VII). Let us therefore use the words of Saint Augustine against Felicianus:

> “Let faith believe this; let understanding not demand it, lest, because it has not found it, it judge it unbelievable, or, having found it, fail to believe it unique” (Augustine, ch. 8).

The same author says in his second letter to Volusianus:

> “If a reason is sought here, it will not be wonderful; if an example is demanded, it will not be unique. Let us grant to God the ability to do something which we admit we cannot investigate. In such matters, the whole explanation of the deed is the power of the one who does it.”

Blessed Hilary says that one must not speak of divine matters according to human or worldly judgment. Hence blessed Ambrose, discussing this very question in his book *On the Sacraments* (*On the Initiation into the Mysteries*, ch. 9), says:

> “Why do we use arguments? Let us use his examples, and by the example of the Incarnation establish the truth of the mystery. Why should we seek here the order of nature in Christ’s body, when Christ himself was born from a virgin contrary to nature?”

Since he invites us to the example of the Incarnation, or of the virgin birth, I think it worthwhile to clarify this likeness briefly, beginning somewhat farther back.

In the holy Scriptures we understand human generation in four ways. The first is that of a solitary man, neither from a man nor from a woman, but from the clay of the earth: Adam. The second is, in a certain sense, contrary to this: from man and woman, producing both men and women; this is the ordinary generation of nearly everyone. The third is again without precedent: from a virgin came a woman, without a man—namely, Eve from Adam. The fourth is likewise singular and unique, made for the sake of all the others and better and more useful than the rest; it is in a certain sense contrary to the third: from a woman who was a Virgin came a man who was a Virgin, namely Christ the Savior of all, born and revealed in our age from Mary.

Of these generations, no one marvels at or considers incredible the one by which men and women are born from man and woman, since it is sustained by daily experience. Yet within it there is something exceedingly marvelous beyond the others: that from two corruptible beings something intact can arise, and that nothing intact can ever arise except from two beings that are not intact—as though contrary arose from contrary.

Solomon declares something utterly incomprehensible to know: how bones are joined together in the womb of a pregnant woman (Eccl. XI). Nor has anyone scarcely ever attacked or accused the generation by which a human being came from one who was not human—Adam formed from clay—which seems in this respect far more wondrous than the others, or the generation by which the virgin Eve was produced from the virgin Adam.

But when Christ, a Virgin, was proclaimed to have been born from the Virgin Mary, the whole world raged against it with countless objections and attempted by force, fraud, and every kind of wickedness to remove this generation entirely. This was wholly unjust, since it is more excellent and useful than all the others, being not only the honor and nobility of all the rest but also their medicine.

For although it drew from the other members of our race only its nature, and derived no honor from them—in fact, it took from them a great abundance of weakness and temptation—it was sufficient in itself through divine virtue for perfect happiness in every respect. The other generations, however, having been raised through this one from beneath the feet of the most wretched of all creatures, the devil, to fellowship with almighty God, so that we might be, as the most blessed apostle Peter says, “partakers of the divine nature” (II Pet. I), would all have perished irrecoverably unless they had used its aid and remedy.

Moreover, when the three singular generations are carefully examined, this one is found to be much nearer and much more similar to the most customary generation, and therefore more credible. For who does not see clearly that the generation from a man and a woman is more similar to this generation, which is from one of those two, than to the generation that is from neither?

Likewise, if we consider the generation by which a woman came from a man alone, it is also very far removed from ordinary experience. It is more familiar and more suited to the common course of nature that a woman should bear a male—for this happens every day—than that a male should give birth to a female.

Nor, perhaps, would anyone call Eve’s generation a birth; for that reason it is even farther removed from ordinary experience. But what of the fact that from the side of a sleeping man—indeed, from the rib from which she was made—she suddenly emerged, contrary to the customary course of nature (Gen. II)? Christ, however, grew gradually, like other human beings, in his mother’s womb for nine months and came forth according to the common law of birth. The exceptions were that his mother suffered no pain in giving birth and that he himself, as befitted such a Son, honored his Mother by preserving her virginal integrity completely through a singular privilege.

For it was not fitting that, because he came to restore what was corrupted and honor what was dishonored, he should violate what was intact or dishonor what was honorable. It was much more fitting that, if Eve, a virgin from a man, had proceeded to violate the world, Christ should proceed from a woman who was a Virgin in order to restore the world.

I add also that all the other generations belong to servants, whereas this one belongs to the Lord. From the others came human beings; from this one, God. God made all the others, so to speak, by command alone—“he spoke, and they were made”—but this one he never ceased from the beginning to promise and prefigure through prophetic oracles, deeds, and especially through the novelty of miracles.

Hence it is written of it as a special work: “Wisdom has built herself a house” (Prov. IX). When all these matters, and many others, are considered properly, this generation ought to be judged sufficiently more credible and more precious than the first two.

But it is worthwhile to see how these matters relate to the question under discussion. For divine Scripture likewise commends to us four substantial changes, or acts of production. The first is that by which everything came to be from nothing. The second is contrary to this: although we do not know it through experience in the same way, we infer by reason that things can return from what they are, insofar as this depends on them, into nothing.

For if all things exist solely because God wills it, and if he should withdraw even slightly his will by which he grants them existence, all things would immediately return to their own nothingness. Thus blessed Augustine says against Felicianus:

> “The creature was brought forth from nothing; and therefore, insofar as it depends upon itself, it must be changed by the quality of its nature from what is into what is not—that is, into nothing—unless perpetual grace should preserve it” (Augustine, ch. IX).

Although, concerning individual accidents, which yield when other accidents supervene, it may not appear that anything else can truly be said except that they become altogether nothing: for if they were something, they would exist in a subject. But when contrary accidents supervene, they can neither remain in their own subject nor pass over into other subjects. They therefore become altogether nothing, unless perhaps someone says that they are changed into those things which supervene.

If that is so, countless examples will present themselves of things that are essentially changed into things that already exist in the same way. Consider, for example, how a very white parchment is stained with the blackest ink: the whiteness immediately yields to the blackness. If the whiteness has been changed into blackness, it has certainly been changed into something that already existed. For it cannot be said that the blackness is then increased by the whiteness being transferred into it, since the ink is no blacker than it was before, nor has the blackness occupied any part of the parchment beyond the ink.

The same may often be found in other cases. Thus departing accidents, as we have said, either become entirely nothing, or, if they are changed, are changed into what supervenes—something highly relevant to our argument—namely, into things that already existed.

The third change is one that we commonly observe: substances pass into substances that did not previously exist, either through the ordinary course of nature or through miracles. Thus a kernel becomes a tree, seed becomes grass, food and drink become flesh and blood; or a staff becomes a serpent, a serpent becomes a staff, and so forth.

The fourth change is that by which what exists passes into what likewise exists. Thus we believe that bread and wine are changed by divine power into Christ’s own body through a power of a singular kind.

Believers readily judge this change to be far better and far more useful than the other three. It is better because what is changed passes into divine flesh, which is the best of all things. It is more useful because Christ established this change as a singular medicine for us, made for the sake of the others.

For the elements were first made from nothing, and through them we did not become blessed. Nor did the other two changes benefit us; rather, they would have brought us into the greatest miseries unless the fourth, coming upon them medicinally, had provided assistance.

Since this change is therefore more honorable and more useful than all the others, and is also much nearer and more similar to the most customary change, it is found to be much more credible than the other two. For since it is as clear as daylight that a change which occurs most commonly from something into something is exceedingly nearer and more similar to a change which likewise occurs from something into something, even if the latter is somewhat more marvelous, than to one which occurs from nothing into something or from something into nothing—how much more credible should this be?

Those two changes have two somethings; the latter changes have only one. They are so far removed from the capacity of our understanding that someone might scarcely even call them changes, and would have the greatest difficulty finding a word—if indeed he could find one at all—with which to express them even somewhat properly.

The other changes concern created substances; this one concerns the Lord. The other changes belong to the remaining creatures; this one the author himself retained for his own body.

God commanded the other changes once, at the beginning, and they were made. But this one he never ceased from the beginning to promise and prefigure through prophetic oracles, deeds, and especially sacrifices and the novelty of miracles. Moreover, with great solemnity and earnestness of prayer, through the words that God himself and our Lord Jesus Christ dictated for this very purpose and that are repeated daily, he provides its effect.

When all these matters, and many others, are properly considered, this change can and ought to be judged much more credible and more precious than those two. For if God made what is more difficult and farther removed from our understanding because he willed it, how could he not also have made what seems in some way easier and more intelligible, if he willed it? No one doubts that God made the former, more difficult thing. Therefore no one ought to doubt that God can make this easier thing, if he wills it.

Or why should God not add this fourth change for the healing of human beings, just as he added the fourth generation—as we have shown—for their restoration to salvation? Just as the supremely good God wished all the good things that ought to exist in creatures to exist in them without envy, so too, through the wondrous beauty of variety, he wished that no fitting mode of generation should be lacking to human beings, and no suitable mode of change should be lacking to things.

Since, then, the proposition has been sufficiently established, as I think—namely, that God made this change if he willed it—the only thing remaining to be proved is the assumption, namely, that he did will it. But since many poisons still remain to be drained away, we reserve that matter for a more suitable place.

For now, then, having refuted the earlier calumnies of the adversaries, let us, if you please, rest here for a little, so that you may recall more carefully what has been said and, as we rise with a new beginning toward what follows, your mind may be renewed with fresh attention.

## HERE BEGINS THE SECOND BOOK

*[Col. 1445]*

## GUITMUNDUS

While I respond to your objections, let anyone who reads this carefully observe that I am not now laboring to overthrow the enemy completely by our arguments, but meanwhile to fortify the Catholic faith against hostile arguments. That will be done later, with God’s help.

For now, however, we wish to distinguish the matter in such a way that we first demonstrate that the hostile argument is weak and can accomplish nothing against our faith. Then, when the adversary has everywhere failed on his own ground, he may finally, with God’s favor, be more completely overthrown by our arguments.

I think this will cause heretical deceit to fall silent more quickly and Catholic truth to shine more clearly. But let these remarks be directed toward those who insist on being satisfied more hastily than the matter permits and who might perhaps criticize us privately for ineffective work because we do not examine all our arguments here.

Now let us proceed with the remaining matters.

## ROGER

Berengarius says: “Christ’s flesh is incorruptible, but the sacraments of the altar, if they are kept for a longer time, can become corrupted; for they appear to putrefy.”

## GUITMUNDUS

O calumnious tongue! O tongue accustomed to blasphemy, more eager proudly to extract its own destruction from the Scriptures of God than to receive, with the faithful, salutary nourishment!

He believed the holy Scriptures when they said that Christ is incorruptible, but he did not believe Christ when he said, “The bread that I will give is my flesh for the life of the world” (John VI); instead, he sets corruption against this.

Let divine bread therefore appear to people who are diseased and corrupted, according to their unbelief, to be corruptible and putrid; and, as it is written, “Let the impious be taken away, lest he ever see the glory of God” (Isa. XXVI). Let him always dream shameful thoughts about God, always devise stumbling-blocks, and let Christ always be for him “a stone of offense and a rock of stumbling” (I Pet. II).

For us, that bread of God from heaven, that Eucharist, that divine manna—which we take from the sacred altars as the flesh of the immaculate Lamb made incapable of suffering, through which we live and are healed from corruption—is never corrupted and never putrefies. For although it renews us from day to day, it never knows aging itself.

Blessed Ambrose agrees with this judgment in his book *On the Sacraments*, in these words (ch. 9):

> “Consider now whether the bread of angels is more excellent, or the flesh of Christ, which is certainly the body of life. The manna was from heaven; this is above heaven. The former belonged to heaven; the latter to the Lord of heaven. The former was subject to corruption if it was kept for another day; the latter is foreign to all corruption. Whoever tastes it reverently cannot experience corruption.”

If, then, it should happen that this appears to someone at some time to be corrupted and putrid through age, and if that person does not believe that what he sees is the Lord’s body, we believe that what happens to him corresponds to his heart. Thus, just as blessed Gregory says concerning Christ as a stranger and the two disciples speaking with him on the road, let what appears outwardly to him be such as he believes inwardly in his heart.

But if he believes that what he sees is the Lord’s body, we believe that one of two things happens to him: either some negligence of his is being revealed as needing correction or punishment—because, insofar as it depended on him, he treated the body of his Lord unworthily or acted disobediently by retaining it too long contrary to ecclesiastical regulations—or else the firmness of his faith is shown to deserve a more abundant reward, since, even against what the eye sees, he does not doubt the matters and power of his Lord or the faith of the universal Church.

We have examples of what we are saying readily available from the divine books. Mary Magdalene, not yet believing that the Lord had risen, saw him, according to her unbelief, as a gardener (John XX). To the disciples who were doubting, he appeared on the very day of the resurrection as a stranger (Luke XXIV).

Here, too, it can be seen how the negligence of believers is punished or corrected. Since they had paid insufficient attention to the prophecies concerning Christ, they deserved first to be punished for their negligence by being called foolish, and then to be corrected when the Scriptures were opened to them.

But how Christ, though incorruptible, deigned to appear as corruptible in order to test and reward the faithful, blessed Gregory explains when he tells of a monk named Martyrius. This monk deserved to carry the Lord Jesus on his own shoulders when he appeared to him in the form of a leper.

“When he who appeared like a leper,” Gregory says, “vanished from his neck, he immediately received from him a sentence of reward: ‘Because you were not ashamed of me on earth, Martyrius, neither will I be ashamed of you in heaven.’”

Therefore, just as our Lord Jesus Christ appeared on earth in a deformed and dreadful form to test and reward Martyrius’s humility or love, so, in order to test and reward the faith of his servants, he is to be believed to appear, whenever this occurs and no unbelief or negligence is being punished or corrected, under the form of that corrupted bread.

And just as Christ showed that the extremely deformed leper was none other than himself when he vanished from Martyrius’s neck, so orthodox prudence knows that in the divine sacraments one must believe that there is nothing other than Christ’s flesh and blood, even if they sometimes appear under the form of bread and wine that seem to be putrefying.

If you object—as is commonly said—that Berengarius did not accept the Lives of the Saints as authoritative, know that, although he does not accept certain Lives of the Saints, I have learned, as I recall, that he never rejected the books of blessed Gregory. For this reason we have accepted blessed Gregory’s *Dialogue* as an authority; in it the matters we have mentioned concerning Martyrius are recorded.

For so great an author would not have written these things unless he himself believed them to be true and judged them worthy of belief by later generations.

Finally, let us run through in our minds the whole dispensation of the Lord’s humanity. It was entirely of such a character that the unbelief of enemies would be more blinded by it and therefore condemned, while the faith of believers would be more greatly increased and therefore crowned.

What of the fact that he wished to be born from the Virgin betrothed to Joseph? Was this not a cause of scandal to his enemies, increasing their deadly impiety, so that they called him the son of a carpenter? Yet it benefited Peter, who believed, by increasing the faith for which he was to be rewarded, since he was not hindered by this from saying, “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God” (Matt. XVI).

And what of the whole weakness of his flesh? Did it not blind the devil so completely that, although he witnessed unprecedented miracles, he rose up to kill him and did not foresee the irreparable losses that would thereby come upon himself?

Yet through that same weakness the faithful are still illuminated by faith, so that, through his help, they are able not to fail amid their own weaknesses; and, believing in the assistance of that same Lord, they dare with ever greater confidence to implore his aid because of the love with which he became weak for them.

What shall I say about his death? Does not the Apostle say that through it Christ is “a stumbling-block to Jews and foolishness to Gentiles, but to Christians Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God” (I Cor. I)?

Therefore, just as when Christ was still mortal and living among human beings, such things occurred concerning his flesh, so, as long as his Church remains mortal until the consummation of the age, something of this kind may appear concerning that same flesh in outward form, for the same benefit of the Church for which those things then occurred concerning it, while its incorruptibility remains unharmed. Through this, unbelievers may always be scandalized and plunged into darkness, while the elect are exercised and more greatly illuminated.

Let people who are corrupt and putrid in mind therefore cease to set corruption and putrefaction against the sacraments of God. Just as Christ’s assumption of the appearance of a stranger, a gardener, or a leper either rebuked or corrected the negligence of the faithful or tested their faith and love, without thereby abolishing the truth of Christ’s essence, so, if putrefaction or anything similarly improper should at some time appear in the sacraments of the Church, it serves—as we have said—to punish or correct the negligence of ministers, or certainly to test faith and love. Yet it cannot abolish the truth of the essence of the Lord’s flesh and blood.

Therefore the Church of God need not fear these stratagems of heretics. She knows that the entire carnal dispensation of her Lord on earth was salvation for her but always a stumbling-block to the reprobate.

## ROGER

They also object that these sacraments can be gnawed or consumed by mice, or by any such animals.

## GUITMUNDUS
I do not at all think that these sacraments can be gnawed by mice or by any irrational animals. If at some time they appear to have been gnawed, the answer may be what we said earlier concerning the gardener, the stranger, or the leper: namely, that they were not gnawed, but that they may appear in such a form either to punish or correct the negligence of the ministers, or to test the faith of those who witnessed it. [Col. 1448D]

[Note: [Col. 1447D] Guitmundus seems to indicate that the sacramental appearances of the Eucharist are not truly corrupted or putrefied, nor can they be gnawed by mice or devoured by other animals, but that these things occur only according to appearance. This is not sufficiently consonant with the principles of sound [Col. 1448D] theology, which holds that, when those appearances themselves truly undergo alteration and corruption and can be eaten by animals, then, as soon as those numerically identical appearances cease to exist, the Lord’s body also ceases to be present under those appearances. See St. Thomas, Part III, Question 77, Articles 3–7.]

But to the claim that they can be consumed by irrational animals, we can answer, for the reasons stated above—that is, to test faith or to condemn or correct the negligence of those responsible for their safekeeping—that irrational animals can approach the body of Christ only as far as human sight can perceive. Thereafter it is either immediately carried away invisibly by the ministry of the angels who are always present to it, or by its own power it is snatched away and [Col. 1449A] established in heaven. The glorious martyr Tarsidus presents himself to us as a suitable witness to this view. While he was carrying the venerable sacrament of the Lord’s body, he was accidentally seized by pagans who came upon him and asked what he was carrying. Choosing to die rather than give the holy thing to dogs (Matthew 7), he earned the crown of a precious death. But when they searched everything with the greatest curiosity, after the Lord’s body had been taken away from heaven, they found absolutely nothing except the linen cloths.

But if someone claims that he saw these things devoured by irrational animals and found within their bodies—for such testimony, even if it does not readily appear worthy of acceptance or an answer, [Col. 1449B] nevertheless, lest we seem to have neglected or evaded anything, an answer may be given. If it pleases Christ, whether for the reasons we have just mentioned or for any others known to him, that these sacraments may be eaten by beasts or birds without suffering corruption: what does this detract from the truth concerning the Lord’s body that we believe? Certainly it is no more harmed by the taste of beasts or birds than by our own taste. Nor does he shrink from the mouths or beaks of beasts or birds for their benefit—the one who lay upon the stone of the tomb and, even after the glory of his resurrection, trod the earth.

For it is perfectly clear, according to God’s ordering, that animate bodies are better than inanimate things, and things endowed with sensation better than things without sensation. I do not think that even the slightest man of learning would oppose this view. Whatever is better is [Col. 1449C] more precious to the good Lord and therefore more honorable. Consequently, the body of any living animal is not less valued by God than earth or stone. But Christ’s own body, as we have already said, lay upon a stone and trod the earth; therefore it does not recoil from the body of any animal on account of some supposed baseness. Accordingly, even if by some divine judgment any irrational animals should be able not only to touch the sacred mysteries but also to devour them, no argument thereby confronts us that could compel us to deny the truth of the Lord’s flesh and blood, which we hold in the sacred mysteries.

Thus, having sufficiently examined this blasphemy as well, let us consider the remaining points. A major question also arises concerning fire, because, as they say, certain canons order the sacred mysteries to be handed over to fire as though they were [Col. 1449D] to be consumed. Yet this is not commanded so that they may be destroyed by burning; rather, they are reverently entrusted to fire as the purest, cleanest, and most worthy of all the elements—the element that purifies all the others, while it itself can neither be defiled by the others nor needs to be purified.

Nevertheless, I would be quite pleased if, whenever some negligence or certainly some new miracle concerning these great mysteries occurred, it happened in this manner. My teacher, an outstanding man whom there is no doubt must be believed, Lord Lanfranc, told me that such a thing happened in Italy when he was a boy. A certain priest, while celebrating Mass, found real flesh upon the altar and real blood in the chalice, in the proper [Col. 1450A] appearance of flesh and blood. Afraid to consume them, he immediately disclosed the matter to his bishop in order to seek advice. The bishop, having summoned many fellow bishops for this purpose, carefully covered the chalice containing that same flesh and blood of the Lord, sealed it, and enclosed it in the middle of the altar, so that it might be preserved forever as one of the greatest relics.

If, however, the sacred mysteries are placed in fire, they are not handed over to fire to be burned, but are faithfully entrusted to that purest element, as I have said, so that they may be concealed from us and immediately restored to the heavenly dwelling. If they should perhaps appear to someone inquisitive to be burned, let him know with complete certainty that the substance of the Lord’s sacrament is in no way consumed by fire; rather, it is snatched away from us as it seeks the things of heaven. But the sensible qualities—which, after the substance has been changed, [Col. 1450B] God in his deepest counsel willed to remain there—display what belongs to them.

Thus color, taste, and odor, and whatever other accidents of the former substance—namely, of bread—have been preserved, undergo what ordinarily happens in bread that has been scorched (*ustulato*) [variant: *jusculato*, “soaked in broth”] or kept for too long. In the same way here also, while the substance of the Lord’s body remains entirely unharmed, those accidents themselves appear outwardly to be somewhat subject to corruption. In this way the exalted character of the heavenly mystery, veiled by the accidents that have been retained, is not openly disclosed to unbelievers, while through the merit of tested faith it is commended more abundantly and graciously to the righteous.

ROGERIUS.

If bread and wine were changed into Christ’s flesh and blood, they say, so many such things have already been devoured that, even if Christ’s body had been as large as an enormous mountain, it would by now have been entirely devoured and consumed. [Col. 1450C]

GUITMUNDUS.

That would indeed seem to follow if we conceded that the Lord’s body is torn limb from limb and eaten by the faithful in such portions that the whole could no longer remain with him without suffering any loss. But since we believe that Christ’s body is eaten by each person in the same way as a voice spoken by one person among a thousand reaches each individual in its entirety—and yet remains in its entirety with the speaker—we confess that the Lord’s body is eaten by each person while nevertheless remaining whole and entire with itself. This objection, therefore, now hinders us in no respect and may fall silent, because, as blessed Augustine and Eusebius of Emesa said: “This grace of God knows how to be distributed; it does not know how to be consumed by distribution.” [Col. 1450D]

ROGERIUS.

It is unfitting for the Lord’s body to be sent into the privy. Yet everything that enters the mouth, as the Savior says, goes into the stomach and is expelled into the privy (Matthew 15). Finally, concerning these sacraments: if, as they say, many loaves and much wine are consecrated, someone could live for a long time eating or drinking nothing else. Where, then, would he have excrement during that period, unless these things entered the privy? These are, for the moment, the arguments from Berengarius that occur to me. After you have answered them, I shall bring forward the authorities.

[Col. 1451A] GUITMUNDUS.

We too believe that the Lord’s body is in no way sent into the privy. But we do not grant that everything entering the mouth goes into the privy. For that saying of the Lord can properly be understood only of foods that are taken to sustain the life of this mortal body. There is no one, for example, who would dare to suspect this of what the Savior ate after his resurrection, any more than of the angels who ate with Abraham (Genesis 18).

Therefore, just as corruptible food, when taken by immortal beings, is rightly believed not to be subject to this law of excretion, so it is impious to suppose that incorruptible food, which is the Lord’s body, when eaten by mortals, is subject to the necessity of excretion. Far be it from us to think that this food, [Col. 1451B] which prepares body and soul for eternal honor, undergoes dishonorable bodily elimination.

But if what we have said is perhaps insufficient for anyone, let him hear what natural philosophers and physicians teach with the greatest certainty concerning our own incorruptible foods. They say that one part of foods and drinks—the part that is more substantial and more corruptible—is expelled through excretion; another, more refined and useful part is distributed through the various parts of the body by nature and is changed into the substance of flesh and blood; another part, refined but less useful, is similarly diffused through the body and evaporates through the pores; while the remaining part, neither so refined nor as substantial as the first, is expelled through the flow of the nostrils, through saliva, or in some similar manner.

If this is so, [Col. 1451C] then not all food that goes into the stomach is expelled into the privy. Nor did the Lord say this in the Gospel. We understand from the Lord’s saying that all food and drink that enters the mouth to sustain the body naturally goes into the stomach. He did not, however, say, “And all of it is expelled into the privy”; he said only, “And it is expelled into the privy,” speaking of the part familiar to everyone. For the present, what we have said concerning this Gospel saying is sufficient for this passage. If anyone wishes the Lord’s saying to be explained to him more fully, let him diligently read the expositions of the Gospels. For now it is enough for us to have said this, lest anyone think that we contradict the Lord’s saying.

Whether [Col. 1451D] the question just stated is more suitably resolved in this way or in some other way, what is sufficient for the discussion undertaken is meanwhile established: not everything that enters the mouth is expelled into the privy. This objection, therefore, is offered to us in vain, since it in no way prevents us from believing that, from the Lord’s table, we receive the Lord’s body and blood, when we know that many other things enter the mouth without going into the privy.

Let us now examine what they add on their own behalf. “Concerning these sacraments,” they say, “if many loaves and much wine are consecrated, someone could live for a long time eating or drinking nothing else. Where, then, would he have excrement during that time, if these things did not go into the privy?”

I readily admit that, through the power of the most holy [Col. 1452A] body, if God so wills it for some reason known to him, someone can be sustained for a long time—not, I say, by a multitude of loaves, but even by a small portion—better than by all the banquets of this world. For if Elijah, through the power of the nourishment he received from two loaves baked under ashes and a little water, ministered by an angel, lived for forty days and as many nights (3 Kings 19), how much more can someone be sustained by the power of this heavenly and divine banquet, in which we receive not loaves baked under ashes and water from the hand of an angel, but the very flesh and blood of the Word of God from the hand of Christ himself, using no other food, if such is God’s will!

Indeed, we also read this concerning certain holy Fathers who, taking absolutely no other food, lived for many years, nourished solely by the Lord’s communion on Sundays. [Col. 1452B]

We can therefore grant that someone may live for a long time through a divine miracle by the power of the Lord’s body; but we altogether deny that excretion can come from it. If any excretion occurs in the meantime, it must necessarily come either from the remains of earlier foods or from the wasting of his own body.

But Berengarius says—and some have answered us on his behalf in this way—that it has now been clearly proved that those nourished by the Eucharist had excrement neither from the remains of earlier foods, since these had already been consumed through the length of so long a period, nor from the wasting of their own flesh, since the customary fatness of the body remained. [Col. 1452C]

O heretical wickedness! Did you dare to prove this by experiment? Did you dare to say that you had proved it? Did you dare to publish this openly? What monstrous audacity! In conducting the experiment, you did not fear the terrifying majesty of God present; in reporting it, you did not fear the indignation that the Christian people would rightly unleash for so great a crime.

Yet I ask when or by whom this was proved. If he says that it was proved in ancient times, since none of the reliable authorities reports it, it must not be believed in any way. But if it was proved in recent times, who proved it? Certainly no one from the Catholic side. For who, believing that this consecrated bread is truly Christ’s body, would think of undertaking so abominable an experiment?

But if he himself, or someone from his party, [Col. 1452D] consecrated many loaves or one very large loaf in order to prove such a thing, we no longer greatly concern ourselves with whatever may have happened to them in the Mass of unbelievers, and especially of those who wished to prove so great a crime. For we necessarily believe that bread and wine pass into the flesh and blood of the Lord only among those who believe that Christ’s words operate such a great reality through divine power. Among those who hold the faith concerning this matter, we both believe and affirm that this change necessarily occurs through Christ’s words.

But if at some time a simple Catholic priest, ignorant of the purpose, was deceived into consecrating several loaves or one very large loaf for the sake of the experiment, or if someone from their party happened to do the same while celebrating Mass [Col. 1453A] with Catholics, we believe that the body of Christ was consecrated. We answer either that it never entered the privy, or that, at the same time as the Lord’s body was invisibly taken away, bread was placed by angels or evil spirits so that it might enter the privy, worthy to deceive and refute the heretics.

For in the *Lives of the Fathers*—which, even if Berengarius does not wish to accept them, I shall nevertheless cite here for the instruction of others—we read that, while a certain most holy Father looked on, God having opened his eyes so that he could see it, an angel invisibly removed the Lord’s body from certain unworthy communicants and offered them a coal, perhaps thereby forearming later generations against this question concerning excretion. This does not mean that he always does this to unworthy communicants, as we shall later show, [Col. 1453B] God willing.

Blessed Augustine also, whom at least Berengarius has never rejected, says in his book *The City of God* (Book XVI, chapter 18) that a similar removal was carried out by apostate spirits in the case of Iphigenia, the virgin daughter of King Agamemnon. He asserts that, when she was about to be sacrificed by her father to the gods, the devil, in order to deceive the wretched people more profoundly through the novelty of the miracle, carried her away and substituted for her a hind taken from elsewhere.

He also reports that, in his own time, great wonders occurred concerning a certain man who seemed, in the form of a horse, to carry grain among beasts of burden, while in the meantime he himself lay snoring as though overcome by a very deep sleep. The devil, having assumed his likeness, then transformed himself before human eyes into a horse and carried the grain.

Therefore, since either the body of the Lord is not made in the Mass of those who do not believe in the power of the [Col. 1453C] Lord’s word, or else, when the Lord’s body has been invisibly removed by divine power or through angelic ministry, bread suitable for excretion may be supplied to the heretics either by angels or by demons, let Berengarius and his followers cease to bark against the Church of God on the basis of such an experiment. For, with the truth of the Lord’s body preserved in every respect in the most holy mysteries, they are themselves more deeply convicted of erring in their most foolish curiosity.

ROGERIUS.

Truly, armed with the sword of God, you have cut down this many-headed serpent of a question with wondrous vigor. And I give thanks to God, because I see that the matter which greatly troubled me has been sufficiently answered.

GUITMUNDUS.

[Col. 1453D] Have you not also heard the point in which he especially prides himself while mocking Catholics?

ROGERIUS.

What point is that?

GUITMUNDUS.

“He says: ‘Christ was never sown or gathered in the fields; but these things were sown and gathered in the fields. How, then, can they be Christ’s body?’”

ROGERIUS.

I had either never heard this argument or it had slipped my mind. I desire you to explain in due order what an appropriate answer to it should be.
