GUITMUNDUS.

The mad mockery of the heretic is plainly laughable. For what human [Col. 1454A] being is there in whose flesh the things sown and gathered in the fields are not changed when eaten? Consequently, all human beings who eat what is sown and gathered in the fields can be said to have been sown and gathered in the fields. Thus Berengarius’s statement is false: “Christ was never sown or gathered in the fields.”

Or, if for this reason no human being is believed to have been sown or gathered in the fields, what is impossible about the things sown and gathered in the fields being changed into Christ’s body, which was neither sown nor gathered in the fields?

But we do not say here that the things which were sown and gathered in the fields are changed. We say that bread is changed into flesh. Bread, however, is never sown or gathered in the fields; rather, the grains from which [Col. 1454B] it is made are sown and gathered. If this is so, then Berengarius’s other statement is also false: “These things were sown and gathered in the fields.”

Let him therefore be laughed at in this matter as well, and let us not fear the empty mocker, since all the ornaments of his objections are easily torn apart, like spiders’ webs, by a simple effort.

ROGERIUS.

Everything you say seems to me worthy of the highest acceptance and embrace with all my heart.

GUITMUNDUS.

These, then, are all the arguments, insofar as we have yet heard them, with which Berengarius and his supporters have so far quibbled against the Church of God as though they were reasons. Since, I think, we have sufficiently demolished them, let us now [Col. 1454C] turn to those passages from the writings of the holy Fathers which they seem to take as their support.

ROGERIUS.

Augustine, in Book III, chapter 9, of *On Christian Doctrine*, calls the food of the Lord’s altar a sign and figure, as they themselves assert, saying:

“But at this time, after the clearest indication of our liberty shone forth through the resurrection of our Lord, we are not even burdened with the operation of those signs that we now understand. Rather, the Lord himself and the apostolic discipline have handed down a few things in place of many—things very easy to perform, most sublime to understand, and most pure in observance—such as the sacrament of baptism and the [Col. 1454D] celebration of the body and blood of the Lord. When each person receives these, being instructed in what they refer to, he recognizes this, so that he may venerate them not with carnal servitude but rather with spiritual liberty. Just as it is a sign of servile weakness to follow the letter and to receive signs in place of the things signified by them, so it is the error of one who wanders badly to interpret signs uselessly.”

You have heard, then, they say, that he calls the sacraments of the altar signs. Then he adds:

“When each person receives these, being instructed in what they refer to, he recognizes this, so that he may venerate them not with carnal servitude but rather with spiritual liberty.”

Have you heard that he says these things are to be venerated not with carnal servitude but with spiritual liberty? And, as though you were asking what it means to venerate signs with carnal servitude, he says:

“To follow the letter and to receive signs in place of the things signified by them is a mark of servile weakness.”

[Col. 1455A] Likewise, later in the same work (Book III, chapter 16):

“But if it appears to command a shameful deed or crime, or to forbid what is useful and beneficent, the expression is figurative. ‘Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you will not have life in yourselves’ (John 6). It seems to command a shameful deed or crime; therefore it is a figure, commanding that we share in the Lord’s passion and that we preserve sweetly and profitably in our memory the fact that his flesh was crucified and wounded for us.”

You have heard, then, they say, the word “figure.” What more do you require? Add also that among all ecclesiastical authorities, and likewise in the collects of the Masses that the Church celebrates everywhere, the bread of the altar is called a sacrament—which is a sacred sign.

GUITMUNDUS.

[Col. 1455B] O men foolishly wise, who either do not understand Augustine, the other holy authors, and the customary language of the Church, or else, with remarkable diligence, perversely distort them! For nowhere in Augustine’s book *On Christian Doctrine* did he call the food of the Lord’s altar a sign or figure; rather, he called the celebration of the Lord’s body a sign—and that is precisely what we too believe. For whenever the celebration of the Lord’s body and blood takes place, we do not indeed kill Christ again; rather, in that celebration and through it we commemorate his death. The celebration itself is therefore a kind of commemoration of Christ’s passion. Now the commemoration of Christ’s passion signifies the passion itself. Thus the celebration of the Lord’s body and blood is a sign of Christ’s passion.

And this is what blessed Augustine says [Col. 1455C]:

> “But in the present time, after the clearest indication of our freedom shone forth through the resurrection of our Lord, we are not burdened even by the operation of those signs which we now understand. Instead, the Lord himself and the apostolic discipline have handed down certain few signs in place of many—signs exceedingly easy to perform, most exalted in meaning, and most chaste in observance—as, for example, the sacrament of baptism and the celebration of the Lord’s body and blood.”

But when he added that “to follow the letter and to accept signs in place of the things signified by them is the mark of servile weakness,” he was speaking of the signs of the Old Testament, which were then under discussion. For it was truly servile and weak merely according to the letter to be circumcised, sacrifice animals, celebrate new moons and Sabbaths, and accept the lamb, the rock, and other such things that signified Christ in place of Christ himself. If Augustine also said this concerning the celebration of the Lord’s body, which he called a sign, we gladly follow him. For when we say that Christ is sacrificed in the celebration of the Lord’s body, no one should understand these words carnally, according to the letter. For Christ, having died once, dies no more; death shall no longer rule over him (Rom. VI). But while we commemorate his passion by celebrating Masses, he who died for us long ago is represented.

Finally, if someone says, “The celebration of the Lord’s body is the Lord’s passion,” we reject him as one who understands carnally. The celebration itself is not the Lord’s passion, but a commemorative sign of the Lord’s passion, which has already been accomplished. [Col. 1456A]

Then, where Augustine goes on to say:

> “But if it appears to command a disgraceful or criminal act, or to forbid something useful and beneficial, the language is figurative: ‘Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you shall not have life in yourselves’ (John VI). It appears to command a disgraceful or criminal act. Therefore it is a figure, commanding that we participate in the Lord’s passion and gently and beneficially store in our memory that his flesh was crucified and wounded for us,”

Augustine himself explains quite carefully elsewhere in what respect it appears to command a disgraceful or criminal act. Let us not follow our own opinion concerning Augustine’s words; let us listen to Augustine himself explaining them most carefully. For, in explaining Psalm 98, he says:

> “What he said seemed hard to them: ‘Unless someone eats my flesh, he shall not have eternal life.’ They received it foolishly; they thought of it carnally, and supposed that the Lord was going to cut off certain pieces from his body and give them to eat. And they said, ‘This is a hard saying.’”

And in his exposition of the Gospel according to John, where he treated these same words at greater length, he pursued this very disgraceful or criminal act which they supposed Christ was commanding, giving an extensive explanation:

> “Does this offend you, because I said, ‘I give you my flesh to eat and my blood to drink’? Surely this offends you. What, then, if you see the Son of Man ascending to where he was before? What does this mean? Here he resolves what had disturbed them; here he disclosed the reason for their offense—here, plainly, if they understood. For they thought that he was going to distribute his body, but he said that he would ascend into heaven, certainly whole. ‘When you see the Son of Man ascending to where he was before,’ then at least you will see that he does not distribute his body in the manner you suppose; then at least you will understand that his grace is not consumed by bites.” [Col. 1456B]

And again:

> “But these men quickly failed when the Lord Jesus spoke such things. They did not believe that he was saying something great and clothing some grace in those words; rather, they understood them as they wished and, in the human manner, supposed that Jesus either could or intended to distribute to believers in him the flesh with which the Word was clothed as though it had been cut into pieces.”

And shortly afterward:

> “What, then? Does the flesh profit nothing? It profits nothing—but only as they understood it. For they understood the flesh as a corpse is torn apart or as meat is sold in a butcher’s market, not as something enlivened by the Spirit.”

And again:

> “It is the Spirit who gives life; the flesh profits nothing—as they understood the flesh, not as I give my flesh to be eaten.”

Thus, clearly, in these words holy Augustine sufficiently declared what disgraceful or criminal act the Lord seemed to command: namely, that which seemed hard to those who heard him. Hence they were offended, because, he says, they “received it foolishly and carnally.” But why foolishly and carnally? Because, he says, they supposed that the Lord was going to cut off certain pieces from his body and give them to eat. They supposed that his grace would be consumed by bites, and that he would distribute to believers the flesh with which the Word was clothed, cut up as a corpse is torn apart or as meat is sold in a butcher’s market, rather than as something enlivened by the Spirit. [Col. 1457A]

This, then, is the disgraceful or criminal act which, as blessed Augustine says, the Lord seemed to command—not because he was actually commanding a disgraceful or criminal act by commanding them to eat his flesh, but because, he says, he seemed to command it to those who supposed that, by commanding this, he necessarily also commanded them to kill him, cut him into pieces, and finally eat his flesh raw or cooked.

“Therefore,” he says, “it is a figure in this expression.” At this point the shadowy disputant perhaps interrupts and rejoices. Do not be premature, shadowy one; do not glory rashly. Attend patiently and carefully to the matter of which this is said to be a figure. “Therefore it is a figure,” Augustine says, “commanding.” What does it command? What does it signify? For it signifies what it commands: “that we participate in the Lord’s passion,” he says, “and gently and beneficially store in our memory that his flesh was crucified and wounded for us.”

Thanks be to God. Whatever, then, that is which Augustine here calls a figure—for it is not so easy to determine from these words what exactly he calls a figure—it is plainly shown to be not the Lord’s body, but his crucifixion and wounding, that is, his killing, and our participation in it: namely, that we should imitate Christ and share in his passion by suffering with him.

The Apostle Paul agrees, saying:

> “Whenever you eat this bread and drink the Lord’s cup, you proclaim the Lord’s death until he comes” (1 Cor. XI). [Col. 1457C]

If we ask what Augustine called a figure here, nothing seems to present itself so fittingly as what the same teacher had said a little earlier: namely, the celebration itself of the Lord’s body and blood.

For these reasons, the Berengarians foolishly and senselessly thrust Augustine’s book *On Christian Doctrine* upon us, although nowhere there is the food of the Lord’s altar called a figure, nowhere a sign. And whatever it is that is there called a sign and a figure is certainly not a sign and figure of the Lord’s body and blood, but of the Lord’s passion and our participation in it. This is demonstrated with complete certainty.

Moreover, if they contentiously assert that the Eucharist itself is called by the Church a sign and a figure—for it is called a sacrament, that is, a sacred sign—what, I ask, will they gain from this, and how will it harm us? We are not afraid to call it a figure and a sacrament.

At this point the shadowy disputant may perhaps answer—as he is accustomed to do: “If it is a figure, how is it truth? If it is a sacrament, how is it truth?” O utterly senseless reasoning of a badly disposed man! Have you not read in the Gospel that Christ himself is called a sign? Simeon says:

> “Behold, this one is appointed for the fall and rising of many in Israel, and as a sign that will be opposed” (Luke II).

And in the *Song of Songs* he himself says to his bride:

> “Set me as a seal upon your heart” (Song VIII).

Isaiah also says:

> “There shall be a root of Jesse, who stands as a sign for the peoples” (Isa. VII).

Therefore, if Christ is a sign—and he is the true Christ and a sign—nothing prevents that which we take from the Lord’s altar, since it is the true body of Christ, from also being called a sign. [Col. 1458A]

“But of what,” you will perhaps ask, “unless it is a sign of the Lord’s body?” I in turn ask you: Of what is Christ a sign? If you answer me, you yourself resolve the question you are asking. If you do not answer me, neither can you compel me to answer it.

Nevertheless, for the instruction of the faithful, I shall say something about this matter as the Lord grants me ability. Because Christ offered himself for us, he became for us a sign of redemption. For every price of transfer is a sign of the thing for which it is the price. Since Christ is our Redeemer, he himself transferred us from death to life; and since he himself is our price, he is the sign of this transfer of ours, that is, of our redemption.

Therefore we rightly believe that, in a similar way, the food of the Lord’s altar is both effective for our salvation, because of the power of the divinity dwelling in it most fully, and, because it is our price, signifying our salvation.

Finally, Christ, the mediator between God and human beings (1 Tim. II), while he always shines forth for us like a rainbow in the clouds, consisting of divine and human substance in the preachers, and while the Father always sees him interceding for us, is a sign of the everlasting covenant between God and human beings, according to what is written:

> “I will set my bow in the clouds, and it shall be a sign of my covenant between me and the earth” (Gen. VII). [Col. 1458C]

The sacred offering of the altar is likewise believed by us to be a sign of this divine covenant and of this most health-giving peace.

Moreover, Christ, who was born of the Virgin, is a sign for us: just as we are reborn in Christ from a virgin mother, whom the Apostle betrothed to one husband as a pure virgin to be presented to Christ (2 Cor. XI)—and she is the Church. As Christ grows, we observe in him the prefiguration of our progress, until we all attain to a perfect man (Eph. IV). He himself casts out demons, restores health, and is completed on the third day. We likewise first drive out vices, then nourish virtues, and in the third stage are perfected.

And what more shall I say, since his entire bodily life in this world, and everything he taught according to the flesh, is set before our Christian life as a sign? For if we say that we remain in Christ, we ought to walk as he walked (1 John II).

To mention something also concerning the end: Christ was crucified, died, was buried, rose again, and finally ascended to the right hand of the Father. Does this not signify for us, according to the Apostle, that each day we should carry our cross, as he commands (Luke IX); each day die to this world; and, having been buried with him, pay no attention to present things, but walk as children of the resurrection in newness of life, so that after the labors of this age we too may ascend to the heavenly kingdoms?

For, as the Apostle says:

> “If we have been planted together in the likeness of his death, we shall also be planted together in the likeness of his resurrection. We know this: that our old man was crucified together with him, so that the body of sin might be destroyed. And all who were baptized into Christ Jesus were baptized into his death, buried with him through baptism into death, so that, just as Christ rose from the dead through the glory of the Father, so we too might walk in newness of life” (Rom. VI). [Col. 1459A]

That after a life well lived we should seek the heavenly realms is attested by the faith of all orthodox Christians. For we know, according to the blessed Apostle, that:

> “If our earthly house of this dwelling is dissolved, we have a dwelling from God, a house not made with hands in the heavens” (2 Cor. V).

In all these things Christ presents to us the sign of his holy Church. Hanging upon the cross, he himself confirmed this by his most holy authority, saying:

> “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” (Matt. XXVII).

But where or when did the Father forsake him, since he himself had said:

> “I am not alone, because the Father is with me” (John VIII),

and again:

> “Father, I know that you always hear me” (John XI)?

In himself, therefore, he undoubtedly prefigured his Church, which had once been forsaken in Adam.

And since, as the blessed Apostle Paul taught us, Christ himself is the head of the Church and the Church is his body (Col. I), his own body—the body which he had taken from the blessed Virgin—is a sign, figure, and sacrament of his body, which is the Church. The body of the Church is born, after the likeness of its head, from the Holy Spirit and the Church, virgin in heart; and from all nations it is gathered into one new man, as from diverse members.

We rightly believe that all these things are signified by that which is taken from the Lord’s altar. To satisfy the matter briefly, without indiscriminately revealing the deepest reasons of the divine mysteries: the universal Church herself is a witness that whenever we receive it, we show that we are Christians, that is, spiritually born. Consequently, we declare that we have been crucified, died, and buried together with our Lord through baptism into death, and that we have also risen together with him. Through it we cast out vices; through it we trust that we are strengthened in new life; and through it we hope that, having been perfected, we shall afterward ascend to the eternal kingdom.

Now that the sacred offering signifies the unity of the body of the Church need not be proved at length. The Apostle Paul sufficiently declares it, saying:

> “The bread which we break, and the cup which we bless, is it not participation in the body and blood of the Lord? Because we, though many, are one in Christ” (1 Cor. X). [Col. 1459D]

Understanding this, blessed Cyprian explains it in a letter to a certain Magnus as follows (*Book I, Letter 6*):

> “Finally, the Lord’s sacrifices themselves declare Christians to be joined together by firm unanimity and inseparable love. For when the Lord calls his body bread, formed by the union of many grains gathered together, he indicates that our people, whom he bore, are united. And when he calls his blood wine, pressed from many clusters and grapes and gathered into one, he likewise signifies our flock, joined together by the mingling of a united multitude.”

Hence blessed Augustine also says concerning John (*Tractate XXVI*):

> “He therefore wishes this food and drink to be understood as the fellowship of his body and members, which is the holy Church.”

And shortly afterward:

> “For this reason, as the holy men of God before us understood, our Lord Jesus Christ entrusted his body and blood to those things which are brought together from many into one. For one thing is made from many grains, and another one thing from many grapes.” [Col. 1460A]

Most fittingly and reasonably, therefore, the sacred offering is called a sign—not only of many other good things, but also of the Lord’s body, that is, of the Church, gathered and joined into one from many human beings, peoples, or nations, like grains crushed between the two Testaments as between an upper and lower millstone—that is, humbled—through the water of baptism and the fire of the Holy Spirit.

But concerning the very body with which the divinity of the Savior was properly clothed, you will find it called a sign openly by any author either nowhere or scarcely anywhere. When, indeed, the Eucharist is called the sacrament of the Lord’s body, we resolve the construction of the words in this way: the Eucharist is the sacrament which is the Lord’s body, so that it is itself truly the Lord’s body, while it is the sacrament of other things, namely, of the good things mentioned above. This is like our customary expressions: “God is the source of goodness,” that is, the source who is goodness; “the fullness of divinity,” that is, the fullness which is divinity; and many other similar expressions.

Or else we understand the words to mean that it is itself the Lord’s body, namely, the proper body of the Word of God, and the sacrament of the Lord’s body, which is the Church, as the blessed Apostle taught. [Col. 1460C]

But if it were found anywhere that even the body with which the Word of God was clothed—a usage which nevertheless appears nowhere, or scarcely anywhere, clearly—were called a sacrament, what harm would this do us, or how would it weaken our faith? Is nothing a sacrament of that of which it is the sacrament? Is nothing a figure of that of which it is the figure?

What, then, does Paul say of the Son of God in his Letter to the Hebrews?

> “Who, being the radiance of glory and the figure of his substance” (Heb. I),

that is, of the Father. Is the Son not what the Father is? Far from it. The Son is altogether what the Father is, and is nothing other than what the Father is. It is therefore false to say that nothing is a figure of that of which it is the figure.

Furthermore, when Christ once taught, performed miracles, and lived most righteously among human beings, eating, drinking, sleeping, and displaying in himself the other properties of our humanity, what else did he signify for us but himself as God and man? And now also, interceding for us, showing his body with its scars to the Father’s face, he signifies that he was born, suffered, rose again for us, and ascended into heaven.

Thus Christ himself is the sacred sign of himself, that is, the sacrament. This same divine offering can likewise signify these same things for us without danger to our faith. Since, then, our Eucharist is found to signify in every respect the same things as Christ does, Christ is likewise the sacrament of those things of which it is the sacrament. [Col. 1461A]

Yet no one on this account says that Christ is Christ’s shadow rather than the true Christ; nor does anyone say that his body is a shadowy and unreal body because it signifies his body, which is the Church, and himself, as we have now shown.

Therefore, let no one say that our Eucharist, because of the significations mentioned above, is a shadow of that Lord’s body which the divinity of the Savior properly assumed, rather than the true and proper body of the Savior himself. For if, because of these significations, it is not the true and proper body of Christ, then, because of the same significations, Christ himself will not be the true Christ.

But far be this from the minds of all, that because Christ is the sacrament of so many and such great goods for us, his truth should thereby in any way be emptied. So likewise, far be it from the hearts of all to deny that our Eucharist is the true and proper body of Christ because it signifies these same goods for us.

Therefore, as I believe, it has been shown sufficiently and abundantly that whatever the adversary brings forward from the writings of blessed Augustine mentioned above, or from the terms “sacrament,” “figure,” and “sign,” which are in use in the Church, does nothing contrary to our faith. How childish he also proves to be in other matters may be clear from this.

ROGERIUS

It is now sufficiently established and proved by you that Christ is the sign of himself. Nevertheless, I desire a fuller explanation of how this can be.

[Col. 1461C] GUITMUNDUS

Why are you surprised at this? The matter is so solemn that no one ought to doubt it. For what human being is there, for example, who, by doing anything at all, or even merely by his spontaneous movement, does not signify that he is alive? Thus it happens that one human being, always the same in substance, can signify himself in different ways according to different actions.

In the same way, Christ is always substantially the same; nevertheless, by performing visible actions, he signifies himself as performing invisible ones. Moreover, by his word, demeanor, or bodily appearance, he signified to those to whom he appeared at various times that he was favorable or angry.

In the same manner, the sacred offering of the altar, although it truly possesses the substance of Christ’s body, can, according to its visible appearance and visible mysteries, signify certain things—either concerning the Lord himself or concerning his Church—without danger to our faith.

ROGERIUS

Continue in the direction you had begun; for concerning these matters it would be utterly insane to doubt any further.

GUITMUNDUS

What especially tends to trouble Berengarius is that, in his exposition of the aforementioned Psalm 98, blessed Augustine says this concerning the Lord’s words to his disciples:

> “When the twelve disciples had remained with him, he instructed them and said to them: ‘It is the Spirit who gives life; the flesh profits nothing. The words that I have spoken to you are spirit and life’ (John VI). You are not going to eat this body that you see, nor drink the blood which those who crucify me are going to pour out.”

“If, then,” says Berengarius, “it is not this body or that blood, it follows that what is taken from the altar is only a shadow and figure of the body and blood.” [Col. 1462A]

If he had carefully considered Augustine’s earlier words in his exposition of the same psalm—or certainly in his exposition of the Gospel, where these same words of the Lord are discussed—he would perhaps never have constructed from them the accusation of this error.

But the unhappy man, long grown old in the plague of heresy and, at the devil’s urging, almost inexplicably entangled in his nets, more willingly applies all the powers of his intellect to snatching at one word, so that, by misunderstanding it, he may seem to fortify the folly he has propagated, than he gives even slight attention to the most provident vigilance of the divine Scriptures, which strongly protests against him.

For in the same psalm blessed Augustine had said earlier:

> “Christ took earth from the earth, because flesh is from the earth; and from Mary’s flesh he received flesh, and in that flesh he walked here, and he gave us that very flesh to eat for salvation.”

If, then, he gave us for salvation the very flesh which he received from Mary’s flesh and in which he walked here, how can he say, “not this body,” unless it is because he gives us that flesh in the same substance, but not this body in the same form? It is as though he were saying: “I shall indeed give you my body, as you have heard, but not according to what you see; that is, not such as you see it—not in this form, not in this appearance which you see.”

Otherwise, why did he add “which you see,” when it would have been sufficient to say “not this,” unless it is because he meant “not this according to essence, but not this according to what you see”? [Col. 1462C]

Finally, so that you may recognize that this is what Augustine understood, consider more attentively what he had blamed in those who were offended, in his exposition of this psalm or of the Gospel. Clearly, they supposed that the substance which they perceived with their eyes would be given to them to eat—not bread, nor anything else.

Augustine says that they received this foolishly and carnally.

“‘For they thought,’ he says, ‘that the Lord would cut off certain pieces from his body and give them to them. They thought that his grace would be consumed by bites, and that he would distribute to believers the flesh with which the Word had been clothed—not whole, as he ascended into heaven, but as though cut up, or as a corpse is torn apart, or as meat is sold in a butcher’s shop—not in the manner in which it is animated by the spirit, that is, not alive. For if it is animated by the spirit,’ it is alive.”

What, then, if they had thought that they would receive the flesh whole, not cut into pieces; not dead, but alive; not as it is sold in a butcher’s shop, but alive, as it is animated by the spirit? Would they have been in error? Certainly not. For they are condemned not because they thought they would eat that flesh—that is, flesh of the same substance—but solely because they thought it would not be whole or alive. Consequently, they would have been entirely free from blame if they had thought that they would eat that same flesh—that is, flesh of the same substance—whole and alive. [Col. 1463A]

If this follows—or rather, since it does follow—see how effectively it completely destroys Berengarius’s position and every shadowy error. Therefore, if the words of Augustine quoted above can be understood in the manner we have explained, most appropriately, with no passage of Scripture contradicting them, indeed with the whole sequence carefully examined, and with the exposition of the Gospel not merely recommending but necessarily compelling this interpretation, what support does Berengarius find in them against us? To speak indulgently, even if these words were ambiguous, they would aid his party no more than ours.

But now, since both the surrounding context of Scripture, the remarkably clear reasoning of the Gospel’s exposition, and the authority of the universal Church support our understanding, let the infection of heretical corruption, having no further refuge here, fall silent. Or certainly, if he believes that he can somehow refute our position or show his own to be better, we are prepared to hear him calmly. We do not wish to evade anything that, with Christ’s help, we cannot examine carefully.

I say this because I believe I have heard that Berengarius reasons as follows concerning the pronoun “this”: “‘This’ is a pronoun; but pronouns signify substance without qualities. Therefore, when he says, ‘not this body,’ he speaks of the substance of the body, not of its qualities.”

Here I am compelled to exclaim, with the prophet and the Apostle: “Where is the learned man? Where is the examiner of words? Where is he who weighs the words of the law?” (Isa. XXXIII). “Has God not made foolish the wisdom of this world?” (1 Cor. I.) [Col. 1463C]

Indeed, I would call this wisdom foolish. For those very grammarians who laid down this kind of rule concerning the properties of the parts of speech also handed down and magnificently praised the figures of speech by which the parts of speech very often depart most appropriately from their proper functions.

Who, speaking or dictating in ordinary usage, would be reproached for saying, “I am not the one I once was,” or “You are not the person you used to be,” when the substance is the same but the qualities are different? Even dialecticians, who weigh words with excessive precision, say and read every day that things differ and that they are the same—not only according to substance, but also according to qualities.

If “ille,” “is,” and “idem” are pronouns, and if, among the most learned, they frequently signify not substance alone but also qualities, why should this pronoun not be able to do the same? Is it because Berengarius, having no other means by which to defend his heresy, dislikes this conclusion?

Nevertheless, certain authorities of the highest standing in the grammatical art held that qualities could be understood figuratively in pronouns, and even that “qualis” and “talis,” which properly signify quality, could be numbered among the pronouns. Let that most accomplished grammarian Donatus, who wished “qualis” and “talis” to be pronouns, see what he has said.

I have no need at present to judge the authorities of the grammatical art, since I can most conveniently use the adversary’s own argument, saying: “It is itself a pronoun. But pronouns signify substance without qualities.” Therefore, when Augustine says, “He walked in that very flesh, and gave that flesh to us to eat for salvation,” he says that we eat the substance of Christ’s flesh, not a figure.

Likewise, “this” is a pronoun. Therefore, when that same Augustine says in his sermon to the newly baptized: “Receive in the bread that which hung upon the cross, and receive in the cup that which was poured from Christ’s side,” he declares that we eat and drink the substance of Christ’s body and blood, not a figure.

Your argument, then, whoever relies upon it—if it is weak, we need not concern ourselves with it. But if it is strong, it benefits us more than you, since you have it only in one place, whereas we have it in many. And since Augustine appears to contradict himself, either he must no longer be accepted, or we must believe him more in his many testimonies than in one. For it is easier for him himself to have erred in one place than for his books to have been corrupted by some falsifier.

Choose, then, whichever alternative you prefer: either this reasoning of yours is weak and accomplishes nothing, or it is strong and greatly benefits us. If it is weak, it proves nothing where it says, “not this body,” that the expression does not refer to the substance. If it is strong, it confirms that where Augustine says, “he gave that very flesh to us to eat,” and, “receive this,” and similar expressions, these must be understood of substance.

Or perhaps you will say: “I will interpret those pronouns in this way: ‘He gave that very flesh to us to eat for salvation,’ that is, he gave us the figure of that flesh; and, ‘receive this in the bread,’ that is, receive the figure of this body in the bread,” and so on.

If you say this, we too interpret your pronoun in the same way, saying: “I will give you not this body, which you see,” that is, “I will give you not the figure of this body; not a shadow, but the truth.” Such an interpretation necessarily follows your interpretations. If, therefore, you accept the figurative interpretation of pronouns against us, how can you refuse to accept the same interpretation against yourself? Either apply it, and your shadows will be taken away from you, or reject it, and it will greatly benefit us.

For if you bring forward the foregoing interpretations of the pronouns against us, you plainly turn against yourself and your shadows the passage you had brought against us. But if you reject them and obstinately insist that pronouns always signify substance, then, as I said, Augustine’s many other statements contradicting this one passage—and contradicting both you and himself—must either not be accepted, or we must believe his many testimonies more than one. Thus we reach the conclusion we desired: we eat the Lord’s body substantially, not as a shadow.

Whichever way you flee, it is evident from these things that if you carefully consider Augustine, the outstanding teacher upon whom you relied most, you completely overthrow, without pause or respite, the plague of this shadowy error. Therefore, having dissolved this slander, let us proceed also to what Berengarius objects from Saint Augustine’s letter to Boniface. In this matter he appears plainly to labor more from love of disputation than from any regard for reason.

For when Saint Augustine says, “Just as the sacrament of Christ’s body is, in a certain manner, Christ’s body, and the sacrament of Christ’s blood is, in a certain manner, Christ’s blood, so the sacrament of faith is faith,” it is not necessary to understand this as referring to the sacraments of our altar. He had been speaking generally about sacraments. For if sacraments did not possess some likeness to the things of which they are sacraments, they would not be sacraments at all. It is from this likeness that sacraments often receive the names of the things themselves.

Then, descending from the genus to the species, he concluded by means of a parallel example what he intended, saying: “Therefore, just as the sacrament of Christ’s body is, in a certain manner, Christ’s body,” and so forth. We may freely understand this as having been said of the manna, or of the bread and wine of Melchizedek (Gen. XIV), or of some of the ancient sacrifices, which were sacraments of Christ’s body and blood. For they can in some manner be called by the names of Christ’s body and blood through a figure, just as the rock is called Christ.

He therefore does not pay sufficient attention to what he is bringing forward. Even if we wish, by way of abundance, to understand this as having been said also of the sacraments of our altar, a faithful and straightforward interpretation is available. Since our sacraments are substantially that which is proper to the Son of God, they are, in a certain manner, through a figure, the very body of Christ whose sacraments they are—that is, the Church.

Augustine confirms this in his exposition of John, in these words (Tract. 26): “This food and drink, therefore, he wishes to be understood as the fellowship of his body and members, which is the holy Church. The sacrament of this reality—that is, of the unity of Christ’s body and blood—is prepared daily in some places, and at fixed intervals of days in others, on the Lord’s table, and is received from the Lord’s table.” [Col. 1465C]

Again, in a certain sermon on the sacraments: “‘He who suffered for us,’ he says, ‘commended to us in this sacrament his blood and body, which he also made us ourselves. For we have become his body, and by his mercy we are what we receive.’”

Behold how he said that the food and drink of the altar are, in a certain manner, the fellowship of the body, which is the Church. He did not say that the food and drink themselves are that fellowship, but the sacrament of that fellowship. And he said that what we receive is, in a certain manner, ourselves, because it is the sacrament of us.

Thus Christ’s proper body is, in a certain manner, through a figure, that body of Christ whose sacrament it is—the Church. Nor is this surprising, since the Lord himself says through the prophet: “He surrounded me with a garment of righteousness, like a bridegroom adorned with a crown and like a bride adorned with her necklaces” (Isa. LXI). He calls himself the bridegroom because he himself is the Bridegroom; he calls himself the bride because he is, in a certain manner, that body of his which is the Church, whose sacrament he himself is.

This interpretation is most aptly commended to us by the following comparison. Just as we call the Lord’s proper body the sacrament of his other body, which is the Church, so we recognize visible baptism as the sacrament of another, invisible baptism. For there is an outward baptism, visible water cleansing the flesh; and there is an inward baptism, invisible faith purifying the soul in a similar manner. The blessed Apostle bears witness to this when he says: “Cleansing their hearts by faith” (Acts XV). And again: “Baptism now saves you—not the removal of dirt from the flesh, but the appeal of a good conscience toward God” (1 Pet. III).

Accordingly, we may understand Augustine’s words quite appropriately and with sound faith as follows: “Just as the sacrament of Christ’s body”—that is, just as the proper body of the Son of God, which is the sacrament of Christ’s body, namely the Church—“is, in a certain manner, Christ’s body,” that is, that body whose sacrament it is, the Church—he himself being the Bridegroom and himself, in a certain manner, the bride—“so the sacrament of faith,” that is, outward baptism, because it is the sign of faith, “is, in a certain manner, faith.”

Saint Peter also offends Berengarius when he says of the Lord: “Whom heaven must receive until the times of the restoration of all things” (Acts III). “If,” says Berengarius, “he must be received by heaven until the end, he never leaves heaven, so that he could at some time be held on earth.”

We believed that Christ reigns in heaven; but this man would imprison him in such a way that, even if he wished to do so bodily, he could not visit this wretched earth until the end. Augustine also says in the book *The City of God* (Book XXII, final chapter) that each of the saints will attain such glory that, wherever his spirit wishes, his body will immediately be present. Berengarius, however, asserts that Christ has been reduced to such impotence that he who raised his body from earth to heaven cannot restore it to earth, even until the end or for an hour. [Col. 1466C]

O excessively blind vanity, and vain blindness! Who, speaking according to ordinary usage, would hesitate to say: “That man remained in that city for so many months or years,” even if he went out of the city each day to attend to his business? In the Gospel it is written of Anna that “she did not depart from the temple” (Luke II), although bodily necessity often called her away.

Therefore, even if we were to say that Christ descends bodily to earth every day, the opposing statement of blessed Peter would not harm us. But far be it from Christian prudence to say that Christ is sacrificed or eaten on earth in such a way that meanwhile he must leave heaven. For he is wholly in heaven while his whole body is truly eaten on earth. That this should not be considered incredible can be demonstrated quite readily by the power of divine omnipotence and by the examples given above, namely those of the voice and the soul.

Who, moreover, could now restrain his laughter on hearing Berengarius interpret the Lord’s own words concerning the sacraments? “‘This,’ he says, ‘is necessarily bread, my body, and this cup is necessarily wine.’”

O most shameless and utterly transparent foolishness, which sees neither what it says nor where it is heading! What necessity is there here for “bread” and “wine” to be understood, when the words could suitably be taken in the opposite way: “This”—with “body” understood—“now no longer bread, is my body”; and “this cup”—with “blood” understood—“now rather no longer wine, is the cup of my blood”?

Or certainly in this way: “This”—understand, “until now bread”—“from this point is my body, not bread”; and “this cup”—understand, “until now wine”—“from this point is my blood, not wine.”

Or, without these implied expressions: the pronoun “this” does not refer back to what was said above, but is merely demonstrative. Therefore the bread and wine previously named in the Gospel are not necessarily to be supplied here at all.

I already pity the man and blush for him. For who, unless he had thus betrayed himself, could believe that a man of such reputation would chatter so childishly and rave so frivolously? But let us see where this great reasoner has arrived through these supposedly necessary implied expressions, what he has accomplished, and what he has gained.

“‘This,’ he says, ‘means that the sacraments of the altar are called bread and wine.’”

Was this, then, the goal of all that labor? Was this the sole purpose for which you poured yourself out so extravagantly, sparing neither your old age nor yourself, so that you might show yourself—rather than an excellent disputant—as a most slanderous caviler; rather than a skilled builder, as the most idle and inept tailor of scraps of every kind?

Who denies this? Who does not readily admit that the sacraments of the Lord’s table are rightly called bread and wine, either because they were formerly bread and wine, or because, having been substantially transformed, they retain the likeness of bread and wine?

Thus the serpent that was made from a staff is called a staff. For it is written: “Aaron’s staff swallowed their staffs” (Exod. VII), that is, the serpent which had been made from Aaron’s staff swallowed their serpents. Likewise, because man was made from it, he is often called earth, dust, and clay. [Col. 1467C]

For the same reason the Apostle says: “The rock was Christ” (1 Cor. X). And in the Psalm it is sung: “I am a worm and not a man” (Ps. XXI), although he was substantially a man and a worm only by likeness. There are many other examples beyond counting.

If, therefore, many things are rightly called by the names of other, entirely different things for either of these reasons, how much more may our sacraments rightly be called bread and wine for both reasons, since they retain much likeness to the things they formerly were, while substantially and properly possessing the reality of the Lord’s body and blood?

Now let us examine what Berengarius boasts that he establishes by the authority of ecclesiastical prayer. “‘The Church,’ he says, ‘prays in a certain Mass as follows: “May your sacraments, O Lord, we beseech you, accomplish in us what they contain, so that what we now enact under a likeness, we may receive in the reality of the things.” Here, therefore, he shows that he does not possess the reality of the things, but only their appearance.’”

Good interpreter, I ask you: the appearance of what things, not their reality? “Of the Lord’s body and blood,” you will say. Very well. Consider carefully what is said and answer me. What is it that “we now enact under a likeness”? “We eat the Lord’s body under a likeness, not substantially,” you will say.

Add what follows: “May we receive it in the reality of the things.” What? Then in the future age shall we truly and substantially eat the Lord’s body and blood? For this is what is prayed: that whatever it is which we now enact under a likeness, we may receive that same thing in reality.

Therefore, if throughout this age we eat Christ’s body under a likeness—that is, as you foolishly claim, as a shadow—it follows that in the other age we shall eat it substantially. Since this is utterly absurd to believe, do not imagine that you yourself remain unaware of how foolishly you interpret the prayer cited above.

Let us therefore examine most carefully, from the beginning of the prayer, what Scripture intends to say: “May your sacraments, O Lord, we beseech you, accomplish in us what they contain.”

We have already said, and have confirmed by the words of the blessed Apostle Paul, that the divine sacraments signify the unity of Christ’s body, which is the Church, and that this is what they contain by signifying it.

The Church therefore prays in these words: “May your sacraments, O Lord, we beseech you, accomplish in us what they contain”—that is, “may they accomplish” that we truly be one body of Christ, one Church, which they signify—“so that what we now enact,” that is, while we eat the body of your Son, “under a likeness,” that is, signify through the figure of so great a sacrament, “we may receive in the reality of the things,” that is, truly be one body of Christ and one Church.

This interpretation, I believe, is possible; it is entirely suitable to Scripture and most useful to us. The blessed Apostle Paul confirms it, and the faith of the whole Church agrees with it. The madness of the adversaries, on the other hand, is supported by no authority; rather, the whole Church flees from it as from deadly poison.

No benefit at all commends their interpretation, nor does the prayer itself; but an intolerable absurdity follows it and wholly rejects it. Who, then, ought in any way to be hindered in favor of a bestial, foolish—indeed impossible—meaning, when he possesses a reasonable and most fitting interpretation, one which all wise people ought to embrace?

“Do you now consider these things sufficient, or do you still require more?”

**ROGERIUS.**

“These things are plainly sufficient for me, indeed more than sufficient; and I marvel that the heretic has been overthrown by his own objections and entangled in his own nets.”

[Col. 1468D]

**GUITMUNDUS.**

“These, then, are the matters which we have found Berengarius accustomed to bring forward against our faith from the books of the blessed Augustine, from the meaning of the word ‘sacrament,’ or from the prayer just examined. If he objects anything else from the blessed Augustine, I say confidently in Christ’s strength that, when carefully considered, it will either support us or at least not be against us.

Let us therefore bring this discussion to an end here, and, if the Lord wills, undertake what remains with a fresh beginning.”

# HERE BEGINS THE THIRD BOOK

[Col. 1469]

[Col. 1469A]

“Thus far the present discourse has dissolved the arguments by which the adversary strove against the Church both by reason and by Scripture. Therefore, since the enemy’s engines have been abundantly frustrated with God’s help, even if we added nothing further, the general practice of the Catholic faith alone ought to suffice for you.

For that faith which is Catholic must be held most firmly, even if it is fiercely attacked. Whoever wishes to be saved, as the holy Fathers have decreed and the whole world unanimously proclaims, must hold the Catholic faith. If it must be retained with the greatest strength when attacked, how much more must it not be abandoned when it is manifestly unconquerable, overcoming everything set against it?

But since many further arguments can, with God’s help, be added both to strengthen our position and to demolish that of the adversaries—and since I know that you eagerly desire them—we shall, with the Lord favoring us in response to your prayers, bring forward additional testimony from the holy Scriptures. Through it the slippery enemy will be more completely overthrown, and the invincible strength of our position will be further demonstrated through his own arguments.

First, therefore, following the order of the questions, let us prove that we eat Christ’s true body in its substance, not in Berengarius’s shadow. Then the discourse will keep watch against those who turn the Lord’s body into bread.”

At the beginning of our discussion, then, since the origin of nearly the whole scandal appears to lie in the blessed Augustine, let us see what that same most noble teacher thought concerning the Church’s sacrifice in his exposition of the title of Psalm XXXIII.

Explaining how David was carried in his own hands before Abimelech, he says:

“Now, brothers, how this can happen in a man, let anyone understand. For who is carried in his own hands? A man may be carried in the hands of others; no one is carried in his own hands. We do not find how this is to be understood literally in David himself, but we do find it in Christ. For Christ was carried in his own hands when, commending his very body, he said: ‘This is my body.’ For he carried that body in his own hands.”

O clearest judgment! O most faithful judgment! O judgment truly worthy of the blessed and most excellent teacher Augustine, from which no one may depart, and to which all must grant the greatest reverence!

“What,” he says, “is not found literally in David and in other human beings is found in Christ.” What is that? “‘Christ was carried,’ he says, ‘in his own hands when, commending his very body, he said: “This is my body.”’”

If this is found in Christ literally—that is, as the words sound—then the body that was carried was not shadow-like, not figurative, but substantial Christ’s body. For if, as these men wish, what was carried in Christ’s hands is understood figuratively and not according to the substance of his body, how is it found in him literally?

Is Christ literally a rock, a lion, a lamb, and a serpent, when he is all these things figuratively? Certainly not. But “in Christ,” he says, “we find how this is to be understood literally.” Otherwise the sentence, which grants concerning Christ what it denied concerning David, cannot be constructed at all.

Therefore, contrary to what these men wish, it is not according to a figure but according to substance. Let every prudent reader carefully observe how decisively all the sophistries of these heretics are excluded by this passage.

Let us suppose, if it pleases you, what the adversaries might say here, so that what follows may become clearer. When Augustine says, “Christ was carried in his own hands,” and then, “He carried that body in his own hands,” suppose our adversaries interpret this on their behalf as follows:

“‘Christ was carried in his own hands,’ that is, only Christ’s shadow or figure, not his substance, was carried in his own hands; and ‘he carried that body,’ that is, the shadow or figure of that body, not its substance.”

If they interpret it this way, we can find the same thing in David and in nearly every human being. For who among human beings could not carry in his hands some representation of himself in which his substance is not present—for example, a statue or a painting?

“But,” he says, “we do not find this in David himself, and no one is carried in his own hands. In Christ, however,” he says, “we find it.”

Since, therefore, he says that what is not found in David and in other human beings is found in Christ; and since both David and other human beings can easily be understood to carry in their hands some representation of themselves in which none of their substance is present, it remains most plainly, without any doubt, to conclude that Christ carried, according to Augustine, not merely a figure or shadow, as our adversaries say, but the substance of his own body.

What will these lovers of shadows answer? Where will these creatures that flee the light prepare a shadow amid such great brightness? Behold, the clearest testimonies of Augustine are recited: there is nothing difficult, nothing ambiguous in them. Let them either explain themselves concerning these passages or cease bringing Augustine forward against us; and, as Augustine bears witness, let them believe with us in the truth of the Lord’s body.

Perhaps they had not noticed that this was written. For if they had attended to it faithfully, they would not still have drawn their heresy from the blessed Augustine. Whatever they seize from him on their behalf, when carefully examined—as we have already said—either supports us or certainly does nothing against us.

But what we have now brought forward destroys them so manifestly that they cannot find any way out by any reasoning. Scripture is so clear, so entirely guarded, that the chatter of these men can find absolutely no argument by which to evade it.

To show its force as briefly as possible: either Christ’s body, which Christ carried and of which he said, “This is my body,” was substantial, or it was merely figurative. But it cannot have been merely figurative, given the preceding statement that what is found in Christ is not found in others. Otherwise it would also be found in others.

For every human being can carry a representation of himself in which none of his substance is present. But “in others,” he says, “it is not found.” “No one,” he says, “is carried in his own hands.” Therefore it was not merely figurative or shadow-like. Consequently, Christ’s body, which he himself carried, was substantial.

I cannot adequately express how much I delight in these words of the blessed Augustine, or how greatly I marvel at the wretched blindness of these men. For they plainly show what that most blessed man wished to be understood in the exposition immediately following of the same Psalm XXXIII, where he said:

“Let us draw near to him, so that we may receive his body and blood. They were darkened by the crucified one; we are enlightened by eating and drinking the crucified one.”

Likewise, elsewhere:

“‘Receive,’ he says, ‘in the bread that which hung upon the cross; and receive in the cup that which was poured from Christ’s side.’”

And in another place:

“These drank what they had previously shed when raging, afterward believing.”

Likewise, in another passage which we have already cited:

“Christ received earth from earth, because flesh is from earth; and he received flesh from Mary’s flesh, and in that flesh he walked here, and he gave us that very flesh to eat for salvation.”

And there are many other passages of this kind in numerous books of his.

Since these men venerate and hold the writings of the blessed Augustine as altogether sacred and inviolate, what can now disturb them—unless perhaps a blindness long rooted in them does so—from believing with us?

But you also, excellent teacher, most blessed Ambrose, spiritual father of the blessed Augustine—whom that most holy man calls holy and blessed in his books; whose authority, as Augustine testifies, the Apostle Paul, revealer of martyrs, commends; whom the blessed Gregory, a truly apostolic man, holds forth; whose teaching the most blessed Benedict, according to Saint Gregory, judged worthy of acceptance, being filled with the spirit of the holy prophets; to whom the glory of the whole Church of Milan bears special witness; whom the whole world rightly embraces with reverence for the sake of the faith—for if so many and such great witnesses had known you to be in error concerning the Catholic faith, they would not have praised you with such acclaim—

Explain, then, what you think concerning the sacraments of the altar.

Certainly, in your book *On the Sacraments* (Book VI, chapter 1), you said:

“Just as our Lord Jesus Christ is the true Son of God—not like other human beings by grace, but as a son by nature, that is, from the substance of the Father—so his true flesh is what we receive, and his true blood is what we drink.”

I therefore hold that you said: “His true flesh is what we receive, and his true blood is what we drink.” But in what sense are they true? Figuratively or substantially? Teach us, through the comparison you have set before us, what kind of truth we are to understand here.

“Just as our Lord Jesus Christ is the true Son of God”—this is still insufficient. For just as righteous human beings are sons of God by grace, he too, insofar as he is human, could be called the true Son of God by grace, although ineffably greater and more excellent than other human beings.

Add what is sufficient: “not like other human beings by grace, but as a son by nature, that is, from the substance of the Father.”

Thus you say that his flesh is true flesh which we receive, and his blood true blood which we drink. But in what sense is it so? That is, not as other things can be called Christ’s flesh and blood because of some grace of signification—for example, the flesh and blood of the paschal lamb sacrificed in Egypt (Exod. XII) could be called Christ’s flesh and blood by the grace of a figure; and in the same way the manna and many other things could be so called—but as flesh and blood by the nature of Christ’s flesh and blood.

The comparison cannot be fitted together in any other way, except that we deny here what he denies there, and affirm here what he affirms there.

Therefore, if we follow this comparison, set forth so explicitly, we confess that what we receive from the altar is substantially Christ’s flesh and blood. For if it had been said: “Just as our Lord Jesus Christ is the true Son of God, so his flesh is true flesh which we receive, and his blood is true blood which we drink,” the statement could still, as has been said, remain ambiguous.

For our Lord Jesus Christ, insofar as he is human, is the true Son of God—but by grace, as we have said, not from the substance of the Father. Accordingly, it could be said: “Thus his flesh is true flesh which we receive,” that is, by the grace of a figure, not through the substance of the flesh; and likewise concerning the blood.

But if the excellent teacher had intended this, he would have added nothing more. What need was there to add something so manifestly contrary to this interpretation?

Now, however, he most carefully added the qualification: “Not like other human beings by grace.” And lest any little cloud of error should remain here, he added: “but as a son by nature.” And lest even this should appear obscure, he explained it more explicitly: “that is, from the substance of the Father.”

By all these most careful qualifications, then, when he adds, “so his true flesh is what we receive, and his true blood is what we drink,” he excludes all the adversaries’ slanderous arguments and shows that Christ’s flesh and blood are substantially what we receive and drink. Therefore, if you do not argue against yourself, blessed Ambrose, you do not dissent from this faith. And if you do not dissent from it, you are certainly more worthy to be imitated than Berengarius.

You have plainly seen what this most noble teacher thinks in this passage concerning the sacraments of the altar, without any concealment. Now observe how briefly he speaks elsewhere in the same book:

“Why do we use arguments? Let us use his examples, and establish the truth of the mystery by the example of the Incarnation. It is clear that the Virgin gave birth contrary to the order of nature, and that this body which we make is from the Virgin. Why do you seek the order of nature in Christ’s body, when Christ himself was born from the Virgin contrary to nature?”

What better or clearer statement could you seek? If the sacraments of the altar were merely the shadow and figure of the Lord’s body, what would occur here contrary to nature? The rock figures Christ not contrary to nature, but rather because of the nature of its firmness; the lamb does so not contrary to nature, but through its nature, that is, through its innocence; and likewise with the other figures of Christ.

It would be lengthy to discuss all the testimonies that we can bring from the blessed Ambrose against Berengarius. We must now pass to other authorities.

The most holy Pope Leo, most ancient and venerable to the entire Church of God, said in a certain sermon (*On the Fast of the Seventh Month*):

“You ought to partake of the sacred table in such a way that you have absolutely no doubt concerning the reality of Christ’s body and blood. For what is received by the mouth is believed by faith. And those who dispute against what they receive answer ‘Amen’ in vain.”

Blessed Cyril likewise, with two hundred bishops at the Synod of Ephesus—which blessed Gregory asserts ought to be received as one of the four Gospels—says as follows:

“We approach the mystical blessings and are sanctified, having been made participants in the holy body and precious blood of Christ, the Redeemer of us all—not as though receiving ordinary flesh, God forbid! nor as sanctified men joined to the Word according to a unity of dignity, nor as though possessing a divine indwelling; but as flesh truly made life-giving and made the very own flesh of the Word himself. For, since he exists as God by nature, he is Life; and because he was united to his own flesh, he confessed that it is life-giving. Therefore, although he says, ‘Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man’ (John 6), we must not regard it as the flesh of one ordinary man from among us. For how could human flesh be life-giving according to its nature? Rather, we confess that it was truly made his own, since for our sake he both became and was called the Son of Man.”

And again:

“If anyone does not confess that the flesh of the Lord is life-giving and the very own flesh of the Word of God the Father, but regards it as belonging to someone else joined to him by dignity, or as though he possessed a divine indwelling, and does not rather confess it to be life-giving because it has been made the own flesh of the Word who is able to give life, let him be anathema.”

But Berengar did not fear the anathema of those two hundred bishops. Like a madman rushing upon his own sword, he incurred the anathema that he himself had pronounced and added with his own mouth at Rome against the sacrament.

Blessed Gregory likewise says in his Homilies on the Gospels (homily 58):

“You have learned what the blood of the Lamb is, not now by hearing but by drinking. That blood is placed upon both doorposts when it is received not only by the mouth of the body but also by the mouth of the heart.”

The same author says in the final book of the Dialogues:

“For this singular victim saves the soul from eternal destruction; through the mystery it restores to us the death of the Only-Begotten. Although, having risen from the dead, he no longer dies, and death shall no longer have dominion over him (Romans 6), nevertheless, living in himself immortally and incorruptibly, he is again offered for us in this mystery of the sacred oblation. For there his body is received, and his flesh is distributed for the salvation of the people. His blood is poured out no longer into the hands of unbelievers but into the mouths of the faithful. Let us therefore consider what kind of sacrifice this is for us: it continually imitates, for our absolution, the passion of the Only-Begotten Son. For what believer could doubt that, at the very hour of the offering, at the priest’s voice the heavens are opened; that in this mystery of Jesus Christ the choirs of angels are present; that the highest and lowest things are joined, earthly things united with heavenly things, and one reality made from visible and invisible things?”

Let these shadow-dwellers now at last impose silence upon themselves, since so many and such great authorities resist them with unanswerable authority. Let them also consider again and again what Saint Jerome teaches in many passages, what Isidore teaches, what Bede teaches, and what all the foremost doctors, both Greek and Latin, teach concerning the Lord’s body; and let them put an end to their error, having so many and such great doctors as their guides. We ought not to examine everything, because of the weariness of a lengthy work, when what we have examined cannot reasonably be contradicted.

Nevertheless, I wish to bring forward blessed Hilary, bishop of Poitiers, almost in his own time a singular pillar of the faith, founder of the most holy Martin, received with the greatest devotion by blessed Augustine and by the doctors who came after him, and likewise by the whole Church of God. I consider it especially useful to examine carefully what this remarkable disputant thinks about the Lord’s Eucharist in the eighth book of *On the Trinity*.

For, disputing against the Arians in order to demonstrate that the Father is substantially in the Son, he proved in the following manner that the Son himself is substantially in us through the Eucharist:

“I now ask those who introduce a unity of will between the Father and the Son whether Christ is in us today through the truth of nature or through agreement of will. For if the Word truly became flesh, and if we truly receive the Word made flesh as food from the Lord, how should he not be considered to remain naturally in us? He both assumed, by being born as man, the nature of our flesh, now inseparable from himself, and mingled the nature of his own flesh with the nature of eternity under the sacrament of the flesh communicated to us.

“Thus we are all one, because the Father is in Christ and Christ is in us. Therefore, whoever denies that the Father is naturally in Christ must first deny that he himself is naturally in Christ or that Christ is in him; for the Father in Christ and Christ in us make us one in these things.

“If, then, Christ truly assumed the flesh of our body, and if that man truly is Christ who was born from Mary, and if we truly receive the flesh of his body under the mystery, we shall be one because the Father is in him and he is in us. How, then, is a unity of will asserted, when the natural possession of the sacrament is the sacrament of perfect unity? We must not speak of the things of God according to human or worldly understanding, nor must perversity be wrung from heavenly words by a violent and imprudent proclamation of an understanding alien to soundness and impious. Let us read what has been written, understand what we have read, and then we shall perform the duty of perfect faith.

“For unless we have learned from him, we speak foolishly and impiously about the natural truth of Christ in us. For he himself says: ‘My flesh is truly food, and my blood is truly drink. Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood remains in me, and I in him’ (John 6). No room for doubt has been left concerning the truth of the flesh and blood. For now, both by the Lord’s own profession and by our faith, it is truly flesh and truly blood; and these things, received and drunk, bring it about that we are in Christ and Christ in us.

“Is this not truth? Let it plainly be untrue for those who deny that Christ Jesus is truly God. He himself is therefore in us through the flesh, and we are in him, since according to what we are, he himself is [what we are is in God]. But that we are in him through the sacrament of the flesh and blood communicated to us, he himself testifies when he says: ‘The world will see me no more, but you will see me, because I live and you will live. On that day you will know that I am in my Father, and you are in me, and I am in you’ (John 14).

“If he had wished only a unity of will to be understood, why did he set out a certain degree and order of consummated unity? Surely it was so that, while he was in the Father by the nature of his divinity, we might be believed to be in him through the bodily birth by which he came into being, and he in turn to be in us through the mystery of his sacraments; and so that perfect unity through the Mediator might be taught: while we remain in him, he remains in the Father; while remaining in the Father, he remains in us; and thus we might advance toward the unity of the Father, since, as he is naturally in the Father, we too might be naturally in him, while he naturally remains in us.

“That this unity is natural in us, he himself testified: ‘Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood remains in me, and I in him’ (John 6). For no one will be in him unless he himself has been in that person; and he alone has him who has received the flesh assumed by him.

“He had already taught the sacrament of this perfect unity above, saying: ‘Just as the living Father sent me and I live because of the Father, so whoever eats my flesh will live because of me’ (ibid.). He lives, therefore, because of the Father; and just as he lives because of the Father, so we live because of his flesh. Every comparison is assumed as a pattern for understanding, so that we may grasp the matter under discussion according to the proposed example.

“This, then, is the cause of our life: that we possess Christ dwelling in us bodily through the flesh; and we shall live through him under the condition by which he lives through the Father. If, therefore, we live naturally according to the flesh through him—that is, having obtained the nature of his flesh—how could he not naturally have the Father in himself according to the spirit, since he lives through the Father?”

I have inserted this entire passage from the aforementioned book of blessed Hilary in sequence so that, once the reasoning of this whole discussion has been examined attentively, it may teach us with unchanging certainty what the blessed Hilary thinks concerning the truth of the Lord’s body that we receive from the altar.

For this remarkable disputant proves that the Father is naturally in the Son—that is, substantially. Otherwise, “naturally” ought not to be understood in this way. The entire controversy with the Arians concerned the substantial unity of the Father and the Son. The most skilled disputant would not have proved this so emphatically unless it had been the issue. He proves it, moreover, by this: that the Son himself is naturally—that is, substantially—in us. For this “naturally” must not be understood in another way either. If it were understood otherwise, the entire argument would totter.

For how could our unity with Christ, if it were not substantial, prove the substantial unity of the Father and Christ? The Arians would instead derive an argument against us from this, asserting that, just as our unity with Christ—which is brought forward to prove the unity of the Father and the Son—is not substantial, so the unity between the Father and the Son ought consequently to be understood in the same way, relying upon the authority of this very man, who says: “Every comparison is assumed as a pattern for understanding, so that we may grasp the matter under discussion according to the proposed example.”

It is therefore established both by the reasoning of the discussion and by the compelling authority of the same man that “naturally” here must be understood as “substantially.”

From this, then, the distinguished disputant constructs a syllogism of the following kind:

If Christ is naturally—that is, substantially—in us, not merely through agreement of will, then the Father is naturally—that is, substantially—in Christ, not merely through agreement of will.

This proposition is accompanied by the assumption, derived from the antecedent, in the following form:

Christ is naturally—that is, substantially—in us, not merely through agreement of will.

He preferred to establish this assumption with remarkable disputative skill by asking a question, as though extracting the answer through interrogation, when he says:

“I now ask those who introduce a unity of will between the Father and the Son whether Christ is in us today through the truth of nature or through agreement of will?”

Then comes the proof of this assumption:

“For if the Word truly became flesh, and if we truly receive the Word made flesh as food from the Lord, how should he not be considered to remain naturally in us? He both assumed, by being born as man, the nature of our flesh, now inseparable from himself, and mingled the nature of his own flesh with the nature of eternity [that is, with what is contained under the sacrament] of the flesh communicated to us.”

The rest of what follows repeats the same point. And as though one might ask, “How do I know that we receive the Word made flesh as food, or that he mingled the nature of his flesh under the sacrament of the flesh communicated to us?” he says:

“No room for doubt has been left concerning the truth of the flesh and blood.”

He then proves why no room for doubt has been left, saying:

“For now, both by the Lord’s own profession and by our faith, it is truly flesh and truly blood.”

How it is truly flesh and truly blood both by the Lord’s profession and by our faith, he had just demonstrated by saying:

“We must not speak of the things of God according to human or worldly understanding, nor must perversity be wrung from heavenly words by a violent and imprudent proclamation of an understanding alien to soundness and impious. Let us read what has been written, understand what we have read, and then we shall perform the duty of perfect faith. For unless we have learned from him, we speak foolishly and impiously about the natural truth of Christ in us. For he himself says: ‘My flesh is truly food, and my blood is truly drink. Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood remains in me, and I in him’ (John 6).”

Here I should like to ask: Who are those who speak about the things of God according to human or worldly understanding? Are they not those who, with their inner lights shut, reason about heavenly mysteries according to the outward senses appropriate to this world? Who, I ask, are those who violently wring an impious understanding from heavenly words? Are they those who read what has been written, as Hilary commands, and understand it simply as they read it, without any addition of their own? Or are they those who torment Scripture, reject what it says, and impose upon it certain figurative meanings according to the inclination of their own hearts?

Certainly, those who understand Scripture simply, as they read it, neither wrench it away nor do violence to it. According to the judgment of blessed Hilary, therefore, those understand the Savior’s words perversely and impiously who, having rejected the simple meaning, transfer them to figures by adding whatever pleases them.

Having therefore proved from these dominical words that “we truly receive the Word made flesh as food from the Lord,” he returns to the assumption of his syllogism and explains how Christ is not merely concordantly but also substantially in us, saying:

“These things, received and drunk, bring it about that we are in Christ and Christ in us. Is this not truth? Let it plainly be untrue for those who deny that Christ Jesus is truly God.”

Everything else that is brought forward up to the conclusion refers to this same point. Then he confidently approaches the conclusion, repeating the assumption together with its proof in a very brief and skillful manner:

“If, therefore, we live naturally according to the flesh through him—that is, having obtained the nature of his flesh—how could he not naturally have the Father in himself according to the spirit, since he lives through the Father?”

Let our shadow-dwellers, then, escape this syllogism of blessed Hilary, if they can. Observe, O shadow-dwellers, that through the food he has received he proves Christ to be substantially in us. When, therefore, we receive this food, we receive the substance of Christ.

For just as it is proved by our receiving the Word made flesh as food from the Lord that Christ is substantially in us, how can this food contain merely the shadow of Christ and not the substance of Christ? Or how can these things, received and drunk, bring it about that Christ becomes substantial in us if they themselves contain nothing but a shadow? How, I ask, if we receive the Word made flesh as food, does it follow that Christ remains substantially in us? What necessity is there in this proof? What logical consequence?

There is no necessity and no consequence that, wherever there is the figure of something, the substance of that same thing must consequently be present. If I were to say to anyone, “Your substance is in this wall because your image is there,” would he not say that I was insane? Nor would anyone at all say, when the legal lamb was eaten, that the substance of Christ was consequently present there, since that lamb was a shadow and figure of Christ.

Who, moreover, would dare to say, when Moses hung the bronze serpent in the desert (Numbers 21), that he hung Christ’s substance there, when that bronze serpent figured Christ’s substance being hung upon the wood? (John 3.)
