Accordingly, if Hilary’s assumption—that Christ is substantially in us—is shown to be established by the fact that we receive the flesh and blood of Christ as food from the Lord, and if these things, received and drunk, bring it about that Christ is in us and that we are naturally one in Christ, having obtained the nature of his flesh, while, as we have shown, that assumption cannot be proved by this unless the food of the Lord truly contains the substance of Christ’s body and blood, it is evident that the most prudent reasoner Hilary, who wished to confirm his assumption by this argument, believed that we receive the substance of the Lord’s body and blood in the food of the Lord—not merely a shadow and figure, as these shadow-dwellers foolishly dream.

To place the force of the entire discussion as briefly as possible before our eyes: blessed Hilary either believed that we eat the Word made flesh in a shadowy manner or substantially. But if he had believed that we eat it in a shadowy manner, that distinguished disputant would never have brought this forward to prove that Christ is substantially in us, since it would have benefited nothing except his opponents. Nor could what he intended in any way be established from it; rather, both he and anyone moderately educated could easily see from it the opposite conclusion, namely, that Christ is not substantially in us.

Since, therefore, this most learned man brought it forward to prove his assumption, he did not believe that we eat the nature of Christ’s flesh in a shadowy manner. He therefore believed that we eat it substantially.

Blessed Augustine mentions this book of the holy Hilary in his own book *On the Trinity* with great veneration. It is therefore plain that he did not judge this argument reprehensible. It is consequently also plain that he held the same faith. Let the disputation of the most blessed and learned Hilary therefore prevail among all the faithful, and let the utterly foolish chatter of the shadow-dwellers fall completely silent.

[Col. 1479A] They are refuted reasonably not only by the authorities mentioned above, but also by many most evident miracles. If they do not accept miracles, they declare themselves enemies of the Church. For the Church was both spread abroad and strengthened especially by miracles. What, after all, is it to invalidate miracles except, so far as lies in one’s power, to remove the Church? For by the same arts, as someone has said, by which an empire is acquired, it is maintained. Therefore, if they refuse to accept its miracles, they show themselves to be enemies of the Church, not its children. And what is more foolish or more senseless than to nullify miracles, when absolutely nothing occurs without a miracle? Would that these babblers, while they shamelessly boast such things, believed that they themselves say nothing at all, since the very fact that they can speak, indeed the very fact that they exist at all, is only through a divine miracle!

But there are those who reply that they do not indeed reject miracles, but maintain that the books in which they are read are apocryphal. O unjust license! Books which the Church of God has read throughout the world for so many ages, under so many doctors, for her edification, and has handed down to be read—these a few less learned and carnal men call apocryphal, with no consideration of reason, merely because they do not please them. Those who gladly embrace pagan histories labor to invalidate Christian histories, which the whole world embraces. Yet, by the very fact that what pleased the universal Church does not please them, and that they obstinately reject what she willingly received, they show themselves not her peaceable sons but manifest enemies. Therefore, let those who wish to be called sons of the Church not reject the books which she receives. On what ground could any Christian call apocryphal the Life of blessed Gregory, which, Rome testifying, was published there, and which so many most holy and learned Roman pontiffs, without a dissentient, have approved until now, and which so many Churches, following their authority, have received up to the present with the agreement of the whole Christian people?

In that same Life it is written that the most blessed Pope Gregory himself, in the presence of the Roman people, withdrew a portion of the Lord’s body from a certain matron when she laughed as she was about to communicate. Having placed it on the altar and immediately poured out a common prayer to God, he showed it before all the people, in the appearance of true flesh, like the little finger, to instruct the matron’s faith, and also that of the people, concerning the truth of the Lord’s flesh. When the woman, now more believing, trembled to communicate because of her horror of the flesh, the pope, as all again suppliantly implored the Lord’s mercy for her, offered her the same particle in its customary appearance of bread.

I also briefly recall that miracle which is read in the Lives of the Fathers, although Berengar hates it, because, with the Lord’s help, it will benefit others. Abbot Daniel relates that a certain old man had innocently fallen into error concerning the Lord’s body. When he had earnestly entreated the Lord with many prayers to remove this doubt, he saw, at the hour of sacrifice, an angel of God upon the altar immolating a child and, as he approached communion, offering him a portion of that child. But, being exceedingly terrified, he hesitated to receive it; then, strengthened in faith, he obtained, with many tears, the appearance of bread.

But who ought not to be moved to admiration and praise of divine goodness by the deeds of our great Father Basil? A Jew, concealed among a large gathering of people, saw a little child being divided in Basil’s hands at the time of sacrifice; he cried out and was therefore baptized. Many other such events, both of our own time and of antiquity, can be related, but I refrain from them. For it is enough briefly to remind Catholics of miracles; perhaps it profits nothing to pursue heretics with a lengthy narration of such things. For with presumptuous speech they tear apart the acts of the holy Fathers, and do not love what has been written or said about them, since they do not know themselves to resemble them in faith.

[Col. 1480B] But what wonder if Berengar and his followers despise the histories of the Fathers when they even contradict the Gospel, saying that one must in no way believe what is there written, that the Lord Jesus entered to the disciples when the doors were shut (John 20)? Yet it is useful for me to have related these things against them, because, whatever they may babble outwardly, their conscience, returning to itself, is shaken and withers. And when we consider how favorably the world everywhere has received these things for so long a time, what the Catholic faith has hitherto been concerning the Lord’s body cannot remain hidden. For if the most learned and holy pontiffs of so long a period, learned and devout abbots, monks, clerics, and the whole people of God had known these things to be contrary to the right faith, why did they not condemn them? Why did they not destroy them? Why did they not at least forbid them to be read? Yet they themselves read them, loved them, and handed them down to be read to this day for the edification of faith. All were heard to favor them; no one was heard or read to have opposed them. Therefore they did not judge them contrary to the right faith. Accordingly, they all held the same faith concerning the Lord’s body. Let our shadow-dwellers, then, either agree with all these persons, corrected by them, or recognize that all of them are irrefragable witnesses to be condemned against themselves. Therefore, their folly, having no further refuge of reason and being overwhelmed by so great a cloud of witnesses, must be wholly silent. Let shadowy impiety, I say, be perpetually shut up in silence where Catholic truth is plainly manifest, while so many foremost witnesses cry out with so clear a voice.

For who could hesitate to call utterly foolish and impious those who are not ashamed, by misinterpreting Holy Scripture at their pleasure, to corrupt it; who count so many venerable and most learned authors as nothing; who now disturb the Church in a matter in which she is known to have had peace with her most savage enemies, the Arians; and who irrationally seek now to invalidate that by which she could fortify herself against those same Arians through the mouth of her Hilary, as by a most certain argument, to the supreme ruin of all Christians? Thus far these things have been said against the shadow-dwellers.

We must now reason against those who, defeated by the Church’s arguments, can no longer deny that the substance of Christ’s body is present in the Lord’s food, but do not at all believe that bread and wine are changed into his flesh and blood by the Savior’s words. Instead, they mingle Christ with bread and wine and thus, as if by a subtler reasoning, have devised another heresy. I call them others, as though held by another error; otherwise they are the same. For at first, wherever and as much as they can, they contend that nothing of the Lord’s body and blood is substantially present in the sacraments; but, driven from that position, they prefer to flee, as we have said, to this impiety rather than humbly to hold the sincere truth with other people.

[Col. 1481A] They offer this cause for their madness: “So that,” they say, “Christ’s flesh may be eaten and his blood drunk by means of bread and wine.” But to what end is that cause alleged? Why can the Lord’s flesh not be eaten and his blood drunk by itself, without the assistance of another body? If they fear the horror of flesh and blood, why does the Church’s answer, given generally through Saint Ambrose in the book *On the Sacraments*, not suffice: that the substances of things are indeed changed, but, because of horror, the former taste, color, and certain other accidents pertaining only to the senses are retained? But if they answer that it cannot happen for the color and taste of one body to be retained in another body, we may briefly set divine power before them. If they concede this, let them end the question. But if they detract from it, let them hear what is written: “Whatever the Lord willed, he did in heaven and on earth” (Psalm 113), besides the many other things with which, at the beginning of this little work, we answered their blasphemies sufficiently and abundantly.

Yet, that the matter may be clear also by examples, let them deign to attend to what is read concerning manna: at the will of the eater, the taste of any foods whatsoever was immediately altered in it. Therefore, to pass over the causes of the higher mystery and the deeper wisdom of the divine counsel (Wisdom 6), insofar as it is granted to my smallness to know them: as there provision was made for the pleasure of carnal men, so here provision is made for the need of the weak; and he who then removed disgust by changing the flavor for many bodies now removes horror by retaining the flavor of one body. Nor is the explanation difficult concerning color and other such accidents, since the Lord himself is read to have shown himself to the disciples in different appearances: at one time displaying his customary color, at another shining transfigured like the sun and snow (Matthew 17), at another presenting himself as a traveler (Luke 24), at another appearing as a gardener (John 20), sometimes exhibiting the appearance of one serving, sometimes assuming the form of one teaching.

But if they flee to those reasons which they are accustomed often to have upon their lips—namely, that it is wrong for Christ to be ground by teeth, wrong for him to be diminished by teeth—we have, I think, sufficiently disposed of these at the beginning of this work. For he who, after the resurrection, as was said, could be touched by hands and lips can also be touched by teeth. Moreover, we denied that the Eucharist is diminished in eating—if indeed it does not please Christ that his body should be divided without some detriment to himself, after the example of voice and soul, which can be wholly in different places—although it appears to happen so, for the sake of the most high mystery, by which so great a matter might be concealed from unbelievers and a useful exercise supplied to believers.

[Col. 1482A] And since they cannot deny that, when a thousand Masses are celebrated at one time in widely differing places, the Lord’s body seems divided because of the different places and yet is not divided at all—for, since it is whole in each Mass, it is not thereby no longer one—why can they not likewise concede that it is perceived as though divided in one mouth, for the exercise of faith, yet suffers no division? Most vainly, then, do they fear this supposed wrong, namely touching the Lord’s body with teeth or diminishing it: the body itself is touchable, and, if it can no longer be divided without detriment to itself, it can appear diminished in this sacrament while remaining indivisible. Therefore, since these causes also have no force, and they offer no others, what madness is it that by their own authority, so to speak, they make Christ breaded (*impanent*) and wined (*invinent*)?

There was reason for Christ’s incarnation for human redemption: the prophets foretold that it would occur, Christ showed that it had occurred, the apostles preached it, and the world believed it. But no reason, as we have shown, requires Christ to be made breaded or wined; the prophets did not foretell it, Christ did not show it, the apostles did not preach it, and the world, except for these very few heretics, did not believe it.

[Col. 1482C] Whence, then, did evil error persuade them of these things? The whole world agrees that, as a rational soul and flesh are one human being, so God and man are one Christ. No one dares say that God and man, bread and wine, are one Christ. Whence, then, comes this new comparison for these people? Why did the Apostle not terrify them when he said: “If anyone should proclaim to you anything besides what we proclaimed to you, let him be anathema” (Galatians 1)? For these men proclaim a Christ made breaded and wined, but the apostles did not proclaim such a Christ. Therefore, by apostolic authority, they incur anathema.

Blessed Ambrose, in the book *On the Sacraments* (*On Initiating into the Mysteries*, ch. 9), discussing these matters at length, taught not that the Lord’s body and blood lie hidden in bread and wine, but that bread and wine are changed into the Lord’s body and blood, saying thus: “If, therefore, there is such power in the word of the Lord Jesus that things which did not exist began to exist, how much more efficacious is it that things which were should exist and be changed into something else?” You hear, therefore, that “they are changed into something else.” Note this carefully, because he did not say “that they should be what they were,” but “that the things which were should exist,” he says, “but be other than what they were.” This seems to be his meaning when he adds, “and be changed into something else,” as if explaining his comparison thus: if the word of the Lord Jesus effected that things which did not exist should begin to exist—that is, that things should exist from not existing, that is, from nothing—how much more efficacious is it that things which were should exist, that is, that these things, namely body and blood, should exist from the things which were, not from nothing? For otherwise this comparison cannot rightly be understood.

The things which were, that is, bread and wine, do exist; but they are not what they were, but have been changed into something else. And this is what he says, “that the things which were should exist”: they should exist in such a way that they are not in themselves but are changed into something else. The same doctor shows this meaning most plainly in the same book, saying: “How many examples do we use to prove that this is not what nature formed, but what blessing consecrated, and that the power of blessing is greater than that of nature, because by blessing even nature itself is changed.” If, therefore, they are not what nature formed, they are not what they were—that is, they are not bread and wine.

[Col. 1483A] From the preceding statement, therefore, and from this one, it is clearly shown that the things which were do exist: that is, the body and blood of Christ are not made here from nothing, but from the things which were. Yet they are not what they were, because they are not what nature formed—that is, they are not bread and wine—but are changed into something else and are what blessing consecrated, namely body and blood, because, he says, nature itself is changed by blessing.

And attend further to the doctor of truth (Ambrose, ibid.): “But if, he says, the word of Elijah had such power as to bring down fire from heaven (3 Kings 18), will not Christ’s word have power to change the appearances of the elements? You have read concerning the works of the whole world: ‘For he spoke, and they were made; he commanded, and they were created’ (Psalm 32). Therefore, can the word of Christ, which was able to make from nothing that which did not exist, not change the things which are into that which they were not? For it is no lesser thing to give new natures to things than to change their natures.” Likewise (*On the Sacraments*, book IV, ch. 5): “This bread is bread before the words of the sacraments; when consecration has been added, from bread the body of Christ comes to be.” And again: “Before it is consecrated, it is bread; but when Christ’s words have been added, it is Christ’s body. Finally, hear him saying: ‘Take and eat of it, all of you; for this is my body.’ And before Christ’s words the chalice is full of wine and water; when Christ’s words have worked, there the blood is made which redeemed the people. Learn, therefore, in how many ways Christ’s word is powerful to change all things. Then the Lord Jesus himself testifies to us that we receive his body and blood. Must we doubt his faithfulness and testimony?” Thus blessed Ambrose.

[Col. 1483D] But Saint Eusebius of Emesa says: “The one and perfect sacrifice is to be esteemed by faith, not judged by appearance or assessed by outward sight, but by inward disposition. Hence heavenly authority confirms it: ‘For my flesh is truly food, and my blood is truly drink’ (John 6). Let every uncertainty of unbelief therefore depart, since he who is the author of the gift is himself also the witness to the truth. For the invisible priest, by his word and by a secret exercise of power, changes visible creatures into the substance of his body and blood, saying: ‘Take and eat; for this is my body.’ And, repeating the sanctification: ‘Take and drink; this is my blood.’ Thus, just as at the command of the Lord who ordered it, the heights of the heavens, the depths of the waves, and the vast expanses of the earth suddenly came into being from nothing, so with equal power in spiritual sacraments, wherever power commands, the effect serves the thing commanded.

“And so that it should not seem new or impossible that earthly and mortal things are changed into the substance of Christ, consider yourself, who have now been reborn in Christ, and the rest.”

Behold how, in very few words, this most holy Father and eminent teacher refutes both heresies. For he destroys the impanators by saying that Christ is by no means hidden in bread and wine, but that visible creatures—that is, bread and wine—are changed into the substance of Christ’s body and blood, and again that earthly and mortal things are changed into Christ’s substance. He likewise disperses the “shadowists” by affirming that these things are changed not into just any creature, but into the substance of Christ’s body and blood.

Again he says—and let no one doubt it—that the primary creatures can, at the nod of power and through the presence of majesty, pass into the nature of the Lord’s body. And again: “When creatures to be blessed with heavenly words are placed upon the sacred altars, before they are consecrated by the invocation of the supreme name, there is the substance of bread and wine; but after Christ’s words, it is Christ’s body and blood. What is remarkable, then, if what he was able to create by his word he is able by his word to change after it has been created? Indeed, it seems a lesser miracle if what he is acknowledged to have made from nothing he can now change, once made, into something better.”

What could be clearer? What more explicit? These things are not held by the common people, for no one has ever been able to say anything more manifest. In a certain Spanish missal [Col. 1484C], which they say Saint Isidore dictated, I found the following in a Mass during the week before Easter:

“All this, Lord, is divine; all of it, Father, is from heaven: changed into the nature of your Son, it is both body and blood. No longer a figure, but the truth; not a mortal creature, but a heavenly nature, granting eternal life to those who eat and an everlasting kingdom to those who drink.”

The Lord Jesus himself destroys these impanators by the word of his mouth when, taking bread, giving thanks, and blessing it, he says: “This is my body.” He does not say, “In this my body is hidden.” Nor does he say, “In this wine is my blood”; rather, he says: “This is my blood.”

Therefore the Church of God rightly separates the same people from herself when, in the very canon of the Mass, she prays according to apostolic tradition:

“Which offering, O God, we ask you to be pleased to make blessed, accredited, ratified, reasonable, and acceptable in every respect, so that it may become for us the body and blood of your most beloved Son, our Lord Jesus Christ.” [Col. 1484D]

Here the prayer is not that the body and blood should be hidden in it, or that the body and blood should come into it, but that the offering itself should become both body and blood. By this prayer Cyprian, Hilary, Ambrose, Augustine, Jerome, Gregory, and all the other ecclesiastical authorities strike down these men with one voice; and all who celebrate Mass and wholeheartedly assent to this prayer do likewise.

As for me, repeatedly reconsidering this doctrine of “impanation,” I cannot adequately express in words how much I marvel at and am indignant over the utterly foolish audacity and insane presumption of these men. For to proceed against divine authorities by human reasoning is madness; to proceed without reason is far greater madness. But to bark continually against God both without reason and contrary to reason is altogether more insane than can be expressed.

These men, worse than the worst, have justified their “shadowist” brethren in comparison with themselves. The latter, unable to rise above the judgment of the senses, may seem to have erred through weakness. But the former, deriving the causes of their error neither from the senses, nor from any reasoning, nor from any Scripture, appear to rave through sheer pride. Nature itself protests against them—the nature they defend with such insistence—for it is impossible to see how another body can be hidden within the solid body of bread. Nature, I say, protests; the sacred Scriptures protest; and they are supported by no testimony of the holy Fathers, no divine oracle, and no miracle. Yet, bestially obstinate, they seem to attack Catholic piety, fortified on every side, for this one reason: lest they appear to have been defeated by it.

O unhappy men whom piety does not conquer! O most unhappy men who, while refusing to submit to piety, are not ashamed to be slaves of impiety! It would seem beneath dignity to answer their plainly evident folly, were it not that, to complete their destruction, their own death does not suffice them, unless they also go about destroying as many others as they can by the basest falsehood.

This, then, is specifically against them. Thereafter, with God’s help, the discussion that follows will strike both of the aforementioned heretics together. Above all, the very division of their heresies should have been sufficient to expose their falsehood: now they contend that nothing of Christ’s flesh and blood is present in God’s sacraments except a shadow and figure; now they contend that the substance of Christ’s flesh and blood lies hidden in them. For the apostolic faith, which alone is the true faith, is not divided between affirmation and denial. The Apostle said: “One Lord, one faith, one baptism” (Ephesians 4). The apostolic faith, therefore, is one alone.

But the empty belief of these men, since what it holds in one false opinion it is shown not to hold in the other, is split between affirmation and denial and therefore is not one. Their belief, then, is not the apostolic faith and consequently is not the true faith. Since they do not possess the apostolic faith, they are also separated from the apostolic Church, and what the Savior says will happen to them: “Every kingdom divided against itself will be laid waste” (Luke 11).

The Berengarians are divided against themselves, as we have shown. But perhaps someone will say: “They are not a kingdom, because they are few.” To this I reply: If they are not a kingdom, they are not the Church of Christ. For the Church of Christ is the kingdom of God, in which God—that is, Christ himself—reigns. But if they are a kingdom, then, because Truth cannot lie, since they are divided against themselves they will be laid waste.

The Prophet foretold of the Catholic Church: “Mount Zion is founded in the joy of the whole earth” (Psalm 47). We see this fulfilled in our Church. But the Berengarian faction is not founded in the joy of the whole earth; indeed, they have not been granted even one little city, or even one little village. They are not, therefore, Mount Zion—that is, the Church.

The same Prophet also says: “Sing to the Lord a new song; sing to the Lord, all the earth” (Psalm 95). Hence blessed Augustine, in his exposition of this verse, dares to say: “If the whole earth is the house of God, whoever does not adhere to the whole earth is a ruin, not a house.” If the Berengarians do not adhere to the whole earth, they are therefore not the house of God, but a ruin.

Isaiah says of the Church of Christ: “Rejoice, barren woman who do not bear; break forth and cry aloud, you who have not been in labor, because the children of the deserted woman are more numerous than those of her who has a husband” (Isaiah 54). The Apostle teaches that she who then had a husband is to be understood as the synagogue of the Jews (Galatians 4), and the barren woman as the Church. Therefore, if the Berengarians are the Church of God, let them show us that their children, after so long a time, are far more numerous than the Jews. The fact that this is not so is evident to everyone.

Again Isaiah says of the Church: “Kings will be your foster fathers” (Isaiah 49). And John says in the Apocalypse: “The kings of the earth will bring their glory into it” (Revelation 21). But which king of the earth has fostered this Berengarian folly? Which king of the earth has brought his glory into it? Some kings once accepted the Arian madness; but no king has accepted the Berengarian madness.

Through Malachi God said: “From the rising of the sun to its setting, my name is great among the nations, and in every place sacrifice is made and a pure offering is offered to my name, because my name is great among the nations, says the Lord of hosts” (Malachi 1). Therefore, if the Lord of hosts calls the offering that is sacrificed and offered to his name in every place, from the rising of the sun to its setting, pure—and since no offering can be pure apart from this one—let Berengar and his followers consider how impure their offering is, which has scarcely obtained a place anywhere, let alone everywhere.

When the prophet Daniel saw the stone cut from the mountain without hands, which struck and shattered the statue at its feet of iron and clay, he interpreted the vision in this way: the four principal kingdoms of the world—namely, the kingdoms of the Chaldeans, Medes, Persians, Greeks, and Romans—were to be struck and shattered by the kingdom of God, which is the Church, during the days of the fourth empire, that is, the Roman Empire, before it ceased to be iron. This is made clear when the same prophet later explains it, saying:

“But in the days of those kingdoms the God of heaven will raise up a kingdom that will never be destroyed, and his kingdom will not be handed over to another people. It will crush and consume all those kingdoms, and it itself will stand forever, according to what you saw: that the stone was cut from the mountain without hands and shattered the iron, clay, bronze, silver, and gold” (Daniel 2). [Col. 1486D]

We see this concerning our Church with the clearest possible evidence. For when the Roman Empire was still iron, she crushed it and the other kingdoms. Even today, as no one can deny, she occupies the house of the Savior in the very house that once belonged to the Roman emperor.

From there, through the blessed Pope Leo (Leo IX), she condemned these Berengarian fabrications soon after their emergence. Then, through the very man who now presides—Lord Pope Gregory (Gregory VII), at that time archdeacon of the Roman See—she convicted Berengar at the Council of Tours and mercifully received Berengar himself, apparently corrected and making satisfaction by an oath sworn with his own hand.

When he returned not long afterward to his vomit, he was again refuted at Rome in a general council through Pope Nicholas of holy memory. Before that venerable assembly of the whole world, Nicholas compelled the same Berengar to swear to the definite words written above and found in many churches, to renounce these insanities with his own mouth, and to burn with his own hands the booklets he had composed in defense of those blasphemies.

It cannot be shown that the Berengarian rabble ever possessed, at any time, not merely the four principal kingdoms, but even one kingdom alone. Or, if it is falsely claimed that they possessed one, their kingdom has now been handed over to another people—that is, to our Catholic people. For our people hold the Roman Empire, together with all kingdoms subject to the Christian name.

Daniel says that the kingdom of God’s people will not be handed over to another people, but will itself stand forever (Daniel 2). The Berengarians, therefore, are not that kingdom which the God of heaven is foretold to raise up. And if they do not belong to the kingdom of the God of heaven, it follows that they belong to the kingdom of the devil.

You see clearly how our Church is confirmed by the prophetic testimonies that resound on every side, while both Berengarian factions are rejected. Concerning these testimonies, blessed Augustine says in the final book of *The City of God* (chapter 25), against certain philosophers:

“If they say that these things must be believed in another way, lest, by saying that what was written is false, they do injury to that God to whom they bear such great witness, they inflict upon him an injury altogether as great, or even greater, if they say that these things must be understood otherwise, not as the world believed—the world whose future faith he himself praised, promised, and fulfilled. Therefore, since they do not believe that he can lie, let them believe that he will do what he promised he would do; and let them believe as the world believed, the world whose future faith he foretold, praised, and promised, and whose faith he has already shown.”

Therefore, if blessed Augustine is as clear to you Berengarians as he usually is, follow his judgment. Believe concerning the body and blood of the Lord what the world believes, and believe as the world believed. For if you believe something else, or believe the same thing in another way, your Augustine tells you that you inflict a grave injury upon God, because you believe concerning Christ otherwise than the world believed—the world whose future faith God foretold, praised, promised, and demonstrated. And if God praised the faith of the world, he surely rejected your fabrications. For there is only one faith that is praiseworthy before God.

Thus what the same blessed Augustine says in the final book of *The City of God* (chapter 5) will rightly befall you:

“If they believed a credible thing, let those who do not believe see how foolish they are. But if the thing is incredible, how has it already been believed throughout the whole world?”

Accordingly, by the judgment of blessed Augustine, you are foolish, since you refuse to believe concerning Christ’s body what is believed throughout the whole world.

Again blessed Augustine says in the fourth book of *On Baptism Against the Donatists* (chapter 6): “What the universal Church holds, and was not instituted by councils but has always been retained, is rightly believed to have been handed down only by apostolic authority.”

And in the seventh book of the same work (chapter 53): “We can assert with the confidence of a secure voice that what has been strengthened by the agreement of the universal Church is so under the governance of the Lord our God and Savior Jesus Christ.”

Therefore, the faith concerning the Lord’s body and blood, which the whole Church has always held and has further strengthened through many general councils, is rightly believed to have been handed down from apostolic authority. For if what the Church has always held, though fortified by no councils, is apostolic, how much more must we believe that what it has both always held and, as I have said, confirmed through many general councils was handed down from apostolic authority.

But the substantial change of the bread and wine of the Lord’s altar into Christ’s body and blood—not, as Berengar raves, that they are merely figures and shadows of the Lord’s body and blood, or that they conceal Christ hidden within them—has been strengthened by the agreement of the universal Church. Therefore, under the guidance of the Lord our God and Savior Jesus Christ, this may be asserted by us with a confident voice.

If opportunity were given, I would gladly discuss this carefully with Berengar himself. He teaches some people that nothing but a shadow and figure of Christ’s body and blood is present in the food of the Lord’s altar, while to others, as though satisfying those who inquire more subtly, he answers that Christ’s body itself is there, but lies hidden in bread. What, then, displeases him in the former opinion, so that, in order to satisfy his questioners, he crosses over to the latter? Or what does he reject in the latter, so that he returns to the former? By moving to the second, he rejects the first; by returning to the first, he condemns the second. Thus, by defending both, he holds neither. Since he hates all the remaining opinions, it follows that he knows absolutely nothing about what he ought to believe concerning these sacraments of the Lord.

From this also arises what we know with certainty: when Berengar and his followers are questioned about their faith by learned Catholics, they either deny in terror what they hold concerning the Lord’s body, or, if they profess it, cannot defend it.

But the deniers of the true faith concerning Christ are met by that terrible sentence of Christ in which he said: “Whoever is ashamed of me and of my words, of him the Son of Man will be ashamed” (Luke 9). And Paul says: “If we deny him, he also will deny us” (2 Timothy 2).

But if they profess the faith and cannot defend it, then—if indeed they are defenders of the true faith—where is what Christ promised his own when he said: “I will give you a mouth and wisdom, which all your adversaries will not be able to resist or contradict” (Luke 21)? If these men were defending the true faith, there would be at least one among them whom all adversaries could not resist. Truth cannot lie, for it made this promise to its own.

Yet none of these men can be found whom our Catholics cannot resist—so completely that the heresiarch Berengar, repeatedly defeated, is held to have renounced these insanities by an oath sworn with his own hand at general councils. It is therefore clear that they are not defenders of the true faith, nor her sons, but adversaries of the Church of Christ.

Moreover, if these men are the Church of Christ, then either the Church did not begin with Christ, or at some later time ceased to exist. For it is well known that, before Berengar went mad, such insanities had never existed. Yet from the time of Christ the Church existed in the apostles and the disciples of the apostles, nor did it ever afterward fail.

Otherwise Scripture would be lying when it cries out through the prophets: “And of his kingdom there will be no end” (Luke 1). The archangel Gabriel would be lying when he said the same thing to blessed Mary. Truth itself would also be lying when it says: “Behold, I am with you always, to the consummation of the age” (Matthew 28). But far be it from us to suppose that Truth could lie, either in its own words or through so many witnesses.

The Church of Christ, therefore, never ceased to exist after Christ. These men are not the Church of Christ—or, if they shamelessly claim that they began from Christ and have persevered to this day, let them show, in accordance with Daniel’s prophecy, that they crushed the four principal kingdoms of the world; let them show that they filled the whole world; let them show that their kingdom was not handed over to another people.

That they cannot do is abundantly clear to everyone, since our people possess the kingdoms of the world and crush these very men by authority and reason. Therefore, let our Church, founded by Christ—not by Berengar, nor begun at Tours or Angers—endure forever from Jerusalem, as Christ commanded and the prophets foretold; and let the insane Berengarian faction, which does not belong to the Church of Christ, be silenced in everlasting confusion.

Now let us also examine whether that proposition which we proved so extensively in the first book can accomplish anything. We proved that if God wishes to make the change of bread and wine that we believe in, he does so. It has now also been assumed and sufficiently proved that God does wish to make it. For the Holy Spirit, through the most holy authorities who are known to have been his temple, has clearly taught this, as we have shown. The incontrovertible authority of the Old and New Testaments has confirmed it; the whole world has universally believed it; and God himself has praised the faith of the world alone.

Let us therefore conclude without hesitation what is most evidently and necessarily established: namely, that God changes bread and wine into the substance of Christ’s body and blood.

Therefore let the new, irrational, false, useless, and contemptible inventions of the most foolish men be silent before all prudent people. Let everything yield, I say, to ecclesiastical faith. For that faith is not recent; it does not belong to this or that man, but to the whole world. It alone is shown to be rational, true, valid, fortified on every side and invincible, most useful, necessary, most joyful, and most honorable.

But where is Christ’s “impanation” read of in the Old or New Testament? By what reasoning, arguments, or miracles is it supported? What necessity, usefulness, or honor is there in “impanating” and “invining” Christ our Lord for no reason?

But as for eating only bread and wine in the figure and shadow of Christ, as these men believe, and eating Christ in the very truth of his substance, who—even the most demented person—could compare the two even for a moment, so far as our usefulness, honor, and excellence are concerned?

For while we believe that the Word of God made flesh is received substantively, without “impanation” and “invination,” in the Lord’s food, and not symbolically; while we hope to live forever through the power of the fullness of eternal life that remains in that same food: what could be conceived as truer than this faith, since it is approved by so many and such great testimonies? What could be more rational?

What, I say, could be more useful, more necessary, or more honorable than this faith? Receiving the pure Christ himself—not a shadow, nor one “impanated”—with the purest reception, enriched by the gift of such great glory, let a person, with the utmost reverent fear, shun sins more intensely; with the utmost ardor of desire, burn more fervently for every righteousness; strive with all his strength to flee the world daily as the enemy of his Lord; and, now made more certain by his promises through so great a pledge, long with unveiled face and with more daring and ardent desire to grasp the very fountain of life, God. [Col. 1490C]

We have already said much against these men, and much more could still be said; but, as I think, these things are sufficient for pious minds. What more would they seek against them, since it has been shown clearly enough that their objections, whether based on reasoning or on Scripture, do not harm our faith, but rather that those very Scriptures are more fully on our side; since their insanities, both individually and collectively, have been utterly destroyed by the testimonies of venerable authorities and by prophetic and evangelical witnesses; and since our faith has been shown everywhere to be most firm, useful, excellent, and supremely necessary?

But what will suffice for the impious, if they refuse to yield after being struck by the hammers of so many arguments harder than stone; if, darker than hell, they cannot be illuminated by the light of so many powerful reasons; or if, like prostitutes, they do not know how to blush at their plainly visible shame? Or if, most like demons, they love the madness they once began with such persistence, hate the truth without cause, and never recover from even the most manifest falsehood?

O most wretched men, worthy of mourning with an immeasurable flood of tears, if such a desire to spread their reputation has seized them that neither the clearest truth, nor their own supreme disgrace, nor love of eternal life, nor eternal damnation can recall them from their public blasphemies! “Return, return, transgressors, to your heart” (Isaiah 46). Why will you die for nothing?

This is not a dispute in which the two sides can lightly be balanced against each other. Here the dispute is not, as in the schools, for victory, nor, as in the courts, for any earthly advantage; rather, before God, the dispute concerns eternal and heavenly life. For everlasting death devours the false side, while eternal life crowns the true.

Therefore weigh your position and ours in a just examination. If you have anything worthy against us, bring it forward; if you do not, yield. Why will you die for nothing?

But why should I pursue these men further? An end must now be placed upon this discussion. For a brief treatment must be given to the two remaining propositions; the matter does not require a lengthy disputation.

## Against Those Who Say That One Part Remains Unchanged on Account of the Unworthy

Of these propositions, one confirms that part of the bread and wine is changed into the flesh and blood of the Lord, while another part is retained unchanged on account of the unworthy. The other asserts that all the bread and wine of the altar is changed into the flesh and blood of the Lord, but that when the unworthy come to communion, it changes back again into bread and wine.

The proponents of both positions refuse to admit that the body and blood of the Lord can be received by unworthy people. Although their errors differ, they nevertheless have one cause. They support it with the same arguments, as follows:

“Christ says,” they declare, “‘Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood remains in me, and I in him’ (John 6). But the unworthy do not remain in Christ, nor does Christ remain in them. For they cannot serve two masters (Matthew 6), nor can they be members both of Christ and of the devil. Therefore,” they say, “they do not eat Christ’s flesh or drink his blood.”

They also try to establish this by an example, namely, that in the *Lives of the Fathers* an angel was said to have appeared to a certain old man when unworthy people approached holy communion, taking away the Lord’s body from them and giving them a coal in its place.

“If such people do not receive the Lord’s flesh and blood,” they say, “then what they receive must either not have been changed or have returned to its former nature.” This, then, is their reasoning, which, with the Lord’s help, must now be answered.

As for the example, it must first be observed that it contributes nothing to their case; indeed, it is wholly opposed to their opinion. For if the bread to be offered to the unworthy remains unchanged, what is the meaning of a coal being given to them rather than bread? And if all the unworthy were fed with a coal, while all the worthy received flesh and blood of the Lord, then no part of the bread remained unchanged.

Or if the flesh and blood were changed into a coal when the unworthy approached, then they were not changed into bread and wine, since a coal is neither bread nor wine. Therefore this example, as I said, destroys their opinion more than it supports it.

For our part, the example seems in no way contrary to us. It could have happened before the man’s eyes that the flesh and blood, in the very form in which they were offered to the righteous, were withdrawn from the unrighteous, and that, to display their iniquity, the same things were offered in the form of a coal.

Or certainly, as I already said above, it could have happened not as a permanent rule, but so that, through the old man, the sinners present might be corrected when their iniquity was revealed to him: the flesh and blood could truly have been withdrawn by the angel, while a coal brought from elsewhere was immediately given. Whichever of these two ways it happened, it could have occurred without contradicting our sound faith.

Let us now approach the Lord’s words: “Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood remains in me, and I in him.” In explaining them, we shall set forth not our own interpretation, but that of blessed Augustine from his book *On the Words of the Lord* (sermon 11).

He says that the words must not be understood universally, but with a certain qualification—namely, in this sense: “Whoever eats Christ’s flesh and drinks his blood remains in Christ, and Christ in him.” But the person who eats in this way is the one who eats worthily. For whoever eats and drinks unworthily eats and drinks judgment upon himself (1 Corinthians 11).

Therefore, if everyone who eats and drinks unworthily eats and drinks judgment upon himself, it must be understood that only the one who eats in another way—that is, worthily—remains in Christ, and Christ in him. Compared with this person, the one who eats unworthily ought not even to be considered to be eating, but rather, insofar as it depends on him, to be trampling upon what he receives.

He eats, therefore, and does not eat. He eats bodily, but does not eat spiritually—not in the right sense, not with the right conduct, not with the charity by which he would eat worthily.

The same applies to the Lord’s words: “Whoever sins against the Holy Spirit will not be forgiven, either in this age or in the age to come” (Matthew 12). These words cannot stand unless they refer to a particular kind of sin. Otherwise, everyone who sins against the Son sins against the Holy Spirit. For no one can offend the Son without also offending the Holy Spirit. But the Lord says: “If anyone speaks a word against the Son, it will be forgiven him.” Therefore the one who sins against the Holy Spirit will also be forgiven.

How, then, is this passage to be understood unless a particular kind of sin against the Holy Spirit is understood—one so great that, by comparison with it, other sins are not said to be against the Holy Spirit?

The same applies to the statement: “Whoever believes and is baptized will be saved” (Mark 16), and to this one: “Everyone who calls upon the name of the Lord will be saved” (Joel 2). Not everyone who believes and is baptized, nor everyone who calls upon the name of the Lord, will be saved; only those who believe with good conduct and call upon the Lord’s name worthily will be saved.

Many other statements of this kind are also found in the sacred Scriptures, and they cannot be properly understood unless they are understood with an appropriate qualification.

Thus that statement with which this discussion began must likewise be understood: “Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood”—that is, worthily—“remains in me, and I in him.”

But that the unworthy—those who do not remain in Christ, and in whom Christ does not remain—nevertheless eat the same flesh and drink the same blood, let us hear the same blessed Augustine saying in the fifth book of *On Baptism Against the Donatists*:

“Just as Judas, to whom the Lord handed the morsel, gave a place to the devil in himself, not by receiving something evil, but by receiving it evilly, so whoever receives the Lord’s sacrament unworthily does not make it evil because he himself is evil, nor does he receive nothing because he does not receive it for salvation. For the body and blood of the Lord were nevertheless present even for those to whom the Apostle said: ‘Whoever eats and drinks unworthily eats and drinks judgment upon himself’” (1 Corinthians 11).

This is Augustine.

Therefore, since the worthy eat the same flesh together with the unworthy, though with different dispositions, and drink the same blood of the Lord; and since the evangelical statement—“Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood remains in me, and I in him”—when properly understood, in accordance with the Apostle and blessed Augustine and by analogy with many such statements, contributes nothing to these men; and since the added example of the old man takes everything away from them; and since there is no basis for this supposed lesson and all their arguments fail, let this wholly new invention of Christian men cease, lest, if they teach otherwise, they incur that apostolic anathema which says: “If anyone announces to you anything apart from what you received, let him be accursed” (Galatians 1).

For what if no unworthy person receives the Lord’s body, and for that reason a portion of the bread remains unchanged on account of the unworthy? Since no one dares to call himself worthy—for it is written: “A person does not know whether he is worthy of love or hatred in his life” (Ecclesiastes 9)—and since no one dares to judge another, for it is written: “Do not praise a person during his life; a person sees the face, but God sees the heart” (Ecclesiasticus 11), no one would confidently dare to confess that the body of the Lord is what he himself, or even the whole people, receives.

And if no one would dare to confess this confidently, then the priest rashly asserts, “This is Christ’s body,” and the people rashly respond, “Amen—that is, it is true,” even though they altogether do not know what it is, since no one knows the merits of all people, whether his own or those of others.

But far be it from us to suppose that the religious confession of the whole Church could in any way be blameworthy. Therefore let each person confidently believe and say, even if he admits himself to be unworthy, that what he receives is Christ’s body.

Furthermore, a priest who is often utterly unworthy celebrates Mass, and he alone consumes all that has been consecrated. But if what this utterly unworthy man was about to receive remained unchanged because of him, then, since he was going to consume the whole of it, none of the bread and wine was changed into Christ’s flesh and blood.

If nothing of the bread and wine was changed on account of the unworthy priest, then the priest’s iniquity would have prevailed—God forbid!—over the words of the Lord and Savior. The faith of the Church would also be false, since it believes that the Lord’s words operate equally through good and bad ministers.

But far be it from all the faithful to believe that a human being’s iniquity could weaken the Savior’s words! Far be it from us to believe that the faith of the Church is false—the faith that alone is praiseworthy before God and believes that Christ’s words operate equally through good and bad ministers.

Therefore what the utterly unworthy priest was about to consume did not remain unchanged on his account. Since he consumes all that has been consecrated, the utterly unworthy priest eats and drinks Christ’s flesh and blood.

Since this is so—or rather, since it is truly so—it is useless to say that a portion of the bread and wine remains unchanged on account of the unworthy. Therefore let this kind of human supposition always be silenced, and let us hold only to what is commended to us in the canon of the Mass.

For it is written there:

“Which offering, O God, we ask you to be pleased to make blessed, accredited, ratified, reasonable, and acceptable in every respect, so that it may become for us the body and blood of your most beloved Son.”

It does not say that a part of it should become the body and blood. Nor did our Lord Jesus Christ, when he said, “Eat from this, all of you,” add: “For a part of it is my body”; he said only: “For this is my body.”

The last point, indeed, would make anyone even moderately educated shudder at hearing it alone: namely, that the flesh and blood of the Lord should, on account of the unworthy, return into bread and wine. For the flesh and blood of the Lord are incorruptible. But what is incorruptible neither is corrupted nor can be corrupted. To lose its own essence and return into corruptible bread and corruptible wine would certainly be a great corruption. Therefore the flesh and blood of the Lord can no longer return into bread and wine. Accordingly, let this error also be buried in eternal silence.

Let both of these men beware of bringing strange fire near the divine altars (Lev. X), lest they die before the Lord. Let them also beware of transgressing the boundaries of their fathers, which they have set for themselves (Prov. XXII): “There are many kinds of food,” as Solomon says, “in the fallow fields of the fathers; others are gathered without judgment” (Prov. XIII). Such foods of doctrine, however, cannot be found in the fallow fields of the fathers. Therefore they are gathered without judgment.

**ROGERIUS.**

As far as I am able to judge, I see that you have pursued everything with the firmest reasoning.

**GUITMUNDUS.**

To show briefly, then, what the whole of our discussion has accomplished: truth does not permit our sacrifice to be merely a shadow or figure of Christ’s flesh and blood, nor to conceal Christ within itself as bread, according to Berengarius; nor does truth permit the substance of the bread and wine to be changed in part while remaining unchanged in part; nor, after the change, is it any longer lawful for it to return to what it had been or to be changed into something else.

It remains, therefore, that this alone, God helping us, is the pure and solid faith: that all that bread and all that wine of the Lord’s altar are so substantially changed through divine consecration into the flesh and blood of Christ that thereafter they can eternally be nothing at all other than the flesh and blood of our Lord and Savior God, Jesus Christ. For such great love let us render eternal thanks to him, who reigns with God the Father and the Holy Spirit, through infinite ages of ages. Amen.

[Col. 1495]

# CONFESSION OF GUITMUND, ARCHBISHOP OF AVERSA

Concerning the Holy Trinity, Christ’s humanity, and the truth of the body and blood of our Lord.

*(Bibliotheca Patrum XVIII, 465.)*

[Col. 1495A] Whenever we wish to think about God, we certainly wish less than we ought; yet we are not capable of as much as we wish—how much less, then, of as much as we ought? If the thought within the human mind cannot discover how to discharge its obligation, what does the outward speech of the mouth pay in full?

Yet, most beloved brother Robert, although our Father does not recognize his Word in our heart as he ought, let us nevertheless, like little children at the breast, or by babbling, show him our devotion. Since it is written, “With the heart one believes unto righteousness, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation” (Rom. X), it is altogether clear that, although the right faith that justifies is held in the heart, confession by the mouth, which saves us, is nevertheless absolutely necessary.

But what will that man say about God who has so far thought something distorted—or perhaps nothing at all—about him? The former is sacrilege deserving eternal condemnation; the latter, if the person in question already uses reason, is evidence of a deadly sleep. Let the heart of a Christian therefore remain vigilant in its contemplation of faith, so that, if necessary, it may know how to open its mouth in confession.

We have briefly previewed these matters in order to demonstrate how necessary knowledge and confession of the faith are, and so that, with the Lord’s help, we might approach the treatment of that same faith with greater freedom.

## On the Unity and Trinity of the Most Holy Divinity

I believe in the eternal Unity of the most holy Divinity; I believe in the coeternal Trinity within that same Unity. For the Creator of all things is one God, yet triune, because he is Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.

[Col. 1495C] I do not say that the very same one is Father, Son, and Holy Spirit; rather, I say that the very same thing is Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. When I say “he himself” (*ipse*), I indicate the person who is Father, Son, or Holy Spirit; but when I say “the same thing” (*ipsum*), I indicate the substance that is God. Thus, in each one, another person is believed; but in the three, only one substance is believed.

Let us now take an example among ourselves by which we may be able, to some small degree, to rise above ourselves. We see a man begetting a son; we see him being the father of a son. If you therefore ask me what that father who begot the son is, I answer: a man. If you ask what the son is, I answer: a man. When I said “man,” I indicated the substance of the father and the son.

[Col. 1496A] You see, therefore, that the substance of the human father and of the human son is the same. For if it were said, “The father is a man, and the son is a horse,” who could think of anything other than a monster or something dreadful? As soon as you heard me speak of different substances in the father and the son, you would not doubt that I was joking or, rather, insane, instead of speaking the truth.

But if you ask again who that person is, I say, “He is that man’s father.” If you ask about the son—who is that person?—I say, “He is that man’s son.” You see, dearest one, that I have assigned different names to the persons, namely “father” and “son,” but in the substance I have indicated one name, namely “man.”

What you see in a human being you can see in many creatures. If, therefore, among creatures there are several persons in one substance, and one substance in several persons, nature requires this—and God brings it about—how much more must it be so in God, who created all things?

Are we then equating the creature with the Creator? Far from it! For although, speaking of creatures, I say of the father that he is a man and of the son that he is a man, and thus the substance of the father and son is one, I say again that a human father and a human son are two human beings.

With God, however, the matter is very different. For I say of the Father that he is God, and of the Son that he is God, and of the Holy Spirit that he is God, yet no one is permitted to believe that there are three gods.

Now, with the consent of him of whom we are speaking, let us speak somewhat more openly about this same Trinity. Let us consider created things and, while admiring the Creator in his creatures, praise him. We see heaven, earth, the sea, and the things that are in them; and we retain in our hearts and confess with our mouths that one God created all these things.

[Col. 1496C] His wholly ineffable wisdom created these things, so great, so numerous, and so marvelous. He himself did not make or create that wisdom, but begot it. For just as we see in our soul that it begets its own counsel, and that this counsel is, as it were, the offspring of the soul which it possesses within itself and through which it works all outward things, so God—in a manner befitting God—begot his Wisdom from himself, through which all things that exist were made by him and are ordered.

This, then, is the Wisdom of God, the Son, begotten God from God. Of him it is said to God the Father: “You have made all things in wisdom” (Ps. CIII). But what would God do through his Wisdom if he did not love that same Wisdom? Or what would he love in it if it likewise did not love him by whom it was begotten?

[Col. 1497A] It is therefore established that love proceeds from the Father to the Son, and from the Son to his Father. This love is the Holy Spirit, who proceeds from both in such a way that he always remains in both, and remains always in both in such a way that he always proceeds from both.

The Son is coeternal with the Father, because the Father never existed without his Wisdom. The Holy Spirit is coeternal with the Father and the Son, because he is the inseparable love of both, sharing their one substance, and has always united them.

The Father knows himself wholly and loves wholly whatever he is; therefore his Wisdom is as great as he himself is, and his love is as great as he himself is. The Son and the Holy Spirit are therefore equal to the Father.

If we wish to think about what the substance of the Father is, let us first think, as far as we can, about what his Wisdom itself is.

[Col. 1497B] It is she who said, “No one comes to the Father except through me” (John XIV), and, “Whoever sees me sees my Father also” (ibid.). In Wisdom, then, we see neither breadth nor length, neither roundness nor any quantity or quality. We find in it no distinctions of different members, as in our body. Nothing bodily, therefore, is found in the essence of Wisdom; whatever is rightly thought about it is wholly spirit.

They are therefore gravely mistaken who attribute the form of a human being to God the Father. Those who do not believe that the Father and the Holy Spirit are such as the Son is are foolish. This Father, Son, and Holy Spirit is wholly everywhere: one God, everywhere unbounded, everywhere undivided.

To understand this to some degree, let us pay closer attention. Let us place before us some very small body, or let us look at our own fingernail, which is at hand, and see, if we can, how God is wholly present in it; if we cannot see this, let us believe it.

[Col. 1497C] In my fingernail I see five regions: upper, lower, right, left, and middle. God has already made all these things through his Wisdom, and even now orders them so that they may subsist.

A part of God’s Wisdom is not present at the right side of the fingernail, another at the left, another at the upper part, another at the lower part, and another at its middle. Rather, just as she operates wholly in all things, so she is wholly present to all of them. Her presence must be understood not locally but in terms of power.

Since at the same hour and moment in which she makes these things she also orders all other things according to her will, she always and simultaneously shows herself to be present in all things.

[Col. 1497D] What we have seen concerning Wisdom—that is, concerning the Son—let us also understand concerning the Father and the Holy Spirit, since we must believe that they are altogether inseparable.

Let us return to the image of God, which is our soul, and see, if possible, the Trinity in unity within it. Our soul is spirit, not body. It possesses in itself and from itself—that is, from its substance—three things: understanding, memory, and will.

Each of these is in all the others, because understanding understands itself, its memory, and its will. Behold: understanding is in memory and in will. Memory remembers itself, its understanding, and its will. Will wills—that is, loves—itself, its understanding, and its memory. Thus they are in all things.

All things, however, are in each one, because by the same reasoning understanding, memory, and will are all simultaneously in one. And these are nothing other than one substance, namely the soul.

Let us therefore speak similarly of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. The Father is life, the Son is Wisdom, and the Holy Spirit is love. Life therefore lives, Wisdom lives, and love lives. Wisdom knows, life knows, and love knows. Love loves, life loves, and Wisdom loves. These three are nothing other than one substance, which is God.

Nevertheless, we must beware lest we wish to equate our soul with our God, lest, while seeking to rise above ourselves toward his likeness, we fall away from him through whom we are.

[Col. 1498B] Just as, therefore, we have seen the image of the one who works in his work, so let us again see how far the thing made differs from the one who made it.

In the soul, understanding, memory, and will are one substance, which is called the mind. Yet understanding is not memory or will; nor is memory understanding or will; nor is will memory or understanding.

For it is one thing in the soul to remember past things, another to understand present things, and another to will what it has remembered and understood. Hence it is understood that these three—understanding, remembering, and willing—are greater in the soul than merely willing, merely understanding, or merely remembering.

[Col. 1498C] Understanding understands itself, memory, and will. Memory remembers itself, understanding, and will. Will wills itself, memory, and understanding.

But in God, whose nature is altogether simple, we do not believe that living is one thing, knowing another, and loving another; nor that these three are more than one, or that one is less than three.

This can be understood as follows. The Father is living, the Son is wise, and the Holy Spirit is loving. The Father too is living, wise, and loving; and so is each one likewise.

Since God’s nature is altogether simple, each is living in such a way as to be life, wise in such a way as to be Wisdom, and loving in such a way as to be love. Each one, therefore, is God; each one is life, Wisdom, and love.

It is inconsistent to believe that in a simple nature life is one thing, Wisdom another, and love another. Let us therefore reduce these three to one and say:

[Col. 1498D] The Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are life, or Wisdom, or love. Thus it is clear that the three are no more than one, nor the one less than three.

Yet we must take care not to confuse the persons. The Father is indeed Wisdom or love, but the Son is nevertheless the Wisdom of the Father, and the Holy Spirit the love of the Father and the Son.

Here a difficult question arises. If the Father is wise and the Son is Wisdom, it is asked whether he is wise by his Wisdom, which is his Son. For every wise person is wise through wisdom.

The answer given is this: Wisdom is of the same reality as essence. If, therefore, the Father is wise through his Son, he has Wisdom from the Son; and consequently he has essence from him as well. The Father, then, would be from the Son, not the Son from the Father.

But the Father is not from the Son; therefore he does not have Wisdom from the Son. The same reasoning applies to the Holy Spirit, who is the love of both.

We must therefore believe that the Father is perfect life, Wisdom, and love from himself; that the Son is perfect life, Wisdom, and love from his Father; and that the Holy Spirit is the same from the Father and the Son.

Adam, before sin, clearly understood this threefold Unity and one Trinity through his soul, the undefiled image of God. The sin committed obscured that light.

[Col. 1499A] The human soul sinned by the will, and the body by the deed. Both therefore died, because sin was committed by both.

Since the human being died through folly, it was necessary that he be brought to life through Wisdom. The Wisdom of God was therefore incarnate, so that human folly might be wiped away.

But human folly killed both the rational soul and the body; whereas the Wisdom of God—that is, the Son—assumed both the rational soul and the body.

And just as the former was made without sin from undefiled earth, so the latter was born without sin from an incorrupt Virgin. God assumed humanity in such a way that neither God was changed into a human being nor the human being absorbed into God.

For if God were changed into a human being, he would no longer be God, but only a human being, and therefore he would not help us.

If, however, the human being were absorbed into God, he would no longer be human, but God alone, and therefore he could not die.

Although many other means by which he might redeem us were available, he wished to die so that he might conquer the devil by justice rather than by power. For it was just that the one who had conquered humanity should be conquered by a human being, and that he should show us with how great a love he restores us.

[Col. 1499C] This is why he is said to have been conceived by the Holy Spirit, because the Holy Spirit is love, and love accomplished this entire mystery.

Thus he became a human being, one person with God, while the proper substance of each was preserved. This human being lived without sin in order to conquer the devil, and endured pains in order to erase human sin.

He worked miracles because he was God; he died because he was human. He raised himself from the dead so that he might be believed to be God; afterward he appeared in palpable flesh so that there would be no doubt that he was human.

He permitted the body that had died on the cross to be buried in the stone; but his living soul, remaining with God, descended into hell—not to suffer, but to rule. After freeing from there those whom he judged worthy, and leaving the others behind, [Col. 1499D] he took up his body again on the third day.

After his body had risen, he remained for forty days with the disciples, appearing to them not continuously but at appointed times, and also eating. On the fortieth day, while they watched, he ascended into heaven.

The fact that he ate after the resurrection was not due to need, but was evidence of the manifest resurrection.

Our Lord Jesus Christ therefore reigns in the glory of the Father. He will come to judge all humanity in the manifestation of his flesh, handing the reprobate over to eternal torments and showing himself to the elect in everlasting joys. In those joys may we reign forever with him, our Lord Jesus Christ, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God, through all ages of ages. Amen.

[Col. 1500A]

## On the Body and Blood of the Lord

Meanwhile, while we journey as exiles from him in this world (II Cor. V), we are nourished on the road by his body and blood, just as he entrusted this mystery to his apostles at the last supper before his death and commanded through them that we who follow should celebrate it frequently.

Faith must therefore be given to the Lord’s words, in which he says: “My flesh is truly food, and my blood is truly drink” (John VI).

With every accursed doubt rejected, let us believe without hesitation that, just as we believe that the only-begotten God, the Son who is God coeternal with the Father, was truly born in our flesh, truly died, truly rose again, truly ascended into heaven, and truly sits at the right hand of his Father, so we truly and wholly eat his real body and blood on the altar after the consecration.

[Col. 1500B] I mean the true and complete body of the Lord, which both rejoices in glory, wholly seated at the Father’s right hand, and is wholly received from the priest’s hands. Even if it is broken into parts, as it were, in each part, however tiny, you have it whole and complete. And if a thousand priests perform this mystery at the same hour and moment, nevertheless in the hands of each one the body of Christ, consecrated whole and complete, is received by each one whole and complete.

Here one may ask why this mystery, or sacrament, or even figure, is called a consecration if it is itself the reality and the truth, and nothing else is signified through it.

I answer that it is both a mystery, because it bears something mystical; and a sacrament, because it conceals within itself something sacred that must be understood; and a figure, because, apart from what is performed bodily, it figures something else spiritual and very necessary.

[Col. 1500C] For what is mystical, sacred, and spiritual is figured through this mystery. Just as we all receive the body of Christ bodily, so we ourselves must become his body by living spiritually—not the body that the Word of God assumed in his own person, which is called the Lord’s body, but that which in the Holy Scriptures is called the Church. Hence Paul says: “He is our head” (Eph. V), and we are his members.

This is why this sacrament is made from bread and wine. Bread is made one from many grains, and wine is poured together into one from many grapes. Similarly, we too are made one body from many grains; through the body and blood of the Lord we are restored by living well and believing with the catholic faith.

Hence Paul also says: “We are all one bread” (I Cor. X).

While preserving these and any other meanings, if there are more, let faith also be preserved, because the body of the Lord itself is believed to be truly present not qualitatively but substantially, so that what the Truth itself testifies to be altogether true, our deceitfulness may not judge to be false or imaginary.

[Col. 1500D] If this body is received unworthily—and it is received unworthily when the soul remains in deadly sins and receives it together with them—judgment is altogether eaten and drunk there.

But when it is received worthily, insofar as human frailty is able, through the grace of God, our soul undoubtedly obtains eternal life through this sacrament. May that life truly be granted to us by our Lord Jesus Christ through his body [Col. 1502A] and blood in the everlasting age. Amen.

[Col. 1501]

# LETTER OF GUITMUND TO ERFASTUS

*(Galland, Bibliotheca Veterum Patrum, XIV, 240.)*

## NOTICE

While Guitmund was still a priest, a certain brother named Erfastus questioned him about the substance and unity of the Holy Trinity, about the mystery of the Lord’s body, and also about the analogies they commonly use—for example, that of the sphere—to establish the unity of the Trinity.

He answers these requests as a sober and cautious theologian ought. The letter has reached us mutilated; we have borrowed it from D’Achery’s *Spicilegium* in order to reprint it.

[Col. 1501B] Brother Guitmund, an unworthy priest, to his most beloved brother Erfastus: may he glory without end in Christ Jesus our Lord.

### I

Having read your letter, brother, I have gathered from the very manner of your inquiries that, chastened by fear of God, you are exercising yourself—not uselessly, as I rejoice—in the wisdom and knowledge of spiritual matters.

Your question about the substance and unity of the eternal Trinity belongs to wisdom. What you added about the mystery of the Lord’s body pertains to knowledge. Likewise, your recalling, in order to establish the unity of the Trinity, an analogy drawn from a temporal thing—namely, the sphere of the sun—also belongs to knowledge.

It is plainly a suitable, beautiful, and most pleasant philosophy, if you persevere in it. For this is not earthly or human, but truly heavenly and divine. It is sweet refreshment for one who labors; after labor, it is perfect blessedness. You do well to seek it diligently, for it will be opened to the one who persistently knocks.

[Col. 1501C] Rejoicing, therefore, in your effort and progress—and intending, if the Lord should will it, at some time to discuss these matters at greater length—I will not delay your questions, but will answer them concisely and briefly, with as much brevity as I can.

### II

In that comparison with the solar sphere, about which you first asked me to reply, observe carefully that it is useful for this purpose: just as the sphere, radiance, and heat produce not three suns but one sun, so you should understand that in the Father, Wisdom, and the Love of both there are not three gods but one divinity.

And just as the sun, which sends forth its radiance, has that radiance altogether coeval with itself, so God the Father has the Son whom he generates from himself, coeternal with himself.

I particularly want you to attend carefully to the fact that the unity of the supreme divinity is established in a way utterly different from what occurs in the sun.

For in the sun, radiance and heat are qualities, whereas the sun itself is substance; consequently, the sun is not the same thing as those two others. The qualities themselves also differ substantially from one another, and indeed produce different effects.

[Col. 1502B] Radiance makes something luminous, while heat makes something hot through its power of operation; they also commonly differ according to place, time, and the things upon which they act.

Often, when the sun is rising, the sun’s radiance is visible where none of its heat at all is felt. At midday, its heat penetrates many solid bodies into which no light whatsoever enters.

Nor are they received by us through the same senses. Radiance is apprehended by sight, heat by touch. Thus, conversely, even someone trembling with intense cold may see the sun’s great light from far away, while a blind person suffering darkness may sometimes wither or grow cheerful under its powerful heat.

### III

These two, then, differ greatly from each other. But the unity of God with his Wisdom and his Love is not so small or, so to speak, so discordant; nor are God’s Wisdom and Love qualities of the divine substance.

Nor do these two differ from one another in such a way. They are called, in a certain sense, one sun because, in the one sun, they are coeval with it and inseparable from it; but what each is in itself is not thereby one and the same in relation to the other, since, as stated above, they differ from each other substantially in every respect.

[Col. 1502C] But the Father, Word, and Spirit—or Father, Wisdom, and Love—are in one God, or are one God, in such a way that whatever each is essentially in itself is one with the others without any separation.

Of the Father and the Son you have our Lord saying in the Gospel: “I am in the Father, and the Father is in me”; “Whoever sees me sees the Father”; and “I and the Father are one.”

The Father does not have the Son from anyone other than himself. For before all creation there was nothing else. Yet, as it is written, all things that were made were made through the Son himself.

If all things that were made were made through him, then he himself was not made, nor did he come from anything else, since there was nothing else; rather, before all things, the Father begot him from himself.
