[Col. 1502D] If the Son was born from the substance of the Father, and since in that substance there is no part—for the first principle is uncompounded and, having itself composed all things, does not know how to be composed at all—then there is likewise no part in the Son. Nothing of him exists except from the Father and in the Father.

Moreover, because the Father’s unity is wholly undivided and never multiplied, it cannot have a plurality of parts.

[Note: [Col. 1503D] “From the Father, moreover.” Acherius had printed: “there is no part: for the first principle is uncompounded; nor . . . . . [Col. 1504D] he himself composed. Likewise, nor . . . . . and in the Father is from the Father. Moreover, unity, etc.”]

[Col. 1503A] The whole, therefore, was born from the whole, without being in any respect greater or less: the same from the same in essence.

For if he has no part, and since he is from that one and in that one, which is already undivided, he differs in no way. For if he is from him, he possesses something of him—or rather, if he himself is something of him, then, since the latter has no part, he possesses or is not merely a part of him but the whole.

If, then, he possesses the whole essence of the Father in himself, he himself is that unmoved essence, since its own undivided simplicity, which knows no part, rejects addition; he differs from it in no essential respect.

[Col. 1503B] Whatever the Father is in essence, therefore, the Son is altogether the same.

### IV

Let the same reasoning also satisfy you concerning the Holy Spirit. Because he is from the Father’s undivided substance without a part, he is one and the same substance with the Father; and because he is from the Son’s undivided substance without a part, he is one and the same substance with the Son.

And since he proceeds simultaneously from the Father and the Son, there are not two processions but one procession, nor are there two Holy Spirits but one Holy Spirit.

Since the substance of the Father and the Son is wholly one and the same, undivided by place or time, the Holy Spirit, proceeding simultaneously from both, proceeds from the other at the very moment that he proceeds from the one.

[Col. 1503C] I understand this to be taught by the Lord in the Gospel, where he says: “When the Paraclete comes, whom I will send to you from the Father.” He said, “I will send from the Father,” as though he were saying: “His procession from me and from the Father is one.”

A little later he says: “He will glorify me, because he will take from what is mine and announce it to you. Everything that the Father has is mine; therefore I said that he will take from what is mine and announce it to you.”

That is: the substance which the Father has is one with mine; therefore, since the Holy Spirit is from us, when he is from the Father, he is from me.

The Holy Spirit, then, is one and the same substance with the Father and the Son. He belongs to both, and his procession from both is one and the same.

[Col. 1503D] Thus these three are in one God, or are one God, in such a way that whatever each is essentially in itself is one with the others without any separation.

### V

Accordingly, when the Son is called the Wisdom or Power of the Father, because knowing or possessing power is essential to him, he is not believed to be a quality of the Father by which the Father is qualified—namely, called wise and strong. Rather, he is the Father’s perfect Wisdom and Power; the Father, individually considered, is perfect Wisdom and Power; the Son, individually considered, is perfect Wisdom and Power; the Holy Spirit, individually considered, is perfect Wisdom and Power.

Together they are not three Wisdoms or powers, but one Wisdom and one Power. The Son is Wisdom from the Father who is Wisdom, Power from the Father who is Power, just as essence from essence, life from life, God from God, light from light.

But because through the Son weakened in the flesh and through the foolishness of his cross we, the weak and foolish, have been made strong and wise, and because he himself was made for us by God Wisdom, Power, and righteousness, so that, justified and strengthened through his weakness and death, we might eventually grow strong enough through him to know the Father, therefore we rightly confess, as though in a special sense, the righteousness, Power, and Wisdom of God.

### VI

Likewise, when the Holy Spirit is called the charity, love, or will of the Father and the Son, he is not therefore believed to be a quality of both, by which they are qualified as loving, willing, or spiritual.

Rather, since each is also the Holy Spirit—for the Father too is spirit, as it is written, “God is spirit,” and the Son according to his divinity is spirit—and since the Father is holy and the Son is holy, there are not three Holy Spirits but one Holy Spirit.

And since each is charity, because “God is love,” and each is love or will, there are nevertheless not three charities, loves, or wills, but one charity, one love, and one will.

Yet we call the one who proceeds from the Father and the Son, as it were properly, the Holy Spirit, charity, love, or will of the Father and the Son. In this way, by giving him in his name what is common to those from whom he is, we designate him to some extent as their own, because, existing from both, he is common to them, consubstantial with them, and the bond of both.

### VII

Thus, although the Father is both essence and principle, the Son likewise essence and principle, and the Holy Spirit also essence and principle, there are not three essences or three principles, but one essence and one principle.

Nevertheless, we speak of these things as though they belonged properly to the Father, so that we may recognize that he is in such a way that he is from himself, and is principle in such a way that he is not from another principle, but only from himself, while the other persons are from him.

For the Son, whatever he is altogether, is not from himself but from the Father. Likewise, the Holy Spirit is not from himself, but whatever he is altogether is from the Father and the Son.

But the Son has from the Father that the Spirit proceeds from the Son. For if whatever he has is from the Father, and he has it from the Father by being born from him, he has from the Father that the Spirit is from him.

[Col. 1504D] The Holy Spirit too, by proceeding from the Father, has from him that he is from him in such a way that he also exists simultaneously from the Son.

Thus each contains all, all are in each, and all are one. Yet, by the definite mystery of reason I have mentioned, certain things are spoken of as though properly of the Father—for example, essential principle; certain things of the Son—for example, righteousness, Power, and Wisdom; and certain things of the Holy Spirit—for example, that he is called the Holy Spirit and is named the love, charity, or will of the Father and the Son.

Thus we understand that, as has been said, the Father is from himself and not from another; that through the Son we have been and will be justified, strengthened, and taught; and that the Holy Spirit proceeds jointly from the Father and the Son.

### VIII

Just as, therefore, they are the same in the essence of their majesty, since they are not separated by an interval of place or time, and are not three powers numerically but one power, so that they are one agent, neither do they differ in the effect of their operation. [Note: [Col. 1505] “They are one agent.” Perhaps: “as one they operate,” and so they do not differ in the effect of their operation.]

For our Lord said: “Whatever the Father does, the Son does likewise,” and not otherwise, because “the Son can do nothing of himself except what he sees the Father doing.”

The same must consequently be understood of the Spirit of both. For although the Son alone assumed humanity, the whole Trinity made that human being and the mystery of the incarnation; the whole Trinity handed him over to death; the whole Trinity raised him up; the whole Trinity exalted him.

[Col. 1505B] In the same way, the whole Trinity made that voice by which the Father alone, speaking to the Son, made himself known: “You are my beloved Son.”

The whole Trinity likewise made the dove and the tongues of fire in which the Holy Spirit appeared either over the Lord when he was baptized or at Pentecost.

Similarly, the two-syllable word that is called “Father,” the three-syllable word that is called “Son,” and the two names by which the Holy Spirit is called, as well as many other utterances—although they separately indicate and present to the hearing the distinct properties of the persons—are nevertheless, like the two-syllable word that is called “God,” which signifies the Trinity as a whole, all equally works of the entire Trinity.

[Col. 1505C] Therefore, even if certain created things properly or mysteriously pertain to the manifestation of the individual persons, it is nevertheless clear that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit differ neither in substance nor in the operation of anything whatsoever.

It is also clear that we contemplate the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit not through different bodily senses but through one and the same pure understanding of the mind, simultaneously, just as we learned from the Truth itself, which says: “Whoever sees me sees the Father.”

IX. To bring our discussion briefly to an end: since the qualities that exist in the sun differ substantially both from the sun itself and from one another, they also differ in their power of acting, according to place and time, and according to their various subjects; absorbed through different senses, they are shown to be widely separated. [Col. 1505D] Yet since the substance of the Father, Wisdom, and Love is altogether one and the same; since in them no quality—not merely a different one, but no quality at all—nor anything whatsoever except one pure essence ought to be conceived; since their works are always, everywhere, and in all things the same, and they are seen simultaneously and inseparably by one and the same understanding of the mind, it is perfectly clear, by the evidence of manifest reason, that the unity of that supreme and indivisible Trinity exists in a manner far different and more truly than it can exist not only in the sun but in any creature whatever.

X. Certainly, when I said above that whatever each of them is essentially is spoken of communally of them all, I said “essentially” for this reason: what is called Father or Begetter, and likewise what is called Son or Word or Image, or what is called the proceeding Holy Spirit, are names not of essence understood in itself but of the distinction or relation of the persons. [Col. 1506A] For, taking care not to confuse the persons, we call the Father “unbegotten,” demonstrating that he is not from another; and, because he is not without the Son, we also call him “Father.”

[Col. 1506B] Likewise, that ineffable vision of the Father, in which the Father beholds himself and all things—that splendor, that light—is called the Son, because it is not from itself but from the Father alone. And since we are able to behold God through some kind of enigma by means of his mirror and image (for our inner man, though darkened, is nevertheless God's image): since, I say, when we see any thing with the mind, whether something outside us or the mind itself, we somehow speak with ourselves about the thing we see and form in the spirit an image most like it, so that, when our mind beholds itself and brings forth within itself, by a kind of examination, a judgment of truth concerning itself, and at last draws forth the light of true understanding, that very acumen of true understanding and offspring of the mind may rightly be called both the word by which it discussed itself and the image or likeness which it formed from contemplating itself, because it itself brought this forth from itself.

In a similar way, through its image, as I have said, which is what we are, we see God through some kind of enigma; and, if we dare to speak of temporal things—or rather, because it is useful for us to do so with respect to temporal things—we somehow conjecture the eternal. In the same way, I say, we believe in our heart that the ineffable light of that paternal vision, eternally from the Father, eternally with the Father, and eternally remaining in the Father, eternally beholding the Father, is the creator of all things, the revealer of the Father, and the same as the Father, because it is from the Father and not from nothing; and that it is the only-begotten Son, the Word, and the Image and Likeness of the Father. According to our capacity we perceive this unto righteousness, and with our mouth we confess it unto salvation.

But we call the Holy Spirit neither unbegotten, because he is not from no one, nor begotten, because he is not from the Father alone. Rather, he proceeds from the Father and the Son, yet is not born from both, because he is equally and in the same manner the Spirit of both; for no one can ever be, equally and in the same manner, the son of two fathers. Nor is he called the Word, Image, or Likeness of both. For although lovers often turn something over in their minds, speak of it with themselves, and form an image of it, and although in speaking and imagining they love it, nevertheless speaking and imagining in us properly belong to vision, not to love. Whatever is to be loved is first spoken of through the mind’s contemplation—what or of what kind it is, or how it is disposed—so that, once this has been determined, it may be loved more certainly.

XI. But what comparison is there between our condition and eternity? I say this so that you may not, with a carnal understanding of words, seek in the Divinity the properties of words exactly as they exist in us. For if you consider the meanings of the words “Father” and “Son,” and the other relational terms when they are spoken of human beings, we ordinarily understand certain accidents of the human beings to whom they are related. Likewise, in the words “begetting” and “proceeding,” we ordinarily understand an action or a passion together with an indication of time.

But we believe in the eternal generation of the Son of God and the procession of the Holy Spirit in such a way that we perceive neither time, nor the action of the begetter, nor the passion of the begotten or proceeding Spirit, nor any accident whatsoever to be present in the divine substance. Therefore, the words of distinction or relation do not properly apply to the Divinity in the same way, nor are they to be understood in God altogether in the same sense as they are in us.

Far be it from us to say that in the eternal Trinity, the one God, before every creature, there existed—because of the limitations of our words—any accident or anything whatsoever apart from the simple Divinity. [Note: [Col. 1507D] “Propter.” I read “praeter.”] [Note: [Col. 1507D] “Propter.” I read “praeter.”] For no creature, however perfect and made in the image of God, can fully express or equal the likeness of the Creator as it is; much less could the words of mortals, which are almost nothing, suffice to explain the nature of the Divinity, which surpasses with ineffable truth every thought of every creature.

XII. We do not therefore say these things about God in order to explain exactly what exists there, but we speak as best we can, in whatever words we possess, lest we seem entirely to suppress in silence what we most certainly believe from the word of the Savior, and what, with Christ’s help, we are able to taste beforehand through enigmas, however faintly and tenuously.

When we desire in some measure to speak of the ineffable, then through these words we indicate—not any accidents of the purest Divinity, but, as it were, the result of the narrowness of human speech—that the Father is not from another, through the name “unbegotten”; that he is not without the one who is from him, through the name “Father”; that the Son is not from himself and exists only from the Father, through the name “Son”; and, in the same way, that the Holy Spirit is not from himself but from the Father and the Son, through the word “proceeding,” as was said above.

XIII. Let it therefore be far from the sons of the holy and universal Church that any carnal mind should imagine within itself any intervals whatsoever in the distinction of the persons. For if this were admitted in the eternal Trinity—God forbid!—then, since this Trinity of persons eternally exists in God before the constitution of all things, the Trinity would falsely be believed—again, God forbid!—to be the creator and origin of all things apart from the one God alone. It would no longer rightly be called a Trinity, but rather a quaternity or quinity, or even more, according to the number of the intervening things or accidents—something equally abhorrent.

Since this is wholly contrary to the Christian religion and supremely opposed to Catholic truth, in the omnipotent, eternal, and simple Trinity, while preserving—as was said—the ineffable distinction of the persons, no taint of accident, no admixture or interposition of any thing whatsoever, is therefore to be admitted. Only one, unique, sincere, and utterly pure Divinity is to be affirmed.

XIV. Whoever, through the stages of faith, as this is granted from above, has now touched God by some inward, most sweet, fiery, and inexpressible taste of the mind, in accordance with the merits of his faith, should rejoice with great trembling and tremble with great joy, sensing his God, as a human being can, to some degree. Yet let him feast in such a way that he does not remain in what he has found, but knocks more vigorously by always seeking, desiring, and praying piously, so that what has been granted may be opened to him more abundantly.

For it is written: “When a man has finished, then he begins.” And again: “Seek his face always.” But whoever is too weak for this should nevertheless not doubt that it is so; meanwhile, let him be patiently nourished in the bosom of faith for the sight of it hereafter.

XV. But if someone wishes to be a violent investigator of eternity, and cannot easily believe that God is triune without number, or distinct in persons without the interposition or admixture of anything, or eternal without extension, or wholly present everywhere without place or position, or great without quantity, good without quality, doing all things without movement, enduring all things without passion, and containing all things without enclosure, let him hear what is written: “Do not seek what is beyond you.” Rather, let him wonder at the things that have been made, and ask himself by what power all these things came forth from nothing.

For they did not come forth by their own power, since they possessed none. If this is so, how did things that were altogether nothing perceive the command of God, who ordered them to be? Or, since they could not simultaneously be and not be, by what intermediate process did they pass from one state to the other? Or, if perhaps he declines to discuss the beginning of the world because it did not yet exist, let him inquire into the origins, growth, changes, and declines of the individual things that come into view each day; let him consider deeply how or why this or that comes about in one manner rather than another.

[Col. 1508D] But if, while carefully investigating even the smallest matters, he should perhaps fail and recognize by experience the truth of the most wise Solomon’s statement:

“All things that are difficult are upon the earth, and the things that are before our eyes we discover only with labor; but who knows the things that are in heaven, unless you give wisdom and send your Holy Spirit from on high?”

—then let him cease, in giant-like arrogance, to storm heaven, and let him humbly believe what . . . [lacuna]

[Col. 1509]

## The Speech of Guitmund, Archbishop of Aversa, to William I, King of the English, when he refused the Bishopric

[Note]

(Bibliotheca Patrum XVIII, p. 468, from Orderic Vitalis, Ecclesiastical History, book V, chapter 17. Its subject is: “Concerning Guitmund, monk of Saint Leufredus, and his most beautiful speech to William, king of England.” Guitmund was a venerable monk of the monastery called the Cross of Helton, where the glorious confessor of Christ, Leufredus, is said to have served the Lord successfully for forty-eight years during the time of Hildebert and Hilperic, the younger kings. Summoned by royal command, he crossed the sea and altogether rejected the burden of ecclesiastical governance offered to him by the king and the nobles of the realm. For he was mature in age, religious, and exceedingly learned in letters; the outstanding evidence of his talent is clearly seen in his book *On the Body and Blood of the Lord against Berengarius*, and in his other little works. When the king therefore asked him to remain with him in England and await a suitable time for promoting him, he deliberated with himself and, showing that his purpose was otherwise, replied to the king:)

[Col. 1509A] Many reasons drive me away from ecclesiastical government, all of which I neither wish nor ought to express individually. First of all, I consider my weaknesses, by which I am incessantly burdened in body and soul. When I have carefully examined them, I greatly fear the divine judgment, grieving that I labor daily on the way of God and waver from the truth. And while I cannot healthfully govern myself, how can I direct the life of others along the way of salvation?

Having carefully surveyed everything with vigilant mind, I do not see by what right I could worthily preside over a group of people whose foreign customs and barbarous speech I do not know, whose fathers, dear parents, and friends you have killed with the sword, or oppressed by dispossessing them and sending them into exile, prison, or unjust and intolerable servitude.

Search the Scriptures and see whether any law decrees that a shepherd chosen by enemies should be violently imposed upon the Lord’s flock. Ecclesiastical election ought first to be made sincerely by the faithful subjects themselves, and afterward, if it is canonical, reverently confirmed by the approval of the Fathers and friends. Otherwise it ought to be corrected with charity.

What you have savagely seized through war and the shedding of much blood—by what right can you distribute it to me and to other despisers of the world, who have voluntarily stripped ourselves of our possessions for Christ, though we are without guilt? The general law of all religious people is to abstain from plunder and, in observance of justice, to refuse to accept booty, even when it is offered.

For Scripture says: “He who sacrifices from an unlawful gain offers a blemished offering” (Ecclesiasticus 34). And shortly afterward: “He who offers a sacrifice from the substance of the poor is like one who slaughters a son in the presence of his father” (ibid.).

As I reflect upon these and similar proclamations of the divine law, I am terrified. I judge all England to be like an immense quantity of booty, and I fear to touch it, together with its treasures, as one would touch a burning fire.

And because God commands each person to love his neighbor as himself, I shall tell you without deceit what has been enjoined upon me from heaven. What I consider useful for myself I also consider salutary for you.

[Col. 1510A] Therefore, let what I say in friendship not appear bitter. But you, vigorous prince, and your fellow soldiers, who have entered with you into grave danger, receive the words of our admonition with kindly hearts.

Consider wisely the works of God throughout all the days of your lives, and fear his judgments, which are incomprehensible, in all your actions. Strive to regulate your life by an even balance according to God’s will, so that the eternal Judge himself may be with you at the final trial.

Do not let flatterers deceive you with empty security, nor let insolent men, because of the favorable events of this present life, persuade you to fall lethally asleep in worldly prosperity. If you defeated the English in battle, do not be proud of this; rather, wage with greater caution the more serious and dangerous struggle against spiritual wickedness, which still remains and daily threatens you.

Changes of kingdoms have frequently occurred throughout the world, as we read scattered through the many fields of Scripture, whose knowledge of letters God has generously granted. Under King Nebuchadnezzar, the Babylonians subdued Judaea, Egypt, and many other kingdoms; but after seventy years they themselves, with their king Belshazzar, were defeated and subjugated by the Medes and Persians, ruled by Darius and his nephew Cyrus.

Then, under Alexander the Great, the Macedonians, after 230 years, defeated Darius, king of the Persians, together with his many legions. Yet they themselves, after some years, were defeated with their king Perseus, when the Roman armies were sending their forces throughout the whole world.

[Col. 1510C] The Greeks, under Agamemnon and Palamedes, besieged Troy and killed Priam, king and son of Laomedon, together with his children Hector, Troilus, Paris, Deiphobus, and Amphimachus. After a ten-year siege they destroyed the famous Phrygian kingdom, laying it waste with fire and sword.

One part of the Trojans, under the leadership of Aeneas, gained the kingdom of Italy; another part, with Antenor, after a long and difficult journey, reached Dacia and settled there, where it has dwelt down to the present day.

[Col. 1511A] The Romans, under Vespasian and Titus, overthrew the kingdom of Jerusalem, which David and his other powerful successors had enriched with the spoils of the Philistines and had exalted after subduing the barbarian nations surrounding it. They destroyed its noble temple 1,089 years after its first construction, when 1,100,000 Jews perished by sword or famine.

The Franks joined the Gauls in the time of the leader Sunno and, having bravely shaken the Roman yoke from their necks, began to reign over them. The English Saxons, under the leaders Hengist and Horsa, took the government from the Britons—who are now called Gauls—by deceit and courage, nearly six hundred years ago.

The Guinili, who had been expelled by lot from the island of Scandinavia, invaded the part of Italy now called Lombardy during the reign of King Alboin, son of Audoin; after resisting the Romans for a long time, they have retained it down to the present.

All these peoples whom I have recalled as rising through victory shortly afterward miserably fell beneath destruction. Afflicted with the same crushing fate as the conquered, they groan irreparably in the sewers of Erebus.

The Normans, under their leader Rollo, wrested Neustria from Charles the Simple and have held it for 190 years, despite the opposition of the Gauls, who often assailed them amid the tumult of war.

What shall I say of the Gepids and Vandals, Goths and Turks, Huns and Heruli? What shall I say of the other barbarians, whose efforts amount to nothing except stealing and plundering and raging continually after peace has been trampled underfoot? They disturb the earth, burn houses, harass the world, scatter wealth, slaughter human beings, defile and unsettle everything.

[Col. 1511C] By these signs the end of the world is foretold, as we are plainly taught by the voice of Truth itself: “Nation will rise against nation and kingdom against kingdom, and there will be great earthquakes in various places, and pestilences and famines” (Mark 13), “and terrors from heaven, and there will be great signs.”

With countless disasters the world is thus continually oppressed.

Having carefully observed these and many similar revolutions in human affairs, let the victor not glory in the ruin of his equal, for he too will not stand except insofar as the disposition of the Creator commands.

I shall now turn my speech to you, O king, and I ask that you kindly receive it for the sake of eternal salvation. None of your fathers before you bore the royal insignia, nor did such great honor come to you by hereditary right, but by the free generosity of almighty God and through the friendship of your kinsman Edward.

Edgar, Aldin, and several others descended from the line of the royal family are, according to the laws of the Hebrews and of other peoples, nearer heirs to the English crown. When these had been removed, the lot of advancement fell to you. But God’s judgment, the more hidden it is, the more terribly it threatens you, that you may render an account of the stewardship entrusted to you.

I have spoken these things to your exalted station from a kindly heart, humbly asking that your mind always remember the last things, and that the prosperity of the present may not entangle you too greatly, since intolerable pain and great mourning and the gnashing of teeth usually follow it.

I commend you, your friends, and your faithful servants to the grace of God. With your permission I intend to return to Normandy, and I leave the rich booty of England to the lovers of the world as though it were refuse.

I love the free poverty of Christ, which Antony and Benedict embraced, more than the riches of the world, which Croesus and Sardanapalus loved too greatly and afterward, miserably perishing, abandoned to their enemies. For Christ, the good shepherd, threatens woe to the rich of this world who here indulge in vain and superfluous pleasures; but to the poor in spirit he promises blessedness in the kingdom of heaven. May he himself grant it to us, he who lives and reigns throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

[Col. 1512B] The king and his nobles, astonished at the steadfastness of the distinguished monk, humbly and devoutly paid him fitting reverence and, having honored him appropriately, ordered him to return to Neustria, where he was to await his presence at whatever place he wished.

It was widely reported that, after Guitmund returned to the enclosure of his monastery, he had preferred monastic poverty to the riches of bishops; that he had called the conquest of England, in the presence of the king and his nobles, an act of plunder; and that he had accused all the bishops and abbots who had been placed over the churches of England against the will of the English of rapacity.

His words, therefore, which were widely disseminated throughout England and carefully discussed, displeased many. Those who scorned to be his followers were inflamed against him by intense envy.

Not long afterward, when John, bishop of Rouen, died, the king and several others chose Guitmund for the archbishopric. But his rivals, whom he had rebuked, hindered him as much as they could from becoming archbishop. Yet they found nothing to allege against him except that he was the son of a priest.

Wishing to be free from all avarice, and preferring to endure poverty among foreigners rather than foster dissensions among his own people, he approached Odilo, the venerable abbot of his monastery, and humbly asked and received permission from him to travel abroad.

The unlearned abbot did not know how great a treasure of wisdom lay hidden in the aforementioned teacher. Thus he easily dismissed from his monastery the philosopher whom he should have desired to retain. Pope Gregory VII received him gladly when he came to him and placed him in charge as a cardinal of the Holy Roman Church; and Pope Urban, having tested him in many matters, solemnly ordained him metropolitan of Aversa.

This city was founded in the time of Pope Leo IX by the Normans who first inhabited Apulia. It was called Aversa by the Romans because it was being built by hostile groups opposed to them. This city, rich in wealth, prompt and warlike through the vigorous energy of the Cisalpine peoples, feared by its enemies and cherished by its loyal dependents and allies, obeys willingly only the pope, at the choice of the Normans. From him it received Guitmund, the sophist, as its bishop, splendidly clothed in the mantle of mystical beauty.

The aforementioned archbishop governed the church entrusted to him for a long time, rejoiced in its freedom from every exaction of mortals through apostolic privileges, diligently taught the people, protected them by his merits and prayers, and, after many struggles in the exercise of the virtues, departed to the Lord.

## Around the Year of the Lord 1089  
### Ebrard, Regular Canon of the Watin Monastery

[Col. 1513]

# Watin Chronicle

(Edited by Dom Martène, *Thesaurus Anecdotorum*, vol. III, col. 797, from the Dunensis manuscript.)

## Preliminary Observations

The other history which we promised for the illumination of Belgian affairs is a brief chronicle of the monastery, or provostship, of Watin, of the order of Saint Augustine. Its author is Ebrard, a regular canon of that place, a disciple of Olfrid the founder, and consequently an eyewitness, who committed to writing events as he had seen them. His work, therefore, although brief, is not to be despised.

Indeed, we hope that what he reports concerning Countess Adela and Robert the Frisian, count and her son; what he reports concerning Drogo and Hubert, bishops of Tarwan; and what he reports concerning the abbots of the monastery of Bergues will be all the more pleasing to every reader because we believe such material is difficult to find elsewhere.

What he testifies to having seen concerning the ruins of the ancient and noble city of the Menapii ought to attract the reader’s attention all the more because it agrees especially well with the testimony of Orosius.

The Dunensis codex from which we copied this work bears only the title *Chronicle of the Guatin Monastery*, with no author named. But the name Ebrard, added to the first page by a later hand, clearly identifies him; nor do we doubt that he was also the author of the following little work concerning the miracle that occurred at Bruges in the year 1088, when Tamardus, a regular canon of Watin, was cured of paralysis through the merits of Saint Donatian. For the style is the same in both works.

That miracle is also mentioned in the *Acts of the Translation of Saint Donatian* in Surius under 14 October, and by Hariulf in book 1 of the *Miracles of Saint Richarius*, in Mabillon’s fifth Benedictine century.

Finally, the noble provostship of Watin continued under the rule of Saint Augustine until the erection of the bishopric of Saint-Omer. At that time it was entirely suppressed, its revenues being assigned to the episcopal table, which eventually passed to the English Fathers of the Society of Jesus.

# Chronicle of the Guatin Monastery

[Col. 1513]

[Col. 1513A] I have resolved, at your command, my father, to undertake a description of the origin of the Guatin church, in which, under the rule of canonical fellowship, I shall speak as the Holy Spirit grants utterance. First I shall set down a description of the place itself; second, traditions of ancient histories, or even those matters known more surely by sight or hearing. Thus, when they have heard of small matters—if such things delight anyone—they may more pleasantly grasp the order of the narrative and understand how, as they say, things gathered piecemeal from the smallest atoms have grown into a bodily mass.

They will also learn that I wish to disclose things long kept silent, to forge new accounts out of old matters, to restore ancient things from new ones, and to mingle not so much inventions as true and certain facts. I think that the ancient Batavi may be joined with the Guatinenses because we occupy their place, build up what they destroyed, and restore what is desolate. We therefore attain and hold, by hereditary right, their name—not borrowed, though altered by a few slight syllables—as will more readily appear on the following page.

But now, so that our undertaking may reach more broadly the sight of those who perceive each particular point, let us enter upon the limits of our discourse.

## 1. The Site of the Monastery

That there was once an extremely ancient town of the Menapii, now called Guatinas or Guatinum, is uncertain to no one who knows, according to the historians, the boundaries of that district or the situation of its territory. These people are also called Batavi by those knowledgeable about history; why this name was given them, as an auspicious sign of some notable matter or event, is unknown.

For Orosius says of them in his *Annals* (book 1), while describing the various situations of places and islands:

> “Britain, an island of the Ocean, extends lengthwise toward the north. To the south it has Gaul, whose nearest shore, as one crosses over, displays a city called the harbor of Rutupi, whence, not far from the Morini situated to the south, it looks toward the Menapii and the Batavi.”  
> [Note: [Col. 1513B] L. reads *aperit* (“opens”), rather than *apparet* (“appears”).]

Since, therefore, we know that the harbor of Rutupi is situated on the southern shore of that same island, and likewise that the Menapii and Batavi extend northward from the Morini, with the same sea dividing them, it is clear that, lying next to one another on the farther shore, they have a view of one another. There can therefore be no doubt that the Guatinenses are rightly called Batavi by writers.

If we pass over that epithet by which, because of a certain native ferocity, they were clearly marked out by authors among the other nations, the evidence cries out of Roman vengeance. The foundations of the walls are visibly torn away, and the buildings are partly ruined. The surviving traces of the ancient destruction testify that, the more they had been feared, the more cruelly they were uprooted by their enemies.

Nor did divine providence yet deem it enough that, at that first moment of overthrow, no pardon at all was granted to the hope of the remnants, even unto utter annihilation [lacuna]; rather, thereafter, through succeeding times, even the fragments of marble came to such desolation that wild beasts made their lairs where destroyed houses, if any had survived, might have restored memorials of habitation.

Thus, consumed by hostile devastation even through the Christian centuries, the place remained empty for so long an age, possessing nothing memorable except the antiquity of its desolate dwelling, which had spread over everything in every direction. Only one church, together with the hut of its cantor, stood out visibly amid brambles and the lairs of serpents, amid thickets and the complaining branches of birds, on the very summit, built in a most wretched fashion.

A very small assembly of the faithful frequently gathered there to hear the solemnities of the Mass. I myself once passed through the place, while still surrounded by courtly bustle, like a mimic stage, though as a cleric I was making a circuit, before the time of my visitation—or of my showing mercy to it—had arrived.

I remember, and it pleases me to remember, the diligence worthy of mention that the priest, Lord Alphuminus, displayed there, with what kindness he received us and how energetically he served us in the necessities that concerned us. One could see a man attentive in the humility of service and charitable, while I sat with the courtesy of modesty; so that one might easily foresee, by a kind of divine presage, the prophetic saying that would later profit us:

> “Behold, how good and how pleasant it is when brothers dwell together in unity!”

This was fulfilled by God’s providence not many years afterward, when the net of conversion drew us both to the harbor of the monastery that was later founded there. It came about that he, as later became clear, assumed the office of governance in that same place, and that after his passing the Guatin church received me, whom he had previously desired with many prayers.

## II. Description of the Place

Then, curious about the new appearance of things, I looked attentively to see what the careful work of the ancients had been in so broad a valley. I pitied the place and pitied its destruction, and expected nothing less than what we see today. Yet it was easily apparent that in its own days it had been famous, since so many monuments of destruction were still preserved there.

For the public and royal roads, converging from both sides, show how great the popular attendance and how great the concourse must once have been. One of these, directed toward us from the broad eastern region, is closed by a stream flowing beneath it. The other begins at a very high lighthouse—once called a watch-house during the winter quarters of the Romans—adjoining the wall of Boulogne and situated at the harbor of the Ocean, looking toward the British island of Deira. From the western side it ends at the same river mentioned above.

The local inhabitants, as ancient report relates, maintain that this river was fordable across both roads. But those who do not credit this prefer to marvel at it rather than believe it. For it is very deep, and by its depth not only supplies abundant fish to the surrounding inhabitants, but is also fit for navigation from the Ocean, which receives it as it flows in through many mouths; it provides both varied wares of merchandise and manifold catches for use.

From its bank a hill rises, its mass gradually increasing with gentle elevation. As it stretches out in a continuous plain toward the east, so it is piled high, with hollows lying to the north and south [Note: [Col. 1515D] The word *cumbae* is understood in different ways by medieval writers: sometimes as a tollhouse, sometimes as a small boat or ship, and sometimes as a sloping place. The last meaning seems most suitable here. —Unless one should read *tumbis*, that is, “mounds.”].

Covered with groves and rich in pastures, it does not produce wine. For this one benefit alone we allow the Gauls to mock us: because we drink fermented juice of grapes after it has been boiled, as though people who drink a milder liquor could not harmlessly awaken to the praises of God.

It is so fertile in fruit-bearing trees and in vegetables of various kinds for the use of those who serve, if it is cultivated, that, whether one wishes to tend useful plants or not, it germinates useless ones with remarkable growth, as though reproving the laborer’s laziness.

Moreover, it is exposed to winds that breathe so healthily that the flowing channel, gathering within itself, does not permit the harmful thickness of the tainted air or of the mists it exhales to coagulate.

## III.

This too is pleasing and worthy of imitation, and, in an insensible thing, almost a living lesson. For it hints, as though by a kind of divine oracle, that those who come together for common life should be formed for advancement according to these principles: namely, that, cultivated by the highest discipline, we should labor in the pursuits of holy living, lest—God forbid!—when we abandon the cultivation of our good purpose, abuses unworthy of our profession break forth.

Once we have gathered the resources of our life at the lofty citadel of the mind, the day, breathing healthily in the west, always sinks the misty shadows of this age into the setting sun. I call them shadows because, as someone swift to flee such darkness has said, whatever appears great in this age ought to be reckoned shadow or dream.

The beauty of the body, the wisdom of letters, the strength of the limbs, the insignia of dignities, and the power of kingship are proved to be shadows and dreams in comparison with that eternal day.

## IV.

Therefore, within the camp of the Church, in the warfare of the apostolic name—which, in the first campaign, initiated us, the poor of Christ, throughout the whole coastal region [Note: [Col. 1516D] From this one may gather that the Watin monastery was the first in those regions belonging to the order of the regular canons of Saint Augustine, which had originated in Gaul not long before. Hence, shortly below, he calls it an unprecedented novelty of the canonical order.]—we must live in such a way that, bound by the bonds of charity, with feet prepared for the Gospel of peace and the sword of the spirit drawn, we may overthrow the powers of the air.

Some we should correct by gentle admonition, others by sterner rebuke; by the example of our life, by our word, and by dwelling together in the city, we should always offer everyone, in every place, a life made more virtuous, as a good fragrance of God. By transmitting similar things to posterity for remembrance, we may be called—and may rightly be, by hereditary right—Batavi, as though heirs of a blessed ancestor, heirs of the primitive apostolic way of life.

And, to add something plausible in a scholastic manner, as knowledgeable people applaud one another, lest we ourselves be barren trees for the advancement of others: perhaps, while we were still absent, we remained as fruit hanging upon these trees; the springs themselves, the mountains themselves, and these groves themselves signified us.

## V. On the Founder of the Watinensian Monastery

Having lingered somewhat longer than seemed necessary over matters that required a brief departure from our subject, let us now bring forward the very founder of our monastery, whom we believe divine mercy caused to be sent from the regions of eastern Flanders to the aforesaid place for the work of God—not merely to lay its external foundations, but, like a wise architect, to arrange living stones of the sanctuary with precision in the spiritual building.

He was a cleric of religious life, adorned with priestly rank, a man worthy—not merely to be called Lord Otfrid—who was so thoroughly instructed in secular literature and divine matters alike that, apart from what we call grammatical learning, the books of the divine writings left by him among us clearly show how diligent an examiner of them he was. He industriously fulfilled every kind of distinction in their service to understanding, as he had heard among scholars concerning the Holy Scriptures.

But perhaps you, eager either to say or to hear something new, may object and reproach me for saying that he painted what was not his own. In this matter I challenge you yourself: “What do you have that you did not receive?” Or are the hidden things of Scripture not to be sought from those who contemplate God’s will more closely with the acuity of their minds? Are we not to follow the footsteps of those to whom divine testimonies have been revealed as they searched them out?

I do not say that an intellect without a teacher is not praiseworthy, but that it is a gift of inspiration and grace. Yet while certain half-learned men have peered through the narrowest cracks into philosophy’s chamber, they judge as contemptible what teachers have gathered unless it has been prepared with an academic flavor. I would rather condemn such men to ridicule, since through deceptive entertainments they prefer to chatter rather than to heed the instruments of the Holy Spirit—namely, the teachings of illustrious men.

Therefore, while he lived among us, we saw him abound in the greater goods of discipline precisely because he did not cloak, by human persuasion, moral instruments either invented or fabricated by himself. Rather, living religiously according to the authority of the Holy Fathers, he shone forth.

## VI. The Founder, Having Visited Various Monasteries, Chose Watinum Above Them

Moreover, because of his love for the preceding manner of life, he visited, with laborious circuit, the various dwellings of coenobites, like a man of desires; but although he had been specially directed to Guatinum, preferring our vegetables, modestly watered, to the wealth of riches and heavily laden dishes [Note: From this you may infer that the food of the first regular canons was exceedingly meager, and that they observed abstinence from meat; this is certainly established sufficiently from other evidence.], he remained fixed in none of them.

In the meantime, like a divine harvester, he gathered into the hive of his mind the most highly reputed elements of canonical discipline, plucked from every source, so that he might carry them into the granary of Holy Church and distribute provisions to those who would labor with him in the threshing, as food for grateful nourishment.

When, therefore, he came to the place described, as though he had completed the course and were about to receive the prize of the contest, he observed the solitude of the woods and judged that he had found a suitable hiding place for private living, protected from the inconvenience of passersby. Yet, as a farsighted provider of future life, he carefully reconsidered its several aspects. Like a bird already near giving birth and anxiously seeking where to place a safe nest, he pondered on one side the violence of the winds and on the other the voracity of the kites; here he anxiously considered whether cranes might at last settle high in the trembling branches, [the precise sense of the final phrase is uncertain] and there whether the leafy shelter would be suitable.

Thus, returning again and again for frequent inspection, and not satisfied with coming back only once or twice, he carefully examined the small dwellings for the sons whom he was already planning, in hope, to bring forth and associate with himself, lest so great an advantage of the place should in any way be wasted.

## VII. He Arranges for the Place to Be Freed from the Jurisdiction of the Bergues Monastery

But when he discovered that it was a dependency of the monastery of Bergues, he referred the matter to a certain eminent man of the province, A., the father, so to speak, of our beginning both in deed and in name. This man's equally honourable wife was, so to speak, the fruitful mother of our foundation. Unable by himself to carry through such a plan, Otfrid explained what he had resolved should be done in the aforesaid, formerly very confined settlement if it were ceded to that man.

Do not suppose that he ventured this with little confidence: was he really to approach, as a stranger approaching a stranger, a man known everywhere by reputation as wicked, proud, disorderly, and raging with something like bestial fury? Or would you not have thought that a man who punished many with chains could somehow, by one means or another, be made gentle toward you?

Yet he clearly dared to do so, and he had the good intention of persuading, rebuking, and teaching such men in every form of instruction, making them perfect so that he might turn them away from evil days. In this he was aided by God, the comforter of the sorrowing, who is able to raise up a son of Abraham, as though living, from a stone.

Although that man had often, with impunity, harmed many through carefully devised acts of wickedness and his habitual inclination to injure, and had frequently fined them without mercy, he is nevertheless to be praised for this: although it is exceedingly rare to learn that he had ever helped anyone in need, even in some small matter, he received this religious man honorably at his first approach, listened to him attentively, treated him with reverence, and, at his urging, willingly offered us possessions, lands, money, ornaments, and even himself above all else for service.

Such was the power of Olfrid’s verbal refinement: by gradually eroding the hardness of the man’s cruelty, it carved the gentle out of the cruel and the thrifty out of the wasteful, correcting his depravity.

When, therefore, he learned of his desire, partly through the prompting of his upright wife [Note: F., “at the prompting of”], and partly because of the unheard-of novelty of the canonical order which he had shortly before proposed should be established there, he devoted himself entirely to this undertaking, so that the place might be granted its freedom together with the annual revenues which he had been accustomed to pay to the men of Bergues. By this maneuver, ingenious as he was, and at the urging of our aforesaid administrator, he made the prudent men cautious by imposing silence.

## VIII. Richarius, a Morinensian Canon, with the Bishop’s Consent, Gave the Altar of Ledringehen

But since we wish no one to remain ignorant—whether those who do not wish to know or those who wish the matter to become known—we should make it clear, just as everyone knows from what lineage he comes, lest the sons who will be born at Guatinum likewise remain ignorant of the monastery’s origin.

A certain Richarius, one of the canons of Saint Mary of Thérouanne, had an altar at Ledringehen serving certain uses. Through that man’s cession, the layman obtained it by his prayers from the late Bishop Drogo, who then granted it to Lord Odfrid.

Not many days later, with its appurtenances and under a suitable arrangement, and with the same aforesaid bishop acting as intermediary, Ermenger, abbot of Bergues, and his monks accepted it for the uses of their monastery, together with the annual solidi which they were owed from Lord Odfrid, our abbot, in exchange for the church of Guatinum. Thus, as possession was exchanged on either side, whichever party had ceded it would thereafter retain the exchanged possession with perpetual security.

When this had been determined in a public synodal assembly, each man, acknowledging firmly and peacefully his own diocese with its proper rights, recognized that the dioceses had been exchanged and that the ratified cessions had been received. Thus we learned that Lord Odfrid had been announced [Note: F., “initiated”] from the very first entrance of his prelacy into the church of Guatinum; and, lest the matter be lost to posterity through concealment, we revive it here in such testimony for remembrance.

## IX. Odfrid First Gathers Disciples

The day had now arrived which he had long desired with a thousand prayers to see [Note: That is, “had eagerly sought”]. Having found the opportunity, he came from the city of the Thérouannais by a direct route to Guatinum, so that he might live canonically with those whom God would call to this harbor of the monastery’s quiet. Having established peace with those whom he found there and having also made an inventory, as the circumstances required, he united in one heart and one soul, with God as mediator, the venerable priest who had hitherto been cantor of that same church and whom, as has been said, we later saw become its prior, and began to live according to the rule.

## X

The aforesaid layman, himself a man of good character, valued this religious community highly. He asked, and obtained with great reverence, that he and his wife be received and enrolled into the fellowship of this brotherhood. Since he was an official of the forests surrounding us, he diligently assisted in the construction of cells, workshops, and necessary buildings, cheerfully managing machines and timber.

At that time the same man also offered forty-eight measures of cultivated land on the southern side beneath Mount Caleti, for the support of our church and for the redemption of himself and his wife. From the beginning he had tended the church like a foster-father tending an exposed child; he had set in order what had been neglected, supported what was lowly, restored what was weak, and splendidly adorned what was ragged. Now, once it had grown and was almost ready to be presented before all, he wished to strengthen it first with the dowry of this offering.

## XI. Various Donations Made at the Beginning of the Foundation

At that time also Lord Odfrid, our provost, gave twenty measures of land in the village of Aissengehem; Richard [Note: This Richard appears to have been the Morinensian canon who had already given the altar of Ledringehen.] the canon gave four measures at Walins; Bernold the canon gave ten measures at Petenham; Bedbert the canon gave five measures at Petenham; Herbert the canon and conversus gave sixteen measures at Sintina; Tainard and Everbold, canons, gave thirty measures; Alfunnius the canon gave ten measures at Brocsela; and Radulf the canon gave ten measures at Sintina.

Of these, we sold Richard’s four measures, as well as the canons Bernold’s and Alfunnius’s ten measures, in order to purchase the allod of John of Arras; and, as will be stated below, we exchanged them for a better possession.

Later, Rodulf the conversus gave thirteen measures of land and himself, together with his entire dwelling, to our church in the village of Ledersela. Gibbodo, a knight of Fleterne, gave twenty measures in the village of Thiggabust.

## XII. Countess Adela of Flanders, Together with Robert the Frisian, Count of Flanders, Confirms Everything and Adds Other Gifts to Those Mentioned Above. Confirmation by Drogo, Bishop of Thérouanne

To ensure that the dignity of eminent persons would not be lacking in confirming what had been begun, he approached Adela, countess of Flanders, namely the widow of Count Baldwin, buried at Lille. He explained to her what had been done and what he desired.

She, being tireless in encouraging advancement toward the better life, immediately went to her son, Count Robert, surnamed the Frisian, and most earnestly persuaded him that it would be good and salutary to assign something to men devoted to such a purpose. She did not desist until both of them had perpetually offered, for the remission of their sins, to God and the saints, for the use of those serving there in continence, the entire manorial estate called Ballenberge, on the western side of Mount Caleti beside the stream Pena, with all its appurtenances; moreover, two sheaves from the whole parish of Guatinum; and, around the churchyard, four day-lands of fiscal land for the attachment of small farms and dwellings.

This was done in the village of Sithiu, at the monastery of Saint Bertin, and was likewise confirmed in a public session of the synod of Thérouanne, with suitable persons standing by, in an episcopal charter with our same church, as is clear to those who wish to know, secured under an unshaken grant of freedom. Drogo the bishop presided, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1072, indiction 10, on the sixth day before the Ides of June, Friday.

## XIII. Countess Adela Laid the Foundations of the Monastery

The woman inspired from heaven was not yet satisfied in spirit. Indeed, she came to Guatinum and, like one of the humbler workers, remained at the task on a low bench among the masons and diggers, enduring the sun beneath the open sky. She laid the foundations of the holy building that still exists today, and, on departing this time, left through the hand of Lord Odfrid, our Father, a considerable sum for the expenses of the builders.

Indeed, so that the work might not be delayed and brought to completion after the funds she had previously sent had been exhausted, she arranged for the amount to be increased repeatedly—not once or twice, but many times—as we have learned from those who knew the matter.

At that time a large sum of money was recklessly and fruitlessly spent on constructing mills at Muggascota, a place which we received as a gift from the count, separated from the forest by the ditch we made.

## XIV. Through the Efforts of the Same Countess, the Land of Olderdesdit Is Acquired

Moreover, several years earlier John of Arras, a powerful man in his own rank and advocate of that province, had assigned to the same noble woman his allod—namely, large lands which he possessed in Flanders—for fifty pounds of solidi. From these lands, after establishing two cattle farms there, she received annual rents according to custom.

But wishing to make a spiritual investment from this usufruct, rather than merely profit from it, she applied her mind attentively to finding a way by which she could give our church perpetual legal possession of those same lands [Note: Add “give,” or something similar.].

They are situated in the parish of Exenboldescappla: twenty-three day-lands called Olderdesdit; and in the parishes of Stenen and Petingham, two hundred day-lands. In total they amount to two hundred and twenty-three day-lands, which we commonly call mansurae.

For this reason she approached John together with our brothers and urged him either to grant the aforesaid allod to the church of Guatinum for the redemption of his sins and those of his wife Ermentrudis, or to sell it at a merciful price.

At last she persuaded him and agreed on a payment: one hundred pounds, and, in addition, ten pounds annually for as long as they lived—namely, one hundred solidi from that church on the feast of Saint Martin and one hundred solidi fifteen days before Easter. The condition was that, when both had died, those ten pounds would thereafter be remitted perpetually to the church of Guatinum, without any claim for repayment, for their absolution.

Thus the devout woman wisely arranged for the purchase price to be more easily reduced to this total; nor could it be done otherwise. Therefore, since she had agreed to the ten annual pounds out of a desire to live longer, she took care to count them out annually.

As part of this debt, she immediately counted toward payment within the total of one hundred pounds the fifty pounds which John had lent her against the aforesaid allod, under the terms of the purchase and sale, just as she had granted them to our church at the beginning of the agreement, John consenting to this. The remaining amount—namely, the other fifty pounds needed to reach one hundred—we paid to him at great expense, scraping it together from every source.

## XV. The Acquisition Was a Heavy Burden for the Monastery

At that time we were so bound by an unbearable debt that, besides the lands we sold, even the books and ornaments of the church were disposed of. It seemed less burdensome to be stripped for a time of movable goods than, in the future, to fail to inherit such an extensive possession for our way of life.

With Count Robert the Frisian acting as intermediary, John publicly consented to and irreversibly approved this agreement in the full court at Pentecost in the fortress of Bergues. When the time came to make the gift and the manumission, however, his wife resisted, as though she were about to lose her dowry. Nevertheless, after she had extorted two ounces of gold from us, she permitted the transaction and lawfully completed it with her husband.

This transfer was made in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1075, indiction 13, on the eighth day before the Kalends of June, Monday of Pentecost, in the village of Bergues, by John of Arras and his wife Ermentrudis, over the relics of the church of Guatinum, in the residence and house of Gontier, the agent and servant of that same John, with the judges whom we call scabini in attendance:

Erembert of Cappla; Fredebold of Uggeshen; Dodinus, son of Tidbold of Werhen; Adalard Tire; Rodulf, son of Everard Nossalim; Lugelmar, son of Stanin, son of Inglemar Stanin; Lugelmar Albus; Ulric, son of Hermi; Eggafrid, son of Arnold of Stenen; Wabrard of Coldelkerke; Arnold, son of Elmenger; Malger, son of Wulfard; Wanka of Petengham; Odfrid, son of Renlof, son of Heregot; Heregot of Petengham; his brother Volrad; Godewin of Petengham; and Walter Voxbalg.

## XVI. Walter, Advocate of Bergues, Confirms It in the Prince’s Name

Since the count was occupied with judicial affairs, Walter, advocate of Bergues, was sent to the judicial court for this purpose. In the presence of the witnesses listed below, he accepted on the count’s behalf, for the use of the church of Guatinum, the gift, the stipulations, and the ratified undertaking, as is customary under the laws.

The witnesses were Walter of Bergues; Eustachius of Mesen; Lambert, his brother; Albert of Bellis; Giselbert, brother of Baldwin of Ghent, who had then come from England; Onulf the steward; Rodbert the cattleman [bouvier, “oxherd”]; Rodulf the chamberlain; Ragenfrid, his brother; Franco of Nivelles; Wago of Arras; Walter, son of Urso of Douai; Goiffrid, castellan of Cassel; Rodulf, his son; Rodulf Sapin; Azo of Stapris; Gerard the scabinus; Gilbodo, scabinus of Fleterne; Arnold, scabinus of Mue; and Arnold of Castra.

From Bergues: Folcrannus, castellan of Bergues; Boldravan, son of Lectra; Baldwin, his brother; Lectra, his brother; Hagabar, son of Stulard; Boldravan, his brother; Wizalo, his brother; Malgor, his brother; Bernold, son of Norbert; Norbert, his brother; Ravan, his brother; Arnold, son of Ravan; Hugo Roda; Odbert, his brother; Hugo Roda of Port; Walter, son of Odfrid; Remgor, son of Arnold the Black; Lugelmar, his son; Everard, son of Everard; Adalim, son of Vemard; Lem., son of Wulfard; Mankel Renger, his brother; Herebert, son of Denes; Bernold, son of Radulf; Gozemar Clenchant; Arnold Uggeshen; Camo of Trembold, son of Eggafrid; Eggafrid, his brother; Erembert, his brother; Erembert, son of Odo; Erembert, son of Onuakim; Reimlof, son of Godild; Hugo, his brother; and Erembold, his brother.

## XVII. John of Arras Confirms the Same Again in the Watinensian Church

After this, on the following day—that is, Tuesday of Pentecost—after the interval of a single night, John came. To lend still greater authority to this transfer, he repeated, in the presence of the judges, lawyers, and witnesses, everything which he had done at Bergues by gift, stipulation, ratification, promise, and surety. He willingly renewed it on the altar for the use of the church of Guatinum, and offered and manumitted it to God and to His saints Nicholas and Richarius [Note: Patrons of the monastery. The first church of Watinum was consecrated to Saint Richarius; when the monastery was built and the old church restored, Saint Nicholas was added as its second patron.].

The young Count Robert, son of Count Robert the Frisian, had been sent for this purpose by his father and grandmother and was present at this second transfer. As those knowledgeable in the law carefully dictated, he accepted for the legal benefit of our church, both by his father’s command and in his place, the gift, the stipulations, and everything else that properly belonged to such a transaction.

## XVIII

Thus the church of Guatinum acquired, through the repeatedly mentioned woman, the allod of John of Arras, which he appeared to possess in the aforesaid parishes. For it we paid, for nine continuous years without remission, the prescribed ten pounds annually, receiving them at his pleasure.

In the tenth year, after his wife had first died, he too was killed; but, after the C scuti of that year had already been paid, [the text is corrupt: “debiti nostri quinque”]. For if you calculate that the lands had cost us somewhat more than two hundred pounds from the beginning of the agreement and thereafter each year, as we have recorded, you will find that before John’s death they had cost us the same amount: add nine times ten pounds to the first one hundred pounds, and once one hundred solidi, and you will easily establish the figure in this record.

I think it will not be harmful to know this as we have set it out above. Indeed, it will be very useful for posterity to know that from that day onward we held the same possession firmly and peacefully.

## XIX. The Watinenses Are Disturbed by Various Calamities

The advances of our church which we have recorded thus far were always sprinkled with some bitterness, lest any benefit, however small, arise without being troubled in some respect, and lest we prove ungrateful for God’s gifts.

First of all, after we had begun to be one heart and one soul in God, the serpent, grudging the unity of the spirit and compelled to change its lodging, left among us serpents, the little vessels friendly to its deceit. Their number in these buildings was so great that they lived in swarms with the resident of that precinct—namely, the cantor of the former church—under the same hut.

Although they did not injure anyone with poisonous bites, they nevertheless polluted the small dwellings and every utensil with their trails [Note: L., “touches”]. At last they attacked the keeper with such an overwhelming invasion that, through excessive annoyance, they compelled him to abandon the place and change his dwelling.

You would have seen them, as those who report the matter assert, so tame that although they naturally used to avoid human encounters out of fear, they nevertheless often crawled forward with some inexplicable boldness between the feet of those sitting together. At other times they threw themselves headfirst from the roof through the tiles or through the opening in the roof of the hut; with a sort of domestic familiarity they climbed into the beds of some people; and, after making a hole, they wound themselves round and round inside the clothing.

Whenever they were discovered there, they did not seek hiding places like creatures caught in the act. Rather, as though dutifully yielding to their masters, they seemed temporarily to give way, from one side, in their changed dwelling.

They also watched for the time of meals, lest either dinner or supper pass without their participation. Sometimes they prepared, like trained creatures, to climb onto the very table, unless they were kept away by force or frightened off.

Thus the days were spent in fear of their sudden entry whenever they were least expected, and the nights were regarded as wholly suspect. For these reptiles, as it became known from those who reported and understood such things, customarily lie in wait for sleepers with open mouths, so that if they observed any opening, as can happen when limbs are loosened in sleep, they might enter human bodies. It was scarcely safe to sleep unless a ball of cleaner cloth had been stuffed around the mouth or the face had been wrapped in a covering.

Whenever, contrary to their nature, they were forced to return to their hiding places by cold or some discomfort of the air, you would see some men armed with stakes and spears, others with poles and stones, besieging the burrows that had been discovered. While some pressed them from above with dung heaps, others received them as they emerged and destroyed them by various deaths.

But when God had perhaps summoned us to this dwelling so that it might be cleansed by a deadly plague—or rather, so that the inner chambers of His dwelling might be cleansed in us—such portents sometimes passed through the innermost parts of our cloister by an unobstructed course, so that they frequently occupied the brothers’ seats, invaded the storerooms, and often blocked the paths of those walking.

## XX

At that time there was among us a certain young brother who, I believe, was bolder than the others through a divine impulse. Whoever he encountered, while others trembled at the mere sight, he punished without mercy.

Since the matter presents itself, I thought it not inappropriate to record a humorous and memorable triumph, so that when older men hear how, under some unknown impulse, a younger age was moved to do something through the steadfastness of simplicity, they may, armed without hesitation by the protection of faith, understand what they themselves may dare in Him who gives power to trample on scorpions and serpents.

One day, while he was sitting in the cloister with some task before him, a serpent of unusual size, at least by comparison with those ordinarily seen, suddenly crawled before his feet. When he noticed it creeping while the others were pale with fear, he immediately attacked it, though unarmed, trusting in the same spiritual impulse that was usual with him. He seized it with his bare hand in the middle, lifted it rigid as though it were a weapon, and pierced a solid wall standing beside him with such ease that it was as if he had thrown some missile in place of the serpent.

When I later asked what he had done with that living dart of his, he replied that it had remained hanging through the pierced wall, on both sides, until he followed it, learned the outcome of the deed, and killed the beast.

I therefore began to marvel, as the matter seemed worthy of wonder. He nevertheless insisted that he had perfectly established that there had not previously been even the smallest opening in that portion of the wall through which the serpent had passed.

Moreover, not relying solely on the credibility of the event, but lest anyone attribute such a thing to a power unknown through slanderous report, he asserted that there are snakes of this kind whose sharply pointed faces would pierce any wooden wall without difficulty if anyone attempted it.

But I would be more inclined to believe the most eloquent historians, who suppose that this serpent, called the dart, lives only in parched Libya or in Arabia’s fertile fields, and that, when it is angered and launches itself, no defensive equipment can preserve one's safety.

Whatever opinions anyone may devise about this event, and whatever excuses anyone may offer for refusing to believe it, I would call it nothing other than a sign of divine power and a hidden presage of some future benefit.

Let no one prejudge that I have fabricated these things as they are committed to writing, since I heard them from the lips of those who, though often terrified, had both the opportunity to see them and the ability to be present.

## XXI

The devil, the seedbed of every iniquity, added temptations against us, being still permitted to stir up arms because our sins demanded it. Having produced a swarm of mice, he infected and defiled all the small workshops with such violent corruption that, apart from what could be eaten according to nature’s ordinary allowance, the bedding of the beds, clothing, towels, altar cloths, divine books, and, without restraint, vessels, wooden chalices, and boxes of sacrificial bread together with the bread itself were ruthlessly gnawed. They scarcely seemed, as was feared, to refrain from human flesh.

Perhaps, however, this impending adversity was a nearby sign of what would follow: after escaping the teeth of unclean animals, we were to be assigned, as indeed happened, to endure the bites of clean ones.

## XXII

For this inconvenience was followed by suspicion, stirred up against us by almost the whole province, and especially by the clergy. We appeared more zealous than others in observing the apostolic commands—namely, in refusing to accept married priests for the celebration of Mass, in avoiding incestuous and simoniacal men, and in observing the other chapters distinguished in the decree of Pope Gregory VII.

For this reason they pursued Lord Odfrid with hatred, insults, and curses as though he were the instigator of this agitation. In addition to the reproaches he suffered outside while preaching the word of God everywhere, the neighboring provincials and clergy threatened us daily at home with slaughter, fires, and deadly destruction.

Thus there were battles outside and fears within; scarcely an hour of security in our life. From one side we feared stones, from another arrows, and from elsewhere flames consuming everything.

## XXIII

But God, foreseeing the dangers to come, placed before us the shield of protection, lest, whenever they descended upon us because our sins demanded it, the whole place should be left desolate without hope.

For the aforesaid woman of outstanding virtue conceived the noble intention of hastening to Rome, to the thresholds of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul. Taking our aforesaid provost with her in that company, she brought him to Gregory VII, of blessed memory.

From him she received, after the cession of the bishop of Thérouanne had been offered, a privilege of Saint Peter solemnly granted for the confirmation of our church. Going safely and returning safely, she brought it all the way to us.

## XXIV

Enriched by these Roman resources, we thought we would live more peacefully. But our adversaries, regarding everything as done to their offense and becoming irritated like a barbed army, rose against us all the more fiercely.

Secretly conferring among themselves, they stirred up the heads of the clergy and the bishop himself. They accused our provost of having received, through a Roman rescript, authority to bind and loose. They claimed that, strengthened by such a privilege, episcopal jurisdiction was being destroyed; that henceforth the bishop would function only in name; that the men of Guatinum would command; that high and low would be reversed; that everything was turned upside down, the head into the tail; that nothing remained except the episcopal mitre; and that all was finished unless Guatinum were completely overthrown.

They raised many similar accusations, enough to compel even the holiest minds to seize the weapons of justice. At last, taking the opportunity provided by an assembly of the clergy, they ordered the privilege to be presented.

It was brought forward and read. Then, as though it were forged, it was dragged and seized with violence and insult, without law and without judgment, and locked in the bishop’s chest. They treated our provost, who had brought it, with insults and stripped him without justification. Without even allowing him further opportunity for defense, they dismissed him condemned without a hearing, according to the cries of the confused tumult.

## XXV

Why should I recount every detail? What grief, disgrace, insults, attacks, threats, terrors, and mockery our church endured in the meantime, while, stripped of its head and clothed in the garments of widowhood, it awaited the time of restoration?

Nevertheless, it was consoled by the steadfastness of the remaining sons, because they bore themselves manfully amid all the misfortunes that had occurred. They did not stray from the royal road of canonical life; rather, acting on behalf of themselves and the place, and judging that nothing could be placed above a Roman decree, they recovered their strength and went to the bishop themselves.

They begged, demanded, and reproached him: Why had he made the church of Guatinum an object of ridicule and acted without law? Why was he attempting, through the machinations of wicked men, to destroy what he himself had made? Why had he dared to take away the privilege, when the church of Guatinum had not presumed to obtain it by furtive usurpation? Its grantor was still alive, and what had been permitted by his own conscience and by the cession of the Roman pontiff ought not to be altered.

They had been convicted by no objection or accusation, yet had been made guilty by pretense rather than testimony. If he wished to examine the guilty, he would find himself to be the one who had inflicted the injury, not those who had suffered it; he would discover himself deserving punishment, while those who had been punished were undeserving of it.

Let him at last be willing to restore what had been taken away, to return the dispossessed to their own jurisdiction with their property restored, and, after shamefully rejecting the father, not to disregard the cause of the orphans.

The Guatinenses had already been proclaimed throughout land and sea by the pride and slander of the wicked—enough, and more than enough. The envious had now advanced to the limit of their oppression. No hope seemed left for the future except the epitaph of misery and weeping.

Yet the wretched ought to become all the more pitiable before the judge in every case precisely because they are oppressed by their rivals. Above all, however, it must be considered that those who impiously act against the divine laws will not long escape unpunished.
