But if these events can be shown to be Neronian times—times which, although they consumed Peter, nevertheless preserved his faith under testimony—then, amid the present disorder, if the reins of even slight injustice are loosened, what else will follow but the shattering of the foundations of the whole faith, despite Truth itself crying out, “I have prayed for you, Peter, that your faith may not fail”? The concluding clause is syntactically corrupt, but reads: “which the impiety of unbelievers left undefiled, [of] the same one whose faith will not cease, even against Truth, to erase covenants.”

## XXVI

The son of the Holy Roman Church, L., a canon of Saint-Omer, was involved in this dispute. We know that he had spent considerable time in the sacred palace with Gregory VII, of venerable memory, and we saw that he had traveled abroad magnificently.

Having opened the written Roman letters, he examined their contents with a sharper understanding, like a familiar associate who had for some time gathered extracts. He then resolved their meaning without difficulty through a sound interpretation, and, closing the mouths of those who resisted, convincingly demonstrated by abundant reasoning that the honored privilege should be restored to the church of Guatinum.

Thus restored and gratefully returned to our former condition, we thereafter learned of no one who attempted to traffic in our freedom through any further disturbance.

## XXVII. The Watinenses’ restraint in adversity. Bishop Drogo of Thérouanne dies

At that time, when numerous councils were being held in various sees throughout Gaul and many things were being corrected by Hugh of Die, legate of the holy Roman Church, the clergy of Morini, through the simplicity of their aged bishop, were behaving with such impunity toward us and others as the circumstances of the time allowed. Nevertheless, we try to excuse them on the grounds that, since we were suffering far less than the envious insinuation of certain people demanded, their spirit scarcely withdrew from us—while preserving episcopal reverence—in our defense.

But in all these matters that some people, as destroyers of peace, were suggesting—matters certainly deserving punishment if we had wished to take vengeance on those who were pressing us—we never on that account offended the venerable gray hairs of so old a priest. Nor, amid such frivolity of conduct, did we appeal to councils or judge with any insolence that a sentence should be hurled against him. With such gentleness we restrained our agitation within ourselves, although amid manifold complaints and the perversities of our accusers he had injured us as our enemies urged him to do.

Indeed, Roman piety—which we supported in this same matter and which is always accustomed to receive those who labor into the lap of mercy—regarded him as one of its veterans. Although he was weakening the condition of the commonwealth in certain respects, it bore with him maternally, because, weighing his simplicity together with his old age, it seemed all the more solicitous and apprehensive for him the more he surpassed others in knowledge and discernment and, being full of days, drew daily nearer to death. In fact, not long afterward he died in the fiftieth year of his episcopate.

## XXVIII. The archdeacon Hubert succeeds him

Hubert, archdeacon of the same Church, was appointed to his see: a man of distinguished learning and worthy of authority, if only—as they say—he could have ruled himself, a matter that has often brought many powerful men to destruction. Once he had obtained the priesthood, he energetically devoted to the maintenance of his Church its possessions and altars, which, together with his failing predecessor, had themselves fallen into decay. Since he intended to restore them as though they were being brought back to life, he began to be regarded by many as a man of good promise, who would provide usefully for the episcopal revenues.

If what he had bestowed had remained preserved, we would to this day be proclaiming his successors fortunate bishops: they would not have lacked the means of support, nor would the patronages of holy places—sold through simony to disgraceful persons and used by their mercenaries to support pitiable means of livelihood—have been dispersed contrary to the Holy Spirit.

## XXIX. How he conducted himself in the episcopate

If, with such beginnings, he had adjusted the rest of his conduct during his episcopate to the places and persons appropriate to the time, he would have suffered fewer misfortunes and possessed more dignity. But when appointing certain persons, relying more on the freedom of grace by which he believed he had been promoted than on discretion, he took the helm of his office disastrously and struck against people of higher rank.

For, after first casting aside several others whom he could have trusted, he ultimately provoked the very prince of all Flanders to his own ruin for this reason. When E., abbot of the monastery of Bergues, had returned from the Council of Poitiers, where he had been deposed by Lord Hugh, the Roman legate, and the monks had graciously obtained permission from the prince, disagreement arose among them. After a dispute had been maintained for a long time, they could not come to an agreement because of their rivalry over advancement.

To settle this matter, the prince summoned W., archbishop of Vienne, who had happened to arrive in those days and was regarded as one of the foremost regular clergy of the monastery of Cluny. He was to determine, by the rule of the canons and on the basis of his advice, whom the prince should appoint as father of the church that had been deprived of its head.

## XXX. The prior of Watten recommends Ad., a monk of Saint-Airy of Verdun, for election as abbot of Bergues

At this assembly our prior put forward Ad., a religiously disciplined monk of the monastery of Saint-Airy of Verdun, under the rule of Saint Benedict.

> **Note:** In the series of the abbots of Bergues there is no one whose name begins in this way; but after Ermengerius there follows Manasses, of whom the necrology of Saint-Airy says: “On the fifth day before the Kalends of May, Manasses, abbot of the monastery of Bergues, died.” John [Iperius] writes above that he was also appointed in succession to Abbot Ermengerius on the authority of the count, whose relative he was. Thus either the author or the copyist suffered a lapse of memory, or Manasses had two names.

The prior said that Ad. had come to our church’s guesthouse a few days earlier in order to visit acquaintances and was staying there, as though sent by God. If it pleased them to promote him, it would be a safe choice, and one could not despair of progress in good conduct under a man who had philosophized strictly in the monastic habit for a considerable time and with such honorable behavior.

He added that grave danger threatened if he consented to those unwilling to live according to the rule: he would share in the sins of others if he did not restrain rebellious and contentious men from acting according to their own judgment. He urged them to recognize that the matter had already reached this point and to take care lest the place suffer harm without a rector, and lest the sacred order that had perished among them return to them, even if only late, through a regular appointment.

## XXXI. The prince of Flanders approves the election

The prince, a man highly capable of reasoning, allowed this to be done, both with the authority of the archbishop and with the assent of his mother, the countess, provided that Ad. could be detached from his monastery by the resignation of his abbot.

When some of the monks persisted to a certain extent in their obstinacy, others, taking a sounder view and considering their salvation with fear of God, set aside personal ambition and, in accordance with the just will and request of the prince, desired that such a man be placed over them.

They therefore returned to the father of the monastery of Saint-Airy of Verdun, whom the prince’s envoys had visited, and reported that the resignation could be secured by no intercession unless the brother returned obediently to the cloister. When the prince had likewise canonically received him after the embassy had been completed, he granted him permission to preside over the monastery of Bergues, with every form of promotion customarily carried out by lay authority removed.

## XXXII. The bishop of Thérouanne refuses to consecrate the elected man

Meanwhile certain [lacuna] monks had approached Hubert, bishop of Thérouanne. Just as they feared that they themselves would be subjected to the law of God, so they opposed the prince’s intention by turning the bishop’s mind against it, using deceptive schemes to prevent, by whatever means, what had been set free from being confirmed.

Although they attempted to achieve what they sought against justice with considerable cunning, their persuasion did them no good, because it brought upon them the hostility of the aforementioned lady and the prince’s son, even if the bishop had learned to exercise the episcopate only for himself.

When the rest of the brothers, in accordance with the canonical decrees, presented their elected man to be consecrated to the pontifical see, Hubert refused. He publicly forbade it, lest such an elected man—because he was not his own—should oppress the church that supported him.

## XXXIII. He excommunicates the prior together with the elected man

Thus, having left unfinished the business for which they had come, he disgracefully drove them from their place of audience, like triflers, to the prince’s insult, and allowed them to return as objects of ridicule.

Nor did he yet consider that he had carried out the impulse of his mind so thoughtlessly. Instead, against the elected man and our prior, who had come with him and seemed to be the adviser in this affair, he imposed the curse of anathema in place of the blessing they had requested.

Nor did he do this only once or twice. Wherever he was accustomed to conduct solemn litanies, he repeatedly proclaimed the bond of excommunication that he had imposed on them, as though commending what he had done to the prince’s memory through repeated scandal and publicizing it to their disgrace.

## XXXIV. The elected man is presented by the prince himself to Hugh of Die for blessing

The prince, wise in the manner of Solomon, restrained his spirit and reserved the matter for the future. He did not protest against the insult in words; but, as the saying goes, “For what you intend, ingenuity is sufficient” (Sallust).

Nor did he alter his purpose in any respect. With the solemnity of a decree, strengthened by the subscriptions of all who had petitioned and supported by his own document, and with the archbishop of Vienne likewise agreeing in his own letters, he sent the same elected man without delay to Lord Hugh of Die, to be ordained for the monastery of Bergues.

When the elected man asked Hugh to release him from the bond imposed by the bishop of Thérouanne, the cardinal is said to have given this reply:

> “I ought to consider rather the cause of the crime inflicted than the punishment of an unjust sentence. A rash sentence can have no force against one who knows inwardly how greatly a pastor’s fictitious condemnation differs; therefore that in which no culpable act was committed has no need of absolution: let him remain in peace and no longer believe himself deprived of apostolic communion.””

## XXXV. After receiving the blessing, he sets out for Rome to be confirmed by the supreme pontiff

After receiving the blessing, they returned to the prince once the business had been completed. Hubert of Thérouanne, however, had not changed his mind and persisted in his former decision. Those whom he had previously deprived of communion, before any securely established authority had been exercised against them, he now marked even more harshly with the wrinkle of anathema because of their contempt for him.

Seeing that the matter was being stirred up further by the bishop’s ingratitude, the prince considered how the Church might be protected, so that he would not suffer loss through the forfeiture of any of the many ecclesiastical benefices he held in the episcopate as a result of this vengeance.

He therefore summoned L., canon of Sithiu, who, as has already been said, was well known among the leading men of the sacred palace. He sent the same abbot swiftly to Rome as his own representative and messenger, and obtained from Lord Pope Gregory for that monastery a most secure privilege against all invasions and exactions.

Not long afterward, however, this privilege, together with the church itself, disastrously opened the way for entering through simony. Since it cannot be briefly explained how this happened, and since it does not pertain to the present matter, I have judged it better to pass over it and proceed with the arrangement of my narrative.

## XXXVI. A serious dispute between the prince of Flanders and the bishop of Thérouanne

Hubert of Thérouanne was still not restrained by the Roman Church’s repudiations. He saw that the abbot had been ordained, as has been said, and that the privilege had been confirmed on his behalf. He also understood that the bond of anathema which he had imposed on the abbot and our prior had been annulled. Yet he anxiously concealed what he should do and where he should turn.

Although he was suspicious of himself lest he reach the outcome toward which the matter was tending, he nevertheless pressed forward what he had once begun, shamelessly piling one thing upon another. The prince, for his part, judged that those who had gone to the cardinals and to Rome were of no help to him; consequently, he too, both personally and through his representatives, unanimously avoided the bishop’s communion—a prohibition which did not harm them. He therefore unanimously avoided the bishop’s communion, both personally and through his representatives.

For this reason he persecuted our prior with greater hatred, alleging that the source of the entire peace that had been destroyed between himself and the prince had grown from the prior: that he had nourished the seed of discord, obstructed reconciliation, and conspired with those who had been deposed by him.

Whenever he could do so under the guise of religious observance, he daily directed the weight of this hostility against our church. We, on the other hand, cut off with every precaution even the smallest opportunities for harm, lest anything cling to us anywhere. Thus we did not even communicate with our prior, although he had been unjustly interdicted by the bishop and although it would otherwise have been honorable to do so.

## XXXVII. The prior voluntarily resigns his priorship in order to calm the bishop

Since no compliance, no dutiful attendance, and no other means could finally soothe his hostile mind, we feared that the little which we seemed to possess might be damaged in some way—or, worse, that the place might be entirely deserted because of these quarrels.

We therefore agreed by common counsel that, following the advice of Lord Pope Gregory VII, our prior should surrender his office. If the matter tended toward a more destructive outcome, or if persons of greater rank united the parties who were at odds with one another, we did not want to be punished for having ignored the fact that these wealthy men had been behaving outrageously toward one another.

For that memorable man, having heard about his arrival and the order of events, had already sent us a page of his writings, strengthened by apostolic freedom. In it he instructed that, with his support before the memory of the apostles, the prior should govern the church for a time. Since he could not altogether avoid giving an account of what had been entrusted to him and what he had received on its behalf, he was to appoint in his place, without delay, a suitable person whom God would assign to the place and who could undertake the whole responsibility.

He himself, released from the honor of the priorship, was to remain in the same order, subject and obedient for fear of almighty God to the man whom he and the brothers’ election placed over them.

## XXXVIII. The bishop delays accepting his resignation

He, desiring in the fear of his heart not to be associated with an honorable title, declared with the greatest devotion that he wished to undertake the name of a private person. He most kindly determined that the cause of the impending danger should be removed, saying that it concerned himself.

A written petition was therefore sent to the same bishop of Thérouanne. In accordance with the interval granted by Lord Pope Gregory, we asked him, since he refused to continue that administration, to appoint another in his place whom we could elect. But the bishop delayed according to his own will and refused for the time being to assist the church’s resignation.

He was cautious in this matter, lest, by removing the prior from his subjection as though he were opposed to fornicators, he should make him more hostile and bolder toward those whom the bishop himself was defending—men whom he had often chastised severely in his zeal for continence.

## XXXIX. A new prior is elected

Once the reason for the delay had become known, we postponed nothing further and elected our man. When our former prior presented him to the pontifical see, he surrendered his office and had the elected person appointed as his successor with every mark of favor, while remaining unharmed himself. He subjected himself to him in complete obedience as a disciple of Christ.

We venerated in him such a grace of humility and glorified God, because just as we had seen him for many years support the monastery’s advancement without false glory, so we recognized that, without grieving over the dignity he had laid down, he retained an upright mind with equanimity.

Formerly, common legumes and dishes of no greater distinction, neither large fish nor large fowl, neither more ambitious clothing nor a softer bed, nor higher-stacked supports, had lifted up his spirit. So now the sighs over what he had lost did not disturb him. For as prior, and afterward as a private person for as long as he lived, he received everything according to the same measure as we did.

## XL

He left among us this memorable pattern of restraint, compounded, so to speak, from the sweetness of a twofold order: that at the beginning no one should be elevated by the dignity of the master’s office, nor should humility burden one placed in a subordinate position with the desire to rise.

For while he was in authority, he wished to preside in such a way that, to the extent that he appeared superior in rank within the order, he bore an equal contempt for himself in humility. Therefore he was able to submit without indignation. The exaltation of his mind had not raised him up when he had shortly before been placed in honor; and, having become lower in rank while remaining in a moderate way of life, he did not disdain to be a disciple, because he had not wished to exalt himself from the place where he had been greater in dignity.

## XLI

He governed the church, from the year in which he founded it—1072 from the Incarnation of Christ—for seven years, eight months, and six days. We have set out in part how many attacks by the envious he endured, because we judged it tedious to record at length the disturbances by which he was almost daily battered on account of his administration of the divine word.

During his time I did not wish, by a condensed account, to retrace the lands that were donated to our place through generosity, so that even the fastidious might learn without burden what it would have been burdensome to seek through individual exceptions in the preceding discussion.

> **Note:** Olfrid died at Ghent and was buried in the monastery of Saint Peter at Blandinium, as we learn from Hariulf’s *Book of the Miracles of Saint Richarius*, chapter 1, where he is called a most holy man and a revelation concerning his glory is reported. His successor was Bernold, the provost, who in 1087 attended the funeral of Saint Arnulf, bishop of Soissons. I believe this is the same Bernard as the provost of Watten who attended the Council of Reims in 1092, where he is mistakenly called provost of Warhem. John Iperius discusses him in the *Chronicle of Saint Bertin*, chapter 39, and also with Bernold, provost of Watten, who in 1114 subscribed the charter of Clarembald concerning possessions granted to the monastery of Saint Bertin at Leustinghen, in volume [illegible] of our *Anecdota*, page 134.

# PREFACE

## Concerning the miracle of a certain canon of Watten cured by Saint Donatian

[Col. 1533]

When, venerable prelate, you had come a few days ago to the ancient city of the Morini on matters of pastoral concern, and, after your arrival had been solemnly welcomed by the public assembly of the clergy and people, you recognized me among the others through the earlier familiarity by which I was accustomed to be known to you. You kindly invited me, asked carefully about my condition and what I was doing there, and I explained it to you: I had already been stripped of secular impediments and had passed over to the regular and apostolic life, for which God is sufficient, in the monastery of Watten.

You received this gladly and paternally. Praising my purpose, you restored me, as I wavered, by the encouragement of your exhortation. Then, in the common conversation that was being held about the consolation of our church, you turned to certain miracles that God had recently wished to perform in it, to the joy of many. As is the custom of a wise man, who investigates more carefully good things heard only once, you learned from the father of my monastery, who was present, how these events had occurred and in what order.

You asked me with very devout insistence to arrange them in writing, so that you might have a place where, rereading the signs of so great a predecessor, you could reconsider his merits and recall how great he is with God. In this way he might direct you as his successor in his metropolitan church and see, reconcile you as shepherd together with your flock, and reconcile you also with his own supreme shepherd.

I embraced this heartfelt desire and had no intention of resisting, lest refusal seem an injury to so great a person. But with the light affection of children—who, when their parents allow them to travel, promise themselves that longer journeys will be easier—I agreed to your wish.

If, while reading, you accept the effectiveness of the commission despite the uncultivated style, do not therefore withdraw from carrying this burden as though it had been lightened. For if any breeze of opposition should blow while you read, you may offer me the apologetic excuse that I am navigating under the oar of the lord archbishop of Reims, not under my own. Thus you will share the danger with me: I shall be at risk because of the weakness of the work’s execution, while you shall be at risk because you ordered it.

Since, therefore, you ordered one who wished to remain hidden to come forth into public view, know the reciter of this little work under this condition: when attacked by vicious men, he too must be defended by you. For there are many—may their Donatian and God be their portion among the saints in light—who, as soon as they learn that I have emerged from the hiding places I chose into such public appearance before you, will weave, I suspect, what accusations and opportunities for harm.

Your acquaintance, which I formerly enjoyed in a way that was pleasing to you, once harmed me in the eyes of certain people. While I was trying to cleanse the Church of their foul greed and lamentable corruption of morals, I nearly perished amid Zeno’s tortures, Plato’s envy, and Socrates’ poison.

Even now I fear that it has not been wholly exhausted: although, through my absence, this aconite had begun to be uprooted, if I appear it may resume its growth from a revived shoot. I am not lying. For, as a certain wise man says, I deny that there is any good that harms its possessor.

Therefore I maintain that the satieties, honors, various riches, and delights of fortune that mortals admire in the world are inferior to the few and measured necessities of the holy Church. For just as the one to whom Christ and the Church are sufficient possesses the whole abundance of riches, so I believe that the one whom the devil and money exalt is always in need.

Because I regard you as a true lover of riches, I arrange these shells of the treasure of this saint’s virtues while sharing them with you. Do not distinguish from which single steward you receive them; retain in yourself only what he presents, so that it may touch the inner parts of your mind with a tasteful savor.

In this, by allowing little ones to come to you, you display the form of humility commanded in the Gospel. Like a man of desires, you heap up within yourself a rich knowledge in hope, with an even greater abundance of varied delights of merchandise, insofar as, without respect of persons, you weigh with impartiality what good each person brings.

Since these things are so, you also arrange yourself and your affairs with the same constancy in your actions. To pass over other matters, before those whom we know to be your neighbors, you rise like a stronger battering ram against the enemies of Mother Church, for the destruction of their fortifications. You scatter some rising storms with the thunder of your word; you calm other whirlwinds of tempests; and wherever you encounter something clouded by ignorance or the darkness of error, you wipe away the gloom and restore it by the hand of teaching to the rule of understanding.

Hence that metropolis of Reims, glorious from the first seedling of the faith and still glorious now under your episcopate, shines clearly in reality as well as in appearance. It excels as a teacher of cities in the height of its governance and likewise in the supreme religious devotion of its ruler and most worthy clergy. As has been experienced in many cases, whenever it finds those shipwrecked in matters of faith, it either drives them away or converts them.

When the character of Reims is so strict and so devoted to preserving honor, trembling seizes my poor pen at the thought of writing anything that might come among those who flourish in Ciceronian eloquence. But since I do not deny that it is right to serve one’s superiors, I submit this writing, whatever it may be, at your command, to be placed in the hands of those who, the greater they are in talent, are, I fear, the more reliable judges in every circumstance.

Therefore let your presence commend this work through its wisdom of expression and elegance of speech, rather than through its style, cause, or subject matter, so that what is alien to the truth of the matter may not, because it had to be written and ought not to have been left unsaid, exclude its fault from pardon.

Moreover, it ought to be received with gratitude to report new signs concerning so great a patron for remembrance. If some of his former signs have perhaps perished through the passage of time, they may have been lost both because of the scarcity of notaries and, as I more readily believe, through the ancient devastation of the church archive over which you preside.

Furthermore, just as servants treasure things for their masters, or children for their parents, so, however small, slight, or rustic the things they bring may be, they are received as the first fruits of their own labor, while those to whom they have been given return a reciprocal service in benefits.

# A MIRACLE CONCERNING A CERTAIN RELIGIOUS OF WATTEN CURED OF HIS ILLNESS BY SAINT DONATIAN

[Col. 1535]

The miracles of the saints—by which they either shone in the world through bodily presence, or those consumed by such afflictions return daily to their bones and memorials—show us what the saints themselves were by the merit of their lives, and invite us to the heavenly homeland to which they have passed to receive heavenly joys.

They live there because they live happily. Having already become citizens of the Jerusalem that will endure, they still visit the guests of this habitation, which will be dissolved, in such a way that they never depart in will from that dwelling in which they truly rest.

They also show that they can obtain what is requested of them, since they grant the petitions of those who ask. If they did not live there happily, they would not be able to give such gifts to those who sigh toward them.

From this common court of angels and human beings, which has already become one commonwealth through adoption, Christ the King presides over the individual peoples. So that his body, which is the Church, may always have vigilant sentinels guarding its pilgrimage and may not carelessly fall into the snares of its envious enemy, he seeks his sheep through these rulers, according to the prophet’s prediction: to bring back what has been cast away, to bind up what has been broken, to restore what has been weakened, and to preserve what is fat and strong.

Among these rulers, he has assigned to us one of the many whom he has glorified through different gifts: Donatian, the most holy confessor, an experienced steward of his household, for the people of our shores; a faithful guide before the flock, a frugal nourisher, a receiver of vows, a cheerful giver in all things, a holy dispenser of abundant healing, and a most holy guardian of lasting salvation.

He shines with miracles not only where the treasure of his venerable body is honored, but has also often become known beyond the limits of his territory through signs of miracles. We have undertaken to make known some memorable examples of these, which earthly preoccupation—always caring for its own concerns, not those of Jesus Christ—has carelessly erased through forgetfulness, rather than any lack of writers having done so.

We have learned that some memorable examples of these were performed three years ago in our church of Watten through the same patron. We trust that the gifts of speech are granted by the one who gives tongues as a gift.

There is therefore a district between the River Leye and the Flemish coast, called Menapia, whose inhabitants are generally called Menapi by historians. It is an ancient and rugged people, whom even the Romans, as the history of the ancients records, were unable to subdue.

This people is not found to have been introduced from some foreign blood, but has the same place as both its settlement and its origin. In ancient times they were divided among themselves by very strong and walled towns, and from the beginning they divided the common dominion of the district into the names Caleti and Batavi.

The district itself extends in length toward the east and is bounded on the west by the River Enula, where it reaches its end. From its bank, as a mound gradually rises, a hill is formed with gentle height; then, sloping down over level ground toward the east, it rises in height through the valleys lying to north and south.

Covered with woods and rich in pasture, it is so fertile in various kinds of vegetables that, whether one wishes to cultivate useful plants or not, it produces useless ones with marvelous growth, as though reproving the laborer’s laziness.

It is also so healthfully exposed to the blowing of the winds that the same channel through which the air of infection or the waters of gathering mists are exhaled does not permit their thickness to coagulate within it.

It is also easy to see how populous and celebrated the place was in former days, since public and royal roads that converge there are still visible. One of these, directed toward us from the spread-out east, is closed by a channel running beneath it; the other, looking toward Britain, ends in a harbor of the Ocean from the west.

On this hill, once a colony of the Batavi according to the testimony of history, our church of Watten is now situated. It was founded from its roots by a certain religious man named Odfrid.

The beginning of the good way of life that he proclaimed there among harsh and uncultivated people gave many souls the opportunity to advance. When, at the time of his first arrival, he saw the solitary place, he loved it as one long desired. He found a little church woven together among brambles and serpents with mean boards. Not long afterward, having obtained episcopal charters, he established a dwelling for clerics there and began to live according to the rule instituted under the holy apostles.

Some people were drawn to him by the novelty of his preaching; others came inspired by devotion and the hidden gift of grace. As the small beginning grew day by day, he founded a larger church and stirred the minds of many toward a purpose of living well. They willingly committed themselves to the common life and, renouncing everything they seemed to possess in the world, made Christ their heir.

Among them, a certain man from the neighborhood named H., a faithful man, offered two young sons at that time and handed them over to the priest mentioned above to be instructed under the yoke of the rule.

The priest received them and nourished them paternally. As they lived under the holy fellowship in accordance with the merit of their lives, he promoted them, as their age permitted, to serve in the sacred orders.

Concerning one of them, named Tamard, God displayed through Saint Donatian a remarkable account of miracles, brilliant in power and clear in splendor, credible in itself and not requiring the testimony of another. Since we have seen these things daily from the beginning, looked upon them daily with our eyes, and handled them daily with our hands, we wish the faithful also to marvel at them with us, venerate them with us, and, although not present, behold them with us in this writing.

When this boy, nine years old, had been offered by his parents to the same monastery, he lived in that holy fellowship according to his measure, regularly under pastoral discipline. Prompt and obedient, he fulfilled the household duties; at the command of the one who instructed him, he readily performed what was enjoined.

When his more advanced age was not yet able to perform some task, he came, as is customary, with his peers to instruct the younger members of God’s household in their appointed portion. He spent a long period under the higher schools, and by God’s providence advanced day by day toward what was better as he was being trained. He passed through adolescence under regular guardianship.

Even then he understood that it was a safe path to live under guides, a safe path to live under rulers, and safe to labor with such laborers. But under the gaze of the Judge who sees all things, what can be safe or self-confident? What can escape the craftsman of his own work? What can evade the sharpness of divine light?

Nothing passes away unseen; nothing comes after unnoticed. He sees all things, penetrates all things, examines all things, judges all things. Nor does he need anyone to testify to him concerning a human being: he himself knows what is in a human being.

Perhaps even in this servant of his, by an invisible judgment, he knew something hidden that he mercifully wished to punish, lest it pass unpunished; or, if it did not deserve punishment for personal guilt, he imposed in him a saving judgment upon our corruption.

When, as has been said, he had passed through childhood and had grown into a larger boy, already reaching the boundaries of burning adolescence, he was struck down by the most acute illness that the Greeks call *paralysis*. His bodily structure collapsed, and from the sole of his foot to the crown of his head one half of him withered.

It was a pitiable sight: a living man bearing the appearance of one joined to the dead. Although the whole mass of his body remained, the illness had seized his entire left side, and one part, dead to its function, had claimed his living limbs for its own service.

Since he could not be well while deprived of himself, he presented to everyone’s eyes a burdensome weight that the disease itself made firm, lest he perish altogether. His languishing limbs lay useless for service and offered only the outer appearance of a human body, suited to no practical use.

Whenever the illness abated for a short time and he had to go to the church or elsewhere, he was lifted by the support of a staff. This living corpse moved slowly and painfully on three supports. At times, when his attendant was absent, he moved himself, with impaired judgment, to other places; the miserable man was often transformed into something crawling on the ground.

His tongue was without function; or, if he drew out anything by stammering, it sounded without sense and was unintelligible. It would take too long to recount each of the miseries and the troubles that so dreadful an illness commonly arouses.

There were days without rest and sleepless nights; the following words concerning the brothers’ continuous attendance are textually incomplete. I recall the greater matters more particularly and pass over the lesser ones.

But I will mention one thing sufficiently worthy of wonder: the living part of his body, which he dragged along as though it were already dead, was strengthened by such power conferred through the illness that it not only did not fail, but sometimes resisted more vigorously than is customary for the weak, even when two or three people were holding him.

Such indomitable strength had never existed in him before the illness, nor did it remain in him afterward once he had recovered his health.

And when the delay of such sufferings had stretched on for nearly three years [Col. 1538C], and the long-established condition of the illness no longer offering any hope of recovery, divine mercy came to those who persisted in their petitions with faith, and showed that the man, though afflicted by the long duration of his suffering, had nevertheless not been abandoned by God’s good pleasure. For when the anniversary feast of Saint Nicholas, our father, had arrived, and a larger crowd of people was gathering to us in his memory, the same brother, moved amid his very torments by a certain liveliness of mind, asked—having been admonished to do so—that he might take part with the other brothers in the common joy which he knew was to be celebrated.

He was led to the nocturnal vigils and devoutly completed the office of readings which he had requested permission to attend. But unable to endure his weakness, he returned to his bed before the others, once the praises had ended. He had scarcely been released into the lightest sleep—such that, as often happens, when one falls asleep easily, one thinks rather that one is keeping watch—when suddenly the whole bed on which he lay was flooded with light [Col. 1538D]. In it he unexpectedly saw two magnificent men coming toward him. An elderly man preceded them with attentive service, as though performing the role of an attendant before such dignity. The two themselves followed behind on either side with the exceedingly decorous bearing of grave persons.

Terrified by the unexpected light, and wholly shaken by the radiance of the forms and garments he had never before seen, the brother, uncertain what to do, tremblingly admired only the presence of those whom he beheld. The man who preceded them, approaching more closely like a familiar visitor, stood beside the little bed and for some time silently examined the condition of the one lying there. When the brother looked more carefully at him as he gazed down upon him, he recognized him as Lord Odfrid, the former prior and founder of our church, who had died two years earlier, splendid in the regular habit.

At once he was lifted up in gladness and relieved by inward joy. He embraced with kisses the unexpected return of the Father whom he had long lost, and, with whatever nod he could manage, he reverently honored that heavenly assembly. Do you not see, then, Father, the affection of your son? Do you not observe the disposition of his mind toward you? If he were able, he would already have anticipated your arrival with greetings; if weakness allowed, he would have responded with joyful services; if his unfree limbs were not stiff, he would have come to meet you with outstretched arms. But now, with the grateful recognition he could offer, he honorably came forward [Col. 1539B]: the son recognized his father, the disciple recognized his teacher, the master of the household recognized his servant, and the faithful heir did not turn away from the one returning from a distant land to his own home. Indeed, he recognized him as the supreme possessor of all things and as his prior.

Since, then, Father, you have come to visit him, command the one whom you remember having once entrusted to yourself. Why have you come forth from that blessed dwelling of yours? Command the young man whom from his earliest age you nourished under your protection. Since, I say, divine providence has led you back to the dwelling of your foundation, command the one whom you left carefully instructed in the rudiments of sacred discipline.

For we know with certainty the reason for which you have come; we know that what you have returned to accomplish is assured; we know that what you are contriving has been firmly agreed upon among those above; and perhaps we know that you have come to restore this sick man to health. But because the brother has words bound within him, for the moment I would gladly take up with you, elder, the role of conversation; I would gladly discuss, with you as witness, the causes of your return. Nor will there be any heavenly offense in this delay, which will be not so much idle as fruitful.

“Advancing,” he says, “from faith to faith, from appearance to appearance, from contemplation to vision, hasten to complete in him what is partial by that which is perfect. Let the effect of perfection appear in him, while the deficiency of health that has been lost is restored.

“But since you do not profess to be a physician, since by your coming you are assisting in this man’s recovery, announce who these highly suitable persons are whom you have brought with you: they dispel the darkness of night in this smoky hut and illuminate the shadowy form [Col. 1539D] without any radiance. Perhaps, just as they appear to be ministers of light, they may also come as healers of this illness.

“To this man sighing for health, whom you know to have been wearied by such prolonged affliction, commend him to whichever of these you wish to have him healed—the one whom you have so often refreshed like a nurse refreshing her child.

“Now, therefore, ask how he is, since, more overwhelmed by the novelty of what has happened than by sleep, he is afraid to speak.”

Then the elder said: “Are you sleeping, son?”

And he replied: “Father, do you think I can sleep, when you see me bound by an impending and so grievous weakness? Sleep has fled from my eyes just as health has fled from my limbs.”

Then the elder said—and he indicated those standing at his side—“Look, son; look, I say, and recognize that this is Saint Donatian of Bruges, who has come to visit you, and do not doubt that that man is the blessed Gudwal, guardian and resident of the monastery of Blandinium.” As he gazed more intently at their radiant faces and episcopal mitres, he impressed upon his memory the forms and qualities of their bodies, and explained their appearance and characteristics to us as though he were still drawing breath from them as living men.

Saint Donatian was of moderate stature, neither exceeding proper height nor diminishing the dignity of his person by excessive shortness. He had broad shoulders, a manly and robust chest, a muscular neck, a round and cheerful face, large eyes shining with brightness, a straight nose, lips clearly defined only at their upper edge [Col. 1540B], a broad forehead, prominent ears, and, around his temples and along the circuit of his forehead, thick gray hairs standing upright in curls. Behind, his hair lay flat, its natural color showing through with only a slight intermixture of white.

The blessed Gudwal, however, was tall, his elegant form rising above the whole surface of his limbs; he was a very old man, mature in age and whitened by the snows of years.

When this had been said, the elder turned toward blessed Donatian and said: “Behold, holy man: God commands you to heal this canon, who at the coming Nativity of Christ will also come to your court at Bruges and bring you as a gift a silver thread weighing two pennies, according to his own measure. Each year, while he lives, he will return when the term has come round and honor your altar with the same offering.”

The saint replied: “I approve.”

“Holy man of God, do you add no further word? You are designated as the physician, and you conclude the promise of healing in a single word? You hear the gift that has been proposed, yet you do not bargain in hope of increasing it; you accept the assurance that health will be accomplished, yet you do not reject the two gifts offered; you have come by such a long road, yet you demand no payment for the journey.

“No Arab, no Indian, no wealthy man sends out the kinds of drugs which you carry, and you value at a cheap price what you have received as a gift. Physicians, however, struggle over different fees; physicians obtain their rewards by different deceptions; physicians thrust themselves forward in different ways; they make promises with many assertions and deceive with many promises. But you, setting aside every ambiguity, using no abundance of words and captured by no greed for payment, say ‘I approve’—five letters and two syllables—and trust that you can heal the whole man.

“Rich is the letter, rich the meaning, rich the reply. Great medicine in a small expression; great health in a brief inscription. You are called Donatian, and you received your name from donation. Give, my lord, a fitting explanation of what you have said; rather, resolve it yourself: ‘I approve’—that is what you said.

“Did you not speak thus, holy man? Then you assert that you were sent by God; you profess yourself to be his courtier. ‘I approve.’ You acknowledge yourself to be a heavenly messenger, moving between the highest and the lowest. ‘I approve.’ You command me to become a physician and entrust this cure to me. ‘I approve.’ You arrange his coming to me and promise that he will remain among my attendants. ‘I approve.’ You intend that he should not appear before God empty-handed and weigh the price of his offering. Therefore, ‘I approve.’

“It remains [Col. 1541A], then, holy man of God, that you now receive the hand into yours and, once he has come to you, send him back healed to his own people. It remains that with your life-giving hand you touch the contracted limb and make its bearer capable of bearing himself. Receive, then, the man lying on his pallet, and return him to us not limping miserably as he usually does.”

The elder took the sick hand of the man lying there and placed it in the saint’s right hand, commending him earnestly in these words:

“Receive, holy man of God, this canon in place of one of your own whom I name to you. Unless he quickly reforms his life, I declare that he is already condemned before God.”

O the depth of the riches of God’s mercy! The man worthy of death does not die; he who ought to be punished is withdrawn from punishment. The sinner is chastised not by judgment but by fear; mercy restrains judgment [Col. 1541B]. A way is opened for the sinner so that he may turn from evil deeds; delay for repentance is granted and offered to one who does not deserve it. Patience announces the hope of recovery and offers it to one who does not expect it.

The guilty man is identified by name in the assembly of the saints, yet the faithful hearer fears to disclose him, lest he be shamed before the gathering of the wicked. What a pure revelation without reproach! What an affectionate visitation without insult! What a gentle admonition without command! The threat chastises the guilty man, not punishment. Conversion is proposed in place of vengeance, and he is taught with true certainty that he may escape the sentence, provided that he does not disregard the condition of reforming.

Moreover, the trustworthy breast of the hearer conceals what has been added, lest he be judged a betrayer of the divine secret. A simple affection trembles to uncover the consciousness of guilt. But, brother, do you not discern this sincerely? Do you not lose the good of your conscience if you turn away from the snare of betrayal the man who desires to perish? Or, if no one is permitted to speak of the secret that he knows, is he at least permitted to speak to the very person about whom he heard it?

For the faith of the blessed spirits is not accused in this matter, in which the spirit of the prophet is confirmed. For he says: “If you do not announce his wickedness to the wicked man, I shall require his blood from your hand.” The Gospel also gives a definite rule of correction, commanding that the sinner be reproved between you and him alone. And the Apostle says: “Your brother, for whom Christ died, will perish through your knowledge.”

Certainly it is not cruelty if you confess it alone to him alone. Indeed, you will be less innocent if, by keeping silent, you allow the brother whom you could win by correcting him to perish. In addition, repeat accordingly the condition that was spoken to you, and you will certainly find an admonition to amend your life. Otherwise, you make yourself a destroyer of the commandment if, by withdrawing and concealing the iron with which a putrid wound can be cut, you hide it.

Hasten, therefore, to win your brother’s soul. If you cause him to turn back, he will certainly not be guilty, for it is written: “Change the command, and it will not be.” The brother, however, wished this to remain silent for the moment, because he silently awaited what revelation concerning himself would be fulfilled. Just as he had been a fellow member of the saints in hearing, so also, with caution, he did not expose the guilty man by disclosing him; for he never wished to tell anyone who he was, except the very man whom the revelation identified.

But, brothers, may we not consider this sinner fortunate—a fortunate transgressor forewarned by a divine oracle and destined to be convicted by such authoritative witnesses? Placed before God in this matter, he will fear to conceal his guilt after the admonition, though until now he had either been ashamed or disdainful of confessing it about himself.

He is plainly fortunate, and he cannot deny it. Indeed, this same negligence places him alongside the holy prophet David. David wished to satisfy God concerning the violation of Uriah’s wife; this man, by confession, disdained to cleanse the bride of Christ whom he had defiled in himself. David took care to conceal more cautiously, by a just silence, the crime he had committed; this man, so that the wound of his soul might not appear, avoided coming into the light, wrapped in the darkness of conscience. David contrived the murder of an innocent man by cunning schemes; this man, by an effort that he could sustain, resolved to die daily, continually striking himself with a wound [Col. 1542B]. David was convicted of his manifest crime by the prophet’s parable; this man, unless he wishes to turn back, is condemned and sentenced in the hearing of the saints by the evil that has been heard.

Both, therefore, were perpetrators of unlawful acts; but one was convicted of a known crime, the other of a hidden one. Both fell into need of God’s mercy and the water of grace, needing reconciliation. Is this sinner therefore more abhorrent because he is lower in rank? Rather, he should be reverently preferred in the form proper to each person, because he wished to be corrected by one possessing royal majesty.

The same brother later told us that, after he had been admonished, he had turned more earnestly toward lamentation before his death.

Meanwhile that heavenly assembly dissolved, and, leaving behind the elder who had come with him, both saints departed [Col. 1542C]. The elder, however, remaining in the same light, stayed behind in the urgency of his concern to arrange certain other domestic matters, and instructed the disciple more fully, with careful teaching, about what he should do next.

“Go,” he said, “son, to our brothers, and announce that their chamberlain, who some time ago was taken from human affairs, is being tormented unbearably. But faithfully indicate that, if they pray for him unanimously, God will shortly grant relief. And, lest they despair of forgiveness, add that through them he will certainly be redeemed from punishment.

“Also add to your assertions that henceforth they must not let the anniversary of Pope Gregory VII pass through negligence, but must solemnly celebrate it every year with conspicuous service, because he confirmed our church by his sign and apostolic decree and promulgated in it, by paternal tradition, the way of living rightly [Col. 1542D]. If they wish to complete this devoutly, affirm without doubt that they will not be deprived of their reward, because he is a holy man and of great merit, and God will receive with abundant thanksgiving what I command to be done for him.”

When the vision of the saints had thus been completed, the elder too departed in the company of the saints’ footsteps, leaving the brother drenched in sweat like water because of the anguish of his spirit. He had scarcely been able to bear the burden of the vision because of its difficulty. Yet it was not so much what he had seen in his mental astonishment—which, though it almost terrified him in his burning state—as the fragrance and the grace of health now hoped for that delightfully refreshed him.

Now, brother, delay no longer. Why are you lying there? Rise, go to the assembly, fulfill the commands. You need no spokesman for yourself: speak for yourself, as far as you are able, what you hold in your mind. Explain yourself what you saw; you yourself—no one can do so more truthfully than you—come into the midst, come forth in public.

There is no need for many words. Your hearers are kindly disposed: they are brothers, and they have often mourned for you in compassion; they have often expressed their affectionate sympathy with your infirmity. They have it in them to weep with you and to rejoice with you; at your pleasure they will impose silence, they will hasten to hear you, they will desire to learn from you, and they will hold their mouths attentive.

You have an impeded tongue; do not be afraid. You will not have to conduct a dialogue, you will not be pressed by questions, you will not have to exchange with them the opportunity to speak. You will have only the voice for narrating, not for answering.

Enter, I say, and explain the matter; explain the end of your sufferings; lay bare the assurance of the restoration of your health [Col. 1543B]; lay bare the dream that you saw, through which the bond of your illness will be loosened; lay bare the promise of this wondrous dispensation, the benefit of an unquestionable cure, and the manifestation of the revelation’s fulfillment in you.

Let them learn from you the certainty of the heavenly ministers. Let them hear who received you: the physician; let them hear where the preparer of effective antidotes has his dwelling-place. Make known the stronghold of Bruges, where, when you arrive, you will find lodging prepared.

Explain more precisely the appointed day; let them prepare the expenses, because your health is ready with Saint Donatian. So that they may wish to lead you, to be healed, to this evangelical innkeeper, and no longer tolerate your weakness, because without doubt you will have him as your healer.

Add also to the praise of this most holy confessor what is appended at the end of the revelation, because it will rightly appear that what was beneficially foretold by the one accompanying you should be attributed to him.

Now the sun was hastening in its course toward the star-bearing citadels,

and the rosy moon was outshining the lesser stars.

Meanwhile the foreign brother was struck by sleep and marveled that he had seen the heavenly beings with greater certainty than he had slept. Immediately, after calculating the order of events, he went as quickly as possible to the confession of what he had seen before the assembly of the brothers. He filled them with wonder and joy, made them more eager because of the promised healing, and stirred them to greater unanimity and hope concerning the heavenly visitation of the place.

In the meantime, as time passed, its course grew longer, and the saving day was eagerly anticipated by the longing mind—the day on which the nativity of our Savior was approaching [Col. 1543D]. Every day he greeted the day of its arrival; every day he greeted the promise of future health. If only the holy station would come, he now spoke confidently. He boasted inwardly of his coming visit, did not reckon the delay of his prolonged suffering, and longed for the day that the Virgin’s offspring, the same Son of God, would sanctify.

He considered his limbs and body, contracted by torture, of no account, so long as the promised day was being sustained—the day that would restore him upright. But it came more slowly than he wished, and one who delays food while serving it is anticipated by the eager desire of the hungry man who sighs for it.

At last, by order of the superior and on the advice of the brothers, his departure having been prepared, he undertook the desired journey and arrived at the stronghold of Bruges, at the saint’s place, three days before the Nativity of the Lord, after much exertion.

On the first night a generous brother received him as a guest. But when the provost learned the reason for his visit, he immediately granted him lodging in his own house. Since the church was adjacent, he could be brought before the saint; and, arranging the services required for his care, the provost left him in the company of suitable brothers who were present with every kindness. He himself went farther away to attend to other matters.

Behold, holy patron, your sick man has been gathered in; every person responsible for his care may rest, since his lodging has been arranged. But now, brother, why do you delay? Why have you come to the station that was appointed? Since you have entered the court of the heavenly magnate Donatian, present yourself before the one whose sight you sought; since you have reached the boundaries of his territory, awaken the recognition of the one whom you have approached.

Go, then, for he does not fail to know that you have come; he already awaits you to come to him, and already knows your face beforehand. But the saint must be sought where he rests. Go, I say, and prostrate yourself before him with a cry for mercy, for without doubt you will find him a gracious intercessor.

This saint is the sweetness of the poor; believe that you have come well. He is the devout consoler of the wretched; trust that you have come well. He is the strength of the weak; take courage, for you have come well. He is your faithful protector; therefore you have come well.

For through him that prophetic saying will be fulfilled in you: “Then the lame man shall leap like a stag, and the tongue of the mute shall be clear.”

When the evening service had been completed and night had begun to draw near—for it was the night preceding the Sunday vigils—he went to the church. There, while he remained for some time fulfilling his prayers [Col. 1544C], he suddenly lost his strength with such a violent shaking that, when he prepared to return, he was in no way able to do so by himself.

For, from some horror poured over him, a hidden heat immediately coursed through the lowest parts of his entrails before the saint [lacuna], and then, spreading outward, began gradually to seize each limb. Consequently his entire body became drenched with a copious flood of sweat. Even after he had recovered his health, this sweat could not be dried from his restored side for many days.

After he had been tormented for some time and could no longer endure his increasing collapse, he was carried from the church back to his bed by the hands of attendants. You would then have seen the man distressed in various ways by the brothers, moving laboriously here and there under certain hidden pressures, doing nothing stable or certain: now lying more suitably, now sitting more comfortably. Yet neither the place provided rest nor the bed afforded repose to limbs so wearied by these many disturbances, so that for a while the attendants feared that, tortured by his pains, he might act madly.

Nevertheless, they did not yield to the varied movements by which the human frame was being reshaped within itself. Rather, now they applied warm remedies to his heat, now supplied coolness to refresh him while he scarcely breathed, and sometimes firmly restrained him when he attempted unsuitable things. Amid all this they marveled that such vigor of health existed in one who was without strength.

Then that side which had lain numb for so long gradually began to grow warm as its stiffness loosened; at frequent intervals a returning power began to tingle through it; the connections of the nerves were restored to their former functions. The hand, together with the arm, and the foot, with repeated attempts at flexion, began to move; the leg returned from the groin. At last, gradually creeping through him, health restored the man on every side, as though after the touch of a physician, from top to bottom, and with a swift leap raised him to his feet among those seated around him [Col. 1545A].

Sorrow was immediately changed into joy, mourning into exultation. Those who a little earlier had stood sadly in compassion now came from every side to rejoice with him.

They tested and touched him. Because of their excessive wonder at the sign, some still doubted, and made repeated trials to determine whether he was truly as he appeared; some tried to see what they had heard, others to hear more than once what they had seen. As though the marvel were always new, they vied with one another in friendly curiosity and astonishment.

He stood in their midst, carrying the proofs of faith, and joyfully explained them to everyone he encountered [Col. 1545B], making them more certain by showing the signs that they saw. Then all of them, each desiring to offer God through him the fruit of devoted service, hastened with him to the church.

But like a new apostolic Aeneas, confident in his steps, he sought neither assistance nor light. Rather, through difficult and winding places, he alone went ahead of all the others. The curious, who ought to have gone ahead in order to assist him, followed. When they found that he had not injured himself at all by striking against anything during the night and the dangerous passage, they marveled even more and glorified God.

To make the firmness of his faith still more evident, he himself descended with great speed, without anyone guiding him, from the upper gallery of the basilica where he had entered, down the staircase, to the altar called the greater altar. There he offered the silver thread, as had been commanded, directly to the saint’s body. In the same place he spent a short time in prayer, inflicting upon himself many prostrations—things he could not have done unless he were well.

By such proofs he satisfied those present, so that they would not believe that this had happened through some momentary impulse. When day had come, he continued to appear healthy in the choir; on that same day he himself, a lively table-server, ministered at table to those who had carried him. With every doubt removed, on the second night he celebrated the Sunday vigils with the full assembly.

On the very day of the Nativity of the Lord, the prelate of the church, at the public service, delivered a credible sermon to the people about all that had occurred, with the same brother bearing witness [Col. 1546B].

It was the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1088, indiction XI. This celebrated miracle was accomplished in the church of Saint Donatian, our father, and was faithfully recounted before the body of that same saint amid great rejoicing of clergy and people, to the praise and glory of God the Father and of his Son Jesus Christ our Lord, who lives and reigns with him and the Holy Spirit for ever and ever. Amen.

Chapter I.—Of the dispute concerning the monasteries, repeatedly pursued, and of the efforts of the bishops of Cologne, frustrated over many years. 291

Chapter III.—The conspiracy jointly made by Cologne and Bremen, and the unjust transfer by the king to them of the abbeys of Corvey, Lorsch, Stavelot, and Juda. 294  
Chapter IV.—A court is held at Trier, where, with the abbot unknown to the matter, the transfer is confirmed. 296  
Chapter V.—Abbot Theodericus and Duke Frederick deliberate together; a fortification is made over Malmedy; they are summoned together to court; but the duke, rejecting the arrangement, complains to the king through an intermediary of the injustice. ibid.  
Chapter VI.—The duke rebukes his nephew Conrad concerning the advocacy of Malmedy and, when Conrad and the abbot are compelled to appear at court, sends Roricus as agent. After Roricus abandons him, Conrad is detained by the king for a long time. 297  
Chapter VII.—The duke’s death, mourning, and misery follow; and, as he had ordered, he is buried at Stavelot. 298  

[Col. 1551D]

Chapter VIII.—The archbishop sends Conrad to claim Malmedy for himself and to choose an abbot; Abbot Theodericus demands from the monks the promise made to him. 299  
Chapter IX.—The people of Malmedy are confirmed by oaths to the bishop; a harsh persecution is directed against our people; the body of our saint is displayed in their midst. ibid.  
Chapter X.—Tegeno is placed over Malmedy as abbot; but our abbot goes to the Lombard margrave Godefridus for assistance. 300  
Chapter XI.—An account of the nature, character, and difference between these two dukes, Frederick and Godefridus. 301  
Chapter XII.—Our abbot restores the holy body to its place; under divine threat he adjures the abbot set over him to depart and abandon what he possesses unjustly. 302  
Chapter XIII.—After becoming duke, Godefridus rightly judges that the saint’s property ought to be restored; but the bishop, delaying, did not consent to do so, and after our church and treasury had been stripped, our claim remained fruitless. ibid.  
Chapter XIV.—The saint’s body is carried to the court at Aachen, where, by order of the bishop, it is received without honor. 303  
Chapter XV.—While we mourn and cry out together with the people, the insolent Bishop of Speyer orders our soil to be carried away; finally, with deep sorrow, we departed from there together with the saint’s body. 304  
Chapter XVI.—The king, seized by a grave illness, promises to restore everything to the saint; the bishop, likewise afflicted by pain, makes the same promise, but soon proceeds otherwise. 305  
Chapter XVII.—After the Archbishop of Trier dies, Anno is found together with the man whom he had unwillingly appointed in his place; and that insolent Bishop of Speyer is beaten like an unclean dog and driven away in disgrace. 306  
Chapter XVIII.—Once again the abbot obtains from the king permission to reclaim his place, returns to Malmedy, and, bringing the saint’s body with him, restrains everyone—monks and laymen alike—under oath to the prelate. 307  
Chapter XIX.—The abbot, coming to Rome, pursues his cases before Pope Alexander, who also sends letters to Cologne on his behalf; but all this was in vain. 308  
Chapter XX.—Gerlasius, the bishop’s agent, again attacks Malmedy in his name, but, after hearing an uncertain report, hastens his return. 309  
Chapter XXI.—The abbot returns from Rome, receiving little help from the apostolic letters; rather, persecution against him and us is renewed through a certain fierce man, Fredelo, and through Gerardus, who later, by God’s judgment, was ruined. ibid.  
Chapter XXII.—The bishop sets out for Rome, and the abbot follows him; the matter is debated before the pope and the senate; finally the cases are settled without any advantage to us. 310
