# WILLIAM CALCULUS, MONK OF JUMIÈGES.

Historical Notice. 777

EIGHT BOOKS OF THE HISTORY OF THE NORTHMEN. 779

Letter to William the Orthodox, King of the English, concerning the deeds of the Northmen’s leaders. Ibid.

BOOK ONE.—How Hasting oppressed Neustria before Rollo’s arrival. 781

CHAPTER I.—How the strength of the Franks, which had long flourished, was altered, so that they themselves were less able to resist the savagery of the pagans. Ibid. [Column 1558]

CHAPTER II.—Concerning the three parts of the world, and in which of them Dacia lies, and concerning its situation. Ibid.

CHAPTER III.—Concerning the origin of the Goths, and where they first lived. Ibid.

CHAPTER IV.—That the Danes descended from the stock of the Goths; why they are called Danes or Northmen; and why the same people multiplied so greatly. 783

CHAPTER V.—How Bier, son of Lothroc, king of Dacia, was expelled from his homeland in the customary manner, together with Hasting, his tutor. 784

CHAPTER VI.—How they came into the kingdom of the Franks and first ravaged the district of Vermandois. Ibid.

CHAPTER VII.—Concerning the destruction of Neustria, which extends across the country from the city of Orléans to Paris. 785

CHAPTER VIII.—How the cities of Paris and Beauvais were destroyed, as well as Poitiers and the other neighboring cities, from the very shore of the Ocean eastward as far as Auvergne. Ibid.

CHAPTER IX.—That, after France had been afflicted by the oppression of the pagans for nearly thirty years, Hasting, sailing to Rome in order to subject it to his lord Bier, was driven by a storm and landed at the Italian city of Luni. 786

CHAPTER X.—How Hasting, supposing Luni to be Rome, captured it by deception because he could not take it by force, and destroyed it. Ibid.

CHAPTER XI.—That the pagans, discovering that the city was not Rome, divided; and that Bier, wishing to return to Denmark, died in Frisia, while Hasting, having made peace with King Charles, received from him the city of Chartres as a stipend and lived there. 787

BOOK TWO.—Containing the deeds of Rollo, the first duke of Normandy. 787

CHAPTER I.—Concerning the nobility and courage of Rollo’s father, and how the young men of Dacia, who had been registered by order of the king for expulsion, came to Rollo and his brother Gurim to ask them to bring aid against the king. Ibid.

CHAPTER II.—How, while Rollo rebelled against the king for five years, the king deceitfully sought peace from him. 789

CHAPTER III.—How the king attacked Rollo’s cities by night; concerning the death of his brother Gurim; and concerning Rollo’s arrival on the island of Scanza with six ships.

CHAPTER IV.—Concerning the warning given to Rollo in a dream that he should seek England, and concerning his victory over the English. 790

CHAPTER V.—Concerning his dream and its interpretation by a certain Christian. 791

CHAPTER VI.—Concerning Alstem, the most Christian king of the English, with whom Rollo entered into a treaty of unbreakable friendship. 792

CHAPTER VII.—Concerning the storm endured by Rollo while sailing from England to the kingdom of the Franks, and how he landed on the shores of the Walgrians. 793

CHAPTER VIII.—How Rollo defeated the rebellious Walgrians, Rainer of Hainaut, and Radebold, prince of Frisia; and concerning the twelve ships loaded with provisions and an equal number filled with armed soldiers, which King Alstem of the English sent him while he was staying there. 794

CHAPTER IX.—How, in the year of the incarnation of the Word 876, Rollo came to Jumièges and then to Rouen; and concerning the peace which Archbishop Franco sought from him and obtained. 796

CHAPTER X.—How Rollo, coming with his men along the channel of the Seine, reached Arques, which is called Hasdans, and there established a certain fortress where he fought against the Franks; and, after killing many, put their duke Rainald to flight; and concerning the destruction of the fortress of Meulan. Ibid.

CHAPTER XI.—By what deception Count Theobald bought the city of Chartres from Hasting, and how Hasting himself, after selling everything, departed abroad and disappeared. 797

CHAPTER XII.—The renewed war of Ragenold, prince of France, against Rollo; concerning Ragenold’s death; the yearly siege of Paris; and the destruction of Bayeux, where Rollo captured a certain maiden named Poppa, by whom he fathered William and her sister Gerloc; and how his army slaughtered the citizens of Évreux, while he himself was besieging Paris with certain others. Ibid.

CHAPTER XIII.—Concerning Elstan (Alstem), king of the English, who through envoys requested his aid against rebels and received it. And that Rollo, returning from there after subduing the English at the king’s request, richly endowed with great gifts and assistance, divided the companions of his army and sent some by the channel of the Seine, others by the Loire, and others by the Gironde, to plunder the intervening provinces with swift navigation. 798 [Column 1559]

CHAPTER XIV.—That Charles, hearing of Rollo’s return, requested and obtained peace from him for three months; and that, when the period had ended, Rollo sent his men all around to plunder as far as Burgundy. Ibid.

CHAPTER XV.—How, while he was besieging the city of Chartres, Richard, duke of the Burgundians, attacked him with his own army and that of the Franks; and, while Rollo resisted bravely, Bishop Antelmus unexpectedly sallied from the city with armed men, carrying the tunic of the holy Mother of God, and attacked him from the rear. Thus Rollo yielded not to the Burgundians but to divine power. 799

CHAPTER XVI.—Concerning the part of the army that entered a certain mountain, and concerning Count Ebal of Poitiers; how he hid in a fuller’s house because of the Northmen. Ibid.

CHAPTER XVII.—That, when Rollo was inflamed with fury and was ravaging France with ever more severe oppression, King Charles gave him his daughter and the coastal land from the river Epte to the Breton borders, as well as Brittany itself for his livelihood, since the land had been plundered and deserted (the aforesaid land was deserted); on the condition, however, that he become a Christian; and that the king, Robert, duke of France, and the other nobles and bishops swore that the same land would be possessed by Rollo and his heirs forever. And that, because Rollo was unwilling to kiss the king’s foot, he ordered one of his soldiers to kiss it. 800

CHAPTER XVIII.—That in the year of the incarnation of the Word 912 Rollo and his army were baptized, and that he gave a portion of the land to the more venerable churches of his province before dividing it among his satraps; and concerning Brenneval, which he gave to Saint Dionysius the Areopagite. 801

CHAPTER XIX.—How he divided the land among his men, rebuilt the destroyed churches and the walls of the cities, and subdued the Bretons who rebelled against him. Ibid.

CHAPTER XX.—Concerning the law he established, that no one should give assistance to a thief; and concerning the peasant and his wife whom he ordered to be hanged because of a stolen knife and ploughshare. 802

CHAPTER XXI.—Concerning the two soldiers of King Charles whom he had punished. Ibid.

CHAPTER XXII.—That, after his wife died without children, he again took Poppa, whom he had had before baptism, as his partner; concerning the oath of loyalty which he made the Northmen and Bretons swear to his son William; and concerning his death. 803

BOOK THREE.—Concerning William, the second duke, son of Rollo. 803

CHAPTER I.—Concerning Duke William’s uprightness of character, and that the Franks envied him because he was extending the boundaries of his duchy on every side; and how he defeated Berenger and Alan, counts of the Bretons, who had rebelled against him. Ibid.

CHAPTER II.—How certain Northmen, led by a treacherous man named Riulf and wishing to expel him completely from the kingdom, were defeated by him with a small troop of soldiers while they were besieging the suburbs of Rouen, at the place that to this day is called the Field of Battle; and that, when he returned victorious from the battle, he learned that a son had been born to him by the most noble maiden Sprota at Fécamp, whom he ordered to be named Richard at baptism. 803

CHAPTER III.—That many counts and leaders from foreign regions, attracted by the fame of his goodness and courage, frequently attended his court, especially Hugh the Great, duke of the Franks; William, count of Poitiers; and Herbert of Vermandois. William asked for and received his sister Gerloc as his wife, while Herbert, at the urging of Hugh the Great, joined his daughter to him in marriage. 805

CHAPTER IV.—How, at the request of King Elstan of the English, he restored Louis to his father’s kingdom and, with Hugh the Great’s support, had him anointed with holy oil and invested with the royal diadem, together with the bishops and the other leading men of the Franks; and that, after five years, the Franks again conspired against him and plotted to expel him from the kingdom. Ibid.

CHAPTER V.—How Louis, compelled by necessity and wishing to enter into a treaty of friendship with Henry, the king beyond the Rhine, could not obtain the king’s consent except through William, marquis of the Northmen. Thus Louis earnestly sought the duke and through him obtained from King Henry the treaty and assistance he desired. 806

CHAPTER VI.—How Duke William, returning from the meeting of the kings, at Louis’s request lifted his son from the sacred font at Laon, and the child was given the name Lothair. Ibid.

CHAPTER VII.—On what occasion Duke William restored the monastery of Jumièges, previously destroyed by the pagans. 807 [Column 1560]

CHAPTER VIII.—Concerning the twelve monks, together with their abbot Martin, taken from the monastery of Saint Cyprian, whom the countess of Poitiers, the duke’s sister, sent to him at his request, so that he might install them in the aforesaid place; and how the duke, wishing to become a monk, was prevented from doing so by that abbot; and concerning the oath of loyalty which he made the Northmen and Bretons swear to his son Richard. Ibid.

CHAPTER IX.—How Herold (Aigrold), king of the Danes, driven from the kingdom by his son Sweyn, came to Normandy with sixty ships and was received by Duke William with suitable honor, the county of Coutances being granted to him by the duke for his protection. 808

CHAPTER X.—How Duke William, moved by the misfortune of Count Herluin, besieged and captured the fortress of Monasteriol, which Arnulf of Flanders had taken from him, and restored it to Herluin. Ibid.

CHAPTER XI.—How Arnulf, saddened by the loss of the town, deceitfully sent Duke William a peaceful message, inviting him to Pinchignac to discuss a treaty of friendship with him. 809

CHAPTER XII.—How four traitors—namely Henry, Balzo, Robert, and Riulf—killed the duke on a certain island of the Somme River at Arnulf’s command; concerning the silver key found in his sash, beneath which in a chest he kept a cowl and a monk’s woolen garment; and how his body was brought back to Rouen. 809

BOOK FOUR.—Concerning the first Richard, son of Duke William. Ibid.

CHAPTER I.—That Richard, still a boy, succeeded his father William. Ibid.

CHAPTER II.—That Louis, king of the Franks, came to Rouen and fraudulently took the boy Richard with him into France, subjecting the duchy of Normandy to his own jurisdiction as though he were the boy’s guardian. 811

CHAPTER III.—That Louis, blinded by Arnulf’s gifts, threatened to burn the knees of Richard, the boy duke of the Northmen. Ibid.

CHAPTER IV.—By what precaution Osmund, the boy’s guardian, freed him from strict custody and, rescuing him from Laon the Fortified, brought him through Senlis to Count Bernard, his maternal uncle. 812

CHAPTER V.—How Bernard the Dane wisely nullified the counsel which Hugh the Great had given Louis against the Northmen. 813

CHAPTER VI.—That Louis, coming to Rouen, was received by Bernard the Dane and the other citizens; and that, at Louis’s command, Hugh the Great ceased ravaging Normandy. Ibid.

CHAPTER VII.—How, through Bernard the Dane’s ingenuity and King Herold of the Danes’ action, Louis, king of the Franks, was captured in the city of Rouen and kept under strict custody. 814

CHAPTER VIII.—That Queen Gerberga, seeking aid from her father Henry, king beyond the Rhine, against the Northmen, did not obtain it; wherefore she gave her son and two bishops as hostages for Louis, her husband the king. 815

CHAPTER IX.—How the Northmen brought their lord Richard back from France, and the hostages were returned; and concerning Herold’s return to Denmark. 816

CHAPTER X.—That Hugh the Great betrothed his daughter Emma to Duke Richard; whereupon King Louis and Count Arnulf of Flanders, terrified, sought the aid of King Otto against Hugh the Great and Duke Richard; and that Otto, after ravaging Hugh the Great’s land, attacked Rouen to conquer it. Ibid.

CHAPTER XI.—How shamefully Emperor Otto, King Louis, and Arnulf of Flanders fled from the siege of Rouen; and concerning the death of Louis himself, whose successor was his son Lothair. 817

CHAPTER XII.—That, when Hugh the Great was approaching death, he commended his son Hugh to the protection of Duke Richard; and that the same duke took Emma, the aforesaid Hugh’s daughter, as his wife after her father’s death. Ibid.

CHAPTER XIII.—That Count Theobald of Chartres gave Queen Gerberga counsel against Duke Richard, and how the same deception was revealed to the duke by two of Theobald’s soldiers. 818

CHAPTER XIV.—How King Lothair, having gathered Duke Richard’s enemies—namely Count Baldwin of Flanders, Geoffrey of Anjou, and Theobald of Chartres—wished to deceive him but could not. 818

CHAPTER XV.—That King Lothair, having captured the city of Évreux, handed it over to Theobald; and how Duke Richard ravaged the county of Chartres and the Dunois; and that Theobald, coming with an army to the estate of Ermentrude, fled from there in disgrace, through the duke’s action, with great loss. 819

CHAPTER XVI.—That Duke Richard requested and effectively obtained the aid of Herold, king of the Danes, against the Franks. 820

CHAPTER XVII.—That, compelled by necessity, King Lothair and Theobald fully restored everything they had seized from Duke Richard; and concerning the conversion of the pagans at the duke’s urging. Ibid.

CHAPTER XVIII.—That, after his wife Emma died without children, the same duke took Gunnor as his wife; and concerning the duke’s descendants. 821

CHAPTER XIX.—How Duke Richard built a church at Fécamp in honor of the Holy Trinity and adorned it with various ornaments; concerning the abbeys of Saint Michael of the Mount and Saint Ouen, which he restored; and that, after Lothair’s death, Hugh Capet was elevated as king, and that after some time, when he too had died, his son Robert succeeded him. Ibid.

CHAPTER XX.—That, as Duke Richard approached death, he placed his son Richard in charge of the Northmen; and concerning his death at Fécamp. 822

BOOK FIVE.—Concerning the second Duke Richard, son of the preceding Richard. 823

CHAPTER I.—Concerning the honorable conduct of the second Richard, both in secular and in divine affairs. Ibid.

CHAPTER II.—How wisely he suppressed the unanimous conspiracy of the peasants, which they were plotting against the peace of the homeland. Ibid.

CHAPTER III.—Concerning the rebellion of William, the duke’s natural brother, to whom he had given the county of Hiémois; and how that same William was captured and later reconciled with his brother, receiving from the duke as a gift the county of Eu together with Lezscenina; and concerning the sons of that William. 824

CHAPTER IV.—That King Ethelred of England, who had married the duke’s sister Emma, sent an army to subjugate Normandy; and how Nigel of Coutances defeated them to the death. 825

CHAPTER V.—That Geoffrey, count of the Bretons, asked for and received as his wife Hadwisa, the sister of Duke Richard, by whom he fathered Alan and Eudo. 826

CHAPTER VI.—Concerning the cruelty of Ethelred, king of the English, toward the Danes who lived peacefully with him in England; and concerning certain young men of the same people who escaped and announced to Sweyn, king of Denmark, the death of their relatives. Ibid.

CHAPTER VII.—That King Sweyn, having gathered an army and arriving in the county of York, dismissed the army and came to Rouen with several ships to seek peace from Duke Richard; and concerning the agreement established between the Northmen and the Danes. And that the Ploracenses, the people of Canterbury, and the people of London surrendered to that king; and concerning King Ethelred’s flight with his wife and sons to Richard, duke of the Northmen. 827

CHAPTER VIII.—Concerning the death of King Sweyn at London; and that Canute, his son, succeeding his father, again moved an army against the English; and concerning Ethelred’s return to England and the Danes’ victory at Assandun. 828

CHAPTER IX.—That, after King Ethelred of the English died, Canute, king of the Danes, took his wife Emma in marriage and fathered by her Harthacnut, who later succeeded him. Ibid.

CHAPTER X.—Concerning the dispute between Duke Richard and Count Odo of Chartres over the fortress of Dreux; and that the same duke fortified the castle of Tillières on the river Avre; and how the Northmen defeated Odo and the two counts who assisted him. 829

CHAPTER XI.—That two pagan kings came from overseas regions to aid Duke Richard against the Franks. Ibid.

CHAPTER XII.—That Robert, king of the Franks, out of fear of the aforesaid kings, established peace between Duke Richard and Odo. 830

CHAPTER XIII.—That Duke Richard took Judith, sister of Geoffrey, count of the Bretons, as his wife, and concerning the offspring he had by her. 831 [Column 1562]

CHAPTER XIV.—How Robert, king of the Franks, with Duke Richard’s assistance, restored the fortress of Melun to Burchard. Ibid.

CHAPTER XV.—That, with Duke Richard’s assistance, Robert, king of the Franks, obtained the duchy of Burgundy, which Henry, its duke, had left to him at his death, against the will of the Burgundians. 832

CHAPTER XVI.—That Rainald, count of the Burgundians beyond the Saône River, married Adeliz, the daughter of Duke Richard. Ibid.

BOOK SIX.—Concerning the third Richard and his brother Robert, namely the sons of the second Richard. 833

CHAPTER I.—That although Richard III held the government of the duchy only briefly, he nevertheless imitated his father’s goodness. Ibid.

CHAPTER II.—Concerning the dispute between him and his brother Robert, and Richard’s death after peace had been made. Ibid.

CHAPTER III.—That Robert succeeded his brother Richard; concerning his character; and concerning the dispute between him and Robert, archbishop. 835

CHAPTER IV.—That the same Duke Robert besieged William of Belême within the fortress of Alençon and forced him to surrender. Ibid.

CHAPTER V.—That Hugh, bishop of Bayeux, son of Count Ralph, wished to hold the fortress of Ivry but could not. 836

CHAPTER VI.—That Count Baldwin of Flanders sought and obtained for his son Baldwin the daughter of Robert, king of the Franks, to his own misfortune, unless Robert, duke of Normandy, should bring him aid; and concerning the death of Robert, king of the Franks, whose successor was his son Henry. Ibid.

CHAPTER VII.—How the same duke helped Henry, king of the Franks, against his mother Constance. 837

CHAPTER VIII.—That Duke Robert, marching against Alan, count of the Bretons, built the fortress of Caruicas (Carrucas) not far from the river Couesnon. 838

CHAPTER IX.—Concerning the abbey of Bec, its first abbot, and its venerable founder Herluin; and concerning his successor Anselm. Ibid.

CHAPTER X.—Concerning the fleet which Duke Robert arranged to send to England in aid of his kinsmen Edward and Alfred, the sons of King Ethelred. 844

CHAPTER XI.—That he sent part of the same fleet to afflict Brittany, and concerning the restoration of peace between him and Alan, count of Brittany. 845

CHAPTER XII.—That Canute, king of the English, through his envoys offered Edward and Alfred half of the English kingdom out of fear of Robert, duke of the Northmen; and that the same duke, setting out for Jerusalem, placed his five-year-old son William in charge of the duchy of Normandy. Ibid.

CHAPTER XIII.—That the same Duke Robert, returning from Jerusalem, died in Christ at the city of Nicaea. 846

BOOK SEVEN.—Concerning Duke William, who subdued England by arms. 847

CHAPTER I.—What hardships the boy William endured at the beginning of his rule because of the perversity of certain men. Ibid.

CHAPTER II.—Concerning the battle between Tustin of Bastenborough and Walchelin of Ferrières, and the death of Osbern, son of Herfast. Ibid.

CHAPTER III.—How Roger of Beaumont, son of Humphrey de Vieilles, defeated Roger of Tosny at his father’s command. 848

CHAPTER IV.—That the same Roger built the abbey of Préaux and married Adelina, daughter of Waleran, count of Meulan. 849

CHAPTER V.—That Henry, king of the Franks, burned the fortress of Tillières, which had been handed over to him by the Northmen for the sake of peace, and also Argentan. 850

CHAPTER VI.—That Turstin Goz wished to hold the fortress of Falaise against Duke William but could not; and concerning his son Richard. Ibid.

CHAPTER VII.—That Malger, son of the second Richard by his second wife Popia (Papia), succeeded Archbishop Robert; and concerning William of Arques. 851
